name: KiloNeRF
head: KiloNeRF: Speeding up Neural Radiance Fields with Thousands of Tiny MLPs
body: KiloNeRF accelerates Neural Radiance Field (NeRF) rendering by three orders of magnitude without sacrificing visual quality by replacing the single large MLP with thousands of independent, small MLPs arranged on a regular 3D grid. Unlike the original NeRF, which queries one deep network for every sample point, KiloNeRF maps 3D positions to specific grid cells, each governed by a lightweight network. This spatial decomposition allows for significant speedups compared to both the original NeRF and other sparse methods like Neural Sparse Voxel Fields (NSVF). Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: A set of N calibrated images with known camera poses; an axis-aligned bounding box (AABB) defined by minimum bounds \mathbf{b}{min} and maximum bounds \mathbf{b}{max} enclosing the scene. Outputs: A set of N{cells} independent MLPs (the "KiloNeRF" model) and an occupancy grid for acceleration. During inference, given a ray \mathbf{r}, the output is the synthesized pixel color C(\mathbf{r}). Data Structures: 1. Network Grid: A uniform 3D grid of resolution \mathbf{r} = (rx, ry, rz) within the AABB. Each cell index \mathbf{i} = (ix, iy, iz) corresponds to a unique MLP with parameters \theta{\mathbf{i}}. The maximum resolution is 16 \times 16 \times 16 = 4096 networks. 2. Occupancy Grid: A second uniform grid with resolution 16 \times \mathbf{r} (upper bounded by 256 \times 256 \times 256). Each cell in this grid is populated with a binary value indicating whether the scene has any content within that cell. 3. Tiny MLP Architecture: Input: Concatenation of positional encoding \gamma(\mathbf{x}) and viewing direction \mathbf{d}. Layers: 4 hidden layers, each with 32 hidden units. Activations: All affine layers use ReLU, except: The input to the penultimate hidden layer has no activation. The output layer for RGB color \mathbf{c} uses Sigmoid activation. Structure: No skip connections. The viewing direction \mathbf{d} is provided as an additional input to the last hidden layer. Outputs: Density \sigma (scalar, independent of \mathbf{d}) and Color \mathbf{c} (RGB vector). Numbered Steps: Stage 1: Teacher Training 1. Train a standard NeRF (the "teacher") on the training images for up to 600,000 iterations. This teacher uses hierarchical sampling and a deep MLP (10 hidden layers, 256/128 units). Stage 2: Occupancy Grid Extraction 2. Instantiate the occupancy grid with resolution 16 \times \mathbf{r}. 3. For each cell in the occupancy grid, sample densities on a 3 \times 3 \times 3 subgrid using the teacher NeRF. 4. Mark a cell as occupied if any evaluated density \sigma > \tau, where \tau = 10. Stage 3: Distillation Training 5. Initialize the KiloNeRF networks \theta{\mathbf{i}} randomly or with small values. 6. For each network \mathbf{i}, randomly sample a batch of 3D points \mathbf{x} inside its corresponding grid cell. 7. Augment these points with viewing directions \mathbf{d} drawn randomly from the unit sphere. 8. Query the teacher NeRF to obtain target density \sigma{teacher} and color \mathbf{c}{teacher}. 9. Query the student KiloNeRF network \theta{\mathbf{i}} to obtain \sigma{student} and \mathbf{c}{student}. 10. Convert densities to alpha values using \alpha = 1 - \exp(-\sigma \delta), where \delta is a fixed distance between samples (e.g., derived from the grid cell size or a constant). 11. Optimize \theta{\mathbf{i}} using an L2 loss between the student's (\alpha{student}, \mathbf{c}{student}) and the teacher's (\alpha{teacher}, \mathbf{c}{teacher}). 12. Apply L2 regularization with weight \lambda = 10^{-6} to the weights and biases of the last two layers of the student networks. 13. Repeat for 150,000 iterations. Stage 4: Fine-tuning 14. Fine-tune all KiloNeRF networks on the original training images using photometric loss (L2 loss between rendered color and ground truth) for 1,000,000 iterations. 15. Use the occupancy grid for Empty Space Skipping (ESS) during this stage. Inference (Rendering): 16. For each ray \mathbf{r}, sample up to K=384 equidistant points. 17. Empty Space Skipping (ESS): For each sample point \mathbf{x}, determine its occupancy grid cell. Only query the KiloNeRF network if the cell is occupied. 18. Network Selection: Determine the network index \mathbf{i} for point \mathbf{x} using spatial binning: \mathbf{i} = \left\lfloor \frac{\mathbf{x} - \mathbf{b}{min}}{(\mathbf{b}{max} - \mathbf{b}{min}) / \mathbf{r}} \right\rfloor where operations are element-wise. 19. Evaluate the selected network: (\mathbf{c}, \sigma) = f{\theta{\mathbf{i}}}(\gamma(\mathbf{x}), \mathbf{d}). 20. Early Ray Termination (ERT): During inference, group queries by distance from the camera. If the transmittance Ti < \epsilon (where \epsilon = 0.01), stop sampling further points for that ray. 21. Compute pixel color via volumetric rendering: C(\mathbf{r}) = \sum{i=1}^{N} Ti \alphai \mathbf{c}i, \quad \alphai = 1 - \exp(-\sigmai \deltai), \quad Ti = \prod{j=1}^{i-1} (1 - \alphaj) where \deltai is the distance between samples. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import torch import torch.nn as nn import math def rayaabbintersect(origin, direction, bmin, bmax): """Compute intersection of ray with AABB. Returns (tnear, tfar).""" t1 = (bmin - origin) / direction t2 = (bmax - origin) / direction tnear = torch.max(torch.min(t1, t2)) tfar = torch.min(torch.max(t1, t2)) return tnear, tfar def positionalencoding(x, numfrequencies=10): """Standard NeRF positional encoding.""" x = x.unsqueeze(-1) scales = torch.tensor([2i for i in range(numfrequencies)], dtype=x.dtype, device=x.device) shaped = x (math.pi scales).reshape(1, 1, -1) return torch.cat([torch.sin(shaped), torch.cos(shaped)], dim=-1).reshape(x.shape[0], -1) class TinyMLP(nn.Module): """KiloNeRF Tiny MLP: 4 hidden layers, 32 units. Input: Encoded Position (3D) + Viewing Direction (3D) Output: Density (1), Color (3)""" def init(self, posencdim, viewencdim): super(TinyMLP, self).init() self.fc1 = nn.Linear(posencdim, 32) self.fc2 = nn.Linear(32, 32) self.fc3 = nn.Linear(32, 32) self.fc4 = nn.Linear(32 + viewencdim, 32) self.densityhead = nn.Linear(32, 1) self.colorhead = nn.Linear(32, 3) def forward(self, posenc, viewdir): # Path 1: Density (independent of view direction) x = torch.relu(self.fc1(posenc)) x = torch.relu(self.fc2(x)) sigma = self.densityhead(x) # Path 2: Color (view direction added at penultimate layer) x = torch.relu(self.fc3(x)) # No activation applied to feature vector input to penultimate layer xwithview = torch.cat([x, viewdir], dim=-1) x = torch.relu(self.fc4(xwithview)) c = torch.sigmoid(self.colorhead(x)) return sigma, c def renderray(rayorigin, raydirection, bmin, bmax, r, networks, occupancygrid, K=384, epsilon=0.01): """Render a single ray using KiloNeRF.""" tnear, tfar = rayaabbintersect(rayorigin, raydirection, bmin, bmax) if tfar < 0.0: return torch.zeros(3) tvals = torch.linspace(tnear, tfar, K) points = rayorigin.unsqueeze(1) + raydirection.unsqueeze(1) tvals.unsqueeze(0) transmittance = 1.0 color = torch.zeros(3) delta = (tfar - tnear) / K for i in range(K): if transmittance < epsilon: break point = points[i] cellsize = (bmax - bmin) / r idx = torch.floor((point - bmin) / cellsize).long() # Clamp indices to grid bounds idx = torch.clamp(idx, 0, torch.tensor(r) - 1) grididx = idx[0] r[1] r[2] + idx[1] r[2] + idx[2] if not occupancygrid[grididx].item(): continue net = networks[grididx] posenc = positionalencoding(point.unsqueeze(0), numfrequencies=10) viewenc = positionalencoding(raydirection.unsqueeze(0), numfrequencies=4) sigma, c = net(posenc, viewenc) alpha = 1.0 - torch.exp(-sigma delta) weight = transmittance alpha color += weight c transmittance = (1.0 - alpha) return color Parameters: Grid Resolution: Largest dimension 16; others chosen for cubic cells. Max 4096 networks. Occupancy Grid Resolution: 16 \times network grid resolution. Max 256^3. Occupancy Threshold \tau: 10. Max Samples K: 384. ERT Threshold \epsilon: 0.01. L2 Regularization Weight: 10^{-6} on last two layers. Optimizer: Adam, LR 5 \times 10^{-4}, batch size 8192 pixels. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Free Space Artifacts: Training KiloNeRF from scratch leads to noticeable artifacts in empty space. View-Dependent Bias: Reducing output features of the last hidden layer to mimic NeRF's view-dependent bias caused visual quality loss due to small network width. Dynamic Parameter Loading: During rendering, a ray traverses different networks, requiring dynamic parameter loading. Memory Overhead: Deploying thousands of MLPs incurs substantial memory overhead compared to a single network. Speedup: KiloNeRF achieves a speedup of 2000x to 2548x compared to the original NeRF. It is approximately two orders of magnitude faster than Neural Sparse Voxel Fields (NSVF). Rendering Time: On an NVIDIA GTX 1080 Ti, KiloNeRF renders in 30ms (BlendedMVS), 26ms (Synthetic-NeRF), 26ms (Synthetic-NSVF), and 91ms (Tanks&Temples). Quality: Visual quality (PSNR, SSIM, LPIPS) is comparable to the original NeRF and NSVF. Memory: Higher memory usage than NeRF due to the storage of thousands of small MLPs. Strengths: Real-time capable rendering; no loss in visual quality; simpler spatial decomposition than DeRF (regular grid vs. Voronoi). Limitations: Requires an AABB; distillation adds training complexity; dynamic network switching requires specialized implementation for optimal speed. KiloNeRF was introduced by Reiser et al. in 2021 at ICCV. It addresses the slow rendering times of NeRF by decomposing the scene into thousands of small MLPs. The method builds on the teacher-student distillation paradigm and incorporates acceleration techniques like Empty Space Skipping and Early Ray Termination, which were previously used in NSVF. It is cited as a key method for accelerating NeRF by three orders of magnitude. name: ProNeRF
head: ProNeRF-12, ProNeRF-32, ProNeRF-8, Projection-Aware Ray Sampling for Fine-Grained Implicit Neural Radiance Fields
body: ProNeRF is a few-point volumetric rendering method that uses a Projection-Aware Sampling (PAS) network to predict sparse 3D sampling points and opacity adjustments, allowing high-quality rendering with significantly fewer samples than standard NeRF. It achieves faster inference than vanilla NeRF with higher quality than HyperReel. Unlike generalizable radiance fields that store all training input images for epipolar feature projection, ProNeRF uses a fixed subset of reference views, eliminating the need for nearest-neighbor projection among all available training views. ProNeRF performs volumetric rendering using a small number of samples Ns (e.g., 8, 12, or 32) guided by a PAS network. The method consists of a PAS network (comprising MLP heads F{\thetac} and F{\thetaf}) and a shading network F{\thetas}. Input: Ray parameters \mathbf{r} = (\mathbf{r}o, \mathbf{r}d) (origin and direction), a set of Nn neighboring reference view colors \{\mathbf{c}^k\}{k=1}^{Nn} from a fixed pool of Nt training views. Output: Rendered pixel color \hat{\mathbf{c}}(\mathbf{r}). 1. Plücker Ray-Point Encoding: The ray is encoded into a vector \mathbf{r}{pr} of size 48 using N{pr}=48 points evenly spaced between near tn and far tf bounds: \mathbf{r}{pr} = [\mathbf{r}d, \mathbf{r}o + \mathbf{r}d \odot \mathbf{t}{nf}, (\mathbf{r}o + \mathbf{r}d \odot \mathbf{t}{nf}) \odot \mathbf{r}d] where \mathbf{t}{nf} is a vector of N{pr} elements, \odot is the Hadamard product, and [\cdot, \cdot] is concatenation. 2. Coarse MLP (F{\thetac}): Consists of 6 fully connected layers with 256 neurons and ELU activations. It takes \mathbf{r}{pr} as input and outputs: Coarse sampling distances \mathbf{T}' = \{t'1, \dots, t'{Ns}\}. Opacity shifts \Deltat and scales Bt. Auxiliary coarse color \hat{\mathbf{c}}c. 3. Color-to-Ray Projections: For each coarse point pi = \mathbf{r}(t'i), lines are traced to the camera centers of Nn neighboring reference views. The colors at these intersections are collected into a projection vector \mathbf{f}{pi} = [\mathbf{c}^1{pi}, \dots, \mathbf{c}^{Nn}{pi}]. 4. Fine MLP (F{\thetaf}): Consists of 6 fully connected layers with 256 neurons and ELU activations. It takes the encoded ray \mathbf{r}'{pr} and the aggregated projections \{\mathbf{f}{p1}, \dots, \mathbf{f}{pNs}\} as input. It outputs: Refinement weights \DeltaT. Auxiliary weights W \in \mathbb{R}^{Ns} (softmax) and M \in \mathbb{R}^{Nn} (sigmoid). Auxiliary fine color \hat{\mathbf{c}}f. 5. Shading Network (F{\thetas}): Consists of 8 fully connected layers with 256 neurons. It takes the refined 3D points \mathbf{x}i = \mathbf{r}o + \mathbf{r}d \odot Ti as input and outputs density \sigmai and color \mathbf{c}i for volumetric rendering. 1. Encode Ray: Compute \mathbf{r}{pr} from \mathbf{r}o, \mathbf{r}d and \mathbf{t}{nf}. 2. Coarse Sampling: Query F{\thetac}(\mathbf{r}{pr}) to obtain \mathbf{T}', \Deltat, Bt, and \hat{\mathbf{c}}c. 3. Projection: For each t'i \in \mathbf{T}', compute pi = \mathbf{r}(t'i). Trace rays from pi to the Nn reference camera centers. Interpolate colors from the reference images to get \mathbf{f}{pi}. 4. Refinement: Query F{\thetaf}([\mathbf{r}'{pr}, \mathbf{f}{p1}, \dots, \mathbf{f}{pNs}]) to obtain \DeltaT, W, M, and \hat{\mathbf{c}}f. 5. Compute Refined Distances: Linearly interpolate between consecutive elements of the expanded set \dot{\mathbf{T}} = \{tn, t'1, \dots, t'{Ns}, tf\} using \DeltaT: Ti = \frac{1}{2} \left( (\dot{T}i + \dot{T}{i+1}) + \Delta{Ti}(\dot{T}{i+2} - \dot{T}i) \right), \quad i=1,\dots,Ns. 6. Adjust Opacity: Compute adjusted opacities \hat{\alpha}i using the original opacities \alphai (derived from \sigmai and distances in T), shifts \Deltat, and scales Bt: \hat{\alpha}i = 1 - \exp(-(\sigmai + \Delta{ti})(t{i+1} - ti) \cdot B{ti}). 7. Render Color: Compute final color using alpha compositing with adjusted opacities: \hat{\mathbf{c}}(\mathbf{r}) = \sum{i=1}^{Ns} \left( \prod{j=1}^{i-1} (1 - \hat{\alpha}j) \right) \hat{\alpha}i \mathbf{c}i. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def pronerfrender(rayorigin, raydirection, refviewcolors, refcameras, tn, tf, Npr, Ns, Nn): import math # Helper: Trace ray from p to camcenter, interpolate color from image def traceandinterpolate(p, camcenter, image, intrinsics): dirtocam = [camcenter[j] - p[j] for j in range(3)] u, v = projecttoimage(p, camcenter, intrinsics) return bilinearsample(image, u, v) # 1. Plücker Ray-Point Encoding tnf = [tn + i (tf - tn) / (Npr - 1) for i in range(Npr)] rd = raydirection ro = rayorigin term2 = [ro[j] + rd[j] t for j in range(3) for t in tnf] term3 = [term2[j] rd[j % 3] for j in range(len(term2))] rpr = rd + term2 + term3 # 2. Coarse Sampling Tprime, deltat, Bt, chatc = Fthetac(rpr) # 3. Color-to-Ray Projections projections = [] for tprime in Tprime: p = [ro[j] + rd[j] tprime for j in range(3)] viewcolors = [] for k in range(Nn): viewcolors.append(traceandinterpolate(p, refcameras[k].center, refviewcolors[k], refcameras[k].intrinsics)) projections.append(viewcolors) # 4. Refinement deltaT, W, M, chatf = Fthetaf(rpr + flatten(projections)) # 5. Refined Distances Tdot = [tn] + Tprime + [tf] T = [] for i in range(Ns): ti = 0.5 ((Tdot[i] + Tdot[i+1]) + deltaT[i] (Tdot[i+2] - Tdot[i])) T.append(ti) # 6. Shading and Opacity Adjustment alphas = [] colors = [] for i in range(Ns): x = [ro[j] + rd[j] T[i] for j in range(3)] sigma, c = Fthetas(x) colors.append(c) deltadist = T[i+1] - T[i] if i < Ns - 1 else tf - T[i] adjalpha = 1.0 - math.exp(-(sigma + deltat[i]) deltadist Bt[i]) alphas.append(adjalpha) # 7. Compositing Ttransmittance = 1.0 cfinal = [0.0, 0.0, 0.0] for i in range(Ns): cfinal = [cfinal[j] + Ttransmittance alphas[i] colors[i][j] for j in range(3)] Ttransmittance = (1.0 - alphas[i]) return cfinal, chatc, chatf Ns: Number of samples. Typical values: 8, 12, 32. N{pr}: Number of Plücker points. Value: 48. N: Maximum exploration samples. Value: 64. Nn: Number of neighboring reference views. Significantly smaller than total training views Nt. Learning Rate: 5 \times 10^{-4}, exponentially decayed for 700,000 iterations. Batch Size: 4,096 rays. \lambda: Auxiliary loss weight. 1 for first 60% of training, 0 afterward. Auxiliary Loss Duration: First 4 \times 10^5 iterations. Pruning: ProNeRF-8 prune adds an MLP head F{\thetam} (same complexity as F{\thetac}) to predict error between \hat{\mathbf{c}}f and \hat{\mathbf{c}}. If error is low, use \hat{\mathbf{c}}f (AVR); otherwise, run F{\thetas}. This adds 3.3 MB memory overhead. Auxiliary Loss: Removing auxiliary loss la causes ~1 dB PSNR drop. Plücker Encoding: Removing Plücker ray-point encoding causes ~0.5 dB PSNR drop. 8 samples. 26.78 dB PSNR on LLFF. >20x faster than NeRF. 12 samples. 27.15 dB PSNR on LLFF. ~15x faster than NeRF. 32 samples. 31.92 dB PSNR on Blender. 3.2 FPS after pruning. Pruned version of ProNeRF-8. 23% faster than standard ProNeRF-8. 26.54 dB PSNR. Speed: 15-23× faster than vanilla NeRF. ProNeRF-8 is >20x faster. ProNeRF-8 prune is 23% faster than ProNeRF-8. Quality: 0.65 dB higher PSNR than NeRF on LLFF. 0.95 dB higher PSNR than HyperReel. Memory: Similar to NeRF. ProNeRF-8 prune adds 3.3 MB overhead. ProNeRF-32 uses 6.3 MB memory. Strengths: High quality with few samples; consistent memory footprint via fixed reference views; fast inference. Limitations: Requires training with auxiliary losses; pruning adds 3.3 MB memory overhead and requires training a complementary MLP head. When to use: When rendering speed is critical but quality must exceed sampler-based methods like HyperReel, and memory is constrained. When not to use: When generalizable rendering across many scenes without per-scene training is required (ProNeRF is not generalizable like IBRNet). ProNeRF was proposed in 2024. It builds on the differentiable approximation of continuous radiance fields [Parent]. It addresses the quality degradation in few-point sampling methods. It is evaluated on LLFF and Blender datasets. name: Quadri-Plane Radiance Fields
head: 4-Plane Representation, Quadri-Plane Model
body: Quadri-Plane Radiance Fields represent a 3D scene using four multi-channel 2D feature planes coupled with a lightweight decoder MLP, designed to enable computationally efficient volumetric super-resolution by leveraging 2D image super-resolution techniques. Unlike standard NeRF which uses a dense MLP for all queries, this method decouples spatial and directional information into explicit planar grids, allowing for faster training and inference while maintaining high-fidelity reconstruction of general scenes. Inputs and Outputs: The method takes a set of training images (low-resolution or high-resolution) and their corresponding camera poses as input. It outputs a differentiable scene representation that can render novel views via volumetric rendering. The core output of the query function is the volume density \sigma and the emitted radiance \mathbf{c} = \{r, g, b\} for a given 3D position \mathbf{p} and viewing direction. Data Structures: The scene representation Ps consists of four 2D feature planes: three positional planes P{xy}, P{xz}, P{yz} aligned with the coordinate axes, and one view-direction plane P{dir} representing the spherical coordinate space of viewing directions. Each positional plane has dimensions N \times N \times C, and the view-direction plane has dimensions N{dir} \times N{dir} \times C. Numbered Steps: 1. Positional Feature Retrieval: For a query point \mathbf{p} = (x, y, z), project \mathbf{p} onto the three positional planes to get 2D coordinates (x, y), (x, z), and (y, z). Retrieve the feature vectors v{xy}, v{xz}, v{yz} from P{xy}, P{xz}, P{yz} respectively using bilinear interpolation. 2. Directional Feature Retrieval: Compute the viewing direction (\thetap, \phip) (azimuth and elevation) for the ray passing through \mathbf{p}. Project this direction onto P{dir} to get 2D coordinates corresponding to (\thetap, \phip). Retrieve the feature vector v{dir} from P{dir} using bilinear interpolation. 3. Positional Feature Aggregation: Compute the aggregated positional feature vector vp by averaging the three positional feature vectors. 4. Density Prediction: Feed vp into the coarse density decoder Dc and the fine density decoder Df to obtain density values \sigmac and \sigmaf. Both Dc and Df are identical MLPs (128 channels, 4 layers). 5. Radiance Prediction: Concatenate all four feature vectors (v{xy}, v{xz}, v{yz}, v{dir}) to form the input vector v{all}. Feed v{all} into the radiance decoder MLP (identical structure to density decoders) to predict the RGB radiance \mathbf{c}. The view-direction plane P{dir} affects radiance but not density, as volume density is view-independent. 6. Volumetric Rendering: Use the predicted \sigma and \mathbf{c} values along sampled rays to compute pixel colors via standard volumetric rendering equations. Formulas: vp = \frac{1}{3} (v{xy} + v{xz} + v{yz}) where v{xy}, v{xz}, v{yz} are the feature vectors retrieved from the positional planes via bilinear interpolation, and vp is the aggregated positional feature vector passed to the density decoders. Parameters: N: Spatial resolution of positional planes. Typical value for low-resolution training on 100px images is N=200. N{dir}: Resolution of the view-direction plane. Set smaller than N (e.g., N{dir}=32) because each pixel's information is relevant to only one point on P{dir} (same viewing direction for all points on a ray), whereas it is relevant to many points on positional planes. C: Number of channels per plane. Typical value is C=48. Decoder MLPs: Fully-connected networks with 128 channels and 4 layers. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: View-Direction Dependency: Omitting P{dir} significantly degrades performance, especially for shiny/reflective objects with non-uniform lighting. PSNR drops from ~29.6 dB to ~23.7 dB in reported experiments. Plane Resolution: Using N too small prohibits high-frequency representation. Using N too large causes artifacts due to insufficient information in low-resolution training images. Directional Plane Resolution: N{dir} must be smaller than N to avoid overfitting to sparse directional information. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import numpy as np def quadriplanequery(p, direction, planes, N, Ndir, C, weightsc, weightsf, weightsr): """ Query the quadri-plane representation for a single point. Args: p: numpy array of shape (3,), 3D position (x, y, z) in [-1, 1] direction: numpy array of shape (3,), viewing direction vector planes: dict containing 'Pxy', 'Pxz', 'Pyz', 'Pdir' Each plane is a numpy array of shape (N, N, C) or (Ndir, Ndir, C) N: spatial resolution of positional planes Ndir: resolution of directional plane C: number of channels weightsc, weightsf, weightsr: list of 4 weight matrices (C, C) for each MLP Returns: sigmac: float, coarse density sigmaf: float, fine density c: numpy array of shape (3,), RGB radiance """ def bilinearinterp(plane, u, v): H, W, C = plane.shape y = u (H - 1) x = v (W - 1) y0, x0 = int(np.floor(y)), int(np.floor(x)) y1, x1 = min(y0 + 1, H - 1), min(x0 + 1, W - 1) yfrac, xfrac = y - y0, x - x0 val00 = plane[y0, x0,:] val01 = plane[y0, x1,:] val10 = plane[y1, x0,:] val11 = plane[y1, x1,:] top = val00 (1 - xfrac) + val01 xfrac bottom = val10 (1 - xfrac) + val11 xfrac return top (1 - yfrac) + bottom yfrac def mlpforward(x, Wlist): for W in Wlist: x = np.maximum(0, x @ W) return x pnorm = (p + 1.0) / 2.0 vxy = bilinearinterp(planes['Pxy'], pnorm[0], pnorm[1]) vxz = bilinearinterp(planes['Pxz'], pnorm[0], pnorm[2]) vyz = bilinearinterp(planes['Pyz'], pnorm[1], pnorm[2]) theta = np.arctan2(direction[1], direction[0]) phi = np.arcsin(direction[2]) udir = (theta + np.pi) / (2 np.pi) vdir = (phi + np.pi / 2) / np.pi vdirfeat = bilinearinterp(planes['Pdir'], udir, vdir) vp = (vxy + vxz + vyz) / 3.0 sigmac = mlpforward(vp, weightsc) sigmaf = mlpforward(vp, weightsf) vall = np.concatenate([vxy, vxz, vyz, vdirfeat], axis=0) c = mlpforward(vall, weightsr) return sigmac, sigmaf, c Time Complexity: Query time is dominated by bilinear interpolation on four planes and a small MLP inference. This is significantly faster than dense MLP-based NeRFs for high-resolution scenes, as the MLP is shallow (4 layers, 128 channels) and the feature lookup is O(1). Memory Complexity: Memory usage is proportional to 4 \times N^2 \times C. For N=200, C=48, this is 4 \times 40000 \times 48 \approx 7.68 MB, which is very compact compared to dense voxel grids or large MLPs. Measured Performance: Training is performed on an NVIDIA A100 GPU using Adam optimizers with learning rates of 0.0005 for the decoder and feature planes, and 0.00005 for the super-resolution model. At each step, 4096 rays are sampled randomly from training images. Scaling: The representation scales well with scene size by increasing N, but is limited by the resolution of the training images. It is specifically designed for volumetric super-resolution, where the planes are upsampled using 2D SR techniques. Strengths: Efficient training and inference; leverages mature 2D SR algorithms; compact memory footprint; good reconstruction quality for general scenes. Limitations: Performance depends heavily on the resolution of training images; may struggle with very high-frequency details if N is not sufficiently large; requires careful tuning of N and N{dir}. When to use it: Use when volumetric super-resolution from low-resolution inputs is required, or when computational efficiency for general scenes is prioritized over view-dependent density modeling. When not to use it: Avoid when high-frequency spatial details are critical and training images are insufficient to populate large N, or when view-dependent density effects are expected. Quadri-Plane Radiance Fields were introduced in "Neural Volume Super-Resolution" (2022). The method builds on the feature plane representation proposed by Chan et al. [9] for human faces and extends it to general scenes by adding a view-direction plane and using coarse/fine decoders inspired by NeRF [32]. It aims to bridge the gap between neural rendering and 2D image super-resolution, allowing for efficient upscaling of 3D scenes from low-resolution inputs. name: Non-Baked Models
head: Hybrid Representations, Learning separate scene features from MLP parameters
body: Non-baked models learn separate scene features from MLP parameters via hybrid representations, enabling smaller MLPs for improved training and inference speed at the cost of increased memory. Unlike baked models that pre-compute and store final MLP outputs to accelerate inference without affecting training time, non-baked models retain the differentiability of the feature-to-output mapping during optimization, improving both phases. Adapts the representation dynamically. Uses sinusoidal activations. Integrates CLIP embeddings. Uses region proposal networks. Focuses on reflection and super-resolution. Improves alignment. Integrates diffusion models. Uses pooling mechanisms. Multi-scale representations. Depth-integrated representation. Ring-based acquisition handling. Optimizes sparsity. Enables scene editing. Uses depth priors. Generative approaches. Implicit Octree Radiance Fields. Instance-specific fields. Multi-input multi-output. Separates lighting. Tensor-based radiance fields. Conditional editing. Handles dynamic scenes. The classification originates from distinguishing NeRF optimization procedures into baked models (pre-computed outputs) and non-baked models (learning separate scene features from MLP parameters). Non-baked models emerged to mitigate memory bottlenecks in standard MLP-based NeRFs by reducing network size, which improves training and inference speed while increasing memory overhead for explicit feature storage. The category encompasses hybrid representations and, pushed further, purely explicit scene representations that omit neural networks entirely; these are included due to their relevance and similarity to NeRF. Common techniques associated with this family include ray termination, space skipping, and hierarchical sampling using coarse and fine MLPs. name: Edit-NeRF
head: EditNeRF
body: Edit-NeRF is a method for user-controlled 3D scene editing that formulates the problem as a joint optimization of NeRF network parameters and latent codes. It solves the limitation of standard NeRFs, which are static and cannot be easily modified by external features, by introducing a modular network architecture with conditional radiance fields. It differs from its siblings by being the first method to execute user-controlled deformation models on NeRF using a shared shape network and instance-specific latent codes, whereas methods like CLIP-NeRF later introduced text/image guidance via CLIP embeddings. Inputs and Outputs: Input: User-provided image conditioning (2D image or sketch) representing the desired edit; initial NeRF weights; category-specific shared shape network parameters. Output: Edited 3D radiance field (density \sigma and color \mathbf{c}) consistent with the user's edit. Data Structures: The shape representation is composed of two networks: 1. Shared Shape Network (F{share}): Category-specific, not conditioned on latent codes. It behaves as a deformation field. 2. Instance-Specific Shape Network (F{inst}): Conditioned on a shape latent code zs. The color network is conditioned on an appearance latent code za (or zc in some notations). Numbered Steps: 1. Initialization: Train the model on multiple instances of the same category to learn underlying part features in an unsupervised manner. 2. Latent Code Optimization: Optimize the latent codes zs and za to minimize the NeRF photometric loss against the user-provided image conditioning. 3. Network Weight Optimization: Optimize the MLP weights of the NeRF networks. 4. Joint Optimization: Optimize both the latent codes (zs, za) and the MLP weights jointly to refine the edit. Formulas: The rendered color \hat{C}(\mathbf{r}, zs, zc) for a ray \mathbf{r} is computed via volumetric rendering: \hat{C}(\mathbf{r}, zs, zc) = \sum{i=1}^{Nc-1} ci \alphai \exp \left( -\sum{j=1}^{i-1} \sigmaj \deltaj \right) where: Nc is the number of samples along the ray. ci is the color at sample i. \alphai = 1 - \exp(-\sigmai \deltai) is the transmittance-derived alpha. \sigmaj is the density at sample j. \deltaj is the distance between samples. Parameters: zs: Shape latent code. za (or zc): Appearance/Color latent code. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Limited Shape Operations: The method only supports adding or deleting local parts of an object; it does not support complex global deformations. Slow Convergence: The editing process is slow due to its iterative optimization nature. Instruct-NeRF2NeRF is a diffusion-based method for editing a NeRF scene guided by text instructions, utilizing InstructPix2Pix. It solves the problem of 3D scene modification by iteratively updating the training dataset with edited images and retraining the NeRF. It differs from its sibling Edit-NeRF by bypassing explicit 3D deformation fields or conditional radiance field architectures, instead relying on 2D image-level diffusion editing to drive 3D consistency. SINE is a method for editing a NeRF scene by editing a single view and applying the edit to the entire scene. It encodes changes in geometry and texture over the original NeRF scene by learning a prior-guided editing field. This field is used to render modified object geometry and color, and a color compositing layer supervised by the single edited view applies the edit on novel views. It is applied on real and synthetic scenes by changing geometry and texture of objects. Time Complexity: Slow due to its iterative optimization nature. Memory Complexity: Requires storing latent codes zs and za per instance/edit. Strengths: Allows user-controlled deformation; modular architecture separates shape and appearance. Limitations: Limited to local part addition/deletion; slow convergence. When to Use: When user-controlled local edits on a category of objects are required and computational time is not the primary constraint. When Not to Use: For global deformations, real-time editing, or when high geometric consistency is critical without additional constraints. Edit-NeRF was proposed by Liu et al. in 2021. It was the first method to execute user-controlled deformation models on NeRF, proposing a modular network's conditional radiance field to guide model editing. It builds on the standard latent-conditioned NeRF architecture but introduces a shared shape network and instance-specific latent codes to enable editing. It was innovated upon by CLIP-NeRF in December 2021, which introduced text/image guidance via CLIP. name: Instruct-NeRF2NeRF
head: Instruct-NeRF2NeRF Baseline
body: Instruct-NeRF2NeRF (IN2N) is a diffusion-based method for editing a Neural Radiance Field (NeRF) scene guided by text instructions, utilizing InstructPix2Pix. It solves the problem of 3D scene modification by iteratively updating the training dataset with edited images and retraining the NeRF. It differs from its sibling Edit-NeRF by bypassing explicit 3D deformation fields or conditional radiance field architectures, instead relying on 2D image-level diffusion editing to drive 3D consistency. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A pre-trained NeRF model representing the original scene, a set of original training images \{Ii\}, and a text instruction T. Output: An edited NeRF model that renders scenes consistent with instruction T. Data Structures: The method does not define new 3D data structures. It operates on the existing NeRF representation (typically a multi-layer perceptron mapping 3D coordinates and viewing directions to color and density) and the 2D image dataset. Algorithm: 1. Initialization: Load the original NeRF model and the original training image dataset. 2. Iterative Editing Loop: a. For each image Ii in the training dataset: i. Pass Ii and the text instruction T to the InstructPix2Pix (IP2P) model. ii. Generate the edited image I'i = \text{IP2P}(Ii, T). b. Replace the original dataset \{Ii\} with the edited dataset \{I'i\}. c. Re-train the NeRF model using the edited dataset \{I'i\}. 3. Convergence: Repeat steps 2a-2c until the edited NeRF converges or a fixed number of iterations is reached. Parameters: Text Instruction T: A natural language string describing the desired edit. Example: "Make it look like it was taken at night.". InstructPix2Pix Model: A fine-tuned Stable Diffusion model capable of following text instructions to edit images. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Lack of Localization: The method applies edits to entire 2D images, lacking the ability to perform precise, localized modifications. Scene Preservation: It sometimes fails to preserve the rest of the scene, resulting in a blurrier scene compared to the original. Global Changes: It may introduce unintended texture and color changes to the entire scene rather than just the target object. Time Complexity: High. Requires iterative retraining of the NeRF after each round of 2D image editing. Memory Complexity: Standard NeRF memory requirements plus storage for the edited image dataset. Performance: Demonstrates high-quality local edit results on real scenes. However, it is slower than methods like Depth-Guided Sequential Editing which avoid integrating a diffusion model into the training loop. Strengths: Simple implementation leveraging existing 2D editing models; intuitive text-based control. Limitations: Poor multi-view consistency due to independent 2D edits; potential for global artifacts and blurring. Instruct-NeRF2NeRF was presented at ICCV 2023. It is the first work to edit a NeRF by iteratively updating the training dataset with edited images generated by a text-based image editing model, specifically InstructPix2Pix. It builds on the capability of generative models to edit 2D images according to text instructions. name: Depth-Guided Sequential Editing
head: ViCA-NeRF, ViCA-NeRF Sequential Editing, View-Consistency-Aware 3D Editing of Neural Radiance Fields, View-Consistency-Aware NeRF
body: Depth-Guided Sequential Editing (ViCA-NeRF) is a two-stage method for editing Neural Radiance Fields (NeRFs) using text instructions, which ensures multi-view consistency by sequentially editing key 2D views and propagating those edits to the rest of the scene via geometric projection and learned regularization. It differs from Instruct-NeRF2NeRF by explicitly enforcing consistency through depth-guided pixel projection and latent code alignment, avoiding the need to integrate a diffusion model into the NeRF training loop, resulting in editing speeds approximately 3 times faster. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: A pre-trained NeRF model (specifically nerfacto from NeRFStudio), a set of input views (images, camera poses, and coarse depth maps rendered from the source NeRF), and a text editing instruction. Outputs: A refined NeRF model representing the edited 3D scene, and a corresponding set of edited 2D images. Data Structures: View Data: Each view i consists of an RGB image Ii, a coarse depth map Di, a camera intrinsic matrix Ki, and a camera pose \xii. Key View Sequence: An ordered list of view indices selected for sequential editing. Modified Mask: A binary mask per view tracking which pixels have already been overwritten by previous projections to prevent overwriting. Parameters: \phi: Maximum desired modified ratio for key view selection, set to \phi = 0.3. lr{thresh}: Reprojection error threshold for valid correspondences, set to 5 pixels. T{warmup}: Warm-up iterations for the diffusion model; 10 for face-centric scenes, 30 for outdoor scenes. T{fine}: Fine-tuning iterations for the NeRF; 10,000 for general scenes, \approx 5,000 for small scenes. T{train}: Initial training iterations for the source NeRF; 30,000. Steps: 1. Source NeRF Training: Train a pre-trained NeRF (e.g., nerfacto) on the original unedited data for T{train} = 30,000 iterations. 2. Depth Extraction: Render coarse depth maps Di for all input views i from the trained source NeRF. 3. Key View Selection: Select a sequence of key views starting from a random view. 4. Sequential Editing and Projection: Iterate through the selected key views in order. Edit Key View: Apply Instruct-Pix2Pix to the current key view j using the text prompt to generate an edited image I'j. A warm-up procedure is applied: run the diffusion process for T{warmup} iterations to shift the main distribution of 2D edits. Geometric Projection: Project the edited pixels from I'j to all other views i (including non-key views and subsequent key views) using the depth maps and camera poses. Calculate 3D points for view i: pi = P^{-1}(Di, Ki, \xii). Reproject pi to view j to find corresponding pixel coordinates. Calculate reprojection error lr. If lr < lr{thresh} (5px), the correspondence is valid. Copy the pixel value from I'j to the corresponding location in view i, but only if that pixel has not yet been modified (checked via the Modified Mask). This creates a "mixup" dataset where edits are mixed but not overwritten. 5. Blending Refinement (Learned Regularization): The projected mixup images may contain noise due to depth inaccuracies. Run the diffusion process (Instruct-Pix2Pix) multiple times on each mixup image. Average the resulting latent codes from these runs. Decode the averaged latent code into a single final image. This corrects noisy depth correspondences and stabilizes the edit, accepting slight image smoothness. 6. NeRF Fine-Tuning: Train the source NeRF on the fully refined, view-consistent edited dataset for T{fine} iterations (10,000 for general, 5,000 for small scenes). 7. Optional Post-Refinement: Re-render images from the fine-tuned NeRF. Apply the blending refinement model (Step 5) again to further improve consistency. Skip this step for large-scale outdoor scenes (e.g., 'campsite', 'farm') as high complexity prevents further consistency improvement. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math import random def depthguidedsequentialediting(sourceneurf, views, textprompt): # Step 1: Train source NeRF on original data for 30,000 iterations # sourceneurf.train(views, iterations=30000) # Step 2: Extract coarse depth maps for all input views depthmaps = {v.id: sourceneurf.renderdepth(v) for v in views} # Step 3: Select a sequence of key views starting from a random view randomstart = random.randint(0, len(views) - 1) keyviewids = [views[i].id for i in range(randomstart, len(views))] + \ [views[i].id for i in range(randomstart)] # Initialize storage for edited images and modification masks editedimages = {v.id: v.image.copy() for v in views} modifiedmasks = {v.id: [[False] v.width for in range(v.height)] for v in views} for keyvid in keyviewids: # Step 4: Edit Key View with warm-up to shift 2D edit distribution warmupiters = 30 if isoutdoorscene(keyvid) else 10 editedkeyimg = ip2pixedit(editedimages[keyvid], textprompt, warmupiters=warmupiters) # Step 4: Geometric Projection to all other views for targetvid in [v.id for v in views if v.id != keyvid]: Dtarget = depthmaps[targetvid] Ktarget = viewsbyid[targetvid].intrinsics xitarget = viewsbyid[targetvid].pose Kkey = viewsbyid[keyvid].intrinsics xikey = viewsbyid[keyvid].pose for y in range(Dtarget.height): for x in range(Dtarget.width): if not modifiedmasks[targetvid][y][x]: # Unproject target pixel to 3D point z = Dtarget[y][x] xcam = (x - Ktarget[0][2]) z / Ktarget[0][0] ycam = (y - Ktarget[1][2]) z / Ktarget[1][1] p = transformpoint([xcam, ycam, z], xitarget) # Reproject 3D point to key view pcam = transformpoint(p, inversepose(xikey)) uk = pcam[0] Kkey[0][0] / pcam[2] + Kkey[0][2] vk = pcam[1] Kkey[1][1] / pcam[2] + Kkey[1][2] lr = math.sqrt((uk - x)2 + (vk - y)2) if lr < 5.0: # Correspondence matching valid threshold if 0 <= uk < editedkeyimg.width and 0 <= vk < editedkeyimg.height: editedimages[targetvid][y][x] = editedkeyimg[vk][uk] modifiedmasks[targetvid][y][x] = True # Blending refinement for the edited key view editedimages[keyvid] = blendrefine(editedkeyimg, textprompt) # Step 5: Blending Refinement for all views to correct noisy depth correspondences refinedimages = {} for vid, img in editedimages.items(): refinedimages[vid] = blendrefine(img, textprompt) # Step 6: Train NeRF on fully refined dataset for 10,000 iterations (5,000 for small scenes) dataset = builddataset(refinedimages, views) sourceneurf.finetune(dataset, iterations=10000) # Step 7: Optional Post-Refinement if not islargeoutdoorscene(): rerendered = sourceneurf.renderall() finalrefined = blendrefineall(rerendered, textprompt) sourceneurf.finetune(finalrefined, iterations=10000) return sourceneurf def transformpoint(p, pose): return pose.R @ p + pose.t def inversepose(pose): return Pose(R=pose.R.T, t=-pose.R.T @ pose.t) def isoutdoorscene(viewid): # Scene classification logic not specified in sources. return False def viewsbyid: # Dictionary mapping view IDs to view objects. pass def builddataset(images, views): # Standard dataset construction. pass def islargeoutdoorscene(): # Scene classification logic not specified in sources. return False def ip2pixedit(image, prompt, warmupiters): # Calls Instruct-Pix2Pix with warm-up steps. pass def blendrefine(image, prompt): # Runs diffusion multiple times, averages latent codes, decodes final image. pass def blendrefineall(images, prompt): # Applies blendrefine to all images. pass Pitfalls: Depth estimation from NeRF is often noisy, yielding incorrect pixel correspondences during projection. Inability to perform large spatial changes (e.g., manipulating existing objects or adding/removing large objects) due to inherited Instruct-Pix2Pix limitations. Blurry results caused by high-frequency information loss (texture on face, beard, hair) when the mixup image passes through the diffusion model, which attempts to reduce introduced noise. Time Complexity: The method is significantly faster than joint training approaches, achieving approximately 3 times faster editing speed compared to Instruct-NeRF2NeRF. Memory Complexity: Requires storing depth maps for all views and the modified masks. The blending refinement step requires multiple passes through the diffusion model's latent space, increasing VRAM usage during the refinement stage. Performance: Evaluated on scenes ranging from faces to outdoor environments, providing higher levels of consistency and detail compared to the state of the art. Strengths: Explicitly enforces multi-view consistency via geometric projection and latent code alignment. Offers improved controllability (by editing key views) and efficiency (less GPU time). Limitations: Inherits limitations from Instruct-Pix2Pix: inability to perform large spatial changes (e.g., adding/removing large objects) and difficulty with highly detailed instructions involving interactions between parts. Blurry results due to high-frequency information loss (texture on face, beard, hair) when the mixup image passes through the diffusion model, which attempts to reduce noise introduced during projection. Post-refinement is ineffective for large-scale outdoor scenes due to high complexity. When to use: Suitable for 3D scene editing and AR applications where multi-view consistency is critical and computational efficiency is desired. Best for scenes where the user can define key views that capture the desired edit. When not to use: Avoid for large-scale outdoor scenes if post-refinement is expected to improve results. Avoid if large spatial manipulations (adding/removing objects) are required. Origin: ViCA-NeRF was introduced as the first view-consistency-aware method for 3D editing with text instructions. History: It builds upon the limitations of Instruct-NeRF2NeRF, which suffers from convergence problems and slower speeds due to iterative diffusion model updates during NeRF training. ViCA-NeRF decouples the editing from the training loop by using geometric and learned regularization in a pre-processing stage. Usage: Evaluated on various scenes and text prompts, ranging from faces to outdoor scenes. Code is available at https://dongjiahua.github.io/VICA-NeRF. name: Geometric Priors and Depth Integration
head: Geometric Regularization, Depth-Guided NeRF, SDF-based NeRF
body: Geometric Priors and Depth Integration methods enhance standard Neural Radiance Fields (NeRF) by incorporating explicit geometric constraints—such as depth maps, surface normals, or Structure-from-Motion (SfM) features—into the optimization loop. Unlike standard NeRF, which relies solely on implicit photometric consistency and often suffers from ambiguous geometry in sparse-view or textureless scenarios, these methods enforce hard boundaries, metric scale, or structural consistency to improve reconstruction fidelity. They distinguish themselves from sibling methods like AdaNeRF or SinNeRF by explicitly modeling the scene's 3D structure (via SDFs, cost volumes, or depth priors) rather than just refining the radiance field's appearance or frequency representation. All methods in this family build on Specific Model Architectures but diverge in how the geometric information is integrated into the optimization loop. The shared mechanism involves augmenting the standard photometric loss with geometric terms or modifying the ray sampling process to respect geometric boundaries. Geometric Loss Functions: Many methods introduce explicit loss terms that penalize deviations from geometric priors. Common forms include: 1. Depth Consistency Loss: Minimizes the difference between the rendered depth (computed as the expected depth along the ray) and a prior depth map D{prior}: L{depth} = \| D{rendered} - D{prior} \|1 2. Normal Smoothness: Encourages surface normals derived from the density field to be smooth or aligned with estimated normals. 3. Epipolar Constraints: Enforces that 3D points reconstructed from matched features in different views lie on the corresponding epipolar lines. Depth-Guided Sampling: Instead of uniform or hierarchical sampling along the entire ray, these methods use depth priors to concentrate samples near the estimated surface. This reduces computational cost and mitigates the "transparent" artifacts common in standard NeRF when geometry is ambiguous. For example, samples are clustered around the depth value predicted by a monocular depth estimator. Signed Distance Fields (SDF): Some variants replace the volumetric density \sigma with a Signed Distance Field (SDF). The rendering integral is modified to integrate weights based on the SDF value relative to a truncation distance tr, effectively creating a thin shell around the surface rather than a volumetric blob. The weight for a sample at distance d is often computed as: w = \sigma\left(\frac{d}{tr}\right) \cdot \sigma\left(-\frac{d}{tr}\right) This allows for direct mesh extraction via Marching Cubes. Integrates explicit SfM constraints (matched features, epipolar geometry) into the NeRF loss to improve geometric accuracy under sparse inputs. It uses sub-pixel rendering and a pyramidal optimization strategy to avoid local minima. Uses monocular depth priors (DepthAnythingV2) to guide learning via Depth Ordering Fidelity Loss and Depth Structural Consistency Regularization. It employs dynamic optimal sampling to handle varying depth levels. Addresses sparse-view ambiguity by modeling geometry through a cascaded 3D cost volume and Transformer-based attention. It extracts view-independent and view-dependent tokens to predict density and color, enabling robust generalization. Replaces density with a Truncated Signed Distance Field (TSDF) for geometry and a radiance field for appearance. It enforces hard boundaries, allowing direct mesh extraction and solving the issue of semi-transparent artifacts. Solves high-disparity synthesis artifacts by using dense depth priors to guide feature fusion and sampling. It leverages predicted depth maps to align features from sparse input views, improving correspondence search. Replaces handcrafted UDF-to-density mappings with a learnable neural network fw that considers 3D context from neighboring points. It learns a robust mapping from local geometric structures to rendering weights, reducing bias and outlier sensitivity. Integrates explicit geometric priors (normal smoothness, bilateral edge-aware constraints) directly into the optimization loop. It unifies physical imaging and geometric constraints for accurate 3D reconstruction under complex imaging conditions. The integration of geometric priors into NeRF-based reconstruction emerged to address the inherent ambiguity of implicit volumetric representations, particularly in sparse-view settings or scenes with low texture. Early NeRF implementations relied on photometric consistency alone, which often resulted in "floaters" or incorrect geometry in unobserved regions. Subsequent works introduced explicit geometric signals such as SfM features, monocular depth estimators, and SDFs to regularize the optimization landscape. This family represents the convergence of traditional multi-view stereo (MVS) techniques with differentiable rendering, allowing for metric-scale reconstruction and direct mesh extraction.

name: SfMNeRF
head: SfM-NeRF
body: SfMNeRF is a method for novel view synthesis and 3D-scene geometry reconstruction using Neural Radiance Fields (NeRF) under sparse input conditions. It improves geometric accuracy and avoids local minima by integrating Structure-from-Motion (SfM) constraints—specifically matched feature positions, epipolar geometry, and multi-view photometric consistency—into the view synthesis training loop. Unlike standard NeRF, which relies solely on implicit photometric consistency, SfMNeRF explicitly constrains the 3D-scene structure using sparse feature matches and epipolar lines, while employing sub-pixel rendering to increase sample density and generalization. SfMNeRF builds on Specific Model Architectures by augmenting the standard NeRF optimization with explicit geometric losses derived from sparse features and multi-view geometry. Inputs: A set of m training images with known camera intrinsics K and global poses [\mathbf{r}i, \mathbf{t}i]. Matched Scale-Invariant Feature Transform (SIFT) correspondences between image pairs. A pyramidal representation of the input images for coarse-to-fine optimization. Outputs: A trained NeRF model (MLP parameters \theta) representing volume density \sigma\theta and color c\theta. Synthesized novel views and depth maps. Camera Intrinsic Matrix (K): 3 \times 3 matrix mapping 3D world coordinates to 2D image coordinates. Relative Pose (T{r \to t}): 4 \times 4 transformation matrix from reference image r to target image t, composed of rotation \mathbf{r} and translation \mathbf{t}. SIFT Features: A set of 2D pixel coordinates in reference and target images, matched across views. Mask Map (M): A binary mask where M(p(k))=1 if point p(k) lies within the minimum bounding rectangle of all matched SIFT features in the reference image, else 0. Depth Map (D): Estimated depth for each pixel, computed via volume rendering integration. 1. Pyramidal Construction: Construct an L-level pyramid for the reference image Ir and target image It. Let I^0r = Ir and I^0t = It. For level n > 0, I^nr and I^nt are downsampled versions of I^{n-1}r and I^{n-1}t with half the resolution. 2. Initialization: Start optimization at the lowest pyramid level L-1. 3. Sub-pixel Sampling: For a selected patch \Omegap in the reference image, generate sub-pixel coordinates p = (x + x{off}, y + y{off}) where x{off}, y{off} \in (0, 1). 4. Ground Truth Interpolation: Compute the ground-truth color \hat{I}(p) for each sub-pixel using bilinear interpolation of the four nearest integer-pixel neighbors in the reference image: \hat{I}(p) = \sum{i \in \{top, bottom\}, j \in \{left, right\}} w^{ij} I(p^{ij}) where w^{ij} is proportional to the inverse Euclidean distance between p and neighbor p^{ij}. 5. Volume Rendering: Input sub-pixel coordinates and viewing directions into the NeRF to render color \tilde{I}(p) and depth D(p). 6. Feature Extraction: Extract SIFT features from the reference and target images and obtain matched correspondences. 7. 3D Coordinate Estimation: For each matched SIFT feature k, compute its 3D coordinate \mathbf{x}s^k in the reference and target views using weighted volume rendering integration: \mathbf{x}s = \sum{j=1}^{Nc} wj (\mathbf{o} + tj \mathbf{d}) where wj = Tj (1 - \exp(-\sigmaj \deltaj)), \deltaj = t{j-1} - tj, and Nc is the number of samples along the ray. 8. Loss Computation: Calculate the following loss terms: Rendering Loss (L{ren}): Mean squared error between rendered sub-pixel color and interpolated ground truth. Position-of-Matches Loss (L{3D}): Squared Euclidean distance between 3D coordinates of matched features in reference and target views. Epipolar Loss (L{epi}): Minimum squared distance between the 3D coordinate of a reference point and points on the epipolar line in the target view. Photometric Consistency Loss (L{pr}): L1 difference between the reference patch and the warped target patch, masked by M. SSIM Loss (L{SSIM}): Structural Similarity index between reference and warped target patches, masked by M. Depth Smoothness Loss (L{ds}): Weighted L1 norm of depth gradients, where weights are determined by image intensity. Depth Prior Loss (L{depth}): (Used in levels n < L-1) L1 difference between current depth and bilinearly interpolated depth from the previous lower-resolution level. 9. Optimization: Minimize the total loss L{total} using the Adam optimizer. 10. Pyramidal Progression: Recursively move to level n-2, using the depth map from level n-1 as a prior via L{depth}, until the "zeroth" level is reached. Rendering Loss: L{ren} = \frac{1}{m} \sum{pi \in \Omegap} \left\| \hat{I}(pi) - \tilde{I}(pi) \right\|2^2 where \hat{I}(pi) is the ground-truth color from interpolation and \tilde{I}(pi) is the synthesized color from NeRF. Position-of-Matched Features Loss: L{3D} = \frac{1}{n} \sum{k=1}^n \|\mathbf{x}s^k - \mathbf{x}{s'}^k\|2^2 where \mathbf{x}s^k and \mathbf{x}{s'}^k are the estimated 3D coordinates of matched SIFT feature k in the reference and target images, respectively. Epipolar Constraint Loss: L{epi} = \mint \left\{ \left\| \mathbf{d}{pr} - \mathbf{d}{pt} \right\|2^2 \right\} where \mathbf{d}{pr} is the 3D coordinate of the point in the reference image, and \mathbf{d}{pt} are the 3D coordinates of points on the epipolar line in the target image. Implausible points on the epipolar line are filtered by color similarity threshold. Warped Pixel Coordinate: \hat{p}t = K T{r \to t} \mathbf{x}p where \mathbf{x}p is the 3D coordinate of pixel p in the reference image, K is the intrinsic matrix, and T{r \to t} = [\mathbf{r}, \mathbf{t}] is the relative pose. Relative Pose Definition: \mathbf{r} = \mathbf{r}t^{-1}, \quad \mathbf{t} = -\mathbf{r}t^{-1}\mathbf{t}t where [\mathbf{r}t, \mathbf{t}t] is the global pose of the target image. Photometric Reconstruction Loss: L{pr} = \sum{p(k) \in \Omegap} M(p(k)) \left| \hat{I}r(p(k)) - \hat{I}t(\hat{p}t(k)) \right| where \hat{I}r is the reference patch color, \hat{I}t(\hat{p}t(k)) is the interpolated color of the warped point in the target image, and M is the binary mask. name: DASNeRF
head: Depth consistency optimization, adaptive sampling, and hierarchical structural fusion for sparse view neural radiance fields
body: DASNeRF is a Neural Radiance Field (NeRF) optimization method designed for sparse-view 3D reconstruction that integrates accurate monocular depth priors to guide learning and reduce lighting artifacts. It distinguishes itself from standard NeRF and other geometric priors by combining a dynamic optimal sampling mechanism with two specific depth regularization terms: Depth Ordering Fidelity Loss and Depth Structural Consistency Regularization. Unlike methods that rely on uniform sampling or simple depth consistency, DASNeRF uses a pre-trained depth estimator (DepthAnythingV2) to extract relative depth ordering and structural continuity constraints, which are enforced via a dynamic boundary adjustment strategy to handle varying depth levels in complex scenes. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: A sparse set of M input images I = \{I1,..., IM\} with corresponding camera poses P = \{p1,..., pM\}. Outputs: A trained implicit radiance field model (MLP) that predicts volumetric density \sigma and color c, and rendered images/depth maps for novel views. Data Structures: Scene Representation: An MLP f\Theta mapping 3D position x and viewing direction d to density \sigma and color c. The input to the MLP is enhanced with position encoding \gamma and a five-dimensional vector containing coordinate and ray information. Depth Prior: A depth map D{V2} estimated by the DepthAnythingV2 model. Sampling Points: A set of N points along a ray, obtained via 3D cone frustum sampling (Mip-NeRF) and a three-layer dynamic sampling mechanism. Parameters: \lambda: Weight for Depth Ordering Fidelity Loss. Default: 0.2. \gamma: Weight for Depth Structural Consistency Regularization. Default: 0.02. \alpha: Hyperparameter for dynamic boundary adjustment. Value: Not given in the sources. m{ar}: Dynamic boundary margin, calculated per pixel pair. m'{ar}: Small boundary value for structural consistency. Value: Not given in the sources. Algorithm Steps: 1. Depth Prior Estimation: For each input image Ii, use the pre-trained DepthAnythingV2 model to estimate the depth map D{V2}^i. DepthAnythingV2 is preferred over MiDaS for its ability to handle transparent/reflective objects and its 10x faster inference speed. The depth data is processed using relative inverse depth. 2. Dynamic Optimal Sampling: For a ray r originating from camera center o with direction d, defined by near tn and far tf boundaries: Employ 3D cone frustum sampling from Mip-NeRF to account for pixel footprint size. Apply a three-layer dynamic sampling mechanism to obtain N sample points t1,..., tN along the ray. For each sample point ti, compute the 3D position xi = o + ti d and the viewing direction d. Construct a five-dimensional input vector for the MLP containing the coordinates and ray information of the sampled points. 3. NeRF Forward Pass: Feed the five-dimensional input vector into the MLP with per-layer input fusion. Each MLP layer l takes two inputs: the features from the previous layer h{l-1} and the processed five-dimensional input information v. The MLP outputs volumetric density \sigmai and color ci for each sample point. 4. Volume Rendering: Compute the transmittance Ti and opacity \alphai for each sample: \alphai = 1 - \exp(-\sigmai \deltai) Ti = \exp\left(-\sum{j=1}^{i-1} \sigmaj \deltaj\right) where \deltai = t{i+1} - ti is the interval between samples. Compute the rendered pixel color \hat{C}(r): \hat{C}(r) = \sum{i=1}^{N} \omegai ci, \quad \text{where } \omegai = Ti \alphai Compute the rendered depth dr for the ray: dr = \sum{i=1}^{N} \omegai ti This depth dr corresponds to a local region P of the RGB image I. 5. Loss Calculation: The total loss is L = L{nerf} + \lambda L{DOF} + \gamma R{DSC}. Photometric Loss (L{nerf}): L{nerf} = \sum{r \in R} \| C(r) - \hat{C}(r) \|2^2 where C(r) is the ground truth pixel color and R is the set of all rays. Depth Ordering Fidelity Loss (L{DOF}): This loss enforces relative depth ordering consistency between the rendered depth dr and the prior depth D{V2}. 1. Identify pairs of 2D pixel coordinates (k1, k2) in the local region such that D{V2}^{k1} \leq D{V2}^{k2} (pixel k1 is closer or equal depth to k2 in the prior). 2. Calculate the dynamic boundary margin m{ar}: m{ar} = \alpha \cdot \frac{1}{N} \sum{i=1}^{N} |dr^{k1}[i] - dr^{k2}[i]| where dr^{k1}[i] and dr^{k2}[i] are the depth values of the i-th sample layer for pixels k1 and k2 respectively. 3. Compute the loss: L{DOF} = \sum{D{V2}^{k1} \leq D{V2}^{k2}} \max(dr^{k1} - dr^{k2} + m{ar}, 0) This penalizes cases where the rendered depth order contradicts the prior, with a margin that adapts to the local depth variance. Depth Structural Consistency Regularization (R{DSC}): This loss enforces continuity of depth values between neighboring pixels if they are continuous in the prior. 1. For each pixel k1, find its k-nearest neighbors KNN(D{V2}^{k1}) based on depth values in a small region of the prior depth map. 2. Compute the loss: R{DSC} = \sum{k1} \sum{D{V2}^{k2} \in KNN(D{V2}^{k1})} \max(|dr^{k1} - dr^{k2}| - m'{ar}, 0) where m'{ar} is a small boundary value accounting for minor depth variations. 6. Optimization: Minimize L with respect to the MLP parameters using gradient descent. Pseudocode: Unverified code. """ # Identify pixel pairs (k1, k2) where depthprior[k1] <= depthprior[k2] # This requires iterating over local regions or using vectorized operations # to find valid pairs. For simplicity, we assume a mask or indices are provided. # Calculate dynamic boundary margin mar # mar = alpha mean(|dr[k1] - dr[k2]|) over samples # Implementation depends on how 'samples' are aggregated per pixel pair # The source uses dr[k1][i] which implies depth at sample layer i # However, rendereddepth is usually a single value per pixel. # The source formula: mar = alpha 1/N sum |dr^k1[i] - dr^k2[i]| # This suggests using the raw sample depths or a specific aggregation. # We will use the rendered depth values for the pair as a proxy for the mean # if sample-wise depth is not explicitly stored in the final output. # Note: The source formula uses dr^k1[i], which might refer to the # contribution of sample i to the depth, or the depth at sample i. # Given dr = sum wi ti, the term |dr^k1[i] - dr^k2[i]| is ambiguous. # It likely refers to the depth value ti weighted by wi, or simply ti. # Let's assume it refers to the sample positions ti for the pixels. # For implementation, we need pairs (k1, k2) # LDOF = sum max(dr[k1] - dr[k2] + mar, 0) # Placeholder for pair selection logic pairs = self.getvaliddepthpairs(depthprior) loss = 0.0 for k1, k2 in pairs: drk1 = rendereddepth[k1] drk2 = rendereddepth[k2] # Dynamic margin calculation # The source sums over N samples. We approximate with the rendered depth difference # or need access to sample-level depths. # Let's assume we have sample depths tvals for these pixels # mar = alpha mean(|tvals[k1] - tvals[k2]|) # This is a simplification. The source says "depth values of the i-th pixel at different sampling layers" # which might mean the depth contribution. # Using rendered depth difference as a proxy for the margin magnitude # if sample-level data is not passed through. # However, to be precise to, we should use sample depths. # Let's assume tvals is available for k1 and k2. mar = alpha torch.mean(torch.abs(tvals[k1] - tvals[k2])) loss += torch.clamp(drk1 - drk2 + mar, min=0) return loss def computestructuralconsistencyloss(self, rendereddepth, depthprior, kneighbors=3): """ Compute Depth Structural Consistency Regularization (RDSC). """ # Find k-nearest neighbors in depth space for each pixel in depthprior # This is computationally expensive. Usually done on a grid. loss = 0.0 # Placeholder for KNN logic neighbors = self.getknndepth(depthprior, kneighbors) for k1, neighborindices in neighbors: drk1 = rendereddepth[k1] for k2 in neighborindices: drk2 = rendereddepth[k2] # Small boundary value m'ar # Value not given. Using a small constant epsilon. marprime = 1e-3 loss += torch.clamp(torch.abs(drk1 - drk2) - marprime, min=0) return loss def trainstep(self, images, poses, tnear, tfar, nsamples): """ Single training step. """ self.mlp.train() totalloss = 0.0 for i, (image, pose) in enumerate(zip(images, poses)): # 1. Get Depth Prior depthprior = self.getdepthprior(image) # 2. Sample Rays # Generate rays from camera pose rayo, rayd = self.generaterays(pose, image.shape) # 3. Sample Points positions, directions, tvals = self.sampleray(rayo, rayd, tnear, tfar, nsamples) # 4. MLP Forward sigma, color = self.forwardmlp(positions, directions) # 5. Volume Render renderedcolor, rendereddepth, weights = self.volumerender(sigma, color, tvals) # 6. Compute Losses # Photometric Loss gtcolor = image.permute(2, 0, 1) # Assuming HWC to CHW lnerf = torch.mean((renderedcolor - gtcolor) 2) # Depth Ordering Fidelity Loss ldof = self.computedepthorderingloss(rendereddepth, depthprior, self.alpha) # Depth Structural Consistency Loss rdsc = self.computestructuralconsistencyloss(rendereddepth, depthprior) # Total Loss loss = lnerf + self.lambdadof ldof + self.gammadsc rdsc totalloss += loss return totalloss / len(images) Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Depth Prior Accuracy: If the monocular depth estimator (DepthAnythingV2) fails on transparent or reflective surfaces, the regularization may introduce artifacts. DepthAnythingV2 is chosen specifically to mitigate this compared to MiDaS. Dynamic Margin Calculation: The dynamic boundary adjustment m{ar} depends on the depth differences at different sampling layers. If the sampling is too coarse, the margin calculation may be inaccurate. Sparse Views: The method is designed for sparse inputs. With very few views, the depth consistency terms are critical, but the photometric loss may be insufficient to constrain the geometry without strong priors. Time Complexity: The method involves an additional forward pass through the DepthAnythingV2 model for each input image during training (or pre-computed). Memory Complexity: Similar to standard NeRF, plus storage for the depth priors. The five-dimensional input fusion does not significantly increase memory usage. Performance: DASNeRF outperforms existing methods in sparse reconstruction details. It is particularly effective in scenes with complex geometries, transparent objects, and intricate details where standard NeRF struggles. Strengths: Improved detail preservation in sparse views. Robustness to lighting variations via dynamic sampling. Effective handling of depth discontinuities and noise through dynamic boundary adjustment. Limitations: Relies on the quality of the monocular depth estimator. Computational cost is higher than standard NeRF due to depth estimation and additional loss calculations. It addresses the limitation of standard NeRF, which typically requires hundreds of images for high-fidelity reconstruction, by enabling sparse-view 3D reconstruction. The method builds on the Neural Radiance Field framework [8] and integrates recent advances in monocular depth estimation (DepthAnythingV2) and Mip-NeRF sampling. It is used in applications requiring rapid depth map generation and practical deployment in fields such as autonomous driving and augmented reality, leveraging the speed and accuracy of DepthAnythingV2. name: GeoNeRF
head: GeoNeRF, A model with two parts: a geometric morphology reasoner and a renderer. The reasoner builds a cascaded cost volume for source view sequences. The renderer infers geometric and appearance representations using a Transformer-based attention mechanism and cascaded cost volumes, then renders fine images
body: GeoNeRF is a multi-view stereo and novel view synthesis method that integrates geometric priors into a radiance field optimization framework. It addresses the ambiguity in sparse-view reconstruction by explicitly modeling geometry through a cascaded cost volume, distinguishing it from standard NeRF which relies solely on volumetric density. Unlike sibling methods that may use explicit SDFs or epipolar constraints, GeoNeRF employs a Transformer-based attention mechanism to refine features extracted from a 3D cost volume, enabling robust generalization to new scenes and fine-tuning for high-fidelity rendering. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: A sequence of N calibrated source views (RGB images). Outputs: Rendered RGB images for novel viewpoints. Data Structures: 1. Feature Pyramid Network (FPN) Features: 2D image features extracted from each source view using a pretrained FPN. 2. Cascaded 3D Cost Volume: A multi-scale 3D tensor constructed via plane sweeping from the 2D features. 3. Feature Tokens: For each query point along a ray, a set of tokens is extracted from the cost volume: One view-independent token. Multiple view-dependent tokens. Algorithm Steps: 1. Feature Extraction: Extract 2D image features from every input view using a pretrained Feature Pyramid Network. 2. Cost Volume Construction: Construct a cascading 3D cost volume for the source view sequences using plane sweeping. 3. Query Point Sampling: For each of the N query points along a ray, extract one view-independent and multiple view-dependent feature tokens from the cost volume. 4. Transformer Refinement: Refine the extracted tokens using a Transformer-based attention mechanism. 5. Density Prediction: Refine the N view-independent tokens through an AutoEncoder to return the N densities along the ray. 6. Color Prediction: Feed the N sets of view-dependent tokens into separate Multi-Layer Perceptrons (MLPs) to extract color for each point. 7. Volume Rendering: Use volume rendering technology to render fine images from the predicted densities and colors. Pseudocode: Unverified code. Returns: Rendered RGB image.
