name: Neural RGB-D Surface Reconstruction
head: Hybrid Scene Representation Network, Neural RGB-D
body: Neural RGB-D Surface Reconstruction is a method for high-quality, metric 3D reconstruction of room-scale scenes from an RGB-D input sequence. It solves the problem of generating clean, watertight meshes from noisy depth data by replacing the standard density-based volumetric representation of NeRF with a hybrid representation: a truncated signed distance field (TSDF) for geometry and a volumetric radiance field for appearance. Unlike standard NeRF which produces semi-transparent artifacts and lacks metric geometry, this method enforces hard boundaries between occupied and free space, enabling direct mesh extraction via Marching Cubes. It builds on Specific Model Architectures by integrating geometric priors directly into the rendering integral rather than as auxiliary losses alone. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: N color frames Ii, corresponding aligned depth frames Di, and initial camera poses Ti. Outputs: Optimized MLP parameters, camera poses, and a triangle mesh extracted from the final TSDF. Data Structures: 1. Shape MLP: A multi-layer perceptron. Input: Sinusoidal positional encoding \gamma(\mathbf{p}) of a 3D query point \mathbf{p}. Output: Truncated signed distance value Di. 2. Radiance MLP: A multi-layer perceptron. Inputs: Sinusoidal positional encoding \gamma(\mathbf{d}) of the viewing direction \mathbf{d}, an intermediate feature vector from the Shape MLP, and a per-frame latent corrective code vector \mathbf{z}i. Output: View-dependent surface radiance \mathbf{c}i. 3. Deformation Field: A 6-layer ReLU MLP acting as a residual correction for pixel locations. 4. Camera Poses: Represented as Euler angles and a translation vector for each frame. 5. Scene Scaling: The scene is scaled such that the truncation region maps to [-1, 1], where positive values are in front of the surface and negative values are behind. Parameters: tr: Truncation distance. Typical value: 5 cm. \lambda1: RGB loss weight. Value: 0.1. \lambda2: Free-space loss weight. Value: 10. \lambda3: Truncation loss weight. Value: 6 \times 10^3. S'f: Number of fine samples. Value: 16. S'c: Coarse sampling rate. One sample for every 1.5 cm of ray length on average. Ray length: Must exceed the largest distance in the scene. Typical range: 4 to 8 meters. Optimizer: ADAM with learning rate 5 \times 10^{-4}. Training iterations: 2 \times 10^5. Batch size: |Pb| = 1024 randomly chosen rays per iteration. Numbered Steps: 1. Initialization: Initialize camera poses Ti using BundleFusion. Initialize MLP weights. 2. Ray Generation & Refinement: For a pixel p in batch b: a. Retrieve the 2D pixel coordinate. b. Apply the deformation field MLP to get a 2D shift vector. c. Add the shift to the pixel coordinate. d. Unproject the corrected 2D coordinate into a 3D ray using the camera pose Ti and intrinsics. 3. Coarse Sampling: Generate S'c sample points along the ray using stratified sampling. 4. Coarse Evaluation: Evaluate the Shape MLP at these S'c points to get signed distance values. 5. Zero-Crossing Search: Search for the zero-crossing (where Di changes sign) in the coarse samples to estimate the surface depth. Pitfall: If the sampling rate S'c is too low, samples may miss the truncation region, causing the zero-crossing to be missed. 6. Fine Sampling: Generate S'f sample points clustered around the identified zero-crossing. 7. Fine Evaluation: Evaluate the Shape MLP and Radiance MLP at all S'c + S'f samples (concatenating outputs from coarse and fine passes). 8. Weight Calculation: For each sample i with signed distance Di, compute the weight wi: wi = \sigma \left( \frac{Di}{tr} \right) \cdot \sigma \left( -\frac{Di}{tr} \right) where \sigma is the sigmoid function. Weights fall to zero as distance from the surface increases. To account for multiple intersections, weights of samples beyond the first truncation region are set to zero. 9. Color Integration: Compute the rendered color \mathbf{C} as a weighted sum: \mathbf{C} = \frac{1}{\sum{i=0}^{K-1} wi} \sum{i=0}^{K-1} wi \cdot \mathbf{c}i where K = S'c + S'f is the total number of samples, and \mathbf{c}i is the radiance output from the Radiance MLP. 10. Loss Computation: Compute the total loss \mathcal{L}(\mathcal{P}) for the batch: \mathcal{L}(\mathcal{P}) = \sum{b=0}^{B-1} \lambda1 \mathcal{L}{rgb}^b(\mathcal{P}) + \lambda2 \mathcal{L}{fs}^b(\mathcal{P}) + \lambda3 \mathcal{L}{tr}^b(\mathcal{P}) RGB Loss: \mathcal{L}{rgb}^b(\mathcal{P}) = \frac{1}{|Pb|} \sum{p \in Pb} (\mathbf{C}p - \hat{\mathbf{C}}p)^2, where \hat{\mathbf{C}}p is the observed color. Free-Space Loss: For samples s between the camera origin and the truncation region (\mathcal{S}p^{fs}): \mathcal{L}{fs}^b(\mathcal{P}) = \frac{1}{|Pb|} \sum{p \in Pb} \frac{1}{|\mathcal{S}p^{fs}|} \sum{s \in \mathcal{S}p^{fs}} (Ds - tr)^2 This forces the MLP to predict tr for free space. Truncation Loss: For samples s within the truncation region (\mathcal{S}p^{tr}): \mathcal{L}{tr}^b(\mathcal{P}) = \frac{1}{|Pb|} \sum{p \in Pb} \frac{1}{|\mathcal{S}p^{tr}|} \sum{s \in \mathcal{S}p^{tr}} (Ds - \hat{D}s)^2 where \hat{D}s is the signed distance observed by the depth sensor along the optical axis. 11. Optimization: Update network parameters \Theta, camera poses Ti, latent codes, and deformation field using ADAM. 12. Mesh Extraction: After training, extract a triangle mesh from the optimized TSDF using Marching Cubes with a spatial resolution of 1 cm. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import numpy as np import torch import torch.nn as nn import torch.nn.functional as F class ShapeMLP(nn.Module): def init(self, inputdim=3, hiddendim=256, outputdim=1): super().init() self.layers = nn.ModuleList([nn.Linear(inputdim, hiddendim)] + [nn.Linear(hiddendim, hiddendim) for in range(4)]) self.out = nn.Linear(hiddendim, outputdim) def forward(self, x): h = x for layer in self.layers: h = F.relu(layer(h)) return self.out(h) class RadianceMLP(nn.Module): def init(self, featuredim=256, viewdim=3, latentdim=16, outputdim=3): super().init() self.layers = nn.ModuleList([nn.Linear(featuredim + viewdim + latentdim, 256)] + [nn.Linear(256, 256) for in range(4)]) self.out = nn.Linear(256, outputdim) def forward(self, feature, viewdir, latentcode): x = torch.cat([feature, viewdir, latentcode], dim=-1) h = x for layer in self.layers: h = F.relu(layer(h)) return self.out(h) class DeformationField(nn.Module): def init(self): super().init() self.layers = nn.ModuleList([nn.Linear(2, 64)] + [nn.Linear(64, 64) for in range(5)]) self.out = nn.Linear(64, 2) def forward(self, x): h = x for layer in self.layers: h = F.relu(layer(h)) return self.out(h) def positionalencoding(x, numfreqbands=10): # Standard NeRF positional encoding freqbands = 2.0 torch.linspace(0, numfreqbands - 1, numfreqbands).to(x.device) out = [x] for freq in freqbands: out.append(torch.sin(x freq)) out.append(torch.cos(x freq)) return torch.cat(out, dim=-1) def renderray(shapemlp, radiancemlp, deformationmlp, pose, intrinsics, pixelcoord, latentcode, tr, Sc, Sf, raylength): # 1. Refine Ray # Deformation field takes 2D pixel coord, returns 2D shift shift = deformationmlp(pixelcoord) refinedcoord = pixelcoord + shift # Unproject to 3D ray (simplified: assume origin and direction from pose/intrinsics) # In practice, this involves camera matrix inversion. # Here we assume a helper unproject exists or is implemented via standard pinhole model. rayorigin, raydirection = unproject(refinedcoord, pose, intrinsics) # 2. Coarse Sampling # Stratified sampling along raylength tcoarse = torch.linspace(0, raylength, Sc) + torch.rand(Sc) / Sc # Simplified stratified # Ensure distinct samples tcoarse = torch.sort(tcoarse)[0] pointscoarse = rayorigin.unsqueeze(0) + tcoarse.unsqueeze(1) raydirection.unsqueeze(0) # Encode points encpointscoarse = positionalencoding(pointscoarse) # 3. Coarse Evaluation Dcoarse = shapemlp(encpointscoarse).squeeze(-1) # Shape: [Sc] # 4. Zero-Crossing Search # Find index where sign changes signs = torch.sign(Dcoarse) zerocrossidx = torch.where(signs[:-1] != signs[1:])[0] if len(zerocrossidx) == 0: # Fallback: use midpoint if no crossing found, or handle error # In practice, one might clamp or extend ray, but sources don't specify fallback logic. # We assume valid input where crossing exists. zerocrossidx = torch.tensor([Sc // 2]) # 5. Fine Sampling # Generate Sf samples around the zero crossing # Estimate depth at crossing (interpolate) idx = zerocrossidx[0] tcross = (tcoarse[idx] + tcoarse[idx+1]) / 2.0 # Generate fine samples around tcross tfine = torch.linspace(tcross - 0.1, tcross + 0.1, Sf) # Range not specified, assume small window pointsfine = rayorigin.unsqueeze(0) + tfine.unsqueeze(1) raydirection.unsqueeze(0) encpointsfine = positionalencoding(pointsfine) # 6. Fine Evaluation Dfine = shapemlp(encpointsfine).squeeze(-1) # Concatenate Dall = torch.cat([Dcoarse, Dfine]) encpointsall = torch.cat([encpointscoarse, encpointsfine]) # 7. Weight Calculation # wi = sigma(Di / tr) sigma(-Di / tr) weights = torch.sigmoid(Dall / tr) torch.sigmoid(-Dall / tr) # Set weights to zero beyond first truncation region (simplified: assume first crossing is the surface) # Logic to identify "first" region requires tracking indices. # Assuming Dall is ordered along ray, we zero out weights after the first peak/zero-crossing. # For simplicity in this self-contained code, we keep all weights as per formula, # but note that implementation must handle multiple intersections. # 8. Radiance Evaluation # Get intermediate feature from shape MLP for fine samples? # Sources say: "intermediate feature output of the shape MLP". # We need to re-evaluate shape MLP or store features. # For simplicity, we assume shape MLP outputs feature too or we re-run. # Let's assume we re-run shape MLP to get feature for fine samples, # and coarse samples might not need radiance if we only integrate fine? # Sources: "integrate color using all Sc + Sf samples". # Re-evaluate shape MLP for all points to get features? # Or assume shape MLP returns (D, feature). # Let's assume Shape MLP returns D only, and we need a separate feature extractor or re-run. # To keep it simple and compliant with "Shape MLP... outputs truncated signed distance", # we might need a separate feature network or assume the last hidden layer is the feature. # Standard practice is to use the last hidden layer of the geometry network as the feature. # We will assume shapemlp has a method or we extract the hidden state. # For this pseudocode, we will assume a helper getfeature or that we re-run. # Let's assume we re-run the forward pass but capture the hidden state. # Simplified: Assume we have a function shapemlpwithfeature # Dall, featuresall = shapemlpwithfeature(encpointsall) # Since we can't modify the class definition easily in this block, # we will assume the radiance MLP takes the D value? No, sources say "intermediate feature". # We will assume the last hidden layer of Shape MLP is the feature. # Re-run Shape MLP to get hidden states hcoarse = encpointscoarse for layer in shapemlp.layers: hcoarse = F.relu(layer(hcoarse)) featurecoarse = hcoarse # Last hidden layer hfine = encpointsfine for layer in shapemlp.layers: hfine = F.relu(layer(hfine)) featurefine = hfine featureall = torch.cat([featurecoarse, featurefine]) # Encode view direction encview = positionalencoding(raydirection.unsqueeze(0).expand(Sall, -1)) # Expand latent code latentexpanded = latentcode.unsqueeze(0).expand(Sall, -1) radiance = radiancemlp(featureall, encview, latentexpanded) # 9. Color Integration # C = sum(wi ci) / sum(wi) color = torch.sum(weights.unsqueeze(1) radiance, dim=0) / torch.sum(weights) return color, Dall, weights def trainstep(shapemlp, radiancemlp, deformationmlp, poses, intrinsics, images, depths, latentcodes, tr, Sc, Sf, raylength, lambdargb, lambdafs, lambdatr, optimizer): optimizer.zerograd() totalloss = 0 batchsize = 1024 # Sample batch of pixels H, W = images[0].shape[1], images[0].shape[2] pixelindices = torch.randint(0, HW, (batchsize,)) frameindices = torch.randint(0, len(images), (batchsize,)) for i in range(batchsize): fidx = frameindices[i] pidx = pixelindices[i] u, v = divmod(pidx, W) pixelcoord = torch.tensor([u, v], dtype=torch.float32) # Get image and depth img = images[fidx][:, v, u] # [3] depthval = depths[fidx][v, u] # Scalar # Get pose and latent code pose = poses[fidx] latent = latentcodes[fidx] # Render colorpred, Dall, weights = renderray( shapemlp, radiancemlp, deformationmlp, pose, intrinsics, pixelcoord, latent, tr, Sc, Sf, raylength) # RGB Loss lossrgb = (colorpred - img).pow(2).mean() # Identify Free Space and Truncation samples # Logic to classify samples based on depth and tr is complex. # Sources define sets Sfs and Str. # Sfs: samples between camera origin and truncation region. # Str: samples within truncation region. # Approximate classification: # If D > tr, it's free space (assuming positive is front). # If |D| < tr, it's truncation region. # Note: Sources say "positive in front of surface". # Free space is "between camera origin and truncation region". # This implies samples with D > tr are free space? # Or samples where the ray hasn't hit the surface yet. # We use the D value to classify. maskfs = Dall > tr masktr = (Dall >= -tr) & (Dall <= tr) lossfs = torch.tensor(0.0) if maskfs.any(): # Target is tr targetfs = torch.fulllike(Dall[maskfs], tr) lossfs = (Dall[maskfs] - targetfs).pow(2).mean() losstr = torch.tensor(0.0) if masktr.any(): # Target is observed signed distance # Need to compute observed signed distance from depth map. # This requires projecting the sample point back to the depth map. # Simplified: assume we have a function getobservedsigneddistance observedD = getobservedsigneddistance(Dall[masktr], pose, intrinsics, depths[fidx]) losstr = (Dall[masktr] - observedD).pow(2).mean() loss = lambdargb lossrgb + lambdafs lossfs + lambdatr losstr totalloss += loss totalloss.backward() optimizer.step() return totalloss.item() InFusionSurf is a NeRF-style RGB-D 3D surface reconstruction framework that refines depth information to enhance reconstruction quality with minimal impact on optimization time, using per-frame intrinsic refinement and TSDF Fusion prior learning. It addresses camera motion-induced blurs in depth frames by correcting the camera intrinsic matrix per frame and accelerates training by pre-training the geometric prior using classical TSDF Fusion. It builds on Neural RGB-D Surface Reconstruction by adding specific intrinsic refinement and a two-stage initialization process. Time Complexity: Training requires 2 \times 10^5 iterations. Each iteration processes 1024 rays. The two-step sampling (coarse + fine) doubles the forward pass cost compared to single-pass methods. Memory Complexity: Depends on the MLP size and the number of samples per ray. The deformation field and latent codes add minor overhead. Measured Performance: On 10 synthetic scenes, the method achieved a Chamfer \ell1 distance of 0.044, IoU of 0.747, Normal Consistency of 0.918, and F-score of 0.924. Strengths: Produces high-quality, metric 3D reconstructions with hard boundaries, avoiding the semi-transparent artifacts common in density-based NeRFs. Robust to noisy depth data by combining color and depth losses. Limitations: Requires RGB-D input. Performance depends on the quality of initial camera poses (initialized via BundleFusion). If coarse sampling is too sparse, the zero-crossing may be missed, leading to reconstruction failure. When to use: When metric 3D mesh reconstruction is required from RGB-D sequences, especially in room-scale scenes. When not to use: When only novel view synthesis is needed without metric geometry, or when only RGB input is available (use standard NeRF or RGB-D methods with monocular depth estimation). Neural RGB-D Surface Reconstruction was proposed by Dejan Azinović, Ricardo Martin-Brualla, Dan B. Goldman, Matthias Nießner, and Justus Thies in 2022. It was presented at CVPR 2022. The method addresses the limitations of neural radiance fields (NeRF) which, while excellent for novel view synthesis, do not reconstruct metric and clean meshes. It builds on the idea of implicit surface representations (SDFs) and integrates them with the differentiable rendering framework of NeRF. It is related to concurrent work such as NeuS. The method is particularly useful for AR/VR applications, teleconferencing, and robotic applications requiring high-fidelity 3D models. name: InFusionSurf
body: InFusionSurf is a NeRF-style RGB-D 3D surface reconstruction framework that refines depth information to enhance reconstruction quality with minimal impact on optimization time, using per-frame intrinsic refinement and TSDF Fusion prior learning. It addresses camera motion-induced blurs in depth frames by correcting the camera intrinsic matrix per frame and accelerates training by pre-training the geometric prior using classical TSDF Fusion. It builds on Neural RGB-D Surface Reconstruction by adding specific intrinsic refinement and a two-stage initialization process. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: A sequence of RGB-D video frames (color images C{u,v}^i and depth maps), initial camera poses [R|t], and initial camera intrinsics (fx, fy, cx, cy). Outputs: A trained hybrid scene representation consisting of a dense feature grid \mathcal{V}^{(feat)}, MLPs for color (MLP^C) and signed distance (MLP^D), per-frame latent embeddings \xii, per-frame intrinsic refinement parameters (s^i, \tau^i), and an image-plane deformation field (from parent method). The final output is a renderable radiance field and a mesh extracted via Marching Cubes. Data Structures: 1. Dense Feature Grid \mathcal{V}^{(feat)}: Layout: 3D array of dimensions Nx \times Ny \times Nz with feature length F. Dimensions: Nx = \lceil Lx/gs \rceil, Ny = \lceil Ly/gs \rceil, Nz = \lceil Lz/gs \rceil, where Lx, Ly, Lz are scene bounds and gs is cell size. Initialization: Zeros. 2. MLPs: MLP^C: Color decoder. 2 hidden layers, 128 nodes each. MLP^D: Signed distance decoder. 2 hidden layers, 128 nodes each. Image-plane deformation MLP (from parent): 2 hidden layers, 64 nodes each. 3. Per-Frame Parameters: Scaling matrix s^i \in \mathbb{R}^{3 \times 3} and translation vector \tau^i \in \mathbb{R}^3 for each frame i. Latent embedding \xii for each frame i. Numbered Steps: 1. Scene Bounds and Grid Setup: Estimate scene bounds Lx, Ly, Lz from depth frames and initial poses. Set cell size gs (default 10cm) and feature length F (default 12). Compute grid dimensions Nx, Ny, Nz and initialize \mathcal{V}^{(feat)} with zeros. 2. Phase 1: TSDF Fusion Prior Learning: Set F=1 for this phase. Construct a TSDF volume from the input depth frames using a standard TSDF Fusion algorithm. Randomly sample grid cells and query their center points p. Query the TSDF volume for the signed distance value D{TSDF}(p). Compute feature vector \phip via trilinear interpolation of the 8 nearest vertices in \mathcal{V}^{(feat)}. Compute predicted signed distance \hat{D}p = MLP^D(\phip). Minimize mean squared error between \hat{D}p and D{TSDF}(p). Optimize only \mathcal{V}^{(feat)} and MLP^D for 3,000 iterations. 3. Phase 2: Progressive Learning (Low-Frequency): Set F=12. Randomly sample ray batches rb. For each ray, sample points Sc every 15.625mm along the ray. Compute normalized image coordinates \varrho{u,v} using initial intrinsics: \varrho{u,v} = \begin{bmatrix} 1/fx & 0 & -cx/fx \\ 0 & -1/fy & cy/fy \\ 0 & 0 & -1 \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} u \\ v \\ 1 \end{bmatrix} (Note: The source table contains a typo \begin{bmatrix} v \\ v \\ 1 \end{bmatrix} and text uses \begin{bmatrix} v \\ u \\ 1 \end{bmatrix}, but standard pinhole projection uses \begin{bmatrix} u \\ v \\ 1 \end{bmatrix}.) Apply per-frame intrinsic refinement to get refined \hat{\varrho}{u,v}^i = s^i \cdot (\varrho{u,v} + \tau^i). Compute ray direction \hat{d}{u,v}^i = [R|t] [\hat{\varrho}{u,v}^i; 1]. Sample points p along \hat{d}{u,v}^i. Compute \phip via trilinear interpolation from \mathcal{V}^{(feat)}. Compute \hat{D}p = MLP^D(\phip). Compute weight \omegap = \sigma(\hat{D}p/tr) \cdot \sigma(-\hat{D}p/tr). Compute color C{p,d}^i = MLP^C(\phip, \Lambda(\hat{d}{u,v}^i), \xii). Compute rendered color \hat{C}r^i = \frac{\sum \omegap C{p,d}^i}{\sum \omegap}. Compute Loss \mathcal{L} (see below). Optimize all parameters for 7,000 iterations. 4. Phase 3: Progressive Learning (High-Frequency): Halve the grid cell size gs (e.g., from 10cm to 5cm). Re-initialize \mathcal{V}^{(feat)} to new dimensions Nx, Ny, Nz with F=12. Sample points Sc as in Phase 2. Identify surfaces in Sc and sample additional points Sf around these surfaces. Use both Sc and Sf for loss computation. Optimize all parameters for 65,000 iterations. Per-Frame Intrinsic Refinement: For each frame i, optimize scaling s^i and translation \tau^i. s^i = \text{diag}(sx^i, sy^i, 1), \tau^i = [\taux^i, \tauy^i, 0]^T. Initialize s^i to identity (1,1,1) and \tau^i to zero. Refined coordinate: \hat{\varrho}{u,v}^i = s^i \cdot (\varrho{u,v} + \tau^i). Loss Function: \mathcal{L} = \lambda{fs} \mathcal{L}{fs} + \lambda{sdf} \mathcal{L}{sdf} + \lambda{rgb} \mathcal{L}{rgb} + \lambda{reg} \mathcal{L}{reg} \mathcal{L}{fs} (Points outside truncation S{fs}): \frac{1}{|rb|} \sum{r \in rb} \frac{1}{|S{fs}|} \sum{p \in S{fs}} (\hat{D}p - tr)^2. \mathcal{L}{sdf} (Points inside truncation S{sdf}): \frac{1}{|rb|} \sum{r \in rb} \frac{1}{|S{sdf}|} \sum{p \in S{sdf}} (\hat{D}p - Dr^i)^2, where Dr^i is the observed depth-derived signed distance. \mathcal{L}{rgb}: \frac{1}{|rb|} \sum{r \in rb} (\hat{C}r^i - C{u,v}^i)^2. \mathcal{L}{reg}: L2 regularization on \xii, s^i, \tau^i, and deformation parameters. Scaling parameters regularized around 1. Parameters: tr = 5cm. \lambda{fs} = 10, \lambda{sdf} = 6 \times 10^3, \lambda{rgb} = 0.5, \lambda{reg} = 0.1. Optimizer: ADAM, lr=5 \times 10^{-4}, decays to 1/10 every 250K iterations, \beta1=0.9, \beta2=0.999. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import torch import torch.nn as nn import numpy as np class InFusionSurf: def init(self, scenebounds, depthframes, colorframes, initialposes, initialintrinsics): self.scenebounds = scenebounds # Lx, Ly, Lz in meters self.depthframes = depthframes self.colorframes = colorframes self.poses = initialposes # [R|t] self.intrinsics = initialintrinsics # fx, fy, cx, cy # Hyperparameters self.gs = 0.1 # 10cm self.F = 12 self.tr = 0.05 # 5cm self.samplinginterval = 0.015625 # 15.625mm # Grid dimensions Nx = int(np.ceil(scenebounds[0] / self.gs)) Ny = int(np.ceil(scenebounds[1] / self.gs)) Nz = int(np.ceil(scenebounds[2] / self.gs)) # Data structures self.Vfeat = torch.zeros(Nx, Ny, Nz, 1) # Phase 1 uses F=1 self.MLPD = MLP(indim=1, h1=128, h2=128, outdim=1) self.MLPC = MLP(indim=12, h1=128, h2=128, outdim=3) self.numframes = len(depthframes) self.scales = torch.ones(self.numframes, 3) # sx, sy, 1 self.translations = torch.zeros(self.numframes, 3) # tx, ty, 0 self.latents = torch.randn(self.numframes, 16) # Example latent dim # Optimizers self.optphase1 = torch.optim.Adam([self.Vfeat] + list(self.MLPD.parameters()), lr=5e-4) self.optphase2 = torch.optim.Adam( [self.Vfeat] + list(self.MLPC.parameters()) + list(self.MLPD.parameters()) + [self.scales, self.translations, self.latents], lr=5e-4) def trilinearinterp(self, V, points): # points: (N, 3) in grid coordinates # Returns (N, F) p = points.float() p000 = torch.floor(p).long() p111 = p000 + 1 w = p - p000.float() c000 = V[p000[:, 0], p000[:, 1], p000[:, 2]] c100 = V[p111[:, 0], p000[:, 1], p000[:, 2]] c010 = V[p000[:, 0], p111[:, 1], p000[:, 2]] c110 = V[p111[:, 0], p111[:, 1], p000[:, 2]] c001 = V[p000[:, 0], p000[:, 1], p111[:, 2]] c101 = V[p111[:, 0], p000[:, 1], p111[:, 2]] c011 = V[p000[:, 0], p111[:, 1], p111[:, 2]] c111 = V[p111[:, 0], p111[:, 1], p111[:, 2]] w000 = (1-w[:,0])(1-w[:,1])(1-w[:,2]) w100 = w[:,0](1-w[:,1])(1-w[:,2]) w010 = (1-w[:,0])w[:,1](1-w[:,2]) w110 = w[:,0]w[:,1](1-w[:,2]) w001 = (1-w[:,0])(1-w[:,1])w[:,2] w101 = w[:,0](1-w[:,1])w[:,2] w011 = (1-w[:,0])w[:,1]w[:,2] w111 = w[:,0]w[:,1]w[:,2] return (w000c000 + w100c100 + w010c010 + w110c110 + w001c001 + w101c101 + w011c011 + w111c111) def getnormalizedcoords(self, u, v, fx, fy, cx, cy): x = (u - cx) / fx y = -(v - cy) / fy z = -1 return torch.stack([x, y, z], dim=-1) def refineintrinsics(self, rho, frameidx): s = self.scales[frameidx] t = self.translations[frameidx] smat = torch.diag(s) rhorefined = smat @ (rho + t.unsqueeze(0)) return rhorefined def computesdfloss(self, points, Dobs, isoutside): Dpred = self.MLPD(self.trilinearinterp(self.Vfeat, points)) target = self.tr if isoutside else Dobs return torch.mean((Dpred - target) 2) def train(self): # Phase 1: TSDF Fusion Prior Learning self.Vfeat = torch.zeros(self.Vfeat.shape[0], self.Vfeat.shape[1], self.Vfeat.shape[2], 1) # Construct TSDF volume from depth frames DTSDF = self.constructtsdfvolume(self.depthframes) for in range(3000): # Sample grid cells, query centers, get DTSDF # Forward MLPD, compute MSE, backward self.optphase1.step() # Phase 2: Progressive Learning self.Vfeat = torch.zeros(self.Vfeat.shape[0], self.Vfeat.shape[1], self.Vfeat.shape[2], 12) for in range(7000): # Sample rays, points Sc every 15.625mm # Compute loss, backward self.optphase2.step() # Phase 3: Progressive Learning self.gs /= 2 Nx, Ny, Nz = int(np.ceil(self.scenebounds[0]/self.gs)), int(np.ceil(self.scenebounds[1]/self.gs)), int(np.ceil(self.scenebounds[2]/self.gs)) self.Vfeat = torch.zeros(Nx, Ny, Nz, 12) for in range(65000): # Sample Sc and Sf, compute loss, backward self.optphase2.step() class MLP(nn.Module): def init(self, indim, h1, h2, outdim): super().init() self.net = nn.Sequential( nn.Linear(indim, h1), nn.ReLU(), nn.Linear(h1, h2), nn.ReLU(), nn.Linear(h2, outdim)) def forward(self, x): return self.net(x) Time Complexity: Training is significantly faster than Neural RGB-D. 75K iterations take ~96 minutes on average, which is 7.3 to 8.7 times faster than Neural RGB-D. Memory Complexity: Uses a dense feature grid. Memory usage scales with Nx Ny Nz F. The grid size is determined by scene bounds and cell size gs. Measured Performance: On ScanNet V2 and synthetic scenes, InFusionSurf outperforms GO-Surf in C-ℓ1, IoU, and F-score with 20% less training time at 20K iterations. It is less effective on normal consistency, indicating that its results contained relatively uneven surfaces. Strengths: Fast training, high-quality geometry reconstruction, handles motion blur in depth frames via intrinsic refinement. Limitations: Relies on simple transformation matrices for intrinsic refinement; does not handle local blurs (object motion, rolling shutter) effectively. Less effective on normal consistency. When to use: Quick reconstruction of complex geometries from RGB-D video with camera motion. When not to use: Scenes with significant local motion blur or rolling shutter effects where uniform intrinsic refinement is insufficient. InFusionSurf was introduced by Seunghwan Lee, Gwanmo Park, Hyewon Son, Jiwon Ryu, and Han Joo Chae from ROKIT Healthcare, Inc.. It was published in 2024. It builds upon Neural RGB-D Surface Reconstruction. It is implemented in PyTorch and evaluated on the ScanNet V2 dataset and synthetic scenes. name: DINER
head: DINER (Depth-aware Image-based NEural Radiance fields), Depth-aware Image-based NEural Radiance fields
body: DINER is a method for novel view synthesis that reconstructs a volumetric scene representation (NeRF) from a sparse set of RGB input views by leveraging predicted dense depth maps. It solves the problem of high synthesis artifacts and geometric failure when the relative distance between source cameras is large, a scenario where implicit correspondence search fails. Unlike sibling methods that rely on sparse landmarks or implicit correspondence, DINER uses dense depth priors to guide feature fusion and sampling, allowing for input views with high disparity and improving sampling efficiency. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: A sparse set of N RGB source images \{I^{(i)}\}{i=1}^N with known camera intrinsics K^{(i)} and extrinsics P^{(i)}. Typical value for N is 4. Outputs: A rendered color \hat{C}(\mathbf{r}) for a target ray \mathbf{r}. Data Structures: Feature Maps: W^{(i)} is a 2D feature map for each source view i, extracted by encoder E. Intermediate Features: V^{(i)} is an intermediate feature vector for view i, output by MLP part f1. Depth Maps: \hat{D}^{(i)} is the predicted depth map for source view i. Method Steps: 1. Depth Estimation: Estimate depth maps \hat{D}^{(i)} for each source view I^{(i)} using a state-of-the-art monocular depth estimation network. 2. Source Feature Extrapolation: Pad each input image I^{(i)} by 64 pixels by repeating border values. Compute positional encoding for normalized pixel coordinates \mathbf{uv} \in [-1, +1]. Use 4 exponentially increasing frequencies starting with 0.5, resulting in an 18-channel map. Set this encoding to 0 for unpadded regions. Concatenate the padded image and positional encoding, then apply the 2D-convolutional encoder E to extract feature maps: W^{(i)} = E(I^{(i)}). 3. Ray Sampling (Depth-Guided): For a target ray \mathbf{r}(t) = \mathbf{o} + t \cdot \mathbf{d}, generate 1000 candidate samples along the ray. Shortlist 25 samples based on depth guidance. Add 15 samples via Gaussian boosting around the shortlisted points. Total samples contributing to final color: 40. Note: Normal maps for backface culling are obtained by calculating central differences on \hat{D}^{(i)} using 3 \times 3 convolutional kernels, filtering out foreground-background edges. 4. Feature Fusion and MLP Processing: For each sample point \mathbf{x}j and view direction \mathbf{d}: Transform \mathbf{x}j and \mathbf{d} into source view coordinates: \mathbf{x}^{(i)} = P^{(i)} \circ \mathbf{x}j \mathbf{d}^{(i)} = R^{(i)} \circ \mathbf{d} where P^{(i)} and R^{(i)} are the extrinsic rotation/translation components. Project \mathbf{x}^{(i)} onto the feature map W^{(i)} using intrinsics K^{(i)} and bilinear interpolation to get feature vector \boldsymbol{\omega}^{(i)}: \boldsymbol{\omega}^{(i)} = W^{(i)}[K^{(i)} \circ \mathbf{x}^{(i)}] Compute the deviation \Delta z between the sample's z-coordinate in camera space and the predicted depth \hat{D}^{(i)}. Condition the NeRF on the positional encoding of \Delta z. Use 6 frequency channels with a base frequency of 1 meter, resulting in a 13-dimensional vector. Concatenate the 13-dimensional \Delta z encoding with the 512-dimensional feature vector \boldsymbol{\omega}^{(i)}. Process \mathbf{x}^{(i)}, \mathbf{d}^{(i)}, \boldsymbol{\omega}^{(i)}, and the encoded \Delta z through the first MLP part f1 to generate intermediate feature vectors V^{(i)}: V^{(i)} = f1(\mathbf{x}^{(i)}, \mathbf{d}^{(i)}, \boldsymbol{\omega}^{(i)}, \Delta z) 5. Aggregation and Rendering: Average pool the intermediate feature vectors across all N views: \text{mean}i V^{(i)}. Process the averaged features through the second MLP part f2 to regress final color \mathbf{c} and opacity \sigma: (\mathbf{c}, \sigma) = f2(\text{mean}i V^{(i)}) Render the final color \hat{C}(\mathbf{r}) using standard volumetric rendering integration: \hat{C}(\mathbf{r}) = \sum{j} Tj (1 - \exp(-\sigmaj \deltaj)) \mathbf{c}j where Tj = \exp\left(-\sum{k=1}^{j-1} \sigmak \deltak\right) and \deltaj = t{j+1} - tj. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import numpy as np def dinerrender(sourceimages, cameraparams, depthestimator, encoder, mlpf1, mlpf2, targetray): """ Renders a single ray using the DINER method. Args: sourceimages: List of N RGB images I^(i). cameraparams: List of N tuples (K^(i), P^(i), R^(i)). depthestimator: Function to predict depth maps. encoder: 2D convolutional network E. mlpf1: First part of NeRF MLP. mlpf2: Second part of NeRF MLP. targetray: Ray tuple (origin o, direction d). Returns: Rendered color c. """ N = len(sourceimages) # Step 1: Depth Estimation depthmaps = [] for i in range(N): dmap = depthestimator(sourceimages[i]) depthmaps.append(dmap) # Step 2: Source Feature Extrapolation featuremaps = [] for i in range(N): # Pad image by 64 pixels paddedimg = padborder(sourceimages[i], 64) # Compute positional encoding for UV coordinates # Normalized to [-1, 1], 4 frequencies starting 0.5 uvcoords = getuvcoords(paddedimg.shape) posenc = positionalencoding(uvcoords, freqs=[0.5, 1.0, 2.0, 4.0]) # Set posenc to 0 for unpadded regions (handled by mask or logic in encoder input) # For implementation, assume posenc is concatenated or masked appropriately # The paper states posenc is set to 0 for unpadded regions. # We assume the encoder handles the concatenation or the input is structured. # Here we assume encoder takes (paddedimg, posenc) or similar. # Simplified: Encoder takes padded image, posenc is part of input processing. # Extract feature map W^(i) # Note: The paper says "positional encoding is set to 0 for all pixels that do not belong to the padded region" # and "Adding positional encodings to the source image before applying the image encoder". # This implies the input to E is [Ipadded; PosEnc] or similar. # We assume E handles the 18-channel posenc addition. Wi = encoder(paddedimg, posenc) featuremaps.append(Wi) # Step 3: Depth-Guided Sampling # Generate 1000 candidates, shortlist 25, add 15 Gaussian -> 40 total # This logic is specific to the sampling strategy. # For a single ray, we need to determine sample points tj. # The paper describes this as a global sampling strategy per ray. # We assume a function depthguidedsample returns 40 points tj. samplepointst = depthguidedsampling(targetray, depthmaps, cameraparams) # Step 4 & 5: Feature Fusion and Rendering # Initialize accumulation variables accumulatedtransmittance = 1.0 accumulatedcolor = np.zeros(3) for tj in samplepointst: xj = targetray.origin + tj targetray.direction viewfeatures = [] for i in range(N): Ki, Pi, Ri = cameraparams[i] # Transform to source view coordinates # Pi is usually [R|t], so x^(i) = Ri xj + ti # The paper uses P^(i) o x. Assuming P includes translation. xi = transformpoint(xj, Pi) di = transformdirection(targetray.direction, Ri) # Project to feature map # Ki o xi implies projection to 2D pixel coordinates uvi = projectpoint(xi, Ki) # Interpolate feature vector w^(i) wi = interpolatefeature(featuremaps[i], uvi) # Compute deviation Delta z # z-coordinate of sample in camera coordinates zsample = xi[2] # Assuming camera z-axis zdepth = getdepthatuv(depthmaps[i], uvi) deltaz = zsample - zdepth # Positional encoding of Delta z # 6 freq channels, base 1m -> 13 dim vector pedeltaz = positionalencodingdeltaz(deltaz, numfreqs=6, basefreq=1.0) # Concatenate wi (512 dim) and pedeltaz (13 dim) # The paper says "concatenated with the 512-dimensional feature vector" # Input to f1: x^(i), d^(i), w^(i), Delta z (encoded) # Note: f1 input dimensions must match. # The paper says "input layer weight dimensions of the MLP are adjusted accordingly" # We assume f1 takes the concatenated vector. inputvec = np.concatenate([wi, pedeltaz]) # Process through f1 Vi = mlpf1(xi, di, inputvec) viewfeatures.append(Vi) # Average pool across views meanV = np.mean(viewfeatures, axis=0) # Process through f2 to get c and sigma c, sigma = mlpf2(meanV) # Volumetric rendering step # deltat is distance between samples. For simplicity, assume uniform or pre-calculated. # In practice, deltaj = t{j+1} - tj. # For the last sample, delta is effectively infinite or handled by termination. # Here we assume deltat is passed or calculated from sample points. # Let's assume we have deltat for the current segment. # Note: The loop structure above processes one sample at a time. # Standard NeRF rendering accumulates. # We need to handle the accumulation correctly. # The loop should iterate through sorted samples. pass # Re-writing the loop for correct accumulation accumulatedtransmittance = 1.0 accumulatedcolor = np.zeros(3) # Sort samples by tj samplepointst.sort() for idx, tj in enumerate(samplepointst): xj = targetray.origin + tj targetray.direction # Calculate deltat if idx < len(samplepointst) - 1: deltat = samplepointst[idx+1] - tj else: deltat = 0.0 # Or a large value if ray continues, but usually clipped viewfeatures = [] for i in range(N): Ki, Pi, Ri = cameraparams[i] xi = transformpoint(xj, Pi) di = transformdirection(targetray.direction, Ri) uvi = projectpoint(xi, Ki) wi = interpolatefeature(featuremaps[i], uvi) zsample = xi[2] zdepth = getdepthatuv(depthmaps[i], uvi) deltaz = zsample - zdepth pedeltaz = positionalencodingdeltaz(deltaz, numfreqs=6, basefreq=1.0) inputvec = np.concatenate([wi, pedeltaz]) Vi = mlpf1(xi, di, inputvec) viewfeatures.append(Vi) meanV = np.mean(viewfeatures, axis=0) c, sigma = mlpf2(meanV) # Update transmittance and color # Tj = exp(-sum{k=1}^{j-1} sigmak deltak) # Weight wj = Tj (1 - exp(-sigmaj deltaj)) weight = accumulatedtransmittance (1.0 - np.exp(-sigma deltat)) accumulatedcolor += weight c accumulatedtransmittance = np.exp(-sigma deltat) # Early termination if transmittance is very low if accumulatedtransmittance < 1e-5: break return accumulatedcolor def padborder(img, size): return np.pad(img, ((size, size), (size, size), (0, 0)), mode='edge') def getuvcoords(shape): h, w = shape[:2] y, x = np.meshgrid(np.linspace(-1, 1, h), np.linspace(-1, 1, w)) return np.stack([x, y], axis=-1) def positionalencoding(uv, freqs): # 4 frequencies starting with 0.5 # Result is 18 channels (4 freqs 2 (sin/cos) 2 (u,v) = 16? # Paper says 18 channels. Maybe includes original UV or different freq count? # Paper: "4 exponentially increasing frequencies starting with 0.5... resulting in a 18-channel map" # 4 freqs 2 (sin/cos) 2 (coords) = 16. # Perhaps it includes the original 2 UV coords? 16+2=18. # Or maybe 5 freqs? "starting with 0.5" and "exponentially increasing". # Let's assume standard PE + UV. pe = [] for f in freqs: for coord in uv: pe.append(np.sin(f coord)) pe.append(np.cos(f coord)) pe = np.stack(pe, axis=-1) # If 18 channels, we might need to add UV or adjust freqs. # Given the ambiguity, we stick to the description: 18 channels. # Implementation detail: Assuming standard sin/cos PE for 2 coords with 4 freqs yields 16 dims. # Adding original UV yields 18. return np.concatenate([uv, pe], axis=-1) def positionalencodingdeltaz(deltaz, numfreqs, basefreq): # 6 frequency channels with base frequency 1 meter -> 13-dimensional vector # Standard PE for 1D: 2 numfreqs + 1 (original) = 13? # 6 freqs 2 = 12. + 1 original = 13. pe = [] for i in range(numfreqs): freq = basefreq (2 i) pe.append(np.sin(freq deltaz)) pe.append(np.cos(freq deltaz)) pe = np.stack(pe, axis=-1) return np.concatenate([np.array([deltaz]), pe], axis=0) def transformpoint(x, P): # P is [R|t] R = P[:3,:3] t = P[:3, 3] return R @ x + t def transformdirection(d, R): return R @ d def projectpoint(x, K): # x is 3D in camera coords # uv = K @ x # Normalize by z xcam = K @ x u = xcam[0] / xcam[2] v = xcam[1] / xcam[2] return np.array([u, v]) def interpolatefeature(W, uv): # Bilinear interpolation # Standard bilinear interpolation implementation pass def getdepthatuv(D, uv): # Sample depth map at uv pass def depthguidedsampling(ray, depthmaps, cameraparams): # Implement the 1000 -> 25 -> 15 sampling logic # This is complex and depends on the specific depth estimator output. # The paper states: "generate 1000 candidate samples... shortlist 25... add 15... summing to 40" # We return a list of 40 t values. pass Parameters: N: Number of source images. Typical value: 4. f1, f2: Parts of the NeRF MLP. f1 input dimensions adjusted to accommodate concatenated features and depth encoding. Loss weights: wl = 1.0, w{vgg} = 0.1, w{ab} = 5.0 (or 1.0 for DTU dataset). Patch size for loss evaluation: 64 \times 64 pixels (Lab downsamples to 8 \times 8). Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Extrapolation: Standard image-based NeRFs suffer from artifacts when rendering outside the source view frustums. DINER handles this by padding input images and using positional encoding. Large Disparity: Implicit correspondence search fails when the distance between source cameras is large. DINER uses dense depth maps instead of sparse landmarks to handle this. Depth Accuracy: Synthesis quality improves with depth accuracy up to a standard deviation of 1mm noise. Higher accuracy yields no further improvement. Rendering Speed: Despite improved sampling, synthesis of a 256 \times 256 image takes two seconds. Time Complexity: Rendering a 256 \times 256 image takes approximately two seconds. This is slower than real-time methods but faster than some previous state-of-the-art generalizable NeRFs due to depth-guided sampling efficiency. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Measured Performance: On the DTU dataset, DINER achieves higher PSNR and SSIM compared to baselines like KeypointNeRF (which is limited to specific classes) and NeuRay. Scaling: The method is designed for sparse inputs (e.g., 4 views) with high relative distance. Strengths: Handles large disparities between source views; dense depth guidance improves geometry estimation and sampling efficiency; reduces median Chamfer distance by 33% and maximum Chamfer distance by a factor of 4 compared to coarse-to-fine sampling with the same number of points. Limitations: Relies on the accuracy of the external depth estimator; synthesis speed is not real-time; limited to scenes where depth can be reasonably estimated. When to use: When input views have high disparity and sparse coverage, and high-quality novel view synthesis is required without per-scene optimization. When not to use: When real-time rendering is required or when depth estimation is unreliable (e.g., textureless regions). DINER (Depth-aware Image-based NEural Radiance fields) was proposed by Malte Prinzler, Justus Thies, and Otmar Hilliges. It was published in CVPR 2023 (arXiv:2211.16630). The method builds on the pixelNeRF pipeline and addresses limitations in previous image-based NeRFs that relied on sparse landmarks or implicit correspondence, which failed for large camera disparities or non-specific object classes. It is used for novel view synthesis of human heads and general objects. DINER: Depth-aware Image-based NEural Radiance fields, https://doi.org/10.1109/cvpr52729.2023.01198, fetched 2026-10-29

name: Volume Rendering Prior (VRPrior)
head: learnable differentiable renderer, neural weight function
body: VRPrior replaces handcrafted, 1D ray-centric equations for mapping unsigned distance fields (UDF) to opaque density with a learnable neural network fw that incorporates 3D context from neighboring points along the ray. It solves the bias and sensitivity to outliers inherent in standard volume rendering formulations by learning a robust mapping from local geometric structures to rendering weights, enabling accurate surface reconstruction from multi-view RGB images without requiring explicit depth supervision during the final optimization stage. VRPrior operates in two distinct phases: Prior Training (learning the mapping function fw) and Generalization (optimizing the scene's UDF and color using the fixed prior). Inputs: During Prior Training: Ground truth meshes \{Sh\}{h=1}^H, random camera views. During Generalization: Multi-view RGB images \{Ij\}{j=1}^J, camera poses. Outputs: Prior Training: Optimized network parameters \thetaw for fw. Generalization: Optimized UDF field fu, color network fc, and rendered RGB/Depth images. The core component is the neural weight function fw, which predicts opaque density \sigman for a query point qn. 1. Neighbor Selection: For each query point qn along a ray, identify M nearest neighbors \{q'm\}{m=1}^M along the same ray. 2. Feature Grouping: The M neighbors are divided into three groups based on their distance to qn: Group 1: M1 = 10 nearest neighbors. Group 2: M2 = 20 next nearest neighbors. Group 3: M3 = 30 furthest neighbors. Total M = M1 + M2 + M3 = 60. 3. Input Features: For each neighbor q'm, the input features are: Unsigned distance: u'm = f{u{gt}}(q'm) (during prior training) or fu(q'm) (during generalization). Sampling interval: \deltam, the distance between q'm and q'{m+1}. 4. Network Architecture fw: Three separate Multi-Layer Perceptrons (MLPs), denoted f{w1}^{(k)} for k \in \{1,2,3\}, process each group independently. Each f{w1}^{(k)} takes the concatenated features (distances and intervals) of its group as input. The parameters of the three f{w1} MLPs are non-shared. The output feature vectors from the three groups are summed. The sum is passed to a final MLP f{w2} with skip connections to predict the opaque density \sigman. 1. Dataset Preparation: For each ground truth shape Sh in the training set: Compute the ground truth UDF f{u{gt}} for all points in space. Sample A=100 random camera views around the shape. 2. Rendering: For each view a of shape h: Shoot rays from the camera. Hierarchically sample N=128 points \{qn\}{n=1}^N along each ray. For each query qn, retrieve the ground truth unsigned distances \{f{u{gt}}(q'm)\}{m=1}^M of its M nearest neighbors along the ray and the sampling intervals \{\deltam\}{m=1}^M. Compute opaque density \sigman = fw(\{\deltam\}, \{f{u{gt}}(q'm)\}) using the current network fw. Compute rendering weights wn = \sigman \times \prod{n'=1}^{n-1} (1 - \sigma{n'}). Render the depth image \tilde{D}a^h = \sum{n'=1}^N w{n'} \times d{n'}, where d{n'} is the depth of point q{n'}. 3. Optimization: Update network parameters \thetaw by minimizing the L2 error between the rendered depth \tilde{D}a^h and the ground truth depth Da^h derived from f{u{gt}}: \min{\thetaw} \sum{h=1}^H \sum{a=1}^A \| Da^h - \tilde{D}a^h \|2^2 Note: RGB images are not used in this phase to prevent the color network from interfering with the geometric prior learning. 1. Initialization: Freeze fw parameters \thetaw. Initialize a UDF field fu (e.g., spherical initialization) and a color network fc. 2. Sampling: For each pixel in the target RGB images, shoot a ray. Hierarchically sample N=128 points \{qn\}{n=1}^N along the ray. 3. Density Prediction: For each query qn: Find M nearest neighbors \{q'm\}{m=1}^M along the ray. Retrieve current UDF values \{fu(q'm)\} and sampling intervals \{\deltam\}. Compute opaque density \sigman = fw(\{\deltam\}, \{fu(q'm)\}) using the frozen fw. 4. Rendering: Compute weights: wn = \sigman \times \prod{n'=1}^{n-1} (1 - \sigma{n'}). Compute rendered color: I' = \sum{n'=1}^N w{n'} \times fc(q{n'}). Compute rendered depth: D' = \sum{n'=1}^N w{n'} \times d{n'}. 5. Optimization: Update fu and fc parameters by minimizing the total loss: \mathcal{L} = \mathcal{L}{rgb} + \lambda \mathcal{L}e Where \mathcal{L}{rgb} = \sum{j=1}^J \| Ij - \tilde{I}j \| (photometric loss) and \mathcal{L}e is the Eikonal loss. 6. Surface Extraction: Extract the zero-level set of the optimized fu as the final mesh surface. Opaque Density: \sigman = fw(\{\deltam\}{m=1}^M, \{f{u{gt}}(q'm)\}{m=1}^M) where q'm \in NN(qn) are the M nearest neighbors of qn along the ray, and \deltam is the sampling interval. Rendering Weight: wn = \sigman \times \prod{n'=1}^{n-1} (1 - \sigma{n'}) Rendered Color: I' = \sum{n'=1}^N w{n'} \times fc(q{n'}) Rendered Depth: D' = \sum{n'=1}^N w{n'} \times d{n'} Prior Training Loss: \min{\thetaw} \sum{h=1}^H \sum{a=1}^A \| Da^h - \tilde{D}a^h \|2^2 Generalization Loss: \mathcal{L} = \mathcal{L}{rgb} + \lambda \mathcal{L}e N=128: Number of hierarchical samples along each ray. A=100: Number of ground truth depth images rendered per shape during prior training. M1=10, M2=20, M3=30: Sizes of the three neighbor groups. \lambda=0.1: Balance weight for the Eikonal loss. Handcrafted Bias: Standard methods using only M=2 neighbors are biased at ray-surface intersections and sensitive to unsigned distance outliers due to small receptive fields and lack of 3D awareness. RGB Interference: Using RGB images during the prior training phase reduces the generalization ability of the learned prior. The prior must be trained solely on depth errors to learn the UDF-to-density mapping. Sampling Bias: Hierarchical sampling can introduce bias in non-intersection regions; an auxiliary point sampling prior may be required to correct sampling density. Time Complexity: The prior training phase requires rendering H \times A depth images, which is computationally expensive but performed once. The generalization phase has similar complexity to standard NeRF/UDF methods but adds the overhead of querying the neighbor-based MLP fw for each sample. Memory Complexity: Requires storing the parameters of fw (three f{w1} MLPs and one f{w2} MLP) and the UDF field fu. Strengths: Robust to unsigned distance outliers; 3D aware due to multi-scale neighborhood aggregation; adaptive to various UDF variants (e.g., sharp corners, large near-surface regions). Limitations: Requires ground truth meshes for prior training; does not generalize to scenes without corresponding training shapes if the prior is not sufficiently diverse. When to use: When reconstructing surfaces from multi-view RGB images where standard UDF methods suffer from bias or noise, and ground truth meshes are available for prior training. When not to use: When real-time inference is critical and the overhead of the neighbor-based MLP is prohibitive, or when no ground truth meshes are available for prior training. VRPrior was introduced in the paper "VRP-UDF: Toward Unbiased Learning of Unsigned Distance Functions From Multi-View Images With Volume Rendering Priors". It addresses limitations in previous differentiable renderers that used handcrafted equations (e.g., NeUDF [2], 2S-UDF [28]) which were biased and not 3D aware. The method builds on the idea of learnable neural rendering frameworks [66–68] and hierarchical volume sampling [69]. It was developed to provide a more robust and scalable way to map UDFs to opaque densities for alpha blending. name: Geometric Structure Constraint
head: Normal Smoothness and Bilateral Edge-Aware Constraint
body: Geometric Structure Constraint is a method that integrates explicit geometric priors directly into the NeRF optimization loop to guide density field learning and improve elevation estimates. Unlike post-processing refinement, it unifies physical imaging and geometric constraints so that radiometric decomposition participates in optimization, enabling more accurate 3D reconstruction under complex satellite imaging conditions. It sets itself apart from siblings by explicitly combining normal smoothness with a bilateral edge-aware constraint to preserve sharp geometric boundaries while smoothing noise. All methods in this family build on Specific Model Architectures but diverge in how the geometric information is integrated into the optimization loop. The shared mechanism involves augmenting the standard photometric loss with geometric terms or modifying the ray sampling process to respect geometric boundaries. Geometric Loss Functions: Many methods introduce explicit loss terms that penalize deviations from geometric priors. Common forms include: 1. Depth Consistency Loss: Minimizes the difference between the rendered depth (computed as the expected depth along the ray) and a prior depth map D{prior}: L{depth} = \| D{rendered} - D{prior} \|1 2. Normal Smoothness: Encourages surface normals derived from the density field to be smooth or aligned with estimated normals. 3. Epipolar Constraints: Enforces that 3D points reconstructed from matched features in different views lie on the corresponding epipolar lines. Depth-Guided Sampling: Instead of uniform or hierarchical sampling along the entire ray, these methods use depth priors to concentrate samples near the estimated surface. This reduces computational cost and mitigates the "transparent" artifacts common in standard NeRF when geometry is ambiguous. For example, samples are clustered around the depth value predicted by a monocular depth estimator. Signed Distance Fields (SDF): Some variants replace the volumetric density \sigma with a Signed Distance Field (SDF). The rendering integral is modified to integrate weights based on the SDF value relative to a truncation distance tr, effectively creating a thin shell around the surface rather than a volumetric blob. The weight for a sample at distance d is often computed as: w = \sigma\left(\frac{d}{tr}\right) \cdot \sigma\left(-\frac{d}{tr}\right) This allows for direct mesh extraction via Marching Cubes. Uses SfM priors for initialization and regularization. Integrates depth and surface normal supervision. Focuses on geometric consistency across views. Combines RGB-D data for surface reconstruction. Uses depth inpainting for novel view synthesis. Applies volume rendering priors for regularization. The Geometric Structure Constraint was proposed in the context of DSM (Digital Surface Model) reconstruction from multi-view satellite images. The method addresses the difficulty of achieving optimal reconstruction results when geometric refinement is applied only as a post-processing step, as illumination and geometry are refined only after the radiance field has been estimated. By decomposing illumination, albedo, and surface normals within the NeRF framework, and modeling sunlight and ambient illumination separately, the method prevents shadow-induced brightness variation from being absorbed into albedo. The geometric branch consists of a normal-smoothing branch and a bilateral edge-aware branch, which play complementary roles in guiding the network to accurately learn the density field distribution. Shading and Geometric Constraint Neural Radiance Field for DSM Reconstruction from Multi-View Satellite Images, https://doi.org/10.3390/rs18071091, fetched 2026-11-05

name: Generative and Style-based Models
head: Generative NeRF, 3D-aware GANs, Style-based Radiance Fields
body: Generative and Style-based Models extend the NeRF paradigm from reconstructing a single static scene to synthesizing novel, high-fidelity 3D-consistent images from a distribution of scenes. They solve the problem of limited training data and the inability of standard NeRF to generalize across a class of objects (e.g., all faces or all cars) by conditioning the radiance field on a latent code. Unlike standard NeRF, which optimizes weights for a fixed scene, these models learn a mapping from a latent space to the scene geometry and appearance, enabling the generation of new instances. They are distinguished from siblings like AdaNeRF and SinNeRF by their explicit use of generative priors (GANs, Diffusion) and style-based conditioning to control appearance attributes and ensure multi-view consistency without requiring explicit 3D supervision. All methods in this family share the mechanism of mapping 6D input coordinates (3D position \mathbf{x} and 2D viewing direction \mathbf{d}) to 4D output values (density \sigma and color \mathbf{c}) using a differentiable neural network. This allows the radiance field to be optimized through the volumetric rendering integral. Input Representation: Raw coordinates \mathbf{x} and \mathbf{d} are rarely used directly due to the spectral bias of MLPs, which struggle to fit high-frequency details. They are mapped to a higher-dimensional space using positional encoding \gamma(\cdot). For a coordinate \mathbf{x}, the encoding includes the original value and sinusoidal functions at increasing frequencies: \gamma(\mathbf{x}) = (\sin(2^0 \pi \mathbf{x}), \cos(2^0 \pi \mathbf{x}), \dots, \sin(2^{L-1} \pi \mathbf{x}), \cos(2^{L-1} \pi \mathbf{x})) where L is the number of frequency bands. Network Topology: The canonical implementation uses two coupled Multi-Layer Perceptrons (MLPs): a density network F\sigma and a color network Fc. 1. Density Network: Takes the encoded position \gamma(\mathbf{x}) as input. It consists of L hidden layers with ReLU activations and skip connections from the input to every 4th layer to preserve low-frequency information. The output is the density \sigma. 2. Color Network: Takes the encoded position \gamma(\mathbf{x}), the raw viewing direction \mathbf{d}, and the intermediate feature vector from the density network (usually the output of the last hidden layer before the density head) as input. It predicts the color \mathbf{c} using a final ReLU or sigmoid activation. Rendering Integration: During training, rays are sampled at points \mathbf{x}i along the ray. The MLPs predict \sigmai and \mathbf{c}i. The pixel color C(\mathbf{r}) is computed via volumetric rendering: C(\mathbf{r}) = \sum{i=1}^N Ti \alphai \mathbf{c}i, \quad \text{where } \alphai = 1 - \exp(-\sigmai \deltai), \quad Ti = \prod{j=1}^{i-1} (1 - \alphaj) and \deltai is the distance between samples. StyleNeRF is a 3D-aware generative model that integrates a neural radiance field (NeRF) into a style-based generator framework to synthesize photo-realistic, high-resolution images with high multi-view consistency from unstructured 2D images. It solves the computational bottleneck of standard NeRF-based generative models by performing volume rendering only at a low resolution to produce feature maps, which are then upsampled in 2D space to high resolution, avoiding the super-computational cost of rendering every pixel via full volume integration. Unlike its siblings HyperNeRFGAN, Latent-NeRF, pi-GAN, and GIRAFFE, StyleNeRF explicitly conditions the NeRF MLP weights on style vectors derived from a mapping network, enabling fine-grained control over appearance attributes while maintaining 3D geometry consistency. HyperNeRFGAN is a generative adversarial network (GAN) architecture that employs a hypernetwork to transform a Gaussian noise vector into the weights of a simplified NeRF target network, enabling 3D-aware image generation without requiring camera position information during training. Unlike standard NeRF which uses a 5D input (position and viewing direction), HyperNeRFGAN uses a 3D input (position only) because the training datasets lack view-dependent characteristics like reflections. It differs from siblings like Latent-NeRF by using a hypernetwork to generate NeRF weights directly, avoiding the complexity of NeRF conditioning mechanisms while maintaining 3D awareness. Latent-NeRF is a method for optimizing Neural Radiance Fields (NeRF) by mapping scene geometry and appearance into a compact latent space, which is then refined using a pre-trained 2D latent diffusion model. It solves the problem of low-frequency artifacts and lack of high-frequency detail in standard NeRF training by leveraging the generative priors of diffusion models. Unlike standard NeRF, which predicts RGB colors directly, Latent-NeRF predicts pseudo-color channels corresponding to latent features, allowing the use of powerful 2D image priors for 3D consistency. pi-GAN is a generative adversarial network (GAN) approach to unsupervised 3D representation learning from 2D images. It conditions an implicit radiance field, represented by a SIREN network, on a noise vector to produce a 5D spatio-angular radiance field, which is rendered via volume rendering to synthesize view-consistent images. It is distinguished from its sibling StyleNeRF and GRAF by using a StyleGAN-inspired mapping network with Feature-wise Linear Modulation (FiLM) to condition the entire SIREN backbone, rather than concatenating latent codes or using separate shape/appearance codes. It outperformed GRAF in image quality and achieved state-of-the-art results on CelebA, Cats, and CARLA datasets. GIRAFFE represents scenes as compositions of N entities (objects plus a background), where each entity possesses a separate neural feature field and an affine transformation. This architecture enables explicit control over the pose, shape, and appearance of individual entities within a generated scene. It distinguishes itself from sibling methods like StyleNeRF and HyperNeRFGAN by decoupling scene composition from the generative process, allowing for variable numbers of objects and independent manipulation of entity attributes via latent codes and transformation parameters. Generative Latent Optimization (GLO) is a training procedure for implicit scene representations where a set of latent codes is jointly optimized with the neural network parameters to minimize a reconstruction loss between rendered outputs and target images. It functions as a discriminator-less GAN, allowing the model to learn a mapping from a fixed latent distribution to the scene space without adversarial training. Unlike standard NeRF training which optimizes only network weights for a fixed scene, GLO treats the latent codes as learnable parameters, enabling the model to capture view-dependent variations or specific scene instances. A 3D-aware generative model that produces animatable and relightable human heads by training on large-scale in-the-wild videos. Deforms feature maps rather than 3D points so lighting and expression changes stay consistent during motion. Builds on a tri-plane generator and introduces a unified animation and lighting representation. Extracts expression coefficients from video to learn a detailed animation space, enabling smooth, controllable head motion and relighting across humans and nonhuman domains. Training a discriminator network in parallel with the super-resolution generator to classify images as ground truth or predicted, using the discriminator's output as a loss term for the generator. Discriminator Loss: L{GAN,D} = - \log(D(x)) - \log(1 - D(G(z))). Generator Loss: L{GAN,G} = - \log(D(G(z))). Here, z is the input over all timesteps, G(z) is the generated result, D(x) is the discriminator score for real data x, and x is replaced by G(z) for fake data. A method for 3D photorealistic style transfer that leverages a hypernetwork to control features of style images as latent codes for scene stylization. HyperNet takes features extracted by StyleEncoder with VGG as input to update the weights of HyperLiner, followed by modifying RGBNet information to update the scene style. Trains a 2D PST network for more realistic scene presentation. Introduces a nearest neighbor feature matching loss to impart detailed style structures onto the original NeRF. Employs a deferred back-propagation technique to optimize with full-resolution images, overcoming GPU memory constraints. Generative NeRF models emerged as an extension of the original NeRF paper, aiming to generalize radiance fields from single-scene reconstruction to multi-scene generation. Early works like GRAF and pi-GAN introduced GAN-based frameworks to learn 3D-aware representations from 2D images. Subsequent developments such as StyleNeRF and HyperNeRFGAN incorporated style-based generators and hypernetworks to improve resolution and controllability. More recent approaches like Latent-NeRF integrate diffusion models for high-fidelity detail synthesis. These methods are widely used in computer graphics for novel view synthesis, 3D asset generation, and style transfer. name: StyleNeRF
head: Style-based 3D-Aware Generator
body: StyleNeRF is a 3D-aware generative model that integrates a neural radiance field (NeRF) into a style-based generator framework to synthesize photo-realistic, high-resolution images with high multi-view consistency from unstructured 2D images. It solves the computational bottleneck of standard NeRF-based generative models by performing volume rendering only at a low resolution to produce feature maps, which are then upsampled in 2D space to high resolution, avoiding the super-computational cost of rendering every pixel via full volume integration. Unlike its siblings HyperNeRFGAN, Latent-NeRF, pi-GAN, and GIRAFFE, StyleNeRF explicitly conditions the NeRF MLP weights on style vectors derived from a mapping network, enabling fine-grained control over appearance attributes while maintaining 3D geometry consistency. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A latent noise vector z \in \mathcal{Z} sampled from a spherical Gaussian distribution, and a camera pose p \in \mathcal{P} defined by pitch and yaw angles. Output: A high-resolution RGB image I \in \mathbb{R}^{H \times W \times 3}. Data Structures: 1. Mapping Network (f): A multi-layer perceptron (MLP) that maps the latent code z to a style vector w in the style space \mathcal{W}. 2. Style-Conditioned NeRF (G): A set of MLPs parameterized by weights modulated by w. The network consists of shared layers for geometry and appearance, followed by task-specific heads. Feature Extraction: \phiw^n(x) computes the n-th layer feature for position x. Density Head (h\sigma): A linear projection or 2-layer MLP predicting density \sigma. Color Head (hc): A linear projection or 2-layer MLP predicting color \mathbf{c}. 3. Upsampling Module: A 2D upsampling operator (e.g., learned upsampler) that increases the resolution of feature maps. Positional Encoding: To handle high-frequency details, input coordinates are mapped using Fourier features. For a coordinate x, the encoding \zeta^L(x) is: \zeta^L(x) = (\sin(2^0 x), \cos(2^0 x), \dots, \sin(2^{L-1} x), \cos(2^{L-1} x)) where L is the number of frequency bands. Network Topology and Style Conditioning: The StyleNeRF representation conditions the NeRF MLPs with style vectors w. The feature at layer n for position x is defined as: \phiw^n(x) = gw^n \circ gw^{n-1} \circ \dots \circ gw^1 \circ \zeta(x) where w = f(z), and gw^i is the i-th layer MLP whose weight matrix is modulated by the style vector w. The network assumes nc > n\sigma, where nc is the depth of the color network and n\sigma is the depth of the density network. The first \min(n\sigma, nc) layers are shared between density and color prediction. Density and color are predicted from the features as: \sigmaw(x) = h\sigma \circ \phiw^{n\sigma}(x) \mathbf{c}w(x, \mathbf{d}) = hc \circ [\phiw^{nc}(x), \zeta(\mathbf{d})] where h\sigma and hc are linear projections or 2-layer MLPs, and \mathbf{d} is the viewing direction. Rendering Approximation: Standard volume rendering is computationally expensive for high resolutions. StyleNeRF approximates the rendering process by early aggregating features into 2D space. The approximate image color is: Iw^{\text{Approx}}(\mathbf{r}) \approx hc \circ [\phiw^{nc, n\sigma}(A(\mathbf{r})), \zeta(\mathbf{d})] where: \phiw^{nc, n\sigma} = gw^{nc} \circ \dots \circ gw^{n\sigma+1} A(\mathbf{r}) = \int0^\infty pw(t) \cdot \phiw^{n\sigma}(\mathbf{r}(t)) dt and pw(t) = \exp\left(-\int0^t \sigmaw(\mathbf{r}(s))ds\right) \cdot \sigmaw(\mathbf{r}(t)) is the probability density of scattering at t. In practice, A(\mathbf{r}) is computed by discretizing the integral and accumulating sampled points along the ray using stratified and hierarchical sampling. To generate high-resolution images, StyleNeRF renders a low-resolution feature map A(\mathbf{r}) and then upsamples it in 2D space: \phiw^{nc, n\sigma}(A(\mathbf{r}H)) \approx \text{Upsample}(\phiw^{nc, n\sigma}(A(\mathbf{r}L))) where \mathbf{r}L and \mathbf{r}H are rays for low- and high-resolution pixels, respectively. Recursive upsampling allows efficient generation of high-resolution images. Training Procedure: StyleNeRF is trained adversarially with a generator G (the StyleNeRF model) and a discriminator D (typically a StyleGAN2 discriminator). The objective is: \minG \maxD \mathbb{E}{x \sim \text{data}}[\log D(x)] + \mathbb{E}{z \sim p(z)}[\log(1 - D(G(z)))] where x is a real image and z is the latent code. Path regularization is applied to the StyleGAN optimization to improve stability. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import torch import torch.nn as nn import torch.nn.functional as F class FourierFeatureEncoder(nn.Module): """Encodes coordinates using Fourier features.""" def init(self, numbands): super().init() self.numbands = numbands # Frequencies: 2^0, 2^1,..., 2^(L-1) self.freqs = torch.pow(2, torch.arange(numbands)) def forward(self, x): # x shape: (..., 3) for position or (..., 3) for direction # Scale by frequencies scaledx = x.unsqueeze(-1) self.freqs.unsqueeze(0) # (..., 3, L) # Sin and Cos sinvals = torch.sin(scaledx torch.pi) cosvals = torch.cos(scaledx torch.pi) # Concatenate encoded = torch.cat([sinvals, cosvals], dim=-1) # (..., 3L2) return encoded class StyleModulatedMLP(nn.Module): """MLP layer with style modulation.""" def init(self, indim, outdim, styledim): super().init() self.indim = indim self.outdim = outdim self.styledim = styledim # Standard linear layer self.linear = nn.Linear(indim, outdim) # Style modulation parameters (gain and bias) self.stylelinear = nn.Linear(styledim, outdim 2) def forward(self, x, w): # x: (..., indim) # w: (..., styledim) out = self.linear(x) # Get scale and shift from style styleparams = self.stylelinear(w).unsqueeze(-2) # (..., 1, outdim2) scale = styleparams[...,:self.outdim] shift = styleparams[..., self.outdim:] # Modulate out = out (1 + scale) + shift return out class StyleNeRF(nn.Module): """StyleNeRF Generator.""" def init(self, latentdim, styledim, posencdim, direncdim, sharedlayers, densitylayers, colorlayers, numbandspos, numbandsdir, lowresh, lowresw): super().init() self.latentdim = latentdim self.styledim = styledim self.posencdim = posencdim self.direncdim = direncdim self.lowresh = lowresh self.lowresw = lowresw # Mapping Network: z -> w self.mappingnet = nn.Sequential( nn.Linear(latentdim, styledim), nn.ReLU(), nn.Linear(styledim, styledim)) # Encoders self.posencoder = FourierFeatureEncoder(numbandspos) self.direncoder = FourierFeatureEncoder(numbandsdir) # Shared layers (geometry and appearance) self.sharedlayers = nn.ModuleList() currentdim = posencdim for i in range(sharedlayers): self.sharedlayers.append(StyleModulatedMLP(currentdim, currentdim, styledim)) currentdim = currentdim # Assuming same dim for simplicity # Density head layers (after shared) self.densitylayers = nn.ModuleList() for i in range(densitylayers): self.densitylayers.append(StyleModulatedMLP(currentdim, currentdim, styledim)) # Color head layers (after shared) # Note: Color head takes shared features + direction encoding self.colorlayers = nn.ModuleList() colorinputdim = currentdim + direncdim for i in range(colorlayers): self.colorlayers.append(StyleModulatedMLP(colorinputdim, colorinputdim, styledim)) colorinputdim = colorinputdim # Assuming same dim # Final heads self.densityhead = nn.Linear(currentdim, 1) # Output sigma self.colorhead = nn.Linear(colorinputdim, 3) # Output RGB # Upsampler (simplified as bilinear for structure, but should be learned) self.upsampler = nn.Upsample(scalefactor=2, mode='bilinear', aligncorners=False) def forward(self, z, cameraposes): """ z: (B, latentdim) cameraposes: (B, 2) containing pitch and yaw Returns: (B, H, W, 3) """ # 1. Map latent to style w = self.mappingnet(z) # (B, styledim) # 2. Generate rays for low resolution # Assume camera is on unit sphere pointing to origin # This is a placeholder for ray generation logic rayso, raysd = generaterays(cameraposes, self.lowresh, self.lowresw) # 3. Sample points along rays # Stratified sampling tvals = stratifiedsampling(numsamples=128) # Placeholder for sampling logic points = rayso.unsqueeze(1) + raysd.unsqueeze(1) tvals.unsqueeze(2) # (B, N, 3) # 4. Encode positions posenc = self.posencoder(points) # (B, N, posencdim) # 5. Compute features through shared layers x = posenc for layer in self.sharedlayers: x = layer(x, w) # (B, N, currentdim) # 6. Compute density sigma = self.densityhead(x).squeeze(-1) # (B, N) sigma = F.relu(sigma) # Ensure non-negative # 7. Compute alpha and transmittance # delta is distance between samples (assume uniform for simplicity) delta = tvals[:, 1] - tvals[:, 0] # (B, N-1) alpha = 1.0 - torch.exp(-sigma delta) # (B, N) transmittance = torch.cumprod(1.0 - alpha + 1e-10, dim=1) # (B, N) transmittance = torch.cat([torch.oneslike(transmittance[:,:1]), transmittance[:,:-1]], dim=1) # 8. Early aggregation: Weighted sum of features # A(r) = integral p(t) phi(t) dt approx sum alphai transmittancei phii weights = alpha transmittance # (B, N) aggregatedfeatures = torch.sum(weights.unsqueeze(-1) x, dim=1) # (B, currentdim) # 9. Upsample features to high resolution # Reshape to (B, C, H, W) for upsampling aggregatedfeatures = aggregatedfeatures.view(B, -1, self.lowresh, self.lowresw) aggregatedfeatureshr = self.upsampler(aggregatedfeatures) # (B, C, H, W) # 10. Generate rays for high resolution raysohr, raysdhr = generaterays(cameraposes, H, W) # 11. Encode directions for high res rays # This step is complex because directions vary per pixel # In practice, directions are computed for each pixel direnchr = self.direncoder(raysdhr) # (B, H, W, direncdim) # 12. Color prediction # Combine aggregated features (upampled) with direction encoding # Note: aggregatedfeatureshr needs to be reshaped to match direnchr featureshr = aggregatedfeatureshr.permute(0, 2, 3, 1) # (B, H, W, C) colorinput = torch.cat([featureshr, direnchr], dim=-1) # (B, H, W, C + direncdim) # Pass through color layers for layer in self.colorlayers: colorinput = layer(colorinput, w) # Final color head rgb = self.colorhead(colorinput) # (B, H, W, 3) rgb = torch.sigmoid(rgb) # Clamp to [0, 1] return rgb def generaterays(cameraposes, H, W): """Placeholder for ray generation logic.""" # Returns rayso (B, 3) and raysd (B, H, W, 3) pass def stratifiedsampling(numsamples): """Placeholder for stratified sampling logic.""" # Returns tvals (B, N) pass Edge Cases and Pitfalls: View Inconsistency: Early aggregation and upsampling sacrifice the inherent consistency of NeRF, leading to view-inconsistent artifacts if not properly mitigated. Upsampling Artifacts: Using LIIF (Local Implicit Image Function) upsampler causes patterns to stick to the same pixel coordinates when the viewpoint changes. Using bilinear interpolation upsampler causes bubble-shape artifacts on feature maps and images. A learned upsampler is recommended to preserve 3D consistency. Precision: The approximation relies on the assumption that upsampling in feature space is equivalent to upsampling in image space, which may not hold for high-frequency details. Time Complexity: StyleNeRF is 100-1000 times more efficient than standard NeRF-based models for generating 1024^2 images because each pixel takes a single forward pass through the network (after feature aggregation) rather than calling the network multiple times for all sampled points on the ray. Memory Complexity: Memory usage is reduced by rendering only at low resolution and upsampling, avoiding the need to cache intermediate results for all sampled points at high resolution. Strengths: High-resolution image synthesis, multi-view consistency, style control, efficiency. Limitations: Sacrifices some 3D consistency due to upsampling, requires careful choice of upsampling operator. When to use: When high-resolution, 3D-consistent image synthesis is required from unstructured 2D images, and computational efficiency is a concern. When not to use: When exact 3D consistency is critical and upsampling artifacts are unacceptable, or when the scene geometry is extremely complex and requires high-frequency sampling. StyleNeRF was proposed in January 2022 by Gu et al.. It builds on the StyleGAN framework and NeRF. It is a highly influential work that focuses on 2D image synthesis by using NeRF to bring 3D awareness to the StyleGAN image synthesis framework. It addresses the challenges of existing approaches that either cannot synthesize high-resolution images with fine details or yield noticeable 3D-inconsistent artifacts. name: HyperNeRFGAN
head: Hypernetwork approach to 3D NeRF GAN
body: HyperNeRFGAN is a generative adversarial network (GAN) architecture that employs a hypernetwork to transform a Gaussian noise vector into the weights of a simplified NeRF target network, enabling 3D-aware image generation without requiring camera position information during training. Unlike standard NeRF which uses a 5D input (position and viewing direction), HyperNeRFGAN uses a 3D input (position only) because the training datasets lack view-dependent characteristics like reflections. It differs from siblings like Latent-NeRF by using a hypernetwork to generate NeRF weights directly, avoiding the complexity of NeRF conditioning mechanisms while maintaining 3D awareness. Inputs and Outputs: Generator Input: A noise vector \mathbf{z} sampled from a Gaussian distribution P{noise}. Generator Output: The weights \theta of the target NeRF model F\theta. Target Model Input: 3D spatial location \mathbf{x} = (x, y, z). Target Model Output: Color \mathbf{c} and volume density \sigma. Discriminator Input: 2D rendered images. Data Structures: The target NeRF model F\theta is a single Multi-Layer Perceptron (MLP). Architecture: It consists of hidden layers with Factorized Multiplicative Modulation (FMM) layers. FMM Layer Layout: An FMM layer takes an input \mathbf{x}{in} of size n{in} and produces an output \mathbf{y} of size n{out}. Shared parameters: Weight matrix W and bias vector b. Modulation parameters: Two matrices A and B generated by the generator G. Dimensions: A is n{out} \times k, B is k \times n{in}. Rank parameter: k controls the rank of the modulation A \times B. Target Network Dimensions: Hidden layer channels: 128 (reduced from standard 256). Network depth: 4 layers (reduced from standard 8) in some experiments. Rank k: 10. Formulas: The FMM layer operation is defined as: \mathbf{y} = W \odot (A \times B) \cdot \mathbf{x}{in} + \mathbf{b} = \tilde{W} \cdot \mathbf{x}{in} + \mathbf{b} where \tilde{W} = W \odot (A \times B). The target NeRF maps spatial location to color and density: F\theta: \mathbf{x} \rightarrow (\mathbf{c}, \sigma) The GAN training objective is a minimax game: \minG \maxD V(D, G) where V = \mathbb{E}{\mathbf{x} \sim P{data}}[\log D(\mathbf{x})] + \mathbb{E}{\mathbf{z} \sim P{noise}}[\log(1 - D(G(\mathbf{z})))] Numbered Steps: 1. Sample a noise vector \mathbf{z} from the base Gaussian distribution P{noise}. 2. Transform \mathbf{z} using the generator G to obtain the weights \theta of the target NeRF model F\theta. 3. Instantiate the target NeRF model F\theta using the generated weights. 4. Render 2D images from the target NeRF model F\theta from a variety of perspectives (camera poses). 5. Evaluate the rendered 2D images using a standard 2D discriminator D. 6. Update the generator G and discriminator D using the GAN minimax objective. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import torch import torch.nn as nn import torch.nn.functional as F class FMMLayer(nn.Module): """Factorized Multiplicative Modulation layer. W, b are shared.
