name: Adversarial Training (GAN)
head: Discriminator Training, GAN Loss
body: Adversarial Training introduces a discriminator network trained in parallel with the radiance field generator to classify rendered images as ground truth or predicted. It distinguishes itself from standard differentiable rendering pipelines by adding a game-theoretic loss term that encourages photorealism and high-frequency detail, addressing the blurriness often associated with pure pixel-wise reconstruction losses. Inputs and Outputs: Generator Input (z): The latent representation or low-resolution input passed through the radiance field network (e.g., super-resolution network) to produce a predicted image G(z). Discriminator Input: Pairs of images consisting of real ground truth images x and generated fake images G(z). Outputs: The generator outputs a rendered image; the discriminator outputs a scalar score D(\cdot) \in [0, 1] indicating the probability that the input is real. Data Structures: Discriminator Network (D): A neural network (typically a CNN in image-based contexts, or adapted for volumetric features) that takes an image as input and outputs a single scalar value. Generator Network (G): The existing radiance field model (e.g., the super-resolution network described in the parent article). Formulas: The discriminator loss L{GAN,D} minimizes the error in distinguishing real from fake data: L{GAN,D} = - \log(D(x)) - \log(1 - D(G(z))) where x is the ground truth image and G(z) is the generated image. The generator loss L{GAN,G} minimizes the discriminator's ability to detect fakes, effectively maximizing the probability that the discriminator classifies generated images as real: L{GAN,G} = - \log(D(G(z))) Parameters: \lambdaG: Weight for the adversarial generator loss in the total objective function. \lambda{M}, \lambda{AO}, \lambda{N}, etc.: Weights for other auxiliary losses (e.g., L1 losses on masks, albedo, normals) which are summed with the GAN loss. Steps: 1. Forward Pass (Generator): Render the image G(z) using the radiance field network from input z. 2. Discriminator Update: a. Compute D(x) for ground truth images x. b. Compute D(G(z)) for generated images G(z). c. Calculate L{GAN,D}. d. Update discriminator weights to minimize L{GAN,D}. 3. Generator Update: a. Compute D(G(z)) using the current discriminator. b. Calculate L{GAN,G}. c. Update generator weights to minimize L{GAN,G} (often combined with other reconstruction losses). Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Training Instability: GAN training is known to be unstable; the discriminator may overpower the generator, leading to mode collapse or vanishing gradients. Loss Balance: The relative weights (\lambda) of the adversarial loss versus reconstruction losses (like L1) must be carefully tuned. A training strategy for predicting lighting conditions in street scenes that addresses depth rendering ambiguity and encourages photorealism through adversarial supervision. It distinguishes itself from standard differentiable rendering pipelines by combining a multi-term hybrid loss (including sky regression, reconstruction, and regularization) with a PatchGAN discriminator, trained in a two-stage process (pre-training followed by joint adversarial training) to stabilize convergence. Complexity: Adds the computational cost of the discriminator network to each training step. The discriminator typically requires fewer parameters than the generator but adds significant overhead to the backward pass if not carefully sized. Performance: Improves perceptual quality and high-frequency details compared to MSE/L1-only training. Strengths: Produces sharper, more realistic textures; reduces blurriness. Limitations: Harder to train; prone to instability; requires careful hyperparameter tuning for loss weights. When to use: When photorealism and high-frequency detail are prioritized over strict pixel-wise accuracy. Originated from Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs) introduced by Goodfellow et al.. In the context of volumetric rendering and super-resolution, it was employed to train a discriminator network in parallel with a super-resolution generator to classify images as ground truth or predicted, using the discriminator's output as a loss term for the generator. name: Lighting Prediction Network Training
head: Hybrid Loss Training for Lighting Prediction
body: A training strategy for predicting lighting conditions in street scenes that addresses depth rendering ambiguity and encourages photorealism through adversarial supervision. It distinguishes itself from standard differentiable rendering pipelines by combining a multi-term hybrid loss (including sky regression, reconstruction, and regularization) with a PatchGAN discriminator, trained in a two-stage process (pre-training followed by joint adversarial training) to stabilize convergence. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: Ground truth lighting parameters (direction f{dir}, intensity f{intensity}), real-world images \{I{real}\} from nuScenes [2] and HoliCity [22] street views, and HDR panoramas. Outputs: Predicted lighting parameters and rendered images \hat{I}{edit}. Data Structures: Discriminator (D): A 5-layer PatchGAN network with spectral norm. Generator: The lighting prediction network (architecture details not specified in sources, but implied to output latent codes and radiance/depth). Loss Weights: \lambda{sky}=1, \lambda{recon}=1, \lambda{transmit}=1, \lambda{reg}=10^{-4}, \lambda{adv}=3 \times 10^{-3}. Numbered Steps: 1. Pre-training: Train the model without the adversarial loss term L{adv} for 50 epochs. 2. Joint Training: Train the model with all loss terms for an additional 50 epochs. 3. Sky Regression Loss (L{sky}): Compute the L1 loss for the latent code. Linearly fade out this specific loss component during the first 50 epochs of the joint training phase. 4. Adversarial Training: Sample real images I{real} and generated images \hat{I}{edit}. Compute discriminator loss LD using hinge loss. Update discriminator D. Compute generator adversarial loss L{adv} based on D(\hat{I}{edit}). 5. Optimization: Update the generator parameters using the total hybrid loss L{hybrid}. Formulas: The final hybrid loss is defined as: L{hybrid} = \lambda{sky} L{sky} + \lambda{recon} L{recon} + \lambda{reg} L{reg} + \lambda{transmit} L{transmit} + \lambda{adv} L{adv} where: L{sky}: Sky regression loss (L1 loss on latent code, faded in first 50 epochs). L{recon}: Radiance and depth reconstruction loss. L{reg}: Regularization loss encouraging the alpha channel of the volume to be binary (0 or 1) to address depth rendering ambiguity. L{transmit}: Sky separation loss. L{adv}: Adversarial supervision loss. The discriminator uses hinge loss: LD = \max(0, 1 - D(I{real})) + \max(0, 1 + D(\hat{I}{edit})) Parameters: Optimizer: Adam. Learning Rate: 3 \times 10^{-4}, decaying by a factor of 0.3 every 30 epochs. Discriminator Batch Size: 1. Total GPU Memory: 20G (8G for network inference, 12G for rendering). Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. optimizer = Adam(params=model.parameters(), lr=3e-4) discriminator = PatchGAN5LayerSpectralNorm() discoptimizer = Adam(params=discriminator.parameters(), lr=3e-4) # Assumed same LR schedule epochspretrain = 50 epochsjoint = 50 totalepochs = epochspretrain + epochsjoint decayfactor = 0.3 decaystep = 30 lambdasky = 1.0 lambdarecon = 1.0 lambdareg = 1e-4 lambdatransmit = 1.0 lambdaadv = 3e-3 for epoch in range(1, totalepochs + 1): # Learning rate decay currentlr = 3e-4 (decayfactor (epoch // decaystep)) setlearningrate(optimizer, currentlr) setlearningrate(discoptimizer, currentlr) for batch in dataloader: # Forward pass predictedlighting, renderedimage = model(batch.input) # Compute losses # Lsky: Sky regression loss (L1 on latent code) # Note: Fade out logic applied here if epoch <= 50 (relative to joint phase start) # Assuming 'epoch' here is global, so joint phase starts at epoch 51 if epoch <= epochspretrain: # Pre-training phase: no adversarial loss lsky = computel1losslatent(predictedlighting, batch.targetlighting) lrecon = computereconstructionloss(renderedimage, batch.targetimage) lreg = computealpharegularization(renderedimage.alpha) ltransmit = computeskyseparation(renderedimage, batch.targetimage) ladv = 0.0 else: # Joint training phase # Linearly fade out L1 loss for latent code in the first 50 epochs of joint training # epoch 51 -> factor 1.0, epoch 100 -> factor 0.0 fadefactor = max(0.0, 1.0 - (epoch - epochspretrain) / epochsjoint) lsky = computel1losslatent(predictedlighting, batch.targetlighting) fadefactor lrecon = computereconstructionloss(renderedimage, batch.targetimage) lreg = computealpharegularization(renderedimage.alpha) ltransmit = computeskyseparation(renderedimage, batch.targetimage) # Adversarial Loss # D is discriminator dreal = discriminator(batch.targetimage) dfake = discriminator(renderedimage.detach()) # Hinge loss for discriminator ldreal = max(0, 1 - dreal) ldfake = max(0, 1 + dfake) ld = ldreal + ldfake # Update Discriminator discoptimizer.zerograd() ld.backward() discoptimizer.step() # Generator adversarial loss (using fake images) dfakegen = discriminator(renderedimage) ladv = max(0, 1 - dfakegen) # Standard GAN generator loss for hinge # Total Hybrid Loss lhybrid = (lambdasky lsky + lambdarecon lrecon + lambdareg lreg + lambdatransmit ltransmit + lambdaadv ladv) # Update Generator optimizer.zerograd() lhybrid.backward() optimizer.step() Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Depth Ambiguity: The regularization loss L{reg} is critical to prevent the volume alpha channel from converging to intermediate values, which causes depth rendering ambiguity. Training Stability: The two-stage training (pre-training then joint) is necessary to stabilize the adversarial training. Memory Constraints: The method requires significant GPU memory (20G total), with rendering consuming the majority (12G). Time Complexity: Not explicitly given, but training involves 4000 epochs in the main paper context (though the specific lighting prediction section details 100 epochs of the specific hybrid loss strategy, the main paper mentions 4000 epochs for the full model including other components). The provided notes specify 50 pre-training + 50 joint epochs for the hybrid loss component. Memory Complexity: 20G GPU memory usage (8G for network inference, 12G for rendering). Strengths: Addresses depth rendering ambiguity via regularization; encourages photorealism via adversarial supervision; handles sky regression ambiguity via fading loss. Limitations: High GPU memory requirement; requires careful tuning of loss weights and learning rate decay. When to use: When generating photorealistic street scene lighting with differentiable rendering and depth ambiguity is a concern. When not to use: When GPU memory is limited (<20G) or when adversarial training instability is unacceptable without careful tuning. Originated in the context of "Neural Light Field Estimation for Street Scenes with Differentiable Virtual Object Insertion". The method combines techniques from differentiable rendering (sky regression, depth reconstruction) with GAN-based adversarial training (PatchGAN discriminator) to improve the realism of predicted lighting in street scenes. It builds on prior work addressing depth rendering ambiguity. name: IRON
head: IRON, Inverse Rendering by Optimizing Neural SDFs and Materials, PIR (Photometric Inverse Rendering), Photometric Inverse Rendering with Shading Cues Modeling and Surface Reflectance Regularization
body: IRON is a neural inverse rendering pipeline that reconstructs high-quality 3D geometry and spatially varying materials from photometric images (multi-view images captured with a collocated flashlight and moving camera). It outputs triangle meshes and material textures compatible with standard graphics pipelines. Unlike standard NeRF variants that optimize density and color directly, IRON uses Signed Distance Fields (SDFs) for geometry and separate neural networks for diffuse, specular, and roughness parameters. It employs a hybrid optimization scheme: a first stage using volumetric radiance field rendering to recover correct topology, followed by a second stage using edge-aware physics-based surface rendering to refine geometry and disentangle materials from lighting. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A set of photometric images captured with a flashlight co-located with the camera. Assumptions include opaque objects, no ambient light, and ignored shadows/inter-reflections. Output: A triangle mesh and material textures (diffuse albedo, specular albedo, roughness). Data Structures: The method uses four Multi-Layer Perceptrons (MLPs) with positional encoding \gamma(\cdot). 1. Neural SDF (F{\Thetas}): Input: 3D position \mathbf{x}. Output: Tuple (S, \mathbf{f}), where S \in \mathbb{R} is the SDF value and \mathbf{f} \in \mathbb{R}^{256} is a local geometric feature descriptor. 2. Neural Diffuse Albedo (F{\Theta\beta}): Input: Position \mathbf{x}, surface normal \mathbf{n}, view direction \mathbf{v} (or normal \mathbf{n} in Stage 2), and feature descriptor \mathbf{f}. Output: Diffuse albedo \beta \in \mathbb{R}^3. 3. Neural Specular Albedo (F{\Theta\kappa}): Input: Position \mathbf{x}, surface normal \mathbf{n}, and feature descriptor \mathbf{f}. Output: Specular albedo \kappa \in \mathbb{R}^3. 4. Neural Roughness (F{\Theta\alpha}): Input: Position \mathbf{x}, surface normal \mathbf{n}, and feature descriptor \mathbf{f}. Output: Roughness \alpha \in \mathbb{R} (small values indicate shiny surfaces, large values indicate matte surfaces). Optimization Stages: Stage 1: Volumetric Radiance Field Rendering This stage initializes the topology (number and location of holes). 1. Treat the neural diffuse albedo network F{\Theta\beta}(\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{n}, \mathbf{v}, \mathbf{f}) as a view-dependent neural radiance field by substituting the view direction -\mathbf{d} for the second normal argument. 2. Optimize F{\Thetas} and F{\Theta\beta} using volumetric rendering. 3. The pixel color C(\mathbf{r}) is computed via the standard volumetric rendering integral: C(\mathbf{r}) = \sum{i=1}^N Ti \alphai \mathbf{c}i, \quad \text{where } \alphai = 1 - \exp(-\sigmai \deltai), \quad Ti = \prod{j=1}^{i-1} (1 - \alphaj) Here, \sigmai is derived from the SDF S, \mathbf{c}i = F{\Theta\beta}(\mathbf{x}i, \mathbf{n}i, -\mathbf{d}i, \mathbf{f}i), and \deltai is the step size. 4. If this stage is skipped, optimization frequently diverges or gets stuck in local minima with incorrect topology. Stage 2: Edge-aware Physics-based Surface Rendering This stage refines geometric details and factorizes materials from lighting. 1. Jointly optimize F{\Thetas}, F{\Theta\beta}, F{\Theta\kappa}, F{\Theta\alpha}, and light intensity L. 2. Use physics-based surface rendering. The light is modeled as a point source: Li(\mathbf{x}) = \frac{L}{\|\mathbf{x} - \mathbf{o}\|^2} where L is light intensity, \mathbf{x} is the surface location, and \mathbf{o} is the light/camera position. 3. Edge Sampling: To handle depth discontinuities, a novel edge sampling algorithm is used. Input: Ray-surface intersection \hat{\mathbf{x}}. Hyperparameters: Max steps K, step size \epsilon, threshold \delta. Algorithm: python def locateedgepoints(xhat, o, K, epsilon, delta): xt = xhat for i in range(1, K + 1): vec = xt - o dist = np.linalg.norm(vec) if dist < 1e-8: return xhat dirvec = vec / dist nt = computenormal(xt) if np.dot(dirvec, nt) < delta: return xt else: projection = nt - np.dot(dirvec, nt) dirvec xt = xt + epsilon projection return "NOT FOUND" def computenormal(x): return computesdfgradient(x) # Computes gradient of SDF network 4. The rendering equation accounts for diffuse and specular components using the optimized material parameters. Parameters: K: Max steps for edge search (Not given in the sources). \epsilon: Step size for edge search (Not given in the sources). \delta: Threshold for edge detection (Not given in the sources). L: Light intensity (Optimized scalar). Pitfalls: Skipping Stage 1 leads to divergence or incorrect topology. The method assumes ideal collocated camera-lighting; deviations cause self-shadowing errors if not handled (addressed in PIR). Inter-reflections are ignored in the original IRON, leading to inaccuracies in concave regions. Time and Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Measured Performance: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Recovers correct topology via volumetric initialization; produces mesh-compatible outputs; handles spatially varying materials. Limitations: Assumes opaque objects; ignores ambient light, self-shadows, and inter-reflections (original version); requires photometric images with collocated flashlight. When to use: When high-quality mesh and texture extraction from photometric image sets is required, and computational resources allow for two-stage optimization. When not: When self-shadows or inter-reflections are significant and cannot be ignored, or when only environmental lighting is available. IRON was proposed by Kai Zhang, Fujun Luan, Zhengqi Li, and Noah Snavely from Cornell University, Adobe Research, and Google Research. It was published in CVPR 2022. The method builds on neural SDF representations (e.g., IDR, NeuS) and neural radiance fields (NeRF). It addresses the limitations of mesh-based inverse rendering by using neural SDFs for flexibility and compactness. A later extension, PIR (Photometric Inverse Rendering), addresses IRON's shortcomings regarding self-shadows and inter-reflections by jointly optimizing light position and using DINO feature regularization. name: Instance-NeRF
head: Instance Neural Radiance Field
body: Instance-NeRF is a learning-based 3D instance segmentation pipeline that extends a pre-trained Neural Radiance Field (NeRF) with an additional instance field component. It takes a pre-trained NeRF model as input and learns to detect all objects within the underlying 3D scene, producing a 3D bounding box, a continuous 3D mask, and a class label for each detected object. Unlike Semantic-NeRF, which relies on 2D semantic priors that are generally consistent across views, Instance-NeRF addresses the challenge of multi-view inconsistent 2D instance masks (where the same object may receive different instance IDs in different views) without relying on 3D bounding volume priors. It achieves this by using a 3D proposal-based mask prediction network (NeRF-RCNN) to generate coarse 3D masks, projecting them to 2D to match and refine multi-view consistent segmentation maps, and then supervising the continuous instance field with these refined 2D masks. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A pre-trained NeRF model F{\Theta\sigma, \Thetac} parameterized by density network weights \Theta\sigma and color branch weights \Thetac, trained on posed RGB images. Output: A continuous instance field G{\Theta\sigma, \Thetai} that produces a view-independent instance label vector at any 3D position, along with 3D bounding boxes, class labels, and discrete 3D masks for detected objects. Data Structures and Layout: The model is parameterized by three components: 1. Density Net (\Theta\sigma): Part of the original NeRF, predicting volume density \sigma. 2. Color Branch (\Thetac): Part of the original NeRF, predicting RGB radiance \mathbf{c}. 3. Instance Branch (\Thetai): The new component, predicting the instance label distribution. The instance field is formulated as G{\Theta\sigma, \Thetai}(\mathbf{x}) = \mathbf{i}, where \mathbf{i} is an L-dimensional vector representing the instance label distribution over L labels, with the first dimension representing the background. Rendering and Sampling: The method uses hierarchical stratified sampling. For each pixel, a ray \mathbf{r}(t) = \mathbf{o} + t\mathbf{d} is formulated, where \mathbf{o} is the camera center and \mathbf{d} is the viewing direction. K quadrature points \{tk\}{k=1}^K are selected along the ray within the traceable volume. The distance between samples is denoted by \deltak. Formulas: The expected color \hat{C}(\mathbf{r}), expected depth \hat{D}(\mathbf{r}), and expected instance logits \hat{I}(\mathbf{r}) are accumulated via numerical quadrature: \hat{C}(\mathbf{r}) = \sum{k=1}^{K} \hat{T}(tk) \alpha(\sigma(tk)\deltak) \mathbf{c}(tk) \hat{D}(\mathbf{r}) = \sum{k=1}^{K} \hat{T}(tk) \alpha(\sigma(tk)\deltak) tk \hat{I}(\mathbf{r}) = \sum{k=1}^{K} \hat{T}(tk) \alpha(\sigma(tk)\deltak) \mathbf{i}(tk) Where: \hat{T}(tk) is the transmittance at sample k. \alpha(\cdot) is the opacity function. \sigma(tk) is the volume density. \mathbf{c}(tk) is the RGB radiance. \mathbf{i}(tk) is the instance label vector at point tk. Training Procedure: 1. 3D Proposal Generation: The method employs a NeRF-RCNN, extended from NeRF-RPN, which takes the extracted radiance and density field of the pre-trained NeRF. NeRF-RCNN outputs 3D bounding boxes, class labels, and discrete 3D masks for each detected object. 2. 2D Segmentation Generation: Existing panoptic segmentation models (specifically Mask2Former) generate 2D panoptic segmentation maps of images rendered from the NeRF. These 2D instance masks are generally multi-view inconsistent. 3. Mask Matching and Refinement: The discrete 3D masks predicted by NeRF-RCNN are projected back to 2D image space from the same camera poses. Instance-NeRF leverages Mask2Former and CascadePSP to match the same instance in 2D segmentation across different views and refine the resultant masks. This process links each 2D instance mask to its corresponding 3D instance to resolve inconsistency. 4. Instance Field Supervision: The resulting multi-view consistent 2D segmentation maps are used to supervise and train the instance field component G{\Theta\sigma, \Thetai}, producing a continuous 3D segmentation. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def traininstancefield(pretrainednerf, cameraposes, consistent2dmasks, K=64): """ Trains the Instance-NeRF instance field using a pre-trained NeRF. Args: pretrainednerf: Pre-trained NeRF model with parameters (Thetasigma, Thetac). cameraposes: List of camera poses for the input images. consistent2dmasks: Multi-view consistent 2D segmentation masks from matching step. K: Number of quadrature points per ray. Returns: Thetai: Trained instance branch parameters. """ # Initialize instance branch parameters Thetai Thetai = initializeparameters() # NeRF-RCNN generates 3D proposals (bounding boxes, class labels, discrete masks) # This step runs once to establish coarse 3D structure for mask matching. discrete3dmasks, boundingboxes, classlabels = nerfrcnnforward(pretrainednerf) # Multi-view mask matching and refinement using CascadePSP and Mask2Former # Projects 3D masks to 2D, matches instances across views, and refines masks. # consistent2dmasks are produced here and used for supervision. for step in range(1000): # for rayorigin, raydirection in generaterays(cameraposes): # # Hierarchical stratified sampling selects K quadrature points {tk} tsamples = stratifiedsample(rayorigin, raydirection, K) # Compute distance between consecutive samples δk delta = diff(tsamples, prepend=tsamples[0]) # Query pre-trained NeRF for density σ and color c sigma = pretrainednerf.querydensity(tsamples) c = pretrainednerf.querycolor(tsamples, raydirection) # Compute 3D positions from ray origins and sample depths positions = rayorigin + tsamples[:, None] raydirection # Query instance field G for instance logits i i = instancefieldforward(positions, Thetai) # Compute opacity α = 1 - exp(-σδ) alpha = 1.0 - exp(-sigma delta) # Compute transmittance T̂(tk) = Π{j=1}^{k-1} (1 - αj) That = cumprod(concat([oneslike(alpha[:,:1]), 1.0 - alpha[:,:-1]], dim=1), dim=1) # Render expected color, depth, and instance logits via quadrature Chat = sum(That alpha c, dim=0) Dhat = sum(That alpha tsamples, dim=0) Ihat = sum(That alpha i, dim=0) # Compute loss against consistent 2D masks loss = computeloss(Chat, Dhat, Ihat, consistent2dmasks) # Backpropagate to update instance branch parameters Thetai = updateparameters(Thetai, loss) return Thetai Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Multi-view Inconsistency: 2D instance masks generated by standard panoptic segmentation models are generally multi-view inconsistent, meaning the same object may be assigned different instance IDs in different views. This can impair performance if not resolved. Instance-NeRF addresses this via the 2D mask matching procedure. Ambiguity in Overlapping Objects: Unlike Panoptic NeRF, which uses 3D bounding volumes as priors, Instance-NeRF does not rely on 3D priors. However, Panoptic NeRF cannot resolve ambiguity when objects belonging to the same class have overlapping bounding volumes. Instance-NeRF avoids this specific ambiguity by not using bounding volume priors, but it must still handle the general case of overlapping instances through the instance field representation. Time Complexity: The method requires an additional forward pass through the instance branch for every sample point along every ray during training and inference. The complexity is dominated by the NeRF-RCNN 3D proposal generation and the multi-view mask matching/refinement step using Mask2Former and CascadePSP. Memory Complexity: Requires storing the parameters for the instance branch \Thetai in addition to the pre-trained NeRF parameters. The discrete 3D masks and intermediate 2D segmentation maps also consume memory during the training pipeline. Strengths: It is one of the first learning-based approaches to generate 3D instance segmentation in NeRF without using ground-truth segmentation as input. It produces satisfactory 3D object masks on complex scenes during test time. It does not rely on 3D priors to address multi-view inconsistency, avoiding the ambiguity issues associated with overlapping bounding volumes. Limitations: The method depends on the quality of the pre-trained NeRF and the external panoptic segmentation models (Mask2Former, CascadePSP). The multi-view inconsistency of 2D instance masks is a significant challenge that requires complex matching and refinement steps. When to use: When 3D instance segmentation is required for a scene represented by a NeRF, and ground-truth 3D instance labels are unavailable. It is suitable for complex scenes where 3D bounding volume priors might fail due to overlapping objects. Instance-NeRF was introduced by Yichen Liu, Benran Hu, Junkai Huang, Yu-Wing Tai, and Chi-Keung Tang from The Hong Kong University of Science and Technology, Carnegie Mellon University, and Dartmouth College. The paper was published in ICCV 2023. It addresses the challenge of 3D instance segmentation in NeRF, a less explored and more challenging task compared to 2D semantic segmentation in NeRF (e.g., Semantic-NeRF). Previous methods like Panoptic NeRF used 3D bounding volumes as priors but struggled with ambiguity in overlapping objects. Instance-NeRF proposes a novel architecture and training approach that generates multi-view consistent 2D segmentation and continuous 3D segmentation without relying on 3D priors. name: MIMO-NeRF
head: MIMO-NeRF-distill, MIMO-NeRF-naive
body: MIMO-NeRF is a neural rendering method that accelerates inference by replacing the standard Single-Input Single-Output (SISO) Multi-Layer Perceptron (MLP) with a Multi-Input Multi-Output (MIMO) MLP. It groups neighboring samples along a ray and processes them simultaneously, reducing the number of MLP evaluations (# Run) required per pixel. Unlike knowledge distillation methods that require training a separate teacher network, MIMO-NeRF can be trained via self-supervised learning using a 3D consistency loss to resolve ambiguities in density and color inherent in grouped predictions. It maintains the original NeRF hyperparameters (sample counts and network width) while achieving superior speed-quality trade-offs compared to methods that reduce sample counts or network width. Inputs and Outputs: The method takes a set of camera views and their poses as input. For each ray \mathbf{r}, it samples Nc coarse points and Nf fine points. The MIMO MLP f{\text{MIMO}} takes a group of Np positions \{\mathbf{x}i, \dots, \mathbf{x}j\} and the ray direction \mathbf{d} as input, and outputs Np colors \{\mathbf{c}i, \dots, \mathbf{c}j\} and densities \{\sigmai, \dots, \sigmaj\}. Data Structures: The network architecture is identical to the baseline NeRF [Parent] except for input/output dimensions. Positional Encoding: Input positions \mathbf{x} \in \mathbb{R}^3 and directions \mathbf{d} \in \mathbb{S}^2 are encoded using positional encoding \gamma(\cdot) [Parent, S1]. \gamma(\mathbf{x}) is 63-dimensional, \gamma(\mathbf{d}) is 27-dimensional. MIMO MLP: Density Network: Takes concatenated encoded positions \gamma(\mathbf{x}i), \dots, \gamma(\mathbf{x}j) (total dimension 63 \times Np) and applies an 8-layer MLP with ReLU activations, 256 hidden units, and skip connections from input to every 4th layer. Output is Np density values \sigma. Color Network: Takes the output of the last hidden layer of the density network (dimension 256), concatenates with encoded directions \gamma(\mathbf{d}) (dimension 27), passes through a 1-layer MLP (ReLU, 128 units), and finally a linear layer to produce Np RGB colors \mathbf{c}. Note: The total parameter count increases because the input dimension of the first layer scales with Np, but the hidden layer size remains constant. Numbered Steps: 1. Grouping: For a ray with N total samples (coarse + fine), group Np neighboring samples starting from the camera. Create N/Np groups. 2. Forward Pass: Apply f{\text{MIMO}} to each group. For group m containing samples i through j (j=i+Np-1), compute: f{\text{MIMO}}: (\mathbb{R}^3)^{Np} \times \mathbb{S}^2 \rightarrow (\mathbb{R}^3 \times \mathbb{R}^+)^{Np} (\mathbf{x}i, \dots, \mathbf{x}j, \mathbf{d}) \mapsto (\mathbf{c}i, \dots, \mathbf{c}j, \sigmai, \dots, \sigmaj) 3. Rendering: Compute pixel color C(\mathbf{r}) using standard volumetric rendering integration with the predicted \sigma and \mathbf{c}. 4. Training Objective: Minimize \mathcal{L}{\text{MIMO}} = \mathcal{L}{\text{pixel}}^{\text{MIMO}} + \lambda \mathcal{L}{\text{3D}}. \mathcal{L}{\text{pixel}}^{\text{MIMO}}: Standard MSE between rendered and ground truth pixel colors. \mathcal{L}{\text{3D}}: 3D consistency loss comprising color and alpha consistency. 5. 3D Consistency Loss: To address ambiguity in grouped predictions, enforce consistency between different reformulated MLPs (or different groups/views). Color 3D Loss: \mathcal{L}{\text{color 3D}} = \sum{m1=1}^{M-1} \sum{m2=m1+1}^M \frac{1}{N} \sum{i=1}^N \left[ \mu{m1}^{m2} \|\mathbf{c}i^{m1} - \text{sg}(\mathbf{c}i^{m2})\|2^2 + \mu{m2}^{m1} \|\text{sg}(\mathbf{c}i^{m1}) - \mathbf{c}i^{m2}\|2^2 \right] Alpha 3D Loss: \mathcal{L}{\text{alpha 3D}} = \sum{m1=1}^{M-1} \sum{m2=m1+1}^M \frac{1}{N} \sum{i=1}^N \left[ \mu{m1}^{m2} \|\alphai^{m1} - \text{sg}(\alphai^{m2})\|2^2 + \mu{m2}^{m1} \|\text{sg}(\alphai^{m1}) - \alphai^{m2}\|2^2 \right] Asymmetric Weight \mu: \mu{m1}^{m2} = \frac{\sqrt{m2} \sqrt{R{\max}}}{\sqrt{R{m1}}} where R{\max} = \max{m \in \{1, \dots, M\}} Rm. Rm are scaling factors for reformulated MLPs. 6. Optimization: Train using Adam optimizer with learning rate 5 \times 10^{-4} and batch size 1024 rays. Pseudocode: Unverified code. (B, Np, 63) xflat = gammax.view(B, -1) # (B, 63Np) h = xflat for i, layer in enumerate(self.densitylayers[:-1]): h = layer(h) if (i + 1) % 4 == 0: # Skip connection to every 4th layer h = h + xflat h = F.relu(h) densities = self.densitylayers-1.view(B, Np, 1) # (B, Np, 1) gammad = positionalencoding(d.unsqueeze(1), Lfreq=4).squeeze(1) # (B, 27) colorinput = torch.cat([h, gammad], dim=-1) # (B, F+27) c = self.colorlayers0 # (B, 128) c = F.relu(c) c = self.colorlayers1.view(B, Np, 3) # (B, Np, 3) return c, densities def compute3dconsistencyloss(c1, c2, a1, a2, R1, R2, Rmax): """ Computes asymmetric 3D consistency loss between two reformulated networks. c1, c2: (B, Np, 3) colors a1, a2: (B, Np, 1) alphas R1, R2: scaling factors for the respective reformulations Rmax: maximum scaling factor across all reformulations """ mu12 = (torch.sqrt(torch.tensor(R2)) torch.sqrt(Rmax)) / torch.sqrt(torch.tensor(R1)) mu21 = (torch.sqrt(torch.tensor(R1)) torch.sqrt(Rmax)) / torch.sqrt(torch.tensor(R2)) lcolor = mu12 F.mseloss(c1, c2.detach()) + mu21 F.mseloss(c1.detach(), c2) lalpha = mu12 F.mseloss(a1, a2.detach()) + mu21 F.mseloss(a1.detach(), a2) return (lcolor + lalpha) / 2.0 def computeloss(colors, densities, gtcolors, alpha, lambda3d=1.0, reformulations=None): lpixel = F.mseloss(colors, gtcolors) if reformulations is not None: # L3D is computed between multiple reformulated networks (M > 1) # using the asymmetric weighting formula from the sources. l3d = 0.0 M = len(reformulations) for m1 in range(M): for m2 in range(m1 + 1, M): c1, a1 = reformulations[m1] c2, a2 = reformulations[m2] R1, R2 = reformulations[m1].get('R', 1), reformulations[m2].get('R', 1) Rmax = max([r.get('R', 1) for r in reformulations]) l3d += compute3dconsistencyloss(c1, c2, a1, a2, R1, R2, Rmax) l3d /= (M (M - 1) / 2) else: l3d = 0.0 # Application of MIMO-NeRF to the TensoRF architecture. It improves inference and training speed without deteriorating image quality by selecting appropriate Np. Parameters: Np (Blender: \le 2, LLFF: \le 4); Tensor ranks R\sigma, Rc (e.g., R\sigma=16, Rc=48). Performance: Improves I-time and T-time of original TensoRF with similar quality. Implementation: Based on official TensoRF source code. Time Complexity: Inference cost is measured by # Run (number of MLP evaluations). # Run = Nc/Np + (Nc+Nf)/Np. For Nc=64, Nf=128, Np=2, # Run is 128 (vs 192 for NeRF). Memory Complexity: Parameter count increases slightly (up to 1.39\times for Np=8). Limitations: Trade-off between speed and quality as Np increases. MIMO-NeRF was introduced in 2023. It addresses the high computational cost of standard NeRF by leveraging parallel processing of ray samples. It builds on the NeRF training loop [Parent] and positional encoding techniques [Parent], modifying the network architecture to accept multiple input positions and produce multiple output colors and densities simultaneously. name: Appearance and Lighting Decomposition
head: Neural Radiance Field Decomposition, Inverse Rendering in NeRF, Material-Lighting Separation
body: Appearance and Lighting Decomposition refers to a family of neural radiance field methods that decouple view-independent geometric and material properties from view-dependent lighting effects to enable physically plausible relighting, appearance editing, and robust reconstruction of specular surfaces. Unlike standard NeRF, which maps 6D coordinates directly to raw color and density, these methods predict intermediate physical attributes (such as normals, roughness, albedo, or reflection directions) and combine them with lighting models or environment maps during the rendering process. This separation resolves the shape-radiance ambiguity inherent in standard NeRF and allows for the accurate modeling of glossy and reflective surfaces that standard architectures fail to capture. All methods in this family build on Specific Model Architectures. While the specific decomposition varies, the core principle is the decoupling of view-independent geometric/material features from view-dependent lighting effects. Input Representation: Raw coordinates \mathbf{x} and \mathbf{d} are mapped to a higher-dimensional space using positional encoding \gamma(\cdot) to mitigate spectral bias. \gamma(\mathbf{x}) = (\sin(2^0 \pi \mathbf{x}), \cos(2^0 \pi \mathbf{x}), \dots, \sin(2^{L-1} \pi \mathbf{x}), \cos(2^{L-1} \pi \mathbf{x})) where L is the number of frequency bands. Network Topology: The canonical implementation uses coupled Multi-Layer Perceptrons (MLPs) modified to output intermediate physical properties rather than raw color. 1. Density/Geometry Network: Takes \gamma(\mathbf{x}) as input. It consists of L hidden layers with ReLU activations and skip connections from the input to every 4th layer. It outputs density \sigma and latent features representing material properties (e.g., normals, roughness, albedo). 2. Appearance/Lighting Network: Takes the latent features, \gamma(\mathbf{x}), and \mathbf{d} (or derived directions like reflection vectors) as input. It computes the final color \mathbf{c} by combining material properties with lighting models (e.g., environment maps, specular models). Rendering Integration: During training, rays are sampled at points \mathbf{x}i. The MLPs predict \sigmai and material properties. The pixel color C(\mathbf{r}) is computed via volumetric rendering: C(\mathbf{r}) = \sum{i=1}^N Ti \alphai \mathbf{c}i, \quad \text{where } \alphai = 1 - \exp(-\sigmai \deltai), \quad Ti = \prod{j=1}^{i-1} (1 - \alphaj) where \deltai is the distance between samples. The color \mathbf{c}i is derived from the decomposed components specific to the child method. Neural Light Field Representations map camera rays directly to RGB color values, bypassing the volumetric ray-marching and alpha-composition steps required by Neural Radiance Fields (NeRF). Unlike NeRF, which requires multiple forward passes per ray to aggregate radiance, these methods achieve novel view synthesis with a single forward pass per ray, enabling rendering speeds that are orders of magnitude faster. Anisotropic Neural Representation Learning (ANRL) is a method for neural volume rendering that models volumetric density and latent features as view-dependent functions using spherical harmonics (SH) to eliminate directional ambiguity. Unlike standard NeRF which assumes isotropic point-sampled features, ANRL replaces the initial MLP output with SH coefficients, allowing the representation to capture anisotropy directly without shape-based sampling parameterization. This approach improves reconstruction quality in scenes with complex lighting or reflective surfaces while maintaining rendering efficiency. Ref-NeRF is a neural radiance field method that improves the representation of specular reflections by replacing NeRF’s parameterization of view-dependent outgoing radiance with a representation of reflected radiance, structured using spatially-varying scene properties. It builds on Specific Model Architectures by decoupling view-independent geometric/material features from view-dependent lighting effects, specifically targeting the failure of standard NeRF to accurately capture glossy surfaces. Unlike its siblings, Ref-NeRF explicitly separates outgoing radiance into diffuse and specular components and reparameterizes the directional input using the reflection of the viewing vector about the local normal vector, enabling smoother interpolation of reflected radiance across scenes with varying materials. The Convex Combination Color Decoder is a method for decomposing view-dependent appearance into a diffuse-like base component and a glossy reflection component, weighted by a geometry-derived coefficient. It solves the problem of modeling specular highlights and environment reflections in neural radiance fields by ensuring that reflection features are utilized at every sample point along a ray, rather than just in image space, which aids convergence when geometry is initially fuzzy. It differs from standard NeRF color decoders by explicitly separating the view-dependent term from a reflection term that utilizes a pre-computed reflection feature \bar{\mathbf{f}}. This method solves the problem of disentangling foreground objects from background environments in a radiance field to enable editable novel view synthesis, where foreground objects can be removed or replaced without corrupting the background. It sets itself apart from sibling methods like Ref-NeRF by explicitly modeling separate background and object radiance fields that are composited via a differentiable one-hot gating mechanism, rather than relying solely on view-dependent lighting models or anisotropic scattering. Unlike Convex Combination Color Decoder which focuses on color mixing, this framework enforces spatial separation through density regularization and Gumbel-Softmax activation. DE-NeRF decomposes lighting, geometry, and appearance to allow relighting of high-frequency environments and appearance editing. It trains a signed distance field (SDF) function using a set of 2D images to reconstruct a display grid as the input scene for the MLP. The scene is decomposed into geometric features and appearance features (diffuse reflection, roughness, specular tint). Geometric features, appearance features, and distance h (from sampling point to grid) are input into four corresponding MLPs to predict diffuse albedo, roughness value, and specular tint. Diffuse reflectance is integrated with the environment map to get diffuse color \mathbf{c}d. A specular lighting MLP Fs is trained to get specular lighting \mathbf{c}l. The specular color \mathbf{c}s is calculated by multiplying \mathbf{c}l with specular hue. The final color \mathbf{c} is calculated as \mathbf{c}s + \mathbf{c}d. On NeRF Synthetic and Shiny Blender data sets, PSNR is 2 points higher than latest papers. NeRFLight is a grid-based neural radiance field architecture designed to achieve real-time view synthesis with a significantly reduced memory footprint compared to standard grid-based methods like Instant-NGP or KiloNeRF. It solves the trade-off between rendering speed and model size by splitting the 3D scene volume into N distinct spatial regions, each utilizing a separate density decoder but sharing a single, compact feature grid. Unlike Instant-NGP, which uses hash grids and multiresolution schemes that can suffer from rendering speed losses due to multiple linear interpolations, NeRFLight avoids hash grids entirely and instead uses multiple density decoders to handle feature collisions, ensuring high frame rates. NeRF-A is a NeRF variant using appearance embeddings (NeRF-A) without transient embeddings for handling varying camera conditions. Train the model with the left half side of the images in the training set and test novel view synthesis on the right half side. Interpolate between appearance embeddings assigned to brighter and darker images for controllable rendering. Quantitative results on classroom image: PSNR 23.52, SSIM 0.907, LPIPS 0.247. Train the material-geometry module first to predict albedo, normal, roughness, metallic, and depth, because the lighting network depends on these properties (e.g., SSRT depends on depth, MLP decoder depends on GBuffers). Train the lighting module second, using the re-rendering loss. The total loss for MGNet is a weighted combination: L{MGNet} = \lambdaa L{albedo} + \lambdan L{normal} + \lambdam L{material} + \lambdad L{depth}. The total loss for LightNet is: L{LightNet} = L{light} + \lambdar L{re-render}. L{light} is the HDR supervision loss function proposed by [Mildenhall et al. 2021]. L{re-render} is an L2 loss between the re-rendered image and the original image. Li et al. [2020]'s rendering layer causes significant artifacts on glossy surfaces. Unlike Li et al. [2020] which discretizes the incident hemisphere to approximate integration, this method leverages differentiable Monte Carlo. NeROIC is a technique using a multi-stage pipeline to recover a relightable NeRF-like model from images of an object captured under multiple unconstrained lighting environments. A method that recovers NeRF-like relightable models of large-scale buildings and historical sites. First stage: recovers geometry while explaining appearance variations due to lighting with latent appearance embeddings. Second stage: extracts normal vectors from this recovered geometry. Third stage: estimates BRDF properties and a spherical harmonic representation of lighting. Decomposes scenes into diffuse albedo, surface normals, a spherical harmonics representation of lighting, and shadows, which can be combined to relight the scene under novel environment illumination. Assumes a Lambertian model. The concept of decomposing appearance and lighting in neural radiance fields emerged as a response to the limitations of standard NeRF in handling specular reflections and complex lighting. Standard NeRF assumes isotropic scattering and maps viewing direction directly to color, which leads to artifacts on glossy surfaces and an inability to separate geometry from material properties. Early works like Ref-NeRF and DE-NeRF introduced explicit material parameters (normals, roughness) and lighting models to address these issues. Subsequent methods like NeRFLight and MGNet explored grid-based decompositions and inverse rendering techniques to estimate lighting and materials from images. The family continues to evolve with methods addressing anisotropy, background decomposition, and efficient rendering. name: NeRFLight
body: NeRFLight is a grid-based neural radiance field architecture designed to achieve real-time view synthesis with a significantly reduced memory footprint compared to standard grid-based methods like Instant-NGP or KiloNeRF. It solves the trade-off between rendering speed and model size by splitting the 3D scene volume into N distinct spatial regions, each utilizing a separate density decoder but sharing a single, compact feature grid. Unlike Instant-NGP, which uses hash grids and multiresolution schemes that can suffer from rendering speed losses due to multiple linear interpolations, NeRFLight avoids hash grids entirely and instead uses multiple density decoders to handle feature collisions, ensuring high frame rates. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A set of training images with known camera poses (oj, dj) defining rays rj(t) = oj + dj t, and a 3D scene volume bounded by a region of interest. Output: A rendered image pixel color C(\mathbf{r}) for a given ray, and a compact model representation (shared feature grid + decoder weights) suitable for inference. Data Structures: 1. Shared Feature Grid: A 3D grid of latent features. The grid is symmetrically configured such that features are placed at multiple spatial positions corresponding to the N regions. This symmetry favors feature pruning after training and allows smooth gradient transitions between neighboring voxels. 2. Density Decoders: N separate Multi-Layer Perceptrons (MLPs), denoted as \thetai for region i \in [1, N]. Each decoder takes features from the shared grid and outputs density \sigma and an intermediate latent representation h. 3. Color Decoder: A single MLP that takes the intermediate representation h, the viewing direction \mathbf{d}, and potentially other lighting parameters to output the final color \mathbf{c}. Numbered Steps: 1. Scene Partitioning: Divide the 3D scene volume into N distinct spatial regions. In the canonical implementation, N=8. 2. Feature Grid Initialization: Create a single shared feature grid. Features are arranged symmetrically across the regions. This configuration forces features to learn a compact representation valid for different parts of the scene, reducing the total number of stored feature values by a factor of N (e.g., 8x reduction) compared to using separate grids per region. 3. Ray Sampling: For a given ray \mathbf{r}, sample points \mathbf{x}j along the ray. 4. Region Identification: Determine which of the N regions a sample point \mathbf{x}j falls into. Let i be the index of the region containing \mathbf{x}j. 5. Feature Lookup: Retrieve the latent features \hat{f}(\mathbf{x}j) from the shared feature grid at position \mathbf{x}j. 6. Density and Latent Prediction: Pass the features \hat{f}(\mathbf{x}j) to the region-specific density decoder \thetai: \sigmaj, hj = \thetai(\hat{f}(\mathbf{x}j)) where \sigmaj is the volume density and hj is the intermediate latent representation. 7. Color Prediction: Pass the intermediate representation hj, the viewing direction \mathbf{d}, and the positional encoding of the position \gamma(\mathbf{x}j) to the color decoder to obtain the color \mathbf{c}j. Note: The parent article specifies that the color network takes latent features, \gamma(\mathbf{x}), and \mathbf{d} [Parent]. 8. Volumetric Rendering: Compute the pixel color C(\mathbf{r}) using deterministic volume integration (as opposed to Monte Carlo integration): C(\mathbf{r}) = \sum{j=1}^{M} Tj \alphaj \mathbf{c}j where \alphaj = 1 - \exp(-\sigmaj \deltaj) is the opacity, Tj = \prod{k=1}^{j-1} (1 - \alphak) is the accumulated transmittance, and \deltaj is the distance between samples [Parent, S1]. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def positionalencoding(x, numbands): """ Computes the positional encoding for input x. x: tensor of shape (..., D) numbands: int L Returns: tensor of shape (..., 2 D L) """ # Implementation of gamma(x) as defined in parent article # gamma(x) = (sin(2^0 pi x), cos(2^0 pi x),..., sin(2^{L-1} pi x), cos(2^{L-1} pi x)) freqbands = 2.0 torch.arange(numbands, dtype=x.dtype, device=x.device) scaledx = x.unsqueeze(-1) freqbands math.pi encoded = torch.cat([torch.sin(scaledx), torch.cos(scaledx)], dim=-1) return encoded def renderray(rayorigin, raydirection, sharedfeaturegrid, densitydecoders, colordecoder, numregions=8): """ Renders a single ray using the NeRFLight architecture. Args: rayorigin: (3,) tensor, origin of the ray oj raydirection: (3,) tensor, direction of the ray dj sharedfeaturegrid: 3D tensor of latent features densitydecoders: list of N MLPs (thetai) colordecoder: MLP for color prediction numregions: int N, number of spatial regions (default 8) Returns: color: (3,) tensor, final pixel color """ # 1. Sample points along the ray # In practice, this involves stratified sampling or hierarchical sampling # For simplicity, assume we have a list of sample points xj and distances deltaj # This part depends on the specific sampling strategy (coarse-to-fine is mentioned in) # Here we assume pre-computed samples for the core NeRFLight logic samples = getraysamples(rayorigin, raydirection) # Placeholder for sampling logic accumulatedcolor = torch.zeros(3) accumulatedtransmittance = 1.0 for sample in samples: xj = sample.position deltaj = sample.distance # 2. Determine region index i for point xj # This requires a mapping from 3D coordinates to region index [1, N] regionindex = getregionindex(xj, numregions) # 3. Lookup features from shared grid # fhat(xj) retrieves features from the shared grid at xj features = lookupsharedgrid(sharedfeaturegrid, xj) # 4. Get density and latent features from region-specific decoder # sigmaj, hj = thetai(fhat(xj)) densitydecoder = densitydecoders[regionindex] sigmaj, hj = densitydecoder(features) # 5. Compute opacity alphaj = 1.0 - torch.exp(-sigmaj deltaj) # 6. Compute color # Color decoder takes hj, gamma(xj), and dj gammaxj = positionalencoding(xj, numbands=10) # Typical L value, not specified in source gammadj = positionalencoding(raydirection, numbands=4) # Typical L value, not specified in source colorj = colordecoder(hj, gammaxj, gammadj) # 7. Accumulate weight = accumulatedtransmittance alphaj accumulatedcolor += weight colorj accumulatedtransmittance = (1.0 - alphaj) # Early termination if transmittance is very low if accumulatedtransmittance < 1e-5: break return accumulatedcolor def getregionindex(x, numregions): """ Determines which of the N regions a 3D point x belongs to. Assumes a simple grid partitioning of the bounding box. """ # Normalize x to [0, 1] range based on scene bounds # This is a placeholder for the specific partitioning logic # The source mentions "symmetrically placed" features, implying a structured grid pass def lookupsharedgrid(grid, x): """ Trilinearly interpolates features from the shared 3D grid at position x. """ # Standard trilinear interpolation pass Parameters: N: The number of regions the volume is split into. In the paper's implementation, N=8. Positional Encoding Bands (L): Not explicitly specified in the sources for NeRFLight, but the parent article defines the general form. Typical values in NeRF variants are L=10 for position and L=4 for direction [Parent]. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Feature Collisions: By sharing the feature grid, features must represent multiple regions. This forces compactness but may lead to ambiguity if the scene has distinct features in different regions that are mapped to the same grid location. NeRFLight handles this by using multiple density decoders. Boundary Artifacts: The symmetry of the feature configuration is designed to favor smooth gradient transitions between neighboring voxels, reducing artifacts at region boundaries. Empty Space: Empty space pruning is applied to accelerate model inference, removing features that do not contribute to the visible scene. Rendering Speed: Achieves real-time performance of up to 181 FPS. Model Size: The model size is approximately 14MB. Efficiency: The FPS/MB ratio is 2x larger than the closest state-of-the-art approach at the time of publication. Memory Footprint: The shared feature grid reduces the total number of stored feature values by a factor of N (8x reduction compared to separate grids). Strengths: High rendering speed, small model size, real-time capability, seamless reconstruction due to symmetric feature configuration. Limitations: The method relies on a fixed number of regions (N=8 in the paper), which may not adapt well to scenes of varying complexity without retraining. It does not use hash grids or multiresolution schemes, which might limit its ability to capture fine details in very large scenes compared to Instant-NGP. When to use: When real-time rendering and low memory footprint are critical, and the scene can be effectively partitioned into a small number of regions. When not to use: For scenes requiring extremely high detail across a vast volume where a fixed partitioning scheme is insufficient, or when dynamic resolution adaptation is needed. NeRFLight was introduced by Rivas-Manzaneque et al. in 2023. It extends grid-based NeRF approaches by addressing the memory footprint issues that prevent deployment on bandwidth-constrained applications. The method builds on the idea of splitting the density field into multiple regions with separate decoders, similar to KiloNeRF, but avoids baking a large number of MLPs by using a shared feature grid. It also leverages deterministic volume integration from [48] to improve accuracy and speed. The approach was evaluated on synthetic and real data, demonstrating state-of-the-art FPS/MB ratios. Rendering Integration: During training, rays are sampled at points \mathbf{x}i. The MLPs predict \sigmai and material properties. The pixel color C(\mathbf{r}) is computed via volumetric rendering: C(\mathbf{r}) = \sum{i=1}^N Ti \alphai \mathbf{c}i, \quad \text{where } \alphai = 1 - \exp(-\sigmai \deltai), \quad Ti = \prod{j=1}^{i-1} (1 - \alphaj) where \deltai is the distance between samples. The color \mathbf{c}i is derived from the decomposed components specific to the child method. Unlike NeRF, which requires multiple forward passes per ray to aggregate radiance, NeLF achieves novel view synthesis with a single forward pass per ray, enabling rendering speeds that are orders of magnitude faster. It differs from sibling methods like NeLF by training with a fixed total parameter budget that is redistributed from many small subnetworks to fewer, wider networks over time, preventing overfitting in early stages while enabling high-fidelity detail reconstruction in later stages. body: Neural Light Field (NeLF) is a scene representation method that maps camera rays directly to RGB color values, bypassing the volumetric ray-marching and alpha-composition steps required by Neural Radiance Fields (NeRF). Unlike NeRF, which requires multiple forward passes per ray to aggregate radiance, NeLF achieves novel view synthesis with a single forward pass per ray, enabling rendering speeds that are orders of magnitude faster. While standard NeLF implementations often use shallow networks, efficient variants like R2L employ deep residual MLPs trained via knowledge distillation from a pre-trained NeRF teacher to maintain high visual fidelity. Inputs and Outputs: The method takes a camera ray, parameterized by its origin \mathbf{o} = (xo, yo, zo) and direction \mathbf{d} = (xd, yd, zd), and outputs a 3D RGB color vector \mathbf{c} = (r, g, b). Data Structures and Layout: 1. Ray Representation: The ray is encoded as a concatenation of spatial coordinates of K sampled points along the ray, forming a 3K-dimensional input vector. In the R2L implementation, K=16. 2. Network Architecture: A deep residual Multi-Layer Perceptron (MLP) G\phi maps the input ray to RGB. Common configurations include width W=256 and depth D=88 (W256D88, ~12M FLOPs) or W=181, D=88 (W181D88, ~6M FLOPs). The network uses extensive residual blocks. 3. Positional Encoding: Inputs are enriched using positional encoding \gamma(\cdot) to mitigate spectral bias. \gamma(\mathbf{x}) = (\sin(2^0 \pi \mathbf{x}), \cos(2^0 \pi \mathbf{x}), \dots, \sin(2^{L-1} \pi \mathbf{x}), \cos(2^{L-1} \pi \mathbf{x})) where L is the number of frequency bands. Training Procedure (Distillation): NeLF is typically trained by distilling knowledge from a pre-trained NeRF teacher model F{\Theta^}. 1. Pseudo Data Generation: Rays are sampled from a uniform distribution U within a viewing bounding box inferred from training camera poses. \begin{aligned} xo &\sim U(x{o,\min}, x{o,\max}), & yo &\sim U(y{o,\min}, y{o,\max}), & zo &\sim U(z{o,\min}, z{o,\max}) \\ xd &\sim U(x{d,\min}, x{d,\max}), & yd &\sim U(y{d,\min}, y{d,\max}), & zd &\sim U(z{d,\min}, z{d,\max}) \end{aligned} The teacher model queries these rays to obtain target RGB values (\hat{r}, \hat{g}, \hat{b}). 2. Loss Function: The NeLF student network G\phi is trained using Mean Squared Error (MSE) loss between its output and the teacher's output. L = \text{MSE}(G\phi(xo, yo, zo, xd, yd, zd), (\hat{r}, \hat{g}, \hat{b})) 3. Hard Example Mining: To focus on high-frequency details, a pool of hard examples (rays with larger loss) is maintained. In each iteration, the top r fraction of batch losses is added to the pool, and r examples are randomly picked from the pool to augment the training batch. Default r=0.2. Rendering: During inference, for each pixel, a ray is defined. K points are evenly spaced along the ray. The concatenated coordinates are fed into G\phi to directly predict the pixel color. name: Point-based Neural Light Field
head: ProLiF point-based representation
body: A neural light field representation that avoids the 3D geometry-agnostic nature of direct ray-to-color mapping by sampling points along the ray and predicting density and color for each point, then accumulating them via volume rendering. It differs from standard NeRF by predicting all densities and colors for a ray's sample points in a single forward pass, enabling efficient batch rendering, though it introduces entanglement between point coordinates that requires specific training schemes to resolve. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A set of input images with known camera poses. For forward-facing cameras, a ray is parameterized by r = (u, v, s, t), where (u, v) are coordinates on the near plane and (s, t) are coordinates on the far plane. Output: A rendered color C \in \mathbb{R}^3 for the ray. Data Structures: Sample Points: D points evenly sampled at predefined depth values \{d0, d1,..., d{D-1}\} between the near and far planes. Ray Parameterization: The ray is represented by the concatenation of all sample point coordinates: (x0, y0,..., x{D-1}, y{D-1}). Network: A Multi-layer Perceptron (MLP) MLP: \mathbb{R}^{2D} \rightarrow \mathbb{R}^{D \times \mathbb{R}^3}. Steps: 1. Sampling: Evenly sample D points at predefined depth values \{d0, d1,..., d{D-1}\} between the near and far planes on the given ray. 2. Parameterization: Concatenate the 2D coordinates of all D sample points into a single vector of size 2D: (x0, y0,..., x{D-1}, y{D-1}). 3. Prediction: Feed the concatenated coordinate vector into the MLP. The network predicts densities \sigmai and colors ci for all D points in a single forward pass. 4. Accumulation: Compute the final pixel color C using volume rendering accumulation: C = \sum{i=0}^{D-1} Ti \alphai ci where: \alphai = 1 - \exp(-\deltai \sigmai) is the opacity of the i-th point. Ti = \prod{j=0}^{i-1} (1 - \alphaj) is the accumulated transmittance up to point i. \deltai is the distance between the i-th and (i+1)-th point. Pitfalls: Entanglement: Simply applying this method causes color and density predictions on a sample point to be entangled with the coordinates of other points on the same ray. Inconsistency: Because the prediction for a 3D point depends on other points on the ray, two rays intersecting at the same 3D point may assign totally different colors and densities, leading to inconsistency in scene geometry and poor generalization to novel views. Efficiency: Unlike NeRF, which requires multiple forward passes for all sample points, this method predicts all densities and colors in a single forward pass. This allows rendering a large batch of rays in one training step and enables fast rendering in both training and inference stages without extensive memory consumption. Limitations: The single-pass design introduces coordinate entanglement, which prevents perfect multi-view consistency if not addressed by additional mechanisms (e.g., progressive training or consistency losses). Origin: Proposed in the "Progressively-connected Light Field Network" (ProLiF) paper. Context: Designed to address the 3D geometry-agnostic nature of direct neural light field mappings, which overfit to input images and fail to generalize to novel views. It builds on the concept of neural light fields but incorporates volume rendering principles to learn multiview consistent scene geometry. name: Progressively-connected Light Field Network (ProLiF) Architecture
body: ProLiF is a neural light field representation that decouples view-independent geometry and material properties from view-dependent lighting, enabling efficient view synthesis by training with a progressively connected architecture. It sets itself apart from standard NeRF or NeLF by replacing a single monolithic MLP with a set of independent subnetworks that are merged during training, enforcing an inductive bias for consistent scene geometry at early stages to prevent overfitting and improve detail reconstruction. ProLiF builds on Specific Model Architectures by decomposing the scene representation into Nk independent subnetworks at training stage k, which are progressively merged to form a single fully-connected MLP by the final stage. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Ray parameters (u, v, s, t) and depth samples. At stage k, the input vector pk consists of sampled x-y coordinates: pk = [x^k0, y^k0, \dots, x^k{Dk-1}, y^k{Dk-1}]. Output: Concatenated color and density values for the sampled points. Data Structures: Subnetworks: At stage k, there are Nk = D \times 2^{-k} subnetworks \Phi^k = \{F^k0, F^k1, \dots, F^k{Nk-1}\}. Hidden Width: Each subnetwork has a hidden width of W \times 2^k, where W is a preset parameter. The total hidden width across all subnetworks remains constant (D \times W) throughout training. Depth Samples: The number of depth samples at stage k is Dk = D \times 2^k. Parameters: D (initial number of subnetworks/depth samples) and W (base hidden width) are preset. Numbered Steps: 1. Initialization (Stage k=0): Initialize N0 = D independent subnetworks. Each subnetwork F^0i has hidden width W. Input coordinates are sampled at D0 = D depth locations. 2. Forward Pass: For each ray, compute sampled x-y coordinates x^ki, y^ki based on ray origin and direction. Each subnetwork F^ki processes its assigned input coordinates to predict density \sigma and color \mathbf{c}. Rendered color is computed via volumetric rendering using the predicted \sigma and \mathbf{c}. 3. Progressive Connection (Merging Subnetworks): At the end of stage k, merge neighboring subnetworks F^k{2i} and F^k{2i+1} into a single subnetwork F^{k+1}i for i \in \{0, \dots, D \times 2^{-(k+1)} - 1\}. Weight Matrix Construction: The new weight matrix W^{k+1}i is constructed by placing the weights of the two merged subnetworks on the diagonal: W^{k+1}i = \begin{bmatrix} W^k{2i} & 0 \\ 0 & W^k{2i+1} \end{bmatrix} This ensures the output z^{k+1}i = [z^k{2i}, z^k{2i+1}] remains unchanged. Bias Vector Construction: The new bias vector is the concatenation of the original biases: b^{k+1}i = [b^k{2i}, b^k{2i+1}]. 4. Depth Subdivision (Input Expansion): When switching from stage k to k+1, the number of depth samples doubles from Dk to D{k+1} = D \times 2^{k+1}. The input vector p changes from pk to p{k+1}, requiring the network to handle double the input dimension. Reparameterization: To maintain output invariance despite the input dimension doubling, the weights and biases of the first and last layers are reparameterized using subdivinputlayers. 5. Final Stage: When k = \log2(D), the network consists of a single fully-connected MLP (\Phi^k = \{F^k0\}). Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def subdivinputlayers(orgweight, orgbias): """ Reparameterizes weights and biases to handle input dimension doubling during depth subdivision, ensuring output invariance. Args: orgweight: numpy array of shape [nsubnetworks, dout, din] orgbias: numpy array of shape [nsubnetworks, dout] Returns: newweight: numpy array of shape [nsubnetworks, dout, 2din] newbias: numpy array of shape [nsubnetworks, dout] """ bias = orgbias # Rearrange weight to separate the two halves of the input dimension # Original shape: [n, o, dc] where c=2 (for x and y coordinates) # Rearranged shape: [n, o, d, c] weight = rearrange(orgweight, 'n o (d c) -> n o d c', c=2) # Concatenate the weight matrix along the input dimension (dim=3) # and scale by 0.5 to maintain the same output magnitude weight = concatenate([weight, weight], dim=3) 0.5 # Rearrange back to the original flattened input dimension format # New shape: [n, o, 2dc] weight = rearrange(weight, 'n o d c -> n o (d c)') return weight, bias def addconnections(orgweight, orgbias): """ Merges neighboring subnetworks by constructing block-diagonal weight matrices. Args: orgweight: numpy array of shape [nsubnetworks, dout, din] orgbias: numpy array of shape [nsubnetworks, dout] Returns: newweight: numpy array of shape [nsubnetworks/2, 2dout, 2din] newbias: numpy array of shape [nsubnetworks/2, 2dout] """ nsubnetworks, dout, din = orgweight.shape newn = nsubnetworks // 2 newweight = np.zeros((newn, 2 dout, 2 din)) newbias = np.zeros((newn, 2 dout)) for i in range(newn): # Merge F{2i} and F{2i+1} into Fi # Construct block-diagonal weight matrix newweight[i,:dout,:din] = orgweight[2 i] newweight[i, dout:, din:] = orgweight[2 i + 1] # Concatenate bias vectors newbias[i,:dout] = orgbias[2 i] newbias[i, dout:] = orgbias[2 i + 1] return newweight, newbias Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Output Invariance: Failure to reparameterize weights during subdivision will cause the network output to change, breaking the progressive training continuity. Precision: The scaling factor of 0.5 in subdivinputlayers is critical for maintaining numerical stability and output consistency. A training strategy that incrementally increases neuron connections across training stages to prevent overfitting and improve detail reconstruction. It sets itself apart from direct MLP training by enforcing an inductive bias for consistent scene geometry at the start, avoiding the overfitting and geometric inaccuracies typical of standard end-to-end optimization. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: The total hidden width remains constant (D \times W) throughout training, but the number of subnetworks decreases while their individual width increases. Measured Performance: Not given in the sources. Scaling: The architecture scales by increasing D (initial subnetworks) and W (base width), with the final network being a single MLP of width D \times W. Strengths: Prevents overfitting in early stages, improves detail reconstruction, and ensures geometric consistency. Limitations: Requires careful reparameterization to maintain output invariance during transitions. When to use: When efficient view synthesis is required with high-quality detail reconstruction, especially in scenarios where standard NeRF might overfit or produce geometric inaccuracies. When not to use: When a simple, single-stage training process is preferred, or when computational resources for managing multiple subnetworks are limited. ProLiF was introduced in a 2022 preprint titled "Progressively-connected Light Field Network for Efficient View Synthesis". It addresses the limitations of standard neural radiance field training by introducing a progressive connection mechanism that starts with sparse, independent subnetworks and merges them over time. name: Progressive Training Scheme
head: Progressive depth sampling, progressive connection merging
body: A training strategy for neural light field networks that incrementally increases neuron connections across training stages to prevent overfitting and improve detail reconstruction. It solves the problem of point coordinate entanglement by starting with sparse, independent subnetworks to ensure point consistency, then progressively densifying connections to increase network capacity for high-quality rendering. It sets itself apart from direct MLP training by enforcing an inductive bias for consistent scene geometry at the start, avoiding the overfitting and geometric inaccuracies typical of standard end-to-end optimization. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A set of training images with known camera poses; a target scene geometry defined by near and far planes. Output: A fully connected Multi-Layer Perceptron (MLP) with learned weights, capable of predicting color and density for any 3D point and viewing direction. Data Structures: The network is structured as a series of stages k=0, \dots, K-1. Subnetworks: At stage k, the network consists of Nk independent subnetworks. Each subnetwork processes coordinates for a specific subset of depth samples. Weights: Weight matrices W and bias vectors b for each layer. During merging, new weights are initialized to zero. Depth Samples: A discrete set of depth planes di between the near and far planes. Parameters: Stages: Total K=5 stages (indexed 0 to 4). Subnetworks at stage k: Nk = 16 \times 2^{-k}. Hidden width per subnetwork: Wk = 32 \times 2^k. Hidden depth: 8 layers for ProLiF, 12 layers for ProLiF-Deep. Depth planes at stage k: Dk = 16 \times 2^k. Activation: SIREN with \omega0 = 30. Optimizer: Adam, initial learning rate 1 \times 10^{-4}, decayed to 2.5 \times 10^{-6} via cosine scheduling. Iterations per stage: t steps (total 1M iterations across all stages). Ray Sampling: 16,384 rays for pixel fitting, 4,096 extra random rays for regularization per iteration. Input Normalization: Coordinates normalized to NDC space. Weight Normalization: Applied to stabilize training. Steps: 1. Initialization (Stage 0): Split the MLP into D0 = 16 separated small subnetworks. Each subnetwork j processes the coordinate of a point at a specific depth dj independently. Points at the same depth on different rays share the same subnetwork. Initialize weights using standard methods (e.g., SIREN initialization). 2. Training Stage 0: Train the independent subnetworks for t steps. Loss function includes pixel fitting and regularization losses (e.g., color consistency, density consistency). 3. Progressive Merging (Stage k to k+1): For k from 0 to K-2: Identify pairs of neighboring subnetworks. Merge two neighboring subnetworks into one single fully connected network. Feature Concatenation: Concatenate the feature vectors of the two subnetworks. Weight Merging: Merge the weight parameters of the two subnetworks. Zero Initialization: Add zero values to the new weight parameters connecting the concatenated features to the next layer. This ensures the merged network initially behaves as two independent networks. Channel Count: Ensure the total channel number in the hidden layers of all points stays unchanged during merging. Depth Subdivision: Interpolate weights in subnetworks of neighboring depth values to process newly added depth samples. The number of sampled depth planes doubles from 16 \times 2^k to 16 \times 2^{k+1}. 4. Training Stage k+1: Continue training with the new architecture for t steps. Repeat steps 3-4 until a single fully connected network processes all input point coordinates (Stage 4). Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def progressivetrainingscheme(numstages=5, stepsperstage=200000): # Initialize parameters numdepthsamples = 16 hiddenwidth = 32 hiddendepth = 8 # or 12 for ProLiF-Deep activation = SIREN(w0=30) optimizer = Adam(lr=1e-4) # Stage 0: Create independent subnetworks # Each subnetwork handles one depth sample subnetworks = [] for i in range(numdepthsamples): # Create a small MLP for depth sample i # Input: 3D coordinate, Output: color/density subnetwork = createmlp(inputdim=3, hiddendim=hiddenwidth, outputdim=4, hiddenlayers=hiddendepth, activation=activation) subnetworks.append(subnetwork) # Train Stage 0 for step in range(stepsperstage): rays = samplerays(16384) # Pixel fitting rays regrays = samplerays(4096) # Regularization rays loss = computeloss(subnetworks, rays, regrays) optimizer.step(loss) # Progressive Merging and Training for k in range(1, numstages): # Double the number of depth samples newdepthsamples = numdepthsamples 2 newsubnetworks = [] # Merge pairs of subnetworks for i in range(0, len(subnetworks), 2): sub1 = subnetworks[i] sub2 = subnetworks[i+1] # Create merged subnetwork # Input: 3D coordinate # Hidden layers: width = hiddenwidth 2 (concatenated features) mergedsubnetwork = createmlp( inputdim=3, hiddendim=hiddenwidth 2, outputdim=4, hiddenlayers=hiddendepth, activation=activation) # Initialize weights from sub1 and sub2 # Copy weights from sub1 to first half of merged weights # Copy weights from sub2 to second half of merged weights # Initialize new cross-connections to zero initializemergedweights(mergedsubnetwork, sub1, sub2) newsubnetworks.append(mergedsubnetwork) subnetworks = newsubnetworks numdepthsamples = newdepthsamples # Train merged subnetworks for step in range(stepsperstage): rays = samplerays(16384) regrays = samplerays(4096) loss = computeloss(subnetworks, rays, regrays) optimizer.step(loss) return subnetworks[0] # Final single fully connected network Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Overfitting: Direct training without the progressive scheme leads to overfitting and failure to reconstruct geometry. Artifacts: Applying regularization losses without the progressive training scheme leaves observable artifacts in rendered images. Precision: Zero initialization of new weights is critical to maintain the inductive bias during merging. Time Complexity: Training requires approximately 28 hours for ProLiF or 35 hours for ProLiF-Deep to complete 1M iterations on a single Nvidia 2080Ti GPU. Memory Complexity: Model size is small (e.g., 8.0MB for LFN-SIREN baseline, ProLiF is comparable or smaller due to efficient representation). Performance: ProLiF outperforms NeRF in speed and image quality, and costs much less memory and time than Nex. Strengths: Correctly reconstructs scene geometry; yields higher quality color and depth maps compared to ablated variants; handles high-frequency details via SIREN. Limitations: Requires careful tuning of stage transitions; regularization is still necessary to avoid noise. When to use: When training neural light field networks for view synthesis, especially when geometry consistency is critical and overfitting is a concern. When not to use: For simple scenes where direct training suffices, or when computational resources are extremely limited and the overhead of multi-stage training is prohibitive. Origin: Proposed in "Progressively-connected Light Field Network for Efficient View Synthesis" (Arxiv, 2022). History: Developed to address the inconsistency in neural light field representations caused by entanglement between point coordinates on a ray. The method builds on the idea of using independent subnetworks to enforce point consistency, gradually increasing capacity. Usage: Used in the ProLiF and ProLiF-Deep architectures for efficient view synthesis.
