name: Anisotropic Neural Representation Learning
head: Anisotropic NeRF, SH-guided anisotropic features
body: Anisotropic Neural Representation Learning (ANRL) is a method for neural volume rendering that models volumetric density and latent features as view-dependent functions using spherical harmonics (SH) to eliminate directional ambiguity. Unlike standard NeRF which assumes isotropic point-sampled features, ANRL replaces the initial MLP output with SH coefficients, allowing the representation to capture anisotropy directly without shape-based sampling parameterization. This approach improves reconstruction quality in scenes with complex lighting or reflective surfaces while maintaining rendering efficiency. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Ray origin \mathbf{o}, direction \mathbf{d}, near/far bounds tn, tf. Output: Pixel color C(\mathbf{r}). Data Structures: The method modifies the first Multi-Layer Perceptron (MLP) of the standard NeRF architecture. 1. Positional Encoding: Input coordinates \mathbf{x} and directions \mathbf{d} are mapped to a higher-dimensional space using positional encoding \gamma(\cdot) to mitigate spectral bias. \gamma(\mathbf{x}) = (\sin(2^0 \pi \mathbf{x}), \cos(2^0 \pi \mathbf{x}), \dots, \sin(2^{L-1} \pi \mathbf{x}), \cos(2^{L-1} \pi \mathbf{x})) where L is the number of frequency bands. 2. SH-MLP (F{SH}): Takes \gamma(\mathbf{x}) as input. It consists of L hidden layers with ReLU activations and skip connections from the input to every 4th layer. Instead of outputting raw density \sigma and latent features, it outputs coefficients for spherical harmonic basis functions. 3. Appearance MLP (Fc): Takes the evaluated view-dependent features, \gamma(\mathbf{x}), and \mathbf{d} as input to compute final color \mathbf{c}. Numbered Steps: 1. Ray Sampling: Sample N points ti along the ray within bounds [tn, tf] in near-to-far order. Define intervals Ii = [ti, t{i+1}]. 2. SH Coefficient Prediction: For each sample point \mathbf{x}i, pass \gamma(\mathbf{x}i) through F{SH} to obtain SH coefficients \mathbf{w}i. 3. Anisotropic Feature Evaluation: Evaluate the SH basis functions at the query viewing direction \mathbf{d} using coefficients \mathbf{w}i to produce view-dependent density \sigmai and latent features \mathbf{f}i. This step captures anisotropy explicitly. 4. Regularization (Training Only): Decompose anisotropic elements from the predicted density and latent features. Apply a point-wise operation to penalize the energy of anisotropy in the geometry representation to prevent over-fitting and shape-radiance ambiguity. 5. Color Computation: Pass \mathbf{f}i, \gamma(\mathbf{x}i), and \mathbf{d} through Fc to obtain color \mathbf{c}i. 6. Volume Rendering: Compute pixel color using the discrete Riemann sum approximation: \hat{C}(\mathbf{r}) = \sum{i=0}^{N} \mathbf{c}i Ti (1 - \exp(-\sigmai (t{i+1} - ti))) where Ti = \exp\left(-\sum{j=0}^{i-1} \sigmaj (t{j+1} - tj)\right) represents occlusion. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import numpy as np def positionalencoding(x, L): """Standard positional encoding for mitigating spectral bias.""" freqbands = 2.0 np.arange(L) np.pi return np.concatenate([np.sin(x freqbands), np.cos(x freqbands)], axis=-1) def shbasis(direction, degree): """Computes SH basis functions for a given direction.""" d = direction / np.linalg.norm(direction) x, y, z = d basis = [] # Degree 0 basis.append(1.0 / np.sqrt(4 np.pi)) # Degree 1 if degree >= 1: invsqrt = 1.0 / np.sqrt(3 np.pi) basis.append(z invsqrt) basis.append(x invsqrt) basis.append(y invsqrt) # Degree 2 (standard compact form) if degree >= 2: invsqrt2 = 1.0 / np.sqrt(5 np.pi) basis.append((3 z2 - 1) invsqrt2) basis.append(x z invsqrt2) basis.append(y z invsqrt2) basis.append((x2 - y2) invsqrt2) basis.append(x y invsqrt2) return np.array(basis) def anisotropicnerfforward(xsamples, d, shmlp, colormlp, degree, tbounds): """Forward pass for Anisotropic Neural Representation Learning.""" N = xsamples.shape[0] L = 10 # Typical number of frequency bands # 1. Positional Encoding gammax = positionalencoding(xsamples, L) # 2. Predict SH Coefficients # shmlp outputs coefficients for density and latent features shcoeffs = shmlp(gammax) # Shape: (N, K) # 3. Evaluate Anisotropic Features shbasisvec = shbasis(d, degree) # Shape: (K,) # Project coefficients onto direction to get view-dependent values # Assuming first half of coefficients are for density, second for features K = shcoeffs.shape[1] mid = K // 2 sigma = np.dot(shcoeffs[:,:mid], shbasisvec) # Shape: (N,) features = np.dot(shcoeffs[:, mid:], shbasisvec) # Shape: (N, F) # 4. Regularization (Training Only) # Specific regularization formula not provided in sources. # lossaniso = computeanisotropypenalty(sigma, features) # 5. Color Computation colors = colormlp(features, gammax, d) # Shape: (N, 3) # 6. Volume Rendering tn, tf = tbounds t = np.linspace(tn, tf, N + 1) deltas = t[1:] - t[:-1] # Transmittance and alpha sigmadelta = sigma deltas alpha = 1.0 - np.exp(-sigmadelta) # Cumulative transmittance Ti transmittance = np.ones(N + 1) for i in range(1, N + 1): transmittance[i] = transmittance[i-1] (1.0 - alpha[i-1]) # Weighted sum: C(r) = sum ci Ti (1 - exp(-sigmai deltai)) weights = transmittance[:-1] alpha color = np.sum(weights[:, np.newaxis] colors, axis=0) return color Parameters: N: Number of samples on the ray within near and far bounds (tn and tf). L: Number of frequency bands for positional encoding. SH Degree: Determines the number of coefficients K = (degree + 1)^2. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Shape-Radiance Ambiguity: Training with only color reconstruction loss causes strong anisotropy and ambiguity. This is mitigated by the point-wise regularization of anisotropy energy. Uses reference images to guide rendering, focusing on appearance consistency across views. Ref-NeRF Uses a convex combination of colors for decoding, ensuring physical plausibility. Convex Combination Color Decoder Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Eliminates directional ambiguity; improves reconstruction quality for anisotropic materials; plug-and-play with various NeRF frameworks. Limitations: Requires regularization to prevent over-fitting of anisotropy; computational cost of SH evaluation. When to Use: Scenes with complex lighting, reflections, or anisotropic materials where standard isotropic NeRF fails. When Not to Use: Simple scenes with diffuse materials where isotropic representation is sufficient. Anisotropic Neural Representation Learning was proposed to address the limitations of standard NeRF in handling directional ambiguity. It builds on the principle of decoupling view-independent geometry from view-dependent lighting [Parent]. The method was introduced in "Improving Neural Volume Rendering via Learning View-Dependent Integral Approximation". name: Ref-NeRF
head: Reflective Neural Radiance Fields, Structured View-Dependent Appearance for Neural Radiance Fields
body: Ref-NeRF is a neural radiance field method that improves the representation of specular reflections by replacing NeRF’s parameterization of view-dependent outgoing radiance with a representation of reflected radiance, structured using spatially-varying scene properties. It builds on Specific Model Architectures by decoupling view-independent geometric/material features from view-dependent lighting effects, specifically targeting the failure of standard NeRF to accurately capture glossy surfaces. Unlike its siblings, Ref-NeRF explicitly separates outgoing radiance into diffuse and specular components and reparameterizes the directional input using the reflection of the viewing vector about the local normal vector, enabling smoother interpolation of reflected radiance across scenes with varying materials. Ref-NeRF modifies the canonical NeRF architecture by introducing a directionless density MLP and a structured directional MLP that outputs physical material properties rather than raw color. The method relies on the assumption that the reflected radiance function is smoother than the raw outgoing radiance when parameterized by the reflection direction, allowing the network to better share appearance information between nearby points. Inputs: 3D spatial coordinate \mathbf{x} \in \mathbb{R}^3. Viewing direction \mathbf{d} \in \mathbb{R}^3 (unit vector). Ground truth RGB image I and camera parameters for training. Outputs: Volume density \sigma. Diffuse color \mathbf{c}d. Tint color \mathbf{s} (specular intensity modulator). Specular color \mathbf{c}s. Material roughness \rho. Surface normal \mathbf{n}'. Bottleneck feature vector \mathbf{b} \in \mathbb{R}^{128}. The implementation uses two coupled Multi-Layer Perceptrons (MLPs): a Spatial MLP (F{spatial}) and a Directional MLP (F{directional}). 1. Spatial MLP (F{spatial}): Input: Positional encoding \gamma(\mathbf{x}). Architecture: L hidden layers with ReLU activations and skip connections from the input to every 4th layer. Output: A tuple (\sigma, \mathbf{c}d, \mathbf{s}, \mathbf{b}, \rho, \mathbf{n}'). Fields: \sigma: Scalar density. \mathbf{c}d: RGB diffuse color. \mathbf{s}: RGB tint color. \mathbf{b}: 128-dimensional bottleneck feature vector. \rho: Scalar roughness. \mathbf{n}': 3D normal vector. 2. Directional MLP (F{directional}): Input: Bottleneck vector \mathbf{b}, Integrated Directional Encoding (IDE) of the reflection direction, and Fresnel term. Output: Specular color \mathbf{c}s (RGB). 1. Positional Encoding: Compute the positional encoding for the spatial coordinate \mathbf{x}: \gamma(\mathbf{x}) = (\sin(2^0 \pi \mathbf{x}), \cos(2^0 \pi \mathbf{x}), \dots, \sin(2^{L-1} \pi \mathbf{x}), \cos(2^{L-1} \pi \mathbf{x})) where L is the number of frequency bands. 2. Spatial Feature Prediction: Pass \gamma(\mathbf{x}) through the Spatial MLP to predict density, material properties, and features: (\sigma, \mathbf{c}d, \mathbf{s}, \mathbf{b}, \rho, \mathbf{n}') = F{spatial}(\gamma(\mathbf{x})). 3. Normal Normalization: Normalize the predicted normal vector to obtain the unit normal \mathbf{n}: \mathbf{n} = \frac{\mathbf{n}'}{\|\mathbf{n}'\|} (Standard normalization required for reflection calculation). 4. Reflection Direction Calculation: Compute the reflection direction \mathbf{r} of the viewing direction \mathbf{d} about the normal \mathbf{n}: \mathbf{r} = 2(\mathbf{n} \cdot \mathbf{d})\mathbf{n} - \mathbf{d}. This reparameterization ensures that the reflected radiance function remains smooth despite variations in surface orientation. 5. Integrated Directional Encoding (IDE): Compute the IDE for the reflection direction \mathbf{r} and roughness \rho. The IDE encodes the distribution of reflection directions towards the environment using a closed-form solution of spherical harmonics convolved with the von Mises-Fisher (vMF) distribution. \text{IDE} = \text{SphericalHarmonics} \otimes \text{vMF}(\mathbf{r}, \rho). The vMF distribution is centered at \mathbf{r} with bandwidth determined by \rho. 6. Fresnel Term Calculation: Compute the Fresnel term to account for viewing angle effects on reflection strength. The directional MLP takes the dot product of \mathbf{n}' and \mathbf{d} as input to account for Fresnel effects: F = \text{Fresnel}(\mathbf{n}' \cdot \mathbf{d}). 7. Specular Color Prediction: Pass the bottleneck vector \mathbf{b}, the IDE, and the Fresnel term through the Directional MLP to predict the specular color: \mathbf{c}s = F{directional}(\mathbf{b}, \text{IDE}, F). 8. Final Color Composition: Combine the diffuse color \mathbf{c}d, the tint color \mathbf{s}, and the specular color \mathbf{c}s using element-wise multiplication and a predefined tone mapping function \gamma{tone}: \mathbf{c} = \gamma{tone}(\mathbf{c}d + \mathbf{s} \odot \mathbf{c}s) where \odot denotes element-wise multiplication. The function \gamma{tone} is a predefined tone mapping function. 9. Volume Rendering: Render the pixel color C(\mathbf{r}) using standard volumetric rendering with the predicted density \sigma and color \mathbf{c}: C(\mathbf{r}) = \sum{i=1}^N Ti \alphai \mathbf{c}i, \quad \text{where } \alphai = 1 - \exp(-\sigmai \deltai), \quad Ti = \prod{j=1}^{i-1} (1 - \alphaj) where \deltai is the distance between samples. Bottleneck dimension: 128. Frequency bands (L): Not given in the sources. Tone mapping function (\gamma{tone}): Predefined, but specific formula not given in the sources. Noisy Normals: Standard NeRF geometry is "foggy" and not tightly concentrated at surfaces, leading to noisy normal vectors that are unsuitable for computing accurate reflection directions. Ref-NeRF addresses this with a novel regularizer on volume density to concentrate density around surfaces and improve normal quality. Specularity on Non-Specular Materials: Ref-NeRF may erroneously assign specularity to non-specular materials (e.g., bread slices in the Toaster object), indicating incomplete comprehension of geometric properties in some cases. Reflection Direction Sensitivity: The accuracy of the reflection direction \mathbf{r} is highly dependent on the accuracy of the predicted normal \mathbf{n}. Errors in \mathbf{n} lead to incorrect reflection directions and thus incorrect specular highlights. Time Complexity: Training time is longer than standard NeRF due to the additional MLP outputs and the computation of IDE and Fresnel terms. Comparison with NRFF shows Ref-NeRF takes approximately 2.44 days for the Ball object and 2.31 days for the Toaster object (vs 2.13 and 1.78 days for NRFF). Memory Complexity: Increased memory usage due to the 128-dimensional bottleneck vector and additional output channels (diffuse, specular, roughness, normal) from the Spatial MLP. Performance: On the evaluated dataset, Ref-NeRF achieves 35.6 dB PSNR and 11.5 degrees Mean Angular Error (MAE) for normals, compared to Mip-NeRF's 30.3 dB PSNR and 59.5 degrees MAE. Strengths: Significantly improves the realism and accuracy of specular reflections; provides interpretable internal representation of outgoing radiance useful for scene editing. Limitations: Struggles with non-specular materials where specularity is incorrectly assigned; relies on accurate normal estimation which is challenging in volumetric representations. When to use: When accurate modeling of glossy/reflective surfaces is required. When not to use: For scenes with predominantly matte materials where the overhead is unjustified, or when normal accuracy is critical but the geometry is highly complex and noisy. Ref-NeRF was introduced by Dor Verbin, Peter Hedman, Ben Mildenhall, Todd Zickler, Jonathan T. Barron, and Pratul P. Srinivasan from Harvard University and Google Research. It was published as arXiv:2112.03907v1 on December 7, 2021. The method was built upon Mip-NeRF to better model reflective surfaces by parameterizing NeRF radiance based on the reflection of the viewing direction about the local normal vector. It addresses the limitation of NeRF-based techniques in accurately capturing glossy surfaces by reparameterizing the directional MLP and introducing a regularizer for volume density. name: Convex Combination Color Decoder
head: Color Decoder
body: The Convex Combination Color Decoder decomposes view-dependent appearance into a view-dependent base component and a glossy reflection component, weighted by a geometry-derived coefficient. It addresses the modeling of specular highlights and environment reflections in neural radiance fields by feeding reflection features into the color decoder at every sample point along a ray, rather than only in image space, which aids convergence when geometry is initially fuzzy. It differs from standard NeRF color decoders by explicitly separating the view-dependent term from a reflection term that utilizes a pre-computed reflection feature \bar{\mathbf{f}}. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: 3D position \mathbf{x}^{(i)}, viewing direction \mathbf{d}, normal \mathbf{n}^{(i)}, bottleneck feature \mathbf{b}^{(i)}, dot product \mathbf{d} \cdot \mathbf{n}^{(i)}, reflected direction \mathbf{d}', and reflection feature \bar{\mathbf{f}}. Outputs: Final color \mathbf{c}(\mathbf{x}^{(i)}, \mathbf{d}) \in \mathbb{R}^3. Data Structures: MLPs g and h: Small Multi-Layer Perceptrons used to compute the view-dependent and reflection color components, respectively. Geometry Encoder: Outputs the raw weighting coefficient and geometry features, which are processed to produce \beta^{(i)} and \mathbf{b}^{(i)}. Reflection Feature \bar{\mathbf{f}}: A feature vector computed by the geometry encoder, fed into the color decoder at every sample point. Steps: 1. Compute Weighting Coefficient: Pass the raw output from the geometry encoder through a sigmoid function to produce \beta^{(i)} \in [0, 1]. 2. Compute Bottleneck Feature: Apply a small MLP to the geometry features to output the bottleneck vector \mathbf{b}^{(i)}. 3. Compute View-Dependent Color Component: Calculate \mathbf{c}v using MLP g with inputs \mathbf{x}^{(i)}, \mathbf{b}^{(i)}, \mathbf{n}^{(i)}, and \mathbf{d}: \mathbf{c}v(\mathbf{x}^{(i)}, \mathbf{d}) = g(\mathbf{x}^{(i)}, \mathbf{b}^{(i)}, \mathbf{n}^{(i)}, \mathbf{d}) 4. Compute Reflection Color Component: Calculate \mathbf{c}r using MLP h with inputs \mathbf{x}^{(i)}, \mathbf{b}^{(i)}, \mathbf{n}^{(i)}, \mathbf{d} \cdot \mathbf{n}^{(i)}, reflected direction \mathbf{d}', and reflection feature \bar{\mathbf{f}}: \mathbf{c}r(\mathbf{x}^{(i)}, \mathbf{d}') = h(\mathbf{x}^{(i)}, \mathbf{b}^{(i)}, \mathbf{n}^{(i)}, \mathbf{d} \cdot \mathbf{n}^{(i)}, \mathbf{d}', \bar{\mathbf{f}}) 5. Compute Final Color: Combine the components using the convex combination: \mathbf{c}(\mathbf{x}^{(i)}, \mathbf{d}) = \beta^{(i)} \mathbf{c}v(\mathbf{x}^{(i)}, \mathbf{d}) + (1 - \beta^{(i)}) \mathbf{c}r(\mathbf{x}^{(i)}, \mathbf{d}') Parameters: \beta^{(i)}: Weighting coefficient, output by geometry encoder + sigmoid. Typical value range [0, 1]. MLPs g, h: Small networks. Sizes not given in the sources. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Fuzzy Geometry: Early in optimization, geometry is fuzzy. Feeding \bar{\mathbf{f}} into the color decoder at every sample (3D space) rather than just in image space is crucial for convergence. Distant Content: Properly downweighting distant content is crucial to prevent aliasing in reflections of distant illumination. A technique to handle inconsistent lighting, transient objects, or weather variations by disentangling scene content from appearance factors, enabling robust reconstruction from unstructured image collections. It introduces learnable per-image latent appearance codes as input to the network alongside samples to explain per-view variability such as lighting, tone, or transient content. This allows the core geometry to be reconstructed while residual factors are absorbed by the appearance codes, enabling rendering with varying lighting/weather by exploring the latent spaces. Introduced in NeRF-in-the-wild, with extensions including GRAF, HaNeRF, and RawNeRF. It is chosen when scene appearance varies significantly across captures due to environmental factors rather than geometry, contrasting with siblings that focus on fixed view-dependent shading or anisotropic material modeling. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Improves convergence when geometry is fuzzy by utilizing reflection features at every sample point. Explicitly models glossy appearance and reflections. Limitations: Requires computation of reflection features \bar{\mathbf{f}} and reflected directions \mathbf{d}'. Sensitive to aliasing in distant reflections if distant content is not properly downweighted. When to use: When modeling glossy/specular appearance and reflections is important. The Convex Combination Color Decoder was introduced in NeRF-Casting. It is inspired by UniSDF. It builds on the specific model architectures described in Appearance and Lighting Decomposition. name: Unified Decompositional and Compositional NeRF Framework
head: Unified Decompositional and Compositional NeRF, Joint Framework for Editable Novel View Synthesis
body: This method solves the problem of disentangling foreground objects from background environments in a radiance field to enable editable novel view synthesis, where foreground objects can be removed or replaced without corrupting the background. It sets itself apart from sibling methods like Ref-NeRF by explicitly modeling separate background and object radiance fields that are composited via a differentiable one-hot gating mechanism, rather than relying solely on view-dependent lighting models or anisotropic scattering. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Camera poses, ray directions \mathbf{d}, and 3D coordinates \mathbf{x} sampled along rays. Output: Composited pixel color C(\mathbf{r}) and decomposed background/object radiance fields. Data Structures: The network consists of a shared backbone and three specific heads. 1. Shared Backbone: A 4-layer Multi-Layer Perceptron (MLP). Input: Positional encoded coordinates \gamma(\mathbf{x}). Output: Generic implicit scene feature vector \mathbf{f}{scene} \in \mathbb{R}^{256}. 2. Heads: Three separate 3-layer MLPs (Background Head, Object Head, Guidance Head). Each head takes \mathbf{f}{scene} as input. Each head outputs density \sigma and color \mathbf{c} for its respective field. 3. Positional Encoding: Coordinates \mathbf{x}: 10 frequency levels. Directions \mathbf{d}: 4 frequency levels. Numbered Steps: 1. Feature Extraction: For a query point \mathbf{x} and direction \mathbf{d}, compute positional encodings \gamma(\mathbf{x}) and \gamma(\mathbf{d}). Pass \gamma(\mathbf{x}) through the Shared Backbone to obtain the latent feature \mathbf{f}{scene}: \mathbf{f}{scene} = \text{Backbone}(\gamma(\mathbf{x})) 2. Radiance Field Prediction: Pass \mathbf{f}{scene} through the three heads to predict parameters for the background (b), object (o), and guidance (g) fields: (\sigmab, \mathbf{c}b) = \text{Head}b(\mathbf{f}{scene}) (\sigmao, \mathbf{c}o) = \text{Head}o(\mathbf{f}{scene}) (\sigmag, \mathbf{c}g) = \text{Head}g(\mathbf{f}{scene}) 3. One-Hot Density Regularization (Background): To constrain uncertain regions in the background, apply a regularization term that encourages the background density to be sparse or one-hot in nature, preventing background leakage into object regions. 4. Gumbel-Softmax Composition (Coarse Stage): To composite the background and object fields, compute one-hot weights using Gumbel-Softmax activation. Let wb and wo be the weights for background and object. wb, wo = \text{GumbelSoftmax}(\text{logits}(\sigmab, \sigmao)) The composited density \sigma and color \mathbf{c} for the coarse stage are: \sigma = wb \sigmab + wo \sigmao \mathbf{c} = wb \mathbf{c}b + wo \mathbf{c}o Note: Directly adding \sigmab and \sigmao without these weights causes the background to collapse to black. 5. Residual Radiance Composition (Fine Stage): Use the Guidance Head's radiance field (\sigmag, \mathbf{c}g) to provide coarse sampling guidance. In the fine stage, the guidance field is merged as residual information. The exact residual merge formula is not given in the sources. 6. 2D In-painting Pseudo Supervision: Apply pseudo-supervision signals to the background radiance field. This involves masking out foreground objects in the input images and using the remaining pixels to supervise the background head, ensuring the background can extrapolate correctly into regions occupied by foreground objects. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import torch import torch.nn as nn import torch.nn.functional as F class SharedBackbone(nn.Module): def init(self): super().init() # 4-layer MLP, output dim 256 self.layers = nn.Sequential( nn.Linear(20, 256), # 10 levels 2 (sin/cos) nn.ReLU(), nn.Linear(256, 256), nn.ReLU(), nn.Linear(256, 256), nn.ReLU(), nn.Linear(256, 256)) def forward(self, x): return self.layers(x) class Head(nn.Module): def init(self): super().init() # 3-layer MLP ending with color and density self.layers = nn.Sequential( nn.Linear(256, 256), nn.ReLU(), nn.Linear(256, 256), nn.ReLU(), nn.Linear(256, 3 + 1) # 3 for color, 1 for density) def forward(self, fscene): out = self.layers(fscene) c = torch.sigmoid(out[:,:3]) sigma = torch.relu(out[:, 3:]) return sigma, c def positionalencoding(x, levels=10): # x shape: [N, 3] # Output shape: [N, 2levels] freqbands = 2.0 torch.linspace(0, levels - 1, levels).to(x.device) x = x.unsqueeze(-1) freqbands x = torch.cat([torch.sin(x), torch.cos(x)], dim=-1) return x def gumbelsoftmax(logits, tau=1.0, hard=False): # Standard Gumbel-Softmax implementation # logits: [N, 2] for background and object gumbels = (-torch.emptylike(logits).exponential().log() + torch.log(torch.emptylike(logits).exponential() + 1e-10)) gumbels = (logits + gumbels) / tau ysoft = F.softmax(gumbels, dim=-1) if hard: index = ysoft.max(dim=-1, keepdim=True)[1] yhard = torch.zeroslike(logits).scatter(-1, index, 1.0) ret = yhard - ysoft.detach() + ysoft else: ret = ysoft return ret class UnifiedNeRF(nn.Module): def init(self): super().init() self.backbone = SharedBackbone() self.headbg = Head() self.headobj = Head() self.headguid = Head() def forward(self, x, d): # x: [N, 3], d: [N, 3] # 1. Positional Encoding: 10 levels for coords, 4 for directions gammax = positionalencoding(x, levels=10) # gammad = positionalencoding(d, levels=4) # Directions used for ray sampling, not passed to heads per # 2. Shared Backbone takes gamma(x) fscene = self.backbone(gammax) # 3. Heads take fscene sigmabg, cbg = self.headbg(fscene) sigmaobj, cobj = self.headobj(fscene) sigmaguid, cguid = self.headguid(fscene) # 4. Gumbel-Softmax Composition (Coarse Stage) logits = torch.stack([sigmabg, sigmaobj], dim=-1) weights = gumbelsoftmax(logits, tau=1.0) # [N, 2] wbg = weights[:, 0].unsqueeze(-1) wobj = weights[:, 1].unsqueeze(-1) sigmacomp = wbg sigmabg + wobj sigmaobj ccomp = wbg cbg + wobj cobj # 5. Residual Composition (Fine Stage) # The guidance field is used for coarse sampling and merged as residual in fine stage. # The exact residual merge formula is not given in the sources. # sigmafine = sigmacomp + sigmaguid # Example merge; implementation varies # cfine = ccomp + cguid return { 'sigma': sigmacomp, 'c': ccomp, 'sigmafine': sigmacomp, 'cfine': ccomp, 'sigmabg': sigmabg, 'cbg': cbg, 'sigmaobj': sigmaobj, 'cobj': cobj, 'sigmaguid': sigmaguid, 'cguid': cguid } Parameters: Backbone Layers: 4. Head Layers: 3 per head. Feature Dimension: 256. Positional Encoding Levels: 10 for coordinates, 4 for directions. Training: End-to-end from scratch, no voxel or geometric initialization. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Background Collapse: Directly adding local object/background radiance fields without Gumbel-Softmax weights causes the background radiance field to collapse to all black. Extrapolation Failure: Disabling 2D in-painting pseudo supervision results in significantly downgraded extrapolation capability in 3D regions occupied by foreground objects. Quality Degradation: Removing residual radiance composition degrades both overall qualitative metrics and background decomposition quality. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Measured Performance: On the ScanNet dataset, the method achieves PSNR 26.1349, SSIM 0.8249, and LPIPS 0.3951. On the ToyDesk dataset, it achieves PSNR 23.1435, SSIM 0.4711, and LPIPS 0.4691. Strengths: Enables explicit editing of foreground objects; disentangles background from foreground effectively. Limitations: Not given in the sources. When to use: Not given in the sources. When not to use: Not given in the sources. The method was introduced in "Learning Unified Decompositional and Compositional NeRF for Editable Novel View Synthesis". The framework is trained end-to-end from scratch, explicitly avoiding voxel feature initialization and geometric initialization. It is evaluated on the ScanNet and ToyDesk datasets against ObjectNeRF and ObjectSDF. name: STensoRRF
head: StensorR, tensorial able relighting radiance field for single-tensor scene representation
body: STensoRRF is a differentiable volume rendering method that represents a 3D scene using a single 4D tensor to enable high-quality novel view synthesis and relighting. It distinguishes itself from standard NeRF architectures by replacing the multi-network feature grid with a decomposed single tensor and explicitly estimating a BRDF value per point to facilitate relighting via spherical Gaussian environment maps. Unlike sibling methods that rely on complex geometric priors or multiple voxel meshes, STensoRRF achieves a 50% faster convergence rate and 1.5x faster rendering speed by combining tensor decomposition with a simplified reflectance equation. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: A set of multi-view images of a scene with unknown illumination; camera poses (\mathbf{o}, \mathbf{d}). Outputs: Rendered pixel colors for new viewpoints; relit images under new illumination conditions; surface normals and BRDF values for geometry. Data Structures: The core representation is a single 4D tensor \mathcal{G}S. Dimensions: The first three dimensions correspond to spatial coordinates (x, y, z). The fourth dimension is the feature vector. Feature Vector Layout: The first element is the volume density \sigma. The remaining elements are appearance features \mathbf{f}. Decomposition: To manage memory and accelerate optimization, the 4D tensor is decomposed into low-rank components using Vector-Matrix (VM) decomposition. This allows efficient retrieval of \sigma and \mathbf{f} given a 3D coordinate. Decoders: Distinct Multi-Layer Perceptrons (MLPs) decode the appearance features \mathbf{f} retrieved from the tensor. 1. Color Network: Decodes \mathbf{f} into view-dependent color \mathbf{c}. 2. Normal Network: Decodes \mathbf{f} into surface normal \mathbf{n}. 3. BRDF Decoder: Decodes \mathbf{f} into a "BRDF value" \beta, which represents the amount of light reflected from the point. Lighting Model: The incident light field (environment map) is simulated using 32 Spherical Gaussians (SGs). The reflected light integral is approximated by combining the BRDF value, the normal vector, and the SG-based lighting field. Rendering and Training Steps: 1. Ray Sampling: For a camera ray \mathbf{r}(t) = \mathbf{o} + t\mathbf{d}, sample N points \mathbf{x}i along the ray. 2. Feature Retrieval: For each \mathbf{x}i, query the decomposed 4D tensor to obtain density \sigmai and appearance features \mathbf{f}i. 3. Decoding: Compute color \mathbf{c}i from \mathbf{f}i. Compute normal \mathbf{n}i from \mathbf{f}i. Compute BRDF value \betai from \mathbf{f}i. 4. Volume Rendering (Training): Render the pixel color C(\mathbf{r}) using standard volumetric rendering to supervise the tensor during initial training: C(\mathbf{r}) = \sum{i=1}^N Ti \alphai \mathbf{c}i, \quad \alphai = 1 - \exp(-\sigmai \deltai), \quad Ti = \prod{j=1}^{i-1} (1 - \alphaj) where \deltai is the distance between samples. 5. Surface Point Estimation: After a certain number of iterations, identify surface points on the ray (e.g., using the density peak or transmittance threshold). 6. Relighting Rendering: For the identified surface points, compute the reflected color using the BRDF value, normal, and SG environment map. This result is used to jointly optimize the tensor field alongside the standard volume rendering loss. 7. Optimization: Iteratively update the 4D tensor parameters by minimizing the difference between rendered pixel colors and real image pixel values. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def stensorrrfforward(rayorigin, raydirection, tnear, tfar, N, sglighting): # 1. Sample points along the ray tvalues = [tnear + i (tfar - tnear) / N for i in range(N)] points = [rayorigin + t raydirection for t in tvalues] densities = [] colors = [] normals = [] brdfvalues = [] for p in points: # 2. Retrieve features from the 4D tensor via VM decomposition sigma, features = vmdecomposelookup(p) # 3. Decode features using distinct MLPs c = colornetwork(features) n = normalnetwork(features) beta = brdfdecoder(features) densities.append(sigma) colors.append(c) normals.append(n) brdfvalues.append(beta) # 4. Volume Rendering for training supervision deltas = [] for i in range(N): if i < N - 1: deltas.append(tvalues[i+1] - tvalues[i]) else: deltas.append(tfar - tvalues[i]) alphas = [1.0 - math.exp(-sigma delta) for sigma, delta in zip(densities, deltas)] transmittances = [] T = 1.0 for a in alphas: transmittances.append(T) T = (1.0 - a) renderedcolor = sum(Ti a c for Ti, a, c in zip(transmittances, alphas, colors)) # 5. Surface Point Estimation surfaceidx = max(range(len(densities)), key=lambda i: densities[i]) if surfaceidx is not None: surfacenormal = normals[surfaceidx] surfacebrdf = brdfvalues[surfaceidx] # 6. Relighting Calculation relitcolor = computereflectedlight(surfacebrdf, surfacenormal, sglighting) return renderedcolor, { 'normal': surfacenormal, 'brdfvalue': surfacebrdf, 'relitcolor': relitcolor, 'depth': tvalues[surfaceidx] } else: return renderedcolor, None def vmdecomposelookup(point): # Reconstructs tensor value from low-rank VM factors return 0.0, [0.0] def colornetwork(features): # MLP decoding color from appearance features return [0.0, 0.0, 0.0] def normalnetwork(features): # MLP decoding normal from appearance features return [0.0, 0.0, 0.0] def brdfdecoder(features): # MLP decoding BRDF value from appearance features return 1.0 def computereflectedlight(brdfvalue, normal, sglighting): # Approximates the reflected light integral using Spherical Gaussians reflectedlight = [0.0, 0.0, 0.0] for sg in sglighting: dotprod = sum(n d for n, d in zip(normal, sg['direction'])) weight = max(0.0, dotprod) for c in range(3): reflectedlight[c] += sg['intensity'][c] brdfvalue weight return reflectedlight Parameters: Spherical Gaussians: 32 SGs are used to fit the environment map. Tensor Dimensions: The tensor is 4-dimensional (3 spatial + 1 feature). Grid resolution not given in the sources. Decomposition Rank: Not given in the sources. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Surface Estimation: The method relies on estimating surface points after a certain number of iterations to decode BRDF and normals. If the density field is noisy or under-converged, surface point identification may fail. BRDF Approximation: The "BRDF value" is a network output approximating reflection properties, not a full analytical BRDF. Convergence: 50% faster convergence rate compared to existing relighting radiation field models. Speed: Rendering and relighting speed is approximately 1.5x faster than previous state-of-the-art models. Memory: Uses a single 4D tensor with VM decomposition, reducing memory overhead compared to methods using multiple voxel meshes or tensors. Strengths: High-quality novel view synthesis; efficient relighting without complex geometric surface properties; fast convergence. Limitations: Relies on a simplified reflectance equation; BRDF is estimated rather than physically modeled; performance depends on the accuracy of the 32 SG environment map fit. STensoRRF (Tensorial Able Relighting Radiance Field for Single-Tensor Scene Representation) was proposed in a preprint published in January 2024. It addresses the limitations of previous radiance field methods that required multiple voxel meshes or tensors for scene representation and complex geometric priors for relighting. By leveraging tensor decomposition and a single 4D tensor, it aims to accelerate training and enable efficient relighting by directly estimating reflection properties (BRDF value) from appearance features. name: Ced-NeRF
body: Ced-NeRF is a compact and efficient method for modeling dynamic neural radiance fields that utilizes a grid-based hybrid representation and a canonical space to model motion. It specifically addresses the problem of overfitting artifacts, such as floaters and noisy geometry, which commonly occur in hybrid representations of dynamic scenes due to fast convergence before accurate motion prediction is achieved. It distinguishes itself from siblings like AdaNeRF and Sparse and Efficient Representations by employing a high-resolution grid for rapid convergence while avoiding separated fields or models that increase training difficulty and slow rendering. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: A set of training images with known camera poses and timestamps t. For rendering, a camera ray \mathbf{r} = \mathbf{o} + s\mathbf{d} defined by origin \mathbf{o}, direction \mathbf{d}, and a specific timestamp t. Outputs: A predicted pixel color \bar{C}(\mathbf{r}). Data Structures: Grid G: A 3D grid of learnable feature vectors. Deformation Network \Phid: A neural network mapping encoded coordinates and timestamp to a deformation vector. Radiance Field Network \Phir: A neural network predicting density \sigma and color \mathbf{c} from grid features and direction. Position Encoding: Ced-NeRF uses two types of encoding: 1. Frequency Encoding \gamma(\cdot): Applied to spatial coordinates \mathbf{x} and viewing direction \mathbf{d} to capture high-frequency details and mitigate spectral bias. \gamma(\mathbf{p}) = (\sin(2^0 \pi \mathbf{p}), \cos(2^0 \pi \mathbf{p}), \dots, \sin(2^{L-1} \pi \mathbf{p}), \cos(2^{L-1} \pi \mathbf{p})) where L is the number of frequency bands. 2. Grid Encoding \gamma{grid}(\cdot): Applied to spatial coordinates \mathbf{x}' to retrieve features from the grid G. This involves determining the closest grid cells and interpolating their features. For example, Instant-NGP selects eight grid cells for linear interpolation. Algorithm Steps: 1. Sample Points: For a camera ray \mathbf{r} = \mathbf{o} + s\mathbf{d}, sample N points \mathbf{r}i = \mathbf{o} + si \mathbf{d} along the ray. 2. Encode Input: Encode the spatial coordinate \mathbf{x}i and timestamp t using frequency encoding \gamma(\cdot). 3. Deform Coordinate: Pass the encoded \mathbf{x}i and t into the deformation network \Phid to predict a deformation vector. Add this to the original coordinate to get the canonical space coordinate \mathbf{x}'i: \mathbf{x}'i = \Phid(\gamma(\mathbf{x}i), \gamma(t)) + \mathbf{x}i. 4. Grid Feature Retrieval: Encode the deformed coordinate \mathbf{x}'i using grid encoding \gamma{grid}(\cdot) to retrieve feature vectors from the grid G. 5. Encode Direction: Encode the viewing direction \mathbf{d} using frequency encoding \gamma(\cdot). 6. Predict Radiance: Pass the grid features (from \mathbf{x}'i) and direction features (from \mathbf{d}) into the radiance field network \Phir to predict density \sigmai and color \mathbf{c}i. 7. Volume Rendering: Compute the final color \bar{C}(\mathbf{r}) using volumetric rendering: \bar{C}(\mathbf{r}) = \sum{i=1}^{N} Ti (1 - \exp(-\sigmai \deltai)) \mathbf{c}i where \deltai is the distance between samples si and s{i+1}, and Ti is the accumulated transmittance: Ti = \prod{j=1}^{i-1} \exp(-\sigmaj \deltaj). Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def cednerfrender(rayorigin, raydirection, timestamp, grid, deformationnet, radiancenet, numsamples, near, far): """ Renders a single ray using the Ced-NeRF method. Args: rayorigin: 3D vector (o) raydirection: 3D vector (d) timestamp: float (t) grid: 3D grid of features deformationnet: Neural network Phid radiancenet: Neural network Phir numsamples: int N near: float, near clipping plane far: float, far clipping plane Returns: predictedcolor: 3D vector """ # 1. Sample points along the ray uniformly samples = [near + i (far - near) / (numsamples - 1) for i in range(numsamples)] predictedcolor = [0.0, 0.0, 0.0] accumulatedtransmittance = 1.0 for i in range(numsamples): # 2. Get spatial coordinate xi xi = rayorigin + samples[i] raydirection # 3. Encode xi and t encx = frequencyencode(xi) enct = frequencyencode(timestamp) # 4. Deform coordinate to canonical space x'i deformation = deformationnet(encx, enct) xprimei = xi + deformation # 5. Retrieve grid features for x'i gridfeatures = gridencode(xprimei, grid) # 6. Encode viewing direction d encd = frequencyencode(raydirection) # 7. Predict density and color sigmai, colori = radiancenet(gridfeatures, encd) # 8. Compute deltai and alphai if i < numsamples - 1: deltai = samples[i+1] - samples[i] else: deltai = 0.0 alphai = 1.0 - exp(-sigmai deltai) # Contribution: Ti alphai ci predictedcolor += accumulatedtransmittance alphai colori # Update transmittance for next sample accumulatedtransmittance = (1.0 - alphai) # Early termination optimization if accumulatedtransmittance < 1e-5: break return predictedcolor def frequencyencode(p, numbands=10): """ Standard positional encoding for NeRF. """ encoded = [p] for i in range(numbands): freq = 2i pi encoded.append(sin(freq p)) encoded.append(cos(freq p)) return encoded def gridencode(xprime, grid): """ Retrieves features from grid G at xprime via tri-linear interpolation. Implementation detail: Find 8 closest grid cells and interpolate. """ ix, iy, iz = floor(xprime) fx, fy, fz = xprime - [ix, iy, iz] f000 = grid[ix, iy, iz] f100 = grid[ix+1, iy, iz] f010 = grid[ix, iy+1, iz] f110 = grid[ix+1, iy+1, iz] f001 = grid[ix, iy, iz+1] f101 = grid[ix+1, iy, iz+1] f011 = grid[ix, iy+1, iz+1] f111 = grid[ix+1, iy+1, iz+1] c00 = lerp(f000, f100, fx) c01 = lerp(f010, f110, fx) c10 = lerp(f001, f101, fx) c11 = lerp(f011, f111, fx) d0 = lerp(c00, c01, fy) d1 = lerp(c10, c11, fy) return lerp(d0, d1, fz) def lerp(a, b, t): return a + t (b - a) Parameters: Grid Cells: The grid resolution is not explicitly given, but the method relies on a "high-resolution grid" for fast convergence. Interpolation: Uses linear interpolation from the 8 closest grid cells to the coordinate. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Overfitting: Hybrid representations for dynamic scenes are prone to overfitting due to fast convergence before accurate motion prediction, leading to artifacts like floaters and noisy geometry on novel views. Ced-NeRF aims to mitigate this through its compact design. Time Complexity: The method achieves fast rendering speeds and rapid convergence (e.g., training in 4 minutes on HyperNeRF scenes) compared to other dynamic NeRF methods. This is attributed to the use of a high-resolution grid which allows for fast convergence, unlike low-resolution grids or sparse voxel grids. Memory Complexity: It is described as "compact," requiring only a small number of additional parameters to construct the hybrid representation. Strengths: Fast training and rendering speeds; high-quality rendering results; outperforms state-of-the-art methods in quality, training, and rendering speed on dynamic scene datasets. Limitations: The source notes that separated fields or models (which Ced-NeRF avoids) increase training difficulty and slow rendering, implying that Ced-NeRF's unified approach is a strength, but the specific limitations of the grid-based approach (e.g., memory usage for very high-resolution grids) are not quantified. When to use: Suitable for dynamic scene reconstruction where fast training and rendering are prioritized, and where artifacts from overfitting in hybrid representations are a concern. Ced-NeRF was proposed to address the issue of overfitting in hybrid representations for dynamic scenes. It builds upon the concept of using a deformation network \Phid to map spatial coordinates and timestamps to a canonical space, a technique previously used in methods like DNeRF. It incorporates explicit-based methods, specifically voxel grids, to accelerate training and rendering, building on the Instant-NGP approach for grid encoding. The method was presented at the AAAI Conference on Artificial Intelligence in 2024. name: Dynamic and Deformable Fields
body: This family builds on Specific Model Architectures and extends static neural radiance fields to model scenes that change over time or undergo non-rigid deformation. It solves the problem of novel-view synthesis for dynamic content by introducing a temporal or deformation dimension to the scene representation. Unlike static methods, these models map 6D inputs (position, direction) plus a time or deformation parameter to radiance properties, often using displacement fields or canonical space mappings to handle motion. All methods in this family map 3D position \mathbf{x}, viewing direction \mathbf{d}, and a temporal or deformation parameter t (or \tau) to density \sigma and color \mathbf{c} using differentiable neural networks or feature grids. Raw coordinates and time are mapped to higher-dimensional spaces using positional encoding \gamma(\cdot) to mitigate spectral bias. The radiance field is optimized by minimizing the difference between rendered pixel colors and ground truth images via differentiable volumetric rendering. NDVG is a fast optimization method for dynamic scene view synthesis that integrates voxel-grid optimization with a deformable radiance field. It replaces heavy MLP computations with fast voxel-grid feature interpolation to enable space-time view synthesis for dynamic scenes captured by a monocular camera. The method consists of a deformation module that maps 3D points from observation space to a canonical space, and a canonical module that models static geometry and density using explicit voxel grids. Unlike static scene applications where occlusion is determined solely by viewing direction, NDVG explicitly models occlusion in dynamic scenes, which is determined by both view direction and motion (time). Choose it when real-time or fast optimization for monocular dynamic capture is required. Fast Per-subject Fine-tuning is a compensation strategy used in generalizable human radiance field models to address artifacts and imperfections that persist for unseen subjects after initial multi-subject training. While the base model learns common representations across a dataset, sparse input views for a new individual often result in low-frequency textures and motion artifacts. This method treats the pre-trained generalizable network as an initialization state and performs rapid optimization of specific parameters on the new subject's data. It distinguishes itself from full retraining by freezing the feature blending network, focusing adaptation only on the deformation field and the radiance field core. Choose it when adapting a pre-trained generalizable model to a new subject with sparse views. Definition: Represents a dynamic surgical scene as a static canonical radiance field and a time-dependent displacement field to handle non-rigid deformations. Step: Preprocessing maps input coordinates and time into Fourier features using positional encoding \gamma(\cdot) before feeding to the networks. Formula: Color and occupancy at time t for point \mathbf{x} are retrieved as F\Theta(\mathbf{x} + G\Phi(\mathbf{x}, t), \mathbf{d}). Layout: The canonical field F\Theta(\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{d}) is an 8-layer MLP with parameters \Theta, mapping coordinates \mathbf{x} \in \mathbb{R}^3 and unit view directions \mathbf{d} \in \mathbb{R}^3 to RGB color \mathbf{c}(\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{d}) \in \mathbb{R}^3 and space occupancy \sigma(\mathbf{x}) \in \mathbb{R}. The displacement field G\Phi(\mathbf{x}, t) is an 8-layer MLP with parameters \Phi, mapping space-time coordinates (\mathbf{x}, t) into the displacement vector between point \mathbf{x} at time t and the corresponding point in the canonical field. Definition: A dynamic neural radiance field approach using two neural networks (static and dynamic) to model measurements from a moving color camera and C-ToF camera pair, enabling high-fidelity novel-view synthesis of dynamic scenes. Step: Blends outputs of static and dynamic networks using a position- and time-dependent blending weight b(\mathbf{x}t, \tau) predicted by the dynamic network to produce blended density \sigma^\text{blend}, radiance Ls^\text{blend}, and radiant intensity Is^\text{blend}. Formula: The RGB radiance is modeled as L{\text{RGB}}(\mathbf{x}, \boldsymbol{\omega}0, \tau) = \int{tn}^{ti} T^{\text{blend}}(\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{x}t, \tau) \sigma^{\text{blend}}(\mathbf{x}t, \tau) Ls^{\text{blend}}(\mathbf{x}t, \boldsymbol{\omega}0, \tau) dt. The ToF radiance is modeled as L{\text{ToF}}(\mathbf{x}, \boldsymbol{\omega}0, \tau) = \int{tn}^{tf} \frac{T^{\text{blend}}(\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{x}t, \tau)^2}{\|\mathbf{x} - \mathbf{x}t\|^2} \sigma^{\text{blend}}(\mathbf{x}t, \tau) Is^{\text{blend}}(\mathbf{x}t, \boldsymbol{\omega}0, \tau) W(2 \|\mathbf{x} - \mathbf{x}t\|) dt. The concept of representing dynamic scenes using neural radiance fields originated with the need to model non-rigid deformations, such as those found in surgical tissues or human motion. Early work, such as that described in, applied this to robotic surgery, representing deformable tissues as a canonical field with a time-dependent displacement field. Concurrently, other approaches like TöRF extended these concepts to integrate Time-of-Flight (ToF) data, using separate static and dynamic networks to handle moving cameras and dynamic scenes. These methods established the foundation for current dynamic NeRF architectures by demonstrating how displacement fields and canonical spaces could effectively model temporal changes. name: Neural Deformable Voxel Grid (NDVG)
body:
Neural Deformable Voxel Grid (NDVG) is a fast optimization method for dynamic scene view synthesis that integrates voxel-grid optimization with a deformable radiance field. It replaces heavy Multi-Layer Perceptron (MLP) computations with fast voxel-grid feature interpolation to enable space-time view synthesis for dynamic scenes captured by a monocular camera. Unlike static scene applications where occlusion is determined solely by viewing direction, NDVG explicitly models occlusion in dynamic scenes, which is determined by both view direction and motion (time). It achieves comparable performance to D-NeRF but trains more than 70× faster. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: A sequence of images \{It\}{t=1}^T with corresponding camera poses \{Tt\}{t=1}^T from a monocular camera. A query consists of a 3D point \mathbf{p}, viewing direction \mathbf{d}, and time instance t. Outputs: Density \sigma and color \mathbf{c} for the query, which are used to render pixel colors via volume rendering. Data Structures: The method uses a hybrid explicit-implicit representation consisting of three 3D feature grids and two light-weight MLPs. 1. Deformation Feature Grid (Gd): Layout: Tensor of shape (Nx, Ny, Nz, Nc). Content: Stores 3D dynamic features for deformation. Access: Trilinear interpolation. 2. Density Grid (G\sigma): Layout: Tensor of shape (N'x, N'y, N'z). Content: Stores density values. Access: Trilinear interpolation followed by softplus activation. 3. Color Feature Grid (Gc): Layout: Tensor of shape (H', W', D', N'c). Content: Stores view-dependent color features. Access: Trilinear interpolation. 4. Deformation MLP (F{	heta^d1}): Architecture: 4 layers, width 64. Input: Concatenation of positional encoding of \mathbf{p}, positional encoding of t, and interpolated feature \hat{\mathbf{f}}^d. Output: Deformation offset \Delta \mathbf{p} and occlusion weight \hat{w}^{occ}. 5. Canonical MLP (F{	heta^c2}): Architecture: 3 layers, width 128. Input: Concatenation of positional encoding of canonical position \mathbf{p}', viewing direction \mathbf{d}, and interpolated feature \hat{\mathbf{f}}^c. Output: Color \mathbf{c}. Parameters: Positional Encoding: Frequency 5 for position and time, 4 for direction. Canonical Time (t{can}): The reference time for the canonical space. Grid Resolutions: Coarse Stage: Deformation module 1,664k voxels; Canonical module 1,024k voxels. Color grid dimension is 3 (RGB). Fine Stage: Deformation module 190^3 voxels; Canonical module 160^3 voxels. Training Iterations: Full Resolution: 10k iterations for coarse stage, 20k for fine stage. Half Resolution: 5k iterations for coarse stage, 10k for fine stage. Optimization: Adam optimizer, 8,192 rays sampled per iteration. Algorithm Steps: 1. Deformation Query: For a query point \mathbf{p} at time t: Perform trilinear interpolation on Gd to get feature \hat{\mathbf{f}}^d = 	ext{interp}(\mathbf{p}, Gd). If t = t{can}, set \Delta \mathbf{p} = \mathbf{0} and \hat{w}^{occ} = 1. Otherwise, input \mathbf{p}, t, and \hat{\mathbf{f}}^d into F{	heta^d1} to regress \Delta \mathbf{p} and \hat{w}^{occ}. Note: \mathbf{p} and t are passed through positional encoding before entering the MLP. 2. Canonical Position: Compute the canonical position \mathbf{p}' = \mathbf{p} + \Delta \mathbf{p}. 3. Density Query: Perform trilinear interpolation on G\sigma to get density value v\sigma = 	ext{interp}(\mathbf{p}', G\sigma). Apply softplus activation: \sigma = 	ext{softplus}(v\sigma). 4. Color Query: Perform trilinear interpolation on Gc to get feature \hat{\mathbf{f}}^c = 	ext{interp}(\mathbf{p}', Gc). Input \mathbf{p}', \mathbf{d}, and \hat{\mathbf{f}}^c into F{	heta^c2} to get color \mathbf{c}. Note: \mathbf{p}' and \mathbf{d} are passed through positional encoding before entering the MLP. In the coarse stage, Gc has dimension 3, and the MLP is bypassed or simplified to directly output RGB. 5. Occlusion Filtering: Filter density and color using the occlusion mask: \sigma' = \sigma 	imes \hat{w}^{occ} and \mathbf{c}' = \mathbf{c} 	imes \hat{w}^{occ}. The occlusion mask \hat{w}^{occ} is 0 if a point is empty in observation space but occupied in canonical space, preventing artifacts where static empty points map to occupied locations. 6. Volume Rendering: Render ray color \hat{C}(\mathbf{r}) using standard volume rendering equation with filtered density \sigma' and color \mathbf{c}'. For a ray \mathbf{r} with K sampled points: \hat{C}(\mathbf{r}) = \sum{k=1}^{K} Tk \alphak \mathbf{c}'k Tk = \exp \left( -\sum{j=1}^{k-1} \sigma'j \deltaj ight), \quad \alphak = 1 - \exp(-\sigma'k \deltak) where \deltak is the distance between adjacent samples. 7. Loss Calculation: Compute total loss L as a weighted sum of components: L = L{photo} + w{ptc} L{ptc} + w{bg} L{bg} + w{d
orm} L{d
orm} + w{d	v} L{d	v} Photometric Loss: L{photo} =  rac{1}{|\mathcal{R}|} \sum{\mathbf{r} \in \mathcal{R}} \| \hat{C}(\mathbf{r}) - C(\mathbf{r}) \|2^2 where \mathcal{R} is the set of rays in a batch. Sampled Point Color Supervision (L{ptc}): Optimizes color of sampled points with top N weights contributing most to rendered color. Background Entropy Loss (L{bg}): Encourages points to concentrate on foreground or background. Deformation L1 Regularization: L{d
orm} =  rac{1}{|\mathcal{R}|} \sum{\mathbf{r} \in \mathcal{R}} \sum{i=1}^{K} \| \Delta \mathbf{p}i \|1 Regularizes deformation based on the prior that most points are static. Total Variation Loss on Deformation Grid: L{d	v} =  rac{1}{|\mathcal{V}|} \sum{\mathbf{v} \in \mathcal{V}} \sum{c \in [Nc]} \sqrt{\Deltax^2(\mathbf{v},c) + \Deltay^2(\mathbf{v},c) + \Deltaz^2(\mathbf{v},c)} where \Deltax^2(\mathbf{v},c) is the squared difference between the c-th element in voxel \mathbf{v}(i,j,k) and voxel \mathbf{v}(i+1,j,k). 8. Training Strategy: Progressive Training: Start training with images close to canonical time, then progressively add images with further time steps to reduce learning difficulty as deformation magnitude increases. Coarse-to-Fine Optimization: 1. Optimize a coarse model (no view-dependence, color grid dim 3) to roughly recover deformation and geometry. 2. Use coarse model to locate object region and filter empty space (bounding box and empty point filtering). 3. Optimize fine model with higher resolution, initialized with coarse weights. Pitfalls and Edge Cases: Occlusion Artifacts: If an empty point in observation space is static (\Delta \mathbf{p}=0) but maps to an occupied location in canonical space, it retrieves non-zero density/color, causing artifacts. This is solved by the explicit occlusion mask \hat{w}^{occ}. Inefficient 4D Grid: Directly storing offsets in a 4D feature grid (3 for \mathbf{p}, 1 for t) is inefficient. NDVG uses a 3D feature grid and a light-weight MLP to decode the feature instead. Resolution Sensitivity: Deformation is more sensitive to resolution than radiance (density and color), so the deformation module grid resolution is set higher than the canonical module. Speed: NDVG achieves comparable performance to D-NeRF using only 20 minutes for training, which is more than 70× faster than D-NeRF. Memory: Uses voxel grids which are generally more memory-efficient than large MLPs for high-resolution scenes, though grid resolution directly impacts memory usage. Strengths: Fast optimization, efficient space-time view synthesis for dynamic scenes, explicit occlusion handling for monocular input. Limitations: Performance depends on the quality of the deformation grid and MLP; may struggle with highly complex deformations if grid resolution is insufficient. When to use: When fast training of dynamic scenes from monocular video is required. When not to use: When multi-view data is available and DeVRF is preferred, or when image quality refinement via look-up tables (V4D) is prioritized over training speed. NDVG was proposed by X. Guo et al. in the paper "Neural Deformable Voxel Grid for Fast Optimization of Dynamic View Synthesis". It is based on the canonical scene framework where a deformation module maps observation space to canonical space, and volume rendering is performed in the canonical space. It builds on voxel-grid optimization techniques used in static radiance fields. Neural Deformable Voxel Grid for Fast Optimization of Dynamic View Synthesis, https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-031-26319-427, fetched 2026-10-26

name: Dynamic Neural Radiance Fields (TöRF)
head: Time-of-Flight Radiance Fields, TöRF
body: TöRF is a dynamic neural radiance field method that reconstructs dynamic scenes by optimizing a neural representation against raw Time-of-Flight (ToF) sensor measurements (phasors) and RGB images, rather than relying on data-driven priors or processed depth maps. It distinguishes itself from sibling methods like Neural Deformable Voxel Grid (NDVG) by explicitly modeling the physics of ToF imaging to handle weakly-reflecting regions and moving cameras, enabling high-fidelity novel-view synthesis from a potentially moving color camera and C-ToF camera pair. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: A set of synchronized RGB images and raw ToF phasor images (in-phase and quadrature components) captured by a moving color camera and a C-ToF camera pair. The ToF data provides phase shift and amplitude measurements. Outputs: A dynamic radiance field capable of rendering novel-view RGB images and synthetic ToF phasor images for arbitrary viewpoints and times. Data Structures: The method uses two multi-layer perceptrons (MLPs): 1. Static Network (F{\theta}^{stat}): A 5D function mapping position \mathbf{x}t and viewing direction \boldsymbol{\omega}0 to static density \sigma^{stat}, static radiance Ls^{stat}, and static radiant intensity Is^{stat}. 2. Dynamic Network (F{\theta}^{dyn}): A 6D function mapping position \mathbf{x}t, viewing direction \boldsymbol{\omega}0, and time \tau to dynamic density \sigma^{dyn}, dynamic radiance Ls^{dyn}, dynamic radiant intensity Is^{dyn}, and a blending weight b(\mathbf{x}t, \tau). Note: The dynamic network does not consume time \tau directly but uses positional encoding to mitigate spectral bias, consistent with the parent family's shared principles. Blending Mechanism: The outputs of the static and dynamic networks are blended using a position- and time-dependent weight b(\mathbf{x}t, \tau) predicted by the dynamic network. This produces the blended density \sigma^{\text{blend}}, blended radiance Ls^{\text{blend}}, and blended radiant intensity Is^{\text{blend}}. The exact blending formula is defined in the source's supplemental document, but conceptually it combines static and dynamic contributions. Rendering Formulas: The method renders two types of observations along a ray \mathbf{x} with direction \boldsymbol{\omega}0 at time \tau: 1. RGB Rendering: L{\text{RGB}}(\mathbf{x}, \boldsymbol{\omega}0, \tau) = \int{tn}^{ti} T^{\text{blend}}(\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{x}t, \tau) \sigma^{\text{blend}}(\mathbf{x}t, \tau) Ls^{\text{blend}}(\mathbf{x}t, \boldsymbol{\omega}0, \tau) dt Where T^{\text{blend}} is the accumulated transmittance. 2. ToF Rendering: L{\text{ToF}}(\mathbf{x}, \boldsymbol{\omega}0, \tau) = \int{tn}^{tf} \frac{T^{\text{blend}}(\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{x}t, \tau)^2}{\|\mathbf{x} - \mathbf{x}t\|^2} \sigma^{\text{blend}}(\mathbf{x}t, \tau) Is^{\text{blend}}(\mathbf{x}t, \boldsymbol{\omega}0, \tau) W(2 \|\mathbf{x} - \mathbf{x}t\|) dt Where W(\cdot) is the system's point spread function (PSF) or weighting function, and the term \frac{1}{\|\mathbf{x} - \mathbf{x}t\|^2} accounts for distance attenuation. The integral limits tn and tf represent the near and far clipping planes of the ray. Optimization: The networks are optimized by minimizing a loss function that compares rendered RGB and phasor outputs against ground truth inputs. The use of raw phasors allows the model to recover geometry in weakly-reflecting regions (e.g., dark objects) where processed depth maps fail, as the model falls back on triangulation cues when phasor magnitudes are small. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Weak Signals: Dark objects result in noisy depth measurements in standard ToF processing; TöRF handles this by modeling raw phasors directly. Moving Cameras: Unlike many NeRF variants that assume static cameras, TöRF supports moving camera rigs by incorporating time \tau into the dynamic network. Accuracy: Provides superior accuracy compared to NSFF [LNSW21] and space-time neural irradiance fields [XHKK21]. Data Efficiency: Reduces the requirement on the number of input views due to the strong geometric cue provided by ToF depth. Hardware Dependency: Requires a synchronized pair of a color camera and a C-ToF camera. Strengths: Handles dynamic scenes with moving cameras; robust to weakly-reflecting surfaces; does not rely on pre-processed depth maps. Limitations: Requires specialized ToF hardware; computational cost of optimizing two networks and rendering ToF physics. TöRF was introduced by Alldieck et al. in 2021. It addresses the limitations of monocular RGB NeRF methods that rely on data-driven priors for dynamic content reconstruction. By integrating raw ToF sensor measurements, it leverages the single-view geometry capability of ToF sensors to improve reconstruction quality. name: Fast Per-subject Fine-tuning
body: Fast Per-subject Fine-tuning is a compensation strategy that addresses artifacts and imperfections for unseen persons by fine-tuning specific network parameters after initial generalizable training. It treats the network optimized on a general dataset as an initialization state and performs rapid optimization on the new subject's data. It distinguishes itself from full retraining by freezing the feature blending network, focusing adaptation only on the deformation field and the generalizable neural radiance field. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Pre-trained parameters for the deformation field MLPd, generalizable radiance field \Phi, and feature blending network MLPB; sparse multi-view images for an unseen subject. Output: Adapted parameters \thetad and \theta\Phi optimized for the unseen subject's geometry and appearance. Data Structures: The model parameters are partitioned into: 1. \thetad: Parameters of the deformation field MLPd. 2. \theta\Phi: Parameters of the generalizable neural radiance field \Phi. 3. \thetaB: Parameters of the feature blending network MLPB. Steps: 1. Initialization: Load pre-trained weights \thetad, \theta\Phi, and \thetaB obtained from training on a general dataset. 2. Freeze Blending Network: Set \thetaB as non-trainable to prevent gradient updates. 3. Optimization Loop: For the unseen subject, optimize \thetad and \theta\Phi using the subject's sparse multi-view images. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def fastpersubjectfinetuning(thetad, thetaphi, thetab, unseensubjectdata): # 1. Freeze feature blending network parameters for param in thetab: param.requiresgrad = False # 2. Initialize optimizer for deformation and radiance field parameters optimizer = Optimizer([thetad, thetaphi]) # 3. Optimization loop for iteration in range(maxiterations): # Not given in the sources. optimizer.zerograd() renderedimages = render(unseensubjectdata, thetad, thetaphi, thetab) loss = computeloss(renderedimages, unseensubjectdata.gtimages) loss.backward() optimizer.step() return thetad, thetaphi, thetab class Optimizer: def init(self, params, lr): self.params = params; self.lr = lr def zerograd(self): for p in self.params: if p.requiresgrad: p.grad = None def step(self): for p in self.params: if p.requiresgrad: p.data -= self.lr p.grad def render(data, thetad, thetaphi, thetab): # Standard differentiable volumetric rendering using thetad, thetaphi, and frozen thetab return [sampleray(ray, thetad, thetaphi, thetab) for ray in data.rays] def computeloss(rendered, groundtruth): return sum((r - g)2 for r, g in zip(rendered, groundtruth)) / len(rendered) def sampleray(ray, thetad, thetaphi, thetab): # Standard ray marching and volume integration return raycolor Parameters: Learning rate: Not given in the sources. Max iterations: Not given in the sources. Edge Cases: Not given in the sources. A meta-learning approach that pretrains a NeRF parameter \thetap^ to easily adapt to unseen subjects by learning common representations from a dataset. Unlike methods that transfer gradients from the support set, it only propagates gradients from the query set to the pretrained model, as the support set is available at test time and adapted via fine-tuning. Choose this when standard meta-learning fails for view synthesis due to GPU batch limits on millions of scene coordinate gradients. Time Complexity: Significantly faster than full retraining because it only optimizes \thetad and \theta\Phi while using pre-trained weights as initialization. Memory Complexity: Requires storing gradients only for \thetad and \theta\Phi, reducing memory footprint during adaptation. Strengths: Effectively removes artifacts and recovers high-frequency details for unseen persons. Efficient adaptation to new identities. Limitations: Not given in the sources. When to use: When sparse input views cause artifacts and lack high-frequency details in generalizable models. When not to use: Not given in the sources. This method was introduced in a framework for efficiently generating human radiance fields from sparse inputs. It addresses the limitation that generalizable models may produce artifacts for specific unseen individuals due to data diversity and sparsity. The approach is inspired by image-based rendering techniques that use adjacent views to refine textures.
