name: Meta-learning Pretraining for Portrait NeRF
head: Meta-learning framework, Pretraining NeRF
body:
A meta-learning approach to pretrain a NeRF model parameter 	hetap^ that can easily adapt to capturing an unseen subject’s appearance and geometry by learning common representations (head geometry, occlusion) from a dataset of subjects. Unlike methods that transfer gradients from the support set, this method only propagates gradients learned from the query set to the pretrained model, as the support set is available at test time and its gradients are adapted via fine-tuning. It addresses the limitation where standard meta-learning algorithms for image classification perform poorly for view synthesis because each update requires gradients from millions of samples across scene coordinates and viewing directions, which do not fit into a single GPU batch. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A dataset of K subjects. For each subject m, a support set Ds (frontal view) and a query set Dq (remaining views). Output: A final pretrained model parameter 	hetap^ = 	heta{p, K-1}. Data Structures: 	heta{p, m}: Global pretrained parameter for subject m. 	heta{m, t}^: Model parameter for subject m at inner iteration t. Ds: Support set (frontal view). Dq: Query set (other views). Parameters: K: Total number of subjects in the training dataset, indexed by m = \{0, \dots, K-1\}. \alpha: Learning rate for the support set update step.  eta: Learning rate for the query set update step. Ns: Number of iterations for updating the model on the support set. Nq: Number of iterations for updating the pretrained parameter using the query set. Steps: 1. Initialize the first subject's pretrained parameter 	heta{p, -1} to random weights. 2. For each subject m from 0 to K-1: a. Initialize the model parameter 	heta{m, 0}^ from the previous subject's pretrained parameter 	heta{p, m-1}. b. Pretrain on Support Set Ds: Iteratively update 	heta{m, t}^ using gradient descent on the L2 loss between the predicted front view and the support set Ds for Ns iterations, using learning rate \alpha. c. Pretrain on Query Set Dq: Iteratively update the current subject's model parameter 	heta{m, t}^ using gradient descent on the loss between prediction and query set Dq for Nq iterations, using learning rate  eta. d. Update Global Pretrained Parameter: Simultaneously update the global pretrained parameter 	heta{p, m, t} using the same gradients computed from the query set Dq for Nq iterations, using learning rate  eta. e. Update the global pretrained parameter for the next subject: Set 	heta{p, m+1} to the final value of 	heta{p, m, t} after Nq iterations. 3. Final Pretrained Model: After visiting all K subjects, the final pretrained model is 	hetap^ = 	heta{p, K-1}. Formulas: Support Set Update (for t = 0, \dots, Ns-1): 	heta{m, t+1}^ = 	heta{m, t}^ - \alpha 
abla{	heta} L{Ds}(f{	heta{m, t}^}) where 	heta{m, 0}^ = 	heta{p, m-1}. Query Set Update (for t = 0, \dots, Nq-1): 	heta{m, t+1}^ = 	heta{m, t}^ -  eta 
abla{	heta} L{Dq}(f{	heta{m, t}^}) 	heta{p, m, t+1} = 	heta{p, m, t} -  eta 
abla{	heta} L{Dq}(f{	heta{m, t}^}) where 	heta{m, 0}^ is the parameter learned from Ds in the previous step, and 	heta{p, m, 0} = 	heta{p, m-1}. Final Pretrained Parameter Update: 	heta{p, m+1} = 	heta{p, m, Nq-1} Note that the update in (3) does not affect the update of the current subject m (i.e., (2)), but the gradients are propagated to the next training subject in subsequent iterations through the pretrained model parameter update in (4). Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def metapretrain(dataset, K, alpha, beta, Ns, Nq): # Helper: Initialize parameters to random weights def randominit(): return [0.0] PARAMSIZE # Standard initialization # Helper: NeRF forward pass predicting color and occupancy def NeRFforward(params, rays): # Standard differentiable rendering forward pass return params # Simplified representation for pseudocode # Helper: L2 loss computation def L2loss(pred, target): return sum((p - t) 2 for p, t in zip(pred, target)) / len(target) # Helper: Gradient computation def computegradient(lossfn, params): # Standard automatic differentiation return [0.0] len(params) # Step 1: Initialize first subject's pretrained parameter to random weights thetapprev = randominit() for m in range(K): thetam = thetapprev # Step 2b: Pretrain on Support Set Ds for t in range(Ns): predds = NeRFforward(thetam, dataset[m].Ds) lossds = L2loss(predds, dataset[m].Ds.targets) gradds = computegradient(lambda: L2loss(NeRFforward(thetam, dataset[m].Ds), dataset[m].Ds.targets), thetam) thetam = [thetam[i] - alpha gradds[i] for i in range(len(thetam))] # Step 2c & 2d: Pretrain on Query Set Dq thetapcurr = thetapprev for t in range(Nq): preddq = NeRFforward(thetam, dataset[m].Dq) lossdq = L2loss(preddq, dataset[m].Dq.targets) graddq = computegradient(lambda: L2loss(NeRFforward(thetam, dataset[m].Dq), dataset[m].Dq.targets), thetam) thetam = [thetam[i] - beta graddq[i] for i in range(len(thetam))] thetapcurr = [thetapcurr[i] - beta graddq[i] for i in range(len(thetapcurr))] # Step 2e: Update global pretrained parameter for the next subject thetapprev = thetapcurr # Step 3: Final Pretrained Model thetapstar = thetapprev return thetapstar Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Standard meta-learning algorithms for image classification perform poorly for view synthesis because each update requires gradients from millions of samples across scene coordinates and viewing directions, which do not fit into a single GPU batch. This method takes many more steps in a single meta-training task for convergence. The method assumes that the order of applying the gradients learned from Dq and Ds are interchangeable, similarly to the first-order approximation in the MAML algorithm. At test time, only a single frontal view of the subject s is available. First, compute the rigid transform (sm, Rm, tm) for the input subject s to map between world and canonical coordinates. Finetune the pretrained model parameter 	hetap^ by repeating the support set update iteration (Equation 1) for the input subject to obtain the optimized model parameter 	hetas^. To render novel views, sample a camera ray in 3D space, warp the ray's 3D coordinates to the canonical space using the subject's rigid transform, and feed the warped coordinate to NeRF to predict color and occupancy. The meshes are for visualization and not used in view synthesis; only the rigid transform is used. Time Complexity: The method requires iterating through K subjects, each involving Ns iterations on the support set and Nq iterations on the query set. Since each update requires gradients from millions of samples, the computational cost per iteration is high, and the method takes many more steps in a single meta-training task for convergence compared to image classification tasks. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Learns common representations (head geometry, occlusion) from a dataset of subjects, allowing for easy adaptation to unseen subjects' appearance and geometry. Only propagates gradients learned from the query set to the pretrained model, as the support set is available at test time and its gradients are adapted via fine-tuning. Limitations: Standard meta-learning algorithms for image classification perform poorly for view synthesis due to the large number of samples required for gradient computation. Requires a dataset of multiple subjects for pretraining. When to use: When there is a dataset of multiple subjects available for pretraining, and the goal is to quickly adapt to a new subject's appearance and geometry using only a single frontal view at test time. When not to use: When there is no dataset of multiple subjects available for pretraining, or when computational resources are limited due to the high cost of gradient computation per iteration. Originated in the paper "Portrait Neural Radiance Fields from a Single Image". The method is designed to address the challenge of capturing an unseen subject's appearance and geometry from a single frontal view by leveraging common representations learned from a dataset of subjects. It builds on the idea of meta-learning, where the model is trained to learn how to learn, allowing for rapid adaptation to new tasks (in this case, new subjects). The method assumes that the order of applying the gradients learned from the query set and support set are interchangeable, similarly to the first-order approximation in the MAML algorithm. Portrait Neural Radiance Fields from a Single Image, https://doi.org/10.48550/arxiv.2012.05903, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial)

name: Scene Representation and Partitioning
body: This family of methods addresses the scalability limits of single-network NeRFs by decomposing the scene into multiple, smaller representations (submodules, blocks, or fields) that are optimized and queried independently. While the parent Scene Representation and Architecture establishes the global mapping from 6D coordinates to radiance properties, these methods partition the domain to enable parallel training, reduce memory footprint, or handle dynamic content. They differ from siblings like Specific Model Architectures by focusing on the structural decomposition of the scene space rather than the internal topology of the neural network itself. MegaNeRF is a framework for training large-scale 3D scenes that support interactive human-in-the-loop fly-throughs, addressing challenges of modeling thousands of images with varying lighting, large model capacities, and fast rendering. It solves the scalability problem of NeRF by decomposing the scene into a set of spatial cells, learning a separate NeRF submodule for each cell, and training them in parallel using geometry-aware pixel data partitioning. Unlike DeRF and KiloNeRF, which use spatial partitioning to speed up inference of a pre-trained single network, MegaNeRF uses spatial partitioning to enable data parallelism for scalable training, as obtaining a pre-trained NeRF for large scales is infeasible. NeRFPlayer is a dynamic scene representation method that decomposes the radiance field into stationary, deforming, and new area components to enable efficient streaming and high-quality rendering of dynamic scenes. It addresses the limitations of existing dynamic NeRF methods, which often suffer from misalignment of moving objects or high computational costs, by explicitly modeling the temporal evolution of scene geometry and appearance. Unlike static scene representations, NeRFPlayer separates the scene into distinct fields to handle static backgrounds, smoothly deforming objects, and newly appearing elements, achieving higher PSNR and significantly faster rendering times compared to baselines like HyperNeRF and DyNeRF. This method partitions 3D space into non-overlapping tiles to enable distributed NeRF training across multiple GPUs. It solves the problem of imbalanced workload distribution, which is a primary bottleneck in multi-GPU systems, by ensuring each partition contains a similar amount of spatial content. Unlike Block-NeRF, which partitions based on training camera positions, this method partitions space directly using a Probability Density Function (PDF) derived from scene geometry, allowing for finer bounding boxes in regions with more content or frequent capture. Definition: A representation for large scenes using multiple blocks and hierarchical Levels of Detail (LODs) to manage representational capacity and resource loading, addressing the limited resolution of single-model approaches. Training Stage: The scene is uniformly partitioned into K blocks \{Bk\}{k=1}^K, each centered at ck=(xk, yk) on the xy plane (ground plane). Only the finest LOD is represented and optimized. For a point \mathbf{p} = (px, py, pz), the corresponding block Bk is determined by its projected xy coordinates \mathbf{p}{proj} = (px, py): \mathbf{p} \in \mathcal{B}k, k = \mathop{\arg \min}\limits{k}\|\mathbf{p}{proj} - \mathbf{c}k\|{\infty} Within block k, the components are: (1) f^k: Hash encoding + MLP decoder for attributes (density, diffuse color, specular feature); (2) \Phi^k: Tiny deferred MLP for view-dependent effects; (3) \psi^k: Proposal MLP for sampling. Rendering Stage: Hierarchical LODs are used. 2 \times 2 blocks are merged into one block between consecutive LODs. For LOD l \in \{1, \dots, L\}, there are K/4^{l-1} blocks. Components per block k at LOD l are: (1) f^{k,l}: Baked texture query (sparse voxel + triplane) for opacity, diffuse color, specular features; (2) \Phi^{k,l}: Tiny deferred MLP for view-dependent effects; (3) \psi^{k,l}: Multi-level occupancy grid for sampling. Parameters: K is the total number of base blocks in the finest LOD. The need for scene partitioning arises from the memory and computational constraints of representing large-scale environments with a single neural network. Early NeRF implementations struggled with urban-scale datasets containing thousands of images. MegaNeRF introduced spatial partitioning to enable parallel training of submodules. Spatial Partitioning for Distributed NeRF refined this by using geometry-based PDFs for balanced distributed training. NeRFPlayer extended decomposition to the temporal domain for dynamic scenes. The Block & LOD approach further optimizes resource loading by baking attributes into textures for rendering. City-on-Web: Real-Time Neural Rendering of Large-Scale Scenes on the Web, https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-031-72970-622, fetched 2026-10-26

name: MegaNeRF
head: Mega-NeRF, Mega-NeRF framework
body: MegaNeRF is a scalable framework for training large-scale 3D neural radiance fields (NeRFs) that supports interactive, human-in-the-loop fly-throughs of urban environments. It addresses the computational infeasibility of training a single NeRF on thousands of images by decomposing the scene into spatial cells, each represented by a separate, specialized NeRF submodule. Unlike methods like DeRF and KiloNeRF that use spatial partitioning primarily to accelerate inference of a pre-trained global network, MegaNeRF uses partitioning to enable data parallelism for scalable training, as obtaining a pre-trained NeRF for large scales is infeasible. It further improves upon NeRF++ by modeling the foreground volume as an ellipsoid rather than a unit sphere to better fit aerial viewpoints and by using camera altitude constraints to avoid querying underground regions. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: A set of M training images with known camera poses (extrinsics and intrinsics) and, optionally, camera altitude measurements. For initialization, Structure-from-Motion (SfM) point clouds or geometry-aware viewpoints are used. Outputs: A set of N independent NeRF submodules, each defined by an MLP \Thetai, and a spatial partitioning scheme (Voronoi cells) defining the region of responsibility for each submodule. Data Structures: 1. Spatial Partitioning: The scene is divided into N spatial cells using Voronoi partitioning based on cluster centroids \bar{c}i. Centroids: \bar{c}i = (\bar{c}{ix}, \bar{c}{iy}, \bar{c}{iz}) for i = 1, \dots, N. The height z of centroids is often fixed to a common value if the altitude variation between camera poses is small relative to latitude/longitude differences. Assignment: Each 3D point p is assigned to the closest submodule index i = \arg \min{j \in \{1, \dots, N\}} \|\bar{c}j - p\|2^2. 2. Submodule MLP: Each submodule i is an MLP \Thetai that maps a 3D position p and viewing direction d to volume density \theta and color r. Signature: \text{MLP}{\Thetai}: (p, d) \rightarrow (r, \theta). 3. Foreground/Background Decomposition: The scene is split into a foreground volume (enclosing camera poses) and a background volume (complement). Foreground: Modeled by an ellipsoid parameterization (extending NeRF++'s inverse sphere). Background: Uses the same 4D outer volume parameterization and raycasting formulation as NeRF++. 4. Training Data Partitioning: A mapping from pixels to submodules. A pixel from a training image is added to the training set of submodule i only if the ray corresponding to that pixel intersects the spatial cell i. 5. Rendering Cache (Optional/Advanced): An octree caching coarse rendering of densities and colors for accelerated inference. Numbered Steps: 1. Initialization: Estimate geometry-aware viewpoints or use SfM point clouds to determine N cluster centroids \bar{c}i. Define the spatial partitioning (Voronoi cells) based on these centroids. Define the foreground ellipsoid bounds and background volume bounds. 2. Data Partitioning (Training Preparation): For each training image k with camera pose Ck: For each pixel u in image k: Construct the ray r{k,u} from the camera center through pixel u. Sample points along r{k,u} within the scene bounds. Identify all spatial cells i that intersect with the ray segment within the scene. Add the pixel (u, k) to the training dataset \mathcal{D}i for each identified submodule i. Note: This reduces the size of each submodule's training set by approximately 10x compared to using all data. 3. Parallel Training: Initialize N independent MLPs \Theta1, \dots, \ThetaN. Train each submodule \Thetai in parallel using its partitioned dataset \mathcal{D}i. Loss function: Standard NeRF photometric loss (MSE between predicted and ground truth pixel colors). Optional: Incorporate per-image appearance embeddings (latent codes) from NeRF-W to handle varying lighting conditions. 4. Inference (Rendering): For a new query ray r: Sample points pt along the ray. Boundary Handling: If a point pt falls within the boundaries of multiple modules (due to overlapping Voronoi regions or proximity to centroids), determine the color and density by combining outputs from relevant NeRFs in proportion to the inverse distance to the cluster centroids. Let wi(p) = \frac{1}{\|\bar{c}i - p\|2^2 + \epsilon} be the weight for module i. Combined density: \theta(p) = \frac{\sum{i \in \text{relevant}} wi(p) \thetai(p)}{\sum{i \in \text{relevant}} wi(p)}. Combined color: r(p) = \frac{\sum{i \in \text{relevant}} wi(p) ri(p)}{\sum{i \in \text{relevant}} wi(p)}. If a point pt is clearly within one cell, query only that submodule \Thetai. Altitude Constraint: Use camera altitude measurements to constrain ray sampling bounds. Terminate rays near ground level to avoid querying underground regions. A parameter z{\text{ground}} indicates the lowest point to keep ray sampling above ground level. Perform standard volume rendering (compositing) using the sampled (r, \theta) values. Interactive Rendering Optimization: Exploit temporal coherence by caching occupancy and color values from nearby previous views. Alternative/Additional: Cache a coarse rendering of densities and colors into an octree for faster lookups. Formulas: Submodule Selection: i = \arg \min{j \in \{1, \dots, N\}} \|\bar{c}j - p\|2^2. Scene Representation: \text{MLP}{\Thetai}: (p, d) \rightarrow (r, \theta). Blending at Boundaries: \theta(p) = \frac{\sum{i} wi(p) \thetai(p)}{\sum{i} wi(p)}, \quad r(p) = \frac{\sum{i} wi(p) ri(p)}{\sum{i} wi(p)} where wi(p) = \frac{1}{\|\bar{c}i - p\|2^2 + \epsilon}. Parameters: N: Number of spatial cells/submodules. Not given in the sources. z{\text{ground}}: Parameter indicating the lowest point to keep ray sampling above ground level. Not given in the sources. \epsilon: Small constant for numerical stability in blending weights. Not given in the sources. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Underground Sampling: Omission of the ground-level parameter (z{\text{ground}}) leads to invalid geometry and wasted computation querying underground regions. Boundary Artifacts: Points near the boundaries of Voronoi cells may be queried by multiple submodules. The blending strategy (distance-weighted) is required to prevent visible seams. Aerial Viewpoint Fit: Using a unit sphere (as in NeRF++) for foreground modeling is less efficient for aerial drone footage than an ellipsoid, which tightly encloses the camera poses and relevant foreground detail. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import numpy as np def initializemeganerf(cameraposes, numclusters): """ Initialize MegaNeRF by clustering camera poses and defining spatial cells. """ # Extract 3D positions from camera poses (e.g., camera centers) cameracenters = extractcameracenters(cameraposes) # Cluster camera centers to find centroids # Using K-Means or similar clustering algorithm centroids = kmeans(cameracenters, k=numclusters) # Define Voronoi cells based on centroids # Each cell i is associated with centroid centroids[i] return centroids def partitiontrainingdata(cameraposes, images, centroids): """ Partition training pixels into submodules based on ray-cell intersection. """ numclusters = len(centroids) trainingdatasets = {i: [] for i in range(numclusters)} for imgidx, (image, camerapose) in enumerate(zip(images, cameraposes)): H, W, = image.shape for u in range(H): for v in range(W): # Construct ray for pixel (u, v) ray = constructray(camerapose, u, v) # Sample points along the ray within scene bounds # Determine which cells the ray intersects intersectingcells = findintersectingcells(ray, centroids) # Add pixel to the training set of intersecting cells for cellidx in intersectingcells: trainingdatasets[cellidx].append((imgidx, u, v)) return trainingdatasets def trainsubmodule(submoduleid, trainingdata, centroids): """ Train a single NeRF submodule on its partitioned data. """ # Initialize MLP for this submodule mlp = initializemlp() for epoch in range(numepochs): for imgidx, u, v in trainingdata: # Get ground truth color gtcolor = getpixelcolor(imgidx, u, v) # Get camera pose camerapose = getcamerapose(imgidx) # Construct ray ray = constructray(camerapose, u, v) # Sample points along ray points = samplepointsalongray(ray) # Query MLP for density and color # Note: In practice, direction d is also passed directions = getviewdirections(camerapose, points) densities, colors = mlp(points, directions) # Compute loss (e.g., MSE) loss = computeloss(colors, gtcolor) # Backpropagate and update MLP updatemlp(mlp, loss) return mlp def renderray(ray, centroids, mlps, zground): """ Render a single ray using the trained MegaNeRF submodules. """ # Sample points along the ray points = samplepointsalongray(ray) # Filter points below ground level points = filterbelowground(points, zground) # Query submodules for each point densities = [] colors = [] for p in points: # Find relevant submodules (those whose centroids are close) # Or simply find the closest one for efficiency, but blending is safer at boundaries relevantindices = findrelevantsubmodules(p, centroids) if not relevantindices: densities.append(0.0) colors.append([0.0, 0.0, 0.0]) continue # Blend outputs from relevant submodules totalweight = 0.0 blendeddensity = 0.0 blendedcolor = np.array([0.0, 0.0, 0.0]) for i in relevantindices: # Calculate weight based on distance to centroid distsq = np.sum((p - centroids[i])2) weight = 1.0 / (distsq + 1e-8) # Query submodule i direction = getviewdirection(ray, p) di, ci = mlpsi blendeddensity += weight di blendedcolor += weight ci totalweight += weight # Normalize if totalweight > 0: blendeddensity /= totalweight blendedcolor /= totalweight else: blendeddensity = 0.0 blendedcolor = np.array([0.0, 0.0, 0.0]) densities.append(blendeddensity) colors.append(blendedcolor) # Perform volume rendering (compositing) finalcolor = volumerender(points, densities, colors) return finalcolor def volumerender(points, densities, colors): """ Standard volume rendering compositing. """ T = 1.0 # Transmittance finalcolor = np.array([0.0, 0.0, 0.0]) for i in range(len(points)): d = densities[i] c = colors[i] # Alpha from density alpha = 1.0 - np.exp(-d) # Contribution contribution = alpha T c finalcolor += contribution # Update transmittance T = (1.0 - alpha) # Early termination if T is very small if T < 1e-4: break return finalcolor A method for large-scale urban reconstruction from aerial drone images using NeRF++ inverse sphere parameterization extended to ellipsoids. It focuses on caching coarse renderings into an octree for faster inference. Link A method that decouples rendering time from scene size by dividing the scene into blocks, each represented by a small MLP, and aligning appearances between adjacent NeRFs for seamless integration. Link Time Complexity: Training is parallelized across N submodules, reducing the training time per GPU by a factor of approximately 10x due to data partitioning. Overall training speed is improved by 3x compared to baseline approaches on existing datasets. Memory Complexity: Each submodule stores a smaller MLP, reducing memory requirements per GPU. However, the total memory across all GPUs is higher than a single global NeRF. The octree cache (if used) adds memory overhead proportional to the scene size. Measured Performance: Achieves a 40x speedup over conventional NeRF rendering while remaining within 0.8 dB in PSNR quality. Improves PSNR by 12% compared to baseline approaches on existing datasets. Scaling: Scales to scenes 1000x larger than prior work (e.g., 150,000 to over 1,300,000 m^2). Rendering time is decoupled from scene size, allowing rendering to scale to arbitrarily large environments. Strengths: Enables training on massive datasets that are infeasible for a single NeRF. Supports interactive fly-throughs. Handles varying lighting via appearance embeddings. Limitations: Requires careful tuning of the ground-level parameter to avoid underground sampling. Boundary artifacts may occur if blending is not handled correctly. MegaNeRF was introduced in 2021/2022 by Xiangli et al.. It was motivated by the need for search-and-rescue applications where drones provide inexpensive means of quickly surveying large areas. The method builds on NeRF++ by replacing the unit sphere foreground model with an ellipsoid and adding altitude constraints. It also incorporates appearance embeddings from NeRF-W. The core insight is that visibility statistics for large-scale scenes show that only a small fraction of training images are visible from any particular scene point, motivating a sparse network structure with specialized parameters for different regions. name: NeRFPlayer
head: Decomposed Neural Radiance Fields, NeRFPlayer Decomposed Neural Radiance Fields
body: NeRFPlayer is a dynamic scene representation method that decomposes the radiance field into stationary, deforming, and new area components to enable efficient streaming and high-quality rendering of dynamic scenes. It addresses the limitations of existing dynamic NeRF methods, which often suffer from misalignment of moving objects or high computational costs, by explicitly modeling the temporal evolution of scene geometry and appearance. Unlike static scene representations, NeRFPlayer separates the scene into distinct fields to handle static backgrounds, smoothly deforming objects, and newly appearing elements, achieving higher PSNR and significantly faster rendering times compared to baselines like HyperNeRF and DyNeRF. NeRFPlayer extends the static scene representation principles by introducing a decomposition mechanism that classifies spatial points into three categories: stationary, deforming, and new. The method uses a hybrid representation backbone (InstantNGP or TensoRF) combined with specific MLPs for deformation and decomposition. Inputs: Camera pose (position and orientation). Viewing direction \mathbf{d}. 3D position \mathbf{x} along the ray. Time t (implicit in the streaming context, though the core decomposition relies on spatial probabilities). Outputs: Rendered pixel color \mathbf{C}. Streaming data updates (new channels) for temporal interpolation. The representation consists of four main components: 1. Decomposition Field (f): Structure: Explicitly cached features (Vf) and a small MLP decoder (Df). Purpose: Predicts the probability of a point belonging to the stationary, deforming, or new area categories. Input: Encoded 3D position \gamma(\mathbf{x}). Output: Probabilities for each area type. 2. Deformation Field (d): Structure: A 4-layer MLP with width 256. Purpose: Predicts the velocity vector \mathbf{v} for deforming points. Input: Encoded 3D position \gamma(\mathbf{x}). Output: Velocity vector \mathbf{v}. 3. Stationary Field (s): Structure: A 2-layer MLP with width 64. Purpose: Predicts density and color for static parts of the scene. Input: Encoded 3D position \gamma(\mathbf{x}). Output: Density \sigma and color \mathbf{c}. 4. Radiance Field (r): Structure: A 4-layer MLP with width 64, sharing the same structure as the decoder in the chosen backbone (InstantNGP or TensoRF). Purpose: Predicts density and color for deforming and new areas. Input: Encoded 3D position \gamma(\mathbf{x}), viewing direction \mathbf{d}, and intermediate features from the backbone. Output: Density \sigma and color \mathbf{c}. Backbone Configuration: InstantNGP: 8 levels, 4 feature dimensions per entry. TensoRF: Follows settings from original TensoRF experiments on LLFF datasets. Streaming Channels (k): Set to 1 for both backbones. 1. Positional Encoding: Encode the 3D position \mathbf{x} using the positional encoding defined in the parent article. 2. Decomposition Probability Calculation: Forward \gamma(\mathbf{x}) through the decomposition field f (features Vf and decoder Df) to obtain probabilities for each area type: stationary, deforming, and new. 3. Deformation Velocity Prediction (Conditional): If the probability of the point being in a dynamic area is below a threshold \tau (default 0.001), set velocity \mathbf{v} = \mathbf{0} and skip the deformation field forwarding for efficiency. Otherwise, forward \gamma(\mathbf{x}) through the deformation field d (4-layer MLP, width 256) to obtain velocity \mathbf{v}. 4. Field Selection and Forward Pass: If the point is classified as "stationary": Forward \gamma(\mathbf{x}) through the stationary field s (2-layer MLP, width 64) to get \sigmas, \mathbf{c}s. If the point is classified as "deforming" or "new": Forward \gamma(\mathbf{x}), \mathbf{d}, and backbone features through the radiance field r (4-layer MLP, width 64) to get \sigmar, \mathbf{c}r. If deforming, apply the velocity \mathbf{v} to adjust the position or feature interpolation. 5. Volumetric Rendering: Compute the pixel color C(\mathbf{r}) using the standard volumetric rendering equation: C(\mathbf{r}) = \sum{i=1}^N Ti \alphai \mathbf{c}i, \quad \text{where } \alphai = 1 - \exp(-\sigmai \deltai), \quad Ti = \prod{j=1}^{i-1} (1 - \alphaj) where \sigmai and \mathbf{c}i are the density and color from the selected field (stationary or radiance) for sample i, and \deltai is the distance between samples. 6. Loss Calculation: The training loss is composed of a reconstruction loss L{rec} and a regularization loss L{reg}: L = L{rec} + \lambda L{reg} where \lambda is a balancing hyper-parameter (default 0.1). Threshold \tau: 0.001. Used to skip deformation field forwarding if probability is low. Deformation Network: 4-layer MLP, width 256. Stationary Field: 2-layer MLP, width 64. Radiance Field: 4-layer MLP, width 64. InstantNGP Levels: 8. InstantNGP Feature Dimensions: 4. Streaming Channels k: 1. Loss Hyper-parameter \lambda: 0.1. Loss Hyper-parameter \alpha: 0.01. Used to penalize deforming areas during training. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def positionalencoding(x, numbands=10): """Standard sinusoidal positional encoding.""" encoded = [] for scale in [2i for i in range(numbands)]: for v in x: encoded.append(math.sin(scale v)) encoded.append(math.cos(scale v)) return encoded def nerfplayerforward(x, d, decompositionfield, deformationfield, stationaryfield, radiancefield, backbone, tau=0.001): """Forward pass for NeRFPlayer.""" gammax = positionalencoding(x) probs = decompositionfield(gammax) # probs[0]: stationary, probs[1]: deforming, probs[2]: new probdynamic = probs[1] + probs[2] usedeformation = probdynamic > tau v = [0.0, 0.0, 0.0] if usedeformation: v = deformationfield(gammax) isstationary = probs[0] > probdynamic if isstationary: sigma, c = stationaryfield(gammax) else: backbonefeatures = backbone(gammax, d) sigma, c = radiancefield(gammax, d, backbonefeatures) return sigma, c def renderray(rayorigin, raydirection, numsamples, nerfplayermodel, tau): """Render a single ray using volumetric rendering.""" tvals = [i / numsamples for i in range(1, numsamples + 1)] sigmalist = [] clist = [] for t in tvals: z = [rayorigin[i] + raydirection[i] t for i in range(3)] sigma, c = nerfplayerforward(z, raydirection, nerfplayermodel.decompositionfield, nerfplayermodel.deformationfield, nerfplayermodel.stationaryfield, nerfplayermodel.radiancefield, nerfplayermodel.backbone, tau) sigmalist.append(sigma) clist.append(c) deltas = [tvals[i] - tvals[i-1] for i in range(1, numsamples)] + [1.0 - tvals[-1]] alphavals = [1.0 - math.exp(-s d) for s, d in zip(sigmalist, deltas)] T = [1.0] for a in alphavals[:-1]: T.append(T[-1] (1.0 - a)) weights = [a t for a, t in zip(alphavals, T)] color = [sum(w c[i] for w, c in zip(weights, clist)) for i in range(3)] return color High FPS Multi-Camera Datasets: Deformation is not used by default for efficiency because modeling every dynamic area as new areas leads to good temporal interpolation performance. Large \alpha (e.g., 1): Over-suppresses deforming areas, leading to blurry moving objects. Small \alpha (e.g., 0.005): Under-suppresses deforming areas, leading to a noisy scene. Recommended Practice: Start with a relatively large \alpha to penalize deforming areas, then gradually decrease \alpha to allow areas to deform. Threshold \tau: If set incorrectly, the decomposition field may fail to skip unnecessary computations, leading to inefficiency. Time Complexity: Training time on Plenoptic Video: 22.797 GPU hours (Ours-InstantNGP), 23.238 (Ours-TensoRF-VM). Rendering time: 5.5 s/img (Ours-InstantNGP), 6 s/img (Ours-TensoRF-VM). Memory Complexity: Depends on the backbone. InstantNGP uses 8 levels with 4 feature dimensions per entry. TensoRF uses CP or VM decomposition. Performance: PSNR on HyperNeRF-vrig (Mean): 22.4 (Ours-InstantNGP), 22.4 (HyperNeRF), 22.2 (Nerfies), 26.3 (NSFF), 16.9 (NV), 20.1 (NeRF). SSIM on HyperNeRF-vrig (Mean): 0.814 (Ours-InstantNGP), 0.814 (HyperNeRF), 0.803 (Nerfies), 0.916 (NSFF), 0.571 (NV), 0.745 (NeRF). Bitrate: TensoRF-CP achieves low bitrate. TensoRF-VM has higher cost but better performance. First frame requires 96 channels for TensoRF-CP and 4 for TensoRF-VM. Strengths: Higher PSNR than HyperNeRF, significantly faster rendering than DyNeRF (12% of the time), better handling of fast-moving objects with TensoRF-VM. Limitations: Slightly lower SSIM than HyperNeRF, generating more accurate but less sharp images. Misalignment issues in HyperNeRF are avoided, but sharpness is traded off. When to Use: When high-quality dynamic scene reconstruction is needed with efficient streaming and rendering, especially for fast-moving objects. When Not to Use: When sharpness is prioritized over accuracy, or when computational resources are extremely limited and streaming is not required. NeRFPlayer was introduced in the paper "NeRFPlayer: A Streamable Dynamic Scene Representation with Decomposed Neural Radiance Fields". It builds on the principles of static NeRFs and dynamic NeRFs like HyperNeRF and DyNeRF, aiming to address their limitations in deformation modeling and efficiency. The method was developed to handle dynamic scenes with varying levels of motion, from static backgrounds to fast-moving objects, by decomposing the scene representation. name: Spatial Partitioning for Distributed NeRF
head: Aspect Ratio Optimization Partitioning, Recursive CDF Partitioning
body: This method partitions 3D space into non-overlapping tiles to enable distributed NeRF training across multiple GPUs. It aims to balance compute by ensuring each partition contains a similar amount of spatial content. Unlike Block-NeRF, MegaNeRF, and NeRFPlayer, which partition based on training camera positions or use uniform grids, this method partitions space directly using a Probability Density Function (PDF) derived from scene geometry, allowing for finer bounding boxes in regions with more content or frequent capture. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A set of 3D points representing the scene geometry, obtained either from Structure from Motion (SfM) sparse points or by discretizing training rays into samples. Output: A set of 2^n non-overlapping axis-aligned bounding boxes (tiles) that partition the scene space, where n is the number of recursive splitting iterations. Data Structures: Point Cloud: A list of 3D coordinates \mathbf{p}i = (xi, yi, zi). Histogram/Bin: A 1D array representing the distribution of points along a specific axis. CDF Array: A 1D array storing the cumulative sum of the histogram values, normalized to [0, 1]. Algorithm Steps: 1. Generate Point Cloud: Create a point cloud from either Structure from Motion (SfM) data or by discretizing training rays into samples. 2. Construct PDF: Compute the Probability Density Function (PDF) for the point cloud distribution along each axis (x, y, z). 3. Compute CDF: Calculate the Cumulative Distribution Function (CDF) along each axis. 4. Identify Candidate Planes: For each axis, identify candidate splitting planes where the CDF equals 0.5. 5. Select Optimal Plane: Evaluate the aspect ratio (ARi) of the resulting partitions for each candidate plane. 6. Split: Divide the current space into two sub-spaces using the selected plane. 7. Recursion: Recursively apply steps 2–6 to each sub-space for n iterations to achieve 2^n partitions. Formulas: CDF Condition: A candidate plane P along axis A is selected if: \text{CDF}A(P) = 0.5 where \text{CDF}A is the cumulative distribution function along axis A. Aspect Ratio (ARi): The metric used to evaluate partition quality. The sources define ARi as the aspect ratio for each partition but do not provide the explicit geometric formula (e.g., ratio of longest to shortest side). The goal is to minimize the deviation of ARi from 1. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def spatialpartition(points, numiterations): if not points or numiterations == 0: return [computeboundingbox(points)] cdfs = {axis: computecdf(points, axis) for axis in 'xyz'} candidates = {axis: findcdfzeropoint(cdfs[axis]) for axis in 'xyz'} bestaxis, bestplane, mindiff = None, None, float('inf') for axis, planeval in candidates.items(): leftpts, rightpts = splitpoints(points, axis, planeval) arleft = computeaspectratio(computeboundingbox(leftpts)) arright = computeaspectratio(computeboundingbox(rightpts)) diff = max(abs(arleft - 1.0), abs(arright - 1.0)) if diff < mindiff: mindiff, bestaxis, bestplane = diff, axis, planeval leftpts, rightpts = splitpoints(points, bestaxis, bestplane) return spatialpartition(leftpts, numiterations - 1) + spatialpartition(rightpts, numiterations - 1) def computecdf(points, axis): if not points: return [] coords = sorted(p[axis] for p in points) n = len(coords) return [(c, (i + 1) / n) for i, c in enumerate(coords)] def findcdfzeropoint(cdfdata): for coord, cdfval in cdfdata: if cdfval >= 0.5: return coord return cdfdata[-1][0] def computeboundingbox(points): if not points: return None return {'min': (min(p[0] for p in points), min(p[1] for p in points), min(p[2] for p in points)), 'max': (max(p[0] for p in points), max(p[1] for p in points), max(p[2] for p in points))} def computeaspectratio(bbox): dims = [bbox['max'][i] - bbox['min'][i] for i in range(3)] mindim = min(dims) return max(dims) / mindim if mindim > 0 else float('inf') def splitpoints(points, axis, planeval): left, right = [], [] for p in points: (left if p[axis] < planeval else right).append(p) return left, right Parameters: numiterations (n): The number of recursive splitting steps. The total number of partitions is 2^n. Typical values are not given in the sources. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Missing SfM Data: For captures lacking point cloud data (e.g., building captures), SfM cannot be used. Imbalanced Workload: Despite the partitioning strategy, imbalanced workload distribution across GPUs remains a bottleneck, potentially due to variations in scene complexity or rendering time per tile. A strategy to partition 3D space into non-overlapping bounding boxes for multi-GPU assignment, aiming to balance compute by ensuring each region contains a similar amount of spatial content. It generates a point cloud via SfM or ray discretization, constructs a PDF, and recursively partitions space by selecting axes that minimize aspect ratio deviation from 1. It is chosen when distributed training of large-scale NeRFs is required to mitigate communication bottlenecks. Pitfall: Imbalanced workload distribution across GPUs remains a bottleneck. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Measured Performance: The method reduces communication costs by over 2× through partition-based volume rendering (tile-based vs. sample-based synchronization). However, multi-GPU communication remains the primary bottleneck due to imbalanced workload distribution. Strengths: Partitions space directly rather than based on camera positions, allowing for finer bounding boxes in regions with more content or frequent capture (level-of-detail property). Versatile across capture types (drone footage, street capture, 360-degree object-centric). Ensures an even distribution of points across tiles. Limitations: Imbalanced workload distribution across GPUs persists, limiting scalability. Requires SfM data or ray discretization. When to Use: Not given in the sources. When Not to Use: Not given in the sources. The method was introduced in NeRF-XL: Scaling NeRFs with Multiple GPUs. It addresses limitations in existing approaches like Block-NeRF and Mega-NeRF, which either partition based on cameras or use uniform spatial partitioning, potentially leading to suboptimal resource utilization. The authors identified that imbalanced workload distribution across GPUs was a significant impediment to effective multi-GPU scaling. The method is part of the NeRF-XL system, which also includes techniques for background modeling and global composition using parallel prefix scans. name: Specific Model Architectures and Extensions
head: Vanilla NeRF, Original NeRF
body: This family represents a scene as a single MLP f\theta(\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{d}) \to (\mathbf{c}, \sigma) that maps a 3D position \mathbf{x} \in \mathbb{R}^3 and a viewing direction \mathbf{d} \in S^2 to an emitted color \mathbf{c} \in \mathbb{R}^3 and a volumetric density \sigma \ge 0. Rendering uses the classical volume rendering integral along rays cast from the camera, with no explicit geometry—geometry emerges from where \sigma is high after photometric optimization on multi-view images. It sets itself apart from its siblings by using a single, monolithic MLP without spatial partitioning or explicit geometric priors, relying entirely on positional encoding and hierarchical sampling to capture scene details. Unlike Mip-NeRF 360 which handles unbounded scenes via contraction, or NeRF-FF which addresses defocus, the original architecture operates within defined near and far ray bounds. Builds on the parent family's shared mechanism of mapping 6D input coordinates (3D position \mathbf{x} and 2D viewing direction \mathbf{d}) to 4D output values (density \sigma and color \mathbf{c}) using a differentiable neural network Scene Representation and Architecture. Specific network topology details (e.g., layer counts, activation functions, skip connection patterns) beyond the general MLP structure are not given in the sources. Extends NeRF quality to unbounded, 360-degree real-world scenes by combining anti-aliased cone-casting with a non-linear scene contraction parameterization. Sets itself apart by introducing a proposal network trained via online distillation and a distortion regularizer to prevent floaters. Choose when handling full 360-degree unbounded geometry. A plug-in strategy that mitigates reconstruction degradation from out-of-focus (defocus blurred) regions by estimating binary image masks to omit out-of-focus pixels during training. Sets itself apart by relying on static ray assumptions, making it compatible with runtime-optimized variants like Instant-NGP and splatfacto. Choose when training on partially blurred data. Specialized for reconstructing large-scale 3D scenes from aerial drone imagery, addressing unbounded space representation and varying camera exposure. Sets itself apart by integrating view frustum sampling for anti-aliasing, a pose optimizer for joint pose refinement, and appearance embeddings to handle exposure discrepancies. Choose for large-scale aerial captures with exposure variations. The specific model architectures described here originate from the foundational NeRF paper (Mildenhall et al., 2020), which introduced the concept of representing a scene as a single MLP f\theta(\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{d}) \to (\mathbf{c}, \sigma). This approach eliminated the need for explicit geometry, allowing geometry to emerge from high-density regions after photometric optimization on multi-view images. The architecture relies on three key innovations: volume rendering as a differentiable encoding mechanism, positional encoding to overcome spectral bias, and hierarchical sampling. Training the original architecture is computationally intensive, requiring 1–2 days on a V100 GPU for a single scene, with render speeds of 0.05–0.3 FPS at 1080p resolution. While later variants like Instant-NGP or Zip-NeRF have significantly improved speed and quality (e.g., PSNR of 28.5+ on Mip-NeRF 360 vs. 25.4 for the original), the vanilla MLP architecture remains the conceptual baseline for understanding implicit neural representations in volume rendering. facebookresearch/NSVF, https://github.com/facebookresearch/NSVF, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial) NeRF — All Variants Cheat Sheet, https://www.chengjianglong.com/ml/3D-NeRFSOTAUpdated.html, fetched 2026-10-29 (unofficial)

name: Mip-NeRF 360
head: Unbounded NeRF, mip360
body: Mip-NeRF 360 extends neural radiance field quality to unbounded, 360-degree real-world scenes where the camera may point in any direction and content exists at arbitrary distances. It solves the problems of aliasing from multi-scale details and the ambiguity of infinite space by combining anti-aliased cone-casting with a non-linear scene contraction parameterization. Unlike its parent Mip-NeRF, which handles bounded scenes, Mip-NeRF 360 maps infinite 3D space into a bounded domain to allocate MLP capacity effectively, and unlike NeRF, it uses online distillation to train a large, high-capacity model efficiently. Inputs and Outputs Inputs: A set of calibrated images with known camera poses (position and orientation) and intrinsics (focal length, pixel size). Outputs: A differentiable neural network model (Proposal MLP and NeRF MLP) that renders novel views by computing pixel colors \mathbf{C}(\mathbf{r}) for any ray \mathbf{r}. Data Structures The method uses two Multi-Layer Perceptrons (MLPs): 1. Proposal MLP: A smaller network predicting only volumetric density \tau. 2. NeRF MLP: A larger network (approximately 15\times the capacity of mip-NeRF) predicting density \tau and color \mathbf{c}. Numbered Steps 1. Scene Parameterization (Contraction): To handle unbounded scenes, 3D coordinates \mathbf{x} are mapped to a bounded domain using a contraction function: \text{contract}(\mathbf{x}) = \begin{cases} \mathbf{x} & \|\mathbf{x}\| \le 1 \\ \left(2 - \frac{1}{\|\mathbf{x}\|}\right) \frac{\mathbf{x}}{\|\mathbf{x}\|} & \|\mathbf{x}\| > 1 \end{cases} This maps the infinite exterior of the unit sphere to the shell between radius 1 and 2, allocating more MLP capacity to nearby content and compressing distant content. 2. Ray Parameterization (Cone-Casting): Instead of sampling points, the ray is divided into intervals Ti = ti, t{i+1}) representing conical frustums. For each interval, the mean \boldsymbol{\mu} and covariance \boldsymbol{\Sigma} of the frustum are computed based on the ray origin, direction, focal length, and pixel size. 3. Integrated [Positional Encoding: The frustum statistics are encoded using integrated positional encoding to provide anti-aliasing: \gamma(\boldsymbol{\mu}, \boldsymbol{\Sigma}) = \left\{ \begin{bmatrix} \left[ \sin(2^\ell \boldsymbol{\mu}) \exp\left(-2^{2\ell-1} \operatorname{diag}(\boldsymbol{\Sigma})\right) \right] \\ \left[ \cos(2^\ell \boldsymbol{\mu}) \exp\left(-2^{2\ell-1} \operatorname{diag}(\boldsymbol{\Sigma})\right) \right] \end{bmatrix} \right\}{\ell=0}^{L-1} where L is the number of frequency bands. High-frequency components are attenuated where the frustum variance is large. 4. Network Forward Pass: The encoded features are passed to the MLPs. The Proposal MLP outputs density \tau^p. The NeRF MLP outputs density \tau and color \mathbf{c}: (\taui, \mathbf{c}i) = \text{MLP}{\text{NeRF}}(\gamma(\mathbf{r}(Ti)); \Theta{\text{NeRF}}) \tau^pi = \text{MLP}{\text{Prop}}(\gamma(\mathbf{r}(Ti)); \Theta{\text{Prop}}) 5. Volume Rendering: The pixel color is computed via alpha compositing: \mathbf{C}(\mathbf{r}) = \sumi wi \mathbf{c}i wi = \left(1 - e^{-\taui(t{i+1}-ti)}\right) e^{-\sum{i' < i} \tau{i'}(t{i'+1}-t{i'})} where \mathbf{C}(\mathbf{r}, \mathbf{t}) is the final rendered pixel color. 6. Hierarchical Sampling (Online Distillation): Coarse Pass: Sample Nc distances t^c uniformly from [tn, tf] (near/far planes). Render coarse image \mathbf{C}^c and compute coarse weights \mathbf{w}^c. Fine Pass: Sample Nf distances t^f from the histogram defined by \mathbf{t}^c and \mathbf{w}^c using inverse transform sampling. Render fine image \mathbf{C}^f. Proposal Supervision: The Proposal MLP is supervised by the histogram weights \mathbf{w}^c generated by the NeRF MLP, rather than by image reconstruction loss. This "online distillation" allows the Proposal MLP to learn the density structure efficiently. 7. Loss Function: The training loss combines coarse and fine reconstruction errors: \mathcal{L}{\text{recon}} = \sum{\mathbf{r} \in \mathcal{R}} \frac{1}{10} \mathcal{L}{\text{recon}}(\mathbf{C}(\mathbf{r}, \mathbf{t}^c), \mathbf{C}^(\mathbf{r})) + \mathcal{L}{\text{recon}}(\mathbf{C}(\mathbf{r}, \mathbf{t}^f), \mathbf{C}^(\mathbf{r})) where \mathcal{L}{\text{recon}} is mean squared error, \mathbf{C}^ is the ground truth color, and \mathcal{R} is the set of training rays. A distortion-based regularizer is also applied to discourage floaters and background collapse. Pseudocode Unverified code. 1.0 / norm) (x / norm)) def integratedpositionalencoding(mu, sigma, numbands): """Computes integrated positional encoding for conical frustums.""" freqbands = 2.0 np.arange(numbands) diagsigma = np.diagonal(sigma, axis1=-2, axis2=-1) attenuation = np.exp(-0.5 (freqbands 2) diagsigma[..., np.newaxis]) sinterm = np.sin(freqbands mu) attenuation costerm = np.cos(freqbands mu) attenuation return np.concatenate([sinterm, costerm], axis=-1) def volumerendering(densities, colors, tintervals): """Computes alpha compositing weights and final color.""" deltas = tintervals[..., 1:] - tintervals[...,:-1] alpha = 1.0 - np.exp(-densities deltas) transmittancethrough = 1.0 - alpha cumprod = np.concatenate([np.oneslike(transmittancethrough[...,:1]), np.cumprod(transmittancethrough[...,:-1], axis=-1)], axis=-1) weights = alpha cumprod color = np.sum(weights[..., np.newaxis] colors, axis=-2) return color, weights def generaterays(images, poses, intrinsics): """Generates ray origins and directions from image grid, poses, and intrinsics.""" h, w = images.shape[:2] fx, fy = intrinsics[0, 0], intrinsics[1, 1] cx, cy = intrinsics[0, 2], intrinsics[1, 2] y, x = np.meshgrid(np.arange(h), np.arange(w), indexing='ij') dirs = np.stack([(x - cx) / fx, (y - cy) / fy, np.oneslike(x)], axis=-1) origins = poses[...,:3, 3] rot = poses[...,:3,:3] dirsworld = np.einsum('...ij,...j->...i', rot, dirs) return origins, dirsworld def computefrustumstats(origins, dirs, tintervals, focallength, pixelsize): """Computes mean and diagonal covariance for conical frustum intervals.""" tmid = (tintervals[...,:-1] + tintervals[..., 1:]) / 2.0 mu = origins[..., np.newaxis,:] + dirs[..., np.newaxis,:] tmid[..., np.newaxis] sigma = np.zeroslike(mu) pixelradius = pixelsize / (2.0 focallength) variance = (1.0 / 12.0) (tintervals[..., 1:]2 + tintervals[..., 1:]tintervals[...,:-1] + tintervals[...,:-1]2) (pixelradius 2) sigma[...,:2] = variance[..., np.newaxis] return mu, sigma def samplefromhistogram(tbins, weights, numsamples): """Inverse transform sampling from discrete histogram.""" cdf = np.cumsum(weights, axis=-1) cdf = cdf / cdf[..., -1:] u = np.random.rand(weights.shape[:-1], numsamples) indices = np.searchsorted(cdf, u, side='right') indices = np.clip(indices, 0, tbins.shape[-1] - 2) tlow = tbins[..., indices] thigh = tbins[..., indices + 1] return tlow + (thigh - tlow) np.random.rand(weights.shape[:-1], numsamples) def computedistortionloss(tintervals, weights): """Standard distortion loss: penalizes spread of weights along ray.""" midpoints = (tintervals[...,:-1] + tintervals[..., 1:]) / 2.0 deltas = tintervals[..., 1:] - tintervals[...,:-1] return np.sum(weights 2 midpoints deltas, axis=-1) def computeproposalloss(proposaldensity, coarseweights): """Supervises proposal density to match coarse weight distribution.""" normweights = coarseweights / (np.sum(coarseweights, axis=-1, keepdims=True) + 1e-8) normproposal = proposaldensity / (np.sum(proposaldensity, axis=-1, keepdims=True) + 1e-8) return np.mean((normproposal - images) 2) lossreconfine = np.mean((colorrenderedfine - images) 2) lossdistortion = np.mean(computedistortionloss(tfine, weightsfine)) totalloss = 0.1 lossreconcoarse + lossreconfine + lambdadist lossdistortion lossproposal = np.mean(computeproposalloss(taupropcoarse, weightscoarse)) return totalloss, lossproposal Parameters Number of frequency bands (L): Not given in the sources. Number of coarse samples (Nc): Not given in the sources. Number of fine samples (Nf): Not given in the sources. Distortion Loss Weight (\lambda): Not given in the sources. Near/Far Planes (tn, tf): Defined by the camera calibration and scene bounds. Edge Cases and Pitfalls Precision: The contraction function maps infinity to a finite radius; care must be taken with numerical stability near \|\mathbf{x}\|=1. Boundaries: The method assumes the scene is unbounded; if the scene is strictly bounded, the contraction may waste capacity on empty space outside the scene. Floaters: Without the distortion regularizer, unbounded scenes suffer from "floaters" (spurious geometry) and background collapse. Replaces the large MLP with Instant-NGP grids and adds specific anti-aliasing mechanisms for faster training and lower error rates. Modifies the distortion loss with a power transformation to more aggressively penalize floaters near the camera. Time Complexity: Training time is approximately 2\times that of mip-NeRF, taking 24-48 hours on the Blender dataset. It accelerates training by 300% compared to NeRF in Detail's learned proposer approach. Memory Complexity: The total model capacity is approximately 15\times larger than mip-NeRF due to the separate Proposal and NeRF MLPs. Performance: NeRF Synthetic (Blender): PSNR = 32.4 \pm 0.4 dB. Mip-NeRF 360 Unbounded Dataset: PSNR = 29.4 \pm 0.4 dB. LLFF Forward-Facing: PSNR = 26.4 \pm 0.4 dB. Strengths: Handles unbounded scenes effectively; reduces mean squared error by 57% compared to mip-NeRF; produces realistic views and detailed depth maps for intricate real-world scenes. Limitations: Poor surface accuracy because it uses a density representation without explicit surface geometry. Slower rendering speed (30+ sec/image at 1080p) compared to grid-based methods like Instant-NGP. Mip-NeRF 360 was introduced in November 2021 as an extension of Mip-NeRF to handle unbounded, 360-degree real-world scenes. It was developed to overcome the limitations of NeRF and mip-NeRF, which struggled with large, unbounded scenes due to aliasing and the ambiguity of infinite space. The method builds on the cone-casting anti-aliasing technique from Mip-NeRF and introduces scene contraction, online distillation, and a distortion regularizer. It is widely used as a baseline for unbounded neural rendering tasks. name: Zip-NeRF
body: Zip-NeRF is a method that integrates scale-aware anti-aliased neural radiance fields with fast grid-based training to achieve lower error rates and faster convergence than prior techniques. It solves the problem of aliasing artifacts in both spatial rendering and the loss function during online distillation, which are particularly prominent when rendering scenes across multiple scales or with sparse sampling. It sets itself apart from its parent Mip-NeRF 360 by replacing the large MLP with an Instant-NGP (iNGP) grid structure and introducing specific anti-aliasing mechanisms (multisampling, downweighting, and interlevel loss) to handle the high-frequency details of grid-based representations. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A set of posed images. Output: A radiance field model capable of rendering anti-aliased images at various scales. Data Structures: Instant-NGP Structure (G\theta): A pyramid of voxel grids and hashes replacing the large MLP used in mip-NeRF 360. Feature Codes: Stored in the grids/hashes. Each level \ell has a resolution n\ell. Proposal Networks: Separate iNGP and MLP structures for each round of proposal sampling. NeRF MLP: Uses a larger view-dependent branch than the standard iNGP. Parameters: Sampling Budget: Two rounds of proposal sampling with 64 samples each, followed by 32 samples in the final NeRF sampling round. Anti-aliased Interlevel Loss Rectangular Pulse Width (r): r = 0.03 in the first proposal round; r = 0.003 in the second round. Anti-aliased Interlevel Loss Multiplier: 0.01. Normalized Weight Decay Multiplier: 0.1 (unless otherwise stated). Scale Factors: [1, 2, 4, 8] for multiscale dataset creation. Algorithm Steps: 1. Multiscale Dataset Creation: For each input image, generate four additional images by bicubically downsampling by scale factors s \in [1, 2, 4, 8]. These act as proxy training/test views with zoomed-out cameras. 2. Initialization: Initialize the Instant-NGP grid pyramid, proposal networks, and NeRF MLP parameters. 3. Multiscale Training Loop: For each training iteration: a. Ray Sampling: Cast rays through the multiscale images. b. Downweighting: When querying the Instant-NGP grid at level \ell with resolution n\ell for a query with filter variance \sigma, apply the downweighting factor \phi(\sigma): \phi(\sigma) = \text{erf}\left(\frac{1}{\sqrt{8\sigma^2 n\ell^2}}\right) This convolves the output with a Gaussian, reducing the impact of higher-resolution features for larger queries. c. Multisampling: Use the anti-aliased multisampling strategy (hexagonal pattern or similar) to sample within the sub-frusta defined by mip-NeRF 360. d. Proposal Sampling: Perform two rounds of proposal sampling (64 samples each) using separate proposal iNGPs/MLPs. e. Final Sampling: Perform the final NeRF sampling round (32 samples). f. Loss Calculation: i. Data Term: Multiply the standard data term (reconstruction loss) by the scale factor s of the current ray/image. ii. Normalized Weight Decay: Calculate the loss \ell for feature codes in the pyramid: \ell = \text{mean}(V\ell^2) where V\ell is the set of grid/hash values at pyramid level \ell. Sum this mean across levels. This penalizes coarse scales more heavily than fine scales. Apply multiplier 0.1. iii. Anti-aliased Interlevel Loss: Impose the interlevel loss on both proposal rounds with pulse width r (0.03 for round 1, 0.003 for round 2) and multiplier 0.01. g. Optimization: Update parameters using JAX. 4. Evaluation: At test time, evaluate each scale factor s \in [1, 2, 4, 8] separately. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def trainzipnerf(images, poses, numiterations=100000): # Initialize Instant-NGP grid pyramid, proposal networks, and NeRF MLP gridpyramid = initializengppyramid() proposalnet1 = initializeproposalnetwork() proposalnet2 = initializeproposalnetwork() nerfmlp = initializenerfmlp(viewdependentbranchsize='large') # Multiscale dataset: bicubically downsample by [1, 2, 4, 8] imagess = [bicubicdownsample(img, s) for s in [1, 2, 4, 8]] for iteration in range(numiterations): for scalefactor in [1, 2, 4, 8]: imgs = imagess[scalefactor - 1] rays = castrays(imgs, poses) for ray in rays: # Helper: Downweight Instant-NGP query def queryngpdownweighted(coord, sigma): value = 0.0 for l in range(gridpyramid.numlevels): nl = gridpyramid.resolution(l) rawval = gridpyramid.query(coord, level=l) phi = math.erf(1.0 / math.sqrt(8 sigma2 nl2)) value += rawval phi return value # Proposal Sampling Round 1 (64 samples) samples1 = sampleproposal(proposalnet1, ray, numsamples=64) # Compute anti-aliased interlevel loss over samples (formula not specified in sources) lossprop1 = computeinterlevelloss(samples1, r=0.03) # Proposal Sampling Round 2 (64 samples) samples2 = sampleproposal(proposalnet2, ray, numsamples=64) lossprop2 = computeinterlevelloss(samples2, r=0.003) # Final NeRF Sampling (32 samples) samplesfinal = samplenerf(nerfmlp, ray, numsamples=32) # Data Loss with scale weighting renderedcolor = renderray(samplesfinal, nerfmlp, queryngpdownweighted) dataloss = meansquarederror(renderedcolor, imgs) scalefactor # Normalized Weight Decay weightdecayloss = 0.0 for l in range(gridpyramid.numlevels): Vl = gridpyramid.getvalues(level=l) weightdecayloss += mean(Vl2) weightdecayloss = 0.1 # Total Loss totalloss = dataloss + 0.01 (lossprop1 + lossprop2) + weightdecayloss updateparameters(totalloss) Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Z-aliasing: Disabling the anti-aliased interlevel loss causes z-aliasing artifacts in video results, though it may have little effect on single-image metrics. Sample Count: The baseline loss (without anti-aliasing) fails catastrophically if fewer than 16 samples are used, whereas the anti-aliased loss degrades gracefully. Weight Decay: Using non-normalized weight decay performs poorly; disabling it reduces accuracy significantly. View-Dependent Branch: Using iNGP’s small view-dependent MLP decreases accuracy; a larger branch is required. A querying scheme to mitigate aliasing where the output of instant-NGP is convolved with a Gaussian. It downweights higher resolution features for larger sized queries. The downweighting factor is \phi(\sigma) = \text{erf}\left(1/\sqrt{8\sigma^2 n\ell^2}\right), where \sigma is the filter variance and n\ell is the grid resolution of level \ell. This is combined with a regularizer that pulls all features towards 0 to reduce the impact of higher resolution features for larger sized queries. Time and Memory Complexity: Training Time: Zip-NeRF trains 24x faster than mip-NeRF 360 (0.89 hrs vs 21.69 hrs on the 360 dataset). It is ~6x slower to train than iNGP (0.89 hrs vs 0.15 hrs). Render Time: 0.9s per image, compared to 7.4s for mip-NeRF 360 and 0.2s for a naive mip-NeRF 360 + iNGP baseline. Measured Performance: 360 Dataset (Table 2): PSNR 28.54, SSIM 0.828, LPIPS 0.189. Outperforms mip-NeRF 360 (PSNR 27.57, SSIM 0.793, LPIPS 0.234) and iNGP (PSNR 25.68, SSIM 0.705, LPIPS 0.302). Multiscale 360 Dataset (Scale 1x): PSNR 28.25, SSIM 0.822, LPIPS 0.198. Multiscale 360 Dataset (Scale 8x): PSNR 32.52, SSIM 0.954, LPIPS 0.037. Error Reduction: 11% reduction in RMSE, 17% in DSSIM, 19% in LPIPS vs mip-NeRF 360 on the 360 dataset. 28% reduction in RMSE, 42% in DSSIM, 37% in LPIPS vs iNGP on the 360 dataset. Strengths and Limitations: Strengths: Significantly faster training than mip-NeRF 360; superior image quality compared to iNGP; robust to low sample counts; handles multiscale generalization well. Limitations: Slower than raw iNGP; render time is higher than iNGP. When to Use: When high-quality, anti-aliased rendering is required for unbounded scenes, and training time is a constraint compared to pure MLP-based NeRFs, but quality is more important than the absolute fastest training time of iNGP. When Not to Use: When absolute minimum training time is required (use iNGP) or when rendering single images with high sample counts where z-aliasing is not a concern (mip-NeRF 360 may suffice, though Zip-NeRF is still better). Zip-NeRF was introduced in the paper "Zip-NeRF: Anti-Aliased Grid-Based Neural Radiance Fields". It builds on the mip-NeRF 360 codebase and incorporates Instant-NGP's grid-based acceleration. The method addresses the divergence between scale-aware anti-aliased NeRFs and fast grid-based NeRF training, unifying them to handle aliasing in both spatial and loss domains. name: Distortion Loss with Power Transformation
head: Power-transformed distortion loss
body: A modification of the mip-NeRF 360 distortion loss that applies a power transformation to metric distance before computing the loss. This curves metric distance to aggressively penalize "floaters" (spurious geometry artifacts) near the camera, which significantly improves the quality of rendered videos. Unlike the standard distortion loss, which treats metric distance linearly, this method maps distance into a normalized space where the gradient is steep near the origin and tapers off, resembling log-distance behavior. The method modifies the computation of the distortion loss term in the training objective by transforming the metric distance variable t before integrating the loss. Inputs: Metric distance t for each sample on a ray. Transformation parameters: scaling factor s and power exponent \lambda. Distortion loss multiplier \alpha. Outputs: Transformed distortion loss value. Data Structures: No specific data structures are required beyond the standard ray sampling buffers (positions, weights, distances) used in differentiable volume rendering. Steps: 1. Retrieve the metric distance t for a sample. 2. Scale the metric distance by a factor s. 3. Apply the power transformation P to the scaled distance: t' = P(t) = (s \cdot t)^{\lambda} Where s is the scaling multiplier and \lambda is the power exponent. 4. Compute the standard distortion loss using the transformed distance t' instead of the raw metric distance t. The standard distortion loss typically involves integrating the absolute difference between the weighted average of distances and the individual distances, weighted by the transmittance and density contributions. 5. Multiply the resulting distortion loss by the multiplier \alpha and add it to the total training loss. Parameters: Scaling factor s: 10000. Power exponent \lambda: -0.25. Distortion loss multiplier \alpha: 0.005. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def computepowertransformeddistortionloss(distances, weights, alpha=0.005, s=10000.0, lambdaval=-0.25): """ Computes the distortion loss using power-transformed metric distances. Args: distances: Array of metric distances t for samples on a ray. weights: Array of normalized weights (density transmittance) for samples. alpha: Multiplier for the distortion loss term. s: Scaling factor for the power transformation. lambdaval: Power exponent for the transformation. Returns: The computed distortion loss value. """ # Step 2: Scale the metric distance scaleddistances = s distances # Step 3: Apply power transformation P(t) = (s t)^lambda # Note: Ensure distances are non-negative to avoid complex numbers if lambda is fractional transformeddistances = scaleddistances lambdaval # Step 4: Compute standard distortion loss on transformed distances # Standard distortion loss is typically: sum(wi |ti - sum(wj tj)|) # Here, we use transformeddistances as ti # Calculate the weighted average of transformed distances # weights must be normalized such that sum(weights) == 1.0 for this to be a valid expectation meantransformeddistance = np.sum(weights transformeddistances) # Compute the absolute difference between each transformed distance and the mean absdiffs = np.abs(transformeddistances - meantransformeddistance) # Weight the differences by the sample weights distortionloss = np.sum(weights absdiffs) # Step 5: Multiply by alpha finalloss = alpha distortionloss return finalloss Edge Cases and Pitfalls: If t=0, t^\lambda with \lambda < 0 results in infinity. In practice, metric distances are strictly positive for samples behind the camera, but care must be taken if samples are exactly at the camera origin. A small epsilon might be needed, though the source does not specify this. The transformation is non-linear, so the interpretation of the loss value changes. It is not directly comparable to the standard distortion loss magnitude. Gradient Scaling is a technique used in differentiable volume rendering to mitigate near-camera overfitting and the formation of "floaters" (spurious geometry artifacts) during radiance field optimization. It addresses the problem of gradient imbalance along rays, where samples far from the camera receive significantly smaller gradients than those near the camera due to the exponential decay of transmittance. Unlike Distortion Loss with Power Transformation, which modifies the loss function to penalize metric distance, Gradient Scaling modifies the optimization process itself by rescaling gradients during backpropagation to ensure uniform gradient magnitude across all samples on a ray. Weight regularization is a loss term applied to neural radiance fields (NeRFs) to suppress geometric noise and cloud-like semi-transparent artifacts that arise when training alters density distributions. It encourages a concentrated density distribution by penalizing pairs of samples with scattered large weights, forcing rays to either have zero weights along the entire ray or consolidate all weights into as small an area as possible [2, unofficial]. Unlike mip-NeRF 360, which optimizes distances to reduce floaters, this method explicitly penalizes weight scattering to maintain clean geometry during optimization. Strengths: Significantly improves the quality of rendered videos by reducing "floaters" near the camera. Limitations: Does not significantly improve test-set metrics on the 360 dataset, as floaters do not tend to contribute much to error metrics computed on still images. Performance: The transformation is computationally inexpensive, involving only basic arithmetic operations. When to use: When video quality is a priority and floaters near the camera are a noticeable artifact. When not to use: When optimizing for standard image-based metrics (e.g., PSNR, SSID) on static datasets, as the improvement is negligible. The power transformation was introduced in the context of mip-NeRF 360 and its extensions, specifically in the Zip-NeRF paper. It was developed to address the issue of "floaters" near the camera in unbounded scene rendering. The method builds on the distortion loss introduced in mip-NeRF 360, adapting it to be more sensitive to errors close to the camera by curving the metric distance space.
