name: Camera Pose and Parameter Optimization
body: This family of methods addresses the problem of optimizing camera parameters (extrinsics and intrinsics) simultaneously with Neural Radiance Field (NeRF) weights, eliminating the reliance on pre-computed Structure-from-Motion (SfM) pipelines like COLMAP. By treating camera poses as learnable parameters, these methods enable 3D reconstruction from sparse or uncalibrated image sets. What sets this family apart from siblings like Time-dependent NeRF with Continuous Camera Motion is the explicit optimization of discrete camera poses per image rather than continuous motion functions, and from Camera Preconditioning by focusing on the joint gradient-based update of poses and scene geometry rather than preconditioning the optimizer for faster convergence. All methods in this family share the core mechanism of differentiable rendering, where the rendered pixel color \hat{C}(r) is a differentiable function of the camera pose P and the NeRF parameters \Theta. The optimization problem is typically formulated as minimizing a loss function \mathcal{L} with respect to both \Theta and P: \min{\Theta, P} \mathcal{L}(\hat{C}(r; \Theta, P), C(r)) where C(r) is the ground-truth pixel color. The gradient \nablaP \mathcal{L} allows the camera pose to be updated via an optimizer (e.g., Adam, SGD) in lockstep with the NeRF weights. Key shared components include: 1. Ray Casting: Computing ray origins \hat{o} and directions \hat{d} from pixel coordinates using current camera estimates. For a pinhole camera model with focal length f and rotation R and translation t: \hat{o} = t \hat{d} = R \begin{pmatrix} (u - W/2)/f \\ -(v - H/2)/f \\ -1 \end{pmatrix} 2. Differentiable Rendering: The volume rendering integral is computed via discrete summation, allowing backpropagation through the ray marching process to the pose parameters. 3. Joint Optimization: Separate optimizers or a combined optimizer are used to update NeRF weights and pose parameters, often with different learning rates to stabilize convergence. Simultaneously optimizes camera poses and NeRF parameters without pre-estimated intrinsics/extrinsics. It solves reconstruction from sparse, forward-facing views where camera parameters are unknown. Unlike baseline NeRF, it treats poses as learnable parameters, achieving NVS quality comparable to baseline NeRF (\DeltaSSIM and \DeltaLPIPS \approx 0.05) without external pose estimation. A two-stage method for 2D X-ray to 3D CT registration. It combines a differentiable neural network similarity loss for global convergence with a Gradient-based Normalized Cross-Correlation (Grad-NCC) loss for local refinement. It leverages network features for coarse alignment and gradient-based correlation for fine-tuning, decoupling the optimization landscape into two phases. Trains NeRFs without precomputed poses by optimizing relative poses between consecutive frames using undistorted monocular depth priors. It differs from global alignment methods by generating a dense point cloud from monocular depth and constraining optimization via point cloud and photometric losses. Creates resilient NeRFs from monocular videos without known poses using self-supervised monocular depth estimation (SMDE) for depth and pose priors. It uses an alternating algorithm to harmonize NeRF outputs with SMDE through error-tolerant regularization, progressively refining geometry and camera parameters. An optimization-based state estimation filter for robot pose estimation within a NeRF using only monocular RGB images. It treats the problem as recursive Bayesian estimation, balancing NeRF-based photometric loss with dynamics prediction loss, and explicitly incorporates system dynamics and uncertainty propagation. A vision-based robot navigation pipeline combining trajectory planning and pose filtering in a receding horizon loop. It solves navigation with uncertain initial poses by continuously replanning trajectories based on updated state beliefs, allowing changes in homotopy classes around obstacles. Optimizes dense flat output waypoints for differentially flat systems (e.g., quadrotors) using first-order gradient descent and NeRF density for implicit obstacle representation. It differs from static waypoint planners by using optimizable waypoints and implicit NeRF obstacles, requiring nonconvex optimization via automatic differentiation. A rigid NeRF registration method that minimizes a photometric loss between rendered images from two NeRFs, using VF and Normalizing Flows to guide ray sampling and generate novel views. Optimize a 6-DoF rigid transformation parameter (rotation and translation) to align the two NeRFs. Minimize a photometric loss (Equation 7 in the full paper) between rendered images from the aligned NeRFs. Use VF and Normalizing Flows to sample novel camera viewpoints and guide ray sampling during optimization. learnable scale factor (added to the 6-DoF parameters to handle unknown scale and illumination changes between scenes). Photometric loss is susceptible to inaccuracies on textureless surfaces. High symmetry can cause convergence to a partially accurate solution that deviates by 180° from the true solution. Partial overlap or moving objects are not explicitly handled and may cause failure. A training strategy that gradually increases the angular distance of sampled target viewpoints from source views to stabilize optimization. Sample noise uniformly from interval [-\beta, +\beta] and add it to original Euler rotation angles of input view poses. Parameter \beta: Grows linearly from 3 to 9 degrees throughout the course of optimization. The problem of optimizing camera poses jointly with NeRF parameters was first explicitly addressed in the context of unknown camera parameters by NeRF with Unknown Camera Parameters, which demonstrated that joint optimization could achieve quality comparable to COLMAP-initialized NeRFs. Subsequent work expanded this to include depth priors (NoPe-NeRF, AltNeRF) and specific applications like medical imaging (Hybrid 2D/3D Registration) and robotics (Vision-Only Pose Filtering, Online Receding Horizon Replanning, NeRF-based Trajectory Optimization). The technique of NeRF registration using Viewshed Fields was introduced in VF-NeRF. name: NeRF with Unknown Camera Parameters
head: Joint Camera Pose and Radiance Field Refinement, Joint Optimization of NeRF and Poses, Joint optimisation of NeRF and camera parameters, NeRF with unknown cameras, NeRF without known camera parameters, NeRF-- (NeRF without known camera parameters)
body: This method simultaneously optimizes the camera poses P and the Neural Radiance Field (NeRF) parameters \theta without requiring pre-estimated camera parameters. It solves the problem of reconstructing 3D scenes from sparse, forward-facing views where camera intrinsics and extrinsics are unknown. Unlike baseline NeRF which relies on external Structure-from-Motion (SfM) pipelines like COLMAP, this approach eliminates the need for pre-estimated camera poses by treating them as learnable parameters. It achieves novel view synthesis (NVS) quality comparable to baseline NeRF (with \DeltaSSIM and \DeltaLPIPS \approx 0.05) but requires no external pose estimation. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: A set of N RGB images \{Ii\}{i=1}^N without associated camera poses or intrinsics. Optionally, depth priors may be used to guide sampling. Outputs: A trained NeRF model F\Theta and optimized camera parameters \{\pii\}{i=1}^N for each image. Data Structures: NeRF Model (F\Theta): A multi-layer perceptron (MLP) mapping 3D coordinates and viewing directions to color and density. Layout: Standard NeRF architecture. Modification: Hidden layer dimension is reduced from 256 to 128 for computational efficiency. Camera Parameters (\pii): For each image i, parameters are \pii = (f, \phii, ti). f: Focal length (scalar, shared across images). \phii: Rotation parameters (axis-angle vector). ti: Translation vector (3D). Depth Priors (Optional): If using depth-guided methods, a pre-trained monocular depth network provides \hat{D}{idpt}. Numbered Steps: 1. Initialization: Initialize NeRF weights \Theta using Kaiming initialization. Initialize all camera poses at the origin, looking in the -z direction. Initialize focal length f to the image width. If using depth priors, initialize learnable linear transformation coefficients si, ki for undistorting depth maps. 2. Ray Casting: For each training iteration: a. Randomly select M pixels from each input image Ii. b. For each pixel p=(u,v), compute the ray origin \hat{o}i and direction \hat{d}{i,p} using current camera estimates \hat{\pi}i = (\hat{f}, \hat{\phi}i, \hat{t}i): \hat{o}i = \hat{t}i \hat{d}{i,p} = \hat{R}i \begin{pmatrix} (u - W/2)/\hat{f} \\ -(v - H/2)/\hat{f} \\ -1 \end{pmatrix} where \hat{R}i is the rotation matrix computed from \hat{\phi}i using Rodrigues' formula. c. Sample K 3D points \{xj\}{j=1}^K uniformly along the ray. In standard implementations, K=128. In depth-guided variants, sampling may be truncated based on depth priors. 3. NeRF Evaluation: Evaluate the NeRF model F\Theta at each sampled point xj to obtain radiance color cj and density \sigmaj. 4. Volume Rendering: Aggregate the predicted radiance and densities along the ray to compute the rendered pixel color \hat{C}(r): \hat{C}(r) = \sum{j=1}^K Tj \alphaj cj where \alphaj = 1 - \exp(-\sigmaj \deltaj) and Tj = \exp(-\sum{l=1}^{j-1} \sigmal \deltal). 5. Loss Computation: Compute the reconstruction loss between rendered colors \hat{C}(r) and ground-truth colors C(r). If depth priors are used, add a self-supervised depth loss: \mathcal{L}{self-depth} = \sum{i} (si \hat{D}{idpt} + ki) - D{infer} where D{infer} is the rendered depth map. 6. Optimization: Minimize the total loss using separate Adam optimizers for NeRF weights, camera poses, and focal lengths. Backpropagate gradients through the differentiable rendering pipeline to update all parameters jointly. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math import random def rodriguesrotation(phi): """Compute rotation matrix from axis-angle vector phi using Rodrigues' formula.""" theta = math.sqrt(phi[0]2 + phi[1]2 + phi[2]2) if theta < 1e-8: return [[1, 0, 0], [0, 1, 0], [0, 0, 1]] k = [phi[0]/theta, phi[1]/theta, phi[2]/theta] cost = math.cos(theta) sint = math.sin(theta) R = [ [cost + k[0]2(1-cost), k[0]k[1](1-cost) - k[2]sint, k[0]k[2](1-cost) + k[1]sint], [k[1]k[0](1-cost) + k[2]sint, cost + k[1]2(1-cost), k[1]k[2](1-cost) - k[0]sint], [k[2]k[0](1-cost) - k[1]sint, k[2]k[1](1-cost) + k[0]sint, cost + k[2]2(1-cost)] ] return R def renderray(rayo, rayd, nerfmodel, numsamples=128): """Render a single ray using volume rendering.""" zvals = [i (1.0 / numsamples) for i in range(numsamples)] pts = [[rayo[0] + rayd[0]z, rayo[1] + rayd[1]z, rayo[2] + rayd[2]z] for z in zvals] samples = [nerfmodel(p, rayd) for p in pts] colors = [s[0] for s in samples] densities = [s[1] for s in samples] deltas = [zvals[i+1] - zvals[i] for i in range(numsamples-1)] deltas.append(1e-3) alphas = [1.0 - math.exp(-densities[i] deltas[i]) for i in range(numsamples)] transmittances = [1.0] for i in range(numsamples-1): transmittances.append(transmittances[-1] (1.0 - alphas[i])) weights = [alphas[i] transmittances[i] for i in range(numsamples)] color = [sum(weights[i] colors[i][c] for i in range(numsamples)) for c in range(3)] return color def trainnerfunknowncameras(images, nerfmodel, numepochs=10000, pixelsperimage=1024): """Jointly optimize NeRF and camera parameters.""" N = len(images) H, W = len(images[0]), len(images[0][0]) f = W phis = [[0.0, 0.0, 0.0] for in range(N)] ts = [[0.0, 0.0, 0.0] for in range(N)] lrnerf, lrpose, lrfocal = 0.001, 0.001, 0.001 for epoch in range(numepochs): if epoch > 0 and epoch % 10 == 0: lrnerf = 0.9954 if epoch > 0 and epoch % 100 == 0: lrpose = 0.9; lrfocal = 0.9 for i in range(N): img = images[i] ulist = [random.randint(0, W-1) for in range(pixelsperimage)] vlist = [random.randint(0, H-1) for in range(pixelsperimage)] Ri = rodriguesrotation(phis[i]) rayo = ts[i] renderedcolors = [] for j in range(pixelsperimage): u, v = ulist[j], vlist[j] dirlocal = [(u - W/2)/f, -(v - H/2)/f, -1.0] rayd = [ Ri[0][0]dirlocal[0] + Ri[0][1]dirlocal[1] + Ri[0][2]dirlocal[2], Ri[1][0]dirlocal[0] + Ri[1][1]dirlocal[1] + Ri[1][2]dirlocal[2], Ri[2][0]dirlocal[0] + Ri[2][1]dirlocal[1] + Ri[2][2]dirlocal[2] ] renderedcolors.append(renderray(rayo, rayd, nerfmodel)) loss = sum((renderedcolors[j][c] - img[vlist[j]][ulist[j]][c])2 for j in range(pixelsperimage) for c in range(3)) / pixelsperimage # Optimizer step: compute gradients w.r.t. nerfmodel, phis[i], ts[i], f # and apply updates: param -= lr grad pass return nerfmodel, phis, ts, f Parameters: Pixels per image (M): 1024. Points per ray (K): 128. Hidden layer dimension: 128. Initial Learning Rate: 0.001 for all optimizers. NeRF LR Decay: Every 10 epochs, multiply by 0.9954. Pose/Focal LR Decay: Every 100 epochs, multiply by 0.9. Training Duration: 10,000 epochs. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Local Minima: Joint optimization may trap into local minima for certain scenes (e.g., Orchids, Room), resulting in inaccurate intrinsics and worse NVS quality compared to baseline. Intrinsic Accuracy: Optimized focal lengths may deviate significantly from ground truth in difficult scenes (e.g., difference of 199.3 and 331.8 in some cases). Parameterizes camera-to-world rotation matrices Ri using 6-dimensional embeddings. The camera location is computed as ti = -Ri \times Ti, where Ti is the published 3D vector of the origin in camera i's reference frame. The pose is represented as a 3x4 matrix (Ri, ti) representing an element of SE(3). Time Complexity: Training is significantly slower than baseline NeRF due to the additional gradients flowing through camera parameters and the larger parameter space. Memory Complexity: Similar to baseline NeRF, with minor overhead for storing camera parameters. Performance: On the Blender Forward Facing (BLEFF) dataset, NeRF-- achieves comparable NVS quality to baseline NeRF (using COLMAP poses) with \DeltaSSIM and \DeltaLPIPS \approx 0.05. Strengths: Eliminates the need for pre-estimated camera poses (e.g., from COLMAP), making it applicable to scenarios where SfM fails or is unavailable. Limitations: Susceptible to local minima, particularly for scenes with limited viewpoint coverage or ambiguous geometry. Convergence is sensitive to initialization and learning rate schedules. Origin: The method was introduced in "NeRF--: Neural Radiance Fields Without Known Camera Parameters". History: Prior methods relied on external SfM pipelines to estimate camera poses before training NeRF. This work demonstrated that camera parameters could be jointly optimized with the radiance field in a fully differentiable manner. Usage: Used in scenarios where camera parameters are unknown or unreliable, such as real-world captured image sequences or synthetic datasets with perturbed poses. name: Hybrid 2D/3D Registration Optimization Pipeline
head: Net+GradNCC, Two-Stage Similarity Optimization
body: The Hybrid 2D/3D Registration Optimization Pipeline is a two-stage method for estimating the 6 Degrees of Freedom (DoF) pose of a 2D X-ray image relative to a 3D CT volume. It combines a differentiable network similarity loss for global convergence with a traditional Gradient-based Normalized Cross-Correlation (Grad-NCC) loss for local refinement. The pipeline optimizes pose parameters \theta (rotation and translation) in two sequential stages. Inputs: 1. Fixed 3D volume V{CT} (CT scan). 2. Moving 2D target image I{target} (X-ray). 3. Initial pose estimate \theta0 (randomly sampled from a distribution, e.g., rotation N(0, 15^\circ), translation N(0, 30 \text{ mm})). 4. Segmentation mask V{Seg} used as input to the network forward pass. Outputs: 1. Optimized pose parameters \theta^. Data Structures: Pose parameters \theta: Represented as rotation and translation components. Loss values: Scalar values LN and L{GNNC} tracked over iterations to monitor convergence. Step 1: Global Optimization (Network Loss) 1. Initialize pose parameters \theta. 2. Generate a Digitally Reconstructed Radiograph (DRR) I{DRR} from V{CT} and current \theta using a differentiable renderer (e.g., ProST). 3. Compute the network similarity loss LN between I{target} and I{DRR} using V{Seg} as network input. 4. Update \theta using Stochastic Gradient Descent (SGD) with momentum 0.9. 5. Use a cyclic learning rate schedule oscillating between 1 \times 10^{-6} and 1 \times 10^{-4} every 100 steps. 6. Monitor convergence by calculating the standard deviation of LN over the last 10 iterations, denoted as std{LN}. 7. If std{LN} < 3 \times 10^{-3}, switch to Step 2. Otherwise, repeat Step 4. Step 2: Local Refinement (Grad-NCC Loss) 1. Compute the Gradient-based Normalized Cross-Correlation loss L{GNNC} between I{target} and I{DRR}. 2. Update \theta using SGD with momentum 0.9. 3. Use a cyclic learning rate schedule oscillating between 1 \times 10^{-3} and 3 \times 10^{-3}. 4. Monitor convergence by calculating the standard deviation of L{GNNC} over the last 10 iterations, denoted as std{L{GNNC}}. 5. If std{L{GNNC}} < 1 \times 10^{-5}, terminate. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def hybrid2d3dregistration(VCT, Itarget, thetainit, VSeg=None): theta = thetainit LNhistory = [] LGNNChistory = [] velocity = 0.0 def getcycliclr(iteration, minlr, maxlr, period): return minlr + (maxlr - minlr) (iteration % period) / period def sgdstep(theta, grad, lr, momentum): nonlocal velocity velocity = momentum velocity - lr grad return theta + velocity def standarddeviation(history): if len(history) < 2: return float('inf') mean = sum(history) / len(history) return (sum((x - mean) 2 for x in history) / len(history)) 0.5 # Stage 1: Global Optimization for iteration in range(100000): # Max iterations based on network training # Generate DRR from VCT and theta using differentiable renderer # Sources do not provide the exact DRR generation implementation. IDRR = generatedrr(VCT, theta) # # Compute network similarity loss LN # Sources do not provide the exact network loss implementation. LN = computenetworkloss(Itarget, IDRR, VSeg) # LNhistory.append(LN) # Compute gradient and update theta with SGD, momentum 0.9 # Sources do not provide the exact gradient computation implementation. gradLN = computegradient(LN) # lr = getcycliclr(iteration, 1e-6, 1e-4, 100) theta = sgdstep(theta, gradLN, lr, 0.9) if len(LNhistory) >= 10: if standarddeviation(LNhistory[-10:]) < 3e-3: break # Stage 2: Local Refinement for iteration in range(100000): IDRR = generatedrr(VCT, theta) # # Compute Grad-NCC loss LGNNC # Sources do not provide the exact Grad-NCC implementation. LGNNC = computegradnccloss(Itarget, IDRR) # LGNNChistory.append(LGNNC) gradLGNNC = computegradient(LGNNC) # lr = getcycliclr(iteration, 1e-3, 3e-3, 100) theta = sgdstep(theta, gradLGNNC, lr, 0.9) if len(LGNNChistory) >= 10: if standarddeviation(LGNNChistory[-10:]) < 1e-5: break return theta Parameters: Momentum: 0.9 for both stages. Stage 1 Learning Rate: Cyclic between 1 \times 10^{-6} and 1 \times 10^{-4}, period 100 steps. Stage 2 Learning Rate: Cyclic between 1 \times 10^{-3} and 3 \times 10^{-3}. Stage 1 Convergence Threshold: std{LN} < 3 \times 10^{-3}. Stage 2 Convergence Threshold: std{L{GNNC}} < 1 \times 10^{-5}. Batch Size: 2 (for training the network component, if applicable). Edge Cases and Pitfalls: The switch criterion relies on the standard deviation of the loss over a small window (10 iterations). If the loss oscillates significantly due to learning rate cycling, premature switching may occur. The method assumes the differentiable renderer (ProST) is available and differentiable with respect to pose parameters. This method performs 6 Degrees of Freedom (DoF) slice-to-volume registration by minimizing the negative Zero-Normalized Cross-Correlation (ZNCC) between a fixed Digitally Reconstructed Radiograph (DRR) and a moving DRR using gradient descent. It serves as the local refinement stage of the Hybrid 2D/3D Registration Optimization Pipeline, leveraging the locally convex loss landscape of ZNCC to converge quickly from random initializations. Unlike the global network-based loss (LN) in its parent pipeline, this method relies on traditional gradient descent with momentum, requiring differentiable DRR generation to compute gradients with respect to pose parameters. Time Complexity: The method requires two sequential optimization phases. Memory Complexity: Depends on the memory footprint of the differentiable renderer and the network. Measured Performance: Tested on 150 simulation studies and 100 real X-ray registrations (cadaver specimens). The method is less sensitive to local textures compared to traditional image-based methods like Grad-NCC alone. Strengths: Combines global convergence of network-based features with local precision of gradient-based correlation. Robust to initial pose errors (rotation N(0, 15^\circ), translation N(0, 30 \text{ mm})). Limitations: Requires a trained network for the first stage. The switch criterion is heuristic. When to use: When robust global alignment is needed before fine-tuning, especially in the presence of local texture ambiguities. When not to use: When computational resources are extremely limited and a single-stage method is preferred, or when the network is not available/trained. The method was introduced in the paper "Generalizing Spatial Transformers to Projective Geometry with Applications to 2D/3D Registration". It addresses the limitations of traditional image-based methods like Grad-NCC, which are sensitive to local textures, and pure differentiable methods that may get stuck in local minima. The pipeline was tested on simulated data from NIH Cancer CT scans and real X-ray images from cadaver specimens. name: Gradient Descent Registration via ZNCC
head: Slice-to-Volume Registration via Gradient Descent, ZNCC-based 6 DoF Registration
body:
This method performs 6 Degrees of Freedom (DoF) slice-to-volume registration by minimizing the negative Zero-Normalized Cross-Correlation (ZNCC) between a fixed Digitally Reconstructed Radiograph (DRR) and a moving DRR using gradient descent. It serves as the local refinement stage of the Hybrid 2D/3D Registration Optimization Pipeline, leveraging the locally convex loss landscape of ZNCC to converge quickly from random initializations. Unlike the global network-based loss (LN) in its parent pipeline, this method relies on traditional gradient descent with momentum, requiring differentiable DRR generation to compute gradients with respect to pose parameters. Inputs: Fixed DRR image I{fixed} generated from ground truth parameters \eta^. Moving DRR image I{moving} generated from initial parameters \eta0. CT Volume data (implicit in DRR generation). Hyperparameters: Learning rates  eta{	heta\phi\gamma},  eta{xyz}, momentum \lambda, maximum iterations N{max}, and convergence threshold. Outputs: Optimized 6 DoF pose parameters \eta{opt} = (	heta, \phi, \gamma, bx, by, bz). The pose is represented as a vector of 6 parameters: \eta = [	heta, \phi, \gamma, bx, by, bz] 	heta, \phi, \gamma: Rotations. bx, by, bz: Translations in millimeters. name: NoPe-NeRF
head: No Pose NeRF
body: NoPe-NeRF is a method for training Neural Radiance Fields (NeRF) without precomputed camera poses, addressing the challenge of optimizing relative poses between consecutive frames using undistorted monocular depth priors. It differs from methods that rely on global alignment or iterative pose refinement by generating a dense point cloud from a monocular depth estimation network and constraining the optimization via a point cloud loss and a photometric loss. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: A sequence of undistorted monocular images; a pre-trained monocular depth estimation network; initial camera pose estimates (often identity or coarse alignment). Outputs: Optimized NeRF model parameters (\Theta) and optimized camera poses (\pii = (Ri, ti)) for each input image. Data Structures: NeRF Model: Standard MLP-based representation mapping 5D coordinates (x, y, z, \theta, \phi) to volume density \sigma and view-dependent color c. Depth Map: A 2D array D \in \mathbb{R}^{H \times W} representing per-pixel depth values from the monocular estimator. Point Cloud: A set of 3D points P = \{(Xj, Yj, Zj)\} generated by unprojecting the depth map using the current camera intrinsics and extrinsics. Numbered Steps: 1. Monocular Depth Estimation: For each input image Ii, pass it through a pre-trained monocular depth estimation network to generate a dense depth map Di. 2. Point Cloud Generation: Unproject the undistorted depth map Di into 3D space using the current camera parameters (intrinsics K and extrinsics Ri, ti) to form a point cloud Pi. Pi = \text{Unproject}(Di, K, Ri, ti) 3. NeRF Rendering: Render the image I{\text{rendered}} from the current NeRF model using the current camera parameters. 4. Loss Computation: Compute two loss terms: Photometric Loss (\mathcal{L}{\text{photo}}): The difference between the rendered image and the input image, typically Mean Squared Error (MSE) or L1 loss. Point Cloud Loss (\mathcal{L}{\text{pc}}): A loss function that constrains the relative poses between consecutive frames by measuring the consistency of the generated point clouds across frames. 5. Joint Optimization: Minimize the total loss \mathcal{L}{\text{total}} = \mathcal{L}{\text{photo}} + \lambda \mathcal{L}{\text{pc}} using gradient descent to update both the NeRF weights \Theta and the camera parameters \pii. The parameter \lambda balances the two losses. 6. Depth Prior Correction: During training, correct the shift parameters and scale of the monocular depth prior to improve its alignment with the NeRF geometry. Formulas: Total Loss: \mathcal{L}{\text{total}} = \mathcal{L}{\text{photo}}(I{\text{rendered}}, I{\text{input}}) + \lambda \mathcal{L}{\text{pc}}(Pi, P{i+1}) where \mathcal{L}{\text{photo}} is typically MSE: \mathcal{L}{\text{photo}} = \frac{1}{N} \sum{p=1}^{N} \| I{\text{rendered}}(p) - I{\text{input}}(p) \|^2 and \mathcal{L}{\text{pc}} constrains the relative poses between consecutive frames. Parameters: \lambda: Weight for the point cloud loss. Not given in the sources. Learning rates: Not given in the sources. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Scale Ambiguity: Monocular depth lacks absolute scale, requiring correction of shift and scale parameters during training. Challenging Trajectories: The method is designed to handle challenging camera trajectories by jointly optimizing the NeRF model and relative poses. Pseudocode: Unverified code. Args: images: List of input images. depthnet: Pre-trained monocular depth estimation network. initialposes: List of initial camera poses [(R, t),...]. lr: Learning rate for joint optimization. epochs: Number of training epochs. lambdapc: Weight for point cloud loss. K: Camera intrinsic matrix. Returns: Optimized NeRF model parameters and camera poses. """ # Initialize NeRF MLP parameters theta theta = initializemlp() # Camera poses: list of (R, t) tensors requiring gradients poses = [pose.clone().requiresgrad() for pose in initialposes] # Joint optimizer for NeRF weights and poses optimizer = torch.optim.Adam(list(theta.parameters()) + poses, lr=lr) for epoch in range(epochs): for i in range(len(images)): # Step 1: Monocular Depth Estimation depthmap = depthnet(images[i]) # Step 2: Point Cloud Generation # Unproject depth map using current camera pose pointsi = unprojectdepth(depthmap, poses[i][0], poses[i][1], K) # Step 3: NeRF Rendering renderedimage = rendernerf(theta, poses[i][0], poses[i][1], K, images[i].shape) # Step 4: Loss Computation # Photometric Loss lossphoto = mseloss(renderedimage, images[i]) losspc = 0.0 if i < len(images) - 1: # Get next frame's point cloud for relative pose constraint depthnext = depthnet(images[i+1]) pointsnext = unprojectdepth(depthnext, poses[i+1][0], poses[i+1][1], K) losspc = pointcloudconsistencyloss(pointsi, pointsnext) totalloss = lossphoto + lambdapc losspc # Step 5: Joint Optimization optimizer.zerograd() totalloss.backward() optimizer.step() # Step 6: Depth Prior Correction # Correct scale and shift of depthmap to align with NeRF geometry # Implementation: differentiable affine transformation optimized jointly depthmap = correctdepthpriorscaleshift(depthmap, poses[i]) return theta, poses def initializemlp(): """Initialize standard NeRF MLP parameters.""" return torch.nn.ModuleDict({ 'density': torch.nn.Linear(3, 1), 'color': torch.nn.Sequential(torch.nn.Linear(3+3, 64), torch.nn.ReLU(), torch.nn.Linear(64, 3)) }) def unprojectdepth(depthmap, R, t, K): """Unproject depth map to 3D point cloud.""" H, W = depthmap.shape u, v = torch.meshgrid(torch.arange(W), torch.arange(H), indexing='xy') ones = torch.oneslike(u) xy = torch.stack([u, v, ones], dim=-1).float() # Back-project to camera space camcoords = torch.matmul(torch.inverse(K), xy.permute(2, 0, 1).reshape(3, -1)) camcoords = camcoords depthmap.reshape(1, -1) # Transform to world space worldcoords = torch.matmul(R, camcoords) + t.reshape(3, 1) return worldcoords.permute(1, 0).reshape(H, W, 3) def rendernerf(theta, R, t, K, imgshape): """Render image from NeRF using volume rendering.""" # Standard differentiable volume rendering integral # Computes ray origins o=t, directions d=Runproject(u,v), samples along ray, # accumulates color and alpha using discrete summation [Parent] return torch.zeros(imgshape) # Placeholder for standard volume rendering implementation def mseloss(rendered, target): """Mean Squared Error loss.""" return torch.mean((rendered - target) 2) def pointcloudconsistencyloss(pointsi, pointsnext): """Compute loss constraining relative poses between consecutive frames.""" # Measures geometric consistency between point clouds of consecutive frames # Implemented as mean squared distance to nearest neighbors after rigid alignment return torch.mean((pointsi - pointsnext) 2) def correctdepthpriorscaleshift(depthmap, pose): """Correct scale and shift of monocular depth prior during training.""" # Applies differentiable affine transformation d' = sd + b # Optimized jointly with pose and NeRF weights s = torch.tensor(1.0, requiresgrad=True) b = torch.tensor(0.0, requiresgrad=True) return s depthmap + b A technique to estimate depth from a single image, providing the initial geometric prior. It sets the stage for NoPe-NeRF by providing the dense point cloud. It is distinct from stereo or LiDAR methods as it operates on single views. When to choose it: when only monocular sequences are available and precomputed poses are missing. [Link to relevant article if available, otherwise leave empty]. A loss function that enforces geometric consistency between point clouds generated from consecutive frames. It is distinct from photometric loss as it operates in 3D space. It sets it apart from pure photometric pose optimization methods by directly constraining relative camera motion via geometry. When to choose it: when training NeRFs without precomputed poses and monocular depth priors are reliable. [Link to relevant article if available, otherwise leave empty]. Time Complexity: Depends on the depth estimation network and the NeRF rendering time. Typically, each iteration involves a forward pass through the depth network and the NeRF. Memory Complexity: Requires storing the depth maps and point clouds for all frames, which can be memory-intensive for large datasets. Measured Performance: Outperforms existing methods in novel view rendering quality and pose estimation accuracy on the Temples and ScanNet datasets. On the LLFF dataset, it achieves 1-2 points higher PSNR for 3, 6, and 9 input views compared to baseline methods. Strengths: Handles challenging camera trajectories; does not require precomputed poses; leverages monocular depth priors for geometric constraints. Limitations: Relies on the accuracy of the monocular depth estimation network; may struggle with scale ambiguity. When to Use: When camera poses are unknown or unreliable, and monocular depth estimation is feasible. When Not to Use: When high-precision precomputed poses are available, or when the scene has significant textureless regions that confuse depth estimation. NoPe-NeRF was proposed by Bian et al. in 2023. It addresses the limitations of previous methods like SC-NeRF, which struggled with large camera movements. The method builds on the idea of using monocular depth priors to guide NeRF optimization, correcting shift and scale parameters during training. It is used in applications requiring novel view synthesis from uncalibrated image sequences, such as indoor scene reconstruction. name: AltNeRF
head: Alternating Depth-Pose Optimization
body: AltNeRF is a framework for creating resilient Neural Radiance Field (NeRF) representations from monocular videos without relying on known camera poses. It solves the problem of suboptimal NeRF reconstruction caused by the lack of explicit 3D supervision and imprecise initial camera poses by using self-supervised monocular depth estimation (SMDE) to generate depth and pose priors. Unlike methods that strictly align rendered depth with priors, AltNeRF uses an alternating algorithm to harmonize NeRF outputs with SMDE through error-tolerant regularization, progressively refining both the scene geometry and camera parameters. AltNeRF comprises two components: the Scene Prior Module (SPM) and the Scene Representation Module (SRM). The SPM provides robust depth and pose estimates as a scene prior, while the SRM refines these initial poses and learns the 3D scene representation, regularized by the depth priors. The refined outputs are fed back to the SPM to improve its performance. Input: Monocular video data V and known camera intrinsics K. Output: A trained NeRF representation fn (density \sigma and color c) and refined camera poses P. Scene Prior Module (SPM) The SPM consists of two networks: 1. Depth Network (fd): Encoder: ResNet-50 with the fully-connected layer removed. Decoder: Ten 3 \times 3 convolutional layers (two per scale) with bilinear up-sampling. Input: Image I. Output: Depth map D. 2. Pose Network (fp): Structure: ResNet-34. Input: Pair of images (It, Is) (target and source). Output: Vector of 9 elements. The first 6 elements are a continuous rotation representation. The last 3 elements are translations. Relative Pose: Predicts P{t \to s}, the transformation from source to target. Scene Representation Module (SRM) 1. NeRF Network (fn): Structure: Eight fully-connected layers with skip connections for density output, and one linear layer for color. Input: 3D point p \in \mathbb{R}^3 and unit viewing direction d \in \mathbb{R}^3. Output: Density \sigma and color c. \alpha: Weight for L1 term in photometric loss. Value: 0.85. \gamma: Scalar hyper-parameter balancing reconstruction and depth regularization losses. Value: 0.08 for LLFF and CO3D; 0.15 for ScanNet and Captures. \epsilon: Tolerance coefficient for error-tolerant depth regularization. Not given in the sources. Sr: Number of SRM iterations per alternation. Value: 50,000. Sp: Number of SPM fine-tuning iterations per alternation. Value: 500. Alternations: Number of full alternating cycles. Value: 2. SPM Pretrain LR: Learning rate for pretraining SPM. Value: 10^{-4}. SPM Fine-tune LR: Learning rate for fine-tuning SPM. Value: 5.0 \times 10^{-5}. SRM NeRF LR: Initial learning rate for NeRF learning in SRM. Value: 10^{-3}, exponentially decays to 10^{-4}. SRM Pose LR: Initial learning rate for pose refinement. Value: 10^{-5}, linearly increases to 2.0 \times 10^{-3} after 1,000 iterations, then exponentially decays to 10^{-5}. 1. SPM Pretraining: Pretrain the SPM (fd, fp) on a large dataset (e.g., NYUv2, VOID) using photometric loss Lp, distilling loss Lr, and edge-aware smoothness loss Ls. Photometric Loss Lp: Lp(It, \hat{I}t) = (1 - \text{SSIM}(It, \hat{I}t)) + \frac{\alpha}{2} (1 - \alpha) \| It - \hat{I}t \|1 where \hat{I}t is the reconstructed target frame warped from source views using predicted depth and pose. Edge-aware Smoothness Loss Ls: Ls = |\partialx D| e^{-|\partialx I|} + |\partialy D| e^{-|\partialy I|} where \partialx and \partialy are image gradients along horizontal and vertical axes. Distilling Loss Lr: Lr = 1 - \text{SSIM}(D, Dr) + 0.1 \times (Er \oplus E / \text{size}(E)) where Dr is a reference depth map from an off-the-shelf estimator, Er and E are occluding boundary maps, and \oplus is the XOR operation. Total SPM Loss: L{pt} = Lp + Lr + 1.0 \times 10^{-3} \times Ls. 2. Pose Initialization: Establish a world coordinate system aligning with the first frame I0 (identity matrix). Calculate initial camera poses Pi using the chain rule: Pi = P{i-1 \to i} \times P{i-1}, where P{i-1 \to i} is the relative transformation predicted by SPM. Use the SPM pose prior P0 as initialization for SRM. Refine by optimizing a residual pose \Delta P. The refined pose is \hat{P} = \Delta P \times P. 3. Alternating Algorithm Workflow: The algorithm cycles through i = 0, \dots, N{alt}-1. Let \Phii be the SPM at step i and \Psii be the SRM. Step 3a: SRM Optimization (Scene Representation Module) Input: Initial pose Pi and depth prior Di. Warmup Learning: Set the learning rate of \Delta P to a low value initially, linearly increasing to the original rate after 1,000 iterations. Run SRM for Sr iterations. The NeRF fn is optimized to minimize: L{sr} = Lc + \gamma \cdot Le where Lc is the reconstruction loss: Lc = \| \hat{C}(r) - C(r) \|2 and Le is the error-tolerant depth regularization loss: Le = H\left( \max \left( \frac{\| \hat{D} - D \|1}{\hat{D} + D} - \epsilon, 0 \right) \right) where H(\cdot) is the Huber loss, \hat{D} is the rendered depth, and D is the depth prior. Rendered Depth \hat{D}(r) for ray r = o + td: \hat{D}(r) = \int{tn}^{tf} T(t) \sigma(t) t \, dt where T(t) = \exp(-\int{tn}^t \sigma(s) ds). Output: Estimated depth \hat{D}{i+1} and improved pose \hat{P}{i+1}. Step 3b: SPM Fine-tuning (Scene Prior Module) Input: \hat{D}{i+1} and \hat{P}{i+1}. Fine-tune SPM for Sp iterations. Use distillation loss Lr replacing reference depth Dr with rendered depth \hat{D}{i+1}. Supervise with total loss L{pt}. Output: Refined depth D{i+1} and pose P{i+1}. 4. Multi-view Consistency Check: Compute uncertainty Ut = \| Dt - D{s \to t} \|1, where D{s \to t} are depth maps warped from nearby source views using predicted poses. Incorporate uncertainty into loss functions (Lr and Le) by weighting them with \text{Softmin}(\cdot) to mitigate unreliable depth estimates. Unverified code. W/2)/K[0,0], -(v - H/2)/K[1,1], -1]) d = d / np.linalg.norm(d) rays.append({'origin': o, 'direction': d, 'gtcolor': frame[v, u]}) return rays def volumerender(rays, sigma, color): # Discrete volume rendering integral: sum T(t) sigma(t) c(t) dt rendered = np.zeros(len(rays)) for j, ray in enumerate(rays): t = np.linspace(0.1, 10.0, 128) dt = t[1] - t[0] T = np.exp(-np.cumsum(sigma[j] dt)) rendered[j] = np.sum(T sigma[j] t dt) return rendered def huberloss(x): return np.where(x < 1.0, 0.5 x2, x - 0.5) def softmin(x): return np.exp(-x) / (np.sum(np.exp(-x)) + 1e-8) def interpolatedepth(depthmap, rays): # Bilinear interpolation of depth map at ray positions return np.array([depthmap[int(r['origin'][1]), int(r['origin'][0])] for r in rays]) def computemultiviewuncertainty(depthmap, pose, frames, K): # Warps depth from neighbors, computes L1 difference, averages 4 smallest # Placeholder for standard multi-view warping logic return np.zeros(len(depthmap)) def distillationloss(preddepth, refdepth): # 1 - SSIM + 0.1 XORboundaryloss return 1.0 - ssim(preddepth, refdepth) + 0.1 xorboundaryloss(preddepth, refdepth) def photometricloss(frames, depthnet, posenet): # Warps frames, computes SSIM + L1 return np.mean((frames[0] - frames[1])2) def smoothnessloss(depthmap): # Gradient-weighted smoothness return np.mean(np.abs(np.gradient(depthmap))) def ssim(a, b): return 1.0 # Standard SSIM implementation def xorboundaryloss(a, b): return 0.0 # Standard boundary XOR implementation def applyresidualpose(P, deltap): return P # Standard 9-vec to 4x4 matrix conversion def WarmupSchedule(initiallr, peaklr, warmupiters): def fn(step): return initiallr + (peaklr - initiallr) min(step, warmupiters) / warmupiters return fn Time Complexity: Training takes 150K–200K total iterations, costing 4.0–6.4 hours on a single RTX 3090 GPU. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Resilient to imprecise camera poses and dynamic objects; leverages complementary strengths of SMDE (robust priors) and NeRF (fine geometry). Limitations: Relies on the quality of the initial SPM priors; alternating algorithm increases training time compared to single-pass methods. When to use: When camera poses are unknown and monocular video data is available. AltNeRF was proposed in 2024 by researchers at The Thirty-Eighth AAAI Conference on Artificial Intelligence. It builds on the BARF approach (Lin et al. 2021) by introducing depth regularization, improved pose initialization, and warmup learning. It addresses the limitations of existing NeRF approaches that suffer from suboptimal outcomes due to lack of explicit 3D supervision and imprecise camera poses. name: Vision-Only Pose Filtering in a NeRF
head: Optimization-based Pose Filter for NeRF, Recursive SE(3) Optimization
body: This method is an optimization-based state estimation filter that estimates the 6-DoF pose and velocities of a robot within a Neural Radiance Field (NeRF) using only onboard monocular RGB images. It addresses the limitation of single-shot pose estimators by treating the problem as recursive Bayesian estimation, balancing a NeRF-based photometric loss with a dynamics prediction loss to provide robustness in low-gradient regions and output state covariance. The method operates as a recursive filter at each timestep t, updating the robot's state belief based on a new image It, the previous action ut, and the prior state estimate. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: Current image It, previous action ut, prior state mean \mu{t-1}, prior state covariance \Sigma{t-1}, pre-trained NeRF model, and a subset of selected pixels I (identified via feature detection). Outputs: Updated state mean \mut, updated state covariance \Sigmat, and the robot pose Tt derived from \mut. Data Structures: State Vector \mut: Contains the robot's position, orientation (represented in SE(3)), and velocities. Covariance Matrix \Sigmat: A symmetric positive-definite matrix representing the uncertainty of the state estimate. Pixel Subset I: A set of 2D image coordinates (u, v) selected using an image feature detector (e.g., ORB) to bias sampling toward areas of high gradient information. Numbered Steps: 1. State Propagation (Prediction): Propagate the state mean and covariance forward using the system dynamics model f and the applied action ut. \mu{t|t-1} = f(\mu{t-1}, ut) A{t-1} = \left. \frac{\partial f(x, ut)}{\partial x} \right|{x=\mu{t-1}} \Sigma{t|t-1} = A{t-1} \Sigma{t-1} A{t-1}^T + Q{t-1} where Q{t-1} is the process noise covariance. 2. Pixel Selection: Select a subset of pixels I from the current image It using an image feature detector (e.g., ORB) to identify points of interest. 3. Optimization (Update): Minimize the cost function J(\mut) with respect to the state \mut to find the posterior mean \mut. The cost function combines a photometric loss and a process loss: J(\mut) = \| CI(Tt) - It(I) \|{St^{-1}}^2 + \| \mu{t|t-1} - \mut \|{\Sigma{t|t-1}^{-1}}^2 where: CI(Tt) represents the predicted pixel values for the selected subset I given the pose Tt (derived from \mut) and the NeRF. It(I) are the observed pixel values from the image It at locations I. St is the measurement noise covariance. The notation \| x \|M^2 = x^T M x denotes the weighted L2 norm. 4. Outlier Rejection: Perform outlier rejection on the per-pixel loss to reduce variance before or during the optimization step. 5. Covariance Update: Compute the posterior covariance \Sigmat using the Hessian of the loss function at the optimized mean: \Sigmat = \left( \left. \frac{\partial^2 J(x)}{\partial x^2} \right|{x=\mut} \right)^{-1} 6. Manifold Projection: During the optimization of \mut, project the pose back onto the SE(3) manifold after every gradient step. This "recursive SE(3)" approach is preferred over optimizing with respect to a reference pose and projecting once, as the multiplication of skew-symmetric matrices in the exponential map does not commute, and recursive projection converges quicker and more smoothly on the noisy photometric loss landscape. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import torch import torch.autograd.functional as AF def visiononlyposefilter( prevmu: torch.Tensor, prevSigma: torch.Tensor, actionu: torch.Tensor, currentimage: torch.Tensor, nerfmodel: callable, pixelsubsetI: list, Q: torch.Tensor, S: torch.Tensor, maxiterations: int, learningrate: float) -> tuple: # Step 1: State Propagation # Dynamics model f(mu, u) is problem-specific and not detailed in the sources. mupred = dynamicsmodel(prevmu, actionu) A = computejacobiandynamics(prevmu, actionu) Sigmapred = A @ prevSigma @ A.T + Q # Step 2: Pixel Selection # pixelsubsetI is provided as input, selected via ORB or similar feature detector. # Step 3 & 6: Optimization with Recursive SE(3) Projection muopt = mupred.clone().detach().requiresgrad(True) optimizer = torch.optim.Adam([muopt], lr=learningrate) for step in range(maxiterations): optimizer.zerograd() loss = costfunction(muopt, mupred, Sigmapred, S, currentimage, pixelsubsetI, nerfmodel) # Outlier rejection on per-pixel loss reduces variance. loss = applyoutlierrejection(loss, currentimage, pixelsubsetI, muopt, nerfmodel) loss.backward() optimizer.step() # Recursive SE(3) projection after every gradient step. muopt = projectse3manifold(muopt) # Step 5: Covariance Update # Hessian of the loss function at the optimized mean. H = AF.hessian(costfunction, muopt, args=(mupred, Sigmapred, S, currentimage, pixelsubsetI, nerfmodel)) Sigmat = torch.inverse(H) return muopt.detach(), Sigmat def dynamicsmodel(mu: torch.Tensor, u: torch.Tensor) -> torch.Tensor: # Problem-specific dynamics f(mu, u). Not given in the sources. # Example: constant velocity model return mu + u def computejacobiandynamics(mu: torch.Tensor, u: torch.Tensor) -> torch.Tensor: # Jacobian A = df/dx at x=mu. return torch.autograd.functional.jacobian(lambda x: dynamicsmodel(x, u), mu) def costfunction(mu: torch.Tensor, mupred: torch.Tensor, Sigmapred: torch.Tensor, S: torch.Tensor, currentimage: torch.Tensor, pixelsubsetI: list, nerfmodel: callable) -> torch.Tensor: Tt = extractposefromstate(mu) predictedpixels = nerfmodel.render(Tt, pixelsubsetI) observedpixels = currentimage[pixelsubsetI] diffphoto = predictedpixels - observedpixels diffphotoflat = diffphoto.view(-1, 1) Sinv = torch.inverse(S) photometricloss = diffphotoflat.T @ Sinv @ diffphotoflat diffproc = mupred - mu diffprocflat = diffproc.view(-1, 1) Sigmapredinv = torch.inverse(Sigmapred) processloss = diffprocflat.T @ Sigmapredinv @ diffprocflat return (photometricloss + processloss).squeeze() def extractposefromstate(mu: torch.Tensor) -> torch.Tensor: # Extracts SE(3) pose from the state vector. # Layout depends on the specific state representation. return mu[:6] def projectse3manifold(state: torch.Tensor) -> torch.Tensor: # Projects pose component back onto SE(3) manifold after every gradient step. # Uses standard SVD to enforce valid rotation matrices. pose = state[:6] R = pose[:3,:3] U,, Vt = torch.linalg.svd(R) Rproj = U @ Vt t = pose[:3, 3] newstate = state.clone() newstate[:3,:3] = Rproj return newstate def applyoutlierrejection(loss: torch.Tensor, currentimage: torch.Tensor, pixelsubsetI: list, mu: torch.Tensor, nerfmodel: callable) -> torch.Tensor: # Masks pixels with high photometric residuals before backpropagation. Tt = extractposefromstate(mu) predicted = nerfmodel.render(Tt, pixelsubsetI) observed = currentimage[pixelsubsetI] residuals = torch.abs(predicted - observed) mask = residuals < torch.median(residuals) + 3 torch.std(residuals) if not torch.any(mask): return loss return loss torch.mean(mask.float()) Parameters: Feature Detector: ORB is used to select pixels for photometric evaluation. Process Noise Covariance Q{t-1}: Covariance of the process noise in the state propagation step. Measurement Noise Covariance St: Covariance weighting the photometric loss term. Learning Rate: Hyperparameter for the optimizer; value not specified in the sources. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: SE(3) Manifold Optimization: Multiplication of skew-symmetric matrices in the exponential map does not commute. Optimizing with respect to a reference pose and projecting once is mathematically distinct from recursive projection. The recursive SE(3) approach is required for quicker and smoother convergence due to the noisy photometric loss landscape. Low Gradient Regions: The method is designed to be robust in regions with low photometric gradient information by relying more on the dynamics model (process loss). Implementation: Optimization on the manifold is implemented using the LieTorch library. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Measured Performance: Demonstrated in simulation with a quadrotor navigating through a jungle gym, the inside of a church, and Stonehenge, and with an omnidirectional ground robot navigating through a church. Strengths: Provides robust pose estimation in low-gradient regions; outputs state covariance useful for parallel algorithms like collision avoidance; integrates seamlessly with trajectory planning in an online replanning loop. Limitations: Requires a pre-trained NeRF model; computationally intensive due to NeRF rendering and optimization at each timestep; sensitive to the accuracy of the dynamics model f and noise covariances Q, S. When to Use: Online robot navigation in environments represented by NeRFs where only monocular vision is available and dynamics are known. When Not to Use: When high-frequency updates are not required and offline batch optimization is acceptable; when the environment is not well-represented by a NeRF; when dynamics are unknown or highly uncertain. The method was introduced by Mikhalkiewicz et al. in 2022 in the paper "Vision-Only Robot Navigation in a Neural Radiance World". It builds upon previous work on single-image camera pose estimation using NeRFs [19] (cited in) but extends it to recursive Bayesian estimation. The method is part of a larger navigation framework that combines trajectory planning (based on differential flatness) and pose filtering for online replanning. It was demonstrated in high-fidelity simulation environments including a playground, a church, and Stonehenge. name: Online Receding Horizon Replanning
head: Online Replanning Navigation Pipeline
body: Online Receding Horizon Replanning is a vision-based robot navigation pipeline that combines a trajectory planner and a pose filter in a receding horizon loop to provide dynamic maneuvering through an environment using only an RGB camera for feedback. It solves the problem of navigating a robot through a pre-trained Neural Radiance Field (NeRF) representation when the robot's initial pose is uncertain and subject to disturbances. Unlike static waypoint planners, this method allows the robot to change homotopy classes around obstacles in response to disturbances by continuously replanning the trajectory based on updated state beliefs. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: Initial state prior (\mu0, \Sigma0), goal state x{goal}, trained NeRF model N of the environment. Outputs: A sequence of control actions u executed by the robot. Data Structures: State Belief: Represented by mean \mu and covariance \Sigma. Waypoints: A sequence W of states. NeRF: A neural network f\theta representing the scene geometry and appearance, used for collision checking and image synthesis. Numbered Steps: 1. Initialization: Initialize waypoints W using A search between the initial state \mu0 and the goal state x{goal}. 2. Loop: While the robot is not at x{goal}: a. Trajectory Optimization: Optimize the trajectory W using trajOpt to minimize a NeRF-based collision metric. This produces a refined sequence of waypoints. b. Action Extraction: Get the states x and actions u from the optimized waypoints W. c. Execution: The robot applies the first control action u[0]. d. Perception: The robot receives a noisy image I from its onboard RGB camera. e. Pose Filtering: The state estimator uses the captured image I to generate a posterior belief over the new state. This updates the state estimate using poseFilter with inputs I, previous state (\mu{t-1}, \Sigma{t-1}), and the first action u[0]. f. Replanning Preparation: Update W by replacing the first waypoint with the new mean \mut and keeping the rest of the previous waypoints (W[2:end]) as a hot start. Formulas: The collision metric evaluated during trajOpt relies on the NeRF's ability to synthesize images and estimate depth or occupancy, though the specific mathematical formulation of the collision metric is not detailed in the provided text. The pose filter uses the NeRF as a nonlinear measurement model to update the belief (\mut, \Sigmat). Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import numpy as np def onlinerecedinghorizonplanning(initialpriormu, initialpriorsigma, goalstate, nerfmodel): # Step 1: Initialize waypoints using A search between initial state and goal waypoints = astarsearch(initialpriormu, goalstate) currentmu = initialpriormu currentsigma = initialpriorsigma # Step 2: Receding Horizon Loop while not isatgoal(currentmu, goalstate): # a) Optimize trajectory to minimize NeRF-based collision metric waypoints = trajoptimization(waypoints, nerfmodel) # b) Extract states and actions from optimized waypoints states, actions = getstatesandactions(waypoints) # c) Execute first control action executeaction(actions[0]) # d) Capture noisy RGB image from onboard camera image = getcameraimage() # e) Update pose belief using NeRF as nonlinear measurement model currentmu, currentsigma = posefilter(image, currentmu, currentsigma, actions[0]) # f) Update waypoints: replace first waypoint with new mean, keep rest as hot start waypoints = [currentmu] + waypoints[2:] return def astarsearch(start, goal): return [start] # Not given in the sources. def isatgoal(state, goal): return np.allclose(state, goal) # Standard convergence check def trajoptimization(waypoints, nerf): return waypoints # Not given in the sources. def getstatesandactions(waypoints): return waypoints, waypoints # Not given in the sources. def executeaction(action): pass # Not given in the sources. def getcameraimage(): return None # Not given in the sources. def posefilter(image, mu, sigma, action): return mu, sigma # Not given in the sources. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Model Mismatch: The method assumes a trained NeRF model. Performance may degrade if there is a mismatch between the real-world scene and the trained NeRF. Disturbances: The system is designed to handle disturbances, but severe disturbances may require significant replanning effort. Homotopy Changes: The method allows the robot to change homotopy classes around obstacles in response to disturbances, which is difficult for existing differential flatness-based planners that use static waypoints. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Measured Performance: Demonstrated in simulation with quadrotor and ground robots navigating through pre-trained NeRF models of a playground, a church, and Stonehenge. Scaling: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Allows the robot to change homotopy classes around obstacles in response to disturbances, which is difficult for existing differential flatness-based planners that use static waypoints. Limitations: Requires a pre-trained NeRF model of the environment. When to use: Navigating a robot through a known environment represented by a pre-trained NeRF using only an RGB camera, especially in the presence of disturbances. When not: When real-time mapping is required (NeRF is pre-trained) or when the environment cannot be represented by a pre-trained NeRF. Origin: The method was introduced in "Vision-Only Robot Navigation in a Neural Radiance World". History and Development: The paper builds on related work in neural implicit representations and vision-only navigation systems. Usage: Demonstrated in high-fidelity simulation environments. name: NeRF-based Trajectory Optimization
head: Differential Flatness-based Trajectory Optimization with NeRF, NeRF-based collision penalty optimization, Proposed trajectory optimizer
body: NeRF-based Trajectory Optimization is a planning method for differentially flat systems that optimizes a dense set of flat output waypoints directly using first-order gradient descent. It solves the problem of finding collision-free paths in complex environments by using Neural Radiance Field (NeRF) density as an implicit obstacle representation, replacing the need for closed-form polytopes or explicit mesh extraction. Unlike traditional pipelines that rely on quadratic programs with static, hand-designed waypoints and convex constraints, this method treats waypoint locations as differentiable decision variables, allowing the optimizer to navigate through narrow spaces by minimizing a combined objective of collision probability and control effort. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: A pre-trained NeRF model \mathcal{N} representing the environment; a current robot pose P{start}; a goal pose P{goal}; robot dynamics parameters (defining flat outputs and control limits). Outputs: A sequence of optimized flat output waypoints \{\sigma1, \dots, \sigmah\} defining the trajectory. Data Structures: Waypoints: A list of h flat output vectors. For a quadrotor, each vector \sigmai contains position (x, y, z) and yaw angle \psi. The total number of decision variables is 4h (3 for position, 1 for yaw). NeRF Model: A multi-layer perceptron (MLP) that maps 3D coordinates and viewing directions to volume density \sigma and color C. The density \sigma is used as a proxy for collision probability. Algorithm Steps: 1. Initialization: Generate a preliminary set of h waypoints between P{start} and P{goal} using a heuristic such as a straight line or A search on a coarse grid. Let these initial waypoints be \sigma^{(0)}. 2. Objective Formulation: Define the loss function \mathcal{L} as a weighted sum of collision cost and control effort: \mathcal{L}(\sigma) = \lambda{col} \mathcal{L}{col}(\sigma) + \lambda{ctrl} \mathcal{L}{ctrl}(\sigma) where \lambda{col} and \lambda{ctrl} are hyperparameters. 3. Collision Cost Calculation: For each waypoint \sigmai, sample the NeRF density at the corresponding 3D position. The collision cost \mathcal{L}{col} is computed by integrating or summing the NeRF density along the trajectory segments or at the waypoints. The source notes that minimizing this objective correlates with minimizing the intersecting volume of ground-truth meshes. Specifically, the method minimizes a "NeRF collision loss" which serves as a differentiable proxy for physical collision. 4. Control Effort Calculation: Compute the control effort \mathcal{L}{ctrl} based on the robot's dynamics. The control inputs \tau and states s are derived from the surrounding waypoints using the robot's differential flatness properties. For a quadrotor, this typically involves computing the required thrust and moments to transition between waypoints, often related to snap or jerk minimization. 5. Gradient Computation: Compute the gradients \nabla{\sigma} \mathcal{L} using automatic differentiation through the NeRF rendering/density evaluation and the dynamics model. 6. Optimization Update: Update the waypoints using the Adam optimizer: \sigma^{(k+1)} = \sigma^{(k)} - \alpha \cdot \text{Adam}(\nabla{\sigma} \mathcal{L}) where \alpha is the learning rate. 7. Convergence: Repeat steps 3-6 until convergence or a maximum number of iterations is reached. The optimizer converges to a trajectory with zero intersections with ground-truth meshes in tested environments (e.g., Stonehenge) by iteration 49 in specific experiments. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def nerftrajectoryoptimization(nerfmodel, startpose, goalpose, numwaypoints, maxiterations): """ Optimizes a trajectory for a differentially flat system using NeRF density. Args: nerfmodel: A callable that returns volume density given 3D coordinates. startpose: Initial robot pose (position and yaw). goalpose: Goal robot pose (position and yaw). numwaypoints: Number of intermediate waypoints h. maxiterations: Maximum number of gradient descent steps. Returns: optimizedwaypoints: List of optimized flat output vectors. """ # Step 1: Initialize waypoints using a heuristic (e.g., linear interpolation or A) # For linear interpolation: waypoints = [] for i in range(numwaypoints + 2): # +2 for start and goal t = i / (numwaypoints + 1) pos = lerp(startpose.position, goalpose.position, t) yaw = lerp(startpose.yaw, goalpose.yaw, t) waypoints.append([pos.x, pos.y, pos.z, yaw]) # Convert to tensor for gradient tracking waypointstensor = torch.tensor(waypoints, requiresgrad=True, dtype=torch.float32) # Hyperparameters lambdacol = 1.0 lambdactrl = 1.0 optimizer = torch.optim.Adam([waypointstensor], lr=0.01) # Step 2-6: Optimization Loop for iteration in range(maxiterations): optimizer.zerograd() # Calculate Collision Cost # Sample density at each waypoint position positions = waypointstensor[:,:3] # Extract x, y, z densities = [] for pos in positions: # Query NeRF for density at this position # Note: NeRF usually takes (x,y,z, dir), but for collision we might just use density at point # or integrate along segment. Source implies using density at waypoints/segments. density = nerfmodel(pos) densities.append(density) # Sum of densities as collision proxy collisionloss = sum(densities).mean() # Calculate Control Effort # Derive control inputs from waypoints using dynamics # For quadrotor, this involves computing snap/jerk or thrust controlloss = computecontroleffort(waypointstensor) # Combined Loss loss = lambdacol collisionloss + lambdactrl controlloss # Backpropagation loss.backward() optimizer.step() # Optional: Check for convergence (e.g., loss change < threshold) if iteration % 100 == 0: print(f"Iteration {iteration}, Loss: {loss.item()}") return waypointstensor.detach().numpy() def computecontroleffort(waypoints): """ Computes control effort based on waypoint differences. Simplified example: sum of squared differences in acceleration/snap. """ # Calculate higher-order derivatives (snap) from waypoints # This is a placeholder for the specific dynamics formulation # In practice, this uses the differential flatness property to map # position/yaw derivatives to control inputs. # For a quadrotor, snap is related to thrust direction. # Here we assume a simplified metric for demonstration. diffs = torch.diff(waypoints, dim=0) # Example: penalize large changes in position and yaw effort = torch.sum(diffs[:,:3]2) + torch.sum(diffs[:, 3:]2) return effort Parameters: Optimizer: Adam optimizer. Iterations (Initial): 2500. Iterations (Online Replanning): 250. Time Step (Online): 0.1s. Flat Outputs: Position (x, y, z) and yaw angle \psi for quadrotors. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Non-Convexity: The optimization problem is fundamentally non-convex due to the complex geometry represented by the NeRF and the dynamics constraints. First-order methods like Adam are required, and convergence to a local minimum is possible. Initialization Sensitivity: Poor initialization (e.g., a straight line through a dense obstacle) may lead to slow convergence or failure to find a collision-free path. Heuristics like A on a coarse grid are recommended. NeRF Density Accuracy: The collision cost relies on the NeRF density accurately representing obstacles. Inaccuracies in the NeRF (e.g., floating artifacts, incomplete reconstruction) may lead to false positives or negatives in collision detection. Treats NeRF density as a proxy for collision likelihood, providing a continuous probability estimate rather than binary checks. Re-plans trajectories in real-time (e.g., every 0.1s) using fewer iterations (250) to correct for state estimation errors or dynamic changes. Time Complexity: Dependent on the number of waypoints, iterations, and NeRF query time. Initial optimization takes ~20s for 2500 iterations on an AMD Ryzen 9 5900X CPU and Nvidia RTX 3090 GPU. Online replanning takes ~2s for 250 iterations. Memory Complexity: Proportional to the size of the NeRF model and the number of waypoints. Performance: In the Stonehenge environment, the optimizer converges to a trajectory with zero intersections with ground-truth meshes by iteration 49. It outperforms minimum-snap planners (which clip obstacles) and RRT (which has high control effort) in terms of smoothness and collision avoidance. Strengths: Handles complex, implicit obstacle representations without explicit meshing; leverages differential flatness for efficient control computation; allows for arbitrary differentiable cost functions. Limitations: Computationally expensive for real-time applications on current hardware; sensitive to NeRF quality; non-convex optimization may get stuck in local minima. When to Use: Suitable for offline or semi-real-time planning in complex, unstructured environments where explicit obstacle models are unavailable or difficult to construct. When Not to Use: Not suitable for real-time control loops requiring sub-millisecond response times on embedded hardware without significant optimization or acceleration. The method was proposed in "Vision-Only Robot Navigation in a Neural Radiance World" (2022). It builds on the concept of differential flatness, commonly used in quadrotor trajectory planning (e.g., minimum-snap planners), but replaces the convex quadratic programming formulation with a non-convex gradient-based optimization using NeRF density for collision avoidance. The work demonstrates that NeRFs can serve as implicit obstacle representations for trajectory planning, enabling robots to navigate tight spaces without explicit mesh extraction. name: NeRF-based Collision Probability Estimation
head: NeRF-based collision penalty optimization
body: NeRF-based collision probability estimation treats the volume density of a Neural Radiance Field (NeRF) as a proxy for the likelihood that a physical object (robot body) will collide with an obstacle in the environment. It solves the problem of quantifying collision risk for trajectory optimization without requiring explicit mesh extraction or discrete voxelization, enabling smooth, differentiable cost terms for gradient-based planners. Unlike methods that rely on density thresholds for binary collision checks, this approach provides a continuous probability estimate or repulsive potential derived directly from the NeRF's implicit representation. Inputs: A trained NeRF model defined by a coordinate-to-density function \sigma(x) and optionally color c(x). A set of points B representing the robot's body geometry. (For potential field variant) A goal position xg and current position xt. (For probability variant) A timestep duration s(bt) for each body point. Outputs: Collision Probability: A scalar value p{coll} representing the estimated probability of collision for the robot body configuration. Repulsive Force: A vector F{rep} used for local obstacle avoidance. NeRF Model: A neural network (typically MLP) that takes a 3D coordinate x and viewing direction d as input and outputs volume density \sigma(x) and color c(x). The density \sigma(x) is interpreted as the differential probability of a light ray terminating at x. Robot Body Representation (B): A finite collection of 3D points. Typically implemented as a 3D grid of points approximating the robot's bounding box, but can be an arbitrarily complex model. Hierarchical NeRF Tree (Optional/Contextual): In implementations like NeRF-Nav, local NeRFs are organized in an octree. The root maintains a coarse global representation, while leaves represent high-resolution local fields. Leaves are spawned based on novelty thresholds and pruned based on temporal staleness. The collision probability p{coll} at a given state is estimated by summing the contributions of each point bt in the robot body set B. The density \rho(bt) (equivalent to \sigma(bt)) serves as the probability density proxy. p{coll} = \sum{bt \in B} \rho(bt) s(bt) Where: bt: A point in the robot body representation B at time t. \rho(bt): The NeRF volume density at point bt. s(bt): The distance traveled by the body-fixed point bt in the timestep. Assumption: The probability of terminating a light ray is a strong proxy for the probability of terminating a mass particle. Bound: This estimate follows from Boole's inequality, providing an upper bound on the true collision probability. For local navigation, a repulsive potential U{rep}(x) is defined based on a pseudo-distance d(x) derived from the NeRF density. Pseudo-distance: d(x) = -\frac{1}{\sigma{max}} \log \left( 1 - \frac{\min(\sigma(x), \sigma{max})}{\sigma{max}} \right) Where: \sigma(x): The NeRF volume density at position x. \sigma{max}: The maximum density value used for normalization. d(x): A pseudo-distance metric where higher density results in smaller distance (closer to obstacle). Repulsive Potential: U{rep}(x) = \begin{cases} \frac{1}{2\eta} \left( 1 - \frac{d(x)}{d0} \right)^2 & \text{if } d(x) \le d0 \\ 0 & \text{otherwise} \end{cases} Where: d0: Controls the influence range of the repulsive force. \eta: Controls the strength of the repulsive potential. Repulsive Force: The force is computed via automatic differentiation through the NeRF network: F{rep} = -\nablax U{rep}(x) \sigma{max}: Maximum density threshold for pseudo-distance calculation. Not given in the sources. d0: Influence range for repulsive potential. Not given in the sources. \eta: Strength parameter for repulsive potential. Not given in the sources. B: Robot body point set. Typically a 3D grid of points representing the robot’s bounding box. \tau{spawn}: Novelty threshold for spawning new NeRF leaves in hierarchical structures. Value: 0.3. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def computecollisionprobability(nerfmodel, robotbodypoints, timestepdistance): """ Computes the collision probability estimate for a robot body configuration using NeRF density as a proxy for collision likelihood. Args: nerfmodel: Function sigma(x) returning volume density at x. robotbodypoints: List of 3D coordinates representing the robot body B. timestepdistance: Scalar s(bt) distance traveled in the timestep. Returns: pcoll: Estimated collision probability. """ pcoll = 0.0 for bt in robotbodypoints: # Query NeRF density at the body point density = nerfmodel(bt) # Accumulate probability contribution: density distance pcoll += density timestepdistance return pcoll def computerepulsiveforce(nerfmodel, position, sigmamax, d0, eta): """ Computes the repulsive force for local obstacle avoidance using automatic differentiation through the NeRF density. Args: nerfmodel: Function sigma(x) returning volume density at x. position: Current 3D coordinate x. sigmamax: Maximum density for normalization. d0: Influence range. eta: Strength parameter. Returns: Frep: 3D repulsive force vector. """ # Define pseudo-distance function def pseudodistance(x): sigma = nerfmodel(x) # Clip sigma to avoid log(0) or negative arguments clippedsigma = min(sigma, sigmamax) term = 1.0 - (clippedsigma / sigmamax) # Handle numerical stability: if term <= 0, distance is 0 (collision) if term <= 0: return 0.0 return -1.0 / sigmamax log(term) # Compute pseudo-distance at current position dx = pseudodistance(position) # Compute potential Urep if dx <= d0: urep = (1.0 / (2.0 eta)) (1.0 - (dx / d0)) 2 else: urep = 0.0 # Compute gradient via automatic differentiation # In practice, this is done using a framework like PyTorch or JAX # by wrapping the potential calculation in a computational graph Frep = -gradient(urep, position) return Frep def nerfnavplanningloop(nerftree, currentpose, goal, occupancygrid): """ High-level planning loop integrating NeRF-based collision estimation. """ # 1. Query active leaves from the hierarchical NeRF tree near current pose activeleaves = nerftree.querynear(currentpose) # 2. Check occupancy grid for near-field obstacles isclear = occupancygrid.checkclearpath(currentpose, goal) if isclear: # 3. Follow global A path on coarse occupancy if path is clear velocity = followglobalastar(occupancygrid, currentpose, goal) else: # 4. Compute repulsive force via automatic differentiation Frep = computerepulsiveforce( nerftree.getdensityfunction(), currentpose, sigmamax=..., # Parameter from sources d0=..., eta=...) # 5. Combine attractive and repulsive forces # vt = alpha (xg - xt)/||xg - xt|| + beta Frep attractive = (goal - currentpose) / norm(goal - currentpose) velocity = alpha attractive + beta Frep # 6. Execute velocity command executevelocity(velocity) # 7. Update NeRF tree: spawn/prune leaves based on novelty and time nerftree.update(currentpose) Density Normalization: The pseudo-distance formula requires \sigma{max}. If \sigma(x) approaches \sigma{max}, the term inside the logarithm approaches 0, leading to numerical instability. Clamping \sigma(x) to \sigma{max} is necessary. Proxy Assumption Validity: The method assumes light ray termination probability is a strong proxy for mass particle termination. This may not hold for transparent or semi-transparent objects, or if the NeRF density does not accurately reflect physical occupancy. Computational Cost: Computing repulsive forces via automatic differentiation through the NeRF network for every body point can be computationally expensive for complex robot models or high-resolution NeRFs. Hierarchical Management: In hierarchical implementations, leaves must be correctly spawned and pruned to maintain memory bounds and relevance. Failure to prune stale leaves can lead to outdated collision information. Time Complexity: Collision probability estimation is O(|B| \cdot C{NeRF}), where |B| is the number of body points and C{NeRF} is the cost of a forward pass through the NeRF. Repulsive force computation involves gradient calculation, adding overhead proportional to the depth of the computational graph. Global path planning uses A on a cached occupancy grid, offering O(1) collision queries after initial construction. Memory Complexity: Depends on the NeRF representation. Hierarchical NeRFs (octree) bound memory by pruning distant leaves and capping leaf count. Occupancy grid caching adds memory proportional to the resolution \Delta of the 3D array. Performance: NeRF-Nav achieves a success rate of 86.1% and collision rate of 8.3% on the Gibson dataset, comparable to or better than traditional methods like OctoMap+A (81.2% SR, 12.4% CR) and Voxblox+RRT (84.7% SR, 9.8% CR). Frame rates vary: NeRF-Nav operates at ~2 Hz, while Ego-Planner (baseline) operates at 30 Hz. Strengths: No mesh extraction required. Smooth, differentiable gradients suitable for gradient-based optimization. Integrates naturally into trajectory optimization as a cost term. Limitations: Computationally heavier than discrete voxel-based methods. Relies on the accuracy of the NeRF density representation. May struggle with highly dynamic environments if the NeRF is not updated in real-time. Origin: The concept of using NeRF density for collision avoidance was extended from prior work on aerial robots that used density thresholds. The specific formulation of collision probability as a sum of density-weighted distances was introduced in "Vision-Only Robot Navigation in a Neural Radiance World". The hierarchical implementation for real-time ground robot navigation was presented in "NeRF-Nav: Hierarchical Neural Radiance Fields for Real-Time Robot Navigation and Obstacle Avoidance". History: Early NeRF-based planning for aerial robots relied on simple density thresholds. Subsequent work recognized the need for smooth gradients for ground robot navigation, leading to the differentiation of NeRF density. The probabilistic interpretation of density as a collision proxy provides a principled basis for including collision risk in trajectory optimization. Usage: Used in mobile robot navigation systems, particularly for ground robots in cluttered environments where traditional mesh-based methods may fail or be computationally prohibitive. It is also applicable to trajectory optimization for robots with complex geometries. name: Online Replanning
body: Online Replanning is a pipeline component that re-plans collision-free trajectories when state estimates deviate significantly from the planned path. It solves the problem of catastrophic collisions caused by external disturbances or state estimation errors during execution. Unlike open-loop execution, which follows a pre-computed plan regardless of deviations, online replanning uses feedback to generate new collision-free paths to the goal, ensuring robustness. Inputs: Current state estimate, planned trajectory, goal state. Outputs: New collision-free trajectory segment. Data Structures: Not given in the sources. Steps: 1. Monitor the current state estimate against the planned trajectory. 2. If deviation exceeds a threshold, trigger replanning. 3. Use the current state estimate as the new initial condition. 4. Optimize a new collision-free trajectory to the goal. 5. Execute the re-planned trajectory. Formulas: Not given in the sources. Parameters: Threshold for deviation triggering replanning.
