name: Surrogate Objective-based Trajectory Planning
head: Ensemble Objective E, SOARNet, Surrogate Objectives for Active Radiance Fields Network, Trajectory Planning with SOARNet
body: Surrogate Objective-based Trajectory Planning selects informative camera poses for training radiance fields without requiring radiance field training or ground-truth mesh access during inference. It solves the active view planning problem by using a deep neural network, SOARNet, to predict surrogate objective scores for candidate poses given monocular images and camera parameters. Unlike in-flight or post-hoc methods that rely on uncertainty estimation from a trained model, this approach is prescriptive and model-agnostic, enabling trajectory generation in seconds rather than hours. It sets itself apart from sibling methods by decoupling view selection from radiance field optimization, allowing for rapid, training-free planning. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: A set of monocular 2D images \hat{M} = \{mk: k \le n\} taken from visited camera poses \hat{C} = \{\hat{c}k: k \le n\}, the camera parameters (extrinsics) for each image, and a set of candidate unvisited poses C^-. The method does not require the image of the unvisited pose or the ground-truth mesh. Outputs: A sequence of selected camera poses \hat{C} up to a budget B, and the predicted surrogate objective scores for visited and candidate poses. Data Structures: SOARNet Architecture: Encoder \mu(\cdot): A ResNet-18 encoder processing the input images \hat{M}. Camera Extrinsics Encoder o(\cdot): A Multi-Layer Perceptron (MLP) taking positionally encoded camera extrinsics. Prediction Heads G(\cdot) and H(\cdot): Simple MLPs for generating objective scores via regression. Output Format: The network outputs a set of scores Fg for g \in \{n, n+1\}, where Fg = \{f{Cg}, f{Qg}, f{Dg}, f{Tg}\}. Fn contains normalized cumulative scores of all poses seen so far. F{n+1} returns normalized cumulative scores for an unseen camera pose c{n+1} conditioned upon visited poses. Formulas: The surrogate objectives are defined as follows: 1. Surface Coverage (fC): Measures the ratio of seen faces to total faces. fC = \frac{1}{J} \sum{j}^{J} \sum{k}^{n} U(Vj^k) Where J is the total number of faces, n is the number of visited poses, U(\cdot) is the Heaviside step function, and Vj^k is an indicator of face j visibility from pose k. 2. Geometric Complexity (fQ): Quantifies variability in mesh surface normals. Not given in the sources. 3. Textural Complexity (fT): Measures photometric variation. Not given in the sources. 4. Ray Diversity (fD): Measures the diversity of viewing rays. Not given in the sources. The SOARNet prediction is formalized as: \text{SOARNet}(\hat{C}, \hat{M}, c{n+1}) = \{Fg: g \in \{n, n+1\}\} The training loss L for SOARNet is the sum of Huber losses on the predictions of each head: L = LG(\hat{F}n, Fn) + LH(\hat{F}{n+1}, F{n+1}) Where LG and LH are Huber losses. Parameters: Budget B: The maximum number of camera poses to select. Initialization Steps n{init}: Set to 3. Ensemble Objective Sequence E: [C, Q, Q, D, D, T]. Training Hardware: NVIDIA RTX8000 GPU, 64GB DRAM, 8 CPUs. Optimizer: Adam with AMSGrad enabled, no weight decay. Learning Rate: 3 \times 10^{-5}. Beta1: 0.9. Beta2: 0.999. Epsilon: 1 \times 10^{-8}. Scheduler: Step size 0.6, \gamma 0.5. Epochs: 12. Batch Size: 8. Algorithm Steps: 1. Initialization: For the first n{init} steps (3 steps), select poses at the extremum along each principal spatial axis (PseudoCoverage). 2. Loop: While the number of selected steps is less than the budget B: a. Determine the current objective index: idx = \text{step} \pmod{\text{len}(E)}. b. Select the objective function f from the ensemble sequence E at index idx. c. For each candidate unvisited pose cz \in C^-: i. Compute the score using SOARNet: Sz = \text{SOARNet}(\hat{C}, \hat{M}, cz). ii. Extract the score corresponding to the selected objective f. d. Select the candidate pose cz with the highest score as the next pose \hat{c}{n+1}. e. Add \hat{c}{n+1} to \hat{C} and its image to \hat{M}. f. Remove \hat{c}{n+1} from C^-. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import numpy as np def getextremumposes(candidateposes, ninit): """ Standard PCA-based extremity selection for initialization.""" posesarray = np.array(candidateposes) mean = np.mean(posesarray, axis=0) cov = np.cov(posesarray.T) eigenvalues, eigenvectors = np.linalg.eigh(cov) principalaxes = eigenvectors[:, -3:] extremumindices = [] for axis in principalaxes: projections = posesarray @ axis extremumindices.append(np.argmax(projections)) extremumindices.append(np.argmin(projections)) selected = [] for idx in extremumindices: if len(selected) < ninit and idx not in selected: selected.append(idx) return [candidateposes[i] for i in selected] def soarnet(images, extrinsics, candidatepose): """ Stub for the trained SOARNet model. Returns predicted scores.""" return { 'Fn': {'fC': 0.0, 'fQ': 0.0, 'fD': 0.0, 'fT': 0.0}, 'F{n+1}': {'fC': 0.0, 'fQ': 0.0, 'fD': 0.0, 'fT': 0.0} } def capturepose(pose): """ Standard environment function to render image and record extrinsics at a given pose.""" return np.zeros((224, 224, 3)), pose def generatetrajectory(images, cameraextrinsics, candidateposes, budget, ensemblesequence, ninit=3): selectedposes = [] visitedimages = list(images) visitedextrinsics = list(cameraextrinsics) candidateset = list(candidateposes) # Initialization phase for step in range(ninit): if step < len(candidateset): nextpose = candidateset[step] selectedposes.append(nextpose) candidateset.remove(nextpose) newimg, newext = capturepose(nextpose) visitedimages.append(newimg) visitedextrinsics.append(newext) # Greedy selection phase step = ninit while len(selectedposes) < budget: idx = step % len(ensemblesequence) objectivename = ensemblesequence[idx] bestscore = -float('inf') bestpose = None for candidate in candidateset: scores = soarnet(visitedimages, visitedextrinsics, candidate) score = scores['F{n+1}'][f'f{objectivename}'] if score > bestscore: bestscore = score bestpose = candidate selectedposes.append(bestpose) candidateset.remove(bestpose) newimg, newext = capturepose(bestpose) visitedimages.append(newimg) visitedextrinsics.append(newext) step += 1 return selectedposes Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision: The use of Huber loss suggests robustness to outliers in objective score predictions. Boundaries: The method relies on the availability of monocular images and camera extrinsics. If extrinsics are inaccurate, the positionally encoded input to the MLP may be misleading. A surrogate objective function measuring the ratio of seen faces to total faces to characterize informative samples for training radiance fields. It optimizes for maximizing the number of unique faces seen across camera poses, given the mesh of an object. It is chosen when surface completeness is the primary goal for reconstruction. Time Complexity: The method provides a significant speed-up, generating trajectories in seconds instead of hours, offering an ~80x speed-up compared to baselines. This is due to the fast inference of SOARNet compared to iterative radiance field training or uncertainty estimation. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Measured Performance: SOARNet outperforms baselines with comparable or better reconstruction qualities. Scaling: The method is model-agnostic, generalizing across fully neural-implicit (e.g., NeRF) to fully explicit approaches (e.g., Plenoxels). Strengths: Training-free, fast, interpretable objectives, model-agnostic. Limitations: Requires a set of candidate poses and monocular images; does not account for radiance field-specific uncertainties during planning. When to use: When rapid view selection is needed without the computational cost of training a radiance field first. When not to use: When the scene geometry is unknown and cannot be approximated by candidate poses, or when high-precision uncertainty quantification is required. The method was introduced in the paper "SO-NeRF: Active View Planning for NeRF using Surrogate Objectives" by Chen Feng et al.. It addresses the limitations of existing active perception methods for radiance fields, which often require in-flight training or post-hoc uncertainty estimation. The work is supported by NSF Awards 2238968 and 2322242. SO-NeRF: Active View Planning for NeRF using Surrogate Objectives, https://doi.org/10.48550/arXiv.2312.03266, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial)

name: MELON
head: Modulo-Equivalent Latent Optimization of NeRF, NeRF with Unposed Images in SO(3)
body: MELON is a differentiable inverse rendering method that jointly optimizes a Neural Radiance Field (NeRF) and camera poses from a set of unposed images. It solves the problem of local minima in the low-dimensional SO(3) latent space by introducing a "modulo loss" that maps the encoder's output to a quotient space, effectively replicating the latent variables to match the object's rotational symmetries. Unlike adversarial approaches such as GNeRF, MELON uses an encoder-decoder architecture with amortized inference, allowing it to perform ab-initio reconstruction without pose initialization or pre-trained CNNs. Does not require a discriminator (unlike GNeRF). Builds on Camera Pose and Extrinsic/Intrinsic Optimization. Siblings include Camera Pose and Parameter Optimization, Time-dependent NeRF with Continuous Camera Motion, Camera Preconditioning, VMRF, SPARF, NeRF Pose and Appearance Optimization, and Test-Time Two-Stage Optimization. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A set of n unposed images \{Ii\}{i=1}^n. The method assumes known camera intrinsics and that cameras point towards the scene origin from a known distance r. Output: A NeRF parameterized by \psi (predicting density \sigma\psi and color c\psi) and a set of camera poses \{Ri\}{i=1}^n in SO(3). Data Structures: NeRF (f\psi): A coordinate-based neural network predicting (c\psi, \sigma\psi) for a given 3D point and viewing direction. Encoder (h\xi): A neural network with weights \xi that maps an input image Ii to a latent pose variable zi in the latent space SO(3). Latent Space (\Omega): Parameterized as SO(3) using azimuth \theta \in SO(2), elevation \phi \in [-\pi/2, \pi/2], and roll \alpha \in SO(2). Replication Order (N): Integer N \in \mathbb{N}^ defining the equivalence relation. Mathematical Formulation: The image formation model is: Ii(p) = C(p; f^, Ri^) where C is the rendering function, f^ = (c^, \sigma^) is the unknown ground truth field, and Ri^ is the unknown ground truth pose. Operations on \Omega are defined for R \sim (\theta, \phi, \alpha): \theta0 + R \sim (\theta0 + \theta, \phi, \alpha) \lambda R \sim (\lambda\theta, \phi, \alpha) for \theta0 \in SO(2), \lambda \in \mathbb{R}. The equivalence relation RN for N \in \mathbb{N}^ is: z RN z' \iff \exists k \in \mathbb{Z}, z = z' + \frac{2k\pi}{N} This creates a quotient space \Omega/RN which is N times smaller than \Omega, replicating cameras along the azimuthal dimension. Algorithm Steps: 1. Initialize: Initialize NeRF parameters \psi and Encoder parameters \xi. Set replication order N. 2. Encode: For each input image Ii, compute the latent estimate zi = h\xi(Ii). 3. Generate Equivalence Class: Compute the equivalence class [zi]{RN} = \{ z \mid z RN zi \}. 4. Render Synthetic Views: For each z \in [zi]{RN}, render a synthetic image C(\cdot; f\psi, z) using the current NeRF. Let \mathcal{C}i^R(\psi, \xi) be the set of these rendered images. 5. Compute Modulo Loss: Calculate the loss as the minimum L2 distance between the input image and any synthetic view in the equivalence class: \mathcal{L}R(\psi, \xi) = \sum{i=1}^n \min \{ \| C - Ii \|2^2 \mid C \in \mathcal{C}i^R(\psi, \xi) \} This loss is a lower bound of the standard L2 loss due to the reflexivity of RN. 6. Optimize: Update \psi and \xi using gradient descent (e.g., Adam) to minimize \mathcal{L}R. 7. Final Pose Estimation: After convergence, for each Ii, the final pose estimate zi^ is: zi^ = \arg \min \{ \| C(\cdot; f\psi, z) - Ii(\cdot) \|2^2 \mid z \in [h{\xi^}(Ii)]{RN} \} where \xi^ is the optimal encoder weight. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import torch import torch.nn as nn import torch.optim as optim def posetorotation(pose): theta, phi, alpha = pose cx, sx = torch.cos(theta), torch.sin(theta) cy, sy = torch.cos(phi), torch.sin(phi) cz, sz = torch.cos(alpha), torch.sin(alpha) R = torch.stack([ cz cy, cz sy sx - sz cx, cz sy cx + sz sx, sz cy, sz sy sx + cz cx, sz sy cx - cz sx, -sy, cy sx, cy cx ]).reshape(3, 3) return R def generaterays(intrinsics, R, T, imageshape): H, W = imageshape f = intrinsics['focallength'] u, v = torch.meshgrid(torch.arange(W), torch.arange(H), indexing='xy') dx = (u - W / 2) / f dy = -(v - H / 2) / f dz = -torch.oneslike(u) directions = torch.stack([dx, dy, dz], dim=-1) directions = torch.einsum('ij,hwj->hwi', R, directions) origins = T.expand(H, W, 3) return origins, directions def volumerender(nerf, origins, directions, numsamples=128, near=0.1, far=10.0): tvals = torch.linspace(near, far, numsamples) zvals = 0.5 (tvals[1:] + tvals[:-1]) points = origins[..., None,:] + directions[..., None,:] zvals[None, None,:] viewdirs = directions.reshape(-1, 3) pointsflat = points.reshape(-1, 3) colors, densities = nerf(pointsflat, viewdirs) colors = colors.reshape(H, W, numsamples, 3) densities = densities.reshape(H, W, numsamples) alpha = 1.0 - torch.exp(-torch.relu(densities) (far - near) / numsamples) weights = alpha torch.cumprod(1.0 - alpha + 1e-10, dim=-2) weights[..., 0] = alpha[..., 0] color = torch.sum(weights[..., None] colors, dim=-2) return color def modulolossstep(nerf, encoder, images, intrinsics, r, N, optimizer): optimizer.zerograd() totalloss = 0 for i, Ii in enumerate(images): zi = encoder(Ii) azimuth, elevation, roll = zi syntheticviews = [] for k in range(N): newazimuth = (azimuth + 2 torch.pi k / N) % (2 torch.pi) latentpose = torch.stack([newazimuth, elevation, roll]) R = posetorotation(latentpose) T = torch.tensor([0, 0, r], device=latentpose.device) rayso, raysd = generaterays(intrinsics, R, T, Ii.shape) renderedview = volumerender(nerf, rayso, raysd) syntheticviews.append(renderedview) dists = [torch.sum((Ii - view) 2) for view in syntheticviews] mindist = min(dists) totalloss += mindist totalloss.backward() optimizer.step() return totalloss.item() def poseestimation(nerf, encoder, images, intrinsics, r, N): poses = [] for Ii in images: zi = encoder(Ii) azimuth, elevation, roll = zi bestpose = None bestdist = float('inf') for k in range(N): newazimuth = (azimuth + 2 torch.pi k / N) % (2 torch.pi) latentpose = torch.stack([newazimuth, elevation, roll]) R = posetorotation(latentpose) T = torch.tensor([0, 0, r], device=latentpose.device) rayso, raysd = generaterays(intrinsics, R, T, Ii.shape) renderedview = volumerender(nerf, rayso, raysd) dist = torch.sum((Ii - renderedview) 2) if dist < bestdist: bestdist = dist bestpose = latentpose poses.append(bestpose) return poses Parameters: Optimizer: Adam. Learning Rate: 10^{-4}. Batch Size: 256 crops (in 1D experiments) or full images. Replication Order (N): Integer N \in \mathbb{N}^. Typical values tested are N \in \{1, 2, 3, 4\}. The method performs best when N is a multiple of the dataset's symmetry order K. Neural Network Architecture (1D): Positional encoding and four fully-connected layers of size 64 with ReLU activation. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Local Minima: The low dimensionality of SO(3) induces local minima. The modulo loss mitigates this by making the loss landscape more convex. Unknown Translation: If both object-to-camera distances and in-plane translations are unknown, the latent space becomes SE(3). MELON fails to jointly infer rotation Ri and translation Ti in this setup. Symmetry Matching: If N does not match the object's symmetry, convergence may be poor. The fractional covering DR(f^) indicates the likelihood of convergence. Time Complexity: Compute time per gradient step increases linearly with the replication order N. For N=1, it takes 23 ms/it; N=2 takes 34 ms/it; N=3 takes 43 ms/it; N=4 takes 52 ms/it. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Performance: On the 'lego' scene with 6 views, MELON achieves a PSNR of 35.4 and a mean angular error of 0.901°, outperforming GNeRF (PSNR 35.3, error 1.21°) and failing COLMAP. Strengths: Does not require CNN pre-training or pose initialization (ab-initio). Does not require a discriminator (unlike GNeRF). Robust to small datasets (works with as few as 6 views). Limitations: Fails when translation is unknown (SE(3)). Requires known intrinsics and object-to-camera distance. MELON was introduced in the paper "MELON: NeRF with Unposed Images in SO(3)". It addresses the limitations of adversarial methods like GNeRF, which require large datasets, complex training schedules, and discriminators. MELON uses amortized inference via an encoder to map images to poses, combined with a modulo loss to handle rotational symmetries. It has been evaluated on the 'NeRF-Synthetic' dataset, RGB-MELON (spheres with quasi-symmetric textures), and real-world datasets (Gold Cape, Ethiopian Head, Toytruck). MELON: NeRF with Unposed Images in SO(3), https://doi.org/10.1109/3dv62453.2024.00084, fetched 2026-10-30

name: Time-dependent NeRF with Continuous Camera Motion
head: COPE-NeRF training, Continuous Optimization of NeRF and poses, Joint Optimization Pipeline, Joint Optimization of Neural Radiance Fields and Continuous Camera Motion
body: This method jointly optimizes a time-dependent Neural Radiance Field (NeRF) and continuous camera motion from monocular video, representing the scene as local Signed Distance Field (SDF) and appearance fields at each time step. Unlike methods that train a single global NeRF mapped via noisy initial transformations, this approach uses local time-dependent representations constrained by consistency losses to avoid local minima. It builds on Camera Pose and Extrinsic/Intrinsic Optimization by modeling camera motion as continuous angular and linear velocities rather than discrete pose parameters. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A sequence of monocular RGB images (video frames) with normalized timesteps t \in [-1, 1]. No initial camera poses or intrinsics are required. Output: A time-dependent NeRF model (\phig, \phic) representing scene geometry and appearance, and a continuous camera motion network (\phiv) providing angular and linear velocities. Derived camera poses for each frame and the full scene geometry in a world coordinate system. Data Structures: 1. Time-dependent SDF Network (\phig): An MLP taking 3D point x \in \mathbb{R}^3 and time t as input, outputting scalar SDF value s \in \mathbb{R}. 2. Time-dependent Appearance Network (\phic): An MLP taking 3D point x \in \mathbb{R}^3, viewing direction d \in \mathbb{R}^2 (in camera coordinates), and time t as input, outputting color c \in \mathbb{R}^3. 3. Camera Motion Network (\phiv): An MLP taking time t as input, outputting angular velocity \omega(t) \in \mathbb{R}^3 and linear velocity v(t) \in \mathbb{R}^3. 4. Sampling: At each iteration, 1024 rays are sampled, with 128 3D points per ray within a pre-defined depth range. Numbered Steps: 1. Initialize Networks: Initialize \phig, \phic, and \phiv. Normalize input timesteps to [-1, 1]. 2. Compute Camera Velocities: For a given time t, compute angular velocity \omega(t) and linear velocity v(t): \omega(t), v(t) = \phiv(t) 3. Integrate Camera Motion: To find the relative transformation from time t to t+l (l>0), use the Euler method with step size \Delta t = l/U (where U=10): R{t \to t+l} = \prod{u=0}^{U-1} \psi(\omega(t + u\Delta t)\Delta t) t{t \to t+l} = \sum{u=0}^{U-1} v(t + u\Delta t)\Delta t where \psi(\cdot): \mathbb{R}^3 \to SO(3) converts rotation angles to a rotation matrix using right-matrix multiplication. 4. Compute Transformation Matrix: Define the transformation P{t1 \to t2} from time t1 to t2: P{t1 \to t2} = \begin{cases} B{t1 \to t2} & \text{if } t1 \le t2 \\ (B{t2 \to t1})^{-1} & \text{otherwise} \end{cases} where B{t1 \to t2} = \begin{bmatrix} R{t1 \to t2} & t{t1 \to t2} \\ 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix} \in \mathbb{R}^{4 \times 4}. 5. Render Color: For a ray r at time t, compute the rendered color \hat{C}t(r) using volume rendering with the SDF s(x,t) = \phig(x,t) and color c(x,t) = \phic(x,d,t). 6. Compute Surface Point: Calculate the expected surface point \tilde{x}(r,t) \in \mathbb{R}^3 for ray r at time t: \tilde{x}(r, t) = \sum{i=1}^K Li \sigmai xi(r, t) where K is the number of samples, Li are weights, \sigmai are opacities, and xi are sample points. 7. Calculate Losses: Rendering Loss (L{rgb}): L{rgb} = \frac{1}{|\Omega|} \sum{r \in \Omega} \|\hat{C}t(r) - Ct(r)\|^2 where \Omega is the set of rays and Ct(r) is the ground truth color. Eikonal Loss (L{eik}): Enforces the Eikonal equation for the SDF: L{eik} = \frac{1}{|X|} \sum{x \in X} \left\| \frac{\partial s(x, t)}{\partial x} - 1 \right\|^2 where X is the set of sampled 3D points. Flow Consistency Loss (L{flow}): Constrains SDF flow to match scene flow derived from camera motion: L{flow} = \frac{1}{|S|} \sum{x \in S} \left\| \frac{\partial s(x,t)}{\partial t} + (\omega(t) \times x + v(t))^T n(x,t) \right\| where S is the set of surface points and n(x) = \nablax s(x,t) is the surface normal. Photometric Consistency Loss (L{photo}): Projects surface points to neighboring frames t+n (n \in \mathcal{N}) and compares colors: \tilde{x}'{t \to t+n}(r, t) = P{t \to t+n} \tilde{x}'(r, t) L{photo} = \frac{1}{|\mathcal{N}||\Omega|} \sum{n,r} \| C{t+n}[K \tilde{x}{t \to t+n}] - Ct(r) \|1 where K is the intrinsic matrix and [\cdot] denotes sampling. SDF Consistency Loss (L{sdf}): Encourages consistency between local SDF and the world frame SDF (where the world frame is the middle time step tw): L{sdf} = \frac{1}{|X|} \sum{x \in X} \| s(x, t) - s(x{t \to tw}, tw) \| where x{t \to tw} is point x transformed to the world frame via P{t \to tw}. 8. Total Loss: L = L{rgb} + \lambda1 L{eik} + \lambda2 L{flow} + \lambda3 L{photo} + \lambda4 L{sdf} Set \lambda4 = 0 for the first 200 epochs to avoid noisy initial transformations, then gradually increase it. 9. Joint Optimization: Update \phiv, \phig, \phic using Adam optimizer with learning rate 0.001. 10. Fine-tuning: After joint optimization, fix the camera motion (derive poses P{t \to tw}), fix t to the world time step tw, drop \lambda2, \lambda3, \lambda4, and fine-tune \phig, \phic using all training frames for 5000 additional epochs with gradually decaying learning rate. Pseudocode: Unverified code. gtcolors)2) sdfgrads = computegradient(phig, surfacepoints, t) leik = np.mean((np.linalg.norm(sdfgrads, axis=1) - 1)2) omega, v = phiv(t) sceneflow = np.cross(omega, surfacepoints) + v sdfflow = computetimederivative(phig, surfacepoints, t) lflow = np.mean(np.linalg.norm(sdfflow[:, None] + sceneflow normals, axis=1)) lphoto = 0.0 if neighborgtcolors is not None: for n in Nintervals: tneighbor = t + n P = computetransformation(phiv, t, tneighbor) homopoints = np.hstack([surfacepoints, np.ones((surfacepoints.shape[0], 1))]) neighborpointshomo = (P @ homopoints.T).T neighborpoints = neighborpointshomo[:,:3] neighboruv = Kintrinsic @ neighborpoints.T neighboruv = neighboruv[:2,:] / neighboruv[2,:] neighborcolors = bilinearsample(neighborgtcolors, neighboruv.T) lphoto += np.mean(np.abs(neighborcolors - Learning rate: 0.001 for Adam during initial joint optimization. Fine-tuning epochs: 5000 additional epochs with gradually decaying learning rate. Sampling: 1024 rays and 128 3D points per ray within a pre-defined depth range. Input normalization: Timesteps normalized from -1 to 1. \lambda4 = 0 for the first 200 epochs. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Noisy Initial Transformations: Early in training, camera poses are noisy. Setting \lambda4 = 0 for the first 200 epochs prevents the SDF consistency loss from hindering convergence. Local Minima: Using a single global NeRF with noisy initial transformations can get stuck in local minima. The time-dependent local representation avoids this. Limitations: Requires monocular video; performance depends on the quality of the continuous motion modeling. When to use: When initial camera poses are unavailable or unreliable, and high-quality geometry reconstruction is needed from monocular video. When not: Not given in the sources. Origin: The method was introduced in "Joint Optimization of Neural Radiance Fields and Continuous Camera Motion from a Monocular Video". History: It builds on SDF-based NeRF models [29] and continuous camera motion modeling. It addresses limitations of prior works like NeRFmm [31] and NoPe-NeRF [2] which either require initial poses or use global NeRFs prone to local minima with noisy transformations. name: Camera Preconditioning
head: CamP (Camera Preconditioning), Camera Preconditioning for Neural Radiance Fields
body: Camera Preconditioning (CamP) is a technique to normalize and decorrelate camera parameters during Neural Radiance Field (NeRF) optimization by transforming the optimization problem from direct camera parameters \boldsymbol{\phi}i to latent preconditioned parameters \tilde{\boldsymbol{\phi}}i, using a preconditioner matrix Pi^{-1} derived from the covariance of projection derivatives. It addresses issues where parameters are correlated or have different units (e.g., translation in world units vs. focal length in pixels), which causes ill-conditioning in naive optimization. Unlike per-parameter scaling or adaptive optimizers like Adam, CamP decouples highly correlated coefficients by using the full covariance matrix, ensuring that parameter updates are scaled according to their sensitivity to the rendered image. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: Initial camera parameters \boldsymbol{\phi}i^0 for each camera i; a set of randomly sampled 3D points within each camera's frustum; hyperparameters \lambda and \mu. Outputs: Preconditioned camera parameters \boldsymbol{\phi}i used in the NeRF forward pass; latent parameters \tilde{\boldsymbol{\phi}}i optimized by the gradient descent algorithm. Data Structures: Camera Parameters (\boldsymbol{\phi}i): A vector containing the specific parameterization for camera i. Common parameterizations include: SE3: 6D screw-axis representation (rotation \mathbf{r}, translation \mathbf{v}). SE3+Focal+Intrinsics: SE3 augmented with focal length (f), principal point (u0, v0), and radial distortion (k1, k2). Focal length residual is multiplicative: f' = f \exp(\Delta f). FocalPose+Intrinsics: Joint pose and focal length parameterization, modified as a residual with respect to initial estimates, plus principal point and radial distortion. SCNeRF: 6D rotation, residual 3D translation (tx, ty, tz), focal lengths (fu, fv), principal point (u0, v0), and radial distortion (k1, k2). Preconditioner (Pi^{-1}): A k \times k matrix where k is the dimension of the camera parameter vector. Computed as Pi^{-1} = (\Sigma{\Pi} + \lambda \text{diag}(\Sigma{\Pi}) + \mu I)^{-1/2}. Covariance Matrix (\Sigma{\Pi}): A k \times k matrix representing the covariance of the derivatives of projected points with respect to camera parameters. Numbered Steps: 1. Point Sampling: For each camera i, sample m points within its view frustum. Sample pixel positions \mathbf{p} = (u, v) uniformly. Sample normalized ray distances d \in [0, 1] uniformly between normalized near and far planes d \sim U(n, f). Unnormalize sampled depths using the power ladder transform of Zip-NeRF, with a curve identical to its ray sampling distribution. 2. Compute Jacobian: Compute the Jacobian matrix J{\Pi} \in \mathbb{R}^{2m \times k} of the projection function \Pi(\mathbf{x}; \boldsymbol{\phi}) with respect to the camera parameters \boldsymbol{\phi} at the current parameter estimate \boldsymbol{\phi}0. The rows correspond to the 2D coordinates of the m projected points. 3. Compute Covariance: Calculate the covariance matrix \Sigma{\Pi} = J{\Pi}^\top J{\Pi}. 4. Compute Preconditioner: Apply dampening to improve conditioning: Pi^{-1} = (\Sigma{\Pi} + \lambda \text{diag}(\Sigma{\Pi}) + \mu I)^{-1/2} where \lambda and \mu are dampening hyperparameters, and I is the identity matrix. 5. Reformulate Optimization: Define latent parameters \tilde{\boldsymbol{\phi}}i such that the actual camera parameters used in the NeRF are \boldsymbol{\phi}i = Pi^{-1} \tilde{\boldsymbol{\phi}}i. This transforms the covariance of the projected points with respect to \tilde{\boldsymbol{\phi}}i to the identity matrix Ik (ZCA whitening). 6. Optimization Loop: For each iteration, compute the loss \mathcal{L} using \boldsymbol{\phi}i = Pi^{-1} \tilde{\boldsymbol{\phi}}i. Update \tilde{\boldsymbol{\phi}}i using an optimizer (e.g., Adam). Shared Intrinsics: If intrinsic parameters are shared across cameras, add a variance loss term \mathcal{L}{\text{shared}} to minimize the variance of these shared parameters. 7. Static Preconditioner: The preconditioner Pi^{-1} is computed once at initialization and kept static during optimization to avoid invalidating the running averages of gradient moments in optimizers like Adam. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import numpy as np def projectpoints(params, points3d): """Standard pinhole projection with optional distortion. Returns 2D coordinates (2m,)""" # Standard differentiable projection implementation for the chosen parameterization pass def computejacobianprojection(params, points3d, eps=1e-5): """Compute Jacobian of projection w.r.t camera parameters via finite differences.""" k = len(params) m = len(points3d) J = np.zeros((2 m, k)) for j in range(k): paramsplus = params.copy() paramsplus[j] += eps projplus = projectpoints(paramsplus, points3d) projminus = projectpoints(params, points3d) J[:, j] = (projplus - projminus) / (2 eps) return J def computepreconditioner(params0, points3d, lambdaval, muval): """Compute the per-camera preconditioner matrix Pinv.""" k = len(params0) J = computejacobianprojection(params0, points3d) Sigma = J.T @ J DampedSigma = Sigma + lambdaval np.diag(np.diag(Sigma)) + muval np.eye(k) eigenvalues, eigenvectors = np.linalg.eigh(DampedSigma) eigenvalues = np.maximum(eigenvalues, 1e-10) Dinvsqrt = np.diag(1.0 / np.sqrt(eigenvalues)) Pinv = eigenvectors @ Dinvsqrt @ eigenvectors.T return Pinv def optimizecameras(camerasdata, points3d, lambdaval, muval, lr, warmupsteps, totalsteps): """Main optimization loop for Camera Preconditioning.""" optimizedlatentparams = [] for cam in camerasdata: phi0 = cam['params0'] camid = cam['id'] # 1. Compute static preconditioner at initialization Pinv = computepreconditioner(phi0, points3d[camid], lambdaval, muval) P = np.linalg.inv(Pinv) # 2. Initialize latent parameters tildephi = P @ phi0 grad = np.zeroslike(tildephi) # 3. Optimization loop for step in range(totalsteps): # Map latent parameters to actual camera parameters phi = Pinv @ tildephi # 4. Compute loss and gradient via differentiable rendering # Standard differentiable volume rendering forward/backward pass loss, gradphi = renderandbackprop(phi, points3d[camid]) # Transform gradient to latent space: dL/d(tildephi) = Pinv^T @ dL/d(phi) grad = Pinv.T @ gradphi # 5. Apply learning rate schedule warmupfactor = min(1.0, step / warmupsteps) cosinedecay = np.cos(np.pi step / (2 totalsteps)) currentlr = lr warmupfactor cosinedecay # 6. Update latent parameters tildephi -= currentlr grad # 7. Handle shared intrinsic variance loss if applicable if cam.get('sharedintrinsics'): sharedloss = computevarianceloss(cam['sharedparams']) gradshared = computegradient(sharedloss, cam['sharedparams']) cam['sharedparams'] -= currentlr gradshared optimizedlatentparams.append(tildephi) return optimizedlatentparams def renderandbackprop(phi, points3d): """Standard differentiable volume rendering. Returns loss and gradient w.r.t phi.""" # Standard differentiable rendering implementation pass def computevarianceloss(sharedparams): """Compute variance loss for shared intrinsic parameters.""" # Standard variance computation over shared parameters pass def computegradient(loss, params): """Compute gradient of loss w.r.t params.""" # Standard automatic differentiation or finite difference gradient pass Parameters: \lambda: Dampening parameter for the diagonal of the covariance matrix. Typical value: 10^{-1}. \mu: Dampening parameter for the identity matrix added to the covariance matrix. Typical value: 10^{-8}. Learning Rate for Camera Parameters: Logarithmically decays from 10^{-3} to 10^{-4} over training. Warmup Multiplier: Cosine-decayed from 10^{-8} to 1 for the first 2500 iterations. Variance Loss Weights (Shared Intrinsics): Focal length 10^{-1}, Principal Point 10^{-2}, Radial Distortion 10^{-2}. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Dynamic Re-parameterization: Avoid updating the preconditioner during optimization. Dynamic updates render the running averages of gradient moments used in optimizers like Adam inaccurate. Lens Distortion: Lens distortion parameters can cause very small changes to dramatically affect point projection, making the covariance matrix ill-conditioned. Dampening parameters \lambda and \mu are especially important in this case. Local Minima: Preconditioning does not always prevent falling into local minima (e.g., white floaters in synthetic NeRF dataset due to bad camera poses). Procrustes Alignment: The Procrustes alignment method breaks when focal length changes significantly, so it is omitted in evaluation. Time Complexity: The preconditioner computation involves eigendecomposition of a k \times k matrix, where k is the number of camera parameters (typically small, e.g., 10-20). Training time is approximately 2 hours on 8 NVIDIA V100 GPUs for 25,000 steps. Memory Complexity: Requires storing the preconditioner matrix Pi^{-1} for each camera (O(k^2) per camera) and the sampled points. Measured Performance: On the perturbed 360 dataset, preconditioning improves PSNR between 4.3 and 6.8 dB for all camera parameterizations. On the perturbed synthetic dataset, FocalPose+Intrinsics with CamP achieves PSNR 28.29, SSIM 0.930, LPIPS 0.064, and camera metrics R=0.420^\circ, p=0.186, f=54.3 px. Strengths: Decorrelates parameter effects and normalizes their scale, leading to improved convergence and accuracy. Handles mixed units and correlated parameters better than per-parameter scaling or Adam. Limitations: Does not guarantee escape from local minima. The preconditioner is computed once at initialization based on the initial camera parameter estimate. Camera Preconditioning (CamP) was introduced by K. Park et al. in the paper "CamP: Camera Preconditioning for Neural Radiance Fields" (ACM Trans. Graph., Vol. 42, No. 6, Article 208, December 2023). It builds on the observation that naive camera parameterizations in NeRF optimization are ill-conditioned due to differences in parameter magnitude (e.g., world units vs. pixels) and spurious correlations. The method draws inspiration from numerical methods, specifically the Zero Component Analysis (ZCA) whitening transform, to design a per-camera preconditioner. It is implemented on top of ZipNeRF and used on datasets like 360, Perturbed-360, Perturbed-Synthetic, and ARKit. CamP: Camera Preconditioning for Neural Radiance Fields, https://doi.org/10.1145/3618321, fetched 2026-10-30

name: SPARF
head: Neural Radiance Fields from Sparse and Noisy Poses, SPARF Joint Pose-NeRF Training Strategy, joint pose-NeRF optimization, pose-NeRF training
body: SPARF is a joint pose-NeRF training strategy designed for novel view synthesis from sparse input views (as few as 3) with noisy camera pose estimates. It solves the problems of overfitting and geometric inconsistency inherent in sparse-view regimes by enforcing multi-view geometry constraints, specifically multi-view correspondence and depth consistency losses, rather than relying solely on photometric loss. Unlike sibling methods that optimize poses and NeRF weights using independent per-image photometric supervision, SPARF explicitly connects training views through pixel correspondences to drive convergence to a globally accurate pose and scene solution. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: n RGB images (typically n=3) with large viewpoint variations and noisy camera pose estimates. No prior on scene shape is assumed. Outputs: Optimized camera poses \hat{P} and NeRF parameters \Theta defining the radiance field. Data Structures and Layouts: Camera Pose P: Represented as a world-to-camera transformation matrix. Translation: A 3D embedding vector t \in \mathbb{R}^3 optimized directly. Rotation: A continuous 6D embedding vector r \in \mathbb{R}^6 optimized directly. The rotation matrix R is recovered from r using a Gram-Schmidt-like process. Given r = [a1^T, a2^T] where a1, a2 \in \mathbb{R}^3, the columns of R = [b1, b2, b3] are computed as: b1 = \frac{a1}{\|a1\|} b2 = \frac{a2 - (a2 \cdot b1)b1}{\|a2 - (a2 \cdot b1)b1\|} b3 = b1 \times b2 NeRF Model: A multi-layer perceptron (MLP) mapping 3D coordinates and viewing directions to color and density. The sources note that for LLFF joint optimization, a single coarse MLP suffices, reducing training time compared to hierarchical sampling. Correspondences: Dense matches q for each pixel p and confidence wp inferred from a pre-trained matching model (e.g., PDC-Net). Numbered Steps: 1. Pre-compute Correspondences: Extract dense matches between all pairs of training views using a pre-trained dense correspondence regression network (e.g., PDC-Net). Filter matches by confidence threshold \gamma = 0.95 (PR operator) and optionally by cyclic consistency < 1.5 pixels. 2. Initialize: Initialize NeRF weights and camera poses (noisy estimates). Set depth sampling bounds. For LLFF, use inverse depth space with lower bound 1/tn = 1 and upper bound 1/tf = 0.05. For DTU/Replica, use metric space [tn, tf]. If poses are noisy, expand depth range by factor \epsilon = 0.3, i.e., [(1-\epsilon)tn, (1+\epsilon)tf]. 3. Staged Training Loop: Iterate for total N iterations (typically 100K for joint optimization). Stage 1 (Iterations 0 to 0.3N): Jointly optimize camera poses \hat{P} and the coarse NeRF MLP \Thetac. Stage 2 (Iterations 0.3N to N): Freeze camera poses \hat{P}. Optimize both coarse and fine NeRF MLPs (\Thetac, \Thetaf) if hierarchical sampling is used. Per-Iteration Procedure: 1. Photometric Loss: Sample x random pixels from all training images. Compute rendered color \hat{I} and photometric loss \mathcal{L}{photo} against ground truth I. 2. Multi-View Correspondence Loss: Sample an image pair (Ii, Ij) and a subset of 1024 matches. For each match (p, q) with confidence wp: Backproject pixel p in Ii to 3D using rendered depth \hat{z}(p; \Theta, \hat{P}i) and pose \hat{P}i. Project the 3D point into view Ij using \hat{P}j to get predicted pixel \hat{q}. Compute re-projection error \rho(\|q - \hat{q}\|^2) using Huber loss \rho. Accumulate \mathcal{L}{MVCorr} = \sum wp \rho(\dots). 3. Depth Consistency Loss: Sample a training view Ii with pose \hat{P}i. Find the closest other training view and compute a virtual "unknown" pose P{un} by interpolating the poses of two close-by training views. Sample 1024 pixels p in Ii. Backproject p to 3D point r{un,y} using \hat{P}i and rendered depth \hat{z}(p; \Theta, \hat{P}i). Project r{un,y} into the virtual view P{un} to get pixel y and depth zy. Compute rendered depth \hat{z}(y; \Theta, P{un}) at y in the virtual view. Calculate visibility mask \gammay = T{un, zy} = \exp \left( -\sum{m'=1}^{m} \sigma{m'} \delta{m'} \right) evaluated at the virtual view ray, where T is accumulated transmittance. \gammay \approx 1 if unoccluded, \approx 0 if occluded. Compute \mathcal{L}{DCons} = \sum \gammay \rho(zy - \hat{z}(y; \Theta, P{un})). Note: Backpropagate through the pseudo-supervision zy and \hat{z}, but not through \hat{P}i. 4. Total Loss: \mathcal{L} = \mathcal{L}{photo} + \lambdac \mathcal{L}{MVCorr} + \lambdad \mathcal{L}{DCons}. 5. Update: Update parameters using Adam optimizer. 4. Loss Weight Decay: After Stage 1 (poses frozen) or from start if poses are fixed, halve \lambdac every 10,000 iterations to gradually increase photometric loss importance and correct geometry errors. Formulas: Volume Rendering: \hat{I}{i,p} = \sum{m=1}^{M} \alpham cm, where \alpham = Tm (1 - \exp(-\sigmam \deltam)) and Tm = \exp \left( -\sum{m'=1}^{m} \sigma{m'} \delta{m'} \right). \deltam = t{m+1} - tm is the distance between adjacent samples. Visibility Mask: \gammay = T{un, zy} = \exp \left( -\sum{m'=1}^{m} \sigma{m'} \delta{m'} \right) evaluated at the unseen view ray. \gammay is close to 1 if no point with large density exists between camera center and 3D point, otherwise close to 0. Rotation Recovery: R = f(r) = [b1, b2, b3], where b1, b2, b3 are computed using a generalized cross product to ensure orthogonality. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import torch import torch.nn as nn import torch.optim as optim def huberloss(error, delta=1.0): abserr = torch.abs(error) quadratic = torch.min(abserr, torch.fulllike(abserr, delta)) return 0.5 quadratic2 + delta (abserr - quadratic) def constructrays(poses, u, v, intrinsics): # u, v are 1D tensors of shape (N,) B, N = u.shape[0], u.shape[0] ones = torch.oneslike(u) pixcoords = torch.stack([u, v, ones], dim=0).unsqueeze(0) # Shape: (1, 3, N) pixcoords = pixcoords / intrinsics[0,:3,:3].unsqueeze(-1) origins = poses[:,:3, 3].unsqueeze(-1).unsqueeze(-1).expand(1, 3, N) directions = torch.bmm(pixcoords, poses[:,:3,:3].transpose(1, 2)).squeeze(0) # Shape: (3, N) directions = directions / torch.norm(directions, dim=0, keepdim=True) return origins, directions def volumerender(nerfmodel, origins, directions, near, far, numsamples): # origins, directions: (B, 3, N) B,, N = origins.shape tvals = torch.linspace(0., 1., numsamples, device=origins.device) # For LLFF, sample in inverse depth space; for DTU/Replica, linear depth. zvals = near (1. - tvals) + far tvals pts = origins.unsqueeze(1) + directions.unsqueeze(1) zvals.view(1, -1, 1) ptsflat = pts.view(B, numsamples, N, 3) dirsflat = directions.unsqueeze(1).expand(-1, numsamples, -1, -1).view(B, numsamples, N, 3) sigmaflat, rgbflat = nerfmodel(ptsflat, dirsflat) sigma = torch.nn.functional.softplus(sigmaflat).view(B, numsamples, N) rgb = rgbflat.view(B, numsamples, N, 3) deltas = zvals[1:] - zvals[:-1] deltainf = torch.tensor(1e10, device=origins.device) deltas = torch.cat([deltas, deltainf]) alpha = 1.0 - torch.exp(-sigma deltas) T = torch.cumprod(1.0 - alpha + 1e-10, dim=1) T = torch.cat([torch.oneslike(T[:,:1]), T[:,:-1]], dim=1) weights = alpha T color = torch.sum(weights.unsqueeze(-1) rgb, dim=1) depth = torch.sum(weights zvals, dim=1) return color, depth, weights, T def project3dtopixel(pts, pose, intrinsics): # pts: (B, 3, N), pose: (B, 3, 4), intrinsics: (B, 3, 3) campts = torch.bmm(pose[:,:3,:3], pts) + pose[:,:3, 3].unsqueeze(-1) pix = torch.bmm(intrinsics, campts) return pix[:, 0,:], pix[:, 1,:], campts[:, 2,:] def interpolatepose(p1, p2, t=0.5): tun = (1 - t) p1[:,:3, 3] + t p2[:,:3, 3] R1 = p1[:,:3,:3] R2 = p2[:,:3,:3] Run = (1 - t) R1 + t R2 b1 = Run[:,:, 0] b1 = b1 / torch.norm(b1, dim=1, keepdim=True) b2raw = Run[:,:, 1] - torch.sum(b1 Run[:,:, 1], dim=1, keepdim=True) b1 b2 = b2raw / torch.norm(b2raw, dim=1, keepdim=True) b3 = torch.cross(b1, b2, dim=1) Run = torch.stack([b1, b2, b3], dim=2) Pun = torch.zeroslike(p1) Pun[:,:3,:3] = Run Pun[:,:3, 3] = tun return Pun def sparfstep(nerfmodel, poses, images, matches, config): B, C, H, W = images.shape optimizernerf, optimizerposes = config['optnerf'], config['optposes'] nerfmodel.train() optimizernerf.zerograd() optimizerposes.zerograd() # 1. Photometric Loss idx = torch.randint(0, H W, (B, config['numphoto'])) u = (idx % W).float() v = (idx // W).float() o, d = constructrays(poses, u, v, config['K']) cphoto,,, = volumerender(nerfmodel, o, d, config['near'], config['far'], config['numsamples']) gt = images[:,:, v.long(), u.long()] lossphoto = torch.mean((cphoto - gt) 2) # 2. Multi-View Correspondence Loss lossmvc = 0.0 pairidx = torch.randint(0, B, (2,)) i, j = pairidx[0], pairidx[1] midx = torch.randint(0, matches[i].shape[0], (config['nummvc'],)) pu, pv = matches[i][midx,:2].T qu, qv = matches[i][midx, 2:4].T w = matches[i][midx, 4] oi, di = constructrays(poses[i:i+1], pu, pv, config['K']), depthi,, = volumerender(nerfmodel, oi, di, config['near'], config['far'], config['numsamples']) pts3d = oi + di depthi.unsqueeze(1) qpredu, qpredv, = project3dtopixel(pts3d, poses[j:j+1], config['K']) error = torch.norm(torch.stack([qpredu - qu, qpredv - qv], dim=1), dim=1) lossmvc = torch.mean(w huberloss(error)) # 3. Depth Consistency Loss lossdc = 0.0 idc = torch.randint(0, B, (1,)).item() kdc = (idc + 1) % B Pun = interpolatepose(poses[idc:idc+1], poses[kdc:kdc+1]) udc, vdc = torch.rand(config['numdc']), torch.rand(config['numdc']) odc, ddc = constructrays(poses[idc:idc+1], udc, vdc, config['K']), depthdc,, = volumerender(nerfmodel, odc, ddc, config['near'], config['far'], config['numsamples']) ptsun = odc + ddc depthdc.unsqueeze(1) yu, yv, zy = project3dtopixel(ptsun, Pun, config['K']) oun, dun = constructrays(Pun, yu, yv, config['K']), depthun,, Tun = volumerender(nerfmodel, oun, dun, config['near'], config['far'], config['numsamples']) tvals = torch.linspace(0., 1., config['numsamples'], device=oun.device) zvalsun = config['near'] (1. - tvals) + config['far'] tvals # Find index of zy in zvalsun for each pixel idxz = torch.argmin(torch.abs(zvalsun.unsqueeze(1) - zy.unsqueeze(0)), dim=0) # Correct indexing for Tun: (B, numsamples, N) -> (numsamples, N) gammay = Tun[0, idxz, torch.arange(config['numdc'])] lossdc = torch.mean(gammay huberloss(zy - depthun)) # Total Loss lambdac = config['lambdac'] lambdad = config['lambdad'] totalloss = lossphoto + lambdac lossmvc + lambdad lossdc totalloss.backward() optimizernerf.step() optimizerposes.step() return totalloss.item(), lossphoto.item(), lossmvc.item(), lossdc.item() Parameters: Training Duration: 100K iterations for joint pose-NeRF refinement. Hardware: ~10 hours on a single A100 GPU. Image Resolution: Resized to 360×600. Samples per Step: 1024 pixel rays for photometric loss, 1024 matches for correspondence loss, 1024 pixels for depth consistency loss. Loss Weights: \lambdac = 10^{-3}, \lambdad = 10^{-3}. On DTU with fixed GT poses, \lambdac = 10^{-4}, \lambdad = 10^{-3}. Optimizer: Adam. NeRF LR: 5 \times 10^{-4} decaying to 1 \times 10^{-4}. Pose LR: 1 \times 10^{-3} decaying to 1 \times 10^{-4}. Positional Encoding: Coarse-to-fine schedule. Joint optimization: frequency width linearly adjusted from 40% to 70% of iterations. Fixed poses: 10% to 50%. Depth Bounds: LLFF: inverse depth [1, 0.05]. DTU/Replica: metric [tn, tf]. Noisy poses: expand by \epsilon=0.3. Correspondence Filter: Confidence \gamma = 0.95, cyclic consistency < 1.5 pixels. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Overfitting: Direct photometric loss causes overfitting to training views, especially with noisy poses. Solved by using multi-view correspondence as the main signal. Occlusion: Depth consistency loss is invalid for occluded pixels or those projected outside the virtual view. Handled by visibility mask \gammay. Training Length: Training longer than necessary with fixed GT poses leads to overfitting. Recommended limits: 50K/70K iterations for 3 views (DTU/Replica/LLFF respectively), 100K/140K for 6 views, 150K/200K for 9 views. Degenerate Geometry: High-frequency positional encodings with standard NeRF on few views lead to degenerate geometry. Coarse-to-fine PE prevents this. General framework for optimizing poses and NeRF parameters jointly. SPARF is a specific instance tailored for sparse views. Camera Pose and Parameter Optimization Uses local optimization and multi-scale features for pose refinement. SPARF uses global multi-view geometry constraints. MELON Models continuous camera motion over time. SPARF assumes static scene with discrete poses. Time-dependent NeRF with Continuous Camera Motion Uses preconditioning to stabilize pose optimization. SPARF uses staged training and specific loss functions. Camera Preconditioning Uses view matching losses. SPARF uses multi-view correspondence and depth consistency. VMRF (View Matching Neural Radiance Fields) Optimizes poses and appearance factors. SPARF focuses on geometry and pose. NeRF Pose and Appearance Optimization Optimizes poses at test time. SPARF optimizes during training. Test-Time Two-Stage Optimization Time Complexity: 100K iterations, ~10 hours on A100 GPU. Memory Complexity: Standard NeRF memory usage plus storage for pre-computed correspondences. Performance: DTU (3 views, noisy poses): PSNR 17.74, SSIM 0.71, LPIPS 0.26, Rot 1.81°, Trans 5.0×100. Outperforms BARF (PSNR 10.71) and SCNeRF (PSNR 12.04). LLFF (3 views, identity poses): PSNR 19.58, SSIM 0.61, LPIPS 0.31, Rot 0.53°, Trans 2.8×100. Outperforms BARF (PSNR 17.47) and SCNeRF (PSNR 17.10). Replica (3 views, COLMAP poses): PSNR 26.98, SSIM 0.88, LPIPS 0.13, Rot 0.15°, Trans 0.36×100. Outperforms DS-NeRF (PSNR 24.75) and SCNeRF (PSNR 22.54). Strengths: Handles sparse views (3 images) and noisy poses effectively. Prevents overfitting through multi-view constraints. Limitations: Requires pre-computed dense correspondences. Performance degrades if correspondences are inaccurate. Limited to static scenes. When to Use: Sparse-view novel view synthesis with noisy initial poses. When Not to Use: Dense-view settings (other methods may be more efficient), dynamic scenes, or when high-quality initial poses are available (fixed pose optimization may suffice). SPARF was introduced in the paper "SPARF: Neural Radiance Fields from Sparse and Noisy Poses". It addresses the challenge of novel view synthesis in the sparse-view regime, where traditional NeRF methods overfit and fail to converge to a globally consistent geometry. The method builds on principles of multi-view geometry, specifically using pixel correspondences and depth consistency to constrain the optimization. It was evaluated on DTU, LLFF, and Replica datasets, setting new state-of-the-art results for few-view synthesis with noisy poses. name: Test-Time Two-Stage Optimization
head: Test-time pose and appearance optimization
body: Test-Time Two-Stage Optimization is a post-training evaluation procedure that first optimizes camera poses and then optimizes appearance embeddings to handle unconstrained image collections with varying lighting and transient objects. It distinguishes itself from sibling methods by decoupling pose refinement and appearance adaptation into two sequential stages, addressing the limitations of methods that optimize only poses (e.g., BARF) or only appearance (e.g., NeRF-W). Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: A pre-trained NeRF model (weights \Theta), a set of test images \{Ii\}, and initial camera pose estimates Pi for the test images. Outputs: Refined camera poses P'i and optimized appearance embeddings Ai for the test images. Data Structures: Pose Parameters: For each test image i, a 6-dimensional vector representing rotation and translation, or a 4 \times 4 transformation matrix. Appearance Embeddings: A learnable vector ai per test image, concatenated with the positional encoding of the 3D point before the density/color MLPs. NeRF Weights: Fixed during optimization. Numbered Steps: 1. Stage 1: Pose Optimization Initialization: Initialize appearance embeddings Ai randomly. Initialize test pose parameters Pi using Procrustes analysis: compute the alignment matrix M between the trained poses of training images and their ground-truth poses, then apply M to the ground-truth test poses. Freezing: Freeze all NeRF network weights \Theta. Optimization: Optimize Pi and Ai jointly using the test images. Sampling: Sample 1024 rays per iteration. For each ray, sample 128 points for the coarse model and 128 points for the fine model. Duration: 20,000 iterations. Learning Rates: 1 \times 10^{-4} for pose parameters Pi; 5 \times 10^{-3} for appearance embeddings Ai. No learning rate decay is applied. 2. Stage 2: Appearance Optimization Freezing: Freeze the refined pose parameters P'i from Stage 1. Re-initialization: Re-initialize the appearance embeddings Ai. Optimization: Optimize only Ai using the test images. Data Splitting: To prevent information leakage, optimize on the left half of the test images and evaluate only on the right half. Duration: 20 epochs. Learning Rates: 1 \times 10^{-1} for appearance embeddings Ai. No learning rate decay is applied. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def testtimetwostageoptimization(nerfmodel, testimages, initialposes, traintrainedposes, traingtposes): """ nerfmodel: Pre-trained NeRF with fixed weights. testimages: List of test images [I1,..., IN]. initialposes: Initial pose estimates for test images. traintrainedposes: Trained poses of training images. traingtposes: Ground-truth poses of training images. """ N = len(testimages) # Stage 1: Pose Optimization # Initialize appearance embeddings randomly appearanceembeddings = [random.randn(1, 256) for in testimages] # Initialize poses using Procrustes analysis: compute alignment matrix M # between traintrainedposes and traingtposes, then apply M to initialposes poses = applyprocrustesalignment(initialposes, traintrainedposes, traingtposes) for iteration in range(20000): rays = samplerays(testimages, poses, numrays=1024) renderedcolors = nerfmodel.render(rays, poses, appearanceembeddings) loss = computeloss(renderedcolors, rays.gtcolors) # Perform optimizer step for poses and appearance embeddings # LRpose = 1e-4, LRappearance = 5e-3 refinedposes = poses # Stage 2: Appearance Optimization # Re-initialize appearance embeddings appearanceembeddings = [random.randn(1, 256) for in testimages] leftimages = testimages[:N//2] rightimages = testimages[N//2:] for epoch in range(20): rays = samplerays(leftimages, refinedposes, numrays=1024) renderedcolors = nerfmodel.render(rays, refinedposes, appearanceembeddings) loss = computeloss(renderedcolors, rays.gtcolors) # Perform optimizer step for appearance embeddings # LRappearance = 1e-1 evalrays = samplerays(rightimages, refinedposes, numrays=1024) evalrendered = nerfmodel.render(evalrays, refinedposes, appearanceembeddings) evalloss = computeloss(evalrendered, evalrays.gtcolors) return refinedposes, appearanceembeddings Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Information Leakage: Optimizing on the same images used for evaluation can lead to overfitting. The method mitigates this by splitting test images into training (left half) and evaluation (right half) sets during Stage 2. Local Minima: Without proper initialization or candidate heads, pose optimization may fall into local minima. Procrustes analysis provides a robust initialization based on training data alignment. Time Complexity: The optimization is performed at test time, adding latency. Stage 1 requires 20,000 iterations, and Stage 2 requires 20 epochs. The number of sampled rays is reduced to 1024 per iteration (from 2048 in training) to speed up computation. Memory Complexity: Requires storing pose parameters and appearance embeddings for all test images. The NeRF weights are frozen, so no additional memory for model weights is needed. Strengths: Handles unconstrained image collections with varying lighting and transient objects effectively. Decoupling pose and appearance optimization improves convergence stability. Limitations: Computationally expensive due to the two-stage optimization process. Requires a pre-trained NeRF model. Performance depends on the quality of the initial pose estimates. When to Use: When dealing with unconstrained image collections where camera poses are not known or are inaccurate, and lighting conditions vary significantly. When Not to Use: When computational resources are limited, or when camera poses are already accurate and lighting is consistent. Test-Time Two-Stage Optimization was introduced in the context of UP-NeRF (Unconstrained Pose-Prior-Free Neural Radiance Fields). It addresses the limitations of previous methods like BARF, which only optimizes poses, and NeRF-W, which only optimizes appearance given fixed poses. UP-NeRF: Unconstrained Pose-Prior-Free Neural Radiance Fields, https://arxiv.org/abs/2311.03784v2, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial)

name: Joint Pose and Radiance Field Optimization
head: Joint Pose Optimization, Unposed NeRF Optimization, Self-Calibration in NeRF
body: Joint Pose and Radiance Field Optimization solves the problem of reconstructing a 3D scene from an unposed image collection by simultaneously optimizing the neural radiance field parameters and the camera extrinsic (and optionally intrinsic) parameters. It distinguishes itself from methods that assume known poses by treating camera poses as learnable variables in the optimization loop, thereby addressing the "chicken-and-egg" problem where pose estimation requires a good scene model and vice versa. This approach builds on Camera Pose and Extrinsic/Intrinsic Optimization by extending the optimization domain to include the scene representation itself. All methods in this family share the core mechanism of differentiable rendering, where the rendered pixel color \hat{C}(r) is a differentiable function of the camera pose P and the NeRF parameters \Theta. The optimization problem is typically formulated as minimizing a loss function \mathcal{L} with respect to both \Theta and P: \min{\Theta, P} \mathcal{L}(\hat{C}(r; \Theta, P), C(r)) where C(r) is the ground-truth pixel color. The gradient \nablaP \mathcal{L} allows the camera pose to be updated via an optimizer (e.g., Adam, SGD) in lockstep with the NeRF weights. Key shared components include: 1. Ray Casting: Computing ray origins \hat{o} and directions \hat{d} from pixel coordinates using current camera estimates. For a pinhole camera model with focal length f and rotation R and translation t: \hat{o} = t \hat{d} = R \begin{pmatrix} (u - W/2)/f \\ -(v - H/2)/f \\ -1 \end{pmatrix} 2. Differentiable Rendering: The volume rendering integral is computed via discrete summation, allowing backpropagation through the ray marching process to the pose parameters. 3. Joint Optimization: Separate optimizers or a combined optimizer are used to update NeRF weights and pose parameters, often with different learning rates to stabilize convergence. RoDynRF enables dynamic scene reconstruction from monocular videos without known camera poses by jointly optimizing intrinsics, extrinsics, and both static and dynamic radiance fields. It distinguishes itself from sibling methods like VMRF and NeRF Pose and Appearance Optimization by explicitly separating static and dynamic components via a two-branch architecture and using motion masks to isolate static geometry for robust pose estimation, thereby handling unposed, in-the-wild video data. See RoDynRF. VMRF is a method for novel view synthesis that learns Neural Radiance Field (NeRF) representations without prior knowledge of camera poses or hand-crafted camera pose distributions. It employs a view matching scheme using unbalanced optimal transport to map features from a rendered image (with a random pose) to a real image, generating a feature transport plan. This plan guides a pose calibration technique that predicts relative pose transformations to rectify randomized poses into estimated real-image poses, which are then used to jointly refine the NeRF and camera parameters. Unlike GNeRF, which estimates absolute poses directly and requires accurate pose distributions, VMRF estimates relative poses, making it robust to out-of-dataset views. See VMRF (View Matching Neural Radiance Fields). This method jointly optimizes camera poses and neural scene representations for unconstrained image collections containing varying illumination and transient occluders, without requiring camera pose priors. It distinguishes itself from standard NeRF optimization by introducing a candidate head for robust pose estimation in "hard-pose" images and a loss scheduling mechanism that transitions from candidate-specific to shared scene representations. It builds on Joint Pose and Radiance Field Optimization by addressing the "chicken-and-egg" problem of pose estimation in unposed data through surrogate tasks and transient-aware supervision. See NeRF Pose and Appearance Optimization. Self-calibrating joint optimization model for NeRF that optimizes unknown poses and camera intrinsic parameters for non-linear camera models such as fish-eye lens models. Use curriculum learning to gradually introduce the nonlinear camera/noise parameters to the joint optimization. The problem of optimizing camera poses alongside radiance fields emerged as a solution to the dependency on Structure-from-Motion (SfM) pipelines, which can fail on textureless or repetitive scenes. Early work such as BARF (Blending ARtifact Free) introduced frequency-aware optimization to stabilize convergence. Jeong et al. introduced a self-calibrating joint optimization model for NeRF (SCNeRF) in August 2021, which optimized unknown poses and intrinsic parameters for non-linear camera models like fish-eye lenses using curriculum learning. GNeRF (March 2021) by Meng et al. used pose as a generative latent code, obtaining coarse poses via adversarial training. These methods laid the groundwork for more complex joint optimization strategies like RoDynRF, VMRF, and NeRF Pose and Appearance Optimization. Neural Radiance Fields in 3D Vision: A Comprehensive Review, https://doi.org/10.26599/cvm.2026.9450535, fetched 2026-10-28

name: RoDynRF
head: Robust Dynamic Radiance Fields
body: RoDynRF enables dynamic scene reconstruction from monocular videos without known camera poses by jointly optimizing intrinsics, extrinsics, and both static and dynamic radiance fields. It distinguishes itself from static pose optimization methods by introducing a two-branch architecture that separates background and moving regions, using motion masks to exclude dynamic pixels during pose estimation to prevent optimization drift. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A sequence of monocular video frames (images) with unknown camera poses and intrinsics. Output: Optimized camera poses (P), intrinsics (K), a static radiance field (\Theta{static}), a dynamic radiance field (\Theta{dynamic}), and a time-conditioned deformation network (\Theta{def}). Data Structures: Static Radiance Field: Standard NeRF representation (MLP or grid) encoding static scene geometry and appearance. Dynamic Radiance Field: Separate representation for moving objects. Deformation Network: A time-conditioned network mapping spatial coordinates and time to deformation vectors. Motion Masks: Binary masks identifying dynamic pixels in each frame. Steps: 1. Initialization: Initialize static and dynamic radiance fields. Initialize camera poses and intrinsics. 2. Motion Masking: Generate motion masks for each frame to identify dynamic regions. These masks are used to exclude dynamic pixels from the pose estimation loss. 3. Coarse-to-Fine Optimization: Employ a coarse-to-fine voxel optimization scheme to stabilize the joint optimization of poses and fields. 4. Joint Optimization Loop: a. Ray Casting: For each pixel, cast a ray using current camera estimates. b. Differentiable Rendering: Compute rendered color \hat{C} by volume rendering through both static and dynamic fields. The dynamic field is deformed using the time-conditioned deformation network based on the current time step. c. Loss Computation: Compute loss \mathcal{L} using only static pixels (masked out dynamic regions) for pose and static field updates. Include reconstruction loss for dynamic pixels for dynamic field updates. d. Gradient Update: Update camera poses, intrinsics, static fields, dynamic fields, and deformation network parameters using an optimizer (e.g., Adam). 5. Refinement: Iterate until convergence. Formulas: Deformation: \mathbf{x}' = \mathbf{x} + \Delta \mathbf{x}(\mathbf{x}, t; \Theta{def}), where \mathbf{x} is the 3D coordinate, t is time, and \Delta \mathbf{x} is the deformation vector. Rendering: \hat{C}(r) = \sum{i=1}^N Ti \alphai ci, where Ti is transmittance, \alphai is opacity, and ci is color, sampled from the deformed dynamic field or static field. Pose Loss: \mathcal{L}{pose} = \sum{p \in \text{static}} || \hat{C}(rp) - C(rp) ||^2, where p are pixels in static regions. Parameters: Learning rates for poses, intrinsics, static fields, dynamic fields, and deformation network. Coarse-to-fine voxel grid resolutions. Time conditioning frequency. Edge Cases: Degenerate Motion: If motion is minimal, motion masks may be unreliable. Use temporal consistency checks or additional constraints. Occlusion: Dynamic objects occluding static background. Ensure motion masks accurately capture occlusion boundaries. Precision: Joint optimization can be unstable. Use different learning rates for poses and fields. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def rodynrfoptimization(frames, initialposes, initialintrinsics): # Initialize fields and deformation network staticnerf = initializenerf() dynamicnerf = initializenerf() deformationnet = initializedeformationnetwork() # Initialize poses and intrinsics poses = copy(initialposes) intrinsics = copy(initialintrinsics) # Coarse-to-fine loop for resolution in coarsetofineresolutions: for epoch in range(maxepochs): for frameidx, frame in enumerate(frames): # Generate motion mask for current frame motionmask = computemotionmask(frame, previousframe) # Ray casting using current poses and intrinsics rays = castrays(frame, poses[frameidx], intrinsics) # Volume rendering # Deform dynamic points based on time deformeddynamicpoints = deformpoints(dynamicpoints, frameidx, deformationnet) # Render static and dynamic components staticcolor = volumerender(rays, staticnerf) dynamiccolor = volumerender(rays, dynamicnerf, deformeddynamicpoints) renderedcolor = staticcolor + dynamiccolor # Compute loss # Exclude dynamic pixels from pose loss staticpixels = maskstaticpixels(motionmask) poseloss = computereconstructionloss(renderedcolor[staticpixels], frame[staticpixels]) dynamicloss = computereconstructionloss(renderedcolor[~staticpixels], frame[~staticpixels]) totalloss = poseloss + dynamicloss # Update parameters updateparameters(poses, intrinsics, staticnerf, dynamicnerf, deformationnet, totalloss) previousframe = frame return poses, intrinsics, staticnerf, dynamicnerf, deformationnet SceneRF is a self-supervised monocular 3D scene reconstruction method trained using only image sequences with poses. It handles large scenes through explicit depth optimization and a novel probabilistic sampling strategy. It achieves the best performance in all metrics for new depth view synthesis, including absolute relative error, root mean square error, and IoU. Time Complexity: High due to joint optimization of poses, intrinsics, and two radiance fields. Coarse-to-fine scheme helps convergence speed. Memory Complexity: High due to storing static and dynamic fields and deformation network. Performance: Robust to unposed, in-the-wild video data. Strengths: Handles dynamic scenes, no need for known poses, robust to motion. Limitations: Computationally expensive, requires careful tuning of motion masks and learning rates. When to use: Dynamic scene reconstruction from monocular video without known poses. When not to use: Static scenes, or when poses are known. RoDynRF was introduced in January 2023. It builds on the static-to-dynamic learning paradigm, first learning static scene representation from multi-view stills, then learning deformation from a few-view dynamic sequence, allowing much faster convergence than fully implicit networks.
