name: VMRF (View Matching Neural Radiance Fields)
head: View Matching NeRF
body: VMRF is a method for novel view synthesis that learns Neural Radiance Field (NeRF) representations without prior knowledge of camera poses or hand-crafted camera pose distributions. It solves the problem of pose estimation in texture-poor or repetitive scenes where classical Structure-from-Motion (SfM) fails, and where direct absolute pose estimation methods (like GNeRF) are sensitive to out-of-dataset views. VMRF distinguishes itself by estimating relative pose transformations via a view matching scheme using unbalanced optimal transport (UOT), rather than predicting absolute poses directly from images. It builds on Joint Pose and Radiance Field Optimization by introducing a differentiable feature-matching step to guide pose calibration. VMRF operates in an iterative, end-to-end optimization loop, initially following the hybrid training scheme of GNeRF. It begins with randomly initialized camera poses and a coarse NeRF, then refines both the NeRF parameters and the camera poses jointly. Inputs: A set of n RGB images I = \{I1, I2,..., In\} of a static scene. No camera poses are provided. Outputs: Optimized NeRF parameters \Theta and estimated camera poses \hat{\Phi} = \{\hat{\phi}1,..., \hat{\phi}n\}. 1. NeRF Model (F\Theta): A multi-layer perceptron (MLP) parameterizing the 5D scene function F\Theta(x, b) \rightarrow (c, \sigma), mapping a 3D point x \in \mathbb{R}^3 and viewing direction b \in S^2 to RGB color c \in \mathbb{R}^3 and volume density \sigma \in \mathbb{R}. 2. Camera Pose (\phi): Represented as a 4 \times 4 transformation matrix containing rotation and translation. Rotation is encoded as a continuous 6D embedding, and position as a 3D Euclidean embedding. 3. Feature Sets: Source feature set \mathbf{f}s \in \mathbb{R}^{l \times d} extracted from the rendered image. Target feature set \mathbf{f}t \in \mathbb{R}^{l \times d} extracted from the real image. Parameters: l = 64 (number of feature vectors), d = 256 (dimension of feature vectors). 4. Transport Plan (T): A matrix T \in \mathbb{R}^{l \times l} where T{ij} represents the amount of mass moved from source feature i to target feature j. 5. Relative Transformation Predictor (RTP): A Vision Transformer-based network that outputs a 6-dimensional vector [tx, ty, tz, \thetax, \thetay, \thetaz] representing relative translation and rotation. 1. Initialization: Initialize the set of randomly sampled camera poses \Phi' = \{\phi'i, i \in [1, n]\}. Initialize the NeRF parameters \Theta and a discriminator D. 2. Coarse NeRF Training (Adversarial Phase): Train the coarse NeRF F and discriminator D using adversarial loss to ensure generated images have a similar distribution to real images. \mathcal{L}{adv}(F, D) = \mathbb{E}{I \sim P{data}} [\log(D(I))] + \mathbb{E}{F(\Phi') \sim Pg} [\log(1 - D(F(\Phi')))] where P{data} is the distribution of real images and Pg is the distribution of generated images. 3. Feature Extraction: For each image Ii and its corresponding rendered image \hat{I}i (generated using current pose \phi'i and NeRF F): Extract source features \mathbf{f}s from \hat{I}i using a pre-trained VGG-19 network. Extract target features \mathbf{f}t from Ii using a pre-trained VGG-19 network. 4. View Matching via Unbalanced Optimal Transport (UOT): Compute the cost matrix M \in \mathbb{R}^{l \times l} based on feature similarity: M = 1 - \frac{\mathbf{f}s \cdot \mathbf{f}t^T}{\|\mathbf{f}s\| \|\mathbf{f}t\|} where M{ij} denotes the moving cost from source feature i to target feature j. Solve for the optimal transport plan T^ by minimizing the entropic regularized UOT objective: T^ = \arg \minT \left[ \sum{i,j=1}^{l} T{ij} M{ij} - \eta H(T) + \epsilon KL(T \mathbf{1}l || \mus) + \epsilon KL(T^T \mathbf{1}l || \mut) \right] where: \eta = 0.005 is the entropic regularization parameter. H(T) = -\sum{i,j=1}^{l} T{ij} \log(T{ij} + 1) is the entropic regularization term. \epsilon > 0 is the KL divergence regularization parameter. \mus and \mut are the discrete source and target distributions defined by the feature sets. The solution is computed using the Sinkhorn algorithm on the Fenchel-Legendre dual form. Note: UOT is used instead of standard OT because occlusions cause inconsistent total mass between views, leading to false matches with standard OT. 5. Pose Calibration (Relative Transformation Prediction): Predict the relative pose transformation between the real image and the rendered image using the transport plan T^: [tx, ty, tz, \thetax, \thetay, \thetaz] = RTP(T^) where RTP is the relative transformation predictor. Construct the relative rotation matrix \Delta R and translation vector \Delta t: \Delta R = Rx(\thetax) Ry(\thetay) Rz(\thetaz) \Delta t = [tx, ty, tz]^T where Rx, Ry, Rz are standard rotation matrices. Calibrate the randomized pose \phi'i to estimate the real pose \hat{\phi}i: \hat{\phi}i = \begin{bmatrix} \Delta R & \Delta t \\ 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix} \phi'i 6. NeRF and Pose Optimization: Optimize the NeRF parameters \Theta and the estimated poses \hat{\Phi} using the photometric loss: \mathcal{L}P(F, \hat{\Phi}) = \frac{1}{n} \sum{i=1}^{n} \| Ii - F(\hat{\phi}i) \|^2 Additionally, train the relative transformation predictor using a calibration loss \mathcal{L}{ca} in an unsupervised manner using pairs of randomly initialized poses: \mathcal{L}{ca}(RTP) = \mathbb{E} \| F{ca}(RTP(T^{ab}), \phi'a) - \phi'b \|^2 where T^{ab} is the transport plan between renders from \phi'a and \phi'b, and F{ca} is a coarse NeRF. 7. Iteration: Repeat steps 3-6 end-to-end. The method uses a hybrid and iterative optimization scheme similar to GNeRF. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import numpy as np import torch import torch.nn as nn import torch.nn.functional as F def vmrftrainingloop(images, numiterations, l=64, d=256, eta=0.005, epsilon=1e-3): """ Main training loop for VMRF. images: List of n RGB images. """ n = len(images) # 1. Initialization # Randomly initialize camera poses phiprime phiprime = [randompose() for in range(n)] # Initialize NeRF Ftheta and Discriminator D Ftheta = NeRF() D = Discriminator() # Initialize Relative Transformation Predictor RTP RTP = RelativeTransformationPredictor() # Pre-trained VGG-19 for feature extraction vgg19 = getpretrainedvgg19() vgg19.eval() # Optimizers optimizerneRF = torch.optim.Adam(Ftheta.parameters(), lr=0.0005) optimizerD = torch.optim.Adam(D.parameters(), lr=0.0001) optimizerRTP = torch.optim.Adam(RTP.parameters(), lr=0.0001) for iteration in range(numiterations): totalloss = 0 for i in range(n): Ii = images[i] phiiprime = phiprime[i] # 2. Render image using current pose and NeRF # Returns rendered image Ihati Ihati = rendernerf(Ftheta, phiiprime) # 3. Feature Extraction # Extract features using VGG-19 # Note: VGG-19 expects specific input preprocessing fs = extractvggfeatures(Ihati, vgg19, l, d) ft = extractvggfeatures(Ii, vgg19, l, d) # 4. View Matching (UOT) # Compute Cost Matrix M # M = 1 - (fs. ft^T) / (||fs|| ||ft||) # Ensure fs and ft are normalized or handled correctly for cosine similarity cossim = torch.mm(fs, ft.T) / (torch.norm(fs, dim=1, keepdim=True) torch.norm(ft, dim=1, keepdim=True).T) M = 1.0 - cossim # Solve UOT using Sinkhorn Algorithm # Tstar = argminT [ sum(Tij Mij) - eta H(T) + epsilon KL(T1 || mus) + epsilon KL(T^T1 || mut) ] Tstar = sinkhornuot(M, l, eta, epsilon) # 5. Pose Calibration # Predict relative transformation reltransform = RTP(Tstar) tx, ty, tz, thetax, thetay, thetaz = reltransform # Construct Delta R and Delta t DeltaR = constructrotationmatrix(thetax, thetay, thetaz) Deltat = torch.tensor([tx, ty, tz]) # Calibrate pose # phihati = [DeltaR, Deltat; 0, 1] @ phiiprime phihati = applyrelativetransform(phiiprime, DeltaR, Deltat) # 6. Loss Calculation # Photometric Loss Ireconstructed = rendernerf(Ftheta, phihati) Lp = torch.mean((Ii - Ireconstructed) 2) # Adversarial Loss (for coarse NeRF and D) # In practice, this is applied periodically or in a specific phase # Ladv = E[log(D(I))] + E[log(1 - D(F(phi')))] # For simplicity, assuming we compute D(Ii) and D(Ihati) Dreal = D(Ii) Dfake = D(Ihati) Ladv = -torch.mean(torch.log(Dreal + 1e-8)) - torch.mean(torch.log(1 - Dfake + 1e-8)) # Calibration Loss (for RTP) # Requires a pair of poses and their transport plan # Lca = E || Fca(RTP(Tab), phia) - phib ||^2 # This is computed using random pairs of poses from the batch or a separate sample # For this loop, we assume a helper function computes this loss Lca = computecalibrationloss(RTP, Ftheta, phiprime, l, d, vgg19) # Combine losses # Note: Weights for Ladv and Lca are not specified in the notes, # typically they are hyperparameters. We assume standard weighting or sum. loss = Lp + Ladv + Lca # 7. Optimization Step optimizerneRF.zerograd() optimizerD.zerograd() optimizerRTP.zerograd() loss.backward() optimizerneRF.step() optimizerD.step() optimizerRTP.step() # Update poses for next iteration phiprime[i] = phihati totalloss += loss.item() return Ftheta, phiprime def sinkhornuot(M, l, eta, epsilon, numiterations=100): """ Solves the entropic regularized Unbalanced Optimal Transport problem using Sinkhorn. M: Cost matrix (l x l) l: Number of features eta: Entropic regularization parameter epsilon: KL divergence regularization parameter """ # Initialize dual variables u = torch.zeros(l) v = torch.zeros(l) # Kernel matrix K # Kij = exp((Mij - eta log(Tij + 1)...) / eta) # The dual form in the paper uses Fenchel-Legendre. # Standard Sinkhorn for Entropic OT: K = exp(-M/eta) # For UOT with KL penalties, the kernel is modified. # Based on, the dual form is solved. # A common implementation for UOT with KL penalties involves: # Kij = exp(-Mij / eta) # Then iteratively update u and v with scaling factors related to epsilon. # Simplified Sinkhorn for Entropic OT (approximation if UOT specifics are complex) # Note: The paper specifies using Sinkhorn on the Fenchel-Legendre dual. # We implement a standard Sinkhorn for demonstration, noting that UOT requires specific scaling. K = torch.exp(-M / eta) # Uniform marginals for initialization (mus, mut are derived from features) # In UOT, marginals are not fixed to 1/l but penalized. # For this pseudocode, we assume a standard Sinkhorn step as a placeholder for the specific UOT solver # which is non-trivial to implement from scratch without the exact dual formulation details. for in range(numiterations): # Standard Sinkhorn update Kscaled = K torch.exp(u.unsqueeze(1)) torch.exp(v.unsqueeze(0)) # This is a placeholder. The actual UOT Sinkhorn involves different updates for u and v # to satisfy the KL constraints. # unew = log(mus) - log(K v) # vnew = log(mut) - log(K^T u) # With KL penalties, the updates are more complex. pass # Return Tstar # Tstar = diag(u) K diag(v) return torch.zeros(l, l) # Placeholder def constructrotationmatrix(thetax, thetay, thetaz): # Rx Rx = torch.tensor([[1, 0, 0], [0, torch.cos(thetax), -torch.sin(thetax)], [0, torch.sin(thetax), torch.cos(thetax)]]) # Ry Ry = torch.tensor([[torch.cos(thetay), 0, torch.sin(thetay)], [0, 1, 0], [-torch.sin(thetay), 0, torch.cos(thetay)]]) # Rz Rz = torch.tensor([[torch.cos(thetaz), -torch.sin(thetaz), 0], [torch.sin(thetaz), torch.cos(thetaz), 0], [0, 0, 1]]) return torch.mm(torch.mm(Rx, Ry), Rz) def extractvggfeatures(image, vgg19, l, d): # Extract l features of dimension d from image using VGG-19 # This involves downsampling or sampling specific feature maps # Not given in sources how exactly l=64 is sampled from VGG-19 output # Assuming a feature extraction module that returns l vectors of dim d return torch.randn(l, d) # Placeholder N: Number of random samples along a camera ray for volume rendering. \Phi': Set of initially randomized camera poses. \Theta: Network parameters of the MLP. l: Number of feature vectors in each feature set. Value: 64. d: Dimension of feature vectors. Value: 256. \eta: Regularization parameter controlling the smoothness of UOT. Value: 0.005. \epsilon: KL divergence regularization parameter. Value: Not given in the sources. Low Texture/Repetitive Patterns: Classical SfM fails here. VMRF avoids this by not relying on SfM. Out-of-Dataset Views: Direct absolute pose estimation (e.g., GNeRF) is disturbed by views beyond the training dataset if the pose distribution is inaccurate. VMRF mitigates this by using relative pose estimation via view matching. Occlusion: Causes inconsistent total mass between source and target feature distributions. Standard OT fails by matching outliers. VMRF uses Unbalanced OT (UOT) with KL divergence penalties to handle this. Time Complexity: The dominant cost is the volume rendering and the UOT computation. UOT via Sinkhorn iterations is O(l^2 \cdot k) where k is the number of iterations. Rendering is O(N \cdot W \cdot H) per image. Memory Complexity: Requires storing the NeRF parameters, the transport plan T (l \times l), and feature sets (l \times d). Performance: VMRF outperforms state-of-the-art methods like GNeRF qualitatively and quantitatively on Synthetic-NeRF and DTU datasets. Strengths: Does not require prior knowledge of camera poses or hand-crafted pose distributions. Robust to out-of-dataset views and low-texture scenes. Limitations: Relies on a pre-trained VGG-19 for feature extraction, which may not capture all semantic details. The UOT optimization adds computational overhead compared to standard OT. VMRF was proposed by Jiahui Zhang, Fangneng Zhan, Rongliang Wu, Yingchen Yu, Wenqing Zhang, Bai Song, Xiaoqin Zhang, and Shijian Lu in 2022. It addresses the limitations of previous pose-free NeRF methods like GNeRF, which required accurate, hand-crafted camera pose distributions for training their inversion networks. VMRF introduces the concept of view matching via unbalanced optimal transport to estimate relative poses, enabling effective NeRF training without prior pose knowledge. It is used in novel view synthesis tasks on Synthetic-NeRF and DTU datasets. VMRF: View Matching Neural Radiance Fields, https://doi.org/10.1145/3503161.3548078, fetched 2026-10-29

name: NeRF Pose and Appearance Optimization
head: UP-NeRF, Unconstrained Pose-prior-Free Neural Radiance Fields
body: This method jointly optimizes camera poses and neural scene representations for unconstrained image collections (varying illumination, transient occluders) without camera pose priors. It sets itself apart from standard NeRF optimization by introducing a candidate head to handle "hard-pose" images and a loss scheduling mechanism to transition from candidate-specific to shared scene representations. Unlike RoDynRF which focuses on dynamic scenes, or VMRF which uses view matching, this method explicitly decouples transient/hard-pose appearance from the global geometry via surrogate tasks. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: A set of N unconstrained images \{Ii\}{i=1}^N with unknown poses \{pi\}, and known intrinsics (focal length f, principal point, resolution W \times H). Ground-truth colors C(r) or deep feature maps F(r). Outputs: Optimized NeRF parameters \Theta (shared MLPs), candidate embeddings \{\elli\}, and camera poses \{pi\}. Data Structures: 1. Shared NeRF: Two MLPs, \Pi{\theta1} and \Pi{\theta2}, parameterizing the scene. \Pi{\theta1}: Input \gammax(r(t)) (positional encoded 3D point), Output [\sigma(t), z(t)] (density, intermediate feature). \Pi{\theta2}: Input [z(t), \gammad(d)] (feature, positional encoded direction), Output c(t) (color). 2. Candidate Head: MLP \Pi{\theta3}. Input [z(t), \elli] (shared feature, image-specific embedding), Output [\sigmai(t), ci(t)] (candidate density, candidate color). 3. Camera Pose: Each pose pi is parameterized as 6 degrees of freedom using the se(3) Lie algebra. 4. Candidate Embeddings: Vector \elli for each image i. Size is adjustable based on pose difficulty. Numbered Steps: 1. Ray Casting: For each pixel (u,v) in image i, compute ray origin \hat{o}i and direction \hat{d}i using current pose estimate pi and intrinsics. \hat{o}i = ti \hat{d}i = Ri \begin{pmatrix} (u - W/2)/f \\ -(v - H/2)/f \\ -1 \end{pmatrix} where pi = (Ri, ti). 2. Sampling: Sample K points tk along the ray r(t) = \hat{o}i + t\hat{d}i using hierarchical sampling (coarse stratified, fine biased). 3. Shared Feature Extraction: For each sample point tk: [\sigma(tk), z(tk)] = \Pi{\theta1}(\gammax(r(tk))) c(tk) = \Pi{\theta2}(z(tk), \gammad(\hat{d}i)) 4. Candidate Feature Extraction: For each sample point tk: [\sigmai(tk), ci(tk)] = \Pi{\theta3}(z(tk), \elli) 5. Joint Volumetric Rendering: Compute candidate rendered color \hat{C}i(r) by combining shared and candidate densities/colors: \hat{C}i(r) = \sum{k=1}^K Ti(tk) \alpha(\sigma(tk)\deltak) c(tk) + \alpha(\sigmai(tk)\deltak) ci(tk) where opacity \alpha(\sigma \delta) = 1 - \exp(-\sigma \delta), distance \deltak = t{k+1} - tk, and transmittance: Ti(tk) = \exp\left( -\sum{k'=1}^{k-1} (\sigma(t{k'}) + \sigmai(t{k'})) \delta{k'} \right) 6. Shared Rendering: Compute shared rendered color \hat{C}(r) using only shared parameters (standard NeRF rendering): \hat{C}(r) = \sum{k=1}^K T(tk) \alpha(\sigma(tk)\deltak) c(tk) where T(tk) = \exp\left( -\sum{k'=1}^{k-1} \sigma(t{k'}) \delta{k'} \right). 7. Loss Scheduling: Calculate training progress l \in [0, 1]. Compute weight w{u,v}(l) using hyperparameters u, v \in [0, 1]: w{u,v}(l) = \begin{cases} 0 & \text{if } l < u \\ \frac{1 - \cos(\pi(l - u)/(v - u))}{2} & \text{if } u \le l < v \\ 1 & \text{if } l \ge v \end{cases} 8. Total Loss: Compute photometric loss \mathcal{L}{rgb} (MSE between ground truth C(r) and rendered color): \mathcal{L} = w{u,v} \mathcal{L}{rgb}(\hat{C}|C) + (1 - w{u,v}) \mathcal{L}{rgb}(\hat{C}i|C) If l < u: \mathcal{L} = \mathcal{L}{rgb}(\hat{C}i|C) (Candidate only). If l \ge v: \mathcal{L} = \mathcal{L}{rgb}(\hat{C}|C) (Shared only). 9. Optimization: Update \Theta, \{\elli\}, and \{pi\} using an optimizer (e.g., Adam) minimizing \mathcal{L}. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def computecandidaterendering(rayorigin, raydirection, candidateembedding, sharedmlp1, sharedmlp2, candidatemlp, numsamples): """ Computes the candidate-specific rendered color for a single ray. """ # 1. Sample points along ray t = samplepoints(rayorigin, raydirection, numsamples) # Hierarchical sampling logic implied points = rayorigin + t raydirection # 2. Extract shared features # gammax and gammad are positional encoding functions encodedpoints = positionalencoding3d(points) sigmashared, z = sharedmlp1(encodedpoints) encodeddirs = positionalencoding3d(raydirection) colorshared = sharedmlp2(concat(z, encodeddirs)) # 3. Extract candidate features candidatedensity, candidatecolor = candidatemlp(concat(z, candidateembedding)) # 4. Compute opacities and transmittance # delta is distance between adjacent samples deltas = t[1:] - t[:-1] # Pad deltas for first sample if necessary, or assume t includes boundaries # Standard NeRF assumes t is sorted. # Opacity alpha = 1 - exp(-sigma delta) alphashared = 1.0 - torch.exp(-sigmashared deltas) alphacandidate = 1.0 - torch.exp(-candidatedensity deltas) # Combined transmittance Ti(tk) depends on sum of shared and candidate densities # Ti(tk) = exp(- sum{k'<k} (sigma(tk') + sigmai(tk')) deltak') # We compute cumulative sum of combined density delta combineddensitydelta = (sigmashared + candidatedensity) deltas # Cumulative sum from end to start for transmittance # Ti(tk) corresponds to transmittance BEFORE sample k # Using torch.cumprod or manual loop # Ti(t1) = 1.0 # Ti(tk) = Ti(t{k-1}) (1 - alphacombined(t{k-1})) alphacombined = 1.0 - torch.exp(-combineddensitydelta) # Transmittance at sample k (before absorption at k) # Ti(tk) = product{j=0}^{k-1} (1 - alphacombinedj) # Note: indices in formula are 1-based. In 0-based tensor: # T[k] = prod{j=0}^{k-1} (1 - alphacombined[j]) # Efficient computation: # 1 - alphacombined is the transmission factor for each segment transmission = 1.0 - alphacombined # Cumulative product of transmissions # T[k] is product of transmissions before k # We need T[k] for each k. # T[0] = 1.0 # T[1] = transmission[0] # T[2] = transmission[0] transmission[1] # Using cumprod on shifted array # Let's compute cumulative product of transmission cumtrans = torch.cumprod(transmission, dim=0) # T[k] = cumtrans[k-1] if k>0 else 1.0 # Prepend 1.0 Ti = torch.cat([torch.oneslike(transmission[0:1]), cumtrans[:-1]]) # 5. Render # Contribution from shared part: Ti(tk) alphashared(tk) colorshared(tk) # Contribution from candidate part: Ti(tk) alphacandidate(tk) candidatecolor(tk) # Note: Formula (5) in source uses alpha(sigma delta) for shared and alpha(sigmai delta) for candidate # and Ti uses sum of sigmas. termshared = Ti alphashared colorshared termcandidate = Ti alphacandidate candidatecolor renderedcolor = torch.sum(termshared + termcandidate, dim=0) return renderedcolor def computesharedrendering(rayorigin, raydirection, sharedmlp1, sharedmlp2, numsamples): """ Computes the shared NeRF rendered color. """ t = samplepoints(rayorigin, raydirection, numsamples) points = rayorigin + t raydirection encodedpoints = positionalencoding3d(points) sigma, z = sharedmlp1(encodedpoints) encodeddirs = positionalencoding3d(raydirection) color = sharedmlp2(concat(z, encodeddirs)) deltas = t[1:] - t[:-1] alpha = 1.0 - torch.exp(-sigma deltas) # Transmittance T(tk) = exp(- sum{k'<k} sigma(tk') deltak') transmission = 1.0 - alpha cumtrans = torch.cumprod(transmission, dim=0) T = torch.cat([torch.oneslike(transmission[0:1]), cumtrans[:-1]]) renderedcolor = torch.sum(T alpha color, dim=0) return renderedcolor def trainstep(images, gtcolors, poses, embeddings, sharedmlp1, sharedmlp2, candidatemlp, u, v, progress): """ Single training step. """ # Initialize gradients #... totalloss = 0.0 for i, (img, gtcolor) in enumerate(zip(images, gtcolors)): # Get current pose and embedding for image i pose = poses[i] embedding = embeddings[i] # Compute ray origins and directions from pose rayorigins, raydirections = getrays(pose, img.shape) # Compute candidate rendering candcolors = [] for origin, direction in zip(rayorigins, raydirections): c = computecandidaterendering(origin, direction, embedding, sharedmlp1, sharedmlp2, candidatemlp, numsamples) candcolors.append(c) candcolors = torch.stack(candcolors) # Compute shared rendering sharedcolors = [] for origin, direction in zip(rayorigins, raydirections): s = computesharedrendering(origin, direction, sharedmlp1, sharedmlp2, numsamples) sharedcolors.append(s) sharedcolors = torch.stack(sharedcolors) # Photometric losses losscand = torch.mean((gtcolor - candcolors) 2) lossshared = torch.mean((gtcolor - sharedcolors) 2) # Loss scheduling weight if progress < u: w = 0.0 elif progress >= v: w = 1.0 else: w = (1.0 - torch.cos(torch.pi (progress - u) / (v - u))) / 2.0 loss = w lossshared + (1.0 - w) losscand totalloss += loss totalloss /= len(images) return totalloss Parameters: u, v: Loss scheduling hyperparameters. Typical values not given in sources. \elli size: Adjustable based on pose difficulty. Learning rates: Separate or combined optimizers, often different rates for pose vs weights. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Hard-pose images: Images with little overlap or unique details may converge to wrong poses if not handled by the candidate head. Transient occluders: The candidate head helps block their influence on pose estimation. Precision: Standard floating-point precision issues in ray marching and transmittance computation apply. A strategy to facilitate stable joint optimization, borrowed from BARF. Using deep feature maps F instead of just color C for training, allowing selective editing and robustness. Time Complexity: Higher than standard NeRF due to the candidate head and dual rendering paths per image. Memory Complexity: Increased by storing candidate embeddings \elli for each image and the candidate head parameters. Strengths: Handles unconstrained internet photo collections (e.g., Phototourism dataset) with varying illumination and transient occluders without pose priors. Limitations: Requires careful tuning of u, v and candidate embedding sizes. May be slower to converge than methods with known poses. When to use: When camera poses are unknown and images are unconstrained (transients, lighting changes). When not to use: When poses are known or images are clean/consistent (standard NeRF is faster and simpler). Originated in the paper "UP-NeRF: Unconstrained Pose-Prior-Free Neural Radiance Fields". It addresses limitations of prior NeRF pose estimation methods (like BARF) which struggle with unconstrained images containing transient occluders or varying illumination. It builds on the concept of surrogate tasks and separate modules for transients. UP-NeRF: Unconstrained Pose-Prior-Free Neural Radiance Fields, https://arxiv.org/abs/2311.03784v2, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial)

name: Sync-NeRF Offset Optimization
head: Joint offset and NeRF optimization, Per-camera Time Offset with Dynamic NeRF, Sync-MixVoxels, Sync-K-Planes
body: Sync-NeRF Offset Optimization addresses the problem of reconstructing dynamic scenes from multi-view videos that are not temporally synchronized. Unlike standard dynamic NeRFs that assume all cameras capture the same scene moment at a given frame index, this method introduces learnable per-camera time offsets to align the temporal axes of unsynchronized inputs. It sets itself apart by treating synchronization as a differentiable optimization problem, jointly refining camera-specific time shifts alongside the neural radiance field parameters. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: A set of K unsynchronized multi-view video sequences. For each camera k \in \{1, \dots, K\}, the input consists of images Ck(r, t) at discrete time indices t. The underlying dynamic NeRF model F\Theta (which may be grid-based or implicit) and its initial parameters \Theta. Outputs: Optimized NeRF parameters \Theta, optimized per-camera time offsets \deltak for each training camera, and optionally a test-time offset \delta{test} for novel view synthesis. Data Structures: Time Offsets (\delta): A vector of learnable parameters, one per camera. Layout: \delta = [\delta1, \delta2, \dots, \deltaK]. Type: Continuous scalar (float). Initialization: \deltak = 0.0 for all k. Calibrated Time (tk): The effective time input to the NeRF for a specific camera and frame. Formula: tk = t + \deltak. Numbered Steps: 1. Initialization: Initialize the learnable time offsets \deltak for all K training cameras to zero. Initialize the NeRF parameters \Theta using the chosen dynamic NeRF baseline (e.g., MixVoxels, K-Planes). 2. Calibration: For each training pixel defined by camera index k, ray r, and frame index t, compute the calibrated time tk: tk = t + \deltak 3. Rendering: Query the dynamic NeRF F\Theta using the calibrated time tk to predict the color and density. The specific query depends on the baseline architecture: For implicit function-based approaches: F\Theta: (x, d, tk) \rightarrow (c, \sigma) For grid-based models (e.g., MixVoxels, K-Planes): F\Theta: (f(x, tk), d) \rightarrow (c, \sigma) where f(x, tk) retrieves the spatial-temporal feature grid at coordinates (x, tk). Render the pixel color \hat{C}(r, t + \deltak) using standard volume rendering integration (numerical quadrature). 4. Loss Computation: Calculate the Mean Squared Error (MSE) between the rendered color \hat{C} and the ground truth color Ck(r, t): \mathcal{L}{RGB} = \sum{k,r,t} \left( \hat{C}(r, t + \deltak) - Ck(r, t) \right)^2 5. Optimization: Minimize \mathcal{L}{RGB} with respect to both the NeRF parameters \Theta and the time offsets \deltak using gradient descent (e.g., Adam). No additional regularizers are required for the offsets. 6. Test-Time Synchronization (Optional): If rendering from a test view that is also unsynchronized, freeze \Theta and \deltak (training offsets) and optimize a specific test offset \delta{test} to minimize reconstruction error for the novel view. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def syncnerfoffsetoptimization(cameras, groundtruthimages, dynamicnerf, numiterations): """ cameras: List of K camera indices. groundtruthimages: Dict mapping (k, t) to image tensor Ck(r, t). dynamicnerf: The dynamic NeRF model FTheta. numiterations: Number of optimization steps. """ # 1. Initialize learnable time offsets deltak for each camera to zero delta = {k: 0.0 for k in cameras} # Initialize optimizer for both NeRF parameters and offsets optimizer = Adam([{'params': dynamicnerf.parameters()}, {'params': list(delta.values())}]) for iteration in range(numiterations): optimizer.zerograd() totalloss = 0.0 # 2. Iterate over all training pixels (k, r, t) for k in cameras: for t in timeindices: # 3. Calculate calibrated time tk = t + deltak tk = t + delta[k] # Get ground truth image for this camera and time Cgt = groundtruthimages[(k, t)] # 4. Compute rendered RGB pixel Chat(r, t + deltak) # This involves ray casting and volume rendering using FTheta # The time input to FTheta is tk Chat = dynamicnerf.render(k, tk) # 5. Compute MSE loss loss = torch.mean((Chat - Cgt) 2) totalloss += loss # 6. Backpropagate and update totalloss.backward() optimizer.step() return dynamicnerf, delta def testtimesync(dynamicnerf, testcamera, testgroundtruth, deltatrain): """ Optimize a specific test offset for a novel view. """ deltatest = 0.0 optimizer = Adam([{'params': [deltatest]}]) for iteration in range(numiterationstest): optimizer.zerograd() # Use frozen trained model and training offsets tk = testgroundtruth.time + deltatrain[testcamera] # Render with test offset Chat = dynamicnerf.render(testcamera, tk + deltatest) Cgt = testgroundtruth.image loss = torch.mean((Chat - Cgt) 2) loss.backward() optimizer.step() return deltatest Parameters: \deltak: Learnable time offset for camera k. Initialized to 0.0. Optimized via gradient descent. Typical Performance: On the Unsynchronized Dynamic Blender Dataset, the Mean Absolute Error (MAE) between predicted offsets and ground truth offsets is approximately 0.01 seconds (less than one-third of a frame at 30 FPS). Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Test View Synchronization: Test views may also be unsynchronized relative to training views. The method requires optimizing a specific test offset \delta{test} with a frozen trained model to resolve this. Unsynchronization Length: Performance degrades with longer unsynchronization lengths (e.g., 1.5\times or 2\times), though the method consistently improves over baselines. Applies Sync-NeRF offset optimization to the MixVoxels baseline. It achieves an MAE of 0.0154 seconds on the Unsynchronized Dynamic Blender Dataset. Applies Sync-NeRF offset optimization to the hybrid K-Planes baseline. It achieves an MAE of 0.0156 seconds on the Unsynchronized Dynamic Blender Dataset. Applies Sync-NeRF offset optimization to the explicit K-Planes baseline. It achieves an MAE of 0.0229 seconds on the Unsynchronized Dynamic Blender Dataset. Time Complexity: The optimization does not introduce additional computational complexity to the grid-based models during rendering, as the time offset is simply added to the time input before grid query. However, the joint optimization of \deltak adds gradient computation overhead for the offset parameters. Memory Complexity: No additional memory is required for the offsets themselves (only K floats), but the method avoids the memory overhead of learning hundreds of individual frame embeddings by using continuous time interpolation. Performance: On the Unsynchronized Dynamic Blender Dataset, Sync-NeRF variants significantly outperform unsynchronized baselines. For example, Sync-MixVoxels achieves a PSNR of 37.11 compared to 31.06 for the baseline MixVoxels. Strengths: Automatically synchronizes videos without manual effort or additional hardware (like timecode systems). Applicable to various dynamic NeRF baselines. Limitations: Does not generalize to causal handheld cameras (future work). May struggle with extreme unsynchronization lengths, though it remains robust. Sync-NeRF was introduced by Kim et al. in 2024 to address the limitation of existing dynamic NeRFs that assume synchronized multi-view inputs. Previous methods fail on unsynchronized data, producing severe artifacts and ghost effects because they employ a single latent embedding for a frame while multi-view images were captured at different moments. The method was verified on the Plenoptic Video Dataset and a newly built Unsynchronized Dynamic Blender Dataset. name: Monocular Depth Estimation Adaptation and Supervision
head: MDE-guided NeRF, Depth-Regularized NeRF, Monocular Depth Priors
body: This family of methods integrates pre-trained monocular depth estimation (MDE) networks into the NeRF training loop to resolve the shape-radiance ambiguity inherent in sparse-view or single-view reconstruction. Unlike standard NeRF which relies solely on RGB photometric supervision, these methods explicitly guide volume sampling, rendering, or optimization using depth maps extracted from a scene-adapted or static monocular network. They distinguish themselves from sibling methods by treating monocular depth not just as a static prior, but as an active supervisory signal that can be adapted to the specific scene geometry (e.g., via fine-tuning or joint optimization) or used to constrain the sampling bounds and loss functions. All methods in this family share the following mechanism: 1. Depth Prior Extraction: A pre-trained MDE network G\phi (e.g., Mannequin Challenge, DiffDP, DPThybrid, Omnidata) is applied to input RGB images I to generate a relative depth map D^. 2. Scale and Shift Alignment: Since MDE outputs are relative and lack absolute scale, a linear alignment is performed between the MDE depth D^ and the NeRF-rendered depth \bar{D} (or ground truth/sparse points). This is typically done per-image or per-patch using least-squares optimization to find scale w and shift q: \min{w, q} \sum{p} \| (w \cdot \text{sg}(D^(p)) + q) - \bar{D}(p) \|^2 where \text{sg}(\cdot) is the stop-gradient operator to prevent gradients from flowing into the frozen MDE network during NeRF updates. 3. Depth Consistency Loss: A loss term L{depth} is added to the total training objective, penalizing the difference between the aligned MDE depth and the NeRF-rendered depth. 4. Sampling Guidance: In some variants, the depth prior is used to clamp the near and far bounds of ray sampling, focusing computation on plausible depths. NerfingMVS integrates learning-based monocular depth priors into NeRF optimization to resolve shape-radiance ambiguity in indoor scenes. It distinguishes itself by combining test-time adaptation of a monocular depth estimator (fine-tuned on sparse SfM+MVS points) with a rendering pipeline that clamps ray bounds based on these priors. This method improves geometric accuracy in sparse-view NeRFs by supervising the distribution of ray termination distances using Earth Mover’s Distance (EMD) rather than direct depth matching. It uses a diffusion-based depth prior and its intrinsic uncertainty map to selectively guide geometry, replacing standard L2 depth losses with a distributional EMD loss weighted by uncertainty. This method integrates a guided depth completion network (e.g., MFFNet) into the NeRF loop to recover dense depth from sparse LiDAR measurements. It sets itself apart by using LiDAR-based completion to provide dense, metrically consistent depth supervision, addressing the sparsity of raw LiDAR data in unbounded real-world scenes. This method aligns pseudo-depth maps from a pre-trained MDE network with NeRF-rendered depth for seen input views. It differs from global scale-fitting approaches by computing local scale and shift parameters per image patch, preventing dominant objects from biasing the depth alignment and preserving local geometric details. DäRF is a framework for robust few-shot NeRF reconstruction that combines NeRF with MDE through online complementary training. It solves ambiguity by jointly optimizing the NeRF and the MDE network at a specific scene, distilling the monocular depth prior to NeRF at both seen and unseen views and finetuning the MDE network with canonical geometry captured by NeRF. This method refines a pre-trained MDE network by using a NeRF model as a geometric prior to resolve ambiguities such as convexity/concavity confusion. It distinguishes itself by explicitly adapting the MDE weights to the specific scene's absolute geometry rather than just using depth as a static supervision signal for the NeRF. This family defines three specific architectural configurations for the FWD framework, distinguished by their depth supervision strategy and the initialization state of the depth estimation module. They address the trade-off between training stability, convergence speed, and reliance on external geometric priors. FWD-U serves as the unsupervised baseline, FWD provides a supervised baseline with pre-trained geometry, and FWD-D bypasses learned depth estimation entirely by using sensor data. ShadowNeuS reconstructs a neural SDF from single-view images under multiple lighting conditions by supervising shadow rays rather than relying solely on camera rays. It solves the problem that standard NeRF does not model rays from the scene to the light source, missing shadow information which contains critical geometry cues via light visibility. NeRF-Supervision generates dense correspondence datasets to train object-centric visual descriptors using only RGB images and NeRFs. It solves the problem of acquiring ground-truth dense correspondences for thin, reflective, or ambiguous objects where traditional RGB-D sensors and MVS fail, using the NeRF's density field to formulate a "distribution-of-depths" approach. GAINS Stage I is the geometry optimization phase of the GAINS pipeline, designed to reconstruct robust 3D shape from sparse RGB images using 2D Gaussian Splatting (2DGS). It solves novel-view artifacts and geometric collapse by augmenting optimization with monocular depth/normal consistency, local depth ranking, and Score Distillation Sampling (SDS) from a latent diffusion model. Definition: A loss function that supervises NeRF geometry at unseen/novel viewpoints by aligning NeRF-rendered depth with monocular depth estimated from the rendered novel view image. Step: For each unseen view l in the set of unseen views U: 1. Sample a patch of the novel viewpoint. 2. Render color \bar{I}l and depth \bar{D}l from NeRF. 3. Extract monocular depth D^l = G\phi(\bar{I}l) from the rendered color image. 4. Compute scale wl and shift ql via least squares between D^l and \bar{D}l. 5. Calculate loss L{unseen}. Parameter: U: Set of unseen view images. P: Randomly sampled patch of pixels. Pitfall: Monocular depth from noisy NeRF rendering may be affected by fine-grained artifacts. However, the MDE model's strong geometric prior is robust against these artifacts, filtering them out. Comparison: Unlike previous methods that only impose priors on input viewpoints (limited by self-occlusion/sparsity), this method applies priors to arbitrary viewpoints, reaching every location. Definition: A composite loss function for adapting a monocular depth estimator to predict scene-specific absolute geometry by enforcing multi-view consistency and local patch-wise scale-shift fitting. Step: Compute the first addend term (scale-shift loss) to force the MDE to adapt towards multiview consistency, reducing its ill-posed nature and aligning its initial global depth prediction with the absolute geometry captured by NeRF. Compute the second addend term (L1 loss with patch-wise scale-shift fitting) to aid the modeling of fine, detailed, local geometry. Optimize the MDE network by minimizing the sum of both terms simultaneously; using only one term performs worse on all metrics than using both in conjunction. Parameter: Scale-shift loss weight and L1 loss weight are required for optimization but values are not specified in this section. Step: Predict uncalibrated disparity of the source view using a monocular depth estimator: De = D(Ir). Define the aligned predicted inverse depth Dr using four parameters a0, a1, a2, a3 and matrices H, V: Dr = a0 De + a1 \mathbf{1}{HW} + a2 H + a3 V. Define H and V as H \times W matrices where for pixel p=(px, py), H(p)=px and V(p)=py. Set weight w(p) to the inverse of the distance between pixel p and the mask centre-of-mass. Perform an additional optimization step to correct Dr to encourage smoothness around the mask, yielding Dr^{smooth}. Parameter: N{depth}: Number of iterations for supervised training on unmasked pixels before applying depth loss. Definition: Aligning monocular depth estimates (range [0,1]) with rendered depth by solving for scale and shift parameters per mini-batch via least-squares optimization. Parameter: q: Shift parameter. Usage: Used to backproject depth and calculate LDC when using monocular cues from Omnidata model. The integration of monocular depth priors into NeRF optimization emerged to address the limitations of sparse-view reconstruction, where photometric consistency alone is insufficient to disambiguate geometry and appearance. Early works like NerfingMVS demonstrated that fine-tuning monocular depth estimators on sparse SfM points could guide volume sampling. Subsequent methods such as DäRF and NeRF-guided MDE Adaptation introduced joint optimization strategies, allowing the MDE network to adapt to the specific scene geometry captured by the NeRF, thereby resolving ambiguities like convexity/concavity confusion. More recent approaches have explored distributional losses like Earth Mover’s Distance to handle the uncertainty in monocular priors, and extended supervision to unseen viewpoints to ensure global geometric coherence. name: NerfingMVS
head: Guided NeRF Optimization for MVS, Guided Optimization of Neural Radiance Fields for Indoor Multi-View Stereo, NeRF with Depth Priors
body: NerfingMVS is a multi-view depth estimation method that integrates learning-based monocular depth priors into the optimization of Neural Radiance Fields (NeRF) to resolve the shape-radiance ambiguity inherent in indoor scenes. Unlike standard NeRF which relies solely on RGB supervision, NerfingMVS explicitly guides volume sampling and rendering using depth maps extracted from a scene-adapted monocular network, allowing for direct optimization over implicit volumes without requiring accurate pixel matching across views. It distinguishes itself from sibling methods by combining a test-time adaptation of a monocular depth estimator (fine-tuned on sparse SfM+MVS points) with a rendering pipeline that clamps ray bounds and weights samples based on these priors. Inputs: A set of multi-view RGB images I. Camera poses (intrinsic and extrinsic) for the input images. A pre-trained monocular depth estimation (MDE) network G\phi (e.g., Mannequin Challenge). Sparse 3D point cloud or sparse depth maps derived from Structure-from-Motion (SfM) and Multi-View Stereo (MVS) using COLMAP. Outputs: Optimized NeRF model parameters \Theta representing the scene's geometry and appearance. Dense depth maps for each input view. Re-rendered RGB images and depth maps. NeRF Model (F\Theta): A multi-layer perceptron (MLP) taking 3D position \mathbf{x} and view direction \mathbf{d} as input, outputting volume density \sigma and RGB color \mathbf{c}. Depth Prior Map (D^): A 2D tensor of shape (H, W) containing relative depth estimates for a specific view, generated by the adapted MDE network. Depth Confidence Map (M): A 2D tensor of shape (H, W) indicating the reliability of the depth prior at each pixel. Ray Bins: The ray is divided into N equal bins. The near and far bounds of these bins are clamped using the depth priors. Tensors for Rendering: rayso: Ray origins, shape [-1, 3]. raysd: Ray directions, shape [-1, 3]. depthpriors: Prior depth values for each ray, shape [-1]. depthconfidences: Confidence values for each ray, shape [-1]. 1. Sparse Reconstruction: Run COLMAP on the input images to obtain camera poses and a sparse 3D point cloud. Project the fused 3D point clouds to each view to acquire sparse depth maps. 2. Depth Prior Adaptation: Fine-tune the pre-trained monocular depth network G\phi on the target scene using the sparse depth maps from COLMAP as ground truth. The network is optimized using a scale-invariant loss to handle the lack of absolute scale in the sparse reconstruction: L(D^ip, D^i{Sparse}) = \frac{1}{n} \sum{j=1}^n \left| \log D^ip(j) - \log D^i{Sparse}(j) + \alpha(D^ip, D^i{Sparse}) \right| where D^ip is the predicted depth, D^i{Sparse} is the sparse depth, and \alpha is a correction term. 3. Ray Preparation: For each training ray, compute the origin \mathbf{o} and direction \mathbf{d} from the camera pose. If NDC (Normalized Device Coordinates) is used, convert rays to NDC space. 4. Depth-Guided Sampling Bounds: Retrieve the depth prior D^ and confidence M for the current view. Use these to clamp the near and far bounds of the ray sampling intervals. Specifically, the ray bounds are adjusted to focus sampling on the depth predicted by the prior, effectively skipping empty space or implausible depths. 5. Volume Rendering: Sample points along the ray within the clamped bounds. Compute density \sigma and color \mathbf{c} for each sample. Render the RGB color \mathbf{C} and depth \mathbf{D} using standard volumetric rendering equations, but weighted by the confidence of the depth prior if applicable. Compute distances between consecutive samples: di = z{i+1} - zi. Scale by ray direction norm: di = di \cdot \|\mathbf{d}\|. Compute alpha: \alphai = 1 - \exp(-\sigmai \cdot di). Compute weights: wi = \alphai \prod{j=1}^{i-1} (1 - \alphaj). Rendered RGB: \mathbf{C} = \sum wi \mathbf{c}i. Rendered Depth: \mathbf{D} = \sum wi zi. 6. Loss Computation: Compute the total loss, which includes the RGB reconstruction loss and a depth consistency loss between the rendered depth and the adapted monocular depth prior. 7. Optimization: Update NeRF parameters \Theta using gradient descent. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import torch import torch.nn.functional as F def nerfingmvsrender(rayso, raysd, depthpriors, depthconfidences, model, Nsamples, near, far): """ Renders rays using NerfingMVS logic. Args: rayso: Tensor of shape [numrays, 3], ray origins. raysd: Tensor of shape [numrays, 3], ray directions. depthpriors: Tensor of shape [numrays], depth prior for each ray. depthconfidences: Tensor of shape [numrays], confidence for each ray. model: The NeRF MLP model. Nsamples: Number of samples per ray. near: Float, absolute near bound (default 0.05). far: Float, absolute far bound (default 0.15). Returns: rgbmap: Tensor of shape [numrays, 3]. depthmap: Tensor of shape [numrays]. accmap: Tensor of shape [numrays]. """ # 1. Define sampling intervals # Divide ray into N equal bins tvals = torch.linspace(0., 1., steps=Nsamples).to(rayso.device) zvals = near (1. - tvals) + far tvals # 2. Clamp bounds using depth priors # NerfingMVS uses depth priors to guide sampling. # The prior depth is used to adjust the sampling range or weight the samples. # Based on, ray bounds are clamped using depth priors. # We assume the prior provides a central depth around which to sample. # A common implementation (from context) involves # perturbing the zvals around the prior depth or limiting the range. # Here we implement a simple clamping/centering based on prior. # Ensure depthpriors are within [near, far] for clamping logic # If prior is outside, clamp to bounds depthpriorsclamped = torch.clamp(depthpriors, min=near, max=far) # Shift zvals to be centered around the depth prior? # Or simply use the prior to define the effective near/far? # The paper says "allowing sampling points only at appropriate depths". # Implementation passes depthpriors to renderrays. # We will assume the sampling is stratified around the prior depth # or the prior is used to filter/weight samples. # For this pseudocode, we will use the prior to define the sampling range # if it's more informative than the fixed near/far, or simply perturb. # Let's use the prior to define the center of sampling, with a fixed spread # spread = (far - near) / 2 spread = (far - near) / 2.0 zvalscentered = depthpriorsclamped.unsqueeze(-1) + (zvals - 0.5) spread # Clamp zvals to [near, far] zvals = torch.clamp(zvalscentered, min=near, max=far) # 3. Sample points and query NeRF pts = rayso.unsqueeze(1) + raysd.unsqueeze(1) zvals.unsqueeze(-1) pts = pts.reshape(-1, 3) # Query NeRF for density and color # model returns raw density and color rawdensity, rawcolor = model(pts) # 4. Compute weights dists = zvals[..., 1:] - zvals[...,:-1] dists = torch.cat([dists, torch.tensor([1e10]).to(rayso.device)], dim=-1) dists = dists torch.norm(raysd.unsqueeze(1), dim=-1) alpha = 1. - torch.exp(-F.relu(rawdensity) dists) # Numerical stability: add 1e-10 to (1-alpha) in cumprod transmittance = torch.cumprod(1. - alpha + 1e-10, dim=-1) transmittance = torch.cat([torch.oneslike(transmittance[...,:1]), transmittance[...,:-1]], dim=-1) weights = alpha transmittance # 5. Render RGB and Depth rgbmap = torch.sum(weights.unsqueeze(-1) rawcolor, dim=-2) depthmap = torch.sum(weights zvals, dim=-1) accmap = torch.sum(weights, dim=-1) # 6. Composite against white background rgbmap = rgbmap + (1. - accmap.unsqueeze(-1)) return rgbmap, depthmap, accmap def nerfingmvstrainstep(rayso, raysd, rgbgt, depthpriors, depthconfidences, model, optimizer): """ Single training step for NerfingMVS. """ optimizer.zerograd() # Render rgbpred, depthpred, acc = nerfingmvsrender( rayso, raysd, depthpriors, depthconfidences, model, Nsamples=64, near=0.05, far=0.15) # Loss 1: RGB Loss (L1 or MSE) rgbloss = F.mseloss(rgbpred, rgbgt) # Loss 2: Depth Consistency Loss # Align rendered depth with depth prior # Use confidence to weight the loss # Note: depthpriors and depthpred are in the same coordinate system if bounds are handled correctly depthloss = torch.mean(depthconfidences torch.abs(depthpred - depthpriors)) totalloss = rgbloss + 0.5 depthloss # Weight for depth loss totalloss.backward() optimizer.step() return totalloss.item(), rgbloss.item(), depthloss.item() depthNrand: Batch size for depth sampling (default 4). depthNiters: Number of iterations for depth prior training (default 151). depthH, depthW: Height and width of the depth image (must be multiples of 16, e.g., 288x384). depthlrate: Learning rate for depth network adaptation (default 4e-4). near: Absolute near bound for ray clipping (default 0.05). far: Absolute far bound for ray clipping (default 0.15). topk: Top-k for consistency error filtering (default 4). Numerical Stability in Cumprod: When computing transmittance, add 10^{-10} to (1-\alpha) to prevent NaNs when \alpha is close to 1. Division by Zero in Disparity: If computing disparity maps, use \max(10^{-10}, \dots) to avoid division by zero when depth or accumulated opacity is zero. Scale Ambiguity: The monocular depth prior is relative. The scale-invariant loss during adaptation helps, but the final NeRF depth may still lack absolute scale unless constrained by the sparse COLMAP points or explicit scale normalization. COLMAP Dependency: The method relies heavily on the quality of COLMAP's sparse reconstruction. Poor pose estimation or sparse points can lead to poor depth priors. Time Complexity: Training time is significantly higher than standard NeRF due to the additional depth prior adaptation step and the complexity of guided sampling. The source notes approximately 3.5 hours on an NVIDIA GeForce RTX 2080 GPU for a ScanNet scene, including COLMAP, depth training, and NeRF training. Memory Complexity: Similar to standard NeRF, but requires storing depth priors and confidences for each ray/view. Chunked rendering is used to avoid OOM errors. Strengths: Improves geometry in textureless or repetitive indoor scenes where standard NeRF suffers from shape-radiance ambiguity. Eliminates the need for explicit pixel matching across views during optimization. Produces more accurate dense depth maps compared to standard NeRF. Limitations: Requires a good initial sparse reconstruction from COLMAP. Performance is dependent on the quality of the monocular depth estimator and its adaptation to the scene. Not suitable for scenes with significant dynamic content or where COLMAP fails to reconstruct poses. When to Use: Indoor multi-view stereo tasks where high-quality geometry and depth are required, and sufficient multi-view overlap exists for COLMAP to work. When Not to Use: Outdoor scenes with large baselines, dynamic scenes, or scenes where COLMAP cannot produce a reliable sparse reconstruction. NerfingMVS was introduced by Yi Wei, Shaohui Liu, Yongming Rao, Wang Zhao, Jiwen Lu, and Jie Zhou in September 2021 at ICCV. The paper, titled "NerfingMVS: Guided Optimization of Neural Radiance Fields for Indoor Multi-View Stereo," addresses the limitations of NeRF in indoor environments, specifically the shape-radiance ambiguity. It builds upon the NeRF framework and integrates principles from multi-view stereo (MVS) and monocular depth estimation. The method was evaluated on ScanNet and Matterport3D datasets. It is based on the PyTorch implementation of NeRF. name: Depth-Guided NeRF Training via Earth Mover’s Distance
head: Depth-guided NeRF via Earth Mover’s Distance, EM D-Guided Sampling, EMD-Guided Depth Supervision for NeRF, EMD-NeRF, EMD-based objective
body: This method improves the geometric accuracy of Neural Radiance Fields (NeRFs) trained on sparse views by supervising the distribution of ray termination distances using Earth Mover’s Distance (EMD) rather than enforcing direct depth matching. Unlike sibling methods such as DäRF which minimize the norm between rendered and prior depth, or SCADE which relies on multiple ambiguous hypotheses, this approach uses a single off-the-shelf diffusion-based depth prior and its intrinsic uncertainty map to selectively guide the NeRF’s geometry without propagating prior inaccuracies. It builds on Monocular Depth Estimation Adaptation and Supervision by replacing standard L2 depth consistency losses with a distributional EMD loss weighted by uncertainty. Inputs: A set of N input RGB images \{Ii\}{i=1}^N (typically N < 20) and their corresponding SfM camera poses. A pre-trained monocular depth estimation (MDE) network, specifically DiffDP. A NeRF model F\Theta initialized with random weights. Outputs: A trained NeRF model F\Theta capable of rendering novel views with accurate geometry. Rendered RGB images and depth maps for novel viewpoints. NeRF Model (F\Theta): A multilayer perceptron (MLP) taking 5D input (x, y, z, \theta, \phi) representing camera position and viewing direction, outputting color c and volume density \sigma. Depth Prior (z0): A relative depth map generated by DiffDP for each input image. Uncertainty Map (u): A pixel-wise uncertainty map derived from the DiffDP denoising process, normalized to [0, 1]. Ray Samples: For each ray, a set of termination distances y = \{y1, \dots, yN\} sampled from the NeRF's predicted distribution. 1. Depth Prior and Uncertainty Extraction: For each input image I, run the DiffDP network to generate the depth prior z0 and the uncertainty map u. DiffDP formulates denoising as p\theta(z{0:T}|I). The uncertainty is derived by comparing estimates at consecutive denoising steps t and t-1. Let c(z{0:T}) be the count of steps where the change exceeds a threshold \tau: c(z{0:T}) = \frac{1}{T} \sum{t=T,\dots,1} \mathbb{I}(|zt - z{t-1}| \ge \tau) The final uncertainty u(z{0:T}|I) combines this temporal uncertainty with spatial consistency using a mirrored image M(I): U(z{0:T}|I) = \frac{c(z{0:T}|I) + M(c(z{0:T}|M(I)))}{2} u(z{0:T}|I) = U(z{0:T}|I) \cdot \| (z0|I) - M(z0|M(I)) \|1 2. NeRF Forward Pass and Weight Calculation: Cast rays through the camera. For each sample i along a ray at distance di, query F\Theta to get density \sigmai. Calculate the transmittance Ti and the weight wi representing the probability that the ray terminates at sample i: Ti = \exp\left(-\sum{j=1}^{i-1} \sigmaj \deltaj\right) wi = Ti (1 - \exp(-\sigmai \deltai)) where \deltai is the distance between adjacent samples. 3. Probability Density Construction: Normalize the weights wi to form a piece-wise constant probability density function (PDF): \hat{w}i = \frac{wi}{\sum{j=1}^{N} wj} Construct the Cumulative Distribution Function (CDF) from \hat{w}i. 4. EMD-Guided Sampling: Sample new ray termination distances y = \{y1, \dots, yN\} from the constructed CDF using inverse transform sampling. These samples represent the NeRF's learned distribution of surface locations. 5. Loss Calculation: Photometric Loss: Compute the L2 loss between the rendered color \hat{C}(r) and the observed color C(r): L{photo} = ||\hat{C}(r) - C(r)||2^2 EMD Depth Loss: Compute the Earth Mover’s Distance between the sampled NeRF distances y and the depth prior z0. Since EMD is non-differentiable, approximate it using Sinkhorn Divergence during training: L{EMD} = EMD(y, z0) Total Loss: Combine the losses weighted by the uncertainty map u, a balancing weight \lambda, and a focal-like exponent \gamma: L = (1 + u)^\gamma L{photo} + \lambda (1 - u)^\gamma L{EMD} Note: Unlike Focal Loss which increases weight for uncertain examples, this method decreases the weight of the depth loss for uncertain pixels (1-u), relying more on photometric supervision when depth is unreliable. 6. Optimization: Update NeRF parameters \Theta using gradient descent. Initialize the scale of the depth priors to 1 and learn the scale with a small learning rate. Unverified code. """ # Run DiffDP denoising process to get intermediate zt # z0 is the final depth estimate ztsequence = diffdpmodel.denoiseprocess(image) # Calculate temporal uncertainty count # Compare zt and z{t-1} diffs = [abs(zt - z{t-1}) for zt, z{t-1} in zip(ztsequence[1:], ztsequence[:-1])] tau = 0.1 # Threshold tau ctemporal = sum([1 if d >= tau else 0 for d in diffs]) / len(diffs) # Spatial consistency using mirrored image mirroredimage = torch.flip(image, dims=[2]) # Assuming H, W dims z0mirrored = diffdpmodel.forward(mirroredimage) z0original = ztsequence[-1] # Mirror the temporal uncertainty of the mirrored image # Simplified: assume we can get c for mirrored cmirrored = computeuncertainty(diffdpmodel, mirroredimage) cmirrored = torch.flip(cmirrored, dims=[1]) # Mirror back to original orientation U = (ctemporal + cmirrored) / 2.0 spatialdiff = torch.abs(z0original - torch.flip(z0mirrored, dims=[1])) u = U torch.mean(spatialdiff, dim=1, keepdim=True) # L1 norm approx return u def nerfforward(rayorigins, raydirections, nerfmodel, near, far, numsamples): """ Standard NeRF forward pass returning weights and samples. name: Depth Completion Network NeRF
head: DCN-NeRF, Depth Completion (MFFNet), Guided depth completion, MFFNet
body: Depth Completion Network NeRF integrates a guided depth completion network into the NeRF training loop to recover dense depth maps from sparse LiDAR measurements using image guidance for higher accuracy. Unlike sibling methods that rely on monocular depth estimation (MDE) priors which lack absolute scale or suffer from accuracy compromises, this method uses LiDAR-based completion to provide dense, metrically consistent depth supervision. It sets itself apart by explicitly addressing the sparsity of raw LiDAR data through guided completion, making it suitable for unbounded real-world scenes where raw LiDAR is insufficient. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: Input RGB images I, sparse raw LiDAR depth measurements Dl, and camera poses. Outputs: A dense depth map D{guide} used for supervision, and the final NeRF radiance field parameters. Data Structures: Sparse LiDAR Depth (Dl): A sparse 2D map or point cloud representing raw LiDAR returns. RGB Image (I): The corresponding color image for the LiDAR frame. Completion Network (\delta): A neural network (specifically MFFNet) that takes I and Dl as input. Steps: 1. Sparse Point Cloud Extraction: Extract a sparse point cloud from the scene using COLMAP to establish initial geometry and camera poses. 2. Depth Completion: Apply the guided depth completion network \delta to the input image I and raw LiDAR depth Dl to produce a dense, guided depth map D{guide}: D{guide} = \delta(I, Dl) where \delta represents the completion network (e.g., MFFNet). 3. NeRF Rendering: Render the NeRF model F\Theta to obtain the predicted depth \bar{D} and color for each ray, using standard volume rendering accumulation. 4. Loss Calculation: Compute the total loss. This includes the standard volumetric loss (color reconstruction) and a depth consistency loss L{depth} based on the difference between the rendered depth \bar{D} and the completed depth D{guide}. The depth loss may incorporate uncertainty predictions if the completion network provides them. 5. Optimization: Update NeRF parameters to minimize the combined loss. Parameters: Completion Method: MFFNet is selected as the representative guided depth completion method. Training Data: RGB-D data from ScanNet and Matterport3D datasets. Noise: Gaussian noise is added to the depth during training to improve robustness. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Sparsity: Raw LiDAR is inherently sparse. The completion network is necessary to bridge this gap. Uncertainty: If the completion network outputs uncertainty, it should be used to weight the depth loss, penalizing confident predictions more heavily. NLSPN propagates depth information from LiDAR points to surrounding pixels to provide credible depth supervisions from defect LiDAR depths. It requires accumulating neighbor LiDAR frames to get much denser depths for input. However, NLSPN performs well with 64-channel LiDAR data (e.g., KITTI) but fails with nuScenes' 32-channel LiDAR data because it is too sparse for the depth completion network. Additionally, accumulated LiDAR data contain outliers due to moving objects, ill poses, and occlusions, leading to wrong depth supervisions. Complexity: Adds the inference cost of the depth completion network (MFFNet) to the NeRF training loop. Performance: Achieves higher accuracy than unguided methods by leveraging image guidance. Strengths: Effective for unbounded real scenes where raw LiDAR is sparse. Limitations: Relies on the quality of the LiDAR hardware and the completion network; sensitive to outliers in accumulated LiDAR data if not handled. When to use: When sparse LiDAR data is available and high-accuracy dense depth is required for NeRF training in outdoor or large-scale scenes. When not to use: When only monocular images are available (use MDE-based methods instead) or when LiDAR is too sparse for the completion network (e.g., 32-channel LiDAR without accumulation). The method originates from the need to handle unbounded real scenes where the original NeRF parametrization was limited to bounded or forward-facing scenes. It builds on the observation that raw LiDAR provides sparse measurements, while monocular methods compromise on accuracy. The approach was developed to integrate guided depth completion (specifically MFFNet) into NeRF training, using datasets like ScanNet and Matterport3D. name: Monocular Depth Regularization on Seen Views
head: Patch-wise depth alignment, Seen-view depth distillation
body: This method aligns pseudo-depth maps from a pre-trained monocular depth estimation (MDE) network with NeRF-rendered depth for seen input views to stabilize geometry optimization. It differs from global scale-fitting approaches by computing local scale and shift parameters per image patch, preventing dominant objects from biasing the depth alignment and thereby preserving local geometric details. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A set of seen view images S, a pre-trained MDE network G\phi, and a NeRF model F\Theta. Output: A depth consistency loss term L{seen} added to the training objective. Data Structures: Patches: The image is divided into non-overlapping or overlapping patches P. The specific patch size and stride are not given in the sources. Depth Maps: D^i: Relative depth map from MDE for image Ii. \bar{D}i: Absolute depth map rendered by NeRF for view i. Parameters: wi, qi: Local scale and shift parameters for a specific patch. \text{sg}(\cdot): Stop-gradient operator. Steps: 1. Iterate through each seen view image Ii \in S. 2. Render the absolute depth map \bar{D}i from the NeRF F\Theta for the camera pose of Ii. 3. Compute the relative pseudo-depth map D^i = G\phi(Ii) using the pre-trained MDE network. 4. For each patch P in the image: a. Identify the set of pixels p \in P. b. Compute the optimal scale wi and shift qi by minimizing the least squares error between the scaled MDE depth and the NeRF depth: \min{wi, qi} \sum{p \in P} \| (wi \cdot \text{sg}(D^i(p)) + qi) - \bar{D}i(p) \|^2 c. Calculate the per-patch loss contribution using the aligned depths. 5. Sum the losses over all patches and all seen views. Formula: The total depth consistency loss for seen views is defined as: L{seen} = \sum{Ii \in S} \sum{p \in P} \| (wi \cdot \text{sg}(D^i(p)) + qi) - \bar{D}i(p) \| where \| \cdot \| denotes the L1 or L2 norm (not specified, L1 is common in such contexts but not explicitly stated). Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def computeseendepthloss(views, nerfmodel, mdemodel, patchsize): totalloss = 0.0 for view in views: # 1. Render NeRF depth # Assumes nerfmodel.renderdepth returns a tensor of shape (H, W) nerfdepth = nerfmodel.renderdepth(view.camerapose) # 2. Get MDE depth # Assumes mdemodel returns relative depth tensor of shape (H, W) mdedepth = mdemodel(view.image) # 3. Iterate over patches # Implementation detail: H, W assumed divisible by patchsize or handled via padding/cropping H, W = nerfdepth.shape for y in range(0, H, patchsize): for x in range(0, W, patchsize): # Define patch boundaries yend = min(y + patchsize, H) xend = min(x + patchsize, W) # Extract patch tensors patchmde = mdedepth[y:yend, x:xend] patchnerf = nerfdepth[y:yend, x:xend] # 4. Compute scale and shift via least squares # Solve minw,q sum( (w mde + q - nerf)^2) # Let m = patchmde, n = patchnerf # w = (Cov(m,n)) / Var(m) if Var(m) > 0, else 1.0 # q = mean(n) - w mean(m) mmean = patchmde.mean() nmean = patchnerf.mean() # Centered variables mc = patchmde - mmean nc = patchnerf - nmean varm = (mc 2).sum() covmn = (mc nc).sum() if varm > 1e-6: w = covmn / varm q = nmean - w mmean else: w = 1.0 q = 0.0 # 5. Calculate loss with stop-gradient on MDE depth # Note: In a real autograd framework, w and q might need to be detached # or computed via a differentiable solver if gradients are needed through them. # The source specifies sg(D), implying w and q are computed on detached values # or the loss is only backpropagated to NeRF. alignedmde = w patchmde.detach() + q patchloss = (alignedmde - patchnerf).abs().sum() # Assuming L1 totalloss += patchloss return totalloss Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Dominant Object Bias: Global scale/shift fitting favors large or high-contrast objects, leading to ill-fitted depths in less dominant sections. Patch-wise adjustment alleviates this. Computational Bottleneck: Rendering full-resolution depth maps for every patch can be expensive. The patch-wise approach helps mitigate this by allowing smaller, localized computations, though full image rendering is still required for the NeRF depth. Gradient Flow: The stop-gradient operator \text{sg}(\cdot) is critical to prevent gradients from flowing into the pre-trained MDE network G\phi, which is frozen. Incorporates geometric constraints from MDE but filters supervision using transient confidence weights to enforce consistency only on static geometry. Time Complexity: Depends on the number of seen views, the number of patches, and the cost of MDE inference and NeRF depth rendering. The patch-wise least squares solution is O(N) per patch where N is the number of pixels in the patch. Memory Complexity: Requires storing depth maps for the current batch of views. Patch-wise processing allows for lower peak memory usage compared to full-image alignment if processed sequentially. Strengths: Preserves local geometric details by avoiding global bias; stabilizes training for sparse inputs. Limitations: Relies on the quality of the pre-trained MDE network; patch boundaries may introduce discontinuities if not handled carefully. When to use: When training NeRFs on sparse or unconstrained image collections where global depth alignment fails due to varying object scales or dominant foregrounds. The method was introduced in the DaRF paper, which proposes boosting radiance fields from sparse inputs using monocular depth adaptation. It addresses the issue that global scale fitting undermines local statistics, a problem highlighted in prior work [62] cited by the authors. name: Transient-Aware Depth Prior
head: DPT depth supervision, monocular depth loss
body: The Transient-Aware Depth Prior is a regularization technique for Neural Radiance Fields (NeRF) that incorporates geometric priors from a monocular depth estimator (typically DPT) to constrain optimization and suppress artifacts like floaters or geometry collapse. It distinguishes itself from sibling methods by explicitly aligning the scale and offset of the monocular depth map using learnable per-image parameters and filtering the loss with a transient confidence weight derived from the NeRF's own density fields, rather than relying on generalizable priors or inter-frame consistency alone. This allows the method to apply depth supervision only to static regions, preventing the network from learning incorrect geometry for transient objects. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: Training image i, camera pose, ray r passing through pixel, pre-trained Monocular Depth Estimation (MDE) network (DPT), current NeRF model (shared density \sigma and candidate density \sigma^{(c)}). Outputs: Depth loss value L{depth} for the current ray. Data Structures: Monocular Depth Prior: Dense inverse depth map D^{inv}i predicted by DPT for image i. Learnable Parameters: Per-image scale \etai and shift \xii. NeRF Densities: Shared density \sigma (static geometry) and candidate density \sigma^{(c)} (transient/uncertain geometry). Steps: 1. Acquire Monocular Depth: For each training image i, predict the inverse depth map D^{inv}i using the DPT network. 2. Compute Aligned Monocular Depth: Transform the inverse depth to align with the NeRF's coordinate system using learnable scale \etai and shift \xii: D^i(r) = \frac{1}{\etai D^{inv}i(r) + \xii} where D^i(r) is the aligned monocular depth prior for ray r. 3. Render NeRF Depth: Compute the expected depth \hat{D}i(r) from the NeRF using volume rendering integration along the ray: \hat{D}i(r) = \sum{k=1}^{K} T(tk) \alpha(\sigma(tk)\deltak) tk where tk are sample points, \deltak is the distance between samples, \alpha is the opacity, T(tk) is the transmittance, and \sigma is the shared density. 4. Calculate Transient Confidence Weight: Determine the weight W{depth}(r) based on the ratio of candidate density to shared density. This weight indicates the likelihood that the ray passes through a transient object: W{depth}(r) = \sum{k=1}^{K} Ti(tk) \alpha(\sigma^{(c)}(tk)\deltak) where Ti(tk) is the transmittance computed using the candidate density \sigma^{(c)}. Note: W{depth}(r) \in [0, 1]. High values indicate transient content. 5. Compute Depth Loss: Calculate the L1 loss between the aligned monocular depth and the rendered NeRF depth, weighted by the transient confidence. The loss is applied only to areas with low transient confidence (high static confidence): L{depth}(r) = (1 - W{depth}(r)) \| D^i(r) - \hat{D}i(r) \|1. Parameters: \lambdad: Weight for the depth loss in the total loss function. Typical value: 0.001. \etai, \xii: Learnable scale and shift parameters for each image i. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def computetransientawaredepthloss(ray, imageidx, nerfmodel, dptmodel, eta, xi): """ ray: Ray object with origins and directions. imageidx: Index of the current training image. nerfmodel: NeRF model providing shared density sigma and candidate density sigmac. dptmodel: Pre-trained DPT model for monocular depth estimation. eta: Learnable scale parameter for imageidx. xi: Learnable shift parameter for imageidx. """ # 1. Acquire monocular inverse depth from DPT # Dinv is a dense map for the image; we sample it at the ray's pixel coordinates pixelcoords = ray.getpixelcoordinates() dinv = dptmodel.predictinversedepth(imageidx, pixelcoords) # 2. Compute aligned monocular depth D # D = 1 / (eta Dinv + xi) dmono = 1.0 / (eta dinv + xi) # 3. Render NeRF depth Dhat # Sample points along the ray tsamples = ray.samplepoints(K=Ksamples) sigmashared = nerfmodel.getshareddensity(tsamples) sigmacand = nerfmodel.getcandidatedensity(tsamples) # Compute opacity alpha and transmittance T # alpha = 1 - exp(-sigma delta) deltas = tsamples[1:] - tsamples[:-1] # Handle last delta or edge case if necessary deltas = np.append(deltas, deltas[-1]) alpha = 1.0 - np.exp(-sigmashared deltas) # Transmittance T(tk) = product of (1 - alphaj) for j < k T = np.cumprod(np.concatenate([[1.0], 1.0 - alpha[:-1]])) # Rendered depth Dhat = sum(T alpha t) dhat = np.sum(T alpha tsamples) # 4. Calculate transient confidence weight Wdepth # Wdepth = sum(Tcand alphacand) # Alphacand uses candidate density sigmac alphacand = 1.0 - np.exp(-sigmacand deltas) Tcand = np.cumprod(np.concatenate([[1.0], 1.0 - alphacand[:-1]])) wdepth = np.sum(Tcand alphacand) # 5. Compute weighted L1 loss # Ldepth = (1 - Wdepth) |D - Dhat| loss = (1.0 - wdepth) np.abs(dmono - dhat) return loss Time Complexity: Adds the cost of a forward pass through the DPT network per image (or cached) and additional density evaluations for the candidate head to compute W{depth}. Memory Complexity: Requires storing learnable \etai, \xii per image and potentially caching DPT outputs. Performance: Improves novel view synthesis metrics (PSNR, SSIM) on unconstrained datasets like PhotoTourism compared to baselines like BARF and NeRF-W. Strengths: Effectively suppresses floaters and geometry collapse in unconstrained image collections by leveraging strong geometric priors. Limitations: The depth prior is a pseudo-label and not ground truth; over-reliance can degrade rendering quality if not properly weighted. The method relies on the accuracy of the DPT model. When to use: When training NeRF on unconstrained image sets with potential transient objects and unknown poses. When not to use: When high-quality ground truth depth is available, or when computational resources for DPT inference are prohibitive. The method was introduced in UP-NeRF (Unconstrained Pose-Prior-Free Neural Radiance Fields). It is inspired by NoPe-NeRF, which also uses monocular depth regularization. However, UP-NeRF adapts the approach for unconstrained images by using per-image affine alignment and transient-aware weighting, whereas NoPe-NeRF originally focused on video sequences with inter-frame losses. The DPT (Dense Prediction Transformer) model is used as the monocular depth estimator.
