Loss Computation if shadowimages is not None: target = shadowimages[b].view(-1)[indices[b]] loss = torch.abs(irradiancefinal - target).mean() totalloss += loss elif rgbimages is not None: # Compute outgoing radiance n = gradsdf rhod, y = self.computematerial(xtilde, n) rhos = self.computespecular(y, ldir, sampledv, n) # C = (rhod + rhos) irradiance (l. n) ldotn = torch.sum(ldir n, dim=-1, keepdim=True) outgoingradiance = (rhod + rhos) irradiancefinal ldotn target = rgbimages[b].view(-1, 3)[indices[b]] loss = torch.abs(outgoingradiance - target).mean() totalloss += loss # Eikonal Loss # Sample random points in space randompoints = torch.randnlike(sampledo) 2.0 # Bounding box assumption sdfrandom = self.sdfnet.sampleandforward(randompoints) gradrandom = torch.autograd.grad(sdfrandom.sum(), randompoints, creategraph=True)[0] eikonal = (torch.norm(gradrandom, dim=-1) - 1.0)2 totalloss += eikonal.mean() return totalloss / B Time Complexity: Training takes approximately 24 hours on a single RTX 2080Ti for 150k iterations. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Performance: Evaluated on synthetic datasets (800x800 resolution) and real capture setups. Strengths: Reconstructs geometry from scratch using shadows, unlike methods that use MVS first. Fully differentiable shadow ray supervision, unlike concurrent works using non-differentiable root finding. Applicable to single-view setups, unlike NeRF which requires multi-view. Handles RGB inputs by modeling material, avoiding the need for explicit shadow segmentation. Limitations: Requires multiple lighting conditions to obtain sufficient shadow observations. Assumes the ground plane position and orientation are known to resolve scale ambiguity. Iterative updating strategy is insufficient for gradients at surface boundaries with abrupt depth changes without the boundary handling mechanism. Transparency and inter-reflections are not modeled. ShadowNeuS was proposed in the paper "ShadowNeuS: Neural SDF Reconstruction by Shadow Ray Supervision". It addresses the limitation of NeRF, which models camera rays but ignores shadow rays (rays from the light source to the scene). The method draws inspiration from NeuS for SDF representation and differentiable rendering techniques. It is used for single-view 3D reconstruction from binary shadow images or RGB images under multiple lights. name: NeRF-Supervision
head: RGB-sensor-only self-supervised pipeline for dense descriptors
body: NeRF-Supervision is a method for generating dense correspondence datasets to train object-centric visual descriptors using only RGB images and Neural Radiance Fields (NeRFs). It solves the problem of acquiring ground-truth dense correspondences for thin, reflective, or ambiguous objects where traditional RGB-D sensors and Multi-View Stereo (MVS) fail. Unlike MVS, which relies on patch-based photometric consistency, NeRF-Supervision uses the NeRF's density field to formulate a "distribution-of-depths" approach, allowing for probabilistic sampling of correspondences and handling of view-dependent appearance. The method operates in three distinct stages: NeRF optimization, dataset generation via density field sampling, and descriptor model training. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A set of RGB images I of an object captured from various viewpoints. Output: A trained dense descriptor model capable of estimating dense object descriptors for unobserved real images. Data Structures: The fundamental unit of training data is a correspondence tuple (Is, us, It, ut): Is, It \in \mathbb{R}^{w \times h \times 3}: Source and target RGB images, where w and h are image width and height. us, ut \in \mathbb{R}^2: Pixel coordinates in the source and target images, respectively. Constraint: The image-forming rays defined by (Is, us) and (It, ut) must intersect the same 3D point in space. Algorithm Steps: 1. NeRF Optimization: Collect RGB images of the object and optimize a NeRF model F\Theta. The NeRF predicts volume density \sigma and view-dependent color c for any 3D point \mathbf{x} and viewing direction \mathbf{d}. 2. Correspondence Dataset Generation: Use the trained NeRF's density field to automatically generate a dataset of dense correspondences. This involves sampling 3D points from the density field and projecting them into multiple camera views to create valid tuples. Distribution-of-Depths Formulation: Unlike methods that rely on a single depth map, this method reformulates correspondence via a distribution-of-depths formulation. The NeRF's density field allows for probabilistic sampling, which handles ambiguity in photometric consistency better than patch-based MVS. 3. Descriptor Training: Train a neural network f\theta with parameters \theta to map an input RGB image I to a dense descriptor field. The network is supervised using the generated tuples (Is, us, It, ut). The descriptor dimensionality is denoted as d. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def nerfsupervisionpipeline(rgbimages, cameraposes): """ Generates dense correspondence data and trains a descriptor model. Args: rgbimages: List of RGB images of the object. cameraposes: Corresponding camera poses for the images. Returns: traineddescriptormodel: A model ftheta mapping images to dense descriptors. """ # Stage 1: Optimize NeRF # FTheta predicts density sigma and color c given position x and view direction d nerfmodel = optimizenerf(rgbimages, cameraposes) # Stage 2: Generate Correspondence Dataset # The dataset consists of tuples (Is, us, It, ut) # where rays from us in Is and ut in It intersect the same 3D point. correspondencedataset = [] # Sample 3D points from the NeRF's density field # This handles ambiguity via density field sampling rather than patch-based consistency for in range(numsamples): # Sample a 3D point P from the density distribution P = sample3dpointfromdensity(nerfmodel) # Project P into multiple camera views to find corresponding pixels # For each pair of views (s, t) that see P: for views, viewt in getviewpairs(cameraposes): us = projecttopixel(P, views) ut = projecttopixel(P, viewt) # Retrieve RGB images Is = getimage(views, rgbimages) It = getimage(viewt, rgbimages) # Add tuple to dataset # Is, It in R^(w x h x 3); us, ut in R^2 correspondencedataset.append((Is, us, It, ut)) # Stage 3: Train Descriptor Model # ftheta maps input RGB image I to dense descriptors of dimensionality d descriptormodel = initializedescriptormodel() for (Is, us, It, ut) in correspondencedataset: # Extract descriptors at specific pixel locations descs = descriptormodel(Is, us) desct = descriptormodel(It, ut) # Compute loss based on correspondence consistency # (Specific loss function depends on the chosen descriptor architecture) loss = computecorrespondenceloss(descs, desct) # Update model parameters theta updateparameters(descriptormodel, loss) return descriptormodel Parameters: w, h: Image width and height. d: Descriptor dimensionality. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Reflective Objects: Standard RGB-D and MVS methods struggle with reflective objects. NeRF-Supervision handles this because the NeRF takes view direction as input for color prediction, allowing it to model view-dependent appearance. Ambiguity: The density field sampling mechanism handles geometric ambiguity better than patch-based photometric consistency used in MVS. Performance: Dense correspondence models trained with this method outperform off-the-shelf learned descriptors by 106% (measured by PCK@3px metric) and outperform a baseline supervised with multi-view stereo by 29%. Strengths: RGB-only: Does not require depth sensors or multiple synchronized cameras. Robustness: Effective for thin and reflective objects (e.g., forks, whisks, strainers) that are challenging for commodity RGB-D cameras or MVS. Application: Enables robots to perform accurate 6-DoF pick and place of challenging objects. Limitations: Requires the optimization of a NeRF for each object, which can be computationally intensive compared to direct MVS. Performance is dependent on the quality of the NeRF reconstruction. NeRF-Supervision was introduced by Lin Yen-Chen, Tsung-Yi Lin, Pete Florence, Jonathan T. Barron, Alberto Rodriguez, and Phillip Isola in 2022. The work addresses the long-standing problem of designing robust visual descriptors invariant to scale, illumination, and pose. While learning-based descriptors have shown superiority over hand-crafted ones, the lack of ground-truth dense correspondence data for challenging objects (particularly thin and reflective ones) has been a bottleneck. This method leverages the recent success of Neural Radiance Fields to provide a self-supervised pipeline for generating such data. name: GAINS Stage I: Shape Estimation
head: GAINS Shape Estimation, GAINS Stage 1
body: GAINS Stage I is the geometry optimization phase of the GAINS pipeline, designed to reconstruct robust 3D shape from a sparse set of input RGB images using 2D Gaussian Splatting (2DGS). It solves the problem of novel-view artifacts and geometric collapse that occur when standard 2DGS losses are applied to sparse inputs by augmenting the optimization with learning-based priors: monocular depth/normal consistency, local depth ranking, and Score Distillation Sampling (SDS) from a latent diffusion model. Unlike its sibling methods that may rely on differentiable volume rendering or MVS priors, GAINS explicitly leverages a pre-trained diffusion model to regularize unseen viewpoints, ensuring the geometry lies on the natural object manifold. Inputs: Sparse set of RGB images \{Ii\}{i=1}^N (typically N \in [4, 16]). Known camera parameters Ci = \{Ki, Ri, ti\} for each view. Pre-trained monocular depth estimator (outputs \hat{D}i). Pre-trained monocular normal estimator (outputs \tilde{N}i). Pre-trained latent diffusion model \epsilon\phi. Optional: Ground-truth alpha masks for outlier removal. Outputs: Optimized 2DGS geometry representation G = \{\muj, Sj, Rj, \sigmaj\}{j=1}^M, where \muj is position, Sj is scaling, Rj is rotation, and \sigmaj is opacity. The scene is represented as a collection of 2D Gaussians. Each Gaussian j stores: \muj \in \mathbb{R}^3: 3D position. Sj \in \mathbb{R}^3: Scaling vector. Rj \in \mathbb{R}^{3 \times 3}: Rotation matrix. \sigmaj \in \mathbb{R}: Opacity. Surface normal nj is derived from Rj. \lambda{DC} = 0.005: Depth consistency weight. \lambda{DR} = 10: Depth ranking weight. \lambda{NC} = 1: Normal consistency weight. \lambda{N} = 0.25: Normal guided loss weight. \lambda{SDS} = 0.0001: Diffusion guidance weight. \lambda{BCE} = 0.75: Binary Cross-Entropy loss weight. \lambda = 0.2: Weight for L1 vs LD-SSIM in color loss (standard 2DGS default, implied by (1-\lambda)L1 + \lambda L{D-SSIM}). Total iterations: 16,000. SDS activation iteration: 10,000. SDS guidance scale: 100. Novel viewpoints sampled: 100. Floater removal interval: Every 1,000 iterations. 1. Initialization: Initialize the 2DGS primitives G using standard initialization procedures for 2DGS. 2. Loss Calculation: For each training iteration, compute the total loss \mathcal{L}{total} as the sum of the following components: A. Re-rendering Loss (\mathcal{L}{col}): Render the image R{geo}(Ci, G) for each input view Ci. Compute: \mathcal{L}{col} = (1 - \lambda) \mathcal{L}1(R{geo}, Ii) + \lambda \mathcal{L}{D-SSIM}(R{geo}, Ii) where \mathcal{L}1 is the L1 loss and \mathcal{L}{D-SSIM} is the D-SSIM loss. B. Depth Distortion Loss (\mathcal{L}{DD}): Optional loss to reduce depth ambiguity by bringing intersected Gaussians closer along each ray. C. Normal Consistency Loss (\mathcal{L}{NC}): Compute surface normals \tilde{N}i from the rendered depth. Compare with normals Ni derived from the Gaussian rotation matrices: \mathcal{L}{NC} = 1 - \frac{1}{M} \sum{j=1}^M Nj^T \tilde{N}j (Note: The source defines \mathcal{L}{NC} = 1 - Ni^T \tilde{N}i, implying an average over primitives or pixels). D. Depth Consistency Loss (\mathcal{L}{DC}): Render depth map Di from G. Obtain monocular depth estimate \hat{D}i from the pre-trained MDE network. Compute the Pearson Correlation Coefficient (PCC) between Di and \hat{D}i: \mathcal{L}{DC} = 1 - \text{PCC}(Di, \hat{D}i) This enforces similarity in depth ordering and relative scale, mitigating hallucinations from MDE. E. Local Depth Ranking Loss (\mathcal{L}{DR}): Add \mathcal{L}{DR} to prevent geometric collapse from hard constraints and alleviate long-range ambiguity. (Specific formula not provided in source, cited as [9]). F. Normal Guided Loss (\mathcal{L}{N}): Obtain reference normals \tilde{N}i from the pre-trained monocular normal estimator. Obtain rendered normals Ni from the Gaussian geometry. Obtain surface normals \hat{N}i from the rendered depth. Compute: \mathcal{L}{N} = \mathcal{L}1(\tilde{N}i, \hat{N}i) + 0.1 \cdot \mathcal{L}1(\tilde{N}i, Ni) + \text{TV}(\tilde{N}i, \hat{N}i) where \text{TV} is the Total Variation loss. G. Diffusion Guidance Loss (\mathcal{L}{SDS}): Condition: Only compute if iteration > 10,000. 1. Sample 100 novel viewpoints Cj. 2. Render geometry R{geo}(Cj, G). 3. Apply forward diffusion to get noisy latents Zj: Zj = \alphat R{geo}(Cj, G) + \sigmat \epsilon where t \sim U(0.02, 0.98) and \epsilon \sim \mathcal{N}(0, I). 4. Compute SDS loss: \mathcal{L}{SDS} = \mathbb{E}{t, \epsilon} w(t) \| \epsilon\phi(Zj; t) - \epsilon \|2^2 where \epsilon\phi is the pre-trained diffusion model predicting noise, and w(t) is the weighting function. H. Outlier Removal Loss (\mathcal{L}{BCE}): Condition: Only if ground-truth alpha masks are provided. Compute Binary Cross-Entropy between the reconstructed alpha mask and the ground truth mask. 3. Optimization Step: Minimize the total loss: \mathcal{L}{total} = \mathcal{L}{col} + \lambda{DD} \mathcal{L}{DD} + \lambda{NC} \mathcal{L}{NC} + \lambda{DC} \mathcal{L}{DC} + \lambda{DR} \mathcal{L}{DR} + \lambda{N} \mathcal{L}{N} + \lambda{SDS} \mathcal{L}{SDS} + \lambda{BCE} \mathcal{L}{BCE} Update parameters of G using gradient descent. 4. Periodic Maintenance: Every 1,000 iterations, apply KNN-based floater removal to prune isolated or erroneous Gaussians. Unverified code. Depth Distortion Loss (LDD) # Optional, reduces depth ambiguity ldd = computedepthdistortionloss(G, rendereddepths) totalloss += lambdadd ldd gradients = accumulategradients(gradients, ldd) # 3. Normal Consistency Loss (LNC) # Compare normals from Gaussian rotation (Ni) with normals from depth (Ntildei) # Note: Source defines LNC = 1 - Ni^T Ntildei lnc = 0 for Rnormal in renderednormals: # Ntildei is derived from depth Ntilde = normalsfromdepth(Rnormal) # Ni is derived from Gaussian rotation Ni = normalsfromgaussianrotation(G) # Assuming element-wise or pixel-wise comparison averaged lnc += 1 - dotproduct(Ni, Ntilde) lnc = lnc / numpixels totalloss += lambdanc lnc gradients = accumulategradients(gradients, lnc) # 4. Local Depth Ranking Loss (LDR) # Prevents geometric collapse ldr = computelocaldepthrankingloss(rendereddepths) totalloss += lambdadr ldr gradients = accumulategradients(gradients, ldr) # 6. Normal Guided Loss (LN) # Uses reference normals from monocular estimator ln = 0 for i, (img, Rdepth) in enumerate(zip(images, rendereddepths)): # Reference normals from monocular normal estimator Nref = normalnet(img) # Surface normals from depth Nsurf = normalsfromdepth(Rdepth) # Rendered normals from Gaussian rotation Nrendered = renderednormals[i] # LN = L1(Nref, Nsurf) + 0.1 L1(Nref, Nrendered) + TV(Nref, Nsurf) term1 = l1loss(Nref, Nsurf) term2 = 0.1 l1loss(Nref, Nrendered) term3 = totalvariation(Nref, Nsurf) ln += term1 + term2 + term3 ln = ln / len(images) totalloss += lambdan ln gradients = accumulategradients(gradients, ln) # 7. It is disabled for the first 10,000 iterations to prevent instability. Sparse View Overfitting: Standard 2DGS losses overfit to captured viewpoints, causing novel-view artifacts. The addition of depth, normal, and diffusion priors mitigates this. MDE Hallucinations: Monocular depth estimators may hallucinate or have systematic biases. The use of PCC (relative scale/order) rather than absolute L1 loss helps mitigate this, along with the diffusion prior. Missing Alpha Masks: If ground-truth alpha masks are not provided, the BCE loss is skipped, and the model assumes the scene includes the background. Time: The optimization runs for 16,000 iterations. The inclusion of SDS loss (after iteration 10,000) adds significant computational cost due to the forward diffusion and noise prediction steps for 100 novel viewpoints per iteration. Memory: Memory usage is dominated by the 2DGS primitives and the storage of the pre-trained models (MDE, Normal Estimator, Diffusion Model) in memory. Hardware: Not specified in the sources. Resolution: Not specified in the sources. Scene: Tested on sparse multi-view captures (4-16 views). Scaling: The method is designed for sparse views, where traditional methods fail. It scales with the number of Gaussians and the complexity of the diffusion model. Strengths: Robust geometry reconstruction from sparse views; prevents novel-view artifacts; leverages strong priors from diffusion models for generalization. Limitations: Computationally expensive due to diffusion guidance; relies on the quality of pre-trained monocular estimators and diffusion models; requires known camera parameters. Use when reconstructing geometry from a sparse set of RGB images (4-16 views) where standard NeRF or 3DGS methods fail due to overfitting or artifacts. Use when high-fidelity geometry is required for subsequent material and lighting estimation (Stage II). Do not use if dense input views are available, as standard 2DGS may suffice and the additional priors add unnecessary complexity. Do not use if computational resources are limited, as SDS guidance is expensive. GAINS (Gaussian-based Inverse Rendering from Sparse Multi-view Captures) was introduced by P. Noras et al. in the paper "GAINS: Gaussian-Based Inverse Rendering from Sparse Multi-view Captures". The method builds on 2D Gaussian Splatting (2DGS) [8], which was chosen over 3DGS for its more accurate geometry reconstruction, essential for material estimation. The pipeline adapts 2DGS for inverse rendering by splitting optimization into two stages: Stage I for geometry and Stage II for material and lighting. Stage I specifically addresses the challenges of sparse views by incorporating priors from latent diffusion models and monocular depth/normal estimation models. GAINS is used for robust and accurate geometry and material property reconstruction from sparse RGB images under known camera intrinsics and extrinsics. name: Monocular Depth Cues
head: MonoSDF Monocular Cues, Omnidata Depth/Normal Priors
body: Monocular Depth Cues is a method that integrates pre-trained monocular geometric priors (depth and surface normal maps) into the training of neural implicit surface reconstruction models (such as MonoSDF) to regularize geometry and improve reconstruction quality from sparse or single views. It differs from sibling methods like NerfingMVS by relying on off-the-shelf monocular predictors (e.g., Omnidata) rather than multi-view stereo consistency or explicit MVS networks, and from Depth-Guided NeRF Training via Earth Mover’s Distance by using direct pixel-wise alignment losses rather than distributional matching. The method addresses the ambiguity of scale and detail in monocular inputs by providing semi-local relative depth and local surface normal cues. Inputs: Input RGB images I. A pre-trained monocular predictor G\phi (specifically Omnidata). A neural implicit surface representation (e.g., MLP or Multi-Resolution Grids). Outputs: Aligned monocular depth map \bar{D} and normal map \bar{N} for each input image. Regularized neural implicit surface reconstruction. Data Structures: Monocular Depth Map (\bar{D}): 2D array of relative depth values. Monocular Normal Map (\bar{N}): 2D array of 3D surface normal vectors. Neural Representation: Stores signed distance field (SDF) or density values queried by rays. Steps: 1. Cue Extraction: Apply the pre-trained predictor G\phi to each input RGB image I to generate a relative depth map \bar{D} and a surface normal map \bar{N}. 2. Scale and Shift Alignment: Align the relative monocular depth \bar{D} with the rendered depth \tilde{D} from the neural model. Since monocular depth lacks absolute scale, find scale w and shift q by minimizing the least-squares error: \min{w, q} \sum{p} \| (w \cdot \text{sg}(\bar{D}(p)) + q) - \tilde{D}(p) \|^2 where \text{sg}(\cdot) is the stop-gradient operator, preventing gradients from flowing into the frozen predictor G\phi. 3. Loss Computation: Compute a depth consistency loss L{depth} penalizing the difference between the aligned monocular depth and the rendered depth, and a normal consistency loss L{normal} penalizing the difference between the aligned monocular normals and the rendered normals (derived from the gradient of the SDF). 4. Optimization: Update the neural implicit surface parameters using the combined loss (RGB, depth, and normal losses). Parameters: Predictor: Omnidata. Resolution: Standard cues are generated at 384×384 resolution. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Scale Ambiguity: Monocular depth is relative; without alignment, the reconstruction scale is undefined. Local vs. Global: Depth cues provide semi-local relative information, while normal cues provide local geometric detail; they are complementary. Resolution Limits: Standard 384×384 cues may lack fine details; higher-resolution variants are available (see Subtopics). A method to generate higher-resolution monocular depth and normal maps by partitioning the input image into overlapping sub-images, predicting cues for each, merging them, and aligning them to recover fine details lost at lower resolutions. It produces cues with more fine details compared to the standard 384×384 resolution cues. It is used in MonoSDF when higher-quality geometric priors are desired. Steps: (1) Partition a high-resolution input image into multiple overlapping sub-images; (2) Predict monocular depth and normal maps for each sub-image using a pretrained predictor (e.g., Omnidata); (3) Merge the predictions from all sub-images into a single high-resolution depth and normal map; (4) Align the merged depth maps using the least-squares alignment formula. Time Complexity: Depends on the inference time of the pre-trained predictor (Omnidata) and the alignment optimization. The divide-and-conquer variant increases inference time due to multiple sub-image predictions and merging overhead. Memory Complexity: Requires storing the monocular depth and normal maps for each input view, plus the neural implicit representation. Performance: On the DTU dataset with 3 input views, methods using monocular cues (MLP and Multi-Res. Grids) produce satisfying reconstructions where they otherwise fail, achieving competitive Chamfer distances (e.g., ~2.0–5.0 mm depending on scene) compared to state-of-the-art methods. Strengths: Improves reconstruction quality for sparse views; provides complementary local (normal) and semi-local (depth) geometric information; easy to integrate via off-the-shelf predictors. Limitations: Relies on the quality of the pre-trained monocular predictor; scale ambiguity requires careful alignment; standard resolution cues may lack fine details. When to use: When training neural implicit surface reconstruction models from sparse or single views and higher-quality geometric priors are desired. The method originates from the MonoSDF paper, which explores the use of monocular geometric cues for neural implicit surface reconstruction. It leverages the Omnidata model for depth and normal prediction. The approach was developed to address the limitations of neural implicit methods that fail to produce satisfying reconstructions without geometric regularization, particularly in sparse-view settings. MonoSDF: Exploring Monocular Geometric Cues for Neural Implicit Surface Reconstruction, https://doi.org/10.52202/068431-1814, fetched 2026-10-26

name: NeRF Editing and Inpainting Procedures
head: NeRF Editing, NeRF Inpainting, 3D Scene Editing
body: NeRF Editing and Inpainting Procedures modify a pre-trained Neural Radiance Field (NeRF) to remove objects, fill occluded regions, or alter appearance and geometry based on user intent [17712-inpainting-and-object-removal.md, 12491-nerf-editing-procedure.md]. Unlike standard training which reconstructs a scene from scratch, these methods optimize existing parameters to satisfy new constraints while maintaining multi-view consistency [17712-inpainting-and-object-removal.md]. They are distinguished from sibling methods by their reliance on external 2D priors (such as inpainted images or diffusion models) to guide 3D optimization, rather than relying solely on multi-view geometry or semantic segmentation alone [17712-inpainting-and-object-removal.md]. All methods in this family operate on a pre-trained NeRF representation f\theta: (\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{d}) \to (\sigma, \mathbf{c}), where \mathbf{x} is a 3D coordinate, \mathbf{d} is the viewing direction, \sigma is volume density, and \mathbf{c} is color [Parent]. The core mechanism involves an optimization loop that minimizes a loss function L to update the NeRF parameters \theta (or a subset thereof). The general optimization objective is: L = L{render} + \lambda{guidance} L{guidance} + \lambda{reg} L{reg} where L{render} is the standard photometric reconstruction loss on visible pixels, L{guidance} incorporates external priors (e.g., 2D inpainted images, diffusion model gradients, or semantic features), and L{reg} prevents artifacts or overfitting. Key shared components include: 1. Masking/Selection: A binary or probabilistic mask M or selection field identifies the region of interest (ROI) or occluded areas. This can be user-defined, derived from semantic segmentation (e.g., LSeg, CLIP), or computed via geometric conflict detection [S1, 14365-repaint-nerf.md, 8658-progressive-inpainting-and-erasing.md]. 2. External Priors: Most methods rely on 2D priors to guide 3D changes. Common priors include: 2D Inpainting: Using models like LaMa or Stable Diffusion to generate color/depth priors for occluded regions [S1, 12405-adaptive-view-selection-for-inpainting.md]. Diffusion Guidance: Using Score Distillation Sampling (SDS) from text-to-image models (e.g., Stable Diffusion) to guide appearance and geometry. Semantic/Text Features: Using CLIP or LSeg to align rendered features with text prompts or semantic labels. 3. View Consistency Enforcement: To prevent flickering or inconsistencies across views, methods enforce multi-view constraints. This is achieved through: Geometric Consistency: Using depth maps or epipolar constraints to ensure warped views align. Gradient-Based Selection: Adapting the reliance on 2D priors vs. multi-view geometry based on local texture gradients [S1, 12405-adaptive-view-selection-for-inpainting.md]. Reference Views: Using a single or multiple inpainted reference views to propagate consistent content [S1, 13952-reference-guided-controllable-inpainting-of-nerfs.md]. Progressive Inpainting-and-Erasing (PERF) reconstructs a panoramic NeRF from a single input panorama by iteratively expanding viewpoint coverage. It solves geometry conflicts between visible and invisible regions by computing conflict masks and erasing inconsistent pixels from supervision. Unlike methods requiring multiple views, PERF generates novel views via inpainting and progressively integrates them. Deceptive-NeRF/3DGS enhances sparse-view reconstruction by densifying input observations with synthetic pseudo-observations generated by a diffusion model during training. It acquires uncertainty through correspondence matching by reprojecting real observations to novel views, enforcing epipolar constraints. It conditions a 2D diffusion model on rendered RGB, depth, and view-consistency uncertainty maps to rectify artifacts. Blended-NeRF edits specific regions of interest (ROI) in an existing NeRF using text prompts and a user-defined 3D bounding box. It initializes a generator NeRF with original weights and blends synthesized content with the original scene using volumetric blending. Unlike methods requiring semantic masks, it operates on any 3D box without learning a new feature space. This procedure enables direct 3D editing by decoupling semantic/geometric selection from appearance rendering using a Distilled Feature Field (DFF). It defines a selection probability p for each 3D point, allowing precise operations like deletion, colorization, and geometric transformation. It avoids iterative gradient descent for the edit itself, relying on a deterministic query-and-transform pipeline during rendering. NeRF-Art is a text-guided method for stylizing pre-trained NeRFs that simultaneously alters appearance and 3D geometry without mesh guidance. It introduces a global-local contrastive learning strategy combined with directional constraints to ensure style adherence and cross-view consistency. This article documents the empirical limitations of the RePaint-NeRF method, specifically regarding computational efficiency, geometric fidelity under significant shape changes, and view-angle consistency. It serves as a reference for failure modes and resource constraints in diffusion-guided NeRF editing. Semantic and Language-Guided Editing modifies NeRFs using high-level semantic cues (text prompts, language instructions, or semantic masks). It solves localized 3D content manipulation while maintaining multi-view consistency. It integrates external semantic priors (e.g., CLIP, LSeg, or diffusion models) into the optimization loop to guide 3D structure and appearance. InNeRF360 combines multiview-consistent 2D priors with 3D diffusion guidance to reconstruct missing or edited regions. It addresses occluded or removed objects by first establishing coherent 2D inpainting across all views, then refining the 3D representation. It differs from direct 3D optimization by decoupling content generation (via 2D inpainting) from 3D reconstruction. Diffusion-guided editing modifies pre-trained NeRFs using text prompts or image instructions by leveraging 2D text-to-image diffusion models as external priors. Unlike sibling methods relying on semantic masks or geometric constraints, this family uses diffusion gradients or iterative image synthesis to guide 3D changes. This family removes unwanted objects or fills occluded regions in a pre-trained NeRF [Parent]. Unlike standard training, these methods optimize NeRF parameters to erase specific masked regions while maintaining geometric and photometric consistency across unmasked views [Parent]. They rely on external 2D priors (such as inpainted images or diffusion models) to guide 3D optimization [Parent]. A strategy employed after the NeRF has been trained on updated data to enhance consistency by generating a more accurate target for each view using the modified Instruct-Pix2Pix with averaging architecture. Use the rendered image as input while continuing to use the mixup image as a condition. 1. Sample an edit code z from the Gaussian distribution. 2. Use the translated NeRF to render the 3D scene conditioned on z. A makeup migration technique based on dynamic NeRF, capable of seamlessly transitioning makeup styles from a standard image to a facial image in various poses and expressions. Guarantees geometric and appearance consistency during the migration. The field of NeRF editing emerged as NeRFs gained popularity for novel view synthesis, with early works focusing on object removal and scene manipulation. Key developments include the introduction of diffusion-guided editing (e.g., RePaint-NeRF, Instruct-NeRF2NeRF) which leveraged 2D generative models to guide 3D optimization [14365-repaint-nerf.md, 15089-instruct-nerf2nerf-optimization.md]. Subsequent methods like Blended-NeRF and NeRF-Art introduced techniques for localized editing and stylization using text prompts and volumetric blending [12273-blended-nerf.md, 13438-nerf-art.md]. Recent advancements focus on improving multi-view consistency through semantic priors and progressive inpainting strategies [8658-progressive-inpainting-and-erasing.md, 14393-semantic-and-language-guided-editing.md]. name: Progressive Inpainting-and-Erasing
head: Conflicted Geometry Detection and Erasing, Inpainting-and-Erasing Strategy, PERF, PERF Algorithm
body: Progressive Inpainting-and-Erasing (PERF) is a method for reconstructing a panoramic Neural Radiance Field (NeRF) from a single input panorama by iteratively expanding the viewpoint coverage. It solves the problem of geometry conflict between visible regions (observed in reference views) and invisible regions (occluded or unseen) by computing a mask of conflicted areas and eliminating them from the NeRF training supervision. Unlike methods that rely on multiple input views or semantic priors, PERF generates novel views via inpainting and progressively integrates them while erasing geometrically inconsistent pixels to ensure 3D consistency. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A single input RGB panorama I{rgb}. Output: A panoramic NeRF representation f{nerf}. Data Structures: NeRF Representation: Instant-NGP. Uses a hash table of size 2^{19} with 16 levels of feature vectors, each having a channel size of 2. Reference Views Set: I{ref}, initialized with the input RGBD panorama. Trajectory Set: \{pk\}, a set of novel view positions generated based on the initial depth map. Formulas: 1. Initial RGBD Estimation: The input I{rgb} is processed to estimate a depth map Id, resulting in an RGBD panorama I{rgbd}. (Specific equation number referenced as Eq. (2) in source, but formula details for depth estimation are not provided in the text; assumes a standard monocular depth estimator is used here). 2. Single-View NeRF Training: The initial NeRF f{nerf} is trained using Id and I{rgb}. (Specific equation number referenced as Eq. (3) in source, but formula details are not provided; assumes standard NeRF volume rendering loss minimization). 3. Invisible Region Mask (m'): For a new view, invisible regions are detected by warping the new view's depth v' to the reference view's coordinate system and comparing it with the reference depth v. m'{ij} = \mathbb{I}(warp(v'{ij}) - v{ij} > \epsilon) where m'{ij} is the mask pixel (1 for invisible, 0 for visible), v{ij} is the reference depth, v'{ij} is the warped depth from the new view, warp(\cdot) is the warping function, \mathbb{I}(\cdot) is the indicator function, and \epsilon is a small threshold value. 4. Conflicted Region Mask (m''): For each reference view I{ref}, conflicted regions are detected by warping the reference depth v to the new view's coordinate system and comparing it with the new view's depth v'. m''{ij} = \mathbb{I}(v{ij} - warp(v'{ij}) > \epsilon) where m''{ij} is the mask pixel (1 for inconsistent/conflicted, 0 for consistent). 5. Final Conflict Mask: The final conflict mask is computed by performing a logic AND operation across the individual masks m'' from all reference views. 6. Collaborative RGBD Inpainting: Invisible regions are inpainted using Stable Diffusion for RGB and a depth estimator for depth stitching. (Specific equation number referenced as Eq. (5) in source, but formula details are not provided; implies using the inpainted RGB and estimated depth to complete the panorama). Parameters: \epsilon: A small value used as a threshold for depth difference. Hash table size: 2^{19}. Levels: 16. Feature vector channel size: 2. Initial training iterations: 10,000 iterations for the single input panorama. New view sampling: 32 new positions with approximately gradually increased distance from the original position. Fine-tuning iterations per new view: 2,000 iterations total. First 100 iterations: Supervision only from the new reference view. Remaining 1,900 iterations: Supervision from all reference views. Optimizer: Adam. Learning rate: Initially 10^{-3}, decayed to 10^{-4} with cosine annealing strategy for each learning stage of a newly sampled view. Ray sampling: 2,048 rays sampled per iteration. Numbered Steps: 1. Estimate the initial depth map Id of the input single panorama I{rgb} to obtain I{rgbd}. 2. Train a single-view NeRF f{nerf} using Id and I{rgb} for 10,000 iterations. 3. Generate trajectories \{pk\} of novel views based on the depth map Id. 4. Initialize the set of reference views I{ref} = \{I{rgbd}\}. 5. Iterate n from 1 to iters (where iters corresponds to the number of new views, e.g., 32): 1. Randomly sample a new camera view p from \{pk\}. 2. Compute the invisible regions according to Eq. (4). 3. Perform collaborative RGBD inpainting using Stable Diffusion and a depth estimator to complete the RGB and depth maps of the invisible regions. 4. For all I{ref} \in I{ref}: 1. Compute the conflicted regions according to Eq. (6). 2. Erase these conflicted regions from the supervision of the NeRF training. 5. Add the new inpainted view to the reference views I{ref}. 6. Fine-tune f{nerf} with the updated I{ref} for 2,000 iterations (100 iterations with only the new view, 1,900 with all views). Pseudocode: Unverified code. Generate novel view trajectories pk = generatetrajectories(Id, numviews=32) # Sample 32 poses at gradually increasing distances from original # 4. Initialize reference views Iref = [Irgbd] # 5. Geometry Conflict: Invisible regions inpainted in one view may conflict with visible regions in another reference view. The erasing mechanism is crucial to prevent this. Precision: The threshold \epsilon must be carefully chosen to allow for small errors while detecting significant conflicts. Boundary Conditions: The warping function must handle occlusions and depth discontinuities correctly. A sub-method that uses Stable Diffusion for RGB inpainting and a depth estimator for depth stitching to complete invisible regions. It is chosen when monocular depth estimation is insufficient and external generative priors are needed. The initial training phase using a single RGBD panorama. It is chosen as the starting point for the progressive expansion. The geometric operation used to detect invisible and conflicted regions by projecting depth maps between camera poses. It is chosen for its efficiency in identifying visibility changes. Time Complexity: The method involves iterative training and inpainting. Training a scene takes about 2 hours on a single Nvidia V100 GPU with 32G memory. Memory Complexity: Uses Instant-NGP representation with a hash table of size 2^{19}. Measured Performance: Evaluated on the Replica dataset (2048x1024 resolution) and in-the-wild data. Strengths: Can reconstruct panoramic NeRFs from a single input view; handles geometry conflicts effectively; ensures 3D consistency through erasing. Limitations: Relies on the quality of the initial depth estimation and the inpainting model. When to use: When only a single panorama is available and a full 3D reconstruction is required. When not to use: When multiple input views are available, or when high-fidelity texture is critical and inpainting artifacts are unacceptable. Origin: Proposed in "PERF: Panoramic Neural Radiance Field From a Single Panorama". History: The method builds on the concept of NeRF [1] and uses Instant-NGP [40] for efficient representation. It addresses the limitation of NeRF requiring multiple views by introducing a progressive inpainting-and-erasing strategy. Usage: Used for reconstructing indoor scenes from single panoramic images, as demonstrated on the Replica dataset and in-the-wild data. name: Deceptive-NeRF/3DGS Pipeline
head: Deceptive-3DGS, Deceptive-NeRF
body: Deceptive-NeRF/3DGS is a sparse-view reconstruction method that enhances NeRF or 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) representations by continuously densifying input observations with synthetic pseudo-observations generated by a diffusion model during training. Unlike methods that rely on ensemble learning, variational inference, or spatial perturbations to estimate uncertainty, this approach acquires uncertainty through correspondence matching by reprojecting real input observations to novel views, thereby enforcing epipolar constraints with minimal additional computation. It sets itself apart by conditioning a 2D diffusion model on rendered RGB images, depth maps, and view-consistency uncertainty maps to rectify artifacts and generate photorealistic pseudo-observations that are filtered by perceptual similarity before being used to retrain the 3D representation. Inputs: A set of W input images I = \{I1, \dots, IW\} with calibrated camera poses. A pre-trained 2D latent diffusion model (e.g., Stable Diffusion) fine-tuned via ControlNet. Outputs: An optimized NeRF or 3DGS representation capable of high-quality novel view synthesis from sparse inputs. The method relies on the standard NeRF/3DGS representation f\theta: (\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{d}) \to (\sigma, \mathbf{c}). Additionally, it maintains: 1. Coarse NeRF: A representation trained on a subset (one-fifth) of input images to simulate sparse-view conditions and generate initial pseudo-observations for diffusion training. 2. Pseudo-Observation Buffer: A collection of generated pseudo-observations PA and their associated metadata (depth DA, uncertainty UA). 3. ControlNet Channels: The diffusion model accepts a 5-channel control map: 3 channels for coarse RGB, 1 for depth, and 1 for uncertainty. 1. Coarse Training: Train a coarse NeRF/3DGS using one-fifth of the input images I. 2. Novel View Sampling: Randomly sample a novel viewpoint A within the bounding box defined by the outermost input views. 3. Rendering: At viewpoint A, render the RGB image \hat{I}A, depth map DA, and transmittance using the coarse NeRF/3DGS. Depth is computed as a weighted sum of distances traveled: \hat{\mathbf{D}} = \sum{k=1}^K \hat{T}(tk)\alpha(\sigma(tk)\deltak) where \hat{T}(tk) is transmittance, \alpha is opacity, \sigma is density, and \deltak is the distance traveled. 4. Uncertainty Map Generation: Identify the nearest input viewpoint B to the novel view A. Warp the ground truth image IB from viewpoint B to viewpoint A using the rendered depth DA and the relative pose R{B \rightarrow A}: I{B \rightarrow A} = \psi(IB; DA, R{B \rightarrow A}) For each pixel p in \hat{I}A, compute the transformed pixel location q in IB: q = K R{B \rightarrow A} DA(p) K^{-1} p where K is the camera parameter matrix. Compute the uncertainty map UA as the squared difference between the warped image and the rendered image: UA = (I{B \rightarrow A} - \hat{I}A)^2. 5. Pseudo-Observation Generation: Generate a pseudo-observation PA using the Deceptive Diffusion Model G: PA = G(\hat{I}A, DA, UA) The model G is a latent diffusion model conditioned on the coarse RGB image, depth, uncertainty, and a text embedding s. 6. Text Embedding Derivation: Generate an initial text prompt s0 using a pre-trained image captioning network. Optimize a shared latent text embedding s^ using textual inversion, shared across all input observations and coarse images. Form the composite feature s = [s0, s^] by concatenating the embeddings. 7. Filtering: Calculate the perceptual similarity between the generated pseudo-observation PA and the input images using the LPIPS metric. Discard the 20% of pseudo-observations with the lowest similarity to avoid generating content far from the original inputs. 8. Accumulation and Re-training: Accumulate the valid pseudo-observations into the training set. Continue training the NeRF/3DGS representation using the combination of real input images and the accumulated pseudo-observations. 9. Iteration: Repeat steps 2–8 until a sufficient number of observations are accumulated to achieve the desired reconstruction quality. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import numpy as np def traindeceptivenerf(inputimages, poses, numepochs, numpseudoviews): """ Trains a NeRF/3DGS using the Deceptive-NeRF pipeline. Args: inputimages: List of W input images. poses: Camera poses for inputimages. numepochs: Number of epochs for coarse training. numpseudoviews: Number of pseudo-views to generate per iteration. Returns: Optimized NeRF/3DGS model. """ # 1. Coarse Training (1/5 of images) subsetsize = len(inputimages) // 5 coarseimages = inputimages[:subsetsize] coarseposes = poses[:subsetsize] coarsemodel = initializenerf(coarseimages, coarseposes) for epoch in range(numepochs): rendered = renderbatchfromnerf(coarsemodel, coarseimages, coarseposes) loss = computerenderingloss(rendered, coarseimages) updatenerfparameters(coarsemodel, loss) # 2. Diffusion Model Setup & Fine-tuning diffusionmodel = ControlNetStableDiffusion(controlchannels=5) trainingquartets = generatetrainingquartets(inputimages, poses) finetunediffusion(diffusionmodel, trainingquartets) # 3. Main (Fine) NeRF Initialization finemodel = initializenerf(inputimages, poses) # 4. Iterative Densification Loop pseudoobservations = [] for iteration in range(numpseudoviews): # Sample novel view A viewA = samplenovelview(poses) # Render from Coarse Model rgbcoarse, depthcoarse = renderfromnerf(coarsemodel, viewA) # Find nearest input view B viewBidx = findnearestinputview(viewA, poses) imgB = inputimages[viewBidx] # Generate Uncertainty Map uncertaintymap = computeuncertainty(imgB, depthcoarse, rgbcoarse, viewA, viewBidx, poses) # Generate Text Embedding textprompt = captionimage(rgbcoarse) latentembedding = optimizetextualinversion(inputimages, rgbcoarse) textembedding = concatenateembeddings(textprompt, latentembedding) # Generate Pseudo-Observation pseudoobs = diffusionmodel(rgbcoarse, depthcoarse, uncertaintymap, textembedding) # Filter Pseudo-Observation (Discard bottom 20% by LPIPS) similarityscores = computelpipsbatch(pseudoobs, inputimages) threshold = np.percentile(similarityscores, 20) if np.mean(similarityscores) >= threshold: pseudoobservations.append(pseudoobs) # Re-train Fine Model with real + pseudo observations trainfinemodel(finemodel, inputimages + pseudoobservations, poses) return finemodel def generatetrainingquartets(inputimages, poses): """ Generates dataset of quartets (Ifine, Icoarse, D, U) for diffusion training. Uses NeRF duos for major data, plus Gaussian noise augmentation. """ dataset = [] # Major dataset: 200 scenes from Hypersim and CO3D (~20k images) scenes = loadscenes(['Hypersim', 'CO3D']) for scene in scenes: # Train coarse NeRF on 1/5 images coarseimgs = scene.images[:len(scene.images)//5] coarsemodel = trainnerf(coarseimgs, scene.poses) coarsergb, coarsedepth = render(coarsemodel, scene.poses) # Train fine NeRF on all images finemodel = trainnerf(scene.images, scene.poses) finergb = render(finemodel, scene.poses) # Compute uncertainty for each view for i in range(len(scene.poses)): viewA = scene.poses[i] viewBidx = findnearestinputview(viewA, scene.poses) imgB = scene.images[viewBidx] warpedB = warpimage(imgB, coarsedepth[i], viewBidx, i, scene.poses) uncertainty = (warpedB - coarsergb[i]) 2 dataset.append((finergb[i], coarsergb[i], coarsedepth[i], uncertainty)) # Data Augmentation: Add Gaussian noise (std=0.3) to 60k Hypersim images noisyimages = addgaussiannoise(scene.images, std=0.3) for i in range(len(scene.images)): # Pair noisy image with original depth; uncertainty is not fed for augmented data dataset.append((scene.images[i], noisyimages[i], scene.depths[i], None)) return dataset def computeuncertainty(imgB, depthA, rgbA, viewA, viewBidx, poses): """Computes UA = (I{B->A} - IA)^2 using epipolar warping.""" K = getcameramatrix(poses) RBA = computerelativepose(poses[viewBidx], poses[0]) warpedB = warpimage(imgB, depthA, viewBidx, 0, poses) uncertainty = (warpedB - rgbA) 2 return uncertainty def warpimage(img, depth, viewsrcidx, viewdstidx, poses): """Warp source image to destination using depth and relative pose.""" K = getcameramatrix(poses) Rsrcdst = computerelativepose(poses[viewsrcidx], poses[viewdstidx]) H = K @ Rsrcdst @ np.linalg.inv(K) # Standard perspective warp using bilinear interpolation over warped coordinates h, w = img.shape[:2] coords = np.meshgrid(np.arange(w), np.arange(h)) coords = np.stack([coords[0].flatten(), coords[1].flatten(), np.ones(wh)], axis=1).T warpedcoords = H @ coords warpedcoords = warpedcoords[:2,:] / warpedcoords[2,:] # Bilinear interpolation omitted for brevity; standard graphics operation return np.zeroslike(img) def finetunediffusion(model, quartets): """Fine-tunes diffusion model using ControlNet objective.""" for batch in quartets: Icoarse, D, U, s = batch z = encodetolatent(Icoarse) t = np.random.randint(1, 1000) epsilon = np.random.normal(0, 1, z.shape) zt = addnoise(z, epsilon, t) prednoise = model.predictnoise(zt, t, Icoarse, D, U, s) loss = np.mean((epsilon - prednoise) 2) updatediffusionparameters(model, loss) def captionimage(rgb): """Generates text prompt s0 using pre-trained captioning network.""" return pretrainedcaptioner(rgb) def optimizetextualinversion(images, coarsergb): """Optimizes shared latent text embedding s via textual inversion.""" sstar = initializerandomembedding() for step in range(100): loss = computetextualinversionloss(sstar, images, coarsergb) sstar = updateembedding(sstar, loss) return sstar def concatenateembeddings(s0, sstar): """Concatenates embeddings to form composite feature s = [s0, s].""" return np.concatenate([s0, sstar], axis=-1) def computelpipsbatch(pseudoobs, referenceimages): """Computes LPIPS perceptual similarity metric.""" scores = [] for ref in referenceimages: # Standard LPIPS metric computation score = lpipsmetric(pseudoobs, ref) scores.append(score) return np.mean(scores) def initializenerf(images, poses): """Initializes NeRF/3DGS parameters theta [Parent].""" return NeRFModel(poses=poses) def renderbatchfromnerf(model, images, poses): """Renders RGB, depth, transmittance for a batch [Parent].""" return model.render(poses) def computerenderingloss(rendered, images): """Computes photometric reconstruction loss Lrender [Parent].""" return np.mean((rendered.rgb - images) 2) def updatenerfparameters(model, loss): """Gradient descent step for NeRF parameters theta [Parent].""" model.optimizer.step(loss) def samplenovelview(poses): """Randomly samples viewpoint within bounding box of input views.""" bounds = computeboundingbox(poses) return randompointinbox(bounds) def renderfromnerf(model, view): """Renders single view RGB and depth [Parent].""" return model.render(view) def findnearestinputview(viewA, poses): """Finds index of input view B closest to A.""" distances = [np.linalg.norm(viewA - p) for p in poses] return np.argmin(distances) def getcameramatrix(poses): """Extracts intrinsic camera matrix K.""" return poses[0].K def computerelativepose(viewB, viewA): """Computes R{B->A} from camera poses.""" return viewA.R @ viewB.R.T def addgaussiannoise(images, std): """Adds Gaussian noise with given standard deviation.""" noise = np.random.normal(0, std, images.shape) return np.clip(images + noise, 0, 1) def loadscenes(datasetnames): """Loads scenes from specified datasets.""" return [Dataset(name) for name in datasetnames] def trainnerf(images, poses): """Trains NeRF on provided images and poses [Parent].""" model = initializenerf(images, poses) for epoch in range(1000): rendered = renderbatchfromnerf(model, images, poses) loss = computerenderingloss(rendered, images) updatenerfparameters(model, loss) return model def render(model, poses): """Renders batch of images and depths [Parent].""" return model.render(poses) def encodetolatent(image): """Encodes image to latent space z using diffusion encoder.""" return pretrainedencoder(image) def addnoise(z, epsilon, t): """Adds noise at diffusion time step t.""" alphat = getalphaschedule(t) return np.sqrt(alphat) z + np.sqrt(1 - alphat) epsilon def getalphaschedule(t): """Returns pre-computed alpha values for time step t.""" return diffusionalphatable[t] def updatediffusionparameters(model, loss): """Gradient descent step for diffusion denoiser epsilontheta.""" model.optimizer.step(loss) def updateembedding(sstar, loss): """Gradient step for textual inversion embedding.""" return sstar - 0.01 np.gradient(loss, sstar) def lpipsmetric(pseudo, ref): """Computes Learned Perceptual Image Patch Similarity.""" return pretrainedlpipsnetwork(pseudo, ref) def trainfinemodel(model, images, poses): """Trains main NeRF on combined real and pseudo observations.""" for epoch in range(500): rendered = renderbatchfromnerf(model, images, poses) loss = computerenderingloss(rendered, images) updatenerfparameters(model, loss) Discard Rate: 20% of pseudo-observations with the lowest LPIPS similarity are discarded. Coarse NeRF Data: Trained on one-fifth of input images. ControlNet Channels: 5 channels (3 RGB, 1 Depth, 1 Uncertainty). Image Resolution: Randomly cropped to 512 \times 512. Gaussian Noise Std: 0.3, added to 60,000 images for data augmentation. Training Dataset Size: 200 scenes, approx. 20,000 images (Hypersim and CO3D). Captioning Efficacy: Image captioning efficacy diminishes for low-quality images or those with pronounced artifacts. Textual inversion is used to optimize a shared latent text embedding to counteract this. Augmentation Data: When training with noisy RGB-depth data augmentation, uncertainty maps are not fed into the diffusion model. Precision: The uncertainty map calculation relies on accurate depth rendering and precise camera pose alignment (K matrix) to ensure valid epipolar constraints. Time Complexity: The method requires training a coarse NeRF, fine-tuning a diffusion model, and iteratively generating pseudo-observations. Memory Complexity: Requires storing the coarse and fine NeRF representations (during dataset generation), the diffusion model, and its ControlNet weights. Performance: On the LLFF dataset with 3 views, Deceptive-NeRF achieves a PSNR of 19.87 and SSIM of 0.436, outperforming PixelNeRF (17.88 PSNR) and MVSNeRF (17.07 PSNR). Deceptive-3DGS achieves 19.95 PSNR. Strengths: Effectively densifies sparse views without requiring dense input data. Enforces 3D consistency via uncertainty maps derived from epipolar geometry. Limitations: Relies on the quality of the pre-trained diffusion model. Computationally intensive due to iterative training and diffusion inference. Deceptive-NeRF/3DGS was introduced by Liu et al. in 2023. It addresses the challenge of high-quality novel view synthesis from sparse input views, a common limitation in NeRF and 3DGS applications. The method leverages the power of 2D diffusion models to "rectify" NeRF renderings, hence the term "deceptive," by generating pseudo-observations that are consistent with the input data and 3D geometry. It builds on the principles of differentiable volume rendering and inverse rendering, specifically focusing on optimization loops that incorporate external 2D priors. name: Blended-NeRF
head: Zero-Shot Object Generation and Blending in Existing Neural Radiance Fields, Blending-NeRF
body: Blended-NeRF is a framework for editing specific regions of interest (ROI) in an existing Neural Radiance Field (NeRF) scene using text prompts and a user-defined 3D bounding box. It differs from generative methods that synthesize objects from scratch (e.g., Dream Fields) by initializing a generator NeRF with the weights of the original scene and blending the synthesized content with the original scene using a novel volumetric blending technique. Unlike methods requiring semantic masks or feature decomposition, it operates on any region defined by a 3D box without learning a new feature space. Inputs: Pre-trained NeRF model F{\thetaO}: (\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{d}) \to (\sigmaO, \mathbf{c}O) representing the original scene. A 3D Region of Interest (ROI) box B localized within the scene. A text prompt y describing the desired edit. A language-image model (e.g., CLIP) with image encoder E{img} and text encoder E{txt}. Outputs: Edited NeRF model F{\thetaE} (implicitly defined by the blending of F{\thetaO} and F{\thetaG}). Rendered views of the edited scene. Data Structures: F{\thetaO}: MLP mapping (\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{d}) to density \sigma and color \mathbf{c}. F{\thetaG}: MLP initialized with weights from F{\thetaO}, mapping (\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{d}) to density \sigmaG and color \mathbf{c}G. B: Axis-aligned 3D box defined by min/max coordinates. \gamma(\mathbf{x}): Sinusoidal positional encoding function. Parameters: \alpha: Hyperparameter for distance smoothing blending strength. Controls the weight given to the original scene vs. the edited scene based on distance from the ROI center. Typical values: 0, 0.5, 2, 4, 10. \lambdaT, \lambdaD: Weights for transmittance and depth losses. \tau: Max transmittance threshold for LT. \rho: Max variance threshold for LD. \epsilon: Small constant for numerical stability in blending. \phi: Non-negative activation function (e.g., ReLU) for densities. S: Sigmoid function. e{max}: Maximum dimension of the ROI box. \gamma{fov}: Camera field of view angle. Numbered Steps: 1. Initialization: Initialize the generator NeRF F{\thetaG} with the weights of the original scene model F{\thetaO}. 2. ROI Localization: Localize the 3D box B inside the scene using a GUI that renders the original NeRF and uses the output depth map for 3D understanding. 3. Training Loop: For each iteration: a. Pose Sampling: Sample a random camera pose around the scene with azimuth/elevation angles (\theta, \phi). The initial distance d from the ROI is calculated as d = \frac{e{max}}{2 \tan(\gamma{fov}/2)}, and the radius is randomly sampled around this value. b. Ray Casting: Cast rays r that pass through the box B. Sample points \mathbf{x}i along these rays. c. Forward Pass (Generator): Query F{\thetaG} for points \mathbf{x}i \in B. For points outside B, set density to zero. d. Rendering: Render the generated content inside the ROI I{ROI} using standard volume rendering on the blended/selected points: C(r) = \frac{\sum{\mathbf{x}i \in B} Ti (1 - e^{-\sigmai \deltai}) \mathbf{c}i}{\sum{\mathbf{x}i \in B} Ti (1 - e^{-\sigmai \deltai})} where Ti = \exp(-\sum{j < i} \sigmaj \deltaj), if \exists \mathbf{x}i \in r s.t. \mathbf{x}i \in B, else 0. e. Loss Calculation: Similarity Loss: L{sim} = -E{img}(I{ROI})^T E{txt}(y). Transmittance Loss: LT = -\min(\tau, \text{mean}(T(P))), where T(P) is the transmittance of the rendered view from pose P. Depth Loss: LD = -\min(\rho, \sigma^2(D(P))), where \sigma^2(D(P)) is the variance of the disparity map of the rendered view from pose P. Total Loss: L{total} = L{sim} + \lambdaT LT + \lambdaD LD. f. Optimization: Update \thetaG to minimize L{total}. g. Augmentations: Use random backgrounds (Gaussian noise, checkerboard, random Fourier textures) to prevent scene diffusion. Use directional dependent prompts by concatenating view-dependent text to the original caption. Gradually introduce LT and LD during training using an annealing strategy to prevent completely transparent or amorphous scenes. 4. Blending (Post-Training): After training, render the final edited scene by blending the sample points generated by F{\thetaO} and F{\thetaG} along each view ray. a. For points outside B, use F{\thetaO}. b. For points inside B, apply distance smoothing blending: f(\mathbf{x}) = 1 - \exp\left(-\alpha \frac{d(\mathbf{x})}{diag}\right) \sigma{blend}(\mathbf{x}) = f(\mathbf{x}) \cdot \sigmaO(\mathbf{x}) + (1 - f(\mathbf{x})) \cdot \sigmaG(\mathbf{x}) \mathbf{c}{blend}(\mathbf{x}) = f(\mathbf{x}) \cdot \mathbf{c}O(\mathbf{x}) + (1 - f(\mathbf{x})) \cdot \mathbf{c}G(\mathbf{x}) where d(\mathbf{x}) is the Euclidean distance from the ROI center, diag is the box diagonal, and \alpha is the smoothing parameter. c. Render the final view xe using standard volume rendering with the blended densities and colors. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import numpy as np def sinusoidalencoding(x, L=10): """High frequency sinusoidal positional encoding.""" freqbands = 2.0 np.arange(L) encoded = [] for l in range(L): freq = freqbands[l] encoded.append(np.cos(freq x)) encoded.append(np.sin(freq x)) return np.concatenate(encoded, axis=-1) def rayboxintersection(origin, direction, boxmin, boxmax): """Returns tmin, tmax for ray-AABB intersection.""" invdir = 1.0 / direction t1 = (boxmin - origin) invdir t2 = (boxmax - origin) invdir tmin = np.maximum(t1, t2).min(axis=1) tmax = np.minimum(t1, t2).max(axis=1) if np.any(tmax < 0) or np.any(tmin > tmax): return np.full(origin.shape[0], -1.0), np.full(origin.shape[0], -1.0) return tmin, tmax def samplecamerapose(r, theta, phi, center): """Samples a camera origin and direction on a sphere around center.""" x = r np.sin(phi) np.cos(theta) + center[0] y = r np.sin(phi) np.sin(theta) + center[1] z = r np.cos(phi) + center[2] origin = np.array([x, y, z]) direction = center - origin direction = direction / np.linalg.norm(direction) return origin, direction def volumerendernormalized(tsamples, sigma, color): """Standard volume rendering with ROI normalization per eq. (4).""" deltat = np.diff(tsamples, axis=1, prepend=np.zeros((tsamples.shape[0], 1))) deltat = np.maximum(deltat, 1e-8) alpha = 1.0 - np.exp(-sigma deltat) oneminusalpha = 1.0 - alpha Tcum = np.oneslike(oneminusalpha) Tcum[:, 1:] = np.cumprod(oneminusalpha[:,:-1], axis=1) contribution = Tcum alpha color numerator = np.sum(contribution, axis=1) denominator = np.sum(Tcum alpha, axis=1) denominator = np.maximum(denominator, 1e-8) renderedcolor = numerator / denominator finalT = Tcum[:, -1] (1 - alpha[:, -1]) return renderedcolor, Tcum, alpha, deltat def blendednerfedit(FthetaG, Bmin, Bmax, textprompt, clipmodel, numiterations, alphasmooth, lambdaT, lambdaD, tau, rho, epsilon): emax = max(Bmax[0] - Bmin[0], Bmax[1] - Bmin[1], Bmax[2] - Bmin[2]) gammafov = np.radians(60) dinit = emax / (2 np.tan(gammafov / 2)) center = (Bmin + Bmax) / 2.0 for in range(numiterations): r = np.random.uniform(dinit 0.8, dinit 1.2) theta = np.random.uniform(0, 2 np.pi) phi = np.random.uniform(-np.pi/2, np.pi/2) raysorigin, raysdirection = samplecamerapose(r, theta, phi, center) tmin, tmax = rayboxintersection(raysorigin, raysdirection, Bmin, Bmax) validmask = tmax > 0 raysorigin = raysorigin[validmask] raysdirection = raysdirection[validmask] tmin = tmin[validmask] tmax = tmax[validmask] numsamples = 128 tsamples = np.linspace(tmin, tmax, numsamples) samples3d = raysorigin[:, np.newaxis,:] + raysdirection[:, np.newaxis,:] tsamples[:,:, np.newaxis] maskinsideB = (samples3d >= Bmin) & (samples3d <= Bmax) maskinsideB = np.all(maskinsideB, axis=2) pointsG = samples3d[maskinsideB] sigmaG = np.zeros((len(raysorigin), numsamples)) colorG = np.zeros((len(raysorigin), numsamples, 3)) if len(pointsG) > 0: posencG = sinusoidalencoding(pointsG) direncG = sinusoidalencoding(raysdirection[maskinsideB[:, 0]]) sigmaGraw, colorGraw = FthetaG(posencG, direncG) sigmaG[maskinsideB] = sigmaGraw colorG[maskinsideB] = colorGraw phiact = lambda x: np.maximum(x, 0) deltat = np.diff(tsamples, axis=1, prepend=np.zeros((tsamples.shape[0], 1))) deltat = np.maximum(deltat, 1e-8) # During training, only FthetaG is used inside B; outside B density is 0 renderedcolor, Tcum,, = volumerendernormalized(tsamples, sigmaG, colorG) roimask = np.any(maskinsideB, axis=1) IROI = renderedcolor[roimask] imgemb = clipmodel.encodeimage(IROI) txtemb = clipmodel.encodetext(textprompt) Lsim = -np.dot(imgemb, txtemb) meanT = np.mean(Tcum[:, -1]) LT = -np.minimum(tau, meanT) troi = tsamples[roimask] disparity = 1.0 / np.maximum(troi, 1e-8) LD = -np.minimum(rho, np.var(disparity)) Ltotal = Lsim + lambdaT LT + lambdaD LD FthetaG.update(Ltotal) diag = np.sqrt(np.sum((Bmax - Bmin)2)) # Post-training blending would re-cast rays and apply f(x) smoothing return renderedcolor Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Scene Diffusion: Using white/black backgrounds during optimization can cause the scene to populate the background. Flat Geometry: In forward-facing scenes, limited viewing intervals can lead to flat billboard geometry. Transparency: Without regularization, the scene can become completely transparent. Use transmittance loss and annealing. View Consistency: Without pose sampling, the object may not be consistent across views. Directional Dependence: The object may look different in different views. Time Complexity: Depends on the number of iterations, number of rays, and number of samples per ray, similar to standard NeRF training. Memory Complexity: Requires storing the weights of F{\thetaO} and F{\thetaG}. Strengths: Can edit any region using a 3D box without semantic masks; blends naturally with the original scene; supports object insertion, replacement, and blending. Limitations: Requires a pre-trained NeRF; relies on CLIP for guidance, which may not always align perfectly with the user's intent; requires tuning of hyperparameters (\alpha, \lambdaT, \lambdaD). When to use: When you want to edit a specific region of an existing NeRF scene using text prompts and a bounding box. When not to use: When you need to generate a new object from scratch without an existing scene (use Dream Fields); when you need semantic segmentation-based editing (use other methods). Blended-NeRF was introduced by Ori Gordon, Omri Avrahami, and Dani Lischinski from The Hebrew University in 2023. It builds on the principles of NeRF [Parent] and Dream Fields, adapting them for local editing of existing scenes. It addresses the challenge of editing local regions in 3D scenes represented by NeRFs, which is difficult due to the implicit nature of the representation. name: NeRF Editing Procedure
head: Feature Field Distillation Editing, DFF-based Editing
body: This procedure enables direct 3D editing of a pre-trained NeRF by decoupling semantic or geometric selection from appearance rendering using a Distilled Feature Field (DFF). It solves the problem of inconsistent multi-view edits by defining a selection probability p for each 3D point based on external feature queries, allowing for precise operations like deletion, colorization, and geometric transformation that respect the underlying scene structure. It sets itself apart from standard optimization-based methods (e.g., RePaint-NeRF) by avoiding iterative gradient descent for the edit itself, instead relying on a deterministic query-and-transform pipeline during rendering. Inputs: Pre-trained NeRF representation f\theta: (\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{d}) \to (\sigma, \mathbf{c}). Pre-trained teacher network (e.g., LSeg or DINO) for feature extraction. User-defined editing parameters: Selection threshold \tau (default not specified, user-defined). Colorization function b(\cdot). Geometric transformation g(\cdot) and its inverse g^{-1}(\cdot). Ray \mathbf{r}(t) = \mathbf{o} + t\mathbf{d} for each pixel. Outputs: Edited image I'. Data Structures: DFF: A field storing feature embeddings or probability scores p for 3D coordinates. In the source, p is calculated by querying the DFF for each point. The exact internal layout of the DFF is not specified, but it outputs a scalar probability p \in [0, 1] representing the likelihood that coordinate \mathbf{x} matches the editing query. NeRF: Standard MLP or grid-based representation storing density \sigma and color \mathbf{c}. Steps: 1. Ray Sampling: Sample points \{\mathbf{x}i\} along the ray \mathbf{r} as in standard volume rendering. 2. Feature Query: For each point \mathbf{x}i, query the DFF to obtain the selection probability pi. 3. Selection Decision: Determine if \mathbf{x}i is "selected" by the edit query: If pi > \tau, \mathbf{x}i is selected. If pi \le \tau, \mathbf{x}i is not selected. Note: The source mentions an alternative mixture approach where results are blended in proportion to p, but the primary procedure uses the threshold. 4. Transform Application: For each point \mathbf{x}i, compute the effective density \sigma'i and color \mathbf{c}'i: Case A: Not Selected: Query the vanilla NeRF: (\sigmai, \mathbf{c}i) = f\theta(\mathbf{x}i, \mathbf{d}). Set \sigma'i = \sigmai, \mathbf{c}'i = \mathbf{c}i. Case B: Selected: Deletion: Set \sigma'i = 0. Color is irrelevant as density is zero. Color Editing: Query the vanilla NeRF for (\sigmai, \mathbf{c}i). Apply colorization function b: \mathbf{c}'i = b(\mathbf{c}i). Keep \sigma'i = \sigmai. Translation / Rescaling: 1. Compute deformed coordinate \mathbf{x}0 = g^{-1}(\mathbf{x}i). 2. Query the DFF for \mathbf{x}0 to get probability p0. 3. If \mathbf{x}0 is selected (p0 > \tau): Query NeRF for (\sigma0, \mathbf{c}0) = f\theta(\mathbf{x}0, \mathbf{d}). Set \sigma'i = \sigma0, \mathbf{c}'i = \mathbf{c}0. 4. If \mathbf{x}0 is not selected: The source does not explicitly define the fallback for the original point \mathbf{x}i in this specific branch, but implies the transformation logic applies primarily when the target location is also within the selected region. If \mathbf{x}0 is not selected, standard behavior for "selected" points (likely querying original \mathbf{x}i) is assumed. 5. Boundary Mixing: If both \mathbf{x}i and \mathbf{x}0 are selected and have non-zero density (e.g., at object boundaries during deformation): Mix colors \mathbf{c}i and \mathbf{c}0 in the ratio of their alphas \alphai and \alpha0. \mathbf{c}'i = \frac{\alphai \mathbf{c}i + \alpha0 \mathbf{c}0}{\alphai + \alpha0} (Derived from "mix their colors... in the ratio of their alphas"). Density handling for mixed points is not explicitly detailed beyond the color mixing instruction. 5. Volume Rendering: Perform standard volume rendering using the modified tuples (\sigma'i, \mathbf{c}'i) along the ray. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def rendereditedray(rayo, rayd, nerfmodel, dffmodel, transformginv, colorfuncb, threshold, isdeletion=False): """ Renders a single ray with editing applied via DFF. """ # 1. Sample points tvals = samplepointsalongray(rayo, rayd) points = rayo + tvals[:, None] rayd # 2. Query DFF for selection probabilities # dffmodel returns a scalar probability p for each point probs = dffmodel(points) # 3. Determine selection mask selected = probs > threshold densities = [] colors = [] for i, (x, p, issel) in enumerate(zip(points, probs, selected)): if not issel: # Case A: Not Selected - Use vanilla NeRF sigma, c = nerfmodel(x, rayd) densities.append(sigma) colors.append(c) else: # Case B: Selected - Apply Transform if isdeletion: # 4-A: Deletion densities.append(0.0) colors.append([0.0, 0.0, 0.0]) # Color irrelevant else: # Query original point for base values sigmaorig, corig = nerfmodel(x, rayd) # Check for geometric transformation (Translation/Rescaling) # Assume transformginv is identity if not a geometric edit xdeformed = transformginv(x) # Query DFF for deformed point pdeformed = dffmodel(xdeformed) isdeformedselected = pdeformed > threshold if isdeformedselected: # Get values from deformed location sigmadef, cdef = nerfmodel(xdeformed, rayd) # 4'-C: Boundary Mixing # Calculate alpha for mixing ratio # Note: Alpha depends on density and step size. # For simplicity in this procedural step, we use density as proxy # or assume pre-computed alpha if available. # The source says "ratio of their alphas". alphaorig = 1.0 - torch.exp(-sigmaorig) # Approximation alphadef = 1.0 - torch.exp(-sigmadef) # Approximation totalalpha = alphaorig + alphadef if totalalpha > 0: worig = alphaorig / totalalpha wdef = alphadef / totalalpha cfinal = worig corig + wdef cdef else: cfinal = corig densities.append(sigmadef) # Use density of deformed point colors.append(cfinal) else: # Deformed point not selected. # Source does not specify fallback for original point in this branch. # Assuming we fall back to original point's edited color if color edit, # or original density if not deletion. if colorfuncb is not None: cfinal = colorfuncb(corig) else: cfinal = corig densities.append(sigmaorig) colors.append(cfinal) # 5. Volume Rendering # Standard alpha compositing accumulatedcolor = 0.0 accumulatedalpha = 0.0 T = 1.0 for sigma, c in zip(densities, colors): alpha = 1.0 - torch.exp(-sigma) weight = T alpha accumulatedcolor += weight c accumulatedalpha += weight T = (1.0 - alpha) return accumulatedcolor A technique to edit specific objects within a NeRF without altering the background, using 2D segmentation masks propagated across views via depth information. It solves the problem where existing methods induce simultaneous changes in both background and foreground, contradicting user intentions to alter distinct objects. It sets itself apart by using depth-based reprojection to ensure multi-view consistency of the segmentation mask, allowing exclusive modification of the target instance while leaving the background intact. A strategy to efficiently warm up the editing process by blending edits directly before the entire editing process, accelerating editing while preserving consistency. It randomly selects a view to edit and projects the edited view onto all other views. The update formula is Ii' = \lambda Ii \odot mw + (1 - \lambda) I{i,j} \odot mw + Ii \odot (1 - mw), where mw is the binary mask for the projected area and \lambda controls the ratio preserved from the original pixel value. An application where scene editing is performed by setting the density inside a proposal bounding box (generated by a Region Proposal Network) to zero when rendering. This effectively removes objects detected by the framework. A simple 3D inpainting method that trains a NeRF using pixel reconstruction loss, guided by 2D inpainted images generated by an MST inpainting network. It relies on standard pixel loss rather than the DFF-based selection mechanism. Time Complexity: Rendering time is dominated by the additional DFF query per sample point. If the DFF is a lightweight network or lookup table, the overhead is minimal compared to the NeRF query. Memory Complexity: Requires storing the DFF in addition to the NeRF. The size of the DFF depends on the feature dimension and spatial resolution, which is not specified in the sources. Strengths: Deterministic editing; no iterative optimization required for the edit itself; supports complex transformations (translation, colorization). Limitations: Relies on the quality of the teacher network (LSeg/DINO) for accurate selection; threshold tuning required. When to use: When precise, non-iterative editing of specific semantic or geometric regions is required. The method originates from "Decomposing NeRF for Editing Via Feature Field Distillation". It utilizes pre-trained teacher networks like LSeg (ViT-L/16 image encoder, CLIP’s ViT-B/32 text encoder) and DINO to generate feature maps for distillation. name: Local Editing via SAM and Depth Propagation
head: Depth-propagated Mask Editing, SAM-based NeRF Editing
body: A technique to edit specific objects within a NeRF without altering the background, using 2D segmentation masks propagated across views via depth information. It solves the problem where existing methods induce simultaneous changes in both background and foreground, contradicting user intentions to alter distinct objects. It sets itself apart by using depth-based reprojection to ensure multi-view consistency of the segmentation mask, allowing exclusive modification of the target instance while leaving the background intact. Inputs: A trained NeRF, a set of input images (views), depth maps for each view, and a user interaction point on a target object in one or more views. Outputs: A modified NeRF where the target object is edited according to a prompt, while the background remains unchanged. Data Structures: Segmentation Mask (M): A 2D binary mask per view, where M{i,j} = 1 if pixel (i,j) belongs to the target object, 0 otherwise. Depth Map (D): A 2D map per view, where D{i,j} is the depth value at pixel (i,j). Camera Parameters: Intrinsic matrix K and extrinsic matrix [R|t] for each view. Steps: 1. Initial Segmentation: Employ the Segment Anything Model (SAM) to derive masks encompassing all components within each image. 2. User Selection: Users pinpoint the target instance with a single point to isolate it from the SAM output. 3. Key View Selection: Designate nearly all views as key views to facilitate propagation. 4. Depth-Based Projection: Utilize depth information to project the identified mask from a source view to a target view progressively. For a pixel (u, v) in the source view with depth d, compute the 3D point P in camera coordinates: P = d \cdot K^{-1} \begin{bmatrix} u \\ v \\ 1 \end{bmatrix}. Transform P to the target camera coordinate system: P' = R{t,s} P + t{t,s}. Project P' to the target image plane: (u', v') = K P'{xy} / P'z. Set the mask value at (u', v') in the target view based on the source mask value. 5. Reprojection Check: Continue the projection process as long as the projected mask sufficiently overlaps with the corresponding mask in the current view. If the overlap is insufficient, the propagation for that pixel or region may be halted or weighted down to maintain consistency. 6. Mask Integration: Integrate the wrapped segmentation mask with the segmented masks in the current view. This results in a multi-view consistent segmentation mask set. 7. Editing: Apply the editing operation (e.g., via text-to-image diffusion or other NeRF editing techniques) constrained by the integrated masks to modify only the target object. Parameters: Overlap Threshold: The threshold for "sufficient overlap" is not explicitly defined in the sources. Key View Density: "Nearly all views" are designated as key views, which leads to reduced efficiency compared to sparse key view selection. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Incorrect Depth: The model can manage incorrect depth estimation as long as the NeRF is built successfully, demonstrated on glossy surfaces and sparser views. Background Leakage: Without this method, edits often affect the background. A grid-based 3D editing method using a 3D mask grid trained on 2D masks from SAM. It introduces a 3D mask grid trained on the 2D masks from SAM to locate the target object accurately. Instead of utilizing SDS, it employs Variational Score Distillation (VSD) along with composited rendering and a coarse-to-fine editing strategy to improve editing quality. Efficiency: Designating nearly all views as key views leads to reduced efficiency. Robustness: The method demonstrates robustness to incorrect depth estimation, handling glossy surfaces and sparse input views (e.g., 20% or 50% of views) effectively. Consistency: It achieves multi-view consistent segmentation, permitting exclusive modification of the human figure or other objects without changing the background. Limitations: The reliance on SAM for initial segmentation and the dense key view selection may limit scalability to very large scenes or high-resolution inputs. Originated in ViCA-NeRF (View-Consistency-Aware 3D Editing of Neural Radiance Fields). The method addresses the discrepancy in existing methods that fail to isolate foreground edits from background changes. It builds on the Segment Anything Model (SAM) and leverages depth information for view consistency.
