name: NeRF-Art
head: Text-Driven Neural Radiance Fields Stylization
body: NeRF-Art is a text-guided method for stylizing pre-trained Neural Radiance Fields (NeRFs) that simultaneously alters both the appearance and the 3D geometry of a scene without requiring mesh guidance. It distinguishes itself from prior approaches by introducing a global-local contrastive learning strategy combined with directional constraints, addressing the insufficiency of direct CLIP similarity supervision in ensuring strong style adherence and cross-view consistency. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A pre-trained NeRF model f\theta: (\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{d}) \to (\sigma, \mathbf{c}), where \mathbf{x} is 3D position, \mathbf{d} is viewing direction, \sigma is volume density, and \mathbf{c} is color [Parent]. A target style text prompt T{\text{target}} and a set of negative style text prompts \{T{\text{neg}}^k\}. Output: Optimized NeRF parameters \theta' that render images matching the target style in both texture and geometry. Data Structures: The method operates on the standard NeRF MLP representation [Parent]. No additional explicit data structures (like grids or meshes) are introduced for the stylization process itself, though the method supports mesh extraction from the final \sigma field for evaluation. Optimization Objective: The optimization minimizes a total loss combining photometric reconstruction, a hybrid global-local contrastive style loss, and a weight regularization term. L = L{\text{rec}} + \lambda{\text{style}} L{\text{style}} + \lambda{\text{reg}} L{\text{reg}} where L{\text{rec}} is the standard photometric reconstruction loss on visible pixels, L{\text{style}} is the hybrid global-local contrastive loss based on CLIP embeddings, and L{\text{reg}} is a weight regularization term. Step-by-Step Method: 1. Ray Marching & Rendering: For each camera ray, sample points along the ray and compute transmittance and density using the current NeRF f\theta. Render the image using the standard volume rendering equation. 2. CLIP Embedding Extraction: Pass the rendered image and text prompts through the CLIP image encoder EI and text encoder ET. Extract the target embedding from the target style prompt, and negative embeddings from pre-defined negative style prompts. Extract the rendered embedding from the generated image. 3. Global-Local Contrastive Loss Calculation: The style loss is defined as a combination of global and local contrastive terms. The global contrastive loss measures similarity between the entire rendered image and the target text, while pushing away from negative texts. To ensure uniformity of style over local details, the contrastive constraint is extended to a local framework by dividing the image into patches. 4. Directional Constraint: A directional constraint is applied to control the trajectory and strength of the style, ensuring consistent application across views. 5. Geometry Stylization and Regularization: To support joint geometry and appearance stylization, constraints on the density field are relaxed. Cloudy artifacts and geometry noise arise easily when the density field is transformed during geometry stylization. A weight regularization term is applied to the NeRF weights to suppress these artifacts. 6. Optimization Loop: Update \theta using gradient descent to minimize the combined loss. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def nerfartstylization(nerfparams, targettext, negativetexts, refimages, cameras, steps, lr, lambdarec, lambdastyle, lambdareg, tau): """ Stylizes a pre-trained NeRF using text-driven contrastive learning. """ # Initialize optimizer optimizer = Optimizer(nerfparams, lr=lr) # Pre-compute CLIP text embeddings targetemb = encodetext(targettext) negembs = [encodetext(txt) for txt in negativetexts] for in range(steps): optimizer.zerograd() totalloss = 0.0 renderedimgs = [] for cam in cameras: rays = generaterays(cam) sigma, color = raymarch(nerfparams, rays) img = volumerender(sigma, color, rays.transmittance) renderedimgs.append(img) if refimages: totalloss += lambdarec sum((r - ref)2 for r, ref in zip(renderedimgs, refimages)) styleloss = 0.0 for img in renderedimgs: imgemb = encodeimage(img) simtarget = cosinesimilarity(imgemb, targetemb) simnegs = [cosinesimilarity(imgemb, neg) for neg in negembs] exptarget = exp(simtarget / tau) expnegs = sum(exp(s / tau) for s in simnegs) styleloss += -log(exptarget / (exptarget + expnegs)) # Local contrastive loss divides image into patches and computes similar contrastive terms # styleloss += computelocalcontrastive(renderedimgs, targetemb, negembs, tau) # Directional constraint controls style trajectory and strength across views # styleloss += computedirectionalloss(renderedimgs, targetemb, cameras) totalloss += lambdastyle styleloss totalloss += lambdareg sum(w2 for w in nerfparams) totalloss.backward() optimizer.step() return nerfparams Parameters: Negative Prompts: Pre-defined styles used as negative samples. Loss Weights (\lambda{\text{rec}}, \lambda{\text{style}}, \lambda{\text{reg}}): Balances reconstruction, style, and regularization. Temperature (\tau): Controls the sharpness of the contrastive loss. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Cloudy Artifacts: Transforming the density field for geometry stylization can easily introduce cloudy artifacts and geometry noise; handled by weight regularization. Insufficient Style Strength: Direct CLIP similarity supervision is insufficient to ensure desired style strength; addressed with contrastive loss. View Consistency: Without proper constraints, style may vary inconsistently across views; enforced via the global-local framework and directional constraints. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Simultaneous geometry and appearance stylization without mesh guidance; strong style adherence via contrastive learning; cross-view consistency. Limitations: Requires careful tuning of regularization to avoid artifacts; dependent on CLIP's style understanding; slower than non-differentiable stylization methods. When to use: When text-driven stylization of both geometry and appearance is needed without mesh data. When not to use: When real-time performance is critical or when mesh-based stylization is preferred. NeRF-Art was introduced by Can Wang, Ruixiang Jiang, Mingming He, Dongdong Chen, and Jing Liao. It addresses the challenge of text-guided NeRF stylization, which is difficult due to the need for simultaneous geometry and appearance transformation. The method builds on the use of large-scale Language-Vision models (CLIP) with NeRF. name: RePaint-NeRF Limitations
head: NeRF editing constraints
body: This article documents the empirical limitations of the RePaint-NeRF method, specifically regarding computational efficiency, geometric fidelity under significant shape changes, and view-angle consistency. It distinguishes these failure modes from the core optimization mechanics detailed in RePaint-NeRF. The method is both time and memory intensive. Generating a high-quality 3D model at the object level requires more than 30 minutes of optimization. Due to these resource demands, the method cannot scale to larger resolutions or larger scenes. Training struggles when the target object shape differs drastically from the source object. In such cases, the edit may be incomplete, failing to fully replace the original geometry. Restricted view angles cause geometric artifacts at image edges during optimization. Objects generated at the periphery may incorrectly combine features from multiple source objects, whereas central regions remain consistent. RePaint-NeRF was introduced in to enable NeRF editing via semantic masks and diffusion model guidance. The limitations described herein were identified during the evaluation of this framework, which uses gradient guidance from a pre-trained 2D diffusion model to regenerate masked parts of the scene. RePaint-NeRF: NeRF Editting via Semantic Masks and Diffusion Models, https://doi.org/10.24963/ijcai.2023/201, fetched 2026-10-26

name: Semantic and Language-Guided Editing
head: Semantic Inpainting, Feature Field Distillation, SDS-based Editing
body: Semantic and Language-Guided Editing modifies neural radiance fields using high-level semantic cues, such as text prompts, language instructions, or semantic masks, rather than relying solely on low-level geometric or photometric constraints. It solves the problem of localized 3D content manipulation—such as object deletion, appearance transformation, or semantic inpainting—while maintaining multi-view consistency and scene integrity. What sets this family apart from sibling methods like NeRF Editing and Inpainting Procedures is the explicit integration of external semantic priors (e.g., CLIP, LSeg, or diffusion models) into the optimization loop to guide the 3D structure and appearance, rather than merely filling in missing geometry or color. All methods in this family operate on a pre-trained NeRF representation f\theta: (\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{d}) \to (\sigma, \mathbf{c}), where \mathbf{x} is a 3D coordinate, \mathbf{d} is the viewing direction, \sigma is volume density, and \mathbf{c} is color [Parent]. The core mechanism involves an optimization loop that minimizes a loss function L to update the NeRF parameters \theta (or a subset thereof) [Parent]. The general optimization objective is: L = L{render} + \lambda{guidance} L{guidance} + \lambda{reg} L{reg} where L{render} is the standard photometric reconstruction loss on visible pixels, L{guidance} incorporates external priors (e.g., 2D inpainted images, diffusion model gradients, or semantic features), and L{reg} prevents artifacts or overfitting. Key shared components include: 1. Masking/Selection: A binary or probabilistic mask M or selection field identifies the region of interest (ROI) or occluded areas, typically user-defined via sketching or language instructions. 2. External Priors: Methods rely on 2D priors to guide 3D changes, commonly using diffusion guidance (e.g., Score Distillation Sampling from text-to-image models) or semantic/text features (e.g., CLIP or LSeg) to align rendered features with prompts. 3. View Consistency Enforcement: To prevent inconsistencies across views, methods enforce multi-view constraints through implicit geometrical and photometric priors embodied by the neural network, which automatically propagates single-view edits to all views. DFF enables 3D semantic segmentation and editable novel-view synthesis by distilling features from a pre-trained 2D teacher network (such as LSeg or DINO) into a neural radiance field [12068-dff-decomposing-nerf-for-editing-via-feature-field-distillat.md]. It solves the problem of decomposing scenes into semantic regions for editing, addressing challenges in surface decomposition, volume decomposition, and handling unobserved parts [12068-dff-decomposing-nerf-for-editing-via-feature-field-distillat.md]. Unlike naive usage of NeRF features which are entangled with low-level factors like color or spatial adjacency, DFF explicitly learns semantic similarity, allowing for multi-view consistent editing such as object deletion or appearance transformation [12068-dff-decomposing-nerf-for-editing-via-feature-field-distillat.md]. Choose this method when explicit semantic decomposition is required for editing, rather than just appearance transfer. Unverified code. def init(self, teachertype='LSeg', useindependentfeature=False): self.teachertype = teachertype self.useindependentfeature = useindependentfeature self.radiancemlp = RadianceMLP(hiddendim=256, interfaces like free-form sketching or language instructions. Given a user-supplied edit in a single reference view, the encoding of a neural field automatically propagates this edit to all views. This propagation promotes consistency between all views thanks to the implicit geometrical and photometric priors embodied by the neural network, preserving the structure of the whole scene. Described in reference [19]. A baseline approach using CLIP for semantic guidance. CLIP provides weak guidance for NeRF optimization; after several epochs, the masked region develops unreasonable textures instead of converging to the target prompt. This method serves as a cautionary example of why diffusion-based guidance (like SDS) is often preferred over simple feature similarity for complex editing tasks. GenN2N introduces a latent distill module to map edited images to edit code vectors. It constrains edit code vectors to a Gaussian distribution through a KL loss. It performs NeRF-to-NeRF translation based on edit codes. It optimizes the translated NeRF using reconstruction loss, adversarial loss, and contrastive loss. CustomNeRF is a method that can utilize images as editing prompts in addition to text prompts. It introduces a local-global iterative editing (LGIE) training scheme to preserve background integrity. It proposes a class-guided regularization to improve consistency across different views. Vox-E is a grid-based method for localized 3D object editing guided by text prompts. It leverages SDS loss for object editing. It introduces a volumetric regularization to preserve the original structure. It optimizes a 3D cross-attention grid based on 2D cross-attention maps. It derives a binary volumetric mask to merge the initial and edited volumetric fields. It enhances the preservation of unaffected areas. Language-Guided Gaussian Editing modifies 2D images with language input using a diffusion model in the masked region generated by a recent 2D segmentation model. It updates attributes of Gaussians again as in the previous NeRF editing work InstructNeRF2NeRF. The concept of semantic inpainting in neural fields was described in reference [19], highlighting the ability to propagate single-view edits to all views via implicit priors. Recent developments in neural rendering have accelerated with synergies to generative approaches such as DreamFusion, which distills 2D generative knowledge to 3D geometry without 3D supervision. Surveys on 3D editing based on NeRF and 3DGS detail the evolution from simple feature distillation (DFF) to complex diffusion-based guidance (SDS, VSD) and grid-based optimizations (Vox-E). name: DFF (Decomposing NeRF for Editing Via Feature Field Distillation)
head: Feature Field Distillation, LSeg-DFF, DINO-DFF
body: DFF enables 3D semantic segmentation and editable novel-view synthesis by distilling features from a pre-trained 2D teacher network (such as LSeg or DINO) into a neural radiance field. It solves the problem that standard NeRF feature spaces are entangled with low-level factors like color or spatial adjacency rather than semantic similarity, making naive decomposition unreliable. Unlike methods that rely on semantic labels during training, DFF achieves this through unsupervised distillation, allowing for zero-shot text-based or image-patch-based editing without retraining the underlying radiance field geometry. Inputs: A set of posed training images Ir with camera poses r. A pre-trained NeRF radiance field f\theta (or a newly trained one). A 2D teacher network (LSeg or DINO) and its associated query mechanism (text prompt for LSeg, image patch for DINO). Outputs: A decomposed NeRF representation consisting of a radiance field (density \sigma and color \mathbf{c}) and a feature field \mathbf{f}. Semantic segmentation probabilities for any 3D point or 2D pixel. Data Structures: The implementation uses two primary neural network architectures: 1. Radiance Field MLP (f\theta): Input: Positional encoded coordinate \mathbf{x} and viewing direction \mathbf{d}. Structure: 8 hidden ReLU layers with 256 dimensions. Outputs: Density \sigma: Linear layer (1 output). Color \mathbf{c}: 3 hidden layers (256 dims) \to Linear layer (3 outputs, RGB). Feature \mathbf{f}: 3 hidden layers (256 dims) \to Linear layer (output dim depends on teacher, e.g., 256 for DINO, 128 for LSeg). Note: In the "branch-based" variant, the feature branch shares the first 8 layers with the radiance field. In the "independent" variant, the feature field is a separate MLP. 2. Independent Feature Field MLP (Optional): Used to avoid retraining the radiance field. Structure: 4 hidden layers. Skip connection: Added at the 3rd layer if positional encoding is used. Input: Positional encoded coordinate \mathbf{x} (and optionally \mathbf{d}). Output: Feature vector \mathbf{f}. Positional Encoding: Input coordinate \mathbf{x}: Length 10. Viewing direction \mathbf{d}: Length 4. Skip connections: Applied to the input coordinate. Sampling Strategy: Coarse MLP: Stratified sampling with Nc = 64 points. Fine MLP: Importance sampling with Nf = 128 points (total 192 points including coarse). Distillation Note: Feature fields are trained using coarse sampling to ensure smoothness. Rendering for editing uses fine sampling. Training Phases: 1. Phase 1: Radiance Field Training (Standard NeRF) Train the radiance field f\theta for 200,000 iterations. Loss: Photometric loss Lp (e.g., L1 or SSIM between rendered and input images). Optimizer: Adam, linearly decaying learning rate from 5 \times 10^{-4} to 8 \times 10^{-5}. Regularization: Gaussian noise added to density. Batch size: 1024 rays (Replica) or 2048 rays (others). Image resolution: 320×240 (Replica) or 1008×756 (others). 2. Phase 2: Feature Field Distillation (Finetuning) Initialize feature branch (either attached to radiance field or independent). Remove Gaussian noise from density. Set learning rate to 1 \times 10^{-4}. Train for 5,000 iterations. Loss: L = Lp + \lambda Lf. Note: Feature loss converges significantly faster than photometric loss; thus, short training is sufficient. Excessively increasing \lambda (e.g., \times 10) degrades view synthesis without improving segmentation. Feature Distillation Loss (Lf): The feature loss minimizes the distance between the rendered feature \mathbf{f}{render} and the target teacher feature \mathbf{f}{img}. Lf = \sum{r} \sum{i \in \text{pixels}} \| \mathbf{f}{render}(r, i) - \mathbf{f}{img}(Ir, r, i) \|^2 Where: \mathbf{f}{img}(Ir, r, i) is the feature map from the teacher network for image Ir at pixel i. Teacher feature maps are resized to the original image size to match the NeRF pixel grid. \mathbf{f}{render} is obtained by volume rendering the feature field \mathbf{f} along the ray, similar to color rendering: \mathbf{f}{render} = \sum{j=1}^{N} Tj (1 - \alphaj) \mathbf{f}j where Tj is the accumulated transmittance and \alphaj is the opacity at sample j. Semantic Probability Calculation: To perform segmentation or editing, the probability p that a 3D point (or rendered pixel) belongs to a query is computed differently for LSeg and DINO. 1. LSeg (Text Query): Encode text label t using LSeg text encoder to get \mathbf{t}{vec}. Compute cosine similarity between rendered feature \mathbf{f}{render} and \mathbf{t}{vec}. Probability p is derived via softmax over all possible labels (Equation 22 in). 2. DINO (Image Patch Query): Select a query patch from an image. Compute patch feature \mathbf{q} by averaging DINO features of all pixels in the patch. Compute cosine similarity between \mathbf{f}{render} and \mathbf{q}. Hard Decomposition: If similarity > \tau (threshold), p=1; else p=0. Note: DINO does not use softmax with negative queries; it uses direct thresholded cosine similarity. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import torch import torch.nn as nn import torch.nn.functional as F import math def positionalencoding(x, numfrequencies): """Standard sine/cosine positional encoding.""" # x: [B, D], returns [B, D 2 numfrequencies] scales = torch.tensor([2 (i / numfrequencies) for i in range(numfrequencies)], device=x.device) x = x.unsqueeze(-1) scales.unsqueeze(0) x = torch.cat([torch.sin(x), torch.cos(x)], dim=-1) return x class RadianceMLP(nn.Module): """8 hidden layers (256 dims), ReLU. Outputs sigma, color, feature.""" def init(self, hiddendim=256): super().init() self.layers = nn.ModuleList([nn.Linear(hiddendim, hiddendim) for in range(8)]) self.sigmalayer = nn.Linear(hiddendim, 1) self.colorlayers = nn.ModuleList([nn.Linear(hiddendim, hiddendim) for in range(3)]) self.colorout = nn.Linear(hiddendim, 3) self.featurelayers = nn.ModuleList([nn.Linear(hiddendim, hiddendim) for in range(3)]) self.featureout = nn.Linear(hiddendim, 128) # Matches LSeg/DINO typical dims def forward(self, xpe, dpe): h = xpe for i, layer in enumerate(self.layers): h = F.relu(layer(h)) if i < 3: # Skip connections at first 3 layers h = torch.cat([h, xpe], dim=-1) sigma = self.sigmalayer(h) c = h for layer in self.colorlayers: c = F.relu(layer(c)) color = self.colorout(c) f = h for layer in self.featurelayers: f = F.relu(layer(f)) feature = self.featureout(f) return sigma, color, feature class IndependentFeatureMLP(nn.Module): """4 layers, skip connection at 3rd if PE used.""" def init(self, hiddendim=256): super().init() self.layers = nn.ModuleList([nn.Linear(hiddendim, hiddendim) for in range(4)]) def forward(self, xpe): h = xpe for i, layer in enumerate(self.layers): h = F.relu(layer(h)) if i == 2: # Skip at 3rd layer h = torch.cat([h, xpe], dim=-1) return h class DFF: def init(self, teachertype='LSeg', useindependentfeature=False, featuredim=128): self.teachertype = teachertype self.useindependentfeature = useindependentfeature self.radiancemlp = RadianceMLP() if useindependentfeature: self.featuremlp = IndependentFeatureMLP() self.teacher = self.loadteacher(teachertype) self.optimizer = None self.lr = 1e-4 self.lambdaf = 1.0 self.threshold = 0.5 # Default for DINO hard decomposition def loadteacher(self, name): # Placeholder for actual LSeg/DINO model loading. # Returns an object with.encodeimage(img),.encodetext(txt),.encodepatch(patch) return None def encodeinput(self, x, d): xpe = torch.cat([x, positionalencoding(x, 10)], dim=-1) dpe = positionalencoding(d, 4) return xpe, dpe def renderray(self, origins, directions, sigmacoarse, colorcoarse, featcoarse, sigmafine, colorfine, featfine, near=0.0, far=1.0): """Standard differentiable volume rendering.""" # Standard ray marching implementation # Compute deltas, alphas, transmittance, weights for coarse and fine # Return rendered color, feature, and accumulated transmittance # For brevity, assumes a standard differentiable renderer is integrated here. # The formula matches: frender = sum(Tj (1 - alphaj) fj) pass def getteacherfeatures(self, image): rawfeatures = self.teacher.encodeimage(image) targetfeatures = F.interpolate(rawfeatures, size=image.shape[2:], mode='bilinear', aligncorners=False) return targetfeatures def computeloss(self, renderedcolor, renderedfeature, targetcolor, targetfeature): lp = F.l1loss(renderedcolor, targetcolor) lf = F.mseloss(renderedfeature, targetfeature) return lp, lf def trainstep(self, images, poses, optimizer): optimizer.zerograd() # Sample rays from images/poses origins, directions, targetcolors = self.samplerays(images, poses, batchsize=1024) # Get teacher features aligned with rays teacherfeats = self.getteacherfeatures(images) targetfeats = self.interpolateteacherfeatures(teacherfeats, origins, directions) # Encode inputs xpe, dpe = self.encodeinput(origins, directions) # Coarse pass (used for feature training) sigmac, colorc, featc = self.radiancemlp(xpe, dpe) # Hierarchical sampling: use coarse weights to sample fine points # Then fine pass xpefine, dpefine = self.encodeinput(fineorigins, finedirections) sigmaf, colorf, featf = self.radiancemlp(xpefine, dpefine) # Render renderedcolor, renderedfeature = self.renderray( origins, directions, sigmac, colorc, featc, sigmaf, colorf, featf) lp, lf = self.computeloss(renderedcolor, renderedfeature, targetcolors, targetfeats) loss = lp + self.lambdaf lf loss.backward() optimizer.step() return loss.item() def editscene(self, querytype, queryvalue, renderfn): if querytype == 'text': queryvec = self.teacher.encodetext(queryvalue) probs = self.computelsegprobability(renderfn, queryvec) elif querytype == 'patch': queryvec = self.teacher.encodepatch(queryvalue) sims = self.computedinosimilarity(renderfn, queryvec) probs = (sims > self.threshold).float() return probs Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Feature Loss Weight: Excessively increasing the feature loss weight (\lambda \times 10) hurts view synthesis quality without improving segmentation. Sampling Mismatch: Using fine sampling for training feature fields introduces high-frequency artifacts. Coarse sampling is preferred for smooth decomposition. Naive NeRF Features: Using hidden layers of the original NeRF (e.g., the 8th layer) for decomposition is not robust; selections leak to regions with similar color/geometry but different semantics. Deletion Artifacts: Deleting foreground objects may leave floating artifacts and blurred volumes in the far distance behind the object. Training Duration: Feature loss converges much faster than photometric loss; 5K iterations is sufficient for distillation. Time Complexity: Distillation phase is short (5,000 iterations) compared to initial training (200,000 iterations). Memory Complexity: Branch-based DFF adds minimal overhead (3 extra layers). Independent DFF adds a separate small MLP (4 layers). Performance: DFF achieves 3D semantic segmentation performance comparable to or better than supervised sparse 3D convolution models (e.g., MinkowskiNet). Strengths: Enables zero-shot text-based and image-patch-based editing. Multi-view consistent results for deletion/extraction, unlike 2D inpainting baselines (LaMa). Independent feature field allows adding semantics to existing NeRFs without retraining geometry. Limitations: Struggles with "volume decomposition" smoothness if fine sampling is used for training features. Deletion can leave artifacts in occluded background regions. Original NeRF features are not semantically meaningful. DFF was introduced in the paper "Decomposing NeRF for Editing Via Feature Field Distillation". It addresses the limitations of editable NeRFs, which previously struggled with surface decomposition, volume decomposition, and estimating unobserved parts. The method leverages pre-trained 2D vision-language models (LSeg) and self-supervised models (DINO) as teachers to distill semantic information into the 3D field, bypassing the need for 3D semantic labels during training. Decomposing NeRF for Editing Via Feature Field Distillation, https://doi.org/10.52202/068431-1694, fetched 2026-10-26

name: InNeRF360
body: InNeRF360 is a 3D scene inpainting and editing method that reconstructs missing or edited regions in a Neural Radiance Field (NeRF) by combining multiview-consistent 2D priors with 3D diffusion guidance. It addresses the problem of generating geometrically and photometrically consistent content for occluded or removed objects by first establishing a coherent 2D inpainting across all views and then refining the 3D representation. It differs from direct 3D optimization methods by decoupling the generation of plausible content (via 2D inpainting) from the 3D reconstruction, using 3D diffusion priors primarily to eliminate artifacts and enforce consistency rather than generating the primary geometry. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: A pre-trained NeRF representation f\theta: (\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{d}) \to (\sigma, \mathbf{c}), a set of input images \{Ii\}, and binary masks \{Mi\} indicating regions to be inpainted or edited. Outputs: An updated NeRF parameter set \theta' representing the scene with inpainted content. Data Structures: Segmentation Mask: A binary mask M{2D} derived from 2D segmentation, refined for view consistency. Inpainted Image: A 2D image I{inpaint} generated by a 2D inpainting model. NeRF Parameters: \theta, typically including MLP weights for density \sigma and color \mathbf{c}. Steps: 1. Multiview Consistent Segmentation Initialization: Initialize segmentations for the target regions using the Segment Anything Model (SAM). Refine these segmentations using depth-warping to ensure they are consistent across multiple views, producing a set of view-consistent 2D masks \{Mi^{\text{consistent}}\}. 2. Multiview 2D Inpainting: Apply a 2D image inpainting model to each view i using the consistent masks \{Mi^{\text{consistent}}\} and the original images \{Ii\}. Generate inpainted images \{Ii^{\text{inpaint}}\} that fill the masked regions with plausible content. 3. NeRF Training from Inpainted Views: Train a new NeRF or fine-tune the existing one using the inpainted images \{Ii^{\text{inpaint}}\} as supervision. The optimization minimizes a photometric reconstruction loss on the inpainted regions to establish the initial geometry and appearance. 4. 3D Diffusion Prior Fine-tuning: Fine-tune the NeRF using 3D diffusion priors to eliminate artifacts and ensure 3D consistency. This involves computing gradients from a 3D diffusion model (typically via Score Distillation Sampling) to guide the NeRF parameters \theta towards distributions consistent with 3D generative priors. Formulas: The exact loss formulation is not given in the sources. The optimization follows the shared parent objective L = L{\text{render}} + \lambda{\text{guidance}} L{\text{guidance}} + \lambda{\text{reg}} L{\text{reg}}, where L{\text{render}} is the standard photometric reconstruction loss on visible pixels, L{\text{guidance}} incorporates the 3D diffusion priors, and L{\text{reg}} prevents artifacts or overfitting NeRF Editing and Inpainting Procedures. Parameters: \lambda{\text{guidance}}: Weight for the diffusion prior loss. Not given in the sources. Learning rate for NeRF optimization. Not given in the sources. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Inconsistency in 2D Inpainting: If the 2D inpainter generates inconsistent content across views, the initial NeRF training may produce geometric artifacts. Over-smoothing: Heavy reliance on diffusion priors may lead to over-smoothed or hallucinated details that deviate from the original scene's texture. Mask Accuracy: The quality of the final inpainting is heavily dependent on the accuracy of the initial SAM segmentation and the subsequent depth-warping refinement. ViCA-NeRF is a method for 3D editing that enhances efficiency and consistency by operating in the latent domain. It differs from standard NeRF editing by focusing on local editing via latent domain refinement rather than direct field optimization. It builds upon IN2N with improvements, initializing and refining a NeRF model within the latent domain using a refinement adapter with residual and self-attention mechanisms. It focuses on editing key views with IP2P, projecting them onto other views, and subsequently refining them with a blending model. It iteratively updates the training set with edited latents and employs a delta module for targeted editing guided by prompts. Time Complexity: The method involves multiple stages: SAM segmentation, depth-warping, 2D inpainting, NeRF training, and 3D diffusion fine-tuning, making the overall process computationally intensive. Memory Complexity: Requires storing the NeRF parameters, intermediate rendered images, and potentially latent representations if latent-domain optimizations are used. Strengths: Produces visually plausible and consistent inpainted content by leveraging strong 2D priors and refining with 3D consistency checks. Limitations: Computationally expensive. Relies on the quality of 2D inpainting, which may struggle with complex occlusions or lack of texture. The 3D diffusion prior may introduce artifacts if not tuned correctly. When to use: When high-quality inpainting of missing regions in a NeRF is required, and computational resources are available for multi-stage optimization. When not to use: For real-time applications or when strict geometric fidelity to the original scene (without generative hallucination) is critical. The method is described in a survey on 3D editing based on NeRF and 3DGS. It represents a trend in 3D editing that combines 2D generative models with 3D scene representations to achieve high-quality results. The pipeline builds on earlier works like IN2N and incorporates advancements in multiview consistency and diffusion priors. name: Diffusion-guided editing
body: Diffusion-guided editing methods modify pre-trained Neural Radiance Fields (NeRFs) using text prompts or image instructions by leveraging 2D text-to-image diffusion models as external priors. Unlike sibling methods that rely on semantic segmentation masks or geometric constraints for inpainting, this family uses diffusion gradients or iterative image synthesis to guide 3D changes. It is distinct from direct gradient-based guidance (like SDS) in variants that use iterative dataset updates, and from single-view guidance in variants that enforce multi-view consistency through iterative retraining [14365-repaint-nerf.md, 15089-instruct-nerf2nerf-optimization.md]. All methods in this family operate on a pre-trained NeRF representation f\theta: (\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{d}) \to (\sigma, \mathbf{c}), where \mathbf{x} is a 3D coordinate, \mathbf{d} is the viewing direction, \sigma is volume density, and \mathbf{c} is color [Parent]. The core mechanism involves an optimization loop that minimizes a loss function L to update the NeRF parameters \theta (or a subset thereof). The general optimization objective is: L = L{render} + \lambda{guidance} L{guidance} + \lambda{reg} L{reg} where L{render} is the standard photometric reconstruction loss on visible pixels, L{guidance} incorporates external priors (e.g., 2D inpainted images, diffusion model gradients, or semantic features), and L{reg} prevents artifacts or overfitting. Key shared components include: 1. Masking/Selection: A binary or probabilistic mask M or selection field identifies the region of interest (ROI) or occluded areas. This can be user-defined, derived from semantic segmentation (e.g., LSeg, CLIP), or computed via geometric conflict detection [S1, 14365-repaint-nerf.md, 8658-progressive-inpainting-and-erasing.md]. 2. External Priors: Most methods rely on 2D priors to guide 3D changes. Common priors include: 2D Inpainting: Using models like LaMa or Stable Diffusion to generate color/depth priors for occluded regions [S1, 12405-adaptive-view-selection-for-inpainting.md]. Diffusion Guidance: Using Score Distillation Sampling (SDS) from text-to-image models (e.g., Stable Diffusion) to guide appearance and geometry. Semantic/Text Features: Using CLIP or LSeg to align rendered features with text prompts or semantic labels. 3. View Consistency Enforcement: To prevent flickering or inconsistencies across views, methods enforce multi-view constraints. This is achieved through: Geometric Consistency: Using depth maps or epipolar constraints to ensure warped views align. Gradient-Based Selection: Adapting the reliance on 2D priors vs. multi-view geometry based on local texture gradients [S1, 12405-adaptive-view-selection-for-inpainting.md]. Reference Views: Using a single or multiple inpainted reference views to propagate consistent content [S1, 13952-reference-guided-controllable-inpainting-of-nerfs.md]. RePaint-NeRF is a framework for editing 3D content in Neural Radiance Fields (NeRF) using text prompts by leveraging a pre-trained diffusion model to guide changes in designated 3D content, ensuring view consistency and scene integrity. It operates by iteratively alternating between two phases: (1) editing the 'dataset' of NeRF input images using an image-conditioned diffusion model, and (2) updating the underlying 3D representation (NeRF) to incorporate the edited images through standard NeRF training. This iterative process allows for the gradual percolation of diffusion priors into the 3D scene, resolving inconsistencies that arise from applying 2D edits independently to each view. It builds on Diffusion-guided editing by using an iterative dataset update scheme rather than direct gradient-based guidance (like SDS) for the NeRF parameters. Instruct-NeRF2NeRF Optimization is a method for editing pre-trained Neural Radiance Fields (NeRFs) using natural language instructions. It solves the problem of modifying 3D scene appearance and geometry without retraining from scratch by leveraging a 2D text-to-image diffusion model as a guidance signal. Unlike sibling methods that may use semantic segmentation or geometric constraints for inpainting, this approach relies on InstructPix2Pix to generate edited views, which are then backpropagated to update the NeRF parameters. It is distinct in its use of classifier-free guidance weights to control edit strength and its lack of a single convergence point due to the stochastic nature of the diffusion model. MALD-NeRF employs a per-scene customization latent diffusion model to generate inpainted images, iteratively updating the training set. It incorporates a masked patch-based adversarial training strategy with adversarial loss and discriminator feature matching losses to refine results. The loss function includes a pixel-level regression loss for reconstruction. Diffusion-guided editing emerged as a solution to the limitations of single-view editing and the inconsistency of applying 2D edits to 3D scenes independently. Early methods relied on Score Distillation Sampling (SDS) for direct gradient guidance, but iterative dataset update schemes like RePaint-NeRF were introduced to better preserve view consistency and scene integrity [14365-repaint-nerf.md]. The field has increasingly focused on exploring inpainting techniques on 3DGS, benefiting from its outstanding rendering efficiency and high-quality scene reconstruction. A survey on 3D editing based on NeRF and 3DGS, https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s11704-025-41176-9, fetched 2026-10-28

name: RePaint-NeRF
head: Iterative DU, Iterative Dataset Update
body: RePaint-NeRF is a framework for editing 3D content in Neural Radiance Fields (NeRF) using text prompts by leveraging a pre-trained diffusion model to guide changes in designated 3D content, ensuring view consistency and scene integrity. It operates by iteratively alternating between two phases: (1) editing the 'dataset' of NeRF input images using an image-conditioned diffusion model, and (2) updating the underlying 3D representation (NeRF) to incorporate the edited images through standard NeRF training. This iterative process allows for the gradual percolation of diffusion priors into the 3D scene, resolving inconsistencies that arise from applying 2D edits independently to each view. It builds on Diffusion-guided editing by using an iterative dataset update scheme rather than direct gradient-based guidance (like SDS) for the NeRF parameters. RePaint-NeRF consists of two distinct stages: Semantic Mask Extraction and Text-to-3D Content Editing. The method takes a pre-captured NeRF scene, its source data (images, camera poses, calibration), and a natural-language instruction as input, and produces an edited NeRF and edited input images. Inputs: Pre-trained NeRF model f\theta (typically Instant-NGP or Nerfacto). Training dataset: Set of images I^0v, camera poses, and calibration parameters (typically from COLMAP). Text instruction cT (e.g., "turn him into Albert Einstein"). Optional: Background prompt c{BGT} (e.g., "leaves" if editing a rose). Outputs: Edited NeRF parameters \theta. Edited dataset images I^iv. NeRF Model: Instant-NGP [Müller et al., 2022] based on multi-resolution hash grid structure. Stores color C and density \sigma [Parent]. Semantic Feature Field: A view-independent feature field s: \mathbf{x} \to \mathbf{f}, where \mathbf{f} is a high-dimensional vector with semantic information. Feature Map: Rendered feature map FI of size H \times W \times 512. Depth Map: Size H \times W \times 1, normalized to range [0, 1]. Mask: Binary mask I{mask}^{H \times W \times 1}. Dataset: List of images I^0v cached separately to serve as conditioning signals. The goal is to extract a view-consistent semantic mask for the target object. 1. Feature Distillation: Distill supervised semantic features from a pre-trained CLIP model using LSeg [Li et al., 2022]. Interpolate all feature maps to size H \times W \times 512. 2. Depth Supervision: Predict rough depth from monocular images using MiDAS [Ranftl et al., 2022]. 3. Optimization: Optimize the feature network s and NeRF parameters to minimize: L{\text{first-stage}} = L{\text{color}} + \lambda{\text{feature}} L{\text{feature}} + \lambda{\text{depth}} L{\text{depth}} where L{\text{color}} is the standard photometric loss, L{\text{feature}} aligns rendered features with CLIP features, and L{\text{depth}} aligns rendered depth with MiDAS predictions: L{\text{depth}} = \sum{r \in R} (D(r) - \hat{D}(r))^2 where D(r) is the depth predicted by MiDAS and \hat{D}(r) is the depth predicted by NeRF. 4. Training Settings: Use Adam optimizer with learning rate 1e-2 and batch size 4096 for 2000 steps. 5. Mask Generation: Render the feature map FI. Compute the mask using a selected patch feature F{\text{patch}} (mean feature of the selected patch) and a similarity function Sim (e.g., cosine similarity) with threshold \alpha: I{mask}^{H \times W \times 1} = 1(Sim(F{\text{patch}}, FI) > \alpha) Patch features are preferred over text features for more accurate segmentation with higher thresholds. The goal is to modify the masked area to conform to the text prompt while preserving the unmasked area and filling "black holes" (previously occluded regions exposed by the edit). 1. Base NeRF Training: Train the NeRF on the original dataset to establish a base model. Use Adan optimizer with learning rate 1e-3 decaying to 1e-4 and batch size 1. Train for 3000 steps. 2. Iterative Update Loop: Alternate between image updates and NeRF updates for up to 10,000 steps (or 30k total iterations in some implementations). Image Update (Editing): For a viewpoint v, edit the current render I^iv using InstructPix2Pix. Inputs: Conditioning image cI = I^0v (original unedited image), text instruction cT, and noisy input zt. Noise: zt is a noised version of I^iv, defined as a linear combination of \mathcal{N}(0,1) and z0 = E(I^iv), following SDEdit. Noise Level: t is chosen randomly from [t{\min}, t{\max}] = [0.02, 0.98]. Sampling: Use DDIM sampling with a fixed number of steps s=20. Output: I^{i+1}v \leftarrow U\theta(I^iv, t; I^0v, cT). Update Dataset: Replace the original image with the edited one: Dataset[v] = I^{i+1}v. NeRF Update: Train the NeRF on a set of random rays sampled from the entire updated dataset (mix of old cached images and newly updated images). Loss: L{\text{render}} (L1 and LPIPS losses). Additional Losses for Masked Region: L{\text{repaint}} = \lambda{\text{unmask}} L{\text{unmask}} + \lambda{\text{clip}} L{\text{clip}} Unmasked Color Loss: Preserves the unmasked region to prevent unwanted diffusion changes: L{\text{unmask}} = \sum{r \in R} (C(r){\text{unmask}} - \hat{C}(r){\text{unmask}})^2 where C(r){\text{unmask}} = C(r) \times 1(I{mask} < 0.5) and \hat{C}(r){\text{unmask}} = \hat{C}(r) \times 1(I{mask} < 0.5). CLIP Loss: Guides the filling of "black holes" (exposed unseen parts) by encouraging similarity with the background prompt: L{\text{clip}} = -Sim(ZI, Z{BGT}) where ZI is the latent feature of the rendered image I and Z{BGT} is the latent feature of the background prompt encoded by CLIP. Training Settings: Adan optimizer, learning rate 1e-3 decaying to 1e-4, batch size 1. Train for 10,000 steps. Unverified code. name: Instruct-NeRF2NeRF Optimization
head: Instruct-NeRF2NeRF optimization process, NeRF Editing via Diffusion Guidance
body: Instruct-NeRF2NeRF is a method for editing pre-trained Neural Radiance Fields (NeRFs) using natural language instructions. It solves the problem of modifying 3D scene appearance and geometry without retraining from scratch by leveraging a 2D text-to-image diffusion model as a guidance signal. Unlike sibling methods that may use semantic segmentation or geometric constraints for inpainting, this approach relies on InstructPix2Pix to generate edited views, which are then backpropagated to update the NeRF parameters. It is distinct in its use of classifier-free guidance weights to control edit strength and its lack of a single convergence point due to the stochastic nature of the diffusion model. Inputs: 1. A pre-trained NeRF model f\theta: (\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{d}) \to (\sigma, \mathbf{c}), typically initialized using the 'nerfacto' model from NeRFStudio trained for 30,000 iterations. 2. A set of input images used for the initial NeRF training. 3. A natural language edit instruction (e.g., "turn the man into a bear"). 4. Classifier-free guidance weights for the diffusion model: sI (image guidance) and sT (text guidance). Outputs: 1. An edited NeRF model with updated parameters \theta that reflects the instruction. The method operates on the standard NeRF representation. No new complex data structures are introduced in the core loop, but the implementation relies on: NeRF Parameters \theta: Stored in the NeRFStudio optimizer state. These must be re-initialized before the editing loop begins. Diffusion Model State: The InstructPix2Pix model weights and the Stable Diffusion autoencoder state. 1. Initialization: Load the pre-trained NeRF. Re-initialize the optimizers in the NeRF training framework to ensure gradients are computed correctly for the editing phase. 2. View Selection: For each optimization iteration, select a single camera view (position \mathbf{x} and direction \mathbf{d}) from the training dataset or a random sampling distribution. 3. Rendering: Render the image \mathbf{I}{render} from the current NeRF f\theta at the selected view. 4. Diffusion Editing: Pass \mathbf{I}{render}, the edit instruction, and guidance weights sI, sT to the InstructPix2Pix model. Generate the edited image \mathbf{I}{edit}. This step uses the public implementation from the Diffusers library. 5. Loss Computation: Compute the photometric loss between the rendered image and the edited image: L{render} = \| \mathbf{I}{render} - \mathbf{I}{edit} \|^2 6. Backpropagation: Backpropagate the loss through the NeRF to update the parameters \theta. The gradient flows from the edited image back to the NeRF weights. 7. Iteration: Repeat steps 2–6 for a specified number of iterations. 8. Termination: Stop optimization at a subjective iteration count. There is no automatic convergence criterion. sI (Image Classifier-Free Guidance): Controls the influence of the input image on the edit. Typical range: 1.3 to 1.75. Specific examples: 1.5 (Tree, Tents, Person, Fig 1, Bear), 1.3-1.5 (Fig 7). sT (Text Classifier-Free Guidance): Controls the influence of the text instruction. Typical range: 6.5 to 12.5. Specific examples: 7.5-12.5 (Tree), 10.0 (Tents), 6.5-7.5 (Person, Fig 1, Bear), 6.5-8.5 (Fig 7). Training Iterations: Small scenes (<100 input images): 3,000 to 4,000 iterations. Large scenes (>200–300 input images): 7,000 to 8,000 iterations. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def instructnerf2nerfedit(nerfmodel, optimizer, inputimages, instruction, sI, sT, maxiterations): """ Edits a NeRF using InstructPix2Pix guidance. Args: nerfmodel: Pre-trained NeRF model ftheta. optimizer: NeRF optimizer (re-initialized before call). inputimages: List of original training images (used for view sampling). instruction: String edit instruction. sI: Image guidance weight. sT: Text guidance weight. maxiterations: Maximum number of optimization steps. Returns: nerfmodel: Edited NeRF model. """ # Re-initialize optimizers as per source optimizer.reset() # InstructPix2Pix model loaded from Diffusers library # model = loadinstructpix2pix() for step in range(maxiterations): # 1. Select a single view # In practice, sample a random index from inputimages idx = random.randint(0, len(inputimages) - 1) cameraparams = getcameraparamsforimage(idx, inputimages) # 2. Render current NeRF view # render() returns color tensor C and depth D Crender, Drender = nerfmodel.render(cameraparams) # 3. Edit the rendered image using InstructPix2Pix # Iedit = InstructPix2Pix(Irender, instruction, sI, sT) Iedit = callinstructpix2pix(Crender, instruction, sI, sT) # 4. Compute Loss # L = || Irender - Iedit ||^2 loss = torch.mean((Crender - Iedit) 2) # 5. Backpropagate optimizer.zerograd() loss.backward() optimizer.step() # Note: Termination is subjective based on iteration count if step % 100 == 0: print(f"Step {step}, Loss: {loss.item()}") return nerfmodel Lack of Convergence: The diffusion model produces temporally varying images. The edit type and strength change over training, so there is no single convergence point. The user must subjectively choose the termination iteration. Texture Blurriness: Using the Stable Diffusion autoencoder on input images causes gradual texture blurriness. The autoencoder creates locally similar but non-3D-consistent textures, leading to blurry renders in the final reconstruction. Double Faces: Single-view diffusion guidance can cause artifacts such as double faces on added objects. View Inconsistency: Edit instructions may only be relevant to certain camera views. For example, if the instruction is "turn the man into a bear," views not prominently featuring the man may produce less or no edit, leading to inconsistency. Spatial Manipulation Limits: The method inherits limitations from InstructPix2Pix, including inability to perform large spatial manipulations or binding between objects. Time: Each iteration requires one NeRF forward pass (rendering) and one diffusion model forward pass (InstructPix2Pix). The diffusion model is significantly more expensive than the NeRF rendering. Total time scales linearly with the number of iterations (3,000–8,000) and the complexity of the diffusion model. Memory: Requires memory for the NeRF parameters, the optimizer state, and the entire InstructPix2Pix/Stable Diffusion model in VRAM. Small Scenes (<100 images): Converges (subjectively) in 3,000–4,000 iterations. Large Scenes (>200-300 images): Converges (subjectively) in 7,000–8,000 iterations. Quality: Edited scenes often contain slightly blurrier textures compared to the original NeRF due to the autoencoder effects. Strengths: Allows editing via natural language without 3D annotations. Simple to implement using existing NeRFStudio and Diffusers libraries. Limitations: Cannot perform large spatial manipulations. Struggles with object binding. Single-view guidance leads to multi-view inconsistencies (e.g., double faces). Quality degrades over long optimization runs. When natural language editing is required. When the scene is relatively small or moderate in size. When the user can tolerate subjective termination and potential blurriness. When strict multi-view consistency is required without post-processing. When large spatial transformations (e.g., moving an object from one side of the room to another) are needed. When high-fidelity texture preservation is critical (due to autoencoder blurring). The method was introduced by Zhizhuo Zhou and Shubham Tulsiani in the paper "Instruct-NeRF2NeRF: Editing 3D Scenes with Instructions". It builds upon the InstructPix2Pix model and the general framework of differentiable rendering. The method leverages the Stable Diffusion autoencoder and InstructPix2Pix implementation from the Diffusers library. It was developed to address the limitations of previous NeRF editing methods that required complex 3D priors or manual segmentation. The authors noted that the diffusion guidance produces temporally varying images, distinguishing it from standard NeRF optimization which has a clear convergence point. It is used for 3D scene editing where users provide text instructions to modify the appearance or content of a NeRF reconstruction. name: Inpainting and Object Removal
head: NeRF Inpainting, 3D Scene Inpainting, Object Removal in NeRFs
body: This family of methods removes unwanted objects or fills occluded regions in a 3D scene represented by a pre-trained Neural Radiance Field (NeRF) [Parent]. Unlike standard NeRF training which reconstructs the entire scene from input views, these methods optimize the NeRF parameters to erase specific masked regions while maintaining geometric and photometric consistency across all unmasked views [Parent]. They are distinguished from sibling methods by their reliance on external 2D priors (such as inpainted images or diffusion models) to guide the 3D optimization, rather than relying solely on multi-view geometry or semantic segmentation alone [Parent]. All methods in this family operate on a pre-trained NeRF representation f\theta: (\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{d}) \to (\sigma, \mathbf{c}), where \mathbf{x} is a 3D coordinate, \mathbf{d} is the viewing direction, \sigma is volume density, and \mathbf{c} is color [Parent]. The core mechanism involves an optimization loop that minimizes a loss function L to update the NeRF parameters \theta (or a subset thereof). The general optimization objective is: L = L{render} + \lambda{guidance} L{guidance} + \lambda{reg} L{reg} where L{render} is the standard photometric reconstruction loss on visible pixels, L{guidance} incorporates external priors (e.g., 2D inpainted images, diffusion model gradients, or semantic features), and L{reg} prevents artifacts or overfitting. Key shared components include: 1. Masking/Selection: A binary or probabilistic mask M or selection field identifies the region of interest (ROI) or occluded areas. This can be user-defined, derived from semantic segmentation (e.g., LSeg, CLIP), or computed via geometric conflict detection. 2. External Priors: Most methods rely on 2D priors to guide 3D changes. Common priors include: 2D Inpainting: Using models like LaMa or Stable Diffusion to generate color/depth priors for occluded regions. Diffusion Guidance: Using Score Distillation Sampling (SDS) from text-to-image models (e.g., Stable Diffusion) to guide appearance and geometry. Semantic/Text Features: Using CLIP or LSeg to align rendered features with text prompts or semantic labels. 3. View Consistency Enforcement: To prevent flickering or inconsistencies across views, methods enforce multi-view constraints. This is achieved through: Geometric Consistency: Using depth maps or epipolar constraints to ensure warped views align. Gradient-Based Selection: Adapting the reliance on 2D priors vs. multi-view geometry based on local texture gradients. Reference Views: Using a single or multiple inpainted reference views to propagate consistent content. A framework that removes objects using a single user-drawn mask and 2D color/depth guidance. It jointly minimizes color and depth losses to ensure consistency, avoiding the artifacts of using multiple inconsistent 2D priors. Addresses inconsistency by adaptively switching between 2D inpainting priors and multi-view geometry based on local texture gradients. It is chosen when maintaining multi-view consistency is critical to prevent flickering in textured regions. Uses a single inpainted reference view to guide geometry and appearance via back-projection and a bilateral solver. It ensures view-dependent effects (VDEs) and avoids the quality deterioration seen in methods requiring multiple inpainted views. The problem of 3D scene inpainting emerged as NeRFs became popular for novel view synthesis, where removing objects or filling holes required more than just 2D image editing. Early approaches adapted 2D inpainting techniques to 3D by optimizing NeRF parameters. The field has evolved to include diffusion-based guidance and reference-guided consistency. NeRF-In: Neural Radiance Field Inpainting via Guided Depth Completion, https://arxiv.org/abs/2203.07112, 2022-03-14 Reference-Guided Controllable Inpainting of NeRFs, https://arxiv.org/abs/2303.13423, 2023-03-23

name: NeRF-In Inpainting Optimization
head: Free-Form NeRF Inpainting with RGB-D Priors, NeRF object removal
body: NeRF-In is a framework for removing unwanted objects or retouching undesired regions in a 3D scene represented by a pre-trained Neural Radiance Field (NeRF). It operates by optimizing the NeRF parameters \Theta using color and depth guidance derived from 2D images, without requiring category-specific training data or procedures. Unlike sibling methods that may rely on multiple inpainted views or semantic segmentation, NeRF-In primarily uses a single user-drawn mask on one view, transferred to other views via video object segmentation, and guides the optimization with inpainted color and completed depth priors. It sets itself apart by jointly minimizing color and depth losses to ensure both visual plausibility and geometric consistency across views. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A pre-trained NeRF model F\Theta: (\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{d}) \to (\sigma, \mathbf{c}), where \mathbf{x} is a 3D coordinate, \mathbf{d} is the viewing direction, \sigma is volume density, and \mathbf{c} is color. A user-chosen camera position ou and a free-form binary mask Mu drawn on the rendered view Iu = F{\Theta{image}}(ou), where Mu = 1 for pixels outside the masked region (background/valid) and Mu = 0 inside (object to remove). Output: Updated NeRF parameters \tilde{\Theta} that remove the unwanted object in the masked region across all rendered views. Data Structures: NeRF Model F\Theta: A multi-layer perceptron (MLP) taking position and direction as input, outputting density and color. The specific architecture (layers, dimensions) is not detailed in the sources, but it supports coarse and fine volume rendering. Camera Trajectory: A set of K camera positions O = \{os \mid s = 1 \dots K\} sampled along a pre-set trajectory (e.g., LLFF test-set trajectory). Masks: Transferred masks M = \{Ms \mid s = 1 \dots K\} for each sampled view, generated by transferring Mu. Guidance Materials: Guiding color images I^G = \{Is^G \mid s = 1 \dots K\}, where Iu^G is the inpainted user view and Is^G for s \neq u are inpainted sampled views. Guiding depth images D^G = \{Ds^G \mid s = 1 \dots K\}, generated via depth completion. Numbered Steps: 1. User Input: The user selects a view ou from the pre-trained NeRF and draws a mask Mu to specify the region to remove. 2. View Sampling: Sample K camera positions O = \{os \mid s = 1 \dots K\} along a pre-set trajectory. 3. Initial Rendering: Render RGB images Is and depth images Ds for all sampled camera positions os \in O using the current NeRF model F\Theta. 4. Mask Transfer: Transfer the user-drawn mask Mu to the sampled views to generate transferred masks M = \{Ms \mid s = 1 \dots K\} using a video object segmentation method (e.g., STCN). 5. Guidance Generation: Generate guiding color images Is^G for each sampled view using an image inpainting method \rho (e.g., MST inpainting network): Is^G = \rho(Is, Ms). Generate guiding depth images Ds^G using a depth completion method \tau (e.g., Fast Bilateral Solver): Ds^G = \tau(Ds, Ms, Is^G). 6. Optimization Setup: Define the set of all views O{all} and outside views O{out}. In the main framework, set O{all} = \{ou\} (the user-chosen view) and O{out} = O (all other sampled views). 7. Loss Computation: Compute the color-guiding loss L{color}(\Theta) and depth-guiding loss L{depth}(\Theta) (see Formulas below). 8. Parameter Update: Optimize the NeRF parameters \Theta to obtain updated parameters \tilde{\Theta} by minimizing the joint loss L{color}(\Theta) + L{depth}(\Theta) using the Adam optimizer for 50,000 steps. Formulas: Volume Rendering: The expected color \hat{C}(\mathbf{r}) of a camera ray \mathbf{r}(t) = \mathbf{o} + t\mathbf{d} is computed via numerical quadrature: \hat{C}(\mathbf{r}) = \sum{i=1}^{N} T(ti)(1 - \exp(-\sigma(ti)\deltai))c(ti) where T(ti) = \exp(-\sum{j=1}^{i-1} \sigma(tj)\deltaj), N is the number of quadrature points, \deltai = t{i+1} - ti, and c(ti), \sigma(ti) are the color and density at point ti produced by F\Theta. Depth Rendering: The rendered depth Df(\mathbf{o}s) is computed by accumulating density \sigma from ray batches during volume rendering. Similarly, Dc(\mathbf{o}s) is the coarse depth. Color-Guiding Loss: The total color-guiding loss is the sum of the all-view color loss and the outside-view color loss: L{color}(\Theta) = L{all}^{color}(\Theta) + L{out}^{color}(\Theta) where: L{all}^{color}(\Theta) = \sum{\mathbf{o} \in O{all}} \| F{\Theta{image}}(\mathbf{o}) - I{\mathbf{o}}^G \|2^2 L{out}^{color}(\Theta) = \sum{\mathbf{o} \in O{out}} \| (F{\Theta{image}}(\mathbf{o}) - I{\mathbf{o}}^G) \odot M{\mathbf{o}} \|2^2 Here, F{\Theta{image}}(\mathbf{o}) is the rendered image at camera position \mathbf{o}, I{\mathbf{o}}^G is the guiding image, and M{\mathbf{o}} is the transferred mask. Note: The source defines L{out}^{color} with the mask M{\mathbf{o}} applied to the difference, implying it measures error only in the masked region (object to remove) for outside views, while L{all}^{color} measures error on the entire user-chosen view. Depth-Guiding Loss: Measures the L2 distance between rendered fine/coarse depth images and guiding depth: L{depth}(\Theta) = \sum{\mathbf{o}s \in O} \left( \| Df(\mathbf{o}s) - D^G(\mathbf{o}s) \|2^2 + \| Dc(\mathbf{o}s) - D^G(\mathbf{o}s) \|2^2 \right) Total Loss: \tilde{\Theta}:= \arg \min{\Theta} L{color}(\Theta) + L{depth}(\Theta) Parameters: K: Number of sampled camera positions/views. Not given in the sources. Batch size: 4,096. Sample points in fine model: 128. Sample points in coarse model: 64. Optimizer: Adam. Optimization steps: 50,000 steps for inpainting. Hardware: Intel i7-7800X CPU and GTX-1080 GPU. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Masked MSE Only: Optimizing only with masked Mean Squared Error (MSE) on the transferred masks without explicit guidance causes the unwanted object to remain in the result. Depth Loss Only: Using only the depth-guiding loss (L{depth}) introduces color noise outside the masked region and loses color information in flat regions. Multiple Color Priors: Using multiple inpainted images as color guidance introduces visual inconsistency between views. The method restricts color guidance to the user-chosen view to maintain consistency. Guidance Artifacts: If the initial 2D inpainting or depth completion contains artifacts, the optimized NeRF may output undesired results. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import torch import torch.nn as nn import torch.optim as optim def nerfininpainting(FTheta, ou, Mu, K, trajectory, numsteps=50000, batchsize=4096): """ NeRF-In Inpainting Optimization Args: FTheta: Pre-trained NeRF model ou: User-chosen camera position Mu: User-drawn mask on view ou (1 for valid, 0 for masked) K: Number of sampled views trajectory: Function or list defining camera positions numsteps: Number of optimization steps batchsize: Batch size for ray sampling Returns: FTildeTheta: Updated NeRF parameters """ # 1. Sample K camera positions O = trajectory(K) # Returns list of K camera positions # 2. Render initial views Islist = [] Dslist = [] for os in O: # Render RGB and Depth using FTheta # Note: Depth is computed by accumulating density Is, Ds = renderview(FTheta, os) Islist.append(Is) Dslist.append(Ds) # 3. Transfer Mask Mlist = [] for i, os in enumerate(O): # Transfer Mu from ou to os using video object segmentation (STCN) # Requires previous frames for context, assuming STCN handles this Ms = transfermaskstcn(Mu, Islist[i], ou, os) Mlist.append(Ms) # 4. Generate Guidance Materials IGlist = [] DGlist = [] for i, os in enumerate(O): # Inpaint color IG = inpaintcolor(Islist[i], Mlist[i]) # rho function (e.g., MST) IGlist.append(IG) # Complete depth DG = completedepth(Dslist[i], Mlist[i], IG) # tau function (e.g., Fast Bilateral) DGlist.append(DG) # 5. Define View Sets Oall = [ou] Oout = O # All sampled views except ou # 6. Optimization Loop optimizer = optim.Adam(FTheta.parameters(), lr=0.0001) # Typical LR, not specified in source for step in range(numsteps): optimizer.zerograd() # Compute Color Loss # Lallcolor: On user-chosen view ou Iurendered = renderview(FTheta, ou)[0] IuG = IGlist[0] # Assuming ou is in O or handled separately; source says Oall={ou} # Note: Source implies IuG is generated from Iu and Mu Lallcolor = torch.mean((Iurendered - IuG) 2) # Loutcolor: On other views Oout, masked Loutcolor = 0.0 for i, os in enumerate(Oout): Isrendered = renderview(FTheta, os)[0] IsG = IGlist[i] Ms = Mlist[i] # Masked MSE diff = (Isrendered - IsG) Ms Loutcolor += torch.mean(diff 2) Lcolor = Lallcolor + Loutcolor # Compute Depth Loss Ldepth = 0.0 for i, os in enumerate(O): # Render fine and coarse depth Df, Dc = renderdepth(FTheta, os) DG = DGlist[i] # L2 distance for fine and coarse depth Ldepth += torch.mean((Df - DG) 2) + torch.mean((Dc - DG) 2) # Total Loss loss = Lcolor + Ldepth loss.backward() optimizer.step() return FTheta A method that removes objects by optimizing a NeRF using posed RGB-D images with 2D masks and 2D inpainted frames from LaMa. It employs confidence-based view selection to automatically exclude inconsistent views during optimization. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Training a new NeRF takes 18-20 hours for 200,000 steps; inpainting optimization takes about 5 hours for 50,000 steps. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Measured Performance: Evaluated on the LLFF dataset and a custom dataset with 24 camera positions per scene. Strengths: No category-specific training data or procedure required; generates visually plausible inpainted results with correct geometry and view consistency. Limitations: Relies on the quality of 2D inpainting and depth completion priors; artifacts in guidance materials can propagate to the 3D result. Using multiple inpainted images as color guidance can introduce visual inconsistency. When to Use: When removing unwanted objects from a pre-trained NeRF without access to category-specific training data or when a single user-drawn mask is sufficient to define the region of interest. When Not to Use: When high-quality 2D inpainting is not available or when the scene requires complex semantic understanding beyond geometric masking. NeRF-In was introduced by Hao-Kang Liu, I-Chao Shen, and Bing-Yu Chen in 2022. It is the first framework to enable free-form inpainting on NeRFs without category-specific training. It builds on the principles of differentiable volume rendering and 2D image inpainting techniques.
