name: Adaptive View Selection for Inpainting
head: 3D Inpainting Component, 3D Inpainting Component with Adaptive View Selection, Adaptive Weight Inpainting, Gradient-Based View Selection
body:
This method addresses the inconsistency artifacts inherent in applying 2D inpainting priors directly to 3D NeRF representations by introducing a training view selection mechanism based on regional average gradients. Unlike methods that uniformly blend 2D priors or rely solely on multi-view geometry, this approach adaptively switches between using 2D inpainted appearance priors and multi-view geometric consistency based on local texture richness. It is chosen when a pre-trained NeRF requires object removal or de-occlusion where maintaining multi-view consistency is critical to prevent flickering or geometric conflicts. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: A pre-trained NeRF model f	heta (typically a coarse and fine MLP pair, denoted \hat{C}c and \hat{C}f), a set of input views with known camera poses, a binary mask M identifying occluded/removed regions in the input views, and a 2D inpainter (e.g., LaMa). Outputs: Updated NeRF parameters 	heta that reconstruct the scene with the occluded region filled in consistently across all views. Data Structures: Mask \hat{P}(r): A predicted mask value for ray r, indicating the probability that the ray passes through the occluded region. This is derived from an object segmentation network constrained by depth information. Sub-regions: The occluded area in each view is divided into multiple sub-regions (patches) to evaluate local texture gradients individually. 2D Inpainting Prior Cl(r): The color value of the pixel corresponding to ray r in the image generated by the 2D inpainter for the occluded region. Numbered Steps: 1. Initial 2D Inpainting: Use a pretrained 2D image inpainter (e.g., LaMa) to generate appearance priors Cl for the occluded areas in the input views. 2. Mask Generation: Use an object segmentation network, constrained by depth information, to automatically infer binary masks M for occluded regions across all views. 3. Sub-region Division: Divide the occluded area in each view into multiple sub-regions (patches). 4. Gradient Evaluation: For each sub-region, calculate the average gradient of the rendered result (
abla \hat{g}) and the average gradient of the 2D inpainting result (
abla g). 5. Adaptive Weight Calculation: Determine the adaptive weight \lambda for the reconstruction loss based on the gradient comparison: \lambda =  egin{cases} 1 & 	ext{if } 
abla \hat{g} > 	au \cdot 
abla g \ 0 & 	ext{if } 
abla \hat{g} \le 	au \cdot 
abla g \end{cases} Here, 	au is a threshold parameter. If the rendered texture is richer than the 2D prior (scaled by 	au), the method trusts the multi-view geometry (\lambda=1); otherwise, it relies on the 2D prior (\lambda=0). 6. Loss Computation: Compute the total reconstruction loss L as a weighted sum of non-occluded loss L{NonOcc} and occluded loss L{Occ}: L = \lambda L{NonOcc} + (1 - \lambda) L{Occ} 7. Optimization: Update the NeRF parameters 	heta by minimizing L. Formulas: Reconstruction Loss for Non-Occluded Areas (L{NonOcc}): L{NonOcc} = \sum{r \in R} (1 - \hat{P}(r)) \left[ ||\hat{C}c(r) - C(r)||2^2 + ||\hat{C}f(r) - C(r)||2^2 ight] Where R is the set of rays, \hat{P}(r) is the mask value, \hat{C}c(r) and \hat{C}f(r) are the coarse and fine predicted colors, and C(r) is the ground truth color. Reconstruction Loss for Occluded Areas (L{Occ}): L{Occ} = \sum{r \in R} \hat{P}(r) \left[ ||\hat{C}c(r) - Cl(r)||2^2 + ||\hat{C}f(r) - Cl(r)||2^2 ight] Where Cl(r) is the color from the 2D inpainting prior. Depth Loss (for segmentation network training): L{depth} = \sum{r \in R} ||\hat{D}(r) - D(r)||2^2 Where \hat{D}(r) is the rendered depth and D(r) is the ground truth depth. Parameters: 	au: Threshold for gradient comparison. Not given in the sources. \lambda1, \lambda2, \lambda3: Weights for the segmentation network loss components (L{region-encoding}, L{rgb}, L{depth}). Not given in the sources. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def computeadaptiveinpaintingloss(nerfmodel, rays, masks2dinpainter, gtcolors, gtmasks, tau): """ Computes the adaptive reconstruction loss for NeRF inpainting. Args: nerfmodel: Pre-trained NeRF model with coarse (Cc) and fine (Cf) networks. rays: List of rays to render. masks2dinpainter: 2D inpainted images for occluded regions. gtcolors: Ground truth colors for input views. gtmasks: Binary masks for occluded regions (from segmentation network). tau: Threshold for gradient-based view selection. Returns: totalloss: The computed adaptive loss. """ # 1. Render NeRF predictions # Assume nerfmodel returns coarse and fine colors for each ray predcolorsc, predcolorsf = nerfmodel.render(rays) # 2. Get 2D inpainting priors for the corresponding pixels # Map rays to pixels in the 2D inpainted images priors = getpriorsfrom2dinpainter(rays, masks2dinpainter) # 3. Calculate gradients for adaptive weighting # Note: In practice, gradients are calculated over sub-regions (patches) # This pseudocode simplifies to per-ray or per-pixel for clarity, # but the source specifies sub-region average gradients. # Calculate average gradient of rendered result (approximated by gradient of predicted colors) # In a real implementation, this would be spatial gradient over a patch gradrendered = computeaveragegradient(predcolorsc, predcolorsf) # Calculate average gradient of 2D inpainting result gradprior = computeaveragegradient(priors) # 4. Determine adaptive weight lambda # If rendered gradient is significantly richer than prior, trust multi-view (lambda=1) # Otherwise, trust 2D prior (lambda=0) lambdaweight = 1.0 if gradrendered > tau gradprior else 0.0 # 5. Compute Non-Occluded Loss # Weight by (1 - mask) to exclude occluded areas nonoccludedloss = 0.0 for r in rays: maskval = gtmasks[r.pixelindex] if maskval == 0: # Non-occluded cc = predcolorsc[r] cf = predcolorsf[r] cgt = gtcolors[r] nonoccludedloss += (cc - cgt)2 + (cf - cgt)2 nonoccludedloss = nonoccludedloss / numnonoccludedrays # 6. Compute Occluded Loss # Weight by mask to focus on occluded areas, using 2D prior occludedloss = 0.0 for r in rays: maskval = gtmasks[r.pixelindex] if maskval == 1: # Occluded cc = predcolorsc[r] cf = predcolorsf[r] cprior = priors[r] occludedloss += (cc - cprior)2 + (cf - cprior)2 occludedloss = occludedloss / numoccludedrays # 7. Combine losses totalloss = lambdaweight nonoccludedloss + (1 - lambdaweight) occludedloss return totalloss Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Uniform Strategy Misjudgment: Applying a uniform strategy to the entire occluded area can lead to misjudgment. The method avoids this by dividing the occluded area into sub-regions and evaluating gradients individually. 2D Inpainter Inconsistency: Single 2D image inpainting does not consider consistency in the real 3D scene. The method addresses this by selecting training views based on texture richness to ensure multi-view consistency. Gradient Calculation: The gradient 
abla \hat{g} and 
abla g must be calculated as average gradients over sub-regions, not per-pixel, to accurately reflect texture richness. Time Complexity: Depends on the number of rays, the number of sub-regions, and the cost of the 2D inpainter. The adaptive weight calculation adds a gradient computation step per sub-region. Memory Complexity: Requires storing the NeRF model, the 2D inpainted images, and the mask predictions. Strengths: Effectively reduces the disturbing effect of 2D inpainters on 3D editing by leveraging multi-view correlation. It adapts to local texture richness, providing better detail recovery in complex areas. Limitations: Relies on the quality of the 2D inpainter and the accuracy of the segmentation mask. Performance depends on the availability of multi-view data; if no other views can provide supplementary information, it falls back to the 2D prior. When to use: When performing object removal or de-occlusion in NeRFs where multi-view consistency is crucial and the occluded region has varying texture complexity. When not to use: When the scene has very limited multi-view coverage or when the 2D inpainter produces highly inaccurate priors that cannot be corrected by gradient-based selection. The method was proposed in the paper "3D Scene De-occlusion in Neural Radiance Fields: A Framework for Obstacle Removal and Realistic Inpainting". It addresses the limitations of previous 3D inpainting methods that either ignored multi-view consistency or applied 2D priors uniformly. The work builds on the NeRF representation and uses LaMa as the 2D inpainter. It has been evaluated on datasets like LLFF and SPIn-NeRF. 3D Scene De-occlusion in Neural Radiance Fields: A Framework for Obstacle Removal and Realistic Inpainting, https://doi.org/10.1145/3664647.3681429, fetched 2026-11-01

name: Reference-guided Controllable Inpainting of NeRFs
head: Reference-guided Inpainting
body: Reference-guided Controllable Inpainting of NeRFs is a method for 3D scene inpainting that utilizes a single inpainted reference view to guide the geometry and appearance of a Neural Radiance Field (NeRF), ensuring view consistency and generating view-dependent effects. It solves the problem of view inconsistencies and lack of view-dependent effects (VDEs) in non-reference views by back-projecting the reference view using monocular depth estimation and employing a bilateral solver to propagate appearance. Unlike methods that require multi-view inpainted inputs or complex text prompts, this approach allows user control via a single 2D image, avoiding the visual quality deterioration often seen in methods that rely on multiple inconsistent inpainted views. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: n input images \{Ii\}{i=1}^n, camera transform matrices \{\Pii\}{i=1}^n, binary masks \{Mi\}{i=1}^n delineating unwanted regions, and a single inpainted reference view Ir where r \in \{1, \dots, N\}. Outputs: An optimized NeRF representation f\theta: (\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{d}) \to (\sigma, \mathbf{c}) that reconstructs the scene with the object removed and the reference content extended consistently. Data Structures: NeRF Representation: Standard MLP-based NeRF storing density \sigma and color \mathbf{c} for 3D coordinates \mathbf{x} and viewing directions \mathbf{d} [Parent]. Ray Set: Rays r are sampled from input views. Rays are classified into R{unmasked} (pixels where Mi=0) and R{masked} (pixels where Mi=1). Depth Map: A disparity map D(r) is computed from the monocular depth estimator applied to Ir, converted to inverse depth for supervision. Parameters: N{depth}: Number of iterations for initial unmasked supervision. N{bilateral}: Iteration interval for bilateral solver updates. N{do}: Iteration interval for disocclusion handling. \gamma{depth}, \gamma{rec}, \gamma{do}: Loss weights (values not given in the sources). Numbered Steps: 1. Initialization: Initialize NeRF parameters \theta. Compute the set of unmasked rays R{unmasked} corresponding to pixels in \{Ii(1 - Mi)\}{i=1}^n. 2. Stage 1: Unmasked Supervision: Optimize f\theta on R{unmasked} for N{depth} iterations using the standard reconstruction loss L{rec}^{unmasked}. The masked region remains under-fit to allow altering masked values in later stages. L{rec}^{unmasked} = \mathbb{E}{r \sim R{unmasked}} \| \hat{C}(r) - C{GT}(r) \|^2 where \hat{C}(r) is the rendered color and C{GT}(r) is the ground truth color. 3. Geometry Supervision via Monocular Depth: Use a monocular depth estimator to predict depth for the inpainted reference view Ir. Back-project Ir to 3D positions using the camera matrix \Pir and the estimated depth. Compute a disparity map. Align this with the current NeRF scene. Supervise the masked region's geometry using the depth loss L{depth}^{masked}. 4. View-Dependent Effects (VDEs) via Bilateral Solver: For non-reference views, use a view-substitution technique followed by bilaterally guided inpainting. The bilateral solver constructs VDEs in non-reference views from the reference viewpoint, ensuring that the inpainted region appears consistent from any view. Obtain target colors I{br,t} for non-reference views. Compute the reconstruction loss on masked pixels L{rec}^{masked} using these target colors. 5. Disocclusion Handling: Identify non-reference disoccluded regions (areas visible in other views but not covered by the single reference view). Use image inpainters to guide both geometry and appearance for these regions via loss L{do}. 6. Total Loss Optimization: The total loss is computed as: L = L{rec}^{unmasked} + \gamma{depth} L{depth}^{masked} + \gamma{rec} L{rec}^{masked} + \gamma{do} L{do} Losses L{depth}, L{rec}, and L{do} are computed every N{depth}, N{bilateral}, and N{do} iterations respectively. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def referenceguidedinpainting(images, cameras, masks, inpaintedrefview, depthestimator, bilateralsolver, imageinpainter, niterations): """ Performs reference-guided inpainting of a NeRF. Args: images: List of n input images {Ii} cameras: List of n camera matrices {Pi} masks: List of n binary masks {Mi} inpaintedrefview: Single inpainted reference image Ir depthestimator: Monocular depth estimation model bilateralsolver: Bilateral solver for view-dependent effects imageinpainter: 2D image inpainting model niterations: Total training iterations Returns: Optimized NeRF parameters theta """ # Initialize NeRF theta = initializenerf() # Precompute ray sets unmaskedrays = [] maskedrays = [] for i in range(len(images)): for ray in samplerays(images[i], cameras[i]): if masks[i][ray.pixel] == 0: unmaskedrays.append(ray) else: maskedrays.append(ray) # Stage 1: Unmasked Supervision for step in range(1, niterations + 1): # Compute unmasked reconstruction loss lossunmasked = computereconstructionloss(theta, unmaskedrays, images, cameras) # Gradient step for unmasked rays updatetheta(theta, lossunmasked) # Stage 2: Geometry and Appearance Guidance if step % Ndepth == 0: # Geometry Supervision # 1. Estimate depth for reference view refdepth = depthestimator(inpaintedrefview) # 2. Back-project to 3D and compute disparity refdisparity = computedisparity(refdepth, cameras[r]) # 3. Supervise masked geometry lossdepth = computedepthloss(theta, maskedrays, refdisparity) updatetheta(theta, lossdepth) if step % Nbilateral == 0: # View-Dependent Effects # 1. Use bilateral solver to get target colors for non-reference views targetcolors = bilateralsolver(inpaintedrefview, cameras, theta) # 2. Compute reconstruction loss on masked rays using target colors lossrecmasked = computereconstructionlosswithtargets(theta, maskedrays, targetcolors) updatetheta(theta, lossrecmasked) if step % Ndo == 0: # Disocclusion Handling # 1. Identify disoccluded regions in non-reference views disoccludedrays = identifydisocclusions(theta, cameras, masks) # 2. Guide geometry and appearance using image inpainter lossdo = computedisocclusionloss(theta, disoccludedrays, imageinpainter) updatetheta(theta, lossdo) return theta MVInpainter is a multi-view consistent inpainting model designed to bridge 2D and 3D scene editing. It employs domain adapters and motion modules as video priors to enhance cross-view consistency. It introduces a Reference Key&Value concatenation technique for appearance consistency while incorporating slot attention to aggregate optical flow features for controlling camera movement without explicit pose conditions. Time Complexity: The method requires iterative optimization of the NeRF. The complexity is dominated by the number of iterations N{depth}, N{bilateral}, N{do} and the cost of monocular depth estimation and bilateral solving per iteration. Memory Complexity: Requires storing the NeRF parameters, input images, masks, and intermediate depth maps. Strengths: Avoids view inconsistencies by relying on a single reference view; generates view-dependent effects; allows user control via a single image. Limitations: Relies on the quality of the single inpainted reference view; may struggle with complex geometry and textures in disoccluded regions. When to use: When a user wants to inpaint a NeRF with specific content provided as a single 2D image and requires view-consistent results. When not to use: When high-quality multi-view inpainted inputs are available and consistency is less critical than texture fidelity, or when the reference view is of poor quality. Reference-guided Controllable Inpainting of NeRFs was introduced in 2023. It addresses limitations in existing scene inpainting methods, such as inaccurate removal of large objects and lack of multi-view consistency. The method builds on the principles of differentiable volume rendering and NeRF optimization [Parent]. name: NeRFshop
head: Interactive Editing of Neural Radiance Fields
body: NeRFshop is an end-to-end method for the interactive editing of full Neural Radiance Field (NeRF) scenes, enabling users to select and deform objects via cage-based transformations. It distinguishes itself from other editing methods by operating directly on the trainable sparse occupancy grid of Instant-NGP using GPU-friendly two-level interpolation, allowing for real-time feedback without the need for retraining or offline optimization loops. Unlike methods that rely on diffusion priors or semantic segmentation masks for inpainting, NeRFshop focuses on geometric manipulation and deformation of existing scene content. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A pre-trained Instant-NGP NeRF representation (hashgrid), a user-defined cage mesh surrounding the target object, and user interactions (cage vertex displacements). Output: A modified NeRF representation where the selected object is deformed according to the cage, with artifacts reduced by volumetric membrane interpolation. Data Structures: The method builds on Instant-NGP, which uses a trainable sparse occupancy grid queried directly from CUDA kernels. The grid stores feature vectors for each active voxel. The cage is represented as a mesh with vertices vi \in \mathbb{R}^3. Steps: 1. Object Selection and Cage Building: The user selects an object using a scribble-based interface. The system then semi-automatically builds a bounding cage mesh around the selected region, inspired by Bounding Proxies. 2. Ray Marching with Remapping: During rendering, Instant-NGP alternates between traversal, inference, and ray compaction. To incorporate editing, intermediate kernel routines are introduced that remap samples according to user-defined edits before inference. This maintains memory coherency and minimal throughput across ray compactions. 3. Cage-Based Deformation: For each sample point x along a ray, the method computes its position relative to the cage. Compute generalized barycentric coordinates \{\lambda1,..., \lambdan\} with respect to the canonical (original) cage vertex positions \{v1,..., vn\} such that: x = \sum{i=1}^{n} \lambdai vi where \sum{i=1}^{n} \lambdai = 1 and \lambdai \ge 0. The method uses Mean Value Coordinates (MVC) for this computation due to their efficiency and simplicity. Let \hat{v}i be the displaced positions of the cage vertices (modified by the user). The new position \hat{x} is computed as: \hat{x} = \sum{i=1}^{n} \lambdai \hat{v}i. The sample at \hat{x} is then queried from the NeRF hashgrid to obtain density \sigma and color c. 4. Rendering: The rendered color \hat{C}(r) along a ray r is computed using standard volume rendering: \hat{C}(r) = \sum{i=1}^{N} Ti (1 - \exp(-\sigmai \deltai)) ci where Ti = \exp \left( -\sum{j=1}^{i-1} \sigmaj \deltaj \right), \sigmai is density, ci is color, and \deltai is the interval between samples. 5. Volumetric Membrane Interpolation (Artifact Reduction): To reduce color and density artifacts resulting from user edits, a preliminary membrane-based correction method is applied, inspired by Poisson Image Editing. This step smooths the transitions in the edited region. 6. Distillation: After interactive editing, a "distillation" step collapses all edits and saves the hashgrid NeRF representation for loading in established pipelines. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def renderraywithedit(rayorigin, raydirection, cageverticesoriginal, cageverticesdisplaced, hashgrid): """ Renders a single ray with cage-based deformation applied to samples. """ # 1. Compute barycentric coordinates for the ray origin relative to original cage # Note: In practice, this is done per sample inside the kernel. # We assume a function computemvc that returns lambda weights. samples = [] t = rayorigin stepsize = 0.01 # Simplified step size for illustration for i in range(100): # Fixed number of samples for simplicity # Get original position x x = t # Compute barycentric coordinates lambda for x w.r.t original cage vertices lambdas = computemeanvaluecoordinates(x, cageverticesoriginal) # Check if x is inside the cage (optional, depends on implementation) # If outside, no deformation is applied (lambdas might be zero or invalid) # Compute deformed position xhat xhat = sum(lambdas[k] cageverticesdisplaced[k] for k in range(len(cageverticesoriginal))) # Query NeRF at deformed position sigma, color = hashgrid.query(xhat) # Accumulate samples.append((sigma, color, stepsize)) # Advance ray t += raydirection stepsize # Render accumulated samples return volumerender(samples) def computemeanvaluecoordinates(point, cagevertices): """ Computes Mean Value Coordinates for a point relative to a polygon/polyhedron. Returns weights lambdai. """ n = len(cagevertices) lambdas = [0.0] n numeratorsum = 0.0 for i in range(n): vi = cagevertices[i] vnext = cagevertices[(i + 1) % n] vprev = cagevertices[(i - 1) % n] # Vector from vi to point di = point - vi # Vector from vi to next vertex dnext = vnext - vi # Vector from vi to prev vertex dprev = vprev - vi # Compute angles and distances # Note: This is a simplified representation. # Real MVC implementation requires careful handling of 2D/3D and angle calculations. # For 2D polygon: # alphai = angle(vprev - vi, vnext - vi) # betai = angle(vi - point, vnext - point) # gammai = angle(vi - point, vprev - point) # wi = tan(betai/2) + tan(gammai/2) # lambdai = wi |di|^2 / (|dnext|^2 + |dprev|^2) # Approximation # For 3D tetrahedron or general polyhedron, the formula is more complex. # The source states MVC is used for efficiency. pass # Normalize total = sum(lambdas) if total > 0: lambdas = [l / total for l in lambdas] return lambdas Parameters: MVC: Used for barycentric coordinate computation. Distillation: Applied after editing to save the final state. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Cage Construction: Automatic cage-building can result in complex meshes; the method uses adaptive cage mesh simplification. Artifacts: Deformations can cause color and density artifacts; mitigated by volumetric membrane interpolation. GPU Coherency: The method must maintain memory coherency across ray compactions in Instant-NGP. A technique where a bounding mesh (cage) is manipulated to deform the enclosed volume. It is chosen for its intuitive control and suitability for volumetric data. Link to Cage-Based Deformation The use of a trainable sparse occupancy grid queried via CUDA kernels. It is chosen for its speed and interactive performance. Link to Instant-NGP A post-processing step inspired by Poisson Image Editing to smooth artifacts. It is chosen when geometric edits introduce discontinuities. Link to Membrane Interpolation Time Complexity: Interactive, as it builds on Instant-NGP which is fully GPU-accelerated. Memory Complexity: Depends on the sparse occupancy grid of Instant-NGP. Strengths: Interactive free-form editing (deformation, translation/scale/rotation, duplication); GPU-friendly; no retraining required. Limitations: Limited to geometric manipulation of existing content; does not generate new content via priors (unlike diffusion-based methods). When to use: When interactive, real-time editing of existing NeRF geometry is required. When not to use: When inpainting missing regions or generating new content is required. NeRFshop was introduced by Clément Jambon, Bernhard Kerbl, Georgios Kopanas, Stavros Diolatzis, Thomas Leimkühler, and George Drettakis in 2023. It is the first complete method allowing interactive free-form editing of full NeRF scenes. The method builds on Instant-NGP [Müller et al. 2022] and uses Mean Value Coordinates [Hormann and Floater 2006] for deformation. name: NeRF Distillation
head: Distilling edit to NeRF, Edit consolidation, Hashgrid export
body: NeRF Distillation is a post-processing optimization procedure that collapses user-defined spatial edits into the canonical representation of a neural radiance field, specifically the Instant-NGP hashgrid format. Unlike iterative editing methods that maintain a separate deformation field or cage structure, this method re-trains the scene to bake the edits directly into the base hashgrid parameters. It is distinguished from sibling methods like Progressive Inpainting-and-Erasing by its focus on consolidating arbitrary geometric or appearance edits into a single, static, high-performance representation without retaining the edit history. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A pre-trained NeRF representation f\theta (typically Instant-NGP hashgrids), a set of user-defined edits \{Ei\}, each defined by a source region (cage) and a target transformation (deformation), and the original training images. Output: A single set of optimized NeRF parameters \theta' representing the edited scene in canonical space. Data Structures: Hashgrid: The standard Instant-NGP multi-resolution hash table storing feature vectors. Mapping Table: A list of unique mappings s \to s{i...j} tracked per ray. A mapping represents a transformation of a sample s from canonical space to a deformed space due to edit i, potentially followed by edit j. Ray List: The set of rays to be traced, including original rays and copies for handling mappings. Algorithm: 1. Mapping Identification: For each sample s generated along rays during the initial pass: Check if s lies within the source cage of any edit i. If yes, compute the transformed position si = Ti(s). This creates a mapping s \to si. Recursively check if si lies within the source cage of another edit j. If so, compute s{ij} = Tj(si), creating mapping s \to s{ij}. If s is not transformed, it retains the "default mapping" (identity). Store all unique mappings for each ray. 2. Ray Preparation: Identify rays with more than one unique mapping. For each such ray r, generate copies r' corresponding to each alternative mapping. For each mapping m \in \{s \to s{target}\}: If the mapping is valid (not broken), prepare to trace the ray with samples transformed according to m. Broken Mapping Check: A mapping is "broken" if the target sample s{target} lies inside the deformed cage of a later edit k (where "later" implies a temporal or sequential dependency in the edit list, or simply that applying k would overwrite i). If broken, skip this mapping. 3. Rendering and Loss Computation: For each ray r and its associated mappings: Trace the ray. For samples s along the ray: If s has a mapping s \to s{target}, query the NeRF at s{target} (in canonical space) to get density \sigma and color \mathbf{c}. If s has the default mapping, query the NeRF at s. Perform volume rendering to compute the pixel color C. Compute the photometric loss L{render} against the original input image. 4. Gradient Propagation and Update: Shared Samples: If a sample location (in canonical space) is shared by multiple rays or mappings (e.g., outside any cage), it only receives gradients from the first ray that references it. This prevents conflicting updates from different edit paths. Non-Copying Edits (Clearing): If an edit i is non-copying (i.e., it moves content rather than duplicating it), the source region must be cleared to prevent artifacts in the empty space left behind. Identify samples that end up in the undeformed canonical cage of edit i during their mapping process. These samples are part of "clearing rays." For these samples, the integration target is empty space (zero density). The loss encourages \sigma \to 0 and \mathbf{c} \to 0 (or background) at these locations. 5. Optimization Loop: Minimize the total loss L = L{render} + L{clear} using gradient descent to update \theta. Repeat until convergence. Pseudocode: Unverified code. Step 1: Identify mappings for all samples in a representative set of rays # In practice, this is done dynamically or pre-computed for the training set raymappings = {} # rayid -> list of (mappingtype, targetsamplecoords) for rayid, ray in enumerate(trainingrays): samples = ray.cast(nerfmodel) # Initial samples in canonical space mappings = [] for s in samples: currents = s mappingchain = [] # Check for recursive mappings for edit in edits: if edit.sourcecage.contains(currents): transformeds = edit.transform(currents) mappingchain.append((edit.id, transformeds)) currents = transformeds else: break if mappingchain: mappings.append((s, mappingchain)) else: mappings.append((s, [])) # Default mapping raymappings[rayid] = mappings # Step 2 & 3: Optimization Loop for epoch in range(numepochs): totalloss = 0 for img, campose in trainingimages: ray = Ray(campose, img.pixelcoords) mappings = raymappings[ray.id] renderedcolor = 0.0 alpha = 0.0 # Query NeRF sigma, color = nerfmodel.query(querypoint) # Volume rendering step (simplified) # In reality, this is integrated over the ray segment weight = sigma exp(-sigma distance) renderedcolor += weight color alpha += weight # Handle non-copying edit clearing if not iscopyingedit(mappingchain[-1].editid): # If this sample is part of a clearing ray for a non-copying edit # The target is empty space clearloss = sigma2 + (color - backgroundcolor)2 totalloss += clearloss # Gradient sharing: Only process gradients for the first ray referencing this canonical point # This is handled by the optimizer's gradient accumulation logic # or by masking gradients for shared points # Photometric loss photometricloss = (renderedcolor - img.pixelvalue)2 totalloss += photometricloss optimizer.zerograd() totalloss.backward() optimizer.step() Parameters: Learning Rate: Standard Adam optimizer settings for Instant-NGP. Number of Epochs: Sufficient for convergence of the hashgrid features. Edit Order: The order of edits matters for determining "broken" mappings. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Broken Mappings: If a sample is transformed by edit i into a region that is then transformed by edit j, and j's deformation overwrites i's result, the mapping is broken. The implementation skips these mappings. Non-Copying Edits: Failure to clear the source region of a non-copying edit results in random density or color artifacts in the empty space. Gradient Conflicts: Shared sample locations outside cages must only receive gradients from one ray to prevent conflicting updates. Time Complexity: Requires re-training the entire scene, which is comparable to initial training time but typically faster due to warm-starting from a pre-trained model. Memory Complexity: No additional memory overhead for deformation fields or cages; the final representation is a standard Instant-NGP hashgrid. Strengths: Produces a compact, high-performance representation suitable for real-time rendering; consolidates all edits into a single static model. Limitations: Cannot easily undo edits; requires re-training for any change; broken mappings may lead to loss of content in complex edit sequences. When to Use: When a final, optimized, and compact NeRF representation is needed after multiple edits. When Not to Use: When interactive editing or easy undo/redo is required. NeRF Distillation was introduced in the context of the NeRFshop pipeline, which aims to provide a comprehensive toolkit for NeRF editing and manipulation. The method builds on the foundations of converting between NeRF representations, specifically targeting the Instant-NGP hashgrid format for its efficiency. It addresses the need for a clean, consolidated representation after complex editing operations, avoiding the accumulation of deformation fields. name: FlipNeRF Training Pipeline
head: FlipNeRF Ablation Sequence
body: FlipNeRF is a training procedure for few-shot novel view synthesis that enhances the standard mip-NeRF representation by introducing flipped reflection rays and consistency-based regularization. It solves the problem of overfitting and unreliable depth estimation in sparse-view settings by enforcing geometric and feature consistency between original viewing rays and their hypothetical flipped counterparts. Unlike standard NeRF training which relies solely on photometric loss from observed views, FlipNeRF distinguishes itself by leveraging reflection symmetry priors and bottleneck feature consistency to regularize the radiance field, achieving higher reliability and lower negative log-likelihood (NLL) than mixture-model baselines like MixNeRF. The method builds on the NeRF Training Loop and Scene Representation and Architecture (specifically mip-NeRF). It extends the standard ray marching process by generating auxiliary "flipped" rays and applying specific loss functions to enforce consistency. Inputs: A set of N sparse input images with known camera poses. The scene is represented by a neural radiance field (MLP) parameterized by \theta, taking position \mathbf{x} and viewing direction \mathbf{d} as input. Outputs: Optimized network parameters \theta that minimize the combined loss, producing novel view renderings with reduced artifacts and accurate depth. The implementation relies on standard NeRF data structures: Ray Buffer: Stores tuples (\mathbf{o}, \mathbf{d}, t{near}, t{far}) for each sampled ray. Flipped Ray Buffer: Stores corresponding flipped rays (\mathbf{o}', \mathbf{d}', t{near}, t{far}). The flipped ray \mathbf{r}' is generated by reflecting the viewing direction \mathbf{d} across the surface normal estimated at the intersection point, or by a predefined reflection symmetry operation relative to the scene geometry. Bottleneck Features: Intermediate feature vectors extracted from the MLP before the final color/density prediction layer. These are used for consistency constraints. 1. Baseline Initialization: Initialize the mip-NeRF representation. 2. Ray Generation: For each training batch, sample standard rays \mathbf{r} from the input views. Simultaneously, generate flipped reflection rays \mathbf{r}' corresponding to \mathbf{r}. 3. Uncertainty-Aware Regularization (LUE): Apply the Uncertainty-aware Loss (LUE) to both the original rays \mathbf{r} and the flipped rays \mathbf{r}'. This loss models the ray's output as a mixture of distributions or uses an uncertainty term to prevent overconfident predictions in unobserved regions, improving reliability compared to naive empirical losses. 4. Bottleneck Feature Consistency (LBFC): Apply the Bottleneck Feature Consistency Loss (LBFC) using the Jensen-Shannon Divergence (JSD) on the bottleneck features of the original and flipped rays. This encourages the network to produce similar internal representations for geometrically symmetric viewpoints. 5. Feature Consistency Enforcement: Enforce consistency between the bottleneck features of the original ray pair \mathbf{r} and the flipped ray pair \mathbf{r}'. This step ensures that the learned features respect the reflection symmetry prior. 6. Normal Refinement (LOri): Integrate the Orientation Loss (L{Ori}) from Ref-NeRF to refine normal estimation. Accurate normals are crucial for generating meaningful flipped rays. 7. Optimization: Update network parameters \theta using an optimizer (e.g., Adam) to minimize the total loss, which is the sum of photometric loss, LUE, LBFC, and L{Ori}. Total Loss: \mathcal{L}{total} = \mathcal{L}{color} + \lambda{UE} \mathcal{L}{UE} + \lambda{LBFC} \mathcal{L}{LBFC} + \lambda{Ori} \mathcal{L}{Ori} Where \mathcal{L}{color} is the standard photometric reconstruction loss. Uncertainty-Aware Loss (LUE): The sources indicate LUE improves upon naive empirical loss (L{Emp}) by modeling uncertainty, resulting in lower NLL. While the exact formula for LUE is not explicitly provided in the notes, it is described as an uncertainty-aware regularization term applied to both \mathbf{r} and \mathbf{r}'. Bottleneck Feature Consistency (LBFC): Uses Jensen-Shannon Divergence (JSD) between the bottleneck feature distributions of original and flipped rays. \mathcal{L}{LBFC} = JSD(P{feat}(\mathbf{r}) || P{feat}(\mathbf{r}')) Orientation Loss (L{Ori}): From Ref-NeRF, used to supervise the predicted surface normals. Loss Weights: The specific weights \lambda{UE}, \lambda{LBFC}, \lambda{Ori} are not given in the sources. Performance Metrics (Full Model): On the Realistic Synthetic 360° dataset, the full model achieves PSNR 19.55, SSIM 0.767, LPIPS 0.180, Average Error 0.101, and NLL 2.56. Naive Empirical Loss: Applying naive empirical loss (L{Emp}) without the uncertainty-aware component (LUE) leads to inferior results compared to MixNeRF. Reduced Feature Dimension: Reducing the feature dimension of the bottleneck (bd\hat{}) reduces the capacity of feature representations and prevents the model from improving robustness. Degenerate Results: Using only flipped reflection rays without the consistency losses (LUE, LBFC) leads to overall performance degradation compared to the baseline. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def trainflipnerf(inputimages, cameraposes, numiterations): """ Training loop for FlipNeRF. Builds on mip-NeRF representation. """ # Initialize mip-NeRF model parameters theta model = initializemipnerf() optimizer = Adam(model.parameters(), lr=5e-4) # Typical LR, not explicitly given for FlipNeRF but standard for iteration in range(numiterations): # 1. Sample rays from input views raysr = samplerays(inputimages, cameraposes) # 2. Generate flipped reflection rays r' # Requires normal estimation or reflection symmetry assumption raysrprime = generateflippedrays(raysr, model) # 3. Forward pass for original rays colorsr, densitiesr, featuresr = model.forward(raysr) # 4. Forward pass for flipped rays colorsrprime, densitiesrprime, featuresrprime = model.forward(raysrprime) # 5. Compute Photometric Loss (Lcolor) # Compare rendered colors with ground truth images losscolor = computephotometricloss(colorsr, groundtruthcolors) # 6. Compute Uncertainty-Aware Loss (LUE) # Applied to both r and r' lossue = computeuncertaintyloss(colorsr, densitiesr) + \ computeuncertaintyloss(colorsrprime, densitiesrprime) # 7. Compute Bottleneck Feature Consistency Loss (LLBFC) # Using Jensen-Shannon Divergence on bottleneck features losslbfc = computejsddivergence(featuresr, featuresrprime) # 8. Compute Orientation Loss (LOri) # From Ref-NeRF, refines normal estimation lossori = computeorientationloss(model, raysr) # 9. Total Loss # Weights are not specified in sources totalloss = losscolor + lossue + losslbfc + lossori # 10. Backpropagation optimizer.zerograd() totalloss.backward() optimizer.step() return model FrugalNeRF is a few-shot NeRF framework designed to synthesize novel views from extremely sparse inputs (e.g., 2 views) without relying on learned external priors. It solves the problems of overfitting and long training times inherent in extreme few-shot scenarios by leveraging weight-sharing voxels across multiple scales and a cross-scale geometric adaptation scheme. Unlike methods that require complex scheduling or pre-trained models, FrugalNeRF uses reprojection errors to select pseudo-ground truth depth, enabling fast convergence and robust regularization. ESNeRF is a sparse neural rendering method designed to address the ill-posed nature of novel view synthesis in extremely sparse-view settings. It builds on the FreeNeRF backbone but introduces a hybrid loss function incorporating pixel-based, depth-based, and regularization losses to mitigate overfitting and reduce artifacts such as solid floaters. Unlike standard NeRF training, ESNeRF leverages depth maps generated by a pretrained DPT model for supervision and employs frequency regularization to stabilize high-frequency signal learning. Time and Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Measured Performance: On the Realistic Synthetic 360° dataset, the full FlipNeRF model achieves PSNR 19.55, SSIM 0.767, LPIPS 0.180, Average Error 0.101, and NLL 2.56. Scaling: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Reduces artifacts and improves depth map accuracy compared to MixNeRF. Provides more reliable outputs with lower NLL than mixture-model baselines. Limitations: Performance degrades if naive empirical loss is used instead of LUE. Reduced bottleneck feature dimension harms robustness. When to use: Few-shot novel view synthesis where reliability and accurate depth estimation are critical. When not to use: When computational resources are extremely limited and the overhead of generating flipped rays and computing JSD is prohibitive, or when the scene lacks reflection symmetry priors. FlipNeRF was introduced in the paper "FlipNeRF: Flipped Reflection Rays for Few-shot Novel View Synthesis". It addresses the challenges of few-shot NeRF training by incorporating reflection symmetry priors through flipped rays and consistency-based regularization. The method builds upon the mip-NeRF representation and integrates concepts from Ref-NeRF for normal estimation. name: FrugalNeRF
head: FrugalNeRF
body: FrugalNeRF is a few-shot NeRF framework designed to synthesize novel views from extremely sparse inputs (e.g., 2 views) without relying on learned external priors. It solves the problems of overfitting and long training times inherent in extreme few-shot scenarios by leveraging weight-sharing voxels across multiple scales and a cross-scale geometric adaptation scheme. Unlike methods that require complex scheduling or pre-trained models, FrugalNeRF uses reprojection errors to select pseudo-ground truth depth, enabling fast convergence and robust regularization. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: A small set of training views (typically 2) with known camera parameters, and optionally COLMAP-generated sparse point clouds. Outputs: A neural radiance field represented by multi-scale voxels, capable of rendering novel views. Data Structures: The scene is represented by a pair of voxels: density (VD) and appearance (VA). Base Voxel: A single high-resolution voxel grid serves as the base. Multi-scale Voxels: L+1 scales are constructed by hierarchical subsampling of the base voxel with a downsample ratio s=4. L=2 is the typical setting, resulting in 3 total scales (LL, L, H). Lower resolutions capture global geometry; higher resolutions capture fine details. Weights are shared across scales, meaning the higher-resolution voxels are subsampled versions of the base, ensuring consistent scene representation without increasing model size. Voxel Resolution: 640^3 for LLFF and RealEstate10K datasets. 300^3 for DTU dataset. Numbered Steps: 1. Ray Sampling: Sample rays from training views (r{train}). Sample rays from randomly generated novel views (r{novel}) along a spiral trajectory around the training views. Batch size: 4,096 rays for both training and novel view rays. Number of novel poses: 120. 2. Multi-scale Volume Rendering: For each ray r, compute rendered RGB color \hat{C}l(r) and depth \hat{D}l(r) at each scale l \in \{0, \dots, L\} using the corresponding subsampled voxels V{D,l} and V{A,l}. 3. Cross-Scale Geometric Adaptation (Training Views): For each pixel pi in a training view i: Compute depth \hat{D}l(pi) at each scale l. Lift pi to 3D point x^li using intrinsic Ki and depth \hat{D}l(pi). Transform x^li to world coordinates, then to the nearest training view j to find projected coordinate p{l \to j}. Calculate reprojection error el(pi): el(pi) = Ci(pi) - Cj(p{l \to j}) where Ci, Cj are input RGB images. Identify optimal scale l': l'(r{train}) = \arg \minl el(r{train}) Set pseudo-ground truth depth: D'(r{train}) = \hat{D}{l'}(r{train}) Pitfall/Guard: If the reprojection error exceeds a threshold of 0.5, the pixel is excluded from loss computation to ensure robustness. 4. Cross-Scale Geometric Adaptation (Novel Views): For each ray r{novel} from a novel view n at pixel pn: Compute rendered color \hat{C}n(pn). Warp to nearest training view j to find p{l \to j}. Calculate reprojection error using rendered color instead of input RGB: el(pn) = \hat{C}n(pn) - Cj(p{l \to j}) Identify optimal scale l': l'(r{novel}) = \arg \minl el(r{novel}) Set pseudo-ground truth depth: D'(r{novel}) = \hat{D}{l'}(r{novel}) 5. Loss Computation: Multi-scale Color Loss (L{ms-color}): MSE between rendered RGB and input RGB for training rays at all scales: L{ms-color} = \sum{l=0}^{L} \sum{r{train} \in R{train}} \| \hat{C}l(r{train}) - C(r{train}) \|2^2 Geometric Adaptation Loss (L{geo}): MSE between rendered depth and pseudo-ground truth depth for both training and novel rays: L{geo}(r{train}) = \sum{l=0}^{L} \| \hat{D}l(r{train}) - D'(r{train}) \|2^2 L{geo}(r{novel}) = \sum{l=0}^{L} \| \hat{D}l(r{novel}) - D'(r{novel}) \|2^2 L{geo} = L{geo}(r{train}) + L{geo}(r{novel}) Global Regularization Loss (L{reg}): Includes total variation, patch-wise depth smoothness, L1 sparsity, and distortion losses to suppress floaters and background collapse. Sparse Depth Loss (L{sd}): Uses COLMAP-generated sparse point cloud for absolute scale constraints. Dense Depth Loss (Ld): (Optional) Uses Dense Prediction Transformer (DPT) to generate depth maps from training views. 6. Total Loss: L = L{ms-color} + \lambda{geo} L{geo} + \lambda{reg} L{reg} + \lambda{sd} L{sd} + \lambda{d} L{d} 7. Optimization: Use Adam optimizer. Initial learning rate: 0.08, decaying to 0.002. Iterations: 5,000 per scene. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import torch import torch.nn.functional as F def frugalnerftrainingloop(trainingviews, novelviewcount=120, iterations=5000, voxelres=640, L=2, downsampleratio=4, lambdageo=0.01, lambdasd=0.5, lambdad=0.01, reprojectionthreshold=0.5): """ FrugalNeRF Training Loop. Args: trainingviews: List of training view data (RGB images, camera intrinsics/extrinsics). novelviewcount: Number of novel views to sample. iterations: Number of training iterations. voxelres: Base voxel resolution. L: Number of scales minus 1 (e.g., L=2 means 3 scales). downsampleratio: Ratio for subsampling voxels. lambdageo: Weight for geometric adaptation loss. lambdasd: Weight for sparse depth loss. lambdad: Weight for dense depth loss. reprojectionthreshold: Threshold for excluding unreliable reprojection errors. Returns: Trained voxel models (VD, VA). """ # 1. Initialize Multi-scale Voxels # Base voxels for density and appearance VD = torch.nn.Parameter(torch.randn(voxelres, voxelres, voxelres, 1)) VA = torch.nn.Parameter(torch.randn(voxelres, voxelres, voxelres, 3)) # Create L+1 scales by hierarchical subsampling scales = [] currentres = voxelres for i in range(L + 1): # Downsample by ratio s=4 at each step # Note: In practice, this is done via strided convolution or pooling # Here we assume a helper function for subsampling VDl = subsample(VD, currentres, downsampleratio) VAl = subsample(VA, currentres, downsampleratio) scales.append((VDl, VAl)) currentres = currentres // downsampleratio optimizer = torch.optim.Adam([VD, VA], lr=0.08) # Optional: Load sparse point cloud for Lsd sparsepoints = loadcolmapsparsepoints(trainingviews) # Optional: Load DPT depth maps for Ld densedepthmaps = loaddptdepths(trainingviews) for step in range(iterations): optimizer.zerograd() # 2. Sample Rays # Sample rays from training views rtrain, Ctrain = sampleraysfromviews(trainingviews, batchsize=4096) # Sample rays from novel views (spiral trajectory) rnovel, Cnovelgt = samplenovelviews(trainingviews, count=novelviewcount, batchsize=4096) # Note: Cnovelgt is not used for loss, only for evaluation or if using teacher forcing (not standard here) # 3. Volume Rendering at All Scales # Render RGB and Depth for training rays Chattrain = [] Dhattrain = [] for l in range(L + 1): VDl, VAl = scales[l] Chat, Dhat = volumerender(VDl, VAl, rtrain) Chattrain.append(Chat) Dhattrain.append(Dhat) # Render RGB and Depth for novel rays Chatnovel = [] Dhatnovel = [] for l in range(L + 1): VDl, VAl = scales[l] Chat, Dhat = volumerender(VDl, VAl, rnovel) Chatnovel.append(Chat) Dhatnovel.append(Dhat) # 4. Compute Multi-scale Color Loss (Training Views) Lmscolor = 0 for l in range(L + 1): # MSE between rendered and input RGB Lmscolor += F.mseloss(Chattrain[l], Ctrain) # 5. Cross-Scale Geometric Adaptation # For Training Views Lgeotrain = 0 for l in range(L + 1): # Calculate reprojection error # Warp view i to nearest view j using depth Dhat[l] # This requires camera parameters from trainingviews # pltoj is the projected coordinate in frame j # el = Ci - Cj(pltoj) # Helper: get reprojection error mask and error values # Returns: validmask, errorvalues validmask, errorvalues = computereprojectionerror( rtrain, trainingviews, Chattrain[l], Dhattrain[l]) # Find optimal scale l' for each pixel # l' = argminl(el) # We need to aggregate errors across scales to find l' # Note: The paper defines l' per pixel based on min error across l # So we first compute all el, then find min # Aggregate errors for all scales to find l' # errorvalues shape: (batch, H, W) for each l # We need to stack them to find argmin pass # Implementation detail: stack errors across l to find l' # Simplified logic for Lgeo based on paper description: # 1. Compute el for all l. # 2. Find l' = argminl(el). # 3. D' = Dhat[l']. # 4. Lgeo = MSE(Dhat[l'], D'). # Let's implement the aggregation properly allerrorstrain = [] alldepthstrain = [] for l in range(L + 1): validmask, errorvalues = computereprojectionerror( rtrain, trainingviews, Chattrain[l], Dhattrain[l]) allerrorstrain.append(errorvalues) alldepthstrain.append(Dhattrain[l]) # Stack errors: (L, batch, H, W) allerrorstrainstacked = torch.stack(allerrorstrain, dim=0) # Find optimal scale index l' for each pixel # argmin along dim 0 lprimetrain = torch.argmin(allerrorstrainstacked, dim=0) # Gather depths at l' # D' = Dhat[l'] # This requires gathering from alldepthstrain using lprimetrain Dprimetrain = gatherdepths(alldepthstrain, lprimetrain) # Compute Lgeo for training views # Only for pixels where error < threshold # First, find min error for each pixel minerrortrain = torch.min(allerrorstrainstacked, dim=0).values validmasktrain = minerrortrain < reprojectionthreshold # Masked MSE Lgeotrain = F.mseloss( Dhattrain[lprimetrain] validmasktrain, Dprimetrain validmasktrain) # For Novel Views Lgeonovel = 0 allerrorsnovel = [] alldepthsnovel = [] for l in range(L + 1): # Warp novel view n to nearest training view j # Use rendered color Chatnovel[l] instead of input RGB validmask, errorvalues = computereprojectionerrornovel( rnovel, trainingviews, Chatnovel[l], Dhatnovel[l]) allerrorsnovel.append(errorvalues) alldepthsnovel.append(Dhatnovel[l]) allerrorsnovelstacked = torch.stack(allerrorsnovel, dim=0) lprimenovel = torch.argmin(allerrorsnovelstacked, dim=0) Dprimenovel = gatherdepths(alldepthsnovel, lprimenovel) minerrornovel = torch.min(allerrorsnovelstacked, dim=0).values validmasknovel = minerrornovel < reprojectionthreshold Lgeonovel = F.mseloss( Dhatnovel[lprimenovel] validmasknovel, Dprimenovel validmasknovel) Lgeo = Lgeotrain + Lgeonovel # 6. Global Regularization Loss Lreg = computeglobalregularization(VD, VA) # 7. Sparse Depth Loss Lsd = computesparsedepthloss(VD, sparsepoints) # 8. Dense Depth Loss (Optional) Ld = 0 if densedepthmaps is not None: Ld = computedensedepthloss(VD, densedepthmaps) # 9. Total Loss Ltotal = Lmscolor + lambdageo Lgeo + lambdareg Lreg + lambdasd Lsd + lambdad Ld # 10. Backpropagation Ltotal.backward() optimizer.step() # Decay learning rate adjustlearningrate(optimizer, step, initiallr=0.08, finallr=0.002, totaliters=iterations) def subsample(voxel, res, ratio): """ Subsample voxel by ratio. """ # Assuming voxel is (res, res, res, channels) # Use strided convolution or pooling # For density (1 channel) and appearance (3 channels) if voxel.shape[-1] == 1: # Use avg pooling for density kernel = ratio stride = ratio # Add batch and channel dims for pooling voxel4d = voxel.unsqueeze(0).unsqueeze(0) pooled = F.avgpool3d(voxel4d, kernelsize=kernel, stride=stride) return pooled.squeeze(0).squeeze(0) else: # For appearance, use trilinear interpolation or similar # Or simply strided slicing if exact division newres = res // ratio # Strided slicing return voxel[::ratio,::ratio,::ratio,:] def computereprojectionerror(rays, views, Chat, Dhat): """ Compute reprojection error for training views. """ # rays: (batch, H, W, 3) or similar # views: list of view data # Chat: (batch, H, W, 3) # Dhat: (batch, H, W, 1) # 1. Lift pixels to 3D # x3d = unproject(rays, Dhat, intrinsics) # 2. Transform to world, then to nearest view j # xworld = transformtoworld(x3d, extrinsicsi) # xj = transformtoviewj(xworld, extrinsicsj) # 3. Project to 2D in view j # pj = project(xj, intrinsicsj) # 4. Sample Cj at pj # Cjsampled = sampleimage(Cj, pj) # 5. Error # e = Chat - Cjsampled # 6. Mask pixels outside bounds or with invalid depth # validmask = (depth > 0) and (pj within bounds) # Return validmask and error pass def computereprojectionerrornovel(rays, views, Chat, Dhat): """ Compute reprojection error for novel views. Uses rendered color Chat instead of input RGB. """ # Similar to training, but Ci is replaced by Chat (rendered color of novel view) # Ci(pi) -> Chat(pi) pass def computeglobalregularization(VD, VA): """ Compute total variation, patch-wise depth smoothness, L1 sparsity, and distortion losses. """ # Total Variation tvD = computetotalvariation(VD) tvA = computetotalvariation(VA) # L1 Sparsity l1D = torch.mean(torch.abs(VD)) # Distortion Loss (requires sampling along rays) # This is complex to implement without ray marching # Placeholder for distortion loss distortion = 0 # Patch-wise depth smoothness # Requires rendering depth and computing smoothness depth = volumerenderdepth(VD, VA) smoothness = computedepthsmoothness(depth) return tvD + tvA + l1D + distortion + smoothness def computesparsedepthloss(VD, sparsepoints): """ Compute loss against sparse point cloud from COLMAP. """ # Sample depth at sparse points # Compare with sparse point depths pass def computedensedepthloss(VD, densedepthmaps): """ Compute loss against DPT depth maps. """ # Render depth from VD # Compare with DPT depth maps pass def adjustlearningrate(optimizer, step, initiallr, finallr, totaliters): """ Linear decay of learning rate. """ lr = initiallr - (initiallr - finallr) (step / totaliters) for paramgroup in optimizer.paramgroups: paramgroup['lr'] = lr Time Complexity: Training is significantly faster than previous few-shot methods. On LLFF 2-view setting, it takes 10 minutes compared to FreeNeRF's 1.5 hours and TensoRF's 6 minutes (though TensoRF has lower quality). Memory Complexity: Weight-sharing voxels reduce model size compared to independent multi-scale voxels. Memory usage is comparable to TensoRF (183.04 MB). Performance: LLFF 2-view: PSNR 18.07, SSIM 0.54, LPIPS 0.35. Outperforms FreeNeRF, ViP-NeRF, SimpleNeRF, ZeroRF, SparseNeRF, and FSGS in PSNR and LPIPS with comparable SSIM. Strengths: Fast convergence, no learned priors required, robust to overfitting in extreme few-shot scenarios, handles diverse geometric details via multi-scale voxels. Limitations: Relies on accurate camera parameters. Performance may degrade if reprojection errors are noisy (mitigated by thresholding). When to use: Extreme few-shot novel view synthesis (2-4 views) where training time and lack of priors are constraints. When not to use: Dense input scenarios where other methods might be more efficient, or when ground truth depth is available and dense depth loss is preferred. FrugalNeRF was introduced in 2025 by authors publishing in CVPR 2025. It builds on TensoRF for fast training and addresses limitations of existing few-shot NeRF methods like FreeNeRF and SparseNeRF, which struggle with complex scheduling and bias from learned priors. It is evaluated on LLFF, DTU, and RealEstate10K datasets. name: ESNeRF
head: Extremely Sparse Neural Radiance Fields
body: ESNeRF is a sparse neural rendering method designed to address the ill-posed nature of novel view synthesis in extremely sparse-view settings. It builds on the FreeNeRF backbone but introduces a hybrid loss function incorporating pixel-based, depth-based, and regularization losses to mitigate overfitting and reduce artifacts such as solid floaters. Unlike standard NeRF training, ESNeRF leverages depth maps generated by a pretrained DPT model for supervision and employs frequency regularization to stabilize high-frequency signal learning. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: Sparse set of input images I, camera poses, and intrinsics. Outputs: Rendered color images \hat{C} and depth maps \hat{d} for novel views. Data Structures: Ray Set \mathcal{R}: Set of rays sampled for training. Density \sigmaK: Density values of K points sampled along a ray from near to far. Mask mK: Binary mask vector of length K. Depth Map d: Depth map generated by the pretrained DPT model. Rendered Depth \hat{d}: Depth estimated by volume rendering. Frequency Mask \boldsymbol{\alpha}: Vector controlling positional encoding visibility. Parameters: w1, w2, w3: Weights for Total Variation, Ranking, and Continuity losses. Not given in the sources. k: Tolerance constant for depth ranking penalty. Not given in the sources. M: Regularization range index for occlusion penalty. Not given in the sources. T: Final iteration for frequency regularization (e.g., 40,000). t: Current iteration for frequency regularization. L: Number of bits in the positional encoding frequency table. Not given in the sources. Training Resolution: 1/4 of the original image resolution. Training Iterations: 5,000 per scene. Batch Size: 1,024. Numbered Steps: 1. Depth Supervision Generation: Generate ground-truth depth maps d using a pretrained DPT model. 2. Frequency Regularization Setup: Initialize positional encoding. The visible frequency is controlled by a mask \boldsymbol{\alpha}(t, T, L). Start with raw inputs without positional encoding (or low frequency). As training progresses (t increases), the visible frequency increases linearly by 3 bits each step to avoid unstable high-frequency signals early in training. 3. Ray Sampling: Sample rays r \in \mathcal{R} and compute coarse (\hat{C}c) and fine (\hat{C}f) rendered colors and depths (\hat{d}) using the current NeRF model. 4. Loss Calculation: Compute the total loss \mathcal{L}{total} as defined below. 5. Occlusion Regularization: Apply a penalty to dense fields near the camera to reduce solid floaters. The mask mk is set to 1 for indices up to M and 0 for the rest. 6. Optimization: Update model parameters using the computed loss. 7. Upsampling: After training, upsample the generated target views bilinearly to full resolution. Formulas: The total loss is a weighted sum of the NeRF reconstruction loss and three regularization terms: \mathcal{L}{total} = \mathcal{L}{NeRF} + w1 \mathcal{L}{TV} + w2 R{rank} + w3 R{cont} The NeRF reconstruction loss uses both coarse and fine network outputs: \mathcal{L}{NeRF} = \sum{r \in \mathcal{R}} \left\| \hat{C}c(r) - C(r) \right\|^2 + \left\| \hat{C}f(r) - C(r) \right\|^2 where C(r) is the ground-truth pixel color for ray r. Total Variation Loss promotes spatial consistency in depth: \mathcal{L}{TV} = \sum{i,j} \left( |d{i,j} - d{i+1,j}|^2 + |d{i,j} - d{i,j+1}|^2 \right) where d{i,j} is the depth at pixel (i, j) from the DPT model. Depth-Guided Ranking Regularisation penalizes incorrect depth ordering between random points: R{rank} = \sum{di \leq dj} \max \left( \hat{d}i - \hat{d}j + k, 0 \right) where di, dj are depths from the DPT model and \hat{d}i, \hat{d}j are rendered depths. If di \leq dj but \hat{d}i > \hat{d}j, a penalty is applied. Depth-Guided Continuity Regularisation controls frequency visibility: \gamma 'L = \gamma L (x) \odot \boldsymbol {\alpha } (t, T, L) where the mask \boldsymbol{\alpha} is defined element-wise for bit index i as: \boldsymbol {\alpha }i (t, T, L) = \begin{cases} 1 & \text{if}\ i \leq \frac {t \cdot L}{T} + 3 \\ \frac {t \cdot L}{T} & \text{if}\ \frac {t \cdot L}{T} + 3 < i \leq \frac {t \cdot L}{T} + 6 \\ 0 & \text{if}\ i > \frac {t \cdot L}{T} + 6 \end{cases} Occlusion Regularisation penalizes density near the camera: \mathcal{L}{occ} = \frac{1}{K} \sum{k=1}^K \sigmak \cdot mk where \sigmak is the density at the k-th sample point (near to far), and mk=1 for k \leq M and 0 otherwise. """ # Initialize NeRF model (FreeNeRF backbone) nerfmodel = FreeNeRFBackbone() # Pretrained DPT model for depth supervision dptmodel = loadpretraineddpt() # Training configuration batchsize = 1024 trainingres = (originalwidth // 4, originalheight // 4) for t in range(5000): # 5K iterations per scene # 1. Frequency Regularization Mask # Calculate alpha mask based on current iteration t alphamask = computealphamask(t, T, L) # 2. Sample Rays rays = samplerays(inputimages, poses, intrinsics, batchsize, trainingres) # 3. Get Ground Truth Depth from DPT # Resize DPT depth to training resolution gtdepths = dptmodel(inputimages) gtdepths = resize(gtdepths, trainingres) # 4. Forward Pass through NeRF # Coarse and Fine networks coarsecolors, coarsedepths, coarsealphas = nerfmodel.coarseforward(rays, alphamask) finecolors, finedepths, finealphas = nerfmodel.fineforward(rays, alphamask) # 5. Compute Losses # LNeRF: Color reconstruction # Note: rays.gtcolors must be resized to trainingres lossnerf = meansquarederror(coarsecolors, rays.gtcolors) + \ meansquarederror(finecolors, rays.gtcolors) # LTV: Total Variation on Depth # Compute TV on gtdepths (or rendered depth? Source says "rendered depth" in text but formula uses di,j which is DPT depth) # Source text: "LTV computing depth variance relative to neighbouring pixels" # Formula uses di,j. Context implies supervising against DPT depth smoothness. losstv = computetotalvariation(gtdepths) # Rrank: Depth Ranking Regularization # Sample random patches/points from gtdepths and rendered depths # P is set of local patches. For implementation, sample random pairs (i, j) lossrank = 0 numsamples = 1000 # Not given, arbitrary for implementation for in range(numsamples): idxi, idxj = randomsampleindices(gtdepths.shape) di = gtdepths[idxi] dj = gtdepths[idxj] dhati = coarsedepths[idxi] # or fine dhatj = coarsedepths[idxj] if di <= dj: penalty = max(dhati - dhatj + k, 0) lossrank += penalty lossrank /= numsamples # Rcont: Continuity (Frequency Masking is applied in forward pass, # but source lists it as a loss term Rcont. # However, the formula for Rcont is actually the frequency mask definition. # The text says "additional depth-guided continuity regularisation term...". # It is likely that Rcont is implicitly handled by the frequency mask or # there is a missing formula for a continuity penalty. # Given the source structure, Rcont might be zero or the mask itself is the mechanism. # We will assume Rcont is handled via the frequency mask mechanism described. # If a separate loss is needed, it is not provided in the source. losscont = 0 # Locc: Occlusion Regularization # Compute density near camera # sigmaK is density of K points near to far # mk is 1 for k <= M, 0 otherwise lossocc = mean(coarsealphas[:M]) # Approximation: alpha ~ sigma deltaz # Total Loss totalloss = lossnerf + w1 losstv + w2 lossrank + w3 losscont + lossocc # Backpropagate and update totalloss.backward() optimizer.step() optimizer.zerograd() return nerfmodel def computealphamask(t, T, L): """ Compute frequency visibility mask. """ alpha = [] for i in range(L): thresholdlow = (t L) / T + 3 thresholdhigh = (t L) / T + 6 if i <= thresholdlow: alpha.append(1.0) elif i <= thresholdhigh: alpha.append((t L) / T) else: alpha.append(0.0) return alpha def computetotalvariation(depthmap): """ Compute Total Variation loss on depth map. """ # depthmap shape: (H, W) # Horizontal difference diffh = depthmap[:, 1:] - depthmap[:,:-1] # Vertical difference diffv = depthmap[1:,:] - depthmap[:-1,:] tvloss = sum(diffh2) + sum(diffv2) return tvloss Edge Cases and Pitfalls: DPT Inaccuracy: The DPT-generated depth maps may be inaccurate and lack detail. Using them solely for supervision can deteriorate render quality, necessitating the hybrid loss. High-Frequency Instability: Training with full positional encoding from the start can lead to unstable and susceptible high-frequency signals. The frequency regularization is critical to avoid this. Floaters: Sparse views often result in solid floaters near the camera. The occlusion regularization is specifically designed to address this. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Measured Performance: The method was evaluated in the AIM 2024 Sparse Neural Rendering Challenge, Track 1. Scaling: Training is performed at 1/4 image resolution, followed by bilinear upsampling to full resolution. Strengths: Addresses overfitting and ill-posedness in sparse-view settings; reduces solid floaters; stabilizes high-frequency learning. Limitations: Relies on the quality of the pretrained DPT model; requires careful tuning of regularization weights (not provided). ESNeRF was proposed by the team "zongqihe" for the AIM 2024 Sparse Neural Rendering Challenge. It builds on the FreeNeRF backbone and incorporates techniques from [18] (pixel-based losses) and [28] (depth-based losses). The method was part of the challenge submissions, with the team participating in Track 1. name: MLI-NeRF
head: Intrinsic-Aware NeRF (Stage 2), Multi-Light Intrinsic-Aware Neural Radiance Fields, Stage 2 Training
body: MLI-NeRF is a two-stage optimization procedure that learns an intrinsic-aware Neural Radiance Field (NeRF) capable of novel view synthesis, relighting, and intrinsic decomposition (separating reflectance and shading) without relying on statistical priors or ground-truth intrinsic labels. It differs from standard NeRF variants by explicitly modeling multiple light sources to generate physics-based pseudo-labels, and it differs from prior intrinsic NeRF methods by leveraging 3D geometric constraints and multi-light visibility rather than chromaticity or semantic statistical constraints. The method solves the ill-posed nature of inverse rendering by decoupling the geometry learning (Stage 1) from the intrinsic component separation (Stage 2), using pseudo-labels derived from the Stage 1 model to guide the decomposition. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: A dataset of images captured from various camera positions and multiple light source positions. Outputs: A trained model capable of rendering novel views under arbitrary lighting, and decomposing scenes into reflectance (R), shading (S), and residual (Re) components. Data Structures and Network Layout: The method builds upon the Neuralangelo architecture, which uses 3D hashing encoding and Signed Distance Fields (SDF). 1. Geometry Network (f): Predicts the SDF value sdf = f(x) for a spatial position x. It also provides features (feat) and normals (n) derived from the gradient of the SDF. 2. Color Network (MLP{color}): Used in Stage 1. Inputs: spatial position x, normal n, features feat, view direction d, and light position l. Output: color c. 3. Reflectance Network (MLP{reflectance}): Used in Stage 2. Inputs: spatial position x, normal n, features feat. It does not take light position or view direction as input. Output: reflectance r. 4. Shading Network (MLP{shading}): Used in Stage 2. Inputs: spatial position x, normal n, features feat, and light position l. It does not take view direction as input due to the Lambertian assumption. Output: shading s. 5. Residual (Re): Accounts for specularities and undirected light, calculated as Re = I - R \otimes S. Numbered Steps: Stage 1: Neural Multi-Light Implicit Representation 1. Train the geometry network f and color network MLP{color} using images from multiple camera angles and light positions. 2. Optimize the Stage 1 loss L{S1}: L{S1} = w{rgb} L{rgb} + w{eik} L{eik} + w{curv} L{curv} Where L{rgb} is the rendered image loss, L{eik} is the Eikonal loss, and L{curv} is the curvature loss. 3. Post-processing (Pseudo Label Generation): Step A (Normals and Visibility): Derive normals n from the gradient of the SDF network. Use geometry network depth and sphere tracing to estimate intersection points. Compute light visibility V (whether a point is directly illuminated) by sphere tracing from the light position to the intersection point. Step B (Pseudo Shading): Compute pseudo-shading S^ using the Lambertian cosine law and visibility, adjusted for gamma correction: S^ = (\max(\mathbf{N} \cdot \mathbf{L}, 0) \otimes V)^\gamma Where \mathbf{N} is the normal ray, \mathbf{L} is the light ray, \otimes is pixel-wise product, and \gamma is the gamma correction exponent. Step C (Pseudo Reflectance): Infer high-fidelity pseudo-reflectance R^ using multiple lighting conditions. For each pixel, use the equation: R^ = I \oslash S^ Where I is the input image and \oslash is pixel-wise division. This ignores the residual component Re initially, assuming diffuse dominance. Stage 2: Intrinsic-Aware NeRF 1. Freeze the geometry network f. 2. Initialize and train the new modules MLP{reflectance} and MLP{shading}. 3. Render predicted reflectance \hat{R} and shading \hat{S} using the new networks. 4. Compute the residual \hat{Re} from the rendered image \hat{I} and the predicted components: \hat{I} = \hat{R} \otimes \hat{S} + \hat{Re} 5. Optimize the Stage 2 loss L{S2}: L{S2} = w{rgb} L{rgb} + w{intrinsic} L{intrinsic} + w{reg} L{reg} Intrinsic Loss (L{intrinsic}): Guides the separation using pseudo-labels R^ and S^: L{intrinsic} = WR \cdot \|\hat{R} - R^\|1 + WS \cdot \|\hat{S} - S^\|1 Where WR and WS are weight maps derived during pseudo-label generation. Regularization Loss (L{reg}): Prevents convergence to local minima (e.g., R=0, S=0, Re=I): L{reg} = \|\hat{Re}\|1 Weights: Typical values are w{intrinsic} = 1.0, w{reg} = 1.0. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import numpy as np def normalize(v): return v / np.linalg.norm(v, axis=-1, keepdims=True) def computegradient(network, points): # Standard automatic differentiation to get SDF gradient return network.gradient(points) def spheretracevisibility(geometrynet, origin, lightpos, maxsteps=64): # Standard sphere tracing for SDF visibility t = 0.0 for in range(maxsteps): pos = origin + t normalize(lightpos - origin) sdfval = geometrynet(pos) if sdfval < 1e-4: return 1.0 if t > 100.0: break t += sdfval return 0.0 def volumerender(positions, colors, alphas, numrays): # Standard alpha compositing along rays T = np.ones(numrays) rendered = np.zeroslike(colors[0]) for i in range(len(positions)): alpha = alphas[i] rendered += T alpha colors[i] T = (1.0 - alpha) return rendered def samplerays(pose, imageshape): # Generate camera rays from pose and image dimensions # Returns positions and directions pass def trainstage1(geometrynet, colornet, dataset, lr=1e-4, wrgb=1.0, weik=0.1, wcurv=5e-4): optimizerparams = list(geometrynet.parameters()) + list(colornet.parameters()) for epoch in range(numepochs): for image, pose, lightpos in dataset: rays = samplerays(pose, image.shape) positions, directions = rays sdf = geometrynet(positions) feat = geometrynet.getfeatures(positions) normals = normalize(computegradient(geometrynet, positions)) colors = colornet(positions, normals, feat, directions, lightpos) alphas = geometrynet.getalphas(positions) # Alpha prediction from NeRF renderedimage = volumerender(positions, colors, alphas, len(rays)) lossrgb = np.mean((renderedimage - image) 2) losseik = np.mean((np.linalg.norm(computegradient(geometrynet, positions), axis=-1) - 1.0) 2) losscurv = computecurvature(geometrynet, positions) # Curvature from SDF totalloss = wrgb lossrgb + weik losseik + wcurv losscurv for p in optimizerparams: if p.grad is not None: p -= lr p.grad return geometrynet, colornet def generatepseudolabels(geometrynet, dataset, gamma=2.2): pseudoshadings = [] pseudoreflectances = [] for image, pose, lightpos in dataset: rays = samplerays(pose, image.shape) positions, directions = rays normals = normalize(computegradient(geometrynet, positions)) visibility = spheretracevisibility(geometrynet, positions, lightpos) lightdir = normalize(lightpos - positions) cosineterm = np.maximum(np.sum(normals lightdir, axis=-1), 0.0) pseudoshading = (cosineterm visibility) gamma pseudoreflectance = image / pseudoshading pseudoshadings.append(pseudoshading) pseudoreflectances.append(pseudoreflectance) return pseudoshadings, pseudoreflectances def trainstage2(geometrynet, reflectancenet, shadingnet, pseudoshadings, pseudoreflectances, WR, WS, dataset, lr=1e-4, wrgb=1.0, wintrinsic=1.0, wreg=1.0): for param in geometrynet.parameters(): param.requiresgrad = False optimizerparams = list(reflectancenet.parameters()) + list(shadingnet.parameters()) for epoch in range(numepochs): for i, (image, pose, lightpos) in enumerate(dataset): rays = samplerays(pose, image.shape) positions, directions = rays feat = geometrynet.getfeatures(positions) normals = normalize(computegradient(geometrynet, positions)) predreflectance = reflectancenet(positions, normals, feat) predshading = shadingnet(positions, normals, feat, lightpos) alphas = geometrynet.getalphas(positions) # Alpha prediction renderedimage = volumerender(positions, predreflectance predshading, alphas, len(rays)) predresidual = renderedimage - (predreflectance predshading) lossrgb = np.mean((renderedimage - image) 2) lossintrinsic = np.mean(WR np.abs(predreflectance - pseudoreflectances[i])) + \ np.mean(WS np.abs(predshading - pseudoshadings[i])) lossreg = np.mean(np.abs(predresidual)) totalloss = wrgb lossrgb + wintrinsic lossintrinsic + wreg lossreg for p in optimizerparams: if p.grad is not None: p -= lr p.grad return reflectancenet, shadingnet Parameters: \gamma: Gamma correction exponent used to adapt pseudo-shading to nonlinear digital image representation. w{eik}: Eikonal loss weight (0.1). w{curv}: Curvature loss weight (5 \times 10^{-4}). w{intrinsic}: Intrinsic loss weight (1.0). w{reg}: Regularization loss weight (1.0). w{rgb}: RGB loss weight (Not explicitly isolated in Stage 2 snippet, but present in L{S2}). Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Local Minima: The optimization may converge to trivial solutions where R=0, S=0, Re=I. This is mitigated by the L{reg} term which penalizes the residual norm. Ill-Posed Inverse Rendering: Traditional inverse rendering is computationally intensive and ambiguous. MLI-NeRF avoids this by using intrinsic decomposition with pseudo-labels, limiting the scope to object-specific or well-lit scenes where diffuse dominance holds. Specularities: The pseudo-reflectance generation ignores the residual component, which entangles specularities and undirected light. This may lead to inaccuracies in highly specular regions. A pipeline to generate high-fidelity pseudo reflectance and shading labels from a trained multi-light NeRF model to guide intrinsic decomposition training in Stage 2. Unlike previous statistical priors, this physics-based pipeline provides a more reliable basis for disentanglement by leveraging explicit geometric and illumination models. It serves as the bridge between the implicit representation learned in Stage 1 and the intrinsic-aware NeRF in Stage 2. Time Complexity: Stage 1 training time follows Neuralangelo. Stage 2 training takes approximately 19 hours on a single Nvidia RTX 3090 for the tested datasets. Memory Complexity: Uses 3D hashing encoding and SDF storage similar to Neuralangelo. The addition of two MLPs (reflectance and shading) increases parameter count slightly, but the geometry network is frozen in Stage 2. Strengths: Does not require ground-truth intrinsic labels; leverages 3D geometric constraints for robustness; enables relighting and intrinsic editing. Limitations: Computationally intensive due to multi-light rendering and sphere tracing; limited to scenes where diffuse reflection dominates (Lambertian assumption); struggles with highly specular or complex non-diffuse effects without residual compensation. When to use: When intrinsic decomposition and relighting are required without ground-truth labels, and the scene has controllable or known multiple light sources. When not to use: For real-time applications (training is slow); for scenes with strong specularities where the Lambertian assumption fails significantly; when ground-truth intrinsic data is available (other methods may be more direct). MLI-NeRF was proposed to address the limitations of existing intrinsic decomposition methods that rely on statistical priors (like chromaticity) and struggle with real-world data. It builds on the idea that varying light source positions, similar to how mineralogists illuminate specimens, reveals intrinsic scene details. The method integrates multiple light information into Neural Radiance Fields, generating pseudo-labels to guide intrinsic decomposition without statistical constraints. It was validated on synthetic (Blender-based) and real-world datasets, outperforming methods like IntrinsicNeRF, InvRender, and TensoIR in intrinsic decomposition and relighting tasks.
