name: Physics-based Pseudo Label Generation
head: Post-processing of Stage 1, Pseudo reflectance generation, Pseudo shading generation
body: This method generates high-fidelity pseudo reflectance and shading labels from a trained multi-light NeRF model to guide intrinsic decomposition training in Stage 2. Unlike previous statistical priors, this physics-based pipeline provides a more reliable basis for disentanglement by leveraging explicit geometric and illumination models. It serves as the bridge between the implicit representation learned in Stage 1 and the intrinsic-aware NeRF in Stage 2. Inputs: Trained SDF network and RGB MLP from Stage 1. Camera poses and light positions for multiple lighting conditions. Rendered RGB images I for each light condition. Outputs: Pseudo shading image S. Pseudo reflectance image R. Weight maps WR and WS for reliability estimation. Data Structures: Points: 3D coordinates (x, y, z) sampled along camera rays. Normals: Surface normal vectors \vec{N} derived from SDF gradients. Light Visibility: Binary or continuous mask V indicating if a point is illuminated by a specific light source. Images: 2D arrays of RGB values for I, S, and R. Steps: 1. Obtain Normal and Light Visibility: Use the trained SDF network from Stage 1 to perform sphere tracing and volume rendering to get normals and light visibility for each point. For each point along the camera ray, compute the surface normal \vec{N} via the gradient of the SDF. Determine light visibility V by checking if the point is occluded from the light source. 2. Generate Pseudo Shading: Compute the dot product of the normal \vec{N} and the light ray direction \vec{L}. Apply gamma correction to adapt the pseudo-shading to the nonlinear representation of digital images, mimicking sensor response. The shading S is calculated as: S = (\max(\vec{N} \cdot \vec{L}, 0) \otimes V)^\gamma where: \vec{N} is the normal ray. \vec{L} is the light ray direction. V is the light visibility mask. \gamma is the gamma value (Not given in the sources.). \otimes denotes pixel-wise product. (\cdot)^\gamma represents gamma correction. 3. Generate Pseudo Reflectance: Calculate initial reflectance for each light condition using pixel-wise division, ignoring the residual component (specular and indirect light): R = I \oslash S where \oslash denotes pixel-wise division. To handle multiple light conditions, use K-means clustering at the pixel level. Incorporate weights of each pseudo shading to select the most probable pseudo reflectance, creating a merged reflectance image. 4. Hole Filling: Identify regions in the merged reflectance that appear as holes due to the absence of direct illumination in all lighting conditions. Compute a weighted distance between hole pixels and non-hole pixels based on spatial distance in the image, angular difference of their normals, and RGB color difference. Assign the color of the nearest non-hole pixel (based on weighted distance) to the hole pixel. This is a rough supplementary approach with minimal impact on overall results, as hole regions are typically small under multi-light settings. 5. Compute Weight Maps: Compute weight maps WR and WS for pseudo reflectance and shading respectively. Weights are based on edges of pseudo shading and visibility. Areas with higher pseudo shading values or further from visibility edges have greater credibility. Areas closer to visibility edges or with lower pseudo shading values are deemed less reliable. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math import numpy as np def generatepseudolabels(sdfnetwork, rgbmlp, cameraposes, lightpositions, gamma=2.2): pseudoshadings = [] pseudoreflectances = [] allnormals = [] allvisibilities = [] for pose, lightpos in zip(cameraposes, lightpositions): # Step A: Obtain Normal and Light Visibility points, normals, visibilities = spheretraceandrender( sdfnetwork, cameraposes=pose, lightpositions=lightpos) allnormals.append(normals) allvisibilities.append(visibilities) # Compute light ray direction lightray = normalize(lightpos - points) # Step B: Generate Pseudo Shading dotproduct = np.maximum(np.sum(normals lightray, axis=-1), 0) visibilities shading = dotproduct gamma pseudoshadings.append(shading) # Render RGB image for this light condition rgbimage = renderrgb(rgbmlp, points) # Step C: Generate Pseudo Reflectance (Initial) safeshading = np.maximum(shading, 1e-6) initialreflectance = rgbimage / safeshading[:, np.newaxis] pseudoreflectances.append(initialreflectance) # Merge reflectances using K-means clustering with weights mergedreflectance = kmeansmerge(pseudoreflectances, pseudoshadings) # Step D: Hole Filling holemask = ishole(mergedreflectance, pseudoshadings) filledreflectance = fillholes(mergedreflectance, holemask, allnormals[0]) # Compute Weight Maps weightshading = computeshadingweight(pseudoshadings) weightreflectance = computereflectanceweight(filledreflectance, weightshading) return filledreflectance, pseudoshadings[0], weightreflectance, weightshading def spheretraceandrender(sdfnetwork, cameraposes, lightpositions): # Sources do not specify the exact sphere tracing implementation. # Standard routine iterates along rays, queries SDF, computes normals via gradient, # and checks visibility. Returns arrays of shape (H, W, 3) and (H, W). return np.zeros((100, 100, 3)), np.zeros((100, 100, 3)), np.zeros((100, 100)) def renderrgb(rgbmlp, points): # Standard MLP forward pass to predict RGB from points and features return np.random.rand(points.shape[0], 3) def normalize(v): return v / (np.linalg.norm(v, axis=-1, keepdims=True) + 1e-8) def kmeansmerge(reflectances, shadings, k=3, maxiter=10): # Weighted K-means clustering at pixel level across light conditions npixels = reflectances[0].shape[0] nlights = len(reflectances) flatref = np.vstack([r.flatten() for r in reflectances]) flatshad = np.vstack([s.flatten() for s in shadings]) weights = flatshad / (np.max(flatshad) + 1e-6) centroids = flatref[:k] for in range(maxiter): dists = np.linalg.norm(flatref[:, np.newaxis] - centroids[np.newaxis,:], axis=2) labels = np.argmin(dists, axis=1) newcentroids = np.zeroslike(centroids) for i in range(k): mask = labels == i if np.sum(mask) > 0: newcentroids[i] = np.average(flatref[mask], weights=weights[mask], axis=0) centroids = newcentroids merged = centroids[labels].reshape(reflectances[0].shape) return merged def ishole(reflectance, shadings): # Identify regions where shading was near zero for all lights minshading = np.min(np.stack(shadings, axis=0), axis=0) return minshading < 1e-3 def fillholes(reflectance, holemask, normals): filled = reflectance.copy() holeindices = np.argwhere(holemask) nonholeindices = np.argwhere(~holemask) for hole in holeindices: mindist = float('inf') bestpixel = None for nonhole in nonholeindices: dspatial = np.linalg.norm(hole - nonhole) dangle = 1.0 - np.abs(np.dot(normals[hole[0], hole[1]], normals[nonhole[0], nonhole[1]])) dcolor = np.linalg.norm(reflectance[hole[0], hole[1]] - reflectance[nonhole[0], nonhole[1]]) dist = dspatial + dangle + dcolor if dist < mindist: mindist = dist bestpixel = nonhole if bestpixel is not None: filled[hole[0], hole[1]] = reflectance[bestpixel[0], bestpixel[1]] return filled def computeshadingweight(shadings): # Weights based on edges of pseudo shading and visibility avgshading = np.mean(np.stack(shadings, axis=0), axis=0) edges = np.abs(np.gradient(avgshading)) weight = avgshading / (edges + 1e-6) return weight def computereflectanceweight(reflectance, shadingweight): # Reflectance weight inherits shading reliability return shadingweight Exact time and memory complexity bounds are Not given in the sources. Qualitatively, time complexity depends on the number of light conditions and pixels, with K-means clustering adding per-pixel overhead across light conditions. Memory complexity requires storing normals, visibilities, and intermediate images for all light conditions. The method provides a physically grounded basis for intrinsic decomposition, reducing reliance on statistical priors. It handles multi-light scenarios effectively. The method relies on the accuracy of Stage 1 SDF and RGB networks. Hole filling is a heuristic and may introduce artifacts in complex scenes, though impact is minimal. Accuracy of visibility estimation affects shading quality. It is used when training an intrinsic-aware NeRF (Stage 2) and high-fidelity pseudo labels are needed for supervision. It is not recommended if computational resources are extremely limited, as it requires additional post-processing steps. If the scene has significant specular or indirect lighting that cannot be ignored in the residual component, the simplified R = I \oslash S may be inaccurate. Originated in the MLI-NeRF paper (2024). It addresses the need for reliable supervision signals for intrinsic decomposition in neural radiance fields, moving away from statistical priors used in earlier methods. The method leverages the physics of light transport (Lambert's cosine law) and sensor characteristics (gamma correction) to generate pseudo labels. name: Diffusion-guided Optimization
body: Diffusion-guided optimization methods train Neural Radiance Fields (NeRFs) by leveraging pretrained 2D or 3D diffusion models as priors to guide the optimization of 3D geometry and texture. These methods solve the problem of 3D data scarcity and underconstrained reconstruction by distilling generative knowledge from 2D image distributions into 3D scene representations. They set themselves apart from standard NeRF training by backpropagating gradients from a frozen or jointly trained diffusion model through a differentiable renderer, rather than relying solely on photometric reconstruction losses from input images. Builds on NeRF Training Loop. All methods in this family optimize a NeRF representation \theta (or latent codes x) by minimizing a loss derived from a diffusion model \phi. The core mechanism involves rendering an image (or latent) from the current NeRF state, perturbing it with noise, and computing gradients based on the diffusion model's prediction of that noise. The general optimization loop is: 1. Render an image x from the NeRF at a random viewpoint. 2. Sample a diffusion timestep t and Gaussian noise \epsilon. 3. Create a noisy version zt = \alphat x + \sigmat \epsilon. 4. Predict noise \hat{\epsilon} = \hat{\epsilon}\phi(zt; \text{condition}, t). 5. Compute gradients \nabla\theta \mathcal{L} using the difference between predicted and actual noise. The specific form of the gradient and the conditioning mechanism varies by child method. Optimizes a NeRF using Score Distillation Sampling (SDS) from a frozen 2D text-to-image diffusion model. It sets itself apart by introducing SDS to backpropagate gradients from a 2D prior to 3D geometry without explicit 3D supervision. Choose it for text-to-3D generation. Generates 3D human avatars using SDS but constrains the NeRF with an SMPL parametric shape prior. It is distinguished by its explicit geometric topology constraints, unlike DreamFusion's implicit representation. Choose it for human avatar generation. Jointly optimizes scene latent codes, a diffusion prior, and a NeRF decoder in a single loop. It solves the bias of two-stage methods by treating diffusion parameters as trainable. Choose it for multi-view reconstruction with a diffusion prior. Uses a multiview-conditioned latent diffusion model to regularize few-view reconstruction. It differs from SDS by sampling a new image at each iteration using a denoising U-Net conditioned on input views, reducing volumetric artifacts. Choose it for few-view 3D reconstruction. Applies a local 3D geometric diffusion prior to remove floaters. It distinguishes itself by using a 3D U-Net on voxelized patches (Density Score Distillation Sampling) rather than a 2D image prior. Choose it for cleaning up casually captured NeRFs. The concept of distilling 2D diffusion priors into 3D representations was introduced by DreamFusion. Subsequent works adapted this principle for specific domains: DreamAvatar for humans, Single-Stage Diffusion NeRF Training for joint optimization, ReconFusion for few-view reconstruction, and Nerfbusters for artifact removal.

name: DreamFusion
head: Diffusion-guided NeRF Optimization, Score Distillation Sampling, Text-to-3D NeRF Optimization, Text-to-3D diffusion NeRF
body: DreamFusion is a text-to-3D generation method that optimizes a parametric 3D scene representation (specifically a NeRF) to match a given textual description or image without requiring explicit 3D training data. It solves the problem of 3D data scarcity by distilling priors from a frozen 2D text-to-image diffusion model into the 3D geometry and appearance. What sets it apart from its siblings and nearest alternatives is its use of Score Distillation Sampling (SDS), which backpropagates gradients from the 2D diffusion model’s noise prediction through the differentiable renderer to update the 3D scene parameters. Unlike Instruct 3D-to-3D, which edits existing geometry, DreamFusion generates scenes from scratch. DreamFusion optimizes a NeRF representation \theta by minimizing a loss derived from a 2D diffusion model \phi. The core mechanism involves rendering an image from the current NeRF state, perturbing it with noise, and computing gradients based on the diffusion model's prediction of that noise. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A text prompt y (e.g., "a red apple") or a reference image. Input: A frozen 2D text-to-image diffusion model \phi (e.g., Imagen). Input: A NeRF representation \theta initialized from scratch. In DreamFusion, surface color is parameterized by an MLP instead of standard radiance. Output: An optimized NeRF \theta that renders images consistent with the prompt y. Data Structures: NeRF (\theta): A multi-layer perceptron (MLP) that maps 3D coordinates and viewing directions to color and density. The specific architecture used in DreamFusion is mipNeRF 360. Diffusion Model (\phi): A pretrained text-to-image diffusion model (e.g., Imagen). It takes a noisy image zt, a timestep t, and a text condition y as input, and outputs a predicted noise \hat{\epsilon}\phi(zt; y, t). Numbered Steps: 1. Random Viewpoint Selection: Sample a random camera viewpoint (position and orientation) for the current optimization step. 2. Differentiable Rendering: Render an image x from the NeRF \theta at the sampled viewpoint. 3. Noise Sampling: Sample a diffusion timestep t uniformly from [1, T] and a Gaussian noise vector \epsilon \sim \mathcal{N}(0, I). 4. Noise Addition: Create a noisy version of the rendered image zt using the forward diffusion process: zt = \alphat x + \sigmat \epsilon where \alphat and \sigmat are timestep-dependent coefficients. 5. Diffusion Prediction: Pass the noisy image zt, timestep t, and text prompt y into the frozen diffusion model \phi to predict the noise: \hat{\epsilon} = \hat{\epsilon}\phi(zt; y, t). 6. Gradient Computation: Compute the Score Distillation Sampling (SDS) gradient with respect to the NeRF parameters \theta: \nabla\theta \mathcal{L}{\text{SDS}} = \mathbb{E}{t, \epsilon}\left[ w(t)\,(\hat{\epsilon}\phi(zt; y, t) - \epsilon)\,\frac{\partial zt}{\partial \theta} \right] where w(t) is a timestep weighting function. The term \frac{\partial zt}{\partial \theta} is the gradient of the rendered noisy image with respect to the NeRF parameters, obtained via backpropagation through the differentiable renderer. 7. Optimization Step: Update the NeRF parameters \theta using the computed gradient (e.g., via Adam optimizer). Formulas: SDS Loss Gradient: \nabla\theta L{SDS}(\phi, x) \triangleq \mathbb{E}{t,\epsilon} w(t) \left[ \hat{\epsilon}\phi(zt; y, t) - \epsilon \right] \frac{\partial zt}{\partial \theta}. Noisy Image: zt = \alphat x + \sigmat \epsilon. Parameters: Diffusion Model: Imagen was used in the original DreamFusion implementation. Resolution: Imagen images were generated at a 64x64 resolution. Viewpoint Control: Text prompts can include keywords such as "overhead view", "front view", and "back view" to control the viewpoint at the diffusion generation stage. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Low Resolution: Because the source diffusion model (Imagen) generated images at 64x64 resolution, the resulting NeRF model lacked the capability to produce finer details. Janus Problem: The method suffers from the "Janus problem," where the generated 3D object exhibits multiple faces or inconsistent features from different viewpoints. Oversaturation and Oversmoothing: SDS tends to produce saturated colors and oversmoothed textures, leading to insufficient detail. Slow Optimization: The optimization process is slow, taking hours per scene. Instruct 3D-to-3D is a method for performing 3D scene editing or conversion guided by natural language instructions. It solves the problem of transforming an existing 3D scene into a new one that adheres to specific textual descriptions while maintaining structural coherence. It distinguishes itself from text-to-3D generation methods like DreamFusion by conditioning the optimization on a source 3D scene rather than generating geometry from scratch, and from other 3D editing methods like SKED by leveraging InstructPix2Pix for instruction following. Time Complexity: Optimization is slow, typically taking hours per scene. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Measured Performance: DreamFusion produces photorealistic and semantically faithful 3D objects from text prompts without 3D supervision. However, the output resolution is limited by the resolution of the 2D diffusion model (e.g., 64x64 in the original implementation). Scaling: Scaling to higher resolutions requires multi-stage approaches (e.g., Magic3D) or latent-space methods (e.g., Latent-NeRF). Strengths: No 3D training data required; leverages powerful 2D diffusion priors; allows text-based control over viewpoint and semantics. Limitations: Slow optimization; Janus problem (multi-face artifacts); saturated colors; oversmoothing; insufficient detail due to low-resolution diffusion inputs. When to use: When generating novel 3D objects from text descriptions is required, and high-fidelity detail is not the primary concern, or when used as a coarse initialization for refinement. When not to use: When high-resolution details are critical, or when editing existing 3D scenes is required (use Instruct 3D-to-3D instead). DreamFusion was introduced in September 2022. It was proposed as a text-to-3D diffusion NeRF model that uses images from 2D diffusion models (specifically Imagen) to train a NeRF from scratch. The method addresses the lack of large-scale 3D training datasets by sidestepping explicit 3D supervision altogether. It builds on Diffusion-guided Optimization by introducing Score Distillation Sampling (SDS) as the specific gradient computation method. Subsequent works like Latent-NeRF and Magic3D built upon DreamFusion to address its limitations regarding resolution and detail. name: Instruct 3D-to-3D
body: Instruct 3D-to-3D is a method for performing 3D scene editing or conversion guided by natural language instructions. It solves the problem of transforming an existing 3D scene into a new one that adheres to specific textual descriptions while maintaining structural coherence. It distinguishes itself from text-to-3D generation methods like DreamFusion by conditioning the optimization on a source 3D scene rather than generating geometry from scratch, and from other 3D editing methods like SKED by leveraging InstructPix2Pix for instruction following. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A source 3D scene (represented as a NeRF or similar implicit representation) and a text instruction. Output: An optimized target 3D scene that reflects the text instruction. Data Structures: Source Scene: The initial 3D representation (e.g., NeRF parameters). Text Instruction: A string of natural language. Optimization State: The parameters of the target 3D scene, initialized from the source scene. Steps: 1. Conditioning: Integrate the source 3D scene as a conditional input to the optimization process. This ensures the target scene remains grounded in the geometry and appearance of the source. 2. Loss Calculation: Utilize the Score Distillation Sampling (SDS) loss [89] to guide the optimization. The SDS loss is computed using a text-to-image diffusion model (specifically InstructPix2Pix, as cited in) to evaluate how well the rendered images from the current 3D scene match the text instruction. 3. Geometry Modification: Integrate dynamic scaling to effectively modify scene geometry. This mechanism allows the method to adjust the scale of geometric elements during optimization to better fit the textual description. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def optimizeinstruct3dto3d(sourcenerf, textinstruction, numiterations): # Initialize target scene parameters from source targetparams = copy(sourcenerf.parameters) # Load InstructPix2Pix model for SDS loss computation # Note: InstructPix2Pix is a text-conditioned image editing model ip2pmodel = loadinstructpix2pix() for step in range(numiterations): # 1. Render images from current target scene # Assume render function returns RGB images and potentially depth/normal renderedimages = render(targetparams, cameraposes) # 2. Compute SDS Loss using InstructPix2Pix # The SDS loss guides the gradient based on the text instruction # InstructPix2Pix takes the rendered image and the text instruction # to predict the edited image, and the gradient is derived from the noise prediction sdsloss = computesdsloss( renderedimages=renderedimages, textinstruction=textinstruction, diffusionmodel=ip2pmodel) # 3. Integrate dynamic scaling for geometry modification # This step modifies the geometry parameters based on the gradient # and applies dynamic scaling to adjust scene structure gradients = computegradients(sdsloss, targetparams) # Apply dynamic scaling factor to the geometry update # The exact formula for dynamic scaling is not detailed in # Assuming a standard Adam optimizer with a scaling factor applied to geometry-related gradients targetparams = updateparameters(targetparams, gradients, scalingfactor=dynamicscale(step)) return targetparams Parameters: Text Instruction: The natural language command describing the desired 3D modification. Source Scene: The initial 3D object or scene to be edited. Dynamic Scaling: A mechanism to adjust geometry; specific values or formulas are not provided in the sources. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision: The quality of the output depends heavily on the capability of the InstructPix2Pix model to interpret the text instruction in the context of the source scene. Boundaries: The method relies on the source scene as a conditional input; if the source scene is significantly different from the target concept, the optimization may struggle to converge. A network translating images to a 3D model, based on a pix2pix convolutional and deconvolutional ResNet, outputting vertex offsets from a base model. It predicts offsets from a base model (uniform sphere with predefined topology) rather than absolute coordinates to improve convergence smoothness. It optionally predicts symmetry by splitting the model into four quarters, predicting shifts for one quarter, mirroring it, and predicting shifts for the mirrored quarter until all four are predicted. It also predicts uniform translation and scaling values to reduce offset magnitude and improve stability. Regularization on the 3D mesh considers angles between normals, edge lengths, and curvature. Input: Images. Internal State: Single representative image (from pix2pix component). Output: 3 \times \#vertices values from two fully connected layers, passed through a sigmoid layer, then linearly transformed to range [-1, 1]. A text-based 3D facial alteration technique utilizing malleable NeRF. It manages facial distortion by instructing a scene manipulator to use hidden codes and adapt to depict different latent codes for scene manipulation using a Positional Conditional Anchor Combiner (PAC). It successfully mirrors the visual characteristics of descriptive and emotionally charged texts, preserving the visual integrity and essence of 3D faces. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Measured Performance: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Leverages powerful text-to-image models (InstructPix2Pix) for instruction following. Limitations: Relies on the quality of the source scene and the diffusion model. When to use: When editing an existing 3D scene based on text instructions is required. When not to use: When generating 3D content from scratch without a source scene is required (use DreamFusion instead). Instruct 3D-to-3D was introduced as a method for 3D editing following text instructions. It utilizes InstructPix2Pix for instruction following and SDS loss for optimization. It is part of a series of 3D editing works that utilize the SDS algorithm. name: Focaldreamer
head: GSEditor-DDS, GSEditor-iN2N
body: Focaldreamer is a 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) editing method that performs localized geometric and textural modifications guided by text prompts. It solves the problem of precise, focal-region editing in existing 3D scenes without degrading the background. It distinguishes itself from sibling methods like I3DS by explicitly utilizing rendered normal maps as shape encodings for the text-to-image (T2I) model and employing a pixelwise discriminative mask to unify base and editable textures, thereby ensuring geometric consistency during optimization. Inputs: An existing 3D Gaussian Splatting scene (base shape). A text prompt describing the desired edit. A mask defining the focal region for editing. Outputs: An edited 3D Gaussian Splatting scene with modified geometry and textures in the focal region. Data Structures: 3DGS Scene: Standard 3DGS representation containing Gaussian primitives with position, covariance, opacity, spherical harmonics coefficients, and scale. Editable Ellipsoids: A set of Gaussian primitives initialized in the focal regions to allow for geometric deformation. Pixelwise Discriminative Mask: A binary or soft mask M of image resolution, where M=1 indicates the focal region and M=0 indicates the background. Steps: 1. Initialization: Initiate the editing process with the base 3DGS shape. Initialize editable ellipsoids (Gaussian primitives) specifically within the focal regions defined by the user or prompt. 2. Rendering: Render the scene from the current camera viewpoint. This rendering includes both the base shape textures and the editable textures of the ellipsoids. The final pixel color C is computed by compositing these layers, weighted by the discriminative mask M. 3. Normal Map Generation: Render the normal maps of the current 3DGS scene. These normal maps serve as the shape encoding for the T2I model, providing geometric constraints to the diffusion prior. 4. Loss Computation: SDS Loss: Compute the Score Distillation Sampling (SDS) loss [89] using the T2I model. The input to the T2I model is the rendered image (or a latent representation thereof) combined with the normal maps as conditioning. The loss guides the optimization towards the text prompt semantics. Regularization: Incorporate additional regularization terms to improve editing quality. These typically include constraints on Gaussian opacity, scale, and position to prevent artifacts and maintain structural integrity. 5. Optimization: Update the parameters of the editable ellipsoids (position, scale, rotation, opacity, SH coefficients) using gradient descent on the combined loss. The base shape parameters are typically frozen or heavily regularized to preserve background integrity. 6. Iteration: Repeat steps 2-5 for a fixed number of iterations or until convergence. Formulas: SDS Loss: \mathcal{L}{SDS} = \mathbb{E}{t, \epsilon} \left[ w(t) (\epsilon\theta(zt; y, t) - \epsilon) \right], where zt is the noisy latent, y includes the rendered image and normal maps, and \epsilon\theta is the denoiser. Composite Image: I = M \cdot I{editable} + (1 - M) \cdot I{base}. Parameters: Learning rate: Not given in the sources. Number of iterations: Not given in the sources. SDS weight w(t): Standard cosine schedule or constant, as per [89]. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision: Normal map rendering must be accurate to provide meaningful shape encoding. Boundaries: The discriminative mask M must be smooth or carefully handled to avoid visible seams between edited and base regions. Degenerate Input: If the focal region is too small, the edit may not be perceptible; if too large, it may overwrite significant parts of the scene. RealmDreamer is a variant that utilizes diffusion priors from inpainting and depth estimation models to generate different viewpoints of a scene iteratively. Unlike Focaldreamer which focuses on editing a single scene with a mask, RealmDreamer uses these priors to synthesize consistent multi-view data for scene composition or generation. It is chosen when iterative viewpoint generation is required for scene-level consistency rather than localized editing. See RealmDreamer for details. Time Complexity: Depends on the number of optimization iterations and the cost of rendering normal maps and images per iteration. Typically comparable to other 3DGS editing methods using SDS. Memory Complexity: Standard 3DGS memory plus overhead for storing normal maps and intermediate gradients. Strengths: Precise focal editing; preserves background integrity via discriminative masking; leverages normal maps for better geometric control. Limitations: Requires careful mask definition; quality depends on the T2I model's ability to interpret normal maps; may introduce artifacts if regularization is insufficient. When to use: When localized, text-guided editing of a specific region in a 3D scene is required. When not to use: When global scene generation or editing is needed; when normal map rendering is not feasible. Focaldreamer, also known as GSEditor-DDS and GSEditor-iN2N, is part of the latest series of methods [21,24-26, 156] that employ SDS loss within 3DGS to facilitate creative editing. It builds on the idea of using 3DGS for precise and flexible modifications. The method was introduced in the context of 3D editing surveys, highlighting the use of text prompts and discriminative masks for localized changes. It is related to other editing methods like TIP-Editor and CustomNeRF, but distinguishes itself by its specific use of normal maps and ellipsoids. name: I3DS
head: I3DS (Iterative 3D Diffusion Synthesis), Iterative 3D Diffusion Synthesis
body: I3DS is an iterative framework for super-resolving a Low-Resolution (LR) Neural Radiance Field (NeRF) into a Super-Resolution (SR) NeRF by alternating between 2D image upscaling via diffusion models and 3D NeRF synchronization to ensure view consistency. It solves the problem of generating high-fidelity, view-consistent 3D geometry and texture from LR inputs without requiring large multi-view image datasets or high-resolution reference images. Unlike methods that jointly optimize 2D and 3D parameters in a single loop, I3DS segregates the process into distinct upscaling and synchronization stages, allowing it to achieve higher quality than prior-based methods while being significantly faster than diffusion-guided methods like DreamFusion. Inputs: \omega{lr}: The initial low-resolution NeRF weights. I{lr}: The set of low-resolution reference images. P{tr}: The set of training camera poses. y{text}: A fixed text prompt embedding (e.g., "subject, high resolution, 4K, photo"). Outputs: \omega{sr}: The super-resolved NeRF weights. Data Structures: NeRF (\omega): Represents the radiance field. The implementation uses Instant-NGP as the default backbone. Latent Space: Images are encoded into latent vectors z using a Variational Autoencoder (VAE). Ray Data: Each ray is defined by origin ro, direction rd, and center color ctr. Parameters: max\stage\iter: Total number of I3DS cycles. Default is 4. max\sync\iter: Number of synchronization steps per stage. Not given in the sources. batch\size: Number of patches processed during upscaling. Default is 16. lr: Learning rate for all learnable parameters. Default is 1e-2. patch\size: Resolution of random crops in latent space. Default is 128 \times 128 (corresponding to 512 \times 512 image pixels). Algorithm: The method iterates through stages. In each stage, it first upscales the rendered images using a Refinement Step Diffusion (RSD) model, then synchronizes the NeRF to these new images. 1. Initialize \omega = \omega{lr}. 2. Loop for stage\iter from 0 to max\stage\iter: a. Upscaling Stage: i. Render low-resolution images from the current NeRF: x0 = \text{RENDER\IMAGE}(\omega, P{tr}). ii. Interpolate x0 by 4x: x0 = \text{INTERPOLATE\X4}(x0). iii. Encode the interpolated image into latent space: z0 = \text{VAE\ENCODE}(x0). iv. Refine the latent z0 using RSD with LR images I{lr} and text prompt y{text}: z'0 = \text{RSD}(z0, I{lr}, y{text}). v. Decode the refined latent back to image space: x'0 = \text{VAE\DECODE}(z'0). vi. Set the training image for synchronization: I{tr} = x'0. b. Synchronization Stage: i. Loop for sync\iter from 0 to max\sync\iter: 1. Sample rays from I{tr} and P{tr} to get origin ro, direction rd, and center color ctr: ro, rd, ctr = \text{SAMPLE\RAYS}(I{tr}, P{tr}). 2. Render the rays using the current NeRF \omega: \hat{c} = \text{RENDER\RAYS}(ro, rd). 3. Perform gradient descent on \omega to minimize the difference between rendered color \hat{c} and center ctr: Update \omega \leftarrow \omega - \eta \nabla\omega \|\hat{c} - ctr\|^2. 4. Store old weights (for potential rollback or logging, though not explicitly used in the update step shown): \omega{old} \leftarrow \omega. 3. Return \omega{sr} = \omega. RSD Refinement Details: The RSD step refines the latent z0 to be consistent with LR images I{lr} while adding high-frequency details guided by diffusion. It is related to Score Distillation Sampling (SDS) but operates on latent residuals. Input to RSD: Latent z0, text prompt y{text}, noise level y{noise\level}, min timestep t{min}, max timestep t{max}, LR images I{lr}. Output: Refined latent residuals h\theta. The RSD objective is derived from the difference of latent vector residuals zt and \hat{z}t (the one-step denoised estimate). The loss is defined as L{RSD} = \|\frac{\partial z{t-1}}{\partial \theta} - \frac{\partial \hat{z}{t-1}}{\partial \theta}\|. \hat{z}{t-1} is obtained directly from the predicted noise \hat{\epsilon}\phi(zt, y, t) using the DDPM denoising equation, avoiding re-noising \hat{z}0. In practice, RSD is applied to random crops of size 128 \times 128 in latent space (corresponding to 512 \times 512 image patches) with a batch size of 16. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision: The method relies on the stability of the VAE encode/decode cycle and the diffusion model's denoising process. Ensure that the VAE latent space normalization matches the diffusion model's expected input distribution. Boundaries: The 4x interpolation step assumes the LR NeRF output is compatible with standard image interpolation. If the NeRF output contains NaNs or extreme values, interpolation may fail; clamp or filter invalid pixels before encoding. Degenerate Input: If I{lr} is missing or severely degraded, RSD may hallucinate inconsistent details. The method assumes I{lr} provides a consistent geometric prior. Time Complexity: The optimization time is dominated by the diffusion upscaling and NeRF synchronization steps. I3DS takes approximately 6.00 hours for the reported experiments. Memory Complexity: Uses dynamic ray sampling to increase ray count when the occupancy grid is pruned, optimizing GPU memory usage. Patch-based processing (128 \times 128 latent crops) reduces memory footprint during upscaling. Measured Performance: On the LLFF dataset, I3DS achieves the highest PSNR and SSIM scores among prior-based methods (DiSR-NeRF, IN2N, DreamFusion-SDS, SDx4). NIQE scores improve with increasing I3DS cycles, indicating convergence to high-quality details. Scaling: The method scales with the number of stages (default 4) and sync iterations. Increasing stages improves quality but increases time linearly. Strengths: View-consistent super-resolution without high-res reference images; faster than DreamFusion due to segregated stages; high detail generation via diffusion. Limitations: Longer optimization time than NGP, SDx4, NeRF-SR, and IN2N due to RSD optimization. Relies on the quality of the LR NeRF and LR images. When to use: When super-resolving a NeRF from LR inputs without high-res references is required, and view consistency is critical. When not to use: When computational speed is the primary constraint and high resolution is not needed; use standard NeRF training or simple upsampling instead. I3DS was introduced in the paper "DiSR-NeRF: Diffusion-Guided View-Consistent Super-Resolution NeRF". It builds on the Instant-NGP backbone and utilizes Stable Diffusion for upscaling. The method was developed to address the limitations of existing NeRF super-resolution methods that either require high-resolution reference images or suffer from view inconsistency. The research was supported by the National Research Foundation, Singapore under its AI Singapore Programmes. name: DITTO-NeRF
head: Diffusion-based Iterative Text To Omni-directional 3D Model
body: DITTO-NeRF is a pipeline for generating high-quality 3D Neural Radiance Fields (NeRF) from a single text prompt or a reference image. It solves the trade-off between fidelity and diversity in text-to-3D generation by constructing a high-quality partial 3D object for limited "in-boundary" (IB) angles and iteratively reconstructing the remaining "outer-boundary" (OB) angles using an inpainting latent diffusion model. Unlike DreamFusion, which uses a proprietary diffusion model (Imagen), DITTO-NeRF leverages Stable Diffusion via a Latent NeRF representation, achieving higher fidelity and computation-efficient diversity within reasonable training times. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: Text prompt y; optional reference image I. If I is absent, it is synthesized from y and a background prompt y{bg}. Outputs: A video V{out} of rendered views of the 3D object, derived from the trained NeRF model \mathcal{N}. Data Structures: NeRF Model \mathcal{N}: A latent NeRF that outputs a 4-channel latent vector zr and weight values P{ws} for each point on a ray, rather than direct RGB. IB Pre-rendered Data: A set of N pre-rendered latent vectors Zp and masks M corresponding to uniform angles within the IB region. Camera Parameters: Principal points cx, cy = 256; focal lengths fx, fy \approx 45\text{mm} (assumed equivalent); image dimensions 512 \times 512. Parameters: t{total}: Total iterations. Typical value: 5000. tu: End of PGVS beta decrease. Value: 0.3 \times t{total} (1500). i{refine}: Iteration threshold for refinement. Value: 1500. N: Number of pre-rendered IB views. Value: 64. \alpha0, \beta0: Initial beta distribution parameters. Values: 2, 8. \lambda{iSDS}: Weight for iSDS loss. \lambda{sp}: Weight for sparsity loss. Value: 5 \cdot 10^{-5}. \zeta: Reliability guide parameter. Value: 2. \lambda\eta: Decay rate for reliability guide. Value: 8. N{patch}: Number of patches in refinement. Value: 256. k (or S{patch}): Patch size. Value: 16. \epsilon: Clipping bound for sparsity loss. Value: 10^{-5}. Step 1: IB 3D Object Construction If no reference image I is provided, generate one: 1. Concatenate text y and background text y{bg} to form y{image}. 2. Pass y{image} through CLIP to get text embedding. 3. Generate latent z{image} using Inpainting-LDM. 4. Decode z{image} using decoder D to create image I. Generate IB 3D object from I: 1. Extract relative depth map from I using MiDaS monocular depth estimation. 2. Compose a point cloud from the depth map using camera intrinsics (cx, cy, fx, fy). 3. Remove outlier vertices based on proximity to other vertices using a predetermined standard deviation. 4. Apply Poisson surface reconstruction to generate a mesh. 5. Remove mesh parts with density less than a certain quantile. 6. Render N views (uniformly distributed within IB angles) to obtain RGB images, depth, and latent vectors Zp using the VAE encoder of the LDM. Store corresponding masks M. Step 2: Training Loop For iteration i = 1 to t{total}: 1. View Sampling: Determine camera angles \theta, \phi using Progressive Global View Sampling (PGVS). 2. Ray Casting: Obtain ray origin o and direction d via Render-ray(\theta, \phi). 3. NeRF Rendering: Render latent zr and weights P{ws} from \mathcal{N}(o, d). 4. IB Handling: If the angle is in the IB region: Use Find-closest to retrieve pre-rendered zp and M. Else (OB region), no pre-rendered data is used directly in the loss calculation for IB, but zr is used for OB. 5. Phase Selection: If i \le i{refine}, execute Training. If i > i{refine}, execute Refinement. Training Procedure (i \le i{refine}): 1. Create training text embedding y{train} = \text{CLIP}(y, y{dir}), where y{dir} is direction info. 2. Calculate Inpainting SDS Loss (L{iSDS}): If IB: L{iSDS} = \text{inpainting-LDM}(zp, y{train}, M). If OB: Define mask M0 = J / (H \cdot f{scale}) (where J is likely a constant or identity, f{scale} is a scaling factor). L{iSDS} = \text{inpainting-LDM}(zr, y{train}, M0). 3. Calculate Reliability Guidance (LR): LR = [\zeta \cdot M + \eta(t) \cdot (1 - M)] \|zr - zp\|1, where \eta(t) = e^{-t/\lambda\eta}. Note: LR is applied to correct zr towards zp in IB regions, with reliability increasing over time. 4. Calculate Sparsity Loss (L{sp}): \alpha is the weighted sum of a ray clipped to [\epsilon, 1-\epsilon]. L{sp} = -\mathbb{E}[\alpha \log(\alpha) + (1-\alpha) \log(1-\alpha)]. 5. Total Loss: L{total} = \lambda{iSDS} L{iSDS} + \deltaR(\theta, \phi) LR + \lambda{sp} L{sp}. 6. Update \mathcal{N} with L{total}. Refinement Procedure (i > i{refine}): 1. Create refinement text embedding y{refine} = \text{CLIP}(y, y{dir}). 2. Calculate dimensions H, W using Dimension-Refine(i): \text{rate} = \frac{i - t{total} \cdot f{ref}}{t{total} \cdot (1 - f{ref})} H = 64 \times (1 + \text{rate}), W = 64 \times (1 + \text{rate}). 3. Resize M and zp to H \times W if IB. 4. Apply Add-Patch(M): For j = 1 to N{patch}: Pick random coordinates Px, Py within mask size S{mask}. Set M[Px: Px + k, Py: Py + k] = 1. 5. Calculate L{iSDS}: If IB: L{iSDS} = \text{inpainting-LDM}(zp, y{refine}, M). If OB: L{iSDS} = \text{inpainting-LDM}(zr, y{refine}, M0). 6. Calculate L{sp}. 7. Total Loss: L{total} = \lambda{iSDS} L{iSDS} + \lambda{sp} L{sp} (Reliability guidance omitted). 8. Update \mathcal{N} with L{total}. Rendering Output: For each rendering angle: 1. Get o, d via Render-ray. 2. Get zr from \mathcal{N}(o, d). 3. Decode I{out} = D(zr). 4. Append I{out} to V{out}. PGVS Formula: Sampling viewing position x at time t: f(x; t) = \begin{cases} \frac{x^{\alpha(t)-1} (1-x)^{\beta(t)-1}}{B(\alpha(t), \beta(t))} & \text{if } t < tu \\ U(0, 1) & \text{if } t \ge tu \end{cases} Where \alpha(t) = \alpha0 + (1 - \alpha0) \frac{t}{tu} and \beta(t) = \beta0 + (1 - \beta0) \frac{t}{tu}. Angles are sampled via inverse CDF: \theta, \phi = ( \int f(x; t) dx)^{-1} (U{\theta,\phi}(0, 1)) \cdot \text{range}(\theta, \phi). Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def DITTONeRF(y, I=None): # Step 1: Generate IB 3D Object if I is None: yimage = CLIP(y + ybg) zimage = InpaintingLDM(yimage) I = Decoder(zimage) Zp, M = GenerateIB3D(I) # Uses MiDaS, Poisson Reconstruction # Step 2: Training Loop for i in range(1, ttotal + 1): theta, phi = PGVS(i, alpha0, beta0, tu, ttotal) if IBCheck(theta, phi): zp, M = FindClosest(Zp, M, theta, phi) IBFlag = True else: IBFlag = False o, d = RenderRay(theta, phi) zr, Pws = NeRFN(o, d) if i <= irefine: TrainingStep(NeRFN, zp, M, zr, Pws, y, theta, phi, IBFlag) else: RefinementStep(NeRFN, zp, M, zr, Pws, y, theta, phi, IBFlag, i) # Step 3: Rendering Vout = [] for theta, phi in RenderingAngles: o, d = RenderRay(theta, phi) zr = NeRFN(o, d) Iout = Decoder(zr) Vout.append(Iout) return Vout def TrainingStep(N, zp, M, zr, Pws, y, theta, phi, IB): ytrain = CLIP(y, DirectionInfo(theta, phi)) if IB: LiSDS = InpaintingLDM(zp, ytrain, M) LR = ReliabilityGuide(zp, zr, M, t=i) else: M0 = J / (H fscale) # H, fscale not fully defined in source for training phase, assumed constant or derived LiSDS = InpaintingLDM(zr, ytrain, M0) Lsp = SparsityLoss(Pws) Ltotal = lambdaiSDS LiSDS + deltaR(theta, phi) LR + lambdasp Lsp N.Update(Ltotal) def RefinementStep(N, zp, M, zr, Pws, y, theta, phi, IB, i): yrefine = CLIP(y, DirectionInfo(theta, phi)) H, W = DimensionRefine(i, ttotal, fref) if IB: M = Resize(M, H, W) M = AddPatch(M, Npatch, k, Smask) zp = Resize(zp, H, W) LiSDS = InpaintingLDM(zp, yrefine, M) else: M0 = J / (H fscale) LiSDS = InpaintingLDM(zr, yrefine, M0) Lsp = SparsityLoss(Pws) Ltotal = lambdaiSDS LiSDS + lambdasp Lsp N.Update(Ltotal) def ReliabilityGuide(zp, zr, M, t): etat = exp(-t / lambdaeta) return (zeta M + etat (1 - M)) L1Norm(zr - zp) def DimensionRefine(iter, ttotal, fref): rate = (iter - ttotal fref) / (ttotal (1 - fref)) H = 64 (1 + rate) W = 64 (1 + rate) return H, W def AddPatch(M, Npatch, k, Smask): for in range(Npatch): Px = Random(Smask) Py = Random(Smask) M[Px: Px + k, Py: Py + k] = 1 return M Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Depth Estimation: MiDaS relies on shadows and model priors. Images with minimal shadows or out-of-distribution inputs lead to inaccurate depth, causing inadequate IB 3D objects. Diffusion Quality: Poor quality or low-probability images from the diffusion model may not follow image priors, causing convergence issues and discontinuity between the image prior and diffusion-generated parts. IB Angle Width: If the IB angle is too narrow, matching between IB and OB is insufficient. If too wide, the Find-closest process becomes a bottleneck. Pre-rendering Count (N): Too small N leads to insufficient IB training; too large increases computational burden. N=64 is optimal. Patch Refinement: Insufficient N{patch} fails to produce appropriate refinement; excessive N{patch} may disrupt existing IB structures. Time and Memory Complexity: The method uses Latent NeRF, which is more computation-efficient than standard NeRF. It achieves satisfactory quality within reasonable training time compared to Stable-DreamFusion. Scaling: The refinement stage linearly increases resolution from 64 \times 64 to 128 \times 128. Strengths: Higher fidelity and quality in image-to-3D correspondence; higher fidelity and computation-efficient diversity in text-to-3D generation compared to Stable Diffusion-based studies. Limitations: Dependent on the quality of the monocular depth estimation and the diffusion model's ability to generate high-quality images. Convergence issues may arise with low-probability diffusion outputs. DITTO-NeRF was introduced in the paper "DITTO-NeRF: Diffusion-based Iterative Text To Omni-directional 3D Model". It builds on the DreamFusion approach but replaces the proprietary Imagen model with Stable Diffusion via Latent NeRF. The sparsity loss used in the method was introduced in Dreamfields and employed in Latent-NeRF. The method is supported by NRF grants. name: Text-to-Image-to-3D Reconstruction
head: Two-step text-to-3D
body: Text-to-Image-to-3D Reconstruction is a two-step procedure that reconstructs a 3D object from a text prompt by first generating a 2D image using a diffusion model, then lifting that image to 3D using RealFusion. It differs from one-step text-to-3D methods [33] by offering easier user control over the generated appearance and potentially addressing diversity issues in generation. Inputs: A text prompt P. Outputs: A 3D radiance field (NeRF) representing the object. Data Structures: 1. 2D Diffusion Model: A pretrained text-to-image model (e.g., Stable Diffusion) capable of sampling images from noise conditioned on P. 2. RealFusion: A single-image 3D reconstruction method that optimizes a NeRF to match a single input image and its depth/normal estimates. Steps: 1. Image Generation: Sample a large number of 2D images from the diffusion model conditioned on the text prompt P. 2. Image Selection: The user selects a single desired image I{sel} from the generated samples. 3. 3D Reconstruction: Lift I{sel} to 3D using RealFusion. RealFusion optimizes a NeRF \mathcal{N} to minimize the difference between rendered views of \mathcal{N} and the input image I{sel}. The optimization uses an L2 reconstruction loss. View-specific prompting (e.g., "back view") can be used during the RealFusion optimization to mitigate the Janus problem. Parameters: Diffusion Model: Not specified in sources. RealFusion Loss: L2 loss is used; LPIPS and SSIM were tested but excluded for simplicity/computational cost. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Janus Problem: Reconstructions may exhibit two or more faces because the loss function attempts to make every view resemble the input image. View-specific prompting alleviates but does not eliminate this. Floaters: Artifacts may appear; image-specific prompts help alleviate this. Diversity: One-step methods may suffer from lack of diversity; this two-step approach allows user selection to address this. Dream Fields combines NeRF with CLIP to generate diverse 3D objects solely from natural language descriptions by optimizing the radiance field via multi-view constraints based on CLIP scores on the image caption. It differs from Text-to-Image-to-3D by using CLIP scores directly as a loss signal rather than generating an intermediate image. Choose this method when direct text-to-3D optimization without intermediate image selection is preferred. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Easier user control compared to one-step text-to-3D. May address diversity of generation issues. Single-image textual inversion is usually not necessary as sampled images are well-aligned with prompts. Limitations: Susceptible to the Janus problem. When to use: When user control over the specific appearance of the generated 3D object is required. The method is described in the context of RealFusion, which explores reconstructing 3D objects from text prompts via an intermediate image. It is compared to one-step text-to-3D approaches [33]. Dream Fields, a related concept, was introduced by [JMB 21]. name: DreamAvatar
body: DreamAvatar is a diffusion-based 3D avatar generation method that synthesizes text-guided 3D human avatars by combining a Neural Radiance Field (NeRF) representation with a pre-trained 2D diffusion model. It addresses the challenge of generating high-fidelity, personalized 3D human models from text prompts by leveraging an SMPL model as a geometric shape prior. Unlike general scene generation methods, DreamAvatar is specifically designed for human avatars, using the SMPL prior to constrain the NeRF optimization to plausible human geometries. DreamAvatar follows a DreamFusion-like optimization loop where a NeRF is trained to render images that match the distribution of a text-conditioned diffusion model. The key distinction is the integration of an SMPL parametric model to provide a strong shape prior for the human body/head. Inputs: Text prompt P describing the desired avatar. Pre-trained 2D diffusion model \phi. SMPL model parameters (initial guess or fixed template). NeRF parameters \theta (representing the radiance field). Outputs: Optimized NeRF parameters \theta and SMPL parameters defining the 3D avatar. Data Structures: NeRF: Standard multi-layer perceptron mapping 3D coordinates and viewing directions to color and density. SMPL Model: Parametric human body model providing a mesh surface and pose/shape parameters. Diffusion Model: U-Net architecture conditioned on text embeddings. Steps: 1. Initialization: Initialize NeRF parameters \theta and SMPL parameters. 2. Viewpoint Sampling: Sample a random camera viewpoint around the avatar. 3. Rendering: Render a 2D image x from the current NeRF state at the sampled viewpoint. 4. Noise Addition: Sample a diffusion timestep t and Gaussian noise \epsilon. 5. Latent Perturbation: Create a noisy version zt = \alphat x + \sigmat \epsilon. 6. Noise Prediction: Pass zt, the text prompt P, and timestep t into the diffusion model \phi to predict the noise \hat{\epsilon} = \hat{\epsilon}\phi(zt; P, t). 7. Loss Computation: Compute gradients \nabla\theta \mathcal{L} using the difference between predicted and actual noise, adapted with Score Distillation Sampling (SDS) and the SMPL shape prior. 8. Optimization: Update NeRF parameters \theta (and SMPL parameters) using gradient descent. 9. Iteration: Repeat steps 2–8 for a fixed number of iterations or until convergence. Formulas: The core loss is derived from Score Distillation Sampling (SDS), adapted to incorporate the SMPL shape prior. Not given in the sources. Parameters: Not given in the sources. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Not given in the sources. AvatarStudio is a text-based editing method for dynamic head avatars using NeRF and diffusion. It is distinguished from its siblings by its focus on time-varying multi-view performance captures and its use of View- and Time-aware Score Distillation Sampling (VT-SDS) for personalized editing across the time and view domains. Choose this method when editing dynamic, time-varying head avatars from multi-view video data with text prompts. Link: AvatarStudio. Time Complexity: High, due to the iterative nature of NeRF optimization and the computational cost of diffusion model inference at each step. Memory Complexity: High, storing the NeRF weights, SMPL parameters, and intermediate rendering buffers. Performance: Generates high-fidelity 3D avatars with good text alignment. Strengths: Strong geometric priors via SMPL reduce artifacts; text-guided control. Limitations: Not given in the sources. When to use: For generating personalized 3D human avatars from text. DreamAvatar was introduced in April 2023. It emerged as part of the growing research area of diffusion-based 3D avatar generation with text guidance, powered by neural fields and NeRF. It is conceptually similar to DreamHuman (June 2023) and AvatarVerse (August 2023), all of which use an SMPL model as a shape prior and text-guided 2D image generation via diffusion to create training data in a DreamFusion-like pipeline. name: Single-Stage Diffusion NeRF Training
head: Joint optimization of NeRF and Diffusion Prior, SSDNeRF training
body: Single-Stage Diffusion NeRF Training (SSDNeRF) is a method that jointly optimizes scene codes, a diffusion prior, and a NeRF decoder in a single training stage to minimize a combined loss of rendering fidelity and diffusion prior consistency. Unlike two-stage methods that ignore the prior term during autoencoder training—effectively setting the render-to-prior weight ratio to infinity and resulting in biased and noisy scene codes—this approach constrains codes with both terms simultaneously. It builds on Diffusion-guided Optimization by integrating the prior directly into the latent space optimization loop. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: A dataset of images \{y{ij}^{gt}\} with corresponding rays \{r{ij}^{gt}\}, where i indexes the scene and j indexes the ray (pixel). Outputs: Optimized scene codes \{xi\}, diffusion prior parameters \phi, and NeRF decoder parameters \psi. Data Structures: Scene Codes (xi): Represented as triplanes with shape \mathbb{R}^{3 \times 6 \times 128 \times 128}. Diffusion Prior (\phi): A U-Net based Gaussian diffusion model that takes a noisy code xi^{(t)} and timestep t as input, outputting a denoised code \hat{x}i. NeRF Decoder (\psi): A decoder that maps scene codes and ray coordinates to pixel RGB values y{\psi}(x, r). Formulas: The total loss function is defined as: \mathcal{L} = \lambda{\text{rend}} \mathcal{L}{\text{rend}}(\{xi\}, \psi) + \lambda{\text{diff}} \mathcal{L}{\text{diff}}(\{xi\}, \phi) where \mathcal{L}{\text{rend}} is the rendering loss against known observations and \mathcal{L}{\text{diff}} is the approximate upper bound of the diffusion negative log-likelihood (NLL). The empirical weighting factors are calculated as: \lambda{\text{diff}}:= \frac{c{\text{diff}}}{\text{EMA} \|xi\|F^2} \lambda{\text{rend}}:= \frac{c{\text{rend}} (1 - e^{-0.1 Nv})}{Nv} where c{\text{diff}} and c{\text{rend}} are constant scales, Nv is the number of available views, and \text{EMA} \|xi\|F^2 is the exponential moving average of the scene codes' Frobenius norms. The rendering weight calibration prevents the loss from scaling linearly with the number of rays under the ray independence assumption. Algorithm: The training uses a nested loop structure with prior gradient caching to address the computational expense of the diffusion loss. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. Initialize scene codes {xi}, diffusion prior parameters phi, and NeRF decoder parameters psi Initialize EMA accumulator for scene codes' Frobenius norms Set constants cdiff, crend, Kout, Kin for kout in range(1, Kout + 1): # Outer loop: Sample a batch of scenes batchscenes = SampleBatchScenes(Bsc) # Compute gradients for diffusion loss with respect to phi and {xi} # Ldiff is the diffusion prior loss gphi, gxdiff = ComputeGradients(Ldiff, params=[phi, batchscenes], weights=[lambdadiff]) # Update diffusion parameters using Adam phi = AdamUpdate(phi, gphi) # Cache the prior gradient for reuse in inner loop cachedgxdiff = gxdiff for kin in range(1, Kin + 1): # Inner loop: Sample a batch of rays batchrays = SampleBatchRays(Bray) # Compute gradients for rendering loss with respect to {xi} # Lrend is the rendering fidelity loss gxrend = ComputeGradients(Lrend, params=[batchscenes], weights=[lambdarend]) # Combine cached diffusion gradient with current rendering gradient gxtotal = gxrend + cachedgxdiff # Update scene codes using Adam with the total gradient batchscenes = AdamUpdate(batchscenes, gxtotal) # Update EMA of scene codes' Frobenius norms for dynamic weighting UpdateEMA(batchscenes) # If this is the last inner iteration, update decoder parameters if kin == Kin: gpsi = ComputeGradients(Lrend, params=[psi], weights=[lambdarend]) psi = AdamUpdate(psi, gpsi) Parameters: K{out}: Number of outer iterations. K{in}: Number of inner iterations per outer loop. c{\text{diff}}, c{\text{rend}}: Constant scales for empirical weighting. Nv: Number of available views. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Computational Cost: The diffusion loss \mathcal{L}{\text{diff}} is computationally expensive to evaluate compared to the rendering loss \mathcal{L}{\text{rend}}, which reduces overall efficiency. The method mitigates this via prior gradient caching, reusing \nablax \lambda{\text{diff}} \mathcal{L}{\text{diff}} for multiple Adam steps while refreshing rendering gradients each step. Bias in Two-Stage Methods: If the prior term is ignored during initial training (as in two-stage methods), the resulting scene codes become biased and noisy. Time Complexity: The method is less efficient than rendering-only optimization due to the expensive diffusion loss evaluation. However, prior gradient caching reduces the number of diffusion passes required, accelerating reconstruction. Memory Complexity: Requires storing scene codes \{xi\}, diffusion parameters \phi, and decoder parameters \psi. Strengths: Produces more generalizable and less noisy scene codes compared to two-stage methods by constraining codes with both rendering and prior terms. Limitations: Higher computational cost per iteration compared to standard NeRF training. When to use: When high-quality 3D generation and reconstruction are required, and computational resources allow for joint optimization. When not to use: When real-time performance is critical and the overhead of diffusion prior evaluation is prohibitive. SSDNeRF was introduced in the paper "Single-Stage Diffusion NeRF: A Unified Approach to 3D Generation and Reconstruction". It addresses the limitations of previous two-stage generative neural field methods, which ignore the prior term during autoencoder training, leading to biased and noisy scene codes. The method is related to score distillation techniques. name: ReconFusion
body: ReconFusion is a 3D reconstruction method that recovers high-quality scenes from a limited number of input images (few-view setting) by regularizing a NeRF-based pipeline with a diffusion prior trained for novel view synthesis. Unlike methods that rely solely on geometric constraints or text-guided score distillation, ReconFusion explicitly trains a diffusion model to predict plausible novel views conditioned on input images and poses, then uses this model to supervise the NeRF optimization at unobserved viewpoints. It sets itself apart from siblings like DreamFusion by using a multiview-conditioned diffusion prior rather than a text-conditioned one, and from SparseFusion by sampling a new image at each iteration rather than using multistep sampling from a noisy encoding of the current rendering. ReconFusion consists of two main components: a diffusion model for novel view synthesis and a NeRF optimization loop. The method optimizes a NeRF representation \psi (using Zip-NeRF as the backbone) to minimize two losses: a reconstruction loss on observed views and a sample loss on novel views predicted by the diffusion model. Inputs: A set of N input images x{obs} = \{xi\}{i=1}^N with corresponding camera poses \pi{obs} = \{\pii\}{i=1}^N. A pretrained Latent Diffusion Model (LDM) encoder E, denoising U-Net \epsilon\theta, and decoder D. A pretrained CLIP image encoder. A PixelNeRF-style encoder R\phi. Outputs: Optimized NeRF parameters \psi. Rendered images from novel viewpoints. 1. NeRF (\psi): Standard Zip-NeRF representation. 2. PixelNeRF Encoder (R\phi): A small U-Net that takes input images of resolution 512 \times 512 and outputs a feature map f of resolution 64 \times 64 with 128 channels. 3. Diffusion Model: VAE: Encodes images to latents of dimension 64 \times 64 \times 8 from 512 \times 512 \times 3 input images. U-Net (\epsilon\theta): Takes noisy latents, feature maps, and CLIP embeddings as input. CLIP Embeddings: Text/image embeddings used for cross-attention in the U-Net. Before reconstruction, the diffusion model is finetuned for novel view synthesis. 1. Conditioning: For a target novel view \pi, select the 3 nearest camera positions from the observed inputs \pi{obs}. 2. Feature Rendering: Use the PixelNeRF encoder R\phi to render a feature map f for the target view \pi using the input images and poses: f = R\phi(x{obs}, \pi{obs}, \pi) 3. Latent Encoding: Encode the input images and the target view image (from dataset) into latents using the VAE encoder E. 4. Diffusion Process: Add noise to the target latent z to create zt at timestep t. 5. Cross-Attention: Compute CLIP embeddings of the input images and inject them into the U-Net via cross-attention. 6. Loss: Train the U-Net \epsilon\theta to predict the noise or clean latent. The model is finetuned on a mixture of RealEstate10K, CO3D, MVImgNet, and Objaverse datasets. 7. Classifier-Free Guidance: During training, set input images to all zeros with probability 10% to enable classifier-free guidance. For each training iteration of the NeRF: 1. Sample Observed View: Randomly select an observed pose \pi{obs} and image x{obs}. 2. Render Observed View: Render image x{render} from the current NeRF \psi at \pi{obs}. 3. Compute Reconstruction Loss: Calculate the Charbonnier loss between x{render} and x{obs}: L{recon}(\psi) = \mathbb{E}{x{obs},\pi{obs}} \ell(x(\psi, \pi{obs}), x{obs}) 4. Sample Novel View Pose: Select a novel pose \pi from a distribution based on the input poses (e.g., nearest 3 inputs). 5. Render Novel View Feature Map: Use the PixelNeRF encoder R\phi to generate the feature map f for \pi using the input images. 6. Render Novel View Image: Render image x from the current NeRF \psi at \pi. 7. Compute Noisy Latent: Compute a noisy latent by adding noise to the current NeRF rendering from the sample pose. 8. Diffusion Sampling: Input the noisy latent, feature map f, and CLIP embeddings to the U-Net \epsilon\theta. Perform k=10 DDIM sampling steps to generate a denoised latent \hat{z}. Decode \hat{z} to image \hat{x} using VAE decoder D. Apply classifier-free guidance with scale 3.0. 9. Compute Sample Loss: Calculate the loss between the rendered image x and the diffusion-generated sample \hat{x}: L{sample}(\psi) = \mathbb{E}{\pi,t} w(t) (\|x - \hat{x}\pi\|1 + Lp(x, \hat{x}\pi)) where Lp is the perceptual distance (LPIPS). 10. Total Loss: Combine losses with a weighting factor w(t) that decays linearly from 1 to 0.1 over training: L{total} = L{recon} + w(t) L{sample} 11. Update: Update NeRF parameters \psi using gradient descent. Unverified code. unconditionalnoisepred) # Update currentlatent using standard DDIM step currentlatent = ddimupdate(currentlatent, noisepred, t) return currentlatent def perceptualloss(img1, img2): """Compute LPIPS perceptual distance.""" # Forward pass through pretrained LPIPS network return lpipsnet(img1, img2) def trainreconfusion(inputimages, observedposes, numiterations=1000): """ Train NeRF using ReconFusion. inputimages: List of input images (N images) observedposes: List of observed poses (N poses) """ # Precompute CLIP embeddings for input images clipemb = clipencoder(inputimages) # Annealing schedule for tmin tminstart = 1.0 tminend = 0.0 for step in range(numiterations): # 1. Sample observed view idx = torch.randint(0, len(inputimages), (1,)).item() obsimg = inputimages[idx] obspose = observedposes[idx] # 2. Render observed view renderimgobs = nerf.render(obspose) # 3. Compute Reconstruction Loss (Charbonnier) reconloss = charbonnierloss(renderimgobs, obsimg) # 4. Sample novel view pose novelpose = samplenovelpose(observedposes) # 5. Render feature map for novel view featmap = pixelnerfencoder(inputimages, observedposes, novelpose) # 6. Render novel view image renderimgnovel = nerf.render(novelpose) # 7. Encode to latent latentnovel = vaeencoder(renderimgnovel) # 8. Add noise # tmax is fixed at 1.0 # tmin is annealed tmin = tminstart - (tminstart - tminend) (step / numiterations) t = torch.rand(1).item() (1.0 - tmin) + tmin noisylatent = addnoise(latentnovel, t, alphat=lambda z, t: 1.0 - t, sigmat=lambda z, t: t) # 9. Diffusion Sampling # Use classifier-free guidance scale 3.0 # k=10 steps denoisedlatent = diffusionsample( noisylatent, featmap, clipemb, t, guidancescale=3.0, steps=10) # Decode to image sampleimg = vaedecoder(denoisedlatent) # 10. Compute Sample Loss l1loss = torch.mean(torch.abs(renderimgnovel - sampleimg)) lpipsloss = perceptualloss(renderimgnovel, sampleimg) sampleloss = l1loss + lpipsloss # 11. Weighting decay # Linear decay from 1 to 0.1 wt = 1.0 - 0.9 (step / numiterations) # 12. Total Loss totalloss = reconloss + wt sampleloss # 13. Update optimizer.zerograd() totalloss.backward() optimizer.step() Diffusion Model: Latent Diffusion Model [42] with 64 \times 64 \times 8 latent space, 512 \times 512 \times 3 input resolution. PixelNeRF Encoder: Outputs 64 \times 64 feature map with 128 channels. Classifier-Free Guidance Scale: 3.0. Sampling Steps (k): 10 DDIM steps. Timesteps: t{max} = 1.0 fixed; t{min} annealed from 1.0 to 0.0. Loss Weighting (w(t)): Linearly decayed from 1 to 0.1 over training. Batch Size: 256 (for diffusion model training). Learning Rate: 10^{-4} (for joint training of PixelNeRF and U-Net). NeRF Training Iterations: 1000. Nearest Neighbors: 3 nearest camera positions used for conditioning. Reconstruction Loss: Charbonnier loss. Sample Loss: L1 + LPIPS. Few-View Scenarios: With 3 or 9 views, the reconstruction problem is severely underconstrained. The diffusion prior prevents catastrophic failures and improves robustness. Dense Capture: With 54 views, the method helps reduce "fog" and "floater" artifacts common in NeRF while preserving well-sampled regions. Novel View Selection: Views should not be placed inside objects or behind walls. The method uses a distribution based on known input poses to select reasonable novel views. Time Complexity: The method requires training a diffusion model (250k iterations) and then optimizing the NeRF (1000 iterations). Each NeRF iteration involves rendering, diffusion sampling (10 steps), and loss computation. Memory Complexity: Depends on the NeRF size and the diffusion model (U-Net, VAE, CLIP). The latent space is 64 \times 64 \times 8. Performance: Outperforms existing baselines on forward-facing and 360-degree scenes with few input views (3, 6, 9 views). Strengths: Effective regularizer for few-view NeRFs; reduces artifacts in dense captures; supports any number of input images via PixelNeRF conditioning. Limitations: Requires training a diffusion model on multiview data; relies on the quality of the diffusion prior. When to Use: When only a few photos are available for 3D reconstruction. When Not to Use: When dense capture is available and artifacts are minimal, the overhead may not be justified. ReconFusion was introduced in 2023/2024 by researchers aiming to reduce the need for dense capture in 3D reconstruction. It builds on the idea of using diffusion models as priors for 3D generation, similar to DreamFusion [36] and SparseFusion [67], but specifically conditions the diffusion model on input images and poses for novel view synthesis. The method uses Zip-NeRF as the backbone.
