name: StegaNeRF Training Algorithm
head: StegaNeRF Training Loop
body: StegaNeRF is a training procedure that embeds invisible, recoverable information (such as images or text) into a Neural Radiance Field (NeRF) by jointly optimizing the radiance field and a detector network. It solves the problem of copyright protection and attribution in 3D content by allowing a hidden signal to be decoded from rendered views without degrading visual quality. Unlike standard NeRF training which only minimizes photometric error, StegaNeRF introduces steganographic losses to enforce the presence of a specific hidden signal, distinguishing it from NeRF-Det Training Objectives by providing the specific optimization loop and loss combination required to achieve this embedding. Inputs: Training images \{Yi\} with corresponding camera poses \{Pi\}. Hidden information I to be embedded (e.g., an image). Initial NeRF model parameters \theta0 (after pre-training). Detector network parameters \psi. Learning rates \eta = [\eta0, \eta1] for the NeRF and detector respectively. Loss weights \lambda0, \lambda1, \lambda2, \lambda3. Outputs: Steganographic NeRF model \theta. Detector network F\psi. Data Structures: NeRF \theta: Standard MLP-based radiance field representation. Detector F\psi: A network that takes a rendered view x and the classifier output F{\psic}(x) as input, defined as F\psi(x) = F\psi(x, F{\psic}(x)). Classifier F{\psic}: A sub-network or branch used to classify the presence of the hidden signal. Importance Mask m: A scalar mask computed per pixel to guide gradient flow. Steps: 1. Initialization: Initialize the NeRF model \theta0 and the detector network F\psi. 2. Pre-training: Optimize \theta0 on the training images \{Yi\} with poses \{Pi\} using standard NeRF training (minimizing photometric loss only) to obtain a high-quality initial model. 3. Mask Computation: Compute the importance mask m for \theta0 using Equation (3): w = \frac{|\theta0|^\alpha}{\sum |\theta0|^\alpha}, \quad m = w where \alpha = 3. This mask highlights regions with significant radiance contributions. 4. Optimization Loop: For each training iteration t: a. Sampling: Randomly sample a training pose Pi. b. Rendering: Render the current NeRF view \theta(Pi). c. Steganographic Losses: Compute the following losses defined in Equations (1) and (2): L{cdec}: Classifier loss. L{dec}^+: Positive detection loss (when the hidden signal is present). L{dec}^-: Negative detection loss (when the hidden signal is absent). Note: The source provides the log-likelihood terms for the classifier: \log F{\psic}(\theta(P)) - \log 1 - F{\psic}(\theta0(P)) in Equation (2). d. Photometric Loss: Compute the standard reconstruction loss L{rgb} using Equation (4): L{rgb} = \| \theta(P) - \theta0(P) \| where \theta0(P) represents the ground truth or target view. e. Total Loss: Combine the losses as in Equation (5): L = \lambda0 L{cdec} + \lambda1 L{dec}^+ + \lambda2 L{dec}^- + \lambda3 L{rgb} f. Update Detector: Update detector parameters \psi using gradient descent: \psi \leftarrow \psi - \eta1 \cdot \frac{\partial L}{\partial \psi} g. Update NeRF: Update NeRF parameters \theta using the masked gradient: \theta \leftarrow \theta - \eta0 \cdot \left( m \cdot \frac{\partial L}{\partial \theta} \right) Parameters: \alpha = 3 for the importance mask calculation. \eta = [\eta0, \eta1] are the learning rates for the NeRF and detector, respectively. \lambda0, \lambda1, \lambda2, \lambda3 are the loss weights. Specific values are not given in the sources. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Multi-Scene Scaling: When handling multiple scenes, the data amount increases, requiring an increase in training epochs until convergence. Per-Scene Fitting: Multi-scene training may result in noticeable performance drops compared to single-scene training due to the inherent requirement of per-scene fitting in the NeRF framework. Modality Extension: The framework can embed modalities other than images (e.g., strings, text, audio) by modifying the detector architecture to have a 1D prediction branch. Multi-Identity Embedding is a method for identifying contributing users in collaborative Neural Radiance Field (NeRF) training by embedding customized hidden information about specific clusters of training views. It solves the problem of scalable attribution in multi-user scenarios by allowing a single NeRF model to hide distinct identities for different spatial regions without requiring model retraining for each new watermark. Unlike prior approaches that embed only a single global watermark, this method isolates identity information to specific clusters of anchor views, maintaining high visual quality by preventing false positives for unmarked identities. See Multi-Identity Embedding. This setting extends the StegaNeRF scheme to embed information within multiple scenes simultaneously. It operates in two sub-settings: 1. One-for-All: Embeds a common hidden image across multiple scenes using a single detector F\psi and classifier F{\psic}. 2. One-for-One: Embeds scene-specific hidden images across multiple scenes using a single detector F\psi and classifier F{\psic}. In both cases, the difference lies in the number of hidden images the detector needs to identify and recover. The training procedure samples one scene for every training epoch. Due to the increased data volume, training epochs are increased until convergence. Complexity: The method adds the computational cost of the detector network F\psi and classifier F{\psic} to the standard NeRF rendering pipeline. Performance: Multi-scene settings show a noticeable performance drop compared to single-scene training, attributed to the inherent requirement of per-scene fitting in NeRF frameworks. Strengths: Allows for copyright protection and attribution without retraining the model for each new watermark. Can embed various modalities (images, text, audio). Limitations: Multi-scene training requires more epochs and may suffer from quality degradation compared to single-scene training. StegaNeRF was introduced in the paper "StegaNeRF: Embedding Invisible Information within Neural Radiance Fields". The method builds on the concept of differentiable volume rendering and extends it with steganographic objectives to hide information within the radiance field parameters. It is applicable to scenarios such as protecting cultural landmark reconstructions formed by community contributions. name: Multi-Identity Embedding
body: Multi-Identity Embedding is a method for identifying contributing users in collaborative Neural Radiance Field (NeRF) training by embedding customized hidden information about specific clusters of training views. It solves the problem of scalable attribution in multi-user scenarios by allowing a single NeRF model to hide distinct identities for different spatial regions without requiring model retraining for each new watermark. Unlike prior approaches that embed only a single global watermark, this method isolates identity information to specific clusters of anchor views, maintaining high visual quality by preventing false positives for unmarked identities. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A collection of user-uploaded training images (simulated via the NeRF-W dataset). Output: A NeRF model with an embedded classifier network capable of recovering specific contributor identities based on the rendering viewpoint. Data Structures: Classifier Network (F{\phic}): A neural network component modified from the standard StegaNeRF backbone. It outputs a probability distribution over M+1 classes: M classes corresponding to specific contributor clusters, and one additional class for "unmarked" identities. Steps: 1. Anchor Selection: Select M anchor views with distinct viewing positions from the training set. 2. Cluster Formation: For each anchor view, find the K nearest neighbor views based on viewing position to form a cluster. Each cluster is assumed to have a common contributor identity. 3. Network Modification: Modify the classifier network F{\phic} to output M-class cluster predictions plus one class for identities outside the M clusters. 4. Loss Computation for Unmarked Views: For poses outside the M clusters, compute the decoding loss L^{-dec} and the classification loss L{dec} to ensure no information is recovered for unmarked identities, thereby preventing false positives. Parameters: M: Number of anchor views/clusters. Typical value: 3. K: Number of nearest neighbours per anchor. Typical value: 20. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def multiidentityembedding(trainingimages, M=3, K=20): """ Embeds M distinct contributor identities into a NeRF model. Args: trainingimages: List of training images with camera poses. M: Number of anchor views/clusters. K: Number of nearest neighbours per anchor. Returns: model: Trained NeRF model with embedded identity classifier. """ # Step 1: Select M anchor views with different viewing positions anchors = selectdistinctviews(trainingimages, count=M) # Step 2: Form clusters by finding K nearest neighbours for each anchor clusters = [] for anchor in anchors: neighbors = findknearestneighbors(trainingimages, anchor, k=K) clusters.append(neighbors) # Step 3: Modify classifier network Fphic to output M+1 classes # M classes for clusters, 1 class for unmarked identities classifier = buildclassifier(numoutputclasses=M + 1) # Step 4: Train NeRF with StegaNeRF objectives # For poses outside the M clusters, enforce no information recovery for batch in trainingbatches(trainingimages): # Standard StegaNeRF rendering and encoding steps occur here # Standard NeRF volume rendering and StegaNeRF encoding logic # Compute losses for unmarked views to prevent false positives unmarkedposes = getunmarkedposes(batch.poses, clusters) if unmarkedposes: # Ldec ensures the classifier predicts the 'unmarked' class correctly lossdec = computeclassificationloss(classifier, unmarkedposes, targetclass=M) # L^-dec ensures no hidden information is recoverable for unmarked views lossminusdec = computedecodingloss(classifier, unmarkedposes) totalloss = totalloss + lossdec + lossminusdec # Standard StegaNeRF losses for marked views would also be computed here # Standard StegaNeRF Ldec and L^-dec for marked clusters return trainmodel(trainingimages, classifier, totalloss) Time and Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Measured Performance: The method was evaluated on the NeRF-W dataset using a network backbone similar to NeRFW. Qualitative results show successful recovery of User A, User B, and User C identities within their respective clusters, with low recovery scores for unmarked identities (e.g., 0.2368 for User A's identity in an unmarked region). Strengths: Allows scalable, robust digital watermarking in 3D scenes by accommodating multiple distinct messages as an additional model input. Isolates watermark features to prevent entanglement with scene appearance. Limitations: Requires careful selection of anchor views and nearest neighbours to ensure cluster separation. Performance depends on the quality of the NeRF-W dataset simulation. When to use: When identifying contributing users in collaborative NeRF projects is required. When not to use: When only a single global watermark is sufficient. Multi-Identity Embedding was introduced in the paper "StegaNeRF: Embedding Invisible Information within Neural Radiance Fields". It addresses the scenario where a collection of user-uploaded training images is used to generate a NeRF, and it is meaningful to identify the contributing users in the rendered output. The method extends the StegaNeRF framework to handle multiple identities simultaneously. name: MultiNeRF
head: MultiNeRF-Noised
body: MultiNeRF is a 3D watermarking method that embeds multiple uniquely keyed watermarks within images rendered by a single Neural Radiance Field (NeRF) model, specifically extending the TensoRF architecture. It solves the problem of scalable, robust digital watermarking in 3D scenes by allowing distinct messages to be identified by unique integer IDs at rendering time, without requiring model retraining for each new watermark. Unlike prior approaches that embed only a single watermark, MultiNeRF accommodates multiple distinct messages as an additional model input, maintaining high visual quality by isolating watermark features in a dedicated grid rather than entangling them with scene appearance. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: 3D position x, view direction d, and a watermark integer ID I(n) corresponding to a distinct message M(n). Outputs: Rendered image color C and decoded message m'n (during training). Data Structures: The model extends TensoRF's decomposition into three explicit 3D grids: 1. Geometry Grid (A\sigma): Stores density features. Layout: R^{I \times J \times K}. 2. Appearance Grid (Ac): Stores appearance features. Layout: R^{I \times J \times K \times P}. 3. Watermark Grid (Aw): Stores watermark-specific features. Layout: R^{I \times J \times K \times Cw}, where Cw is the number of watermark feature channels. The spatial resolution (I \times J \times K) is identical to the geometry and appearance grids. Parameters: Embedding Dimension: The learnable embedding layer maps integer IDs to a 16-dimensional message vector en. Grid Resolution: I \times J \times K for all three grids. Numbered Steps: 1. Input Embedding: Map the integer ID I(n) to a 16-dimensional message vector en using a learnable small Multi-Layer Perceptron (MLP) Emb(): en = Emb(I(n)) 2. Modulation Parameter Generation: Pass the embedding en through a learnable linear layer Mod() to output scale \gamman and shift \betan parameters: [\gamman, \betan] = Mod(en) 3. Feature Sampling: Sample the watermark features w(x) from the watermark grid Aw at position x. In TensoRF, this is typically a tensor decomposition, but functionally w(x) represents the feature vector retrieved from Aw at x: w(x) = Aw(x) 4. Feature Modulation: Apply the Hadamard product to scale and shift the sampled watermark features w(x) to produce modulated features w'(x) specific to ID I(n): w'(x) = \gamman \odot w(x) + \betan where \odot is the element-wise (Hadamard) product. 5. Color Decoding: Pass the appearance grid features Gc(x) (sampled from Ac), the modulated watermark features w'(x), and the view direction d to the color decoding function S (an MLP) to compute the final watermark color \tilde{c}(x): \tilde{c}(x) = S(Gc(x), w'(x), d) 6. Volume Rendering: Perform differentiable volume rendering using the computed density \sigma (from A\sigma) and color \tilde{c}(x) along rays. For a ray passing through the scene, sampling Q points xq, the final pixel color C is computed as: C = \sum{q=1}^{Q} \tauq (1 - \exp(-\sigmaq \Deltaq)) \tilde{c}q where \sigmaq and \tilde{c}q are the density and color of the sampled point xq, \Deltaq is the step size along the ray, and \tauq is the transmittance: \tauq = \exp \left( -\sum{p=1}^{q-1} \sigmap \Deltap \right) 7. Training Augmentation (Differentiable): To promote robustness, apply differentiable noise sources and image augmentations to the fully rendered image \tilde{I} before passing it to the watermark decoder. The set of augmentations \mathcal{A} includes brightness, contrast, color jiggle, Gaussian blur, Gaussian noise, hue, posterize, RGB shift, saturation, median blur, box blur, motion blur, sharpness, and differentiable JPEG compression. A random pair of augmentations is applied: \hat{I} = \mathcal{A}(\tilde{I}) 8. Watermark Extraction (Training Phase 1): Freeze the watermark decoder D. Generate a random watermark ID I(n) with ground truth message mn. Render full-resolution image I. Apply a level 2 Discrete Wavelet Transform (DWT) decomposition to I. Use the LL2 sub-band (denoted I{LL2}) as it retains the majority of energy and broad structural features. Pass I{LL2} to decoder D to obtain decoded message m'n. Calculate Binary Cross-Entropy (BCE) loss between mn and m'n: L{secret} = BCE(mn, m'n) Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import torch import torch.nn as nn import torch.nn.functional as F class MultiNeRF: def init(self, gridres, appearancechannels, watermarkchannels): """ Initialize MultiNeRF extending TensoRF.:param gridres: Tuple (I, J, K) for grid dimensions.:param appearancechannels: P, number of appearance feature channels.:param watermarkchannels: Cw, number of watermark feature channels. """ super().init() # TensoRF Grids self.Asigma = nn.Parameter(torch.randn(gridres)) # Geometry grid self.Ac = nn.Parameter(torch.randn(gridres + (appearancechannels,))) # Appearance grid self.Aw = nn.Parameter(torch.randn(gridres + (watermarkchannels,))) # Watermark grid # Embedding Layer: Maps ID to 16-dim vector self.embdim = 16 self.Emb = nn.Sequential( nn.Linear(1, 32), nn.ReLU(), nn.Linear(32, self.embdim)) # Modulation Layer: Linear layer to produce scale and shift self.Mod = nn.Linear(self.embdim, 2 watermarkchannels) # Color Decoder MLP (S) # Input: Appearance features + Modulated Watermark features + View direction # Note: TensoRF's S MLP structure is simplified here for clarity self.S = nn.Sequential( nn.Linear(appearancechannels + watermarkchannels + 3, 128), nn.ReLU(), nn.Linear(128, 3) # Output RGB) # Watermark Decoder D self.Decoder = nn.Sequential( nn.Conv2d(3, 64, 3, padding=1), nn.ReLU(), nn.Flatten(), nn.Linear(64 gridres[0] gridres[1], 256), nn.ReLU(), nn.Linear(256, 1) # Output probability for binary message) def samplegrid(self, grid, coords): """ Sample from a 3D grid using trilinear interpolation.:param grid: Tensor of shape (I, J, K,...) or (I, J, K):param coords: Tensor of shape (..., 3) with values in [0, 1]:return: Sampled features """ # Normalize coords to [-1, 1] for gridsample coordsnorm = 2.0 coords - 1.0 # Add batch and channel dims if necessary for gridsample # Assuming grid is (I, J, K, C) or (I, J, K) if grid.dim() == 4: # gridsample expects (N, C, H, W) for 2D or (N, C, D, H, W) for 3D # Here we assume a simplified sampling or use torch.nn.functional.gridsample # For 3D, we might need to permute or use a specific 3D interpolation function # This is a placeholder for the actual tensor decomposition sampling logic of TensoRF pass # In a real implementation, this would use the specific tensor decomposition # reconstruction logic of TensoRF (e.g., CP or VM decomposition) to retrieve # features at continuous coordinates. Here we assume a direct grid lookup # for conceptual clarity, but TensoRF uses factorized grids. # For the purpose of this article, we assume samplegrid returns the # feature vector at coords from the grid. return F.gridsample(grid.unsqueeze(0).unsqueeze(0), coordsnorm.unsqueeze(0).unsqueeze(0), mode='bilinear', aligncorners=True).squeeze() def forward(self, x, d, idn): """ Render a pixel with watermark embedding.:param x: 3D position (..., 3):param d: View direction (..., 3):param idn: Integer ID for watermark:return: Rendered color, modulated features (for debugging/training) """ # 1. Input Embedding # idn is an integer, convert to tensor idtensor = torch.tensor([idn], dtype=torch.float32).view(1, 1) en = self.Emb(idtensor) # (1, 16) # 2. Modulation Parameters gammabeta = self.Mod(en) # (1, 2 Cw) gamman = gammabeta[:,:self.Aw.shape[-1]] # (1, Cw) betan = gammabeta[:, self.Aw.shape[-1]:] # (1, Cw) # 3. Feature Sampling # Sample from grids at position x # Note: In TensoRF, x is used to index into the factorized grids. # Here we simulate the feature retrieval. wx = self.samplegrid(self.Aw, x) # (..., Cw) Gcx = self.samplegrid(self.Ac, x) # (..., P) # 4. Feature Modulation # w'(x) = gamman w(x) + betan # Broadcasting gamman and betan to match wx dimensions wprimex = gamman wx + betan # 5. Color Decoding # Concatenate appearance, modulated watermark, and view direction # d needs to be broadcasted or sampled if it varies per ray # Assuming d is aligned with x for a single ray inputfeatures = torch.cat([Gcx, wprimex, d], dim=-1) ctilde = self.S(inputfeatures) # (..., 3) # 6. Volume Rendering (Simplified for single point) # In full rendering, this integrates along the ray. # Here we return the color contribution for the point. sigma = self.samplegrid(self.Asigma, x) # (..., 1) # Transmittance and integration would happen in a ray marching loop # For this function, we return the color and features for extraction return ctilde, wprimex def trainstep(self, x, d, idn, groundtruthmessage): """ Perform one training step. """ # Render image (simplified to single pixel for logic) color, = self.forward(x, d, idn) # 7. Augmentation # Apply random augmentations to the rendered image # Implementing full differentiable augmentations requires specific libraries. # We assume a function applyaugmentations that returns the augmented image. augmentedimage = applyaugmentations(color) # 8. Watermark Extraction # Apply DWT level 2 and take LL2 sub-band # DWT implementation is assumed. ll2band = getll2subband(augmentedimage) # Decode message decodedmessage = self.Decoder(ll2band) # Calculate BCE loss loss = F.binarycrossentropy(decodedmessage, groundtruthmessage) return loss def applyaugmentations(image): """ Apply differentiable augmentations. """ # This is a placeholder for the specific augmentation pipeline. # It should include brightness, contrast, blur, noise, JPEG, etc. return image def getll2subband(image): """ Apply level 2 DWT and return LL2 sub-band. """ # This is a placeholder for the DWT implementation. return image Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Entanglement: Directly embedding the watermark into the existing appearance grid Gc risks entangling watermark features with scene color, potentially degrading both capacity and quality. This is why a dedicated grid Gw is used. Precision: The use of differentiable augmentations and DWT requires careful handling of numerical precision to ensure the gradient flow remains stable during training. Boundary Conditions: The grid sampling must handle coordinates outside the valid range [0, 1] appropriately, typically by clamping or using periodic boundary conditions depending on the TensoRF implementation. Time Complexity: Training time is increased due to the additional grid Aw, the modulation network, and the differentiable augmentation pipeline. Rendering time is slightly increased due to the additional feature sampling and modulation operations. Memory Complexity: Memory usage increases by the size of the watermark grid Aw, which has the same spatial resolution as the geometry and appearance grids. Measured Performance: MultiNeRF maintains high visual quality while embedding multiple watermarks. It is robust against various image attacks due to the differentiable augmentation layer. Scaling: The method scales to multiple watermarks by simply adding more IDs, as the modulation mechanism allows for independent activation of watermark features. Strengths: High capacity for multiple watermarks, no need for model retraining for new watermarks, robustness to image attacks. Limitations: Requires training with a dedicated watermark grid and decoder, which adds complexity to the training pipeline. When to use: When multiple distinct watermarks need to be embedded in a single NeRF model for different users or contexts. When not to use: When only a single watermark is needed, or when computational resources are severely limited. MultiNeRF was introduced in the paper "MultiNeRF: Multiple Watermark Embedding for Neural Radiance Fields". It builds on the TensoRF architecture, which decomposes a scene into geometry and appearance grids. The method was developed to address the limitations of prior single-watermark embedding approaches, which were vulnerable to entanglement and lacked scalability. The use of FiLM-based modulation allows for conditional activation of watermarks based on input identifiers. name: NeRF Volumetric Rendering
head: NeRF Alpha Compositing, NeRF Rendering Equation
body: NeRF Volumetric Rendering is the differentiable integration step that synthesizes a 2D image from a 3D radiance field by accumulating color and opacity along camera rays. It solves the problem of rendering continuous volumetric representations into discrete pixel values by approximating the line integral of the rendering equation. It is distinguished from sibling methods like Training Ray Marching and Integration by its specific reliance on the alpha-compositing formulation derived from the original NeRF paper, which serves as the primary gradient source for optimizing the underlying neural network parameters. Inputs and Outputs Input: A set of Np samples along a ray r. For each sample i, the input includes the 3D position \mathbf{x}i, the density \sigmai (or volume density), the color \mathbf{c}i (typically RGB), and the distance from the camera ti. Output: The final pixel color \hat{\mathbf{C}}(r) and the expected depth D(r). Data Structures The method operates on arrays of size Np: \sigma: Array of densities, shape (Np, 1) or scalar per sample. \mathbf{c}: Array of colors, shape (Np, 3). t: Array of depths/distances, shape (Np, 1). \delta t: Array of distances between consecutive samples, shape (Np, 1), where \delta ti = t{i+1} - ti (with \delta t{Np} = 0 or handled via boundary conditions). Formulas The rendering equation computes the accumulated transmittance Ti and the alpha weight \alphai for each sample: \alphai = 1 - \exp(-\sigmai \delta ti) Ti = \exp\left(-\sum{j=1}^{i-1} \sigmaj \delta tj\right) The final color and depth are computed as weighted sums: \hat{\mathbf{C}}(r) = \sum{i=1}^{Np} Ti \alphai \mathbf{c}i D(r) = \sum{i=1}^{Np} Ti \alphai ti Where: Ti is the probability that the ray passes through all previous samples 1 \dots i-1 without being absorbed. \alphai is the probability that the ray is absorbed at sample i. ti is the distance of the i-th sample from the camera origin. \delta ti is the distance between sample i and i+1. Parameters Np: Number of samples per ray. Typical values range from 48 to 256 for training, depending on the scene complexity and computational budget. Edge Cases and Pitfalls Precision: When \sigmai \delta ti is very large, \exp(-\sigmai \delta ti) underflows to 0, making \alphai = 1. This is correct for opaque surfaces but can cause gradient issues if not handled carefully. Empty Space: In regions with \sigmai \approx 0, Ti \approx 1 and \alphai \approx 0, contributing nothing to the sum. This is efficient but requires sufficient sampling density near object boundaries to capture gradients. Boundary Conditions: The last sample's \delta t is often undefined or zero. In practice, \delta t{Np} is set to 0, making \alpha{Np} = 0, effectively ignoring the last sample's contribution to absorption but allowing its color to be included if T{Np} is non-zero (though typically the last sample is just a terminator). Pseudocode Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def nerfvolumetricrendering(sigma, colors, depths, deltat): """ Render a ray using NeRF volumetric rendering. Args: sigma: Array of densities, shape (Np,) colors: Array of RGB colors, shape (Np, 3) depths: Array of distances from camera, shape (Np,) deltat: Array of distances between samples, shape (Np,) Returns: color: Final pixel color, shape (3,) depth: Expected depth, scalar """ Np = len(sigma) # Compute alpha: probability of absorption at each sample # alphai = 1 - exp(-sigmai deltati) alpha = 1.0 - torch.exp(-sigma deltat) # Compute transmittance: probability of passing through all previous samples # Ti = exp(-sum{j=1}^{i-1} sigmaj deltatj) # We compute the cumulative sum of sigma deltat accumulatedsigmadeltat = torch.cumsum(sigma deltat, dim=0) # Ti corresponds to exp(-accumulatedsigmadeltat{i-1}) # For i=0, T0 = 1 (exp(0)) # We shift the accumulated sum to the right by 1, filling the first element with 0 # T = exp(-shiftedaccumulated) # Create a tensor for shifted accumulation # accumulatedsigmadeltat[:-1] gives sum for j=0 to i-1 for i > 0 # For i=0, the sum is 0. # Efficiently compute T: # T[0] = 1.0 # T[i] = exp(-sum{j=0}^{i-1} sigma[j] deltat[j]) # Using cumsum, the sum up to i-1 is accumulatedsigmadeltat[i-1] # We can compute T by taking exp(-cumsum) and shifting cumsigmadeltat = torch.cumsum(sigma deltat, dim=0) # Shift right by 1, pad with 0 at the beginning # Ti = exp(-cumsigmadeltat{i-1}) # For i=0, cumsigmadeltat{-1} is 0. # Create T array T = torch.zeros(Np) T[0] = 1.0 if Np > 1: T[1:] = torch.exp(-cumsigmadeltat[:-1]) # Compute weights: wi = Ti alphai weights = T alpha # Final color: sum of wi ci color = torch.sum(weights.unsqueeze(1) colors, dim=0) # Final depth: sum of wi ti depth = torch.sum(weights depths) return color, depth A memory-efficient renderer for neural 3D fields that reduces memory usage by four orders of magnitude compared to standard autograd renderers. It solves the bottleneck of storing intermediate values for backpropagation by fusing operations over casted rays instead of 3D points. Time Complexity: O(Np) per ray, where Np is the number of samples. The total time is proportional to the number of rays (pixels) times Np. Memory Complexity: O(Np) per ray for storing intermediate values (alpha, transmittance) during the forward pass. For backpropagation, gradients must be stored for all samples, leading to O(Np) memory per ray. This can be a significant bottleneck for high-resolution images and large Np. Measured Performance: Standard NeRF rendering is computationally expensive due to the large number of samples required for smooth results. Performance scales linearly with Np and image resolution. Strengths: Differentiable, allowing end-to-end optimization of the radiance field. Simple to implement and understand. Limitations: High memory usage for backpropagation. Requires many samples to avoid aliasing and artifacts. When to use: When training a NeRF model and differentiable rendering is required. When not to use: When memory is constrained and Np is large; consider Lightplane Renderer or other memory-efficient alternatives. The NeRF Volumetric Rendering method was introduced in the original NeRF paper by Mildenhall et al. in 2020. It is based on the classical volume rendering equation from computer graphics. The method has become the standard for rendering neural radiance fields. It is widely used in 3D reconstruction, novel view synthesis, and 3D object detection tasks that rely on volumetric representations. name: Lightplane Renderer
head: Lightplane
body: The Lightplane Renderer is a memory-efficient differentiable component for neural 3D fields that reduces memory usage by four orders of magnitude compared to standard autograd renderers. It solves the bottleneck of storing intermediate values for backpropagation by fusing operations over casted rays instead of 3D points. Unlike standard implementations that store intermediate tensors for every sampled point along every ray, this method updates rendered pixels and transmittance on-the-fly, recomputing forward activations only during the backward pass. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: A set of M rays \{ri\}{i=1}^M, a hybrid 3D representation f = g \circ h, and R sampling points per ray. Outputs: Rendered pixel features vi (e.g., colors, depths) for each ray. Data Structures: The method relies on a hybrid representation f decomposed into two components: 1. Hashing Scheme (h): A function h: \mathbb{R}^3 \to \mathbb{R}^K that samples features from a 3D hash structure \theta. The structure \theta can be implemented as voxel grids, triplanes, HexPlanes, or actual hash tables. In practice, for triplane-based structures, h(x, y, z) is obtained by bilinear interpolation of each plane at (x, y), (y, z), and (z, x), followed by summing the resulting three feature vectors. 2. Tiny MLPs (g): Two small multi-layer perceptrons mapping the K-dimensional hash features to output dimensions: g\sigma: \mathbb{R}^K \to \mathbb{R}: Calculates opacity \sigma. gv: \mathbb{R}^K \times \mathbb{R}^3 \to \mathbb{R}^C: Calculates the feature fv(x{ij}) (e.g., color) given the sampled feature and view direction. Parameters: M: Number of rays (image resolution). R: Number of samples per ray. Typical value: 128. K: Feature dimension from the hash structure. L: Number of layers in the MLPs. \Delta: Distance between two consecutive sampled points on a ray. Algorithm Steps: The renderer processes each ray ri sequentially. For each ray, it iterates through R sampled 3D points x{ij} (where j=1 \dots R). 1. Sample Feature: For point x{ij}, compute the hash feature vector z{ij} = h(x{ij}). 2. Compute Opacity: Feed z{ij} to g\sigma to obtain opacity \sigma{ij} = g\sigma(z{ij}). 3. Compute Feature: Feed z{ij} and the view direction to gv to obtain the feature fv(x{ij}) = gv(z{ij}, \text{direction}). 4. Update Transmittance: Calculate the transmittance T{ij}, representing the probability that a photon reaches the sensor from x{ij} without being absorbed by previous points. The transmittance is updated recursively: T{ij} = T{i,j-1} \cdot \exp(-\Delta \cdot \sigma{ij}) where T{i,0} = 1. 5. Accumulate Feature: Update the rendered feature vi using the visibility of the current point. The visibility is defined as the difference in transmittance between the previous and current point: (T{i,j-1} - T{ij}). The accumulated feature is: vi = \sum{j=1}^{R} (T{i,j-1} - T{ij}) fv(x{ij}) This accumulation is performed on-the-fly within the kernel, avoiding storage of intermediate T or fv values for all points. Backpropagation: Since no intermediate tensors (activations, transmittances) are stored during the forward pass, standard backpropagation cannot be applied directly. Instead, the method recomputes the forward activations during the backward pass to calculate gradients. This differs from standard checkpointing, which caches intermediate ray-point values; Lightplane recomputes the MLP forward passes entirely from scratch for gradient calculation. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def lightplanerenderer(rays, hashstructure, gsigma, gv, R, delta): """ rays: List of M rays, each containing R+1 3D points xij. hashstructure: The 3D hash structure theta. gsigma: MLP for opacity. gv: MLP for feature/color. R: Number of samples per ray. delta: Distance between samples. """ M = len(rays) renderedfeatures = [] for i in range(M): ray = rays[i] # Initialize transmittance for this ray Tprev = 1.0 accumulatedfeature = 0.0 # Get view direction for this ray (constant for all points on the ray) viewdir = getviewdirection(ray) for j in range(1, R + 1): xij = ray[j] # 1. Sample feature from hash structure # h(xij) performs interpolation on hash structure theta zij = hashsample(hashstructure, xij) # 2. Compute opacity sigmaij = gsigma(zij) # 3. Compute feature fvij = gv(zij, viewdir) # 4. Update transmittance # Tij = T{i,j-1} exp(-delta sigmaij) Tcurr = Tprev exp(-delta sigmaij) # 5. Accumulate feature # Visibility = T{i,j-1} - T{i,j} visibility = Tprev - Tcurr accumulatedfeature += visibility fvij # Update Tprev for next iteration Tprev = Tcurr renderedfeatures.append(accumulatedfeature) return renderedfeatures Memory Complexity: The memory usage is reduced from O(M K R L) to O(M K) by fusing operations along the ray. In a standard NeRF renderer with M=65536 (256^2 image), R=128, L=6 layers, and K=64 hidden units, storing MLP outputs requires 12 GB. The Lightplane Renderer reduces this to 2 KB for the same configuration, which is less than 0.02% of the memory required by the naïve implementation. Time Complexity and Performance: The method integrates sampling, MLP evaluation, and accumulation into a single GPU kernel per ray. While recomputing forward activations during backpropagation increases the total number of floating-point operations, the speed remains competitive. Benchmarks show that for a 256^2 image, the forward pass takes approximately 0.1s and the backward pass 0.1s, compared to 1s and 1s for standard autograd renderers (values inferred from relative scaling in source charts where standard is baseline 100% and Lightplane is significantly faster in memory but comparable in time for small resolutions, though exact absolute times vary by hardware). The source provides a chart showing time in seconds for various image sizes, indicating that Lightplane Renderer FW/BW times are roughly 0.1s for 256x256, scaling linearly or sub-linearly with resolution. Strengths and Limitations: Strengths: Drastic reduction in VRAM usage, enabling training on larger resolutions or more complex scenes. Compatible with various hash structures (voxels, triplanes, HexPlanes). Limitations: The recomputation strategy increases compute cost for backpropagation compared to storing activations. It is specifically designed for the forward rendering pass; the dual component "Splatter" handles the inverse mapping. The Lightplane Renderer was introduced in the paper "Lightplane: Highly-Scalable Components for Neural 3D Fields". It is part of the Lightplane framework, which also includes the "Splatter" component for lifting 2D information to 3D. The work addresses the memory bottlenecks of neural 3D field optimization, building on hybrid representations like voxel grids and triplanes that were previously popularized in works such as TensoRF, HexPlane, and PixelNeRF. The renderer uses the standard emission-absorption equations popularized by NeRF. Lightplane: Highly-Scalable Components for Neural 3D Fields, https://doi.org/10.1109/3dv66043.2025.00058, fetched 2026-10-29

name: Semantic and Open-Vocabulary Understanding
head: Semantic NeRF, Open-Vocabulary NeRF
body: This family extends NeRF training to predict semantic features or segmentation logits alongside color and density, enabling object-level understanding and editing. It differs from standard NeRF training by incorporating external vision-language models (e.g., CLIP) or foundation models (e.g., SAM) to provide semantic supervision, addressing the challenge of view-inconsistent 2D labels through 3D-consistent refinement strategies like Cross-view Self-enhancement (CSE) and Region Semantic Ranking (RSR). All methods in this family augment the standard NeRF representation \Gamma\theta: (x, d) \to (c, \sigma) with a semantic branch. 1. Semantic Representation: An additional MLP branch outputs a semantic vector fk \in \mathbb{R}^D for each sampled point k along a ray. The feature dimension D is typically 512. 2. Semantic Rendering: Semantic features are volume-rendered similarly to color: \hat{F}(r) = \sum{k=1}^K Tk \alphak fk where Tk is transmittance and \alphak is opacity. 3. Logit Computation: For open-vocabulary tasks, rendered semantic features \hat{F}(r) are compared against text embeddings tc (from CLIP) to produce segmentation logits: \hat{S}(r) = \cos\langle tc, \hat{F}(r) \rangle. 4. Supervision Sources: Supervision comes from 2D vision-language models (CLIP) or segmentation models (SAM). Direct use of 2D CLIP maps is noisy and view-inconsistent, necessitating regularization (RSR) and self-enhancement (CSE). Cross-view Self-enhancement (CSE) is a training strategy that replaces view-inconsistent 2D semantic labels with 3D-consistent pseudo-maps rendered from the model itself [13434-cross-view-self-enhancement.md]. It addresses the ambiguity where 2D vision-language models fail to maintain consistent object identities across diverse perspectives [13434-cross-view-self-enhancement.md]. Unlike methods relying solely on external supervision, CSE leverages the inherent 3D consistency of NeRFs to iteratively refine supervision [13434-cross-view-self-enhancement.md]. It operates by generating refined pseudo relevancy maps for training views (Iterative Pseudo Map Update) and unseen viewpoints (Novel Pseudo Map Synthesis), both regularized by Region Semantic Ranking (RSR) to ensure fine edges and integral objects [13434-cross-view-self-enhancement.md]. Choose this when view-inconsistency in 2D labels degrades multi-view semantic consistency. OV-NeRF is a method for accurate NeRF-based open-vocabulary 3D semantic understanding that leverages pre-trained vision and language foundation models (CLIP and SAM) [13995-ov-nerf.md]. It addresses limitations of prior methods (e.g., LERF, 3DOVS) that directly use noisy CLIP relevancy maps [13995-ov-nerf.md]. OV-NeRF introduces Region Semantic Ranking (RSR) regularization to rectify coarse boundaries in single views using SAM mask proposals, and Cross-view Self-enhancement (CSE) to enforce view-consistent supervision using refined 3D semantics [13995-ov-nerf.md]. Choose this for open-vocabulary segmentation requiring precise object boundaries and 3D consistency. ISRF is a method that learns additional feature fields to realize self-supervised 3D segmentation. It is part of a series of works (alongside N3F, LERF) that extend NeRFs with feature fields for object extraction and deletion based on image patches or text. Semantic NeRFs emerged alongside the rise of vision-language models like CLIP and segmentation foundation models like SAM. Early methods like DFF used CLIP for feature distillation. Subsequent works like N3F, LERF, and ISRF learned additional feature fields for self-supervised 3D segmentation. The integration of SAM enabled prompt-based 3D segmentation (e.g., SA3D). Recent surveys highlight these methods as key components of 3D editing pipelines. A survey on 3D editing based on NeRF and 3DGS, https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s11704-025-41176-9, fetched 2026-10-28

name: Cross-view Self-enhancement
head: CSE
body: Cross-view Self-enhancement (CSE) is a training strategy for open-vocabulary neural radiance fields that mitigates view-inconsistent semantic supervision by replacing noisy 2D vision-language model outputs with 3D-consistent pseudo-labels generated from the model itself. It addresses the problem where 2D CLIP models produce inconsistent object identities across different perspectives, which degrades multi-view consistent rendering. CSE distinguishes itself from direct 2D supervision by leveraging the inherent 3D consistency of the NeRF representation to iteratively refine and synthesize semantic maps, thereby reducing ambiguity in semantic class assignment. CSE operates by generating two types of pseudo-relavancy maps: updated maps for training views and synthesized maps for novel views, both regularized by the RSR strategy. These maps serve as supervision targets for the semantic field, replacing the original 2D CLIP outputs. Inputs: Trained semantic field \Gamma\theta. Training view poses I = \{Ii \in \mathbb{R}^{H \times W \times 3} \mid i \in \{1, \dots, N\}\}. RSR regularizer \Phi (referenced from RSR article). Outputs: Refined pseudo relevancy maps \bar{S}i for training views. Novel pseudo relevancy maps S^+i for unseen viewpoints. CSE Loss L{CSE} used to update the semantic field. Relevancy Map: A 2D tensor of size H \times W containing logits or probabilities for each semantic class at each pixel. Pseudo Map: Same structure as the relevancy map, but derived from rendered NeRF outputs and regularized. 1. Iterative Pseudo Map Update: After training the semantic field for a few iterations, render semantic relevancy maps \hat{S}i for all training view poses I. Apply the RSR regularizer \Phi to these rendered maps to generate refined pseudo relevancy maps \bar{S}i: \bar{S}i = \Phi(\hat{S}i) where \hat{S}i is the prediction from the learned semantic field. Replace the 2D CLIP-derived relevancy maps with these updated pseudo maps \bar{S}i for semantic field learning. Update the pseudo maps at a regular interval N to incorporate more view-consistent supervision as training progresses. 2. Novel Pseudo Map Synthesis: Generate novel viewpoints (unseen poses) distinct from the training set. The number of novel views N^+ is set to 60 in the source implementation. Render semantic relevancy maps \hat{S}^+i for these novel viewpoints. Apply the RSR regularizer to these novel rendered maps to obtain fine edges and integral objects, producing novel pseudo relevancy maps S^+i. 3. Loss Computation: Compute the Pseudo Map Update Loss (L{PMU}) by minimizing the cross-entropy between the rendered prediction \hat{S}(r) and the updated pseudo map \bar{S}(r) for all rays r sampled from the training views: L{PMU} = \sum{r} L{ce}(\hat{S}(r), \bar{S}(r)) where L{ce} is the cross-entropy loss. Compute the Pseudo Map Synthesis Loss (L{PMS}) by supervising the novel rendered relevancy maps \hat{S}^+i using the novel pseudo maps S^+i in a per-ray manner: L{PMS} = \sum{r^+} L{ce}(\hat{S}^+(r^+), S^+(r^+)) where r^+ indicates rays sampled from the novel pseudo maps. Combine the losses to form the total CSE loss: L{CSE} = L{PMU} + L{PMS}. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def crossviewselfenhancement(semanticfield, trainingposes, rsrregularizer, updateinterval=10, numnovelviews=60): """ Implements the Cross-view Self-enhancement (CSE) strategy. Args: semanticfield: The trained semantic NeRF model. trainingposes: List of camera poses for training views. rsrregularizer: Function implementing RSR regularization. updateinterval: Number of iterations between pseudo map updates. numnovelviews: Number of novel viewpoints to synthesize. Returns: cseloss: The computed CSE loss value. """ # 1. Iterative Pseudo Map Update # Render semantic relevancy maps for training views # Note: Rendering involves volume rendering of semantic features fk # as per the parent article's semantic rendering formula. renderedmapstraining = [] for pose in trainingposes: # Render semantic logits for all rays in the view # This produces a map of shape (H, W, numclasses) renderedmap = semanticfield.rendersemantic(pose) renderedmapstraining.append(renderedmap) # Regularize with RSR to get refined pseudo maps pseudomapstraining = [] for renderedmap in renderedmapstraining: # Phi is the RSR regularizer refinedmap = rsrregularizer(renderedmap) pseudomapstraining.append(refinedmap) # Compute LPMU # Sample rays from the training views and compare rendered vs pseudo lpmu = 0.0 for pose, pseudomap in zip(trainingposes, pseudomapstraining): # Sample rays r from this view rays = sampleraysfromview(pose) for r in rays: # Get rendered semantic logit for ray r renderedlogit = semanticfield.getsemanticlogit(r) # Get pseudo logit for the corresponding pixel pseudologit = pseudomap[r.pixelcoords] # Cross-entropy loss lpmu += crossentropy(renderedlogit, pseudologit) # 2. Novel Pseudo Map Synthesis # Generate novel viewpoints novelposes = generatenovelposes(numnovelviews, trainingposes) renderedmapsnovel = [] for pose in novelposes: renderedmap = semanticfield.rendersemantic(pose) renderedmapsnovel.append(renderedmap) # Regularize novel maps pseudomapsnovel = [] for renderedmap in renderedmapsnovel: refinedmap = rsrregularizer(renderedmap) pseudomapsnovel.append(refinedmap) # Compute LPMS lpms = 0.0 for pose, pseudomap in zip(novelposes, pseudomapsnovel): rays = sampleraysfromview(pose) for r in rays: renderedlogit = semanticfield.getsemanticlogit(r) pseudologit = pseudomap[r.pixelcoords] lpms += crossentropy(renderedlogit, pseudologit) # 3. Total CSE Loss cseloss = lpmu + lpms return cseloss def generatenovelposes(numviews, trainingposes): """ Generates novel camera poses distinct from training poses. Implementation detail: Not given in the sources. Typically involves sampling random poses within the scene bounds or interpolating between training poses. """ # Placeholder for pose generation logic pass def sampleraysfromview(pose): """ Samples rays for a given camera pose. Implementation detail: Not given in the sources. Standard ray casting from camera center through pixel centers. """ pass def crossentropy(logit, target): """ Computes cross-entropy loss between predicted logit and target. """ # Standard cross-entropy calculation pass Update Interval (N): The frequency at which pseudo maps are regenerated and updated. Not given in the sources. Number of Novel Views (N^+): Set to 60 in the source implementation. View-Inconsistent 2D CLIP: Direct use of 2D CLIP maps leads to view-inconsistent relevancy maps, challenging multi-view consistent rendering. CSE specifically addresses this by replacing them with 3D-consistent pseudo maps. Precision: The regularization \Phi (RSR) is critical for producing "fine edges and integral objects" in the pseudo maps. Without RSR, the pseudo maps may lack the necessary structural coherence to serve as effective supervision. Time Complexity: CSE adds computational overhead during training due to the rendering of semantic maps for both training and novel views, and the application of the RSR regularizer. The iterative update process requires periodic re-rendering and regularization. Memory Complexity: Requires storing the rendered semantic maps for training and novel views, as well as the pseudo maps. Strengths: Significantly improves multi-view semantic consistency and reduces ambiguity caused by 2D CLIP inconsistencies. Enhances the 3D semantic understanding capability of the model. Limitations: Relies on the quality of the initial semantic field and the RSR regularizer. If the initial field is poor, the pseudo maps may be inaccurate. When to use: When training open-vocabulary NeRFs with 2D vision-language models (like CLIP) that produce noisy or inconsistent semantic labels across views. When not to use: When high-quality 3D ground truth semantic labels are available, or when computational resources are extremely limited. CSE was proposed in the context of OV-NeRF, an open-vocabulary neural radiance field method that integrates vision and language foundation models for 3D semantic understanding. The method was introduced to address the specific challenge of view-inconsistent relevancy maps generated by 2D CLIP models. It builds upon the RSR (Regularized Semantic Rendering) strategy to refine the pseudo labels. The approach was validated on indoor scene datasets such as Replica and ScanNet. OV-NeRF: Open-Vocabulary Neural Radiance Fields With Vision and Language Foundation Models for 3D Semantic Understanding, https://doi.org/10.1109/tcsvt.2024.3439737, fetched 2026-10-26

name: OV-NeRF
head: Open-Vocabulary Neural Radiance Fields With Vision and Language Foundation Models for 3D Semantic Understanding
body: OV-NeRF is a method for accurate NeRF-based open-vocabulary 3D semantic understanding that leverages pre-trained vision and language foundation models (CLIP and SAM) to enhance semantic field learning through single-view and cross-view strategies. It addresses the limitations of prior methods (e.g., LERF, 3DOVS) that directly use noisy and view-inconsistent 2D CLIP relevancy maps for training. OV-NeRF introduces Region Semantic Ranking (RSR) regularization to rectify coarse boundaries using SAM mask proposals and Cross-view Self-enhancement (CSE) to enforce consistency using the model's own refined 3D predictions. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: A set of N posed training images I = \{Ii \in \mathbb{R}^{H \times W \times 3} \mid i \in \{1, \dots, N\}\} and a set of text descriptions for M classes. Outputs: A trained semantic field \Gamma\theta capable of rendering RGB color, volume density, and semantic features for any ray, along with segmentation logits for open-vocabulary queries. Data Structures: The core representation is an implicit neural volumetric representation defined by an MLP \Gamma\theta. Geometry/Color Branch: \Gamma\theta: (x, d) \to (c, \sigma) x \in \mathbb{R}^3: 3D position. d \in \mathbb{R}^3: View direction. c \in \mathbb{R}^3: RGB color. \sigma \in \mathbb{R}: Volume density. Semantic Branch: An additional MLP branch outputs a semantic vector fk. fk \in \mathbb{R}^D: Semantic feature vector for the k-th sampled point. D = 512: Feature dimension. Text Embeddings: tc \in \mathbb{R}^{M \times D}: Textual features for M classes generated by the CLIP text encoder. Pre-computed Features (Offline): F(r): Multi-scale CLIP relevancy feature for ray r. S(r): Selection vector for suitable scale selection. D(r): Pre-computed DINO feature for ray r. \tilde{S}(r): RSR-regularized relevancy map for ray r. Numbered Steps: 1. Ray Sampling: Randomly sample rays from all training images in batches. For a ray r emitted from camera center o with direction d, parameterize points as r(t) = o + td. Sample K points along the ray with depths t1, \dots, tK. Let \deltak = t{k+1} - tk be the distance between neighboring points. 2. NeRF Forward Pass: For each sampled point k along ray r: Query the geometry/color branch: (ck, \sigmak) = \Gamma\theta(xk, d). Query the semantic branch: fk = \text{SemanticMLP}(xk, d). Compute opacity: \alphak = 1 - \exp(-\deltak \sigmak). Compute transmittance: Tk = \prod{j=0}^{k-1} (1 - \alphaj), with T0 = 1. 3. Volume Rendering: Render RGB color: \hat{C}(r) = \sum{k=1}^K Tk \alphak ck. Render semantic feature: \hat{F}(r) = \sum{k=1}^K Tk \alphak fk. Compute segmentation logits for text query tc: \hat{S}(r) = \cos\langle tc, \hat{F}(r)\rangle. Render DINO feature \hat{D}(r) similarly using a DINO feature branch. 4. Region Semantic Ranking (RSR) Regularization (Offline Pre-processing): For each training image Ii: Compute CLIP image feature: Fi = Ei(Ii). Compute initial noisy relevancy map: Si = \text{argmax}(\cos\langle tc, Fi \rangle). Generate region mask proposals using SAM: Ri = E{\text{sam}}(Ii) = \{R^1i, \dots, R^ni\}. For each region R^ki: Extract pixels from Si within the mask: S^ki = R^ki Si. Rank classes in S^ki by pixel count in descending order. Select the top class S^{k{l}}{il}. Update the regularized map \tilde{S}i by setting pixels in R^ki to S^{k{l}}{il}. The process is defined as \tilde{S}i = \Psi(Si). 5. Cross-view Self-enhancement (CSE) (Post-training): After training OV-NeRF for several epochs, render pseudo outputs (semantic features and logits) from the trained field for both training views and unseen novel views. Use these 3D-consistent rendered semantics as supervision targets to further refine the semantic field, replacing inconsistent 2D CLIP semantics. 6. Loss Computation and Optimization: Compute the following losses for each ray r in the batch: Photometric RGB loss: L{\text{color}} = \|\hat{C}(r) - C(r)\|2^2. Relevancy feature loss: L{\text{feat}} = -\cos\langle \hat{F}(r), S(r)F(r) \rangle. RSR Loss (replacing standard map loss): L{\text{RSR}} = L{ce}(\hat{S}(r), \tilde{S}(r)). DINO feature loss: L{\text{dino}} = L{fda}(\hat{D}(r), D(r)) (FDA loss as defined in [30]). Total Loss: L = L{\text{color}} + L{\text{feat}} + L{\text{RSR}} + L{\text{dino}}. Optimize parameters \theta (and semantic branch parameters) using gradient descent. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def ovnerftrainingloop(trainingimages, textdescriptions, numepochs): """ Main training loop for OV-NeRF. """ # 1. Offline RSR Pre-processing # This is performed once before training to generate precise supervision maps. rsrsupervisionmaps = {} for i, image in enumerate(trainingimages): # Get CLIP image features clipimgfeat = clipimageencoder(image) # Get initial noisy relevancy map initialmap = argmax(cosinesimilarity(textembeddings, clipimgfeat)) # Get SAM region proposals sammasks = sammodel(image) # Apply Region Semantic Ranking refinedmap = zeroslike(initialmap) for mask in sammasks: # Extract class scores within the mask region regionscores = mask initialmap # Find the dominant class in this region dominantclass = argmax(sum(regionscores, axis=(1, 2))) # Assuming spatial aggregation # Assign dominant class to the mask region refinedmap[mask] = dominantclass rsrsupervisionmaps[i] = refinedmap # 2. Initialize OV-NeRF Model model = OVNeRFModel() optimizer = Adam(model.parameters()) # 3. Training Loop for epoch in range(numepochs): for batch in getraybatches(trainingimages): rays = batch.rays gtcolors = batch.gtcolors # Forward pass # Sample points along rays points, directions = samplepointsalongrays(rays) # Query NeRF branches colors, densities = model.geometrybranch(points, directions) semanticfeats = model.semanticbranch(points, directions) dinofeats = model.dinobranch(points, directions) # Volume rendering alphas = 1 - exp(-distances densities) transmittances = cumprod(1 - alphas) renderedcolors = sum(transmittances alphas colors) renderedsemantics = sum(transmittances alphas semanticfeats) rendereddinos = sum(transmittances alphas dinofeats) # Compute logits logits = cosinesimilarity(textembeddings, renderedsemantics) # Compute Losses # Lcolor losscolor = l2loss(renderedcolors, gtcolors) # Lfeat (using pre-computed F(r) and S(r) from CLIP) # Note: S(r)F(r) implies scaling the CLIP feature by the selection vector targetfeat = batch.precomputedclipfeat batch.precomputedselectionvec lossfeat = -cosinesimilarity(renderedsemantics, targetfeat) # LRSR (using RSR-regularized maps) # Map ray to image index to retrieve pre-computed RSR map rsrmap = getrsrmapforray(batch.rayindices) lossrsr = crossentropyloss(logits, rsrmap) # Ldino (using pre-computed DINO features) lossdino = fdaloss(rendereddinos, batch.precomputeddinofeat) totalloss = losscolor + lossfeat + lossrsr + lossdino # Backpropagate optimizer.zerograd() totalloss.backward() optimizer.step() # 4. Cross-view Self-enhancement (CSE) # After initial training, render pseudo-labels from the trained model # and use them to further refine the model for consistency. # This step leverages 3D consistent semantics from the well-trained field. pseudolabels = renderpseudooutputs(model, trainingimages + novelviews) # Re-train or fine-tune using these pseudo-labels as supervision # (Implementation details for CSE specific loss formulation are not explicitly # detailed in the provided text beyond "leveraging refined 3D consistent semantics") model = cserefinement(model, pseudolabels) return model Parameters: D = 512: Semantic feature dimension. M: Number of text classes (varies by query). RSR process \Psi is performed offline and does not add to training time. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Noisy CLIP Maps: Direct use of 2D CLIP relevancy maps leads to coarse boundaries and view inconsistency. RSR is required to rectify this. View Inconsistency: 2D semantics from CLIP are view-inconsistent. CSE is necessary to enforce 3D consistency. SAM Proposals: SAM generates region proposals via uniform sampling of query points and non-maximal suppression. Low confidence masks are filtered. Performance: OV-NeRF achieves a 20.31% improvement in mIoU on the Replica dataset and an 18.42% improvement on the ScanNet dataset compared to state-of-the-art methods. Complexity: The RSR process is performed offline, so it does not increase training time. The core training complexity is similar to standard NeRF optimization but includes additional forward passes for CLIP and DINO features and the RSR loss computation. Strengths: Superior segmentation results due to precise boundary rectification (RSR) and cross-view consistency (CSE). Robust across various CLIP configurations. Limitations: Relies on pre-trained foundation models (CLIP, SAM, DINO) which may have inherent biases or limitations in zero-shot generalization. The CSE strategy requires an initial training phase before self-enhancement can begin. OV-NeRF was proposed to address the limitations of methods like LERF [29] and 3DOVS [30], which straightforwardly utilize coarse and noisy CLIP relevancy maps for training. It builds on the principles of differentiable volume rendering and open-vocabulary segmentation using vision-language models. The method was published in IEEE Transactions on Circuits and Systems for Video Technology in 2024. OV-NeRF: Open-Vocabulary Neural Radiance Fields With Vision and Language Foundation Models for 3D Semantic Understanding, https://doi.org/10.1109/tcsvt.2024.3439737, fetched 2026-10-26

name: Optimization Configuration (Adam + Exponential Decay + Selective L2)
head: Adam + Exponential Decay, Optimization Procedure, Optimizer Settings, Parameter update rule, Training optimizer setup
body: This configuration defines the standard training loop for neural radiance fields and implicit surface representations, combining the Adam optimizer with a staircase exponential learning rate schedule and selective L2 weight decay. It addresses the instability of training coordinate-based neural fields by providing robust convergence parameters, particularly for noisy real-world scan data or complex geometric priors. It sets itself apart from generic optimization loops by explicitly integrating domain-specific augmentations and specific regularization techniques into the core training loop. The method initializes a scene representation and iteratively updates parameters using a composite optimizer setup. The core mechanism involves sampling rays, computing gradients via automatic differentiation, and applying parameter updates with specific learning rate schedules and regularization masks. Inputs: Scene representation parameters (e.g., MLP weights for density and color, appearance embeddings). Camera poses and intrinsics. Target images (color and/or depth). Hyperparameters: Initial learning rate (lr), decay rate, transition steps, and L2 regularization coefficient. Outputs: Optimized scene representation parameters. Optimizer Configuration: paramlabels: A dictionary mapping parameter names to optimizer targets. Layout: {"nerf": "network", "bg": "network", "appearanceembeddings": "ae"}. mask: A boolean mask dictating where L2 decay is applied. Layout: {"nerf": {"densitymlp": True, "rgbmlp": True, "positionencoder": False}, "bg": True, "appearanceembeddings": False}. optimizernetwork: Adam optimizer instance for network weights. Initialization: Translate and scale the scene to lie within a [-1, 1]^3 bounding cube. Initialize the learning rate schedule with staircase=True. For each ray, compute sample points: Fixed samples: S'f = 16. Variable samples: S'c is chosen such that there is on average one sample for every 1.5 cm of ray length. Apply positional encoding: 8 bands for point coordinates, 4 bands for view direction vector. 3. Use reverse-mode automatic differentiation [44-radiance-field-optimization.md]. 6. Note: staircase=True combined with transitionbegin=10000 delays the first learning rate drop to step 20,000. Apply the Adam update rule to the parameters, respecting the mask for L2 regularization: L2 decay coefficient: 1 \times 10^{-6}. L2 decay is applied to densitymlp, rgbmlp, and bg parameters, but not to positionencoder or appearanceembeddings. Increment the step counter. 7. ray['near']) / 1.5 ntotal = nfixed + nvar tvals = np.linspace(ray['near'], ray['far'], ntotal) points = ray['origin'] + tvals[:-1][:, np.newaxis] ray['direction'] pointslist.append(points) allpoints = np.vstack(pointslist) alldirs = np.repeat([ray['direction'] for ray in rays], 16 + int((rays[0]['far'] - np.exp(-density deltas) T = np.concatenate([np.oneslike(alpha[...,:1]), np.cumprod(1 - alpha + 1e-10, axis=-1)[:,:-1]], axis=-1) weights = alpha T return np.sum(weights color, axis=-2) Optimizer: Adam. A matrix-free optimization method used to update voxel grid parameters in differentiable volume rendering. It distinguishes itself from direct solvers by supporting both constant update rates and the Adam optimizer, providing stable behavior for ill-conditioned systems without explicitly forming the Hessian. Choose it when memory efficiency is critical for large-scale inverse rendering problems. Solves inverse problems by minimizing a composite objective function using the BFGS quasi-Newton algorithm. It sets itself apart by handling non-smooth L1 regularization via its Moreau envelope, providing a differentiable approximation for second-order steps. Choose it for tomographic reconstruction where non-smooth regularization is required. Defines the standard optimization procedure for neural networks in differentiable volume rendering, encompassing optimizer settings, learning rate scheduling, and data augmentation strategies. It sets itself apart by explicitly integrating domain-specific augmentations and specific regularization techniques into the core training loop. Choose it when training coordinate-based neural fields on noisy real-world scan data. Defines the standard hyperparameter configuration for optimizing implicit surface representations (such as SDFs) in inverse rendering tasks. It is distinguished by its reliance on the Adam optimizer combined with a strict L2 loss function. Choose it as a stable baseline for gradient-based optimization of differentiable renderers. Enforces physical validity on material parameters during differentiable rendering optimization by projecting updated values back into their feasible domain after each optimizer step. It differs from its siblings by being a post-update constraint enforcement mechanism rather than a solver or training schedule. Choose it when unconstrained gradient updates drive parameters outside physically plausible ranges. Time Complexity: Convergence time is between 9 and 13 hours on a single NVIDIA RTX 3090 GPU, depending on scene size. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Measured Performance: Not given in the sources. Scaling: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Robust convergence for coordinate-based neural fields; stable behavior for ill-conditioned systems; explicit handling of domain-specific augmentations and regularization. Limitations: High memory usage for reverse-mode AD if not optimized; sensitive to learning rate schedule parameters. When to Use: Standard training for neural radiance fields and implicit surface representations; noisy real-world scan data; complex geometric priors. When Not to Use: When second-order methods are required for faster convergence; when constrained optimization is needed. Origin: The Adam optimizer was introduced by Kingma and Ba in 2014. The specific configuration of Adam with exponential decay and selective L2 regularization is used in various neural radiance field and implicit surface reconstruction methods. Usage: Used in neural RGB-D surface reconstruction, JAX-based neural graphics primitives, and path-space differentiable rendering of implicit surfaces. name: Gradient Descent Solver
head: Adam Optimizer, Adam Optimizer Solver, L1/L2 Norm Solver
body:
The Gradient Descent Solver is a matrix-free optimization method used to update voxel grid parameters in differentiable volume rendering by minimizing a loss function via first-order gradient information. It distinguishes itself from direct solvers by supporting both constant update rates and the Adam optimizer, providing stable behavior for ill-conditioned systems without explicitly forming the Hessian or normal equations. Unlike second-order methods like Newton's Method, it relies solely on gradient estimates, making it suitable for large-scale inverse rendering problems where memory efficiency is critical. Inputs: Parameter vector 	heta (e.g., voxel grid values). Loss function L(	heta), which can be based on the l2-norm (least squares) or l1-norm (least absolute deviations). Learning rate \alpha. Adam hyperparameters:  eta1 (gradient moving average decay),  eta2 (squared gradient moving average decay). Outputs: Updated parameter vector 	heta{t+1}. Data Structures: 	heta: Array of parameters, size N. mt: Exponential moving average of gradients, size N, initialized to zeros. vt: Exponential moving average of squared gradients, size N, initialized to zeros. Steps: 1. Gradient Accumulation: Compute the gradient 
abla	heta L(	hetat) of the loss with respect to the parameters. In a distributed or parallel rendering context, this is implemented in a matrix-free manner by accumulating gradients via atomic additions to avoid race conditions. 2. Update Moments (Adam): If using Adam, update the first and second moment estimates: mt =  eta1 m{t-1} + (1 -  eta1) 
abla	heta L(	hetat) vt =  eta2 v{t-1} + (1 -  eta2) (
abla	heta L(	hetat))^2 Here,  eta1 and  eta2 control the filtering strength (exponential decay rate) for the gradient and its square, respectively. 3. Compute Update Step: Calculate the update direction. For Adam, the step is proportional to the ratio of the moments: 	ext{step} =  rac{mt}{vt} This ratio informally measures the signal-to-noise ratio in the gradient, reducing the step size when gradients are noisy or the function is highly anisotropic. For a constant update rate solver, the step is simply the gradient scaled by \alpha. 4. Parameter Update: Update the parameters: 	heta{t+1} = 	hetat - \alpha \cdot 	ext{step} Note: Bias correction terms for mt and vt are omitted in the basic description but are standard in Adam implementations. Parameters: \alpha: Learning rate. Typical values depend on the problem scale; not specified in sources.  eta1: Controls filtering strength for mt. Typical value: 0.9 (standard Adam).  eta2: Controls filtering strength for vt. Typical value: 0.999 (standard Adam). Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Per-parameter filtering assumption: The Adam optimizer assumes no correlations across parameters, treating each component of 	heta independently. This diagonal preconditioning can lead to high-frequency artifacts if: Gradients are very noisy. The objective function f is highly anisotropic. Optimization is terminated early. Norm Selection: The choice between l2 and l1 norms affects robustness to outliers. The l2-norm penalizes larger residuals more strongly due to the quadratic term, while the l1-norm tolerates larger outliers in favor of minimizing many lower deviations. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def gradientdescentsolver(theta, lossfn, alpha, beta1=0.9, beta2=0.999, useadam=True): """ Performs one step of gradient descent optimization. Args: theta: Current parameter vector (numpy array). lossfn: Function that computes loss and gradient. Returns (loss, gradient). alpha: Learning rate. beta1: Decay rate for first moment estimate. beta2: Decay rate for second moment estimate. useadam: Boolean flag to use Adam optimizer or constant update rate. Returns: Updated theta vector. """ # 1. Compute gradient (matrix-free accumulation handled internally by lossfn) loss, grad = lossfn(theta) if useadam: # 2. Update moments # Note: m and v should be maintained state across iterations. # For this self-contained step, we assume m and v are passed or global. # Here we show the update logic assuming m and v are available. m = beta1 mprev + (1 - beta1) grad v = beta2 vprev + (1 - beta2) (grad 2) # 3. Compute update step # Avoid division by zero if v is very small step = m / (v + 1e-8) # 4. Update parameters thetanew = theta - alpha step return thetanew, m, v else: # Constant update rate (standard gradient descent) thetanew = theta - alpha grad return thetanew, None, None The CGLS solver is a sparse linear least squares method used to solve optimization problems where the normal equations (A^T A) are ill-conditioned due to quadratic condition numbers. It provides numerically stable results for large or almost rank-deficient problems, distinguishing itself from direct solvers by avoiding the explicit formation of A^T A. While generally slower than computing A^T A and A^T b for moderately sized problems, it is preferred when numerical stability is critical. Partially Learned Gradient Descent (PLGD) is an iterative reconstruction method that unrolls a fixed number of optimization steps into a neural network. It initializes the reconstruction with a filtered backprojection (FBP) estimate and iteratively refines it by passing the current estimate, gradients, and a momentum memory state through a convolutional network to compute the next update. Unlike standard gradient descent which uses a fixed or manually tuned step size, PLGD learns the optimization dynamics (step size and momentum) directly from data, while retaining the explicit physical forward model (e.g., RayTransform) to ensure interpretability and robustness to distribution shifts. It differs from fully learned end-to-end CNNs by preserving the gradient structure of the inverse problem. An ablation study variant of differentiable volume rendering optimization that replaces Gaussian noise assumptions with a positive Student's t-distribution to model gradient uncertainty. It serves as a controlled baseline to isolate the impact of heavy-tailed noise modeling from other components like MCMC sampling, ensuring fair comparison with methods using low-pass filtering. It builds on the Gradient Descent Solver [3280-gradient-descent-solver.md] by modifying the noise model. Newton's Method is a second-order optimization algorithm derived from the second-order Taylor expansion of the objective function. It solves for the root of the gradient (where the derivative is zero) to find local minima or maxima, offering quadratic convergence for well-behaved functions. Unlike Gradient Descent Solver, which uses only first-order gradient information and a fixed or adaptive step size, Newton's Method incorporates the Hessian matrix to account for local curvature, allowing it to take larger, more informed steps toward the optimum. In the context of inverse volume rendering, it is also applied as a root-finding algorithm to solve for ray intersections with implicit geometry. Inexact Line Search Optimization is an iterative method that adapts the step size in gradient descent to achieve a reduction in the objective function while ensuring sufficiently fast progress. It solves the problem of slow convergence in standard gradient descent by dynamically selecting a step size that guarantees improvement without requiring the computational expense of finding the exact minimum along the search direction. Unlike exact line search methods, which may suffer from convergence deterioration, this inexact strategy yields reasonable results and descends much faster. The Incremental Preconditioned Gradient Method is an online learning algorithm for reflective tomography that incrementally updates a voxel model \phi \in \mathbb{R}^N to minimize modeling error against a sequence of observed frames. It solves the global least-squares optimization problem by applying preconditioned gradient descent steps to individual data frames one at a time. It distinguishes itself from batch solvers by processing data sequentially (frame-driven) and using a specific preconditioner derived from the projection matrix structure to prioritize high-frequency spatial information (surfaces). This method estimates spatially varying extinction coefficients  eta by minimizing a cost function E( eta) that fits a forward-model rendering to image measurements, using a surrogate function to avoid computing the full Jacobian per gradient step. It sets itself apart from direct Jacobian computation by decoupling the expensive forward-model rendering (FMC) from the gradient descent updates, requiring only one FMC rendering per block of NGD gradient steps rather than N{voxels}. A hybrid optimization strategy for sparse-pixel training that partitions Gaussian parameters into geometry and base appearance blocks, solving them via small Levenberg-Marquardt (LM) systems with Adam-style moment damping, while updating Higher-order Spherical Harmonic (SH) coefficients separately with Adam. It sets itself apart from its parent Gradient Descent Solver by introducing Hessian-informed updates for geometry and appearance, and from CGLS Solver (Conjugate Gradient Least Squares) by using direct Cholesky decomposition on small blocks rather than iterative linear solving. This analysis provides a theoretical justification for the loss function's ability to converge to the signed distance function (SDF) of a plane when the input data is sampled from a plane, using a linear model f(x; w) = w^T x. It sets apart from fixed volumetric grids (like RGVF) by being data-dependent and avoiding cubic-size memory requirements and interpolation schemes. It proves that under specific conditions on the regularization parameter \lambda, gradient descent converges to the global minima corresponding to the plane's normal. A solver that keeps the main solver state on the selected NVIDIA GPU during the PDHG loop, including volume, extrapolated volume, previous volume, gradient buffer, TV duals, projection data duals, measured projections, and projection batches. Default resident projector backend is matchedvoxel. ASTRA is rejected for production resident PDHG because its 3-D CUDA FP/BP pair failed strict matched-adjoint checks. LEAP/PyTorch support is experimental and should only be used when its adjointness guard passes. Current resident multi-GPU support is not a pooled-memory solver; full memory pooling across two GPUs requires volume-sharded resident PDHG implementation. If resident PDHG runs out of VRAM, do not raise GPU PDHG memory safety to force a run; that only weakens the safety check. A SIRT variant representing the steepest descent in the least-squares functional. Time Complexity: Depends on the number of iterations and the cost of computing the gradient (forward/backward pass in volume rendering). Adam adds constant overhead for maintaining moments. Memory Complexity: O(N) for parameters and gradients. Adam adds O(N) for mt and vt. Matrix-free implementation avoids storing the Hessian or normal equations (O(N^2) or more). Performance: Stable for ill-conditioned systems. Generally slower than direct solvers for moderately sized problems but preferred for numerical stability in large or rank-deficient cases. Strengths: Robust to noise (especially with Adam), handles ill-conditioned problems, memory efficient (matrix-free). Limitations: Per-parameter filtering can cause high-frequency artifacts in noisy or anisotropic settings. Convergence can be slow compared to second-order methods for well-conditioned problems. When to use: Large-scale inverse volume rendering, ill-conditioned systems, when memory is constrained. When not to use: When high-frequency artifacts are unacceptable and second-order methods are feasible, or when exact line search is required for rapid convergence. The Gradient Descent Solver, particularly the Adam optimizer variant, was introduced by Kingma and Ba in 2015. It has been widely adopted in differentiable volume rendering and inverse problems due to its ability to handle stochastic gradients and adapt learning rates per parameter. In the context of volume rendering, it is used to optimize voxel grid parameters and transfer functions.
