name: CGLS Solver (Conjugate Gradient Least Squares)
head: Sparse Linear Least Squares Solver
body: The CGLS solver is a sparse linear least squares method used to solve optimization problems where the normal equations (A^T A) are ill-conditioned due to quadratic condition numbers. It provides numerically stable results for large or almost rank-deficient problems, distinguishing itself from direct solvers by avoiding the explicit formation of A^T A. While generally slower than computing A^T A and A^T b for moderately sized problems, it is preferred when numerical stability is critical. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Matrix A (implicitly available via matrix-vector products), vector b. Output: Solution vector x minimizing \|Ax - b\|^2. Data Structures: Vectors x, p, r, Ap of size n (dimension of the solution space). Scalar parameters \alpha, \beta. Algorithm Steps: 1. Initialize x0 = 0. 2. Compute initial residual r0 = b - A x0 = b. 3. Set initial search direction p0 = r0. 4. For k = 0, 1, \dots until convergence: a. Compute matrix-vector product Apk = A pk. b. Compute step size \alphak = \frac{rk^T rk}{pk^T A pk}. c. Update solution x{k+1} = xk + \alphak pk. d. Update residual r{k+1} = rk - \alphak A pk. e. Check convergence: if \|r{k+1}\| is sufficiently small, stop. f. Apply Jacobi preconditioning. Let M be the diagonal of A^T A (or an approximation thereof). The preconditioned residual \tilde{r} is computed as \tilde{r}i = ri / M{ii}. g. Compute \betak = \frac{\tilde{r}{k+1}^T \tilde{r}{k+1}}{rk^T rk}. h. Update search direction p{k+1} = \tilde{r}{k+1} + \betak pk. Parameters: Convergence tolerance: Not given in the sources. Preconditioner: Jacobi preconditioner. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Ill-conditioning: The method is specifically chosen to handle ill-conditioned systems where normal equations fail. Rank deficiency: Provides stable results for almost rank-deficient problems. Performance: Slower than normal equation approaches for moderately sized problems. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def cglssolve(Amatvec, b, maxiter=1000, tol=1e-6): """ Solves min ||Ax - b||^2 using CGLS with Jacobi preconditioning. Amatvec: function that computes A v for a vector v. b: target vector. """ n = len(b) x = [0.0] n r = [b[i] for i in range(n)] # r = b - Ax, initially x=0 p = [r[i] for i in range(n)] # Compute diagonal of A^T A for Jacobi preconditioning # Note: In practice, this requires computing A^T A diagonal or approximating it. # If A is not explicitly available, this step might be an approximation. # Here we assume we can compute the diagonal of A^T A. diagAtA = [0.0] n for i in range(n): # Compute i-th column of A, then its norm squared coli = Amatvec([1.0 if j == i else 0.0 for j in range(n)]) diagAtA[i] = sum(coli[j]2 for j in range(n)) # Avoid division by zero for i in range(n): if diagAtA[i] == 0: diagAtA[i] = 1.0 rdotr = sum(r[i]2 for i in range(n)) for k in range(maxiter): Ap = Amatvec(p) pAp = sum(p[i] Ap[i] for i in range(n)) if pAp == 0: break alpha = rdotr / pAp # Update x for i in range(n): x[i] += alpha p[i] # Update r rdotrnew = 0.0 for i in range(n): r[i] -= alpha Ap[i] rdotrnew += r[i]2 if rdotrnew < tol: break # Jacobi Preconditioning rtilde = [r[i] / diagAtA[i] for i in range(n)] rtildedotrtilde = sum(rtilde[i]2 for i in range(n)) beta = rtildedotrtilde / rdotr # Update p for i in range(n): p[i] = rtilde[i] + beta p[i] rdotr = rdotrnew return x This method recovers missing pixels in a rendered volume image by solving a regularized least-squares optimization problem using the Conjugate Gradient algorithm. It allows reconstruction from a subset of pixels, reducing total rendering time compared to full volume rendering. It differs from its parent CGLS Solver (Conjugate Gradient Least Squares) by explicitly defining the regularization term H via B-spline convolution and the sampling matrix S for pixel dropping, whereas the parent focuses on the general numerical stability of the least-squares formulation. The Symmetric Least Squares Solver solves the linear system Ax = b where A is a symmetric matrix, typically arising from the normal equations A^T A in least-squares problems. It differs from the parent CGLS Solver by explicitly computing the pseudoinverse via Singular Value Decomposition (SVD) rather than using iterative conjugate gradients. This approach provides a direct solution suitable for small, dense symmetric systems (e.g., 3 \times 3) where numerical stability via eigenvalue thresholding is required, contrasting with the iterative nature of Conjugate Gradient Solver for Compressive Volume Rendering. Adaptive Grid Optical Tomography is a volumetric reconstruction method that represents the 3D density field using an adaptive octree grid of piecewise constant basis functions, allowing for higher effective resolution and better memory efficiency than uniform grids by using fewer basis functions in uniform regions. It solves the problem of reconstructing dynamic, semi-transparent phenomena (such as smoke and flames) from multi-view video sequences by iteratively refining the grid resolution only where the reconstruction error is high, combined with a visual hull constraint to restrict the solution space. Unlike uniform grid approaches, which quickly exhaust memory limits for high-resolution multi-camera setups, this method uses 20-25% of the memory while achieving comparable accuracy. Solves Hc = \eta by performing Cholesky decomposition of H, followed by forward and backward substitution. This is used when H is positive-definite and symmetric, such as the Hankel matrix of the biased moment vector. Addresses problems when solving outer vertices of very sparse parent voxels that lack enough neighboring child voxels to create a linear system of equations. It solves sparse cases using the scalar field expansion method described in Appendix B of the source. A pitfall is that Singular Value Decomposition (SVD) often results in incorrect values for these sparse cases, with resulting values being both positive (outside bounds) and negative (inside the model). Time Complexity: Generally slower than computing A^T A and A^T b for moderately sized problems. Memory Complexity: Sparse, as it avoids forming A^T A explicitly. Numerical Stability: Provides numerically more stable results for very large or almost rank-deficient problems compared to normal equations. Strengths: Handles ill-conditioned systems better than normal equations. Limitations: Slower for moderate problem sizes. When to Use: When A^T A is ill-conditioned or rank-deficient. When Not to Use: For moderately sized problems where speed is prioritized over stability. The CGLS solver is based on the work by Paige and Saunders [PS82], as cited in. It is used in transfer function optimization for comparative volume rendering. name: Conjugate Gradient Solver for Compressive Volume Rendering
head: CG Solver, Compressive Volume Rendering with Conjugate Gradient Solver, Global CG Solver
body: This method recovers missing pixels in a rendered volume image by solving a regularized least-squares optimization problem using the Conjugate Gradient algorithm. It allows reconstruction from a subset of pixels, reducing total rendering time compared to full volume rendering. It differs from its parent CGLS Solver (Conjugate Gradient Least Squares) by explicitly defining the regularization term H via B-spline convolution and the sampling matrix S for pixel dropping, whereas the parent focuses on the general numerical stability of the least-squares formulation. Inputs: Y: The observed rendered image vector (size N \times 1, where N = \text{imageWidth} \times \text{imageHeight}). S: The binary sampling matrix (size N \times N). \lambda: Regularization parameter. \phi: The basis function (univariate uniform centered cubic B-spline \beta3(t), tensor-producted to 2D). Outputs: x: The reconstructed full-resolution image vector (size N \times 1). Data Structures: x, r, p, b: Vectors of size N (floats). A: Implicitly defined as S^T S + \lambda H. H: Convolution matrix defined by H{p,q} = \langle \phi(\cdot - jp), \phi(\cdot - jq) \rangle{L^2}. Formulas: The optimization problem is: \minx \|Sx - y\|2^2 + \lambda x^T H x The linear system to solve is: (S^T S + \lambda H)x = S^T y Let A = S^T S + \lambda H and b = S^T y. Steps: 1. Initialize x0 to zeros. 2. Compute b = S^T Y. Note that S^T acts as an upsampling operator inserting zeros at missing pixel locations. 3. Initialize residual r0:= b - A x0 and search direction p0:= r0. 4. Iterate for k = 0, 1, \dots: a. Calculate step size \alphak:= \frac{rk^T rk}{pk^T A pk}. b. Update solution x{k+1}:= xk + \alphak pk. c. Update residual r{k+1}:= rk - \alphak A pk. d. If r{k+1} is sufficiently small (convergence criterion), exit loop. e. Calculate \betak:= \frac{r{k+1}^T r{k+1}}{rk^T rk}. f. Update search direction p{k+1}:= r{k+1} + \betak pk. g. Increment k. 5. Return x{k+1}. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def dot(a, b): return sum(ai bi for ai, bi in zip(a, b)) def applyS(x, Smap): # Smap: list of (outputindex, inputindex) where S[outputindex, inputindex] = 1 # Sx is downsampling: returns vector of observed pixel values return [x[idx] for, idx in Smap] def applyST(y, Smap, N): # S^T inserts zeros at missing pixels res = [0.0] N for i, (, idx) in enumerate(Smap): res[idx] = y[i] return res def convolveH(x, kernel, N): # Hx is equivalent to convolving the image with a 2D kernel phi # phi is the tensor product of univariate uniform centered cubic B-spline beta3 H = int(math.sqrt(N)) W = H img = [x[iW:(i+1)W] for i in range(H)] kh, kw = len(kernel), len(kernel[0]) out = [[0.0]W for in range(H)] for i in range(H): for j in range(W): val = 0.0 for ki in range(kh): for kj in range(kw): ni, nj = i + ki - kh//2, j + kj - kw//2 if 0 <= ni < H and 0 <= nj < W: val += img[ni][nj] kernel[ki][kj] out[i][j] = val return [v for row in out for v in row] def solvecompressivevolumerendering(Y, Smap, lambdareg, phikernel, maxiter=100, tol=1e-6): N = len(Y) x = [0.0] N b = applyST(Y, Smap, N) r = b[:] p = r[:] rdot = dot(r, r) for k in range(maxiter): # Ap = (S^T S + lambda H) p pdown = applyS(p, Smap) Sp = applyST(pdown, Smap, N) Hp = convolveH(p, phikernel, N) Ap = [Spi + lambdareg Hpi for Spi, Hpi in zip(Sp, Hp)] pdotAp = dot(p, Ap) if pdotAp == 0: break alpha = rdot / pdotAp x = [xi + alpha pi for xi, pi in zip(x, p)] r = [ri - alpha Api for ri, Api in zip(r, Ap)] rdotnew = dot(r, r) if math.sqrt(rdotnew) < tol: break beta = rdotnew / rdot p = [ri + beta pi for ri, pi in zip(r, p)] rdot = rdotnew return x Edge Cases and Pitfalls: The global solver is too slow for real-time rendering due to high data transfer between CPU and GPU for FFT convolution and cuBLAS dot products. FFT-based convolution requires memory to be copied back and forth between CPU and GPU, decreasing performance. cuBLAS dot product operations require memory copy for each iteration, significantly reducing performance. The matrix S has size (imageWidth \times imageHeight) by (imageWidth \times imageHeight). Time Complexity: The reconstruction time is almost constant regardless of the number of features or pixels added, while total rendering time increases with features/pixels. However, the global solver is computationally expensive and performance depends on image size and iteration count. Memory Complexity: Requires storage for vectors x, r, p, b and intermediate results for S^T S and H operations. FFT-based convolution requires additional memory for transforms. Performance: Volume rendering using 100% of the pixels takes more time than the compressive rendering method. The global reconstruction process is too slow to interact with the volume renderer in real-time due to CPU-GPU data transfers. Strengths: Acceptable image quality for reconstructed images. Can significantly reduce rendering time by using a subset of pixels. Limitations: Poor performance for real-time interactive rendering due to data transfer overheads. This method is described in the thesis "GPU-based Compressive Volume Rendering". It builds on the concept of compressive sensing applied to volume rendering, utilizing the Conjugate Gradient solver to recover missing pixel data. The regularization term H is defined using cubic B-splines. GPU-based Compressive Volume Rendering, https://doi.org/10.11575/prism/5366, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial)

name: Symmetric Least Squares Solver
body: The Symmetric Least Squares Solver solves the linear system Ax = b for a symmetric matrix A using an SVD-based pseudoinverse. It returns the solution vector x and the squared residual error \|Ax - b\|^2. Inputs: A: A symmetric matrix (stored as upper triangular elements). b: A vector of the same dimension as A. svd\tol: Tolerance for SVD convergence or singular value classification. svd\sweeps: Number of iterations for the SVD algorithm. pinv\tol: Threshold for inverting eigenvalues; eigenvalues below this magnitude are treated as zero to ensure numerical stability. Outputs: x: The solution vector. residual: The squared residual error \|Ax - b\|^2. Data Structures: SMat3: A symmetric 3 \times 3 matrix stored with 6 floats: m00, m01, m02, m11, m12, m22. Mat3: A general 3 \times 3 matrix stored with 9 floats. Vector3: A 3-element vector. Steps: 1. SVD Decomposition: Call getSymmetricSvd(A, VTAV, V, svdtol, svdsweeps) to compute the eigenvectors V and the diagonalized eigenvalues VTAV. 2. Pseudoinverse Calculation: Call pseudoinverse(out pinv, VTAV, V, pinvtol) to compute the pseudoinverse matrix A^+ by inverting the eigenvalues in VTAV and thresholding those below pinvtol. 3. Solution: Compute x = A^+ b using matrix-vector multiplication. 4. Residual: Calculate and return \|Ax - b\|^2. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def solvesymmetricleastsquares(Auppertri, b, svdtol, svdsweeps, pinvtol): # Step 1: SVD Decomposition # getSymmetricSvd computes eigenvectors V and eigenvalues for symmetric A # Not given in the sources: specific iterative diagonalization routine. V, eigenvalues = getsymmetricsvd(Auppertri, svdtol, svdsweeps) # Step 2: Compute Pseudoinverse # Invert eigenvalues, thresholding near-zero values lambdainv = [1.0 / lam if abs(lam) > pinvtol else 0.0 for lam in eigenvalues] # Aplus = V diag(lambdainv) V^T pinv = computepseudoinversematrix(V, lambdainv) # Step 3: Solve for x x = matvecmul(pinv, b) # Step 4: Compute Residual Error ||Ax - b||^2 residual = calcerror(Auppertri, x, b) return x, residual def getsymmetricsvd(Auppertri, tol, sweeps): """ Computes eigenvectors V and eigenvalues for symmetric A. Not given in the sources: specific Givens/Jacobi rotation logic. Returns: (V: 3x3 matrix, eigenvalues: list of 3 floats) """ # Not given in the sources: specific iterative diagonalization routine. pass def computepseudoinversematrix(V, lambdainv): """ Computes V diag(lambdainv) V^T explicitly. V: 3x3 matrix (list of lists) lambdainv: list of 3 floats Returns: 3x3 matrix """ pinv = [[0.0] 3 for in range(3)] for i in range(3): for j in range(3): val = 0.0 for k in range(3): val += V[i][k] lambdainv[k] V[j][k] pinv[i][j] = val return pinv def matvecmul(M, v): """Matrix-vector multiplication M v""" n = len(M) result = [0.0] n for i in range(n): for j in range(n): result[i] += M[i][j] v[j] return result def calcerror(Auppertri, x, b): """Computes ||Ax - b||^2""" A = uppertritofull(Auppertri) Ax = matvecmul(A, x) diff = [Ax[i] - b[i] for i in range(3)] return sum(d d for d in diff) def uppertritofull(uppertri): """Converts [m00, m01, m02, m11, m12, m22] to 3x3 matrix""" m00, m01, m02, m11, m12, m22 = uppertri return [ [m00, m01, m02], [m01, m11, m12], [m02, m12, m22] ] Parameters: pinvtol: Threshold for inverting eigenvalues. Eigenvalues with magnitude less than this are treated as zero. Typical value not given in the sources. svdtol: Tolerance for SVD convergence. Typical value not given in the sources. svdsweeps: Number of sweeps for the SVD algorithm. Typical value not given in the sources. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Singular/Ill-conditioned Matrices: The pinvtol parameter handles near-zero eigenvalues, preventing division by zero and stabilizing the solution. Symmetry Assumption: The method assumes A is symmetric, as the decomposition and storage format rely on this property. Dimensionality: The implementation is specific to 3 \times 3 matrices (SMat3, Vector3). Solves the overdetermined linear system Ax = b for a non-symmetric matrix A by explicitly forming the normal equations A^T A x = A^T b. Choose when A is not symmetric. Computes the pseudoinverse of a symmetric matrix from its eigenvectors and diagonal eigenvalues, handling near-zero eigenvalues via a threshold to ensure numerical stability. This is the core linear algebra primitive used by the Symmetric Least Squares Solver. Reconstructs spatially varying volume properties by solving the ill-conditioned linear system Wa = o using Conjugate Gradient minimization on the GPU, avoiding explicit storage of the large sparse matrix W. Choose for large-scale volume rendering where explicit SVD is too expensive. Strengths: Provides a direct solution for symmetric systems; handles singular or ill-conditioned matrices via eigenvalue thresholding. Limitations: Explicitly forms the pseudoinverse, which is computationally expensive for large matrices; limited to symmetric matrices. When to Use: Small, dense, symmetric linear systems (e.g., local optimization steps in dual contouring) where stability is critical. When Not to Use: Large, sparse systems where iterative methods are preferred. The method is implemented in the DualContouringCSharp repository by tuckbone. It is used in the context of dual contouring for implicit surface reconstruction, where small symmetric linear systems arise from optimizing vertex positions. tuckbone/DualContouringCSharp, https://github.com/tuckbone/DualContouringCSharp, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial)

name: General Least Squares Solver
body: The General Least Squares Solver addresses the overdetermined linear system Ax = b for a non-symmetric matrix A. It solves this by explicitly forming the normal equations A^T A x = A^T b, thereby reducing the problem to solving a symmetric system. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Matrix A (non-symmetric), vector b. Output: Solution vector x, residual error scalar. Data Structures: A: Dense matrix. A^T: Transpose of A. A^T A: Symmetric matrix. A^T b: Vector. x: Solution vector. Steps: 1. Compute the transpose of A, denoted A^T, using a standard matrix transpose operation. 2. Compute the product A^T A using a matrix multiplication routine optimized for the form A^T A. 3. Compute the product A^T b using a matrix-vector multiplication routine. 4. Solve the symmetric system (A^T A) x = A^T b using the Symmetric Least Squares Solver (SVD-based pseudoinverse method). 5. Return the solution x and the residual error. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def solvegeneralleastsquares(A, b, svdtol, svdsweeps, pinvtol): # Step 1: Transpose A At = [[A[j][i] for j in range(len(A))] for i in range(len(A[0]))] # Step 2: Compute A^T A n = len(At) AtA = [[sum(At[i][k] A[k][j] for k in range(len(A))) for j in range(n)] for i in range(n)] # Step 3: Compute A^T b Atb = [sum(At[i][j] b[j] for j in range(len(b))) for i in range(n)] # Step 4: Solve symmetric system (A^T A)x = A^T b using SVD-based pseudoinverse x = solvesymmetric(AtA, Atb, svdtol, svdsweeps, pinvtol) # Step 5: Calculate residual error ||Ax - b|| Ax = [sum(A[i][j] x[j] for j in range(len(x))) for i in range(len(A))] residual = sum((Ax[i] - b[i])2 for i in range(len(b)))0.5 return x, residual def solvesymmetric(AtA, Atb, svdtol, svdsweeps, pinvtol): # Computes pseudoinverse of AtA via SVD and solves for x # Uses getSymmetricSvd and pseudoinverse routines internally # Returns solution vector x # (Implementation details delegated to the symmetric solver component) return x Parameters: svdtol: Tolerance for SVD decomposition in the symmetric solver. Not given in the sources. svdsweeps: Number of Jacobi sweeps for SVD. Not given in the sources. pinvtol: Tolerance for pseudoinverse calculation. Not given in the sources. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Not given in the sources. The Normal Equations Solver addresses the overdetermined linear system Ax = b by explicitly forming the symmetric positive semi-definite matrix A^T A and vector A^T b, then solving the resulting square system. It is distinguished from matrix-free iterative methods (like CGLS) by its direct assembly of the normal equations. Not given in the sources. The method relies on the Symmetric Least Squares Solver for the final step, which uses SVD-based pseudoinverse calculation. tuckbone/DualContouringCSharp, https://github.com/tuckbone/DualContouringCSharp, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial)

name: Normal Equations Solver
head: A^T A Solver, Least Squares via Normal Equations
body: The Normal Equations Solver addresses the overdetermined linear system Ax = b by explicitly forming the symmetric positive semi-definite system A^T A x = A^T b and solving it using a standard linear solver. It is distinguished from iterative methods (like CGLS) and direct factorizations of the original matrix (like QR) by its reliance on the explicit construction of the Hessian matrix A^T A. While generally the fastest alternative for small-to-medium systems, it is prone to numerical instability if the system matrix A is ill-conditioned. Inputs and Outputs: Input: System matrix A \in \mathbb{R}^{m \times n} (where m \gg n) and vector b \in \mathbb{R}^m. Output: Solution vector x \in \mathbb{R}^n. Data Structures: Matrix A: Stored in Compressed Sparse Row (CSR) format to allow efficient sequential querying of non-zero entries for the i-th voxel (row). Matrix A^T A: A band matrix with non-zero entries only on the main diagonal and two diagonals four rows/columns away from the main diagonal. The distance of four arises from the separate handling of RGB\alpha channels. Due to symmetry, only the upper triangular part is stored. Vector A^T b: Standard dense or sparse vector representation. Steps: 1. Assemble A^T A and A^T b: Compute the sparse matrix-matrix product A^T A and the sparse matrix-vector product A^T b using a linear algebra library (e.g., Eigen on CPU, cuSPARSE on GPU) or custom matrix-free compute code. 2. Solve the Symmetric System: Solve the ordinary least squares problem A^T A x = A^T b using a dense or sparse linear least squares solver (e.g., QR, LLT, LDLT). 3. Constraint Handling: The standard normal equations solver does not enforce box constraints 0 \le xi \le 1. If the unconstrained solution violates these constraints, apply truncation: x'i = \max\{\min\{xi, 1\}, 0\}. If explicit constraint enforcement is required, a constrained quadratic programming solver (e.g., ADMM via OSQP) should be used instead. Pseudocode (Matrix-free GPU Assembly): Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def assemblenormalequations(voxels, ATAuppertri): # Initialize ATAuppertri as a band matrix structure for i in range(len(voxels)): j = computecolumnindex(voxels[i]) # From Subsec. 3.2 w = computeinterpolationweight(voxels[i]) # From Subsec. 3.2 # Atomically add to upper triangular part of A^T A ATAuppertri[j, j] += (1 - w)2 ATAuppertri[j+1, j+1] += w2 ATAuppertri[j+1, j] += (1 - w) w # Compute A^T b similarly return ATAuppertri Formulas: Normal Equations: A^T A x = A^T b. Condition Number Relationship: \text{cond}(A^T A) = \text{cond}(A). The source text states this equality, noting that computing A^T A results in many arithmetic additions and potentially very large values, which leads to numerical instability. Truncation: x'i = \max\{\min\{xi, 1\}, 0\}. Parameters: Precision: 32-bit floating point is typical. For a dataset with 1.76 \cdot 10^6 voxels, storing A in CSR format requires almost 7 GiB of memory. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Ill-conditioning: The condition number relationship \text{cond}(A^T A) = \text{cond}(A) leads to potential numerical instability due to accumulated arithmetic operations and large matrix values. Rank Deficiency: A^T A is often nearly rank deficient because certain transfer function values are hardly referenced by voxel values, or rank deficient if no values fall within a certain range. Solvers like QR may require pivoting for stability. GPU Atomic Contention: While atomic additions on GPU for assembling A^T A might theoretically cause write conflicts and slowdowns, in practice this method proved to be one of the fastest solutions. Addresses the box-constrained least squares problem (0 \le xi \le 1) by formulating it as a quadratic programming (QP) problem. It differs from direct unconstrained solvers by explicitly handling constraints (often via ADMM) and differs from iterative solvers by relying on the explicit construction of the Hessian Q = A^T A. Time Complexity: Generally the fastest alternative for small-to-medium systems where A^T A is small enough to fit in memory and be solved directly. Memory Complexity: Storing A is expensive (e.g., ~7 GiB for 1.76 \cdot 10^6 voxels with 32-bit floats), but A^T A is usually quite small and can be stored in dense or sparse format. Strengths: Fast assembly and solution for small systems; leverages highly optimized dense linear algebra libraries for the final solve step. Limitations: Prone to stability issues if A is ill-conditioned due to the condition number relationship; does not natively support box constraints without post-processing or external QP solvers. When to Use: When A^T A is small enough to be stored and solved directly, and numerical stability is not a primary concern or the matrix is well-conditioned. When Not to Use: When A is ill-conditioned (use QR or iterative methods); when explicit box constraints are required (use Normal Equations-based Solver with QP). The method originates from the formulation of ordinary least squares problems in volume rendering transfer function optimization. It is discussed in the context of comparing solver strategies for optimizing RGB\alpha values, where the system matrix A is tall and skinny (m \gg n). The approach is noted as the most straightforward solution, with implementations supporting CPU (Eigen), GPU (cuSPARSE), and matrix-free Vulkan compute. name: Normal Equations-based Solver
head: A^T A Solver, Constrained Least Squares, Least Squares via Normal Equations, Quadratic Programming Solver (Box-Constrained)
body: The Normal Equations-based Solver addresses the box-constrained least squares problem \forall i \in [1,...,n]: 0 \le xi \le 1 by formulating it as a quadratic programming (QP) problem. It differs from direct unconstrained solvers by explicitly handling the box constraints via the Alternating Direction Method of Multipliers (ADMM). Unlike iterative least-squares solvers that avoid forming the normal equations, this method explicitly constructs the Hessian Q = A^T A, which shares the drawback of quadratic condition number amplification. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Matrix A (size m \times n), vector b (size m), and constraint bounds [0, 1] for each element of x. Output: Vector x (size n) minimizing the constrained objective. Data Structures: Exact layouts and bit packing are not given in the sources. The method stores Q = A^T A and c = -A^T b as sparse structures to exploit sparsity. Steps: 1. Construct the quadratic programming parameters by computing Q = A^T A and c = -A^T b. 2. Formulate the objective as \minx \frac{1}{2} x^T Q x + c^T x subject to 0 \le xi \le 1 for all i \in [1,...,n]. 3. Solve the constrained QP problem using an ADMM solver (e.g., OSQP). 4. The ADMM method splits the objective into a data term and a prior term, alternating between subproblems and maintaining a dual variable u to enforce consensus. Formulas: Objective: \minx \frac{1}{2} x^T Q x + c^T x, where x \in \mathbb{R}^n, Q \in \mathbb{R}^{n \times n}, and c \in \mathbb{R}^n. Hessian: Q = A^T A, where A \in \mathbb{R}^{m \times n}. Linear term: c = -A^T b, where b \in \mathbb{R}^m. Constraints: 0 \le xi \le 1 for all i \in [1,...,n]. Parameters: Typical values are not given in the sources. Solver: OSQP. Hardware: CPU implementation is standard; a GPU implementation exists but offers no significant speed-up for the small matrix sizes resulting from normal equations. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Ill-conditioning: The condition number of Q is the square of the condition number of A, making the method prone to stability issues for large, ill-conditioned systems. Convexity: The ordinary least squares problem is convex, as the Hessian H(x) = 2 A^T A is positive semi-definite. Truncation fallback: If constraints are not enforced explicitly by the solver, values are truncated via x'i = \max\{\min\{xi, 1\}, 0\}. The ADMM Solver is an optimization method for solving separable minimization problems of the form \minx f(x) + g(x) by splitting the objective into a data term f(x) and a prior term g(x). It differs from direct solvers by decoupling these terms into alternating subproblems, allowing specialized solvers for each component, and differs from primal-dual methods by explicitly maintaining a dual variable u to enforce consensus between the split variables. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. The solver exploits sparsity in the problem definition. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Performance: For the small size of A^T A resulting from normal equations, no significant speed-up was observed with GPU implementations compared to CPU implementations. Strengths: Handles box constraints explicitly; leverages sparse solvers. Limitations: Prone to stability issues if the matrix is ill-conditioned due to the quadratic condition number. When to use: When box constraints are required and the system size is small enough to avoid severe ill-conditioning. When not to use: For very large, ill-conditioned systems where avoiding A^T A is preferable. The method is based on formulating box-constrained least squares as a quadratic programming problem, a technique used in opacity optimization approaches [GRT13, AZD17]. The ADMM method was first introduced by Boyd et al. [BPC∗ 11] for solving convex optimization problems. The OSQP solver library [SBG∗ 20] is commonly used for this purpose. name: ADMM Solver
head: Alternating Direction Method of Multipliers, Standard ADMM
body: The ADMM Solver is an optimization method for solving separable minimization problems of the form \minx f(x) + g(x) by splitting the objective into a data term f(x) and a prior term g(x). It differs from direct solvers by decoupling these terms into alternating subproblems, allowing specialized solvers for each component, and differs from primal-dual methods by explicitly maintaining a dual variable u to enforce consensus between the split variables. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Objective functions f(x) and g(x); linear operator D (identity I for standard form); penalty parameter \rho > 0; initial guesses x^0, z^0, u^0. Output: Optimal variable x. Data Structures: Vectors x, z, u \in \mathbb{R}^n. Scalar \rho. Integer iteration counter k. Steps: 1. Initialize: Set k=0. Initialize x^0, z^0, u^0. 2. Check Convergence: If convergence criteria met, return x^k. 3. Update x: Solve for x^{k+1} by minimizing the augmented Lagrangian with respect to x: x^{k+1} = \operatorname{argmin}x f(x) + \frac{\rho}{2} \|Dx - z^k + u^k\|^2 For D=I, this simplifies to the proximal operator: x^{k+1} = \text{prox}{\rho f}(x^k - u^k). 4. Update z: Solve for z^{k+1} by minimizing the augmented Lagrangian with respect to z: z^{k+1} = \operatorname{argmin}z g(z) + \frac{\rho}{2} \|Dx^{k+1} - z + u^k\|^2 For D=I, this simplifies to the proximal operator: z^{k+1} = \text{prox}{\rho g}(x^{k+1} + u^k). 5. Update Dual: Update the scaled dual variable u: u^{k+1} = u^k + Dx^{k+1} - z^{k+1} When D=I, this becomes u^{k+1} = x^k + x^{k+1} - z^{k+1}. 6. Increment: Set k \leftarrow k+1 and return to Step 2. Formulas: Augmented Lagrangian: L(x, z, u) = f(x) + g(z) + \frac{\rho}{2} \|Dx - z + u\|^2. Proximal Operator: \text{prox}{\lambda h}(y) = \operatorname{argmin}x h(x) + \frac{1}{2\lambda} \|x - y\|^2. Standard ADMM (when D=I): x^{k+1} = \text{prox}{\rho f}(x^k - u^k) z^{k+1} = \text{prox}{\rho g}(x^{k+1} + u^k) u^{k+1} = x^k + x^{k+1} - z^{k+1} Parameters: \rho: Penalty parameter. Typical values are not given in the sources. \lambda: Used in the standard form definition, effectively equivalent to \rho in the scaled form. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision issues may arise if \rho is too large or too small, affecting convergence speed. The x-update may require iterative solvers like Conjugate Gradient (CG) when D is not easily invertible, as implemented in the Reconstruction ToolKit (RTK). Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def admmsolver(f, g, D, rho, x0, z0, u0, maxiter=1000, tol=1e-6): """ Solves minx f(x) + g(Dx) using ADMM. """ x = x0.copy() z = z0.copy() u = u0.copy() for k in range(maxiter): # Update x: argminx f(x) + (rho/2) ||Dx - z + u||^2 if Disidentity(D): xnew = proxfscaled(x - u, rho) else: # Solve quadratic subproblem; typically via Conjugate Gradient xnew = solvexsubproblem(f, D, rho, z, u) # Update z: argminz g(z) + (rho/2) ||Dxnew - z + u||^2 znew = proxgscaled(D(xnew) + u, rho) # Update dual: u^{k+1} = u^k + Dx^{k+1} - z^{k+1} unew = u + D(xnew) - znew # Check convergence if vectornorm(xnew - x) < tol and vectornorm(znew - z) < tol and vectornorm(unew - u) < tol: return xnew x = xnew z = znew u = unew return x def proxfscaled(y, rho): """Computes prox{rho f}(y) = argminx f(x) + (rho/2)||x - y||^2.""" return proxf(y, rho) def proxgscaled(y, rho): """Computes prox{rho g}(y) = argminz g(z) + (rho/2)||z - y||^2.""" return proxg(y, rho) def proxf(y, lambdaval): """Standard proximal operator for f: argminx f(x) + 1/(2lambda)||x - y||^2.""" # Implementation depends on f. For L2 data term f(x)=0.5||Ax-p||^2, solve linear system. raise NotImplementedError("Proximal operator for f must be provided.") def proxg(y, lambdaval): """Standard proximal operator for g: argminz g(z) + 1/(2lambda)||z - y||^2.""" # Example for L1 norm g(x)=||x||1: soft thresholding return softthreshold(y, lambdaval) def softthreshold(y, threshold): return sign(y) max(abs(y) - threshold, 0) def solvexsubproblem(f, D, rho, z, u): """Solves x = argminx f(x) + (rho/2)||Dx - z + u||^2.""" # Uses Conjugate Gradient as implemented in RTK raise NotImplementedError("x-subproblem solver must be provided.") def Disidentity(D): return D is None or D == 'I' def vectornorm(v): return (sum(val2 for val in v))0.5 This method solves the L1 shearlet regularized Computed Tomography (CT) reconstruction problem using the Alternating Direction Method of Multipliers (ADMM). It is designed to produce high-quality reconstructions from limited-angle or sparse sinogram data by enforcing sparsity in the shearlet domain while maintaining data consistency. It differs from standard Filtered Backprojection (FBP) by incorporating a non-linear prior that preserves edges and reduces artifacts, and it differs from other ADMM solvers by specifically structuring the proximal operators for shearlet sparsity and non-negativity constraints. Time Complexity: Depends on the cost of evaluating f, g, and their proximal operators, and the number of iterations to convergence. Each iteration involves one evaluation of D and its transpose (if needed for the x-update). Memory Complexity: O(n) for storing x, z, u and intermediate vectors. Measured Performance: Implemented in the Reconstruction ToolKit (RTK) as an ADMM total variation-regularized solver with conjugate gradient (CG) method. Scaling: Scales well with problem size if subproblems can be solved efficiently. Strengths: Handles non-smooth priors (like L1) effectively; decouples complex objectives. Limitations: Convergence can be slow for ill-conditioned problems; requires careful tuning of \rho. When to use: When the objective function is separable into a data term and a prior term, and proximal operators are available or easy to compute. When not to use: When the problem is not separable or proximal operators are expensive to compute. The ADMM method is a proximal algorithm used for volume reconstruction, particularly in Computed Tomography (CT). It is implemented in the Reconstruction ToolKit (RTK), a high-performance toolkit for 3D cone beam reconstruction based on ITK. The method is part of a broader class of proximal algorithms for solving inverse problems. name: L1 Shearlet Regularized CT Reconstruction (ADMM)
head: ADMM Shearlet Reconstruction, Bubba et al. Algorithm
body: This method solves the L1 shearlet regularized computed tomography (CT) reconstruction problem using the Alternating Direction Method of Multipliers (ADMM). It minimizes a composite objective consisting of a weighted L1 norm of shearlet coefficients and a quadratic data fidelity term, subject to non-negativity constraints on the image. It sets itself apart from standard filtered backprojection by enforcing sparsity in the shearlet domain to handle limited-angle artifacts, and from its parent ADMM Solver by specifically structuring the proximal steps for shearlet shrinkage and non-negativity clamping. Inputs and Outputs: Input: y (measured sinogram), radon (forward Radon projection operator R), shearlet (shearlet transform operator SH). Output: f (reconstructed image volume). Data Structures: f: Image tensor, shape matching the backprojected image bp. bp: Backprojected image tensor, shape matching f. sc: Shearlet coefficients of bp, shape matching shf. u1, z1: Dual and primal variables for shearlet constraint, shape matching sc. u2, z2: Dual and primal variables for non-negativity constraint, shape matching bp. cgy: Right-hand side vector for the conjugate gradient linear system. w: Weight vector for the L1 norm, shape matching shf. Parameters: p0: Data fidelity weight. Typical value: 0.02. p1: Regularization weight. Typical value: 0.1. numiterations: Number of ADMM iterations. Not given in the sources. maxiter: Maximum iterations for the inner Conjugate Gradient solver. Typical value: 50. nscales: Number of shearlet scales. Typical value: 5. w calculation: w = 3^{\text{scales}} / 400, reshaped to (1, -1, 1, 1) for broadcasting. Algorithm Steps: 1. Initialization: Initialize u2, z2, u1, z1, f to zero tensors with shapes matching bp and sc respectively. Compute initial backprojection bp = radon.backward(y). Compute initial shearlet coefficients of backprojection sc = shearlet.forward(bp). Compute weights w = 3nscales / 400 and reshape to broadcastable dimensions (1, -1, 1, 1). 2. ADMM Loop (for i in range(numiterations)): Compute CG RHS: cg\y = p0 \cdot bp + p1 \cdot \text{shearlet.backward}(z1 - u1) + (z2 - u2) Solve for f (Primal Update): Solve the linear system for f using Conjugate Gradient Least Squares (CGLS): \minf \left( p0 \cdot \| R f - y \|2^2 + (1 + p1) \cdot \| f \|2^2 \right) This is equivalent to solving: (p0 \cdot R^T R + (1 + p1) \cdot I) f = cg\y Using the solver: f = cg(lambda x: p0 radon.backward(radon.forward(x)) + (1 + p1) x, f.clone(), cgy, maxiter=50). Shearlet Transform: Compute shearlet coefficients of the new f: sh\f = \text{shearlet.forward}(f) Update z1 (Shearlet Proximal Step): Apply soft-thresholding (shrinkage) to update the primal variable for the shearlet constraint: z1 = \text{shrink}(sh\f + u1, \frac{p0}{p1} \cdot w) Update z2 (Non-negativity Proximal Step): Project onto the non-negative orthant: z2 = \max(0, f + u2) Implemented as z2 = (f + u2).clampmin(0). Update Dual Variables: u1 = u1 + sh\f - z1 u2 = u2 + f - z2 Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def l1shearletadmm(y, radon, shearlet, numiterations=100, maxcgiter=50): p0 = 0.02 p1 = 0.1 nscales = 5 bp = radon.backward(y) sc = shearlet.forward(bp) u2 = zeroslike(bp) z2 = zeroslike(bp) u1 = zeroslike(sc) z1 = zeroslike(sc) f = zeroslike(bp) w = (3 nscales) / 400 w = reshape(w, (1, -1, 1, 1)) def linearop(x): return p0 radon.backward(radon.forward(x)) + (1 + p1) x for i in range(numiterations): cgy = p0 bp + p1 shearlet.backward(z1 - u1) + (z2 - u2) f = conjugategradient(linearop, f.clone(), cgy, maxiter=maxcgiter) shf = shearlet.forward(f) threshold = (p0 / p1) w z1 = shrink(shf + u1, threshold) z2 = clamp(f + u2, min=0.0) u1 = u1 + shf - z1 u2 = u2 + f - z2 return f def zeroslike(tensor): return fulllike(tensor, 0.0) def fulllike(tensor, val): return [val] tensor.size def conjugategradient(A, x0, b, maxiter): x = x0.copy() r = b - A(x) p = r.copy() rsold = dot(r, r) for in range(maxiter): Ap = A(p) alpha = rsold / dot(p, Ap) x = x + alpha p r = r - alpha Ap rsnew = dot(r, r) if sqrt(rsnew) < 1e-6: break p = r + (rsnew / rsold) p rsold = rsnew return x def shrink(a, b): return clamp(abs(a) - b, min=0.0) sign(a) def clamp(tensor, min=None, max=None): if min is not None: tensor = maximum(tensor, min) if max is not None: tensor = minimum(tensor, max) return tensor Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision: The implementation supports single and half precision. Relative error between single and half precision for the Shepp-Logan phantom is 1.40 \cdot 10^{-4}, and reconstruction MSE error difference is negligible (2.0566 \cdot 10^{-4} vs 2.0567 \cdot 10^{-4}). Limited Angles: The method is designed for limited-angle tomography where R represents forward projection with limited angles. Numerical Stability: The inner CG solver requires a well-conditioned system. The term (1+p1)I acts as a regularization term to ensure invertibility. A GPU-based cone-beam CT reconstruction method that uses TIGRE for forward/backward projections and an ADMM solver with restarted GMRES for the x-update step to handle numerical mismatch between TIGRE's Ax and A^Tb operators. It sets itself apart from its parent L1 Shearlet Regularized CT Reconstruction (ADMM) by returning to TIGRE reconstruction physics, using matched A and A^T operators from TIGRE, and employing GMRES to solve the linear system arising from the ADMM x-update due to potential numerical mismatch between the forward and adjoint operators. Time Complexity: The dominant cost per iteration is the forward/backward Radon projections and the shearlet transform, plus the conjugate gradient solve. The CG solve converges in up to maxiter (50) steps per ADMM iteration. Memory Complexity: Requires storage for f, bp, sc, u1, z1, u2, z2, and cgy. Measured Performance: On a Tesla V100 GPU, the implementation runs in 1.6 seconds per reconstruction, compared to 2.5 minutes on an Intel i7 CPU in the original paper, representing a 125x speedup. With batch processing, the average time is 1.2 seconds per image. Strengths: All operations (including shearlet transforms) are performed on the GPU, maximizing execution speed. No CPU-GPU memory copies occur in the main loop. Supports batch processing for parallel sinogram handling. Limitations: Performance depends on the convergence of the inner CG solver. The method is specific to L1 shearlet regularization and may not be optimal for other priors. The method is based on the work of Bubba et al. [4], who proposed solving the L1 shearlet regularized CT reconstruction problem as a preprocessing step for deep learning-based inverse problems. The original implementation was on CPU, but a GPU-accelerated version using TorchRadon was developed to leverage modern hardware. The algorithm uses the Alternating Direction Method of Multipliers (ADMM) to decouple the data fidelity term from the sparsity-promoting shearlet prior and the non-negativity constraint. name: TomoAnchor V3 Z-Sharded ADMM-GMRES
head: V3 solver
body: A GPU-based cone-beam CT reconstruction method that uses TIGRE for forward/backward projections and an ADMM solver with restarted GMRES for the x-update step to handle numerical mismatch between TIGRE's Ax and A^Tb operators. It sets itself apart from its parent L1 Shearlet Regularized CT Reconstruction (ADMM) by returning to TIGRE reconstruction physics, using matched A and A^T operators from TIGRE, and employing GMRES to solve the linear system arising from the ADMM x-update due to potential numerical mismatch between the forward and adjoint operators. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Projection data y, forward projection operators As, backprojection operators Bs, weight matrix W, regularization parameter \rho, and initial volume estimate x. Output: Reconstructed volume x, split into shards xs. Data Structures: ShardedVolume: A dataclass with fields shards (tuple of arrays), volumeshards (tuple of VolumeShard objects), and xp (array library, default np). Numbered Steps: 1. Initialization: Initialize volume x and shards xs. Verify that the number of arrays matches the number of volume shards, raising ValueError if mismatched. Verify that shard local shape matches array shape, raising ValueError if tuple(int(value) for value in array.shape) != tuple(int(value) for value in shard.localshape). 2. ADMM Loop: For each ADMM iteration: a. x-update: Solve the linear system using restarted GMRES. The core matrix-vector product computes the global projection first, then the shard-wise residual. b. z-update: Update auxiliary variables based on current x and dual variable u. c. u-update: Update dual variable u based on current x and z. 3. Termination: Check convergence criteria (e.g., relative change in x, residual norm). If converged, stop; otherwise, return to step 2. Formulas: Each matvec computes the global projection first, then the shard output: y = \sums As xs \text{out}s = Bs W^2 y + \rho (G^T G x)s where As is the forward projection for shard s, Bs is the backprojection for shard s, W is the weight matrix, \rho is the regularization parameter, G is a linear operator, xs is the shard of volume x, and y is the global projection. Parameters: Residency mode: Determines host/device data management. stagedtigre: Production default. Uses stock TIGRE NumPy wrappers with pinned/staged host buffers. Preserves TIGRE physics but is not strict GPU-resident. devicetigre: Strict native bridge backend. Keeps ADMM-GMRES solver vectors host-resident, streams one z-shard at a time to GPU, and calls TIGRE CUDA kernels through the TomoAnchor native CuPy device-pointer bridge. Requires running python tools/buildtigredevicebackend.py --preflight-only then python tools/buildtigredevicebackend.py --tigre-source tools/TIGRE. devicetigreresident: Full CuPy-resident backend. Keeps all V3 solver shards on selected GPUs. Only appropriate when the whole ADMM-GMRES state fits in aggregate VRAM. auto: Uses devicetigre only when available, otherwise stagedtigre unless strict residency is required. Number of GMRES restarts: Not given in the sources. Tolerance for GMRES convergence: Not given in the sources. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Mismatch between the number of arrays and volume shards raises a ValueError. Mismatch between shard local shape and array shape raises a ValueError. Numerical mismatch between TIGRE's Ax and A^Tb operators necessitates GMRES instead of CG. The volume is split only along the z-axis; slabs are not reconstructed independently. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def admmgmresxupdate(xshards, As, Bs, W, rho, G): # Compute global projection y = sums As xs y = sum(Asi for i in range(len(xshards))) # Compute RHS for each shard: outs = Bs W^2 y + rho (G^T G x)s rhs = [] for i in range(len(xshards)): rhsi = Bsi + rho (G.T @ G @ xshards[i]) rhs.append(rhsi) # Define matvec for the linear system def matvec(vshards): vproj = sum(Asi for i in range(len(vshards))) return Bs[i + rho (G.T @ G @ vshards[i]) for i in range(len(vshards))] # Note: The sources do not provide the GMRES solver implementation. # A standard restarted GMRES implementation should be used here. xnew = gmresrestarted(matvec, rhs, xshards) return xnew Strengths: Uses TIGRE for accurate forward and backward projections, handles numerical mismatch between operators using GMRES, supports GPU acceleration via residency modes. Limitations: Numerical mismatch between operators may require careful tuning of GMRES parameters, residency modes may impact performance and memory usage. When to Use: Suitable for cone-beam CT reconstruction where TIGRE's physics are desired and GPU acceleration is needed. When Not to Use: Not suitable when strict GPU residency is required and the whole ADMM-GMRES state does not fit in aggregate VRAM, or when TIGRE's numerical mismatch cannot be handled by GMRES. Originated as part of the TomoAnchor V3 project, which aims to provide a flexible and efficient framework for CT reconstruction. The method builds on the L1 Shearlet Regularized CT Reconstruction (ADMM) algorithm, adapting it to use TIGRE for projections and GMRES for the x-update step. It is used in research and production environments for high-quality CT reconstruction. alidarbandi/TomoAnchor-V3, https://github.com/alidarbandi/TomoAnchor-V3, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial)

name: Symmetric Pseudo-Inverse Calculation
head: Pseudoinverse Calculation
body: Computes the pseudoinverse of a symmetric matrix given its eigenvectors and diagonal eigenvalues, handling near-zero eigenvalues via a threshold to ensure numerical stability. Unlike the General Least Squares Solver which processes arbitrary matrices, this method exploits symmetry to reconstruct the inverse directly from the eigen-decomposition, reducing arithmetic operations and memory footprint. It serves as the core linear algebra primitive for the Symmetric Least Squares Solver, enabling the solution of symmetric linear systems where the matrix may be singular or ill-conditioned. Inputs: V: A 3 \times 3 matrix of eigenvectors (stored as columns), where A = V D V^T. d: A length-3 array of diagonal eigenvalues [d0, d1, d2]. tol: A scalar threshold for singularity detection. Outputs: A^+: A 3 \times 3 pseudoinverse matrix. Data Structures: V: Stored as a 3 \times 3 array where V{ik} denotes the element at row i, column k. d: Stored as a length-3 array. A^+: Stored as a 3 \times 3 array with explicit fields for all 9 elements. Steps: 1. Thresholded Inversion: For each eigenvalue dk (k \in \{0,1,2\}), compute the inverted value dk^+: dk^+ = \begin{cases} 0 & \text{if } |dk| < tol \text{ or } |1/dk| < tol \\ 1/dk & \text{otherwise} \end{cases} This prevents division by zero or amplification of noise when eigenvalues are near zero. 2. Reconstruction: Compute the pseudoinverse A^+ using the eigenvectors and inverted eigenvalues. Since A = V D V^T, then A^+ = V D^+ V^T. The elements of A^+ are calculated as: A^+{ij} = \sum{k=0}^{2} V{ik} dk^+ V{jk} Explicitly for a 3 \times 3 matrix, all 9 elements are computed directly to preserve symmetry without relying on triangular mirroring: \begin{aligned} A^+{00} &= V{00}d0^+V{00} + V{01}d1^+V{01} + V{02}d2^+V{02} \\ A^+{01} &= V{00}d0^+V{10} + V{01}d1^+V{11} + V{02}d2^+V{12} \\ A^+{02} &= V{00}d0^+V{20} + V{01}d1^+V{21} + V{02}d2^+V{22} \\ A^+{10} &= V{10}d0^+V{00} + V{11}d1^+V{01} + V{12}d2^+V{02} \\ A^+{11} &= V{10}d0^+V{10} + V{11}d1^+V{11} + V{12}d2^+V{12} \\ A^+{12} &= V{10}d0^+V{20} + V{11}d1^+V{21} + V{12}d2^+V{22} \\ A^+{20} &= V{20}d0^+V{00} + V{21}d1^+V{01} + V{22}d2^+V{02} \\ A^+{21} &= V{20}d0^+V{10} + V{21}d1^+V{11} + V{22}d2^+V{12} \\ A^+{22} &= V{20}d0^+V{20} + V{21}d1^+V{21} + V{22}d2^+V{22} \end{aligned} Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. class Matrix3x3: def init(self): self.m00 = 0.0; self.m01 = 0.0; self.m02 = 0.0 self.m10 = 0.0; self.m11 = 0.0; self.m12 = 0.0 self.m20 = 0.0; self.m21 = 0.0; self.m22 = 0.0 def pinv(x, tol): """Thresholded inverse of a scalar.""" if abs(x) < tol or abs(1.0 / x) < tol: return 0.0 return 1.0 / x def symmetricpseudoinverse(V, d, tol): """ Computes pseudoinverse of symmetric matrix A = V diag(d) V^T. Args: V: List of lists (3x3), eigenvectors (columns). d: List (length 3), eigenvalues [d0, d1, d2]. tol: Float, singularity threshold. Returns: Matrix3x3, the pseudoinverse A+. """ # Step 1: Thresholded inversion of eigenvalues d0 = pinv(d[0], tol) d1 = pinv(d[1], tol) d2 = pinv(d[2], tol) # Step 2: Reconstruct A+ = V diag(d+) V^T Out = Matrix3x3() # Row 0 Out.m00 = V[0][0]d0V[0][0] + V[0][1]d1V[0][1] + V[0][2]d2V[0][2] Out.m01 = V[0][0]d0V[1][0] + V[0][1]d1V[1][1] + V[0][2]d2V[1][2] Out.m02 = V[0][0]d0V[2][0] + V[0][1]d1V[2][1] + V[0][2]d2V[2][2] # Row 1 Out.m10 = V[1][0]d0V[0][0] + V[1][1]d1V[0][1] + V[1][2]d2V[0][2] Out.m11 = V[1][0]d0V[1][0] + V[1][1]d1V[1][1] + V[1][2]d2V[1][2] Out.m12 = V[1][0]d0V[2][0] + V[1][1]d1V[2][1] + V[1][2]d2V[2][2] # Row 2 Out.m20 = V[2][0]d0V[0][0] + V[2][1]d1V[0][1] + V[2][2]d2V[0][2] Out.m21 = V[2][0]d0V[1][0] + V[2][1]d1V[1][1] + V[2][2]d2V[1][2] Out.m22 = V[2][0]d0V[2][0] + V[2][1]d1V[2][1] + V[2][2]d2V[2][2] return Out Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Singularity: If an eigenvalue is exactly zero, pinv returns 0, effectively removing that dimension from the solution space. Numerical Stability: The condition |1/x| < tol handles cases where x is very small but non-zero, preventing overflow or extreme noise amplification. Symmetry Preservation: The output matrix is explicitly symmetric by direct calculation of all 9 elements, avoiding reliance on triangular mirroring. Computes the pseudo-inverse of a 3 \times 3 symmetric matrix using eigen-decomposition, specifically designed for minimizing distance to a midpoint in dual contouring contexts. It uses auxiliary arrays w for inverse eigenvalues and u for eigenvectors. A key variant feature is the handling of degenerate cases: if two dominant eigenvalues are close (ratio > 0.2), it may return a pre-computed expectedNorm instead of computing the full inverse, optimizing for planar surfaces. Time Complexity: O(1) for fixed 3 \times 3 matrices, dominated by the 9 multiplications and additions for reconstruction. Memory Complexity: O(1), requiring storage for the input V, d, and output A^+. Strengths: Numerically stable for symmetric matrices; handles singular systems gracefully via thresholding; efficient for small fixed-size matrices. Limitations: Only applicable to symmetric matrices; requires pre-computed eigendecomposition; threshold selection (tol) is critical and problem-dependent. When to use: When solving symmetric linear systems Ax=b where A is derived from quadratic error functions and may be rank-deficient. When not to use: For non-symmetric matrices or when A is guaranteed to be full-rank and well-conditioned. Originated in the context of dual contouring and implicit surface reconstruction, where symmetric quadratic error functions are minimized. It leverages the mathematical property that the pseudoinverse of a symmetric matrix can be computed via its eigendecomposition, avoiding the more expensive general SVD. tuckbone/DualContouringCSharp, https://github.com/tuckbone/DualContouringCSharp, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial) ChessQian/DualContouring, https://github.com/ChessQian/DualContouring, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial)

name: GPU Volume Reconstruction via Conjugate Gradient
head: Implicit Matrix Solution, Ray Marching Back-Projection
body: This method reconstructs spatially varying volume properties (albedo, emission, extinction) by solving the ill-conditioned linear system Wa = o using Conjugate Gradient (CG) minimization on the GPU. It avoids explicit storage of the large sparse matrix W by implicitly computing matrix-vector products via ray marching. Inputs: Target images o (observation pixels). Initial volume estimate a (stored in 3D textures). Camera poses and intrinsics. Optional: Per-pixel constraint weights, visual hull masks, regularization weights. Outputs: Reconstructed volume properties a (albedo, emission, extinction) in 3D textures. Data Structures: Volume Properties (a): Stored in 3D textures representing vectors. Fields correspond to albedo, emission, and extinction. Precision can be 16-bit to reduce bandwidth. Target Images (o): 2D textures or buffers. Residual (c): 2D buffer storing Wa - o. Gradient/Direction Vectors: 3D textures for volume updates. Formulas: The objective is to minimize the quadratic error function: E(a) = ||Wa - o||^2 With regularization terms \Omega(a): E{reg}(a) = ||Wa - o||^2 + \lambdaL ||La||^2 + \lambda0 ||a||^2 + \lambda1 ||a - 1||^2 Where: W is the sparse rendering matrix. L is the Laplacian operator. \lambdaL, \lambda0, \lambda1 are user-defined weights (typically weak, e.g., 2^{-9}). Constraint weights wp are applied per pixel by multiplying the residual vector: minimize || (Wa - o) \odot wp ||^2. Numbered Steps: 1. Initialization: Initialize a (e.g., zeros or previous estimate). Compute initial gradient g0 = W^T(Wa0 - o). Set search direction p0 = -g0. 2. Iteration Loop: For k = 0, 1, \dots until convergence: a. Forward Pass (Wpk): Render the volume with properties pk to generate an image via ray marching. b. Back-Projection (W^T(Wpk)): Distribute the rendered image back to the volume voxels via ray marching with accumulation. c. Step Size: Compute \alphak = \frac{pk^T pk}{pk^T W^T W pk}. d. Update Solution: a{k+1} = ak + \alphak pk. e. Update Residual: g{k+1} = gk + \alphak W^T W pk. f. Convergence Check: If ||g{k+1}|| < \epsilon, stop. g. Beta: Compute \betak = \frac{g{k+1}^T g{k+1}}{gk^T gk}. h. Update Direction: p{k+1} = g{k+1} + \betak pk. Pseudocode: The core operations are implemented as shaders. The unified ray marching loop handles both forward (rendering) and backward (back-projection) passes. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def solvevolumecg(targetimages, initialvolume, maxiter=100, tol=1e-6): a = initialvolume.copy() # Compute initial gradient: g = W^T(Wa - o) Wa = raymarchforward(a) residualimg = Wa - targetimages g = raymarchbackward(residualimg) p = -g.copy() pdotp = dotproduct(p, p) for k in range(maxiter): if pdotp < tol: break # Compute W^T(Wp) Wp = raymarchforward(p) WTWp = raymarchbackward(Wp) pdotWTWp = dotproduct(p, WTWp) if pdotWTWp == 0: break alpha = pdotp / pdotWTWp a = a + alpha p g = g + alpha WTWp newpdotp = dotproduct(g, g) if newpdotp < tol: break beta = newpdotp / pdotp p = g + beta p pdotp = newpdotp return a def raymarchforward(volumeproperties): outputimage = zeroslike(targetimageshape) for pixel in allpixels: ray = getcameraray(pixel) accumulatedtransmittance = 1.0 accumulatedradiance = 0.0 tmin, tmax = ray.intersectvolume() t = tmin while t < tmax: position = ray.origin + t ray.direction emission = textureread3d(volumeproperties.emission, position) extinction = textureread3d(volumeproperties.extinction, position) weight = accumulatedtransmittance (1.0 - exp(-extinction)) accumulatedradiance += weight emission accumulatedtransmittance = exp(-extinction) t += ray.stepsize outputimage[pixel] = accumulatedradiance return outputimage def raymarchbackward(imageresidual): volumegradient = zeroslike(volumeproperties) # Interleaved 6x6 pattern to avoid synchronization stalls from data scattering # Process pixels in blocks, advancing by 6 each round to minimize conflicts for offsety in range(6): for offsetx in range(6): for y in range(offsety, height, 6): for x in range(offsetx, width, 6): pixel = (x, y) ray = getcameraray(pixel) residual = imageresidual[pixel] accumulatedbackproj = 0.0 accumulatedtransmittance = 1.0 tmin, tmax = ray.intersectvolume() t = tmin while t < tmax: position = ray.origin + t ray.direction extinction = textureread3d(volumeproperties.extinction, position) weight = accumulatedtransmittance (1.0 - exp(-extinction)) accumulatedbackproj += weight residual accumulatedtransmittance = exp(-extinction) t += ray.stepsize texturewriteadd3d(volumegradient, position, accumulatedbackproj) return volumegradient def dotproduct(u, v): return sum(u[i] v[i] for i in range(len(u))) def textureread3d(tex, pos): return tex.sample(pos) def texturewriteadd3d(tex, pos, val): tex[pos] = tex[pos] + val def zeroslike(shape): return [0.0] shape def getcameraray(pixel): return CameraRay(pixel, intrinsics, extrinsics) Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Synchronization Stalls: Data scattering during back-projection (texture writes) causes stalls because neighboring rays write to the same voxels. Precision: Use 16-bit textures instead of 32-bit to reduce bandwidth and speed up computation by ~25%. Resolution Mismatch: Albedo and emission can use lower resolution than extinction to accelerate computation and reduce memory, though this may affect quality. Refractive Rays: For non-constant refractive indices, use arbitrary integration curves computed via Euler forward scheme. Visual Hulls: Limit solution domain to voxels with non-zero extinction (for albedo/emission) or user-defined masks (for extinction) to improve quality and performance. Time Complexity: Depends on the number of CG iterations and the cost of ray marching per iteration. Memory Complexity: O(Nv) for volume storage, where Nv is the number of voxels. Performance: 16-bit textures provide ~25% speedup. Interleaved pixel pattern provides ~10% speedup by reducing synchronization stalls. Strengths: Handles large sparse systems without explicit matrix storage. Flexible regularization. Supports refraction and visual hulls. Limitations: Ill-conditioned systems may require careful regularization. Synchronization issues in back-projection can limit parallel efficiency. When to Use: When reconstructing volume properties from multiple views and explicit matrix storage is infeasible. When Not to Use: When high precision is critical and 16-bit textures are insufficient. This method was introduced in "Property and Lighting Manipulations for Static Volume Stylization Using a Painting Metaphor" (2014). It builds on the linearity of light transport and the sparsity of the rendering operator. The use of Conjugate Gradient for volume reconstruction allows for efficient optimization of volume properties without the memory overhead of direct matrix inversion. name: Adaptive Grid Optical Tomography
head: Adaptive Tomography, Adaptive reconstruction algorithm, Octree-based Optical Tomography, Octree-based adaptive CT
body: Adaptive Grid Optical Tomography is a volumetric reconstruction method that represents the 3D density field using an adaptive octree grid of piecewise constant basis functions, allowing for higher effective resolution and better memory efficiency than uniform grids by using fewer basis functions in uniform regions. It solves the problem of reconstructing dynamic, semi-transparent phenomena (such as smoke and flames) from multi-view video sequences by iteratively refining the grid resolution only where the reconstruction error is high, combined with a visual hull constraint to restrict the solution space. Unlike uniform grid approaches, which quickly exhaust memory limits for high-resolution multi-camera setups, this method uses 20-25% of the memory while achieving comparable accuracy. Inputs: A synchronized multi-video sequence of nc cameras. Camera calibration parameters (intrinsics and extrinsics) for all cameras. A set of background images for each camera. A visual hull (or silhouette masks) for each camera, derived from the background-subtracted foreground images. Outputs: A sparse system matrix S representing the projection of the current octree basis functions onto the image planes. A coefficient vector a representing the density values of the active basis functions. The final adaptive octree structure defining the 3D density field. Sparse Matrix S: Layout: Index-stored sparse matrix (coordinate format). Stores two indices (row, column) and the matrix value for each non-zero entry. Rows: Correspond to pixels in the image plane across all cameras. Total rows np is the number of pixels in one frame multiplied by the number of cameras nc. Columns: Correspond to basis functions (octree leaves) in the 3D volume. Entries: S{ij} is the integral of basis function \phij over the ray/pixel area for pixel i. Non-zero only if the support of \phij projects onto pixel i. Octree Node Structure: Used to track the splitting process and identify geometry. Fields: splitlevel: Integer, depth from the root of the octree. leafindex: Integer, the index the leaf would have in a uniformly split octree under a fixed traversal order (e.g., Morton order). This structure allows the algorithm to determine the position and size of new basis functions generated during splitting and to compute the integral values for the new columns of S. Coefficient Vector a: Vector of density coefficients corresponding to the columns of S. Constrained to be non-negative (ai \ge 0). Residual Vector r: r = p - S a, where p is the background-subtracted pixel vector. k: Number of basis functions to split per iteration. Typical value: \sqrt{nb}, where nb is the current number of basis functions. Max Split Level: Maximum depth of the octree. Stopping criterion based on the Nyquist limit: splitting stops if a basis function projects to less than two pixels in all images. Non-negative Constraint: Applied during the solver step. 1. Preprocessing (Background Subtraction): Record background images for all cameras. Compute the median background image and standard deviation per pixel for each camera. Classify pixels as foreground or background based on the standard deviation. For foreground pixels, subtract the background value. For background pixels, set the value to zero. This computes the target vector p (representing p{original} - b) in advance. 2. Initialization: Initialize a uniform grid of box basis functions at the coarsest level (root of the octree). Construct the initial sparse projection matrix S where rows correspond to pixels and columns to basis functions. S{ij} is non-zero if basis function \phij projects onto pixel pi. Apply Visual Hull Restriction to S (see Substeps 2.1 and 2.2 below) to remove columns corresponding to basis functions with non-zero support completely outside the visual hull. 2.1. Visual Hull Restriction (Column Pruning): For each camera, create a binary vector marking basis functions that have non-zero support in the camera's silhouette (generalized cone). Compute the element-wise logical AND of all camera binary vectors to find the intersection of generalized cones (the visual hull). Restrict matrix S to only include columns (basis functions) that are inside the visual hull intersection. Keep all rows (pixels), even those outside the silhouette, to ensure accurate boundary representation. 2.2. Visual Hull Restriction (Row Handling): Note: Rows corresponding to pixels outside the silhouette are kept but will have zero entries in the right-hand side vector p (after background subtraction). The basis functions on the boundary of the visual hull are likely to be split, allowing the boundary to be represented accurately. 3. Adaptive Iteration Loop: Repeat the following steps until convergence or maximum split level is reached: Step 1: Solve for Coefficients Solve the linear least squares system using the CGLS (Conjugate Gradient Least Squares) solver. The system is: S a = p. In every iteration of CGLS, project the solution to the subspace of non-negative solutions by setting all negative entries of the solution vector a to zero. The theoretical least squares solution is given by: a = (S^T S)^{-1} S^T (p - b) where p is the background-subtracted pixel vector and b is the background (already subtracted in preprocessing, so effectively p in the code represents p{orig}-b). Step 2: Compute Residual and Error Measure Compute the residual error vector: r = p - S a Project the residual error onto the basis functions to get a measure of where to split. For each basis function \phij, compute the error measure e{\phij}: e{\phij} = \frac{\sum{i} S{ij} |ri|}{n{\phij}} where the sum is over all pixels i for which S{ij} \neq 0, and n{\phij} is the number of cameras in which basis function \phij is visible (i.e., the number of non-zero entries in column j of S). Note: This formula weights the residual by the projection strength S{ij} to provide a better measure than simply summing absolute residuals. Step 3: Split Basis Functions Identify the k basis functions with the largest error measures e{\phij}. k is typically set to \sqrt{nb}, where nb is the current number of basis functions. Split the selected k basis functions uniformly. For box basis functions, this involves replacing the column in matrix S with columns for the new sub-boxes (children in the octree). For linear basis functions, asymmetric basis functions must be introduced where splitting levels overlap. Update matrix S: Remove the columns corresponding to the split basis functions. Insert new columns for the new basis functions. Recalculate the integral values for the new columns using the octree node structure (split level and leaf index). Re-apply Visual Hull Restriction to the updated matrix S to ensure new basis functions outside the visual hull are removed. Step 4: Termination Check Check if the estimate is good enough. Stop splitting if: A maximum split level is reached. A basis function projects to less than two pixels in all images (Nyquist limit). If not converged, go back to Step 1. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def adaptivegridopticaltomography(cameras, backgroundimages, maxsplitlevel): """ Reconstructs a 3D density field from multi-view video using adaptive octree grid. Args: cameras: List of camera objects with calibration and projection functions. backgroundimages: List of background images for each camera. maxsplitlevel: Maximum depth of the octree. Returns: octree: The final adaptive octree structure. coefficients: The density coefficients for the active basis functions. """ # 1. Preprocessing # Compute median background and standard deviation per pixel medianbackgrounds = [] stddevs = [] for camidx, cam in enumerate(cameras): bgimg = backgroundimages[camidx] medianbg = computemedian(bgimg) std = computestd(bgimg) medianbackgrounds.append(medianbg) stddevs.append(std) # Classify pixels and compute target vector p (p - b) # p is a flattened vector of all pixels across all cameras p = [] for camidx, cam in enumerate(cameras): currentframe = getcurrentframe(cam) # Assuming this is called per iteration or pre-loaded bg = medianbackgrounds[camidx] std = stddevs[camidx] campixels = [] for pixel in currentframe: if isforeground(pixel, bg, std): campixels.append(pixel - bg) else: campixels.append(0.0) p.extend(campixels) p = np.array(p) # 2. Initialization # Initialize uniform grid of box basis functions (root level) octree = Octree(rootlevel=0) # Construct initial sparse matrix S # Rows = pixels, Cols = basis functions S = buildsparsematrix(cameras, octree) # Apply Visual Hull Restriction S = applyvisualhullrestriction(S, cameras, octree) # Initialize coefficients vector a nbasis = S.shape[1] a = np.zeros(nbasis) # 3. Adaptive Iteration Loop while True: # Step 1: Solve for coefficients using CGLS with non-negative constraint a = cglssolve(S, p, a, nonnegative=True) # Step 2: Compute Residual and Error Measure r = p - S @ a e = computeerrormeasure(S, r) # Step 3: Split Basis Functions nbasis = S.shape[1] k = int(np.sqrt(nbasis)) # Identify k basis functions with largest error splitindices = gettopkindices(e, k) # Check termination criteria (Nyquist limit) cansplit = True for idx in splitindices: basisfunc = octree.getbasisfunction(idx) if basisfunc.projectstolessthan2pixels(cameras): cansplit = False break if basisfunc.splitlevel >= maxsplitlevel: cansplit = False break if not cansplit: break # Split the selected basis functions # This updates the octree and the matrix S S, octree, a = splitbasisfunctions(S, octree, a, splitindices, cameras) # Re-apply Visual Hull Restriction S = applyvisualhullrestriction(S, cameras, octree) # Check for convergence (e.g., max iterations or residual norm) if isconverged(r, S): break return octree, a def buildsparsematrix(cameras, octree): """ Builds the projection matrix S. Sij = integral of basis function phij over the ray/pixel area for pixel i. """ # Implementation details omitted for brevity, but involves ray-tracing # each basis function through each camera to compute integrals. pass def applyvisualhullrestriction(S, cameras, octree): """ Removes columns (basis functions) that are completely outside the visual hull. """ # For each camera, create a binary vector of basis functions inside the silhouette binaryvectors = [] for cam in cameras: vec = np.zeros(S.shape[1]) for j in range(S.shape[1]): if basisfunctioninsilhouette(octree.getbasisfunction(j), cam): vec[j] = 1 binaryvectors.append(vec) # Element-wise logical AND hullmask = np.ones(S.shape[1]) for vec in binaryvectors: hullmask = hullmask & vec # Keep only columns where hullmask is 1 S = S[:, hullmask.astype(bool)] return S def computeerrormeasure(S, r): """ Computes ephij = sum(Sij |ri|) / nphij """ nphi = np.array([np.countnonzero(S[:, j]) for j in range(S.shape[1])]) # Avoid division by zero nphi[nphi == 0] = 1 # Sum of weighted absolute residuals for each basis function # S is sparse, so we can use sparse matrix operations weightedabsr = S.multiply(np.abs(r)) # Element-wise multiplication if supported, else loop sumweighted = weightedabsr.sum(axis=0) e = sumweighted / nphi return e def splitbasisfunctions(S, octree, a, splitindices, cameras): """ Splits the basis functions at the given indices. Removes old columns, adds new columns for children. """ # Remove old columns mask = np.ones(S.shape[1], dtype=bool) mask[splitindices] = False S = S[:, mask] # Remove old coefficients a = np.delete(a, splitindices) # Add new columns for children newbasisfunctions = [] for idx in splitindices: parent = octree.getbasisfunction(idx) children = parent.split() # Returns list of new basis functions newbasisfunctions.extend(children) # Update octree octree.addchildren(newbasisfunctions) # Build new columns for S newScols = [] for child in newbasisfunctions: col = computecolumnforbasisfunction(child, cameras) newScols.append(col) newScols = np.columnstack(newScols) # Append new columns to S S = np.hstack([S, newScols]) # Append new coefficients (initialized to 0 or interpolated) a = np.append(a, np.zeros(len(newbasisfunctions))) return S, octree, a def cglssolve(S, p, a, nonnegative=False): """ Solves min ||Sa - p||^2 using Conjugate Gradient Least Squares. If nonnegative is True, projects a to non-negative subspace in each iteration. """ # Standard CGLS algorithm # r = p - Sa # pvec = S^T r #... iterative updates... # If nonnegative: a = max(a, 0) after each update pass Time and Memory Complexity: Memory: The method uses 20-25% of the memory required by a uniform grid approach. A uniform grid with 8 cameras at 320x240 resolution reaches the 2 GB memory limit on a 32-bit machine quickly, whereas the adaptive grid mitigates this by using fewer basis functions. Time: The method is more computationally intensive per iteration than filtered backprojection. The complexity involves solving a sparse linear system (CGLS) and updating the sparse matrix S during splitting. The number of non-zero elements in S is O(\sqrt{nb} \cdot np) per row, where nb is the number of basis functions and np is the number of pixels. Scaling: The number of basis functions grows sub-exponentially with the number of iterations when k = \sqrt{nb}. The method allows for higher resolution input images and reconstructed models compared to uniform grids due to the memory savings. Strengths and Limitations: Strengths: Higher effective resolution than uniform grids for the same memory budget. Handles dynamic scenes (time-varying volumetric models). Mathematically sound error projection heuristic (though noted as heuristic in future work). Accurate visual hull computation up to the pixel level. Limitations: More computationally intensive per iteration than traditional methods like filtered backprojection. The error projection is a heuristic; a mathematically sound error projection is identified as future work. Splitting linear basis functions requires introducing asymmetric basis functions, complicating the implementation. Non-negative constraint is enforced by projection, which may not be optimal for all basis function types (e.g., wavelets). When to Use: Reconstructing thin smoke and flames volumetrically from synchronized multi-video recordings. Scenes where memory is a constraint for high-resolution multi-camera setups. Dynamic scenes requiring adaptive resolution. When Not to Use: When computational speed is more critical than memory usage or resolution. When the scene does not benefit from adaptive resolution (e.g., uniformly dense volumes). Origin: The method was presented by Ivo Ihrke and Marcus Magnor from the Max-Planck-Institut für Informatik, Saarbrücken, Germany. It was published in 2005 in the Eurographics proceedings. History and Development: The method builds upon a basic computerized tomography (CT) technique presented in [IM04] (Ihrke and Magnor, 2004), which used an algebraic formulation for fire reconstruction. The adaptive grid approach was developed to overcome the memory limitations of uniform grids and to improve reconstruction quality for dynamic phenomena. Future work mentioned in the source includes deriving a mathematically sound error projection, using wavelet bases, and modeling occluding objects in flames and smoke. Usage: Used for reconstructing dynamic volumetric models of flames and thin smoke from multi-camera video sequences. Applicable to other tomography problems, such as real X-ray data, as suggested by the authors. Adaptive Grid Optical Tomography, https://core.ac.uk/works/26024869, fetched 2026-11-03
