name: Matrix-Free PCG Solver
head: Implicit normal operator PCG, Triangle-Structured Matrix-Free PCG Solver, Vertex-Block Preconditioned PCG
body: The Matrix-Free PCG Solver is a method for solving the global normal system Hx=g arising in closed-form radiance-field optimization. It evaluates the matrix-vector product Hu directly from rasterization records without constructing the global observation or normal matrices H. Unlike factorization-based solvers that explicitly assemble and decompose the normal matrix, this variant maintains smaller GPU memory by never materializing A and H. It builds on the CGLS Solver by providing a numerically stable solution to the least squares problem while avoiding the ill-conditioning of explicit normal equation assembly. Inputs: Set of calibrated RGB images \{Ik\}{k=1}^K. Rasterization records R containing, for each valid pixel p{k,r} in view k: Triangle vertex indices \{i{s,k,r}\}{s=0}^2. Observation vectors \{\phi{s,k,r}\}{s=0}^2 (SH basis evaluations at the pixel). Weight w{k,r} (grazing-angle down-weighting). Global SH regularizer \Lambda, composed of vertex blocks \Lambdai \in \mathbb{R}^{q \times q} for each vertex i. Tolerance \delta: Prescribed relative residual tolerance for PCG termination. T{max}: Maximum iteration count for PCG (typically 300). Outputs: Estimated appearance coefficients X^ \in \mathbb{R}^{q Nv \times 3}, where Nv is the number of vertices and q is the SH dimension per channel. Vertex Blocks: The solution vector X and right-hand side G are partitioned by vertex. Gi \in \mathbb{R}^{q \times 3} stores the accumulated RHS for vertex i. Preconditioner Blocks: Pi \in \mathbb{R}^{q \times q} stores the diagonal block of the normal matrix for vertex i. Cholesky Factors: Li \in \mathbb{R}^{q \times q} such that Pi = Li Li^\top. PCG Vectors: X^{(\tau)} (solution), r (residual), p (search direction), z (preconditioned residual), h (normal product result). Construct the right-hand side G and the vertex-block preconditioner P. 1. Initialize Gi = 0 for all vertices i=1 \dots Nv. 2. Initialize Pi = \Lambdai for all vertices i=1 \dots Nv. 3. For each view k = 1 \dots K: 4. For each valid pixel p{k,r} in view k: 5. For each vertex s \in \{0, 1, 2\} of the covering triangle: 6. Let i{s,k,r} be the vertex index. 7. Update RHS: G{i{s,k,r}} \leftarrow G{i{s,k,r}} + w{k,r} \phi{s,k,r} Ik(p{k,r})^\top. 8. Update Preconditioner: P{i{s,k,r}} \leftarrow P{i{s,k,r}} + w{k,r} \phi{s,k,r} \phi{s,k,r}^\top. 9. For each vertex i = 1 \dots Nv: 10. Compute Cholesky factor Li such that Pi = Li Li^\top. 11. Return G and \{Li\}{i=1}^{Nv}. Evaluate the matrix-vector product h = Hu without forming H. 1. For each vertex i = 1 \dots Nv: 2. Initialize hi = \Lambdai ui. 3. For each view k = 1 \dots K: 4. For each valid pixel p{k,r} in view k: 5. For each vertex s \in \{0, 1, 2\}: 6. Let i{s,k,r} be the vertex index. 7. Update: h{i{s,k,r}} \leftarrow h{i{s,k,r}} + w{k,r} \phi{s,k,r} \left( \sum{t=0}^2 \phi{t,k,r}^\top u{i{t,k,r}} \right). 8. Assemble h from blocks hi. 9. Return h. Solve H X^{(\tau)} = G^{(\tau)} using Preconditioned Conjugate Gradients. 1. Initialize X^{(\tau)} = 0. 2. Set g \leftarrow G^{(\tau)}, r \leftarrow g, \eta \leftarrow \|g\|2^2. 3. Solve P z = r for z: For each vertex i, solve Li Li^\top zi = ri using forward/backward substitution. 4. Set p \leftarrow z, \sigma \leftarrow r^\top z. 5. For t = 1 \dots T{max}: 6. h \leftarrow \text{TriangleNormal}(p). 7. \alpha \leftarrow \sigma / (p^\top h). 8. X^{(\tau)} \leftarrow X^{(\tau)} + \alpha p. 9. r \leftarrow r - \alpha h. 10. If \|r\|2^2 \le \delta^2 \eta, break. 11. Solve P z = r for z (using \{Li\}). 12. \sigma{new} \leftarrow r^\top z. 13. \beta \leftarrow \sigma{new} / \sigma. 14. p \leftarrow z + \beta p. 15. \sigma \leftarrow \sigma{new}. 16. End For. RHS Accumulation: G{i{s,k,r}} \leftarrow G{i{s,k,r}} + w{k,r} \phi{s,k,r} Ik(p{k,r})^\top. Preconditioner Accumulation: P{i{s,k,r}} \leftarrow P{i{s,k,r}} + w{k,r} \phi{s,k,r} \phi{s,k,r}^\top. Cholesky Decomposition: Pi = Li Li^\top. Regularization Term: hi \leftarrow \Lambdai ui. Pixel Contribution to Normal Product: h{i{s,k,r}} \leftarrow h{i{s,k,r}} + w{k,r} \phi{s,k,r} \left( \sum{t=0}^2 \phi{t,k,r}^\top u{i{t,k,r}} \right). Termination Condition: \sum{i=1}^{Nv} \|Gi^{(\tau)} - Hi Xi^{(\tau)}\|2^2 \le \delta \sum{i=1}^{Nv} \|Gi^{(\tau)}\|2^2. \delta: Relative residual tolerance. Tighter tolerances reduce final residual error but require more iterations. T{max}: Maximum iterations. Set to 300 in evaluations to prevent infinite loops on ill-conditioned systems. Ill-conditioning: Without adaptive SH regularization, weakly supported SH components cause ill-conditioning, making the unregularized system difficult to solve within T{max} iterations. Memory: The method processes views sequentially during matrix-free evaluation, so peak memory does not grow with the number of views K. Memory Complexity: M{GPU} = O(Nv q + HW q). Peak memory depends on vertices and image resolution, not the number of views K. Computational Complexity: Setup: O(KHWq^2 + Nv q^3). Per Iteration: O(KHWq + Nv q^2). Total solve time grows linearly with K. Strengths: Maintains smaller GPU memory than factorization-based solvers by never materializing A and H. The vertex-block preconditioner preserves coupling among all SH coefficients of the same vertex, improving numerical efficiency over scalar Jacobi preconditioners. Limitations: Requires T{max} iterations; convergence depends on the conditioning provided by adaptive SH regularization. Accuracy: At tight stopping tolerances, the residual MAE approaches that of the explicitly assembled factorization-based solver, confirming high numerical accuracy. The Matrix-Free PCG Solver was introduced in CF-Splat: Closed-Form Triangle Splatting with Mesh Priors. It addresses the computational and memory costs of explicitly constructing the global normal matrix H for large-scale scenes. The method exploits the three-vertex support of each pixel to evaluate the normal operator directly from rasterization records. name: Partially Learned Gradient Descent
head: Learned Gradient Descent, Learned iterative reconstruction, Partially learned gradient descent without regularizer, Unrolled Optimization with Learned Updates, Unrolled optimization
body: Partially Learned Gradient Descent (PLGD) is an iterative reconstruction method that unrolls a fixed number of optimization steps into a neural network. It initializes the reconstruction with a filtered backprojection (FBP) estimate and iteratively refines it by passing the current estimate, gradients, and a momentum memory state through a convolutional network to compute the next update. Unlike standard gradient descent which uses a fixed or manually tuned step size, PLGD learns the optimization dynamics (step size and momentum) directly from data, while retaining the explicit physical forward model (e.g., RayTransform) to ensure interpretability and robustness to distribution shifts. It differs from fully learned end-to-end CNNs by preserving the gradient structure of the inverse problem. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Noisy measurement data y (e.g., sinograms), initial estimate x0 (typically FBP of y), and the forward operator \mathcal{A} (and its adjoint \mathcal{A}^). Output: Reconstructed volume x. Parameters: Number of iterations n{iter}, number of memory channels n{memory}, network weights W1, b1, W2, b2, W3, b3. Data Structures: State Tensor x: Shape [batch, height, width, 1]. Memory Tensor s: Shape [batch, height, width, nmemory], initialized to zeros. Network Weights: W1: [3, 3, C{in}, 32], b1: [1, 1, 1, 32] W2: [3, 3, 32, 32], b2: [1, 1, 1, 32] W3: [3, 3, 32, n{memory} + 1], b3: [1, 1, 1, n{memory} + 1] Where C{in} is the number of input channels to the network (2 for "No Regularizer" variant, 3 for "With Regularizer" variant). Algorithm Steps: 1. Initialization: Compute x0 = \text{FBP}(y). Initialize s = 0 with shape [batch, height, width, nmemory]. Normalize the forward operator \mathcal{A} and its pseudoinverse by the operator norm \|\mathcal{A}\| for scale invariance: \mathcal{A}{norm} = \frac{1}{\|\mathcal{A}\|} \mathcal{A}, \mathcal{A}{pinv} = \mathcal{A}{pinv} \cdot \|\mathcal{A}\|. 2. Iteration Loop (i = 0 to n{iter}-1): Compute Gradients: Forward projection: y{pred} = \mathcal{A}(x). Data Gradient: For linear models: g{data} = \mathcal{A}^(y - y{pred}). For nonlinear models (e.g., CT with attenuation): y{pred} = \exp(-\mu{water} \cdot \mathcal{A}(x)), then g{data} = \mu{water} \cdot \mathcal{A}^(y - y{pred}). Regularization Gradient (optional, see variants): g{reg} = \mathcal{R}^(x), where \mathcal{R}^ is the adjoint of the regularizer (e.g., Laplacian: (\partial0^ \partial0 + \partial1^ \partial1)(x)). Concatenate Inputs: Form input tensor u by concatenating along the channel axis: No Regularizer: u = \text{concat}(x, g{data}, s). With Regularizer: u = \text{concat}(x, g{data}, g{reg}, s). Neural Network Update: Layer 1: h1 = \text{ReLU}(W1 u + b1). Layer 2: h2 = \text{ReLU}(W2 h1 + b2). Layer 3 (Linear): h3 = W3 h2 + b3. Split Output: Step size: dx = h3[:,:,:, 0:1]. New Memory: s{new} = \text{ReLU}(h3[:,:,:, 1:]). Update State: s \leftarrow s{new}. x \leftarrow x + dx. 3. Training (if learning weights): Loss: Mean Squared Error between final x and ground truth x{true}: \text{Loss} = \frac{1}{N} \sum{b=1}^{N} \sum{i,j} (x{b,i,j} - x{true,b,i,j})^2. Optimizer: RMSProp with inverse time decay. Starter learning rate: 10^{-3}. Decay rate: 1.0. Decay steps: 500. Staircase: True. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def partiallylearnedgradientdescent(x0, y, operatoradjoint, operatorforward, niter, nmemory, useregularizer=False, muwater=0.02, operatornorm=1.0, w1=None, b1=None, w2=None, b2=None, w3=None, b3=None): """ Implements Partially Learned Gradient Descent. Args: x0: Initial estimate tensor [batch, H, W, 1] y: Measurement tensor [batch, Hsin, Wsin, 1] operatoradjoint: Function computing A^(residual) operatorforward: Function computing A(x) niter: Number of unrolled iterations nmemory: Number of memory channels useregularizer: Boolean, whether to include regularization gradient in input muwater: Attenuation coefficient for nonlinear forward model operatornorm: Norm of the forward operator for scaling w1, b1, w2, b2, w3, b3: Convolutional weights and biases Returns: x: Final reconstruction tensor """ import numpy as np # Initialize memory state s to zeros batchsize = x0.shape[0] H, W = x0.shape[1], x0.shape[2] s = np.zeros((batchsize, H, W, nmemory)) x = x0.copy() # Ensure weights are provided if w1 is None: raise ValueError("Weights must be provided or initialized.") for i in range(niter): # 1. Compute forward projection ypred = operatorforward(x) / operatornorm # 2. Compute data gradient # Nonlinear model: ypred = exp(-muwater A(x)) # Residual: y - ypred # Gradient: muwater A^(y - ypred) residual = y - np.exp(-muwater ypred) gradx = operatoradjoint(residual) muwater # 3. Compute regularization gradient (if enabled) if useregularizer: gradreg = computelaplacianadjoint(x) updateinput = np.concatenate([x, gradx, gradreg, s], axis=-1) else: updateinput = np.concatenate([x, gradx, s], axis=-1) # 4. Neural Network Layers h1 = np.maximum(0, conv2d(updateinput, w1) + b1) h2 = np.maximum(0, conv2d(h1, w2) + b2) h3 = conv2d(h2, w3) + b3 # 5. Split output dx = h3[:,:,:, 0:1] snew = np.maximum(0, h3[:,:,:, 1:]) # 6. Update states s = snew x = x + dx return x def conv2d(x, W, stride=(1, 1)): """Standard 2D convolution with SAME padding.""" # x: [B, H, W, Cin], W: [kh, kw, Cin, Cout] # Returns: [B, H, W, Cout] B, H, W, Cin = x.shape kh, kw,, Cout = W.shape out = np.zeros((B, H, W, Cout)) for b in range(B): for cout in range(Cout): for h in range(H): for w in range(W): hstart = max(0, h - kh // 2) hend = min(H, h + (kh + 1) // 2) wstart = max(0, w - kw // 2) wend = min(W, w + (kw + 1) // 2) patch = x[b, hstart:hend, wstart:wend,:] out[b, h, w, cout] = np.sum(patch W[:,:,:, cout]) return out def computelaplacianadjoint(x): """ Computes the adjoint of the Laplacian operator: (partial0.adjoint partial0 + partial1.adjoint partial1)(x) Implemented as a discrete convolution kernel. """ # Kernel for 2D Laplacian adjoint (which is the Laplacian itself for symmetric operators) # Standard 5-point stencil: # 0 -1 0 # -1 4 -1 # 0 -1 0 kernel = np.array([[[[0, -1, 0], [-1, 4, -1], [0, -1, 0]]]]) # Expand kernel for batch/channel dimensions if necessary # Assuming x is [B, H, W, 1], kernel should be [3, 3, 1, 1] kernelexpanded = np.expanddims(kernel, axis=-1) return conv2d(x, kernelexpanded) Parameters: n{memory}: Number of memory channels. Typical value: 5. n{iter}: Number of unrolled iterations. Typical value: 10. n{angles}: Number of projection angles. Typical value: 30. \mu{water}: Attenuation coefficient. Typical value: 0.02. photons{per\pixel}: For Poisson noise simulation. Typical value: 10,000. \epsilon: Small constant for log/noise. Value: 1/photons{per\pixel}. Noise level: 5% of mean absolute data value. Pitfalls: Nonlinear Saturation: The exponential function in the nonlinear forward model can saturate if the input is not scaled correctly or if \mu{water} is incorrect. Ensure proper scaling of the forward projection before applying exp. Momentum Sign: The memory state s is updated using ReLU, ensuring it remains non-negative. This prevents oscillatory behavior from negative momentum values. Operator Norm: Failure to normalize the operator by its norm can lead to scale-dependent convergence issues. The operator and pseudoinverse must be scaled by \|\mathcal{A}\| and 1/\|\mathcal{A}\| respectively. Includes a Tikhonov-like regularization term (adjoint of partial derivatives) in the network input concatenation. Input channels are n{memory} + 3 (estimate, data gradient, regularization gradient, memory). Weights W1 shape: [3, 3, nmemory + 3, 32]. A technique to reuse samples from the previous gradient-descent iteration at the current iteration by merging reservoirs from current and previous iterations, treating different iterations as different frames. Handles sign changes by reusing both positive and negative samples for both reservoirs. M{cap} is typically 32 for base color, 16 otherwise. A recursive inference step to refine noisy primitive positions by updating offsets \Delta \mui based on previous estimation \Delta \mu{prev}. Update rule: \Delta \mui^k = \text{Tanh}(\mathcal{D}{pos}(\mathbf{f}i)) \cdot v{size}, where \mathbf{f}i = \mathcal{F}(\mui^{init} + \Delta \mui^{k-1}). Stabilizes at a stationary point. On Waymo dataset, first inference increases PSNR by ~0.46 dB, subsequent updates maintain stable PSNR of 23.78 dB. Time Complexity: Linear in the number of unrolled iterations n{iter}. Each iteration involves one forward projection, one adjoint projection, and a small convolutional network pass. Memory Complexity: Proportional to n{memory} channels for the state tensor s, plus the memory for the convolutional weights. Performance: Outperforms standard gradient descent and FBP in terms of reconstruction quality (PSNR/SSIM) on medical imaging and phantom data. Strengths: Retains physical model interpretability; learns adaptive step sizes and momentum; robust to noise. Limitations: Requires training data to learn the network weights; inference speed depends on n{iter} and network depth; sensitive to operator norm scaling. When to use: When a physics-based model is available but standard optimization converges slowly or gets stuck in local minima, and end-to-end learning is undesirable due to lack of interpretability. Partially Learned Gradient Descent originates from the field of learned iterative reconstruction for medical imaging and tomography. It was developed to bridge the gap between model-based iterative reconstruction (which is interpretable but slow/hard to tune) and end-to-end deep learning (which is fast but lacks physical guarantees). The method unrolls the optimization steps of gradient descent into a neural network, allowing the network to learn the update rule (step size and momentum) while keeping the data fidelity term fixed. It is implemented in the learnedgradienttomography repository. adler-j/learnedgradienttomography, https://github.com/adler-j/learnedgradienttomography, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial) Parameter-space ReSTIR for Differentiable and Inverse Rendering, https://doi.org/10.1145/3588432.3591512, fetched 2026-10-27 EVolSplat: Efficient Volume-based Gaussian Splatting for Urban View Synthesis, https://doi.org/10.1109/CVPR52734.2025.01054, fetched 2026-11-03

name: Velocity Reconstruction (VelRecon)
head: VelRecon
body: Velocity Reconstruction (VelRecon) is an optimization-based method for estimating 3D velocity fields from temporal sequences of volumetric density fields. Unlike tracer-based techniques (e.g., tomographic PIV) that require specialized hardware and physical tracers, VelRecon is a tracer-free approach that infers motion directly from captured video data by solving a constrained primal-dual optimization problem. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Volumetric density fields at two consecutive time steps, \rho{t-2} and \rho{t-1}. Output: Estimated velocity field u{t-1} at time step t-1. Data Structures: The method operates on voxel grids representing the density and velocity fields. Exact bit-packing or memory layout details are not given in the sources. Algorithm Steps: VelRecon solves the velocity estimation problem using a fast primal-dual approach. The optimization is governed by Equations (11)–(13) as constraints and solved via Equations (14)–(16). The iterative procedure is as follows: 1. Initialize iteration loop for k from 0 to \text{maxIter}. 2. Update the velocity estimate u{t-1}^{k+1} using the proximal operator of the constraint function g, a scaling parameter \gamma, and an auxiliary variable Xk. Formula: u{t-1}^{k+1} = \text{prox}{\gamma g} (u{t-1}^k - \gamma Xk). 3. Update the auxiliary variable Y{k+1} using a momentum term \theta and the difference between the current and previous velocity estimates. Formula: Y{k+1} = u{t-1}^{k+1} + \theta (u{t-1}^{k+1} - u{t-1}^k). 4. Compute the residual r{k+1} as the difference between the current and previous velocity estimates. Formula: r{k+1} = u{t-1}^{k+1} - u{t-1}^k. 5. Update the error threshold e by adding 3 times the absolute value of the new residual to the previous error. Formula: e{k+1} = ek + 3 |r{k+1}|. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def zeroslike(arr): # Returns an array of zeros with the same shape as arr return [[0.0 for in range(len(row))] for row in arr] def proximaloperatorg(x, gamma): # Computes prox{gammag}(x) enforcing physical constraints from # Exact formulation not provided in sources return x def VelRecon(rhotminus2, rhotminus1, maxiter, gamma, theta): uprev = zeroslike(rhotminus1) X = zeroslike(rhotminus1) e = 0.0 for k in range(maxiter): # Step 2: Update velocity estimate ucurr = proximaloperatorg(uprev - gamma X, gamma) # Step 3: Update auxiliary variable with momentum Y = ucurr + theta (ucurr - uprev) # Step 4: Compute residual r = ucurr - uprev # Step 5: Update error threshold e = e + 3.0 abs(r) # Update for next iteration uprev = ucurr # Note: Dual variable X update rule is not specified in the provided notes return ucurr Parameters: \gamma: Scaling parameter for the proximal operator. Value not given in sources. \theta: Momentum term. Value not given in sources. \text{maxIter}: Maximum number of iterations. Value not given in sources. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision issues may arise if the proximal operator is not well-conditioned. Boundary conditions for the velocity field are not explicitly detailed in the sources. This variant recovers the roughness texture of a metallic plate from a single reference image using noisy gradients. It employs 16 samples per pixel for the primal update and 1 sample per pixel for the gradient update. The method uses Adam optimization with hyperparameters \alpha = 0.01 and \beta1 = 0.2. Time and Memory Complexity: The method uses a fast primal-dual approach, suggesting linear or near-linear complexity with respect to the number of voxels per iteration. Memory complexity is proportional to the storage of density fields, velocity fields, and auxiliary variables. Measured Performance: Specific performance metrics (FPS, accuracy) are not provided in the sources. Strengths and Limitations: The method is tracer-free and does not require specialized hardware or complex camera setups. It couples density and velocity reconstruction in a physics-constrained manner for robustness. Solving the optimization problem at each step may be computationally intensive compared to direct methods. The accuracy relies on the quality of the input density fields. When to Use: Use when estimating fluid motion from monocular video without access to tracer particles or specialized PIV hardware. Origin: The method is described in the context of physics-based differentiable rendering for fluid modeling. It is part of a coupled density and velocity estimation framework where velocity reconstruction is called to estimate velocity fields from previous density fields to perform advection. History and Development: The approach contrasts with traditional tracer-based methods like tomographic PIV, synthetic aperture PIV, and structured-light PIV, which require careful particle choice and complex setups. VelRecon represents a tracer-free alternative leveraging differentiable rendering and optimization. Usage: Used in differentiable rendering frameworks for fluid simulation and reconstruction from monocular video. name: Reparameterized Stochastic Gradient Descent
head: Reparameterized SGD, Reparameterized Stochastic Gradient Descent for Parameter Optimization
body: Reparameterized Stochastic Gradient Descent (Reparam-SGD) is an optimization technique designed to find altered scattering parameters (g, \sigmas) that minimize the error between a rendered image and a target image. It addresses the problem of SGD getting trapped in local minima with small gradients caused by low-frequency lighting, which leads to solutions that generalize poorly to high-frequency lighting. It sets itself apart from standard SGD by reparameterizing the search space to regularize the error surface and using sequential 1D searches to escape ill-conditioned regions. Inputs: Target image I0. Initial guess for scattering parameters (g, \sigmas). Error function d(g, \sigmas) defined in (Eq. 21 in source), where I0 is the input image. Outputs: Optimized scattering parameters (g^, \sigmas^). Data Structures: Parameters: g (anisotropy factor), \sigmas (scattering coefficient). Reparameterized variable: \tilde{\sigma}s (reduced scattering coefficient). Formulas: The reparameterization replaces the horizontal axis with the reduced scattering coefficient: \tilde{\sigma}s:= (1 - g)\sigmas This ensures both axes (g and \tilde{\sigma}s) have the same units and regularizes the error surface. Steps: 1. Reparameterize: Transform the search space from (g, \sigmas) to (g, \tilde{\sigma}s) using the formula above. 2. First 1D Search: Fix \sigmas and perform a one-dimensional SGD search to find \tilde{\sigma}s that minimizes the error d. This step selects an equivalence class based on the order-1 similarity relation. 3. Second 1D Search: Keep the found \tilde{\sigma}s fixed and perform another one-dimensional SGD search to find the best \sigmas within the selected equivalence class. 4. Result: The pair (g, \sigmas) from the second step is the solution. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def reparameterizedsgd(targetimage, initialg, initialsigmas, errorfunction, learningrate, numiterations): """ Performs reparameterized SGD to optimize scattering parameters. Args: targetimage: The target image I0. initialg: Initial guess for anisotropy factor g. initialsigmas: Initial guess for scattering coefficient sigmas. errorfunction: Function d(g, sigmas) computing error between rendered and target image. learningrate: Step size for SGD. numiterations: Number of iterations for each 1D search. Returns: Optimized g and sigmas. """ # Step 1: Reparameterize initial guess # Note: The source defines the search space transformation but does not explicitly # state if the initial sigmas is converted. We assume the search operates on # the reparameterized space for the first variable. currentg = initialg currentsigmas = initialsigmas # Calculate initial reduced scattering coefficient currenttildesigmas = (1 - currentg) currentsigmas # Step 2: First 1D Search - Optimize tildesigmas while fixing sigmas # The source states: "fix sigmas and look for tildesigmas that minimizes the error" # However, tildesigmas depends on both g and sigmas. # The source implies a coordinate descent approach in the reparameterized space. # To keep sigmas constant while changing tildesigmas, g must change. # But the source says "fix sigmas" for the first step. This implies the # optimization variable is tildesigmas, and sigmas is held constant. # If sigmas is constant, changing tildesigmas implies changing g. # Let's re-read carefully: "First, we fix sigmas and look for tildesigmas... # Then, we search for the best parameter point within this class by keeping # tildesigmas fixed and performing another 1D search to find the best sigmas." # Interpretation: # Step 2a: Optimize tildesigmas. Since sigmas is fixed, this effectively # optimizes g. But the variable is named tildesigmas. # Let's follow the source's variable naming strictly. # Optimization 1: Minimize error w.r.t tildesigmas, keeping sigmas constant. # Since tildesigmas = (1-g)sigmas, and sigmas is constant, # varying tildesigmas is equivalent to varying g. # However, the source calls the variable tildesigmas. # Let's implement the search on the variable tildesigmas directly, # deriving g from it if needed for the error function, or vice versa. # The error function d is defined on (g, sigmas). # We need to express d in terms of (g, tildesigmas). # sigmas = tildesigmas / (1 - g) # So d(g, tildesigmas) = d(g, tildesigmas / (1 - g)) # But the source says "fix sigmas" in step 1. # If sigmas is fixed, and we search for tildesigmas, we are searching for g. # Let's assume the "1D SGD" operates on the specific variable mentioned. # Step 2: Fix sigmas, optimize tildesigmas. # This implies we vary tildesigmas. Since sigmas is fixed, g must vary. # g = 1 - tildesigmas / sigmas currenttildesigmas = (1 - currentg) currentsigmas currentsigmasfixed = currentsigmas for i in range(numiterations): # Compute gradient of error w.r.t tildesigmas # We need d(derror / dtildesigmas) # Using chain rule: derror / dtildesigmas = (derror / dg) (dg / dtildesigmas) # g = 1 - tildesigmas / sigmas # dg / dtildesigmas = -1 / sigmas # Calculate error and gradients at current state # Note: In practice, gradients are obtained via Monte Carlo simulations # We assume a function getgradients(g, sigmas) returns (gradg, gradsigmas) # Current parameters for error function evaluation currg = 1 - currenttildesigmas / currentsigmasfixed currsigmas = currentsigmasfixed # Get gradients of error d w.r.t original parameters gradg, gradsigmas = getgradients(currg, currsigmas, targetimage) # Gradient w.r.t tildesigmas # derror / dtildesigmas = gradg (-1 / sigmas) + gradsigmas 0 # Because sigmas is fixed, gradsigmas term is 0 for this step? # No, the error function d(g, sigmas) depends on both. # But we are optimizing tildesigmas. # sigmas is constant. g changes. # So we only care about the effect of changing g. # derror / dtildesigmas = (derror / dg) (dg / dtildesigmas) gradtildesigmas = gradg (-1 / currentsigmasfixed) # Update tildesigmas currenttildesigmas -= learningrate gradtildesigmas # Guard: Ensure physical validity # g must be in [-1, 1], sigmas > 0 # g = 1 - tildesigmas / sigmas # If g goes out of bounds, clamp or handle appropriately # This is a pitfall not explicitly detailed in sources, but necessary for implementation # Step 3: Second 1D Search - Optimize sigmas while keeping tildesigmas fixed currenttildesigmasfixed = currenttildesigmas for i in range(numiterations): # Current g derived from fixed tildesigmas and variable sigmas # g = 1 - tildesigmas / sigmas # We need gradient w.r.t sigmas # derror / dsigmas = (derror / dg) (dg / dsigmas) + (derror / dsigmas) # dg / dsigmas = tildesigmas / sigmas^2 currg = 1 - currenttildesigmasfixed / currentsigmas currsigmas = currentsigmas gradg, gradsigmas = getgradients(currg, currsigmas, targetimage) # Gradient w.r.t sigmas gradsigmastotal = gradg (currenttildesigmasfixed / (currentsigmas 2)) + gradsigmas # Update sigmas currentsigmas -= learningrate gradsigmastotal # Guard: sigmas must be positive if currentsigmas <= 0: currentsigmas = 1e-6 # # Final parameters finalg = 1 - currenttildesigmasfixed / currentsigmas finalsigmas = currentsigmas return finalg, finalsigmas def getgradients(g, sigmas, targetimage): """ Computes gradients of the error function d(g, sigmas) using Monte Carlo simulations. This is a placeholder for the specific Monte Carlo gradient estimation method. """ # Implementation details for Monte Carlo gradient estimation are not provided in the source # This function must return (gradg, gradsigmas) pass Parameters: Learning rate: Not given in the sources. Number of iterations: Not given in the sources. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Low-frequency lighting: Creates large regions where the error function is close to zero with very small gradients, dominated by Monte Carlo or measurement noise. Standard SGD gets trapped here. Local Minima: Solutions found in low-error regions under low-frequency lighting may generalize poorly to high-frequency lighting. Physical Validity: Parameters g and \sigmas must remain within physical bounds (e.g., \sigmas > 0, g \in [-1, 1]). A reparameterization technique for optimizing translucent material properties that resolves ambiguities caused by similarity equivalence classes. It sets itself apart from standard gradient descent by warping the non-linear parameter space to separate indistinguishable parameter sets, thereby preventing the optimization from stalling in ill-conditioned regions. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Measured Performance: The method finds solutions that generalize better to high-frequency lighting compared to standard SGD, which gets trapped in local minima under low-frequency lighting. Strengths: Regularizes the error surface; avoids local minima caused by low-frequency lighting; improves generalization to high-frequency lighting. Limitations: Relies on Monte Carlo simulations for gradients, which can be noisy. When to use: When optimizing scattering parameters (g, \sigmas) for translucent materials, especially under low-frequency lighting conditions where standard SGD fails to generalize. When not to use: When high-frequency lighting is not a concern and standard SGD converges sufficiently. Origin: The method is described in the paper "High-order similarity relations in radiative transfer". History: The paper discusses the application of forward rendering for optically dense and forward-scattering materials. Usage: Used for inverse rendering of translucent materials, specifically optimizing scattering parameters. name: Similarity-Based Inverse Rendering
head: Inverse Rendering Reparameterization
body: Similarity-Based Inverse Rendering is a reparameterization technique for optimizing translucent material properties that resolves ambiguities caused by similarity equivalence classes. It sets itself apart from standard gradient descent by warping the non-linear parameter space to separate indistinguishable parameter sets, thereby preventing the optimization from stalling in ill-conditioned regions. Inputs: Target image I{target}. Initial material parameters \theta0 = (g, \sigmas) (ascent ratio and scattering coefficient). Forward rendering function R(\theta) that computes the rendered image for parameters \theta. Outputs: Optimized material parameters \theta^ that minimize the error between rendered and target images. Data Structures: Parameter vector \theta: Stores the scattering properties to be optimized. Warped parameter vector \phi: The transformed search space coordinates. Method: The method relies on the principle that different sets of parameters can produce visually similar appearances (similarity equivalence classes), creating flat or ambiguous regions in the error landscape. 1. Identify Ambiguity Locations: Use similarity theory to determine where in the parameter space equivalence classes exist. Similarity theory provides relations between parameters (e.g., between g and \sigmas) that yield identical or near-identical radiance fields. 2. Apply Non-Linear Warp: Transform the original parameters \theta into a warped space \phi using a non-linear mapping W. This mapping is designed such that points belonging to the same equivalence class in \theta-space are separated in \phi-space, effectively "stretching" the ambiguous regions. The exact functional form of W is derived from the high-order similarity relations in radiative transfer. Let \phi = W(\theta). 3. Gradient Descent in Warped Space: Perform optimization in the \phi space. Compute the gradient of the error function E(\phi) = ||R(W^{-1}(\phi)) - I{target}||^2 with respect to \phi. Update \phi using a standard optimizer (e.g., SGD or Adam). Map the updated \phi back to \theta for rendering or constraint checking if necessary. Pitfalls: Ill-Conditioning: Without warping, the optimization is ill-conditioned because gradients vanish or become misleading within equivalence classes. Inverse Mapping: If the warp W is not bijective, recovering \theta from \phi may be ambiguous or impossible. The sources describe this as a "proof-of-concept," implying the specific invertibility conditions depend on the chosen similarity relations. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. The method adds a non-linear transformation step per iteration but does not change the cost of the forward rendering, which is the dominant factor. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Requires storage for the parameter vector and its warped counterpart. Strengths: Greatly improves the efficiency of gradient descent algorithms by resolving ambiguities that stall standard optimization. Limitations: Described as a "proof-of-concept," suggesting it may not be a general-purpose solver without specific derivation of similarity relations for the material class. When to use: When optimizing translucent materials where similarity equivalence classes are known or can be derived, and standard gradient descent fails to converge due to parameter ambiguity. The method originates from the work on high-order similarity relations in radiative transfer. It was proposed as a solution to the difficulty of inverse rendering of translucent media, where the search space is high-dimensional and the presence of equivalence classes makes the problem ill-conditioned. The authors note that forward rendering is their main application, but this approach has the potential to benefit a wide range of future applications in simulating and acquiring volume-based appearance. name: Large Steps reparameterization
head: Nicolet et al. 2021 method, Nicolet et al. Large Steps, Shape Reconstruction with Large Steps
body:
Large Steps reparameterization is a gradient preconditioning technique for inverse rendering of geometry that handles sparse silhouette gradients and prevents mesh topology errors such as flipped triangles. It achieves fast convergence by preconditioning the bias of gradient steps toward smooth solutions without enforcing smoothness in the final result. It sets itself apart from standard optimizers by treating the optimization as a spatiotemporal process using Laplacian smoothing and infinity-norm filtering. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Current vertex positions x \in \mathbb{R}^{3N} (where N is the number of vertices), Laplacian matrix L \in \mathbb{R}^{3N 	imes 3N}, hyperparameter \lambda > 0, and the gradient of the loss function with respect to x, denoted 
ablax f. Output: Updated vertex positions x. Data Structures: Laplacian Matrix (L): A sparse matrix representing the mesh connectivity. For a standard cotangent Laplacian, L{ij} depends on the angles opposite the edge connecting vertices i and j. The matrix is symmetric and positive semi-definite. Reparameterized Variable (u): u \in \mathbb{R}^{3N}, defined as u = (I + \lambda L)x. Optimizer State (mu, vu): First and second moment estimates for u, initialized to zero vectors of size 3N. Parameters: \lambda: Controls the strength of regularization introduced by the Laplacian matrix. Typical values are not specified in the sources; implementation notes suggest it may require adjustment depending on the rendering engine (e.g., Mitsuba 3 vs. nvdiffrast). \alpha: Learning rate for the UniformAdam optimizer.  eta1,  eta2: Exponential decay rates for moment estimates (standard Adam defaults: 0.9, 0.999). \epsilon: Numerical stability constant (standard Adam default: 10^{-8}). Steps: 1. Reparameterization: Compute the transformed variable u from the current geometry x: u = (I + \lambda L)x 2. Gradient Transformation: Compute the gradient with respect to u using the chain rule. Since u = (I + \lambda L)x, the Jacobian is  rac{\partial x}{\partial u} = (I + \lambda L)^{-1}. The gradient for u is: 
ablau f = (I + \lambda L)^{-1} 
ablax f Note: In practice, this involves solving a linear system (I + \lambda L) 
ablau f = 
ablax f. 3. UniformAdam Update: Perform an update on u using the UniformAdam variant of Adam. Let g = 
ablau f. Update biased first moment estimate: mu \leftarrow  eta1 mu + (1 -  eta1) g Update biased second raw moment estimate: vu \leftarrow  eta2 vu + (1 -  eta2) g^2 (element-wise square) Compute bias-corrected estimates: \hat{m}u =  rac{mu}{1 -  eta1^t}, \quad \hat{v}u =  rac{vu}{1 -  eta2^t} where t is the time step. Key Difference: Instead of dividing by \sqrt{\hat{v}u} + \epsilon, UniformAdam uses the infinity norm of the second moment vector. Let V{\infty} = \max(\hat{v}u) (the maximum element-wise value). The update step \Delta u is: \Delta u = -\alpha  rac{\hat{m}u}{\sqrt{V{\infty}} + \epsilon} Note: The source describes replacing component-wise division by vt with component-wise max \|vt\|\infty. This implies the denominator is a scalar derived from the max norm, applied to the entire vector update, or potentially element-wise if interpreted as scaling. The text "component-wise max ||vt||∞" is slightly ambiguous. Standard interpretation of "infinity norm" is a scalar. However, "component-wise division... replaced with component-wise max" suggests the denominator might be treated as a scalar broadcast or the operation is vector-wise. Given "UniformAdam... same as Adam except...", and Adam is element-wise, replacing the element-wise denominator with a scalar max-norm makes it a "uniform" step size direction. We assume the denominator is the scalar \sqrt{\max(\hat{v}u)} + \epsilon. Update u: u \leftarrow u + \Delta u 4. Inverse Reparameterization: Convert the updated u back to the physical space x: x = (I + \lambda L)^{-1} u Note: This involves solving the linear system (I + \lambda L) x = u. Gradient Transformation: gradu = (I + lambda L)^-1 gradx # Solve A gradu = gradx gradu = spsolve(A, gradx) # 3. "Component-wise max" usually doesn't make sense for a scalar. # It likely means the denominator is the scalar max norm. # If it meant element-wise, it would say "element-wise max". # "Infinity norm" is a scalar. denominator = np.sqrt(vinf) + epsilon deltau = -alpha mhat / denominator unew = u + deltau # 4. Inverse Reparameterization: x = (I + lambda L)^-1 unew # Solve A xnew = unew xnew = spsolve(A, unew) return xnew, munew, vunew Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Singular Matrix: The matrix (I + \lambda L) is positive definite if \lambda > 0 and L is positive semi-definite, so it is invertible. However, for very large meshes, solving the linear system can be computationally expensive. Iterative solvers (e.g., Conjugate Gradient) are recommended. Precision: The inversion of (I + \lambda L) can be sensitive to numerical precision if \lambda is very small or very large. Boundary Conditions: The Laplacian matrix L depends on the mesh connectivity. Degenerate triangles or flipped triangles in the input mesh can lead to incorrect Laplacian values. The method aims to prevent flipped triangles, but the initial mesh must be valid. Hyperparameter Tuning: The value of \lambda and the learning rate \alpha are critical and may need adjustment based on the specific rendering engine and scene complexity. Time Complexity: The dominant cost is solving the linear system (I + \lambda L) y = b twice per step (once for gradient transformation, once for inverse reparameterization). Using direct solvers, this is O(N^3) in the worst case, but for sparse meshes, iterative solvers can achieve O(N) to O(N \log N) depending on the condition number. Memory Complexity: O(N) to store the sparse Laplacian matrix and the optimizer states. Strengths: Prevents flipped triangles and tangled meshes by smoothing gradients. Allows for higher learning rates due to the preconditioning. Limitations: Requires the computation and storage of the Laplacian matrix. The choice of \lambda is non-trivial and may require tuning. When to use: Shape reconstruction in inverse rendering where mesh topology preservation is critical and gradients are sparse (e.g., silhouette-based optimization). When not to use: When the mesh topology is fixed and known to be robust, or when computational resources are extremely limited and iterative linear solves are too slow. The Large Steps reparameterization was introduced by Nicolet et al. in 2021. It was designed to address the instability of gradient-based optimization for mesh reconstruction, where gradients are concentrated on sparse silhouettes, leading to local vertex perturbations that cause flipped triangles. The method is described as a spatiotemporal optimizer that uses Laplacian smoothing and an infinity norm as filters. It has been adopted in subsequent work, such as MRD, which uses Mitsuba 3 for implementation. name: Newton's Method
head: Newton-Raphson method, Newton-Raphson method for inverse rays, Root Finding Based Algorithm
body: Newton's Method is a second-order optimization algorithm derived from the second-order Taylor expansion of the objective function. It solves for the root of the gradient (where the derivative is zero) to find local minima or maxima, offering quadratic convergence for well-behaved functions. Unlike Gradient Descent Solver, which uses only first-order gradient information and a fixed or adaptive step size, Newton's Method incorporates the Hessian matrix to account for local curvature, allowing it to take larger, more informed steps toward the optimum. In the context of inverse volume rendering, it is also applied as a root-finding algorithm to solve for ray intersections with implicit geometry. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Current parameter vector \thetat, objective function f(\theta), gradient function g(\theta) = \nabla f(\theta), Hessian function H(\theta) = \nabla^2 f(\theta). Output: Updated parameter vector \theta{t+1}. Data Structures: \theta \in \mathbb{R}^n: Parameter vector. g \in \mathbb{R}^n: Gradient vector. H \in \mathbb{R}^{n \times n}: Hessian matrix. v \in \mathbb{R}^n: Newton direction vector. \alpha \in \mathbb{R}: Step length scalar. Numbered Steps: 1. Compute Gradient and Hessian: Evaluate the gradient g(\thetat) and the Hessian matrix H(\thetat) at the current point \thetat. 2. Check Positive Semi-Definiteness (PSD): Verify if H(\thetat) is positive semi-definite. If not, apply Hessian modification to ensure PSD, or use a trust region method. 3. Compute Newton Direction: Solve the linear system H(\thetat) v = -g(\thetat) for v. The update direction is v = -H^{-1}(\thetat)g(\thetat). Note: For root-finding applications (e.g., inverse rays), solve JF(xn)(x{n+1} - xn) = -F(xn) for the root approximation x{n+1}, where JF is the Jacobian of the residual function F. 4. Determine Step Length: In standard Newton's Method, a fixed step size \gamma is often used, or \alpha=1 is assumed if the quadratic approximation is valid. In Newton Conjugate Gradient, \alpha is derived analytically by minimizing the quadratic approximation along v: \alpha = - \frac{g(\thetat)^T v}{v^T H(\thetat) v}. 5. Apply Trust Region (Optional but Recommended): To prevent divergence if the Hessian is not well-conditioned, truncate the step: \alpha = \min(\alpha, \Delta \|v\|^{-1}), where \Delta is the trust region radius. 6. Update Parameters: \theta{t+1} = \thetat + \alpha v. Formulas: Second-Order Taylor Expansion: f(\theta) \approx f(\thetat) + g(\thetat)^T (\theta - \thetat) + \frac{1}{2} (\theta - \thetat)^T H(\thetat) (\theta - \thetat) Optimality Condition (Root of Gradient): \frac{d}{d\theta} f(\theta) = 0 \approx g(\thetat) + H(\thetat)(\theta - \thetat) Newton Direction: v = -H^{-1}(\thetat)g(\thetat) Update Rule: \theta{t+1} = \thetat - \gamma H^{-1}(\thetat)g(\thetat) Newton Conjugate Gradient Step Length: \alpha = - \frac{g(\theta)^T v}{v^T H(\theta) v} Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import numpy as np def norm(v): return sum(x2 for x in v)0.5 def dot(a, b): return sum(xy for x, y in zip(a, b)) def ensurepsd(H): # Shift diagonal until positive semi-definite mineig = np.linalg.eigvalsh(H).min() if mineig < 0: H = H + (-mineig + 1e-6) np.eye(len(H)) return H def solvelinearsystem(A, b): return np.linalg.solve(A, b) def hessvectorproduct(theta, v, grad, eps=1e-5): # Central difference approximation return (grad(theta + eps v) - grad(theta - eps v)) / (2 eps) def newtonmethod(theta, f, grad, hess, maxiter=100, tol=1e-6, trustradius=None): for t in range(maxiter): g = grad(theta) H = hess(theta) if norm(g) < tol: break H = ensurepsd(H) v = solvelinearsystem(H, -g) alpha = 1.0 if trustradius is not None: if norm(v) > 1e-12: alpha = min(alpha, trustradius / norm(v)) else: alpha = 0.0 theta = theta + alpha v return theta def newtonconjugategradient(theta, f, grad, hess, maxiter=100, tol=1e-6): v = -grad(theta) r = v for t in range(maxiter): Hv = hessvectorproduct(theta, v, grad) g = grad(theta) numerator = -dot(g, v) denominator = dot(v, Hv) if abs(denominator) < 1e-12: break alpha = numerator / denominator theta = theta + alpha v rnew = r - alpha Hv if norm(rnew) < tol: break beta = dot(rnew, rnew) / dot(r, r) v = rnew + beta v r = rnew return theta Parameters: \gamma: Step size multiplier (often 1 in pure Newton, but used in damped variants). \Delta: Trust region radius. \epsilon: Perturbation magnitude for central-difference Hessian-vector product approximation. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Hessian Inversion Cost: Computing, storing, and inverting the full Hessian H \in \mathbb{R}^{n \times n} is O(n^3) and requires O(n^2) memory, becoming a bottleneck in high-dimensional problems. Negative Definiteness: If the Hessian is not positive semi-definite, the Newton direction may point towards a maximum or saddle point, causing divergence. This is handled by Hessian modification (ensuring PSD) and trust region step truncation. Root Finding Failure: In inverse ray tracing, naive Newton-Raphson can fail if the starting point is not close to the root or if the Jacobian is singular. Quasi-Newton methods utilize second-order information for optimization by approximating the Hessian matrix using zero- or first-order information. Unlike Newton's Method, which requires explicit computation of the Hessian, these methods build an approximation iteratively. In the context of differentiable rendering, they are distinguished by their sensitivity to noise; while they can converge on smooth tasks, they often fail on noisy derivative estimations common in rendering without specific damping or line-search modifications. Naive Newton fails if the Hessian is not positive semi-definite (PSD), as negative eigenvalues can flip the gradient vector and cause divergence. This is handled by ensuring positive semi-definiteness via Hessian modification and step truncation to a trust region: \alpha = \min(\alpha, \Delta \|v\|^{-1}). For example, in a negated 2D Gaussian convolution, analytic Hessians can be computed and compared with estimates, with mean error within 1 \times 10^{-4} for 100 samples across the interval (-3,3)^2. An upgrade to Newton's method that solves for the Newton direction iteratively using conjugate directions and determines the step length scalar \alpha. It avoids explicit Hessian inversion by solving H(\theta)v = -g(\theta) iteratively. The direction v and residual r are initialized to the negative gradient (v0 = r0 = -g(\thetat)). The step length is derived from the Taylor expansion derivative set to zero: \alpha = - \frac{g^T(\theta)v}{v^T H(\theta)v}. The residual is updated as r{t+1} = rt - \alpha H(\thetat) vt, and the new direction is computed using the Fletcher-Reeves formula: \beta = \frac{r{t+1}^T r{t+1}}{rt^T rt} and v{t+1} = r{t+1} + \beta vt. Time Complexity: O(n^3) per iteration for standard Newton's Method due to Hessian inversion. Newton Conjugate Gradient reduces this to O(n^2) per iteration if Hessian-vector products are O(n), but requires multiple iterations to converge to the Newton direction. Memory Complexity: O(n^2) for storing the Hessian matrix. Convergence: Quadratic convergence near the optimum for well-behaved functions. Strengths: Fast convergence near the solution; accounts for curvature. Limitations: High computational cost for large n; sensitive to non-PSD Hessians; requires smooth, differentiable objective functions. When to Use: Small to medium-scale optimization problems where the Hessian is affordable to compute and invert; when high precision is required near the optimum. When Not to Use: Large-scale problems where Hessian storage is prohibitive. The method can also fail in certain situations, such as poor starting points or singular Jacobians. Newton's Method is one of the most-used second-order optimizers, derived from the second-order Taylor expansion of the objective function. It has been applied to several optimization tasks in vision and graphics. The Newton-Raphson method is also a standard method for finding approximations of the roots of functions, such as in inverse ray tracing for volume rendering. Hessian-vector product approximations, such as central differences, have been discussed by Pearlmutter and Werbos to avoid explicit Hessian computation. name: Quasi-Newton Methods (BFGS/LBFGS)
head: BFGS, BFGS/LBFGS Optimization, LBFGS
body: Quasi-Newton methods utilize second-order information for optimization by approximating the Hessian matrix using zero- or first-order information. Unlike Newton's Method, which requires explicit computation of the Hessian, these methods build an approximation iteratively. In the context of differentiable rendering, they are distinguished by their sensitivity to noise; while they can converge on smooth tasks, they often fail on noisy derivative estimations common in rendering without specific damping or line-search modifications. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Objective function f(\theta), initial parameter vector \theta0, initial Hessian approximation H0 (or inverse B0), and step size parameters. Output: Optimized parameter vector \theta^. Data Structures: \theta: Parameter vector of size d (often large, e.g., neural network weights). H or B: d \times d matrix approximating the Hessian or its inverse. Storing this explicitly is O(d^2), which is prohibitive for large d, leading to the use of Limited Memory variants. Steps: 1. Initialization: Set \theta0, H0 = I (identity matrix), and iteration counter k=0. 2. Gradient Evaluation: Compute the gradient gk = \nabla f(\thetak). In rendering, this may be sampled (stochastic) or analytic. 3. Search Direction: Compute search direction pk. For BFGS (Inverse Hessian Approximation Bk): pk = -Bk gk. For BFGS (Hessian Approximation Hk): Solve Hk pk = -gk. 4. Line Search: Determine step size \alphak satisfying Wolfe conditions (e.g., Armijo-Wolfe). Update \theta{k+1} = \thetak + \alphak pk. 5. Curvature Update: Compute difference vectors: sk = \theta{k+1} - \thetak yk = g{k+1} - gk 6. Hessian Update: Update the approximation B{k+1} (or H{k+1}) using the BFGS rank-2 update formula: B{k+1} = Bk + \frac{yk yk^T}{yk^T sk} - \frac{Bk sk sk^T Bk}{sk^T Bk sk} Note: If yk^T sk \leq 0, the update is skipped to maintain positive definiteness. 7. Iteration: Increment k. If convergence criteria are not met, return to Step 2. Parameters: Line search tolerance: Standard Wolfe conditions. Damping: Used in "Damped BFGS" to handle non-positive semi-definite (non-PSD) Hessians or noisy gradients. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Noisy Derivatives: Vanilla BFGS, BFGS with Armijo-Wolfe line search, and LBFGS only converge for smooth tasks (e.g., QUAD task) but fail on noisy derivative estimations typical in rendering. Non-PSD Hessians: The method assumes the Hessian is positive semi-definite. If the estimated Hessian is not PSD, convergence may fail unless damping is applied. Memory: Standard BFGS requires O(d^2) storage. For large-scale problems (e.g., neural networks), this is impractical. Pseudocode (BFGS with Inverse Hessian Approximation): Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def bfgsupdate(B, s, y): """ Update inverse Hessian approximation B using BFGS formula. B: d x d matrix s: d x 1 vector (step) y: d x 1 vector (gradient difference) """ sy = dot(s, y) if sy <= 1e-10: # Guard against non-positive curvature return B Bs = matvec(B, s) yBs = dot(y, Bs) # BFGS Rank-2 Update term1 = outer(y, y) / sy term2 = outer(Bs, Bs) / yBs return B + term1 - term2 def solvebfgs(f, gradf, theta0, maxiter=1000, tol=1e-6): d = len(theta0) theta = theta0.copy() B = identity(d) # Initial inverse Hessian approximation for k in range(maxiter): g = gradf(theta) # Check convergence if norm(g) < tol: break # Search direction p = -matvec(B, g) # Line search (simplified backtracking for brevity, # sources specify Armijo-Wolfe) alpha = linesearcharmijowolfe(f, theta, p, g) # Update parameters thetanew = theta + alpha p # Update Hessian approximation s = thetanew - theta gnew = gradf(thetanew) y = gnew - g B = bfgsupdate(B, s, y) theta = thetanew return theta A variant of BFGS that modifies the update step to handle cases where the Hessian is not positive semi-definite or gradients are noisy. It was tested in differentiable rendering contexts but did not improve convergence over vanilla BFGS for tasks beyond the smooth QUAD task. A variant that uses adaptive finite differences to estimate gradients or Hessians within the BFGS framework. Like Damped BFGS, it was tested for noisy derivative estimation in rendering but failed to change convergence behavior for other tasks compared to standard methods. An optimization algorithm used to solve configuration selection objectives by approximating gradients and Hessians via least squares. It generates a search direction from these approximations and solves a system of linear equations to update variables. It is prone to producing unreasonable resource allocation on complex scenes due to poor initial assumption values and inherent approximation errors in the least-squares estimation. Time Complexity: Each iteration requires O(d^2) operations for the matrix-vector product and update in standard BFGS. LBFGS reduces this to O(m \cdot d) where m is the memory limit. Memory Complexity: Standard BFGS is O(d^2), which is prohibitive for large neural networks. LBFGS is O(m \cdot d). Convergence: Superlinear convergence for smooth, convex problems. Limitations: Highly sensitive to noise in gradient estimation. Vanilla variants fail on noisy rendering derivatives. Requires careful handling of non-PSD Hessians. When to use: Smooth optimization problems where second-order information provides significant acceleration and memory constraints allow O(d^2) or limited memory storage. When not to use: Noisy derivative estimation (e.g., stochastic rendering gradients) without damping or specialized line searches. Quasi-Newton methods, specifically the BFGS family, are well-established optimization algorithms. They were tested in the context of differentiable rendering to leverage second-order information while avoiding the explicit computation of the Hessian. The family includes vanilla BFGS, BFGS with Armijo-Wolfe line search, and LBFGS. Variants like Damped BFGS and Adaptive Finite Difference BFGS were also explored in this context. name: Inexact Line Search Optimization
head: Line Search
body: Inexact Line Search Optimization is an iterative method that adapts the step size in gradient descent to achieve a reduction in the objective function while ensuring sufficiently fast progress. It solves the problem of slow convergence in standard gradient descent by dynamically selecting a step size that guarantees improvement without requiring the computational expense of finding the exact minimum along the search direction. Unlike exact line search methods, which may suffer from convergence deterioration, this inexact strategy yields reasonable results and descends much faster. Inputs: xk: Current point (e.g., feature opacity values) at iteration k. dk: Descent direction at iteration k. f(\cdot): Objective function to minimize (e.g., visibility-weighted saliency error). M: Maximum iteration count for the line search. Outputs: \gammam: The chosen step size. x{k+1}: The updated point xk + \gammam dk. Data Structures: Integer counter m: Tracks the current power of 2 for the step size. Integer M: Upper bound for m. Algorithm Steps: 1. Initialize m = 0 and set M to the maximum iteration count. 2. Check the condition: f(xk + \gamma{m+1} dk) < f(xk + \gammam dk) where \gammam = 2^m. 3. If the condition is met AND m < M - 1: Increment m \leftarrow m + 1. Repeat step 2. 4. Otherwise (condition fails OR m = M - 1): Terminate the line search. Set the chosen step size to \gammam. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def inexactlinesearch(xk, dk, f, M): """ Performs inexact line search to find step size gamma. Args: xk: Current point (vector). dk: Descent direction (vector). f: Objective function callable. M: Maximum iteration count. Returns: gamma: The chosen step size. """ m = 0 gammam = 1 # 2^0 while m < M - 1: gammanext = gammam 2 fcurrent = f(xk + gammam dk) fnext = f(xk + gammanext dk) if fnext < fcurrent: m = m + 1 gammam = gammanext else: break return gammam Parameters: M: Maximum iteration count. \gammam: Step size defined as 2^m. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: If the objective function evaluation is expensive, the overhead of multiple evaluations may outweigh the benefits of faster convergence. The method assumes the objective function allows for meaningful comparison between f(xk + \gamma{m+1} dk) and f(xk + \gammam dk). Parallel Inexact Line Search is a variant that evaluates the objective function at different candidate points in parallel along the line search direction to accelerate optimization on multi-core processors. It differs from the sequential version by always evaluating all candidate points and picking the one with the least objective function value, whereas the sequential version terminates early if the condition is not met. It is beneficial when the objective function evaluation is more expensive than the overhead of parallel processing, such as when computing visibility fields requires a pass of slice-based volume rendering. Algorithm Steps: 1. Generate a list of M step sizes S = \{\gamma0, \gamma1,..., \gamma{M-1}\} where \gammam = 2^m. 2. Evaluate f(xk + \gammam dk) in parallel for each \gammam in S using multiple threads. 3. Find the index m of the minimum f(xk + \gammam dk), and \gammam is the chosen step size. Pitfalls: The number of threads should not exceed the number of processor cores to avoid performance impact from sharing cores. Parallel search is only beneficial when objective function evaluation is more expensive than thread overhead. Golden-Section Search is a gradient-free iterative optimization algorithm used to locate the minimum of a unimodal function by successively narrowing the search range. It is employed to efficiently search for optimal bandwidth parameters in Anisotropic Fourier Features Mapping, replacing computationally prohibitive brute-force grid searches. Unlike its siblings, it reduces the number of expensive network training runs from polynomial to logarithmic time by leveraging the golden ratio and requires no gradient calculations. Choose it when optimizing bandwidth parameters in neural implicit representations without gradient access. Golden-Section Search Time Complexity: The sequential version performs up to M evaluations of the objective function. The parallel version performs M evaluations simultaneously, reducing wall-clock time for the line search phase but increasing total computational work if thread overhead is significant. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Performance: Compared to standard gradient descent, line search takes many fewer iterations to converge to a desired target. It descends much faster than gradient descent. Strengths: Adapts step size to achieve reduction in objective function while making sufficiently fast progress. Avoids convergence deterioration associated with exact line search methods. Limitations: Requires multiple evaluations of the objective function per iteration. Parallel version has overhead from thread management. When to use: When objective function evaluation is expensive (e.g., involves volume rendering passes) and parallel hardware is available. When faster convergence than standard gradient descent is needed. When not to use: When objective function evaluation is cheap, making parallel overhead unjustified. When exact minimum is required (though inexact is preferred for stability). The method was introduced in the context of transfer function optimization for volume rendering, specifically for optimizing feature opacities based on a combined model of visibility and saliency. It was proposed to reduce the number of iterations required in optimization compared to standard gradient descent. The approach is based on the work of Vrahatis et al. [2000] and Zhou et al. [2006], citing advantages of inexact strategies over exact methods. name: Golden-Section Search
head: 2D Golden-Section Search, GSS for Bandwidth, GSS-based bandwidth searching scheme, Golden-Section Search (GSS) for Bandwidth, Golden-Section Search (GSS) for Bandwidth Selection, Linear GSS
body: Golden-Section Search (GSS) is a gradient-free iterative optimization algorithm used to locate the minimum of a unimodal function by successively narrowing the range of values inside which the minimum is known to exist. In the context of volume rendering and neural implicit representations, it is specifically employed to efficiently search for optimal bandwidth parameters in Anisotropic Fourier Features Mapping (AFFM), replacing computationally prohibitive brute-force grid searches. Unlike its siblings, it reduces the number of expensive network training runs from polynomial time to logarithmic time by leveraging the golden ratio to shrink the search interval, requiring no gradient calculations with respect to the bandwidth. Inputs and Outputs: Input: An initial search interval [a, b] for 1D, or an initial search box [a1, b1] \times [a2, b2] for 2D, containing the optimal bandwidth(s). A cost function that returns the training loss or validation error for a given bandwidth, which requires a full network training run to evaluate. Output: The estimated optimal bandwidth \beta^ (or pair \beta^1, \beta^2) and the final search interval/box. Data Structures: 1D Case: Two scalar values a, b representing the current search interval bounds. Two scalar values x1, x2 representing the candidate points within the interval. 2D Case: Four scalar values a1, b1, a2, b2 representing the current search box bounds. Four candidate points forming a grid of 4 pairs. Constants: Golden ratio conjugate \phi = \frac{\sqrt{5}-1}{2} \approx 0.618. Complementary ratio 1-\phi \approx 0.382. Numbered Steps (1D Linear GSS): 1. Initialize the search interval [a, b]. 2. Calculate two candidate points: x1 = a + (1-\phi)(b-a) x2 = a + \phi(b-a) Note: x1 is at 0.382 and x2 is at 0.618 of the interval. 3. Evaluate the cost function at x1 and x2 by training the network with these bandwidths. 4. Compare the costs: If cost(x1) < cost(x2), the minimum lies in [a, x2]. Set b = x2 and x2 = x1. Recalculate x2 using the new interval. The old x1 is reused, saving one evaluation. If cost(x1) \ge cost(x2), the minimum lies in [x1, b]. Set a = x1 and x1 = x2. Recalculate x1 using the new interval. The old x2 is reused. 5. Repeat steps 3-4 until convergence or a fixed number of iterations is reached. Numbered Steps (2D GSS): 1. Initialize the search box [a1, b1] \times [a2, b2]. 2. Define the 1D split points for each dimension using \phi and 1-\phi. 3. Generate 4 candidate pairs by combining the split points of dimension 1 with those of dimension 2. 4. Evaluate the cost for all 4 candidates. 5. Identify the candidate C{best} with the lowest cost. 6. Shrink the search box. The new bounds for each dimension are determined by the coordinates of C{best} and the previous bounds, effectively reducing the box area by a factor of \phi^2 (approx 0.618^2). Specifically, if C{best} is at (x^1, x^2), the new interval for dimension 1 is determined by the subset of previous candidates that contained x^1, and similarly for dimension 2. 7. Repeat steps 2-6 until convergence. Formulas: 1D Interval Width: After k iterations, the width of the search interval is (0.618)^k. 1D Evaluations: The number of network trainings is k + 1. 2D Box Area: After k iterations, the parameter box area is 0.618^{2k}. 2D Evaluations: The number of network trainings is 3^k + 1. Parameters: Iterations: Empirically, 5 iterations are sufficient to achieve good practice convergence. Shrinkage Factor: 0.618 (golden ratio conjugate) for 1D; 0.618^2 for 2D area reduction. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Non-Unimodal Functions: GSS assumes the cost function is unimodal within the search interval. If the loss landscape has multiple local minima, GSS may converge to a suboptimal local minimum. Evaluation Cost: Each evaluation requires a full network training run, which is expensive. The algorithm's efficiency relies on minimizing these evaluations. Precision: The reuse of candidates relies on precise interval updates. Floating-point errors in interval boundary calculations can accumulate, though the logarithmic convergence rate mitigates this over the typical 5 iterations. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def goldensectionsearch1d(costfunc, a, b, maxiter=5): """ Performs 1D Golden-Section Search. costfunc: A function that takes a bandwidth beta and returns the training loss. a, b: Initial search interval [a, b]. maxiter: Maximum number of iterations. Returns: The estimated optimal bandwidth. """ phi = (math.sqrt(5) - 1) / 2.0 # ~0.618 invphi = 1.0 - phi # ~0.382 # Initialize candidates x1 = a + invphi (b - a) x2 = a + phi (b - a) # Evaluate initial candidates f1 = costfunc(x1) f2 = costfunc(x2) for in range(maxiter): if f1 < f2: # Minimum is in [a, x2] b = x2 x2 = x1 f2 = f1 x1 = a + invphi (b - a) f1 = costfunc(x1) else: # Minimum is in [x1, b] a = x1 x1 = x2 f1 = f2 x2 = a + phi (b - a) f2 = costfunc(x2) # Return the better of the two if f1 < f2: return x1 else: return x2 def goldensectionsearch2d(costfunc, a1, b1, a2, b2, maxiter=5): """ Performs 2D Golden-Section Search. costfunc: A function that takes a tuple (beta1, beta2) and returns the training loss. a1, b1: Initial search interval for dimension 1. a2, b2: Initial search interval for dimension 2. maxiter: Maximum number of iterations. Returns: The estimated optimal bandwidth tuple (beta1, beta2). """ phi = (math.sqrt(5) - 1) / 2.0 invphi = 1.0 - phi # Initial candidates for dimension 1 x11 = a1 + invphi (b1 - a1) x21 = a1 + phi (b1 - a1) # Initial candidates for dimension 2 x12 = a2 + invphi (b2 - a2) x22 = a2 + phi (b2 - a2) # Generate 4 candidates candidates = [ (x11, x12), (x11, x22), (x21, x12), (x21, x22) ] # Evaluate all 4 costs = [costfunc(c) for c in candidates] for in range(maxiter): # Find best candidate bestidx = costs.index(min(costs)) bestc = candidates[bestidx] # Shrink bounds based on best candidate (1D logic per dimension) if bestc[0] == x11: b1 = x21 x21 = x11 x11 = a1 + invphi (b1 - a1) else: a1 = x11 x11 = x21 x21 = a1 + phi (b1 - a1) if bestc[1] == x12: b2 = x22 x22 = x12 x12 = a2 + invphi (b2 - a2) else: a2 = x12 x12 = x22 x22 = a2 + phi (b2 - a2) # Regenerate candidates and evaluate only the new ones newcandidates = [(x11, x12), (x11, x22), (x21, x12), (x21, x22)] newcosts = [] for i, c in enumerate(newcandidates): if c == candidates[bestidx]: # Reuse best candidate from previous iteration newcosts.append(costs[bestidx]) else: newcosts.append(costfunc(c)) candidates = newcandidates costs = newcosts # Return the best candidate from the last iteration bestidx = costs.index(min(costs)) return candidates[bestidx] The 1D variant of the algorithm. It is chosen when a single bandwidth parameter needs to be optimized. It reduces the search space exponentially by the golden ratio. The extension to two dimensions. It is chosen when two bandwidth parameters (e.g., spatial and angular) need to be optimized simultaneously. It reduces the search box area by the square of the golden ratio per iteration. Time Complexity: Reduces the number of searches from polynomial time (in grid search) to logarithmic time. Specifically, for 1D, the interval width decreases as (0.618)^k. For 2D, the area decreases as 0.618^{2k}. Memory Complexity: Low. It only stores the current search interval/box and a few candidate points. Measured Performance: In a neural relighting task with the 'kneeling knight' imageset (253 reflectance images), 2D GSS provided a 7x speed-up over Grid search. Strengths: Gradient-free (avoids expensive gradient calculations w.r.t bandwidth), no need for initial point selection, saves function evaluations per iteration. Limitations: Assumes unimodality. Convergence is slower than Newton's method if gradients are available, but in this context, gradients are not available or too expensive. When to use: When optimizing bandwidth parameters for Fourier feature mappings in neural rendering, where each evaluation is a full network training. When not to use: When the cost function is not unimodal or when gradients are cheap and available. It was developed to address the computational overload of brute-force grid search for bandwidth selection in AFFM. The method leverages the mathematical properties of the golden ratio to efficiently narrow down the search space for optimal bandwidths in both spatial and angular domains.
