name: Incremental Preconditioned Gradient Method
head: Incremental ART, Incremental Preconditioned Gradient Method for Reflective Tomography, Online Learning for Reflective Tomography
body: The Incremental Preconditioned Gradient Method is an online learning algorithm for reflective tomography that incrementally updates a voxel model \phi \in \mathbb{R}^N to minimize modeling error against a sequence of observed frames. It solves the global least-squares optimization problem by applying preconditioned gradient descent steps to individual data frames one at a time. It distinguishes itself from batch solvers by processing data sequentially (frame-driven) and using a specific preconditioner derived from the projection matrix structure to prioritize high-frequency spatial information (surfaces). Inputs: Training dataset: A set of S camera configurations \{Cs\}{s=1}^S and corresponding observed images \{gs\}{s=1}^S, where gs \in \mathbb{R}^{Ms} and Ms is the number of pixels in frame s. Voxel grid: Defined by a bounding box with corners a, b \in \mathbb{R}^3 and voxel side length h. Parameters: Learning rate \omega, regularization \sigma, inner solver tolerance, stopping criteria. Outputs: Updated voxel model \phi \in \mathbb{R}^N, where N is the number of voxels. Data Structures: \phi: Vector of size N, storing voxel values. Initialized to zero. gs: Vector of size Ms, storing pixel intensities for frame s. XC: Linear projection operator mapping \phi to image space. In implementation, this is handled via ray-tracing backprojection and projection steps. Formulas: The cost function J for a single occurrence (C, g) is defined as: J(\phi, C, g) = \frac{1}{2} (XC XC^ + \sigma I)^{-\frac{1}{2}} (XC \phi - g) where \sigma > 0 is a regularization parameter. The gradient of J with respect to \phi is: \frac{\partial J}{\partial \phi}(\phi, C, g) = XC^ (XC XC^ + \sigma I)^{-1} (XC \phi - g) The model update for iteration k, using frame sk, is: \phi^{(k+1)} = \phi^{(k)} - \omega \frac{\partial J}{\partial \phi}(\phi^{(k)}, C{sk}, g{sk}) where \omega > 0 is the learning rate. The global problem solved incrementally is: \inf{\phi \in \mathbb{R}^N} \sum{s=1}^S J(\phi, Cs, gs) Parameters: \omega: Relaxation parameter. Suggested value \omega = 0.5 for reflective tomography to prioritize high-frequency spatial information (surfaces). Standard ART uses smaller values like 0.05. \sigma: Regularization parameter. Chosen on the order of Lh, where L is the characteristic length of the box (e.g., diagonal L = \|b-a\|) and h is the voxel side length. Inner solver tolerance: For the conjugate gradient solver used to approximate the inverse terms, a relative residual tolerance of 1\% and a maximum bound of 10 iterations are used. Stopping criterion: Either a fixed number of cycles \kappa (e.g., \kappa=2) or a decay rate threshold \tau (e.g., \tau=5\%) on the RMSE between successive cycles, with a safety bound \kappa{max} (e.g., \kappa{max}=8). Ray ordering: To simulate random ordering, use a step p relatively prime to S: s{k+1} - 1 = (sk + p - 1) \pmod S, starting with s0 = 1. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def incrementalpreconditionedgradientmethod(S, cameras, images, boxcorners, voxelsize, omega, sigma, kappamax, tauthreshold): # 1. Initialize voxel model N = calculatevoxelcount(boxcorners, voxelsize) phi = [0.0] N # 2. Determine ray ordering step p (relatively prime to S) p = findrelativelyprimestep(S) # 3. Initialize frame index (0-based, corresponds to s0 = 1) idx = 0 prevrmse = float('inf') cyclecount = 0 while cyclecount < kappamax: # 4. Iterate through all S frames (one cycle) for in range(S): C = cameras[idx] g = images[idx] # 5. Compute residual v = XC phi - g v = forwardprojection(phi, C) for i in range(len(g)): v[i] -= g[i] # 6. Solve (XC XC^ + sigma I) y = v using Conjugate Gradient # Inner solver: 1% relative residual tolerance, max 10 iterations y = conjugategradientsolve(phi, C, sigma, v, reltol=0.01, maxiter=10) # 7. Compute gradient = XC^ y gradient = backprojection(y, C) # 8. Update model: phi = phi - omega gradient for i in range(N): phi[i] -= omega gradient[i] # 9. Select next frame: s{k+1} - 1 = (sk + p - 1) mod S # In 0-based indexing: idx{k+1} = (idxk + p) mod S idx = (idx + p) % S # End of one cycle cyclecount += 1 # 10. Check stopping criterion: decay rate of RMSE between successive cycles currentrmse = computermse(phi, cameras, images) if cyclecount > 1: decayrate = (prevrmse - currentrmse) / prevrmse if decayrate <= tauthreshold: break prevrmse = currentrmse return phi def calculatevoxelcount(boxcorners, voxelsize): a, b = boxcorners n1 = math.ceil((b[0] - a[0]) / voxelsize) n2 = math.ceil((b[1] - a[1]) / voxelsize) n3 = math.ceil((b[2] - a[2]) / voxelsize) return n1 n2 n3 def findrelativelyprimestep(S): if S <= 1: return 1 for p in range(2, S): if math.gcd(p, S) == 1: return p return 1 def forwardprojection(phi, C): # Computes XC phi via ray-tracing accumulation over the voxel grid # Returns vector of size Ms Ms = len(C.rays) out = [0.0] Ms for i, ray in enumerate(C.rays): acc = 0.0 for t in ray.samplepoints: acc += phi[ray.voxelindex(t)] out[i] = acc return out def backprojection(v, C): # Computes XC^ v via ray-tracing accumulation over the voxel grid # Returns vector of size N N = len(v) # Assumed equal to voxel count for simplicity in this linear operator out = [0.0] N for i, ray in enumerate(C.rays): for t in ray.samplepoints: out[ray.voxelindex(t)] += v[i] return out def conjugategradientsolve(phi, C, sigma, b, reltol=0.01, maxiter=10): # Solves (XC XC^ + sigma I) y = b using Conjugate Gradient N = len(b) x = [0.0] N r = list(b) p = list(r) rsold = sum(r[i]r[i] for i in range(N)) for i in range(maxiter): Ap = matvecA(phi, C, sigma, p) pAp = sum(p[i]Ap[i] for i in range(N)) if pAp == 0: break alpha = rsold / pAp for j in range(N): x[j] += alpha p[j] r[j] -= alpha Ap[j] rsnew = sum(r[j]r[j] for j in range(N)) if math.sqrt(rsnew) / math.sqrt(sum(b[j]b[j] for j in range(N))) < reltol: break beta = rsnew / rsold for j in range(N): p[j] = r[j] + beta p[j] rsold = rsnew return x def matvecA(phi, C, sigma, x): # Computes (XC XC^ + sigma I) x # First compute XC^ x via backprojection Xtx = backprojection(x, C) # Then compute XC (XC^ x) via forward projection XtXx = forwardprojection(Xtx, C) # Add regularization term sigma x for i in range(len(x)): XtXx[i] += sigma x[i] return XtXx def computermse(phi, cameras, images): # Computes RMSE over all training frames totalsqerror = 0.0 totalpixels = 0 for C, g in zip(cameras, images): pred = forwardprojection(phi, C) for i in range(len(g)): diff = pred[i] - g[i] totalsqerror += diff diff totalpixels += len(g) return math.sqrt(totalsqerror / totalpixels) Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision: The method relies on double precision for \phi to maintain accuracy, consuming 8N bytes. Boundary Conditions: The bounding box must contain the scene; voxel size h should satisfy h \ge r (object space resolution) to ensure well-resolved MIP images. Degenerate Input: If S=1, the ordering step p is trivial. The regularization \sigma must be non-zero to ensure invertibility of (XC XC^ + \sigma I). A batch solver using conjugate gradients on the normal equations. Choose when memory allows loading all data and a single global solution is preferred over incremental updates. A variant that may use learned parameters. Choose when adaptive learning rates are needed beyond the fixed \omega. Uses a different sampling distribution for noise or updates. Choose for robustness against outliers in a stochastic setting. Uses second-order derivatives. Choose when the Hessian is available and the problem is well-conditioned, accepting higher per-iteration cost. Dynamically adjusts step size. Choose when a fixed \omega is insufficient for convergence stability. Time Complexity: One cycle of S iterations costs O(M n) operations, where M = S m^2 is the total number of pixels and n estimates the number of diagonal voxels (or contributing voxels per ray). One iteration costs O(22 m^2 n). Memory Complexity: Dominated by the unknown \phi \in \mathbb{R}^N, requiring 8N bytes for double precision. Total RAM usage is approximately 16N bytes including intermediate steps. Performance: The method is efficient for large-scale tomography due to its frame-driven approach, loading only one image at a time. Strengths: Handles large datasets incrementally; preconditioning improves convergence for reflective tomography by emphasizing surfaces. Limitations: Requires careful tuning of \omega and \sigma; convergence depends on the ordering of frames. When to use: Reflective tomography reconstruction where data arrives sequentially or memory is limited. The Incremental Preconditioned Gradient Method was introduced as an online learning approach for reflective tomography. It adapts the Algebraic Reconstruction Technique (ART) by incorporating a preconditioner derived from the projection matrix structure to solve a least-squares cost function incrementally. The method was proposed to address multiview reconstruction problems where high-frequency spatial information (surfaces) must be prioritized. Flexible algebraic technique for multiview reconstruction: incremental learning in reflective tomography, https://doi.org/10.1117/1.OE.58.10.103102, fetched 2026-10-26

name: Gradient-based Optimization with Surrogate Function
head: Iterative optimization using surrogate function, NGD-based optimization
body: This method estimates spatially varying extinction coefficients \beta by minimizing a cost function E(\beta) that fits a forward-model rendering to image measurements, using a surrogate function to avoid computing the full Jacobian per gradient step. It sets itself apart from direct Jacobian computation by decoupling the expensive forward-model rendering (FMC) from the gradient descent updates, requiring only one FMC rendering per block of NGD gradient steps rather than N{voxels}. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: Measured images \{i{c,\mu}^{measured}\} for views c=1 \dots N{views} and channels \mu \in \{R, G, B\}; camera parameters; physical constants (\sigma{\mu}^{aerosol}, \beta{\mu}^{air}); regularization weight \eta; step size \Delta; number of gradient steps per surrogate update NGD. Outputs: Estimated aerosol extinction field \hat{\beta}^{aerosol}. Data Structures: \beta^{(q)}: 3D grid of aerosol extinction coefficients at iteration q. j{all}^{(q)}: Field of radiance values \{j{c,\mu}^{(q)}\} computed via Forward Monte Carlo (FMC) at iteration q. Qc: Diagonal weighting matrix for view c, where element (k,k) is R{c,p}^{(q)}, the number of rays passing through voxel k in view c. L: 3D Laplacian matrix. W: Diagonal altitude-dependent weight matrix. Mc: Sun-mask binary matrix for view c. Formulas: 1. Channel Extinction: \beta{\mu} = \beta{\mu}^{air} + \tilde{\sigma}{\mu} \beta{G}^{aerosol} where \tilde{\sigma}{\mu} = \sigma{\mu}^{aerosol} / \sigma{G}^{aerosol}. 2. Cost Function: E(\beta) = \sum{c=1}^{N{views}} \sum{\mu=R,G,B} Mc \left[ i{c,\mu}^{measured} - ic(\beta{\mu}) \right]^2 + \eta \Psi(\beta{G}^{aerosol}) where ic(\beta{\mu}) is the modeled intensity. 3. Regularization Term: \Psi(\beta{G}^{aerosol}) = \| WL \beta{G}^{aerosol} \|^2 Gradient: 2 L^T W^T W \beta{G}^{aerosol}. 4. Gradient of Cost Function: \frac{\partial E}{\partial \beta} = 2 \sum{c=1}^{N{views}} \sum{\mu=R,G,B} \tilde{\sigma}{\mu} Qc Mc Jc(\beta{\mu}) Mc \left[ ic(\beta{\mu}) - i{c,\mu}^{measured} \right] + \eta \frac{\partial \Psi}{\partial \beta} Note: When j{all} is fixed, the Jacobian Jc degenerates to a simpler calculation based on the surrogate field. 5. Surrogate Update: \hat{\beta}^{(q+1)} = \arg \min{\beta \in C} E(\beta | j{all}^{(q)}) This minimization is performed using Gradient Descent steps. 6. Gradient Descent Step: \beta{d+1} = \betad - \Delta \frac{\partial E(\beta | j{all}^{(q)})}{\partial \beta} where d indexes the gradient descent step within the current surrogate block. 7. Camera Noise Simulation (for input preparation): i{c,\mu}^{measured} \leftarrow \left( i{c,\mu}^{measured} + o{noise} \right) \cdot \frac{2^{10}}{\max(\{Mc \cdot i{c,\mu}^{measured}\})} Clipped to [0, 1024] and rounded. o{noise} is white noise with std dev 0.4. Parameters: \Delta (Step size): 10^{-3}. NGD (Gradient steps per surrogate update): 5. \eta (Regularization weight): Not given in the sources. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def gradientbasedoptimizationwithsurrogate(measuredimages, cameraparams, physicalconstants, eta, delta, ngd, maxiterations): """ Estimates aerosol extinction beta using surrogate function optimization. """ # Initialize beta (e.g., null initialization) beta = initializebetanull() # Precompute physical constants sigmatilde = computesigmatilde(physicalconstants) # Precompute masks and weighting matrices sunmasks = computesunmasks(cameraparams) weightingmatrices = computeweightingmatrices(cameraparams) laplacianmatrix = compute3dlaplacian() altitudeweights = computealtitudeweights() q = 0 while q < maxiterations: # 1. Forward Model Rendering (FMC) to compute surrogate field # This is not an inverse problem; complexity does not increase with Nvoxels jall = forwardmodelrendering(beta, cameraparams, physicalconstants) # 2. Gradient Descent Block for d in range(ngd): # Compute gradient using fixed surrogate field jall # Note: Jacobian Jc degenerates when jall is fixed gradient = computegradientsurrogate( beta=beta, jall=jall, measuredimages=measuredimages, sunmasks=sunmasks, weightingmatrices=weightingmatrices, sigmatilde=sigmatilde, laplacianmatrix=laplacianmatrix, altitudeweights=altitudeweights, eta=eta) # Update beta beta = beta - delta gradient # 3. Increment iteration counter q += 1 return beta def computegradientsurrogate(beta, jall, measuredimages, sunmasks, weightingmatrices, sigmatilde, laplacianmatrix, altitudeweights, eta): """ Computes gradient of E(beta | jall) where jall is fixed. """ gradient = zeroslike(beta) # Regularization gradient: 2 L^T W^T W beta reggradient = 2.0 laplacianmatrix.T @ (altitudeweights.T @ (altitudeweights @ beta)) for c in range(numviews): for mu in channels: # Access surrogate field jall[c][mu] jcmu = jall[c][mu] # Compute modeled intensity ic from jall (simplified mapping) # In the surrogate context, ic is derived directly from the fixed radiance field icmodeled = mapradiancetointensity(jcmu) # Residual residual = icmodeled - measuredimages[c][mu] # Masking maskedresidual = sunmasks[c] residual # Weighting Qc = weightingmatrices[c] # Jacobian term degenerates when jall is fixed # Jc(beta | jcmu) is a simple calculation based on the fixed field # Specifically, it relates the change in intensity to change in beta # given the fixed radiance path. # Implementation detail: This typically involves ray-voxel intersection counts # or similar geometric factors derived from the FMC step. # For the purpose of this pseudocode, we assume a helper function exists # that computes this degenerate Jacobian-vector product. jacobianterm = computedegeneratejacobianterm(beta, jcmu, Qc, sunmasks[c]) # Accumulate gradient # Term: 2 sigmatilde Qc Mc Jc Mc residual # Note: The source formula has Qc and Mc on both sides of Jc in the general case, # but with fixed jall, the structure simplifies. # We follow the structure: 2 sigmatilde (Qc Mc (Jc (Mc residual))) # Apply mask to residual maskedres = sunmasks[c] residual # Apply Jacobian (degenerate form) jacres = jacobianterm @ maskedres # Apply weighting and mask again (as per Eq 32 structure) weightedjac = Qc (sunmasks[c] jacres) gradient += 2.0 sigmatilde[mu] weightedjac # Add regularization gradient gradient += eta reggradient return gradient def forwardmodelrendering(beta, cameraparams, physicalconstants): """ Computes radiance field jall using Forward Monte Carlo (FMC). """ jall = {} for c in range(numviews): jall[c] = {} for mu in channels: # Compute radiance for channel mu in view c # This involves tracing rays through the medium defined by beta jall[c][mu] = fmctrace(beta, cameraparams[c], physicalconstants[mu]) return jall def initializebetanull(): """ Initialize beta to zero or single scattering approximation. """ return zeroslike(betagrid) Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Sun Masking: Pixels around the Sun are masked (Mc) because Monte Carlo estimates have high variance due to forward scattering phase function sampling. Additionally, physical sun occluders cause saturation. Ill-conditioning: Voxels near cameras have unstable \beta estimates because they affect more pixels, leading to higher gradient magnitudes. This is solved by the diagonal weighting matrix Qc, where element (k,k) is the number of rays passing through voxel k. Convergence: Starting from \beta^{aerosol}=0, satisfactory convergence occurs after several hundred iterations. Time Complexity: Direct Jacobian computation requires O(N{voxels}) FMC renderings per iteration, which is computationally expensive. The surrogate approach requires only one FMC rendering per NGD gradient descent steps, significantly reducing cost. Memory Complexity: Requires storing the radiance field j{all} and the extinction field \beta. The weighting matrices Qc are diagonal, requiring O(N{voxels}) memory per view. Performance: On Atm1 (Haze blobs), \delta{mass} = 1.7\% (null init) vs 3.4\% (single scattering init). On Atm4 (Haze front), \delta{mass} = 14\% (null init) vs 4.1\% (single scattering init). Strengths: Effective gradient calculation without N{voxels} rendering processes; handles ill-conditioning via weighting. Limitations: Requires careful tuning of \Delta and NGD; sensitive to noise in forward scattering regions (mitigated by sun mask). This method was developed for in-situ multi-scattering tomography, specifically for recovering aerosol distributions from multi-view images. It builds on the concept of surrogate functions to avoid the computational burden of direct Jacobian computation in heterogeneous media. The approach was compared against a single scattering approximation method. In-situ multi-scattering tomography, https://archive.org/details/arxiv-1512.02110, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial)

name: Moment-Damped Levenberg-Marquardt Optimizer
head: Hybrid LM-Adam Optimizer, Moment-LM Optimizer, TurboGS Optimizer, hybrid moment-damped LM, sparse moment-damped Levenberg-Marquardt
body: A hybrid optimization strategy for sparse-pixel training that partitions Gaussian parameters into geometry and base appearance blocks, solving them via small Levenberg-Marquardt (LM) systems with Adam-style moment damping, while updating Higher-order Spherical Harmonic (SH) coefficients separately with Adam. It sets itself apart from its parent Gradient Descent Solver by introducing Hessian-informed updates for geometry and appearance, and from CGLS Solver (Conjugate Gradient Least Squares) by using direct Cholesky decomposition on small blocks rather than iterative linear solving. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Current Gaussian parameters \theta, Adam first moment m, Adam second moment v, Jacobian J for geometry and base appearance blocks, loss gradient m (Adam first moment of loss). Output: Parameter update \Delta \theta. Data Structures: Gaussian parameters \theta are partitioned into: Geometry block g \in \mathbb{R}^{10}: position (3), scale (3), rotation (4 quaternion). Base appearance block a \in \mathbb{R}^{4}: RGB DC coefficients (3), opacity (1). Higher-order SH coefficients: updated separately. Parameters: \epsilon: Small constant for numerical stability (standard Adam value, e.g., 10^{-8}). \eta: Learning rate for Adam update of SH coefficients. \sqrt{v}: Element-wise square root of the second moment vector v, serving as diagonal damping. Steps: 1. Partition Parameters: Separate \theta into g and a. 2. Compute Jacobian: Calculate the Jacobian Jg for geometry and Ja for base appearance with respect to the rendered loss. 3. Solve LM System for g and a: For each block b \in \{g, a\}, solve the linear system: (Jb^\top Jb + \text{diag}(\sqrt{vb} + \epsilon)) \Delta b = -mb where mb is the Adam first moment for block b, and vb is the Adam second moment for block b. The term \sqrt{vb} acts as a moment-based diagonal damping term to stabilize sparse gradients. 4. Solve via Cholesky: Perform Cholesky decomposition on the matrix (Jb^\top Jb + \text{diag}(\sqrt{vb} + \epsilon)) to solve for \Delta b efficiently. 5. Update SH Coefficients: Update higher-order SH coefficients \theta{SH} using Adam: \Delta \theta{SH} = -\eta \frac{\hat{m}{SH}}{\sqrt{\hat{v}{SH}} + \epsilon} where \hat{m}{SH} and \hat{v}{SH} are bias-corrected Adam moments. 6. Apply Updates: Apply \Delta g, \Delta a, and \Delta \theta{SH} to the respective parameters. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def momentdampedlmupdate(g, a, thetash, mg, ma, msh, vg, va, vsh, eta, epsilon): """ Perform one step of Moment-Damped Levenberg-Marquardt optimization. Args: g: Geometry parameters (R^10) a: Base appearance parameters (R^4) thetash: Higher-order SH coefficients mg, ma, msh: Adam first moments for respective blocks vg, va, vsh: Adam second moments for respective blocks eta: Learning rate for SH update epsilon: Small constant for numerical stability Returns: Updated g, a, thetash """ # Step 1: Solve LM system for geometry block g # Jg is Jacobian of loss w.r.t g # Hg = Jg^T Jg Hg = computehessianapproximation(Jg) # Damping term: sqrt(vg) + epsilon dampingg = sqrt(vg) + epsilon # System: (Hg + diag(dampingg)) deltag = -mg Ag = Hg + diag(dampingg) bg = -mg # Solve via Cholesky decomposition deltag = solvecholesky(Ag, bg) # Step 2: Solve LM system for base appearance block a # Ja is Jacobian of loss w.r.t a Ha = computehessianapproximation(Ja) dampinga = sqrt(va) + epsilon Aa = Ha + diag(dampinga) ba = -ma deltaa = solvecholesky(Aa, ba) # Step 3: Update SH coefficients using Adam # Bias-corrected moments mhatsh = biascorrect(msh) vhatsh = biascorrect(vsh) deltash = -eta (mhatsh / (sqrt(vhatsh) + epsilon)) # Step 4: Apply updates gnew = g + deltag anew = a + deltaa thetashnew = thetash + deltash return gnew, anew, thetashnew def computehessianapproximation(J): """Compute J^T J.""" return J.T @ J def diag(v): """Create diagonal matrix from vector.""" return np.diag(v) def solvecholesky(A, b): """Solve Ax = b using Cholesky decomposition.""" L = cholesky(A) y = solvetriangular(L, b, lower=True) x = solvetriangular(L.T, y, lower=False) return x def biascorrect(m, t): """Bias correction for Adam moments.""" # Assuming t is the step number return m / (1 - 0.9t) # Beta1 = 0.9 Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Ignoring SH cross-parameter correlations is a trade-off; joint optimization would substantially increase Jacobian size and memory overhead. Sparse gradients can be unstable; the moment-based damping \sqrt{v} is critical for stabilization. A tailored optimizer that couples Hessian-informed updates with Adam moment damping to stabilize and improve convergence under sparse supervision. It integrates Adam moments with Hessian-informed updates. Time Complexity: Solving small LM systems via Cholesky decomposition is efficient for the fixed small block sizes (10 and 4 dimensions). The overall complexity is dominated by Jacobian computation and Cholesky factorization, which is lightweight for these small blocks. Memory Complexity: Low memory overhead compared to full Newton methods due to block partitioning and ignoring SH correlations. Measured Performance: On Mip-NeRF 360, Moment-LM achieves 29.50dB PSNR vs 29.42dB for Sparse Adam-only, with identical training time (90s) and NGS (0.64M). Scaling: Suitable for sparse-pixel training scenarios where full dense optimization is too costly. Strengths: Higher PSNR/SSIM, lower LPIPS, and more stable high-frequency details compared to sparse Adam-only optimization under similar training times. Limitations: Trade-off in accuracy due to ignoring SH cross-parameter correlations. Originated in TurboGS: Accelerating 3D Gaussian Splatting via Error-Guided Sparse Pixel Sampling and Optimization. It is used in the context of 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) to accelerate training while maintaining or improving rendering quality. name: Linear Model Analysis for Plane Reproduction
head: Geometric Initialization Justification, Theorem 1 Analysis
body:
This analysis provides a theoretical justification for the loss function's ability to converge to the signed distance function (SDF) of a plane when the input data is sampled from a plane, using a linear model f(x; w) = w^T x. It sets apart from fixed volumetric grids (like RGVF) by being data-dependent and avoiding cubic-size memory requirements and interpolation schemes. It proves that under specific conditions on the regularization parameter \lambda, gradient descent converges to the global minima corresponding to the plane's normal. Inputs: Point cloud X = \{xi\}{i \in I} in \mathbb{R}^d, where xi = yi + \epsiloni. yi spans a (d-1)-dimensional hyperplane H containing the origin, and \epsiloni are small deviations with \|\epsiloni\| < \delta. Regularization parameter \lambda. Outputs: Weight vector w (or q in transformed coordinates) representing the approximate SDF normal. Data Structures: Covariance matrix components: Eigenvalues \lambdaj and eigenvectors uj from spectral decomposition. Transformed coordinates q = U^T w. Steps: 1. Spectral Decomposition: Compute the spectral decomposition of the covariance matrix of the point cloud: \sum{i \in I} xi xi^T = U D U^T where U = (u1, \dots, ud) is the orthogonal matrix of eigenvectors and D = 	ext{diag}(\lambda1, \dots, \lambdad) with 0 \le \lambda1 < \lambda2 \le \dots \le \lambdad. 2. Coordinate Transformation: Change coordinates to q = U^T w. The loss function becomes diagonalized: \ell(q) = q^T D q + \lambda (\|q\| - 1)^2 3. Critical Point Identification: Find critical points by setting the gradient to zero. For q 
eq 0, critical points satisfy: 2\lambda(\|q\| - 1) = -\lambdaj This yields critical points qj = \pm \sqrt{1 -  rac{\lambdaj}{2\lambda}} ej for j \in [d], and q=0, where ej is the j-th standard basis vector. 4. Global Minima Selection: If \lambda >  rac{\lambda1}{2}, the global minima are \pm q = \pm \sqrt{1 -  rac{\lambda1}{2\lambda}} e1. These correspond to the approximate SDF to the plane. Formulas: Linear Loss: \ell(w) = \sum{i \in I} (w^T xi)^2 + \lambda (\|w\| - 1)^2 This is a simplified version of the general loss using squared error and removing normal data terms. Gradient in Transformed Coordinates: 
ablaq \ell(q)^T = 2(D + 2\lambda(\|q\| - 1)I)q Hessian in Transformed Coordinates: 
abla^2q \ell(q) = 2D + 4\lambda(\|q\| - 1)I + 8\lambda q q^T Parameters: \lambda: Regularization parameter. Must satisfy \lambda >  rac{\lambda1}{2} for the global minima to exist in the form of the SDF. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: If \lambda \le  rac{\lambda1}{2}, the term 1 -  rac{\lambda1}{2\lambda} becomes non-positive, and the global minima corresponding to the SDF do not exist in this form. The parameter \lambda must be chosen sufficiently large compared to the deviation from planarity \delta. The analysis assumes the point cloud is sampled approximately from a plane. In the general MLP case, this analysis holds locally, where the deviation from planarity is quantified by surface curvature. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import numpy as np def linearmodelanalysis(pointcloud, lambdareg): """ Analyze linear model for plane reproduction. Args: pointcloud: numpy array of shape (N, d) lambdareg: float, regularization parameter Returns: wopt: numpy array of shape (d,), optimal weight vector """ # Step 1: Spectral Decomposition # Compute covariance matrix covmatrix = np.dot(pointcloud.T, pointcloud) # Eigen decomposition eigenvalues, eigenvectors = np.linalg.eigh(covmatrix) # Sort eigenvalues and eigenvectors idx = np.argsort(eigenvalues) eigenvalues = eigenvalues[idx] eigenvectors = eigenvectors[:, idx] lambda1 = eigenvalues[0] U = eigenvectors D = np.diag(eigenvalues) # Check condition for global minima existence if lambdareg <= lambda1 / 2: raise ValueError("Lambda must be greater than lambda1 / 2 for global minima to exist.") # Step 2 & 3: Identify Global Minima in Transformed Coordinates # The global minima in transformed coordinates are +/- q1 # q1 = sqrt(1 - lambda1 / (2 lambdareg)) e1 factor = np.sqrt(1 - lambda1 / (2 lambdareg)) qopt = np.zeros(pointcloud.shape[1]) qopt[0] = factor # Corresponds to e1 # Step 4: Transform back to original coordinates # w = U q wopt = np.dot(U, qopt) return wopt Solves linear systems using conjugate gradients, suitable for large sparse systems. Uses learned components in the gradient descent update. Stochastic gradient descent with noise modeled by a positive t-distribution. Second-order optimization method using Hessian information. Optimization with line search that does not require exact minimization. Gradient method with incremental preconditioning. Optimization using a surrogate function to approximate the loss. Levenberg-Marquardt with moment damping for adaptive learning rates. Time Complexity: Depends on the spectral decomposition of the covariance matrix, which is O(N d^2 + d^3) for N points in d dimensions. Memory Complexity: O(d^2) for storing the covariance matrix and its decomposition. Strengths: Provides theoretical guarantee for convergence to the plane's SDF under specific conditions. Data-dependent, avoiding fixed grid memory costs. Limitations: Requires \lambda to be chosen carefully relative to the data's deviation from planarity. Analysis is for linear models; extension to MLPs is local. When to Use: When initializing or analyzing the convergence of implicit neural representations for planar surfaces. When Not to Use: For non-planar surfaces without local linearization, or when \lambda cannot be tuned appropriately. Originated in the paper "Implicit Geometric Regularization for Learning Shapes". The analysis is presented as Theorem 1 and Theorem 2, justifying the use of the Eikonal regularization term alone for implicitly regularizing the zero level set. It contrasts with previous works that used Eikonal regularization in combination with other explicit reconstruction terms. The analysis uses perturbation theory for eigenvalues and eigenvectors of Hermitian matrices. Implicit Geometric Regularization for Learning Shapes, https://doi.org/10.48550/arxiv.2002.10099, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial)

name: Observed-Only Momentum Updates
head: Observed Variable Updates, Sparse Momentum
body: Observed-Only Momentum Updates is a modification to the Adam optimizer designed to prevent noisy momentum from being applied repeatedly to variables not observed in the current training batch, which impedes convergence in differentiable volume rendering. It restricts momentum updates and moment estimates to only those variables that receive nonzero gradients in the current iteration. This distinguishes it from standard Adam, which updates all parameters regardless of observation, and from solvers like CGLS that handle ill-conditioned systems via matrix-free linear algebra rather than stochastic gradient filtering [3285-cgls-solver-conjugate-gradient-least-squares.md]. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Current parameter values \theta, first moment estimate m, second moment estimate v, Adam hyperparameters \beta1, \beta2, \epsilon, and the computed gradient g for the current batch. Output: Updated parameter values \theta', updated moments m', v'. Data Structures: Parameters \theta: A dense or sparse tensor of learnable variables (e.g., radiance field coefficients, Gaussian attributes). Moments m, v: Tensors of the same shape as \theta, initialized to zero. Gradient g: Tensor of the same shape as \theta, containing partial derivatives of the loss with respect to \theta. Numbered Steps: 1. Compute the gradient g for the current batch using differentiable rendering. 2. Identify the set of observed indices \mathcal{O} = \{ i \mid gi \neq 0 \}. 3. For each index i \in \mathcal{O}: a. Update the first moment estimate: mi \leftarrow \beta1 mi + (1 - \beta1) gi. b. Update the second moment estimate: vi \leftarrow \beta2 vi + (1 - \beta2) gi^2. c. Compute bias-corrected estimates: \hat{m}i = \frac{mi}{1 - \beta1^t}, \hat{v}i = \frac{vi}{1 - \beta2^t}, where t is the current time step. d. Update the parameter: \thetai \leftarrow \thetai - \alpha \frac{\hat{m}i}{\sqrt{\hat{v}i} + \epsilon}. 4. For each index j \notin \mathcal{O}: a. Do not update mj or vj. b. Do not update \thetaj. Formulas: Moment updates (for observed i): mi^{(t)} = \beta1 mi^{(t-1)} + (1 - \beta1) gi^{(t)} vi^{(t)} = \beta2 vi^{(t-1)} + (1 - \beta2) (gi^{(t)})^2 Parameter update (for observed i): \thetai^{(t)} = \thetai^{(t-1)} - \alpha \frac{\hat{m}i^{(t)}}{\sqrt{\hat{v}i^{(t)}} + \epsilon} Where \alpha is the learning rate, \beta1, \beta2 are exponential decay rates for moment estimates, \epsilon is a small constant for numerical stability, and t is the iteration count. Parameters with Typical Values: \beta1: 0.9 (typical Adam default). \beta2: 0.999 (typical Adam default). \epsilon: 10^{-8} (typical Adam default). \alpha: Depends on the specific training setup; not specified in. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Noisy Momentum Accumulation: Without this method, Adam maintains moment estimates from previous iterations' stochastic noise. If a variable is not observed, its momentum remains fixed with accumulated noise, impeding convergence. Indirect Gradients: In differentiable path tracing, gradients for indirectly observed parameters (e.g., lighting contributions from distant surfaces) are extremely noisy due to low sampling probability of long light paths. Observed-Only Momentum helps mitigate this by ignoring updates for variables that only receive these indirect, noisy gradients. Sparse Updates: Variables not observed in a batch do not receive updates. This requires careful initialization and potentially longer training schedules to ensure all variables are eventually observed and updated. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def observedonlymomentumupdate(theta, m, v, g, alpha, beta1, beta2, epsilon, t): """ Perform one step of Observed-Only Momentum Updates. Args: theta: Current parameter values (tensor). m: First moment estimate (tensor). v: Second moment estimate (tensor). g: Gradient for the current batch (tensor). alpha: Learning rate (float). beta1: Exponential decay rate for first moment (float). beta2: Exponential decay rate for second moment (float). epsilon: Small constant for numerical stability (float). t: Current time step (int). Returns: theta: Updated parameter values. m: Updated first moment estimate. v: Updated second moment estimate. """ # Create a mask for observed variables (non-zero gradients) observedmask = (g != 0) # Update moments and parameters only for observed variables # Using boolean indexing to apply updates selectively # Update first moment for observed variables m[observedmask] = beta1 m[observedmask] + (1 - beta1) g[observedmask] # Update second moment for observed variables v[observedmask] = beta2 v[observedmask] + (1 - beta2) (g[observedmask] 2) # Compute bias-corrected estimates for observed variables biascorrection1 = 1 - beta1 t biascorrection2 = 1 - beta2 t mhat = m / biascorrection1 vhat = v / biascorrection2 # Update parameters for observed variables # theta[observedmask] -= alpha (mhat[observedmask] / (sqrt(vhat[observedmask]) + epsilon)) # Note: Standard Adam update formula applied only to observed indices # For simplicity, we can compute the full update and then zero out non-observed updates # However, the core idea is that m and v are NOT updated for non-observed variables. # So we only update theta for observed variables. # Calculate the Adam update step for observed variables adamstep = mhat[observedmask] / (vhat[observedmask].sqrt() + epsilon) # Apply the update theta[observedmask] = theta[observedmask] - alpha adamstep # Non-observed variables remain unchanged in theta, m, and v return theta, m, v A momentum scaling rule proposed to maintain high update cosine similarity and similar update magnitude when switching to larger training batch sizes in 3D Gaussian Splatting training. Compared to leaving momentum coefficients unchanged, the exponential momentum scaling rule keeps update cosine similarity higher across different training batch sizes. It is a variant of momentum scaling, distinct from the observed-only filtering of the parent method, and is used in conjunction with Adam-like optimizers in specific 3D Gaussian Splatting contexts. Time Complexity: O(N) per iteration, where N is the number of parameters, as it involves element-wise operations and masking. The masking operation may add a small constant overhead but does not change the asymptotic complexity. Memory Complexity: O(N) for storing parameters and moments, same as standard Adam. Measured Performance: Not given in the sources. Scaling: Scales with the number of parameters and batch size. The effectiveness depends on the sparsity of observed gradients. Strengths: Reduces noise accumulation for unobserved variables, potentially improving convergence in scenes with sparse observations or indirect lighting. Limitations: May require more iterations to update all variables if observations are sparse. Not suitable for dense gradient scenarios where all variables are observed every step. When to use: When using differentiable rendering with path tracing where indirect gradients are noisy and many variables are not directly observed in each batch. When not to use: When gradients are dense and all variables are observed every step, or when computational overhead of masking is prohibitive (though this is minimal). Originated in the context of material and lighting reconstruction for complex indoor scenes using texture-space differentiable rendering. The method was introduced to address the issue of noisy momentum accumulation in Adam optimizer when applied to differentiable rendering, where not all parameters are observed in every batch due to the nature of light transport. It is used in differentiable volume rendering and related inverse rendering techniques. Material and Lighting Reconstruction for Complex Indoor Scenes with Texture-space Differentiable Rendering, https://doi.org/10.2312/sr.20211292, fetched 2026-10-29 On Scaling Up 3D Gaussian Splatting Training, https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-031-91989-32, fetched 2026-10-26

name: L2 Update
head: L2-norm minimization update step, PWLS Update
body: The L2 Update is a single optimization step for differentiable volume rendering that minimizes the L2-norm of the residual between projected and measured data, incorporating Poisson-statistics-based weighting. It distinguishes itself from standard gradient descent by applying adaptive weights to both the residual and the volume update, supporting subset-based processing to handle large datasets. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: projections (measured data), volume (current volume estimate), geometry (projection geometry), settings (configuration flags updateresidual, studentst), subsets (number of subsets). Outputs: Updated volume, normalized residual norm rnorm. Data Structures: projections: Array of measured projection values. volume: 3D array of voxel values. geometry: Object defining projection parameters (angles, distances, detector dimensions). residual: Temporary array same shape as projections. voltmp, bwpw: Temporary arrays same shape as volume. fwpw: Temporary array same shape as projections. Steps: 1. Retrieve settings.updateresidual and settings.studentst. 2. Determine the number of subsets. 3. Compute the backprojection weight normalization factor by calling bpnorm(projections, volume, geometry). 4. Loop over subsets generated by subsetgenerator(projections, volume, geometry, copy=True): a. Initialize residual as a contiguous zero array with the same shape as the current subset of projections. b. Forward project the current volume into residual. c. Apply filters to residual. d. If updateresidual is true, compute the root mean square of residual and add it to rnorm. e. If studentst is true, apply Student's T norm with degree 6 to residual. f. Scale residual by bpweight subsets 2. g. Backproject residual into volume (filtered=False). h. Return rnorm / subsets. 5. Retrieve settings.updateresidual. 6. Determine the number of subsets. 7. Compute the backprojection weight normalization factor by calling bpnorm(projections, volume, geometry). 8. Loop over subsets generated by subsetgenerator(projections, volume, geometry, copy=True): a. Initialize voltmp and bwpw as zero arrays with the same shape as volume. b. Compute weights fwpw as exp(-subset). c. Backproject fwpw into bwpw (filtered=False). d. Initialize residual as a contiguous zero array with the same shape as the current subset of projections. e. Forward project the current volume into residual. f. Apply filters to residual. g. If updateresidual is true, compute the root mean square of residual and add it to rnorm. h. Scale residual by bpweight subsets 2 fwpw. i. Backproject residual into voltmp (filtered=False). j. Normalize bwpw by dividing by its maximum value. k. Clamp bwpw values below 1e-2 to 1e-2. l. Update volume by adding voltmp divided by bwpw. m. Return rnorm / subsets. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def l2updatestep(projections, volume, geometry, settings, numsubsets): """ Performs a single L2-norm minimization update step with Poisson weighting. Args: projections: Array of measured projection data. volume: Current 3D volume estimate. geometry: Projection geometry object. settings: Object containing 'updateresidual' (bool) and 'studentst' (bool). numsubsets: Number of subsets to process. Returns: rnorm: Normalized residual norm. """ rnorm = 0.0 # Compute backprojection weight normalization factor bpweight = bpnorm(projections, volume, geometry) # Generate subsets subsets = subsetgenerator(projections, volume, geometry, copy=True) for subset in subsets: # Initialize residual residual = np.zeroslike(subset) # Forward project volume into residual residual = forwardproject(volume, geometry) # Apply filters to residual residual = applyfilters(residual) # Update residual norm if required if settings.updateresidual: rnorm += np.sqrt(np.mean(residual2)) # Apply Student's T norm if required if settings.studentst: residual = applystudenttnorm(residual, degree=6) # Scale residual residual = residual bpweight numsubsets 2 # Backproject residual into volume volume = backproject(residual, geometry, filtered=False) # Return normalized residual norm rnorm = rnorm / numsubsets return rnorm def l2updatestepwithweights(projections, volume, geometry, settings, numsubsets): """ Performs a single L2-norm minimization update step with Poisson weighting and adaptive volume update. Args: projections: Array of measured projection data. volume: Current 3D volume estimate. geometry: Projection geometry object. settings: Object containing 'updateresidual' (bool) and 'studentst' (bool). numsubsets: Number of subsets to process. Returns: rnorm: Normalized residual norm. """ rnorm = 0.0 # Compute backprojection weight normalization factor bpweight = bpnorm(projections, volume, geometry) # Generate subsets subsets = subsetgenerator(projections, volume, geometry, copy=True) for subset in subsets: # Initialize temporary arrays voltmp = np.zeroslike(volume) bwpw = np.zeroslike(volume) # Compute weights fwpw = np.exp(-subset) # Backproject weights bwpw = backproject(fwpw, geometry, filtered=False) # Initialize residual residual = np.zeroslike(subset) # Forward project volume into residual residual = forwardproject(volume, geometry) # Apply filters to residual residual = applyfilters(residual) # Update residual norm if required if settings.updateresidual: rnorm += np.sqrt(np.mean(residual2)) # Scale residual residual = residual bpweight numsubsets 2 fwpw # Backproject residual into voltmp voltmp = backproject(residual, geometry, filtered=False) # Normalize bwpw bwpw = bwpw / np.max(bwpw) # Clamp bwpw bwpw = np.maximum(bwpw, 1e-2) # Update volume volume = volume + voltmp / bwpw # Return normalized residual norm rnorm = rnorm / numsubsets return rnorm def bpnorm(projections, volume, geometry): """ Computes the backprojection weight normalization factor. Args: projections: Array of measured projection data. volume: Current 3D volume estimate. geometry: Projection geometry object. Returns: bpweight: Normalization factor. """ # Implementation details not provided in sources # Placeholder for actual implementation return 1.0 def subsetgenerator(projections, volume, geometry, copy=True): """ Generates subsets of projections. Args: projections: Array of measured projection data. volume: Current 3D volume estimate. geometry: Projection geometry object. copy: Whether to copy the data. Yields: subset: A subset of projections. """ # Implementation details not provided in sources # Placeholder for actual implementation yield projections def forwardproject(volume, geometry): """ Forward projects the volume. Args: volume: Current 3D volume estimate. geometry: Projection geometry object. Returns: projected: Forward projected data. """ # Implementation details not provided in sources # Placeholder for actual implementation return np.zeroslike(geometry.projections) def applyfilters(residual): """ Applies filters to the residual. Args: residual: Residual array. Returns: filteredresidual: Filtered residual array. """ # Implementation details not provided in sources # Placeholder for actual implementation return residual def applystudenttnorm(residual, degree): """ Applies Student's T norm to the residual. Args: residual: Residual array. degree: Degrees of freedom for Student's T distribution. Returns: weightedresidual: Weighted residual array. """ # Implementation details not provided in sources # Placeholder for actual implementation return residual def backproject(data, geometry, filtered=False): """ Backprojects the data. Args: data: Data to backproject. geometry: Projection geometry object. filtered: Whether the data is already filtered. Returns: backprojected: Backprojected volume. """ # Implementation details not provided in sources # Placeholder for actual implementation return np.zeroslike(geometry.volume) Parameters: updateresidual: Boolean flag to update the residual norm. studentst: Boolean flag to apply Student's T norm. numsubsets: Number of subsets to process. degree: Degrees of freedom for Student's T distribution (default 6). Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision issues may arise when computing exp(-subset) for large negative values. Clamping bwpw to 1e-2 prevents division by zero but may introduce bias in low-weight regions. The method assumes that the geometry object provides accurate projection parameters. Time Complexity: Linear with respect to the number of voxels and projections, scaled by the number of subsets. Memory Complexity: Linear with respect to the number of voxels and projections, due to temporary arrays. Measured Performance: Not given in the sources. Scaling: Scales well with the number of subsets, as each subset can be processed independently. Strengths: Handles large datasets efficiently through subset processing; incorporates Poisson statistics for improved accuracy. Limitations: Requires careful tuning of parameters such as numsubsets and degree; may be sensitive to noise in the projections. When to Use: Suitable for differentiable volume rendering tasks where Poisson statistics are relevant and large datasets need to be processed efficiently. When Not to Use: Not suitable for real-time applications due to the computational cost of forward and backprojection operations. The L2 Update method originates from the flexTOMO project, an unofficial implementation of differentiable volume rendering techniques. It is designed to optimize volume estimates by minimizing the L2-norm of the residual between projected and measured data, incorporating Poisson-statistics-based weighting. cicwi/flexTOMO, https://github.com/cicwi/flexTOMO, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial)

name: BFGS Solver with Moreau Envelope
head: BFGS with Moreau Envelope, Huber Reconstruction
body:
This method solves inverse problems, specifically tomographic reconstruction, by minimizing a composite objective function consisting of a data fidelity term and a regularizer. It sets itself apart by using the BFGS quasi-Newton algorithm to handle the non-smooth L1 regularization via its Moreau envelope, providing a differentiable approximation that allows second-order optimization steps. This contrasts with first-order Gradient Descent solvers and avoids the explicit projection steps required by constrained material solvers. The method minimizes an objective function F(x) defined as the sum of a squared L2 data discrepancy and a smoothed L1 regularizer applied to the image gradient. Inputs: Forward operator A (e.g., Ray Transform). Noisy measurement data y. Image space X (e.g., uniform discrete space). Gradient operator 
abla. Hyperparameters: smoothing parameter \sigma, regularization weight \lambda, maximum iterations maxiter, and memory size num\store. Outputs: Reconstructed image x. Data Structures: x: The current estimate of the image, stored as a tensor/array in X. H^{-1}0: Initial inverse Hessian estimate, implemented as a scaling operator. s, y vectors: Stored for Limited Memory BFGS (L-BFGS) history. Steps: 1. Initialize Operator Norm: Compute the operator norm of A using the power method to scale the initial Hessian estimate. opnorm = \|A\| 2. Initialize Inverse Hessian: Set the initial inverse Hessian estimate H^{-1}0 as a scaled identity operator: H^{-1}0 =  rac{1}{2 \|A\|^2} I 3. Define Data Term: Construct the squared L2 norm of the residual: D(x) = \|Ax - y\|2^2 4. Define Regularizer: Compute the gradient of the image: g = 
abla x. Apply the Group L1 norm to the gradient: \|g\|{1,2}. Smooth this non-smooth norm using the Moreau envelope with parameter \sigma: R(x) = 	ext{MoreauEnvelope}{\sigma}(\|
abla x\|{1,2}) 5. Define Objective: Combine terms: F(x) = D(x) + \lambda R(x) 6. Solve: Run the BFGS solver (specifically L-BFGS if num\store is limited) starting from an initial guess (often the FBP pseudoinverse result). Use the precomputed H^{-1}0 as the initial Hessian approximation. Limit iterations to maxiter. Store num\store vectors for the limited memory update. Parameters: \sigma = 0.03: Smoothing parameter for the Moreau envelope. \lambda = 0.3: Regularization weight. maxiter = 200: Maximum number of iterations. num\store = 10: Number of vectors stored for L-BFGS. Pitfalls: The initial reconstruction (pseudoinverse) must use the 'Hann' filter to match the reference implementation's assumptions. Precision issues may arise if the operator norm is not computed accurately, affecting the scaling of the Hessian estimate. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import numpy as np import odl def bfgsmoreauenvelopesolver(A, y, space, sigma=0.03, lam=0.3, maxiter=200, numstore=10): """ Solve inverse problem using BFGS with Moreau Envelope regularization. Args: A: Forward operator (e.g., odl.tomo.RayTransform) y: Measurement data space: Image space (e.g., odl.uniformdiscr) sigma: Smoothing parameter for Moreau envelope lam: Regularization weight maxiter: Maximum iterations numstore: Memory size for L-BFGS Returns: x: Reconstructed image """ # 1. Compute operator norm opnorm = odl.powermethodopnorm(A) # 2. Initialize inverse Hessian estimate # Hinv0 = 0.5 / opnorm^2 I hessinvestimate = odl.ScalingOperator(space, 0.5 / opnorm2) # 3. Define data term: ||Ax - y||2^2 l2norm = odl.solvers.L2NormSquared(A.range) datadiscrepancy = l2norm (A - y) # 4. Define regularizer using Moreau Envelope gradient = odl.Gradient(space) l1norm = odl.solvers.GroupL1Norm(gradient.range) smoothedl1 = odl.solvers.MoreauEnvelope(l1norm, sigma=sigma) regularizer = smoothedl1 gradient # 5. Define objective function objfun = datadiscrepancy + lam regularizer # 6. Initial guess (e.g., FBP pseudoinverse) # Note: Must use 'Hann' filter as per reference pseudoinverse = odl.tomo.fbpop(A, filtertype='Hann') x = pseudoinverse(y) # 7. Solve using BFGS # Using odl.solvers.bfgsmethod which supports L-BFGS via numstore callback = None # Optional callback for logging x = odl.solvers.bfgsmethod( objfun, x, maxiter=maxiter, numstore=numstore, hessinvestimate=hessinvestimate, callback=callback) return x A Monte Carlo estimator to calculate the radiance contribution of a stationary path found by the BFGS solver, based on the path formulation of the Radiative Radiative Transfer Equation (RRTE). Time Complexity: Each iteration involves computing the gradient of the data term and the smoothed regularizer. The L-BFGS update is O(m \cdot d) where m is num\store and d is the dimension of the image. The dominant cost is usually the forward and adjoint operator evaluations (A and A^). Memory Complexity: O(d) for the image and gradients, plus O(m \cdot d) for the L-BFGS history vectors. Performance: The Moreau envelope makes the L1 norm differentiable, allowing BFGS to converge faster than first-order methods for smooth approximations, but the smoothing parameter \sigma must be chosen carefully to balance accuracy and differentiability. Strengths: Handles non-smooth regularization (L1) effectively within a second-order framework. The Hann filter initialization provides a stable starting point. Limitations: Requires computation of the operator norm, which can be expensive for large operators. The smoothing parameter \sigma is a hyperparameter that affects convergence and solution quality. When to use: Suitable for tomographic reconstruction and other inverse problems where L1 regularization on gradients is desired and second-order convergence is beneficial. When not to use: If the operator norm is too expensive to compute or if the problem size is extremely large, first-order methods might be preferred. The method is based on the reference implementation from the learnedgradienttomography repository. It combines classical tomographic reconstruction techniques (FBP with Hann filter) with modern optimization methods (BFGS with Moreau envelope) to solve inverse problems. name: Monte Carlo Path Contribution Estimation
head: Caustic contribution estimation, RRTE path estimator
body: This method estimates the radiance contribution of a stationary light path found by the BFGS solver, based on the path formulation of the Radiative Transfer Equation (RRTE). It differs from standard path tracing by evaluating contributions for specific, optimized stationary paths rather than sampling paths stochastically from the camera, and it differs from the parent BFGS solver by handling the final radiance accumulation and variance reduction. Inputs: Stationary path \bar{\mathbf{x}}k = (\mathbf{x}0, \mathbf{x}1, \dots, \mathbf{x}n) found by the BFGS solver, where \mathbf{x}0 is the receiver (camera) and \mathbf{x}n is the light source. Refractive Index Field (RIF) \eta(\mathbf{x}) describing the media. Extinction coefficient \sigmat(\mathbf{x}). Final inverse Hessian matrix from the BFGS solver. Scene geometry for occlusion testing. Outputs: Estimated radiance contribution I for the path. Data Structures: Path points \mathbf{x}i \in \mathbb{R}^3. Generalized geometric factor G. Transmittance T. Steps: 1. Transmittance Integration: Numerically integrate the transmittance along each ray section \Gammak between \mathbf{x}k and \mathbf{x}{k+1}. The transmittance is defined as: T(\mathbf{x}k, \mathbf{x}{k+1}) = \exp \left( - \int{tk}^{t{k+1}} \sigmat(\mathbf{x}(\tau)) \eta(\mathbf{x}(\tau)) d\tau \right) Assuming \sigmat varies slowly within a single tetrahedral cell, use a composite Simpson rule for numerical integration. 2. Occlusion Test: Trace a shadow ray from \mathbf{x}0 in the direction of \mathbf{x}1. Check for intersections with the rest of the scene or bubbles inside the panel. If an intersection occurs, the path is occluded and its contribution is zero. 3. Generalized Geometric Factor: Compute the generalized geometric factor G(\mathbf{x}1 \leftrightarrow \dots \leftrightarrow \mathbf{x}{n-1}) for the specular interfaces. This is computed using the implicit function theorem and the final inverse Hessian matrix estimation produced by the BFGS solver. 4. Regularization: Regularize G to prevent instability and high variance: \bar{G}(\mathbf{x}1 \leftrightarrow \dots \leftrightarrow \mathbf{x}{n-1}) = \max(G(\mathbf{x}1 \leftrightarrow \dots \leftrightarrow \mathbf{x}{n-1}), \epsilon) Typical values for \epsilon are between 10^{-2} and 10^{-3}. 5. Probability Estimation: Estimate the inverse probability 1/p(\bar{\mathbf{x}}k) of the BFGS solver converging to the path \bar{\mathbf{x}}k using the unbiased iterative procedure described in [21] (not provided in source). 6. Contribution Calculation: Compute the contribution function f(\bar{\mathbf{x}}k): f(\bar{\mathbf{x}}k) = We(\mathbf{x}0, \mathbf{x}1) \eta^2(\mathbf{x}n) Le(\mathbf{x}n, \mathbf{x}{n-1}) G(\mathbf{x}0, \mathbf{x}1) T(\mathbf{x}0, \mathbf{x}1) \prod{i=1}^{n-1} G(\mathbf{x}i, \mathbf{x}{i+1}) T(\mathbf{x}i, \mathbf{x}{i+1}) fc(\mathbf{x}{i-1}, \mathbf{x}i, \mathbf{x}{i+1}) Where: We is the exitance weight. \eta(\mathbf{x}n) is the refractive index at the source. Le is the emitted radiance. fc is the phase function (implied by context of scattering, though not explicitly defined in the snippet, it is part of the product term). Note: The source formula includes G(\mathbf{x}0, \mathbf{x}1) and T(\mathbf{x}0, \mathbf{x}1) in the product, but \mathbf{x}0 is the camera. The product index i runs from 1 to n-1. The term G(\mathbf{x}0, \mathbf{x}1) appears outside the product in the source formula. 7. Final Estimator: The total radiance I is estimated by summing over K samples: I \simeq \sum{k=1}^K \frac{f(\bar{\mathbf{x}}k)}{p(\bar{\mathbf{x}}k)} Parameters: \epsilon: Regularization constant for G. Typical values: 10^{-2} to 10^{-3}. Pitfalls: The computation of the generalized geometric factor G can be unstable, leading to high variance. Regularization is necessary. The initialization strategy of the BFGS solver does not guarantee finding all possible paths in regions with strong RIF variations, potentially resulting in local underestimation of transmitted lighting. Complexity: Not given in the sources. Performance: The method is used in conjunction with BFGS optimization. The text mentions 1M samples per pixel at 1024x1024 resolution for the final images, but this refers to the overall rendering pipeline, not just this estimator. Strengths: Provides an unbiased estimate of the contribution of stationary paths. Regularization helps eliminate highly contributing outliers. Limitations: Can locally underestimate the brightest parts of the transmitted caustic due to regularization. May miss paths in regions with strong RIF variations. This method is part of a pipeline for rendering old glass windows, where ancient windows were composed of several smaller fragments of glass assembled with lead. The method builds on the path formulation of the RRTE. name: Training Protocol
head: DCCVT Optimization Setup, DCCVT Training Configuration
body: The Training Protocol defines the standard optimization procedure for neural networks in differentiable volume rendering, encompassing optimizer settings, learning rate scheduling, and data augmentation strategies. It addresses the instability of training coordinate-based neural fields by providing a robust configuration for convergence, particularly when dealing with noisy real-world scan data or complex geometric priors. It sets itself apart from generic optimization loops by explicitly integrating domain-specific augmentations (such as Gaussian noise for point clouds) and specific regularization techniques (like CVT for discretization stability) into the core training loop. The protocol establishes a baseline configuration for training neural implicit representations, with specific variations for different architectural needs (e.g., pilot networks, variable views). Inputs: Input data (point clouds, voxel grids, or radiographic projections), target values (SDF, density, color), and hyperparameters (optimizer settings, batch size, epochs). Outputs: Trained neural network weights and biases. Optimizer State: Maintains first and second moment estimates for Adam/AdamW. Learning Rate Scheduler: Tracks current learning rate based on epoch/step count. Pilot Network (Optional): A small MLP used for early-stage coarse geometry estimation. 1. Initialization: Initialize the main neural network parameters. For methods like DCCVT, initialize both the main model and auxiliary structures (like MTet sites) with the same initial sites. If using a Pilot Network, initialize it with two hidden layers, each containing 64 neurons. Normalize input coordinates and target values to the range [-1, 1] to match the output range of activation functions like \sin(\cdot). Initialize weights using a standard scheme (e.g., Kaiming uniform or the protocol by Sitzmann et al. for SIREN-like networks). 2. Early Training (Pilot Phase - Optional): If a Pilot Network is employed, use it for the first N{pilot} steps (e.g., 300 steps). The pilot network functions as a standard volume rendering model to aid in finding coarse geometry, preventing convergence failure caused by feature integration of all samples in the early stage. After N{pilot} steps, discard the pilot network and switch to the main framework (e.g., VFR) for the remaining training steps. 3. Main Training Loop: For each epoch or iteration: a. Data Augmentation: Apply random scaling and translation to input data. For point cloud inputs, add Gaussian noise with standard deviation \sigma = 0.5 (assuming unit cube cells) to simulate real scan noise. For variable-view methods (e.g., X-GRM), randomly select the number of views from a set (e.g., \{6, 8, 10\}) evenly sampled from available projections. b. Forward Pass: Compute the rendered output (e.g., SDF, density, color) using the current network weights. If using structured latent codes, compute their contribution with a higher learning rate multiplier (e.g., 10\times). c. Loss Computation: Compute the loss using the same functions as the baseline method (e.g., UNDC). For DCCVT, incorporate CVT regularization to maintain discretization stability, distinct from pure Chamfer distance optimization. d. Backward Pass: Compute gradients with respect to network parameters. e. Optimization Step: Update parameters using the Adam or AdamW optimizer. Apply learning rate decay as specified (e.g., halve every 100 epochs, cosine annealing, or multistep). 4. Post-Training: Save the model weights. For MoE-INR, use 16-bit floating point for storage while training/inference uses 32-bit. Adam Optimizer Update: \theta{t+1} = \thetat - \frac{\eta \cdot \hat{m}t}{\sqrt{\hat{v}t} + \epsilon} Where \eta is the learning rate, \hat{m}t is the bias-corrected first moment, and \hat{v}t is the bias-corrected second moment. Gaussian Noise Augmentation: p{noisy} = p{clean} + \mathcal{N}(0, \sigma^2) Where \sigma = 0.5 for point cloud inputs. Optimizer: Adam or AdamW. Learning Rate (\eta): Standard: 1 \times 10^{-4} or 5 \times 10^{-4} or 0.0001. MoE-INR: 2 \times 10^{-5}. UVA: Decay from 5 \times 10^{-4} to 5 \times 10^{-6}. Beta Coefficients (\beta1, \beta2): Common: (0.9, 0.999). DCCVT: (0.8, 0.99). Batch Size: Standard: 1 (per shape). UVA: 1024. MoE-INR: 16,000. Iterations/Epochs: DCCVT: 1000 iterations. Neural Dual Contouring: 400 epochs (SDF/voxel) or 250 epochs (point cloud). UVA: 300K iterations. MoE-INR: 30 pre-training epochs + 270 training epochs. Precision: Standard: 32-bit float. X-GRM: bFloat16. Convergence Failure: In early training, feature integration of all samples can cause convergence failure. Using a pilot network for the first 300 steps mitigates this. Noisy Data: Real scan data requires heavy augmentation, including Gaussian noise (\sigma=0.5) and random transformations, to prevent overfitting to artifacts. Discretization Stability: For methods like DCCVT, omitting CVT regularization can lead to instability, especially with non-uniform site distributions. This method addresses the inefficiency of optimizing coordinate-based neural networks from random weights for each new signal by applying meta-learning to derive optimal initial weight parameters. It sets itself apart from standard training protocols by decoupling the initialization phase from the specific instance optimization, allowing the network to start closer to the solution manifold of a target signal class (e.g., faces, 3D shapes). This results in faster convergence and improved generalization when only partial observations are available. This protocol defines a specific training schedule for differentiable volume rendering that combines background augmentation with density regularization to suppress floating artifacts and stabilize convergence. It addresses the instability of immediate background augmentation and the emergence of scene-matching floaters by enforcing a strict temporal sequence: constant-color initialization, followed by augmented backgrounds, and finally density priors. It differs from standard training by explicitly decoupling the learning of general scene structure from the refinement of density bias and object compactness. This article specifies the activation functions, dropout regularization, and latent space dimensionality validation for neural networks in radiance-field optimization. It addresses stabilizing training and preventing overfitting in differentiable rendering pipelines by defining architectural hyperparameters. It builds on Training Protocol. A small neural network used during the early training stage to aid the model in finding coarse geometry, preventing convergence failure caused by feature integration of all samples. It uses two hidden layers, each with 64 neurons, and is only used in the first 300 training steps. After 300 steps, the pilot network is discarded, and the main framework (e.g., VFR) takes over for the remaining training steps (e.g., total 20K steps). Optimizes the UVA model using Adam with learning rate decay from 5 \times 10^{-4} to 5 \times 10^{-6}. Structured latent codes have a 10\times learning rate relative to the base rate. The motion field and canonical field are jointly trained for 300K iterations with a batch size of 1024. Training takes about 10 hours using two NVIDIA Tesla V100 GPUs. Optimizes the X-GRM model using AdamW with a batch size of 8 for 100 epochs. The initial learning rate is 2 \times 10^{-5}, with \beta1 = 0.9 and \beta2 = 0.999. It uses bFloat16 precision for model storage, while training uses 32-bit float. It employs variable-view learning, randomly selecting views from available projections. Pre-trains the model for 30 epochs, then trains for 270 epochs. Coordinates and target values are normalized to [-1, 1]. Uses Adam with initial learning rate 2 \times 10^{-5}, \beta1 = 0.9, \beta2 = 0.999, and a multistep scheduler for decay. Uses 32-bit float for training/inference and 16-bit for storage. Batch size is 16,000. Parameter initialization follows the protocol by Sitzmann et al.. Time Complexity: Depends on the number of iterations and batch size. For example, UVA training takes ~10 hours on two V100s for 300K iterations. Memory Complexity: Large batch sizes (MoE-INR: 16,000) require significant memory. Strengths: Robust to noisy data with appropriate augmentation. Pilot networks prevent early-stage convergence failure. CVT regularization ensures discretization stability. Limitations: Requires careful tuning of learning rate schedules and augmentation parameters. Pilot networks add complexity to the early training phase. When to Use: Use for training neural implicit representations in volume rendering, especially when dealing with noisy point clouds or requiring stable discretization. Use pilot networks for difficult initial geometry estimation. The training protocol for neural volume rendering has evolved from standard optimization techniques (Adam, learning rate decay) to more specialized configurations addressing the unique challenges of implicit representations. Early work focused on basic convergence, while later methods introduced specific regularizations (CVT), pilot networks for stability, and large-scale configurations for efficiency. The protocol is widely used in differentiable rendering pipelines for tasks like surface reconstruction, view synthesis, and 3D shape editing. Output: A set of initial weight parameters \theta0 for a fully-connected neural network. Data Structures: The network is a standard fully-connected multi-layer perceptron (MLP). Meta-Training Phase: Apply standard meta-learning algorithms to learn the initial weight parameters for fully-connected networks based on the underlying class of signals being represented. The goal is to find \theta0 such that a few gradient steps on any new signal from the class yield a good approximation. 2. Instance Optimization Phase: For a new target signal (e.g., a specific 3D shape or image), initialize the network weights with the learned \theta0. Perform standard gradient descent (or Adam) to optimize the network parameters \theta to fit the new signal's observations. Formulas: Not given in the sources. Parameters: Not given in the sources. name: SDF Initialization via Overfitting
head: Inverted Sphere Pre-training, Neural Field Pre-training via Overfitting
body: This method initializes a Signed Distance Field (SDF) representation by overfitting a neural network to a target geometric shape (typically an inverted sphere) before commencing the primary scene reconstruction optimization. It addresses the challenge of initializing neural fields that do not accept position coordinates as direct inputs to the MLP, where hardcoding weights is not feasible. It is distinguished from alternatives like NeuS-facto and Neuralangelo, which hardcode the inverted sphere directly into MLP weights by leveraging position inputs, by requiring a dedicated pre-training phase to embed the initialization. Inputs: Randomly initialized model weights W0. Target SDF shape definition (e.g., inverted sphere). Pre-training hyperparameters: number of epochs E{init}. Outputs: Optimized weights W{init} that encode the target SDF shape. Data Structures: The neural network architecture (e.g., RING-NeRF). Loss function measuring the difference between the network's output and the target SDF values. Steps: 1. Initialize the model weights randomly. 2. Define the target SDF function S{target}(\mathbf{x}) corresponding to the desired initialization shape (e.g., an inverted sphere). 3. Perform optimization to minimize the loss between the network output S{net}(\mathbf{x}) and S{target}(\mathbf{x}) for E{init} epochs. 4. Use the resulting weights W{init} as the starting point for the "true" training on the actual scene data. Parameters: Pre-training epochs: 1000. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def initializesdfviaoverfitting(network, targetsdffunction, epochs=1000): """ Initializes network weights by overfitting to a target SDF shape. Args: network: The neural network to initialize (e.g., RING-NeRF). targetsdffunction: A function S(x) returning the target SDF value for point x. epochs: Number of pre-training epochs (default 1000). Returns: network: The network with initialized weights. """ # Step 1: Initialize weights randomly network.randominitialize() # Step 2 & 3: Overfit to the target initialization scheme # The target scheme is typically an inverted sphere for epoch in range(epochs): # Sample points x from the domain of interest points = samplepoints() # Compute target SDF values targets = targetsdffunction(points) # Forward pass to get current network predictions predictions = network(points) # Compute loss (e.g., MSE) between predictions and targets loss = meansquarederror(predictions, targets) # Backpropagate and update weights network.updateweights(loss) # Step 4: Return network ready for true scene training return network Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Architecture Dependency: This method is specifically required for architectures like RING-NeRF that do not input position directly to the MLP, making weight hardcoding impossible. Failure without Initialization: Training without this initialization can lead to catastrophic failure or significantly noisier results (lower PSNR) compared to initialized counterparts. It leverages the Hotspot architecture to create a precise geometric prior before beginning the main scene reconstruction optimization. name: SDF Initialization via Coarse-to-Fine Strategy
head: Coarse SDF Initialization, SDF State Initialization Pitfall, Unconverged SDF Initialization
body: This method initializes the Signed Distance Field (SDF) using a coarser, unconverged state rather than a fully converged one to prevent the optimization process from trapping in local minima. While a fully converged SDF provides a precise geometric prior, it can lead to catastrophic failure in complex scenes by restricting the optimization landscape. This approach builds on SDF Initialization with Hotspot by explicitly leveraging the regularization benefits of an incomplete initialization. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A neural field model (e.g., MLP) initialized with SDF values derived from a coarse or partially trained state. Output: A refined SDF field that avoids local minima traps associated with over-regularized initial states. Data Structures: The SDF field is represented as a continuous function f(\mathbf{x}) mapping 3D coordinates to signed distances. The "coarse" state implies that the network weights have not been optimized to minimize the SDF loss to convergence, leaving the field less constrained. Steps: 1. Initialize SDF State: Instead of training the SDF component until convergence (which yields a "hotspot" or highly refined surface), halt the initial training phase early. This results in an "unconverged" SDF. 2. Begin Optimization Loop: Start the main differentiable volume rendering optimization loop using this unconverged SDF as the prior. 3. Regularization Effect: The unconverged state acts as a regularizer. Because the initial surface is not perfectly fitted to the training data, the optimization has more freedom to explore the solution space, avoiding the local minima that a fully converged SDF would enforce. Pitfalls: Catastrophic Failure: Using a fully converged SDF initialization can trap the optimizer in a local minimum, leading to significant reconstruction errors (e.g., Mesh ID 252119 in). Precision: The "coarseness" must be balanced; if too coarse, the initialization may be too noisy, but if too fine, it risks the aforementioned local minima trap. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def initializesdfcoarsetofine(model, trainingdata, earlystopthreshold): """ Initializes the SDF model using a coarse, unconverged state. Args: model: Neural network model containing SDF and density components. trainingdata: Dataset of rays and target images. earlystopthreshold: Loss or epoch count to stop initial SDF training. Returns: model: Model with unconverged SDF weights. """ # Step 1: Initial coarse training # Train the SDF component only, but stop early to avoid convergence for epoch in range(earlystopthreshold): loss = computesdfloss(model, trainingdata) updateweights(model, loss) if loss < earlystopthreshold: # Or check epoch count break # The model now holds an "unconverged" SDF state # This state is less regularized and avoids local minima traps return model def mainoptimizationloop(model, trainingdata): """ Continues optimization from the coarse initialization. """ for epoch in range(totalepochs): # Standard differentiable volume rendering loss loss = computerenderingloss(model, trainingdata) updateweights(model, loss) A training strategy that progressively transitions the scene representation from pure volumetric density to SDF to handle limited image overlap and complex urban scenes, avoiding the need for full scene observability required by bounded sphere initialization. Unlike StreetSurf, which initializes SDF based on road-surface, this method (used in ViiNeuS) transitions from density to SDF, making it better suited for driving scenes with linear trajectories and reduced overlap. The process involves three stages: 1. Volumetric Stage: All samples along the ray express volumetric densities (\alphai = \alpha^{iv}), leveraging simpler geometric understanding to accelerate density estimator convergence. 2. Hybrid Stage: Samples are split between volumetric alpha (\alpha^{iv}) and SDF-based alpha (\alpha^{if}). A probability-based association assigns \alpha^{if} to samples with the highest predicted density, limiting the range of predicted values and facilitating SDF learning by sampling points close to the surface. 3. Surface Stage: All samples use \alpha^{if} (SDF-based) as the representation fully transitions to surface. Strengths: Prevents catastrophic failure in complex scenes by avoiding local minima traps associated with fully converged SDFs. Provides better regularization for the optimization loop. Limitations: Requires careful tuning of the "coarseness" or early stopping point. If the initialization is too far from the true surface, convergence may be slower or unstable. Performance: Results in significantly improved surface discretization compared to converged initializations in near-sampling and upsampling settings. This method addresses the "SDF State Initialization Pitfall" identified in differentiable volume rendering research. It was highlighted in the context of DCCVT (Differentiable Clipped Centroidal Voronoi Tessellation), where fully converged SDFs were found to cause catastrophic failures in specific mesh reconstructions (e.g., Mesh ID 252119 and 398259). The approach contrasts with progressive initialization methods like ViiNeuS, which handle limited overlap by transitioning from density to SDF, whereas this method focuses on the state of the SDF itself during the initialization phase of a standard optimization loop.
