head: Hardware-in-the-loop Training
body: This method trains a data-driven surrogate model using experimentally captured phase-to-intensity data to predict light propagation from a Spatial Light Modulator (SLM) to multiple target planes. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A dataset of phase patterns \Phi (2D or 3D) and their corresponding captured intensity images I at eight specific propagation distances. Output: A trained neural network model M\theta that predicts intensity I{pred} given an input phase \Phi. Data Structures: Phase Patterns: Stored as 2D arrays representing phase values. Intensity Images: Captured by the camera at the target planes. Region of Interest (ROI): The effective usable area is defined as 880 \times 1600 pixels, cropped from the full 1920 \times 1080 resolution due to laser uniformity and modulator efficiency. Steps: 1. Dataset Construction: Collect 5860 phase patterns. These include 2D phases generated via stochastic gradient descent, higher-order gradient descent, and double-phase amplitude encoding, as well as true 3D phases derived from the Flying Planes mesh-wave field-hologram dataset. 2. Data Capture: For each phase pattern, record the resulting intensity at eight target planes located at distances d \in \{10.00, 10.07, 10.14, 10.21, 10.28, 10.35, 10.42, 10.49\} cm from the SLM. 3. Preprocessing: To mitigate anti-aliasing, magnify the wave field by a factor of two in both dimensions and apply a fill factor of 0.93. Perform grid interpolation to handle spatial transformations. 4. Optimization Loop: Train the model on a single NVIDIA RTX 4090 GPU with a batch size of one for twenty epochs, utilizing the Adam optimizer with a learning rate of 0.0005. Formulas: The specific mathematical formulation of the surrogate network is not given in the sources. Parameters: Optimizer: Adam. Learning Rate: \eta = 0.0005. Batch Size: B = 1. Epochs: E = 20. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Anti-aliasing: Addressed by 2× magnification and a 0.93 fill factor. Boundary/ROI: The usable area is restricted to 880 \times 1600 pixels due to laser uniformity and modulator efficiency limits. Pseudocode: Unverified code. name: Camera-Calibrated Learned Wave Propagation Model
head: Camera-Calibrated Model, Learned Forward Model
body: The Camera-Calibrated Learned Wave Propagation Model is a data-driven surrogate for numerical propagation operators (such as the Angular Spectrum Method) used within differentiable holographic optimization loops. It solves the problem of model mismatch between idealized physics simulations and real-world optical hardware, specifically accounting for spatial light modulator (SLM) non-linearities, optical aberrations, stray light, and limited diffraction efficiency. Unlike analytical models that assume perfect free-space propagation, this learned model maps input phase patterns directly to captured multi-plane intensity images, providing a more accurate gradient signal for phase-aware gradient descent (PAGD). The method replaces the analytical forward propagation step in the optimization loop with a neural network trained to predict the intensity distribution at multiple depth planes given an input phase pattern. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A phase-only hologram (or phase pattern) displayed on the SLM. Output: Predicted intensity images at 8 target depth planes. Data Structures: The model architecture details are not provided in the primary source text, which refers to supplementary materials for specific network layers and hyperparameters. The training data consists of pairs: Phase: Phase-only holograms generated from 2D and 3D targets. Target: Multi-plane intensity images captured from a physical prototype display. Training Procedure: 1. Dataset Acquisition: Use the "Flying Planes" dataset, which contains 1,000 randomly generated 3D scenes in OBJ format. These scenes include corresponding complex-valued wave fields, RGB-Depth images, and phase-only holograms generated via various encoders (DPAC, SGD, PAGD with ASM). The 3D primitives are sampled with random position, rotation, and scale from the DIV2K dataset textures. 2. Physical Data Collection: Display numerous phase patterns (derived from 2D and 3D targets in the dataset) on a prototype SLM. Capture the resulting light field at 8 distinct target planes using a camera. 3. Model Adaptation: Adapt the learned wave propagation model architecture from Choi et al.. Crucially, introduce an extra low-pass filter within the model to suppress high-frequency phase noise. 4. Loss Minimization: Train the model using the phase and multi-plane image pairs. The objective is to minimize the discrepancy between the model's predicted intensities and the physically captured intensities. The loss function compares the scaled reconstructed field ur with the target field ut. Parameters: Target Planes: 8 planes. Dataset Size: 1,000 scenes. Low-pass Filter: Applied to suppress high-frequency phase noise. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: High-Frequency Noise: Without the extra low-pass filter, high-frequency phase noise may degrade the model's accuracy. Hardware Specificity: The model is calibrated to a specific prototype optical system; it does not generalize to different hardware configurations without retraining. Angular Spectrum Method (ASM) is a free-space propagation operator that models parallel wave propagation between planes without paraxial approximations. It treats the field as a superposition of plane waves, making it exact for any distance and angle under sampling constraints. It is chosen when analytical accuracy is required without hardware calibration, unlike the learned model which captures real-world optical imperfections. Angular Spectrum Method (ASM) Accuracy: The learned model provides a Peak Signal-to-Noise Ratio (PSNR) improvement of 2 dB compared to the analytical Angular Spectrum Method (ASM) baseline. Computational Cost: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Captures real-world imperfections (aberrations, SLM non-linearities, stray light) that numerical models like ASM struggle to replicate. Limitations: Requires physical data collection and training; does not provide a differentiable physics-based gradient in the traditional sense but rather a learned gradient. The method originates from research into full 3D holographic displays, specifically addressing the limitations of numerical propagation operators in differentiable holography. It builds on the work of Choi et al.. The approach is part of a broader effort to mesh-represent and learning-empower hologram synthesis for full 3D holographic displays. name: Angular Spectrum Method (ASM)
head: Free-space propagation operator
body: The Angular Spectrum Method (ASM) is a free-space propagation operator used to model the parallel propagation of a wave field from one plane to another without approximations. It solves the problem of accurately reconstructing or propagating a complex optical field U0(x0, y0) to a target plane at distance z by treating the field as a superposition of plane waves. Unlike the Fresnel Method, which relies on paraxial approximations, ASM calculates the wavefield by propagating plane waves in different directions, making it exact for any propagation distance and angle, provided the sampling conditions are met. Inputs and Outputs: Input: The complex optical field U0(x0, y0) at the source plane (z=0), the propagation distance z, and the wavelength \lambda. Output: The reconstructed complex wavefield Ur(x, y) at the target plane (z). Data Structures: The input field is represented as a 2D grid of complex numbers. The angular spectrum is represented as a 2D grid of complex numbers in the frequency domain (kx, ky). The transfer function is a 2D grid of complex numbers with the same dimensions as the angular spectrum. Parameters: \lambda: Wavelength of the light. k = \frac{2\pi}{\lambda}: Wavenumber. z: Propagation distance. \Delta x, \Delta y: Spatial sampling intervals in the source plane. \Delta kx, \Delta ky: Frequency sampling intervals, where \Delta kx = \frac{2\pi}{Nx \Delta x} and \Delta ky = \frac{2\pi}{Ny \Delta y} for an Nx \times Ny grid. Steps: 1. Fourier Transform: Compute the 2D Fourier Transform of the input field U0(x0, y0) to obtain the Angular Spectrum A0(kx, ky). A0(kx, ky) = \mathcal{F} \{ U0(x0, y0) \} Note: The exact definition involves a normalization factor depending on the Fourier Transform convention. The source defines the inverse transform with a factor of \frac{1}{2\pi}, implying the forward transform does not include it, or uses a symmetric convention. We follow the standard DFT implementation where the forward transform sums without normalization and the inverse divides by N or uses \frac{1}{2\pi} factors as per the specific mathematical definition. The source equation (8) shows the continuous integral with \frac{1}{2\pi}, but equation (11) uses operator notation \mathcal{F} and \mathcal{F}^{-1}. In discrete implementation, standard FFT libraries are used. 2. Apply Transfer Function: Multiply the Angular Spectrum A0(kx, ky) by the propagation phase factor (transfer function) H(kx, ky; z). H(kx, ky; z) = \exp \left( j kz z \right) where kz = \sqrt{k^2 - kx^2 - ky^2} This step assumes k^2 \ge kx^2 + ky^2. If kx^2 + ky^2 > k^2, the term under the square root is negative, resulting in an evanescent wave which decays exponentially. In many practical implementations for propagating fields, these components are zeroed out or handled via complex kz. The source states the assumption k^2 \ge kx^2 + ky^2. 3. Inverse Fourier Transform: Compute the 2D Inverse Fourier Transform of the product to obtain the reconstructed wavefield Ur(x, y). Ur(x, y) = \mathcal{F}^{-1} \left\{ A0(kx, ky) \exp \left( j \sqrt{k^2 - kx^2 - ky^2} z \right) \right\} Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import numpy as np def angularspectrummethod(U0, z, wavelength, dx, dy): """ Propagates a complex optical field U0 using the Angular Spectrum Method. Args: U0: 2D numpy array (complex128) representing the input field. z: float, propagation distance. wavelength: float, wavelength of light. dx: float, spatial sampling interval in x. dy: float, spatial sampling interval in y. Returns: Ur: 2D numpy array (complex128) representing the propagated field. """ Ny, Nx = U0.shape k = 2 np.pi / wavelength # Create frequency grid # FFT shift centers zero frequency at the center of the array kx = np.fft.fftfreq(Nx, d=dx) 2 np.pi ky = np.fft.fftfreq(Ny, d=dy) 2 np.pi # Create 2D meshgrid KX, KY = np.meshgrid(kx, ky) # Calculate kz # kz = sqrt(k^2 - kx^2 - ky^2) # If kx^2 + ky^2 > k^2, kz becomes imaginary (evanescent waves) # For standard propagation, we often set these to 0 or handle them. # The source assumes k^2 >= kx^2 + ky^2. kzsq = k2 - KX2 - KY2 # Handle evanescent waves: if kzsq < 0, kz is imaginary. # exp(j kz z) will decay. # We use complex sqrt to handle negative arguments correctly. kz = np.sqrt(kzsq) # Transfer function H = np.exp(1j kz z) # Step 1: Fourier Transform A0 = np.fft.fft2(U0) # Step 2: Multiply by transfer function Apropagated = A0 H # Step 3: Inverse Fourier Transform Ur = np.fft.ifft2(Apropagated) return Ur Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Evanescent Waves: If kx^2 + ky^2 > k^2, kz is imaginary. The source assumes k^2 \ge kx^2 + ky^2. In practice, high-frequency components beyond the cutoff must be handled, typically by zeroing them or allowing exponential decay. Sampling: The spatial sampling \Delta x, \Delta y must satisfy the Nyquist criterion for the highest spatial frequency present in the field to avoid aliasing. The frequency grid must cover the relevant bandwidth. Computational Cost: ASM requires two 2D Fourier Transforms, making it more computationally intensive than the Fresnel Method. A differentiable computational model that simulates the physical propagation of light from a Spatial Light Modulator (SLM) to a camera sensor, incorporating learnable parameters to account for system-specific imperfections such as polarization, SLM curvature, beam profiles, higher diffraction orders, crosstalk, and Lookup Table (LUT) non-linearity. It sets itself apart from standard Angular Spectrum Method (ASM) implementations by explicitly modeling the superposition of zero and first-order diffraction patterns through a neural network (U-Net) and calibrating these parameters against experimental data, thereby compensating for unmodeled physical effects in compact optical setups. HOASM is a differentiable wave propagation model that separates the propagation of zero-order and first-order diffraction terms to handle them differently before feeding them into a neural network. It builds on Angular Spectrum Method (ASM) by introducing a specific preprocessing step for the first-order term involving grid patterning and sinc weighting, distinguishing it from standard ASM which propagates all orders together. Time Complexity: O(N \log N) due to the use of Fast Fourier Transforms (FFT), where N is the number of pixels in the 2D grid. Memory Complexity: O(N) for storing the input field, angular spectrum, and transfer function. Measured Performance: The source notes that ASM is more computationally intensive than the Fresnel Method because it requires two Fourier Transforms and does not use approximations that might allow for faster, single-transform methods. Strengths: Exact solution for free-space propagation; no paraxial approximation; works for large angles and short distances. Limitations: Computationally more expensive than Fresnel or Fresnel-Kirchhoff approximations; sensitive to sampling rates; requires handling of evanescent waves. When to use: When high accuracy is required, especially for near-field propagation or large angles where Fresnel approximations fail. When not to use: When computational speed is critical and the paraxial approximation is valid (use Fresnel Method instead). The Angular Spectrum Method is a fundamental technique in wave optics and digital holography. It is based on the principle that any optical field can be decomposed into a sum of plane waves (its angular spectrum). The method was developed as an exact solution to the Helmholtz equation for free-space propagation. It is widely used in computer-generated holography (CGH) and digital holographic reconstruction. The method is cited in recent advances in processing and rendering algorithms for CGH and in mesh-represented hologram synthesis. name: Camera-Calibrated Differentiable Holographic Model
head: Camera-Calibrated Differentiable Model for Holography, Camera-calibrated model, Differentiable holographic model
body: A differentiable computational model that simulates the physical propagation of light from a Spatial Light Modulator (SLM) to a camera sensor, incorporating learnable parameters to account for system-specific imperfections such as polarization, SLM curvature, beam profiles, higher diffraction orders, crosstalk, and Lookup Table (LUT) non-linearity. It sets itself apart from standard Angular Spectrum Method (ASM) implementations by explicitly modeling the superposition of zero and first-order diffraction patterns through a neural network (U-Net) and calibrating these parameters against experimental data, thereby compensating for unmodeled physical effects in compact optical setups. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: SLM digital input pattern s (scalar per pixel), propagation distance z, wavelength \lambda. Outputs: Predicted image intensity Iz at the sensor plane. Data Structures: SLM Pattern s: 2D array of integers (e.g., 0-255) representing digital drive values. Diffraction Orders G0, G1: Complex-valued 2D arrays representing the zero-order and first-order diffraction patterns generated by the SLM. Propagated Fields f{ASM}: Complex-valued 2D arrays resulting from ASM propagation. U-Net: A neural network architecture (separate instance for each color channel) taking stacked complex fields as input and outputting real-valued intensity. Learnable Parameters: a1, a2: Scalars (per color channel) for the linear LUT model. k{xt}: 5x5 convolution kernel (per color channel) for crosstalk. M{color}: 3x3 matrix for camera color balance. Formulas: 1. SLM Phase with Crosstalk and LUT: The phase \phi\lambda(s) off the SLM for wavelength \lambda given input s is modeled as: \phi\lambda(s) = k{xt} (a1 \cdot s + a2) where denotes convolution, a1, a2 are learnable linear LUT parameters, and k{xt} is a learned 5x5 convolution kernel representing field fringing (crosstalk). 2. Diffraction Pattern Generation: The SLM phase is converted into complex diffraction patterns G0 (zero-order) and G1 (first-order). The specific mapping from phase to G0, G1 relies on the physics of the SLM modulation, typically involving Fourier components of the phase profile. 3. Angular Spectrum Propagation: Each diffraction order is propagated independently to distance z using the Angular Spectrum Method (ASM), building on Angular Spectrum Method (ASM): f{ASM}(G, z) = \mathcal{F}^{-1} \{ G \cdot H{ASM}(z) \} where G is the diffraction order pattern (G0 or G1), H{ASM}(z) is the ASM transfer kernel, and \mathcal{F}^{-1} is the inverse Fourier transform. 4. Intensity Prediction via U-Net: The propagated zero-order field f{ASM}(G0, z) and first-order field f{ASM}(G1, z) are stacked and passed through a U-Net to predict the final image intensity: Iz = \text{Unet}(f{ASM}(G0, z), f{ASM}(G1, z)) A separate U-Net is learned for each color channel to handle color-specific unmodeled system aspects. Numbered Steps: 1. Calibration Phase (Parameter Learning): 1. Pre-calculate 882 SLM patterns from a dataset of images using the standard ASM propagation model. 2. Capture these patterns using the experimental camera at 10 mm increments from z=90 mm to z=120 mm. 3. Debayer the camera data and apply an affine transform to align the image coordinates with the SLM grid. 4. Initialize learnable parameters: a1, a2 (LUT), k{xt} (crosstalk kernel), and M{color} (3x3 color calibration matrix). 5. Perform gradient descent using PyTorch to minimize the L1 loss between the model output Iz and the captured camera data. 6. This method avoids physical apertures (4f systems) by modeling the 0th and 1st orders explicitly and using a U-Net to compensate for residual unmodeled effects. SLM Crosstalk: LCoS SLMs exhibit field fringing due to elastic forces in the LC layer. This is modeled as a convolution (k{xt}) on the phase. Failure to model this leads to blurred phase and reduced hologram quality. LUT Validity: The SLM pattern s must be constrained to the range where the LUT is valid (e.g., 0-255). Values outside this range must be wrapped after every optimization step. Color Deviation: Simultaneous RGB holography is an overdetermined problem (3x more output pixels than SLM degrees of freedom). This can lead to color deviations and desaturation if not addressed by the perceptual loss and calibrated model. Time Complexity: Hologram generation optimization takes approximately 2 minutes per 2D hologram on an Nvidia A6000 GPU. 3D hologram computation time scales proportionally to the number of depth planes. Memory Complexity: Requires memory for the SLM pattern, propagated fields, and the U-Net parameters. The U-Net is separate for each color channel. Strengths: Enables simultaneous color computer-generated holography in a compact setup without bulky optics or filters, suitable for VR/AR displays. Reduces depth replicas and high-frequency out-of-focus light by using extended phase range SLMs and modeling higher orders. Limitations: Calibration is time-consuming (2-3 days on A6000). The method relies on the accuracy of the U-Net to capture unmodeled system imperfections, which may not generalize perfectly to different hardware without re-calibration. When to Use: When generating simultaneous color holograms in a compact optical setup where physical filtering of higher diffraction orders is impractical. When Not to Use: When high coherence lasers are required (this method uses SLEDs to reduce speckle) or when a 4f system is already present to filter diffraction orders. The method was developed to address the mismatch between simulated holograms and experimental captures in simultaneous color computer-generated holography. It builds on the Angular Spectrum Method (ASM) and incorporates insights from Gopakumar et al. [2021] regarding higher-order angular spectrum models. The use of SLEDs (Superluminescent Light Emitting Diodes) to reduce speckle is based on work by Deng and Chu [2017]. The specific implementation details, including the U-Net architecture and calibration procedure, are described in the source paper. name: Modified High Order Angular Spectrum Method (HOASM)
body: HOASM is a differentiable wave propagation model that separates the propagation of zero-order and first-order diffraction terms to handle them differently before feeding them into a neural network. It builds on Angular Spectrum Method (ASM) by introducing a specific preprocessing step for the first-order term involving grid patterning and sinc weighting, distinguishing it from standard ASM which propagates all orders together. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Complex field U(x,y) at the source plane (e.g., SLM), propagation distance z, wavelength \lambda, and SLM parameters (pixel size p, resolution). Output: Single-channel intensity image I(x,y) at the sensor plane. Data Structures: Complex Field: 2D array of complex numbers representing the wavefront. U-Net Input: Stacked real and imaginary parts of the propagated zero-order and first-order fields. U-Net Architecture: Downsampling path: 4 layers. Channels: Start with 4 input channels. First layer maps to 32 channels. Each subsequent downsampling layer doubles the channel count (32 \to 64 \to 128 \to 256). Upsampling path: 4 layers. Output: Single channel (intensity). Steps: 1. Zero-Order Propagation: Propagate the zero-order component of the complex field using the standard Angular Spectrum Method (ASM). 2. First-Order Preparation: a. Compute the Fourier transform of the complex field. b. Zero-pad the Fourier transform. c. Pattern the zero-padded Fourier transform into a 3 \times 3 grid. d. Zero out the center Fourier transform of this grid. e. Weight the Fourier representation of the first-order term with a sinc function. 3. First-Order Propagation: Propagate the weighted first-order term to the sensor plane using ASM. 4. Post-Processing: Down-sample and crop the resulting first-order field. 5. Stacking: Split the complex fields of both the zero-order and first-order into their real and imaginary parts. Stack these four components (Real0, Imag0, Real1, Imag1) to form the input tensor for the neural network. 6. Neural Network Inference: Feed the stacked tensor into a U-Net to produce a single-channel output representing the intensity of the propagated wavefront. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def hoasmpropagate(complexfield, z, wavelength, pixelsize, slmresolution): """ Propagates a complex field using the Modified High Order Angular Spectrum Method. Args: complexfield: 2D array of complex numbers (SLM pattern). z: Propagation distance. wavelength: Wavelength of light. pixelsize: Size of SLM pixels. slmresolution: Tuple (width, height) of SLM resolution. Returns: intensity: 2D array of intensity values. """ # Step 1: Separate zero-order and first-order components # Note: The source does not specify the exact mathematical separation formula. # Assuming standard decomposition or that the input field is already separated. # For the purpose of this implementation, we assume 'complexfield' contains the # relevant components or that the separation is implicit in the grid patterning step. # Step 2: Propagate Zero-Order using ASM zeroorderpropagated = asmpropagate(complexfield, z, wavelength, pixelsize) # Step 3: Prepare and Propagate First-Order # Compute Fourier Transform fourierfield = fft2(complexfield) # Zero-pad the Fourier transform # Padding size is not explicitly defined in sources. # Assuming padding to a size suitable for 3x3 grid patterning. paddedfourier = zeropad(fourierfield, targetshape=getpaddedshape(fourierfield)) # Pattern into 3x3 grid gridfield = patternintogrid(paddedfourier, gridsize=3) # Zero out the center Fourier transform of the grid centeridx = gridsize // 2 gridfield[centeridx, centeridx] = 0 # Weight with sinc function # The exact sinc function parameters (e.g., width) are not given. # Assuming a standard sinc function centered at the grid location. sincweight = sincfunction(gridfield.shape) weightedfirstorder = gridfield sincweight # Propagate weighted first-order using ASM firstorderpropagated = asmpropagate(weightedfirstorder, z, wavelength, pixelsize) # Step 4: Down-sample and crop the first-order field firstorderprocessed = downsampleandcrop(firstorderpropagated) # Step 5: Split and Stack # Split zero-order into real and imaginary parts zeroreal = real(zeroorderpropagated) zeroimag = imag(zeroorderpropagated) # Split first-order into real and imaginary parts firstreal = real(firstorderprocessed) firstimag = imag(firstorderprocessed) # Stack: [Real0, Imag0, Real1, Imag1] inputtensor = stack([zeroreal, zeroimag, firstreal, firstimag], axis=-1) # Step 6: U-Net Inference intensity = unetforward(inputtensor) return intensity def asmpropagate(field, z, wavelength, pixelsize): """ Standard Angular Spectrum Method propagation. """ # Compute spatial frequencies # Standard ASM implementation details (frequency grid calculation) are assumed. fx, fy = computefrequencygrid(field.shape, pixelsize) # Compute transfer function # H(fx, fy) = exp(i 2 pi z sqrt(1/lambda^2 - fx^2 - fy^2)) # Handling evanescent waves (imaginary argument) is standard ASM practice. transferfunction = computeasmtransferfunction(fx, fy, z, wavelength) # Propagate fieldfft = fft2(field) propagatedfft = fieldfft transferfunction propagatedfield = ifft2(propagatedfft) return propagatedfield def unetforward(inputtensor): """ U-Net forward pass. Architecture: 4 downsampling layers, 4 upsampling layers. Channels: 4 -> 32 -> 64 -> 128 -> 256 ->... -> 1 """ # Standard U-Net implementation details (convolutions, pooling, skip connections) are assumed. # The source specifies the channel progression and layer counts. model = buildunet(inputchannels=4, outputchannels=1) return model(inputtensor) Parameters: SLM Resolution: 1920 x 1080 pixels. SLM Pixel Size: 8 µm x 8 µm. Propagation Distance: 100 mm. SLM Phase Range: Red: 2.4\pi. Green: 5.9\pi. Blue: 7.4\pi. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Sinc Weighting: The exact parameters of the sinc function used to weight the first-order term are not specified in the sources. Implementers must determine appropriate width/normalization. Grid Patterning: The method of patterning the zero-padded Fourier transform into a 3 \times 3 grid is described but not mathematically detailed. Zero-Order Separation: The method for separating the zero-order and first-order terms from the initial complex field is not explicitly defined. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Performance: The method is designed for differentiable rendering in virtual environments, specifically for simultaneous color holography. Strengths: Allows for separate handling of diffraction orders, potentially improving accuracy or training stability in neural holography. Limitations: Requires a neural network (U-Net) for final intensity prediction, adding computational overhead compared to pure analytical ASM. HOASM is implemented as a modified version of the High Order Angular Spectrum Method (HOASM) as described by Gopakumar et al. [2021]. It was developed for use in simultaneous color computer-generated holography, specifically within the context of the "Simultaneous Color Holography" project. The method is used to simulate wave propagation from a Spatial Light Modulator (SLM) to a sensor plane, incorporating experimental calibration for specific SLM hardware (Holoeye Pluto-2.1-Vis-016). name: Gerchberg-Saxton Algorithm
head: Iterative Phase Optimization, iterative phase retrieval
body:
The Gerchberg-Saxton algorithm is an iterative optimization method used to compute phase-only holograms by determining object point phase values that cause interference resulting in constant amplitude across the hologram plane. It solves the problem of phase-only display constraints where the eye does not detect image phase, allowing the algorithm to treat object phases as free variables to satisfy amplitude constraints on the display. It is distinguished from its parent, Phase-Aware Gradient Descent (PAGD), by its specific use of back-and-forth propagation with hard amplitude constraints rather than gradient-based loss minimization, and from its sibling, Camera-Calibrated Wave Propagation Model Training, by being a direct analytical iterative solver rather than a learned model. Inputs: Target image intensity distribution (implicitly defining the required amplitude on the hologram plane). Hologram plane resolution and geometry. Propagation model (typically Fresnel or Fraunhofer diffraction, implemented via Fourier transforms). Outputs: Phase-only hologram H (complex field with unit amplitude and optimized phase). Data Structures: Complex field array Uo representing the object plane. Complex field array Uh representing the hologram plane. Phase array \phio for object points. Steps: 1. Initialization: Initialize the complex field on the hologram plane Uh^{(0)} with the target amplitude A{target} and a random or zero phase distribution. Alternatively, initialize the object plane field and propagate to the hologram plane. 2. Forward Propagation: Propagate the current hologram plane field Uh^{(k)} to the object plane Uo^{(k)} using the appropriate diffraction integral (e.g., Fourier transform for far-field). 3. Object Plane Constraint: Replace the amplitude of the object plane field Uo^{(k)} with the target object amplitude (or keep it as is if the target is on the hologram plane, depending on the specific formulation; the standard GS for holograms often enforces amplitude on the hologram plane directly). Note: The source describes propagating back and forth between object and hologram planes while enforcing amplitude constraints at each plane. In the context of phase-only holograms for displays, the constraint is typically that the hologram plane amplitude must be constant (uniform) because the SLM can only modulate phase. 4. Hologram Plane Constraint: Propagate the object plane field Uo^{(k)} back to the hologram plane Uh^{(k+1)}. Enforce the amplitude constraint on Uh^{(k+1)} by setting its amplitude to the required constant value (e.g., 1.0) while preserving its calculated phase. 5. Iteration: Repeat steps 2-4 for N iterations. 6. Final Output: The final phase distribution of the hologram plane field is extracted as the hologram H = \arg(Uh^{(N)}). Formulas: Let Uh be the complex field on the hologram plane and Uo be the complex field on the object plane. Propagation from hologram to object: Uo = \mathcal{P}(Uh) Propagation from object to hologram: Uh' = \mathcal{P}^{-1}(Uo) Amplitude constraint enforcement on the hologram plane: Uh^{(k+1)} = A{target} \cdot \exp(i \cdot \arg(Uh')) Where A{target} is the constant required amplitude (often 1 for phase-only). Parameters: Number of iterations: Typically 10-100. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Speckle: Iteratively optimized holograms tend to include undesirable high-frequency noise or speckle. Computational Expense: The method is computationally expensive due to the need for many iterations. Local Minima: The algorithm may converge to local minima, resulting in suboptimal holograms. Modern variations add error compensation and define "do not care" regions to increase performance. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def gerchbergsaxton(targetamplitudehologram, numiterations, propagationfunc, inversepropagationfunc): """ Computes a phase-only hologram using the Gerchberg-Saxton algorithm. Args: targetamplitudehologram: 2D array of the desired amplitude on the hologram plane. numiterations: Number of GS iterations. propagationfunc: Function to propagate field from hologram to object plane. inversepropagationfunc: Function to propagate field from object to hologram plane. Returns: phasehologram: 2D array of the computed phase-only hologram. """ # Initialize hologram plane field with target amplitude and random phase # Random phase initialization is standard to break symmetry; # source implies starting with some field and propagating. hologramfield = targetamplitudehologram np.exp(1j np.random.uniform(0, 2 np.pi, targetamplitudehologram.shape)) for k in range(numiterations): # Forward propagation: Hologram -> Object objectfield = propagationfunc(hologramfield) # The source mentions enforcing amplitude constraints at each plane. # In standard hologram generation, the object plane constraint is often the target image intensity. # However, the specific quote says "find values phio that cause the object points to interfere # such that the required amplitude values of H are constant". This implies the constraint is on H. # If there is a constraint on the object plane (target image), it would be applied here. # Since the source emphasizes constant amplitude on H, we assume the object plane constraint # is either the target image amplitude or simply preserving the phase from the previous step # if no object constraint is defined. # Standard GS for holograms often uses: Object Amplitude = Target Image Amplitude. # Let's assume a target object amplitude is available or derived. # If not specified, we preserve the phase from the forward pass. # To be implementable, we assume a target object amplitude exists or is the magnitude of the current field. # Given the source text focuses on constant amplitude on H, we will apply the H constraint. # If an object constraint exists, it would be: objectfield = targetobjectamplitude exp(1j angle(objectfield)) # Backward propagation: Object -> Hologram hologramfieldnew = inversepropagationfunc(objectfield) # Enforce amplitude constraint on Hologram plane # The goal is constant amplitude on H hologramfield = targetamplitudehologram np.exp(1j np.angle(hologramfieldnew)) # Extract phase phasehologram = np.angle(hologramfield) return phasehologram An iterative algorithm to design Computer-Generated Holograms (CGHs) by finding a phase distribution on the hologram plane that approximates a target focal pattern, used to generate multiple simultaneous focal points for voxel positioning. It differs from the base Gerchberg-Saxton algorithm by introducing a weighting function w that is iteratively updated to control convergence and improve uniformity among reconstructed focal points. It is chosen for its high uniformity and simplicity based on iterative FFT operations. Steps: 1. Initialize amplitude ah(x,y) as uniform values on the hologram plane. 2. Form initial phase \phih by inverse Fourier transform of the complex amplitude constructed with the target pattern. 3. In iteration step k, constrain the reconstructed plane amplitude to the desired distribution at(
ux, 
uy) using the weighting function w^{(k+1)}: ur^{(k+1)}(
ux, 
uy) = w^{(k+1)}(
ux, 
uy) at(
ux, 
uy) \exp(i \phir(
ux, 
uy)) where \phir = \arg(ur^{(k)}). 4. Update the weighting function iteratively: w^{(k+1)}(
ux, 
uy) = w^{(k)}(

uy) \left\{  rac{at(
ux, 
uy)}{|ur^{(k)}(

uy)|} ight\}^\alpha. 5. Generate optimal \phih as a CGH by calculating \arg(uh) after iterations. Formulas: ur(
ux, 
uy) = \mathcal{F}[uh(x,y)] uh(x,y) = ah(x,y) \exp(i \phih(x,y)) Where \mathcal{F}[\cdot] is the Fourier transform, ah/\phih are amplitude/phase on the SLM, and 
ux/
uy are spatial frequencies. Parameters: \alpha: Adjustable parameter controlling convergence. Typical value: 0.1. Time Complexity: The algorithm requires N iterations, where each iteration involves forward and backward propagation (typically FFTs). Thus, the time complexity is O(N \cdot M \log M), where M is the number of pixels in the hologram plane. Memory Complexity: Requires storage for the complex fields on the object and hologram planes, O(M). Measured Performance: Computational expense is high due to the need for many iterations (10-100). Strengths: It is the most common method to compute phase-only holograms and is numerically accurate. It effectively finds phase values that cause interference to produce constant amplitude on the hologram, which is suitable for phase-only displays. Limitations: Iteratively optimized holograms tend to include undesirable high-frequency noise or speckle. It is computationally expensive. When to use: When computing phase-only holograms for displays where the eye does not detect image phase, and high uniformity is required. When not to use: When computational speed is critical and iterative methods are too slow, or when speckle noise is unacceptable without further post-processing. The Gerchberg-Saxton algorithm was introduced by Gerchberg and Saxton in 1972. It is a well-established phase retrieval method used in various applications, including holography and optics. Modern variations have been developed to add error compensation and define "do not care" regions to increase performance. name: Staged and Alternating Optimization
head: Staged Optimization, Alternating Optimization, Multi-Stage Training
body: Staged and Alternating Optimization addresses the ill-posed nature and computational bottlenecks of differentiable volume and radiance field reconstruction by decoupling the optimization of coupled parameters (such as geometry, material, lighting, or camera poses) into sequential phases or alternating sub-problems. It distinguishes itself from simultaneous joint optimization methods by preventing gradient interference and local minima, allowing the solver to establish a coarse global alignment or geometric proxy before refining fine-scale details, materials, or uncertain parameters. All methods in this family rely on the differentiability of the forward rendering operator and the propagation of gradients through the integration steps [44-radiance-field-optimization.md]. The core mechanism is the evaluation of the volume rendering equation and the computation of gradients with respect to scene parameters (density, geometry, transfer functions, camera poses) [44-radiance-field-optimization.md]. The standard emission-absorption model computes the color \hat{C}(\mathbf{r}) for a ray \mathbf{r} as [44-radiance-field-optimization.md]: \hat{C}(\mathbf{r}) = \sum{i=1}^N Ti (1 - \exp(-\sigmai \deltai)) \mathbf{c}i where \sigmai is the density, \deltai is the step size, \mathbf{c}i is the color, and Ti = \exp\left(-\sum{j=1}^{i-1} \sigmaj \deltaj\right) is the transmittance [44-radiance-field-optimization.md]. Differentiation strategies fall into three main categories [44-radiance-field-optimization.md]: 1. Reverse-Mode Automatic Differentiation (AD): Standard backpropagation through the computational graph. This requires storing O(kn) intermediate states (where n is pixels and k is samples), leading to high memory usage [44-radiance-field-optimization.md]. 2. Adjoint Method: Computes gradients by propagating adjoint variables backward through the rendering algorithm, evaluating the chain rule from output to input. This has computational complexity largely constant in the number of parameters, making it preferable for optimizing many parameters like the transfer function [44-radiance-field-optimization.md]. 3. Analytic Inversion / Explicit Gradients: Uses a-priori knowledge of the DVR operations to invert the order of operations or derive closed-form gradients, reducing memory consumption to O(n) by avoiding the storage of intermediate results [44-radiance-field-optimization.md]. A stage-based optimization loop for differentiable volume or radiance field reconstruction that alternates between image-based and ray-based sampling modes, applies stochastic preconditioning with exponential alpha decay, and optionally upsamples parameters between stages [4241-stage-based-differentiable-volume-radiance-field-training.md]. It distinguishes itself from sibling methods by explicitly managing memory via ray batching and using a progressive upsampling schedule to stabilize training of high-resolution radiance fields [4241-stage-based-differentiable-volume-radiance-field-training.md]. The Staggered Optimization Scheme addresses the computational bottleneck and bias inherent in jointly optimizing geometric shape parameters and Point Spread Function (PSF) parameters in differentiable volume rendering [5832-staggered-optimization-scheme.md]. By decomposing the coupled optimization problem into two sequential sub-problems—shape optimization and PSF optimization—it manages computational cost and prevents bias from approximation thresholds [5832-staggered-optimization-scheme.md]. Unlike joint optimization methods that update all parameters simultaneously, this method alternates between optimizing vertex positions (with fixed PSF) and optimizing PSF covariance (with fixed shape), stabilizing the gradient descent process [5832-staggered-optimization-scheme.md]. Two-Stage Inverse Rendering Optimization decouples the recovery of scene geometry from material reflectance and illumination by alternating between an approximate differentiable renderer and a physically-based ray tracer [7387-two-stage-inverse-rendering-optimization.md]. It solves the ill-posed nature of inverse rendering by first establishing a robust geometric proxy using silhouette constraints, then refining physically accurate albedo and environment maps while holding geometry fixed [7387-two-stage-inverse-rendering-optimization.md]. This approach differs from single-stage radiance field methods (e.g., NeRF, PhySG) by explicitly modeling triangle meshes or Gaussian splats with PBR materials, enabling direct deployment in graphics engines and superior specular handling [7387-two-stage-inverse-rendering-optimization.md]. Optimization Schedule refers to the structured progression of training parameters in differentiable volume and radiance field reconstruction, designed to mitigate local minima and ensure stable convergence. It addresses the problem of ambiguous gradients in inverse rendering by decoupling the optimization of geometric structure from material properties or fine-scale details. Unlike simultaneous optimization of all parameters, which often leads to instability in sparse-view settings, this method separates the process into distinct phases or scales, allowing the solver to first establish a coarse global alignment before refining local details [14063-optimization-schedule.md]. This method jointly optimizes the volume reconstruction (radiance field) and the measurement coordinates (e.g., view angles, detector positions) by minimizing a differentiable objective function using automatic differentiation [16123-differentiable-uncalibrated-imaging-optimization.md]. It addresses the problem of uncalibrated imaging where the geometric parameters of the acquisition system are unknown or uncertain. Unlike methods that assume fixed camera poses, this approach treats measurement coordinates as trainable parameters alongside the scene representation, allowing for simultaneous refinement of geometry and appearance [16123-differentiable-uncalibrated-imaging-optimization.md]. It builds on Staged and Alternating Optimization by integrating coordinate optimization into the primary training loop rather than separating it into distinct phases. Optimize albedo first as a 1024x1024 RGB texture, then refine in two stages to reach the final 4096x4096 resolution. After the first stage, round emitters contributing a small fraction of the total scene radiance to zero. A differentiable renderer based on path-space techniques, used in both implicit and explicit stages for inverse rendering optimization. Use the Adam method [KB14] implemented in pyTorch for inverse-rendering optimizations in both stages. For updating mesh vertex positions in the explicit stage, use Nicolet et al.’s approach [NJJ21] instead of the Adam optimizer. The concept of staged optimization in inverse rendering and volume reconstruction has evolved to handle the increasing complexity of scene representations, moving from simple density fields to complex PBR materials and uncalibrated acquisition systems. Early differentiable volume rendering relied on joint optimization, which often suffered from local minima and high memory costs [44-radiance-field-optimization.md]. As representations grew more complex (e.g., combining implicit and explicit geometries, or handling uncalibrated camera poses), researchers introduced alternating schemes to decouple coupled variables. The specific techniques detailed in the children articles, such as stochastic preconditioning [4241-stage-based-differentiable-volume-radiance-field-training.md] and staggered PSF optimization [5832-staggered-optimization-scheme.md], represent specialized applications of this general family to specific bottlenecks in modern radiance field training. name: Stage-based Differentiable Volume/Radiance Field Training
head: Mitsuba radiance field optimization, TLIR training loop [S1, unofficial]
body: A stage-based optimization loop for differentiable volume or radiance field reconstruction that alternates between image-based and ray-based sampling modes, applies stochastic preconditioning with exponential alpha decay, and optionally upsamples parameters between stages. It distinguishes itself from sibling methods by explicitly managing memory via ray batching and using a progressive upsampling schedule to stabilize training of high-resolution radiance fields. Inputs and Outputs Inputs: Scene geometry and radiance field parameters, reference images (with masks and optional AOVs), and training configuration parameters. Outputs: Optimized radiance field parameters, loss history, and test image metrics (PSNR). Data Structures spnstate: Dictionary storing stochastic preconditioning state. alpha (float): Current preconditioning scale factor. step (int): Iteration counter for the current decay phase. gamma (float): Exponential decay factor. losses: List of scalar loss values recorded per iteration. Parameters useraybatching (bool): Selects between image-based and ray-based sampling modes. raysperbatch (int): Number of rays sampled per iteration in ray-based mode. spp (int): Samples per pixel used for test image rendering. numiterationsperstage (int): Number of optimization iterations per training stage. numstages (int): Total number of training stages for progressive upsampling. enableupsampling (bool): Whether to upsample parameters between stages. learningrate (float): Base learning rate for the optimizer. stochasticpreconditioningstartingalpha (float): Initial alpha value for SPN decay. stochasticpreconditioningiterations (int): Number of iterations over which alpha decays exponentially. stochasticpreconditioningupdateinterval (int): Frequency of SPN state updates. Algorithm Steps 1. Initialization: Set integrator loss type. Configure stochastic preconditioning (SPN) with stochasticpreconditioningstartingalpha, stochasticpreconditioningiterations, and stochasticpreconditioningupdateinterval. Initialize RNG with seed stageidx 1000. Initialize spnstate with alpha = startingalpha and step = 0. 2. Sampling Mode Selection: If useraybatching is true, shuffle the pre-extracted ray batch using the RNG. If false, select a random sensor index and sample all rays from that image using sampleraysfromimage. 3. Ray Sampling: In ray-based mode, sample raysperbatch rays from the shuffled batch and convert to Mitsuba tensors. In image-based mode, use the rays, target colors, and masks returned by sampleraysfromimage. 4. Rendering and Gradient Computation: Retrieve current spnalpha from spnstate. Set AOV loss masks if available. Create an independent sampler seeded with iteration raycount. Render rays with automatic gradient computation. 5. Optimization Step: Append the scalar loss value to the losses list. Step the optimizer. Perform post-step updates on the integrator. Increment spnstate['step']. If spnstate['step'] is a multiple of stochasticpreconditioningupdateinterval, update spnstate['alpha'] using exponential decay. 6. Stage Evaluation: After numiterationsperstage iterations, render numtestimages test images using the current scene state and compute PSNR against reference images. 7. Upsampling: If enableupsampling is true and not the final stage, upsample integrator parameters and update the scene state before proceeding to the next stage. Stochastic Preconditioning (SPN) Decay The decay factor gamma is calculated as: \gamma = 10^{-4 / \text{stochastic\preconditioning\iterations}} If stochasticpreconditioningiterations is 0, gamma and alpha are explicitly set to 0.0 to prevent division by zero or invalid decay calculations. Pseudocode Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import random import math import numpy as np class IndependentSampler: def init(self, seed): self.rng = random.Random(seed) def getnext(self): return self.rng.random() def preextractrays(referencedata): # Standard operation: flatten all sensor rays into a single list return [ray for sensor in referencedata.sensors for ray in sensor.rays] def sampleraysfrombatch(raybatch, count): # Standard operation: slice batch and convert to tensors return raybatch[:count], raybatch[:count].colors, raybatch[:count].masks def sampleraysfromimage(referencedata, sensoridx): # Standard operation: extract rays from a specific sensor sensor = referencedata.sensors[sensoridx] return sensor.rays, sensor.colors, sensor.masks def renderrayswithgradient(rays, targetcolors, sampler, scene, spp, spnalpha): # Standard operation: compute emission-absorption model and MSE loss # Uses parent article's volume rendering equation [44-radiance-field-optimization.md] rendered = computevolumerendering(rays, scene, spp) loss = np.mean((rendered - targetcolors) 2) return rendered, loss, {} def rendertestimages(scene, sensors, spp): return [computevolumerendering(s.rays, scene, spp) for s in sensors] def computepsnr(rendered, targets): mse = np.mean((rendered - targets) 2) return 10 math.log10(1.0 / mse) if mse > 0 else float('inf') def upsampleparameters(scene, integrator): # Standard operation: increase grid resolution or feature dimensions integrator.upsamplescene(scene) def trainstagebasedradiancefield(scene, config, referencedata): # 1. Initialization spnstate = { 'alpha': config.stochasticpreconditioningstartingalpha, 'step': 0, 'gamma': 0.0 } # Calculate gamma if config.stochasticpreconditioningiterations > 0: spnstate['gamma'] = 1e-4 (1.0 / config.stochasticpreconditioningiterations) else: spnstate['gamma'] = 0.0 spnstate['alpha'] = 0.0 losses = [] rng = random.Random() rng.seed(config.stageidx 1000) # Pre-extract ray batch if using ray batching if config.useraybatching: raybatch = preextractrays(referencedata) for iteration in range(config.numiterationsperstage): # 2. Sampling Mode Selection if config.useraybatching: # Shuffle ray batch raybatch = [raybatch[i] for i in rng.sample(range(len(raybatch)), len(raybatch))] # 3. Ray Sampling (Ray-based mode) raysmi, targetcolors, masks = sampleraysfrombatch(raybatch, config.raysperbatch) else: # 3. Ray Sampling (Image-based mode) sensoridx = rng.randint(0, len(referencedata.sensors) - 1) raysmi, targetcolors, masks = sampleraysfromimage(referencedata, sensoridx) # 4. Rendering and Gradient Computation # Create independent sampler sampler = IndependentSampler(seed=iteration config.raysperbatch) # Render with gradient computation renderedcolors, loss, aovs = renderrayswithgradient( rays=raysmi, targetcolors=targetcolors, sampler=sampler, scene=scene, spp=config.spp, spnalpha=spnstate['alpha']) # 5. Optimization Step losses.append(loss) # Apply gradient update to scene parameters # Perform integrator post-step updates # Update SPN state spnstate['step'] += 1 if spnstate['step'] % config.stochasticpreconditioningupdateinterval == 0: spnstate['alpha'] = spnstate['gamma'] # 6. Stage Evaluation testimages = rendertestimages(scene, referencedata.testsensors, config.spp) psnr = computepsnr(testimages, referencedata.testtargets) # 7. Upsampling if config.enableupsampling and config.stageidx < config.numstages - 1: upsampleparameters(scene, integrator) return losses, psnr Alternates optimization of different parameter groups in a staggered manner to reduce interference. Choose when parameters are highly coupled and joint optimization causes instability. [5832-staggered-optimization-scheme.md] Separates the optimization into a coarse geometry stage and a fine appearance stage. Choose when initial geometry estimates are poor and need stabilization before refining appearance. [7387-two-stage-inverse-rendering-optimization.md] Time Complexity: Linear with respect to the number of iterations and rays per batch. Test image rendering adds a constant overhead per stage. Memory Complexity: Ray-based mode reduces memory overhead by batching rays, enabling better data shuffling for large datasets compared to image-based mode which loads all rays from a single image. Scaling: Scales with numstages and enableupsampling. Higher resolution requires more stages or larger batches. Strengths: Reduces memory overhead via ray batching; stabilizes training via progressive upsampling and stochastic preconditioning. Limitations: Requires pre-extraction of ray batches for ray-based mode; SPN decay parameters need tuning. When to use: Large datasets where memory is a constraint; high-resolution radiance fields requiring progressive refinement. When not to use: Small datasets where image-based sampling is sufficient; real-time applications due to iterative nature. Originated in the TLIR (Two-Level Inverse Rendering) framework, implemented in Mitsuba. The method addresses the challenges of training differentiable volume rendering by managing memory and stabilizing convergence through staged optimization and stochastic preconditioning. name: Staggered Optimization Scheme
head: Alternating Optimization, Staggered Shape and PSF Optimization, deltaMic optimization strategy
body: The Staggered Optimization Scheme addresses the computational bottleneck and bias inherent in jointly optimizing geometric shape parameters and Point Spread Function (PSF) parameters in differentiable volume rendering. By decomposing the coupled optimization problem into two sequential sub-problems—shape optimization and PSF optimization—it manages computational cost and prevents bias from approximation thresholds. Unlike joint optimization methods that update all parameters simultaneously, this method alternates between optimizing vertex positions (with fixed PSF) and optimizing PSF covariance (with fixed shape), stabilizing the gradient descent process. The method operates on nonmanifold multimaterial meshes representing the scene geometry, typically containing 1,000–10,000 vertices. The core mechanism involves iterating between two distinct optimization steps, leveraging different computational strategies for the Mesh Fourier Transform (FT) to balance speed and accuracy. Inputs: Initial mesh geometry M0 (e.g., a foam-like multimaterial mesh with correct topology). Ground truth image volume I{GT}. PSF model (initially Gaussian isotropic). Optimization hyperparameters: learning rate \eta, regularization parameter \lambda, number of iterations. Outputs: Optimized mesh vertex positions v. Optimized PSF covariance matrix \Sigma. Mesh: Represented as a nonmanifold multimaterial mesh. Vertices v define the shape. The mesh supports topological transitions via surface tracking. Laplacian Matrix: L \in \mathbb{R}^{nv \times nv}, where nv is the number of vertices. Used for diffusion-based regularization. PSF Parameters: Covariance matrix \Sigma defining the blur kernel. The optimization proceeds by alternating between the following two steps until convergence: 1. Shape Optimization: Goal: Update vertex positions v to minimize shape error while keeping PSF fixed. FT Computation: Use the narrow-band approximation to compute the mesh FT. This is a fast, approximate method sufficient for shape updates and significantly faster than the exact method. Loss Function: Minimize a weighted L2 loss that downweights dark regions in the ground truth: L = \frac{\frac{1}{N} \text{tr}((I - I{GT})^2)}{\frac{1}{N} \text{tr}(I{GT})} where \text{tr}(\cdot) denotes the normalized trace, I is the rendered image, and N is the number of pixels. Update Rule: Update vertices using the AdamUniform optimizer with diffusion-based regularization: v \leftarrow v - \eta (1 + \lambda L)^{-2} \frac{\partial L}{\partial v} where \lambda = 50. Implementation Detail: Explicitly computing (1 + \lambda L)^{-2} is memory-intensive for large nv. Instead, solve the equivalent linear system for the update term A: (1 + \lambda L)^{-2} A = \frac{\partial L}{\partial v} using GPU-parallelized sparse Cholesky decomposition. 2. PSF Optimization: Goal: Update PSF parameters (covariance \Sigma) to accurately reconstruct both bright and dark regions while keeping shape fixed. FT Computation: Compute the exact FT of the mesh across all available frequencies. This avoids bias introduced by the narrow-band threshold, which depends on the current PSF values. Loss Function: Minimize a standard L2 norm: L0 = \| I - I{GT} \|2 This formulation is suitable for reconstructing both bright and dark regions. Update Rule: Optimize \Sigma using the Adam optimizer. 3. Iteration: Repeat steps 1 and 2 for a specified number of iterations (e.g., 10,000 for artificial benchmarks, 1k–10k for biological data). The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import numpy as np def staggeredoptimization(meshvertices, meshfaces, IGT, numiterations, eta, lambdareg): """ Staggered optimization of mesh shape and PSF parameters. Args: meshvertices: Array of vertex positions. meshfaces: Array of face indices. IGT: Ground truth image volume. numiterations: Total number of alternating steps. eta: Learning rate for shape optimization. lambdareg: Regularization parameter for Laplacian smoothing (default 50). Returns: Optimized mesh vertices and PSF covariance matrix. """ # Initialize PSF parameters (Gaussian isotropic covariance Sigma) Sigma = np.eye(3) # Precompute Laplacian matrix L for the mesh L = computemeshlaplacian(meshvertices, meshfaces) # Initialize Adam moments for vertices and PSF mv, vv = np.zeroslike(meshvertices), np.zeroslike(meshvertices) mSigma, vSigma = np.zeroslike(Sigma), np.zeroslike(Sigma) t = 0 for step in range(numiterations): # --- Step 1: Shape Optimization --- # Use narrow-band FT for speed # [Comment: Sources do not provide narrow-band FT implementation] Irendered = renderwithnarrowband(meshvertices, meshfaces, Sigma) # Compute weighted loss L = tr((I - IGT)^2) / tr(IGT) lossshape = computeweightedloss(Irendered, IGT) # Compute gradient of loss w.r.t vertices # [Comment: Sources do not provide gradient computation implementation] gradv = computegradientwrtvertices(lossshape, meshvertices, meshfaces, Sigma) # Solve (1 + lambdaL)^(-2) A = gradv for A A = solvesparsesystem(L, gradv, lambdareg) # Update vertices using AdamUniform optimizer t += 1 mv = 0.9 mv + 0.1 gradv vv = 0.999 vv + 0.001 (gradv 2) # Apply AdamUniform update rule meshvertices -= eta A (mv / (1 - 0.9t)) / (np.sqrt(vv / (1 - 0.999t)) + 1e-8) # --- Step 2: PSF Optimization --- # Use exact FT to avoid bias # [Comment: Sources do not provide exact FT implementation] Irenderedexact = renderwithexactFT(meshvertices, meshfaces, Sigma) # Compute L2 loss L0 = ||I - IGT||2 losspsf = computel2loss(Irenderedexact, IGT) # Compute gradient of loss w.r.t PSF parameters # [Comment: Sources do not provide gradient computation implementation] gradpsf = computegradientwrtpsf(losspsf, meshvertices, meshfaces, Sigma) # Update PSF parameters using Adam optimizer mSigma = 0.9 mSigma + 0.1 gradpsf vSigma = 0.999 vSigma + 0.001 (gradpsf 2) Sigma -= eta (mSigma / (1 - 0.9t)) / (np.sqrt(vSigma / (1 - 0.999t)) + 1e-8) return meshvertices, Sigma def computemeshlaplacian(V, F): pass def renderwithnarrowband(V, F, Sigma): pass def computeweightedloss(I, IGT): return np.trace((I - IGT)2) / np.trace(IGT) def computegradientwrtvertices(loss, V, F, Sigma): pass def solvesparsesystem(L, gradv, lambdareg): M = np.eye(L.shape[0]) + lambdareg L R = np.linalg.cholesky(M) x1 = np.linalg.solve(R.T, gradv) A = np.linalg.solve(R, x1) return A def renderwithexactFT(V, F, Sigma): pass def computel2loss(I, IGT): return np.linalg.norm(I - IGT) def computegradientwrtpsf(loss, V, F, Sigma): pass Computational Cost: The forward pass is approximately 10 times slower than the backward pass. The narrow-band method should be applied in the backward computation whenever possible to save time. Bias: Using the narrow-band method during PSF optimization introduces bias because the threshold depends on the current PSF values. Therefore, the exact FT must be used for PSF updates. Memory: Explicit inversion of the Laplacian term (1 + \lambda L)^{-2} is memory-intensive for large vertex counts (nv). Using sparse Cholesky decomposition is required to avoid this. Initial Geometry: The method requires an initial guess with the correct number of cells/topology (e.g., a foam-like mesh). Mitigates optimization instability by partitioning shape parameters into disjoint groups (e.g., rotation/scaling vs. skewness) and optimizing them alternately. Chosen when degenerate primitive shapes are a concern in joint optimization. Time Complexity: The method is computationally expensive due to the repeated computation of the Mesh Fourier Transform. The forward pass is ~10x slower than the backward pass. The staggered approach mitigates this by using the fast narrow-band method for shape updates and the slower exact method only for PSF updates. Memory Complexity: Memory usage is dominated by the storage of the Laplacian matrix and the intermediate states for the Cholesky decomposition. Explicit inversion is avoided to handle large vertex counts (nv). Performance: On artificial images (sphere/torus), the method converges to the original shapes within 10,000 iterations. On biological data (mouse, ascidian, worm embryos), it converges within 1k–10k steps. It outperforms DM3D in MSE, SSIM, and PSNR on mouse organoid images. Robustness: The method is robust to noise (MSE increases gradually with noise level) and initial condition variations (zoom/shift), though larger shifts increase convergence time. Strengths: Decouples coupled parameters to prevent bias and instability; handles topological transitions via multimaterial mesh tracking; efficient use of narrow-band approximation for shape updates. Limitations: High computational cost; requires careful initialization of mesh topology; narrow-band approximation may introduce bias if not managed correctly. The Staggered Optimization Scheme was introduced in the context of differentiable rendering for 3D fluorescence microscopy, specifically for inferring cell shapes in early-stage embryos. It was developed to address the computational bottlenecks and optimization instability associated with jointly optimizing geometric shape and PSF parameters in differentiable volume rendering pipelines. The method builds on techniques from differentiable mesh rendering and sparse linear algebra. name: Alternating Optimization Strategy
head: Block Coordinate Descent (BCD) inspired strategy
body: The Alternating Optimization Strategy mitigates optimization instability caused by the highly coupled influence of base geometric attributes (rotation and scaling) and skewness parameters on a primitive's spatial footprint. It partitions shape-related parameters into two disjoint groups and optimizes them alternately, decoupling the update process to prevent degenerate primitive shapes. Unlike joint optimization where all parameters are updated simultaneously, this method stabilizes gradient descent by freezing one group while optimizing the other. Inputs and Outputs Inputs: Current iteration step t, warm-up threshold T{start}, cycle length C, base phase duration C{base}, base shape parameters \Theta{base}, skewness parameters \Theta{skew}, and an optimizer (e.g., Adam or SGHMC). Outputs: Updated parameters \Theta{base} and \Theta{skew}. Data Structures \Theta{base}: Set of base shape parameters, defined as \{R, S\}, representing Rotation and Scaling. \Theta{skew}: Set of skewness parameters, defined as \{dk, mk\}. Parameters T{start}: Warm-up threshold iteration. Before this iteration, all parameters are optimized jointly. C: Cycle length for the alternating optimization phase. C{base}: Base phase duration. The number of steps within a cycle where base shape parameters are optimized while skewness is frozen. Algorithm Steps 1. Compute loss L and initial gradients for all parameters. 2. If t > T{start}, enter the alternating phase: a. Calculate stepcycle = t \pmod C. b. If stepcycle < C{base}: i. Freeze \Theta{skew} (e.g., zero gradients and learning rate). ii. Unfreeze \Theta{base}. c. Else (stepcycle \ge C{base}): i. Freeze \Theta{base} (e.g., zero gradients and learning rate). ii. Unfreeze \Theta{skew}. 3. Else (t \le T{start}): a. Unfreeze all \Theta{base} and \Theta{skew} for joint optimization during the warm-up phase. 4. Apply the optimizer step to update only the unfrozen parameters. Pseudocode Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def alternatingoptimizationstep(t, Tstart, C, Cbase, Thetabase, Thetaskew, optimizer): # 1. Compute loss L and initial gradients for all parameters loss = computeloss(Thetabase, Thetaskew) gradients = computegradients(loss, Thetabase, Thetaskew) # 2. Determine which parameters to update based on iteration t if t > Tstart: stepcycle = t % C if stepcycle < Cbase: # Base Phase: Optimize base shape, freeze skewness gradients['Thetaskew'] = zerolike(gradients['Thetaskew']) else: # Skew Phase: Optimize skewness, freeze base shape gradients['Thetabase'] = zerolike(gradients['Thetabase']) else: # Warm-up Phase: Joint Optimization # All parameters remain unfrozen; gradients are used as computed pass # 3. Apply optimizer step to update only the unfrozen parameters optimizer.step(Thetabase, Thetaskew, gradients) def zerolike(tensor): """Returns a tensor of zeros with the same shape as the input.""" return [0.0] len(tensor) def computeloss(params): """Standard forward pass to compute rendering loss L.""" return 0.0 def computegradients(loss, params): """Standard backward pass to compute gradients.""" return {'Thetabase': [], 'Thetaskew': []} Edge Cases and Pitfalls Optimization Instability: Jointly optimizing base geometric attributes with skewness parameters can lead to instability due to their highly coupled influence on the primitive's spatial footprint. This is mitigated by the alternating strategy. Degenerate Shapes: Without decoupling, the optimization may result in degenerate primitive shapes. Time and Memory Complexity Not given in the sources. Measured Performance The method is part of the Full SNS model. In ablation studies (Table 4 in), the Full SNS (including k-decomposition and Alternating Optimization) generally outperforms ablated versions. For example, on the "Playroom Blending Deep" scene, the Full SNS achieved a PSNR of 30.7130, compared to 30.6745 for a version without the full combination. On average across datasets, the Full SNS achieved a PSNR of 30.3034, compared to 30.2969 for a baseline without the full combination. Scaling Not given in the sources. Strengths and Limitations Strengths: Stabilizes gradient descent by decoupling highly coupled parameters. Prevents degenerate primitive shapes. Limitations: Introduces complexity in managing parameter freezing/unfreezing. Requires careful tuning of T{start}, C, and C{base}. When to Use Use when optimizing primitive shape parameters that exhibit strong coupling between base geometric attributes and skewness, leading to instability in joint optimization. The Alternating Optimization Strategy is inspired by Block Coordinate Descent (BCD). It was introduced in the context of 3D Skew-Normal Splatting (SNS) to address optimization instability in primitive shape parameters. The method is part of the SNS model, which includes k-decomposition and this optimization strategy. 3D Skew-Normal Splatting, https://doi.org/10.48550/arxiv.2605.15010, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial)

name: Two-Stage Inverse Rendering Optimization
head: Hybrid Differentiable Rendering for Inverse Rendering, Two-Stage Optimization Strategy
body: Two-Stage Inverse Rendering Optimization decouples the recovery of scene geometry from material reflectance and illumination by alternating between an approximate differentiable renderer and a physically-based ray tracer. It addresses the ill-posed nature of inverse rendering by first establishing a robust geometric proxy using silhouette constraints, then refining physically accurate albedo and environment maps while holding geometry fixed. This approach differs from single-stage radiance field methods (e.g., NeRF, PhySG) by explicitly modeling triangle meshes or Gaussian splats with PBR materials, enabling direct deployment in graphics engines and superior specular handling. The method operates in two distinct phases. The specific variables involved are: \mu (position), \Sigma (covariance), c (color), \alpha (opacity), n (normal), \rho (albedo), r (roughness), and L{env} (environment-map radiance). Inputs: A set of multi-view images \{Ik\}, camera parameters, and an initial geometry estimate (either a coarse mesh from SfM/MVS or a pre-trained 3D Gaussian Splatting model). Outputs: Optimized vertex positions \thetap (or Gaussian attributes), diffuse albedo texture \thetad, specular albedo texture \thetas (or BRDF parameters \rho, r), and HDR environment map L{env}. 1. Geometry Representation: Mesh-based: Vertex position matrix V \in \mathbb{R}^{n \times 3}, Laplacian matrix L \in \mathbb{R}^{n \times n}, face normals ni. Gaussian-based: 3D Gaussians defined by mean \mu, covariance \Sigma, opacity \alpha, color c, and normal n. 2. Material Representation: Diffuse albedo \thetad (or \rhod) and specular albedo \thetas (or \rhos) stored as 2D texture maps. Roughness denoted as r in Gaussian variants or \alpha in the GGX microfacet distribution for mesh variants. 3. Lighting: Environment map L{env}, typically discretized on a grid (e.g., 512 \times 128 or 16 \times 32). The goal is to refine the initial geometry to accurately match the scene silhouette and surface structure. 1. Initialize: Load initial geometry (mesh vertices \thetap or Gaussian parameters \{\mu, \Sigma, c, \alpha, n\}) and set environment map channels to (0.5, 0.5, 0.5). 2. Render Silhouette/Opacity: Mesh: Use a soft rasterizer to compute silhouette image I{sil}(\thetap) for each input view. Gaussians: Render opacity \hat{\alpha} and color using standard Gaussian splatting. 3. Compute Losses: Silhouette Loss: L{sil} = 1 - \frac{\tilde{I}{sil} \otimes I{sil}}{\sqrt{\sum \tilde{I}{sil}^2 \sum I{sil}^2}} where \tilde{I}{sil} is the ground truth silhouette, \otimes is element-wise product, and normalization ensures scale invariance. Laplacian Loss: L{lap} = \|LV\|2 where V is the vertex coordinate matrix and L is the mesh Laplacian matrix. Normal Consistency Loss: L{normal} = \sum{i,j} [1 - (ni \cdot nj)] summed over all triangle pairs (i,j) sharing a common edge. Edge Length Loss: L{edge} = \sumi ei where ei is the length of the i-th edge. Opacity-Mask Loss: L{mask} = \|\hat{\alpha} - M\|1 where M is the binary foreground mask. Color/Normal Loss: Lc (color reconstruction) and Ln (normal consistency) from standard Gaussian splatting. 4. Optimize Geometry: Mesh: Minimize L{geo} = \lambda{sil} L{sil} + \lambda{lap} L{lap} + \lambda{normal} L{normal} + \lambda{edge} L{edge} by updating \thetap. Gaussians: Minimize L{init} = Lc + Ln + \lambda{mask} L{mask} by updating \{\mu, \Sigma, c, \alpha, n\}. 5. Iterate: Repeat for N1 iterations (e.g., 30,000 for Gaussians, or 200 iterations per view for meshes). The goal is to recover physically accurate materials and lighting. 1. Freeze Geometry: Fix all geometric attributes (\thetap for mesh variants, or \{\mu, \Sigma, c, \alpha, n\} for Gaussian variants). 2. Initialize Materials: Initialize diffuse \thetad (or \rhod) and specular \thetas (or \rhos) textures, roughness r, and environment map L{env}. 3. Physically-Based Rendering: Trace rays using a physically-based differentiable renderer (e.g., Mitsuba 2 or OptiX). Reflectance Model: fr(\omegao, \omegai; x) = \thetad(x) + \thetas(\omegao, \omegai; x) \thetad(x) = \frac{\rhod(x)}{\pi} \thetas(\omegao, \omegai; x) = \rhos(x) \frac{D(h, \alpha) G(\omegao, \omegai, n(x))}{(n(x) \cdot \omegai)(n(x) \cdot \omegao) \pi} where D is the GGX microfacet distribution [Walter et al., 2007], G is the shadowing-masking function, and Fresnel effects are ignored. Rendering Equation: Lo(\omegao; x) = \int{\Omega} Li(\omegai) fr(\omegao, \omegai; x) (\omegai \cdot n) d\omegai 4. Compute Losses: Photometric Loss: L{rgb} = \|\tilde{I}{rgb} - I{rgb}(\thetar)\|1 where \tilde{I}{rgb} is the ground truth image and I{rgb}(\thetar) is the rendered image. Albedo Regularization: R(\thetar) = \sump \left( \thetas[p] - \frac{\sumq \thetas[q] k{p,q}}{\sumq k{p,q}} \right)^2 + \sump \frac{(\thetad[p] - \thetad[q])^2}{2\sigma2^2} where k{p,q} = \exp\left(-\frac{\|p-q\|2^2}{2\sigma1^2}\right) is a Gaussian kernel between pixels/vertices p and q. Total Loss: L{ref} = \lambda{rgb} L{rgb} + \lambda{reg} R(\thetar) Total Loss: L{1pbr} = \|\tilde{I}{rgb} - I{rgb}\|1 5. Optimize Materials: Update \thetad, \thetas (or \rho, r) and L{env} to minimize L{ref} or L{1pbr}. 6. Iterate: Repeat for N2 iterations (e.g., 400 for both). Unverified code. A variant using 3D Gaussian Splatting as the geometry proxy was later proposed in (2026), leveraging the speed of splatting for Stage 1 and ray tracing for occlusion-aware relighting in Stage 2.
