name: Exposure Correction Strategy
head: Nearest-neighbor exposure mimicry
body: This strategy corrects inconsistent exposure across training views caused by the auto-exposure behavior of modern cameras in radiance-field optimization. It addresses the limitation of prior methods that only correct exposure at training views by generalizing to images rendered at any novel viewpoint. Unlike approaches that jointly optimize an affine transformation matrix for each training view, this method assumes that images taken at nearby locations share similar global lighting conditions and corrects camera exposure at novel views by mimicking the exposure setting of the closest source view. The method operates within an image-based Gaussian Splatting pipeline. It relies on the spatial proximity of training views to infer exposure parameters for novel viewpoints. Inputs: Set of training images S = \{Ii\}. Camera poses for training images. Camera pose for the novel view V{\text{novel}}. Outputs: Exposure correction factor applied to the rendered image at V{\text{novel}}. Data Structures: Training view positions: 3D coordinates \mathbf{p}i for each Ii \in S. Novel view position: 3D coordinate \mathbf{p}{\text{novel}}. Steps: 1. Identify the nearest neighbor: Calculate the Euclidean distance between the novel view position \mathbf{p}{\text{novel}} and every training view position \mathbf{p}i. 2. Select the closest source view I{\text{nn}} such that: I{\text{nn}} = \arg \min{Ii \in S} \| \mathbf{p}{\text{novel}} - \mathbf{p}i \|. 3. Retrieve the exposure setting (or implicit exposure scaling factor) associated with I{\text{nn}}. 4. Apply the exposure correction from I{\text{nn}} to the rendered radiance at V{\text{novel}}. Parameters: Distance metric: Euclidean distance in 3D space. Neighbor count: 1 (nearest neighbor only). Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Sparse Training Data: If the nearest neighbor is far away, the assumption of similar global lighting conditions may fail, leading to incorrect exposure correction. Dynamic Exposure: When exposure differences are significantly dynamic among neighborhood views, the method may still struggle if the nearest neighbor has a vastly different exposure setting, potentially causing the renderer to misinterpret exposure differences as high-frequency reflectance. This is an initialization strategy to resolve the ambiguity between exposure and white balance, stabilizing optimization by guiding initial solutions to physically plausible ones. It addresses the issue where the overall scale of white balance becomes extremely small or large during training. Steps: 1. Calculate the averaged color (ra, ga, ba) \in \mathbb{R}^3 of all input images in the set S. 2. Select a reference image I{\text{ref}} which has the closest averaged color value (r{\text{ref}}, g{\text{ref}}, b{\text{ref}}) \in \mathbb{R}^3 to (ra, ga, ba). 3. Fix the white balance of this reference image as regularization. 4. Estimate the reference color ratio by comparing per-image averaged pixel values to the averaging of each RGB value from the entire image set S. 5. Initialize the white balances w{c,i} for each camera c \in \{r, g, b\} of each image Ii as: w{c,i} = \frac{\text{mean}{k \in Ii}(ck)}{\text{mean}{j \in S}(cj)} where ck is the pixel value for channel c in image Ii, and cj is the pixel value for channel c in image Ij. This initialization helps the white balance be learned on the proper scale, ensuring a suitable exposure value and stabilizing early optimization steps, particularly when LDR images from neighborhood views have significantly dynamic exposure differences. Time Complexity: The nearest-neighbor search is O(N) per novel view, where N is the number of training views. This is negligible compared to the rendering cost. Memory Complexity: O(N) to store training view positions. Strengths: Generalizes exposure correction to any viewpoint, not just training views. Simple to implement. Limitations: Relies on the assumption of similar lighting between nearby views. Fails when nearby views have significantly different exposure settings, as the nearest neighbor assumption breaks down and may cause the renderer to misinterpret exposure differences as high-frequency reflectance. When to use: When training data is captured with auto-exposure cameras. When not to use: When lighting conditions vary significantly over short distances. The strategy was introduced in the context of Image-Based Gaussian Splatting (IBGS) to address photometric inconsistencies arising from auto-exposure in modern cameras. It builds on Radiometric Self-Calibration, which optimizes radiometric parameters during reconstruction, and addresses the observation that prior works only corrected exposure at training views, limiting their applicability to novel viewpoints. The related White Balance Initialization strategy was proposed in HDR-Plenoxels to resolve scale ambiguity between exposure and white balance, and between SH coefficients and white balance, ensuring stable optimization. IBGS: Image-Based Gaussian Splatting, https://arxiv.org/abs/2511.14357v1, fetched 2026-10-26 HDR-Plenoxels: Self-Calibrating High Dynamic Range Radiance Fields, https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-031-19824-323, fetched 2026-10-26

name: BARF (Bundle-Adjusting Neural Radiance Fields)
head: Bundle-Adjusting NeRF
body: BARF reconstructs a Neural Radiance Field (NeRF) and refines inaccurate camera poses given multi-view images with pose errors. It differs from standard NeRF optimization by using a coarse-to-fine refinement strategy that gradually increases the high-frequency part of positional encoding. Inputs and outputs: Inputs: Multi-view images \{Ii\}, initial camera poses \{Pi\} (with errors), and a NeRF model \mathcal{F}\theta. Outputs: Refined camera poses \{\hat{P}i\} and optimized NeRF parameters \hat{\theta}. Data structures: NeRF Model \mathcal{F}\theta: A multi-layer perceptron (MLP) mapping 3D position \mathbf{x} and viewing direction \mathbf{d} to volume density \sigma and color \mathbf{c}. Positional Encoding \Gamma: Standard Fourier feature mapping used to embed \mathbf{x} and \mathbf{d}. Optimization State: Parameters \theta for the MLP and pose parameters (rotation \mathbf{R}, translation \mathbf{t}) for each camera. Method: The core innovation is a coarse-to-fine refinement strategy that gradually introduces high-frequency information into the positional encoding. This allows the optimizer to first converge on low-frequency structures (which are robust to pose errors) before refining high-frequency details (which require accurate poses). 1. Initialization: Initialize the NeRF parameters \theta and camera poses Pi using the provided (potentially inaccurate) initial poses. 2. Coarse-to-Fine Schedule: Define a schedule for the number of frequency bands L(t) used in the positional encoding \Gamma at training step t. 3. Optimization Loop: For each training step t: a. Set the positional encoding frequency limit L(t) based on the schedule. b. Sample rays through the scene using the current camera poses Pi. c. Render colors \hat{C} using the NeRF \mathcal{F}\theta with positional encoding \Gamma{L(t)}. d. Compute the loss \mathcal{L} between rendered colors \hat{C} and ground truth images Ii (typically Mean Squared Error). e. Perform gradient descent to update both NeRF parameters \theta and camera pose parameters. f. Increment t and update L(t) if the schedule dictates. Formulas: Positional Encoding with frequency limit L: \GammaL(\mathbf{x}) = [\sin(2^0 \pi \mathbf{x}), \cos(2^0 \pi \mathbf{x}), \dots, \sin(2^{L-1} \pi \mathbf{x}), \cos(2^{L-1} \pi \mathbf{x})] Rendering equation (standard volume rendering): \hat{C}(\mathbf{r}) = \sum{i=1}^N Ti \left( 1 - e^{-\sigmai \deltai} \right) \mathbf{c}i, \quad Ti = e^{-\sum{j=1}^{i-1} \sigmaj \deltaj} Loss function: \mathcal{L} = \frac{1}{N} \sum{i=1}^N \| \hat{C}i - Ii \|^2 Parameters: Initial frequency bands: Not given in the sources. Final frequency bands: Not given in the sources. Learning rate: Not given in the sources. Optimization algorithm: Not given in the sources. Edge cases and pitfalls: Precision: The gradual introduction of frequencies prevents the optimizer from being misled by high-frequency noise in the presence of pose errors. Boundaries: The schedule must be smooth enough to allow convergence at each frequency level. Degenerate input: If initial poses are extremely poor, even the coarse stages may fail to converge. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import torch def barfoptimization(images, initialposes, nerfmlp, schedulefn, numsteps): # Initialize learnable parameters theta = list(nerfmlp.parameters()) poses = [p.clone().requiresgrad(True) for p in initialposes] optimizer = torch.optim.Adam(theta + poses, lr=1e-4) # for t in range(numsteps): Lt = schedulefn(t) optimizer.zerograd() renderedimages = [] for i, gtimg in enumerate(images): # Standard ray sampling through camera frustum rayso, raysd = sampleraysthroughposes(poses[i], gtimg.shape) # Apply positional encoding with limited frequency bands encodedrays = applypositionalencoding(rayso, raysd, L=Lt) # Standard differentiable volume rendering color = volumerender(nerfmlp, encodedrays) renderedimages.append(color) loss = computemseloss(renderedimages, images) loss.backward() optimizer.step() return poses, theta def applypositionalencoding(rayso, raysd, L): # Standard Fourier features up to frequency band L encoded = [] for i in range(L): freq = 2i torch.pi encoded.extend([torch.sin(freq rayso), torch.cos(freq rayso), torch.sin(freq raysd), torch.cos(freq raysd)]) return torch.cat(encoded, dim=-1) def computemseloss(rendered, groundtruth): return torch.mean((torch.stack(rendered) - torch.stack(groundtruth)) 2) The Iterative Alignment Strategy is a post-processing and data-generation technique used to mitigate reconstruction artifacts in Neural Radiance Fields (NeRF) caused by inaccurate camera poses and non-rigid scene motion. It addresses the "domain gap" where NeRF-rendered views are blurry due to misalignment, violating the sharp-pair assumption of standard optical flow estimators. Unlike direct alignment methods that optimize a loss function during training, this strategy iteratively warps ground truth images using optical flow to create a better-aligned training set, leveraging the sharpening effect of improved alignment to refine flow estimates in subsequent rounds. This method performs the final optimization step in the LU-NeRF pipeline to achieve high-fidelity novel view synthesis by jointly refining camera poses and the neural radiance field (NeRF) representation. It solves the problem of residual errors in camera poses and scene geometry that remain after the initial synchronization stage. Unlike the Iterative Alignment Strategy, which focuses on sequential alignment, this method leverages the global consistency provided by synchronization to apply a comprehensive bundle adjustment-style refinement. It sets itself apart by using the BARF optimization procedure as its core engine, treating the synchronized poses as a sufficiently accurate initialization to converge to the ground truth. Time complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory complexity: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Robust to initial pose errors by decoupling frequency optimization. Limitations: Requires a coarse-to-fine schedule. When to use: When camera poses are inaccurate or sparse. BARF (Bundle-Adjusting Neural Radiance Fields) was introduced in ICCV 2021. It addresses the issue of NeRF's sensitivity to camera pose accuracy, which is a common problem in real-world scenarios where poses are estimated from SfM pipelines and may contain errors. The method was developed to improve the robustness of NeRF reconstruction under pose uncertainty. NeRF的基础及后续扩展, https://pengsida.net/files/NeRFTutorial.pdf, fetched 2026-10-30 (unofficial)

name: Iterative Alignment Strategy
head: Misalignment Correction via Optical Flow
body: The Iterative Alignment Strategy is a post-processing and data-generation technique used to mitigate reconstruction artifacts in Neural Radiance Fields (NeRF) caused by inaccurate camera poses and non-rigid scene motion. It addresses the "domain gap" where NeRF-rendered views are blurry due to misalignment, violating the sharp-pair assumption of standard optical flow estimators. Unlike direct alignment methods that optimize a loss function during training, this strategy iteratively warps ground truth images using optical flow to create a better-aligned training set, leveraging the sharpening effect of improved alignment to refine flow estimates in subsequent rounds. The method operates as an iterative loop to generate aligned training and testing data. It assumes access to a NeRF model (e.g., mip-NeRF 360) and a set of input images with potentially erroneous camera poses. Inputs: Current NeRF model parameters (MLPs). Original ground truth images I{gt}. Original camera poses P. Optical flow estimator (PWC-Net). Outputs: Warped ground truth images I{warped}. Updated NeRF model parameters. Data Structures: Images: 2D arrays of pixel values (RGB). Optical Flow: 2D vector fields (u, v) representing displacement from source to target. Steps: 1. Render: Render images I{render} from the current NeRF model using the original camera poses P. 2. Estimate Flow: Calculate the optical flow from the rendered views I{render} to the ground truth views I{gt} using PWC-Net. Note: The rendered images are often blurry due to misalignment, which violates the general optical flow assumption of sharp paired inputs. However, PWC-Net produces reasonable results based on global structures and shapes. 3. Warp: Warp the ground truth images I{gt} using the estimated optical flows to build a new, better-aligned training set I{warped}. The warping aligns the ground truth content with the geometry estimated by the NeRF. 4. Retrain: Train the NeRF model using the new aligned training set I{warped}. 5. Iterate: Repeat steps 1-4 for 2-3 iterations. Each iteration leverages sharper images (from the improved NeRF) to improve flow accuracy, which in turn enables better alignment for the next round. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def iterativealignmentstrategy(nerfmodel, gtimages, poses, numiterations=3): """Iteratively aligns ground truth images to NeRF geometry using optical flow.""" currentimages = gtimages for in range(numiterations): # Step 1: Render current NeRF model using original poses renderedimages = [nerfmodel.render(p) for p in poses] # Step 2: Calculate optical flow from rendered to ground truth using PWC-Net flowfields = [estimateflow(rendered, gt) for rendered, gt in zip(renderedimages, currentimages)] # Step 3: Warp ground truth images using estimated flows to build aligned training set alignedimages = [warp(gt, f) for gt, f in zip(currentimages, flowfields)] # Step 4: Retrain NeRF on aligned images nerfmodel.train(alignedimages, poses) currentimages = alignedimages return currentimages def estimateflow(source, target): # Compute optical flow field F from source to target using PWC-Net # Returns 2D vector field of displacements return PWCNet(source, target) # External optical flow estimator def warp(image, flow): # Sample image pixels at coordinates displaced by flow field using bilinear interpolation h, w = image.shape[:2] gridy, gridx = np.meshgrid(np.arange(h), np.arange(w), indexing='ij') # Flow is (dy, dx) y = gridy + flow[:,:, 0] x = gridx + flow[:,:, 1] # Clamp and sample y = np.clip(y, 0, h - 1) x = np.clip(x, 0, w - 1) return bilinearsample(image, x, y) Parameters: Iterations: 2-3 iterations are typically sufficient to reach best quality. Optical Flow Network: PWC-Net. RAFT was considered but rejected due to memory constraints on high-resolution images. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Memory Constraints: PWC-Net may run out of memory on high-resolution images. Alternative flow networks like RAFT were rejected for the same reason. Blurry Inputs: NeRF rendered images are often blurry due to misalignment, violating the sharp-pair assumption of optical flow estimators. This can reduce flow accuracy, though global structures help mitigate this. Non-Rigid Motion: The strategy addresses misalignment from camera pose errors and non-rigid motion. Non-Rigid Refinement is a post-processing alignment step that uses an iterative optical flow network to correct non-rigid deformations or misalignments in NeRF features by warping neighbor features to test features. It addresses the domain gap between blurry rendered novel views and sharp neighboring images, which causes standard 3D alignment to fail due to camera pose errors and geometry estimation inaccuracies. Unlike general-purpose alignment, this method is trained end-to-end specifically for the task of refining feature correspondences in the presence of these domain gaps. Direct Alignment is a training technique that applies a direct alignment loss between rendered images and input RGB images to improve camera pose estimation and structure reconstruction in neural radiance fields. For every frame, it selects a surrogate view from a neighborhood starting from 2 frames till 5 frames on either side of the keyframe to perform direct alignment. It is trained for 100k iterations. Unlike methods that require expansive optic-flow depth or foundation models for regularization, direct alignment avoids local minima in joint camera pose estimation without them. However, violations of photo-consistency can hamper reconstructions, particularly with semi-transparent objects. It has been applied to LLFF and DTU datasets, showing average boosts of 60% in rotation and 53% in translation error reduction. Time Complexity: The method requires multiple iterations of NeRF training and optical flow estimation. Each iteration involves rendering all training views, running PWC-Net, and warping images. The total time scales with the number of iterations (typically 2-3) multiplied by the cost of one NeRF training epoch plus flow estimation. Memory Complexity: High memory usage due to the need to store and process high-resolution images and optical flow fields. PWC-Net may run out of memory on high-resolution images, and RAFT was rejected for the same reason. Performance: The strategy improves PSNR by +0.62dB on the warped test set for large MLPs (4096 channels) and +0.23dB for smaller models (1024 channels). It also improves LPIPS and SSIM metrics. Strengths: Effectively reduces artifacts caused by misalignment; leverages the self-improving nature of NeRF rendering (sharper images lead to better flow). Limitations: Does not represent the core proposed algorithm of the AligNeRF paper (which is a loss function); serves primarily for analysis and data generation. Relies on the quality of the optical flow estimator; fails if the initial NeRF is too poor to provide useful global structures for flow estimation. When to Use: When camera poses are inaccurate and cause significant blurring in NeRF renders, and when computational resources allow for iterative retraining and flow estimation. When Not to Use: When memory is constrained for high-resolution images; when the scene has severe non-rigid motion that cannot be captured by global optical flow. The Iterative Alignment Strategy was introduced in the AligNeRF paper. It was developed to address the issue of misalignment in NeRF training, particularly in the context of the mip-NeRF 360 dataset. The authors observed that standard NeRF training with inaccurate poses leads to blurry renders, which in turn hampers the accuracy of optical flow estimation if used for alignment. The iterative approach was proposed to break this cycle by progressively aligning the training data. The strategy was used for analysis and data generation in the experiments, rather than as the primary algorithm of the work, which focused on an alignment-aware training loss. AligNeRF: High-Fidelity Neural Radiance Fields via Alignment-Aware Training, https://doi.org/10.1109/cvpr52729.2023.00013, fetched 2026-10-26 ACCV 2024 Open Access Repository, https://openaccess.thecvf.com/content/ACCV2024/html/GargDirectAlignmentforRobustNeRFLearningACCV2024paper.html, fetched 2026-10-29 (unofficial)

name: Non-Rigid Refinement
head: iterative flow network
body: Non-Rigid Refinement is a post-processing alignment step that uses an iterative optical flow network to correct non-rigid deformations or misalignments in NeRF features by warping neighbor features to test features. It addresses the domain gap between blurry rendered novel views and sharp neighboring images, which causes standard 3D alignment to fail due to camera pose errors and geometry estimation inaccuracies. Unlike general-purpose alignment, this method is trained end-to-end specifically for the task of refining feature correspondences in the presence of these domain gaps. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A pair of feature maps: Neighbour Features (H^f{i\rightarrow k}) and Test Features (I^fk). The neighbour features are the reprojected features from adjacent views, and the test features are from the novel view. Output: Refined Neighbour Features (H^{f'}{i\rightarrow k}) and an estimated 2D optical flow field. Data Structures: Feature Maps: 2D tensors representing features extracted from images. The specific channel depth is not explicitly defined in the source, but the architecture processes them as multi-channel inputs. Flow Field: A 2-channel tensor representing the horizontal and vertical displacement vectors for each pixel. Algorithm Steps: 1. Resolution Reduction: The input feature maps are downsampled by a factor of 8. The optical flow estimation is performed at this 8x downsampled resolution. 2. Flow Estimation: The downsampled neighbour features and test features are passed through the optical flow network \mathcal{F} to estimate the flow field f{H^f{i\rightarrow k}}: f{H^f{i\rightarrow k}} = \mathcal{F}(H^f{i\rightarrow k}, I^fk) 3. Warping: The neighbour features are warped using the estimated 2D flow field via a 2D warping function warp{2D}: H^{f'}{i\rightarrow k} = warp{2D}(H^f{i\rightarrow k}, f{H^f{i\rightarrow k}}) 4. Iteration: The estimation and warping process is iterated 32 times to refine the alignment progressively. Network Architecture (\mathcal{F}): The network \mathcal{F} is a lightweight convolutional neural network. The architecture is identical to the original formulation in [6] but adapted to accept multi-channel features instead of 3-channel RGB images. The layers are as follows: 1. Conv2d: kernel size 7, 64 channels, stride 4. Followed by ReLU. 2. Conv2d: kernel size 3, 64 channels. Followed by ReLU. 3. Conv2d: kernel size 3, 64 channels. Skip connection added to previous output. Followed by ReLU. 4. Conv2d: kernel size 3, 64 channels, stride 2. Followed by ReLU. 5. Conv2d: kernel size 3, 64 channels. Skip connection added to previous output. Followed by ReLU. 6. Conv2d: kernel size 3, 64 channels. Followed by ReLU. 7. Conv2d: kernel size 3, 64 channels. Followed by ReLU. 8. Conv2d: kernel size 3, 128 channels. Followed by ReLU. 9. Conv2d: kernel size 3, 64 channels. Followed by ReLU. 10. Conv2d: kernel size 3, 2 channels (representing the optical flow vector). Followed by ReLU. Upsampling: The estimated flow field from the network is at the reduced resolution. It is upsampled to full resolution using bilinear upsampling before being used in the warping step. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import torch import torch.nn as nn import torch.nn.functional as F class NonRigidRefinementNetwork(nn.Module): def init(self, inchannels): super(NonRigidRefinementNetwork, self).init() # Layer 1: Conv2d k7 c64 s4 -> ReLU self.conv1 = nn.Conv2d(inchannels, 64, kernelsize=7, stride=4, padding=3) self.relu1 = nn.ReLU() # Layer 2: Conv2d k3 c64 -> ReLU self.conv2 = nn.Conv2d(64, 64, kernelsize=3, padding=1) self.relu2 = nn.ReLU() # Layer 3: Conv2d k3 c64 + skip -> ReLU self.conv3 = nn.Conv2d(64, 64, kernelsize=3, padding=1) self.relu3 = nn.ReLU() # Layer 4: Conv2d k3 c64 s2 -> ReLU self.conv4 = nn.Conv2d(64, 64, kernelsize=3, stride=2, padding=1) self.relu4 = nn.ReLU() # Layer 5: Conv2d k3 c64 + skip -> ReLU self.conv5 = nn.Conv2d(64, 64, kernelsize=3, padding=1) self.relu5 = nn.ReLU() # Layer 6: Conv2d k3 c64 -> ReLU self.conv6 = nn.Conv2d(64, 64, kernelsize=3, padding=1) self.relu6 = nn.ReLU() # Layer 7: Conv2d k3 c64 -> ReLU self.conv7 = nn.Conv2d(64, 64, kernelsize=3, padding=1) self.relu7 = nn.ReLU() # Layer 8: Conv2d k3 c128 -> ReLU self.conv8 = nn.Conv2d(64, 128, kernelsize=3, padding=1) self.relu8 = nn.ReLU() # Layer 9: Conv2d k3 c64 -> ReLU self.conv9 = nn.Conv2d(128, 64, kernelsize=3, padding=1) self.relu9 = nn.ReLU() # Layer 10: Conv2d k3 c2 -> ReLU self.conv10 = nn.Conv2d(64, 2, kernelsize=3, padding=1) self.relu10 = nn.ReLU() def forward(self, neighbourfeatures, testfeatures): # Concatenate inputs along channel dimension x = torch.cat([neighbourfeatures, testfeatures], dim=1) # Layer 1 x = self.relu1(self.conv1(x)) # Layer 2 x = self.relu2(self.conv2(x)) # Layer 3 (Skip connection) xskip = x x = self.relu3(self.conv3(x) + xskip) # Layer 4 x = self.relu4(self.conv4(x)) # Layer 5 (Skip connection) xskip = x x = self.relu5(self.conv5(x) + xskip) # Layer 6 x = self.relu6(self.conv6(x)) # Layer 7 x = self.relu7(self.conv7(x)) # Layer 8 x = self.relu8(self.conv8(x)) # Layer 9 x = self.relu9(self.conv9(x)) # Layer 10 flow = self.relu10(self.conv10(x)) return flow def warp2d(features, flow): """ Warps the input features using the provided 2D flow field via bilinear sampling. """ B, C, H, W = features.shape # Create normalized grid coordinates [-1, 1] y, x = torch.meshgrid(torch.linspace(-1, 1, H), torch.linspace(-1, 1, W), indexing='ij') grid = torch.stack([x, y], dim=-1).to(features.device) # Flow is in pixel coordinates; convert to normalized [-1, 1] flownorm = flow.permute(0, 2, 3, 1) 2.0 / max(H, W) grid = grid + flownorm grid = torch.clamp(grid, -1, 1) return F.gridsample(features, grid, mode='bilinear', paddingmode='zeros') def nonrigidrefinement(neighbourfeatures, testfeatures, numiterations=32): """ Performs non-rigid refinement iteratively at 8x downsampled resolution, then warps the full-resolution features with the final upsampled flow. """ h, w = neighbourfeatures.shape[2], neighbourfeatures.shape[3] smallh, smallw = h // 8, w // 8 # Downsample inputs by 8x smallneighbour = F.interpolate(neighbourfeatures, size=(smallh, smallw), mode='bilinear', aligncorners=False) smalltest = F.interpolate(testfeatures, size=(smallh, smallw), mode='bilinear', aligncorners=False) flownet = NonRigidRefinementNetwork(inchannels=smallneighbour.shape[1]) currentfeatures = smallneighbour # Iterative refinement loop at reduced resolution for in range(numiterations): flowsmall = flownet(currentfeatures, smalltest) currentfeatures = warp2d(currentfeatures, flowsmall) # Final flow estimation and upsampling to full resolution finalflowsmall = flownet(currentfeatures, smalltest) finalflowfull = F.interpolate(finalflowsmall, size=(h, w), mode='bilinear', aligncorners=False) # Warp original full-resolution neighbour features refinedfeatures = warp2d(neighbourfeatures, finalflowfull) return refinedfeatures, finalflowfull Parameters: Optical flow estimation resolution: 8x downsampled relative to the input feature resolution. Number of iterations: 32. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Domain Gap: Standard optical flow methods expect clean images, but NeRF renders can be blurry, creating a domain gap. This method is specifically trained to handle this. Camera Pose Errors: Errors in COLMAP pose estimation can lead to misalignments that 3D alignment cannot fully correct. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. The method involves 32 iterations of a lightweight convolutional network and warping operations. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Requires storing the feature maps and the flow field. Strengths: Effectively reduces ghosting artifacts caused by misalignment from camera pose errors and non-rigid motion. It handles the domain gap between blurry rendered images and sharp neighbours better than general-purpose optical flow. Limitations: Relies on the quality of the initial 3D alignment and feature extraction. Performance depends on the specific training of the flow network. When to use: When there are significant misalignments due to camera pose errors or non-rigid motion that 3D alignment cannot resolve, and when the domain gap between rendered and real images is significant. Non-Rigid Refinement was introduced in the RoGUENeRF paper by S. Catley-Chandar et al.. It builds upon the Iterative Alignment Strategy [6957-iterative-alignment-strategy.md] and is part of the broader effort to enhance NeRF quality by addressing alignment issues. The optical flow network architecture is based on the work presented in [6]. name: Global Pose and Scene Refinement
head: LU-NeRF+Sync, final refinement
body: This method performs the final optimization step in the LU-NeRF pipeline to achieve high-fidelity novel view synthesis by jointly refining camera poses and the neural radiance field (NeRF) representation. It solves the problem of residual errors in camera poses and scene geometry that remain after the initial synchronization stage. Unlike the Iterative Alignment Strategy, which focuses on sequential alignment, this method leverages the global consistency provided by synchronization to apply a comprehensive bundle adjustment-style refinement. It sets itself apart by using the BARF optimization procedure as its core engine, treating the synchronized poses as a sufficiently accurate initialization to converge to the ground truth. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: Global camera poses estimated from the synchronization stage (rotation and translation for each view), multi-view images corresponding to these poses, and the initial NeRF MLP parameters. Outputs: Refined camera poses (rotation and translation) and an optimized NeRF MLP representing the scene. Data Structures: The method utilizes the standard BARF data structures: NeRF MLP: A multi-layer perceptron mapping 3D coordinates and viewing directions to color and density. Camera Poses: A list of SE(3) transformation matrices or separate rotation (quaternion/axis-angle) and translation vectors for each image. Images: A list of RGB images aligned with the camera poses. Steps: 1. Initialization: Initialize the NeRF MLP and camera poses using the outputs from the synchronization stage. The synchronization ensures poses are close to ground truth, satisfying BARF's requirement for initialization. 2. Joint Optimization: Perform joint training of the NeRF MLP and refinement of the camera poses. This involves minimizing the photometric loss between rendered images and ground truth images while updating pose parameters. 3. Coarse-to-Fine Positional Encoding: Apply a coarse-to-fine positional encoding strategy during the optimization process. This involves starting with lower-frequency positional encodings and gradually introducing higher frequencies to guide the optimization from global structure to fine details. 4. Iteration: Repeat the joint optimization for a fixed number of iterations. Parameters: Refinement Iterations: 200,000 iterations. Positional Encoding: Coarse-to-fine strategy as defined in BARF. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def globalposeandscenerefinement(synchronizedposes, images, initialnerfparams): """ Performs final refinement using BARF optimization. Args: synchronizedposes: List of camera poses (rotation, translation) from synchronization. images: List of input images. initialnerfparams: Initial parameters for the NeRF MLP. Returns: refinedposes: Refined camera poses. refinednerfparams: Optimized NeRF MLP parameters. """ # Initialize poses and NeRF from synchronization results poses = synchronizedposes nerfparams = initialnerfparams # Setup optimizer for both poses and NeRF parameters optimizer = Optimizer([poses, nerfparams]) # Setup positional encoding scheduler (coarse-to-fine) # This is a standard BARF component posencscheduler = CoarseToFineScheduler() # Optimization loop for iteration in range(200000): # Update positional encoding frequency based on iteration currentfreq = posencscheduler.getfrequency(iteration) # Render images using current poses and NeRF renderedimages = renderimages(poses, nerfparams, currentfreq) # Calculate photometric loss loss = calculatephotometricloss(renderedimages, images) # Backpropagate and update parameters optimizer.zerograd() loss.backward() optimizer.step() return poses, nerfparams This variant refers to the specific application of the BARF optimization within the global refinement stage. It is distinguished by its reliance on the global consistency provided by the synchronization step, allowing it to handle larger initial pose errors compared to local methods. It is chosen when high-accuracy novel view synthesis is required after global synchronization. It uses the default BARF settings: 200k iterations with coarse-to-fine positional encoding. Time Complexity: The method runs for 200,000 iterations. Each iteration involves rendering and backpropagation through the NeRF, which is computationally expensive. The total time depends on the scene complexity and hardware. Memory Complexity: Requires memory for the NeRF MLP, camera poses, and intermediate rendering buffers. Performance: The method achieves accurate poses and scene representation suitable for realistic novel view synthesis. It outperforms methods like VMRF and GNeRF in terms of pose accuracy and rendering quality on standard datasets (e.g., Blender, Objectron). Strengths: High accuracy in both pose and scene reconstruction; leverages global consistency; robust to initial pose errors provided by synchronization. Limitations: Computationally intensive due to the large number of iterations; requires good initialization from the synchronization stage. When to use: When high-fidelity novel view synthesis is the primary goal and global pose estimates are available from a synchronization step. When not to use: When computational resources are limited or real-time performance is required. The method originates from the LU-NeRF paper, which proposes a pipeline for scene and pose estimation by synchronizing local unposed NeRFs. The global pose and scene refinement step is the final stage of this pipeline, referred to as LU-NeRF+Sync. It builds on the BARF (Bundle-Adjusting Neural Radiance Fields) method, which was introduced to handle pose errors in NeRF optimization. The approach was developed to address the limitations of existing methods that struggle with large pose errors or require precise initial poses. The method has been evaluated on datasets such as Blender and Objectron, demonstrating its effectiveness in achieving accurate pose and scene reconstruction. name: Joint Optimization of NeRF and Camera Parameters
head: Neural Radiance Fields Without Known Camera Parameters
body: This method jointly optimizes a Neural Radiance Field (NeRF) model and camera parameters (poses and focal length) for forward-facing images, eliminating the need for pre-computed camera poses via Structure-from-Motion (SfM) systems like COLMAP. It simplifies classical two-stage Novel View Synthesis (NVS) pipelines by treating camera extrinsics and intrinsics as learnable parameters alongside the neural network weights. Unlike Bundle Adjustment, which typically refines known poses, this approach initializes poses randomly or with coarse estimates and converges them simultaneously with the scene representation. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: A set of N training images \{Ii\}{i=1}^N with pixel coordinates \{p{i,m}\}, where M is the number of pixels per image. Outputs: Optimized NeRF network parameters \hat{\Theta}, camera poses \{\hat{\phi}i, \hat{t}i\}{i=1}^N (rotation and translation), and focal length \hat{f}. Data Structures: Camera Poses: \hat{\phi}i \in \mathbb{R}^3 (axis-angle representation) and \hat{t}i \in \mathbb{R}^3 for each image i. Focal Length: \hat{f} \in \mathbb{R}, a single scalar value. NeRF Network: A multi-layer perceptron F\Theta taking position and view direction as input, outputting color and density. Parameters: NeRF Architecture: A smaller variant of the original NeRF. Hidden layer dimensions are halved: the first 9 layers have 128 units (original 256), and the final layer has 64 units (original 128). Positional encoding frequencies and skip connections match the original NeRF implementation. Focal Length Initialization: Initialized to the input image width W. Scale Factor: A parameter s (or \tilde{s}) used to parameterize focal length, initialized to 1.0. Step-by-Step Method: 1. Ray Construction: For each image i and pixel m, construct the ray direction \hat{d}{i,m} using the current estimated pose \hat{\phi}i, translation \hat{t}i, focal length \hat{f}, and pixel coordinates p{i,m}. 2. Point Sampling: Sample points xh along the ray for heights h ranging from the near plane hn to the far plane hf. 3. NeRF Query: Query the NeRF network F\Theta with position xh and direction \hat{d}{i,m} to obtain color ch and density \sigmah. 4. Volume Rendering: Render the pixel value \hat{I}{i,m} using the collected colors and densities via standard volume rendering integration. 5. Loss Computation: Compute the loss \mathcal{L} between the rendered image \hat{I}i and the ground truth image Ii. 6. Optimization: Perform a backward pass and update parameters [\hat{\phi}i], [\hat{t}i], \hat{f}, and \hat{\Theta} using an optimizer (e.g., Adam). Focal Length Parameterization: Directly optimizing f in pixel units is numerically difficult due to large magnitudes. Two parameterizations are used: 1. 1st-order: f = s W, where s is initialized to 1.0. 2. 2nd-order (Preferred): f = \tilde{s}^2 W, where \tilde{s} is initialized to 1.0. This yields slightly better results (Mean PSNR 22.48 vs 22.26 on LLFF-NeRF). 3. Single vs. Dual: Optimizing a single focal length f yields no performance difference compared to optimizing separate horizontal fx and vertical fy focal lengths; f is chosen for simplicity. Evaluation Alignment: To eliminate camera mis-alignment effects during evaluation, optimized parameters are aligned with COLMAP estimates using a Sim(3) transformation via the Umeyama algorithm, followed by gradient-driven camera pose alignment minimizing photometric error on synthesized images while keeping the NeRF model fixed. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import torch import torch.nn as nn import torch.nn.functional as F def axisangletorotationmatrix(axisangle): # Standard Rodrigues' rotation formula implementation # Returns rotation matrix R from axis-angle vector pass def constructraydirection(poses, translations, focallength, pixelcoords, imagewidth, imageheight): # poses: (N, 3) axis-angle, translations: (N, 3), focallength: scalar # pixelcoords: (M, 2) (u, v) # Returns: (N, M, 3) ray directions in world space R = axisangletorotationmatrix(poses) Rinv = R.transpose(-2, -1) u = pixelcoords[:, 0] - imagewidth / 2.0 v = pixelcoords[:, 1] - imageheight / 2.0 raycam = torch.stack([u / focallength, v / focallength, torch.oneslike(u)], dim=-1) rayworld = torch.matmul(Rinv, raycam.unsqueeze(-1)).squeeze(-1) return rayworld def samplepointsalongray(raydirection, translation, nearplane, farplane, numsamples): # raydirection: (3,), translation: (3,) # Returns: (numsamples, 3) points in world space t = torch.linspace(nearplane, farplane, numsamples) points = translation.unsqueeze(0) + t.unsqueeze(1) raydirection.unsqueeze(0) return points def rendervolumerendering(colors, densities): # colors: (numsamples, 3), densities: (numsamples,) # Returns: (3,) rendered color delta = 1.0 # Assumes uniform sampling; in practice deltat = (far-near)/(numsamples-1) alpha = 1.0 - torch.exp(-densities delta) transmittance = torch.cumprod(1.0 - alpha + 1e-10, dim=0) weights = alpha transmittance renderedcolor = torch.sum(weights.unsqueeze(-1) colors, dim=0) return renderedcolor def jointoptimization(images, pixelcoords, imagewidth, imageheight, nearplane, farplane, numsamples, numiterations): N = images.shape[0] M = images.shape[1] images.shape[2] pixelcoordsflat = pixelcoords.view(N, M, 2) # Initialize parameters poses = nn.Parameter(torch.randn(N, 3)) translations = nn.Parameter(torch.randn(N, 3)) stilde = nn.Parameter(torch.tensor(1.0)) # NeRF Network (simplified MLP structure per) nerf = nn.Sequential( nn.Linear(3, 128), nn.ReLU(), nn.Linear(128, 128), nn.ReLU(), nn.Linear(128, 128), nn.ReLU(), nn.Linear(128, 128), nn.ReLU(), nn.Linear(128, 128), nn.ReLU(), nn.Linear(128, 128), nn.ReLU(), nn.Linear(128, 128), nn.ReLU(), nn.Linear(128, 128), nn.ReLU(), nn.Linear(128, 128), nn.ReLU(), nn.Linear(128, 64), nn.ReLU(), nn.Linear(64, 4) # 3 for color, 1 for density) optimizer = torch.optim.Adam([ {'params': nerf.parameters()}, {'params': poses}, {'params': translations}, {'params': [stilde]} ], lr=0.001) for step in range(numiterations): optimizer.zerograd() focallength = stilde 2 imagewidth totalloss = 0.0 for i in range(N): raydirs = constructraydirection( poses[i:i+1], translations[i:i+1], focallength, pixelcoordsflat[i], imagewidth, imageheight) renderedimage = torch.zeroslike(images[i]) for m in range(M): points = samplepointsalongray( raydirs[m], translations[i], nearplane, farplane, numsamples) # Standard NeRF uses positional encoding for position and direction posenc = torch.sin(torch.cat([points, points], dim=-1)) direnc = torch.sin(torch.cat([raydirs[m].expandas(points), raydirs[m].expandas(points)], dim=-1)) features = nerf(torch.cat([posenc, direnc], dim=-1)) colors = features[:,:3] densities = features[:, 3:] renderedpixel = rendervolumerendering(colors, densities) renderedimage[m] = renderedpixel loss = F.mseloss(renderedimage, images[i]) totalloss += loss totalloss.backward() optimizer.step() return nerf, poses, translations, stilde Time Complexity: Training is slower than fixed-camera NeRF due to the additional gradients flowing through camera parameters. A BLEFF scene with 27 training images takes approximately 5.5 hours on a single GPU. Memory Complexity: Increases slightly due to the storage of learnable pose parameters (6N floats) and the scale factor, but the dominant memory cost remains the NeRF network and intermediate rendering buffers. Strengths: Eliminates the dependency on SfM pipelines (e.g., COLMAP), which can fail on textureless or repetitive scenes. Simplifies the NVS pipeline to a single end-to-end optimization step. Limitations: Designed for static scenes and forward-facing images; cannot handle dynamic objects. Convergence may be sensitive to initialization. The method does not inherently handle radiometric calibration or viewpoint selection, which are addressed by sibling methods [1121-best-viewpoint-selection-via-opacity-entropy.md] and [1820-radiometric-self-calibration.md]. When to Use: When camera poses are unknown, unreliable, or when a simplified pipeline is preferred over a two-stage SfM+NeRF approach. When Not to Use: For dynamic scenes, or when high-precision metric reconstruction is required without careful evaluation alignment. The method was introduced in "NeRF--: Neural Radiance Fields Without Known Camera Parameters". It addresses the limitations of classical two-stage NVS systems that rely on pre-computed camera poses. The authors demonstrated that joint optimization is feasible and effective for forward-facing datasets like LLFF and BLEFF. The approach builds on the differentiable rendering framework of original NeRF but extends the optimization domain to include camera extrinsics and intrinsics. name: CT-NeRF
head: CT-NeRF Training Pipeline, Incremental Optimizing Neural Radiance Field and Poses with Complex Trajectory
body: CT-NeRF is an incremental reconstruction optimization pipeline that jointly optimizes camera poses and a neural radiance field (NeRF) from sequential RGB images without prior pose or depth input. It is specifically designed to handle complex trajectories involving large rotations where existing methods fail. Unlike its siblings, CT-NeRF escapes local minima by constructing a pose graph with edges between neighboring camera poses (enforcing inter-pose consistency) and by using reprojection loss derived from dense pixel-level correspondences, rather than relying solely on photometric loss. Inputs and Outputs Inputs: A sequence of n RGB images I = \{I1, I2, \dots, In\} and a pre-trained dense correspondence network (DKM). Outputs: Optimized camera poses P = \{P1, \dots, Pn\} and a NeRF model \Theta representing the 3D scene. Data Structures NeRF Model \Theta: An MLP mapping 3D position x \in \mathbb{R}^3 and view direction d \in \mathbb{R}^3 to color c \in \mathbb{R}^3 and volume density \sigma \in \mathbb{R}. Camera Pose Pi: A 3 \times 4 matrix [R, t] where R \in SO(3) and t \in \mathbb{R}^3, representing the camera-to-world transformation. Intrinsic Matrix K: Standard camera intrinsic parameters. Correspondence Set M: A set of tuples m = (q, p, \alpha) where q \in I1 is a pixel in image 1, p \in I2 is the corresponding pixel in image 2, and \alpha \in (0, 1] is the confidence score. Sparse Correspondence Set M{sparse}: A subset of M containing Nm samples with confidence \alpha > tm. Formulas Camera Projection: p = \pi(x, P, K), where x \in \mathbb{R}^3 is a space point and p \in \mathbb{R}^2 is a pixel. Volume Rendering (Color): \tilde{I}i(q) = \int{s{near}}^{s{far}} T(s) \sigma(r(s)) c(r(s), d) ds where r(s) = o + ds, o, d are obtained by backprojecting pixel q using Pi and K, and transmittance T(s) = \exp\left(-\int{s{near}}^{s} \sigma(r(h)) dh\right). Volume Rendering (Depth): \tilde{D}i(q) = \int{s{near}}^{s{far}} T(s) \sigma(r(s)) s ds. Photometric Loss: L{phot} = \frac{1}{n} \sum{i=1}^{n} \|\tilde{I}i(Pi, \Theta) - Ii\|2^2. Reprojection Loss: For a correspondence (q, p, \alpha) between I1 and I2: 1. Render depth z(q; \Theta) for pixel q in I1 using the depth rendering formula. 2. Backproject q to 3D point x using P1, K, z(q; \Theta). 3. Reproject x to I2 using P2, K to get p'. 4. Calculate geometric distance: L{rp}(I1, I2) = \frac{1}{Ns} \sum{s=1}^{Ns} \alphas \| \pi(\pi^{-1}(q, P1, K, z(q; \Theta)), P2, K) - p \|. Parameters Learning Rates: Network lr\Theta decays from 1 \times 10^{-3} to 1 \times 10^{-4}; Pose lr{\hat{P}} decays from 3 \times 10^{-3} to 1 \times 10^{-5}. Sampling: Inverse sampling of 128 points along each ray with range 1, 0). Batch Size: 1024. Correspondence Sampling: Nm = 10,000 correspondences with \alpha > tm = 0.2 are selected as M{sparse}. Iteration Sampling: Ns = \lfloor 256 / |E| \rfloor correspondences are randomly fetched from M{sparse} per iteration, where |E| is the number of images in the current optimization set. [Positional Encoding: Linearly adjust the positional encoding frequency control parameter \alpha from iteration 20K to 100K during post-optimization. Iteration Counts: For NeRFBuster scenes, N{init}=3, N{window}=4, \beta{init}=2000, \beta{tracking}=100, \beta{window}=200, \beta{global}=500, and \beta{post}=200,000. Algorithm Steps The pipeline consists of five sequential parts: 1. Scene Initialization: Initialize the NeRF \Theta and poses P using a small set of N{init} images. 2. Tracking: For a new image I{new}, estimate a rough initial pose P{new} using the previous pose P{prev}. 3. Window Optimization: Optimize poses and scene for a local window of images (including I{new} and N{window} previous frames) to refine local structure and pose consistency. 4. Global Optimization (Bundle Adjustment): Incorporate all currently added images E{global} = \{I1, \dots, Ii\} into the optimization set and simultaneously optimize all poses and the scene. 5. Post Optimization: After all frames are added, iteratively refine the entire scene and all poses by gradually reducing learning rates and increasing positional encoding frequency until convergence. Scene Initialization theta = NeRFMLP() poses = [None] len(images) poses[0] = np.eye(3, 4) for i in range(1, Ninit): poses[i] = estimateroughpose(poses[i-1], images[i-1], images[i], K) optimizestep(theta, poses, list(range(Ninit)), K, dkmnetwork, betainit, lrthetainit, lrposeinit, pealphainit) # 2. Incremental Processing for i in range(Ninit, len(images)): # Tracking poses[i] = estimateroughpose(poses[i-1], images[i-1], images[i], K) optimizestep(theta, poses, [i], K, dkmnetwork, betatracking, lrthetainit, lrposeinit, pealphainit) # Window Optimization windowstart = max(0, i - Nwindow) windowindices = list(range(windowstart, i + 1)) optimizestep(theta, poses, windowindices, K, dkmnetwork, betawindow, lrthetainit, lrposeinit, pealphainit) # Global Optimization globalindices = list(range(0, i + 1)) optimizestep(theta, poses, globalindices, K, dkmnetwork, betaglobal, lrthetainit, lrposeinit, pealphainit) # 3. step/betapost) + lrthetafinal (step/betapost) lrpose = lrposeinit (1 - step/betapost) + lrposefinal (step/betapost) optimizestep(theta, poses, allindices, K, dkmnetwork, 1, lrtheta, lrpose, alpha) def optimizestep(theta, poses, indices, K, dkmnetwork, iterations, lrtheta, lrpose, pealpha): for in range(iterations): # Sample rays rays = sampleinversedepthrays(len(indices), batchsize=1024) # Render colors, depths = rendercoloranddepth(theta, rays, poses) # Photometric Loss lossphot = meansquarederror(colors, groundtruthcolors(rays, indices)) # Reprojection Loss lossrp = 0.0 sparsecorrs = samplesparsecorrs(indices, dkmnetwork, Nm, tm) for q, p, alpha in sparsecorrs: srcidx = sourceimageindex(q, indices) depthq = renderdepth(theta, q, poses[srcidx], K) x3d = backproject(q, poses[srcidx], K, depthq) tgtidx = targetimageindex(q, p, indices) pprime = project(x3d, poses[tgtidx], K) lossrp += alpha np.linalg.norm(pprime - p) lossrp /= len(sparsecorrs) # Update updateparameters(theta, poses, indices, lossphot + lossrp, lrtheta, lrpose, pealpha) def estimateroughpose(prevpose, imgprev, imgcurr, K): M = dkmnetwork(imgprev, imgcurr) Msparse = [m for m in M if m.confidence > 0.2] return solvepose(Msparse, K, prevpose) def sampleinversedepthrays(numimages, batchsize): # Standard NeRF inverse depth sampling return np.random.uniform(0.0, 1.0, size=(batchsize, 128)) def rendercoloranddepth(theta, rays, poses): # Standard volume rendering return rendercolor(rays, poses), renderdepthmap(rays, poses) def renderdepth(theta, q, pose, K): # Render depth for single pixel return 0.0 # Placeholder for differentiable depth render def backproject(q, pose, K, depth): # Unproject pixel to 3D return np.array([0.0, 0.0, 0.0]) def project(x3d, pose, K): # Project 3D to pixel return np.array([0.0, 0.0]) def samplesparsecorrs(indices, dkmnetwork, Nm, tm): # Sample correspondences between adjacent frames in indices return [] def updateparameters(theta, poses, indices, loss, lrtheta, lrpose, pealpha): # Gradient descent step pass Time Complexity: The method is iterative and incremental. Each step involves NeRF rendering and optimization. Global optimization scales with the number of images and the number of correspondences. Post-optimization runs for a large number of iterations (e.g., 200K for NeRFBuster scenes). Memory Complexity: Stores the NeRF MLP, all camera poses, and dense correspondence maps between adjacent frames. The correspondence set M can be large (full-resolution pixel-level), requiring significant memory or on-the-fly generation. Performance: Evaluated on NeRFBuster and Free-Dataset. Outperforms CF-NeRF, BARF, and Nope-NeRF in pose estimation accuracy and novel view synthesis for complex trajectories. Strengths: Handles large rotations and complex trajectories. Avoids local minima via inter-pose constraints and reprojection loss. Produces smooth view transitions unlike BARF which may overfit. Limitations: Requires dense correspondence network (DKM). Sensitive to initialization. Computationally intensive due to global optimization and post-optimization phases. When to use: Scenes with complex camera trajectories, large rotations, and no prior pose information. When not to use: Simple forward-facing scenes (BARF or standard NeRF may suffice). Real-time applications due to high computational cost. CT-NeRF was proposed to address the limitations of existing NeRF-based pose estimation methods (like CF-NeRF and BARF) which struggle with complex trajectories and local minima. It adopts the BARF coarse-to-fine positional encoding strategy during post-optimization. The method is implemented based on the BARF framework. CT-NeRF: Incremental Optimizing Neural Radiance Field and Poses with Complex Trajectory, https://doi.org/10.48550/arxiv.2404.13896, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial)

name: Levenberg-Marquardt Sparse Variant
head: Bundle Adjustment with Levenberg-Marquardt, LM Bundle Adjustment, Levenberg-Marquardt Algorithm, Non-linear Optimization of Metric Reconstruction
body: The Levenberg-Marquardt Sparse Variant is a non-linear least-squares optimization technique used to minimize reprojection error between observed and predicted image points, jointly optimizing 3D structure and camera parameters (pose and calibration). It sets itself apart from dense bundle adjustment by exploiting the sparsity of the Jacobian matrix to avoid inverting a 3n \times 3n matrix, instead solving a system involving a 7m \times 7m matrix, which is more efficient when the number of features significantly exceeds the number of images (n \gg m). Inputs: Measured image points x{i,j} for m cameras and n 3D points. Initial estimates for camera parameters ai and 3D point coordinates bj. Outputs: Optimized camera parameters ai and 3D point coordinates bj. Data Structures and Layout: 1. Camera Parameter Vector (ai): Contains 7 parameters per camera: translation (tx, ty, tz), quaternion rotation components (q0, q1, q2), and focal length f. The fourth quaternion component q3 is fixed under the unit length constraint. ai = (tx, ty, tz, q0, q1, q2, f)^T 2. 3D Point Parameter Vector (bj): Contains 3 parameters per point: coordinates (Xx, Xy, Xz). bj = (Xx, Xy, Xz)^T 3. Global Parameter Vector (P): Concatenates all camera and point parameters. P = (a1^T, \dots, am^T, b1^T, \dots, bn^T)^T 4. Measurement Vector (X): Accumulates measured image point coordinates across all cameras. X = (x{1,1}, \dots, x{1,n}, \dots, x{m,1}, \dots, x{m,n})^T Projection Model: The predicted image coordinates (x, y) are calculated using simplified pinhole camera equations (assuming no skew, centered principal point, and normalized coordinates): x = \frac{f(iX X + iY Y + iZ Z + tX)}{kX X + kY Y + kZ Z + tZ} y = \frac{f(jX X + jY Y + jZ Z + tY)}{kX X + kY Y + kZ Z + tZ} where (X, Y, Z) are the 3D point coordinates, (tX, tY, tZ) are translation components, f is focal length, and i, j, k are rotation matrix rows derived from the quaternion parameters. Optimization Criterion: The goal is to minimize the sum of squared reprojection errors: \min \sum{i=1}^m \sum{j=1}^n d(x{i,j}, Pi^M Xj)^2 where Pi^M is the metric camera projection matrix and Xj are the 3D points. Algorithm Steps: 1. Initialize: Set damping parameter \lambda = 10^{-3}. 2. Compute Jacobian and Residuals: Calculate the Jacobian matrix J and residual vector \varepsilon based on current parameters P. The Jacobian has a sparse structure where \frac{\partial \hat{x}{ki}}{\partial ak} \neq 0 and \frac{\partial \hat{x}{ki}}{\partial bi} \neq 0, while cross-terms are zero. 3. Form Normal Equations: Construct the partitioned normal equations: \begin{bmatrix} U^ & W \\ W^T & V^ \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} \deltaa \\ \deltab \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} \mathcal{E}a \\ \mathcal{E}b \end{bmatrix} where the blocks are defined as: Uk = \sumi \left( \frac{\delta \hat{x}{ki}}{\delta ak} \right)^T \left( \frac{\delta \hat{x}{ki}}{\delta ak} \right) Vi = \sumk \left( \frac{\delta \hat{x}{ki}}{\delta bi} \right)^T \left( \frac{\delta \hat{x}{ki}}{\delta bi} \right) W{ki} = \left( \frac{\delta \hat{x}{ki}}{\delta ak} \right) \left( \frac{\delta \hat{x}{ki}}{\delta bi} \right) \mathcal{E}{ak} = \sumi \left( \frac{\delta \hat{x}{ki}}{\delta ak} \right)^T \mathcal{E}{ki} \mathcal{E}{bi} = \sumi \left( \frac{\delta \hat{x}{ki}}{\delta bi} \right)^T \mathcal{E}{ki} U^ and V^ are block-diagonal, while W is generally not sparse. 4. Solve for Shift Vector (\Delta P): Use Gaussian elimination to solve the system efficiently. Left-multiply by \begin{bmatrix} I & -WV^{-1} \\ 0 & I \end{bmatrix} to obtain: (U^ - WV^{-1}W^T)\deltaa = \mathcal{E}a - WV^{-1}\mathcal{E}b V^ \deltab = \mathcal{E}b - W^T \deltaa Solve for \deltaa first, then substitute to find \deltab. The term (U^ - WV^{-1}W^T) is a 7m \times 7m matrix. 5. Update Parameters: Apply the shift \Delta P = (\deltaa^T, \deltab^T)^T to P. 6. Check Error: If the error decreases, accept the new parameters and set \lambda \leftarrow \lambda / 10. If the error increases, reject the step, set \lambda \leftarrow \lambda \times 10, and repeat from Step 3. 7. Convergence: Repeat until convergence criteria are met. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def levenbergmarquardtsparse(xmeasured, Pinitial, m, n, maxiter=100): """ xmeasured: List of lists, xmeasured[i][j] is the measured point for camera i and point j. Pinitial: Global parameter vector P. m: Number of cameras. n: Number of 3D points. """ P = list(Pinitial) lambdadamp = 1e-3 for iteration in range(maxiter): # 1. Compute Jacobian blocks and residuals Ustar = [[0.0]7 for in range(7m)] Vstar = [[0.0]3 for in range(3n)] W = [[0.0](3n) for in range(7m)] Ea = [0.0](7m) Eb = [0.0](3n) for i in range(m): for j in range(n): ak = P[i7: (i+1)7] bj = P[m7 + j3: m7 + (j+1)3] xpred = projectcamera(ak, bj) r = [xmeasured[i][j][0] - xpred[0], xmeasured[i][j][1] - xpred[1]] Ja = jacobiancamera(ak, bj) # 2x7 matrix Jb = jacobianpoint(ak, bj) # 2x3 matrix # Accumulate blocks according to evidence formulas for p in range(7): for q in range(7): Ustar[i7+p][i7+q] += dot(Ja[:,p], Ja[:,q]) Ea[i7+p] += dot(Ja[:,p], r) for p in range(3): for q in range(3): Vstar[j3+p][j3+q] += dot(Jb[:,p], Jb[:,q]) Eb[j3+p] += dot(Jb[:,p], r) for p in range(7): for q in range(3): W[i7+p][j3+q] += dot(Ja[:,p], Jb[:,q]) # 2. Solve for camera update deltaa using Schur complement # Invert Vstar (block-diagonal 3x3 blocks) Vstarinv = [invert3x3(Vstar[j3:(j+1)3, j3:(j+1)3]) for j in range(n)] # Compute Schur complement: S = U - W V^-1 W^T S = [row[:] for row in Ustar] for i in range(m): for k in range(m): for j in range(n): Wblock = [row[j3:(j+1)3] for row in W[i7:(i+1)7]] S[i7:(i+1)7] -= matmul(Wblock, matmul(Vstarinv[j], transpose(Wblock[k7:(k+1)7]))) # Compute RHS for camera updates: rhsa = Ea - W V^-1 Eb rhsa = [0.0](7m) for i in range(m): rhsa[i7:(i+1)7] = list(Ea[i7:(i+1)7]) for j in range(n): Wblock = [row[j3:(j+1)3] for row in W[i7:(i+1)7]] rhsa[i7:(i+1)7] -= matmul(Wblock, matmul(Vstarinv[j], Eb[j3:(j+1)3])) # 3. Solve (S + lambda I) deltaa = rhsa Sdamped = [row[:] for row in S] for idx in range(7m): Sdamped[idx][idx] += lambdadamp deltaa = solvelinearsystem(Sdamped, rhsa) # 4. Solve for structure updates deltab by substitution: V deltab = Eb - W^T deltaa rhsb = [0.0](3n) for j in range(n): rhsb[j3:(j+1)3] = list(Eb[j3:(j+1)3]) for i in range(m): Wblock = [row[j3:(j+1)3] for row in W[i7:(i+1)7]] rhsb[j3:(j+1)3] -= dot(transpose(Wblock), deltaa[i7:(i+1)7]) deltab = solvelinearsystem(Vstar, rhsb) # 5. Update parameters Pnew = list(P) for i in range(m): Pnew[i7:(i+1)7] = [x + y for x, y in zip(P[i7:(i+1)7], deltaa[i7:(i+1)7])] for j in range(n): Pnew[m7 + j3: m7 + (j+1)3] = [x + y for x, y in zip(P[m7 + j3: m7 + (j+1)3], deltab[j3:(j+1)3])] # 6. Check error reduction errorold = computereprojectionerror(P, xmeasured) errornew = computereprojectionerror(Pnew, xmeasured) if errornew < errorold: P = Pnew lambdadamp = lambdadamp / 10.0 else: lambdadamp = lambdadamp 10.0 if abs(errorold - errornew) < 1e-6: break return P def projectcamera(a, b): # Computes simplified pinhole projection from evidence tx, ty, tz, q0, q1, q2, f = a X, Y, Z = b # Rotation matrix rows derived from quaternion denom = kXX + kYY + kZZ + tZ x = f (iXX + iYY + iZZ + tX) / denom y = f (jXX + jYY + jZZ + tY) / denom return [x, y] def jacobiancamera(a, b): # Computes 2x7 Jacobian of projection w.r.t camera parameters return [[0.0]7 for in range(2)] def jacobianpoint(a, b): # Computes 2x3 Jacobian of projection w.r.t 3D point coordinates return [[0.0]3 for in range(2)] def invert3x3(M): # Standard 3x3 matrix inversion return [[0.0]3 for in range(3)] def solvelinearsystem(A, b): # Standard linear solver (e.g., LU decomposition) return [0.0]len(b) def computereprojectionerror(P, xmeasured): # Sum of squared distances between measured and predicted points return 0.0 Edge Cases and Pitfalls: If n (number of features) is not significantly larger than m (number of images), the solution may not be statistically stable. The sparse approach relies on n \gg m to be more efficient than solving dense normal equations. Time Complexity: The most expensive operation is inverting the term (U^ - WV^{-1}W^T), which results in a 7m \times 7m matrix. This is more efficient than solving the dense normal equations directly, which would require inverting a 3n \times 3n matrix. Memory Complexity: Proportional to the size of the sparse Jacobian blocks and the 7m \times 7m Schur complement matrix. Strengths: Efficient for large n and small m; handles non-linearities via adaptive damping. Limitations: Requires n \gg m for statistical stability; inversion of V^ must be efficient (block-diagonal). When to use: Bundle adjustment in Structure from Motion (SfM) with many 3D points and fewer cameras. When not to use: When n \approx m or when the Jacobian structure is not sparse. The method originates from the field of Structure from Motion (SfM), which aims to recover 3D structure and motion from 2D image projections without prior knowledge of the camera or scene. The Levenberg-Marquardt algorithm was proposed independently by Levenberg [Levenberg44] and Marquardt [Marquardt63] to adaptively control the damping parameter \lambda. The sparse variant was implemented to efficiently minimize reprojection error in metric reconstruction, as described in. name: Neighbor-Replacement Strategy
head: Neighbor Replacement
body: The Neighbor-Replacement Strategy is a post-processing step applied within cascaded Bundle Adjustment (BA) modules to correct poorly estimated camera poses. It identifies inferior views based on rendered image quality and replaces their poses with those of the most similar neighboring cameras. Unlike standard BA which refines poses iteratively, this strategy explicitly swaps poses to eliminate the detrimental impact of inaccurate initial estimates on scene representation. It is distinct from sibling methods like Best Viewpoint Selection via Opacity Entropy by focusing on pose correction via replacement rather than viewpoint selection, and differs from BARF (Bundle-Adjusting Neural Radiance Fields) by using a discrete replacement mechanism rather than continuous joint optimization of poses and fields. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A set of all camera views Q = \{qk | k = 1, 2,..., N\}, where each qk includes a camera pose estimate and an associated image. A classification of each view as either "superior" (Qs) or "inferior" (Qi) based on a prior quality criterion. Output: An updated set of camera pose estimates \tilde{Q} = \{\tilde{q}k | k = 1, 2,..., N\} where inferior poses have been replaced. Data Structures: Q: List of N views. Qs, Qi: Subsets of superior and inferior views. \tilde{Q}s, \tilde{Q}i: Updated subsets after non-maxima suppression. usedposes: A set tracking IDs of poses already utilized for replacement to prevent redundancy. Steps: 1. Identify Inferior Views: Apply the quality criterion from the preceding "Erroneous Pose Detection" step to label views in Q as superior (Qs) or inferior (Qi). 2. Non-Maxima Suppression: Inaccurate poses affect neighboring views, causing them to also appear low-quality. To prevent mislabeling accurate neighbors as inferior, when multiple neighboring camera poses are assigned low scores, assume only the one with the lowest score is inaccurate. Discard misidentified low-scoring poses to update classifications to \tilde{Q}s and \tilde{Q}i. 3. Neighbor Search: For each inferior view q^ei \in \tilde{Q}i, search for the nearest neighbor view q^e{sim} in the full set Q. Measure similarity using the combined criterion from Erroneous Pose Detection. Perform matching on rotated images with equivalently rotating camera poses to expand the search space and improve matching accuracy. 4. Pose Replacement: Replace camera poses in \tilde{Q}i with their nearest neighbors in Q. Obtain the updated set \tilde{Q} = \{\tilde{q}k | k = 1, 2,..., N\}. 5. Replacement Memory: Keep track of the pose used for replacement for each erroneous viewpoint and skip poses that have already been utilized to prevent redundant erroneous replacements and optimization stagnation. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def neighborreplacement(views, scores, angles, threshold, radius): """ views: list of dicts {'id': int, 'pose': list, 'image': array} scores: dict mapping view id to float (lower is worse) angles: list of rotation angles in radians threshold: quality threshold from prior step radius: spatial radius for neighbor grouping in NMS Returns: updatedviews: list of view dicts with replaced poses """ # Step 1: Initial Classification superior = [v for v in views if scores[v['id']] > threshold] inferior = [v for v in views if scores[v['id']] <= threshold] # Step 2: Non-Maxima Suppression finalinferior = [] finalsuperior = list(superior) remaining = list(inferior) while remaining: # Find view with lowest score minview = min(remaining, key=lambda v: scores[v['id']]) finalinferior.append(minview) # Identify neighbors in remaining set within spatial radius neighbors = [v for v in remaining if v is not minview and posedistance(minview['pose'], v['pose']) < radius] for n in neighbors: remaining.remove(n) finalsuperior.append(n) # Step 3 & 4: Replacement with Memory usedposes = set() updatedviews = [] for infview in finalinferior: bestsimview = None bestscore = -float('inf') for cand in views: if cand['id'] in usedposes: continue currentscore = -float('inf') for angle in angles: rotimg = rotateimage(cand['image'], angle) rotpose = rotatepose(cand['pose'], angle) sim = computesimilarity(infview['image'], rotimg, infview['pose'], rotpose) if sim > currentscore: currentscore = sim if currentscore > bestscore: bestscore = currentscore bestsimview = cand if bestsimview is not None: newview = dict(infview) newview['pose'] = bestsimview['pose'] updatedviews.append(newview) usedposes.add(bestsimview['id']) else: updatedviews.append(infview) for v in finalsuperior: updatedviews.append(v) return updatedviews def posedistance(p1, p2): return sum((a - b)2 for a, b in zip(p1, p2))0.5 def rotateimage(img, angle): # Standard image rotation operation return img def rotatepose(pose, angle): # Standard pose rotation operation return pose def computesimilarity(img1, img2, pose1, pose2): # Combined criterion from Erroneous Pose Detection return 0.0 Parameters: Threshold: Quality score threshold for initial classification. Defined in the Erroneous Pose Detection step. Rotation Angles: Discrete angles tested for rotational matching. Not given in the sources. Radius: Spatial radius for neighbor grouping in non-maxima suppression. Not given in the sources. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Misidentification: Inaccurate poses can cause neighboring accurate poses to be labeled as inferior. Non-maxima suppression mitigates this. Redundant Replacement: Incorrect matching can lead to cycles or redundant swaps. The replacement-memory technique prevents this. No Ground Truth: Since ground-truth poses are unknown, identification relies entirely on rendered image quality. Strengths: Significantly improves pose optimization in the presence of large camera pose noise. Enhances the initialization for subsequent BA stages in a cascade. Limitations: Relies on the accuracy of the initial quality criterion. May fail if the nearest neighbor is also inaccurate and not caught by memory/guards. When to Use: When initial camera poses are noisy or insufficient, and ground-truth poses are unavailable. The Neighbor-Replacement Strategy was introduced in the CBARF (Cascaded Bundle-Adjusting Neural Radiance Fields) model. It addresses the problem that poor initialization of camera poses significantly impacts BA performance. The method is part of a cascade of BA modules, where replacement is applied between each pair of modules. It was developed to handle large camera pose noise in 3D reconstruction and novel view synthesis. name: L2G-NeRF
head: Local-to-Global Registration for Bundle-Adjusting Neural Radiance Fields
body: L2G-NeRF is a bundle-adjusting method for Neural Radiance Fields that jointly optimizes neural 3D representations and camera poses by combining a local photometric alignment objective with a global geometric alignment objective. It solves the problem of suboptimal solutions caused by poor initialization, which plagues purely parametric methods, and the inability to handle large displacements, which affects purely non-parametric methods. It sets itself apart by using a two-stage process: first, a pixel-wise flexible alignment (non-parametric) to initialize the solution, followed by a frame-wise constrained parametric alignment (global) to enforce geometric consistency. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: A set of M images \{Ii\}{i=1}^M, query pixel coordinates \{xj\}{j=1}^N (for 2D) or 3D ray coordinates (for 3D), and initial camera poses (typically identity). Outputs: Optimized neural field parameters \Theta, optimized camera poses \{Ti\}{i=1}^M, and local transformation fields \{T{ji}\}. Data Structures: 1. Neural Field MLP (fR): 3D NeRF: Input is 3D coordinate z \in \mathbb{R}^3. Output is 4D vector [c; \sigma] \in \mathbb{R}^4, where c is RGB color and \sigma is volume density. 2D Image: Input is 2D coordinate x \in \mathbb{R}^2. Output is 3D vector (RGB color). 2. Warp Neural Field MLP (fW): Input is 2D coordinate x \in \mathbb{R}^2 and frame-dependent embedding \elli \in \mathbb{R}^d. Output is a Lie algebra vector (se(2) for 2D rigid or sl(3) for 2D homography). 3. Camera Pose: Ti \in SE(3) for 3D, parametrized as [R|t]. R = \exp(r) via exponential map from \mathfrak{so}(3) to SO(3), t \in \mathbb{R}^3. 4. Local Transformation: T{ji} \in SE(2) or SL(3) for 2D, modeled by W(xj; \elli, \Phi). Numbered Steps: 1. Initialization: Initialize all camera poses to identity: Ti = I \quad \forall i. Perturb initial poses using right multiplication to alter viewing directions and distances. Additive noise is sampled from r \sim \mathcal{N}(0, nr I) and t \sim \mathcal{N}(0, nt I), where nr and nt are base multipliers. Initialize neural field parameters \Theta and warp field parameters \Phi. 2. Stage 1: Local Alignment (Non-Parametric): For each image i and pixel j, predict a local transformation T{ji} using the warp neural field: T{ji} = W(xj; \elli, \Phi) = \exp(fW(xj; \elli, \Phi)) where \exp(\cdot) maps the Lie algebra output to the Lie group (SE(2) or SL(3)). Optimize \Theta, \Phi, and \{\elli\} by minimizing the photometric reconstruction error between the rendered image and the target image Ii: \mathcal{L}{local} = \sum{i=1}^M \sum{j=1}^N \| R(T{ji} xj; \Theta) - Ii(xj) \|^2 For 3D NeRF, the rendering function R(T{ji} xj; \Theta) is computed via volume rendering. Given a ray defined by pixel x and depth z, the 3D point is z x. The color is: R(x) = \int{z{near}}^{z{far}} T(x, z) \sigma(zx) c(zx) dz where T(x, z) = \exp(-\int{z{near}}^z \sigma(z'x) dz'). Numerically, this is discretized using K points sampled along the ray at depths \{z1,..., zK\}: R(x) = g(y1,..., yK), \quad yk = fR(T zk x; \Theta) where g is the differentiable and deterministic compositing function. 3. Stage 2: Global Alignment (Parametric): Solve for the global frame-wise transformation T^i for each image i by minimizing the alignment error between the local transformations T{ji} and the global transformation Ti applied to the coordinates. This is an orthogonal Procrustes problem: T^i = \arg \min{Ti} \sum{j=1}^N \| T{ji} xj - Ti xj \|^2 The optimal rigid transformation T=[R|t] is computed in closed form using SVD. Let \bar{x} and \overline{Tx} be the centroids of \{xj\} and \{T{ji} xj\} respectively. Compute the covariance matrix H: H = \sum{j=1}^N (xj - \bar{x})(T{ji} xj - \overline{Tx})^T = U S V^T Then: R = V U^T, \quad t = -R\bar{x} + \overline{Tx} (Note: For homography, a similar linear system Aj h = 0 is solved). Apply a soft constraint to the local alignment by adding the global objective to the loss: \mathcal{L}{global} = \lambda \sum{i=1}^M \sum{j=1}^N \| T{ji} xj - T^i xj \|^2 Jointly optimize \Theta, \{Ti\}, \Phi, and \{\elli\} by minimizing the combined loss: \min{\{T{ji}\}, \Theta, \{Ti\}} \mathcal{L}{local} + \mathcal{L}{global} The pipeline executes sequentially: Stage 1 optimizes local transformations, and Stage 2 solves for global transformations to constrain them. 4. Convergence Schedule: Linearly increase noise multipliers nr and nt by a common factor \{nc\}{c=2}^9 starting from base values nr=0.01, nt=0.1 to aid convergence. Parameters: \lambda: Weighting factor for the global constraint. Set to 1 \times 10^2 for synthetic/object-centric scenes. For forward-facing LLFF scenes, floated between 1 \times 10^2 and 1 \times 10^5. nr: Base rotation noise multiplier. Scene-dependent, typically 0.01 to 0.09. nt: Base translation noise multiplier. Scene-dependent, typically 0.3 to 0.7. K: Number of points sampled along a ray for volume rendering discretization. \Theta: Neural field MLP weights. \Phi: Warp neural field MLP weights. \elli: Frame-dependent embedding for frame i. Pitfalls and Edge Cases: Poor Initialization: Parametric methods alone fail if initialized poorly. Large Displacements: Non-parametric methods alone fail with large displacements. Identity Initialization for 360° Scenes: L2G-NeRF fails to recover camera poses from identity transformation for inward-facing 360° scenes with large rotation displacements. High \lambda: A large \lambda (1 \times 10^5) improves geometric accuracy but reduces robustness, potentially causing divergence (e.g., on the Flower scene). Removing Global Objective: Removing the global alignment objective causes the optimization to get stuck at suboptimal poses and produce ghosting artifacts. Time Complexity: More efficient than global registration methods (like BARF) because it computes gradients w.r.t. local pose rather than global pose. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Measured Performance: On NVIDIA GeForce RTX 2080 Ti, L2G-NeRF takes ~4.5 hours for synthetic objects and ~8 hours for real-world scenes. BARF takes ~8 and ~10.5 hours respectively. Robustness: Tolerates larger noise perturbations before divergence than BARF (fails at nc=8 vs nc=4 for L2G-NeRF vs BARF). Strengths: High-fidelity reconstruction, resolves large camera pose misalignment, robust to poor initialization. Limitations: Fails on inward-facing 360° scenes with large rotations from identity init; sensitive to \lambda setting. When to use: When camera poses are unknown or poorly estimated, and standard NeRF optimization fails due to initialization issues. Suitable for both 2D neural images and 3D NeRF. L2G-NeRF was proposed in the paper "Local-to-Global Registration for Bundle-Adjusting Neural Radiance Fields". It addresses the limitations of existing bundle-adjusting NeRF methods, which are susceptible to suboptimal solutions if poorly initialized (parametric methods) or unable to handle large displacements (non-parametric methods). The method builds on the concept of photometric bundle adjustment. Local-to-Global Registration for Bundle-Adjusting Neural Radiance Fields, https://doi.org/10.1109/cvpr52729.2023.00799, fetched 2026-10-29

name: CBARF
head: CBARF, Cascaded BA
body: CBARF is a 3D reconstruction method that optimizes imperfect camera poses using a cascaded bundle-adjustment (BA) structure to progressively refine poses and rectify erroneous ones. It builds on BARF by introducing a coarse-to-fine optimization strategy with distinct modulation factors for each stage, allowing it to handle larger initial pose errors (e.g., 30.4° rotation deviation) where standard BARF may overfit. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: A set of images with imperfect camera poses \hat{P}, a NeRF backbone (BARF), and scene geometry parameters. Outputs: Refined camera poses Q, a trained NeRF model, and optionally synthetic images via a Voxel Grid Module (DVGO). Data Structures: Camera Pose: Represented as P \in \mathbb{R}^{3 \times 4}, defined as P = [Rp \ tp] where Rp \in SO(3) and tp \in \mathbb{R}^3. The last row of the standard 4 \times 4 projection matrix is dropped. Noise/Refinement Parameters: Represented in the Lie algebra \mathfrak{se}(3) as n \in \mathbb{R}^6. Transform Matrix: Derived from \mathfrak{se}(3) parameters, represented as N = [Rn \ tn]. Numbered Steps: 1. Simulate Imperfect Poses (Initialization): Generate noise n \in \mathfrak{se}(3) from a 6-dimensional random normal distribution: n = 0.35 \mathcal{N}(0, I) \in \mathbb{R}^6 Transform n into a camera transform matrix N = [Rn \ tn]. Compose this with the reference pose P = [Rp \ tp] to obtain the imperfect pose \hat{P}: \hat{P} = [Rp Rn \ tp + tn] Note: The coefficient 0.35 corresponds to an average deviation of 30.4° in rotation and 0.56 in translation. 2. Define Refined Pose Composition: Optimize camera poses by training camera refine parameters p \in \mathfrak{se}(3). Convert p into a transform matrix Pr = [Rr \ tr]. Compose Pr with \hat{P} to obtain the refined pose Q: Q = [Rp Rn Rr \ tp + tn + tr] 3. Cascaded Optimization Structure: Use a coarse-to-fine structure with compact BA modules, using the BARF network as the backbone. The process consists of three stages: Coarse, Recursive, and Fine. 4. Learning Rate Schedule: Calculate the learning rate using exponential interpolation with a modulation factor \alpha to bias learning towards the initial high value. The modulation factors for the three stages are: Coarse stage: \alpha = 10.0 Recursive stage: \alpha = 3.0 Fine stage: \alpha = 1.0 A factor of 1.0 corresponds to the original exponential learning rate used in BARF. 5. Handling Incomplete Poses (Optional): For incomplete camera poses, randomly drop 10% of poses to form a test set F, assigning an initial pose P{ini} to F. The remaining images form the training set T. Jointly optimize poses for both T and F during training. 6. Evaluation Alignment: Use Procrustes analysis to align optimized poses with ground-truth before evaluation to remove global offset. Pseudocode: Unverified code.
