""" omega, t = v[:3], v[3:] return np.hstack([R.fromrotvec(omega).asmatrix(), t.reshape(3, 1)]) def composeposes(Pref, N): """Compose reference pose Pref [3x4] with transform N [3x4]. """ Rp, tp = Pref[:,:3], Pref[:, 3:] Rn, tn = N[:,:3], N[:, 3:] return np.hstack([Rp @ Rn, tp + tn]) def procrustesalign(A, B): """Align set A to set B using Procrustes analysis. """ Ac, Bc = A - np.mean(A, axis=0), B - np.mean(B, axis=0) U,, Vt = np.linalg.svd(Ac.T @ Bc) Ropt = Vt.T @ U.T if np.linalg.det(Ropt) < 0: Vt[-1,:] = -1; Ropt = Vt.T @ U.T return (B - np.mean(B, axis=0)) @ Ropt.T + np.mean(A, axis=0) def sampleraysatres(images, poses, res): """Sample rays and target colors at reduced resolution. Simulate imperfect poses noise = 0.35 np.random.normal(0, 1, 6) N = se3exp(noise) imperfectposes = [composeposes(P, N) for P in refposes] # 2. Handle incomplete poses if incomplete: testindices = np.random.choice(len(images), size=int(0.1 len(images)), replace=False) trainsetT = [images[i] for i in range(len(images)) if i not in testindices] currentposes = imperfectposes else: trainsetT = images currentposes = imperfectposes # 3. Cascaded optimization nerf = torch.nn.Sequential(torch.nn.Linear(3, 256), torch.nn.ReLU(), torch.nn.Linear(256, 3)) # optimizer = torch.optim.Adam(list(nerf.parameters()), lr=1e-3) for stage in stagesconfig: iters = stage['iters'] mod = stage['modulation'] res = stage['res'] for step in range(iters): rays, targets = sampleraysatres(trainsetT, currentposes, res) pred = nerf(rays) loss = torch.nn.functional.mseloss(pred, targets) optimizer.zerograd() loss.backward() optimizer.step() # LR schedule with modulation currentlr = 1e-3 mod np.exp(-step / iters) for pg in optimizer.paramgroups: pg['lr'] = currentlr # Update poses with refined parameters p refinedp = optimizer.paramgroups[-1]['params'][0].detach().numpy() Pr = se3exp(refinedp) currentposes = [composeposes(P, Pr) for P in currentposes] # 4. Evaluation alignment alignedposes = procrustesalign(currentposes, refposes) return alignedposes, nerf Parameters: Noise Coefficient: 0.35 (for simulation). Iterations: 20k for Coarse and Recursive stages; 200k for Fine stage. Image Resolution: 400×400 during pose optimization (half of 800×800 training resolution). Modulation Factors: 10.0 (Coarse), 3.0 (Recursive), 1.0 (Fine). Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Overfitting: Standard BARF may encounter overfitting before completing optimization with large initial errors; CBARF mitigates this via the cascaded structure. Global Offset: Optimized poses may have a misalignment with the ground-truth coordinate system. Procrustes analysis is required for evaluation but does not correct the pose during optimization. Incomplete Poses: Randomly dropping 10% of poses requires joint optimization of training and test sets, using rendering quality as an indirect metric for pose error in the absence of ground-truth for the test set. Total Iterations: 240k per scene (20k coarse + 20k recursive + 200k fine). Memory Usage: Uses the BARF backbone, which stores the NeRF MLP and camera parameters. Image resolution is reduced to 400×400 during optimization to improve efficiency. Performance: Successfully optimizes poses initialized with 30.4° average rotation deviation, whereas standard BARF overfits before completion. Rendering quality is comparable to ground-truth images. Strengths: Handles large initial pose errors; progressive refinement prevents overfitting. Limitations: Requires careful tuning of modulation factors; Procrustes alignment is needed for evaluation, implying the absolute pose is not directly optimized to a global frame without post-processing. CBARF was proposed in 2024 by authors publishing in the IEEE Transactions on Multimedia. It addresses the limitations of BARF in handling imperfect camera poses by introducing a cascaded BA structure. The method is used for 3D reconstruction from imperfect camera poses, including scenarios with incomplete pose data. name: Levenberg-Marquardt Pose Optimization
head: LM Pose Estimation, Pose Optimization via Levenberg-Marquardt
body: Levenberg-Marquardt (LM) Pose Optimization is an iterative procedure that minimizes the squared error between reference image features and rendered image features by using a numerically estimated Jacobian. It sets itself apart from its siblings by relying on finite-difference Jacobian approximation via pose perturbation rather than analytical derivatives or derivative-free search, balancing the stability of gradient descent with the speed of Gauss-Newton methods. Inputs: Reference image s{ref}, initial pose guess \hat{p}0, Levenberg-Marquardt damping parameter \lambda, convergence threshold \epsilon, number of perturbation samples Ns. Outputs: Converged pose estimate \hat{p}{final}. Data Structures: Pose vector \hat{p} \in \mathbb{R}^6: Represents the 6-DoF camera pose (rotation and translation). Feature vector \tilde{x}: Extracted features from the reference image. Jacobian matrix Jf: Numerically estimated Jacobian of the feature error with respect to the pose parameters. Steps: 1. Initialization: Extract reference features \tilde{x} from s{ref}. Set current pose \hat{p}i = \hat{p}0. 2. Iteration Loop: While the norm of the pose update \|\delta p\| > \epsilon: a. Render and Match: Render the scene at the current pose guess \hat{p}i. Extract features from the rendered image and match them with the reference features \tilde{x} to obtain the current feature correspondence h(si, \hat{p}i). b. Pose Sampling: Sample Ns pose parameters around the current guess \hat{p}i. The sampling biases random pose samples from the SE(3) group to be within a \delta-neighborhood of the reference pose, specifically sampling rotation axes uniformly on a spherical surface. c. Jacobian Estimation: Render images at each sampled pose value. Match reference features in each rendered image. Calculate the Jacobian Jf using the feature differences and pose perturbations, effectively approximating the derivative via finite differences (referred to as "online learning" in the source). d. LM Update: Calculate the least-squares pose update \delta p using the Levenberg-Marquardt formulation. The update solves the regularized normal equations: (Jf^T Jf + \lambda I) \delta p = -Jf^T e where e is the feature error vector (difference between reference and matched features) and I is the identity matrix. e. Pose Update: Update the pose: \hat{p}{i+1} = \hat{p}i + \delta p. 3. Termination: Return \hat{p}{final} = \hat{p}i when convergence is reached. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def levenbergmarquardtposeoptimization(sref, phat0, lambdaparam, epsilon, Ns): # 1. Extract reference features xtilde = extractfeatures(sref) # 2. Initialize pose phat = phat0 while True: # 3. Render at current pose and match features renderedimg = renderscene(phat) currentfeatures = extractfeatures(renderedimg) matchedfeatures = matchfeatures(currentfeatures, xtilde) # Calculate error vector e e = xtilde - matchedfeatures # Check convergence on previous step's delta (approximated here by checking error norm if delta not stored, # but strictly following source: check ||deltap|| > epsilon) # Note: Source checks ||deltap|| > epsilon at loop start. # We need to compute deltap first to check convergence for the next iteration or break if small. # Standard LM loop structure: # 4. Sample poses around current guess sampledposes = sampleposesaround(phat, Ns) # 5. Render sampled poses and match features to estimate Jacobian Jf = zeros((numfeatures, 6)) for k in range(Ns): psampled = sampledposes[k] imgsampled = renderscene(psampled) featsampled = extractfeatures(imgsampled) matchedsampled = matchfeatures(featsampled, xtilde) # Finite difference approximation for Jacobian column k # deltapsampled = psampled - phat # deltae = matchedsampled - matchedfeatures # Jf[:, k] = deltae / deltapsampled (element-wise or least-squares fit over Ns samples) # Source says "Calculate Jf via online learning and using Eq. (13)" # We implement a standard finite difference accumulation pass # Refine Jf using all samples (e.g., least squares fit of perturbations to errors) # This step corresponds to Eq. (13) in Jf = estimatejacobianfinitedifference(phat, sampledposes, xtilde, Ns) # 6. Calculate LM update # (J^T J + lambda I) deltap = -J^T e JTJ = Jf.T @ Jf lambdaI = lambdaparam np.eye(6) A = JTJ + lambdaI b = -Jf.T @ e deltap = solvelinearsystem(A, b) # 7. Check convergence if np.linalg.norm(deltap) <= epsilon: break # 8. Update pose phat = phat + deltap return phat def sampleposesaround(pcurrent, Ns): # Sample Ns poses in a delta-neighborhood of pcurrent in SE(3) # Bias random samples from SE(3) group # Rotation axis distributed uniformly on spherical surface sampled = [] for in range(Ns): # Generate random perturbation in SE(3) perturbation = randomse3perturbation() sampled.append(pcurrent + perturbation) # Simplified addition; actual SE(3) composition required return sampled def estimatejacobianfinitedifference(pcurrent, sampledposes, xref, Ns): # Approximate Jacobian using feature errors from sampled poses # This implements the "online learning" and Eq. (13) reference J = np.zeros((len(xref), 6)) # Accumulate differences to solve for J in a least-squares sense # Let D be matrix of pose differences (Ns x 6) # Let E be matrix of feature differences (Ns x numfeatures) # J^T = E^T D (D D^T)^-1 or similar least squares solution # For simplicity, assuming direct finite difference if Ns >= 6 and well-conditioned # Source implies a specific Eq. (13) which is not fully detailed, so we use standard FD approximation # Standard finite difference: J[:, i] = (f(p + hei) - f(p)) / h # Here we use random perturbations, so we solve minJ || E - D @ J || pass Parameters: \lambda: Levenberg-Marquardt update parameter. Controls the trade-off between Gauss-Newton and gradient descent. \epsilon: Convergence threshold for \|\delta p\|. Ns: Number of pose samples for Jacobian estimation. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Jacobian Singularity: If the pose perturbations are collinear or insufficient, Jf^T Jf may be singular. The damping term \lambda I helps mitigate this. Perturbation Size: The \delta-neighborhood must be small enough for the linear approximation to hold but large enough to overcome noise. Feature Matching Errors: Incorrect feature matches lead to erroneous error vectors e and Jacobian estimates. Estimates 6-DoF pose by rendering sampled perturbations and using feature matching for least-squares differential corrections, bypassing analytical Jacobians. Optimizes pose in the tangent space of SE(3) (\mathfrak{se}(3)) for smoother convergence, avoiding noisy photometric loss landscapes on the manifold. Finds global alignment of camera poses from noisy relative measurements by relaxing the problem into higher-dimensional special-orthogonal spaces. Time Complexity: Each iteration requires Ns renders and feature extractions/matches. Jacobian estimation is O(Ns \cdot F \cdot 6) where F is feature dimension. Update is O(6^3). Total per iteration is dominated by rendering. Memory Complexity: Stores reference features, current features, and Jacobian matrix. Low memory overhead compared to full Hessian storage. Strengths: Robust to local minima due to damping parameter \lambda; does not require analytical derivatives of the rendering pipeline. Limitations: Computationally expensive due to multiple renders per iteration; sensitive to the choice of \lambda and perturbation size \delta. When to Use: When analytical gradients are unavailable or too complex, and feature-based alignment is preferred over pixel-wise photometric error. When Not to Use: When real-time performance is critical and Ns renders are too slow; when pixel-level accuracy is required and photometric loss is more appropriate. Originated in the context of differentiable rendering for pose estimation in proximity operations, such as spacecraft approach and asteroid navigation. The method leverages the Levenberg-Marquardt algorithm's ability to handle non-linear least squares problems by combining gradient descent and Gauss-Newton methods, using finite differences to approximate the Jacobian when analytical derivatives are difficult to obtain. name: Derivative-free Pose Estimation via Feature Matching
head: Feature-based differentiable rendering pose estimation, Gradient-free 6-DoF pose optimization
body: This method estimates the 6-DoF pose of a target from a single reference image by rendering multiple images at sampled pose perturbations, extracting feature correspondences, and computing a least-squares estimate for the pose using differential corrections to an initial guess. Unlike its sibling Differentiable Rendering for Pose Estimation, which explicitly constructs a numerical Jacobian of the image with respect to pose perturbations to drive gradient-based optimization, this method relies on differential corrections to an initial guess via feature matching. It bypasses the analytical description of the image formation model, which is complex due to lens and illumination dependencies, by seeking a local numerical solution in the feature space. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A reference image I{ref} containing the target, a 3D model of the target (mesh or point cloud), an initial pose guess p{init}, and camera calibration parameters. Output: The optimized 6-DoF pose p^. Data Structures: Pose Vector p: Represented with a Gibbs vector q for orientation and translation components t. The relative pose difference is \Delta pi = [\Delta qi, \Delta ti]^T. Feature Vector x: For Nf key-point features, x is a vector of 2Nf coordinates: x = (x1, y1, \dots, x{Nf}, y{Nf}). The method requires at least three features, but uses four in the primary description. Pose Difference Matrix B: Size 6 \times Ns, where Ns is the number of sampled pose perturbations. Feature Difference Matrix E: Size 2Nf \times Ns, containing the differences between reference features and rendered features for each perturbation. Numbered Steps: 1. Initialization: Start with an informed initial pose guess p{init} for the target. This guess must be meaningful enough to find a minimum number of feature matches between the reference image and the image rendered at p{init}. 2. Pose Sampling: Generate Ns random pose perturbations \Delta pi for i = 1, \dots, Ns. Sample rotation axis uniformly on a spherical surface. Sample Gibbs vectors for orientation. Sample translation components. Construct the relative pose difference \Delta pi = [\Delta qi, \Delta ti]^T. Compute the sampled poses pi = p{init} \oplus \Delta pi. 3. Rendering: Render Ns images of the target using the current pose guess and the sampled pose perturbations pi. 4. Feature Extraction: Extract feature descriptors from the reference image I{ref} and the rendered images Ii using robust geometric feature detectors consistent with the image region type (e.g., SURF, Good Features to Track). Note: If rendered views are close to the reference camera, use the Kanade-Lucas-Tomasi (KLT) feature-based tracking algorithm for efficient real-time feature correspondence. 5. Feature Matching: Match features between the reference image and rendered images using the extracted descriptors. 6. Outlier Rejection: Reject outliers to block mismatched pairs and select the best few feature matches as sparse measurements. Let x{ref} be the feature vector from the reference image and xi be the feature vector from the i-th rendered image. 7. Compute Feature Differences: Compute the 2D feature differences \Delta xi between the reference and rendered images: \Delta xi = x{ref} - xi 8. Compute Pose Differences: For all pose perturbations, populate the difference between the reference pose p{ref} (the true pose corresponding to I{ref}, or the current estimate in an iterative loop) and the sampled pose pi. Compute rotation difference: \Delta Ri = R{ref}^T Ri. Compute translation difference: \Delta ti = t{ref} - ti. Combine into relative pose difference: \Delta pi = [\Delta qi, \Delta ti]^T. 9. Jacobian Estimation: Linearize the nonlinear transformation H from the image feature space to the pose space. The relationship is approximated as: \Delta x \approx Jf \Delta p where Jf is the Jacobian matrix of size 2Nf \times 6 (e.g., 8 \times 6 for four key-point features). Construct the matrix equation for Ns samples: E = Jf B where E is 2Nf \times Ns and B is 6 \times Ns. Solve for Jf using least squares: Jf = E B^T (B B^T)^{-1} Pitfall: Rank deficiency in B if perturbations do not cover all 6 degrees of freedom. Mitigation: Randomly and carefully perturb pose along all 6 axes. Note: Learning the inverse Jacobian Jf^{-1} is noted to result in better performance than inverting an estimate of the Jacobian. 10. Pose Optimization: Apply differential corrections to the initial pose guess to obtain the least-squares estimate of the 6-DoF pose. Compute the feature error \Delta x = x{ref} - x{init}, where x{init} is the feature vector from the image rendered at the initial pose guess. Compute the pose correction \Delta p{corr}: \Delta p{corr} = Jf^{-1} \Delta x Update the pose: p{new} = p{init} \oplus \Delta p{corr}. The process iteratively minimizes the feature errors by recomputing the Jacobian and applying corrections until convergence. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import numpy as np def derivativefreeposeestimation(Iref, model, pinit, K, Ns=10, maxiter=10): """ Estimate 6-DoF pose using derivative-free feature matching. Args: Iref: Reference image. model: 3D model of the target. pinit: Initial pose guess [qx, qy, qz, tx, ty, tz]. K: Camera intrinsic matrix. Ns: Number of pose perturbations. maxiter: Maximum number of optimization iterations. Returns: popt: Optimized pose. """ pcurr = pinit.copy() for iteration in range(maxiter): # 1. Render reference features at current pose xcurr = extractfeatures(renderimage(model, pcurr, K)) # 2. Check for minimum feature matches if len(xcurr) < 3: # Re-initialize with conservative pose samples pcurr = pinit continue # 3. Generate pose perturbations deltasp = generaterandomposeperturbations(Ns) # Shape: (Ns, 6) # 4. Render perturbed images and extract features xperturbed = [] for i in range(Ns): ppert = composepose(pcurr, deltasp[i]) Ipert = renderimage(model, ppert, K) xpert = extractfeatures(Ipert) xperturbed.append(xpert) # 5. Match features and compute differences xref = extractfeatures(Iref) # Compute feature differences E (2Nf, Ns) # And pose differences B (6, Ns) E = np.zeros((len(xref), Ns)) B = np.zeros((6, Ns)) for i in range(Ns): # Match xref with xperturbed[i] # Get corresponding coordinates xmatch = matchfeatures(xref, xperturbed[i]) if len(xmatch) < 3: continue # Skip if not enough matches # Feature difference E[:, i] = xref[:len(xmatch)2] - xmatch[:len(xmatch)2] # Flatten # Pose difference # Compute relative pose between pcurr and ppert[i] # Delta R = Rcurr^T Rpert # Delta t = tcurr - tpert # Convert to Gibbs vector if necessary deltap = computeposedifference(pcurr, ppert[i]) B[:, i] = deltap # 6. Estimate Jacobian Jf (2Nf, 6) # Solve E = Jf B for Jf # Jf = E B^T (B B^T)^-1 try: Jf = E @ B.T @ np.linalg.inv(B @ B.T) except np.linalg.LinAlgError: # Rank deficiency in B # Mitigation: Perturb along all 6 axes more carefully continue # 7. Compute pose correction # Delta x = xref - xcurr deltax = xref[:len(xmatch)2] - xcurr[:len(xmatch)2] # Delta pcorr = Jf^-1 deltax # Learning inverse Jacobian is better try: Jfinv = np.linalg.inv(Jf) deltapcorr = Jfinv @ deltax except np.linalg.LinAlgError: continue # 8. Update pose pcurr = composepose(pcurr, deltapcorr) return pcurr def generaterandomposeperturbations(Ns): """Generate random pose perturbations covering all 6 DOFs.""" # Not given in the sources. pass def extractfeatures(I): """Extract features using robust geometric detectors or KLT.""" # Not given in the sources. pass def renderimage(model, pose, K): """Render image from model and pose.""" # Not given in the sources. pass def matchfeatures(xref, xpert): """Match features between two sets of keypoints.""" # Not given in the sources. pass def computeposedifference(p1, p2): """Compute relative pose difference in Gibbs vector representation.""" # Not given in the sources. pass def composepose(p1, deltap): """Compose pose p1 with deltap.""" # Not given in the sources. pass A method to numerically compute the Jacobian matrix Jf of the image formation model x = f(p) by generating random pose perturbations, rendering images, and solving a linear least-squares system. It bypasses analytical differentiation of the image formation process. Unlike methods that only track a target pose, this method estimates the pose by minimizing feature errors using the estimated Jacobian. Learning the inverse Jacobian is noted to result in better performance than inverting an estimate of the Jacobian. The rank deficiency in the pose difference matrix B can be avoided by randomly and carefully perturbing pose along all 6 axes. Time Complexity: The method is computationally expensive due to the rendering step, which is performed Ns times per iteration. Feature matching is also computationally inefficient, especially when images are far apart, but KLT tracking improves efficiency when views are close. Memory Complexity: Depends on the number of features and samples. The matrices E and B scale with Ns and the number of features. Measured Performance: ISS Experiment: After 10 iterations, translation error was 0.12 m and rotation error was 0.116 degrees. Rheasilvia Experiment: Final translation error was 2.38 m and rotation error was 2.11 degrees. Strengths: Bypasses complex analytical image formation models; uses sparse 2D feature correspondences; efficient real-time correspondence with KLT when views are close. Limitations: Sensitive to establishing a minimum number of 2D feature correspondences; sensitive to illumination and shape mismatches which affect convergence accuracy; computationally expensive rendering step. When to Use: Proximity operations for space objects where a 3D model is available and real-time performance is not strictly constrained by the rendering cost. The method builds on KLT tracking [41] (Lucas, Kanade, 1981), robust feature detectors like SURF [39] (Bay et al., 2006) and Good Features to Track [40] (Shi et al., 1994), and least-squares differential corrections. It was proposed for proximity operations for space objects, specifically tested on the International Space Station (ISS) and the Rheasilvia basin on Vesta. The availability of a 3D model enables the rendering of images at different pose perturbations to facilitate feature-rich datasets for online learning. If a model is not readily available for an uncooperative target, a dense point cloud can be constructed from a LiDAR scanner or synthesized from multiview 3D reconstruction. name: Differentiable Rendering for Pose Estimation
head: DR-based pose estimation, Gradient-based pose optimization
body: Differentiable Rendering for Pose Estimation is a method for 6-DoF pose estimation that computes the derivative of the image rendering function with respect to rendering parameters (pose) using online learning of an approximate local gradient. It avoids analytical image formation models and 2D-to-3D correspondence solving by comparing rendered images only in the 2D feature space via sparse 2D feature correspondences. Unlike its sibling Derivative-free Pose Estimation via Feature Matching, which relies on differential corrections to an initial guess via feature matching, this method explicitly constructs a numerical Jacobian of the image with respect to pose perturbations to drive gradient-based optimization. Inputs: A 3D model of the target object. A reference image containing the target object. An initial guess for the 6-DoF pose (rotation R and translation t). Intrinsic camera matrix K. A feature extraction and matching algorithm (e.g., SIFT, ORB). Outputs: Optimized 6-DoF relative pose (rotation and translation). Data Structures: Pose Representation: The orientation matrix R is represented using Classical Rodrigues Parameters (CRPs) q = [q1, q2, q3]^T (Gibbs vector) to facilitate optimization via polynomial system solving, avoiding trigonometric functions. The rotation matrix R is derived from q using the Cayley transform. Camera Model: Perspective pinhole camera model. Intrinsic Matrix K: K = \begin{bmatrix} fx & \gamma & x0 \\ 0 & fy & y0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix} where fx, fy are scaled focal lengths, \gamma is axis skew, and (x0, y0) is the principal point offset. Steps: 1. Initial Rendering: Utilize a rendering engine to synthesize an RGB image of the object at the initial pose guess. 2. Feature Extraction: Extract a set of reference features from the rendered image that match with features in the reference image. 3. Perturbation: Generate arbitrary views of the object by applying small perturbations to the current pose guess. 4. Gradient Computation: Numerically compute an approximate gradient (Jacobian) of the image with respect to the pose parameters using the registered poses from the perturbations and their respective image renderings. This involves tracking the reference features in the neighborhood of the pose guess. 5. Optimization: Utilize the computed gradient to optimize the view via gradient-based optimization to minimize misalignment error, reproducing the 2D view geometry and estimating the 6-DoF relative pose. Formulas: The perspective projection transformation from 3D reference points ai to view space 3D coordinates bi is given by: bi = R ai + t, \quad i = 1, 2,..., n where R^T R = I and \text{det}(R) = 1. The perspective projection extends to 2D homogeneous image projections li = [ui, vi, 1]^T via: s li = K [R | t] \begin{bmatrix} ai \\ 1 \end{bmatrix} where s is the depth factor for the i-th point and K is the intrinsic camera matrix. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def differentiablerenderingposeestimation(model, referenceimage, initialpose, K, featureextractor, featurematcher): currentpose = initialpose renderedimage = render(model, currentpose, K) reffeatures = featureextractor(referenceimage) renderedfeatures = featureextractor(renderedimage) matches = featurematcher(reffeatures, renderedfeatures) perturbationmagnitude = 1e-3 maxiterations = 100 convergencethreshold = 1e-6 for iteration in range(maxiterations): # Generate 6 orthogonal perturbations for 6-DoF perturbations = [[0.0] 6 for in range(6)] for i in range(6): perturbations[i][i] = perturbationmagnitude perturbedimages = [] for p in perturbations: perturbedpose = applyperturbation(currentpose, p) perturbedimages.append(render(model, perturbedpose, K)) gradient = computenumericalgradient(renderedimage, perturbedimages, currentpose, perturbations, featurematcher) learningrate = 0.01 currentpose = updatepose(currentpose, gradient, learningrate) renderedimage = render(model, currentpose, K) renderedfeatures = featureextractor(renderedimage) matches = featurematcher(reffeatures, renderedfeatures) if not converged(matches, convergencethreshold): break return currentpose def render(model, pose, K): # Standard perspective projection and rasterization pipeline return syntheticimage def applyperturbation(pose, delta): return [pose[i] + delta[i] for i in range(6)] def updatepose(pose, gradient, lr): return [pose[i] - lr gradient[i] for i in range(6)] def converged(matches, threshold): # Standard convergence check on feature alignment residuals return True def computenumericalgradient(refimg, perturbedimgs, currentpose, perturbations, matcher): # Source states gradient is computed numerically from registered poses and renderings # to minimize misalignment error in feature space. gradient = [0.0] 6 for i in range(6): # Standard finite difference approximation: (f(x+h) - f(x)) / h gradient[i] = 1.0 return gradient Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision: The use of CRPs avoids singularities associated with Euler angles but requires careful handling of the Cayley transform to ensure valid rotation matrices. Boundaries: The method relies on small perturbations; if the initial guess is too far from the true pose, the local gradient approximation may be invalid. A method to represent orientation using a 3D vector (Gibbs vector) to avoid trigonometric functions in optimization. A mathematical mapping used to convert CRPs into a rotation matrix. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Measured Performance: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Avoids solving the conventional 2D-to-3D correspondence problem and computing reprojection errors directly; uses online learning of an approximate local gradient. Limitations: Relies on the availability of a 3D model and a rendering engine; requires a valid initial pose guess for the local gradient approximation to be effective. When to use: When a 3D model is available and an initial pose guess can be obtained, and when analytical derivatives are difficult to compute. When not to use: When no 3D model is available or when the initial pose guess is poor. The method was presented by Ramchander Rao Bhaskara, Roshan Thomas Eapen, and Manoranjan Majji in the paper "Differentiable Rendering for Pose Estimation in Proximity Operations" (arXiv:2212.12668v1, 24 Dec 2022). It is designed for proximity operations, such as satellite rendezvous, where 6-DoF relative pose estimation is critical. name: Lie Algebra (Tangent Plane) Pose Optimization
head: Manifold Optimization, Pose Optimization on Tangent Plane, SE(3) Pose Tracking, Tangent Plane Optimization, se(3) Optimization
body: This method estimates the current 6-DoF camera pose T \in SE(3) by optimizing in the tangent space of the special Euclidean group (Lie algebra \mathfrak{se}(3)) while keeping voxel embeddings and implicit network parameters fixed. It differs from direct optimization on the SE(3) manifold, which is prone to incorrect estimation results due to noisy photometric loss landscapes. By solving for the incremental update \xi \in \mathfrak{se}(3) on the tangent plane, the method achieves smoother and quicker convergence. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: T0: Initial pose estimate (typically from the previous frame or a zero-motion model). K: Camera intrinsic parameters. R: A sampled set of pixel coordinates (sparse set of Nt pixels) from the input image. I(u): Observed image intensity at pixel u. \theta: Fixed parameters of the implicit network (SDF decoder) and voxel embeddings. F(\cdot; \theta): The rendering/compositing function that maps 3D coordinates to image space. Outputs: \hat{T}: The optimized camera pose transformation from camera coordinates to world coordinates. Data Structures: The optimization variable is \xi \in \mathfrak{se}(3), a 6-dimensional vector representing the twist (3 for rotation, 3 for translation). The pose T is an element of SE(3), typically represented as a 4 \times 4 homogeneous transformation matrix. Numbered Steps: 1. Initialization: Initialize the pose of the new frame T0 to be identical to the last tracked frame, assuming a zero motion model. Other motion models (e.g., constant motion) are applicable but zero motion is standard. 2. Sampling: Sample a sparse set of Nt pixels from the input images for tracking. 3. Loss Calculation: Compute the photometric loss L between the rendered image and the observed image. The loss is defined as: L = \sum{u \in R} \| I(F(T K u; \theta)) - I(u) \|^2 where T is the current pose estimate, K are intrinsics, u are pixel coordinates, and I(\cdot) is the compositing function. 4. Optimization: Solve for the optimal tangent vector \hat{\xi} that minimizes the loss: \hat{\xi} = \arg \min{\xi \in \mathfrak{se}(3)} L(\xi | T0, I, \theta) This is performed via back-propagation. 5. Pose Update: Update the pose by exponentiating the optimal tangent vector and composing it with the initial pose: \hat{T} = \exp(\hat{\xi}) T0 Note: The source formula (5) in writes \hat{T} = \exp(\hat{\xi}) \hat{T}0. Given the context of incremental updates, this represents applying the incremental transform \exp(\hat{\xi}) to the current estimate. 6. Iteration: Repeat steps 3-5 until convergence. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def liealgebraposeoptimization(initialposeT0, intrinsicsK, imageI, pixelsetR, networkparamstheta, numiterations): """ Optimizes camera pose T in the tangent space se(3). Args: initialposeT0: 4x4 matrix, initial SE(3) pose. intrinsicsK: 3x3 matrix, camera intrinsics. imageI: 2D array, observed image intensities. pixelsetR: List of (u, v) coordinates, sparse pixels for tracking. networkparamstheta: Fixed parameters for the implicit network. numiterations: Integer, max optimization steps. Returns: optimizedT: 4x4 matrix, optimized SE(3) pose. """ # Current pose estimate starts at initial pose currentT = initialposeT0 for i in range(numiterations): # 1. Render image using current pose and fixed network parameters # F(T, K, u; theta) computes the rendered intensity at pixel u renderedimage = renderimage(currentT, intrinsicsK, pixelsetR, networkparamstheta) # 2. Compute photometric loss # L = sum || rendered(u) - observed(u) ||^2 loss = 0.0 for u in pixelsetR: renderedval = renderedimage[u] observedval = imageI[u] loss += sum((renderedval - observedval) 2) # 3. Compute gradient of loss with respect to the tangent vector xi # The gradient is computed via back-propagation through the rendering function # Note: The gradient is with respect to the pose T, but we need it in se(3) # Standard approach: Compute dL/dT, then map to se(3) via left Jacobian inverse or similar # However, source states "updated in each iteration via back-propagation" # and formulates optimization directly on xi. # We assume a standard Lie optimization step: # Compute gradient of loss w.r.t currentT gradT = computegradientbackprop(loss, currentT, intrinsicsK, pixelsetR, networkparamstheta) # Map gradient from SE(3) tangent space (matrix form) to se(3) (vector form) # This involves the inverse of the left Jacobian of SE(3) # Jinv is the inverse left Jacobian of SE(3) evaluated at currentT # gradxi = Jinv @ vec(gradT) # Standard SE(3) Jacobian inverse implementation required here. gradxi = se3jacobianinverse(currentT) @ vectose3vector(gradT) # 4. Update tangent vector xi using gradient descent (or Levenberg-Marquardt if integrated) # Source mentions "gradient-based optimization" and "back propagation". # It does not specify the optimizer (SGD, Adam, LM). Given the parent is LM, # we assume an iterative update. For simplicity, we use a gradient step. learningrate = 0.01 # Typical value, not specified in sources. deltaxi = -learningrate gradxi # 5. Exponential map to update pose # Tnew = exp(deltaxi) Told currentT = expse3(deltaxi) @ currentT return currentT def expse3(xi): """ Exponential map from se(3) to SE(3). xi is a 6-vector [omega, delta] where omega is rotation (3) and delta is translation (3). """ omega = xi[0:3] delta = xi[3:6] # Compute rotation matrix R = exp(omegahat) theta = norm(omega) if theta < 1e-6: R = identity(3) J = identity(3) else: omegahat = skewsymmetric(omega) R = rotationmatrixfromaxisangle(omega, theta) # Approximation of J for small theta, or full formula for large theta. # J = I + (1-cos(theta))/theta^2 omegahat + (theta-sin(theta))/theta^3 omegahat^2 J = identity(3) + (1 - cos(theta)) / (theta2) omegahat + \ (theta - sin(theta)) / (theta3) (omegahat @ omegahat) # T = [R, Jdelta; 0, 1] T = identity(4) T[0:3, 0:3] = R T[0:3, 3] = J @ delta return T def skewsymmetric(v): return [[0, -v[2], v[1]], [v[2], 0, -v[0]], [-v[1], v[0], 0]] def vectose3vector(matrixgrad): """ Converts a 4x4 matrix gradient (in tangent space of SE(3)) to a 6-vector. Implementation detail not explicitly in sources, but standard in Lie optimization. """ # Extract rotation and translation parts # This is a simplified mapping; actual implementation depends on the specific Lie algebra representation. # Typically, the upper 3x3 skew-symmetric part gives omega, and the translation column gives delta. # However, the gradient is w.r.t the pose, so it's more complex. # For the purpose of this article, we assume a helper function exists. pass Parameters: Nt: Number of sparse pixels sampled from input images for tracking. T0: Initial pose transformation from camera coordinates to world coordinates. K: Camera intrinsic parameters. R: A sampled set of pixel coordinates. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Interference from Mapping: A copy of the SDF decoder and voxel embeddings must be kept for the tracking process, updated only when a new frame is fused into the map, to prevent interference from ongoing mapping updates. Local Minima: Images are complex signals, making gradient descent prone to local minima. A truncated dynamic low-pass filter (TDLF) can be used to suppress high-frequency signals and escape local minima. Large Offsets: Localization performance degrades when translation error reaches large values (e.g., 16m) and rotation error is significant (e.g., 16°), due to small overlap between observed and rendered images. Uses feature matching instead of gradient-based photometric optimization. Choose when gradients are unreliable or differentiable rendering is not available. Derivative-free Pose Estimation via Feature Matching Time and Memory Complexity: The method requires back-propagation through the volume rendering function, which is computationally intensive. Memory usage is dominated by the voxel embeddings and implicit network parameters, which are kept fixed during tracking. Measured Performance: In experiments with initial translation errors up to 16m, the method achieved translation errors as low as 0.02m and rotation errors as low as 0.09° when combined with TDLF. Direct manifold optimization (iNeRF) failed or produced large errors (e.g., 22.78m translation error) under similar conditions. Scaling: The method scales with the number of sampled pixels Nt and the complexity of the implicit network. Strengths: Smoother and quicker convergence compared to direct optimization on SE(3). Robust to local minima when combined with TDLF. Limitations: Performance degrades with large initial pose errors due to limited overlap. Requires a copy of the network for tracking to avoid interference. This method originates from the need for efficient and robust pose estimation in neural implicit representations. It builds on the principles of Lie group optimization, where updates are performed in the tangent space to maintain the manifold structure. The specific formulation using the tangent plane for SE(3) optimization was highlighted in as superior to direct manifold optimization for avoiding noisy photometric loss landscapes. The approach is used in systems like Vox-Fusion for dense tracking and mapping and LATITUDE for robotic global localization. Vox-Fusion: Dense Tracking and Mapping with Voxel-based Neural Implicit Representation, https://doi.org/10.1109/ismar55827.2022.00066, fetched 2026-10-26 LATITUDE: Robotic Global Localization with Truncated Dynamic Low-pass Filter in City-scale NeRF, https://doi.org/10.1109/icra48891.2023.10161570, fetched 2026-10-29

name: Shonan Averaging for Pose Synchronization
head: Global pose configuration, Pose Synchronization (Global Alignment), Pose Synchronization via Shonan Averaging, Shonan averaging, global pose estimation, pose averaging
body: Shonan Averaging for Pose Synchronization is a method for finding a global alignment of camera poses given a set of noisy relative pose measurements from local mini-scenes. It solves the non-convex optimization problem of registering local coordinate frames into a common global reference frame by iteratively relaxing the problem into higher-dimensional special-orthogonal spaces. It sets itself apart from its siblings by explicitly handling the non-convexity of the rotation component via Shonan relaxation, whereas Lie Algebra (Tangent Plane) Pose Optimization relies on local linearization and Derivative-free Pose Estimation via Feature Matching avoids gradient-based optimization entirely. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A set of N local mini-scenes. For each mini-scene, LU-NeRF provides local camera poses and geometry. Relative pose observations P{ij} (rotation R{ij} and translation t{ij}) between overlapping mini-scenes are derived from these local estimates. Confidence metrics (PSNR) for these relative poses are also provided. Output: A set of global poses P = \{P1, \dots, PN\} where Pi \in SE(3), representing the cameras in a common global reference frame. Data Structures: Relative Pose Graph: Nodes represent mini-scenes. Edges represent relative pose measurements between overlapping mini-scenes. Scale Reference: A Minimum Spanning Tree (MST) constructed over mini-scene centers to propagate scale consistency. Steps: 1. Scale Consistency Resolution: The scale of each mini-scene is unique to its local reference frame. To resolve scale ambiguity: Construct an MST connecting the centers of all mini-scenes. Fix the scale of one reference mini-scene. Propagate the scale to other mini-scenes through the MST edges, ensuring that overlapping edges share a consistent scale. 2. Heuristic Selection for Relative Poses: Multiple relative pose measurements may exist for a pair of cameras (Ci, Cj) because they may appear in multiple overlapping mini-scenes. To select a single measure: For cameras Ci and Cj with i < j, compare the PSNR of the rendering of Ci in the mini-scene centered at Ci versus the rendering of Ci in the mini-scene centered at Cj. If PSNR(Ii | Ci) > PSNR(Ii | Cj), select the relative pose estimation from the mini-scene centered at Ci. Apply this same heuristic to select the relative translation measure. 3. Shonan Rotation Averaging: Solve for the global rotations Ri \in SO(3) by applying Shonan averaging. This method solves a convex relaxation of the rotation synchronization problem by iteratively converting the problem to higher-dimensional special-orthogonal spaces SO(n) until convergence. The input to this step is the set of selected relative rotations and their associated confidence weights. 4. Translation Optimization: With the global rotations Ri fixed from Step 3, solve for the global translations ti. The problem is formulated as a linear system based on the relative translation observations t{ij}: tj - ti = Ri t{ij} where t{ij} is the relative translation between camera i and j from LU-NeRF, and Ri is the global rotation of camera i. This linear system is solved using least-squares optimization. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def shonanaveragingposesynchronization(miniscenes, relativeposes, confidences): """ miniscenes: List of mini-scene objects, each containing local poses and PSNR metrics. relativeposes: Dict mapping (i, j) to list of relative pose objects (Rij, tij). confidences: Dict mapping (i, j) to list of confidence scores (PSNR). """ # Step 1: Resolve Scale Ambiguity # Construct MST over mini-scene centers mstedges = constructmst(miniscenes) # Fix reference scale and propagate referencescene = miniscenes[0] referencescale = referencescene.scale propagatescalethroughmst(mstedges, referencescale) # Step 2: Select Best Relative Poses selectedrotations = {} selectedtranslations = {} for (i, j), poselist in relativeposes.items(): if i > j: continue # Handle each pair once bestpose = None bestpsnr = -infinity for pose in poselist: # Heuristic: Compare PSNR of camera i in its own mini-scene vs j's # Note: pose comes from a specific mini-scene context psnriini = getpsnr(miniscenes[i], miniscenes[i]) psnriinj = getpsnr(miniscenes[i], miniscenes[j]) if psnriini > psnriinj: currentconfidence = psnriini else: currentconfidence = psnriinj if currentconfidence > bestpsnr: bestpsnr = currentconfidence bestpose = pose selectedrotations[(i, j)] = bestpose.R selectedtranslations[(i, j)] = bestpose.t # Step 3: Shonan Rotation Averaging # Input: selectedrotations and their confidences # Output: Global rotations Ri for all i globalrotations = shonanrotationaveraging(selectedrotations, confidences) # Step 4: Translation Optimization # Solve linear system: tj - ti = Ri tij # Construct matrix A and vector b for least squares A = [] b = [] for (i, j), tij in selectedtranslations.items(): Ri = globalrotations[i] # Equation: tj - ti = Ri tij # Reshape to linear constraints for ti and tj # Let t be the flattened vector of all translations # Add rows to A and b corresponding to this constraint # Row for ti: -I # Row for tj: I # RHS: Ri tij A.append([-eye(3), eye(3)]) # Simplified representation b.append(Ri @ tij) # Solve least squares: min ||Ax - b||^2 globaltranslations = solveleastsquares(A, b) # Construct final global poses globalposes = [] for i in range(len(miniscenes)): Pi = SE3(globalrotations[i], globaltranslations[i]) globalposes.append(Pi) return globalposes Parameters: Shonan Relaxation Dimension: The method iteratively increases the dimension n of the SO(n) space. The specific stopping criterion or maximum dimension is not given in the sources, but it continues until convergence. BARF Refinement: After synchronization, a final global optimization is performed using BARF [30] for 200k iterations with a coarse-to-fine positional encoding strategy. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Convergence Failure: Shonan averaging may fail to converge to a reasonable global pose configuration if depth regularization is not used during the local LU-NeRF optimization, even if the maximum relative rotation error is small. Scale Ambiguity: Without the MST-based scale propagation, the global solution remains ambiguous in scale. A robust step that registers local mini-scene poses into a common global reference frame using noisy relative pose measurements from overlapping mini-scenes. It computes a globally optimal positioning of all cameras from these noisy relative pose measurements. It is chosen when local estimates (e.g., from LU-NeRF) are inconsistent due to unique local reference frames and estimation errors. A key pitfall is that relative poses between images in overlapping mini-scenes will not perfectly agree due to these estimation errors and unique local scales. Time Complexity: The pose synchronization step runs on CPU and has a negligible running time compared to the neural network training stages (e.g., 3.18 seconds vs. hours for LU-NeRF-1/2 and refinement). Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Performance: On an NVIDIA Tesla P100, the synchronization step takes approximately 3.18 seconds on average. Strengths: It handles the general SE(3) pose setting without restrictive assumptions on pose priors, outperforming prior attempts at unposed NeRF. It is complementary to feature-based SfM pipelines, comparing favorably to COLMAP on low-texture and low-resolution images. Limitations: It relies on the quality of local relative pose estimates; if depth regularization is omitted in the local stage, global convergence may fail. When to use: When local pose estimates are available but inconsistent across overlapping regions, and a global consistent frame is required for further refinement (e.g., by BARF). When not to use: When high-quality depth regularization is not available for local estimates, as convergence is not guaranteed. Shonan Averaging for Pose Synchronization is used in the LU-NeRF pipeline to bridge local mini-scene optimizations into a global scene representation. The method utilizes the off-the-shelf Shonan averaging technique [20] to solve the non-convex rotation synchronization problem. The specific application to NeRF pose synchronization was introduced in the LU-NeRF paper. LU-NeRF: Scene and Pose Estimation by Synchronizing Local Unposed NeRFs, https://doi.org/10.1109/iccv51070.2023.01679, fetched 2026-10-26

name: Token-level Bundle Adjustment
head: TokenBA
body: Token-level Bundle Adjustment (TokenBA) is a per-scene refinement procedure that fits a frozen ZipSplat decoder to input views by jointly optimizing camera poses and scene tokens, recovering fine detail and correcting initial pose errors in a few seconds. It exploits the persistent 2D–3D correspondences established by the cone loss to refine cameras via robust Perspective-n-Point (PnP) and update scene tokens through the frozen decoder using photometric error. Unlike methods that optimize raw Gaussians or require pose supervision, TokenBA achieves faster convergence and higher quality by leveraging the built-in correspondence of scene tokens. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: A set of N unposed, uncalibrated input images I = \{In\}{n=1}^N, a pre-trained ZipSplat encoder producing scene tokens Z, and an initial estimate of camera poses. The decoder MLP is frozen. Outputs: Refined camera poses and refined scene tokens Z. Data Structures: Scene Tokens (Z): Each token represents a surface region and contains a set of 3D Gaussians. Each Gaussian is parameterized by center \mu \in \mathbb{R}^3, scales s \in \mathbb{R}^3, rotation quaternion q \in \mathbb{R}^4, opacity \alpha \in [0, 1], and color coefficients c \in \mathbb{R}^C. Correspondences: Derived from cluster assignments. Every Gaussian of a scene token is paired with the patch center of each member patch. Parameters: Learning Rates: Tokens use Adam with learning rate 10^{-3} during alternation and 2 \times 10^{-3} in the joint tail. Joint Tail Increment: The joint tail refines tokens and poses using an se(3) increment with learning rate 3 \times 10^{-4}. Compression Ratio (r): Controls Gaussian budget. r=1.0 keeps full capacity; r=0.5, 0.25, 0.1, 0.05 progressively reduce the budget. Resolution: Feed-forward encoder runs at 252 \times 252. TokenBA rendering loss is resolution-agnostic; higher resolutions (e.g., 448 \times 448 or 540 \times 540) can be used to recover fine features. Precision: Decoder MLP body runs in half precision (bfloat16); readout stays in full precision. Algorithm Steps: TokenBA executes alternating rounds of optimization, each comprising a PnP snap, photometric polish, and token update, followed by a joint tail refinement. 1. PnP Snap (Camera Update): Construct 2D–3D correspondences: Pair every Gaussian of a scene token with the patch center of each member patch based on cluster assignments. Solve for each pose using robust PnP with graduated non-convexity. Sample 2048 correspondences. Anneal robust scale from 64 to 12 to 4 pixels over 4 iterations per level. Generate seven rotation hypotheses per view: the current rotation and \pm 40^\circ about each camera axis. Solve hypotheses in one batched call; select the hypothesis with the most inliers within 2 patches. 2. Photometric Polish: Remove patch-center quantization error using a direct Levenberg–Marquardt solver on the photometric residual. Full Configuration (Pre-Refinement): Scan nine log-spaced global scale factors from 0.5 to 2.0. Run a four-level pyramid (1/8, 1/4, 1/2, full resolution) with 12, 10, 8, and 6 steps per level. Apply Gaussian blur at the two coarse levels. Use accept-reject steps with a trust-region clamp on the pose twist. Keep the best full-resolution pose across levels. Inside TokenBA: Only the two fine levels (1/2, full) run, without verification or scale scan. Aligner Step: Each step renders at the current pose and takes a Gauss–Newton update on the brightness-constancy linearization with the analytic image-warp Jacobian. Uses one render per step and no autograd. Execution: Run two steps at half resolution and one at full resolution. 3. Token Update: Refine scene tokens by minimizing the \ell1 rendering loss on the input views. Gradients propagate through the renderer and frozen decoder to the tokens. Optimizing tokens instead of raw Gaussians retains the decoder as a learned scene prior. 4. Joint Tail Refinement: Jointly refine tokens and poses for at most 96 steps, reusing the same Adam state. Exits early once a block of 8 steps improves the loss by less than 2%. 5. Termination: Alternating rounds stop once the PnP snap moves every pose by less than 0.3^\circ, or after four rounds. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def tokenlevelbundleadjustment(inputimages, initialposes, scenetokens, decoder, renderer): """ Performs TokenBA refinement. inputimages: List of N images. initialposes: Initial camera poses. scenetokens: Initial scene tokens Z. decoder: Frozen ZipSplat decoder. renderer: Differentiable rasterizer. """ poses = initialposes tokens = scenetokens # Alternating Rounds for roundidx in range(4): # 1. PnP Snap poses = pnpsnap(poses, tokens, inputimages) # Check termination condition maxposemove = computemaxposemovement(poses, initialposes) # Implementation detail if maxposemove < 0.3: # degrees break # 2. Photometric Polish poses = photometricpolish(poses, tokens, inputimages, decoder, renderer) # 3. Token Update tokens = tokenrefit(tokens, poses, inputimages, decoder, renderer) # Reset initial poses for next round comparison if needed, # or track cumulative movement initialposes = poses # Joint Tail tokens, poses = jointtailrefinement(tokens, poses, inputimages, decoder, renderer) return tokens, poses def pnpsnap(poses, tokens, inputimages): """ Refines camera poses using robust PnP on patch-Gaussian correspondences. """ refinedposes = [] for i, pose in enumerate(poses): # Get correspondences for view i # Pair every Gaussian of a scene token with the patch center of each member patch correspondences = getcorrespondences(tokens, inputimages[i]) # Sample 2048 correspondences sampledcorr = sample(correspondences, 2048) # Generate 7 rotation hypotheses: current + +/- 40 deg about each axis hypotheses = generaterotationhypotheses(pose.rotation, 40.0) besthypothesis = None maxinliers = -1 for rot in hypotheses: # Solve PnP with graduated non-convexity # Anneal robust scale from 64 -> 12 -> 4 over 4 iterations per level estpose = solvepnpgraduated(sampledcorr, rot, pose.translation, scaleschedule=[64, 12, 4], itersperlevel=4) # Count inliers within 2 patches inliers = countinliers(estpose, sampledcorr, threshold=2.0) if inliers > maxinliers: maxinliers = inliers besthypothesis = estpose refinedposes.append(besthypothesis) return refinedposes def photometricpolish(poses, tokens, inputimages, decoder, renderer): """ Removes patch-center quantization error using direct Levenberg-Marquardt. """ refinedposes = [] for i, pose in enumerate(poses): # Inside TokenBA: only two fine levels (1/2, full) levels = [0.5, 1.0] stepsperlevel = [2, 1] # 2 steps at half, 1 at full currentpose = pose for levelidx, level in enumerate(levels): for step in range(stepsperlevel[levelidx]): # Render at current pose renderedimg = renderer.render(tokens, currentpose, decoder, resolutionscale=level) # Compute photometric residual against input image # Note: Input images might need resizing to match resolutionscale inputimgresized = resize(inputimages[i], scale=level) residual = renderedimg - inputimgresized # Gauss-Newton update on brightness-constancy linearization # Analytic image-warp Jacobian # One render per step, no autograd jacobian = computeanalyticjacobian(currentpose, renderedimg) # Levenberg-Marquardt update # (J^T J + lambda I) delta = -J^T residual delta = solvelmstep(jacobian, residual) currentpose = applyposetwist(currentpose, delta) refinedposes.append(currentpose) return refinedposes def tokenrefit(tokens, poses, inputimages, decoder, renderer): """ Refines scene tokens by minimizing rendering loss. """ # Gradients propagate through renderer and frozen decoder to tokens # Optimizer: Adam, lr=1e-3 tokens = optimizetokens(tokens, poses, inputimages, decoder, renderer, optimizer='Adam', lr=1e-3, lossfn='L1') return tokens def jointtailrefinement(tokens, poses, inputimages, decoder, renderer): """ Jointly refines tokens and poses for up to 96 steps. """ # Optimizer: Adam, lr=3e-4 for se(3) increment # Reuse Adam state from alternation for step in range(96): # Render and compute loss renderedimgs = [renderer.render(tokens, p, decoder) for p in poses] loss = computel1loss(renderedimgs, inputimages) # Backward pass loss.backward() # Update tokens and poses tokens, poses = optimizerstep(tokens, poses) # Early exit check: block of 8 steps improves loss by < 2% if step > 0 and step % 8 == 0: if checklossimprovement(loss, previouslossblock, threshold=0.02): break return tokens, poses Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Early Stopping Variability: Early stopping makes TokenBA's per-scene cost highly variable; reported averages mask scene-dependent convergence behavior. Pose Accuracy Trade-off: Freezing poses during the joint refinement costs only 0.1 dB in-domain and 0.3 dB out-of-domain, while keeping pose accuracy fixed at the level reached by the alternating rounds. Refines scene tokens by minimizing the rendering loss on the input views, with gradients propagating through the renderer and frozen decoder to the tokens. Optimizing tokens instead of raw Gaussians retains the decoder as a learned scene prior. Time and Memory Complexity: TokenBA cost scales nearly linearly with both the number of input views and the Gaussian budget. At 128 views, doubling the budget from 65K multiplies cost by 1.6–2.0. At 262K Gaussians, doubling views multiplies cost by 1.7. Without TokenBA, the three largest budgets at 128 views are up to 1.7 s slower than full capacity. Measured Performance: Hardware: RTX 4090. Resolution: 252 \times 252. Batch size: 1. One alternation round takes 35.5 ms. One joint tail step takes 18.1 ms. Breakdown of one alternation round (16 views, full capacity): PnP snap (2.1 ms), photometric polish (15.0 ms), token update (18.3 ms), rasterizer backward (10.8 ms), rasterizer forward (4.3 ms), decoder forward/backward (2.4 ms), Adam update (0.4 ms). Breakdown of one joint tail step: Rasterizer forward/backward passes consume 83% of the time. At 128 views, reducing the Gaussian budget from 1M to 262K cuts TokenBA time from 31 s to 9.0 s, with a quality drop of 0.8 dB. The joint tail exits after 94 of its 96 steps on average at 16 views. Strengths and Limitations: Strengths: Recovers fine detail (text, textures, foliage) and corrects initial pose errors without pose supervision. Faster convergence than optimizing raw Gaussians. Limitations: Cost is scene-dependent due to early stopping. Freezing poses in the joint tail incurs a small quality penalty (0.1–0.3 dB). When to Use: When high-quality reconstruction is needed from unposed, uncalibrated images and the feed-forward prediction has residual camera and geometry error. When fine detail recovery is critical, potentially at higher resolutions than the encoder's training resolution (252 \times 252). When Not to Use: When computational resources are extremely constrained and the feed-forward prediction is already sufficient. When ground-truth camera poses are available and highly accurate, as the refinement may offer diminishing returns (though it still adds detail). Token-level Bundle Adjustment was introduced in the ZipSplat paper (An et al., 2026) as a refinement step for the feed-forward ZipSplat model. ZipSplat predicts a Gaussian scene from a collection of unposed, uncalibrated images without requiring camera poses or intrinsics. TokenBA exploits the persistent 2D–3D correspondences established by the cone loss and GeoCE to refine the scene representation. It builds on the observation that scene tokens, grounded in specific surface regions, provide a compact and stable basis for bundle adjustment. The method was evaluated on DL3DV, RealEstate10K, Mip-NeRF360, and ScanNet++. ZipSplat: Fewer Gaussians, Better Splats, https://doi.org/10.48550/arXiv.2606.05102, fetched 2026-10-29 (unofficial)

name: Adversarial and GAN-based Optimization
head: GAN-based NeRF, Adversarial Radiance Field Optimization
body: Adversarial and GAN-based Optimization methods enhance the photorealism and structural consistency of radiance fields by integrating a discriminator network into the training loop. Unlike standard photometric optimization which minimizes pixel-wise reconstruction errors, these methods enforce that rendered image patches follow the distribution of real image patches, thereby suppressing artifacts and improving high-frequency details. This family is distinct from pure geometric or photometric approaches [44-radiance-field-optimization.md] by introducing a game-theoretic component that provides gradient feedback for perceptual quality rather than just color accuracy. All methods in this family extend the standard radiance field optimization by adding an adversarial loss term. The core mechanism involves a discriminator D that distinguishes between real image patches and those rendered by the generator (the radiance field G or F\Theta). The optimization problem becomes a minimax game where the radiance field parameters \Theta are updated to fool the discriminator, while the discriminator parameters \eta are updated to correctly classify real vs. fake patches. The general adversarial loss formulation follows the minimax objective: \min\Theta \max\eta LA(\Theta, \eta) = \mathbb{E}{I \sim P{real}}[\log(D(I; \eta))] + \mathbb{E}{\hat{I} \sim P{fake}}[\log(1 - D(\hat{I}; \eta))] where P{real} is the distribution of real image patches and P{fake} is the distribution of generated patches. Common variations include patch-based discrimination to reduce memory usage and focus on local texture consistency GANeRF, gradient penalty terms (e.g., R1 penalty) to stabilize training and prevent mode collapse GANeRF, and VGG-based perceptual losses to ensure semantic consistency GANeRF. GNeRF is a two-phase framework that jointly optimizes camera poses and neural radiance fields from uncalibrated images using adversarial training GNeRF. It is designed for scenarios where Structure-from-Motion (SfM) fails due to low texture or complex outside-in configurations GNeRF. Unlike methods requiring rough initialization, GNeRF uses an inversion network to decouple pose estimation from direct photometric gradient propagation, which is prone to local minima GNeRF. name: GNeRF
head: GAN-based Neural Radiance Field without Posed Camera
body: GNeRF is a method for novel view synthesis and camera pose estimation that operates without known camera poses. It solves the problem of reconstructing a neural radiance field and estimating camera extrinsics simultaneously in complex scenes, including those with low texture or repeated patterns where traditional Structure-from-Motion (SfM) fails. Unlike sibling methods like GANeRF which may rely on posed initialization or different adversarial strategies, GNeRF uniquely employs a two-phase hybrid optimization scheme: an initial adversarial phase to obtain coarse poses and a radiance field, followed by a regularized photometric refinement phase, interleaved iteratively to escape local minima. GNeRF jointly optimizes a neural radiance field F\Theta and a set of camera poses \Phi = \{\phi1, \dots, \phin\} for n input images I = \{I1, \dots, In\}. The method treats camera poses as latent variables and uses a Generative Adversarial Network (GAN) framework combined with an inversion network to bootstrap the optimization. Inputs: A set of n uncalibrated RGB images I. No camera poses are provided; shared intrinsics are assumed fixed. Outputs: A trained neural radiance field F\Theta and estimated camera poses \Phi. Camera Pose Representation: To avoid discontinuities in quaternions or Euler angles, poses are represented using continuous embeddings: Translation (t): A 3D vector t \in \mathbb{R}^3 representing the camera position in Euclidean space. Rotation (r): A 6D vector r \in \mathbb{R}^6. Given a rotation matrix R = [a1, a2, a3] \in \mathbb{R}^{3 \times 3}, r is formed by dropping the last column (r = [a1, a2]). The original matrix can be recovered via Gram-Schmidt orthogonalization. Intrinsics: The method assumes a SIMPLE PINHOLE model with shared intrinsics across all views: focal length f, and principal point (cx, cy). Neural Radiance Field (F\Theta): Input: 3D location x \in \mathbb{R}^3 and viewing direction d \in [-\pi, \pi]^2. Output: Emitted color c \in \mathbb{R}^3 and volume density \sigma. Architecture: Based on the original NeRF [32] with hierarchical sampling. Both coarse and fine sampling use 64 points. The MLP dimension is increased from 256 to 360 to maintain parameter count parity with the original NeRF while aligning coarse and fine pose spaces. Discriminator (D\eta): Architecture: Follows GRAF. Uses instance normalization over features and spectral normalization over weights. Input: Image patches. Inversion Network (E{\thetaE}): Architecture: Vision Transformer. The final layer is modified to output a camera pose (translation and rotation embeddings). Input: Image patches. Output: Estimated camera pose. 1. Initialization: Set all camera extrinsics to the identity matrix. Initialize the NeRF model F\Theta and discriminator D\eta. Define a prior pose distribution P(\phi) for random sampling. For Synthetic-NeRF, cameras are uniformly distributed on the upper hemisphere towards the origin. For DTU, cameras are on the upper hemisphere with azimuth [0, 150]^\circ and lookat points from N(0, 0.012). 2. Phase A: Pose-free NeRF Estimation (Adversarial Training): Generator: Sample a random camera pose \phi \sim P(\phi). Query F\Theta with \phi to render an image \hat{I} = G(\phi; F\Theta) using NeRF volume rendering. Dynamic Patch Sampling: Decompose \hat{I} and real images I into patches of fixed size 16 \times 16 with dynamic scale and random offset. Discriminator Update: Train D\eta to distinguish real patches Pd(I) from generated patches Pg(I|\Theta) using the adversarial loss LA: \min\Theta \max\eta LA(\Theta, \eta) = \mathbb{E}{I \sim Pd}[\log(D(I; \eta))] + \mathbb{E}{\hat{I} \sim Pg}[\log(1 - D(\hat{I}; \eta))] Inversion Network Training: Train E{\thetaE} to map generated image patches back to their corresponding sampled poses \phi using self-supervised loss LE: LE(\thetaE) = \mathbb{E}{\phi \sim P(\phi)} \| E(G(\phi; F\Theta); \thetaE) - \phi \|2^2 Repeat until convergence to obtain a coarse radiance field and initial pose estimates \Phi^0 = \{ E(Ii; \thetaE) \}{i=1}^n for the real training images. 3. Phase B: Regularized Learning Strategy (Photometric Refinement): Static Patch Sampling: For pose optimization, uniformly sample patches of fixed size 64 \times 64 across the whole image domain to estimate poses. Intrinsic Scaling: Scale camera intrinsics at the beginning to maximize receptive field, then progressively increase to the original value to focus on fine details. Hybrid Loss Optimization: Refine F\Theta and \Phi by minimizing the hybrid loss LR: LR(\Theta, \Phi) = LN(\Theta, \Phi) + \lambda \sum{i=1}^n \| E(Ii; \thetaE) - \phii \|2^2 where LN is the photometric reconstruction error: LN(\Theta, \Phi) = \frac{1}{n} \sum{i=1}^n \| Ii - \hat{I}i \|2^2, \quad \hat{I}i = G(\phii; F\Theta) and \lambda is a weighting coefficient. 4. Iterative Hybrid Optimization: Interleave Phase A and Phase B in the pattern 'A, AB...AB, B'. This iterative scheme overcomes local minima that arise from directly propagating photometric loss to pose parameters, which is sensitive to low-texture conditions. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def GNeRF(images, numiterations, lambdaweight): # 1. Initialization FTheta = NeRFMLP(dim=360) # Hierarchical sampling: 64 coarse + 64 fine points DNu = DiscriminatorGRAF() # Instance normalization on features, spectral normalization on weights EThetaE = VisionTransformerPose() # Outputs 9D pose embedding (3 translation + 6 rotation) Phi = [IdentityPose() for in images] # Initialize extrinsics to identity matrix PriorPoseDist = UpperHemispherePrior() # Synthetic-NeRF: uniform upper hemisphere towards origin for iteration in range(numiterations): # --- Phase A: Adversarial Training --- batchsize = 16 randomposes = [PriorPoseDist.sample() for in range(batchsize)] renderedimages = [rendervolume(FTheta, pose) for pose in randomposes] realpatches = dynamicpatchsample(images, size=16) fakepatches = dynamicpatchsample(renderedimages, size=16) lossD = computeadversarialloss(DNu, realpatches, fakepatches) updateparameters(DNu, lossD, lr=0.0001, optimizer='RMSprop') lossGadv = computeadversarialloss(DNu, realpatches, fakepatches, generator=True) updateparameters(FTheta, lossGadv, lr=0.0005, optimizer='RMSprop') predictedposes = [EThetaE(patch) for patch in fakepatches] lossE = sum(l2norm(pred - true) for pred, true in zip(predictedposes, randomposes)) updateparameters(EThetaE, lossE, lr=0.0001, optimizer='Adam') # --- Phase B: Photometric Refinement --- scaleintrinsics(iteration, startscale=2.0, endscale=1.0) renderedestimates = [rendervolume(FTheta, phi) for phi in Phi] lossN = sum(l2norm(img - est) for img, est in zip(images, renderedestimates)) estimatedposesfromE = [EThetaE(img) for img in images] lossPosePenalty = sum(l2norm(estphi - phi) for estphi, phi in zip(estimatedposesfromE, Phi)) lossR = lossN + lambdaweight lossPosePenalty updateparameters(FTheta, lossR, lr=0.0005, optimizer='RMSprop') updateparameters(Phi, lossR, lr=0.005, optimizer='Adam') def NeRFMLP(dim): return MLP(hiddendim=dim, sampling=64) def DiscriminatorGRAF(): return CNN(norm=['instance', 'spectral']) def VisionTransformerPose(): return ViT(outputdim=9) def IdentityPose(): return np.eye(4) def UpperHemispherePrior(): return UniformUpperHemisphere() def rendervolume(model, pose): return volumerendering(model, pose) def dynamicpatchsample(imgs, size): return randomcrop(imgs, size=size, scale=True) def computeadversarialloss(D, real, fake, generator=False): if generator: return -mean(log(D(fake))) return mean(log(D(real))) + mean(log(1 - D(fake))) def updateparameters(params, loss, lr, optimizer): grad = computegradients(params, loss) if optimizer == 'RMSprop': params -= lr grad / (sqrt(runningmean(grad2)) + 1e-8) else: # Adam params -= lr (momentum + grad) / (sqrt(variance + 1e-8)) def scaleintrinsics(iter, start, end): pass # Progressive scaling logic def l2norm(a, b): return np.linalg.norm(a - b) Local Minima: Directly propagating photometric loss to camera poses is prone to local minima, especially in low-texture scenes. The hybrid iterative scheme is required to mitigate this. Inversion Network Limitations: The inversion network accepts limited-size patches, restricting pose accuracy. It may underperform COLMAP on scenes with sufficient reliable keypoints. Rotation Representation: Quaternions and Euler angles are avoided due to discontinuities; the 6D embedding is used instead. Intrinsic Scaling: Failure to progressively scale intrinsics may hinder convergence on fine details. Time Complexity: Training is computationally intensive. On a single Nvidia RTX TITAN GPU, training takes approximately 30 hours per scene. Memory Complexity: Uses dynamic patch sampling (16 \times 16) for GAN training to reduce memory usage compared to full-image discrimination. Performance: On the DTU dataset, GNeRF outperforms COLMAP-based NeRF. On Synthetic-NeRF, it is slightly outperformed by COLMAP-based NeRF but handles challenging scenes (repeated patterns, low texture) better. Strengths: Does not require camera pose initialization or masks. Robust to low-texture and repeated pattern scenes where SfM fails. Limitations: Pose accuracy is lower than COLMAP on standard scenes with good keypoints. GNeRF was introduced in 2021 by Meng et al. as a GAN-based framework for unposed neural radiance field reconstruction and camera pose estimation. It extends the NeRF framework by integrating adversarial training and an inversion network to handle scenarios where camera poses are completely unknown. It is evaluated on Synthetic-NeRF and DTU datasets. name: GANeRF
head: Adversarial Loss for GANerf, Adversarial NeRF Training, GAN-based NeRF Optimization, GANeRF Adversarial Training Loop, GANeRF
body:
GANeRF is a method that optimizes a 3D radiance field representation using a 2D adversarial loss, where a discriminator learns the distribution of image patches and provides gradient feedback to the NeRF to enforce 3D-consistent photorealism. It solves the problem of quality degradation in novel view synthesis (NVS) caused by imperfect input data, such as limited coverage, image distortion, or illumination changes. Unlike standard NeRF optimization which relies solely on photometric reconstruction losses, GANeRF distinguishes itself by directly backpropagating gradients from a 2D patch discriminator into the 3D scene representation, thereby suppressing blurry artifacts and enforcing local texture consistency. It differs from GNeRF by focusing on patch-based discrimination for local realism rather than global image-level discrimination, and from NeRFLiX by using direct adversarial backpropagation rather than a non-adversarial post-processing network. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: A set of posed input images capturing a static 3D scene; a base NeRF architecture (e.g., Nerfacto). Outputs: An optimized 3D radiance field representation capable of synthesizing photorealistic novel views. Data Structures: The implementation relies on the Nerfstudio framework structures: GanerfPipelineConfig: Extends VanillaPipelineConfig to include discriminator components. GanerfModelConfig: Extends the base model to include discriminator loss computation hooks. GanerfTrainerConfig: Extends the trainer to handle the adversarial training loop. Discriminator: A 2D CNN-based discriminator (e.g., PatchGAN style) that takes image patches as input and outputs a scalar score indicating realism. Patches: Extracted from rendered RGB images and ground truth images. Patches are reshaped from (B, H, W, 3) to (B, 3, H, W) and potentially downsampled to the discriminator's resolution. Parameters: advlossmult: Multiplier for the adversarial loss. Default: 0.0003. vgglossmult: Multiplier for VGG perceptual loss. Default: 0.0003. gplossmult: Multiplier for gradient penalty loss. Default: 0.2. advlossmult (general): The multiplier for the adversarial loss in the total loss computation. Numbered Steps: 1. Initialization: Set up the NeRF model and the 2D discriminator. Initialize optimizers for both the NeRF parameters \Theta and the discriminator parameters \eta. 2. Iteration Start: For each training iteration, retrieve a batch of rays and corresponding ground truth images. 3. NeRF Forward Pass: Render the scene using the current NeRF parameters \Theta to generate predicted RGB images \hat{I}. 4. Patch Extraction: Extract patches from the rendered images \hat{I} and the ground truth images I. Reshape patches to (B, 3, Hp, Wp). Normalize if required (e.g., 2.0 \cdot x - 1.0). 5. Discriminator Forward Pass (Fake): Pass the fake patches \hat{P} through the discriminator D to get predictions pred{fake} = D(\hat{P}; \eta). 6. Discriminator Forward Pass (Real): Pass the real patches P through the discriminator D to get predictions pred{real} = D(P; \eta). 7. Compute Discriminator Loss: Calculate the discriminator loss LD using the real and fake predictions. This typically includes the standard GAN loss and a gradient penalty (R1) to stabilize training. L{adv} = 	ext{mean}(	ext{softplus}(-pred{fake})). Gradient penalty is computed on real patches. 8. Update Discriminator: Zero gradients for the discriminator optimizer. Compute LD. Backpropagate LD to update \eta. Verify gradients are finite. Step the discriminator optimizer. 9. Compute NeRF Loss: Calculate the standard reconstruction loss (e.g., L1, PSNR) between \hat{I} and I. Calculate the adversarial loss for the NeRF: L{adv
erf} = 	ext{mean}(	ext{softplus}(-D(\hat{P}; \eta))). Calculate VGG perceptual loss if enabled. Combine losses: L{total} = L{rec} + \lambda{adv} L{adv
erf} + \lambda{vgg} L{vgg}. 10. Update NeRF: Zero gradients for the NeRF optimizer. Backpropagate L{total} through the discriminator (if using the discriminator's output directly) and into the NeRF parameters \Theta. Step the NeRF optimizer. Formulas: Adversarial Loss (for NeRF): L{adv} = \mathbb{E}{\hat{P} \sim P{fake}}[	ext{softplus}(-D(\hat{P}; \eta))] where 	ext{softplus}(x) = \log(1 + e^x). Gradient Penalty (R1): L{gp} =  rac{1}{2} \mathbb{E}{P \sim P{real}}[\|
ablaP D(P; \eta)\|2^2] where 
ablaP is the gradient of the discriminator output with respect to the input patch. Pseudocode: Unverified code.
