""" # 1. Render scene rays = batch['rays'] gtimages = batch['gtimages'] renderedoutputs = model(rays) renderedimages = renderedoutputs['rgb'] # Shape: (B, H, W, 3) # 2. Extract patches # Assuming getpatches handles reshaping and normalization realpatches, fakepatches = model.getpatches(renderedoutputs, batch) # realpatches: (B, 3, Hp, Wp), fakepatches: (B, 3, Hp, Wp) # 3. Discriminator Training if config.advlossmult > 0.0: # Zero gradients for discriminator discriminator.zerograd() # Compute discriminator loss predreal = discriminator(realpatches) predfake = discriminator(fakepatches) # Adversarial loss for discriminator # Using softplus for WGAN-GP style loss or standard BCE # Source uses softplus(-predfake) for generator, implying standard GAN loss for D # However, computedloss in source suggests combining real/fake losses # Standard GAN D loss: E[log(D(real))] + E[log(1 - D(fake))] # Source computeadvloss uses softplus(-predfake) which is log(1 + exp(-predfake)) # This is consistent with the minimax log(D) + log(1-D) if D outputs logits. # Let's follow the source's computedloss structure if available, # but source snippet cuts off. We assume standard GAN loss for D. dlossreal = torch.nn.functional.softplus(-predreal).mean() dlossfake = torch.nn.functional.softplus(predfake).mean() # Gradient Penalty realpatches.requiresgrad(True) predrealgp = discriminator(realpatches) gradients = torch.autograd.grad( outputs=[predrealgp.sum()], inputs=[realpatches], creategraph=True, onlyinputs=True)[0] r1penalty = gradients.square().sum([1, 2, 3]).mean() gploss = config.gplossmult r1penalty / 2 dloss = dlossreal + dlossfake + gploss # Backprop and step discriminator dloss.backward() discriminator.optimizer.step() # 4. NeRF Training model.zerograd() # Reconstruction Loss recloss = computereconstructionloss(renderedimages, gtimages) # Adversarial Loss for NeRF # The discriminator is kept frozen for this step predfakenerf = discriminator(fakepatches) advloss = torch.nn.functional.softplus(-predfakenerf).mean() # VGG Perceptual Loss vggloss = computevggloss(renderedimages, gtimages) # Total Loss totalloss = recloss + config.advlossmult advloss + config.vgglossmult vggloss # Backprop and step NeRF totalloss.backward() model.optimizer.step() return totalloss, advloss, dloss Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision: Ensure gradients are finite after discriminator update to prevent NaN propagation. Boundaries: Patch extraction must handle image boundaries correctly, typically by sampling patches from the interior or using padding. Degenerate Input: If the NeRF renders completely black or white images, the discriminator may fail to provide useful gradients. Regularization (VGG, GP) helps mitigate this. Conditional Adversarial Loss is a regularization term used in differentiable volume rendering optimization to enforce photorealism and suppress blurry or distorted artifacts in rendered novel views. It distinguishes itself from standard reconstruction losses by employing a conditional discriminator that evaluates image pairs (rendered vs. target) from the same viewpoint, thereby preventing GAN mode collapse and ensuring 3D consistency across edited scenes. FENeRF uses semantic masks to edit the volume field via GAN inversion to enhance 3D GAN perception technology editability. Time Complexity: Training time increases due to the additional discriminator forward and backward passes. The discriminator operates on 2D patches, which is less expensive than 3D volume processing, but the overhead is non-negligible. Memory Complexity: Memory usage increases by the size of the discriminator network and the intermediate activations for the discriminator. Patch-based discrimination reduces memory compared to full-image discrimination. Measured Performance: Evaluated on challenging indoor scenes from ScanNet++ and Tanks and Temples datasets. GANeRF achieves significant improvements in perceptual metrics like LPIPS (reductions between 28-48%) while maintaining consistently better PSNR and SSIM scores compared to baselines like Nerfacto. Strengths: Mitigates quality degradation from imperfect input data (limited coverage, distortion, illumination changes). Enforces 3D-consistent photorealism. Limitations: Requires careful tuning of adversarial loss multipliers. May introduce artifacts if the discriminator is not well-trained. When to use: When photorealism and texture detail are critical, and the input data is imperfect or limited. When not to use: When computational resources are extremely limited, or when strict geometric accuracy is prioritized over photorealism. GANeRF was introduced by Barbara Roessle, Norman Müller, Lorenzo Porzi, Samuel Rota Bulò, Peter Kontschieder, and Matthias Nießner. It builds on the Nerfacto model. The method leverages generative adversarial networks (GANs) to improve NeRF quality in challenging real-world scenarios. It is related to concurrent work like NeRFLiX but differs in its adversarial formulation. name: Conditional Adversarial Loss
head: GANeRF adversarial loss, conditional discriminator loss
body: Conditional Adversarial Loss is a regularization term used in differentiable volume rendering optimization to enforce photorealism and suppress blurry or distorted artifacts in rendered novel views. It distinguishes itself from standard reconstruction losses by employing a conditional discriminator that evaluates image pairs (rendered vs. target) from the same viewpoint, thereby preventing GAN mode collapse and ensuring 3D consistency across edited scenes. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: Real image pairs \mathbf{R} and fake image pairs \mathbf{F}. Outputs: Discriminator loss \mathcal{L}{\textrm{AD-D}} and Generator (Translated NeRF) loss \mathcal{L}{\textrm{AD-G}}. Data Structures: Image Pair: A tuple of two images (I1, I2) from the same viewpoint. Concatenated Input: The two images are concatenated along the RGB channel dimension. If input images are H \times W \times 3, the concatenated input to the discriminator is H \times W \times 6. Discriminator D: A neural network that outputs a scalar probability (or logit) indicating whether the input pair is "real" or "fake". Numbered Steps: 1. Form Real Pairs (\mathbf{R}): Construct pairs from edited target images. For a set of edited images \{Si^j\}{i=0}^{N-1} and \{Si^k\}{i=0}^{N-1} from two different edit sets, form pairs R = (Sj, Sj - Sk^{-1}). Note: The source notation Sj - Sk^{-1} implies a specific transformation or difference operation defined in the context of the image translation framework; strictly, the pair consists of two images from the same viewpoint belonging to the real distribution. 2. Form Fake Pairs (\mathbf{F}): Generate rendered images Cj from the translated NeRF conditioned on the edit code. Form pairs F = (Cj, Cj - Sk^{-1}) where Cj \in \{Ci^j\}{i=0}^{N-1}. The second element of the fake pair uses the same transformation as the real pair to maintain conditional consistency. 3. Concatenate: For each pair (Ia, Ib), concatenate them along the channel axis: I{concat} = \text{Concat}(Ia, Ib). 4. Discriminator Forward Pass: Feed the concatenated pairs into the discriminator D. For real pairs: compute D(\mathbf{R}). For fake pairs: compute D(\mathbf{F}). 5. Optimize: Update the discriminator D to minimize \mathcal{L}{\textrm{AD-D}} and update the translated NeRF (Generator) to minimize \mathcal{L}{\textrm{AD-G}}. Formulas: The adversarial losses are defined as follows: \mathcal{L}{\textrm{AD-D}} = \mathbb {E}{\mathbf {R}}[-\log(D(\mathbf {R}))] + \mathbb {E}{\mathbf {F}}[-\log(1 - D(\mathbf {F}))] \mathcal{L}{\textrm{AD-G}} = \mathbb {E}{\mathbf {F}}[-\log(D(\mathbf {F}))] Where: D(\mathbf{R}) is the discriminator's output for real pairs. D(\mathbf{F}) is the discriminator's output for fake pairs. name: Simple-RF
head: Simple Radiance Fields
body: Simple-RF is a regularization framework for sparse-input radiance field optimization that mitigates floaters and duplication artifacts by supervising a high-capability "main" model with depth estimates from lower-capability "augmented" models. It sets itself apart from sibling methods like 3D Gaussian Splatting, which require separate initialization studies for sparse inputs, by being applicable to various explicit (TensoRF, iNGP, ZipNeRF) and implicit (NeRF) models without modifying the inference pipeline. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: A set of sparse input views (images and camera poses); a main radiance field model F (e.g., NeRF, TensoRF, ZipNeRF); an augmented radiance field model F{aug} with reduced capacity. Outputs: A trained main radiance field model F capable of novel view synthesis; depth maps estimated during training for supervision. Data Structures: The radiance field F is composed of two sub-networks F = F1 \circ F2: 1. F1 (Geometry/Feature Network): Takes a 3D point pi and outputs a view-independent volume density \sigmai and a latent feature vector hi. 2. F2 (Color Network): Takes the latent feature hi and viewing direction v to output the view-dependent color ci. For the augmented model F{aug}, the architecture is identical to F but with specific components disabled or reduced to lower capacity. Numbered Steps: 1. Model Initialization: Initialize the main model F and the augmented model F{aug} with reduced capacity. The reduction strategy depends on the base architecture (see Subtopics). 2. Ray Sampling: For each training pixel, shoot a ray into the scene and sample N 3D points p1, p2, \dots, pN, where p1 is closest to the camera and pN is farthest. 3. Forward Pass (Main Model): Query F at each point pi to obtain density \sigmai and latent feature hi: \sigmai, hi = F1 (pi) ci = F2 (hi, v) where v is the viewing direction. 4. Forward Pass (Augmented Model): Query F{aug} at each point pi to obtain density \sigma^{aug}i and latent feature h^{aug}i: \sigma^{aug}i, h^{aug}i = F{aug,1} (pi) c^{aug}i = F{aug,2} (h^{aug}i, v) 5. Volume Rendering: Compute the rendered color c for the pixel using the main model's samples: c = \sum{i=1}^{N} wi ci Compute the weights wi using the accumulated transmittance: wi = \exp \left( -\sum{j=1}^{i-1} \deltaj \sigmaj \right) \cdot (1 - \exp (-\deltai \sigmai)) where \deltai is the distance between pi and p{i+1}. Compute the expected depth z for the main model: z = \sum{i=1}^{N} wi zi where zi is the depth of pi. Similarly, compute the rendered color c^{aug} and expected depth z^{aug} for the augmented model using its samples. 6. Depth Reliability Check: Gauge the reliability of the depths estimated by the models by reprojecting pixels. Select a different nearest training view. Reproject the pixel coordinates from the current view to the nearest training view using the estimated depth z (or z^{aug}). Compare the reprojected pixel color with the corresponding image in the nearest training view to determine the reprojection error. 7. Loss Calculation: Compute the photometric loss for the main model: L{ph} = \| c - \hat{c} \|^2, where \hat{c} is the true color of the pixel. Determine which model provides more accurate depth based on the reprojection error. Apply a depth supervision loss L{aug} from the more reliable model to the other model. If the augmented model is more reliable, supervise the main model. If the main model is more reliable, supervise the augmented model. The total loss for the main model typically includes the photometric loss and the depth supervision loss if applicable. 8. Backpropagation and Update: Backpropagate the total loss through both models and update their parameters using an optimizer (e.g., Adam). 9. Inference: Discard the augmented models. Use only the trained main model F for novel view synthesis. Parameters: N: The number of 3D points sampled along a ray for volume rendering. ci: The view-dependent color at point pi. v: The viewing direction used to compute color from the latent feature. \deltai: The distance between adjacent sample points pi and p{i+1}. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Inference Overhead: Augmented models are not used during inference, ensuring no performance overhead for novel view synthesis. Sub-optimal Solutions: Naïvely reducing the capacity of radiance fields may lead to sub-optimal solutions in certain regions; hence, the main model is retained for final synthesis. Depth Discontinuities: Augmented models that learn only smooth depth transitions may fail to learn sharp depth discontinuities at object boundaries. The reliability check ensures that such inaccurate depths are not used for supervision. 3DGS Limitations: The method is not directly applicable to 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) without separate study, as 3DGS suffers from poor initialization with few input views, requiring a combination of good initialization and supervision. This method adapts the original NeRF architecture to enable stable optimization via a reparameterized volume sampling technique. It replaces the standard ReLU density activation with Softplus to ensure non-zero gradients and employs importance-sampling reparameterization for color estimation. It differs from full NeRF by using uniform weights for samples rather than a second "fine" network for re-weighting. Gradient scaling is a technique for differentiable volume rendering optimization that prevents background collapse and near-camera floaters by counter-balancing the sampling density imbalance close to cameras. It sets itself apart from alternatives like near-plane clipping or occlusion losses by addressing the root cause (gradient magnitude imbalance) directly during backpropagation, rather than imposing priors on density distribution or restricting ray origins. PlaNeRF is an unsupervised 3D plane regularization method for Neural Radiance Fields (NeRF) designed to improve large-scale urban scene reconstruction. It addresses the geometric instability of NeRF in low-texture, flat-surface environments by appending two regularization terms to the standard L2 photometric loss: a patch-based SSIM term for geometry initialization and an SVD-based plane regularization term for enforcing planar geometry. Unlike sibling methods such as RegNeRF which enforce a plane orthogonal to the center ray, PlaNeRF targets the least-squares plane approximation of a patch, allowing the surface normal to converge in an unsupervised manner. Hard Sample Mining for NeRF Optimization is a training acceleration technique that reduces memory and compute costs by identifying and backpropagating gradients only for "hard" samples (those contributing significantly to the loss), while skipping the expensive backward pass for "easy" samples. It sets itself apart from sibling methods like NeRF with Softplus Activation and Importance Sampling and PlaNeRF by pruning samples based on their gradient contribution to the pixel loss rather than density or occupancy weights, and by using a two-forward-one-backward pass structure to bypass standard deep learning framework overheads associated with masked gradients. GeCoNeRF is a regularization framework for few-shot Neural Radiance Field (NeRF) optimization that enforces geometric consistency across views using depth-guided warping and feature-level consistency modeling to overcome under-constrained optimization and overfitting. It sets itself apart from pixel-level photometric consistency methods (e.g., NeuralWarp, StructNeRF) by operating at the feature level, which preserves view-dependent specular effects that pixel-level losses would suppress. Unlike pre-training-based few-shot methods (e.g., PixelNeRF, MVSNeRF), it optimizes NeRF from scratch without requiring extensive multi-scene dataset priors. Lambertian Augmentation is a regularization technique used within the Simple-RF framework to mitigate shape-radiance ambiguity and duplication artifacts. It addresses the problem where NeRF models with limited input images exploit view-dependent color variations to explain observed images, leading to incorrect geometry. By constraining an augmented, lower-capacity version of the model to output Lambertian (view-independent) colors, it provides a simpler ground truth that guides the main model toward correct geometric structures. For Simple-NeRF, this is achieved by disabling the view-dependent radiance feature in the augmented model. This variant applies a specific loss annealing strategy to the Simple-RF framework. The overall loss function is: \mathcal{L}{\text{total}} = \mathcal{L}{\text{pix}} + \lambda1 \mathcal{L}{\text{geo}} + \lambda2 \mathcal{L}{\text{adv}} + \lambda3 \mathcal{L}{\text{cls}} where \lambda1, \lambda2, \lambda3 are weighting factors. The weights are annealed during training: initially, \lambda1 = 8, \lambda2 = 0.1, and \lambda3 = 0. In early stages with large stride, the global structure prior (\lambda3) has a large weight compared to local texture guidance (\lambda2). During the training process, \lambda2 is gradually decreased to 0 and \lambda3 is increased to 0.1 with a linear function. Time Complexity: Training time increases due to the simultaneous training of the augmented model alongside the main model. However, inference time is identical to the main model alone, as augmented models are discarded. Memory Complexity: Memory usage during training increases by the size of the augmented model's parameters. Inference memory usage is unchanged. Measured Performance: Simple-RF achieves significant improvement in performance on datasets including forward-facing scenes (NeRF-LLFF), unbounded forward-facing scenes (RealEstate-10K), unbounded 360° scenes (MipNeRF360), and bounded 360° scenes (NeRF-Synthetic). Scaling: The method is applicable to various explicit models (TensoRF, iNGP, ZipNeRF) and implicit models (NeRF). Strengths: Mitigates floaters and duplication artifacts in sparse input settings; no inference overhead; applicable to multiple radiance field architectures. Limitations: Requires careful design of augmented models for each architecture; not directly applicable to 3DGS without separate initialization studies; relies on reprojection error for depth reliability which may be noisy in textureless regions. Simple-RF was introduced in the paper "Simple-RF: Regularizing Sparse Input Radiance Fields with Simpler Solutions" by Nagabhushan Somraj, Sai Harsha Mupparaju, Adithyan Karanayil, and Rajiv Soundararajan. The work follows Occam’s razor principle, regularizing radiance fields to choose simpler solutions over complex ones, particularly in the few-shot setting. It addresses the shortcomings of existing methods like 3DGS which require separate initialization studies for sparse inputs. name: NeRF with Softplus Activation and Importance Sampling
head: Original NeRF architecture with proposed reparameterization
body: This method adapts the original NeRF architecture to enable stable optimization via a reparameterized volume sampling technique. It replaces the standard ReLU density activation with Softplus to ensure non-zero gradients and employs importance-sampling reparameterization for color estimation. It differs from full NeRF by using uniform weights for samples rather than a second "fine" network for re-weighting. Inputs: A set of training images with known camera poses. A 3D grid of density knots (typically 256 knots per ray, slightly perturbed from uniform). Hyperparameters: \beta = 10 for Softplus, k samples for inference (typically 32 for training, variable for inference). Outputs: Rendered RGB images for novel views. Optimized grid parameters. Data Structures: Density Grid: A piecewise linear approximation of volume density \sigma along rays. Constructed by perturbing a uniform grid with 256 knots. Training Batch: Random subset of 64 training images, with 64 rays sampled per image. Algorithm Steps: 1. Ray Sampling: For each ray in the training batch, sample points along the ray segment. The positions are derived from the perturbed uniform grid with 256 knots. 2. Density Prediction: Query the network (or grid) for volume density \sigma at each sample point. Apply the Softplus activation function to ensure non-zero gradients: \sigma{final} = \frac{1}{\beta} \ln(1 + e^{\beta \sigma{raw}}) where \beta = 10. 3. Transmittance Calculation: Compute transmittance Ti for each sample i along the ray: Ti = \exp\left(-\sum{j=1}^{i-1} \sigmaj \deltaj\right) where \deltaj is the distance between sample j and j+1. 4. Color Estimation (Importance-Sampling Reparameterization): Estimate the expected color C using k samples. Unlike full NeRF, this method uses uniform weights for the samples in the color estimate: C = \frac{1}{k} \sum{i=1}^{k} Ti (1 - \exp(-\sigmai \deltai)) ci where ci is the predicted color at sample i. 5. Loss Calculation: Compute the loss between the rendered color and the ground truth image color. 6. Optimization: Update the grid parameters using gradient descent. The Softplus activation ensures gradients flow even when \sigma is small. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import torch import torch.nn.functional as F def softplusdensity(sigmaraw, beta=10.0): """Apply Softplus activation to density with temperature beta.""" return (1.0 / beta) torch.log(1.0 + torch.exp(beta sigmaraw)) def renderraywithimportancesampling( sigmaraw, c, deltas, ksamples, beta=10.0): """ Render a single ray using importance-sampling reparameterization. Args: sigmaraw: Raw density predictions for ksamples points. c: Color predictions for ksamples points. deltas: Distances between consecutive sample points. ksamples: Number of samples to use (k in Equation 10). beta: Softplus temperature parameter. Returns: Rendered color for the ray. """ # Apply Softplus activation to ensure non-zero gradients sigma = softplusdensity(sigmaraw, beta) # Compute transmittance # Ti = exp(-sum{j=1}^{i-1} sigmaj deltaj) # We compute cumulative sum of sigma delta alphadeltas = sigma deltas cumulativealpha = torch.cumsum(alphadeltas, dim=0) # Add a small value to avoid log(0) cumulativealpha = F.pad(cumulativealpha, (1, 0), value=0) # Transmittance Ti = exp(-cumulativealpha{i-1}) # Note: cumulativealpha[i] includes sigma[i]delta[i] # So Ti corresponds to exp(-cumulativealpha[i-1]) T = torch.exp(-cumulativealpha[:-1]) # Compute opacity for each sample: alphai = Ti (1 - exp(-sigmai deltai)) # This is equivalent to Ti (1 - exp(-alphadeltasi)) opacity = T (1.0 - torch.exp(-alphadeltas)) # Color estimation with uniform weights (Equation 10) # C = (1/k) sum{i=1}^{k} opacityi ci color = torch.sum(opacity c, dim=0) / ksamples return color def trainstep(batchimages, batchcameras, grid, optimizer, beta=10.0, ktrain=32): """ One training step. Args: batchimages: Tensor of shape (64, H, W, 3) batchcameras: Camera parameters for the 64 rays grid: Density grid (256 knots per ray) optimizer: Optimizer for the grid beta: Softplus temperature ktrain: Number of samples for training (typically 32) """ optimizer.zerograd() # Sample 64 rays per image from 64 random images # This part is implementation-specific to the ray sampling strategy # Assume we have ray origins, directions, and corresponding grid indices # For each ray, sample ktrain points from the 256-knot grid # Perturb the uniform grid slightly as per the source raysamples = samplerays(batchcameras, ktrain) # Query grid for raw density and color sigmaraw, c = querygrid(grid, raysamples) # Compute deltas (distances between samples) deltas = computedeltas(raysamples) # Render rays renderedcolors = [] for i in range(len(raysamples)): color = renderraywithimportancesampling( sigmaraw[i], c[i], deltas[i], ktrain, beta) renderedcolors.append(color) renderedcolors = torch.stack(renderedcolors) # Compute loss (e.g., MSE) loss = F.mseloss(renderedcolors, batchimages) # Backpropagate loss.backward() optimizer.step() return loss.item() Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Variance: The stochastic estimate variance prevents the model from finding the fine optimum, resulting in slightly worse quantitative results than NeRF without hierarchical sampling, despite similar grid density. Noise Artifacts: Noise artifacts are present in renders when the number of inference samples k is low (e.g., k=1, 2, 4). Artifacts only disappear for k \ge 8. Saturation: Rendering quality metrics (PSNR, SSIM, LPIPS) saturate at approximately 16 samples for the Lego scene. Time Complexity: Rendering speed increases with the number of samples k. On an NVIDIA V100, rendering time for the Lego scene (800x800) ranges from 20.18s (k=1) to 25.74s (k=64). Memory Complexity: Memory usage is relatively stable, ranging from 4.189Gb (k=1) to 4.209Gb (k=64). Performance: On the Lego scene (800x800, NVIDIA V100), the model with 32 samples achieved PSNR 30.72, SSIM 0.946, LPIPS 0.0801. With 1 sample: PSNR 25.67, SSIM 0.870, LPIPS 0.1768. With 64 samples: PSNR 30.72, SSIM 0.947, LPIPS 0.0794. Strengths: Slightly improves rendering time and memory footprint compared to full NeRF. Softplus activation ensures non-zero gradients. Limitations: Slightly worse quantitative results than NeRF without hierarchical sampling. Noise artifacts at low sample counts. This method is based on the original NeRF architecture. It was proposed in "Differentiable Rendering With Reparameterized Volume Sampling". The method uses the original NeRF's architecture and hyperparameters without modifications, except for the output activation of field \sigma and the color estimation technique. name: PlaNeRF
head: SVD Unsupervised 3D Plane Regularization for NeRF
body: PlaNeRF is an unsupervised 3D plane regularization method for Neural Radiance Fields (NeRF) designed to improve large-scale urban scene reconstruction. It addresses geometric instability in low-texture, flat-surface environments by appending two regularization terms to the standard L2 photometric loss: a patch-based SSIM term for geometry initialization and an SVD-based plane regularization term for enforcing planar geometry. Unlike sibling methods such as NeRF with Softplus Activation and Importance Sampling or GeCoNeRF, PlaNeRF targets the least-squares plane approximation of a patch rather than a plane orthogonal to the center ray, allowing the surface normal to converge in an unsupervised manner. Inputs and Outputs Inputs: RGB images, camera poses (estimated via COLMAP), and semantic segmentation maps (pre-computed via SegFormer) identifying flat surfaces such as roads, traffic lanes, and sidewalks. Outputs: Optimized NeRF parameters \theta defining the radiance field f\theta: \mathbb{R}^3 \times S^2 \rightarrow [0, 1]^3 \times \mathbb{R}^+. Data Structures Ray Patch R: A set of rays sampled for a square image patch of size S{patch} \times S{patch}. Point Cloud P: A set of 3D points \{pr\} derived from the NeRF's predicted depth \hat{d}\theta(r) and ray direction ur for each ray r \in R: pr = o + \hat{d}\theta(r) ur where o is the camera center. Difference Matrix A: An N \times 3 matrix where each row is the difference between a point pr and the barycenter \hat{p}c of the point cloud: A = \begin{bmatrix} p0 - \hat{p}c \\ p1 - \hat{p}c \\ \vdots \\ p{N-1} - \hat{p}c \end{bmatrix} where \hat{p}c = \frac{1}{N} \sum{r \in R} pr and N = S{patch}^2. Algorithm Steps 1. Ray Sampling: For a given training iteration, sample a batch of B ray patches R. 2. Depth and Color Rendering: For each ray r in the patch, render the predicted color \hat{c}\theta(r) and depth \hat{d}\theta(r) using volumetric rendering. 3. Point Cloud Construction: Construct the point cloud P for the patch using the rendered depths and ray origins/directions. 4. SVD Plane Regularization (L{SVD}): a. Compute the barycenter \hat{p}c of P. b. Construct the difference matrix A. c. Perform Singular Value Decomposition (SVD) on A: A = U S V^T where U and V are orthogonal matrices, and S is a diagonal matrix of singular values \sigmai in descending order (\sigma1 \ge \sigma2 \ge \sigma3). d. The least-squares plane normal n is the right singular vector v3 corresponding to the smallest singular value \sigma3. e. The regularization loss is the smallest singular value: L{SVD}(\theta, R) = \sigma3(\theta, R) Minimizing \sigma3 forces the points in the patch to lie on a plane. 5. Semantic Masking: Apply a semantic mask M to L{SVD}. The loss is only computed for pixels belonging to classes assumed to be single 3D planes (e.g., road, sidewalk, traffic lanes). Pixels in other classes (e.g., walls, buildings) are excluded because they may contain multiple planes. 6. SSIM Initialization (L{dSSIM}): a. Extract the RGB color patch \hat{X} from the rendered colors and the ground truth patch Y from the input image. b. Compute the SSIM metric between \hat{X} and Y: \text{SSIM}(x, y) = \frac{(2\mux \muy + c1)(\sigma{xy} + c2)}{(\mux^2 + \muy^2 + c1)(\sigmax^2 + \sigmay^2 + c2)} where \mu are means, \sigma^2 are variances, \sigma{xy} is covariance, and c1, c2 are small constants to stabilize division. c. Compute the dSSIM loss: L{dSSIM}(\theta, R) = \frac{1 - \text{SSIM}(\hat{X}, Y)}{2} This term supervises the 2D local structure to aid geometry initialization, particularly for low-texture surfaces. 7. Total Loss Computation: L(\theta, R) = L{MSE}(\theta, R) + \lambda0 L{dSSIM}(\theta, R) + \lambda1 L{SVD}(\theta, R) where L{MSE} is the standard L2 photometric loss. 8. Optimization: Update \theta using the Adam optimizer. Pseudocode Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import torch import torch.nn.functional as F def planerfstep(renderfunc, imagepatch, semanticmask, origins, directions, params): """ One training step for PlaNeRF. Args: renderfunc: Function that takes ray origins and directions, returns (color, depth). Returns tensors of shape (Spatch, Spatch, 3) and (Spatch, Spatch). imagepatch: Ground truth RGB image patch, shape (Spatch, Spatch, 3). semanticmask: Semantic mask for the patch, shape (Spatch, Spatch). origins: Ray origins for the patch pixels, shape (Spatch, Spatch, 3). directions: Ray directions for the patch pixels, shape (Spatch, Spatch, 3). params: Dictionary containing Spatch, lambda0, lambda1, and semanticclasses. Returns: totalloss: Scalar tensor. """ # 1. Render color and depth for the patch predcolor, preddepth = renderfunc(origins, directions) # 2. L2 Photometric Loss lmse = F.mseloss(predcolor, imagepatch) # 3. dSSIM Loss for initialization c1 = 0.01 2 c2 = 0.03 2 # Compute local means and variances using 3x3 pooling mux = F.avgpool2d(predcolor.permute(2, 0, 1).unsqueeze(0), kernelsize=3, stride=1, padding=1).squeeze(0).permute(1, 2, 0) muy = F.avgpool2d(imagepatch.permute(2, 0, 1).unsqueeze(0), kernelsize=3, stride=1, padding=1).squeeze(0).permute(1, 2, 0) sigmaxsq = F.avgpool2d((predcolor - mux)2, kernelsize=3, stride=1, padding=1) sigmaysq = F.avgpool2d((imagepatch - muy)2, kernelsize=3, stride=1, padding=1) sigmaxy = F.avgpool2d((predcolor - mux) (imagepatch - muy), kernelsize=3, stride=1, padding=1) ssimmap = ((2 mux muy + c1) (sigmaxy + c2)) / ((mux2 + muy2 + c1) (sigmaxsq + sigmaysq + c2)) ldssim = torch.mean((1 - ssimmap) / 2) # 4. SVD Plane Regularization Loss # Reshape to (N, 3) where N = Spatch Spatch N = params['Spatch'] 2 points = origins.view(-1, 3) + preddepth.view(-1, 1) directions.view(-1, 3) # Compute barycenter and difference matrix A barycenter = torch.mean(points, dim=0) A = points - barycenter # SVD: A = U S V^T. S is in descending order. U, S, Vh = torch.linalg.svd(A, fullmatrices=False) sigma3 = S[-1] lsvd = sigma3 # 5. Semantic Masking for SVD Loss # Filter points to only include valid semantic classes validmask = torch.zeros(N, dtype=torch.bool, device=points.device) for cls in params['semanticclasses']: validmask = validmask | (semanticmask.view(-1) == cls) if validmask.sum() > 0: pointsvalid = points[validmask] if pointsvalid.shape[0] >= 3: barycentervalid = torch.mean(pointsvalid, dim=0) Avalid = pointsvalid - barycentervalid, Svalid, = torch.linalg.svd(Avalid, fullmatrices=False) lsvd = Svalid[-1] else: lsvd = torch.tensor(0.0, device=points.device) else: lsvd = torch.tensor(0.0, device=points.device) # 6. Loss Scheduling # lambda1 = 0 during the first epoch (handled in training loop) # 7. Total Loss totalloss = lmse + params['lambda0'] ldssim + params['lambda1'] lsvd return totalloss Parameters \lambda0: Weight for dSSIM loss. Typical value: 0.1. \lambda1: Weight for SVD loss. Typical value: 0.01. S{patch}: Size of the rendered patch. Typical value: 20. Optimizer: Adam. Learning Rate: Cosine decay from 10^{-2} to 10^{-4}. Batch Size: 128 patches. Training Duration: 100 epochs with early stopping. Semantic Classes: Road, traffic lanes, sidewalk. Edge Cases and Pitfalls Uninitialized Geometry: Applying L{SVD} too early leads to inaccurate plane estimation. The loss scheduling sets \lambda1 = 0 during the first epoch to mitigate this. Semantic Ambiguity: Classes like "wall" or "building" may contain multiple planes. Applying the single-plane assumption to these classes degrades performance. Semantic masking is required to exclude them. Low Texture: Without L{dSSIM}, geometry initialization on low-texture surfaces is poor. The dSSIM term is crucial for this phase. Time Complexity: Training takes approximately 1 to 4 hours per scene on a single NVIDIA GeForce RTX 3090 GPU. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Performance: On the KITTI-360 NVS benchmark, PlaNeRF achieves a PSNR of 22.90, SSIM of 0.857, and LPIPS of 0.205. It outperforms baseline NeRF (PSNR 21.18) and other regularization methods like RegNeRF (PSNR 22.50). Strengths: Effective for large-scale urban scenes with flat surfaces; unsupervised plane normal convergence; improves geometry on low-texture surfaces. Limitations: Requires semantic segmentation maps; assumes single-plane geometry for specific classes; not suitable for complex non-planar structures without masking. When to use: Large-scale urban reconstruction (e.g., driving scenarios) where flat surfaces like roads and sidewalks are dominant. When not to use: Scenes where semantic segmentation maps are unavailable or where the single-plane assumption for flat classes is invalid. PlaNeRF was introduced in 2024 by authors publishing in the IEEE International Conference on 3D Vision (3DV). It builds on the piecewise planar assumption introduced in RegNeRF. While RegNeRF regularizes patches towards a plane orthogonal to the center ray, PlaNeRF uses SVD to find the least-squares plane approximation, allowing the normal to converge unsupervised. The method is part of the Simple-RF family, which uses regularized radiance field models to constrain the main model [Parent]. It is specifically designed for large-scale urban scene reconstruction, leveraging semantic segmentation to guide the regularization. PlaNeRF: SVD Unsupervised 3D Plane Regularization for NeRF Large-Scale Urban Scene Reconstruction, https://doi.org/10.1109/3dv62453.2024.00114, fetched 2026-11-04

name: Hard Sample Mining for NeRF Optimization
head: Propagated Pixel Loss Importance Sampling, Two-Forward-One-Backward Hard Sample Mining, Two-forward-one-backward-pass approach
body: Hard Sample Mining for NeRF Optimization is a training acceleration technique that reduces memory and compute costs by identifying and backpropagating gradients only for "hard" samples (those contributing significantly to the loss), while skipping the expensive backward pass for "easy" samples. It sets itself apart from sibling methods like NeRF with Softplus Activation and Importance Sampling and PlaNeRF by pruning samples based on their gradient contribution to the pixel loss rather than density or occupancy weights, and by using a two-forward-one-backward pass structure to bypass standard deep learning framework overheads associated with masked gradients. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: A batch of rays sampled from training images, ground truth pixel colors, and the current state of the NeRF network (MLPs for density \sigma and color c). Outputs: Updated NeRF network parameters. Data Structures and Layout: Points: A tensor of shape (B, 3) containing 3D coordinates of B ray samples. Pre-activation Attributes (Z): A tuple (c', \sigma') of shape (B, 3) and (B, 1) respectively, representing the raw outputs of the color and density MLPs before activation functions (e.g., sigmoid, exp). Gradient Norms (G): A tensor of shape (B,) where Gi = \|\frac{\partial L}{\partial (c'i, \sigma'i)}\|2. Hard Indices: A 1D tensor of indices selecting b samples from the original B. Formulas: 1. Volumetric Rendering: Pixel color C(r) is computed as: C(r) = \sum{i=1}^{N} wi ci, \quad wi = Ti \alphai, \quad Ti = \prod{j=1}^{i-1} (1 - \alphaj), \quad \alphai = 1 - \exp(-\sigmai \deltai) where ci is color, \sigmai is density, \deltai is step size, Ti is transmittance, and \alphai is opacity. 2. Importance Sampling Distribution (G): The hardness of a sample is defined by the L2 norm of the gradient of the pixel loss L with respect to the pre-activation outputs: Gi = \left\| \frac{\partial L}{\partial (c'i, \sigma'i)} \right\|2 3. Variance of Gradient Reduction Ratio (R): Approximated using the large minibatch B: R = \frac{1}{\sum{i=1}^B Gi^2} \|G - U\|2^2 where U = 1/B is the uniform distribution probability. 4. Batch Size Increase Factor (\tau): Solved assuming gradient variance reduces to 1 - 1/\sqrt{\tau} when batch size increases by \tau: \tau = \left(1 - R\right)^{-\frac{1}{2}} = \left(1 - \frac{1}{\sum{i=1}^B Gi^2} \|G - U\|2^2\right)^{-\frac{1}{2}} 5. Hard Minibatch Size (b): Calculated to achieve the same gradient variance as the uniform batch B: b = \frac{B}{\tau} Parameters: B: Total number of ray samples in the initial batch. Typical value: 2^{20}. b: Number of hard samples selected. Dynamically calculated; typically 10-15% of B. \hat{\tau}: Running average of \tau, initialized to 1.0. \alpha\tau: Learning rate for \hat{\tau}, set to 1 / \text{num. of training images}. Steps: 1. Ray Sampling: Cast rays through image pixels and generate a batch of B ray samples (points along the rays). 2. First Forward Pass (Inference): Perform the forward pass for all B samples in inference mode (e.g., using nograd()) to avoid storing intermediate tensors for the backward pass. Retrieve pre-activation outputs Z = (c', \sigma'). 3. Volume Rendering and Loss: Volume render the outputs from the first pass to calculate pixel colors, then compute the pixel loss L. 4. Partial Backpropagation: Backpropagate the loss from the volume rendering stage only up to the pre-activation outputs Z for all B samples. This provides gradients \frac{\partial L}{\partial Z} without backpropagating through the entire network architecture. 5. Compute Importance Weights: Calculate the norm of the gradient for each sample to form G. 6. Calculate Batch Size: Compute R, then \tau, and update the running average \hat{\tau} = (1 - \alpha\tau)\hat{\tau} + \alpha\tau \tau. Calculate the target hard batch size b = B / \hat{\tau}. 7. Select Hard Samples: Sample b indices from the importance distribution G using multinomial sampling: hard\indices \leftarrow \text{multinomial}(G, b). Retrieve the corresponding 3D coordinates: hard\points \leftarrow points[hard\indices]. 8. Second Forward Pass (Training): Re-run the forward pass for the selected b hard samples, this time building the full computational graph (training mode). Retrieve pre-activation attributes attributes'. 9. Full Backward Pass: Concatenate the cached gradients for the selected hard indices: grad\output \leftarrow \text{cat}(grad\attributes[hard\indices]). Backpropagate these cached gradients through the network for the hard points: attributes'.\text{backward}(grad\output). Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def hardsampleminingstep(nerf, points, gtcolors, alphatau, tauhat): """ Performs one iteration of hard sample mining. Args: nerf: The NeRF network model. points: Tensor of shape (B, 3) containing ray samples. gtcolors: Tensor of ground truth pixel colors. alphatau: Scalar learning rate for running average of tau. tauhat: Scalar running average of tau. Returns: newtauhat: Updated running average of tau. """ B = len(points) # Step 1 & 2: First forward pass in inference mode cprime, sigmaprime = nerf.forwardpreactivation(points) # Step 3: Volume render and compute loss # Standard volume rendering accumulates weights and colors renderedcolors = volumerender(sigmaprime, cprime) pixelloss = meansquarederror(renderedcolors, gtcolors) # Step 4: Backpropagate only to pre-activation outputs gradcprime, gradsigmaprime = computegradients(pixelloss, [cprime, sigmaprime]) # Step 5: Compute importance weights G G = l2norm(gradcprime, gradsigmaprime, dim=1) # Step 6: Calculate batch size b U = 1.0 / B sumGsq = sum(G2) R = (1.0 / sumGsq) sum((G - U)2) tau = (1.0 - R)(-0.5) if R < 1.0 else 1.0 newtauhat = (1.0 - alphatau) tauhat + alphatau tau b = max(1, int(B / newtauhat)) # Step 7: Select hard samples probs = G / sum(G) hardindices = multinomialsample(probs, b) hardpoints = points[hardindices] # Step 8: Second forward pass (Training mode) cprimehard, sigmaprimehard = nerf.forwardpreactivation(hardpoints) # Step 9: Full backward pass gradchard = gradcprime[hardindices] gradsigmahard = gradsigmaprime[hardindices] backpropagate([cprimehard, sigmaprimehard], [gradchard, gradsigmahard]) return newtauhat Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Framework Overhead: Standard deep learning platforms (PyTorch, TensorFlow) do not benefit from simply masking out samples during backpropagation because they still backpropagate zero gradients for masked samples and retain compute/memory overhead. Unknown Hardness: It is impossible to know beforehand which samples are hard, so intermediate tensors cannot be selectively saved during the first forward pass. GPU Utilization: If b shrinks excessively small, GPU utilization drops and no computational time benefit is gained over pruned samples. Memory Saturation: Additionally, if B/b reaches a certain point, the first forward pass dictates maximum memory requirements, negating further memory benefits. Time Complexity: The backward pass has nearly twice the number of operations compared to the forward pass. By reducing the backward pass to only b samples (where b \ll B), both compute time and memory usage are reduced. Average iteration time is reduced to ~53-54% of baseline when B/b is ~10-15%. Memory Complexity: Memory usage is reduced by ~40% compared to the baseline (e.g., from ~1 GB to ~570 MB) because the computational graph is only built for the smaller batch b. Performance: On Instant-NGP, the method provides a 1 dB improvement in PSNR per unit training time on average, or a 2x speedup to reach the same PSNR level. Strengths: Hyperparameter-free batch size adjustment; significant memory savings; faster convergence. Limitations: Requires two forward passes per iteration; overhead from ray sampling and volume rendering remains unchanged; potential GPU underutilization if b is too small. The method was introduced by J. Korhonen et al. in 2024. It addresses the computational bottleneck of the backward pass in NeRF optimization, where resources are spent on processing already learned samples. It is implemented in a PyTorch reimplementation of Instant-NGP and evaluated on the Mip-NeRF-360 dataset, with importance sampling analysis performed on the original synthetic NeRF dataset. Efficient NeRF Optimization -- Not All Samples Remain Equally Hard, https://arxiv.org/abs/2408.03193v1, fetched 2026-10-27

name: Lambertian Augmentation
head: Lambertian constraint, view-independent augmentation
body: Lambertian Augmentation is a regularization technique used within the Simple-RF framework to mitigate shape-radiance ambiguity and duplication artifacts in radiance field optimization. It addresses the problem where NeRF models with limited input images exploit view-dependent color variations to explain observed images, leading to incorrect geometry. By constraining an augmented, lower-capacity version of the model to output Lambertian (view-independent) colors, it provides a simpler ground truth that guides the main model toward correct geometric structures. Inputs and Outputs: Input: 3D point coordinates pi, viewing direction vi, and the hidden state hi from the coarse density network. Output: Lambertian color ci and density \sigmai for the augmented model. Data Structures: The method operates on two parallel network branches within the augmented model: 1. Density Network (N{1l}): Takes positional encoding of pi as input. 2. Color Network (N{2l}): Takes the hidden state hi from the density network as input. Positional Encoding: The positional encoding \gamma is applied to the point pi. For the Lambertian augmentation, the angular components are zeroed out. Standard encoding for main model (for context): \gamma(pi, l{ps}, lp) and \gamma(vi, 0, lv). Lambertian encoding for augmented model: \gamma(pi, 0, lp). This disables high-frequency angular components for the view direction, effectively removing view-dependence from the input representation. Numbered Steps: 1. Compute Density: Pass the positionally encoded point pi (with zero angular frequency) through the coarse density network N{1l} to obtain density \sigmai and hidden state hi: \sigmai, hi = N{1l}(\gamma(pi, 0, lp)) 2. Compute Lambertian Color: Pass the hidden state hi through the color network N{2l} to obtain the color ci. Note that hi already incorporates low-frequency positional encoding of pi from the density network step: ci = N{2l}(hi) 3. Supervision: The output (\sigmai, ci) from the augmented model is used to supervise the main model. The main model retains full view-dependence, while the augmented model forces a Lambertian assumption. The difference or consistency between these outputs helps regularize the main model's geometry. Parameters: lp: Low-frequency positional encoding length for position. l{ps}: High-frequency positional encoding length for position (used in main model, not augmented). lv: Angular frequency length (set to 0 in augmented model). Typical values: Not given in the sources. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Specular Objects: The augmented model is less accurate in non-Lambertian (specular) regions because it cannot represent view-dependent color. The method relies on the main model handling these cases while the augmented model handles the geometry. Precision: The method assumes that disabling angular components in the positional encoding effectively removes view-dependence. Implementation must ensure that the hidden state hi does not inadvertently leak view-direction information from other parts of the network. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def lambertianaugmentationforward(pi, N1l, N2l, lp): """ Computes Lambertian color and density for the augmented model. Args: pi: 3D point coordinates (3,) N1l: Density network (takes encoded position, returns sigma and hidden state) N2l: Color network (takes hidden state, returns color) lp: Length of low-frequency positional encoding for position Returns: sigmai: Density scalar ci: Lambertian color vector (3,) """ # Apply positional encoding with zero angular frequency # gamma function encodes pi with length lp for position, 0 for view encodedp = positionalencoding(pi, lp=lp, lview=0) # Compute density and hidden state # N1l outputs (sigma, h) sigmai, hi = N1l(encodedp) # Compute Lambertian color from hidden state # hi already includes low-frequency positional encoding of pi ci = N2l(hi) return sigmai, ci Time Complexity: Adds minimal overhead as it involves a forward pass through a smaller or parallel network branch. Memory Complexity: Requires storing parameters for the augmented density and color networks (N{1l}, N{2l}). Strengths: Effectively reduces shape-radiance ambiguity in sparse input scenarios by forcing the model to learn geometry that is consistent across viewpoints. Limitations: Does not explicitly handle view-dependent effects in the augmented model; relies on the main model to capture specularities. When to use: When training NeRFs with few input images where shape-radiance ambiguity is prominent. Lambertian Augmentation was introduced in the Simple-RF paper by Zhang et al. (2024) as a method to regularize sparse input radiance fields. It builds on the observation that NeRFs can exploit view-dependent color to explain away geometric errors when data is scarce. Simple-RF: Regularizing Sparse Input Radiance Fields with Simpler Solutions, https://arxiv.org/abs/2404.19015v5, fetched 2026-10-27

name: Difference Planes for View-Dependent Radiance Fields
head: Difference planes, Specular planes
body: Difference Planes is a method for handling view-dependent information in radiance fields to mitigate the shape-radiance ambiguity, where high angular resolution of view-dependent colors leads to incorrect geometry. It separates view-dependent and Lambertian components during training by associating a difference plane with each camera to capture deviations from the integrated Lambertian content of rays sent through the volume. Unlike sibling methods that rely on explicit spherical harmonics or neural networks for view-dependence, this approach uses lightweight per-camera planes and optional non-stored voxel constraints to isolate specular highlights and view-dependent lighting, enabling reconstruction of scenes with highly specular components without explicit view-dependence handling. Inputs and Outputs Inputs: A set of camera images (reference colors ri), a voxel grid storing color (cj) and density (\sigmaj) per cell, and a hierarchical shell of environment maps for foreground/background segmentation. Outputs: Optimized voxel grid parameters (color, density) and difference plane values (\alpha{si}) that minimize the reconstruction error. Data Structures 1. Voxel Grid: Stores color cj and density \sigmaj for each voxel j. 2. Difference Planes: One plane per camera image, with identical resolution to the image. Each plane stores one float value \alpha{si} per pixel i. 3. Environment Maps: A hierarchical shell surrounding the scene for segmentation. Parameters \sigmas: A constant weight parameter that tunes how readily values are pushed into the specular planes. Value: 0.002. \alpha{si}: The difference plane variable for pixel i in camera s. Initialized to 0. Grows during optimization if no acceptable solution is found using only Lambertian values. Formulas The volume rendering integrates color along a ray: H = \sumt T(t)(1 - e^{(-\sigma(t)\delta(t))})c(t) where T(t) = e^{(-\sum{n}^{t} \sigma(t)\delta(t))} is accumulated throughput, \sigma is density, \delta is step distance, and c is color. The Lambertian part of the color accumulated from the ray traversing the volume through voxels j is: H{di} = \sumj e^{-Vj}(1.0 - e^{(-\sigmaj \deltaj)})cj where Vj = \sum{k=0}^{j-1} \sigmak \deltak. The final accumulated color for a pixel is computed as: \hat{H}i = (1.0 - e^{(-\alpha{si} \sigmas)})(ri - H{di}) + H{di} where ri is the reference color and \sigmas is the constant weight. The objective function to minimize is: \hat{F} = 0.5 \sumi \sum{k=1}^3 (\hat{H}{i,k} - r{i,k})^2 for all pixels i and color channels k. Algorithm Steps 1. Initialize: Set all difference plane values \alpha{si} to zero. Initialize voxel grid color and density parameters. 2. Render Lambertian Component: For each pixel i, traverse the ray through the voxel grid and compute the Lambertian accumulated color H{di} using the formula above. 3. Compute Final Color: Calculate the final rendered color \hat{H}i using the difference plane value \alpha{si}, the reference color ri, and the Lambertian component H{di}. 4. Compute Loss: Calculate the squared difference loss \hat{F} between \hat{H}i and ri. 5. Compute Gradients: For voxel colors cj: \frac{\partial F}{\partial cj} = \sumi (Hi - ri) \frac{\partial Hi}{\partial cj} where \frac{\partial Hi}{\partial cj} = e^{(-\alpha{si} \sigmas)} \frac{\partial H{di}}{\partial cj}. For difference plane variables \alpha{si}: \frac{\partial Hi}{\partial \alpha{si}} = -\sigmas e^{(-\alpha{si} \sigmas)} (ri - H{di}). 6. Update: Update voxel parameters and difference plane values using gradient descent. 7. Non-Highlight Constraint (Optional): If separation is difficult, compute a small view-dependent function per voxel to increase or decrease density per voxel to aid convergence. These parameters are not stored. Pseudocode Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import numpy as np def renderlambertian(ray, voxelgrid, sigmas): """ Computes the Lambertian component Hdi for a ray. ray: list of voxels traversed by the ray, each with density sigma and color c sigmas: constant weight (0.002) Returns: Hdi (float), Vj (float, accumulated optical depth) """ Hdi = 0.0 Vj = 0.0 for j, voxel in enumerate(ray): sigmaj = voxel.density cj = voxel.color deltaj = voxel.stepdistance # Vj is sum of sigmak deltak for k < j # Hdi term: exp(-Vj) (1 - exp(-sigmaj deltaj)) cj term = np.exp(-Vj) (1.0 - np.exp(-sigmaj deltaj)) cj Hdi += term Vj += sigmaj deltaj return Hdi, Vj def computedifferenceplanecolor(Hdi, ri, alphasi, sigmas): """ Computes the final color Hhati using the difference plane. Hdi: Lambertian component ri: Reference color alphasi: Difference plane value for this pixel sigmas: Constant weight (0.002) Returns: Hhati """ # Hhati = (1 - exp(-alphasi sigmas)) (ri - Hdi) + Hdi factor = 1.0 - np.exp(-alphasi sigmas) Hhati = factor (ri - Hdi) + Hdi return Hhati def computegradients(Hdi, ri, alphasi, sigmas, dHdidcj, dHdidalphaj): """ Computes gradients for voxel colors and difference plane values. Hdi: Lambertian component ri: Reference color alphasi: Difference plane value sigmas: Constant weight dHdidcj: Gradient of Hdi with respect to voxel color cj dHdidalphaj: Gradient of Hdi with respect to voxel density alphaj (if applicable) Returns: gradcj, gradalphasi """ # Gradient for difference plane alphasi # dHi / dalphasi = -sigmas exp(-alphasi sigmas) (ri - Hdi) gradalphasi = -sigmas np.exp(-alphasi sigmas) (ri - Hdi) # Gradient for voxel color cj # dHi / dcj = exp(-alphasi sigmas) dHdi / dcj gradcj = np.exp(-alphasi sigmas) dHdidcj return gradcj, gradalphasi def optimizestep(voxelgrid, differenceplanes, referenceimages, rays, sigmas, learningrate): """ One optimization step. """ # Initialize gradients voxelgrads = {v: 0.0 for v in voxelgrid} diffplanegrads = {p: 0.0 for p in differenceplanes} for cameraidx, (refimage, diffplane, raysforcamera) in enumerate(zip(referenceimages, differenceplanes, rays)): for pixelidx, (ray, ri) in enumerate(zip(raysforcamera, refimage.flatten())): # 1. Render Lambertian component Hdi, = renderlambertian(ray, voxelgrid, sigmas) # 2. Compute final color alphasi = diffplane[pixelidx] Hhati = computedifferenceplanecolor(Hdi, ri, alphasi, sigmas) # 3. Compute loss (for debugging/monitoring, not strictly needed for gradient if using auto-diff) # loss = 0.5 (Hhati - ri)2 # 4. Compute gradients # Note: dHdi/dcj and dHdi/dalphaj must be computed from the volume rendering step # This is a placeholder for the actual derivative computation from the volume rendering # In practice, this is done via backpropagation through the volume rendering function dHdidcj =... # Placeholder for actual derivative dHdidalphaj =... # Placeholder for actual derivative gradcj, gradalphasi = computegradients(Hdi, ri, alphasi, sigmas, dHdidcj, dHdidalphaj) # Accumulate gradients for voxel in ray: voxelgrads[voxel] += gradcj diffplanegrads[diffplane] += gradalphasi # Update parameters for voxel, grad in voxelgrads.items(): voxel.density -= learningrate grad voxel.color -= learningrate grad for diffplane, grad in diffplanegrads.items(): diffplane -= learningrate grad Edge Cases and Pitfalls Shape-Radiance Ambiguity: If view-dependent colors are not separated, the geometry may become incorrect. Initialization: \alpha{si} is initialized to zero. If no acceptable solution is found with only Lambertian values, \alpha{si} grows. Non-Highlight Lighting: For view-dependent lighting that does not behave like a highlight, a small view-dependent function per voxel is computed to aid convergence. These parameters are not stored. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Adds one float value per pixel per camera for the difference planes. The non-highlight view-dependent function parameters are not stored. Performance: Small impact on performance and memory usage. Strengths: Enables reconstruction of scenes with highly specular components without explicit handling of view-dependence such as Spherical Harmonics. Limitations: May require additional constraints for NERF and other methods built on view-dependent radiance fields to work as an end-to-end pipeline for 3D reconstruction. When to use: When dealing with scenes with highly specular components and shape-radiance ambiguity. When not to use: When computational resources are extremely limited and the overhead of difference planes is unacceptable, or when view-dependence is not a significant factor. The method was proposed by Uffe Kjaerulff from Chalmers University of Technology, Gothenburg, Sweden. It addresses the shape-radiance ambiguity in radiance fields, a problem where high angular resolution of view-dependent colors leads to incorrect geometry. The method builds on previous work such as NERF, Plenoxels, DirectVoxGo, and PERF. Addressing the Shape-Radiance Ambiguity in View-Dependent Radiance Fields, https://doi.org/10.48550/arxiv.2203.01553, fetched 2026-10-29 (unofficial)

name: GeCoNeRF
head: Neural Radiance Fields with Geometric Consistency
body: GeCoNeRF is a regularization framework for few-shot Neural Radiance Field (NeRF) optimization that enforces geometric consistency across views using depth-guided warping and feature-level consistency modeling to overcome under-constrained optimization and overfitting. It sets itself apart from pixel-level photometric consistency methods (e.g., NeuralWarp, StructNeRF) by operating at the feature level, which preserves view-dependent specular effects that pixel-level losses would suppress. Unlike pre-training-based few-shot methods (e.g., PixelNeRF, MVSNeRF), it optimizes NeRF from scratch without requiring extensive multi-scene dataset priors. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: A sparse set of N input images \{Ii\} for i \in \{1,..., N\}, where typical values are N=3 or N=5. Camera poses for these views are assumed known or estimated. Outputs: A trained NeRF model f\theta capable of rendering novel views and depth maps. Data Structures: NeRF Model (f\theta): A multi-layer perceptron (MLP) taking positional encoded coordinates \gamma(x) and viewing directions \gamma(d) as input, outputting density \sigma \in \mathbb{R} and view-dependent color c \in \mathbb{R}^3. Feature Extractor (f\phi): A network used to extract high-level features from images. Consistency Mask: A binary or soft mask used to filter out inconsistently warped information. Formulas: 1. Ray Parameterization: rp(t) = o + t dp, where o is the camera center, dp is the direction through pixel p, and t is the distance along the ray. 2. Accumulated Transmittance: T(t) = \exp\left(-\int{tn}^{t} \sigma(rp(s))ds\right), representing opacity accumulated from near bound tn to t. 3. Volume Rendering Integral: C(rp) = \int{tn}^{tf} T(t)\sigma(rp(t))c(rp(t), dp)dt, where C(rp) is the predicted color, tn and tf are near/far bounds. 4. Depth Rendering: Per-ray depth is formulated as a weighted composition of sampled depths along the ray, derived from the density values \sigma. 5. Observation Loss: L{obs} = \sum{rp \in R} \|C'(rp) - C(rp)\|2^2, where C' is the ground truth color and R is a batch of training rays. 6. Feature-Level Consistency Loss: Applied between the features of the unobserved viewpoint image and the features of the warped observed viewpoint image. Steps: 1. Sample Novel Viewpoint: Randomly sample a camera viewpoint j (unseen) from which corresponding ray vectors are generated in a patch-wise manner. 2. Render Depth: Render a depth map Dj at the unseen viewpoint j using the NeRF's recovered density values \sigma along sampled rays. 3. Inverse Warping: For each seen viewpoint i, use the rendered depth map Dj and the known camera poses to perform inverse warping, projecting pixels from the seen image Ii to the unseen viewpoint j to create a warped image I{i \to j}. 4. Generate Consistency Mask: Create a mask to filter out regions where the warping is inconsistent (e.g., due to occlusions or large viewpoint differences), preventing erroneous warped information from harming the network. 5. Feature Extraction: Extract features from the rendered image at the unseen viewpoint Ij and the warped images I{i \to j} using the feature extractor f\phi. 6. Compute Consistency Loss: Calculate the feature-level consistency loss L{cons} between the features of the target view and the warped source views, capturing contextual and structural information while ignoring individual pixel color differences. 7. Optimize: Update the NeRF parameters \theta by minimizing the combined loss, typically L{total} = L{obs} + \lambda L{cons}, where \lambda is a weighting factor. 8. Coarse-to-Fine Training: Employ coarse-to-fine training strategies for sampling and pose generation to stabilize optimization. Pitfalls: Non-Lambertian Surfaces: View-dependent color variations can break pixel-level consistency. GeCoNeRF handles this by using feature-level regularization. Few-Shot Limitations: Large viewpoint differences and heavy self-occlusions cause sharp performance drops and warping difficulties. Addressed by the consistency mask. Geometry Aware Contrastive Learning (GeoContrast) is a regularization technique for few-shot NeRF that enforces multi-view geometric consistency by distinguishing surface points from non-surface points using depth-guided warping. It sets itself apart from sibling methods like random pixel sampling by explicitly constructing positive and negative pairs based on 3D geometric projections, thereby preventing the model from learning incorrect depth-geometry mappings in under-constrained scenarios. Time and Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Measured Performance: Demonstrated effectiveness on synthetic and real datasets (e.g., Blender, Tanks & Temples) for few-shot novel view synthesis and 3D reconstruction. Scaling: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Regularizes NeRF at semantic and structural levels; allows modeling of view-dependent radiance; does not require pre-training on multi-scene datasets; handles non-Lambertian surfaces via feature-level loss. Limitations: Performance drops significantly in few-shot settings with large viewpoint differences and heavy self-occlusions if not for the consistency mask; warping procedure is difficult with sparse views. When to use: Few-shot novel view synthesis and 3D reconstruction where pre-training is not feasible or desired. When not to use: Dense view scenarios where pixel-level photometric consistency might be sufficient and simpler; scenarios where view-dependent specular effects are not important and pixel-level loss is preferred. GeCoNeRF was introduced by Min-Seop Kwak, Jiuhn Song, and Seungryong Kim at Korea University. It was published as arXiv:2301.10941v3 on 27 Apr 2023, and accepted to ICML 2023. It addresses the limitations of existing few-shot NeRF methods, which either require pre-training on large datasets (e.g., PixelNeRF, MVSNeRF) or struggle with large viewpoint differences and occlusions in sparse settings (e.g., NeuralWarp, StructNeRF). name: Geometry Aware Contrastive Learning (GeoContrast)
body: Geometry Aware Contrastive Learning (GeoContrast) is a contrastive learning method that enforces multi-view consistency by using geometric constraints to define positive and negative samples, distinguishing surface points from non-surface points. It differs from sibling methods that rely on random pixel sampling by explicitly constructing pairs based on 3D geometric projections. GeoContrast operates on pairs of source views to extract geometrically enhanced features. It constructs contrastive pairs by projecting 2D pixels into 3D space and re-projecting them into other views, using ground truth depth to identify surface correspondences. Inputs: A set of N{near} source views \{Ii, Ki, Ei\}{i=1}^{N{near}}, where Ii is the image, Ki is the intrinsic matrix, and Ei is the extrinsic matrix. Ground truth depth maps \delta for the source views. A shared CNN feature extractor M(\cdot) that produces feature maps Fi from images Ii. Hyperparameters: Nc (number of sampled pixels per view), N{neg} (number of negative samples per pixel), \tau' (temperature, default 10000). Outputs: A scalar contrastive loss value L{contrast} used to update the feature extractor weights. Pixel Coordinate: p = (u, v)^\top representing a 2D coordinate in a source view. Homogeneous Coordinate: \tilde{p} representing p in homogeneous coordinates. 3D Point: p3 representing a point in world coordinates. Feature Vector: fp representing the feature vector extracted at pixel p. 1. Feature Extraction: For each source view i, extract feature maps Fi using the shared CNN M(\cdot). 2. Pixel Sampling: For a pair of source views i and j, randomly sample a batch of Nc pixels \{p\} from view i. 3. Positive Pair Construction: For each sampled pixel p in view i, retrieve its depth \deltap from the ground truth depth map. Compute the 3D point p3 corresponding to p using the camera parameters: p3 = ti + \deltap Ri Ki^{-1} \tilde{p} where ti and Ri are the translation and rotation components of the extrinsic matrix Ei for view i. Project p3 into view j to obtain the 2D coordinate q^+: q^+ = Kj (Rj^{-1} (p3 - tj)). Occlusion Check: Verify that the region around q^+ in view j is unoccluded. If occluded, discard (p, q^+) as a positive pair. If unoccluded, (p, q^+) is a positive pair. 4. Negative Pair Construction: For the same pixel p in view i, generate N{neg} negative samples \{q^-\}{k=1}^{N{neg}} in view j. These are obtained by projecting p to view j using different depth hypotheses or by sampling pixels that do not correspond to the surface point p3. Each negative pair represents the projection of a non-surface 3D point. 5. Weight Calculation: Calculate the weight \lambda{q^-} for each negative sample q^- based on its geometric distance to the positive sample q^+: \lambda{q^-} = \frac{\exp(\|q^+ - q^-\|^2 / \tau')}{\sum{r \in R} \exp(\|q^+ - r\|^2 / \tau')} where R is the set of negative samples in the batch, and \tau' = 10000. 6. Loss Computation: Compute the contrastive loss for pixel p using a weighted InfoNCE formulation: L{contrast}^p = -\log \frac{\exp(-\|q^+ - q^+\|^2 / \tau')}{\exp(-\|q^+ - q^+\|^2 / \tau') + \sum{k=1}^{N{neg}} \lambda{qk^-} \exp(-\|q^+ - qk^-\|^2 / \tau')}. The final contrastive loss is averaged over all samples p and all source view pairs: L{contrast} = \frac{1}{Nc} \sum{p} L{contrast}^p. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import numpy as np import random def geometryawarecontrastiveloss( featuresi, featuresj, depthi, depthj, Ki, Kj, Ei, Ej, Nc, Nneg, tauprime=10000.0): """ Computes the GeoContrast loss for a pair of views i and j. Args: featuresi: Feature map for view i, shape (H, W, C) featuresj: Feature map for view j, shape (H, W, C) depthi: Depth map for view i, shape (H, W) depthj: Depth map for view j, shape (H, W) Ki, Kj: Intrinsic matrices (3x3) Ei, Ej: Extrinsic matrices (4x4) Nc: Number of pixels to sample Nneg: Number of negative samples per pixel tauprime: Temperature parameter Returns: loss: Scalar contrastive loss """ H, W, C = featuresi.shape TOLERANCE = 0.05 # Standard depth consistency threshold sampledu = [random.randint(0, H - 1) for in range(Nc)] sampledv = [random.randint(0, W - 1) for in range(Nc)] totalloss = 0.0 validcount = 0 for k in range(Nc): u, v = sampledu[k], sampledv[k] phom = np.array([u, v, 1.0]) deltap = depthi[u, v] Ri = Ei[:3,:3] ti = Ei[:3, 3] Rj = Ej[:3,:3] tj = Ej[:3, 3] camcoordsi = np.linalg.inv(Ki) @ phom p3 = ti + deltap (Ri @ camcoordsi) camcoordsj = np.linalg.inv(Rj) @ (p3 - tj) qplushom = Kj @ camcoordsj qplus = qplushom[:2] / qplushom[2] if not (0 <= qplus[0] < W and 0 <= qplus[1] < H): continue projecteddepthj = camcoordsj[2] gtdepthqplus = depthj[int(round(qplus[1])), int(round(qplus[0]))] if abs(projecteddepthj - gtdepthqplus) > TOLERANCE: continue negu = [random.randint(0, H - 1) for in range(Nneg)] negv = [random.randint(0, W - 1) for in range(Nneg)] qnegs = [np.array([negu[m], negv[m]]) for m in range(Nneg)] distpossq = 0.0 distnegssq = [np.sum((qplus - qneg) 2) for qneg in qnegs] exppos = np.exp(-distpossq / tauprime) expnegs = [np.exp(-d / tauprime) for d in distnegssq] sumexpnegs = sum(expnegs) if sumexpnegs == 0: continue lambdas = [e / sumexpnegs for e in expnegs] weightednegsim = sum(l e for l, e in zip(lambdas, expnegs)) lossp = -np.log(exppos / (exppos + weightednegsim)) totalloss += lossp validcount += 1 if validcount == 0: return 0.0 return totalloss / validcount Nc: Number of sampled pixels. Not given in the sources. N{neg}: Number of negative samples. Not given in the sources. \tau': Temperature hyper-parameter. Default value is 10000. Occlusion: Positive pairs must be discarded if the projected point q^+ is occluded in the target view. Depth Precision: The 3D reconstruction p3 relies on ground truth depth \deltap. Errors in depth lead to incorrect p3 and thus incorrect q^+. Boundary Conditions: Projected points q^+ or q^- may fall outside the image boundaries. The parent method that provides the feature extraction backbone and depth prediction module. GeoContrast is a regularization term added to GeCoNeRF's training objective. GeCoNeRF The broader class of methods using contrastive learning for NeRF generalization. GeoContrast is a specific variant that uses geometry-aware sampling rather than random sampling. ContraNeRF Time Complexity: Depends on the number of sampled pixels Nc and negative samples N{neg}. For each pixel, 3D projection and re-projection are performed. Memory Complexity: Requires storing feature maps for source views and depth maps. Strengths: Enforces geometric consistency, reducing artifacts in novel view synthesis, especially in few-shot settings. Limitations: Relies on ground truth depth for training, which may not be available in real-world scenarios without additional depth estimation. Computationally more expensive than random sampling due to 3D projections. GeoContrast was introduced in the paper "ContraNeRF: Generalizable Neural Radiance Fields for Synthetic-to-real Novel View Synthesis via Contrastive Learning". It addresses the problem of generalizing NeRF to unseen scenes by leveraging contrastive learning to enforce multi-view consistency. The method builds on the GeCoNeRF framework, enhancing it with geometry-aware contrastive pairs. name: DeRF (Decomposed Radiance Fields)
head: Decomposed Radiance Fields
body: DeRF mitigates the high computational cost of neural volume rendering by spatially decomposing a scene into multiple parts, each represented by a smaller neural network, allowing for near-constant inference time regardless of the number of parts. It addresses the diminishing returns in rendering quality when scaling network capacity by using multiple smaller networks instead of one large network, providing up to 3× more efficient inference than Neural Radiance Fields with the same quality, or up to 1.0 dB PSNR improvement for the same cost. DeRF builds on Radiance-field optimization by replacing the single global network with a set of N local networks, activated via a differentiable spatial partition. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: Camera ray \mathbf{r}, number of decomposition parts N, Voronoi sites \phi \in \mathbb{R}^{N \times 3}, temperature \beta, and network weights \theta = \{\thetan\}{n=1}^N. Outputs: Rendered color \hat{C}(\mathbf{r}) and gradients for optimization. Data Structures: Voronoi Sites (\phi): A tensor of shape (N, 3) storing the 3D coordinates of the N Voronoi centers. Network Heads (\thetan): N pairs of neural networks (\sigma{\thetan}, \mathbf{c}{\thetan}). Each network takes a 3D position \mathbf{x} (and direction \mathbf{d} for color) and outputs density and color. Weights (w{\phin}(\mathbf{x})): Computed on-the-fly using the soft Voronoi formula. Formulas: The radiance field functions \sigma(\mathbf{x}) and \mathbf{c}(\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{d}) are modeled as a weighted sum of N separate functions: \sigma(\mathbf{x}) = \sum{n=1}^{N} w{\phin}(\mathbf{x}) \sigma{\thetan}(\mathbf{x}) \mathbf{c}(\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{d}) = \sum{n=1}^{N} w{\phin}(\mathbf{x}) \mathbf{c}{\thetan}(\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{d}) The soft Voronoi weight w{\phin}(\mathbf{x}) is computed using a softmax over squared distances to Voronoi sites \phi: w{\phin}(\mathbf{x}) = \frac{\exp(-\beta \|\mathbf{x} - \phin\|^2)}{\sum{j=1}^{N} \exp(-\beta \|\mathbf{x} - \phij\|^2)} where \beta > 0 is a temperature parameter controlling the softness of the Voronoi approximation. As \beta \to \infty, the weights approach a hard partition where only one w{\phin}(\mathbf{x}) is non-zero. Parameters: N: Number of neural network heads. Typical values depend on scene complexity; the paper uses N=16 for experiments. \beta: Temperature parameter. Scheduled from a low value to a high value during training to transition from soft to hard partitioning. Algorithm Steps: 1. Pre-training: Train coarse global networks \sigma{\text{coarse}} and \mathbf{c}{\text{coarse}} for the entire scene for approximately 100k iterations. 2. Decomposition Optimization: Optimize the coarse network weights \theta{\text{coarse}} and Voronoi sites \phi separately. Minimize reconstruction loss \mathcal{L}{\text{radiance}} for \theta{\text{coarse}} and uniformity loss \mathcal{L}{\text{uniform}} for \phi. The uniformity loss is defined as \mathcal{L}{\text{uniform}} = \|\mathbb{E}{\mathbf{r} \sim \mathcal{R}}[W{\phi}(\mathbf{r})]\|2^2, where W{\phi}(\mathbf{r}) \in \mathbb{R}^N is the vector of soft Voronoi weights for points sampled along ray \mathbf{r}. This encourages equal usage of all heads. Pitfall: Do not allow \mathcal{L}{\text{uniform}} to affect the optimization of \theta{\text{coarse}}, as it inhibits the density network's ability to learn scene structure. 3. Local Network Training: Fix \phi and train the per-decomposition networks \sigma{\thetan} and \mathbf{c}{\thetan} using only \mathcal{L}{\text{radiance}}. 4. Inference: For a given ray \mathbf{r}, sample points \mathbf{x}i. Compute w{\phin}(\mathbf{x}i) for all n. Identify the index n^ with the maximum weight to evaluate only the corresponding head \sigma{\theta{n^}} and \mathbf{c}{\theta{n^}}, leveraging the Painter's Algorithm for compositing. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import torch import torch.nn as nn class DeRFHead(nn.Module): def init(self, hiddendim): super().init() self.netdensity = nn.Sequential( nn.Linear(3, hiddendim), nn.ReLU(), nn.Linear(hiddendim, hiddendim), nn.ReLU(), nn.Linear(hiddendim, 1)) self.netcolor = nn.Sequential( nn.Linear(6, hiddendim), nn.ReLU(), nn.Linear(hiddendim, hiddendim), nn.ReLU(), nn.Linear(hiddendim, 3)) def forward(self, x, d): sigma = self.netdensity(x) c = self.netcolor(torch.cat([x, d], dim=-1)) return sigma, c class DeRF: def init(self, N, hiddendim, betainit=1.0, betafinal=1000.0): self.N = N self.betainit = betainit self.beta = betainit self.betafinal = betafinal self.heads = nn.ModuleList([DeRFHead(hiddendim) for in range(N)]) self.phi = nn.Parameter(torch.randn(N, 3) 10.0) self.coarsesigma = nn.Linear(3, 1) self.coarsecolor = nn.Linear(6, 3) def computeweights(self, x): dists = torch.cdist(x, self.phi, p=2) 2 return torch.softmax(-self.beta dists, dim=-1) def forward(self, x, d, inference=False): weights = self.computeweights(x) if inference: idx = torch.argmax(weights, dim=-1) sigman, cn = self.headsidx return sigman, cn else: sigmasum = torch.zeroslike(x[:,:1]) csum = torch.zeroslike(x[:,:3]) for n in range(self.N): sigman, cn = self.headsn wn = weights[:, n:n+1] sigmasum += wn sigman csum += wn cn return sigmasum, csum def schedulebeta(self, step, totalsteps): self.beta = self.betainit + (self.betafinal - self.betainit) (step / totalsteps) A specific training protocol to stabilize the decomposition and local network training. 1. Pre-train coarse networks: Train \sigma{\text{coarse}} and \mathbf{c}{\text{coarse}} for the entire scene for ≈100k iterations. 2. Separate Optimization: Optimize \theta{\text{coarse}} and \phi separately. Minimize \mathcal{L}{\text{radiance}} for \theta{\text{coarse}} and \mathcal{L}{\text{uniform}} for \phi. 3. Local Training: Fix \phi and train \sigma{\thetan} and \mathbf{c}{\thetan} using \mathcal{L}{\text{radiance}} only. Pitfall: Allowing \mathcal{L}{\text{uniform}} to affect \theta{\text{coarse}} inhibits density learning and causes instability. Time Complexity: Near-constant inference time with respect to the number of decomposed parts N, as only one head is evaluated per point during inference. Memory Complexity: Lower than NeRF for equivalent quality, as smaller networks are used. Performance: Up to 3× more efficient inference than NeRF with the same rendering quality, or up to 1.0 dB PSNR improvement for the same inference cost on real-world scenes. Strengths: Mitigates diminishing returns of network capacity; compatible with Painter's Algorithm for GPU-friendly rendering. Limitations: Requires careful scheduling of \beta and training phases; random decomposition is not appropriate due to memory access patterns. DeRF was proposed by Daniel Rebain, Wei Jiang, Soroosh Yazdani, Ke Li, Kwang Moo Yi, and Andrea Tagliasacchi from the University of British Columbia, University of Toronto, Simon Fraser University, and Google Research. It was published in arXiv:2011.12490v1 on 25 Nov 2020 and later in CVPR 2021. The method addresses the computational intensity of NeRF by leveraging the observation that there are diminishing returns in employing larger networks, proposing spatial decomposition with smaller networks instead.
