name: Dual Rendering Equation Optimization
head: Deformable Radiance Field Optimization, Volume Rendering and Optimization, Volume and Surface Rendering Loss
body: Dual Rendering Equation Optimization (DREO) is a differentiable volume rendering method that jointly optimizes scene geometry and appearance by minimizing a combined loss derived from two distinct rendering equations: one for volumetric density accumulation and one for surface reflectance. Unlike standard NeRF which relies solely on volumetric integration, DREO explicitly models surface normals and BRDF properties to enable relighting. It differs from Deformable and Dynamic Fields by focusing on the dual-equation loss formulation rather than temporal deformation fields, and from Surface-SDF Representation by using a neural radiance field tensor optimized via volume rendering integrals rather than explicit signed distance functions. The method optimizes a scene tensor (representing density, color, and BRDF parameters) by jointly minimizing losses from two rendering passes. Inputs: Camera poses, input images C{gt}, and optionally ground truth normals n{gt}. Outputs: Optimized scene tensor parameters, rendered colors, and surface normals. The scene is represented as a tensor field encoding density \sigma, color c, and BRDF parameters. Specific internal layouts (e.g., voxel grid vs. MLP) are not detailed in the primary source. 1. Volume Rendering Pass: Emit a ray r(t) = o + td from origin o in direction d. Sample N points along the ray. Compute density-weighted color accumulation using the volume rendering equation: C{vl}(r) = \sum{i=1}^{N} Ti (1 - \exp(-\sigmai \deltai)) ci, \quad Ti = \exp(-\sum{j=1}^{i-1} \sigmaj \deltaj) where \deltai is the distance between consecutive samples. 2. Surface Rendering Pass: For surface points x, compute the reflected radiance L(x, d). Approximate the surface integral of the reflectance equation using the incident light field Li(x, d) and normal n: L(x, d) = bval \cdot Li(x, d) (n \cdot d) where bval is the BRDF value decoded by a decoder B{dec}. 3. Loss Evaluation: Compute the total loss combining surface rendering, volume rendering, and normal consistency: loss = \lambda1 || L(x, d) - C{gt} ||2^2 + \lambda2 || C{vl}(r) - C{gt} ||2^2 + \lambda3 || n - n{gt} ||2^2 where \lambda1, \lambda2, \lambda3 are loss weights. 4. Optimization: Update the scene tensor parameters to minimize the loss. Schedule: Set \lambda1 = 0 during early iterations before the scene surface is obtained. Once a threshold is reached, gradually decrease \lambda2 in subsequent iterations. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def dualrenderingoptimization(cameras, gtcolors, gtnormals, numiterations, surfacethreshold, decayrate, lambda1init, lambda2init, lambda3init): # Initialize scene tensor parameters (density sigma, color c, BRDF decoder weights) sceneparams = initializesceneparameters() lambda1 = lambda1init lambda2 = lambda2init lambda3 = lambda3init for iteration in range(numiterations): # Sample camera rays and points along them rays = sampleraysfromcameras(cameras) points = samplepointsalongrays(rays, numsamples=128) # Query scene tensor for density, color, and normal sigma, c, n = queryscenetensor(sceneparams, points) # Compute distances between consecutive samples deltas = computesegmentlengths(points) # Volume Rendering Pass T = 1.0 Cvl = 0.0 for i in range(len(points)): alpha = 1.0 - exp(-sigma[i] deltas[i]) Cvl += T alpha c[i] T = exp(-sigma[i] deltas[i]) # Surface Rendering Pass # Compute incident light field Li(x, d) from environment or precomputed field Li = computeincidentlightfield(points, rays.direction) bval = decodebrdf(sceneparams, points) Lsurf = bval Li dot(n, rays.direction) # Loss Evaluation lossvol = meansquarederror(Cvl, gtcolors) losssurf = meansquarederror(Lsurf, gtcolors) lossnorm = meansquarederror(n, gtnormals) if gtnormals is not None else 0.0 totalloss = lambda1 losssurf + lambda2 lossvol + lambda3 lossnorm # Optimization Step # Compute gradients w.r.t. scene parameters and apply optimizer step gradients = computegradients(totalloss, sceneparams) sceneparams = optimizerstep(sceneparams, gradients) # Loss Weight Schedule if iteration > surfacethreshold: lambda1 = 1.0 lambda2 = decayrate return sceneparams \lambda1, \lambda2, \lambda3: Loss weights for surface rendering, volume rendering, and normal consistency, respectively. bval: BRDF value decoded by the BRDF decoder B{dec}. Ti: Discretization calculation of transmittance. Early Training: Surface loss (\lambda1) must be zero initially because the scene surface is not yet well-defined; enabling it too early leads to poor convergence. Lighting Approximation: The surface integral is approximated using an incident light field, which may introduce errors if the lighting is complex or dynamic. BRDF Decoder: The choice of BRDF model (e.g., simplified Disney principle-based) depends on the scene dataset characteristics. This method synthesizes a 3D volumetric texture (specifically cloud volumes) from a single input photograph by minimizing an energy function that measures the distance between the input image pixel blocks and the rendered voxel blocks. It adapts the patch-based texture synthesis technique of Kwatra et al. to the 3D volume domain, treating voxel blocks as the fundamental units of synthesis. Unlike standard volume rendering which uses fixed parameters, this method optimizes the voxel values themselves to match visual evidence. It is distinguished from its parent Dual Rendering Equation Optimization by explicitly solving for the volume geometry/appearance via an Expectation-Maximization (EM) framework rather than optimizing only lighting parameters. This variant renders Gaussians twice using a differentiable rasterizer: once for the C-ToF view to compute the quad loss, and once for the RGB view to compute the color loss. It enables joint optimization of depth and color from multi-view data, leveraging the complementary information from both modalities. This variant processes full images instead of randomly sampled subsets for reconstruction, using 8-10 reference views per task. It employs recursive control variates to reduce primal rendering overhead, requiring ~4-8 times fewer samples than plain DRT to reach similar quality, while the adjoint phase runtime remains identical. Control variates alleviate the need for large sample counts required by L1 loss to mitigate loss function bias. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Performance: The dual-equation approach requires two rendering passes per iteration, increasing computational cost compared to single-equation methods. Strengths: Joint optimization of volume and surface cues improves reconstruction quality. Explicit BRDF modeling enables relighting. Limitations: The method requires careful scheduling of loss weights and depends on the incident light field approximation. BRDF modeling requires dataset-specific decoder tuning. When to Use: Not given in the sources. When Not to Use: Not given in the sources. Dual Rendering Equation Optimization was introduced in the paper "STensoRRF: Tensorial Able Relighting Radiance Field for Single-Tensor Scene Representation". The method builds on the principles of neural radiance fields (NeRF) and differentiable rendering, extending them to include surface reflectance modeling. It addresses the limitations of standard NeRF in handling complex lighting and geometry by incorporating a surface rendering equation alongside the volume rendering equation. name: Texture Optimization for Volume Synthesis
head: Kwatra et al. method adaptation
body: This method synthesizes a 3D volumetric texture (specifically cloud volumes) from a single input photograph by minimizing an energy function that measures the distance between the input image pixel blocks and the rendered voxel blocks. It adapts the patch-based texture synthesis technique of Kwatra et al. to the 3D volume domain, treating voxel blocks as the fundamental units of synthesis. Unlike standard volume rendering which uses fixed parameters, this method optimizes the voxel values themselves to match visual evidence. It is distinguished from its parent Dual Rendering Equation Optimization by explicitly solving for the volume geometry/appearance via an Expectation-Maximization (EM) framework rather than optimizing only lighting parameters. Inputs: I{ph}: Input photograph (2D image). V{ex}: Example cloud volume database containing N example volumes. C{ex} = \{C1, \dots, CK\}: Set of K voxel blocks extracted from V{ex}. Each block has dimensions w \times w \times Nz. L0^, La^: Optimized lighting parameters obtained by solving a nonlinear least square problem. Outputs: V: Synthesized cloud volume. Data Structures: Voxel Block (zV): A 3D array of size w \times w \times Nz representing density/extinction values. Rendered Image Block (zI): A 2D array of size w \times w representing pixel values. Vector z: Concatenation of rendered image block and voxel block: z = \{zI, zV\}. Vector xp: Concatenation of input image pixel block xp^I and corresponding voxel block xp^V: xp = \{xp^I, xp^V\}. Distance Metric d(xp, z): d(xp, z) = \|xp^V - zV\|^2 + \lambda \|xp^I - zI\|^2 where \lambda is a relative weighting coefficient (default 100). Algorithm Steps: 1. Preprocessing: Extract voxel blocks C{ex} from the example database V{ex}. Ensure grid resolution in the Z-direction is equal to Nz. Render all example volumes in V{ex} using L0^ and La^ to populate the set of candidate vectors z. 2. Sorting: Sort all voxel blocks in the order in which incident sunlight reaches them. This ensures that transmittance \tau can be calculated for voxels closer to the sun first. 3. Optimization Loop (EM Steps): Repeat until energy converges or a specified number of iterations is reached: E-step (Expectation Step): Minimize energy with respect to xp (specifically xp^V) keeping zp fixed. This results in a least squares problem. The derivative of the energy function E(x; \{z\}) = \sum{p \in X{ph}} d(xp, zp) with respect to xp^V is set to zero. The solution simplifies to a weighted average computation of neighbor voxel blocks. Update xp^V and accumulate the best zp^V into the corresponding voxels in V. M-step (Maximization Step): Minimize energy with respect to zp keeping xp fixed. This involves searching for the closest vector zp from the set of all vectors z. Acceleration Strategy: Since searching all K vectors is expensive, use a two-pass search: 1. For each xp^V, find k nearest neighbor vectors z1^V, \dots, zk^V from the database using the FLANN library. 2. Render each zi^V to compute zi^I. 3. Search for the closest vector zp from the set \{z1, \dots, zk\} based on the distance metric d(xp, z). Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def synthesizevolume(inputimage, examplevolumes, lightingparams, sundirection, w, Nz, kneighbors, lambdaweight, maxiterations, tolerance): # 1. Preprocessing: Extract voxel blocks from example database voxelblocksdb = [] for vol in examplevolumes: for y in range(0, vol.shape[0] - w + 1, w): for x in range(0, vol.shape[1] - w + 1, w): voxelblocksdb.append(vol[y:y+w, x:x+w,:]) volh, volw = inputimage.shape[:2] cols = volw // w rows = volh // w volume = [[[0.0] Nz for in range(cols)] for in range(rows)] # 2. Sorting: Sort blocks by sunlight incidence order sortedindices = sorted(range(rows cols), key=lambda i: (i // cols) sundirection[0] + (i % cols) sundirection[1]) # 3. Optimization Loop for iteration in range(maxiterations): totalenergy = 0.0 for idx in sortedindices: r, c = idx // cols, idx % cols ystart, xstart = r w, c w xpI = inputimage[ystart:ystart+w, xstart:xstart+w] xpV = volume[r][c] # --- E-step --- # Minimize energy w.r.t xp^V keeping zp fixed. # Results in a least squares problem solved by a weighted average of neighbor voxel blocks. neighbors = getneighbors(volume, r, c, rows, cols, w, Nz) xpV = weightedaverage(xpV, neighbors) volume[r][c] = xpV # --- M-step --- # Find closest zp from candidates using acceleration. xpVflat = [v for row in xpV for col in row for v in col] kindices = findknearestneighbors(xpVflat, voxelblocksdb, kneighbors) bestcandidate = None mindist = float('inf') for i in kindices: candV = voxelblocksdb[i] candI = renderblock(candV, lightingparams, sundirection) distV = sum((a - b)2 for a, b in zip(xpVflat, [v for row in candV for col in row for v in col])) distI = sum((a - b)2 for a, b in zip([v for row in xpI for col in row for v in col], [v for row in candI for col in row for v in col])) dist = distV + lambdaweight distI if dist < mindist: mindist = dist bestcandidate = candV volume[r][c] = bestcandidate totalenergy += mindist if totalenergy < tolerance: break return volume def renderblock(zV, lightingparams, sundirection): # Computes transmittance and radiance along the sun direction h, w, Nz = zV.shape out = [[0.0] w for in range(h)] # Standard volume rendering accumulation return out def getneighbors(vol, r, c, rows, cols, w, Nz): # Returns adjacent voxel blocks in the synthesized volume neighbors = [] for dr in [-1, 0, 1]: for dc in [-1, 0, 1]: if dr == 0 and dc == 0: continue nr, nc = r + dr, c + dc if 0 <= nr < rows and 0 <= nc < cols: neighbors.append(vol[nr][nc]) return neighbors def weightedaverage(current, neighbors): # Returns the weighted average of the current block and its neighbors if not neighbors: return current avg = [[[0.0]Nz for in range(w)] for in range(w)] count = 1 for n in neighbors: for i in range(w): for j in range(w): for k in range(Nz): avg[i][j][k] += n[i][j][k] count += 1 for i in range(w): for j in range(w): for k in range(Nz): avg[i][j][k] = (current[i][j][k] + avg[i][j][k]) / count return avg def findknearestneighbors(query, db, k): # Standard k-NN search dists = [sum((a - b)2 for a, b in zip(query, vec)) for vec in db] return sorted(range(len(dists)), key=lambda i: dists[i])[:k] Parameters: \lambda: Relative weighting coefficient for the pixel difference term. Default value is 100. k: Number of nearest neighbors searched in the M-step acceleration strategy. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Transmittance Calculation: Requires voxel values of blocks closer to the sun to be computed first. Incorrect sorting order leads to incorrect lighting/shadowing. Computational Cost: Rendering zV for every candidate is expensive. The k-nearest neighbor acceleration is critical for feasibility. Boundary Conditions: The method assumes specific boundary handling for the weighted average in the E-step. An extension of the texture optimization method to synthesize a cloud volume such that rendered images from two orthogonal directions (e.g., xy and xz planes) match two input images. It augments the vector xp and z to include pixel values from the second image plane (I{xz}). The distance metric becomes: d(xp, z) = \|xp^V - zV\|^2 + \lambda \|xp^I - zI\|^2 + \mu \|xp^{I{xz}} - zI^{I{xz}}\|^2 where \mu is a relative weighting coefficient (e.g., 10 in experiments). A method to synthesize a new texture patch Pn by pasting an example patch En from an input image I{in} into the output I{out}, ensuring boundary matching to avoid feature mismatches. It uses an overlap region to initialize optimized kd-trees for accelerating approximate nearest neighbors (ANN) search. The matching condition is d(\partial(Pn), \partial(En)) < \eta, where \partial(\cdot) is the boundary zone and \eta is a prescribed constant. A probability density function (PDF) is computed based on the L2 distance of boundaries, and a patch is randomly chosen according to the PDF, then pasted and blended. Time Complexity: The method is iterative (EM steps). Each iteration involves rendering k candidate blocks per pixel block. Rendering is O(Nz) per block. The ANN search is O(K \log K) or better with FLANN. Overall complexity is high due to repeated rendering. Memory Complexity: Requires storing the example volume database and pre-rendered candidates. Memory scales with K \times w^2 \times Nz. Performance: On a desktop PC (Intel Core-i7 4790 3.60 GHz), preprocessing takes about 4 minutes for 137 example volumes. Synthesis time depends on resolution and iteration count. Strengths: Produces visually consistent textures that match input photographs. Limitations: Computationally expensive due to rendering in the loop. Requires a database of example volumes. The method is based on the texture optimization technique proposed by Kwatra et al. [11] (referenced in). It was adapted for 3D cloud volume synthesis by Iwasaki, Dobashi, and Okabe in 2017. The approach leverages the similarity between 2D patch-based synthesis and 3D voxel-based synthesis, extending the EM framework to volumetric data. name: Two-Phase Method
body: The Two-Phase Method is a synthesis technique designed to ensure both geometric and appearance continuity in synthesized results, particularly for complex texture and geometry. It decouples the patch selection process into two stages: first filtering candidates for geometric continuity, then selecting one for appearance continuity. The method operates on a set of candidate patches derived from an exemplar volume. It requires a density field V^{(d)} and a color feature field V^{(f)} from the exemplar, along with a shading map to guide lighting consistency. Inputs: Candidate patch set \mathcal{P} (filtered by shading similarity). Exemplar density field V^{(d)}. Exemplar color feature field V^{(f)}. Synthesis target patch Pn. Outputs: Selected patch P{selected} from \mathcal{P}. Data Structures: Patches are represented as 3D voxel blocks. Density field V^{(d)} stores scalar density values. Color feature field V^{(f)} stores color/feature vectors. Steps: 1. Phase 1: Geometry-based Synthesis For each candidate patch Pi \in \mathcal{P}, calculate the geometric continuity error against the target Pn using the density field V^{(d)}. Select a subset of kg candidate patches that exhibit the highest geometric continuity. 2. Phase 2: Appearance-based Synthesis For each of the kg candidates from Phase 1, calculate the appearance continuity error against the target Pn using the color feature field V^{(f)}. Select the single patch P{selected} that best matches the target in color features. Formulas: Geometric Error Eg(Pi, Pn): Not given in the sources. Appearance Error Ea(Pi, Pn): Not given in the sources. Parameters: kg: Number of candidates retained after Phase 1. Not given in the sources. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Boundary artifacts may occur if patches are not constrained at scene edges. Precision issues in density or color feature comparison may lead to suboptimal selections. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def twophasesynthesis(targetpatch, candidatepatches, densityfield, colorfield): # Phase 1: Geometry-based Synthesis geometricerrors = [] for patch in candidatepatches: err = boundaryl2(patch, targetpatch, densityfield) geometricerrors.append((patch, err)) geometricerrors.sort(key=lambda x: x[1]) kg = 10 # Not given in the sources topcandidates = [x[0] for x in geometricerrors[:kg]] # Phase 2: Appearance-based Synthesis appearanceerrors = [] for patch in topcandidates: err = boundaryl2(patch, targetpatch, colorfield) appearanceerrors.append((patch, err)) bestpatch, = min(appearanceerrors, key=lambda x: x[1]) return bestpatch def boundaryl2(patch1, patch2, field): """Computes L2 distance between boundary voxels of two patches using a field.""" # Not given in the sources # Standard implementation: mean squared difference of boundary voxels b1 = field[patch1.boundaryindices] b2 = field[patch2.boundaryindices] return ((b1 - b2) 2).mean() A variant for textures without sharp boundaries that introduces an edge error factor into the synthesis process to measure and balance average edge discontinuities. It calculates edge errors Ee by measuring average edge discontinuities for composed textures, considering that discontinuities along an edge come from 2 vertical pairs of adjacent cube faces (e.g., A(E)-C(E) and C(N)-D(N) for edge a1-b2-c3-d4). For each face of a cube, errors of the 4 edges are calculated from all cubes having the same color on the adjacent face, collecting the 2 face errors of the 12 edges from all combinations once and only once. The accumulated synthesis error is Es = pi \times Ei + pe \times Ee, where Ei is the inside error, Ee is the edge error, and pi, pe are weights set as the inverse of their cutting path size to balance the errors. The method ensures geometric and appearance continuity, which is crucial for complex texture and geometry. Performance details such as time and memory complexity are not explicitly provided in the sources. The method is suitable for synthesizing large-scale scenes with reasonable lighting. The Two-Phase Method was proposed in the context of NeRF Synthesis with Shading Guidance. It addresses high-dimensional texture synthesis problems inspired by traditional exemplar-based methods. name: General Radiance Field Rendering via MLP
head: MLP Radiance Field with Aggregated Features
body: This method renders novel views by training a Multi-Layer Perceptron (MLP) to predict volumetric density and RGB color for 3D points, forming a "General Radiance Field" (GRF). It differs from standard Neural Radiance Fields (NeRF) by using aggregated 3D point features as the primary spatial input to the MLP, rather than raw 3D coordinates, while retaining the viewing direction as a secondary input. It solves the problem of generalizable 3D representation and rendering from 2D images without requiring explicit 3D ground truth data. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: A set of 2D images with known camera poses. For rendering, the inputs are a 3D point p and a viewing direction Vp. Outputs: Volumetric density \sigma(t) and RGB color c(t) for points along a ray, resulting in a rendered 2D image pixel value. Data Structures: Aggregated Point Features (\bar{F}p): A feature vector representing the 3D point p. The exact dimension and generation method are not specified in the source, but it replaces the raw coordinate vector [x, y, z] used in NeRF. Viewing Direction (Vp): A 3D vector [xv, yv, zv] representing the direction from the camera center to point p. MLP: A neural network architecture strictly following the design in NeRF [29]. It takes the concatenated input [\bar{F}p, Vp] and outputs density and color. Numbered Steps: 1. Positional Encoding: Apply the positional encoding function \gamma(\cdot) proposed in NeRF [29] to both the aggregated point features \bar{F}p and the viewing direction Vp. \text{input} = [\gamma(\bar{F}p), \gamma(Vp)] 2. MLP Forward Pass: Feed the encoded input into the MLP to predict the volumetric density \sigma and RGB color c for the query point. [\sigma, c] = \text{MLP}(\text{input}) 3. Ray Casting: For each pixel in the target image, cast a ray from the camera center through the pixel into the 3D space. 4. Hierarchical Sampling: Estimate the volume rendering integral using numerical quadrature with a hierarchical sampling strategy, strictly following the method in NeRF [29]. This involves sampling points along the ray, potentially using coarse and fine networks (though the source states the MLP design follows NeRF, it does not explicitly detail the two-network hierarchy, only that the strategy is followed). 5. Volume Rendering: Compute the final pixel color rgb by integrating the density and color along the ray: rgb = \int{tn}^{tf} T(t) c(t) \sigma(t) dt where the transmittance T(t) is: T(t) = \exp\left(-\int{tn}^{t} \sigma(s) ds\right) Here, tn and tf are the near and far clipping planes, c(t) is the color at point t, and \sigma(t) is the volume density at point t. 6. Optimization: Minimize the L2 loss between the rendered RGB values and the ground truth RGB values from the input images. The entire network is trained end-to-end. Parameters: Loss Function: L2 loss between rendered and ground truth RGB. Positional Encoding: As defined in NeRF [29]. Sampling: Hierarchical sampling strategy as defined in NeRF [29]. Typical Values: Not given in the sources. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision: Not given in the sources. Boundaries: The ray integration is bounded by near and far clipping planes (tn, tf). Degenerate Input: Not given in the sources. A neural network representation that replaces costly recursive path tracing for indirect illumination by learning a continuous function for visibility and outgoing radiance. Time and Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Measured Performance: On ShapeNetv2 chair and car classes, the method (GRF) achieved a PSNR of 22.65. For comparison, SRNs achieved 24.48. Other metrics (SSIM, LPIPS, etc.) are provided in the source but not detailed here beyond the PSNR comparison. Scaling: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Can synthesize novel 2D images directly by querying points along light rays, trainable only with 2D images without requiring 3D data. Limitations: The source does not specify limitations compared to NeRF other than the architectural difference in input. When to use: When a general radiance field representation is desired that leverages aggregated features rather than raw coordinates. When not: When raw coordinate-based spatial encoding is preferred or when higher PSNR is required (SRNs performed better in the cited experiment). The method was introduced in the paper "GRF: Learning a General Radiance Field for 3D Representation and Rendering". It builds on the principles of Radiance-field optimization [44-radiance-field-optimization.md] and specifically adapts the MLP architecture from NeRF [4972-neural-radiance-fields.md]. The key innovation is the substitution of raw 3D coordinates with aggregated point features as the input to the radiance field MLP. GRF: Learning a General Radiance Field for 3D Representation and Rendering, https://doi.org/10.1109/iccv48922.2021.01490, fetched 2026-10-26

name: Visibility and Outgoing Radiance MLP
body: This method replaces costly recursive path tracing for indirect illumination by learning continuous functions for visibility and outgoing radiance, enabling efficient view synthesis and inverse rendering. It differs from its parent General Radiance Field Rendering via MLP by explicitly decoupling the visibility term and the outgoing radiance field into separate learnable MLPs, avoiding the need for expensive sphere tracing during forward rendering. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: Observed images, geometry (surface points \mathbf{x}, normals \mathbf{\hat{n}}), and viewing/lighting directions (\boldsymbol{\omega}i, \boldsymbol{\omega}o). Outputs: Visibility value v and outgoing radiance Lo. Data Structures: The method utilizes two primary MLPs: 1. Visibility MLP (V): Maps surface point location \mathbf{x} and direction \boldsymbol{\omega}i to visibility v. 2. Outgoing Radiance Field MLP (R): Maps surface point location \mathbf{\hat{x}}, normal \mathbf{\hat{n}}, and viewing direction \boldsymbol{\omega}o to outgoing radiance Lo. Both networks share the same architecture: 4 layers with 512 hidden units. Positional Encoding: Input coordinates are encoded using positional encoding: 3D locations: 10 frequency components. Directions: 4 frequency components [G: Standard positional encoding \gamma(p) = [\sin(2^0 \pi p), \cos(2^0 \pi p), \dots, \sin(2^{L-1} \pi p), \cos(2^{L-1} \pi p)]]. Training Procedure: 1. Visibility MLP Training: Train V using a small number of sampled rays above surface points to learn occlusion. 2. Outgoing Radiance Field Training: Train R using a view synthesis method [27] from observed images and geometry. 3. Rendering: Query R to obtain the outgoing radiance of the second intersection (cumulative result of multiple bounces): Lo(\mathbf{\hat{x}'}, -\boldsymbol{\omega}i) = R(\mathbf{\hat{x}'}, \mathbf{\hat{n}'}, -\boldsymbol{\omega}i) \quad (6) Parameters: Optimizer: Adam. Learning Rate: 5 \times 10^{-4}. Framework: PyTorch. Loss Function: The full loss in the final stage is: \ell = \lambda{\text{recon}}\ell{\text{recon}} + \lambda{\text{KL}}\ell{\text{KL}} + \lambda{\text{s}}\ell{\text{s}} \quad (12) \lambda{\text{recon}} = 1.0 \lambda{\text{KL}} = 0.01 \lambda{\text{s}} = 0.1 Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import torch import torch.nn as nn import torch.optim as optim class PositionalEncoding(nn.Module): def init(self, numfreqcomponents): super().init() self.numfreqcomponents = numfreqcomponents def forward(self, x): # x shape: (..., D) # Output shape: (..., D 2 numfreqcomponents) freqbands = 2.0 torch.arange(self.numfreqcomponents, device=x.device).float() xexpanded = x.unsqueeze(-1) freqbands.unsqueeze(0) # (..., D, numfreq) xsin = torch.sin(xexpanded) xcos = torch.cos(xexpanded) return torch.cat([xsin, xcos], dim=-1).view(x.shape[0], -1) class VisibilityMLP(nn.Module): def init(self, locfreq=10, dirfreq=4): super().init() self.locenc = PositionalEncoding(locfreq) self.direnc = PositionalEncoding(dirfreq) # Input dim: 3210 + 324 = 60 + 24 = 84 inputdim = 3 2 locfreq + 3 2 dirfreq hiddendim = 512 self.layers = nn.Sequential( nn.Linear(inputdim, hiddendim), nn.ReLU(), nn.Linear(hiddendim, hiddendim), nn.ReLU(), nn.Linear(hiddendim, hiddendim), nn.ReLU(), nn.Linear(hiddendim, hiddendim), nn.ReLU(), nn.Linear(hiddendim, 1) # Output v) def forward(self, x, omegai): # x: (N, 3), omegai: (N, 3) xenc = self.locenc(x) omegaienc = self.direnc(omegai) combined = torch.cat([xenc, omegaienc], dim=-1) return self.layers(combined).squeeze(-1) class OutgoingRadianceMLP(nn.Module): def init(self, locfreq=10, dirfreq=4): super().init() self.locenc = PositionalEncoding(locfreq) self.normenc = PositionalEncoding(dirfreq) # For normal self.direnc = PositionalEncoding(dirfreq) # For viewing direction # Input dim: 3210 + 324 + 324 = 60 + 24 + 24 = 108 inputdim = 3 2 locfreq + 3 2 dirfreq + 3 2 dirfreq hiddendim = 512 self.layers = nn.Sequential( nn.Linear(inputdim, hiddendim), nn.ReLU(), nn.Linear(hiddendim, hiddendim), nn.ReLU(), nn.Linear(hiddendim, hiddendim), nn.ReLU(), nn.Linear(hiddendim, hiddendim), nn.ReLU(), nn.Linear(hiddendim, 3) # Output Lo (RGB)) def forward(self, xhat, nhat, omegao): # xhat: (N, 3), nhat: (N, 3), omegao: (N, 3) xenc = self.locenc(xhat) nenc = self.normenc(nhat) omegaoenc = self.direnc(omegao) combined = torch.cat([xenc, nenc, omegaoenc], dim=-1) return self.layers(combined) def trainvisibilitymodel(): model = VisibilityMLP() optimizer = optim.Adam(model.parameters(), lr=5e-4) # 1. Train using a small number of sampled rays above surface points # 2. Minimize visibility prediction error against ground truth occlusion pass def trainradiancemodel(): model = OutgoingRadianceMLP() optimizer = optim.Adam(model.parameters(), lr=5e-4) # 1. Train using view synthesis method [27] from observed images and geometry # 2. Minimize loss: l = 1.0 lrecon + 0.01 lKL + 0.1 ls pass Re-parameterizes visibility as an MLP to avoid time-consuming sphere tracing during forward rendering. It is trained using a small number of sampled rays above surface points. Time Complexity: Training takes approximately 1 hour for the second stage and 2 hours for the third stage on a single RTX 3090 GPU. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Provides a compact and continuous representation of visibility, significantly reducing rendering time compared to recursive path tracing. Limitations: Requires pre-trained geometry and observed images for training. When to use: When efficient view synthesis and inverse rendering are required, and recursive path tracing is too slow. When not to use: When high-fidelity dynamic indirect illumination without pre-training is needed. The method originates from "Modeling Indirect Illumination for Inverse Rendering" (CVPR 2022). It addresses the computational bottleneck of calculating indirect illumination via recursive path tracing by learning it as a continuous function. name: Visibility Parameterization
head: Mixture of Logistics Visibility, NeuRay Visibility Parameterization, Visibility from occlusion probability
body: Visibility Parameterization is a method to represent the visibility function v(z) along a ray as a continuous, differentiable function using a neural network. It solves the problem of expensive ray tracing or sphere tracing for occlusion by replacing discrete sampling with a learned probability distribution. It sets itself apart from recursive path tracing by avoiding iterative ray-surface intersection tests, instead decoding a feature vector into a mixture of logistic distributions that directly yields the occlusion probability. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A feature vector \mathbf{g} (decoded from an input view's feature map) and a depth z along the ray originating from the location of \mathbf{g}. Output: The visibility value v(z), the occlusion CDF t(z), and the hitting probability density hi for sample points. Data Structures: Visibility Feature Map \mathbf{G}: A 2D map where each element is a feature vector \mathbf{g}. MLP Decoder: A neural network that takes \mathbf{g} and outputs parameters for the mixture of logistics: means \{\mui\}, standard deviations \{\sigmai\}, and mixing weights \{wi\}. Parameters: Nl: Number of logistic distributions in the mixture. Typical value: 2. Kt: Number of sample points on the test ray. Formulas: 1. Visibility Definition: v(z) = 1 - t(z) where t(z) is the occlusion probability CDF. 2. Occlusion CDF (Mixture of Logistics): t(z;\{\mui,\sigmai,wi\})=\sum {i=1}^{N{l}} wi S\left(\frac{z-\mui}{\sigmai}\right) where S(\cdot) is the sigmoid function, \mui is the mean, \sigmai is the standard deviation, and wi is the mixing weight with \sum wi = 1. 3. Alpha Value (from CDF): The alpha value \alphak for a sample point at depth zk is derived from the CDF. While the source defines hitting probability using \alphak, the alpha value itself is typically the probability of hitting the surface within the interval ending at zk. Based on the hitting probability formula, \alphak represents the probability mass at step k. In the context of the coarse-to-fine variant, alpha is explicitly defined as: \alpha(z0, z1) = \frac{t(z1) - t(z0)}{1 - t(z0)}. For the standard hitting probability, \alphak is the probability of the k-th interval. 4. Hitting Probability Density: h{i}=\prod {k=1}^{i-1} (1-\alpha k)\alpha i where \alphak is the alpha value derived from the distribution for the k-th interval. 5. Final Color Aggregation: \bm {c}=\sum {i=1}^{Kt} \bm {c}{i} h{i} where \bm {c}{i} is the local feature/color at sample point i. Steps: 1. Decode the visibility feature vector \mathbf{g} using an MLP to obtain parameters \{\mui, \sigmai, wi\} for i=1 \dots Nl. 2. For a given depth z, compute the occlusion CDF t(z) using the mixture of logistics formula. 3. Compute visibility v(z) = 1 - t(z). 4. For rendering, compute alpha values \alphak for sample intervals along the ray. 5. Compute hitting probabilities hi using the product formula. 6. Aggregate colors \bm{c}i weighted by hi to produce the final pixel color. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def sigmoid(x): """Standard sigmoid function.""" return 1.0 / (1.0 + math.exp(-x)) def computeocclusioncdf(z, params): """ Compute the occlusion CDF t(z) for a given depth z. Args: z: float, depth along the ray. params: dict containing 'mus', 'sigmas', 'weights' lists of length Nl. Returns: float: t(z), the cumulative occlusion probability. """ mus = params['mus'] sigmas = params['sigmas'] weights = params['weights'] Nl = len(mus) tz = 0.0 for i in range(Nl): # S((z - mui) / sigmai) term = sigmoid((z - mus[i]) / sigmas[i]) tz += weights[i] term return tz def computevisibility(z, params): """ Compute visibility v(z) = 1 - t(z). Args: z: float, depth along the ray. params: dict containing mixture parameters. Returns: float: v(z), the visibility value. """ tz = computeocclusioncdf(z, params) return 1.0 - tz def computealphainterval(tz0, tz1): """ Compute alpha value for a depth interval (z0, z1). Formula: (t(z1) - t(z0)) / (1 - t(z0)) Args: tz0: float, CDF at start of interval. tz1: float, CDF at end of interval. Returns: float: alpha value. """ if 1.0 - tz0 == 0: return 0.0 return (tz1 - tz0) / (1.0 - tz0) def renderray(samplepointsdepths, samplecolors, params): """ Render a ray by aggregating colors weighted by hitting probabilities. Args: samplepointsdepths: list of floats [z1, z2,..., zKt]. samplecolors: list of color vectors [c1, c2,..., cKt]. params: dict containing mixture parameters. Returns: float: final color c (scalar for simplicity, or vector sum). """ Kt = len(samplepointsdepths) finalcolor = 0.0 # Precompute CDFs for all sample points to get alphas # Note: The formula hi = prod(1-alphak) alphai implies alphai # is the probability of hitting at step i. # We need alpha for each interval. Let's assume intervals are defined # by consecutive sample points. # Compute t(z) for all points tvalues = [computeocclusioncdf(z, params) for z in samplepointsdepths] # Compute alpha for each interval (zi, z{i+1})? # The source formula hi = prod{k=1}^{i-1} (1-alphak) alphai # suggests alphai is associated with the i-th sample/interval. # Standard volume rendering alpha is often defined per interval. # Let's compute alphai as the probability of the i-th segment. # Using the interval formula: alpha(zi, z{i+1}) alphas = [] for i in range(Kt - 1): z0 = samplepointsdepths[i] z1 = samplepointsdepths[i+1] t0 = tvalues[i] t1 = tvalues[i+1] alphai = computealphainterval(t0, t1) alphas.append(alphai) # The last point's alpha is not defined by an interval in this loop. # However, the hitting probability formula uses alphai. # In standard NeuRay, alphai is often derived from the CDF difference # normalized by remaining transparency. # Let's assume the hitting probability hi corresponds to the sample point i. # If Kt samples, there are Kt-1 intervals. # The source says hi for depth interval (zi, z{i+1}). # So h1 corresponds to interval (z1, z2)? Or (z0, z1)? # Source: "hi for depth interval (zi, z{i+1})". # And c = sum ci hi. # This implies hi is the weight for color ci. # Let's re-read carefully: "hi for depth interval (zi, z{i+1})". # And "c = sum{i=1}^{Kt} ci hi". # This indexing is slightly ambiguous. Usually, hi is the probability # of the ray terminating at or within the i-th interval. # Let's stick to the explicit formula: hi = prod{k=1}^{i-1} (1-alphak) alphai. # This requires alpha1, alpha2,..., alpha{Kt}. # We computed alphas for intervals (z1, z2)... (z{Kt-1}, z{Kt}). # We need alpha for the first interval (z1, z2) to be alpha1? # Or is alphai the alpha associated with sample point i? # In NeuRay, alpha is often computed as: # alpha(z0, z1) = (t(z1) - t(z0)) / (1 - t(z0)) # This is the probability of hitting in (z0, z1) given survival up to z0. # Let's assume sample points are z1... zKt. # Intervals are (z1, z2), (z2, z3),..., (z{Kt-1}, z{Kt}). # And perhaps a final interval or the last point is handled differently. # Given the source formula hi = prod{k=1}^{i-1} (1-alphak) alphai, # h1 = alpha1. # h2 = (1-alpha1) alpha2. # We need alpha1... alpha{Kt}. # Let's define alphai as the alpha for the interval ending at zi? # Or starting at zi? # Source: "alpha value derived from the distribution". # And "hi for depth interval (zi, z{i+1})". # This suggests hi is the weight for the interval (zi, z{i+1}). # But the sum is over ci. Or in the interval? # Usually ci is the color at sample point zi. # Let's assume the standard interpretation: # alphai is the probability of the i-th sample point being the hit. # This is often computed as: # alphai = (t(zi) - t(z{i-1})) / (1 - t(z{i-1})) # with z0 = 0 (or near field). # Let's implement this standard interpretation which matches the formula structure. # Define z0 = 0 (or minimum depth) zprev = 0.0 tprev = computeocclusioncdf(zprev, params) hittingprobs = [] for i in range(Kt): zcurr = samplepointsdepths[i] tcurr = tvalues[i] # Alpha for the interval (zprev, zcurr) # This alpha represents the probability of hitting in this interval # given survival up to zprev. alphai = computealphainterval(tprev, tcurr) # Hitting probability hi # hi = alphai prod{k=1}^{i-1} (1-alphak) # We can compute this iteratively. if i == 0: hi = alphai else: # hi = h{i-1} / (1 - alpha{i-1}) alphai ? Better to compute product. # Let's compute product explicitly for clarity prodsurvival = 1.0 for k in range(i): # We need alphak for k < i # We didn't store them. Let's store them. pass # Let's rewrite loop to store alphas pass # Rewritten loop alphaslist = [] tprev = computeocclusioncdf(0.0, params) # Assuming start at 0 for i in range(Kt): zcurr = samplepointsdepths[i] tcurr = tvalues[i] alphai = computealphainterval(tprev, tcurr) alphaslist.append(alphai) tprev = tcurr hittingprobs = [] for i in range(Kt): alphai = alphaslist[i] prodsurvival = 1.0 for k in range(i): prodsurvival = (1.0 - alphaslist[k]) hi = prodsurvival alphai hittingprobs.append(hi) # Aggregate finalcolor = 0.0 for i in range(Kt): finalcolor += samplecolors[i] hittingprobs[i] return finalcolor Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision: The product formula for hitting probabilities can suffer from underflow if many intervals have high alpha values. Use log-space arithmetic or iterative updates if numerical stability is an issue. Boundaries: The CDF t(z) must be non-increasing and 0 \le v(z) \le 1. The mixture of logistics ensures t(z) is monotonic if weights are positive and sum to 1. Degenerate Input: If \sigmai is very small, the logistic distribution becomes a step function, potentially causing discontinuities in gradients. Add a small epsilon to \sigmai during training. A method to accelerate rendering by computing a coarse hitting probability \hat{h}i from NeuRay to identify relevant sample points, avoiding feature aggregation on empty points. It sets itself apart by using input view visibility to estimate test ray occupancy without full fine-grained sampling. Choose it when rendering speed is critical and the scene has large empty regions. Link: NeuRay (hypothetical link to main NeuRay article). Definition: Uses a coarse hitting probability \hat{h}i to identify points with large probability, sampling fine points only around these locations for feature aggregation. Steps: 1. Compute alpha value \tilde{\alpha} in depth range (z0, z1) on an input ray. 2. Compute coarse alpha \hat{\alpha}i for point pi on test ray. 3. Compute coarse hitting probability \hat{h}i. 4. Use \hat{h}i to identify points with large probability. 5. Sample fine points around these locations for feature aggregation. Formulas: 1. Alpha Value on Input Ray: \tilde {\alpha }(z0,z1)=\frac {t(z1)-t(z0)}{1-t(z0)}. 2. Coarse Alpha: \hat {\alpha }{i}=\frac {\sum {j}\tilde {\alpha }{i,j}(z{i,j},z{i,j}+li) v{i,j}}{\sum {j} v{i,j}} where j indexes input views, z{i,j} is depth on view j, li is distance to next point, and v{i,j} is visibility. 3. Coarse Hitting Probability: \hat {h}{i}=\prod {k=1}^{i-1} (1-\hat {\alpha }k)\hat {\alpha }i. Parameters: li: Distance between point pi and its subsequent point p{i+1} on the test ray. Pitfalls: The consistency loss \ell{consist} = \frac{1}{Kt}\sum{i=1}^{Kt} CE(\tilde{h}i, hi) is used to enforce consistency between coarse and fine hitting probabilities. Time Complexity: Rendering is faster than sphere tracing because it avoids iterative ray-surface intersection tests. The MLP decoding is O(Nl) per sample point. Memory Complexity: Requires storing the visibility feature map \mathbf{G} and the MLP parameters. Measured Performance: On synthetic objects, NeuRay achieves higher PSNR and SSIM than baselines like PixelNeRF and MVSNeRF. On real objects (DTU), it also shows improvements. Strengths: Compact representation, differentiable, avoids expensive tracing. Limitations: Requires training on input views; generalization depends on the number of input views and the quality of the feature map. When to use: When indirect illumination needs to be modeled efficiently and differentiability is required. When not to use: If real-time rendering with very limited memory is required and the scene is simple enough for traditional ray tracing. Originated in the paper "Neural Rays for Occlusion-aware Image-based Rendering" (CVPR 2022) by and "Modeling Indirect Illumination for Inverse Rendering" (CVPR 2022) by. It was developed to address the computational cost of sphere tracing in inverse rendering and image-based rendering. It is used in general radiance field rendering via MLPs, specifically in the NeuRay framework. name: Tetra-NeRF
head: Tetrahedra Field
body: Tetra-NeRF is a radiance field representation that replaces uniform voxel grids or sparse point clouds with a dense set of non-overlapping tetrahedra generated by Delaunay triangulation of an input point cloud. It solves the problem of empty regions in sparse point-based methods and the fixed-resolution limitations of voxel-based methods by providing a continuous, adaptive representation that is naturally denser near surfaces. Unlike Point-NeRF which requires growing the point cloud during training to fill gaps, Tetra-NeRF uses a fixed set of points and constant parameter count, ensuring the representation complexity does not grow. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A point cloud (typically from Structure from Motion/SfM like COLMAP) and camera poses. Output: Novel view images synthesized via volumetric rendering. Data Structures: 1. Point Cloud: A set of 3D points P. Each point has a position and an initial feature vector. Feature Vector: Size 64. Initialization: Dimensions 0-3: RGBA color values from the point cloud, rescaled to [0, 1]. Original points have \alpha=1; randomly added points have \alpha=0. Dimensions 4-63: Uniformly sampled from [-10^{-4}, 10^{-4}]. 2. Tetrahedra Field: A set of non-overlapping tetrahedra \mathcal{T} covering the convex hull of P, generated via Delaunay triangulation. 3. Acceleration Structure: An acceleration structure (e.g., OptiX) for fast ray-triangle intersection to identify intersected tetrahedra. 4. MLP: Density/Appearance MLP: 3 layers, hidden size 128, Kaiming uniform initialization. Color MLP: Concatenate appearance features with ray direction encoded via Fourier features, pass through a single linear layer to get raw RGB. Numbered Steps: 1. Point Cloud Preprocessing: If the number of points |P| > 10^6, subsample to 10^6 points randomly. If |P| \le 10^6 (e.g., Blender dataset), add |P|/2 random points to prevent edge artifacts. To add a random point: Sample x0 \in P, a random normal n, and \alpha \sim \mathcal{N}(\bar{d}, \bar{d}^2/4), where \bar{d} is the average spacing of P. Add x = x0 + \alpha n. 2. Triangulation: Perform Delaunay triangulation on P to generate the set of tetrahedra \mathcal{T}. 3. Ray Casting and Intersection: For each pixel in a virtual view, project a ray r from the camera plane. Compute intersections between r and all faces of tetrahedra in \mathcal{T} using an acceleration structure (e.g., OptiX). Limit to the first 512 intersected triangles per ray. Determine the corresponding tetrahedra and order them along the ray to allow marching. 4. Barycentric Coordinate Computation: For each ray-tetrahedron intersection, compute the 2D barycentric coordinates \lambda{2D} with respect to the triangle face. Obtain the 3D barycentric coordinates \lambda{3D} for the tetrahedron by setting the coordinate for the vertex opposite to the intersected face to 0. For a query point x inside a tetrahedron, compute its barycentric coordinates \lambda by linearly interpolating between the barycentric coordinates of the two ray-tetrahedron intersections. Alternatively, compute \lambda directly via volume ratios: \lambda = \left(\frac{V{x234}}{V{1234}}, \frac{V{1x34}}{V{1234}}, \frac{V{12x4}}{V{1234}}, \frac{V{123x}}{V{1234}}\right) where V{1234} is the volume of the tetrahedron and V{x234} etc. are volumes formed by replacing one vertex with x. 5. Feature Interpolation: Interpolate the feature vectors fv at the four vertices of the containing tetrahedron using \lambda: fx = \sum{i=1}^{4} \lambdai f{vi} This yields the feature vector fx for the query point x. 6. Network Query: Pass fx through the 3-layer MLP (hidden size 128) to compute raw density \bar{\sigma} and appearance features a. Encode the ray direction d using Fourier features. Concatenate a and the encoded d, then pass through the single linear layer to get raw RGB color \bar{c}. 7. Activation: Map raw density to volume density: \sigma = \text{softplus}(\bar{\sigma}). Map raw color to RGB: c = \text{sigmoid}(\bar{c}). 8. Sampling: Coarse Stage: Use stratified uniform sampling along the ray, limited to the space occupied by tetrahedra. Fine Stage: Use density weights from the coarse stage to bias sampling towards potential surfaces. Use the same network as the coarse stage. Merge coarse and fine samples. 9. Rendering: Compute accumulated weights \bar{w}i for each sample i: \bar{w}i = (1 - \exp (-\sigmai \deltai))\exp \left(-\sum{j=1}^{i-1}\sigmaj \deltaj\right) where \deltai = ti - t{i-1}. Normalize weights to wi and render final color C: \mathbf {C} = \sum {i=1}^{N} Ti (1 - \exp (\sigma i \delta i))\mathbf {c}i, \quad Ti = \exp (-\sum {j=1}^{i-1} \sigmaj \deltaj) Backpropagate MSE loss to update features and MLP weights. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import numpy as np def softplus(x): return np.log1p(np.exp(-np.abs(x))) + np.maximum(x, 0) def sigmoid(x): return 1 / (1 + np.exp(-x)) def tetravolume(a, b, c, d): return np.abs(np.dot(a - d, np.cross(b - d, c - d))) / 6.0 def computebarycentriccoords(v1, v2, v3, v4, x): V = tetravolume(v1, v2, v3, v4) if V == 0: return np.array([0.25, 0.25, 0.25, 0.25]) return np.array([ tetravolume(x, v2, v3, v4) / V, tetravolume(v1, x, v3, v4) / V, tetravolume(v1, v2, x, v4) / V, tetravolume(v1, v2, v3, x) / V ]) def raytriangleintersect(rayo, rayd, a, b, c): edge1 = b - a edge2 = c - a h = np.cross(rayd, edge2) det = np.dot(edge1, h) if abs(det) < 1e-8: return None, None invdet = 1.0 / det s = rayo - a u = np.dot(s, h) invdet if u < 0 or u > 1: return None, None q = np.cross(s, edge1) v = np.dot(rayd, q) invdet if v < 0 or u + v > 1: return None, None t = np.dot(edge2, q) invdet if t > 1e-6: return t, np.array([1.0 - u - v, u, v]) return None, None def raytetraintersect(rayo, rayd, v1, v2, v3, v4): faces = [(v1, v2, v3), (v1, v2, v4), (v1, v3, v4), (v2, v3, v4)] ts = [] lambdas = [] for a, b, c in faces: t, lam = raytriangleintersect(rayo, rayd, a, b, c) if t is not None: ts.append(t) # Map triangle barycentrics to tet barycentrics (opposite vertex gets 0) if np.allclose([a, b, c], [v1, v2, v3]): tetlam = np.array([lam[0], lam[1], lam[2], 0.0]) elif np.allclose([a, b, c], [v1, v2, v4]): tetlam = np.array([lam[0], lam[1], 0.0, lam[2]]) elif np.allclose([a, b, c], [v1, v3, v4]): tetlam = np.array([lam[0], 0.0, lam[1], lam[2]]) else: tetlam = np.array([0.0, lam[0], lam[1], lam[2]]) lambdas.append(tetlam) if len(ts) >= 2: idx = np.argsort(ts) return ts[idx[0]], ts[idx[1]], lambdas[idx[0]], lambdas[idx[1]] return None, None, None, None def inversecdfsample(weights, tmin, tmax, numsamples): cdf = np.cumsum(weights) cdf /= cdf[-1] u = np.random.uniform(0, 1, numsamples) indices = np.searchsorted(cdf, u) tfine = tmin + (tmax - tmin) u return np.sort(tfine) def tetranerfforward(rayorigin, raydirection, tetrahedra, vertexfeatures, mlpdensityappearance, mlpcolor, numcoarsesamples=64, numfinesamples=48): # 1. Find intersected tetrahedra and compute segments tetsegments = [] for idx, tet in enumerate(tetrahedra): v1, v2, v3, v4 = tet tin, tout, lamin, lamout = raytetraintersect(rayorigin, raydirection, v1, v2, v3, v4) if tin is not None: tetsegments.append((idx, tin, tout, lamin, lamout)) # Limit to 512 triangles/tetrahedra as per source tetsegments = sorted(tetsegments, key=lambda x: x[1])[:512] if not tetsegments: return np.array([0.0, 0.0, 0.0]) # 2. Coarse Sampling bounds tmin = max(0.0, min(seg[1] for seg in tetsegments)) tmax = max(seg[2] for seg in tetsegments) coarset = np.linspace(tmin, tmax, numcoarsesamples) coarsesigma = [] coarsec = [] coarseweights = [] for tq in coarset: # Find containing tetrahedron segment tetidx = -1 lamq = None for i, (idx, tin, tout, lamin, lamout) in enumerate(tetsegments): if tin <= tq <= tout: tetidx = idx # Linear interpolation of barycentric coordinates along ray frac = (tq - tin) / (tout - tin) lamq = (1.0 - frac) lamin + frac lamout break if tetidx == -1: coarsesigma.append(0.0) coarsec.append([0.0, 0.0, 0.0]) coarseweights.append(0.0) continue tet = tetrahedra[tetidx] v1, v2, v3, v4 = tet feats = vertexfeatures[tetidx] # (4, 64) # Interpolate features fx = np.dot(lamq, feats) # MLP: Density and Appearance rawsigma, appearance = mlpdensityappearance(fx) sigma = softplus(rawsigma) # MLP: Color # Fourier encoding placeholder for direction encodeddir = np.concatenate([np.sin(raydirection 2np.arange(10)), np.cos(raydirection 2np.arange(10))]) rawc = mlpcolor(np.concatenate([appearance, encodeddir])) c = sigmoid(rawc) coarsesigma.append(sigma) coarsec.append(c) coarsesigma = np.array(coarsesigma) coarsec = np.array(coarsec) # 3. Compute coarse weights for fine sampling bias deltas = np.diff(np.concatenate([[0], coarset])) alphacoarse = 1 - np.exp(-coarsesigma deltas) transmittancecoarse = np.exp(-np.cumsum(coarsesigma deltas)) weightscoarse = alphacoarse transmittancecoarse # 4. Fine Sampling finet = inversecdfsample(weightscoarse, tmin, tmax, numfinesamples) finesigma = [] finec = [] for tq in finet: tetidx = -1 lamq = None for idx, tin, tout, lamin, lamout in tetsegments: if tin <= tq <= tout: tetidx = idx frac = (tq - tin) / (tout - tin) lamq = (1.0 - frac) lamin + frac lamout break if tetidx == -1: finesigma.append(0.0) finec.append([0.0, 0.0, 0.0]) continue tet = tetrahedra[tetidx] v1, v2, v3, v4 = tet feats = vertexfeatures[tetidx] fx = np.dot(lamq, feats) rawsigma, appearance = mlpdensityappearance(fx) sigma = softplus(rawsigma) encodeddir = np.concatenate([np.sin(raydirection 2np.arange(10)), np.cos(raydirection 2np.arange(10))]) rawc = mlpcolor(np.concatenate([appearance, encodeddir])) c = sigmoid(rawc) finesigma.append(sigma) finec.append(c) finesigma = np.array(finesigma) finec = np.array(finec) # 5. Merge and Render allt = np.concatenate([coarset, finet]) allsigma = np.concatenate([coarsesigma, finesigma]) allc = np.concatenate([coarsec, finec]) sortidx = np.argsort(allt) allt = allt[sortidx] allsigma = allsigma[sortidx] allc = allc[sortidx] deltas = np.diff(np.concatenate([[0], allt])) alpha = 1 - np.exp(-allsigma deltas) transmittance = np.exp(-np.cumsum(allsigma deltas)) weights = alpha transmittance finalcolor = np.sum(weights[:, None] allc, axis=0) return finalcolor Parameters: Feature Vector Size: 64. MLP Hidden Sizes: 128. Batch Size: 4,096 random rays. Optimizer: RAdam. Learning Rate: Exponential decay from 10^{-3} to 10^{-4} in 300k steps. Max Intersections: 512 triangles per ray. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Fixed Triangle Limit: Limiting to 512 triangles can degrade results in large scenes or those with fine-grained tetrahedralization, as more intersections may be needed. Mitigation: Consider more triangles at the cost of runtime. Edge Artifacts: With low point counts, some pixels on edges may not intersect any tetrahedra, causing artifacts. Mitigation: Add randomly generated points near the original point cloud. Empty Regions: Unlike Point-NeRF, Tetra-NeRF does not suffer from empty regions due to sparse points because the triangulation covers the convex hull continuously. Time Complexity: Depends on the number of tetrahedra, vertices, and scene structure. Training speed ranges from 15k to 30k rays per second on a single NVIDIA A100 GPU. Memory Complexity: Fixed number of parameters. Feature vectors are stored at vertices. The number of parameters stays constant during training, unlike Point-NeRF or Plenoxels which grow complexity. Strengths: Adaptive resolution (denser near surfaces), continuous representation avoiding empty regions, fixed parameter count. Limitations: Performance degrades if the fixed triangle intersection limit (512) is insufficient for the scene complexity. When to Use: When a high-quality point cloud (e.g., from SfM) is available, and adaptive resolution is desired without the overhead of growing representations or fixed grid resolutions. When Not to Use: In very large scenes where the fixed intersection limit causes significant artifacts, or when no initial point cloud is available. Tetra-NeRF was introduced in the paper "Tetra-NeRF: Representing Neural Radiance Fields Using Tetrahedra". It builds on the idea of using classical surface reconstruction methods (Delaunay triangulation) to create a dense, non-overlapping tetrahedral mesh from a point cloud, extending the triangle-rendering pipeline to neural radiance fields. It addresses limitations of MLP-based NeRFs (costly queries, hard to modify) and voxel/grid-based methods (fixed resolution, non-local effects) by storing features freely in 3D space on a tetrahedral mesh. name: Light Field and Lumigraph Methods
head: Opacity Light Field Volume Viewing, Unstructured Lumigraph Rendering
body: Light Field and Lumigraph Methods synthesize novel views by treating a set of key views as an opacity light field parameterized on a geometric proxy surface. The method uses unstructured lumigraph rendering (ULR) to visualize the opacity field interactively on standard graphics hardware. Inputs and outputs: Input consists of a triangular mesh (geometric proxy) and a set of RGBA key views with corresponding camera parameters. The output is a rendered novel view image. Data structures: The method stores the triangular mesh proxy, RGBA key view textures, and a pre-computed BSP tree for back-to-front triangle traversal. Numbered steps: 1. For each mesh vertex v, determine the set of visible key views. A key view is visible if all neighboring triangles around v are completely unoccluded in that view. 2. For each vertex v, select the k (k \le 3) visible views closest to the new viewing direction \mathbf{d}. These are designated as the closest views for vertex v. 3. Compute blending weights for the closest views using unstructured lumigraph interpolation, assigning higher weights to views closer to \mathbf{d}. 4. Render each triangle by blending the key views from the closest views of its three vertices, amounting to blending up to nine textures per triangle. Formulas and parameters: The exact ULR interpolation formula is not provided in the sources. The method uses a fixed maximum of k=3 closest views per vertex. Edge cases and pitfalls: Triangles must be rendered in back-to-front order to ensure correct alpha blending; a BSP tree for the geometric proxy is pre-computed and traversed during rendering. For geometric proxies with relatively small occlusions, considering all camera views for blending at each vertex yields higher image quality at a slight performance cost. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def renderopacitylightfield(mesh, keyviews, cameraparams, newviewdirection): # Pre-compute BSP tree for back-to-front triangle traversal bsptree = computebsptree(mesh) renderedimage = emptyimage() for triangle in traversebacktofront(bsptree): v1, v2, v3 = triangle.vertices # Step 1 & 2: Find visible and closest views for each vertex closestv1 = getclosestvisibleviews(v1, mesh, keyviews, cameraparams, newviewdirection, k=3) closestv2 = getclosestvisibleviews(v2, mesh, keyviews, cameraparams, newviewdirection, k=3) closestv3 = getclosestvisibleviews(v3, mesh, keyviews, cameraparams, newviewdirection, k=3) # Step 3: Compute blending weights using ULR interpolation w1 = computeulrweights(closestv1, newviewdirection) w2 = computeulrweights(closestv2, newviewdirection) w3 = computeulrweights(closestv3, newviewdirection) # Step 4: Blend up to nine textures per triangle via GPU hardware tricolor = blendtriangletextures(triangle, [closestv1, closestv2, closestv3], [w1, w2, w3]) rasterizetriangle(triangle, tricolor) return renderedimage def getclosestvisibleviews(vertex, mesh, keyviews, cameraparams, viewdirection, k=3): visibleviews = [] for view in keyviews: neighbors = getneighboringtriangles(vertex, mesh) # A key view is visible if all neighboring triangles around v are completely unoccluded if all(not isoccluded(tri, view, cameraparams) for tri in neighbors): visibleviews.append(view) # Sort by angular distance to viewdirection, return top k visibleviews.sort(key=lambda v: dotproduct(v.direction, viewdirection), reverse=True) return visibleviews[:k] def computeulrweights(views, viewdirection): # Higher blending weights are assigned to views closer to d weights = [1.0 - dotproduct(v.direction, viewdirection) for v in views] total = sum(weights) return [w / total for w in weights] if total > 0 else [1.0 / len(views)] len(views) def blendtriangletextures(triangle, closestviewspervertex, weightspervertex): # Blends up to nine textures per triangle (3 vertices 3 closest views) # Carried out solely by graphics hardware using standard barycentric interpolation and alpha compositing pass def dotproduct(a, b): return sum(x y for x, y in zip(a, b)) def isoccluded(triangle, view, cameraparams): # Standard ray-triangle intersection test from camera center through triangle pass def computebsptree(mesh): # Standard BSP tree construction for mesh pass def traversebacktofront(bsptree): # Standard recursive BSP traversal pass def emptyimage(): # Initialize output buffer pass def rasterizetriangle(triangle, color): # Standard GPU rasterization pass def getneighboringtriangles(vertex, mesh): # Standard adjacency lookup pass Local Light Field Fusion (LLFF) is a method designed to produce photorealistic novel views for well-sampled, forward-facing scenes by predicting a discretized frustum-sampled RGB\alpha grid (Multiplane Image or MPI) for each input view. It differs from its siblings, such as Neural Lumigraph Rendering and Instant Neural Opacity Light Fields, by explicitly generating per-view MPI representations that are subsequently blended, rather than optimizing a single global implicit field or using a fixed light field parameterization. Neural Lumigraph Rendering (NLR) is a neural rendering framework that jointly optimizes an implicit signed distance function (SDF) for geometry and a radiance field for appearance, supervised exclusively by posed 2D images. It enables the export of view-dependent textured meshes for real-time rasterization, achieving rendering speeds two orders of magnitude faster than standard neural volume rendering methods like NeRF while maintaining comparable image quality. Unlike sibling methods that rely on dense volumetric sampling or local light field fusion, NLR uses sphere tracing on an SDF to find the surface and applies unstructured lumigraph rendering to blend projective textures, preserving view-dependent effects without runtime volumetric integration. Instant Neural Opacity Light Fields (i-NOLF) is a real-time neural rendering method that represents scenes as local neural opacity light fields to achieve one-query-per-pixel rendering. It combines spatial hash encoding with light field properties to avoid the computational overhead of hundreds of neural network forward passes per pixel, which is typical in standard neural radiance fields. Unlike its siblings, i-NOLF decouples the outgoing radiance into view-independent diffuse and view-dependent specular components, using a cached density texture for efficient hit-point estimation and Perfect Spatial Hashing (PSH) specifically for the specular encoder to balance memory efficiency and rendering speed. A technique to generate high-quality light field representation and integrate it into the GPU-based raycasting pipeline to provide novice audiences access to interactive volume renditions. The method is interactive on PCs using current graphics hardware, as texture blending is carried out solely by the GPU. Rendering each triangle blends up to nine textures (3 vertices \times 3 closest views). Considering all camera views for blending at each vertex yields higher image quality at a slight performance cost, particularly for proxies with small occlusions. Exact time and memory complexity metrics are not given in the sources. The method originates from image-based volume rendering research that parameterizes an opacity light field on a proxy surface. It builds on the system by Vlasic et al. and Unstructured Lumigraph Rendering (ULR) to visualize the opacity light field interactively. In volume visualization, the approach has been adapted to handle volumetric data, providing interactive capabilities for novice users by integrating high-quality light field representations into GPU-based raycasting pipelines. name: Local Light Field Fusion
head: LFLF, LLFF, Layered Light Field Fusion
body: Local Light Field Fusion (LLFF) is a view synthesis method designed for producing photorealistic novel views for well-sampled, forward-facing scenes. It differs from its siblings by using a trained 3D convolutional network to directly predict a discretized frustum-sampled RGB\alpha grid (Multiplane Image or MPI) for each input view, then rendering novel views by alpha compositing and blending nearby MPIs. Unlike Neural Lumigraph Rendering which optimizes a separate network per scene, LLFF applies a single trained network to predict the MPIs directly from input images. Inputs: A set of input images from a forward-facing capture. Outputs: High-resolution novel view images. Data Structures: MPI (Multiplane Image): A discretized frustum-sampled RGB\alpha grid representing color and opacity at specific depth intervals within the camera frustum. 3D Convolutional Network: A trained neural network that takes an input image and outputs the parameters for the MPI planes. Steps: 1. Input Preparation: Collect a set of input images from a forward-facing scene. 2. MPI Prediction: Pass each input image through the trained 3D convolutional network to predict the RGB and \alpha values for the discretized frustum-sampled planes for that specific view. 3. Novel View Rendering: To render a novel viewpoint: a. Identify the nearby input views whose predicted MPIs are relevant to the novel viewpoint. b. Warp or project the MPIs from these nearby input views into the coordinate system of the novel viewpoint. c. Perform alpha compositing of the warped MPIs to combine the color and opacity information. d. Blend the results from the different MPIs to produce the final image. Parameters: Disparity Limit: The method provides a sampling guideline not to exceed 64 pixels of disparity between input views. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: High Disparity: The method frequently fails to estimate correct geometry in datasets with up to 400-500 pixels of disparity between views, as it exceeds the 64-pixel guideline. Inconsistency: Blending between different scene representations (MPIs) for rendering different views can result in perceptually-distracting inconsistency and repeated edges. Artifacts: The method exhibits banding artifacts on object edges and ghosting artifacts in complex geometry (e.g., masts, internal structures). Time Complexity: All compared single-scene methods take at least 12 hours to train per scene, whereas LLFF processes a small input dataset in under 10 minutes. Memory Complexity: LLFF produces a large 3D voxel grid for every input image, resulting in enormous storage requirements (over 15GB for one "Realistic Synthetic" scene). Strengths: Fast processing time; capable of recovering fine details in geometry and appearance (e.g., non-Lambertian reflectance, fine rigging) for well-sampled forward-facing scenes. Limitations: High storage requirements; fails with high disparity (>64 pixels); perceptual inconsistencies due to blending; artifacts like banding and ghosting. When to use: When fast processing of well-sampled, forward-facing scenes is required and storage is not a constraint. When not to use: For scenes with large baseline disparities, or when storage efficiency and view consistency are critical. Local Light Field Fusion (LLFF) was introduced as a method for view synthesis, specifically targeting forward-facing captures of real scenes. It was compared against baselines such as Scene Representation Networks (SRN) and Neural Volumes (NV). SRN is limited by selecting only a single depth and color per camera ray, while NV is limited by its explicit 128^3 voxel grid. LLFF was shown to outperform these baselines in qualitative and quantitative metrics for suitable scenes, although it suffered from storage and consistency issues. A sibling method that optimizes a separate network per scene. It is chosen when per-scene optimization is feasible and higher view consistency is required than LLFF can provide. See Neural Lumigraph Rendering. A sibling method focusing on instant rendering capabilities. It is chosen when speed of inference is critical. See Instant Neural Opacity Light Fields. NeRF: Representing scenes as neural radiance fields for view synthesis, http://www.matthewtancik.com/nerf, fetched 2026-10-27 Neural Radiance Fields-Comprehensive Survey, https://zenodo.org/records/7597137, fetched 2026-10-26

name: Light Field Representation
head: Light Field Rendering, Lumigraph Rendering
body: Light field representation is a technique that generates a high-quality parameterization of the light field to enable interactive volume rendering via GPU-based raycasting. It solves the problem of computational complexity in direct volume rendering by pre-computing radiance information in a lower-dimensional representation, allowing novice users to access interactive frame rates. It sets itself apart from direct raycasting by decoupling the expensive integration step from the rendering loop, trading memory for speed, and differs from Fourier domain methods by operating in spatial coordinates rather than frequency space. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A 3D volumetric dataset (scalar or vector field) and a set of camera viewpoints. Output: A light field representation (typically a 4D or 5D data structure) and a GPU shader pipeline capable of raycasting through this representation. Data Structures: The light field is typically represented as a 4D function L(u, v, s, t), where (u, v) parameterize the position on a view plane (or camera plane) and (s, t) parameterize the position on a ray plane (or aperture plane) [S1, implied by standard light field theory and context of two-plane parameterization in siblings]. The exact bit-packing and memory layout are implementation-specific, but generally involve storing radiance values at discrete grid points in the (u, v, s, t) space. Steps: 1. Sampling: Sample the volumetric data along rays corresponding to a grid of viewpoints and directions. This creates a set of 2D images (views) or a 4D texture. 2. Integration: For each sampled ray, compute the accumulated radiance and opacity using volume rendering integration (e.g., standard DVR). 3. Storage: Store the integrated radiance values in the light field data structure. 4. Rendering: During interactive rendering, for a new viewpoint, interpolate the radiance values from the pre-computed light field based on the ray's intersection with the parameterization planes. Formulas: The light field L(u, v, s, t) represents the radiance traveling through point (u, v) on the view plane in the direction defined by (s, t) on the ray plane. The rendered image I(x, y) for a camera at position (u, v) is obtained by integrating along the rays defined by (s, t): I(x, y) = \int L(u, v, s, t) \, ds \, dt In discrete implementations, this becomes a summation over the sampled (s, t) grid. Parameters: Grid resolution for (u, v) and (s, t): Determines the quality and memory usage. Not given in the sources. Interpolation method: Bilinear or trilinear interpolation is common. Not given in the sources. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Memory Usage: The 4D nature of the light field can lead to high memory consumption for large volumes or high-resolution views. Aliasing: Insufficient sampling in the light field parameterization can cause aliasing artifacts in novel views. Occlusion: Standard light field representations may struggle with complex occlusions if not explicitly modeled (e.g., via opacity). This method parameterizes a light field using two planes, \pi{xy} and \pi{uv}, and learns a re-parameterization (local affine transforms) to align the neural network's interpolation kernels with the object surface \pi{st}. It solves the problem of misaligned interpolation kernels in standard two-plane parameterizations, which degrades view synthesis quality when the distance between the view plane and the object surface is large. It sets itself apart from standard two-plane methods by explicitly optimizing the embedding space to minimize the discrepancy between the parameterized coordinates and the true surface coordinates. Time Complexity: Rendering time is O(1) per pixel relative to the volume size, depending only on the interpolation cost in the light field. Pre-computation is O(N) where N is the number of sampled rays. Memory Complexity: O(U \times V \times S \times T) where U, V are view plane resolutions and S, T are ray plane resolutions. This can be very large. Measured Performance: Enables interactive frame rates for novice audiences on GPU hardware. Strengths: High rendering speed, suitability for interactive applications. Limitations: High memory usage, potential quality loss if sampling is insufficient or parameterization is poor. When to use: When interactive performance is critical and memory is available. When not to use: For very large volumes where memory is constrained, or when dynamic scenes require frequent updates. The technique was introduced by Rezk-Salama et al. to provide novice audiences with access to interactive volume renditions by integrating high-quality light field representation into a GPU-based raycasting pipeline. It builds on the broader field of light field rendering and lumigraph techniques.
