name: Two-plane light field parameterization with re-parameterization
head: Local affine transform embedding, Ray-space embedding
body: This method parameterizes a light field using two planes, \pi{xy} and \pi{uv}, and learns a re-parameterization (local affine transforms) to align the neural network's interpolation kernels with the object surface \pi{st}. It solves the problem of misaligned interpolation kernels in standard two-plane parameterizations, which degrades view synthesis quality when the distance between the view plane and the object surface is large. It sets itself apart from standard two-plane methods by explicitly optimizing the embedding space to minimize the discrepancy between the parameterized coordinates and the true surface coordinates. Inputs: A set of input images with known camera poses. A scene geometry (implicitly or explicitly defined, e.g., via a textured plane \pi{st} or a voxel grid). Two initial parameterization planes: \pi{xy} (view plane) and \pi{uv} (viewpoint plane). Outputs: A re-parameterized light field representation where rays are mapped to a latent space aligned with the object surface. A neural network (MLP) that maps the re-parameterized ray coordinates to color and density. Data Structures: Ray Representation: A ray r is defined by its origin on \pi{xy} and its intersection with \pi{uv}. Voxel Grid: For subdivided models, a 3D grid of voxels \upsilon is used to cover the scene space (e.g., NDC space). Embedding Network: An MLP that takes the re-parameterized ray coordinates as input and outputs the ray's color and density. Steps: 1. Initial Parameterization: Define \pi{xy} and \pi{uv}. For the Stanford Light Field dataset, \pi{xy} is set to z = -1 and \pi{uv} is set to z = 0. Scale camera positions to lie between [-0.25, 0.25] in x and y. Scale pixel coordinates on \pi{uv} to lie between [-1, 1]. For each ray r originating at (\hat{x}, \hat{y}) on \pi{xy} and passing through a point (\hat{s}, \hat{t}) on the object surface \pi{st}, calculate its intersection (\hat{u}, \hat{v}) with \pi{uv} using similar triangles: \hat{u} - \hat{x} = (\hat{s} - \hat{x}) \frac{z{uv}}{z{st}} \hat{v} - \hat{y} = (\hat{t} - \hat{y}) \frac{z{uv}}{z{st}} where z{st} and z{uv} are the depths of \pi{st} and \pi{uv} respectively, and the depth of \pi{xy} is assumed to be 0. 2. Re-parameterization (Subdivided Model): For a subdivided model, re-parameterize each ray r within a voxel \upsilon. Transform space so that the voxel center lies at the origin. Intersect the transformed ray with the voxel’s front and back planes. Take the xy coordinates of these intersections as the parameterization, which lie within the range [-\text{voxel width}, +\text{voxel width}] in all dimensions. 3. Learning Re-parameterization: Learn a re-parameterization that moves \pi{uv} towards \pi{st}, reducing the distance z{st} - z{uv}. The finite capacity of the light field MLP drives the embedding network to map rays intersecting the same 3D point to the same point in latent space. This process aligns the color network's interpolation kernels with the object surface \pi{st}. Parameters: Stanford Light Field Dataset: \pi{xy} at z = -1, \pi{uv} at z = 0. Camera positions scaled to [-0.25, 0.25] in x and y. Pixel coordinates on \pi{uv} scaled to [-1, 1]. Real Forward-Facing and Shiny Datasets: Experiments performed in NDC space. A 32^3 voxel grid covers all NDC space, except for CD/Lab scenes which use a coarser 4^3 grid. Pitfalls: If the distance z{st} - z{uv} is large, the difference between (\hat{u}, \hat{v}) and (\hat{s}, \hat{t}) increases, causing the network's interpolation kernels to become misaligned with the object surface, degrading reconstruction quality. Not given in the sources. This method originates from the paper "Learning Neural Light Fields with Ray-Space Embedding Networks". It addresses the limitations of standard two-plane parameterization by introducing a learnable re-parameterization to improve view synthesis quality. Learning Neural Light Fields with Ray-Space Embedding Networks, https://doi.org/10.48550/arxiv.2112.01523, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial)

name: Neural Lumigraph Rendering
head: Neural Radiance Fields with SDF export, SIREN-based Neural Rendering
body:
Neural Lumigraph Rendering (NLR) is a neural rendering framework that jointly optimizes an implicit Signed Distance Function (SDF) for shape and a radiance field for appearance, supervised exclusively by posed 2D images. It distinguishes itself from standard volumetric rendering methods like NeRF by exporting a triangular mesh with view-dependent textures, enabling real-time rasterization via OpenGL while maintaining state-of-the-art image quality. Unlike Local Light Field Fusion which relies on explicit light field parameterization, NLR learns an implicit neural representation that is subsequently discretized for rendering. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: A set of m multi-view 2D images I \in \mathbb{R}^{m 	imes w 	imes h 	imes 3} and corresponding binary object masks M \in \mathbb{R}^{m 	imes w 	imes h} (where 1 marks foreground). Camera poses are defined by view matrix V \in \mathbb{R}^{4 	imes 4} and projection matrix P \in \mathbb{R}^{4 	imes 4}. Outputs: Optimized parameters 	heta (SDF) and \phi (appearance); optionally, a triangular mesh and projective textures for real-time rendering. Data Structures: SDF Network S: A SIREN (Sinusoidal Representation Network) MLP with 5 layers and 256 hidden units each. Input: position x \in \mathbb{R}^3. Output: scalar S(x; 	heta) \in \mathbb{R}. Radiance Field Network E: A SIREN MLP with 5 layers and 256 hidden units each. Input: position x \in \mathbb{R}^3, view direction rd \in \mathbb{R}^3, and local normal n \in \mathbb{R}^3. Output: RGB color E(x, rd, n; 	heta, \phi) \in \mathbb{R}^3. Fourier Features: The view direction rd is embedded using Fourier features \{\sin(2k\pi rd), \cos(2k\pi rd) \mid k \in 1 \dots 4\} before entering E. Numbered Steps: 1. Ray Generation: For a pixel at relative projection plane location u \in [-1, 1]^2, compute ray origin ro and direction rd: ro = (V^{-1} \cdot [0, 0, 1, 0]^T){x,y,z} rd = 
u((P \cdot V)^{-1} \cdot [ux, uy, 0, 1]^T) where 
u(\omega) = \omega{x,y,z} / \|\omega{x,y,z}\| is vector normalization. 2. Sphere Tracing: Find the zero-level set S0 closest to the camera along the ray using iterative updates: x0 = ro x{i+1} = xi + S(xi)rd The surface point is S0 = \{xn \mid S(xn) \approx 0\} for step count n=16. A small residual |S(xn)| < 0.005 is tolerated. To save memory, gradients are retained only for the last step n. 3. Normal Computation: Compute the local normal n via automatic differentiation of the SDF at the surface point: n = 
ablax S(xn; 	heta). 4. Appearance Sampling: Sample the radiance field at the surface point: c = E(xn, rd, n; 	heta, \phi). 5. Loss Calculation: Minimize the total loss L = LR + wE LE + wM LM + wS LS: Reconstruction Loss (LR): L1 error for foreground pixels Uf = U \cap S0 \cap \{U \mid MU = 1\}: LR =  rac{1}{|U|} \sum{c \in I{Uf}} |E(x, rd, n; 	heta, \phi) - c|. Eikonal Loss (LE): Enforces metric properties for sphere tracing by regularizing the gradient of S to unit length. Random points xr are uniformly sampled from a cube encapsulating the object's bounding unit radius sphere: LE =  rac{1}{|U|} \sum{xr} (\|
ablax S(xr; 	heta)\|2^2 - 1)^2. Soft Mask Loss (LM): Restricts coarse shape to object mask boundaries for non-foreground pixels U \setminus Uf. S{min} is the minimum SDF value along the ray: LM =  rac{1}{\alpha |U|} \sum{m \in M{U \setminus Uf}} 	ext{BCE}(	ext{sigmoid}(-\alpha S{min}), m) where \alpha is a softness parameter. Smoothness Loss (LS): Linearizes angular behavior to prevent overfitting: LS =  rac{1}{|U|} \sum \|
abla^2{rd} E(x, rd, n; 	heta, \phi)\|2^2. 6. Optimization: Parameters 	heta and \phi are optimized using the Adam solver with initial learning rate 10^{-4}, decreased by factor of 2 every 40,000 batches, for 150,000 batches. Batch size is 50,000 rays. Weights: wE = 0.1, wM = 100, wS = 0.01. 7. Mesh Extraction (Optional for Real-Time): Voxelize S at 512^3 resolution and extract mesh using marching cubes. Offset the iso-surface by 0.5% of the object radius in the outside direction. Resample E to synthesize projective textures Ti for N camera poses. 8. Real-Time Rendering (NLR-RAS): Rasterize the mesh using OpenGL. Compute angles 	aui between the rendering camera ray and rays to each projective texture viewpoint. Blend contributions from the first k=5 textures sorted by 	aui ascending: \hat{w}i =  rac{1}{	aui} \left(1 -  rac{	aui}{	auk}ight) wi =  rac{\hat{w}i}{\sum{j=1}^k \hat{w}j}. Discard occluded textures by setting wi=0 if the pre-rendered depth indicates occlusion. Parameters: n=16: Sphere tracing steps. wE = 0.1, wM = 100, wS = 0.01: Loss weights. \alpha: Softness parameter for mask loss. Hidden units: 256 per layer. Layers: 5. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Overfitting: SIRENs tend to overfit to training views. Mitigated by large batch size (50,000) and uniform ray distribution. High-Frequency Artifacts: Large values of wS cause high-frequency artifacts in S. Initialization: S is initialized to a unit sphere of radius 0.5 by pretraining to a procedural shape. Defines the end-to-end differentiable optimization objective for the Neural Lumigraph Representation (NLR++), which jointly reconstructs shape via a Signed Distance Function (SDF) and appearance via a radiance field from posed 2D images. It distinguishes itself from standard volumetric rendering losses by introducing a soft mask loss on the SDF minimum along rays and a specific training schedule that decouples shape approximation from feature refinement to accelerate convergence. Time Complexity: Training is slower than some baselines; NLR is slower to converge in shape reconstruction than MetaNLR++ and IDR. Memory Complexity: Model size is compact. On DTU scan 65 at 1600x1200, NLR-ST is 2.07 MB and NLR-RAS is 34.68 MB, compared to NeRF's 2.27 MB and IDR's 11.13 MB. Performance: NLR-ST (sphere-traced) renders at 13s per image on DTU scan 65, while NLR-RAS (rasterized) achieves real-time performance (>60 fps at HD). This is 10x faster than NeRF (150s). Image Quality: NLR-RAS achieves 33.33 dB PSNR on DTU Scan 65, comparable to NeRF (34.87 dB) and superior to Colmap (32.13 dB) and IDR (33.50 dB). Strengths: Real-time rendering capability via mesh export; high image quality; compact model size; view-dependent textures. Limitations: Slower convergence during training compared to some implicit surface methods; requires posed images and masks. Neural Lumigraph Rendering was introduced by Kellnhofer et al. in CVPR 2021. It builds on sinusoidal representation networks (SIREN) and unstructured lumigraph rendering techniques from Buehler et al.. Fourier features were adopted from prior work. The method was implemented in PyTorch and rendered using OpenGL. name: NLR++ Training Loss and Supervision
head: NLR++, NLR++ Loss, NLR++ Optimization
body: NLR++ Training Loss and Supervision defines the end-to-end differentiable optimization objective for the Neural Lumigraph Representation (NLR++), which jointly reconstructs shape via a Signed Distance Function (SDF) and appearance via a radiance field from posed 2D images. It distinguishes itself from standard volumetric rendering losses by introducing a soft mask loss on the SDF minimum along rays and a specific training schedule that decouples shape approximation from feature refinement to accelerate convergence. Inputs and Outputs Inputs: A batch of k \le N input images \{In\}{n=1}^k, their corresponding binary object masks \{Mn\}{n=1}^k, and viewpoint parameters \{Cn\}{n=1}^k. The model parameters are \Phi\theta (SDF), E\xi (encoder), D\psi (decoder), and \Gamma\zeta (aggregator). Outputs: A synthesized target image \hat{I}t, a rendered mask \hat{M}t, and the updated model parameters after minimizing the total loss. Data Structures SDF (\Phi\theta): An implicit function mapping 3D coordinates to signed distance values. Initialized as a unit sphere of radius 0.5 using a pre-trained SIREN. Radiance Field: Defined by the encoder E, decoder D, and aggregator \Gamma, which map view-dependent features to color. Ray Sampling: For each pixel p, a ray is traced from the camera center defined by Ct. Numbered Steps 1. Batch Sampling: For each training iteration, sample a set of k \le N images \{In\}{n=1}^k from the available N input images. 2. Target Selection: Designate one image as the primary ground-truth target It, with its mask Mt and viewpoint Ct. 3. Multi-Target Gradient Computation: To improve gradient accuracy and utilize GPU memory, treat l < k images in the batch as target images. Compute gradients for each of these l targets using the other images in the batch as input context. 4. Synthesis: Generate the synthesized target image \hat{I}t and rendered mask \hat{M}t from viewpoint Ct using the NLR++ image formation model. 5. Loss Calculation: Compute the total loss \mathcal{L} as the sum of image reconstruction loss, soft mask loss, and eikonal regularization. 6. Scheduled Shape Supervision: Enforce shape-related losses (\mathcal{L}M and \mathcal{L}E) only for the first t1 iterations, and then every t2 iterations thereafter. This allows initial shape approximation before refining with better feature encoding. 7. Optimization: Update parameters \Theta = [\xi, \psi, \zeta, \theta] using the Adam optimizer. Formulas The total loss is defined as: \mathcal{L}(\{\hat{I}t, \hat{M}t\}, \{It, Mt\}, \Phi\theta) = \mathcal{L}R(\hat{I}t, \{It, Mt\}) + \lambda1 \mathcal{L}M(\Phi\theta, Mt) + \lambda2 \mathcal{L}E(\Phi\theta) 1. Image Reconstruction Loss (\mathcal{L}R): A masked L1 loss on rendered images: \mathcal{L}R(\hat{I}t, \{It, Mt\}) = \frac{1}{P} \sum{p | Mt[p]=1} |It[p] - \hat{I}t[p]| where P is the number of pixels where Mt[p]=1. 2. Soft Mask Loss (\mathcal{L}M): Applied to bootstrap neural shape learning from object masks: \mathcal{L}M(\Phi\theta, Mt) = \frac{1}{\alpha \sum{p | Mt[p]=0 \lor \Phi{\min}[p]<\tau} Mt[p]} \sum{p | Mt[p]=0 \lor \Phi{\min}[p]<\tau} \text{BCE}(\text{sigmoid}(-\alpha \Phi{\min}[p]), Mt[p]) where: \Phi{\min}[p] is the minimum SDF value along the ray traced from pixel p. \tau is a threshold for whether the zero level set L0(\Phi\theta) has been intersected. \alpha is a softness hyperparameter. \text{BCE}(y, \hat{y}) = -[y \log(\hat{y}) + (1-y) \log(1-\hat{y})] is the Binary Cross Entropy. 3. Eikonal Regularization (\mathcal{L}E): Enforces the eikonal constraint on randomly sampled points pi in a unit cube containing the scene: \mathcal{L}E(\Phi\theta) = \frac{1}{P} \sum{i=0}^{P} ||(||\nabla{pi} \Phi\theta(pi)||^2 - 1)||^22 Parameters \alpha: Softness hyperparameter for mask loss. Starting value: 50. \tau: Threshold for zero level set intersection. Starting value: 1 \times 10^{-3}. \lambda1: Weight for mask loss. Calculated as 1 \times 10^2 / \alpha. \lambda2: Weight for eikonal regularization. Starting value: 3. t1: Number of initial iterations to enforce shape losses. Starting value: 50. t2: Frequency (in iterations) to enforce shape losses after t1. Starting value: 7. Learning Rates: Adam optimizer with starting LR 1 \times 10^{-4} for \Phi and 5 \times 10^{-4} for E, D, \Gamma. Pseudocode Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def trainnlrplusplus(batchimages, batchmasks, batchcameras, modelparams, optimizer, hyperparams): """ Performs one training step for NLR++. Args: batchimages: List of k images {In} batchmasks: List of k masks {Mn} batchcameras: List of k camera parameters {Cn} modelparams: Parameters [xi, psi, zeta, theta] for E, D, Gamma, Phi optimizer: Adam optimizer instance hyperparams: Dict containing alpha, tau, lambda1, lambda2, t1, t2, l, k Returns: lossvalue: Scalar loss value """ k = len(batchimages) l = hyperparams['l'] # Number of target images in batch, l < k t1 = hyperparams['t1'] t2 = hyperparams['t2'] currentiter = getcurrentiteration() # Global iteration counter # Select l target images from the batch # In practice, this might be random or sequential; here we assume indices 0 to l-1 targetindices = list(range(l)) totalloss = 0.0 for idx in targetindices: It = batchimages[idx] Mt = batchmasks[idx] Ct = batchcameras[idx] # 1. Synthesize target image and mask # Uses the NLR++ image formation model with current modelparams # The model takes other images in the batch as context if needed, # but typically It is synthesized from Ct and the global representation. # Note: The source implies gradients are computed for It from other images, # meaning the context images are used to build the feature representation. contextimages = [batchimages[i] for i in range(k) if i != idx] Ihatt, Mhatt = synthesizeimage( viewpoint=Ct, contextimages=contextimages, params=modelparams) # 2. Compute Image Reconstruction Loss (Masked L1) # Only compute over pixels where Mt[p] == 1 maskpixels = getmaskedpixels(Mt) lrloss = 0.0 count = 0 for p in maskpixels: lrloss += abs(It[p] - Ihatt[p]) count += 1 if count > 0: lrloss /= count else: lrloss = 0.0 # 3. Compute Soft Mask Loss (Shape Loss) # Only enforced if currentiter <= t1 OR currentiter % t2 == 0 lmloss = 0.0 if currentiter <= t1 or currentiter % t2 == 0: # Find minimum SDF along ray for each pixel # This requires dense sampling of Phitheta along rays phiminvalues = [] validmasksum = 0.0 for p in range(Mt.height Mt.width): # Check condition: Mt[p] == 0 OR Phimin[p] < tau # We need Phimin[p] to check the condition, so we compute it first ray = getrayfrompixel(p, Ct) phimin = findminsdfalongray(ray, modelparams.phi) if Mt[p] == 0 or phimin < hyperparams['tau']: phiminvalues.append(phimin) validmasksum += Mt[p] # Note: Mt[p] is 0 or 1. # If Mt[p]==0, it adds 0 to sum? # Formula says: sum{p|...} Mt[p]. # If Mt[p]==0, term is 0. # If Mt[p]==1, term is 1. # But the condition includes Mt[p]==0. # Let's re-read formula: # sum{p | Mt[p]=0 v Phimin[p]<tau} Mt[p] # If Mt[p]=0, Mt[p] is 0. So it contributes 0 to denominator. # If Mt[p]=1 and Phimin < tau, it contributes 1. # If Mt[p]=1 and Phimin >= tau, it is excluded. # If Mt[p]=0, it is included in sum but adds 0. # So denominator is effectively count of pixels where Mt[p]=1 AND Phimin < tau. # Wait, if Mt[p]=0, the term Mt[p] is 0. # So the denominator is sum of Mt[p] for valid p. # This effectively counts pixels where Mt[p]=1 and Phimin < tau. # However, the numerator sums BCE for ALL valid p. # If Mt[p]=0, BCE(sigmoid(-alphaphi), 0). # If Mt[p]=1, BCE(sigmoid(-alphaphi), 1). pass # Recalculate denominator correctly based on formula denominatorsum = 0.0 numeratorsum = 0.0 for p in range(Mt.height Mt.width): ray = getrayfrompixel(p, Ct) phimin = findminsdfalongray(ray, modelparams.phi) if Mt[p] == 0 or phimin < hyperparams['tau']: # Add to denominator sum: Mt[p] denominatorsum += Mt[p] # Add to numerator sum: BCE(sigmoid(-alpha phimin), Mt[p]) sigval = sigmoid(-hyperparams['alpha'] phimin) bceval = binarycrossentropy(sigval, Mt[p]) numeratorsum += bceval if denominatorsum > 0: lmloss = numeratorsum / (hyperparams['alpha'] denominatorsum) else: lmloss = 0.0 # 4. Compute Eikonal Regularization (Shape Loss) # Only enforced if currentiter <= t1 OR currentiter % t2 == 0 leloss = 0.0 if currentiter <= t1 or currentiter % t2 == 0: # Sample P random points in unit cube points = samplerandompoints(hyperparams['P'], bounds=[-1, 1]) gradnormsqsum = 0.0 for pi in points: grad = computegradient(modelparams.phi, pi) normsq = dot(grad, grad) leloss += pow(normsq - 1, 2) leloss /= len(points) # 5. Combine Losses loss = lrloss + hyperparams['lambda1'] lmloss + hyperparams['lambda2'] leloss totalloss += loss # Average loss over l targets totalloss /= l # 6. Backpropagation optimizer.zerograd() totalloss.backward() optimizer.step() return totalloss def findminsdfalongray(ray, phi): """ Finds the minimum SDF value along a ray. Requires dense sampling. """ # Sample points along the ray # Typically from near to far plane samples = samplealongray(ray, numsamples=256) # Example count minval = infinity for p in samples: val = phi(p) if val < minval: minval = val return minval Edge Cases and Pitfalls Compute Bottleneck: \mathcal{L}M requires finding the minimum of \Phi\theta along a ray, which necessitates dense sampling of the network and accounts for most of the compute time of each forward pass. Precision: The threshold \tau must be small enough to detect the zero level set but large enough to avoid noise. The softness parameter \alpha controls the sharpness of the mask boundary; if too high, gradients may become unstable. Degenerate Input: If no pixels satisfy the condition Mt[p]=0 \lor \Phi{\min}[p]<\tau, the denominator in \mathcal{L}M becomes zero. The implementation must handle this division by zero case (e.g., by setting loss to 0 or adding a small epsilon). MetaNLR++ uses meta-learning to learn a prior over feature encoding, decoding, aggregation, and shape representation by optimizing the initial network weights \Theta0 for fast convergence on unseen scenes. It differs from standard NLR++ by using the Reptile algorithm to update \Theta0 based on inner-loop optimization on sampled tasks. The meta-learning objective is to find initial weights \Theta0^ that minimize the expected loss after m optimization steps on an unseen scene T: \Theta0^ = \arg \min{\Theta0} \mathbb{E}{T \sim \mathcal{T}} [\mathcal{L}(\Thetam(\Theta0, T))]. The update rule is \Theta0^{j+1} = \Theta0^j + \beta(\Thetam(\Theta0^j, Tj) - \Theta0^j), where \beta is the meta-learning rate (starting value 1 \times 10^{-1}) and m is the fixed number of inner-loop steps. This approach significantly reduces training time; for example, on the ShapeNet chairs split, MetaNLR++ reaches 30dB PSNR in 1.5 minutes compared to NLR++'s 3.6 minutes. Time Complexity: The training is dominated by the dense sampling required for \mathcal{L}M, which accounts for most of the compute time per forward pass. The multi-target batching strategy adds forward passes to \Gamma and D, which are fast to evaluate. Memory Complexity: The number of target images l treated as targets in the batch is limited by GPU memory. Performance: On the ShapeNet dataset, NLR++ is slower to converge than MetaNLR++. For instance, on the chairs split, NLR++ takes 3.6 minutes to reach 30dB PSNR, while MetaNLR++ takes 1.5 minutes. Strengths: The scheduled shape supervision allows for faster initial convergence by decoupling shape approximation from feature refinement. The use of CNN encoder/decoder increases the receptive field of the image loss, allowing for more meaningful gradients. Limitations: The dense sampling for \mathcal{L}M is computationally expensive. NLR++ without meta-learning converges slower than MetaNLR++. When to Use: Use NLR++ when a standard neural lumigraph representation is needed without the overhead of meta-learning setup. Use MetaNLR++ when rapid convergence on unseen scenes is critical. NLR++ was introduced as an end-to-end differentiable neural lumigraph representation optimized to reconstruct target views from a set of input images using a CNN encoder/decoder and a signed distance function (SDF) for shape. It serves as the baseline for MetaNLR++, which improves upon it using meta-learning. The method was developed to enable real-time export of view-dependent textured meshes from posed 2D images. The implementation details, including hyperparameters and training schedules, are described in the supplementary material of the source paper. Experiments were conducted on Nvidia Quadro RTX8000 and RTX6000 GPUs. Fast Training of Neural Lumigraph Representations using Meta Learning, https://doi.org/10.48550/arxiv.2106.14942, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial)

name: Instant Neural Opacity Light Fields
head: Neural Opacity Light Field, PSH Implementation for i-NOLF
body: Instant Neural Opacity Light Fields (i-NOLF) is a real-time neural rendering method that represents scenes as local neural opacity light fields to achieve one-query-per-pixel rendering. It combines spatial hash encoding with light field properties to avoid the computational overhead of hundreds of neural network forward passes per pixel, which is typical in standard NeRF-based renderers. Unlike Local Light Field Fusion which relies on explicit light field structures, and Neural Lumigraph Rendering which uses neural radiance fields on lumigraphs, i-NOLF decouples diffuse and specular components and uses a proxy geometry with opacity refinement to handle complex details like hair and boundaries efficiently. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: A surface mesh or proxy geometry M, view direction v, and ray origin. Outputs: Final outgoing radiance color c and opacity \alpha. Data Structures: 1. Density Texture Cubes: A set of small dense texture cubes representing the density field. Base Grid: Uniform indexing grid of resolution b (Typical value: 128) to index valid grid cells. Valid Cubes Table: Maps valid grid cells to addresses in a table of valid cubes. Cube Content: Uniform grid of resolution r (Typical value: 16) storing queried densities. Storage: Moved to texture memory for hardware-accelerated linear interpolation. 2. Hash Tables: Specular Hash Encoder (Es): Uses Perfect Spatial Hashing (PSH). Stores features only for voxels surrounding hit points. Diffuse Hash Encoder (Ed): Uses standard hash grid encoding. 3. Neural Networks: Specular MLP (Fs): Takes Es(p), view direction v, and coarse opacity \alphac as input. Outputs specular color cs and opacity \alpha. Diffuse MLP (Fd): Takes Ed(p) as input. Outputs diffuse color cd and specular tint t. Numbered Steps: 1. Hit Point Estimation: Perform ray marching on the cached density texture cubes to find the ray-object hit point Ph. To avoid noisy hit points on object boundaries or hair (common in standard NeRF blending), select the sample point with the largest blending weight wi as the hit point. Accumulate sample weights into a coarse opacity \alphac for the ray. The blending weight is defined as: wi = Ti (1 - \exp(-\sigmai \deltai)) where \sigmai is the density, \deltai is the distance between adjacent samples, and Ti = \exp(-\sum{j=1}^{i-1} \sigmaj \deltaj) is the transmittance. 2. Feature Encoding: Encode the hit point coordinate Ph to a feature vector Es(Ph) using the specular hash encoder Es. Encode the hit point coordinate Ph to a feature vector Ed(Ph) using the diffuse hash encoder Ed. 3. Network Inference: Specular Path: Concatenate Es(Ph), the normalized view direction v (in 3D Cartesian space), and the coarse opacity \alphac. Pass this through the Specular MLP Fs: Fs: (Es(p), v, \alphac) \rightarrow (cs, \alpha) This outputs the view-dependent specular color cs and the refined opacity \alpha. Diffuse Path: Pass Ed(Ph) through the Diffuse MLP Fd: Fd: Ed(p) \rightarrow (cd, t) This outputs the view-independent diffuse color cd and the specular tint t. 4. Radiance Combination: Combine the diffuse and specular components to obtain the final outgoing radiance c: c = cd + t \cdot cs This decoupling helps keep specular effects during compression and leverages the compressibility of the residual specular component. 5. Training: Optimize parameters of hash grids Es, Ed and networks Fs, Fd using an L2 loss on a batch of N rays sampled according to an optimizable error map: L = \frac{1}{N} \sum{i=1}^N (\|c - c{gt}\|^2 + \|\alpha - \alpha{gt}\|^2) where c{gt} and \alpha{gt} are ground truth color and alpha values. Apply the Adam optimizer with the same parameter settings as i-NGP. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def normalize(v): mag = math.sqrt(v[0]2 + v[1]2 + v[2]2) return (v[0]/mag, v[1]/mag, v[2]/mag) def lerp(a, b, t): return a + t (b - a) def trilinearinterp(v000, v100, v010, v110, v001, v101, v011, v111, fx, fy, fz): fx, fy, fz = max(0.0, min(1.0, fx)), max(0.0, min(1.0, fy)), max(0.0, min(1.0, fz)) c00 = lerp(v000, v100, fx) c10 = lerp(v010, v110, fx) c01 = lerp(v001, v101, fx) c11 = lerp(v011, v111, fx) return lerp(lerp(c00, c10, fy), lerp(c01, c11, fy), fz) def hashfunc(p, tablesize): return hash(p) % tablesize def standardhashgridlookup(p, hashtable): idx = hashfunc(p, len(hashtable)) return hashtable[idx] def renderray(rayorigin, raydirection, densitycubes, cuberes, hashtables, offsettables, hashtabled, offsettabled, Fs, Fd): currentpos = rayorigin transmittance = 1.0 coarseopacity = 0.0 maxweight = -1.0 hitpoint = rayorigin stepsize = 0.01 numsteps = 100 for i in range(numsteps): gx, gy, gz = currentpos[0] / cuberes, currentpos[1] / cuberes, currentpos[2] / cuberes baseidx = int(gx) 10000 + int(gy) 100 + int(gz) cubedata = densitycubes.get(baseidx) if cubedata is not None: fx, fy, fz = gx % 1.0, gy % 1.0, gz % 1.0 density = trilinearinterp(cubedata, fx, fy, fz) else: density = 0.0 deltai = stepsize sigmai = density weight = transmittance (1.0 - math.exp(-sigmai deltai)) transmittance = (1.0 - weight) coarseopacity += weight if weight > maxweight: maxweight = weight hitpoint = currentpos currentpos = (currentpos[0] + raydirection[0] stepsize, currentpos[1] + raydirection[1] stepsize, currentpos[2] + raydirection[2] stepsize) # PSH Encoding for Specular corners = [(int(math.floor(hitpoint[0])), int(math.floor(hitpoint[1])), int(math.floor(hitpoint[2])))] indicess = [hashfunc(c, len(hashtables)) + offsettables[hashfunc(c, len(offsettables))] for c in corners] Es = trilinearinterp([hashtables[idx] for idx in indicess], hitpoint[0] % 1.0, hitpoint[1] % 1.0, hitpoint[2] % 1.0) # Standard Hash Grid Encoding for Diffuse Ed = standardhashgridlookup(hitpoint, hashtabled) # Network Inference viewdir = normalize(raydirection) cs, alpha = Fs(Es, viewdir, coarseopacity) cd, t = Fd(Ed) # Radiance Combination c = (cd[0] + t cs[0], cd[1] + t cs[1], cd[2] + t cs[2]) return c, alpha Parameters: M: Surface mesh or proxy geometry. S^2: Sphere of unit vectors representing view directions. Es: Spatial hash encoder for specular component. Ed: Extra spatial hash encoder for diffuse component. v: Normalized view direction in 3D Cartesian space. cs: View-dependent specular color output. \alpha: Refined opacity output. \alphac: Coarse opacity accumulated from sample weights. \deltai: Distance between adjacent samples. cd: Diffuse color output. t: Specular tint output. N: Number of rays in a batch. c{gt}: Ground truth color. b: Resolution of base uniform indexing grid (Typical: 128). r: Resolution of each density texture cube (Typical: 16). Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Proxy Geometry Ambiguity: Learning an opacity light field with a bounding box as proxy geometry is difficult because spatially adjacent points have similar encoded features but different lumispheres (one-to-many mapping). Noisy Hit Points: Standard NeRF hit depth estimation generates noisy hit points on object boundaries and hair objects. The largest blending weight strategy mitigates this. Memory Efficiency: PSH is used for specular because it offers superior memory efficiency and speed, while diffuse is cached in texture cubes, making the hash grid sufficient for diffuse. An ultra-fast renderer that marries opacity light fields with i-NGP to conduct one-query-per-ray rendering, avoiding redundant computational overhead. It uses density texture cubes for fast hit point estimation and decouples diffuse/specular components for efficient encoding. A caching mechanism representing the density field as a set of small dense texture cubes to skip empty space and accelerate hit point estimation (ray marching) by leveraging hardware-accelerated linear interpolation in texture memory. It uses a base uniform indexing grid (resolution b=128) to index valid cells, which map to a table of valid cubes (resolution r=16). Hit point estimation takes less than 0.1ms for a 1920x1080 image. Time Complexity: One-query-per-ray rendering, significantly faster than standard NeRF which requires hundreds of forward passes per pixel. Hit point estimation takes less than 0.1ms for 1920x1080. Memory Complexity: Uses Perfect Spatial Hashing (PSH) for specular to improve memory efficiency and speed. Diffuse is cached in texture cubes. Hash tables store features only for voxels surrounding hit points, allowing finer grid resolution with acceptable parameter scale. Performance: Achieves real-time rendering speeds suitable for cloud platforms and interactive applications. Strengths: Ultra-fast rendering, handles complex details (hair, boundaries) better than standard NeRF hit estimation, memory efficient via PSH and texture cubes. Limitations: Requires proxy geometry M. Learning with poor proxy geometry (e.g., simple bounding boxes) can lead to artifacts due to one-to-many mappings. Slightly degraded rendering quality compared to non-optimized NeRF due to approximations. When to Use: Real-time neural rendering, cloud rendering platforms, scenes with complex geometry and view-dependent effects. When Not to Use: Scenes where proxy geometry is unavailable or highly inaccurate, or when maximum possible rendering quality is prioritized over speed. i-NOLF was introduced in the paper "NEPHELE: A Neural Platform for Highly Realistic Cloud Radiance Rendering" by Luo et al. in 2023. It builds on the i-NGP renderer [Müller et al. 2022] and aims to accelerate real-time neural rendering by combining opacity light fields with instant neural graphics primitives. The method addresses the computational bottlenecks of standard NeRF rendering and the limitations of multiresolution hash encoding on GPUs. NEPHELE: A Neural Platform for Highly Realistic Cloud Radiance Rendering, https://arxiv.org/abs/2303.04086v1, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial)

name: Generalizable Radiance Fields
body: Generalizable Radiance Fields solve the problem of per-scene optimization latency by learning a data prior from a large-scale dataset, enabling immediate novel view synthesis on unseen scenes without iterative training. They differ from standard radiance-field optimization methods by replacing per-scene gradient descent with a feedforward neural network that aggregates multi-view features or cost volumes to predict density and color directly. Generalizable radiance fields share the goal of bypassing per-scene optimization by learning a representation from a large-scale dataset that can be adapted to unseen objects or scenes. This is achieved by learning generalizable geometric priors from source images, typically obtained using feature volumes or transformer-based attention modules to aggregate source view information. Recent methods also leverage deep multiview stereo (MVS) strategies to enforce generalization within the NeRF or 3D Gaussian Splatting pipelines. NeRF-SDP is a generalizable neural radiance field designed for high-fidelity novel view synthesis with sparse sampling points NeRF-SDP. It differs from sibling methods by explicitly incorporating monocular depth estimation for geometry features and a depth-encoded ray transformer to maintain quality with fewer sampling points NeRF-SDP. Choose it when balancing rendering speed and quality is critical for sparse input views NeRF-SDP. IBRNet is a feedforward neural network for generalizable view synthesis that bypasses per-scene optimization by learning a data prior from a training set IBRNet. It differs from sibling methods by using a Ray Transformer to predict density directly from aggregated multi-view features IBRNet. Choose it when a data-driven prior from a large training set is available for fast inference on unseen scenes IBRNet. A generalizable approach aiming to learn a representation from a large-scale dataset that can be fine-tuned for unseen objects, using feature volumes to obtain generalizable geometric priors. A scene representation architecture that combines 2D feature planes (tri-planes) and a 3D voxel grid to improve reconstruction quality while maintaining compact parameter counts. Ablation on Synthetic-NeRF dataset: Tri-plane (13.7M, 31.44 PSNR, 0.949 SSIM), Voxel (13.6M, 32.35 PSNR, 0.956 SSIM), Hybrid (13.2M, 32.64 PSNR, 0.958 SSIM). Compared to a pure 2D tri-plane representation (13.7M params, 31.44 PSNR, 0.949 SSIM) and a pure 3D voxel representation (13.6M params, 32.35 PSNR, 0.956 SSIM), the hybrid grid uses 13.2M parameters to achieve 32.64 PSNR and 0.958 SSIM, confirming superior compactness and quality. Original implicit radiance field representations lack cross-scene generalization capabilities and typically overlook relations between views, requiring long per-scene optimization. To mitigate this, methods following a generalizable approach aim to learn a representation from a large-scale dataset that can be fine-tuned and adapted to unseen objects or scenes. This is achieved by learning generalizable geometric priors from source images, obtained using feature volumes or transformer-based attention modules to aggregate source view information. Recent methods further enforce generalization by leveraging deep multiview stereo (MVS) strategies incorporated into the original NeRF and 3D Gaussian Splatting pipelines. name: NeRF-SDP
body: NeRF-SDP is an efficient generalizable neural radiance field that achieves high-fidelity novel view synthesis with sparse sampling points by incorporating scene depth perception via geometry feature extraction and a depth-encoded ray transformer. It solves the problem of balancing rendering speed and quality in generalizable NeRFs, where existing methods either rely on complex networks leading to inefficient rendering or use simpler networks and fewer sampling points leading to artifacts. It differs from its siblings, such as IBRNet, by explicitly using monocular depth estimation to extract geometry features during the feature extraction stage and employing a depth-encoded ray transformer to infer volume density, thereby maintaining quality with fewer sampling points. Inputs: A set of N reference images Ii for i=1, \dots, N. Outputs: A rendered image for a target camera pose, derived from volume density \sigma and color c along rays. Data Structures: Feature Volume (V^fi): A 3D tensor representing features for a single view, derived from the total feature map Fi. Cost Volume (Vc): A 3D tensor constructed from multiple feature volumes, encoding multi-view consistency. Depth Probability Volume (Vp): A 3D tensor where each voxel contains the probability of a surface existing at that depth layer. 3D Feature Volume (F{cv}): A 3D tensor containing aggregated features for volume rendering, derived from the cost volume. Geometry Feature Map (F^{geo}i): A 2D map per view containing geometric priors. Texture Feature Map (F^{fe}i): A 2D map per view containing appearance priors. Steps: 1. Geometry Feature Extraction: For each reference image Ii, a pre-trained monocular depth estimation model H{mono} estimates the relative depth map \tilde{D}i. This depth map is passed through a shared feature extraction network G{fe} to calculate the geometry feature map F^{geo}i: F^{geo}i = G{fe}(H{mono}(Ii)), \quad i = 1, \dots, N The output F^{geo}i has the same spatial dimensions as the input image but encodes geometric structure. 2. Texture Feature Extraction: For each reference image Ii, a network extracts the texture feature map F^{fe}i. 3. Feature Concatenation: Concatenate the texture feature map F^{fe}i and the geometry feature map F^{geo}i of the i-th view to form the total feature map Fi: Fi = \text{Concat}(F^{fe}i, F^{geo}i) Concatenation occurs along the channel dimension. 4. Feature Volume Construction: Obtain a feature volume V^fi for each view using its total feature map Fi. This is typically achieved by extruding the 2D feature map along the depth axis using a fixed set of depth planes. 5. Cost Volume Construction: Construct the cost volume Vc from the set of feature volumes \{V^fi\}: Vc = \frac{1}{N} \sum{i=1}^{N} (V^fi - \bar{V}^f)^2 where \bar{V}^f denotes the mean feature volume of the N views, and the square is an element-wise operation. 6. Depth Probability and 3D Feature Volume Generation: Use a 3D CNN network to convert the cost volume Vc into a depth probability volume Vp and a 3D feature volume F{cv}. 7. Depth and Confidence Estimation: Calculate the estimated depth d and confidence interval s on a ray r from the depth probability volume Vp: d = \sum{j=1}^{L} pj dj s = \sum{j=1}^{L} pj (dj - d)^2 Here, d and s represent the estimated depth and confidence interval on ray r. pj and dj represent the depth probability in Vp and the depth value at the j-th layer on ray r, respectively. L is the number of depth layers. 8. Volume Density Inference: Use a Depth-Encoded Ray Transformer (DERT) to infer the volume density \sigma of each query point. The DERT aggregates features from N views for each point and uses the estimated depth d and confidence s as positional encodings or inputs to guide density prediction, allowing for accurate reconstruction with fewer sampling points. 9. Volume Rendering: Render the image by integrating color and density along rays using the inferred \sigma and color c. Parameters: N: Number of reference views. L: Number of depth layers/hypotheses. Typical Performance: On the dataset in, NeRF-SDP achieves PSNR 26.95dB in 5.16s. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Monocular depth accuracy affects geometry features; inaccurate estimates may lead to artifacts. Extreme sparsity may challenge generalization. Element-wise operations in cost volume construction and depth estimation require careful numerical precision handling. Constructs a 3D cost volume from multiple input views to enable generalizable NeRFs by encoding multi-view consistency. It differs from standard NeRFs by replacing per-ray MLP optimization with a differentiable 3D convolutional encoding of a pre-computed cost volume, and from other generalizable methods by explicitly using homographic warping for feature alignment. Choose it when multi-view consistency is critical and homographic warping is applicable. Rendering time is efficient compared to other generalizable NeRFs, achieving 5.16s per image versus 7.44s for MVSNeRF and 15.48s for IBRNet. Memory complexity is not given in the sources. Measured performance on the comparison dataset shows NeRF-SDP achieves PSNR 26.95dB, outperforming MVSNeRF (25.33dB) and IBRNet (26.29dB). Strengths include high fidelity with sparse sampling points, efficient rendering, and improved geometry understanding via scene depth perception. Limitations include reliance on a pre-trained monocular depth estimation model and potential failure when depth estimation is unreliable. Use it when high-quality novel view synthesis is required from sparse input views with limited rendering resources. Avoid it when per-scene optimization is acceptable and higher accuracy is needed, or when input views are dense. NeRF-SDP was proposed by researchers from Shanghai Jiao Tong University, China. It was published in 2023. The method addresses the challenge of balancing rendering speed and quality in generalizable NeRFs by introducing scene depth perception. It is the first generalizable method to use estimated depth during the feature extraction stage. NeRF-SDP: Efficient Generalizable Neural Radiance Field with Scene Depth Perception, https://doi.org/10.1145/3595916.3626380, fetched 2026-10-30

name: Cost Volume Construction for Neural Radiance Fields
head: Homographic warping cost volume, Variance-based cost volume
body: This method constructs a 3D cost volume from multiple input views to enable generalizable neural radiance fields by encoding multi-view consistency. It infers scene geometry and appearance without per-scene optimization by warping 2D features from input views to a reference view across a range of depths and aggregating their variance. It replaces per-ray MLP optimization with a differentiable 3D convolutional encoding of a pre-computed cost volume, and uses homographic warping for feature alignment rather than simple depth projection or attention mechanisms. Inputs: N input views, each an image Ii \in \mathbb{R}^{Hi \times Wi \times 3} for i=1 \dots N. Camera parameters for each view i: intrinsic matrix Ki, rotation matrix Ri, translation vector ti. A reference view (typically view 1) with parameters K1, R1, t1. A set of discrete depth values g defining the scanning volume. Hyperparameters: feature channel count C, number of input views N. Outputs: Cost volume P with spatial dimensions matching the downsampled reference view, depth steps, and feature channels. Neural feature volume S = B(P), where B is a 3D CNN (see Subtopics). Data Structures: Feature maps Fi: Extracted via CNN, layout \mathbb{R}^{Hi/4 \times Wi/4 \times C}. Warped feature maps F{i,g}: Same layout as Fi, aligned to reference view coordinates. Cost volume P: 4D tensor with dimensions corresponding to reference view spatial resolution (downsampled by 4), depth steps, and feature channels. Steps: 1. Feature Extraction: For each input view Ii, pass through a deep CNN with down-sampling convolutional layers to extract a high-dimensional feature map Fi \in \mathbb{R}^{Hi/4 \times Wi/4 \times C}. The CNN typically uses stride-2 convolutions to achieve the 1/4 resolution reduction. 2. Homographic Warping: For each view i and each depth sample g: a. Compute the homographic deformation matrix Qi(g) to warp features from view i to the reference view at depth g: Qi(g) = Ki Ri R1^T + \frac{(t1 - ti)n}{n1} \mathbf{1}^T K1^{-1} Where Ki, K1 are intrinsic matrices, Ri, R1 are rotation matrices, ti, t1 are translation vectors, n is the normal vector, n1 is the depth component of n, and \mathbf{1} is a vector of ones. For a fixed depth g in the reference frame, n is typically [0,0,1]^T and n1 = g. b. Warp the feature map Fi to the reference view at depth g using bilinear interpolation: F{i,g}(a, b) = Fi(Qi(g)[a, b, 1]^T) where (a, b) is the pixel position in the reference view. 3. Cost Volume Aggregation: For each voxel at position (a, b, g) in the cost volume, collect the warped feature vectors from all N views and compute the variance across the views to determine the cost feature vector P(a, b, g): P(a, b, g) = \text{Var}(F{i,g}(a, b)) \text{Var}(\cdot) is computed channel-wise. For each channel c, P(a, b, g)c = \frac{1}{N} \sum{i=1}^N (F{i,g}(a, b)c - \muc)^2, where \muc is the mean across views for channel c. This results in a vector of size C. 4. Neural Encoding: Process the cost volume P with a 3D CNN B with a UNet structure to extract scene geometry and appearance characteristics, producing a neural feature volume S = B(P). Parameters: C: The desired number of feature channels in the extracted feature maps. N: The total number of input views used to compute the variance in the cost volume. Depth range and sampling count: Not given in the sources. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Occlusions: Homographic warping assumes consistent depth; occlusions cause mismatches in warped features, increasing variance incorrectly. Precision: Bilinear interpolation during warping introduces smoothing, potentially losing high-frequency details. Camera Parameters: Accurate K, R, t are critical; errors lead to misalignment and incorrect cost volume. A variant step where the cost volume P is processed by a 3D CNN B with a UNet structure to extract scene geometry and appearance characteristics, producing a neural feature volume S = B(P). This step transforms the raw variance-based cost features into a high-dimensional feature space where channels represent distinct attributes (lighting, textures, materials), enabling inference of volume density and brightness dependent on viewpoint. It sets itself apart by adding a learnable 3D convolutional encoder to the static cost volume, allowing the network to refine geometric and appearance cues before rendering. Choose this when high-fidelity rendering of complex materials and lighting is required, as opposed to using the raw cost volume directly. Time Complexity: Dominated by feature extraction (O(N \cdot H \cdot W \cdot C)) and warping (O(N \cdot D \cdot H \cdot W \cdot C)). Memory Complexity: O(N \cdot D \cdot H \cdot W \cdot C) to store intermediate warped features or the final cost volume. Performance: Enables fast novel view synthesis as it avoids per-scene optimization. Strengths: Generalizable to unseen scenes; leverages multi-view consistency; differentiable end-to-end. Limitations: Sensitive to camera calibration errors; struggles with occlusions and non-Lambertian surfaces; resolution limited by the cost volume size and warping accuracy. When to use: Sparse view synthesis, real-time applications where per-scene optimization is too slow. When not to use: Scenes with significant occlusions, dynamic content, or when high-precision depth is required without additional regularization. Originated in the context of generalizable neural radiance fields, specifically in the work by (2024/2025). It builds on earlier work in multi-view stereo and homography-based warping [37] (cited in) and UNet-based 3D CNNs [38] (cited in). The method addresses the limitation of traditional NeRFs that require per-scene optimization, by introducing a cost volume that encodes multi-view consistency, allowing for generalizable rendering. Rugularizing generalizable neural radiance field with limited-view images, https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s40747-024-01696-6, fetched 2026-10-29

name: IBRNet
head: Instant Neural Graphics Primitives with Image-Based Rendering Networks
body: IBRNet is a feedforward neural network method for novel view synthesis that generalizes to unseen scenes without per-scene optimization. It differs from standard NeRF and siblings like NeRF-SDP by replacing iterative volume rendering optimization with a CNN-based feature extraction and a Ray Transformer that predicts density directly from multi-view features. It builds on Generalizable Radiance Fields by using a data prior learned from a large dataset to bypass scene-specific training. The input consists of a target camera pose and N source images from the training set with similar viewing directions. The output is the density \sigma for query points along rays from the target camera. The feature volume is implicitly constructed via feature aggregation. No explicit 3D grid is stored, and features are projected from 2D image features. The Ray Transformer is a sequence model that processes concatenated features along a ray. 1. View Selection: For a target view, the method selects N source views from the training set with the most similar viewing directions. 2. Feature Extraction: A CNN extracts feature maps Fi from each of the N source images. 3. Query Point Projection: For a query point x along a ray from the target camera, the method projects x onto each source image i using the known camera matrix Ki to obtain pixel coordinates. 4. Feature Sampling: The method samples the color ci and feature vector fi from the CNN features at the projected coordinates for each view i. 5. Feature Refinement and Weighting: Each feature fi is passed through an MLP to produce a refined multi-view aware feature f'i and a pooling weight wi. 6. Feature Aggregation: The method computes the aggregated feature F{agg} for point x by summing the refined features weighted by wi: F{agg}(x) = \sum{i=1}^{N} wi f'i This step is repeated for all query points along the ray. 7. Ray Transformer Processing: The method concatenates the aggregated features F{agg}(x) for all query points along the ray into a sequence. This sequence is fed into a Ray Transformer. 8. Density Prediction: The Ray Transformer outputs the density \sigma for each query point. Color prediction details are not provided in the sources. The number of source views N is not given in the sources. The CNN backbone is not given in the sources. The MLP dimensions are not given in the sources. View selection relies on choosing N source views with the most similar viewing directions. Projection accuracy depends on camera calibration. IBRNet is limited by COLMAP for camera pose estimation. A denoising method that incorporates inter-view and spatial awareness to enhance noise robustness, achieving state-of-the-art results in burst denoising under challenging conditions like large motion and high noise. It avoids per-scene training by building on IBRNet, which generalizes to unseen scenes with minimal input. Feedforward inference is significantly faster than iterative NeRF optimization. Memory usage depends on the number of source views N and the CNN feature size, with no explicit 3D volume storage required. The method is widely used in benchmarks for view synthesis. It reduces the number of iterations compared to per-scene NeRF. Generalization to unseen scenes without per-scene optimization and fast inference are primary strengths. Limitations include the requirement for a training dataset and performance dependence on the availability of similar source views. The method should be used for novel view synthesis where per-scene optimization is too slow. It is not suitable for scenes with no similar training views. IBRNet was published in February 2021 as a NeRF-adjacent method for view synthesis. It was introduced to address the slow training speed of NeRF by using a feedforward model to learn a data prior. It is widely used in benchmarks. name: 2D-3D Hybrid Feature Grid
head: Hybrid Tri-Plane and Voxel Grid
body: The 2D-3D Hybrid Feature Grid is a scene representation architecture that combines 2D feature planes (tri-planes) and a 3D voxel grid to improve reconstruction quality while maintaining compact parameter counts. It addresses the trade-off between the geometric expressiveness of 3D voxels and the computational efficiency of 2D planes. Compared to a pure 2D tri-plane representation and a pure 3D voxel representation, the hybrid grid achieves superior compactness and quality, using fewer parameters to reach higher PSNR and SSIM scores. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A set of source images used for training; a query ray defined by origin \mathbf{o} and direction \mathbf{d} for rendering. Output: Volume density \sigma and view-dependent color \mathbf{c} for sample points along the ray. Data Structures: The representation consists of a hybrid feature grid \Psi. While the specific layout of the 2D tri-planes is not detailed in the provided sources, the 3D component is defined as a 3D volume of dimension f \times d^3. Feature Grid \Psi: A 3D volume storing features. Density Features fd: A vector in \mathbb{R}^4. Appearance Features fc: A vector in \mathbb{R}^8. Positional Encoding \gamma(\cdot): Applied to the view direction \mathbf{d}, using 6 frequencies. Parameters: d = 256: The final grid resolution dimension for the 3D component. fd \in \mathbb{R}^4: Number of density feature channels. fc \in \mathbb{R}^8: Number of appearance feature channels. N\gamma = 6: Number of frequencies in the positional encoding function \gamma(\cdot). Steps: 1. Ray Sampling: Sample points pi along the ray. 2. Feature Interpolation: Obtain features f for each sample point pi by trilinearly interpolating the feature grid \Psi. 3. Feature Splitting: Split the interpolated features into density features fd and appearance features fc. 4. Density Prediction: Process density features fd through a small MLP \pid to produce density \sigmai: \sigmai = \pid(fd) 5. Color Prediction: Concatenate appearance features fc with the viewpoint encoding \gamma(\mathbf{d}) and process through a small MLP \pic to produce color \mathbf{c}i: \mathbf{c}i = \pic(fc, \gamma(\mathbf{d})) Pitfalls: Hardware Efficiency: The number of features for each network must be a multiple of four to maximize texture efficiency, as one hardware-accelerated texture read fetches four channel values. Precision: Not given in the sources. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def queryhybridgrid(grid, point, viewdirection): """ Query the 2D-3D hybrid feature grid for density and color. Args: grid: The 3D feature volume Psi of dimension f x d^3. point: 3D coordinate (x, y, z) of the sample point. viewdirection: 3D view direction vector d. Returns: sigma: Volume density. color: View-dependent color. """ # 1. Trilinearly interpolate features from the 3D grid # Note: The sources describe a hybrid grid but only provide # implementation details for the 3D voxel part's interpolation. # The 2D tri-plane contribution is not specified in the pseudocode # or detailed layout in the sources. features = trilinearinterpolate(grid, point) # 2. Split features into density and appearance components # Based on, fd is R^4 and fc is R^8. # Assuming features are concatenated as [fd, fc] or similar. # The exact split logic (e.g., indices) is not given in sources. fd = features[0:4] fc = features[4:12] # 3. Predict density using MLP pid # pid is a small MLP. Implementation details of pid are not given. sigma = mlpdensity(fd) # 4. Predict color using MLP pic # Apply positional encoding with 6 frequencies to viewdirection viewencoding = positionalencoding(viewdirection, numfrequencies=6) # Concatenate fc and viewencoding inputcolor = concatenate(fc, viewencoding) # pic is a small MLP. Implementation details of pic are not given. color = mlpcolor(inputcolor) return sigma, color A model architecture combining a 3D feature grid with small MLP decoders to leverage hardware texture interpolation and cache coherence for efficient real-time rendering. It uses a 3D feature grid \psi of dimension f \times d^3 and small MLPs \pid and \pic for density and color, respectively. This design achieves higher computational efficiency due to better cache coherence for sampling. It is critical to use multiples of four for the number of features for each network to maximize texture efficiency, as one hardware-accelerated texture read fetches four channel values. The grid resolution is set to d=256, with fd \in \mathbb{R}^4 and fc \in \mathbb{R}^8. The view direction \mathbf{d} is encoded using a positional encoding function \gamma(\cdot) with 6 frequencies. To address aliasing artifacts and high-resolution query costs in virtual reality, a hierarchy of feature grids is introduced by trilinearly downsampling the full-resolution grid to multiple levels of lower resolutions, similar to mipmaps. Time and Memory Complexity: Memory: The hybrid grid uses 13.2M parameters, which is fewer than the tri-plane (13.7M) and voxel (13.6M) representations. The 3D component has a resolution of 256^3. Time: The compact representation leads to better cache coherence, improving computational efficiency. Sparsity loss can improve rendering time in both training and inference with a minor decrease in reconstruction quality. Measured Performance: Synthetic-NeRF Dataset: Tri-plane: 13.7M params, 31.44 PSNR, 0.949 SSIM. Voxel: 13.6M params, 32.35 PSNR, 0.956 SSIM. Hybrid: 13.2M params, 32.64 PSNR, 0.958 SSIM. Dynamic Scene Reconstruction (D-NeRF/HyperNeRF): Ours-B2 (w/o sparsity loss): 6.4m train time, 3.3 fps inference, 32.69 PSNR, 0.958 SSIM. Ours-B2 (w/ sparsity loss): 6.1m train time, 3.8 fps inference, 32.64 PSNR, 0.958 SSIM. Ours-B8 (w/o sparsity loss): 14.7m train time, 2.2 fps inference, 33.60 PSNR, 0.964 SSIM. Ours-B8 (w/ sparsity loss): 13.9m train time, 2.7 fps inference, 33.59 PSNR, 0.964 SSIM. Strengths and Limitations: Strengths: Superior compactness and quality compared to pure 2D or 3D representations. Efficient real-time rendering potential due to hardware texture interpolation and cache coherence. Limitations: Not given in the sources. When to Use: Use when high reconstruction quality is needed with compact parameter counts. Use when real-time rendering efficiency is critical, leveraging hardware texture interpolation. The 2D-3D Hybrid Feature Grid was introduced in "Binary Radiance Fields". It was developed to improve radiance field reconstruction quality while maintaining compact feature encoding. The hardware-guided variant was presented in "Neural Assets: Volumetric Object Capture and Rendering for Interactive Environments". name: General Radiance Field (GRF)
body: General Radiance Field (GRF) is a neural rendering method that learns a 3D scene representation by extracting local features from 2D input images and projecting them into a canonical 3D space. It operates in canonical space rather than view-space, distinguishing it from methods like Generalizable Radiance Fields. The network models 3D geometry and appearance by constructing an internal representation for each point in 3D space and rendering appearance and geometry from an arbitrary position. Inputs: 1. A set of M input images with their corresponding camera poses and intrinsics: \{(I1, \xi1, K1), \dots, (IM, \xiM, KM)\}, where Im is the image, \xim is the pose, and Km is the intrinsic matrix. 2. A query 3D point p = \{xp, yp, zp\} in canonical space. 3. A query viewpoint Vp = \{x{vp}, y{pv}, z{pv}\} representing the camera position from which the point is observed. Outputs: 1. Predicted RGB color values \{rp, gp, bp\}. 2. Predicted volumetric density dp. The method utilizes a neural network architecture composed of four distinct components: 1. Feature Extractor: A Convolutional Neural Network (CNN) with an encoder-decoder structure that processes 2D images to extract pixel-level features. 2. Reprojector: A geometric module that transforms 2D features extracted from input images into the 3D canonical space corresponding to the query point p. 3. Aggregator: A module that combines features reprojected from multiple input views into a single general feature vector for point p. 4. Neural Renderer: A Multi-Layer Perceptron (MLP) based on the NeRF architecture that maps the aggregated general features and viewpoint information to density and color. 1. Preprocessing Input Images: For each input image Im, the camera's 3D location (xyz coordinates) is stacked (duplicated) to each pixel of the image. This allows the feature extractor to be explicitly aware of the pixel's relative position in 3D space. 2. Feature Extraction: The preprocessed images are passed through the shared CNN feature extractor. Skip connections between the encoder and decoder are used to preserve high-frequency local features, while fully connected layers in the middle learn global features. This produces a set of 2D feature maps, one for each input image. 3. Reprojection: For a given query point p, the 2D features from each input image Im are reprojected back to the 3D location of p. This aligns the features from different viewpoints to the same canonical coordinate. 4. Aggregation: The reprojected features from all M views are aggregated. An attention mechanism is integrated to handle visual occlusions implicitly, weighting features from visible views higher than those from occluded views. This results in a single general feature vector for point p. 5. Radiance Field Query: The aggregated general feature vector, along with the query viewpoint Vp, is fed into the NeRF MLP. The MLP predicts the density dp and color \{rp, gp, bp\} for point p. 6. Volume Rendering: To render a final pixel color for a camera ray, multiple points along the ray are sampled. The volume rendering equation is used to integrate the predicted densities and colors of these points to obtain the final pixel RGB value. The network fW with learnable parameters W is defined as: (rp, gp, bp, dp) = fW \left( (I1, \xi1, K1), \dots, (IM, \xiM, KM), (xp, yp, zp), (x{vp}, y{pv}, z{pv}) \right) Where: (rp, gp, bp, dp) are the predicted RGB value and volumetric density of point p observed from viewpoint Vp. fW is the network with learnable parameters W. (Im, \xim, Km) are the m-th image, pose, and intrinsics. (xp, yp, zp) are the coordinates of the query point p. (x{vp}, y{pv}, z{pv}) are the coordinates of the query viewpoint Vp. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math import numpy as np class GRF: def init(self, numimages, featureextractor, aggregator, renderer): self.numimages = numimages self.featureextractor = featureextractor self.aggregator = aggregator self.renderer = renderer def extract2dfeatures(self, images, camerapositions): # images: [M, H, W, 3], camerapositions: [M, 3] # Stack camera position to each pixel camposexpanded = np.expanddims(np.expanddims(camerapositions, axis=1), axis=1) camposstacked = np.broadcastto(camposexpanded, (images.shape[0], images.shape[1], images.shape[2], 3)) inputtensor = np.concatenate([images, camposstacked], axis=-1) return self.featureextractor(inputtensor) def reprojectfeatures(self, features2d, querypoints, cameraposes, Kmatrices): # features2d: [M, H, W, C] # querypoints: [N, 3] # cameraposes: [M, 4, 4] # Kmatrices: [M, 3, 3] N = querypoints.shape[0] M = features2d.shape[0] C = features2d.shape[-1] reprojected = np.zeros((M, N, C)) for m in range(M): camposeinv = np.linalg.inv(cameraposes[m]) phom = np.hstack([querypoints, np.ones((N, 1))]) pcamhom = (camposeinv @ phom.T).T pcam = pcamhom[:,:3] K = Kmatrices[m] pcamproj = (K @ pcam.T).T u = pcamproj[:, 0] / pcamproj[:, 2] v = pcamproj[:, 1] / pcamproj[:, 2] z = pcamproj[:, 2] unorm = (u / (features2d.shape[2] - 1)) 2 - 1 vnorm = (v / (features2d.shape[1] - 1)) 2 - 1 grid = np.stack([unorm, vnorm], axis=-1).reshape(1, 1, N, 2) featm = features2d[m].reshape(1, features2d.shape[1], features2d.shape[2], C) sampled = np.squeeze(gridsample(featm, grid)) reprojected[m] = sampled.T return reprojected def aggregatefeatures(self, reprojectedfeatures, querypoints): # reprojectedfeatures: [M, N, C] # querypoints: [N, 3] return self.aggregator(reprojectedfeatures, querypoints) def queryradiancefield(self, aggregatedfeatures, querypoints, queryviewpoints): # aggregatedfeatures: [N, Cagg] # querypoints: [N, 3] # queryviewpoints: [N, 3] inputdata = np.concatenate([aggregatedfeatures, querypoints, queryviewpoints], axis=-1) output = self.renderer(inputdata) color = output[:,:3] density = output[:, 3:4] return color, density def render(self, images, camerapositions, cameraposes, Kmatrices, raysorigins, raysdirections, numsamples): # raysorigins: [H, W, 3], raysdirections: [H, W, 3] tvals = np.linspace(0.0, 1.0, numsamples) points = raysorigins[:,:, np.newaxis,:] + raysdirections[:,:, np.newaxis,:] tvals[np.newaxis, np.newaxis,:, np.newaxis] H, W, N = points.shape[:3] pointsflat = points.reshape(-1, N, 3) features2d = self.extract2dfeatures(images, camerapositions) reprojected = self.reprojectfeatures(features2d, pointsflat, cameraposes, Kmatrices) aggregated = self.aggregatefeatures(reprojected, pointsflat) viewpointsflat = np.broadcastto(camerapositions[np.newaxis,:,:], (HW, N, 3)).reshape(-1, 3) color, density = self.queryradiancefield(aggregated, pointsflat, viewpointsflat) deltas = np.diff(tvals) delta = np.concatenate([deltas, [1e10]]) delta = np.broadcastto(delta[np.newaxis, np.newaxis,:], (H, W, N)).reshape(-1, N) alpha = 1.0 - np.exp(-density delta) T = np.cumprod(1.0 - alpha + 1e-10, axis=1) T = np.concatenate([np.oneslike(T[:,:1]), T[:,:-1]], axis=1) weights = alpha T renderedcolor = np.sum(weights[:,:, np.newaxis] color, axis=1) return renderedcolor.reshape(H, W, 3) def gridsample(inputtensor, grid): # Standard bilinear sampling implementation omitted for brevity; # assumes standard library or framework implementation. pass Number of Input Images (M): Not specified in the sources. CNN Architecture: Details are in the appendix of the source paper; not specified here. MLP Architecture: Based on NeRF; specific layer sizes not given in the provided notes. Lighting Sensitivity: Using raw RGB values as pixel features is sub-optimal because they are sensitive to lighting conditions and environmental noise. Camera Intrinsics/Rotations: Stacking additional camera rotation and intrinsics to each pixel does not noticeably improve performance. Occlusions: The attention mechanism in the aggregator implicitly handles visual occlusions by weighting features from visible views. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Performance: Extensive experiments demonstrate the effectiveness of the approach, but specific metrics are not provided in the notes. Strengths: Operates in canonical space, allowing for generalizable features across views. The use of CNNs for feature extraction provides robustness to lighting variations. Limitations: The method relies on accurate camera poses and intrinsics. The performance of the CNN feature extractor is critical and its optimal design is not detailed in the source. General Radiance Field (GRF) was introduced by Alex Trevithick and Bo Yang in October 2020. It is similar to pixelNeRF but operates in canonical space rather than view-space. The method models 3D geometries as a general radiance field, taking 2D images with camera poses and intrinsics as input, constructing an internal representation for each point of the 3D space, and rendering appearance and geometry from an arbitrary position. name: Closed-Form Color Field Estimation
head: Closed-form color estimation
body: Closed-form color field estimation is a rendering-independent technique that computes the color field solely from a given density field and posed training images in closed form. It decouples shape and radiance to reduce the shape-radiance ambiguity inherent in Neural Radiance Fields (NeRF). Unlike general geometric priors such as total variation or sparsity losses, this method is scene-adaptive and guided by photometric loss, directly supervising the density field through color consistency. Inputs: A 3D density field \sigma(\mathbf{v}) defined on a grid or explicit representation. A set of posed training images providing camera centers \mathbf{o}k and projection matrices Pk. The degree of the spherical harmonics basis L. Outputs: A color field \hat{\mathbf{c}}(\mathbf{v}) represented by spherical harmonics coefficients for every 3D point \mathbf{v} in the scene. Data Structures: Spherical Harmonics Coefficients: For each 3D point \mathbf{v}, store a vector of coefficients h\ell^m for \ell \in [0, L] and m \in [-\ell, \ell]. Transmittance Values: Precomputed or on-the-fly transmittance Tk(\mathbf{v}) from each camera k to point \mathbf{v} along the viewing direction. Algorithm Steps: 1. Represent Color: Represent the color at each 3D point \mathbf{v} observed from direction \mathbf{d} as a linear combination of spherical harmonics basis functions up to degree L: F{\mathbf{v},\mathbf{d}} = \sum{\ell=0}^L \sum{m=-\ell}^\ell h\ell^m Y\ell^m(\mathbf{d}). 2. Estimate Coefficients: Estimate each coefficient h\ell^m by approximating the spherical integral using Monte Carlo sampling over directions \mathbf{d}k observed in the posed training images. The integral is approximated by dividing by the direction probability density function pd(\mathbf{d}k). 3. Weight by Transmittance: Weight the observed colors by the transmittance Tk(\mathbf{v}) to handle occlusion, ensuring only visible geometry contributes to the color estimation. 4. Residual Correction: Apply a residual color estimation scheme to handle non-uniformly distributed views and compensate for directional sampling bias. Formulas: The coefficient h\ell^m is estimated as: h\ell^m \approx \frac{1}{K} \sum{k=1}^K \frac{Tk(\mathbf{v}) F{\mathbf{v},\mathbf{d}k} Y\ell^m(\mathbf{d}k)}{pd(\mathbf{d}k)} where F{\mathbf{v},\mathbf{d}k} is the observed color at pixel location corresponding to \mathbf{d}k, Tk(\mathbf{v}) is the transmittance from camera k to \mathbf{v}, Y\ell^m(\mathbf{d}) is the spherical harmonics basis function, pd(\mathbf{d}) is the direction PDF, and K is the number of Monte Carlo samples (directions). Parameters: L: Degree of the spherical harmonics basis. Controls angular resolution of the color field. Typical values in NeRF literature are 3 or 4. pd(\mathbf{d}): Probability density function of observation directions. Assumed uniform over the sphere: pd(\mathbf{d}) \equiv \frac{1}{4\pi}. K: Number of Monte Carlo samples (directions) drawn from posed training images to approximate the integral for each SH coefficient. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Occlusion: Points occluded by foreground geometry will have low transmittance Tk(\mathbf{v}), reducing their contribution to the color field. Non-uniform Views: If training views are clustered, the Monte Carlo approximation of the spherical integral will be biased. Precision: Accumulating weights in floating point can lead to precision issues for points with many observations; use double precision for accumulation if necessary. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import numpy as np def closedformcolorestimation(densitygrid, cameraposes, images, L): """ densitygrid: 3D numpy array of sigma(v) cameraposes: list of tuples (ok, Pk) where ok is camera center and Pk is projection matrix images: list of 2D numpy arrays of observed colors L: Degree of spherical harmonics Returns: shcoeffs: 2D numpy array of shape (numvoxels, (L+1)^2) """ numvoxels = densitygrid.size numcoeffs = (L + 1) 2 shaccum = np.zeros((numvoxels, numcoeffs), dtype=np.float64) samplecounts = np.zeros(numvoxels, dtype=np.float64) pd = 1.0 / (4.0 np.pi) # Uniform direction PDF for k, (ok, Pk) in enumerate(cameraposes): img = images[k] # Standard ray marching over the grid to collect points and transmittance for u in range(img.shape[1]): for v in range(img.shape[0]): raydir = Pk.unproject(u, v) rayorig = ok points, transmittances = raymarch(rayorig, raydir, densitygrid) for pt, T in zip(points, transmittances): if T < 1e-6: continue observedcolor = img[v, u] dk = pt - ok dk /= np.linalg.norm(dk) # Standard SH basis evaluation for l=0..L, m=-l..l basis = evaluateshbasis(dk, L) # Accumulate weighted contributions weight = (T observedcolor basis) / pd idx = getvoxelindex(pt, densitygrid) shaccum[idx] += weight samplecounts[idx] += 1 # Normalize by K (number of samples per point) safecounts = np.maximum(samplecounts, 1.0) shcoeffs = shaccum / safecounts[:, np.newaxis] return shcoeffs def evaluateshbasis(d, L): """Evaluates spherical harmonics basis functions Yl^m(d) for l=0..L, m=-l..l.""" # Standard implementation depends on SH convention (e.g., Nayar, Healy) # Returns flattened array of basis values pass def raymarch(origin, direction, densitygrid): """Traces a ray through a 3D grid, returning points and transmittances.""" # Standard volumetric ray marching implementation pass def getvoxelindex(point, densitygrid): """Maps a 3D point to a voxel index in the grid.""" # Standard coordinate-to-index mapping pass Memory Complexity: O(N \cdot (L+1)^2) to store the SH coefficients for all points, where N is the number of 3D points (voxels). Strengths: Decouples shape and radiance, reducing ambiguity. Provides a photometric regularization term that is adaptive to the scene geometry. Limitations: Requires a pre-existing density field. Not given in the sources. When to use: As a regularization term for explicit NeRF representations like Plenoxels and Direct Voxel Grid Optimization (DVGO). When not to use: Not given in the sources. The method was proposed to address the shape-radiance ambiguity in Neural Radiance Fields (NeRF). It was introduced in the paper "Reducing Shape-Radiance Ambiguity in Radiance Fields with a Closed-Form Color Estimation Method". The authors note that existing regularization methods (TV, sparsity, distortion) are based on general assumptions and are not adaptive to specific scenes. This method was applied to explicit NeRF representations, specifically Plenoxels and DVGO, demonstrating improvements on NeRF Synthetic, LLFF, and DTU datasets.
