name: Surface-SDF Representation
body: Surface-SDF Representation methods reconstruct 3D geometry and appearance by modeling the scene as a continuous implicit surface defined by a Signed Distance Function (SDF), rather than a volumetric density field [6060-neus.md][10715-volsdf.md]. This approach disentangles geometry from appearance, enabling high-fidelity surface reconstruction and direct mesh extraction [6060-neus.md][7385-surface-nerf.md]. It differs from standard NeRF-like methods by enforcing geometric consistency through the SDF constraint, and from explicit mesh methods by avoiding explicit mesh extraction during the training phase, instead rendering differentiable images directly from the implicit field [6060-neus.md]. Builds on Radiance-field optimization. All methods in this family represent scene geometry using a learnable SDF f(\mathbf{x}), compute surface normals as \mathbf{n} = \nabla f(\mathbf{x}) / \|\nabla f(\mathbf{x})\|, and convert SDF values into a probability distribution (e.g., via sigmoid or Laplace CDF derivatives) to compute segment alphas and transmittance along rays [6060-neus.md][10715-volsdf.md][12440-instant-nsr.md]. NeuS represents a surface as the zero-level set of an SDF and trains it using a novel volume rendering scheme to avoid geometric bias inherent in standard volume rendering [6060-neus.md]. It solves the problem of reconstructing high-quality 3D surfaces from multi-view 2D images by combining the robustness of neural radiance fields with the geometric precision of implicit SDFs [6060-neus.md]. Unlike siblings that also use SDFs, NeuS introduces a specific S-density formulation based on the derivative of the sigmoid function to ensure unbiased surface reconstruction in the first-order approximation [6060-neus.md]. Choose it when high-quality surface reconstruction from multi-view images is needed without explicit mesh extraction during training [6060-neus.md]. Surface NeRF converts a pre-trained Neural Radiance Field (NeRF) into a 3D mesh and a surface light field, reducing per-pixel rendering cost by evaluating the NeRF only at the surface isosurface rather than via volumetric raycasting [7385-surface-nerf.md]. It achieves this by extracting an isosurface from the density field and optimizing both the geometry and the network parameters to maintain image quality, reducing per-pixel computational cost from 226 MFLOPS to 1.7 MFLOPS and runtime by more than 100x compared to baseline NeRF [7385-surface-nerf.md]. Choose it when rendering speed is critical and a pre-trained NeRF is available, as it reduces per-pixel cost by evaluating the network only at the isosurface [7385-surface-nerf.md]. VolSDF is a neural inverse rendering method that decouples geometric representation and appearance by modeling scene density as a function of a learnable Signed Distance Function (SDF) [10715-volsdf.md]. It solves the problem of noisy, low-fidelity geometry reconstruction inherent in standard density-based NeRF approaches, where geometry is extracted via arbitrary level sets of generic density functions [10715-volsdf.md]. Unlike siblings that model geometry as a function of density, VolSDF provides a useful inductive bias for geometry, bounds opacity approximation error, and enables efficient unsupervised disentanglement of shape and appearance [10715-volsdf.md]. Choose it when disentanglement of shape and appearance is required, or when stable geometry gradients and opacity error bounds are needed [10715-volsdf.md]. Instant-NSR is a neural surface reconstruction method that improves 3D geometry quality by incorporating a Signed Distance Function (SDF) representation into a hash-encoded neural network framework [12440-instant-nsr.md]. It solves the convergence instability inherent in applying SDFs to hash coding by employing a Truncated Signed Distance Function (TSDF) via a sigmoid output activation [12440-instant-nsr.md]. It sets itself apart from its sibling NeuS by using the spatial hashing acceleration of Instant-NGP while retaining NeuS's SDF-based rendering formulation, and from Surface NeRF by its specific handling of hash-grid numerical overflow through truncation [12440-instant-nsr.md]. Choose it when fast training and inference are required via hash-grid acceleration, and numerical stability with hash coding is a concern [12440-instant-nsr.md]. Originated from the integration of neural implicit fields with inverse volume rendering. VolSDF [10715-volsdf.md] was one of the early works to explicitly model the SDF for volume rendering, aiming to overcome the ambiguity of density-based representations. NeuS [6060-neus.md] and Surface NeRF [7385-surface-nerf.md] further refined this by introducing specific architectures and optimization strategies (such as hierarchical sampling and alternating optimization) to stabilize training and improve geometric fidelity. Instant-NSR [12440-instant-nsr.md] later adapted the approach for hash-grid acceleration. These methods are primarily used in multi-view stereo reconstruction, 3D asset creation, and augmented reality applications where accurate geometry is as important as photorealistic appearance [6060-neus.md][7385-surface-nerf.md][10715-volsdf.md][12440-instant-nsr.md]. Not given in the sources.

name: NeuS
head: NeuS, Learning Neural Implicit Surfaces by Volume Rendering for Multi-view Reconstruction
body:
NeuS is a neural surface reconstruction method that represents a scene geometry as the zero-level set of a learnable Signed Distance Function (SDF) and trains it using a novel volume rendering scheme. It solves the problem of inherent geometric bias (errors) in reconstructed surfaces that occurs when standard volume rendering is naively applied to SDF-associated density. Unlike Surface NeRF which uses occupancy grids, or VolSDF which uses a fixed variance, NeuS introduces an unbiased volume rendering formulation with a trainable sharpness parameter, allowing for high-quality surface extraction without foreground mask supervision. NeuS builds on Radiance-field optimization by replacing the density-outputting MLP with an SDF-outputting MLP. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A set of posed RGB images \{Ik\} of a 3D object. Output: A reconstructed triangular mesh extracted from the learned SDF zero-level set, and rendered novel views. Data Structures: The scene is represented by two Multi-Layer Perceptrons (MLPs): 1. SDF Network (f): Maps spatial position \mathbf{x} \in \mathbb{R}^3 to a scalar signed distance value d = f(\mathbf{x}). Architecture: 8 hidden layers, hidden size 256. Activation: Softplus with  eta=100 (replacing ReLU). Skip connection: From input to the output of the 4th layer. Output: Tuple (d, \mathbf{g}) where d is the SDF value and \mathbf{g} \in \mathbb{R}^{15} is a geometry feature vector. 2. Color Network (c): Maps position \mathbf{x}, viewing direction \mathbf{v}, normal \mathbf{n}, and feature \mathbf{g} to RGB color. Architecture: 4 hidden layers, hidden size 256. Inputs: Spatial location \mathbf{p}, view direction \mathbf{v}, normal \mathbf{n} = 
abla f(\mathbf{p}), and feature \mathbf{g}. Positional Encoding: Applied to \mathbf{p} (6 frequencies) and \mathbf{v} (4 frequencies). 3. Variance Network: A single learnable parameter variance (or scalar s) controlling the sharpness of the SDF-to-alpha conversion. Inverse temperature: inv\s = \exp(variance 	imes 10.0). Clipped to [10^{-6}, 10^6] to prevent numerical instability. Numbered Steps: 1. Ray Sampling: For a camera ray \mathbf{p}(t) = \mathbf{o} + t\mathbf{v}, sample n points. NeuS uses hierarchical sampling: Uniformly sample 64 points initially. Perform importance sampling for k=4 iterations, adding 16 points per iteration, totaling 128 points. For the 'w/o mask' setting, sample an extra 32 points outside the bounding sphere to represent the background using NeRF++. 2. SDF and Gradient Query: For each sampled point \mathbf{p}i, query the SDF network to get f(\mathbf{p}i) and the geometry feature \mathbf{g}i. Compute the normal \mathbf{n}i = 
abla f(\mathbf{p}i) / \|
abla f(\mathbf{p}i)\|. 3. Alpha Computation (Unbiased Volume Rendering): Compute the opacity \alphai for the segment between section points qi and q{i+1} using the cumulative distribution function (CDF) of the S-density. Define the S-density function (derivative of Sigmoid): \phis(x) =  rac{s e^{-sx}}{(1 + e^{-sx})^2} where s is a trainable parameter (or derived from variance). Define the Sigmoid CDF: \Phis(x) =  rac{1}{1 + e^{-sx}} Compute alpha for segment i: \alphai = \max\left(  rac{\Phis(f(qi)) - \Phis(f(q{i+1}))}{\Phis(f(qi))}, 0 ight). Note: 10^{-5} is added to numerator and denominator to prevent division by zero. Alternative Implementation (Instant-NSR-PL): Uses a dynamic inv\s and cosine annealing for better convergence: python def getalpha(sdf, normal, dirs, dists, cosannealratio): invs = clip(exp(variance 10.0), 1e-6, 1e6) truecos = dot(dirs, normal) # Cosine annealing for early training stability itercos = -(relu(-truecos 0.5 + 0.5) (1 - cosannealratio) + relu(-truecos) cosannealratio) estimatednextsdf = sdf + itercos dists 0.5 estimatedprevsdf = sdf - itercos dists 0.5 prevcdf = sigmoid(estimatedprevsdf invs) nextcdf = sigmoid(estimatednextsdf invs) p = prevcdf - nextcdf c = prevcdf alpha = clip((p + 1e-5) / (c + 1e-5), 0.0, 1.0) return alpha 4. Color Computation: Compute the color ci at the midpoint pi = \mathbf{o} +  rac{ti + t{i+1}}{2}\mathbf{v} using the Color Network with inputs \mathbf{p}i, \mathbf{v}, \mathbf{n}i, \mathbf{g}i. 5. Volume Rendering: Accumulate color along the ray using standard alpha compositing: C(\mathbf{o}, \mathbf{v}) = \sumi Ti ci where Ti = \prod{j < i} (1 - \alphaj) is the transmittance. 6. Loss Calculation: Minimize the total loss: \mathcal{L} = \mathcal{L}{	ext{color}} +  eta \mathcal{L}{	ext{eikonal}} \mathcal{L}{	ext{color}}: Huber loss between rendered color and ground truth pixel. \mathcal{L}{	ext{eikonal}}: Regularizes the SDF gradient magnitude to 1: \mathcal{L}{	ext{eikonal}} =  rac{1}{mn} \sum{k,i} (\|\mathbf{n}{k,i}\| - 1)^2. 7. Optimization: Train using ADAM optimizer. Learning rate: Linear warmup from 0 to 5 	imes 10^{-4} in first 5k iterations, then cosine decay to minimum 2.5 	imes 10^{-5}. Total iterations: 300k. Weight normalization is used to stabilize training. Parameters: s (or variance): Trainable sharpness parameter. Standard deviation of \phis is 1/s, approaching 0 as training converges.  eta: Weight for Eikonal loss. Typical value not explicitly stated in sources, but described as indispensable. Softplus  eta: 100. initval: Initial value for variance parameter. modulate: Boolean to enable modulation of inv\s during training. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Geometric Bias: Naive application of standard volume rendering to SDF density causes inherent geometric errors. NeuS formulation avoids this in the first-order approximation. Spectral Bias: Random initialization causes axis-aligned artifacts due to positional encoding spectral bias. Geometric initialization avoids this. Textureless Regions: Textureless areas are ambiguous and may fail to reconstruct correctly. Numerical Stability: inv\s must be clipped to [10^{-6}, 10^6]. HAME-NeRF is a two-stage framework for extracting high-fidelity, textured surface meshes from RGB images by defining volume density as a Secant Hyperbolic Function applied to a Signed Distance Function (SDF). It builds on NeuS by introducing a spatially-varying sharpness parameter  eta(\mathbf{x}) learned via an MLP, which enhances flexibility for complex surfaces compared to methods using fixed  eta values. Unlike NeuS which focuses on differentiable volume rendering for surface representation, HAME-NeRF explicitly optimizes a mesh through differentiable rendering and iterative refinement, achieving superior geometric accuracy and visual quality on synthetic benchmarks compared to NeRF2Mesh. D-NeuS is a volume rendering-based neural implicit surface reconstruction method that recovers fine-level geometric details by extending NeuS with two additional loss functions: a geometry bias loss and a multi-view feature consistency loss. It addresses the ambiguity in geometry and appearance representation inherent in volume rendering by ensuring consistency between the rendered surface points (derived from alpha compositing) and the underlying signed distance field (SDF) zero-crossings. Unlike its parent NeuS, which suffers from geometry bias due to the non-linear transformation of SDF to density, D-NeuS explicitly penalizes this bias and enforces feature consistency on surface points rather than all sampled points, distinguishing it from siblings like HAME-NeRF and NeuS2. NeuS2 is a fast neural surface reconstruction approach for multi-view RGB input that achieves two orders of magnitude improvement in training speed over NeuS without compromising reconstruction quality, applicable to both static and dynamic scenes. It sets itself apart by parameterizing the neural network-encoded Signed Distance Field (SDF) using multi-resolution hash tables of learnable feature vectors, as introduced in Instant-NGP, and by calculating second-order derivatives using a novel lightweight formula tailored to ReLU-based MLPs to leverage CUDA parallelism and reduce memory footprint. HF-NeuS is an improvement on NeuS that separates low-frequency details into a base SDF and high-frequency details into a displacement function to increase reconstruction quality. It builds on NeuS by addressing the smoothness limitations of standard implicit SDF representations, which often fail to capture sharp geometric features. NeuDA is a neural implicit surface reconstruction method that utilizes hierarchical deformable anchors to encode local geometry, building on the NeuS [6060-neus.md] framework. It distinguishes itself by replacing standard positional encoding with Hierarchical Positional Encoding (HPE) and employing a shallower SDF network (4 layers vs. 8 for NeuS). This design achieves high-fidelity surface reconstruction with lower computational cost and sharper surfaces compared to siblings like HAME-NeRF, D-NeuS, NeuS2, and HF-NeuS. SparseNeus is a method improving NeuS for sparse-view SDF reconstruction using a geometry encoding volume with learnable image features as a hybrid representation method. Time Complexity: NeuS is slower than standard NeRF because SDF queries require more network evaluations per ray (gradient computation). Rendering a 1600x1200 image takes ~320 seconds on an Nvidia 2080Ti GPU in default settings, or ~60 seconds with sphere tracing acceleration. On an A100 GPU at 1080p, it renders at 0.8 ± 0.2 FPS. Memory Complexity: Requires storing two MLPs (SDF and Color) and their gradients. The SDF network is 8 layers, Color is 4 layers. Performance: On the NeRF Synthetic dataset, NeuS achieved PSNR = 28.4 ± 0.8 dB. On the DTU dataset, it achieved the most accurate surface reconstruction with Chamfer distance = 0.62 ± 0.08 mm. Strengths: Unbiased surface reconstruction; high geometric accuracy; works without foreground mask supervision; robust optimization for complex structures. Limitations: Slow training and rendering speed compared to hash-encoded variants; struggles with textureless regions; sensitive to initialization (requires geometric init to avoid artifacts). When to use: When high-quality, watertight surface meshes are required from multi-view images and training time is not the primary constraint. When not to use: When real-time rendering is needed (use Instant-NSR or NeuS2) or when input views are very sparse (use SparseNeus). NeuS was introduced in 2021 by Yen-Chen Lin et al. in the paper "NeuS: Learning Neural Implicit Surfaces by Volume Rendering for Multi-view Reconstruction". It was developed to address the limitations of previous implicit surface representations (like UNISURF) and the geometric bias inherent in applying standard NeRF volume rendering to SDFs. The method combines the robustness of volume rendering with the accuracy of SDF-based surface extraction. It has become a foundational method for neural surface reconstruction, leading to numerous variants such as Instant-NSR, NeuS2, and HF-Neus. name: HAME-NeRF
head: High Accuracy Mesh Extraction Leveraging Neural Radiance Fields
body: HAME-NeRF is a two-stage framework for extracting high-fidelity, textured surface meshes from RGB images by defining volume density as a Secant Hyperbolic Function applied to a Signed Distance Function (SDF). It builds on NeuS by introducing a spatially-varying sharpness parameter \beta(\mathbf{x}) learned via an MLP, which enhances flexibility for complex surfaces compared to methods using fixed \beta values. Unlike NeuS which focuses on differentiable volume rendering for surface representation, HAME-NeRF explicitly optimizes a mesh through differentiable rendering and iterative refinement, achieving superior geometric accuracy and visual quality on synthetic benchmarks compared to NeRF2Mesh. HAME-NeRF operates in two stages: initialization of geometry and appearance using a grid-based NeRF, followed by mesh refinement via differentiable rendering. Inputs: A set of N RGB images with known camera poses. Outputs: A textured triangular mesh (vertices, faces, and diffuse/specular textures) and a learned scene representation. 1. Geometry Representation: Multi-resolution feature grid E^{\text{geo}} storing spatial features for SDF computation. A shallow MLP that maps features from E^{\text{geo}} to the SDF value. 2. Appearance Representation: Multi-resolution feature grid E^{\text{app}} storing spatial features for appearance. MLP1: Maps E^{\text{app}}(\mathbf{x}) to diffuse color \mathbf{c}d and specular feature \mathbf{f}s. MLP2: Maps \mathbf{f}s and view direction \mathbf{d} to specular color \mathbf{c}s. MLP\beta: Maps spatial coordinates \mathbf{x} to the sharpness parameter \beta(\mathbf{x}). 3. Mesh Data: Vertices \mathbf{V} with per-vertex offsets learned during refinement. Faces \mathbf{F} with adaptive resolution based on rendering error. The volume density \sigma is derived from the SDF and the spatially varying parameter \beta(\mathbf{x}): \sigma(\text{SDF}, \beta) = \frac{1}{4\beta} \cdot \frac{1}{\cosh^2\left(\frac{\text{SDF}}{2\beta}\right)} \quad (2) where \beta(\mathbf{x}) is output by MLP\beta(\mathbf{x}). Appearance is decomposed into diffuse and specular components: \mathbf{c}d, \mathbf{f}s = \psi(\text{MLP}1(E^{\text{app}}(\mathbf{x}))) \quad (4) \mathbf{c}s = \psi(\text{MLP}2(\mathbf{f}s, \mathbf{d})) \quad (4) \mathbf{c} = \mathbf{c}d + \mathbf{c}s \quad (5) where \psi denotes a sigmoid activation, \mathbf{f}s encodes specular information, and \mathbf{d} is the view direction. \lambda{\text{elk}}: Weight for the Eikonal Loss. \lambda\beta: Weight for the Beta Regularization Loss. Typical values: Not given in the sources. 1. Train Grid-based NeRF: Initialize a grid-based NeRF structure with an SDF component. Compute SDF using E^{\text{geo}} and a shallow MLP. Compute density \sigma using Equation (2). Compute appearance using Equations (4) and (5). 2. Optimize: Minimize the total loss (defined below) to converge the NeRF representation. 3. Extract Coarse Mesh: Apply Marching Cubes to the converged SDF field to generate an initial coarse mesh. 1. Differentiable Rendering: Use a differentiable rasterizer to render the current mesh and compute the photometric rendering loss against input images. 2. Vertex Optimization: Optimize vertex positions by learning per-vertex offsets using gradients from the pixel-wise rendering loss. 3. Adaptive Mesh Resolution: Identify faces with high rendering errors using k-means clustering. Subdivide high-error faces to increase resolution. Simplify low-error regions to decrease resolution. 4. Iterate: Repeat the refinement loop (rendering, vertex optimization, adaptive resolution) until convergence. 5. Unbounded Scene Handling: For unbounded scenes, partition the environment into regions of progressively lower resolution away from the center and apply regularization terms for smooth surfaces and bounded vertex displacements. efficiency and accuracy. Beta Instability: Without regularization, \beta(\mathbf{x}) may vary unstably. The L1 penalty \lambda\beta |\beta(\mathbf{x})| is used to prevent this. Precision: The density formula involves division by \beta. If \beta approaches zero, numerical instability may occur. The sources do not specify a lower bound for \beta, but the regularization encourages smooth transitions. The parent method that introduced differentiable volume rendering for surface representation using SDFs. HAME-NeRF extends this by optimizing a mesh directly and learning spatially varying \beta. See NeuS. A baseline method that applies Marching Cubes directly to a density field. HAME-NeRF improves upon this by using an SDF for mesh extraction and adaptive mesh refinement. See NeRF2Mesh. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Training involves two stages: NeRF initialization and mesh refinement. The refinement stage includes iterative k-means clustering and mesh subdivision, which may increase computational cost compared to static NeRF methods. Memory Complexity: Uses multi-resolution feature grids for geometry and appearance, which are memory-efficient compared to dense voxel grids. The mesh size adapts to scene complexity. Measured Performance: On the NeRF-Synthetic dataset, HAME-NeRF outperforms NeRF2Mesh in Chamfer Distance, Normal Consistency, PSNR, and visual quality. On the Mip-NeRF 360 dataset, it achieves comparable, though slightly lower, performance than NeRF2Mesh. Strengths: High-fidelity surface extraction, spatially varying sharpness control, adaptive mesh resolution, and compatibility with real-time graphics via mesh output. Limitations: Slightly lower performance on complex real-world scenes (Mip-NeRF 360) compared to NeRF2Mesh. Requires careful tuning of loss weights \lambda{\text{elk}} and \lambda\beta. When to use: When high-quality, editable 3D meshes are required for real-time rendering or simulation, and the scene is well-lit or pre-baked lighting is acceptable. When not to use: For unbounded scenes with extreme dynamic range or complex lighting without pre-baking, as the method relies on baked lighting. HAME-NeRF was proposed to address the difficulty of extracting accurate and editable 3D meshes from NeRFs, which are inherently volumetric and incompatible with polygonal meshes needed for real-time graphics and simulation. The method builds on the NeRF2Mesh pipeline but introduces an SDF-based density modeling and a learned spatially varying \beta parameter. It was evaluated on the NeRF-Synthetic and Mip-NeRF 360 datasets. HAME-NeRF: High Accuracy Mesh Extraction Leveraging Neural Radiance Fields, https://zenodo.org/records/18469075, fetched 2026-10-26

name: D-NeuS
head: Details recovering Neural implicit Surface reconstruction
body: D-NeuS is a volume rendering-based neural implicit surface reconstruction method that recovers fine-level geometric details by extending NeuS with two additional loss functions: a geometry bias loss and a multi-view feature consistency loss. It addresses the ambiguity in geometry and appearance representation inherent in volume rendering by ensuring consistency between the rendered surface points (derived from alpha compositing) and the underlying signed distance field (SDF) zero-crossings. Unlike its parent NeuS, which suffers from geometry bias due to the non-linear transformation of SDF to density, D-NeuS explicitly penalizes this bias and enforces feature consistency on surface points rather than all sampled points, distinguishing it from siblings like HAME-NeRF and NeuS2. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: A set of multi-view images of a static scene. Outputs: A trained implicit neural network representing the scene geometry (SDF) and appearance (radiance), from which a mesh can be extracted. Data Structures and Network Layout: 1. Geometry Network (f): An MLP mapping \mathbb{R}^3 \to \mathbb{R}. Architecture: 8 hidden layers, each with 256 units. Skip connections: From input to the output of the 4th hidden layer. Initialization: Weights initialized to approximate the SDF field of a unit sphere. 2. Radiance Network (g or c): An MLP mapping spatial position, view direction, normal, and feature vector to color \mathbb{R}^3. Architecture: 4 hidden layers, each with 256 units. Inputs: Spatial point \mathbf{x}, view direction \mathbf{v}, normal \mathbf{n}, and feature vector \mathbf{z}. 3. Position Encoding: Spatial coordinates \mathbf{x}: 6 frequencies. View direction \mathbf{v}: 4 frequencies. 4. Feature Consistency: Feature channels: Nc = 32. Neighboring views: Nv = 2 source views compared against each reference view. Mathematical Formulation: The surface \mathcal{S} is defined as the zero-level set of the SDF f: \mathcal{S} = \{ \mathbf{x} \in \mathbb{R}^3 \mid f(\mathbf{x}) = 0 \} \quad (1) A 3D point on a ray from camera center \mathbf{o} with direction \mathbf{v} is: \mathbf{x}(t) = \mathbf{o} + t\mathbf{v}, \quad t \ge 0 \quad (2) The normal \mathbf{n} is computed via automatic differentiation of the SDF: \mathbf{n} = \nabla f(\mathbf{x}) The opaque density \sigma(t) is derived from the SDF using a sigmoid function \Phis: \sigma(t) = \max \left( -\frac{d\Phis}{dt}(f(\mathbf{x}(t))), 0 \right) \quad (5) where \Phis(x) = (1 + e^{-sx})^{-1} and s^{-1} is a trainable standard deviation. Numbered Steps: 1. Sampling: For each iteration, sample 512 rays. For each ray, generate 64 coarse points, 64 fine points, and 32 additional points outside the unit sphere (following NeRF++ strategy). 2. SDF Evaluation: Query the geometry network f for all sampled points to obtain SDF values f(\mathbf{x}(t)). 3. Density and Alpha Compositing: Compute density \sigma(t) using Eq. (5). Perform volume rendering to accumulate color Cr and alpha weights w(t). 4. Surface Point Interpolation: Find the first zero-crossing of the SDF along the ray. Instead of recursive ray tracing, use locally differentiable linear interpolation between adjacent sampled points where the SDF sign changes to estimate the surface point \mathbf{x}s. 5. Feature Extraction: Extract feature vectors \mathbf{z} from the geometry network f at the surface point \mathbf{x}s. 6. Loss Calculation: Photometric Loss: Standard difference between rendered color and ground truth. Eikonal Loss: Regularizes the gradient of the SDF to be unit length. Weight \alpha = 0.1. Geometry Bias Loss: Generate additional distance maps during rendering. Back-project these distances to 3D points. Penalize the absolute SDF values predicted by f at these points to encourage consistency between the rendered surface and the implicit surface. Weight \beta varies by stage. Multi-view Feature Consistency Loss: Compare feature vectors \mathbf{z} of the surface point \mathbf{x}s from the reference view with those from Nv=2 neighboring source views. Use CNNs for robust feature representation. Weight \gamma varies by stage. 7. Optimization: Update network weights using the Adam optimizer. 8. Mesh Extraction: After training, apply Marching Cubes to the SDF field f in a bounding box of size 512^3 voxels. Pseudocode: Unverified code. MS-NeuS integrates the Multi-Space (MS) module into the NeuS framework to address multi-view inconsistency, specifically improving novel view synthesis and the reconstruction of mirror surfaces. It distinguishes itself from its parent D-NeuS by focusing on view-dependent appearance consistency via sub-space decomposition rather than explicit geometric bias or feature consistency losses. Time Complexity: Training takes approximately 19 hours on a single NVIDIA Titan RTX for 300k iterations. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Scaling: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Recovers high-accuracy surface geometry, especially fine details and complex scenes. Limitations: Computationally expensive training and inference (7 mins per image). Relies on multi-view consistency which may struggle with highly reflective or textureless surfaces without additional priors (though MS-NeuS addresses this). When to use: When high-fidelity geometric reconstruction is required from multi-view images, particularly for complex scenes with fine details. When not: When real-time rendering is required or when only a small number of views are available (though it uses neighboring views, sparse views may degrade performance). D-NeuS builds upon the NeuS method, which itself was designed to improve geometric reconstruction quality by using a signed distance field (SDF) representation. The key insight of D-NeuS is the analysis of geometry bias arising from the transformation of SDF to density for volume rendering, and the proposal of a novel constraint to regularize this bias. It also incorporates multi-view feature consistency using CNNs, inspired by MVSDF, to recover fine local geometric details. The method was evaluated on the DTU and BlendedMVS datasets. name: MS-NeuS
head: Multi-Space NeuS
body: MS-NeuS integrates the Multi-Space (MS) module into the NeuS framework to resolve multi-view inconsistency for novel view synthesis and improve the reconstruction of mirror surfaces. It distinguishes itself from its parent D-NeuS by enforcing view-dependent appearance consistency through feature sub-space decomposition rather than explicit geometric bias or multi-view feature consistency losses. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Multi-view images of a scene containing reflective or mirror surfaces. Output: A neural implicit signed distance function (SDF) and a view-dependent radiance field for novel view synthesis. Data Structures: The method extends the NeuS architecture by replacing the standard feature representation with an MS module. Sub-spaces: The feature space is partitioned into K independent sub-spaces. Feature Dimension: d denotes the dimensionality of features within each sub-space. Hidden Dimension: h denotes the hidden dimension of the associated MLPs. Parameter Layout: The source reports grid parameters and MLP parameters separately using the notation "A|B". Algorithm: 1. Initialization: Initialize the NeuS backbone (SDF MLP and Color MLP) and the MS module parameters. 2. Sampling: For each pixel, sample points along the camera ray through the scene volume. 3. Sub-space Decomposition: Query the MS module to project scene coordinates into K sub-spaces, yielding decomposed features instead of a single monolithic feature vector. 4. Rendering: Perform volumetric rendering by aggregating the decomposed features to compute density and view-dependent color. 5. Optimization: Minimize the standard NeuS loss functions (photometric, SDF, etc.) while the MS module implicitly enforces multi-view consistency across the decomposed sub-spaces. Parameters: K = 4: Number of sub-spaces. d = 16: Feature dimension per sub-space. h = 32: Hidden dimension of the MLPs. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Geometric Cleanliness: The method struggles to reconstruct clean geometry because the MS module is primarily designed for novel view synthesis and lacks explicit geometric constraints on the sub-spaces. Mirror Surfaces: While it reconstructs mirror geometry better than standard NeuS, artifacts may persist due to the absence of geometric regularization within the sub-spaces. Geo-NeuS introduces multi-view constraints for SDF supervised by a NeRF, specifically a multi-view geometry constraint supervised by a sparse point cloud and a multi-view photometric consistency constraint. Time and Memory Complexity: Memory: MS-NeuS requires more parameters than the baseline NeuS. On the synthesized dataset, NeuS uses 0.16 \times 10^{-1} M parameters, while MS-NeuS uses 0.37 \times 10^{-1} M parameters. Time: The method performs multiple volumetric rendering operations per pixel, making time consumption dependent on the importance sampling strategy and backbone network inference. Measured Performance: On a synthesized dataset with circle paths: PSNR: MS-NeuS achieves 28.65, compared to NeuS 25.86. SSIM: MS-NeuS achieves 0.859, compared to NeuS 0.831. LPIPS: MS-NeuS achieves 0.195, compared to NeuS 0.258. Strengths and Limitations: Strengths: Significantly improves novel view synthesis quality and reconstructs better geometry for mirror surfaces compared to standard NeuS. Limitations: Fails to produce clean geometry due to the absence of geometric constraints on the sub-spaces. MS-NeuS is a generalization of the MS-NeRF scheme applied to the NeuS framework. It was developed to solve multi-view inconsistency for novel view synthesis, particularly in scenes with reflective surfaces. The implementation is based on the NeuS code from [66] (cited in). name: NeuS2
head: NeuS2 Dynamic Reconstruction, NeuS2 Static Reconstruction
body: NeuS2 is a fast neural surface reconstruction approach for multi-view RGB input that achieves two orders of magnitude improvement in training speed over NeuS without compromising reconstruction quality, applicable to both static and dynamic scenes. It sets itself apart by parameterizing the neural network-encoded Signed Distance Field (SDF) using multi-resolution hash tables of learnable feature vectors, as introduced in Instant-NGP, and by calculating second-order derivatives using a novel lightweight formula tailored to ReLU-based MLPs to leverage CUDA parallelism and reduce memory footprint. Inputs: Multi-view RGB images. For dynamic scenes, a sequence of such views. Outputs: A neural implicit surface representation (SDF and color) parameterized by multi-resolution hash encodings. Data Structures: Multi-resolution Hash Table: A set of hash tables, one for each resolution level l \in \{0, \dots, L-1\}, mapping 3D coordinates to learnable feature vectors. MLP: A ReLU-based Multi-Layer Perceptron that takes the hashed features as input and outputs the SDF value and color. Parameters: Training time for dynamic scenes: up to 20 seconds per frame. Typical training time for static scenes: minutes. Steps: 1. Hash Encoding: For a given 3D point \mathbf{x}, query the multi-resolution hash tables to retrieve feature vectors at different resolutions and combine them. 2. MLP Forward Pass: Pass the combined features through the ReLU-based MLP to predict the SDF value d(\mathbf{x}) and color c(\mathbf{x}). 3. Second-Order Derivative Calculation: Compute the second-order derivatives of the SDF required for the surface constraint using a novel lightweight formula tailored to ReLU-based MLPs to enable efficient CUDA implementation with a small memory footprint. 4. Progressive Learning (Static): Optimize the multi-resolution hash encodings from coarse to fine to stabilize and expedite training convergence. 5. Incremental Learning (Dynamic): Train the first frame of the sequence. For subsequent frames, sequentially fine-tune the representation, exploiting similarity in shape and appearance. If the movement between consecutive frames is large, predict a global transformation to roughly align the frames before learning the representation of the new frame, addressing issues where occluded regions get stuck in the previous frame's SDF. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def neuus2trainstatic(images, hashtables, mlp, numlevels): # Initialize hash tables and MLP weights for level in range(numlevels): # Progressive learning: optimize coarse to fine for image in images: # Sample points along rays (standard volume rendering step) points = samplerays(image) # Hash encoding features = [queryhashtable(hashtables[l], points) for l in range(numlevels)] combinedfeatures = combinefeatures(features) # MLP forward pass sdf, color = mlp(combinedfeatures) # Volume rendering to get pixel colors renderedcolor = volumerender(points, sdf, color) # Compute loss against ground truth image loss = colorloss(renderedcolor, image) + sdfconstraint(sdf) # Compute gradients # Second-order derivative calculation uses lightweight formula for ReLU MLPs # Update hash table features and MLP weights optimizer.step(loss) def neuus2traindynamic(sequences, hashtables, mlp): # Train first frame neuus2trainstatic(sequences[0], hashtables, mlp) for i in range(1, len(sequences)): # Estimate rigid transformation to align current frame with previous frame # using standard point cloud registration (e.g., SVD on matched features) transformation = estimaterigidalignment(sequences[i-1], sequences[i]) # Apply transformation to camera poses or points alignedsequence = applyalignment(sequences[i], transformation) # Fine-tune representation for the new frame neuus2trainstatic(alignedsequence, hashtables, mlp) Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Large Movements in Dynamic Scenes: If the movement between consecutive frames is large, occluded regions may get stuck in the previous frame's SDF. The method addresses this by predicting a global transformation to align frames. Precision: The method aims to reduce memory footprint and computational cost, but specific precision details are not provided. Time Complexity: Two orders of magnitude faster than NeuS. Over 3x faster than Voxurf. 100x faster than Neuralangelo. Memory Complexity: Reduced memory footprint due to the lightweight calculation of second-order derivatives. Measured Performance: Static scenes reconstructed in minutes; dynamic scenes up to 20 seconds per frame. Strengths: Fast training, high-quality geometry, applicable to both static and dynamic scenes. Limitations: Not explicitly stated in the sources. When to Use: When fast training of neural implicit surfaces is required for multi-view reconstruction, especially for dynamic scenes. When Not to Use: When extremely dense geometry is required and training time is not a constraint (Neuralangelo might be better). NeuS2 was proposed as a fast neural surface reconstruction approach to address the long training time of NeuS, which takes an extremely long time (8 hours) and makes it almost impossible to apply to dynamic scenes with thousands of frames. It builds on the multi-resolution hash encodings introduced in Instant-NGP. The method was presented in the paper "NeuS2: Fast Learning of Neural Implicit Surfaces for Multi-view Reconstruction". name: HF-NeuS
head: High-Frequency NeuS
body: HF-NeuS is an improvement on NeuS that separates low-frequency details into a base SDF and high-frequency details into a displacement function to increase reconstruction quality. Inputs and Outputs: The method takes multi-view images as input and outputs a reconstructed 3D surface and appearance. Data Structures: Geometry is decoupled into a base SDF for low-frequency details and a displacement function for high-frequency details. The specific network architecture for the displacement function is not given in the sources. Numbered Steps: The optimization procedure follows the NeuS volume rendering framework. The specific steps for HF-NeuS are not detailed in the sources. Formulas: Not given in the sources. Parameters: Not given in the sources. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Not given in the sources. A framework that decouples geometry (SDF) and appearance (light field) from calibrated multi-view images, using volume rendering to generate images and minimizing the difference between rendered and input images. It utilizes the NeuS volume rendering framework to render 2D images based on the neural implicit SDF and light field. Steps: Define a ray r(s) = o + sv for s \ge 0, where o is the camera center and v is the unit direction vector. Uniformly sample 500 points per iteration in the bounding volume \Omega for the L{off} calculation. Formulas: T(t) = \exp\left(-\int{sn}^{t} \sigma(r(u)) du\right) where T(t) is the accumulated transmittance along the ray. L = L{color} + \alpha L{eikonal} + \beta L{mask} + \gamma L{off} where \alpha, \beta, and \gamma are weights. L{eikonal} = \frac{1}{\#X} \sum{p \in X} (\|\nablax \Phi(p)\|^2 - 1)^2 where X is the sample point set on rays. L{off} = \frac{1}{\#\Omega} \sum{x \in \Omega} \psi(\Phi(x), \beta0) where \Omega is the bounding volume and \beta0 is 100. Time and Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Measured Performance: HF-NeuS outperformed the baseline NeRF model and provided theoretical and experimental justifications for its SDF-based scene density implementation. It greatly increased reconstruction quality compared to standard NeuS. Strengths and Limitations: The primary strength is improved geometric reconstruction quality by separating low-frequency and high-frequency details. The specific computational overhead of the displacement function is not quantified in the sources. When to use it: Use when high-frequency geometric details are required and standard NeuS reconstruction quality is insufficient. HF-NeuS was introduced in June 2022. It is an improvement on NeuS. Concurrently, other methods like Geo-NeuS and SparseNeus were introduced to address multi-view constraints and sparse-view reconstruction, respectively. name: SparseNeus
head: SparseNeuS
body: SparseNeuS is a neural rendering-based method for surface reconstruction from multi-view images that generalizes to new scenes and works with sparse inputs (as few as 2 or 3 images). It improves upon NeuS by introducing a geometry encoding volume with learnable image features as a hybrid representation, allowing it to recover surfaces in a coarse-to-fine manner without requiring dense views or time-consuming per-scene optimization from scratch. Unlike NeuS, which suffers from distorted and incomplete geometry with only three images due to radiance ambiguity, SparseNeuS produces high-quality, complete meshes by leveraging generalizable priors learned from image features. The pipeline consists of three parts: Geometry reasoning, Appearance prediction, and Per-scene fine-tuning. Inputs: N input images \{Ii\}{i=0}^{N-1} (typically N=3). Camera parameters for each input image. A bounding box covering the region of interest, defined in the camera coordinate system of the centered input image and gridded into regular voxels. Outputs: A Signed Distance Function (SDF) field representing the surface geometry. Synthesized views of the scene. 1. Geometry Encoding Volume (M): A 3D sparse convolutional volume implemented with a U-Net-like architecture using torchsparse. Coarse Volume: Resolution 96 \times 96 \times 96. Fine Volume: Resolution 192 \times 192 \times 192. 2. Cost Volume (B): A 3D volume where each voxel v stores the variance of projected features. 3. Feature Maps (Fi): 2D feature maps extracted from input images Ii using a Feature Pyramid Network (FPN). 4. SDF Prediction Network (f\theta): An MLP that takes 3D coordinates and interpolated features from M as input to predict SDF values. This stage constructs cascaded geometry encoding volumes to recover surfaces in a coarse-to-fine manner. 1. Feature Extraction: Extract 2D feature maps \{Fi\}{i=0}^{N-1} from the input images \{Ii\}{i=0}^{N-1} using a 2D feature extraction network (FPN). 2. Projection: For each vertex v of the bounding box, project it to each feature map Fi using the camera parameters of image Ii. Let \pii(v) denote the projected pixel location. Obtain the features Fi(v) = Fi(\pii(v)) by interpolation. 3. Cost Volume Construction: Calculate the variance of all projected features for each vertex v to build the cost volume B: B(v) = \operatorname{Var}\left( \{Fi(v)\}{i=0}^{N-1} \right) where \operatorname{Var} computes the variance across the N feature vectors. 4. Geometry Encoding Volume Generation: Apply a sparse 3D CNN \Psi to the cost volume B to obtain the geometry encoding volume M: M = \Psi(B). 5. Surface Extraction (Coarse): For an arbitrary 3D location q, apply positional encoding \operatorname{PE} to its 3D coordinates. Interpolate the features from the coarse geometry encoding volume M{\text{coarse}}(q). Concatenate \operatorname{PE}(q) and M{\text{coarse}}(q) and pass them through the coarse SDF prediction network f{\theta, \text{coarse}} to predict the SDF s(q). 6. Surface Extraction (Fine): Use the coarse geometry to guide the fine level. Interpolate features from the fine geometry encoding volume M{\text{fine}}(q) (which is constructed similarly to M{\text{coarse}} but at higher resolution). Concatenate \operatorname{PE}(q) and M{\text{fine}}(q) and pass them through the fine SDF prediction network f{\theta, \text{fine}} to predict the refined SDF s(q). This stage predicts colors and renders synthesized views. 1. Color Blending: Use a multi-scale color blending module to predict colors by aggregating information from the input images. The module uses a patch-based blending strategy with a patch size of 5 \times 5. 2. Volume Rendering: Combine the estimated geometry (SDF) with the predicted colors to render synthesized views using volume rendering. The rendering loss is minimized between the rendered view and the ground truth view. This stage improves the obtained geometry with fine-grained details. 1. Consistency-Aware Loss: Introduce a consistency-aware fine-tuning scheme to control inconsistent regions caused by occlusion and noise. The loss function includes a rendering loss and a consistency term that encourages consistent SDF values for points behind visible surfaces. 2. Optimization: Optimize the model using the same N input images without adding new images. The optimization runs for 10k iterations. 3. SDF Rescaling: Use a hyperparameter \tau to rescale the SDF value of sampled points behind visible surfaces. This encourages SDF values to be far from 0, avoiding uncontrollable free surfaces when extracting the 0-level set. Unverified code. """ self.N = N self.coarseres = coarseres self.fineres = fineres self.patchsize = patchsize # Feature extraction network (FPN) self.featureextractor = FeaturePyramidNetwork() # Sparse 3D CNN for geometry encoding volume # Implemented with U-Net-like architecture using torchsparse self.sparsecnn = Sparse3DCNN() # SDF prediction networks self.sdfcoarse = SDFPredictionMLP() self.sdffine = SDFPredictionMLP() # Color blending module self.colorblender = MultiScaleColorBlending(patchsize) # Hyperparameter for SDF rescaling self.tau = 1.0 # Value not specified in sources, placeholder def extractfeatures(self, images): """ Extract 2D feature maps from input images.:param images: Tensor of shape (N, C, H, W):return: List of feature maps {Fi} """ return self.featureextractor(images) def projectfeatures(self, vertices, featuremaps, cameraparams): """ Project vertices to feature maps and interpolate features.:param vertices: Tensor of shape (V, 3) containing 3D coordinates of bounding box vertices.:param featuremaps: List of feature maps {Fi} of shape (N, C, H, W).:param cameraparams: Camera parameters for each image.:return: Tensor of shape (V, N, C) containing projected features Fi(v). Stage 2: Train fine level networks while keeping coarse fixed. """ # Extract features featuremaps = self.extractfeatures(images) # Define bounding box and vertices vertices = getboundingboxvertices(cameraparams[0], self.coarseres) # Project features projectedfeatures = self.projectfeatures(vertices, featuremaps, cameraparams) # Build cost volume costvolume = self.buildcostvolume(projectedfeatures) # Build coarse geometry encoding volume Mcoarse = self.buildgeometryencodingvolume(costvolume) # Train coarse SDF network for i in range(iterations): # Sample points points = samplepoints(vertices) # Predict SDF sdf = self.predictsdfcoarse(points, Mcoarse) # Compute loss (rendering loss) loss = computerenderingloss(sdf, images, cameraparams) loss.backward() self.sdfcoarse.step() # Build fine geometry encoding volume (guided by coarse) # Note: Sources say fine volume is constructed similarly, guided by coarse # Implementation detail: Re-project or refine vertices based on coarse SDF? # Sources say "coarse level to refine the geometry", implying the fine volume # is built on a refined bounding box or with higher resolution. verticesfine = getboundingboxvertices(cameraparams[0], self.fineres) projectedfeaturesfine = self.projectfeatures(verticesfine, featuremaps, cameraparams) costvolumefine = self.buildcostvolume(projectedfeaturesfine) Mfine = self.buildgeometryencodingvolume(costvolumefine) # Train fine SDF network for i in range(iterations): points = samplepoints(verticesfine) sdf = self.predictsdffine(points, Mfine) loss = computerenderingloss(sdf, images, cameraparams) loss.backward() self.sdffine.step() def finetune(self, images, cameraparams, iterations=10000): """ Per-scene fine-tuning. """ # Use the same three input images # Optimize model (likely just the SDF networks or specific parameters) for i in range(iterations): # Sample points points = samplepoints() # Predict SDF sdf = self.predictsdffine(points, Mfine) # Compute consistency-aware loss loss = computeconsistencyawareloss(sdf, images, cameraparams, self.tau) loss.backward() # Update parameters # Note: Sources say "Optimizes the model", implying some parameters are updated # It is not specified which parameters are frozen. # Assuming SDF networks are updated. self.sdffine.step() class FeaturePyramidNetwork(nn.Module): def init(self): super().init() # FPN implementation pass def forward(self, x): return self.featuremaps class Sparse3DCNN(nn.Module): def init(self): super().init() # U-Net-like architecture using torchsparse pass def forward(self, x): return self.output class SDFPredictionMLP(nn.Module): def init(self): super().init() # MLP layers pass def forward(self, x): return self.sdf def positionalencoding(x): # Standard positional encoding pass def interpolatefeatures(featuremap, pixellocs): # Bilinear interpolation pass def interpolatevolume(volume, points): # Trilinear interpolation pass def sdftoalpha(sdf): # Convert SDF to opacity pass def computeweights(alphas): # Compute ray marching weights pass def computerenderingloss(sdf, images, cameraparams): # Render and compare with ground truth pass def computeconsistencyawareloss(sdf, images, cameraparams, tau): # Rendering loss + consistency term # Consistency term encourages SDF values behind visible surfaces to be far from 0 # using tau to rescale pass N: Number of input images. Typically 2 or 3. \Psi: Sparse 3D CNN used to aggregate the cost volume. \tau: Hyperparameter to rescale the SDF value of sampled points behind visible surfaces. Value: Not specified in the sources. batchsize: Number of rays processed per training iteration. Value: 512. coarsevolumeresolution: 3D grid resolution for the coarse geometry encoding volume. Value: 96 \times 96 \times 96. finevolumeresolution: 3D grid resolution for the fine geometry encoding volume. Value: 192 \times 192 \times 192. patchsize: Spatial size of patches used in the patch-based blending strategy. Value: 5 \times 5. coarsetrainingiterations: Number of iterations for the first training stage. Value: 150k. finetrainingiterations: Number of iterations for the second training stage. Value: 150k. finetuningiterations: Number of iterations for per-scene fine-tuning. Value: 10k. finetuningtime: Approximate wall-clock time for 10k iteration fine-tuning. Value: 20 mins. Radiance Ambiguity: With sparse views (e.g., 3 images), radiance ambiguity can cause distorted and incomplete geometry in methods like NeuS and MVSNerf. SparseNeuS mitigates this through generalizable priors and consistency-aware fine-tuning. Weak Textures: Conventional MVS methods like COLMAP fail with weak textures. SparseNeuS produces more complete meshes for such objects. Background Noise: DTU dataset images contain large black backgrounds with considerable noise. SparseNeuS uses a simple threshold on zero RGB values as a prior to encourage empty geometry predictions in these regions. Per-Scene Optimization Requirements: Unlike IDR, SparseNeuS does not require extra object masks for per-scene optimization. Unlike MVSNerf, SparseNeuS successfully fine-tunes with only three input images, whereas MVSNerf fails under the same condition. A stage that further improves the obtained geometry with fine-grained details using a consistency-aware fine-tuning scheme. It optimizes the model using the same input images without adding new ones, running for 10k iterations. Time Complexity: The generic model training involves two stages of 150k iterations each. Per-scene fine-tuning takes 10k iterations, approximately 20 minutes. Memory Complexity: Uses sparse 3D CNNs with resolutions 96 \times 96 \times 96 and 192 \times 192 \times 192. Memory efficiency is improved by using center-cropped images (512 \times 640) for training and sparse convolutions. Performance: Outperforms state-of-the-art methods (PixelNeRF, IBRNet, MVSNerf, IDR, NeuS, VolSDF, UniSurf, COLMAP) on DTU and BlendedMVS datasets with 3 input images. Strengths: Generalizes to new scenes, works with sparse views (2-3 images), produces high-quality complete meshes, avoids radiance ambiguity issues of NeuS and MVSNerf, does not require object masks. Limitations: Requires known camera parameters. Performance depends on the quality of the 2D feature extraction network. When to Use: When only sparse multi-view images are available and generalization to new scenes is required. When Not to Use: When dense views are available and per-scene optimization is acceptable (e.g., NeuS might be simpler). When camera parameters are unknown. SparseNeuS was introduced by Xiaoxiao Long, Cheng Lin, Peng Wang, Taku Komura, and Wenping Wang from The University of Hong Kong, Tencent Games, and Texas A&M University. It was published on arXiv on 2 Aug 2022. The method was trained on 75 non-overlapping scenes from the DTU dataset and tested on 15 DTU scenes and 7 challenging scenes from the BlendedMVS dataset. It addresses the limitations of existing neural reconstruction approaches that heavily depend on dense views and require time-consuming per-scene optimization, lacking generalization. name: SparseNeuS Per-Scene Fine-Tuning
head: Fine-Tuning Networks, Per-Scene Optimization, SparseNeuS, SparseNeuS Network Architecture and Sampling
body: SparseNeuS Per-Scene Fine-Tuning is a method for refining a neural surface reconstruction from sparse input views by optimizing the geometry encoding volume and SDF network directly for a specific scene. It differs from the generic SparseNeuS inference by discarding the 2D feature extraction and 3D sparse CNN networks, replacing the CNN-based blending network with a lightweight MLP, and employing a consistency-aware color loss to handle occlusions and noise. This approach leverages the initialization from the generic network inference to fast converge to a high-quality surface. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: A set of N input images, camera poses, and the pre-trained generic SparseNeuS model parameters (specifically the fine-level geometry encoding volume and the SDF network f\theta). Outputs: Optimized fine-level geometry encoding volume, optimized SDF network f\theta, and the reconstructed 3D surface. Data Structures: Geometry Encoding Volume: A 3D grid storing latent features for spatial locations. SDF Network (f\theta): An MLP with 4 hidden layers and hidden size 256. Blending Network (fc'): A tiny MLP with 3 hidden layers and hidden size 256. Positional Encoding: Applied to 3D locations (6 frequencies) and view directions (4 frequencies). Numbered Steps: 1. Initialization: Load the pre-trained generic SparseNeuS model. Discard the 2D feature extraction network and the 3D sparse CNN networks. Keep the fine-level geometry encoding volume and the SDF network f\theta. 2. Network Replacement: Replace the CNN-based blending network used in the generic setting with a tiny MLP network fc'. This MLP outputs blending weights for a query 3D position q. 3. Sampling: Adopt a hierarchical sampling strategy similar to NeuS. Sample 64 coarse points and 64 fine points along each query ray. 4. Blending Weight Calculation: For each query 3D position q, compute the blending weights \{wi^q\}{i=0}^{N-1} using the tiny MLP fc'. The inputs to fc' are: PE(q): Positional encoding of the 3D position q. PE(d): Positional encoding of the ray direction d. nq: Surface normal at q. s(q): Predicted SDF value at q. M(q): Interpolated geometry encoding feature at q from the fine-level volume. The formula is: \{wi^q\}{i=0}^{N-1} = fc'(PE(q), PE(d), nq, s(q), M(q)) where N is the number of input images. 5. Loss Computation: Compute the total loss, which includes the consistency-aware color loss and other terms (e.g., sparseness loss). Consistency-Aware Color Loss: This loss automatically detects regions lacking consistent projections across views (due to occlusion or noise) and excludes them from optimization. The loss is defined as: \mathcal{L}{color} = \sum{r \in \mathbb{R}} O(r) \cdot \mathcal{D}{pix}(C(r), \tilde{C}(r)) + \sum{r \in \mathbb{R}} O(r) \cdot \mathcal{D}{pix}(C(r), \tilde{C}(r)) (Note: The source text for the full formula is truncated, but it involves an observation mask O(r), rendered color C(r), and target color \tilde{C}(r).) Sparseness Loss: Includes a scaling parameter \tau. 6. Optimization: Directly optimize the fine-level geometry encoding volume and the SDF network f\theta using the computed losses. Parameters: SDF Network: 4 hidden layers, hidden size 256. Blending Network (fc'): 3 hidden layers, hidden size 256. Positional Encoding: 6 frequencies for 3D locations, 4 frequencies for view directions. Sampling: 64 coarse samples, 64 fine samples. Loss Weights: \alpha = 0.1, \beta = 0.02 for total loss. SDF Scaling (\tau): 100 for sparseness loss. Consistency-Aware Color Loss: \lambda0 = 0.01, \lambda1 = 0.015 by default. Data Preparation: Threshold \tau = 10 for detecting invalid black regions in images, followed by dilation and erosion. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Ratio Tuning: The ratio \lambda0 / \lambda1 in the consistency-aware color loss affects surface completeness vs. cleanliness. Decreasing the ratio keeps more regions, while increasing it excludes more regions for cleaner surfaces. Noise and Occlusion: Regions with inconsistent projections across views (due to occlusion or image noise) can lead to inaccurate and distorted surfaces if not handled by the consistency-aware loss. Background: Images may contain large black backgrounds and considerable noise, requiring threshold-based denoising and mask processing. Time Complexity: Faster than generic SparseNeuS inference due to the replacement of the CNN-based blending network with a smaller MLP. Memory Complexity: Reduced memory footprint compared to generic SparseNeuS as the 2D feature extraction and 3D sparse CNN networks are discarded during fine-tuning. Performance: Fast convergence to high-quality surfaces due to initialization from the generic network inference. Strengths: Handles sparse views effectively; consistency-aware loss improves robustness to noise and occlusion; lightweight blending network speeds up optimization. Limitations: Requires per-scene optimization, which may be slower than single-shot inference methods; performance depends on the quality of the generic initialization. When to Use: When high-quality surface reconstruction is needed from sparse views and per-scene optimization is feasible. When Not to Use: When real-time inference is required or when input views are dense (other methods may be more efficient). SparseNeuS was introduced to address the challenge of neural surface reconstruction from sparse views. The per-scene fine-tuning method builds upon the generic SparseNeuS framework, which uses a hybrid representation of geometry encoding volume and learnable image features. The method was developed to improve the quality and speed of surface reconstruction by leveraging the initialization from the generic model and optimizing it for specific scenes. It is used in applications requiring high-fidelity 3D reconstruction from limited camera views, such as in the DTU dataset evaluations. SparseNeuS: Fast Generalizable Neural Surface Reconstruction from Sparse Views, https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-031-19824-313, fetched 2026-10-26

name: NeuDA
head: NeuDA (Neural Deformable Anchor), Neural Deformable Anchor
body: NeuDA is a neural implicit surface reconstruction method that utilizes hierarchical deformable anchors to encode local geometry, building on the NeuS [6060-neus.md] framework. It distinguishes itself by replacing standard positional encoding with Hierarchical Positional Encoding (HPE) and employing a shallower SDF network (4 layers vs. 8 for NeuS). This design achieves high-fidelity surface reconstruction with lower computational cost and sharper surfaces compared to siblings like HAME-NeRF, D-NeuS, NeuS2, and HF-NeuS. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: A set of training images with known camera poses, optional foreground masks, and a 3D bounding box defining the scene volume. Outputs: A signed distance function (SDF) f(x), a predicted normal vector \hat{n}(x), a geometric feature z(x), and a color C(r) for any ray r. Data Structures: 1. Hierarchical Deformable Anchors \psi(G): Arranged into L levels (default L=8). Each level l contains Tl coordinate vectors (anchors) \mathbf{p}n \in \mathbb{R}^3. At the coarsest level (l=0), T0 = 16. For finer levels, T{l} = T{l-1} \times 1.38. Initialized uniformly at the vertices of a voxel grid G covering the scene. These anchors are learnable parameters optimized during training. 2. SDF Network \mathcal{F}: A 4-layer Multi-Layer Perceptron (MLP). Hidden layer size: 256. Input: Hierarchical Positional Encoding \mathcal{H}(p). Output: Tuple (f(x;\theta), \hat{n}(x;\theta), z(x;\theta)). 3. Color Network: Follows the NeuS architecture. 4-layer MLP with hidden layer size 256. Inputs: Geometric feature z(x;\theta), view direction, and potentially other features. Algorithm Steps: 1. Anchor Initialization: Initialize the set of deformable anchors \psi(G) uniformly distributed at the vertices of a voxel grid G. 2. Hierarchical Positional Encoding (HPE): For a target point p, retrieve the L levels of anchors. For each level l \in \{0, \dots, L-1\}: Let \mathbf{p}l be the set of anchor points at level l. Apply frequency encoding to each coordinate of each anchor point \mathbf{p}n individually. The frequency encoding function for level l is: \gamma(\mathbf{p}{n,l}) = (\sin(2^l \pi \mathbf{p}{n,l}), \cos(2^l \pi \mathbf{p}{n,l})) This returns a 6-dimensional embedding for each anchor. Interpolate these embeddings based on the spatial proximity of the target point p to the anchors \mathbf{p}{n,l} to obtain a local embedding vector \phi(\hat{\mathbf{p}}l) for level l. Concatenate the multi-level embedding vectors to form the hierarchical positional encoding: \mathcal{H}(p) = (\phi(\hat{\mathbf{p}}0), \phi(\hat{\mathbf{p}}1), \dots, \phi(\hat{\mathbf{p}}{L-1})). 3. SDF and Feature Prediction: Feed the encoded hierarchical feature \mathcal{H}(p) into the SDF network \mathcal{F}: \mathcal{F}(x; \theta) = \mathcal{F}(\mathcal{H}(p); \theta) = (f(x;\theta), \hat{n}(x;\theta), z(x;\theta)) where f is the signed distance, \hat{n} is the predicted normal, and z is the geometric feature. 4. Volume Rendering: Sample points along rays. Compute transmittance T{r,i} and alpha \alpha{r,i} using the SDF values f(x{r,i}) and a density function (typically derived from f via a sigmoid or similar function as in NeuS, though the specific density function formula is not explicitly detailed in the provided notes, it is implied by the rendering pipeline). Render the color C(r) using the color network. 5. Loss Computation: Compute the total loss \mathcal{L} as a weighted sum of four terms: Color Loss (\mathcal{L}c): Mean absolute error between rendered color C(r) and ground truth \hat{C}(r): \mathcal{L}c = \frac{1}{|\mathcal{R}|} \sum{r \in \mathcal{R}} \| C(r) - \hat{C}(r) \|. Eikonal Regularization (\mathcal{L}{reg}): Ensures the gradient of the SDF has unit magnitude: \mathcal{L}{reg} = \frac{1}{|\mathcal{R}|N} \sum{r,i} (\|\nabla f(\mathcal{H}(p{r,i}))\|2 - 1)^2 where N is the number of sample points per ray. Normal Regularization (\mathcal{L}{norm}): Ties the SDF gradient to the predicted normal \hat{n}{r,i}: \mathcal{L}{norm} = \sum{r,i} T{r,i} \alpha{r,i} \| \nabla f(\mathcal{H}(p{r,i})) - \hat{n}{r,i} \|. Mask Loss (\mathcal{L}{mask}): Binary Cross Entropy (BCE) between the mask label mr and accumulated alpha: \mathcal{L}{mask} = \text{BCE}(mr, \sumi^n T{r,i} \alpha{r,i}). Total Loss: \mathcal{L} = \mathcal{L}c + \lambda{eik}\mathcal{L}{reg} + \lambda{norm}\mathcal{L}{norm} + \lambda{mask}\mathcal{L}{mask}. 6. Optimization: Use the Adam optimizer. Train for 300,000 iterations. Decay learning rate from 5 \times 10^{-4} to 2.5 \times 10^{-5} using a cosine decay scheduler. Parameters: L: Total number of anchor grid levels. Default: 8. \lambda{eik}: Eikonal loss weight. Value: 0.1. \lambda{norm}: Normal regularization loss weight. Value: 3 \times 10^{-5}. \lambda{mask}: Mask loss weight. Value: 0.1. Positional encoding frequencies: 8 frequencies for deformable anchors, 4 frequencies for view directions. Pitfalls and Edge Cases: Anchor Levels: Using too many hierarchical levels (e.g., L=10) can introduce redundant information that harms SDF approximation, leading to slightly lower performance (higher Chamfer Distance) than L=8. Standard Deviation Interpretation: Standard deviation curves of the SDF gradient may not directly reflect global reconstruction quality. For instance, Instant-NeuS yields a slightly better mean Chamfer Distance than NeuS despite having a higher standard deviation. Time and Memory Complexity: NeuDA uses a shallower SDF network (4 layers) compared to NeuS (8 layers), reducing computational cost. The HPE produces a low-dimensional embedding compared to standard Multi-Level Positional Encoding (ML-PE), which reduces memory overhead for feature storage. Measured Performance: On the DTU dataset (w/o mask setting), NeuDA achieves a mean Chamfer Distance (CD) of 0.67, outperforming Instant-NeuS (0.80) and NeuS (0.76). With mask, it achieves 0.65, outperforming Instant-NeuS (0.79). Surface Sharpness: NeuDA achieves the lowest standard deviation value compared to NeuS and Instant-NeuS, indicating sharper surfaces with less time cost. Strengths: High-fidelity reconstruction, sharper surfaces, lower computational cost due to shallower network and efficient encoding. Limitations: The method relies on empirical validation without strict mathematical proof for the deformable anchor mechanism. NeuDA was introduced in the paper "NeuDA: Neural Deformable Anchor for High-Fidelity Implicit Surface Reconstruction". It builds upon the NeuS [6060-neus.md] framework, which was designed to improve geometric reconstruction quality in volume rendering. NeuDA specifically addresses the limitations of standard positional encoding and deep networks by introducing deformable anchors and hierarchical encoding. NeuDA: Neural Deformable Anchor for High-Fidelity Implicit Surface Reconstruction, https://doi.org/10.1109/cvpr52729.2023.00819, fetched 2026-10-26

name: Surface NeRF
head: NeRF surf, Surface rendering via NeRF
body: Surface NeRF (SNeRF) converts a pre-trained Neural Radiance Field (NeRF) into a 3D mesh and a surface light field, reducing per-pixel rendering cost by evaluating the NeRF only at the surface isosurface rather than via volumetric raycasting. It differs from its siblings NeuS, VolSDF, and Instant-NSR by starting from an existing volume-rendered NeRF and extracting a mesh via isosurface extraction, whereas the siblings learn the SDF and radiance jointly from scratch using differentiable volume rendering. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A pre-trained NeRF network \mathcal{N} mapping 3D position \mathbf{x} and view direction \mathbf{v} to color \mathbf{c} and density \sigma, and a set of posed input images. Output: A refined 3D mesh (isosurface) and a surface light field representation enabling fast rendering. Data Structures: Density Grid: A regular 3D grid storing density values \sigma, initialized by evaluating the pre-trained NeRF at grid vertices. NeRF Network: The original MLP parameters, finetuned during the optimization process. Parameters: Isosurface Threshold: 50, as suggested by the original NeRF paper. Optimization Iterations: 5000. Samples per Pixel: 1, compared to 128 in baseline volume rendering. Steps: 1. Initialization: Evaluate the pre-trained NeRF on a regular 3D grid to construct the input density field. 2. Mesh Extraction: Extract an isosurface from the density field at the fixed threshold (50) to serve as the initial geometry. This surface is an accurate but noisy model of the subject shape. 3. Finetuning Setup: Since the NeRF was trained under the assumption of volume rendering, it must be finetuned to produce good results when evaluated only at the surface. 4. Optimization Loop: Perform 5000 iterations of alternating optimization: a. NeRF Step: Take one gradient step on the NeRF network while holding the density grid fixed. The optimizer is Adam. The loss is the original NeRF L2 loss between rendered colors and input images. b. Grid Step: Take one gradient step on the density grid while holding the NeRF network fixed. The optimizer is standard gradient descent. 5. Rendering: Render the isosurface using Rasterize-then-Splat (RtS). The NeRF network produces shaded colors \mathbf{C}k for the surface points, effectively acting as a surface light field. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def surfacenerfoptimization(pretrainednerf, inputimages, gridresolution, threshold=50, iterations=5000, rays=None): # Step 1: Initialize density grid by evaluating NeRF at grid vertices densitygrid = evaluatenerfongrid(pretrainednerf, gridresolution) # Step 2: Extract initial isosurface at threshold mesh = extractisosurface(densitygrid, threshold) # Initialize optimizers nerfoptimizer = Adam(pretrainednerf.parameters()) gridoptimizer = SGD(densitygrid.parameters()) for i in range(iterations): # Step 4a: Optimize NeRF (hold grid fixed) nerfoptimizer.zerograd() renderedcolors = rendersurfacelightfield(pretrainednerf, mesh, rays) loss = computel2loss(renderedcolors, inputimages) loss.backward() nerfoptimizer.step() # Step 4b: Optimize Density Grid (hold NeRF fixed) gridoptimizer.zerograd() # The source does not specify the exact gradient computation for the grid; # it states to optimize the density grid directly via gradients from rendering. loss.backward() gridoptimizer.step() return mesh, pretrainednerf def evaluatenerfongrid(nerf, resolution): grid = np.zeros((resolution, resolution, resolution)) for x in range(resolution): for y in range(resolution): for z in range(resolution): pos = gridtoworld(x, y, z, resolution) grid[x, y, z] = nerf(pos, None).density return grid def extractisosurface(grid, threshold): # Standard Marching Cubes algorithm extracts vertices and faces from a scalar field at the threshold return marchingcubes(grid, threshold) def rendersurfacelightfield(nerf, mesh, rays): colors = [] for ray in rays: point, normal = raymeshintersect(ray, mesh) if point is not None: viewdir = ray.direction color = nerf(point, viewdir).color colors.append(color) else: colors.append(np.zeros(3)) return np.array(colors) def raymeshintersect(ray, mesh): # Standard ray-triangle intersection returns closest hit or (None, None) closestt = np.inf closestpoint = None closestnormal = None for triangle in mesh.faces: t, hitpoint = intersectraytriangle(ray.origin, ray.direction, triangle) if 0 < t < closestt: closestt = t closestpoint = hitpoint closestnormal = triangle.normal return closestpoint, closestnormal def computel2loss(rendered, target): return np.mean((rendered - target) 2) def gridtoworld(x, y, z, resolution): # Maps integer grid coordinates to normalized 3D space [-1, 1]^3 return np.array([x / (resolution - 1) 2 - 1, y / (resolution - 1) 2 - 1, z / (resolution - 1) 2 - 1]) def intersectraytriangle(origin, direction, triangle): # Möller–Trumbore algorithm v1, v2, v3 = triangle.vertices edge1 = v2 - v1 edge2 = v3 - v1 h = np.cross(direction, edge2) a = np.dot(edge1, h) if -0.00001 < a < 0.00001: return np.inf, None f = 1.0 / a s = origin - v1 u = f np.dot(s, h) if u < 0.0 or u > 1.0: return np.inf, None q = np.cross(s, edge1) v = f np.dot(direction, q) if v < 0.0 or u + v > 1.0: return np.inf, None t = f np.dot(edge2, q) if t > 0.00001: return t, origin + t direction return np.inf, None Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Optimizer Instability: Adam is unstable for optimizing the density grid because the isosurface does not constrain all grid values at each iteration. Standard gradient descent is used for the grid instead. Complex Geometry: On complex scenes like Fern, the extremely complex isosurface limits quality improvement over the fixed surface baseline. The method loses 0.9 PSNR compared to full volume rendering on such scenes. Closed-Form Requirement: The method requires a closed-form evaluation function for the surface, which may not be available for all surface representations (e.g., some subdivision schemes). Occlusion Handling: The splatting step currently assumes a single surface at each pixel, which may cause artifacts in highly occluded regions. Computational Cost: Reduces per-pixel computational cost from 226 MFLOPS (volume rendering) to 1.7 MFLOPS (SNeRF). This achieves a runtime cost reduction of more than 100× compared to baseline NeRF rendering. Quality: On the Lego dataset, SNeRF achieves a PSNR of 29.61, which is within 0.3 of the baseline NeRF PSNR of 29.91. It improves 2.2 PSNR over the baseline without surface optimization (SNeRF fixed, PSNR 27.44). On the Fern dataset, SNeRF achieves a PSNR of 23.52, losing 0.9 PSNR to full volume rendering (24.38). It improves only 0.1 PSNR over the fixed surface baseline (23.41). Strengths: Significant reduction in rendering time; works with any surface that can be expressed as a non-differentiable sampling and a differentiable evaluation function. Limitations: Quality degradation on scenes with extremely complex isosurfaces; requires a closed-form evaluation function; assumes a single surface at each pixel during splatting. Surface NeRF was introduced in the paper "Differentiable Surface Rendering via Non-Differentiable Sampling". It builds on the original NeRF work and aims to address the long rendering times associated with volumetric raycasting by converting the volume representation into a surface representation. The method leverages the Rasterize-then-Splat (RtS) technique for differentiable surface rendering.
