name: VolSDF
head: Neural Scene Representation with SDF and Volumetric Rendering, SDF-based Neural Volume Rendering
body: VolSDF is a neural inverse rendering method that decouples geometric representation from appearance by modeling scene geometry via a learnable Signed Distance Function (SDF) and deriving volume density from it. It solves the problem of noisy, low-fidelity geometry reconstruction inherent in previous methods that modeled geometry as an arbitrary level set of a generic density function. Unlike density-based NeRF or mesh-based surface rendering, VolSDF provides a theoretical upper bound on opacity error and facilitates stable convergence by using the Cumulative Distribution Function (CDF) of a Laplace distribution to convert SDF values into density. Inputs and Outputs Inputs: A set of multi-view images with known camera poses. Outputs: A rendered image for a novel view, a reconstructed 3D mesh (extracted from the SDF zero-level set), and material parameters (in extended variants like SupeRVol). Data Structures The method uses two Multi-Layer Perceptrons (MLPs): 1. Geometry MLP (f{\Thetag}): Input: 3D coordinate \mathbf{x} \in \mathbb{R}^3. Output: A tuple (s, \mathbf{f}{geo}) where: s \in \mathbb{R} is the signed distance value S(\mathbf{x}). \mathbf{f}{geo} \in \mathbb{R}^{256} is a learned local geometric feature descriptor. 2. Appearance MLP (f{\Thetac}): Input: 3D coordinate \mathbf{x}, surface normal \mathbf{n}, view direction \mathbf{v}, and potentially geometric features \mathbf{f}{geo}. Output: Radiance color \mathbf{c} \in \mathbb{R}^3 (or BRDF parameters in extended versions). Numbered Steps 1. Ray Definition: For a pixel, define a ray \mathbf{r}(t) = \mathbf{o} + t\mathbf{d}, where \mathbf{o} is the camera origin and \mathbf{d} is the view direction. 2. Sampling: Sample N discrete points t1, t2, \dots, tN along the ray within the bounding volume. VolSDF employs an iterative sampling algorithm based on opacity error bounds to concentrate samples near the surface. 3. SDF Evaluation: For each sample point \mathbf{x}i = \mathbf{r}(ti), query the geometry MLP to obtain the signed distance S(\mathbf{x}i) and geometric features \mathbf{f}{geo}(\mathbf{x}i). 4. Density Conversion: Convert the SDF value S(\mathbf{x}i) to volume density \sigma(\mathbf{x}i) using the Laplace CDF transformation: \sigma(\mathbf{x}) = \frac{1}{2} - \frac{1}{2} \text{erf}\left( \frac{S(\mathbf{x}) - \mu}{\sqrt{2} \lambda} \right) where \mu = 0 is the mean and \lambda is the learnable scale parameter of the Laplace distribution. 5. Normal Computation: Compute the surface normal \mathbf{n} at \mathbf{x}i by numerically differentiating the SDF: \mathbf{n} = \frac{\nabla S(\mathbf{x}i)}{\|\nabla S(\mathbf{x}i)\|}. 6. Radiance Estimation: Query the appearance MLP with \mathbf{x}i, \mathbf{n}, view direction \mathbf{v}, and \mathbf{f}{geo}(\mathbf{x}i) to obtain the color \mathbf{c}i. 7. Volume Rendering Integration: Compute the accumulated transmittance Tj and the final pixel color C(\mathbf{o}, \mathbf{d}) using discrete quadrature: Tj = \exp\left( -\sum{q=1}^{j-1} \sigmaq \deltaq \right) C(\mathbf{o}, \mathbf{d}) = \sum{j=1}^{N} Tj (1 - \exp(-\sigmaj \deltaj)) \mathbf{c}j where \deltaj = t{j+1} - tj is the distance between samples. Alternatively, a trapezoidal rule approximation may be used: Lp \approx \sum{i=1}^{m-1} \frac{(t{i+1} - ti)}{2} w(ti) L(\mathbf{x}(ti), \mathbf{n}(ti), \mathbf{v}). Parameters N: Number of discrete points used to approximate the ray integral. \lambda: Scale parameter of the Laplace distribution, learned during optimization. \mu: Mean of the Laplace distribution, fixed at zero. Edge Cases and Pitfalls Reflectance Limitations: Standard VolSDF bakes material and lighting into the radiance network, meaning it cannot recover reflectance properties or handle dynamic lighting; self-shadows are absent in colocated camera-light setups. Geometry Fidelity: Previous methods using arbitrary level sets of generic density functions resulted in noisy, low-fidelity geometry; VolSDF addresses this but requires accurate sampling near the zero-level set. Precision: The opacity error bound relies on accurate SDF gradients; numerical instability in gradient computation can affect normal accuracy. Time Complexity: Dependent on the number of samples N per ray and the depth of the MLPs. The iterative sampling algorithm adds overhead but reduces the required N for high fidelity compared to uniform sampling. Memory Complexity: Requires storing two MLPs (geometry and appearance) and their gradients. The geometry MLP outputs a 256-dimensional feature vector, increasing memory usage compared to scalar-only density networks. Performance: VolSDF outperforms baselines like NeRF and NeRF++ on challenging multi-view datasets (DTU, BlendedMVS) in terms of geometry reconstruction quality. Strengths: Decouples geometry and appearance; provides theoretical bounds on opacity error; yields high-quality, clean meshes from the SDF zero-level set. Limitations: Cannot inherently model complex lighting or material variations without extensions (e.g., SupeRVol); sensitive to sampling density near the surface. VolSDF was introduced by L. Yariv et al. as a novel parameterization for density in neural volume rendering. It was developed to address the limitations of NeRF, which models geometry as a function of volume density, leading to noisy reconstructions. VolSDF inverts this relationship, modeling density as a function of geometry (SDF). The method leverages the Laplace CDF to provide an inductive bias for geometry and allows for efficient unsupervised disentanglement of shape and appearance. It has been extended in subsequent work, such as SupeRVol, to include super-resolution shape and reflectance estimation. SupeRVol: Super-Resolution Shape and Reflectance Estimation in Inverse Volume Rendering, https://arxiv.org/abs/2212.04968v2, fetched 2026-10-26 PIR: Photometric Inverse Rendering with Shading Cues Modeling and Surface Reflectance Regularization, https://doi.org/10.1109/3dv66043.2025.00055, fetched 2026-10-26 Volume Rendering of Neural Implicit Surfaces, https://lioryariv.github.io/volsdf/, fetched 2026-10-29 (unofficial)

name: Instant-NSR
head: Neural Surface Reconstruction with Hash
body: Instant-NSR is a neural surface reconstruction method that accelerates training using Hash encoding while improving geometry quality by incorporating a Signed Distance Function (SDF) representation during optimization. It builds on Radiance-field optimization and Surface-SDF Representation by adapting the NeRF architecture to predict SDF values instead of density, and employs a Truncated SDF (TSDF) formulation to ensure numerical stability when combined with hash grids. Unlike NeuS, which uses multi-resolution hash grids but may suffer from convergence issues with large temperature parameters, Instant-NSR explicitly truncates the SDF range to prevent gradient explosion. Inputs: A set of calibrated images with known camera poses. Outputs: A neural network representing the scene geometry (SDF) and appearance, capable of rendering novel views and extracting a 3D mesh. Data Structures: 1. Hash Grid: A multi-resolution hash table mapping spatial coordinates to feature vectors, identical to the structure in Instant-NGP. It provides the front-end feature encoding for input points. 2. Neural Network: A small MLP that takes the hashed features as input and outputs the SDF value f(\mathbf{x}) and color \mathbf{c}. The architecture follows the SDF-based design of NeuS rather than the density-based design of Instant-NGP. Algorithm Steps: 1. Sampling: For each pixel in a training image, cast a ray and sample N points \mathbf{x}i along the ray segment within the camera frustum. 2. Hash Encoding: Encode each point \mathbf{x}i using the multi-resolution hash grid to obtain feature vectors. 3. SDF Prediction: Pass the hashed features through the MLP to predict the raw SDF value f(\mathbf{x}i) and color \mathbf{c}i. 4. TSDF Truncation: Apply a sigmoid function \pi(\cdot) to the raw SDF output to truncate it to the range [-1, 1]. This prevents numerical overflow when the temperature parameter b is large. The transformation is defined as: \pi(f(\mathbf{x})) = \frac{1 - e^{-bf(\mathbf{x})}}{1 + e^{-bf(\mathbf{x})}} where b is a temperature parameter. Note: The source text presents this specific formula for \pi(f(x)) which maps the real line to (-1, 1), effectively acting as a scaled tanh or a specific sigmoid variant for truncation. 5. Probability Distribution: Compute the cumulative density distribution \phib using the truncated SDF value \pi(f(\mathbf{x})). This replaces the standard NeRF/NeuS formulation to ensure stability: \phib(f(\mathbf{x})) = \frac{b e^{-b\pi(f(\mathbf{x}))}}{(1 + e^{-b\pi(f(\mathbf{x}))})^2} This \phib is used to compute the weight w(t) for volume rendering. 6. Rendering: Render the image using the standard volume rendering equation with the computed weights and colors. 7. Loss Computation: Calculate the total loss as a weighted sum of rendering loss and eikonal loss. 8. Optimization: Update the network parameters (hash grid and MLP weights) using gradient descent. Formulas: TSDF Mapping: \pi(f(\mathbf{x})) = \frac{1 - e^{-bf(\mathbf{x})}}{1 + e^{-bf(\mathbf{x})}} \quad \text{} Weight Distribution: \phib(f(\mathbf{x})) = \frac{b e^{-b\pi(f(\mathbf{x}))}}{(1 + e^{-b\pi(f(\mathbf{x}))})^2} \quad \text{} Eikonal Loss: Enforces that the gradient magnitude of the SDF is 1 everywhere: L{eik} = \frac{1}{M} \sum{j=1}^{M} (\|\nabla f(\mathbf{x}j)\|2^2 - 1)^2 where M is the number of sampled points and \nabla f(\mathbf{x}j) is the gradient of the SDF at point \mathbf{x}j. Total Loss: L{total} = \alpha L{render} + \beta L{eik} where L{render} is the rendering loss (e.g., L1 or L2 between rendered and ground truth images) and \alpha, \beta are hyperparameters. Parameters: b: Temperature parameter for the TSDF truncation and distribution. Not given in the sources. \alpha: Weighting factor for rendering loss. Chosen via cross-validation. \beta: Weighting factor for eikonal loss. Chosen via cross-validation. TSDF Range: Values are effectively constrained between -1 and 1 by the sigmoid function \pi(\cdot). Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Numerical Instability: In standard SDF-based methods, increasing b causes -bf(\mathbf{x}) to become a large positive number, making e^{-bf(\mathbf{x})} approach infinity, leading to network divergence. Instant-NSR solves this by using the TSDF truncation \pi(f(\mathbf{x})), which bounds the exponent. Convergence: Applying raw SDF representations to hash coding frameworks can cause convergence problems. The TSDF formulation is critical for stable training in this context. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def instantnsrforward(rayorigins, raydirections, hashgrid, mlp, b): """ Forward pass for Instant-NSR. Args: rayorigins: Tensor of shape (H, W, 3), camera origins. raydirections: Tensor of shape (H, W, 3), normalized ray directions. hashgrid: Multi-resolution hash grid structure. mlp: Neural network predicting SDF and color from hashed features. b: Temperature parameter for TSDF truncation. Returns: renderedimage: Tensor of shape (H, W, 3). sdfvalues: Tensor of sampled SDF values. """ # 1. Sample points along rays (standard volume rendering sampling) # Assume samplepoints returns points p of shape (N, 3) and depths t of shape (N,) points, depths = samplepointsalongrays(rayorigins, raydirections) # 2. Hash Encode points # hashencode returns feature vectors for all points features = hashencode(points, hashgrid) # 3. Predict SDF and Color # mlp takes features and returns (sdf, color) # sdfraw shape: (N,), color shape: (N, 3) sdfraw, color = mlp(features) # 4. TSDF Truncation # Apply sigmoid-like truncation to bound SDF to (-1, 1) # pi(f) = (1 - exp(-bf)) / (1 + exp(-bf)) expterm = torch.exp(-b sdfraw) sdftruncated = (1 - expterm) / (1 + expterm) # 5. Compute Weight Distribution phib # phib = b exp(-b pi(f)) / (1 + exp(-b pi(f)))^2 expphi = torch.exp(-b sdftruncated) denominator = (1 + expphi) 2 phib = (b expphi) / denominator # 6. Volume Rendering # Compute weights w(t) using phib and depth intervals # This follows the standard NeRF/NeuS volume rendering integration # wi = phib(f(xi)) exp(-sum(phib(f(xj)) deltaj)) # Rendered color = sum(wi colori) renderedimage = volumerender(phib, depths, color) return renderedimage, sdfraw def computeloss(renderedimage, gtimage, sdfraw, points): """ Compute total loss for Instant-NSR. Args: renderedimage: Rendered image tensor. gtimage: Ground truth image tensor. sdfraw: Raw SDF values from network. points: Sampled 3D points. Returns: totalloss: Scalar loss value. """ # Rendering Loss lrender = torch.mean((renderedimage - gtimage) 2) # Eikonal Loss # Compute gradient of SDF w.r.t. spatial coordinates # gradsdf shape: (N, 3) gradsdf = computegradient(sdfraw, points) # Leik = mean((||gradsdf||^2 - 1)^2) gradnormsq = torch.sum(gradsdf 2, dim=1) leik = torch.mean((gradnormsq - 1) 2) # Total Loss # alpha and beta are hyperparameters chosen via cross-validation alpha = 1.0 # Placeholder, should be tuned beta = 1.0 # Placeholder, should be tuned totalloss = alpha lrender + beta leik return totalloss Uses SDF and volume rendering but may lack the specific TSDF truncation mechanism for hash grids found in Instant-NSR. Choose when simpler SDF integration is sufficient. Link Another SDF-based method. Compare based on specific loss formulations and encoding strategies. Link One of the earlier methods to introduce SDF into NeRF. Instant-NSR improves upon this by using hash encoding for speed and TSDF for stability. Link Time Complexity: Accelerated training compared to standard NeRF due to Hash encoding (similar to Instant-NGP). Memory Complexity: Depends on the size of the hash grid and MLP, similar to Instant-NGP. Performance: Demonstrates commendable performance in novel-view synthesis and competitive 3D reconstruction results compared to commercial MVS software like Reality Capture in agricultural contexts. Strengths: Fast training due to hash encoding; improved geometry quality via SDF; numerical stability via TSDF. Limitations: Requires careful tuning of hyperparameters \alpha and \beta via cross-validation. When to use: When fast training and high-quality geometry reconstruction are required, particularly in scenarios where standard SDF-NeRF methods suffer from numerical instability. Instant-NSR was explored in the context of high-fidelity 3D reconstruction of plants using Neural Radiance Fields. It builds upon the principles of Instant-NGP for speed and NeuS for SDF-based rendering, introducing Truncated SDF (TSDF) to resolve convergence issues inherent in applying SDF representations to hash coding frameworks. The method was tested on datasets of indoor and outdoor orchards (pitahaya, grape, orange, fig). High-fidelity 3D Reconstruction of Plants using Neural Radiance Field, https://arxiv.org/abs/2311.04154v1, fetched 2026-10-27

name: Physical and Material Priors
body: Physical and Material Priors methods incorporate physical laws (such as ray refraction) or material properties into the differentiable rendering pipeline to recover underlying scene properties like geometry, lighting, and optical constants. They are distinguished from siblings by their focus on recovering physical optical properties rather than just appearance, building on Radiance-field optimization. Recovers a 3D refractive index field and luminance from single-view refracted images by optimizing neural fields. It differs from standard methods by modeling light propagation through varying refractive indices using ODEs instead of fixed-step volumetric integration. Chosen when recovering optical constants from refracted measurements is required. Reconstructs geometry, material properties, and lighting by optimizing differentiable rendering parameters. It is distinguished by its focus on recovering physical optical properties (e.g., extinction coefficients, reflectance) rather than just static radiance. Chosen when optimizing underlying optical properties is required. Reconstructs spatially varying optical properties (absorption, scattering, phase function) and the light field of participating media from posed RGB images by enforcing the Radiative Transfer Equation (RTE) as a physics-informed constraint. It differs from surface-based inverse rendering by enforcing light transport locally throughout the volume. Chosen when physically complete volumetric light transport is required without restrictive assumptions such as homogeneous media. Extends differentiable volume rendering by integrating physical sensor models and geometric priors to solve inverse problems where optical assumptions fail or data is sparse. It differs from standard radiance field optimization by replacing or augmenting the emission-absorption model with physics-based signal formation equations. Chosen when optical assumptions fail or data is sparse. A framework that jointly optimizes triangle mesh, Physically-Based (PBR) material, and High Dynamic Range (HDR) light probe from pre-trained neural fields by combining neural field reconstruction with differentiable rasterization/ray tracing. It obtains a Neural Radiance Cache (NRC) from a pre-trained neural field to model indirect illumination, uses the trained neural field to initialize Differentiable Marching Tetrahedrons (DMTet), and integrates the NRC into a ray tracing pipeline to compute global illumination via single-bounce differentiable MC ray tracing. Unlike previous inverse rendering methods based on textured meshes that bake indirect illumination into materials, JOC separates indirect illumination effects from material. Unlike NVDIFFRECMC which only considers direct lighting due to noise and iteration time costs of multi-bounce path tracing, JOC captures global illumination. The input neural field must be capable of synthesizing novel views and estimating depth via ray casting. Not given in the sources. Joint Optimization of Triangle Mesh, Material, and Light from Neural Fields with Neural Radiance Cache, https://doi.org/10.48550/arxiv.2305.16800, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial)

name: Refractive Index Tomography using Neural Fields
head: Neural Field Recovery, Single-View Refractive Index Tomography
body: Refractive Index Tomography using Neural Fields (RNTF) is a method to recover a 3D refractive index field (\eta) and a luminance field from single-view refracted image measurements by optimizing neural fields that represent these quantities. It differs from standard differentiable volume rendering by modeling light propagation through a continuous medium with spatially varying refractive index using ray tracing governed by Fermat's principle, rather than assuming straight-line paths or constant index. It builds on Physical and Material Priors by explicitly parameterizing the material property (refractive index) as a neural field and integrating the physical equations of motion for light rays. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: A single refracted image (or set of measurements), camera parameters (field of view fovangle, resolution res), and an optional initial refractive index estimate ninit. Outputs: A trained neural network representing the 3D refractive index field \eta(\mathbf{x}) and optionally a luminance/emission field L(\mathbf{x}). Data Structures: Ray Input Array: Shape [batchsize, 6 + numaux]. The first 3 elements are the ray position (x, y, z), the next 3 are the ray direction (dx, dy, dz), and the remaining elements are auxiliary data. ODE State y: Shape [batchsize, statedim]. statedim is 6 for path-only tracing (position + direction) or 7 for luminance tracing (position + direction + luminance). Parameters: svals: Array of path length values at which to evaluate the ray-traced path integral. Passed to the ODE solver. lam: Regularization weight for the boundary term in the loss function. res: Resolution of the ray grid, determining the number of rays as res^2. fovangle: Field of view angle in degrees, used to calculate aperture points and ray directions. ninit: Initial refractive index at the starting position, used to scale the initial ray direction magnitude. lrinit, lrfinal: Initial and final learning rates for the optimizer. numiters: Total number of training iterations. Numbered Steps: 1. Initialize Rays: Generate ray origins and directions based on camera parameters (fovangle, res). Normalize the ray direction and scale its magnitude by the initial refractive index ninit at the starting position to ensure correct physical propagation, as the ODE uses raydir / eta. 2. Define Neural Fields: Instantiate two neural networks (e.g., MLPs): predicteta: Takes 3D position \mathbf{x} as input and outputs the scalar refractive index \eta(\mathbf{x}) and its gradient \nabla \eta(\mathbf{x}). predictlum: Takes 3D position \mathbf{x} as input and outputs the luminance/emission L(\mathbf{x}) at that point. 3. Define ODE Function: Define the derivative function for the ray tracing ODE. The state y contains [\mathbf{r}, \mathbf{d}, l] (position, direction, luminance). The derivatives with respect to path length s are: \frac{d\mathbf{r}}{ds} = \frac{\mathbf{d}}{\eta} \frac{d\mathbf{d}}{ds} = \nabla \eta \frac{dl}{ds} = L (or \frac{L}{\eta^2} for radiance adjustment depending on the specific variant renderfn vs renderfnrad). 4. Integrate ODE: Use an ODE solver (e.g., jax.experimental.ode.odeint) to integrate the ODE function over the path length values svals. The initial state y0 is constructed by concatenating the initialized ray position, direction, and auxiliary data (initial luminance if applicable). 5. Extract Results: Extract the final ray positions (raytrace) and integrated luminance (raylum) from the integration result. Move the ray trace to the last axis if necessary. 6. Compute Loss: Calculate the loss between the rendered luminance/image and the target measurements. Include a regularization term weighted by lam for boundary conditions. 7. Optimize: Use gradient descent (e.g., Adam) via jax.valueandgrad and applygradients to update the parameters of the neural fields (predicteta, predictlum). Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import jax import jax.numpy as jnp from jax.experimental.ode import odeint def predictetagradfn(x): """ Neural network that takes position x and returns eta and gradient of eta. x shape: [N, 3] Returns: eta shape [N], etagrad shape [N, 3] """ # Implementation depends on specific MLP architecture (e.g., flax.nn.MLP) # This is a placeholder for the actual network call raise NotImplementedError def predictlumfn(x): """ Neural network that takes position x and returns luminance. x shape: [N, 3] Returns: lum shape [N] """ # Implementation depends on specific MLP architecture raise NotImplementedError def odefnlum(y, s): """ ODE function for ray tracing with luminance. y shape: [batchsize, 7] -> [posx, posy, posz, dirx, diry, dirz, lum] s: scalar path length Returns: dy/ds shape [batchsize, 7] """ raypos = y[...,:3] raydir = y[..., 3:6] # Reshape for network input if necessary rayposflat = jnp.reshape(raypos, [-1, 3]) # Get refractive index and its gradient eta, etagrad = predictetagradfn(rayposflat) # Get luminance lum = predictlumfn(rayposflat) # Compute derivatives # ddsraypos = raydir / eta # Note: eta is [N], raydir is [N, 3]. Need to broadcast eta. ddsraypos = raydir / eta[:, None] # ddsraydir = etagrad ddsraydir = etagrad # ddsraylum = lum # For radiance adjustment variant (renderfnrad), use: lum / eta^2 ddsraylum = lum[:, None] # Concatenate derivatives out = jnp.concatenate([ddsraypos, ddsraydir, ddsraylum], axis=-1) return out def renderfnrad(rays, predicteta, predictlum, svals): """ Renders refracted image using neural fields. rays shape: [batchsize, 6 + numaux] predicteta: function returning (eta, etagrad) from position predictlum: function returning lum from position svals: array of path lengths Returns: raytrace, raylum """ # Initialize ODE state y0 # rays[...,:3] is pos, rays[..., 3:6] is dir # Assuming initial luminance is 0 or derived from rays if present # For luminance tracing, statedim is 7 raypos = rays[...,:3] raydir = rays[..., 3:6] # Initial luminance might be 0 or passed in rays if numaux > 0 # Assuming no initial luminance in rays for simplicity, or 0 initiallum = jnp.zeroslike(raypos[..., 0]) # Concatenate to form y0: [pos, dir, lum] y0 = jnp.concatenate([raypos, raydir, initiallum[:, None]], axis=-1) # Integrate ODE # odeint expects function(y, t) -> dy/dt # Here s is the independent variable (path length) ysol = odeint(odefnlum, y0, svals) # ysol shape: [len(svals), batchsize, 7] # Extract final state finalstate = ysol[-1] raytrace = finalstate[...,:3] # Final positions raylum = finalstate[..., 6] # Final luminance # Move raytrace to last axis if needed by downstream code # raytrace shape: [batchsize, 3] return raytrace, raylum def lossfn(renderedlum, targetlum, lam, bdval, Xreg): """ Computes loss with data fidelity and boundary regularization. """ # Data fidelity term (e.g., MSE) dataloss = jnp.mean((renderedlum - targetlum) 2) # Boundary regularization term # Xreg are boundary points, bdval is expected eta at boundary # This is a simplified placeholder; actual implementation in uses getXbd and specific logic # Typically involves predicting eta at Xreg and comparing to bdval etaatreg = predictetafn(Xreg) # Assuming predictetafn returns just eta bdloss = jnp.mean((etaatreg - bdval) 2) totalloss = dataloss + lam bdloss return totalloss Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Ray Direction Scaling: The initial ray direction magnitude must be scaled by the initial refractive index ninit to ensure correct physical propagation, as the ODE uses raydir / eta. Precision: For simulations like dark matter, tight ODE tolerances (rtol=1e-10, atol=1e-10) are required to ensure precision. Radiance Adjustment: The variant renderfnrad adjusts the luminance integrand by dividing by \eta^2, whereas renderfn does not. This accounts for radiance adjustment according to the index of refraction. Focuses on recovering optical properties like albedo and normals, often assuming straight-line paths or simpler scattering models. RNTF specifically handles refraction in continuous media. Link Uses physics-informed neural networks (PINNs) to solve the radiative transfer equation, often for participating media. RNTF uses ray tracing ODEs for non-participating or weakly participating media with varying index. Link Incorporates multiple sensor types or strong physical priors to constrain the inverse problem. RNTF primarily uses single-view refracted images. Link Time Complexity: Depends on the number of training iterations, the number of rays (res^2), the number of ODE steps (len(svals)), and the cost of evaluating the neural networks. ODE integration is typically the most expensive part per iteration. Memory Complexity: Proportional to the number of rays and the depth of the ODE integration (if storing all steps) or the memory required for the neural network parameters and gradients. Measured Performance: Tested on NVIDIA RTX A6000 GPU. Specific performance metrics (FPS, convergence time) are not provided in the sources. Scaling: Scales with resolution res (number of rays) and the complexity of the neural networks (depth, width). Strengths: Can recover continuous 3D refractive index fields from single views; handles smooth variations and complex geometries implicitly via the neural field. Limitations: Requires careful tuning of ODE tolerances and regularization; may be slow to converge; single-view setup can lead to ambiguities. When to use: Gas flow recovery, smooth refractive field recovery, dark matter halo recovery simulations. When not to use: When high-speed real-time rendering is required, or when the medium is highly scattering (participating media) where the radiative transfer equation is more appropriate. The method is based on the paper "Single-View Refractive Index Tomography using Neural Fields". It was built and tested on Ubuntu 22.04 and NVIDIA RTX A6000 GPU. The code uses JAX, Flax, and Optax. Applications include gas flow recovery, smooth refractive field recovery, and dark matter halo recovery simulations. brandonyzhao/rtnf, https://github.com/brandonyzhao/rtnf, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial)

name: VDN-NeRF
head: View-Dependence Normalization, View-Dependence Normalization NeRF, Ours
body: VDN-NeRF is a method for training neural radiance fields (NeRFs) to achieve high-quality geometry under non-Lambertian surface and dynamic lighting conditions. It resolves the shape-radiance ambiguity by normalizing view-dependent radiance variations through self-distillation of invariant features encoded within the NeRF itself. Unlike methods that explicitly model complex underlying factors of view-dependence (such as specularities or dynamic illumination), VDN-NeRF aligns the view-dependence of different scenes to a uniform level, allowing a single optimal network capacity to ensure good view synthesis and prevent geometric degradation. VDN-NeRF builds on Neural Radiance Fields and Surface-SDF Representation by introducing a parallel feature stream and a distillation network to normalize view-dependent color variations. Inputs: A set of posed 2D images Ik of a scene. Outputs: A trained SDF network f, a radiance function c, a feature function F, and a distillation network \psi. The system produces rendered images and depth maps for novel views. 1. SDF Network f: Predicts the Signed Distance Function f(x) for a point x \in \mathbb{R}^3. The zero-level set S = \{x \mid f(x) = 0\} represents the scene geometry. 2. Radiance Function c: A 4-layer Multi-Layer Perceptron (MLP) with a hidden dimension of 256. It maps coordinate x and viewing direction v to an RGB value: c: \mathbb{R}^3 \times S^2 \rightarrow \mathbb{R}^3. 3. Feature Function F: A 4-layer MLP with a hidden dimension of 256, identical in architecture to c. The feature function F is instantiated in parallel to the radiance function c, and its outputs are volume-rendered to produce \Psi(o, v). 4. Distillation Network \psi: A monocular depth prediction network. It uses a DenseNet161 backbone (specifically WaveletMonodepth) and takes a rendered image I{kr} as input to predict rendered depth \hat{d}{rk} and intermediate feature maps. The density \rho(t) at a point p(t) along a ray parameterized by t is derived from the SDF f and a scaling factor \Phis: \rho(t) = \max\left(\frac{s}{\Phis(f(p(t)))} \frac{-d}{dt}(f(p(t))), 0\right) where s is a scaling factor. The accumulated transmittance T(t) is: T(t) = \exp\left(-\int0^t \rho(\tau) d\tau\right) The weight function w(t) for volume rendering is: w(t) = T(t)\rho(t) The standard color rendering C for a ray (o, v) is: C(o, v) = \int0^{+\infty} w(t) c(p(t), v) dt The feature rendering \Psi(o, v) is defined similarly using the feature function F: \Psi(o, v) = \int0^{+\infty} w(t) F(p(t), v) dt 1. Instantiate Networks: Initialize f, c, F, and \psi. Pretrain \psi on in-domain data (different from training and test scenes) for a few epochs to ensure efficient convergence during joint training. 2. Sample Points: For each image Ik in a batch of size n, sample points pi along rays using hierarchical sampling (as in NeuS). 3. Compute Features and Radiance: For each sample point pi and viewing direction vi, compute the SDF value f(pi), density \rhoi, and the outputs of the radiance function c(pi, vi) and feature function F(pi, vi). 4. Volume Render: Compute the rendered color and the rendered feature \Psi(oi, vi) for each ray. 5. Distillation Prediction: Pass the rendered image I{kr} (or the input image Ik) through the distillation network \psi to obtain the normalized feature map \bar{\psi}l(Ik) from the l-th layer. The operational choice sets l=1, using features from the first Conv block of the distillation encoder. 6. Compute Losses: Calculate the joint training objective \mathcal{L}: \mathcal{L} = \lambda{\text{color}} \mathcal{L}{\text{color}} + \lambda{\text{vdn}} \mathcal{L}{\text{vdn}} + \lambda{\text{reg}} \mathcal{L}{\text{reg}} Color Loss (\mathcal{L}{\text{color}}): L1 loss between rendered color and input image Ik. If masks Mk are available, the loss is weighted by the mask: \mathcal{L}{\text{color}} = \frac{1}{n} \sum{i=1}^n \| C(oi, vi) - I{k,i} \|1 \cdot M{k,i} Otherwise, use the standard L1 loss: \mathcal{L}{\text{color}} = \frac{1}{n} \sum{i=1}^n \| C(oi, vi) - I{k,i} \|1 View-Dependence Normalization Loss (\mathcal{L}{\text{vdn}}): L1 loss between the rendered feature \Psi(oi, vi) and the normalized distillation feature \bar{\psi}l(Ik)[pi]: \mathcal{L}{\text{vdn}} = \frac{1}{n} \sum{i=1}^n \| \Psi(oi, vi) - \bar{\psi}l(Ik)[pi] \|1 Regularization Loss (\mathcal{L}{\text{reg}}): Eikonal loss regularizing the gradient of the SDF network to be unit length: \mathcal{L}{\text{reg}} = \frac{1}{mn} \sum{i,j} (\|\nabla f(p{i,j})\| - 1)^2 where m is the number of point samples per ray. 7. Update: Minimize \mathcal{L} using gradient descent. The distillation network \psi is optionally frozen during training if its prediction discrepancy with self-supervision is small, reducing training time. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def trainvdnnerf(images, poses, batchsize=512, numsteps=300000): # Initialize networks f = SDFNetwork() # Predicts f(x) c = RadianceNetwork() # 4-layer MLP, dim 256 F = FeatureNetwork() # 4-layer MLP, dim 256 psi = DistillationNetwork() # WaveletMonodepth with DenseNet161 # Pretrain psi on in-domain data for a few epochs pretraindistillationnetwork(psi, indomaindata) optimizer = Optimizer([f.parameters(), c.parameters(), F.parameters(), psi.parameters()]) for step in range(numsteps): # Sample batch of images batchimages, batchposes = samplebatch(images, poses, batchsize) totalloss = 0 for img, pose in zip(batchimages, batchposes): # 1. Sample points along rays using hierarchical sampling points, directions, tvals = samplerays(pose, hierarchical=True) # 2. Compute SDF and Density sdfvals = f(points) # Compute density rho(t) from SDF gradient and scaling factor Phis # rho(t) = max( (s / Phis(f(p))) (-d/dt f(p)), 0) densities = computedensityfromsdf(sdfvals, points, tvals) # 3. Compute Transmittance and Weights transmittance, weights = computetransmittanceandweights(densities) # 4. Compute Radiance and Feature Outputs radianceoutputs = c(points, directions) featureoutputs = F(points, directions) # 5. Volume Render Color and Feature renderedcolor = sum(weights radianceoutputs) renderedfeature = sum(weights featureoutputs) # 6. Distillation Network Prediction # psi takes the rendered image or input image to predict depth features # We use the input image Ik for distillation feature extraction distillationfeatures = psi(img) # Extract normalized feature from layer l=1 (first Conv block) normalizedfeature = distillationfeatures[1] # 7. Compute Losses # Color Loss (L1) colorloss = meanl1(renderedcolor, img) # VDN Loss (L1 between rendered feature and normalized distillation feature) # Note: normalizedfeature must be aligned with point samples pi vdnloss = meanl1(renderedfeature, normalizedfeature) # Eikonal Regularization # Sample additional points for gradient regularization regpoints = samplerandompoints() gradf = computegradient(f, regpoints) eikonalloss = meansquarederror(norm(gradf) - 1.0) # Joint Loss loss = lambdacolor colorloss + lambdavdn vdnloss + lambdareg eikonalloss # 8. Backpropagate optimizer.zerograd() loss.backward() optimizer.step() totalloss += loss.item() if step % 1000 == 0: print(f"Step {step}, Loss: {totalloss}") # Optional: Freeze psi if discrepancy is small if checkdistillationdiscrepancy(psi) < threshold: psi.requiresgrad = False Hyperparameters: \lambda{\text{color}}, \lambda{\text{vdn}}, \lambda{\text{reg}} are weighting factors (values not explicitly given in sources, but standard practice applies). Batch size is 512. Layer Selection: The operational choice for the distillation layer index l is 1 (first Conv block of the encoder). Pitfall - Distillation Update: If the distillation network's prediction discrepancy is small, it can be frozen to save time. Pitfall - Mask Handling: If foreground masks Mk are available, the color loss is masked. If not, the standard L1 loss is used. The source notes that masks are defined as Mk for input and \hat{M}k = \sum w{k,j} for rendered. Precision: The method relies on the stability of the depth prediction network \psi. Pretraining \psi is critical for convergence. Time Complexity: Training takes approximately 300,000 steps, converging in about 11 hours on a single NVIDIA RTX 3090 GPU. Memory Complexity: Uses 4-layer MLPs with hidden dimension 256 for c and F, plus a DenseNet161 backbone for \psi. Memory usage is comparable to standard SDF-based NeRFs (like NeuS) with the added overhead of the distillation network features. Performance: On the BlendedMVS dataset, VDN-NeRF achieves an IoU of 0.854, L1 Chamfer Distance of 0.397, L2 Chamfer Distance of 0.827, Normal Consistency of 0.845, and f-score of 0.834. Strengths: Improves geometry quality under non-Lambertian surfaces and dynamic lighting without changing the volume rendering pipeline. It aligns the optimal network capacity across scenes, preventing shape-radiance ambiguity from degrading geometry. Limitations: Requires pretraining the distillation network. The method assumes that depth-prediction features are sufficiently view-invariant, which may not hold for all extreme view-dependent phenomena. When to Use: When high-quality geometry is required for scenes with specularities, dynamic lighting, or non-Lambertian materials, and when using a baseline NeRF/SDF method. VDN-NeRF was proposed by Bingfan Zhu, Yanchao Yang, Xulong Wang, Youyi Zheng, and Leonidas Guibas from Zhejiang University, The University of Hong Kong, and Stanford University. It was published in CVPR 2023 (arXiv:2303.17968v1, March 31, 2023). The work addresses the fundamental issue in NeRF reconstruction where geometry is often poor due to shape-radiance ambiguity, particularly under varying lighting and non-Lambertian surfaces. It builds upon the NeuS method. VDN-NeRF: Resolving Shape-Radiance Ambiguity via View-Dependence Normalization, https://doi.org/10.1109/CVPR52729.2023.00012, fetched 2026-10-29

name: Inverse Rendering and Optical Properties
head: Inverse Volume Rendering, Differentiable Volume Rendering, Neural Reflectance Fields
body: Inverse rendering and optical properties methods reconstruct physical scene parameters—such as volume density, extinction coefficients, albedo, or environmental illumination—from a set of observed images. Unlike forward rendering, which computes images from known geometry and materials, these methods treat the rendering equation as an optimization problem where the scene parameters are the variables. This family is distinguished from standard differentiable volume rendering by its explicit focus on recovering physically meaningful material properties (e.g., via adjoint derivatives or neural field residuals) rather than merely optimizing a black-box radiance field. All methods in this family share the core mechanism of differentiating the forward rendering operator to propagate gradients from image space to scene parameter space. The general optimization objective is: \min{\theta} \mathcal{L}(\theta) = \sum{i} \| I{rendered}(\theta) - I{ref}^{(i)} \|^2 where \theta represents the scene parameters (e.g., density grid values, neural network weights, or lighting coefficients). The gradient \nabla\theta \mathcal{L} is computed using either backpropagation through a differentiable path tracer or by solving the adjoint of the rendering equation. The forward operator must be differentiable with respect to \theta, allowing the use of gradient-based optimizers like Adam. This method optimizes a 3D volume density grid to match reference images using differentiable path tracing [1523-volumetric-inverse-rendering-with-differentiable-path-tracin.md]. It accounts for direct and indirect illumination by integrating the adjoint method into the path tracing loop, allowing differentiability through stochastic sampling events [1523-volumetric-inverse-rendering-with-differentiable-path-tracin.md]. Choose this when you need to reconstruct complex volumetric properties (extinction/scattering) from multiple viewpoints while maintaining physical accuracy through path replay backpropagation [1523-volumetric-inverse-rendering-with-differentiable-path-tracin.md]. Neural Radiosity represents the outgoing radiance field as a neural network and optimizes its parameters by minimizing the residual of the rendering equation [6755-neural-radiosity.md]. It solves global illumination by treating the rendering equation as a fixed-point problem, making it independent of specific camera viewpoints during training [6755-neural-radiosity.md]. Choose this when you want to compute global illumination without relying on rasterizers or path tracers, and when viewpoint independence is desired [6755-neural-radiosity.md]. NeRV reconstructs a 3D scene representation from images under unconstrained, known lighting, enabling view synthesis and relighting with indirect illumination [10246-nerv-neural-reflectance-and-visibility-fields.md]. It extends NeRF by representing the scene as a 3D field of oriented particles that absorb and reflect light, parameterized by neural networks [10246-nerv-neural-reflectance-and-visibility-fields.md]. Choose this when you need to support arbitrary environment lighting and one-bounce global illumination, using a learned neural visibility field to reduce light transport simulation complexity [10246-nerv-neural-reflectance-and-visibility-fields.md]. Definition: An optimization method that estimates scene optical properties (position, scale, rotation, cross-section, spherical harmonic coefficients) from images using gradient-based optimization with adjoint derivatives of the forward pass. Step: Start optimization with a small number of primitives and gradually generate new primitives to add detail. Parameter: Optimizer: Bound Adam (an improved Adam optimizer that respects parameter boundaries). Loss function: L1 error, D-SSIM, plus regularization terms for anisotropy and density of small primitives. Definition: A 3D representation for inverse rendering where the scene is represented as a field of volume density, surface normals, and Bidirectional Reflectance Distribution Functions (BRDFs). Step: Augment NeRF with an additional MLP to model lighting. Model BRDFs with spherical Gaussians. Incorporate SDF-based representation in the model. Introduce regularization to stabilize normals from NeRF's foggy geometry. Pitfall: These methods suffer from extremely time-consuming optimization and slow rendering speed. Definition: Optimizes environmental illumination instead of volume properties to match desired volume appearance. Volume properties (emission, albedo, extinction) are assumed spatially varying but fixed during this optimization. The concept of inverse rendering has roots in computer vision and graphics, aiming to recover scene properties from images. Recent advances have leveraged neural fields and differentiable rendering to make this process more tractable. The use of adjoint derivatives for volumetric inverse rendering was highlighted in work on volumetric ray-traced primitives, which allows for noiseless and efficient rendering of scattering media. Reflectance fields, which model BRDFs and lighting via neural networks, have been surveyed as a key approach for inverse rendering, though they face challenges in optimization time and rendering speed. Light reconstruction, as an alternative to modifying volume properties, has been explored in the context of volume stylization, where environmental illumination is optimized to match desired appearances. Don’t Splat your Gaussians: Volumetric Ray-Traced Primitives for Modeling and Rendering Scattering and Emissive Media (2025), https://qiita.com/matumu20/items/67b33681dc97ccbcc849, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial) Recent Advances and Trends in Learning‐Based 3D Representations, https://doi.org/10.1111/cgf.70530, fetched 2026-10-26 Property and Lighting Manipulations for Static Volume Stylization Using a Painting Metaphor, https://doi.org/10.1109/TVCG.2014.13, fetched 2026-10-26

name: Volumetric Inverse Rendering with Differentiable Path Tracing
head: Differentiable Volumetric Inverse Rendering, Differentiable Volumometric Path Tracing Optimization, Mitsuba 3 Volumetric Inverse Rendering, Mitsuba 3 Volumetric Inverse Rendering Tutorial, Volumetric Inverse Rendering with Differentiable Path Replay Backpropagation, Volumetric Path Tracing with Adjoint Differentiation
body: Volumetric Inverse Rendering with Differentiable Path Tracing is a technique to optimize a 3D volume density (extinction/scattering) stored on a regular grid to match a set of synthetic reference images. It accounts for direct and indirect illumination by using path replay backpropagation to compute derivatives of delta tracking and volumetric multiple scattering. It sets itself apart from its siblings by explicitly optimizing physical volume parameters (grid-based extinction) using a differentiable path tracer (specifically prbvolpath) rather than neural field representations. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: A set of reference images I{ref}^{(i)} captured from N viewpoints; a scene geometry (typically a container with a null BSDF); an initial volume density grid \sigmat; and optimization hyperparameters (learning rate, iterations, resolution). Outputs: An optimized volume density grid \sigmat that minimizes the difference between rendered images and reference images. Data Structures: Volume Grid: A 3D tensor of shape (V, V, V, 1) representing the extinction coefficient \sigmat. In Mitsuba 3, this is stored as a TensorXf accessed via the key 'object.interiormedium.sigmat.data'. Scene Parameters: Traversed via mi.traverse(scene) to identify differentiable tensors. Algorithm Steps: 1. Sensor Setup: Create N sensors (typically N=5 for simple scenes, up to 50-100 for complex ones) placed on a half-circle around the origin. For each sensor i \in [0, N-1]: Calculate angle: \thetai = \frac{180.0}{N} \cdot i - 90.0. Create rotation transform Ry(\thetai) around the Y-axis. Create look-at transform from target [0,0,0] to camera origin [0,0,4] with up vector [0,1,0]. Combine transforms: T{to\world} = Ry(\thetai) \cdot T{look\at}. Load sensor with type 'perspective', FOV 45, film resolution 64 \times 64, and 'tent' filter. 2. Reference Rendering: Render the reference scene (containing the ground-truth volume) using the prbvolpath integrator for each sensor with S{ref} samples per pixel (SPP). Store results in I{ref}. Typical S{ref} = 512. 3. Optimization Scene Initialization: Create a scene with a uniform volume grid of resolution V{init} \times V{init} \times V{init} (e.g., 16^3). Initialize \sigmat to a low constant value (e.g., 0.002). This facilitates optimization by making it easier to increase density than to remove parts of a very dense volume. Set the container's BSDF to 'null' to make it invisible. Set the volume scale parameter to 40.0. This scales the extinction range to [10^{-6} \cdot \text{scale}, \text{scale}]. 4. Optimizer Setup: Traverse the scene to extract the volume data key: key = 'object.interiormedium.sigmat.data'. Initialize an Adam optimizer with learning rate \eta = 0.02. Assign the volume data to the optimizer: opt[key] = params[key]. 5. Optimization Loop: For each iteration it from 0 to I{count}-1: Initialize totalloss = 0.0. For each sensor j from 0 to N-1: Render the scene using mi.render(scene, params, sensor=sensors[j], spp=S{opt}, seed=it). Compute L2 loss: Lj = \text{mean}((I{rendered} - I{ref}^{(j)})^2). Backpropagate gradients: dr.backward(Lj). Take a gradient step: opt.step(). Clamp density values: opt[key] = dr.clip(opt[key], 1e-6, 1.0). Update scene parameters: params.update(opt). Accumulate loss: totalloss += Lj. 6. Volume Upsampling (Multi-resolution): After initial optimization at low resolution, upsample the volume grid to a higher resolution (e.g., 64^3). Use dr.resample(opt[key], shape=(64, 64, 64, 1), filter='linear'). Note: dr.upsample is also used in some implementations, but resample with a linear filter is preferred to avoid negative values from cubic overshoot. Update parameters: params.update(opt). The optimizer automatically resets internal state (e.g., momentum) when the tensor size changes. Continue optimization with increased SPP (e.g., S{opt} = 8 \cdot S{ref}). Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import drjit as dr import mitsuba as mi mi.setvariant('cudaadrgb') def setupsensors(sensorcount=5): from mitsuba import ScalarTransform4f as T sensors = [] for i in range(sensorcount): angle = 180.0 / sensorcount i - 90.0 sensorrotation = T().rotate([0, 1, 0], angle) sensortoworld = T().lookat(target=[0, 0, 0], origin=[0, 0, 4], up=[0, 1, 0]) sensors.append(mi.loaddict({ 'type': 'perspective', 'fov': 45, 'toworld': sensorrotation @ sensortoworld, 'film': { 'type': 'hdrfilm', 'width': 64, 'height': 64, 'filter': {'type': 'tent'} } })) return sensors def renderreferenceimages(sceneref, sensors, refspp=512): return [mi.render(sceneref, sensor=sensors[i], spp=refspp) for i in range(len(sensors))] def createoptimizationscene(vres=16, scale=40.0): scenedict = { 'type': 'scene', 'integrator': {'type': 'prbvolpath'}, 'object': { 'type': 'cube', 'bsdf': {'type': 'null'}, 'interior': { 'type': 'heterogeneous', 'sigmat': { 'type': 'gridvolume', 'grid': mi.VolumeGrid(dr.full(mi.TensorXf, 0.002, (vres, vres, vres, 1))), 'toworld': mi.ScalarTransform4f().translate(-1).scale(2.0) }, 'scale': scale } }, 'emitter': {'type': 'constant'} } return mi.loaddict(scenedict) def optimizevolume(scene, sensors, refimages, iterationcount=20, spp=8): params = mi.traverse(scene) key = 'object.interiormedium.sigmat.data' opt = mi.ad.Adam(lr=0.02) opt[key] = params[key] params.update(opt) for it in range(iterationcount): totalloss = 0.0 for sensoridx in range(len(sensors)): img = mi.render(scene, params, sensor=sensors[sensoridx], spp=spp, seed=it) loss = dr.mean(dr.square(img - refimages[sensoridx])) dr.backward(loss) opt.step() opt[key] = dr.clip(opt[key], 1e-6, 1.0) params.update(opt) totalloss += loss return scene, params def upsamplevolume(opt, key, newshape=(64, 64, 64, 1)): opt[key] = dr.resample(opt[key], shape=newshape, filter='linear') An unbiased method for estimating gradients with respect to scattering volume parameters using differential ratio tracking with a majorant, avoiding separate medium control density hyperparameters. Time Complexity: Depends on the number of sensors, iterations, SPP, and volume resolution. Each iteration requires rendering N views. Memory Complexity: Proportional to the volume grid size (V^3) and the number of sensors. Performance: Measured on standard hardware using Mitsuba 3. Initial low-resolution optimization (16^3) is fast, while high-resolution (64^3) with high SPP is computationally expensive. Strengths: Multi-resolution approach improves convexity and recovers both shape and detail. Path replay backpropagation handles indirect illumination and multiple scattering. Limitations: Requires multiple viewpoints to constrain the volume. Initialization to low density is critical. Upsampling requires careful filter choice to avoid negative densities. When to use: When optimizing physical volume parameters (extinction/scattering) for novel view synthesis or reconstruction from multi-view images. When not to use: When single-view reconstruction is required, or when neural field representations are preferred over grid-based volumes. This method is implemented in Mitsuba 3 using the prbvolpath integrator, heterogeneous volume plugin, and gridvolume plugin. It is documented in the Mitsuba 3 tutorial for volumetric inverse rendering. The approach builds on differentiable path tracing techniques, specifically utilizing path replay backpropagation for efficient gradient computation in participating media. facebookresearch/volumetricprimitives, https://github.com/facebookresearch/volumetricprimitives, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial) Volumetric inverse rendering - Mitsuba 3, https://mitsuba.readthedocs.io/en/stable/src/inverserendering/volumeoptimization.html, fetched 2026-10-29 (unofficial) Volumetric inverse rendering, https://mitsuba.readthedocs.io/en/latest/src/inverserendering/volumeoptimization.html, fetched 2026-10-29 (unofficial)

name: Inverse Rendering with Differential Trackers
head: Differential ratio tracking, Unbiased inverse volume rendering
body: Inverse Rendering with Differential Trackers is an unbiased method for estimating gradients with respect to the parameters of scattering volumes (density \sigmat, albedo \alpha) to minimize a re-rendering objective function in inverse rendering. It sets itself apart from standard free-flight sampling by using differential ratio tracking with a majorant of 1.01 \sigmat, which avoids the need for a separate medium control density hyperparameter and reduces computation cost. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: Reference images, initial values for medium properties (density \sigmat, albedo \alpha, emission Le), camera parameters, illumination conditions, and an isotropic phase function. Outputs: Optimized medium properties (\sigmat, \alpha) that minimize the difference between rendered and reference images. Data Structures: Medium Properties: Stored on a regular grid with fields for extinction coefficient \sigmat, scattering albedo \alpha, and emission Le. Path State: Stores the current position, direction, throughput, and accumulated optical depth along the path. Algorithm Steps: 1. Initialization: Use a coarse-to-fine approach for initialization unless specified otherwise. 2. Stage 1 (Emissive Fit): Optimize only for emission Le to fit a nonphysical, emissive volume. 3. Stage 2 (Albedo Fit): Set medium emission Le to zero and optimize for scattering albedo \alpha such that all color originates from lighting and the reconstructed albedo. 4. Gradient Estimation: Use differential ratio tracking with a majorant of 1.01 \sigmat to compute gradients. This involves tracing one additional recursive path for each training path. 5. Optimization: Use gradient-based optimization (Adam or SGD with momentum) to update medium properties. Formulas: Majorant: M = 1.01 \sigmat. Objective: Minimize a re-rendering objective function over medium parameters. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def inverserenderingwithdifferentialtrackers(referenceimages, initialsigmat, initialalpha, numiterations=1000, learningrate=0.01): sigmat = initialsigmat.copy() alpha = initialalpha.copy() Le = initialalpha sigmat # Initial emissive guess # Stage 1: Fit emissive volume for i in range(numiterations // 2): renderedimage = differentiablevolumerender(sigmat, alpha, Le) loss = meansquarederror(renderedimage, referenceimages) gradLe = computegradientdifferentialtracking(sigmat, alpha, Le, loss) Le = Le - learningrate gradLe # Stage 2: Optimize albedo Le = 0.0 # Set emission to zero for i in range(numiterations // 2, numiterations): renderedimage = differentiablevolumerender(sigmat, alpha, Le) loss = meansquarederror(renderedimage, referenceimages) gradalpha = computegradientdifferentialtracking(sigmat, alpha, Le, loss) alpha = alpha - learningrate gradalpha return sigmat, alpha def differentiablevolumerender(sigmat, alpha, Le): # Standard differentiable volume rendering integration image = zeroslike(referenceimages) for each pixel: ray = castray(pixel) throughput = 1.0 radiance = 0.0 for step in range(64): # Maximum path length sigma = samplegrid(sigmat, ray.position) alphaval = samplegrid(alpha, ray.position) L = samplegrid(Le, ray.position) s = samplefreeflight(sigma) T = exp(-sigma s) radiance += throughput T (L + sigma alphaval phasefunction(ray.direction)) throughput = T ray.position += ray.direction s image[pixel] = radiance return image def computegradientdifferentialtracking(sigmat, alpha, Le, loss): # Trace primary path with actual density primarypath = tracepath(sigmat, alpha, Le, maxlength=64) # Trace recursive path with majorant density for gradient estimation majorantsigma = 1.01 sigmat recursivepath = tracepath(majorantsigma, alpha, Le, maxlength=64) # Compute gradient using path replay backpropagation ratio gradient = pathreplaybackpropagation(primarypath, recursivepath, loss) return gradient def tracepath(sigma, alpha, Le, maxlength): # Standard differentiable path tracing loop path = [] throughput = 1.0 for in range(maxlength): sigmatval = samplegrid(sigma, currentposition) s = samplefreeflight(sigmatval) T = exp(-sigmatval s) path.append({'s': s, 'T': T, 'throughput': throughput, 'sigma': sigmatval}) throughput = T if throughput < 1e-4: break return path def pathreplaybackpropagation(primarypath, recursivepath, loss): # PRB gradient computation using ratio of PDFs gradient = zeroslike(sigma) for step in range(len(primarypath)): p = primarypath[step] r = recursivepath[step] ratio = p['sigma'] / r['sigma'] # Differential ratio tracking weight gradient += loss ratio p['throughput'] return gradient Parameters: Maximum path length: 64 vertices. Majorant factor: 1.01. Optimizer: Adam or SGD with momentum. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: High gradient variance: Free-flight sampling gradients are prone to large outliers, causing persistent thin 'haze' artifacts around reconstructed volumes when using Adam optimizer. Defensive sampling: Eliminates large outliers but does not sufficiently reduce overall variance, exposing similar haze artifacts. Optimizer choice: SGD fails to converge due to gradient outliers, filling empty regions with artifacts. Adam suppresses these outliers via adaptive step sizes, allowing convergence despite high variance. Time Complexity: Linear time complexity in path length. Memory Complexity: Constant memory complexity. Performance: The recursive path amounts to an overhead of ~20% compared to pure free-flight sampling in the path replay backpropagation framework. Strengths: Unbiased gradient estimation, no need for medium control density hyperparameter, efficient parallel optimization of millions of parameters. Limitations: High gradient variance can lead to artifacts if not handled by appropriate optimizer (Adam) or initialization scheme. When to use: When unbiased gradient estimation is required for inverse rendering of participating media, and computational resources allow for the ~20% overhead of recursive path tracing. When not to use: When real-world, imperfect data is used without domain-specific assumptions, as the method focuses on synthetic scenes with known parameters. Origin: Based on Path Replay Backpropagation framework by Vicini et al. [2021b]. History: Developed to address severe issues in existing gradient estimation methods, which led to biased and high-variance gradients. Usage: Implemented in Mitsuba 2 [Nimier-David et al. 2019]. Unbiased inverse volume rendering with differential trackers, https://doi.org/10.1145/3528223.3530073, fetched 2026-11-01

name: Neural Radiosity
head: Full-gradient method, Residual-based optimization
body:
Neural Radiosity is an inverse rendering technique that solves the rendering equation by representing the outgoing radiance field as a neural network and optimizing its parameters to minimize the residual between the left-hand side (LHS) and right-hand side (RHS) of the equation. Unlike Volumetric Inverse Rendering with Differentiable Path Tracing, which relies on differentiable path tracing to compute gradients, Neural Radiosity treats the rendering equation as a self-supervised loss function, allowing for direct optimization of scene properties without explicit light transport simulation per step. It differs from NeRV (Neural Reflectance and Visibility Fields) by optimizing the radiance residual directly rather than learning separate reflectance and visibility fields. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: Scene geometry (meshes), material properties (BRDF parameters, diffuse/specular reflectance), and initial network parameters 	heta. Outputs: A trained neural network L	heta(x, \omegao) representing the outgoing radiance field. Data Structures: Neural Network: A Multi-Layer Perceptron (MLP) with 6 fully-connected layers and 512 neurons per hidden layer. Network Inputs: Surface location x. Outgoing direction \omegao. Surface normal at x. Diffuse and specular reflectance at x. Multi-resolution learnable feature vectors from sparse grids (optional, for high-frequency details). Sampling Buffers: Location samples \{xj\}{j=1}^N uniformly distributed on scene surfaces. Outgoing direction samples \{\omega{o,j}\}{j=1}^N uniformly distributed on the unit hemisphere (or sphere for two-sided BSDFs). Incident direction samples \{\omega{i,j,k}\}{k=1}^M uniformly distributed on the hemisphere for each (xj, \omega{o,j}). Algorithm Steps: 1. Initialize: Set network parameters 	heta and learning rate \eta. 2. Sample: For each optimization step, sample N location vectors \{xj\} uniformly on all scene surfaces and N outgoing directions \{\omega{o,j}\} uniformly over the hemisphere. 3. Sample Incident Directions: For each pair (xj, \omega{o,j}), sample M incident directions \{\omega{i,j,k}\}{k=1}^M uniformly over the hemisphere. 4. Compute Residual: Calculate the residual r	heta(xj, \omega{o,j}) for each sample. The residual is the difference between the LHS and RHS of the rendering equation: r	heta(x, \omegao) = L	heta(x, \omegao) - E(x, \omegao) - \int{H^2} fr(x, \omegai, \omegao) L	heta(x'(x, \omegai), -\omegai) (n \cdot \omegai) d\omegai where: L	heta(x, \omegao) is the network's predicted outgoing radiance. E(x, \omegao) is the emitted radiance. fr(x, \omegai, \omegao) is the BRDF. x'(x, \omegai) is the closest surface intersection of the ray originating at x with direction \omegai. n is the surface normal. The integral is estimated via Monte Carlo integration using the M incident samples. 5. Compute Loss: Estimate the loss \mathcal{L}(	heta) as the mean squared norm of the residual over all samples: \mathcal{L}(	heta) \approx  rac{1}{N} \sum{j=1}^{N}  rac{r	heta(xj, \omega{o,j})^2}{p(xj, \omega{o,j})} where p(xj, \omega{o,j}) is the sampling density. 6. name: Differentiable Neural Radiosity
head: DNR
body: Differentiable Neural Radiosity (DNR) is a method for solving the differential rendering equation using a neural network to represent the differential radiance field. It addresses the problem of computing gradients of rendered images with respect to arbitrary scene parameters (such as geometry, material properties, or illumination) by minimizing the residual of the differential rendering equation. Unlike traditional differentiable rendering methods that simulate light transport per optimization step, DNR pre-trains a neural network to cache the differential radiance distribution, enabling view-independent gradient computation with constant time and memory complexity relative to path length. It distinguishes itself from Radiative Backpropagation (RB) by avoiding quadratic time complexity in path length and from Path Replay Backpropagation (PRB) and Automatic Differentiation (AD) by not requiring the storage of per-bounce data or complete light path construction. Inputs: Scene geometry, materials (BRDFs), and illumination. A set of scene parameters p with respect to which derivatives are desired (e.g., BRDF roughness, diffuse albedo, index of refraction). A pre-trained primal radiance network L\phi. Outputs: A trained neural network \partialp L\theta(x, \omegao) representing the differential radiance field. Gradients \partialp Ik for inverse rendering tasks. Data Structures: 1. Primal Radiance Network (L\phi): A neural network with fixed parameters \phi that approximates the outgoing radiance L(x, \omegao). Exact layout and sizes are not given in the sources. 2. Differential Radiance Network (\partialp L\theta): A neural network with learnable parameters \theta that approximates the differential radiance \partialp L(x, \omegao). Exact layout and sizes are not given in the sources. 3. Scene Parameters (p): A vector of parameters defining the scene state. Formulas: The differential rendering equation is derived by differentiating the standard rendering equation with respect to p: \partialp L(x, \omegao) = \partialp E(x, \omegao) + \int{H^2} f(x, \omegai, \omegao) \partialp L(x'(x, \omegai), -\omegai) d\omegai^\perp + \int{H^2} \partialp f(x, \omegai, \omegao) L(x'(x, \omegai), -\omegai) d\omegai^\perp Where: L(x, \omegao) is the outgoing radiance. E(x, \omegao) is the emitted radiance. f(x, \omegai, \omegao) is the BRDF. x'(x, \omegai) is the next intersection point along direction \omegai. H^2 is the projected solid angle hemisphere. \partialp denotes the derivative with respect to parameter set p. The residual r\theta is defined as the difference between the left-hand side (LHS) and right-hand side (RHS) of the differential equation, using the neural network approximations: r\theta(x, \omegao) = \partialp L\theta(x, \omegao) - \partialp E(x, \omegao) - \int{H^2} f(x, \omegai, \omegao) \partialp L\theta(x'(x, \omegai), -\omegai) d\omegai^\perp - \int{H^2} \partialp f(x, \omegai, \omegao) L\phi(x'(x, \omegai), -\omegai) d\omegai^\perp The loss function is the L2 norm of this residual: \mathcal{L}(\theta) = \| r\theta \|^2 Steps: 1. Pre-train Primal Radiance: Train the network L\phi to approximate the primal radiance field L(x, \omegao) for the given scene. Fix parameters \phi. 2. Initialize Differential Network: Initialize the network \partialp L\theta with parameters \theta. 3. Compute Residual: For a sample point x and direction \omegao: a. Query L\phi to get incident primal radiance L\phi(x'(x, \omegai), -\omegai). b. Compute \partialp f(x, \omegai, \omegao) analytically or via automatic differentiation of the BRDF function with respect to p. c. Compute \partialp E(x, \omegao) analytically or via automatic differentiation. d. Query \partialp L\theta at x'(x, \omegai) to get \partialp L\theta(x'(x, \omegai), -\omegai). e. Evaluate the integrals over the hemisphere H^2. f. Calculate the residual r\theta(x, \omegao) using the formula above. 4. Optimize: Minimize \mathcal{L}(\theta) with respect to \theta using gradient descent. 5. Inverse Optimization: For a new inverse rendering task, use the pre-trained \partialp L\theta to compute gradients \partialp Ik for the measurement equation: \partialp Ik = \intA \int{H^2} Wk(x, \omega) \partialp L\theta(x, \omega) d\omegai^\perp dx Use the pre-trained network to compute gradients for inverse optimization tasks. Parameters: \theta: Learnable parameters of the differential radiance network. \phi: Fixed parameters of the primal radiance network. p: Scene parameters (e.g., roughness, albedo). Typical values: Not given in the sources. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Visibility Discontinuities: The method ignores visibility-related discontinuities (occlusions) for simplicity. Pre-training Dependency: The accuracy of the differential gradients depends on the quality of the pre-trained primal radiance network L\phi. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import torch import torch.nn as nn class DifferentiableNeuralRadiosity: def init(self, primalnetwork, differentialnetwork): self.primalnetwork = primalnetwork self.differentialnetwork = differentialnetwork self.primalnetwork.eval() for param in self.primalnetwork.parameters(): param.requiresgrad = False def computeresidual(self, x, wo, p, sceneops, numsamples=100): # LHS: differential radiance at current point dLtheta = self.differentialnetwork(x, wo) # Differential emission dE = sceneops.computeemissionderivative(x, wo, p) # Sample directions in hemisphere H^2 wisamples, cosweights = sceneops.samplehemisphere(wo, numsamples) # RHS integral 1: f dLtheta term1 = torch.zeroslike(dLtheta) for i in range(numsamples): wi = wisamples[i] xprime = sceneops.traceray(x, wi) dLprime = self.differentialnetwork(xprime, -wi) f = sceneops.brdf(x, wi, wo) term1 += f dLprime cosweights[i] # RHS integral 2: df/dp Lphi term2 = torch.zeroslike(dLtheta) dfdp = sceneops.computebrdfderivative(x, wisamples, wo, p) for i in range(numsamples): wi = wisamples[i] xprime = sceneops.traceray(x, wi) Lphi = self.primalnetwork(xprime, -wi) term2 += dfdp[i] Lphi cosweights[i] # Residual rtheta = dLtheta - dE - term1 - term2 residual = dLtheta - dE - term1 - term2 return residual def train(self, optimizer, numiterations, sceneops): for in range(numiterations): optimizer.zerograd() x, wo, p = sceneops.sampletrainingdata() residual = self.computeresidual(x, wo, p, sceneops) loss = torch.norm(residual) 2 loss.backward() optimizer.step() def computeinversegradients(self, p, sceneops): # Integrate differential radiance over pixel area and hemisphere to get dIk/dp # Implementation depends on specific pixel sampling strategy pass Optimizes scene parameters by minimizing the distance between rendered and reference images, using a neural network to cache the differential radiance field. It amortizes global light transport costs and avoids independent simulations per step. Represents the differential radiance field using learnable feature vectors at mesh vertices, reducing memory consumption and avoiding grid artifacts by leveraging geometric priors. Time Complexity: Constant in path length given pre-trained networks, as it queries the network at the first intersection rather than building complete light paths. In contrast, PRB and AD are linear in path length, and RB is quadratic. Memory Complexity: Constant in path length, similar to RB and PRB, as it does not store per-bounce data in an adjoint transcript. Measured Performance: Gradient computation time per iteration is 0.002s, compared to 0.009s for RB, 0.017s for PRB, and 0.088s for AD. View-Independence: Provides view-independent solutions, meaning sensor parameter changes do not require recomputation unless sensor parameters are being optimized. Strengths: Faster convergence, lower gradient computation time, view-independence, constant complexity in path length. Limitations: Ignores visibility-related discontinuities (occlusions), which can lead to incorrect gradients. Requires pre-training of the primal radiance network. Differentiable Neural Radiosity was introduced by Saeed Hadadan and Matthias Zwicker from the University of Maryland, College Park, USA. The method was published as a preprint on arXiv in January 2022. It builds on the concept of Neural Radiosity, which uses a neural network to solve the rendering equation, by extending it to the differential rendering equation. The method aims to provide a more efficient and accurate way to compute gradients for inverse rendering problems compared to existing differentiable rendering techniques. name: Inverse Rendering with Neural Radiosity
body: Inverse rendering with Neural Radiosity optimizes scene parameters p by minimizing an objective function z(\cdot) that measures the distance between a candidate rendered image and a reference image. It distinguishes itself from differentiable path tracing methods by caching the differential radiance distribution in a neural network, which amortizes the cost of resolving global light transport and avoids independent light transport simulations per optimization step. Inputs: Scene parameters p (e.g., roughness, position, emission intensity). Reference image. Pre-trained primal radiance network L\phi. Differential radiance network \partialp L\theta. Camera geometry and scene primitives. Outputs: Optimized scene parameters p. Updated networks \partialp L\theta and L\phi. Data Structures: Neural Networks: MLPs with 6 fully-connected layers and 512 neurons per hidden layer. Network Inputs: Position x, outgoing direction \omegao, surface normal, diffuse reflectance, and specular reflectance. Sparse Grids: Multiresolution learnable feature vectors stored in sparse grids within the scene. Sampling: Hemispherical samples \omega{i,j,k} for incident directions, importance sampled from emitter directions and BSDF distributions in primal space. Steps: 1. Compute a non-differentiable candidate primal rendering y = g(p) and calculate the loss z (e.g., L2 or L1 distance) between y and the reference image. 2. Compute the derivative of the loss with respect to the pixels of the primal image, \frac{\partial z}{\partial y}. 3. Compute the gradient of the rendered image with respect to parameters, \frac{\partial y}{\partial p}, equivalent to the measurement vector [\partialp I0 \dots \partialp In]. Trace rays from the sensor to find the first hit point x, query the differential radiance network \partialp L\theta, and integrate over the surface area A and hemisphere H^2: \partialp I{k,\theta} = \intA \int{H^2} Wk(x, \omega) \partialp L\theta(x'(x, \omega)) \, dx \, d\omega{i\perp} where Wk is the window function and x'(x, \omega) is the point on the surface visible from x in direction \omega. 4. Compute the total gradient of the loss w.r.t. parameters \frac{\partial z}{\partial p} by multiplying the gradients from steps 2 and 3: \frac{\partial z}{\partial p} = \frac{\partial z}{\partial y} \cdot \frac{\partial y}{\partial p}. 5. Update scene parameters p using an optimizer (e.g., Adam) and a learning rate. 6. Fine-tune the networks \partialp L\theta and L\phi to adapt to the new parameter state. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def inverserenderingstep(p, Iref, Lphi, dLtheta, camera, scene, optimizer, lr): # Step 1: Primal rendering y = renderprimal(p, Lphi, camera, scene) # loss = computeloss(y, Iref) # e.g., L2 or L1 distance # Step 2: Pixel gradient dzdy = computegradient(loss, y) # # Step 3: Differential radiance integration dydp = 0.0 for each pixel k: x, omega = traceray(camera, k) # dL = dLtheta(x, omega) # Query network integral = integrate(Wk(x, omega) dL, over=A, over=H2) # dydp += integral # Step 4: Gradient accumulation dzdp = dzdy dydp # # Step 5: Parameter update p = optimizer.step(p, dzdp, lr) # # Step 6: Network fine-tuning or RHS fallback if userhsfallback: # Use RHS of differential solution instead of fetching gradients from dLtheta # RHS adapts faster with one extra ray-tracing step using updated parameters pass # else: finetunenetworks(dLtheta, Lphi, p) # return p, dLtheta, Lphi Formulas: The differential radiance is reparameterized to separate the network output from the differential emission term: \partialp L\theta(x, \omegao) = N\theta(x, \omegao) + \partialp E(x, \omegao) where N\theta is the network output and E is emission. The residual of the differential rendering equation r\theta is defined as: r\theta(x, \omegao) = N\theta(x, \omegao) - T\{N\theta + \partialp E\}(x, \omegao) - T'\{N\phi + E\}(x, \omegao) where T and T' are transport operators. The transport operators are defined as integrals over the hemisphere H^2: T\{\partialp L\theta\}(x, \omegao) = \int{H^2} f(x, \omegai, \omegao) \partialp L\theta(x'(x, \omegai), -\omegai) \, d\omega{i\perp} T'\{L\phi\}(x, \omegao) = \int{H^2} \partialp f(x, \omegai, \omegao) L\phi(x'(x, \omegai), -\omegai) \, d\omega{i\perp} where f is the BSDF and L\phi is the primal radiance. Parameters: Sampling: Importance sample emitter directions and BSDF distributions in primal space to obtain incident directions \omegai. Samples are detached (static w.r.t. perturbations in scene parameters). Optimizer: Adam. Network Architecture: 6 fully-connected layers, 512 neurons per hidden layer. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Fine-tuning Bottleneck: Fine-tuning networks after every parameter update is computationally expensive. Mitigation: Keep networks intact in their initial state and use the Right-Hand Side (RHS) of the differential solution instead of fetching gradients from \partialp L\theta. The RHS adapts faster to parameter changes because it requires only one extra ray-tracing step with updated parameters, updating terms \partialp f and f in scattering integrals. This introduces bias but improves performance. Gradient Computation: All gradient terms, including \partialp f and \partialp E, are computed using automatic differentiation frameworks during optimization. Performs volumetric inverse rendering by jointly optimizing a neural medium field and a neural light field. It uses a Volumetric Radiance Error (VRE) loss to integrate radiance along primary viewing rays, counteracting oversmoothing from local constraints, and amortizes global light transport resolution. Time Complexity: Avoids the high cost of differentiating through generic Monte Carlo rendering by using an adjoint-like approach with a cached neural representation. Fine-tuning networks at every iteration is a bottleneck. Using the RHS approximation reduces this cost but introduces bias. Memory Complexity: Requires storing two neural networks (primal and differential) and sparse feature grids. The computation graph size is vastly reduced compared to generic differentiable path tracing. Performance: Efficient for scenes where global light transport is complex, as it amortizes the transport solution. Suitable for optimizing material properties (e.g., roughness) and illumination. Strengths: Avoids independent light transport simulations per scene instance; handles global illumination via the neural network; reduces computation graph size. Limitations: Fine-tuning bottleneck if not using the RHS approximation; potential bias from using the RHS approximation; requires pre-training of the primal radiance network. The method is based on "Differentiable Neural Radiosity" by Hadadan et al. (2022). It builds on the Neural Radiosity method by Hadadan et al. (2021). The approach was developed to address the computational costs of differentiable rendering by caching the differential radiance distribution in a neural network.
