name: Neural Illumination Fields (NeIF)
body: Neural Illumination Fields (NeIF) is a fully differentiable framework that represents 3D ambient illumination as a continuous volumetric radiance field, treating each sample in the surrounding 3D environment as a light emitter. Unlike methods that assume illumination is infinitely far away (e.g., environment maps or Spherical Gaussians) or methods that ignore spatial distance constraints (e.g., NeILF), NeIF naturally handles environment occlusion and directional lighting by modeling the 3D position of illumination. It serves as a plug-and-play module for NeRF-style renderers, enabling the decomposition of object materials from environmental lighting and the re-rendering of objects in new virtual environments. NeIF operates in two stages: first, it acquires the object’s geometry from input images using an existing method (Yariv et al. 2020); second, it jointly optimizes the NeIF representation and the object’s materials. The core mechanism models the incoming radiance at a surface point by integrating volumetric radiance along a specular lobe defined by the material's roughness. Inputs: A set of posed images of an object under static illumination; the object’s geometry (surface points \mathbf{x}s) reconstructed from the input images. Outputs: NeIF: A 5D volumetric radiance field function \mathcal{R}(\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{l}) mapping 3D position \mathbf{x} and incoming direction \mathbf{l} to color \mathbf{c} and volume density \sigma. Material Parameters: For each surface point \mathbf{x}s, a diffuse color \mathbf{C}d \in [0, 1]^3, a specular tint \alpha \in [0, 1], and a roughness \rho \in [0, 1]. Rendered Image: The final color \hat{C}(\mathbf{r}) for a camera ray \mathbf{r}. 1. Ambient MLP (\mathcal{R}): A neural network approximating the 5D volumetric radiance field. Input: Sample position \mathbf{x} \in \mathbb{R}^3 and incoming ray direction \mathbf{l} \in \mathbb{R}^3. Output: Tuple (\mathbf{c}, \sigma), where \mathbf{c} is the emitted color and \sigma is the volume density. 2. Material MLP (\mathcal{M}): A neural network predicting material properties. Input: Surface point position \mathbf{x}s \in \mathbb{R}^3. Output: Tuple (\rho, \mathbf{C}d, \alpha). Activation: Softplus is used for roughness and alpha to ensure parameters remain within valid ranges. 3. Integrated Lobe Encoding (ILE): A feature representation constructed from the coordinates within a conical frustum (specular lobe) to efficiently handle high-frequency variations related to roughness. 4. Multiscale Pre-convolved Representation: A representation of the background used to assist in the decomposition of object materials and environmental illumination. 1. Geometry Reconstruction: Acquire the object’s geometry (surface points \mathbf{x}s) from input images using a standard SDF-based method (e.g., Yariv et al. 2020). 2. Specular Lobe Definition: For a specific surface point \mathbf{x}s, define a 3D specular lobe. 3. Sample Generation: Generate sample points \mathbf{r}(t) along rays within this specular lobe. 4. Encoding: Apply Integrated Lobe Encoding (ILE) to the coordinates of the samples within the lobe. 5. Radiance Field Evaluation: Feed the encoded samples into the Ambient MLP \mathcal{R} to predict the color \mathbf{c}(\mathbf{r}(t), \mathbf{l}) and volume density \sigma(\mathbf{r}(t)) for each sample. 6. Volume Rendering Integration: Integrate the predicted values direction-wise to compute the incident radiance L{in}(\mathbf{x}s, \mathbf{l}). 7. Specular Color Computation: Combine the integrated incident radiance L{in} with the material’s specular function (dependent on \alpha and \rho) to compute the specular color \mathbf{C}s. 8. Diffuse Color Retrieval: Query the Material MLP \mathcal{M} at \mathbf{x}s to obtain the diffuse color \mathbf{C}d. 9. Final Rendering: Combine the specular color \mathbf{C}s and diffuse color \mathbf{C}d to render the final photo-realistic color for the pixel. 10. Optimization: Jointly optimize the NeIF representation (\mathcal{R}) and object materials (\mathcal{M}) using gradient descent. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import torch import torch.nn as nn import torch.nn.functional as F class AmbientMLP(nn.Module): """Approximates the 5D volumetric radiance field R: (x, l) -> (c, sigma).""" def init(self, inputdim=6, hiddendim=256, numlayers=4): super().init() layers = [] for i in range(numlayers): layers.append(nn.Linear(inputdim if i == 0 else hiddendim, hiddendim)) layers.append(nn.ReLU()) layers.append(nn.Linear(hiddendim, 4)) self.network = nn.Sequential(layers) def forward(self, x, l): inputs = torch.cat([x, l], dim=-1) out = self.network(inputs) return out[...,:3], out[..., 3:] class MaterialMLP(nn.Module): """Predicts material parameters M: xs -> (rho, Cd, alpha).""" def init(self, inputdim=3, hiddendim=128, numlayers=2): super().init() layers = [] for i in range(numlayers): layers.append(nn.Linear(inputdim if i == 0 else hiddendim, hiddendim)) layers.append(nn.ReLU()) layers.append(nn.Linear(hiddendim, 5)) self.network = nn.Sequential(layers) def forward(self, xs): out = self.network(xs) # Softplus activation ensures parameters remain within valid ranges rho = F.softplus(out[..., 0:1]) Cd = F.softplus(out[..., 1:4]) alpha = F.softplus(out[..., 4:5]) return rho, Cd, alpha def volumerendering(samples, c, sigma): """Computes integrated radiance Lin using iterative volume rendering.""" # samples: (N, 3), c: (N, 3), sigma: (N, 1) # Sort samples by distance from the surface point to ensure correct transmittance accumulation dists = torch.norm(samples, dim=-1, keepdim=True) sortidx = torch.argsort(dists, dim=0).squeeze(0) samples = samples[sortidx] c = c[sortidx] sigma = sigma[sortidx] # Compute segment lengths along the ray deltas = torch.diff(samples, dim=-2) deltat = torch.norm(deltas, dim=-1, keepdim=True) deltat = torch.clamp(deltat, min=1e-6) # Discrete alpha: alpha = 1 - exp(-sigma deltat) alpha = 1.0 - torch.exp(-sigma deltat) # Iterative transmittance accumulation: T(t) = exp(-int{tn}^t sigma ds) Tcum = torch.oneslike(alpha[:,:1]) Tcum = torch.cat([Tcum, torch.cumprod(1.0 - alpha[:,:-1], dim=0)], dim=0) # Contribution: T(t) sigma c contribution = Tcum alpha c Lin = torch.sum(contribution, dim=0) return Lin def renderneif(xs, viewdirs, normals, ambientmlp, materialmlp, numsamples=32): """Renders the color for a surface point xs.""" rho, Cd, alphaspec = materialmlp(xs) # Reflection direction lr # viewdirs points from camera to surface, so incoming light direction is -viewdirs lr = 2.0 torch.sum(normals -viewdirs, dim=-1, keepdim=True) normals + viewdirs lr = F.normalize(lr, dim=-1) # Sample directions within specular lobe (width defined by roughness rho) phi = torch.rand(numsamples, 1) 2 torch.pi costheta = 1.0 - rho torch.rand(numsamples, 1) sintheta = torch.sqrt(torch.clamp(1.0 - costheta2, min=0.0)) localdirs = torch.cat([sintheta torch.cos(phi), costheta, sintheta torch.sin(phi)], dim=-1) # Rotate local cone to align with lr samplesr = F.normalize(lr + localdirs rho, dim=-1) # Evaluate NeIF: R(x, l) -> (c, sigma) # l is the direction from surface to sample ldirs = samplesr - xs ldirs = F.normalize(ldirs, dim=-1) c, sigma = ambientmlp(samplesr, ldirs) # Volume render to get Lin Lin = volumerendering(samplesr, c, sigma) # Compute specular color Cs by multiplying Lin with the material's function # Exact material function not specified in sources Cs = Lin alphaspec (1.0 - rho) # Final color: combine specular and diffuse C = Cd + Cs return C Roughness (\rho): Controls the width of the specular lobe. Range [0, 1]. Near/Far Bounds (tn, tf): Ideally tn \to 0 and tf \to \infty. Material MLP Activation: Softplus for roughness and alpha to ensure positivity. Material-Light Ambiguity: Without background guidance ("w/o BG"), the method reconstructs geometrically correct results but fails to disentangle material and light, resulting in incorrect white balance (e.g., ambiguity between a red object and red incident light). Roughness Limits: As roughness increases, novel views gradually become blurred, even when the roughness becomes extremely large that exceeds the maximum scale of the pre-convolved representation. Near-field Lighting: Methods like Ne-Env assume all radiance comes from infinite distance, leading to poor decomposition for nearby illumination that varies dramatically with position. Time Complexity: The method involves evaluating a neural network for every sample in the specular lobe and performing volume rendering integration. Memory Complexity: Requires storing the parameters for the Ambient MLP and Material MLP. Strengths: Handles environment occlusion and directional lighting naturally; provides photo-realistic views; allows for material editing (roughness, diffuse color); works as a plug-and-play module for existing NeRF pipelines (e.g., Mip-NeRF). Limitations: Struggles with material-light decomposition without background guidance; difficult to model ambient illumination in complex scenarios without sufficient constraints; computationally more expensive than environment map-based methods due to volumetric integration. When to Use: When realistic specular reflections and accurate environmental lighting decomposition are required, especially for placing objects into new NeRF-style environments. When Not to Use: When computational resources are extremely limited and approximate lighting (environment maps) is sufficient; when background information is unavailable and high-fidelity material-light separation is critical. Neural Illumination Fields (NeIF) was proposed to address the limitations of previous illumination representations. Traditional methods like environment maps and Spherical Gaussians assume illumination is infinitely far away, failing to handle environment occlusion and directional lighting practically. Follow-up methods like NeILF modeled incident illumination maps for each surface point but ignored spatial distance constraints, leading to material-lighting ambiguity in complex 3D environments. NeIF builds on the success of Neural Radiance Fields (NeRF) and their ability to recover detailed geometry and material, extending this to a fully differentiable framework for 3D ambient illumination. It was demonstrated as a plug-and-play module for Mip-NeRF, allowing objects to have a better sense of belonging in new 3D environments. name: Multi-Sensor and Physical Priors
body: This family adapts differentiable volume rendering to non-ideal imaging conditions and multi-modal sensor data by replacing or augmenting the standard emission-absorption model with physics-based signal formation equations. Both methods optimize scene representations by backpropagating gradients through a modified rendering operator tailored to specific sensor physics. They replace standard emission-absorption integration with physics-specific accumulation: rigid motion deformation for optical blur DP-NeRF and azimuth-plane summation for SAR Radar Fields, minimizing reconstruction losses against observed inputs. Reconstructs sharp 3D scenes from blurred inputs using 3D physical priors instead of 2D pixel-wise optimization, ensuring geometric and appearance consistency across views. Choose when inputs have known camera poses but suffer from motion or defocus blur. Extends radiance fields to Synthetic Aperture Radar imagery by integrating radar signal contributions across rays in an azimuth plane sharing the same range distance. Choose when reconstructing volumetric surface models from multiple SAR measurements. NeuRAD is a neural rendering method for Autonomous Driving (AD) that integrates camera and LiDAR sensor models. name: DP-NeRF
head: Deblurred Neural Radiance Field with Physical Scene Priors, Rigid Blur Kernel (RBK) & SE(3) Fields
body: DP-NeRF is a framework for reconstructing clean 3D scenes from blurred input images (camera motion blur and defocus blur) by imposing two physical priors derived from the image acquisition process. It differs from prior methods like Deblur-NeRF by using 3D physical priors instead of 2D pixel-wise independent ray optimization, ensuring geometric and appearance consistency across views. Unlike Deblur-NeRF, which predicts a single blurred color, DP-NeRF employs two blurred color predictions to enable a coarse-to-fine optimization strategy. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: A set of blurred RGB images B{sp} with known camera poses (calibrated via COLMAP). Outputs: A trained "sharp" NeRF model capable of rendering clean novel views. Data Structures: The method relies on the standard NeRF representation (MLPs for density \sigma and color \mathbf{c}) augmented with two specific modules: 1. Rigid Blurring Kernel (RBK): Encoding Branch (E): MLP with 4 fully-connected linear layers, each 64 dimensions, ReLU activation. Decoding Branches (W, R, L): Each consists of one linear layer with 32 dimensions and an output linear layer. Outputs: ms: Motion weights, channel dimension k (hyper-parameter controlling the number of rigid camera motions). Normalized such that \sum{i=0}^{k} m{s,i} = 1. rs: Rigid motion parameters, channel dimension 3k. vs: View-specific parameters, channel dimension 3k. Input: View information ls embedded with 64 channels. 2. Adaptive Weight Proposal (AWP): Uses Feature Modulation (FM) and a Motion Feature Aggregation Module (MAM). Inputs: Depth features of samples for transformed rays, viewing direction, and view information. Outputs: Refined composition weights \tilde{m}q for each pixel. Numbered Steps: 1. Coarse Scene Initialization: Train a pure NeRF for 1200 iterations to obtain a coarse scene representation. 2. RBK Processing: For each view, embed view information ls into 64 dimensions. Pass ls through Encoding Branch E. Pass the encoded features through Decoding Branches W, R, L to generate ms, rs, vs. Predict a scene-wise screw axis Sq \in \mathbb{R}^6 via MLP T\Psi(ls), decompose it into rotation axis rq and angle vq, and convert them to rotation matrix e{rq} and translation matrix pq using Rodrigues' formula. Transform ray r to rq = e{rq} r + pq. Compute a coarse blurred color prediction \hat{B}{sp} using the deformation field and the NeRF samples. 3. AWP Processing: For each ray, compute depth features for the transformed samples. Aggregate motion features using MAM based on depth features, viewing direction, and view information. Refine the composition weights using Feature Modulation. Compute a fine blurred color prediction \tilde{B}{sp}. 4. Loss Calculation: Compute the coarse reconstruction loss Lc = ||B{sp} - \hat{B}{sp}|| and fine reconstruction loss Lf = ||B{sp} - \tilde{B}{sp}||. Calculate the exponential decay weight \lambda for the current iteration ec: \alpha = -\log(\lambdas / \lambdae) / (ef - ei) \lambda = \lambdas \exp(\alpha(ec - ei)) where ei is the initial iteration (1200), ef is the final iteration (200,000), \lambdas = 0.9, and \lambdae = 0.1. Compute the final loss: L{final} = \lambda Lc + (1 - \lambda) Lf. 5. Joint Optimization: Optimize the RBK, AWP, and the sharp NeRF parameters jointly using the Adam optimizer. Use only the reconstruction loss from the blurred input as supervision. Train for 200,000 iterations total. 6. Inference: Render clean novel views using only the trained sharp NeRF model, ignoring the RBK and AWP modules. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import torch import torch.nn as nn import torch.nn.functional as F def rodrigues(axis, angle): """Convert rotation axis and angle to rotation matrix using Rodrigues' formula.""" axis = F.normalize(axis, dim=-1) c = torch.cos(angle) s = torch.sin(angle) t = 1 - c x, y, z = axis[..., 0:1], axis[..., 1:2], axis[..., 2:3] R = torch.zeroslike(axis).expand(-1, -1, 3) R[..., 0, 0] = t x2 + c R[..., 0, 1] = t x y - s z R[..., 0, 2] = t x z + s y R[..., 1, 0] = t x y + s z R[..., 1, 1] = t y2 + c R[..., 1, 2] = t y z - s x R[..., 2, 0] = t x z - s y R[..., 2, 1] = t y z + s x R[..., 2, 2] = t z2 + c return R class RBK(nn.Module): def init(self, k): super().init() self.k = k self.enc = nn.Sequential( nn.Linear(64, 64), nn.ReLU(), nn.Linear(64, 64), nn.ReLU(), nn.Linear(64, 64), nn.ReLU(), nn.Linear(64, 64), nn.ReLU()) self.W = nn.Sequential(nn.Linear(64, 32), nn.Linear(32, k)) self.R = nn.Sequential(nn.Linear(64, 32), nn.Linear(32, 3 k)) self.L = nn.Sequential(nn.Linear(64, 32), nn.Linear(32, 3 k)) def forward(self, ls): h = self.enc(ls) ms = self.W(h) rs = self.R(h) vs = self.L(h) ms = F.softmax(ms, dim=-1) return ms, rs, vs class AWP(nn.Module): def init(self): super().init() self.mam = nn.Linear(64 + 3 + 64, 32) self.fm = nn.Linear(32, 1) def forward(self, depthfeatures, viewdir, viewinfo): feat = torch.cat([depthfeatures, viewdir, viewinfo], dim=-1) motionfeat = self.mam(feat) weights = torch.sigmoid(self.fm(motionfeat)) return weights class DPNeRF: def init(self, k=10, ncoarse=64, nfine=64): self.k = k self.ncoarse = ncoarse self.nfine = nfine self.neuralnerf = nn.Sequential( nn.Linear(3, 256), nn.ReLU(), nn.Linear(256, 256), nn.ReLU(), nn.Linear(256, 128), nn.ReLU(), nn.Linear(128, 4) # [sigma, r, g, b]) self.rbk = RBK(k) self.awp = AWP() self.lambdas = 0.9 self.lambdae = 0.1 self.ei = 1200 self.ef = 200000 def volumerender(self, sigma, c, tvals): """Standard volume rendering equation.""" dists = tvals[..., 1:] - tvals[...,:-1] alpha = 1.0 - torch.exp(-sigma dists) trans = torch.cumsum(alpha[...,:-1], dim=-1) weights = alpha (1.0 - trans + 1e-10) color = torch.sum(weights.unsqueeze(-1) c, dim=-2) return color def applyrigidmotion(self, rayo, rayd, rs, vs, ms): """Apply SE(3) transformation to rays using Rodrigues' formula.""" # rs: [B, 3k], vs: [B, 3k], ms: [B, k] # Reshape for batch processing rs = rs.view(-1, self.k, 3) vs = vs.view(-1, self.k, 3) ms = ms.view(-1, self.k, 1) # Normalize angles to [0, pi] for Rodrigues angles = torch.norm(vs, dim=-1, keepdim=True) axes = vs / (angles + 1e-8) Rq = rodrigues(axes, angles) Tq = rs # Translation component # Transform ray origins and directions rayodeformed = torch.einsum('bki,bn->bnki', Rq, rayo) + Tq.unsqueeze(1) rayddeformed = torch.einsum('bki,bn->bnki', Rq, rayd) # Weighted composition of deformed rays ms = ms.unsqueeze(1) rayofinal = torch.sum(ms rayodeformed, dim=2) raydfinal = torch.sum(ms rayddeformed, dim=2) return rayofinal, raydfinal def computeblurredcolor(self, rayo, rayd, tnear, tfar, viewinfo): tvals = torch.linspace(tnear, tfar, self.ncoarse + self.nfine) xyz = rayo.unsqueeze(0) + rayd.unsqueeze(0) tvals.unsqueeze(1) # Standard NeRF forward pass out = self.neuralnerf(xyz.view(-1, 3)) sigma = torch.relu(out[...,:1]).view(xyz.shape[:-1]) c = torch.sigmoid(out[..., 1:4]).view(xyz.shape[:-1], 3) # RBK: Coarse prediction ms, rs, vs = self.rbk(viewinfo) rayodeform, rayddeform = self.applyrigidmotion(rayo, rayd, rs, vs, ms) xyzdeform = rayodeform.unsqueeze(0) + rayddeform.unsqueeze(0) tvals.unsqueeze(1) outdeform = self.neuralnerf(xyzdeform.view(-1, 3)) sigmadeform = torch.relu(outdeform[...,:1]).view(xyzdeform.shape[:-1]) cdeform = torch.sigmoid(outdeform[..., 1:4]).view(xyzdeform.shape[:-1], 3) Bhat = self.volumerender(sigmadeform, cdeform, tvals) # AWP: Fine prediction depthfeatures = tvals.unsqueeze(-1) # Depth proxy viewdir = rayd.unsqueeze(0).expandas(depthfeatures) weights = self.awp(depthfeatures, viewdir, viewinfo) Btilde = self.volumerender(sigma, c, tvals) weights return Bhat, Btilde def trainstep(self, rayo, rayd, tnear, tfar, viewinfo, gtblurredrgb, currentiter): Bhat, Btilde = self.computeblurredcolor(rayo, rayd, tnear, tfar, viewinfo) Lc = torch.norm(gtblurredrgb - Bhat) Lf = torch.norm(gtblurredrgb - Btilde) alpha = -torch.log(torch.tensor(self.lambdas / self.lambdae)) / (self.ef - self.ei) lam = self.lambdas torch.exp(alpha (currentiter - self.ei)) Lfinal = lam Lc + (1 - lam) Lf return Lfinal Parameters: \lambdas: Initial weight for coarse-to-fine optimization, set to 0.9. \lambdae: Final weight for coarse-to-fine optimization, set to 0.1. k: Hyper-parameter controlling the number of rigid camera motions in the RBK. Output channel dimensions for ms, rs, vs are k, 3k, 3k respectively. Nc, Nf: Number of coarse and fine samples, set to 64 each. Learning Rate: Exponentially decays from 5 \times 10^{-4} to 8 \times 10^{-5}. Optimizer: Adam with default parameters. Image Resolution: Resized to 600 \times 400. Total Iterations: 200,000. RBK Training Start: After 1200 iterations of pure NeRF training. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Object Motion Blur: The model assumes a static scene. It fails to reconstruct correct geometry for moving objects because it lacks multi-view data for a specific time instance. Complex Depth/Textures: The RBK alone may lose detail in regions with complex depth or similar textures; the AWP is required to refine these areas. Depth Prior Inaccuracy: Blur in each image makes predicted depth inaccurate and inconsistent across multiple views, hindering the usability of external depth priors. Time Complexity: Training involves joint optimization of NeRF, RBK, and AWP. The coarse-to-fine strategy stabilizes training but adds computational overhead due to the two parallel prediction paths (RBK and AWP) per ray. Memory Complexity: Standard NeRF memory usage plus overhead for RBK and AWP parameters. The RBK parameters are view-dependent but not ray-dependent, keeping memory usage manageable compared to per-pixel kernel methods. Performance: DP-NeRF achieves significant improvements in PSNR, SSIM, and LPIPS over Naive NeRF and Deblur-NeRF on synthetic and real scenes with camera motion and defocus blur. Strengths: Ensures 3D geometric and appearance consistency by using 3D physical priors (RBK) instead of 2D pixel-wise optimization. Handles both camera motion and defocus blur. Limitations: Cannot handle object motion blur due to the static scene assumption. Requires calibrated camera poses (COLMAP). DP-NeRF is a NeRF framework for reconstructing clean 3D scenes from blurred inputs. It was developed to address the limitations of previous deblurring NeRF methods, specifically Deblur-NeRF, which relied on 2D pixel-wise independent ray optimization that broke 3D consistency. The method builds on the standard NeRF framework and incorporates physical priors derived from the camera blurring process. It is used for novel view synthesis on synthetic and real scenes with blur. name: Radar Fields
head: SAR Radiance Fields
body: Radar Fields is a differentiable rendering framework that extends radiance fields to Synthetic Aperture Radar (SAR) imagery, enabling the learning of volumetric surface models from multiple SAR measurements. Unlike optical radiance fields that integrate radiance along individual rays, Radar Fields integrates radar signal contributions across all rays within a given azimuth plane that share the same range distance. This method solves the problem of 3D reconstruction from SAR data by adapting the volume rendering equation to the specific physics of SAR image formation, where the integration dimension is swapped from the ray direction to the azimuth direction. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: A collection of SAR images of a scene from different viewpoints; satellite poses (positions and orientations). Outputs: A learned surface model of the scene, represented as a Digital Surface Model (DSM) or implicit function, and optionally surface properties like specularity. Data Structures: Surface Model: The surface is defined by a Digital Surface Model (DSM) function dsm: [0, 1]^2 \rightarrow [0, 1] mapping 2D coordinates to height. The implicit function is defined as F(x) = z - dsm(x, y) for x=(x,y,z) \in [0,1]^3. Implementation: The DSM is rasterized into an image where each pixel represents the height value, and these pixel values are directly optimized during training. Subpixel heights are estimated using bilinear interpolation of the nearest values, and surface normals are computed accordingly. Ray Data: For each azimuth plane, a set of rays rj is defined by origin oj and direction vj. Distance samples di are fixed by the SAR range sampling. Parameters: Specularity Parameter (\theta): Used in the reflection model s = -\langle v|n \rangle^\theta. \theta=1 corresponds to a Lambertian surface; larger values represent specular surfaces. This parameter can be learned alongside the surface location. Training Hyperparameters: 10,000 optimization steps; initial learning rate 1.0, reduced to 0.1 at epoch 5,000, and to 10^{-2} at step 8,000. Azimuth planes are sampled uniformly and batched in groups of 64, with 256 rays sampled per azimuth plane. Algorithm Steps: 1. Ray Sampling: For a given azimuth plane, sample a set of rays rj with origins oj and directions vj. The distance sampling di is fixed by the SAR data's range resolution. 2. Ray Origin Perturbation: To improve optimization performance, perturb the ray origin. Let wj be the vector orthogonal to vj inside the azimuth plane. The perturbed origin is \tilde{o}j = oj + n wj, where n \sim \mathcal{N}(0, 1). 3. Signal Computation: For each ray rj and distance sample di, compute the sensed signal s{rj}(di). This involves evaluating the density \sigma{i,j} and normal n{i,j} at the intersection point, and applying the reflection model: s{rj}(di) = -T{i,j} \sigma{i,j} \langle vj | n{i,j} \rangle^\theta where T{i,j} is the transmittance along ray j up to sample i. 4. Azimuth Integration: Batch all rays belonging to the same azimuth plane. Compute the total signal for a pixel at distance di by summing the contributions from all rays j in that plane: s(di) = \sumj s{rj}(di) = \sumj -T{i,j} \sigma{i,j} \langle vj | n{i,j} \rangle^\theta Note that the index j (ray) is summed over, while i (distance) defines the pixel. 5. Loss Computation: Compare the rendered signal s(di) with the observed SAR intensity I. For single-channel single-look intensity images, model the speckle noise as multiplicative: I = n \times R, where R is the noise-free reflectance and n \sim \Gamma(1, 1). Minimize the difference between the rendered signal and the observed intensity. 6. Optimization: Back-propagate the loss to update the DSM pixel values and the specularity parameter \theta. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import torch import torch.nn as nn import math class RadarField: def init(self, dsmimage, cameraposes, azimuthplanes): """Initialize Radar Field.""" self.dsm = nn.Parameter(dsmimage.clone().float()) self.theta = nn.Parameter(torch.tensor(1.0)) self.cameraposes = cameraposes self.azimuthplanes = azimuthplanes def getsurfacenormal(self, x, y): """Compute surface normal from DSM using finite differences.""" h = self.dsm[y, x] dzdx = (self.dsm[y, x + 1] - self.dsm[y, x - 1]) / 2.0 dzdy = (self.dsm[y + 1, x] - self.dsm[y - 1, x]) / 2.0 normal = torch.stack([-dzdx, -dzdy, torch.oneslike(h)], dim=-1) return torch.nn.functional.normalize(normal, dim=-1) def renderazimuthplane(self, azimuthplane, rays, distancesamples): """Render signal for a single azimuth plane by integrating across rays.""" renderedsignal = torch.zeroslike(distancesamples) for j, (origin, direction) in enumerate(rays): # Perturb ray origin: wj orthogonal to vj in azimuth plane w = getorthogonalvector(direction, azimuthplane) nnoise = torch.randn(1) perturbedorigin = origin + nnoise w accumulatedopacity = torch.zeroslike(distancesamples) for i, di in enumerate(distancesamples): # Sample point at fixed distance point = perturbedorigin + di direction x, y = projecttodsm(point) # Get density and normal sigma = computedensity(self.dsm, x, y) normal = getsurfacenormal(x, y) # Compute transmittance T{i,j} accumulatedopacity[i] += sigma (distancesamples[min(i+1, len(distancesamples)-1)] - distancesamples[i]) T = torch.exp(-accumulatedopacity[i]) # Compute reflection signal cosangle = torch.dot(direction, normal) signal = -T sigma torch.pow(cosangle, self.theta) # Accumulate across rays for the same distance sample renderedsignal[i] += signal return renderedsignal def forward(self, azimuthplaneidx): """Forward pass for optimization.""" azimuthplane = self.azimuthplanes[azimuthplaneidx] rays = samplerays(azimuthplane, numrays=256) distancesamples = getsarrangesamples(azimuthplane) rendered = self.renderazimuthplane(azimuthplane, rays, distancesamples) observed = getobservedsarintensity(azimuthplane) # Loss computation with speckle noise model loss = torch.mean((rendered - observed) 2) return loss def computeloss(rendered, observed): """Compute loss based on multiplicative speckle noise model.""" return torch.mean((rendered - observed) 2) def getorthogonalvector(v, planenormal): return torch.cross(v, planenormal) def projecttodsm(point): x, y, z = point return x, y def computedensity(dsm, x, y): return torch.abs(torch.linalg.norm(torch.stack([ (dsm[y, x+1] - dsm[y, x-1])/2, (dsm[y+1, x] - dsm[y-1, x])/2, torch.oneslike(x) ]))) def samplerays(azimuthplane, numrays): return [(torch.rand(3), torch.rand(3)) for in range(numrays)] def getsarrangesamples(azimuthplane): return torch.linspace(0, 1, 256) def getobservedsarintensity(azimuthplane): return torch.rand(256) Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Fixed Sampling: Unlike NeRF, fixed uniform sampling along rays is not possible because the sampling step is defined by the SAR range sampling. Noise must be added to the ray origin instead. Multi-bounce Effects: Signals from double or multiple bounces appear at incorrect positions (e.g., signal from A->B->receiver appears at C). The generic case violates the zero-doppler assumption, requiring batching multiple azimuth planes, which is highly unfeasible without strong priors. Complex Data: SAR raw data stores complex numbers separating amplitude and phase. The method primarily focuses on intensity images, but phase contains satellite-target path delay modulo the wavelength. Time Complexity: The computational complexity remains similar to standard radiance fields on average, with the primary difference being the batching requirement. All rays of a given azimuth plane must be batched together during computation. Memory Complexity: Not explicitly given, but batching all rays in an azimuth plane may increase memory usage compared to per-ray processing in optical NeRF. Performance: Reconstruction errors are in the order of 10^{-2} pixels relative to ground pixel resolution. Strengths: Enables 3D reconstruction from SAR data, which has day-night and cloud-penetrating capabilities. Does not prescribe geometric configuration, allowing opportunistic acquisitions. Limitations: Multi-bounce effects are not fully handled in the generic case. Requires batching rays by azimuth plane, which may limit scalability. Radar Fields was introduced in the paper "Radar Fields: An Extension of Radiance Fields to SAR". The method extends the concept of radiance fields to Synthetic Aperture Radar (SAR) imagery. SAR systems use side-looking geometry and emit electromagnetic pulses, receiving echoes backscattered by the ground surface. The resulting images are complex-valued, with amplitude related to ground reflectivity and angle, and phase containing path delay information. The method was developed to leverage the widespread availability of SAR data for global 3D reconstruction. name: LiDAR-NeRF
head: LiDAR Neural Radiance Fields, LiDAR-NeRF Framework, LiDAR-NeRF with iNGP, LiDAR-NeRF with standard NeRF, Neural Radiance Fields for LiDAR
body: LiDAR-NeRF is a differentiable end-to-end framework for novel LiDAR view synthesis that leverages a neural radiance field to jointly learn geometry and 3D point attributes (distance, intensity, ray-drop probability) without explicit 3D reconstruction. It reformulates NeRF to model LiDAR sensor characteristics, synthesizing realistic geometry (distance), intensity, and ray-drop probability. Unlike traditional NeRFs which focus on individual pixels and ignore local information leading to poor geometry in low-texture areas, LiDAR-NeRF incorporates structural regularization to preserve local details. It outperforms explicit 3D reconstruction and ray-tracing baselines because explicit methods neglect crucial LiDAR features like beam penetration through glass and loss due to surface material/normal direction. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A set of LiDAR point clouds from multiple viewpoints. These are converted into 360-degree range pseudo images (range images) where each pseudo-pixel represents the distance between the LiDAR receiver and a world point hit by a laser beam. Output: A synthesized novel LiDAR view consisting of a range image (distance), an intensity map, and a ray-drop probability map. Data Structures: The radiance field is represented by a function f(x, \theta) that outputs three values: 1. Density \sigma 2. Expected distance d 3. A two-channel feature map containing intensity i and ray-drop probability p. Preprocessing: 1. Centering: Center the LiDAR point clouds by subtracting the origin of the global world coordinate system from the scene’s central frame. 2. Scaling: Scale the scene frames by a factor such that the region of interest falls within a unit cube, which is required by most positional encodings used in NeRFs. 3. Ray Direction Calculation: For each pseudo-pixel (h, w) in the H \times W range pseudo image, calculate the laser viewing direction \theta using angular coordinates (\alpha, \beta): \begin{pmatrix} \alpha \\ \beta \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} |f{up}| - h fv H^{-1} \\ -(2w - W) \pi W^{-1} \end{pmatrix} where fv = |f{down}| + |f{up}| is the vertical field-of-view. 4. Coordinate Transformation: Transform ray origin o and viewing direction \theta to the global world coordinate system so sampled points t are consistent across multiple LiDAR frames. Rendering Process: For a ray r, sample N points ti along the ray. Calculate the distance between adjacent samples \deltai = t{i+1} - ti. Compute accumulated transmittance Ti = \exp(-\sum{j=1}^{i-1} \sigmaj \deltaj). The rendered expected depth \hat{D}(r), intensity I(r), and ray-drop probability \hat{P}(r) are computed as: \hat{D}(r) = \sum{i=1}^{N} Ti (1 - \exp(-\sigmai \deltai)) ti I(r) = \sum{i=1}^{N} Ti (1 - \exp(-\sigmai \deltai)) ii \hat{P}(r) = \sum{i=1}^{N} Ti (1 - \exp(-\sigmai \deltai)) pi where ii is the intensity feature and pi is the ray-drop probability feature at sample i. Loss Function: The total loss is defined as: L{total} = L{distance} + \lambda1 L{intensity}(r) + \lambda2 L{raydrop}(r) + \lambda3 L{reg} where: L{distance}(r) = \sum{r \in R} || \hat{D}(r) - D(r) ||1 L{intensity}(r) = \sum{r \in R} || I(r) - I{gt}(r) ||2^2 L{raydrop}(r) = \sum{r \in R} || \hat{P}(r) - P{gt}(r) ||2^2 R is the set of training rays. Structural Regularization: Standard geometry regularization (smoothness-loss, TV-loss) is ineffective in large-scale scenes where differences between neighboring points are significant. Standard gradient loss is dominated by rich-texture areas. LiDAR-NeRF proposes a structural regularization strategy that restricts gradient loss to low-texture areas (e.g., ground) to guide NeRF geometry. L{reg} = || \hat{G}M(R) - GM(R) ||1 where GM(\cdot) denotes the gradient operation with a low-texture areas mask. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def computeaccumulatedtransmittance(sigma, deltas): """Ti = exp(-sum{j=1}^{i-1} sigmaj deltaj)""" T = [1.0] for i in range(1, len(sigma)): T.append(T[-1] math.exp(-sigma[i-1] deltas[i-1])) return T def queryradiancefield(point, direction): """Returns (sigma, expecteddistance, intensity, raydropprobability) from the trained MLPs.""" # Implementation depends on the specific network architecture (e.g., hash grid + MLP or standard MLP) # Returns the four predicted values for the given 3D point and viewing direction. pass def samplepointsalongray(origin, direction, numsamples): """Samples points ti along the ray and returns positions and inter-sample distances.""" # Assumes uniform sampling along the ray direction for simplicity tvals = [i (1.0 / numsamples) for i in range(1, numsamples + 1)] samples = [(origin[0] + t direction[0], origin[1] + t direction[1], origin[2] + t direction[2]) for t in tvals] deltas = [tvals[i] - tvals[i-1] for i in range(1, len(tvals))] deltas.insert(0, tvals[0]) return samples, deltas, tvals def renderlidarview(rayorigins, raydirections, coarsesamples, finesamples): """Renders depth, intensity, and ray-drop probability for a batch of rays.""" rendereddepths, renderedintensities, renderedraydrops = [], [], [] for origin, direction in zip(rayorigins, raydirections): # Coarse pass samples, deltas, tvals = samplepointsalongray(origin, direction, coarsesamples) sigma, d, intensity, raydrop = [], [], [], [] for x in samples: s, dist, ival, pval = queryradiancefield(x, direction) sigma.append(s); d.append(dist); intensity.append(ival); raydrop.append(pval) T = computeaccumulatedtransmittance(sigma, deltas) weights = [T[i] (1.0 - math.exp(-sigma[i] deltas[i])) for i in range(len(sigma))] depth = sum(w tvals[i] for w, i in zip(weights, range(len(tvals)))) intensityout = sum(w intensity[i] for w, i in zip(weights, range(len(intensity)))) raydropout = sum(w raydrop[i] for w, i in zip(weights, range(len(raydrop)))) rendereddepths.append(depth) renderedintensities.append(intensityout) renderedraydrops.append(raydropout) return rendereddepths, renderedintensities, renderedraydrops def computestructuralregularizationloss(rendereddepth, groundtruthdepth, lowtexturemask): """Lreg = || GM(R) - GM(Rgt) ||1""" # Apply gradient mask to restrict regularization to low-texture areas gradrendered = [abs(rendereddepth[i] - rendereddepth[i-1]) if mask else 0.0 for i, mask in enumerate(lowtexturemask)] gtgrad = [abs(groundtruthdepth[i] - groundtruthdepth[i-1]) if mask else 0.0 for i, mask in enumerate(lowtexturemask)] return sum(abs(a - b) for a, b in zip(gradrendered, gtgrad)) / len(lowtexturemask) A specialized neural network design for LiDAR-based NeRF that jointly learns geometry and 3D point attributes (distance, intensity, ray-drop probability) without explicit 3D reconstruction. It distinguishes itself from standard NeRF variants by integrating a 3D sparse UNet for LiDAR geometry encoding with a multi-resolution hash grid for density prediction, enabling efficient processing of sparse LiDAR point clouds. Choose this architecture when efficient processing of sparse LiDAR data is required for differentiable LiDAR view synthesis. Builds on LiDAR-NeRF by providing the specific network components required for differentiable LiDAR view synthesis. Time and Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Measured Performance: LiDAR-NeRF (w iNGP): Implemented based on torch-ngp. Optimized per scene using a single NVIDIA GeForce RTX 3090 GPU. Total of 30k steps. Coarse network samples 768 samples per ray; fine network samples 64 samples per ray. Hash encoding finest resolution: 32768. Patch-wise training with patch size 2x8 and mask gradients smaller than threshold 0.1. LiDAR-NeRF (w NeRF): Implemented based on nerf-pytorch. Optimized for 400k iterations with batch size 2048. Coarse network samples 64 times; fine network samples 128 times. Highest frequency of coordinates set to 2^{15}. Strengths and Limitations: Strengths: Enables end-to-end optimization without explicit 3D reconstruction or game engine usage. Produces realistic LiDAR patterns by accounting for beam penetration through glass and loss due to surface material/normal direction. Outperforms explicit 3D reconstruction and ray-tracing baselines (LiDARsim, PCGen). Limitations: Standard geometry regularization techniques (smoothness-loss, TV-loss) are ineffective in large-scale scenes. Standard gradient loss is dominated by rich-texture areas, making it insufficient for guiding geometry in low-texture regions without structural regularization. When to use: Use for novel LiDAR view synthesis where realistic geometry, intensity, and ray-drop probability are required, particularly where explicit reconstruction fails to capture LiDAR-specific artifacts. LiDAR-NeRF was introduced by Tang Tao, Longfei Gao, Guangrun Wang, Yixing Lao, Peng Chen, Hengshuang Zhao, Dayang Hao, Xiaodan Liang, Mathieu Salzmann, and Kaicheng Yu in "LiDAR-NeRF: Novel LiDAR View Synthesis via Neural Radiance Fields" (arXiv:2304.10406v2, July 14, 2023). The work addresses the challenge that traditional model-based LiDAR simulators suffer from limited scalability and fail to produce realistic LiDAR patterns, while traditional NeRFs are not directly applicable to point clouds. The authors established an object-centric synthesis approach for traffic objects to validate the framework. name: LidaRF Network Architecture
head: LidaRF
body: The LidaRF network architecture is a specialized neural network design for LiDAR-based Neural Radiance Fields (NeRF) that jointly learns geometry and 3D point attributes (distance, intensity, ray-drop probability) without explicit 3D reconstruction. It distinguishes itself from standard NeRF variants by integrating a 3D sparse UNet for LiDAR geometry encoding with a multi-resolution hash grid for density prediction, enabling efficient processing of sparse LiDAR point clouds. This method builds on LiDAR-NeRF by providing the specific network components required for differentiable LiDAR view synthesis. Inputs: A set of LiDAR points (3D coordinates). Sampled 3D positions along rays for volume rendering. Outputs: Density values (\sigma) for each sampled position. A 15-dimensional density embedding for each sampled position. RGB color values for each sampled position (via the color network, which uses the density embedding). 1. Hash Grid (for Proposal Sampler and Density Network) Structure: A multi-resolution hash table mapping 3D coordinates to feature vectors. Layout: Levels: L levels of resolution. Resolution per Level: Minimum resolution N{min}, Maximum resolution N{max}. Feature Dimension: F{hash} dimensions per level. Encoding: Hash encoding maps 3D positions to specific entries in the grid. 2. Sparse Voxel Grid (for LiDAR Encoding) Structure: A 3D grid of cells. Size: 512 \times 512 \times 512 cells. Cell Content: Mean 3D position of LiDAR points falling within the cell. Empty cells are ignored by sparse convolution. 3. Sparse UNet Features Encoder Layers: Feature dimensions [32, 64, 96, 128]. Decoder Layers: Feature dimensions [128, 96, 64, 64]. Output: LiDAR features from the final decoder layer. 4. MLP Layers Proposal Sampler MLP: 2 layers, 16 hidden features. Density Network MLP: 2 layers, 64 hidden features. Color Network MLP: 2 layers, 64 hidden features (implied by context of predicting RGB from embedding). 1. Scene Bounding Sphere Definition: Define a sphere bounding the scene. The diameter is the maximum distance between any two camera positions in the training log plus 50 meters. 2. LiDAR Point Voxelization: Input: All LiDAR points. Process: Voxelize points into a 512 \times 512 \times 512 grid. Feature Assignment: For each non-empty cell, compute the mean 3D position of the LiDAR points contained within it. This mean position serves as the initial feature for the cell. 3. LiDAR Geometry Encoding (Sparse UNet): Input: The voxelized LiDAR features. Process: Pass features through a 3D sparse UNet. Encoder: Applies sparse convolutions with feature dimensions [32, 64, 96, 128]. Decoder: Applies sparse convolutions with feature dimensions [128, 96, 64, 64]. Skip Connections: Integrate skip connections and multi-level feature fusion between encoder and decoder stages. Output: LiDAR features from the final layer of the UNet. 4. Proposal Sampling: Structure: Two consecutive "fused" MLPs. Hash Grid Parameters: Minimum resolution: 16. Levels: 5. Feature dimension per level: 2. MLP: 2 layers, 16 hidden features. Distinction: First MLP set: Maximum hash grid resolution 512. Second MLP set: Maximum hash grid resolution 1024. Process: 1. Query hash encoding for 3D positions. 2. Pass hash features through the fused MLP to predict density. 3. Use the predicted density to sample points (proposal sampling). 5. Density Network Processing: Hash Grid Parameters: Minimum resolution: 16. Maximum resolution: 4096. Levels: 16. Feature dimension per level: 2. MLP Parameters: 2 layers, 64 hidden features. Process: 1. Compute hash encoding for sampled 3D positions. 2. Query hash features from the grid. 3. Concatenate hash features with LiDAR features (output from Step 3). 4. Pass concatenated features through the Density Network MLP. Output: Density value (\sigma). 15-dimensional density embedding. 6. Color Network Processing: Input: Density embedding (from Step 5) and potentially other attributes (implied by context of RGB prediction). MLP Parameters: 2 layers, 64 hidden features. Output: RGB value for the sampled position. Hash Encoding: Standard multi-resolution hash encoding is used. For a position \mathbf{x}, the feature is computed by hashing \mathbf{x} to indices in grids of varying resolutions Nl for l=1 \dots L, and interpolating the features at those indices. Loss Weights: The optimization uses a weighted loss function with the following weights: \lambda1 = 0.0005 \lambda2 = 1 \lambda3 = 0.005 \lambda4 = 1 Unnormalized Scale Epsilon Values: Used for normalization or scaling in the loss/optimization: \epsilon{0t} = 10\text{m} \epsilon{t} = 100\text{m} \epsilon{0o} = 1\text{m} \epsilon{o} = 0.15\text{m} \epsilon{n} = 0.15\text{m} \epsilon{a} = 1.5\text{m} Scheduling Rates: \alphat = 1.00004 \alphao = 0.99995 Optimization Parameters: Algorithm: RAdam. Iterations: 100,000. Learning Rate: Initial 0.01, reduced to 0.0001. Scheduler max limit 50,000 iterations. Sampling: 4,096 points per iteration. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import torch import torch.nn as nn import torchsparse import torchsparse.nn as spnn class LidaRFNetwork(nn.Module): def init(self): super(LidaRFNetwork, self).init() # 1. Proposal Sampler # Two consecutive fused MLPs with hash encoding # Shared params: minres=16, levels=5, featdim=2, mlplayers=2, mlphidden=16 self.proposalsampler1 = FusedMLPHash( minres=16, maxres=512, levels=5, featdim=2, mlphidden=16) self.proposalsampler2 = FusedMLPHash( minres=16, maxres=1024, levels=5, featdim=2, mlphidden=16) # 2. LiDAR Encoding (Sparse UNet) # Encoder dims: [32, 64, 96, 128] # Decoder dims: [128, 96, 64, 64] self.lidarencoder = SparseUNet( inchannels=1, # Mean position scalar or vector? Note says "mean 3D positions", likely 3 channels or processed separately. # Assuming 3 channels for 3D mean position for simplicity, or 1 if processed as scalar features. # Source says "cell features represented by the mean 3D positions". # Sparse UNet typically takes tensor. Let's assume 3 channels. encoderdims=[32, 64, 96, 128], decoderdims=[128, 96, 64, 64]) # 3. Memory: The hash grid memory usage depends on the number of levels and resolutions. The density network uses 16 levels with 2-dim features, and the proposal sampler uses 5 levels with 2-dim features. Hash encoding is O(1) per query. The MLPs are small (2 layers, 16-64 hidden units), so they are fast. The LidaRF network architecture was introduced in the paper "LidaRF: Delving into Lidar for Neural Radiance Field on Street Scenes". LidaRF is part of the LiDAR-NeRF framework, which aims to synthesize novel LiDAR views using neural radiance fields. It builds on previous work in NeRF and LiDAR processing, integrating sparse convolution and hash encoding for efficiency and accuracy. Used in autonomous driving and street scene reconstruction, specifically for novel view synthesis of LiDAR data. name: Deformable and Dynamic Fields
body: Deformable and Dynamic Fields extend static radiance field optimization to model scenes that change over time or undergo non-rigid deformation. Unlike static methods that assume fixed geometry, these methods introduce a temporal or deformation component to map input coordinates to a canonical space, enabling novel view synthesis for moving or deforming objects. They are distinguished from static voxel methods and static MLP-based methods by their explicit handling of motion through learned warp fields or displacement mappings. All methods in this family rely on the differentiability of the forward rendering operator and the propagation of gradients through the integration steps. The core mechanism evaluates the volume rendering equation and computes gradients with respect to scene parameters (density, geometry, transfer functions, camera poses). The standard emission-absorption model computes the color \hat{C}(\mathbf{r}) for a ray \mathbf{r} as: \hat{C}(\mathbf{r}) = \sum{i=1}^N Ti (1 - \exp(-\sigmai \deltai)) \mathbf{c}i where \sigmai is the density, \deltai is the step size, \mathbf{c}i is the color, and Ti = \exp\left(-\sum{j=1}^{i-1} \sigmaj \deltaj\right) is the transmittance. Differentiation strategies fall into three main categories: 1. Reverse-Mode Automatic Differentiation (AD) uses standard backpropagation through the computational graph. 2. The Adjoint Method computes gradients by propagating adjoint variables backward through the rendering algorithm, evaluating the chain rule from output to input. 3. Analytic Inversion or Explicit Gradients uses a-priori knowledge of the DVR operations to invert the order of operations or derive closed-form gradients, reducing memory consumption to O(n) by avoiding the storage of intermediate results. Neural Volumes (NV) synthesizes novel views of dynamic scenes by optimizing a deep 3D convolutional network to predict a discretized RGB\alpha voxel grid and a 3D warp field [912-neural-volumes.md]. It solves the problem of rendering semi-transparent, dynamic objects (such as smoke or hair) from sparse multi-view video input without requiring explicit geometry reconstruction or depth sensors [912-neural-volumes.md]. Unlike implicit radiance fields that map coordinates to color via MLPs, NV uses an explicit voxel grid, trading memory for rendering speed and interpretability [912-neural-volumes.md]. It sets itself apart from static voxel methods by introducing a learnable warp field to model non-rigid motion and from MLP-based methods by avoiding the prohibitive computational cost of evaluating deep networks at every ray-marching step [912-neural-volumes.md]. EndoNeRF is a method for deformable surgical scene reconstruction that utilizes a canonical radiance field and a time-dependent displacement field, optimized with stereo depth-cueing and supervision. It addresses the challenge of reconstructing non-rigid tissue dynamics in endoscopic videos by mapping input space-time coordinates to a static canonical space via a learned displacement field. Unlike static radiance field methods, it explicitly models temporal deformation, allowing for the querying of radiance and density at any continuous time step. A computational framework to efficiently reconstruct a temporally coherent sequence of fluid density fields from monocular video, aligning density fields with input images while conforming to physical priors [10672-fluid-motion-reconstruction-framework.md]. An adaptation of the binary feature encoding technique applied to time-aware voxel features to enable highly compact reconstruction of dynamic scenes without conventional dense feature encoding. 1. Initialize TiNeuVox base model with time-aware voxel features. 2. Replace conventional feature encoding with binary feature encoding on the voxel grid. 3. Train the model on dynamic scene datasets (D-NeRF, HyperNeRF). 4. Evaluate storage size and reconstruction metrics. TiNeuVox-S on D-NeRF (synthetic): Size reduced from 7.63 MB to 0.59 MB; PSNR drops from 31.03 to 28.68; SSIM drops from 0.957 to 0.938. TiNeuVox-B on D-NeRF (synthetic): Size reduced from 47.51 MB to 3.88 MB; PSNR drops from 33.02 to 31.23; SSIM drops from 0.972 to 0.961. TiNeuVox-B on HyperNeRF (real): Size reduced from 47.85 MB to 3.90 MB; PSNR drops from 24.20 to 23.87; MS-SSIM drops from 0.835 to 0.826. Achieves 0.6 MB storage for the synthetic jumpingjacks dynamic scene. The need for dynamic scene representation arises from the limitations of static NeRF-like methods in capturing temporal variations. Neural Volumes [912-neural-volumes.md] was among the early works to introduce explicit voxel grids with warp fields for dynamic scenes. EndoNeRF [5540-endonerf.md] later adapted these concepts for the specific challenges of endoscopic surgery, such as non-rigid tissue deformation and limited viewpoint coverage. name: Neural Volumes
head: Deformable Volumes, Neural Volumes: Learning Dynamic Renderable Volumes from Images, Volumetric Reconstruction with Ray Potentials
body: Neural Volumes (NV) is a method for synthesizing novel views of dynamic scenes by optimizing a deep 3D convolutional network to predict a discretized RGB\alpha voxel grid and a 3D warp field. It solves the problem of rendering semi-transparent, non-rigidly deforming objects (such as smoke or hair) from sparse multi-view video inputs without requiring explicit geometry or texture maps. It differs from previous ray potential works by modeling voxel transparency rather than occupancy probability, focusing on rendering rather than reconstruction. It uses an explicit voxel grid decoded from a latent code, avoiding the prohibitive computational cost of evaluating large MLPs at every ray-marching step. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: A set of K synchronized, calibrated RGB images from different viewpoints for each time instant (typically K=3 orthogonal views). Outputs: A rendered RGB image for a novel camera pose, and a latent code z representing the scene state. Data Structures: 1. Voxel Grid (V): A discrete 3D grid of size D \times D \times D (typically 128^3) storing RGBA values. Layout: Tensor Y \in \mathbb{R}^{D \times D \times D \times 4}. Values: \mathbf{V}{\text{rgb}} \in \mathbb{R}^3 (color) and \mathbf{V}{\alpha} \in \mathbb{R} (differential opacity, range [0, \infty]). 2. Warp Grid (W): A discrete 3D grid of size Nw \times Nw \times Nw (typically 32^3) storing inverse warp vectors. Layout: Tensor storing the inverse transformation W^{-1}(\mathbf{x}) for each voxel center. 3. Latent Code (z): A vector z \in \mathbb{R}^{256} representing the scene state at a specific time instant. Network Architecture: 1. Encoder: A CNN processes each of the K input images through dedicated branches. Outputs are concatenated and encoded into the parameters of a diagonal 256-dimensional Gaussian (\mu, \sigma). 2. Latent Sampling: An instance z is sampled from the Gaussian using the reparameterization trick. 3. Decoder: A 3D convolutional network (or linear basis decoder) maps z to the Voxel Grid V and the Warp Grid W. Activation: Softplus is used to ensure non-negative opacity values. Rendering (Differentiable Ray Marching): For a camera ray \mathbf{r}, the color \hat{C}(\mathbf{r}) and accumulated opacity \hat{A}(\mathbf{r}) are computed by marching through the warped voxel grid. 1. Warping: For a sample point \mathbf{x} along the ray, the inverse warp field W^{-1}(\mathbf{x}) is sampled. This maps the world-space position to a position in the template (canonical) space. Note: The warp field can be modeled as a mixture of affine transformations in warp space. 2. Sampling: The RGBA values are sampled from the Voxel Grid at the warped position: (\mathbf{c}, \alpha) = V(W^{-1}(\mathbf{x})). 3. Accumulation: Values are accumulated front-to-back using alpha blending: \hat{C}(\mathbf{r}) = \sum{j} \mathbf{c}j \cdot \alphaj \cdot \prod{k<j} (1 - \alphak) \hat{A}(\mathbf{r}) = 1 - \prod{j} (1 - \alphaj) where \mathbf{c}j and \alphaj are the color and differential opacity at the j-th sample. Training: The system is trained end-to-end by minimizing the reconstruction loss between the rendered image and the input image. Loss Function: \mathcal{L}(\theta) = \| I{\text{rgb}} - I^{\text{rgb}} \|2^2 + \beta \cdot D{KL}(z \| \mathcal{N}(0,1)) + \lambda{tv} J{tv}(\mathbf{V}{\alpha}) + \lambdaB JB(I{\alpha}) \| I{\text{rgb}} - I^{\text{rgb}} \|2^2: L2 pixel reconstruction error. D{KL}(z \| \mathcal{N}(0,1)): KL-divergence regularization for the latent code. J{tv}(\mathbf{V}{\alpha}): Total variation regularization on opacity to encourage sharp boundaries. JB(I{\alpha}): Beta distribution prior on accumulated opacity to encourage binary transparency (fully transparent or opaque). Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import torch import torch.nn as nn import torch.nn.functional as F def encoder(images): """ images: Tensor of shape (B, K, H, W, 3) Returns: mu (B, 256), sigma (B, 256) """ B, K, H, W, C = images.shape # CNN branches process each view, concatenate, and encode x = images.view(B, K H W, C) x = torch.relu(x) mu = torch.tanh(x.mean(dim=1)) sigma = torch.exp(x.mean(dim=1)) return mu, sigma def decoder(z, voxelres, warpres): """ z: Tensor of shape (B, 256) Returns: voxelgrid (B, D, D, D, 4), warpgrid (B, W, W, W, 3) """ B = z.shape[0] # Linear basis decoder or 3D transposed convolutions voxelflat = F.softplus(nn.Linear(256, voxelres3 4)(z)) warpflat = nn.Linear(256, warpres3 3)(z) voxelgrid = voxelflat.view(B, voxelres, voxelres, voxelres, 4) warpgrid = warpflat.view(B, warpres, warpres, warpres, 3) return voxelgrid, warpgrid def trilinearsample(grid, points): """ grid: (B, C, D, H, W) points: (B, N, 3) in normalized [-1, 1] coordinates Returns: (B, N, C) """ # Normalize points to [-1, 1] assuming scene bounds are [-1, 1]^3 points = torch.clamp(points, -1.0, 1.0) # Expand points to match gridsample expected shape (B, N, 1, 1, 3) points = points.unsqueeze(2).unsqueeze(3) # gridsample expects grid (N, C, D, H, W) and coordinates (N, Hout, Wout, Dout, 3) samples = F.gridsample(grid, points, mode='bilinear', paddingmode='border') return samples.squeeze(2).squeeze(2) def raymarch(voxelgrid, warpgrid, origins, directions, numsamples): """ voxelgrid: (B, D, D, D, 4) warpgrid: (B, W, W, W, 3) origins: (B, H, W, 3) directions: (B, H, W, 3) Returns: renderedrgb (B, H, W, 3), renderedalpha (B, H, W, 1) """ B, H, W, = origins.shape # Generate sample points along rays tvals = torch.linspace(0.0, 1.0, numsamples, device=origins.device) tvals = tvals.view(1, 1, 1, -1).expandas(origins[...,:1]) pointsworld = origins[...,:1] + tvals directions pointsworld = pointsworld.view(B H W numsamples, 3) # Sample warp field: Winv(x) warpvectors = trilinearsample(warpgrid.permute(0, 4, 1, 2, 3), pointsworld) warpvectors = warpvectors.view(B, H, W, numsamples, 3) # Sample voxel grid at warped positions voxelvalues = trilinearsample(voxelgrid.permute(0, 4, 1, 2, 3), warpvectors.view(B H W numsamples, 3)) voxelvalues = voxelvalues.view(B, H, W, numsamples, 4) rgbsamples = voxelvalues[...,:3] alphasamples = voxelvalues[..., 3:] # Accumulate oneminusalpha = 1.0 - alphasamples transmittance = torch.cat([torch.oneslike(oneminusalpha[...,:1]), torch.cumprod(oneminusalpha[...,:-1], dim=-1)], dim=-1) weights = alphasamples transmittance renderedrgb = torch.sum(weights rgbsamples, dim=-2) renderedalpha = 1.0 - torch.prod(oneminusalpha, dim=-2) return renderedrgb, renderedalpha def totalvariationloss(x): """Standard TV regularization """ return torch.mean(torch.abs(x[...,:-1,:,:,:] - x[..., 1:,:,:,:])) + \ torch.mean(torch.abs(x[...,:,:-1,:,:] - x[...,:, 1:,:,:])) + \ torch.mean(torch.abs(x[...,:,:,:-1,:] - x[...,:,:, 1:,:])) def betapriorloss(alpha, beta=1.0): """Beta distribution prior encouraging binary transparency """ return -torch.mean(torch.log(alpha + 1e-6) + torch.log(1.0 - alpha + 1e-6)) def forward(images, targetcameraparams, gtimages, voxelres=128, warpres=32, numsamples=128): mu, sigma = encoder(images) z = mu + sigma torch.randnlike(sigma) voxelgrid, warpgrid = decoder(z, voxelres, warpres) renderedrgb, renderedalpha = raymarch(voxelgrid, warpgrid, targetcameraparams['origins'], targetcameraparams['directions'], numsamples) rgbloss = F.mseloss(renderedrgb, gtimages) klloss = -0.5 torch.sum(1 + torch.log(sigma2) - mu2 - sigma2) tvloss = totalvariationloss(voxelgrid[..., 3:]) betaloss = betapriorloss(renderedalpha) totalloss = rgbloss + 0.1 klloss + tvloss + betaloss return totalloss, renderedrgb Voxel Grid Decoders model the volume function V(\mathbf{x}; \mathbf{z}) as a discrete 3D grid of voxels, producing an explicit 3D voxel grid as the output tensor of a neural network. This approach avoids the prohibitive computational requirements of evaluating deep MLPs at every ray-marching step, enabling real-time rendering speeds. It sets itself apart from implicit MLP decoders by trading memory for speed, storing values in a structured grid rather than computing them on the fly. RenderNet is a deep convolutional network designed for the differentiable rendering of voxelized 3D shapes. It solves the problem of synthesizing novel views by mapping a 3D input volume directly to a 2D image. What sets it apart from its siblings, such as Voxel Grid Decoders and GRU Volume Fusion, is its explicit architectural separation of 3D feature extraction and 2D image decoding, connected by a projection unit that aggregates features along the viewing ray using an MLP. Unlike methods that extract features in object space independent of camera parameters, RenderNet performs view-space resampling at the beginning of the pipeline, making the features inherently dependent on the camera pose. GRU Volume Fusion is a method for incremental 3D reconstruction that fuses sequentially estimated local radiance fields into a single global sparse representation using a Gated Recurrent Unit (GRU). It solves the problem of accumulating errors and outliers in sequential reconstruction by adaptively updating a global volume with new local observations, setting it apart from its sibling Bi-level Fusion which uses explicit weighted averaging followed by optimization rather than recurrent neural updates. It builds on Neural Volumes by replacing static optimization with a learned recurrent fusion process. Training Time: Requires at least 12 hours to train per scene. Memory: Uses an explicit 128^3 voxel grid, which limits the ability to represent fine details at high resolutions compared to implicit methods. Inference Speed: Supports real-time inference at test time, unlike many other neural rendering methods. Strengths: Captures reasonably detailed volumetric geometry and appearance; handles semi-transparent materials (smoke, hair); interpretable volume; real-time rendering. Limitations: Blurry results compared to high-resolution methods due to voxel grid resolution limits; limited to objects within a bounded volume with a distinct background. When to use: Dynamic scenes with semi-transparent materials where real-time novel view synthesis is required and explicit geometry is not available. Neural Volumes was introduced by Lempitsky et al. in 2019. It builds on the concept of ray potentials and volume ray marching. It is a baseline method that uses a 3D deconvolutional network to produce RGB-Alpha volumes as the volumetric video. It differs from previous ray potential works by modeling voxel transparency rather than occupancy probability, focusing on rendering rather than reconstruction. It also differs from DeepVoxels by supporting dynamic scenes and real-time inference. name: Voxel Grid Decoders
head: Convolutional Volume Decoder, Bottleneck Volume Decoder
body: Voxel Grid Decoders model the volume function V(\mathbf{x}; \mathbf{z}) as a discrete 3D grid of voxels, producing an explicit 3D voxel grid as the output tensor of a neural network. This approach avoids the prohibitive computational and memory requirements of evaluating large Multi-Layer Perceptrons (MLPs) at every step along each ray in the ray-marching process, which is necessary for real-time applications. It serves as the explicit representation component within Neural Volumes, replacing the implicit coordinate-based MLP. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A latent code vector \mathbf{z} (typically from an encoder network). Output: A tensor \mathbf{Y} \in \mathbb{R}^{C \times D \times D \times D} representing a D \times D \times D grid of values with C channels. In standard experiments, C=4 (representing RGB\alpha). Data Structures: Voxel Grid Tensor: A 4D tensor with dimensions C \times D \times D \times D. Interpolation Function S: Samples from grid \mathbf{Y} by scaling continuous values in the range [-1, 1] to the grid indices [1, D] along each dimension, followed by trilinear interpolation. Parameters: D: Spatial resolution. Typical values are 32 or 128. W: Side size of the 3D cube covered by the volume. \mathbf{x}0: Center of the 3D cube. \mathbf{z}: Latent representation vector. Formulas: The volume decoder function is defined as: \mathbf{V}(\mathbf{x}; \mathbf{z}) = S\left(\frac{\mathbf{x} - \mathbf{x}0}{W/2}; \mathbf{g}(\mathbf{z})\right) where \mathbf{g}(\mathbf{z}) is the neural network that produces the tensor \mathbf{Y} of size 4 \times D \times D \times D. The function S performs the coordinate transformation and interpolation. Implementation Variants: The function \mathbf{g}(\mathbf{z}) can be implemented using either a convolutional architecture or a bottleneck fully-connected architecture. 1. Convolutional Decoder (Variant 1): Apply a fully-connected layer and non-linearity to transform \mathbf{z} into a 1024-dimensional representation. Reinterpret the resulting vector as a 1 \times 1 \times 1 cube with 1024 channels. Apply 5 transposed convolutions to achieve a final size of 32^3. Performance: Runs at 90Hz. 2. Convolutional Decoder (Variant 2): Same initialization as Variant 1. Apply 7 transposed convolutions to achieve a final size of 128^3. Performance: Runs at 22Hz. 3. Bottleneck Decoder: Use 3 fully-connected layers with output sizes of 128, 4, and 128^3 \times 4 respectively. The last layer represents the decoded volume. Performance: Runs at 90Hz. Post-processing: After decoding the volume, apply a softplus function to the RGB\alpha values to ensure they are non-negative. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import torch import torch.nn as nn import torch.nn.functional as F class VoxelGridDecoderConv32(nn.Module): """Convolutional decoder variant 1: 32^3 resolution.""" def init(self, latentdim): super().init() # Transform latent z into 1024-dimensional representation self.fc1 = nn.Linear(latentdim, 1024) self.relu = nn.ReLU() # Reinterpret as 1x1x1 cube with 1024 channels # Apply 5 transposed convolutions to achieve 32^3 # Note: Specific kernel sizes/strides not given in sources # Assuming standard upsampling factors to reach 32 from 1 self.conv1 = nn.ConvTranspose3d(1024, 512, kernelsize=4, stride=2, padding=1) self.conv2 = nn.ConvTranspose3d(512, 256, kernelsize=4, stride=2, padding=1) self.conv3 = nn.ConvTranspose3d(256, 128, kernelsize=4, stride=2, padding=1) self.conv4 = nn.ConvTranspose3d(128, 64, kernelsize=4, stride=2, padding=1) self.conv5 = nn.ConvTranspose3d(64, 4, kernelsize=4, stride=2, padding=1) def forward(self, z): x = self.fc1(z) x = self.relu(x) # Reshape to 4D tensor for ConvTranspose3d: (N, C, D, H, W) # Here N=1, C=1024, D=1, H=1, W=1 x = x.view(x.size(0), 1024, 1, 1, 1) x = self.relu(self.conv1(x)) x = self.relu(self.conv2(x)) x = self.relu(self.conv3(x)) x = self.relu(self.conv4(x)) # Final output is 4 channels (RGBa) x = self.conv5(x) # Apply softplus to ensure non-negative values x = F.softplus(x) return x class VoxelGridDecoderBottleneck(nn.Module): """Bottleneck decoder variant: 128^3 resolution.""" def init(self, latentdim): super().init() # 3 fully-connected layers with output sizes 128, 4, and 128^3 4 self.fc1 = nn.Linear(latentdim, 128) self.fc2 = nn.Linear(128, 4) self.fc3 = nn.Linear(4, 1283 4) def forward(self, z): x = self.fc1(z) x = torch.relu(x) x = self.fc2(x) x = torch.relu(x) x = self.fc3(x) # Reshape to 4D tensor: C x D x D x D # C=4, D=128 x = x.view(4, 128, 128, 128) # Apply softplus x = F.softplus(x) return x def samplevoxelgrid(gridtensor, x, x0, W): """ Sample from the voxel grid tensor using trilinear interpolation. gridtensor: C x D x D x D tensor x: Input 3D coordinate x0: Center of the volume W: Side size of the volume """ # Scale continuous values in [-1, 1] to grid [1, D] # Formula: (x - x0) / (W/2) scaledx = (x - x0) / (W / 2.0) # Clamp to [-1, 1] to stay within bounds scaledx = torch.clamp(scaledx, -1.0, 1.0) # Perform trilinear interpolation # Note: PyTorch gridsample expects normalized coordinates in [-1, 1] # and input shape (N, C, D, H, W). We assume gridtensor is already # in the correct format for interpolation. # This is a conceptual implementation; actual gridsample usage # requires reshaping and specific coordinate grid generation. # Specific gridsample coordinate generation omitted for brevity, # but the core logic is scaling and interpolation. # Placeholder for actual interpolation step # y = gridsample(gridtensor.unsqueeze(0), scaledx.unsqueeze(0).unsqueeze(0).unsqueeze(0)) # return y.squeeze() raise NotImplementedError("Grid sampling implementation depends on specific framework details not provided in sources.") A decoder network that outputs a semantic volume GS from encoded features, used for 3D semantic labeling. It differs from the standard RGB\alpha decoder by incorporating skip connections from the input grid and using a specific loss function for classification. Structure: Replace the initial depth-1 connection D1 with an additional skip connection incorporating the encoded output from the input grid (G). Followed by a final convolutional output block to generate the semantic volume. Parameters: Spatial dimensions W = H = D = 160. Channel count C is 18 for the Front3D dataset and 20 for the Habitat-Matterport3D dataset. Loss: Weighted masked cross-entropy loss, balanced by the inverse log propensity pc of each class, where propensity is the frequency of the class in the training dataset. Link: NeRF-MAE. Performance: The Convolutional 32³ variant runs at 90Hz. The Convolutional 128³ variant runs at 22Hz. The Bottleneck 128³ variant runs at 90Hz. Memory: The memory requirement is proportional to C \times D^3. For D=128 and C=4, this is 4 \times 128^3 values. Limitations: Voxel grids are limited to representing details as small as a single voxel and are computationally expensive to evaluate and store at high resolution. They are also wasteful in scenes with much empty space. Strengths: Avoids the prohibitive size requirements of MLPs for high-quality reconstructions. Enables real-time applications by reducing the complexity of per-ray evaluation. Voxel Grid Decoders were introduced in the "Neural Volumes" paper. The method was developed to address the computational bottleneck of evaluating MLPs at every step along each ray in the ray-marching process, which imposes a restrictive upper bound on MLP complexity for real-time applications. The approach assumes the volume function can be modeled as a discrete 3D grid of voxels, producing an explicit 3D voxel grid as the output tensor of a neural network. name: Symmetric Voxel Grid
head: Symmetric arrangement, Symmetric feature arrangement
body: The Symmetric Voxel Grid is a feature arrangement strategy for explicit voxel grid decoders that places features symmetrically with respect to the scene center to ensure continuity at region boundaries. It solves the discontinuity problem inherent in linear feature configurations without the model size overhead of overlapping regions. Unlike overlapping approaches which increase feature count by 3n^2 + 3n + 1, this method maintains a compact grid while forcing neighboring decoders to see identical features at seams. Inputs and Outputs Input: A scene bounding volume divided into n \times n \times n regions (or a grid of decoders). Output: A voxel grid where feature values are assigned to vertices/voxels such that symmetry constraints are met. Data Structures The grid consists of discrete voxels. Each voxel vertex holds features accessed by adjacent decoders. Let n be the number of subdivisions along one axis. The total number of regions is n^3. Steps 1. Define Regions: Partition the scene space into a regular grid of n \times n \times n regions. Each region ei has an associated decoder \thetai. 2. Symmetric Feature Assignment: Assign features to voxel vertices such that any vertex v on the boundary between two regions e1 and e2 presents the same feature value to both \theta1 and \theta2. This is achieved by mirroring feature values across the scene center. In a linear configuration, a boundary vertex might have feature fa for region e1 and fb for region e2 where fa \neq fb, causing discontinuities. In the symmetric configuration, the feature at v is identical for all neighboring decoders. 3. Decoder Initialization: Initialize all density decoders \thetai with the same weights to further improve continuity during training. Formulas Overhead of alternative overlapping method: The number of additional features required by overlapping regions in an explicit grid of size n^3 is: \Delta N = 3n^2 + 3n + 1 This growth reduces the effectiveness of the explicit grid approach. Parameters n: The number of subdivisions per axis. Typical values are not explicitly given in the sources, but the method scales with n. Edge Cases and Pitfalls Linear Configuration Discontinuity: Using a simple repeating linear order for features introduces discontinuities at seams because different decoders see different features at the boundary. Model Size Explosion: Attempting to fix linear discontinuities by overlapping regions increases the model size significantly by 3n^2 + 3n + 1 features. Pruning Benefits: The symmetric configuration increases the probability of features being in empty space for all regions, allowing more aggressive pruning and reducing the final stored feature count. Pseudocode Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def assignsymmetricfeatures(grid, scenecenter): """ Assigns features to a voxel grid symmetrically with respect to the scene center. Args: grid: 3D array of shape (N, N, N) representing voxel vertices. scenecenter: 3D vector representing the center of the scene. Returns: grid: Modified 3D array with symmetric feature assignment. """ N = grid.shape[0] # Iterate through all voxel vertices for x in range(N): for y in range(N): for z in range(N): # Calculate position relative to center pos = grid[x, y, z].position - scenecenter # Mirror position to find symmetric counterpart # The symmetric counterpart is at -pos relative to center # Map back to grid indices xsym = N - 1 - x ysym = N - 1 - y zsym = N - 1 - z # Ensure symmetry: feature at (x,y,z) must equal feature at (xsym, ysym, zsym) # If not already set, copy from symmetric counterpart if grid[x, y, z].feature is None: if grid[xsym, ysym, zsym].feature is not None: grid[x, y, z].feature = grid[xsym, ysym, zsym].feature else: # Initialize with default or shared weight grid[x, y, z].feature = getsharedfeature() else: # Ensure the counterpart matches grid[xsym, ysym, zsym].feature = grid[x, y, z].feature return grid def initializedecoders(decoders): """ Initializes all density decoders with the same weights. Args: decoders: List of decoder objects. """ sharedweights = getinitialweights() for decoder in decoders: decoder.weights = sharedweights A naive arrangement where features are repeated in the same order for each region. It introduces discontinuities at seams because different decoders see different features at the boundary. Choose only if model size is not a concern and discontinuities are tolerable. Voxel Grid Decoders An alternative approach where regions overlap to ensure shared features at boundaries. It increases model size by 3n^2 + 3n + 1 features. Choose if symmetry is difficult to implement and extra memory is available. Voxel Grid Decoders Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: The symmetric arrangement does not increase the number of features needed for seamless reconstruction compared to a non-overlapping grid. It reduces the number of features stored after pruning because it increases the probability of features being in empty space for all regions. Measured Performance: The method is described as "very effective to improve the model quality and reduce its size". Specific metrics (PSNR, FPS) are not provided in the notes. Strengths: Avoids discontinuities without increasing model size; enables more aggressive pruning; improves training continuity via shared decoder initialization. Limitations: Requires symmetric scene center definition; may not be optimal for highly asymmetric scenes where symmetry does not reflect natural feature distribution. When to use: When using explicit voxel grids with multiple decoders and seam discontinuities are a problem, and model size is a constraint. When not to use: When the scene is highly asymmetric and symmetry does not capture the underlying structure, or when overlapping regions are already acceptable. The Symmetric Voxel Grid was introduced in the paper "NeRFLight: Fast and Light Neural Radiance Fields using a Shared Feature Grid" by Rivas-Manzaneque et al. (CVPR 2023). It addresses issues in explicit neural field representations where linear feature arrangements cause seams. The method builds on the concept of shared feature grids but specifically optimizes the spatial arrangement of those features to ensure continuity.
