name: RenderNet Architecture
head: RenderNet
body: RenderNet is a deep convolutional network designed for the differentiable rendering of voxelized 3D shapes. It solves the problem of synthesizing novel views by mapping a 3D input volume directly to a 2D image. What sets it apart from its siblings, such as Voxel Grid Decoders and GRU Volume Fusion, is its explicit architectural separation of 3D feature extraction and 2D image decoding, connected by a projection unit that aggregates features along the viewing ray using an MLP. Unlike methods that extract features in object space independent of camera parameters, RenderNet performs view-space resampling at the beginning of the pipeline, making the features inherently dependent on the camera pose. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A 3D voxel grid representing the shape. Output: A 2D rendered image (RGB or grayscale) and optionally other modalities (e.g., albedo, normals). Data Structures and Layout: The network consists of four main stages: 3D Input Encoder, 3D Residual Blocks, Projection Unit, and 2D Decoder. 1. 3D Input Encoder: A sequence of 3D convolutions. Layer 1: Channels \{8\}, Kernel \{5\}, Stride \{2\}. Layer 2: Channels \{16\}, Kernel \{3\}, Stride \{2\}. Layer 3: Channels \{16\}, Kernel \{3\}, Stride \{1\}. 2. 3D Residual Blocks: Ten 3D residual blocks follow the encoder. Each block consists of two 3D convolutions with a shortcut connection adding the input to the output. 3. Projection Unit: Resizes the tensor from dimensions W \times H \times 32 \times 16 to W \times H \times (32 \cdot 16). Applies a 1 \times 1 convolution with the same number of channels (32 \cdot 16 = 512). This projects all voxels along the X-axis (ray direction) to a single high-dimensional feature vector, analogous to an accumulation function. 4. 2D Decoder: 2D Residual Blocks: Ten 2D residual blocks follow the projection unit. Similar to 3D blocks but using 2D convolutions. Intermediate Conv: A 4 \times 4 convolution with 32 \cdot 8 = 256 channels. Final 2D Residual Blocks: Five 2D residual blocks. Output Convs: A series of 2D convolutions with channels \{32 \cdot 4, 32 \cdot 2, 32, 16, 3 \text{ (or } 1 \text{ for greyscale)}\}, kernel sizes \{4, 4, 4, 4, 4\}, and strides \{1, 2, 2, 2, 1\}. Steps: 1. Resampling: Resample the input 3D volume to view space using a perspective camera transform. The X-axis of the resampled volume corresponds to ray directions, and the YZ-axes correspond to image coordinates. 2. 3D Feature Extraction: Process the resampled volume with the 3D Input Encoder and 3D Residual Blocks to extract semantic features, reducing spatial dimensions. 3. Ray Projection: Use the Projection Unit to project all voxels along the X-axis to a single high-dimensional feature vector (512-channel 2D projection). 4. 2D Upsampling: Upsample the 2D projection to the target resolution using the 2D Decoder (2D Residual Blocks and Output Convs). 5. Multi-modal Output (Optional): To generate additional modalities (e.g., normal maps), create a branch of 2D convolution layers starting at the first strided up-convolution layer (Layer 2 of Output Convs) and train it jointly with the main branch. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def rendernet(inputvolume3d, cameraparams): # Step 1: Resample to view space viewspacevolume = resampletoviewspace(inputvolume3d, cameraparams) # X-axis: ray directions, YZ-axes: image coordinates # Step 2: 3D Input Encoder x = conv3d(viewspacevolume, outchannels=8, kernelsize=5, stride=2) x = conv3d(x, outchannels=16, kernelsize=3, stride=2) x = conv3d(x, outchannels=16, kernelsize=3, stride=1) # Step 3: 3D Residual Blocks (10 blocks) for in range(10): x = residualblock3d(x) # Step 4: Projection Unit # Resize from WxHx32x16 to WxHx(3216) x = resizetensor(x, newshape=(x.shape[0], x.shape[1], 32 16)) # 1x1 Convolution with the same number of channels x = conv1x1(x, outchannels=32 16) # Step 5: 2D Decoder # 2D Residual Blocks (10 blocks) for in range(10): x = residualblock2d(x) # Intermediate Conv: 4x4, 256 channels x = conv2d(x, outchannels=256, kernelsize=4, stride=1) # Final 2D Residual Blocks (5 blocks) for in range(5): x = residualblock2d(x) # Output Convs x = conv2d(x, outchannels=128, kernelsize=4, stride=1) x = conv2d(x, outchannels=64, kernelsize=4, stride=2) # Multi-modal branch can be attached here x = conv2d(x, outchannels=32, kernelsize=4, stride=2) x = conv2d(x, outchannels=16, kernelsize=4, stride=2) rgboutput = conv2d(x, outchannels=3, kernelsize=4, stride=1) return rgboutput def resampletoviewspace(volume, cameraparams): # Resamples 3D volume to view space using perspective camera transform # X-axis aligns with ray directions, YZ-axes align with image coordinates pass def conv3d(x, outchannels, kernelsize, stride): # Applies a 3D convolution with specified output channels, kernel size, and stride pass def resizetensor(x, newshape): # Resizes tensor dimensions to newshape (e.g., flattening last two dimensions) pass def conv1x1(x, outchannels): # Applies a 1x1 convolution with specified output channels pass def conv2d(x, outchannels, kernelsize, stride): # Applies a 2D convolution with specified output channels, kernel size, and stride pass def residualblock3d(x): # Applies two 3D convolutions with a shortcut connection adding input to output pass def residualblock2d(x): # Applies two 2D convolutions with a shortcut connection adding input to output pass Parameters: Projection output channels: 512. Input volume dimensions: Not given in the sources. Target image resolution: Not given in the sources. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: The architecture supports arbitrary input and output dimensions during and after training, but the specific dimensions provided in the notes are for the training dataset. The projection unit assumes a specific tensor shape (W \times H \times 32 \times 16) before resizing, which may require padding or cropping if the input volume dimensions do not align with the expected feature map size after the 3D encoder. Definition: An alternative model for comparison against RenderNet. Layout: The 3D input encoder consists of 3D convolutions with channels \{64, 128, 256, 512\}, kernel sizes \{4, 4, 4, 4\}, and strides \{2, 2, 2, 2\}, using parametric ReLU. This is followed by a fully-connected layer mapping tensors to a 200-dimensional vector and a sigmoid activation. Lighting and pose parameters are directly concatenated to the shape latent vector. The decoder consists of 2D convolutions with 4×4 kernels, channels \{512, 512, 256, 256, 128, 128, 64, 64, 32, 32, 16, 1\}, and strides \{2, 1, 2, 1, 2, 1, 2, 1, 2, 1, 2, 1\}. When to choose: Use when comparing against the standard RenderNet pipeline or when explicit pose/lighting conditioning via latent vector concatenation is required. Time and Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Measured Performance: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Enables learning different rendering styles; effective for synthesizing novel viewpoints for faces captured from a single viewpoint; allows multi-modal output sharing high-level information. Limitations: View-space resampling at the beginning makes features dependent on camera parameters, unlike object-space feature extraction methods. When to use: When differentiable rendering of voxelized 3D shapes is required, particularly for novel view synthesis of faces or bodies. When not to use: When object-space feature independence is preferred, or when explicit modeling of occlusion through absorption coefficient and alpha blending is required. RenderNet was introduced as a deep convolutional network for differentiable rendering from 3D shapes. The architecture enables differentiable rendering of voxelized 3D shapes by combining a 3D and a 2D convolutional part connected by a projection unit. It has been applied to scene relighting, novel view synthesis, facial and body reenactment, and photorealistic avatars. The projection unit has also been extended to controllable neural voxel rendering for handling high-frequency and complex textures. name: GRU Volume Fusion
head: Fusing Volumes for Global Reconstruction, NeRFusion, Recurrent Fusion Module, Recurrent Neural Fusion
body: GRU Volume Fusion is a method for incremental 3D reconstruction that fuses sequentially estimated local radiance fields into a single global sparse representation using a Gated Recurrent Unit (GRU). It solves the problem of accumulating errors and outliers in sequential reconstruction by adaptively updating a global volume with new local observations, setting it apart from its sibling Bi-level Fusion which uses explicit weighted averaging followed by optimization rather than recurrent neural updates. It builds on Neural Volumes by replacing static optimization with a learned recurrent fusion process. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A sequence of local sparse feature volumes \{\mathcal{V}t\}, where each \mathcal{V}t represents the local radiance field estimated from the t-th frame's input images. The global volume \mathcal{V}0^g is initialized (typically to zeros or a small random value). Output: The final global sparse feature volume \mathcal{V}T^g after processing T frames. This volume conditions density and color MLPs for rendering. Data Structures: Local Volume \mathcal{V}t: A sparse 3D tensor containing feature vectors for voxels visible in frame t. The sparsity pattern is determined by the camera pose and geometry estimation for that frame. Global Volume \mathcal{V}t^g: A sparse 3D tensor of the same spatial resolution and feature dimension as \mathcal{V}t. It stores the accumulated global features. Voxels not covered by the current local volume \mathcal{V}t remain unchanged from \mathcal{V}{t-1}^g. Gate Volumes (zt, rt): Sparse 3D tensors of the same shape as \mathcal{V}t^g, containing values in [0, 1] for the update and reset gates. Candidate Volume \tilde{\mathcal{V}}t^g: Sparse 3D tensor of the same shape as \mathcal{V}t^g, containing candidate feature updates. Network Components: Three deep neural networks with sparse 3D convolution layers are used: 1. Mz: Computes the update gate. Ends with a sigmoid activation. 2. Mr: Computes the reset gate. Ends with a sigmoid activation. 3. Mt: Computes the candidate volume. Ends with a tanh activation. Numbered Steps: For each frame t = 1, \dots, T: 1. Input: Take the local sparse volume \mathcal{V}t and the previous global volume \mathcal{V}{t-1}^g. 2. Compute Update Gate: Concatenate the previous global volume and the local volume along the feature dimension: [\mathcal{V}{t-1}^g, \mathcal{V}t]. Pass this through Mz to get the update gate zt: zt = Mz([\mathcal{V}{t-1}^g, \mathcal{V}t]) 3. Compute Reset Gate: Pass the same concatenated input through Mr to get the reset gate rt: rt = Mr([\mathcal{V}{t-1}^g, \mathcal{V}t]) 4. Compute Candidate Volume: Element-wise multiply the previous global volume by the reset gate: rt \mathcal{V}{t-1}^g. Concatenate this result with the local volume: [rt \mathcal{V}{t-1}^g, \mathcal{V}t]. Pass this through Mt to get the candidate volume \tilde{\mathcal{V}}t^g: \tilde{\mathcal{V}}t^g = Mt([rt \mathcal{V}{t-1}^g, \mathcal{V}t]) 5. Update Global Volume: Combine the previous global volume and the candidate volume using the update gate: \mathcal{V}t^g = (1 - zt) \mathcal{V}{t-1}^g + zt \tilde{\mathcal{V}}t^g 6. Sparse Application: Steps 2-5 are applied only to voxels covered by the local volume \mathcal{V}t. All other voxels in the global volume remain unchanged from \mathcal{V}{t-1}^g. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def gruvolumefusion(localvolumes: List[SparseTensor], initialglobal: SparseTensor, Mz: SparseCNN, Mr: SparseCNN, Mt: SparseCNN) -> SparseTensor: """ Incrementally fuses local sparse volumes into a global volume using GRU. Args: localvolumes: List of sparse 3D tensors Vt, one per frame. initialglobal: Sparse 3D tensor V0^g, initialized to zeros or small random values. Mz, Mr, Mt: Sparse 3D CNN networks for update, reset, and candidate gates. Returns: Final global sparse volume VT^g. """ globalvolume = initialglobal for t, localvol in enumerate(localvolumes): # Identify voxels present in the local volume # Note: Sparse tensors handle this implicitly; operations are only defined on existing entries. # Concatenation must align sparse indices. # 1. Compute Update Gate zt # Concatenate along feature dimension. Only voxels in localvol are processed. # Voxels in globalvolume but not in localvol are ignored for this step. zt = Mz(concat(globalvolume, localvol)) # 2. Compute Reset Gate rt rt = Mr(concat(globalvolume, localvol)) # 3. Compute Candidate Volume Vtilde # Element-wise multiply reset gate with previous global volume resetglobal = elementwisemultiply(rt, globalvolume) # Concatenate with local volume candidateinput = concat(resetglobal, localvol) # Apply tanh activation via Mt candidatevol = Mt(candidateinput) # 4. Update Global Volume # Vt^g = (1 - zt) V{t-1}^g + zt Vtilde # Note: For voxels not in localvol, zt and candidatevol are undefined/zero. # The update should only affect voxels in localvol. # Voxels not in localvol remain as globalvolume. # Create a mask or use sparse operations to update only relevant voxels # In a sparse tensor implementation, we can construct a new global volume # by merging the unchanged parts and the updated parts. # Update voxels present in localvol updatedglobal = merge(globalvolume, elementwisemultiply(elementwisemultiply(1 - zt, globalvolume), elementwisemultiply(zt, candidatevol)), mask=localvol.indices) globalvolume = updatedglobal return globalvolume Parameters: The network is generalizable and pre-trained across scenes, allowing it to handle arbitrary scene scales and arbitrary numbers of input images. Typical training datasets: ScanNet, DTU, Google Scanned Object. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Sparsity Alignment: The concatenation and element-wise operations must correctly handle the sparse structure. Voxels present in the global volume but not in the local volume must be preserved without modification. Initialization: The initial global volume \mathcal{V}0^g must be properly initialized (e.g., zeros) to avoid biasing the first update. Precision: Using sparse 3D CNNs requires careful handling of memory and computation for large scenes to maintain real-time performance. An online 3D reconstruction method that represents geometry using implicit neural volumes, combining local-level fusion for efficient depth map integration and global-level fusion framed as neural rendering for consistent reconstruction. It solves the problem of accumulating errors and outliers in sequential reconstruction by first fusing latent codes via weighted averaging and then optimizing the global volume against depth measurements. It sets itself apart from its sibling GRU Volume Fusion by using explicit weighted averaging of latent codes followed by an optimization step, rather than recurrent neural network updates. Time Complexity: The recurrent fusion runs in real-time at 22 fps. Memory Complexity: Uses sparse 3D representations, which are memory-efficient for large-scale scenes with sparse observations. Measured Performance: Achieves state-of-the-art quality on both large-scale indoor and small-scale object scenes, with substantially faster reconstruction than NeRF and other recent methods. Outperforms baseline NeRF, NeRFingMVS, and MVSNeRF on ScanNet, DTU, and NeRF Synthetic datasets. Strengths: Real-time incremental reconstruction, handles arbitrary scene scales and numbers of input images, adaptive feature updating. Limitations: Requires pre-training on a diverse dataset for generalization. Quality can be further boosted by fine-tuning the predicted voxel features per scene. When to use: Large-scale scene reconstruction from image sequences where real-time or near-real-time incremental updates are needed. When not to use: When high-quality single-scene optimization is preferred over incremental reconstruction, or when no pre-trained model is available and per-scene training is not feasible. GRU Volume Fusion, also known as NeRFusion, was introduced in 2022. It combines the advantages of NeRF and TSDF-based fusion techniques to achieve efficient large-scale reconstruction and photo-realistic rendering. The method was trained end-to-end with only rendering losses on a combination of scenes from the ScanNet, DTU, and Google Scanned Object datasets. It addresses the challenges of reconstructing and rendering large-scale indoor scenes from RGB images, which are crucial for applications in AR/VR, e-commerce, and robotics. name: Bi-level Fusion
head: BNV-Fusion, BNVF, Local- and Global-level Fusion, local + global fusion
body: Bi-level Fusion is an online 3D reconstruction method that represents geometry using implicit neural volumes, combining local-level fusion for efficient depth map integration and global-level fusion framed as neural rendering for consistent reconstruction. It solves the problem of accumulating errors and outliers in sequential reconstruction by first fusing latent codes via weighted averaging and then optimizing the global volume against depth measurements. It sets itself apart from its sibling GRU Volume Fusion by using explicit weighted averaging of latent codes followed by an optimization step, rather than recurrent neural network updates. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: A sequence of depth maps Dt, camera extrinsic parameters T{ct}^w, and the current global implicit volume Vw^{t-1} with associated weight volume W^{t-1}. Outputs: The updated global implicit volume Vw^t and weight volume W^t. Data Structures: Implicit Neural Volume (Vw): A 3D grid of latent codes where the voxel resolution is 2 cm, meaning each latent code represents the geometry of a 2\text{cm}^3 volume around its position. Weight Volume (W): A 3D grid of weights, where values are set to the number of 3D points associated with a voxel. Decoder: An MLP with 4 fully connected layers with sizes [128, 128, 128, 1] that maps a latent code and a 3D position to an SDF value. Numbered Steps: 1. Local-level Fusion: 1. Transform the single-view neural volume V{ct}^s from camera coordinates to world coordinates using the camera extrinsic parameters: Vw^s = T{ct}^w V{ct}^s. 2. Update the global implicit volume Vw and weight volume W using weighted averaging of the latent codes: Vw^t = \frac{W^{t-1} Vw^{t-1} + W{ct}^s Vw^s}{W^{t-1} + W{ct}^s} W^t = W^{t-1} + W{ct}^s where Vw and W denote the global implicit volume and its weight, respectively. The superscript t-1 and t means prior update and post update. The superscript s denotes single-view source. 2. Global-level Fusion: 1. Randomly sample a set of pixels in the depth map. The method samples 5000 pixels per image in each iteration. 2. Along the ray unprojected from each sampled pixel, sample N 3D points \{x0, x1,..., xn\} using hierarchical sampling: more points are sampled closer to the measured surface. Coarse-level sampling: 5 3D points per meter. Fine-level sampling: 20 3D points per meter. 3. Transform the 3D points to world coordinates. 4. Extract SDF values si from the global volume Vw using trilinear interpolation of decoder outputs. 5. Compute the projective TSDF \bar{s}i for each 3D point given a depth measurement p on the ray: \bar{s}i = \min(\max(\|p - xi\|2, -\delta), \delta) where \delta is the truncation threshold. 6. Optimize the global volume Vw to minimize the discrepancy between decoded SDF values si and projective TSDF values \bar{s}i: \argmin{Vw} \sum{i=0}^{n} \|si - \bar{s}i\|1 where si is the SDF value decoded from the neural volume Vw. 7. The optimization uses the Adam optimizer for 5 iterations for each image. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math import random def bilevelfusion(Vwprev, Wprev, depthmap, cameraextrinsic, depthencoder, decoder, intrinsics, delta): # Step 1: Local-level Fusion # Encode depth map to single-view neural volume Vcst Vcst = depthencoder(depthmap) # Transform single-view volume to world coordinates Vws = transformvolumecoords(Vcst, cameraextrinsic) # Compute source weight volume (number of 3D points per voxel) Wcst = computeweightvolume(Vws) # Weighted averaging of latent codes Vw = (Wprev Vwprev + Wcst Vws) / (Wprev + Wcst) W = Wprev + Wcst # Step 2: Global-level Fusion sampledpixels = random.samplepixels(depthmap, numpixels=5000) for iteration in range(5): totalloss = 0.0 paramgrads = {} for u, v in sampledpixels: p = depthmap[v, u] rayorigin, raydirection = unprojectpixel(u, v, p, intrinsics) # Hierarchical sampling: coarse 5 pts/m, fine 20 pts/m points3d = samplealongray(rayorigin, raydirection, p, coarsedensity=5, finedensity=20) for point in points3d: latentcode = getlatentcode(Vw, point) si = decoder(latentcode, point) # Projective TSDF dist = abs(p - sum(r c for r, c in zip(raydirection, point))) sbari = min(max(dist, -delta), delta) totalloss += abs(si - sbari) # Accumulate gradients for Adam optimizer grad = computegradient(si, sbari, decoder, Vw, point) accumulategrads(paramgrads, grad) # Update parameters using Adam Vw = adamstep(Vw, paramgrads, lr=0.001) return Vw, W def transformvolumecoords(V, Tcw): # Apply extrinsic matrix to voxel centers return V.applytransform(Tcw) def computeweightvolume(Vws): # Count number of 3D points associated with each voxel return Vws.countpoints() def randomsamplepixels(depthmap, numpixels): h, w = depthmap.shape return [(random.randint(0, w-1), random.randint(0, h-1)) for in range(numpixels)] def unprojectpixel(u, v, depth, intrinsics): fx, fy = intrinsics['fx'], intrinsics['fy'] cx, cy = intrinsics['cx'], intrinsics['cy'] x = (u - cx) depth / fx y = (v - cy) depth / fy z = depth rayorigin = [0.0, 0.0, 0.0] raydirection = [x, y, z] normval = math.sqrt(sum(c2 for c in raydirection)) raydirection = [c / normval for c in raydirection] return rayorigin, raydirection def samplealongray(rayorigin, raydirection, depth, coarsedensity, finedensity): points = [] maxdist = depth # Coarse sampling along the ray coarsestep = 1.0 / coarsedensity for d in range(0, int(maxdist coarsedensity)): point = [rayorigin[i] + raydirection[i] d coarsestep for i in range(3)] points.append(point) # Fine sampling near the measured surface finestep = 1.0 / finedensity startfine = max(0, int(maxdist coarsedensity) - 10) endfine = int(maxdist coarsedensity) + 10 for d in range(startfine, endfine): point = [rayorigin[i] + raydirection[i] d finestep for i in range(3)] points.append(point) return points def getlatentcode(Vw, point): return Vw.interpolate(point) def decoder(latentcode, point): x = latentcode + point for size in [128, 128, 128]: x = math.tanh(sum(a b for a, b in zip(x, [1.0]len(x)))) # Simplified linear+activation return x[-1] # Final layer outputs scalar SDF def computegradient(si, sbari, decoder, Vw, point): # Standard backpropagation gradient computation return (si - sbari) 1.0 def accumulategrads(grads, grad): for k in grad: grads[k] = grads.get(k, 0.0) + grad[k] def adamstep(params, grads, lr, beta1=0.9, beta2=0.999, eps=1e-8): # Simplified Adam update step return {k: params[k] - lr grads[k] for k in params} Parameters: Voxel Resolution: 2 cm. Latent Code Dimension: 8. Decoder Architecture: MLP with 4 fully connected layers with sizes [128, 128, 128, 1]. Sampling Density: Coarse-level: 5 3D points per meter; Fine-level: 20 3D points per meter. Pixels Sampled: 5000 pixels per image in each iteration. Optimization Iterations: 5 iterations for each image. Optimizer: Adam optimizer. Truncation Threshold (\delta): Defined in the projective TSDF formula, but a specific numerical value is not given in the sources. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Depth Noise: Severe depth noise causes discontinuities between neighboring implicit voxels. Trilinear interpolation among neighboring implicit voxels is used to improve border consistency, but discontinuities may still occur. Initialization: Global-level fusion initialized by local-level fusion converges in 5 iterations. Initialized randomly, it takes much longer to converge and remains inferior even after 20 iterations. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Measured Performance: On a 1080Ti GPU, encoding + local-level fusion takes 0.1s total; global-level fusion for 2 iterations takes 0.5s; overall runs at ~2 fps. DI-Fusion runs at 10 fps on the same device. Scaling: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Outperforms TSDF-Fusion, iMAP, and DI-Fusion on ICL-NUIM and ScanNet datasets in accuracy, completeness, and F1 score, demonstrating robustness to synthetic noise and better generalization to diverse indoor scenes. The combination of local- and global-level fusion significantly improves reconstruction quality compared to using either alone. Limitations: Slower than traditional volumetric fusion approaches (e.g., InfiniTAM v3 runs at over 30 fps on a mobile device). Severe noise can still cause discontinuities despite trilinear interpolation. When to Use: Online 3D reconstruction where global consistency is important and depth noise is present. Bi-level Fusion was introduced in the paper "BNV-Fusion: Dense 3D Reconstruction using Bi-level Neural Volume Fusion". It is an online 3D reconstruction method that uses implicit neural volumes to represent geometry. The method was evaluated on the augmented ICL-NUIM dataset, 3D Scene Dataset, and ScanNet validation set (312 sequences). For ScanNet, every 10th frame was used as input, and ground truth meshes were used as pseudo ground truth. The depth encoder and shape decoder were trained using object CAD models from two categories (chairs and lamps) in ShapeNet. BNV-Fusion: Dense 3D Reconstruction using Bi-level Neural Volume Fusion, https://doi.org/10.1109/CVPR52688.2022.00607, fetched 2026-10-30

name: EndoNeRF
body: EndoNeRF is a method for reconstructing deformable surgical scenes using a canonical radiance field and a time-dependent displacement field, optimized with stereo depth-cueing and supervision. It addresses non-rigid tissue reconstruction in endoscopic video by mapping input space-time coordinates to a static canonical space via a learned deformation, allowing standard volume rendering to operate on the displaced points. It explicitly models temporal deformation through a displacement field rather than a static 3D volume or explicit voxel grid, and differs from fluid dynamics-focused methods by leveraging endoscopic stereo cues. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: A sequence of endoscopic images (stereo pairs) with known camera poses and timestamps \tau. Outputs: A rendered image \hat{C}(\mathbf{r}) for a given ray \mathbf{r} and time \tau, and the underlying scene representation (canonical field and deformation field). Data Structures: 1. Canonical Radiance Field (F\Theta): An MLP that maps a 3D position \mathbf{x} and viewing direction \mathbf{d} to density \sigma and color \mathbf{c}. Architecture: 8 fully connected ReLU layers, each with 256 channels. Input encoding: Positional encoding (Fourier features) for input coordinates \mathbf{x} and time \tau. 2. Time-Dependent Displacement Field (G\Phi): An MLP that maps a 3D position \mathbf{x} and time \tau to a 3D displacement vector \Delta \mathbf{x}. Input encoding: Positional encoding for \mathbf{x} and \tau. Method Steps: 1. Ray Sampling: For a camera ray \mathbf{r}(t) = \mathbf{o} + t\mathbf{d} at time \tau, sample points along the ray using stereo depth-cueing ray marching. 2. Deformation Mapping: For each sample point \mathbf{x}i = \mathbf{r}(ti), query the displacement field to find the corresponding location in the canonical space: \mathbf{x}'i = \mathbf{x}i + G\Phi(\mathbf{x}i, \tau) where G\Phi(\mathbf{x}i, \tau) is the displacement between point \mathbf{x}i at time \tau and its corresponding point in the canonical field. 3. Field Query: Query the canonical radiance field F\Theta at the displaced location \mathbf{x}'i with viewing direction \mathbf{d} to obtain density \sigmai and color \mathbf{c}i: (\sigmai, \mathbf{c}i) = F\Theta(\mathbf{x}'i, \mathbf{d}) 4. Volume Rendering: Compute the final color \hat{C}(\mathbf{r}) using the standard differentiable volume rendering equation: \hat{C}(\mathbf{r}) = \sum{i=1}^N Ti (1 - \exp(-\sigmai \deltai)) \mathbf{c}i where \deltai is the step size and Ti = \exp\left(-\sum{j=1}^{i-1} \sigmaj \deltaj\right) is the transmittance. 5. Optimization: Minimize the L2 photometric reconstruction loss between rendered images and ground truth stereo images. The optimization is supervised by stereo depth-cueing, which provides depth constraints to regularize the deformation field and improve reconstruction quality. Parameters: MLP Layers: 8 fully connected layers. MLP Channels: 256 per layer. Activation: ReLU. Loss: L2 photometric reconstruction loss. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Resource Consumption: EndoNeRF optimizes an entire spatial-temporal field, resulting in significant time and resource consumption. Topology Changes: The displacement field approach assumes topology preservation; it may struggle with significant changes in scene topology (e.g., tissue tearing). A framework for spatio-temporal reconstruction of objects from few X-ray projections, consisting of a canonical volume assigning density to every point in 3D space and a deformation field returning a displacement for every point as a function of time. It allows querying the neural radiance field at continuous temporal and spatial locations. The deformation field is posed as a B-spline field whose time-dependent weights are obtained from a neural network, using cubic B-splines with fixed control points and time-varying weights to impose a smooth efficient prior. The canonical volume is trained using a hybrid method where projection loss is supplemented by volumetric loss based on high-fidelity X-CT data typically available at initial and final timesteps. The deformation field is trained jointly for all timesteps and with all available data. It is preferred to train the canonical volume on the final step of deformation where the maximum amount of material is present in the field of view to map material seen in projections to the canonical volume. This framework assumes deformations preserve topology. Time Complexity: High. Optimizing an entire spatial-temporal field results in significant time consumption. Memory Complexity: High. The 8-layer, 256-channel MLP for both the canonical field and displacement field requires substantial memory. Strengths: Yields high-quality non-rigid reconstruction in surgical scenes. Can model complex tissue deformations. Limitations: Significant time and resource consumption. Struggles with changes in scene topology. Inference speed may be insufficient for clinical demands compared to factorized methods like Lerplane. When to Use: When high-quality reconstruction of deformable tissue is required and computational resources are available. When Not to Use: When real-time inference is required or when scene topology changes significantly. EndoNeRF emerged as a promising solution for deformable surgical scene reconstruction, utilizing NeRF with tool-guided ray casting, stereo depth-cueing ray marching, and stereo depth-supervised optimization. It was introduced to address the limitations of previous methods in handling non-rigid tissue deformation in endoscopic video. The method builds on the principles of differentiable volume rendering and radiance field optimization. Efficient Deformable Tissue Reconstruction via Orthogonal Neural Plane, https://doi.org/10.1109/tmi.2024.3388559, fetched 2026-10-26 Neural rendering enables dynamic tomography, https://doi.org/10.48550/arxiv.2410.20558, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial)

name: Fluid Motion Reconstruction Framework
head: Fluid Motion Reconstruction Pipeline, FluidMotionRestruction
body: The Fluid Motion Reconstruction Framework is a computational pipeline for reconstructing temporally coherent fluid density fields from monocular video sequences. It combines differentiable rendering for image alignment with physics-based coupled estimation to ensure temporal coherence. It builds on differentiable volume rendering principles Deformable and Dynamic Fields and explicitly models fluid dynamics and velocity to maintain physical plausibility over time. Inputs: A sequence of monocular fluid images \{I\}, where It is the image at time t. Outputs: A sequence of fluid density fields \{\rho\}. Parameters: t is the time index, t \in \mathbb{N}0, t \le F, where F is the total number of frames. The framework operates in two main components: a differentiable rendering component and a coupled density and velocity estimation component. 1. Initialization: Reconstruct the initial fluid density fields \rho1 and \rho2 using the differentiable rendering component. This aligns the volumetric representation with the first two input images I1 and I2. 2. Temporal Propagation: For subsequent frames t > 2, compute the estimated fluid density \tilde{\rho}t using the coupled density and velocity estimation component. This step ensures that fluid flows adhere to underlying physical priors. 3. Refinement: Given the estimated density \tilde{\rho}t, correct the final fluid density \rhot via the differentiable renderer using the target image It. This aligns the physically plausible estimate with the observed image data. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def fluidmotionreconstruction(images): # images: list of monocular fluid images [I1,..., IF] F = len(images) densities = [] # Step 1: Initialize first two frames using differentiable rendering rho1 = differentiablerender(images[0]) rho2 = differentiablerender(images[1]) densities.extend([rho1, rho2]) # Step 2 & 3: Iterate through remaining frames for t in range(2, F): # Coupled density and velocity estimation for temporal coherence rhotilde = coupleddensityvelocityestimation(densities[t-1], densities[t-2]) # Differentiable rendering correction for image alignment rhot = differentiablerender(rhotilde, images[t]) densities.append(rhot) return densities def differentiablerender(targetimage, density=None): # Standard differentiable volume rendering optimization # Minimizes rendering loss against targetimage using the emission-absorption model. # Gradients propagate through the volume rendering equation to update density and velocity. # [Comment] The exact optimization solver and loss function are not provided in the sources. return density if density is not None else targetimage def coupleddensityvelocityestimation(prevrho, prevprevrho): # [Comment] The exact physics-based coupled estimation formulation is not provided in the sources. # It enforces fluid flows to adhere to underlying physical priors for temporal coherence. return prevrho Not given in the sources. The framework is described in research on physics-based differentiable rendering for fluid modeling. It addresses the challenge of reconstructing dynamic fluid scenes from limited monocular input by integrating physical constraints with differentiable rendering. name: HDR-NeRF
head: High Dynamic Range Neural Radiance Fields
body: HDR-NeRF is a method for high dynamic range (HDR) view synthesis that recovers an HDR radiance field from a set of low dynamic range (LDR) training images captured with variable exposure times. It solves the problem of limited sensor dynamic range by modeling the physical imaging process as two implicit functions: a radiance field that encodes scene radiance (values from 0 to +\infty) and a learned tone mapper that predicts pixel values from radiance and exposure time. Unlike baseline NeRF, which is limited to low dynamic range outputs, HDR-NeRF enables the generation of novel HDR views and novel LDR views under arbitrary exposures, while avoiding the ghost artifacts common in traditional multi-exposure stack-based HDR synthesis when the camera is hand-held. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: A set of LDR images \{Ii\} captured from various camera poses Pi with known exposure times \Delta ti. The exposure is defined as the product of exposure time and radiance. Outputs: An HDR radiance field capable of rendering novel views at arbitrary exposure times, producing both HDR radiance values and tone-mapped LDR pixel values. Data Structures: The method consists of two neural network modules: 1. Radiance Field (F): An eight-layer Multi-Layer Perceptron (MLP) with 256 channels per layer. It maps a 5D input (ray origin \mathbf{o}=(x,y,z) and ray direction \mathbf{d}=(\theta,\phi)) to a 4D output: HDR radiance \mathbf{e} \in 0, \infty) and density \sigma. 2. Tone Mapper: Three separate one-layer MLPs, each with 128 channels. These process the Red, Green, and Blue channels independently because RGB channels are tone-mapped with different Camera Response Functions (CRFs). The tone mapper takes the radiance \mathbf{e} and exposure time \Delta t as inputs to predict the final pixel color \mathbf{c}. [Positional Encoding: To handle high-frequency variations in color and geometry, positional encoding is applied to the ray origins and ray directions, identical to the baseline NeRF strategy. Sampling Strategy: The method optimizes two models: a coarse model and a fine model, where densities from the coarse model bias the sampling of the fine model. The coarse model samples 64 points along each ray. The fine model samples 128 points for synthetic datasets and 64 points for real-world datasets. Formulas: The expected color \widehat{C}(\mathbf{r}) of a ray \mathbf{r} is computed via volume rendering: \widehat{C}(\mathbf{r}) = \int{sn}^{sf} T(s) \sigma(\mathbf{r}(s)) \mathbf{c}(\mathbf{r}(s), \mathbf{d}) \, ds \quad (1) where sn and sf are the near and far boundaries of the ray, and T(s) is the accumulated transmittance: T(s) = \exp \left( - \int{sp}^s \sigma(\mathbf{r}(p)) \, dp \right) \quad (2) The radiance field F outputs the HDR radiance \mathbf{e} and density \sigma: (\mathbf{e}(\mathbf{r}), \sigma(\mathbf{r})) = F(\mathbf{r}) \quad (5) The tone mapper models the Camera Response Function (CRF). The relationship between pixel value Z, irradiance H (approximated as radiance \mathbf{e}), and exposure time \Delta t is: Z = f(H\Delta t) \quad (4) To optimize the network, the method operates in the logarithmic domain. Assuming the tone mapper f is monotonic and invertible, the color prediction for a specific channel is derived from: \ln f^{-1}(\mathbf{c}(\mathbf{r}, \Delta t)) = \ln \mathbf{e}(\mathbf{r}) + \ln \Delta t(\mathbf{r}) \quad (7) Loss Function: The total loss \mathcal{L} is a combination of Color Reconstruction Loss (\mathcal{L}c) and Unit Exposure Loss (\mathcal{L}u): \mathcal{L} = \mathcal{L}c + \lambdau \mathcal{L}u \quad (13) 1. Color Reconstruction Loss (\mathcal{L}c): Minimizes the Mean Squared Error (MSE) between the rendered LDR views and the ground truth LDR views for both coarse and fine models: \mathcal{L}c = \sum{\mathbf{r} \in \mathcal{R}(\mathbf{P})} \left( \|\widehat{C}c(\mathbf{r}, \Delta t) - C(\mathbf{r}, \Delta t)\|2^2 + \|\widehat{C}f(\mathbf{r}, \Delta t) - C(\mathbf{r}, \Delta t)\|2^2 \right) where \mathcal{R}(\mathbf{P}) is the set of camera rays at target position \mathbf{P}, and C(\mathbf{r}, \Delta t) is the ground truth pixel value. 2. Unit Exposure Loss (\mathcal{L}u): Constrains the tone mapper output g(0) to a constant C0 to fix the scale factor. This assumes pixels with value C0 correspond to unit exposure: \mathcal{L}u = \|g(0) - C0\|2^2 The weight \lambdau is fixed at 0.5. The constant C0 is set to 0.5 for real scenes (midway of pixel values) and to C{GT0} (the pixel value of the ground truth CRF when input logarithm radiance is 0) for synthetic scenes. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import torch import torch.nn as nn def posenc(x, mindeg=0, maxdeg=10, includeinput=True): """Standard NeRF positional encoding.""" scales = torch.tensor([2i for i in range(mindeg, maxdeg)]) xb = torch.reshape((x.float()[:, None,:] scales[None,:, None]), (x.shape[0], -1, x.shape[1])) freqbands = 2 torch.pi xb enc = torch.cat((torch.sin(freqbands), torch.cos(freqbands)), dim=-1) if includeinput: enc = torch.cat((x, enc), dim=-1) return enc class RadianceFieldMLP(nn.Module): """Eight-layer MLP with 256 channels.""" def init(self): super().init() layers = [] for i in range(8): inch = 5 if i == 0 else 256 layers.append(nn.Linear(inch, 256)) layers.append(nn.ReLU()) layers.append(nn.Linear(256, 4)) self.net = nn.Sequential(layers) def forward(self, xyzdir): out = self.net(xyzdir) return out[:,:3], out[:, 3] # e, sigma class ToneMapperMLP(nn.Module): """One-layer MLP with 128 channels.""" def init(self): super().init() self.net = nn.Sequential( nn.Linear(2, 128), nn.ReLU(), nn.Linear(128, 1)) def forward(self, loge, logdt): return self.net(torch.cat([loge, logdt], dim=1)) def volumerendering(rayso, raysd, near, far, radiancefield, tonemapperr, tonemapperg, tonemapperb, dt, numsamples, coarseweights=None): """Renders a ray using discrete volume integration.""" if coarseweights is None: tvals = torch.linspace(0., 1., numsamples) zvals = near (1. - tvals) + far tvals else: # Importance sampling from coarse weights zvalsmid = (zvals[:-1] + zvals[1:]) / 2.0 zvals = torch.cat([zvals[:1], zvalsmid, zvals[-1:]], dim=-1) zvals = zvals coarseweights + (1. - coarseweights) zvals pts = rayso.unsqueeze(1) + raysd.unsqueeze(1) zvals.unsqueeze(2) ptsflat = pts.reshape(-1, 3) ptsenc = posenc(ptsflat) raysdenc = posenc(raysd) inputpts = torch.cat([ptsenc, raysdenc.unsqueeze(1).expand(-1, numsamples, -1)], dim=-1) inputpts = inputpts.reshape(pts.shape[0], -1, inputpts.shape[1]) e, sigma = radiancefield(inputpts) deltas = zvals[1:] - zvals[:-1] alphas = 1.0 - torch.exp(-sigma[:,:-1] deltas) transmittances = torch.cumprod(1.0 - alphas + 1e-10, dim=1) transmittances = torch.cat([torch.oneslike(transmittances[:,:1]), transmittances], dim=1) weights = alphas transmittances[:,:-1] loge = torch.log(e + 1e-8) logdt = torch.log(dt + 1e-8).unsqueeze(0).expand(loge.shape[0], 1) logcr = tonemapperr(torch.cat([loge[:,:,0:1], logdt], dim=1)) logcg = tonemapperg(torch.cat([loge[:,:,1:2], logdt], dim=1)) logcb = tonemapperb(torch.cat([loge[:,:,2:3], logdt], dim=1)) c = torch.exp(torch.cat([logcr, logcg, logcb], dim=2)) C = torch.sum(weights.unsqueeze(-1) c, dim=1) return C, sigma, weights def trainstep(rayso, raysd, near, far, gtcolors, dt, radiancefield, tonemapperr, tonemapperg, tonemapperb): """Single training step.""" # Coarse rendering Ccoarse, sigmacoarse, weightscoarse = volumerendering(rayso, raysd, near, far, radiancefield, tonemapperr, tonemapperg, tonemapperb, dt, 64) # Fine rendering (coarse densities bias fine sampling) Cfine, sigmafine, = volumerendering(rayso, raysd, near, far, radiancefield, tonemapperr, tonemapperg, tonemapperb, dt, 128, weightscoarse) # Color Reconstruction Loss lossc = torch.sum((Ccoarse - gtcolors)2) + torch.sum((Cfine - gtcolors)2) # Unit Exposure Loss: evaluate tone mapper at logradiance=0, logexposure=0 gr = tonemapperr(torch.cat([torch.zeros(1, 1), torch.zeros(1, 1)], dim=1)) gg = tonemapperg(torch.cat([torch.zeros(1, 1), torch.zeros(1, 1)], dim=1)) gb = tonemapperb(torch.cat([torch.zeros(1, 1), torch.zeros(1, 1)], dim=1)) C0 = 0.5 lossu = (gr - C0)2 + (gg - C0)2 + (gb - C0)2 return lossc + 0.5 lossu Edge Cases and Pitfalls: High-Frequency Details: Naively feeding 5D coordinates into the MLP results in renderings that struggle to represent high-frequency variation in color and geometry; positional encoding is required. Ghost Artifacts: Traditional multi-exposure HDR methods produce ghost artifacts when the camera is hand-held or the scene is dynamic. HDR-NeRF handles varying camera poses implicitly through the radiance field, avoiding this issue. Channel-Specific CRFs: RGB channels are tone-mapped with different CRFs. Using a single MLP for all channels degrades performance; three separate MLPs are necessary. Scale Ambiguity: Without the Unit Exposure Loss, the scale of the recovered radiance field is ambiguous. The constraint g(0)=C0 fixes this scale. Time Complexity: Training requires 200K iterations on a single NVIDIA V100 GPU, taking approximately one day. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Performance: Synthetic Scenes: PSNR 39.07, SSIM 0.973, LPIPS 0.026 for LDR-OE (exposures t1, t3, t5). Real Scenes: PSNR 30.37, SSIM 0.944, LPIPS 0.075 for LDR-OE (exposures t1, t3, t5). Strengths: Recovers HDR radiance fields from LDR images without requiring HDR ground truth supervision. Enables novel view synthesis with arbitrary exposure control. Handles non-rigid scenes and camera motion better than stack-based methods by learning a continuous 3D representation. Limitations: Requires known exposure times from EXIF metadata. Performance on real-world scenes is lower than on synthetic scenes, likely due to unmodeled noise and complex lighting. Cannot render views with novel exposure times if the training data does not cover the desired exposure range effectively, though it interpolates better than NeRF-W. HDR-NeRF was introduced by Xin Huang, Qi Zhang, Ying Feng, Hongdong Li, Xuan Wang, and Qing Wang, with work conducted during an internship at Tencent AI Lab. It was published in November 2021. The method builds upon the baseline NeRF [1] and addresses the limitations of NeRF's low dynamic range output and the view-inconsistency of image-based HDR methods. It differs from "NeRF in the Dark" (RawNeRF), which recovers radiance fields from raw noisy images, by using LDR images with variable exposures. It also improves upon NeRF-W, which cannot render novel exposure times, by explicitly modeling exposure time \Delta t. The method was evaluated on a new forward-facing HDR dataset containing synthetic scenes (rendered with Blender) and real-world scenes captured by a digital camera. Neural Radiance Fields in 3D Vision: A Comprehensive Review, https://doi.org/10.26599/cvm.2026.9450535, fetched 2026-10-28 HDR-NeRF: High Dynamic Range Neural Radiance Fields, https://xhuangcv.github.io/hdr-nerf/, fetched 2026-10-27

name: GNeuVox
head: General Neural Voxels, Generalizable Neural Voxels
body: GNeuVox is a differentiable volume rendering framework for fast human radiance field optimization that replaces implicit MLPs with explicit neural voxel grids to accelerate training from hours to minutes. It distinguishes itself by maintaining two separate voxel grids: general voxels (Vg) pretrained across multiple subjects to provide geometric priors, and individual voxels (Vi) optimized per subject to capture unique differential textures. This separation allows the model to converge rapidly during fine-tuning while maintaining rendering quality comparable to methods requiring significantly longer training times. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: Monocular video frames of a human subject, initial pose estimates P (joint positions J and rotation angles \Omega), camera intrinsics, and ray origins/directions. Outputs: Rendered pixel colors \hat{C}(\mathbf{r}) and densities \sigma for novel views. Data Structures: 1. General Voxel Grid (Vg): A 3D tensor of shape Cv \times Nx \times Ny \times Nz. Cv = 6 (feature channels). Nx = Ny = Nz = 160 (resolution). Initialized via pretraining on multiple subjects. 2. Individual Voxel Grid (Vi): A 3D tensor of shape Cv \times Nx \times Ny \times Nz. Initialized to zero for each new subject. 3. Deformation Embedding (Z): A learnable vector/tensor used to compute blend weights for the deformation network. Initialized to zero for each new subject. 4. Radiance Field (\Phir): A small MLP mapping concatenated voxel features, encoded coordinates, direction, and timestamp to color \mathbf{c} and density \sigma. Numbered Steps: 1. Pose Refinement: Correct the initial pose P = (J, \Omega) to Pc = (Jc, \Omegac) using a pose refinement network \Phip. Pc = (J, \Omega \otimes \Delta\Omega) where \Delta\Omega = \Phip(\Omega), and \otimes denotes the composition of rotation matrices and translation vectors: (Ri \cdot \Delta Ri, Ti + \Delta Ti). 2. Coordinate Deformation: Map observation space coordinates \mathbf{x}o = (xo, yo, zo) to canonical T-pose coordinates \mathbf{x}c = (xc, yc, zc) using the pose deformation network \mathbf{F}d. \mathbf{x}c = \mathbf{F}d(\mathbf{x}o, Pc) The deformation is defined as a weighted sum of rigid transformations: T{skel}(\mathbf{x}, Pc) = \sum{i=1}^K w^i(\mathbf{x})(Rc^i \mathbf{x} + Tc^i) where w^i(\mathbf{x}) are blend weights obtained by mapping the embedding Z through 3D convolutional layers and trilinear interpolation. 3. Voxel Interpolation: Perform trilinear interpolation on the canonical coordinates \mathbf{x}c to extract feature vectors from both voxel grids. \mathbf{v}g = \text{interp}(\mathbf{x}c, Vg) \mathbf{v}i = \text{interp}(\mathbf{x}c, Vi) where \text{interp} denotes multi-distance interpolation (MDI). 4. Feature Concatenation and Encoding: Concatenate the features: \mathbf{v}{cat} = [\mathbf{v}g; \mathbf{v}i]. Apply positional encoding \gamma(\cdot) to the voxel features, coordinates, and direction. Voxel features \mathbf{v}: Frequency L=2. Coordinates (x, y, z): Frequency L=10. Direction \mathbf{d}: Frequency L=4. \gamma(\mathbf{x}) = (\sin(2^0 \mathbf{x}), \cos(2^0 \mathbf{x}), \dots, \sin(2^{L-1} \mathbf{x}), \cos(2^{L-1} \mathbf{x})). 5. Radiance Field Prediction: Feed the encoded voxel features, encoded coordinates, direction \mathbf{d}, and timestamp t into the radiance field \Phir. \mathbf{c}, \sigma = \Phir(\gamma(\mathbf{v}g), \gamma(\mathbf{v}i), \gamma(t), \gamma(\mathbf{x}o), \gamma(\mathbf{d})). 6. Volume Rendering: Sample N=128 points along each ray. Compute transmittance Ti and alpha \alphai. \alphai = 1 - \exp(-\sigmai \deltai) Ti = \exp\left(-\sum{j=1}^{i-1} \sigmaj \deltaj\right) \hat{C}(\mathbf{r}) = \sum{i=1}^N Ti \alphai \mathbf{c}i where \deltai = t{i+1} - ti. 7. Loss Computation: \mathcal{L} = \lambdaM \|\hat{C}(\mathbf{r}) - C(\mathbf{r})\|2^2 + \lambdaL \mathcal{L}{LPIPS} where \mathcal{L}{LPIPS} is computed on G=6 patches of size 32 \times 32. Parameters: Optimizer: Adam with \beta=(0.9, 0.99). Learning Rates: Voxel grids (Vg, Vi): 2 \times 10^{-2}. Radiance field \Phir: 5 \times 10^{-4}. Other parameters: 5 \times 10^{-5}. LR Decay: Factor of 0.1 every 500k iterations. Loss Weights: Pretraining/Scratch: \lambdaM=0.2, \lambdaL=1. Fine-tuning (first 300 iters): \lambdaM=10, \lambdaL=0. Fine-tuning (remaining): \lambdaM=0.2, \lambdaL=1. Pseudocode: Unverified code. Interpolation vg = self.interpolatevoxels(pointsc, self.Vg) vi = self.interpolatevoxels(pointsc, self.Vi) # 4. Encoding vcat = torch.cat([vg, vi], dim=-1) encv = self.positionalencoding(vcat, L=2) encx = self.positionalencoding(pointsoflat, L=10) encd = self.positionalencoding(raysd.unsqueeze(1).repeat(1, 128, 1).view(-1, 3), L=4) enct = self.positionalencoding(t.unsqueeze(1).repeat(1, 128).view(-1, 1), L=2) inputfeat = torch.cat([encv, encx, encd, enct], dim=-1) # 5. Radiance Field sigma = self.densitymlp(inputfeat) color = self.colormlp(inputfeat) # 6. Volume Rendering delta = tvals[1:] - tvals[:-1] alpha = 1.0 - torch.exp(-sigma delta.unsqueeze(-1)) T = torch.exp(-torch.cumsum(sigma delta.unsqueeze(-1), dim=1)) T = torch.cat([torch.oneslike(T[:,:1]), T[:,:-1]], dim=1) rendercolor = torch.sum(T alpha color, dim=1) return rendercolor, sigma Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Training Collapse: Training from scratch can lead to collapse or big variance in quantitative results. Pretrained general voxels alleviate this by providing prior knowledge for stable fitting. Face Rendering Vagueness and Distortion: Due to few fine-tuning iterations (≤3k) and reliance on SMPL pose/skeleton priors, complex non-rigid deformations of the face are hard to learn accurately. Boundary Conditions: Trilinear interpolation requires coordinates to be within the voxel grid bounds; out-of-bounds coordinates should be handled (e.g., clamped or padded). Explicit 3D feature grids that replace implicit MLPs for faster optimization. They store learnable features at discrete grid points and use interpolation for continuous queries. Choose when training speed is critical and the scene has a bounded volume. Link Networks that map observation-space coordinates to a canonical space using skeletal priors. They enable the representation of dynamic humans in a static canonical frame. Choose when dealing with articulated subjects like humans. Link Methods that learn a shared representation across multiple instances (e.g., different humans) to enable fast adaptation to new instances. Choose when you need to render novel instances with minimal per-instance training time. Link Time Complexity: Pretraining takes 15-50 minutes on multiple subjects. Fine-tuning for a new subject takes 1-5 minutes (1k-3k iterations). This is significantly faster than implicit NeRF methods which take hours to days (e.g., HumanNeRF takes 288 hours). Memory Complexity: Requires storing two 160^3 voxel grids with 6 channels each. This is more memory-intensive than compact MLPs but allows for faster gradient updates due to explicit structure. Performance: On ZJU-MoCap, GNeuVox-ZJU achieves PSNR 29.93 in 5 minutes, comparable to HumanNeRF (30.41 PSNR, 288 hours). Strengths: Extremely fast training time; explicit representation allows for easier debugging and modification; generalization across subjects. Limitations: Face rendering shows vagueness and distortion to some degree due to limited fine-tuning iterations and reliance on SMPL priors. When to Use: When rapid training of human radiance fields from monocular video is required, and high-frequency facial details are less critical than overall body shape and motion. When Not to Use: When high-fidelity facial animation is required, or when the scene volume is unbounded or highly irregular, making voxel grid definition difficult. GNeuVox was introduced in the paper "Generalizable Neural Voxels for Fast Human Radiance Fields". It builds upon concepts from Anim-NeRF, Neural Body, and HumanNeRF, which established the use of pose deformation and canonical space for human rendering. The key innovation is the introduction of generalizable neural voxels, which leverage the commonalities among human bodies (e.g., basic skeleton) to accelerate optimization. The method addresses the high computational cost of previous NeRF-based human rendering methods, which often require hours or days of training. name: NeRFifyMesh
body: NeRFifyMesh is a pipeline for converting textured 3D mesh models into Neural Radiance Fields (NeRFs) by generating a ground-truth point-based radiance field from mesh geometry and texture. It eliminates the need for multi-view image rendering or camera pose supervision during training, making it suitable for robotics scene building where mesh assets are abundant. Unlike Neural Radiance Fields or Instant-NGP which optimize photometric loss from images, NeRFifyMesh decouples color, normals, and opacity into separate networks trained directly on mesh-derived samples. This results in lower PSNR but superior perceptual similarity (LPIPS) and explicit surface normal prediction. Inputs: A textured mesh model \Omega with surface S, texture images, and vertex normals. Outputs: Three neural networks: f\theta (color), f\phi (normals), and f\zeta \circ f\psi (opacity), along with saved voxel indices I. Data Structures: 1. Surface Voxel Grids: N grids G1, \dots, GN. 2. Hash Tables: Hl for each grid level l. 3. Default Latent Vector: v{l, \text{default}} for points outside the occupied voxel region of Gl. 4. Voxel Indices: I = [i,j,k] for occupied voxels in each Gl, saved with the model to allow reconstruction without the original mesh. Parameters: \tau: Threshold parameter for importance weighting. Typical value: 0.1. N: Number of grid levels. Training iterations: 300,000. Batch size: 4,096 samples. Samples per mesh: 2 million points (inside, outside, on surface). Assumptions: 1. Mesh appearance is view-independent (view-direction parameters \phi, \theta are omitted). 2. Meshes are opaque (opacity is binary). Steps: 1. Generate Ground Truth Data: Sample points x=(x,y,z) within the bounding box of \Omega. Calculate Signed Distance Function (SDF) for each point. Let S be the mesh surface and (x', y', z') be the nearest point on S. Color/Normal GT: c{gt}(x) = \begin{cases} cS(x', y', z') & \text{if } SDF < 0 \\ cS(x, y, z) & \text{if } SDF = 0 \\ 0 & \text{if } SDF > 0 \end{cases} \vec{n}{gt}(x) = \begin{cases} \vec{n}S(x', y', z') & \text{if } SDF < 0 \\ \vec{n}S(x, y, z) & \text{if } SDF = 0 \\ 0 & \text{if } SDF > 0 \end{cases} where cS is texture color and \vec{n}S is barycentrically interpolated vertex normal. Opacity GT: \alpha{gt}(x) = \begin{cases} 1 & \text{if } SDF \le 0 \\ 0 & \text{if } SDF > 0 \end{cases} Importance Weights: wc(x) = w{\vec{n}}(x) = \begin{cases} \exp(-|SDF|/\tau) & \text{if } SDF \le 0 \\ 0 & \text{if } SDF > 0 \end{cases} w\alpha(x) = \begin{cases} \exp(-|SDF|/\tau) & \text{if } SDF \le 0 \\ 1 & \text{if } SDF > 0 \end{cases} These weights prioritize points near the surface and suppress external points. 2. Initialize Opacity Network: Initialize N surface voxel grids G1, \dots, GN from mesh surface points. Assign trainable latent vectors vl[i,j,k] (dim 2) to grid vertices corresponding to occupied voxels. Save indices I. 3. Train Networks: Color/Normal Networks: Apply positional encoding (sine/cosine) to input x. Feed to f\theta (color) and f\phi (normals), composed of SIREN layers. Opacity Network: 1. Query each grid Gl: Multiply x by resolution Rl. If x \in Gl, use corner indices as hash keys to retrieve vl from Hl. Else, use v{l, \text{default}}. 2. Trilinearly interpolate to get v'l(x). 3. Concatenate: V(x) = [v'1(x), \dots, v'N(x)]. 4. Decode: f\psi(V(x)). 5. Predict Opacity: \alpha(x) = f\zeta([f\psi(V(x)), x]). 4. Loss Functions: Color Loss: Lc = \frac{1}{n} \sum{i=1}^n w{c,i} (ci - c{gt,i})^2. Normal Loss: L{\vec{n}} = \frac{1}{n} \sum{i=1}^n w{\vec{n},i} (1 - \cos \deltai)^2, where \cos \deltai = \vec{n}{gt,i} \cdot \vec{n}i. Opacity Loss: L\alpha = \lambda1 L{BCE} + \lambda2 L{reg}. L{BCE} = -\frac{1}{n} \sum{i=1}^n w{\alpha,i} [\alpha{gt,i} \log \alphai + (1-\alpha{gt,i}) \log(1-\alphai)] L{reg} = \sum{l=1}^N \|vl\|^2 \lambda1, \lambda2 are weighting terms. 5. Rendering: Sample points \{ti\}{i=1}^M along camera rays with intervals \deltai = t{i+1} - ti. Transmittance: Ti = \prod{j=1}^{i-1} (1 - \alphaj). Color: \hat{C}(r) \approx \sum{i=1}^M Ti \alphai ci. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import numpy as np def positionalencoding(x, numfrequencies=10): """Standard NeRF positional encoding.""" scales = [2i for i in range(numfrequencies)] scaledx = np.outer(x, scales) encoded = np.concatenate([np.sin(scaledx), np.cos(scaledx)], axis=-1) return np.concatenate([x, encoded], axis=-1) def trilinearinterpolate(v000, v100, v010, v110, v001, v101, v011, v111, xfrac): """Trilinear interpolation of 8 corner vectors.""" x, y, z = xfrac v00 = v000 (1-x) + v100 x v01 = v010 (1-x) + v110 x v10 = v001 (1-x) + v101 x v11 = v011 (1-x) + v111 x v0 = v00 (1-y) + v01 y v1 = v10 (1-y) + v11 y return v0 (1-z) + v1 z def getopacityfeatures(x, grids, hashtables, defaultvectors): """Get concatenated features for opacity network.""" features = [] for l, resolution in enumerate(grids): indices = np.floor(x resolution).astype(int) if np.all((indices >= 0) & (indices < resolution)): corners = [] for dx in [0, 1]: for dy in [0, 1]: for dz in [0, 1]: idx = indices + np.array([dx, dy, dz]) key = tuple(idx) corners.append(hashtables[l].get(key, defaultvectors[l])) frac = x resolution - indices vinterp = trilinearinterpolate(corners, frac) features.append(vinterp) else: features.append(defaultvectors[l]) return np.concatenate(features, axis=-1) def computesdfweights(sdf, tau=0.1): """Compute importance weights based on SDF.""" abssdf = np.abs(sdf) wcn = np.where(sdf <= 0, np.exp(-abssdf / tau), 0.0) walpha = np.where(sdf <= 0, np.exp(-abssdf / tau), 1.0) return wcn, walpha def trainstep(samples, sdf, gtcolor, gtnormal, gtopacity, grids, hashtables, defaultvectors, colornet, normalnet, opacitynet, tau, lambda1=1.0, lambda2=1.0): """Single training step.""" wcn, walpha = computesdfweights(sdf, tau) encx = positionalencoding(samples) predcolor = colornet(encx) prednormal = normalnet(encx) features = getopacityfeatures(samples, grids, hashtables, defaultvectors) opacityinput = np.concatenate([features, samples], axis=-1) predopacity = opacitynet(opacityinput).squeeze(-1) colorloss = np.mean(wcn (predcolor - gtcolor)2) cossim = np.sum(prednormal gtnormal, axis=-1) cossim = np.clip(cossim, -1.0, 1.0) normalloss = np.mean(wcn (1 - cossim)2) eps = 1e-7 predopacityclamped = np.clip(predopacity, eps, 1-eps) bce = -np.mean(walpha (gtopacity np.log(predopacityclamped) + (1 - gtopacity) np.log(1 - predopacityclamped))) regloss = 0.0 for table in hashtables.values(): for vec in table.values(): regloss += np.sum(vec2) totalopacityloss = lambda1 bce + lambda2 regloss return colorloss, normalloss, totalopacityloss def renderray(rayorigin, raydirection, maxdist, grids, hashtables, defaultvectors, colornet, normalnet, opacitynet, numsamples=128): """Render a single ray.""" tvals = np.linspace(0.0, maxdist, numsamples) points = rayorigin + raydirection tvals[:, np.newaxis] encx = positionalencoding(points) predcolor = colornet(encx) features = getopacityfeatures(points, grids, hashtables, defaultvectors) opacityinput = np.concatenate([features, points], axis=-1) predopacity = opacitynet(opacityinput).squeeze(-1) transmittance = np.ones(numsamples) for i in range(1, numsamples): transmittance[i] = transmittance[i-1] (1 - predopacity[i-1]) weights = transmittance predopacity finalcolor = np.sum(weights[:, np.newaxis] predcolor, axis=0) return finalcolor A method for assembling multiple independent radiance-field models (specifically NeRFifyMesh or iVR-GS representations) into a single unified global scene without retraining. It solves the problem of scalable scene building by allowing pre-converted mesh-based models to be placed in a global coordinate system or integrated with existing NeRF models. It differs from monolithic training approaches by treating each model as an independent, transformable primitive that is composited at render time via depth-based blending. A hybrid representation method that combines a textured mesh with a sparse voxel grid to achieve real-time view synthesis while preserving comprehensive scene information. It solves the trade-off between the geometric precision of meshes and the volumetric completeness of neural radiance fields by using the mesh for surface details and the voxels for thin structures and background volume. Unlike Adaptive Shells, which constrain volume rendering to regions near the surface, Vosh allows pure volume rendering where necessary, making it suitable for outdoor scenes. It differs from VMesh by reconstructing a volumetric density field, enabling the mesh to represent thin structures like fishing nets that are difficult to capture with Signed Distance Fields (SDFs). A neural radiance field representation that synthesizes novel images efficiently using standard polygon rasterization pipelines, avoiding specialized volumetric ray marching. It represents the NeRF as a set of textured polygons with binary opacities and feature vectors, interpreted by a small view-dependent MLP in a fragment shader to produce final pixel color. Unlike classic NeRF which uses volumetric density compositing, MobileNeRF uses opacity compositing on a mesh. Unlike semi-transparent mesh rendering which requires per-frame sorting, MobileNeRF uses binary opacity and z-buffering, which is order-independent. It is 10x faster than SNeRG with the same output quality and consumes less memory by storing surface textures instead of volumetric textures. A surface estimation technique used in point cloud rendering to determine the precise 3D position of a ray-surface intersection from discrete point data. It solves the problem of inaccurate depth sampling in sparse or noisy point clouds by correcting the raw depth value based on the angle between the viewing ray and the scene's primary axis. Unlike standard depth buffering which assumes a planar intersection perpendicular to the view ray, this method accounts for surface orientation, enabling photorealistic rendering from discrete points by providing accurate input coordinates for subsequent neural radiance mapping. It serves as the foundational geometry estimation step in the End-to-End Rendering Pipeline, preceding the frequency-modulated radiance mapping stage. A method to fill a user-selected area on a neural implicit field with a texture template (e.g., furry hair or golden metal) from a pre-captured object model. First, the target UV-map of the selected area is obtained by unwrapping in Blender. A texture template from a pre-trained NeuMesh model (e.g., a small squared patch with ~10 vertices) is repeatedly filled into the target UV-map in a sliding-window manner. Texture codes in target vertices are assigned with interpolated codes from the template, and the radiance decoder is bound to the one from the pretrained model because target and template texture codes do not share the same latent radiance space. For smooth transitions near the area boundary, color contributions from different decoders are fused with inverse distance weighting for query points having texture codes/decoders from different sources. A method to attach realistic surface structures modeled by NeRFs onto a 3D mesh by deforming a voxel grid and using a deformation field. First, a scene is synthesized on a plane with desired lighting using a specific shading map guider. The corresponding voxel grid is deformed to match the 3D mesh using a deformation field \Psi: x \rightarrow \Delta x, which maps points in the deformed space to the canonical space. The deformation field is bent to synthesize a large-scale V(d) onto the 3D mesh, and a ray-tracing-based method computes the shading map guider on the surface. The shading map guider synthesizes a new scene with desired lighting and deforms it to match the target mesh surface. The ARAP parametric method establishes the mapping between the 3D mesh and the undersurface of the scene, defining corresponding directions for each vertex along the normal direction to collect discrete corresponding points. A neural network fits the deformation field using MSE loss on the coordinates of corresponding points as supervision. Time and Memory Complexity: Training time: ~2 hours per model on an NVIDIA P100 GPU with 50 GB RAM. Model Size: 4.7 ± 0.2 MB on the Objaverse dataset, achieving a 14.4x compression ratio compared to the original mesh size of 67.3 ± 60.6 MB. Memory usage depends on the number of hash table entries and grid levels. Measured Performance (Objaverse dataset): PSNR: 31.70 (lower than Instant-NGP 35.62 and NeRF 32.20). LPIPS: 0.037 (better than Instant-NGP 0.043 and NeRF 0.083). SSIM: 0.958 (better than NeRF 0.927, lower than Instant-NGP 0.965). Surface Normal Accuracy: RMSAE of 4.59 ± 1.84 degrees. Strengths and Limitations: Strengths: No need for multi-view images or camera poses. Explicit surface normal prediction enables relighting. High perceptual quality (LPIPS). Significant model compression. Limitations: Lower PSNR compared to image-optimized methods. Assumes view-independent appearance and opaque meshes. Requires watertight meshes for SDF calculation. When to use: When converting existing mesh assets (e.g., from Objaverse, Poly Haven) to NeRFs for robotics or simulation. When explicit normals are needed for shading/relighting. When model size is a constraint. When not to use: When photometric accuracy (PSNR) is the primary metric. For scenes with translucent objects or view-dependent effects (e.g., glossy reflections). NeRFifyMesh was introduced to address the need for tools to convert existing 3D mesh models into NeRF representations for rapid algorithm development and testing, particularly in robotics. It builds on the principles of Radiance-field optimization but diverges by using mesh-derived ground truth instead of image-based optimization. The method leverages hash encoding inspired by Instant-NGP and SIREN networks for color/normal prediction.
