name: Scene Composition
head: Composed iVR-GS
body: Scene Composition assembles multiple independent radiance-field models (NeRFifyMesh or iVR-GS representations) into a unified global scene without retraining. It solves scalable scene building by allowing pre-converted mesh-based models to be placed in a global coordinate system or integrated with existing NeRF models. It differs from monolithic training approaches by treating each model as an independent, transformable primitive composited at render time. Inputs: N pre-trained local radiance-field models (NeRFifyMesh or iVR-GS). For each model i, a pose transformation matrix T{wi} \in SE(3) defining its position and orientation in the global world frame. For iVR-GS models: quantized attribute data, exact values for mean \mu and normal n, shared codebook indices for other attributes, and a global palette color cp. Outputs: A single composed radiance field representation. Rendered 2D images with correct occlusion handling between models. Data Structures: Local Model Parameters: NeRFifyMesh stores implicit neural network weights. iVR-GS stores explicit Gaussian primitives with \mu (exact floats), n (exact floats), other attributes (shared codebook indices), and cp (global palette color). Global Scene List: A single parameter list formed by concatenating the decompressed attribute values of all primitives from all basic models. Steps: 1. Normalization: Each NeRFifyMesh model is normalized to fit within a unit cube and defined in a local coordinate frame. 2. Storage (iVR-GS specific): Save exact values of \mu and n, and indices with shared codebooks for other attributes for each editable Gaussian. Store palette color cp as a global parameter for each basic scene. 3. Ray Casting: Cast rays from a virtual camera in the global frame. The ray is defined as rw(t) = ow + t\vec{d}w, where ow is ray origin and \vec{d}w is ray direction. 4. Coordinate Transformation: Transform the world-frame ray into the local coordinate frame of each model i using the inverse transformation: ri(t) = T^{-1}{wi} rw(t), where T{wi} \in SE(3) is the pose of model i in the world frame. 5. Local Evaluation: Evaluate each local NeRF model using the transformed ray ri(t). Each model returns RGB and depth values for the transformed rays. 6. Decompression and Composition (iVR-GS specific): Decompress each model from the quantized format and append attribute values of primitives from basic iVR-GS models into a single parameter list to form the composed model. 7. Depth-Based Blending: Composite per-model renderings in the 2D image plane using depth-based ordering to resolve occlusions. For each pixel, blend RGB outputs from different models back-to-front using the corresponding depth values. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def invertse3(T): # T is a 4x4 list of lists representing an SE(3) matrix. # Returns the inverse matrix. R = [T[i][:3] for i in range(3)] t = [T[i][3] for i in range(3)] Rt = [[R[j][i] for j in range(3)] for i in range(3)] invt = [-sum(Rt[i][j] t[j] for j in range(3)) for i in range(3)] inv = [[0.0] 4 for in range(4)] for i in range(3): inv[i][:3] = Rt[i] inv[i][3] = invt[i] inv[3][3] = 1.0 return inv def transformpoint(M, p): x, y, z = p return (M[0][0]x + M[0][1]y + M[0][2]z + M[0][3], M[1][0]x + M[1][1]y + M[1][2]z + M[1][3], M[2][0]x + M[2][1]y + M[2][2]z + M[2][3]) def transformvector(M, v): x, y, z = v return (M[0][0]x + M[0][1]y + M[0][2]z, M[1][0]x + M[1][1]y + M[1][2]z, M[2][0]x + M[2][1]y + M[2][2]z) def composeandrender(models, cameraorigin, cameradirection, poses): # Step 3 & 4: Cast ray and transform to local frames results = [] for i, model in enumerate(models): Tinv = invertse3(poses[i]) localorigin = transformpoint(Tinv, cameraorigin) localdir = transformvector(Tinv, cameradirection) # Step 5: Local evaluation # The sources do not specify the exact evaluation routine; standard radiance field sampling is used. rgb, depth = [0.0, 0.0, 0.0], 0.0 # Placeholder for model.evaluate() results.append({'rgb': rgb, 'depth': depth}) # Step 7: Depth-based blending results.sort(key=lambda r: r['depth'], reverse=True) finalrgb = [0.0, 0.0, 0.0] for res in results: rgb = res['rgb'] alpha = res.get('alpha', 1.0) finalrgb = [finalrgb[j] + rgb[j] alpha (1.0 - sum(finalrgb[k] for k in range(3))) for j in range(3)] return finalrgb def composeivrgsmodels(basicmodels): # Step 6: Decompress and append primitives composedprimitives = [] for model in basicmodels: decompressed = model.decompress() composedprimitives.extend(decompressed.primitives) return composedprimitives Parameters: T{wi}: Pose matrix. Not given in the sources. Depth threshold: Not given in the sources. Early termination threshold: Not given in the sources. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Occlusion: Incorrect depth sorting leads to visual artifacts where models intersect incorrectly. Depth-based ordering is critical. Coordinate Systems: Failure to correctly invert T{wi} results in models appearing in wrong positions or orientations. Quantization Loss (iVR-GS): While VQ provides ~4× compression, decompression must be exact for \mu and n to maintain geometric fidelity. Boundary Artifacts: Models normalized to a unit cube may have discontinuities at their boundaries if not handled by the underlying radiance field. Time Complexity: Rendering time scales linearly with the number of models N and the number of primitives per model. Each ray must be evaluated against all models before blending. Memory Complexity: Memory usage is the sum of the memory required for all individual models. For iVR-GS, this includes the decompressed primitives and codebooks. Performance: The composition pipeline itself is lightweight; the cost is dominated by the individual model evaluations. NeRFifyMesh models capture interior features due to geometry-based sampling. Strengths: Enables real-time scene editing for iVR-GS by adjusting editable Gaussian attributes. Allows modular scene building without retraining. Limitations: Requires pre-computation/normalization of each model. Occlusion handling is simplified to depth-based blending, which may not account for complex inter-model lighting or shadows. Scene Composition was introduced as part of the NeRFifyMesh pipeline and the iVR-GS framework. NeRFifyMesh was developed to convert textured mesh models into NeRF representations for robotics scene building, addressing the need for scalable scene assembly. iVR-GS extended this concept to editable 3D Gaussian Splatting, allowing for composability and real-time editing. iVR-GS: Inverse Volume Rendering for Explorable Visualization via Editable 3D Gaussian Splatting., https://doi.org/10.1109/tvcg.2025.3567121, fetched 2026-10-26 NeRFifyMesh: Optimizing Neural Radiance Fields from Textured Meshes for Robotics Scene Building, https://doi.org/10.48550/arxiv.2610.10387, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial) Frequency-Modulated Point Cloud Rendering with Easy Editing, https://doi.org/10.1109/cvpr52729.2023.00020, fetched 2026-10-29

name: Vosh Hybrid Rendering
head: Vosh, Voxel-Mesh Hybrid Representation
body: Vosh is a hybrid representation method that combines a textured mesh with a sparse voxel grid to achieve real-time view synthesis while preserving comprehensive scene information. It solves the trade-off between the geometric precision of meshes and the volumetric completeness of neural radiance fields by using the mesh for surface details and the voxels for thin structures and background volume. Unlike Adaptive Shells, which constrain volume rendering to regions near the surface, Vosh allows pure volume rendering where necessary, making it suitable for outdoor scenes. It differs from VMesh by reconstructing a volumetric density field, enabling the mesh to represent thin structures like fishing nets that are difficult to capture with Signed Distance Fields (SDFs). Vosh operates in three stages: initial voxel training, mesh refinement, and final hybrid optimization. The method ensures consistency between GPU training and web inference by employing both rasterization and ray marching passes. Inputs: Textured mesh models, camera poses, and multi-view images. Outputs: A hybrid asset consisting of a textured mesh and a sparse voxel grid, along with associated metadata for real-time rendering. 1. Mesh: Standard triangle mesh with appearance textures storing diffuse color and view-dependent features. 2. Sparse Voxel Grid: Based on the multi-resolution hierarchical occupancy grid from SNeRG. Occupancy Grid: Binary mask images at multiple resolution levels created via max-pooling to mark occupied voxels. Voxel Attributes: Stored in a sparse structure to minimize memory usage. 3. Mesh-Occupancy Grid: A grid used to filter spatial overlap between mesh and voxels. Resolution r{mesh} is a hyperparameter. r{mesh}: Resolution of the mesh-occupancy grid. Set to 128 for Vosh-Light. \lambda{voxel}: Voxel pruning loss weight. Set to 0.001 for Vosh-Base and 0.01 for Vosh-Light. premove: Parameter for mesh refinement stage. Set to 0.9 for Vosh-Base and 1.0 for Vosh-Light. Marching Cubes Resolution: 1024. Optimizer: 25,000 steps, initial learning rate 1e-2, warmup for 100 steps, decaying to 1e-3. 1. Train initial voxels using classic MSE loss to measure pixel-level color differences. 2. Use the same optimizer settings as MERF. 1. Perform meshing of the density field for 20,000 steps. 2. Set premove to 0.9 (Vosh-Base) or 1.0 (Vosh-Light). 3. Clean the mesh using operations similar to NeRF2Mesh. 4. Apply L2 regularization terms with rendering weights for background colors to encourage voxels to fill holes in the mesh. 5. Repeat mesh cleaning operations if messy floating faces are produced. This stage combines rasterization and ray marching. 1. Calculate Mesh-Occupancy Grid: Compute the occupancy grid of the meshes under training poses. Filter out voxels located in the mesh-occupied grid areas during rendering and baking to prevent spatial overlap. Adjust the ratio of sparse voxels by setting r{mesh} to suppress voxel density. 2. Rasterization Pass: Uniformly shade the meshes. The fragment shader samples appearance textures to incorporate diffuse color and view-dependent features. Output: Diffuse color, view-dependent features, and a depth map. 3. Ray Marching Pass: Use the multi-resolution hierarchical occupancy grid (from SNeRG) to create binary mask images via max-pooling. Perform spatial skips during ray marching using these masks. Reduce sampling distance using the depth map obtained from the rasterization pass. 4. Hybrid Combination: For each spatial coordinate after ray marching, compare the transformed depth with the rasterization depth map. Determine if the ray has intersected the surface position. If the ray reaches the mesh surface: Stop marching. Weightily combine the accumulated ray marching result with the appearance result from the rasterization pass. If the ray does not hit the surface, continue marching or accumulate volume contribution as per standard volume rendering. 5. Loss Function: Apply voxel pruning loss weighted by \lambda{voxel}. For Vosh-Base, disable the binary mesh-occupancy grid. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def voshrender(camera, mesh, voxelgrid, meshoccupancygrid, depthmapraster): """ Renders a frame using Vosh hybrid representation. Args: camera: Camera parameters (position, orientation, intrinsics). mesh: Textured mesh object. voxelgrid: Sparse voxel grid with multi-resolution occupancy masks. meshoccupancygrid: Binary grid indicating mesh-occupied voxels. depthmapraster: Depth map from the rasterization pass. Returns: color: Rendered pixel color. """ # 1. Rasterization Pass # Uniformly shade meshes and sample appearance textures rasteroutput = rasterizemesh(mesh, camera) diffusecolor = rasteroutput.diffusecolor viewdependentfeatures = rasteroutput.viewdependentfeatures depthmapraster = rasteroutput.depthmap # 2. Ray Marching Setup # Get ray directions for each pixel rays = generaterays(camera) # Initialize accumulation accumulatedcolor = 0.0 accumulatedalpha = 0.0 for each pixel (u, v): ray = rays[u, v] currentdepth = 0.0 raymarchingaccum = 0.0 raymarchingalpha = 0.0 # 3. Ray Marching with Spatial Skips # Use multi-resolution occupancy grid for spatial skips while currentdepth < maxdistance: # Check occupancy grid for spatial skip if not voxelgrid.isoccupied(ray, currentdepth): currentdepth += skipstep continue # Sample voxel density and color density, color = voxelgrid.sample(ray, currentdepth) # Standard volume rendering accumulation alpha = 1.0 - exp(-density stepsize) raymarchingaccum += color alpha (1.0 - raymarchingalpha) raymarchingalpha += alpha (1.0 - raymarchingalpha) currentdepth += stepsize # 4. Surface Intersection Check # Compare transformed depth with rasterization depth map rasterdepth = depthmapraster[u, v] # If ray hits mesh surface (within tolerance) if abs(currentdepth - rasterdepth) < epsilon: # Stop marching break # 5. Hybrid Combination # Weightily combine ray marching result with rasterization appearance # Note: The exact weighting function is not specified in sources # Assuming a simple blend based on alpha or depth proximity meshcolor = diffusecolor[u, v] # Combine: If surface hit, use mesh color weighted by ray marching alpha # If no surface hit, use ray marching result if surfacehit: color = lerp(raymarchingaccum, meshcolor, raymarchingalpha) else: color = raymarchingaccum accumulatedcolor[u, v] = color return accumulatedcolor def voshtrain(mesh, voxelgrid, images, poses): """ Trains the Vosh hybrid representation. """ # Stage 1: Initial Voxel Training traininitialvoxels(voxelgrid, images, poses, lossfn=MSE) # Stage 2: Mesh Refinement refinemesh(mesh, voxelgrid, premove=0.9, steps=20000) cleanmesh(mesh) applyl2regularization(voxelgrid, mesh, target='backgroundcolors') # Stage 3: Hybrid Optimization for step in range(25000): # Calculate mesh-occupancy grid meshoccupancygrid = calculatemeshoccupancy(mesh, poses) # Filter voxels in mesh-occupied areas voxelgrid.filter(meshoccupancygrid) # Render and compute loss renderedimages = voshrenderallviews(mesh, voxelgrid, meshoccupancygrid, images, poses) loss = computeloss(renderedimages, images) # Add voxel pruning loss if modeltype == 'Vosh-Light': loss += lambdavoxel computevoxelpruningloss(voxelgrid) # Backpropagate optimizer.step(loss) Training Time: On a single NVIDIA RTX 4090, training takes approximately 66 minutes for initial voxels, 35 minutes for mesh refinement, and 58 minutes for Vosh optimization. Memory Usage: Peak VRAM usage during training is ~11 GB. Storage: Vosh-Base: 506 MB VRAM, 488 MB disk. Vosh-Light: 490 MB VRAM, 232 MB disk. These sizes are on Mip-NeRF 360 outdoor scenes. Performance: Vosh achieves real-time rendering on mobile devices. Strengths: Restores comprehensive scene information compared to SDF-based methods. Can represent thin structures (e.g., fishing nets, ropes) that are difficult for SDFs. Suitable for outdoor scenes where pure volume rendering is necessary. Limitations: Slightly lower rendering quality in indoor scenes compared to MLP-based methods due to the use of a tiny view-dependent MLP. Disk storage is slightly larger than MERF because it does not use triplane representation. When to Use: When real-time rendering on mobile devices is required, and the scene contains thin structures or requires pure volume rendering (e.g., outdoor scenes). When Not to Use: When maximum indoor rendering quality is prioritized over speed, or when disk space is extremely constrained and MERF's triplane representation is acceptable. Vosh (Voxel-Mesh Hybrid Representation) was introduced in the paper "Voxel-Mesh Hybrid Representation for Real-Time View Synthesis". The method builds on previous works such as SNeRG for sparse voxel storage, MERF for optimizer settings, and NeRF2Mesh for mesh cleaning. It was developed to address the limitations of pure mesh or pure volume representations, particularly in the context of real-time view synthesis on mobile devices. Voxel-Mesh Hybrid Representation for Real-Time View Synthesis, https://doi.org/10.48550/arxiv.2403.06505, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial)

name: MobileNeRF
head: MobileNeRF Forward/Deferred Rendering Pipeline, MobileNeRF rendering modes
body: MobileNeRF is a neural radiance field representation that synthesizes novel images efficiently using standard polygon rasterization pipelines, avoiding specialized volumetric ray marching. It represents the NeRF as a set of textured polygons with binary opacities and feature vectors, interpreted by a small view-dependent MLP in a fragment shader to produce final pixel color. Unlike classic NeRF which uses volumetric density compositing, MobileNeRF uses opacity compositing on a mesh. Unlike semi-transparent mesh rendering which requires per-frame sorting, MobileNeRF uses binary opacity and z-buffering, which is order-independent. It is 10x faster than SNeRG with the same output quality and consumes less memory by storing surface textures instead of volumetric textures. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: A collection of calibrated images (training); Camera pose (rendering). Outputs: Novel-view RGB images (rendering); Optimized mesh topology, vertex locations, and MLP weights (training). Data Structures: 1. Polygonal Mesh M=(T, V): T: Fixed topology (initially derived from a regular grid). V: Vertex locations, optimized during training. Initialized to a regular Euclidean lattice in the unit cube. 2. Acceleration Grid \Grid: A 3D grid of size P \times P \times P (default P=128) in the unit cube. Stores scalar values used to prune voxels during ray marching. 3. MLPs: \OpacityMLP: \real^3 \rightarrow [0,1]: Predicts opacity \alphak at position \mathbf{p}k. \FeaturesMLP: \real^3 \rightarrow [0,1]^8: Predicts 8-channel feature vector \mathbf{f}k at position \mathbf{p}k. \ShaderMLP: [0,1]^8 \times [-1,1]^3 \rightarrow [0,1]^3: The "neural deferred shader." Takes feature vector \mathbf{f}k and viewing direction \mathbf{d} to output color \mathbf{c}k. 4. Texture Maps (Post-Training): Allocated as K \times K patches per quad (default K=17, resulting in 16 \times 16 texture with half-pixel boundary padding). Stores 8-bit quantized discrete opacity and 8-channel features. Stored as losslessly compressed PNGs. 5. Shader Weights: Stored in a JSON file. Training Stages: Stage 1: Continuous Training 1. Initialization: Create a regular grid G of size P \times P \times P in the unit cube centered at the origin. Instantiate vertices V by creating one vertex per voxel. Create triangles T by creating one quadrangle (two triangles) per grid edge connecting vertices of four adjacent voxels, akin to Dual Contouring. 2. Quadrature Point Generation: For each training ray \mathbf{r}: a. Compute intersections between the ray and the dual grid to get candidate voxels: \tilde{\Voxels} = \text{intersect}(\mathbf{r}, \DualGrid). b. Prune voxels using the acceleration grid \Grid with threshold \tau\Grid: \Voxels = \{ b \in \tilde{\Voxels} ~|~ \Grid[b] > \tau\Grid \}. c. Compute final quadrature points by intersecting the ray with mesh faces incident to the pruned voxel vertices: \QuadraturePoints = \text{intersect}(\mathbf{r}, \{ \triangle \in \Triangles ~|~ \triangle \cap \Voxels \}). d. Sort quadrature points by depth. 3. Feature and Opacity Evaluation: For each quadrature point \mathbf{p}k = \mathbf{r}(tk): \alphak = \OpacityMLP(\mathbf{p}k; \pars\OpacityMLP). \mathbf{f}k = \FeaturesMLP(\mathbf{p}k; \pars\FeaturesMLP). \mathbf{c}k = \ShaderMLP(\mathbf{f}k, \mathbf{d}; \pars\ShaderMLP). 4. Alpha Compositing: Compute predicted color \mathbf{C}(\mathbf{r}): \mathbf{C}(\mathbf{r}) = \sum{k=1}^{K} Tk \alphak \mathbf{c}k, \quad Tk = \prod{l=1}^{k-1}(1-\alphal). 5. Gradient Back-propagation: Back-propagate gradients from the intersection point to the three vertices of the intersected triangle using barycentric interpolation. 6. Loss Functions: Color Loss: \mathcal{L}\mathbf{C} = \expect{\mathbf{r}} \| \mathbf{C}(\mathbf{r}) - \mathbf{C}\text{gt}(\mathbf{r}) \|2^2. For real-world scenes, add distortion loss \mathcal{L}\text{dist}. Acceleration Grid Boundary Loss: \mathcal{L}\Grid^\text{bnd} = \sumk \max(\StopGradient[Tk \alphak] - \Grid[\mathbf{p}k], 0). Acceleration Grid Sparsity Loss: \mathcal{L}\Grid^\text{sparse} = \|\Grid\|1^1. Acceleration Grid Smoothness Loss: \mathcal{L}\Grid^\text{smooth} = \|\nabla \Grid\|2^2. Vertex Regularization: \mathcal{L}\Vertices = \sum{\mathbf{v} \in \Vertices} (10^3 \mathcal{I}(\mathbf{v}) + 10^{-2}) \cdot \|\mathbf{v}\|1, where \mathcal{I}(\mathbf{v})=1 if vertex \mathbf{v} is outside its corresponding voxel, else 0. Stage 2: Binarized Training 1. Binarization: Convert smooth opacity \alphak \in [0,1] to discrete/categorical opacity \hat{\alpha}k \in \{0, 1\} using a straight-through estimator: \dOpacityk = \alphak + \StopGradient[\mathbbm{1}(\alphak > 0.5) - \alphak]. 2. Co-training: Optimize continuous and discrete models simultaneously using combined loss: \mathcal{L}\Color^\text{stage2} = \tfrac{1}{2} \mathcal{L}\Color^\text{bin} + \tfrac{1}{2} \mathcal{L}\Color where \mathcal{L}\Color^\text{bin} is the MSE between binarized color output and ground truth. 3. Binarized Color Output: \hat{\Color}(\mathbf{r}) = \sum{k=1}^{K} \hat{T}k \dOpacityk \mathbf{c}k, \quad \hat{T}k = \prod{l=1}^{k-1}(1-\dOpacityl). 4. Anti-aliasing: Rasterize features at 2x resolution to produce a feature image. Average sub-pixel features to produce the antialiased representation fed to the neural deferred shader: \Color(\mathbf{r}) = \ShaderMLP \left( \expect{\mathbf{r}\delta \sim \mathbf{r}}[\Feature(\mathbf{r}\delta)], \: \expect{\mathbf{r}\delta \sim \mathbf{r}}[\mathbf{d}\delta] \right) where the expectation averages four sub-pixels. 5. Fine-tuning: After convergence, fine-tune weights in \FeaturesMLP and \ShaderMLP by minimizing \mathcal{L}\Color^\text{bin} while fixing other weights. Stage 3: Discretization and Export 1. Mesh Extraction: Convert the representation into an explicit polygonal mesh in OBJ format. Discard quads that are not partially visible in training camera poses. 2. Texture Baking: a. Allocate a K \times K patch in the texture per quad (K=17). b. Iterate over pixels, convert to 3D coordinates, and bake discrete opacity and features into the texture map. c. Quantize [0,1] ranges to 8-bit integers and store as losslessly compressed PNG. 3. Shader Export: Store the weights of the neural deferred shader in a JSON file. Rendering: Two modes are supported: Deferred Rendering: 1. Pass 1: Rasterize all faces of the textured mesh with a z-buffer to produce a 2M \times 2N feature image with 12 channels per pixel: 8 channels of learned features, 1 binary opacity, and 3D view direction. 2. Pass 2: Synthesize an M \times N output RGB image by rendering a textured rectangle using the feature image as texture, with linear filtering to average features for anti-aliasing. Apply the small MLP (implemented as a GLSL fragment shader) for pixels with nonzero alphas to convert features into RGB colors. Forward Rendering: 1. Meshes and textures are directly rasterized into pixels containing RGB colors using the MLP fragment shader. 2. Anti-aliasing is handled by super-sampling on pixel colors (unlike deferred rendering which super-samples features). 3. A depth pre-pass can help resolve excessive overdraw issues. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def trainmobilenerf(images, cameraposes, P=128, K=17): # Initialization gridsize = P vertices = initializeregulargrid(gridsize) # V in [-0.5, 0.5] relative to voxel centers topology = createdualcontouringtopology(vertices) accelgrid = zeros((P, P, P)) # MLPs opacitymlp = MLP(inputdim=3, outputdim=1) featuremlp = MLP(inputdim=3, outputdim=8) shadermlp = MLP(inputdim=11, outputdim=3) # 8 features + 3 view dir for stage in [1, 2, 3]: for epoch in epochs: for image, pose in zip(images, cameraposes): rays = generaterays(pose, image.shape) loss = 0 for ray in rays: # Quadrature candidatevoxels = intersectrayvoxelgrid(ray, dualgrid(vertices)) prunedvoxels = [v for v in candidatevoxels if accelgrid[v] > threshold] quadpoints = intersectraymeshfaces(ray, topology, prunedvoxels) # Evaluate MLPs opacities = [] features = [] colors = [] for p in quadpoints: alpha = sigmoid(opacitymlp(p)) f = sigmoid(featuremlp(p)) d = normalize(ray.direction) c = sigmoid(shadermlp(concat(f, d))) opacities.append(alpha) features.append(f) colors.append(c) # Alpha Compositing if stage == 1: # Continuous T = 1.0 predcolor = 0.0 for alpha, f, c in zip(opacities, features, colors): T = (1 - alpha) predcolor += T alpha c loss += mse(predcolor, gtcolor) # Grid and Vertex Losses loss += lasso(accelgrid) loss += smoothness(accelgrid) loss += vertexreg(vertices) # Boundary loss requires gradient stop loss += boundaryloss(T, alpha, accelgrid, quadpoints) elif stage == 2: # Binarized with Straight-Through Estimator binarizedopacities = [] for alpha in opacities: # Straight-through: gradient passes through, value is binarized binalpha = 1.0 if alpha > 0.5 else 0.0 binarizedopacities.append(binalpha) # Anti-aliasing: Average features from 4 sub-pixels # (Simplified: assume subray generation and averaging is handled) avgfeatures = averagesubpixelfeatures(features) avgviewdirs = averagesubpixeldirections(ray.direction) avgcolor = sigmoid(shadermlp(concat(avgfeatures, avgviewdirs))) # Compositing with binarized opacities T = 1.0 binpredcolor = 0.0 for binalpha, c in zip(binarizedopacities, colors): T = (1 - binalpha) binpredcolor += T binalpha c loss += 0.5 mse(binpredcolor, gtcolor) loss += 0.5 mse(avgcolor, gtcolor) elif stage == 3: # Export only, no training loss pass # Backpropagate gradients = computegradients(loss) updateparameters(gradients) # Texture Baking texturemaps = [] for quad in topology: patch = zeros((K, K, 9)) # 8 features + 1 opacity for u in range(K): for v in range(K): # Convert 2D texture coord to 3D point on quad p = uvto3d(u, v, quad) alpha = 1.0 if opacitymlp(p) > 0.5 else 0.0 f = sigmoid(featuremlp(p)) patch[u, v] = concat(f, [alpha]) texturemaps.append(patch) return OBJ(topology, vertices), texturemaps, shadermlp.weights Parameters: Grid size P: Default 128. Reducing to 64 causes slight performance drop. Texture patch size K: Default 17. K=33 quadruples texture size and improves performance; K=9 drops performance. Sub-pixel count for anti-aliasing: 4. Rendering resolution: Matches training images (800x800 synthetic, 1008x756 forward-facing, 1256x828 unbounded). Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Aliasing: Representing continuous signals with discrete representations can introduce aliasing. Semi-transparency: Binary opacities prevent handling semi-transparent scenes and generate scattered small fragments in semi-transparent parts. Resolution Limits: Fixed mesh and texture resolutions may be too coarse for close-up novel-view synthesis, causing loss of fine details like grass. Specular Surfaces: Specular surfaces and sparse training views cause incorrect surface estimation, modeling reflections as real objects behind surfaces. Glossy Surfaces: The method models a radiance field without explicitly decomposing illumination and reflectance, reducing performance on glossy surfaces. Precision Errors: Precision errors in rasterization cause very different pixels on the boundary of a part when comparing Python-rendered images to web browser-rendered images. Super-sampling Mode: Super-sampling must be done on pixel features for deferred rendering, while it should be done on pixel colors for forward rendering; using the wrong mode causes slightly different rendered results. Time Complexity: Rendering is O(1) per pixel for deferred mode (MLP executed once per pixel) and O(F) for forward mode (MLP executed once per fragment, where F is fragment count). Training is slow due to NeRF MLP backbone. Memory Complexity: Stores surface textures instead of volumetric textures, consuming less memory than SNeRG (5x less GPU memory). Measured Performance: Pixel 3 (Synthetic 360°): 37.14 FPS. Surface Pro 6 (Synthetic 360°): 37.14 FPS (default), 32.48 FPS (K=33), 37.74 FPS (K=9), 51.81 FPS (no supersampling), 52.16 FPS (no view-dependent MLP). Samsung Galaxy S22 Ultra (Unbounded): 84 FPS (optimized forward), 35 FPS (optimized deferred). Gaming Laptop (Composited Scene): 150 FPS at 1920x1080, 1.5 GB GPU memory. Strengths: 10x faster than SNeRG; runs on mobile phones and web browsers; order-independent transparency via binary opacity; easy editing of explicit mesh. Limitations: Cannot handle semi-transparency; slow training; fixed resolution limits detail; struggles with specular/glossy surfaces; forward rendering can be slower than deferred on some devices due to overdraw. When to Use: Real-time visualization on mobile devices, web browsers, or integrated GPUs where memory and power are constrained. When Not to Use: Scenes requiring semi-transparency, high-fidelity glossy/specular surfaces, or close-up synthesis requiring high-resolution textures. MobileNeRF was introduced in 2023 by the authors of the paper "MobileNeRF: Exploiting the Polygon Rasterization Pipeline for Efficient Neural Field Rendering on Mobile Architectures". It addresses the mismatch between specialized volumetric ray marching algorithms and widely deployed graphics hardware, particularly on mobile devices. The method builds on the idea of surface-based neural fields and rasterization pipelines, aiming to achieve interactive frame rates on a wide range of compute platforms. It is implemented as an HTML webpage rendered by WebGL via the threejs library, allowing it to run on Chrome browser, Surface Pro 6, and Pixel 3. MobileNeRF: Exploiting the Polygon Rasterization Pipeline for Efficient Neural Field Rendering on Mobile Architectures, https://doi.org/10.1109/cvpr52729.2023.01590, fetched 2026-10-26 NeRF的基础及后续扩展, https://pengsida.net/files/NeRFTutorial.pdf, fetched 2026-10-30 (unofficial)

name: Coordinate Rectification for Point Cloud Rendering
head: Surface Coordinate Estimation
body: Coordinate Rectification is a surface estimation technique used in point cloud rendering to determine the precise 3D position of a ray-surface intersection from discrete point data. It solves the problem of inaccurate depth sampling in sparse or noisy point clouds by correcting the raw depth value based on the angle between the viewing ray and the scene's primary axis. Unlike standard depth buffering which assumes a planar intersection perpendicular to the view ray, this method accounts for surface orientation, enabling photorealistic rendering from discrete points by providing accurate input coordinates for subsequent neural radiance mapping. It serves as the foundational geometry estimation step in the End-to-End Rendering Pipeline, preceding the frequency-modulated radiance mapping stage. The method estimates the 3D surface coordinate \mathbf{x} for each pixel by rasterizing the point cloud to a depth buffer and applying a geometric correction factor. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Point cloud P = \{\mathbf{p}1, \mathbf{p}2, \dots, \mathbf{p}N\} where \mathbf{p}k \in \mathbb{R}^3; Camera parameters (position \mathbf{o}, ray direction \mathbf{d}); Image resolution H \times W. Output: Estimated surface coordinates \mathbf{x} \in \mathbb{R}^3 for each pixel. Data Structures: Point Cloud: List of N points. Each point \mathbf{p}k has coordinates (\mathbf{p}k^x, \mathbf{p}k^y, \mathbf{p}k^z). Depth Buffer: A 2D array z \in \mathbb{R}^{H \times W} storing the corrected depth value for each pixel. Pixel Coordinates: Array I \in \mathbb{R}^{H \times W \times 2} representing pixel centers in normalized device coordinates. Steps: 1. Coordinate Transformation: Transform the point cloud P from world space to normalized device coordinate (NDC) space such that \mathbf{p}k \in [-1, 1] \times [-1, 1] \times [z{near}, z{far}]. Simultaneously, transform the pixel coordinates I to the same NDC space, where each pixel center \mathbf{I}{i,j} \in [-1, 1]^2. 2. Disk Expansion: For each point \mathbf{p}k, define a disk of radius rk in the xOy plane (the plane perpendicular to the z-axis) centered at (\mathbf{p}k^x, \mathbf{p}k^y). The radius rk is typically determined by the point's local density or a fixed splatting radius. 3. Depth Buffer Query: For each pixel (i, j), find the depth value \mathbf{z}{i,j} corresponding to the nearest point whose disk covers the pixel. This is calculated as: \mathbf{z}{i,j} = \mink{\mathbf{p}^zk}, \quad \text{subject to } (\mathbf{p}k^x - \mathbf{I}{i,j}^x)^2 + (\mathbf{p}k^y - \mathbf{I}{i,j}^y)^2 < rk^2 where \mathbf{z}{i,j} is the depth of the nearest disk covering pixel \mathbf{I}{i,j}. If no disk covers the pixel, the depth is undefined or set to a default value. 4. Angle Calculation: Compute the angle \theta between the normalized viewing ray direction \mathbf{d} and the scene's z-axis (pointing to the center of the scene). Let \mathbf{z}{axis} be the unit vector (0, 0, 1) in the local coordinate system aligned with the scene's primary axis. Then: \theta = \arccos(\mathbf{d} \cdot \mathbf{z}{axis}). 5. Coordinate Rectification: Calculate the estimated 3D surface coordinate \mathbf{x} using the rectification formula: \mathbf{x} = \mathbf{o} + \frac{z}{\cos \theta} \times \mathbf{d} where: \mathbf{x} is the estimated surface coordinate. \mathbf{o} is the camera position. \mathbf{d} is the normalized ray direction. z is the depth value \mathbf{z}{i,j} obtained from the depth buffer. \theta is the angle between the ray and the z-axis. Parameters: rk: Disk radius for point \mathbf{p}k. Not given in the sources. [G: Typically a small constant or derived from point spacing]. z{near}, z{far}: Clipping plane distances in NDC space. Not given in the sources. [G: Standard camera frustum parameters]. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Division by Zero: If \theta = \pi/2 (ray perpendicular to the z-axis), \cos \theta = 0, leading to division by zero. This occurs when viewing the scene edge-on relative to the z-axis. A small epsilon or clamping of \cos \theta is required. Occlusion: The depth buffer query finds the nearest point in z-depth among those covering the pixel. If the point cloud is sparse, this may not represent the true surface, leading to artifacts. Noise: Noisy point clouds can cause incorrect depth values, harming rendering quality. The source mentions an optional preprocessing module for denoising and completion to mitigate this. I^x)^2 + (p^y - I^y)^2 < rk^2 dx = p[0] - pixelcenter[0] dy = p[1] - pixelcenter[1] if dx2 + dy2 < pointradius2: if p[2] < minz: minz = p[2] found = True if found: depthbuffer[i, j] = minz # Step 4: Calculate angle theta for each ray # zaxis is (0, 0, 1) zaxis = np.array([0.0, 0.0, 1.0]) # Dot product of raydirections and zaxis # raydirections shape: (H, W, 3) dotproduct = np.sum(raydirections zaxis, axis=-1) # Shape (H, W) # Clip to avoid numerical errors in arccos dotproduct = np.clip(dotproduct, -1.0, 1.0) theta = np.arccos(dotproduct) # Shape (H, W) # Step 5: Coordinate Rectification # x = o + (z / cos(theta)) d # cos(theta) can be zero if theta is pi/2 costheta = np.cos(theta) # Avoid division by zero # Use a small epsilon to prevent division by zero epsilon = 1e-6 costhetasafe = np.where(np.abs(costheta) < epsilon, epsilon np.sign(costheta), costheta) # Scale factor for each pixel scalefactor = depthbuffer / costhetasafe # Shape (H, W) # Expand scalefactor to (H, W, 3) to multiply with raydirections scalefactor3d = np.expanddims(scalefactor, axis=-1) # Shape (H, W, 1) # Calculate surface coordinates # raydirections shape: (H, W, 3) offset = scalefactor3d raydirections # Shape (H, W, 3) surfacecoords = camerao + offset # Shape (H, W, 3) return surfacecoords, depthbuffer This is a complete rendering framework that uses Coordinate Rectification as its first stage. It consists of three stages: Surface Estimation (using Coordinate Rectification), Radiance Mapping (using AFNet to predict raw RGB and feature vectors), and Refinement (using a U-Net to predict offsets). The final RGB is the sum of raw RGB and offsets. It is trained with L2 loss and perceptual loss. This variant is chosen when a full photorealistic rendering pipeline from point clouds is required, integrating neural radiance fields with explicit geometry. Time Complexity: The rasterization step (finding the nearest point for each pixel) is O(H \times W \times N) in the naive implementation, where H, W are image dimensions and N is the number of points. This can be optimized with spatial data structures (e.g., k-d trees, grids) to reduce the search space. The rectification formula is O(H \times W). When Not to Use: When the point cloud is extremely noisy or sparse without preprocessing, or when real-time performance is critical and the O(H \times W \times N) rasterization is too slow. name: Progressively Deblurring Radiance Field (PDRF)
body: PDRF is a method for reconstructing high-quality radiance fields from blurry source images by using a progressively deblurring scheme that accurately models blur with 3D scene context and uses efficient importance sampling for fast optimization. It sets itself apart from prior deblurring methods like Deblur-NeRF by incorporating 3D features into the blur estimation process, avoiding the limitation of purely 2D coordinate-based blur prediction, and by using a Coarse Ray Renderer (CRR) to enable efficient importance sampling that remains valid for dynamic ray generation. Inputs: A set of V blurry source images and their camera poses. A radiance field implicit function F mapping 3D coordinates and view directions to color and density. An implicit function H for blur estimation. Inputs to H: View embedding l, 2D pixel coordinate x, canonical blur kernel location x'k, and optional features \emptyset. Outputs: A trained radiance field F and blur estimator H. Rendered clean images for novel views. Radiance Field Implicit Function F: Maps (X, d) to (c, \sigma). X \in \mathbb{R}^3: 3D coordinate. d \in \mathbb{R}^3: View direction. c \in \mathbb{R}^3: Color. \sigma \in \mathbb{R}: Density. Uses positional embedding \gammaL with L frequency bands. Blur Estimation Implicit Function H: Inputs: View embedding l, 2D pixel coordinate x, canonical blur kernel location x'k, and optional features \emptyset. Outputs: Offsets \Delta o{x'k}, \Delta x'k, and blur weight h'(x^k). Learnable Parameters for Coarse Blur Estimation: Canonical blur kernel location x'k: Shape \mathbb{R}^{V \times P \times 2}. V: Number of source views. P: Number of clean pixels (rays) needed to render a single blurry pixel (kernel size). 2: 2D coordinate dimensions. View embedding l: Shape \mathbb{R}^{V \times K}. K: Embedding size. 1. Initialize Radiance Field: Define the implicit function F that maps embedded 3D coordinates and view directions to color and density. (ci, \sigmai) = F(\gammaL(Xi), \gammaL(d)) where Xi = o + ti d is the voxel location, o is the ray origin, ti is the travel distance, and \gammaL is the embedding function. 2. Coarse Blur Estimation (Stage 1): For each pixel x in a source view, query the implicit function H with the view embedding l, pixel coordinate x, and canonical location x'k to predict offsets and weights: \Delta o{x'k}, \Delta x'k, h'(x^k) = H(l, x, x'k, \emptyset) Compute the coarse ray parameters: x^k = x'k + \Delta x'k o{x^k} = o + \Delta o{x'k} r{x^k} = o{x^k} + t d{x^k} This stage generates a coarse set of P rays per blurry pixel based on 2D coordinates. 3. Coarse Ray Tracing (CRR): Trace the coarse rays r{x^k} through the radiance field F to obtain features and density estimates. The Coarse Ray Renderer (CRR) aggregates features from the underlying radiance field instead of rendering individual voxels to provide fast estimation for the next stage and the fine renderer. 4. Refined Blur Estimation (Stage 2): Refine the coarse blur estimations by incorporating the 3D features obtained from the CRR into the blur modeling. This update allows H to account for 3D scene context, improving blur accuracy over the purely 2D coarse stage. 5. Fine Voxel Rendering (FVR): Perform importance sampling based on the density estimation provided by the CRR. Use a larger network and denser predictions for high-quality view synthesis. The Fine Voxel Renderer (FVR) focuses on quality, leveraging the efficient sampling enabled by CRR. 6. Blurry Observation Modeling: Model the blurry observation \tilde{C}(rx) as a convolution between clean pixels C(r{xi}) and blur kernel weights h(xi): \tilde{C}(rx) = \sum{xi \in N(x)} C(r{xi}) h(xi) \quad \text{s.t.} \quad \sum{xi \in N(x)} h(xi) = 1 Here, N(x) denotes neighboring pixel locations, and P = |\{xi\}| is the kernel size. 7. Volume Rendering: Compute the rendered color \hat{C}(rx) for a ray rx using standard volume rendering: \hat{C}(rx) = \sum{i=1}^{N} Ti (1 - \exp(-\sigmai \deltai)) ci Ti = \exp\left(-\sum{j=1}^{i-1} \sigmaj \deltaj\right) where \deltai is the distance between samples, and \{\sigmai, Ti\} are current and cumulative densities. 8. Optimization: Update F by constraining the rendered blurry observation \hat{C}(rx) to match the observed blurry image \tilde{C}(rx). Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import numpy as np class Ray: def init(self, origin, direction): self.origin = origin self.direction = direction class MLP: """Standard multi-layer perceptron for implicit functions.""" def init(self, indim, outdim, hiddendims=[256, 256]): self.weights = [np.random.randn(indim, hiddendims[0])] for i in range(1, len(hiddendims)): self.weights.append(np.random.randn(hiddendims[i-1], hiddendims[i])) self.weights.append(np.random.randn(hiddendims[-1], outdim)) def forward(self, x): for w in self.weights[:-1]: x = np.maximum(0, x @ w) return x @ self.weights[-1] def computedirection(pose, pixelcoord): """Compute ray direction from camera pose and pixel coordinates.""" return np.array([pixelcoord[0], pixelcoord[1], 1.0]) def importancesample(ray, densitysamples, numsamples=64): """Sample points along ray based on density using inverse CDF sampling.""" tvals = np.linspace(0, 1, numsamples) return tvals def mseloss(pred, target): return np.mean((pred - target) 2) def pdrfoptimization(sourceimages, cameraposes, numviews, kernelsize, embeddingsize, numiterations): V = numviews P = kernelsize K = embeddingsize # Initialize learnable parameters canonicalkernellocs = np.random.randn(V, P, 2) viewembeddings = np.random.randn(V, K) # Initialize implicit functions F = MLP(indim=7, outdim=4) H = MLP(indim=K + 2 + 2P, outdim=2P + 1) for iteration in range(numiterations): viewidx = np.random.randint(0, V) image = sourceimages[viewidx] pose = cameraposes[viewidx] l = viewembeddings[viewidx] xprimek = canonicalkernellocs[viewidx] for y in range(image.shape[0]): for x in range(image.shape[1]): pixelcoord = np.array([x, y]) # Step 2: Coarse Blur Estimation hinput = np.concatenate([l, pixelcoord, xprimek.flatten()]) houtput = H.forward(hinput) deltao = houtput[:P3] deltax = houtput[P3:2P] hprime = houtput[2P:] xstar = xprimek + deltax.reshape(P, 2) ostar = pose.origin + deltao.reshape(P, 3) dstar = np.stack([computedirection(pose, xstar[i]) for i in range(P)]) rays = [Ray(ostar[i], dstar[i]) for i in range(P)] # Step 3: CRR coarsedensity = np.array([F.forward(np.concatenate([ray.origin, ray.direction]))[3] for ray in rays]) coarsefeatures = np.array([F.forward(np.concatenate([ray.origin, ray.direction]))[:3] for ray in rays]) # Step 4: Refined Blur Estimation refinedinput = np.concatenate([l, pixelcoord, xprimek.flatten(), coarsefeatures.flatten()]) refinedoutput = H.forward(refinedinput) refinedweights = refinedoutput[-P:] # Step 5: FVR tfine = importancesample(rays[0], coarsedensity) finesamples = np.array([rays[0].origin + t rays[0].direction for t in tfine]) renderedcolor = np.mean(F.forward(np.concatenate([finesamples, rays[0].direction]))[:3]) # Step 6 & 7: Blurry Observation & Volume Rendering blurryobs = np.sum(renderedcolor refinedweights) / np.sum(refinedweights) loss = mseloss(blurryobs, image[y, x]) # Step 8: Optimization # loss.backward() # optimizer.step() return F, H P: The number of clean pixels (rays) needed to render a single blurry pixel, representing the blur kernel size. It should be minimal to reduce cost. V: The number of source views. K: The embedding size for view embeddings. L: The number of frequency bands in the positional embedding \gammaL. Dynamic Ray Generation: Voxel pruning strategies used in acceleration methods like Instant-NGP are not applicable to dynamic ray generation for blurred images because gradients only propagate on parts of the ray, leading to sub-optimal learning. Static Ray Assumption: Previous acceleration methods relying on explicit density volumes assume static rays lead to good density approximation, which is not true when images are blurred. 2D Limitation: Predicting pixel-wise blur based solely on 2D image coordinates (as in Deblur-NeRF) limits blur modeling capacity due to the lack of 3D scene context. Computational Cost: Deblur-NeRF is P times slower than NeRF because P pixels need to be ray-traced to render a single blurry pixel. Time Complexity: PDRF is 15X faster than previous State-of-the-Art methods (specifically Deblur-NeRF). This is achieved by using the Coarse Ray Renderer (CRR) for efficient feature/density estimation and importance sampling, avoiding the P-fold ray tracing cost of Deblur-NeRF. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Measured Performance: PDRF achieves better performance on both synthetic and real scenes compared to Deblur-NeRF. Strengths: Accurately models blur with 3D scene context. Fast optimization due to efficient importance sampling and CRR. Robust to blur commonly observed in wild images. Limitations: Requires a two-stage blur estimation process. Relies on learnable parameters for canonical blur kernel locations and view embeddings. When to use: When reconstructing radiance fields from blurry source images where 3D context is important for accurate blur modeling and computational efficiency is required. When not to use: When source images are clean and standard NeRF optimization is sufficient, or when explicit density volume pruning is desired (as it is incompatible with dynamic ray generation for blur). Origin: PDRF was proposed by Cheng Peng and Rama Chellappa from Johns Hopkins University. Paper: "PDRF: Progressively Deblurring Radiance Field for Fast and Robust Scene Reconstruction from Blurry Images". Date: The arXiv preprint was published on 17 Aug 2022. History and Development: PDRF addresses the limitations of previous deblurring methods like Deblur-NeRF, which lack 3D context and are computationally intensive. It builds on the concept of implicit functions for blur modeling and integrates it with efficient radiance field rendering techniques like CRR and FVR. Usage: Used for 3D scene reconstruction from blurry images, with applications in robotics, site model construction, AR/VR, and e-commerce. PDRF: Progressively Deblurring Radiance Field for Fast Scene Reconstruction from Blurry Images, https://doi.org/10.1609/aaai.v37i2.25295, fetched 2026-10-26 PDRF: Progressively Deblurring Radiance Field for Fast and Robust Scene Reconstruction from Blurry Images, https://doi.org/10.48550/arxiv.2208.08049, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial)

name: Geometry Pseudo Label via Image Warping
head: Image Warping for Geometry Pseudo Labels, Self-supervised Geometry Pseudo Labeling
body: This method reconstructs reasonable 3D geometry from a single reference view by propagating depth information to unseen views through image warping, serving as pseudo ground truth labels to prevent overfitting and collapse in single-view NeRF training. It sets itself apart from standard NeRF [4972-neural-radiance-fields.md] by introducing explicit geometric consistency constraints derived from multi-view projection, rather than relying solely on photometric reconstruction loss. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: A single reference view image I{ref} with known camera intrinsics K{ref} and extrinsics; a set of unseen view images I{unseen} with known intrinsics K{unseen} and extrinsics; the current predicted depth map Z{ref} for the reference view. Outputs: Pseudo depth labels for the unseen views; a geometry consistency loss \mathcal{L}{geo} used to update the radiance field. Data Structures: Depth Map: A 2D array of floating-point values representing depth Z for each pixel in the reference view. Camera Matrices: K (3 \times 3 intrinsic matrix), T (4 \times 4 transformation matrix representing the relative pose between reference and unseen views). Numbered Steps: 1. Forward Warping: For each pixel pi(xi, yi) in the reference view I{ref} with depth Zi, compute the corresponding pixel pj(xj, yj) in the j-th unseen view I{unseen} using the projection equation: pj = K{\text{unseen}} T (K^{-1}{\text{ref}} Zi pi) Here, pi and pj are treated as homogeneous coordinates. T is the transformation matrix from the reference camera frame to the unseen camera frame. 2. Occlusion Handling (Painter’s Algorithm): If multiple points from the reference view project to the same pixel location in the unseen view, select the point with the smallest depth value as the valid warping result. This handles occlusions by prioritizing closer geometry. 3. Backward Warping: Reproject the unseen views back to the reference view using the warped depth information to enforce geometry consistency. This creates a bidirectional consistency check. 4. Smoothness Regularization: Calculate the self-supervised inverse depth smoothness loss \mathcal{L}{\text{smooth}} to regularize uncertain regions in the warped results. This loss is calculated on a downscaled resolution. 5. Loss Computation: Combine the forward and backward warping errors with the smoothness term to form the total geometry pseudo label loss \mathcal{L}{geo}. Formulas: Projection: pj = K{\text{unseen}} T (K^{-1}{\text{ref}} Zi pi) Where: pi, pj: Homogeneous pixel coordinates in reference and unseen views. Zi: Depth value at pixel pi in the reference view. K{ref}, K{unseen}: Intrinsic camera matrices. T: Extrinsic transformation matrix from reference to unseen view. Smoothness Loss: \mathcal{L}{\text{smooth}}(di) = e^{-\nabla^2 \mathcal{I}(\mathbf{x}i)} \left( |\partial{xx} di| + |\partial{xy} di| + |\partial{yy} di| \right) Where: di: The depth map. \mathcal{I}(\mathbf{x}i): The RGB pixel value at location \mathbf{x}i. \nabla^2 \mathcal{I}(\mathbf{x}i): The Laplacian of the pixel value at location \mathbf{x}i. \partial{xx}, \partial{xy}, \partial{yy}: Second-order spatial derivatives of the depth map. Total Geometry Loss: \mathcal{L}{geo} = \mathcal{L}1(d1, f(d2)) + \mathcal{L}1(f(d1), d2) + \lambda4 \mathcal{L}{smooth} Where: d1, d2: Depth maps of two views (reference and unseen). f(\cdot): The image warping function using the current view's depth information. \lambda4: Weight for the smoothness term, empirically set to 0.1. \mathcal{L}1: L1 loss function. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def computegeometrypseudolabelloss(depth1, depth2, K1, K2, T1to2, lambda4=0.1, image1=None, image2=None): """ Computes the geometry pseudo label loss using image warping. Args: depth1, depth2: 2D lists of floats, depth maps for two views. K1, K2: 3x3 lists of lists, intrinsic matrices. T1to2: 4x4 list of lists, extrinsic transformation from view 1 to view 2. lambda4: Float, weight for smoothness loss. image1, image2: 2D lists of floats, RGB images for Laplacian computation. Returns: totalloss: Float, the computed geometry loss. """ # Forward warp: depth1 -> depth2 frame warpeddepth2 = warpdepth(depth1, K1, K2, T1to2) # Backward warp: depth2 -> depth1 frame T2to1 = inversematrix(T1to2) warpeddepth1 = warpdepth(depth2, K2, K1, T2to1) lossforward = meanabsoluteerror(depth2, warpeddepth2) lossbackward = meanabsoluteerror(depth1, warpeddepth1) smoothloss = 0.0 if image1 is not None and image2 is not None: # Downscale for smoothness loss as per d1ds = downscale2d(depth1, factor=2) d2ds = downscale2d(depth2, factor=2) img1ds = downscale2d(image1, factor=2) img2ds = downscale2d(image2, factor=2) smoothloss = computesmoothnessloss(d1ds, img1ds) + computesmoothnessloss(d2ds, img2ds) return lossforward + lossbackward + lambda4 smoothloss def warpdepth(depthmap, Ksrc, Kdst, Tsrctodst): """ Warps depth map from source view to destination view. Uses Painter's Algorithm for occlusion handling. """ H, W = len(depthmap), len(depthmap[0]) Kinvsrc = inversematrix(Ksrc) warped = [[float('inf')] W for in range(H)] for y in range(H): for x in range(W): z = depthmap[y][x] if z <= 0: continue # Homogeneous pixel psrc = [float(x), float(y), 1.0] # 3D point in src camera: Kinv [x,y,1] Z ray = matrixvectormultiply(Kinvsrc, psrc) point3d = [ray[0]z, ray[1]z, ray[2]z] # Transform to dst camera point3dh = point3d + [1.0] pointdsth = matrixvectormultiply(Tsrctodst, point3dh) pointdst = pointdsth[:3] # Project to dst image: Kdst pointdst pdsth = matrixvectormultiply(Kdst, pointdst) if pdsth[2] <= 0: continue u = pdsth[0] / pdsth[2] v = pdsth[1] / pdsth[2] if 0 <= u < W and 0 <= v < H: if pointdsth[2] < warped[int(v)][int(u)]: warped[int(v)][int(u)] = pointdsth[2] return warped def computesmoothnessloss(depth, image): """ Computes self-supervised inverse depth smoothness loss. """ H, W = len(depth), len(depth[0]) laplacian = computelaplacian(image) total = 0.0 count = 0 for y in range(1, H-1): for x in range(1, W-1): dxx = depth[y][x+1] - 2depth[y][x] + depth[y][x-1] dyy = depth[y+1][x] - 2depth[y][x] + depth[y-1][x] dxy = 0.25 (depth[y-1][x-1] - depth[y-1][x+1] - depth[y+1][x-1] + depth[y+1][x+1]) weight = math.exp(-laplacian[y][x]) total += weight (abs(dxx) + abs(dxy) + abs(dyy)) count += 1 return total / count if count > 0 else 0.0 def inversematrix(M): """Computes inverse of a 4x4 matrix using standard Gaussian elimination.""" n = len(M) aug = [row[:] + [1.0 if i == j else 0.0 for j in range(n)] for i, row in enumerate(M)] for i in range(n): pivot = aug[i][i] for j in range(2n): aug[i][j] /= pivot for k in range(n): if k != i: factor = aug[k][i] for j in range(2n): aug[k][j] -= factor aug[i][j] return [row[n:] for row in aug] def matrixvectormultiply(M, v): return [sum(M[i][j] v[j] for j in range(len(v))) for i in range(len(M))] def downscale2d(arr, factor): H, W = len(arr), len(arr[0]) return [[arr[ifactor][jfactor] for j in range(W//factor)] for i in range(H//factor)] def computelaplacian(image): H, W = len(image), len(image[0]) lap = [[0.0]W for in range(H)] for y in range(1, H-1): for x in range(1, W-1): lap[y][x] = (image[y-1][x] + image[y+1][x] + image[y][x-1] + image[y][x+1] - 4image[y][x]) return lap def meanabsoluteerror(pred, target): H, W = len(pred), len(pred[0]) total = 0.0 count = 0 for y in range(H): for x in range(W): if target[y][x] != float('inf'): total += abs(pred[y][x] - target[y][x]) count += 1 return total / count if count > 0 else 0.0 Parameters: \lambda4: 0.1. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Occlusion: When multiple points project to the same pixel, the Painter’s Algorithm selects the smallest depth. Uncertain Regions: Projected results may contain uncertain regions due to occlusion or depth prediction errors. The smoothness loss helps regularize these. Misalignment: Small misalignments in the predicted depth map can cause large errors when projected to other views. Resolution: The smoothness loss is calculated on a downscaled resolution. A self-supervised task to classify points as visible or occluded along a ray to enhance 3D geometry prediction, without requiring multi-view geometry ground truth. Along a camera ray trajectory, points sampled prior to reaching the first surface point are categorized as visible, whereas points sampled beyond the first surface point are classified as occluded. To find the first surface point, the multiplication of SRDF values between adjacent sampled points is computed; when \tilde{d}{\Omega}^i \cdot \tilde{d}{\Omega}^{i+1} \le 0, the first surface lies within that interval, labeling points before it as visible (1) and after as occluded (0). The same logic is applied to SDF predictions. Labels are only assigned if SRDF and SDF agree; points with divergent classifications are omitted. A visibility probability V{pred} is predicted from the SRDF branch, and binary cross-entropy loss L{vis} is computed between V{pred} and the ground truth V{gt}. The visibility ground truth is defined as: V{gt}= \begin{cases} 1, & \text { if } (V^{\text{SRDF}} = 1) \& (V^{\text{SDF}} = 1) \\ 0, & \text { if } (V^{\text{SRDF}} = 0) \& (V^{\text{SDF}} = 0) \end{cases} This provides 3D space priors that directly influence SRDF and SDF learning. Strengths: Provides explicit geometric supervision in single-view settings, preventing collapse and improving 3D shape reconstruction. Limitations: Relies on accurate camera calibration and depth prediction. Uncertain regions due to occlusion can still introduce errors. When to use: Single-view NeRF training where depth supervision is needed but ground truth depth is unavailable. Originated in the SinNeRF paper, which proposes training NeRF from a single image by propagating depth information to unseen views. The method addresses the issue that simple depth supervision from a single view cannot produce reasonable 3D shapes without additional consistency constraints. name: Semantic Pseudo Label with Global Structure Prior
head: DINO-ViT CLS Token Loss
body: This method enforces semantic consistency between a reference view and unseen rendered views in radiance field optimization by using a pre-trained Vision Transformer (ViT) as a global structure prior. Unlike methods that rely on pixel-wise alignment or projected image embeddings, it extracts a single [CLS] token from DINO-ViT to represent the entire image, making the supervision robust to pixel-wise misalignment between views. It builds on Radiance-field optimization. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: A reference view image I{ref}, a rendered view image I{unseen} (patch B), and the DINO-ViT model. Outputs: A scalar loss value \mathcal{L}{\text{cls}} used to update the radiance field parameters. Data Structures: DINO-ViT Model: A self-supervised Vision Transformer trained on ImageNet. It outputs a sequence of tokens for each input image. CLS Token: The first token in the ViT output sequence, serving as a global representation of the input image. Steps: 1. Feature Extraction: Pass the reference view patch A and the unseen view patch B through the pre-trained DINO-ViT model. 2. Token Selection: Extract the [CLS] token from the output of the ViT for both patches. Let f{\text{vit}}(A) be the [CLS] token for patch A and f{\text{vit}}(B) be the [CLS] token for patch B. 3. Loss Calculation: Compute the L2 distance (squared Euclidean distance) between the two extracted [CLS] tokens. Formula: The semantic loss is defined as: \mathcal{L}{\text{cls}} = ||f{\text{vit}}(A) - f{\text{vit}}(B) ||^2 where f{\text{vit}}(\cdot) denotes the extraction of the [CLS] token from the DINO-ViT output, and A and B are patches from the reference view and an unseen view, respectively. Parameters: ViT Model: DINO-ViT. Training Data for ViT: ImageNet. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Misalignment: The method is designed to be robust to pixel-wise misalignment between views because the [CLS] token captures global semantic content rather than local pixel details. Patch Selection: A and B are patches. The specific size or selection criteria for these patches are not detailed in the provided sources, though they correspond to regions in the reference and unseen views. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def computesemanticloss(referencepatch, unseenpatch, dinovitmodel): """ Computes the semantic pseudo-label loss using DINO-ViT CLS tokens. Args: referencepatch (Tensor): Image patch from the reference view. unseenpatch (Tensor): Image patch from the rendered unseen view. dinovitmodel (nn.Module): Pre-trained DINO-ViT model. Returns: Tensor: Scalar loss value. """ # Extract features using DINO-ViT # The model returns a sequence of tokens; we take the first one (CLS token) reffeatures = dinovitmodel(referencepatch) unseenfeatures = dinovitmodel(unseenpatch) # Extract the [CLS] token (assumed to be the first token in the sequence) # Assuming standard ViT output shape [batch, seqlen, dim], # we select index 0 for the CLS token. clsref = reffeatures[:, 0,:] clsunseen = unseenfeatures[:, 0,:] # Compute L2 distance squared # Using torch.norm or direct subtraction depending on framework, # here we use explicit squared L2 norm. diff = clsref - clsunseen loss = torch.sum(diff 2) return loss This variant uses DiNO-ViT features to establish semantic correspondences between source and target objects, typically for appearance transfer or alignment. It differs from the global structure prior by operating on pixel-level features and cosine similarity rather than global [CLS] tokens and L2 distance. It is chosen when fine-grained semantic matching between specific parts of objects is required. Definition: Uses DiNO-ViT features to establish semantic correspondences between source and target objects. Steps: 1. Randomly render 100 images per object. 2. Sample 5,000 non-background pixels from each image to compute features and affinities. 3. For each sampled pixel, compute cosine similarity to all feature descriptors in the source NeRF. 4. If objects are not pre-aligned, optimize rotation and translation of the target object to roughly align it with the source object. Formula: Cosine similarity between feature vectors f1 and f2: \operatorname{sim}(f1, f2) = \frac{\langle f1, f2 \rangle}{||f1|| \cdot ||f2||} Pitfalls: Performance decreases on un-textured images because DiNO was trained on natural images. Edge loss (washed-out details) can occur due to 2D-to-3D mapping noise. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Robust to pixel-wise misalignment; provides semantic-level supervision. Limitations: Relies on the quality of the pre-trained ViT; may not capture fine-grained geometric details. When to use: When semantic consistency is more important than pixel-perfect alignment, or when dealing with views that have significant misalignment. When not to use: When fine-grained geometric accuracy is required without additional geometric priors. The method was introduced in SinNeRF. It leverages the property that Vision Transformers (ViT) capture semantic appearance after self-supervised pre-training, making them robust to misalignment. It builds on the observation that deep networks can learn invariant representations of content and style. name: Tensorial and Low-Rank Representations
head: Tensor Factorization, Tensor Decomposition Radiance Fields
body: Tensorial and Low-Rank Representations address the high memory consumption and overfitting issues inherent in dense voxel-based radiance fields by modeling the scene as a factorized 4D tensor [3026-tensorf.md]. Unlike Direct Voxel Grid Optimization, which stores independent features per voxel, this family exploits the low-rank structure of geometry and appearance to correlate the entire field, reducing space complexity from O(n^3) to O(n) or O(n^2). It sets itself apart from NeRF by replacing multi-layer perceptrons (MLPs) with compact vector and matrix factors, enabling significantly faster reconstruction and smaller model sizes [3026-tensorf.md]. All methods in this family represent the radiance field as a low-rank tensor decomposition, typically using Canonical Polyadic (CP) or Vector-Matrix (VM) formats [3026-tensorf.md]. The core mechanism replaces the implicit function of an MLP or the dense grid of a voxel field with a set of global mode vectors and matrices [3026-tensorf.md]. For a 4D radiance field \mathcal{F}(x, y, z, \theta), where (x,y,z) are spatial coordinates and \theta represents view-dependent parameters, the field is approximated by a sum of rank-1 components [3026-tensorf.md]. In the Vector-Matrix (VM) decomposition, the density \sigma and appearance features \mathbf{c} are computed by interpolating mode vectors and matrices [3026-tensorf.md]. For a component r, the density contribution is a sum of terms like \mathbf{v}X(x) \cdot \mathbf{M}{YZ}(y,z), where \mathbf{v} is a vector and \mathbf{M} is a matrix [3026-tensorf.md]. This structure allows for efficient trilinear interpolation and differentiable rendering [3026-tensorf.md]. The training process typically employs a coarse-to-fine strategy [3453-tensorf-reconstruction-optimization.md]. Optimization begins at a low resolution N0^3 (e.g., 128^3) and upsamples the tensor factors at specific iteration steps (e.g., 2000, 3000, 4000) using linear interpolation for vectors and bilinear interpolation for matrices [3453-tensorf-reconstruction-optimization.md]. Regularization is critical to prevent overfitting; L1 norm loss on factors encourages sparsity, while Total Variation (TV) loss promotes smoothness, particularly for datasets with few views or imperfect capture [3453-tensorf-reconstruction-optimization.md]. Models the radiance field as a factorized 4D tensor using CP or VM decomposition. It sets itself apart from implicit MLPs and sparse voxels by achieving superior memory efficiency through global mode vectors and matrices. Choose it for fast reconstruction and compact storage. The iterative gradient-based procedure to fit tensorial fields to multi-view images. It sets itself apart by enforcing structural regularization (L1/TV) on factors and using dynamic coarse-to-fine upsampling. Choose it for the standard training loop. Jointly refines camera poses and scene geometry using only 2D image supervision. It sets itself apart by integrating spectral filtering to avoid local optima caused by the lack of spectral bias in voxels. Choose it when camera poses are unknown. A computationally optimized configuration of the Strivec method. It sets itself apart by reducing multi-scale levels and top-k candidates during ray sampling for faster training and inference. Choose it when speed is prioritized over maximum detail capture. An explicit representation for dynamic 3D scenes that decomposes a 4D spacetime grid into six learned feature planes. It sets itself apart by pairing spatial planes with spatio-temporal planes to capture entangled space-time dynamics. Choose it for dynamic novel view synthesis. A 3D reconstruction framework combining tensor-based representation with frequency-driven regularization. It sets itself apart by applying a dynamic frequency mask to prioritize low-frequency information in early training stages. Choose it for few-shot reconstruction. Creates multiple levels of detail from a trained finest-resolution radiance field model. It sets itself apart by leveraging the compressibility of rank-residual models and merging blocks with adapted deferred MLPs. Choose it for efficient rendering of large composed scenes. The concept of tensor decomposition for radiance fields was introduced by TensoRF, which demonstrated that radiance fields exhibit low-rank structures in both geometry and appearance. Prior methods like NeRF relied on MLPs, which are memory-efficient but slow to train, while voxel-based methods like Direct Voxel Grid Optimization were fast but memory-intensive. TensoRF bridges this gap by using tensor factorization to achieve both speed and compactness [3026-tensorf.md]. The joint optimization variant addresses the instability of optimizing poses with voxel-based representations by leveraging the spectral bias and smoothness properties of the tensor factors [11498-joint-optimization-of-camera-pose-and-decomposed-low-rank-te.md]. TensoRF: Tensorial Radiance Fields, https://arxiv.org/abs/2203.09517, 2022-03-18

name: TensoRF
head: TensoRF (Tensorial Radiance Field Representation), TensoRF Representation, TensoRF Representation and Reconstruction, Tensor Factorization for NeRF, Tensorial Radiance Field Representation, Tensorial Radiance Fields
body: TensoRF models a 3D radiance field as a factorized 4D tensor, replacing the implicit MLPs of NeRF with explicit, low-rank tensor grids for density and appearance. It sets itself apart from sibling methods like Strivec by using global tensor factorization rather than local sparse grids, and from HexPlane by employing full 3D vector-matrix decomposition rather than planar projections. It achieves significantly faster training and smaller model sizes than implicit NeRF and concurrent explicit methods like Plenoxels, while maintaining high rendering quality. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: Multi-view images with known camera poses; scene bounding box. Outputs: Optimized tensor factors for geometry (G\sigma) and appearance (Gc); rendered RGB images. Data Structures: The method uses two grids: 1. Geometry Grid (G\sigma): A 3D tensor of shape I \times J \times K storing scalar density values directly. 2. Appearance Grid (Gc): A 4D tensor of shape I \times J \times K \times P storing P-dimensional appearance features. These grids are decomposed using CANDECOMP-PARAFAC (CP) or Vector-Matrix (VM) factorization. The parameters are: Geometry Factors: For each component r \in \{1, \dots, R\sigma\} and mode m \in \{X, Y, Z\}: \mathbf{v}{\sigma,r}^m: 1D vector of length Nm (where NX=I, NY=J, NZ=K). \mathbf{M}{\sigma,r}^{m'}: 2D matrix of shape N{m'} \times N{m''}, where \{m, m', m''\} = \{X, Y, Z\}. Appearance Factors: For each component r \in \{1, \dots, Rc\} and mode m \in \{X, Y, Z\}: \mathbf{v}{c,r}^m: 1D vector of length Nm. \mathbf{M}{c,r}^{m'}: 2D matrix of shape N{m'} \times N{m''}. \mathbf{b}r: 1D vector of length P. There are 3Rc such vectors. Global Appearance Dictionary (\mathbf{B}): A matrix of shape P \times 3Rc, formed by stacking all \mathbf{b}r vectors as columns. Formulas: The interpolated component value for mode X at location \mathbf{x}=(x,y,z) is: \mathcal{A}r^X(\mathbf{x}) = \mathbf{v}r^X(x) \mathbf{M}r^{YZ}(y, z) where \mathbf{v}r^X(x) is linearly interpolated along the X-axis, and \mathbf{M}r^{YZ}(y, z) is bilinearly interpolated in the YZ plane. Similar formulas apply for modes Y and Z. The density grid value is the sum of interpolated components: \mathcal{G}\sigma(\mathbf{x}) = \sum{r=1}^{R\sigma} \sum{m \in XYZ} \mathcal{A}{\sigma,r}^m(\mathbf{x}) \quad (13) The appearance feature vector is computed by concatenating all interpolated appearance components into a vector of size 3Rc and multiplying by \mathbf{B}: \mathcal{G}c(\mathbf{x}) = \mathbf{B} \left( \bigoplus{r=1}^{Rc} \bigoplus{m \in XYZ} \mathcal{A}{c,r}^m(\mathbf{x}) \right) \quad (14) where \oplus denotes concatenation. The final density \sigma and color c are: \sigma = \mathcal{G}\sigma(\mathbf{x}) c = S(\mathcal{G}c(\mathbf{x}), \mathbf{d}) where S is a decoding function (MLP or Spherical Harmonics) and \mathbf{d} is the viewing direction. Differentiable volume rendering computes pixel color C by marching along a ray, sampling Q points, and accumulating transmittance \tauq = \exp(-\sum{p=1}^{q-1} \sigmap \Deltap): C = \sum{q=1}^Q \tauq (1 - \exp(-\sigmaq \Deltaq)) cq \quad (16) where \sigmaq, cq are density and color at sample q, and \Deltaq is the ray step size. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import torch import torch.nn.functional as F def linearinterp1d(vec, coord): """Linear interpolation of a 1D vector at coordinate coord.""" coord = torch.clamp(coord, 0, vec.shape[0] - 1 - 1e-6) i0 = coord.long() i1 = torch.clamp(i0 + 1, max=vec.shape[0] - 1) w = coord - i0.float() return vec[i0] (1 - w) + vec[i1] w def bilinearinterp2d(mat, coordy, coordz): """Bilinear interpolation of a 2D matrix at coordinates (y, z).""" coordy = torch.clamp(coordy, 0, mat.shape[0] - 1 - 1e-6) coordz = torch.clamp(coordz, 0, mat.shape[1] - 1 - 1e-6) j0 = coordy.long() k0 = coordz.long() j1 = torch.clamp(j0 + 1, max=mat.shape[0] - 1) k1 = torch.clamp(k0 + 1, max=mat.shape[1] - 1) wy = coordy - j0.float() wz = coordz - k0.float() v00 = mat[j0, k0] v01 = mat[j0, k1] v10 = mat[j1, k0] v11 = mat[j1, k1] v0 = v00 (1 - wy) + v10 wy v1 = v01 (1 - wy) + v11 wy return v0 (1 - wz) + v1 wz def evaluatesh(features, directions): """Standard spherical harmonics evaluation for 3rd order (P=27).""" # Standard SH basis evaluation mapping features and directions to RGB return torch.zeroslike(directions) # Placeholder for standard SH math def mlpdecoder(features, directions): """2-layer MLP decoder with 128 hidden units and ReLU.""" x = F.relu(torch.nn.Linear(27, 128)(features)) x = F.relu(torch.nn.Linear(128, 128)(x)) return torch.sigmoid(torch.nn.Linear(128, 3)(x)) def evaluatetensorf(x, d, params): """ x: (B, 3) coordinates d: (B, 3) viewing directions params: dict containing tensor factors Returns: sigma (B,), color (B, 3) """ # Extract factors vsigmaX = params['vsigmaX'] # (N0, Rsigma) MsigmaYZ = params['MsigmaYZ'] # (N0, N1, Rsigma) #... other geometry factors similarly... Bmat = params['B'] # (P, 3Rc) sigma = torch.zeros(x.shape[0], device=x.device) for r in range(params['Rsigma']): ax = linearinterp1d(vsigmaX[:, r], x[:, 0]) bilinearinterp2d(MsigmaYZ[:,:, r], x[:, 1], x[:, 2]) sigma += ax # Add modes Y and Z similarly... # Appearance appfeatures = [] for r in range(params['Rc']): # Mode X appfeatures.append(linearinterp1d(params['vcX'][:, r], x[:, 0]) bilinearinterp2d(params['McYZ'][:,:, r], x[:, 1], x[:, 2])) # Mode Y appfeatures.append(linearinterp1d(params['vcY'][:, r], x[:, 1]) bilinearinterp2d(params['McXZ'][:,:, r], x[:, 0], x[:, 2])) # Mode Z appfeatures.append(linearinterp1d(params['vcZ'][:, r], x[:, 2]) bilinearinterp2d(params['McXY'][:,:, r], x[:, 0], x[:, 1])) appvec = torch.stack(appfeatures, dim=1) # (B, 3Rc) Gc = appvec @ Bmat.T # (B, P) if params['decodertype'] == 'SH': color = evaluatesh(Gc, d) else: color = mlpdecoder(Gc, d) return sigma, color Parameters: N0: Initial grid resolution. Typical value: 128. P: Number of appearance features. Typical value: 27 (3rd-order SH coefficients). R\sigma, Rc: Number of components. Configuration examples: 48, 96, 192, 384. Learning Rate: 0.02 for tensor factors, 0.001 for MLP decoder. Optimizer: Adam. Batch Size: 4096 pixel rays. Upsampling Steps: 2000, 3000, 4000, 5500, 7000. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Overfitting: In regions with few views, the model may overfit. Mitigated by L1 norm loss on factors and Total Variation (TV) loss. TV loss is preferred for datasets with few images (e.g., LLFF) or imperfect capture (e.g., Tanks and Temples). Local Minima: Coarse-to-fine upsampling helps avoid local minima. Precision: Trilinear interpolation is computed efficiently by interpolating factors directly, avoiding the cost of evaluating 8 voxel values. A multi-scale tensor decomposition that achieves superior compactness by separating frequencies across hierarchical levels using a tree structure. Choose when maximum compactness is required. A regularization method for sparse views that uses a secondary low-capacity model to provide depth priors. Choose when training with very few input views to mitigate floaters. A framework for simultaneous multi-scene optimization using higher-order tensor decomposition. Choose when optimizing multiple scenes in parallel or for cross-scene editing. A representation using sparsely distributed, compactly factorized local tensor feature grids. Choose when scene sparsity is high and global tensors are inefficient. Time and Memory Complexity: Space complexity is reduced from O(n^3) (dense grid) to O(n) with CP decomposition or O(n^2) with VM decomposition, where n is the grid dimension. Training speed is comparable to Plenoxels and significantly faster than implicit NeRF models. Measured Performance: Hardware: Single Tesla V100 GPU (16GB). Synthetic NeRF (300^3 voxels, 30k steps): TensoRF-VM-192: PSNR 33.14, SSIM 0.963, Time 17.4 min, Size 71.8 MB. TensoRF-CP-384: PSNR 31.56, Time 25.2 min, Size 3.9 MB. NSVF (300^3 voxels, 30k steps): TensoRF-VM-192: PSNR 36.52, SSIM 0.982. Tanks & Temples (300^3 voxels, 30k steps): TensoRF-VM-192: PSNR 28.56, SSIM 0.920. LLFF (Forward-facing): TensoRF-VM-96: PSNR 26.73, SSIM 0.839, Time 25.43 min, Size 179.7 MB. Strengths and Limitations: Strengths: Extremely compact model size (CP variant < 4MB), fast reconstruction (< 30 min for most variants), high rendering quality (VM variant outperforms NeRF), standard PyTorch implementation without custom CUDA kernels. Limitations: VM variant requires more memory than CP. When to Use: Use when training speed and model compactness are critical. Use when a standard implementation without custom kernels is preferred. TensoRF was introduced by Anpei Chen, Zexiang Xu, Andreas Geiger, Jingyi Yu, and Hao Su in the paper "Tensorf: Tensorial Radiance Fields" presented at ECCV 2022. It was developed to address the computational inefficiency and large memory footprint of MLP-based NeRFs and concurrent explicit methods like Plenoxels. The method leverages tensor factorization (CP and VM) to decompose the 4D radiance field into low-rank components, enabling efficient trilinear interpolation and differentiable rendering. It has been widely used as a baseline for subsequent low-rank and tensor-based radiance field research.
