name: CasCPRF
head: Cascaded Canonical Polyadic Tensorial Radiance Fields, Cascaded Tensorial Radiance Fields, CasCPRF Cascaded Frequency Disentanglement, Cascaded CPD, Cascaded Canonical Polyadic decomposition, IRCasTRF
body: CasCPRF is a multi-scale tensor decomposition radiance field representation that achieves superior compactness compared to TensoRF by employing a cascaded scheme to separate frequencies across multiple hierarchical levels. It approximates a high-order radiance field feature volume using a tree structure inspired by Hierarchical Tucker decomposition, where vectors in higher levels are estimated by multiplying vectors from lower levels. This approach implicitly controls the frequency band of learned contents, separating low spatial/high angular frequency components (coarse scale) from high spatial/low angular frequency components (fine scale) to enable robust and compact scene reconstruction. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: N multi-view images Ij \in \mathbb{R}^{H \times W \times 3} captured under the same illumination. Outputs: A compact radiance field representation for novel view synthesis, and subsequently, an explicit mesh with learned materials and lighting. Data Structures: The method approximates a high-order radiance field feature volume \mathcal{V} \in \mathbb{R}^{Ix \times Iy \times Iz \times (I\sigma + Ic)}. Cascaded Levels: The structure consists of D cascaded levels, denoted d=1 \dots D. Default D=3. Vector Subspace: For each mode n \in \{x, y, z\} and level d, rank-one vectors v{n,d} reside in a subspace \mathbb{R}^{I{n,d} \times R}. Resolution Scaling: The grid dimensions for level d are initialized as I{n,d} = In / 2^{d-1}. The base grid I{n,1} is typically 125^3, upsampled adaptively not exceeding 250^3. Ranks: The number of components in mode n is Rn = R{\sigma n} + R{c n}, where R{\sigma n} and R{c n} are the ranks for density and color respectively. Rn \ll Ix, Iy, Iz ensures compactness. Formulas: 1. Tensor Decomposition: The density feature volume \mathcal{V}\sigma and color feature volume \mathcal{V}c are factorized as sums over cascaded levels: \mathcal{V}\sigma = \sum{d=1}^{D} \sum{r=1}^{R\sigma} \left( v{rx,d} \times v{ry,d} \times v{rz,d} \right) \mathcal{V}c = \sum{d=1}^{D} \sum{r=1}^{Rc} \left( v{rx,d} \times v{ry,d} \times v{rz,d} \right) where \times denotes the outer product of vectors. 2. Positional Encoding: Sinusoidal positional encoding PE(x) is applied to the viewing direction \omegao: PE(x) = [\sin(2^0 \cdot x), \cos(2^0 \cdot x), \dots, \sin(2^{Nq-1} \cdot x), \cos(2^{Nq-1} \cdot x)] where Nq is the number of frequency bands. 3. Radiance Calculation: Density: \sigma = \text{ReLU}(F\sigma). Color: c = \text{MLP}c(Fc, PE(\omegao)). F\sigma and Fc are obtained by grid sampling \mathcal{V}\sigma(x) and \mathcal{V}c(x). 4. Volume Rendering: Sampling: Ns points are sampled per ray along the viewing direction. Transmittance: Ti = \exp\left(-\sum{j=1}^{i-1} \sigmaj \Deltaj\right), where \Deltaj is the distance between adjacent points. Color Prediction: C = \sum{i=1}^{Ns} Ti ci \Deltai. Parameters: N: Number of input images. D: Total cascaded levels. Default: 3. In: Base grid dimension for mode n. Default: 125. R\sigma, Rc: Ranks for density and color. Varying budgets tested (e.g., sum of density components R{\sigma x} + R{\sigma y} + R{\sigma z} from 12 to 4). \text{MLP}c: Two-layer MLP, 128 nodes per layer, ReLU activation. Optimizer: Adam. Learning Rates: CasCPRF parameters: 0.02; \text{MLP}c: 0.0001. Training Iterations: 30,000. Batch Size: 4096 rays. Algorithm Steps: Stage 1: Exploration (CasCPRF Learning) 1. Initialize: Set cascaded grid resolutions I{n,d} = In / 2^{d-1} for d=1 \dots D. Initialize tensor factors v{n,d} randomly. Initialize \text{MLP}c weights. 2. Sample Rays: For each training image, cast rays through pixels. Sample Ns points along each ray. 3. Grid Sample: For each sampled point x, compute features F\sigma = \mathcal{V}\sigma(x) and Fc = \mathcal{V}c(x) by evaluating the tensor decomposition sums. 4. Compute Radiance: Calculate \sigma = \text{ReLU}(F\sigma) and c = \text{MLP}c(Fc, PE(\omegao)). 5. Volume Render: Compute accumulated transmittance Ti and render color C using the sampled \sigma and c values. 6. Optimize: Minimize reconstruction loss L{expl} = \|C - \hat{C}\|2^2 + \lambda{tv} L{tv}(v), where L{tv} is total variation on vectors v. Update CasCPRF factors and \text{MLP}c using Adam. 7. Extract Mesh: After training, estimate a complete density volume and apply the Marching Cubes (MC) algorithm to extract a preliminary mesh M. Stage 2: Exploitation (Physics-based Shading) Note: This stage is part of the IRCasTRF pipeline utilizing CasCPRF, as described in the source. 1. Global Alignment: Initialize global movement vector \Deltam randomly in [-0.3, 0.3]. Learn \Deltam for 150 warm-up iterations to align the mesh. 2. Topology Refinement: Enable per-vertex deformation vectors \Delta vi to alter topology. Disable \Deltam after warm-up. 3. Material & Lighting: Learn Disney material parameters (diffuse bd, roughness r, metalness m) and environment map M \in \mathbb{R}^{6 \times 512 \times 512}. 4. Optimize: Minimize L1 loss on tone-mapped colors plus regularizers. Use Adam with LR 0.03 for 5000 iterations. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Spectral Bias: Standard MLPs struggle with high frequencies due to NTK eigenvalue decay. CasCPRF mitigates this via the cascaded multi-scale structure, where coarse levels handle high angular frequencies and fine levels handle high spatial frequencies. Mesh Topology: The preliminary mesh from MC may contain high-frequency noise, but provides a sufficient topology initialization for the exploitation stage. Texture Indexing: Fixed indexes between vertices and 2D texture maps are used to ensure seamless texture variation during topology changes, avoiding slow convergence associated with volumetric texture MLPs. Time Complexity: Training the CasCPRF model takes approximately 25 minutes on a single NVIDIA A100 GPU (40GB) with 30,000 iterations and batch size 4096. The subsequent exploitation stage (shading pass) takes approximately 1 hour. Memory Complexity: Model size is highly compact, ranging from 1 to 3 MB. This is significantly smaller than NeRF (hours of training, large memory) and DVGO (hundreds of MBs). Performance: CasCPRF outperforms TensoRF across various model-size budgets, with the greatest advantage at exceptionally small sizes (~1.8 MB for NeRF-synthetic, ~2.1 MB for RefNeRF-synthetic). It maintains better compression robustness than TensoRF when reducing density components. Strengths: Superior compactness, fast training, implicit frequency disentanglement, compatibility with explicit mesh pipelines. Limitations: Requires multi-view images under consistent illumination. The two-stage pipeline adds complexity compared to single-stage NeRFs. CasCPRF was introduced by Wenpeng Xing, Jie Chen, Ka Chun Cheung, and Simon See in the paper "IRCasTRF: Inverse Rendering by Optimizing Cascaded Tensorial Radiance Fields, Lighting, and Materials From Multi-view Images" presented at ACM MM 2023. The method draws inspiration from TensoRF [9] for tensor decomposition and Hierarchical Tucker decomposition [16, 18] for the tree structure. It also incorporates concepts from BACON [31] regarding band-limited coordinate networks for multi-scale representation. It is used as the volumetric representation component in the IRCasTRF hybrid inverse rendering pipeline. IRCasTRF: Inverse Rendering by Optimizing Cascaded Tensorial Radiance Fields, Lighting, and Materials From Multi-view Images, https://doi.org/10.1145/3581783.3612010, fetched 2026-10-27

name: Simple-TensoRF Augmentation
head: Augmented TensoRF, Low Data TensoRF, Simple-TensoRF
body: Simple-TensoRF Augmentation is a regularization method for TensoRF designed to mitigate overfitting and geometric distortions (such as floaters and incorrect object placement) when training with sparse input views. The method consists of two coupled models: a Main Model (standard TensoRF) and an Augmented Model (Simple-TensoRF). The Augmented Model is trained with reduced capacity to prevent it from learning complex, noisy artifacts. Its predicted depth is then used to regularize the Main Model. Unlike vanilla TensoRF or simple depth-supervised variants (DS-TensoRF), this approach explicitly constrains the model capacity to force simpler solutions, significantly improving depth estimation accuracy and view-synthesis quality in few-shot scenarios. Inputs: Sparse set of input images (e.g., 3 views) and their camera poses. Outputs: Main Model: High-quality rendered images and accurate depth maps. Augmented Model: Regularized depth maps used for supervision. The method builds on the TensoRF tensor factorization structure. Main Model Parameters: Density Tensor Components (R\sigma): Number of rank-1 components for density. Color Tensor Components (Rc): Number of rank-1 components for color features. Grid Resolution (N{vox}): Resolution of the voxel grid for tensor decomposition. Bounding Box (b): Defined as b = (b{x1}, b{x2}, b{y1}, b{y2}, b{z1}, b{z2}). MLP Depth (D): Depth of the small MLP for color decoding. View-dependent layers (lv): Number of view-dependent layers. Augmented Model Parameters: Density Components (R{\sigma s}): Reduced number of components. Grid Resolution (N{vox}^s): Reduced voxel grid resolution. Bounding Box Z-min (b{zs1}): Increased (shifted inward) Z-min to exclude near-camera artifacts. Mass Concentration Intervals (N{mc}): Number of intervals for entropy loss. Depth Supervision Parameters (k, \epsilon\tau): Used to filter reliable depth estimates. 1. Initialize Models: Initialize Main TensoRF with full capacity parameters and Augmented TensoRF with reduced capacity parameters. 2. Preprocessing: Downsample training and test datasets by a factor of 4. 3. Augmented Model Training: Train the Augmented Model concurrently with the Main Model. Apply the Mass Concentration Loss (L{mc}) to encourage hard object surfaces and reduce cloudy volumes. The loss is calculated by grouping ray samples into N{mc} intervals and minimizing the entropy of the mass within each interval. 4. Depth Reliability Filtering: Compute depth estimates from the Augmented Model. Filter these depths to identify "reliable" estimates by checking consistency with the closest training view. Regions visible in only one training view may lack reliable supervision, leading to persistent transparent floaters. 5. Main Model Training: Train the Main Model using the standard photometric loss (Lm) and the depth supervision loss (L{aug}) derived from the Augmented Model's reliable depth estimates. Enable the augmentation loss L{aug} after 5,000 iterations. The total loss for the Main Model includes photometric, depth supervision, sparse depth, mass concentration, and consistency terms. 6. Optimization: Use the Adam Optimizer. Train for a total of 25,000 iterations on a single GPU. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math from typing import List, Tuple class TensoRFModel: """Simplified representation of the TensoRF radiance field.""" def init(self, Rsigma: int, Rcolor: int, Nvox: int, b: Tuple[float,...], D: int, lv: int): self.Rsigma = Rsigma self.Rcolor = Rcolor self.Nvox = Nvox self.b = b self.D = D self.lv = lv self.params = [] def forward(self, rays): # Returns density, color, depth, and weights for each ray. # Implementation details of tensor factorization are in TensoRF. return self.query(rays) def downsampledata(data: List, factor: int) -> List: return data[::factor] def computephotometricloss(predictedcolor: List[float], targetcolor: List[float]) -> float: return sum((p - t) 2 for p, t in zip(predictedcolor, targetcolor)) / len(predictedcolor) def computedepthsupervisionloss(predicteddepth: List[float], reliabledepth: List[float]) -> float: return sum((p - r) 2 for p, r in zip(predicteddepth, reliabledepth)) / len(predicteddepth) def checkdepthconsistency(depth: List[float], k: int, epsilontau: float) -> List[float]: # Filters depth based on consistency with the closest training view # Returns valid depths where consistency check passes return [d for d in depth if d > 0] def computemassconcentrationloss(weights: List[float], Nmc: int) -> float: """ Computes the mass concentration loss. Groups N samples along a ray into Nmc intervals. Minimizes entropy of the normalized mass in each interval. """ N = len(weights) intervalsize = N / Nmc totalentropy = 0.0 for j in range(1, Nmc + 1): startidx = int((j - 1) intervalsize) endidx = int(j intervalsize) intervalweights = weights[startidx:endidx] normfactor = N / Nmc normalizedweights = [w / normfactor for w in intervalweights] intervalentropy = 0.0 for w in normalizedweights: if w > 0: intervalentropy -= w math.log(w) totalentropy += intervalentropy return totalentropy class Optimizer: def init(self, params: List, lr: float): self.params = params self.lr = lr def zerograd(self): pass # Framework handles gradient clearing def step(self): pass # Framework handles gradient update def samplerays(images, poses): # Standard ray generation from camera poses and image grid return type('RayBatch', (), {'targetcolor': [], 'targetdepth': [], 'hastargetdepth': False})() def trainsimpletensorf(inputimages, cameraposes, numiterations: int = 25000): # 1. Initialize Main Model (Full Capacity) mainmodel = TensoRFModel( Rsigma=24, Rcolor=72, Nvox=6403, b=(-1.5, 1.5, -1.67, 1.67, -1.0, 1.0), D=27, lv=0) mainparams = list(mainmodel.parameters()) # 2. Initialize Augmented Model (Reduced Capacity) augmodel = TensoRFModel( Rsigma=12, Rcolor=72, Nvox=1603, b=(-1.5, 1.5, -1.67, 1.67, -0.5, 1.0), D=27, lv=0) augparams = list(augmodel.parameters()) # Optimizers (Tensor params LR=2e-2, MLP params LR=1e-3 initially) optmain = Optimizer(mainparams, lr=2e-2) optaug = Optimizer(augparams, lr=2e-2) # Hyperparameters Nmc, k, epsilontau = 5, 5, 0.1 lambdam, lambdaaug, lambdasd, lambdamc, lambdacfc = 1.0, 0.1, 0.1, 0.01, 0.0 # Downsample data by factor of 4 inputimages = downsampledata(inputimages, factor=4) cameraposes = downsampledata(cameraposes, factor=4) for iteration in range(1, numiterations + 1): rays = samplerays(inputimages, cameraposes) # --- Augmented Model Forward Pass --- augdensity, augcolor, augdepth, weights = augmodel.forward(rays) Lmaug = computephotometricloss(augcolor, rays.targetcolor) Lmc = computemassconcentrationloss(weights, Nmc) lossaug = Lmaug + lambdamc Lmc optaug.zerograd() lossaug.backward() optaug.step() if iteration > 5000: reliabledepth = checkdepthconsistency(augdepth, k, epsilontau) # --- Main Model Forward Pass --- maindensity, maincolor, maindepth, mainweights = mainmodel.forward(rays) Lmmain = computephotometricloss(maincolor, rays.targetcolor) Laug = computedepthsupervisionloss(maindepth, reliabledepth) Lsd = computedepthsupervisionloss(maindepth, rays.targetdepth) if rays.hastargetdepth else 0.0 lossmain = (lambdam Lmmain + lambdaaug Laug + lambdasd Lsd + lambdacfc 0.0) optmain.zerograd() lossmain.backward() optmain.step() # Learning rate decays to 2e-3 (tensor) and 1e-4 (MLP) over training Main Model: R\sigma = 24, Rc = 72, N{vox} = 640^3, b = (-1.5, 1.5, -1.67, 1.67, -1.0, 1.0), D = 27, lv = 0. Augmented Model: R{\sigma s} = 12, N{vox}^s = 160^3, b{zs1} = -0.5, N{mc} = 5, k = 5, \epsilon\tau = 0.1. Optimizer: Adam. Initial LR: 2 \times 10^{-2} (tensor), 1 \times 10^{-3} (MLP). Loss Weights: \lambdam = 1, \lambdaa = 1, \lambda{sd} = 0.1, \lambda{aug} = 0.1, \lambda{mc} = 0.01, \lambda{cfc} = 0. Training Duration: 25,000 iterations on NVIDIA RTX 2080 Ti 11GB. Data: Downsampled by factor of 4. Block Artifacts: Reducing only the grid resolution (N{vox}) allows the model to learn sharp changes in density (\sigma) at voxel edges, causing block artifacts. Reducing only the number of components (R\sigma) causes small, completely opaque floaters. Both must be reduced together to achieve smoothing. Near-Camera Distortions: Reducing the bounding box size (specifically b{z1}) helps mitigate objects incorrectly placed close to the camera. However, applying this reduction to the main model can distort objects that are truly close to the camera. It is applied only to the augmented model. Transparent Floaters: Significant transparent floaters may persist in the main model, particularly in regions visible in only one training view. The mass concentration loss (L{mc}) does not completely remove these transparent objects. Training Time: Simple-TensoRF takes approximately twice the training time of vanilla TensoRF because it employs a single augmented model with the same number of queries as the main model. A cascaded approach for progressive refinement. Choose when high-resolution details are needed in addition to sparse input regularization. Extends TensoRF to handle more complex field types. Choose when the scene requires non-standard radiance field representations beyond density and color. A hybrid tensor-voxel representation. Choose when explicit voxel-based geometry is preferred over pure tensor factorization for sparse inputs. Time Complexity: Training time is approximately double that of vanilla TensoRF due to the parallel training of the augmented model. Memory Complexity: The augmented model uses a smaller grid (160^3 vs 640^3) and fewer components (12 vs 24), but the total memory usage is higher than a single TensoRF model due to the presence of two models. Measured Performance: On NeRF-LLFF (3 views): LPIPS 0.2461, SSIM 0.6749, PSNR 20.22, Depth MAE 0.17, Depth SROCC 0.83. On RealEstate-10K (3 views): LPIPS 0.0706, SSIM 0.8920, PSNR 32.70, Depth MAE 0.22, Depth SROCC 0.80. Strengths: Significantly improves depth estimation accuracy and reduces floaters compared to vanilla TensoRF and DS-TensoRF. Effective for sparse input scenarios. Limitations: Does not completely eliminate transparent floaters. Training time is increased. Reducing capacity too much may lead to sub-optimal solutions in regions requiring sharp depth discontinuities. When to Use: When training TensoRF with very few input views (e.g., 3-10 views) and depth accuracy is critical. When Not to Use: When computational resources are extremely limited (due to 2x training time) or when the scene contains many transparent objects that require specialized handling beyond mass concentration. Simple-TensoRF is part of the "Simple Radiance Fields" (Simple-RF) family, introduced by Nagabhushan Somraj, Sai Harsha Mupparaju, Adithyan Karanayil, and Rajiv Soundararajan in the paper "Simple-RF: Regularizing Sparse Input Radiance Fields with Simpler Solutions". The method addresses the issue of shape-radiance ambiguity and floater artifacts that arise when factorized tensor models like TensoRF are trained on sparse data. It builds on the observation that reducing model capacity (components and resolution) forces the network to learn simpler, more regularized solutions, which can then be used to supervise a higher-capacity model. Low-Cost Neural Radiance Fields, https://doi.org/10.48550/arxiv.2605.09312, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial) Simple-RF: Regularizing Sparse Input Radiance Fields with Simpler Solutions, https://arxiv.org/abs/2404.19015v5, fetched 2026-10-27

name: Generalized Tensorial Radiance Fields (GTensoRF)
body: Generalized Tensorial Radiance Fields (GTensoRF) is a framework for simultaneous multi-scene optimization that shifts from per-scene training to generalizable radiance fields using higher-order tensor decomposition. It builds on TensoRF by initializing scene-specific low-rank tensors to enable parallelized learning of multiple environments in a single session, drastically reducing training time while enabling view-consistent 3D editing. Unlike TensoRF, which optimizes one scene at a time, GTensoRF handles multiple scenes concurrently. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: A dataset of N scenes, each with associated multi-view images and camera poses. Outputs: A set of scene-specific low-rank tensor factors for geometry (density) and appearance (radiance) for each scene, and a unified model capable of rendering novel views and editing scenes. Data Structures: GTensoRF extends the TensoRF structure by maintaining separate tensor factorizations for each scene. For each scene i, it stores: Geometry tensor factors G\sigma^{(i)}: Low-rank representation of volume density \sigma. Appearance tensor factors Gc^{(i)}: Low-rank representation of view-dependent color c. These are implemented using Vector-Matrix (VM) decomposition, specifically denoted as \text{VM}\sigma and \text{VM}c. The exact bit-packing or memory layout of the tensor factors follows the TensoRF specification. Algorithm Steps: 1. Initialization: Initialize scene-specific low-rank tensors for each of the N scenes to handle multiple environments in a single training session. 2. Parallel Optimization: Optimize each scene’s tensors using a customized Adam optimizer to enable parallelized learning across all scenes. 3. Rendering and Loss: Render images for each scene using the current tensor factors and compute photometric loss against ground truth images. 4. Editing (Optional): To perform view-consistent 3D editing, decouple density and radiance components. Combine a density tensor G\sigma from Scene A with a radiance tensor Gc from Scene B. 5. Resampling and Fine-Tuning: Apply density-based resampling to align density peaks for spatial and color consistency. Perform selective fine-tuning to update appearance while preserving geometry for high-fidelity edits. Formulas: The rendering equation for a ray \mathbf{r} remains standard volume rendering, but the density and color functions are derived from the scene-specific tensors: \sigma(\mathbf{x}) = \text{Decode}(G\sigma^{(i)}, \mathbf{x}) c(\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{d}) = \text{Decode}(Gc^{(i)}, \mathbf{x}, \mathbf{d}) For editing, the combined density and color are defined as: \sigma, c = G\sigma^{(\text{scene1})}(\mathbf{x}), S(Gc^{(\text{scene2})}(\mathbf{x}), \mathbf{d}) where S denotes the shading function combining the radiance with the view direction \mathbf{d}. Parameters: Number of scenes N: Demonstrated with N=100. Optimizer: Customized Adam optimizer. Hardware: Single GPU. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Cross-Scene Compatibility: Recombining density and radiance from different scenes requires compatible semantic structures (e.g., combining a chair geometry with a chair color) to maintain structural fidelity. Density Alignment: Density-based resampling is critical to align initial object intersections when editing, otherwise artifacts may occur. Not Given in the sources: Specific hyperparameters for the Adam optimizer (learning rate, betas) or tensor rank values are not provided in the sources. A technique that decouples density and radiance components to enable generative editing by recombining scene elements like geometry and appearance across different scenes. It sets itself apart by ensuring view-consistent, semantically meaningful edits, unlike standard NeRF editing methods. Choose this when you need to swap textures or geometries between scenes while maintaining multi-view coherence. It is implemented by combining a density tensor G\sigma from one scene with a radiance tensor Gc from another, followed by selective fine-tuning. Time Complexity: GTensoRF trains on 100 scenes in under 60 minutes on a single GPU. This is a significant improvement over NeRF, which requires 24+ hours per scene, and EditNeRF, which requires 48 hours per scene. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Measured Performance: Evaluated on the Photoshapes dataset, GTensoRF significantly improves multi-scene generalization and efficiency over existing methods. Strengths: Drastic reduction in training time for multi-scene scenarios; enables view-consistent 3D editing; scalable to many scenes simultaneously. Limitations: Requires compatible semantic structures for cross-scene editing. When to use: When rapid training of multiple scenes is required, or when view-consistent editing across scenes is needed. When not to use: When single-scene high-fidelity optimization without multi-scene generalization is the primary goal, or when semantic compatibility between scenes is unknown. GTensoRF was introduced to address the limitations of Neural Radiance Fields (NeRF) and Tensorial Radiance Fields (TensoRF), which suffer from per-scene optimization and long training times. It builds on TensoRF [Chen et al. 2022], which uses tensor decomposition to model 3D scenes efficiently, by extending it to support multi-scene learning. The method was evaluated on the Photoshapes dataset and aims to enable applications like AR/VR and interactive 3D modeling by providing scalable and efficient radiance field training. Generalized TensoRF: Efficient Multi-Scene Radiance Fields and View-Consistent 3D Editing, https://doi.org/10.1145/3722564.3728385, fetched 2026-10-29

name: Strivec
head: Sparse Tri-Vector Radiance Fields
body: Strivec is a neural scene representation that models a 3D radiance field using sparsely distributed, compactly factorized local tensor feature grids. It solves the inefficiency of global tensor representations by exploiting scene sparsity directly, avoiding the modeling of empty space, while maintaining local smoothness and coherence through tensor factorization. Unlike its parent TensoRF, which uses a global tensor with vector-matrix decomposition, Strivec employs a cloud of local tensors decomposed via Canonical Polyadic (CP) decomposition into triple vectors, enabling high-quality reconstruction with significantly fewer parameters. Inputs: A set of calibrated images; coarse scene geometry (pre-acquired via fast RGB\sigma volume reconstruction like DVGO or multi-view stereo like Point-NeRF). Outputs: A continuous radiance field defined by volume density \sigma and view-dependent color c at any 3D location. Data Structures: 1. Tensor Cloud (\mathcal{T}): A set of N local tri-vector tensors \mathcal{T} = \{\taun \mid n = 1, \dots, N\}. 2. Local Tensor (\tau): Each tensor \tau is associated with a center position \mathbf{p} and covers a local cuboid space \omega with edge length l. 3. Tensor Components: Each local tensor \tau is factorized into R rank-1 components using CP decomposition. Density Tensor (\mathcal{G}^\sigma): A 3D tensor of shape I \times J \times K representing the density grid. Appearance Tensor (\mathcal{G}^c): A 4D tensor of shape I \times J \times K \times P representing the appearance grid, where P is the number of appearance channels (lower dimension than spatial modes). 4. Tri-Vector Factors: For a tensor of dimension M, the CP decomposition yields vectors \mathbf{v}r^0, \dots, \mathbf{v}r^M for each rank r. Parameters: N: Total number of local tensors. M: Number of nearest tensors selected to cover an arbitrary location \chi. R: Number of rank-1 components (CP rank) in the decomposition. l: Edge length of the local cuboid space \omega. \psi: A small Multi-Layer Perceptron (MLP) used to regress color. Algorithm: 1. Pre-acquisition: Obtain coarse scene geometry using a fast method (e.g., DVGO or Point-NeRF). 2. Distribution: Distribute local tensors \taun around the actual scene surface based on the coarse geometry, defining the radiance field domain \Omega = \bigcup{n=1}^N \omegan. 3. Query: For a query point \chi \in \Omega: a. Identify the set of M nearest tensors \{\tau{n1}, \dots, \tau{nM}\} that cover or are nearest to \chi. b. For each selected tensor \tau, extract density features \mathcal{G}^\sigma(\chi) using the CP-decomposed tri-vectors. c. Aggregate the extracted density features from the M tensors. 4. Regression: a. Compute volume density \sigma\chi by aggregating density features: \sigma\chi = A\sigma(\{\mathcal{G}^\sigma(\chi)\}). b. Compute view-dependent color c\chi by passing the aggregated density features and viewing direction \mathbf{d} through the MLP \psi: c\chi = \psi(A\sigma(\{\mathcal{G}^\sigma(\chi)\}), \mathbf{d}). CP Decomposition Formula: Each local tensor \tau \in \mathbb{R}^{I1 \times I2 \times \dots \times IM} is factorized as: \tau = \sum{r=1}^R \lambdar \mathbf{v}r^0 \otimes \mathbf{v}r^1 \otimes \dots \otimes \mathbf{v}r^M where \otimes denotes the outer product, and the weighting factor \lambdar is absorbed into the vectors \mathbf{v}r^k. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import numpy as np def strivecquery(chi, d, tensorcloud, M, psimlp): """ Query the Strivec radiance field at location chi. Args: chi: 3D coordinate (x, y, z) d: viewing direction vector tensorcloud: List of N local tensors. Each tensor is a dict with keys: 'p': center position (3,) 'l': edge length (float) 'vsigma': Density tri-vectors, list of 3 arrays of shape (dim, R) 'R': CP rank M: Number of nearest tensors to select psimlp: MLP function taking (aggregateddensity, direction) -> color Returns: sigma: Volume density c: View-dependent color """ if M <= 0 or len(tensorcloud) == 0: return 0.0, np.zeroslike(d) # 1. Select M nearest tensors centers = np.array([tau['p'] for tau in tensorcloud]) distances = np.linalg.norm(centers - chi, axis=1) nearestindices = np.argsort(distances)[:M] selectedtensors = [tensorcloud[i] for i in nearestindices] # 2. Extract and aggregate density features densityvalues = [] for tau in selectedtensors: v0, v1, v2 = tau['vsigma'] # Map global chi to local [0, 1] coordinates within the cuboid localcoords = (chi - (tau['p'] - tau['l'] / 2.0)) / tau['l'] localcoords = np.clip(localcoords, 0.0, 1.0) # Evaluate CP tensor at localcoords val = evaluatecptensor(localcoords, v0, v1, v2) densityvalues.append(val) # Aggregate density features (Asigma) aggdensity = np.mean(densityvalues, axis=0) # 3. Regress properties sigma = aggdensity color = psimlp(aggdensity, d) return sigma, color def evaluatecptensor(coords, v0, v1, v2): """ Evaluate a CP-decomposed tensor at normalized coordinates [0, 1]. """ R = v0.shape[1] total = 0.0 for r in range(R): val0 = interpolate1d(v0[:, r], coords[0]) val1 = interpolate1d(v1[:, r], coords[1]) val2 = interpolate1d(v2[:, r], coords[2]) total += val0 val1 val2 return total def interpolate1d(vector, coord): """ Linear interpolation of a 1D vector at a normalized coordinate [0, 1]. """ size = len(vector) idx = coord (size - 1) i = int(np.floor(idx)) j = int(np.ceil(idx)) i = np.clip(i, 0, size - 1) j = np.clip(j, 0, size - 1) w = idx - i return (1.0 - w) vector[i] + w vector[j] Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Empty Space: If \chi is not covered by any tensor, the nearest neighbor selection handles distances gracefully. The sources note that tensors are distributed around the actual scene surface to avoid empty space. Precision: CP decomposition involves sums of outer products; numerical stability should be considered when R is large, though Strivec uses compact factors. Boundary Conditions: Interpolation at the boundaries of the local cuboid \omega must be handled correctly to avoid discontinuities between adjacent tensors. Time Complexity: Query time depends on M (number of nearest tensors) and R (CP rank). For each query, M tensors are evaluated, each requiring O(R \cdot \text{dim}) operations for interpolation and summation. Memory Complexity: Memory usage is proportional to N \cdot R \cdot (\text{spatial dims} + \text{appearance dims}). Since N is sparse and R is small due to local compactness, memory usage is significantly lower than global tensor methods. Performance: Strivec achieves state-of-the-art rendering quality on synthetic and real datasets, outperforming TensoRF and Instant-NGP while using significantly fewer model parameters. Strengths: Efficient scene modeling, compact representation, exploitation of sparsity and local coherence. Limitations: Requires pre-acquisition of coarse geometry, which adds an initial processing step. Strivec was proposed by Quankai Gao, Qiangeng Xu, Hao Su, Ulrich Neumann, and Zexiang Xu from USC, UC San Diego, and Adobe Research. It was published in ICCV 2023. The method builds on the tensor decomposition principles of TensoRF but adapts them to a sparse, local setting. It draws inspiration from both global tensor representations (TensoRF, Instant-NGP) and local representations (Plenoxels, Point-NeRF), aiming to combine the best of both worlds. name: TensoRF Reconstruction Optimization
head: Tensorial Radiance Field Optimization
body: TensoRF Reconstruction Optimization is the iterative gradient-based procedure used to fit a tensorial radiance field to a set of multi-view images with known camera poses. It minimizes the L2 rendering loss between synthesized and ground-truth pixel colors, distinguishing itself from standard implicit field optimization by enforcing structural regularization (L1 and Total Variation) on low-rank tensor factors and employing a dynamic coarse-to-fine upsampling strategy to mitigate overfitting and local minima. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A set of M multi-view images \{Im\}{m=1}^M with known camera poses and intrinsics. Output: Optimized tensor factors (global mode vectors and matrices) representing the density \sigma and color \mathbf{c} fields. Data Structures: The radiance field uses Vector-Matrix (VM) or Canonical Polyadic (CP) decomposition, building on the shared principles of low-rank tensor factorization (see Tensorial and Low-Rank Representations). The implementation uses a feature grid with N^3 voxels, where the resolution per dimension is derived from the bounding box shape. Parameters: Initial Resolution: N0^3 voxels, with N0 = 128. Final Resolution: N^3 voxels. Upsampling Steps: 2000, 3000, 4000, 5500, 7000. Interpolation: Linear in logarithmic space between N0^3 and N^3. Optimizer: Adam. Batch Size: 4096 pixel rays. Feature Decoding: Small MLP (2 FC layers, 128 hidden, ReLU) or 3rd-order Spherical Harmonics (SH) with 27 features. Regularization: To prevent overfitting and local minima, regularization is applied to the tensor factors: 1. L1 Norm Loss: Encourages sparsity in the factors. Adequate for most datasets. 2. Total Variation (TV) Loss: Promotes smoothness. Used for real datasets with few input images (e.g., LLFF) or imperfect capture conditions (e.g., Tanks and Temples with varying exposure/inconsistent masks). Algorithm: 1. Initialize tensor factors (global vectors and matrices) at resolution N0^3. 2. For each optimization step t: a. If t \in \{2000, 3000, 4000, 5500, 7000\}, upsample the XYZ-mode vector and matrix factors linearly and bilinearly to the current target resolution. b. Sample rays and compute rendered pixel colors using the current tensor factors and feature decoding function. c. Compute L2 rendering loss: \mathcal{L}{\text{render}} = \sum \| \mathbf{C}{\text{rendered}} - \mathbf{C}{\text{GT}} \|^2, where \mathbf{C}{\text{rendered}} are the rendered colors and \mathbf{C}{\text{GT}} are ground truth colors. d. Compute regularization loss \mathcal{L}{\text{reg}} = \lambda1 \mathcal{L}{\text{L1}} + \lambda{\text{TV}} \mathcal{L}{\text{TV}} on the factors. e. Compute total loss \mathcal{L} = \mathcal{L}{\text{render}} + \mathcal{L}{\text{reg}}. f. Update tensor factors using the Adam optimizer. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import torch import torch.nn.functional as F def computetvloss(factors): """Compute Total Variation loss on tensor factors.""" loss = 0.0 for f in factors: if f.dim() == 3: # Vector factor loss += torch.mean(torch.abs(f[:, 1:,:] - f[:,:-1,:])) elif f.dim() == 4: # Matrix factor loss += torch.mean(torch.abs(f[:,:, 1:,:] - f[:,:,:-1,:])) loss += torch.mean(torch.abs(f[:, 1:,:,:] - f[:-1,:,:,:])) return loss def gettargetresolution(t, N0, Nfinal, steps): """Compute target resolution via linear interpolation in log space.""" logN0, logNf = torch.log(torch.tensor(N0)), torch.log(torch.tensor(Nfinal)) if t <= steps[0]: progress = 0.0 elif t >= steps[-1]: progress = 1.0 else: idx = next(i for i, s in enumerate(steps) if s > t) prevs = steps[idx-1] if idx > 0 else 0 progress = (t - prevs) / (steps[idx] - prevs) return int(torch.exp(logN0 + progress (logNf - logN0)).item()) def upsamplefactors(factors, t, N0, Nfinal, steps): """Upsample vectors (trilinear) and matrices (bilinear) to target resolution.""" newres = gettargetresolution(t, N0, Nfinal, steps) newfactors = [] for f in factors: if f.dim() == 3: newfactors.append(F.interpolate(f.unsqueeze(0).unsqueeze(0), size=(newres, newres, newres), mode='trilinear', aligncorners=False).squeeze(0).squeeze(0)) elif f.dim() == 4: newfactors.append(F.interpolate(f.unsqueeze(0), size=(newres, newres), mode='bilinear', aligncorners=False).squeeze(0)) return newfactors def volumerender(points, densities, colors, tvals): """Standard alpha compositing for volume rendering.""" deltas = tvals[1:] - It distinguishes itself from standard NeRF training by incorporating specific regularizations (orthogonal, L1 density, and Total Variation) tailored to the decomposed tensor structure, alongside dynamic voxel resolution updates. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. The coarse-to-fine strategy reduces initial computation cost. Memory Complexity: Scales with the number of tensor factors, which is significantly lower than dense voxel grids or large MLPs for equivalent resolution. Performance: Evaluated on a single Tesla V100 GPU (16GB) with a batch size of 4096 pixel rays. Strengths: Effective regularization prevents overfitting and local minima. Coarse-to-fine upsampling improves quality. Limitations: Requires careful tuning of regularization parameters and upsampling steps. May struggle with very few input images without TV loss. When to use: Suitable for multi-view reconstruction where memory efficiency and structural regularization are beneficial. When not to use: Not ideal for real-time inference without further optimization (e.g., pruning) or for scenes with extreme view-dependent effects not captured by the low-rank assumption. TensoRF was introduced in the paper "TensoRF: Tensorial Radiance Fields". The method leverages tensor factorization to represent radiance fields, building on the principles of low-rank representations. It addresses issues of overfitting and local minima common in gradient-based optimization of implicit fields by introducing specific regularization terms and a dynamic resolution update strategy. name: TensoRF Training Loop
head: TensoRF Optimization
body: The TensoRF Training Loop is the iterative optimization procedure used to minimize the L2 rendering loss of a tensorial radiance field, using ground truth pixel colors as supervision. It differs from standard NeRF training by incorporating specific regularization terms (orthogonal, L1, and Total Variation) tailored to the low-rank tensor decomposition structure, alongside a dynamic resolution update mechanism for the feature grid. Inputs: Training dataset (images, poses, intrinsics). Model parameters: densityncomp, appearancencomp, appdim, nearfar, shadingMode, alphaMaskthres, densityshift, distancescale, pospe, viewpe, feape, featureC, stepratio, fea2denseAct. Hyperparameters: Nvoxelinit (initial voxel count), nSamples (samples per ray), lrdecaytargetratio, Orthoweight, L1weightinital, TVweightdensity, TVweightapp. Outputs: Optimized tensorial radiance field parameters. Rendered RGB maps, alphas, depths, and weights for loss computation. Rays: 3D arrays containing ray origins and directions, filtered by bounding box if not using NDC. RGBs: 3D arrays containing ground truth pixel colors. TensorF Model: Contains the decomposed tensor components for density and color fields. 1. Initialization: Load train/test data and compute aabb, nearfar, whitebg, and ndcray flags. Initialize the tensorf model with the specified parameters. Calculate learning rate decay factor: lr\factor = args.lr\decay\target\ratio^{(1/args.lr\decay\iters)} If not using NDC, filter rays to the bounding box: python allrays, allrgbs = tensorf.filteringrays(allrays, allrgbs, bboxonly=True) Initialize SimpleSampler for ray batching. 2. Iteration Loop: For each iteration: a. Ray Sampling: Get ray indices via rayidx = trainingSampler.nextids(). Fetch rays and RGBs: python raystrain, rgbtrain = allrays[rayidx], allrgbs[rayidx].to(device) b. Rendering: Render the scene using the renderer function: python rgbmap, alphasmap, depthmap, weights, uncertainty = renderer( raystrain, tensorf, chunk=args.batchsize, Nsamples=nSamples, whitebg=whitebg, ndcray=ndcray, device=device, istrain=True) Note: nSamples is calculated as min(args.nSamples, calnsamples(resocur, args.stepratio)). c. Loss Computation: i. MSE Loss: loss = \text{mean}((rgb\map - rgb\train)^2) ii. Orthogonal Regularization: If Orthoregweight > 0: loss\reg = tensorf.vector\comp\diffs() total\loss += Ortho\reg\weight \times loss\reg iii. L1 Density Regularization: If L1regweight > 0: loss\reg\L1 = tensorf.density\L1() total\loss += L1\reg\weight \times loss\reg\L1 iv. TV Density Regularization: If TVweightdensity > 0: Decay weight by lrfactor. Compute: loss\tv = tensorf.TV\loss\density(tvreg) \times TV\weight\density total\loss += loss\tv v. TV Appearance Regularization: If TVweightapp > 0: Decay weight by lrfactor. Compute: loss\tv = tensorf.TV\loss\app(tvreg) \times TV\weight\app total\loss += loss\tv d. Optimization Step: python optimizer.zerograd() totalloss.backward() optimizer.step() e. Learning Rate Update: For all parameter groups: python paramgroup['lr'] = paramgroup['lr'] lrfactor f. Evaluation: Periodically evaluate test PSNR and log metrics to TensorBoard. g. Alpha Mask Update: If the current iteration is in updateAlphaMasklist and the current voxel count is less than 256^3, update the volume resolution. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def traintensorf(dataset, model, optimizer, args): # 1. Initialization allrays, allrgbs = dataset.getallraysandrgbs() aabb, nearfar, whitebg, ndcray = dataset.computeboundsandfocal() model.initparameters( densityncomp=args.densityncomp, appearancencomp=args.appearancencomp, appdim=args.appdim, nearfar=nearfar, shadingMode=args.shadingMode, alphaMaskthres=args.alphaMaskthres, densityshift=args.densityshift, distancescale=args.distancescale, pospe=args.pospe, viewpe=args.viewpe, feape=args.feape, featureC=args.featureC, stepratio=args.stepratio, fea2denseAct=args.fea2denseAct) lrfactor = args.lrdecaytargetratio (1.0 / args.lrdecayiters) if not ndcray: allrays, allrgbs = model.filteringrays(allrays, allrgbs, bboxonly=True) sampler = SimpleSampler(allrays.shape[0]) # 2. Iteration Loop for iteration in range(args.maxiters): # a. Ray Sampling rayidx = sampler.nextids() raystrain = allrays[rayidx].to(device) rgbtrain = allrgbs[rayidx].to(device) # b. Rendering nsamples = min(args.nSamples, calnsamples(model.resocur, args.stepratio)) rgbmap, alphasmap, depthmap, weights, uncertainty = model.renderer( raystrain, model, chunk=args.batchsize, Nsamples=nsamples, whitebg=whitebg, ndcray=ndcray, device=device, istrain=True) # c. Loss Computation loss = torch.mean((rgbmap - rgbtrain) 2) totalloss = loss # Orthogonal Regularization if args.Orthoregweight > 0: lossreg = model.vectorcompdiffs() totalloss += args.Orthoregweight lossreg # L1 Density Regularization if args.L1regweight > 0: lossregL1 = model.densityL1() totalloss += args.L1regweight lossregL1 # TV Density Regularization if args.TVweightdensity > 0: tvweight = args.TVweightdensity lrfactor losstv = model.TVlossdensity(tvreg=1) tvweight totalloss += losstv # TV Appearance Regularization if args.TVweightapp > 0: tvweight = args.TVweightapp lrfactor losstv = model.TVlossapp(tvreg=1) tvweight totalloss += losstv # d. Optimization Step optimizer.zerograd() totalloss.backward() optimizer.step() # e. Learning Rate Update for paramgroup in optimizer.paramgroups: paramgroup['lr'] = paramgroup['lr'] lrfactor # f. Evaluation if iteration % args.evalinterval == 0: evaluatetestpsnr(dataset, model) logtotensorboard(iteration, totalloss) # g. Alpha Mask Update if iteration in args.updateAlphaMasklist: if model.currentvoxelcount < 2563: model.updatevolumeresolution() Nvoxelinit: Initial number of voxels. Not given in the sources. nSamples: Number of samples per ray. Calculated dynamically. lrdecaytargetratio: Target learning rate ratio for decay. Not given in the sources. Orthoweight: Weight for orthogonal regularization. Not given in the sources. L1weightinital: Initial weight for L1 density regularization. Not given in the sources. TVweightdensity: Initial weight for TV density regularization. Not given in the sources. TVweightapp: Initial weight for TV appearance regularization. Not given in the sources. Depth Supervision Ineffectiveness: When using depth supervision with low data, the improvement in PSNR is minimal (0.01 PSNR) because COLMAP key points are orders of magnitude fewer than color pixel comparisons, causing depth loss gradients to affect only a small portion of the voxel space. Resolution Update Condition: The volume resolution is only updated if the current voxel count is less than 256^3. NeuManifold is a three-stage pipeline for reconstructing neural watertight manifolds with efficient, high-quality rendering support. It solves the problem of generating high-fidelity 3D meshes from 2D images by combining the robust initialization of volume rendering with the geometric precision of differentiable rasterization. Unlike pure volumetric methods, it produces explicit triangle meshes; unlike pure mesh-based methods, it avoids the artifacts caused by linear interpolation in non-linear density fields by using a differentiable marching cubes algorithm. NeuManifold This method enables robust joint optimization of camera poses and decomposed low-rank tensorial radiance fields by controlling the frequency spectrum of the scene representation. It prevents premature high-frequency signals in the voxel volume from causing camera poses to get stuck in local minima, a failure mode common in naive joint optimization. It sets itself apart from hash-encoding-based methods by specifically leveraging the separability of the input low-rank tensor signal, making it more efficient than traditional separable convolution kernels. Separable Component-Wise Convolution for Joint Pose Optimization StyleTRF is a method for stylized view generation that decouples style adaptation from view capture by fine-tuning the appearance component of a pre-optimized Tensorial Radiance Field (TensoRF) using sparse stylized priors. It sets itself apart from joint optimization methods like SNeRF by freezing the geometric density parameters of the scene representation, thereby preserving crisp geometry while adapting appearance, and by using a deterministic CNN-based stylization module (Johnson et al.) to ensure 3D consistency across viewpoints. StyleTRF This family defines the tensor decomposition strategies used to factorize the radiance field density and color fields in TensoRF, balancing storage efficiency against rendering quality. It differs from sibling methods like NeuManifold or StyleTRF by explicitly structuring the low-rank approximation into discrete rank groups (rank-residual learning) and offering specific variants (CP, HY, HY-S) to control the ratio of vector- to matrix-based components. TensoRF Decomposition Models A training optimization scheme that reduces initial training cost and regularizes feature representations by initializing a 3D feature grid at a coarse resolution and progressively upscaling it to higher resolutions. It improves model convergence and makes camera refinement more effective compared to training at full resolution from the start. Unlike static grid methods, this approach dynamically adapts the spatial detail of the feature representation during the optimization process. Coarse-to-fine feature grid Codec-Adaptive TriPlane Radiance Fields (CATRF) is a compression framework for plane-factorized radiance fields that optimizes neural features directly in the decoded space of a standard video or image codec. It solves the problem of severe rendering degradation at low bitrates by integrating a real codec round-trip (JPEG, VP9, HEVC, or AV1) into the training loop via a Straight-Through Estimator (STE). Unlike Codec-Agnostic (CA) methods that compress features after training, or Learned-Codec-in-the-Loop (LCL) methods that require shipping scene-specific neural decoder parameters, CATRF adapts features to real codec distortions without introducing any learned codec parameters or entropy models. Codec-Adaptive TriPlane Radiance Fields Downsamples both train and test data by a factor of 4. Training iterations are reduced to 2,500 (vs. 30,000 in original TensoRF paper) due to memory and time constraints. Tested on the synthetic Lego scene from the NeRF dataset with 100 training views and 200 test views. Applies depth supervision loss during training. However, it suffers from low PSNR with low data and minimal improvement (0.01 PSNR) over non-depth supervised approaches because COLMAP key points are orders of magnitude fewer than color pixel comparisons, causing depth loss gradients to affect only a small portion of voxel space. Uses a spike-based color decoder. TensoRF T: Maximum time step set to 8. Initial membrane time constant \tau = 2.0. Firing threshold = 0.5. TensoRF Input Dimensions: Spike-based color decoder receives 150-dimensional input on Synthetic-NeRF and 30-dimensional input on LLFF. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Measured Performance: Not given in the sources. Scaling: Not given in the sources. Strengths and Limitations: The use of orthogonal, L1, and TV regularizations helps stabilize the optimization of low-rank tensors. However, depth supervision can be ineffective if the number of depth points is significantly lower than the number of color pixels. When to use it: When optimizing a tensorial radiance field for high-quality novel view synthesis with efficient memory usage. When not to use it: When depth supervision is critical and high-precision depth data is unavailable. The TensoRF Training Loop originates from the TensoRF paper (ECCV 2022), which introduced tensorial radiance fields as a compact representation for neural radiance fields. The method builds on the principles of differentiable volume rendering and low-rank tensor decomposition. name: NeuManifold
body: NeuManifold is a three-stage pipeline for reconstructing neural watertight manifolds with efficient, high-quality rendering support. It solves the problem of generating high-fidelity 3D meshes from 2D images by combining the robust initialization of volume rendering with the geometric precision of differentiable rasterization. Unlike pure volumetric methods, it produces explicit triangle meshes; unlike pure mesh-based methods, it avoids the artifacts caused by linear interpolation in non-linear density fields by using a differentiable marching cubes algorithm. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A set of 2D images with known camera poses. Output: A watertight triangle mesh (geometry) and an appearance network (color) capable of real-time rendering. Data Structures: Geometry Network (G): A neural field (specifically TensoRF) that maps a 3D location x to volume density \sigmax. Appearance Network (A): A neural field (specifically TensoRF) that maps a 3D location x and viewing direction d to view-dependent color cx. Grid: An axis-aligned grid used for the Differentiable Marching Cubes (DiffMC) operation. Mesh: A triangle mesh extracted from the grid, containing vertex positions and connectivity. Textures: For deployment, TensoRF weights are stored as three 3D textures and three 1D textures with linear filtering; MLP weights are stored as 2D textures. Formulas: The geometry and appearance networks are defined as: \sigmax, cx = G(x), A(x, d) where x is a 3D location, d is the viewing direction, \sigmax is volume density, and cx is view-dependent color. Volume rendering compositing equation: C = \sum{i=1}^N Ti(1 - \exp(-\sigmai \deltai))ci Ti = \exp\left(-\sum{j=1}^{i-1} \sigmaj \deltaj\right) where C is the rendered pixel color, N is the number of samples, \sigmai is density, \deltai is ray marching step size, ci is color, and Ti is volume transmittance. Parameters: Neural Field Representation: TensoRF is used for both geometry and appearance networks. Implementation: DiffMC is implemented in CUDA for optimal GPU performance. Steps: 1. Stage 1: Initialization by Volume Rendering. Train the geometry network G and appearance network A using differentiable volume rendering to establish a strong initialization. Sample rays through the scene. Query G(x) for density \sigma and A(x, d) for color c. Compute pixel colors C using the volume rendering compositing equation. Optimize network weights to minimize rendering loss. 2. Stage 2: Manifold Generation & Optimization. Use the pretrained network weights from Stage 1 as initialization. Optimize object topology, geometry, and appearance simultaneously using differentiable rasterization. Apply Differentiable Marching Cubes (DiffMC) on an axis-aligned grid. DiffMC extracts meshes using conventional Marching Cubes and provides gradients for mesh vertices relative to the grid. Feed the resulting mesh into nvdiffrast to render 2D images. Use the rendering loss to update the geometry and appearance networks. 3. Stage 3: Geometry and Appearance Fine-tuning (Optional). Fine-tune only the positions of mesh vertices and the appearance network to minimize rendering loss. This preserves original robust edge connections, maintaining watertightness. Note that this step may occasionally introduce self-intersections. 4. Rendering Deployment. Implement neural networks as GLSL shaders for integration into modern rendering engines. Rasterize triangles in the vertex shader. Compute TensoRF and MLPs using modelspace coordinates and viewing directions in the fragment shader. Use Supersample Anti-Aliasing (SSAA) or Multisample Anti-Aliasing (MSAA) to handle aliasing from undersampling high-frequency features. Pitfalls and Edge Cases: DMTet Artifacts: DMTet produces severe artifacts (peaks and valleys) when extracting meshes from density fields due to reliance on linear interpolation between tetrahedra vertices, which is inadequate for non-linear density fields. This issue is not present with SDF. Self-Intersections: Stage 3 fine-tuning may introduce self-intersections. Grid Alignment: While DiffMC is less susceptible to non-linear data issues, geometries not aligned with the grid axis may still exhibit some artifacts, though significantly smoother than DMTet. Time Complexity: DiffMC is implemented in CUDA for optimal GPU performance and is approximately 20 times faster than DMTet. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Performance: The method achieves high-quality mesh reconstruction, photorealistic rendering quality, and real-time rendering support. Strengths: Produces watertight, manifold, and intersection-free meshes; handles non-linear density fields better than tetrahedra-based methods; supports real-time rendering via GLSL shaders. Limitations: Stage 3 may introduce self-intersections; SSAA has higher computational cost. When to use: When high-quality, watertight manifold meshes are required with efficient rendering support. When not to use: When SDF-based representations are available and DMTet artifacts are not a concern (though DiffMC is still faster). NeuManifold was proposed to integrate the advantages of volumetric and mesh-based methods. The authors observed that with proper initialization, mesh-based methods can converge to a more favorable state, enabling the reconstruction of high-quality meshes. The method addresses the limitations of DMTet in handling non-linear density fields by introducing DiffMC, a differentiable marching cubes algorithm operating on an axis-aligned grid. The work cites TensoRF as the state-of-the-art neural field representation used in this context. name: Separable Component-Wise Convolution for Joint Pose Optimization
head: Component-wise Separable Convolution, Edge-Guided Loss Mask, Efficient 3D Filtering, Randomized 2D/3D Filtering, Separable Component-wise Convolution of Gaussian Filters
body: This method enables robust joint optimization of camera poses and decomposed low-rank tensorial radiance fields by controlling the frequency spectrum of the scene representation. It prevents premature high-frequency signals in the voxel volume from causing camera poses to get stuck in local minima, a failure mode common in naive joint optimization. It sets itself apart from hash-encoding-based methods by specifically leveraging the separability of the input low-rank tensor signal, making it more efficient than traditional separable convolution kernels. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: Decomposed low-rank tensor representation of the radiance field (typically factorized into axial components), 2D supervision images (ground truth views), and camera poses (initial estimates). Outputs: Refined camera poses and optimized decomposed tensor parameters. Data Structures: The method operates on the decomposed low-rank tensor structure used in TensoRF, where the 3D volume is represented as a product of lower-dimensional axial tensors (e.g., V \approx A \times B \times C). The specific bit-packing or memory layout of these factors is inherited from the parent TensoRF Training Loop. Algorithm Steps: 1. Spectral Control via 3D Filtering: Apply separable component-wise convolution of Gaussian filters on the decomposed 3D tensor volume. This directly controls the spectrum of the radiance field, smoothing high-frequency noise that destabilizes pose optimization. 2. 2D Supervision Smoothing: Apply separable component-wise convolution of Gaussian filters on the 2D supervision images. This creates "smoothed 2D supervision" to match the spectral properties of the filtered 3D field. 3. Joint Optimization: Use the filtered radiance field and smoothed supervision for the joint optimization of camera poses and the decomposed voxel representation. 4. Randomized Kernel Scaling: Use randomly scaled kernel parameters for the Gaussian filters during training. This variability is introduced to ensure stability and robustness in the optimization process. 5. Edge-Guided Loss Mask: Apply an edge-guided loss mask to the optimization objective. This technique is proposed to further ensure stability and robustness in the optimization process. Formulas and Parameters: Gaussian Filter: The core operation is a convolution with a Gaussian kernel. The specific kernel size (k) and standard deviation (\sigma) are not explicitly detailed in the provided text but are implied to be configurable. Randomized Scaling: The kernel parameters (likely \sigma or k) are randomly scaled at each step or epoch. Separability: The method utilizes the separability of the input signal (the decomposed tensor) to achieve an equivalent effect to brute-force 3D convolution with little computational overhead. This implies that instead of convolving the full 3D volume, the convolution is applied component-wise to the factorized tensors, exploiting their structure. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def generategaussiankernel1d(sigma): """Generates a normalized 1D Gaussian kernel.""" radius = max(1, int(3 sigma)) x = list(range(-radius, radius + 1)) kernel = [math.exp(-0.5 (xi / sigma) 2) for xi in x] total = sum(kernel) return [k / total for k in kernel] def convolve1d(signal, kernel): """Convolves a 1D signal with a kernel using zero-padding.""" n = len(signal) klen = len(kernel) pad = klen // 2 padded = [0.0] pad + signal + [0.0] pad result = [] for i in range(n): val = 0.0 for j in range(klen): val += padded[i + j] kernel[j] result.append(val) return result def applyseparablecomponentwiseconvolution(tensorfactors, sigma): """Applies 1D Gaussian convolution to each axial factor of the decomposed tensor.""" filteredfactors = [] kernel = generategaussiankernel1d(sigma) for factor in tensorfactors: filteredfactors.append(convolve1d(factor, kernel)) return filteredfactors def smooth2dimages(images, sigma): """Applies separable 2D Gaussian smoothing to a list of images.""" kernel1d = generategaussiankernel1d(sigma) smoothedimages = [] for img in images: smoothedrows = [convolve1d(row, kernel1d) for row in img] cols = list(zip(smoothedrows)) smoothedcols = [convolve1d(col, kernel1d) for col in cols] smoothedimg = list(zip(smoothedcols)) smoothedimages.append(smoothedimg) return smoothedimages def renderviews(tensorfactors, poses): """Renders 2D views from decomposed tensor factors and camera poses.""" # Standard volume rendering or tensor factor evaluation given poses. return [rendersingleview(factor, pose) for factor, pose in zip(tensorfactors, poses)] def rendersingleview(factor, pose): # Evaluates the radiance field at camera ray origins and integrates. return [[0.0 for in row] for row in factor] def computeedgeguidedloss(rendered, target, edgemask): """Computes edge-guided mean squared error loss.""" totalloss = 0.0 count = 0 for rrow, trow, erow in zip(rendered, target, edgemask): for rval, tval, eval in zip(rrow, trow, erow): diff = rval - tval totalloss += diff diff eval count += 1 return totalloss / max(count, 1) def updateparameters(poses, tensorfactors, gradients, lr=0.01): """Updates parameters using gradient descent.""" # Standard parameter update step. for i in range(len(poses)): poses[i] = [p - lr g for p, g in zip(poses[i], gradients[i])] for i in range(len(tensorfactors)): tensorfactors[i] = [v - lr g for v, g in zip(tensorfactors[i], gradients[i])] return poses, tensorfactors def jointposeoptimization(tensorfactors, images, poses, edgemask, numiterations=50000): """Main loop for joint optimization with randomized filtering.""" basesigma = 1.0 for step in range(numiterations): # Randomly scale kernel parameter for stability scale = 0.5 + (step % 100) / 100.0 # Deterministic pseudo-random scaling for reproducibility currentsigma = basesigma scale # Step 1: Filter 3D tensor volume filteredfactors = applyseparablecomponentwiseconvolution(tensorfactors, currentsigma) # Step 2: Filter 2D supervision images smoothedimages = smooth2dimages(images, currentsigma) # Step 3: Optimize renderedviews = renderviews(filteredfactors, poses) loss = computeedgeguidedloss(renderedviews, smoothedimages, edgemask) # Gradients are computed via standard backpropagation through the rendering and filtering operations. gradients = computegradients(loss, poses, tensorfactors) poses, tensorfactors = updateparameters(poses, tensorfactors, gradients) return poses, tensorfactors def computegradients(loss, poses, tensorfactors): # Standard autodiff routine. Returns gradients for poses and tensor factors. return [[0.0] for in poses], [[0.0] for in tensorfactors] Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Premature High Frequencies: Naively applying joint optimization on voxel-based NeRFs leads to dramatic failure because premature high-frequency signals in the voxel volume curse the camera poses to get stuck in local minima. Inapplicability to Hash Encoding: This method is specifically designed for decomposed low-rank tensors and is not directly applicable to multi-resolution hash encoding, which requires different interpolation schemes or curriculum learning. Time Complexity: The method is more efficient than traditional separable convolution kernels because it utilizes the separability of the input signal (the decomposed tensor). It achieves an equivalent effect to brute-force 3D convolution with little computational overhead. Memory Complexity: Inherits the memory complexity of the underlying TensoRF representation, which uses decomposed low-rank tensors instead of dense 3D grids. Performance: The proposed framework requires only 50k training iterations, whereas previous methods typically need 200k iterations. It demonstrates superior performance in novel view synthesis and rapid convergence for optimization. Strengths: Robust joint pose refinement, efficient spectral control, rapid convergence. Limitations: Not applicable to hash-based representations. Origin: The method was proposed in the paper "Improving Robustness for Joint Optimization of Camera Pose and Decomposed Low-Rank Tensorial Radiance Fields". History: It addresses the challenge of joint optimization of camera poses and radiance fields, which is prone to local minima due to high-frequency artifacts. The method builds on the TensoRF representation. Usage: It is used in the Joint-TensoRF project for robust joint pose refinement. name: StyleTRF
head: StyleTRF (S3)
body: StyleTRF is a method for stylized view generation that decouples style adaptation from view capture by fine-tuning the appearance component of a pre-optimized Tensorial Radiance Field (TensoRF) using sparse stylized priors. It sets itself apart from joint optimization methods like SNeRF by freezing the geometric density parameters of the scene representation, thereby preserving crisp geometry while adapting appearance, and by using a deterministic CNN-based stylization module (Johnson et al.) to ensure 3D consistency across viewpoints. Inputs: A set of posed ground-truth images of a scene. A reference style image. Camera poses (obtained via COLMAP for real scenes or Blender for synthetic scenes). Outputs: A fine-tuned TensoRF representation capable of rendering stylized novel views. Data Structures: The scene is represented using the VM-48 variant of TensoRF, which employs Vector-Matrix decomposition (a special case of Block Term Decomposition). Density Tensor (T\sigma): Stores volumetric density. These parameters are frozen during the style adaptation phase. Appearance Tensor (TC): Stores color/appearance vectors. These parameters are optimized during the style adaptation phase. Voxel Grid: The effective resolution starts at 128^3 and is upsampled to 640^3 for real-world scenes (or 300^3 for synthetic scenes). Interpolation: Bi-linear interpolation is used for matrices, and linear interpolation is used for vectors within the VM-decomposed representation during ray queries and upsampling. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def styletrf(groundtruthimages, cameraposes, styleimage): # Phase 1: Pre-optimization of TensoRF # Initialize VM-48 representation: density grid (128^3) and appearance grid (128^3) densitygrid = createvoxelgrid(shape=(128, 128, 128)) appearancegrid = createvoxelgrid(shape=(128, 128, 128)) optimizer = Adam(parameters=[densitygrid, appearancegrid], lr=0.02) for iteration in range(15000): # Sample 4096 rays from camera poses rays = generaterays(cameraposes, count=4096) # Render colors using volumetric rendering renderedcolors = volumetricrender(densitygrid, appearancegrid, rays) # Calculate losses l1loss = meanabsoluteerror(renderedcolors, groundtruthimages[rays]) tvloss = computetvloss(densitygrid, appearancegrid) totalloss = l1loss + tvloss # Update parameters optimizer.step(totalloss) # Upsampling schedule: start at 2000, every 1000 until 5000 if 2000 <= iteration <= 5000 and iteration % 1000 == 0: densitygrid = upsamplegrid(densitygrid, factor=2) appearancegrid = upsamplegrid(appearancegrid, factor=2) optimizer.lr = 0.02 # Re-initialize LR after upsampling # Phase 2: Preprocessing Stylization Module # Train Johnson et al. CNN for the specific style on COCO2014 dataset # Note: Sources do not provide implementation details for the CNN training loop. stylizationcnn = traincnn(styleimage, dataset="COCO2014") # Phase 3: Generate and Stylize Priors # Render sparse novel views (20-30 views in spiral trajectory) novelcameras = generatespiraltrajectory(count=30) novelviews = volumetricrender(densitygrid, appearancegrid, novelcameras) # Stylize these views using the pre-trained CNN stylizedpriors = [stylizationcnn(view) for view in novelviews] # Phase 4: Fine-tuning Appearance # Freeze density parameters densitygrid.requiresgrad = False # Optimize only appearance vectors using stylized priors appearanceoptimizer = Adam(parameters=[appearancegrid], lr=0.02) for iteration in range(1000): rays = generaterays(novelcameras, count=len(stylizedpriors)) renderedcolors = volumetricrender(densitygrid, appearancegrid, rays) styleloss = meanabsoluteerror(renderedcolors, stylizedpriors) appearanceoptimizer.step(styleloss) return densitygrid, appearancegrid def volumetricrender(densitygrid, appearancegrid, rays): """ Computes color C from transmittance tauq, color cq, density sigma, and step size Delta. C = sum{q=1}^{Q} tauq cq tauq = product{p=1}^{q-1} exp(-sigmap Deltap) """ colors = [] for ray in rays: color = 0.0 transmittance = 1.0 # Q samples along the ray (0-based indexing maps to 1-based formula) for q in range(ray.Q): sigmaq = querygrid(densitygrid, ray.position[q]) cq = querygrid(appearancegrid, ray.position[q]) deltaq = ray.stepsize[q] color += transmittance cq transmittance = exp(-sigmaq deltaq) colors.append(color) return colors def computetvloss(densitygrid, appearancegrid): """ LTV = (1/N) sum( sqrt(Delta^2 Tsigma) + 0.1 sqrt(Delta^2 TC)) Delta^2 is squared difference between neighboring values. N is total number of parameters. Density and appearance weighted in ratio 10:1. """ N = densitygrid.numel() + appearancegrid.numel() tvsigma = sum((densitygrid[i] - densitygrid[i+1])2 for i in range(N-1)) tvC = sum((appearancegrid[i] - appearancegrid[i+1])2 for i in range(N-1)) return (1/N) (sqrt(tvsigma) + 0.1 sqrt(tvC)) Formulas: Volumetric Rendering: C = \sum{q=1}^{Q} \tauq cq where \tauq = \prod{p=1}^{q-1} \exp(-\sigmap \Deltap). C is the final color, \tauq is the transmittance, cq is the color, \sigma is the density, and \Delta is the step size. Total Variation Loss: L{TV} = \frac{1}{N} \sum \left( \sqrt{\Delta^2 T\sigma} + 0.1 \sqrt{\Delta^2 TC} \right) where \Delta^2 is the squared difference between neighboring values in the tensors, N is the total number of parameters in the TensoRF representation T, T\sigma represents the density value, and TC represents the appearance value. The density and appearance are weighted in a ratio of 10:1. Parameters: TensoRF Variant: VM-48 (Vector-Matrix decomposition). Optimizer: Adam. Learning Rate: 0.02 (re-initialized to 0.02 after upsampling). Voxel Grid Resolution: Effective resolution starts at 128^3. Upsampled every 1000 iterations starting at iteration 2000 until 5000 iterations, reaching 640^3 for real-world scenes and 300^3 for synthetic scenes. Training Iterations (Pre-optimization): 15,000 iterations. Training Iterations (Style Fine-tuning): 1,000 iterations. Rays per Iteration: 4,096 rays. Number of Stylized Priors: 20–30 (or 30–40) randomly sampled camera positions around the object. Stylization Module: Johnson et al. [20] (trained on COCO2014). Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Optimizing from scratch (Strategy S1): Fails because stylized priors may not share exact geometry with ground truth, leading to geometric artifacts. Unconstrained optimization (Strategy S2): Optimizing both density and appearance simultaneously leads to fuzzy geometry and artifacts in thin structures because limit-free optimization alters geometry components. Stylization Module Choice: Using Gatys et al. [10] causes inconsistencies across nearby viewpoints because it starts with white noise and depends on initialization/optimizer, making it unreliable for 3D consistency. Micro-details: Strategy S2 struggles to capture micro-details and may lose geometry. Time Complexity: Pre-optimization of TensoRF: 10–15 minutes. Stylization Module Training (per style): ~20 minutes. Style Fine-tuning: 40–50 seconds. Rendering (800x800 image): 4–5 seconds. Memory Complexity: Memory footprint of TensoRF VM-48: 10–15 MB. Strengths: Decouples style adaptation from view capture. Preserves crisp geometry by freezing density. Fast style adaptation (40–50 seconds). Low memory footprint compared to MLP-based NeRFs (~1GB). Stable stylization across close-by viewpoints using Johnson et al.. Limitations: Requires pre-optimization of the scene. Relies on the quality of the sparse priors; insufficient priors may lead to incomplete style transfer. When to use: When crisp geometry preservation is critical and fast style adaptation is desired. When 3D consistency across viewpoints is required. When not to use: When joint optimization of geometry and style is preferred (e.g., if the style implies geometric changes). When real-time training is required (pre-optimization takes 10-15 mins). StyleTRF was introduced in the paper "StyleTRF: Stylizing Tensorial Radiance Fields" presented at ICVGIP’22 in December 2022. It builds upon the TensoRF representation [6] and the Johnson et al. stylization method [20]. It addresses limitations in previous methods like SNeRF [29], which uses Gatys et al. [10] and joint optimization, leading to higher training times and potential 3D inconsistencies. name: TensoRF Decomposition Models
head: CP model, HY model, HY-S model, Rank-Residual Decomposition Models (CP, HY-S)
body: This family defines the tensor decomposition strategies used to factorize the radiance field density and color fields in TensoRF, balancing storage efficiency against rendering quality. It differs from sibling methods like NeuManifold or StyleTRF by explicitly structuring the low-rank approximation into discrete rank groups (rank-residual learning) and offering specific variants (CP, HY, HY-S) to control the ratio of vector- to matrix-based components. The core mechanism is Rank-Residual Decomposition, where the radiance field is approximated as a sum of M groups of components. Each group m contains a specific number of rank components for density and color. The decomposition supports two types of components: 1. Vector-based (CP): Uses only 1D vectors for each spatial dimension. 2. Matrix-based (HY): Uses 1D vectors for one dimension and 2D matrices for the other two, allowing for higher local correlation capture with fewer total ranks. The total field value at a point is the sum of contributions from all groups. The model size is controlled by the number of groups M and the rank distribution within each group. The decomposition is optimized using an Adam optimizer with different learning rates for factorized matrices and singular values. Reconstructs a radiance field by factorizing geometry and appearance into n components (one per input view) using Vector-Matrix (VM) decomposition and a global appearance dictionary. It differs from the standard TensoRF families by binding components to specific views to enable robust point cloud fusion. Uses only vector-based rank components. It requires higher ranks (96 for density, 384 for color) to achieve quality, leading to higher GPU memory usage and slower querying, but offers lower storage. Uses both vector- and matrix-based components. It reduces the required number of ranks (64 vector/16 matrix for density; 256 vector/64 matrix for color), thereby reducing GPU memory usage at the cost of slightly higher storage. A scalable variant of HY that allows adjustable model size. It starts with 96 vector components for both density and color, then gradually appends matrix components (4, 16, 32, 64) across 5 groups, enabling flexible trade-offs between quality and resource usage. The Rank-Residual Decomposition models were introduced in "Compressible-Composable NeRF Via Rank-Residual Decomposition". The work addresses the limitations of the standard TensoRF VM decomposition, which requires a fixed 1:1 ratio of vector- to matrix-based ranks, limiting flexibility in model size control. The HY decomposition allows arbitrary adjustment of this ratio, and the HY-S model provides a scalable range of model sizes without requiring retraining for optimal configurations.
