name: Factorized Radiance Field with Fixed View-Dependent Components
head: Point Cloud Fusion NeRF, VM Decomposition NeRF
body: This method reconstructs a radiance field from sparse input views by factorizing geometry and appearance tensors into a fixed number of components equal to the number of input views (n), rather than a small fixed constant. It differs from TensoRF by binding each tensor component to a specific input view, enabling robust point cloud fusion that substitutes inaccurate depth-derived points with accurate ones from other views. The approach uses Vector-Matrix (VM) decomposition for spatial factors and a global appearance dictionary to abstract commonalities across the scene. Inputs: n input views, each containing an RGB image, a depth map, and camera parameters (intrinsic matrix K, rotation matrix R, translation vector t). Hyperparameters: \lambda{depth} (balance between color and depth loss), \omega{reg} (L1 regularization weight), P (feature decoding MLP dimension, set to 27), N0 (initial grid size, set to 128), N (final grid size), Q (number of shading points per ray). Outputs: Rendered RGB images and depth maps for novel viewpoints. 1. Geometry Grid (G\sigma) A factorized 3D tensor representing volume density \sigma. It is decomposed into n components, one per input view. Each component r (1 \le r \le n) consists of: Three 1D vectors: v{\sigma,r}^X \in \mathbb{R}^I, v{\sigma,r}^Y \in \mathbb{R}^J, v{\sigma,r}^Z \in \mathbb{R}^K. Three 2D matrices: M{\sigma,r}^{XY} \in \mathbb{R}^{I \times J}, M{\sigma,r}^{XZ} \in \mathbb{R}^{I \times K}, M{\sigma,r}^{YZ} \in \mathbb{R}^{J \times K}. The grid dimensions are I \times J \times K. 2. Appearance Grid (Gc) A factorized 3D tensor representing color c. It is also decomposed into n components. Each component r involves: Three 1D vectors: v{c,r}^X \in \mathbb{R}^I, v{c,r}^Y \in \mathbb{R}^J, v{c,r}^Z \in \mathbb{R}^K. Three 2D matrices: A{c,r}^X \in \mathbb{R}^{I \times J}, A{c,r}^Y \in \mathbb{R}^{J \times K}, A{c,r}^Z \in \mathbb{R}^{I \times K}. Note: The source defines A{c,r}^X = v{c,r}^X \circ M{c,r}^{XY}, implying the matrices are derived from vector-matrix outer products or similar factorizations, but stored as distinct factors in the decomposition sum. Three basis vectors: b{3r-2}, b{3r-1}, b{3r} \in \mathbb{R}^P. 3. Global Appearance Dictionary (B) A matrix of size P \times 3n formed by stacking the 3n basis vectors br. 1. NDC Mapping: Map depth values to Normalized Device Coordinate (NDC) space to ensure all visible locations fit within a predetermined cubic space. 2. Point Cloud Generation: For each input view r, map every 2D pixel location xp to a 3D world location xw using the camera parameters: xw = R^{-1} (K^{-1} xp D - t) where D is the depth value at xp. 3. Grid Assignment: Geometry: For each point xw from view r, identify the corresponding voxel indices (i,j,k) in the I \times J \times K grid. Set the elements of v{\sigma,r}^X, v{\sigma,r}^Y, v{\sigma,r}^Z and M{\sigma,r}^{XY}, M{\sigma,r}^{XZ}, M{\sigma,r}^{YZ} corresponding to these projections to 1. All other elements are set to 0. Appearance: For the same projections, assign the average RGB color of the projected points to the elements of A{c,r}^X, A{c,r}^Y, A{c,r}^Z. Assign random values to v{c,r}^X, v{c,r}^Y, v{c,r}^Z. 4. Dictionary Initialization: Initialize the basis vectors br (and thus matrix B). To render a pixel, march along a ray and sample Q shading points xq with step size \Deltaq. 1. Density Interpolation: Calculate \sigmaq = G\sigma(xq) using trilinear interpolation of the factorized geometry grid. For a single component r, the interpolated value is: A{\sigma,r}(x) = v{\sigma,r}(x) M{\sigma,r}(y, z) (Generalizing to 3D via the sum of modes). 2. Color Interpolation: Calculate the feature vector fq by concatenating the interpolated appearance factors for component r, then multiplying by the dictionary B: fq = B \oplus [A{c,r}(xq)]{r} The color cq is obtained by passing fq through a feature decoding MLP S: cq = S(fq, dq) where dq is the view direction at xq. 3. Volume Rendering: Compute the pixel color C and transmittance \tauq: \tauq = \exp\left(-\sum{p=1}^{q-1} \sigmap \Deltap\right) C = \sum{q=1}^{Q} \tauq (1 - \exp(-\sigmaq \Deltaq)) cq \tau{Q+1} = \exp\left(-\sum{p=1}^{Q} \sigmap \Deltap\right) (Background color is typically added as \tau{Q+1} c{bg}, though not explicitly detailed in the source, the formula for C is given as above). The model is optimized using a composite loss function L: L = L{RGB} + \lambda{depth} L{depth} 1. RGB Loss (L{RGB}): L{RGB} = \|C - \hat{C}\|2^2 + \omega{reg} L{reg} where \hat{C} is the ground truth color, and L{reg} is the L1 regularization term applied to all tensor factors to promote sparsity and eliminate floaters. 2. Depth Loss (L{depth}): L{depth} = \|D - \hat{D}\|2^2 where D is the rendered depth and \hat{D} is the ground truth depth. Training starts with a grid of size N0^3 (N0=128). The grid is upsampled at specific training steps (2000, 3000, 4000, 5500, 7000) to the final size N^3. Upsampling is performed by linearly and bilinearly upsampling the XYZ-mode vector and matrix factors. Unverified code. F = torch.cat([ interpolate2d(self.AcX, x, y, dim1=1, dim2=2).flatten(), interpolate2d(self.AcY, y, z, dim1=1, dim2=2).flatten(), interpolate2d(self.AcZ, x, z, dim1=1, dim2=2).flatten() ], dim=-1) # Shape (batch, 3n) # Multiply by Dictionary B # B is (P, 3n). F is (batch, 3n). # Result: (batch, P) features = torch.matmul(F, self.B.T) # Pass through MLP colors = self.mlp(features) return colors def renderray(self, rayorigins, raydirections, tnear, tfar, Q=128): """ Render a batch of rays. """ # Sample points tvals = torch.linspace(tnear, tfar, Q).unsqueeze(0) # (1, Q) tvals = tvals.expand(rayorigins.shape[0], -1) # (batch, Q) # Interpolate tvals to match ray directions? # Standard: xq = o + tq d points = rayorigins.unsqueeze(1) + tvals.unsqueeze(2) raydirections.unsqueeze(1) # (batch, Q, 3) # Normalize points to grid coordinates [0, I], [0, J], [0, K] # Assuming points are in world space, need inverse transform to grid space # This step depends on the specific NDC mapping, omitted for brevity xgrid, ygrid, zgrid = worldtogrid(points) # Get density and color sigma = self.getdensity(xgrid, ygrid, zgrid) # (batch, Q) colors = self.getcolor(xgrid, ygrid, zgrid, raydirections) # (batch, Q, 3) # Volume rendering deltas = tvals[:, 1:] - tvals[:,:-1] deltas = torch.cat([deltas, torch.zeroslike(deltas[:,:1])], dim=1) alpha = 1.0 - torch.exp(-sigma deltas) T = torch.cumprod(torch.exp(-sigma deltas), dim=1) T = torch.cat([torch.oneslike(T[:,:1]), 1.0 - T], dim=1) weights = alpha T[:,:-1] C = torch.sum(weights.unsqueeze(2) colors[:,:-1], dim=1) return C def loss(self, predcolor, preddepth, gtcolor, gtdepth): Lrgb = torch.mean((predcolor - gtcolor)2) + self.omegareg torch.mean(torch.abs(self.vsigmaX)) # Simplified reg Ldepth = torch.mean((preddepth - gtdepth)2) return Lrgb + self.lambdadepth Ldepth Time and Memory Complexity: Memory: Scales with n \times (I \cdot J + J \cdot K + I \cdot K) for geometry and appearance matrices, plus P \times 3n for the dictionary. Since n is the number of views, memory grows linearly with the number of input views, unlike TensoRF which uses a fixed small number of components. Time: Rendering involves interpolating factors for each sample point. The number of components n adds a summation loop during density/color calculation. Measured Performance: LLFF Dataset (2 views): PSNR 17.83, SSIM 0.5512, LPIPS 0.3832. LLFF Dataset (4 views): PSNR 20.86, SSIM 0.5967, LPIPS 0.3247. DTU Dataset (0% noise): PSNR 19.34, SSIM 0.7431, LPIPS 0.2576. DTU Dataset (10% depth noise): PSNR 16.63, SSIM 0.4144, LPIPS 0.5561. Strengths and Limitations: Strengths: Robust to inaccurate depth values through point cloud fusion; eliminates floaters via L1 regularization; performs well on sparse views. Limitations: Performance degrades with noisy depth maps (e.g., 10% noise significantly reduces PSNR). Memory usage increases with the number of input views. When to Use: Sparse view reconstruction where depth maps are available but potentially noisy. Scenes where view-dependent appearance can be abstracted into a global dictionary. Origin: The method was introduced in the paper "Depth-Guided Robust and Fast Point Cloud Fusion NeRF for Sparse Input Views" presented at the Thirty-Eighth AAAI Conference on Artificial Intelligence (AAAI-24). History and Development: It builds upon TensoRF but modifies the decomposition to fix the number of components to the number of input views, enabling explicit point cloud fusion. It uses NDC normalization similar to DSNeRF. Usage: Implemented in PyTorch, optimized on NVIDIA RTX 4090 GPU with a batch size of 4096 pixel rays. name: Vector-Matrix-Matrix (VMM) Factorization
head: VMM decomposition
body: Vector-Matrix-Matrix (VMM) factorization is a compact representation technique for light field tensors that models radiance and geometry by decomposing feature probes into shared core factors and probe-specific basis factors. It distinguishes itself from standard CP decomposition by introducing a hybrid structure where a Vector-Matrix (VM) core captures multilinear interactions shared across local probes, while a Matrix (M) basis factor handles individual probe details, enabling efficient spatial sharing and multi-scale pyramid storage. Input: A set of L discrete spherical probes \mathcal{T} = \{\taul \in \mathbb{R}^{H \times W \times D}\}{l=1}^L, where each probe \taul represents a D-layered spherical grid located at position pl. Output: A continuous feature field \taul(\mathbf{x}) for any 3D coordinate \mathbf{x}, reconstructed via weighted blending of neighboring probes. The decomposition utilizes three types of factor tensors. The layout and typical resolutions for optimization are: 1. Core Vector (\ddot{V}{c,r}): Shape: \mathbb{R}^D Role: Shared among all local probes; captures depth interactions. Resolution: Starts at 64, upscaled to 1024 during optimization. 2. Core Matrix (\ddot{M}{c,r}): Shape: \mathbb{R}^{H \times W} Role: Shared among all local probes; captures angular interactions. Resolution: Starts at (64, 128), upscaled to (128, 256) during optimization. 3. Basis Matrix (M{l,r}): Shape: \mathbb{R}^{H \times W} Role: Specific to probe l; designated exclusively for each individual probe. Resolution: Fixed at (256, 512) during optimization. Parameters: R: Number of factor components (rank). Set to 32. F: Number of basis factor components reduced via a linear layer before aggregation. Set to 2. D: Dimension of the core vector (depth of spherical grid). H, W: Spherical dimensions of the matrix factors, providing full angular coverage. To query values on the low-dimensional factors, the input 3D coordinate \mathbf{x} = (x, y, z) is transformed into local normalized depth and spherical coordinates relative to a probe center p: \tilde{t} = \|\mathbf{x} - p\|2 t = \frac{1}{\tilde{t} + 1} \tilde{\mathbf{v}} = \left( \arccos \left( \frac{z}{\tilde{t}} \right), \arctan \left( \frac{y}{x} \right) \right) Here, t represents the normalized depth, and \tilde{\mathbf{v}} represents the spherical angles. The discrete tensor element \taul^{ijk} for probe l at indices i, j, k is factorized as a sum of R scalar products using the Hadamard product (\circ): \taul^{ijk} = \sum{r=1}^R \ddot{V}{c,r}^k \circ \ddot{M}{c,r}^{ij} \circ M{l,r}^{ij} Where: \ddot{V}{c,r} \in \mathbb{R}^D is the core vector component r for core index c. \ddot{M}{c,r} \in \mathbb{R}^{H \times W} is the core matrix component r for core index c. M{l,r} \in \mathbb{R}^{H \times W} is the basis matrix component r for probe l. c, l are core and basis factor indices respectively. i, j, k denote the three modes (angular and depth). For continuous field reconstruction, linear interpolation (\cdot) is applied to each vector and matrix when querying a target position \mathbf{x}: \taul(\mathbf{x}) = \sum{r=1}^R \ddot{V}{c,r}(\mathbf{x}) \circ \ddot{M}{c,r}(\mathbf{x}) \circ M{l,r}(\mathbf{x}) To simplify computation, scalar values are concatenated into an R-channel vector: \ddot{V}c(\tilde{t}c) = [\ddot{V}{c,1}(\tilde{t}c), \dots, \ddot{V}{c,R}(\tilde{t}c)]. Similarly for \ddot{M}c and Ml. The combined feature for probe l at \mathbf{x} is denoted as Gl(\mathbf{x}) = \ddot{V}c(\tilde{t}c) \circ \ddot{M}c(\tilde{v}c) \circ Ml(vl). The final tensor value is recovered via summation: \taul(\mathbf{x}) = \sum Gl(\mathbf{x}), though a neural decoder may be included instead. 1. Neighbor Selection: For a target camera center, select K neighboring feature probes based on the distance between the target camera center and the probe centers. Use \hat{L}=16 neighboring basis factors for representation. 2. Coordinate Transformation: For each selected probe l and target point \mathbf{x}, compute local coordinates t and \tilde{\mathbf{v}} using the transformation equations above. 3. Factor Interpolation: Perform linear interpolation on the core vector \ddot{V}{c,r}, core matrix \ddot{M}{c,r}, and basis matrix M{l,r} using the local coordinates to obtain interpolated values \ddot{V}{c,r}(\mathbf{x}), \ddot{M}{c,r}(\mathbf{x}), and M{l,r}(\mathbf{x}). 4. Weighted Blending: Apply efficient weighted blending on each factor group (core and basis) across the K selected probes. This is done before performing the final matrix multiplication to avoid multiplying factors for each probe individually. 5. Factor Multiplication: Compute the Hadamard product of the blended core vector, blended core matrix, and blended basis matrix for each rank r. 6. Summation: Sum the results over all R ranks to obtain the feature tensor \taul(\mathbf{x}). 7. Decoding (Optional): Pass the aggregated features through a neural network \Phi to predict density \alphai and blended radiance weights w{i,l}. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import numpy as np def vmmfactorizationquery(probes, corevectors, corematrices, basismatrices, targetpoint, probecenters, weights): """ Reconstructs the feature tensor at a target point using VMM factorization. Args: probes: List of probe indices selected (size K). corevectors: Tensor of shape (C, R, D) - Core vectors for C cores. corematrices: Tensor of shape (C, R, H, W) - Core matrices for C cores. basismatrices: Tensor of shape (L, R, H, W) - Basis matrices for L probes. targetpoint: 3D coordinate (x, y, z). probecenters: Array of probe center coordinates (L, 3). weights: Blending weights for the K selected probes (K,). Returns: featuretensor: Reconstructed feature tensor (R,). """ K = len(probes) R = corevectors.shape[1] D = corevectors.shape[2] H, W = corematrices.shape[2], corematrices.shape[3] # Initialize blended factors # Blended core vector: (R, D) blendedcorevec = np.zeros((R, D)) # Blended core matrix: (R, H, W) blendedcoremat = np.zeros((R, H, W)) # Blended basis matrix: (R, H, W) blendedbasismat = np.zeros((R, H, W)) for k in range(K): probeidx = probes[k] probecenter = probecenters[probeidx] w = weights[k] # 1. Coordinate Transformation distsq = np.sum((targetpoint - probecenter) 2) ttilde = np.sqrt(distsq) t = 1.0 / (ttilde + 1.0) # Spherical coordinates # Handle edge case where ttilde is 0 to avoid division by zero if ttilde < 1e-8: theta = 0.0 phi = 0.0 else: theta = np.arccos(targetpoint[2] / ttilde) phi = np.arctan2(targetpoint[1], targetpoint[0]) # 2. Linear Interpolation of Factors # Note: In practice, this involves trilinear/bilinear interpolation on the grids. # Here we assume helper functions for interpolation. # Interpolate Core Vector (D dimension) # Core vector index c is typically fixed or selected based on scene scale. # Assuming c=0 for simplicity as per typical single-core usage in examples. c = 0 interpcorevec = interpolatelinear(corevectors[c], t, D) # Interpolate Core Matrix (H, W dimensions) interpcoremat = interpolatebilinear(corematrices[c], theta, phi, H, W) # Interpolate Basis Matrix (H, W dimensions) interpbasismat = interpolatebilinear(basismatrices[probeidx], theta, phi, H, W) # 3. Weighted Blending blendedcorevec += w interpcorevec blendedcoremat += w interpcoremat blendedbasismat += w interpbasismat # 4. Factor Multiplication (Hadamard Product) # Result shape: (R, H, W) -> then sum over H,W to get (R,) or keep as tensor # The formula sums over R. The output is typically a feature vector per rank. # However, the formula shows taul(x) = sumr (V o M o M). # This results in a tensor of shape (H, W) if we sum over R? # No, the formula is element-wise in i,j,k. # Let's follow the vector concatenation description: # Gl(x) = Vc(x) o Mc(x) o Ml(x) -> This is element-wise product of vectors/matrices. # If V is (R, D), Mc is (R, H, W), Ml is (R, H, W). # The product is (R, H, W). # Then taul(x) = sumr Gl(x)? No, sumr is over the rank dimension. # The formula: taul^{ijk} = sumr V^k o M^{ij} o M^{ij}. # This implies the output is a scalar per (i,j,k) if we sum over r? # Actually, V is (R, D), Mc is (R, H, W), Ml is (R, H, W). # The Hadamard product is element-wise. # So for each rank r, we have a matrix (H,W) and a vector (D). # The result is a tensor (R, H, W, D)? No. # Let's look at Eq 5: taul^{ijk} = sumr V{c,r}^k o M{c,r}^{ij} o M{l,r}^{ij}. # i,j are spatial/angular, k is depth. # V{c,r}^k is a scalar (k-th element of vector r). # M{c,r}^{ij} is a scalar. # M{l,r}^{ij} is a scalar. # So for each r, we compute a scalar product. # Then we sum over r. # The result is a tensor of shape (H, W, D). # Re-evaluating based on "concatenate all scalar values into an R-channel vector" # This suggests the final output might be kept as R channels before summation or decoding. # But the formula explicitly sums over R. # Implementation of the sum over R: # We have blendedcorevec (R, D), blendedcoremat (R, H, W), blendedbasismat (R, H, W). # We need to compute sumr (corevecr corematr basismatr). # Expand dimensions for broadcasting # corevec: (R, 1, 1, D) # coremat: (R, H, W, 1) # basismat: (R, H, W, 1) # This is complex to broadcast directly to (H, W, D). # Instead, iterate or use einsum. # Using einsum: # V: (R, D) # Mc: (R, H, W) # Mb: (R, H, W) # Result: sumr (V{r,k} Mc{r,i,j} Mb{r,i,j}) for each i,j,k # This results in a tensor of shape (H, W, D). # However, the text says "Gl(x) = Vc o Mc o Ml... recover taul(x) using a simple sum operation". # If Gl is (R, H, W) [assuming D is handled separately or V is part of the matrix? No, V is vector]. # Let's stick to the formula: # taul(x) is a tensor of shape (H, W, D). # Efficient computation: # 1. Element-wise multiply coremat and basismat: (R, H, W) # 2. Multiply by corevec: (R, H, W, D) -> broadcast V over H,W # 3. Sum over R: (H, W, D) product = blendedcoremat blendedbasismat # (R, H, W) # Expand V to (R, 1, 1, D) productexpanded = product[:,:,:, np.newaxis] blendedcorevec[:, np.newaxis, np.newaxis,:] # (R, H, W, D) featuretensor = np.sum(productexpanded, axis=0) # (H, W, D) return featuretensor def interpolatelinear(tensor, t, dim): """Placeholder for linear interpolation along dimension dim.""" # In practice, this maps t to indices and interpolates. # For VMM, t is normalized depth. return tensor[int(t (tensor.shape[0]-1))] # Simplified for pseudocode def interpolatebilinear(tensor, theta, phi, H, W): """Placeholder for bilinear interpolation on spherical grid.""" # Map theta, phi to i, j indices i = int((theta / np.pi) (H - 1)) j = int(((phi + np.pi) / (2 np.pi)) (W - 1)) return tensor[i, j] # Simplified Division by Zero: When the target point coincides with a probe center, \tilde{t} = 0. The formula for t involves division by \tilde{t}+1, which is safe, but the spherical coordinate calculation \arccos(z/\tilde{t}) requires handling \tilde{t}=0 explicitly to avoid NaNs. Precision: Linear interpolation on low-resolution core factors (starting at 64) may introduce aliasing if not upscaled properly. The method uses progressive upscaling to mitigate this. Boundary Conditions: The spherical coordinates \theta and \phi must be correctly mapped to the matrix indices H and W to ensure full angular coverage. Time Complexity: The factorization reduces the complexity of storing and querying light field tensors. By sharing core factors, the number of parameters is significantly reduced compared to storing full tensors for each probe. The weighted blending before multiplication reduces the number of matrix multiplications from K \times R to 1 \times R (after blending). Memory Complexity: The memory usage is dominated by the core factors (shared) and the basis factors (per probe). With R=32, D=1024, H=128, W=256 for cores and H=256, W=512 for basis, the memory footprint is compact relative to the scene size. Strengths: Compactness: Achieves compact encoding while preserving locality. Efficiency: Fast reconstruction and aliasing-free rendering via soft localization and blending. Multi-scale: Stores 3D points in a multi-scale pyramid (mipmaps) format, modeling nearby areas at higher resolution and distant areas at lower resolution. Limitations: Resolution Dependency: Performance depends on the resolution of the core and basis factors. Lower resolutions may lose detail. Probe Selection: Requires selecting K neighboring probes, which adds computational overhead during query time. When to Use: Suitable for novel view synthesis in scenes with arbitrary scales where compact representation and efficient rendering are prioritized. Origin: The Vector-Matrix-Matrix (VMM) factorization was introduced in the paper "NeLF-Pro: Neural Light Field Probes for Multi-Scale Novel View Synthesis". Development: It was developed to improve grid-based representations for handling scenes with arbitrary scales within a compact and efficient framework. It builds on the concept of light field feature probes and introduces a novel factorization technique to uncover hidden relationships and patterns within the scene. Usage: It is used in novel view synthesis tasks, particularly for large-scale scenes like Google Earth, KITTI360, and City Walk, as demonstrated in the evaluation section of the source paper. NeLF-Pro: Neural Light Field Probes for Multi-Scale Novel View Synthesis, https://doi.org/10.1109/cvpr52733.2024.01875, fetched 2026-10-27

name: Multiscale Tensor Decomposition
body: Multiscale Tensor Decomposition (MTD) is a radiance field representation method that decomposes 3D tensors into plane and line features at multiple resolutions to reconstruct scenes from coarse to fine scales. It improves shape and appearance reconstruction accuracy and convergence speed over single-scale TensoRF while using fewer parameters. Unlike TensoRF, which performs decomposition at a single scale, MTD leverages multiscale representations to explore local smoothness at varying scales, allowing higher-resolution representations to capture richer details with fewer total parameters. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A 3D point x = (x, y, z), a view direction d, and camera parameters. Output: Density \sigma and color c (diffuse and specular components) for the point. Data Structures: The representation consists of L levels. At each level l, the 3D tensor is decomposed into: Three plane feature maps: F{xy}^l, F{xz}^l, F{yz}^l with resolution Nl \times Nl. Three line feature vectors: F{z}^l, F{y}^l, F{x}^l with length Nl. The total number of parameters is determined by the number of levels, base resolution, growth factor, and feature channels per level. Parameters: N{min}: Base resolution (e.g., 16). N{max}: Maximum resolution (e.g., 512). L: Total number of levels (e.g., 16). b: Growth factor, calculated as b = \exp\left(\frac{\ln N{max} - \ln N{min}}{L-1}\right). C{app}: Feature channels for appearance field (e.g., 4). C{den}: Feature channels for density field (e.g., 2). Spatial MLP: 3 layers, 256 hidden units, ReLU activation. Directional MLP: 6 layers, 256 hidden units, ReLU activation. Steps: 1. Calculate Resolution: For each level l \in [0, L-1], compute the resolution Nl: Nl = \lfloor N{min} b^l \rfloor 2. Feature Extraction: For a point x at level l: Decompose coordinates into 2D projections (x, y), (x, z), (y, z) and 1D projections z, y, x. Perform linear interpolation (bilinear for planes, linear for lines) on the feature maps/vectors: f{xy}^l = \text{Interp2D}(F{xy}^l, (x, y)) f{z}^l = \text{Interp1D}(F{z}^l, z) (Similarly for f{xz}^l, f{y}^l, f{yz}^l, f{x}^l). Compute the feature vector for level l by element-wise multiplication (Hadamard product) of the corresponding plane and line features. For example, for the xyz component: f{xyz}^l = f{xy}^l \odot f{z}^l 3. Concatenation and Spatial MLP: Concatenate feature vectors from all levels: f{concat} = [f{xyz}^0, \dots, f{xyz}^{L-1}, \dots] (including all permutations if using the full decomposition structure described in TensoRF, i.e., f{xyz}, f{xzy}, f{yzx} etc., though the text highlights f{xyz} specifically for the sum). Feed f{concat} into the Spatial MLP to predict parameters P. P includes: diffuse color cd, specular weight s, normal n, bottleneck feature b, and parameters for specular encoding ai, \lambdai, \mui. 4. Density Prediction: Sum the feature vectors from all levels for the density field. Apply softplus activation: \sigma = \text{softplus}\left(\sum{l=0}^{L-1} f{den}^l\right) 5. Color Prediction: Construct an encoded feature vector g by concatenating encoded view direction features (using the Rendering Equation Encoding or similar method described in the source). Feed g and the bottleneck feature b (from P) into the Directional MLP to predict specular color cs. Predict diffuse color cd and specular weight s from the Spatial MLP output P. Compute final color: c = \text{Sigmoid}(cd + s \odot cs) 6. Volume Rendering (Optional/Integrated): For a ray sampled at points xi with depth ti and interval \Deltai: Compute composition weights: wi = \exp\left(-\sum{j=0}^{i-1} \sigmaj \Deltaj\right) (1 - \exp(-\sigmai \Deltai)) Only compute colors for points where wi exceeds a predefined threshold to reduce cost. Rendered pixel color: \hat{c} = \sumi wi ci Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import torch import torch.nn as nn import torch.nn.functional as F class MultiscaleTensorDecomposition(nn.Module): def init(self, Nmin=16, Nmax=512, L=16, Capp=4, Cden=2): super().init() self.Nmin = Nmin self.Nmax = Nmax self.L = L self.Capp = Capp self.Cden = Cden # Calculate growth factor b # b = exp((ln(Nmax) - ln(Nmin)) / (L - 1)) self.b = torch.exp((torch.log(torch.tensor(Nmax)) - torch.log(torch.tensor(Nmin))) / (L - 1)) # Initialize feature maps and vectors for all levels # For each level l, we need 3 plane maps and 3 line vectors # Dimensions: [L, 3, Nl, Nl] for planes, [L, 3, Nl] for lines self.planefeatures = nn.ParameterList() self.linefeatures = nn.ParameterList() for l in range(L): Nl = int(torch.floor(self.Nmin (self.b l))) # Plane features: [3, Nl, Nl, Capp] for appearance, [3, Nl, Nl, Cden] for density? # The text implies separate fields or shared structure. # Assuming separate feature sets for density and appearance as per "Model scene density and appearance fields separately" # However, standard TensoRF MTD often shares the decomposition structure. # Let's assume we store features for both fields or combine them. # Based on "4 feature channels for appearance and 2 for density", we store: # Appearance planes: [3, Nl, Nl, Capp] self.planefeatures.append(nn.Parameter(torch.randn(3, Nl, Nl, Capp))) # Appearance lines: [3, Nl, Capp] self.linefeatures.append(nn.Parameter(torch.randn(3, Nl, Capp))) # Density planes: [3, Nl, Nl, Cden] self.planefeatures.append(nn.Parameter(torch.randn(3, Nl, Nl, Cden))) # Density lines: [3, Nl, Cden] self.linefeatures.append(nn.Parameter(torch.randn(3, Nl, Cden))) # Spatial MLP: 3 layers, 256 hidden # Input size: L (sum of feature vector dims). # If we concatenate fxyz, fxzy, fyzx for each level, and Capp channels. # The text says "concatenate the output feature vectors from all levels... fed into spatial MLP" # Let's assume input dim is L Capp 3 (for the 3 permutations) or just L Capp if simplified. # Standard TensoRF uses 3 permutations. inputdim = L Capp 3 self.spatialmlp = nn.Sequential( nn.Linear(inputdim, 256), nn.ReLU(), nn.Linear(256, 256), nn.ReLU(), nn.Linear(256, 256) # Output P) # Directional MLP: 6 layers, 256 hidden # Input: encoded view direction g + bottleneck b # Output: specular color components self.directionalmlp = nn.Sequential( nn.Linear(256, 256), # Assuming g and b are projected to 256 nn.ReLU(), nn.Linear(256, 256), nn.ReLU(), nn.Linear(256, 256), nn.ReLU(), nn.Linear(256, 256), nn.ReLU(), nn.Linear(256, 256), nn.ReLU(), nn.Linear(256, 256), nn.ReLU(), nn.Linear(256, 3) # Specular color RGB) def getresolution(self, l): return int(torch.floor(self.Nmin (self.b l))) def interpolate(self, planefeat, linefeat, coord2d, coord1d): """ planefeat: [3, N, N, C] linefeat: [3, N, C] coord2d: [B, 2] (x, y) normalized to [0, 1] coord1d: [B, 1] (z) normalized to [0, 1] """ N = planefeat.shape[2] # Bilinear interpolation for plane # Normalize coords to [-1, 1] for gridsample x, y = coord2d[:, 0], coord2d[:, 1] xynorm = torch.stack([x, y], dim=-1) 2 - 1 xynorm = xynorm.unsqueeze(1).unsqueeze(1) # [B, 1, 1, 2] # gridsample expects input [N, C, H, W] # planefeat is [3, N, N, C] -> permute to [3, C, N, N] pfeatperm = planefeat.permute(0, 3, 1, 2) # Sample for each of the 3 planes fxy = F.gridsample(pfeatperm[0], xynorm, aligncorners=True).squeeze(-1).squeeze(-1) # [B, C] fxz = F.gridsample(pfeatperm[1], xynorm, aligncorners=True).squeeze(-1).squeeze(-1) # Using x,z coords? # Note: The text says fxy = Interp2D(Fxy, xxy). # We need to map 2D coords correctly for each plane. # For Fxz, coords are (x, z). For Fyz, coords are (y, z). # Simplified: Assume helper handles coordinate mapping # Here we just return the interpolated result structure return fxy # Placeholder for actual interpolation logic per plane def forward(self, x, d): """ x: [B, 3] coordinates d: [B, 3] view directions """ B = x.shape[0] allfeatures = [] densitysum = 0 for l in range(self.L): Nl = self.getresolution(l) # Access features for this level # Appearance features are at indices 0,1,2,3 (3 planes, 3 lines) # Density features are at indices 4,5,6,7 # This indexing is complex in the simplified init. # Let's assume we have separate lists for App and Den # Extract 2D and 1D coords # xxy = [x, y], xxz = [x, z], xyz = [y, z] # zcoord = z, ycoord = y, xcoord = x # Interpolate Appearance Features # fxy, fxz, fyz (planes) and fz, fy, fx (lines) # Calculate fxyz = fxy fz # Calculate fxzy = fxz fy # Calculate fyzx = fyz fx # Concatenate appearance features for this level # fapplevel = [fxyz, fxzy, fyzx] flattened # fapplevel shape: [B, 3 Capp] # Interpolate Density Features # fdenlevel = sum of feature vectors at all levels? # Text: "density sigma is the result of the softplus activation of the sum of the feature vectors at all levels" # This implies we sum the interpolated features across levels for density. # For now, let's just collect appearance features for the Spatial MLP # And accumulate density features #... Implementation details for interpolation omitted for brevity, # assuming standard bilinear/linear interpolation functions... pass # Concatenate all level appearance features # fconcat shape: [B, L 3 Capp] # P = SpatialMLP(fconcat) # P contains cd, s, n, b, ai, lambdai, mui # Density calculation # sigma = softplus(sum of density features from all levels) # Color calculation # g = encodeviewdirection(d, P) # cs = DirectionalMLP(g, b) # c = Sigmoid(cd + s cs) return sigma, c This variant integrates the MTD representation with a specific volume rendering pipeline. It models density and appearance fields separately using two MTD representations. Density \sigmai is the softplus of the sum of feature vectors at all levels. Color composition weights wi are computed based on densities and sampling intervals \Deltai. To reduce computational cost, colors are only computed for sampled points where wi exceeds a predefined threshold. The final color is a weighted sum of predicted colors. The specular color is predicted by a directional MLP fed with an encoded feature vector g and a bottleneck feature b, while diffuse color and specular weight are predicted by the spatial MLP. The spatial MLP has 3 layers and the directional MLP has 6 layers. Complexity: Time complexity is proportional to the number of levels L and the resolution Nl at each level for interpolation. Memory complexity is proportional to the total number of parameters in the plane and line features across all levels. Performance: MTD achieves better view synthesis quality than single-scale TensoRF with fewer parameters. For example, a configuration with 16 levels, max resolution 512, and 4 feature channels uses 8.5M parameters, compared to 13M parameters for single-scale TensoRF with resolution 300 and 48 channels. Convergence: Scene geometry appears fast in coarse-scale representations, leading to faster convergence than single-scale representations. Strengths: Better exploration of local smoothness at varying scales; fewer parameters for high-resolution details; faster convergence. Limitations: More complex implementation due to multiple scales; interpolation overhead at multiple resolutions. When to use: When high-quality reconstruction of wide-ranging computer vision tasks (nature scenes) is required with limited parameters and faster training convergence. When not to use: When computational resources for interpolation at multiple scales are constrained, or if single-scale accuracy is sufficient. Multiscale Tensor Decomposition was proposed in the paper "Multiscale Tensor Decomposition and Rendering Equation Encoding for View Synthesis" (CVPR 2023). It was developed to address the limitations of single-scale tensor decomposition in TensoRF, which performs decomposition only at a single scale. The method draws inspiration from multiscale methods in computer vision [1, 14, 16, 26, 27] and aims to represent scenes from coarse to fine scales. It differs from Multiresolution Hash Encoding (MHE), which uses multiresolution to mitigate hash collisions, by using multiresolution to explore local smoothness at varying scales. name: Coarse-to-fine feature grid
head: Progressive Upscaling of Feature Grids, Coarse-to-fine grid optimization
body: A training optimization scheme that reduces initial training cost and regularizes feature representations by initializing a 3D feature grid at a coarse resolution and progressively upscaling it to higher resolutions. It improves model convergence and makes camera refinement more effective compared to training at full resolution from the start. Unlike static grid methods, this approach dynamically adapts the spatial detail of the feature representation during the optimization process. Inputs and Outputs Input: Initial coarse feature grid parameters (matrices and vectors), current iteration count, target final resolution. Output: Updated feature grid parameters at the current resolution stage. Data Structures The method operates on the 3D feature grid components defined in the parent TensoRF Decomposition Models. These typically consist of: Feature Matrices: 2D tensors representing features along specific axes (e.g., X, Y, Z). Feature Vectors: 1D tensors representing scalar or vector features at grid nodes. Numbered Steps 1. Initialization: Initialize the 3D feature grid with a coarse resolution. 2. Start Optimization: Begin model optimization with an initial grid resolution of d = 32. 3. Iterative Upscaling: Check if the current iteration count is a multiple of 5,000. If yes, upsample the grid to a resolution that is two times larger in each dimension. Apply bi-linear upscaling to the feature matrices. Apply linear upscaling to the feature vectors. Initialize the new grid entries with interpolated values from the coarse grid. 4. Repeat: Continue the optimization and upscaling process every 5,000 iterations. 5. Termination: Stop upscaling when the final dimension reaches d = 256 or the desired fine resolution determined by scene complexity. Formulas Upsampling Interval: Upsampling occurs at iterations k where k \mod 5000 = 0. Resolution Progression: d{new} = 2 \times d{old}. Matrix Upscaling: Bi-linear interpolation is used for 2D feature matrices. Vector Upscaling: Linear interpolation is used for 1D feature vectors. Parameters Initial Resolution (d{init}): 32. Final Resolution (d{final}): 256 or determined by scene complexity (input DVR or IR images). Upsampling Frequency: Every 5,000 iterations. Upsampling Factor: 2x per step. Edge Cases and Pitfalls Scene Complexity: If the scene is simple, a lower final resolution may suffice, reducing memory usage. Camera Refinement: Coarse-to-fine optimization is critical for effective camera refinement; skipping it may lead to poor pose estimation. Precision: Bi-linear and linear upscaling preserve continuity but may introduce smoothing artifacts if the scene has high-frequency details not captured by the coarse grid. Uses manifold-based representations for unbounded environments, often combined with coarse-to-fine strategies for better convergence. Focuses on pose optimization, where coarse-to-fine grids help stabilize camera refinement. Applies style-based transformations, potentially benefiting from progressive grid upscaling for multi-scale detail. The foundational representation that uses the feature grids optimized by this method. Time Complexity: Reduces initial training cost by starting with a smaller grid. Total training time may increase due to upscaling steps, but convergence is faster. Memory Complexity: Scales with the cube of the resolution (d^3). Starting at d=32 significantly reduces peak memory usage compared to starting at d=256. Measured Performance: Effective for static and dynamic scenes, improving novel view synthesis quality. Strengths: Regularizes the optimization process, prevents overfitting in early stages, and improves camera refinement. Limitations: Requires careful tuning of upscaling frequency and final resolution. When to Use: When training cost is a concern, or when camera refinement is critical. When Not to Use: For very simple scenes where full resolution can be trained quickly, or when real-time inference is prioritized over training time. Originated in the context of TensoRF and HexPlane representations to address the high computational cost of training large 3D feature grids. It was adopted in ViSNeRF for efficient multidimensional neural radiance field representation and in Neural Assets for volumetric object capture. The method builds on the observation that coarse-to-fine optimization stabilizes gradient descent and improves generalization. name: Codec-Adaptive TriPlane Radiance Fields
head: CATRF, SCL, Standard-Codec-in-the-Loop
body: Codec-Adaptive TriPlane Radiance Fields (CATRF) is a compression framework for plane-factorized radiance fields that optimizes neural features directly in the decoded space of a standard video or image codec. It solves the problem of severe rendering degradation at low bitrates by integrating a real codec round-trip (JPEG, VP9, HEVC, or AV1) into the training loop via a Straight-Through Estimator (STE). Unlike Codec-Agnostic (CA) methods that compress features after training, or Learned-Codec-in-the-Loop (LCL) methods that require shipping scene-specific neural decoder parameters, CATRF adapts features to real codec distortions without introducing any learned codec parameters or entropy models. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A pre-trained plane-factorized radiance field backbone (TensoRF for static scenes, DVGO for dynamic scenes). Output: A compressed bitstream of the radiance field features decodable by standard codecs, and the ability to render the scene from this compressed representation. Data Structures: The method operates on plane-factorized radiance fields. The scene is represented by three orthogonal feature planes P = \{P{xy}, P{xz}, P{yz}\} and a 3D density grid D. Each feature plane P{ax} (where ax \in \{xy, xz, yz\}) has layout P{ax} \in \mathbb{R}^{C \times H \times W}, where C is the channel dimension, and H, W are height and width. The density grid is D \in \mathbb{R}^{Dy \times Dx \times Dz}. These tensors are quantized and packed into 2D canvases (images with integer pixel values) suitable for standard codecs. The default packing format is FlattenGray, which avoids cross-channel mixing to reduce codec artifact sensitivity. Quantization uses AbsMax quantization by default. Channelwise quantization is avoided as it increases bitrate by ~45x. Parameters: Codec: Off-the-shelf codecs (JPEG, VP9, HEVC, AV1). Total-variation regularization weight (\lambda{tv}): Controls the trade-off between codec compatibility and high-frequency detail preservation. Default value: 5 \times 10^{-5}. Cache refresh interval (M): The number of training steps before the cached decoded planes are refreshed. Default value: 128. Algorithm Steps: The method employs a two-stage pipeline: 1. Backbone Training: Train the vanilla backbone (TensoRF for static, DVGO for dynamic) for each scene or video segment to convergence. 2. SCL Finetuning: Finetune the radiance fields using the Standard-Codec-in-the-Loop (SCL) framework under a fixed codec configuration. During the SCL finetuning phase, each training step proceeds as follows: 1. Quantize and Pack: Quantize the multi-channel appearance planes and density grid into 2D canvases using AbsMax quantization and FlattenGray packing. 2. Codec Round-Trip: Encode the canvases using the selected standard codec, then decode them to obtain reconstructed features. 3. Unpack and Dequantize: Unpack the decoded canvases back into feature planes and dequantize them. 4. Render and Loss: Render the radiance fields from the decoded features to compute the reconstruction loss. 5. Regularization: Apply spatial total-variation and temporal-consistency regularization terms to encourage smoother, codec-friendly patterns. The total loss includes the reconstruction loss and \lambda{tv} \times \text{TV}(P). 6. Backpropagation: Pass gradients across the entire codec round-trip using a Straight-Through Estimator (STE). The codec is treated as a black box with an identity gradient (i.e., \frac{\partial L}{\partial \text{Input}} = \frac{\partial L}{\partial \text{Output}}). 7. Caching: Cache the decoded planes across training steps to avoid per-minibatch codec round trips. The cache is refreshed every M steps. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import torch import torch.nn as nn import numpy as np class StraightThroughCodec(nn.Module): """ A module that performs a codec round-trip and passes gradients through it using a Straight-Through Estimator (STE). """ def forward(self, inputtensor): # Forward pass: encode then decode bitstream = codecencode(inputtensor) outputtensor = codecdecode(bitstream) # STE: Gradient flows as if output == input return outputtensor class CATRF: def init(self, backbone, codecconfig, lambdatv=5e-5, cacherefreshinterval=128): self.backbone = backbone # TensoRF or DVGO self.codec = StraightThroughCodec() self.lambdatv = lambdatv self.cacherefreshinterval = cacherefreshinterval self.stepcount = 0 self.cacheddecodedplanes = None self.cachedbitstream = None # Packing and Quantization helpers self.packingformat = "FlattenGray" self.quantization = "AbsMax" def quantizeandpack(self, planes, densitygrid): """ Quantize feature planes and density grid into 2D canvases. Uses AbsMax quantization and FlattenGray packing. """ # FlattenGray: Flatten channels and spatial dims into 2D image-like structure # AbsMax: Scale each plane by its absolute maximum value to [0, 255] range (uint8) canvases = [] for plane in planes: # plane shape: (C, H, W) absmax = plane.abs().max() if absmax == 0: absmax = 1e-8 normalized = plane / absmax # Pack into 2D canvas (implementation detail of FlattenGray) canvas = packflattengray(normalized) canvases.append(canvas) # Pack density grid similarly if needed, or handle separately # For simplicity, assuming density is packed into a canvas too densitycanvas = packdensitygrid(densitygrid) canvases.append(densitycanvas) return canvases def unpackanddequantize(self, decodedcanvases): """ Unpack decoded canvases back to feature planes and dequantize. """ planes = [] for i, canvas in enumerate(decodedcanvases[:-1]): # Last one is density # Unpack FlattenGray normalized = unpackflattengray(canvas) # Dequantize: multiply back by absmax (stored or recomputed) # Note: In practice, absmax needs to be transmitted or stored. # For the purpose of the loop, we assume the codec preserves the structure # and we recover the scale factor. # In a real implementation, the quantization scale factors must be # stored in the bitstream or derived from the decoded data. # Here we assume a simplified recovery. plane = normalized self.absmaxcache[i] planes.append(plane) densitygrid = unpackdensitygrid(decodedcanvases[-1]) return planes, densitygrid def computetvregularization(self, planes): """ Compute spatial total variation regularization. """ tvloss = 0.0 for plane in planes: # plane shape: (C, H, W) # TV = sum(|dx| + |dy|) dx = plane[:,:, 1:] - plane[:,:,:-1] dy = plane[:, 1:,:] - plane[:,:-1,:] tvloss += dx.abs().mean() + dy.abs().mean() return tvloss def trainstep(self, rays, gtimages): """ One training step. """ # 1. Get current planes from backbone planes, densitygrid = self.backbone.getplanesanddensity() # 2. Check cache refreshcache = False if self.cacheddecodedplanes is None or self.stepcount % self.cacherefreshinterval == 0: refreshcache = True if refreshcache: # Quantize and Pack canvases = self.quantizeandpack(planes, densitygrid) # Codec Round-Trip bitstream = codecencode(canvases) decodedcanvases = codecdecode(bitstream) # Unpack and Dequantize decodedplanes, decodeddensity = self.unpackanddequantize(decodedcanvases) # Cache results self.cacheddecodedplanes = decodedplanes self.cacheddensity = decodeddensity self.cachedbitstream = bitstream # Store absmax for dequantization recovery # In practice, this requires storing metadata. # For the loop, we assume the backbone can re-quantize or we store scales. # Here we assume the decoded planes are already in the correct scale # relative to the backbone's expected input range, or we adjust. # The paper states "dequantize the reconstructed features", implying # the codec operates on quantized values. We must recover the scale. # Let's assume we stored the scales during packing. self.absmaxcache = [p.abs().max().item() for p in planes] # Use cached decoded planes for rendering # Note: The backbone's internal planes are not used for rendering in this step, # only for the next packing step. planestorender = self.cacheddecodedplanes densitytorender = self.cacheddensity # 3. Render renderedimages = self.backbone.render(planestorender, densitytorender, rays) # 4. Compute Loss reconstructionloss = mseloss(renderedimages, gtimages) tvloss = self.computetvregularization(planestorender) totalloss = reconstructionloss + self.lambdatv tvloss # 5. Backpropagate totalloss.backward() self.stepcount += 1 return totalloss.item() def optimize(self, dataloader, epochs): """ Two-stage optimization. Stage 1: Train backbone to convergence. Stage 2: Finetune with SCL. """ # Stage 1 self.backbone.traintoconvergence(dataloader) # Stage 2 for epoch in range(epochs): for rays, gtimages in dataloader: self.trainstep(rays, gtimages) self.optimizer.step() self.optimizer.zerograd() Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Codec Sensitivity: Feature planes are highly sensitive to codec distortions (quantization, block transforms, in-loop filtering). Training without codec exposure (Codec-Agnostic) causes severe rendering degradation at low bitrates. Bitrate vs. Quality: Standard codecs are sensitive to artifacts. CATRF adapts to various quality levels, operating at lower bitrates with modest detail loss or higher bitrates for sharper edges. Quantization Choice: Channelwise quantization increases bitrate by ~45x and is unsuitable for streaming. FlattenGray with AbsMax quantization is the default. Cache Refresh: The cache refresh interval M balances training time and bitrate. M=128 is the empirical default. Time and Memory Complexity: The memory footprint is dominated by the encoded feature planes. On the NeRF Synthetic dataset, CATRF uses 70.04 MB total, with 69.95 MB for encoded feature planes, 0.05 MB for feature vectors, and 0.04 MB for hash embeddings. It requires 0 MB for neural codec parameters, entropy model parameters, anchor features, and MLPs. Measured Performance: Static Scenes: CATRF-JPEG achieves a 43% BD-rate reduction over state-of-the-art LCL compression methods. On NeRF Synthetic, it achieves a 23% bitrate reduction over CNC at matched PSNR. On Tanks and Temples, it achieves a 43% bitrate saving over CNC. Dynamic Scenes: CATRF achieves BD-rate reductions of 40.5% (AV1), 63.3% (HEVC), and 51.8% (VP9) compared to TeTriRF on the N3D dataset. It achieves 17% bitrate savings over HAC++ and 39% BD-rate reduction over GIFStream. Decoding Speed: CATRF-HEVC reconstructs radiance fields at 138 FPS, compared to 2.94 FPS for GIFStream and 0.35 FPS for HAC++. This is because CATRF reconstruction is neural-free, relying only on standard-codec decoding. Strengths: No need to transmit scene-specific decoding parameters (unlike LCL). Neural-free reconstruction (unlike 3DGS methods). High decoding throughput. Limitations: Requires a two-stage training process. Relies on the quality of the underlying backbone (TensoRF/DVGO). When to Use: Volumetric content delivery, free-viewpoint video streaming, 3D video playback, and telepresence. CATRF was introduced as the first standard-codec-in-the-loop (SCL) training framework for plane-factorized radiance fields. It overturns the prevailing assumption that the codec must be differentiable, instead treating the real codec round trip as a black box and using STE to pass gradients. It differs from Learned-Codec-in-the-Loop (LCL) methods like NeRFCodec and CNC, which require learned neural codecs and entropy models, and from Codec-Agnostic (CA) methods that compress features after training. name: TensoRF with Density-Shift Fix
head: Corrected TensoRF, Corrected TensoRF Density Parameterization, Density shift correction, Novelty I, TensoRF density shift correction
body: TensoRF with Density-Shift Fix is a parameter correction for the TensoRF [13296-tensorf-decomposition-models.md] density parameterization that prevents the density field from collapsing to zero during training. It replaces the default configuration (\Delta = -10, s = 25) which causes degenerate attenuation geometry and zero gradient flow, with a corrected configuration (\Delta = 0, s = 1) that stabilizes volumetric reconstruction and thresholding. Unlike the default TensoRF which may achieve high photometric fidelity (PSNR 32.0 dB) but unstable geometry, this fix yields stable volumetric errors across adjacent percentiles. Inputs: TensoRF model parameters \theta (including feature planes/lines Pi, Li and MLP weights). Camera poses and intrinsics. Target images I. Outputs: Corrected volumetric density field \sigma(x). Optimized model parameters \theta. Data Structures: TensoRF Model: Uses Vector-Matrix (VM) decomposition. Feature planes Pi (size: 48 \times 48 \times 48 per axis, 27-dim features). Feature lines Li (size: 16 per axis, VM rank-16). MLP: 2 \times 128 hidden units, ReLU activation, 6 frequencies. Scene AABB: x \in [-2.5, 3.5], y \in [-1.5, 1.5], z \in [-2.0, 1.5]. Voxel grid: 64^3 voxels (\approx 3.75 mm per voxel). Parameters: \Delta (density shift): Corrected value is 0 (Default is -10). s (distance scale): Corrected value is 1 (Default is 25). \lambda1 (sparsity weight): 1 \times 10^{-4}. \lambda2 (TV regularization weight): 1 \times 10^{-5}. Formulas: The corrected density \sigma(x) at position x is computed as: \sigma(x) = \text{ReLU}(f\theta(x) + \Delta) \cdot s where f\theta(x) is the raw output of the TensoRF density network. With the correction (\Delta=0, s=1): \sigma(x) = \text{ReLU}(f\theta(x)) The total loss function is: \mathcal{L} = \mathcal{L}{\text{photo}} + \lambda1 \mathcal{L}{\text{sparse}} + \lambda2 \mathcal{L}{\text{TV}} where \mathcal{L}{\text{photo}} = \text{MSE}(\hat{I}, I), \mathcal{L}{\text{sparse}} is an \ell1 penalty on density, and \mathcal{L}{\text{TV}} is total variation regularization on density planes: \mathcal{L}{\text{TV}} = \sumi \left( \|\Deltah Pi\|1 + \|\Deltav Pi\|1 \right) where \Deltah, \Deltav are horizontal and vertical finite differences. Steps: 1. Initialize TensoRF model parameters \theta using Kaiming initialization. This yields f\theta(x) \in [-c, c] where c \approx 1. 2. Set density shift \Delta = 0 and scale s = 1 in the TensoRF configuration. 3. Render views using the corrected density parameterization \sigma(x) = \text{ReLU}(f\theta(x)). 4. Compute photometric loss \mathcal{L}{\text{photo}}, sparsity loss \mathcal{L}{\text{sparse}}, and total variation loss \mathcal{L}{\text{TV}}. 5. Update parameters \theta via gradient descent to minimize \mathcal{L}. 6. After training, perform a threshold sweep on the resulting density field for volumetric extraction (e.g., Marching Cubes). Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def correctedtensorfdensity(fthetax, delta=0, s=1): """ Computes the corrected density for TensoRF. Args: fthetax: Raw output of the TensoRF density network (tensor). delta: Density shift scalar. Default 0. s: Distance scale scalar. Default 1. Returns: sigma: Corrected density field (tensor). """ # Apply density shift and scale shifted = fthetax + delta scaled = shifted s # Apply ReLU activation sigma = max(scaled, 0) return sigma def traincorrectedtensorf(model, images, poses, lambda1=1e-4, lambda2=1e-5, iterations=3000): """ Trains TensoRF with the density-shift fix. Args: model: TensoRF model instance. images: Target images. poses: Camera poses. lambda1: Sparsity regularization weight. lambda2: Total variation regularization weight. iterations: Number of training steps. """ # Ensure corrected parameters are set model.setdensityparams(delta=0, s=1) for i in range(iterations): # Render current view renderedimages = model.render(poses) # Compute photometric loss lphoto = mseloss(renderedimages, images) # Compute sparsity loss (L1 on density) densityfield = model.getdensityfield() lsparse = l1norm(densityfield) # Compute Total Variation loss on density planes ltv = computetotalvariation(model.densityplanes) # Total loss loss = lphoto + lambda1 lsparse + lambda2 ltv # Backpropagate and update loss.backward() model.optimizer.step() model.optimizer.zerograd() # Optional: Log metrics if i % 100 == 0: print(f"Iter {i}: Loss={loss.item()}, PSNR={psnr(renderedimages, images)}") return model Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Dead-Zone Failure: Using the default \Delta = -10 with Kaiming initialization (f\theta(x) \in [-1, 1]) results in f\theta(x) + \Delta \in [-11, -9]. The ReLU output is zero, gradients are zero, and density remains zero throughout training. Photometric vs. Geometric Fidelity: The default parameterization may achieve high PSNR (32.0 dB) because the appearance MLP can still update, but the density field remains uniformly zero, leading to unstable marching cubes results (e.g., 204% error at p=97). Threshold Sensitivity: The corrected version stabilizes errors across adjacent percentiles (e.g., 13.8% at p=99 and 14.3% at p=97 on patient LIDC-IDRI-0001), confirming that the parameterization is a prerequisite for downstream reconstruction quality. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Measured Performance: On patient LIDC-IDRI-0001, the corrected method achieves 13.8% error at one percentile and 14.3% at an adjacent percentile. The default method achieves 8.0% error at p=99 but 204% at p=97. Strengths: Restores gradient flow immediately; stabilizes volumetric reconstruction; robust to variation in initialization range c. Limitations: May reduce photometric fidelity (PSNR) compared to the default configuration which can "learn" to reproduce pixel intensities via the appearance branch despite zero density. When to Use: When stable volumetric extraction (e.g., for medical nodule volumetry) is required, and the default TensoRF density collapse is observed. When Not to Use: When only photometric rendering quality is needed and geometric consistency is not critical. Origin: Identified in "Sparse-View Lung Nodule Volumetry from Digitally Reconstructed Radiographs via AReT: Anatomy-Regularized TensoRF". History: The default TensoRF parameterization (\Delta = -10, s = 25) was found to cause a critical failure mode where density collapses to zero due to the interaction with Kaiming initialization. The fix (\Delta = 0, s = 1) was proposed as "Novelty I" in this work. Usage: Applied in medical imaging, specifically for lung nodule volumetry from sparse-view X-ray projections (LIDC-IDRI dataset). Sparse-View Lung Nodule Volumetry from Digitally Reconstructed Radiographs via AReT: Anatomy-Regularized TensoRF, https://doi.org/10.48550/arxiv.2606.02639, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial)

name: Joint Optimization of Camera Pose and Decomposed Low-Rank Tensorial Radiance Fields
head: Joint TensoRF
body: Joint TensoRF is a method for the joint refinement of camera poses and scene geometry represented by decomposed low-rank tensors, using only 2D image supervision. It solves the problem that naive joint optimization on voxel-based radiance fields leads to suboptimal solutions because voxel-based methods lack the spectral bias inherent in MLPs, causing them to overemphasize sharp edges and get trapped in local optima. Unlike TensoRF, which assumes known camera poses, this method integrates efficient spectral filtering into the training loop to enable stable pose optimization. Inputs: A set of 2D images with initial camera poses and intrinsics; a decomposed low-rank tensor representation of the radiance field. Outputs: Refined camera poses and an optimized radiance field. Data Structures: The scene is represented by decomposed low-rank tensors. For density \sigma and color features \mathbf{c}, the method uses mode vectors and matrices. The core mechanism applies convolutional Gaussian filters on these fields to control the frequency spectrum during training. Algorithm Steps: 1. Initialization: Initialize the decomposed low-rank tensor factors and camera poses. 2. Spectral Filtering (Coarse-to-Fine): Apply convolutional Gaussian filters to both the 2D supervision images and the 3D radiance fields to enable a coarse-to-fine training schedule. Efficient 3D Convolution: Leverage the decomposition property of the low-rank tensor to achieve an equivalent effect to brute-force 3D convolution with minimal computational overhead. The convolution is applied to the individual mode vectors and matrices. Filter Parameters: Use Gaussian kernels with randomly scaled parameters during training to improve robustness. 3. Rendering: Render the filtered 2D images from the current camera poses using differentiable volume rendering. 4. Loss Computation: Compute the loss between the rendered images and the ground truth 2D images. Smoothed 2D Supervision: Apply smoothing to the supervision images to reduce high-frequency noise that could destabilize pose optimization. Edge-Guided Loss Mask: Use an edge-guided loss mask to focus optimization on structural details, improving stability. 5. Optimization: Update both the camera poses and the tensor factors using gradient descent. The joint optimization is performed for 50,000 iterations. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math import random def applygaussian2d(image, kernelsize, sigma): """Apply 2D Gaussian filter for smoothed supervision.""" kernel = [math.exp(-0.5 ((i - kernelsize//2)2) / sigma2) for i in range(kernelsize)] blurred = [] for row in image: blurredrow = [] for j in range(len(row)): acc = sum(row[max(0, j-kernelsize//2):min(len(row), j+kernelsize//2+1)] kernel[max(0, kernelsize//2-j):min(len(kernel), kernelsize//2+1-j)]) blurredrow.append(acc) blurred.append(blurredrow) return blurred def applygaussian3dseparable(factors, kernelsize, sigma): """Leverage decomposition to apply 3D Gaussian filter efficiently.""" kernel = [math.exp(-0.5 ((i - kernelsize//2)2) / sigma2) for i in range(kernelsize)] filteredfactors = [] for factor in factors: if len(factor.shape) == 1: filteredfactors.append([sum(factor[max(0, i-kernelsize//2):min(len(factor), i+kernelsize//2+1)] kernel[max(0, kernelsize//2-i):min(len(kernel), kernelsize//2+1-i)] for i in range(len(factor)))]) else: filteredfactors.append([[sum(row[max(0, j-kernelsize//2):min(len(row), j+kernelsize//2+1)] kernel[max(0, kernelsize//2-j):min(len(kernel), kernelsize//2+1-j)] for j in range(len(row))) for row in factor]]) return filteredfactors def computeedgemask(image): """Generate edge-guided loss mask.""" return [[1.0 if abs(image[i][j] - image[i][j+1]) > 0.1 else 0.0 for j in range(len(image[0])-1)] for i in range(len(image))] def volumerender(factors, pose): """Differentiable volume rendering using interpolated tensor factors.""" return [sum(f p for f, p in zip(factors, pose)) / len(factors)] def jointoptimization(images, initialposes, initialfactors, numiterations=50000): poses = initialposes factors = initialfactors lr = 0.01 # Standard learning rate kernelsize = 3 basesigma = 1.0 for step in range(numiterations): # 1. Spectral Filtering & Smoothed Supervision currentsigma = basesigma (0.5 + 0.5 random.random()) filteredimages = [applygaussian2d(img, kernelsize, currentsigma) for img in images] # 2. Efficient 3D Convolution on Tensor Factors filteredfactors = applygaussian3dseparable(factors, kernelsize, currentsigma) # 3. Rendering renderedimages = [volumerender(filteredfactors, pose) for pose in poses] # 4. Loss Computation with Edge-Guided Mask totalloss = 0.0 for rendered, gt in zip(renderedimages, filteredimages): mask = computeedgemask(gt) totalloss += sum((r - g)2 for r, g in zip(rendered, gt)) / len(rendered) # 5. Optimization gradsposes = [lr random.random() for in poses] # Gradient computation placeholder gradsfactors = [lr random.random() for in factors] poses = [p - g for p, g in zip(poses, gradsposes)] factors = [f - g for f, g in zip(factors, gradsfactors)] return poses, factors Parameters: Training iterations: 50,000. Previous methods typically require 200,000 iterations. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Local Optima: Naive joint optimization on voxel-based NeRFs easily leads to suboptimal solutions due to the lack of spectral bias, which causes the model to overemphasize sharp edges. The proposed Gaussian filtering and coarse-to-fine schedule are critical to avoid this. Precision: The efficiency relies on the decomposition property; if the rank is too high, the computational overhead of the "efficient" convolution may approach that of brute-force 3D convolution. Time Complexity: The method reduces training time by 25% compared to previous MLP-based methods. This is attributed to the efficient spectral filtering algorithm which requires only a single reusable voxel grid. Memory Complexity: Inherits the low memory usage of decomposed low-rank tensors (TensoRF). Performance: Achieves superior performance in novel view synthesis and rapid convergence. Strengths: Robust joint pose refinement; efficient computation via separable component-wise convolution; reduced training iterations (50k vs 200k). Limitations: Requires careful tuning of filter parameters and edge-guided masks for stability. Joint TensoRF was proposed by Bo-Yu Cheng, Wei-Chen Chiu, and Yu-Lun Liu from National Yang Ming Chiao Tung University. It addresses the limitations of voxel-based NeRFs in joint pose optimization, which lack the spectral bias of MLPs. The method builds on the TensoRF framework [3026-tensorf.md] and incorporates techniques from TensoRF Reconstruction Optimization for upsampling. The source code is available at https://github.com/Nemo1999/Joint-TensoRF. name: Strivec Fast Variant
head: Multi(0.6, 0.3) with TopK=2
body: The Strivec Fast Variant is a computationally optimized configuration of the Strivec method, designed to accelerate training and inference while maintaining competitive rendering quality. It achieves this by reducing the number of multi-scale levels and the number of top-k candidates considered during ray sampling. It serves as a faster alternative to the standard Strivec configuration, offering a speed profile closer to Vector-Matrix (VM) decomposition while outperforming Canonical Polyadic (CP) decomposition in efficiency. Builds on Tensorial and Low-Rank Representations. The method builds on the shared principles of Tensorial and Low-Rank Representations, specifically using sparse tri-vector radiance fields. The "Fast Variant" is defined strictly by its hyperparameters rather than a change in the underlying mathematical formulation of the radiance field. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Camera poses, image observations, and the specified hyperparameters (scales, TopK). Output: Rendered images and optimized tensor factors. Data Structures: The radiance field is represented using a multi-scale tri-vector structure. The specific configuration for the Fast Variant is: Number of Scales: 2. Scale Lengths: The tensor lengths for the two scales are 0.6 and 0.3. TopK: The number of top-k candidates selected per sample point along a ray is 2. Formulas: Not given in the sources. Steps: 1. Initialization: Initialize the tri-vector tensor factors for the two scales with lengths 0.6 and 0.3 as an ablation variant of the default 3-scale configuration. 2. Ray Sampling: For each ray, sample points along the path. 3. Sparse Selection: For each sample point, identify the relevant tensor components by selecting only the top 2 candidates (TopK=2) based on their relevance or magnitude. 4. Interpolation and Rendering: Interpolate the values from the selected tensor components to compute density and color, then perform volume rendering. 5. Optimization: Update the tensor factors using gradient descent, applying regularization as per the parent method's principles. Parameters: numscales: 2. scalelengths: [0.6, 0.3]. topk: 2. Note: The standard Strivec model uses 3 scales (0.15, 0.3, 0.6) and TopK=4. The Fast Variant reduces these to accelerate computation. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Reducing TopK from 4 to 2 reduces the computational load significantly but may slightly impact the ability to capture high-frequency details if the scene is complex. Reducing scales from 3 to 2 simplifies the multi-resolution hierarchy, which may affect the smoothness of the rendered output compared to the 3-scale variant. This is the standard multi-scale configuration of Strivec, serving as the baseline from which the Fast Variant is derived. It uses 3 scales with tensor lengths of 0.15, 0.3, and 0.6. It typically employs 24 appearance components by default. This configuration provides more smoothness and better rendering quality than single-scale counterparts, consistent with findings in iNGP. A multi-scale model with 24 components outperforms a single-scale model with more parameters. The benefit of adding more components becomes marginal when the number reaches 48. Time and Memory Complexity: The Fast Variant reduces computation by lowering the number of tensor ranks and the number of TopK candidates per sample point. This results in faster training and inference times compared to the standard Strivec configuration and TensoRF-CP. Measured Performance: Evaluated on the NeRF Synthetic dataset: Training Time: 959 seconds. Inference Time: 1.67 seconds per iteration. Parameters: 6.20 Million. PSNR: 33.09. Comparison: vs. TensoRF-CP: Faster training (959s vs 1914s), faster inference (1.67s/it vs 2.01s/it), more parameters (6.20M vs 0.98M), but higher PSNR (33.09 vs 31.56). vs. TensoRF-VM: Similar training time (959s vs 915s), slightly slower inference (1.67s/it vs 1.60s/it), significantly fewer parameters (6.20M vs 17.95M), and comparable PSNR (33.09 vs 33.14). Strengths and Limitations: Strengths: Achieves a balance between speed and quality. It becomes faster than CP and close to VM in speed, while maintaining competitive quality. It improves quality, training time, and compactness together with proper hyper-parameters. Limitations: The reduction in scales and TopK may limit the model's capacity to learn very high-frequency details compared to the full 3-scale, TopK=4 configuration. The Strivec method (Sparse Tri-Vector Radiance Fields) was introduced in 2023. The Fast Variant is an ablation study result from the same work, demonstrating that reducing the number of scales and TopK candidates accelerates the method without significant quality loss. The method is part of the broader family of tensorial and low-rank representations for neural radiance fields. name: HexPlane
body: HexPlane is an explicit representation for dynamic 3D scenes that decomposes a 4D spacetime grid into six learned feature planes spanning pairs of coordinate axes (e.g., XY, ZT). It solves the memory and data-sparsity challenges of dynamic novel view synthesis by replacing implicit MLPs with a factorized structure that shares information across timesteps, achieving training speeds over 100× faster than implicit baselines like DyNeRF while matching image quality. Unlike TensoRF which uses vector-matrix decomposition for static 3D volumes, HexPlane extends this to 4D by pairing spatial planes with spatio-temporal planes to capture entangled space-time dynamics. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: A set of posed images with timestamps \{(Ik, \mathbf{c}k, tk)\}, where \mathbf{c}k is the camera pose and tk is the time. Outputs: A radiance field model capable of rendering novel views at arbitrary poses and times. Data Structures: The representation consists of two HexPlanes (one for opacity, one for appearance features) and a small MLP. 1. HexPlane: Defined by six feature planes (matrices) and three fusion matrices. Six planes: \mathbf{M}^{XY}, \mathbf{M}^{XZ}, \mathbf{M}^{YZ} (spatial) and \mathbf{M}^{XT}, \mathbf{M}^{YT}, \mathbf{M}^{ZT} (spatio-temporal). Dimensions: \mathbf{M}^{XY} \in \mathbb{R}^{Nx \times Ny}, \mathbf{M}^{XT} \in \mathbb{R}^{Nx \times Nt}, etc. Nx, Ny, Nz are spatial resolutions; Nt is temporal resolution. Fusion Matrices: \mathbf{V}^{R1 F}, \mathbf{V}^{R2 F}, \mathbf{V}^{R3 F} where Ri is the rank and F is the feature dimension. 2. MLP: A tiny multi-layer perceptron taking appearance features, position, and view direction to output RGB color. 3. Emptiness Voxel: A tiny 3D voxel grid indicating empty regions, computed by taking the maximum opacity across all time steps. Query Function: For a 4D point (x, y, z, t), the feature vector \mathbf{f} \in \mathbb{R}^F is computed by projecting the point onto the six planes, aggregating the six resulting feature vectors, and multiplying by the fusion matrices. The formula is: D(x, y, z, t) = (\mathbf{P}{xy\bullet}^{XYR1} \odot \mathbf{P}{xt\bullet}^{ZTR1}) \mathbf{V}^{R1F} + (\mathbf{P}{xz\bullet}^{XZR2} \odot \mathbf{P}{yt\bullet}^{YTR2}) \mathbf{V}^{R2F} + (\mathbf{P}{yz\bullet}^{YZR3} \odot \mathbf{P}{xt\bullet}^{XTR3}) \mathbf{V}^{R3F} Where: \mathbf{P}{xy\bullet}^{XYR1} is a vector of size R1 obtained by bilinearly interpolating the plane \mathbf{M}^{XY} at (x,y). \mathbf{P}{xt\bullet}^{ZTR1} is a vector of size R1 obtained by bilinearly interpolating the plane \mathbf{M}^{ZT} at (z,t). \odot denotes element-wise multiplication. \mathbf{V}^{R1F} is a matrix of size R1 \times F. Training Pipeline: 1. Initialization: Start with low spatial resolution (e.g., 32^3 or 64^3). 2. Coarse-to-Fine: Gradually upsample the grid resolution at specific iterations (e.g., doubling at 70k, 140k, 210k iterations for Plenoptic Video). 3. Emptiness Voxel Update: Periodically compute the emptiness voxel by evaluating opacities across time and taking the maximum. 4. Sampling: Use importance sampling (e.g., global-median-based or temporal-difference-based) to sample points along rays. 5. Rendering: Perform differentiable volume rendering using the queried opacity and color. 6. Loss: Minimize photometric loss plus regularization: \mathcal{L} = \frac{1}{|\mathcal{R}|} \sum{\mathbf{r} \in \mathcal{R}} \|C(\mathbf{r}) - \hat{C}(\mathbf{r})\|2^2 + \lambda{reg} \mathcal{L}{reg} Where \mathcal{L}{reg} includes Total Variation (TV) loss on planes and depth smooth loss. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import numpy as np def bilinearinterpolate(grid, u, v): """ Perform bilinear interpolation on a 2D grid. grid: shape (H, W) u, v: float coordinates in [0, 1] Returns: interpolated value """ h, w = grid.shape uidx = u (w - 1) vidx = v (h - 1) u0 = int(np.floor(uidx)) v0 = int(np.floor(vidx)) u1 = np.clip(u0 + 1, 0, w - 1) v1 = np.clip(v0 + 1, 0, h - 1) u0 = np.clip(u0, 0, w - 1) v0 = np.clip(v0, 0, h - 1) wu = uidx - u0 wv = vidx - v0 val = (1 - wu) (1 - wv) grid[v0, u0] + \ (1 - wu) wv grid[v1, u0] + \ wu (1 - wv) grid[v0, u1] + \ wu wv grid[v1, u1] return val def queryhexplane(x, y, z, t, planes, fusionmatrices): """ Query the HexPlane representation for a 4D point. x, y, z, t: float coordinates in [0, 1] planes: dict containing PXY, PXZ, PYZ, PXT, PYT, PZT Each tensor has shape (Dim1, Dim2, Ri) fusionmatrices: list of [V1, V2, V3] where Vi is shape (Ri, F) Returns: feature vector of shape (F,) """ # Term 1: XY and ZT planes vecxy = np.array([bilinearinterpolate(planes['PXY'][:,:,r], x, y) for r in range(planes['PXY'].shape[2])]) veczt = np.array([bilinearinterpolate(planes['PZT'][:,:,r], z, t) for r in range(planes['PZT'].shape[2])]) fused1 = vecxy veczt term1 = fused1 @ fusionmatrices[0] # Term 2: XZ and YT planes vecxz = np.array([bilinearinterpolate(planes['PXZ'][:,:,r], x, z) for r in range(planes['PXZ'].shape[2])]) vecyt = np.array([bilinearinterpolate(planes['PYT'][:,:,r], y, t) for r in range(planes['PYT'].shape[2])]) fused2 = vecxz vecyt term2 = fused2 @ fusionmatrices[1] # Term 3: YZ and XT planes vecyz = np.array([bilinearinterpolate(planes['PYZ'][:,:,r], y, z) for r in range(planes['PYZ'].shape[2])]) vecxt = np.array([bilinearinterpolate(planes['PXT'][:,:,r], x, t) for r in range(planes['PXT'].shape[2])]) fused3 = vecyz vecxt term3 = fused3 @ fusionmatrices[2] return term1 + term2 + term3 def samplepointsalongray(origin, direction, nsamples, tnear=0.0, tfar=1.0): """ Linearly sample points along a ray. Standard implementation. """ tvals = np.linspace(tnear, tfar, nsamples) points = origin + tvals[:, np.newaxis] direction return points def mlpdecoder(features, point, viewdir): """Tiny MLP decoder.""" x = np.concatenate([features, point, viewdir]) h = np.maximum(0, x @ np.ones((x.shape[0], 16))) return h @ np.ones((16, 3)) def renderray(rayorigin, raydirection, t, opacityplanes, opacityfusion, appearanceplanes, appearancefusion, nsamples): """ Volume render a single ray. """ points = samplepointsalongray(rayorigin, raydirection, nsamples) opacities = [] appearances = [] for p in points: x, y, z = p opfeat = queryhexplane(x, y, z, t, opacityplanes, opacityfusion) sigma = opfeat[0] opacities.append(sigma) if sigma > 0.1: apfeat = queryhexplane(x, y, z, t, appearanceplanes, appearancefusion) appearances.append(apfeat) else: appearances.append(np.zeros(3)) colors = [] for i, p in enumerate(points): if len(appearances) > i and np.linalg.norm(appearances[i]) > 0: color = mlpdecoder(appearances[i], p, raydirection) colors.append(color) else: colors.append(np.zeros(3)) # Standard volume rendering compositing alphas = 1.0 - np.exp(np.array(opacities)) transmittance = np.cumprod(1.0 - alphas) weights = alphas np.concatenate([[1.0], transmittance[:-1]]) finalcolor = np.sum(np.array(colors) weights[:, np.newaxis], axis=0) return finalcolor Parameters: Spatial Resolution (N): Typically 128^3 to 512^3. Temporal Resolution (T): Typically 32 to 300. Rank (R): Number of basis functions. Typical values: 8, 12, 16, 24, 48, 96. Larger R improves quality but increases memory and computation; too large causes overfitting. Plenoptic Video Appearance: R1=48, R2=24, R3=24. Plenoptic Video Opacity: R1=24, R2=12, R3=12. D-NeRF Appearance: R1=R2=R3=48. D-NeRF Opacity: R1=R2=R3=24. Learning Rate: 0.02 for feature planes, 0.001 for MLP/VRF. Optimizer: Adam (\beta1=0.9, \beta2=0.99). Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Unbounded Scenes: HexPlane is limited to bounded scenes because grid sampling fails for out-of-boundary points. Fast Motion: Degraded results occur when objects move too fast or observations are too sparse. Color Jittering: Explicit representations are prone to artifacts; strong regularization (TV loss) is required. NDC Artifacts: Using Normalized Device Coordinates (NDC) assumes bounded x,y and can cause artifacts at extreme views. A dynamic scene representation consisting of a series of feature volumes, one for each gear level G, instead of a unified 4D volume. Each gear describes regions of a certain scale of motion, while purely spatial features are shared. The feature vector for gear G at space-time coordinate (x,t) is computed as f^G(x, t) = B1(h1(x, y) \odot k^G1(z, t)) + B2(h2(x, z) \odot k^G2(y, t)) + B3(h3(y, z) \odot k^G3(x, t)), where hj are shared spatial embedding functions, k^Gj are gear-specific spatio-temporal embeddings, and Bj are shared linear transforms. A continuous gear score is computed via g(x, t) = 1^\top (h'1(x, y) \odot k'1(z, t)) + 1^\top (h'2(x, z) \odot k'2(y, t)) + 1^\top (h'3(y, z) \odot k'3(x, t)). Typical parameters are M=32 for the spatio-temporal embedding dimension and N{\text{gear}}=4 gear levels. Memory Complexity: Reduced from O(N^3 T F) to O(N^2 R + N T R + R F). For N=512, T=32, F=3, a naive 4D volume requires 48GB, while HexPlane requires only ~200MB. Time Complexity: Querying requires six bilinear interpolations and vector-matrix products, making it significantly faster than MLP-based methods. Performance: On the Plenoptic Video dataset, HexPlane achieves 29.47 PSNR in 12 GPU hours (112× speedup over DyNeRF). With fewer iterations (100k), it achieves 29.26 PSNR in 2 GPU hours (672× speedup). On D-NeRF, it achieves 31.04 PSNR in 11 minutes. Strengths: High efficiency, low memory footprint, no need for deformation fields, robust to various fusion mechanisms and coordinate systems. Limitations: Limited to bounded scenes (unless spherical coordinates are used), sensitive to sparse observations and fast motion, requires strong regularization to avoid artifacts. HexPlane was introduced by Ang Cao and Justin Johnson from the University of Michigan, Ann Arbor, in January 2023. It was developed to address the limitations of implicit representations (like T-NeRF and DyNeRF) which are slow due to numerous MLP evaluations and struggle with memory usage for dynamic scenes. The method builds on the principles of tensor decomposition used in TensoRF but adapts them for 4D spacetime by using paired spatial and spatio-temporal feature planes.
