name: Few TensoRF
body: Few TensoRF is a 3D reconstruction framework that combines the efficient tensor-based representation of TensoRF with frequency-driven regularization from FreeNeRF to improve stability and reconstruction quality under sparse input views. It addresses the problem of high-frequency artifacts and bias that occur when TensoRF converges too rapidly on high-frequency components during few-shot training. By applying a dynamic frequency mask to tensor components, Few TensoRF forces the model to prioritize low-frequency information in early training stages, enhancing data efficiency without sacrificing the fast training times characteristic of the parent method. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs consist of a sparse set of images, camera poses, and intrinsics. Outputs are the factorized radiance field grids and rendered novel views. Data Structures: The radiance field is modeled using two distinct grids employing Vector-Matrix (VM) decomposition: a geometry grid G\sigma for density \sigma and an appearance grid Gc for features. Density and features are derived via trilinear interpolation at location x as \sigma(x) = G\sigma(x) and \mathbf{c}{feat}(x) = Gc(x). Final color is computed as c = S(\mathbf{c}{feat}(x), \mathbf{d}), where \mathbf{d} is the viewing direction and S is a pre-selected function like a small MLP or spherical harmonics. Tensor Decomposition: The appearance grid decomposes as Gc(x) = \sum{r=1}^{Ro} (A^X{c,r} \circ b^{3r-2} + A^Y{c,r} \circ b^{3r-2} + A^Z{c,r} \circ b^{3r}), where Ro is rank, r is the index, A are tensor components, b are basis vectors, and \circ is the combination operation. The density grid G\sigma follows a similar VM structure. Frequency Masking: To mitigate over-fast convergence in high-frequency components, a dynamic frequency mask \alpha(t, T, L) is applied to density components A and appearance components Ac. The masked component is A'L(t, T; x) = AL(x) \odot \alpha(t, T, L), where \odot is element-wise multiplication. The mask value for the i-th bit is \alphai(t, T, L) = \begin{cases} 1 & \text{if } i \le \frac{t \cdot L}{T} \\ \frac{t \cdot L}{T} - \lfloor \frac{t \cdot L}{T} \rfloor & \text{if } \frac{t \cdot L}{T} < i \le \frac{t \cdot L}{T} + 6 \\ 0 & \text{if } i > \frac{t \cdot L}{T} + 6 \end{cases}. Here t is the current iteration, T is total iterations, and L is the component length. If t \ge T, the mask returns a tensor of ones. Algorithm Steps: 1. Initialize G\sigma and Gc with VM decomposition factors. 2. For each training iteration t from 1 to T: a. Sample rays and compute \sigma(x) and \mathbf{c}{feat}(x) via trilinear interpolation from the grids. b. Compute \alpha(t, T, L) for both density and appearance components based on t and T. c. Apply the mask to tensor factors A and Ac using element-wise multiplication. d. Render the image using volume rendering integration. e. Compute loss against ground truth images. f. Backpropagate and update the tensor factors. 3. After training, render novel views using the final factors. Parameters: T is the total training iterations, aligning with approximately 10–15 minutes of optimization. L is the length of the tensor component being masked. S is the color prediction function (MLP or SH). Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Rapid convergence in high-frequency components hinders the exploration of low-frequency information, causing bias and undesired high-frequency artifacts in sparse scenarios. Time complexity maintains the fast training time of TensoRF, approximately 10–15 minutes. Memory complexity inherits the low memory footprint of the VM decomposition from TensoRF. On the Synthesis NeRF benchmark, Few TensoRF improves average PSNR from 21.45 dB (standard TensoRF) to 23.70 dB, with a fine-tuned version reaching 24.52 dB. On the THuman 2.0 dataset, it achieves 27.37–34.00 dB PSNR with only eight input images. Strengths include high data efficiency for few-shot inputs, prevention of high-frequency artifacts, and retention of real-time rendering speed. Limitations include reliance on the frequency mask schedule and performance tied to the specific few-shot regime. Few TensoRF was introduced by authors from FPT University, Ho Chi Minh City, Vietnam, in a paper published in March 2026. It builds directly on TensoRF and incorporates regularization techniques from FreeNeRF to address the limitations of tensor-based radiance fields in sparse view settings. Few TensoRF: Enhance the Few-shot on Tensorial Radiance Fields, https://doi.org/10.48550/arxiv.2603.25008, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial)

name: LOD Generation
head: Hierarchical LOD creation
body: LOD Generation creates multiple levels of detail from a trained finest-resolution radiance field model to reduce resource usage for distant scene blocks while maintaining high-quality rendering from elevated viewpoints. It avoids the prohibitive cost and appearance inconsistency of retraining the entire scene from scratch at lower resolutions. By leveraging the compressibility of rank-residual models, it also enables dynamic LOD adjustment per object to balance rendering quality and storage/performance in composed scenes. The method operates on a scene decomposed into blocks with an associated deferred MLP. It generates coarser LODs by merging fine-grained blocks and adapting the query function. Inputs: Trained finest-resolution model consisting of submodels (query functions f^k) and a shared deferred MLP \Phi. Scene geometry divided into M \times M blocks. Virtual grid storing rendering attributes, simulated during training. Outputs: A hierarchy of LOD models, where LOD l consists of merged blocks and adapted parameters. Baked texture assets for rendering. Data Structures: Virtual Grid: Stores rendering attributes (density, color features) for each block; resolution is downsampled by a factor of 2 for each LOD level. Submodels: Contain the frozen query function f^k for each block or merged block group. Deferred MLP (\Phi^{k,l}): A shared MLP retrained for each LOD level l to map the downsampled features to final radiance. Steps: 1. Virtual Grid Simulation: During the initial training of the finest LOD, simulate a virtual grid to store rendering attributes for each block. 2. Block Merging: To generate LOD l, merge 2^l \times 2^l fine blocks into a single coarser block (specifically 2 \times 2 for LOD 1). 3. Grid Downsampling: Downsample the resolution of the virtual grid within each merged block by a factor of 2 relative to the previous LOD level. 4. Freeze Query Function: Freeze the training of the query function f^k within the submodels corresponding to the merged blocks. 5. Retrain Deferred MLP: Retrain a new shared deferred MLP \Phi^{k,l} across the merged blocks. 6. Joint Optimization: Jointly optimize the frozen submodels and the newly trained deferred MLP \Phi^{k,l} to ensure consistency and quality at the lower resolution. 7. Baking: For LOD l, bake the 2^l \times 2^l merged blocks into a single texture asset, retaining samples with opacity and weight values above a certain threshold. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. class MLP: def init(self): self.weights = [0.0] def forward(self, features): return sum(f w for f, w in zip(features, self.weights)) def backward(self, loss): self.weights = [w - 0.01 (loss - self.forward([])) for w in self.weights] def generatelodhierarchy(finemodel, sceneblocks, maxlodlevel): lodmodels = {} currentblocks = sceneblocks currentgrid = finemodel.virtualgrid for l in range(1, maxlodlevel + 1): # Step 2: Merge 2^l x 2^l blocks (factor 2 per level) mergedblocks = [currentblocks[i:i+4] for i in range(0, len(currentblocks), 4)] # Step 3: Downsample virtual grid resolution by factor of 2 downsampledgrid = downsamplegrid(currentgrid, factor=2) # Step 4: Freeze query functions f^k in submodels frozenfunctions = [block.queryfunction for block in mergedblocks] # Step 5: Retrain new shared deferred MLP Phi^{k,l} newdeferredmlp = MLP() # Step 6: Jointly optimize submodels and deferred MLP for step in range(1000): features = [f(downsampledgrid.sample) for f in frozenfunctions] radiance = newdeferredmlp.forward(features) loss = computemse(radiance, downsampledgrid.targets) newdeferredmlp.backward(loss) lodmodels[l] = { 'blocks': mergedblocks, 'frozenfunctions': frozenfunctions, 'deferredmlp': newdeferredmlp, 'grid': downsampledgrid } currentblocks = mergedblocks currentgrid = downsampledgrid return lodmodels def downsamplegrid(grid, factor): newdata = [[grid.data[i][j] for j in range(0, len(grid.data[i]), factor)] for i in range(0, len(grid.data), factor)] return {'resolution': grid['resolution'] // factor, 'data': newdata} def computemse(pred, target): return sum((p - t) 2 for p, t in zip(pred, target)) / len(pred) Parameters: Merge Factor: Typically 2 \times 2 for adjacent LOD levels. Downsampling Factor: 2 per LOD level. LOD Level (l): Integer indicating the coarseness, where LOD 0 is the finest resolution. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Appearance Consistency: Retraining from scratch for extrapolated views causes inconsistency; freezing query functions mitigates this. Resource Usage: Distant blocks should use higher LODs to save resources. Baking Threshold: Samples with opacity and weight values above a certain threshold are retained during baking to ensure quality. A scene composition technique that dynamically adjusts the model size (LOD) per object to balance rendering quality and storage/performance, leveraging the compressibility of rank-residual models. It assigns the full model to primary objects requiring high detail and truncates the model to a smaller LOD for secondary/scaled-down objects. This allows composing objects in a scene using their respective LODs. For example, a high LOD model size of 68.9 MB can be reduced to 1.5 MB for a low LOD model, demonstrated on bulldozer objects from nerf-synthetic composed into a barn scene from Tanks And Temples. Time Complexity: Generating LODs is significantly faster than retraining from scratch, as it freezes query functions and only retrains the deferred MLP. Memory Complexity: Higher LODs use less memory due to downsampled virtual grids and merged blocks. Dynamic LOD adjustment can reduce model size from 68.9 MB to 1.5 MB. Performance: Enables efficient rendering of large-scale scenes by reducing resource usage for distant blocks. Strengths: Avoids retraining from scratch; maintains appearance consistency; supports dynamic scene composition. Limitations: Requires simulating a virtual grid during the initial training stage. Quality depends on proper optimization of the deferred MLP. LOD Generation was introduced to ensure high-quality rendering from elevated viewpoints and reduce resource usage for distant scene blocks. It addresses the challenge of rendering large scenes captured from aerial or top-down perspectives, where appearance consistency across separately trained models is difficult to ensure. The method builds on the principles of tensorial and low-rank representations, specifically utilizing the compressibility of rank-residual models. name: Hierarchical Semantic Guidance
body: Hierarchical Semantic Guidance (HSG) is a supervision method for radiance-field optimization that enforces semantic consistency across views by aligning coarse-to-fine semantic content with coarse-to-fine scene representations. It solves the problem where standard CLIP-based semantic loss fails during early training because rendered images are blurred (low-frequency) while ground-truth images are high-resolution, causing a sharp drop in cosine similarity. Unlike direct depth supervision or standard photometric loss, HSG dynamically adjusts the spatial resolution of the semantic comparison to match the learning stage of the neural field. Inputs and Outputs: The method takes a randomly selected known camera pose, the current state of the radiance field model, and the ground-truth image Ci corresponding to that pose as inputs. It outputs a scalar semantic loss value used to update the radiance field parameters. Data Structures: The image is represented as C \in \mathbb{R}^{H \times W \times 3} where H and W are height and width. The sampling grid is defined as P(si) = \{(u, v) \mid u \in [0, H, \text{stride} = si], v \in [0, W, \text{stride} = si]\}. The CLIP encoder outputs a feature vector \phi \in \mathbb{R}^D. Parameters: s{max} is the maximum sampling stride, typically set to 0.1 \cdot \min(H, W). N{hsg} is the number of iterations until full pixels are sampled, typically 50% of total training iterations. i is the current training iteration index. Steps: 1. Randomly select a known camera pose from the training set. 2. Render an image \hat{C}{sem} from the selected pose using the current radiance field model. 3. Compute the current sampling stride si using the iteration index i: si = \max\left(\left\lceil s{max} \cdot \frac{1 + \cos((i/N{hsg})\pi)}{2} \right\rceil, 1\right) where \lceil \cdot \rceil denotes the ceiling operation. 4. Define the pixel sampling grid P(si) with spacing si. 5. Sample pixels from the rendered image \hat{C}{sem} and the ground-truth image Ci using the grid P(si) to obtain downsampled versions \hat{C}{sem}^{sampled} and Ci^{sampled}. 6. Encode the sampled images using the CLIP image encoder f{clip} to obtain feature vectors \phi{sem} = f{clip}(\hat{C}{sem}^{sampled}) and \phii = f{clip}(Ci^{sampled}). 7. Compute the semantic loss as 1 - \text{cosine\similarity}(\phi{sem}, \phii). Pseudocode: Unverified code. """ # Standard volume rendering along rays from the camera pose renderedimage = renderfn(pose) # Shape: (H, W, 3) # Compute current stride si ratio = iteration / nhsg cosineval = math.cos(ratio math.pi) stridefloat = smax (1 + cosineval) / 2 si = max(math.ceil(stridefloat), 1) # Sample pixels using the coarse-to-fine grid P(si) uindices = list(range(0, h, si)) vindices = list(range(0, w, si)) sampledrendered = renderedimage[uindices][:, vindices] # Shape: (len(u), len(v), 3) sampledgt = gtimage[uindices][:, vindices] # Standard CLIP preprocessing: resize to 224x224, normalize to [-1, 1] renderedclip = clipencoder.preprocess(sampledrendered) gtclip = clipencoder.preprocess(sampledgt) # Encode features phisem = clipencoder.encode(renderedclip) phii = clipencoder.encode(gtclip) # Compute cosine similarity loss similarity = torch.cosinesimilarity(phisem, phii, dim=0) loss = 1.0 - similarity return loss Edge Cases and Pitfalls: CLIP semantic consistency is limited for multi-resolution images; cosine similarity decreases sharply with down-sampling rate, especially in complex real-world scenes. The stride si is clamped to a minimum of 1 to ensure full pixel sampling eventually. If the rendered image is completely black or white, CLIP features may be uninformative. name: Hybrid Explicit-Implicit Representations
body: Hybrid Explicit-Implicit Representations address the trade-off between the memory efficiency of explicit structures and the continuous flexibility of implicit neural decoders in radiance field optimization. This family balances memory efficiency and rendering speed by leveraging cheap lookups for feature retrieval while maintaining the ability to model complex scene geometry and appearance. The core mechanism involves two components: an Explicit Feature Storage (V) and a Decoder (D). 1. Explicit Feature Storage (V): A data structure holding feature vectors, commonly implemented as voxel grids or hash tables. Basis vectors are not detailed in the sources. 2. Decoder (D): A function that maps the retrieved feature vector vp to physical properties. Specific decoder architectures are not detailed in the sources. Algorithm Steps: 1. Initialize Storage: Construct the explicit feature storage V. Specific initialization procedures are not detailed in the sources. 2. Feature Retrieval: For a query point p = (x, y, z) in 3D space, retrieve the corresponding feature vector vp from V. If V is a voxel grid, perform tri-linear interpolation of the surrounding voxel features to obtain vp. If V is a hash table, compute the hash of p and retrieve the associated feature vector. 3. Decoding: Pass the feature vector vp through the decoder D to predict the volume density \sigma(p) and color c(p, d), where d is the viewing direction. 4. Rendering: Use standard volume rendering integration along rays passing through the scene, summing the contributions of \sigma and c weighted by transmittance. Parameters: Storage Type: Voxel grid or hash table. Interpolation Method: Tri-linear interpolation is standard for voxel grids. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision: Tri-linear interpolation assumes continuous variation between voxels; sharp discontinuities may require higher resolution or specialized handling. Boundaries: Points outside the defined storage domain must be handled (e.g., clamping, zero-padding, or out-of-bounds flags). Degenerate Input: Empty regions in the scene may result in sparse feature storage, requiring efficient sparse data structures or padding strategies. A general framework combining explicit feature storage with an implicit decoder to balance memory efficiency and rendering speed. Uses explicit voxel grids for density inference and implicit MLPs for color inference to achieve real-time performance. Decomposes scenes into a low-quality triangle mesh, a view-dependent displacement map, and a compressed NeRF model in a hash table to enable real-time rendering on edge devices by leveraging distinct graphics hardware units. Refines coarse shape and appearance from an implicit stage by converting the continuous implicit field into a discrete mesh and jointly optimizing vertex positions and SVBRDF maps. Combines a voxel grid and a triangle mesh to achieve real-time view synthesis on mobile devices, converting portions of the volumetric density field into a surface mesh based on rendering quality differences. Definition: MERF is a volumetric scene representation that achieves real-time rendering of large-scale scenes in a browser by combining a sparse feature grid and high-resolution 2D feature planes, with a lossless baking procedure to convert the optimized parameterization into a fast rendering format. It uses a unified radiance field representation with two different underlying parameterizations: one for optimization (NGP hash grid) and one for rendering (baked binary occupancy grid and triplanes). Steps: During optimization, MERF uses the NGP hash grid structure to compress the parameterization, allowing for differentiable sparsification and providing an inductive bias that aids convergence. After optimization, it queries the recovered NGP to explicitly bake out the MERF and create a binary occupancy grid to accelerate rendering. Performance: MERF achieves better image quality for the same amount of compression as SNeRG++, matching the output of a SNeRG++ model that is over 17x larger. Compared to TensoRF, MERF speeds up query time by removing the need for matrix multiplication and halves memory bandwidth consumption. Definition: NeRF-Editing is the first mesh-based shape deformation method, leveraging explicit representations for scene geometry edits and implicit representations for realistic rendering effects. Steps: It extracts an explicit triangular mesh from the NeRF, enables intuitive user-driven deformations through the classic ARAP deformation method, generates a tetrahedral mesh around the triangular mesh to propagate deformations spatially, employs tetrahedral vertex interpolation to transform discrete deformations into a continuous field, and ensures rays passing through the mesh bend according to user adjustments. Hybrid representations emerged to address the limitations of pure Neural Radiance Fields (NeRF), which are compute-intensive for real-time rendering, and pure explicit methods, which lack the flexibility of continuous representations. The concept of storing features in a structured format (voxel grids, hash tables) and decoding them via lightweight networks was introduced to balance memory efficiency and rendering speed. Notable implementations include MERF, which introduces a baking procedure to transition from an optimized hash-grid representation to a real-time renderable format. Other historical details or sibling comparisons are not detailed in the sources. head: Explicit-Implicit Hybrid
body: Hybrid Representation is a framework for radiance field optimization that combines explicit feature storage with an implicit decoder to efficiently reconstruct and render scenes, addressing the computational expense of pure implicit NeRFs. It sets itself apart from siblings like DVGO by providing a general architectural pattern where spatial features are stored in a discrete structure (e.g., voxel grid, hash table) and decoded via a neural network, rather than relying solely on dense voxel grids or purely implicit MLPs. Inputs: A set of training images with known camera poses. A scene bounding box defining the spatial domain. Outputs: A trained Explicit Feature Storage V. A trained Decoder D. A rendered image for a given query ray. Data Structures: 1. Explicit Feature Storage (V): Voxel Grid: A 3D array of dimensions Dx \times Dy \times Dz where each cell stores a feature vector of dimension F. Hash Table: A mapping from spatial coordinates to feature vectors, requiring a hash function H and a capacity C. Basis Vectors: A set of learned basis functions or matrices. 2. Decoder (D): Typically a Multi-Layer Perceptron (MLP) or Spherical Harmonics (SH) coefficients. Algorithm Steps: 1. Initialize Storage: Construct the explicit feature storage V (e.g., voxel grid, hash table, or basis vectors). 2. Feature Retrieval: For a query point p = (x, y, z) in 3D space, retrieve the feature vector vp from V. If V is a voxel grid, perform tri-linear interpolation of the surrounding voxel features to obtain vp. If V is a hash table, compute the hash of p and retrieve the associated feature vector. 3. Decoding: Pass vp through the decoder D to predict volume density \sigma(p) and color c(p, d), where d is the viewing direction. The decoder D can be an MLP or Spherical Harmonics. 4. Rendering: Use standard volume rendering integration along rays passing through the scene, summing the contributions of \sigma and c weighted by transmittance. Formulas: Baking Implicit NeRF into Multi-resolution Voxel Mesh: The scene space is divided into a three-level voxel grid based on adaptive resolution. The voxel side length is defined as sk = \frac{S}{2^k} where S is the maximum side length of the scene and k=0, 1, 2 correspond to LOD0 (512³), LOD1 (256³), and LOD2 (128³). Radiation field sampling collects Ns = 8 uniform sampling points xp within each voxel V{i,j,k}. The voxel properties are calculated through the pre-trained implicit NeRF model F\theta with Fourier encoding \gamma(\cdot): c{i,j,k} = \frac{1}{Ns} \sum{p=1}^{Ns} F\theta(\gamma(xp)) \sigma{i,j,k} = \frac{1}{Ns} \sum{p=1}^{Ns} F\theta(\gamma(xp)) where c{i,j,k} and \sigma{i,j,k} are the averaged color and density for voxel (i,j,k). Parameters: Storage Type: Voxel grid, hash table, or basis vectors. Decoder Type: MLP or Spherical Harmonics. Interpolation Method: Tri-linear interpolation is standard for voxel grids. Typical Values: Not given in the sources. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision: Tri-linear interpolation is standard for voxel grids. Boundaries: Points outside the defined storage domain must be handled (e.g., clamping, zero-padding, or out-of-bounds flags). Degenerate Input: Empty regions in the scene may result in sparse feature storage, requiring efficient sparse data structures or padding strategies. HybridNeRF is a radiance field optimization method that combines explicit surface representations with implicit volumetric modeling to address computational expenses and enable efficient reconstruction and rendering. A technique to replace the computational bottleneck of MLP inference in implicit NeRF by pre-calculating voxel properties (color and density) into a multi-resolution voxel grid structure. Spatial division divides scene space into a three-level voxel grid based on adaptive resolution. The voxel side length is defined as sk = \frac{S}{2^k} where S is the maximum side length of the scene and k=0, 1, 2 correspond to LOD0 (512³), LOD1 (256³), and LOD2 (128³). Radiation field sampling collects Ns = 8 uniform sampling points xp within each voxel V{i,j,k}. The voxel properties are calculated through the pre-trained implicit NeRF model F\theta with Fourier encoding \gamma(\cdot): c{i,j,k} = \frac{1}{Ns} \sum{p=1}^{Ns} F\theta(\gamma(xp)) \sigma{i,j,k} = \frac{1}{Ns} \sum{p=1}^{Ns} F\theta(\gamma(xp)) Time and Memory Complexity: Memory: Depends on the explicit storage structure, scaling with D^3 \times F for voxel grids or the number of active entries for hash tables. Time: Feature retrieval operates in O(1) time for both structures, while decoding complexity depends on the decoder architecture, such as O(L \cdot F^2) for an MLP with L layers. Measured Performance: Hybrid representations address the computational expense of pure implicit NeRFs by enabling efficient reconstruction and rendering. Strengths and Limitations: Strengths: Addresses the computational expense of pure implicit NeRFs. Efficient reconstruction and rendering. Limitations: Tri-linear interpolation may struggle with sharp discontinuities, requiring higher resolution or specialized handling. When to Use: When efficient radiance field reconstruction and rendering are required, balancing implicit compactness with explicit speed. Hybrid representations were developed to efficiently reconstruct and render radiance fields, addressing the slow training and rendering speed of pure implicit NeRFs. The framework leverages explicit features stored in structures like voxel grids, hash tables, or basis vectors, decoded by MLPs or spherical harmonics. name: HybridNeRF
head: Hybrid Surface-Volume NeRF
body: HybridNeRF is a radiance field optimization method that combines explicit surface representations with implicit volumetric modeling to achieve high-fidelity novel-view synthesis at real-time frame rates. It addresses the computational expense of pure implicit NeRFs and the reconstruction limitations of pure surface-based methods by rendering most of the scene as thin surfaces while modeling challenging regions (thin structures, semi-opaque areas) volumetrically using spatially-varying surfaceness parameters \beta(\mathbf{x}). Unlike prior work that treats surfaceness as a global parameter, HybridNeRF learns \beta in a spatially adaptive manner, allowing it to improve error rates by 15–30% compared to state-of-the-art baselines while achieving at least 36 FPS for 2K×2K virtual-reality resolutions. Inputs: A set of calibrated images with known camera poses. Outputs: A rendered image for a target camera pose, and trained model parameters (SDF MLP, color MLP, surfaceness grid). Data Structures: 1. SDF and Color Networks: Two separate multi-layer perceptrons (MLPs). The SDF network takes 3D coordinates and features as input and outputs a signed distance value f(\mathbf{x}). The color network takes 3D coordinates, features, and viewing direction as input and outputs color \mathbf{c}. 2. Feature Grids: Dense multi-resolution 3D feature grids in combination with multi-resolution triplanes. These store features for 3D sample locations. 3. Surfaceness Grid: A 3D grid of size 512^3 storing scalar values for \beta(\mathbf{x}). 4. Proposal Network: A small network similar to Nerfacto used to improve sampling efficiency by predicting likely surface locations. Parameters: \beta(\mathbf{x}): Surfaceness parameter. Initially uniform, then spatially varying. \etai: Per-sample loss weight for Eikonal regularization, typically set to 1. Algorithm Steps: 1. Initialization: Initialize the SDF network, color network, feature grids, and the surfaceness grid. Set all values in the surfaceness grid to a uniform constant \beta. 2. Phase 1: Global Surfaceness Training: Train the model using a VolSDF-like approach. Sample points along rays. Compute the Eikonal loss to regularize the SDF gradient magnitude to 1: \mathcal{L}{\text{Eik}}(\mathbf{r}):= \sum{i=0}^{N-1} \etai (\|\nabla f(\mathbf{x}i)\| - 1)^2, where \mathbf{x}i are sample points along ray \mathbf{r}, and \etai = 1. Convert SDF f(\mathbf{x}) to density \sigma{\text{SDF}}(\mathbf{x}) using the global \beta: \sigma{\text{SDF}}(\mathbf{x}):= \beta \Psi(f(\mathbf{x})\beta). Render the image using standard volume rendering integration. Optimize network weights and the uniform \beta value. 3. Phase 2: Spatially-Varying Surfaceness Transition: Transition from the global \beta to position-dependent \beta(\mathbf{x}) values. Initialize the 512^3 surfaceness grid with the converged global \beta value. Enable gradient updates for the surfaceness grid values. Continue training with the same loss functions, but now \beta is queried from the grid at each sample location \mathbf{x}i: \beta(\mathbf{x}i) = \text{GridQuery}(\mathbf{x}i). The surfaceness grid is queried via nearest-neighbor interpolation. This allows the model to maintain high surfaceness (thin surfaces) in most of the scene while lowering \beta (more volumetric) in regions with thin structures or semi-opaque areas to preserve quality. 4. Rendering: For a given camera ray, use sphere tracing to identify sample locations, leveraging the fact that the model behaves as a valid SDF in >95% of the scene. At each sample point \mathbf{x}i: Query features from the multi-resolution grids. Query \beta(\mathbf{x}i) from the 512^3 grid using nearest-neighbor interpolation. Compute density: \sigma{\text{SDF}}(\mathbf{x}i) = \beta(\mathbf{x}i) \Psi(f(\mathbf{x}i)\beta(\mathbf{x}i)). Compute color \mathbf{c}(\mathbf{x}i) from the color network. Perform volume rendering integration using the computed densities and colors. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import numpy as np def laplacecdf(s): """Computes the CDF of a standard Laplace distribution.""" return 0.5 np.exp(-s) if s > 0 else 1.0 - 0.5 np.exp(s) def computedensity(sdfval, beta): """Converts SDF value and surfaceness to density.""" return beta laplacecdf(sdfval beta) def querysurfacenessgrid(x, grid, bounds=1.0): """Queries the 512x512x512 surfaceness grid via nearest-neighbor interpolation.""" # Map world coordinates x in [-bounds, bounds]^3 to grid indices [0, 511] idx = np.round((x + bounds) / (2 bounds) 511).astype(int) idx = np.clip(idx, 0, 511) return grid[idx[0], idx[1], idx[2]] def computegradient(network, x): """ Computes spatial gradient of the SDF network at x.""" eps = 1e-4 grad = np.zeros(3) for d in range(3): xp = x.copy(); xp[d] += eps xm = x.copy(); xm[d] -= eps grad[d] = (network(xp) - network(xm)) / (2 eps) return grad def trainphase1(images, poses, sdfnet, colornet, featgrids, betaglobal, epochs): """Phase 1: Train with globally uniform surfaceness.""" for in range(epochs): for img, pose in zip(images, poses): rays = generaterays(pose) pts = proposalsample(rays, sdfnet, featgrids) sdfvals = sdfnet(pts, featgrids) colors = colornet(pts, featgrids, rays.dirs) dens = computedensity(sdfvals, betaglobal) rendered = volumerender(rays, dens, colors) lossrgb = mse(rendered, img) eik = sum((np.linalg.norm(computegradient(sdfnet, p)) - 1)2 for p in pts) total = lossrgb + eik updateparams(sdfnet, colornet, featgrids, betaglobal, total) def trainphase2(images, poses, sdfnet, colornet, featgrids, surfgrid, betaglobal, epochs): """Phase 2: Transition to spatially-varying surfaceness.""" surfgrid[:] = betaglobal for in range(epochs): for img, pose in zip(images, poses): rays = generaterays(pose) pts = proposalsample(rays, sdfnet, featgrids) sdfvals = sdfnet(pts, featgrids) colors = colornet(pts, featgrids, rays.dirs) betas = np.array([querysurfacenessgrid(p, surfgrid) for p in pts]) dens = computedensity(sdfvals, betas) rendered = volumerender(rays, dens, colors) lossrgb = mse(rendered, img) eik = sum((np.linalg.norm(computegradient(sdfnet, p)) - 1)2 for p in pts) total = lossrgb + eik updateparams(sdfnet, colornet, featgrids, surfgrid, total) def render(camerapose, surfgrid, sdfnet, colornet, featgrids, maxdist=10.0, eps=1e-4): """Renders an image using sphere tracing.""" rays = generaterays(camerapose) img = np.zeros(rays.origin.shape) for i, ray in enumerate(rays): t = 0.0 samples = [] while t < maxdist: p = ray.origin + t ray.dir sdfval = sdfnet(p, featgrids) if abs(sdfval) < eps: samples.append(p) break t += max(sdfval, eps) beta = querysurfacenessgrid(p, surfgrid) samples.append((p, computedensity(sdfval, beta))) img[i] = volumerenderray(ray, samples) return img Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision: Sphere tracing relies on the SDF property \|\nabla f(\mathbf{x})\| \approx 1. Boundaries: The surfaceness grid is finite (512^3). Points outside the grid bounds must be handled, typically by clamping or assuming a default \beta. Degenerate Input: Thin structures and semi-opaque areas require lower \beta values. A method that interprets MLP outputs as a signed distance field (SDF) and regularizes the gradient norm to 1 using Eikonal loss. It serves as the foundation for the SDF representation in HybridNeRF. A method that uses a proposal network to improve sampling efficiency in neural radiance fields. HybridNeRF uses a similar proposal network. A technique for featurizing 3D locations using 2D planes. HybridNeRF uses this for feature storage. Time Complexity: Rendering is accelerated by sphere tracing, which requires far fewer samples per ray than uniform volumetric sampling, as the model behaves as a valid SDF in >95% of the scene. Memory Complexity: The model uses dense multi-resolution 3D feature grids, multi-resolution triplanes, and a 512^3 surfaceness grid. Measured Performance: HybridNeRF improves error rates by 15–30% compared to state-of-the-art baselines, including rasterization-based approaches, while achieving real-time framerates (at least 36 FPS) for virtual-reality resolutions (2K×2K). Strengths: High rendering efficiency due to surface-like behavior in most of the scene; high fidelity in challenging regions (thin structures, semi-opaque areas) due to volumetric modeling; real-time performance. Limitations: Requires careful tuning of the surfaceness grid and Eikonal loss. When to use: When real-time rendering is required and the scene contains a mix of solid surfaces and thin/semi-opaque structures. When not to use: For scenes that are entirely volumetric (e.g., smoke, fire) or entirely solid without thin structures, pure volumetric or pure surface methods may be more appropriate. HybridNeRF was proposed by Haithem Turki et al. in 2024. It builds on previous work in surface-based neural fields, such as VolSDF, which interprets MLP outputs as SDFs. The key innovation is the introduction of spatially-varying surfaceness parameters \beta(\mathbf{x}), replacing the global \beta used in prior work. The method was evaluated on the Eyeful Tower dataset and other commonly used view synthesis datasets. HybridNeRF: Efficient Neural Rendering via Adaptive Volumetric Surfaces, https://doi.org/10.1109/cvpr52733.2024.01858, fetched 2026-10-26

name: Hybrid Multi-Space Module
head: Hybrid MS Module, MS module for grid-based methods, MS-NeRF Hybrid MS Module, MS-TensoRF, MS-iNGP, multi-space iNGP
body: The Hybrid Multi-Space Module extends grid-based Neural Radiance Field (NeRF) methods to handle scenes with complex light paths, such as reflections and refractions, by decomposing the rendering process into multiple sub-spaces. Unlike pure feature-field approaches that are incompatible with high-performance grid structures, this module integrates a small "Gate" MLP to compute composition weights while using multiple radiance fields (density and color) within the explicit grid backbone. It sets itself apart from siblings like Hybrid Representation by explicitly modeling K distinct radiance fields for sub-spaces rather than just feature fields, enabling accurate rendering of virtual images and refractive surfaces in grid-based frameworks like iNGP and TensoRF. The method modifies the standard grid-based NeRF pipeline by introducing a parallel "Gate" MLP branch and expanding the output layer to support K sub-spaces. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: Sampled 3D points \{pi\} along a ray, ray direction d, explicit grid parameters V (from the parent Hybrid Explicit-Implicit Representations), and positional encoding \gamma(pi). Outputs: Final rendered color C and optional per-sub-space color maps \{Ck\}. Data Structures: 1. Explicit Grid (V): Inherits the layout from the parent method (e.g., hash table or voxel grid) storing feature vectors. 2. Gate MLP (\ThetaG): A small Multi-Layer Perceptron with parameters \ThetaG. Input dimension: Dimension of positional encoding \gamma(p). Hidden layer dimension: h. Output dimension: d (feature vector size for gating). 3. Radiance Fields Branch: The main grid-based NeRF backbone. Output: For each sub-space k \in \{1, \dots, K\}, outputs density \sigma{ik} and color c{ik} for point pi. Parameters: K: Total number of sub-spaces. Typical value: 4. d: Dimension of output features for the Gate MLP. Typical value: 8. h: Hidden layer dimension of the Gate MLP. Typical value: 32. \gamma(\cdot): Positional encoding function (as defined in standard NeRF literature, e.g., Eq. 1). Algorithm Steps: 1. Initialize Gate MLP: Construct a small MLP \ThetaG with hidden dimension h and output dimension d. Initialize it similarly to the main branch's MLP but with smaller capacity. 2. Query Gate Features: For each sampled point pi and view direction d: Compute positional encoding \gamma(pi). Pass \gamma(pi) and d through \ThetaG to obtain a feature vector fi \in \mathbb{R}^d. Note: One feature vector is recorded per position due to model capacity constraints. 3. Query Radiance Fields: For each sampled point pi and view direction d: Retrieve the base feature vector v{pi} from the explicit grid V using query function Q(V, pi) (as defined in the parent Hybrid Explicit-Implicit Representations). Pass v{pi} and d through the main radiance field decoder to predict K pairs of density and color: \{(\sigma{i1}, c{i1}), \dots, (\sigma{iK}, c{iK})\}. 4. Multi-Space Integration (Color Maps): Perform volumetric rendering along the ray for each sub-space k independently. Use the densities \{\sigma{ik}\}i and colors \{c{ik}\}i to compute transmittance and opacity. Integrate to form K color maps \{Ck\}, where Ck is the color contribution of sub-space k. Formula: Ck = \sum{i=1}^{N} Ti (1 - e^{-\sigma{ik} \deltai}) c{ik}, where Ti is the accumulated transmittance up to point i, and \deltai is the distance between samples (Standard volume rendering integration). 5. Multi-Space Integration (Feature Maps): Perform volumetric rendering using the Gate features \{fi\} and the sub-space densities \{\sigma{ik}\}i. Compute K feature maps \{Fk\} for each sub-space. Formula: Fk = \sum{i=1}^{N} Ti (1 - e^{-\sigma{ik} \deltai}) fi (Eq. 5). 6. Decode Composition Weights: Decode the pixel-wise composition weight map \{wk\} from the feature maps \{Fk\}. Formula: wk = \text{Softmax}(Fk) or a similar normalization ensuring \sumk wk = 1 (Eq. 6). Note: The source describes decoding from Fk but does not specify the exact activation function in the text; Softmax is the standard interpretation for weight maps in this context. 7. Compose Final Output: Combine the K color maps \{Ck\} using the decoded weights \{wk\}. Formula: C = \sum{k=1}^{K} wk Ck (Eq. 7). Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def hybridmultispacerender(rayorigin, raydirection, gridV, gatemlp, radiancedecoder, K, d, h): """ Renders a single ray using the Hybrid Multi-Space Module. Args: rayorigin: (3,) float32, origin of the ray. raydirection: (3,) float32, normalized direction of the ray. gridV: Explicit feature storage (e.g., HashGrid or VoxelGrid). gatemlp: Small MLP with hidden dim h, output dim d. radiancedecoder: Main decoder mapping grid features + direction to K (sigma, color) pairs. K: Number of sub-spaces. d: Output dimension of gatemlp. h: Hidden dimension of gatemlp. Returns: finalcolor: (3,) float32, rendered color. """ # 1. Sample points along the ray # Standard sampling strategy (e.g., uniform or proposal-based) # Returns N points pi, distances deltai, and transmittance Ti points, deltas, transmittance = samplepoints(rayorigin, raydirection) N = len(points) # 2. Compute Gate Features # Apply positional encoding gamma to each point gammapoints = positionalencoding(points) # Shape: (N, Dgamma) # Concatenate view direction if required by gatemlp input definition # Source says "maps each 3D positions {gamma(pi)}... and view directions d" # Assuming gatemlp takes [gamma(p), d] or similar. # If d is constant for the ray, broadcast it. directions = np.broadcastto(raydirection, (N, 3)) gateinput = np.concatenate([gammapoints, directions], axis=-1) # Pass through Gate MLP # gatemlp is a simple MLP: Linear -> Activation -> Linear gatefeatures = gatemlp(gateinput) # Shape: (N, d) # 3. Query Radiance Fields for K sub-spaces # Retrieve base features from grid gridfeatures = gridV.query(points) # Shape: (N, Dgrid) # Predict K densities and K colors # radiancedecoder outputs K pairs of (sigma, color) # sigma: (N, K), color: (N, K, 3) sigmas, colors = radiancedecoder(gridfeatures, raydirection) # 4. Multi-Space Integration for Color Maps {Ck} # Initialize color maps for each sub-space colormaps = np.zeros((K, 3)) # 5. Multi-Space Integration for Feature Maps {Fk} # Initialize feature maps for each sub-space featuremaps = np.zeros((K, d)) # Accumulate contributions # Ti is transmittance BEFORE point i # Opacity alphai = 1 - exp(-sigmai deltai) # Contribution = Ti alphai value for k in range(K): sigmak = sigmas[:, k] # (N,) colork = colors[:, k,:] # (N, 3) # Compute opacity alphak = 1.0 - np.exp(-sigmak deltas) # Compute weight for each sample in sub-space k # wsamplei = Ti alphai sampleweights = transmittance alphak # (N,) # Accumulate Color Map Ck # Ck += sum(sampleweights colork) colormaps[k] += np.sum(sampleweights[:, np.newaxis] colork, axis=0) # Accumulate Feature Map Fk # Fk += sum(sampleweights gatefeatures) featuremaps[k] += np.sum(sampleweights[:, np.newaxis] gatefeatures, axis=0) # Update transmittance for next point # T{i+1} = Ti (1 - alphai) transmittance = (1.0 - alphak) # 6. Decode Composition Weights {wk} # Decode weights from feature maps Fk # Source: "decode the pixel-wise composition weight map {wk} from {Fk}" # Assuming a softmax over the K feature maps for the pixel # featuremaps shape: (K, d) # We need a scalar weight per sub-space. # Standard practice is to reduce Fk to a scalar (e.g., sum or linear proj) then softmax. # Source does not specify reduction. We assume a linear projection to scalar followed by softmax. # Let's assume a simple sum reduction for Fk to scalar sk, then softmax. scalarfeatures = np.sum(featuremaps, axis=1) # (K,) weights = softmax(scalarfeatures) # (K,) # 7. Compose Final Result # C = sum(wk Ck) finalcolor = np.sum(weights[:, np.newaxis] colormaps, axis=0) return finalcolor def softmax(x): ex = np.exp(x - np.max(x)) return ex / ex.sum(axis=0) Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision: Tri-linear interpolation in the underlying grid V assumes continuous variation; sharp discontinuities in sub-space boundaries may require higher grid resolution. Boundaries: Points outside the defined storage domain must be handled (e.g., clamping or zero-padding) as per the parent method's requirements. Degenerate Input: Empty regions in the scene may result in sparse feature storage. The hybrid module relies on the efficiency of the underlying sparse data structure (hash table/voxel grid) to handle this. Weight Decoding: The exact reduction of feature maps Fk (size d) to scalar weights wk is not explicitly defined in the source text, only that they are "decoded". Implementation requires a choice (e.g., linear projection or sum). An implementation of the Hybrid Multi-Space Module integrated with Instant Neural Graphics Primitives (iNGP). It uses the iNGP hash grid and proposal estimator. Choose when rendering unbounded scenes with reflections/refractions requiring fast convergence. An implementation of the Hybrid Multi-Space Module integrated with Tensor Decomposition-based NeRF (TensoRF). It uses 2D/3D tensor grids. Choose when rendering bounded scenes with complex light paths where memory efficiency of tensor decomposition is prioritized. Time Complexity: Dominated by the grid queries and the small Gate MLP. The Gate MLP is significantly smaller than the main radiance field MLP, adding minimal overhead. Memory Complexity: Increases by the size of the Gate MLP and the storage for K radiance fields. For MS-TensoRF, parameters are split between grid and MLP. Example: MS-TensoRF-grid uses 5.60e-2M grid parameters and 4.60e-2M MLP parameters. Measured Performance: On the MS-TensoRF-grid ablation, the method achieved PSNR 32.07 and SSIM 0.932. In Mip-NeRF 360-based experiments, it showed a 4.15 dB PSNR improvement over baselines with minimal extra cost. Strengths: Compatible with high-performance grid-based methods (iNGP, TensoRF); handles reflections and refractions effectively; small Gate MLP keeps parameter count low. Limitations: Requires tuning of K, d, h; performance depends on the underlying grid's ability to resolve sub-space boundaries. When to use: Scenes with complex light paths (mirrors, glass) where grid-based methods are preferred for speed/memory. When not to use: Simple scenes without multi-space effects, where standard grid-based NeRF suffices. The Hybrid Multi-Space Module was introduced in "MS-NeRF: Multi-Space Neural Radiance Fields". It addresses the limitation of previous multi-space modules that relied on MLP-based feature fields, which are not compatible with the high-performance grid-based representations (like iNGP and TensoRF) that dominate modern NeRF optimization. By decomposing the multi-space composition information into a small MLP branch (Gate) and modeling the sub-spaces using multiple radiance fields within the grid, it enables efficient rendering of reflective and refractive surfaces in grid-based frameworks. name: DVGO (Deep Voxel Grids)
head: Deep Voxel Grids, Direct Voxel Grid Optimization
body: DVGO is a super-fast radiance field method that uses a hybrid representation: explicit for density inference and implicit for color inference, chosen for its potential for real-time applications. It speeds up NeRF by replacing the density MLP with voxel grids, allowing for efficient trilinear interpolation and volume rendering. Unlike completely implicit NeRF representations which are not fast enough for real-time applications due to querying costs, DVGO achieves competitive results and speed by leveraging the efficiency of grid-based explicit representations for density. DVGO operates in two stages: a coarse stage and a fine stage. The coarse stage uses two explicit volumes for density and color, while the fine stage refines the density grid and replaces the color volume with a feature grid and a shallow MLP for view-dependent color. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: Camera parameters (ray origin o and direction d), near and far planes, scene images (for supervision). Outputs: Rendered color \hat{C}(r) for each ray r. Data Structures: 1. Coarse Stage: V^{(\sigma,c)}: A 3D voxel grid storing raw density values \ddot{\sigma}^{(c)}. Dimensions: Nx \times Ny \times Nz. Initialized with zero raw density to prevent suboptimal geometry. V^{(rgb,c)}: A 3D voxel grid storing color values c^{(c)}. Dimensions: Nx \times Ny \times Nz. 2. Fine Stage: V^{(\sigma,f)}: A higher-resolution 3D voxel grid storing raw density values \ddot{\sigma}^{(f)}. Initialized with the optimized coarse geometry V^{(\sigma,c)}. V^{(feat,f)}: A 3D voxel grid storing color features. Dimensions: Nx \times Ny \times Nz. MLP{\Theta{rgb}}: A shallow multi-layer perceptron for view-dependent color inference. Algorithm Steps: 1. Ray Sampling: For a pixel-rendering ray r, sample n points xi between pre-defined near and far planes. Let \deltai be the distance between adjacent sampled points. 2. Coarse Stage Query (Optional/Initial): Query density: \ddot{\sigma}^{(c)} = \text{interp}(x, V^{(\sigma,c)}). Query color: c^{(c)} = \text{interp}(x, V^{(rgb,c)}). Activate density: \sigma^{(c)} = \text{softplus}(\ddot{\sigma}^{(c)}) = \log(1 + \exp(\ddot{\sigma}^{(c)} + b)), where b is a shift hyperparameter. 3. Fine Stage Query: Density Retrieval: Interpolate raw density from the refined grid: \ddot{\sigma}^{(f)} = \text{interp}(x, V^{(\sigma,f)}) where \text{interp} denotes trilinear interpolation. Density Activation: Apply shifted softplus to obtain final density: \sigma = \text{softplus}(\ddot{\sigma}^{(f)}) = \log(1 + \exp(\ddot{\sigma}^{(f)} + b)) where b is a hyperparameter. Feature Retrieval: Interpolate color features from the feature grid: v = \text{interp}(x, V^{(feat,f)}) where v \in \mathbb{R}^C. Color Decoding: Map the color feature to a view-dependent color emission using the shallow MLP: c^{(rgb)} = MLP{\Theta{rgb}}(v, x, d) Positional encoding is applied to encode x and d for the MLP{\Theta{rgb}}. 4. Volume Rendering: Calculate light termination probability (opacity) for each point: \alphai = 1 - \exp(-\sigmai \deltai) where \sigmai is the density at point i and \deltai is the distance to the adjacent point. Calculate accumulated transmittance: Ti = \prod{j=1}^{i-1} (1 - \alphaj) with T1 = 1. Accumulate results into a single color \hat{C}(r): \hat{C}(r) = \sum{i=1}^{n} Ti \alphai ci + T{n+1} c{bg} where ci is the color at point i, and c{bg} is a pre-defined background color. Parameters: b: A shift hyperparameter in the softplus activation function for density. Grid Resolution: Nx, Ny, Nz for coarse and fine grids. MLP Architecture: Shallow MLP for color decoding. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Initialization: V^{(\sigma,c)} must be initialized with zero raw density to prevent suboptimal geometry. Precision: Trilinear interpolation assumes continuous variation between voxels; sharp discontinuities may require higher resolution. Boundaries: Points outside the defined storage domain must be handled (e.g., clamping, zero-padding, or out-of-bounds flags). Degenerate Input: Empty regions in the scene may result in sparse feature storage, requiring efficient sparse data structures or padding strategies. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import numpy as np def softplus(x, b=0.0): """Shifted softplus activation.""" return np.log(1 + np.exp(x + b)) def trilinearinterpolate(grid, points): """ Perform trilinear interpolation for points in a 3D grid. grid: np.array of shape (Nx, Ny, Nz) or (Nx, Ny, Nz, C) points: np.array of shape (N, 3) with coordinates in [0, 1] relative to grid bounds Returns: interpolated values. If grid has C channels, returns (N, C). """ Nx, Ny, Nz = grid.shape[:3] coords = points np.array([Nx - 1, Ny - 1, Nz - 1]) x0, y0, z0 = np.floor(coords).astype(int) x1, y1, z1 = np.ceil(coords).astype(int) x0 = np.clip(x0, 0, Nx - 1) x1 = np.clip(x1, 0, Nx - 1) y0 = np.clip(y0, 0, Ny - 1) y1 = np.clip(y1, 0, Ny - 1) z0 = np.clip(z0, 0, Nz - 1) z1 = np.clip(z1, 0, Nz - 1) fx, fy, fz = coords - np.floor(coords) def getval(x, y, z): return grid[x, y, z] v000 = getval(x0, y0, z0) v100 = getval(x1, y0, z0) v010 = getval(x0, y1, z0) v110 = getval(x1, y1, z0) v001 = getval(x0, y0, z1) v101 = getval(x1, y0, z1) v011 = getval(x0, y1, z1) v111 = getval(x1, y1, z1) w000 = (1-fx)(1-fy)(1-fz) w100 = fx(1-fy)(1-fz) w010 = (1-fx)fy(1-fz) w110 = fxfy(1-fz) w001 = (1-fx)(1-fy)fz w101 = fx(1-fy)fz w011 = (1-fx)fyfz w111 = fxfyfz return (w000v000 + w100v100 + w010v010 + w110v110 + w001v001 + w101v101 + w011v011 + w111v111) def dvgorenderray(rayorigin, raydirection, nearplane, farplane, Vsigmaf, Vfeatf, mlprgb, b, bgcolor, numsamples=128): """ Render a single ray using the fine stage of DVGO. Args: rayorigin: (3,) array raydirection: (3,) array nearplane: float farplane: float Vsigmaf: 3D grid of raw densities Vfeatf: 3D grid of color features mlprgb: function taking (features, position, direction) -> color b: shift hyperparameter for softplus bgcolor: (3,) array numsamples: int Returns: color: (3,) array """ # 1. Sample points along the ray t = np.linspace(nearplane, farplane, numsamples) points = rayorigin + t[:, np.newaxis] raydirection # 2. Query Density rawdensities = trilinearinterpolate(Vsigmaf, points) densities = softplus(rawdensities, b) # 3. Query Color Features and Decode features = trilinearinterpolate(Vfeatf, points) # Positional encoding is applied to points and direction colors = np.zeros((numsamples, 3)) for i in range(numsamples): colors[i] = mlprgb(features[i], points[i], raydirection) # 4. Volume Rendering # Calculate delta distances correctly deltas = np.full(numsamples, (farplane - nearplane) / (numsamples - 1)) # Calculate alpha alphas = 1 - np.exp(-densities deltas) # Calculate transmittance Ti = prod{j=1}^{i-1} (1 - alphaj) transmittances = np.ones(numsamples) for i in range(1, numsamples): transmittances[i] = transmittances[i-1] (1 - alphas[i-1]) # Accumulate color contribution = transmittances[:, np.newaxis] alphas[:, np.newaxis] colors accumulatedcolor = np.sum(contribution, axis=0) # Add background: T{n+1} = Tn (1 - alphan) finaltransmittance = transmittances[-1] (1 - alphas[-1]) finalcolor = accumulatedcolor + finaltransmittance bgcolor return finalcolor The general class of methods combining explicit and implicit storage. DVGO is a specific instance using voxel grids for density and MLPs for color. See Hybrid Explicit-Implicit Representations. A sibling method that may use different explicit storage mechanisms (e.g., hash tables) or decoder structures. See Hybrid Representation. Time Complexity: Faster than completely implicit NeRF representations because querying density from voxel grids is efficient compared to MLP evaluation for every sample point. The coarse stage allows fast convergence, and the fine stage provides high-quality reconstruction. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Measured Performance: DVGO demonstrates super-fast radiance field capabilities, suitable for real-time applications. It achieves competitive results and speed when compared to other hybrid representations. Strengths: Real-time potential, efficient density computation, dual-stage design for flexibility in level of detail. Limitations: Memory usage scales with grid resolution; view-dependent color requires an MLP, which is slower than direct color lookup but faster than full NeRF. When to Use: When real-time or near real-time rendering is required, and the scene can be represented with sufficient resolution in voxel grids. DVGO (Direct Voxel Grid Optimization) was proposed as a method to speed up NeRF by replacing the density MLP with voxel grids. It is part of a family of "super fast radiance fields" that use hybrid representations (implicit for light field, explicit for density field). It has been used in applications such as ActiveRMAP for active mapping and planning. The method builds on the principles of neural radiance fields but optimizes for query efficiency. ActiveRMAP: Radiance Field for Active Mapping And Planning, https://doi.org/10.48550/arxiv.2211.12656, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial) NeRF Synthesis with Shading Guidance, https://link.springer.com/chapter/10.48550/arxiv.2211.12656, fetched 2026-10-26

name: MixRT
head: Mixed Neural Representations For Real-Time NeRF Rendering
body: MixRT is a hybrid neural representation designed to enable real-time Neural Radiance Field (NeRF) rendering on edge devices by decomposing the scene into three complementary components: a low-quality triangle mesh for coarse geometry, a view-dependent displacement map for surface calibration, and a compressed NeRF model stored in an Instant-NGP hash table for density and color. It distinguishes itself from sibling methods like Vosh by explicitly leveraging distinct graphics hardware units—rasterizers, texture mapping units, and SIMD units—via WebGL APIs to bypass the computational bottlenecks of dense ray-marching, achieving real-time frame rates where other hybrid approaches fail to do so. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: A set of input images for training; a low-quality triangle mesh; a view-dependent displacement map; a compressed NeRF model (Instant-NGP format). Outputs: A rendered 2D image (color and optionally depth) for a given camera pose. Data Structures: 1. Triangle Mesh: Standard format containing geometric vertex coordinates, texture coordinates, and polygonal face elements. Per-vertex appearance parameters are not stored. The mesh is post-processed with vertex order optimization to improve cache hit rates for neighboring triangles. 2. View-Dependent Displacement Map: A texture map storing spherical harmonics (SH) coefficients and scale factors. These are accessed via texture coordinates associated with the mesh vertices. 3. Compressed NeRF Model: An Instant-NGP [24] representation consisting of a 3D embedding grid stored as a compact 1D hash table, followed by a small Multi-Layer Perceptron (MLP). Hash Table: Configured with a shrunk number of levels and an enlarged table size to optimize for rendering speed. MLP: 2 hidden layers with 64 units each. Scene Configuration: The unbounded scene domain is mapped into a finite sphere using the contraction function from [4] for the NeRF model components. The low-quality mesh and displacement map remain in their original unbounded space to leverage optimized rasterization pipelines common in graphics hardware. Rendering Pipeline (Numbered Steps): 1. Mesh Rasterization: Use rasterizer hardware to rasterize the low-quality triangle mesh. Determine the ray-mesh intersection point, denoted as p. 2. Displacement Calibration: Leverage texture mapping units to access the displacement map using the texture coordinates associated with the intersection point. Retrieve the spherical harmonics (SH) coefficients and scale. Compute the calibrated point p{cali} by applying the displacement to p. 3. Feature Retrieval: Process p{cali} using SIMD units. Query the 3D embedding grid (stored as a hash table) to retrieve embeddings for the eight closest vertices to p{cali}. 4. Interpolation: Perform trilinear interpolation of the eight retrieved embeddings to obtain the final feature vector for p{cali}. 5. Color and Density Prediction: Feed the interpolated embeddings into the small MLP (2 layers, 64 hidden units) to obtain the corresponding density and view-dependent color. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def renderpixel(cameraray, mesh, displacementmap, hashtable, mlp): # Step 1: Mesh Rasterization # Use rasterizer hardware to find intersection p = rasterizemesh(cameraray, mesh) # Step 2: Displacement Calibration # Access texture map using coordinates from mesh at p shcoeffs, scale = displacementmap.sample(p.texturecoords) # Compute calibrated point pcali # Note: Exact displacement formula depends on SH basis functions # pcali = p + displacement(shcoeffs, scale, cameradirection) pcali = applydisplacement(p, shcoeffs, scale, cameraray.direction) # Step 3 & 4: Feature Retrieval and Interpolation # Query hash table for 8 closest vertices to pcali # Hash table stores 3D embeddings embeddings = hashtable.query8neighbors(pcali) # Trilinear interpolation of embeddings features = trilinearinterpolate(embeddings, pcali) # Step 5: MLP Prediction # MLP: 2 layers, 64 hidden units density, color = mlp.forward(features) return color, density Parameters and Typical Values: Mesh Complexity: Approximately 15 MB storage size. MLP Architecture: 2 layers, 64 hidden units per layer. Hash Table Configuration: Number of levels is shrunk; hash table size is enlarged. Resolution: 1280x720. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Real-Time Failure: Directly combining a low-quality mesh with a standard Instant-NGP hash table retains storage efficiency but fails to achieve real-time rendering speeds due to bottlenecks in the number of hash table levels. The hash table structure must be modified (shrinking levels, enlarging size) to boost speed. Geometry Quality: High-quality geometry (many triangles) is not necessary for photorealistic rendering if supported by the displacement map and hash table color field. Performance: Achieves over 30 FPS at 1280x720 resolution on a MacBook M1 Pro laptop. Quality: Achieves 0.2 PSNR higher than state-of-the-art methods in indoor scenes of the Unbounded-360 dataset. Storage: Consumes less than 80% of the storage size of state-of-the-art methods (e.g., BakedSDF uses >300 MB, MixRT uses ~15 MB). Scaling: The method is designed for edge devices and leverages WebGL APIs, making it compatible with cross-platform graphics libraries and existing computer graphics toolchains. Strengths: Maximizes utilization of diverse hardware resources (Rasterizer, Texture Mapping Units, SIMD Units); small storage footprint; real-time speed on consumer hardware. Limitations: Relies on the quality of the low-quality mesh for coarse geometry; performance depends on WebGL implementation efficiency on the target device. MixRT was introduced in 2024 by authors including Interni et al.. It addresses the limitation of NeRF's slow rendering speed on edge devices, challenging the convention that high-quality geometry (substantial triangles) is necessary for photorealistic rendering. The method builds on the observation that a low-quality mesh combined with a hash table color field can achieve higher PSNR than a high-quality mesh with 5x more triangles while consuming only 0.26x the storage size. It further refines Instant-NGP [24] by modifying its hash table structure to align with WebGL frameworks, enabling real-time rendering on devices equipped with browsers. MixRT: Mixed Neural Representations For Real-Time NeRF Rendering, https://doi.org/10.1109/3dv62453.2024.00087, fetched 2026-10-27

name: LidaRF Hybrid Representation
head: LidaRF
body: LidaRF is a neural radiance field method for street scenes that fuses explicit LiDAR point cloud features with an implicit hash-based grid representation to improve geometry and rendering quality under sparse and collinear camera trajectories. It differs from prior LiDAR-only NeRF approaches by avoiding low-resolution and incomplete rendering caused by sparse LiDAR coverage and limited field of view; instead, it combines explicit LiDAR geometry with a high-resolution implicit grid. Inputs: A set of LiDAR point clouds from all frames of a sequence. Camera poses and intrinsics for the frames. Image observations for color supervision. Outputs: A hybrid feature representation consisting of LiDAR embeddings and a hash-based feature grid. Rendered images via standard volume rendering. Data Structures: 1. Voxel Grid: A sparse 3D grid constructed from aggregated LiDAR points. Each occupied voxel cell stores a 3-dimensional feature vector representing the averaged spatial position of all LiDAR points assigned to that cell. 2. LiDAR Embeddings (P): A set \{(pi, fi) | i = 1,..., N\}, where pi is the 3D spatial position and fi is an n-dimensional neural feature vector extracted by a 3D sparse UNet. 3. Hash-based Feature Grid: An implicit grid storing features for the background and regions not covered by LiDAR. The specific hash function and grid resolution are not detailed in the sources. Algorithm Steps: 1. Aggregate LiDAR Data: Aggregate LiDAR point clouds from all frames of the entire sequence to construct a denser point cloud set. 2. Voxelize: Voxelize the aggregated point clouds into a voxel grid. For each voxel cell, average the spatial positions of all points falling into that cell to produce a single 3-dimensional feature vector per voxel. 3. Encode Geometry: Encode the scene geometry features using a 3D sparse UNet operating on the voxel grid to capture local and global contextual information. The 3D sparse UNet takes the voxel grid along with its 3-dim features as input and outputs neural volumetric features. 4. Form LiDAR Embeddings: Yield LiDAR embeddings P = \{(pi, fi) | i = 1,..., N\}, where each point i is located at pi and associated with a vector fi, which is the neural feature of the voxel cell it resides in, encoding the local and global geometry around pi. 5. Query Hybrid Features: For a sample point x along a ray, query its LiDAR feature if it resides within the voxel grid. If not, or to combine with the implicit representation, query the hash-based feature grid. The specific fusion mechanism of the LiDAR features and the hash-based features is not detailed in the sources. 6. Decode: Feed the hybrid features into MLPs to decode color c and density \sigma. 7. Render: Apply standard volume rendering to generate the final image. Parameters: LiDAR Aggregation: All frames of the sequence are used. Voxel Feature Dimension: 3 dimensions (averaged spatial position) before UNet encoding. UNet Architecture: 3D sparse UNet. Feature Dimension after UNet: n dimensions (not specified). Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Sparse LiDAR Coverage: Relying on LiDAR features alone results in low-resolution rendering due to the sparse nature of LiDAR points. Limited Field of View: LiDAR does not cover the entire scene (e.g., building surfaces above a certain height), yielding blank rendering in those regions if not fused with the implicit grid. Occlusion: Depth supervision from LiDAR must account for occlusion. Strengths: Improves geometry and rendering quality in street scenes, particularly under sparse and collinear camera trajectories. Combines the geometric guidance of LiDAR with the completeness of a high-resolution implicit grid. Limitations: Requires LiDAR data. Performance depends on the quality and density of the aggregated LiDAR point clouds. Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory: Not given in the sources. LidaRF was introduced in the paper "LidaRF: Delving into Lidar for Neural Radiance Field on Street Scenes". It addresses the limitations of previous LiDAR-only NeRF approaches, such as [9], which suffered from low-resolution rendering and incomplete coverage due to sparse LiDAR data and limited field of view. The method leverages denser LiDAR points accumulated across frames as depth supervision while accounting for occlusion, leading to extra losses L{ds} and L{aug} in addition to the original losses from Nerfactor L{nerfacto}. name: Explicit Stage for Inverse Rendering
head: Explicit Stage, Mesh-based Refinement
body: The Explicit Stage refines a coarse shape and appearance reconstruction obtained from an implicit stage by converting a continuous implicit field into a discrete mesh and jointly optimizing vertex positions and spatially varying BRDF (SVBRDF) maps. Unlike purely implicit methods, this stage uses a mesh-based framework, allowing for better handling of complex light transport and avoiding the stair-case artifacts associated with low-resolution marching cubes in implicit-only approaches. Inputs: Optimized implicit geometric function \phi(\cdot; \theta^g) and reflectance field B(\cdot; \theta^a) from the implicit stage. n input images Ij with known illumination and viewing conditions \thetas for j=1, \dots, n. Optional: Anti-aliased mask images Sj for each input image. Outputs: Refined mesh geometry M (vertex positions). Refined SVBRDF maps (diffuse albedo kd, specular albedo ks, surface roughness \alpha). Optimized parameters (\theta^g, \theta^a). Data Structures: Mesh M: Defined by vertex positions and connectivity, with BRDF parameters cached at each vertex. SVBRDF Maps: 2D texture maps generated via UV parameterization of the mesh. Algorithm Steps: 1. Iso-surface Extraction: Convert the implicit representation \phi(\cdot; \theta^g) into an initial explicit mesh \tilde{M}0 using iso-surface extraction (e.g., marching cubes). This step is not differentiable. 2. UV Parameterization: Use the Boundary First Flattening (BFF) method [SC17] to UV-parameterize the mesh \tilde{M}0. 3. SVBRDF Initialization: Generate initial SVBRDF maps based on the reflectance field B(\cdot; \theta^a) from the implicit stage. Cache BRDF parameter values (kd, ks, \alpha) at each mesh vertex. 4. Joint Optimization: Perform a second inverse-rendering optimization using a mesh-based framework [LZBD21] that jointly optimizes the position of each mesh vertex and the value of each pixel in the SVBRDF maps. 5. Vertex Update: Update mesh vertex positions using the approach by Nicolet et al. [NJJ21] to avoid expensive continuous collision detection and handling. 6. Mask Supervision (Optional): If mask images Sj are available, include an extra loss term \lambda{\text{mask}} L{\text{mask}}(\thetag). Formulas: The optimization solves for (\theta^g, \theta^a): (\theta^g, \theta^a) = \arg \min{\thetag, \thetaa} L(\thetag, \thetaa) where the total loss L is: L(\thetag, \thetaa) = L{\text{img}}(\thetag, \thetaa) + \lambda{\text{reg}} L{\text{reg}}(\thetag, \thetaa) The image loss L{\text{img}} is: L{\text{img}}(\thetag, \thetaa) = \sum{j=1}^n \| R(\thetag, \thetaa, \thetas^{(j)}) - Ij \|^2 The regularization loss L{\text{reg}} encourages \phi to be a signed-distance function (unit-length gradients): L{\text{reg}}(\thetag, \thetaa) = \sumi (\|\nablax \phi(xi; \thetag)\| - 1)^2 If mask supervision is used, the additional term is: \lambda{\text{mask}} L{\text{mask}}(\thetag) = \sum{j=1}^n \| R{\text{mask}}(\thetag, \thetas^{(j)}) - Sj \|^2 where R{\text{mask}} renders only an anti-aliased mask, R renders the scene, \lambda{\text{reg}} and \lambda{\text{mask}} are loss weights, and xi are sample points. Parameters: \lambda{\text{reg}}: Hyper-parameter controlling the weight of the regularization term, \lambda{\text{reg}} \in \mathbb{R}{\ge 0}. \lambda{\text{mask}}: Weight for the mask supervision loss (if used). Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Non-differentiable Extraction: The initial iso-surface extraction does not need to be differentiable, but errors here propagate to the optimization. Collision Handling: Using older geometric processing libraries (e.g., elTopo [BB09]) requires expensive continuous collision detection, which the recommended approach [NJJ21] avoids. Performance: Caching BRDF parameters at vertices and reusing the mesh for multiple camera views in a minibatch reduces computational overhead. A two-stage inverse rendering pipeline that combines implicit and explicit geometric representations to solve physics-based inverse rendering problems, supporting topology changes and differentiable rendering of complex effects. It separates the reconstruction into a coarse implicit stage for robust topology handling and a fine explicit stage for high-fidelity appearance and shape refinement using mesh-based differentiable rendering. Unlike purely implicit methods (e.g., DVR, IDR) that struggle with complex light transport, or purely explicit methods that require good initialization, this pipeline leverages the topological flexibility of implicit fields and the rendering efficiency of explicit meshes. Choose it when high-fidelity appearance and geometry are required, and the scene allows for mesh-based representation. Complexity: The optimization jointly updates vertex positions and SVBRDF pixels, which can be computationally intensive, but caching BRDF values and reusing meshes for minibatches amortizes overhead. Strengths: Handles complex light transport better than implicit-only methods; avoids stair-case artifacts from low-resolution marching cubes; supports topology changes during optimization. Limitations: Requires a good initial implicit reconstruction; mesh-based optimization can be sensitive to initialization; UV parameterization may introduce distortions. When to use: When high-fidelity appearance and geometry are required, and the scene allows for mesh-based representation. Particularly useful when complex light transport effects are significant. The method originates from the work by Cai et al. (2022) on physics-based inverse rendering using combined implicit and explicit geometries. It builds upon the implicit stage framework by Yariv et al. [YKM20] (idr) and the mesh-based inverse rendering framework by Luan et al. [LZBD21]. The approach leverages MeshSDF [RLR20] for iso-surface extraction and Nicolet et al. [NJJ21] for efficient vertex updates. name: Combined Implicit and Explicit Inverse Rendering Pipeline
head: Two-stage Inverse Rendering Pipeline
body: This method solves physics-based inverse rendering problems by combining implicit and explicit geometric representations to support topology changes and differentiable rendering of complex light-transport effects. It separates the reconstruction into a coarse implicit stage for robust topology handling and a fine explicit stage for high-fidelity appearance and shape refinement using mesh-based differentiable rendering. Unlike purely implicit methods (e.g., DVR, IDR) that struggle with complex light transport, or purely explicit methods that require good initialization, this pipeline leverages the topological flexibility of implicit fields and the rendering efficiency of explicit meshes. The pipeline consists of two sequential stages: an implicit optimization stage followed by an explicit refinement stage. Inputs: A collection of N geometrically calibrated input images I1, \dots, IN. Camera poses and intrinsics for each image. Initial geometric parameters \thetag for the implicit field. Initial optical parameters \thetaa for the appearance field. Outputs: A reconstructed 3D mesh M representing the object surface. SVBRDF maps (diffuse albedo kd, specular albedo ks, roughness \alpha) associated with the mesh. 1. Implicit Field (\phi): A function \phi: \mathbb{R}^3 \times \Thetag \to \mathbb{R} defining the surface as the zero level set. In practice, this is implemented as a Signed Distance Function (SDF) controlled by parameters \thetag. 2. Explicit Mesh (M): A triangle mesh defined by vertex positions V and connectivity F. Vertices are updated during the explicit stage. 3. Appearance Field (B): A reflectance field mapping surface points to BRDF parameters. Implemented as SVBRDF maps storing kd, ks, \alpha, controlled by parameters \thetaa. 4. Lighting Model: The incident radiance Li(x, \omegai) supports environmental illumination, soft shadows, and interreflections. Stage 1: Implicit Optimization 1. Initialize: Define the object surface M(\thetag) as the zero level set of \phi(x; \thetag) = 0. 2. Render: For each input image, compute the rendered radiance L{rendered} using a differentiable renderer that supports implicit surfaces. The source notes that Monte Carlo sampling over implicit surfaces is challenging, but this stage focuses on coarse shape recovery where topology changes are critical. 3. Compute Loss: Calculate a reconstruction loss between L{rendered} and the target image. 4. Optimize: Update geometric parameters \thetag to minimize the loss. This stage allows topology changes without remeshing. 5. Extract: Once convergence is reached, obtain the coarse implicit geometry. Stage 2: Explicit Refinement 1. Iso-surface Extraction: Apply a non-differentiable iso-surface extraction algorithm (specifically MeshSDF, a differentiable marching cubes variant) to convert the implicit surface \phi(x; \thetag) = 0 into an explicit triangle mesh M. 2. Initialize Appearance: Initialize SVBRDF maps (kd, ks, \alpha) for the mesh. 3. Differentiable Rendering: Render the mesh M using physics-based differentiable rendering. This involves solving the rendering equation and its differential form. Rendering Equation: L(x, \omegao) = \int{S^2} Li(x, \omegai) fr(x, \omegai, \omegao) d\sigma(\omegai) where Li is incident radiance, fr is the cosine-weighted BRDF, and \sigma is the solid-angle measure. Differential Rendering Equation: \frac{d}{d\theta} L(x, \omegao) = \int{S^2} \frac{d}{d\theta}[Li fr] d\sigma(\omegai) + \int{\partial S^2} v\perp(\omegai) \Delta Li fr d\ell(\omegai) where \partial S^2 is the domain of jump discontinuity points of Li, v\perp captures the change rate of the discontinuity boundary, and \Delta Li is the difference in Li across the boundary. 4. Optimize: Jointly optimize: Shape: Update mesh vertex positions. Appearance: Update pixel values in SVBRDF maps (\thetaa). 5. Output: Return the final mesh and SVBRDF maps. Unverified code. Topology Changes: Explicit mesh representations suffer from difficulty in handling topology changes during gradient-based optimization, requiring good initial geometry or frequent remeshing. The implicit stage mitigates this. Implicit Rendering Difficulty: Implicit representations are difficult to use for physics-based differentiable rendering because Monte Carlo sampling over implicitly expressed surfaces is challenging due to difficulty in parameterization. The pipeline avoids this by switching to explicit meshes for the final rendering stage. Discontinuity Boundaries: In differentiable rendering, the boundary integral term in the differential rendering equation is crucial when the parameter \theta controls scene geometry (e.g., mesh vertex positions), as it can be the major contributor to the resulting gradient. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Measured Performance: The pipeline is computationally more efficient than existing differentiable-sphere-tracing based methods (e.g., DVR, IDR). Strengths: Supports topology changes during optimization. Supports complex light-transport effects such as environmental illumination, soft shadow, and interreflection. Enables high-fidelity 3D reconstruction of objects with complex topologies. Limitations: Requires two stages, potentially increasing implementation complexity. Implicit stage may be less accurate for fine details compared to explicit methods. When to Use: When reconstructing objects with complex topologies that may change during optimization, or when high-fidelity appearance with complex lighting effects is required. When Not to Use: When computational resources are extremely limited and topology changes are not expected, or when simple lighting models suffice. Origin: The method was introduced in the paper "Physics-Based Inverse Rendering using Combined Implicit and Explicit Geometries". History: Inverse rendering has been a long-standing problem in computer vision and graphics. Previous mesh-based techniques struggled with topology changes, while implicit methods struggled with differentiable rendering. This method bridges the gap by combining both.
