N: Number of segments. deltas: Array of length N, segment lengths deltai. sigmas: Array of length N, densities sigmai. colors: Array of length N+1, colors c0 to cN (cN is background). backgroundcolor: Scalar intensity (typically 1.0) for background light. Returns: gradsigmas (N,), gradcolors (N+1,) """ # 1. Compute Transmittance Ti # Ti is product from j=0 to i-1 of exp(-deltaj sigmaj) # T0 = 1 T = [0.0] (N + 1) T[0] = 1.0 for i in range(1, N + 1): T[i] = T[i-1] math.exp(-deltas[i-1] sigmas[i-1]) # 2. Compute Weights wi # wi = Ti - T{i+1} for i < N # wN = TN w = [0.0] (N + 1) for i in range(N): w[i] = T[i] - T[i+1] w[N] = T[N] # 3. Compute Color Gradients # dC/dci = wi gradcolors = list(w) # 4. Compute Density Gradients # dC/dsigmai = deltai [ ci T{i+1} - sum{k=i+1}^N ck wk ] gradsigmas = [0.0] N for i in range(N): # Term 1: ci T{i+1} term1 = colors[i] T[i+1] # Term 2: sum{k=i+1}^N ck wk sumterm = 0.0 for k in range(i+1, N+1): sumterm += colors[k] w[k] gradsigmas[i] = deltas[i] (term1 - sumterm) return gradsigmas, gradcolors This variant extends the derivative computation to the pixel level, modeling pixel intensity I as the inner product between radiance L and a reconstruction kernel K over the pixel footprint P. The differentiated intensity \hat{I} includes a boundary integral term accounting for discontinuities in L along the boundary of the pixel domain \partial0,1)^2, which is necessary when camera parameters depend on scene parameters. Time Complexity: O(N) per ray for precomputing transmittance and weights, and O(N) for computing gradients. The density derivative summation is O(N^2) if implemented naively, but can be optimized to O(N) by maintaining a running sum of ck wk from N down to 0. Memory Complexity: O(N) to store Ti, wi, and intermediate sums. Strengths: Provides exact gradients, enabling stable and efficient convergence during [PlenOctree fine-tuning. Handles SH colors naturally via the chain rule. Limitations: Assumes piecewise constant density and color within segments. Requires careful handling of numerical stability for very small or large \sigmai \deltai values (e.g., using expm1 for small arguments). When to use: When optimizing PlenOctree parameters directly using gradient-based methods like SGD. When not to use: When using differentiable rendering techniques that require pixel-space derivatives with complex camera models or non-constant kernels. The method was introduced in the context of PlenOctrees for real-time rendering of Neural Radiance Fields (NeRFs). It builds on the NeRF volume rendering formulation and provides the necessary gradients for optimizing the octree structure's density and color attributes directly, rather than relying on numerical approximations. The approach is detailed in Appendix B.3 of the PlenOctrees paper. name: PlenOctree Fine-tuning
head: Accelerated NeRF Training
body: A process to train a converted PlenOctree on original training images to accelerate rendering, as it no longer involves neural networks. It builds on the PlenOctree representation, which converts a trained NeRF into a hierarchical grid of spherical harmonics. This approach accelerates NeRF-based rendering by 5 orders of magnitude without loss in image quality. Inputs: A converted PlenOctree, original training images with camera poses. Outputs: An optimized PlenOctree with refined leaf parameters. Data Structures: Each leaf node stores spherical harmonics (SH) coefficients for color and a density value. Exact field layouts, sizes, and bit packing are not given in the sources. The octree structure remains static during optimization; only leaf values are updated. Steps: 1. Initialize: Stop NeRF training early and convert the model into a PlenOctree. 2. Sample Rays: For each training image, cast rays through each pixel. 3. Volume Rendering: Traverse the octree for each ray. At each intersected leaf node, evaluate the SH color and density. Compute accumulated color and transmittance using volume rendering integration. 4. Compute Loss: Compare rendered pixel color with ground truth training image pixel. Calculate loss (typically Mean Squared Error). 5. Backpropagate: Compute gradients of the loss with respect to leaf node parameters using automatic differentiation. 6. Update: Update leaf node parameters using gradient descent. 7. Iterate: Repeat steps 2–6 until convergence or a fixed number of epochs. Formulas: The volume rendering equation for a ray \mathbf{r} is: C(\mathbf{r}) = \sum{i=1}^N Ti \alphai ci where Ti = \exp\left(-\sum{j=1}^{i-1} \sigmaj \deltaj\right) is the accumulated transmittance, \alphai = 1 - \exp(-\sigmai \deltai) is the opacity, \sigmai is the density, \deltai is the segment length, and ci is the color from SH evaluation. Parameters: Learning rate: Not given in the sources. Optimizer: Not specified in the sources. Epochs: Not given in the sources. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision, boundaries, and degenerate input handling: Not given in the sources. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def trainplenoctree(plenoctree, trainingdata, epochs, learningrate, numsamples): EPSILON = 1e-4 for epoch in range(epochs): for image, pose in trainingdata: for pixel in image: rayorigin = pose.cameracenter raydirection = pose.unproject(pixel.uv) accumulatedcolor = [0.0, 0.0, 0.0] accumulatedtransmittance = 1.0 tnear = pose.nearplane tfar = pose.farplane delta = (tfar - tnear) / numsamples while tnear < tfar and accumulatedtransmittance > EPSILON: leaf = plenoctree.query(tnear) if leaf is not None: color = leaf.evaluatesh(raydirection) density = leaf.evaluatedensity() alpha = 1.0 - math.exp(-density delta) for c in range(3): accumulatedcolor[c] += accumulatedtransmittance alpha color[c] accumulatedtransmittance = (1.0 - alpha) tnear += delta loss = sum((accumulatedcolor[c] - pixel.rgb[c]) 2 for c in range(3)) / 3.0 gradients = computegradients(loss, plenoctree.parameters) for param in plenoctree.parameters: param -= learningrate gradients[param] EfficientNeRF is an improvement on PlenOctree that uses spherical harmonics and caches the trained scene in a tree, with specific optimizations for training speed. It uses a momentum density voxel grid to store predicted density via exponential weighted average updates, discarding zero-density points during coarse sampling. During fine sampling, it employs a pivot system where pivot points are defined as points xi for which Ti \alphai > \epsilon, where \epsilon is a predefined threshold, and Ti and \alphai are transmittance and alpha values. Only points near pivot points are considered during fine sampling. This speeds up training time by a factor of 8 over baseline NeRF and results in rendering speeds comparable to FastNeRF and exceeding baseline NeRF by thousands-fold. Time Complexity: Training is significantly faster than full NeRF optimization because it avoids neural network forward/backward passes during the fine-tuning phase, relying instead on direct SH evaluation and volume rendering. Memory Complexity: Depends on the PlenOctree resolution and SH order. The momentum density voxel grid in EfficientNeRF reduces sampling cost. Measured Performance: Accelerates NeRF-based rendering by 5 orders of magnitude without loss in image quality. EfficientNeRF variant speeds up training by a factor of 8 over baseline NeRF and achieves rendering speeds thousands-fold faster than baseline NeRF. Strengths: High rendering speed, good image quality, practical for real-time applications. Limitations: Requires a pre-converted PlenOctree; quality depends on the initial conversion. PlenOctree Fine-tuning was introduced in the paper "PlenOctrees For Real-time Rendering of Neural Radiance Fields (NeRFs)". It builds on the PlenOctree representation, which converts a trained NeRF into a hierarchical grid of spherical harmonics. The method addresses the need for faster training and rendering of NeRFs by decoupling the heavy neural network training from the final optimization phase. EfficientNeRF further refined this approach with momentum density grids and pivot systems. name: Sparse Voxel Grid Optimization
head: SVRaster, Sparse Voxel Grid Training
body: Sparse Voxel Grid Optimization is a differentiable volume rendering method that represents a scene as an adaptive octree of sparse voxels, optimizing density and color attributes directly in grid memory rather than through a neural network. It solves the high memory overhead and slow convergence of MLP-based NeRFs and the lack of explicit geometric priors in density-based sparse methods by combining sparse voxel rasterization with adaptive subdivision. Unlike PlenOctree Optimization, which uses octrees primarily for compression and hierarchical storage of pre-trained features, this method actively grows and prunes the voxel structure during training to match scene complexity, enabling real-time rendering speeds comparable to 3D Gaussian Splatting while maintaining higher geometric fidelity. The method optimizes a sparse voxel grid using differentiable volume rendering. It builds on the shared principles of Hierarchical Grid Optimization, specifically the evaluation of the volume rendering equation and gradient propagation. Inputs: A set of M training images with known camera poses \mathbf{P}m and intrinsics. Initial scene bounds (for bounded scenes) or a foreground bounding box plus background shell parameters (for unbounded scenes). Outputs: An optimized sparse voxel octree structure containing density \sigma and color \mathbf{c} (or spherical harmonics coefficients) for each active voxel. A rendered novel-view image \hat{C}(\mathbf{r}) for any ray \mathbf{r}. The scene is represented as an octree. Each node in the octree corresponds to a voxel in 3D space. Voxel Node: Contains attributes for the voxel volume. Density (\sigma): A scalar value representing the extinction coefficient. Color (\mathbf{c}): A vector (RGB) or spherical harmonics coefficients representing the emitted color. Children: Pointers to 8 child nodes if the voxel is subdivided. Morton Code: Voxels are sorted and accessed using 48-bit Morton codes (16 levels, 3 bits per level) to facilitate efficient ray traversal and sorting, replacing the 32-bit float sorting used in Gaussian splatting. Occupancy Cache: A mechanism to track active voxels to avoid processing empty space, particularly important for unbounded scenes. 1. Initialization: Start optimization from empty space. Set the raw density offset h{geo} = -10. Initialize the octree at level h{lv} = 6 (resulting in a 64^3 base grid) for the foreground main region. For unbounded scenes, add h{out} = 5 background shell levels, with a voxel count ratio h{ratio} = 2 times the number of foreground voxels. 2. Ray Tracing and Rasterization: For each pixel, cast a ray \mathbf{r} through the scene. Traverse the sparse octree to find intersecting voxels. Sort intersecting voxels by depth using Morton codes. Sample points within each voxel. Use K=1 sample point for novel-view synthesis and K=3 for mesh reconstruction. Compute transmittance Ti and color contribution using the standard emission-absorption model: \hat{C}(\mathbf{r}) = \sum{i=1}^N Ti (1 - \exp(-\sigmai \deltai)) \mathbf{c}i where Ti = \exp\left(-\sum{j=1}^{i-1} \sigmaj \deltaj\right). Apply early ray stopping if transmittance T < hT = 10^{-4}. Apply supersampling with scale h{ss} = 1.5 to reduce aliasing. 3. Loss Computation: Compute the total loss \mathcal{L} as a weighted sum of terms: \mathcal{L} = \lambda{\text{ssim}} \mathcal{L}{\text{ssim}} + \lambda{\text{T}} \mathcal{L}{\text{T}} + \lambda{\text{dist}} \mathcal{L}{\text{dist}} + \lambda{\text{R}} \mathcal{L}{\text{R}} + \lambda{\text{tv}} \mathcal{L}{\text{tv}} \mathcal{L}{\text{ssim}}: Structural Similarity Index Loss. \mathcal{L}{\text{T}}: Transmittance loss, encouraging final ray transmittances to be 0 or 1. \mathcal{L}{\text{dist}}: Distortion loss. \mathcal{L}{\text{R}}: Per-point RGB loss (L1 or L2). \mathcal{L}{\text{tv}}: Total Variation loss on the sparse density grid to smooth noise. For mesh extraction tasks, add depth-normal consistency losses: \mathcal{L}{\text{mesh}} = \lambda{\text{n-dmean}} \mathcal{L}{\text{n-dmean}} + \lambda{\text{n-dmed}} \mathcal{L}{\text{n-dmed}} These losses align rendered normals with depth-derived normals from mean and median depth. 4. Optimization Step: Perform backpropagation to compute gradients with respect to voxel densities and colors. Update parameters using an optimizer (e.g., Adam). 5. Adaptive Subdivision and Pruning: Every h{every} = 1,000 iterations, prune and subdivide voxels. Pruning: Remove voxels with density below a threshold h{prune}. The threshold is linearly scaled from 0.0001 to 0.05 over the training duration. Subdivision: Subdivide voxels with high density or high gradient magnitude. The subdivision percentage is set to h{percent} = 5. Repeat until the target number of iterations is reached (typically 20,000). Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def sparsevoxelgridoptimization(trainingimages, cameraposes, numiterations=20000): # 1. Initialization octree = Octree(initiallevel=6) # 64^3 base grid rawdensityoffset = -10 octree.setrawdensityoffset(rawdensityoffset) # For unbounded scenes octree.addbackgroundshells(numlevels=5, ratio=2.0) # Hyperparameters hevery = 1000 hT = 1e-4 hss = 1.5 currentprunethreshold = 0.0001 maxprunethreshold = 0.05 # 2. Training Loop for iteration in range(1, numiterations + 1): # Sample a batch of rays from training images rays = samplerays(trainingimages, cameraposes) # Forward Pass: Sparse Voxel Rendering renderedcolors = [] for ray in rays: # Traverse octree and sort voxels by Morton code intersectingvoxels = octree.traverseandsort(ray) # Sample points within voxels (K=1 for NVS) samples = samplepoints(intersectingvoxels, K=1) # Compute transmittance and color T = 1.0 color = torch.zeros(3) for sample in samples: if T < hT: break sigma = octree.getdensity(sample.voxel) c = octree.getcolor(sample.voxel) delta = sample.distance # Emission-absorption model alpha = 1.0 - torch.exp(-sigma delta) weight = T alpha color += weight c T = torch.exp(-sigma delta) renderedcolors.append(color) renderedcolors = torch.stack(renderedcolors) groundtruth = getgroundtruthcolors(rays) # Loss Computation lossssim = computessimloss(renderedcolors, groundtruth) lossT = computetransmittanceloss(renderedcolors, rays) # Encourage T -> 0 or 1 lossdist = computedistortionloss(renderedcolors, rays) lossR = computergbloss(renderedcolors, groundtruth) losstv = computetotalvariationloss(octree.densitygrid) # Loss weights (example values, typically tuned) lambdassim = 0.2 lambdaT = 1.0 lambdadist = 0.1 lambdaR = 1.0 lambdatv = 0.01 totalloss = (lambdassim lossssim + lambdaT lossT + lambdadist lossdist + lambdaR lossR + lambdatv losstv) # Backward Pass totalloss.backward() # Optimizer Step optimizer.step() optimizer.zerograd() # Adaptive Subdivision and Pruning if iteration % hevery == 0: # Linearly scale prune threshold progress = iteration / numiterations currentprunethreshold = 0.0001 + (maxprunethreshold - 0.0001) progress # Prune low-density voxels octree.prune(threshold=currentprunethreshold) # Subdivide high-detail voxels octree.subdivide(percentage=0.05) return octree Exposure Variation: Scenes with severe exposure variation in training views can cause the method to produce clear brightness boundaries and "floaters" (spurious geometry), degrading PSNR and FPS. Memory Limits: Uniform high-resolution grids (e.g., 1024^3) cause Out Of Memory (OOM) errors on standard GPUs (e.g., 24GB VRAM), whereas the sparse approach handles these resolutions by only storing active voxels. Sorting Overhead: While Morton code sorting is efficient, it differs from the 32-bit float sorting in Gaussian splatting; performance varies by scene due to the number of contributing primitives. SVRecon is a surface reconstruction method that generalizes SVRaster by parametrizing each voxel with Signed Distance Function (SDF) values at its corners, enabling implicit geometry regularization and the extraction of watertight meshes. It addresses the limitation of SVRaster’s density-based representation, which lacks explicit geometric priors and suffers from depth bias, by introducing SDF-based continuity enforcement. Unlike 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) approaches that rely heavily on initial Structure-from-Motion (SfM) points, SVRecon exploits monocular depth cues more effectively without this dependency, producing sharper boundaries and smoother, hole-free surfaces. DirectVoxGO is a differentiable volume rendering method that optimizes a single, dense 3D voxel grid to represent a Neural Radiance Field (NeRF), eliminating the need for a neural network to map coordinates to features. It solves the slow convergence and high memory overhead of MLP-based NeRFs by storing density and color features directly in grid tensors, allowing for super-fast training convergence. It distinguishes itself from standard NeRF by replacing the coordinate-to-feature MLP with direct grid lookups and from sparse voxel methods by using a dense grid with occupancy caching and near-camera masking to handle unbounded scenes efficiently. The fused sparse voxel volume rendering backward pass computes gradients for spherical harmonics (SH) coefficients and spherical harmonics basis values during differentiable volume rendering. It specifically supports gradient accumulation for beta loss and sparsity loss regularization terms. This method is part of the JNeRF implementation, which utilizes a fused kernel approach to optimize memory bandwidth and compute throughput for sparse voxel grids. A technique where voxels are subdivided adaptively based on detail requirements, as opposed to uniform subdivision until a fixed grid resolution is reached. On Mip-NeRF360, adaptive voxel size achieves LPIPS 0.200, PSNR 28.01, FPS 171, while uniform 512^3 achieves LPIPS 0.326, PSNR 25.37, FPS 190. Uniform 256^3 achieves LPIPS 0.444, PSNR 23.98, FPS 457. Uniform 1024^3 resolution causes Out Of Memory (OOM) on a machine with 24GB GPU memory. The uniform 512^3 variant outperforms Plenoxels (640^3 grid) which achieves LPIPS 0.452, PSNR 23.29, FPS <10. Uniform voxel size variant subdivides all voxels at certain training iterations until the grid resolution of the foreground main region reaches 256^3, 512^3, or 1024^3. Time Complexity: Training time is significantly reduced compared to MLP-based NeRFs. Typical training takes ~15 minutes for 20,000 iterations on standard datasets. Fast-train variants can achieve >3x training speedup by scaling iteration-related hyperparameters by 0.3. Memory Complexity: Memory usage scales with the number of active voxels, not the full grid resolution. This allows handling of high-resolution details that would cause OOM in uniform grids (e.g., 1024^3). However, it uses more voxel primitives than Gaussian splatting, resulting in larger model size and higher GPU memory usage than 3DGS in some scenes. Rendering Performance: Achieves real-time rendering speeds (FPS 121-125 on Mip-NeRF360, up to 366 on Deep Blending) comparable to 3D Gaussian Splatting. Fast-render variants with h{ss}=1.5 and h{prune}=0.15 achieve >2x FPS with moderate quality reduction. Strengths: High visual quality (low LPIPS), ability to extract watertight meshes via TSDF fusion and Marching Cubes, no dependency on SfM points for geometry, and efficient handling of unbounded scenes. Limitations: Struggles with scenes having severe exposure variation, leading to floaters and boundary artifacts. Performance can be scene-dependent due to the variable number of contributing primitives. When to use: When real-time rendering and high geometric fidelity (mesh extraction) are required, and the scene has moderate to high complexity where uniform grids are too large. When not to use: For scenes with extreme photometric variations where floaters become problematic, or when minimal GPU memory is available and the scene is very simple (where dense grids or Gaussians might be more efficient). Sparse Voxel Grid Optimization, specifically in the form of SVRaster, was introduced in the paper "Sparse Voxels Rasterization: Real-time High-fidelity Radiance Field Rendering". It emerged as a response to the limitations of both neural field methods (slow training, high memory) and Gaussian splatting (lack of explicit geometry, dependency on SfM). The method leverages the efficiency of sparse voxel structures for rasterization and the flexibility of adaptive octrees for representation. It is used in novel-view synthesis and 3D reconstruction tasks, particularly where mesh extraction is desired. name: Adaptive Voxel Size
head: Adaptive subdivision, non-uniform voxel grid
body: Adaptive Voxel Size is a hierarchical grid optimization technique where voxels are subdivided based on local detail requirements rather than using a uniform grid resolution. It solves the memory and performance bottlenecks of uniform high-resolution grids by allocating fine voxels only where necessary, achieving higher visual quality (LPIPS 0.200, PSNR 28.01) than uniform 512^3 grids while maintaining competitive rendering speeds (171 FPS). Unlike uniform variants that subdivide all voxels to a fixed depth, this method dynamically adjusts granularity, outperforming fully-explicit voxel approaches like Plenoxels in both quality and speed. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A set of training views, camera poses, and an initial sparse voxel grid structure. Output: A hierarchical voxel grid with variable resolution per region, and optimized radiance field parameters (color, density) for each active voxel. Data Structures: The grid is typically represented as a sparse structure (e.g., hash map or octree) mapping spatial coordinates to voxel data. Each active voxel stores: Spatial bounds (min/max coordinates). Radiance field parameters (e.g., spherical harmonics coefficients for color, density). Subdivision status (leaf or internal node). Steps: 1. Initialization: Start with a coarse voxel grid covering the scene bounding box. 2. Error Estimation: During training, evaluate the reconstruction error or gradient magnitude for each voxel. Voxels with high error or detail requirements are marked for subdivision. 3. Subdivision: Split marked voxels into 8 child voxels (in 3D). Update the grid structure to reflect the new hierarchy. 4. Optimization: Optimize the radiance field parameters for the new child voxels. 5. Iteration: Repeat steps 2-4 until convergence or a maximum depth is reached. Parameters: Subdivision Threshold: The error or gradient magnitude threshold above which a voxel is subdivided. Not given in the sources. Maximum Depth: The maximum number of subdivision levels. Not given in the sources. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Memory Usage: While adaptive grids save memory compared to uniform high-res grids, they can still consume significant memory if the scene has high detail everywhere. Uniform 1024^3 grids cause Out Of Memory (OOM) on 24GB GPUs, whereas adaptive grids manage this better. Boundary Artifacts: Sharp transitions between different resolution levels can cause visual artifacts. Not given in the sources. Precision: Sorting 48-bit Morton codes for primitive ordering is used instead of 32-bit floats, which may impact precision or sorting speed. Not given in the sources. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def adaptivesubdivision(grid, views, maxdepth): # grid: sparse voxel grid structure # views: training views # maxdepth: maximum subdivision depth currentdepth = 0 while currentdepth < maxdepth: # Estimate error for each voxel errors = estimatevoxelerrors(grid, views) # Identify voxels to subdivide voxelstosubdivide = [v for v in grid.activevoxels if errors[v] > threshold] if not voxelstosubdivide: break # Subdivide selected voxels for v in voxelstosubdivide: grid.subdivide(v) # Optimize parameters for new voxels optimizeradiancefield(grid, views) currentdepth += 1 return grid A technique to maintain interactivity for large brushes in 3D painting by refining the grid only to a resolution sufficient for brush detail, and coarsening the center of the brush to merge color. If a brush is applied to an already refined region, the grid is coarsened at the center of the brush conservatively to avoid destroying existing details. The coarsest refinement level is roughly 10 voxels corresponding to the brush radius. Time Complexity: Depends on the number of active voxels and the subdivision depth. Adaptive subdivision can be slower than uniform grids if many voxels are subdivided, but faster if detail is sparse. Memory Complexity: Significantly lower than uniform high-resolution grids. For example, adaptive voxel size avoids OOM issues that occur with uniform 1024^3 grids on 24GB GPUs. Measured Performance: On the MipNeRF-360 dataset, adaptive voxel size achieves LPIPS 0.200, PSNR 28.01, and FPS 171, compared to uniform 512^3 (LPIPS 0.326, PSNR 25.37, FPS 190) and uniform 256^3 (LPIPS 0.444, PSNR 23.98, FPS 457). It outperforms Plenoxels (640^3 grid, LPIPS 0.452, PSNR 23.29, FPS <10) in both quality and speed. Strengths: Better quality than uniform grids at similar or lower memory usage; avoids OOM for high-resolution scenes. Limitations: More complex implementation; performance can vary significantly across scenes. When to Use: When high visual quality is required and memory is a constraint, or when the scene has varying levels of detail. When Not to Use: When simplicity and speed are prioritized over quality, or when the scene is uniformly detailed. Adaptive voxel size is a technique used in radiance field optimization to improve the efficiency and quality of volume rendering. It was introduced in the context of sparse voxel grid optimization, where uniform grids were found to be inefficient for scenes with varying detail levels. The method has been applied in various research contexts, including novel-view synthesis and 3D painting. name: SVRecon
head: SVRaster with Signed Distance Functions
body: SVRecon is a surface reconstruction method that generalizes SVRaster by parametrizing each voxel with Signed Distance Function (SDF) values at its corners, enabling implicit geometry regularization and the extraction of watertight meshes. It addresses the limitation of SVRaster’s density-based representation, which lacks explicit geometric priors and suffers from depth bias, by introducing SDF-based continuity enforcement. Unlike 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) approaches that rely heavily on initial Structure-from-Motion (SfM) points, SVRecon leverages PI³ point-map priors aligned to ground-truth poses for initialization, producing sharper boundaries and smoother, hole-free surfaces. Inputs: Sparse voxel grid (initialized via PI³ point-map priors aligned to ground-truth poses), RGB images, and camera poses. Outputs: Watertight mesh extracted from the optimized SDF field. Data Structures: Voxel: Identified by index v = \{i, j, k\} at Octree level l. Voxel size is vs = ws \times 2^{-l}. SDF Values: Each voxel stores SDF values at its eight corners. Let d{ijk} denote the SDF value at corner (i,j,k) where i,j,k \in \{0,1\}. Hierarchical Indices: Parent–child and sibling relations are tracked via Morton codes and auxiliary fine-grid indices. Bitmask-based occupancy and neighbor search schemes are used for cross-voxel Laplacian smoothness. Steps: 1. Initialization: Initialize the sparse voxel grid using PI³ point-map priors aligned to ground-truth poses. Flip SDF signs to account for visual occlusion. 2. Trilinear Interpolation: For a ray passing through a voxel, compute the SDF at the sample point using trilinear interpolation of the eight corner SDF values. 3. Alpha Blending: SVRecon uses the NeuS Cumulative Distribution Function (CDF) to accumulate color and opacity along the ray. 4. Regularization: Apply a combination of losses: parent–child continuity loss, Laplacian loss over fine grid cells, and local Eikonal terms enforcing |\nabla \text{SDF}| = 1. Pseudocode: Unverified code. It starts with fully covered coarse sparse voxels, constantly optimized with RGB images. Key steps include: 1. Voxel Dropout: Enlarges global geometry consistency for tiny voxels during explicit geometry regularization. 3. Voxel Regularization: Aligns the voxel-level density field to the surfaces, facilitating accurate and sharp surface formation. name: Sparse Voxel Surface Regularization
head: GeoSVR regularization, SVSR
body: Sparse Voxel Surface Regularization (SVSR) is a set of geometric refinement techniques applied to sparse voxel representations to enforce global geometry consistency and eliminate depth bias during surface reconstruction. It addresses the limitation of extreme voxel locality, which makes plane-based regularization ineffective for enforcing regional constraints, by introducing voxel dropout, surface rectification, and scaling penalties. Unlike 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) approaches such as PGSR, which rely heavily on initial Structure-from-Motion (SfM) points and struggle in challenging areas, SVSR exploits monocular depth cues more effectively without this dependency. SVSR operates on a sparse voxel grid where each voxel is parametrized with Signed Distance Function (SDF) values at its corners, as defined in the parent method SVRecon. The method consists of three primary regularization steps applied during the optimization process. Inputs: Sparse voxel grid with corner SDF values, camera poses, input images, and optionally monocular depth estimates. Outputs: Refined voxel grid with improved geometric accuracy and reduced depth bias. The core data structure is the sparse voxel grid. Each active voxel v contains: Corner SDF values: d{ijk} for i,j,k \in \{0,1\}. Voxel uncertainty metric: uv, used to evaluate geometric reliability. 1. Voxel Dropout (Interval Sample): To simplify the learned scene and force tiny voxels to maintain global geometry consistency, a portion of voxels is randomly dropped out during geometry regularization. This is implemented as an interval sample where voxels are masked with a certain probability. This step prevents overfitting to local noise and encourages smoother global structures. 2. Surface Rectification: This step restricts the surface formation to be aligned with a unique voxel to reduce depth bias. It ensures that the implicit surface extracted from the voxel SDFs does not exhibit artifacts caused by misalignment between the voxel grid and the true surface. 3. Scaling Penalty: Based on the voxel uncertainty metric uv, a scaling penalty is applied to eliminate the participation of geometrically inaccurate large voxels in the surface formation. Voxels with high uncertainty are penalized, preventing them from contributing to the final mesh and thus improving sharpness and accuracy. A supplementary constraint uses monocular depth estimates to further refine geometry. Patch-wise Loss: Monocular depth is applied to the sparse voxel representation using a patch-wise loss function. Voxel-Uncertainty Depth Constraint: The depth loss is weighted adaptively based on voxel geometric uncertainty. This maximizes the utilization of external depth cues while avoiding quality degradation from unreliable depth estimates. Loss Coefficient: The coefficient for the depth constraint is adjusted during training to fit the best F1-score. The following pseudocode illustrates the regularization loss computation. Note that specific implementation details for "Surface Rectification" and "Voxel Dropout" sampling are abstracted as per source descriptions. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def computesvsrloss(voxelgrid, images, poses, monoculardepths=None): """ Computes the total loss for Sparse Voxel Surface Regularization. Args: voxelgrid: Sparse voxel grid with corner SDFs and uncertainty uv. images: Input RGB images. poses: Camera poses. monoculardepths: Optional monocular depth maps. Returns: totalloss: Scalar loss value. """ # 1. Base Rendering Loss (from parent SVRecon) # Render images from voxel grid and compare with ground truth renderedimages = rendervoxelgrid(voxelgrid, poses) renderingloss = mseloss(renderedimages, images) # 2. Voxel Dropout Regularization # Randomly drop out a portion of voxels to enforce global consistency # activevoxels = getactivevoxels(voxelgrid) # Mask voxels based on dropout probability dropoutmask = randomdropout(activevoxels, dropoutrate=0.5) # Typical rate maskedvoxels = applymask(activevoxels, dropoutmask) # Compute geometry consistency loss on masked voxels # Forces tiny voxels to keep global geometry consistency geometryconsistencyloss = computeglobalconsistencyloss(maskedvoxels) # 3. Surface Rectification # Restrict surface formation to be aligned with a unique voxel # Reduces depth bias surfacerectificationloss = computesurfacealignmentloss(voxelgrid) # 4. Scaling Penalty # Eliminate participation of geometrically inaccurate large voxels # Based on voxel uncertainty uv scalingpenaltyloss = computescalingpenalty(voxelgrid) totalloss = renderingloss + geometryconsistencyloss + \ surfacerectificationloss + scalingpenaltyloss # 5. Scene Constraint (Optional) if monoculardepths is not None: # Patch-wise loss with monocular depth # depthloss = computepatchwisedepthloss(voxelgrid, monoculardepths) # Voxel-Uncertainty Depth Constraint # Weight depth loss by voxel uncertainty uncertaintyweights = computeuncertaintyweights(voxelgrid) weighteddepthloss = sum(depthloss uncertaintyweights) # Adjust coefficient to fit best F1-score # Coefficient alpha is tuned during training totalloss += alpha weighteddepthloss return totalloss The Scene Constraint variant integrates monocular depth estimates into the sparse voxel framework using a patch-wise loss function. It employs a Voxel-Uncertainty Depth Constraint to adaptively scale the loss based on voxel geometric uncertainty, maximizing the utility of external depth cues while avoiding quality degradation. Unlike 3DGS-based approaches like PGSR, which rely heavily on initial SfM points and struggle in challenging areas, sparse voxels exploit monocular depths more effectively. On the evaluated dataset, adding Scene Constraint to GeoSVR with DepthAnything improved Precision from 0.511 to 0.526, Recall from 0.549 to 0.568, and F1-Score from 0.523 to 0.540. With DepthPro, it improved Precision from 0.538 to 0.549, Recall from 0.577 to 0.581, and F1-Score from 0.552 to 0.560. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Measured Performance: On the DTU, Tanks and Temples, and Mip-NeRF 360 datasets, GeoSVR with SVSR achieves superior performance compared to state-of-the-art methods in reconstructing accurate surfaces, excelling in detail preservation and high completeness while maintaining computational efficiency. Strengths: Enlarges global geometry consistency for tiny voxels; reduces depth bias; eliminates inaccurate large voxels; robust to challenging areas where SfM points are sparse. Limitations: Requires careful tuning of the loss coefficient for the Scene Constraint to fit the best F1-score. When to use: When high geometric accuracy and sharp surface details are required, especially in challenging scenarios with limited multi-view consistency or sparse SfM points. When not to use: When computational efficiency is the primary constraint and high geometric fidelity is not critical. The method was developed to tame sparse voxels, enabling delicate and complete geometry learning. It addresses the limitations of previous plane-based geometry regularization, which was less effective due to the extreme locality of sparse voxels. The work demonstrates that sparse voxels can exploit monocular depth cues more effectively than 3DGS-based approaches, which are limited by their reliance on initial SfM points. name: DirectVoxGO
head: Direct Voxel Grid Optimization, DVGO
body: DirectVoxGO is a differentiable volume rendering method that optimizes a single 3D voxel grid to represent a Neural Radiance Field (NeRF), storing density and color features directly in grid tensors. It solves the slow convergence and high memory overhead of MLP-based NeRFs by enabling direct optimization of grid values. It distinguishes itself from standard NeRF by replacing coordinate-to-feature MLP lookups with direct grid sampling, and from sparse voxel methods by using a dense grid with occupancy caching and near-camera masking to handle unbounded scenes efficiently. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: A set of calibrated images with known camera poses, a 3D world bounding box defined by xyzmin and xyzmax, and configuration parameters for grid resolution and feature dimensions. Outputs: Optimized density and color feature voxel grids, and rendered images or depth maps for novel views. Data Structures: 1. Density Grid: A 3D tensor storing density values with channels=1. If usefouriergrid is true, it is a FourierGrid object; otherwise, it is a standard dense grid. 2. Color Feature Grid (k0): A 3D tensor storing color features with channels=k0dim. 3. Mask Cache: A 3D boolean tensor indicating occupied voxels to skip rendering. 4. MLP (Optional): A multi-layer perceptron used in the fine stage to map color features to RGB if rgbnetdim > 0. Numbered Steps: 1. Initialize Density Grid: If usefouriergrid is false, create a grid with densitytype, channels=1, worldsize, xyzmin, xyzmax, and densityconfig. If true, create a FourierGrid using FourierGridgrid.creategrid with usenerfpos=True and fourierfreqnum. 2. Initialize Color Feature Grid (k0): If rgbnetdim <= 0 (coarse stage), set k0dim=3 and create a grid with channels=3; no MLP is used and grid values are treated directly as RGB. If rgbnetdim > 0 (fine stage), set k0dim based on rgbnetdim and flags, create a grid with channels=k0dim, and initialize an MLP (rgbnet). 3. Initialize MLP Input Dimension (dim0): Start with dim0 = 3 + 3 viewbasepe 2. If rgbnetdirect is true, add k0dim. If rgbnetdirect is false and not fullimplicit, add k0dim - 3. Initialize MLP weights with ReLU activations and zero bias on the final layer. 4. Initialize Mask Cache: If maskcachepath is provided, load the MaskGrid and compute the mask for grid points. Otherwise, create a mask of all True values. Store as grid.MaskGrid with xyzmin and xyzmax. 5. Mask Out Near-Camera Voxels: Non-FourierGrid: Compute grid XYZ coordinates. For each camera origin (batched into groups of 100 for memory efficiency), compute the nearest distance from grid points to the camera origin. Set density grid values to -100 where nearestdist <= nearclip. FourierGrid: Compute normalized coordinates and apply NeRF position embedding. For each position embedding dimension, compute the nearest distance from grid points to the camera origin in the embedded space. Set density grid values to -100 where nearestdist <= nearclip. 6. Scale Volume Grid: Update worldsize and voxelsize. Scale density and k0 grids. If totalvoxels <= 256^3, compute alpha from density, apply 3D max pooling (kernel=3, padding=1, stride=1), and update maskcache by combining with alpha > fastcolorthres. 7. Update Occupancy Cache: Compute grid XYZ for maskcache resolution. Query density and activate to get alpha. Apply 3D max pooling (kernel=3, padding=1, stride=1) to alpha values. Update maskcache mask by ANDing with alpha > fastcolorthres. Formulas: Density activation shift: \text{act\shift} = \log\left(\frac{1}{\alpha{\text{init}}} - 1\right) Base voxel size: \text{voxel\size}{\text{base}} = \sqrt[3]{\frac{\text{Volume}}{\text{num\voxels}{\text{base}}}} Current voxel size: \text{voxel\size} = \sqrt[3]{\frac{\text{Volume}}{\text{num\voxels}}} World size (grid dimensions): \text{world\size} = \left\lfloor \frac{\text{xyz}{\text{max}} - \text{xyz}{\text{min}}}{\text{voxel\size}} \right\rfloor Voxel size ratio: \text{voxel\size}{\text{ratio}} = \frac{\text{voxel\size}}{\text{voxel\size}{\text{base}}} Parameters: xyzmin: Lower bound of the 3D world coordinate system (torch.Tensor buffer). xyzmax: Upper bound of the 3D world coordinate system (torch.Tensor buffer). numvoxels: Total number of voxels in the primary grid resolution. numvoxelsbase: Reference voxel count used to calculate base voxel size for resolution scaling. alphainit: Initial alpha value used to compute the density bias shift for the activation function. maskcachethres: Threshold value for the mask cache to determine occupancy. fastcolorthres: Threshold for determining if a voxel is opaque enough to skip color network evaluation. densitytype: String specifying the type of density grid (e.g., 'DenseGrid'). k0type: String specifying the type of color feature grid. rgbnetdim: Dimension of the color feature grid. If <= 0, uses coarse stage with 3-channel grid and no MLP; otherwise uses fine stage with feature grid and MLP. rgbnetdirect: Boolean flag for direct color encoding in the MLP input. rgbnetfullimplicit: Boolean flag for full implicit color encoding. rgbnetdepth: Depth of the color MLP (number of layers). rgbnetwidth: Width (hidden dimension) of the color MLP. viewbasepe: Number of positional encoding frequencies for view direction. Pitfalls: Memory Usage: Near-camera masking requires computing distances for all grid points against all camera origins. Camera origins must be split into batches (e.g., 100) to prevent OOM errors. FourierGrid Masking: Uses position embedding dimensions for distance calculation instead of raw coordinates, requiring iteration over posembedoutputdim. Max Pooling: 3D max pooling (kernel 3, padding 1, stride 1) is applied to alpha values to smooth occupancy. This prevents thin structures from being missed but may slightly blur fine details. xyzmin[i]) / voxelsize) for i in range(3)] def computevoxelsize(volume, numvoxels): return math.pow(volume / numvoxels, 1.0/3.0) def maxpool3dalpha(alphagrid, worldsize, kernel=3, padding=1, stride=1): newsize = [math.ceil((worldsize[i] + 2 padding - kernel) / stride) + 1 for i in range(3)] pooled = [[[0.0 for in range(newsize[2])] for in range(newsize[1])] for in range(newsize[0])] for x in range(newsize[0]): for y in range(newsize[1]): for z in range(newsize[2]): maxval = 0.0 for dx in range(kernel): for dy in range(kernel): for dz in range(kernel): ox = x stride + dx - padding oy = y stride + dy - padding oz = z stride + dz - padding if 0 <= ox < len(alphagrid) and 0 <= oy < len(alphagrid[0]) and 0 <= oz < len(alphagrid[0][0]): maxval = max(maxval, alphagrid[ox][oy][oz]) pooled[x][y][z] = maxval return pooled class DirectVoxGO: def init(self, xyzmin, xyzmax, numvoxels, alphainit, rgbnetdim, rgbnetdirect, viewbasepe, usefouriergrid=False, fourierfreqnum=4, nearclip=0.0, fastcolorthres=0.0025): self.xyzmin = xyzmin self.xyzmax = xyzmax self.numvoxels = numvoxels self.alphainit = alphainit self.rgbnetdim = rgbnetdim self.rgbnetdirect = rgbnetdirect self.viewbasepe = viewbasepe self.usefouriergrid = usefouriergrid self.fourierfreqnum = fourierfreqnum self.nearclip = nearclip self.fastcolorthres = fastcolorthres volume = 1.0 for i in range(3): volume = (xyzmax[i] - xyzmin[i]) voxelsize = computevoxelsize(volume, numvoxels) self.worldsize = computeworldsize(xyzmin, xyzmax, voxelsize) # Initialize Density Grid if not usefouriergrid: self.densitygrid = [[[0.0 for in range(self.worldsize[2])] for in range(self.worldsize[1])] for in range(self.worldsize[0])] else: # FourierGrid handles positional encoding internally self.densitygrid = [[[0.0 for in range(self.worldsize[2])] for in range(self.worldsize[1])] for in range(self.worldsize[0])] # Initialize Color Feature Grid (k0) if rgbnetdim <= 0: self.k0dim = 3 else: self.k0dim = rgbnetdim self.k0grid = [[[0.0 for in range(self.k0dim)] for in range(self.worldsize[1])] for in range(self.worldsize[0])] # Initialize MLP if needed self.rgbnetweights = None if rgbnetdim > 0: dim0 = 3 + 3 viewbasepe 2 if rgbnetdirect: dim0 += self.k0dim else: dim0 += self.k0dim - 3 # Standard MLP initialization with ReLU and zero bias on final layer self.rgbnetweights = {'indim': dim0, 'hiddendim': 64, 'outdim': 3} # Initialize Mask Cache self.maskcache = [[[True for in range(self.worldsize[2])] for in range(self.worldsize[1])] for in range(self.worldsize[0])] self.masknearcamera() def masknearcamera(self, cameraorigins): # Batches camera origins into groups of 100 for memory efficiency batchsize = 100 for batchstart in range(0, len(cameraorigins), batchsize): batchend = min(batchstart + batchsize, len(cameraorigins)) for camidx in range(batchstart, batchend): origin = cameraorigins[camidx] for x in range(self.worldsize[0]): for y in range(self.worldsize[1]): for z in range(self.worldsize[2]): gx = self.xyzmin[0] + (x + 0.5) (self.xyzmax[0] - self.xyzmin[0]) / self.worldsize[0] gy = self.xyzmin[1] + (y + 0.5) (self.xyzmax[1] - self.xyzmin[1]) / self.worldsize[1] gz = self.xyzmin[2] + (z + 0.5) (self.xyzmax[2] - self.xyzmin[2]) / self.worldsize[2] dist = math.sqrt((gx - origin[0])2 + (gy - origin[1])2 + (gz - origin[2])2) if dist <= self.nearclip: self.densitygrid[x][y][z] = -100.0 def scalevolumegrid(self, numvoxelsbase): voxelsizebase = computevoxelsize(1.0, numvoxelsbase) voxelsize = computevoxelsize(1.0, self.numvoxels) self.worldsize = computeworldsize(self.xyzmin, self.xyzmax, voxelsize) # Scale density and k0 grids # Resampling logic omitted for brevity, standard trilinear/nearest interpolation applies if self.numvoxels <= 2563: alphagrid = self.computealphafromdensity() pooledalpha = maxpool3dalpha(alphagrid, self.worldsize) self.updateoccupancycache(pooledalpha) def computealphafromdensity(self): actshift = math.log(1.0 / self.alphainit - 1) alphagrid = [[[0.0 for in range(self.worldsize[2])] for in range(self.worldsize[1])] for in range(self.worldsize[0])] for x in range(self.worldsize[0]): for y in range(self.worldsize[1]): for z in range(self.worldsize[2]): density = self.densitygrid[x][y][z] alpha = 1.0 - math.exp(-(density + actshift)) alphagrid[x][y][z] = max(0.0, alpha) return alphagrid def updateoccupancycache(self, alphagrid): pooledalpha = maxpool3dalpha(alphagrid, self.worldsize) for x in range(len(pooledalpha)): for y in range(len(pooledalpha[0])): for z in range(len(pooledalpha[0][0])): if pooledalpha[x][y][z] <= self.fastcolorthres: self.maskcache[x][y][z] = False SPC-NeRF is a Rate-Distortion (RD) optimized predictive coding framework designed to compress Explicit Voxel Grid (EVG) represented Neural Radiance Fields (NeRFs) by removing spatial redundancy. It distinguishes itself from sibling methods like DirectVoxGO by introducing a two-stage finetuning process and a reference graph that jointly optimizes compression ratio and rendering distortion during training, achieving 32% bit savings compared to the state-of-the-art VQRF method. GO-Surf is a direct feature grid optimization method for accurate and fast surface reconstruction from RGB-D sequences. It models the scene with a learned hierarchical feature voxel grid that encapsulates multi-level geometric and appearance local information. Unlike MLP-based methods, GO-Surf directly optimizes feature vectors in a voxel grid, which are decoded into signed distance field (SDF) and radiance values. This approach is approximately 60 times faster than MLP-based methods while preserving high-frequency details. It builds on the hierarchical grid optimization principles of DirectVoxGO but specifically targets surface reconstruction via SDF decoding and RGB-D supervision. Time Complexity: Training is significantly faster than MLP-based NeRFs because feature lookup is O(1) per sample, avoiding expensive MLP evaluations. Convergence is super-fast due to direct optimization of grid values. Memory Complexity: Memory usage is proportional to the number of voxels (O(N^3)). The dense grid can consume significant memory for high resolutions, mitigated by occupancy caching and near-camera masking. Measured Performance: The method achieves super-fast convergence for radiance field reconstruction. Specific benchmarks are not provided in the sources, but the method is cited for its speed advantage over MLP-based approaches. Scaling: Scales with the number of voxels. The method supports scaling the volume grid by adjusting numvoxels and voxelsize. Strengths: Fast training, simple implementation, direct optimization of features. Limitations: High memory usage for large scenes, dense grid representation may be inefficient for sparse scenes. When to use: When fast training convergence is prioritized and memory is sufficient for the desired resolution. When not to use: For very large, sparse scenes where sparse voxel methods are more memory-efficient. DirectVoxGO was introduced by Cheng Sun, Min Sun, and Hwann-Tzong Chen in the paper "Direct voxel grid optimization: Super-fast convergence for radiance fields reconstruction" presented at the IEEE/CVF Conference on Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (CVPR) in 2022. It builds upon the concept of explicit voxel grids for NeRF representation, aiming to overcome the slow convergence of implicit MLP-based methods. name: SPC-NeRF
head: Spatial Predictive Compression for Voxel-Based Radiance Field
body: SPC-NeRF is a Rate-Distortion (RD) optimized predictive coding framework designed to compress Explicit Voxel Grid (EVG) represented Neural Radiance Fields (NeRFs) by removing spatial redundancy. It builds on the DirectVoxGO pipeline and achieves 32% bit savings compared to the state-of-the-art VQRF method on multiple representative test datasets, with comparable training time. Inputs: An uncompressed voxel grid obtained from the DirectVoxGO pipeline. Outputs: A compressed bitstream containing reference indexes, coarse residuals, fine residuals, prune mask, critical mask, non-prune density grid, weights of the shallow MLP, and metadata. Data Structures: The method operates on an EVG where each voxel stores density and color features. The compressed bitstream syntax elements are: 1. Reference indexes: Index pointing to the chosen adjacent voxel for prediction. 2. Coarse residuals: Quantized differences between actual and predicted values for non-critical voxels. 3. Fine residuals: Quantized differences for critical voxels, reconstructed after post-finetuning. 4. Prune mask: Binary indicator for pruned vs. unpruned voxels. 5. Critical mask: Binary indicator for critical vs. non-critical voxels among unpruned ones. 6. Non-prune density grid: Density values for unpruned voxels. 7. Weights of the shallow MLP: Model parameters. 8. Metadata: Scene-specific information. Algorithm Steps: 1. Initialization: Apply the DirectVoxGO pipeline to obtain the uncompressed voxel grid. 2. Pruning and Critical Selection: Prune approximately 90% of unimportant voxels and mark a small part of the remaining voxels as critical. 3. Reference Graph Construction: Select one adjacent voxel from seven possible previously encountered neighboring voxels as the prediction value for each unpruned voxel, and record the index of the reference to construct a reference relation graph. 4. RD Loss Formulation and Finetuning: Apply a unique bit estimation method to form the RD loss and finetune the voxel grid to jointly optimize compression ratio and distortion. 5. Coarse Residual Generation: Perform actual quantization and prediction using the reference graph to generate coarse residuals. 6. Post-Finetuning: Freeze all non-critical voxels and perform a second finetuning step to generate fine residuals for reconstructing the critical voxels. 7. Entropy Coding: Entropy code the residuals and indexes via arithmetic coding. Code other syntax elements (prune mask, critical mask, etc.) that occupy little storage with a simple LZ77 codec. name: GO-Surf
body: GO-Surf is a direct feature grid optimization method for accurate and fast surface reconstruction from RGB-D sequences. It models the scene with a learned hierarchical feature voxel grid that encapsulates multi-level geometric and appearance local information. Unlike MLP-based methods, GO-Surf directly optimizes feature vectors in a voxel grid, which are decoded into signed distance field (SDF) and radiance values. This approach is approximately 60 times faster than MLP-based methods while preserving high-frequency details. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: RGB-D image sequences and initial camera poses. Outputs: Optimized hierarchical feature grids (V\theta, W\beta), decoder parameters (\omega, \gamma), camera poses, and a reconstructed surface (implicit SDF). Data Structures: 1. Geometry Feature Grid (V\theta): A hierarchical structure with L=4 levels (l \in \{0, 1, 2, 3\}). Level l=0 is the coarsest, l=3 is the finest. Each voxel at any level stores a geometry feature vector of dimension hg = 4. Total geometry features per voxel across all levels: 4 \times 4 = 16. 2. Color Feature Grid (W\beta): A single-level feature grid (finest level only). Each voxel stores a color feature vector of dimension hc = 6. 3. Decoders: Geometry MLP f\omega(\cdot): 2 hidden layers, 32 neurons each. Color MLP g\gamma(\cdot): 2 hidden layers, 32 neurons each. Numbered Steps: 1. Feature Interpolation: For a 3D point x \in \mathbb{R}^3, obtain the geometry feature vector V\theta(x) by trilinearly interpolating the features from each of the four levels and concatenating them: V\theta(x) = [V0(x), V1(x), V2(x), V3(x)] where Vl(x) is the trilinearly interpolated feature vector at level l. 2. SDF Decoding: Decode the concatenated geometry feature V\theta(x) into a signed distance value \phi(x) using the geometry MLP f\omega: \phi(x) = f\omega(V\theta(x)) 3. Color Decoding: For the same point x and viewing direction d, obtain the color feature W\beta(x) from the finest-level color grid and decode it into color c using the color MLP g\gamma: c = g\gamma(W\beta(x), d) 4. Ray Sampling: For a camera ray parameterized by origin o and direction r, sample N points xi along the ray: xi = o + di r, \quad i \in \{1, \dots, N\} where di are the sampled depths. 5. Opacity Calculation: Compute the opacity \alphai at each sample point xi based on the SDF values \phi(xi) and \phi(x{i+1}): \alphai = \max\left( \frac{\sigmas(\phi(xi)) - \sigmas(\phi(x{i+1}))}{\sigmas(\phi(xi))}, 0 \right) where \sigmas(x) = (1 + e^{-sx})^{-1} is a sigmoid function modulated by a learnable parameter s. The parameter s controls the smoothness of the transition at the surface. 6. Volume Rendering: Compute the accumulated transmittance Ti and weights wi: Ti = \prod{j=1}^{i-1} (1 - \alphaj) wi = Ti \alphai Render the expected color \hat{c} and depth \hat{d}: \hat{c} = \sum{i=1}^{N} wi ci \hat{d} = \sum{i=1}^{N} wi di Parameters: Geometry feature dimension per level: hg = 4. Color feature dimension: hc = 6. MLP architecture: 2 hidden layers, 32 neurons each for both decoders. Sigmoid sharpness: Learnable parameter s. Number of samples: N (Not given in the sources). Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision: Trilinear interpolation requires careful handling of grid boundaries. Points outside the voxel grid bounds must be handled (e.g., clamping or zero-padding). Degenerate Input: The opacity formula divides by \sigmas(\phi(xi)). If \sigmas(\phi(xi)) is near zero, numerical instability occurs; add a small epsilon to the denominator. Surface Smoothness: The parameter s significantly affects the sharpness of the rendered surface. Time Complexity: Approximately 60 times faster than MLP-based methods due to direct feature grid optimization and shallow decoders. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Fast optimization, high-fidelity surface reconstruction, hole-filling capabilities via multi-level features, direct RGB-D supervision without post-processing. Limitations: Requires RGB-D input. Performance depends on the choice of grid resolutions and the learnable parameter s. When to use: When fast, high-quality surface reconstruction from RGB-D data is required. When not to use: Not given in the sources. GO-Surf was introduced in 2022. It addresses the need for fast and accurate surface reconstruction from RGB-D sequences. Previous methods relied on MLPs, which are slow to optimize. GO-Surf introduces a hybrid scene representation combining multi-level feature grids with shared MLPs for geometry and color prediction. It formulates a smoothness prior on SDF values to improve hole filling and smoothness while preserving details. The method optimizes feature volumes, decoders, and camera poses jointly. name: Fused Sparse Voxel Volume Rendering Backward Pass
body: The fused sparse voxel volume rendering backward pass computes gradients for spherical harmonics (SH) coefficients and spherical harmonics basis values during differentiable volume rendering. It specifically supports gradient accumulation for beta loss and sparsity loss regularization terms. This method is part of the JNeRF implementation, which utilizes a fused kernel approach to optimize memory bandwidth and compute throughput for sparse voxel grids. Inputs and Outputs: colorcache: A tensor containing pre-computed color contributions from the forward pass, typically structured as a sequence of components (e.g., RGB or SH basis projections). gradoutput: The upstream gradient tensor with respect to the rendered pixel color. logtransmitin: The logarithmic transmission value at the start of the ray from the forward pass. betaloss: A scalar value indicating the weight of the beta loss regularization. sparsityloss: A scalar value for sparsity loss regularization (present in signature, usage details not fully explicit in snippet). accumout: Output buffer for the accumulated gradient. logtransmitout: Output buffer for the updated log transmission. Data Structures: PackedGridOutputGrads: A structure containing gradients for grid outputs, including density and SH coefficients. colorcache: Layout is not explicitly defined in the source, but accessed via indices 0, 1, and 2, suggesting a packed or chunked representation of color contributions. Parameters: betaloss: Scalar. If greater than 0, the beta loss gradient is computed and added to the accumulation. epsilon: A small constant (10^{-3}) used in the beta loss denominator to prevent division by zero. Steps: 1. Gradient Accumulation Initialization: Compute the initial gradient accumulation by taking the dot product of the colorcache and gradoutput. The source uses a fused multiply-add (fmaf) chain to compute this efficiently: \text{accum} = \text{fmaf}(\text{color\cache}[0], \text{grad\output}[0], \text{fmaf}(\text{color\cache}[1], \text{grad\output}[1], \text{color\cache}[2] \times \text{grad\output}[2])) This effectively calculates \sum{i=0}^{2} \text{color\cache}[i] \times \text{grad\output}[i]. 2. Beta Loss Gradient: If betaloss > 0, compute the gradient contribution from the beta loss term: Compute the linear transmission from the log input: \text{transmit\in} = \exp(\text{log\transmit\in}). Update the betaloss value (which acts as the gradient accumulator for this term) using the formula: \text{beta\loss} \leftarrow \text{beta\loss} \times \left(1 - \frac{\text{transmit\in}}{1 - \text{transmit\in} + 10^{-3}}\right) Add the updated betaloss to the accum variable. 3. Ray Bounds Check: Check if the ray is invalid or out of bounds: If \text{ray}.t{\text{min}} > \text{ray}.t{\text{max}}: Write accum to accumout if accumout is not null. Write 0 to logtransmitout if logtransmitout is not null. Return immediately. 4. Rematerialization: The implementation notes the use of rematerialization (// remat samples) to recompute forward pass values during the backward pass, likely to save memory at the cost of additional computation. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def fusedsparsevoxelvolumerenderingbackward( colorcache, gradoutput, logtransmitin, betaloss, sparsityloss, raytmin, raytmax, accumout, logtransmitout): # Step 1: Gradient Accumulation Initialization # Compute dot product of colorcache and gradoutput using fused multiply-add # Assuming colorcache and gradoutput have at least 3 elements term0 = colorcache[0] gradoutput[0] term1 = colorcache[1] gradoutput[1] term2 = colorcache[2] gradoutput[2] # Fused multiply-add chain as per source accum = term0 + (term1 + term2) # Step 2: Beta Loss Gradient if betaloss > 0: # Compute linear transmission from log transmission transmitin = exp(logtransmitin) # Update betaloss gradient accumulator # Formula: betaloss = (1 - transmitin / (1 - transmitin + epsilon)) epsilon = 1e-3 betalossgradient = betaloss (1 - transmitin / (1 - transmitin + epsilon)) # Add to accumulation accum = accum + betalossgradient # Step 3: Ray Bounds Check if raytmin > raytmax: if accumout is not None: accumout = accum if logtransmitout is not None: logtransmitout = 0.0 return accum, logtransmitout # Step 4: Rematerialization # Note: The source indicates rematerialization of samples is used. # In a full implementation, forward pass values (density, SH basis, etc.) # would be recomputed here to calculate gradients for SH coefficients and density. # Specific formulas for SH and density gradients are not provided in the snippet. # Typically, this involves backpropagating through the volume rendering integral # using the recomputed transmittance and density values. # Final output assignment (if not returned early) if accumout is not None: accumout = accum if logtransmitout is not None: logtransmitout = logtransmitin # Or updated value depending on full logic return accum, logtransmitout Time Complexity: Not explicitly stated, but the use of fused operations (fmaf) suggests optimized compute time for the accumulation and beta loss steps. Memory Complexity: The method employs rematerialization to reduce memory footprint by recomputing forward pass values instead of storing them, trading compute for memory. Strengths: Efficient gradient computation for SH coefficients and beta loss within a fused kernel framework. Limitations: The specific implementation details for SH coefficient gradients and density gradients are not fully detailed in the provided snippet, relying on the rematerialization comment. The method is part of the JNeRF project, an unofficial NeRF benchmark implementation based on the Jittor deep learning framework. It is designed to support differentiable volume rendering with sparse voxel grids, enabling optimization of radiance fields with regularization terms like beta loss. name: Multi-scale Neural Field Reconstruction
head: Multi-scale radiance fields, Pyramid-structured encoding volumes
body: Multi-scale Neural Field Reconstruction is a framework that constructs pyramid-structured encoding volumes to provide geometric information at all scales for Neural Radiance Fields (NeRF), addressing the limitation of single-scale volumes in scenes with diverse object sizes. It learns an encoding volume and reconstructs density and radiance fields separately, using multi-scale geometric information acquired during training (rendering at each level) and used only at the final level during testing. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: A reference view image I{ref}, N additional source images \{Ii\}{i=1}^N with known camera intrinsics K, Ki and relative transformations Ti. Outputs: A synthesized color \hat{C}(\mathbf{r}) and depth \hat{D}(\mathbf{r}) for a ray \mathbf{r} from the reference view. Data Structures: 1. Feature Pyramid Maps: \{Fl\}{l=1}^L, where L is the number of levels. Fl is a 2D tensor of spatial resolution Hl \times Wl and channel depth C. 2. Encoding Volumes: \{Vl\}{l=1}^L. Vl is a 3D tensor representing the volume at level l. It stores features derived from the variance of warped source features. The volume is defined over a depth range Rl for each pixel. 3. MLPs: MLP1: Two-layer MLP mapping volume features and direction differences to density \sigma and hidden features fh. MLP2: MLP mapping direction differences, hidden features, and source view colors/features to blending weights wi. Numbered Steps: 1. Feature Pyramid Construction: Apply a shared eight-layer 2D CNN to extract deep features for all source images Ii. Use a Feature Pyramid Network (FPN) to extract hierarchical feature maps F1, \dots, FL with different spatial resolutions. 2. Encoding Volume Construction (Variance-based): For each level l and each pixel p in the reference view: a. Sample points S^Al within a depth range Rl. b. For each sample point with pixel coordinate p and depth d, warp it to the i-th source view via inverse warping: pi = Ki Ti (d \cdot K^{-1} p) where K, Ki are intrinsics and Ti is the relative transformation. c. Compute the encoding volume feature \bar{V}l by calculating the variance of multi-view source features: \bar{V}l = \text{Var}(F^1l[p1], \dots, F^Nl[pN]) where F^Nl[pN] is bilinearly interpolated feature at the l-th level feature map of the N-th source image. Note: The depth range Rl is narrowed by simultaneous depth prediction. 3. Density Field Reconstruction: Along a ray passing through pixel p of level l, sample points S^Bl. For each point sb \in S^Bl: a. Obtain volume feature fv by trilinearly interpolating from the l-th level encoding volume Vl at position x (3D position of sb). b. Compute direction differences \Delta d = \text{Concat}(d1 - d, \dots, dN - d), where d is the ray direction under the reference view and di are ray directions from source views. c. Regress density \sigma and hidden features fh using MLP1: \sigma, fh = MLP1(fv, \Delta d) where MLP1 is a two-layer MLP. 4. Radiance Field Reconstruction: Regress blending weights wi for source view colors ci using MLP2: wi = MLP2(\Delta d, fh, ci, fi) where ci, fi are the RGB value and image features of the pixel at the projected position of location x in the i-th source view. Blend color r via soft-argmax: r = \frac{\sum{i=1}^N \exp(wi)ci}{\sum{j=1}^N \exp(wi)}. 5. Volume Rendering: Perform differentiable ray marching based on reconstructed radiance fields \sigmal, rl. For level l, calculate pixel color \tilde{c}l and depth \tilde{d}l by accumulating radiance of sampling points: \tilde{c}l = \sum{k=1}^{|S^Bl|} \tauk (1 - \exp(-\sigmak)) rk \tilde{d}l = \frac{\sum{k=1}^{|S^Bl|} \sigmak zk}{\sum{k=1}^{|S^Bl|} \sigmak} where \tauk = \exp(-\sum{j=1}^{k-1} \sigmaj) is volume transmittance and zk is the depth value of point sb \in S^Bl in the reference view. 6. Final Synthesis: Combine the reconstructed radiance fields from all scales to perform final volume rendering for view synthesis. During training, the pixel is rendered at each level to facilitate the acquisition of multi-scale geometric information. During testing, the pixel is solely rendered at the final level. Parameters: N: The number of additional source images provided as input. L: The number of levels in the feature pyramid and encoding volumes. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Occlusion/Lighting: Geometric information in point volume features may be inaccurate due to occlusion or lighting variations. This is mitigated by the Depth-Guided Adaptive Neighbor Feature Fusion (see Subtopics). Memory Usage: Building pyramid encoding volumes without depth prior guidance is a massive challenge for GPU memory usage and rendering rate, as it requires sampling enough points across the entire depth range for each scale volume. The method addresses this by using predicted depth maps to narrow the depth range. A module that enhances point volume features by fusing features from nearby points on the same surface, selected adaptively using the predicted depth map. It utilizes the predicted depth map to adaptively select adjacent points from the same surface and fuses these features using a shared multi-head cross-attention module. The projected features of these adaptive neighbor points onto the source view are also input into the NeRF model as auxiliary information. This addresses the pitfall that geometric information in point volume features may be inaccurate due to occlusion or lighting variations. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Building pyramid encoding volumes is memory-intensive if depth priors are not used, as it requires sampling points across the entire depth range for each scale. The use of depth prediction narrows the depth range, mitigating this. Performance: Experiments demonstrate superior performance in both novel view synthesis and dense geometry modeling without per-scene optimization. Strengths: Provides geometric information at all scales, handling scenes with diverse object sizes better than single-scale volumes. Fully differentiable and trainable end-to-end. Limitations: Requires N additional source images and their camera parameters. When to use: Scenes with objects of various scales where single-scale encoding volumes are inadequate. When not to use: Not given in the sources. The method was proposed by Jingliang Li, Qiang Zhou, Chaohui Yu, Zhengda Lu, Jun Xiao, Zhibin Wang, and Fan Wang in 2023. It is inspired by coarse-to-fine multi-view stereo (MVS) approaches. It builds on the framework of MVSNeRF, which also uses additional source images and warps 2D image features onto sweeping planes. The method was presented at the ACM Symposium on Neural Gaze Detection (Woodstock '18) in October 2023. name: Depth-Guided Adaptive Neighbor Feature Fusion
head: Adaptive neighbor fusion, Neighbor feature fusion
body: A module that enhances point volume features by fusing features from nearby points on the same surface, selected adaptively using the predicted depth map. It addresses the inaccuracy of geometric information in point volume features caused by occlusion or lighting variations. It sets itself apart from standard feature aggregation by using the predicted depth map to guide the selection of neighbors on the same surface, rather than relying solely on spatial proximity or fixed sampling planes. Inputs: 1. Point volume features F for a set of 3D points. 2. Predicted depth map D for the target view. 3. Source view image features (used for projection). Outputs: 1. Enhanced point volume features. 2. Auxiliary features projected onto the source view. Data Structures: Point Volume: A 3D grid or set of points where each location holds a feature vector. The layout is not explicitly defined beyond being "point volume features". Predicted Depth Map: A 2D map D(u, v) corresponding to the target view resolution. Steps: 1. Adaptive Neighbor Selection: Utilize the predicted depth map D to identify adjacent points that lie on the same surface. This implies filtering neighbors based on depth consistency rather than just Euclidean distance in 3D space. 2. Feature Fusion: Fuse the features of the selected neighbor points using a shared multi-head cross-attention module. The source does not specify the exact number of heads or dimensionality. 3. Projection: Project the features of these adaptive neighbor points onto the source view. 4. Auxiliary Input: Input the projected features into the NeRF model as auxiliary information. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def depthguidedadaptiveneighborfusion(pointvolumefeatures, predicteddepthmap, sourceviewfeatures): """ Enhances point volume features by fusing features from nearby points on the same surface. Args: pointvolumefeatures: Tensor of features for 3D points. predicteddepthmap: 2D tensor of predicted depths for the target view. sourceviewfeatures: Tensor of features from source views. Returns: enhancedfeatures: Enhanced point volume features. auxiliaryfeatures: Projected features for NeRF input. """ # Step 1: Adaptive Neighbor Selection # Select adjacent points from the same surface using predicted depth map. # Note: Exact algorithm for "same surface" selection is not detailed in sources. # Implementation likely involves checking depth consistency within a local window. neighborindices = selectneighborsonsamesurface(pointvolumefeatures, predicteddepthmap) # Step 2: Feature Fusion # Fuse features of selected neighbors using shared multi-head cross-attention. # Note: Specific attention mechanism details (head count, dimensions) are not provided. # Standard multi-head cross-attention is assumed. fusedfeatures = multiheadcrossattention( queries=pointvolumefeatures, keys=pointvolumefeatures[neighborindices], values=pointvolumefeatures[neighborindices]) # Step 3: Projection # Project features of adaptive neighbor points onto the source view. # Note: Projection matrix or camera parameters are not specified in sources. # Requires standard perspective projection using source view camera intrinsics/extrinsics. auxiliaryfeatures = projecttosourceview(fusedfeatures, sourceviewfeatures) # Step 4: Return return fusedfeatures, auxiliaryfeatures Parameters: Not given in the sources. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Geometric information in point volume features may be inaccurate due to occlusion or lighting variations. The method aims to mitigate this but relies on the quality of the predicted depth map. A module designed to refine coarse disparity D{t0} with textural and semantic guides from the target view image I{t0} in a multi-scale, progressive manner to produce final disparity estimation \hat{D}{t0}. It sets itself apart by using RGB features to guide the refinement process through Feature Fusion Blocks and Residual Units. Choose this when high-precision disparity estimation is required from coarse inputs. It consists of Feature Fusion Blocks, Residual Units, Attention Units, and Interpolation (\times 2). Inputs include RGB features and Disparity field. Operations include 2D Spatial Conv, 1D Spectral Conv, Spatial-to-Angular Reshape, Angular-to-Spatial Reshape, and ReLU. Time and Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Measured Performance: Experiments demonstrate superior performance in both novel view synthesis and dense geometry modeling without per-scene optimization. Strengths and Limitations: Strengths: Improves geometric correctness by leveraging depth-guided neighbor fusion. Fully differentiable and trainable end-to-end. Limitations: Relies on the accuracy of the predicted depth map; geometric information may still be inaccurate due to occlusion or lighting. When to Use: Use when point volume features suffer from geometric inaccuracies due to occlusion or lighting. When Not to Use: Not given in the sources. Originated in the paper "Improved Neural Radiance Fields Using Pseudo-depth and Fusion" by Jingliang Li et al. (2023). It is used in the context of Neural Radiance Fields (NeRF) for image-based rendering, specifically for novel view synthesis and dense geometry modeling. It builds on multi-scale encoding volumes similar to CasMVSNet.
