name: Plenoxels
head: Radiance Fields without Neural Networks, Yu et al. 2022
body: Plenoxels is a method for fast radiance field reconstruction that replaces the multilayer perceptron (MLP) used in NeRF with an explicit sparse voxel grid storing density and spherical harmonic (SH) coefficients. It solves the problem of high computational overhead in neural radiance fields by enabling direct data access and significantly faster optimization and rendering. Unlike NeRF, which relies on implicit neural networks to map coordinates to density and color, Plenoxels fits these features directly onto the voxel grid, achieving training speeds hundreds of times faster while maintaining comparable image quality. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: A set of N calibrated images with known camera poses (intrinsics and extrinsics). Optional: a depth prior from a foundation model (e.g., VGGT) for pre-pruning. Outputs: Optimized sparse voxel grids for density (V^D) and SH coefficients (V^{SH}), and rendered novel view images. Data Structures: The scene is represented by two sparse 3D voxel grids: 1. Density Grid (V^D): Stores a single scalar density value \sigma per voxel. 2. SH Grid (V^{SH}): Stores spherical harmonic coefficients for color. Each voxel stores 9 coefficients per color channel (R, G, B), totaling 27 coefficients, plus the density, for 28 float values per vertex. The SH coefficients k{\ell m} correspond to degree \ell{max}=2. The grid resolution is typically 128 \times 128 \times 128 for synthetic scenes (NeRF-Synthetic, TanksAndTemple) and 512 \times 512 \times 128 for forward-facing scenes (LLFF). The grid bounds are typically defined in world space, e.g., [-1, 1]^3 or aligned to the scene bounding box. Numbered Steps: 1. Initialization: Initialize the voxel grids V^D and V^{SH} with zeros or small random values. If using depth priors, prune empty voxels first. 2. Ray Generation: For each pixel in the target image, generate a ray \mathbf{r}(t) = \mathbf{o} + t\mathbf{d}, where \mathbf{o} is the camera origin and \mathbf{d} is the normalized direction vector. 3. Ray Marching: Sample points along the ray within the grid bounds. Compute entry (t{min}) and exit (t{max}) distances using the slab method. Divide the interval [t{min}, t{max}] into N steps (e.g., N=100) with step size \deltai. For each sample point \mathbf{x}i at distance ti: a. Density Sampling: Retrieve \sigma(\mathbf{x}i) by trilinearly interpolating the 8 neighboring voxels in V^D. Apply ReLU to ensure non-negativity: \sigma(\mathbf{x}i) = \text{ReLU}(\text{interp}(\mathbf{x}i, V^D)) b. Color Sampling: Retrieve SH coefficients \mathbf{k}(\mathbf{x}i) by trilinearly interpolating the 8 neighboring voxels in V^{SH} for each RGB channel. Compute the color \mathbf{c}i by evaluating the SH basis functions \mathbf{Y}(\mathbf{d}) at the view direction \mathbf{d}: \mathbf{c}i = \text{ReLU}\left( \sum{\ell=0}^{\ell{max}} \sum{m=-\ell}^{\ell} \mathbf{k}{\ell m}(\mathbf{x}i) \mathbf{Y}{\ell}^m(\mathbf{d}) \right) Note: The SH basis functions for degree 2 are fixed constants. 4. Volume Rendering: Compute the final color \hat{C}(\mathbf{r}) using the standard volume rendering equation: \hat{C}(\mathbf{r}) = \sum{i=1}^N Ti (1 - \exp(-\sigmai \deltai)) \mathbf{c}i where transmittance Ti = \exp\left(-\sum{j=1}^{i-1} \sigmaj \deltaj\right). Early Termination: If Ti < \text{stop\thresh} (e.g., 0.01), terminate marching. Background: If no background layers are defined, add \exp(-\sum \sigmaj \deltaj) \times \text{background\brightness} to the result. 5. Optimization: Minimize the Mean Squared Error (MSE) loss between rendered and ground truth colors: \mathcal{L}{\text{MSE}} = \frac{1}{|\mathcal{R}|} \sum{\mathbf{r} \in \mathcal{R}} \| \mathbf{C}(\mathbf{r}) - \hat{C}(\mathbf{r}) \|2^2 Regularization: Apply Total Variation (TV) loss to smooth density and SH coefficients: \mathcal{L}{\text{TV}}(V^D) = \frac{1}{|V|} \sum{\mathbf{v} \in V} \sqrt{\Deltax^2(\mathbf{v}) + \Deltay^2(\mathbf{v}) + \Deltaz^2(\mathbf{v})} \mathcal{L}{\text{TV}}(V^{SH}) = \frac{1}{|V|} \sum{\mathbf{v} \in V} \sum{d \in [D]} \sqrt{\Deltax^2(\mathbf{v}, d) + \Deltay^2(\mathbf{v}, d) + \Deltaz^2(\mathbf{v}, d)} where \Deltax(\mathbf{v}) is the difference between voxel \mathbf{v} and its neighbor in the x-direction. Gradient Scaling: Use transmittance-based gradient scaling to suppress near-camera floaters. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import numpy as np def evaluateshbasis(direction, degree=2): """Evaluate spherical harmonic basis functions for degree 2.""" x, y, z = direction return np.array([ 0.28209479177387814, z 0.488602511902919923, z2 0.94617469575756008 - 0.315391565252520045, -0.488602511902919978 x, -0.488602511902919978 y, -1.09254843059207896 z x, -1.09254843059207896 z y, 0.546274215296039478 (x2 - y2), 0.546274215296039478 (2 x y) ]) def trilinearinterpolate(grid, pos, gridsize, boundsmin, boundsmax): """Trilinearly interpolate value from a 3D grid.""" normpos = (pos - boundsmin) / (boundsmax - boundsmin) gridpos = normpos (gridsize - 1) gridpos = np.clip(gridpos, 0, gridsize - 1) ix, iy, iz = np.floor(gridpos).astype(int) fx, fy, fz = gridpos - ix ixnext = np.minimum(ix + 1, gridsize[2] - 1) iynext = np.minimum(iy + 1, gridsize[1] - 1) iznext = np.minimum(iz + 1, gridsize[0] - 1) v000 = grid[iz, iy, ix] v100 = grid[iz, iy, ixnext] v010 = grid[iz, iynext, ix] v110 = grid[iz, iynext, ixnext] v001 = grid[iznext, iy, ix] v101 = grid[iznext, iy, ixnext] v011 = grid[iznext, iynext, ix] v111 = grid[iznext, iynext, ixnext] c00 = v000 (1 - fx) + v100 fx c10 = v010 (1 - fx) + v110 fx c01 = v001 (1 - fx) + v101 fx c11 = v011 (1 - fx) + v111 fx c0 = c00 (1 - fy) + c10 fy c1 = c01 (1 - fy) + c11 fy return c0 (1 - fz) + c1 fz def generaterays(imageshape, camerapose, fov=0.7): """Generate rays for a batch of pixels given camera pose and FOV.""" H, W = imageshape[:2] u = np.linspace(0, 1, W) v = np.linspace(0, 1, H) U, V = np.meshgrid(u, v) aspect = W / H x = (U - 0.5) aspect np.tan(fov / 2) y = (V - 0.5) np.tan(fov / 2) z = -np.oneslike(x) directions = np.stack([x, y, z], axis=-1) directions = directions / np.linalg.norm(directions, axis=-1, keepdims=True) origins = np.broadcastto(camerapose[:3, 3], (H, W, 3)) return origins, directions def renderray(rayorigin, raydirection, densitygrid, shgrid, gridsize, boundsmin, boundsmax, numsamples=100, stopthresh=0.01): """Render a single ray using Plenoxels.""" rayinv = 1.0 / raydirection tmin = np.max(np.minimum((boundsmin - rayorigin) rayinv, (boundsmax - rayorigin) rayinv)) tmax = np.min(np.maximum((boundsmin - rayorigin) rayinv, (boundsmax - rayorigin) rayinv)) if tmin > tmax: return np.array([0.0, 0.0, 0.0]), 0.0 tvals = np.linspace(tmin, tmax, numsamples + 1)[1:] positions = rayorigin + raydirection tvals[:, np.newaxis] deltas = np.diff(np.concatenate([[0], tvals])) accumulatedcolor = np.zeros(3) transmittance = 1.0 shbasis = evaluateshbasis(raydirection) for i in range(numsamples): pos = positions[i] sigma = trilinearinterpolate(densitygrid, pos, gridsize, boundsmin, boundsmax) sigma = max(sigma, 0.0) if sigma < 1e-5: continue shcoeffsr = trilinearinterpolate(shgrid[0], pos, gridsize, boundsmin, boundsmax) shcoeffsg = trilinearinterpolate(shgrid[1], pos, gridsize, boundsmin, boundsmax) shcoeffsb = trilinearinterpolate(shgrid[2], pos, gridsize, boundsmin, boundsmax) colorr = max(np.dot(shcoeffsr, shbasis), 0.0) colorg = max(np.dot(shcoeffsg, shbasis), 0.0) colorb = max(np.dot(shcoeffsb, shbasis), 0.0) color = np.array([colorr, colorg, colorb]) attenuation = sigma deltas[i] alpha = 1.0 - np.exp(-attenuation) weight = transmittance alpha accumulatedcolor += weight color transmittance = (1.0 - alpha) if transmittance < stopthresh: break return accumulatedcolor, 1.0 - transmittance def trainplenoxels(images, poses, densitygrid, shgrid, gridsize, boundsmin, boundsmax, lr=0.01, epochs=1000): """Simplified training loop.""" params = [densitygrid, shgrid] for epoch in range(epochs): loss = 0.0 for img, pose in zip(images, poses): origins, directions = generaterays(img.shape, pose) renderedcolors = [] for o, d in zip(origins.flatten(), directions.flatten()): c, = renderray(o, d, densitygrid, shgrid, gridsize, boundsmin, boundsmax) renderedcolors.append(c) renderedimg = np.array(renderedcolors).reshape(img.shape) mse = np.mean((renderedimg - img)2) loss += mse # Backpropagation step (e.g., using a standard optimizer like Adam) # optimizer.zerograd() # mse.backward() # optimizer.step() print(f"Epoch {epoch}, Loss: {loss}") Plenoxels Optimization Configuration defines the hyperparameter settings and training protocols required to optimize the voxel opacity (\sigma) and spherical harmonic (SH) coefficients of a sparse 3D grid representation. It solves the problem of efficiently converging to high-fidelity radiance fields without neural networks by selecting appropriate gradient-based optimizers and learning rate schedules. It is distinguished from sibling methods like Explicit Radiance Fields and Coarse-to-Fine Optimization with Pruning by its specific reliance on RMSProp for SH coefficients and its robustness to learning rate schedule variations, while building on the differentiable volume rendering principles of Hierarchical Grid Optimization. Coarse-to-Fine Optimization with Pruning is a hierarchical training strategy for 3D radiance fields represented as voxel grids. It solves the problem of efficiently initializing and refining high-resolution scene representations by starting with a coarse dense grid, pruning unoccupied regions, and iteratively subdividing the remaining voxels to higher resolutions. It sets itself apart from static grid methods by dynamically adapting the voxel structure to scene complexity during training, building on the general framework of Hierarchical Grid Optimization. HDR-Plenoxels is a voxel-based volume rendering method that reconstructs 3D High Dynamic Range (HDR) radiance fields, scene geometry, and varying camera settings from multi-view Low Dynamic Range (LDR) images. It extends Plenoxels by introducing a differentiable tone-mapping module that models the in-camera imaging pipeline (ISP), including white balance and Camera Response Functions (CRF), allowing for self-calibration and controllable rendering. Unlike NeRF, which uses implicit neural networks, HDR-Plenoxels uses explicit sparse voxel grids with spherical harmonics, achieving rendering speeds two orders of magnitude faster than NeRF. This variant optimizes the rendering kernel for real-time performance. It applies standard early termination on ray marching, stopping when accumulated transmittance is lower than 1%. It accesses SH coefficients using a data pointer to the first dimension and a fixed stride to prefetch memory addresses for the rest of the dimensions, speeding up the trilinear interpolation kernel. The sampling step is doubled to decrease overall sample points. SH coefficients and density information are stored in a sparse 3D array with a full-scale mask, with coefficients stored in contiguous memory space. Unlike the original Plenoxels which uses one CUDA warp (32 threads) per ray with memory coalescing, this method simplifies to launching one kernel per ray, as the original coalescing incurred large computational cost exceeding its benefits. Time Complexity: Training is significantly faster than NeRF, often by a factor of hundreds, due to the elimination of MLP inference and the use of direct memory access. Training a single scene takes approximately 10 minutes. Memory Complexity: Memory usage is proportional to the grid resolution and the number of SH coefficients. A 128^3 grid with 28 floats per voxel requires \approx 128^3 \times 28 \times 4 \text{ bytes} \approx 188 \text{ MB}, which is manageable but scales cubically. Performance depends excessively on spatial resolution, leading to enormous memory footprint if high resolution is required. Performance: On an Intel Core i7-7700HQ and GTX 1060 at 1024x768 resolution, single-threaded CPU rendering took ~7.8s, while OpenMP (4 threads) took ~1.4s. Rendering speeds are two orders of magnitude faster than NeRF. Strengths: Fast training and rendering; no neural network overhead; suitable for consumer devices. Limitations: Suffers from densely localized acquisitions, with PSNR drops up to 8 points compared to methods with MLP components (like DVGO or Instant-NGP). Lacks the generalization capability of MLPs for unseen regions. Memory consumption is higher than hash-based methods for very large scenes. Plenoxels was introduced by Alex Yu, Sara Fridovich-Keil, Matthew Tancik, et al. in December 2021. It was published at CVPR 2022. The method demonstrated that the primary contribution of NeRF models is the volumetric rendering of new views given point-wise densities and color, rather than the density and color MLPs themselves. name: Plenoxels Optimization Configuration
head: Plenoxels optimizer settings, RMSProp vs SGD for Plenoxels
body: Plenoxels Optimization Configuration defines the hyperparameter settings, specifically the choice of gradient-based optimizer and learning rate schedules, required to train the sparse voxel grid representation of Plenoxels. It solves the problem of efficiently converging voxel opacity (\sigma) and spherical harmonic (SH) coefficients from multi-view images without neural networks. It sets itself apart from its siblings by focusing on the specific numerical stability and convergence properties of optimizing SH coefficients, which are more sensitive to optimizer choice than standard neural network weights. The optimization procedure updates the voxel parameters using gradient descent. The inputs are multi-view images and camera poses; the output is the optimized voxel grid containing opacity values and SH coefficients. Data Structures: Voxel Grid: A 3D grid of resolution N^3 (typically 256^3). Voxel Data: Each voxel stores: Opacity \sigma: A single scalar value. SH Coefficients: A vector of coefficients representing view-dependent color. The number of coefficients depends on the degree L of the spherical harmonics. For degree L, there are (L+1)^2 coefficients per color channel (RGB). Parameters: Optimizer: RMSProp is the recommended default. SGD is an alternative but yields lower quality. Learning Rate (LR): Base learning rates for \sigma and SH coefficients. Schedule: Delayed Schedule: The learning rate for \sigma is delayed (starts later or increases slower) relative to SH coefficients. This yields the best results. Constant Schedule: Constant learning rates for both \sigma and SH. Mixed: Constant for SH, Delayed for \sigma. Steps: 1. Initialization: Initialize voxel \sigma and SH coefficients. Common initialization involves setting \sigma to small positive values and SH coefficients to zero or based on average view color. 2. Sampling: For each training step, sample rays through the voxel grid. 3. Rendering: Compute the rendered color and opacity for each ray using volume rendering integration with trilinear interpolation for SH coefficients and \sigma. 4. Loss Calculation: Compute the loss between rendered and ground truth images (e.g., L1 or MSE). 5. Backpropagation: Compute gradients for \sigma and SH coefficients. 6. Update: Apply the optimizer update step. If using RMSProp, maintain a running average of squared gradients for each parameter. If using SGD, update parameters directly by subtracting the learning rate times the gradient. Formulas: Volume Rendering: C(r) = \sum{i=1}^n Ti (1 - \exp(-\sigmai \deltai)) ci where Ti = \exp(-\sum{j=1}^{i-1} \sigmaj \deltaj), \deltai is the segment length, \sigmai is the opacity, and ci is the color computed from SH coefficients at direction \omega. RMSProp Update: vt = \rho v{t-1} + (1-\rho) gt^2 \thetat = \theta{t-1} - \frac{\eta}{\sqrt{vt + \epsilon}} gt where \rho is the decay rate (typically 0.99), \eta is the learning rate, gt is the gradient, and \epsilon is a small constant for numerical stability. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def optimizeplenoxels(voxelgrid, images, cameras, optimizertype='RMSProp', lrschedule='delayed'): # Initialize optimizer if optimizertype == 'RMSProp': optimizer = RMSProp(voxelgrid.parameters(), lr=0.001) elif optimizertype == 'SGD': optimizer = SGD(voxelgrid.parameters(), lr=0.001) else: raise ValueError("Unsupported optimizer") # Learning rate schedules # Delayed schedule: SH LR is constant, Sigma LR starts later or is smaller # Constant schedule: Both LRs are constant # Implementation of specific schedule logic depends on framework for epoch in range(numepochs): for image, camera in zip(images, cameras): # Forward pass renderedimage = render(voxelgrid, camera) # Loss calculation loss = computeloss(renderedimage, image) # Backward pass optimizer.zerograd() loss.backward() # Update parameters optimizer.step() # Adjust learning rates if using dynamic schedules if lrschedule == 'delayed': adjustlrsigma(optimizer, epoch) Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Optimizer Choice: Using SGD for both \sigma and SH results in significantly lower PSNR (29.35 vs 30.57) and SSIM (0.932 vs 0.950). Learning Rate Schedule: A constant schedule for both parameters yields lower quality (PSNR 30.13) compared to a delayed schedule for \sigma (PSNR 30.57). Precision: SH coefficients can be sensitive to learning rate variations; RMSProp helps stabilize this. A technique composed of two steps: space carving and opaque voxels optimization, used to generate neural radiance fields based on plenoxels. It uses spherical harmonics of degree 9 to render the shading of each voxel. Running the implementation maincarvesph.py takes approximately 4 minutes on a single GPU. Time Complexity: Depends on the number of rays sampled and the resolution of the voxel grid. The optimization is generally faster than neural radiance fields due to the lack of MLP evaluation. Memory Complexity: Proportional to the number of voxels and the number of SH coefficients per voxel. For a 256^3 grid with degree 3 SH, this is manageable on modern GPUs. Measured Performance: On 8 synthetic NeRF scenes at 256^3 resolution, RMSProp for both SH and \sigma achieves PSNR 30.57, SSIM 0.950, LPIPS 0.065. SGD for both drops to PSNR 29.35, SSIM 0.932, LPIPS 0.087. Strengths: RMSProp provides better convergence for SH coefficients. The method is robust to variations in optimizer and schedule, though RMSProp with delayed schedule is optimal. Limitations: SGD is less effective, particularly for SH coefficients. When to Use: Use RMSProp with a delayed learning rate schedule for \sigma for best results. Use SGD only if computational resources for RMSProp are constrained, accepting lower quality. Plenoxels Optimization Configuration originates from the Plenoxels paper, which introduced a novel approach for fast radiance field reconstruction from sparse views using voxel grids without neural networks. The specific optimization settings were derived from empirical evaluation on synthetic NeRF scenes. The method builds on the assumption that voxel opacity and SH coefficients can be optimized directly using gradient-based methods. name: Plenoxels Training with Progressive Growing
head: Progressive Growing for Plenoxels
body: A training procedure for Plenoxels that uses progressive growing of the receptive field size to optimize a 3D voxel grid from multi-view images, incorporating TV loss and beta loss for regularization. It differs from static grid optimization by starting with a coarse, downsampled representation and refining it, which reduces training time and improves convergence stability. Inputs: Multi-view images (imgs), camera parameters (transformmatrices, cameraanglex), grid dimensions (gridsize), and hyperparameters (lr, tv, beta, steps, numberofrays, numsamples, deltastep, pointsdistance, progressivegrowing). Outputs: Optimized voxel grid gridcellsfull containing RGB and opacity values. Data Structures: gridcellsfull: Tensor of shape (X, Y, Z, 4). The last dimension stores cell information (RGB + Alpha). Initialized with requiresgrad=True. gridcoords: Tensor of shape (X \cdot Y \cdot Z, 3) storing the 3D coordinates of each voxel center. pointsdistance: Scalar defining the physical distance between grid points (default 0.0125). receptivefieldssizes: List of odd integers from 93 down to 3 (inclusive). Algorithm: 1. Initialization: Create gridcellsfull of shape gridsize + (4) on the target device. Initialize gridcellsfullgrad (accumulator for absolute gradients) to zeros of the same shape. Set receptivefieldssizes = [93, 91, \dots, 3]. Set stepsperfield = 5. 2. Training Loop: Iterate i from 0 to steps - 1. 3. Receptive Field Configuration: Calculate fieldindex = \lfloor i / \text{steps\per\field} \rfloor. If fieldindex < length(receptivefieldssizes), set receptivefieldsize = receptivefieldssizes[fieldindex]. Else, set receptivefieldsize = 1. 4. Grid Sub-sampling (Progressive Growing): If receptivefieldsize > 1 AND progressivegrowing is True: Calculate stride = \max(1, \lfloor \text{receptive\field\size} / 4 \rfloor). Calculate startindex = \lfloor \text{receptive\field\size} / 2 \rfloor. Extract sub-grid gridgrid from gridcellsfull using slice [startindex::stride, startindex::stride, startindex::stride]. Reshape gridgrid to gridindices (flattened spatial indices). Update pointsdistance = pointsdistanceoriginal stride. Compute gridcells by averaging gridcellsfull over the receptive field using averagepool3dgrid (implemented via 3D convolution with a uniform kernel). Else (static or final refinement): Set gridcells = gridcellsfull. Set gridindices = gridcellsfull.reshape(-1, 3) (or equivalent coordinate mapping). Set pointsdistance = pointsdistanceoriginal. 5. Ray Sampling: Call samplecameraraysbatched with transformmatrices, cameraanglex, imgs, numberofrays, numsamples, deltastep, evenspread, cameraray=False, and device. Returns samplesinterval (ray samples), pixelstorays (ground truth colors), camerapositions, raydirections. 6. Normalization and Voxel Assignment: Normalize samples: Call normalizesamplesforindecies with gridindices and samplesinterval using pointsdistance to get normalizedsamplesforindecies (coordinates in voxel index space). Clip gridcells to [0, 1]. Get nearest voxels: Call getnearestvoxels with normalizedsamplesforindecies and clipped gridcells. Inside getnearestvoxels: Round normalizedsamplesforindecies to nearest integer indices. Check bounds using findoutofbound. Fix out-of-bounds indices using periodic boundary conditions (fixoutofbounds) or mask them. Returns nearest (voxel values) and mask (boolean tensor indicating valid samples). Zero out invalid samples: nearest = nearest mask.unsqueeze(-1). 7. Rendering: Reshape nearest to (B, \text{number\of\rays}, \text{num\samples}, 4). Compute pixel colors: Call computealphaweightedpixels(nearest) to perform volume rendering (alpha compositing). Reshape pixelscolor to (B \cdot \text{number\of\rays}, \text{num\samples}). 8. Loss Computation: MSE Loss: mseloss = \text{MSE}(\text{pixels\color}, \text{pixels\to\rays}). loss = mseloss. TV Loss: If tv > 0 AND receptivefieldsize < 19: tvloss = tv tvloss(gridcells). loss = loss + tvloss. Beta Loss (Entropy Regularization): If beta > 0: Extract alpha channel: \alpha = \text{nearest}[:,:,:, -1]. betaloss = beta \text{mean}(\log(\alpha + 0.0001) - \log(1 - \alpha + 0.0001)). loss = loss + betaloss. 9. Optimization: optimizer.zerograd(). loss.backward(). optimizer.step(). 10. Gradient Accumulation: gridcellsfullgrad += \text{abs}(\text{grid\cells\full.grad}). 11. Checkpointing: Detach gridcellsfull to CPU. Save dictionary containing grid (gridcellsfull), gridgrad (gridcellsfullgrad), and param (device, numberofrays, numsamples, deltastep, evenspread, cameraray, pointsdistance, gridsize) to savepath. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import torch import torch.nn.functional as F import torch.nn as nn def trilinearinterpolation(normalizedsamplesforindecies, selectedpoints, gridcells): """ Trilinear interpolation of grid values at sample points.:param normalizedsamplesforindecies: Tensor (N, 3):param selectedpoints: Tensor (N, 8, 3) indices of 8 corners:param gridcells: Tensor (X, Y, Z, 4):returns: Tensor (N, 4) """ inteplationfrac = torch.frac(normalizedsamplesforindecies) # Selection based on corner indices provided in selectedpoints # Indices 4-7 are ceil corners, 0-3 are floor corners (based on doc comment) selection0 = gridcells[selectedpoints[:, 4:, 0], selectedpoints[:, 4:, 1], selectedpoints[:, 4:, 2]] selection1 = gridcells[selectedpoints[:,:4, 0], selectedpoints[:,:4, 1], selectedpoints[:,:4, 2]] # Interpolate along X inteplationfracstep = inteplationfrac[:, 0].unsqueeze(-1).unsqueeze(-1) newstep = (selection1 inteplationfracstep) + (selection0 (1 - inteplationfracstep)) del selection0, selection1 # Interpolate along Y inteplationfracstep = inteplationfrac[:, 1].unsqueeze(-1).unsqueeze(-1) newstep = (newstep[:,:2] inteplationfracstep) + (newstep[:, 2:] (1 - inteplationfracstep)) # Interpolate along Z inteplationfracstep = inteplationfrac[:, 2].unsqueeze(-1) newstep = (newstep[:, 0] inteplationfracstep) + (newstep[:, 1] (1 - inteplationfracstep)) return newstep def findoutofbound(indecies, grid): """ Checks if indices are within grid bounds [0, X), [0, Y), [0, Z).:param indecies: Tensor (N, 3):param grid: Tensor (X, Y, Z,...):returns: Boolean Tensor (N,) True if inside bounds """ idx1, idx2, idx3 = indecies[:, 0], indecies[:, 1], indecies[:, 2] X, Y, Z, = grid.shape idx1ok = (idx1 >= 0) & (idx1 < X) idx2ok = (idx2 >= 0) & (idx2 < Y) idx3ok = (idx3 >= 0) & (idx3 < Z) return idx1ok & idx2ok & idx3ok def fixoutofbounds(indices, grid): """ Fixes out of bounds indices using periodic boundary conditions.:param indices: Tensor (N, 3):param grid: Tensor (X, Y, Z,...):returns: Tuple of Tensors (idx1, idx2, idx3) fixed indices """ idx1, idx2, idx3 = indices[:, 0], indices[:, 1], indices[:, 2] X, Y, Z, = grid.shape idx1 = idx1 % X idx2 = idx2 % Y idx3 = idx3 % Z return idx1, idx2, idx3 def getnearestvoxels(normalizedsamplesforindices, grid): """ Gets nearest voxel values for normalized sample indices.:param normalizedsamplesforindices: Tensor (N, 3):param grid: Tensor (X, Y, Z, 4):returns: Tuple (values Tensor (N, 4), mask Tensor (N,)) """ indices = torch.round(normalizedsamplesforindices).to(torch.long) outofbounds = findoutofbound(indices, grid) # Fix out of bounds for indexing idx1, idx2, idx3 = fixoutofbounds(indices, grid) values = grid[idx1, idx2, idx3] return values, outofbounds def averagepool3dgrid(gridcellsfull, receptivefieldsize): """ Averages grid cells over a receptive field using 3D convolution.:param gridcellsfull: Tensor (X, Y, Z, 4):param receptivefieldsize: int (odd):returns: Tensor (X, Y, Z, 4) """ # Permute to (1, 4, X, Y, Z) for conv3d tensor = gridcellsfull.permute(3, 0, 1, 2).unsqueeze(0).float() # Create uniform kernel kernelvalue = 1.0 / (receptivefieldsize 3) kernel = torch.full((1, 1, receptivefieldsize, receptivefieldsize, receptivefieldsize), kernelvalue, device=tensor.device) kernel = kernel.repeat(4, 1, 1, 1, 1) # Repeat for 4 channels # Convolve with padding to maintain size result = F.conv3d(tensor, kernel, padding=receptivefieldsize // 2, groups=4) # Permute back to (X, Y, Z, 4) result = result.squeeze(0).permute(1, 2, 3, 0) return result def trainplenoxelsprogressive(gridcellsfull, gridcoords, optimizer, imgs, transformmatrices, cameraanglex, steps, numberofrays, numsamples, deltastep, pointsdistanceoriginal, tv, beta, progressivegrowing, device): """ Main training loop for Plenoxels with progressive growing. """ receptivefieldssizes = list(range(93, 2, -2)) # 93 down to 3 stepsperfield = 5 gridcellsfullgrad = torch.zeroslike(gridcellsfull) for i in range(steps): # 1. Determine receptive field fieldindex = i // stepsperfield if fieldindex < len(receptivefieldssizes): receptivefieldsize = receptivefieldssizes[fieldindex] else: receptivefieldsize = 1 # 2. Configure Grid and Sampling if receptivefieldsize > 1 and progressivegrowing: stride = max(1, receptivefieldsize // 4) startindex = int(receptivefieldsize / 2) # Extract sub-grid gridgrid = gridcellsfull[startindex::stride, startindex::stride, startindex::stride] gridindices = gridgrid.reshape(-1, 3) # Placeholder for coordinate mapping logic pointsdistance = pointsdistanceoriginal stride # Average pool to get current representation gridcells = averagepool3dgrid(gridcellsfull, receptivefieldsize) else: gridcells = gridcellsfull gridindices = gridcoords # Placeholder pointsdistance = pointsdistanceoriginal # 3. Sample Rays (Placeholder for external function) # samplesinterval, pixelstorays, camerapositions, raydirections = samplecameraraysbatched(...) # For implementation completeness, we assume these are available samplesinterval = torch.rand((imgs.shape[0], numberofrays, numsamples, 3), device=device) # pixelstorays = torch.rand((imgs.shape[0], numberofrays, 3), device=device) # # 4. Normalize Samples # normalizedsamplesforindecies = normalizesamplesforindecies(gridindices, samplesinterval, pointsdistance) # Assuming simple scaling for demonstration if gridindices are coordinates normalizedsamplesforindecies = samplesinterval / pointsdistance # 5. Get Nearest Voxels clippedgrid = torch.clamp(gridcells, 0, 1) nearest, mask = getnearestvoxels(normalizedsamplesforindecies, clippedgrid) # Zero out invalid samples nearest = nearest mask.unsqueeze(-1).float() # 6. Render # Reshape for rendering: (B, rays, samples, 4) nearestreshaped = nearest.reshape(imgs.shape[0], numberofrays, numsamples, 4) # Compute Alpha Weighted Pixels (Placeholder for volume rendering logic) # pixelscolor = computealphaweightedpixels(nearestreshaped) # Simple sum for demonstration if alpha is not used, or standard compositing alphas = torch.sigmoid(nearestreshaped[..., 3:]) # Assuming last channel is logit alpha rgbs = nearestreshaped[...,:3] # Standard volume rendering: C = sum(Ti ci (1 - exp(-sigmai deltai))) # Simplified for placeholder: weighted sum weights = alphas (1 - alphas) # Placeholder weights pixelscolor = torch.sum(rgbs weights, dim=2) pixelscolor = pixelscolor.reshape(imgs.shape[0] numberofrays, numsamples) # Shape mismatch fix for loss calc # 7. Compute Loss # Note: pixelstorays shape is (B, rays, 3). pixelscolor is (Brays, samples). # This implies a mismatch in the source description or a specific sampling strategy. # Assuming pixelstorays is expanded or sampled to match numsamples for MSE. # Assuming pixelstorays is replicated or sampled to match numsamples for the sake of valid code pixelstoraysexpanded = pixelstorays.repeatinterleave(numsamples, dim=0).reshape(imgs.shape[0] numberofrays, numsamples, 3) mseloss = nn.functional.mseloss(pixelscolor, pixelstoraysexpanded) loss = mseloss # TV Loss if tv > 0 and receptivefieldsize < 19: # TV Loss: Sum of absolute differences between adjacent voxels tvlossval = torch.mean(torch.abs(gridcells[...,:-1,:] - gridcells[..., 1:,:])) + \ torch.mean(torch.abs(gridcells[...,:-1,:,:] - gridcells[..., 1:,:,:])) + \ torch.mean(torch.abs(gridcells[...,:-1,:,:,:] - gridcells[..., 1:,:,:,:])) tvloss = tv tvlossval loss = loss + tvloss # Beta Loss if beta > 0: alpha = nearest[..., -1] # Last channel # Clamp for log stability alphaclamped = torch.clamp(alpha, min=0.0001, max=0.9999) betaloss = beta (torch.log(alphaclamped) - torch.log(1 - alphaclamped)).mean() loss = loss + betaloss # 8. Optimize optimizer.zerograd() loss.backward() optimizer.step() # 9. Accumulate Gradients if gridcellsfull.grad is not None: gridcellsfullgrad += torch.abs(gridcellsfull.grad) return gridcellsfull, gridcellsfullgrad Parameters: lr: Learning rate for Adam optimizer. Default: 0.0075. tv: Strength of Total Variation loss. Default: 10^{-5}. Set to 0 to disable. beta: Strength of Beta loss (entropy regularization on alpha). Default: 5 \times 10^{-3}. Set to 0 to disable. steps: Total training steps. Default: 500. numberofrays: Rays per camera. Default: 128. numsamples: Samples per ray. Default: 600. deltastep: Distance between samples. Default: 0.0125. pointsdistance: Grid spacing. Default: 0.0125. gridsize: Grid dimensions. Default: [256, 256, 256] if not specified. The code clips grid values to [0, 1] before querying, but getnearestvoxels returns a mask to zero out samples outside the grid boundaries. Precision: The torch.frac function is used for interpolation fractions. Ensure normalizedsamplesforindecies are correctly scaled relative to pointsdistance. A variant where the voxel grid resolution is doubled at specific checkpoints during training, rather than using a shrinking receptive field on a fixed grid. The initial number of voxels is set to \lfloor M(f)/2 \rfloor. At each checkpoint, voxel grids V(\text{density})(f) and V(\text{feat})(f) are resized by trilinear interpolation to match the new dimensions N(f)x, N(f)y, N(f)z and voxel size s(f). Strengths: Faster convergence, better quality, handles coarse-to-fine details effectively. Limitations: Requires careful tuning of stepsperfield and receptivefieldssizes. Static mode (no progressive growing) may be simpler but slower or less stable. Originated from the Plenoxels framework, which optimizes voxel opacity and spherical harmonic coefficients [Parent]. name: Joint Finetuning for Vector-Quantized Radiance Fields
head: VQ-DVGO, VQ-Plenoxels, VQ-TensoRF finetuning
body: Joint finetuning is a post-compression optimization procedure applied to vector-quantized radiance fields to recover rendering quality lost during voxel pruning and codebook initialization. It adapts gradient-based optimization to the constraints of vector-quantized structures, building on Plenoxels Optimization Configuration. The method recovers rendering quality in compressed radiance field representations through a sequence of pruning, initialization, and joint optimization. Inputs: A pre-trained radiance field model (DVGO, Plenoxels, or TensoRF), training images, camera poses, and a pruning quantile for cumulative score rates. Outputs: A vector-quantized radiance field model with recovered rendering quality and up to 100× lower storage cost compared to uncompressed models. The data structures depend on the specific variant being finetuned: 1. DVGO Model: Density grid, feature grid, and a shallow MLP for color estimation. 2. Plenoxels Model: Density grid and a feature grid filled with spherical harmonic coefficients. 3. TensoRF Model: Virtual grid for importance scoring, with points projected onto density and feature tri-planes by aggregating along each axis. 1. Pruning: Prune less important voxels according to the quantile of the cumulative score rate. 2. Codebook Initialization: Use only the pruned voxels for codebook initialization. 3. Joint Finetuning: Begin joint finetuning with method-specific learning rates and exponential decay schedules. The specific parameters for each variant are as follows: DVGO (VQ-DVGO) Density grid learning rate: 8 \times 10^{-2}. Feature grid and shallow MLP learning rate: 1.6 \times 10^{-3}. Decay schedule: Exponential decay, scaling learning rates by 0.3 every 10,000 iterations. Duration: 10,000 iterations. Batch size: 8,192 rays per iteration. Plenoxels (VQ-Plenoxels) Duration: 25,600 iterations, equivalent to two epochs in the original Plenoxels training. Scheduler reset: Reset to the sixth epoch of the original setting. TensoRF (VQ-TensoRF) Learning rate: 5 \times 10^{-3} for all density tri-planes, feature tri-planes, and the shallow MLP. Decay schedule: Exponential decay, scaling learning rate by 0.3 every 30,000 iterations. Duration: 10,000 iterations. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def jointfinetune(model, trainingdata, config): # 1. Pruning scores = computevoxelimportance(model) threshold = sorted(scores)[int(config['pruningquantile'] len(scores))] model.prunevoxelsbelow(threshold) # 2. Codebook Initialization model.initializecodebookfromprunedvoxels() # 3. Joint Finetuning numiterations = config['numiterations'] lrdensity = config['lrdensity'] lrfeature = config['lrfeature'] lrmlp = config['lrmlp'] decayfactor = config['decayfactor'] decayinterval = config['decayinterval'] raysperiter = config['raysperiter'] currentlrs = {'density': lrdensity, 'feature': lrfeature, 'mlp': lrmlp} for iteration in range(numiterations): # Sample rays rays = sampleraysfromdataset(trainingdata, raysperiter) # Forward pass rendered = model.forward(rays) groundtruth = rays.gtimages # Compute loss loss = sum((r - g) 2 for r, g in zip(rendered, groundtruth)) / len(rendered) # Backward pass gradients = computegradients(loss, model.parameters()) # Update parameters for name, param in model.parameters().items(): param -= currentlrs[name] gradients[name] # Learning rate decay if config['variant'] == 'plenoxels': # Scheduler reset to sixth epoch is handled by external configuration pass else: if (iteration + 1) % decayinterval == 0: for name in currentlrs: currentlrs[name] = decayfactor return model Pruning Threshold: The quantile of the cumulative score rate must be chosen carefully to balance compression ratio and quality recovery. [Not given in the sources.] Scheduler Reset: For Plenoxels, the learning rate scheduler is reset to the sixth epoch of the original setting. Precision and Boundaries: Standard differentiable rendering precision limits apply during gradient computation through the quantized grids. A post-baking optimization step that refines only texel colors for 3,000 iterations while freezing geometry and view-dependent color parameters. It distinguishes itself from continuing neural teacher training by eliminating hash collisions inherent in the original hash grid and leveraging a larger parameter count (5–29× more) to exceed the teacher's performance. Choose this when recovering rendering quality after compression into a texture atlas is required. Storage Cost: Achieves up to 100× lower storage cost compared to uncompressed models while preserving rendering quality. Performance: Effectively preserves rendering quality, including fine details, compared to the uncompressed model. Computational Cost: Finetuning duration varies by variant: 10,000 iterations for DVGO and TensoRF, and 25,600 iterations for Plenoxels. Scalability: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Significant compression with minimal quality loss; recovers quality lost during quantization. Limitations: Performance depends on the underlying grid structure (e.g., hash grids for DVGO) and the chosen pruning quantile. Joint finetuning for vector-quantized radiance fields was introduced in "Compressing Volumetric Radiance Fields to 1 MB". The method addresses the challenge of compressing neural radiance fields while maintaining high rendering quality by applying targeted gradient-based optimization after quantization and pruning. name: Atlas Finetuning with Sparse Adam
head: Atlas Finetune Procedure, Atlas Finetuning, Atlas Optimization, Sparse Adam Finetuning, Baked + finetune, Texel finetune
body: Atlas Finetuning with Sparse Adam is a post-baking optimization step that recovers rendering quality lost during the quantization, pruning, and compression of a neural radiance field into a texture atlas. It treats the baked atlas as an initialization and refines only the texel colors for 3,000 iterations, freezing geometry and view-dependent color parameters. This method distinguishes itself from continuing neural teacher training by eliminating hash collisions inherent in the original hash grid and leveraging a larger parameter count (5–29× more parameters) to exceed the teacher's performance. Inputs and Outputs Input: A baked, BC7-compressed texture atlas (dequantized to FP16), frozen geometry (surfel positions/scales), frozen view-dependent color coefficients, and training images. Output: An optimized atlas texture where only the texel RGB values have been updated. Data Structures Atlas Texture: A 2D texture storing FP16 values. The layout is determined by the bake and texel allocation stage, which assigns specific tile sizes to surfels based on rate-distortion trade-offs. Optimizer State: Lazy sparse Adam state maintained only for texel rows that receive gradients, storing first and second moment estimates in BF16 precision to reduce memory usage. Parameters Iterations: 3,000. Learning Rate: 1 \times 10^{-3}. Optimizer Hyperparameters: \beta1 = 0.9, \beta2 = 0.999. Loss Weights: L1 loss weight 1.0, D-SSIM loss weight 0.2. Loss Function: L = L1 + 0.2(1 - SSIM). Algorithm Steps 1. Dequantization: Convert the baked BC7-compressed atlas into a trainable FP16 texture. 2. Freeze Non-Texel Parameters: Explicitly freeze the geometry (surfel positions and scales) and view-dependent color coefficients. 3. Differentiable Rasterization Setup: Configure the renderer to use the exact inference atlas fetch logic: Forward pass performs rect transform, coordinate clamping, and bilinear interpolation to fetch texel colors. Backward pass scatters the residual gradient from the bilinear read into the four contributing texels. 4. Sparse Optimization Loop: For each iteration from 1 to 3,000: Render the scene using the current atlas and frozen parameters to generate a predicted image. Compute the loss L = L1 + 0.2(1 - SSIM) against the ground truth training image. Compute gradients with respect to the atlas texels. Identify the set of texel rows touched by the current view (gradient sparsity is typically 5–7% of rows). Update only the touched texels using the Sparse Adam optimizer with BF16 moment storage. Continue the learning rate schedule from the teacher training phase; do not restart. Pseudocode Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def atlasfinetune(atlastexture, frozengeometry, frozenviewcolor, trainingdataset, iterations=3000, lr=1e-3, beta1=0.9, beta2=0.999, eps=1e-8): optimizerstate = {} for step in range(iterations): gtimage, camera = next(trainingdataset) predictedimage = bilinearatlasfetch(atlastexture, frozengeometry, frozenviewcolor, camera) loss = meanabsoluteerror(predictedimage, gtimage) + 0.2 (1.0 - structuralsimilarity(predictedimage, gtimage)) gradients = computegradients(loss, atlastexture) touchedrows = [r for r in range(atlastexture.shape[0]) if any(gradients[r] != 0)] for rowidx in touchedrows: if rowidx not in optimizerstate: optimizerstate[rowidx] = {'mean': zeroslike(atlastexture[rowidx], dtype='bf16'), 'var': zeroslike(atlastexture[rowidx], dtype='bf16')} state = optimizerstate[rowidx] gradrow = gradients[rowidx] state['mean'] = bf16(beta1 state['mean'] + (1 - beta1) gradrow) state['var'] = bf16(beta2 state['var'] + (1 - beta2) (gradrow 2)) meanhat = state['mean'] / (1 - beta1 (step + 1)) varhat = state['var'] / (1 - beta2 (step + 1)) atlastexture[rowidx] = atlastexture[rowidx] - lr meanhat / (sqrt(varhat) + eps) return atlastexture def bilinearatlasfetch(texture, geometry, viewcolor, camera): uvcoords = maptouv(geometry, camera) uvcoords = clamp(uvcoords, 0.0, 1.0) return bilinearinterpolate(texture, uvcoords) def computegradients(loss, texture): return scatterbilineargradients(loss, texture) def meanabsoluteerror(pred, gt): return sum(abs(pred - gt)) / len(pred) def structuralsimilarity(pred, gt): return 1.0 - sum(abs(pred - gt)) / (len(pred) 3) def zeroslike(tensor, dtype): return tensor 0 def bf16(tensor): return tensor.to('bf16') def sqrt(tensor): return tensor 0.5 Edge Cases and Pitfalls Unfreezing Geometry: Unfreezing geometry during finetuning degrades quality, costing 0.18 dB PSNR and 0.009 LPIPS, even at 0.1× the learning rate. This is because moving surfels invalidates the binding between texels and scene positions established at bake time. Unfreezing View-Dependent Color: Jointly training view-dependent color with the atlas costs 2.7 dB PSNR. Unfreezing view-dependent color alone is neutral (0.01 dB tie), but joint training is ill-posed because the view-dependent term can cancel against the residual. Precision: Optimizer moments are stored in BF16 to halve memory usage. Time Complexity: The finetuning stage costs a few minutes per scene. The sparse update ensures that only 5–7% of texel rows are processed per iteration, reducing computational load compared to dense updates. Memory Complexity: Memory usage is reduced by half compared to dense Adam due to BF16 moment storage and lazy allocation for touched rows only. Performance: The finetuned atlas surpasses the neural teacher model by +0.24 to +0.47 dB PSNR and improves LPIPS by 0.025–0.026 on all benchmarks. It also improves SSIM on two of three datasets. Scaling: The method scales with the number of surfels and the sparsity of the gradient. The sparse update avoids the "slow random walk" that degrades the atlas when untouched texels are updated by dense optimizers. Strengths: Eliminates hash collisions present in the original hash grid; leverages higher parameter count (13× average) for better representation; low memory overhead; fast convergence. Limitations: Requires a prior bake step; only refines color, not geometry or view-dependence; sensitive to learning rate if geometry is accidentally unfrozen. Atlas Finetuning with Sparse Adam was introduced in the paper "Bake It Till You Make It: Ultrafast Spatial Texture-Atlas Splatting". It addresses the quality loss inherent in baking neural radiance fields into texture atlases due to quantization, Nyquist clamping, and pruning. The method was developed to allow real-time rendering of high-quality radiance fields by offloading the heavy neural network evaluation to a texture lookup, while recovering the lost fidelity through targeted optimization. name: Plenoxels Training
head: Plenoxels Training Implementation
body: Plenoxels Training is the optimization procedure that produces the final sparse voxel grid representation from input images. It builds on Plenoxels Optimization Configuration by executing gradient-based updates to persist learned opacity (\sigma) and spherical harmonic (SH) coefficients. The implementation saves the final voxel grid at a fixed resolution of 128 \times 128 \times 128 after approximately 30 minutes of training on a single GPU. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A dataset of multi-view images with known camera poses. Output: A saved voxel grid file containing the optimized sparse voxels, where each voxel stores coordinates, density values, and SH coefficients. Data Structures: The output is a sparse voxel grid consisting of two primary components: 1. Coordinates: The 3D spatial positions of the active voxels. 2. Features: The radiance field parameters for each active voxel, specifically the density (\sigma) and the spherical harmonic coefficients representing view-dependent color. Steps: 1. Initialization: Initialize the voxel grid parameters (\sigma and SH coefficients) based on the configuration defined in Plenoxels Optimization Configuration. 2. Rendering: Render images from the training views using differentiable volume rendering. 3. Loss Computation: Calculate the difference between rendered images and ground truth images using a photometric loss. 4. Optimization: Update the voxel parameters using a gradient-based optimizer to minimize the loss. 5. Iteration: Repeat steps 2-4 for the specified number of iterations. 6. Saving: Upon completion, save the final optimized voxel grid to disk. Formulas: The discrete volume rendering integral accumulates color C along a ray: C = \sum{i=1}^{N} Ti (1 - e^{-\sigmai \deltai}) ci where Ti = \prod{j=1}^{i-1} e^{-\sigmaj \deltaj} is the transmittance, \sigmai is the opacity, ci is the color from SH coefficients, \deltai is the step size, and N is the number of steps. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def trainplenoxels(dataset, config): # Initialize voxel grid parameters (opacity sigma and SH coefficients) # Standard initialization based on parent configuration voxelparams = initializeparameters(config.initialresolution) # Setup gradient-based optimizer # Standard optimizer setup (e.g., Adam or SGD) optimizer = torch.optim.Adam(voxelparams.parameters(), lr=config.learningrate) # Training loop for iteration in range(config.totaliterations): # Sample batch of training views imagesgt, cameras = dataset.samplebatch(config.batchsize) # Render images from current voxel grid state # Differentiable volume rendering: ray marching through sparse voxels # accumulating opacity and color based on stored features imagespred = rendervoxelgrid(voxelparams, cameras) # Compute loss between rendered and ground truth images # Standard photometric loss (e.g., L2 or MSE) loss = torch.mean((imagespred - imagesgt) 2) # Backpropagate and update voxel parameters optimizer.zerograd() loss.backward() optimizer.step() # Log metrics or save intermediate checkpoints if iteration % config.saveinterval == 0: savecheckpoint(voxelparams, iteration) # Save final optimized voxel grid # Serialization of sparse voxel coordinates and features savefinalgrid(voxelparams, path="./savedgrids/") return voxelparams def rendervoxelgrid(voxelparams, cameras): renderedimages = [] for camera in cameras: rays = generaterays(camera) image = volumerenderrays(rays, voxelparams) renderedimages.append(image) return renderedimages def volumerenderrays(rays, voxelparams): # Iterative ray marching: for each ray, step through grid cells, # query sparse voxels for sigma and SH coefficients, accumulate color/opacity # using the volume rendering integral. No recursion used. return rays.castandaccumulate(voxelparams) def generaterays(camera): # Standard camera projection to generate ray origins and directions return camera.generaterays() def initializeparameters(resolution): # Standard parameter initialization return torch.nn.ParameterDict() def savecheckpoint(params, iteration): # Standard checkpoint saving pass def savefinalgrid(params, path): # Standard grid serialization pass Parameters and Typical Values: Final Resolution: The output voxel grid is saved at a resolution of 128 \times 128 \times 128. Hardware: Training is benchmarked on a single GPU, specifically an NVIDIA RTX 3090. Duration: The training process takes approximately 30 minutes on a single GPU. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Not given in the sources. This variant uses the trained Plenoxels grid as input for 3D classification tasks. It employs 3D convolutional networks (e.g., ResNet variants) implemented with spatially sparse convolutional layers. The input to the network consists of the sparse voxel coordinates and their features (SH coefficients and density values). Training uses the SGD optimizer with an initial learning rate of 0.1, cosine annealing for 100K iterations, and a batch size of 16 on a single RTX 3090 GPU. Data augmentation includes geometric transformations (random rotation, coordinate dropout, horizontal flip, uniform translation, scaling) and feature-level jittering. A unique augmentation involves substituting the background of a scene with backgrounds from other scenes while preserving the foreground. Time Complexity: Training takes approximately 30 minutes on a single GPU. Memory Complexity: Depends on the sparsity of the voxel grid and the resolution (128^3 final grid). Strengths: Fast training time; produces a compact, sparse representation suitable for downstream tasks like classification. Limitations: Performance is tied to the specific hardware (RTX 3090) and configuration. Plenoxels Training was introduced as part of the Plenoxels framework, which aims to represent radiance fields using sparse voxels and spherical harmonics to enable fast rendering and training. The implementation details, including the 30-minute training time on a single GPU, were documented in the associated repository. The method has been extended to support perception tasks, such as 3D classification, by leveraging the sparse voxel features directly in convolutional networks. nissmar/Radiance-Fields, https://github.com/nissmar/Radiance-Fields, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial) PeRFception: Perception using Radiance Fields, https://doi.org/10.48550/arxiv.2208.11537, fetched 2026-10-26

name: Voxel optimization (F2Plenoxels)
head: Depth-guided voxel pre-pruning with SH regularization
body: F2Plenoxels is a voxel radiance field optimization method designed for few-shot view synthesis that eliminates neural networks by using depth-guided voxel pre-pruning and spherical harmonic (SH) regularization. It improves upon baseline Plenoxels by significantly reducing floaters and cluttered artifacts while maintaining high geometry accuracy and appearance fidelity. Inputs: Pruned voxel grids for density (VD) and SH coefficients (V{SH}), input images I = \{In\}{n=1}^S, camera intrinsics K = \{Kn\}{n=1}^S, and extrinsics P = \{Pn\}{n=1}^S. Outputs: Optimized voxel grids VD and V{SH}. Data Structures: VD: Density voxel grid. Initialized to zeros. V{SH}: Spherical Harmonic coefficient voxel grid. Initialized to zeros. R: Batch of training rays. C: Batch of corresponding target colors. Parameters: Training duration: E = 10 epochs. Iterations per epoch: N = 2560. Batch size: 5000 rays. SH degree: 2. SH regularization iterations: T = 1280. Density learning rate: Delayed exponential decay, scaled by 15, initial delay 3000 steps, decays to 0.05 at step 50000. SH learning rate: Pure exponential decay, initial 0.01, decays to 5 \times 10^{-6} at step 50000. Total Variation (TV) regularization weights (\lambda\sigma for density, \lambdak for SH): Blender dataset: \lambda\sigma = 5 \times 10^{-4}, \lambdak = 5 \times 10^{-2}. LLFF dataset: \lambda\sigma = 2.5 \times 10^{-3}, \lambdak = 2.5 \times 10^{-2}. Algorithm: 1. Initialize VD \leftarrow 0, V{SH} \leftarrow 0. 2. Retrieve all training rays and colors: R, C \leftarrow \text{GetAllTrainingRays}(K, P, I). 3. For epoch e from 1 to E: 4. Shuffle R, C. 5. For iteration n from 1 to N: 6. Calculate global iteration count: i \leftarrow (e - 1) \times N + n. 7. Sample batch: R, C \leftarrow \text{GetBatchTrainingRays}(R, C). 8. If i \le T: Apply SH regularization to V{SH}. 9. Render ray colors: \hat{C} \leftarrow \text{VolumeRendering}(R, VD, V{SH}). 10. Compute loss: \mathcal{L}{MSE} \leftarrow \text{MSELoss}(\hat{C}, C). 11. Update VD and V{SH} using RMSProp optimizer with specified learning rate schedules. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def voxeloptimization(VD, VSH, K, P, I, E=10, N=2560, batchsize=5000, T=1280): # Initialization VD = zeroslike(VD) VSH = zeroslike(VSH) # Get all rays and colors Rall, Call = GetAllTrainingRays(K, P, I) # Optimizer setup (RMSProp) optimizerD = RMSProp(VD, lrscheduledensity) optimizerSH = RMSProp(VSH, lrscheduleSH) for e in range(1, E + 1): # Shuffle rays for this epoch Rall, Call = ShuffleAllTrainingRays(Rall, Call) for n in range(1, N + 1): i = (e - 1) N + n # Get batch Rbatch, Cbatch = GetBatchTrainingRays(Rall, Call, batchsize) # SH Regularization (only in initial iterations) if i <= T: VSH = SHRegularization(VSH, lambdak) # Forward pass Chat = VolumeRendering(Rbatch, VD, VSH) # Loss computation loss = MSELoss(Chat, Cbatch) # Backward pass and update optimizerD.zerograd() optimizerSH.zerograd() # Note: The source mentions TV regularization weights lambdasigma and lambdak # but does not explicitly show the TV loss term in the pseudocode snippet. # Assuming TV loss is added to the total loss if applicable, or handled # within the regularization step. Based on "4.1.4 Implementation details", # TV regularization is enabled. We add it here for completeness. tvlossdensity = TotalVariation(VD) lambdasigma tvlosssh = TotalVariation(VSH) lambdak totalloss = loss + tvlossdensity + tvlosssh totalloss.backward() optimizerD.step() optimizerSH.step() return VD, VSH Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Near-camera overfitting: Methods using depth priors like ReVoRF can produce blurriness due to near-camera overfitting. F2Plenoxels mitigates this through its specific depth-guided pre-pruning. Artifacts: Without proper regularization, methods like DNGaussian (3DGS-based) may produce cluttered needle-like artifacts. F2Plenoxels avoids these. Precision: The method relies on accurate depth priors for pre-pruning; incorrect depth estimates may lead to incorrect voxel pruning. Performance: F2Plenoxels achieves better SSIM than other few-shot NeRF-based methods on the LLFF dataset and is superior in PSNR and LPIPS compared to other NeRF-based methods, though slightly inferior to some 3DGS-based methods in specific metrics. Comparison: It significantly reduces floaters compared to Plenoxels, MixNeRF, and SynergyNeRF. It produces less blurriness than ReVoRF. It avoids cluttered needle-like artifacts present in DNGaussian. It improves geometry accuracy and appearance fidelity over baseline Plenoxels. Its depth constraints are finer than SparseNeRF, VGOS, DiffusioNeRF, and FrugalNeRF, resulting in better texture details. Efficiency: The method is built on Plenoxels' codebase and uses RMSProp. Training time is reported on a single NVIDIA Quadro P5000 GPU. Specific training times are not given in the notes for F2Plenoxels, but Plenoxels baseline is 12 mins. F2Plenoxels was introduced in the paper "F2Plenoxels: fast voxel radiance fields without neural networks for few-shot view synthesis". It builds on the Plenoxels framework. The method is evaluated on the Blender (Mildenhall et al. 2020) and LLFF (Mildenhall et al. 2019) datasets. name: RGB-D Plenoxel Mapping
head: RGB-D Plenoxel
body: RGB-D Plenoxel Mapping is a dense mapping algorithm that extends the Plenoxel voxel-based radiance field representation to incorporate depth data from an RGB-D sensor. It solves the problem of geometric ambiguity in gradient-less regions and outward-facing scenes, which standard NeRF-based methods fail to capture accurately. Unlike sparse tracking methods that rely on feature points, this method utilizes all available image and model information for smoother, more accurate trajectories. It builds on Plenoxels Optimization Configuration by adding depth constraints to the optimization process. The method derives analytical derivative equations for mapping in a voxel-based radiance field based on RGB-D data and implements the optimization in CUDA for fast computation. Inputs: RGB-D image pair (color C, depth D) from a camera pose P. Pre-existing Plenoxel radiance field model (voxel grid with opacity \sigma and spherical harmonic coefficients). Outputs: Updated Plenoxel model parameters (refined geometry and appearance). Refined camera pose P' (in the context of tracking). Data Structures: Voxel grid storing radiance field parameters. The specific layout is inherited from the base Plenoxel representation. CUDA kernels for rendering and gradient computation. Steps: 1. Rendering: Render the predicted RGB and depth values for the current camera pose using the radiance field rendering equations. 2. Loss Computation: Compute the photometric difference between the observed RGB-D data and the rendered values. 3. Gradient Derivation: Use the derived analytical derivative equations for the voxel-based radiance field with RGB-D data to compute gradients. 4. Optimization: Update the model parameters (and/or camera pose) using gradient-based optimization. 5. Implementation: Execute steps 1-4 in CUDA to leverage the speed of the Plenoxel model, which is more than two magnitudes faster than the original NeRF algorithm. The optimization minimizes the photometric difference between the observed image and the image rendered from the estimated pose. Parameters: Not given in the sources. Outward-facing scenes: Standard NeRF fails to capture geometry; depth sensors ensure accurate geometry. name: Volumetric Dense Image-to-Model Tracking
head: Camera Tracking, Rendering-based optimization
body: Volumetric Dense Image-to-Model Tracking is a pose optimization algorithm that tracks camera motion by aligning a query image to a pre-existing volumetric dense map using radiance field rendering equations. It serves as a fine-level localization method to correct odometry noises by minimizing the photometric difference between the observed image and the image rendered from the estimated pose. Unlike sparse tracking, which relies on a subset of feature points, this method utilizes all available image and model information, resulting in smoother and more accurate trajectories. Inputs: 1. Current odometry estimate (initial camera pose T{init}). 2. Query image I{obs} (RGB-D or RGB). 3. Volumetric dense map (e.g., RNR-Map or Plenoxel grid) containing latent codes or voxel attributes. Outputs: 1. Optimized camera pose T{opt}. Data Structures: The method operates on a voxel-based radiance field representation. The map stores latent codes at each grid location which are decoded into radiance properties (color, density). The specific layout of the latent codes is defined by the parent mapping algorithm [7820-rgb-d-plenoxel-mapping.md]. Algorithm Steps: 1. Initialization: Initialize the optimization variables with the current odometry estimate T{init}. 2. Rendering: Render an image I{render} from the estimated pose using the radiance field rendering equations and the map's decoder. This involves sampling the voxel grid along camera rays and aggregating color and density values. 3. Loss Calculation: Compute the photometric loss L between the rendered image I{render} and the observed image I{obs}. For RGB-D data, the loss may incorporate depth consistency. 4. Gradient Derivation: Derive the analytical derivatives of the rendering equations with respect to the camera pose parameters. This allows for efficient gradient-based optimization without numerical differentiation. 5. Optimization: Update the camera pose T to minimize the photometric loss L using an iterative optimizer (e.g., Gauss-Newton or Levenberg-Marquardt). 6. Convergence: Repeat steps 2-5 until convergence or a maximum number of iterations is reached. The final pose is T{opt}. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def volumetricdensetracking( map: RadianceFieldMap, queryimage: Image, initialpose: Pose, maxiterations: int = 10, learningrate: float = 0.01) -> Pose: """ Tracks camera pose by optimizing alignment between rendered and observed images. Args: map: The volumetric dense map (e.g., RNR-Map or Plenoxel grid). queryimage: The observed RGB-D or RGB image. initialpose: The initial camera pose estimate from odometry. maxiterations: Maximum number of optimization steps. learningrate: Step size for the optimizer. Returns: Optimized camera pose. """ currentpose = initialpose for i in range(maxiterations): # Render image from current pose using the map # This involves ray marching through the voxel grid and decoding latent codes renderedimage = renderimage(map, currentpose) # Calculate photometric loss between rendered and observed image # For RGB-D, this may include depth term; for RGB, color term only loss = computephotometricloss(renderedimage, queryimage) # Compute gradient of loss with respect to pose parameters # Uses analytical derivatives derived from radiance field rendering equations gradient = computeposegradient(map, currentpose, queryimage) # Update pose currentpose = updatepose(currentpose, gradient, learningrate) # Check for convergence (e.g., loss change < threshold) if isconverged(loss, i): break return currentpose Parameters: Tracking Frequency: 5 Hz. Optimizer: Gradient-based (specific algorithm not detailed, but analytical derivatives are used). Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Gradient-less Regions: Dense mapping/tracking requires assumptions for areas with no gradients, as photometric optimization may fail or drift. The parent RGB-D Plenoxel Mapping addresses this by incorporating depth data [7820-rgb-d-plenoxel-mapping.md]. Odometry Noise: While designed to correct odometry, large initial errors may lead to local minima if the optimization landscape is non-convex. Computational Cost: Rendering-based optimization is computationally heavy compared to direct latent code utilization, but is kept efficient by the speed of the underlying Plenoxel model. Time Complexity: The tracking operates at 5 Hz. The underlying Plenoxel model is more than two magnitudes faster than original NeRF algorithms, enabling real-time tracking. Memory Complexity: Depends on the size of the volumetric dense map (RNR-Map or Plenoxel grid). The map stores latent codes for the entire scene. Strengths: High accuracy and smooth trajectories due to using all image/model information (dense) rather than sparse features. Real-time capable (5 Hz). Robust to odometry noise. Limitations: Computationally more intensive than sparse tracking or direct latent code localization. Requires a pre-existing dense map. Performance degrades in textureless or gradient-less regions without depth data. When to use: When high-accuracy, smooth camera trajectory estimation is required in a known environment with a pre-built dense volumetric map, and computational resources allow for 5 Hz rendering-based optimization. When not to use: When real-time performance >5 Hz is critical and sparse tracking is sufficient, or when no dense map is available. The method originates from research into efficient radiance field representations for practical applications like robotics and XR, which often struggle with the computational cost of original NeRF. It builds upon the Plenoxel model, which uses a voxel grid representation instead of neural networks for faster inference. The specific implementation of tracking via analytical derivatives in a voxel-based radiance field using RGB-D data was presented in. The application of this tracking to the RNR-Map (Renderable Neural Radiance Map) for visual navigation was detailed in. The approach contrasts with sparse tracking methods that use only a subset of points. name: Plenoxel
body: Plenoxel is a volume rendering method that represents a scene as a sparse 3D grid of voxels, calculating color and opacity via trilinear interpolation during ray casting without using neural networks. It solves the problem of high computational cost in neural radiance fields by relaxing the PlenOctrees assumption of constant opacity and spherical harmonic (SH) coefficients inside each voxel, instead defining a continuous function throughout the volume. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A sparse 3D voxel grid containing learnable parameters; camera poses and viewing directions. Output: Rendered HDR color image \hat{C}(\mathbf{r}) for given rays \mathbf{r}. Data Structures: The scene is represented by a voxel grid. Each vertex of the voxel grid stores a 28-dimensional vector: 1. SH Coefficients: 27 values, corresponding to 9 coefficients per color channel (R, G, B) for degree-2 spherical harmonics. 2. Opacity: 1 scalar value \sigma. Algorithm Steps: 1. Initialization: Initialize voxel opacities \sigma to 0.1 and color coefficients to grey by adding an offset of 0.5 to the SH coefficients. 2. Ray Definition: For each pixel, define a ray \mathbf{r} = \mathbf{o} + t\mathbf{d}, where \mathbf{o} is the camera center and \mathbf{d} is the normalized viewing direction. 3. Sampling: Sample N points along the ray at regular intervals \deltai = t{i+1} - ti. 4. Interpolation: For any 3D point (x, y, z) and normalized viewing angle (vx, vy, vz) within the voxel grid, trilinearly interpolate the color \mathbf{c}i and opacity \sigmai from the eight nearby voxel vertices. 5. Rendering: Compute the accumulated transmittance Ti and the final color using the volume rendering integral: \hat{C}(\mathbf{r}) = \sum{i=1}^{N} Ti \left( 1 - \exp(-\sigmai \deltai) \right) \mathbf{c}i where the transmittance is defined as: Ti = \exp\left( -\sum{j=1}^{i-1} \sigmaj \deltaj \right) 6. Optimization: Directly optimize the voxel opacities and SH coefficients using gradient-based optimizers, without neural network backpropagation through a MLP. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def renderplenoxel(rayorigin, raydirection, voxelgrid, numsamples, bounds): """ Renders a single ray using Plenoxel representation. Args: rayorigin: 3D vector (o) raydirection: 3D vector (d), normalized voxelgrid: Sparse 3D grid storing 28D vectors per vertex numsamples: Integer N bounds: Tuple (xmin, xmax, ymin, ymax, zmin, zmax) defining the grid extent Returns: color: 3D vector (RGB) alpha: Float (accumulated opacity) """ # 1. Ray-AABB intersection tmin, tmax = intersectaabb(rayorigin, raydirection, bounds) if tmin > tmax: return [0.0, 0.0, 0.0], 0.0 # 2. Sample points at regular intervals delta = (tmax - tmin) / numsamples tvalues = [tmin + i delta for i in range(numsamples + 1)] accumulatedtransmittance = 1.0 finalcolor = [0.0, 0.0, 0.0] for i in range(numsamples): ti = tvalues[i] pointpos = rayorigin + raydirection ti # 3. Trilinear Interpolation ci, sigmai = trilinearinterpolate(voxelgrid, pointpos, raydirection) # 4. Volume Rendering Step weight = 1.0 - math.exp(-sigmai delta) finalcolor = [finalcolor[k] + accumulatedtransmittance weight ci[k] for k in range(3)] accumulatedtransmittance = math.exp(-sigmai delta) # Early termination if transmittance is negligible if accumulatedtransmittance < 1e-5: break return finalcolor, 1.0 - accumulatedtransmittance def intersectaabb(o, d, bounds): xmin, xmax, ymin, ymax, zmin, zmax = bounds # Handle parallel rays and compute entry/exit distances tx1 = (xmin - o[0]) / d[0] if d[0] != 0 else float('-inf') tx2 = (xmax - o[0]) / d[0] if d[0] != 0 else float('inf') ty1 = (ymin - o[1]) / d[1] if d[1] != 0 else float('-inf') ty2 = (ymax - o[1]) / d[1] if d[1] != 0 else float('inf') tz1 = (zmin - o[2]) / d[2] if d[2] != 0 else float('-inf') tz2 = (zmax - o[2]) / d[2] if d[2] != 0 else float('inf') tmin = max(min(tx1, tx2), min(ty1, ty2), min(tz1, tz2)) tmax = min(max(tx1, tx2), max(ty1, ty2), max(tz1, tz2)) return tmin, tmax def trilinearinterpolate(grid, pos, dir): # Map world position to grid coordinates (assumes unit spacing for simplicity) ix, iy, iz = int(math.floor(pos[0])), int(math.floor(pos[1])), int(math.floor(pos[2])) fx, fy, fz = pos[0] - ix, pos[1] - iy, pos[2] - iz # Boundary check if ix < 0 or iy < 0 or iz < 0 or ix >= grid.shape[0]-1 or iy >= grid.shape[1]-1 or iz >= grid.shape[2]-1: return [0.0, 0.0, 0.0], 0.0 # Fetch 8 vertices v000 = grid[ix, iy, iz] v100 = grid[ix+1, iy, iz] v010 = grid[ix, iy+1, iz] v110 = grid[ix+1, iy+1, iz] v001 = grid[ix, iy, iz+1] v101 = grid[ix+1, iy, iz+1] v011 = grid[ix, iy+1, iz+1] v111 = grid[ix+1, iy+1, iz+1] def lerp(a, b, t): return a + t (b - a) # Interpolate along x c00 = [lerp(v000[k], v100[k], fx) for k in range(28)] c01 = [lerp(v010[k], v110[k], fx) for k in range(28)] c10 = [lerp(v001[k], v101[k], fx) for k in range(28)] c11 = [lerp(v011[k], v111[k], fx) for k in range(28)] # Interpolate along y c0 = [lerp(c00[k], c01[k], fy) for k in range(28)] c1 = [lerp(c10[k], c11[k], fy) for k in range(28)] # Interpolate along z result = [lerp(c0[k], c1[k], fz) for k in range(28)] return result[:3], result[27] Parameters: Initial Opacity: 0.1. Initial Color Offset: 0.5 added to initialize color to grey. Sampling: N points sampled at regular intervals. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Training Instability: SH coefficients can change significantly during training, leading to instability. The grey initialization offset mitigates this. Boundary Conditions: Trilinear interpolation requires valid voxel neighbors. Points outside the sparse grid bounds must be handled (e.g., treated as transparent or background). Precision: The product \sigmai \deltai must be dimensionless; ensure \sigma is in inverse world units and \delta is in world units to avoid overflow or underflow in the exponential term. A radiance representation using Spherical Harmonics (SH) in a voxel grid to model HDR irradiance, exploiting SH's ability to implicitly express non-Lambertian effects and span all colors over every direction of a sphere. It follows the standard Plenoxel interpolation and rendering pipeline but is specifically configured for High Dynamic Range output, often followed by an explicit tone mapping stage to convert HDR radiance to LDR images. Time Complexity: Rendering requires O(N) trilinear interpolations per ray, where N is the number of samples. This is significantly faster than neural network queries (MLPs) used in standard NeRF, which involve multiple matrix multiplications per sample. Memory Complexity: Memory usage is proportional to the number of voxels in the sparse grid. Each voxel vertex stores 28 floats (27 SH + 1 opacity). Performance: Plenoxels optimized with Instant-NGP algorithms achieve training speeds 2 orders of magnitude faster than JNeRF, with no loss in visual quality on standard benchmarks. Strengths: No neural network overhead; efficient ray marching; continuous representation avoids artifacts from piecewise constant assumptions. Plenoxel was proposed by Fridovich-Keil et al. in 2022. It was introduced as a NeRF model without neural networks, representing the scene as a sparse 3D grid. It relaxes the PlenOctrees assumption [YLT 21] by using trilinear interpolation to define a continuous function throughout the volume, directly optimizing voxel opacities and SH coefficients.
