name: Plenoxels Training Configuration (PeRFception variants)
head: PeRFception-CO3D training, PeRFception-ScanNet training
body: This configuration defines the specific hyperparameters, initialization strategies, and training schedules required to optimize Plenoxels for the CO3D and ScanNet datasets, as implemented in the PeRFception framework. It addresses dataset-specific challenges such as sparse observation, motion blur, and background ambiguity by modifying learning rates, loss weights, and voxel initialization methods. It differs from standard Plenoxels configurations by employing distinct initialization pipelines for ScanNet (depth-based) versus CO3D (default), disabling background rendering for indoor scenes, and applying a sparsity loss ten times stronger than the default. The method optimizes voxel opacity (\sigma) and spherical harmonic (SH) coefficients using gradient-based optimization. The implementation relies on the official Plenoxels PyTorch implementation with custom CUDA kernels. Inputs: Training images resized to 640 \times 480 resolution. Ground truth camera parameters (intrinsics and extrinsics). Ground truth depth maps (required for ScanNet initialization). Scene mask indicating foreground/background (ScanNet treats all points as foreground). Outputs: Optimized voxel grid containing density values (\sigma) and 9-dimensional SH coefficients per RGB channel. The voxel grid is a 3D structure. For ScanNet, the initial resolution is 256^3. The grid stores: 1. Density (\sigma): Scalar value per voxel. 2. Spherical Harmonics (SH): 9 coefficients per RGB channel (27 values total per voxel). Initialization depends on the dataset variant: PeRFception-CO3D: Uses the default Plenoxels initialization. PeRFception-ScanNet: 1. Depth Unprojection: Unproject depth maps into a point cloud using ground truth camera parameters. 2. Outlier Filtering: Discretize the point cloud into coarse voxels with a size of 5 cm. Perform connected component analysis to identify disconnected voxels. Remove disconnected voxels, which are likely outliers due to noisy depth observations. 3. Grid Initialization: Initialize the 256^3 voxel grid using the refined point cloud. 1. Blur Detection (ScanNet only): Automatically exclude scenes with severe motion blur using OpenCV's blur detection algorithm with a threshold of 10. Scenes with too few frames after filtering are considered defective. 2. Warm-up Phase: Skip foreground rendering for the first 1,000 training steps to stabilize training. 3. Optimization Loop: Run for 51,200 iterations. 4. Voxel Pruning: At iteration 25,600, prune voxels whose density values fall below 1.28. 5. Background Rendering: CO3D: Enable background rendering. ScanNet: Disable background rendering; all points are treated as foreground. The optimization minimizes a composite loss function. The specific weights and learning rates are: Learning Rates: Density values (\sigma): 30. Spherical Harmonic coefficients: 10^{-2}. Loss Weights (\lambda): Total Variation (TV) loss for foreground densities: 5.0 \times 10^{-5}. Total Variation (TV) loss for foreground SH coefficients: 5.0 \times 10^{-3}. Total Variation (TV) loss for background colors: 1.0 \times 10^{-3}. Total Variation (TV) loss for background densities: 1.0 \times 10^{-3}. Beta loss: 10^{-5}. Sparsity loss: 10^{-10} (10 times larger than the default configuration). Other Parameters: Background brightness: 0.5. The following pseudocode outlines the training loop and initialization for the PeRFception variants. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def trainplenoxelsperfception(datasettype, scenes, device='cuda'): """ Trains Plenoxels using PeRFception-specific configurations. Args: datasettype: 'CO3D' or 'ScanNet' scenes: List of scene data (images, depth, camera params) device: Hardware device """ for scene in scenes: # 1. Pre-processing and Initialization if datasettype == 'ScanNet': # Check for motion blur if isblurry(scene.images, threshold=10): continue # Skip scene # Initialize voxel grid from depth pointcloud = unprojectdepth(scene.depthmaps, scene.cameras) pointcloud = filteroutliers(pointcloud, voxelsize=0.05) # 5cm voxelgrid = initializegridfrompointcloud(pointcloud, resolution=256) backgroundrendering = False else: # CO3D voxelgrid = initializegriddefault() # Standard Plenoxels init backgroundrendering = True # 2. Hyperparameters lrdensity = 30.0 lrsh = 1e-2 lambdatvdensityfg = 5.0e-5 lambdatvshfg = 5.0e-3 lambdatvcolorbg = 1.0e-3 lambdatvdensitybg = 1.0e-3 lambdabeta = 1.0e-5 lambdasparsity = 1.0e-10 bgbrightness = 0.5 prunethreshold = 1.28 pruneiteration = 25600 totaliterations = 51200 warmupsteps = 1000 # 3. Optimization Loop for step in range(totaliterations): # Sample rays rays = samplerays(scene) # Render if step < warmupsteps: # Skip foreground rendering during warmup renderedcolor = renderbackgroundonly(rays, voxelgrid, bgbrightness) else: renderedcolor = renderfull(rays, voxelgrid, bgbrightness, backgroundrendering) # Compute Loss targetcolor = rays.targetcolor lossrecon = mseloss(renderedcolor, targetcolor) # Total Variation Losses losstvfgdensity = tvloss(voxelgrid.density, foregroundmask=True) losstvfgsh = tvloss(voxelgrid.sh, foregroundmask=True) losstvbgcolor = 0.0 losstvbgdensity = 0.0 if backgroundrendering: losstvbgcolor = tvloss(voxelgrid.bgcolor) losstvbgdensity = tvloss(voxelgrid.bgdensity) losstv = (lambdatvdensityfg losstvfgdensity + lambdatvshfg losstvfgsh + lambdatvcolorbg losstvbgcolor + lambdatvdensitybg losstvbgdensity) lossbeta = betaloss(voxelgrid) losssparsity = sparsityloss(voxelgrid) totalloss = lossrecon + losstv + lambdabeta lossbeta + lambdasparsity losssparsity # Backpropagate totalloss.backward() # Update parameters updateoptimizer(voxelgrid.density, lr=lrdensity) updateoptimizer(voxelgrid.sh, lr=lrsh) # Pruning if step == pruneiteration: prunevoxels(voxelgrid, threshold=prunethreshold) Defines the data preparation pipeline for ScanNet, using depth-based initialization and CPU-cached ray batches to handle sparse observations and motion blur artifacts. Extends the PERF algorithm with difference planes and Cauchy loss to mitigate shape-radiance ambiguity, separating view-independent density from view-dependent appearance. Time Complexity: Training takes up to 30 minutes per scene on a single RTX 3090 GPU. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Performance: The configuration is tuned for the CO3D (18,618 scenes) and ScanNet (1,513 scenes, 16 excluded) datasets. Strengths: Stabilizes training via warm-up and specific learning rates; handles ScanNet's noisy depth data through robust outlier filtering; improves sparsity control via increased sparsity loss weight. Limitations: Resolution does not directly correlate with average rendering quality on ScanNet (tested at 128, 256, 512). Fails to render unobserved parts reliably if camera poses are too distant from training views. When to use: When training Plenoxels on CO3D or ScanNet datasets where standard configurations fail to converge or produce artifacts due to sparse data or motion blur. The PeRFception variants were introduced in the PeRFception paper. The framework builds on the Plenoxels method, which uses PyTorch with custom CUDA kernels. The specific configurations for CO3D and ScanNet were developed to address the unique characteristics of these datasets, such as object-centric variability in CO3D and indoor scene sparsity/noise in ScanNet. name: PeRFception-ScanNet Data Generation
body: This method defines the data preparation pipeline for training Plenoxels on the ScanNet dataset, addressing specific challenges such as motion blur from auto-exposure, sparse observation of room geometries, and the resulting "floater" artifacts in empty space. It builds on Plenoxels Training Configuration (PeRFception variants) and differs from standard configurations by initializing the voxel grid with unprojected depth maps rather than a dense grid, and by pre-generating and caching ray batches in CPU memory to optimize bandwidth utilization. Inputs: Raw ScanNet video streams and unprojected depth maps provided with ScanNet. Outputs: A compressed dataset of ray batches and initialized voxel grids (occupying ~35GB disk space). Data Structures: Ray Batches: Pre-generated batches of rays, stored in CPU memory. Voxel Grid: Initialized using unprojected depth maps. Steps: 1. Frame Selection: For each scene, uniformly sample up to 1,500 image frames. If a scene has fewer than 1,500 images, use all available frames. 2. Blur Filtering: For scenes with fewer than 1,500 images, filter out blurry frames using a low variance of the Laplacian metric. 3. Ray Generation: Generate batches of rays for the selected frames. 4. Memory Caching: Load the generated ray batches into CPU memory to ensure efficient memory bandwidth utilization during training. 5. Voxel Initialization: Initialize the voxel grid using the unprojected depth maps provided in ScanNet, rather than starting from a dense voxel grid. 6. Outlier Filtering: Apply connected component analysis to the unprojected point clouds derived from the depth maps to filter out disconnected outlier points. Parameters: maxframes: 1,500 (uniformly sampled). blurthreshold: Not given in the sources. Pitfalls: Motion Blur: ScanNet videos are captured with auto-exposure enabled, leading to motion blur in many frames that results in poor scene geometries if not filtered. Floaters: In room-centric datasets like ScanNet, fewer images observe the same part of the space, causing standard Plenoxels reconstruction to create excessive voxels (floaters) in empty space to minimize image reconstruction loss. The depth-based initialization mitigates this. Partial SRFs are generated by optimizing Sparse Radiance Fields (SRFs) on only a small number of images (1 or 3) randomly sampled from all 400 available views for each shape. These partial SRFs serve as input to the learning pipeline (e.g., SuRFNet) to generate whole SRFs, whereas Whole SRFs are optimized using the entire set of 400 views. This allows for the creation of multiple partial SRF variants per object, facilitating 3D learning setups that treat radiance fields as 3D data structures. Storage: The resulting PeRFception-ScanNet dataset occupies approximately 35GB, compared to the original 966GB required for ScanNet video streams, achieving a 96.4% compression rate. Performance: Pre-generating and caching ray batches in CPU memory improves training efficiency by optimizing memory bandwidth utilization. Quality: The depth-based initialization and outlier filtering lead to stable and more accurate reconstruction, reducing the generation of floaters in empty space. This method is part of the PeRFception project, which focuses on perception using radiance fields. It adapts the Plenoxels optimization configuration for the ScanNet dataset, which consists of indoor room scans captured with handheld cameras. The approach addresses the specific challenges of indoor scenes, such as auto-exposure induced blur and sparse viewpoint coverage. name: PERF with Cauchy Loss and Hierarchical Planes
head: Implementation details for PERF additions, PERF additions, PERF with difference planes and Cauchy loss
body: This method extends the PERF (Plenoxels Optimization Framework) algorithm by introducing difference planes and a Cauchy loss function to mitigate shape-radiance ambiguity in view-dependent radiance fields. It sets itself apart from standard PERF by explicitly separating view-independent density from view-dependent appearance using hierarchical difference planes, while using a robust loss function to handle outliers and sparse real-world data. The method operates within a non-linear least-squares optimization framework. It augments the standard Plenoxels representation with additional "difference planes" and modifies the loss function. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: Camera poses and intrinsics (calibrated via COLMAP), input images, initial Plenoxels grid. Outputs: Optimized Plenoxels grid (density and base color), difference planes (view-dependent color residuals), and per-voxel weights for the loss function. Data Structures: 1. Plenoxels Grid: Standard 3D voxel grid storing density and base color coefficients. 2. Difference Planes: A set of 2D planes (feature maps) corresponding to the hierarchical levels. These store view-dependent color residuals. 3. Weight Buffer: A buffer storing one float per voxel, representing the per-voxel weight for the Cauchy loss. Hierarchical Structure: The method uses four hierarchical levels. The highest level has a resolution of 256^3. The resolution of the added difference planes follows camera resolutions through hierarchical steps, approximately matching the voxel resolution at any given level. Values for each new hierarchical level are upsampled using linear interpolation from the previous level. Formulas: 1. Difference Planes (Equation 4 in): These planes capture the residual view-dependent color information not captured by the base Plenoxels. The exact formulation of Equation 4 is not provided in the source text, but it is added to the rendering pipeline. 2. Cauchy Loss with Per-Voxel Weight (Equation 7 in): Lc = \sum{i} wi \cdot \log\left(1 + \frac{(I{pred} - I{gt})^2}{\epsilon}\right) Where wi is the per-voxel weight, I{pred} is the predicted pixel color, I{gt} is the ground truth pixel color, and \epsilon is a small constant. The source mentions a constant w = 0.0001 is added to the baseline case for fair comparison. The exact value of \epsilon is not specified in the provided text. 3. Visibility Loss (Equation 8 in): Ls = \lambdas (-4(T - 0.5)^2 + 1) Where T is the total visibility for each ray, and \lambdas = 0.1. This term helps mitigate smoke-like artifacts and keeps real scenes sparse. Parameters: Hierarchical Levels: 4. Highest Level Resolution: 256^3. Visibility Loss Weight (\lambdas): 0.1. Baseline Cauchy Loss Weight: 0.0001 (used for fair comparison with baseline PERF). Algorithm Steps: 1. Calibration: Calibrate scenes using COLMAP. 2. Initialization: Initialize the Plenoxels grid and difference planes. 3. Hierarchical Optimization: a. For each hierarchical level (starting from the second level, as the first is initialized differently): i. Run Algorithm 1 and Equation 6 from PERF once at the beginning of the level. ii. Compute per-voxel weights and store them in a buffer. iii. Upsample difference planes from the previous level using linear interpolation. b. In each iteration of the optimization: i. Evaluate the Cauchy loss (Equation 7) using the pre-computed per-voxel weights. ii. Evaluate the visibility loss (Equation 8). iii. Update the Plenoxels grid and difference planes using non-linear least-squares optimization. Baseline Comparison: To ensure a fair comparison with baseline PERF, the Cauchy loss must be added with a constant weight w = 0.0001 to the baseline case. For real scenes, the extra overhead is 20-30%. The table values for real scenes show mixed results (Material is faster, Ignatius and Family are slower), which aligns with the stated overhead range. Limitations: Additional overhead for real scenes, requires careful calibration (COLMAP). name: Clonoxels
head: Cloning-Plenoxels
body: Clonoxels is a voxel-based radiance field framework that automatically detects repeated objects within a scene using instance and semantic segmentation, aligns them via rigid registration, and shares voxel features between instances to improve reconstruction quality and reduce storage requirements. It sets itself apart from standard Plenoxels by introducing intra-scene information sharing, allowing gradients to propagate to 3D regions unseen within training images and enabling the recovery of hidden structures by drawing information from other instances of the same object. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: Training images with known camera parameters (intrinsics and extrinsics), instance segmentation masks, and semantic labels for the training set. Outputs: A shared voxel feature grid, learnable rigid transformation parameters (poses) for each instance, and scalar color correction values. The final output can be rendered images or extracted 3D meshes via marching cubes. Data Structures: 1. Baseline Grid: A regular 3D voxel grid storing opacity values \sigma and view-dependent color c represented as spherical harmonic (SH) coefficients (9 per color channel), following the Plenoxels baseline. 2. Object Subgrid: An axis-aligned bounding cube (AABB) of voxels assigned to a specific detected instance. Features are stored at the vertices of this subgrid. 3. Transformation Parameters: For each instance, a learnable rigid transformation defined by a rotation matrix R \in SO(3) derived from a learnable quaternion, a center of rotation o \in \mathbb{R}^3, and a translation vector t \in \mathbb{R}^3. 4. Color Correction: A single scalar voxel feature \Delta c per subgrid voxel, applied equally to all three RGB channels. Formulas: Volume Rendering: The color \hat{C} of a camera ray x(t) = xo + t \hat{d} is computed as: \hat{C}(x) = \int{tn}^{tf} V(t) \sigma(x(t)) c(x(t), \hat{d}) dt where V(t) is the transmittance: V(t) = e^{-\int0^t \sigma(x(s)) ds} Rigid Transformation: Each vertex v of an object's feature subgrid F is transformed to v': v' = R(v - o) + o + t Color Correction: The final color c' is: c' = c + \Delta c \cdot \mathbf{1} where \mathbf{1} = (1, 1, 1)^T. The result is clamped to [0, 1]. Loss Functions: Reconstruction Loss: L{recon} = ||C - \hat{C}||2^2. Total Variation Loss: L{TV} (used for regularization). Feature Similarity Loss: L{feat} = \lambda{feat} ||F' - \hat{F}||1, where F' is the transformed subgrid of one instance, \hat{F} is the subgrid of another instance of the same class, and \lambda{feat} is a weighting coefficient. L1 is used for outlier tolerance. Algorithm Steps: 1. Instance Detection and Ranking: Use instance segmentation (e.g., Mask2Former or SAM2 with YOLOv10 boxes) and semantic labels on training images to extract objects. Rank semantic classes by instance count and retain only masks corresponding to the most numerous class to prioritize repetitions. 2. 3D Localization and Subgrid Definition: Project the 2D masks into 3D space using multi-view consistency. Assign voxels to define axis-aligned bounding cubes (Object Subgrids) for each instance. 3. Initial Scene Optimization: Optimize the entire scene's baseline features (\sigma, c) using L{recon} and L{TV} to build an initial representation. 4. Pose Estimation (Feature Sharing Setup): Cull low-density voxels to ensure pose optimization stability. Optimize only the transformation parameters (R, o, t) for each instance using L{feat} until convergence to align the subgrids of repeated objects. 5. Joint Optimization: Reintroduce L{recon} and L{TV}. Continue updating features and transformations jointly so that instances exchange information while pose refinement is informed by photometric cues. 6. Rendering: Query the shared feature grid. For a given instance, apply its learned transformation to map the shared features to its local coordinate system. Apply the scalar color correction \Delta c to handle lighting differences (shadows, specular highlights). Pseudocode: Unverified code. Instance Detection and Ranking instances = detectinstances(masks, semanticlabels) # Extract objects via instance/semantic segmentation topclassinstances = rankandselecttopclass(instances) # Sort by count, keep most numerous class # 2. 3D Localization and Subgrid Definition subgrids = {} for inst in topclassinstances: subgrids[inst.id] = projectto3d(inst.mask, trainingimages.cameras) # Multi-view backprojection to AABB # 3. Initial Scene Optimization optimizerbaseline = torch.optim.Adam(scenedata.parameters()) for in range(1000): # Standard convergence loop optimizerbaseline.zerograd() lossrecon = torch.sum((renderray(scenedata, trainingimages) - trainingimages.targets)2) losstv = computetotalvariationloss(scenedata) (lossrecon + losstv).backward() optimizerbaseline.step() # 4. Pose Estimation scenedata = culllowdensity(scenedata, threshold=0.15) # Remove voxels with sigma < threshold optimizertransforms = torch.optim.Adam([t.parameters() for t in subgrids.values()]) referenceinstance = topclassinstances[0] # Select reference instance for Fhat for in range(500): # Standard convergence loop optimizertransforms.zerograd() lossfeat = 0 for inst in topclassinstances: q = F.normalize(inst.transform.q) R = quaterniontomatrix(q) vprime = (R @ (inst.vertices - inst.transform.o).T).T + inst.transform.o + inst.transform.t Fprime = F.gridsample(scenedata.features.unsqueeze(0), vprime.unsqueeze(0), mode='bilinear', paddingmode='border').squeeze(0) Fhat = subgrids[referenceinstance.id].features lossfeat += lambdafeat torch.norm(Fprime - Fhat, p=1) lossfeat.backward() optimizertransforms.step() # 5. Joint Optimization optimizerjoint = torch.optim.Adam(list(scenedata.parameters()) + [t.parameters() for t in subgrids.values()]) for in range(1000): optimizerjoint.zerograd() lossrecon = torch.sum((renderray(scenedata, trainingimages) - trainingimages.targets)2) lossfeat = 0 for inst in topclassinstances: q = F.normalize(inst.transform.q) R = quaterniontomatrix(q) vprime = (R @ (inst.vertices - inst.transform.o).T).T + inst.transform.o + inst.transform.t Fprime = F.gridsample(scenedata.features.unsqueeze(0), vprime.unsqueeze(0), mode='bilinear', paddingmode='border').squeeze(0) Fhat = subgrids[referenceinstance.id].features lossfeat += lambdafeat torch.norm(Fprime - Fhat, p=1) totalloss = lossrecon + lossfeat totalloss.backward() optimizerjoint.step() return scenedata, subgrids Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Lighting Differences: Direct feature sharing fails under different lighting (shadows, specular highlights). The scalar correction \Delta c is essential. Per-channel corrections are not used to maintain memory savings. Symmetric Objects: Rigid pose registration may struggle with highly symmetric objects, which are sensitive to pose initialization. Visual Differences: Semantically similar objects may have significant visual differences, compromising feature sharing gains. Precision: Calculations assume 32-bit floating-point precision. Memory: Significantly reduces memory footprint by storing only one instance's features and propagating them via learned poses and color corrections. Memory savings are reported as absolute values (e.g., 13.3 MB to 23.6 MB saved) and percentages (e.g., 66.0% to 76.4% of voxels with \sigma > 0.15). Quality: Improves reconstruction quality, particularly for occluded novel views. Clonoxels reduces MSE by 21% in occluded novel view rendering compared to the baseline by drawing information from other objects. Color Correction Impact: Using the scalar color correction \Delta c improves MSE (0.022 vs 0.039), PSNR (26.9 vs 24.2), and SSIM (0.85 vs 0.83) compared to not using it. Denoising: The method imposes constraints on geometry and appearance, reducing noisy artifacts and producing cleaner 3D geometry suitable for mesh extraction. Limitations: Performance degrades if repeated objects have significant visual differences or if objects are highly symmetric. Clonoxels (Cloning-Plenoxels) was introduced by O. Camilleri, M. Volino, and A. Hilton in 2026. It builds on the Plenoxels framework, which optimizes voxel opacity and spherical harmonic coefficients. The method addresses the limitations of standard voxel-based radiance fields by leveraging intra-scene repetition to enhance reconstruction and reduce storage, offering a practical path for efficient and accurate reconstruction of complex scenes. name: Plenoxels Transmittance Offset
head: High transmittance offset
body: Plenoxels Transmittance Offset is an optimization technique applied to Plenoxels that adds a high transmittance offset to the density parameters to ensure high rendering quality across various scene scaling factors k. It sets itself apart from the baseline Plenoxels configuration by addressing the convergence failure of standard density rectification methods when scene scales vary, a problem where baseline models suffer significant quality degradation at large k. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Plenoxels voxel grid containing spherical harmonic (SH) coefficients for radiance and density; scene scaling factor k; baseline learning rates \eta{init} = 0.05 and \eta{final} = 0.005. Output: Optimized voxel grid parameters yielding high PSNR across scales, specifically correcting the quality drop seen in baseline models at k \ge 1. Data Structures: The method operates on the existing Plenoxels voxel grid. Each voxel stores SH coefficients. The density \sigma is queried via trilinear interpolation of these coefficients. Method Steps: 1. Initialize: Set up the Plenoxels voxel grid with SH coefficients. Configure the optimizer with initial learning rate \eta{init} = 0.05 and final learning rate \eta{final} = 0.005. 2. Density Query: For a given ray, sample the voxel grid using trilinear interpolation to obtain the raw density value \sigma{raw}. 3. Activation and Offset: Apply the exponential activation function to the raw density and add a high transmittance offset \tau to ensure high transmittance (low opacity) initially or throughout optimization: \sigma = \exp(\sigma{raw}) + \tau The sources define this as a "high transmittance offset" but do not provide the exact numerical value of \tau or the specific formula for its calculation, noting only that it is "high" and "needed even at k=1". In practice, this offset is typically a small positive constant added to the density to prevent the exponential from collapsing to zero or to maintain a baseline transparency level. 4. Rendering: Compute transmittance T and color C using standard volume rendering integration with the modified \sigma. 5. Optimization: Update voxel coefficients using gradient-based optimization with the specified learning rate schedule. Parameters: \eta{init} = 0.05 \eta{final} = 0.005 Transmittance Offset \tau: Value not given in the sources. Described as "high". Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Insufficiency of Exp Activation: Using only the exponential activation (\sigma = \exp(\sigma{raw})) is insufficient for convergence at various scene scales. Baseline Failure: The baseline Plenoxels model (using ReLU or exp without offset) suffers significant quality drops at large k (e.g., PSNR 13.05 vs 32.25 at k=10 on Blender Chair). Learning Rate: The reduced learning rate (\eta{init} = 0.05, \eta{final} = 0.005) is used in conjunction with the offset; the baseline with ReLU uses a larger rate. This variant highlights that rectifying \sigma with exp activation alone is insufficient for convergence at various scene scales; a high transmittance offset is needed even at k=1. It serves as a prerequisite step, indicating that the offset is the critical differentiator from a simple exp-activated baseline. Time and Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Measured Performance: On the Blender dataset, the method significantly outperforms the baseline Plenoxels at large scene scaling factors k: Chair: At k=1, baseline PSNR 31.80 vs. method 31.89. At k=10, baseline 13.05 vs. method 32.25. Ship: At k=1, baseline 28.16 vs. method 28.25. At k=10, baseline 11.27 vs. method 28.21. Other Objects: Similar trends observed for other Blender objects (e.g., Ours vs Default at k=10: 34.93 vs 13.03 for one object, 31.69 vs 11.64 for another). Strengths and Limitations: Strengths: Maintains high rendering quality across various scene scaling factors k, preventing the severe quality degradation seen in baseline models at large k. Limitations: The specific value of the offset is not detailed, making reproducibility dependent on heuristic tuning. When to Use: Use when optimizing Plenoxels for scenes with varying or large scaling factors k where baseline models fail to converge or produce low-quality renders. The method originates from the work on "Alpha Invariance: On Inverse Scaling Between Distance and Volume Density in Neural Radiance Fields". It addresses the issue where forcing rays to be bounded within predetermined global near and far planes produces significantly worsened rendering quality, as shown in related tables. The technique is part of a broader effort to stabilize Plenoxels optimization under scene scaling variations. head: Low-frequency view-dependent function, Per-voxel environment map
body: This method addresses the shape-radiance ambiguity in view-dependent radiance fields by distinguishing surface points from arbitrary volume points using a low-frequency approximation of outgoing radiance. Unlike standard Plenoxels which may struggle with complex view-dependent lighting that lacks clear Lambertian components, this technique assigns a small per-voxel environment map to capture low-frequency view dependence, thereby improving geometry reconstruction. It sets itself apart by integrating a Cauchy loss weighted by the error of this low-frequency approximation into the optimization framework. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: A hierarchical voxel grid where each voxel has an associated density \sigma. Camera poses and colors are available for ray marching. Outputs: A buffer of weights w (one float per voxel) representing the error cost, which is used to modulate the Cauchy loss during optimization. Data Structures: Per-voxel Environment Map: Each voxel stores a small environment map of size 8 \times 4 pixels. This map represents a low-frequency view-dependent function. Weight Buffer: A buffer storing one float per voxel, containing the pre-computed error cost w. Parameters: \lambdac: Controls the overall loss magnitude. Value is 0.05 for artificial scenes and 0.01 for real scenes. \lambdan: Controls the weight of the cost function in the Cauchy loss. Value is 10 for both artificial and real scenes. Steps: 1. Population of View-Dependent Function: For each voxel, populate its 8 \times 4 environment map by iterating over all cameras. Project the voxel to the camera, trace visibility, map to spherical coordinates (\theta, \phi), and accumulate the projected color weighted by visibility into the environment map bin. Sum the total visibility. 2. Normalization: Normalize the environment map by dividing each bin by the total visibility sum T{sum} over all spherical coordinates \theta \in [0, \pi] and \phi \in [-\pi, \pi]. 3. Error Calculation: Calculate the error E for the voxel by comparing the reference color in each camera with the color predicted by the environment map for the corresponding direction, weighted by visibility. 4. Weight Storage: Store the resulting error cost w (derived from E) in a buffer. This step is executed once at the beginning of each hierarchical level, except the first. 5. Loss Evaluation: In each optimization iteration, evaluate the Cauchy loss using the pre-computed weights w from the buffer. Formulas: The error E for a voxel is calculated as: E = \sum{k} \frac{1}{X} \sum{i} Tk (ci - pi)^2 where: k indexes the cameras. i indexes the color channels. X is a normalization factor (implied by the summation structure, likely related to the number of samples or channels, though exact definition of X is not explicitly detailed beyond its presence in the formula). Tk is the visibility to camera k. ci is the reference color in camera k for channel i. pi is the predicted color from the environment map for the corresponding direction and channel i. The weight w is derived from this error E. The Cauchy loss Lc is defined as: Lc = \lambdac \sum{i} \log(1 + \lambdan w \sigmai^2) where: \sigmai is the density for voxel i. w is the error cost from the environment map evaluation. \lambdac and \lambdan are the parameters defined above. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def populatevoxelenvmap(voxel, cameras, envmapsize=(8, 4)): """ Populates the 8x4 environment map for a single voxel. Returns the normalized environment map and the total visibility sum. """ envmap = zeros(envmapsize) Tsum = 0.0 for camera in cameras: # Project voxel to camera space p = projectvoxeltocamera(voxel, camera) # Trace visibility from camera to voxel T = tracevisibility(voxel, camera) # Map voxel direction to spherical coordinates (theta, phi) theta, phi = maptosphericalcoordinates(voxel, camera) # Map spherical coordinates to env map indices # Assuming uniform sampling over [0, pi] for theta and [-pi, pi] for phi # and envmapsize is (8, 4) # Note: Exact mapping logic (e.g., scaling) is not specified, # but typically involves normalizing theta and phi to [0, 1] and scaling to indices. # Assuming a standard equirectangular-like projection mapping: u = int((phi + pi) / (2 pi) envmapsize[1]) v = int(theta / pi envmapsize[0]) # Clamp indices to valid range u = clamp(u, 0, envmapsize[1] - 1) v = clamp(v, 0, envmapsize[0] - 1) # Accumulate color weighted by visibility envmap[v, u] += T p.color Tsum += T # Normalize the environment map if Tsum > 0: envmap = envmap / Tsum return envmap, Tsum def calculateerror(envmap, cameras, voxel): """ Calculates the error E for a voxel based on its environment map. """ errorsum = 0.0 totalsamples = 0 for camera in cameras: # Project voxel to camera space to get direction p = projectvoxeltocamera(voxel, camera) # Trace visibility Tk = tracevisibility(voxel, camera) # Get reference color ci = camera.getcoloratprojection(p) # Get predicted color from environment map theta, phi = maptosphericalcoordinates(voxel, camera) u = int((phi + pi) / (2 pi) envmap.shape[1]) v = int(theta / pi envmap.shape[0]) u = clamp(u, 0, envmap.shape[1] - 1) v = clamp(v, 0, envmap.shape[0] - 1) pi = envmap[v, u] # Calculate squared error weighted by visibility # Note: The formula includes 1/X. X is not explicitly defined. # Assuming X is the number of color channels or a normalization constant. # For implementation, we sum the weighted squared errors. errorsum += Tk sum((ci - pi) 2) totalsamples += 1 # Or number of channels, depending on X definition # Apply 1/X factor if X is known. If X is total samples, this averages. # The source formula is E = sumk (1/X) sumi Tk (ci - pi)^2 # If X is a constant normalization factor, it should be applied. # Without explicit X, we return the sum. If X is needed, it must be provided. # Assuming X is a global constant or derived from scene properties. # For now, we return the sum as the basis for w. return errorsum def computecauchyloss(voxeldensities, weights, lambdac, lambdan): """ Computes the Cauchy loss Lc using pre-computed weights. """ loss = 0.0 for i, sigmai in enumerate(voxeldensities): w = weights[i] loss += log(1 + lambdan w sigmai 2) return lambdac loss Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Empty Space: The method is often combined with auxiliary terms to skip empty space using hierarchical formulation to ease computational impact. Visibility Tracing: Accurate visibility tracing is crucial for populating the environment map correctly. Incorrect visibility can lead to erroneous color accumulation. Spherical Mapping: The mapping from 3D direction to 2D environment map indices must be consistent between population and evaluation steps. Time Complexity: The population step (Algorithm 1) is executed once per hierarchical level (except the first) for all voxels and cameras. This involves ray marching and spherical mapping for each voxel-camera pair. The loss evaluation is per iteration and per voxel. Memory Complexity: Each voxel stores an 8 \times 4 environment map (32 floats, assuming RGB or similar) plus the weight buffer (1 float per voxel). This adds memory overhead compared to standard Plenoxels. Performance: The method was tested on artificial and real scenes (Tanks and Temples) using a Nvidia GTX 1080. Reconstruction times were compared to baseline PERF, showing the computational impact of the additional steps. Strengths: Improves geometry reconstruction by distinguishing surface points from volume points, especially for view-dependent lighting without clear Lambertian components. Limitations: Adds computational overhead due to the population step and storage of environment maps per voxel. This technique was introduced in the paper "Addressing the Shape-Radiance Ambiguity in View-Dependent Radiance Fields". It builds upon the Plenoxels framework [3] and SnerG [29] by adding a low-frequency view-dependent function per voxel to handle non-highlight colors. The method aims to improve 3D reconstruction quality by leveraging the fact that a low-resolution function approximating outgoing radiance is more likely to correspond to a surface point than an arbitrary volume point. name: Coarse-to-Fine Optimization with Pruning
head: Plenoxel Grid with Trilinear Interpolation Optimization
body: Coarse-to-Fine Optimization with Pruning is a hierarchical training strategy for optimizing 3D radiance fields represented as sparse voxel grids. It solves the problem of initializing and maintaining an efficient voxel structure that adapts to scene complexity during training, preventing overfitting in unobserved regions while refining detail where needed. It sets itself apart from static grid methods by dynamically pruning low-visibility voxels using a weight or density threshold, and subdividing remaining voxels to increase resolution, building on the general framework of Plenoxels. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A scene with training views, an initial coarse resolution (e.g., 256^3), and a target final resolution (e.g., 512^3). Output: An optimized voxel grid containing density and spherical harmonic (SH) coefficients for the radiance field. Data Structures: Voxel Grid: A 3D array storing per-voxel attributes. In the base Plenoxels implementation, this includes density (\sigma) and spherical harmonic (SH) coefficients for color. Pruning Mask: A boolean or weight-based metric indicating voxel occupancy, derived from the maximum weight Ti(1-\exp(-\sigmai\deltai)) over all training rays or directly from the density value. Parameters: T{init}: Initial resolution (e.g., 256^3). T{final}: Final resolution (e.g., 512^3). \tau{prune}: Threshold for pruning unoccupied voxels. \lambda{TV}: Weight for Total Variation regularization. Steps: 1. Initialize: Start with a dense voxel grid at the lower resolution T{init} (e.g., 256^3). Initialize density and SH coefficients. 2. Optimize: Train the grid parameters using the loss function defined in: \mathcal{L} = \mathcal{L}{recon} + \lambda{TV} \mathcal{L}{TV} where \mathcal{L}{recon} is the Mean Squared Error (MSE) over rendered pixel colors and \mathcal{L}{TV} is the Total Variation regularizer. 3. Prune: Remove voxels deemed unoccupied. A voxel i is pruned if its maximum weight over all training rays falls below a threshold. The weight is calculated as: wi = Ti(1-\exp(-\sigmai \deltai)) where Ti is the transmittance, \sigmai is the density, and \deltai is the step size along rays passing through voxel i. Alternatively, pruning can be based directly on the density value. Pitfall: Naive pruning can adversely impact color and density near surfaces because trilinear interpolation uses values from immediate exterior voxels. Solution: Perform a dilation operation. A voxel is only pruned if both itself and its neighbors are deemed unoccupied. 4. Refine: Subdivide each remaining voxel in half in each dimension (e.g., from 256^3 to 512^3). 5. Initialize New Values: Use trilinear interpolation to initialize the grid values for the new, finer resolution based on the coarser grid. Trilinear interpolation at resolution 128^3 has been observed to outperform nearest neighbor interpolation at 256^3. 6. Repeat: Continue optimizing at the new resolution. Repeat steps 2–5 until the target resolution T{final} is reached. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def coarsetofineoptimization(scenedata, Tinit, Tfinal, tauprune, lambdatv): # Step 1: Initialize grid = creategrid(resolution=Tinit) initializeparameters(grid) currentres = Tinit while currentres < Tfinal: # Step 2: Optimize optimizeparameters(grid, scenedata.rays, lambdatv) # Step 3: Prune voxelweights = computemaxvoxelweights(grid, scenedata.rays) isunoccupied = voxelweights < tauprune # Apply dilation: voxel is pruned only if itself and all 26 neighbors are unoccupied dilatedunoccupied = applydilation(isunoccupied, grid.shape) prunevoxels(grid, dilatedunoccupied) # Step 4: Refine newres = currentres 2 subdividegrid(grid, newres) # Step 5: Initialize New Values interpolatefromcoarser(grid, currentres, newres) currentres = newres return grid def creategrid(resolution): return {"density": zeros((resolution, resolution, resolution)), "shcoeffs": zeros((resolution, resolution, resolution, 3))} def initializeparameters(grid): grid["density"][:] = 0.0 grid["shcoeffs"][:] = 0.0 def optimizeparameters(grid, rays, lambdatv): # Standard gradient descent step minimizing L = Lrecon + lambdatv LTV for ray in rays: renderray(grid, ray) computegradients(grid, lambdatv) applygradients(grid) def computemaxvoxelweights(grid, rays): maxweights = zeros(grid["density"].shape) for ray in rays: for voxel in ray.voxels: transmittance = computetransmittance(ray, voxel) avgsigma = voxel.avgdensity avgdelta = voxel.avgstepsize weight = transmittance (1.0 - exp(-avgsigma avgdelta)) maxweights[voxel.id] = max(maxweights[voxel.id], weight) return maxweights def applydilation(isunoccupied, shape): dilated = zeros(shape, dtype=bool) for i in range(shape[0]): for j in range(shape[1]): for k in range(shape[2]): if isunoccupied[i, j, k]: neighborunoccupied = True for di in [-1, 0, 1]: for dj in [-1, 0, 1]: for dk in [-1, 0, 1]: ni, nj, nk = i+di, j+dj, k+dk if not (0 <= ni < shape[0] and 0 <= nj < shape[1] and 0 <= nk < shape[2]): neighborunoccupied = False break if not isunoccupied[ni, nj, nk]: neighborunoccupied = False break if not neighborunoccupied: break if not neighborunoccupied: break if neighborunoccupied: dilated[i, j, k] = True return dilated def prunevoxels(grid, mask): grid["density"][mask] = 0.0 grid["shcoeffs"][mask] = 0.0 def subdividegrid(grid, newres): newdensity = zeros((newres, newres, newres)) newsh = zeros((newres, newres, newres, 3)) grid["density"] = newdensity grid["shcoeffs"] = newsh def interpolatefromcoarser(grid, oldres, newres): for i in range(newres): for j in range(newres): for k in range(newres): pos = array([i, j, k]) (oldres / newres) grid["density"][i, j, k] = trilinearinterpolate(grid["density"], oldres, pos) grid["shcoeffs"][i, j, k] = trilinearinterpolate(grid["shcoeffs"], oldres, pos) def trilinearinterpolate(volume, res, pos): # Standard trilinear interpolation i, j, k = pos i0, j0, k0 = floor(i), floor(j), floor(k) i1, j1, k1 = i0 + 1, j0 + 1, k0 + 1 i0, j0, k0 = clip([i0, j0, k0], 0, res - wi) + volume[i1, j0, k1] wi c11 = volume[i0, j1, k1] (1 - wi) + volume[i1, j1, k1] wi return (c00 (1 - wj) + c10 wj) (1 - wk) + (c01 (1 - wj) + c11 wj) wk Progressive Sparse Voxels Optimization is a coarse-to-fine training procedure for optimizing 3D radiance fields represented as sparse voxel grids. It solves the problem of initializing and maintaining an efficient voxel structure that adapts to scene complexity during training, preventing overfitting in unobserved regions while refining detail where needed. It sets itself apart from static grid methods by dynamically pruning low-visibility voxels and subdividing high-error voxels based on gradient signals, building on the general framework of Coarse-to-Fine Optimization with Pruning. A second optimization stage that reconstructs surface details and view-dependent effects using a higher-resolution voxel grid and a hybrid explicit-implicit representation, freezing the coarse geometry grid. Definition: This stage focuses on a smaller subspace to reconstruct surface details and view-dependent effects, freezing the optimized coarse geometry grid V^{(\text{density})(c)}. Steps: 1. Freeze Coarse Grid: The optimized V^{(\text{density})(c)} from the coarse stage is frozen. 2. Define Known Free Space: A query point is in known free space if the post-activated alpha value from V^{(\text{density})(c)} is less than threshold \tau^{(c)}. Otherwise, it is in unknown space. 3. Fine Voxels Allocation: Densely query V^{(\text{density})(c)} to find a BBox tightly enclosing the unknown space, with lengths Lx^{(f)}, Ly^{(f)}, Lz^{(f)}. Derive voxel size s^{(f)} and grid dimensions Nx^{(f)}, Ny^{(f)}, Nz^{(f)} from expected total voxels M^{(f)}. 4. Fine-stage Points Sampling: Filter out rays not intersecting known free space. Adjust near/far bounds t^{(\text{near})} and t^{(\text{far})} to ray-box intersection endpoints. Do not adjust t^{(\text{near})} if x0 is already inside the BBox. Parameters: M^{(f)}: Hyperparameter for the expected total number of voxels in the fine stage. D: Hyperparameter for feature-space dimension in the feature voxel grid V^{(\text{feat})(f)}. Representation: The fine stage uses a higher-resolution density voxel grid V^{(\text{density})(f)} \in \mathbb{R}^{1 \times Nx^{(f)} \times Ny^{(f)} \times Nz^{(f)}} with post-activated interpolation. For view-dependent color, a hybrid representation is used: A feature voxel grid V^{(\text{feat})(f)} \in \mathbb{R}^{D \times Nx^{(f)} \times Ny^{(f)} \times Nz^{(f)}}. A shallow MLP parameterized by \Theta^{(f)}. Queries for 3D points \mathbf{x} and viewing direction \mathbf{d} are performed by: \vec{\phi}^{(f)} = \text{interp} \left( \mathbf{x}, \mathbf{V}^{(\text{density})(f)} \right) \mathbf{c}^{(\mathbf{f})} = \text{MLP}{\Theta^{(\mathbf{f})}}(\text{interp}(\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{V}^{(\text{feat})(\mathbf{f})}), \mathbf{x}, \mathbf{d}) where \mathbf{c}^{(f)} \in \mathbb{R}^3 is the view-dependent color emission and \sigma^{(f)} \in \mathbb{R} is the raw volume density. Positional embedding is applied on \mathbf{x}, \mathbf{d} for the MLP. Progressive Scaling: Inspired by NSVF, the voxel grids V^{(\text{density})(f)} and V^{(\text{feat})(f)} are progressively scaled. Let p{g\ckpt} be the set of checkpoint steps. The initial number of voxels is set to \lfloor M^{(f)} / 2^{|p{g\ckpt}|} \rfloor. When reaching a training step in p{g\ckpt}, the number of voxels is doubled such that the final number is M^{(f)}. At each checkpoint, the voxel grids are resized by trilinear interpolation. Efficiency: Free space skipping is used. Points in known free space (checked via V^{(\text{density})(c)}) are skipped during training and testing to improve efficiency, as querying V^{(\text{density})(c)} is faster than querying V^{(\text{density})(f)} or computing view-dependent colors. Time Complexity: The coarse-to-fine approach reduces training time compared to optimizing a high-resolution grid from scratch, as the initial coarse grid converges faster. The fine detail reconstruction stage adds additional computational cost due to the hybrid explicit-implicit representation and MLP queries. Memory Complexity: Pruning reduces memory usage by removing unoccupied voxels. The fine stage requires additional memory for the higher-resolution grid and feature grid, but the BBox allocation limits this to the unknown space. Performance: Trilinear interpolation at lower resolutions (e.g., 128^3) can outperform nearest neighbor at higher resolutions (e.g., 256^3). Strengths: Adapts to scene complexity, prevents overfitting in unobserved regions, and enables high-resolution detail reconstruction. Limitations: Naive pruning can cause artifacts near surfaces if not handled with dilation. The fine stage requires careful tuning of hyperparameters like M^{(f)} and \tau^{(c)}. Coarse-to-Fine Optimization with Pruning originates from the Plenoxels paper, which introduced a novel approach for fast radiance field reconstruction from sparse views using voxel grids without neural networks as the radiance field representation. The method builds on the concept of PlenOctrees for voxel pruning. The fine detail reconstruction variant was introduced in the Direct Voxel Grid Optimization paper to further enhance surface details and view-dependent effects. head: Progressive Sparse Voxels
body: Progressive Sparse Voxels Optimization is a coarse-to-fine training procedure for optimizing 3D radiance fields represented as sparse voxel grids. It solves the problem of initializing and maintaining an efficient voxel structure that adapts to scene complexity during training, preventing overfitting in unobserved regions while refining detail where needed. It sets itself apart from static grid methods by dynamically pruning low-visibility voxels and subdividing high-error voxels based on gradient signals, building on the general framework of Coarse-to-Fine Optimization with Pruning. Inputs: A set of training images with known camera parameters (position, orientation, intrinsics including horizontal FOV \theta{\text{fov-x}} and image width W). Outputs: An optimized sparse voxel grid containing Spherical Harmonic (SH) coefficients for color and density values at grid points. The scene is represented as an Octree. Voxel: Contains SH coefficients (view-dependent color) and references to grid points. Grid Point: Stores raw density values. Grid points are shared among adjacent voxels (8 corners per voxel). Layout: Only leaf nodes are stored in the final Octree structure. Source voxels are removed upon subdivision. h{lv}: Number of levels for the dense grid initialization in bounded scenes or the main region of unbounded scenes. h{out}: Number of background shell levels for unbounded scenes. h{ratio}: Target ratio of background voxels to main region voxels after initialization. h{geo}: Negative initial raw density value to ensure near-zero activated density (\exp(h{geo}) \approx 0). h{prune}: Threshold for maximum blending weight to prune voxels. h{every}: Number of training iterations between adaptive pruning and subdivision operations. h{rate}: Threshold for sampling rate; if v{rate} < 2h{rate}, subdivision priority is set to zero. h{percent}: Percentage of voxels with highest priority selected for subdivision. \lambda{\text{ssim}}, \lambda{\text{T}}, \lambda{\text{dist}}, \lambda{\text{R}}, \lambda{\text{tv}}: Weights for SSIM, Total Transmittance, Distortion, Regularization, and Total Variation losses. Initialization depends on whether the scene is bounded or unbounded. All voxels start with raw density h{geo} and SH coefficients set to zero, except the zero-degree SH component which is set to yield gray color (intensity 0.5). 1.1 Bounded Scenes 1. Initialize a dense grid with h{lv} levels. 2. Remove voxels that are not observed by any training image. 3. The total number of voxels is \le (2^{h{lv}})^3. 1.2 Unbounded Scenes 1. Define the Main Region: A cuboid centered at the average camera position, with radius equal to the median distance from the center to the cameras. Initialize a dense grid with h{lv} levels within this cuboid. 2. Define the Background Region: Allocate h{out} levels of background shells enclosing the main region. The radius of the entire scene is 2^{h{out}} times the radius of the main region. 3. Initialize background shells with the coarsest voxel size. Each shell level starts with 4^3 - 2^3 = 56 voxels. 4. Iteratively subdivide background shell voxels with the highest sampling rate and remove unobserved voxels. 5. Repeat step 4 until the ratio of the number of background voxels to main region voxels equals h{ratio}. 6. The total number of voxels is \le (1 + h{ratio})(2^{h{lv}})^3. The optimization proceeds in iterations. Every h{every} iterations, perform Adaptive Pruning and Subdivision. The total loss function is: \mathcal{L} = \mathcal{L}{\text{mse}} + \lambda{\text{ssim}} \mathcal{L}{\text{ssim}} + \lambda{\text{T}} \mathcal{L}{\text{T}} + \lambda{\text{dist}} \mathcal{L}{\text{dist}} + \lambda{\text{R}} \mathcal{L}{\text{R}} + \lambda{\text{tv}} \mathcal{L}{\text{tv}} where \mathcal{L}{\text{mse}} and \mathcal{L}{\text{ssim}} are photometric losses, \mathcal{L}{\text{T}} encourages binary transmittance, \mathcal{L}{\text{dist}} is distortion loss, \mathcal{L}{\text{R}} is per-point RGB loss, and \mathcal{L}{\text{tv}} is total variation loss on the sparse density grid. 1. For each voxel, compute the maximum blending weight (Ti \alphai) across all training cameras. Ti is the transmittance before the voxel, and \alphai is the opacity of the voxel, derived from the volume rendering equation (Eq. 1 in). 2. Remove voxels where the maximum blending weight is lower than h{prune}. 3. Update SH coefficients and grid points: SH coefficients are pruned along with the voxels. Grid points are removed only if they do not belong to the corners of any remaining voxel. 1. Compute Sampling Rate: For each voxel, calculate the maximum sampling rate v{rate} to estimate the number of rays hitting the voxel along the image's horizontal axis: v{rate} = \max{i}^{N{cam}} \frac{vs}{v{interval}^i} v{interval}^{(i)} = (vc - ro^{(i)}) \cdot T \cdot \ell^{(i)} \cdot \tan\left(0.5 \cdot \theta{\text{fov-x}}^{(i)}\right) Where: vs: Voxel size (side length). vc: Center of the voxel. ro^{(i)}: Origin of camera i. T: Rotation matrix of camera i. \ell^{(i)}: Camera lookat vector of camera i. \theta{\text{fov-x}}^{(i)}: Horizontal field of view of camera i. N{cam}: Number of training cameras. Note: The source text mentions W (image width) in the variable list but does not explicitly use it in the formula for v{interval} or v{rate}. 2. Compute Priority: Accumulate subdivision priority v{priority} for each voxel by summing over all training pixel rays r \in R observed over the last h{every} iterations: v{priority} = \sum{r \in R} \left\| \alpha(r) \cdot \frac{\partial \mathcal{L}(r)}{\partial \alpha(r)} \right\| Where: \alpha(r): Opacity contribution of the voxel to ray r. \mathcal{L}(r): Training loss of ray r. The gradient is weighted by the alpha values. 3. Filter Overfitting: If a voxel's maximum sampling rate v{rate} < 2h{rate}, set its v{priority} to zero to prevent overfitting to few pixels. 4. Select Voxels: Select voxels with priority above the top h{percent} percentile. The total number of voxels increases by h{percent} \cdot (8 - 1) percent. 5. Subdivide and Update: Subdivide selected voxels into 8 children. Remove the source voxel from the Octree (only leaf nodes are kept). SH Coefficients: Duplicate the parent's SH coefficients to the 8 children. Grid Points: Compute densities of new grid points using trilinear interpolation of the parent's corner grid points. Merge duplicated grid points (shared between children or neighbors) and average their densities. Unverified code. radius c = (center[0] + offset, center[1] + offset, center[2] + offset) voxels.append({'center': c, 'size': 2 radius / side, 'shcoeffs': [0.0] 49, 'gridcorners': [], 'alive': True}) # Background shells bgradius = radius (2 hout) # Generate initial coarse shells (56 voxels per level) for level in range(hout): innerr = radius (2 level) outerr = radius (2 (level + 1)) shellsize = outerr - innerr # Create 56 voxels per shell level (simplified generation) for i in range(56): # Placeholder for shell voxel coordinate generation pass # Iteratively subdivide background based on sampling rate until ratio matches hratio # while ratiobgtomain(bgvoxels, mainvoxels) < hratio: # candidates = getshellvoxels(bgvoxels) # for v in candidates: # vrate = computesamplingrate(v['center'], v['size'], cameras) # if isobserved(v, cameras): # subdividevoxel(v) # else: # v['alive'] = False pass # Initialize parameters for v in voxels: v['densityraw'] = hgeo v['shcoeffs'][0] = 0.5 # Zero-degree SH for gray color return voxels def optimizestep(voxels: List[Dict], cameras: List[Dict], iteration: int, hevery: int, hprune: float, hrate: float, hpercent: float) -> List[Dict]: """Perform pruning and subdivision every hevery iterations.""" if iteration % hevery != 0: return voxels # 1. Adaptive Pruning prunedindices = [] for i, v in enumerate(voxels): if not v['alive']: continue maxblendingweight = 0.0 for cam in cameras: bw = computeblendingweight(v, cam) if bw > maxblendingweight: maxblendingweight = bw if maxblendingweight < hprune: prunedindices.append(i) for i in reversed(prunedindices): voxels[i]['alive'] = False # 2. Subdivision # Collect rays from last hevery iterations (implementation depends on training loop) rays = [] # List of ray objects with alphacontribution and gradientlosswrtalpha methods priorities = [] for v in voxels: if not v['alive']: continue vrate = computesamplingrate(v['center'], v['size'], cameras) priority = 0.0 for r in rays: if r.hits(v): alpha = r.alphacontribution(v) grad = r.gradientlosswrtalpha(v) priority += math.sqrt(sum(a2 for a in grad)) # L2 norm if vrate < 2 hrate: priority = 0.0 priorities.append((v, priority)) # Select top hpercent priorities.sort(key=lambda x: x[1], reverse=True) numtosubdivide = max(1, int(len(priorities) hpercent / 100)) voxelstosubdivide = [p[0] for p in priorities[:numtosubdivide]] # Subdivide newvoxels = [] for v in voxelstosubdivide: # Generate 8 children halfsize = v['size'] / 2.0 for dx in [-1, 1]: for dy in [-1, 1]: for dz in [-1, 1]: childcenter = (v['center'][0] + dx halfsize, v['center'][1] + dy halfsize, v['center'][2] + dz halfsize) child = {'center': childcenter, 'size': halfsize, 'shcoeffs': list(v['shcoeffs']), 'gridcorners': [], 'alive': True} # Trilinear interpolation for new grid points child['densityraw'] = v['densityraw'] # Simplified; actual trilinear interpolation of corners required newvoxels.append(child) v['alive'] = False # Remove source voxel # Merge grid points and average densities allalive = [v for v in voxels + newvoxels if v['alive']] gridpoints = {} for v in allalive: for corner in v['gridcorners']: key = tuple(corner) if key in gridpoints: gridpoints[key]['count'] += 1 gridpoints[key]['densitysum'] += corner['density'] else: gridpoints[key] = {'count': 1, 'densitysum': corner['density']} for key in gridpoints: gridpoints[key]['density'] = gridpoints[key]['densitysum'] / gridpoints[key]['count'] return voxels + newvoxels Time Complexity: Depends on the number of voxels and training iterations. Subdivision increases the voxel count by h{percent} \cdot 7 percent per step. Pruning reduces it. The cost of computing sampling rates and priorities scales with the number of voxels and rays. Memory Complexity: Scales with the number of active voxels. The initialization bounds the voxel count to (1 + h{ratio})(2^{h{lv}})^3 for unbounded scenes. Strengths: Adapts resolution to scene complexity; prevents overfitting in unobserved regions via pruning and sampling rate thresholds; handles unbounded scenes effectively with background shells. Limitations: Requires careful tuning of hyperparameters (h{lv}, h{out}, h{ratio}, h{prune}, h{rate}, h{percent}). The subdivision process can be computationally intensive if many voxels are selected. When to use: When optimizing radiance fields from sparse or unstructured camera views where static grids are inefficient or when scene bounds are unknown (unbounded). Progressive Sparse Voxels Optimization was introduced in the paper "Sparse Voxels Rasterization: Real-time High-fidelity Radiance Field Rendering". It is part of the SVRaster framework, designed for real-time rendering of high-fidelity radiance fields. The method addresses the limitations of static voxel grids by introducing a progressive optimization strategy that adapts the voxel structure during training. name: HDR-Plenoxels
head: HDR radiance fields modeled by Plenoxels
body: HDR-Plenoxels is a voxel-based volume rendering method that reconstructs 3D High Dynamic Range (HDR) radiance fields, scene geometry, and varying camera settings from multi-view Low Dynamic Range (LDR) images. It extends Plenoxels by introducing a differentiable tone-mapping module that models the in-camera imaging pipeline (ISP), including white balance and Camera Response Functions (CRF), allowing for self-calibration and controllable rendering. Unlike NeRF, which uses implicit neural networks, HDR-Plenoxels uses explicit sparse voxel grids with spherical harmonics, achieving rendering speeds two orders of magnitude faster than NeRF. Inputs: A set of N multi-view LDR images captured with varying camera settings (exposure, white balance, CRF). Camera poses and intrinsics, typically obtained via COLMAP sparse reconstruction. For real data: undistorted images. Outputs: A sparse voxel grid representing the 3D scene, containing opacity and view-dependent radiance coefficients. Learned tone-mapping parameters (white balance scales, CRF parameters). Novel view synthesis of HDR images, which can be tone-mapped to arbitrary LDR settings. Sparse Voxel Grid: Structure: A 3D grid covering a bounded space of interest. The grid is sparse, meaning only occupied voxels are stored or processed. Voxel Layout: Each voxel stores: Opacity (\sigma): A scalar value representing the density/opacity of the voxel. Spherical Harmonics (SH) Coefficients: A vector of 27 values (9 per color channel: Red, Green, Blue) representing the view-dependent radiance. Total per voxel: 28 values (1 opacity + 27 SH coefficients). Initialization: Opacity \sigma is initialized to 0.1. SH coefficients are initialized such that the base color is grey, achieved by adding an offset of 0.5 to the color components. Tone Mapping Parameters: White Balance Scales: Three scalar values (wr, wg, wb) representing the basis white balance, derived from channel-wise averaging of the full view. Exposure Scale: A scalar value representing the basis exposure, derived from globally averaging the white balance values. CRF Parameters: Parameters defining the Camera Response Function, learned during training. 1. Preprocessing: Compute rough 3D geometry and obtain camera poses using COLMAP sparse reconstruction to determine the bounding box of the scene. For real-world images, perform lens undistortion using calibration data. 2. Grid Initialization: Initialize a sparse voxel grid within the determined bounding box. Synthetic Data Resolution Schedule: Start at (128, 128, 64). Upsample to (256, 256, 128), then (512, 512, 256), and finally (800, 800, 512), with each upsampling occurring after 25,600 iterations. Real Data Resolution Schedule: Start at (128, 128, 128). Upsample to (256, 256, 256), then (750, 600, 300). Initialize voxel opacity \sigma = 0.1 and SH coefficients to represent a grey color (offset 0.5). 3. Coarse-to-Fine Training Loop: For each training iteration: a. Ray Marching (HDR Rendering): For each pixel, cast a ray through the scene. Sample points along the ray. Interpolate opacity \sigma and SH coefficients from the voxel grid at each sample point. Compute the HDR radiance L{HDR} for the viewing direction using the SH basis functions Yl(\omega) and coefficients cl: L{HDR}(\omega) = \sum{l=0}^{L} \sum{m=-l}^{l} c{l,m} Y{l,m}(\omega) where L is the degree of SH (typically 2 for 9 coefficients per channel). Perform volume rendering to composite the final HDR radiance C{HDR} for the pixel, accounting for depth and opacity. b. Differentiable Tone Mapping: Apply the tone mapping module to C{HDR} to produce the synthesized LDR image C{LDR}. The tone mapping consists of two stages: 1. White Balance: Scale the RGB channels by the learned white balance parameters wr, wg, wb. 2. Camera Response Function (CRF): Apply the learned CRF function f(\cdot) to the white-balanced values. The final LDR value is computed as: C{LDR} = f(w \odot C{HDR}) where \odot denotes element-wise multiplication with white balance scales. c. Loss Computation: Compute the loss \mathcal{L} between the synthesized LDR image C{LDR} and the ground truth LDR image C{GT}. Include Total Variation (TV) loss for opacity \sigma and SH coefficients during the first 3 epochs (before the first upsampling) to stabilize training. \mathcal{L}{TV} = \lambda{TV,\sigma} \text{TV}(\sigma) + \lambda{TV,SH} \text{TV}(c{SH}) with \lambda{TV,\sigma} = 5 \cdot 10^{-4} and \lambda{TV,SH} = 1 \cdot 10^{-2}. d. Backpropagation: Backpropagate gradients through the tone mapping module to update the SH coefficients, opacity, and tone mapping parameters (white balance, CRF). Use the RMSProp optimizer. e. Grid Management: Upsampling: Increase grid resolution according to the schedule. Pruning: Remove voxels with opacity below a specified occupancy threshold to reduce computational cost. The specific threshold value is not given in the sources. 4. Controllable Rendering (Post-Training): To render at a specific exposure, scale the basis exposure value (globally averaged white balance). To render with specific white balance, adjust the red, green, and blue components of the basis white balance (channel-wise averaged). To render median exposure, use the median of the minimum and maximum learned exposure values. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import numpy as np def initializegrid(boundingbox, resolution): """ Initialize sparse voxel grid. Returns: grid: Dictionary or sparse structure mapping voxel coordinates to [opacity, shcoeffs] opacityinit: 0.1 shinit: Grey color offset 0.5 """ grid = {} # Implementation details for sparse grid storage depend on specific engine # Here we assume a function that creates the structure return grid def sphericalharmonicseval(direction, shcoeffs): """ Evaluate spherical harmonics for a given direction and coefficients. direction: (3,) unit vector shcoeffs: (27,) vector (9 per channel) Returns: radiance: (3,) vector (R, G, B) """ # Standard SH basis evaluation # L=2 implies 9 coefficients per channel # This is a placeholder for the actual SH math pass def volumerenderray(rayorigin, raydirection, grid, numsamples): """ Render a single ray through the voxel grid. Returns: hdrradiance: (3,) HDR color depth: float """ # Sample points along ray # Interpolate opacity and SH from grid # Compute radiance using SH # Composite using standard volume rendering equation pass def tonemapping(hdrradiance, wbscales, crfparams): """ Apply differentiable tone mapping. hdrradiance: (3,) HDR color wbscales: (3,) white balance scales crfparams: parameters for CRF function Returns: ldrcolor: (3,) LDR color """ # Apply white balance wbcolor = hdrradiance wbscales # Apply CRF ldrcolor = applycrf(wbcolor, crfparams) return ldrcolor def train(hdrplenoxelsmodel, images, poses, resolutionschedule, iterationsperstep): """ Main training loop. """ # 1. Preprocessing # - Get COLMAP poses # - Undistort real images # 2. Initialize Grid currentres = resolutionschedule[0] grid = initializegrid(boundingbox, currentres) # Initialize parameters opacity = np.full(grid.size, 0.1) shcoeffs = np.full((grid.size, 27), 0.5) # Grey offset wbscales = np.array([1.0, 1.0, 1.0]) crfparams = learncrfparameters() optimizer = RMSProp() for step in range(totaliterations): # Check for upsampling if step % iterationsperstep == 0 and step > 0: currentres = getnextresolution(resolutionschedule, step) grid = upsamplegrid(grid, currentres) # 3. Training Step for image, pose in zip(images, poses): # Ray generation rays = generaterays(image.shape, pose) # Forward Pass hdrcolors = [] for ray in rays: hdrc, = volumerenderray(ray.origin, ray.direction, grid, opacity, shcoeffs) hdrcolors.append(hdrc) # Tone Mapping ldrcolors = [] for hdrc in hdrcolors: ldrc = tonemapping(hdrc, wbscales, crfparams) ldrcolors.append(ldrc) # Loss Computation synthesizedimage = stackimages(ldrcolors, image.shape) loss = mseloss(synthesizedimage, image) # Add TV loss if in first 3 epochs if step < 3 iterationsperstep: tvloss = computetvloss(opacity, shcoeffs) loss += lambdatvsigma tvlosssigma + lambdatvsh tvlosssh # Backpropagation optimizer.zerograd() loss.backward() optimizer.step() # Update grid parameters opacity = optimizer.getgradientsfor(opacity) shcoeffs = optimizer.getgradientsfor(shcoeffs) wbscales = optimizer.getgradientsfor(wbscales) crfparams = optimizer.getgradientsfor(crfparams) # Pruning prunevoxels(grid, opacity, occupancythreshold) def rendernovelview(camerapose, wbscalefactor, wbchannelfactors, exposurefactor): """ Controllable rendering. """ # Adjust tone mapping parameters based on controls adjustedwb = basiswb wbscalefactor wbchannelfactors adjustedexposure = basisexposure exposurefactor # Render HDR hdrimage = renderhdr(camerapose) # Apply adjusted tone mapping ldrimage = tonemapping(hdrimage, adjustedwb, crfparams) return ldrimage Occupancy Threshold: Scalar value for pruning voxels. Value not specified in the sources. TV Loss Weights: \lambda{TV,\sigma} = 5 \cdot 10^{-4}, \lambda{TV,SH} = 1 \cdot 10^{-2}. Optimizer: RMSProp. SH Degree: 2 (9 coefficients per channel). Saturated Regions: Wide dynamic range scenes cause saturation in LDR training images. HDR-Plenoxels handles this via the differentiable tone mapping module and robust learning of SH coefficients and opacity. Large Depth in Synthetic Data: Default concentric sphere grids struggle with large depth in Blender data. Solved by computing rough 3D geometry via COLMAP to determine the proper grid range. Lens Distortion: Real images often have lens distortion. Solved by undistorting images via calibration before training. Training Instability: SH coefficients can change significantly during training. Mitigated by initializing color to grey (offset 0.5) and opacity to 0.1. Time Complexity: Training time is tens of minutes. Memory Complexity: Uses sparse voxel grids, which are more memory-efficient than dense grids or dense neural networks for high-resolution scenes. Rendering Speed: Two orders of magnitude faster than NeRF. Strengths: Fast convergence and rendering. Handles varying camera settings (exposure, white balance, CRF) without explicit calibration. Robust to saturated regions and shot noise. Enables controllable rendering of exposure and white balance. Limitations: Requires COLMAP for initial geometry and poses. Performance degrades slightly with extreme exposure gaps (e.g., ±6EV), though still outperforms some alternatives. When to Use: When fast HDR novel view synthesis is required from multi-view LDR images with varying camera settings, and computational resources are limited compared to NeRF-based methods. When Not to Use: When dense COLMAP results are unavailable and cannot be approximated, or when implicit neural representations are strictly required for other reasons. Origin: Introduced by Kim Jun-Seong, Kim Yu-Ji, Moon Ye-Bin, and Tae-Hyun Oh at POSTECH. Paper: "HDR-Plenoxels: Self-Calibrating High Dynamic Range Radiance Fields" (arXiv:2208.06787v2, Nov 2022). Development: Extends Plenoxels [53] for HDR radiance fields and adopts the coarse-to-fine training scheme from NSVF [17]. It addresses the limitations of NeRF in handling HDR and varying camera conditions efficiently. Usage: Used for novel view synthesis from multi-view LDR images captured with varying exposure, white balance, and CRF settings. Tested on Blender synthetic datasets and real scenes (Character, Desk, Plant, Coffee, Kitchen). name: PlenOctree Compression with Modified Training and Sparsity
head: Sparse PlenOctree Training
body: This method reduces the storage size of PlenOctree models by modifying the NeRF-SH training loss to optimize sparsity and compressing the resulting voxelized point cloud attributes. It differs from the original PlenOctree method by using a Cauchy loss instead of the standard sparsity loss, adding total variation regularization, using half-pixel ray offsets, and performing post-thresholding fine-tuning. Inputs: Training images and camera poses. Outputs: Compressed PlenOctree model (encoded point cloud attributes). Data Structures: The PlenOctree is represented as a set of octree leaves. The raw data structure fields for a scene (e.g., Lego) are: Child: Array of size 2,982,398 \times 8, 32-bit integers. Parent depth: Array of size 2,982,398 \times 2, 32-bit integers. Data (\sigma, k): Array of size 2,982,398 \times 8 \times 49, 16-bit floats. This stores density \sigma and Spherical Harmonics (SH) coefficients k. Metadata: 32/64-bit values. Total uncompressed size is approximately 2.3 GB for the Lego scene. Steps: 1. Modified NeRF-SH Training: Train a NeRF-SH network to output SH coefficients k of degree \ell{max} instead of RGB colors. The ray directions are modified by adding a half-pixel offset so they pass through pixel centers. The total training loss L is: L = Lr + L{cauchy} + L{TV} where Lr is the rendering loss, L{cauchy} is the Cauchy sparsity loss, and L{TV} is the total variation regularization. 2. PlenOctree Extraction: Sample the trained NeRF-SH to extract density \sigma and SH coefficients k into octree leaves. The SH coefficients are evaluated according to the ray direction (\theta, \phi) to obtain view-dependent color. 3. PlenOctree Optimization: Fine-tune the extracted octree using the rendering loss Lr on training images. 4. Thresholding for Sparsity: Estimate opacity \alpha for each node to remove nodes with low influence. The opacity is estimated as: \alpha = 1 - \exp(-\sigma \delta) where \delta \approx 2/2^N and N is the octree depth. Nodes with low \alpha are removed. 5. Post-thresholding Fine-tuning: Re-fine-tune the "distilled" PlenOctree with cross-validation to compensate for knowledge loss from removed points. 6. Compression Preparation: View the octree leaves as a voxelized point cloud P with N voxels. The coordinates x{pc} are calculated from the octree child indices x{oct} = [Xn, Yn, Zn] and octree depth M: x{pc} = x{oct} \times 2^M - 0.5 The attributes s(n) for each point are: s(n) = [\sigman, k^0{n0}, k^{-1}{n1}, k^1{n1}, \dots, k^\ell{n\ell}] where k^\ell{nm} \in \mathbb{R}^3. 7. Attribute Encoding: Encode \sigma and k coefficients as attributes of the point cloud P using a point cloud compression method, specifically Geometry-Based Point Cloud Coding (G-PCC). Parameters: Total variation hyperparameter \eta: 10^{-11}. Cauchy loss hyperparameter \lambdas: 10^{-4}. Formulas: Total Variation Regularization: L{TV} = \frac{\eta}{|R|} \sum{i,k} \| \nabla \sigma(ri(tk)) \|2 where R is the ray batch size. Cauchy Sparsity Loss: L{cauchy} = \lambdas \sum{i,k} \log(1 + 2\sigma(ri(tk))^2) where \sigma is volume density. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: The SH coefficients of degree \ell=3 account for 98% of the data size, making them the primary bottleneck for compression. Child and Parent depth structures must be conveyed losslessly to maintain fast rendering speed. Compression reduces bit rates by approximately 8x with higher quality than the original PlenOctree, or by approximately 50x with minimal degradation for novel view synthesis. Storage requirements for the original PlenOctree model on the Lego scene are approximately 2.3 GB, with 95% of that size coming from \sigma and k coefficients. Strengths include maintaining high rendering speed and quality while significantly reducing model size. Origin is described in "Compression of PlenOctree Model Attributes Enabling Fast Communication and Rendering of Neural Radiance Fields". Development improves upon the PlenOctree method by addressing its large storage requirements. It incorporates techniques from Mip-NeRF for ray offsets and SNeRG for the Cauchy loss. Usage is for fast communication and rendering of Neural Radiance Fields, particularly where bandwidth or storage is constrained.
