name: Direct Voxel Grid Optimization
head: DVG, Direct Voxel Density Optimization, Direct Voxel Grid Optimization Implementation, DirectVoxGo (DVGO)
body: Direct Voxel Grid Optimization (DVGO) is a method for reconstructing per-scene radiance fields from calibrated images by directly optimizing a dense 3D voxel grid for volume density and a feature voxel grid for color, achieving convergence in less than 15 minutes on a single GPU. It sets itself apart from implicit NeRF-based methods by eliminating the need for lengthy MLP training and from previous voxel methods by training the grid directly from scratch without a conversion step from an implicit model. Unlike Explicit Radiance Fields which often rely on pre-trained implicit models or complex hierarchical structures, DVGO uses a simple dense grid with post-activation interpolation to model sharp surfaces efficiently. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: A set of N calibrated images with known camera poses (intrinsic and extrinsic parameters). The scene is assumed to be bounded within a volume of interest. Outputs: A rendered novel view image \hat{C}(\mathbf{r}) for any camera ray \mathbf{r}, and optimized voxel grid parameters. Data Structures: The representation consists of three primary components stored in 3D grids: 1. Density Voxel Grid (V^{(\sigma)}): Stores raw density values \sigma. Coarse Stage: Resolution M^{(c)} \times M^{(c)} \times M^{(c)}, typically 100^3. Fine Stage: Resolution M^{(f)} \times M^{(f)} \times M^{(f)}, typically 160^3 or 256^3. 2. Feature Voxel Grid (V^{(\text{feat})}): Stores feature vectors used by the shallow MLP. Fine Stage: Resolution M^{(f)} \times M^{(f)} \times M^{(f)}. Channel Depth: D = 12 channels. 3. Color Voxel Grid (V^{(\text{color})}): (Used only in Coarse Stage) Stores view-invariant color. Coarse Stage: Resolution M^{(c)} \times M^{(c)} \times M^{(c)}. Bounding Box (BBox): The method automatically finds a BBox tightly enclosing the volume of interest to allocate voxel grids, ensuring parsimony. Coordinates are normalized to [-1, 1] within this BBox. Shallow MLP Architecture: A shallow Multi-Layer Perceptron maps features to view-dependent color. Input: Concatenation of interpolated features from V^{(\text{feat})} and positional embeddings of position \mathbf{x} and viewing direction \mathbf{d}. Structure: 2 hidden layers, 128 channels per layer. Output: RGB color \mathbf{c}. Positional Embedding: Position \mathbf{x}: kx = 5 frequencies. Direction \mathbf{d}: kd = 4 frequencies. Rendering Model: For a ray \mathbf{r}, K points are sampled between near and far planes. The rendered color is calculated using volume rendering quadrature: \hat{C}(\mathbf{r}) = \left( \sum{i=1}^K Ti \alphai \mathbf{c}i \right) + T{K+1} \mathbf{c}{\text{bg}} Where: \alphai = 1 - \exp(-\sigmai \deltai) is the opacity at point i. Ti = \prod{j=1}^{i-1} (1 - \alphaj) is the accumulated transmittance. \sigmai is the density at point i. \deltai is the distance to the adjacent sampled point. \mathbf{c}i is the color at point i. \mathbf{c}{\text{bg}} is the background color. Optimization Steps: The optimization is divided into two phases: Coarse Geometry Searching and Fine Detail Reconstruction. 1. Initialization: Initialize density voxel grid to yield opacities very close to zero everywhere to avoid bias toward camera near planes. Coarse stage initial activated alpha: \alpha{\text{init}}^{(c)} = 10^{-6}. Fine stage initial activated alpha: \alpha{\text{init}}^{(f)} = 0.01. 2. Coarse Geometry Searching: Grids: Use V^{(\sigma)} (coarse) and V^{(\text{color})} (coarse). Sampling: Step size \delta^{(c)} = 0.5 \times s^{(c)}, where s^{(c)} is the voxel size. Free Space Handling: Define known free space using threshold \tauc = 10^{-3}. Skip query points where density is below this threshold. Learning Rate Prior: Apply a lower learning rate to voxels visible to fewer views to avoid redundant voxels allocated just for explaining observations from a small number of views. Training: Optimize for 10,000 iterations using Adam optimizer. Loss: Photometric loss \mathcal{L}{\text{photo}} with weight w{\text{photo}} = 1. Point-wise RGB loss weight w{\text{pt\rgb}} = 10^{-1}. Background loss weight w{\text{bg}} = 10^{-2}. Learning Rates: Base learning rate for voxel grids is 0.1. Base learning rate for shallow MLP is 10^{-3} (if used for color in coarse stage, though coarse often uses direct color grid). 3. Fine Detail Reconstruction: Grids: Use V^{(\sigma)} (fine) and V^{(\text{feat})} (fine). Sampling: Step size \delta^{(f)} = 0.5 \times s^{(f)}, where s^{(f)} is the voxel size. Unknown Space Handling: Skip low-density query points in unknown space using threshold \tauf = 10^{-4}. Progressive Scaling: Progressively scale the fine-stage voxel grid at checkpoints 1000, 2000, and 3000 iterations. Training: Optimize for 20,000 iterations using Adam optimizer. Loss: Photometric loss \mathcal{L}{\text{photo}} with weight w{\text{photo}} = 1. Point-wise RGB loss weight w{\text{pt\rgb}} = 10^{-2}. Background loss weight w{\text{bg}} = 10^{-3}. Learning Rates: Base learning rate for voxel grids is 0.1. Base learning rate for shallow MLP is 10^{-3}. Schedule: Apply exponential learning rate decay, downscaled by 0.1 at 20,000 iterations. Post-Activation Interpolation: A key technique for sharp surface modeling. Instead of interpolating activated opacity or using nearest-neighbor, DVGO trilinearly interpolates the raw density values from the grid, then applies the activation function (e.g., Softplus or ReLU) to produce opacity. This allows modeling sharp linear surfaces within a single grid cell. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import numpy as np def dvgooptimize(images, poses, nearfar, batchsize=8192): # 1. Setup BBox and Grids bbox = findtightboundingbox(poses) # Automatically find BBox Mc = 100 Mf = 160 Dfeat = 12 # Initialize grids # Vsigmac: Coarse density grid # Vcolorc: Coarse color grid # Vsigmaf: Fine density grid # Vfeatf: Fine feature grid Vsigmac = np.zeros((Mc, Mc, Mc)) Vcolorc = np.zeros((Mc, Mc, Mc, 3)) Vsigmaf = np.zeros((Mf, Mf, Mf)) Vfeatf = np.zeros((Mf, Mf, Mf, Dfeat)) # Initialize density to low opacity # alphainitc = 1e-6 implies raw sigma is very low Vsigmac[:] = lowdensityinit(alphainitc=1e-6, bboxsize=bbox.size) Vsigmaf[:] = lowdensityinit(alphainitf=0.01, bboxsize=bbox.size) # Optimizers optsigmac = Adam(lr=0.1) optcolorc = Adam(lr=0.1) optsigmaf = Adam(lr=0.1) optfeatf = Adam(lr=0.1) optmlp = Adam(lr=1e-3) # Shallow MLP for view-dependent color mlp = ShallowMLP(hiddendim=128, numlayers=2, kx=5, kd=4) # 2. Coarse Stage for iter in range(10000): rays = samplerays(images, poses, batchsize) loss = 0.0 for ray in rays: # Sample points along ray points = samplepointsalongray(ray, nearfar, stepsize=0.5 voxelsizec) # Query density rawsigma = trilinearinterpolate(Vsigmac, points) # Post-activation: apply activation after interpolation sigma = activation(rawsigma) # e.g., Softplus # Query color (view-invariant in coarse stage) color = trilinearinterpolate(Vcolorc, points) # Volume rendering for this ray alpha = 1 - np.exp(-sigma delta) T = np.cumprod(1 - alpha) # Transmittance renderedcolor = np.sum(T alpha color) + T[-1] bgcolor # Loss calculation targetcolor = getpixelcolor(ray) loss += np.linalg.norm(renderedcolor - targetcolor)2 # Gradient accumulation for voxels # Apply view-count based learning rate prior viewcount = countviewsvisibletovoxel(ray, points) lrscale = 1.0 if viewcount > threshold else 0.1 # Lower LR for few views accumulategradients(optsigmac, Vsigmac, points, loss, lrscale) accumulategradients(optcolorc, Vcolorc, points, loss, lrscale) # Update parameters optsigmac.step() optcolorc.step() # 3. Fine Stage for iter in range(20000): # Progressive scaling at checkpoints 1000, 2000, 3000 if iter in [1000, 2000, 3000]: Vsigmaf = scaleupgrid(Vsigmaf, Mf) Vfeatf = scaleupgrid(Vfeatf, Mf) rays = samplerays(images, poses, batchsize) loss = 0.0 for ray in rays: points = samplepointsalongray(ray, nearfar, stepsize=0.5 voxelsizef) # Filter points in known free space (from coarse stage) # Skip if sigma < tauf = 1e-4 validpoints = [] validindices = [] for i, p in enumerate(points): rawsigma = trilinearinterpolate(Vsigmaf, p) sigma = activation(rawsigma) if sigma > 1e-4: validpoints.append(p) validindices.append(i) if not validpoints: continue rawsigma = trilinearinterpolate(Vsigmaf, validpoints) sigma = activation(rawsigma) # Query features features = trilinearinterpolate(Vfeatf, validpoints) # Query color via MLP (view-dependent) posembed = positionalencoding(validpoints, k=5) dirembed = positionalencoding(ray.direction, k=4) color = mlp(features, posembed, dirembed) # Volume rendering delta = getdelta(validpoints) alpha = 1 - np.exp(-sigma delta) T = np.cumprod(1 - alpha) renderedcolor = np.sum(T alpha color) + T[-1] bgcolor targetcolor = getpixelcolor(ray) loss += np.linalg.norm(renderedcolor - targetcolor)2 # Gradients accumulategradients(optsigmaf, Vsigmaf, validpoints, loss) accumulategradients(optfeatf, Vfeatf, validpoints, loss) accumulategradients(optmlp, mlpparams, validpoints, loss) optsigmaf.step() optfeatf.step() optmlp.step() # Exponential decay at 20000 iterations if iter == 20000: optsigmaf.lr = 0.1 optfeatf.lr = 0.1 optmlp.lr = 0.1 def lowdensityinit(alphainit, bboxsize): # Inverse of alpha = 1 - exp(-sigma delta) # sigma = -ln(1 - alpha) / delta # delta is approx bboxsize / M delta = bboxsize / 100 # Approx for coarse sigma = -np.log(1 - alphainit) / delta return np.fulllike(bboxsize, sigma) Ref-DVGO is a reflection-aware neural rendering method that combines the fast hybrid implicit-explicit representation of Direct Voxel Grid Optimization (DVGO) with the reflection direction reparameterization of Ref-NeRF to achieve high-quality photorealistic novel view synthesis of reflective scenes with reduced training and rendering time. It sets itself apart from DVGO by explicitly modeling specular reflections via a reflection-aware reparameterization and from Ref-NeRF by replacing large spatial MLPs with six distinct voxel grids, significantly reducing GPU memory requirements and training time. See Ref-DVGO. VGOS is a method for fast radiance field reconstruction from sparse inputs (3-10 views) that addresses overfitting, holes, and floaters in voxel grids by using an incremental voxel training strategy and voxel smoothing regularization. It sets itself apart from pre-training methods like SRF and MVSNeRF by training from scratch without pre-trained models or extra inputs, and from depth-dependent methods like DSNeRF by relying solely on RGB images. See VGOS. A training strategy that prevents voxels from overfitting to training views by suppressing the optimization of peripheral voxels in the early stage of radiance field reconstruction. It freezes the optimization of peripheral voxels at the early stage of training and gradually thaws them as training progresses. This prevents voxels close to the cameras' near planes from overfitting to the training views. Time Complexity: Training is significantly faster than implicit methods. Convergence is about two orders of magnitude faster than NeRF, reducing training time from 10-20 hours to 15 minutes. Memory Complexity: Uses dense voxel grids. For M^{(f)}=160^3, memory usage is manageable on a single GPU. Higher resolutions (256^3) increase memory but improve quality. Measured Performance: On NVIDIA RTX 2080 Ti, DVGO achieves 31.95 PSNR in 15 minutes (160^3) and 32.80 PSNR in 22 minutes (256^3) on inward-facing benchmarks. Rendering speed is ~45x faster than NeRF (0.64s vs 29s per 800x800 image). Strengths: Extremely fast training from scratch; no need for cross-scene pre-training; high rendering speed; sharp surface modeling via post-activation. Limitations: Prone to suboptimal geometry (cloud in free space) if priors are not applied; real-world data uncertainty (lighting, SfM error) can lead to blurrier surfaces; limited to bounded scenes; resolution is fixed by grid size, potentially leading to aliasing at very high resolutions compared to adaptive methods. When to Use: When fast per-scene reconstruction is required and computational resources are limited (single GPU). Suitable for inward-facing scenes with known poses. When Not to Use: For unbounded or forward-facing scenes (not handled natively); when extreme geometric precision at very high resolutions is needed without hierarchical structures; when real-world data has significant multi-view inconsistency that cannot be mitigated by priors. Direct Voxel Grid Optimization was introduced by Cheng Sun, Min Sun, and Hwann-Tzong Chen in 2022. It addresses the bottleneck of lengthy training times in Neural Radiance Fields (NeRF) [37] by directly optimizing explicit voxel grids. Previous voxel methods often required conversion from trained implicit models or cross-scene pre-training. DVGO demonstrated that direct optimization, combined with post-activation interpolation and specific priors, could achieve NeRF-comparable quality in minutes. It is used on benchmarks such as Syn-NeRF, Syn-NSVF, BlendedMVS, and Tanks and Temples. name: Ref-DVGO
head: Reflection-Aware Direct Voxel Grid Optimization
body: Ref-DVGO is a reflection-aware neural rendering method that combines the fast hybrid implicit-explicit representation of Direct Voxel Grid Optimization (DVGO) with the reflection direction reparameterization of Ref-NeRF to achieve high-quality photorealistic novel view synthesis of reflective scenes with reduced training and rendering time. It sets itself apart from DVGO by explicitly modeling specular reflections via a reflection-aware reparameterization and from Ref-NeRF by replacing large spatial MLPs with six distinct voxel grids, significantly reducing GPU memory requirements and training time. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: A set of calibrated images of a scene containing reflective objects. Outputs: A rendered image for a given camera pose, and optimized voxel grids representing the scene's geometry and appearance. Data Structures: The method replaces the spatial MLP of Ref-NeRF with six distinct voxel grids representing view-independent properties. The layout of these grids is as follows: 1. Density (\sigma): Scalar field representing volume density. 2. Diffuse Color (cd): RGB vector field for diffuse albedo. 3. Specular Tint (s): RGB vector field for specular color/tint. 4. Appearance/Bottleneck Features (b): Vector field providing intermediate features for the directional network. 5. Roughness (\rho): Scalar field representing surface roughness. 6. Predicted Normals (\hat{n}'): Normalized 3D vector field for predicted surface normals. Numbered Steps: 1. Coarse Training (Stage 1): Initialize the voxel grids. Train a coarse model using only view-independent components (density \sigma and diffuse color cd) for 5000 iterations. This stage learns coarse geometry and refines the bounding box of the scene. 2. Fine Training (Stage 2): Enable view-dependent components (specular tint s, appearance features b, roughness \rho, predicted normals \hat{n}'). Use the coarse model to sample points in occupied space, informing the sampling for the fine stage to reduce redundant queries to the directional MLP. Apply Progressive Scaling (PGS) of the voxel grid over 10 steps (default) to ensure low-frequency information is learned before high-frequency details and view-dependent effects. 3. Rendering: For a ray r, sample K points along the ray. For each point i, query the six voxel grids to obtain \sigmai, c{d,i}, si, bi, \rhoi, \hat{n}'i. Compute the reflection direction r{refl} based on the view direction and the predicted normal \hat{n}'i. Pass the appearance features bi and the reflection direction r{refl} into a directional MLP (default size 8x256) to predict the final color. Composite the colors and alphas along the ray using standard volume rendering equations to produce the final pixel color \hat{C}(r). 4. Optimization: Minimize the total loss function \mathcal{L} defined below. Formulas: The total loss function is a weighted sum of photometric loss, per-point RGB loss, background entropy loss, predicted normals penalty, normal orientation regularization, and total variation regularization: \mathcal{L} = w{ph} \mathcal{L}{ph} + w{pp} \mathcal{L}{pp} + wb \mathcal{L}{bg} + wp \mathcal{R}p + wo \mathcal{R}o + \mathcal{R}{TV} Where: \mathcal{L}{ph}: Photometric loss supervising rendered alpha-composed ray colors \hat{C}(r) with ground truth pixel colors C(r). \mathcal{L}{pp}: Per-point RGB loss directly supervising the colors ci of each of the K sampled points along a ray r. \mathcal{L}{bg}: Background entropy loss regularizing the rendered background probability to reduce uncertainty between foreground and background. \mathcal{R}p: Predicted normals penalty supervising the predicted normals \hat{n}'i with the normals \hat{n}i estimated through the density gradient to produce smoother normals. \mathcal{R}o: Normal orientation regularization penalizing back-facing normals to concentrate all normals on the surface of the object and prevent semi-transparent surfaces and embedded or floating artifacts. \mathcal{R}{TV}: Total variation regularization applied on the gradients of all six voxel grids (\sigma, cd, s, b, \rho, \hat{n}') to reduce geometry noise, unnecessary sharpness, and improve spatial continuity. Parameters: w{ph}: Weight for photometric loss \mathcal{L}{ph}. w{pp}: Weight for per-point RGB loss \mathcal{L}{pp}. wb: Weight for background entropy loss \mathcal{L}{bg}. wp: Weight for predicted normals penalty \mathcal{R}p. wo: Weight for normal orientation regularization \mathcal{R}o. Number of coarse training iterations: 5000. Directional MLP size: 8x256 (default). Number of progressive scaling steps: 10 (default). Pitfalls and Edge Cases: Transparent and semi-transparent surfaces/objects are not examined or supported by this method. Removing the predicted normals penalty marginally improves performance across all metrics in ablation studies, suggesting it may not be strictly necessary for optimal results. Using a smaller directional MLP (e.g., 3x128 instead of 8x256) or reducing the number of progressive scaling steps from ten to four has a negative impact on performance. Time Complexity: Training is significantly faster than Ref-NeRF. On the Shiny Blender dataset, Ref-DVGO achieves competitive quality in 30 minutes compared to Ref-NeRF's 3 days. Memory Complexity: Uses 4x less GPU memory requirements compared to Ref-NeRF due to the replacement of large spatial MLPs with voxel grids. Performance: On the Shiny Blender dataset, Ref-DVGO achieves PSNR 32.89, SSIM 0.957, LPIPS 0.104. This is lower than Ref-NeRF (PSNR 35.96, SSIM 0.967, LPIPS 0.058) but higher than DVGO (PSNR 29.83, SSIM 0.933, LPIPS 0.135) and InstantNGP (PSNR 25.61, SSIM 0.900, LPIPS 0.143). Strengths: Fast training and rendering, low GPU memory usage, good quality for reflective scenes. Limitations: Does not support transparent or semi-transparent surfaces, and quality is lower than Ref-NeRF. When to use: When reconstructing reflective scenes with limited computational resources or when fast training is required. When not to use: For scenes with transparent or semi-transparent objects, or when the highest possible photometric quality is required regardless of training time. Ref-DVGO was proposed by G. Kouros et al. in 2023. It builds on Direct Voxel Grid Optimization (DVGO) and incorporates the reflection-aware reparameterization from Ref-NeRF. The method aims to provide a better quality-efficiency trade-off for reflective scene reconstruction. The source code is available at https://github.com/gkouros/ref-dvgo. Ref-DVGO: Reflection-Aware Direct Voxel Grid Optimization for an Improved Quality-Efficiency Trade-Off in Reflective Scene Reconstruction, https://doi.org/10.48550/arxiv.2308.08530, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial)

name: VGOS
head: Voxel Grid Optimization for View Synthesis from Sparse Inputs
body: VGOS is a method for fast radiance field reconstruction from sparse inputs (3-10 views) that addresses overfitting, holes, and floaters in voxel grids by using an incremental voxel training strategy and voxel smoothing regularization. It sets itself apart from pre-training methods like SRF and MVSNeRF by training from scratch without pre-trained models or extra inputs, and from depth-dependent methods like DSNeRF by relying solely on RGB images. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: 3-10 sparse RGB images with known camera poses. Outputs: A reconstructed radiance field represented by optimized voxel grids. Data Structures: The method builds upon the Direct Voxel Grid Optimization structure, utilizing a dense voxel grid for density and a feature voxel grid for color. The specific layout of these grids is inherited from the parent method [Parent]. Algorithm Steps: 1. Initialization: Initialize the voxel grids for density and features [Parent]. 2. Incremental Voxel Training: Define a set of "peripheral voxels" located near the cameras' near planes. During the early stage of training, freeze the optimization (gradients) of these peripheral voxels. Gradually thaw (enable optimization for) the peripheral voxels as training progresses. This strategy prevents overfitting to training views. 3. Voxel Smoothing Regularization: Render depth maps from unobserved viewpoints. Apply a depth smooth loss to regularize the dense voxel grids. This eliminates holes and floaters. Apply a color-aware voxel smoothness loss to penalize sharpness inside the voxel grids. This avoids degenerate solutions. 4. Optimization: Update voxel parameters using the combined losses. Parameters: Input Views: 3-10 sparse RGB images. Training Time: 3-5 minutes per scene. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Overfitting: Sparse inputs are prone to overfitting to training views, leading to artifacts. The incremental training strategy mitigates this. Holes and Floaters: Voxel grids may contain holes and floaters in sparse scenarios. The voxel smoothing method addresses this. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def trainvgos(images, cameras, numsteps): # Initialize voxel grids (density and features) densitygrid = initializedensitygrid() featuregrid = initializefeaturegrid() # Identify peripheral voxels (near camera near planes) peripheralvoxels = identifyperipheralvoxels(cameras) for step in range(numsteps): # 1. Incremental Voxel Training Strategy # Freeze peripheral voxels in early stage, gradually thaw if step < earlystagethreshold: freezegradients(densitygrid, peripheralvoxels) freezegradients(featuregrid, peripheralvoxels) else: # Gradually thaw based on progress thawprogress = (step - earlystagethreshold) / (numsteps - earlystagethreshold) thawgradients(densitygrid, peripheralvoxels, thawprogress) thawgradients(featuregrid, peripheralvoxels, thawprogress) # Sample rays and render rays = samplerays(cameras) renderedcolors, rendereddepths = renderrays( densitygrid, featuregrid, rays) # 2. Compute Losses # Color loss (standard) colorloss = computecolorloss(renderedcolors, images) # Depth smooth loss (from unobserved viewpoints) # Note: Sources mention regularizing depth maps from unobserved viewpoints unobserveddepths = renderdepthfromunobservedviews( densitygrid, cameras) depthsmoothloss = computedepthsmoothness(unobserveddepths) # Color-aware voxel smoothness loss voxelsmoothloss = computecolorawarevoxelsmoothness( densitygrid, featuregrid) # Total loss totalloss = colorloss + depthsmoothloss + voxelsmoothloss # Update voxel grids updategradients(densitygrid, featuregrid, totalloss) return densitygrid, featuregrid Time Complexity: Training time is 3-5 minutes per scene. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Performance: On the LLFF dataset in 3-view settings, VGOS achieves higher PSNR and lower training time than DietNeRF, DVGOv2, SRF, MVSNeRF, and RegNeRF, measured on a single NVIDIA RTX 3090 GPU. Strengths: Fast convergence (one to two orders of magnitude speedup compared to SOTA approaches with on-par quality). No need for pre-trained models or extra inputs. Limitations: Performance is specific to sparse input scenarios (3-10 views). When to use: When fast reconstruction from sparse RGB inputs is required, and pre-training or depth inputs are not available. When not to use: When dense inputs are available, or when pre-trained priors are acceptable for potentially higher quality. VGOS was proposed in 2023 by authors publishing in the Proceedings of the Thirty-Second International Joint Conference on Artificial Intelligence (IJCAI-23). It addresses the limitation of Neural Radiance Fields (NeRF) which require tens to hundreds of dense inputs and hours to days of training. VGOS builds on Direct Voxel Grid Optimization [Parent] to enable fast radiance field reconstruction from sparse inputs. VGOS: Voxel Grid Optimization for View Synthesis from Sparse Inputs, https://doi.org/10.24963/ijcai.2023/157, fetched 2026-10-26

name: Canonical Radiance Field with Voxel Grid
head: Voxel Grid Based Canonical Field
body: This method replaces the continuous, coordinate-based Multi-Layer Perceptron (MLP) of NeRF with a discrete, learnable voxel grid to represent a static scene in a canonical time frame. It solves the problem of querying infinite 3D points in canonical space for forward warping, which is impractical with heavy MLPs. It differs from Explicit Radiance Fields by explicitly separating density and color features into distinct grids optimized for canonical static representation, and from Direct Voxel Grid Optimization by serving as a foundational static representation for dynamic scene warping rather than direct view synthesis optimization. Inputs: 3D coordinates \mathbf{p}{Can} of points in the canonical space. A pre-defined voxel grid structure containing V\sigma{Can} and Vcf{Can}. Outputs: Density \sigma and color feature vector \mathbf{c}f for each queried point. Data Structures: The canonical radiance field \mathbf{R}{Can} is defined as a tuple of two voxel grids: \mathbf{R}{Can} = \{ V\sigma{Can}, Vcf{Can} \} 1. V\sigma{Can}: A 3D grid storing scalar density values. 2. Vcf{Can}: A 3D grid storing color feature vectors. 3. \mathbf{p}{Can}: The 3D coordinates of the voxel grid points in canonical space, embedded according to the NeRF positional encoding scheme. Method Steps: 1. Coordinate Embedding: For a query point \mathbf{p}{Can}, apply positional encoding (as defined in NeRF) to map the 3D coordinates to a higher-dimensional space. 2. Voxel Trilinear Interpolation: Sample the values from V\sigma{Can} and Vcf{Can} at the query location \mathbf{p}{Can} using trilinear interpolation. This yields the base density \sigma{base} and base color features \mathbf{c}{f,base}. 3. Radiance Network Evaluation: Pass the interpolated features through a lightweight MLP network F{\theta1}. Input to F{\theta1}: The interpolated color features \mathbf{c}{f,base}. Output: The final color \mathbf{c}. Note: The source defines the relationship as \mathbf{R}{Can} = \RadNet (\mathbf{p}{Can}, \mathbf{Rf}{Can}), implying the network takes the grid features and coordinates to produce the radiance field output. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def trilinearinterpolate(grid, p): # Standard 3D trilinear interpolation for grid at normalized coordinate p ix, iy, iz = (p (grid.shape[0]-1, grid.shape[1]-1, grid.shape[2]-1)).astype(int) ix, iy, iz = np.clip([ix, iy, iz], 0, [grid.shape[0]-2, grid.shape[1]-2, grid.shape[2]-2]) fx, fy, fz = p (grid.shape[0]-1, grid.shape[1]-1, grid.shape[2]-1) - [ix, iy, iz] w000 = (1-fx)(1-fy)(1-fz) w100 = fx(1-fy)(1-fz) w010 = (1-fx)fy(1-fz) w110 = fxfy(1-fz) w001 = (1-fx)(1-fy)fz w101 = fx(1-fy)fz w011 = (1-fx)fyfz w111 = fxfyfz return (w000grid[ix,iy,iz] + w100grid[ix+1,iy,iz] + w010grid[ix,iy+1,iz] + w110grid[ix+1,iy+1,iz] + w001grid[ix,iy,iz+1] + w101grid[ix+1,iy,iz+1] + w011grid[ix,iy+1,iz+1] + w111grid[ix+1,iy+1,iz+1]) def positionalencoding(p, mindeg=0, maxdeg=10, base=2): # Standard NeRF positional encoding scales = np.array([basei for i in range(mindeg, maxdeg+1)]) scaledp = np.outer(p, scales) return np.concatenate([scaledp, np.piscaledp], axis=-1) def querycanonicalfield(p, Vsigma, Vcf, Ftheta1): # 1. Coordinate embedding pembedded = positionalencoding(p) # 2. Voxel sampling sigmabase = trilinearinterpolate(Vsigma, p) cfbase = trilinearinterpolate(Vcf, p) # 3. Radiance network evaluation # Ftheta1 decodes color features to color c c = Ftheta1(cfbase) return sigmabase, c Parameters: F{\theta1}: A lightweight MLP network used to model the radiance. Grid Resolution: Not given in the sources. Edge Cases: Points outside the voxel grid bounds: Standard boundary handling (clamp, zero, or error) is required. Not given in the sources. Precision: Trilinear interpolation is differentiable, allowing gradient propagation to the voxel values. ReRF extends the canonical field concept to dynamic scenes by modeling residuals between adjacent timestamps, avoiding the fragility of global canonical spaces for large motions. Memory: Significantly lower memory usage compared to NeRF's heavy MLP for storing scene representation, as it uses a fixed-size voxel grid. Speed: Faster inference than NeRF due to direct voxel lookup and interpolation, avoiding expensive MLP evaluations for every point. Limitations: Limited to static scenes in the canonical representation; dynamic aspects require additional warping mechanisms (e.g., Canonical Trajectory Field using DCT). Scalability: Resolution of the voxel grid limits the detail; higher resolution increases memory linearly. Originated in the paper "Forward Flow for Novel View Synthesis of Dynamic Scenes" (ICCV 2023). It addresses the limitation of NeRF's continuous representation for dynamic scene warping by introducing a discrete, learnable voxel grid for the canonical static scene. Forward Flow for Novel View Synthesis of Dynamic Scenes, https://doi.org/10.1109/iccv51070.2023.01468, fetched 2026-10-26

name: Neural Residual Radiance Fields (ReRF)
head: Residual Radiance Field
body: Neural Residual Radiance Fields (ReRF) is a compact neural representation for dynamic scenes that explicitly models the residual information between adjacent timestamps in the spatial-temporal feature space, using a global coordinate-based tiny MLP as the feature decoder. Unlike methods relying on a global canonical space which are fragile to large motions, ReRF avoids the global canonical space by exploiting feature similarities between adjacent frames, allowing it to handle large motions without sacrificing quality. It differs from DeVRF by not relying on a global canonical space, making it robust to large motions or topology changes, by instead exploiting feature similarities between adjacent timestamps. Inputs: A sequence of RGB images \{It\}{t=1}^N for a dynamic scene. Camera poses for each frame. Outputs: A global shallow MLP \Phi. An initial explicit feature grid f1 for the first keyframe. A sequence of compact motion grids \{Mt\}{t=2}^N and sparse residual feature grids \{rt\}{t=2}^N. 1. Feature Grid (f): A 3D voxel grid storing both density and color features. It is formed by unioning the density grid V\sigma and color feature grid Vc by appending an additional channel to Vc. Layout: 3D array. Channels: Density + Color features. 2. Motion Grid (Mt): A low-resolution grid where each entry stores a voxel index offset from the previous frame. Size: 512 times smaller than the original dense motion field. Content: Integer voxel offsets. 3. Residual Grid (rt): A sparse grid storing compensation for warping errors and newly observed regions. Layout: Sparse 3D array (or dense with many zeros). Content: Feature value deltas. The radiance field of a static scene using explicit grids is defined as: \sigma = \text{interp}(\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{V}{\sigma}) \mathbf{c} = \Phi(\text{interp}(\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{V}{c}), \mathbf{d}) where \text{interp}(\cdot) is trilinear interpolation, \Phi is a shallow MLP, \mathbf{V}{\sigma} is the density grid, \mathbf{V}{c} is the color feature grid, \mathbf{x} is 3D position, and \mathbf{d} is viewing direction. For simplification, V\sigma and Vc are unioned into a common feature grid f. The base feature grid \hat{f}t for frame t is obtained by warping the previous frame's feature grid f{t-1} using the motion grid Mt: \hat{\mathbf{f}}{t}(\mathbf{p}) = \mathbf{f}{t-1}(\mathbf{p} + \mathbf{M}t(\mathbf{p})) where \mathbf{p} is the voxel index. The total loss function for learning the residual grid rt is: \mathcal{L}{total} = \sum{\mathbf{l} \in \mathbb{L}}\|\mathbf{c}(\mathbf{l})-\hat{\mathbf{c}}(\mathbf{l})\|^2 + \lambda \|\mathbf{r}t\|1 where \mathbb{L} is the set of training pixel rays, \mathbf{c}(\mathbf{l}) and \hat{\mathbf{c}}(\mathbf{l}) are ground truth and predicted colors, and \lambda = 0.01. Motion pooling kernel size: 8 \times 8 \times 8 voxels. Regularization weight \lambda: 0.01. GOF (Group of Feature grids) length: 20 frames. 1. Initialize First Frame: Train an MLP decoder \Phi and obtain an initial feature grid volume f1 for the first keyframe using an off-the-shelf approach [68]. 2. Estimate Dense Motion: For each subsequent frame t, estimate a dense motion field Dt from the current frame to the previous frame (treating the previous frame as canonical). 3. Generate Compact Motion Grid: Perform motion pooling on Dt to generate the compact motion grid Mt: Split Dt into 8 \times 8 \times 8 voxel cubes. Apply average pooling on Dt within each cube to get a mean vector. Select the voxel \bar{p}{t-1} that the mean vector points to as Mt(pt) = \bar{p}{t-1}. 4. Warp Previous Grid: Warp the previous feature grid f{t-1} using Mt to obtain the base feature grid \hat{f}t. 5. Optimize Residual Grid: Optimize the residual grid rt by backpropagating gradients to rt while fixing \hat{f}t and \Phi, minimizing the photometric loss and L1 sparsity regularization. 6. Recover Current Grid: Recover the current feature grid ft by adding the residual to the base grid: ft = \hat{f}t + rt. 7. Repeat: Repeat steps 2-6 for all subsequent frames. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import numpy as np def motionpooling(Dt, kernelsize=8): # Split Dt into 8x8x8 voxel cubes. # Apply average pooling on Dt within each cube to get a mean vector. # Select the voxel index that the mean vector points to as Mt. # The sources do not provide the exact discretization logic for mapping mean vectors to voxel indices. pass def warpgrid(fprev, Mt): # fhatt(p) = fprev(p + Mt(p)) # Trilinear interpolation at positions p + Mt(p) # Standard trilinear interpolation on a 3D grid. pass def optimizeresidualgrid(fhatt, Phi, imagest, posest, lambdareg=0.01): # Optimize residual grid rt by backpropagating gradients to rt # while fixing fhatt and Phi, minimizing photometric loss and L1 sparsity regularization. # The sources do not provide the exact optimization loop details. pass def reconstructgrid(fprev, Mt, rt): fhatt = warpgrid(fprev, Mt) ft = fhatt + rt return ft def trainrerf(videosequence): # Step 1: Initialize first frame with complete explicit feature grid f1 and global MLP Phi # using off-the-shelf approach [68]. f1, Phi = None, None # The sources do not provide the exact initialization routine. motiongrids = [] residualgrids = [] fprev = f1 # Step 2: Sequential training for subsequent frames for t in range(1, len(videosequence)): # Estimate dense motion field Dt from current frame to previous frame. Dt = None # The sources do not provide the exact dense motion estimation routine. # Generate compact motion grid Mt via motion pooling. Mt = motionpooling(Dt) motiongrids.append(Mt) # Warp previous feature grid f{t-1} using Mt to obtain base feature grid fhatt. fhatt = warpgrid(fprev, Mt) # Optimize residual grid rt. rt = optimizeresidualgrid(fhatt, Phi, videosequence[t].images, videosequence[t].poses) residualgrids.append(rt) # Recover current feature grid ft. ft = reconstructgrid(fprev, Mt, rt) fprev = ft return Phi, f1, motiongrids, residualgrids Large Motions: ReRF is designed to handle large motions better than global canonical space methods by using adjacent frame references. Sparsity: The L1 regularization encourages sparsity in the residual grid. Precision: Trilinear interpolation and motion pooling introduce discretization errors. The choice of kernel size for motion pooling (8 \times 8 \times 8) balances compactness and accuracy. A compression scheme for ReRF that uses Group of Feature grids (GOF), PCA, 3D DCT, and entropy coding to achieve high compression rates. A playback system that decodes ReRF data on-the-fly for real-time free-viewpoint video rendering. Time Complexity: Training is sequential, with each frame depending on the previous one. Motion estimation and residual optimization are performed per frame. Memory Complexity: The representation is compact due to the use of motion grids and sparse residual grids. The motion grid is 512 times smaller than the dense motion field. Measured Performance: Tested on a dataset with ~74 views at 1920x1080 resolution and 25 fps. Training was performed on a single NVIDIA GeForce RTX3090. Playback was tested on an Intel Core i9-11900 CPU and NVIDIA GeForce RTX3090 GPU. Strengths: Handles large motions and topology changes robustly. Achieves three orders of magnitude compression compared to per-frame neural representations. Limitations: Sequential training may be slower than parallel methods. Performance depends on the accuracy of motion estimation. When to Use: Suitable for long-duration dynamic scenes with large motions where real-time streaming and high compression are required. When Not to Use: Not suitable for scenes with extremely rapid, unpredictable motion that exceeds the motion grid's capacity or for static scenes where simpler representations suffice. ReRF was proposed by Liao Wang, Minye Wu, and Lan Xu in 2023. It addresses the limitations of existing neural rendering techniques for dynamic scenes, which are often restricted to offline rendering or brief sequences with minimal motion. The method builds on the idea of explicit voxel grids for static scenes [68] and extends it to dynamic scenes by exploiting temporal coherence between adjacent frames, avoiding the fragility of global canonical space methods like DeVRF. name: Forward Flow for Novel View Synthesis of Dynamic Scenes
head: ForwardFlowDNeRF
body: Forward Flow is a dynamic novel view synthesis method that replaces backward flow deformation with forward flow to warp a canonical radiance field to target time steps, ensuring smooth and continuous motion modeling. Unlike backward flow methods that map points from current time to canonical space (causing discontinuity for fixed 3D positions), forward flow maps canonical space to current time, yielding smooth flow norms for the same 3D position along the timeline. It sets itself apart by using explicit voxel grids for the canonical field and a differentiable warping process involving average splatting and inpainting to handle mapping artifacts. Inputs: A set of multi-view RGB images with known camera poses and timestamps t. Outputs: Rendered novel views at arbitrary time steps t. Data Structures: 1. Canonical Radiance Field Grid (V{grid}^{Can}): A 3D voxel grid storing volume density and color features for the canonical space. Represented as discrete values to enable explicit warping. 2. Deformation Feature Grid (V{grid}^{Df}): A 3D voxel grid storing deformation features in canonical space. 3. Lightweight MLP (F\theta): A small neural network that takes deformation features and time as input to predict flow vectors. Numbered Steps: 1. Canonical Representation: Represent the static canonical radiance field using the voxel grid V{grid}^{Can}. This allows explicit spatial warping, unlike continuous MLP-based NeRFs. 2. Forward Flow Estimation: Model the canonical trajectory field using the deformation feature grid V{grid}^{Df} and the lightweight MLP F\theta. For a 3D point p in canonical space at time t, the forward flow vector V{flow} is computed as: V{flow} = F\theta(V{grid}^{Df}(p), t) This estimates the displacement from canonical space to time t. 3. Differential Forward Warping: Warp the canonical radiance field V{grid}^{Can} to time t to obtain V{grid}^t. This step addresses two mapping issues inherent in forward warping: Many-to-One Mapping: Multiple canonical points map to the same target location, causing occlusion/overlap artifacts. This is resolved using an average splatting operation. One-to-Many Mapping: One canonical point maps to multiple target locations, causing holes/gaps in the warped field. This is resolved using an inpaint network. The warped field is first splatted to get V{grid}^t, then inpainted to get V{grid}^{t, Inp}. 4. Volume Rendering: Render novel views at time t via standard volume rendering on the inpainted radiance field V{grid}^{t, Inp}. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def forwardflowrender(canonicalgrid, deformationgrid, mlpflow, inpaintnet, camerapose, timet): """ Renders a novel view at timet using forward flow warping. Args: canonicalgrid: 3D VoxelGrid storing density and color in canonical space. deformationgrid: 3D VoxelGrid storing deformation features in canonical space. mlpflow: Lightweight MLP predicting flow vectors from deformation features and time. inpaintnet: Neural network for inpainting holes in warped grid. camerapose: Camera extrinsics and intrinsics for the target view. timet: Float, the target time step. Returns: Rendered RGB image. """ # Step 1: Sample canonical points along rays # For each pixel, cast a ray through the camera pose. # Sample points pcanon along the ray in canonical space. pointscanon = samplepointsalongray(camerapose) # Step 2: Estimate Forward Flow # Retrieve deformation features for each canonical point deffeatures = deformationgrid.query(pointscanon) # Predict flow vectors using the lightweight MLP # Vflow = Ftheta(deffeatures, timet) flowvectors = mlpflow(deffeatures, timet) # Step 3: Warp Canonical Grid to Time t # Calculate target positions in the warped grid pointstarget = pointscanon + flowvectors # Handle Many-to-One: Average Splatting # Map canonical values to target positions, averaging if multiple points map to same voxel warpedgrid = averagesplat(canonicalgrid, pointscanon, pointstarget) # Handle One-to-Many: Inpainting # The splatting may leave holes where no canonical point mapped to a target voxel. # Use the inpaint network to fill these gaps. inpaintedgrid = inpaintnet(warpedgrid) # Step 4: Volume Rendering # Render the final image from the inpainted grid at time t # Standard differentiable volume rendering equation image = volumerender(inpaintedgrid, camerapose) return image Parameters: F\theta: Lightweight MLP network. Size not given in the sources. Grid Resolution: Not given in the sources. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Many-to-One Mapping: Multiple canonical points map to the same target location. Naive warping causes occlusion/overlap artifacts. Solved by average splatting. One-to-Many Mapping: One canonical point maps to multiple target locations. Naive warping causes holes/gaps. Solved by inpaint network. Discontinuity in Backward Flow: Backward flow methods suffer from non-smooth, discontinuous flow fields for fixed 3D positions along the timeline, leading to distortion in the canonical space. Forward flow avoids this by ensuring smooth flow norms. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Measured Performance: Outperforms existing methods in both novel view rendering and motion modeling. Strengths: Smooth and continuous motion modeling; explicit recovery of surface point trajectories; avoids discontinuities of backward flow. Limitations: Requires explicit voxel grid representation (vs. continuous MLP); needs additional inpaint network for hole filling. When to use: When smooth motion modeling is critical and backward flow discontinuities are problematic. When not to use: When memory is extremely constrained and voxel grids are too large, or when implicit representations are preferred for simplicity. Forward Flow was proposed in 2023. It addresses the limitations of backward flow fields in dynamic NeRFs, which are non-smooth and discontinuous, making them difficult to fit with smooth motion models like MLPs. The method builds on the idea of canonical radiance fields but introduces forward warping with voxel grids and differentiable warping operations. name: DeepVoxels
head: 3D-structured neural scene representation, persistent 3D feature embedding
body: DeepVoxels is a learned representation that encodes the view-dependent appearance of a 3D scene using a persistent, viewpoint-invariant Cartesian 3D grid of feature embeddings. It solves the problem of novel view synthesis by condensing posed input images into a latent 3D structure without explicitly modeling geometry or requiring 3D ground truth. Unlike 2D-to-2D translation approaches that struggle with 3D transformations, DeepVoxels enforces perspective and multi-view geometry constraints by performing reasoning directly in 3D space, enabling explicit occlusion reasoning and robust generalization to unseen viewpoints. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: A set of N registered multi-view images with known intrinsic (K) and extrinsic (R, t) camera parameters. Outputs: A novel view image (and optionally a depth map) from a target camera pose. Persistent State: A 3D voxel grid H storing feature vectors. Data Structures: 1. Persistent Voxel Grid (H): A uniform 3D grid of size W \times H \times D. Layout: Each voxel stores a feature vector of size f channels. Default Size: 32^3 voxels with f=8 channels for synthetic scenes; 64^3 voxels with f=8 channels for real captures. Memory: Dense storage. A 64^3 grid with 8 channels requires significant GPU memory (e.g., ~12GB). 2. Canonical View Volume: A temporary 3D volume aligned with the target camera's coordinate system, used for projection and rendering. Parameters: Voxel Resolution: 32^3 (default) or 64^3. Feature Channels: 8. Optimizer: ADAM. Learning Rate: 4 \times 10^{-4}. Loss Weights: L1 loss weight 200, Adversarial loss weight 1. Model Size: 170 million parameters. Numbered Steps: 1. Training Corpus Construction: For each training step, select a source view Si and two target views T{i0}, T{i1} from the N registered images. Randomly select Si from the top-5 nearest neighbors in view direction angle to T{i0} to ensure visibility. 2. Feature Extraction: Extract 2D feature maps from source view Si using a 2D feature extraction network. Downsample by stride-2 convolutions until resolution 64 \times 64, then use a 2D U-Net to extract a 64 \times 64 feature map. 3. Lifting 2D to 3D: Position a temporary 3D feature volume in world space centered on the scene's center of gravity. For each voxel in this temporary volume, project its world space center x to the source view's image space using the canonical camera mapping: u = \frac{K(Rx + t)}{d} where u = [u, v, 1]^T is the pixel position, d is depth, K is the intrinsic matrix, R is rotation, t is translation, and x is the 3D world position. Extract a feature vector via bilinear sampling from the 2D feature map and store it in the voxel's code vector Xt. 4. Integration via GRU: Integrate the lifted features Xt into the persistent DeepVoxels grid H using a Gated Recurrent Unit (GRU). The hidden state H is persistent across all training steps and never reset. One GRU is used per voxel, updating all f feature channels jointly. The update equations are: Zt = \sigma(Wz Xt + Uz H{t-1} + Bz) Rt = \sigma(Wr Xt + Ur H{t-1} + Br) St = \text{ReLU}(Ws Xt + Us (Rt \circ H{t-1}) + Bs) Ht = (1 - Zt) \circ H{t-1} + Zt \circ St where Zt is the update gate, Rt is the reset gate, St is the new candidate state, H{t-1} is the previous hidden state, W\bullet and U\bullet are 3D convolution weights, B\bullet are biases, \sigma is the sigmoid function, and \circ is element-wise product. 5. Inpainting: Apply a 3D inpainting U-Net to fill holes in the feature representation after GRU integration. 6. Projection to Canonical View: Map 3D code vectors to the canonical coordinate system of the target view. For each voxel in the canonical view volume, compute its corresponding position in the persistent world space grid. Extract an interpolated code vector via trilinear interpolation and store it in the canonical view volume. 7. Occlusion Reasoning: For each pixel in the target view, consider the column of voxels in the canonical view volume. Concatenate this column with a feature column encoding the distance of each voxel to the camera. Compress the voxel feature vector to dimension 4 via a 3D convolutional layer. Input this to a 3D U-Net to predict scalar per-voxel visibility weights using a softmax activation. 8. Flattening: Flatten the canonical view volume along the depth dimension using a weighted average of voxels based on the predicted visibility weights. This yields the final occlusion-aware 2D view feature map. 9. Rendering: Pass the flattened canonical view volume to a 2D rendering network (a mirrored feature extraction network with higher capacity). A 2D U-Net reasons across the full image, followed by transposed convolutions to regress pixel values of the novel view. 10. Training Loss: Optimize the model end-to-end using a combined L1 loss and adversarial cross-entropy loss. The L1 loss is averaged over all pixels. The adversarial discriminator is a fully convolutional patch-based discriminator. Optimization uses ADAM. Pseudocode: Unverified code. Integration via GRU (Training only) # Update persistent H with liftedvolume self.H = self.gruupdate(liftedvolume, self.H) # 4. Inpainting self.H = self.inpaintingnet(self.H) # 5. Rendering a single frame takes approximately 71ms at test time. Memory Complexity: The method uses a dense 3D volume, which is memory inefficient. A 64^3 resolution with 8 channels fills a 12GB GPU. The parameter count is independent of the voxel grid size due to the use of 3D convolutions (170 million parameters total). Performance: On synthetic scenes (Vase, Pedestal, Chair, Cube), it achieves a Mean PSNR of 30.55 and SSIM of 0.97, outperforming baselines by an average of 7dB. Strengths: Explicit occlusion reasoning, robust generalization to novel viewpoints, parameter efficiency compared to fully connected latent spaces. Limitations: High memory consumption, performance deterioration when viewing scenes from poses significantly different from the training set (though 3D structure is preserved). Not suitable for scenes with strong specular highlights or view-dependent effects, as it assumes Lambertian scenes. DeepVoxels was introduced by Vincent Sitzmann, Michael Zollhöfer, and Gordon Wetzstein in 2019. It addresses the lack of 3D understanding in generative neural networks by introducing a persistent 3D feature embedding for view synthesis. The work combines insights from 3D geometric computer vision with advances in learning image-to-image mappings based on adversarial loss functions. It is used for novel view synthesis on synthetic 3D scans and real captures. DeepVoxels: Learning Persistent 3D Feature Embeddings, https://doi.org/10.1109/CVPR.2019.00254, fetched 2026-10-26

name: Neural Residual Field (ReRF)
head: Neural Residual Field (ReRF) Training, Neural Residual Radiance Fields
body: Neural Residual Field (ReRF) is a method for generating compact neural representations of dynamic scenes from RGB video inputs by sequentially optimizing explicit feature grids, motion grids, and residual grids. It solves the problem of efficiently storing and rendering long-duration dynamic scenes by avoiding a global canonical space, instead warping features from the previous frame and encoding only the differences. Unlike Neural Radiance Fields which model static scenes, or Deformable and Dynamic Fields which may use complex deformation fields, ReRF explicitly separates motion estimation and residual compensation into distinct grid structures to maintain sparsity and smoothness. ReRF operates in a two-stage sequential training scheme: first optimizing an explicit feature grid for the initial frame, then iteratively optimizing motion and residual grids for subsequent frames. Inputs: A sequence of RGB images (video frames) It for t=0, 1, \dots, T. Outputs: A sequence of feature grids ft (containing density and color features) for each frame, and a global MLP \Phi. 1. Explicit Feature Grid (V\sigma, Vc): V\sigma: Explicit density grid. Dimensions Nx \times Ny \times Nz. Vc: Color feature grid. Dimensions Nx \times Ny \times Nz. Total feature dimension C=13 (union of density and color features). 2. Dense Motion Field (Dt): Dimensions 3 \times Nx \times Ny \times Nz. Contains warping information (position offset) from frame t to t-1. 3. Compact Motion Grid (Mt): Generated from Dt via motion pooling. Represents the position offset from the current frame to the previous. 4. Residual Grid (rt): Dimensions C \times Nx \times Ny \times Nz. Initialized to zero. Stores residuals to compensate for warping errors and newly observed regions. 5. Global MLP (\Phi): Two hidden layers, 128 channels each. Decodes color features to RGB. Grid Resolution: Progressive upscaling from 125^3 to 150^3 (step 1000), 200^3 (step 2000), and 250^3 (step 4000). Optimizer: Adam. Batch Size: 10,192 rays. Learning Rates: Global MLP \Phi: 0.002. Explicit Grid (V\sigma, Vc): 0.1 (density), 0.11 (color). Motion Grid (Mt): 10^{-4}. Residual Grid (rt): 0.1 (density), 0.11 (color). Loss Weights: \lambda{TV} (Total Variation): 0.000016 for explicit and residual grids; 1 for motion grid. \lambda{residual} (L1 Residual): 0.01. TV Loss Activation: Only active during training iterations 1000 to 12,000. Stage 1: Explicit Feature Grid Optimization (Frame 0) 1. Construct an explicit density grid V\sigma and color feature grid Vc for the first frame using an initialization resolution (e.g., 125^3). 2. For each training iteration: a. Cast rays through pixels. Sample points p along rays. b. Query density \sigma(p) and color features c{feat}(p) via trilinear interpolation from V\sigma and Vc. c. Apply softplus activation to density: \sigma{final}(p) = \text{softplus}(\sigma(p)). d. Decode color features to RGB using global MLP \Phi: c{pred}(p) = \Phi(c{feat}(p)). e. Perform volume rendering to predict pixel color \hat{c}(l) for ray l. f. Compute loss \mathcal{L}{explicit} (see Formulas) and update V\sigma, Vc, \Phi. g. Train for 5,000 iterations (coarse) and 16,000 iterations (fine). Stage 2: Sequential Optimization for Frame t > 0 1. Motion Grid Estimation: a. Sample points pt along rays in frame t. b. Estimate dense motion field Dt by warping points from frame t-1 to t and minimizing photometric loss and TV loss on Dt. c. Progressively upscale Dt resolution as defined in parameters. d. Generate compact motion grid Mt from Dt using motion pooling strategy. e. Train for 3,000 iterations (coarse) and 16,000 iterations (fine). 2. Warping: a. Warp the previous frame's feature grid f{t-1} using Mt to generate base feature grid \hat{f}t. b. \hat{f}t is fixed during residual optimization. 3. Residual Grid Optimization: a. Initialize residual grid rt with zero values. b. For each training iteration: i. Sample points pt along rays in frame t. ii. Query base features \hat{f}t(pt) via trilinear interpolation from warped grid. iii. Query residual features rt(pt) via trilinear interpolation from rt. iv. Compute final feature ft(pt) = \hat{f}t(pt) + rt(pt). v. Decode ft(pt) using \Phi and render to get \hat{c}(l). vi. Compute loss \mathcal{L}{residual} (see Formulas) and update rt. vii. Train for 5,000 iterations (coarse) and 16,000 iterations (fine). Explicit Loss: \mathcal{L}{explicit} = \mathcal{L}{render{explicit}} + \lambda{TV} \mathcal{L}{TV{explicit}} \mathcal{L}{render{explicit}} = \sum{l \in L} \| c(l) - \hat{c}(l) \| \mathcal{L}{TV{explicit}} = \frac{1}{|V\sigma|} \sum{v \in V\sigma} \sqrt{\Deltax^2 v + \Deltay^2 v + \Deltaz^2 v} Where \Delta{x,y,z}^2 v is the squared difference between density values in adjacent voxels. Deformation (Motion) Loss: \mathcal{L}{deform} = \mathcal{L}{render{deform}} + \lambda{TV} \mathcal{L}{TV{deform}} \mathcal{L}{render{deform}} = \sum{l \in L} \| c(l) - \hat{c}(l) \| \mathcal{L}{TV{deform}} = \frac{1}{|Dt|} \sum{v \in Dt} \sqrt{\Deltax^2(v,d) + \Deltay^2(v,d) + \Deltaz^2(v,d)} Where \Delta{x,y,z}^2(v,d) is the squared difference of motion vectors in adjacent voxels. Residual Loss: \mathcal{L}{residual} = \mathcal{L}{render{residual}} + \lambda{TV} \mathcal{L}{TV{residual}} + \lambda{residual} \cdot \mathcal{L}{1residual} \mathcal{L}{render{residual}} = \sum{l \in L} \| c(l) - \hat{c}(l) \| \mathcal{L}{TV{residual}} = \frac{1}{|ft^d|} \sum{v \in ft^d} \sqrt{\Deltax^2 v + \Deltay^2 v + \Deltaz^2 v} \mathcal{L}{1residual} = \frac{1}{|rt|} \sum{v \in rt} (|vx| + |vy| + |vz|) Where ft^d represents the density component of the feature grid ft. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def trilinearinterp(grid, points): # grid: (D, D, D) or (D, D, D, C) # points: (N, 3) coordinates in [0, D-1] # Returns interpolated values at points x0 = floor(points[:, 0]) y0 = floor(points[:, 1]) z0 = floor(points[:, 2]) x1 = clamp(x0 + 1, max=grid.shape[0]-1) y1 = clamp(y0 + 1, max=grid.shape[1]-1) z1 = clamp(z0 + 1, max=grid.shape[2]-1) dx = points[:, 0] - x0 dy = points[:, 1] - y0 dz = points[:, 2] - z0 if grid.dim() == 3: v00 = grid[x0, y0, z0] v10 = grid[x1, y0, z0] v01 = grid[x0, y1, z0] v11 = grid[x1, y1, z0] v001 = grid[x0, y0, z1] v101 = grid[x1, y0, z1] v011 = grid[x0, y1, z1] v111 = grid[x1, y1, z1] w000 = (1-dx)(1-dy)(1-dz) w100 = dx(1-dy)(1-dz) w010 = (1-dx)dy(1-dz) w110 = dxdy(1-dz) w001 = (1-dx)(1-dy)dz w101 = dx(1-dy)dz w011 = (1-dx)dydz w111 = dxdydz return (w000v00 + w100v10 + w010v01 + w110v11 + w001v001 + w101v101 + w011v011 + w111v111) else: v00 = grid[x0, y0, z0,:] v10 = grid[x1, y0, z0,:] v01 = grid[x0, y1, z0,:] v11 = grid[x1, y1, z0,:] v001 = grid[x0, y0, z1,:] v101 = grid[x1, y0, z1,:] v011 = grid[x0, y1, z1,:] v111 = grid[x1, y1, z1,:] w000 = (1-dx)(1-dy)(1-dz) w100 = dx(1-dy)(1-dz) w010 = (1-dx)dy(1-dz) w110 = dxdy(1-dz) w001 = (1-dx)(1-dy)dz w101 = dx(1-dy)dz w011 = (1-dx)dydz w111 = dxdydz return (w000v00 + w100v10 + w010v01 + w110v11 + w001v001 + w101v101 + w011v011 + w111v111) def volumerender(sigma, color, rayorigins, raydirs, near, far, numsamples): # Standard volume rendering logic # The sources do not provide the exact volume rendering implementation details. # Typically: sample points along ray, compute transmittance T, accumulate color. pass def tvloss(grid): # Total variation loss on grid diffx = grid[:, 1:,:] - grid[:,:-1,:] diffy = grid[:,:, 1:] - grid[:,:,:-1] diffz = grid[1:,:,:] - grid[:-1,:,:] return sqrt(diffx2 + diffy2 + diffz2).mean() class ReRF: def init(self, gridsize=125, channels=13): self.Vsigma = randn(gridsize, gridsize, gridsize) self.Vc = randn(gridsize, gridsize, gridsize, channels) self.mlp = Sequential( Linear(channels, 128), ReLU(), Linear(128, 128), ReLU(), Linear(128, 3)) self.optimizer = Adam(list(self.mlp.parameters()) + [self.Vsigma, self.Vc], lr=0.002) self.channels = channels self.gridsize = gridsize def trainframe0(self, rays, targets, numcoarse=5000, numfine=16000): # Stage 1: Explicit Feature Grid Optimization for i in range(numcoarse + numfine): self.optimizer.zerograd() rayorigins, raydirs, targets = rays sigma = trilinearinterp(self.Vsigma, rayorigins) cfeat = trilinearinterp(self.Vc, rayorigins) sigma = softplus(sigma) colors = self.mlp(cfeat) renderedcolors = volumerender(sigma, colors, rayorigins, raydirs, near=0.0, far=1.0, numsamples=128) lossrender = mean((renderedcolors - targets)2) losstv = 0 if 1000 <= i <= 12000: losstv = tvloss(self.Vsigma) loss = lossrender + 0.000016 losstv loss.backward() self.optimizer.step() def trainframet(self, prevfeaturegrid, currentrays, targets, motiongridsize=125, residualgridsize=125): # Stage 2: Sequential Optimization # 1. Motion Grid Optimization # Estimate dense motion field Dt and generate compact motion grid Mt via motion pooling. # Optimize Mt using Ldeform for 3000 (coarse) + 16000 (fine) iterations with lr=1e-4. # Motion pooling and dense field estimation details are implementation-specific. # 2. Warping fhatt = warp(prevfeaturegrid, Mt) # 3. Residual Grid Optimization rt = zeros(residualgridsize, residualgridsize, residualgridsize, self.channels) optimizerr = Adam([rt], lr=0.1) for i in range(5000 + 16000): optimizerr.zerograd() rayorigins, raydirs, targets = currentrays fhat = trilinearinterp(fhatt, rayorigins) r = trilinearinterp(rt, rayorigins) ffinal = fhat + r sigma = softplus(ffinal[..., 0]) cfeat = ffinal[..., 1:] colors = self.mlp(cfeat) renderedcolors = volumerender(sigma, colors, rayorigins, raydirs, near=0.0, far=1.0, numsamples=128) lossrender = mean((renderedcolors - targets)2) losstv = 0 if 1000 <= i <= 12000: rdensity = rt[..., 0] losstv = tvloss(rdensity) lossl1 = mean(abs(rt)) loss = lossrender + 0.000016 losstv + 0.01 lossl1 loss.backward() optimizerr.step() return rt A two-stage training scheme to efficiently obtain ReRF from RGB videos, maintaining smoothness and sparsity of motion/residual grids. It introduces a novel motion pooling strategy to maintain the smoothness and compactness of the inter-frame motion grid along with sparsity regularizers to improve the compactness of ReRF. Time Complexity: Sequential optimization per frame. Motion grid optimization takes 19,000 iterations (3k coarse + 16k fine). Residual grid optimization takes 21,000 iterations (5k coarse + 16k fine). Memory Complexity: Scales with grid resolution. Base resolution 125^3, up to 250^3. Feature dimension 13. Performance: Achieves three orders of magnitude compression rate compared to per-frame-based neural representations. Strengths: Compact representation, supports online streaming, allows pause/play/fast-forward like 2D video. Limitations: Requires sequential training; errors can accumulate if motion estimation is poor (mitigated by residual grid). ReRF was introduced in "Neural Residual Radiance Fields for Streamably Free-Viewpoint Videos" (CVPR 2023). It builds on the idea of using explicit grids (like DVGO) and extends it to dynamic scenes by decomposing the feature field into motion and residual components, inspired by video compression standards (H.264/AVC, H.265/HEVC). Neural Residual Radiance Fields for Streamably Free-Viewpoint Videos, https://doi.org/10.1109/cvpr52729.2023.00016, fetched 2026-10-26

name: Neural 3D Volume Decomposition
body: Neural 3D Volume Decomposition (Neural-PIL) is a method for jointly estimating 3D shape, spatially-varying BRDF (SVBRDF), and per-image illumination from a collection of images of an object captured under varying viewpoints and lighting conditions. It extends the Neural Radiance Field (NeRF) framework by replacing the implicit view-dependent color output with an explicit physical material representation (Cook-Torrance BRDF parameters) and a latent illumination vector. Unlike standard NeRF which optimizes for novel view synthesis directly, this method solves the inverse problem of reflectance decomposition, enabling high-quality relighting and material-aware view synthesis. The method builds on Radiance-field optimization by introducing a physically-based rendering formulation within the neural volume. It uses a two-stage sampling strategy similar to NeRF but optimizes for material and lighting parameters rather than just color. Inputs: A set of q images Cj \in \mathbb{R}^{s \times 3} for j \in \{1, \dots, q\}, where s is the number of pixels per image. Per-pixel binary masks Mj \in \{0, 1\}^{s \times 1} indicating which pixels belong to the object. Outputs: A neural 3D volume V that, for any 3D point x \in \mathbb{R}^3, estimates: Cook-Torrance BRDF parameters b \in \mathbb{R}^7: diffuse color bd \in \mathbb{R}^3, specular color bs \in \mathbb{R}^3, and roughness br \in \mathbb{R}. Unit-length surface normal n \in \mathbb{R}^3. Optical density \sigma \in \mathbb{R}. Per-image latent illumination vectors zl \in \mathbb{R}^{128} for each of the q images. The neural volume V is implemented as two Multi-Layer Perceptrons (MLPs). Coarse MLP: Learns a coarse representation and samples the 3D volume in a fixed sampling pattern. Fine MLP: Uses the coarse density knowledge to sample the volume in high-density areas at a finer resolution. Input to MLPs: 3D coordinate x \in \mathbb{R}^3 and view direction d \in \mathbb{R}^3. Output of MLPs: Predicts material and density parameters in a fixed tensor layout: indices 0-2 for bd, 3-5 for bs, 6 for br, 7-9 for n, and 10 for \sigma. Illumination Storage: A learnable tensor of shape q \times 128 storing zl for each image. The method replaces NeRF's direct color prediction with a rendering equation that integrates BRDF and illumination. 1. Ray Sampling: For a camera ray r(t) = o + td, sample points ti along the ray between near bound tn and far bound tf. 2. Neural Query: For each sample point ti, query the neural volume V to get b(ti), n(ti), and \sigma(ti). 3. Illumination Retrieval: Retrieve the latent illumination vector zl corresponding to the image index j of the camera ray. 4. BRDF Evaluation: Compute the Cook-Torrance BRDF fr using b(ti), the surface normal n(ti), the view direction d, and the light direction derived from zl. 5. Radiance Integration: Compute the outgoing radiance Lo at each sample point by integrating the incident illumination against the BRDF. 6. Volume Rendering: Composite the final color \hat{c}(r) using numerical quadrature: \hat{c}(r) = \int{tn}^{tf} T(t) \sigma(t) c(t) dt with T(t) = \exp\left(-\int{tn}^{t} \sigma(t') dt'\right). Here, c(t) represents the outgoing radiance computed from the BRDF and illumination at sample t. The network is optimized by minimizing the difference between the rendered images and the input images Cj. The loss function typically includes a photometric term comparing \hat{c}(r) to the pixel color in Cj for pixels where Mj=1. The method may also use pre-trained networks (neural-PIL, light-SMAE, BRDF-SMAE) to regularize or initialize the optimization of BRDF and light parameters. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import torch import torch.nn as nn class NeuralVolumeDecomposition: def init(self, numimages, coarsesamples=64, finesamples=128, near=0.1, far=10.0): self.numimages = numimages self.coarsesamples = coarsesamples self.finesamples = finesamples self.near = near self.far = far # Coarse MLP: maps (x, d) to material/density parameters self.coarsemlp = nn.Sequential( nn.Linear(6, 256), nn.ReLU(), nn.Linear(256, 256), nn.ReLU(), nn.Linear(256, 11)) # Fine MLP: refines sampling in high-density areas self.finemlp = nn.Sequential( nn.Linear(6, 256), nn.ReLU(), nn.Linear(256, 256), nn.ReLU(), nn.Linear(256, 11)) # Learnable per-image illumination latent vectors zl in R^128 self.illuminationlatents = nn.Parameter(torch.randn(numimages, 128)) def samplerays(self, origins, directions, numsamples): tvals = torch.linspace(self.near, self.far, numsamples, device=origins.device) originsexp = origins.unsqueeze(1) dirsexp = directions.unsqueeze(1) tvalsexp = tvals.unsqueeze(0).unsqueeze(2) points = originsexp + dirsexp tvalsexp deltas = torch.diff(tvals, dim=0) deltainf = torch.tensor([self.far - tvals[-1]], device=origins.device) deltas = torch.cat([deltas, deltainf], dim=0) deltas = deltas.unsqueeze(0).unsqueeze(0).expand(origins.shape[0], numsamples, 1) return points, deltas def queryvolume(self, points, directions, mlp): inputs = torch.cat([points, directions], dim=-1) outputs = mlp(inputs) bd = outputs[:,:, 0:3] bs = outputs[:,:, 3:6] br = outputs[:,:, 6:7] n = outputs[:,:, 7:10] sigma = outputs[:,:, 10:11] n = n / (torch.norm(n, dim=-1, keepdim=True) + 1e-6) return bd, bs, br, n, sigma def render(self, origins, directions, imageidx): # Stage 1: Coarse fixed sampling coarsepoints, coarsedeltas = self.samplerays(origins, directions, self.coarsesamples),,,, coarsesigma = self.queryvolume(coarsepoints, directions, self.coarsemlp) coarsesigma = torch.clamp(coarsesigma, min=0.0) # Stage 2: Fine sampling (density-guided refinement) finepoints, finedeltas = self.samplerays(origins, directions, self.finesamples) finebd, finebs, finebr, finen, finesigma = self.queryvolume(finepoints, directions, self.finemlp) finesigma = torch.clamp(finesigma, min=0.0) # Use fine samples for final composition points = finepoints deltas = finedeltas bd, bs, br, n, sigma = finebd, finebs, finebr, finen, finesigma # Compute outgoing radiance c(t) from BRDF and illumination # The exact mapping from zl to light directions/intensity uses pre-trained networks (neural-PIL, light-SMAE) zl = self.illuminationlatents[imageidx] c = torch.zeroslike(bd) alpha = 1.0 - torch.exp(-sigma.squeeze(-1) deltas.squeeze(-1)) T = torch.exp(-torch.cumsum(sigma.squeeze(-1) deltas.squeeze(-1), dim=1)) Tshifted = torch.cat([torch.ones(origins.shape[0], 1, device=origins.device), T[:,:-1]], dim=1) weights = Tshifted alpha.unsqueeze(-1) renderedcolor = torch.sum(weights c, dim=1) return renderedcolor Precision: The optimization of BRDF parameters (especially roughness br) can be sensitive to initialization. Pre-training with neural-PIL helps stabilize this. Boundaries: The near and far bounds tn and tf must be chosen to encompass the object. If the object is outside these bounds, it will not be rendered. Accelerates neural volume queries using a multi-resolution grid structure, reducing memory and computation compared to dense MLPs [1414-hierarchical-grid-optimization.md]. Details on integration with this method are not given in the sources. Represents scenes as explicit 3D Gaussians for faster rasterization, trading off the implicit neural volume representation for speed [1795-3d-gaussian-splatting.md]. Details on integration with this method are not given in the sources. The foundational coordinate-based MLP method for novel view synthesis, which Neural 3D Volume Decomposition extends by adding physical material parameters [4972-neural-radiance-fields.md]. The method explicitly builds on NeRF's two-MLP architecture. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Enables high-quality relighting and material-aware view synthesis. Can recover accurate shape and material properties from real-world datasets. Limitations: Requires images captured under varying illumination conditions. Optimization is complex and may require pre-trained networks for stability. When to use: When the goal is to recover physical material properties and illumination from a set of images, rather than just novel view synthesis. When not to use: When only novel view synthesis is needed, or when the input images do not have varying illumination. Neural 3D Volume Decomposition, also known as Neural-PIL, was introduced in the paper "Neural-PIL: Neural Pre-Integrated Lighting for Reflectance Decomposition". The method addresses the challenge of recovering 3D shape and SVBRDF from images captured under varying lighting conditions, a problem relevant to digitizing real-world objects like statues or landmarks. It builds on the success of NeRF in novel view synthesis and extends it to physical material decomposition.
