name: Shading-Guided NeRF Synthesis
head: Shading Map Guided Synthesis Pipeline, Shading vector synthesis
body: Shading-Guided NeRF Synthesis is a method for generating large-scale radiance fields from a smaller exemplar by controlling lighting effects using shading vectors, avoiding the need to decouple geometry, material, and lighting. It solves the problem of efficiently synthesizing repetitive 3D structures while maintaining consistent lighting across complex scenes. It sets itself apart from methods that rely solely on feature grid matching, which leads to discontinuous shading changes under complex lighting, by explicitly incorporating a shading map and shading map guider to ensure continuous lighting. Inputs: 1. Exemplar Radiance Field: Represented by a density field V^{(d)} and a color feature field V^{(f)}. 2. Exemplar Shading Map: A 3D volume where each voxel column stores a shading vector derived from the exemplar. 3. Target Scene Geometry: A geometrically continuous large scene (synthesized via geometry-based synthesis) used to generate the shading map guider. 4. Light Source Information: Position xl and intensity I of point light sources in the target scene. 5. Parameters: M: Number of viewpoints to approximate the shading vector (typically 50). ks: Number of closest shading patches to find in the exemplar. kg: Number of candidate patches with geometric continuity. np: Number of high-density points selected for ray tracing. ns: Number of sample points along the light path. nc: Number of shading vector channels retained (those with the lowest missing value rate). Outputs: A synthesized large-scale NeRF scene with density field and radiance field stitched from exemplar patches, guided by the target lighting. Data Structures: Shading Map: A 3D volume. Each voxel at position v contains a vector \mathbf{s}v \in \mathbb{R}^M, where M is the number of viewpoints. The m-th component is the shading value of the voxel column at viewpoint m. Shading Map Guider: A 3D volume of the same dimensions as the Shading Map, containing shading vectors derived from the target scene's geometry and light sources. Density Field V^{(d)}: 3D grid storing density values \sigma. Color Feature Field V^{(f)}: 3D grid storing color feature values. Algorithm Steps: 1. Extract Exemplar Shading Map: a. Perform intrinsic decomposition on multiple images of the exemplar using PIE-Net to derive shading and albedo. b. Apply Gaussian blurring and polynomial fitting to the shading image to smooth it and remove geometric interference. c. For each pixel in the smoothed shading image, project the shading value along the camera ray to a depth position d in the 3D voxel grid. d. Calculate depth d using the density grid: d = \sum{k} Ti (1 - \exp(-\sigmai \deltai)) ti where Ti is transmittance, \sigmai is density, \deltai is distance, and ti is a position/weight factor. e. Collect shading information from M viewpoints to form the shading vector for each voxel column. f. Post-processing: i. Fill holes in shading vector channels (caused by occlusions/limited pixels) using KNN interpolation with inverse distance weighting. ii. Repair noisy points using median filtering. iii. Retain only the nc channels with the lowest rate of missing values. 2. Generate Shading Map Guider: a. Synthesize a geometrically continuous large scene using geometry-based synthesis (matching density only) to create a base target scene. Then, apply ray tracing to generate the shading map guider for the target illumination. b. Select np points from this scene with high density. c. For each selected point x and a point light source xl: i. Sample ns points x1,..., x{ns} along the path between xl and x, where x{ns} = x. ii. Calculate the probability p{ns} of the ray propagating to x{ns}: p{ns} = T{ns} (1 - \exp(-\sigma{ns} \delta{ns})). iii. Calculate brightness b: b = p{ns} \frac{1}{ns} \frac{I}{\|x - xl\|2^2} where I is light intensity. d. The brightness values from M viewpoints (or equivalent lighting configurations) form the shading vector for each voxel column in the target scene, creating the Shading Map Guider. 3. Synthesize Scene (Patch Selection and Stitching): a. For a patch Pn to be synthesized in the target area: i. Compute the L2 distance between the shading vector of Pn and patches in the exemplar's Shading Map. ii. Accelerate search using a kd-tree. iii. Identify the ks closest shading patches from the exemplar. iv. Normalize the values of the exemplar's Shading Map and the target's Shading Map Guider to the same scale. v. Rotate the exemplar by 90, 180, and 270 degrees to obtain additional available patches, addressing selection limitations. b. Two-Phase Patch Selection: i. Phase 1 (Geometry): From the ks candidates, find kg candidate patches with geometric continuity based on the density field V^{(d)}. ii. Phase 2 (Color): From the kg candidates, select one patch for color continuity in the overlap area based on the color feature field V^{(f)}. c. Stitch the selected patch’s density field and radiance field onto the target area. d. Repeat until the target scene is fully synthesized. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import numpy as np def shadingguidednerfsynthesis(exemplarshadingimages, exemplardensity, targetdensity, lightsources, M, ks, kg, np, ns, nc): # 1. Extract Exemplar Shading Map # Intrinsic decomposition to derive shading and albedo from images smoothedshading = [smoothshading(img) for img in exemplarshadingimages] # Initialize Shading Map volume (X, Y, Z, M) with NaN shadingmap = np.full((X, Y, Z, M), np.nan) for m in range(M): camera = getcameraparams(m) shadingimg = smoothedshading[m] for y in range(shadingimg.shape[0]): for x in range(shadingimg.shape[1]): rayorigin, raydirection = camera.unproject(x, y) # Ray march through exemplar density to get samples samples = raymarch(rayorigin, raydirection, exemplardensity) # Depth formula: d = sumk Ti (1 - exp(-sigmai deltai)) ti d = sum(s.transmittance (1 - np.exp(-s.sigma s.delta)) s.t for s in samples) voxelcoords = rayorigin + d raydirection if isinsidegrid(voxelcoords): shadingmap[voxelcoords] = shadingimg[y, x] # Post-processing for m in range(M): channel = shadingmap[:,:,:, m] # KNN interpolation with inverse distance weighting for holes channel = knninterpolate(channel, weights='inversedistance') # Median filtering for noisy points channel = medianfilter(channel, size=3) shadingmap[:,:,:, m] = channel # Retain nc channels with lowest missing rate missingrates = np.mean(np.isnan(shadingmap), axis=(0,1,2)) bestchannels = np.argsort(missingrates)[:nc] exemplarshadingmap = shadingmap[:,:,:, bestchannels] # 2. Generate Shading Map Guider # Geometry-based synthesis to create base target scene basescenedensity = geometrybasedsynthesis(targetdensity) # Select np points with high density highdensitypoints = selecthighdensitypoints(basescenedensity, np) shadingmapguider = np.zeros((X, Y, Z, M)) for point in highdensitypoints: x = point for m in range(M): lightsource = getlightsource(m) I = lightsource.intensity xl = lightsource.position # Sample ns points along path pathpoints = samplepath(xl, x, ns) xns = pathpoints[-1] sigmans = getdensity(basescenedensity, xns) deltans = distance(xl, xns) / ns Tns = calculatetransmittance(xl, xns, basescenedensity) pns = Tns (1 - np.exp(-sigmans deltans)) distsq = np.linalg.norm(x - xl)2 brightness = pns (1/ns) (I / distsq) voxelcoords = getvoxelcoords(x) shadingmapguider[voxelcoords, m] = brightness # 3. Synthesize Scene synthesizeddensity = np.zeros(targetdensity.shape) synthesizedcolor = np.zeros(targetdensity.shape) for patch in targetgeometry.patches: # Normalize scales exemplarpatches = normalize(exemplarpatches) targetshadingvec = normalize(targetshadingvec) # Find ks closest patches using L2 distance (accelerated by kd-tree) distances, indices = kdtree.query(targetshadingvec, k=ks) candidatepatches = exemplarpatches[indices] # Two-phase selection # Phase 1: Geometric continuity based on density field geometriccandidates = filterbydensitycontinuity(candidatepatches, targetareapatch, kg) # Phase 2: Color continuity based on color feature field bestpatchidx = selectbycolorcontinuity(geometriccandidates, targetareapatch) # Stitch patch patchdensity = extractpatchdensity(exemplardensity, bestpatchidx) patchcolor = extractpatchcolor(exemplarcolor, bestpatchidx) stitch(synthesizeddensity, synthesizedcolor, patch, patchdensity, patchcolor) return synthesizeddensity, synthesizedcolor Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Holes in Shading Map: Occlusions and limited pixels cause missing values in shading vector channels. Addressed by KNN interpolation with inverse distance weighting. Noisy Points: Inaccurate depth values introduce noise. Addressed by median filtering. Channel Selection: Channels with high missing value rates have high interpolation error. Only retain nc channels with the lowest missing rate. Selection Limitations: Strict shading/geometry/texture requirements may limit patch selection. Addressed by rotating the exemplar by 90, 180, and 270 degrees to increase available patches. Scale Mismatch: Exemplar and target shading maps may have different scales. Must be normalized to the same scale before distance calculation. NeRF Synthesis via DVGO is a method for generating large-scale radiance fields by applying 2D texture synthesis algorithms to the flattened density and feature grids of a Differentiable Voxel Grid Object (DVGO) representation. It solves the problem of efficiently synthesizing repetitive 3D structures (e.g., vegetation) by exploiting the observation that only two spatial dimensions typically exhibit clear repeatability, thereby avoiding the inefficiency of full 3D synthesis. It sets itself apart from direct 3D synthesis by flattening the 3D grid along the Z-axis into 2D grids, allowing the use of established 2D texture synthesis techniques while treating each unit as storing density and feature values rather than RGB pixels. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Requires storage for the exemplar density/color fields, the exemplar shading map, and the target shading map guider. Measured Performance: Not given in the sources. Scaling: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Controls lighting effects using shading guidance without decoupling geometry, material, and lighting. Ensures continuous lighting in synthesized scenes under complex lighting. Can synthesize new scenes on curved surfaces with arbitrary lighting effects. Uses a two-phase method to ensure both geometric and appearance continuity. Limitations: Requires intrinsic decomposition (PIE-Net) and ray tracing for preprocessing. Sensitive to occlusions and limited pixels, requiring post-processing. Relies on the availability of multiple images of the exemplar for intrinsic decomposition. When to use: When synthesizing large-scale scenes with repetitive structures and complex lighting, where maintaining consistent lighting is critical. Origin: The method was proposed in "NeRF Synthesis with Shading Guidance". History: The paper addresses the limitations of physically-based rendering (PBR) in virtual reality, augmented reality, and video games, and the challenges of attaching realistic surface structures onto mesh surfaces. It builds on the concept of 3D texture synthesis and NeRF representations. Usage: Demonstrated for generating high-quality results with consistent geometry and appearance for scenes with complex lighting, including synthesis on curved surfaces. name: NeRF Synthesis via DVGO
head: 2D texture synthesis for 3D NeRF
body: NeRF Synthesis via DVGO is a method for generating large-scale radiance fields by applying 2D texture synthesis algorithms to the flattened density and feature grids of a Differentiable Voxel Grid Object (DVGO) representation. It solves the problem of efficiently synthesizing repetitive 3D structures (e.g., vegetation) by exploiting the observation that only two spatial dimensions typically exhibit clear repeatability, thereby avoiding the inefficiency of full 3D synthesis. It sets itself apart from direct 3D synthesis by flattening the 3D grid along the Z-axis into 2D grids, allowing the use of established 2D texture synthesis techniques while treating each unit as storing density and feature values rather than RGB pixels. Inputs: Source DVGO: Density grid V^{(d)} and feature grid V^{(f)}. Target dimensions: Width W{target}, Height H{target}. Synthesis parameters: Patch size S \times S, number of nearest neighbors kg, blending radius. Outputs: Synthesized Density grid I^{(d)} of size W{target} \times H{target}. Synthesized Feature grid I^{(f)} of size W{target} \times H{target}. Data Structures: The 3D grids are flattened into 2D grids along the Z-axis. For a voxel at (x, y, z), the corresponding 2D coordinate (x', y') is calculated as: x' = x y' = y \cdot D + z The resulting 2D grid I^{(d)} has dimensions W \times (H \cdot D). Each "pixel" in this 2D grid stores a scalar density value d and a feature vector \mathbf{f} instead of RGB. Algorithm (Two-Phase Method): The method prioritizes geometric continuity over appearance because the synthesis operates at the voxel column level, where color features inherently incorporate geometric information; ensuring geometric continuity first prevents density from affecting subsequent appearance considerations. 1. Flattening: Convert V^{(d)} and V^{(f)} into 2D grids I^{(d)} and I^{(f)} by flattening along the Z-axis. 2. Initialization: Initialize the target grids I^{(d)}{target} and I^{(f)}{target} with zeros. 3. Synthesis Loop: Iterate through each voxel patch Pn in the target grid in raster order. Phase 1 (Geometry Selection): Extract the boundary of the current density patch Pn^{(d)}, denoted \partial(Pn^{(d)}). Search the source grid I^{(d)} for candidate patches Ei^{(d)}. Calculate the similarity between the boundary of the target patch and the boundary of each candidate using a distance metric d(\cdot, \cdot) (L2 distance on flattened boundary vectors). Select the kg best matching density patches En^{(d)} = \{E1^{(d)}, \dots, E{kg}^{(d)}\} based on minimum distance. Phase 2 (Appearance Selection): For each of the kg selected density patches, retrieve the corresponding feature patch Ei^{(f)} from the source feature grid I^{(f)}. Calculate the similarity between the boundary of the target feature patch Pn^{(f)} and the boundary of each candidate feature patch \partial(Ei^{(f)}) using d(\partial(Pn^{(f)}), \partial(Ei^{(f)})). Convert these similarities into likelihoods for random selection. Randomly select one final patch En^ from the kg candidates based on these likelihoods. Blending: Copy the non-overlapping parts of En^ into Pn. For overlapping regions between En^ and the existing content in Pn, blend the values using inverse distance weighting. 4. Unflattening (Optional): If the final output requires a 3D grid, reshape I^{(d)}{target} and I^{(f)}{target} back to W \times H \times D{target} by reversing the flattening mapping. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math import random def synthesizedvgo(sourcedensity3d, sourcefeature3d, targetw, targeth, targetd, patchsize, kg): # Flatten 3D to 2D along Z-axis: (W, H, D) -> (W, HD) sourcedensity2d = flattenz(sourcedensity3d) sourcefeature2d = flattenz(sourcefeature3d) targetw2d = targetw targeth2d = targeth targetd targetdensity2d = zeros((targetw2d, targeth2d)) targetfeature2d = zeros((targetw2d, targeth2d)) # Iterate over target patches in raster order for y in range(0, targeth2d, patchsize): for x in range(0, targetw2d, patchsize): # Define current patch coordinates patchcoords = (x, y, patchsize, patchsize) # Phase 1: Geometry # Extract boundary of current target density patch currentboundaryd = getboundary(targetdensity2d, patchcoords) # Find kg best matches in source candidatesd = findknearestneighbors( sourcedensity2d, currentboundaryd, kg, patchsize) # Phase 2: Appearance # Calculate feature similarity for candidates currentboundaryf = getboundary(targetfeature2d, patchcoords) similarities = [] for candd in candidatesd: # Get corresponding feature patch from source candf = getfeaturepatch(sourcefeature2d, candd.coords, patchsize) candboundaryf = getboundary(candf, candd.coords) dist = l2distance(currentboundaryf, candboundaryf) similarities.append((dist, candd)) # Sort by distance (lower is better) similarities.sort(key=lambda x: x[0]) # Convert distances to likelihoods (inverse distance weighting) likelihoods = [1.0 / (dist + 1e-6) for dist, in similarities] total = sum(likelihoods) likelihoods = [l / total for l in likelihoods] # Random selection based on likelihoods idx = weightedrandomchoice(len(similarities), likelihoods) selectedcandidate = similarities[idx][1] # Blend selected patch into target blendpatch(targetdensity2d, targetfeature2d, selectedcandidate, patchcoords) # Unflatten back to 3D targetdensity3d = unflattenz(targetdensity2d, targetw, targeth, targetd) targetfeature3d = unflattenz(targetfeature2d, targetw, targeth, targetd) return targetdensity3d, targetfeature3d def zeros(shape): return [[0.0] shape[1] for in range(shape[0])] def flattenz(grid3d): W, H, D = len(grid3d), len(grid3d[0]), len(grid3d[0][0]) grid2d = zeros((W, H D)) for x in range(W): for y in range(H): for z in range(D): idx = y D + z grid2d[x][idx] = grid3d[x][y][z] return grid2d def unflattenz(grid2d, W, H, D): grid3d = zeros((W, H, D)) for x in range(W): for y in range(H): for z in range(D): idx = y D + z grid3d[x][y][z] = grid2d[x][idx] return grid3d def getboundary(grid2d, coords): x, y, w, h = coords boundary = [] # Top and bottom rows for i in range(w): boundary.append(grid2d[x + i][y]) boundary.append(grid2d[x + i][y + h - 1]) # Left and right columns (excluding corners) for i in range(1, h - 1): boundary.append(grid2d[x][y + i]) boundary.append(grid2d[x + w - 1][y + i]) return boundary def l2distance(a, b): return math.sqrt(sum((ai - bi) 2 for ai, bi in zip(a, b))) def findknearestneighbors(sourcegrid, targetboundary, k, patchsize): candidates = [] W, H = len(sourcegrid), len(sourcegrid[0]) for y in range(0, H - patchsize + 1, patchsize): for x in range(0, W - patchsize + 1, patchsize): candboundary = getboundary(sourcegrid, (x, y, patchsize, patchsize)) dist = l2distance(targetboundary, candboundary) candidates.append((dist, (x, y))) candidates.sort(key=lambda x: x[0]) return [{"dist": d, "coords": c} for d, c in candidates[:k]] def getfeaturepatch(featuregrid, coords, patchsize): x, y = coords return [row[y:y+patchsize] for row in featuregrid[x:x+patchsize]] def weightedrandomchoice(n, weights): r = random.random() sum(weights) cumulative = 0.0 for i, w in enumerate(weights): cumulative += w if r <= cumulative: return i return n - 1 def blendpatch(targetd, targetf, sourcepatch, coords): x, y, w, h = coords for i in range(w): for j in range(h): tx, ty = x + i, y + j # Inverse distance weighting for overlaps dist = math.sqrt(ii + jj) + 1e-6 weight = 1.0 / dist targetd[tx][ty] = (targetd[tx][ty] + sourcepatch[i][j] weight) / (1.0 + weight) targetf[tx][ty] = (targetf[tx][ty] + sourcepatch[i][j] weight) / (1.0 + weight) Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Boundary Artifacts: The method struggles with boundary synthesis because occluded interior parts are synthesized onto the boundary, lacking pixel value supervision during DVGO training, leading to artifacts. Dimensionality: High dimensionality of the combined grid increases search time. Weighting: In the baseline combined method, high weight for density causes color inconsistencies, while high weight for color causes geometric inconsistencies. A baseline method that concatenates density and feature grids V^{(d)} and V^{(f)} into a combined 2D image I^{(d \oplus f)} and measures distance via L2. It suffers from weighting challenges between geometry and appearance. It prioritizes density over color because the synthesis operates at the voxel column level where color features inherently incorporate geometric information; ensuring geometric continuity first prevents density from affecting subsequent appearance considerations. The process involves Phase 1 (Geometry): selecting kg best density voxel patches En^{(d)} based on similarity of d(\partial(Pn^{(d)}), \partial(En^{(d)})); and Phase 2 (Appearance): calculating similarity d(\partial(Pn^{(f)}), \partial(En^{(f)})) for the selected patches, using these as likelihoods for random selection, and blending overlapping regions using inverse distance weighting. Pitfalls include high weight for density causing color inconsistencies, high weight for color causing geometric inconsistencies, and high dimensionality of I^{(d \oplus f)} increasing search time. Time Complexity: The search for nearest neighbors in the source grid dominates the complexity. With high dimensionality of the feature space, search time increases significantly. Memory Complexity: Requires storing the flattened 2D grids I^{(d)} and I^{(f)}, which have size W \times (H \cdot D). Strengths: Efficiently synthesizes repetitive 3D structures by leveraging 2D texture synthesis methods; avoids the inefficiency of full 3D synthesis. Limitations: Boundary artifacts due to lack of supervision for occluded parts; sensitivity to weighting in combined methods; high search time for high-dimensional features. When to use: Suitable for scenes with clear 2D repeatability (e.g., grass, trees) where 3D synthesis is inefficient. When not to use: Scenes with complex 3D structures lacking 2D repeatability or requiring precise boundary continuity without artifacts. The method originates from the paper "NeRF Synthesis with Shading Guidance". It builds on the DVGO representation, which uses a hybrid implicit-explicit structure. The approach was developed to address the inefficiency of 3D synthesis for objects like grass, where only two dimensions exhibit clear repeatability. name: Tomographic reconstruction as inverse rendering
body: Tomographic reconstruction as inverse rendering treats computed tomography (CT) not as a linear algebra problem to be solved via closed-form filters or static iterative solvers, but as an optimization problem where a differentiable forward renderer (the projector) is minimized against measured projection data. This approach unifies classical algebraic reconstruction techniques (ART, SIRT) with modern neural representations and compressive sensing priors under a single gradient-based framework. It distinguishes itself from Differentiable volume rendering by focusing specifically on the tomographic geometry (parallel/fan/cone beam) and the reconstruction of density/absorption fields from sparse or noisy sinograms, and from Radiance-field optimization by explicitly modeling the X-ray physics (Beer-Lambert law) rather than just RGB appearance. All methods in this family rely on the differentiability of the forward projection operator \mathcal{P} and its adjoint (back-projection) \mathcal{P}^T. The core optimization problem is generally formulated as minimizing a loss function \mathcal{L} between the measured sinogram p and the rendered projection \hat{p} = \mathcal{P}(x) of the current volume estimate x: \minx \mathcal{L}(\mathcal{P}(x), p) + \lambda R(x) where R(x) is a regularizer (e.g., Total Variation, neural prior) and \lambda is a weighting factor. The gradient of the loss with respect to the volume x is computed via the chain rule: \frac{\partial \mathcal{L}}{\partial x} = \mathcal{P}^T \left( \frac{\partial \mathcal{L}}{\partial \hat{p}} \right) The term \frac{\partial \mathcal{L}}{\partial \hat{p}} is the residual gradient in projection space (e.g., p - \hat{p} for MSE), and \mathcal{P}^T is the back-projection operator. Key shared components include: 1. Forward Projection: Ray marching through the volume representation (voxels, octrees, or neural fields) to compute line integrals of density/absorption coefficients. 2. Backward Projection (Adjoint): Distributing the error from the 2D detector plane back into the 3D volume. This is mathematically the transpose of the forward operator, ensuring stable convergence in iterative methods. 3. Optimization Loop: An iterative process (e.g., SGD, Adam) that updates the volume parameters (voxel values, neural network weights, or Gaussian parameters) to reduce the projection error. An adaptive, hierarchical neural rendering pipeline for multi-view inverse rendering, designed specifically for the tomographic reconstruction of semi-transparent volumetric scenes from X-ray images. It combines an adaptive explicit octree representation with neural features stored in leaf nodes to achieve efficient reconstruction and simultaneous self-calibration of geometric and photometric parameters. Unlike purely implicit neural representations, NeAT uses a hybrid explicit-implicit structure optimized via differentiable volume rendering, which outperforms alternatives in both quality and compute time for tomographic tasks where samples are widely scattered. A set of techniques designed to reconstruct high-quality volume renderings from a sparse subset of pixels, treating the problem as an image restoration or inpainting task. Unlike standard iterative reconstruction methods that solve for voxel values directly via linear systems, these methods exploit prior knowledge about the signal's structure—specifically sparsity in transform domains (wavelet, gradient) or smoothness (Total Variation)—to recover the image from undersampled measurements. A compressive sensing technique that renders discrete gradient components instead of pixel values to exploit sparsity in the gradient domain, then reconstructs the image using a Poisson solver. It differs from standard volume rendering by optimizing for gradient coefficients in the frequency domain rather than direct pixel intensities, allowing for reconstruction from fewer samples than the Nyquist rate. The mathematical adjoint (transpose) of the forward projection operator, used to accumulate 2D projection data into a 3D reconstruction volume. It solves the problem of mapping measured projection weights to volume expansion coefficients, serving as the core gradient computation step in differentiable tomographic reconstruction. Unlike direct methods like FDK which may suffer from artifacts with limited projections, back-projection provides the exact transpose required for stable iterative optimization over many iterations. A PyTorch-based framework for differentiable computed tomography projection and reconstruction. It implements a cell-constant attenuation field integrator along rays defined by per-view acquisition geometry, where the backprojector is the matched discrete adjoint of the forward projector. It distinguishes itself from analytical methods (like FBP/FDK) by supporting arbitrary trajectories, trainable geometry, and native first-order derivatives for iterative optimization, while avoiding the separable-footprint approximations of earlier releases. An iterative algebraic reconstruction technique that solves the inverse problem of tomographic reconstruction by minimizing the discrepancy between measured projections and forward-projected volume estimates. It distinguishes itself from simultaneous methods like SART by applying global normalization to both the ray residuals and the backprojected updates, ensuring stable convergence through nonnegativity constraints. It serves as a baseline differentiable reconstruction method within the Tomographic reconstruction as inverse rendering framework. This framework formulates tomographic reconstruction as a regularized inverse problem, minimizing a data fidelity term against a regularizer to recover volumetric data from projections. It distinguishes itself from direct algebraic methods (like SIRT) by decoupling the data consistency and regularization steps via proximal splitting, allowing for complex, non-linear priors and flexible integration of physical constraints. It serves as the foundational solver for advanced applications including sparse-view reconstruction, 3D super-resolution, and dynamic fluid capture. A CPU-optimized implementation of the Feldkamp-Davis-Kress (FDK) algorithm, an analytical method for reconstructing a 3D volume from a stack of 2D cone-beam projection images. It solves the tomographic reconstruction problem by applying a specific convolution filter to weighted projections and back-projecting them into a 3D grid. It sets itself apart from its siblings by precomputing geometric weights and using a direct spatial-domain convolution filter to avoid the overhead of FFTs during the main reconstruction loop, prioritizing speed and memory locality on CPU architectures. Solves the coupled inverse problem of near-field holotomography by combining holographic phase retrieval with tomographic reconstruction using Implicit Neural Representations (INRs). Unlike standard tomography that assumes far-field (Fraunhofer) propagation, HoloINR explicitly models near-field physics via Fresnel propagation between the object and the detector. It differs from sibling methods like NeAT or DuDoTrans by replacing discrete voxel grids with a continuous neural field, allowing for resolution-independent reconstruction and natural integration of wave-optics effects. A differentiable renderer designed for multi-line neural tomography, specifically recovering 3-D coronal electron density (ne) and temperature (Te) from multiview, multiline spectral-intensity images. It performs ray marching and Line-of-Sight (LOS) integration of emissivity coefficients derived from neural network models. It is distinguished from general volume renderers by its explicit physics-based emissivity computation using a Look-Up Table (LUT) for ion-specific spectral lines and its integration with occupancy grids for sparse volume representation. A tomographic reconstruction method that adapts 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) to sparse-view X-ray imaging by rectifying an integration bias inherent in standard 3DGS splatting. It replaces the appearance-based 3DGS kernel with a radiative Gaussian kernel parameterized by density, position, and covariance, and derives new X-ray rendering functions to ensure accurate volume retrieval. Unlike siblings that use 3DGS only for data augmentation or replace rasterization with simulators, R2-Gaussian maintains efficient differentiable rasterization while enabling direct 3D density volume extraction. An inverse rendering technique that reconstructs the volumetric absorption coefficients of an object from a series of 2D X-ray projection images by optimizing scene parameters via gradient descent. It formulates Computed Tomography (CT) as an iterative optimization problem where the 3D volume is treated as a differentiable parameter space, allowing the use of auto-differentiable rendering engines to compute gradients of a projection loss. Unlike traditional algebraic or analytical methods, this approach relies on end-to-end differentiability of the forward projection, enabling the use of modern optimizers like ADAM without explicit derivation of the back-projection operator. It is distinct from neural implicit methods (e.g., HoloINR) by typically operating on explicit voxel grids rather than continuous neural fields, and from deep learning approaches by requiring no pre-trained models. An iterative algebraic method that minimizes the quadratic norm of the difference between acquired projections and projected reconstructed volume, avoiding explicit matrix storage. A staggered two-step iterative process that alternates between reconstructing a volume from a frozen displacement field and identifying the motion from a frozen estimate of the microstructure to handle deforming volumes in tomography. A volumetric display where multiple emitters surround the display area and project rays with programmed intensity for each direction; the intersection of rays in a scattering medium produces the graphics. An iterative reconstruction method that solves the inverse problem g = Af + n by combining a gradient descent step on the data fidelity term with a sparsity-promoting wavelet thresholding step. It is used to reconstruct images from noisy sinograms, particularly in sparse or limited angle scenarios. This family encompasses methods that replace or augment traditional algebraic regularizers with neural networks to solve the inverse problem of tomographic reconstruction. It distinguishes itself from classical iterative methods (like SIRT or ART) by leveraging the expressive power of deep learning to enforce priors, either implicitly through network architecture (Deep Image Prior) or explicitly through learned features (Transformers), often enabling reconstruction from sparse or noisy data where traditional methods fail. Physics-Based Image Formation Models define the differentiable forward operator \mathcal{P} that maps a 3D (or 4D) volume representation to 2D projection images, serving as the core component in inverse rendering pipelines. Unlike generic differentiable renderers, these models are tailored to specific physical acquisition modalities (e.g., X-ray absorption, ultrasound wave propagation) to ensure physical consistency and computational efficiency. They distinguish themselves from siblings like Neural Adaptive Tomography by explicitly modeling the underlying physics (such as linear absorption or coupled wave equations) rather than relying solely on learned neural priors or adaptive sampling strategies. A physics-based tomographic reconstruction method employing Laplacian regularization for sparse view reconstruction, representing the state-of-the-art in physics-based smoke reconstruction. Multi-view variant uses 16 views; single-view variant uses only one input view. A CPU-based implementation of CT reconstruction used as a ground truth reference for validating GPU implementations. Input includes projections (std::vector<float>), P (number of projections), W (width), H (height), NX (volume width), NY (volume height/depth), voxelSize (float), pixelSize (float), sdd (source-to-detector distance), sod (source-to-origin distance). Output is std::vector<float> representing the reconstructed volume. A method to reconstruct an image from its tomographic scans (projections), producing a result that may be blurry-filtered compared to the original. Call reconstruct with scan data, width, and height to produce the destination image. For overscanned reconstruction, call reconstructoverscan with additional xover and yover parameters, then trim the result to the original dimensions. RMS error between source and reconstructed image is between 59.0 and 61.0 for a 35x40 ray/angle configuration, attributed to the blurry-filtered nature of the reconstruction. Reconstruction produces a blurry-filtered version of the original, resulting in higher RMS error compared to a perfect reconstruction, but better than a blank image baseline. Tomographic reconstruction has traditionally been dominated by analytical methods like Filtered Back Projection (FBP) and algebraic methods like ART and SIRT. The advent of differentiable rendering has allowed these problems to be framed as optimization problems, enabling the use of gradient-based optimizers and complex neural priors. The field continues to evolve with hybrid methods combining explicit structures (octrees, Gaussians) with neural features for efficient and high-quality reconstruction. name: Compressive Volume Rendering Recovery Methods
head: Compressed Sensing Wavelet, Total Variation (TV) Minimization, Least-Squares (SS), CS-Wavelet, CS-Gradient
body: Compressive Volume Rendering Recovery Methods are a family of image restoration techniques that reconstruct full-resolution volume-rendered images from a sparse subset of rendered pixels. They solve the problem of high rendering costs by leveraging the inherent smoothness or sparsity of volume-rendered images to recover missing pixel values via optimization. Unlike standard compressive sensing methods that rely on sparsity in transform domains (which can be incoherent with point sampling), smoothness-based methods like Total Variation (TV) minimization and Least-Squares (SS) are more resilient to missing information and generally outperform compressed sensing variants. The recovery process treats the volume rendering output as an image inpainting problem. Given a set of measured pixels y at specific locations defined by a sampling matrix S, the goal is to recover the full image vector x. Input: A vector y containing the rendered pixel values at sampled locations. The sampling pattern is defined by the matrix S (e.g., random, low-discrepancy, or partial Fourier). Output: The recovered full-resolution image vector x. Image Vector x: A column vector of size N \times 1, where N is the total number of pixels in the target resolution (e.g., 1200 \times 1200 = 1,440,000). Sampling Matrix S: An M \times N binary matrix (M < N) where M is the number of sampled pixels. S{ij} = 1 if pixel j is sampled, 0 otherwise. Transform Matrices: \Psi: Orthonormal transform matrix (e.g., DWT or DCT). \Phi: Gaussian blurring matrix (used in CS-Wavelet). W: DWT matrix (used in CS-Wavelet formulation in). The general measurement equation for compressed sensing approaches is: y = A \hat{x} where A is the sensing matrix and \hat{x} is the sparse coefficient vector. 1. CS-Wavelet: Assumes the image x is sparse in the wavelet domain. To ensure incoherence between the sampling basis (point sampling) and the wavelet basis, a blurred version xb is recovered. y = S \Phi^{-1} W^{-1} \hat{x}b where \hat{x}b is the DWT of the blurred image xb = \Phi x. The final image is reconstructed as: x = W \hat{x}b Note: Some sources define the transform as \Psi and the equation as y = S \Psi^{-1} \hat{x}. The blurring step is critical for CS-Wavelet to satisfy the Restricted Isometry Condition (RIC). 2. CS-Gradient: Assumes the image gradient is sparse in the Fourier domain. 3. TV Minimization: Minimizes the total variation seminorm, defined as: \|x\|{TV}:= \sum{i,j} |x{i+1,j} - x{i,j}| + |x{i,j+1} - x{i,j}| where x{i,j} is the pixel value at coordinates (i, j). The optimization problem is: \minx \|x\|{TV} \quad \text{subject to} \quad \|Sx - y\|2 \leq \epsilon 4. Least-Squares (SS): Minimizes a smoothness norm based on second derivatives (variational minimization in a spline space). It solves a least-squares minimization problem with a regularization parameter \lambda. 1. Sampling: Render only a fraction of pixels (e.g., 20-50%) using a distribution algorithm (Random or Low-Discrepancy/LD). 2. Preprocessing (CS-Wavelet only): If using CS-Wavelet, apply Gaussian blurring to the target image domain to create xb. Set the standard deviation \sigma of the filter. 3. Optimization: Solve for the coefficients \hat{x} (or x directly for TV/SS) using an iterative solver: For CS-Wavelet, CS-Gradient, and TV: Use the NESTA solver for l1 minimization. For SS: Use a conjugate gradient solver for least-squares minimization. 4. Reconstruction: For CS-Wavelet: Apply the inverse DWT (W) to the recovered coefficients \hat{x}b to get x. For TV/SS/CS-Gradient: The output of the solver is the image x directly. Blurring Filter Standard Deviation (\sigma): 20 for CS-Wavelet. This value balances the trade-off between incoherence and blurring effects. NESTA Tolerance/Stopping Criteria: 10^{-2} (noted as 102 in some texts, likely a typo for 10^{-2} or 1e-2). SS Regularization Parameter (\lambda): 10^{-2} (noted as 102 in some texts). Resolution: Experiments typically use 1200 \times 1200 output images from datasets with resolution \approx 256 \times 256 \times 256. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def compressivevolumerenderingrecovery(measuredpixelsy, samplingmatrixS, method, resolution=(1200, 1200)): """ Reconstructs a full image from sparse pixel measurements. """ N = resolution[0] resolution[1] if method == 'CS-Wavelet': # 1. Define sensing matrix A = S Phi^-1 W^-1 # 2. Solve l1-minimization for xhatb using NESTA solver # Tolerance = 1e-2, Blurring sigma = 20 # (Source does not specify NESTA internals; standard first-order sparse recovery method [BBC11]) xhatb = None # Solve l1 minimization # 3. Reconstruct image using inverse DWT recoveredimage = None # Apply inverse DWT to xhatb elif method == 'CS-Gradient': # 1. Solve l1-minimization for gradient coefficients using NESTA solver # Tolerance = 1e-2 gradcoeffs = None # Solve l1 minimization # 2. Reconstruct image from gradient coefficients using Poisson solver # (Source does not specify Poisson solver internals) recoveredimage = None # Solve Poisson equation for gradient elif method == 'TV': # 1. Solve TV minimization: min ||x||TV s.t. ||Sx - y||2 <= epsilon using NESTA solver # Tolerance = 1e-2 # (Source does not specify TV solver internals) recoveredimage = None # Solve TV minimization elif method == 'SS': # 1. Solve Least-Squares minimization with smoothness prior using Conjugate Gradient solver # Regularization parameter lambda = 1e-2 # (Source does not specify SS solver internals) recoveredimage = None # Solve least-squares minimization else: raise ValueError("Unknown method") return recoveredimage High Missing Pixel Rates: CS-Wavelet and CS-Gradient deteriorate quickly when the fraction of missing pixels is high. CS-Wavelet is particularly sensitive to pixel distribution; random distribution leads to strong speckling artifacts. Non-Smooth Images: TV and SS methods fail on images with high and low frequencies alike (e.g., synthetic textures). They cannot produce acceptable recovery even with 10% missing pixels if the image lacks smoothness. Blurring Sensitivity: CS-Wavelet requires careful tuning of the Gaussian blurring filter variance (\sigma), which must be adjusted case-by-case. Directional Artifacts: Low-Discrepancy (LD) distribution in CS-Wavelet can exhibit directional artifacts. Renders discrete gradient components instead of pixel values to exploit sparsity in the Fourier domain, then reconstructs the image using a Poisson solver. It differs from standard volume rendering by optimizing for gradient coefficients in the frequency domain rather than direct pixel intensities, allowing for reconstruction from fewer samples than the Nyquist rate. Treats the entire image as a single unit for inverse rendering recovery, solving for missing pixel values by running a solver over the full image domain simultaneously. It addresses the problem of recovering high-quality volumes from images with high missing pixel rates. Renders a full-resolution image by tracing rays for only a sparse subset of pixels and reconstructing the remaining pixels using an image representation model. It extends the two-step compressive rendering proposal by Sen and Darabi by replacing compressed sensing with a smoothness-based recovery approach. A regularized inverse problem solver for CT reconstruction that addresses sparse sampling and noise. It alternates between gradient descent on the data fidelity term and sparsity-promoting soft-thresholding in the Haar wavelet domain. It is a specific instance of ISTA adapted for tomographic geometry. Time Complexity: Depends on the solver. CS-Wavelet is the slowest because it requires evaluating forward and inverse DWT at every iteration. TV and CS-Gradient have comparable performance trends. SS is the fastest due to the efficiency of the least-squares solver. Memory Complexity: Requires storing the full image vector x (N pixels) and the sampling matrix S (M \times N). For 1200 \times 1200, N \approx 1.44 \times 10^6. Measured Performance: Head Dataset (600x600): 1754.92s recovery time. Head Dataset (900x900): 3955.13s. Head Dataset (1200x1200): 7067.32s. Engine Dataset (600x600): 1093.61s. Engine Dataset (900x900): 2442.28s. Engine Dataset (1200x1200): 4249.44s. GPU TV-L1: 30 FPS for 320x240 resolution using iterative conjugate gradient solver. Strengths: Smoothness-based methods (TV, SS) are more resilient to missing information than CS-based methods and produce high-quality recovery with as little as 20% of pixels. SS is sharper in boundary regions; TV preserves edges better. Limitations: Performance degrades with high missing pixel rates for CS methods. All methods struggle with non-smooth images. CS-Wavelet is sensitive to pixel distribution and blurring parameters. When to Use: Use TV or SS for general volume rendering where smoothness is expected and high missing pixel rates are acceptable. Use CS-Wavelet/Gradient only if strict sparsity priors are justified and pixel distribution can be controlled (LD preferred for CS-Wavelet, Random for CS-Gradient). Compressive Volume Rendering was initially proposed by Sen and Darabi [SD11] for compressive rendering, leveraging the theory of compressed sensing. The specific methods discussed (CS-Wavelet, CS-Gradient, TV, SS) were further explored and compared by Liu and Alim. The NESTA solver used for l1 minimization was introduced by Becker, Bobin, and Candès [BBC11]. The concept of using pixel shuffling based on Fibonacci numbers for distribution was introduced by Anderson [And93]. Least-squares linear systems have a long history of GPU acceleration [PF05]. name: Compressive Gradient Rendering
head: CS-Gradient, Compressed Sensing Gradient, Gradient Recovery via CS, Gradient-based Compressive Rendering
body: Compressive Gradient Rendering is a compressive volume rendering method that recovers high-quality images from sparse pixel samples by exploiting the sparsity of image gradients in the Discrete Fourier Transform (DFT) domain. Unlike sibling methods such as CS-Wavelet which suffer from coherence issues with random sampling, this approach renders discrete gradient components (x1, x2) instead of pixel values, solves an l1-minimization problem to recover the gradient's DFT, and reconstructs the image using a Poisson solver. It is distinguished by its use of the Fourier basis, which is inherently incoherent with point sampling, allowing for robust recovery when the fraction of missing pixels is moderate, though performance deteriorates significantly when missing pixels are high. Inputs: A set of m sampled pixel locations \Omega in an image of size N \times N (where m \ll N^2). The measured horizontal gradient values \mathbf{y}1 at these locations. The measured vertical gradient values \mathbf{y}2 at these locations. A reconstruction kernel basis (e.g., bilinear B-spline or Mitchell-Netravali cubic). Outputs: The reconstructed image \mathbf{x} of size N \times N. Data Structures: \mathbf{S}: The sensing matrix of size m \times N^2. It selects the m sampled locations. \mathbf{F}^{-1}: The inverse 2D Discrete Fourier Transform (DFT) matrix of size N^2 \times N^2. \hat{\mathbf{x}}1, \hat{\mathbf{x}}2: The 2D DFT coefficients of the horizontal and vertical gradient components, respectively. \mathbf{y}1, \mathbf{y}2: Measured gradient vectors of size m \times 1. Parameters: \epsilon: Tolerance for the l1-minimization solver. A typical value is 10^{-2}, providing a tradeoff between recovery quality and runtime. Kernel type: Bilinear B-spline or Mitchell-Netravali cubic. Steps: 1. Gradient Rendering: Render the horizontal gradient component x1 and vertical gradient component x2 from the volume data. This is achieved by differentiating the pixel reconstruction kernel used during ray casting. Alternatively, render the image using a box filter and apply a finite differencing scheme to obtain the gradients. 2. Sampling Gradients: Measure the horizontal gradient values at the m sampled locations \Omega to form the vector \mathbf{y}1. Similarly, measure the vertical gradient values to form \mathbf{y}2. 3. Formulate Sensing Model: The relationship between the measured gradients and the DFT of the gradients is given by \mathbf{y}1 = \mathbf{S}\mathbf{F}^{-1}\hat{\mathbf{x}}1 and \mathbf{y}2 = \mathbf{S}\mathbf{F}^{-1}\hat{\mathbf{x}}2. Here \mathbf{S} is the sampling matrix, \mathbf{F}^{-1} is the inverse 2D DFT matrix, and \hat{\mathbf{x}}1, \hat{\mathbf{x}}2 are the DFTs of the horizontal and vertical gradients. The matrix \mathbf{A} = \mathbf{S}\mathbf{F}^{-1} is a partial Fourier matrix with the Restricted Isometry Property (RIC) and low coherence with point sampling. 4. Recover Horizontal Gradient DFT (\hat{\mathbf{x}}1): Solve the l1-minimization problem to find the sparsest approximation of the horizontal gradient's DFT: \min \|\hat{\mathbf{x}}1\|1 \quad \text{subject to} \quad \|\mathbf{S}\mathbf{F}^{-1}\hat{\mathbf{x}}1 - \mathbf{y}1\|2 \leq \epsilon. This problem is typically solved using an iterative solver such as NESTA. 5. Recover Vertical Gradient DFT (\hat{\mathbf{x}}2): Solve the analogous l1-minimization problem for the vertical gradient. 6. Reconstruct Image via Poisson Solver: Recover the pixel values \mathbf{x} from the gradient components \hat{\mathbf{x}}1 and \hat{\mathbf{x}}2. Compute the inverse DFT of \hat{\mathbf{x}}1 and \hat{\mathbf{x}}2 to obtain the spatial gradient fields. Apply a Poisson solver with Dirichlet boundary conditions to the divergence of the gradient field to solve for \mathbf{x}. The approach follows Pérez et al. [PGB03]. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import numpy as np from scipy.fft import fft2, ifft2 from scipy.sparse import diags, kron, eye from scipy.sparse.linalg import spsolve def compressivegradientrendering(sampledindices, N, y1, y2, epsilon=1e-2): """ Reconstructs an image from sampled gradient measurements using Compressive Gradient Rendering. Args: sampledindices: Array of shape (m, 2) containing (row, col) indices of sampled pixels. N: Image resolution (N x N). y1: Horizontal gradient values at sampled locations (shape (m,)). y2: Vertical gradient values at sampled locations (shape (m,)). epsilon: Tolerance for l1 minimization. Returns: x: Reconstructed image of shape (N, N). """ m = len(sampledindices) # Gradient rendering is performed by differentiating the reconstruction kernel # or using a box filter with finite differencing. # y1 and y2 are assumed to be pre-computed from the volume data. # 1. Construct sensing matrix S (m x N^2) flatindices = sampledindices[:, 0] N + sampledindices[:, 1] S = np.zeros((m, N N)) for i in range(m): S[i, flatindices[i]] = 1.0 # 2. Solve l1 minimization for horizontal gradient DFT xhat1 = solvel1(S, N, y1, epsilon) # 3. Solve l1 minimization for vertical gradient DFT xhat2 = solvel1(S, N, y2, epsilon) # 4. Reconstruct image from gradients via Poisson solver gradx = np.real(ifft2(xhat1.reshape(N, N))) grady = np.real(ifft2(xhat2.reshape(N, N))) x = poissonsolver(gradx, grady, N) return x def solvel1(S, N, y, epsilon): """ Solves min ||xhat||1 s.t. ||S @ Finv @ xhat - y||2 <= epsilon using Iterative Soft-Thresholding Algorithm (ISTA). """ xhat = np.zeros(N N) stepsize = 1.0 # Lipschitz constant for S @ Finv is 1.0 maxiter = 1000 threshold = epsilon 0.1 # Heuristic threshold for sparsity for in range(maxiter): # Compute spatial gradient from DFT coefficients spatialgrad = np.real(ifft2(xhat.reshape(N, N))) # Compute residual: S @ spatialgrad - y residual = S @ spatialgrad.flatten() - y # Compute gradient of data fidelity: F @ S^T @ residual errorspatial = S.T @ residual grad = np.real(fft2(errorspatial.reshape(N, N))) # Proximal gradient step xhatnew = xhat - stepsize grad # Soft thresholding xhat = np.sign(xhatnew) np.maximum(np.abs(xhatnew) - threshold, 0) return xhat def poissonsolver(gradx, grady, N): """ Solves for x given horizontal gradient gradx and vertical gradient grady. Uses Dirichlet boundary conditions. """ # Compute divergence of the gradient field: div(g) = d(gx)/dx + d(gy)/dy divg = np.zeros((N, N)) # d(gx)/dx using central differences for interior, forward/backward for boundaries divg[:, 1:-1] += (gradx[:, 2:] - gradx[:,:-2]) / 2.0 divg[:, 0] = gradx[:, 1] - gradx[:, 0] divg[:, -1] = gradx[:, -1] - gradx[:, -2] # d(gy)/dy divg[1:-1,:] += (grady[2:,:] - grady[:-2,:]) / 2.0 divg[0,:] = grady[1,:] - grady[0,:] divg[-1,:] = grady[-1,:] - grady[-2,:] # Construct 2D Laplacian matrix (5-point stencil) e = np.ones(N) T = diags([-1, 2, -1], [-1, 0, 1], shape=(N, N), format='csr') A = kron(eye(N), T) + kron(T, eye(N)) # Apply Dirichlet BCs: remove boundary rows/columns interiorindices = [] for i in range(1, N - 1): for j in range(1, N - 1): interiorindices.append(i N + j) Ainterior = A[np.ix(interiorindices, interiorindices)] binterior = divg.flatten()[interiorindices] # Solve linear system xinterior = spsolve(Ainterior, binterior) # Reconstruct full image x = np.zeros((N, N)) for idx, flatidx in enumerate(interiorindices): x[flatidx // N, flatidx % N] = xinterior[idx] return x Edge Cases and Pitfalls: High Missing Pixel Fraction: Performance deteriorates quickly when the fraction of missing pixels is high. Boundary Conditions: The Poisson solver requires boundary conditions. Solver Tolerance: The tolerance \epsilon must be chosen carefully; 10^{-2} is recommended as a tradeoff between quality and runtime. Time Complexity: Dominated by the l1-minimization solver (e.g., NESTA) and the Poisson solver. The l1 minimization is iterative and scales with the number of samples m and image size N. Memory Complexity: Requires storage for the DFT coefficients (O(N^2)) and the sensing matrix operations. Measured Performance: The method shows improvement over CS-Wavelet and Sen and Darabi's approach [SD11] in terms of recovery quality for moderate missing pixel fractions. Strengths: Exploits sparsity in the Fourier domain, which is inherently incoherent with point sampling, avoiding the coherence issues of wavelet-based methods. Gradient components are often sparser in the Fourier domain than the image itself. Limitations: Deteriorates significantly with high percentages of missing pixels. Requires solving two l1-minimization problems and a Poisson solver, which can be computationally expensive. When to Use: Suitable for compressive volume rendering when the fraction of missing pixels is moderate and high coherence with the sampling basis is a concern. When Not to Use: When the fraction of missing pixels is very high, or when computational resources are limited and iterative solvers are prohibitive. Compressive Gradient Rendering was introduced as part of the broader field of Compressive Volume Rendering. It extends the idea of Sen and Darabi [SD11] by rendering gradient components instead of the image itself. The method leverages the Restricted Isometry Property (RIC) of random partial Fourier matrices, which are known to have low coherence with point sampling. The approach was developed to address coherence issues found in CS-Wavelet methods and to exploit the natural sparsity of gradients in the Fourier domain. The Poisson solver step follows the approach of Pérez et al. [PGB03]. The method is discussed in the context of tomographic reconstruction as inverse rendering and is a key component of Compressive Volume Rendering Recovery Methods. name: Laplacian Projection
head: Laplacian Regularization for Sparse View Reconstruction
body:
Laplacian Projection is a physics-based tomographic reconstruction method designed to recover volumetric properties, such as extinction coefficients, from sparse-view or single-view input data. It addresses the ill-posed nature of sparse-view reconstruction by enforcing smoothness on the spatial distribution of volume properties, specifically targeting smoke and spray imaging where limited angular data leads to noisy or artifact-ridden results. It distinguishes itself from standard Tikhonov regularization by directly penalizing the second-order spatial derivatives (curvature) of the volume field, thereby preserving sharp features better while suppressing high-frequency noise. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A set of N 2D projection images (views) of the volume. The method supports both single-view (N=1) and multi-view (N=16) configurations. Output: A 3D volume grid representing the reconstructed physical property (e.g., extinction coefficient). Data Structures: The volume is represented as a 3D grid. In the experimental setup, the resolution is 128 	imes 196 	imes 128. The state is typically optimized iteratively to minimize a cost function comprising a data fidelity term and a Laplacian regularization term. Method Steps: 1. Initialization: Initialize the 3D volume field V (e.g., with zeros or a prior estimate). 2. Forward Projection: Render the current volume estimate V to generate synthetic 2D projections P{syn} for each input view angle. This involves integrating the volume along rays, potentially using directional samples. The source notes that 30 directional samples are recommended as an optimal balance between accuracy and performance for pre-computation or rendering steps. 3. Error Calculation: Compute the difference between the synthetic projections P{syn} and the observed input views P{obs}. 4. Regularization Term Calculation: Compute the Laplacian of the volume field, 
abla^2 V. The Laplacian operator 
abla^2 is the sum of second-order partial derivatives with respect to spatial coordinates x, y, z: 
abla^2 V =  rac{\partial^2 V}{\partial x^2} +  rac{\partial^2 V}{\partial y^2} +  rac{\partial^2 V}{\partial z^2} This term penalizes curvature, enforcing smoothness. 5. Optimization Step: Update the volume field V by minimizing the combined cost function: E(V) = \| P{syn} - P{obs} \|^2 + \lambda \| 
abla^2 V \|^2 where \lambda is the regularization weight. The update can be performed using gradient-based optimization or projection-based iterative solvers. 6. Iteration: Repeat steps 2-5 until convergence or a maximum number of iterations is reached. The source investigates iteration limits of 250, 1000, and 5000 to analyze quality-efficiency trade-offs. Parameters: Number of views: 1 (single-view) or 16 (multi-view). Directional samples: 30 (recommended for optimal balance). Volume resolution: 128 	imes 196 	imes 128 (as used in experiments). Iteration limit: Variable (250, 1000, 5000 tested). Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Sparse views can lead to significant artifacts if regularization is too weak. Over-regularization may blur sharp features, though Laplacian projection is noted to preserve them better than Tikhonov methods. Precision issues may arise in the calculation of second-order derivatives on discrete grids. Time Complexity: Depends on the number of iterations and the cost of forward projection and Laplacian computation. The source notes that 30 directional samples are used for pre-computation, suggesting a fixed cost per iteration related to rendering. Memory Complexity: Proportional to the volume grid size (128 	imes 196 	imes 128) and the number of views. Performance: Evaluated on an NVIDIA GeForce RTX 2080 Ti GPU using the ScalarFlow dataset (300×531 pixels). It is described as state-of-the-art for physics-based smoke reconstruction. Strengths: Effective for sparse-view reconstruction; preserves sharp features better than Tikhonov regularization; suitable for smoke and spray imaging. Limitations: Performance depends on the choice of regularization parameter \lambda and iteration count; may be computationally intensive for high-resolution volumes or large numbers of views. When to use: When reconstructing volumetric media like smoke from limited angular data and preserving sharp features is important. When not to use: When high computational resources are unavailable or when the input data is dense and standard methods suffice. Laplacian Projection is a physics-based tomographic reconstruction technique that has been applied to smoke reconstruction, representing the state-of-the-art in this specific domain. It was evaluated against methods like 3D Gaussian Splatting and other physics-based approaches using the ScalarFlow dataset. The method leverages the physical properties of volumetric media to constrain the reconstruction problem, making it particularly effective for scenes with limited view angles. name: Laplacian Regularization
head: Laplacian Regularization for Sparse View Reconstruction
body: Laplacian Regularization is a physics-based tomographic reconstruction technique that enforces smoothness on the spatial distribution of volume properties (such as extinction coefficients) by penalizing their Laplacian. It addresses the ill-posed nature of sparse-view reconstruction, particularly in smoke and spray imaging, where limited angular data leads to noisy or artifact-ridden results. It distinguishes itself from standard Tikhonov regularization by directly penalizing the second-order spatial derivatives (curvature) of the volume field, thereby preserving sharp features better while suppressing high-frequency noise. Inputs: A set of N training view images I = \{Ii \in \mathbb{R}^M\}{i=1}^N. Associated camera poses P = \{\phii \in \mathbb{R}^{3 \times 4}\}{i=1}^N. A neural radiance field parameterized by \Theta, denoted F\Theta(p, \theta) = (g \circ f(p, \theta), h \circ f(p)), which outputs color c and density \sigma for a point p and direction \theta. Outputs: Optimized parameters \Theta that minimize the total loss, including the Laplacian regularization term. Data Structures: The volume is represented implicitly by the neural network F\Theta. The regularization is applied to the output density field \sigma\Theta(x) defined over the domain [-1, 1]^3. Formulas: The Laplacian regularization term R{Lap}(\Theta) is defined as the integral of the absolute Laplacian of the density field over the volume: R{Lap}(\Theta) = \int{[-1,1]^3} |\Deltax \sigma\Theta(x)| dx where \Delta = \text{div} \cdot \nabla is the Laplacian operator. In practice, this integral is approximated by a discrete sum over a 3D grid of resolution N \times N \times N with spacing \delta: R{Lap}(\Theta) \approx \sum{i=1}^N \sum{j=1}^N \sum{k=1}^N |\Deltax \sigma\Theta(\delta i, \delta j, \delta k)| \delta^3 where \sigma\Theta(\delta i, \delta j, \delta k) is the density value at grid point (\delta i, \delta j, \delta k). Steps: 1. Initialize training view images I and camera poses P. 2. Define the neural radiance field F\Theta mapping spatial coordinates and viewing directions to color and density. 3. For each training iteration: a. Cast rays through the scene using camera poses P. b. Sample points along rays and query F\Theta to obtain density \sigma\Theta and color c. c. Render the view and compute the photometric loss against ground truth images I. d. Compute the Laplacian regularization term R{Lap}(\Theta) by evaluating the density field on a 3D grid and calculating the discrete Laplacian magnitude. e. Update \Theta to minimize the combined loss (photometric + regularization). Parameters: Grid resolution N: Not given in the sources. Grid spacing \delta: Not given in the sources. Regularization weight: Not given in the sources. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: The discrete approximation assumes a uniform grid over [-1, 1]^3. Boundary conditions for the Laplacian calculation are not specified. The absolute value |\cdot| makes the term non-differentiable at zero, which may require subgradient methods or smoothing in implementation. Time Complexity: Depends on the number of grid points N^3 for regularization and the number of rays/samples for rendering. Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Requires storing the neural network parameters and potentially the 3D grid for regularization evaluation. Not given in the sources. Strengths: Improves continuity and generates smooth geometry representations, reducing severe noise compared to baselines. Limitations: Relies on the assumption that the volume field is smooth; may oversmooth sharp discontinuities if the weight is too high. Not given in the sources. name: Multi-parameter Regularization with Center-Axis Constraint
head: Multi-Parameter Regularized Inversion for Axisymmetric Tomography, Tikhonov with axis constraint
body: This method stabilizes the ill-posed inverse reconstruction of local extinction coefficients and radiative source terms from infrared radiance data in axisymmetric sprays. It combines a global second-order Tikhonov smoothness penalty with a specific center-axis constraint (zero-gradient condition) to suppress numerical artifacts near the symmetry axis that plague single-penalty Abel-type inversions. Unlike single regularization terms which cause artifacts near the axis, this multi-penalty model preserves physical features by utilizing regularization matrices with different null spaces. Inputs: Line-of-sight IR radiance measurements I{meas}. Differential Infrared Thermography (DIT) emissivity \epsilon{DIT}. Threshold for weakly radiating regions \epsilon{thresh}. Outputs: Local extinction coefficient \sigmaa(r). Local radiative source term S(r). Data Structures: Radial grid points ri for i = 1 \dots N, where r1 = 0 is the symmetry axis. Vectors \mathbf{\sigma}a and \mathbf{S} of size N. Regularization matrices \mathbf{R}1 (global smoothness) and \mathbf{R}2 (axis constraint). Step 1: Reconstruct Local Extinction Coefficient Use the DIT emissivity \epsilon{DIT} to reconstruct the local extinction coefficient \sigmaa(r). The DIT technique provides integrated emissivity, which is inverted to obtain attenuation information. Step 2: Formulate the Inverse Problem for Source Term The local radiative source term S(r) is recovered by solving the attenuated line-of-sight integral of the Radiative Transfer Equation (RTE). The problem is ill-posed and sensitive to measurement noise, particularly near the symmetry axis. Step 3: Apply Multi-Parameter Regularization Stabilize the inversion by minimizing an objective function that combines two penalty terms: 1. Global Smoothness Penalty: Second-order Tikhonov regularization to suppress high-frequency oscillations caused by measurement noise. 2. Center-Axis Constraint: A constraint imposing the zero-gradient condition \frac{\partial S}{\partial r} = 0 at r=0, required by axisymmetry. The objective function J to minimize is: J(\mathbf{S}) = \| \mathbf{A}\mathbf{S} - \mathbf{b} \|^2 + \lambda1 \| \mathbf{R}1 \mathbf{S} \|^2 + \lambda2 \| \mathbf{R}2 \mathbf{S} \|^2 Where: \mathbf{A} is the system matrix representing the line-of-sight integration operator. \mathbf{b} is the vector of measured radiance data. \mathbf{R}1 is the second-order difference matrix for global smoothness. \mathbf{R}2 is the matrix enforcing the zero-gradient condition at the axis. \lambda1 and \lambda2 are regularization parameters. Step 4: Boundary Masking Apply a mask based on \epsilon{DIT} to exclude weakly radiating regions below a prescribed threshold \epsilon{thresh}. This reduces boundary fluctuations that appear near the outer boundary where the extinction coefficient becomes small. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def multiparamregularization(radiancedata, ditemissivity, threshold): """ Reconstructs local source term S and extinction coefficient sigmaa using multi-parameter regularization with center-axis constraint. """ N = len(radiancedata) # Step 1: Reconstruct extinction coefficient from DIT # Note: Exact inversion formula for DIT to sigmaa is not provided in sources. # Assuming a standard inversion or lookup based on DIT emissivity. sigmaa = reconstructextinctionfromdit(ditemissivity) # Step 2: Construct system matrix A for the RTE line-of-sight integral # A[i, j] represents the path length contribution of radial bin j to measurement i. A = buildabelprojectionmatrix(radiancedata, sigmaa) b = radiancedata # Step 3: Construct regularization matrices # R1: Second-order Tikhonov (global smoothness) R1 = secondorderdifferencematrix(N) # R2: Center-axis constraint (zero-gradient at r=0) # Enforces S[0] - S[1] = 0 or similar discrete zero-gradient condition R2 = axisconstraintmatrix(N) # Step 4: Solve the regularized least squares problem # Minimize ||AS - b||^2 + lambda1 ||R1S||^2 + lambda2 ||R2S||^2 # This is equivalent to solving the normal equations: # (A^T A + lambda1 R1^T R1 + lambda2 R2^T R2) S = A^T b # Standard regularization parameters are not specified in sources. lambda1 = 1.0 # Placeholder value lambda2 = 1.0 # Placeholder value # Construct the combined system matrix # Using standard linear algebra operations. ATA = A.T @ A R1TR1 = R1.T @ R1 R2TR2 = R2.T @ R2 M = ATA + lambda1 R1TR1 + lambda2 R2TR2 rhs = A.T @ b # Solve for S S = solvelinearsystem(M, rhs) # Step 5: Apply boundary masking # Exclude regions where DIT emissivity is below threshold mask = ditemissivity > threshold S[~mask] = 0.0 # Or keep previous estimate, depending on implementation return S, sigmaa def secondorderdifferencematrix(N): """ Creates a matrix for second-order differences (smoothness penalty). """ R = zeros((N-2, N)) for i in range(N-2): R[i, i] = 1 R[i, i+1] = -2 R[i, i+2] = 1 return R def axisconstraintmatrix(N): """ Creates a matrix enforcing zero gradient at the axis (r=0). Assumes r[0] is the axis. """ R = zeros((1, N)) # Enforce S[0] - S[1] = 0 (zero first derivative approximation) # Or S[0] = S[1] R[0, 0] = 1 R[0, 1] = -1 return R Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Semi-convergence: Iterative techniques like ART suffer from slow convergence and semi-convergence, where the solution diverges as measurement noise is amplified. Boundary Fluctuations: Fluctuations appear near the outer boundary where the extinction coefficient becomes small, because the local radiance is obtained from the ratio of the radiative source term to the extinction coefficient. Axis Artifacts: Single global regularization terms cause numerical artifacts near the symmetry axis due to Abel-type inversion sensitivity. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Solving the linear system depends on the sparsity of the matrices and the solver used. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Depends on the size of the system matrix \mathbf{A} and regularization matrices. Strengths: Improves reconstruction near the axis without significantly influencing the overall radial distribution compared to single Tikhonov regularization. Suppresses high-frequency oscillations and non-physical artifacts near the symmetry axis. Limitations: Remaining fluctuations can still appear near the outer boundary where extinction is small. Requires careful selection of regularization parameters \lambda1 and \lambda2 (values not specified). When to use: For tomographic reconstruction of IR radiance from axisymmetric sprays in hot environments, particularly when high accuracy near the symmetry axis is required and measurement noise is present. When not to use: For non-axisymmetric flows where the center-axis constraint is invalid. The method was introduced to address the limitations of single-penalty regularization in axisymmetric spray tomography. It builds on the concept that multi-penalty models with different null spaces can preserve various physical features of the target. The framework combines Differential Infrared Thermography (DIT) with multi-parameter regularized inversion to directly solve the Radiative Transfer Equation (RTE). Numerical phantom studies, including configurations relevant to evaporating cold sprays and flashing jets, demonstrated the method's accuracy under well-defined conditions and noisy measurement scenarios. name: Global Solver
body: The Global Solver is a compressive volume rendering reconstruction method that treats the entire image as a single unit for inverse rendering recovery. It solves for missing pixel values by running a solver over the full image domain simultaneously, contrasting with block-based partitioning strategies. It addresses the problem of recovering high-quality volumes from images with high missing pixel rates. Inputs and Outputs: Input: volume rendering image with missing pixels. Output: reconstructed full-resolution image. Data Structures: The method operates on the entire image matrix as a single entity without partitioning it into blocks. Steps: 1. Initialize the solver for the entire image domain. 2. Set the iteration parameter, which can be fixed to a constant value or controlled via a flag to run until a desired solution is reached. 3. Execute the iterative solver loop. 4. Inside the loop, perform the convolution process, identified as the most time-consuming operation. 5. Update the image data iteratively until the fixed iteration count is met or the convergence flag indicates a desired solution is arrived at. Parameters: Number of iterations: Affects solver performance; can be fixed or set via a flag to run multiple times until a desired solution is arrived at. Pitfalls: FFT-based convolution overhead: Using Fast Fourier Transform (FFT) for convolution causes memory to be copied back and forth from CPU to GPU for each iteration, resulting in very slow reconstruction time. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def globalsolver(image, missingmask, maxiterations=None, convergenceflag=False): """Reconstructs the entire image globally with the solver running the entire image at once.""" currentimage = image.copy() if convergenceflag: # Allow the solver to run multiple times until it arrives at a desired solution while not checkconvergence(currentimage, missingmask): currentimage = updateimage(currentimage, missingmask) else: # Fixed number of iterations parameter for in range(maxiterations): currentimage = updateimage(currentimage, missingmask) return currentimage def updateimage(image, missingmask): # Perform convolution process, which is the most time-consuming operation # Using FFT-based convolution causes memory to be copied back and forth from CPU to GPU for each iteration # Apply standard convolution operation to the image matrix convolved = applystandardconvolution(image) # Update missing pixels while preserving known pixels updated = image.copy() updated[missingmask] = convolved[missingmask] return updated def checkconvergence(image, missingmask): # Check if the solver has arrived at a desired solution # Compare residual or error against a threshold return True def applystandardconvolution(image): # Standard convolution operation # In practice, this applies a kernel to the image matrix return image # Placeholder for actual convolution logic A parallel implementation that partitions the image into mutually exclusive blocks to reduce global memory access and improve performance using shared memory. It differs from the Global Solver by processing blocks independently, allowing for different numbers of iterations per block based on local convergence criteria. Time Complexity: High, as the convolution process is the most time-consuming operation. Memory Access: Inefficient when using FFT-based convolution due to frequent CPU/GPU memory transfers. Measured Performance: Reconstruction time of approximately 124 milliseconds (about 10 frames per second) when 60% of pixels are missing (40% present). The global solver takes 119 milliseconds using only 60% pixels. Scaling: Not well suited for interactivity due to the high reconstruction time. Strengths: Provides a global solution for the entire image, maintaining consistency across the full domain. Limitations: Very slow reconstruction time compared to local solvers; for example, the Local Solver takes 5.6 milliseconds for the same task, making it 24 times faster. When to use: When global consistency is prioritized over speed and interactivity is not required. When not to use: When interactive frame rates are needed. The Global Solver was proposed in a thesis on GPU-based compressive volume rendering as one of two parallel approaches to reconstruction, the other being the Local Solver. It builds on gradient solver techniques previously demonstrated by Liu and Alim et al., who measured reconstruction times using a CPU. The method was developed to address the limitations of CPU-based reconstruction and to provide a baseline for comparing block-based optimizations.
