name: Differential Infrared Thermography (DIT)
head: DIT thermography
body: Differential Infrared Thermography (DIT) is a technique used to estimate the transmittance (e^{-\delta{max}}) of a transmissive target from the Radiative Transfer Equation (RTE) to avoid the direct inversion of the ill-posed integral source term. It simplifies the 3-D spray structure as a thin slab layer to measure the local attenuation coefficient by comparing measurements with two different radiating backgrounds, assuming the target's temperature/radiance remains constant between measurements. It sets itself apart from full volumetric tomography by providing an effective apparent temperature and total optical depth (TOD) without resolving the internal line-of-sight distribution, serving as a preprocessing step to recover the local extinction coefficient for subsequent RTE solving. Inputs and Outputs Inputs: Two raw IR images of the spray field: I{meas,1} and I{meas,2}. Two corresponding background radiance images (chamber radiation without spray): I{bg,1} and I{bg,2}. Assumption: The spray field remains statistically consistent (local attenuation coefficient and source term are identical) between the two measurements. Outputs: Integrated slab emissivity \varepsilon{DIT}(x). Total Optical Depth (TOD) \delta{max}(x). Local extinction coefficient profile \alpha(r) (via Abel inversion). Effective DIT radiance I{DIT} and associated temperature. Data Structures Images: 2D arrays of radiance values. Discretized Spray Cross-Section: Represented as concentric rings indexed by j. Geometric Kernel Matrix K: A matrix where element K{ij} corresponds to the path length of the i-th ray passing through the j-th concentric ring. Vectors: \Delta: Vector of known Total Optical Depths (TOD) derived from \delta{max}(x). A: Unknown vector of radial extinction coefficients \alpha(r). Formulas The Radiative Transfer Equation (RTE) relating measured radiance to local properties is: I{meas} = I{bg} e^{-\delta{max}} + \int{0}^{S{max}} j(s) e^{-\delta(s)} ds Where: I{meas} is observed radiance. I{bg} is background radiance. j(s) is the local emission source term. s is the coordinate along the ray path of total length S{max} (background at s=0, detector at s=S{max}). \delta(s) is the local optical depth (LOD), i.e., cumulative attenuation from position s to the detector. \delta{max} is the total optical depth (TOD) of the medium along the entire line of sight. Under the thin slab approximation, the integral term reduces, and the measured images are expressed as: I{meas,1}(x) = I{bg,1} (1 - \varepsilon{DIT}(x)) + \varepsilon{DIT}(x) I{DIT}(x) \quad (13a) I{meas,2}(x) = I{bg,2} (1 - \varepsilon{DIT}(x)) + \varepsilon{DIT}(x) I{DIT}(x) \quad (13b) The integrated spray emissivity \varepsilon{DIT} is calculated from the four measured images: \varepsilon{DIT}(x) = \frac{I{meas,2} - I{meas,1}}{I{bg,2} - I{bg,1}} \quad (14) The maximum optical depth \delta{max}(x) is determined from the emissivity using the Beer-Lambert law approximation: \delta{max}(x) = -\ln(1 - \varepsilon{DIT}(x)) \quad (12b) Under the assumption of axisymmetry, the total optical depth \delta{max}(x) is the Abel transform of the local extinction-coefficient profile \alpha(r): \delta{max}(x) = 2 \int{x}^{r{max}} \frac{\alpha(r) r}{\sqrt{r^2 - x^2}} dr \quad (16) The continuous integral is approximated by a finite sum in linear algebraic form: \Delta = K A \quad (17) Where \Delta is the vector of TOD, A is the unknown vector of radial extinction coefficient \alpha(r), and K is the geometric kernel matrix. Steps 1. Acquire two raw IR images of the spray, I{meas,1} and I{meas,2}, corresponding to two different background conditions I{bg,1} and I{bg,2}, while ensuring the spray field remains statistically consistent. 2. Acquire background images I{bg,1} and I{bg,2} (chamber radiation without spray). 3. Calculate the integrated slab emissivity \varepsilon{DIT}(x) for each pixel/position x using Equation (14). 4. Calculate the Total Optical Depth (TOD) \delta{max}(x) using Equation (12b). 5. Discretize the spray cross-section into concentric rings. Construct the geometric kernel matrix K where K{ij} is the path length of the i-th ray through the j-th ring. 6. Solve the linear system \Delta = K A for the unknown vector A (radial extinction coefficient \alpha(r)). 7. (Optional/Contextual) Calculate the DIT radiance I{DIT} from Eq. (13a) or (13b) and convert to temperature. Pseudocode Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import numpy as np from scipy.special import erf # Placeholder for Abel inversion solver if not using linear algebra directly def computeditemissivity(Imeas1, Imeas2, Ibg1, Ibg2): """ Computes the integrated slab emissivity epsilonDIT from four images. """ # Equation 14 epsilonDIT = (Imeas2 - Imeas1) / (Ibg2 - Ibg1) return epsilonDIT def computetotalopticaldepth(epsilonDIT): """ Computes the maximum optical depth deltamax from emissivity. """ # Equation 12b # Guard against log(0) or log(negative) due to noise epsilonclamped = np.clip(epsilonDIT, 0, 1 - 1e-6) deltamax = -np.log(1 - epsilonclamped) return deltamax def abelinversionlinear(deltamaxvector, geometry): """ Solves for radial extinction coefficient alpha(r) using the linear algebraic form of the Abel transform. Parameters: deltamaxvector: 1D array of TOD values for each ray position x. geometry: Object or matrix K containing path lengths. Returns: alphavector: 1D array of radial extinction coefficients alpha(r). """ # Construct geometric kernel matrix K # Kij corresponds to the path length of the i-th ray passing through the j-th concentric ring. # This requires knowledge of the discretization of the spray cross-section into concentric rings. K = geometry.constructkernelmatrix() # Equation 17: Delta = K A # Solve for A (alpha vector) # Note: This system may be ill-conditioned; regularization might be required in practice. # Using least squares or pseudo-inverse if K is not square or invertible. alphavector = np.linalg.lstsq(K, deltamaxvector, rcond=None)[0] return alphavector def rundit(Imeas1, Imeas2, Ibg1, Ibg2, geometry): """ Full DIT pipeline. """ # Step 1 & 2: Inputs are already acquired # Step 3: Calculate emissivity epsilonDIT = computeditemissivity(Imeas1, Imeas2, Ibg1, Ibg2) # Step 4: Calculate TOD deltamax = computetotalopticaldepth(epsilonDIT) # Step 5 & 6: Invert Abel transform to get extinction coefficient alphar = abelinversionlinear(deltamax, geometry) return epsilonDIT, deltamax, alphar Parameters Background Variation: The two background conditions must be sufficiently different to ensure numerical stability in the division (I{bg,2} - I{bg,1}). Statistical Consistency: The spray structure must not change significantly between the two measurements. Edge Cases and Pitfalls Effective Temperature: DIT temperature does not represent local spray temperature because the 3-D structure is simplified as a thin slab. It represents an effective apparent temperature associated with the region where the Local Optical Depth (LOD) is of the order of unity, based on the Eddington–Barbier approximation. Optically Thick Cold Vapor: For optically thick cold vapor sprays in a warm environment, the DIT temperature is an effective temperature associated mainly with the outer spray region where the line-of-sight depth (LOD) is of the order of unity. Uncertainty from Drift: If the spray structure or chamber radiation changes significantly between the two DIT measurements, the estimated emissivity and subsequent reconstruction contain additional uncertainty. Scattering: The method neglects scattering effects produced by dispersed sprays. Time Complexity: The core DIT calculation (emissivity and TOD) is O(N) where N is the number of pixels. The Abel inversion via linear algebra is O(M^3) or O(M^2) depending on the solver, where M is the number of radial rings. Memory Complexity: O(N) for images, O(M^2) for the kernel matrix K. Strengths: Avoids direct inversion of the ill-posed integral source term of the RTE. Provides a robust estimate of the extinction coefficient profile which is a prerequisite for solving the full RTE. Limitations: Cannot recover internal radiance or temperature distribution of optically thick sprays on its own. The "temperature" is an effective value, not a local physical temperature. Sensitive to temporal variations in the spray or background between the two acquisitions. When to use: When estimating the extinction coefficient profile for axisymmetric sprays to enable subsequent RTE solving, and when the spray is statistically stable over the acquisition time of the two frames. When not to use: When local temperature distribution is required directly, or when the spray is highly dynamic/non-axisymmetric. Differential Infrared Thermography (DIT) was originally used in spray studies to avoid direct inversion of the ill-posed integral term of the RTE. Key references include Lamanna et al. (2013) and Golzke et al. (2016). The technique assumes that attenuation is caused exclusively by particles (originally soot, but applied to sprays with micrometer-scale droplets) and relies on the Eddington–Barbier approximation for interpreting the resulting temperature. It is often used as a component of a larger tomographic reconstruction pipeline where the extinction coefficient derived from DIT is used to solve for the local source term. Tomographic Reconstruction of Infrared Radiance from Axisymmetric Sprays in a Hot Environment Using Multi-Parameter Regularization, https://doi.org/10.21203/rs.3.rs-10907544/v1, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial)

name: Differential Rendering for CT Reconstruction
head: Differentiable Rendering for CT Reconstruction, Differentiable Volume Rendering Reconstruction, Gradient-based Volumetric Reconstruction, Inverse Rendering for CT, Iterative Differential CT
body: Differential Rendering for CT Reconstruction is an inverse rendering technique that reconstructs the volumetric absorption coefficients of an object from a series of 2D X-ray projection images by optimizing scene parameters via gradient descent. It formulates Computed Tomography (CT) as an iterative optimization problem where the Mean Squared Error (MSE) between differentially rendered images and reference projections is minimized. Unlike traditional algebraic reconstruction techniques or deep learning-based methods, this approach relies on fully auto-differentiable rendering engines to compute gradients directly from the rendering equation, allowing for end-to-end optimization without pre-trained models. It sets itself apart from siblings like DiffVox by utilizing a specific multi-view iterative rotation strategy with fixed 45° steps and ADAM optimization. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: Reference projection images (Ground Truth) acquired at various rotation angles; initial scene parameters \pi including rotation angle and volume data \sigma; optimization hyperparameters (N{rot}, N{iter}, LR, \beta1, \beta2, \epsilon). Outputs: Optimized 3D volume data (absorption coefficient matrix \sigma). Data Structures: Voxel Grid: A 3D grid representation of the object, specifically a 16 \times 16 \times 16 grid. Absorption Coefficient (\sigma): A scalar value per voxel. Value 1 means fully absorbing; 0 means no absorption. Non-zero values (10^{-4}) are assigned if surface data is present in the bounding box subdivision. Scene Parameters (\pi): Contains the current rotation angle and the current state of the volume data \sigma. Update Buffer (\sigma{update}): A non-absorbing matrix (volume data) used to update the scene parameters. Initialized to zero in the first run. Mathematical Formulation: The core principle is differentiating the rendering function with respect to the absorption coefficient matrix \pi0 (representing \sigma): \frac{\partial}{\partial \pi0} \iint f(x, y; \pi) \, dx \, dy = \frac{\partial Ii}{\partial \pi0} Where: \pi0 is the absorption coefficient matrix of the volumetric object. f(x, y; \pi) is the rendering function mapping scene parameters to image coordinates. Ii is the pixel value in the rendered image. Algorithm Steps: 1. Initialize: Set N{rot} (number of 45° rotations) and N{iter} (iterations per rotation). Initialize the absorption coefficient parameter matrix \pi0 with constant entries (e.g., 0 or 0.001). 2. Loop over Rotations (i from 0 to N{rot}-1): a. Calculate Angle: Compute rotation angle as (i \times 45.0) \pmod{360}. b. Load Scene: Create scene object using parameters \pi and current rotation. c. Render Reference: Forward render the scene to create the target image (I{ref}). d. Initialize Update Buffer: If \sigma{update} is null, initialize it as a zero-filled array matching the length of the reference volume \sigma data. e. Update Volume: Apply \sigma{update} to the scene volume parameters. f. Loop over Iterations (j from 0 to N{iter}-1): i. Differential Render: Render the scene using the differentiable renderer to get the current image (I{curr}) and compute gradients. ii. Calculate Loss: Compute MSE between I{curr} and I{ref}: L = \frac{1}{N} \sum{k=1}^{N} (I{curr, k} - I{ref, k})^2 iii. Backpropagate: Compute gradients of the loss with respect to scene parameters (\frac{\partial L}{\partial \pi}). iv. Gradient Step: Update parameters using the ADAM optimizer. g. Update Buffer: After the iteration loop, update \sigma{update} with the optimized \sigma data from the scene volume. 3. Convergence: Repeat until N{rot} rotations are complete or convergence is reached (no further changes in scene parameters). Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def differentialctreconstruction(Nrot, Niter, initialsigma, lr, beta1, beta2, epsilon): """ Reconstructs volumetric data using differential rendering. Args: Nrot: Number of 45-degree rotations (e.g., 40 for 360 degrees). Niter: Number of optimization iterations per rotation (e.g., 40). initialsigma: Initial absorption coefficient matrix (e.g., zeros or 0.001). lr: Learning rate for ADAM (0.002). beta1: ADAM beta1 (0.9). beta2: ADAM beta2 (0.99). epsilon: ADAM epsilon (1e-8). Returns: Optimized sigma volume. """ sigma = initialsigma.copy() sigmaupdate = None # ADAM state variables m = np.zeroslike(sigma) v = np.zeroslike(sigma) t = 1 for i in range(Nrot): rotationangle = (i 45.0) % 360.0 # Construct scene geometry, camera, detector, and volume buffer scene = createscene(sigma, rotationangle) # Render image without gradient tracking imageref = forwardrender(scene) if sigmaupdate is None: sigmaupdate = np.zeroslike(sigma) scene.volume.sigma = sigmaupdate for j in range(Niter): # Render image and compute gradients w.r.t scene.volume.sigma imagecurr = differentialrender(scene) loss = mean((imagecurr - imageref) 2) # Backpropagate loss through the computational graph gradients = computegradients(loss, scene.volume.sigma) # ADAM update step m = beta1 m + (1 - beta1) gradients v = beta2 v + (1 - beta2) (gradients 2) mhat = m / (1 - beta1 t) vhat = v / (1 - beta2 t) sigma = scene.volume.sigma - lr mhat / (np.sqrt(vhat) + epsilon) scene.volume.sigma = sigma t += 1 sigmaupdate = scene.volume.sigma.copy() return sigmaupdate def createscene(sigma, rotationangle): # Standard operation: constructs scene geometry, camera, detector, and volume buffer return {'volume': {'sigma': sigma}, 'rotation': rotationangle} def forwardrender(scene): # Standard operation: renders image without gradient tracking return render(scene, requiresgrad=False) def differentialrender(scene): # Standard operation: renders image and computes gradients w.r.t scene.volume.sigma return render(scene, requiresgrad=True) def computegradients(loss, params): # Standard operation: backpropagates loss through the computational graph return loss.backward(params) def zeroslike(tensor): # Standard operation: creates a tensor of zeros with the same shape return np.zeroslike(tensor) def mean(tensor): # Standard operation: computes arithmetic mean return np.mean(tensor) def sqrt(tensor): # Standard operation: computes element-wise square root return np.sqrt(tensor) Parameters: Learning Rate (LR): 0.002. Beta1 (\beta1): 0.9. Beta2 (\beta2): 0.99. Epsilon (\epsilon): 10^{-8}. Nrot: 40 (covering 360° in 45° steps). Niter: 40 iterations per rotation. Resolution: 256x256 pixels. Sample Count: 10 samples per pixel. Initial Absorption Coefficient: 0.001 (for reference) or 0 (for optimization start). Edge Cases and Pitfalls: High GPU Memory Usage: Auto-differential volume rendering requires significant GPU memory. High resolutions or sample counts cause out-of-memory errors. Mitigation: Use lower resolution (256x256) and sample count (10). Noise in Reference Images: Noise in forward-rendered reference images propagates into the optimized volume, causing "noise clouds". Edge Artifacts: Undesired clouds around volume edges may be caused by interpolation algorithms or reference image noise. Loss Spikes at Rotation Start: The MSE loss function shows descending spikes at the start of each new 45° rotation during the first full 360° because the full geometry is not yet known to the optimizer. Convergence Threshold: The loss function converges around an MSE of 0.0010 after the first full rotation. Time Complexity: The method is iterative and computationally expensive. Total reconstruction time can exceed 15 hours for 40 rotations and 40 iterations per rotation on an Nvidia RTX 3090. The mean time per 45° rotation is 23.441 minutes. Memory Complexity: High GPU memory usage (>90% utilization) due to the storage of gradients and intermediate rendering states for auto-differentiation. This limits the feasible resolution and sample count. Performance: On an AMD Ryzen 9 3950X and Nvidia RTX 3090, the algorithm is slow but produces reliable results. Strengths: Works without pre-trained models; leverages existing differentiable rendering engines (e.g., Mitsuba 2); provides a proof-of-concept for inverse rendering in CT. Limitations: High memory consumption limits resolution; noisy reference images degrade reconstruction quality; slow convergence; sensitive to initial geometric assumptions during early rotations. When to Use: Suitable for proof-of-concept demonstrations, small-scale volumetric reconstruction where high precision is not critical, or when traditional reconstruction methods fail due to complex lighting/material interactions that can be modeled in a differentiable renderer. When Not to Use: For large-scale clinical CT scans requiring high resolution and speed; when GPU memory is constrained; when reference images are extremely noisy. The method was implemented using the Mitsuba 2 framework and a specific fork (master @f4bc83c68f). It builds upon the work of Zhao et al. [ZJL20] for mathematical insights into differentiable volume rendering and Hochhauser et al. [Hoc22] for X-ray spectrum rendering. The approach is part of the broader field of differentiable rendering, which seeks to make rendering pipelines differentiable with respect to scene parameters, enabling inverse problems like shape and material estimation. Differential Rendering for Computed Tomography, https://www.cg.tuwien.ac.at/research/publications/2022/Vucenovic2022/Vucenovic2022-Bachelor%20thesis.pdf, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial)

name: DiffVox
head: Differentiable Voxel-based X-ray Rendering
body: DiffVox is a self-supervised framework for Cone-Beam Computed Tomography (CBCT) reconstruction that directly optimizes a discrete voxel grid representation using physics-based differentiable X-ray rendering. It solves the sparse-view reconstruction problem by parameterizing the unknown volume as a voxel grid and using differentiable forward models (Siddon's method or trilinear interpolation) to render 2D projections, enabling gradient-based optimization of the 3D volume. Unlike traditional iterative methods that suffer from sparse-view artifacts or neural field approaches that are computationally prohibitive, DiffVox achieves high-quality reconstructions with significantly faster runtimes. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: A set of N 2D X-ray projection images (ground truth intensities I\mu) with known acquisition geometry (source and detector positions). The number of views N is typically sparse (e.g., 5–60 views). Outputs: A reconstructed 3D voxel grid \hat{\mu} of linear attenuation coefficients (LACs). Data Structures: Voxel Grid \hat{\mu}: A 3D tensor of dimensions Dx \times Dy \times Dz representing the volume. In experiments, this is 501 \times 501 \times 501 with isotropic spacing of 0.1 mm. The values represent unactivated LACs. Ray Set \mathcal{R}: A set of photon beams sampled from the projection images. Each ray \vec{r} is defined by its origin, direction, and the corresponding ground truth intensity I\mu(\vec{r}). Algorithm Steps: 1. Initialization: Initialize the voxel grid \hat{\mu} with zeros. Alternatively, it can be initialized with an estimate from Nesterov or SIRT to reduce runtime. 2. Activation: Apply the Softplus activation function to \hat{\mu} prior to rendering to ensure non-negative LACs, as physical attenuation coefficients must be non-negative. \mu{\text{active}} = \text{Softplus}(\hat{\mu}, \beta) where \beta = 20. 3. Ray Sampling: Randomly sample a batch of rays \mathcal{R} from all available projection images without replacement, using uniform probability. The batch size is limited by GPU memory (e.g., |\mathcal{R}| = 5.5 \times 10^5 for Siddon's method, 1.8 \times 10^6 for trilinear interpolation). 4. Differentiable Forward Rendering: Compute the rendered intensities I{\hat{\mu}}(\vec{r}) for each ray in the batch using one of two differentiable forward models: Siddon's Method: Computes the exact line integral through the voxel grid according to the discrete Beer-Lambert law. Trilinear Interpolation: Approximates the volume density at ray points using trilinear interpolation, effectively allowing non-intersected voxels to influence the pixel intensity. For this method, M=500 points are sampled per ray. 5. Loss Calculation: Compute the total loss \mathcal{L} using the photometric loss (L1 norm) and Total Variation (TV) regularization: \mathcal{L}(\hat{\mu}) = \frac{1}{|\mathcal{R}|} \sum{\vec{r} \in \mathcal{R}} \|I{\mu}(\vec{r}) - I{\hat{\mu}}(\vec{r})\|1 + \lambda{\text{TV}} \text{TV}(\hat{\mu}) where \lambda{\text{TV}} = 25 for Siddon's method and \lambda{\text{TV}} = 15 for trilinear interpolation. 6. Optimization: Update \hat{\mu} using the Adam optimizer with an initial learning rate of 1, linearly decaying to 0 over 50 iterations. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import torch import torch.nn.functional as F def softplus(x, beta=20): """Applies Softplus activation to ensure non-negative LACs.""" return F.softplus(x, beta=beta) def computetv(volume): """Computes Total Variation regularization term.""" diffx = torch.abs(volume[:, 1:,:,:] - volume[:,:-1,:,:]) diffy = torch.abs(volume[:,:, 1:,:] - volume[:,:,:-1,:]) diffz = torch.abs(volume[:,:,:, 1:] - volume[:,:,:,:-1]) return torch.sum(diffx) + torch.sum(diffy) + torch.sum(diffz) def samplerays(projectionindices, geometry, batchsize): """Uniformly samples rays without replacement from available projections.""" numavailable = len(projectionindices) if batchsize > numavailable: batchsize = numavailable indices = torch.randperm(numavailable)[:batchsize] rays = geometry.rays[indices] gtintensities = geometry.gtintensities[indices] return rays, gtintensities def rendersiddon(volume, rays, sourcepos, detectorpos): """Siddon's method: computes exact line integrals through the voxel grid.""" # Standard differentiable Siddon implementation: # 1. Compute ray-voxel grid intersections # 2. Accumulate mu pathlength for intersected voxels # 3. Apply Beer-Lambert law: I = I0 exp(-accumulation) # Returns rendered intensities (batchsize,) accumulation = torch.zeros(rays.shape[0], device=rays.device) #... standard autograd-compatible Siddon grid traversal... # Implementation uses exact ray-marching kernels rendered = torch.exp(-accumulation) return rendered def rendertrilinear(volume, rays, sourcepos, detectorpos, M=500): """Trilinear interpolation: samples M points along each ray and integrates.""" t = torch.linspace(0, 1, M, device=rays.device).unsqueeze(0) points = rays[:,:3].unsqueeze(1) + t rays[:, 3:6].unsqueeze(1) # Trilinear interpolation at points values = F.gridsample(volume.unsqueeze(0), points.unsqueeze(1), mode='bilinear', aligncorners=False).squeeze() # Integrate along ray pathlength = 1.0 / M accumulation = torch.sum(values pathlength, dim=1) rendered = torch.exp(-accumulation) return rendered def diffvoxreconstruction(projections, geometry, numiters=50, lambdatv=15.0): """Main DiffVox reconstruction loop.""" # 1. Initialize voxel grid with zeros volume = torch.zeros((501, 501, 501), requiresgrad=True) # 2. Setup Adam optimizer optimizer = torch.optim.Adam([volume], lr=1.0) # 3. Optimization loop for i in range(numiters): # Linearly decay learning rate to 0 over 50 iterations currentlr = 1.0 (1 - i / numiters) for paramgroup in optimizer.paramgroups: paramgroup['lr'] = currentlr # 3.1 Sample rays rays, gtintensities = samplerays(projectionindices, geometry, batchsize=550000) # 3.2 Forward pass (Trilinear example) renderedintensities = rendertrilinear(volume, rays, geometry.source, geometry.detector, M=500) # 3.3 Compute Loss # L1 photometric loss l1loss = torch.mean(torch.abs(gtintensities - renderedintensities)) # Total Variation regularization tvloss = computetv(volume) # Combined loss loss = l1loss + lambdatv tvloss # 3.4 Backward pass optimizer.zerograd() loss.backward() optimizer.step() return volume Parameters: Softplus \beta: 20. Adam Learning Rate: Initial 1, linearly decaying to 0 over 50 iterations. TV Regularization Weight (\lambda{\text{TV}}): 25 for Siddon's method, 15 for trilinear interpolation. Trilinear Sampling Points (M): 500 points per ray. Batch Size: Limited by GPU memory; 5.5 \times 10^5 rays for Siddon, 1.8 \times 10^6 for trilinear. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Overfitting with Siddon's Method: Siddon's method exactly computes line integrals, which can lead to overfitting in sparse-view settings because it does not allow ground truth pixels to supervise non-intersected voxels. Mitigation via Trilinear Interpolation: Trilinear interpolation mitigates overfitting by approximating second-order effects (like scatter) and allowing rendered pixel intensities to be influenced by voxels not directly intersected by the ray, providing self-supervision to more voxels. Initialization: Initializing with zeros is standard, but initializing with Nesterov or SIRT estimates can reduce runtime. Time Complexity: DiffVox is an order of magnitude faster than neural field methods (e.g., SAX-NeRF, NAF). Memory Complexity: Depends on the voxel grid resolution (501^3 in experiments) and batch size of rays. Measured Performance: On a single NVIDIA RTX A6000 GPU, for 60-view reconstruction: DiffVox (Siddon): 45.1 minutes. DiffVox (Trilinear): 39.1 minutes. SAX-NeRF: 10.3 hours. NAF: 30.6 hours. Nesterov (traditional): \le 5 minutes. Quality: DiffVox outperforms baselines in SSIM, PSNR, PCC, and MSE for sparse views (\le 20). For 30-60 views, SAX-NeRF achieves higher PSNR than DiffVox. Siddon's method achieves higher accuracy than trilinear interpolation but with moderately increased runtime. Strengths: High-quality reconstructions in sparse-view regimes (\le 20 views), fast convergence, ability to use well-validated reconstruction algorithms for initialization. Limitations: Slower than traditional iterative methods (e.g., Nesterov \le 5 min) for all view counts; Siddon's method prone to overfitting in sparse settings without sufficient TV regularization. DiffVox was presented in a paper by Mohammadhossein Momeni, Vivek Gopalakrishnan, Neel Dey, Polina Golland, and Sarah Frisken from Brigham and Women's Hospital and MIT CSAIL. It builds on Siddon's method (1985), Total Variation regularization (1992), and the Adam optimizer (2015). It is used for CBCT reconstruction from sparse X-ray views, particularly in regimes where traditional and neural methods fail (\le 20 views). name: Shape from Projections via Differentiable Forward Projector
head: CTDR, Differentiable Forward Projector for CT
body: This method estimates 3D shapes represented by a triangular mesh directly from tomographic projection data. It treats tomographic reconstruction as a rendering process, extending a differentiable rasterizer to optimize the 3D geometry. Unlike volumetric approaches, it operates directly on surface meshes, distinguishing it from volumetric differentiable renderers like DiffVox or emissivity-based methods like EmissivityRenderer. Inputs: A 3D triangular mesh (vertices and faces). Tomographic projection data (2D sinograms or projection images). Projection geometry parameters (source position, detector position, orientation). Outputs: Optimized 3D triangular mesh that minimizes the difference between simulated projections and input data. Data Structures: Mesh: List of vertices (3D coordinates) and faces (indices into vertices). Projections: 2D arrays representing intensity values. Geometry: Parameters defining the X-ray source and detector for each view. Steps: 1. Initialization: Start with an initial guess of the 3D mesh. 2. Forward Projection: For each view, simulate the projection of the current mesh through the X-ray geometry. This involves calculating the path length of rays through the mesh triangles. 3. Loss Calculation: Compare the simulated projections with the input tomographic data. Compute a loss function (e.g., Mean Squared Error). 4. Backpropagation: Compute gradients of the loss with respect to the mesh vertices using the differentiable forward projector. 5. Optimization: Update the mesh vertices using an optimizer (e.g., Adam) to minimize the loss. 6. Iteration: Repeat steps 2-5 until convergence or a maximum number of iterations is reached. Formulas: Loss: L = \sum{i} (P{sim}^{(i)} - P{true}^{(i)})^2 where P{sim} is the simulated projection and P{true} is the true projection. Gradient: \frac{\partial L}{\partial V} where V are the mesh vertices. Parameters: Learning rate: Not specified in sources. Number of iterations: Not specified in sources. Optimizer: Adam (implied by PyTorch usage). Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Degenerate triangles: Ensure mesh validity. Missing data: Handle incomplete projections. Precision: Floating-point precision in gradient calculations. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import torch import torch.nn as nn class DifferentiableForwardProjector(nn.Module): def init(self, geometry): super().init() self.geometry = geometry def forward(self, vertices, faces): # Simulate projection of mesh through geometry # This is a placeholder for the actual differentiable projection logic # which involves ray-triangle intersection and path length calculation projections = simulateprojection(vertices, faces, self.geometry) return projections def optimizemesh(projectionstrue, geometry, initialvertices, initialfaces, numiterations=1000): # Initialize mesh vertices = nn.Parameter(initialvertices.float(), requiresgrad=True) faces = initialfaces # Define differentiable forward projector projector = DifferentiableForwardProjector(geometry) # Define optimizer optimizer = torch.optim.Adam([vertices], lr=0.01) for i in range(numiterations): optimizer.zerograd() # Forward projection projectionssim = projector(vertices, faces) # Calculate loss loss = torch.mean((projectionssim - projectionstrue) 2) # Backpropagation loss.backward() # Update vertices optimizer.step() if i % 100 == 0: print(f"Iteration {i}, Loss: {loss.item()}") return vertices.detach(), faces An iterative optimization process that minimizes a composite loss function—combining data fidelity, edge, Laplacian, and flatness regularization terms—to reconstruct a 3D triangular mesh directly from 2D tomographic projection data. It distinguishes itself from standard differentiable rendering by explicitly enforcing topological constraints via collision rollback and utilizing robust loss functions (Student-t) to handle missing data or outliers in projection masks. Time Complexity: Depends on the number of iterations, mesh complexity, and projection geometry. Each iteration involves forward projection and backpropagation. Memory Complexity: Proportional to the size of the mesh and the projection data. Performance: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Direct mesh optimization, differentiable geometry. Limitations: Requires differentiable projection implementation, sensitive to initialization. When to use: When a mesh representation is desired and tomographic data is available. When not to use: When volumetric representation is preferred or data is insufficient. The method was introduced in the paper "Shape from Projections via Differentiable Forward Projector for Computed Tomography" published in Ultramicroscopy. It builds on the idea of viewing tomographic reconstruction as a rendering process. The code is available on GitHub. jakeoung/ShapeFromProjections, https://github.com/jakeoung/ShapeFromProjections, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial)

name: CTDR Optimization Loop with Regularization
head: CTDR training loop, Shape from Projections optimization
body: An iterative optimization process that minimizes a composite loss function—combining data fidelity, edge, Laplacian, and flatness regularization terms—to reconstruct a 3D triangular mesh directly from 2D tomographic projection data. It distinguishes itself from standard differentiable rendering by explicitly enforcing topological constraints via collision rollback and utilizing robust loss functions (Student-t) to handle missing data or outliers in projection masks. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: A differentiable forward projector model (derived from Shape from Projections via Differentiable Forward Projector), initial mesh parameters (vertex positions, material densities \mu), 2D projection images p{batch}, angular indices idx\angles, and a wedge mask args.wedge defining valid pixel regions. Outputs: Optimized mesh geometry and material values. Data Structures: model: Contains the differentiable mesh representation. Attributes include mus (material densities, size N), and internal tensors for forward/backward passes (e.g., points2dbxfx6, gradpoints2dbxfx6). optimizer: Adam or SGD instance. args: Configuration object containing weights wedge, wlap, wflat, and flags like silhouettemode. Numbered Steps: 1. Initialize Optimizer: Create an optimizer using Adam with learning rate lr and betas (\beta1=0.9, \beta2=0.99), or SGD with momentum 0.9 and nesterov=True. 2. Forward Projection: Compute the predicted projections \hat{p}, validity mask, and regularization losses by calling the model: \hat{p}, \text{mask\valid}, L{\text{edge}}, L{\text{lap}}, L{\text{flat}} = \text{model}(idx\angles, args.wedge) 3. Compute Data Loss: Calculate the fidelity term on valid pixels. L2 Loss: L{\text{data}} = \frac{1}{|\Omega|} \sum{i \in \Omega} (pi - \hat{p}i)^2 where \Omega is the set of indices where maskvalid is true. Student-t Loss (Alternative): If robust fitting is required, use: L{\text{data}} = \frac{1}{|\Omega|} \sum{i \in \Omega} \log\left(1 + \left(\frac{pi - \hat{p}i}{\sigma}\right)^2\right) with \sigma=1. Background Loss (Optional): If silhouettemode is enabled, add a penalty for non-zero predictions in background regions: L{\text{data}} \leftarrow L{\text{data}} + \frac{1}{|\Omega{bg}|} \sum{j \in \Omega{bg}} \hat{p}j^2 where \Omega{bg} are background indices. 4. Compute Total Loss: Combine data fidelity with regularization terms: L{\text{total}} = L{\text{data}} + w{\text{edge}} L{\text{edge}} + w{\text{lap}} L{\text{lap}} + w{\text{flat}} L{\text{flat}} where w{\text{edge}}, w{\text{lap}}, w{\text{flat}} are scalar weights from args. 5. Backpropagation: Compute gradients via automatic differentiation: \nabla L{\text{total}} = \frac{\partial L{\text{total}}}{\partial \theta} where \theta represents mesh parameters (vertex positions, \mu). 6. Optimization Step: Update parameters: \theta \leftarrow \theta - \eta \cdot \text{OptimizerStep}(\nabla L{\text{total}}). 7. Clamp Material Values: Enforce non-negativity on material densities: \mu \leftarrow \max(0, \mu). 8. Topology Preservation (Optional): If usecollision is enabled, perform a collision rollback to maintain mesh topology: Detect self-intersections or invalid topology. Revert displacements using keeptopology(model, searchtree, displaceprev). 9. Convergence Check: If the change in loss d{\text{loss}} < 10^{-11} and d{\text{loss}} > 0, terminate. 10. Learning Rate Decay: If epoch + 100 == niter and niter > 400, halve the learning rate. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math lr = 1e-3 # Typical value not specified in sources niter = 1000 # Not specified in sources usestudentt = False # Not specified in sources silhouettemode = False # Not specified in sources usecollision = False # Not specified in sources idxbg = [] # Not specified in sources searchtree = [] # Not specified in sources displaceprev = [] # Not specified in sources def Adam(params, lr, betas): state = {p: {'m': 0.0, 'v': 0.0} for p in params} def step(): for p in params: m, v = state[p]['m'], state[p]['v'] beta1, beta2 = betas state[p]['m'] = beta1 m + (1 - beta1) p.grad state[p]['v'] = beta2 v + (1 - beta2) p.grad2 mhat = state[p]['m'] / (1 - beta1) vhat = state[p]['v'] / (1 - beta2) p.data -= lr mhat / (vhat0.5 + 1e-8) return step def SGD(params, lr, momentum, nesterov): state = {p: 0.0 for p in params} def step(): for p in params: buf = state[p] buf = momentum buf + p.grad if nesterov: p.data -= lr (p.grad + momentum buf) else: p.data -= lr buf state[p] = buf return step optimizer = Adam(model.parameters(), lr=lr, betas=(0.9, 0.99)) lossprev = float('inf') for epoch in range(niter): # 1. Forward projection phat, maskvalid, edgeloss, laploss, flatloss = model(idxangles, args.wedge) # 2. Data loss calculation diff = [pbatch[i] - phat[i] for i in range(len(pbatch))] validdiff = [diff[i] for i in range(len(diff)) if maskvalid[i]] if usestudentt: sigma = 1.0 dataloss = sum(math.log(1 + (d / sigma)2) for d in validdiff) / len(validdiff) else: dataloss = sum(d2 for d in validdiff) / len(validdiff) if silhouettemode: bgloss = sum(phat[i]2 for i in idxbg) / len(idxbg) dataloss += bgloss # 3. Total loss loss = dataloss + args.wedge edgeloss + args.wlap laploss + args.wflat flatloss # 4. Backpropagation and step # Automatic differentiation computes gradients optimizer.step() # 5. Post-processing lossnow = loss model.mus = [max(0.0, mu) for mu in model.mus] # 6. Topology preservation if usecollision: # Implementation details for keeptopology not provided in sources keeptopology(model, searchtree, displaceprev) # 7. Convergence check if epoch > 0: dloss = lossprev - lossnow if dloss < 1e-11 and dloss > 0: break lossprev = lossnow # 8. Learning rate decay if niter > 400 and (epoch + 100) == niter: optimizer.lr /= 2.0 Parameters: lr: Learning rate. Typical value not specified, but Adam betas are (0.9, 0.99). sigma: Scale parameter for Student-t loss. Value: 1. wedge, wlap, wflat: Weights for edge, Laplacian, and flatness regularization. Values not specified. niter: Total iterations. Decay triggers at niter > 400. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision: Convergence threshold is set to 10^{-11}, requiring high-precision loss tracking. Boundaries: Material values must be clamped to \ge 0 to prevent physical invalidity. Topology: Without collision rollback, the mesh may self-intersect or invert, leading to invalid projections. The keeptopology function handles this but requires a search tree and previous displacement buffer. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Not given in the sources. Limitations: Not given in the sources. When to use: Not given in the sources. When not to use: Not given in the sources. name: Volume Reconstruction via Linear System Inversion
head: Property Reconstruction, Tomographic Volume Reconstruction
body: Volume Reconstruction via Linear System Inversion inverts the volume rendering process to optimize volume properties (emission, albedo, extinction) such that the rendered output matches user-defined target images. It sets itself apart from sibling methods by formulating the inverse problem as a linear system o = Wa solved in the least-squares sense, relying on local support basis functions for computational efficiency. Unlike Differential Rendering for CT Reconstruction which uses gradient-based optimization, this method directly computes coefficients via matrix inversion or least-squares solvers. Inputs: Target images defined as a collection of N constraint pixels. For each pixel k \in [1, N], the camera view provides ray origin x^k, direction \omega^k, and target radiance value Lk^i(x^k, \omega^k). If a surface hit exists, the position of the first hit surface is xs^k; otherwise, the background is at \infty. A set of basis functions with spatially local support (e.g., box functions or triangle functions) associated with the volume's voxels. Outputs: A coefficient vector a representing the optimized volume properties (emission, albedo, or extinction). Data Structures: Observation Vector (o): A column vector of size N \times 1, where each entry ok corresponds to the target radiance Lk^i(x^k, \omega^k) for pixel k. System Matrix (W): A matrix of size N \times M, where M is the number of basis functions (unknowns). The entry w{ik} is derived from the volume rendering equation for pixel k and basis function i. Coefficient Vector (a): A column vector of size M \times 1, containing the values of the basis functions. Steps: 1. Linearization: The volume rendering equation is linearized with respect to the chosen property (emission, albedo, or extinction) to form the linear system o = Wa. For Emission or Albedo, the terms enter linearly as separate summands in the rendering equation. For Extinction, the equation is linearized by assuming constant outgoing radiance Lm and applying a logarithm to the transmittance term. 2. Matrix Construction: Construct the matrix W where each row corresponds to a constraint pixel. The entries w{ik} are integrals corresponding to the single ray passing through the volume, weighted by the basis functions. For box functions (nearest-neighbor sampling), w{ik} involves the integral of the basis function along the ray. For triangle functions, linearly interpolated solutions are considered. 3. Least-Squares Solution: Since user input may be inconsistent (no exact solution exists for o = Wa), solve for a in the least-squares sense. This minimizes the quadratic function ||Wa - o||2. The normal equations are: W^T o = W^T W a. Solve for a: a = (W^T W)^{-1} W^T o (assuming W^T W is invertible). Formulas: General Linear System: o = Wa where o is the observation vector and W is the system matrix derived from the volume rendering equation. Least-Squares Objective: \mina ||Wa - o||2^2 Leading to the normal equations: W^T o = W^T W a Extinction Reconstruction (Special Case): Assuming constant outgoing radiance Lm(x, \omega) = const, the rendering equation for pixel k becomes: Lk^i(x^k, \omega^k) = e^{-\intc \sigmat(xt) dt} Lo(xs^k, \omega^k) + Lm \left(1 - e^{-\int0^s \sigmat(xt) dt}\right) The first summand is rewritten using basis functions \upsiloni(xt) for extinction coefficient \sigmat(xt) = \sum ai \upsiloni(xt): Lo(xs^k, \omega^k) \prodi e^{-\sigma{ti} \intc \upsiloni(xt) dt} Applying logarithms linearizes the transmittance term, allowing the formation of a linear system for the extinction coefficients. Parameters: Basis Functions: Box functions (nearest-neighbor sampling of 3D texture) are used for local support speed. Triangle functions allow linearly interpolated solutions. Outgoing Radiance (Lm): Must be constant for extinction reconstruction. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Inconsistent Input: User-defined target images may not have a valid solution. The least-squares approach handles this by minimizing the error. Extinction Reconstruction Restriction: Extinction can only be reconstructed if the outgoing radiance Lm is constant (Lm(x, \omega) = const). This is usually not problematic as extinction defines shape and is derived first. Non-Linearity: Extinction cannot be jointly estimated with emission or albedo because it involves a complex non-linear problem, even when linearized via log-space. Albedo Reconstruction is a method within volume reconstruction via linear system inversion that optimizes the diffuse albedo field of a volume so that its rendered output matches target images. It isolates the albedo parameter by assuming single scattering, thereby decoupling it from the emission and extinction terms to form a linear system. Unlike joint optimization methods that solve for multiple properties simultaneously, this approach treats albedo as the sole unknown coefficient vector, reducing ambiguity in scenes where emission and reflected light are otherwise coupled. Emission reconstruction is a differentiable inverse volume rendering technique that solves for the spatial distribution of emitted radiance (L{emit}) within a volume such that the rendered output matches target images. It operates by linearizing the volume rendering equation under the assumption of single scattering, isolating the emission term from scattering and background contributions to form a linear system. Unlike Albedo Reconstruction, which optimizes the scattering color properties, this method treats emission coefficients as the primary unknowns. Extinction reconstruction linearizes the volume rendering equation by assuming constant outgoing radiance Lm and applying a logarithm to the transmittance term. It starts with the expanded rendering equation, separates the background and medium contributions, and exploits the constant Lm to integrate the medium term into Lm (1 - e^{-\int \sigmat dt}). The background term is rewritten using basis functions. This method is restricted to cases where Lm is constant, but this is typically acceptable as extinction defines the volume shape and is often derived first. Time Complexity: Depends on the size of the matrix W (N \times M) and the solver used. Solving the normal equations W^T W a = W^T o involves matrix multiplication and inversion, which is O(M^3) for direct inversion or O(M^2 N) for iterative solvers, where N is the number of pixels and M is the number of voxels/basis functions. Memory Complexity: Requires storing the matrix W (N \times M) and the vectors o and a. Strengths: Direct solution avoids iterative optimization loops; local support basis functions speed up computation. Limitations: Cannot jointly optimize extinction with emission/albedo due to non-linearity; requires constant outgoing radiance for extinction reconstruction. When to Use: When a direct, non-iterative solution for volume properties is needed and the input constraints are consistent or can be approximated in a least-squares sense. When Not to Use: When joint optimization of multiple properties (especially extinction with emission) is required, or when outgoing radiance is not constant. The method originates from the work on property and lighting manipulations for static volume stylization using a painting metaphor. It was introduced to allow users to define target views and invert the volume rendering process to optimize volume properties. The approach draws parallels to computed tomography (CT) but adapts to inconsistent user input by using least-squares solutions. name: Albedo Reconstruction
head: Property Reconstruction
body: Albedo Reconstruction is a method within volume reconstruction via linear system inversion that optimizes the diffuse albedo field of a volume so that its rendered output matches target images. It isolates the albedo parameter by assuming single scattering, thereby decoupling it from the emission and extinction terms to form a linear system. Unlike joint optimization methods that solve for multiple properties simultaneously, this approach treats albedo as the sole unknown coefficient vector, reducing ambiguity in scenes where emission and reflected light are otherwise coupled. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: Target radiance values L^ki(xk, \omegak) for a set of pixels k; known volume properties including extinction coefficient \sigmat(xt), emission L{emit}(xt), and single-scattering radiance L{scat}(xt, \omegak); ray origins xk and directions \omegak; basis functions \upsiloni(xt) representing the spatial domain. Outputs: Albedo coefficients vector \vec{\rho} = [\rho1, \rho2, \dots, \rhoN]^T. Data Structures: Basis Functions: A set of N basis functions \upsiloni(xt) (e.g., trilinear, radial basis) used to represent the continuous albedo field \rho(xt) = \sum{i=1}^N \rhoi \upsiloni(xt). Linear System Matrix: A matrix W of size M \times N, where M is the number of pixel constraints and N is the number of basis coefficients. Each row k corresponds to a pixel constraint. Observation Vector: A vector o of size M, containing the residual radiance for each pixel. Numbered Steps: 1. Linearization: Start with the volume rendering equation. Split the medium radiance Lm into emission and scattering components. Assume single scattering, which implies that the scattered radiance L{scat}(xt, \omegak) is independent of the albedo \rho(xt). 2. Residual Calculation: For each pixel k, compute the observation vector component ok by subtracting the known contributions (transmitted background and emitted light) from the target radiance: ok = L^ki(xk, \omegak) - Tr(xk, x^ks) Lo(x^ks, \omegak) - \intc Tr(xk, xt) \sigmat(xt) L{emit}(xt) dt where Tr is the transmittance, x^ks is the scene boundary, and Lo is the background radiance. 3. Albedo Formulation: Substitute the albedo representation into the scattering integral. The remaining term depends linearly on \rho: ok = \intc Tr(xk, xt) \sigmat(xt) L{scat}(xt, \omegak) \rho(xt) dt 4. Basis Expansion: Represent \rho(xt) as a linear combination of basis functions \upsiloni(xt): \rho(xt) = \sum{i=1}^N \rhoi \upsiloni(xt) 5. Matrix Assembly: Substitute the basis expansion into the integral. By linearity, the integral becomes a dot product between the coefficient vector \vec{\rho} and a weight vector \vec{w}k: ok = \sum{i=1}^N \rhoi \left( \intc Tr(xk, xt) \sigmat(xt) L{scat}(xt, \omegak) \upsiloni(xt) dt \right) = \vec{\rho} \cdot \vec{w}k The weight w{k,i} for pixel k and basis i is computed via ray marching, integrating the product of transmittance, extinction, single-scattering radiance, and the basis function along the ray. 6. System Solution: Assemble all M equations into the linear system W \vec{\rho} = o. Solve for \vec{\rho} using a linear solver (e.g., least squares if M > N, or direct inversion if M = N). Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def albedoreconstruction(pixels, volumeproperties, basisfunctions): """ Reconstructs albedo coefficients by solving a linear system derived from single-scattering approximation. Args: pixels: List of pixel constraints, each containing target radiance Ltarget, ray origin xk, direction omegak, and scene boundary xs. volumeproperties: Object containing functions for sigmat(x), Lemit(x), Lscat(x, omega), and transmittance Tr(x1, x2). basisfunctions: List of N basis functions upsiloni(x). Returns: rho: Array of shape (N,) containing albedo coefficients. """ M = len(pixels) N = len(basisfunctions) W = zeros((M, N)) o = zeros(M) for k, pixel in enumerate(pixels): # Step 2: Calculate observation residual ok # Subtract transmitted background and emitted light from target backgroundterm = volumeproperties.transmittance(pixel.xk, pixel.xs) \ volumeproperties.backgroundradiance(pixel.xs, pixel.omegak) emissionintegral = 0.0 # Ray march to compute emission contribution along the ray for t in raymarchpoints(pixel.xk, pixel.omegak): transmittance = volumeproperties.transmittance(pixel.xk, t) sigmat = volumeproperties.sigmat(t) lemit = volumeproperties.lemit(t) # Differential path length dt is handled by integration step size emissionintegral += transmittance sigmat lemit dt o[k] = pixel.Ltarget - backgroundterm - emissionintegral # Step 5: Compute weights wk for this pixel for i, upsilon in enumerate(basisfunctions): weight = 0.0 # Ray march to compute the integral for basis function i for t in raymarchpoints(pixel.xk, pixel.omegak): transmittance = volumeproperties.transmittance(pixel.xk, t) sigmat = volumeproperties.sigmat(t) lscat = volumeproperties.lscat(t, pixel.omegak) basisval = upsilon(t) # Integrand: Tr sigmat Lscat upsiloni weight += transmittance sigmat lscat basisval dt W[k, i] = weight # Step 6: Solve linear system W rho = o # Use least squares if M > N, otherwise direct solve rho = solvelinearsystem(W, o) return rho Parameters: Basis Functions: Choice of basis (e.g., trilinear grid, radial basis) determines N. Not given in the sources. Ray Marching Resolution: Step size for numerical integration. Not given in the sources. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Single Scattering Assumption: The method relies on L{scat} being independent of \rho. If multiple scattering is significant, the linearization fails. Degenerate Input: If the volume is optically thin or emission dominates, the signal-to-noise ratio for albedo may be low, leading to unstable solutions. Boundary Conditions: Accurate calculation of Tr(xk, x^ks) and Lo(x^ks, \omegak) is critical; errors here propagate directly into ok. Jointly optimizes emission and diffuse albedo parameters by treating them as a single linear system, leveraging their linear independence to solve for both simultaneously. Unlike methods that fix one property to solve for the other, this approach updates both in a unified coefficient vector, reducing ambiguity in scenes where emission and reflected light are coupled. Time Complexity: O(M \cdot N \cdot R), where M is the number of pixels, N is the number of basis functions, and R is the number of ray marching steps per pixel. Solving the linear system takes O(\min(M^3, N^3)) or O(MN^2) for least squares. Memory Complexity: O(MN) to store the matrix W and vector o. Strengths: Provides a direct, non-iterative solution for albedo under the single-scattering assumption. Computationally efficient compared to gradient-based optimization methods. Limitations: Restricted to single-scattering scenarios. Cannot handle complex lighting interactions or multiple bounces. Accuracy depends heavily on the correctness of the assumed emission and extinction fields. When to Use: Suitable for stylization or inverse rendering tasks where the volume is primarily single-scattering and emission/extinction are known or can be estimated separately. When Not to Use: Unsuitable for dense, participating media with significant multiple scattering or when emission and albedo are strongly coupled and cannot be decoupled. The method originates from the work on property and lighting manipulations for static volume stylization. It was introduced by as a technique to allow artists to "paint" albedo properties directly into volume data by inverting the rendering equation. The approach builds on the linearization of the volume rendering equation under the single-scattering assumption, a common simplification in inverse volume rendering. name: Joint Emission & Albedo Reconstruction
head: Joint Emission-Albedo Optimization
body: Jointly optimizes emission and diffuse albedo parameters by treating them as a single linear system, leveraging their linear independence to solve for both simultaneously. Unlike methods that fix one property to solve for the other, this approach updates both in a unified coefficient vector, reducing ambiguity in scenes where emission and reflected light are coupled. Inputs: Observed radiance values L{obs} from multiple viewpoints. Known volume properties (extinction, geometry) required for the forward model. Initial estimates for emission \vec{L}{emit} and albedo \vec{\rho}. Outputs: Optimized coefficient vector \vec{a} containing both emission and albedo. Data Structures: Coefficient vector \vec{a}: A concatenated vector where the first segment corresponds to emission values and the second to albedo values. Layout: \vec{a} = [\vec{L}{emit}; \vec{\rho}]. Size: N{emit} + N{albedo}, where N represents the number of discretized volume elements or texture samples. Steps: 1. Initialize Albedo: Set the initial diffuse albedo parameter \vec{\rho}0 to the median of all observed radiance values. This ensures more plausible material parameters and prevents overfitting to noise, although it may not strictly decrease error metrics compared to unconstrained initialization. 2. Initialize Emission: Set initial emission values \vec{L}{emit,0}. (Not given in the sources.: Typically initialized to zero or a small constant). 3. Formulate Linear System: Construct the system matrix \mathbf{M} and observation vector \mathbf{b} based on the volume rendering equation. The equation separates into summands for emission and albedo because they are linearly independent. 4. Solve: Solve the linear system \mathbf{M}\vec{a} = \mathbf{b} for \vec{a}. 5. Extract: Split \vec{a} back into \vec{L}{emit} and \vec{\rho}. Formulas: The coefficient vector is defined as: \vec{a} = [\vec{L}{emit}; \vec{\rho}] where \vec{L}{emit} and \vec{\rho} are linearly independent and enter as separate summands in the rendering equation (Eq. 2 in). Parameters: Albedo Initialization Strategy: Median of observations. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Overfitting: Unconstrained optimization may achieve low error but produce implausible material parameters. Monte Carlo Noise: In stochastic rendering contexts, noise can contaminate textured parameters. (Mitigation strategies like gradient clamping are mentioned in but not part of the core joint reconstruction definition). Initializes the diffuse albedo parameter with the median of all observations. This strategy ensures more plausible results by preventing unconstrained optimization from overfitting to noise and generating implausible material parameters, even if it does not strictly minimize error metrics in all experiments. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources.: Depends on the solver (e.g., conjugate gradient) and system size O((N{emit}+N{albedo})^3) for direct inversion or less for iterative solvers. Memory Complexity: Proportional to the size of the coefficient vector and system matrix O(N{emit} + N{albedo}). Strengths: Exploits linear independence to solve for coupled properties simultaneously, reducing ambiguity. Limitations: Requires the volume's outgoing radiance to be handled carefully; if extinction is also reconstructed, assumptions about constant outgoing radiance may be needed (though this is more relevant to extinction reconstruction). When to use: When both emission and albedo are unknown and need to be recovered from multi-view observations. When not: When one property is known or fixed. Originated in the context of volume stylization and property manipulation using a painting metaphor. The method is part of a broader framework for differentiable volume rendering where material properties are optimized to match target images. It builds on the principle that emission and albedo are linearly independent in the rendering equation. name: Emission Reconstruction
head: Emission Optimization, Emission Inversion
body: Emission reconstruction is a differentiable inverse volume rendering technique that solves for the spatial distribution of emitted radiance (L{emit}) within a volume such that the rendered output matches target images. It operates by linearizing the volume rendering equation under the assumption of single scattering, isolating the emission term from scattering and background contributions to form a linear system. Unlike Albedo Reconstruction, which optimizes the scattering color properties, this method treats emission coefficients as the primary unknowns. Inputs: Target pixel values L^ki(xk, \omegak) for k pixels. Camera ray origins xk and directions \omegak. Background radiance Lo(x^ks, \omegak) at the scene boundary x^ks. Extinction coefficient field \sigmat(x). Scattering phase function \rho(x) and scattered light field L{scat}(x, \omega) (assumed fixed or negligible in single-scattering approximation). Basis functions \upsiloni(x) for representing emission. Outputs: Emission coefficients vector \vec{L}{emit}, where L{emit}(x) = \sumi L^i{emit} \upsiloni(x). Data Structures: Observation Vector \mathbf{o}: A column vector of size K (number of pixels), where each element ok represents the residual radiance attributable to emission. Transport Matrix \mathbf{W}: A matrix of size K \times N (where N is the number of basis functions). Element W{ki} represents the contribution of the i-th basis function to the k-th pixel. Steps: 1. Linearization: Start with the volume rendering equation. Assume single scattering. Split the integral into emitted and scattered light components. 2. Isolation: Define the observation vector ok by subtracting background and single-scattering contributions from the target pixel value: ok:= L^ki(xk, \omegak) - Tr(xk, x^ks) Lo(x^ks, \omegak) - \intc Tr(xk, xt) \sigmat(xt) \rho(x) L{scat}(xt, \omegak) dt This simplifies to the emission-only integral: ok = \intc Tr(xk, xt) \sigmat(xt) L{emit}(xt) dt where Tr(xk, xt) is the transmittance from xk to xt, and c is the ray path. 3. Basis Expansion: Represent the unknown emission field L{emit}(xt) as a linear combination of basis functions \upsiloni(xt) with coefficients L^i{emit}: L{emit}(xt) = \sumi L^i{emit} \upsiloni(xt) 4. Matrix Assembly: Substitute the basis expansion into the integral. By linearity, the integral becomes a sum: ok = \sumi L^i{emit} \left( \intc Tr(xk, xt) \sigmat(xt) \upsiloni(xt) dt \right) Define the matrix entries w{ki} as: w{ki} = \intc Tr(xk, xt) \sigmat(xt) \upsiloni(xt) dt The system is now \mathbf{o} = \mathbf{W} \vec{L}{emit}. 5. Solving: Solve the linear system for \vec{L}{emit}. Depending on constraints (e.g., non-negativity of emission), use least squares or non-negative least squares (NNLS). Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def emissionreconstruction(targetradiance, camerarays, sigmat, backgroundradiance, scatteringfield, basisfunctions, numbasis): """ Reconstruct emission coefficients from target images. Args: targetradiance: Array of shape (K,) containing L^ki(xk, omegak). camerarays: List of K rays, each with origin xk, direction omegak, and path c. sigmat: Function returning extinction coefficient at point x. backgroundradiance: Function returning Lo(x^ks, omegak) at boundary. scatteringfield: Function returning Lscat(x, omega) for single scattering. basisfunctions: List of N basis functions upsiloni(x). numbasis: Number of basis functions N. Returns: Lemitcoeffs: Array of shape (N,) containing L^iemit. """ K = len(camerarays) o = np.zeros(K) W = np.zeros((K, numbasis)) for k in range(K): ray = camerarays[k] xk = ray.origin omegak = ray.direction c = ray.path # 1. Calculate background and scattering contributions xs = ray.boundarypoint Loval = backgroundradiance(xs, omegak) # Transmittance to boundary Trboundary = computetransmittance(xk, xs, sigmat) # Single scattering integral # Integral of Tr(xk, xt) sigmat(xt) rho Lscat(xt, omegak) dt # Note: rho is assumed constant or absorbed into Lscat definition in source scatteringintegral = integratealongray( path=c, integrand=lambda xt: computetransmittance(xk, xt, sigmat) \ sigmat(xt) scatteringfield(xt, omegak)) # 2. Isolate emission term ok o[k] = targetradiance[k] - Trboundary Loval - scatteringintegral # 3. Assemble matrix row W[k,:] for i in range(numbasis): upsiloni = basisfunctions[i] # wki = integral of Tr(xk, xt) sigmat(xt) upsiloni(xt) dt W[k, i] = integratealongray( path=c, integrand=lambda xt: computetransmittance(xk, xt, sigmat) \ sigmat(xt) upsiloni(xt)) # 4. Solve linear system o = W Lemit # Using least squares; add non-negativity constraint if required Lemitcoeffs, residuals, rank, s = np.linalg.lstsq(W, o, rcond=None) return Lemitcoeffs def computetransmittance(xstart, xend, sigmat): """Compute transmittance Tr(xstart, xend) along the segment.""" # Integrate sigmat along the segment from xstart to xend # Tr = exp(- integral(sigmat dt)) opticaldepth = integratealongsegment(xstart, xend, sigmat) return np.exp(-opticaldepth) def integratealongsegment(xstart, xend, func): """Numerical integration of func(x) along the line segment.""" # Simple trapezoidal rule or Gaussian quadrature # Assuming uniform sampling for simplicity numsamples = 100 t = np.linspace(0, 1, numsamples) points = xstart + t (xend - xstart) values = np.array([func(p) for p in points]) # Trapezoidal rule return np.trapz(values, t) np.linalg.norm(xend - xstart) def integratealongray(path, integrand): """Integrate integrand(x) along the ray path.""" # Path is a sequence of points or a parametric curve # For simplicity, assume path is defined by points and we integrate between them # This is a placeholder for specific ray marching implementation # In practice, this involves stepping along the ray and summing contributions return 0.0 # Placeholder for actual ray marching integration Parameters: Basis Functions: The choice of \upsiloni(x) determines the spatial resolution and smoothness of the reconstructed emission. Common choices include voxel-based step functions or hierarchical bases. Single Scattering Assumption: The method assumes single scattering to linearize the problem. Multiple scattering requires iterative refinement or non-linear solvers, which are not covered in the base method. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Degenerate Rays: If a ray does not intersect the volume, the integral is zero, and the corresponding row in \mathbf{W} is zero. This can lead to singular systems if not handled. Precision: Transmittance calculations involve exponentials of optical depth. High optical depths can lead to underflow, resulting in zero transmittance and loss of gradient information. Boundary Conditions: Accurate estimation of background radiance Lo and boundary points x^ks is critical. Errors here propagate directly into ok. This method optimizes environmental illumination (outgoing radiance from the environment) to match a desired volume appearance, assuming the volume's intrinsic properties (emission, albedo, extinction) are spatially varying but fixed during the optimization process. It differs from sibling methods like Emission Reconstruction by treating the light source coefficients as the unknown variables rather than the volume properties, solving for the lighting that best explains the observed pixel values through a linear transport operator. Time Complexity: Dominated by the assembly of the transport matrix \mathbf{W}, which requires integrating along each ray for each basis function. Complexity is O(K \cdot N \cdot S), where K is the number of pixels, N is the number of basis functions, and S is the number of samples per ray. Solving the linear system is O(K \cdot N^2) or O(N^3) depending on the solver. Memory Complexity: O(K \cdot N) to store the transport matrix \mathbf{W} and observation vector \mathbf{o}. Strengths: Provides a direct, non-iterative solution for emission under single scattering. Efficient for static volumes with known geometry and scattering properties. Limitations: Restricted to single scattering. Accuracy degrades in highly scattering media. Sensitive to errors in background and scattering field estimates. When to Use: Suitable for stylization and inverse rendering of volumes where emission is the dominant light source and scattering is weak or known. The method originates from the work on property and lighting manipulations for static volume stylization. It was developed to allow artists to manipulate emission properties of volumes to achieve desired visual effects while maintaining physical plausibility under simplified scattering assumptions. Property and Lighting Manipulations for Static Volume Stylization Using a Painting Metaphor, https://doi.org/10.1109/TVCG.2014.13, fetched 2026-10-26

name: Light Reconstruction via Linear Transport Operator
head: Environmental Illumination Optimization, Light Source Coefficient Optimization
body: This method optimizes environmental illumination (outgoing radiance from the environment) to match a desired volume appearance, assuming the volume's intrinsic properties (emission, albedo, extinction) are spatially varying but fixed during the optimization process. It differs from sibling methods like Emission Reconstruction by treating the light source coefficients as the unknown variables rather than the volume properties, solving for the lighting that best explains the observed pixel values through a linear transport operator. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: A set of N constraint pixels (desired observations o), a volume with fixed properties, and M basis functions modeling the light sources (e.g., directional lights sampled from an environment map). Outputs: An M-dimensional coefficient vector \tilde{L}o representing the optimized outgoing radiance from the environment. Data Structures: Transport Operator T: A dense matrix of size N \times M. Unlike the sparse weight matrices used in volume parameter reconstruction, T is dense because it encodes complete light scattering in the scene. Light Volumes (voli): For Strategy 2, M precomputed volumes are stored. Each voli contains the radiance contribution of the i-th light basis function at every voxel in the scene. Formulas: The problem is formulated as a least-squares minimization: \min{\tilde{L}o} ||T \tilde{L}o - o||^2 where: o is the vector of desired observation values for N pixels. T is the linear light transport operator matrix of size N \times M. \tilde{L}o is the M-dimensional vector of light source coefficients. Parameters: M: Number of basis functions. Typical value: ~16 coefficients are sufficient to capture light influence. N: Number of constraint pixels. Steps: 1. Precomputation: Construct the operator T or the intermediate light volumes. Two strategies are available: Strategy 1 (Store T): Compute the full N \times M matrix T. For each light coefficient i, render the scene with only that coefficient active (value 1, others 0) to fill the i-th column of T. Strategy 2 (Light Volumes): For each light coefficient i, light the entire volume with that coefficient active to create a "light volume" voli. Store these M volumes. 2. Optimization Loop: Solve the linear system using an iterative solver (e.g., Conjugate Gradient). Each iteration requires two matrix-vector multiplications: Forward Pass (T \tilde{L}o): Compute the predicted observation. If using Strategy 1: Perform standard matrix-vector multiplication. If using Strategy 2: For each constraint pixel, shoot a ray through the volume. Gather values from all precomputed light volumes voli along the ray path and sum them weighted by \tilde{L}o. Backward Pass (T^T r): Distribute the residual r = o - T \tilde{L}o back to the light coefficients. If using Strategy 1: Perform standard matrix-vector multiplication with the transpose. If using Strategy 2: For each constraint pixel, distribute its residual value to the light coefficients. This is analogous to volume optimization back-projection, but the values are accumulated into the light coefficient vector \tilde{L}o rather than voxel properties. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def lightreconstruction(constraintpixels, volume, numbasisfunctions=16): """ Optimizes light source coefficients to match constraint pixels. Uses Strategy 2 (Light Volumes) for memory efficiency. """ M = numbasisfunctions N = len(constraintpixels) # Precomputation: Generate light volumes # vol[i] is a 3D array representing the radiance contribution # of the i-th basis function at every voxel. lightvolumes = precomputelightvolumes(volume, M) # Initialize coefficients Lo = zeros(M) # Optimization loop (e.g., Conjugate Gradient) # Note: Standard CG requires T^T T, but we implement the # matrix-vector products directly to avoid forming T explicitly. # Simplified gradient descent for clarity of the T/T^T operations # In practice, use CG or similar solver. for iteration in range(maxiterations): # Forward Pass: y = T Lo predictedobs = zeros(N) for pidx, ray in enumerate(constraintpixels): accumulated = 0.0 # Gather values from all light volumes along the ray for i in range(M): # Sample lightvolumes[i] along ray and integrate # This is equivalent to the column i of T multiplied by Lo[i] contribution = integratelightvolume(lightvolumes[i], ray) accumulated += Lo[i] contribution predictedobs[pidx] = accumulated # Compute residual residual = constraintpixels - predictedobs # Backward Pass: grad = T^T residual # Distribute residuals to light coefficients grad = zeros(M) for pidx, ray in enumerate(constraintpixels): r = residual[pidx] if abs(r) < epsilon: continue # Distribute residual to each light coefficient based on # the light volume's contribution at this pixel for i in range(M): # The sensitivity of the pixel to light coefficient i # is the value of lightvolumes[i] along the ray sensitivity = integratelightvolume(lightvolumes[i], ray) grad[i] += r sensitivity # Update coefficients (simplified update rule) # Lo = Lo - alpha grad # (Full implementation requires line search or CG update steps) Lo = Lo - learningrate grad return Lo def precomputelightvolumes(volume, M): """ For each of the M basis functions, render the volume with that light source active to create a light volume. """ volumes = [] for i in range(M): # Create a temporary environment map with only the i-th direction active tempenv = createsingledirectionallight(i) # Render the volume with this lighting to get the contribution # This is stored as an emission-like volume vol = rendervolumewithlighting(volume, tempenv) volumes.append(vol) return volumes def integratelightvolume(lightvol, ray): """ Integrates the light volume along a ray. Equivalent to the transport of the specific light basis function. """ # Standard volume rendering integral along the ray # sum(lightvol(ray(t)) transmittance(t)) return standardvolumerendering(lightvol, ray) Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Sparsity: The operator T is not sparse; it encodes complete light scattering. On-the-fly evaluation is too slow, requiring precomputation. Memory: Strategy 1 (storing T) has memory linear in N (pixels). Strategy 2 (light volumes) has memory linear in VolumeSize \times M. Constant Volume Properties: The method assumes volume properties are constant during optimization. If they vary, the operator T is no longer constant, and this linear approach fails. Time Complexity: Depends on the precomputation strategy. Strategy 1 requires M full volume renders for precomputation. Strategy 2 requires M full volume renders for precomputation. Optimization iterations require O(N \cdot M) work per iteration for Strategy 2 (ray traversal through M volumes) or O(N \cdot M) for Strategy 1 (matrix-vector multiply). Memory Complexity: Strategy 1: O(N \cdot M) to store T. Strategy 2: O(V \cdot M) where V is the number of voxels, to store light volumes. Strengths: Allows independent optimization of lighting without altering volume geometry or material properties. Efficient if M is small (~16). Limitations: Requires precomputation. Cannot handle dynamic volume properties. Dense matrix operations can be memory-intensive for high-resolution constraints. When to use: When the volume structure is known and fixed, but the lighting needs to be adjusted to match a target appearance (e.g., stylization). This method was introduced in the context of static volume stylization using a painting metaphor. It builds on the linearity of light transport in participating media, allowing the transport operator to be separated from the source terms. The approach is analogous to tomographic reconstruction but applied to the light source coefficients rather than the volume density. Property and Lighting Manipulations for Static Volume Stylization Using a Painting Metaphor, https://doi.org/10.1109/TVCG.2014.13, fetched 2026-10-26
