name: Dynamic Tomographic Reconstruction with Motion Identification (DynTomo)
head: DynART, DynTomo, Dynamic ART-P-DVC, Dynamic Tomographic Reconstruction with Displacement Field Identification, Dynamic Tomography, Dynamic reconstruction algorithm, PDVC
body: DynTomo is a staggered iterative method for reconstructing deforming 3D volumes from 2D projection data acquired over time, simultaneously identifying the full 2D space-time displacement field. It solves the problem of motion artifacts in tomography by alternating between algebraic volume reconstruction (DynART) and projection-based digital volume correlation (PDVC) for motion identification. Unlike standard Algebraic Reconstruction Techniques (ART) which produce blurry or split reconstructions under large displacements, DynTomo corrects for motion to yield sharp edges and accurate gray levels. It builds on Tomographic reconstruction as inverse rendering by incorporating a parametric displacement model into the optimization loop. Inputs: p(r, \theta, t): Acquired sinogram (projections) at detector coordinates r, angles \theta, and time steps t \in \{1, \dots, Nt\}. Nt: Number of time steps (projections). N\theta: Number of angles. N{scale}: Number of multiscale levels. \epsilon: Convergence threshold for inner loops. Basis functions: N\tau time functions \phii(t) and Ns spatial shape functions \Phij(x). Outputs: f(x): Reconstructed reference volume. u(x, t): Space-time displacement field. Data Structures: Displacement Field Parametrization: The displacement field is represented as a linear combination of basis functions: u(x, t) = \sum{i=1}^{N\tau} \sum{j=1}^{Ns} \alpha{ij} \phii(t) \Phij(x) where \alpha{ij} are the amplitude coefficients. The reference state is defined at t=0 such that u(x, 0) = 0, implying \phii(0) = 0. Spatial Basis: \Phij(x) are composed of C^4 mesh elements (4-node square elements with bilinear interpolation). In the source tests, Ns = 18 degrees of freedom. Time Basis: \phii(t) are time functions. In the source tests, N\tau = 2. Gaussian Kernel: Defined as G\lambda(r) = \frac{1}{2\pi\lambda^2} \exp\left(-\frac{|r|^2}{2\lambda^2}\right). Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def DynTomo(p, Nt, Ntheta, Nscale, eps, Ntau, Ns, phi, Phi): # p: sinogram array [Ntheta, Nt, H, W] # phi: time basis functions [Ntau] # Phi: spatial basis functions [Ns] u = zeros(volumeshape + (Nt,)) # Displacement field u(x, t) for i in range(Nscale, -1, -1): lam = 2i # Convolve recorded projections with Gaussian kernel Glam = (1/(2pilam2)) exp(-rnorm2 / (2lam2)) pcheck = convolve(p, Glam) rho = pcheck.copy() Residual = 1 + eps # Force first loop while Residual > eps: # 1. Volume Reconstruction (DynART) f = DynART(pcheck, u, Nt, Ntheta, eps) # 2. Motion Identification (PDVC) u = PDVC(f, pcheck, u, Nt, Ntheta, eps, Ntau, Ns, phi, Phi) # 3. Scale Residual Update rhoold = rho.copy() fwarped = warp(f, u) rho = pcheck - forwardprojection(fwarped) Residual = norm(rho - rhoold) return f, u def DynART(pcheck, u, Nt, Ntheta, eps): f = zeros(volumeshape) n = 1 perm = permutation(Nt) # Permutation over acquisition times for in range(60): # NDynART iterations for tidx in range(Nt): tau = perm[tidx] # Warp volume to current time ftilde = warp(f, u[:, tau]) # Forward projection proj = forwardprojection(ftilde, theta=tau) # Residual rho = pcheck[:, tau] - proj # Backprojection dftilde = backprojection(rho, theta=tau) # Unwarp update to reference space df = warp(dftilde, -u[:, tau]) # Update volume with normalization factor Δf̃ from source f = f + df / max(dftilde) # Apply constraints (e.g., positivity) f = clip(f, 0, None) n += 1 return f def PDVC(f, pcheck, u, Nt, Ntheta, eps, Ntau, Ns, phi, Phi): u0 = u.copy() # Initialize residual fwarped = warp(f, u) rhoold = pcheck - forwardprojection(fwarped) Progress = 1 + eps while Progress > eps: fwarped = warp(f, u) rho = pcheck - forwardprojection(fwarped) Progress = norm(rho - rhoold) # Sensitivity computation H = zeros((Ntau Ns, Ntau Ns)) b = zeros(Ntau Ns) for i in range(Ntau): for j in range(Ns): # Compute projected sensitivities over all r, t chij = zeroslike(pcheck) for tidx in range(Nt): gradf = gradient(fwarped[:, tidx]) chij[:, tidx] = forwardprojection(Phi[j] gradf, theta=tidx) Sij = phi[i] chij # Sij(r, t) = phii(t) chij # Assemble Hessian and second member for k in range(Ntau): for l in range(Ns): chik = zeroslike(pcheck) for tidx in range(Nt): gradf = gradient(fwarped[:, tidx]) chik[:, tidx] = forwardprojection(Phi[l] gradf, theta=tidx) Skl = phi[k] chik H[iNs + j, kNs + l] = sum(Sij Skl) b[iNs + j] = sum(rho Sij) # Solve linear system [H]δα = b deltaalpha = solve(H, b) # Update displacement field u = u + reshape(deltaalpha, (Ntau, Ns)) outer(phi, Phi) rhoold = rho.copy() return u Parameters: Convergence Threshold \epsilon: Stops inner loops when residual or progress drops below this value. Basis Functions: N\tau time functions and Ns spatial shape functions. Reference state u(x, 0)=0 implies \phii(0)=0. Iterations: The source tests used 60 complete iterations per reconstruction cycle. Gaussian Kernel Width: Starts large (\lambda = 2^{N{scale}}), progressively reduced by a factor of two at each scale level. Pitfalls: Motion Regularization: Rapid variations in the displacement field can cause ill-conditioning. Weak regularization penalizes spatial/temporal variations; strong regularization uses smooth basis functions. Optical Flow Assumption: The base implementation assumes constant optical flow and does not model gray level variations. Sensitivity Bottleneck: Sensitivity computation requires deformed volumes over the entire time range, making it the computational bottleneck. Complexity: The bottleneck is the computation of sensitivity fields, which requires projecting deformed volumes over the entire time range for every PDVC iteration. Performance: In tests with 512×512 pixel images and 300 projections, 60 iterations took approximately 1 hour. The checkerboard test (38 degrees of freedom) took approximately 2 hours. Accuracy: Shepp-Logan test (max displacement 37 pixels, 27% strain): Displacement error standard deviation of 3.10 pixels after 60 iterations. Checkerboard test (max strain ~25%): Displacement error standard deviation < 1.2 pixel after 60 iterations. Strengths: Produces sharp edges and correct gray levels even with large displacements, unlike standard ART which produces blurry reconstructions with split parts. Limitations: Assumes constant optical flow; not robust to gray level variations without extension. Computationally expensive due to sensitivity calculation. Usage: Applicable to in situ mechanical tests, synchrotron beam-lines, and data assimilation. DynTomo was introduced in 2018 by. It is derived from Algebraic Reconstruction Techniques (ART) coupled with Projection-based Digital Volume Correlation (P-DVC). The method was designed to handle large displacements and strains in dynamic tomography, such as those found in in situ mechanical testing. It was tested on numerical phantoms (Shepp-Logan and checkerboard) with parallel projection geometry. Dynamic Tomographic Reconstruction of Deforming Volumes, https://doi.org/10.3390/ma11081395, fetched 2026-10-26

name: Physics-Based Image Formation Models
body: Physics-Based Image Formation Models define the differentiable forward operator \mathcal{P} that maps a 3D (or 4D) volume representation to 2D projection images, serving as the core component in inverse rendering pipelines. Unlike generic differentiable renderers, these models are tailored to specific physical acquisition modalities (e.g., X-ray absorption, ultrasound wave propagation) to ensure physical consistency and computational efficiency. They distinguish themselves from siblings like Neural Adaptive Tomography by explicitly modeling the underlying physics (such as linear absorption or coupled wave equations) rather than relying solely on learned neural priors or adaptive sampling strategies. All methods in this family rely on the differentiability of the forward projection operator \mathcal{P} and its adjoint (back-projection) \mathcal{P}^T. The core optimization problem is generally formulated as minimizing a loss function \mathcal{L} between the measured sinogram p and the rendered projection \hat{p} = \mathcal{P}(x) of the current volume estimate x: \minx \mathcal{L}(\mathcal{P}(x), p) + \lambda R(x) where R(x) is a regularizer and \lambda is a weighting factor. The gradient of the loss with respect to the volume x is computed via the chain rule: \frac{\partial \mathcal{L}}{\partial x} = \mathcal{P}^T \left( \frac{\partial \mathcal{L}}{\partial \hat{p}} \right) The term \frac{\partial \mathcal{L}}{\partial \hat{p}} is the residual gradient in projection space (e.g., p - \hat{p} for MSE), and \mathcal{P}^T is the back-projection operator. Key shared components include: 1. Forward Projection: Ray marching through the volume representation (voxels, octrees, or neural fields) to compute line integrals of density/absorption coefficients. 2. Backward Projection (Adjoint): Distributing the error from the 2D detector plane back into the 3D volume. 3. Optimization Loop: An iterative process (e.g., SGD, Adam) that updates the volume parameters (voxel values, neural network weights, or Gaussian parameters) to reduce the projection error. Represents a continuously deforming 3D object as a 4D density function h(x, y, z, t), discretized into Nk static frames [3268-space-time-image-formation-model.md]. It differs from warp-based methods by treating time as a direct dimension of the density field, allowing for topology changes but potentially suffering from temporal inconsistency [3268-space-time-image-formation-model.md]. Choose this when reconstructing dynamic objects where deformation is complex and topology changes are expected [3268-space-time-image-formation-model.md]. A differentiable forward model for synthesizing ultrasound B-mode images by solving coupled forward and backward wave amplitude equations across voxel interfaces using a sparse linear system [5511-b-mode-image-reconstruction.md]. It distinguishes itself from standard ray-marching volume rendering by modeling wave physics rather than simple line integrals of density [5511-b-mode-image-reconstruction.md]. Choose this for differentiable ultrasound rendering where acoustic wave propagation physics are critical [5511-b-mode-image-reconstruction.md]. Reconstruction of a 3D density field from images using an optical absorption-only model, reducing the problem to a linear optimization problem solvable via DiffDVR. Step: Multi-resolution optimization: Start with volume resolution 32^3. Double the resolution in each dimension after 10 iterations. Perform optimization for 50 iterations at the highest resolution. Formula: Loss function: Same L{\text{total}} as TF reconstruction, but the smoothing prior is computed on reconstructed volume densities in 3D with \lambda = 0.5. Parameter: Views: 64 uniformly sampled views on a surrounding sphere. Image Resolution: 512^2. Reconstructed Volume Resolution: 256^3. Step size: 0.2 voxels during reconstruction. Optimizer: Adam with batch size 8 and learning rate 0.3. Number: Performance comparison for human skull dataset: ASTRA takes 53 seconds, DiffDVR takes ~12 minutes, Mitsuba takes multiple hours. The family originates from the application of differentiable rendering techniques to tomographic reconstruction. Early work focused on adapting standard volume rendering pipelines (like DiffDVR) to inverse problems, demonstrating that absorption-only models could be solved using differentiable optimizers, though at higher computational cost than algebraic methods. The field has since expanded to include specialized physics-based models for modalities like ultrasound, where simple ray-tracing is insufficient to capture wave phenomena B-mode Image Reconstruction. Differentiable Direct Volume Rendering, https://arxiv.org/abs/2107.12672v1, fetched 2026-10-26

name: Space-Time Image Formation Model
head: 4D density function model
body: The Space-Time Image Formation Model represents a continuously deforming 3D object as a 4D density function h(x, y, z, t), discretized into a sequence of Nk frames, each treated as an approximately static 3D volume. It formulates tomographic reconstruction for dynamic scenes as a block-diagonal linear system, solving for each frame's volume independently within the forward projection operator. Unlike warp-based methods that separate geometry into a canonical form and a dynamic transformation, this approach uses a single unified representation to directly regress dynamic properties, making it tolerant of topology changes but prone to time inconsistency. Inputs: Np: Total number of captured projection images. Nk: Number of reconstructed frames (time steps), where Nk \le Np. N\theta: Number of projections contributing to each frame. Typically N\theta = Np / Nk. M: Number of pixels in a single projection image. Nv: Number of voxels in the 3D grid for each frame. Outputs: \mathbf{f}: The reconstructed 4D density volume, represented as a vector in \mathbb{R}^{Nv Nk}. Data Structures: The 4D density volume is described by a column vector \mathbf{f} composed of Nk sub-vectors \mathbf{f}t, where each \mathbf{f}t \in \mathbb{R}^{Nv} represents the 3D volume at the t-th time step: \mathbf{f} = \{\mathbf{f}0, \mathbf{f}1, \dots, \mathbf{f}{Nk-1}\} The measured data is a vector \mathbf{p} containing the sinogram data for all frames: \mathbf{p} = \{\mathbf{p}0, \mathbf{p}1, \dots, \mathbf{p}{Nk-1}\} where \mathbf{p}t \in \mathbb{R}^{N\theta M} is the vector of measured data for frame t. Formulas: The tomography problem is expressed as a linear system \mathbf{A} \mathbf{f} = \mathbf{p}. The matrix \mathbf{A} is a block diagonal matrix where each block \mathbf{A}t \in \mathbb{R}^{N\theta M \times Nv} models the Radon transform operator for the N\theta projections contributing to the t-th frame: \mathbf{A} = \begin{pmatrix} \mathbf{A}0 & & & \\ & \ddots & & \\ & & \mathbf{A}t & \\ & & & \ddots \\ & & & & \mathbf{A}{Nk-1} \end{pmatrix} The forward projection for each frame computes \hat{\mathbf{p}}t = \mathbf{A}t \mathbf{f}t. Steps: 1. Discretization: Divide the temporal domain into Nk frames. 2. Projection Assignment: Assign N\theta unique projection angles to each frame. The total number of projections Np is distributed such that N\theta = Np / Nk. All projection angles are unique across the entire sequence. 3. Forward Projection: For each frame t, compute the predicted measurements \hat{\mathbf{p}}t by applying the Radon transform matrix \mathbf{A}t to the current volume estimate \mathbf{f}t. 4. Optimization: Minimize the loss function defined in the parent framework to update \mathbf{f}. 5. Reconstruction: Solve the ill-posed inverse problem to recover \mathbf{f}. Parameters: Nk: Number of reconstructed frames. Constraint: Nk \le Np. N\theta: Number of projections per frame. Typical value: N\theta = Np / Nk. N{min}: Minimum number of projections for acceptable quality. Values such as N{min} = 10 are noted for achieving results. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Ill-posedness: The problem is ill-posed, especially when few projections are used per frame (N\theta is small). Time Inconsistency: Independent frame reconstruction can lead to temporal discontinuities. Sampling Strategy: The sampling strategy is decoupled from the magnitude of deformation. The number of reconstructed frames Nk is independent of the number of capture rounds and can be chosen post-capture. Static Assumption: The model assumes each frame is approximately static. If deformation is too rapid within a frame's time window, reconstruction quality degrades. Models dynamic scenes by extending the query space to include time as a direct input, omitting explicit deformation networks. Unlike warp-based methods, it uses a single unified function to regress dynamic properties, tolerating topology changes but suffering from time inconsistency. Time Complexity: Depends on the number of frames Nk and the cost of the Radon transform \mathbf{A}t. Memory Complexity: O(Nv Nk) to store the 4D volume vector \mathbf{f}. Strengths: Tolerant of topology changes; sampling strategy is decoupled from deformation magnitude; Nk can be chosen post-capture. Limitations: Prone to time inconsistency; ill-posed with few projections per frame; assumes approximate static geometry per frame. When to use: When topology changes are expected, or when post-capture choice of temporal resolution is desired. When not to use: When high temporal consistency is required without additional regularization, or when deformation is too rapid for the "static frame" assumption. The Space-Time Image Formation Model was introduced in the context of space-time tomographic reconstruction of deforming objects. It addresses the challenge of reconstructing 3D objects that undergo continuous deformation over time by discretizing the 4D density function into static frames. The approach allows for the reconstruction of dynamic scenes using a sequence of projections, where each frame is reconstructed from a subset of the total projections. Space-Time Tomographic Reconstruction of Deforming Objects, https://vccimaging.org/Publications/Zang2020Thesis/Zang2020Thesis.pdf, fetched 2026-10-30 (unofficial)

name: Space-time representations
body: Space-time representations model dynamic scenes by extending the query space of the rendering function to include time, omitting the explicit deformation network used in warp-based methods. Unlike warp-based approaches that separate geometry into a static canonical form and a dynamic transformation, space-time methods use a single unified function to directly regress dynamic properties by conditioning a 3D representation with a time component. This approach is tolerant of topology changes and can model a wider range of motion but is prone to time inconsistency. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A query tuple q = (p, \mathbf{d}, t), where p \in \mathbb{R}^3 is the spatial position, \mathbf{d} is the viewing direction, and t is the time coordinate. Output: A property vector \xi (e.g., color, density, or feature vector). Data Structures: The representation is implemented as either a neural implicit model conditioned on a time variable, a set of 3D Gaussians with time-dependent parameters, or an explicit feature grid. Algorithm: 1. Define the Query Function: The method uses a single unified function to directly regress dynamic properties. Two common formulations exist: Formulation A (Time in Main Function): f{\theta}: (\gamma(p, \mathbf{d}, t)) \rightarrow \xi \quad (12) Here, \gamma is an encoding function that processes position, direction, and time jointly, and \xi is the output property. Formulation B (Time in Encoding): f: (\text{enc}(p, t), [\text{enc}(\mathbf{d})]) \rightarrow \xi \quad (13) Here, the encoding function \text{enc} depends on time, while the main network f processes the encoded spatial and directional features. 2. Discretize Time: Divide the time interval into equally spaced time slots. 3. Compute Features at Time Slots: Compute features at these discrete time slots using an MLP-based neural network or an explicit feature grid. 4. Interpolate for Arbitrary Time: Compute the feature of a point p \in \mathbb{R}^3 at any time t by interpolating between the features of the neighboring time slots. 5. Enforce Time Consistency (Optional): Enforce time consistency locally by using flow fields, which define forward and backward mappings between neighboring time steps when available. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def queryspacetimerepresentation(p, d, t, timeslots, encnet, mainnet): """ Query a space-time representation for a property at position p, direction d, and time t. Implements Formulation B: time-dependent encoding with interpolation between slots. """ # 1. Find neighboring time slots k = 0 while k < len(timeslots) - 1 and timeslots[k + 1] <= t: k += 1 tk = timeslots[k] tk1 = timeslots[min(k + 1, len(timeslots) - 1)] # 2. Compute features at neighboring slots using an MLP or feature grid featk = encnet(concatenate(p, tk)) featk1 = encnet(concatenate(p, tk1)) # 3. Interpolate features for arbitrary time t alpha = (t - tk) / (tk1 - tk) if tk1 != tk else 0.0 interpolatedfeat = featk + alpha (featk1 - featk) # 4. Encode direction (static) encd = encnet(d) # 5. Main network regression xi = mainnet(concatenate(interpolatedfeat, encd)) return xi Parameters: Time slots: Equally spaced intervals used to discretize the time domain for feature computation. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Time Inconsistency: Due to the flexibility of the representation, the model may produce inconsistent results across time, especially if the number of observations is limited. Models temporal changes by learning a temporally global 3D canonical representation and a learnable, time-dependent deformation field. Sets itself apart by explicitly separating geometry and appearance, ensuring long-term correspondence. Choose when topology is stable and long-term consistency is critical. A failed design that models temporal changes by storing a static feature matrix for each spatial point and computing features via an inner product with time-dependent basis functions. It differs by attempting to represent the entire volume as a linear combination of static basis volumes, which proved intractable due to memory and artifacts. Time Complexity: Using grid interpolation between time slots decreases the computational burden and enables faster training compared to evaluating an MLP at every time step. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Tolerant of topology changes; can model a wider range of motion than warp-based methods; omits the explicit deformation network. Limitations: Prone to time inconsistency; performance depends on the number of observations available. When to Use: When the scene undergoes topology changes or when a simpler pipeline without explicit deformation fields is preferred. When Not to Use: When long-term temporal consistency is critical, as the representation is prone to time inconsistency. Space-time representations emerged as an alternative to warp-based dynamic scene representations, aiming to simplify the modeling of dynamic scenes by directly incorporating time into the query space. The approach builds on the idea of conditioning 3D representations with time, allowing for a unified function to regress dynamic properties. Recent advances have explored both neural implicit models and explicit feature grids to implement this paradigm. Recent Advances and Trends in Learning‐Based 3D Representations, https://doi.org/10.1111/cgf.70530, fetched 2026-10-26

name: Warp-based Dynamic Scene Representation
head: Deformation-based representations, Warp-based methods, Warping-based Dynamic Scene Representation
body: Warp-based dynamic scene representations model temporal changes by learning a temporally global 3D canonical representation and a learnable, time-dependent deformation field to warp canonical space to match observed scenes at each timestep. This approach ensures long-term correspondence, allowing for consistent novel view synthesis and smooth interpolation in the time dimension. Unlike Space-time representations, which extend the query space to include time directly, warp-based methods explicitly separate geometry and appearance into a static component and a deformation component. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A 3D point p in the deformed (observed) space, camera parameters \mathcal{C}, viewing direction \mathbf{d}, and time t. Output: An implicit field value \xi (e.g., density, color) at the queried location. Data Structures: Deformation Network T: A function mapping points from the deformed space to the canonical space (backward warp) or vice versa (forward warp). It is typically implemented as a Multi-Layer Perceptron (MLP). Alternatively, it can be modeled explicitly using polynomial bases, Fourier transforms, or learned basis functions. Static Representation F: A function that infers the implicit field from the canonical point p'. Steps: 1. Learn Canonical Representation: Learn a temporally global 3D representation (canonical space) that captures the static geometry and appearance of the scene. 2. Learn Deformation Field: Learn a deformation field T that maps points between the canonical space and the deformed space at specific time steps. Backward Warp: Map deformed states back to the canonical representation (p \rightarrow p'). Forward Warp: Alternatively, map from canonical space to dynamic time steps (p' \rightarrow p) to ensure smooth and continuous deformation. 3. Render: Query the static representation F at the warped canonical point p' to obtain the field value \xi. Formulas: The rendering function f is defined as the composition of the deformation network T and the static representation F: f = F \circ T Specifically, the mapping is formalized as: T: (p, \mathcal{C}0) \rightarrow p' F: p'[\mathbf{d}; \mathcal{C}] \rightarrow \xi Where: T is the deformation network mapping point p to its canonical counterpart p'. F is the static representation inferring the implicit field from p'. \mathcal{C}0 is the canonical camera configuration. \mathbf{d} is the viewing direction. \mathcal{C} is the camera parameters. \xi is the output field value. Parameters: Not given in the sources. Pitfalls and Edge Cases: Discontinuous Mapping: Backward warps often result in discontinuous mappings because various object configurations can occupy the same spatial location at different time steps. Forward warps are preferred to mitigate this. Topology Changes: Warp-based methods struggle with topology changes, limiting their applicability primarily to object-level modeling where the object maintains a consistent structure over time. DeVRF is a warp-based method that combines an explicit voxel-based canonical 3D volumetric grid with a 4D deformation field. It sets itself apart by using a static-to-dynamic learning paradigm: it first learns the static scene representation from multi-view stills, then learns the deformation from a few-view dynamic sequence. This approach allows for much faster convergence than fully implicit networks and simplifies learning 4D voxel deformation fields with limited dynamic data. Choose it when efficient learning of non-rigid motion is required with limited dynamic views. Strengths: Ensures long-term correspondence, allowing consistent novel view synthesis and smooth interpolation in the time dimension. Limitations: Struggles with topology changes, limiting applicability to object-level modeling with consistent structure. Backward warps can cause discontinuities. Complexity: Not given in the sources. Performance: Not given in the sources. Warp-based methods were introduced as a class of space-time representations that condition the representation with a time component. They model geometry and appearance as a continuous function of both space and time. Key references include [PSB 21, PSH 21, TTG 21, LDZY24, WYF 24, YGZ 24] for warping-based methods and [GSD 23] for forward warp approaches. Recent Advances and Trends in Learning‐Based 3D Representations, https://doi.org/10.1111/cgf.70530, fetched 2026-10-26

name: DeVRF
head: DeVRF, A method that designs a static-dynamic learning paradigm to simplify learning 4D voxel deformation fields using only a few dynamic sequences
body: DeVRF adapts NeRF-like volume rendering frameworks with explicit 3D representations to dynamic scenes by combining an explicit voxel-based canonical 3D volumetric grid with a 4D deformation field. It solves the problem of efficiently learning non-rigid motion in dynamic scenes by employing a static-to-dynamic learning paradigm: first learning the static scene representation from multi-view stills, then learning the deformation from a few-view dynamic sequence. This approach allows for much faster convergence than fully implicit networks and simplifies the learning of 4D voxel deformation fields using limited dynamic data. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: Multi-view static images for static initialization, a few-view dynamic video sequence for deformation learning, and camera poses for ray generation. Outputs: A canonical 3D voxel grid representing the static scene appearance and geometry, and a 4D deformation field mapping canonical space to observed space at specific times. Data Structures: 1. Canonical 3D Volumetric Grid: An explicit voxel-based grid storing features (e.g., density, color) for the static scene structure. The exact resolution and bit-packing are not specified in the sources. 2. 4D Deformation Field: A network or function that takes a 3D spatial coordinate (x, y, z) and a time coordinate t as input, and outputs a 3D displacement vector (\Delta x, \Delta y, \Delta z). Numbered Steps: 1. Static Initialization: Learn the static scene representation from multi-view still images using an explicit 3D voxel-based canonical grid. This establishes the baseline geometry and appearance without temporal dynamics. 2. Deformation Learning: Using a few-view dynamic sequence, learn the 4D deformation field that warps the canonical space to match the observed dynamic scenes at each timestep. 3. Rendering: During rendering, sample points along rays. Apply the deformation transform (querying the 4D deformation field with the sample point's 3D coordinates and the current time t) to warp the point from canonical space to the observed space. Query the canonical voxel grid at the warped position to retrieve features (density, color). 4. Optimization: Optimize the deformation field parameters to minimize the difference between rendered images and the dynamic input sequence. Formulas: Let p = (x, y, z) be a point in canonical space and t be the time. The deformation field D computes the displacement: p' = p + D(p, t) where p' is the point in the observed space at time t. The radiance C and density \sigma are then queried from the canonical voxel grid at p': C, \sigma = \text{GridQuery}(p') [G: The exact mathematical formulation of the deformation network architecture is not given in the sources.] Parameters: Static-to-Dynamic Ratio: The method relies on a significant portion of static initialization followed by dynamic refinement. Specific ratios are not given in the sources. Dynamic Sequence Length: A few-view dynamic sequence is used. The exact number of frames is not given in the sources. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Overfitting: Model training is prone to overfitting when modeling dynamic non-rigid scenes with 4D deformation fields on discrete voxels due to network parameter constraints. Time Information: Modeling time information and capturing point motion at different scales are challenges for voxel features in dynamic scenes. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def renderdevrfray(rayorigin, raydirection, timet, canonicalgrid, deformationnet): """ Renders a single ray for DeVRF. """ tmin, tmax = 0.0, 100.0 # Scene bounds numsamples = 128 stepsize = (tmax - tmin) / numsamples accumulatedcolor = [0.0, 0.0, 0.0] accumulatedalpha = 0.0 densitiessofar = 0.0 for i in range(numsamples): t = tmin + i stepsize pcanonical = [rayorigin[j] + t raydirection[j] for j in range(3)] # Apply deformation to get observed space point displacement = deformationnet(pcanonical, timet) pobserved = [pcanonical[j] + displacement[j] for j in range(3)] # [G: Standard trilinear interpolation on the canonical grid returns density and color] density, color = canonicalgrid.query(pobserved) # Standard volume rendering accumulation alpha = 1.0 - math.exp(-density stepsize) weight = alpha math.exp(-densitiessofar) accumulatedcolor = [accumulatedcolor[j] + weight color[j] for j in range(3)] accumulatedalpha += weight densitiessofar += density stepsize if accumulatedalpha > 0.99: break return accumulatedcolor def traindevrfr(staticimages, dynamicvideo, canonicalgridinit, deformationnetinit): """ Two-stage training process. """ # Stage 1: Static Initialization for staticview in staticimages: rendered = renderdevrfray(staticview.rayorigin, staticview.raydirection, 0.0, canonicalgridinit, deformationnetinit) # Mean squared error loss loss = sum((rendered[j] - staticview.image[j])2 for j in range(3)) / 3.0 # Standard gradient descent update for canonicalgridinit # Stage 2: Dynamic Deformation Learning for frame in dynamicvideo: rendereddynamic = renderdevrfray(frame.rayorigin, frame.raydirection, frame.time, canonicalgridinit, deformationnetinit) loss = sum((rendereddynamic[j] - frame.image[j])2 for j in range(3)) / 3.0 # Standard gradient descent update for deformationnetinit Enables dynamic scene reconstruction from monocular videos without known camera poses by jointly optimizing intrinsics, extrinsics, and both static and dynamic radiance fields. It uses a two-branch architecture and motion masks. Choose when camera poses are unknown. RoDynRF A foundational method for dynamic NeRF using a time-conditioned deformation network. Choose for implicit representations with known poses. D-NeRF Time Complexity: Faster convergence than fully implicit networks due to the explicit voxel-based canonical grid and static initialization. Specific training times are not given in the sources, but the method claims significant acceleration in optimization. Memory Complexity: Uses an explicit voxel-based canonical 3D volumetric grid, which is generally more memory-efficient than fully implicit networks for high-resolution scenes, but the exact memory footprint is not given in the sources. Performance: On synthetic datasets, DeVRF-dynamic achieved a PSNR of 34.29 dB and SSIM of 0.982, with GPU memory usage of 4.4 GB and training time of 0.13 hours. On real-world datasets, it achieved a PSNR of 31.68 dB and SSIM of 0.972, with GPU memory usage of 6.6 GB and training time of 0.18 hours. Strengths: Fast convergence, simplified learning process for 4D deformation fields, high rendering quality. Limitations: Prone to overfitting on non-rigid scenes due to parameter constraints. Requires multi-view static images for initialization and a few-view dynamic sequence. When to use: When you have multi-view static images and a short dynamic sequence, and need fast convergence and high quality. When not to use: For scenes with complex non-rigid motion where overfitting is a concern, or when only monocular video is available without static initialization. DeVRF was proposed by Liu et al. in 2022. It was designed to address the challenges of applying voxel features to dynamic scenes, specifically modeling time information and capturing point motion at different scales. The method builds on the potential of voxel-based representations but introduces a static-dynamic learning paradigm to simplify the learning of 4D deformation fields. It is used in the context of dynamic scene reconstruction and novel view synthesis for dynamic scenes. name: Fixed Basis for Time Axis
head: Basis Function Volume Representation, Static Feature Matrix with Time Basis
body: A failed design for dynamic scene representation that models temporal changes by storing a static feature matrix for each spatial point and computing features at time t via an inner product with time-dependent basis functions. It differs from successful methods like HexPlane by attempting to represent the entire spatiotemporal volume as a linear combination of static basis volumes, which proved computationally intractable due to excessive memory requirements and reconstruction artifacts. Inputs: Spatial dimensions X, Y, Z. Number of time basis functions Rt. Feature dimension F. Time parameter t. Outputs: Feature vector \mathbf{V}t \in \mathbb{R}^F for a specific spatial location and time t. Data Structures: The naive representation stores a static feature matrix for every spatial point. Basis Volumes Stack (\hat{\mathbf{V}}): A tensor of shape \mathbb{R}^{XYZF \times Rt}. This can be viewed as a stack of Rt basis volumes \hat{\mathbf{V}}i, where each \hat{\mathbf{V}}i has shape \mathbb{R}^{XYZF}. Time Coefficients (\mathbf{f}(t)): A vector of shape \mathbb{R}^{Rt} containing the values of the basis functions at time t. Numbered Steps: 1. Define Basis Functions: Construct the vector \mathbf{f}(t) using a set of sine and cosine functions, similar to positional encoding in neural radiance fields. The standard definition is: \mathbf{f}(t) = [1, \sin(t), \cos(t), \sin(2t), \cos(2t), \sin(4t), \cos(4t), \dots] Legendre or Chebyshev polynomials were also explored as alternatives. 2. Compute Features (Naive Approach): For a spatial location (x,y,z), retrieve the feature matrix \mathbf{M}{xyz} \in \mathbb{R}^{F \times Rt} from \hat{\mathbf{V}}. Compute the feature vector at time t using the inner product: \mathbf{V}t = \sum{i=1}^{Rt} \mathbf{f}(t)i \cdot \hat{\mathbf{V}}i(x,y,z) = \hat{\mathbf{V}}(x,y,z) \cdot \mathbf{f}(t) where \hat{\mathbf{V}}(x,y,z) is the slice of the basis stack at (x,y,z) with shape \mathbb{R}^{F \times Rt}. 3. Memory Optimization (Tensor Decomposition): Due to the memory cost of the naive approach, tensor decomposition is applied to factorize the volume into smaller components. The representation is factorized into matrices M{XY}, M{XZ}, M{YZ} and vectors vX, vY, vZ, each augmented with an additional dimension Rt. M{XY}^T \in \mathbb{R}^{XY \times Rt}. vX^T \in \mathbb{R}^{X \times Rt}. Similar structures are used for M{XZ}, M{YZ}, vY, vZ. 4. Compute Features (Decomposed Approach): a. Multiply \mathbf{f}(t) with the transposed decomposition matrices and vectors along the last dimension (Rt) to obtain time-specific matrices \mathbf{M} and vectors \mathbf{v}. b. Use the resulting \mathbf{M} and \mathbf{v} to calculate features following the HexPlane feature aggregation equation (Eq. 1 in). 5. Training Regularization: a. Apply a weighted L1 loss to regularize the time-decomposed components M{Tr} and v{Tr}. Higher weights are assigned to high-frequency coefficients to encourage smoothness. b. Use smoothly bandwidth annealing during training to gradually introduce high-frequency components. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import numpy as np def computebasisvector(t, numfreqs=4): """ Computes the basis function vector f(t). Args: t: float, time parameter. numfreqs: int, number of frequency pairs (excluding DC). Returns: f: np.array of shape (2 numfreqs + 1,) """ f = [1.0] for i in range(1, numfreqs + 1): f.append(np.sin(i t)) f.append(np.cos(i t)) return np.array(f) def getfeaturesnaive(x, y, z, t, basisstack, ft): """ Naive feature retrieval from the full basis stack. Args: x, y, z: int, spatial coordinates. t: float, time. basisstack: np.array of shape (X, Y, Z, F, Rt). ft: np.array of shape (Rt,). Returns: Vt: np.array of shape (F,). """ # Retrieve feature matrix for point (x,y,z): shape (F, Rt) featurematrix = basisstack[x, y, z,:,:] # Inner product: (F, Rt) dot (Rt,) -> (F,) Vt = np.dot(featurematrix, ft) return Vt def getfeaturesdecomposed(x, y, z, t, MXY, MXZ, MYZ, vX, vY, vZ, ft, Ydim, Zdim): """ Feature retrieval using tensor decomposition. Args: x, y, z: int, spatial coordinates. t: float, time. MXY: np.array of shape (XY, Rt). MXZ: np.array of shape (XZ, Rt). MYZ: np.array of shape (YZ, Rt). vX: np.array of shape (X, Rt). vY: np.array of shape (Y, Rt). vZ: np.array of shape (Z, Rt). ft: np.array of shape (Rt,). Ydim, Zdim: int, spatial dimensions for index flattening. Returns: Vt: np.array of shape (F,). """ # Map 3D coordinates to 2D indices for matrices # Assuming row-major flattening for XY, XZ, YZ xyidx = x Ydim + y xzidx = x Zdim + z yzidx = y Zdim + z # Get time-specific components by multiplying with ft # MXYt: shape () -> scalar for this xy MXYt = np.dot(MXY[xyidx,:], ft) MXZt = np.dot(MXZ[xzidx,:], ft) MYZt = np.dot(MYZ[yzidx,:], ft) vXt = np.dot(vX[x,:], ft) vYt = np.dot(vY[y,:], ft) vZt = np.dot(vZ[z,:], ft) # Combine using HexPlane Eq. 1 logic # Note: The exact combination formula (Eq 1) is not fully detailed in the provided text, # but typically involves combining these projected features. # The sources state features are calculated "following Eq 1" of the parent HexPlane paper. # The exact aggregation formula is not provided in the notes, so it is omitted here. Vt = np.zeros(27) # Placeholder shape matching F=27 return Vt Parameters: Rt: Number of time basis functions. Typical value: 32. F: Feature dimension. Typical value: 27. Basis function frequencies: Powers of 2 (1, 2, 4, \dots) are used in the sine/cosine series. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Memory Overflow: The naive implementation requires enormous GPU memory. For X=Y=Z=128, Rt=32, F=27, storage is ~7GB, and training memory reaches ~30GB due to back-propagation and Adam optimizer states. Performance: Extremely slow due to memory I/O bottlenecks when reading/writing large volumes. Visual Artifacts: Severe color jittering and distortions occur in the rendered output. Degenerate Input: Fails to produce satisfactory results when objects move too fast or when there are too few observations to synthesize details. The successful method that replaced this design. It uses a different feature aggregation strategy to avoid the memory and artifact issues of the fixed basis approach. An alternative sibling method that uses explicit deformation networks instead of basis functions or static feature planes. Time Complexity: Extremely high due to memory I/O bottlenecks in the naive implementation. The decomposed version reduces memory footprint but adds computational overhead for the tensor contractions. Memory Complexity: Naive: O(XYZF Rt). Example: 7GB for 128^3 volume. Decomposed: Significantly reduced by factorizing into M{XY}, M{XZ}, M{YZ}, vX, vY, vZ. Strengths: Conceptually simple; leverages traditional time-series basis function approaches. Limitations: Proven to be a "failed design" due to intractable memory usage, slow training/inference speeds, and poor visual quality (color jittering, distortions). When to use: Not recommended for production. Included primarily as a cautionary example of what not to do in dynamic scene representation. This method was explored as part of the development of HexPlane, a fast representation for dynamic scenes. The authors initially attempted to model dynamic scenes by extending the query space with time using fixed basis functions, similar to positional encoding. However, they found this approach computationally infeasible and visually inferior, leading to the development of the HexPlane architecture which uses feature planes instead of a full 3D basis stack. The design is discussed in Section 9.1 of the HexPlane paper as a "Failed Design for Dynamic Scenes". HexPlane: A Fast Representation for Dynamic Scenes, https://doi.org/10.1109/cvpr52729.2023.00021, fetched 2026-10-26

name: B-mode Image Reconstruction
head: Image Formation Model
body: B-mode Image Reconstruction is a differentiable forward model for synthesizing ultrasound B-mode images from volumetric data, primarily used in differentiable ultrasound rendering. It distinguishes itself from standard ray-marching volume rendering by modeling coupled forward and backward wave amplitudes across voxel interfaces using a sparse linear system, rather than simple line integrals of density. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A 3D volumetric representation of tissue acoustic properties, specifically reflection coefficients R and transmission coefficients T. Output: A 2D B-mode image where pixel intensity corresponds to echo amplitude first differences, mapped to beam angle and depth. Data Structures: The core data structure is a sparse matrix A representing the coupled recursion relations for wave amplitudes. For a depth of N voxels, the matrix has dimensions (2N+2) \times (2N+2). The matrix is strictly banded with at most three non-zero entries per row, resulting in O(N) non-zero elements. The indices r (row) and c (column) are defined for i = 0, \dots, N-1 and r, c = 0, \dots, 2N+1. body: This method reconstructs a 2D slice from parallel projections by modeling the slice as a 1D piecewise constant function defined by n parameters. It solves for these parameters by minimizing a constrained quadratic criterion that compares model projections against measured data. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Measured parallel projection data p for a specific 2D slice. Output: A vector of n parameters defining the 1D piecewise constant model of the slice. Data Structures: The model represents the 2D slice as a function constant along one axis and piecewise constant along the orthogonal axis. Model Parameters: A vector \theta \in \mathbb{R}^n containing the values for each of the n zones. Zones: The domain is partitioned into n contiguous zones. Steps: 1. Model Definition: Define the 1D piecewise constant model f(x; \theta) for the slice, where \theta contains n parameters representing the values of n zones. 2. Forward Projection: Compute the theoretical projection \hat{p}(\theta) of the model f(x; \theta) using parallel ray geometry. 3. Criterion Formulation: Construct a quadratic criterion J(\theta) measuring the difference between the measured data p and the model projection \hat{p}(\theta): J(\theta) = \| p - \hat{p}(\theta) \|^2 4. Regularization: Since the quadratic criterion J(\theta) is non-differentiable due to the piecewise constant nature of the model, apply one of three proposed regularization techniques to handle this non-differentiability. 5. Constrained Minimization: Solve for the optimal parameters \theta^ by minimizing the regularized criterion subject to constraints: \min\theta J{reg}(\theta) \quad \text{subject to constraints} 6. Noise Analysis (Optional): Compute the covariance matrix of the estimated parameter vector \theta to analyze sensitivity to noise in the input data. Pseudocode: Unverified code. name: Noise Sensitivity Analysis via Covariance Matrix
head: Covariance-based Noise Sensitivity, Parameter Noise Analysis
body: This method analyzes the sensitivity of the reconstructed parameter vector to noise present in the input projection data by computing the covariance matrix of the parameters. It builds on 1D Slice Reconstruction with Piecewise Constant Model, where a 2D slice is modeled as a 1D piecewise constant function with n parameters, and reconstruction is achieved by minimizing a constrained quadratic criterion. While the parent method solves for the parameters, this analysis quantifies the uncertainty and stability of those solutions in the presence of measurement noise. Inputs and Outputs: Input: The reconstructed parameter vector \mathbf{p} (of size n) obtained from the piecewise constant model, and the covariance matrix \mathbf{C} of this vector. Output: The covariance matrix \mathbf{C}, which characterizes the noise sensitivity of each parameter and their correlations. Data Structures: \mathbf{p}: A 1D array of length n, containing the estimated values of the piecewise constant parameters. \mathbf{C}: An n \times n symmetric matrix. The diagonal elements C{ii} represent the variance of the i-th parameter, and off-diagonal elements C{ij} represent the covariance between parameters i and j. Steps: 1. Reconstruction: Perform the 1D slice reconstruction to obtain the parameter vector \mathbf{p}. This involves minimizing a constrained quadratic criterion. Note that the criterion is non-differentiable, so regularization techniques may be applied. 2. Covariance Determination: Compute the covariance matrix \mathbf{C} of the parameter vector \mathbf{p} with respect to the noise in the input data. The specific mathematical derivation of \mathbf{C} depends on the linearization of the forward projection model and the noise statistics of the input data, which are not detailed in the provided sources. 3. Sensitivity Analysis: Use \mathbf{C} to analyze the sensitivity of each parameter. The standard deviation of the i-th parameter is \sigmai = \sqrt{C{ii}}. High values indicate high sensitivity to noise. Parameters: Not given in the sources. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: The non-differentiability of the quadratic criterion requires regularization, which may affect the accuracy of the covariance estimation if not properly accounted for. The sources do not specify how the noise statistics of the input data are modeled or incorporated into the covariance calculation. Pseudocode: Unverified code. Args: p: numpy array of shape (n,), reconstructed parameter vector. C: numpy array of shape (n, n), covariance matrix of the parameters. Returns: stddevs: numpy array of shape (n,), standard deviations of each parameter. correlations: numpy array of shape (n, n), correlation matrix. """ # Calculate standard deviations from the diagonal of the covariance matrix stddevs = np.sqrt(np.diag(C)) # Calculate correlation matrix for normalized sensitivity # Correlation(i, j) = Cov(i, j) / (std(i) std(j)) stddevssafe = np.where(stddevs == 0, 1e-10, stddevs) # Avoid division by zero correlations = C / np.outer(stddevssafe, stddevssafe) return stddevs, correlations Recovers constant absorption (\sigma) and source (q) parameters from a sequence of intensity measurements by fitting a linear recurrence relation I{k+1} = a Ik + b. It is chosen when the data consists of a 1D sequence of intensity measurements with known step size ds. The method validates that intensity.size() >= 3 and ds > 0. It calculates sums Sx, Sy, S{xx}, S{xy} over k=0 to N-2 where N = \text{intensity.size()} - 1, with x = Ik and y = I{k+1}. The determinant D = N S{xx} - Sx^2 is computed; if |D| \le 10^{-14}, the result is invalid. The coefficients are a = (N S{xy} - Sx Sy) / D and b = (Sy - a Sx) / N. name: Regularization of Non-Differentiable Quadratic Criterion
head: Regularization for Piecewise Constant Model
body: This method addresses the non-differentiability of the quadratic criterion used in 1D slice reconstruction with a piecewise constant model. It applies regularization techniques to handle the optimization problem where the objective function is not smooth, enabling stable parameter estimation. Inputs: Measured projection data vector y. Forward operator matrix F mapping the unknown radial field x to the projection space. Regularization weight parameter \mu2. Outputs: Reconstructed radial field vector x. Data Structures: x: Vector of size n (number of parameters in the 1D piecewise constant model). F: Matrix of size m \times n (where m is the number of projections). L2: Second-order finite-difference operator matrix of size n \times n. Formulas: The objective function \Phi(x) combines data fidelity and a smoothness penalty: \Phi(x) = \|Fx - y\|2^2 + \mu2^2 \|L2 x\|2^2 where: \|Fx - y\|2^2 is the data fidelity term. \mu2^2 \|L2 x\|2^2 is the Tikhonov regularization term. L2 is defined as: L2 = \frac{1}{\Delta r^2} \begin{bmatrix} 1 & -2 & 1 & 0 & \cdots & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & -2 & 1 & \cdots & 0 \\ \vdots & & & \ddots & & \vdots \\ 0 & \cdots & 0 & 1 & -2 & 1 \end{bmatrix} \Delta r is the radial step size. Steps: 1. Expand the objective function terms into quadratic forms: \|Fx - y\|2^2 = x^T F^T Fx - 2x^T F^T y + y^T y \mu2^2 \|L2 x\|2^2 = \mu2^2 x^T L2^T L2 x 2. Combine the expanded terms to form the full objective function: \Phi(x) = x^T F^T Fx - 2x^T F^T y + y^T y + \mu2^2 x^T L2^T L2 x 3. Compute the derivative of \Phi(x) with respect to x and set it to zero to find the minimum: \frac{\partial \Phi}{\partial x} = 2F^T Fx - 2F^T y + 2\mu2^2 L2^T L2 x = 0 4. Rearrange into the regularized normal equation: (F^T F + \mu2^2 L2^T L2) x = F^T y Define B^T = F^T F + \mu2^2 L2^T L2. The equation becomes: B^T x = F^T y 5. Solve the linear system B^T x = F^T y using Cholesky factorization of B^T. 6. Determine the optimal regularization weight \mu2 using the L-curve method: Scan \mu2 over a range (e.g., 10^{-10} to 10^{-2} with Nk = 201 steps). For each \mu{2,k}, solve for xk. Compute the residual norm R(\mu{2,k}) = \|Fxk - y\|2 and the regularization norm P(\mu{2,k}) = \|L2 xk\|2. Plot \log{10} R(\mu{2,k}) vs \log{10} P(\mu{2,k}) to form the L-curve. Select the \mu2 corresponding to the corner of the L-curve as the optimal value. Parameters: \mu2: Regularization weight. Typical scanning range is 10^{-10} to 10^{-2} with 201 steps for L-curve analysis. Edge cases and pitfalls: The second-order operator L2 acts globally and does not explicitly enforce the physical center-axis condition (\partial x / \partial r |{r=0} = 0) for axisymmetric fields, leading to inaccuracies near the symmetry axis. A regularization technique to mitigate noise amplification in direct and iterative inversions by adding a second-order smoothness penalty to the objective function. It stabilizes the reconstruction but fails to explicitly impose the zero-gradient condition at the center axis of axisymmetric fields. Time Complexity: Solving the linear system via Cholesky factorization is O(n^3) for dense matrices, though F^T F and L2^T L2 may have structure. The L-curve search requires solving the system Nk times (e.g., 201 times). Memory Complexity: Requires storage for F, L2, and the factorized matrix B^T. Strengths: Mitigates noise amplification observed in direct and iterative inversions. Limitations: Does not enforce the physical center-axis condition (\partial x / \partial r |{r=0} = 0), causing inaccuracies near the symmetry axis in axisymmetric tomography. The method originates from tomographic reconstruction of a 2D slice from parallel projections using a 1D piecewise constant model. The quadratic criterion for this model is non-differentiable, necessitating regularization techniques. Single-parameter Tikhonov regularization was proposed as a standard approach to handle noise amplification. name: Iterative Solvers
head: Conjugate Gradient on the Normal Equations, Landweber, Landweber Iteration, Landweber Iteration Solver
body: Iterative solvers reconstruct volumetric data by minimizing the discrepancy between measured sinograms and forward-projected volume estimates through repeated updates. They are implemented as specialized algorithms (Conjugate Gradient, CGNE, Landweber) that exploit the linear structure of the Radon transform for efficient computation. They distinguish themselves from general Differentiable CT Execution Model approaches by providing optimized, mathematically grounded solvers tailored to tomographic inverse problems. Iterative solvers operate on the linear system Ax = b, where A is the forward projection operator (Radon transform), x is the volume to reconstruct, and b is the measured sinogram. The core mechanism relies on the differentiability of the forward operator \mathcal{P} and its adjoint (back-projection) \mathcal{P}^T. Inputs: radon: An object defining the geometry (angles, detector count, beam type) and providing forward() and backprojection() methods. sino: The measured sinogram tensor, shape (N{batch}, N{angles}, N{detectors}). guess: Initial volume estimate tensor, shape (N{batch}, D, D, D) or similar. alpha (Landweber only): Step size parameter. maxiter / iterations: Number of optimization steps. Outputs: rec: Reconstructed volume tensor, same shape as guess. Volume (x): 3D tensor (e.g., D \times D \times D) representing density/absorption coefficients. Sinogram (p): 2D or 3D tensor representing line integrals. Residual (r): Difference between measured sinogram and forward-projected volume. Landweber iteration is an iterative solver for CT reconstruction. It updates the volume estimate by moving in the direction of the back-projected residual. Step Size Estimation: The step size \alpha is estimated using power iteration on the operator A^T A, typically scaled by 0.95 to ensure stability. Update Rule: x{k+1} = xk + \alpha \mathcal{P}^T (p - \mathcal{P}(xk)) Where: xk is the volume estimate at iteration k. \mathcal{P}(xk) is the forward projection (synthetic sinogram). p is the measured sinogram. \mathcal{P}^T(\cdot) is the back-projection operator. \alpha is the step size. Pseudocode (Landweber): Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def landwebersolve(radon, sino, guess, maxiter, alpha): """ Solve tomography reconstruction using Landweber iteration. Args: radon: Radon object with forward() and backprojection() methods. sino: Measured sinogram tensor. guess: Initial volume estimate tensor (zeros). maxiter: Number of iterations. alpha: Step size (estimated via power iteration, typically < 2/sigmamax^2). Returns: rec: Reconstructed volume. """ x = guess.clone() for in range(maxiter): # Forward projection: compute synthetic sinogram sinopred = radon.forward(x) # Compute residual in projection space residual = sino - sinopred # Back-projection of residual to update volume update = radon.backprojection(residual) x = x + alpha update return x CGNE solves the normal equations A^T A x = A^T b using the Conjugate Gradient method. Update Rule: The algorithm applies standard CG to the system M x = c where M = A^T A and c = A^T b. 1. Initialize x0, r0 = c - M x0, p0 = r0. 2. For k = 0, 1, \dots: \alphak = \frac{rk^T rk}{pk^T M pk} x{k+1} = xk + \alphak pk r{k+1} = rk - \alphak M pk \betak = \frac{r{k+1}^T r{k+1}}{rk^T rk} p{k+1} = r{k+1} + \betak pk Where M pk = A^T (A pk) requires two projections (forward then back-projection). Pseudocode (CGNE): Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def cgnesolve(radon, sino, guess, maxiter): """ Solve tomography reconstruction using Conjugate Gradient on Normal Equations. Args: radon: Radon object. sino: Measured sinogram. guess: Initial volume estimate. maxiter: Maximum iterations. Returns: rec: Reconstructed volume. """ x = guess.clone() # Compute initial residual r = A^T b - A^T A x c = radon.backprojection(sino) Ax = radon.forward(x) Mx = radon.backprojection(Ax) r = c - Mx p = r.clone() # r^T r (standard dot product) rdot = sum(r r) for in range(maxiter): # Compute M p = A^T (A p) Ap = radon.forward(p) Mp = radon.backprojection(Ap) # alpha = (r^T r) / (p^T M p) pMp = sum(p Mp) alpha = rdot / pMp # x = x + alpha p x = x + alpha p # r = r - alpha M p r = r - alpha Mp rdotnew = sum(r r) # beta = (rnew^T rnew) / (r^T r) beta = rdotnew / rdot # p = r + beta p p = r + beta p rdot = rdotnew return x Step Size (\alpha): For Landweber, typically estimated as 0.95 \times \frac{2}{\sigma{max}^2} where \sigma{max} is found via power iteration. Iterations: 500 is a common default for convergence in test settings. Batch Processing: All solvers support batch processing, allowing multiple volumes to be reconstructed in parallel on GPU. Precision: Half-precision (16-bit) storage provides speedups of >125× but may introduce numerical instability; single precision is safer for convergence. Step Size Selection: If \alpha is too large in Landweber, the iteration diverges. Ill-Conditioning: CGNE may struggle with ill-conditioned systems (e.g., sparse views) without regularization. SIRT updates all voxels simultaneously using normalized residuals, improving convergence stability in limited-angle or sparse-view scenarios compared to unnormalized methods like ART. This framework decomposes the optimization into independent proximal sub-problems, enabling the handling of non-smooth regularization (e.g., Total Variation) and large-scale linear systems using primal-dual splitting or stochastic sampling. ART updates the volume estimate one angle (or ray set) at a time, avoiding explicit storage of the system matrix by iteratively applying back-projection of residuals. An iterative reconstruction method using PyTorch's automatic differentiation to minimize the mean squared error between simulated and measured projections. It initializes the volume as a tensor with requiresgrad=True, uses an Adam optimizer (default lr=1e-2), and runs for a specified number of iterations (default 50). Memory Complexity: Requires storing the volume, sinogram, and intermediate vectors (residuals, search directions). Batch processing increases memory linearly with batch size. Performance: On a Tesla V100, TorchRadon's iterative solvers are >40× faster than Astra Toolbox in single precision, and >125× faster in half precision. Quality: In test settings, Landweber achieved an MSE of 1.39 \cdot 10^{-4} and CGNE achieved 4.42 \cdot 10^{-5}, outperforming FBP (2.22 \cdot 10^{-4}). Strengths: Handles sparse views and noise better than FBP; supports regularization; differentiable. Limitations: Not given in the sources. In the context of differentiable volume rendering and deep learning, libraries like TorchRadon have implemented these solvers to leverage GPU acceleration and automatic differentiation, enabling their use in end-to-end trainable pipelines. The integration of these solvers allows for hybrid reconstruction methods combining physics-based models with deep learning priors. name: SIRT (Simultaneous Iterative Reconstruction Technique)
head: Iterative Inversion, SIRT Reconstruction, Simultaneous Iterative Reconstruction Algorithm
body: SIRT is a global algebraic iterative reconstruction method that solves the discrete linear system Af = b arising from tomographic projection data by updating the volume estimate simultaneously for all projection lines. It reduces computational cost compared to line-by-line methods (like ART) and improves convergence robustness in noisy conditions by normalizing residuals and updates using row and column sums of the system matrix. Unlike direct inversion methods which fail under noise, SIRT provides a stable solution by treating the reconstruction as a simultaneous correction across the entire dataset. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Projection data (sinogram) y \in \mathbb{R}^M, forward projection operator A: \mathbb{R}^N \to \mathbb{R}^M, number of iterations K, relaxation parameter \omega (or step size), and volume shape N. Output: Reconstructed volume vector x{\text{rec}} \in \mathbb{R}^N. Data Structures: x{\text{rec}}: Reconstruction vector, initialized to zeros, shape A.\text{domain\shape}. y: Sinogram vector, shape A.\text{range\shape}. R: Row preconditioner vector, shape M (number of rays). C: Column preconditioner vector, shape N (number of voxels). A: Forward projection operator. A^T: Backward projection operator (transpose of A). Preconditioner Calculation: The row preconditioner R normalizes each ray residual by its total intersected length. The column preconditioner C normalizes the backprojected update by accumulated voxel sensitivity. 1. Compute R: Rj = \frac{1}{(A \mathbf{1})j} \quad \text{for } j=1,\dots,M where \mathbf{1} is a vector of ones with shape A.\text{domain\shape}. Clamp R to prevent division by zero: Rj \leftarrow \min(Rj, \frac{1}{\epsilon}) where \epsilon is a small constant (e.g., ts.epsilon). 2. Compute C: Ci = \frac{1}{(A^T \mathbf{1})i} \quad \text{for } i=1,\dots,N where \mathbf{1} is a vector of ones with shape A.\text{range\shape}. Clamp C: Ci \leftarrow \min(Ci, \frac{1}{\epsilon}). Iterative Update: The generalized update rule for the unknown vector x at iteration k+1 is: x^{(k+1)} = \max\left(0, x^{(k)} + \omega C A^T R (y - A x^{(k)})\right) where: \omega is the relaxation parameter (step size). R is the diagonal matrix with entries R{jj}. C is the diagonal matrix with entries C{ii}. The \max(0, \cdot) operation enforces nonnegativity. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def sirt(y, A, AT, numiters, stepsize, epsilon): """ Simultaneous Iterative Reconstruction Technique (SIRT). Args: y: Sinogram vector (M,) A: Forward projection function, takes (N,) returns (M,) AT: Backward projection function, takes (M,) returns (N,) numiters: Number of iterations stepsize: Relaxation parameter omega epsilon: Small constant to prevent division by zero Returns: xrec: Reconstructed volume vector (N,) """ # Initialize reconstruction vector to zeros # Note: domainshape is inferred from the output of AT(torch.ones(M)) or provided # For this implementation, we assume we can create a zeros vector of the correct size. # In practice, A.domainshape is needed. Here we assume it is known or derived. # Let's assume we have a function to get domain shape or it is passed. # Since A is an operator, we assume we can create a zeros vector of shape A.domainshape. # If not, we might need to infer it from AT(y) shape. # For clarity, we assume xrec is initialized to zeros of shape N. # We need to know N. Let's assume we have a way to get N. # In the tomosipo example, A.domainshape is used. # Here, we will assume we can create a zeros vector of the correct size. # Let's assume we have a variable N for the number of voxels. # If not, we can infer N from the shape of AT(y). # Initialize xrec to zeros # We need to know the shape of the volume. # Let's assume we have a function getdomainshape() or it is passed. # For the sake of this pseudocode, we assume we can create a zeros vector of the correct size. # We will use a placeholder for the shape, but in a real implementation, this must be known. # Let's assume we have a variable 'domainshape' available. # Initialize xrec to zeros with shape A.domainshape xrec = zeroslike(AT(y)) # This assumes AT(y) has the same shape as the volume, which is true for the transpose operator. # Compute row preconditioner R # R = 1 / (A ones) onesdomain = oneslike(xrec) forwardones = A(onesdomain) R = 1.0 / forwardones # Clamp R to prevent division by zero R = minimum(R, 1.0 / epsilon) # Compute column preconditioner C # C = 1 / (A^T ones) onesrange = oneslike(y) backwardones = AT(onesrange) C = 1.0 / backwardones # Clamp C to prevent division by zero C = minimum(C, 1.0 / epsilon) # Iterate for k in range(numiters): # Compute residual residual = y - A(xrec) # Scale residual by R scaledresidual = R residual # Backproject scaled residual backprojected = AT(scaledresidual) # Scale backprojected update by C update = C backprojected # Update volume xrec = xrec + stepsize update # Enforce nonnegativity xrec = maximum(xrec, 0.0) return xrec Parameters: numiters: Number of reconstruction iterations. Typical value: 100. Some studies use 1000 to ensure convergence. stepsize (\omega): Relaxation parameter or learning rate. Default value: 10^{-2}. epsilon: Small constant to clamp preconditioners. Exact numerical value is not specified in the sources. volshape: Dimensions of the output volume. Typical value: (96, 96, 96). Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Division by Zero: Preconditioners R and C must be clamped to prevent division by zero when rays or voxels have zero intersected length. Semi-convergence: Iterative approaches often exhibit semi-convergence even in noise-free conditions, leading to potential inaccuracies if not stopped at the optimal iteration. Nonnegativity: The \max(0, \cdot) operation is crucial for enforcing physical nonnegativity constraints. SART is an iterative algebraic reconstruction technique that solves the discrete linear system Af = b arising from tomographic projection data by updating the volume estimate simultaneously for all rays in a subset of projections. It improves upon single-ray methods (like ART) by normalizing the backprojection by the number of rays intersecting each voxel, which reduces streak artifacts and accelerates convergence. It is distinguished from its sibling SIRT by the order of normalization: SART normalizes the residual by the ray's total intersected length before backprojecting, whereas SIRT normalizes the backprojected update by the voxel's total intersected length. It is preferred over direct methods like FDK for limited projection scenarios and over Conjugate Gradient (CG) for sparse-view settings due to better convergence properties in matrix-free implementations. A classical Simultaneous Iterative Reconstruction Technique (SIRT) implementation using a custom backprojector, without autodiff. It initializes the volume to zeros and iteratively computes the forward projection, residual error, backprojection of the residual, and volume update using a step size. The step size is typically 10^{-2}. Time Complexity: O(K \cdot (M + N)) per iteration, where K is the number of iterations, M is the number of rays, and N is the number of voxels. Each iteration involves one forward projection and one backward projection. Memory Complexity: O(N + M) for storing the volume, sinogram, and preconditioners. Measured Performance: In a 128x128x128 volume with 100 projections, SIRT converges in 100 iterations. In a 96x96x96 volume with 30 iterations, it produces reconstructions comparable to FDK but with different artifact profiles. Scaling: SIRT scales well with the number of projections and voxels, but the number of iterations required for convergence can be high. Strengths: Robust to noise, handles incomplete data well, enforces nonnegativity. Limitations: Slow convergence compared to direct methods, requires careful tuning of the relaxation parameter. When to Use: Limited projection scenarios, sparse-view settings, noisy data. When Not to Use: When fast reconstruction is required and data is complete and noise-free. SIRT was developed as a global algebraic reconstruction technique to overcome the failure of direct inversion in noisy conditions. It is based on the work of Andersen and Kak (1984) and is widely used in tomographic applications. The method is implemented in various libraries, including tomosipo and custom implementations. It is used in medical imaging, industrial CT, and scientific tomography.
