name: Iterative Reconstruction (SIRT via Autodiff)
head: Gradient Descent Reconstruction
body: This method performs tomographic reconstruction by treating the volume estimation as a differentiable optimization problem, using automatic differentiation to minimize the mean squared error between simulated and measured projections. It differs from standard SIRT (Simultaneous Iterative Reconstruction Technique) by replacing explicit algebraic matrix operations with gradient descent via an autodiff engine, allowing for easier integration of custom physics constraints or differentiable regularizers. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: Measured projections as a tensor of shape (N, H, W) where N is the number of angles and H, W are detector dimensions. Projection geometry parameters defining source-detector distances and angles (e.g., DSO, DSD, detector pixel size, and a list of N angles). Volume dimensions D \times D \times D. Outputs: Reconstructed volume as a tensor of shape (D, D, D) representing the estimated attenuation coefficients. Data Structures: volume: A PyTorch tensor of shape (D, D, D) initialized with zeros or a prior estimate. It must have requiresgrad=True to track gradients. optimizer: An Adam optimizer instance initialized with the volume parameters. Numbered Steps: 1. Initialization: Create a tensor volume of shape (D, D, D) with requiresgrad=True. Initialize an Adam optimizer with volume as the parameter and lr=1e-2. 2. Iteration Loop: For k = 1 to iters: a. Zero Gradients: Call optimizer.zerograd() to clear previous gradients. b. Forward Projection: Compute simulated projections P{sim} from the current volume using a differentiable forward projector F(\cdot) defined by the geometry. P{sim} = F(\text{volume}). c. Loss Computation: Calculate the Mean Squared Error (MSE) between the simulated projections P{sim} and the measured projections P{meas}. d. Backpropagation: Compute gradients of the loss with respect to the volume: \nabla{\text{volume}} L = \frac{\partial L}{\partial \text{volume}}. This is handled automatically by the autodiff engine. e. Optimization Step: Update the volume parameters using the optimizer. Adam applies adaptive learning rates internally rather than a fixed step size. Formulas: L = \frac{1}{NHW} \sum{i=1}^{N} \sum{j=1}^{H} \sum{l=1}^{W} (P{sim}[i,j,l] - P{meas}[i,j,l])^2 where L is the loss, N is the number of angles, H and W are detector dimensions, and P{sim} and P{meas} are the simulated and measured projection tensors respectively. Parameters: lr: Learning rate, typically 1 \times 10^{-2}. iters: Number of optimization steps, default 50. geometry: Object containing DSO (Source-to-Object), DSD (Source-to-Detector), detector resolution, and angles. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Degenerate Input: If projections are all zeros or constant, the gradient may vanish, leading to no update. Initialize with a small random noise or a prior estimate (e.g., FDK) to break symmetry. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import torch import torch.nn.functional as F def iterativereconstructionautodiff(projections, geometry, volshape, iters=50, lr=1e-2): """ Reconstruct volume using SIRT-like gradient descent via autodiff. Args: projections: Tensor [N, H, W] of measured projections. geometry: Object with forwardproject method. volshape: Tuple (D, D, D) for volume dimensions. iters: Number of optimization steps. lr: Learning rate for Adam optimizer. Returns: Reconstructed volume tensor [D, D, D]. """ # Initialize volume tensor with gradients enabled volume = torch.zeros(volshape, requiresgrad=True, device=projections.device) # Initialize Adam optimizer optimizer = torch.optim.Adam([volume], lr=lr) for step in range(iters): # Zero gradients from previous step optimizer.zerograd() # Forward projection: simulate projections from current volume estimate simulatedprojections = geometry.forwardproject(volume) # Compute loss: Mean Squared Error between simulated and measured projections loss = F.mseloss(simulatedprojections, projections) # Backpropagate to compute gradients on the volume loss.backward() # Update volume parameters optimizer.step() return volume.detach() ACID is an iterative reconstruction framework that stabilizes an unstable deep reconstruction neural network by combining it with a Compressed Sensing (CS)-based sparsity-promoting module. It minimizes an objective function balancing neural network output consistency, data fidelity, residual error energy, and sparsity. ACID searches for a solution good in three aspects: image sparsity, big-data-driven prior, and iterative calibration to eliminate unexplained residual data. It differs from standard sparsity-minimization reconstruction by incorporating a data-driven deep prior (\Phi) to fill gaps where sparsity alone may not yield a unique solution, especially when the measurement matrix does not satisfy the Restricted Isometry Property (RIP). Unlike traditional iterative reconstruction which searches for a feasible solution within the space of sparse solutions, ACID simultaneously optimizes for sparsity, data-driven priors, and residual calibration. A method that uses an implicit neural network to represent the 3D volume density field, optimizing the network parameters to fit the 2D projection images while jointly optimizing the 3D orientation (pose) of each projection. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Performance: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Easy to integrate custom constraints (e.g., non-negativity, sparsity) by modifying the loss function. No need to explicitly derive or implement the backprojection matrix. Limitations: Convergence depends heavily on the learning rate and the condition number of the problem. May get stuck in local minima if the initial guess is poor. When to Use: When custom physics constraints are needed, or when integrating with deep learning components (e.g., neural networks as priors). When Not to Use: For standard CT reconstruction with no special constraints, where FDK or algebraic methods are faster and sufficient. This approach leverages the automatic differentiation capabilities of deep learning frameworks (like PyTorch) to solve inverse problems traditionally addressed by algebraic reconstruction techniques. The specific implementation described here uses a cone-beam forward projector and Adam optimizer to minimize projection error. ayush-chauhan-1202/physics-aware-ct-reconstruction, https://github.com/ayush-chauhan-1202/physics-aware-ct-reconstruction, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial)

name: ACID (Adversarial Calibration Iterative Deep learning)
head: ACID scheme, ACID workflow, Adversarial Calibration Iterative Deep learning, Adversarial Convergence Iterative Deep learning
body: ACID is an iterative reconstruction framework that stabilizes an unstable deep reconstruction neural network by combining it with a Compressed Sensing (CS)-based sparsity-promoting module. It minimizes an objective function balancing neural network output consistency, data fidelity, residual error energy, and sparsity. ACID searches for a solution good in three aspects: image sparsity, big-data-driven prior, and iterative calibration to eliminate unexplained residual data. It differs from standard sparsity-minimization reconstruction by incorporating a data-driven deep prior (\Phi) to fill gaps where sparsity alone may not yield a unique solution, especially when the measurement matrix does not satisfy the Restricted Isometry Property (RIP). Unlike traditional iterative reconstruction which searches for a feasible solution within the space of sparse solutions, ACID simultaneously optimizes for sparsity, data-driven priors, and residual calibration. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: p^{(0)} \in \mathbb{R}^m: Original measurement data (projections). A: System matrix (forward model, e.g., Radon transform for CT, Fourier transform for MRI). \Phi(\cdot): A pre-trained deep neural network (recon-net) that maps measurement data to an image. H \in \mathbb{R}^{N \times N}: Sparse transform matrix (e.g., discrete gradient for TV) and its adjoint H^. Hyperparameters: \lambda > 0, \mu \ge 0, \xi > 0. Outputs: f^{(k)}: Reconstructed image estimate at iteration k. Data Structures: p^{(k)}: Residual error vector in the projection domain, size m. f^{(k)}: Image estimate vector, size N. \bar{f}^{(k)} = H f^{(k)}: Transformed image vector, size N. Parameters: \lambda: Hyperparameter weighting the data fidelity term (measured noise energy). \mu: Hyperparameter weighting the residual error energy in the projection domain. \xi: Hyperparameter weighting the sparsity term \|Hf\|1. \varepsilon = \xi/\lambda: Effective threshold for soft-thresholding, matching system tolerance level. M1 = \frac{\lambda}{1+\lambda+\mu}. M2 = \frac{1+\mu}{\lambda}. M = \frac{M1}{M2} = \frac{1+\mu}{1+\lambda+\mu} < 1. s: Number of components spanning the s-sparse space of Hf^. \sigma: A constant such that the artifact norm is bounded by (1-\sigma)\|f^\|. Formulas: The objective function minimized is: L(p,f):= \frac{1}{2}\|\Phi(Af+p)-f\|2^2 + \frac{\lambda}{2}\|p^{(0)}-Af-p\|2^2 + \frac{\mu}{2}\|p\|2^2 + \xi\|Hf\|1 where p is the residual error in the projection domain (p=p^{(0)}-Af). The iterative update equations are: p^{(k+1)} \cong \frac{\lambda(p^{(0)}-Af^{(k)})}{1+\lambda+\mu} f^{(k+1)} \cong H^ S\varepsilon \left( H \left( f^{(k)} + \frac{1+\mu}{\lambda}\Phi(p^{(k+1)}) \right) \right) The soft-thresholding kernel S\varepsilon(x) is defined as: S\varepsilon(x) = \begin{cases} 0 & \text{if } |x| < \varepsilon \\ x - \text{sgn}(x)\varepsilon & \text{otherwise} \end{cases} For Total Variation (TV) minimization using a non-unitary discrete gradient transform H, the image update f^{(k+1)} at pixel (iw, ih) is computed as: f^{(k+1)}{(iw,ih)} = \frac{1}{4} \sum{\text{neighbors}} S^{-1}\varepsilon \left( f^{(k+1/2)}{(iw,ih)}, f^{(k+1/2)}{\text{neighbor}} \right) where the intermediate image variable is f^{(k+1/2)} = f^{(k)} + \frac{1+\mu}{\lambda}\Phi(p^{(k+1)}). The pseudo-inverse soft-thresholding kernel S^{-1}\varepsilon(va, vb) is defined as: S^{-1}\varepsilon(va, vb) = \begin{cases} \frac{va+vb}{2} & \text{if } |va-vb| \le \varepsilon \\ va - \frac{\varepsilon}{2} & \text{if } va-vb > \varepsilon \\ va + \frac{\varepsilon}{2} & \text{if } va-vb < -\varepsilon \end{cases} Numbered Steps: 1. Initialize: Set initial image estimate f^{(0)}. A common initialization is the output of the neural network on the initial data: f^{(0)} = \Phi(p^{(0)}). Note that \Phi(p^{(0)}) can be decomposed into ground truth f^, observable artifact f^{(ob,0)}, and null-space artifact f^{(nl,0)}. 2. Iterate for k = 0, 1, \dots until convergence: a. Residual Update: Compute the residual error p^{(k+1)} using the forward model A and previous estimate f^{(k)}: p^{(k+1)} = M1 (p^{(0)} - A f^{(k)}) where M1 = \frac{\lambda}{1+\lambda+\mu}. b. Network Prediction: Pass the residual through the recon-net to get the update direction: \Delta f{\text{net}} = \Phi(p^{(k+1)}) c. Intermediate Image: Compute the intermediate variable: f^{(k+1/2)} = f^{(k)} + M2 \Delta f{\text{net}} where M2 = \frac{1+\mu}{\lambda}. d. Sparsity Projection (CS Step): i. Transform to sparse domain: \bar{f}^{(k+1/2)} = H f^{(k+1/2)}. ii. Apply soft-thresholding: \bar{f}^{(k+1)} = S\varepsilon(\bar{f}^{(k+1/2)}). iii. Transform back: If H is unitary, f^{(k+1)} = H^ \bar{f}^{(k+1)}. If H is non-unitary (e.g., TV gradient), compute f^{(k+1)} using the pixel-wise pseudo-inverse formula involving neighbors. ACID handles this by introducing sparsity priors via H and deep priors via \Phi. Non-Unitary Transform: The discrete gradient transform H used in TV minimization is non-unitary and not invertible. The method handles this by interpreting the adjoint H^ as a pseudo-inverse in the iterative framework, using the specific pixel-wise update rule. RIP Violation: If the Restricted Isometry Property (RIP) or robust Null-Space Property (rNSP) is not satisfied, ACID may converge to an image with a nonzero null-space component. However, this is also true for sparsity-promoting algorithms alone; ACID reduces the feasible solution space via the deep prior. Unstable Network: If the network is not ideal and produces substantial artifacts, convergence is still guaranteed as long as the relative error is under control (less than 100%) in the L2 norm. Noise Floor: For noise-free measurements, if \varepsilon \to 0, then the observable artifact norm \|f^{(ob,\infty)}\| \to 0. The parameter \varepsilon should match the system tolerance level. Convergence: The Lipschitz constant of ACID for CT and MRI monotonically decreases and converges to a constant scale with respect to the number of iterations. The observable artifact norm is bounded by \|f^{(ob,\infty)}\| < \frac{(1-\sigma)s M2}{\sigma \varepsilon}. The general bound for artifact norm at step k+1 is \|f^{(ob,k+1)}\| < (1-\sigma) \left[ (1-M\sigma)^k M1 \|f^{(ob,0)}\| + \frac{1-(1-M\sigma)^{k+1}}{M\sigma} M1 \varepsilon s \right]. Performance: In CT cases using Ell-50, the maximum output-to-input variation ratio against additive white Gaussian noise (zero mean, 11-30 HU std dev) was 0.229. In MRI cases using DAGAN, the maximum output-to-input variation ratio against additive white Gaussian noise was 3.023. Strengths: ACID stabilizes unstable deep reconstruction networks and is resilient against adversarial attacks. It outperforms sparsity-promoting algorithms that do not utilize big-data-driven priors, specifically in recovering nonzero null-space components. Limitations: Convergence to a solution with nonzero null-space components is possible if RIP/rNSP is not satisfied, though the deep prior reduces the feasible space compared to sparsity alone. Usage: Used for few-view CT imaging and sparse sampling MRI reconstruction. Specifically applied in tomographic reconstruction, sparse-view CT, and low-dose spectral CT contexts. ACID was introduced to stabilize deep tomographic reconstruction methods which are often unstable due to the "troublesome kernel" of deep learning models. It builds on the concept of using Compressed Sensing (CS) to promote sparsity and combines it with a data-driven prior from a neural network. The method was developed to address cases where standard sparsity-promotion algorithms fail to provide unique solutions, particularly when the measurement matrix does not satisfy RIP. The theoretical analysis demonstrates that ACID converges to a solution in the intersection of measured data, sparse solutions, and data-driven solutions. name: INR Tomography with Joint Alignment
head: INR Tomography Optimization with Pose Alignment, Implicit Neural Representation Tomography, Joint Alignment and Reconstruction, Self-supervised INR Tomography, Self-supervised INR reconstruction
body: A fully self-supervised tomographic reconstruction algorithm that uses an Implicit Neural Representation (INR) to jointly optimize the 3D volume density field and the full 3D pose (orientation and in-plane translation) for each projection image. Unlike conventional voxel-grid methods that require interpolation during rotation and struggle with multi-GPU parallelization, this method represents the volume as a continuous neural network, enabling arbitrarily fine sampling and projection at any orientation without interpolation. It is particularly suited for heterogeneous materials where supervised training data is unavailable, solving for complete sample pose rather than relying on pre-estimated shifts or single tilt angles. Inputs: A tilt series of M 2D projection images I^{exp}{i,j}, where i \in \{1, \dots, N\} is the pixel index and j \in \{1, \dots, M\} is the tilt index. The nominal tilt angle \thetaj for each image is assumed known. Outputs: The weights of the INR volume representation and the optimized pose parameters for each tilt image. Data Structures: 1. INR Model: A fully-connected neural network (MLP) with periodic activation functions. Input: 3D coordinate vector \mathbf{r} = [x, y, z]^T. Output: Scalar intensity value \phi. 2. Pose Parameters: For each tilt image j, a set of learnable parameters: z1j, z3j: Learnable Euler angles representing tilt axis oscillation and rotation around the beam axis. \delta xj, \delta yj: Learnable scalars representing in-plane translation shifts along the x and y axes. 3. Optimization State: INR weights W. Pose parameters \mathbf{P}j = [z1j, z3j, \delta xj, \delta yj]^T for j=1 \dots M. Formulas: The total loss function is: L = L{pixel} + \alpha L{TV} where \alpha is the total variation regularization weight. The pixel loss is defined as: L{pixel} = \frac{1}{MN} \sum{j=1}^{M} \sum{i=1}^{N} \text{smoothL1}(I^{exp}{i,j} - I^{pred}{i,j}) The smoothL1 loss function is: \text{smoothL1}(x) = \begin{cases} 0.5x^2/\beta & \text{if } |x| < \beta \\ |x| - 0.5\beta & \text{otherwise} \end{cases} where \beta = 0.07 is the crossover point hyperparameter. The predicted intensity I^{pred}{i,j} for pixel i in image j is computed by integrating the INR output along a ray: 1. Define a base ray \mathbf{r}0(t) = [0, 0, t]^T (along the z-axis). 2. Apply in-plane shifts \delta xj, \delta yj to the ray origin in the image plane. 3. Apply rotation R(\mathbf{p}j) to the ray direction and origin, where R(\mathbf{p}j) = R(z3j) R(\thetaj) R(z1j). Here R(\thetaj) is the nominal rotation around the tilt axis, and R(z1j), R(z3j) are the learned corrections. 4. Sample discrete points \mathbf{r}k along the transformed ray. 5. Evaluate \phi(\mathbf{r}k) using the INR. 6. Integrate \phi along the ray to obtain I^{pred}{i,j}. Algorithm Steps: 1. Initialization: Initialize INR weights W randomly (or pre-trained on SIRT). Initialize pose parameters \mathbf{P}j to identity/zero (nominal pose). 2. Sampling: For each training step, sample a batch of pixels from the tilt series. The batch size is 1024 pixels per GPU. 3. Forward Pass: a. For each pixel (i, j) in the batch, construct the ray based on current pose \mathbf{P}j and nominal angle \thetaj. b. Sample K points along the ray. K starts small and ramps up over the first few epochs. c. Evaluate INR at these points to get intensities. d. Integrate intensities to predict I^{pred}{i,j}. 4. Loss Calculation: Compute L{pixel} using the smoothL1 formula. Compute L{TV} (Total Variation) on the INR outputs if regularization is active. Compute total loss L. 5. Backpropagation: Compute gradients \frac{\partial L}{\partial W} and \frac{\partial L}{\partial \mathbf{P}j} using automatic differentiation. 6. Update: Update W and \mathbf{P}j using the Adam optimizer. 7. Validation (Optional): If SNR is high, split data into 80% training / 20% validation. Monitor L{pixel} on validation set. Stop if loss increases. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import torch import torch.nn as nn import torch.optim as optim class PeriodicActivation(nn.Module): """Periodic activation function for INR.""" def init(self, omega0): super().init() self.omega0 = omega0 def forward(self, x): return torch.sin(self.omega0 x) class INRVolume(nn.Module): """Fully connected neural network representing the 3D volume.""" def init(self, inputdim=3, outputdim=1, hiddendim=256, numlayers=8, omega0=30.0): super().init() self.layers = nn.ModuleList() self.omega0 = omega0 # Input layer self.layers.append(nn.Linear(inputdim, hiddendim)) self.layers.append(PeriodicActivation(omega0)) # Hidden layers for in range(numlayers - 2): self.layers.append(nn.Linear(hiddendim, hiddendim)) self.layers.append(PeriodicActivation(omega0)) # Output layer self.layers.append(nn.Linear(hiddendim, outputdim)) def forward(self, x): for layer in self.layers: x = layer(x) return x def computerotationmatrix(z1, theta, z3): """ Compute rotation matrix R(z3) R(theta) R(z1). Assumes standard Euler angle conventions compatible with the source. R(theta) is rotation around the tilt axis (typically Y or X depending on setup). For this implementation, we assume a generic rotation composition. Note: Exact axis definitions for z1, theta, z3 must match the experimental setup. Typically: z1 is tilt axis wobble, theta is nominal tilt, z3 is in-plane rotation. """ # Placeholder for specific rotation matrix construction based on axis definitions. # The source specifies R(z3j)R(thetaj)R(z1j). # We assume rotations are around specific axes (e.g., Z, Y, Z or similar). # For a generic implementation, one must define the axes. # Let's assume standard Z-Y-Z or similar. The source does not specify axes explicitly, # but implies a composition of three rotations. # We will use a generic rotation composition function. pass def sampleray(rayorigin, raydirection, numsamples): """Sample points along a ray.""" t = torch.linspace(0, 1, numsamples) points = rayorigin.unsqueeze(1) + t.unsqueeze(0).unsqueeze(2) raydirection.unsqueeze(1) return points def integrateray(points, inrmodel): """Evaluate INR and integrate along ray.""" intensities = inrmodel(points) # Shape: [numsamples, 1] # Simple trapezoidal or midpoint integration # Assuming points are uniformly spaced dy = 1.0 / (points.shape[0] - 1) # Normalized step size integral = torch.trapz(intensities.squeeze(-1), dx=dy) return integral def smoothl1loss(input, target, beta=0.07): diff = input - target absdiff = torch.abs(diff) loss = torch.where(absdiff < beta, 0.5 diff2 / beta, absdiff - 0.5 beta) return torch.mean(loss) def totalvariationloss(inrmodel, coordinates): """Compute Total Variation regularization on INR outputs.""" # Evaluate INR at coordinates outputs = inrmodel(coordinates) # Compute gradient of outputs w.r.t coordinates # This is computationally expensive. Often approximated or computed via autodiff. # For simplicity, we assume a helper function exists or use torch.autograd.grad gradoutputs = torch.autograd.grad(outputs.sum(), coordinates, creategraph=True)[0] tv = torch.mean(torch.norm(gradoutputs, dim=1)) return tv def traininrtomography(tiltimages, nominalangles, numepochs=150, numgpus=16): """ Main training loop for INR Tomography with Joint Alignment. """ # Hyperparameters lrinr = 8e-6 lrpose = 5e-2 beta = 0.07 alphatv = 1e-4 batchsizepergpu = 1024 warmupepochs = 10 # Initialize INR inr = INRVolume() # Initialize Pose Parameters # M tilt images M = len(tiltimages) N = tiltimages[0].shape[0] # Assuming square images NxN # Learnable pose parameters: [z1, z3, dx, dy] for each tilt poseparams = nn.Parameter(torch.zeros(M, 4)) # Optimizers optimizerinr = optim.Adam(inr.parameters(), lr=lrinr) optimizerpose = optim.Adam([poseparams], lr=lrpose) # Learning rate schedulers schedulerinr = optim.lrscheduler.CosineAnnealingLR(optimizerinr, Tmax=numepochs) # Warmup for inr # Scheduler for pose can be constant or scaled # Distributed Data Parallel setup would go here # inr = DDP(inr) for epoch in range(numepochs): # Warmup logic if epoch < warmupepochs: currentlr = lrinr (epoch + 1) / warmupepochs for paramgroup in optimizerinr.paramgroups: paramgroup['lr'] = currentlr # Sample batch of pixels # Randomly select batchsizepergpu pixels from the tilt series # Flatten images to 1D array of pixels # Indices: (imageidx, pixelidx) batchindices = samplebatchindices(M, N, batchsizepergpu) optimizerinr.zerograd() optimizerpose.zerograd() totalloss = 0.0 numsamples = 0 for idx in batchindices: imgidx, pixidx = idx # Get experimental intensity expintensity = tiltimages[imgidx][pixidx] # Get nominal angle theta = nominalangles[imgidx] # Get current pose parameters z1, z3, dx, dy = poseparams[imgidx] # Construct ray # 1. Base ray along Z rayorigin = torch.tensor([0.0, 0.0, 0.0]) raydirection = torch.tensor([0.0, 0.0, 1.0]) # 2. Apply shifts dx, dy to origin (in-plane) # Assuming x,y are in-plane, z is beam rayorigin[0] += dx rayorigin[1] += dy # 3. Apply rotations R(z3) R(theta) R(z1) # Note: Exact rotation matrix construction depends on coordinate system # We assume a helper function that applies these rotations to the ray rayorigin, raydirection = applyposetransform(rayorigin, raydirection, z1, theta, z3) # 4. Sample points along ray # Number of samples ramps up with epoch numsamplesray = rampupsamples(epoch) points = sampleray(rayorigin, raydirection, numsamplesray) # 5. Evaluate INR intensities = inr(points) # 6. Integrate predintensity = integrateray(points, inr) # 7. Compute Loss pixelloss = smoothl1loss(predintensity, expintensity, beta) totalloss += pixelloss numsamples += 1 # Average loss totalloss /= numsamples # Add Total Variation regularization # Sample a subset of coordinates for TV calculation to save memory # Or compute on the batch coordinates # For simplicity, we assume TV is computed on the batch # tvloss = totalvariationloss(inr, batchcoordinates) # totalloss += alphatv tvloss # Backpropagate totalloss.backward() # Update optimizerinr.step() optimizerpose.step() # Scheduler step schedulerinr.step() # Validation check if needed # if epoch % 10 == 0: # valloss = evaluatevalidation(inr, poseparams, valdata) # if valloss > bestvalloss: # break return inr, poseparams Parameters: Network Architecture: Fully-connected neural network with periodic activation functions. Hidden dimension and number of layers are hyperparameters; the source notes that this architecture required the least hyperparameter tuning to converge to high spatial frequencies. Loss Function: smoothL1 loss with \beta = 0.07. Regularization: Total Variation (TV) loss with weight \alpha. For phantom data, \alpha = 1 \times 10^{-4}. Learning Rate (INR Weights): 8 \times 10^{-6}. Learning Rate (Pose Parameters): 5 \times 10^{-2}. Batch Size: 1024 pixels per GPU. Global batch size 16384 with 16 GPUs. Optimizer: Adam. LR Schedule: Warmup for 10 epochs, then cosine-annealing. Sampling: Number of sampling points per ray starts small and ramps up over the first few epochs. Initialization: Random initialization is sufficient for self-supervision. Pre-training on a converged SIRT reconstruction can speed up convergence. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Interpolation: Conventional voxel-grid methods require interpolation during rotation, which is difficult to parallelize across multiple GPUs because the volume must be instantiated across each GPU. The INR method avoids this by using precisely rotated projection vectors. Overfitting: In high SNR scenarios, the model may overfit to noise. Mitigation involves splitting data into 80% training and 20% validation, and stopping training when validation loss increases. Parallelization: The method is parallelizable via Distributed Data Parallel (DDP). Gradients are averaged across GPUs, and the learning rate is scaled by the square root of the number of GPUs. Coordinate System: The exact definition of the rotation matrices R(z1j), R(\thetaj), R(z3j) depends on the experimental setup (e.g., tilt axis orientation). The source specifies the composition order but not the specific axes for each angle, which must be derived from the hardware configuration. Time Complexity: Reconstruction speed scales nearly linearly with the number of GPUs. For 150 epochs on a full dataset using 16 GPUs, reconstruction takes approximately 2 hours. Without multi-GPU systems, speed depends heavily on volume size and single-GPU performance. Memory Complexity: Memory usage is dominated by the INR model size and the batch of sampled coordinates. Since the volume is not stored as a grid, memory usage is independent of the voxel grid resolution, allowing for high-resolution representations without proportional memory increase. Strengths: Self-supervised: No training data from similar samples required. Joint Alignment: Optimizes full 3D pose (orientation and in-plane translation) for each projection. Missing Wedge Inpainting: Acts as a regularizer to fill in missing information. Denoising: Regularization helps denoise low-dose datasets. No Interpolation: Allows arbitrarily fine sampling and projection at any orientation. Limitations: Computationally intensive per epoch compared to analytical methods like SIRT, though parallelization mitigates this. Requires careful tuning of regularization parameter \alpha. Convergence may be slow without pre-training or good initial alignment. When to Use: Suitable for heterogeneous materials, beam-sensitive samples (low dose), and datasets with significant misalignment or missing wedges where supervised methods are impractical. When Not to Use: When computational resources are severely limited (single CPU, no GPU) and real-time reconstruction is required, or when high-quality training data from similar samples is available and supervised methods are preferred. The method was proposed in the paper "Missing Wedge Inpainting and Joint Alignment in Electron Tomography through Implicit Neural Representations". It addresses limitations of conventional voxel-grid tomographic reconstruction, which requires interpolation and struggles with parallelization, and supervised deep learning methods that require training data. The approach leverages the properties of Implicit Neural Representations (INRs) to provide a continuous, differentiable volume representation that can be optimized jointly with projection poses. It is implemented in the open-source Python package quantEM. The method is applicable to HAADF STEM data, where image intensity depends linearly on the projected potential. name: Iterative Algebraic Reconstruction (LSQR)
head: 3D Helical CT Reconstruction via LSQR, 3D Helical Cone-Beam CT Image Reconstruction using LSQR, Helical CT LSQR, Iterative Backprojection Reconstruction, LSQR Reconstruction
body: Iterative Algebraic Reconstruction using LSQR solves the linear inverse problem \mathbf{A}\mathbf{X} = \mathbf{B} for 3D helical cone-beam CT, reconstructing a 3D voxel density grid \mathbf{X} from 2D X-ray projection measurements \mathbf{B}. Unlike direct methods such as Back-projection or FastFDK, LSQR iteratively minimizes the residual error by leveraging the adjoint of the forward projection operator, making it suitable for large-scale, sparse systems where explicit matrix storage is infeasible. It distinguishes itself from other iterative solvers like Iterative Solvers by specifically employing the Least Squares QR algorithm to handle the ill-conditioned nature of helical ray-voxel intersection matrices. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Measured projection data \mathbf{B} (sinogram) of size N{pa} \times N{det} \times N{slice}, and system geometry parameters (source-to-object distance, source-to-detector distance, detector pitch, helical shift, angular span). Output: Reconstructed 3D volume \mathbf{X} of size N{vox} \times N{vox} \times N{vox} (typically 512^3). Data Structures: Volume Grid \mathbf{X}: A contiguous 1D array of float32 values representing the voxel densities, mapped to a 3D grid of resolution N{vox} \times N{vox} \times N{vox}. In the reference implementation, N{vox} = 512, occupying ~536.87 MB. Projection Data \mathbf{B}: A contiguous 1D array of float32 values representing line integrals for each detector pixel at each angle. Size: N{pa} \times N{det} \times N{slice}. Ray Geometry: Implicitly defined by the helical trajectory. For angle i, the source position (x1, y1, z1) and detector ray endpoints are calculated using trigonometric functions of the angular span and helical shift. Parameters (Reference Values): N{vox} (npix): 512 N{pa}: 473 (projections) N{det}: 512 (detector columns) N{slice}: 512 (detector rows) Span: 640^\circ Detector Pitch (d): 0.8 mm Source-to-Object Distance (scob): 166.641 mm Source-to-Detector Distance (scd): 1238.157 mm Helical Shift: 0.136 mm per angle Relaxation Factor: 0.05 (used in backprojection scaling) Max Iterations: 20 Algorithm Steps: The reconstruction follows an iterative loop where each iteration processes all projection angles to update the volume estimate. 1. Initialization: Initialize the volume buffer \mathbf{X} to zero. 2. Iteration Loop: For iter = 0 to max\iterations - 1: a. Angle Loop: For each projection angle i from 0 to N{pa} - 1: i. Data Transfer: Copy the projection slice \mathbf{B}i (size N{det} \times N{slice}) from host memory to device memory. ii. Adjoint Kernel Launch: Launch the adjointkernel CUDA kernel. Grid Dimensions: \left(\frac{N{det}+15}{16}, \frac{N{slice}+15}{16}\right) Block Dimensions: (16, 16) Operation: For each detector element (j, k) at angle i, calculate the ray path through the volume. Accumulate the measured projection value p into the intersected voxels. The contribution is scaled by the relaxation factor and the pixel length. Ray Calculation: Source position: x1 = scob \cdot \sin(\thetai), y1 = -scob \cdot \cos(\thetai), z1 = z{start} - i \cdot shift (where \thetai = \frac{span \cdot \pi}{N{pa} \cdot 180}). Detector point: p1 = (\frac{N{det}}{2} - (0.5 + k)) \cdot d, p3 = z1 + (\frac{N{slice}}{2} - (j + 0.5)) \cdot d. Ray direction components derived from source-to-detector vector. Intersection with voxel grid boundaries determines the path length and voxel indices (m1, m2, m3). b. Synchronization: After all angles are processed, synchronize the device to ensure all atomic updates to \mathbf{X} are complete. 3. Normalization: Multiply every voxel in \mathbf{X} by the normalization factor \frac{1}{N{pa}} (or 1/473) to scale the accumulated backprojected values. 4. Output: Save \mathbf{X} as a binary file. name: Distributed CT Reconstruction with TIGRE
head: Distributed Ax/Atb, Distributed Full-Data Operator, Distributed TIGRE, DistributedFullDataTigrePool, TomoAnchor-V3
body: Distributed CT Reconstruction with TIGRE is a multiprocessing framework that parallelizes the forward projection (Ax) and backprojection (A^Tb) operators of the TIGRE library across multiple GPUs using shared memory and process pools. It solves the computational bottleneck of large-scale tomographic reconstruction by partitioning projection angles across worker processes, allowing independent GPU execution while maintaining a consistent global data view through shared memory buffers. Unlike spatial decomposition methods that partition the volume, this method partitions the measurement space (angles), making it suitable for iterative reconstruction algorithms that require repeated forward and backprojection operations. Inputs: volume: 3D numpy array of shape (nz, ny, nx) and dtype float32. projections: 3D numpy array of shape (numangles, detrows, detcols) and dtype float32. angles: 1D numpy array of projection angles in radians. geometryparams: Parameters defining the CT geometry (source-detector distance, detector pixels, voxel size, etc.). gpuids: List of GPU indices to use. Outputs: projections: Result of forward projection (Ax). volume: Result of backprojection (A^Tb). residual: Scalar value for residual squared norm. WorkerShard A dataclass defining the assignment of angles to a specific worker/GPU. workerid (int): Unique identifier for the worker process. gpuid (int): CUDA device ID assigned to this worker. start (int): Start index (inclusive) in the angles array. stop (int): Stop index (exclusive) in the angles array. angles (np.ndarray): Subset of projection angles assigned to this shard. SharedArraySpec Specification for shared memory buffers. name (str): Unique name for the shared memory segment. shape (tuple): Shape of the numpy array. dtype (np.dtype): Data type (e.g., np.float32). Shared Memory Buffers volumeshared: Single shared array of shape volumeshape (nz, ny, nx), dtype float32. Used to store the global volume accessible by all workers. projectionbuffers: Dictionary mapping workerid to a shared array. Shape: (shard.count, detrows, detcols). Each worker writes its partial projection results here. partialvolumebuffers: Dictionary mapping workerid to a shared array. Shape: volumeshape (nz, ny, nx). Each worker accumulates its partial backprojection result here. 1. Initialization: Validate inputs: Ensure len(gpuids) > 1 and len(angles) > 0. Partition angles into shards using partitionangleshards. Each shard is assigned to a unique GPU from gpuids. Create shared memory buffers (volumeshared, projectionbuffers, partialvolumebuffers) using multiprocessing.sharedmemory.SharedMemory with create=True. Spawn worker processes using mp.getcontext("spawn") to ensure clean state isolation. For each shard, create a worker process with arguments: shard metadata, geometry params, subset of angles, shared array specs, and command/result queues. Start all worker processes. 2. Forward Projection (Ax): Copy input volume to volumeshared using np.copyto. Dispatch 'forward' command to all workers via their command queues. Wait for all workers to respond via result queues with timeout QUEUEPOLLSECONDS. Gather results: For each shard, copy self.projectionbuffers[shard.workerid] to output[shard.start: shard.stop]. 3. Backprojection (A^Tb): Validate input projections shape matches self.projectionshape. For each shard, copy projectionarray[shard.start: shard.stop] to self.projectionbuffers[shard.workerid]. Dispatch 'backproject' command to all workers. Wait for all workers to respond. Reduce results: Initialize volume = zeros(volumeshape, dtype=float32). For each shard, add self.partialvolumebuffers[shard.workerid] to volume. 4. Normal Operator (A^T A): Copy volume to volumeshared. Dispatch 'normal' command to workers. Workers call tigre.Ax to compute a local projection, then tigre.Atb on that local projection with backprojectiontype='matched'. Reduce results: Initialize result = zeros(volumeshape, dtype=float32). For each shard, add self.partialvolumebuffers[shard.workerid] to result. 5. Residual Squared: Copy volume to volumeshared and projections to projectionbuffers as in Backprojection. Dispatch 'residualsquared' command. Workers compute local residual squared norm: value = sum((localprojection - projectionbuffer)^2) using float64 accumulation. Reduce results: Sum response.get('value', 0.0) from all workers to get totalvalue. Forward Projection: y = Ax. Backprojection: x = A^T b. Normal Operator: z = A^T A x. Residual Squared: R = \sum{i} ( (Ax)i - bi)^2. QUEUEPOLLSECONDS: Timeout in seconds for resultqueue.get() in the master wait loop. PROCESSJOINTIMEOUTSECONDS: Timeout in seconds for process.join() during shutdown. backprojectiontype: String parameter passed to tigre.Atb, set to 'matched' for backproject and normal operations. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import numpy as np import multiprocessing as mp from multiprocessing import sharedmemory import tigre from tigre.utilities import gpu QUEUEPOLLSECONDS = 30.0 # Not given in sources PROCESSJOINTIMEOUTSECONDS = 10.0 # Not given in sources class WorkerShard: def init(self, workerid, gpuid, start, stop, angles): self.workerid = workerid self.gpuid = gpuid self.start = start self.stop = stop self.angles = angles class DistributedTigrePool: def init(self, gpuids, angles, geometryparams, volumeshape, detpixels): self.gpuids = gpuids self.angles = angles self.geometryparams = geometryparams self.volumeshape = volumeshape self.detpixels = detpixels self.projectionshape = (len(angles), detpixels[0], detpixels[1]) if len(gpuids) <= 1: raise ValueError("Requires at least two GPUs") if len(angles) == 0: raise ValueError("Requires at least one projection angle") self.shards = self.partitionangleshards(angles, gpuids) self.volumeshared = self.createsharedarray("vol", volumeshape, np.float32) self.projectionbuffers = {} self.partialvolumebuffers = {} for shard in self.shards: projshape = (shard.stop - shard.start, detpixels[0], detpixels[1]) self.projectionbuffers[shard.workerid] = self.createsharedarray( f"proj{shard.workerid}", projshape, np.float32) self.partialvolumebuffers[shard.workerid] = self.createsharedarray( f"pvol{shard.workerid}", volumeshape, np.float32) self.workers = [] self.commandqueues = {} self.resultqueues = {} for shard in self.shards: cmdq, resq = mp.Queue(), mp.Queue() self.commandqueues[shard.workerid] = cmdq self.resultqueues[shard.workerid] = resq p = mp.Process( target=distributedtigreworker, args=(shard, geometryparams, self.volumeshared, self.projectionbuffers, self.partialvolumebuffers, cmdq, resq)) p.start() self.workers.append(p) def createsharedarray(self, name, shape, dtype): shm = sharedmemory.SharedMemory(create=True, size=np.prod(shape) dtype.itemsize) return np.ndarray(shape, dtype=dtype, buffer=shm.buf) def partitionangleshards(self, angles, gpuids): shards = [] numangles = len(angles) numgpus = len(gpuids) anglespergpu = numangles // numgpus remainder = numangles % numgpus startidx = 0 for i, gpuid in enumerate(gpuids): count = anglespergpu + (1 if i < remainder else 0) shards.append(WorkerShard( workerid=i, gpuid=gpuid, start=startidx, stop=startidx + count, angles=angles[startidx:startidx + count])) startidx += count return shards def forward(self, volume): np.copyto(self.volumeshared, np.ascontiguousarray(volume, dtype=np.float32), casting='no') for shard in self.shards: self.commandqueues[shard.workerid].put({'op': 'forward'}) self.waitforresponses() output = np.zeros(self.projectionshape, dtype=np.float32) for shard in self.shards: np.copyto(output[shard.start:shard.stop], self.projectionbuffers[shard.workerid], casting='no') return output def backproject(self, projections): for shard in self.shards: np.copyto(self.projectionbuffers[shard.workerid], np.ascontiguousarray(projections[shard.start:shard.stop], dtype=np.float32), casting='no') for shard in self.shards: self.commandqueues[shard.workerid].put({'op': 'backproject'}) self.waitforresponses() volume = np.zeros(self.volumeshape, dtype=np.float32) for shard in self.shards: volume += self.partialvolumebuffers[shard.workerid] return volume def normal(self, volume): np.copyto(self.volumeshared, np.ascontiguousarray(volume, dtype=np.float32), casting='no') for shard in self.shards: self.commandqueues[shard.workerid].put({'op': 'normal'}) self.waitforresponses() result = np.zeros(self.volumeshape, dtype=np.float32) for shard in self.shards: result += self.partialvolumebuffers[shard.workerid] return result def residualsquared(self, volume, projections): np.copyto(self.volumeshared, np.ascontiguousarray(volume, dtype=np.float32), casting='no') for shard in self.shards: np.copyto(self.projectionbuffers[shard.workerid], np.ascontiguousarray(projections[shard.start:shard.stop], dtype=np.float32), casting='no') for shard in self.shards: self.commandqueues[shard.workerid].put({'op': 'residualsquared'}) totalvalue = 0.0 for shard in self.shards: res = self.resultqueues[shard.workerid].get(timeout=QUEUEPOLLSECONDS) totalvalue += float(res.get('value', 0.0)) return totalvalue def waitforresponses(self): for shard in self.shards: try: res = self.resultqueues[shard.workerid].get(timeout=QUEUEPOLLSECONDS) if not isinstance(res, dict) or res.get('status') != 'ok': raise RuntimeError(f"Invalid response from worker {shard.workerid}") except mp.queues.Empty: if not self.workers[shard.workerid].isalive(): raise RuntimeError(f"Worker {shard.workerid} died unexpectedly") def distributedtigreworker(shard, geoparams, volshm, projbuffers, pvolbuffers, cmdq, resq): volarr = np.ndarray(volshm.shape, dtype=np.float32, buffer=volshm.buf) projarr = projbuffers[shard.workerid] pvolarr = pvolbuffers[shard.workerid] gpuids = gpu.GpuIds() gpuids.devices = [int(shard.gpuid)] geo = buildtigregeometry(geoparams) while True: command = cmdq.get() operation = str(command.get('op', '')).strip().lower() if operation == 'close': break elif operation == 'forward': result = tigre.Ax(np.ascontiguousarray(volarr, dtype=np.float32), geo, shard.angles, gpuids=gpuids) np.copyto(projarr, np.asarray(result, dtype=np.float32), casting='no') elif operation == 'backproject': result = tigre.Atb(np.ascontiguousarray(projarr, dtype=np.float32), geo, shard.angles, backprojectiontype='matched', gpuids=gpuids) np.copyto(pvolarr, np.asarray(result, dtype=np.float32), casting='no') elif operation == 'normal': localproj = tigre.Ax(np.ascontiguousarray(volarr, dtype=np.float32), geo, shard.angles, gpuids=gpuids) result = tigre.Atb(np.ascontiguousarray(localproj, dtype=np.float32), geo, shard.angles, backprojectiontype='matched', gpuids=gpuids) np.copyto(pvolarr, np.asarray(result, dtype=np.float32), casting='no') elif operation == 'residualsquared': localproj = tigre.Ax(np.ascontiguousarray(volarr, dtype=np.float32), geo, shard.angles, gpuids=gpuids) residual = np.asarray(localproj, dtype=np.float32) - np.asarray(projarr, dtype=np.float32) value = float(np.sum(np.asarray(residual, dtype=np.float64) 2)) resq.put({'status': 'ok', 'value': value}) continue resq.put({'status': 'ok', 'workerid': shard.workerid, 'gpuid': shard.gpuid}) def buildtigregeometry(params): # Constructs TIGRE geometry object from parameters. # Implementation details not provided in sources. pass Process Context: Uses spawn context, which does not inherit open file descriptors or GPU contexts from the parent, ensuring clean state isolation. Shared Memory Cleanup: Shared memory segments must be explicitly closed and unlinked to prevent OS resource leaks. Worker Death: If a worker process exits unexpectedly, the master detects this via Empty exception from resultqueue.get() and checks process.isalive(). A RuntimeError is raised with the dead PIDs. Invalid Response: If the response from a worker is not a dictionary or has status != 'ok', a RuntimeError is raised. Shape Mismatch: Volume and projection arrays must match self.volumeshape and self.projectionshape respectively. A ValueError is raised if they do not. Non-Contiguous Arrays: Input arrays are converted to contiguous float32 arrays before passing to TIGRE or shared memory copy. Cancellation: Cancellation is checked only during the wait loop. OperationCancelled is raised only after the current GPU call completes. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Communication Overhead: Data exchange uses shared memory buffers (volumeshared, projectionbuffers, partialvolumebuffers) to avoid network overhead in single-node multi-GPU setups. Strengths: Simple load balancing by partitioning angles across GPUs. Leverages TIGRE's optimized CUDA kernels. Limitations: Requires at least two GPUs and at least one projection angle. Volume and projection arrays must match specified shapes. When to Use: Single-node multi-GPU systems where the volume fits in shared memory and the bottleneck is projection/backprojection speed. When Not to Use: Multi-node distributed setups without shared memory support. Origin: This method is part of the TomoAnchor-V3 framework. History: It was introduced as a distributed computing framework for tomographic forward and backprojection operators using multiple GPUs via shared memory and multiprocessing. Usage: Used in computed tomography (CT) reconstruction, particularly for iterative algorithms like MBIR (Model-Based Iterative Reconstruction) that require repeated forward and backprojection operations. alidarbandi/TomoAnchor-V3, https://github.com/alidarbandi/TomoAnchor-V3, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial)

name: Inverse Rendering for PET Image Reconstruction
head: Differentiable PET Reconstruction, PET Inverse Rendering
body: Inverse Rendering (IR) for Positron Emission Tomography (PET) reconstructs the highest-resolution spatial distribution of a radioactive tracer (the emission image) from measured sinograms by inverting a differentiable forward rendering process. Unlike traditional algebraic methods or standard Maximum Likelihood Expectation Maximization (MLEM), this approach treats reconstruction as a gradient-based optimization problem where the forward model simulates photon detection via hybrid Monte Carlo sampling coupled with an analytical projector. It sets itself apart by leveraging physical differentiability to directly optimize voxel values against measured data, achieving superior resolution (clearly separating 0.7 mm hot-spots) and intensity accuracy compared to MLEM and deep learning baselines. The method reconstructs the 3D emission image \mathbf{I} by minimizing the discrepancy between the measured sinogram \mathbf{M} and a rendered sinogram \mathcal{R}(\mathbf{I}) generated by a differentiable forward model. Input: Measured sinogram data \mathbf{M}, representing coincident photon detection events. Output: Reconstructed emission image \hat{\mathbf{I}}, a 3D volume representing the spatial distribution of the radiotracer. Emission Image (\mathbf{I}): A 3D voxel grid representing the radioactive tracer distribution f(x, y, z). Sinogram (\mathbf{M}): A 4D dataset indexed by LOR parameters (s, \theta, z, \delta). s: Distance between the axial axis and the projection of the Line of Response (LOR) onto the transaxial plane. \theta: Angle between the projection and the transaxial axis (y-axis). z: Axial coordinate of the midpoint between the two detectors of the LOR. \delta: Tangent of the angle between the LOR and the transaxial plane. The set of all LORs is specified by (s, \theta, z, \delta) \in \mathbb{R}^{M \times 4}, where M is the number of crystal pairs. Time-of-Flight (TOF) Bins: For TOF-capable scanners, each LOR is divided into multiple bins symmetrically centered around the LOR midpoint. The forward model simulates the PET acquisition process. It uses hybrid Monte Carlo sampling to estimate line integrals of the source distribution along each LOR. For Time-of-Flight (TOF) rendering, the LOR is divided into n TOF bins. For the i-th TOF bin, the rendered sinogram value is estimated by sampling the emission image at various points within the image domain. The Monte Carlo estimator for the rendered sinogram \mathcal{R}(\mathbf{I}) is defined as: \mathcal{R}(\mathbf{I}) = p(s, \theta, z, \delta) = \frac{1}{m} \sum{i=1}^n \sum{j=1}^m fi\left(s \cdot \cos(\theta) - tj \cdot \sin(\theta), \, s \cdot \sin(\theta) + tj \cdot \cos(\theta)\right) Where: \mathcal{R}(\mathbf{I}) is the rendered sinogram value for a specific LOR. n is the total number of TOF bins. m is the total number of sampling points in the i-th TOF bin. fi is the voxel value of the emission image at the sampled location. tj denotes the projection of the LOR in the transaxial plane from the axial position z, corresponding to the j-th sampling point. The coordinates (s \cdot \cos(\theta) - tj \cdot \sin(\theta), s \cdot \sin(\theta) + tj \cdot \cos(\theta)) map the LOR geometry to the 2D transaxial plane coordinates for sampling. The reconstruction is performed by minimizing a loss function \mathcal{L} that measures the alignment between the rendered sinogram \mathcal{R}(\mathbf{I}) and the measured sinogram \mathbf{M}. 1. Initialize: Start with an initial estimate of the emission image \mathbf{I}^0. 2. Forward Pass: Compute the rendered sinogram \mathcal{R}(\mathbf{I}^k) using the forward rendering operator described above. 3. Loss Calculation: Compute the loss \mathcal{L}(\mathbf{M}; \mathcal{R}(\mathbf{I}^k)). The source specifies Mean Squared Error (MSE) as an example. \hat{\mathbf{I}} = \operatorname{argmin}{\mathbf{I}} \mathcal{L}(\mathbf{M}; \mathcal{R}(\mathbf{I})) 4. Gradient Computation: Compute the gradient of the loss with respect to the emission image \mathbf{I}^k. This requires differentiating the forward rendering operator \mathcal{R} with respect to each voxel. The differentiable forward rendering process provides the estimation of how a change in sinogram y can be achieved by modifying voxel values. 5. Update: Update the emission image using gradient descent: \mathbf{I}^{k+1} = \mathbf{I}^k - \eta \frac{\partial \mathcal{L}}{\partial \mathbf{I}^k} Where: \eta is the learning rate. \frac{\partial \mathcal{L}}{\partial \mathbf{I}^k} is the gradient propagated from the loss function at iteration k. 6. Iterate: Set \mathbf{I}^k = \mathbf{I}^{k+1} and repeat until convergence or a maximum number of iterations is reached. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def inverserenderingpet(measuredsinogram, lorparams, numiterations, learningrate, numtofbins, numsamplesperbin): """ Reconstructs PET emission image using inverse rendering. Args: measuredsinogram: List of lists of shape (M, numtofbins) containing measured sinogram data M. lorparams: List of tuples (s, theta, z, delta) for M crystal pairs. numiterations: Number of optimization steps. learningrate: Step size eta for gradient descent. numtofbins: Number of TOF bins n. numsamplesperbin: Number of sampling points m per TOF bin. Returns: reconstructedimage: 3D list representing the emission image I. """ M = len(lorparams) # Initialize emission image I^0 with zeros imgdim = 100 emissionimage = [[[0.0 for in range(imgdim)] for in range(imgdim)] for in range(imgdim)] for k in range(numiterations): # 1. Forward Pass: Compute rendered sinogram R(I^k) renderedsinogram = [[0.0 for in range(numtofbins)] for in range(M)] for l in range(M): s, theta, z, delta = lorparams[l] for i in range(numtofbins): # Iterate over TOF bins # Generate sampling points tj along the LOR projection samplingpointst = [float(j) 2.0 - float(numsamplesperbin) for j in range(numsamplesperbin)] binsum = 0.0 for j in range(numsamplesperbin): tj = samplingpointst[j] # Map to 2D transaxial plane coordinates xprime = s math.cos(theta) - tj math.sin(theta) yprime = s math.sin(theta) + tj math.cos(theta) # Sample voxel value fi at (xprime, yprime) at axial position z # Clamp to image bounds xidx = int(max(0, min(imgdim - 1, xprime))) yidx = int(max(0, min(imgdim - 1, yprime))) zidx = int(max(0, min(imgdim - 1, z))) fi = emissionimage[xidx][yidx][zidx] binsum += fi # Average over m samples renderedsinogram[l][i] = binsum / numsamplesperbin # 2. Loss Calculation: Compute MSE loss loss = 0.0 count = 0 for l in range(M): for i in range(numtofbins): diff = measuredsinogram[l][i] - renderedsinogram[l][i] loss += diff diff count += 1 loss = loss / count # 3. Gradient Computation: Backpropagate through forward render # dL/dR for MSE is 2(R - M) / (M N) dLdR = [[0.0 for in range(numtofbins)] for in range(M)] for l in range(M): for i in range(numtofbins): dLdR[l][i] = 2.0 (renderedsinogram[l][i] - measuredsinogram[l][i]) / count # Accumulate gradients into emission image gradientimage = [[[0.0 for in range(imgdim)] for in range(imgdim)] for in range(imgdim)] for l in range(M): s, theta, z, delta = lorparams[l] for i in range(numtofbins): gradval = dLdR[l][i] / numsamplesperbin samplingpointst = [float(j) 2.0 - float(numsamplesperbin) for j in range(numsamplesperbin)] for j in range(numsamplesperbin): tj = samplingpointst[j] xprime = s math.cos(theta) - tj math.sin(theta) yprime = s math.sin(theta) + tj math.cos(theta) xidx = int(max(0, min(imgdim - 1, xprime))) yidx = int(max(0, min(imgdim - 1, yprime))) zidx = int(max(0, min(imgdim - 1, z))) gradientimage[xidx][yidx][zidx] += gradval # 4. Update: I^{k+1} = I^k - eta dL/dI^k for x in range(imgdim): for y in range(imgdim): for z in range(imgdim): emissionimage[x][y][z] = emissionimage[x][y][z] - learningrate gradientimage[x][y][z] return emissionimage Learning Rate (\eta): The step size for gradient descent. Number of TOF Bins (n): Determines the temporal resolution of the forward model. Number of Sampling Points (m): The number of Monte Carlo samples per TOF bin. Scanner Geometry: Defined by (s, \theta, z, \delta) for each of the M crystal pairs. Ambiguity: The inverse problem is inherently ambiguous; gradient-based optimization finds a local minimum. Precision: The Monte Carlo estimator introduces noise. Boundaries: Sampling coordinates must be clamped to the image domain to prevent out-of-bounds access. Time Complexity: The forward pass involves Monte Carlo sampling for each LOR and TOF bin. Complexity is proportional to M \times n \times m, where M is the number of LORs, n is the number of TOF bins, and m is the number of samples per bin. The backward pass requires similar complexity for gradient accumulation. Memory Complexity: Requires storing the 3D emission image \mathbf{I} and the sinogram \mathbf{M}. Intermediate gradients also require memory proportional to the image size. Measured Performance: In tests with a simulated hot-spot phantom, the IR model achieved clear separation for hot-spots with a minimum diameter of 0.7 mm, whereas MLEM only demonstrated optimal separation for 0.8 mm. The IR model also showed higher pixel intensity accuracy in gray matter and nearly no intensity in white matter compared to MLEM. Strengths: Higher resolution than MLEM; outperforms DNN-based methods in some metrics; physically grounded differentiable model. Limitations: Computationally expensive due to Monte Carlo sampling and iterative optimization; solution is ambiguous without regularization; sensitive to initialization. When to Use: High-resolution PET reconstruction where physical accuracy is prioritized over speed. When Not to Use: Real-time applications requiring fast reconstruction. Inverse Rendering for PET was introduced by W. Jakob, B. Nicolet, Y. Li, Z. Wang, W. Tan, and Amirhossein Goldan. The work leverages Physically-Based Differentiable Rendering (PBDR) techniques, which have been used to differentiate image formation processes with respect to millions of parameters. This approach is similar to training a neural network but uses physical simulation instead of a learned model. The method aims to outperform Maximum Likelihood Expectation Maximization (MLEM) and Deep Neural Networks (DNNs) in PET image reconstruction. name: Deep Learning and Neural Representations
body: This family addresses the ill-posed inverse problem of tomographic reconstruction by replacing or augmenting traditional discrete voxel grids with neural networks, leveraging their expressive power to recover 3D density fields from sparse, noisy, or limited-angle projections. It distinguishes itself from sibling methods like Compressive Volume Rendering Recovery Methods and Iterative Solvers by optimizing continuous function parameters (network weights) rather than discrete voxel values, enabling high-resolution reconstruction from minimal data and simultaneous self-calibration of geometric parameters. See Tomographic reconstruction as inverse rendering for the shared differentiable forward projection, adjoint back-projection, and iterative optimization framework. This family encompasses methods that utilize deep neural networks to solve the inverse problem of tomographic reconstruction, mapping measured projection data (sinograms) directly or iteratively to a 3D volume estimate [8282-deep-learning-and-neural-architectures.md]. Unlike classical analytical methods (e.g., Filtered Back-Projection) or iterative algebraic techniques, these methods leverage the expressive power of neural architectures to regularize the ill-posed nature of the inverse Radon transform, particularly in sparse-view or noisy regimes [8282-deep-learning-and-neural-architectures.md]. They are distinguished from Neural Radiance Fields and Implicit Neural Representations by their explicit focus on tomographic geometry (Radon transforms) and often their ability to produce explicit voxel-based or parametric density volumes suitable for quantitative analysis, rather than just view-dependent rendering [8282-deep-learning-and-neural-architectures.md]. This family applies Implicit Neural Representations (INRs) to tomographic reconstruction, replacing discrete voxel grids with continuous functions parameterized by neural networks. It solves the ill-posed inverse problem of recovering 3D density fields from sparse, noisy, or limited-angle X-ray projections by leveraging the differentiability of the rendering pipeline. Unlike traditional discrete methods, these approaches optimize network weights directly, allowing for high-resolution reconstruction from minimal data and enabling simultaneous self-calibration of geometric and photometric parameters. Definition: HybridCT is a computationally efficient method for practical cloud tomography that combines deep learning and linear algebra to reconstruct cloud extinction volumes from multi-angle imaging observations. It combines a retrieval emulator with a reconstruction stage: (1) the retrieval is emulated using a deep learning U-Net architecture which is trained to map multi-angle radiance measurements into optical thickness values. (2) the reconstruction stage takes these multi-angle optical thickness values as input and uses SART (Simultaneous Algebraic Reconstruction Technique) to computationally reconstruct the cloud extinction volume. Steps: 1. Emulate retrieval using a deep learning U-Net architecture trained to map multi-angle radiance measurements into optical thickness values. 2. Take the multi-angle optical thickness values as input and use SART to computationally reconstruct the cloud extinction volume. Parameters: The method is demonstrated using synthetic multi-angle images representing the viewing angle geometry of the Multi-angle Imaging Spectroradiometer (MISR) onboard the Terra spacecraft at its red channel wavelength of 670 nm. Usage: Designed for practical cloud tomography using synthetic cloud fields from Large Eddy Simulations and synthetic multi-angle radiance fields rendered using the 3D Monte Carlo radiative transfer model MYSTIC and the libRadtran library. The method is used in practical cloud tomography to reconstruct cloud extinction volumes from multi-angle imaging observations. name: Deep Learning and Neural Architectures
head: DL-based Tomographic Reconstruction, Neural Inverse Solvers
body: This family encompasses methods that utilize deep neural networks to solve the inverse problem of tomographic reconstruction, mapping measured projection data (sinograms) directly or iteratively to a 3D volume estimate. Unlike classical analytical methods (e.g., Filtered Back-Projection) or iterative algebraic techniques, these methods leverage the expressive power of neural architectures to regularize the ill-posed nature of the inverse Radon transform, particularly in sparse-view or noisy regimes. They are distinguished from Neural Radiance Fields and Implicit Neural Representations by their explicit focus on tomographic geometry (Radon transforms) and often their ability to produce explicit voxel-based or parametric density volumes suitable for quantitative analysis, rather than just view-dependent rendering. All methods in this family rely on the differentiability of the forward projection operator \mathcal{P} and its adjoint (back-projection) \mathcal{P}^T. The core optimization problem is generally formulated as minimizing a loss function \mathcal{L} between the measured sinogram p and the rendered projection \hat{p} = \mathcal{P}(x) of the current volume estimate x: \minx \mathcal{L}(\mathcal{P}(x), p) + \lambda R(x) where R(x) is a regularizer (e.g., Total Variation, neural prior) and \lambda is a weighting factor. The gradient of the loss with respect to the volume x is computed via the chain rule: \frac{\partial \mathcal{L}}{\partial x} = \mathcal{P}^T \left( \frac{\partial \mathcal{L}}{\partial \hat{p}} \right) The term \frac{\partial \mathcal{L}}{\partial \hat{p}} is the residual gradient in projection space (e.g., p - \hat{p} for MSE), and \mathcal{P}^T is the back-projection operator. Key shared components include: 1. Forward Projection: Ray marching through the volume representation (voxels, octrees, or neural fields) to compute line integrals of density/absorption coefficients. 2. Backward Projection (Adjoint): Distributing the error from the 2D detector plane back into the 3D volume. This is mathematically the transpose of the forward operator, ensuring stable convergence in iterative methods. 3. Optimization Loop: An iterative process (e.g., SGD, Adam) that updates the volume parameters (voxel values, neural network weights, or Gaussian parameters) to reduce the projection error. Uses a neural network as an implicit regularizer, optimizing both the network weights and a latent variable. It distinguishes itself by requiring no external training data, relying instead on the network architecture's bias toward natural images. Adapts 3D Gaussian Splatting for X-ray tomography by correcting integration bias in the splatting kernel. It enables efficient differentiable rasterization and direct 3D density extraction, unlike standard 3DGS which is appearance-based. A fully differentiable U-Net based architecture that maps sinograms directly to volumes via a differentiable back-projection layer. It learns a generalizable mapping, unlike Deep Image Prior which optimizes per-instance. Decomposes the inverse Radon transform into a hierarchy of sparse connection layers, transitioning from the sinogram domain to the image domain. It avoids the parameter explosion of fully connected networks by using sparse connectivity. Applies self-attention mechanisms to capture long-range dependencies in volumetric data, addressing the local receptive field limitations of convolutions. Definition: A generator network G(r, z) that maps a sinogram r and a latent vector z to a reconstructed image, used for optimization in the inverse problem. Layout: The input sinogram r passes through an Embedding Conv 2D layer and a sequence of U-Net Blocks. The latent vector z is processed by a 'Modified Block' and integrated into the network. The architecture is analogous to the end-to-end reconstruction model but includes this latent injection mechanism. Definition: A supervised learning approach to map MRI intensities to acoustic impedance values Z(x, y, z) using a multi-layer perceptron (MLP) fitted to paired data of MRI intensities and reference impedance values from literature. Parameter: Reference impedance values from literature [4,5,6,14] are used for supervised training. Pitfall: MRI intensities do not correspond directly to physical quantities such as density or acoustic impedance; they reflect a complex combination of tissue-specific properties (water content, fat concentration, relaxation times) modulated by the acquisition sequence. This makes impedance reconstruction from MRI fundamentally ill-posed. The application of deep learning to tomographic reconstruction has evolved from post-processing denoising to end-to-end inverse solvers. Early works focused on using CNNs to denoise Filtered Back-Projection (FBP) outputs. Subsequent developments introduced differentiable forward/backward operators to embed the physics of the Radon transform directly into the network architecture, allowing for end-to-end training. The introduction of neural priors (Deep Image Prior) and novel differentiable renderers (3DGS adaptations) has further expanded the family to handle sparse-view and quantitative reconstruction tasks. name: Deep Image Prior Reconstruction
head: DIP Reconstruction, DRP Denoising
body: Deep Image Prior Reconstruction is an iterative tomographic reconstruction method that uses a neural network as an implicit regularizer to optimize an intermediate latent variable and network weights against measured sinogram data. It distinguishes itself from supervised neural architectures by decoupling the latent variable update from the network weight optimization, allowing the network architecture itself to act as a dynamic prior without external training data. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A sparse or noisy sinogram p (measured projection data). Output: A reconstructed 3D volume estimate x. Data Structures: The method maintains the following state variables: 1. PriorModel: A neural network that maps a latent tensor to the volume space. 2. Latent Variable z: An intermediate tensor updated via the data consistency term. 3. Projector: An object implementing the forward projection operator \mathcal{P} and its adjoint (back-projection) \mathcal{P}^T. 4. Optimizer: An Adam optimizer instance managing the gradients of the PriorModel parameters. 5. Loss: An MSE loss function. Algorithm Steps: The reconstruction proceeds in an alternating optimization loop consisting of outer epochs and inner steps. 1. Initialization: Initialize the PriorModel if not provided and move it to the device. Initialize the Adam optimizer with the PriorModel's parameters and a learning rate lr. Compute an initial estimate of the volume by applying Filtered Back Projection (FBP) to the sinogram p and detaching it from the computation graph: z = \text{FBP}(p).\text{detach}(). Set hyperparameters: number of outer epochs E, number of inner steps K, and latent update step size \beta. 2. Outer Loop (Epochs): For each epoch from 0 to E-1: Compute the current volume estimate: x = \text{PriorModel}(z). Compute the data consistency residual: \delta = \text{projector.backward}(p - \text{projector.forward}(x)). Update the latent variable: z = x + \beta \cdot \delta. 3. Inner Loop (Network Weight Optimization): For each inner step from 0 to K-1: Compute the forward projection of the current volume estimate: \hat{p} = \text{projector.forward}(\text{PriorModel}(z)). Compute the Mean Squared Error (MSE) loss between the predicted projections and the measured sinogram: \mathcal{L} = \text{MSE}(\hat{p}, p). Perform backpropagation to compute gradients with respect to the PriorModel parameters. Perform one Adam optimizer step to update the parameters. 4. Final Output: After completing all epochs, the final reconstruction is obtained by passing the final latent variable z through the prior network: x{\text{final}} = \text{PriorModel}(z). Parameters: E (epochs): Number of outer optimization epochs. Default: 250. K (innersteps): Number of Adam optimization steps per outer epoch. Default: 50. \beta (beta/stepsize): Step size for the latent variable update. Default: 0.25. lr: Learning rate for the Adam optimizer. Default not specified in the sources. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision: The FBP initialization must be detached from the computation graph to prevent gradients from flowing through it during the latent update. Boundaries: The projector must handle rays passing outside the volume bounds correctly, typically by contributing zero to the integral. Degenerate Input: If the sinogram p is extremely sparse or noisy, the FBP initialization may be poor, potentially leading to slow convergence or local minima. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import torch import torch.nn as nn import torch.optim as optim import numpy as np def deepimagepriorreconstruction(sinogramp, projector, priormodel=None, epochs=250, innersteps=50, beta=0.25, lr=0.01): """ Reconstructs a volume from sinogram data using Deep Image Prior. Args: sinogramp: Tensor of measured projections. projector: Object with methods forward(x) and backward(residual). priormodel: Neural network mapping latent z to volume x. If None, initialized. epochs: Number of outer epochs. innersteps: Number of inner Adam steps per epoch. beta: Step size for latent variable update. lr: Learning rate for Adam optimizer. Returns: Reconstructed volume tensor. """ # Standard U-Net initialization for volumetric prior if priormodel is None: priormodel = nn.Sequential( nn.Conv3d(1, 64, 3, padding=1), nn.ReLU(), nn.Conv3d(64, 1, 3, padding=1)) priormodel.train() optimizer = optim.Adam(priormodel.parameters(), lr=lr) # Standard FBP algorithm: filter sinograms and back-project into 3D volume z = fbp(sinogramp).detach() lossfn = nn.MSELoss() for in range(epochs): # Outer Loop: Update Latent Variable z x = priormodel(z) residual = sinogramp - projector.forward(x) delta = projector.backward(residual) z = x + beta delta # Inner Loop: Optimize PriorModel weights for in range(innersteps): phat = projector.forward(priormodel(z)) loss = lossfn(phat, sinogramp) optimizer.zerograd() loss.backward() optimizer.step() # Final reconstruction output = priormodel(z) return output def fbp(sinogram): # Standard FBP: apply ramp filter in frequency domain, then back-project # sinogram shape: [numprojections, numdetectors] # Returns 3D volume tensor numproj, numdet = sinogram.shape volume = torch.zeros((1, numdet, numdet, numdet), device=sinogram.device) for i in range(numproj): # Simple back-projection for demonstration; production FBP applies ramp filter angle = i np.pi / numproj volume[0,:,:,:] += sinogram[i,:] return volume / numproj This variant, proposed by Xu et al., proposes an unsupervised neural network for image reconstruction of gradient-domain volumetric photon density estimation, specifically for volumetric photon mapping. It utilizes a variant of GradNet with an encoded shift connection and a separated auxiliary feature branch that includes volume-based auxiliary features such as transmittance and photon density. The network is designed to smooth images at a global scale while preserving high-frequency details on a small scale. It produces higher-quality results than previous works such as L1, L2, or standard GradNet. However, it cannot reconstruct images with strong noise and tends to over-blur some features. While originally developed for volumetric photon mapping, the method is noted as straightforward to extend to other tasks like beam radiance estimation. Time Complexity: The method is computationally intensive due to the alternating optimization loop. Each epoch involves one forward/backward pass for the latent update and K forward/backward passes for the network weight update. The total number of forward projections per epoch is K+1. Memory Complexity: Memory usage is dominated by the storage of the PriorModel parameters, the latent variable z, and the intermediate tensors during backpropagation. Measured Performance: Specific quantitative metrics (PSNR, SSIM) are not provided in the sources for general scenes. Strengths: Unsupervised nature (no ground truth needed); effective regularization for sparse-view tomography; leverages the natural image bias of CNNs. Limitations: Computationally expensive due to iterative optimization. Poor FBP initialization can lead to slow convergence or local minima. When to use: Sparse-view or limited-angle tomography where traditional methods produce severe artifacts. When not to use: High-noise scenarios where the prior may over-smooth or fail to converge. Deep Image Prior Reconstruction was introduced as an application of the Deep Image Prior concept to tomographic reconstruction. The DIP concept demonstrates that the architecture of a convolutional neural network itself acts as a powerful prior for natural images. In the context of tomography, the method was adapted to handle the inverse problem of reconstructing 3D volumes from 2D projections. The specific implementation detailed in the sources is associated with the DiffTomo project. The variant for gradient-domain volumetric photon mapping was proposed by Xu et al., building upon earlier work on GradNet.
