name: R2-Gaussian
head: Rectified Radiative Gaussians
body: R2-Gaussian is a tomographic reconstruction method that adapts 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) to sparse-view X-ray imaging by rectifying an integration bias inherent in standard 3DGS splatting. It replaces the appearance-based 3DGS kernel with a radiative Gaussian kernel parameterized by density, position, and covariance, and derives new X-ray rendering functions to ensure accurate volume retrieval. Unlike siblings that use 3DGS only for data augmentation or replace rasterization with simulators, R2-Gaussian maintains efficient differentiable rasterization while enabling direct 3D density volume extraction. Inputs: Sparse-view X-ray projections (sinogram data), camera poses, and initial Gaussian parameters. Outputs: A set of optimized 3D Gaussian parameters representing the density field, and a reconstructed 3D volume. Data Structures: The core representation is a set of N 3D Gaussians. Each Gaussian i is defined by: 1. Position: \mui \in \mathbb{R}^3 2. Covariance: \Sigmai \in \mathbb{R}^{3 \times 3} (symmetric positive definite) 3. Central Density: \sigmai \in \mathbb{R} (isotropic attenuation coefficient) 4. Opacity/Alpha: \alphai \in [0, 1] (standard 3DGS parameter, though the radiative kernel focuses on density) Step 1: Initialization Initialize the Gaussian parameters using the analytical Filtered Back-Projection (FBP) or Feldkamp-Davis-Kress (FDK) method. This provides a coarse density estimate to bootstrap the optimization. Step 2: Forward Projection (X-ray Rasterization) For each view, render the projection by mapping 3D Gaussians to 2D Gaussians on the detector plane. 1. Local Affine Approximation: For a ray r(t) = o + td, approximate the 3D Gaussian transformation to the 2D image plane using a local affine approximation. 2. Rectification: Standard 3DGS splatting overlooks a covariance-related scaling factor when projecting a 3D Gaussian to 2D, leading to integration bias. R2-Gaussian derives new X-ray rendering functions that correct this bias. The rendered pixel value I(r) in logarithmic space is computed as the line integral of the density \sigma(r(t)): I(r) = \int{tn}^{tf} \sigma(r(t)) dt where tn, tf are the near and far bounds of the ray segment covered by the Gaussian. 3. Alpha Compositing: The 2D Gaussians are composited using standard alpha blending to produce the final projection image \hat{p}. Step 3: Loss Computation Compute the photometric loss between the measured X-ray projection p and the rendered projection \hat{p}. The raw pixel value I'(r) follows the Beer-Lambert Law: I'(r) = I0 \exp\left(-\int{tn}^{tf} \sigma(r(t)) dt\right) Tomography transforms this to logarithmic space for linearization: I(r) = \log I0 - \log I'(r) = \int{tn}^{tf} \sigma(r(t)) dt \quad \text{} The loss \mathcal{L} is computed as a photometric loss between the rendered and measured log-intensity. Step 4: Optimization Optimize the Gaussian parameters (\mui, \Sigmai, \sigmai) using photometric losses. 1. Compute the gradient of the loss with respect to the rendered projections: \frac{\partial \mathcal{L}}{\partial \hat{p}}. 2. Back-propagate through the differentiable rasterizer to obtain gradients for Gaussian parameters. 3. Voxel-based Regularization: Use a CUDA-based differentiable voxelizer to extract a 3D volume from the Gaussians during training. This allows the application of voxel-based regularizers to the extracted volume, improving reconstruction quality. Step 5: Volume Extraction After optimization, extract the final 3D density volume using the CUDA-based differentiable voxelizer. Pitfalls: Integration Bias: Using standard 3DGS splatting without rectification leads to inconsistent volumetric properties queried from different views, hampering accurate density retrieval. Affine Approximation Degradation: The local affine approximation used in splatting can degrade quantitative accuracy and complicate nonlinear geometric corrections. A tomography reconstruction setup that uses the volumetrically consistent rasterizer to recover the underlying 3D density field \sigma(x) from 2D images. It requires no changes to the alpha computation process and avoids the affine approximation used in standard 3DGS splatting, providing a more accurate forward rendering model for tomography. Speed: R2-Gaussian is significantly faster than NeRF-based solutions. On the IntraTomo dataset, it achieves 34.56 dB PSNR in 3 minutes (10k iterations) and 35.01 dB in 10 minutes (30k iterations). Comparison: It is 12x faster than the most efficient NeRF-based solution (NAF) and converges to optimal results in 15 minutes, improving PSNR by 0.6 dB compared to SOTA methods. Performance Metrics: IntraTomo: 33.19 dB, 138 min NAF: 33.99 dB, 32 min SAX-NeRF: 34.45 dB, 792 min R2-Gaussian (10k iters): 34.56 dB, 3 min R2-Gaussian (30k iters): 35.01 dB, 10 min Strengths: High efficiency, direct 3D density volume extraction, bias-free training pipeline. Limitations: Relies on the accuracy of the local affine approximation for splatting, which may degrade quantitative accuracy in complex geometries. R2-Gaussian was introduced in 2024 as the first 3DGS-based framework for sparse-view tomographic reconstruction. It addresses the under-explored potential of 3DGS in volumetric reconstruction tasks like X-ray CT. The method was developed to overcome the limitations of previous approaches that either treated 3DGS solely as data augmentation for traditional algorithms (e.g., FDK) or replaced efficient rasterization with CT simulators. name: End-to-End Reconstruction Model Architecture
head: Simultaneous Reconstruction and Denoising Model, End-to-end differentiable architecture, Sinogram-Based Tomography Reconstruction, g(r) model
body: This method is an end-to-end differentiable deep learning architecture that directly maps a noisy sinogram into a denoised 3D reconstruction, combining the reconstruction and denoising steps to mitigate noise amplification caused by the ill-conditioning of the Radon transform. It differs from traditional Filtered Back-Projection (FBP) by replacing the fixed linear filtration with a trainable neural network, and from pure post-processing methods by learning the physics of the acquisition geometry implicitly through the differentiable back-projection operator. Unlike Deep Image Prior Reconstruction which optimizes a static network's weights per instance, this model learns a generalizable mapping from sinogram to volume via joint optimization of its parameters. The model, denoted as g(r), consists of two U-Net instances (g1 and g2) connected by the Radon back-projection operator A^T. The architecture is defined by the composition: g(r) = g2 (A^T g1 (r)) where r is the noisy sensor reading (sinogram), g1 is a U-Net that processes the sinogram, A^T is the transpose of the discrete Radon transform (back-projection), and g2 is a U-Net that processes the back-projected images to produce the final reconstruction. Input: A noisy sinogram r. Output: A denoised 3D reconstruction volume. The model comprises two U-Net architectures, g1 and g2. The specific configuration depends on the model size (XXS, XS, S, S-64, M, L, XL, XXL). U-Net Block Structure: Each U-Net is composed of down-sampling and up-sampling blocks. 1. Down-sampling Block: Consists of a strided convolution followed by a sequence of residual blocks. 2. Up-sampling Block: Takes the output of the previous block. Doubles the resolution using bilinear up-sampling. Concatenates the result with the skip connection from the corresponding down-sampling block at the same resolution. Weights the concatenated channels using channel attention. Shrinks the number of channels via a 1 \times 1 convolution. Processes the result via a sequence of residual blocks. Residual Block Channels: The number of channels in residual blocks is doubled every two strided convolutions. The first block of XXS, XS, and S models uses 32 channels. The first block of S-64, M, L, XL, and XXL models uses 64 channels. Model Sizes and Residual Blocks: The number of residual blocks per U-Net block depends on the resolution and model size. Let N{res}(size, resolution) be the number of residual blocks for a given model size and resolution: | Resolution | XXS | XS | S | M | L | XL | XXL | |:--- |:--- |:--- |:--- |:--- |:--- |:--- |:--- | | 256 | 1 | 1 | 1 | 2 | 2 | 3 | 5 | | 128 | 1 | 1 | 1 | 1 | 2 | 3 | 5 | | 64 | 2 | 1 | 1 | 1 | 2 | 3 | 5 | | 32 | - | 2 | 2 | 1 | 2 | 3 | 5 | | 16 | - | - | 2 | 1 | 2 | 3 | 5 | | 8 | - | - | - | 2 | 3 | 5 | 9 | | 16 | - | - | - | 2 | 3 | 4 | 6 | | 32 | - | - | 2 | 2 | 3 | 4 | 6 | | 64 | - | 2 | 2 | 2 | 3 | 4 | 6 | | 128 | 2 | 2 | 2 | 2 | 3 | 4 | 6 | | 256 | 1 | 2 | 2 | 2 | 4 | 4 | 6 | Note: "-" indicates the resolution is not applicable or not used for that model size. Channel Counts for Back-Projection: The smallest end-to-end model (XXS for g1, S-64 for g2) uses 16 channels for the Radon back-projection input. Other end-to-end models use 32 channels. 1. Sinogram Embedding (g1 Input): The input sinogram r passes through an "Embedding Conv 2D" layer. The output passes through a U-Net Block. This sequence is repeated for multiple U-Net Blocks to form the g1 network. The specific number of blocks and their resolutions follow the U-Net architecture defined by the chosen model size (e.g., S-64). The final convolution of g1 reduces the number of channels to the back-projection channel count (16 or 32). 2. Radon Back-Projection: The multi-channel output of g1 is transformed into images using the Radon back-projection operator A^T. Each channel of the output from g1 is treated as a separate sinogram and back-projected into an image. 3. Positional Encoding: The output of A^T (shape (ch, 256, 256)) is concatenated with a 4-dimensional positional embedding (shape (4, 256, 256)) in the first layer of g2. This positional embedding is processed by a "Pos Features Conv 2D" layer to encode pixel coordinates. 4. Reconstruction and Denoising (g2): The concatenated input (back-projected images + positional features) is processed by a sequence of U-Net Blocks to form the g2 network. The architecture of g2 follows the same U-Net structure as g1, but with potentially different dimensions (e.g., S-64). Blocks with multiple inputs (e.g., skip connections) up-sample each input to the largest resolution using bilinear up-sampling, then concatenate all inputs on the channel dimension. The model is trained end-to-end by jointly optimizing the parameters of g1 and g2 to minimize an image reconstruction loss. The differentiability of the Radon back-projection operator A^T allows gradients to flow from the loss in the image space, through g2, through A^T, through g1, and back to the input sinogram r. Unlike Gradient-Aware ResNet Reconstruction, it treats the input as a static noisy image rather than conditioning on the explicit Radon matrix. name: ResNet-Based CT Reconstruction
head: CNN Reconstruction, Deep Learning CT Reconstruction, Learned Post-Processing, Learned Post-Processing with ResNet
body: ResNet-Based CT Reconstruction is a learned post-processing method that maps noisy filtered backprojection (FBP) reconstructions directly to ground truth images, learning to suppress artifacts and noise. It differs from Gradient-Aware ResNet Reconstruction by treating the input as a static noisy image rather than conditioning on the explicit Radon matrix. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Noisy FBP reconstruction f{BP} (2D image tensor). Output: Cleaned reconstruction f{pred} (2D image tensor). Data Structures: ResNet: A convolutional neural network model instance. inputs: Tensor of shape (batchsize, channels, height, width). targets: Tensor of shape (batchsize, channels, height, width) containing ground truth images. Training Procedure: 1. Dataset Generation: Create synthetic ground truth images f{true} consisting of 5 to 20 overlapping ellipses of varying sizes. Generate sinograms from f{true} using a projector and projection geometry. Add noise to sinograms. Reconstruct noisy sinograms using filtered backprojection (FBP) to obtain f{BP}. 2. Model Initialization: Initialize the ResNet() model. 3. Loss Function: Define the loss as Mean Squared Error (MSE) between the network output and the ground truth: L = \text{MSE}(f{pred}, f{true}). 4. Optimization: Use the Adam optimizer with a learning rate of 0.001. 5. Training Loop: Iterate for numepochs (default 10). For each batch: forward pass outputs = model(inputs.float()). Compute loss loss = criterion(outputs, targets.float()). Backpropagate loss.backward(). Update weights optimizer.step(). 6. Evaluation: Evaluate on a validation set. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import torch import torch.nn as nn import torch.optim as optim class ResNet(nn.Module): def init(self, inchannels=1, outchannels=1): super().init() self.conv1 = nn.Conv2d(inchannels, 32, kernelsize=3, padding=1) self.relu = nn.ReLU() self.conv2 = nn.Conv2d(32, outchannels, kernelsize=3, padding=1) def forward(self, x): return self.conv2(self.relu(self.conv1(x))) def trainresnetct(model, trainloader, numepochs=10, batchsize=32, lr=0.001): criterion = nn.MSELoss() optimizer = optim.Adam(model.parameters(), lr=lr) model.train() for epoch in range(numepochs): for inputs, targets in trainloader: optimizer.zerograd() # Zero gradients before backward pass outputs = model(inputs.float()) loss = criterion(outputs, targets.float()) loss.backward() optimizer.step() def inferresnetct(model, inputs): model.eval() with torch.nograd(): return model(inputs.float()) Parameters: lr: Learning rate, default 0.001. batchsize: Training batch size, default 32. numepochs: Number of training epochs, default 10. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Not given in the sources. Extends standard ResNet by conditioning on the explicit Radon matrix A, incorporating geometric projection constraints directly during reconstruction. Not given in the sources. The method originates from the use of convolutional neural networks (CNNs) for medical image reconstruction, specifically leveraging ResNet architectures for artifact suppression in CT. It builds on the concept of learned post-processing, where traditional reconstruction methods (like FBP) are used to generate an initial estimate, which is then refined by a deep learning model. name: Gradient-Aware ResNet Reconstruction
head: Gradient-Conditioned Reconstruction
body: Gradient-Aware ResNet Reconstruction extends standard ResNet-based CT reconstruction by conditioning the neural network on the explicit Radon matrix A (the forward projection operator). This allows the network to incorporate geometric projection constraints directly during reconstruction, rather than treating the input as a static noisy image. It differs from pure post-processing methods by using acquisition geometry to guide denoising and artifact suppression. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A tuple (f, g), where f is the current image estimate (initially the noisy filtered backprojection) and g is the Radon matrix A. Output: A tuple containing the concatenated image-gradient tensor and the Radon matrix g. Data Structures: The Radon matrix A is passed explicitly as g. A boolean flag sparsesvd controls sparse SVD computation during matrix construction, defaulting to True. Gradient utilities (applyDx, applyDy, applyDxTrans, applyDyTrans) implement finite differences using np.diff with boundary padding to handle image edges. Algorithm Steps: 1. Gradient Computation: The gradient method computes the gradient of the data fidelity term. It projects f using A, computes A^T(Af), permutes the result, and triggers a backward pass on the mean to extract \nablaf. The output is reshaped to match the input image dimensions. 2. Concatenation: The image f and computed gradient are concatenated along the channel dimension: x{\text{cat}} = \text{cat}(f, \nablaf, \text{dim}=1). 3. Output: The module returns the concatenated tensor and the Radon matrix g for subsequent processing steps. 4. Training Loop: The model is trained via supervised learning. Inputs and targets are passed through the model, a loss (e.g., MSE) is computed, and gradients are backpropagated to update weights. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import torch import torch.nn as nn class GradientAwareResNet(nn.Module): def init(self): super().init() self.resnet = nn.Sequential( nn.Conv2d(2, 64, 3, padding=1), nn.ReLU(), nn.Conv2d(64, 1, 3, padding=1)) def gradient(self, f, g): # f: image estimate [B, 1, H, W] # g: Radon matrix A [B, Nproj, Ndet] Afg = torch.matmul(g, f.view(f.shape[0], -1)).view(f.shape) ATAtg = (g.transpose(-2, -1).squeeze(0) @ Afg).permute(0, 2, 1) ATAtg.mean().backward() out = f.grad.permute(0, 2, 1).reshape(f.shape) return out def forward(self, x): f, g = x grad = self.gradient(f, g) return (torch.cat((f, grad), dim=1), g) def trainstep(model, inputs, targets, optimizer, criterion): optimizer.zerograd() outputs = model(inputs) loss = criterion(outputs, targets.float()) loss.backward() optimizer.step() Parameters: sparsesvd: Boolean flag in explicitradon to control sparse SVD computation. Default: True. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision: The gradient computation relies on matrix operations with the Radon matrix, which can be memory-intensive for large datasets. Boundaries: The finite difference utilities use np.diff with boundary padding, implying zero-padding or similar boundary handling must be consistent with the projection geometry. Incorporates the Radon transform and its gradient directly into a learned iterative framework. It merges traditional optimization with neural network flexibility, allowing the model to adaptively learn prior constraints from inverse problems theory, unlike pure post-processing which only corrects final images. Choose this variant when iterative refinement with physics-informed priors is required over direct end-to-end mapping. See ResNet-Based CT Reconstruction. Time Complexity: Depends on the size of the Radon matrix A and the ResNet depth. The gradient computation involves matrix-vector multiplications (A and A^T), which scales with the number of projection angles and detector samples. Memory Complexity: Requires storing the explicit Radon matrix A and intermediate gradient tensors. The concatenation of f and grad doubles the channel dimension input to the ResNet. Strengths: Incorporates physical constraints (geometry) directly into the learning process, potentially leading to more accurate reconstructions than methods ignoring the projection model. Limitations: Requires explicit access to the Radon matrix, which may not be available or feasible to store for very large datasets. This method originates from the inverse-problems-CT-scans repository by imanfs. It builds on the concept of using ResNets for CT reconstruction [8264-resnet-based-ct-reconstruction.md] by conditioning the network on the forward projection operator. The source code includes utilities for wavelet thresholding and iterative thresholding, indicating a broader context of inverse problem solving in CT. imanfs/inverse-problems-CT-scans - GitHub, https://github.com/imanfs/inverse-problems-CT-scans, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial)

name: Hierarchical CT Reconstruction via Domain Transform
head: Hierarchical DL framework, Hierarchical DL reconstruction, Hierarchical Deep Learning Tomographic Reconstruction, Hierarchical Domain Transform Decomposition, Hierarchical decomposition of domain transforms, Partial line integral domain transform
body: Hierarchical CT Reconstruction via Domain Transform is a deep learning framework that solves large-scale inverse problems, such as tomographic reconstruction, by decomposing the non-local, space-variant integral transform into a sequence of simpler, local hierarchical steps. Unlike brute-force fully connected networks that require intractable parameter counts for full-scale data, this method avoids dense connectivity by introducing virtual intermediate data representations (partial line integrals). It sets itself apart from siblings like Deep Image Prior Reconstruction, R2-Gaussian, End-to-End Reconstruction Model Architecture, and Transformer-based Architectures by explicitly constructing a homotopy-like continuum of data domains (from line integrals to partial line integrals to voxels) rather than relying on implicit neural priors or direct end-to-end mapping of the full sinogram to the image. Input: A sinogram p(r, \theta) representing line integrals, with dimensions Nr radial bins and N\theta projection angles. For the reference implementation, Nr = 512 and N\theta = 512. Output: A reconstructed image f(x, y) (or f(r, t) at \theta=0) with dimensions Nx \times Ny. For the reference implementation, 512 \times 512. The method operates on a hierarchy of stages L=0 to L=N. Each stage L holds data in the partial line integral domain, defined by three dimensions: 1. Depth bins (Nt): Represents depth resolution along the projection ray. 2. Projection angles (N\theta): The number of angular views. 3. Radial bins (Nr): The number of detector channels. The data tensor at stage L has shape (Nt^{(L)}, N\theta^{(L)}, Nr^{(L)}). The total data size is kept approximately constant across stages: Nt^{(L)} \times N\theta^{(L)} \times Nr^{(L)} \approx \text{Constant}. Reference Dimension Progression (2D, 512^2 output): L=0 (Input Sinogram): (1, 512, 512) L=1: (2, 256, 512) L=2: (8, 64, 512) L=3: (32, 16, 512) L=4: (128, 4, 512) L=5 (Output Image): (512, 1, 512) The ratio of depth bins to projection angles between stages does not need to be a power of two or an integer, as the network is trained to perform resampling and interpolation of the data between hierarchical stages. The forward model is the Fredholm integral equation of the first kind: p(v) = \int K(u,v)f(u)du where K(u,v) = \delta(ux \cos v\theta + uy \sin v\theta - vr) is the Dirac delta kernel for parallel-beam geometry, u=(ux, uy) are image coordinates, and v=(vr, v\theta) are projection coordinates. The method introduces a virtual intermediate representation q\alpha(v, t) using a window function \Pi(\cdot): q\alpha(v,t) = \int K(u,v)f(u)\Pi\left(\frac{t-u}{\alpha}\right)du where: \alpha is a scale factor controlling the window size. t is a parameter specifying the location of the window (depth). \Pi(x) = 1 for x < 0.5 and 0 elsewhere. In the limit \alpha \to \infty, q\alpha(v,t) = p(v) (line integral domain). In the limit \alpha \to 0, the window becomes a Dirac delta impulse, yielding the voxel domain f(u). \alpha (Scale Factor): Controls the width of the integration window. Decreases from \infty (input) to 0 (output) across stages. \Pi(x): Rectangular window function. Neighborhood Size: For sparse connection layers, each input neuron connects to a small neighborhood of output neurons. Empirical size: 3 \text{ depths} \times 5 \text{ angles} \times 3 \text{ radial bins}. Number of Stages (L): On the order of O(\log n), where n is the data dimension (512 \times 512). 1. Define Hierarchy: Determine the sequence of data dimensions (Nt, N\theta, Nr) for stages L=0 to L=N. 2. Initialize Network: Construct L sparse connection layers. 3. Initialize Weights: Initialize sparse connection weights to all ones. Initialize convolution kernels (if used) with the Glorot uniform initializer. 4. Pre-training (Optional): Train each sparse connection layer individually using synthetic noise data to initialize weights to a reasonable magnitude. This reduces total training time but does not affect the final loss function. 5. End-to-End Training (Noise-Based): Generate training pairs: Computer-generated white Gaussian random noise patterns f{noise} and their forward projections p{noise} using distance-driven projection. Compute intermediate labels q{\alpha}^{(L)} for each stage using Filtered Back Projection (FBP) on the noise patterns onto non-isotropic voxel grids corresponding to stage L dimensions. Train the network to minimize Mean Squared Error (MSE) between the network output and the intermediate labels. Vanishing Gradient Handling: During end-to-end training, update only one layer per iteration while freezing others. Select the layer randomly at each iteration. Linear Constraint: Exclude non-linear activation units during this phase to constrain the network to learning a linear inverse operator, preventing it from learning noise appearance as a prior. 6. End-to-End Training (Clinical Refinement): Generate training pairs from clinical CT images: Reproject clinical images to create sinograms with added random noise. Include non-linear activation units (e.g., ReLU) in convolutional layers to learn non-linear priors. Train end-to-end using MSE loss. 7. Reconstruction: For a new sinogram, pass it through the trained network. The final stage L=N outputs the reconstructed image f(x,y) where \theta=0 and \alpha corresponds to the voxel size. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import numpy as np class SparseConnectionLayer: """ Implements a sparse fully-connected layer where each input neuron connects only to a small neighborhood of output neurons. Forward operator: product of input data and sparse matrix. Backpropagation operator: product of transpose of sparse matrix and gradient. """ def init(self, inputshape, outputshape, neighborhood): self.inputshape = inputshape self.outputshape = outputshape self.neighborhood = neighborhood self.buildsparsity() self.weights = np.ones(len(self.rows)) # Initialized to all ones def buildsparsity(self): rows, cols = [], [] for i in range(np.prod(self.inputshape)): incoords = np.unravelindex(i, self.inputshape) for dt in range(-self.neighborhood[0]//2, self.neighborhood[0]//2 + 1): for dtheta in range(-self.neighborhood[1]//2, self.neighborhood[1]//2 + 1): for dr in range(-self.neighborhood[2]//2, self.neighborhood[2]//2 + 1): outcoords = (incoords[0] + dt, incoords[1] + dtheta, incoords[2] + dr) if 0 <= outcoords[0] < self.outputshape[0] and \ 0 <= outcoords[1] < self.outputshape[1] and \ 0 <= outcoords[2] < self.outputshape[2]: rows.append(np.ravelmultiindex(outcoords, self.outputshape)) cols.append(i) self.rows = np.array(rows) self.cols = np.array(cols) def forward(self, x): batchsize = x.shape[0] flatx = x.reshape(batchsize, -1) flatout = np.zeros((batchsize, np.prod(self.outputshape))) for b in range(batchsize): for idx in range(len(self.rows)): flatout[b, self.rows[idx]] += self.weights[idx] flatx[b, self.cols[idx]] return flatout.reshape(batchsize, self.outputshape) def backward(self, gradout): batchsize = gradout.shape[0] flatgradout = gradout.reshape(batchsize, -1) flatgradin = np.zeros((batchsize, np.prod(self.inputshape))) for b in range(batchsize): for idx in range(len(self.rows)): flatgradin[b, self.cols[idx]] += self.weights[idx] flatgradout[b, self.rows[idx]] return flatgradin.reshape(batchsize, self.inputshape) def createhierarchicalnetwork(stagedims, neighborhood=(3, 5, 3)): layers = [] for i in range(1, len(stagedims)): inputdims = stagedims[i-1] outputdims = stagedims[i] layer = SparseConnectionLayer(inputdims, outputdims, neighborhood) layers.append(layer) # Optional convolutional layers (L1: 1D kernel size 512; L2-L5: 2D 3x3 kernels with ReLU) are inserted here. return layers def trainhierarchicalnetwork(layers, sinograms, noiseimages, numiterations=1000, batchsize=20): for iteration in range(numiterations): layeridx = np.random.randint(0, len(layers)) noisebatch = noiseimages[np.random.choice(len(noiseimages), batchsize)] # Distance-driven forward projection operator sinogrambatch = np.zeroslike(noisebatch) predictions = layers[layeridx].forward(sinogrambatch) loss = np.mean((predictions - noisebatch) 2) gradout = 2 (predictions - noisebatch) / (predictions.size) gradin = layers[layeridx].backward(gradout) # SGD weight update step # layers[layeridx].weights -= learningrate gradient Vanishing Gradients: During end-to-end training, gradients may vanish across the deep hierarchy. This is mitigated by updating only one layer per iteration while freezing others. Parameter Explosion: Implementing the transforms as fully connected layers would require 512^4 \approx 69 billion parameters per stage, which is intractable. The sparse connection layer reduces the parameter count to O(n \log n). Noise Learning: If non-linear activations are used during noise-based training, the network may learn to reproduce noise artifacts as prior information. Using linear activations constrains the network to learn the linear inverse operator. Dimension Ratios: The ratio of depth bins to projection angles between stages does not need to be an integer, but the network must be trained to handle the resampling. Time Complexity: The computational complexity scales linearly with data size, even for extension to three dimensions, due to sparse network connections between hierarchical levels. Memory Complexity: The number of parameters scales as O(n \log n) for 2D and O(n^2 \log n) for 3D, where n is the data dimension. For a 512 \times 512 2D image, the network uses ~42 million parameters, which is 0.06% of the 69 billion parameters required by a fully connected layer. Measured Performance: In the reference implementation, training took ~4 hours for pre-training individual layers and ~1 day for end-to-end refinement on an NVIDIA Tesla V100 GPU. Strengths: Scalable to full-size problems (e.g., 512^4 system matrix); avoids brute-force dense networks; does not rely on direct or iterative inversion techniques. Limitations: Requires synthetic noise data for initial training; clinical refinement is needed for optimal image quality; currently demonstrated primarily for 2D parallel-beam geometry. When to Use: When reconstructing large-scale tomographic data where traditional iterative methods are too slow and fully connected deep learning models are intractable. When Not to Use: For small-scale problems where analytical methods (FBP) are sufficient and fast, or when hardware constraints prevent the training of deep hierarchical networks. The hierarchical approach was conceived independently of the AUTOMAP approach. Prior attempts using supervised learning relied on brute-force fully connected networks limited to 128^4 system matrix sizes, which could not practically scale to realistic data sizes like 512^4 or 512^6. This method was introduced to solve such large-scale inverse problems by decomposing the domain transform into hierarchical stages. It is applicable to other imaging problems such as emission and magnetic resonance reconstruction. Deep learning tomographic reconstruction through hierarchical decomposition of domain transforms., https://doi.org/10.1186/s42492-022-00127-y, fetched 2026-10-26

name: Transformer-based Architectures
head: Transformer-based Neural Representations, Vision Transformers in Volume Rendering
body: Transformer-based architectures apply self-attention mechanisms to capture long-range dependencies in volumetric data, addressing the local receptive field limitations of convolutions in volume rendering. They are distinct from sibling methods like DuDoTrans (which integrates transformers into iterative tomographic loops) and Generalizable Radiance Fields via Transformer Attention (which focuses on cross-view aggregation for generalization) by primarily leveraging the global context of attention to recover large-scale structures, denoise, or aggregate multi-view features directly. All methods in this family rely on the differentiability of the forward projection operator \mathcal{P} and its adjoint (back-projection) \mathcal{P}^T. The core optimization problem is generally formulated as minimizing a loss function \mathcal{L} between the measured sinogram p and the rendered projection \hat{p} = \mathcal{P}(x) of the current volume estimate x: \minx \mathcal{L}(\mathcal{P}(x), p) + \lambda R(x) where R(x) is a regularizer (e.g., Total Variation, neural prior) and \lambda is a weighting factor. The gradient of the loss with respect to the volume x is computed via the chain rule: \frac{\partial \mathcal{L}}{\partial x} = \mathcal{P}^T \left( \frac{\partial \mathcal{L}}{\partial \hat{p}} \right) The term \frac{\partial \mathcal{L}}{\partial \hat{p}} is the residual gradient in projection space (e.g., p - \hat{p} for MSE), and \mathcal{P}^T is the back-projection operator. Key shared components include: 1. Forward Projection: Ray marching through the volume representation (voxels, octrees, or neural fields) to compute line integrals of density/absorption coefficients. 2. Backward Projection (Adjoint): Distributing the error from the 2D detector plane back into the 3D volume. This is mathematically the transpose of the forward operator, ensuring stable convergence in iterative methods. 3. Optimization Loop: An iterative process (e.g., SGD, Adam) that updates the volume parameters (voxel values, neural network weights, or Gaussian parameters) to reduce the projection error. DuDoTrans is a dual-domain transformer architecture designed for sparse-view CT reconstruction, addressing the ill-posed nature of tomographic inversion when projection data is limited. It distinguishes itself from standard transformer-based reconstruction methods by explicitly operating in both the image domain (via Swin Transformer blocks) and the projection domain (via differentiable forward/back-projection), leveraging window-based multi-head self-attention to reduce computational complexity while maintaining global context. This method addresses the problem of generalizing neural radiance field representations to unseen objects or scenes without requiring per-scene optimization. It solves the limitation of standard NeRFs, which overfit to specific training views, by learning generalizable geometric priors from source images. It sets itself apart from sibling methods like DuDoTrans and Transformer-based Tomographic Reconstruction by focusing on cross-view feature aggregation via attention mechanisms rather than iterative tomographic inversion or specific architectural variants like Ray Transformers. Transformers compute pairwise attention over input tokens to capture long-range dependencies that convolutions miss. The Vision Transformer (ViT) adapts this architecture for images by treating fixed-size patches as tokens. In volume rendering, they are used for super-resolution and denoising, where their ability to attend across the full spatial extent of a subvolume helps recover large-scale structures that local convolutions miss. Transformer-based Tomographic Reconstruction is a deep learning technique that reconstructs 3D single-photon emission computed tomography (SPECT) images using a slice-by-slice transformer network (SSTrans-3D). It addresses the considerable artifacts caused by incomplete projection data in image reconstruction. It differs from siblings like DuDoTrans and DIOR by relying on a pure transformer architecture rather than combining deep learning with iterative optimization. Definition: A transformer architecture that infers volume density by incorporating relative depth differences as position encoding, rather than absolute positions. Steps: 1. Sample M points pm on ray r with depths tm. 2. Calculate relative depth encoding Em for each point using \deltam. 3. Element-wise add Em to point feature fm. 4. Pass through self-attention and feed-forward network to predict volume density \sigmam. Parameters: K: Length of the position encoding feature vector. Details: The relative depth \deltam is calculated as \deltam = \frac{tm - d}{u(t{far} - t{near})}, where d is the estimated depth, t{near} and t{far} are the near and far plane depths, and u is a hyperparameter controlling the range. The position encoding Em uses sinusoidal functions with frequencies \omegak = \frac{1}{10000^{2i/K}} for even/odd indices k. Definition: A proposer network constrained to reduce computational cost, using a single transformer block for encoder and decoder with a single attention head. Layout: Features are projected to 16-D. A single transformer block is used for the encoder. A single transformer block is used for the decoder. A single attention head is used. Context: This architecture is used in NeRF sampling to propose points for coarse and fine networks, reducing the overhead compared to fully connected layers while maintaining reasonable cost. Definition: Using Masked Auto Encoder combined with a 3D transformer-based architecture to learn a generalized representation capable of reconstructing unseen scenes. Context: This approach scales self-supervised NeRF training by leveraging geometric cues from sparse inputs, enabling transfer learning and generalization to new scenes without per-scene optimization. Definition: A large feedforward transformer model that encodes sparse-view X-ray projections into compact latent tokens and fuses them across views to reconstruct a 3D CT volume density field. Steps: 1. Encode each X-ray projection Ii independently using a feature extractor F{enc} (specifically DINO) to produce patch features Hi: Hi = F{enc}(Ii) for i = 1, \dots, K. 2. Inject camera geometry into the encoded features by applying ModLN with Plücker ray embeddings Ri: \tilde{H}i = ModLN(Hi, Ri) for i = 1, \dots, K. 3. Concatenate the modulated features from all K views and process them through a 16-layer Fusion ViT (similar to ViT-B) using all-to-all self-attention F{fuse} to produce fused features \{F1, \dots, FK\}. Parameters: Fusion ViT depth: 16 layers, architecture similar to ViT-B. Encoder backbone: DINO transformer. Camera embedding: Plücker ray embedding Ri, derived from the cross product between camera location and ray direction, independent of scale, camera position, and focal length. Definition: A model using Transformers for volume rendering, processing ray-depth-ordered feature sequences from multiple source views. Steps: 1. Processes ray-depth-ordered feature sequences from multiple source views. 2. Uses alternating pooling and ray-wise attention layers. 3. Enables effective joint feature aggregation and ray marching. Context: NeRFormer is geometry-free and does not produce the scene's density function directly, nor does it rely on geometric inductive biases, distinguishing it from standard NeRF models. Transformer architectures have been adapted for volume rendering to overcome the local connectivity constraints of Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs). The Vision Transformer (ViT) was originally proposed for image classification. In the context of Neural Radiance Fields (NeRF), transformers have been used for view aggregation, sampling proposal, and generalizable reconstruction. The integration of transformers into tomographic reconstruction, such as in DuDoTrans and SSTrans-3D, addresses the ill-posed nature of sparse-view problems by leveraging global attention to recover missing information. name: DuDoTrans
head: DuDoTransModel
body: DuDoTrans is a dual-domain transformer architecture designed for sparse-view CT reconstruction, addressing the ill-posed nature of tomographic inversion when projection data is limited. It distinguishes itself from standard transformer-based reconstruction methods by explicitly operating in both the image domain (via Swin Transformer blocks) and the projection domain (via differentiable forward/back-projection), leveraging window-based multi-head self-attention to reduce computational complexity while maintaining global context. DuDoTrans integrates a Swin Transformer into the iterative optimization loop of differentiable tomographic reconstruction. The network processes 2D projection images (sinograms) or reconstructed volume slices, using windowed attention to model local structures efficiently. Input: A batch of 2D images (sinograms or volume slices) with shape (B, H, W, C), where B is batch size, H, W are spatial dimensions, and C is the number of channels (typically 1 for grayscale sinograms). Output: A refined 2D image tensor of shape (B, H, W, C). In the full reconstruction pipeline, these outputs are aggregated or used to update the 3D volume estimate via the differentiable forward/back-projection operators defined in the parent article. The core data structure is the Swin Transformer Block, which relies on specific tensor layouts for relative position bias. 1. Relative Position Bias Table (relativepositionbiastable) Type: Parameter tensor (learnable weights). Shape: ((2Wh - 1)(2Ww - 1), \text{num\heads}). Initialization: Zeros, followed by truncated normal distribution with standard deviation 0.02. Purpose: Stores learnable biases for relative spatial positions within an attention window. 2. Relative Position Index (relativepositionindex) Type: Buffer tensor (constant, not updated during training). Shape: (Wh Ww, Wh Ww). Content: Integer indices mapping each pair of positions in the window to an entry in relativepositionbiastable. windowsize: Height and width of the attention window. Default: (7, 7). shiftsize: Shift size for shifted window partitioning. If 0, non-shifted windows are used. Default: 0. mlpratio: Ratio of MLP hidden dimension to embedding dimension. Default: 4.0. qkscale: Override for the scaling factor of Query and Key vectors. If None, defaults to dk^{-0.5} where dk is the head dimension. The input tensor is partitioned into non-overlapping windows to enable local attention. 1. Reshape input x \in \mathbb{R}^{B \times H \times W \times C} to (B, H/Ws, Ws, W/Ws, Ws, C), where Ws is the window size. 2. Permute dimensions to (B, H/Ws, W/Ws, Ws, Ws, C). 3. Flatten spatial window dimensions to obtain windows x{win} \in \mathbb{R}^{(B \cdot \frac{H}{Ws} \cdot \frac{W}{Ws}) \times Ws \times Ws \times C}. Let N{win} = B \cdot \frac{H}{Ws} \cdot \frac{W}{Ws} be the number of windows. Compute the index mapping for relative positions within each window. 1. Generate coordinates: coordsh = \text{arange}(Wh), coordsw = \text{arange}(Ww). 2. Create meshgrid and flatten to shape (2, Wh Ww). 3. Compute relative coordinates: relative\coords = coords\flatten[:,:, \text{None}] - coords\flatten[:, \text{None},:]. 4. Permute to shape (Wh Ww, Wh Ww, 2). 5. Shift indices to ensure non-negative values: relative\coords[:,:, 0] += Wh - 1 relative\coords[:,:, 1] += Ww - 1 6. Map to 1D index: relative\coords[:,:, 0] = 2Ww - 1. 7. Sum to get final index: relative\position\index = \text{sum}(relative\coords, \text{axis}=-1). Result shape: (Wh Ww, Wh Ww). Compute attention within each window. 1. Linear Projection: Compute qkv = \text{Linear}(x{win}). Reshape to (N{win}, N, 3, \text{num\heads}, C/\text{num\heads}) where N = Ws^2. Permute to (3, N{win}, \text{num\heads}, N, C/\text{num\heads}) to separate Q, K, V. 2. Scale Q: q = q \cdot \text{scale}, where \text{scale} = \text{qk\scale} or dk^{-0.5}. 3. Attention Scores: attn = q \cdot k^T. Shape: (N{win}, \text{num\heads}, N, N). 4. Add Bias: Retrieve bias: bias = \text{table}[relative\position\index]. Shape: (N, N, \text{num\heads}). Reshape/Permute bias to (\text{num\heads}, N, N). Add to attention scores: attn = attn + bias. 5. Softmax: Apply softmax along the last dimension (key dimension). 6. Dropout: Apply attention dropout. 7. Output: Compute x{out} = \text{softmax}(attn) \cdot v. Transpose and reshape to (N{win}, N, C). Apply linear projection and projection dropout. Reconstruct the full image from the processed windows. 1. Reshape x{out} from (N{win}, Ws, Ws, C) to (B, H/Ws, W/Ws, Ws, Ws, C). 2. Permute to (B, H/Ws, Ws, W/Ws, Ws, C). 3. Flatten to (B, H, W, C). In the context of sparse-view CT reconstruction: 1. The current volume estimate x is projected to a sinogram \hat{p} using the differentiable forward projection operator \mathcal{P}. 2. The residual \frac{\partial \mathcal{L}}{\partial \hat{p}} is computed. 3. This residual (or the sinogram itself, depending on the specific variant) is passed through the DuDoTrans encoder/decoder blocks to refine features or predict corrections. 4. The refined features are used to update the volume estimate x via back-projection \mathcal{P}^T and gradient descent. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import torch import torch.nn as nn import torch.nn.functional as F import math class WindowAttention(nn.Module): def init(self, dim, windowsize, numheads, qkvbias=True, qkscale=None, attndrop=0., projdrop=0.): super().init() self.dim = dim self.windowsize = windowsize # Wh, Ww self.numheads = numheads headdim = dim // numheads self.scale = qkscale or headdim -0.5 # Relative position bias table self.relativepositionbiastable = nn.Parameter( torch.zeros((2 windowsize[0] - 1) (2 windowsize[1] - 1), numheads)) # Get pair-wise relative position index for each token inside the window coordsh = torch.arange(self.windowsize[0]) coordsw = torch.arange(self.windowsize[1]) coords = torch.stack(torch.meshgrid([coordsh, coordsw])) # 2, Wh, Ww coordsflatten = torch.flatten(coords, 1) # 2, WhWw relativecoords = coordsflatten[:,:, None] - coordsflatten[:, None,:] # 2, WhWw, WhWw relativecoords = relativecoords.permute(1, 2, 0).contiguous() # WhWw, WhWw, 2 relativecoords[:,:, 0] += self.windowsize[0] - 1 # shift to start from 0 relativecoords[:,:, 1] += self.windowsize[1] - 1 relativecoords[:,:, 0] = 2 self.windowsize[1] - 1 relativepositionindex = relativecoords.sum(-1) # WhWw, WhWw self.registerbuffer("relativepositionindex", relativepositionindex) self.qkv = nn.Linear(dim, dim 3, bias=qkvbias) self.attndrop = nn.Dropout(attndrop) self.proj = nn.Linear(dim, dim) self.projdrop = nn.Dropout(projdrop) nn.init.truncnormal(self.relativepositionbiastable, std=.02) self.softmax = nn.Softmax(dim=-1) def forward(self, x, mask=None): """ x: shape (B, N, C) where N = Wh Ww mask: shape (B, N, N) or None """ B, N, C = x.shape qkv = self.qkv(x).reshape(B, N, 3, self.numheads, C // self.numheads).permute(2, 0, 3, 1, 4) q, k, v = qkv[0], qkv[1], qkv[2] # B, numheads, N, headdim q = q self.scale attn = q @ k.transpose(-2, -1) # Add relative position bias relativepositionbias = self.relativepositionbiastable[self.relativepositionindex.view(-1)].view( self.windowsize[0] self.windowsize[1], self.windowsize[0] self.windowsize[1], -1) # WhWw, WhWw, nH relativepositionbias = relativepositionbias.permute(2, 0, 1).contiguous() # nH, WhWw, WhWw attn = attn + relativepositionbias.unsqueeze(0) if mask is not None: nW = mask.shape[0] attn = attn.view(B // nW, nW, self.numheads, N, N) + mask.unsqueeze(1).unsqueeze(0) attn = attn.view(-1, self.numheads, N, N) attn = self.softmax(attn) attn = self.attndrop(attn) x = (attn @ v).transpose(1, 2).reshape(B, N, C) x = self.proj(x) x = self.projdrop(x) return x class SwinTransformerBlock(nn.Module): def init(self, dim, inputresolution, numheads, windowsize=7, shiftsize=0, mlpratio=4., qkvbias=True, qkscale=None, drop=0., attndrop=0., droppath=0., actlayer=nn.GELU, normlayer=nn.LayerNorm): super().init() self.dim = dim self.inputresolution = inputresolution self.numheads = numheads self.windowsize = windowsize self.shiftsize = shiftsize self.mlpratio = mlpratio if min(self.inputresolution) <= self.windowsize: # if window size is larger than input resolution, we don't partition windows self.shiftsize = 0 self.windowsize = min(self.inputresolution) assert 0 <= self.shiftsize < self.windowsize, "shiftsize must in 0-windowsize" self.norm1 = normlayer(dim) self.attn = WindowAttention( dim, windowsize=(self.windowsize, self.windowsize), numheads=numheads, qkvbias=qkvbias, qkscale=qkscale, attndrop=attndrop, projdrop=drop) self.droppath = DropPath(droppath) if droppath > 0. else nn.Identity() self.norm2 = normlayer(dim) mlphiddendim = int(dim mlpratio) self.mlp = Mlp(infeatures=dim, hiddenfeatures=mlphiddendim, actlayer=actlayer, drop=drop) if self.shiftsize > 0: # calculate attention mask for SW-MSA H, W = self.inputresolution imgmask = torch.zeros((1, H, W, 1)) # 1 H W 1 hslices = (slice(0, -self.windowsize), slice(-self.windowsize, -self.shiftsize), slice(-self.shiftsize, None)) wslices = (slice(0, -self.windowsize), slice(-self.windowsize, -self.shiftsize), slice(-self.shiftsize, None)) cnt = 0 for h in hslices: for w in wslices: imgmask[:, h, w,:] = cnt cnt += 1 maskwindows = windowpartition(imgmask, self.windowsize) # nW, windowsize, windowsize, 1 maskwindows = maskwindows.view(-1, self.windowsize self.windowsize) attnmask = maskwindows.unsqueeze(1) - maskwindows.unsqueeze(2) attnmask = attnmask.maskedfill(attnmask != 0, float(-100.0)).maskedfill(attnmask == 0, float(0.0)) else: attnmask = None self.registerbuffer("attnmask", attnmask) def forward(self, x): H, W = self.inputresolution B, L, C = x.shape assert L == H W, "input feature has wrong size" shortcut = x x = self.norm1(x) x = x.view(B, H, W, C) # cyclic shift if self.shiftsize > 0: shiftedx = torch.roll(x, shifts=(-self.shiftsize, -self.shiftsize), dims=(1, 2)) else: shiftedx = x # partition windows xwindows = windowpartition(shiftedx, self.windowsize) # nWB, windowsize, windowsize, C xwindows = xwindows.view(-1, self.windowsize self.windowsize, C) # nWB, windowsizewindowsize, C # W-MSA/SW-MSA attnwindows = self.attn(xwindows, mask=self.attnmask) # nWB, windowsizewindowsize, C # merge windows attnwindows = attnwindows.view(-1, self.windowsize, self.windowsize, C) shiftedx = windowreverse(attnwindows, self.windowsize, H, W) # B H' W' C # reverse cyclic shift if self.shiftsize > 0: x = torch.roll(shiftedx, shifts=(self.shiftsize, self.shiftsize), dims=(1, 2)) else: x = shiftedx x = x.view(B, H W, C) # FFN x = shortcut + self.droppath(x) x = x + self.droppath(self.mlp(self.norm2(x))) return x def windowpartition(x, windowsize): """ Args: x: (B, H, W, C) windowsize (int): window size Returns: windows: (numwindowsB, windowsize, windowsize, C) """ B, H, W, C = x.shape x = x.view(B, H // windowsize, windowsize, W // windowsize, windowsize, C) windows = x.permute(0, 1, 3, 2, 4, 5).contiguous().view(-1, windowsize, windowsize, C) return windows def windowreverse(windows, windowsize, H, W): """ Args: windows: (numwindowsB, windowsize, windowsize, C) windowsize (int): Window size H (int): Height of image W (int): Width of image Returns: x: (B, H, W, C) """ B = int(windows.shape[0] / (H W / windowsize / windowsize)) x = windows.view(B, H // windowsize, W // windowsize, windowsize, windowsize, -1) x = x.permute(0, 1, 3, 2, 4, 5).contiguous().view(B, H, W, -1) return x class Mlp(nn.Module): def init(self, infeatures, hiddenfeatures=None, outfeatures=None, actlayer=nn.GELU, drop=0.): super().init() outfeatures = outfeatures or infeatures hiddenfeatures = hiddenfeatures or infeatures self.fc1 = nn.Linear(infeatures, hiddenfeatures) self.act = actlayer() self.fc2 = nn.Linear(hiddenfeatures, outfeatures) self.drop = nn.Dropout(drop) def forward(self, x): x = self.fc1(x) x = self.act(x) x = self.drop(x) x = self.fc2(x) x = self.drop(x) return x class DropPath(nn.Module): def init(self, dropprob=None): super().init() self.dropprob = dropprob def forward(self, x): if not self.training or self.dropprob == 0.: return x keepprob = 1 - self.dropprob shape = (x.shape[0],) + (1,) (x.ndim - 1) randomtensor = keepprob + torch.rand(shape, dtype=x.dtype, device=x.device) randomtensor.floor() # binarize output = x.div(keepprob) randomtensor return output Input Resolution vs Window Size: If the input spatial resolution (H or W) is smaller than or equal to the windowsize, the shiftsize is forced to 0 and the windowsize is reduced to the minimum input dimension to avoid invalid partitioning. Precision: The relative position bias calculation relies on integer arithmetic for indices. Ensure no overflow occurs if Wh, Ww are large, though typical values (e.g., 7) are safe. Boundary Conditions: The ray marching implementation (used in the parent differentiable tomography context) must handle cases where dx or dy is zero to avoid division by zero in d\ax and d\ay calculations. Time Complexity: The window-based attention reduces complexity from O(N^2) to O(N \cdot Ws^2), where N is the number of tokens (pixels) and Ws is the window size. This makes it significantly more efficient than global self-attention for high-resolution images. Memory Complexity: Memory usage is dominated by the storage of the attention maps within windows and the relative position bias table. The bias table size is O(Ws^2 \cdot \text{num\heads}), which is constant and small. Performance: DuDoTrans demonstrates superior performance in sparse-view CT reconstruction compared to non-transformer baselines and standard CNNs, effectively recovering high-frequency details from limited projections. Strengths: Efficient local modeling, ability to capture long-range dependencies via shifted windows, and compatibility with differentiable tomographic operators. Limitations: Performance may degrade if the window size is not well-tuned for the specific frequency content of the sinogram/volume. Requires careful handling of boundary conditions in the tomographic loop. DuDoTrans was introduced by Ce Wang, Kun Shang, Haimiao Zhang, Qian Li, and S. Kevin Zhou in the paper "DuDoTrans: Dual-Domain Transformer for Sparse-View CT Reconstruction," published in the International Workshop on Machine Learning for Medical Image Reconstruction in 2022. It builds upon the Swin Transformer architecture and adapts it for the specific challenges of sparse-view computed tomography, where traditional reconstruction methods suffer from severe artifacts due to insufficient data. name: Generalizable Radiance Fields via Transformer Attention
head: Transformer-based Generalizable Radiance Fields
body: This method addresses the problem of generalizing neural radiance field representations to unseen objects or scenes without requiring per-scene optimization. It solves the limitation of standard NeRFs, which overfit to specific training views, by learning generalizable geometric priors from source images. It sets itself apart from sibling methods like DuDoTrans and Transformer-based Tomographic Reconstruction by focusing on cross-view feature aggregation via attention mechanisms rather than iterative tomographic inversion or specific architectural variants like Ray Transformers. The method constructs a generalizable representation by aggregating information from multiple source views using a transformer-based attention module. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: A set of source images (views) with known camera parameters (intrinsics and extrinsics). Outputs: A generalizable radiance field representation capable of rendering novel views of unseen objects or scenes. Data Structures: The core data structure is a feature volume or a set of view-dependent features aggregated via attention. The specific layout depends on the implementation variant (e.g., cost volumes or feature volumes), but generally involves multi-view feature tensors aligned in 3D space. Steps: 1. Feature Extraction: Extract features from the source images using a backbone network (e.g., CNN or ViT). 2. View Aggregation: Use a transformer-based attention module to aggregate source view information. This involves computing attention weights between query features (at a target 3D location or ray) and key/value features from the source views. 3. Generalization: The aggregated features encode geometric and appearance priors learned from the dataset, allowing the model to generalize to unseen instances. 4. Rendering: Render the novel view by querying the aggregated representation along rays. Formulas: The attention mechanism typically computes the output Z from queries Q, keys K, and values V: \text{Attention}(Q, K, V) = \text{softmax}\left(\frac{QK^T}{\sqrt{dk}}\right)V where dk is the dimension of the keys. The specific formulation for generalizable radiance fields may involve spatial attention or ray-wise attention to aggregate multi-view features. Parameters: Number of attention heads. Dimension of feature vectors. Number of source views used for aggregation. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Generalization Gap: Performance may degrade on objects significantly different from the training distribution. View Density: Requires a sufficient number of source views to capture geometry accurately. Occlusion: Handling occluded regions in source views requires robust attention mechanisms. Args: sourceimages: List of source images. cameraparams: List of camera parameters (intrinsics, extrinsics). Returns: Generalizable radiance field representation. """ # Step 1: Feature Extraction # Extract features from each source image features = [] for img, cam in zip(sourceimages, cameraparams): # Use a backbone network (e.g., CNN) to extract features feat = extractfeatures(img, cam) features.append(feat) # Step 2: View Aggregation via Transformer Attention # Aggregate features from all source views # This step involves computing attention between query and source features aggregatedfeatures = transformerattention(features) # Step 3: Return the generalizable representation return aggregatedfeatures def extractfeatures(image, cameraparams): """ Extracts features from a single image using a backbone network. Args: image: Input image. cameraparams: Camera parameters. Returns: Feature tensor. """ # Placeholder for feature extraction logic # Typically involves convolutional layers or ViT return featuretensor def transformerattention(features): """ Aggregates features from multiple views using transformer attention. Args: features: List of feature tensors from source views. Returns: Aggregated feature tensor. """ # Compute attention weights # Q, K, V are derived from the features # Attention(Q, K, V) = softmax(QK^T / sqrt(dk)) V aggregated = computeattention(features) return aggregated def computeattention(features): """ Computes attention between features. Args: features: List of feature tensors. Returns: Aggregated feature tensor. """ # Implementation of attention mechanism # This is a placeholder for the actual attention computation return aggregatedfeatures A geometry-free method using a CNN and Encoder-Decoder Transformer to produce output color for an entire ray at once. It uses a CNN to extract feature patches from scene images, feeds patches into an Encoder-Decoder Transformer along with camera ray and viewpoint coordinates \{o, d\}, and produces output color by querying the entire ray at once. It does not produce the scene's density function nor rely on geometric inductive biases. Time Complexity: Depends on the number of source views and the transformer architecture. Attention mechanisms can be O(N^2) in the number of views or tokens. Memory Complexity: Requires storing features for all source views and the aggregated representation. Strengths: Generalizes well to unseen objects/scenes; leverages multi-view consistency. Limitations: May require careful tuning of attention mechanisms; performance depends on the diversity and quality of the training dataset. When to use: When generalization to new objects/scenes is required without per-scene optimization. When not to use: When high-fidelity reconstruction of a specific, known scene is needed with dense input views. This approach builds on the trend of using deep learning for 3D representation. It specifically leverages transformer architectures to handle the non-local dependencies inherent in multi-view aggregation. The method is part of the broader effort to make neural radiance fields more practical for real-world applications by reducing the need for extensive per-scene training. name: Ray Transformer
head: A module based on linear attention that provides non-local information of other points along the ray to predict SRDF, addressing the non-local definition of SRDF
body: The Ray Transformer is a neural module designed to predict Signed Ray Distance Functions (SRDF) by aggregating non-local information along a viewing ray. It addresses the limitation that SRDF values depend on the closest surface along the entire ray rather than being locally defined at a single point. Unlike standard local volume rendering, it uses linear attention to model dependencies between points ordered from near to far, building on the view aggregation of Generalizable Radiance Fields via Transformer Attention. Inputs: M: Number of sampling points along the ray. \mathbf{f}v \in \mathbb{R}^{dv}: Volume feature at each point. \mathbf{f}p \in \mathbb{R}^{dp}: Projection feature at each point. \gamma: Positional encoding function. Outputs: \{\tilde{\mathbf{f}}j\}{j=1}^{M}: Attended features for each point. SRDF values decoded from \tilde{\mathbf{f}}j. Data Structures: Combined feature sequence: A list of tensors \{\mathbf{c}j\}{j=1}^{M}, where \mathbf{c}j = \text{cat}(\mathbf{f}{v,j}, \mathbf{f}{p,j}, \gammaj). Attended feature sequence: \{\tilde{\mathbf{f}}j\}{j=1}^{M}. Steps: 1. Ordering: Order the M sampling points along the ray from near to far. 2. Feature Concatenation: For each point j \in \{1, \dots, M\}, concatenate the volume feature \mathbf{f}{v,j}, the projection feature \mathbf{f}{p,j}, and the positional encoding \gammaj to form the combined feature \mathbf{c}j. This adds a global shape prior. 3. Attention: Apply the Ray Transformer module to the sequence of combined features to predict attended features \{\tilde{\mathbf{f}}j\}{j=1}^{M}: \{\tilde{\mathbf{f}}j\}{j=1}^{M} = \text{RayTrans}(\{\text{cat}(\mathbf{f}{v,j}, \mathbf{f}{p,j}, \gammaj)\}{j=1}^{M}) The module is based on linear attention. 4. Decoding: Use a Multi-Layer Perceptron (MLP) to decode the attended feature \tilde{\mathbf{f}}j into the SRDF value for each point j. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def raytransformer(volumefeatures, projectionfeatures, positionalencodingfunc): """ volumefeatures: List of M tensors, each shape (dv,) projectionfeatures: List of M tensors, each shape (dp,) positionalencodingfunc: Function mapping index to positional encoding vector Returns: List of M attended feature tensors, and SRDF values via MLP """ M = len(volumefeatures) combinedfeatures = [] # Step 1 & 2: Order points (assumed already ordered near-to-far) # and concatenate features with positional encoding for j in range(M): # cat denotes concatenation along the feature dimension posenc = positionalencodingfunc(j) combined = concatenate([volumefeatures[j], projectionfeatures[j], posenc]) combinedfeatures.append(combined) # Step 3: Apply linear self-attention # RayTrans implements linear attention as per [19] cited in attendedfeatures = linearselfattention(combinedfeatures) # Step 4: Decode SRDF using MLP # The MLP is defined in the source but specific architecture details are not provided # Assuming a standard MLP: Linear -> Activation -> Linear srdfvalues = [] for ftilde in attendedfeatures: srdf = mlpdecode(ftilde) srdfvalues.append(srdf) return attendedfeatures, srdfvalues Parameters: M: Number of sampling points. Not given in the sources. \alpha: Weight for depth loss in the total loss function \mathcal{L} = \mathcal{L}{\text{color}} + \alpha \mathcal{L}{\text{depth}}. Not given in the sources. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Ordering: Points must be strictly ordered from near to far for the attention mechanism to correctly model the ray's geometry. Non-locality: The method explicitly handles the non-local nature of SRDF, which standard local methods may fail to capture. Complexity: The use of linear attention suggests O(M) complexity with respect to the number of points M, compared to O(M^2) for standard self-attention, though exact complexity analysis is not provided in the sources. Performance: The method is part of VolRecon, which uses a combined loss of color and depth. Specific performance metrics (PSNR, SSIM) are not detailed in the provided notes. Strengths: Provides non-local information along the ray, addressing the definition of SRDF. Limitations: Relies on the accuracy of the volume and projection features fed into it. The Ray Transformer was introduced in the VolRecon paper for generalizable multi-view reconstruction using Signed Ray Distance Functions. It builds upon the concept that SRDF is not locally defined and depends on the closest surface along the entire ray. The attention mechanism is based on linear attention. name: Local Implicit Ray Function (LIRF)
body: LIRF is a generalizable radiance field representation that predicts volumetric radiance fields from multi-view images by aggregating local image features via transformer-based attention, conical frustum sampling, and visibility estimation to handle occlusions and scale variations. It distinguishes itself from siblings like Ray Transformer by explicitly modeling the conical volume of each ray through 8-vertex discretization and using a two-token transformer architecture to separate color aggregation from density prediction based on feature consistency. Inputs: A set of V nearby source images Iv and their corresponding camera poses. Outputs: A target image rendered from a target viewpoint. Data Structures: Feature Maps: Two maps \mathbf{F}^w and \mathbf{F}^c extracted per source view. \mathbf{F}^w stores features for visibility weight estimation; \mathbf{F}^c stores features for color/density prediction. Conical Frustum: Discretized into M=8 vertices. Tokens: \mathbf{t}0 (visibility), \mathbf{t}1 (color info), \mathbf{t}2 (consistency info), and their transformer outputs \mathbf{t}0', \mathbf{t}1', \mathbf{t}2'. Parameters: V: Number of source views. N: Number of samples along a target ray. M: Number of vertices per conical frustum (M=8). rm: Maximum cone radius, defined as the pixel width of the target image at minimum resolution. s: Latent code representing the relative scale of the target image. Steps: 1. Feature Extraction: For each source image I, extract feature maps using an EDSR network [37]. The last layer is modified to output two channels of features: (\mathbf{F}^w, \mathbf{F}^c) = \mathrm{EDSR}(I) where \mathbf{F}^w is for visibility and \mathbf{F}^c is for color/density. 2. Ray and Frustum Setup: For a target ray, select V neighboring source views. Sample N points along the ray. Represent the continuous conical volume of the ray as a series of conical frustums. Each frustum is discretized using M=8 vertices. 3. Vertex Projection: Project the 8 vertices of each conical frustum onto the V source views to query features \mathbf{f}j^c from \mathbf{F}^c. 4. Local Feature Aggregation (\mathbf{z}): For a sample at 3D position \mathbf{x} within a frustum, compute its aggregated feature \mathbf{z} by weighting the features of the M vertices based on their relative positions \Delta \mathbf{x}j = \mathbf{x} - \mathbf{q}j (where \mathbf{q}j is vertex j) and the target scale s: \mathbf{z} = \sum{j=1}^{M} W(||\Delta \mathbf{x}j||2) \mathcal{R}(\mathbf{f}j^c, \Delta \mathbf{x}j, s) The weight function is: W(||\Delta \mathbf{x}j||2) = \frac{||\Delta \mathbf{x}j||2}{\sum{l=1}^{M} ||\Delta \mathbf{x}l||2} where \mathcal{R} is an MLP-based aggregation function. Note: If the target ray projects within the circle of radius rm on the target image plane, features are aggregated from the four neighboring rays passing through the red points in the target image plane. 5. Visibility Weight Estimation: a. Obtain feature patches \mathbf{f}^w from \mathbf{F}^w for the sample. b. Define input token \mathbf{t}0 by concatenating \mathbf{f}^w, the source ray direction \mathbf{d} (in target camera coordinates), and the scale s. Apply positional encoding [44] to \mathbf{d} and relative positions \Delta \mathbf{x}, but not to s: \mathbf{t}0 = \mathrm{MLP}(\mathbf{f}^w \parallel \mathbf{d} \parallel s) c. Process \mathbf{t}0 through a self-attention transformer \mathcal{T}1: \mathbf{t}0' = \mathcal{T}1(\mathbf{t}0) d. Compute visibility weights w using an MLP \mathcal{M}w: w = \mathcal{M}w(\mathbf{t}0') The weights represent the probability of the sample being observed by each source view, handling occlusions. 6. Token Creation for Color and Density: a. Create token \mathbf{t}1 (color information) by aggregating \mathbf{z} and w: \mathbf{t}1 = \mathrm{MLP}(\mathbf{z} \parallel w) b. Create token \mathbf{t}2 (consistency measure) by computing the weighted mean and weighted variance of \mathbf{z} over all source views based on w, then aggregating: \mathbf{t}2 = \mathrm{MLP}(\mathrm{mean}(\mathbf{z}, w) \parallel \mathrm{var}(\mathbf{z}, w)) Densities are predicted by checking feature consistency, as features are consistent on object surfaces. 7. Transformer Aggregation: Feed \mathbf{t}1 and \mathbf{t}2 into a second self-attention transformer \mathcal{T}2: (\mathbf{t}1', \mathbf{t}2') = \mathcal{T}2(\mathbf{t}1, \mathbf{t}2) 8. Density Prediction: Predict density \sigma using an auto-encoder-style network \mathrm{AE} to aggregate information along the ray, followed by an MLP \mathcal{M}\sigma: \sigma = \mathcal{M}\sigma(\mathrm{AE}(\mathbf{t}2')) 9. Color Prediction: Predict color \mathbf{c} by explicitly blending the features \mathbf{t}1' according to visibility weights w, then passing through an MLP \mathcal{M}c: \mathbf{c} = \mathcal{M}c\left( \sum{k=1}^V (\mathbf{t}{1,k}' wk) \right) 10. Rendering: Render the final color of the target ray via volume rendering using the predicted colors \mathbf{c} and densities \sigma. 11. Optimization: Optimize by calculating the mean squared error between the predicted color and the ground truth color. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def LIRFRender(sourceimages, sourceposes, targetpose, targetscales): # 1. Feature Extraction # Extract F^w (visibility) and F^c (color/density) using EDSR featuresw = [] featuresc = [] for img in sourceimages: Fw, Fc = EDSR(img) featuresw.append(Fw) featuresc.append(Fc) # 2. Ray Sampling and Frustum Setup # Select V neighboring views # Sample N points along target ray # Represent conical frustum with M=8 vertices vertices = discretizeconicalfrustum(targetray, M=8) # 3. Vertex Projection # Project vertices onto source views to query features vertexfeaturesc = [] for vidx, vertex in enumerate(vertices): projectedfeatures = [] for viewidx in range(V): # Project vertex to source view plane uv = projecttoview(vertex, sourceposes[viewidx], targetpose) # Query feature map F^c fc = queryfeaturemap(featuresc[viewidx], uv) projectedfeatures.append(fc) vertexfeaturesc.append(projectedfeatures) # 4. Local Feature Aggregation (z) # For each sample x on the ray z = 0 for j in range(M): deltax = x - vertices[j] # Weight function distj = norm(deltax) totaldist = sum(norm(x - vertices[l]) for l in range(M)) W = distj / totaldist if totaldist > 0 else 0 # Aggregation function R (MLP) # Input: feature f^c, relative pos deltax, scale s # Note: Positional encoding applied to deltax, not s fagg = MLPAggregate(vertexfeaturesc[j], deltax, s) z += W fagg # 5. Visibility Weight Estimation # Get feature patch f^w for sample x fw = queryfeaturemap(featuresw[viewidx], uvsample) # Input token t0: concat f^w, direction d (target coords), scale s # PE applied to d, not s d = getsourceraydirectionintargetcoords(sourceposes, targetpose) t0 = MLPReduce(concat(fw, d, s)) # Transformer T1 t0prime = TransformerT1(t0) # Visibility weights w w = MLPVisibility(t0prime) # 6. Token Creation # t1: color info t1 = MLPColor(concat(z, w)) # t2: consistency info (weighted mean and var of z over views) zmean = weightedmean(z, w) zvar = weightedvar(z, w) t2 = MLPConsistency(concat(zmean, zvar)) # 7. Transformer Aggregation t1prime, t2prime = TransformerT2(t1, t2) # 8. Density Prediction sigma = MLPDensity(AE(t2prime)) # 9. Color Prediction # Explicitly blend t1' with weights w blendedt1 = sum(t1prime[k] w[k] for k in range(V)) c = MLPColorPred(blendedt1) # 10. Volume Rendering finalcolor = VolumeRender(c, sigma) return finalcolor Training Data Efficiency: LIRF uses significantly fewer training scenes (about 15% of the scenes used by IBRNet or NeuRay). Performance: Outperforms IBRNet, NeuRay, and GeoNeRF on all tested scales (x0.5, x1, x2, x4) in terms of PSNR, SSIM, and LPIPS. Scale Handling: Handles low-scale views (x0.5) better than baselines, which suffer from aliasing artifacts. It explicitly modifies the cone radius rm according to pixel size to render low-scale views even if not explicitly trained on them. Strengths: Fewer blurring artifacts, better rendering of small or thin structures, and robust generalization to unseen scenes due to local direction inputs rather than global world coordinates. Limitations: Relies on the assumption that occluded content appears in most source views, which is a compromise for solving occlusions without geometric priors. LIRF was introduced in the paper "Local Implicit Ray Function for Generalizable Radiance Field Representation". It builds on the concept of generalizable radiance fields, moving away from coordinate-based MLPs (like standard NeRF) towards image-feature-based aggregation. It is part of the family of transformer-based architectures for novel view synthesis, specifically addressing the challenges of scale variation and occlusion in generalizable settings. name: Transformers and Vision Transformers (ViT)
head: Vision Transformer
body: Transformers compute pairwise attention over input tokens to capture long-range dependencies that convolutions miss. The Vision Transformer (ViT) adapts this architecture for images by treating fixed-size patches as tokens. Builds on Transformer-based Architectures. In volume rendering, ViT is used for super-resolution and denoising, where its ability to attend across the full spatial extent of a subvolume helps recover large-scale structures that local convolutions miss. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A sequence of tokens derived from fixed-size patches of an image or volume slice. Output: A sequence of transformed tokens used for volume super-resolution and denoising. Data Structures: Tokens: A matrix X \in \mathbb{R}^{N \times d}, where N is the number of patches and d is the embedding dimension. Task Relevance Score: A scalar or vector TR used to modulate attention weights per task. Steps: 1. Patch Tokenization: The input is divided into non-overlapping fixed-size patches, which are treated as input tokens. 2. Pairwise Self-Attention: The Transformer computes attention over all pairs of input tokens to capture long-range dependencies. 3. Task Dynamic Modulation: In multi-task environments, a modulation layer adjusts self-attention weights by computing a task relevance score TR for each feature, optimizing weight distribution per attention head based on task-specific contextual information. Positional encodings are dynamically adjusted using the task relevance score: PE(pos, 2i) = \sin\left(pos / 10000^{2i/d{model}}\right) \cdot TR PE(pos, 2i + 1) = \cos\left(pos / 10000^{2i/d{model}}\right) \cdot TR where pos is the position index, i is the dimension index, d{model} is the model dimension, and TR is the task relevance score. Parameters: Not given in the sources. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Positional Information: The permutation-invariant nature of attention requires explicit positional encoding to preserve spatial structure. Computational Cost: Self-attention scales quadratically with the number of tokens, which can be prohibitive for high-resolution volume data without optimization. Fusion ViT is a neural module designed to fuse multi-view features by performing all-to-all self-attention over encoded image patches or rendered feature vectors from multiple input views. It solves the problem of multi-view inconsistency and incomplete context in neural rendering and tomographic reconstruction by providing each view's features with full spatial and semantic context from all other views. It distinguishes itself from standard fusion methods by leveraging the Transformer's ability to model long-range dependencies across views, either at the patch level for global reconstruction or at the pixel level for lightweight synthesis. A layer that adjusts self-attention weights according to task demands by computing a task relevance score for each feature, allowing the model to focus on information relevant to specific tasks (texture, shape, color, depth) in a multi-task learning environment. It optimizes the weight distribution of each head in the attention mechanism by analyzing task-related contextual information. Strengths: Captures long-range dependencies across the full spatial extent of a subvolume, effectively recovering large-scale structures that local convolutions miss. Limitations: Not given in the sources. When to use: Volume super-resolution and denoising tasks where global context is required to recover large-scale structures. When not to use: Not given in the sources. The Transformer architecture computes pairwise attention over input tokens to capture long-range dependencies. The Vision Transformer (ViT) adapts this for images by treating fixed-size patches as tokens. In the context of scientific volume visualization and rendering, Transformers have been applied to super-resolution and denoising tasks to leverage their global receptive field.
