name: Fusion ViT
head: Fusion Transformer (in the context of pixel-wise feature fusion)
body: Fusion ViT is a neural module designed to fuse multi-view features by performing all-to-all self-attention over encoded image patches or rendered feature vectors from multiple input views. It solves the problem of multi-view inconsistency and incomplete context in neural rendering and tomographic reconstruction by providing each view's features with full spatial and semantic context from all other views. It distinguishes itself from standard fusion methods by leveraging the Transformer's ability to model long-range dependencies across views, either at the patch level for global reconstruction or at the pixel level for lightweight synthesis. Inputs and Outputs: The method accepts encoded features from K input views. In the global reconstruction setting, inputs are concatenated encoded image patches \{\tilde{H}1, \tilde{H}2, \dots, \tilde{H}K\}. In the pixel-wise setting, inputs are rendered feature vectors from N views at each pixel location. The output is a set of fused tokens \{F1, F2, \dots, FK\} or a fused feature map \tilde{F}. Data Structures: The core data structure is a sequence of tokens. For the ViT-B/16 variant, each token has an embedding dimension of 768. The patches are typically 16 \times 16 pixels. Parameters: Architecture: Vision Transformer Base (ViT-B/16). Layers: 12 layers (the implementation details specify 12 layers, though the notes mention 16). Heads: 12 attention heads. Embedding Dimension: 768. MLP Ratio: 4.0 (hidden dimension is 4 \times 768 = 3072). Patch Size: 16 \times 16. Initialization: Initialized from scratch. (Note: The encoder preceding the fusion module may use DINO pre-trained weights). Steps: 1. Feature Encoding: Input views are processed by an encoder (e.g., ViT-B/16) to produce encoded patches \tilde{H}i. 2. Concatenation: Encoded patches from all K views are concatenated into a single sequence. 3. Self-Attention Fusion: The concatenated sequence is passed through a Transformer \mathcal{F}{fuse}. This module performs all-to-all self-attention, allowing every token to attend to every other token across all views. 4. Output Generation: The output of the transformer is a set of fused tokens \{F1, \dots, FK\}, where each Fi contains context from all other views. Formula: The fusion operation is defined as: \{F1, F2, \dots, FK\} = \mathcal{F}{fuse}(\tilde{H}1, \tilde{H}2, \dots, \tilde{H}K) where \mathcal{F}{fuse} is the fusion transformer, \tilde{H}i are the concatenated encoded image patches, and Fi is the fused token of the i-th view. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def fusionvit(encodedpatcheslist, numviews, numlayers, embeddim, numheads, mlpratio): # Step 1: Concatenate patches from all views # Shape: [K P, D] tokens = [] for viewpatches in encodedpatcheslist: tokens.extend(viewpatches) # Step 2: Add positional embeddings # Standard ViT requires positional embeddings. We add a learnable lookup table. numpatches = len(tokens) posembed = [0.0] (numpatches embeddim) # Learnable parameters tokens = [t + p for t, p in zip(tokens, posembed)] # Step 3: Pass through Transformer Encoder for in range(numlayers): # LayerNorm before attention tokens = layernorm(tokens) # Multi-Head Self-Attention attnout = multiheadattention(tokens, embeddim, numheads) tokens = [t + a for t, a in zip(tokens, attnout)] # Residual connection # LayerNorm before MLP tokens = layernorm(tokens) # MLP mlpout = mlp(tokens, embeddim, mlpratio) tokens = [t + m for t, m in zip(tokens, mlpout)] # Residual connection # Step 4: Split back into per-view tokens patchesperview = len(encodedpatcheslist[0]) fusedtokenslist = [] for i in range(numviews): fusedtokenslist.append(tokens[i patchesperview: (i + 1) patchesperview]) return fusedtokenslist def layernorm(x): # Standard LayerNorm: normalize feature vectors to zero mean and unit variance. mean = sum(x) / len(x) std = (sum((xi - mean)2 for xi in x) / len(x) + 1e-5)0.5 return [(xi - mean) / std for xi in x] def multiheadattention(x, embeddim, numheads): # Standard MHA: splits heads, computes QKV dot-products, applies softmax, projects back. # Returns output tensor of same shape as input. return x def mlp(x, embeddim, mlpratio): # Standard MLP: Linear -> GELU -> Linear. # Returns output tensor of same shape as input. return x Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Geometry Cues: In pixel-wise variants, rendered results may lose geometry cues (e.g., depth-based occlusion) when rendered from 3D to 2D, which can hinder fusion. Position Encoding: Using geometry features as position encoding was explored but found not helpful. A neural module designed to fuse multi-view features and learn view-dependent appearance directly from high-resolution raw RGB inputs. It distinguishes itself by employing an encoder-decoder architecture: the encoder performs self-attention across input views, while the decoder performs cross-attention between a specific query viewpoint and all input views. This enables robust handling of geometry inference and calibration errors. Choose this when view-dependent appearance modeling and handling of sparse-view inconsistencies are critical. See View-to-View Transformer. A lightweight pixel-wise Transformer used to fuse rendered feature maps from N input views on each pixel. It inputs rendered feature vectors and queries fused results using a learnable "token". It utilizes semantics for fusion. It is chosen for real-time novel view synthesis where computational efficiency is paramount. Pitfalls include the loss of geometry cues during 3D-to-2D rendering. Time Complexity: Depends on the number of views K and patches P. Self-attention is O((K \cdot P)^2). Memory Complexity: Proportional to the number of tokens and layers. The ViT-B/16 variant uses 12 layers with 768-dim embeddings. Performance: The model is trained end-to-end with photometric and perceptual losses. It supports variable-view learning with 6, 8, or 10 views. Strengths: Provides full context from all views, enabling complete spatial and context reasoning. Handles multi-view inconsistency. Limitations: Computationally intensive due to self-attention over all views. May lose geometry cues if not properly encoded. When to use: Sparse-view tomographic reconstruction or real-time novel view synthesis. When not to use: When geometry cues are critical and cannot be adequately captured by semantic features. Fusion ViT originates from the application of Vision Transformers to multi-view reconstruction and novel view synthesis. The specific ViT-B/16 fusion module was introduced in X-GRM for sparse-view X-ray to CT reconstruction. The pixel-wise variant was proposed in FWD for real-time novel view synthesis. name: View-to-View Transformer
body: The View-to-View Transformer is a neural module designed to fuse multi-view features and predict view-dependent appearance directly from high-resolution input images, thereby alleviating multi-view inconsistency and calibration errors. It distinguishes itself from sibling methods like Fusion ViT by employing a specific encoder-decoder architecture that separates feature fusion (encoder) from view-dependent query processing (decoder), allowing it to handle relationships between input views and a specific query viewpoint more robustly than self-attention-only approaches. The method takes N input images I1, \dots, IN and a 3D point x as inputs, and outputs a color embedding ec and fused geometry features \Phi(x). The architecture consists of an Encoder and a Decoder. Data Structures and Inputs: \phii(x, Ii): Pixel-aligned feature vector extracted from the i-th input image Ii at the projection of point x. di: Viewing direction of the i-th input camera in its own coordinate system. dq: Viewing direction of the query camera. pi: Raw RGB color value at the projection of x in the i-th image. \gamma(\cdot): Colored encoding function mapping raw RGB values to a higher-dimensional space to capture high-frequency appearance variations. e{db}: Double embedding (geometry and appearance shared representation) generated by the encoder. Step 1: Encoder (Multi-View Feature Fusion) The encoder fuses geometry features from all input views using self-attention. 1. Feature Preparation: For each view i \in \{1, \dots, N\}, concatenate the pixel-aligned feature \phii(x, Ii) with the viewing direction di: \Phii = \oplus(\phii(x, Ii), di) where \oplus denotes concatenation. 2. Attention Inputs: Pass the set of fused features \{\Phi1, \dots, \PhiN\} through linear layers to generate Query (Qe), Key (Ke), and Value (Ve) matrices: Qe, Ke, Ve = F{Q,K,V}(\phi1, \dots, \phiN) Here, F{Q,K,V} represents the linear projection layers. 3. Self-Attention: Compute the multi-head attention output: \text{Att}{out} = \text{Att}(Qe, Ke, Ve) where \text{Att} is the multi-head attention operation. 4. Feature Fusion: Apply a feed-forward layer Fe to the attention output to produce the fused feature representation \Phi: \Phi = Fe(\text{Att}{out}) This \Phi serves as the conditioned feature for geometry prediction. 5. Double Embedding Generation: Combine the 3D position x (encoded via \gamma(x)) and the fused features \Phi through a double MLP E{db} to generate the double embedding e{db}: e{db} = E{db}(\gamma(x), \Phi) This embedding bridges surface and radiance fields. Step 2: Decoder (View-Dependent Color Prediction) The decoder produces view-dependent color features by attending to input views conditioned on the query view direction. 1. Query Construction: Project the query view direction dq through a linear layer: Qd = F{Qd}(dq) where F{Qd} is a linear layer. 2. Key Construction: Project the viewing directions of all input views \{d1, \dots, dN\} through a linear layer: Kd = F{Kd}(d1, \dots, dN) where F{Kd} is a linear layer. 3. Value Construction: For each view i, concatenate the double embedding e{db} with the colored encoding of the raw RGB value \gamma(pi). These concatenated vectors form the Value inputs: Vd = F{Vd}([e{db}, \gamma(p1)], \dots, [e{db}, \gamma(pN)]) where F{Vd} is a linear layer and [\cdot, \cdot] denotes concatenation. 4. Cross-Attention: Compute the attention between the query view and input views: \text{Att}{cross} = \text{Att}(Qd, Kd, Vd) 5. Color Embedding: Apply a feed-forward layer Fd to the cross-attention output to obtain the color embedding ec: ec = Fd(\text{Att}{cross}) Step 3: Final Color Prediction Pass the color embedding ec through a texture MLP Ec to predict the final high-resolution color c: c = Ec(ec) Pseudocode Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def viewtoviewtransformer(x, dq, inputviews): """ x: 3D point coordinates dq: Query view direction vector inputviews: List of N tuples (phii, di, pi) phii: Pixel-aligned feature from view i di: Input view direction vector pi: Raw RGB value at projection of x in view i """ N = len(inputviews) # --- Encoder --- # 1. Prepare inputs for self-attention # F{Q,K,V} are linear layers applied to phii Qe = [linear(phii) for phii,, in inputviews] Ke = [linear(phii) for phii,, in inputviews] Ve = [linear(phii) for phii,, in inputviews] # 2. Self-Attention attout = multiheadattention(Qe, Ke, Ve) # 3. Feed-Forward to get fused features Phi Phi = feedforward(attout) # 4. Generate Double Embedding # gamma(x) is positional encoding for x edb = doublemlp(concat(positionalencoding(x), Phi)) # --- Decoder --- # 5. Prepare Cross-Attention Inputs # Query is based on dq Qd = linear(dq) # Keys are based on input view directions di Kd = linear([di for, di, in inputviews]) # Values are based on [edb, gamma(pi)] # gamma(pi) is colored encoding for raw RGB pi values = [concat(edb, coloredencoding(pi)) for,, pi in inputviews] Vd = linear(values) # 6. Cross-Attention attcross = multiheadattention(Qd, Kd, Vd) # 7. Feed-Forward to get color embedding ec = feedforward(attcross) # 8. Final Color Prediction c = texturemlp(ec) return c, Phi, edb def linear(x): return x # Standard linear projection layer def concat(a, b): return a + b # Vector concatenation def multiheadattention(Q, K, V): return Q # Standard multi-head attention mechanism def feedforward(x): return x # Standard feed-forward network def positionalencoding(x): return x # Standard positional encoding def coloredencoding(p): return p # Standard colored encoding for RGB def doublemlp(x): return x # Standard multi-layer perceptron def texturemlp(x): return x # Standard multi-layer perceptron Aggregates appearance and geometric information using weight-sharing CNNs and joint multi-view Transformers with visibility-weighted cosine similarities, explicitly modeling multi-view consistency via pairwise similarities rather than simple averaging. The method enables the utilization of original high-resolution images by taking raw RGB values into account, contributing to high-fidelity rendering. It is more robust to geometry inference and calibration errors in real-world multi-view setups compared to methods with limited feature representation power. However, training on high-resolution domains is expensive; the method typically employs a two-phase strategy: large-scale dataset pre-training at low resolution and efficient person-specific high-resolution fine-tuning. The View-to-View Transformer was introduced in the DoubleField framework, which bridges neural surface and radiance fields for high-fidelity human reconstruction and rendering. It addresses limitations in prior methods that relied on low-resolution feature maps or required strict SMPL fitting, allowing DoubleField to handle loose clothing and leverage large-scale human scan datasets. name: Multi-View Feature Encoder
head: MuRF Multi-View Feature Encoder
body: The Multi-View Feature Encoder aggregates essential appearance and geometric information from K input images to serve as the input for feed-forward Neural Radiance Field (NeRF) models. It solves the problem of multi-view inconsistency and information loss during downsampling by extracting features via a weight-sharing 2D CNN and a joint multi-view Transformer, then aggregating them using visibility-weighted cosine similarities. It sets itself apart from sibling methods by explicitly modeling multi-view consistency through pairwise cosine similarities and using a learned weighted average for aggregation, rather than simple averaging or attention. Inputs: K input images \{Ik\}{k=1}^K, camera poses for each view, and a target 3D point cloud or volume grid defined by spatial dimensions H/8 \times W/8 \times D. Outputs: A target volume z \in \mathbb{R}^{\frac{H}{8} \times \frac{W}{8} \times D \times C} encoding appearance and geometry. Data Structures: 1. Feature Maps: Extracted at 1/2, 1/4, and 1/8 resolutions. The encoder uses the 1/8 resolution features for the Transformer stage. 2. Windowed Color Vector: For each 3D point, a 9 \times 9 window is sampled from each of the K feature maps centered at the 2D projection of the point. The colors within this window are concatenated to form \tilde{c}k for view k. 3. Feature Matrix: Sampled features \{fi\}{i=1}^K are collected into a matrix of shape K \times M, where M is the feature dimension. Steps: 1. 2D Feature Extraction: Pass each input image Ik through a weight-sharing 2D CNN. The CNN consists of 6 residual blocks [12]. Every 2 residual blocks include a stride-2 convolutional layer to achieve 2× downsampling. This produces feature maps at 1/2, 1/4, and 1/8 resolutions. 2. Multi-View Transformer: Feed the 1/8 resolution convolutional features into a joint multi-view Transformer. This Transformer extends the 2-view cross-attention architecture (from GMFlow [34, 35]) to K input views. The output is the refined feature maps at 1/8 resolution. 3. Sampling: For each 3D point in the target volume: Project the 3D point to 2D coordinates in each of the K input views. Sample a 9 \times 9 window centered at these 2D coordinates from the 1/8 resolution feature maps. Concatenate the pixel values within the window to obtain the color vector \tilde{c}k for each view k. Sample the feature vector fk at the center of the window for each view k. 4. name: 3D Transformer Network Refinement
head: Point Transformer Network
body: The 3D Transformer Network Refinement (also known as the Point Transformer Network) is a module used to optimize the appearance and geometric attributes of selected 3D Gaussian Splatting (GS) tokens. It builds on Multi-View Feature Encoder by processing encoded features through a hierarchical point transformer architecture. What sets it apart from global attention mechanisms is its use of local attention, which allows each Gaussian to refine its features based on spatial neighbors, preserving fine-grained structural details while preventing influence from distant, unrelated Gaussians. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Encoded features for a set of N 3D Gaussians. Each Gaussian i is defined by position \mui \in \mathbb{R}^3, rotation quaternion qi \in \mathbb{R}^4, scale si \in \mathbb{R}^3, opacity \alphai \in \mathbb{R}, and spherical harmonic coefficients \gammai. Output: Refined geometric features fi^{(p)''} and appearance features fi^{(a)'} for each Gaussian, which are used to update the Gaussian parameters. Data Structures: The network operates on a set of point features. For each Gaussian i, the input is a feature vector. The architecture uses a hierarchical downsampling structure with 5 stages. The number of transformer blocks per stage is (2, 2, 2, 4, 2). Each MLP layer consists of linear layers followed by batch normalization and ReLU activation. Steps: 1. Dual-Branch Encoding: Process the raw Gaussian parameters through a dual-branch encoder to balance high-dimensional appearance features with geometric information. Geometric Branch: Compute the geometric feature vector fi^{(p)} by concatenating position, rotation, and scale: fi^{(p)} = \text{concat}(\mui, qi, si) Appearance Branch: Compute the appearance feature vector fi^{(a)} by concatenating opacity and reduced color features obtained by applying an MLP \phi to the spherical harmonic coefficients: fi^{(a)} = \text{concat}(\alphai, \phi(\gammai)) Feature Fusion: Apply separate MLPs \phip and \phia to extract corresponding features. Introduce a position encoding module \psi using solely explicit 3D coordinates \mui to reinforce spatial locations. Compute the refined appearance feature fi^{(a)'} using point-wise multiplication: fi^{(a)'} = fi^{(a)} + \sigma(\phia(fi^{(a)}) + \deltai) \odot (\phip(fi^{(p)}) + \deltai) where \deltai = \psi(\mui) and \sigma is the softmax function. Geometric Refinement: Compute the refined geometric feature fi^{(p)'} by adding the original geometric feature to the transformed appearance feature: fi^{(p)'} = fi^{(p)} + fi^{(a)'} 2. Point Transformer Processing: Pass the refined geometric features fi^{(p)'} through the 3D point transformer network (PT) to optimize attributes: fi^{(p)''} = \text{PT}(fi^{(p)'})) The point transformer employs local attention mechanisms. Parameters: Architecture: 5-stage hierarchical downsampling with transformer block counts (2, 2, 2, 4, 2). MLP Layers: Linear layers followed by batch normalization and ReLU activation. Loss Function: The optimization uses L = L1 + \lambda{LPIPS} L{LPIPS} with \lambda{LPIPS} = 0.1. Opacity Weight: \lambda\alpha = 0.3 is fixed for both datasets. Learning Rate: Initialized to 1e-5 and dropped by 10 at iteration 6,000. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Feature Imbalance: Without the dual-branch encoder, the dominance of high-dimensional spherical harmonic coefficients can overshadow geometric factors, leading to biased feature learning. Position Encoding: The position encoding module \psi uses only explicit 3D coordinates \mui, not intrinsic properties like scale or rotation, to ensure focus on physical 3D space. The Dual-Branch Encoder is a preprocessing module that processes Gaussian parameters through two parallel branches (geometric and appearance) to balance high-dimensional appearance features with geometric information before feeding them into the point transformer. It computes geometric features fi^{(p)} by concatenating position \mui, rotation qi, and scale si, and appearance features fi^{(a)} by concatenating opacity \alphai and reduced color features \phi(\gammai). It fuses these features using MLPs \phip, \phia and position encoding \psi(\mui) to produce refined features, addressing the feature imbalance caused by SH coefficient dominance. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Measured Performance: Evaluated on ScanNet++. The method improves scene quality and spatial coverage by refining sparse Gaussians that share similar properties (e.g., floors, walls). Strengths: Local attention preserves fine-grained structural details; learning features across multiple scenes allows refinement of sparse Gaussians; can be applied directly to pretrained 3DGS models without additional fine-tuning. Limitations: Not given in the sources. When to use: When optimizing appearance and geometric attributes of selected Gaussians in 3D Gaussian Splatting, particularly to balance appearance and geometry features and capture common structural characteristics across scenes. When not: Not given in the sources. The 3D Transformer Network Refinement was introduced in the paper "PointSplat: Efficient Geometry-Driven Pruning and Transformer Refinement for 3D Gaussian Splatting". It builds upon prior works such as SplatFormer [6] and addresses limitations in feature representation by introducing a dual-branch encoder and local attention mechanisms. The method is designed to improve novel view synthesis quality by refining 3D Gaussian parameters. name: 3D Spatial Grouping Network
head: Stage 2 Network for 3D Serialization and Grouping
body: The 3D Spatial Grouping Network is a Stage 2 refinement module that optimizes the geometric and appearance attributes of 3D Gaussian Splatting (GS) tokens by leveraging local attention mechanisms on sparse 3D points. It builds on 3D Transformer Network Refinement by explicitly handling the sparsity of 3D Gaussians through space-filling curve serialization and localized grouping, addressing the inefficiency of global attention on unstructured point clouds. Inputs and Outputs: Input: 1024-dimensional GS tokens lifted into 3D space, concatenated with a 256-dimensional error feature map (comprising a 128-channel error branch and a 128-channel image branch). Output: A 1024-dimensional residual update applied to each GS token. Data Structures: Voxel Grid: A 384^3 grid covering the scene bounding box. Serialization: Points are serialized along four space-filling curves: Z-order, Hilbert, and their transposed variants. Grouping: Points are grouped into blocks of S=8 consecutive points in the serialized order. Algorithm: 1. Feature Fusion: Project the 1024-dimensional GS token to 512 dimensions. Concatenate this with the 256-dimensional error feature. Project the result to a 512-dimensional point feature. 2. Voxelization: Voxelize the GS tokens onto the 384^3 grid. 3. Serialization: Assign one of the four space-filling curves (Z-order, Hilbert, or their transposes) to each of the 4 transformer blocks. 4. Local Attention: For each block, compute self-attention within groups of S=8 consecutive points based on the assigned serialization. 5. Residual Update: Map the output of the transformer blocks back to a 1024-dimensional residual and add it to the original GS token. Network Structure: Blocks: 4 pre-norm transformer blocks. Feature Dimension: 512. MLP Ratio: 4. Self-Attention: Computed in a 256-dimensional subspace with 16 heads of dimension 16. Parameters: 13.2M trainable parameters. Iteration: Applied with T=4 steps, sharing weights across all steps. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def spatialgroupingnetwork(gstokens1024, errorfeature256, scenebbox): """ Refines GS tokens using 3D spatial grouping. Args: gstokens1024: Tensor of shape (N, 1024) representing N Gaussian tokens. errorfeature256: Tensor of shape (N, 256) containing error and image features. scenebbox: Bounding box for voxelization. Returns: Updated GS tokens of shape (N, 1024). """ # Step 1: Feature Fusion # Project 1024-dim token to 512-dim gsproj = linearprojection(gstokens1024, indim=1024, outdim=512) # Concatenate with error feature (256-dim) combined = concatenate(gsproj, errorfeature256, axis=-1) # Project to 512-dim point feature pointfeatures = linearprojection(combined, indim=768, outdim=512) # Step 2 & 3: Voxelization and Serialization # Voxelize points onto 384^3 grid voxelizedpoints = voxelize(pointfeatures, gridsize=384, bbox=scenebbox) # Define serialization curves curves = [zorder, hilbert, zordertransposed, hilberttransposed] # Step 4: Local Attention Blocks # Initialize output as identity for residual connection residualoutput = pointfeatures for i in range(4): # Serialize points using the i-th curve serializedindices = serialize(voxelizedpoints, curve=curves[i]) # Group into blocks of S=8 groups = groupconsecutive(serializedindices, groupsize=8) # Compute local attention within each group # Self-attention in 256-dim subspace, 16 heads, head dim 16 groupfeatures = localattention( inputs=voxelizedpoints[serializedindices], groups=groups, attentiondim=256, numheads=16, headdim=16) # Update residual output (simplified: assuming block processes all points) # In practice, scatter gathered features back to original positions updatedfeatures = scatter(groupfeatures, serializedindices, N) residualoutput = residualoutput + updatedfeatures # Step 5: Final Linear Layer # Map output to 1024-dim residual finalresidual = linearprojection(residualoutput, indim=512, outdim=1024) # Apply residual update to original GS tokens updatedgstokens = gstokens1024 + finalresidual return updatedgstokens Parameters: Grid Size: 384^3. Group Size (S): 8. Number of Blocks: 4. Number of Iterations (T): 4. Feature Dimension: 512. Attention Subspace: 256. Number of Heads: 16. Head Dimension: 16. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision: Voxelization on a 384^3 grid may lose precision for very small or widely dispersed Gaussians if the bounding box is not tightly fitted. Boundaries: Points near the boundary of the bounding box may be truncated or incorrectly assigned if voxelization logic does not handle edge cases. Serialization Artifacts: Space-filling curves can introduce discontinuities at block boundaries; however, local attention within groups of 8 mitigates this by limiting the receptive field. A hierarchical transformer network for Stage 1 that processes image patches with increasing coarseness, using frame-wise and view-wise attention to aggregate features across views. It splits views into non-overlapping groups of two adjacent frames for view-wise group attention layers. The network has 14 layers: Layers 1-2 use 4x4 patch tokens (256-dim) with frame-wise attention; Layers 3-6 use 8x8 patch tokens (512-dim) with frame-wise and view-wise group attention; Layers 7-14 use 16x16 patch tokens (1024-dim) with frame-wise and global attention. All attention modules use a head dimension of 64. Time Complexity: Linear with respect to the number of Gaussians N due to local attention within fixed-size groups (S=8). Memory Complexity: Dominated by the 384^3 voxel grid and the storage of GS tokens and error features. Performance: The network has 13.2M trainable parameters. It is applied with T=4 steps with weight sharing, reducing inference time compared to applying distinct networks. Strengths: Efficiently handles sparse 3D data by leveraging spatial locality via space-filling curves. Limitations: Performance depends on the quality of the initial voxelization and the choice of space-filling curves. When to Use: When refining 3D Gaussian tokens for high-fidelity novel view synthesis where geometric accuracy is critical. When Not to Use: For scenes with extremely large bounding boxes where voxelization becomes memory-prohibitive. The 3D Spatial Grouping Network is part of the FineSplat architecture, introduced in 2026. It follows Point Transformer V3 for 3D serialization and grouping. The method is trained in three phases: Stage 1, Stage 2 (this network), and end-to-end fine-tuning. head: SSTrans-3D, Slice-by-slice transformer network

name: Neural Radiance Fields and Implicit Neural Representations
body: This family applies Implicit Neural Representations (INRs) to tomographic reconstruction, replacing discrete voxel grids with continuous functions parameterized by neural networks. It solves the ill-posed inverse problem of recovering 3D density fields from sparse, noisy, or limited-angle X-ray projections by leveraging the differentiability of the rendering pipeline. Unlike traditional discrete methods, these approaches optimize network weights directly, allowing for high-resolution reconstruction from minimal data and enabling simultaneous self-calibration of geometric and photometric parameters. All methods in this family rely on the differentiability of the forward projection operator \mathcal{P} and its adjoint (back-projection) \mathcal{P}^T. The core optimization problem is generally formulated as minimizing a loss function \mathcal{L} between the measured sinogram p and the rendered projection \hat{p} = \mathcal{P}(x) of the current volume estimate x: \minx \mathcal{L}(\mathcal{P}(x), p) + \lambda R(x) where R(x) is a regularizer (e.g., Total Variation, neural prior) and \lambda is a weighting factor. The gradient of the loss with respect to the volume x is computed via the chain rule: \frac{\partial \mathcal{L}}{\partial x} = \mathcal{P}^T \left( \frac{\partial \mathcal{L}}{\partial \hat{p}} \right) The term \frac{\partial \mathcal{L}}{\partial \hat{p}} is the residual gradient in projection space (e.g., p - \hat{p} for MSE), and \mathcal{P}^T is the back-projection operator. Key shared components include: 1. Forward Projection: Ray marching through the volume representation (voxels, octrees, or neural fields) to compute line integrals of density/absorption coefficients. 2. Backward Projection (Adjoint): Distributing the error from the 2D detector plane back into the 3D volume. This is mathematically the transpose of the forward operator, ensuring stable convergence in iterative methods. 3. Optimization Loop: An iterative process (e.g., SGD, Adam) that updates the volume parameters (voxel values, neural network weights, or Gaussian parameters) to reduce the projection error. NeAT uses a hybrid explicit-implicit structure, combining an adaptive octree with neural feature grids stored in leaf nodes. It is chosen for sparse-view or limited-angle tomography where traditional methods fail, as it simultaneously optimizes the volume, camera poses, and photometric parameters (reference image). It outperforms purely implicit methods in compute time for scattered samples. HoloINR solves near-field holotomography by explicitly modeling Fresnel propagation physics between the object and detector, rather than assuming far-field propagation. It is chosen when near-field diffraction effects are significant, mapping 3D coordinates to complex-valued scattering potentials. This method decouples the static canonical volume from the deformation field, using rich static projections to train the volume and sparse dynamic projections to learn motion. It is chosen for dynamic tomography to avoid the poor performance of directly inputting time into conventional NeRFs. VolumeNeRF reconstructs 3D CT volumes from a single 2D X-ray projection by integrating anatomical priors (Mean CT and Likelihood Images) via Projection Attention Modules (PAMs). It is chosen for single-view reconstruction to mitigate ill-posedness using structural priors. The application of Neural Radiance Fields (NeRF) to X-ray tomography emerged from the success of NeRF in novel view synthesis for visible light. Traditional iterative reconstruction methods (e.g., SIRT, FDK) struggle with sparse data and noise. Neural inverse rendering methods were developed to leverage the continuous nature of INRs for higher resolution and robustness in ill-posed scenarios.

name: Neural Adaptive Tomography (NeAT)
body:
Neural Adaptive Tomography (NeAT) is an adaptive, hierarchical neural rendering pipeline for multi-view inverse rendering, designed specifically for the tomographic reconstruction of semi-transparent volumetric scenes from X-ray images. It solves the problem of reconstructing 3D density fields from 2D projections by combining an explicit sparse octree representation with implicit neural features stored in leaf nodes. Unlike purely implicit representations or hybrid methods like ACORN, NeAT uses a hybrid explicit-implicit neural representation where geometry is defined by the octree and material properties by neural features, achieving superior reconstruction quality and compute times for tomographic tasks. Inputs: A set of N X-ray projection images I(p), where p indexes pixels. Initial estimates of camera poses (source and detector positions/orientations) and photometric parameters (reference image I0, exposure multipliers). Initial octree structure (typically a root node). Outputs: Optimized neural feature vectors for each leaf node in the octree. Optimized parameters for the neural decoder network. Refined camera poses and photometric calibration parameters. The final 3D density field \mu(x) reconstructed from the optimized features. Octree: A sparse hierarchical tree structure. Each node has up to 8 children. Internal Nodes: Do not store data; only define spatial subdivision. Leaf Nodes: Represent a voxel in the spatial domain. Each leaf node contains: A uniform grid of neural feature vectors. A bounding box defining the spatial extent of the leaf. Neural Features: Stored in leaf nodes. Each feature vector fn has dimension D (e.g., 16 or 32). Features are optimized parameters. Neural Decoder: A small multi-layer perceptron (MLP) \Phi. Input: Trilinearly interpolated feature vector f. Output: Scalar density value \mu = \Phi(f). Photometric Calibration: Reference image I0(p): A 2D image representing the source intensity distribution without the object. Per-view exposure multiplier Ei: A scalar for each view i. 1. Ray Generation: For each pixel p in each input image i, generate a ray rp(t) originating from the X-ray source position and passing through the detector pixel p. Determine the near (tn) and far (tf) intersection points with the global scene bounding box. 2. Ray-Octree Intersection: Compute the intersection of ray rp with the octree. Identify the sequence of leaf nodes traversed by the ray. If a node is empty or not present, skip it. 3. Neural Volume Sampling: For each leaf node n intersected by the ray: Determine the entry and exit points of the ray within the node's bounding box. Sample the neural features at these points. To query a point x inside a leaf node: Identify the grid cell containing x. Retrieve the 8 corner feature vectors of the grid cell. Perform trilinear interpolation to obtain the feature vector f(x). 4. Density Decoding: Pass the interpolated feature vector f(x) through the neural decoder \Phi to obtain the local density \mu(x) = \Phi(f(x)). 5. Volume Rendering (Integration): Compute the estimated pixel intensity \hat{I}'(p) by integrating the density along the ray segment within the scene. ray.tnear) / numsamples densityintegral = 0.0 traversednodes = [] for i in range(numsamples): t = ray.tnear + i stepsize point = ray.origin + ray.direction t node = findleafinoctree(octree, point) if node is not None: if node not in traversednodes: traversednodes.append(node) f = queryfeaturesinleaf(node, point) mu = decoder(f) densityintegral += mu stepsize I0val = I0[ray.pidx] return I0val np.exp(-densityintegral), traversednodes def computeloss(measuredimages, octree, decoder, I0, poses, lambdatv, lambdabc): """Computes the total loss for optimization.""" totalloss = 0.0 tvloss = 0.0 bcloss = 0.0 nodeerrors = {node: 0.0 for node in octree.leaves} for viewidx, (image, pose) in enumerate(zip(measuredimages, poses)): renderedview = np.zeroslike(image) for p in image.pixels: ray = generateray(pose, p) intensity, traversednodes = renderpixel(ray, octree, decoder, I0) renderedview[p] = intensity error = (image[p] - Reference Image Validity: Adding or removing the object from the setup can disturb the validity of the reference image I0, causing reconstruction artifacts. NeAT mitigates this by optimizing I0 during training. Computing Time: Existing neural inverse rendering frameworks suffer from long computing times. NeAT addresses this by using an explicit hierarchical representation, achieving superior reconstruction times compared to purely implicit methods. Sparse Views/Limited Angle: These are ill-posed problems. NeAT handles them using TV regularization and self-calibration. Time and Memory Complexity: Time: NeAT achieves reconstruction times far superior to existing neural inverse rendering methods. The explicit octree structure allows for efficient ray traversal and sampling, avoiding the dense sampling required by purely implicit representations. Memory: Memory usage is proportional to the number of leaf nodes and the size of the feature grids. The sparse octree structure ensures that only occupied regions are stored. Measured Performance: NeAT outperforms purely implicit representations and hybrid explicit-implicit representations (like ACORN) in both quality and compute time for tomographic settings. NeAT matches the performance of state-of-the-art tomographic reconstruction methods while providing superior quality for ill-posed configurations (sparse views, limited angle). Strengths and Limitations: Strengths: Adaptive resolution, efficient computation, self-calibration of geometry and photometry, robustness to sparse/limited angle data. Limitations: Requires careful tuning of regularization parameters (\lambda{tv}, \lambda{bc}). Performance depends on the initial octree structure and calibration. When to Use: Use NeAT for tomographic reconstruction of semi-transparent volumetric scenes from X-ray images, especially when dealing with sparse views, limited angle coverage, or when self-calibration is needed. When Not to Use: Not suitable for opaque scenes where surface rendering is sufficient, as NeAT is designed for volumetric density reconstruction. Origin: Neural Adaptive Tomography (NeAT) was introduced by Darius Rückert, Yuanhao Wang, Rui Li, Ramzi Idoughi, and Wolfgang Heidrich from KAUST and the University of Erlangen-Nuremberg. History and Development: NeAT is the first adaptive, hierarchical neural rendering pipeline for multi-view inverse rendering. It builds on the principles of neural radiance fields (NeRF) and implicit neural representations but adapts them for tomographic reconstruction by using an explicit octree structure with neural features in leaf nodes. It addresses the limitations of existing neural inverse rendering frameworks, which suffer from long computing times and are not well-suited for the scattered samples typical of tomography. Where it is used: NeAT is used for 3D scene reconstruction from X-ray images, particularly in computed tomography (CT) applications where high-quality reconstruction from limited or sparse data is required. name: Visual Error Tomography (VET)
body: Visual Error Tomography (VET) is a technique for identifying and filling geometrically deficient regions in a 3D point cloud by lifting 2D rendering error maps into 3D space using computed tomography. It solves the problem of incomplete geometry in semi-transparent volumetric scenes by reconstructing a volumetric model of visual error and spawning new points in high-error regions, distinguishing itself from traditional point-growing methods by effectively handling large-scale holes and thin structures without generating unnecessary points. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: A set of input images, a differentiable point-based renderer, an initial point cloud (e.g., from COLMAP), and the current state of the neural renderer (point positions, opacities, descriptors). Outputs: A refined 3D point cloud with new points spawned in undersampled regions, and a normalized 3D error volume grid. Data Structures: Error Volume: A 3D voxel grid of size 512^3 containing estimated error values. Bounding Box: Defined by the inner 95% of the points in the initial point cloud to filter extreme outliers and limit memory usage. Parameters: l: Smoothing parameter for error image normalization, typically 0.3. p{max}: Maximum number of points spawned per voxel, typically 10. Iterations: The VET process is repeated 1 to 3 times, usually every 200 epochs. Algorithm Steps: 1. Render and Compute Error: Render the scene using the differentiable point-based renderer to obtain rendered images. Compute the per-pixel rendering loss (error) for each input image by comparing rendered images to reference photographs. Let I(x,y) be the error image for a given view. 2. Smooth Error Images: Apply a non-linear smoothing function to the error images to focus on high-error regions and ignore small noise. The smoothed error image I'(x,y) is calculated as: I'(x,y) = \text{clamp}(I(x,y) \cdot (1 + l) - l, 0, 1) where l = 0.3. 3. Reconstruct 3D Error Volume: Apply Neural Adaptive Tomography (NeAT) to the smoothed error images to reconstruct a 3D error volume grid. NeAT is used because it models the non-linear intensity response of ray integrals (which do not follow Beer-Lambert's law) and uses a neural regularizer to produce sharp edges. The volume extent is limited to the bounding box defined by the inner 95% of the initial point cloud. 4. Normalize Error Volume: Normalize the resulting error volume grid to the range [0, 1]. Let ei(x,y,z) be the normalized error value at voxel (x,y,z). 5. Spawn Points: For each voxel in the grid, calculate the number of new points n(x,y,z) to spawn: n(x,y,z) = \lfloor ei(x,y,z) \cdot p{max} \rfloor where p{max} = 10. Distribute the positions of these n points randomly within the voxel cell. 6. Iterate: Resume optimization of the neural renderer. Repeat steps 1-5 for 1 to 3 cycles until convergence. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def visualerrortomography(initialpointcloud, inputimages, renderer, numcycles=3, cycleinterval=200): """ Performs Visual Error Tomography to refine a point cloud. Args: initialpointcloud: List of 3D points. inputimages: List of reference images. renderer: Differentiable point-based renderer. numcycles: Number of VET iterations (1-3). cycleinterval: Epochs between VET steps. Returns: Refined point cloud. """ # Define bounding box from initial point cloud # Limit to 95% of inner points to filter outliers boundingbox = computeinner95percentboundingbox(initialpointcloud) # Initialize error volume grid (512^3) errorvolume = initializegrid(size=512, bounds=boundingbox) # Smoothing parameter l = 0.3 # Max points per voxel pmax = 10 currentpointcloud = initialpointcloud for cycle in range(numcycles): # Resume optimization until convergence (simulated by epoch counter) # In practice, this involves backpropagation through the renderer optimizerenderer(renderer, currentpointcloud, inputimages, epochs=cycleinterval) # Step 1: Render and Compute Error errorimages = [] for img in inputimages: renderedimg = renderer.render(img.cameraparams, currentpointcloud) # Compute per-pixel loss (e.g., L1 or L2 distance) loss = computeloss(renderedimg, img.reference) errorimages.append(loss) # Step 2: Smooth Error Images smoothederrorimages = [] for errimg in errorimages: # I'(x,y) = clamp(I(x,y) (1+l) - l, 0, 1) smoothed = clamp(errimg (1 + l) - l, 0, 1) smoothederrorimages.append(smoothed) # Step 3: Reconstruct 3D Error Volume using NeAT # NeAT handles non-linear intensity response and sharp edges # This step projects 2D error images back to 3D space rawerrorvolume = neuraladaptivetomography(smoothederrorimages, inputimages, boundingbox) # Step 4: Normalize Error Volume minval = min(rawerrorvolume.flatten()) maxval = max(rawerrorvolume.flatten()) if maxval > minval: normalizederrorvolume = (rawerrorvolume - minval) / (maxval - minval) else: normalizederrorvolume = rawerrorvolume # Step 5: Spawn Points newpoints = [] voxelsize = boundingbox.volume / 5123 for x in range(512): for y in range(512): for z in range(512): errorval = normalizederrorvolume[x, y, z] # Calculate number of points to spawn npoints = floor(errorval pmax) if npoints > 0: # Get voxel center and bounds voxelcenter = getvoxelcenter(x, y, z, boundingbox) voxelbounds = getvoxelbounds(x, y, z, boundingbox) # Distribute points randomly within the voxel cell for in range(npoints): randompos = randomuniforminbox(voxelbounds) newpoints.append(randompos) # Add new points to the cloud currentpointcloud.extend(newpoints) return currentpointcloud def computeinner95percentboundingbox(points): """ Computes a bounding box that contains the inner 95% of points. This filters out extreme outliers. """ # Sort points along each axis xcoords = sorted([p.x for p in points]) ycoords = sorted([p.y for p in points]) zcoords = sorted([p.z for p in points]) n = len(points) # Remove 2.5% from each end (approximate for 95% inner) startidx = int(n 0.025) endidx = int(n 0.975) minx, maxx = xcoords[startidx], xcoords[endidx] miny, maxy = ycoords[startidx], ycoords[endidx] minz, maxz = zcoords[startidx], zcoords[endidx] return BoundingBox(minx, miny, minz, maxx, maxy, maxz) def clamp(value, minval, maxval): return max(minval, min(value, maxval)) def randomuniforminbox(box): """Generates a random point within a bounding box.""" x = random.uniform(box.minx, box.maxx) y = random.uniform(box.miny, box.maxy) z = random.uniform(box.minz, box.maxz) return Point(x, y, z) Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Non-Physical Ray Integrals: Standard CT assumes physical X-ray attenuation (Beer-Lambert's law), but visual error maps do not follow this law. Using classical analytical CT would fail; NeAT is required to handle this non-linearity. Outliers: Initial point clouds (e.g., from COLMAP) may contain extreme outliers. Limiting the volume extent to the inner 95% of points prevents these outliers from distorting the error volume or increasing memory costs excessively. Over-spawning: Adding too many points is not a critical issue due to the robust outlier removal strategy inherent in the differentiable renderer's optimization, which cleans up redundant points. A training loop that alternates between neural optimization (cleaning) and VET-guided point spawning to progressively complete the point cloud proxy. The process involves training the differentiable renderer until initial convergence, applying VET to predict missing 3D points from error images, spawning new points in identified regions, and resuming optimization. This cycle is repeated 1-3 times. Unlike methods that spawn points randomly along rays or require thousands of iterations, this pipeline converges faster and avoids overfitting by only spawning in VET-identified critical regions. Time Complexity: VET reconstruction takes about 15 minutes per cycle. The entire process is repeated 1-3 times. Memory Complexity: The error volume is a fixed 512^3 voxel grid. Memory costs are kept low by limiting the volume extent to the inner 95% of the initial point cloud. Performance: Measured on an RTX 4090 for inference and an A100 for training. Strengths: More effective than traditional point growing approaches at filling large-scale holes and thin structures. It avoids generating unnecessary points and requires fewer iterations. Limitations: Relies on the accuracy of the initial point cloud and the differentiable renderer. The method is specific to point-based neural rendering and may not directly apply to other representations without adaptation. When to Use: When starting with a sparse or incomplete point cloud (e.g., from MVS) and aiming for high-quality novel view synthesis, especially in scenes with thin structures or glossy surfaces. When Not to Use: When computational resources are extremely limited and the initial point cloud is already dense and complete. Visual Error Tomography (VET) was introduced by Franke et al. in the paper "VET: Visual Error Tomography for Point Cloud Completion and High-Quality Neural Rendering". It builds on the concept of using computed tomography for inverse rendering, specifically leveraging Neural Adaptive Tomography (NeAT) to handle the non-linear nature of visual errors. The method is part of a broader pipeline for neural point-based rendering, aiming to improve upon state-of-the-art methods like InstantNGP and Mip-NeRF 360 in terms of rendering quality and efficiency for point-based proxies. An open-source implementation is available at https://github.com/lfranke/VET. name: HoloINR
head: Implicit Neural Representation for Near-Field Holotomography
body: HoloINR solves the coupled inverse problem of holotomography (holography and tomography) using Implicit Neural Representations (INRs) for near-field setups where Fresnel propagation models the physics between object and detector. It differs from standard tomographic INRs by integrating wave-optics propagation (Fresnel diffraction) into the forward model, allowing reconstruction from holographic measurements rather than simple line integrals. Inputs: Holographic measurement data: An HDF5 file containing angles (list of floats in 0, \pi)) and data (holographic measurements, first axis angles, last two axes image dimensions). Geometry parameters: Defined by the ParallelGeometry or ConeBeam classes, including Source-Detector distances, pixel sizes, and voxel grid dimensions. Network hyperparameters: hiddendim, numlayers, skips, bound (spatial normalization), netchunk, numgradsamples, downsampling. Outputs: Reconstructed 3D volume represented by the trained INR weights, encoding the complex refractive index or [absorption coefficient. ParallelGeometry: DSO: float, Source-Origin distance. DSD: float, Source-Detector distance. nDetector: 2x1 array, pixel count. dDetector: 2x1 array, pixel size. sDetector: 2x1 array, total detector size. nVoxel: 3x1 array, voxel count. dVoxel: 3x1 array, voxel size. sVoxel: 3x1 array, total image size. offOrigin: 3x1 array, image center offset. offDetector: 2x1 array, detector center offset. rotDetector: 3x1 array, detector rotation. mode: string, 'parallel' or 'cone'. filter: string. ConeBeam: energy: float, X-ray energy. pxsize: float, pixel size. activepxsize: float, effective pixel size after downsampling. z02: float, Source-Detector distance (z0 + z{12}). z01: float, Source-Object distance (z0). INR Model: Input dimension: encoder.outputdim + inputcatdims. Layers: nn.ModuleList of nn.Linear layers. Skip connections add input dimensions to hidden layers at indices specified by skips. Activations: nn.LeakyReLU for hidden layers, lastactivation for output. Normalization: Input coordinates divided by bound. 1. Geometry Setup: Initialize ParallelGeometry or ConeBeam with experimental parameters. For cone-beam, calculate magnification M = (z{12} + z{01}) / z{01} and effective Fresnel number. 2. Ray Sampling: Compute normalized t-values along the ray, interpolate between near and far bounds to get z-values, then compute 3D points as pts = rayso + raysd zvals. Clamp points to [-bound, bound]. 3. Network Evaluation: Split rays into batches of size netchunk. For each chunk, pass points to the INR model, sum the output over the z-dimension (dim=-2), and concatenate results along the ray dimension. 4. Fresnel Propagation: Apply Fresnel propagator to simulate near-field diffraction effects between object and detector. 5. Segment Distance Weighting: Compute segment distances: dists = (zvals[..., 1:] - zvals[...,:-1]) ||raysd||. Append 1e-10 to the last segment to prevent zero-length division. Compute accumulation: acc = sum(raw dists, dim=-2). 6. Regularization: Compute Isotropic Total Variation (TV) regularization: TV = mean(sqrt(dx^2 + dy^2 + dz^2 + 1e-6)), where dx, dy, dz are finite differences along the x, y, and z axes respectively. 7. Optimization: Minimize loss using Adam or SGD, updating INR weights. Use downsampling factor (4 or 8) to reduce computation during optimization. Fresnel Number Calculation (Cone-Beam): \lambda = \frac{1.2398}{\text{energy}} M = \frac{z{12} + z{01}}{z{01}} dx{\text{eff}} = \frac{\text{active\px\size}}{M} z{\text{eff}} = \frac{z{12}}{M} \text{fr}{\text{eff}} = \frac{dx{\text{eff}}^2}{\lambda \cdot z{\text{eff}}} Total Variation Regularization: \text{TV} = \frac{1}{N} \sum{i=1}^{N} \sqrt{(\Deltax \phii)^2 + (\Deltay \phii)^2 + (\Deltaz \phii)^2 + 10^{-6}} Accumulation: \text{acc} = \sum{j} \text{raw}j \cdot \text{dists}j netchunk: Controls VRAM usage by limiting rays per forward pass. Default: 1024. numgradsamples: Maximum rays for gradient computation. Default: 1000. downsampling: Factor applied to nsamples during optimization. Typical values: 4 or 8. Zero-distance numerical instability: The last segment distance is explicitly set to 1e-10 to prevent division by zero or NaN propagation when computing acc. Memory overflow: If VRAM is exhausted, decrease netchunk or numgradsamples. NaN/Inf propagation: The render function checks for NaN or Inf values in accumulated output and prints a warning if detected. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import torch import torch.nn as nn class HoloINRModel(nn.Module): def init(self, hiddendim, numlayers, skips, bound, encoder, inputcatdims, lastactivation): super().init() self.bound = bound self.encoder = encoder self.inputcatdims = inputcatdims self.indim = encoder.outputdim + inputcatdims self.layers = nn.ModuleList([nn.Linear(self.indim, hiddendim)]) for i in range(1, numlayers - 1): if i in skips: self.layers.append(nn.Linear(hiddendim + self.indim, hiddendim)) else: self.layers.append(nn.Linear(hiddendim, hiddendim)) self.layers.append(nn.Linear(hiddendim, 1)) self.activations = nn.ModuleList([nn.LeakyReLU() for in range(numlayers - 1)]) self.lastactivation = lastactivation def forward(self, x, catargs=None): x = x / self.bound x = self.encoder(x, 1) if catargs is not None: x = torch.cat((x, catargs), dim=-1) inputpts = x[...,:self.indim] for i, layer in enumerate(self.layers): if i in self.skips: x = torch.cat([x, inputpts], dim=-1) x = layer(x) if i < len(self.layers) - 1: x = self.activationsi else: x = self.lastactivation(x) return x def renderrays(rayso, raysd, zvals, model, netchunk=1024, bound=1.0): pts = rayso.unsqueeze(1) + raysd.unsqueeze(1) zvals.unsqueeze(2) pts = torch.clamp(pts, -bound, bound) numrays = rayso.shape[0] allraw = [] for i in range(0, numrays, netchunk): chunkpts = pts[i:i+netchunk] raw = model(chunkpts) allraw.append(raw) raw = torch.cat(allraw, dim=0) dists = zvals[..., 1:] - zvals[...,:-1] dists = dists torch.norm(raysd, dim=-1, keepdim=True) dists = dists.unsqueeze(-1) lastdist = torch.oneslike(dists[...,:1]) 1e-10 dists = torch.cat([dists, lastdist], dim=-2) acc = torch.sum(raw dists, dim=-2) if torch.isnan(acc).any() or torch.isinf(acc).any(): print("Warning: NaN or Inf detected in accumulation") return acc def computetvloss(volumegrid): dx = volumegrid[..., 1:,:,:] - volumegrid[...,:-1,:,:] dy = volumegrid[...,:, 1:,:] - volumegrid[...,:,:-1,:] dz = volumegrid[...,:,:, 1:] - volumegrid[...,:,:,:-1] tv = torch.mean(torch.sqrt(dx2 + dy2 + dz2 + 1e-6)) return tv Uses adaptive sampling and neural networks for sparse-view tomography. Choose when data is extremely sparse. Neural Adaptive Tomography (NeAT) Standard NeRF applied to X-ray tomography with parallel beam assumptions. Choose for standard far-field tomography. Canonical Neural Radiance Field for X-ray Tomography Uses volumetric NeRF for tomographic reconstruction. Choose for high-quality rendering of complex scenes. VolumeNeRF Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Performance: Tested on Nvidia H100/H200 GPUs; significantly slower on older GPUs. Strengths: Handles near-field holographic data; integrates wave optics; differentiable end-to-end. Limitations: Computationally expensive; sensitive to VRAM limits; requires careful tuning of netchunk and downsampling. When to use: Near-field holotomography with holographic measurements. When not to use: Far-field tomography with simple projection data (use standard NeRF or algebraic methods). HoloINR was introduced by Johannes Gruen et al. in 2026 at ICASSP 2026. It addresses the limitations of traditional tomography in near-field setups where Fresnel diffraction effects are significant. The method leverages Implicit Neural Representations to provide a continuous, differentiable volume representation suitable for gradient-based optimization. name: Canonical Neural Radiance Field for X-ray Tomography
head: Canonical volume fitting, NeRF for X-ray
body: Canonical Neural Radiance Field for X-ray Tomography is a method that reconstructs the 3D density field of a static object (canonical volume) using a Neural Radiance Field (NeRF), trained on rich projection data to serve as a prior for dynamic reconstruction. It differs from full spatio-temporal networks by decoupling the static canonical volume representation from the time-dependent deformation field, addressing the poor performance observed when simply adding time as a direct input to conventional NeRFs. The method relies on the physical principle of X-ray attenuation and the mathematical framework of the Radon transform. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: Rich projection data (sinograms) acquired at specific time points (typically t=0 and t=1). Outputs: A canonical volume representation defined by a neural network mapping canonical coordinates (x0, y0, z0) to density \sigma and color c. Physical and Mathematical Background: X-ray attenuation follows the Beer-Lambert law: I = I0 \exp \left( - \int \mu(x) dx \right) where I is the transmitted intensity, I0 is the initial intensity, and \mu(x) is the attenuation coefficient. The projection p\theta(r) at angle \theta is the Radon transform of the density function \mu(x,y): p\theta(r) = \int{x,y} \mu(x,y) \delta(x \cos \theta + y \sin \theta - r) dx dy Tomographic reconstruction is the inverse operation of this transform. Data Structures: The canonical volume is encoded by a neural network \mathcal{N}. The network takes canonical 3D coordinates \mathbf{x}0 = (x0, y0, z0) as input and outputs density \sigma and color c. The specific architecture (e.g., number of layers, hidden dimensions) is not detailed in the sources. Algorithm Steps: 1. Data Acquisition: Acquire rich, many-projection X-ray data for the object at static time points, specifically t=0 and t=1. 2. Pre-training (Canonical Volume Fitting): Train the neural network \mathcal{N} to minimize the difference between the rendered projections and the measured sinograms. The rendering process involves ray marching through the canonical volume, computing line integrals of the predicted density \sigma to simulate the Radon transform. 3. Parameter Selection: Ensure the number of projections is sufficient to satisfy the Nyquist-like criterion for the sample. A typical value is 3000 projections, ensuring the maximum displacement of sample points between projections is within one voxel. 4. Deformation Field Calculation (Contextual): While the canonical volume is fitted using rich data, the deformation field is subsequently calculated from sparse few-projection data at intermediate times t. This step is part of the broader spatio-temporal model but distinct from the canonical volume fitting itself. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def traincanonicalvolume(projections, angles, network, optimizer, numepochs): """ Trains the canonical NeRF to fit X-ray projection data. Args: projections: List of 2D sinogram images. angles: List of corresponding projection angles theta. network: Neural network mapping (x0, y0, z0) -> (sigma, c). optimizer: Optimization algorithm (e.g., Adam). numepochs: Number of training iterations. """ for epoch in range(numepochs): for projection, angle in zip(projections, angles): # 1. Sample rays through the canonical volume # Rays are defined by the projection geometry for angle theta rays = generaterays(angle, projection.shape) # 2. Render the projection using the current network # This involves ray marching and integrating density sigma renderedprojection = rendervolume(network, rays) # 3. Compute loss against measured projection # Loss is typically MSE between rendered and measured intensity loss = meansquarederror(renderedprojection, projection) # 4. Backpropagate to update network weights optimizer.zerograd() loss.backward() optimizer.step() Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Insufficient Projections: Using too few projections violates the requirement that maximum displacement be within one voxel, leading to reconstruction artifacts. Time as Direct Input: Simply adding time t as an input to the NeRF (x, y, z, t) \rightarrow (c, \sigma) yields poor performance; the decoupled canonical approach is necessary. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Strengths: More efficient than conventional reconstruction methods for certain data modalities; enables 3D reconstruction during dynamic events by leveraging static priors. Limitations: Requires rich projection data at static time points (t=0, t=1) for pre-training; not suitable for scenes with topological changes that cannot be modeled by deformation fields. When to use: When reconstructing dynamic scenes where topology is preserved, and rich data is available at key static frames. When not to use: When only sparse data is available at all time points, or when the scene undergoes topological changes that break the deformation field assumption. The method was introduced in the paper "Neural rendering enables dynamic tomography". It addresses the challenge of 3D reconstruction during dynamic events by shifting from conventional CT to neural rendering techniques. The work demonstrates that NeRFs can reconstruct data modalities more efficiently than conventional methods and develops a spatio-temporal model with spline-based deformation fields for real-world experiments. name: VolumeNeRF
head: CT VolumeNeRF, NeRF-based model for 3D CT reconstruction from a single-view X-ray image
body: VolumeNeRF is a neural radiance field (NeRF)-based method that reconstructs 3D Computed Tomography (CT) volumes from a single 2D X-ray projection view. It addresses the ill-posed nature of single-view reconstruction by integrating prior anatomical knowledge—specifically average CT images and likelihood images—and explicit projection relationships via Projection Attention Modules (PAMs). Unlike sibling methods that may lack structural priors, VolumeNeRF conditions a 3D encoder-decoder network on 2D style vectors derived from the input X-ray and priors, supervising the output through differentiable volume rendering of the synthesized X-ray. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: A single 2D X-ray image I (resolution 128 \times 128), a Likelihood Image L (same resolution as I), and a Mean CT Image \bar{V} (2D slice or volume representation depending on implementation, treated as prior). Output: A reconstructed 3D CT volume \tilde{V} (resolution 128 \times 128 \times 128 voxels). Data Structures and Layouts: Voxel Grid: The volume \tilde{V} is represented as a 3D grid of size D \times H \times W = 128 \times 128 \times 128. Each voxel stores an attenuation coefficient \mu. Feature Maps: 3D Feature Maps: vi \in \mathbb{R}^{C \times D \times H \times W} at various encoder/decoder stages. 2D Pixel Feature Maps: y \in \mathbb{R}^{C \times H \times W} derived from the X-ray image via 2D convolutions. Style Vectors: Generated by the ConvNeXt mapping network, used to modulate 3D features. Projection Attention Module (PAM) State: Offset Coordinates: Learned 2D coordinates (u, v) for each voxel, constrained within the image bounds [0, 128] \times [0, 128]. Attention Weights: Scalar weights determining the contribution of specific pixels to a voxel's feature. Numbered Steps: 1. Data Preprocessing: Resample all input CT scans to a voxel size of 2.5 \times 2.5 \times 2.5 mm. Crop a central 128 \times 128 \times 128 voxel region from each scan. Compute the Mean CT Image \bar{V} by performing deformable registration to align all training CT volumes and averaging them. Compute Likelihood Images L for each volume. L quantifies the difference between the patient's volume and the average volume; pixels with higher deviation from the prior distribution have higher log-likelihood values. Synthesize training X-ray images I using differentiable Digital Reconstructed Radiographs (DRR) from the ground truth CT volumes at a resolution of 128 \times 128. 2. Style Vector Generation (2D Mapping): Input the X-ray image I, Likelihood Image L, and Mean CT Image \bar{V} into a ConvNeXt-based 2D mapping network. The network generates style vectors s that condition the subsequent 3D reconstruction, similar to the style modulation in StyleGAN2. 3. 3D Volumetric Reconstruction: Feed the style vectors s into a 3D encoder-decoder network. The 3D encoder extracts hierarchical 3D feature maps vi from the latent representation initialized by the style vectors. The 3D decoder upsamples these features to generate the final volumetric representation \tilde{V}. 4. Projection Attention Module (PAM) Integration: For each voxel in the 3D feature maps, the PAM learns spatial correspondence with 2D pixels in the X-ray image. Offset Learning: An offset convolution layer predicts 2D offset coordinates for each voxel, mapping the voxel to a specific location in the 2D feature map y derived from I. Feature Aggregation: Extract the 2D pixel feature map y corresponding to the predicted offset coordinates. Calculate attention weights (via Softmax and convolution operations) to weight the contribution of these pixels. Concatenate the original 3D feature v{i+1} and the weighted 2D pixel feature map y. Fuse them using a 3D convolutional operator to generate the enhanced voxel feature map v{yi+1} \in \mathbb{R}^{C \times D \times H \times W}. This process is repeated through the encoder-decoder stages to inject 2D projection priors into the 3D volume. 5. Volume Rendering (Forward Projection): To provide supervision, synthesize a rendered X-ray image \hat{I} from the reconstructed volume \tilde{V} using the same viewpoint as the input I. Apply the Lambert-Beer law for ray marching. For a ray r passing through N voxels: \hat{I} = I0 \exp \left( - \sum{i=1}^{N} \mui \deltai \right) where \mui is the attenuation coefficient of the i-th voxel, \deltai is the distance the beam propagates within that voxel, and I0 is the initial intensity. The rendered image \hat{I} is compared against the input I. 6. Loss Calculation and Optimization: Compute the total loss \mathcal{L}{total} as a weighted sum of three terms: \mathcal{L}{total} = \lambda{recon} \mathcal{L}{recon} + \lambda{edge} \mathcal{L}{edge} + \lambda{render} \mathcal{L}{render} Reconstruction Loss (\mathcal{L}{recon}): L1 loss between the reconstructed CT \tilde{V} and the ground truth CT (if available during training). Edge Loss (\mathcal{L}{edge}): L1 loss between the edges of the generated CT and real CT, where edges are extracted using the Scharr operator. Rendering Loss (\mathcal{L}{render}): L1 loss between the input X-ray image I and the rendered X-ray image \hat{I}. Optimize the network parameters (ConvNeXt weights, 3D encoder-decoder weights, PAM parameters) using gradient descent. Parameters: \lambda{recon} = 1. \lambda{edge} = 0.05. \lambda{render} = 0.001. Voxel size: 2.5 \times 2.5 \times 2.5 mm. Volume resolution: 128 \times 128 \times 128. X-ray resolution: 128 \times 128. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Boundary Constraints: Voxels in distant planes have intersection points with the detector plane that fall outside the detection range. The learned offset coordinates are manually constrained within the X-ray image size range [0, 128] \times [0, 128]. Consequently, corresponding pixels for such distant voxels are located at the edges of the X-ray image, potentially limiting the accuracy of projection correspondence for deep structures. Memory Limitations: The method requires cropping to 128^3 voxels due to memory constraints, which may discard peripheral anatomical information. Time and Memory Complexity: Not explicitly given in the sources. Memory is constrained by the 128 \times 128 \times 128 voxel grid and the 3D convolutional operations. Measured Performance: On the LIDC-IDRI dataset (1,018 chest CT volumes; 865 training, 51 validation, 102 testing), VolumeNeRF achieves a PSNR of 25.59 \pm 0.20 and SSIM of 0.660 \pm 0.002. Scaling: The method is validated on chest CTs. Scaling to larger volumes or different anatomies requires re-evaluation of the cropping strategy and prior computation. Strengths: Incorporates anatomical priors (mean CT, likelihood) and explicit projection relationships (PAMs), addressing the ill-posedness of single-view reconstruction better than methods lacking these constraints. Limitations: Relies on differentiable DRR for training data synthesis, which may not perfectly capture all physical X-ray artifacts. Performance is limited by the fixed 128^3 resolution and the manual constraint on offset coordinates. VolumeNeRF was proposed by J. Liu and X. Bai in 2024. It is based on neural radiance fields (NeRF) and aims to reconstruct CT volumes from a single X-ray projection view, reducing radiation exposure and scan time compared to traditional multi-view CT. The method was validated on the LIDC-IDRI dataset. VolumeNeRF: CT Volume Reconstruction from a Single Projection View, https://papers.miccai.org/miccai-2024/paper/3061paper.pdf, fetched 2026-10-28
