name: Online Monocular Neural 3D Reconstruction with Geometric Priors
head: MonoNeuralFusion, MonoNeuralFusion Online Pipeline, Online Reconstruction System
body: Online Monocular Neural 3D Reconstruction with Geometric Priors (MonoNeuralFusion) is an incremental surface mapping system that reconstructs 3D geometry from monocular RGB sequences by maintaining and refining a sparse feature volume. It solves the problem of real-time, globally coherent 3D reconstruction from a single camera by decoupling the pipeline into a parallel mapping thread for feature volume construction and an optimization thread for volume rendering refinement. Unlike offline dense voxel methods (e.g., Atlas) or purely depth-estimation approaches, MonoNeuralFusion uses a sparse representation guided by geometric priors (predicted normals) to achieve high normal consistency and lower Chamfer distance while operating online. The method builds on Neural Radiance Fields and Implicit Neural Representations by using a neural radiance field f\omega to represent the scene, but optimizes it incrementally using geometric constraints. Inputs: Monocular RGB image sequence, camera intrinsics, and estimated camera extrinsics (poses). Outputs: A surface mesh (extracted via Marching Cubes) and a refined neural radiance field representation. 1. Sparse Feature Volume: A 3D grid storing multi-level image features extracted by a 2D CNN encoder (MnasNet) and processed by a 3D sparse CNN. The volume is sparse, meaning it only stores features for occupied voxels, reducing memory usage compared to dense grids. 2. Keyframe Database: Stores selected keyframes, their poses, and associated predicted normal maps. 3. Neural Radiance Field (f\omega): A neural network parameterized by \omega that maps 3D coordinates and viewing directions to color and density. Initialized randomly from a zero-mean Gaussian distribution. 1. Mapping Thread (Feature Volume Construction) 1. Receive an incoming RGB frame with its pose. 2. Determine if the frame is a keyframe. A frame is selected as a keyframe if the distance to the last keyframe > \taud = 0.1 OR the rotation angle from the last keyframe > \taua = 15^\circ. 3. If a keyframe is selected: a. Predict the normal map for the image using an out-of-the-box Omnidata model. b. Insert the keyframe and its normal map into the Keyframe Database. c. Maintain a sliding window of keyframes. When the window size reaches K = 9, construct the Sparse Feature Volume using all images in the window and their camera parameters. d. Apply Marching Cubes to the current Sparse Feature Volume to extract an initial surface mesh. 2. Optimization Thread (Volume Rendering Refinement) 1. Run in parallel with the Mapping Thread. 2. Select B = 9 optimization keyframes from the Keyframe Database. 3. Randomly sample M = 512 pixels on each of the selected keyframes. 4. For each sampled pixel, cast a ray through the scene. 5. Perform volume rendering to compute the rendered color and depth. This involves: a. Coarse sampling: Sample Nc = 16 points along the ray. b. Importance sampling: Sample Ni = 16 points along the ray based on coarse densities. c. Compute the final color and depth using the accumulated density and color from f\omega. 6. Compute the loss function \mathcal{L}, which includes photometric loss and a normal consistency loss weighted by 0.05. 7. Use the Adam optimizer to refine the scene representation parameters (\omega) for T = 100 iterations. 3. Per-Scene Fine-Tuning (Optional) 1. After the online process, or for specific high-fidelity requirements, optimize the entire scene. 2. Sample M = 512 pixels on each of B = 9 images. 3. Use Nc = Ni = 32 sampling points per ray. 4. Optimize for T = 5,000 iterations. The optimization minimizes a loss function. While the exact composite loss formula is not fully detailed in the provided text, the components are specified: Photometric loss component weight: \lambda{lo} = 0.8 (using L1 loss). Normal consistency loss weight: 0.05. Clamp threshold \tau = 0.2 used in NISR training. The gradient is computed via backpropagation through the volume rendering operator and the neural network f\omega. \taud = 0.1: Distance threshold for keyframe selection. \taua = 15^\circ: Rotation threshold for keyframe selection. K = 9: Sliding window size for feature volume construction. B = 9: Number of optimization keyframes per loop. M = 512: Number of pixels sampled per keyframe for optimization. Nc = 16: Coarse sampling points per ray (online). Ni = 16: Importance sampling points per ray (online). T = 100: Online optimization iterations per loop. Nc = Ni = 32: Sampling points per ray (fine-tuning). T = 5,000: Fine-tuning iterations. Normal weight: 0.05. \lambda{lo} = 0.8: L1 loss weight. \tau = 0.2: Clamp threshold. Learning rate: 0.001 (Adam optimizer). Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import numpy as np class MonoNeuralFusion: def init(self): # Parameters self.taud = 0.1 self.taua = 15.0 # degrees self.K = 9 self.B = 9 self.M = 512 self.Nccoarse = 16 self.Nifine = 16 self.Tonline = 100 self.normalweight = 0.05 self.lr = 0.001 # Data Structures self.keyframedatabase = [] # List of dicts: {'rgb': img, 'pose': pose, 'normal': normal} self.slidingwindow = [] self.sparsefeaturevolume = None self.fomega = None # Neural Radiance Field, initialized randomly from zero-mean Gaussian # Optimizer self.optimizer = Adam(self.fomega.parameters(), lr=self.lr) def iskeyframe(self, currentframe, lastkeyframe): dist = distance(currentframe.pose, lastkeyframe.pose) rotangle = rotationangle(currentframe.pose, lastkeyframe.pose) return dist > self.taud or rotangle > self.taua def mappingthreadstep(self, currentframe): # 1. Check if keyframe if not self.keyframedatabase: iskf = True else: lastkf = self.keyframedatabase[-1] iskf = self.iskeyframe(currentframe, lastkf) if iskf: # 2. Predict Normal normalmap = predictnormals(currentframe.rgb) # Using Omnidata # 3. Update Database self.keyframedatabase.append({ 'rgb': currentframe.rgb, 'pose': currentframe.pose, 'normal': normalmap }) # 4. Sliding Window Construction self.slidingwindow.append(currentframe) if len(self.slidingwindow) >= self.K: # Construct Sparse Feature Volume self.sparsefeaturevolume = constructsparsevolume( self.slidingwindow, cameraintrinsics=currentframe.intrinsics) # Extract Mesh mesh = marchingcubes(self.sparsefeaturevolume) # Reset window or keep sliding? Text implies "sliding window", # usually means we keep the last K. # For simplicity, we assume we rebuild with the last K. self.slidingwindow = self.slidingwindow[-self.K:] # Note: Optimization thread runs in parallel, so we don't wait for it here. def optimizationthreadstep(self): if len(self.keyframedatabase) < self.B: return # 1. Select B frames selectedframes = selectrandomframes(self.keyframedatabase, self.B) # 2. Sample Pixels # For each selected frame, sample M pixels for in range(self.Tonline): loss = 0.0 gradients = [] for frame in selectedframes: # Randomly sample M pixels u, v = randomsamplepixels(frame.rgb.shape, self.M) for i in range(self.M): # 3. Ray Casting and Volume Rendering ray = castray(frame.pose, frame.intrinsics, u[i], v[i]) # Coarse Sampling coarsepoints = samplealongray(ray, self.Nccoarse) coarsedensities, coarsecolors = self.fomega(coarsepoints, ray.directions) # Importance Sampling finepoints = importancesample(coarsedensities, ray, self.Nifine) finedensities, finecolors = self.fomega(finepoints, ray.directions) # Composite Color and Depth renderedcolor, rendereddepth = composite(finepoints, finedensities, finecolors, ray) # 4. Loss Computation gtcolor = frame.rgb[u[i], v[i]] gtnormal = frame.normal[u[i], v[i]] # Photometric Loss (L1) colorloss = l1loss(renderedcolor, gtcolor) # Normal Consistency Loss # Predict normal from rendered depth or volume gradient prednormal = predictnormalfromvolume(rendereddepth, self.sparsefeaturevolume) normalloss = l1loss(prednormal, gtnormal) # Combined Loss batchloss = colorloss + self.normalweight normalloss loss += batchloss # Accumulate gradients (conceptual) gradients.append(batchloss) # 5. Update Parameters loss.backward() self.optimizer.step() self.optimizer.zerograd() def finetuning(self): # Select all keyframes or a subset selectedframes = self.keyframedatabase Ncfine = 32 Nifine = 32 Tfine = 5000 for in range(Tfine): loss = 0.0 for frame in selectedframes: u, v = randomsamplepixels(frame.rgb.shape, self.M) for i in range(self.M): ray = castray(frame.pose, frame.intrinsics, u[i], v[i]) # Fine sampling coarsepoints = samplealongray(ray, Ncfine) coarsedensities, = self.fomega(coarsepoints, ray.directions) finepoints = importancesample(coarsedensities, ray, Nifine) finedensities, finecolors = self.fomega(finepoints, ray.directions) renderedcolor, = composite(finepoints, finedensities, finecolors, ray) gtcolor = frame.rgb[u[i], v[i]] colorloss = l1loss(renderedcolor, gtcolor) # Normal loss also applied prednormal = predictnormalfromvolume(rendereddepth, self.sparsefeaturevolume) gtnormal = frame.normal[u[i], v[i]] normalloss = l1loss(prednormal, gtnormal) loss += colorloss + self.normalweight normalloss loss.backward() self.optimizer.step() self.optimizer.zerograd() def selectrandomframes(database, B): return random.sample(database, B) def randomsamplepixels(shape, M): h, w = shape[:2] u = np.random.randint(0, h, M) v = np.random.randint(0, w, M) return u, v def l1loss(pred, gt): return np.mean(np.abs(pred - gt)) Degenerate Input: If the camera does not move significantly (distance < 0.1 and rotation < 15^\circ), no keyframes are selected, and the feature volume is not updated. This requires sufficient camera motion for reconstruction. Precision: The method relies on accurate pose estimation. Errors in extrinsic parameters will propagate into the feature volume construction and volume rendering. Memory: While sparse, the feature volume can still grow large for extensive scenes. The sliding window approach limits the volume size to K=9 frames at a time, but the optimization thread may need to access a larger database. Uses adaptive sampling and neural fields for tomography. Chooses this when high-resolution internal structure is needed from limited angles. Neural Adaptive Tomography (NeAT) Uses holographic principles for neural implicit representations. Chooses this when dealing with light field or holographic data. HoloINR Maps views to a canonical space for X-ray tomography. Chooses this for X-ray specific applications with rigid objects. Canonical Neural Radiance Field for X-ray Tomography Uses volume rendering with NeRF for general 3D reconstruction. Chooses this when dense, offline reconstruction is acceptable and no online constraint exists. VolumeNeRF Time Complexity: The online system runs in parallel threads. Mapping thread complexity depends on the number of keyframes and the cost of normal prediction and feature volume construction. Optimization thread complexity is O(T \cdot B \cdot M \cdot (Nc + Ni)) per loop, where T is iterations, B is keyframes, M is pixels, and Nc, Ni are sampling points. Memory Complexity: Sparse feature volume size is proportional to the number of occupied voxels in the sliding window (K=9 frames). This is significantly less than dense voxel grids used by methods like Atlas. Measured Performance: On the TUM RGB-D dataset, the method achieves Chamfer Distance = 0.107, F-score = 0.375, Normal Consistency = 0.806, Abs Rel = 0.062, Abs Diff = 0.108, and \delta < 1.25 = 0.959. Runtime: Normal prediction takes ~61.48ms per keyframe. Feature volume construction takes ~34.35ms per local fragment (9 keyframes) on an Nvidia RTX 3090 GPU. Fine-tuning Time: Per-scene fine-tuning typically takes less than 9 minutes. Strengths: High normal consistency, globally coherent reconstruction, online capability, lower Chamfer distance compared to other online methods. Limitations: Requires accurate camera poses. Performance depends on the quality of the normal prediction model. Recall is comparable to offline dense methods but may be lower due to sparsity. MonoNeuralFusion was introduced in the paper "MonoNeuralFusion: Online Monocular Neural 3D Reconstruction with Geometric Priors". It builds upon previous work in neural surface reconstruction such as NeuralRecon and TransformerFusion, aiming to improve normal consistency and online efficiency. The method uses MnasNet for 2D feature extraction and a 3D sparse CNN for feature processing. It was evaluated on the ScanNet and TUM RGB-D datasets. name: Stretched Sinograms for Neural Tomographic Reconstruction
head: Stretched Sinograms
body: Stretched Sinograms is a direct reconstruction method for limited-angle electron tomography that preprocesses tilt views by stretching them perpendicular to the tilt axis by a factor of \sec(\theta), then feeds the stretched views into a 2-D U-Net to directly output a 3-D reconstruction, avoiding backprojection. It differs from sibling methods like Neural Radiance Fields and Implicit Neural Representations by operating on explicit 2-D image channels rather than implicit continuous fields, and from Deep Learning and Neural Architectures by incorporating a geometric preprocessing step (stretching) specifically designed to compensate for the missing wedge in limited-angle tomography before the neural network processes the data. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A 3-D tensor of 2-D tilt views y \in \mathbb{R}^{n{\text{view}} \times nh \times nw}, assumed to be log-normalized and related to the object density via the Radon transform. The views cover a limited angular range (-\theta, +\theta) where \theta < 90^\circ. Output: A 3-D reconstruction volume \hat{x} \in \mathbb{R}^{nd \times nh \times nw}. Data Structures: Tilt View Tensor (y): Shape (n{\text{view}}, nh, nw). Stretched Sinogram (y{\text{stretched}}): Shape (n{\text{view}}, nh, nw). U-Net Input: Treated as a 2-D image with n{\text{view}} input channels. U-Net Output: Treated as a 2-D image where the channel dimension corresponds to the depth dimension nd of the output volume. Parameters: n{\text{view}}: Number of tilt views. nh, nw: Height and width of each tilt view. \theta: Maximum tilt angle in the range (-\theta, +\theta). nd: Depth of the output volume. n{\text{pixel}} = nd \times nh \times nw: Total number of pixels in the output reconstruction. Optimizer: Adam with learning rate 0.001. Normalization: Instance Normalization before every ReLU layer. Steps: 1. Stretching: For each tilt view y(\theta, \cdot, \cdot), stretch the image in the direction perpendicular to the tilt axis by a factor of \sec(\theta). The image size (nh \times nw) is preserved. Bilinear interpolation is used, treating the center of each image as the origin. 2. Coordinate Transformation: If the tilt axis is parallel to the \hat{y} axis (stretching along \hat{x}), the stretched view is computed as: y{\text{stretched}}(\theta, i, j) = y(\theta, i, j \sec \theta) where i, j are natural coordinates indexing rows and columns, with (-1, -1) at the upper left and (+1, +1) at the bottom right. 3. Matrix Formulation: The stretching operation can be represented as a sparse linear operator S such that y{\text{stretched}} = Sy, mapping the raw views tensor to the stretched views tensor. 4. Network Input Preparation: Treat the stretched sinogram y{\text{stretched}} as a 2-D image with K = n{\text{view}} input channels. 5. Neural Reconstruction: Pass the stretched sinogram through a 2-D U-Net architecture f\omega. 6. Volume Assembly: Treat the output channel dimension of the U-Net as the depth dimension of the output volume \hat{x}. 7. Training: Train the network using stochastic gradient descent on the Mean Squared Error (MSE) objective: l(\omega) = \frac{1}{2 n{\text{pixel}}} \| x - f\omega(Sy) \|^2 where x is the ground truth volume. 8. Optimization: Use the Adam optimizer with a step-size of 0.001. Use early stopping based on validation set error to select the network for test-set evaluation. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import torch import torch.nn as nn import torch.nn.functional as F def stretchsinogram(y, theta): """ Stretches each tilt view in the sinogram by sec(theta) perpendicular to the tilt axis. Args: y: Tensor of shape (nview, nh, nw). Log-normalized tilt views. theta: Maximum tilt angle in radians. Returns: ystretched: Tensor of shape (nview, nh, nw). """ nview, nh, nw = y.shape stretchfactor = 1.0 / torch.cos(torch.tensor(theta)) # Create coordinate grids in natural coordinates (-1 to 1) # i corresponds to rows (height), j corresponds to columns (width) icoords = torch.linspace(-1, 1, nh, device=y.device) jcoords = torch.linspace(-1, 1, nw, device=y.device) # Create meshgrid: I is (nh, nw), J is (nh, nw) I, J = torch.meshgrid(icoords, jcoords, indexing='ij') # Stretch along the x-axis (columns/j) assuming tilt axis is parallel to y-axis # Formula: ystretched(theta, i, j) = y(theta, i, j sec(theta)) # We need to map the output grid coordinates back to the input grid coordinates Jinput = J / stretchfactor # Stack coordinates for gridsample: (N, H, W, 2) # gridsample expects coordinates in [-1, 1] grid = torch.stack((Jinput, I), dim=-1) # Expand y to have a batch dimension for gridsample if necessary, # or process per view. gridsample works on (N, C, H, W). # Here, each view is a channel? No, y is (nview, nh, nw). # We treat each view as a separate sample in a batch for gridsample, # or reshape to (nview, 1, nh, nw). yreshaped = y.unsqueeze(1) # (nview, 1, nh, nw) # Perform bilinear interpolation # gridsample requires grid of shape (N, H, W, 2) # We need to broadcast grid to match nview views gridexpanded = grid.unsqueeze(0).expand(nview, -1, -1, -1) ystretchedreshaped = F.gridsample( yreshaped, gridexpanded, mode='bilinear', paddingmode='zeros', aligncorners=True) # Remove channel dimension: (nview, nh, nw) ystretched = ystretchedreshaped.squeeze(1) return ystretched class StretchedSinogramReconstructor(nn.Module): def init(self, nview, nd, nh, nw): super(StretchedSinogramReconstructor, self).init() # 2-D U-Net architecture # Input channels: nview (number of tilt views) # Output channels: nd (depth of the volume) self.unet = UNet2D(inchannels=nview, outchannels=nd) def forward(self, y, theta): """ Reconstructs 3D volume from stretched sinogram. Args: y: Tensor of shape (nview, nh, nw) theta: Maximum tilt angle in radians Returns: xhat: Tensor of shape (nd, nh, nw) """ # Step 1: Stretch the sinogram ystretched = stretchsinogram(y, theta) # Step 2: Pass through U-Net # U-Net expects input shape (N, Cin, H, W). # We treat the batch dimension as 1, and channels as nview. # ystretched is (nview, nh, nw). Reshape to (1, nview, nh, nw). ystretchedbatch = ystretched.unsqueeze(0) # U-Net output shape: (1, nd, nh, nw) unetoutput = self.unet(ystretchedbatch) # Step 3: Extract volume # Remove batch dimension: (nd, nh, nw) xhat = unetoutput.squeeze(0) return xhat class UNet2D(nn.Module): """ Simplified 2-D U-Net with Instance Normalization before ReLU. """ def init(self, inchannels, outchannels): super(UNet2D, self).init() # Encoder self.enc1 = self.block(inchannels, 64) self.enc2 = self.block(64, 128) self.enc3 = self.block(128, 256) self.enc4 = self.block(256, 512) self.pool = nn.MaxPool2d(2) # Bottleneck self.bottleneck = self.block(512, 1024) # Decoder self.up4 = nn.ConvTranspose2d(1024, 512, 2, stride=2) self.dec4 = self.block(1024, 512) self.up3 = nn.ConvTranspose2d(512, 256, 2, stride=2) self.dec3 = self.block(512, 256) self.up2 = nn.ConvTranspose2d(256, 128, 2, stride=2) self.dec2 = self.block(256, 128) self.up1 = nn.ConvTranspose2d(128, 64, 2, stride=2) self.dec1 = self.block(128, 64) self.final = nn.Conv2d(64, outchannels, 1) def block(self, inchannels, outchannels): return nn.Sequential( nn.Conv2d(inchannels, outchannels, 3, padding=1), nn.InstanceNorm2d(outchannels), nn.ReLU(inplace=True), nn.Conv2d(outchannels, outchannels, 3, padding=1), nn.InstanceNorm2d(outchannels), nn.ReLU(inplace=True)) def forward(self, x): # Encoder e1 = self.enc1(x) e2 = self.enc2(self.pool(e1)) e3 = self.enc3(self.pool(e2)) e4 = self.enc4(self.pool(e3)) # Bottleneck b = self.bottleneck(self.pool(e4)) # Decoder d4 = self.dec4(torch.cat([self.up4(b), e4], dim=1)) d3 = self.dec3(torch.cat([self.up3(d4), e3], dim=1)) d2 = self.dec2(torch.cat([self.up2(d3), e2], dim=1)) d1 = self.dec1(torch.cat([self.up1(d2), e1], dim=1)) return self.final(d1) def trainstretchedsinogram(model, y, xgt, theta, optimizer, npixel): """ Training step for Stretched Sinogram reconstruction. Args: model: StretchedSinogramReconstructor instance y: Input tilt views tensor (nview, nh, nw) xgt: Ground truth volume tensor (nd, nh, nw) theta: Maximum tilt angle optimizer: Adam optimizer npixel: Number of pixels in output volume (nd nh nw) """ optimizer.zerograd() # Forward pass xhat = model(y, theta) # Compute MSE loss loss = (1.0 / (2.0 npixel)) torch.sum((xgt - xhat) 2) # Backward pass loss.backward() optimizer.step() return loss.item() Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Normalization: Using Batch Normalization instead of Instance Normalization results in significantly higher test time error, likely because the U-Nets are trained with a batch size of 1. Tilt Axis Orientation: The formula y{\text{stretched}}(\theta, i, j) = y(\theta, i, j \sec \theta) assumes the tilt axis is parallel to the \hat{y} axis (stretching along \hat{x}). For arbitrary tilt axes, the formula must be adjusted to stretch along a linear combination of i and j. Limited Angle: The method is designed for limited-angle tomography where \theta < 90^\circ. The stretching compensates for the missing wedge but may introduce artifacts if the angle is too large or if the assumption of parallel beam geometry is violated. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Measured Performance: The method was evaluated on a 992×1000×1000 test set volume extracted from FIB-SEM images of fly brain tissue, broken into 124 non-overlapping patches of size 32×512×512. Inference and backpropagation were performed on a single ASUS RTX3090 Turbo 24GB GPU. Forward/backward projections for comparison methods were distributed across 64 CPUs. Scaling: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Direct reconstruction without explicit backprojection; handles limited-angle tomography effectively; avoids artifacts associated with traditional FBP in limited-angle scenarios. Limitations: Requires paired training data (tilt views and ground truth volumes); performance depends on the quality of the U-Net architecture and training; limited to parallel beam geometry assumptions. When to use: Limited-angle electron tomography where traditional methods like FBP suffer from severe artifacts due to the missing wedge. When not to use: Full-angle tomography (where FBP is sufficient and faster); non-parallel beam geometries without modification. Origin: Proposed by Kyle Luther and H. Sebastian Seung from the Princeton Neuroscience Institute and Princeton Computer Science Department. Paper: "Stretched sinograms for limited-angle tomographic reconstruction with neural networks" (arXiv:2306.10201v1, 16 Jun 2023). History and Development: The method builds on the idea of using convolutional neural networks for tomographic reconstruction, specifically addressing the limitations of limited-angle data by geometrically preprocessing the sinogram before neural processing. Usage: Demonstrated on simulated tilt views from 3-D images of fly brain tissue acquired with Focused Ion Beam Scanning Electron Microscopy (FIB-SEM). Stretched sinograms for limited-angle tomographic reconstruction with neural networks, https://arxiv.org/abs/2306.10201v1, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial)

name: Diffusive INR (DINR)
head: Diffusion-regularized Implicit Neural Representation, Diffusive Computed Tomography Inversion Framework
body: DINR is a sparse-view computed tomography (CT) reconstruction method that regularizes an Implicit Neural Representation (INR) using a pretrained diffusion model prior to suppress noise and artifacts in raw projection data. It addresses the ill-posed inverse problem of sparse-view CT, where insufficient projection views cause severe artifacts in traditional methods like Filtered Back Projection (FBP). Unlike standard INRs, which suffer from spectral bias toward low-frequency components and instability under sparse supervision, DINR incorporates a proximal formulation that integrates denoised diffusion outputs into the INR loss. It differs from sibling methods like DD3IP by replacing the UNet-based volume representation with an INR, enabling resolution-independent and memory-efficient posterior mean estimation. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: S: A 3D coordinate grid (cubic lattice) defining the volumetric domain. y: Sparse-view parallel-beam CT projection data (sinogram). A: Sparse-view parallel beam projector matrix. A^ y: The analytical solution (FBP estimate) of the projection data. \thetaT: Pretrained diffusion model weights. \omega: Scaling parameter for noise injection (typically 0.002). \rho: Regularization parameter for the proximal term (chosen such that the ratio of the proximal term to the data-fidelity term is 1 \times 10^{-6} or 1 \times 10^{-5} depending on the specific experimental setup). \eta: Stochasticity control variable in [0, 1] for DDIM sampling. \alpha{1:T}: Decreasing sequence in (0, 1]^T parameterizing the reverse diffusion process. Outputs: x0: The final reconstructed 3D volume tensor of attenuation coefficient values. Data Structures: INR Model (F\phi): A neural network (typically an MLP) parameterized by weights \phi. It maps spatial coordinates S and the FBP estimate A^ y to attenuation coefficient values. The input to F\phi is the concatenation or combination of coordinates S and the low-frequency prior A^ y. Diffusion Model (D\theta): A pretrained denoising model (e.g., UNet) parameterized by weights \theta, conditioned on the projection data y. Projector (A): Implemented as a distance-driven parallel-beam projector (e.g., via Tomosipo/ASTRA toolbox). Formulas: 1. Forward Model: y = Ax + n, where x is the 3D tensor of attenuation coefficients, A is the projection matrix, and n is additive noise. 2. Proximal Loss (L\phi): Used to update INR weights \phi: L\phi (S, y, \hat{x}t, \rho) = \text{MSE} (AF\phi (S, A^ y), y) + \rho \text{MSE} (\hat{x}t, F\phi (S, A^ y)) where \hat{x}t is the denoised estimate from the diffusion model at step t. 3. DDIM Sampling Step: \text{DDIM}\theta (\hat{x}t, \eta):= \sqrt{\alpha{t-1}} \hat{x}t + \sqrt{1 - \alpha{t-1}} \eta \epsilon + (1 - \eta) \epsilon\theta where \epsilon is spherically interpolated Gaussian noise and \epsilon\theta is the noise removed by the denoising model D\theta. 4. Initialization of Reverse Process: xT \leftarrow \sqrt{\alphaT} A^ y + \sqrt{1 - \alphaT} \epsilon w where w is a scaling factor related to \omega. Algorithm Steps: 1. Initialize the 3D coordinate grid S, the sparse-view parallel beam projector A, and the sparse-view CT projection y. 2. Compute the FBP estimate A^ y. 3. Initialize the INR weights \phiT by minimizing the standard MSE loss without the diffusion prior (\rho=0): \phiT \leftarrow \arg \min\phi \{L\phi (S, y, -, \rho = 0)\} where L\phi (S, y, -, \rho = 0) = \text{MSE} (AF\phi (S, A^ y), y). 4. Load the pretrained diffusion model weights as \thetaT. 5. Initialize the volume estimate xT using the formula: xT \leftarrow \sqrt{\alphaT} A^ y + \sqrt{1 - \alphaT} \epsilon w where \epsilon is Gaussian noise and w is the scaling parameter \omega. 6. Iterate the diffusion reverse process for t = T down to 1: a. Update Diffusion Model: Update the diffusion model parameters \theta{t-1} by minimizing the data consistency loss between the projected INR reconstruction and the measured projections: \theta{t-1} \leftarrow \arg \min\theta \{\text{MSE} (A D\theta (xt |y), y)\}. b. Denoise: Generate the denoised estimate \hat{x}t by applying the updated diffusion model D{\theta{t-1}} to the current latent xt conditioned on y: \hat{x}t \leftarrow D{\theta{t-1}} (xt |y). c. Update INR: Update the INR parameters \phi{t-1} by minimizing the proximal loss L\phi (S, y, \hat{x}t, \rho), which incorporates the diffusion prior estimate \hat{x}t and the regularization parameter \rho. d. Compute Next Latent: If t = 1: Compute the final output x{t-1} by evaluating the final INR F{\phi{t-1}} at the coordinate grid S with the FBP estimate A^ y: x{t-1} \leftarrow F{\phi{t-1}} (S, A^ y). If t > 1: Compute the next latent x{t-1} using the DDIM sampler with the updated diffusion model \theta{t-1}, the INR output F{\phi{t-1}} (S, A^ y), and the noise scaling factor \eta: x{t-1} \leftarrow \text{DDIM}{\theta{t-1}} (F{\phi{t-1}} (S, A^ y), \eta). 7. Return the final reconstruction x0. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def DINR(S, y, A, Astary, thetaT, alphaT, omega, rho, eta, T): """ S: 3D coordinate grid y: sparse-view CT projection A: parallel beam projector Astary: FBP estimate (A y) thetaT: pretrained diffusion model weights alphaT: diffusion schedule parameter at step T omega: scaling parameter for noise injection rho: regularization parameter for proximal loss eta: stochasticity control for DDIM T: total number of diffusion timesteps """ # 1. Initialize INR weights with standard MSE loss (rho=0) # Lphi(S, y, -, rho=0) = MSE(A Fphi(S, Astary), y) phiT = minimizemse(Fphi, S, y, A, Astary) # 2. Initialize diffusion model weights theta = thetaT # 3. Initialize volume estimate xT # xT = sqrt(alphaT) Astary + sqrt(1 - alphaT) epsilon omega epsilon = samplegaussiannoise(S.shape) xt = sqrt(alphaT) Astary + sqrt(1 - alphaT) epsilon omega # 4. Iterate reverse diffusion process for t in range(T, 0, -1): # a. Update diffusion model weights theta{t-1} # Minimize MSE(A Dtheta(xt | y), y) # Note: Dtheta is the denoising model parameterized by theta theta = minimizemsediffusion(Dtheta, xt, y, A, theta) # b. Compute denoised estimate xhatt xhatt = Dtheta(xt, y, theta) # c. Update INR weights phi{t-1} # Minimize Lphi(S, y, xhatt, rho) # Lphi = MSE(A Fphi(S, Astary), y) + rho MSE(xhatt, Fphi(S, Astary)) phi = minimizeproximalloss(Fphi, S, y, A, Astary, xhatt, rho, phi) # d. Compute next latent x{t-1} if t == 1: # Final output xt = Fphi(S, Astary, phi) else: # DDIM sampling step # DDIMtheta(xhatt, eta) = sqrt(alpha{t-1}) xhatt + sqrt(1 - alpha{t-1}) eta epsilon + (1 - eta) epsilontheta # epsilontheta is the noise removed by Dtheta, which is (xt - Dtheta(xt, y, theta)) epsilontheta = xt - Dtheta(xt, y, theta) epsilonnext = samplesphericalgaussiannoise(S.shape) alphatminus1 = getalphaschedule(t - 1) # Assuming alpha schedule is known xt = sqrt(alphatminus1) xhatt + \ sqrt(1 - alphatminus1) eta epsilonnext + \ (1 - eta) epsilontheta return xt Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Spectral Bias: Standard INRs exhibit strong spectral bias toward low-frequency components, leading to poor reconstruction of high-frequency structure under sparse supervision. DINR mitigates this by incorporating the diffusion prior. Initialization: The initialization of xT uses the FBP estimate A^ y corrupted with noise. The scaling parameter \omega controls the regularization by scaling the values of A^ y relative to the noise variance. Parameter Tuning: The parameter \rho must be chosen carefully. In experiments, it was set such that the ratio of the proximal term to the data-fidelity term was 1 \times 10^{-6} or 1 \times 10^{-5}. The parameter \omega was set to 0.002. Time Complexity: The method involves iterative optimization of both the diffusion model weights \theta and the INR weights \phi at each diffusion timestep t. This makes it computationally expensive compared to single-pass methods like FBP or standard INR training. Memory Complexity: The INR representation is memory-efficient and resolution-independent compared to voxel-based methods like DD3IP, as it only stores the neural network weights rather than a 3D grid. Performance: DINR delivers superior performance, reduces reconstruction artifacts, and achieves gains in PSNR and SSIM compared to traditional methods (FBP) and state-of-the-art sparse-view techniques (DD3IP, Siren). It performs on par with MBIR with a qGGMRF prior in sparse-view settings and outperforms it in the ultra-sparse regime. Strengths: High-quality reconstruction from sparse views, resolution-independent representation, ability to integrate learned priors with traditional inverse problem formulations. Limitations: Computationally intensive due to the iterative nature of the diffusion process and the joint optimization of \theta and \phi. Requires a pretrained diffusion model. When to use: Sparse-view CT reconstruction, particularly when data is extremely limited (e.g., 5-33 views) and high-quality microstructural characterization is required. When not to use: When computational resources are limited or when full-view data is available (FBP or standard INR may suffice). DINR was proposed in the paper "Regularizing INR with Diffusion Prior for Self-Supervised 3D Reconstruction OF Neutron Computed Tomography Data". It builds upon the DD3IP framework and the use of Implicit Neural Representations (INRs) for inverse imaging problems. The method is designed for sparse-view parallel-beam neutron CT reconstruction of concrete microstructures. It addresses the limitations of standard INRs (spectral bias) and traditional methods (artifacts in sparse views) by combining the flexibility of INRs with the powerful generative prior of diffusion models. Regularizing INR with Diffusion Prior for Self-Supervised 3D Reconstruction OF Neutron Computed Tomography Data, https://doi.org/10.1109/ICASSP55912.2026.11464479, fetched 2026-10-26

name: Self-Calibrating Differentiable NLOS Inverse Rendering
head: Differentiable transient rendering with self-calibration, Phasor-field NLOS inverse rendering, Self-Calibrating, Fully Differentiable NLOS Inverse Rendering
body: Self-Calibrating Differentiable NLOS Inverse Rendering is a fully-differentiable end-to-end pipeline for reconstructing hidden scenes from time-resolved non-line-of-sight (NLOS) measurements. It solves the problem of reconstruction artifacts and inversion ambiguities inherent in traditional NLOS imaging by automatically self-calibrating imaging parameters during the reconstruction process, eliminating the need for manual selection of filtering functions and parameters. Unlike volumetric back-projection methods or explicit polygonal mesh approaches, this method estimates an implicit geometric representation (surface points and normals) from volumetric intensities and refines the reconstruction by minimizing the error between simulated and measured illumination via gradient descent. The method operates in two domains: time and frequency. It begins with a phasor-field diffraction reconstruction to generate an initial volumetric intensity, extracts an implicit geometry from this volume, and then uses differentiable transient rendering to simulate the measurement, optimizing parameters to match the input data. Input: Measurement matrix H(xl, xs, t), representing time-resolved illumination captured at points xs on a visible relay wall from a laser beam emitted at point xl. Output: Volumetric intensity I{pf}, implicit geometry G (surface points and normals), and optimized imaging parameters \Theta{pf}, \ThetaG, \Theta{ls}. 1. Measurement Matrix H: A 3D array indexed by laser position xl, sensor position xs, and time t. In the frequency domain, this is transformed into phasors H(xl, xs, \Omega) via Fourier transform. 2. Volumetric Intensity I{pf}: The output of the phasor-field reconstruction, representing the estimated density of hidden objects. 3. Implicit Geometry G: A set of surface points and their associated normals, estimated from I{pf} without defining a polygonal mesh. 4. Parameters: \Theta{pf}: Parameters for the phasor-field reconstruction. \ThetaG: Parameters defining the implicit geometry. \Theta{ls}: Parameters for the differentiable transient rendering (light source and sensor models). 1. Phasor-Field Reconstruction: Transform the time-resolved measurement matrix H(xl, xs, t) into the frequency domain to obtain phasors H(xl, xs, \Omega). Apply a filtering function to the noisy phasor data. Perform NLOS imaging using a phasor-field diffraction method to compute the initial volumetric intensity I{pf} = R{pf}(P(H; \Theta{pf})). Here, P denotes the projection/processing and R{pf} the reconstruction operator. 2. Implicit Geometry Estimation: Estimate the implicit geometry G (surface points and normals) from the volumetric intensity I{pf} using a differentiable estimator D: G = D(I{pf}). This step avoids explicit surface mesh definition. 3. Differentiable Transient Rendering: Render the time-resolved illumination HR from the estimated geometry G using differentiable path-space transient rendering: HR = R(G; \ThetaG, \Theta{ls}). This simulates the light transport from the hidden scene back to the relay wall, accounting for the optimized parameters. 4. Optimization: Compute the loss \mathcal{L} between the measured illumination H and the rendered illumination HR: \mathcal{L} = \sum \| H - HR \|^2 + \Gamma where \Gamma represents regularization terms. Perform gradient descent to update the imaging parameters \Theta{pf}, \ThetaG, \Theta{ls} by minimizing \mathcal{L}. The geometry G is computed during the forward pass, while parameters are updated during the backward pass. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def selfcalibratingnlosinverserendering(H): """ H: Measurement matrix H(xl, xs, t) Returns: Optimized parameters and reconstructed geometry """ # Step 1: Phasor-Field Reconstruction # Transform time-domain measurements to frequency domain (phasors) Hphasor = fouriertransform(H) # Apply filtering to phasors (details of filter not specified in source) Hfiltered = applyfilter(Hphasor) # Reconstruct initial volumetric intensity # Thetapf are initial parameters for phasor-field reconstruction Ipf = phasorfieldreconstruction(Hfiltered, thetapf) # Step 2: Estimate Implicit Geometry # Estimate surface points and normals from volumetric intensity G = estimateimplicitgeometry(Ipf) # Step 3 & 4: Differentiable Rendering and Optimization # Define loss function def lossfunction(thetapf, thetaG, thetals): # Re-render volumetric intensity with updated parameters Ipfnew = phasorfieldreconstruction(Hfiltered, thetapf) # Re-estimate geometry with updated parameters Gnew = estimateimplicitgeometry(Ipfnew) # Render simulated time-resolved illumination from geometry HR = differentiabletransientrendering(Gnew, thetaG, thetals) # Compute loss # Gamma is regularization term L = sumsquarederror(H, HR) + regularizationterm(Gnew) return L # Initialize parameters thetapf = initializeparameters('pf') thetaG = initializeparameters('G') thetals = initializeparameters('ls') # Gradient descent optimization while not converged: L = lossfunction(thetapf, thetaG, thetals) gradients = computegradients(L, thetapf, thetaG, thetals) # Update parameters thetapf = update(thetapf, gradients['thetapf']) thetaG = update(thetaG, gradients['thetaG']) thetals = update(thetals, gradients['thetals']) # Check convergence if checkconvergence(L): break return thetapf, thetaG, thetals, estimateimplicitgeometry(phasorfieldreconstruction(Hfiltered, thetapf)) Memory Limitations: Computing derivatives of time-resolved radiometric data severely limits the number of unknown parameters that can be handled in differentiable methods. This method addresses this by coupling phasor-field reconstruction with differentiable rendering, but memory constraints remain a factor. Visibility Changes: Handling visibility changes in a differentiable manner is difficult and can lead to non-differentiable discontinuities. Noise: The method is designed to be robust in the presence of noise, providing consistent geometric estimations under varying capture conditions. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Limited by the need to compute derivatives of time-resolved radiometric data, which restricts the number of unknown parameters. Strengths: Self-calibrates imaging parameters automatically via gradient descent, removing the need for manual parameter selection. Provides more geometric detail than previous surface-based methods and is robust to noise. Limitations: Bounded by memory limitations inherent in differentiable transient rendering. When to use: When high-quality reconstruction of hidden scenes is required without manual tuning of filtering parameters, and when implicit geometry representation is preferred over explicit meshes. The method was introduced by Kiseok Choi, Inchul Kim, Dongyoung Choi, Julio Marco, Diego Gutierrez, and Min H. Kim. It builds upon wave-based NLOS imaging methods that use diffractive phasor-based frameworks to formulate NLOS reconstruction as a virtual line-of-sight problem. It also integrates concepts from differentiable rendering pipelines in path space. The code is available at https://github.com/KAIST-VCLAB/nlos-inverse-rendering.git. name: Tomographic Image Synthesis for Layered 3D
head: Attenuation-based Light Field Synthesis, Layered 3D, Tomographic Image Synthesis for Multi-Layer HDR Displays, Tomographic Optimization, Tomographic reconstruction for attenuation displays
body: Tomographic Image Synthesis for Layered 3D is a method to optimally construct volumetric or layered attenuators to emit a target light field by minimizing the difference between emitted and target light fields subject to physical constraints on attenuation, using iterative tomographic reconstruction. It solves the inverse problem of determining the attenuation map \mu(x,y) that, when backlit, produces a desired 4D light field l(u,a). Unlike heuristic methods that blur target images to rear layer resolution, this method formulates the synthesis as a constrained linear least-squares optimization problem, proving that existing dual-layer architectures are near-optimal in the least-squares sense. It extends conventional parallax barriers to multiple disjoint layers, increasing spatial resolution, depth of field, and brightness for 3D displays, and enabling high dynamic range (HDR) for 2D displays. Inputs: Target light field l(u, a), parameterized on a relative two-plane system where u is the spatial coordinate on the slab bisector and a is the ray orientation slope. Display geometry: number of layers Nl, layer thickness/separation, and spatial resolution (e.g., 384x512 pixels per layer). Physical constraints: limited layer contrast (attenuation bounds). Outputs: Attenuation maps \mun(x, y) for each layer n \in \{1, \dots, Nl\}, defined as continuously-varying functions nonzero only within the slab dimensions |x| < w/2, |y| < h/2. Light Field: Stored as a 4D array l(u, a) with spatial resolution (e.g., 384x512) and angular resolution (e.g., 7x7 views). Attenuation Map: Represented using a series expansion into a set of normalized linear basis functions rather than a discrete voxel grid to ensure smoother reconstructions and mitigate discrete ray sampling artifacts. Projection Matrix: A sparse matrix A mapping the basis function coefficients to the light field samples. The matrix is stored directly in memory, limiting the maximum display dimensions and layer count by available system RAM. The forward model is based on the Beer-Lambert law. For a single slab, the transmitted intensity I of a ray along path C is: I = I0 e^{-\intC \mu(\mathbf{r}) d\mathbf{r}} where I0 is incident intensity and \mu(\mathbf{r}) is the attenuation map. The logarithm of the normalized intensity \bar{l} is defined as: \bar{l} = \ln\left(\frac{I}{I0}\right) = -\intC \mu(\mathbf{r}) d\mathbf{r} This integral is the Radon transform p(u, a) of the attenuation map. Thus, the emitted light field is: l(u, a) = -p(u, a) For layered displays, the total attenuation is the sum of the attenuations of individual layers (assuming negligible scattering and reflection between layers). The inverse problem is to find \mu such that the emitted light field matches the target. This is solved as a constrained linear least-squares optimization: \min{\mathbf{x}} \| A \mathbf{x} - \mathbf{b} \|^2 \quad \text{subject to} \quad \mathbf{x}{min} \le \mathbf{x} \le \mathbf{x}{max} where \mathbf{x} represents the coefficients of the basis functions for the attenuation maps, A is the projection matrix (Radon transform), and \mathbf{b} is the target light field (log-intensity). The constraints \mathbf{x}{min}, \mathbf{x}{max} enforce physical limits on layer contrast (attenuation values). Light Field Resolution: 384x512 spatial pixels by 7x7 angular views. Layer Count (Nl): Typically 3-5 layers in demonstrations. Field of View: ±5 degrees. Basis Functions: Normalized linear basis functions. 1. Preprocessing: Convert the target light field l{target}(u, a) to log-intensity space: \mathbf{b} = \ln(l{target}). Evaluate color channels independently. 2. Matrix Construction: Construct the sparse projection matrix A that maps the chosen basis function coefficients to the light field samples. This involves computing line integrals through the basis functions for each ray (u, a). 3. Optimization: Solve the constrained linear least-squares problem using a sparse, constrained, large-scale trust region method (e.g., Coleman and Li 1996). Initialize \mathbf{x} (e.g., zeros or heuristic guess). Iterate until convergence (typically 8-14 iterations). Enforce constraints \mathbf{x}{min} \le \mathbf{x} \le \mathbf{x}{max} at each step. 4. Post-processing: Convert the optimized coefficients \mathbf{x} back to attenuation maps \mun(x, y) for each layer. 5. Rendering (Verification): Render the synthesized light field using POV-Ray as 7x7 oblique projections. Apply a depth-dependent 4D antialiasing filter by rendering each view with a limited depth of field (finite aperture camera) to approximate combined anti-aliasing and display prefiltering. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def tomographicsynthesis(targetlightfield, numlayers, spatialres, angularres, basisfunctions, constraints): """ Synthesize layered attenuation maps for a target light field. Args: targetlightfield: 4D array [u, v, theta, phi] or flattened vector b. numlayers: Number of attenuator layers Nl. spatialres: (width, height) of each layer. angularres: (numviewsu, numviewsa) of light field. basisfunctions: Set of normalized linear basis functions phii(x,y). constraints: Tuple (xmin, xmax) for attenuation bounds. Returns: attenuationmaps: List of Nl 2D arrays representing mun(x,y). """ # 1. Preprocessing: Convert target to log-intensity # Assuming targetlightfield is in linear intensity space b = log(targetlightfield) # 2. Construct Projection Matrix A # A maps basis coefficients to light field samples. # A is sparse. Each row corresponds to a ray (u, a). # Each column corresponds to a basis function coefficient. # Aij = integral of basisfunctionj along rayi A = constructprojectionmatrix(spatialres, angularres, basisfunctions) # 3. Solve Constrained Least-Squares # Minimize ||Ax - b||^2 subject to xmin <= x <= xmax # Using sparse constrained trust-region method (Coleman & Li) xopt = solveconstrainedlsqr(A, b, constraints.xmin, constraints.xmax) # 4. Reconstruct Attenuation Maps # xopt contains coefficients for all layers combined # Split xopt into Nl segments corresponding to each layer's basis functions attenuationmaps = [] for layeridx in range(numlayers): layercoeffs = xopt[layeridx numbasisperlayer: (layeridx + 1) numbasisperlayer] mu = reconstructfrombasis(layercoeffs, basisfunctions) attenuationmaps.append(mu) return attenuationmaps def constructprojectionmatrix(spatialres, angularres, basisfunctions): """ Construct the sparse Radon transform matrix A. """ # Determine all rays (u, a) in the light field parameterization rays = generaterays(spatialres, angularres) numrays = len(rays) numbasis = len(basisfunctions) # Initialize sparse matrix A = SparseMatrix(numrays, numbasis) for i, ray in enumerate(rays): for j, phi in enumerate(basisfunctions): # Compute line integral of basis function phi along ray integral = computelineintegral(phi, ray) A[i, j] = integral return A def computelineintegral(basisfunction, ray): """ Compute the integral of a basis function along a specific ray path. Ray is defined by u (position on slab) and a (slope). """ # Integrate basisfunction over the path C defined by the ray # In flatland (2D cross-section), this is a 1D integral path = ray.path return integrate(basisfunction, path) Color Crosstalk: The standard implementation evaluates color channels independently, neglecting color crosstalk between layers. Incorporating crosstalk increases memory requirements and computation time significantly. Flip Animations: For uncorrelated multi-view imagery (flip animations), direct application of the optimization leads to significant crosstalk. A spatial downsampling constraint must be added to yield accurate results with enhanced contrast. Filtering Artifacts: Linear reconstruction filters applied to the logarithm of the light field do not correspond to the same filters applied to the light field directly. Memory Limits: Storing the sparse projection matrix directly in memory limits the maximum display dimensions, image resolution, and number of layers by system capacity. Matrix-free optimization can mitigate this but may increase computation time. Physical Assumptions: Scattering and reflection losses are assumed negligible. Interreflections between layers are ignored, though in practice they may not lead to visual artifacts if ambient lighting is controlled. Time Complexity: The optimization requires solving a large, sparse system of equations. It is not real-time; typical optimization takes 12 minutes for 5 layers on a 2.4 GHz Intel Core 2 workstation with 8 GB RAM. Convergence is typically achieved in 8-14 iterations. Memory Complexity: Proportional to the size of the sparse projection matrix, which depends on the number of light field samples and basis functions. Limited by system RAM. Strengths: Produces qualitatively optimal decompositions for dual-layer HDR displays, confirming existing heuristics. Extends naturally to multiple disjoint layers, increasing spatial resolution, depth of field, and brightness compared to parallax barriers. Limitations: Computationally expensive; not suitable for dynamic content without significant acceleration (e.g., GPU, precomputed inverses). Limited by physical constraints of layer contrast and separation. When to Use: Static images or pre-rendered content for multi-layer HDR or 3D attenuation displays. When Not to Use: Real-time dynamic applications without hardware acceleration; scenes with significant inter-layer scattering or reflection that cannot be neglected. Origin: Proposed by Wetzstein et al. in 2011. History: The method builds on tomographic reconstruction principles [Herman 1995] and light field parameterization [Chai et al. 2000]. It was developed to address the limitations of heuristic image synthesis methods for layered displays, such as parallax barriers and integral imaging, by providing a mathematically optimal solution in the least-squares sense. Usage: Demonstrated on hardware prototypes consisting of five printed transparency layers separated by clear acrylic sheets, illuminated by a backlight. name: Basic GPU D2VR Framework
head: D2VR Framework
body: The Basic GPU D2VR Framework is a method for GPU-accelerated Direct Volume Rendering (D2VR) that reconstructs a 3D volume from 2D projections distributed around a circular orbit. It specifically enables the reconstruction of image-aligned volume slices in front-to-back order, a structural requirement that facilitates occlusion culling and empty space skipping during rendering. It differs from general GPU ray casting by explicitly managing the geometric relationship between projection sets and viewing vectors to maintain slice alignment for acceleration techniques. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A set of M 2D projection images. Output: A rendered 3D volume visualization. Data Structures: The framework organizes projections into two sets: a Viewing set (V-set) and a Support set (S-set). These sets are used to reconstruct two corresponding texture stacks: the Viewing stack (V-stack) and the Support stack (S-stack). Parameters: N: The desired volume resolution dimension (N \times N \times N). M: The number of projections. For maximal volume resolution N^3 without aliasing using parallel beam data, M = \frac{\pi}{2} \cdot N projections are required. Viewing Angle Constraint: The viewing vector must be tilted within \pm 45^\circ perpendicular to the reference plane (e.g., the x-z plane) when using the projective texture method. Method Steps: 1. Projection Organization: Distribute M projections around a circular orbit. If the projections are perpendicular to the x-z plane, classify them based on their alignment with the viewing vector. 2. Viewing Vector Check: Determine if the current viewing vector is within the \pm 45^\circ range perpendicular to the x-z plane. If within range: Proceed with the Projective Texture Method. If outside range: Switch to the Texture Spreading Method or provide an orthogonal set of projections (e.g., around the x-y plane). 3. Stack Assignment (Projective Texture Method): Rotate the volume proxy polygons so that one slice set is perpendicular and the other is orthogonal to the viewing vector. Define the perpendicular slices as the Viewing (V) stack and the orthogonal slices as the Support (S) stack. Divide the projections into the V-set (projections more perpendicular to the V-stack) and the S-set (projections more perpendicular to the S-stack). 4. Reconstruction: Reconstruct the S-stack from the S-set projections. Reconstruct the V-stack from the V-set projections. The reconstruction aims to produce image-aligned volume slices. 5. Rendering Preparation: The reconstructed slices are arranged in front-to-back order relative to the viewing direction to enable occlusion culling. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Viewing Angle Exceedance: If the viewing vector exceeds the \pm 45^\circ limit, the projective texture method fails to maintain alignment. The implementer must either switch methods or provide additional orthogonal projection sets. Tuy’s Condition: If a single method is to be used for all viewpoints, two orthogonal half-orbits of projections, equally spaced in angle, must be provided to satisfy Tuy’s condition for exact 3D reconstruction. Extends the basic framework with occlusion culling and empty space skipping for interactive speeds. Complexity: Not given in the sources. Performance: The framework is designed to enable occlusion culling, which optimizes rendering performance by skipping empty space. Limitations: The method is constrained by the viewing angle (\pm 45^\circ) when using the projective texture approach, requiring specific projection arrangements or method switches for other angles. Memory: The gradient-from-samples (GFS) approach, mentioned as a related technique in the source, reduces memory bandwidth in the accumulator by reconstructing only density values and estimating gradients from volume samples, though it slows down the rendering procedure. The framework was introduced in the context of GPU-accelerated volume rendering from 2D projections. It relies on Tuy’s condition for exact 3D reconstruction from projection data. name: GPU-Accelerated D2VR
head: GPU D2VR with occlusion culling
body: A GPU-accelerated implementation of Direct 2D Volume Rendering (D2VR) that incorporates occlusion culling and empty space skipping to achieve interactive or near-interactive rendering speeds. It builds on the RapidCT framework but generalizes it to allow reconstruction of arbitrary oriented volumes and incorporates acceleration techniques to limit reconstruction effort to visible/non-occluded samples. The method extends the GPU-accelerated filtered backprojection approach used in RapidCT. It performs ray advancement in a single fragment shader loop, allowing for non-linear ray effects. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: 2D projection images (sinogram data), camera orientation parameters defining an arbitrary image plane. Outputs: Rendered 2D volume image. Data Structures: Projection images stored in GPU texture memory. Volume data structure aligned with the arbitrary image plane. Depth correction factors applied during backprojection. Algorithm Steps: 1. Filtering: Filter acquired images along their columns using a ramp filter (e.g., Shepp-Logan, RamLak) in the frequency domain. 2. Backprojection: Backproject filtered data into the volume. For cone-beam geometry, multiply weights w{ij} by a depth correction factor: w{ij}(d) = w{ij} \frac{a^2}{d^2} where a is a constant and d is the depth. 3. Volume Alignment: Generate a matrix of samples exactly aligned with the arbitrary image plane, generalizing the CT framework to support arbitrary orientations. 4. Ray Casting: Run the entire ray advancement in a single fragment shader loop. 5. Acceleration: Apply occlusion culling and empty space skipping to limit reconstruction effort to only visible and non-occluded samples. Parameters: Filter type: Shepp-Logan, RamLak. Target framerate: 2 frames/s and more for realistic dataset sizes. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Arbitrary orientation requires precise alignment of the sample matrix with the image plane. Depth correction factor must be correctly applied for cone-beam geometry. Performance: Enables framerates of 2 frames/s and more for realistic dataset sizes. Strengths: Interactive or near-interactive speed; supports arbitrary volume orientations; efficient via occlusion culling and empty space skipping. Limitations: Original D2VR method was comparatively slow; this implementation addresses that but performance depends on dataset size and acceleration effectiveness. The method builds on the RapidCT framework for GPU-accelerated CT reconstruction. It was proposed to address the slow rendering speed of the original D2VR method, which was a shortcoming for clinical deployment. The work is part of the Volume Graphics 2006 conference proceedings. name: GPU D2VR Acceleration Methods
body: This family encompasses techniques designed to optimize the Direct Volume Ray Casting (D2VR) pipeline on Graphics Processing Units (GPUs) by leveraging hardware-specific features such as early Z-culling. The primary problem it solves is the computational bottleneck inherent in fragment-based volume rendering, where the high cost of shading often negates the benefits of hardware occlusion culling. What sets this family apart is its focus on the ratio between computational effort per fragment and the potential for early termination; methods are evaluated based on how effectively their shading complexity interacts with early Z-cull mechanisms to achieve interactive or near-interactive rendering speeds. The core principle shared by all methods in this family is the exploitation of the GPU's early Z-cull mechanism. Early Z-culling discards fragments that are occluded by previously rendered fragments closer to the camera, thereby saving shading computations. However, the effectiveness of this optimization is contingent upon the computational effort required per fragment. If the shading logic is too lightweight, the overhead of the cull check and fragment processing may offset the savings gained from skipping shading for occluded fragments. Therefore, acceleration strategies are most beneficial when the fragment shader performs significant computation, such as gradient estimation or complex transfer functions, which increases the "computational effort ratio". The spreading method distributes volume data across multiple fragments or uses a rendering approach that results in a longer, more computationally intensive fragment shader. It is chosen when high shading complexity (e.g., density and gradient calculations) is required, as it benefits significantly from early Z-culling due to the high cost of shading each fragment. Compared to projective texture mapping, it achieves better speed-ups in scenarios where occlusion is frequent because the savings from skipping expensive shading outweigh the culling overhead. The projective texture method maps volume data onto geometric primitives using texture mapping, imposing relatively light rendering efforts on individual fragments. It is chosen for simpler shading requirements or when hardware texture sampling is highly optimized. It benefits less from early Z-culling compared to the spreading method because the low computational effort per fragment means the advantage gained from skipping shading is minimal, potentially being offset by the fixed costs of fragment processing. The analysis of these acceleration methods originates from research on GPU-accelerated D2VR frameworks, specifically detailed in the paper "GPU-Accelerated D2VR". The study was conducted on an AMD Athlon 2.2GHz dual-core PC with 1GB RAM and a GeForce 6800 GT, using CT datasets with viewport sizes of 128x128 or 256x256. The work highlights the trade-off between shading complexity and hardware culling efficiency, noting a speedup factor of 1.5 for density-only D2VR over density+gradient D2VR, indicating that additional shading costs reduce the effectiveness of acceleration. name: Analysis and Diagnostics
body: Analysis and Diagnostics methods evaluate the quality, stability, and information content of tomographic reconstructions without necessarily updating the volume parameters. They solve the problem of verifying reconstruction success and diagnosing artifacts by analyzing the relationship between the measured sinogram and the reconstructed volume. Unlike iterative solvers that minimize a loss function to find the best volume estimate, these methods provide diagnostic metrics (such as SNR or error volumes) or algebraic characterizations (such as null space analysis) to assess the reliability of the reconstruction process. All methods in this family rely on the differentiability of the forward projection operator \mathcal{P} and its adjoint (back-projection) \mathcal{P}^T. The core optimization problem is generally formulated as minimizing a loss function \mathcal{L} between the measured sinogram p and the rendered projection \hat{p} = \mathcal{P}(x) of the current volume estimate x: \minx \mathcal{L}(\mathcal{P}(x), p) + \lambda R(x) where R(x) is a regularizer (e.g., Total Variation, neural prior) and \lambda is a weighting factor. The gradient of the loss with respect to the volume x is computed via the chain rule: \frac{\partial \mathcal{L}}{\partial x} = \mathcal{P}^T \left( \frac{\partial \mathcal{L}}{\partial \hat{p}} \right) The term \frac{\partial \mathcal{L}}{\partial \hat{p}} is the residual gradient in projection space (e.g., p - \hat{p} for MSE), and \mathcal{P}^T is the back-projection operator. Key shared components include: 1. Forward Projection: Ray marching through the volume representation (voxels, octrees, or neural fields) to compute line integrals of density/absorption coefficients. 2. Backward Projection (Adjoint): Distributing the error from the 2D detector plane back into the 3D volume. This is mathematically the transpose of the forward operator, ensuring stable convergence in iterative methods. 3. Optimization Loop: An iterative process (e.g., SGD, Adam) that updates the volume parameters (voxel values, neural network weights, or Gaussian parameters) to reduce the projection error. Explicit Radon Transform Analysis constructs and analyzes the explicit forward projection matrix A for a given scanning geometry to diagnose the ill-posedness of tomographic reconstruction. It identifies the singular values and the null space of the operator, revealing volumetric perturbations that are invisible to the measurements. Unlike iterative solvers that approximate the inverse, this method provides a direct algebraic characterization of the information loss in sparse or limited-angle scenarios. This method selects the optimal set of projection angles \thetai for tomographic reconstruction by minimizing the posterior entropy of the inferred 3D volume given the projections, H(\mathcal{D}|\mathcal{X}). It operates on the principle that maximizing the joint entropy of the projections H(\mathcal{X}) reduces the uncertainty of the underlying data, which is achieved by minimizing the sum of pairwise mutual information (MI) terms between all projection pairs. Unlike sibling methods that focus on reconstruction speed or specific geometric approximations, this approach is information-theoretic, deriving angle configurations that maximize data diversity based on statistical assumptions about the volume and noise. It is distinct from Compressive Volume Rendering Recovery Methods by explicitly modeling the correlation structure between projections via Gaussian priors, and from FastFDK by optimizing the acquisition geometry rather than the reconstruction kernel. Signal-to-Noise Ratio (SNR) for Tomography is a metric used to evaluate the robustness of a tomographic reconstruction method against acquisition noise. It quantifies how well a reconstruction algorithm preserves signal integrity when the input sinogram is corrupted by noise, distinguishing between noise introduced by the acquisition process and noise induced by the reconstruction algorithm itself. Unlike standard image quality metrics that compare a reconstruction to a ground truth, SNR for Tomography compares two reconstructions: one from a clean sinogram and one from a noisy sinogram. This sets it apart from metrics like SSIM or MSE which measure fidelity to an ideal target, as SNR specifically isolates the method's sensitivity to input perturbations. Error Volume Analysis is a diagnostic technique for tomographic reconstruction that visualizes the residual error between the measured projection data (tilt-series) and the synthetic projections generated from the current volume estimate. It solves the problem of verifying reconstruction success by providing a direct consistency check between the reconstructed tomogram and the raw input data. Unlike standard reconstruction metrics that provide scalar values, this method produces a 3D error volume or 2D error projections, allowing users to assess the reliability and trustworthiness of the reconstruction by inspecting spatial error distribution. It is distinct from sibling methods like Back-projection or Iterative Solvers because it does not update the volume parameters but rather analyzes the output of the reconstruction process to detect artifacts, misalignments, or insufficient regularization. The family of Analysis and Diagnostics methods in tomographic reconstruction emerged from the need to quantify the reliability of inverse solutions, particularly in limited-angle or sparse-view scenarios where standard reconstruction algorithms may produce ambiguous or artifact-ridden results. Early work focused on algebraic approaches, such as the analysis of the Radon transform's null space, to understand the fundamental limits of information recovery. As computational power increased, information-theoretic approaches, such as mutual information minimization for angle selection, were developed to optimize acquisition protocols. More recently, with the rise of differentiable rendering and inverse rendering, diagnostic tools like Error Volume Analysis have become integral to verifying the consistency of learned volumetric representations against raw sensor data. These methods are widely used in electron tomography, medical CT, and computational imaging to validate reconstruction pipelines and guide experimental design. name: Explicit Radon Transform Analysis
head: Radon Matrix Analysis, Sparse-View Radon Transform Null Space Analysis
body: Explicit Radon Transform Analysis constructs and analyzes the explicit forward projection matrix A (or operator RV) for a given scanning geometry to diagnose the invertibility and stability of tomographic reconstruction. Unlike black-box differentiable rendering which relies on gradient descent, this method explicitly exposes the linear algebra structure of the forward operator, allowing for the computation of singular values and the identification of the null space. It is distinct from Optimal Projection Angle Selection via Mutual Information Minimization because it analyzes the operator's spectral properties directly rather than optimizing information metrics, and from Signal-to-Noise Ratio (SNR) for Tomography by focusing on structural ambiguity (null space) rather than noise propagation. Inputs: Scanning geometry parameters: number of angles n{angles}, maximum angle range \theta{max}, number of samples per ray n{samples}, and detector dimensions v{large}, h{large}. Volume dimensions: v{small}, h{small} (or 3D extent w). Optional: sparsesvd flag to determine if full or sparse SVD is computed. Outputs: The explicit Radon transform matrix A (size M \times N, where M is total detector pixels and N is total volume voxels). Singular values W of the matrix A. Visualization of the sparsity pattern of A. Data Structures: Matrix A: A sparse matrix where A{ij} represents the contribution of voxel j to detector pixel i. The layout corresponds to the discretized line integrals. Singular Values W: A vector of length \min(M, N) representing the decay of the operator's energy. Steps: 1. Geometry Setup: Define the volume geometry (volgeom) and projection geometry (projgeom) based on input parameters n{angles}, \theta{max}, n{samples}, v{large}, h{large}. 2. Matrix Construction: Call the explicit Radon transform function explicitradon (or equivalent constructor) with the geometry parameters and sparsesvd=False to generate the matrix A and its singular values W. Note: In practice, this may involve creating a sinogram using a library like ASTRA Toolbox (createsinogram) and extracting the underlying projector matrix. 3. Spectral Analysis: Compute the Singular Value Decomposition (SVD) of A to obtain W. Analyze the decay of W to determine the effective rank and condition number of the system. 4. Null Space Identification: Identify the null space \mathcal{N}(RV) defined as: \mathcal{N}(RV) = \{ \delta V \mid RV(\delta V) = 0 \} where RV is the sparse-view Radon operator. Vectors in this null space represent volumetric perturbations invisible to the projections. 5. Visualization: Use imshow to visualize the matrix A to observe the sparsity pattern corresponding to the scanning geometry (e.g., sparse vs. limited angles). Formulas: The sparse-view Radon transform is defined as the concatenation of Radon operators along K projection directions V = \{v1, \dots, vK\}: RV(V) = (R{v1}(V), \dots, R{vK}(V)) \in \mathbb{R}^{K \times h \times w} where V is the attenuation field, Rv is the line-integral operator along direction v, and K is the number of views. For dense views (K \to \infty), R is injective. For sparse views (finite K, e.g., K \in \{10, 20, 25\}), RV is strongly underdetermined, and \mathcal{N}(RV) is non-trivial. Parameters: nangles: Number of projection angles. Typical values: 10, 20, 25, 45. maxangle: Maximum angular range. Typical values: \pi (sparse, full rotation) or limited ranges (limited angle). nsamples: Number of samples per ray. vsmall, hsmall: Volume dimensions. vlarge, hlarge: Detector dimensions. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Memory: Explicitly storing A requires O(M \times N) memory, which is prohibitive for high-resolution 3D volumes. Sparse matrix formats are required. Ill-posedness: In sparse-view or limited-angle scenarios, the singular value decay is slow, indicating high ill-posedness. Regularization is necessary for reconstruction. Numerical Precision: Small singular values may be dominated by noise, requiring truncation in SVD. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import numpy as np import matplotlib.pyplot as plt def explicitradonanalysis(nangles, maxangle, nsamples, vsmall, hsmall, vlarge, hlarge, sparsesvd=False): """ Constructs the explicit Radon matrix and analyzes its properties. """ # 1. Setup Geometry # volgeom defines the 3D volume grid volgeom = { 'voxelsize': (1.0, 1.0, 1.0), 'volumesize': (vsmall, hsmall, 1), # Assuming 2D slice for simplicity or 3D 'origin': (0, 0, 0) } # projgeom defines the detector and ray configuration projgeom = { 'detectorsize': (hlarge, vlarge), 'numpixels': (hlarge, vlarge), 'numangles': nangles, 'anglerange': maxangle, 'rayspacing': 1.0 } # 2. Construct Projector Matrix A # This step creates the explicit linear operator mapping volume to sinogram # In practice, this might use astra.projector.create or similar projectorid = createprojector('cuda', projgeom, volgeom) # Library-specific call to build matrix # Initialize a dummy volume to determine matrix dimensions if needed dummyvol = np.zeros((vsmall, hsmall, 1)) # Create the explicit matrix A # A is of shape (numdetectorpixels, numvoxels) A = projectorid.getmatrix(dummyvol) # 3. Compute Singular Values if sparsesvd: # Use sparse SVD for large matrices U, S, Vt = sparse.linalg.svds(A, k=min(100, np.min(A.shape))) W = S else: # Full SVD (only feasible for small matrices) U, S, Vt = np.linalg.svd(A, fullmatrices=False) W = S # 4. Visualize Sparsity Pattern plt.figure() plt.imshow(A.toarray() if hasattr(A, 'toarray') else A, cmap='hot') plt.title(f"Radon Matrix Sparsity (n={nangles}, maxangle={maxangle})") plt.xlabel("Voxel Index") plt.ylabel("Detector Pixel Index") plt.show() # 5. Analyze Null Space # The null space is spanned by the right singular vectors corresponding to zero (or near-zero) singular values nullspacethreshold = 1e-6 nullspacevectors = Vt[W < nullspacethreshold,:] return A, W, nullspacevectors Analyzes the operator when K is small (e.g., 10-25 views) but the angular range is full (\pi). Characterized by a non-trivial null space due to insufficient angular sampling. Analyzes the operator when the angular range is restricted (e.g., \theta{max} < \pi). Characterized by directional artifacts and a null space that depends on the missing angular sector. Sparse-view (fixed \theta{max}=\pi, varying K) vs. Limited-angle (fixed K, varying \theta{max}) exhibit different singular value decay patterns and null space structures. Time Complexity: Constructing the explicit matrix A is O(M \times N) where M is detector pixels and N is voxels. SVD is O(\min(M^2 N, M N^2)) for full SVD, making it infeasible for large volumes. Sparse SVD reduces this but still requires significant memory. Memory Complexity: O(M \times N) for the explicit matrix. This is the primary limitation, restricting the method to low-resolution volumes or 2D slices. Strengths: Provides exact diagnostic information about the forward operator's invertibility and null space. Useful for designing regularizers that penalize null-space components. Limitations: Not scalable to high-resolution 3D volumes due to memory constraints. Does not provide a reconstruction itself, only analysis. Originating from the mathematical analysis of the Radon transform in computed tomography, this method was applied to 3D Gaussian tomography to diagnose optimization drift and null-space ambiguities in sparse-view settings. The explicit matrix construction and SVD analysis are implemented in inverse problems toolboxes like the ASTRA Toolbox. It is used to understand why sparse-view reconstructions fail and how to constrain the solution space.
