name: Optimal Projection Angle Selection via Mutual Information Minimization
head: Information theoretic projection angle selection, Information-Theoretic Angle Selection, Information-theoretic tomography angle selection, MI-based angle optimization, Mutual Information Optimization, Optimal Projection Angles
body: This method selects the optimal set of projection angles \thetai for tomographic reconstruction by minimizing the posterior entropy of the inferred 3D volume H(\mathcal{D}|\mathcal{X}). It operates on the principle that maximizing the joint entropy of the observed projections H(\mathcal{X}) reduces the uncertainty about the underlying data, assuming the noise entropy H(\mathcal{X}|\mathcal{D}) is independent of angle choice. Unlike Explicit Radon Transform Analysis which relies on geometric completeness, or Signal-to-Noise Ratio (SNR) for Tomography which focuses on measurement fidelity, this approach uses information theory to quantify redundancy between views. It sets itself apart by approximating higher-order statistical dependencies as pairwise mutual information (MI), allowing for efficient numerical optimization of angle configurations. Inputs: N: The number of desired projection angles. \Sigma: The covariance matrix of the 3D data distribution (often assumed axisymmetric Gaussian \sigma^2 I for analytical simplification). \sigma0: The standard deviation of additive i.i.d. Gaussian noise in the projections. Geometry type: Parallel beam or Cone beam (determines periodicity and Fourier coefficients). Cone angle \phi (for cone beam): Defined by source-to-origin distance L and data spread \sigma, where \tan(\phi/2) = \sigma/L. Outputs: A set of optimal angles \Theta = \{\theta1, \dots, \thetaN\} that minimizes the sum of pairwise mutual information terms. Fourier Coefficients Table (A): A lookup table mapping cone angles \phi to Fourier coefficients ak for k=0,\dots,6. Structure: Array of shape (M, 7), where M is the number of discrete cone angles (e.g., 4 for \phi \in \{10^\circ, 15^\circ, 20^\circ, 25^\circ\}). Fields: a0, a1, a2, a3, a4, a5, a6. Default values (for \varepsilon = 0.1): \phi=10^\circ: [0.66, -0.02, -0.46, -0.01, -0.13, 0.0, -0.01] \phi=15^\circ: [0.67, -0.05, -0.43, -0.03, -0.12, -0.01, -0.01] \phi=20^\circ: [0.69, -0.10, -0.39, -0.05, -0.10, -0.01, -0.02] \phi=25^\circ: [0.73, -0.16, -0.29, -0.07, -0.08, -0.02, -0.02]. 1. Define Pairwise Mutual Information Function: Calculate the mutual information I(\alpha{ij}) between two projections separated by angular distance \alpha{ij} = |\thetaj - \thetai|. Analytical Form (Axisymmetric Gaussian): For an axisymmetric Gaussian prior with noise ratio \varepsilon = \sigma0^2/\sigma^2: I(\alpha{ij}) = -\frac{1}{2} \ln \left( 1 - \frac{\cos^2 \alpha{ij}}{(1 + \varepsilon)^2} \right) where \alpha{ij} is in radians. General Form (Non-axisymmetric): If \Sigma is not axisymmetric, use: I(\alpha{ij}|\Sigma) = -\frac{1}{2} \ln \left( 1 - \frac{(\mathbf{b}i^T \Sigma \mathbf{b}j)^2}{(\sigma0^2 + \mathbf{b}i^T \Sigma \mathbf{b}i)(\sigma0^2 + \mathbf{b}j^T \Sigma \mathbf{b}j)} \right) where \mathbf{b}i = [1, 0]^T and \mathbf{b}j = [\cos \alpha{ij}, \sin \alpha{ij}]^T are direction vectors. Surrogate Form (Cone Beam Approximation): For cone beam geometries, the MI function is approximated using a Fourier series surrogate to capture decorrelation at \pi: I(\alpha) = -\frac{1}{2} \log \left( \sum{k=0}^{6} ak \cos(k\alpha) \right) where coefficients ak are retrieved from the Fourier Coefficients Table based on the cone angle \phi. 2. Formulate Optimization Objective: The goal is to maximize the joint entropy H(\mathcal{X}). Using the pairwise approximation: H(\mathcal{X}) \approx \sum{i=1}^N H(\mathcal{X}i) - \sum{1 \le i < j \le N} I(\mathcal{X}i; \mathcal{X}j) Since marginal entropies H(\mathcal{X}i) are constant with respect to angle selection, minimizing the total pairwise MI minimizes the posterior entropy: \min{\Theta} \sum{1 \le i < j \le N} I(\thetaj - \thetai). 3. Numerical Optimization: Optimize the angles \thetai \in [0, 2\pi) to minimize the surrogate MI sum. Odd N: The optimal angles are uniformly distributed: \thetai = \frac{2\pi i}{N}, \quad i=0,\dots,N-1. Even N (Parallel Beam): Angles divide the half-circle: \thetai = \frac{\pi i}{N}, \quad i=0,\dots,N-1 Note: Due to symmetry I(\pi)=I(0), angles \theta and \theta+\pi are redundant. Even N (Cone Beam): To increase angular separation and reduce MI, reflect some angles into the opposite half-circle. This requires numerical optimization using the surrogate Fourier form, as the simple uniform distribution is suboptimal when I(\pi) < I(0). 4. Monte Carlo Verification (Optional): To validate the MI model for specific cone angles: 1. Sample N{mc}=100,000 points (x,y) from \mathcal{N}(0, I). 2. Apply cone beam projection transform: \tilde{r} = \left\| x + (x-s) \frac{L-x \cdot n}{(x-s) \cdot n} - Ln \right\| where s = [L\sin\theta, -L\cos\theta] and n = [-\sin\theta, \cos\theta]. 3. Add Gaussian noise \sigma0=0.1 to obtain r1, r2. 4. Compute correlation \rho and MI: I(\alpha) = -0.5 \log(1 - \rho). Unverified code. """ epsilon = (sigma0 / sigmadata) 2 term = (np.cos(alpha) 2) / ((1 + epsilon) 2) # Clamp term to < 1 to avoid log(0) or complex numbers due to precision term = np.minimum(term, 1.0 - 1e-10) return -0.5 np.log(1 - term) def calculatepairwisemiconesurrogate(alpha, coeffs): """ Calculates surrogate MI for cone beam using Fourier coefficients. alpha: angular separation in radians. coeffs: list of 7 coefficients [a0,..., a6]. """ sumcos = 0.0 for k, a in enumerate(coeffs): sumcos += a np.cos(k alpha) # Clamp to avoid log of negative number sumcos = np.maximum(sumcos, 1e-10) return -0.5 np.log(sumcos) def optimizeanglesparallel(N): """ Returns optimal angles for parallel beam. """ if N % 2 != 0: # Odd N: Uniform distribution over 2pi return np.linspace(0, 2 np.pi, N, endpoint=False) else: # Even N: Uniform distribution over pi (half-circle) return np.linspace(0, np.pi, N, endpoint=False) def optimizeanglescone(N, coneangledeg, coeffs): """ Returns optimal angles for cone beam. For even N, this requires numerical optimization. Here we provide the analytical odd case and a placeholder for even case optimization. """ if N % 2 != 0: return np.linspace(0, 2 np.pi, N, endpoint=False) else: # For even N, simple uniform over pi is suboptimal. # The source states: "higher angular separation can be achieved by reflecting some angles" # This requires a numerical solver (e.g., scipy.optimize.minimize) # minimizing sum{i<j} calculatepairwisemiconesurrogate(thetaj - thetai, coeffs). # Implementation details for the solver are not provided in the source. raise NotImplementedError("Numerical optimization required for even N cone beam.") def verifymicone(theta1, theta2, L, sigmadata, sigma0): """ Monte Carlo verification of MI for cone beam. """ Nmc = 100000 # 1. Sample points points = np.random.normal(0, 1, (Nmc, 2)) # 2. Define geometry for theta1 and theta2 # Source uses theta1=0 for reference, but general case requires rotation # Simplified for alpha = theta2 - theta1 # Note: Full implementation of Eq. 8 for arbitrary theta requires rotating points # or rotating source/plane vectors. The source sets theta1=0. # We assume alpha is the relative angle. # 3. Project (Simplified axisymmetric case logic from source text) # The source derives I(alpha) via correlation rho. # We use the surrogate formula for the final result as it is the optimization target. pass Noise Level (\varepsilon): The Fourier coefficients in Table 3 are tabulated for \varepsilon = 0.1. If noise levels differ significantly, the coefficients may need re-tabulation or scaling. Parallel Beam Symmetry: For parallel beams, I(\pi) = I(0). This forces all odd Fourier coefficients ak (k=1,3,\dots) to be zero. The MI function has period \pi. Cone Beam Decorrelation: For cone beams, I(\pi) < I(0). This necessitates non-zero odd coefficients to model the reduction in MI at \pi. Periodicity: The angular distance \alpha{ij} is symmetric (\alpha{ij} = \alpha{ji}) and periodic with 2\pi (or \pi for parallel). Precomputation: Calculating Fourier coefficients via Monte Carlo (N=100,000 samples) is computationally expensive but done once per cone angle configuration. Optimization: For odd N, complexity is O(1) (direct formula). For even N with cone beams, it requires numerical optimization, complexity depends on the solver but scales with N^2 for the MI sum evaluation. Memory: Minimal. Requires storing N angles and a small 7 \times M coefficient table. The method identifies 0^\circ and 90^\circ as optimal for N=2 parallel projections, consistent with minimizing MI. For cone beams, the method demonstrates that reflecting angles into the opposite half-circle for even N yields better angular separation than simple half-circle uniform distribution. Strengths: Provides a principled, information-theoretic basis for angle selection. Handles both parallel and cone beam geometries. Simple analytical solutions for odd N. Limitations: Relies on the assumption that higher-order mutual information can be approximated by pairwise terms. Assumes Gaussian priors for the analytical form. The surrogate Fourier approximation may lose accuracy for extreme cone angles or noise levels not covered in the table. This method originates from the work on "Neural rendering enables dynamic tomography". It applies information theory to the problem of selecting projection angles in tomographic reconstruction, specifically within the context of neural rendering and differentiable rendering. The approach builds on the postulate that minimizing the posterior entropy H(\mathcal{D}|\mathcal{X}) is equivalent to maximizing the joint entropy of projections H(\mathcal{X}). It distinguishes itself from photographic NeRF angle selection (which separates views by 180^\circ) by recognizing that X-ray projections at \theta and \theta+\pi are not identical in cone beam geometry, leading to different optimal configurations. name: Signal-to-Noise Ratio (SNR) for Tomography
head: rapport signal sur bruit
body: Signal-to-Noise Ratio (SNR) for Tomography is a metric used to evaluate the robustness of a tomographic reconstruction method against acquisition noise. It quantifies how well a reconstruction algorithm preserves signal integrity when the input sinogram is corrupted by noise, distinguishing between noise introduced by the acquisition process and noise induced by the reconstruction algorithm itself. Unlike standard image quality metrics that compare a reconstruction to a ground truth, SNR for Tomography compares two reconstructions: one from a clean sinogram and one from a noisy sinogram. This sets it apart from metrics like SSIM or MSE which measure fidelity to an ideal target, as SNR specifically isolates the method's sensitivity to input perturbations. Inputs and Outputs: Input 1: A clean sinogram R\theta(\rho) (ideal, noise-free acquisition). Input 2: A noisy sinogram R\theta^{noise}(\rho) (acquired with additive noise). Input 3: The reconstruction algorithm \mathcal{R} (e.g., Back Projection, Fourier Reconstruction). Output: The SNR value in decibels (dB), representing the robustness of \mathcal{R}. Data Structures: Sinogram: A 2D array where rows correspond to projection angles \theta and columns to detector positions \rho. Reconstructed Image: A 2D or 3D array of pixel/voxel intensities. Noise Model: Acquisition noise is modeled as additive white Gaussian noise. To generate the noisy sinogram, random noise values are added to each value R\theta(\rho) of the clean sinogram. The noise amplitude is proportional to the signal intensity: R\theta^{noise}(\rho) = R\theta(\rho) + \epsilon where \epsilon is a random value uniformly distributed between -(A/2)R\theta(\rho) and +(A/2)R\theta(\rho). The parameter A represents the noise level percentage; a typical value cited is A = 10\%. Step-by-Step Method: 1. Generate Noisy Sinogram: Apply the noise model described above to the clean sinogram R\theta(\rho) using a specified noise level A (e.g., 10%). 2. Reconstruct Clean Image: Apply the reconstruction algorithm \mathcal{R} to the clean sinogram to obtain the ideal reconstruction J. 3. Reconstruct Noisy Image: Apply the same reconstruction algorithm \mathcal{R} to the noisy sinogram to obtain the noisy reconstruction JB. 4. Compute Mean Squared Error (MSE): Calculate the MSE between the ideal input image I{in} (which corresponds to J in the context of comparing robustness, or the ground truth if available, but the text defines SNR as comparing J and JB) and the noisy output image I{out} (which corresponds to JB). The formula is: mse(I{in}, I{out}) = \frac{\sum{p=1}^{N} (I{in}(p) - I{out}(p))^2}{N} where I{in} is the ideal image, I{out} is the noisy image, and N is the number of pixels. 5. Calculate SNR: Compute the SNR using the ratio of the mean intensity of the ideal image to the MSE, expressed in decibels: snr(I{in}, I{out}) = 10 \log{10} \left( \frac{\bar{I}{in}^2}{mse(I{in}, I{out})} \right) Note: The source text provides the formula as \log(\frac{\bar{I}{in}}{mse}) but explicitly states it is expressed in decibels and gives the context of power ratio. Standard SNR in dB is 10 \log{10}(\text{Power Ratio}). The text formula (2.23) is written as \log(\frac{\bar{I}{in}}{mse}) which is dimensionally inconsistent if not squared or if log base is not specified. However, looking at standard definitions and the context of "power average signal over noise", and the fact that MSE is variance-like, the standard definition is 10 \log{10}(\frac{\mu^2}{\sigma^2}). The text says "ratio between the average intensity... and the MSE". Let's stick to the text's explicit formula structure but correct for dB conversion if implied. The text says: "Il estime alors la puissance moyenne du signal par dessus le bruit... (formule 2.23)". Formula 2.23 is: snr(I{in}, I{out}) = \log(\frac{\bar{I}{in}}{mse(I{in}, I{out})}). This is likely a typo in the source for 10 \log{10}(\frac{\bar{I}{in}^2}{mse}) or similar. Given the values (6.33 dB), we assume the standard dB conversion. The source explicitly writes the log without base or coefficient in the equation block, but the text says "decibel". We will use the standard interpretation of the text's intent: 10 \log{10}(\frac{\bar{I}{in}^2}{mse}). Correction: The source text (2.23) literally says log ( Iinbar / mse). This is physically incorrect for dB. However, we must follow the source. If the source defines it this way, we cite it. But wait, if A=10\%, and SNR is 6.33 dB, let's check. If the formula is just \log{10}(\dots), it's not dB. If it's 10 \log{10}, it is. The text says "expressed in decibel on a logarithmic scale". We will assume the standard 10 \log{10} factor is implied by the unit "dB" despite the potentially simplified notation in the source equation. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import numpy as np def generatenoisysinogram(cleansinogram, noiselevelpercent=0.10): """ Adds uniform noise to the sinogram based on the method in. Noise is uniform between -(A/2)R and +(A/2)R. """ A = noiselevelpercent # Generate random noise uniform in [-A/2, A/2] noise = np.random.uniform(-A/2, A/2, size=cleansinogram.shape) # Scale noise by the signal value noisysinogram = cleansinogram + (noise cleansinogram) return noisysinogram def computemse(imagein, imageout): """ Computes Mean Squared Error between two images. """ N = imagein.size mse = np.sum((imagein - imageout) 2) / N return mse def computesnrtomography(reconstructionfunc, cleansinogram, noisysinogram): """ Computes SNR for Tomography as defined in. """ # Step 1 & 2: Reconstruct clean image J J = reconstructionfunc(cleansinogram) # Step 3: Reconstruct noisy image JB JB = reconstructionfunc(noisysinogram) # Step 4: Compute MSE between J (ideal) and JB (noisy) # Note: The source defines Iin as ideal and Iout as noisy output mseval = computemse(J, JB) # Step 5: Compute SNR in dB # Source formula 2.23: log(Iinbar / mse). # Text states it is in decibels. Standard dB is 10log10(Power). # Power is proportional to mean^2. # We implement the standard interpretation of the text's intent for dB. meanIin = np.mean(J) # Avoid division by zero if mseval == 0: return float('inf') # Using 10 log10 for decibels as per text description "expressed in decibel" # and standard SNR definition, assuming the source equation omitted the 10 and square for brevity or had a typo. snrdb = 10 np.log10((meanIin 2) / mseval) return snrdb Parameters: A: Noise level percentage. Typical value: 10\%. Edge Cases: Zero MSE: If the reconstruction is identical for clean and noisy inputs (perfect noise immunity), MSE is 0, leading to infinite SNR. Negative Intensities: If the reconstruction algorithm produces negative values, the mean intensity \bar{I}{in} might be small or zero, affecting the SNR calculation. The noise model assumes positive sinogram values for the multiplicative noise scaling. A metric evaluating how a denoiser strategy increases the contrast between a Region of Interest (ROI) and a uniform background. It is used to assess the effectiveness of denoising in cryo-electron tomography. CNR = \frac{lf - lu}{\frac{1}{\sqrt{N{pr}}} \sqrt{0.5(r^2f + r^2u)}} where N{pr} is the number of paired regions selected to compute the CNR, lf and r^2f refer to the mean and variance in the selected regions containing features, and lu and r^2u are the mean and variance in the selected uniform regions. Time Complexity: The SNR calculation itself is O(N) where N is the number of pixels in the reconstructed volume, as it involves computing MSE and mean values. The dominant cost is the reconstruction of the two volumes (clean and noisy), which depends on the specific reconstruction algorithm (e.g., Back Projection is O(N \cdot M) where M is the number of projections). Memory Complexity: Requires storing two reconstructed volumes (clean and noisy) and the two sinograms. O(N) for volumes. Measured Performance: In a comparison of robustness to 10% additive Gaussian noise on sinograms, Back Projection achieved an SNR of 6.33 dB, while Fourier Reconstruction achieved -0.44 dB. This indicates Back Projection is significantly more robust to acquisition noise than Fourier Reconstruction in this context. Strengths: Directly measures robustness to acquisition noise, independent of reconstruction-induced noise. Simple to compute once reconstructions are available. Limitations: Does not measure absolute image quality (fidelity to ground truth), only relative robustness. Sensitive to the choice of noise model and level. When to use: When comparing reconstruction algorithms for their stability against noisy input data. When not to use: When absolute accuracy or structural similarity to a ground truth is the primary concern (use SSIM, MSE, or PSNR instead). The metric is defined in the context of tomographic reconstruction quality and precision assessment. It originates from French-language research on tomographic algorithms and applications, specifically a thesis or report titled "Précision et qualité en reconstruction tomographique: algorithmes et applications". The method is used to compare the robustness of different reconstruction techniques, such as Back Projection and Fourier Reconstruction, against acquisition noise. name: Contrast-to-Noise Ratio (CNR)
body: Contrast-to-Noise Ratio (CNR) is a quantitative metric used to evaluate the quality of volume-rendered images by measuring the distinguishability of a feature of interest from its surrounding background relative to the noise level. It serves as a diagnostic tool for validating reconstruction algorithms, interpolation methods, and denoising strategies, particularly in scenarios where visual assessment is insufficient. Unlike Signal-to-Noise Ratio (SNR), which measures the robustness of a reconstruction to acquisition noise by comparing clean and noisy sinograms, CNR focuses on the perceptual contrast of specific structures within the final rendered volume [Parent]. The calculation of CNR requires defining Regions of Interest (ROIs) on the rendered volume and computing statistical moments of the intensity values within those regions. Two distinct formulations are documented in the literature, corresponding to different application domains (tomosynthesis vs. cryo-electron tomography). Inputs: 1. Rendered volume or image I. 2. Definition of ROIs: Feature ROI(s): Regions containing the structure of interest. Background ROI(s): Regions containing uniform background or homogeneous areas. 3. (Optional) Number of paired regions N{pr} if using the paired formulation. Outputs: A scalar value representing the Contrast-to-Noise Ratio. No complex data structures are required. The method operates on scalar intensity values extracted from the volume at specific voxel coordinates defined by the ROIs. Intensity Array: A 1D array or list of pixel/voxel values vi for each ROI. Statistics: Mean (\mu or l) and Standard Deviation (\sigma or r) of the intensity values in each ROI. Two primary formulas exist. The choice depends on the specific implementation context described in the sources. Formula 1: Standard Difference-of-Means (Tomosynthesis/General) Used in for evaluating interpolation and sampling in breast tomosynthesis. CNR = \frac{\mu{feat} - \mu{BG}}{\sigma{BG}} Where: \mu{feat}: Mean pixel value in the Region of Interest (ROI) over the feature (e.g., a 5.0 mm disk). \mu{BG}: Mean pixel value in the background ROI. \sigma{BG}: Mean of the standard deviations in the background ROIs. Note: If multiple background ROIs are used, \sigma{BG} is the average of their individual standard deviations. Formula 2: Paired Variance-Based (Cryo-ET/Denoising) Used in for evaluating denoising strategies in cryo-electron tomography. CNR = \frac{lf - lu}{\frac{1}{\sqrt{N{pr}}} \sqrt{0.5(r^2f + r^2u)}} Where: N{pr}: Number of paired regions selected to compute the CNR. lf: Mean intensity in the selected regions containing features. r^2f: Variance in the selected regions containing features. lu: Mean intensity in the selected uniform (background) regions. r^2u: Variance in the selected uniform regions. ROI Selection: Critical for reproducibility. In, ROIs are drawn over a specific phantom feature (5.0 mm disk) and surrounding background. In, regions are manually labeled on different slices of the reconstructed tomogram. Number of Paired Regions (N{pr}): In, this is a user-defined parameter for the number of samples taken to estimate the metric. The following implementation covers the standard formulation (Formula 1) which is more common in general volume rendering diagnostics, with a note on the paired variant. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def calculatecnrstandard(featurevalues, backgroundvalueslist): """ Calculates CNR using the standard difference-of-means formula. Args: featurevalues (list of float): Intensity values in the feature ROI. backgroundvalueslist (list of list of float): List of intensity arrays for each background ROI. Returns: float: The CNR value. """ # 1. Calculate mean of feature ROI if not featurevalues: return 0.0 mufeat = sum(featurevalues) / len(featurevalues) # 2. Calculate mean and standard deviations of background ROIs bgmeans = [] bgstds = [] for bgvals in backgroundvalueslist: if not bgvals: continue meanval = sum(bgvals) / len(bgvals) bgmeans.append(meanval) # Calculate standard deviation if len(bgvals) < 2: stdval = 0.0 else: variance = sum((x - meanval) 2 for x in bgvals) / (len(bgvals) - 1) stdval = math.sqrt(variance) bgstds.append(stdval) if not bgstds: return 0.0 # 3. Calculate mean background mean and mean background std dev muBG = sum(bgmeans) / len(bgmeans) sigmaBG = sum(bgstds) / len(bgstds) # 4. Compute CNR # Guard against division by zero if sigmaBG == 0: return 0.0 cnr = (mufeat - muBG) / sigmaBG return cnr def calculatecnrpaired(featuremeans, featurevariances, uniformmeans, uniformvariances, npr): """ Calculates CNR using the paired variance-based formula. Args: featuremeans (list of float): Mean intensities for feature regions. featurevariances (list of float): Variances for feature regions. uniformmeans (list of float): Mean intensities for uniform regions. uniformvariances (list of float): Variances for uniform regions. npr (int): Number of paired regions. Returns: float: The CNR value. """ if npr == 0: return 0.0 # Average the means and variances across the selected regions lf = sum(featuremeans) / len(featuremeans) r2f = sum(featurevariances) / len(featurevariances) lu = sum(uniformmeans) / len(uniformmeans) r2u = sum(uniformvariances) / len(uniformvariances) # Numerator numerator = lf - lu # Denominator # sqrt(0.5 (r2f + r2u)) / sqrt(Npr) # Note: Source formula: 1/sqrt(Npr) sqrt(0.5 (r2f + r2u)) denominator = (1.0 / math.sqrt(npr)) math.sqrt(0.5 (r2f + r2u)) if denominator == 0: return 0.0 cnr = numerator / denominator return cnr 1. Zero Noise/Uniform Background: If the background is perfectly uniform (\sigma{BG} = 0), the denominator in Formula 1 becomes zero. The implementation must handle this, typically by returning 0 or a maximum value depending on convention. 2. ROI Definition Bias: The metric is highly sensitive to ROI placement. In, the background ROIs must be drawn in the surrounding area, not overlapping the feature. In, manual labeling introduces subjectivity. 3. Anisotropic Resolution: In tomosynthesis, the z-direction has coarser resolution than xy. CNR calculations should account for this, as features may spread in z, affecting \mu{feat} and \sigma{BG}. 4. Paired Region Count: In Formula 2, N{pr} must be consistent across comparisons. A small N{pr} leads to high variance in the metric estimate. Time Complexity: O(N), where N is the total number of pixels/voxels in the defined ROIs. The calculation involves simple statistical aggregations (mean, variance). Memory Complexity: O(N) to store the intensity values of the ROIs, or O(1) if computed on-the-fly during rendering/analysis. Strengths: Provides an objective, numerical basis for comparing rendering configurations (e.g., interpolation methods, sampling distances). Effective for evaluating denoising performance by quantifying contrast preservation vs. noise reduction. Limitations: Does not account for human visual perception directly (unlike SSIM or VDP). Sensitive to ROI selection bias. In, it is noted that CNR alone is insufficient; it is often used alongside Smoothness and FWHM to provide a complete picture of image quality. When to use: When optimizing volume rendering parameters (sampling, interpolation) or evaluating denoising algorithms where quantitative comparison is needed. When not to use: When subjective visual quality is the primary concern, or when the background is not well-defined/uniform. CNR is a standard metric in medical imaging and scientific visualization. In the context of volume rendering diagnostics, it has been applied to: 1. Breast Tomosynthesis (DBT): Used to validate and compare interpolation methods (Linear, Cubic, Nearest-Neighbor, Sinc with various windows) and sampling distances. Studies showed that optimized parameters (e.g., Hamming window with BF(z)=2, sampling 0.025 mm) significantly improved CNR compared to default settings. 2. Cryo-Electron Tomography (cryo-ET): Used to evaluate adaptive differentiable grids and denoising strategies. It measures how well a denoiser increases contrast between features and background. The metric is often part of a suite of quantitative image analysis metrics, including Smoothness and FWHM, to objectively evaluate volume rendering quality. Optimization of Breast Tomosynthesis Visualization through 3D Volume Rendering, https://doi.org/10.3390/jimaging6070064, fetched 2026-10-26 Adaptive differentiable grids for cryo-electron tomography reconstruction and denoising, https://doi.org/10.1093/bioadv/vbad131, fetched 2026-10-27

name: Error Volume Analysis
head: Error Volume Visualization Enhancement, Error projection enhancement, Reconstruction Error Visualization
body: Error Volume Analysis is a diagnostic technique for tomographic reconstruction that visualizes the residual error between the measured projection data (tilt-series) and the synthetic projections generated from the current volume estimate. It solves the problem of verifying reconstruction success by providing a direct consistency check between the reconstructed tomogram and the raw input data. Unlike standard reconstruction metrics that provide scalar values, this method produces a 3D error volume or 2D error projections, allowing users to assess the reliability and trustworthiness of the reconstruction by inspecting spatial error distribution. It is distinct from sibling methods like Back-projection or Iterative Solvers because it does not update the volume parameters but rather analyzes the output of the reconstruction process to detect artifacts, misalignments, or insufficient regularization. The method operates by computing the discrepancy between the input tilt-series and the forward-projected volume, then reconstructing this discrepancy into a 3D error volume. Inputs: P{orig}: The original measured tilt-series (set of 2D projection images at various angles). V{est}: The estimated 3D volume (tomogram) obtained from a reconstruction algorithm (e.g., SART, SART+TV+NLM). \mathcal{P}: The forward projection operator (ray marching). Outputs: E{vol}: The reconstructed error volume. E{proj}: Enhanced error projection images (optional intermediate visualization). Data Structures: Tilt-Series: A list of 2D arrays (images) corresponding to projection angles. Volume: A 3D grid of voxel values (density/absorption coefficients). Error Volume: A 3D grid of the same dimensions as V{est}, initialized to zero. Steps: 1. Compute Synthetic Projections: For each angle \thetai in the tilt-series, compute the synthetic projection \hat{p}i by forward projecting the estimated volume V{est}: \hat{p}i = \mathcal{P}(V{est}, \thetai) 2. Calculate Re-projection Error Images: Compute the absolute difference between the original projection pi and the synthetic projection \hat{p}i for each angle: ei = | pi - \hat{p}i | The set \{ei\} forms the "error tilt-series". 3. Reconstruct Error Volume: Apply a tomographic reconstruction algorithm (specifically SART in the source implementation) to the error tilt-series \{ei\} to generate the initial error volume E{raw}: E{raw} = \text{Reconstruct}(\{ei\}) 4. Enhance Error Visualization (Post-processing): To make significant error contributions visible, apply the following steps to E{raw} (or to the individual error projections ei before reconstruction, as the source implies enhancing the projections to pronounce structural features): Gaussian Blur: Apply a 3 \times 3 Gaussian blur to smooth noise. E{blurred} = \text{GaussianBlur}(E{raw}, \sigma=1) Thresholding: Threshold intensity values below 1/8 of the maximum value in the volume/projection. E{thresh}[v] = \begin{cases} E{blurred}[v] & \text{if } E{blurred}[v] > \frac{1}{8} \max(E{blurred}) \\ 0 & \text{otherwise} \end{cases} Gamma Correction: Adjust the gamma value to 2.0 to shift mid-tones to brighter values, enhancing visibility of lower-magnitude errors. E{final}[v] = E{thresh}[v]^{\frac{1}{2.0}} 5. Interpretation: Successful Reconstruction: The error volume should be uniformly distributed and not correlated with the features of the reconstructed volume. Misalignment/Artifacts: Visible structures in the error volume (e.g., diagonal smudges corresponding to fiducials) indicate misalignment or reconstruction errors. Regularization Effect: In non-regularized reconstructions (e.g., SART only), the error volume may contain structures resembling the object (e.g., virus particles), indicating that the model has not fully captured the data. In regularized reconstructions (e.g., SART+TV+NLM), the error should present practically no structure correlated to the volume. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Limited Angle Artifacts: If the reconstructed volume has the same width as the projection images, rays at the borders intersect the volume for shorter distances at high tilt angles. Horizontal padding is required to ensure uniform ray path lengths. The padded volume width vw should be rounded up to the next even value (e.g., for width 1024, padded width is 2568). Noise Sensitivity: The raw error images can be very noisy. The Gaussian blur and thresholding steps are critical to suppress high-frequency noise and highlight structural errors. Regularization Masking: Heavy regularization may hide reconstruction errors by forcing the volume to be smooth, potentially masking misalignments. The error volume analysis helps verify if the regularization is appropriate. A method to evaluate reconstruction precision by computing the correlation between two volumes reconstructed from split projection sets, used because only one copy of the volume exists in tilt-series cryo-ET. It is chosen when a quantitative resolution estimate is needed, though it is less reliable for absolute resolution in tilt-series than in single-particle analysis. Definition: FSC measures the similarity between two independent reconstructions in Fourier space. Steps: 1. Split the even and odd projections of the tilt-series into two sets. 2. Reconstruct two independent volumes, V1 and V2, from these sets. 3. Compute the Fourier transforms F1 and F2 of V1 and V2. 4. Calculate the FSC for each radial shell ri in Fourier space. Formula: FSC(ri) = \frac{\sum ri F1(ri) F2(ri)}{\sqrt{\sum |F1(ri)|^2 \sum |F2(ri)|^2}} where ri is the voxel element in Fourier space at radius r, and F1(ri) and F2(ri) are the complex structure factors of the first and second volume, respectively. Parameters: Resolution Threshold: The reconstruction resolution is defined as the highest frequency where the FSC remains above a given threshold. The source uses FSC = 0.5 because FSC = 0.143 cannot distinguish resolution for some methods in tilt-series cryo-ET. Pitfalls: FSC values may be unreliable for absolute resolution estimation in tilt-series cryo-ET due to high residual noise. FSC may rank methods highly that produce consistent but wrong structures across the two reconstructions. Time Complexity: The method requires one additional forward projection pass for each angle in the tilt-series and one additional tomographic reconstruction pass (SART) on the error images. The complexity is dominated by the reconstruction step, typically O(N \cdot M \cdot K) where N is the number of voxels, M is the number of projections, and K is the number of SART iterations. Memory Complexity: Requires storing the original tilt-series, the estimated volume, and the error volume. The error volume has the same size as the estimated volume. Strengths: Provides intuitive visual feedback on reconstruction quality; detects misalignments and regularization issues; allows for direct comparison between different reconstruction strategies (e.g., with/without regularization). Limitations: Computationally expensive due to the additional reconstruction step; interpretation requires experience to distinguish between noise and structural errors; not a quantitative metric like FSC. When to use: During iterative reconstruction to monitor convergence and diagnose artifacts; for final validation of reconstruction quality. When not to use: When only a scalar quality metric is needed; when computational resources are extremely limited. Error Volume Analysis was introduced in the context of GPU-accelerated 3D tomographic reconstruction for cryogenic electron microscopy (cryo-ET). It addresses the need for a direct consistency check between the reconstruction and the raw input projection images, which is particularly important in noisy and limited-angle tomographic data. The method builds on the principle that a successful reconstruction should reproduce the input projections, and any significant deviation (error) should be uncorrelated with the object's structure if the reconstruction is accurate and regularized appropriately. name: Back-projection
head: Adjoint Backprojection, Adjoint Projection, Cone Beam Adjoint, FDK Backprojection (CPU/PyTorch Path), Radon backprojection (parallel)
body: Back-projection is the adjoint (transpose) of the forward projection operator \mathcal{P}, used to map 2D projection data (sinograms) or projection-space gradients back into a 3D volume representation. It solves the inverse problem of tomographic reconstruction by redistributing measured ray integrals along their corresponding geometric paths into the voxel grid. Unlike forward projection, which integrates density along rays to produce a 2D image, back-projection scatters 2D values into 3D space, effectively blurring the data if unfiltered. It is the core differentiable operator required for iterative optimization and gradient-based reconstruction, ensuring stable convergence when paired with forward projection. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A sinogram/projection tensor p of shape [B, P, H, W] (spatial) or [B, P, H, W/2+1] (Fourier-space), and geometric parameters defining the ray paths (source positions, detector orientations, or ray anchors/directions). Output: A 3D volume tensor x of shape [B, D, H{rec}, W{rec}] or [B, D, H{rec}, W{rec}/2+1] (Fourier-space). Data Structures: Ray Specification: Defined by ray anchors \mathbf{t} \in \mathbb{R}^D and directions \mathbf{n} \in \mathbb{R}^D. Volume Grid: Defined by origin \mathbf{x}0, spacing \mathbf{\Delta}, and dimensions \mathbf{Q} (knotspec). Interpolation State: For GPU implementations, pending voxel values and indices are stored in registers or local memory to minimize atomic contention. Numbered Steps: 1. Coordinate Transformation: For each projection pixel coordinate \mathbf{k}{proj} = (kr, kc), compute the corresponding 3D coordinate in the volume space. In Fourier-space methods, extend to 3D: \mathbf{k}{3D} = (kc, kr, 0). In spatial methods, compute the ray path from source to detector element. Apply inverse rotation/translation matrices to map detector coordinates to volume coordinates: \mathbf{k}{rec} = \mathbf{R}^{-1} \mathbf{k}{3D}. 2. Interpolation Kernel Selection: Determine the interpolation order order \in \{0, 1, 2\}. order=0: Voxel-based (nearest neighbor). order=1: Trilinear (3D) or bilinear (2D). order=2: Higher-order box splines or tricubic (Catmull-Rom). 3. Scatter Accumulation: Distribute the projection value p into the volume. Spatial Domain: For each ray, iterate through voxels intersected by the ray. For each voxel, compute the interpolation weights based on the fractional distance of the ray within the voxel. Accumulate the weighted projection value into the voxel using atomic addition. Formula: x{\mathbf{q}} \leftarrow x{\mathbf{q}} + w \cdot p. Fourier Domain: Accumulate the projection value into the 3D Fourier volume at the transformed coordinate \mathbf{k}{rec} using 3D interpolation kernels in transpose mode. For trilinear, distribute to the 2 \times 2 \times 2 neighborhood. For tricubic, distribute to the 4 \times 4 \times 4 neighborhood. 4. Gradient Computation (Differentiable Back-projection): To compute \frac{\partial \mathcal{L}}{\partial x}, pass the residual gradient \frac{\partial \mathcal{L}}{\partial \hat{p}} through the back-projection operator. To compute gradients w.r.t. geometry (source/detector positions), apply the chain rule through the interpolation derivatives, scattering gradients back to the camera parameters. Shift gradients are computed using phase modulation derivatives: \frac{\partial P}{\partial \mathbf{s}} = -i2\pi\mathbf{k}{proj}P(\mathbf{k}{proj}). Pseudocode (Spatial Cone-Beam Adjoint): Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def rayboxintersect(rayo, rayd, box): # box: [minx, maxx, miny, maxy, minz, maxz] # Handle zero direction components to avoid division by zero invd = torch.where(rayd.abs() > 1e-8, 1.0 / rayd, torch.zeroslike(rayd)) t1 = (box[0] - rayo[0]) invd[0] t2 = (box[1] - rayo[0]) invd[0] t3 = (box[2] - rayo[1]) invd[1] t4 = (box[3] - rayo[1]) invd[1] t5 = (box[4] - rayo[2]) invd[2] t6 = (box[5] - rayo[2]) invd[2] tmin = torch.maximum(torch.minimum(t1, t2), torch.maximum(torch.minimum(t3, t4), torch.minimum(t5, t6))) tmax = torch.minimum(torch.maximum(t1, t2), torch.minimum(torch.maximum(t3, t4), torch.maximum(t5, t6))) tmin = torch.clamp(tmin, min=0.0) return tmin, tmax def coneadjoint(projections, sources, detectors, box, nsamples, volumeshape, voxelsize): """ Computes the adjoint of the cone-beam forward projection. Args: projections: Tensor [B, 1, views, rows, cols] sources: Tensor [views, 3] detectors: Tensor [views, rows, cols, 3] box: Tensor [6] (minx, maxx, miny, maxy, minz, maxz) nsamples: int volumeshape: tuple (Z, Y, X) voxelsize: float or Tensor [3] Returns: volume: Tensor [B, 1, Z, Y, X] """ batch,, views, rows, cols = projections.shape volume = torch.zeros(batch, 1, volumeshape, device=projections.device) z, y, x = volumeshape for view in range(views): src = sources[view] detplane = detectors[view] projview = projections[:, 0, view] raysd = detplane - src rayso = src.expandas(raysd) raysdnorm = raysd / (raysd.norm(dim=-1, keepdim=True) + 1e-8) tmin, tmax = rayboxintersect(rayso, raysdnorm, box) valid = tmax > tmin # Step along rays tvals = torch.linspace(0, 1, nsamples, device=projections.device) tsampled = tmin.unsqueeze(-1) + tvals.unsqueeze(0) (tmax - tmin).unsqueeze(-1) points = rayso.unsqueeze(1) + tsampled.unsqueeze(-1) raysdnorm.unsqueeze(1) # Convert to voxel coordinates voxelcoords = points / voxelsize ix, iy, iz = voxelcoords[..., 0], voxelcoords[..., 1], voxelcoords[..., 2] # Clamp to volume bounds for interpolation ix = torch.clamp(ix, 0, x - 1) iy = torch.clamp(iy, 0, y - 1) iz = torch.clamp(iz, 0, z - 1) # Trilinear weights dx = ix - ix.floor() dy = iy - iy.floor() dz = iz - iz.floor() w000 = (1-dx)(1-dy)(1-dz) w100 = dx(1-dy)(1-dz) w010 = (1-dx)dy(1-dz) w110 = dxdy(1-dz) w001 = (1-dx)(1-dy)dz w101 = dx(1-dy)dz w011 = (1-dx)dydz w111 = dxdydz # Scatter weighted values to 8 neighboring voxels #... (Implementation detail omitted for brevity; see GPU kernels) pass return volume Parameters: detcount: Number of detector pixels. For exact reconstruction of pixels outside the inscribed circle in a 512x512 image, detcount = ceil(sqrt(2) 512). angles: Array of sampling angles. For parallel beam, equally spaced in 0, \pi). order: Interpolation order (0, 1, 2). nsamples: Number of samples per ray. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Atomic Contention: Using atomicAdd for scatter accumulation is a major bottleneck on GPUs. Keeping pending voxels in registers minimizes atomics. Unfiltered Blurring: Unfiltered back-projection creates a blurred image due to low-frequency noise accumulation. Boundary Conditions: Volumes often require a 1-voxel zero-padding border to handle interpolation at edges without bounds checks. Precision: Relative error compared to reference implementations (e.g., Astra Toolbox) is 8.07 \times 10^{-4} for forward projection and 4.12 \times 10^{-5} for back-projection. Generates 2D projections from a 3D [volume by sampling central slices in Fourier space, implementing the Central Slice Theorem. It is the mathematical adjoint to back-projection. Maps projection weights to volume expansion coefficients using a single kernel launch per angle with a 1D NDRange, avoiding complex local memory tiling. Performs filtered backprojection using OpenCL global memory buffers, explicitly including the ramp filtering step in the GPU path. Accelerates backprojection by leveraging OpenCL image objects for hardware-accelerated bilinear interpolation of pre-filtered data. Computes 2D/3D back-projections exclusively in the Fourier domain using RFFT format, achieving 1–2 orders of magnitude speedup over spatial-domain libraries. Computes gradients of the projection error with respect to camera parameters by scattering gradients back to the source/detector positions. Materializes the full forward projection matrix for parallel-beam CT, enabling direct algebraic solutions and explicit adjoint verification. Time Complexity: O(Nv \cdot Nr \cdot Ns), where Nv is the number of views, Nr is the number of rays per view, and Ns is the number of samples per ray. In Fourier space, complexity is dominated by FFTs: O(N^3 \log N). Memory Complexity: O(Nv \cdot Nr) for storing projection data and O(Nx \cdot Ny \cdot Nz) for the volume buffer. Explicit Radon Matrix Construction requires O(Nv \cdot Nr \cdot Nx \cdot Ny \cdot Nz), which is prohibitive for large volumes. Performance: TorchRadon is up to 125× faster than Astra Toolbox for parallel/fan-beam projections due to GPU batch operations. Fourier-space methods show 1–2 orders of magnitude improvement over torch-fourier-slice. Strengths: Differentiable, stable for iterative optimization, efficient on GPUs. Limitations: Unfiltered BP is blurry. FDK yields worse results than iterative methods (e.g., SART) with limited projections. Atomic contention in spatial back-projection can limit throughput. Back-projection is the inverse of the Radon transform, forming the basis of analytical tomographic reconstruction methods like Filtered Back-Projection (FBP). It was historically implemented on CPUs and later optimized for GPUs using CUDA and OpenCL. Recent developments focus on making back-projection fully differentiable for integration into deep learning pipelines, enabling end-to-end optimization of volume representations and camera parameters.
