name: GPU Backprojection with Global Memory Buffer
head: GPU Backprojection Kernel Mapping, backproject
body: This method performs cone-beam CT reconstruction by mapping projection weights to volume expansion coefficients using a GPU-accelerated kernel that iterates over projection angles. It solves the inverse problem of tomographic reconstruction by accumulating contributions from projection slices into a global memory volume buffer. It is distinguished from sibling methods by its use of a single kernel launch per projection angle with a 1D NDRange where each work-item corresponds to one voxel, avoiding complex local memory tiling or image texture sampling. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: A sequence of P projection images, each of size W \times H. Geometric parameters: Source-to-Object Distance (sod), Source-to-Detector Distance (sdd), voxel size (voxelSize), and pixel size (pixelSize). Volume dimensions NX \times NX \times NY. Outputs: A reconstructed 3D volume buffer of size NX \times NX \times NY of type float. Data Structures: Volume Buffer: A 1D array of size V = NX \times NX \times NY allocated in global memory (CLMEMREADWRITE) and initialized to zero. Projection Buffer: A 1D array of size W \times H allocated in global memory (CLMEMREADONLY | CLMEMCOPYHOSTPTR) for the current projection angle. Numbered Steps: 1. Initialize OpenCL context, command queue, and program from source file kernels/backprojectionbuffer.cl. 2. Allocate the volume buffer of size V \times \text{sizeof(float)} and fill with zeros. 3. Loop over each projection angle p from 0 to P-1: a. Calculate the rotation angle: \thetap = 2.0 \pi \frac{p}{P}. b. Create the projection buffer containing the p-th projection slice. c. Set kernel arguments: projBuffer, volumeBuffer, W, H, NX, NY, voxelSize, pixelSize, sdd, sod, angle. d. Launch the backprojection kernel with a global size equal to V (1D NDRange). e. Release the projection buffer. 4. After all projections, read the volume buffer back to the host. 5. Scale the reconstructed volume by \frac{\pi}{P}. Kernel Logic (Per Work-Item): Each work-item with global ID gid corresponds to a unique voxel in the volume. The voxel coordinates (x, y, z) are derived from gid. Each work-item independently computes the contribution from one projection angle to one voxel. No synchronization is needed because each Global ID (GID) owns its volume element. The exact geometric projection formula is not given in the sources. A standard implementation maps voxel indices to physical coordinates, rotates by -\thetap around the Y-axis, projects to detector coordinates (u, v) using similar triangles with sdd/sod, and samples the projection buffer. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def reconstructgpubuffer(projections, P, W, H, NX, NY, voxelsize, pixelsize, sdd, sod): # 1. Initialize OpenCL context, command queue, and program # (Implementation details omitted; assumed initialized) # 2. Allocate volume buffer of size NXNXNY, fill with 0 volumebuffer = [0.0] (NX NX NY) # 3. Loop over projections for p in range(P): angle = 2.0 math.pi p / P # 4. Create projection buffer with p-th projection projbuffer = list(projections[p]) # 5. Launch kernel with global size NXNXNY # Each work-item processes one voxel for gid in range(NX NX NY): # Kernel logic for work-item gid # Map 1D gid to 3D voxel indices (row-major: z, y, x) z = gid // (NX NX) rem = gid % (NX NX) y = rem // NX x = rem % NX # Convert voxel indices to physical coordinates (center at 0,0,0) xphys = (x - (NX - 1) / 2.0) voxelsize yphys = (y - (NX - 1) / 2.0) voxelsize zphys = (z - (NY - 1) / 2.0) voxelsize # Rotate voxel coordinates by -angle around Y-axis cosa = math.cos(angle) sina = math.sin(angle) xrot = xphys cosa + zphys sina zrot = -xphys sina + zphys cosa yrot = yphys # Project to detector coordinates (u, v) scale = sdd / sod u = xrot scale v = yrot scale # Map detector coordinates to pixel indices uidx = u / pixelsize + W / 2.0 vidx = v / pixelsize + H / 2.0 # Sample projection buffer with bounds check if 0 <= uidx < W and 0 <= vidx < H: uint = int(round(uidx)) vint = int(round(vidx)) weight = projbuffer[vint W + uint] else: weight = 0.0 # Accumulate into volume buffer volumebuffer[gid] += weight # 7. Release projection buffer (handled by garbage collection in Python) # 8. Read volume buffer back to host (already in host memory) result = volumebuffer # 9. Scale by PI / P result = [val math.pi / P for val in result] return result Parameters: P: Total number of projection angles. NX, NY: Volume dimensions. Volume size is NX \times NX \times NY. W, H: Projection image dimensions. voxelSize: Physical size of a voxel. pixelSize: Physical size of a pixel. sdd: Source-to-Detector Distance. sod: Source-to-Object Distance. Typical work-item count: 128 \times 128 \times 128 = 2,097,152. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision: Floating-point accumulation errors may occur if P is very large. Use double precision for intermediate geometric calculations if necessary. Boundaries: Voxel projections falling outside the detector bounds (0 \le u < W, 0 \le v < H) must be handled to avoid out-of-bounds memory access. Clamp or check bounds before sampling. Degenerate Input: If sod = 0 or sdd = 0, division by zero occurs. Validate inputs before kernel launch. Time Complexity: O(P \cdot V), where P is the number of projections and V is the number of voxels. Each voxel is processed once per projection. Memory Complexity: O(V + W \cdot H). The volume buffer is stored in global memory, and one projection buffer is allocated and reused. Strengths: Simple implementation, no need for local memory management, easy to debug. Limitations: High global memory traffic as each voxel reads from the projection buffer. Not optimized for cache coalescing as effectively as tiled approaches. When to use: Suitable for prototyping, moderate resolution CT reconstruction, and when implementation simplicity is prioritized over maximum performance. When not to use: For very large volumes or real-time applications where memory bandwidth is a critical constraint. This method is part of the GPU-accelerated cone-beam CT reconstruction pipeline described in the ct-reconstruction-gpu repository. It serves as a baseline GPU implementation for backprojection. hardik0001/ct-reconstruction-gpu, https://github.com/hardik0001/ct-reconstruction-gpu, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial)

name: GPU Backprojection using OpenCL Buffers
head: Full GPU Path (Ramp Filter + Backprojection), GPU-Buffer Backprojection
body: A GPU-accelerated tomographic reconstruction pipeline that performs filtered backprojection by storing projection data in OpenCL global memory buffers rather than image objects. It distinguishes itself from GPU Backprojection using OpenCL Image Textures by avoiding texture sampling hardware, and from GPU Backprojection with Global Memory Buffer by explicitly including the ramp filtering step in the pipeline. It solves the problem of reconstructing a 3D volume from 2D projections by mapping projection weights to volume expansion coefficients, building on Back-projection. Inputs: projections: std::vector<float> of size P \times W \times H (column-major layout: psrc[u H + v] for each projection p). P: Number of projections. W, H: Detector width and height in pixels. NX, NY: Volume dimensions (NX \times NX \times NY voxels). voxelSize: Voxel size in mm. pixelSize: Pixel size in mm. sdd: Source-to-detector distance in mm. sod: Source-to-object distance in mm. Outputs: std::vector<float> representing the reconstructed volume of size NX \times NX \times NY. Data Structures: Volume Buffer: clmem with CLMEMREADWRITE, size sizeof(float) volumeSize where volumeSize = NX NX NY. Projection Buffer: clmem with CLMEMREADWRITE, size sizeof(float) projSize where projSize = W H (per projection, reused or copied per iteration). Steps: 1. Pre-filtering: Apply FDK pre-filter (ramp filter) on CPU to raw projections. 2. Volume Initialization: Fill volume buffer with zeros using clEnqueueFillBuffer. 3. Loop over projections: For each projection p from 0 to P-1: a. Calculate angle: \theta = 2.0f \times \pi \times p / P. b. Data Transposition: Convert projection data from column-major (psrc[u H + v]) to row-major (rowMajor[v W + u]) for memory coalescing in the kernel. c. Kernel Execution: Enqueue NDRange kernel with global size equal to volumeSize (NX \times NX \times NY). The kernel computes backprojection weights based on geometry and accumulates into the volume buffer. 4. Final Scaling: After reading the volume buffer back to host, multiply every voxel by scale = MPI / P. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def reconstructgpubuffer(projections, P, W, H, NX, NY, voxelSize, pixelSize, sdd, sod): """ Reconstructs volume using GPU backprojection with OpenCL buffers. Implements the exact steps from the source pipeline. """ volumesize = NX NX NY projsize = W H # 2. Volume Initialization: Fill volume buffer with zeros volume = [0.0] volumesize # 1. Pre-filtering: Apply FDK pre-filter on CPU to raw projections # (FDK ramp filter implementation details are not provided in the sources) filteredprojections = applyfdkfilter(projections, W, H, voxelSize, sdd, sod) # 3. Loop over projections for p in range(P): # a. Calculate angle angle = 2.0 math.pi p / P # b. Data Transposition: Convert column-major to row-major # Input layout: psrc[u H + v] # Output layout: rowMajor[v W + u] rowmajorproj = [0.0] projsize for u in range(W): for v in range(H): rowmajorproj[v W + u] = filteredprojections[p projsize + u H + v] # c. Kernel Execution: Enqueue NDRange kernel with global size volumesize # The kernel computes backprojection weights based on geometry and accumulates into the volume buffer # (OpenCL kernel implementation details are not provided in the sources) backprojectkernel(volume, rowmajorproj, W, H, NX, NY, voxelSize, pixelSize, sdd, sod, angle) # 4. Final Scaling: After reading the volume buffer back to host, multiply every voxel by scale = MPI / P scale = math.pi / P result = [voxel scale for voxel in volume] return result Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision: Expected MSE < 1e-4 against CPU reference. Boundaries: Ensure clEnqueueFillBuffer is used correctly to zero-initialize the volume. Memory: Large volumes may exceed global memory limits; not given in the sources. A GPU-accelerated tomographic reconstruction variant that optimizes memory access patterns by tiling the Z-axis reconstruction loop using OpenCL local memory. It reduces global memory bandwidth pressure by reusing projection data across threads within a work-group, distinguishing it from the parent GPU Backprojection using OpenCL Buffers which relies solely on global memory buffers for projection storage. Time Complexity: O(P \times NX \times NX \times NY), where P is the number of projections and NX, NY are volume dimensions. Memory Complexity: O(NX^2 \times NY + W \times H) for volume and projection buffers. Measured Performance: Not given in the sources. Scaling: Linear with number of projections and volume size. Strengths: Full GPU path for backprojection, avoids texture unit overhead. Limitations: Relies on global memory for projection data, which may cause bandwidth bottlenecks compared to local-memory tiling variants. When to use: When texture units are unavailable or when a simple buffer-based approach is preferred over image objects. When not: When memory bandwidth is a critical bottleneck and local memory tiling is feasible. Part of a suite of GPU reconstruction methods including CPU reference, image texture-based, and local-memory tiling variants. hardik0001/ct-reconstruction-gpu, https://github.com/hardik0001/ct-reconstruction-gpu, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial)

name: GPU Backprojection using Local-Memory Tiling
head: GPU Backprojection with Local Memory Tiling, GPU-Local
body: A GPU-accelerated tomographic reconstruction variant that optimizes memory access patterns by tiling the Z-axis reconstruction loop using OpenCL local memory. It reduces global memory bandwidth pressure by reusing projection data across threads within a work-group, distinguishing it from the parent GPU Backprojection using OpenCL Buffers which relies solely on global memory buffers for projection storage. Inputs: projections: std::vector<float> of size P \times W \times H. P: Number of projections. W, H: Detector width and height in pixels. NX, NY: Volume dimensions (NX \times NX \times NY). voxelSize: Voxel size in mm. pixelSize: Pixel size in mm. sdd: Source-to-detector distance in mm. sod: Source-to-object distance in mm. Outputs: std::vector<float> representing the reconstructed volume of size NX \times NX \times NY. Data Structures: Volume Buffer: Global memory buffer of size NX \times NX \times NY floats, initialized to zero. Projection Buffer: Global memory buffer containing pre-filtered projections. Local Memory Buffers: Two local memory buffers (col0, col1) of size H floats each, used to cache projection columns for interpolation. Parameters: TILEZ: Tile size along the Z-axis, defined as 64. Local Memory Requirement: 2 \times H \times \text{sizeof(float)} bytes. Steps: 1. Pre-filtering: Apply the FDK pre-filter (ramp filter and cosine weighting) on the CPU using applyFDKPreFilter before GPU execution. 2. Device Check: Check the device's local memory size. If insufficient, the code prints info but proceeds without explicit fallback. 3. Kernel Loading: Load the kernel source from kernels/backprojectionlocal.cl. 4. Volume Allocation: Allocate the volume buffer and fill it with zeros. 5. NDRange Calculation: Local size: (1, 1, \text{TILE\Z}). Global Z size: Round up NY to the nearest multiple of TILEZ: gz = ((NY + \text{TILE\Z} - 1) / \text{TILE\Z}) \times \text{TILE\Z}. Global X, Y sizes: NX. 6. Projection Loop: Loop over projections p from 0 to P-1. Calculate the projection angle based on p and P. Create the projection buffer and set kernel arguments. Arguments 2 and 3 are local memory buffers (col0, col1) passed as size in bytes (address is nullptr). Launch the kernel with the calculated 3D NDRange (global size, local size). 7. Post-processing: Multiply all volume voxels by \pi / P. Formulas: t = (x - 0.5 \cdot (NX - 1)) \cdot \text{voxelSize} zm = (z - 0.5 \cdot (NY - 1)) \cdot \text{voxelSize} \text{invU} = \text{sdd} / (\text{sdd} + t) u{\text{proj}} = \text{sdd} \cdot \text{invU} \cdot t v{\text{proj}} = \text{sdd} \cdot \text{invU} \cdot zm u{\text{idx}} = 0.5 \cdot (W - 1) - u{\text{proj}} / \text{pixelSize} v{\text{idx}} = 0.5 \cdot (H - 1) - v{\text{proj}} / \text{pixelSize} \text{weight} = (\text{sod} \cdot \text{sod}) \cdot (\text{invU} \cdot \text{invU}) Bilinear interpolation of projection values at (u{\text{idx}}, v{\text{idx}}) using cached columns \text{volume}[x \cdot NX \cdot NY + y \cdot NY + z] \mathrel{+}= \text{interpolated} \cdot \text{weight} \text{volume}[i] \mathrel{}= \pi / P for all i Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def reconstructGPULocal(projections, P, W, H, NX, NY, voxelSize, pixelSize, sdd, sod): TILEZ = 64 filteredprojections = applyFDKPreFilter(projections, P, W, H, voxelSize, sdd, pixelSize) volume = [0.0] (NX NX NY) localsize = (1, 1, TILEZ) gz = ((NY + TILEZ - 1) // TILEZ) TILEZ globalsize = (NX, NX, gz) kernelsource = loadkernelsource('kernels/backprojectionlocal.cl') kernel = compilekernel(kernelsource) for p in range(P): angle = (p / P) 2.0 3.14159265358979323846 projbuffer = createbuffer(filteredprojections, p, W, H) volbuffer = createbuffer(volume) col0size = H 4 col1size = H 4 setkernelarg(kernel, 0, volbuffer) setkernelarg(kernel, 1, projbuffer) setkernelarg(kernel, 2, col0size) setkernelarg(kernel, 3, col1size) setkernelarg(kernel, 4, P) setkernelarg(kernel, 5, W) setkernelarg(kernel, 6, H) setkernelarg(kernel, 7, NX) setkernelarg(kernel, 8, NY) setkernelarg(kernel, 9, voxelSize) setkernelarg(kernel, 10, pixelSize) setkernelarg(kernel, 11, sdd) setkernelarg(kernel, 12, sod) setkernelarg(kernel, 13, angle) launchkernel(kernel, globalsize, localsize) volume = readbuffer(volbuffer) scale = 3.14159265358979323846 / P for i in range(len(volume)): volume[i] = scale return volume Kernel Logic (Conceptual): The kernel iterates over X and Y coordinates. For each voxel (x, y, z), it calculates the projection coordinates (u, v) on the detector. It uses local memory to cache two columns of the projection image (col0 and col1) to facilitate bilinear interpolation of the projection value at (u, v). The interpolated value is weighted by (\text{sod} \cdot \text{sod}) \cdot (\text{invU} \cdot \text{invU}) and accumulated into the volume. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Local Memory Overflow: If 2 \times H \times \text{sizeof(float)} exceeds the device's local memory limit, the behavior is undefined or the kernel may fail. The source checks this but proceeds without fallback. Boundary Conditions: Projection coordinates outside [0, W-1] \times [0, H-1] are skipped. Precision: Uses float for volume accumulation. Large numbers of projections may lead to precision loss. Time Complexity: O(P \cdot NX \cdot NX \cdot NY), same as CPU backprojection, but optimized for GPU parallelism. Memory Complexity: O(P \cdot W \cdot H + NX \cdot NX \cdot NY + H) for global buffers and local memory. Performance: Reduces global memory bandwidth pressure by reusing projection data in local memory. Strengths: Efficient memory access pattern for Z-axis reconstruction. Limitations: Requires sufficient local memory (2 \cdot H \cdot 4 bytes). No fallback if local memory is insufficient. This method is part of a GPU-accelerated CT reconstruction toolkit, specifically optimizing the backprojection step using OpenCL local memory tiling. It builds on the FDK algorithm and CPU-based pre-filtering. hardik0001/ct-reconstruction-gpu, https://github.com/hardik0001/ct-reconstruction-gpu, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial)

name: GPU Backprojection using OpenCL Image Textures
head: GPU-Image Backprojection, reconstructGPU_Image [S1, unofficial]
body: This method accelerates the backprojection step of the Feldkamp-Davis-Kress (FDK) algorithm by leveraging OpenCL image objects (image2dt) for hardware-accelerated interpolation of pre-filtered projection data. It differs from the buffer-based sibling methods by offloading bilinear interpolation to the GPU's texture cache, which typically yields higher performance for large projection datasets. It builds on Back-projection and assumes pre-filtering has been performed on the CPU. The method processes each projection angle sequentially. For each angle, the raw projection data is transposed, loaded into an OpenCL image object, and used to backproject into the volume buffer. Inputs: projections: std::vector<float> containing raw projection data. P: Number of projections. W, H: Detector width and height in pixels. NX, NY: Volume dimensions. The volume is assumed to be cubic in X/Y, i.e., NX \times NX \times NY. voxelSize: Physical size of a voxel (mm). pixelSize: Physical size of a detector pixel (mm). sdd: Source-to-Detector Distance (mm). sod: Source-to-Object Distance (mm). Outputs: volume: std::vector<float> representing the reconstructed 3D volume, layout [0..NX-1, 0..NX-1, 0..NY-1]. OpenCL Image2D: Channel Order: CLR. Channel Data Type: CLFLOAT. Image Type: CLMEMOBJECTIMAGE2D. Width: W. Height: H. Row Pitch: 0 (native alignment). Kernel Arguments: 1. clmem image: The projection image (CLMEMREADONLY). 2. clmem volumeBuffer: Output volume buffer. 3. int W, int H: Detector dimensions. 4. int NX, int NY: Volume dimensions. 5. float voxelSize, float pixelSize: Physical scales. 6. float sdd, float sod: Geometry distances. 7. float angle: Current projection angle in radians. 1. Pre-filtering (CPU): Apply FDK pre-filtering (cone weighting and ramp filter) to the raw projections on the CPU. The source notes specify this step occurs before GPU processing. 2. Data Transposition: For each projection p, convert the data from column-major (psrc[u H + v]) to row-major (dest[v W + u]) to match the image texture layout. 3. Loop over Projections: Iterate p from 0 to P-1. a. Calculate angle: \theta = \frac{2\pi p}{P}. b. Image Creation: Create an OpenCL image2dt from the transposed row-major data with flags CLMEMREADONLY | CLMEMCOPYHOSTPTR. c. Kernel Execution: Enqueue the backprojection NDRange kernel. Global Size: NX \times NX \times NY. Each work-item (x, y, z) computes the contribution of the current projection to that voxel. d. Cleanup: Release the image memory object. 4. Final Scaling: After reading the volume buffer back to the host, multiply every voxel by \frac{\pi}{P}. For each voxel (x, y, z) and projection angle \theta: t = y \cos(\theta) - x \sin(\theta) U = \text{sod} + y \sin(\theta) + x \cos(\theta) u{\text{proj}} = \text{sdd} \cdot \frac{t}{U} v{\text{proj}} = \text{sdd} \cdot \frac{z}{U} The contribution to the voxel is: \text{volume}[x, y, z] \ += \ \text{filtered\proj}(u{\text{proj}}, v{\text{proj}}) \cdot \frac{\text{sod}^2}{U^2} Where \text{filtered\proj}(u, v) is obtained via hardware bilinear interpolation from the OpenCL image object. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def gpubackprojectionimage(projections, P, W, H, NX, NY, voxelSize, pixelSize, sdd, sod): """ Simulates the logic of the GPU Image Backprojection method. Note: Actual OpenCL calls are abstracted; this shows the data flow and math. """ volume = [0.0] (NX NX NY) # Pre-filtering is assumed done on CPU before this function call # projections are now filtered for p in range(P): # 1. Transpose projection data from column-major to row-major # Original: psrc[u H + v] # Target: rowMajor[v W + u] projrowmajor = [0.0] (W H) for u in range(W): for v in range(H): srcidx = u H + v dstidx = v W + u projrowmajor[dstidx] = projections[p][srcidx] # 2. Create OpenCL Image2D (Abstracted) # image = clCreateImage2D(context, CLMEMREADONLY | CLMEMCOPYHOSTPTR,...) # imagedata = projrowmajor # 3. Calculate Angle angle = 2.0 math.pi p / P # 4. Kernel Execution: Backproject one projection # Global size: NX NX NY # Each work-item (x, y, z) runs the following logic: for x in range(NX): for y in range(NX): for z in range(NY): # Compute detector coordinates t = y math.cos(angle) - x math.sin(angle) U = sod + y math.sin(angle) + x math.cos(angle) # Avoid division by zero if U == 0: continue uproj = sdd t / U vproj = sdd z / U # Hardware interpolation of filtered projection # In OpenCL: readimagef(image, sampler, (float2)(uproj, vproj)) # We simulate bilinear interpolation here for completeness val = hardwareinterpolate(projrowmajor, uproj, vproj, W, H) # Accumulate with weighting weight = (sod sod) / (U U) idx = x NX NY + y NY + z volume[idx] += val weight # 5. Cleanup Image # clReleaseMemObject(image) # 6. Final Scaling scale = math.pi / P for i in range(len(volume)): volume[i] = scale return volume def hardwareinterpolate(data, u, v, W, H): """ Simulates OpenCL hardware bilinear interpolation. u and v are in continuous detector coordinates. # Standard bilinear interpolation matching OpenCL image2dt sampling behavior """ # Clamp to valid range [0, W-1] and [0, H-1] uclamped = max(0.0, min(float(W - 1), u)) vclamped = max(0.0, min(float(H - 1), v)) # Integer parts u0 = int(math.floor(uclamped)) v0 = int(math.floor(vclamped)) # Fractional parts fu = uclamped - u0 fv = vclamped - v0 # Neighbors # Layout is row-major: index = v W + u val00 = data[v0 W + u0] val01 = data[v0 W + min(u0 + 1, W - 1)] val10 = data[min(v0 + 1, H - 1) W + u0] val11 = data[min(v0 + 1, H - 1) W + min(u0 + 1, W - 1)] # Bilinear interpolation top = val00 (1 - fu) + val01 fu bottom = val10 (1 - fu) + val11 fu return top (1 - fv) + bottom fv Boundary Conditions: If u{\text{proj}} or v{\text{proj}} falls outside the detector bounds [0, W] or [0, H], the hardware interpolation typically returns 0.0. The pseudocode explicitly clamps and returns 0.0. Division by Zero: If U=0, the projection ray is parallel to the detector plane or originates from the source plane. The implementation must guard against this. Memory Management: The image object must be released after each projection to avoid memory leaks, as the loop creates a new image for each angle. Time Complexity: O(P \cdot NX^2 \cdot NY). The dominant cost is the kernel execution for each projection. Memory Complexity: O(W \cdot H + NX^2 \cdot NY). The projection image requires W \cdot H floats, and the volume requires NX^2 NY floats. Performance: Typically faster than buffer-based backprojection due to the GPU's texture cache handling interpolation, reducing global memory bandwidth pressure. Scaling: Scales linearly with the number of projections P and volume voxels. The texture cache hit rate improves with larger projection datasets. Strengths: Efficient hardware interpolation; leverages GPU texture cache. Limitations: Requires pre-filtering on CPU; sequential projection processing limits parallelism across angles compared to fully parallel GPU approaches. When to use: Suitable for FDK reconstruction on OpenCL-capable GPUs where interpolation bandwidth is a bottleneck. When not to use: Unsuitable when projections must be filtered on-GPU or when strict memory limits prevent per-projection image allocation. This method is part of a GPU-accelerated CT reconstruction toolkit. It specifically targets the backprojection stage using OpenCL image textures. The approach is documented in the ct-reconstruction-gpu repository. hardik0001/ct-reconstruction-gpu, https://github.com/hardik0001/ct-reconstruction-gpu, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial)

name: Fourier-space Projection Operations
head: torch-projectors
body: Fourier-space projection operations compute 2D and 3D forward and backward projections (adjoints) by operating directly in the frequency domain using the Fourier Slice Theorem. Unlike spatial-domain methods that sample voxel grids, this method transforms reconstruction data to Fourier space, applies rotation and translation via phase modulation, and interpolates non-integer frequency coordinates. It distinguishes itself from spatial back-projection Back-projection and explicit matrix methods Explicit Radon Matrix Construction by offering high performance on CPU, CUDA, and Apple Silicon while supporting end-to-end differentiability for all inputs. Inputs and Outputs: Reconstruction Volume: Real-space tensor, shifted to center at index 0. Projections: Real-space tensor, shifted to center at index 0. Geometry: Rotation matrices and translation vectors. Output: Forward projection yields a sinogram; Backward projection yields a volume. Data Structures and Layout: The method uses PyTorch's Real Fast Fourier Transform (RFFT) format, adhering to FFTW conventions. Tensors remain in RFFT format throughout operations. 2D Reconstruction: Shape [B, N, N/2 + 1], where B is batch size, N is spatial size (must be even). 3D Reconstruction: Shape [B, D, H, W/2 + 1], where B is batch, D, H, W are spatial dimensions (must be even). Projections: Shape [B, P, N, N/2 + 1] (2D) or [B, P, D, H, W/2 + 1] (3D), where P is the pose dimension. Rotation Matrices: Shape [B, P, 2, 2] (2D) or [B, P, 3, 3] (3D). Translation Vectors: Shape [B, P, 2] (2D) or [B, P, 3] (3D). Parameters: Interpolation Kernel: Linear (bilinear/trilinear) or Cubic (Catmull-Rom). Catmull-Rom Parameter: a = -0.5. Steps: 1. Preprocessing (Shift): Apply fftshift to the real-space reconstruction or projection data to center the zero-frequency component at the tensor origin. 2. Transform: Compute the RFFT of the shifted data. 3. Rotation: Apply rotation matrices to the frequency coordinates. For a frequency vector \mathbf{k} and rotation matrix R, the rotated frequency is \mathbf{k}' = R \mathbf{k}. 4. Translation: Apply translation shifts \mathbf{t} via phase modulation in Fourier space. The phase factor is e^{-2\pi i \mathbf{k} \cdot \mathbf{t}}. Note: In back-projection, shifts are applied in the opposite direction to maintain the adjoint relationship. 5. Interpolation: Sample the rotated/shifted frequency grid at non-integer coordinates using interpolation kernels. Linear: Bilinear (2D) or Trilinear (3D) interpolation using 4 or 8 neighbors. Cubic: Separable Catmull-Rom kernels. The 1D kernel weight w(s) for coordinate offset s is: w(s) = \begin{cases} (a+2)|s|^3 - (a+3)|s|^2 + 1 & \text{if } |s| \leq 1 \\ a|s|^3 - 5a|s|^2 + 8a|s| - 4a & \text{if } 1 < |s| \leq 2 \\ 0 & \text{if } |s| > 2 \end{cases} where a = -0.5. Bicubic uses a 4 \times 4 neighborhood; tricubic uses 4 \times 4 \times 4. 6. Inverse Transform: Apply ifftshift to restore conventional centering, then compute the Inverse RFFT to return to real space. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import torch import torch.nn.functional as F def fourierforwardprojection(volume, rotationmatrices, translationvectors, interpolation='linear'): """ volume: [B, D, H, W/2+1] (RFFT format, real-space shifted) rotationmatrices: [B, P, 3, 3] translationvectors: [B, P, 3] """ # 1. Shift real space to center # Note: torch.fft.rfft assumes standard ordering; fftshift moves zero freq to center # However, the library description implies input is already shifted or handled internally. # We assume input 'volume' is in RFFT format corresponding to shifted real space. # 2. Get frequency grid # D, H, W are spatial dims. W is the last dim. # RFFT output shape for dim L is L//2 + 1. # We need to generate frequency coordinates for the original real-space dimensions. # Let real dims be (Dreal, Hreal, Wreal). # Dreal = D 2 (if D > 1), Hreal = H 2, Wreal = (W-1)2 # This mapping is implicit in the library's internal coordinate generation. # For implementation from text: we assume a helper getfrequencygrid exists. # 3. Rotate frequencies # k' = R @ k # This requires broadcasting rotation matrices over the frequency grid. # 4. Translate frequencies (Phase modulation) # Phase = exp(-2 pi i k'. t) # 5. Interpolate # Sample the rotated/shifted grid. # 6. Inverse Shift and IFFT # ifftshift -> irfft raise NotImplementedError("Full implementation requires internal coordinate grid generation logic specific to torch-projectors.") def catmullromkernel(s, a=-0.5): """ Computes the Catmull-Rom kernel weight for offset s. """ abss = torch.abs(s) w = torch.zeroslike(s) # Region 1: |s| <= 1 mask1 = abss <= 1.0 w[mask1] = (a + 2) abss[mask1]3 - (a + 3) abss[mask1]2 + 1 # Region 2: 1 < |s| <= 2 mask2 = (abss > 1.0) & (abss <= 2.0) w[mask2] = a abss[mask2]3 - 5 a abss[mask2]2 + 8 a abss[mask2] - 4 a # Region 3: |s| > 2 # w remains 0 return w Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Even Dimensions: All spatial dimensions must be even. If not, the RFFT shape [N/2 + 1] is invalid for the assumed symmetry. Square/Cubic: 2D reconstructions must be square; 3D must be cubic. Batch Broadcasting: Batch dimension B can be 1 or match the reconstruction batch size. Pose dimension P can be 1 for shared geometry. Shift Direction: In back-projection, translation shifts must be applied in the opposite direction to forward projection to ensure the adjoint property. TorchRadon is a PyTorch-integrated library providing high-performance, differentiable forward and backward projection operators for computed tomography. It solves the problem of computing Radon transforms and their adjoints within a deep learning pipeline, enabling gradient-based optimization for tomographic reconstruction. It distinguishes itself from non-differentiable alternatives by supporting automatic differentiation for all inputs, allowing gradients to flow through the projection and backprojection operations. Computes the Radon transform (sinogram) of a batch of multi-channel images by rotating the image and summing along one axis for each angle. It differs from TorchRadon by providing a specific implementation of the direct projection operator within the torchskradon library, focusing on explicit rotation and summation steps rather than optimized Fourier-space approximations. Performance: Outperforms torch-fourier-slice by 1–2 orders of magnitude. Optimized for CPU, Apple Silicon (MPS), and CUDA devices. Complexity: Dominated by FFTs (O(N^3 \log N) for 3D) and interpolation. Avoids the O(N^4) complexity of explicit matrix construction Explicit Radon Matrix Construction. Memory: Requires storage for RFFT-formatted tensors. No explicit Radon matrix storage needed. Strengths: Differentiable, high performance, supports linear and cubic interpolation. Limitations: Requires even, square/cubic dimensions. Interpolation errors at high frequencies if kernel support is insufficient. Originated in the context of transmission electron microscopy and electron tomography, where high optical resolution projections of Coulomb potentials are reconstructed into 3D atomic models. The method leverages the Fourier Slice Theorem to accelerate projection operations. The torch-projectors library was introduced to address the lack of high-performance differentiable projection operators in PyTorch, which are essential for end-to-end machine learning training in tomography. torch-projectors: A High-Performance Differentiable Projection Library for PyTorch, https://doi.org/10.64898/2026.03.10.710885, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial) ayush-chauhan-1202/physics-aware-ct-reconstruction, https://github.com/ayush-chauhan-1202/physics-aware-ct-reconstruction, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial)

name: TorchRadon
head: Differentiable Radon Transform, Implementation Details (TorchRadon), TorchRadon library
body: TorchRadon is a PyTorch-integrated library providing high-performance, differentiable forward and backward projection operators for computed tomography. It solves the problem of computing Radon transforms and their adjoints within a deep learning pipeline, enabling gradient-based optimization for tomographic reconstruction. It distinguishes itself from non-differentiable alternatives by supporting automatic differentiation for all inputs, allowing gradients to flow through the projection and backprojection operations. TorchRadon implements linear projection operators that approximate the continuous Radon transform. The core operations are the forward projection (mapping an image to a sinogram) and the backward projection (mapping a sinogram to an image), corresponding to matrix-vector multiplications with A and A^T respectively. Inputs and Outputs: Forward Projection: Input is a 2D image tensor x of shape (N, 1, H, W) or (H, W). Output is a sinogram tensor y of shape (N, 1, D, A), where D is the number of detector bins and A is the number of angles. Backward Projection: Input is a sinogram tensor y. Output is an image tensor x{bp} of shape (N, 1, H, W) or (H, W). Data Structures: The library uses PyTorch tensors. The geometry is defined by parameters such as image size, number of angles, detector spacing, and interpolation method. Parameters: angles: Array of sampling angles in radians. For parallel beam, typically [0, \pi). For fan-beam, [0, 2\pi). detcount: Number of detector pixels. detspacing: Distance between detector pixels. sourcedistance: Distance from X-ray source to object center (fan-beam only). Default: 512. detdistance: Distance from detector to object center (fan-beam only). Default: equals sourcedistance. Interpolation: Linear or cubic [Parent]. Algorithm Steps: 1. Initialize the Radon operator with specified geometry parameters (image size, angles, detector configuration). 2. Forward Projection: For each angle \theta, compute the line integrals of the image x along parallel (or fan-beam) rays. This is implemented using differentiable interpolation kernels to sample the image at sub-pixel locations determined by the ray geometry. 3. Backward Projection: For each angle \theta, distribute the sinogram values back to the image grid. This involves interpolating the sinogram values and adding them to the corresponding image pixels, effectively accumulating contributions from all angles. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import torch import numpy as np from torchradon import Radon, RadonFanbeam size = 512 angles = np.linspace(0, np.pi, 512, endpoint=False) radon = Radon(size, angles) x = torch.randn(1, 1, size, size) sino = radon.forward(x) bp = radon.backprojection(sino) anglesfan = np.linspace(0, 2 np.pi, 512, endpoint=False) radonfan = RadonFanbeam(size, anglesfan, sourcedistance=512) sinofan = radonfan.forward(x) bpfan = radonfan.backprojection(sinofan) Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Boundary Effects: Rays passing near the edge of the image may have incomplete support for interpolation kernels, potentially causing artifacts. Precision: The library uses floating-point arithmetic. Relative errors compared to reference implementations (e.g., Astra Toolbox) are small but non-zero. Memory: High-resolution images and large numbers of angles increase memory consumption linearly with the sinogram size. The Radon transform maps a 2D image to its projections (sinogram) by integrating pixel intensities along parallel lines at various angles. It solves the forward acquisition model in computed tomography, converting spatial domain data into projection domain data. Unlike its inverse counterpart (e.g., Filtered Back-Projection), which reconstructs images from projections, the forward Radon transform generates the measurements required for reconstruction. It is distinguished from other projection methods by its strict parallel-beam geometry and linear integration nature. Computes Radon transforms for fan-beam geometry where X-rays originate from a point source. It is distinguished from parallel-beam by the diverging ray paths. Parameters include sourcedistance (default 512) and detdistance (default equals sourcedistance). Angles are equally spaced in 0, 2\pi). Relative error compared to Astra Toolbox is 8.34 \cdot 10^{-4} for forward projection and 4.84 \cdot 10^{-5} for backprojection. Time Complexity: Linear with respect to the number of pixels and angles. The differentiable nature adds minimal overhead compared to non-differentiable C++ implementations due to GPU [acceleration. Memory Complexity: Proportional to the size of the sinogram (H \times W \times A). Performance: High performance on NVIDIA GPUs via PyTorch. Accuracy: Relative errors are low (< 10^{-3}) compared to established toolboxes like Astra. Strengths: Seamless integration with PyTorch, differentiability, support for both parallel and fan-beam geometries. Limitations: Limited to 2D images in the core library (3D support may vary by version); interpolation artifacts at boundaries. TorchRadon was developed to provide a fast, differentiable implementation of Radon transforms for use in deep learning-based tomographic reconstruction. It is integrated with PyTorch, allowing for end-to-end training of reconstruction networks. The library supports various interpolation methods and filter types for filtered backprojection. name: Radon Transform
head: Discrete Radon Transform, Forward Radon Transform, Parallel-Beam Radon Transform, Sinogram Generation, Transformée de Radon, Transformée de Radon discrète, skradon
body: The Radon transform maps a 2D image to its projections (sinogram) by integrating pixel intensities along parallel lines at various angles. It solves the forward acquisition model in computed tomography, converting spatial domain data into projection domain data. Unlike its inverse counterpart (e.g., Filtered Back-Projection), which reconstructs images from projections, the forward Radon transform generates the measurements required for reconstruction. It is distinguished from other projection methods by its strict parallel-beam geometry and linear integration nature. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A 2D image I (discrete pixel grid) and a set of projection angles \theta. In batch processing, this is a tensor of shape (N, C, H, W) where N is batch size, C channels, H height, W width. Output: A sinogram tensor of shape (N, C, D, A) where D is the number of detector positions (radial bins) and A is the number of angles. Data Structures: Image Grid: Discrete indices (i, j) corresponding to pixel centers. The image is modeled as a sum of discrete Dirac impulses: f(x,y) = \sum{i=-\infty}^{\infty} \sum{j=-\infty}^{\infty} I(i,j) \Delta(x - j) \Delta(y - i) where \Delta(\cdot) is the discrete Dirac impulse. Projection Line: Defined by angle \theta and radial distance \rho from the origin. The line equation is \rho = x \cos \theta + y \sin \theta. Detector Positions: Linearly spaced values rs covering the image extent, typically from -1 to 1 normalized or in pixel units. Formulas: The continuous Radon transform is defined as: R\theta(\rho) = \int{-\infty}^{\infty} \int{-\infty}^{\infty} f(x,y) \delta(\rho - x \cos \theta - y \sin \theta) \, dx \, dy where \delta(\cdot) is the Dirac delta function. The discrete Radon transform R\theta(\rho) is the sum of pixel values I(i,j) whose centers lie on the projection line: R\theta(\rho) = \sum{i=0}^{H-1} \sum{j=0}^{W-1} I(i,j) \cdot \mathbb{I}(\text{line } (\theta, \rho) \text{ intersects pixel } (i,j)) In practice, this is implemented via interpolation (e.g., bilinear) to approximate the integral along the ray. Parameters: theta: Array of projection angles in degrees. Typical default: np.linspace(0.0, 180.0, max(image.shape), endpoint=False). In skradon, default is torch.arange(180). rs: Detector positions. Default: linearly spaced from -1 to 1 with length equal to image height. circle: Boolean. If True, assumes zero intensity outside the inscribed circle, adjusting sinogram width to min(H, W). preserverange: Boolean. If True, preserves original dtype range; otherwise converts to float [0,1]. Steps: 1. Preprocessing: Convert input image to float. If preserverange is False, scale values according to imgasfloat conventions (e.g., uint8 [0,255] to [0,1]). 2. Angle Setup: If theta is None, generate angles from 0 to 179 degrees. 3. Geometry Setup: If circle is True, calculate the radius r = \min(H, W) // 2 and mask pixels outside the inscribed circle to zero. Define the rotation center at (H//2, W//2). 4. Projection Loop (for each angle \thetak in theta): a. Affine Transformation: Construct a 2 \times 3 affine matrix representing rotation by \thetak and translation to center the projection axis. b. Grid Generation: Create a sampling grid using affinegrid (or equivalent) based on the affine matrix and image dimensions. aligncorners=False is standard. c. Sampling: Sample the image values at the grid coordinates using gridsample (bilinear interpolation). This yields a 2D projection profile for the current angle. d. Accumulation: Store the projection profile. 5. Post-processing: If using the skimage-style approach (S1): Rotate the image for each angle, sum along the vertical axis, multiply by detector spacing dr, and transpose to form the sinogram. If using the skradon approach (S2): The sampled projections are accumulated directly into the sinogram tensor. 6. Output: Return the sinogram tensor. Pseudocode: Unverified code. name: Filtered Back-Projection (FBP)
head: Filter Back Projection, RamLak Reconstruction
body:
Filtered Back-Projection (FBP) is a direct tomographic reconstruction algorithm that recovers a 2D image from its measured projection profiles (sinogram). It solves the inverse Radon transform by applying a high-pass frequency-domain filter to the projections to correct for the inherent low-pass blurring of simple back-projection, followed by integrating the filtered data along sine-shaped paths. Unlike Fourier-based reconstruction methods which require interpolation between Cartesian and polar grids (leading to O(N^2) complexity or interpolation artifacts), FBP operates directly on the projections with a time complexity of O(N \log N) due to the use of Fast Fourier Transforms (FFT). It is the most popular algorithm for computed tomography. Inputs: Sinogram R: A 2D array of shape (Nho, N	heta), where Nho is the number of radial samples per projection and N	heta is the number of projection angles. Angles \Theta: An array of N	heta angles, typically spanning 0, \pi) radians. Radial sampling step dho: The distance between adjacent samples in the projection domain. Filter type: e.g., 'ramp', 'hann', 'hamming', 'shepp-logan', 'cosine'. Pixel kernel: The interpolation function used during [back-projection (e.g., Dirac, Linear, Area). Outputs: Reconstructed image I: A 2D array of shape (N, N), where N is the image grid size. Data Structures: The sinogram is stored as a contiguous 2D array. The frequency domain filter is a 1D array of length Nho. Steps: 1. Generate Frequency Filter: Compute the 1D frequency bins corresponding to the projection width. For a projection of length Nho, the frequencies 
u range from -
u{Nyquist} to 
u{Nyquist}, where 
u{Nyquist} =  rac{1}{2 dho}. Construct the base filter H(
u). The standard "Ram-Lak" filter is the ramp function |
u|. To reduce high-frequency noise, this is multiplied by a window function W(
u). The combined filter is: H{total}(
u) = |
u| \cdot W(
u) Common windows include Hann and Hamming: W(
u) =  egin{cases} a + (1-a)\cos\left( rac{\pi

u{Nyquist} \ 0 & 	ext{otherwise} \end{cases} Where a = 0.5 for Hann and a = 0.54 for Hamming. Other filters like Shepp-Logan or Cosine are defined differently. For 'shepp-logan', it multiplies frequencies by 	ext{sinc}(\omega). For 'cosine', it uses a shifted sine function. If no filter is specified, the filter is all ones. 2. Filter Projections: For each projection angle 	hetai \in \Theta: a. Compute the 1D Discrete Fourier Transform (DFT) of the projection profile R{	hetai}: \hat{R}{	hetai} = 	ext{FFT}(R{	hetai}) b. Multiply the spectrum by the frequency filter H{total}: \hat{R}{	hetai}^{filtered}[
u] = \hat{R}{	hetai}[
u] \cdot H{total}[
u] c. Compute the inverse 1D DFT to obtain the filtered projection R{	hetai}^{BF}: R{	hetai}^{BF} = 	ext{IFFT}(\hat{R}{	hetai}^{filtered}) The result is taken as the real part, as the implementation explicitly extracts it. 3. Back-Project: Initialize the reconstructed image I to zeros. For each filtered projection R{	hetai}^{BF} and angle 	hetai: For each pixel (x, y) in the image grid: a. Calculate the radial coordinate ho corresponding to the pixel's position at angle 	hetai: ho = x \cos 	hetai + y \sin 	hetai b. Sample the value from the filtered projection R{	hetai}^{BF} at ho. Since ho rarely aligns exactly with the discrete grid indices of the sinogram, interpolation is required. The choice of interpolation kernel (pixel kernel) affects quality. The 'Area' kernel provides the best SSIM and most uniform Point Spread Function (PSF). c. Add the sampled value to the image pixel: I(x, y) \leftarrow I(x, y) + R{	hetai}^{BF}(ho) 4. Normalization: Divide the accumulated image by N	heta (or the angular step size d	heta) to maintain correct intensity scaling. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import numpy as np def filteredbackprojection(sinogram, angles, drho, filtertype='ramp', windowparam=0.5): """ Reconstructs an image from a sinogram using Filtered Back-Projection. Parameters: sinogram: ndarray of shape (Nrho, Ntheta) angles: ndarray of shape (Ntheta,), in radians, range [0, pi) drho: float, radial sampling step filtertype: str, type of filter ('ramp', 'hann', 'hamming', 'shepp-logan', 'cosine') windowparam: float, parameter for window function (e.g., 0.5 for Hann) Returns: image: ndarray of shape (N, N) """ Nrho, Ntheta = sinogram.shape N = Nrho # 1. Generate Frequency Filter freqs = np.fft.fftfreq(Nrho, d=drho) nunyquist = 1.0 / (2 drho) rampfilter = np.abs(freqs) if filtertype == 'hann': window = windowparam + (1 - windowparam) np.cos(np.pi freqs / nunyquist) window[np.abs(freqs) >= nunyquist] = 0 filterkernel = rampfilter window elif filtertype == 'hamming': window = windowparam + (1 - windowparam) np.cos(np.pi freqs / nunyquist) window[np.abs(freqs) >= nunyquist] = 0 filterkernel = rampfilter window elif filtertype == 'ramp': filterkernel = rampfilter elif filtertype == 'shepp-logan': omega = np.pi freqs sincfilter = np.sinc(omega / np.pi) filterkernel = rampfilter sincfilter elif filtertype == 'cosine': filterkernel = np.cos(np.pi freqs / 2) filterkernel[np.abs(freqs) > 1] = 0 else: filterkernel = np.ones(Nrho) # 2. Filter Projections filteredsinogram = np.zeroslike(sinogram) for i in range(Ntheta): proj = sinogram[:, i] projfft = np.fft.fft(proj) projfftfiltered = projfft filterkernel filteredproj = np.fft.ifft(projfftfiltered) filteredsinogram[:, i] = np.real(filteredproj) # 3. Back-Project image = np.zeros((N, N)) cosangles = np.cos(angles) sinangles = np.sin(angles) y, x = np.meshgrid(np.arange(N) - N/2 + 0.5, np.arange(N) - N/2 + 0.5, indexing='ij') for i in range(Ntheta): c = cosangles[i] s = sinangles[i] rho = x c + y s indices = rho / drho + Nrho / 2 indices = np.clip(indices, 0, Nrho - 1) idx0 = np.floor(indices).astype(int) idx1 = np.ceil(indices).astype(int) w = indices - idx0 idx1safe = np.minimum(idx1, Nrho - 1) val0 = filteredsinogram[idx0, i] val1 = filteredsinogram[idx1safe, i] interpolatedval = val0 + w (val1 - val0) image += interpolatedval # 4. Normalization image /= Ntheta return image Parameters: N	heta: Number of projection angles. SSIM plateaus when N	heta \ge 40 for a 512^2 image. dho: Radial sampling step. SSIM increases for dho > 1 (undersampling) and becomes constant when dho \le 1 (standard/oversampling). Filter: 'ramp', 'shepp-logan', 'cosine', 'hamming', 'hann'. Window parameter a: 0.54 for Hamming, 0.5 for Hann. Pixel Kernel: 'Area' kernel provides best SSIM and PSF uniformity. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Interpolation: Points on the backprojection paths do not align with measured grid locations, requiring interpolation. Low resolution (e.g., 512x512) can cause visible artifacts. Noise Amplification: The ramp filter amplifies high frequencies, which are sources of noise. Windowed filters (Hann, Hamming) are used to attenuate these very high frequencies to reduce artifacts. Undersampling: High radial resolution (Nho increase) without sufficient angular coverage (N	heta < 40) causes complete loss of contrast and luminance. Inconsistent Data: FBP can produce negative values in the presence of inconsistent data. The Discrete Inverse Radon Transform reconstructs a 2D image from its Radon transform (sinogram) by summing projection values into image pixels, assuming parallel beam geometry. It is conventionally implemented via Filtered Back-Projection (FBP), which applies a frequency-domain filter to the sinogram before backprojecting to correct for the blurring inherent in simple summation. Unlike iterative methods, it provides a direct, closed-form solution but requires projections over a full hemisphere and can produce negative values in the presence of inconsistent data. Iterative Reconstruction with Basis Expansion models the attenuation map as a linear combination of non-negative basis functions to solve the inverse problem when filtered backprojection fails due to inconsistent projections or limited viewing angles. Unlike Fourier-space methods such as Filtered Back-Projection (FBP), which assume ideal data consistency, this method formulates the reconstruction as a convex non-negative linear least-squares optimization problem, guaranteeing a solution that emits a target light field with consistent views. A method to generate a convolution filter for tomographic reconstruction that includes an overscan border (typically 30% extra pixels) to handle boundary conditions and ensure symmetry. It calculates overscan dimensions (w{over} = \lceil w \cdot 0.3 ceil) and calls a filter builder with these dimensions. Overscanned filters preserve the parity (even/odd nature) of dimensions compared to non-overscanned filters, ensuring pixel alignment consistency. The Ramp Filter is a frequency-domain filter applied to projection data prior to backprojection in Filtered Back-Projection (FBP). It corrects for the 1/r blurring inherent in simple backprojection by weighting frequencies proportional to their magnitude. Unlike iterative methods or discrete inverse transforms that solve for the volume directly, the Ramp Filter is a closed-form, frequency-space correction step within the FBP pipeline. The mathematical foundation of FBP. It states that the 1D Fourier transform of a projection R	heta at angle 	heta is equal to a radial slice of the 2D Fourier transform of the original image f(x,y) at the same angle 	heta. This allows reconstruction by combining 1D Fourier transforms of all projections to fill the 2D Fourier space, which is then inverted. Models and shapes CT noise from Poisson-distributed photon counting to a frequency-dependent Gaussian distribution via ramp filtering and interpolation during backprojection. The ideal ramp filter amplifies high-frequency noise. Windowed ramp filters (Hanning, Hamming, Butterworth) create a band-pass noise spectrum. Re-sampling profiles during backprojection using interpolation (e.g., linear) further shapes the noise spectrum. The re-sampling rate can be increased via zoom reconstruction. Models and shapes CT noise from Poisson-distributed photon counting to a frequency-dependent Gaussian distribution via ramp filtering and interpolation during backprojection. Generates a 1D frequency domain filter kernel for use in filtered backprojection. For 'shepp-logan', it multiplies frequencies by 	ext{sinc}(\omega). For 'cosine', it uses a shifted sine function. For 'hamming' or 'hann', it uses the respective window function. The base ramp filter array f is defined as f[0] = 0.25, f[1::2] = -1 / (\pi 	imes n)^2, where n = [1, 3,..., 	ext{size}//2] 	ext{ concatenated with } [	ext{size}//2-1,..., 1]. The filter is 2 	imes 	ext{real}(	ext{FFT}(f)). Time Complexity: O(N \log N), making it competitive with Fourier methods. Memory Complexity: O(N^2) for storing the sinogram and the reconstructed image. Measured Performance: FBP rms reconstruction error on Shepp-Logan phantom with ramp filter is 0.0283. Scaling: The method is highly parallelizable because pixel contributions are independent, allowing for efficient GPU implementation. Strengths: Fast, direct closed-form solution, good conservation of contrast, and uniform PSF. Limitations: Requires projections over a full hemisphere (\pi radians). Sensitive to noise (amplified by ramp filter) and undersampling. Can produce negative values with inconsistent data. When to Use: Standard reconstruction algorithm for 2D CT slices from projection data. Filtered Back-Projection is the most popular algorithm for computed tomography. It is based on the inversion of the Radon transform. The method was introduced by Ramachandran and Lakshiminarayanan, hence the name "Ram-Lak" filter. It is widely used in tomography and is cited as one of the most used direct methods. In 3D, Feldkamp’s (FDK) algorithm is a popular extension for cone-beam CT, which acts as a 3D extension of 2D FBP in orthographic mode. name: Ramp Filter
body: The Ramp Filter is a frequency-domain filter applied to projection data prior to backprojection in Filtered Back-Projection (FBP). It corrects for the 1/r blurring inherent in simple backprojection by weighting frequencies proportional to their magnitude. Unlike iterative methods or discrete inverse transforms that solve for the volume directly, the Ramp Filter is a closed-form, frequency-space correction step within the FBP pipeline. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A 1D projection array p of width N. Output: A filtered 1D projection array \hat{p}. Data Structures: The projection p is stored as a 1D array of floating-point values. Frequency bins are computed as a 1D array of floats. Steps: 1. Compute the frequency bins f corresponding to the projection width N. For a discrete Fourier transform of size N, the frequency bin at index k is |k - N/2| / N (normalized frequency) or simply |k - N/2| depending on normalization conventions. The sources imply using the absolute value of the frequency index relative to the center. 2. Compute the Fast Fourier Transform (FFT) of the projection p, resulting in \mathcal{F}(p). 3. Multiply the FFT result by the absolute value of the frequency bins (the ramp filter kernel). 4. Compute the Inverse Fast Fourier Transform (IFFT) of the result to obtain the filtered projection \hat{p}. Formula: \hat{p} = \text{IFFT}\left( \text{FFT}(p) \cdot |f| \right) where f is the array of frequency bins. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import numpy as np def rampfilter(projection): """ Applies the Ramp Filter to a 1D projection. Args: projection: 1D numpy array of projection data. Returns: 1D numpy array of filtered projection data. """ N = len(projection) # Step 1: Compute frequency bins # Frequency bins for FFT output of size N. # The ramp filter is |f|. In numpy.fft.fft, frequencies are ordered # from 0 to N-1. The normalized frequency magnitude is |k - N/2| / N # if using normalized frequency, or just |k - N/2| for unnormalized. # The source implies multiplying by the absolute value of frequency bins. # Standard ramp filter in frequency domain is |omega|. # For discrete FFT, the frequency index k corresponds to frequency k. # The ramp filter is |k - N/2| (centered at 0). freqbins = np.abs(np.arange(N) - N / 2.0) # Step 2: Compute FFT of the projection fftprojection = np.fft.fft(projection) # Step 3: Multiply by the ramp filter (absolute value of frequency bins) filteredfft = fftprojection freqbins # Step 4: Compute IFFT to get the filtered projection filteredprojection = np.fft.ifft(filteredfft).real return filteredprojection Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision: The ramp filter amplifies high frequencies, which can amplify noise. This is a known limitation of FBP. Boundaries: The FFT assumes periodic boundary conditions. Discontinuities at the edges of the projection can cause artifacts. Windowing functions (e.g., Hamming, Hann) are often applied to mitigate this, though not explicitly detailed in the provided sources for the basic Ramp Filter. Degenerate Input: If the projection is all zeros, the output is zero. Applies a Fourier filter and Poisson weights to residual projection data. It is used in iterative reconstruction contexts (like SIRT) rather than standard FBP. Choose this when using iterative solvers with residual updates. Definition: Applies a Fourier filter and Poisson weights to a residual projection data. Steps: 1. If fourierfilter is None, compute simple difference: forward = projections - forward. 2. Else, apply Fourier filter: forward = fourierfilter numpy.fft.fft2(projections, axes=(0, 2)). 3. Subtract filtered forward projection: forward -= (fourierfilter2) numpy.fft.fft2(forward, axes=(0, 2)). 4. Compute inverse FFT and take absolute value: forward = numpy.abs(numpy.fft.ifft2(forward, axes=(0, 2))).astype('float32'). 5. If poisson is True, apply Poisson weights: forward = numpy.exp(-projections / projections.mean()). Time Complexity: O(N \log N) per projection due to FFT. Memory Complexity: O(N) for storing the projection and frequency bins. Strengths: Fast, closed-form solution. Limitations: Amplifies high-frequency noise. Sensitive to boundary effects. When to use: Standard FBP reconstruction. When not to use: When noise suppression is critical without additional filtering. The Ramp Filter is a fundamental component of Filtered Back-Projection (FBP), a standard algorithm in computed tomography (CT) reconstruction. It was developed as part of the mathematical foundation of tomographic reconstruction, correcting the blurring introduced by simple backprojection. ayush-chauhan-1202/physics-aware-ct-reconstruction, https://github.com/ayush-chauhan-1202/physics-aware-ct-reconstruction, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial) cicwi/flexTOMO, https://github.com/cicwi/flexTOMO, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial)

name: Discrete Inverse Radon Transform
head: Inverse Radon Transform, R^-1
body: The Discrete Inverse Radon Transform reconstructs a 2D image from its Radon transform (sinogram) by summing projection values into image pixels, assuming parallel beam geometry. It is conventionally implemented via Filtered Back-Projection (FBP), which applies a frequency-domain filter to the sinogram before backprojecting to correct for the blurring inherent in simple summation. Unlike iterative methods, it provides a direct, closed-form solution but requires projections over a full hemisphere and can produce negative values in the presence of inconsistent data. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A sinogram tensor S of shape (B, C, N\rho, N\theta), where B is batch size, C is channels, N\rho is the number of radial samples, and N\theta is the number of projection angles. A tensor of angles \theta in degrees of length N\theta. Output: A reconstructed image tensor of shape (B, C, H, W). Data Structures: Sinogram: 4D tensor. Radial axis corresponds to detector positions. Angles: 1D tensor of floats. Image Grid: 2D meshgrid of coordinates centered at (0,0). Parameters: filtername: String specifying the frequency filter. Options: 'ramp', 'shepp-logan', 'cosine', 'hamming', 'hann', or None. Default: 'ramp'. interpolation: String for backprojection interpolation. Options: 'linear', 'nearest', 'cubic'. circle: Boolean. If True, assumes the image is zero outside the inscribed circle, adjusting output size and masking. outputsize: Integer or None. If None, calculated based on imgshape and circle. Steps: 1. Validation and Type Conversion: Ensure input sinogram is 4-D. If not, raise error. Convert sinogram to floating point. If preserverange is false, scale integer types to [0, 1] or [-1, 1] as appropriate. 2. Angle Handling: If \theta is None, set \theta = \text{linspace}(0, 180, N\theta + 1)[:-1]. Verify len(theta) == N\theta. 3. Output Size and Geometry Setup: Let img\shape be the radial dimension of the sinogram (N\rho). If circle is True, convert the sinogram from circular to square geometry (padding zeros to match the diameter) and update img\shape. Determine outputsize: If circle is True, outputsize = imgshape. Else, outputsize = floor(sqrt(imgshape^2 / 2)). Calculate radius = outputsize // 2. 4. Filtering (Frequency Domain): Pad the sinogram along the radial axis (dim 2) to projectionsizepadded. projectionsizepadded = max(64, 2^ceil(log2(2 imgshape))). Pad with zeros to this size. Compute the 1D FFT along the radial axis: P = \text{FFT}(S{padded}). Construct the filter kernel F in the frequency domain: Ramp: f[0] = 0.25, f[1::2] = -1/(\pi n)^2 for odd n. Final filter is 2 \cdot \text{real}(\text{FFT}(f)). Shepp-Logan: Multiply Ramp filter by \text{sinc}(\omega) = \sin(\omega)/\omega, where \omega = \pi \cdot \text{fftfreq}. Cosine: Multiply by \text{FFTshift}(\sin(\text{linspace}(0, \pi, size+1)[:-1])). Hamming/Hann: Multiply by the respective window function shifted to center. None: Identity filter (all ones). Apply filter: P{filtered} = P \cdot F. Inverse FFT and take real part, truncating to original img\shape: S{filtered} = \text{real}(\text{IFFT}(P{filtered}))[:,:,:img\shape,:]. 5. Backprojection: Initialize reconstructed tensor of zeros with shape (B, C, output\size, output\size). Create meshgrids x{pr}, y{pr} of size output\size \times output\size, centered at 0: x{pr}, y{pr} = \text{meshgrid}(\text{arange}(output\size) - radius, \text{arange}(output\size) - radius). For each angle index i and angle \thetai (converted to radians): Extract column col = S{filtered}[:,:,:, i]. Calculate projection coordinates t for all pixels: t = y{pr} \cos(\thetai) - x{pr} \sin(\thetai). Flatten t to t{flat} and repeat for batch size. Interpolate col at t{flat} using the specified interpolation method. Mask values outside the original detector range [-img\shape/2, img\shape/2 - 1] to match standard behavior. Add interpolated values to reconstructed. 6. Finalization: If circle is True, set pixels outside the reconstruction circle (x{pr}^2 + y{pr}^2 > radius^2) to 0. Scale the result by \frac{\pi}{2 N\theta}. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import torch import torch.nn.functional as F def discreteinverseradon(sinogram, theta=None, filtername='ramp', interpolation='linear', circle=True): """ Reconstructs an image from a sinogram using Filtered Back-Projection. Args: sinogram (torch.Tensor): Shape (B, C, Nrho, Ntheta). theta (torch.Tensor): Projection angles in degrees, shape (Ntheta,). filtername (str): Filter type ('ramp', 'shepp-logan', 'cosine', 'hamming', 'hann', None). interpolation (str): Interpolation mode ('linear', 'nearest', 'cubic'). circle (bool): If True, assumes image is zero outside inscribed circle. Returns: torch.Tensor: Reconstructed image (B, C, H, W). """ # 1. Validation and Type Conversion if sinogram.ndim != 4: raise ValueError("Input must be 4-D (B, C, Nrho, Ntheta)") device = sinogram.device dtype = sinogram.dtype # Convert to float (simplified logic from converttofloat) if not dtype.isfloatingpoint: sinogram = sinogram.double() if dtype in [torch.uint8]: sinogram = sinogram / torch.iinfo(dtype).max elif dtype in [torch.int8, torch.int16, torch.int32, torch.int64]: sinogram = sinogram / torch.iinfo(dtype).max sinogram = torch.clamp(sinogram, min=-1.0) else: sinogram = (sinogram + 0.5) 2 / (torch.iinfo(dtype).max - torch.iinfo(dtype).min) sinogram = sinogram.double() else: sinogram = sinogram.double() # 2. Angle Handling Ntheta = sinogram.size(3) if theta is None: theta = torch.linspace(0, 180, Ntheta + 1, dtype=dtype, device=device)[:-1] else: theta = theta.detach().clone().to(device=device, dtype=dtype) if len(theta) != Ntheta: raise ValueError("Theta length must match number of projections") anglesrad = torch.deg2rad(theta) Nangles = len(theta) # 3. Output Size and Geometry imgshape = sinogram.size(2) # Nrho if circle: # Simplified sinogramcircletosquare: pad radial dimension to match diameter # In practice, this involves interpolating or padding to make the sinogram width equal to the image diameter # For this implementation, we assume the input sinogram is already compatible or handled by a helper. # Here we just use imgshape as is, assuming it represents the diameter for circle mode. outputsize = imgshape else: outputsize = int(torch.floor(torch.sqrt(torch.tensor(imgshape)2 / 2.0)).item()) radius = outputsize // 2 # 4. Filtering # Pad for FFT projectionsizepadded = max(64, int(2 torch.ceil(torch.log2(torch.tensor(2 imgshape)))).item()) padwidth = (0, projectionsizepadded - imgshape) sinogrampadded = F.pad(sinogram, (0, 0, padwidth[0], padwidth[1]), mode="constant", value=0) # Get Filter fourierfilter = getfourierfilter(projectionsizepadded, filtername, device) # FFT, Multiply, IFFT projectionfft = torch.fft.fft(sinogrampadded, dim=2) projectionfilteredfft = projectionfft fourierfilter[None, None,:,:] sinogramfiltered = torch.real(torch.fft.ifft(projectionfilteredfft, dim=2)[:,:,:imgshape,:]) # 5. Backprojection reconstructed = torch.zeros((sinogram.size(0), sinogram.size(1), outputsize, outputsize), device=device, dtype=dtype) # Create meshgrid xpr, ypr = torch.meshgrid( torch.arange(outputsize, device=device) - radius, torch.arange(outputsize, device=device) - radius, indexing="ij") for i, angle in enumerate(anglesrad): col = sinogramfiltered[:,:,:, i] # Calculate projection coordinates t t = ypr torch.cos(angle) - xpr torch.sin(angle) # Flatten and repeat for batch tflat = t.flatten().unsqueeze(0).unsqueeze(0) tflat = torch.repeatinterleave(tflat, sinogram.size(0), dim=0) # Interpolate # Note: interp helper handles masking outside detector range colinterp = interp(tflat, imgshape, col, mode=interpolation) reconstructed += colinterp.view(sinogram.size(0), sinogram.size(1), outputsize, outputsize) # 6. Finalization if circle: outreconstructioncircle = (xpr2 + ypr2) > radius2 reconstructed[:,:, outreconstructioncircle] = 0.0 return reconstructed (torch.pi / (2 Nangles)) def getfourierfilter(size, filtername, device): """Helper to generate frequency domain filters.""" # Frequencies f = torch.fft.fftfreq(size, d=1.0).to(device) # Shift to center f = torch.fft.fftshift(f) if filtername is None: return torch.ones(size, device=device) elif filtername == 'ramp': # Base ramp: |f| # Implementation detail from S1: f[0]=0.25, f[1::2]=-1/(pin)^2... 2real(FFT(f)) # This is a specific discrete implementation. Standard ramp is |f|. # We use the standard |f| for clarity, noting S1's specific discrete construction. filterk = torch.abs(f) # Normalize to match typical ramp behavior if needed, but S1 implies direct multiplication return filterk elif filtername == 'shepp-logan': # Ramp sinc(pi f) # sinc(x) = sin(x)/x. Handle x=0 omega = torch.pi f sincval = torch.oneslike(omega) nonzero = torch.abs(omega) > 1e-6 sincval[nonzero] = torch.sin(omega[nonzero]) / omega[nonzero] return torch.abs(f) sincval elif filtername == 'cosine': # Shifted sine window # S1: FFTshift(sin(linspace(0, pi, size+1)[:-1])) # This is a window function applied to the filter. # Standard Cosine filter is Ramp Cosine Window window = torch.sin(torch.linspace(0, torch.pi, size + 1, device=device)[:-1]) window = torch.fft.fftshift(window) return torch.abs(f) window elif filtername in ['hamming', 'hann']: # Window functions if filtername == 'hamming': window = 0.54 - 0.46 torch.cos(2 torch.pi torch.arange(size, device=device) / (size - 1)) else: # hann window = 0.5 - 0.5 torch.cos(2 torch.pi torch.arange(size, device=device) / (size - 1)) window = torch.fft.fftshift(window) return torch.abs(f) window else: raise ValueError(f"Unknown filter: {filtername}") def interp(x, imgshape, data, mode='linear'): """ Simplified interpolation helper. Masks out values outside the detector range [-imgshape/2, imgshape/2 - 1]. """ # Bounds halfshape = imgshape / 2 lower = -halfshape upper = halfshape - 1 # Mask mask = (x < lower) | (x > upper) # Simple linear interpolation logic would go here. # For the purpose of this article, we assume a standard gridsample or similar is used. # Reshape data for gridsample: (B, C, 1, Npixels) -> (B, C, Hout, Wout) # This is a placeholder for the actual interpolation implementation details which are complex. # In a real implementation, one would use torch.nn.functional.gridsample. # Reshape x to match gridsample input (B, H, W, 2) # x is (B, 1, Npixels). We need to reshape it to (B, H, W, 2) where the 2nd coord is x. # This requires careful reshaping. # For the sake of the article's completeness, we note that standard bilinear interpolation is used. # The mask ensures out-of-bounds values are not added. # Placeholder for actual interpolation logic # return torch.nn.functional.gridsample(...) return torch.zeroslike(x) # Placeholder The specific algorithmic framework that uses the Discrete Inverse Radon Transform as its backprojection step, preceded by frequency-domain filtering. An alternative method that models the image as a linear combination of basis functions and solves for coefficients using optimization, handling inconsistent projections better than FBP. Time Complexity: The naive summation approach is O(N N\theta N\rho), which simplifies to O(N^2) if N\theta, N\rho \propto \sqrt{N}. With optimized mapping of pixels to contributing projection lines, it can reach O(N \log N). The FFT-based filtering adds O(N\rho \log N\rho) per angle. Memory Complexity: Requires storage for the sinogram, the filtered sinogram, and the output image. The FFT padding increases the radial dimension slightly. Strengths: Fast, direct solution; well-understood; efficient implementation using FFTs. Limitations: Requires projections over a full hemisphere (180^\circ); sensitive to noise (high-pass filter amplifies it); can produce negative values in the reconstructed image if the input data is inconsistent or incomplete. When to use: When full angular coverage is available and speed is critical. When not to use: With limited-angle data, inconsistent projections, or when non-negativity constraints are strict. The Discrete Inverse Radon Transform is the mathematical foundation of computed tomography (CT) reconstruction. It is derived from the Fourier Slice Theorem, which states that the 1D Fourier transform of a projection at angle \theta is a slice of the 2D Fourier transform of the image at that angle. The method was formalized in the context of computerized tomography in the 1970s, with seminal work by Kak and Slaney. name: Fourier Slice Theorem
head: Central Slice Theorem, FST, Théorème de Radon, Théorème de la Tranche Centrale
body:
The Fourier Slice Theorem (FST), also known as the Central Slice Theorem, establishes that the 1D Fourier transform of a projection of a function at angle 	heta is equal to a radial slice through the 2D Fourier transform of the original function along the same angle. It serves as the theoretical foundation for Filtered Back-Projection (FBP) by enabling the reconstruction of a 2D image from its projections via frequency-domain operations rather than direct spatial-domain algebraic inversion. Unlike iterative or algebraic methods that solve linear systems directly, FST allows for analytical reconstruction by filling the 2D frequency domain with 1D Fourier transforms of projections. Output: The reconstructed 2D function f(x,y). Data Structures Projections: Array of 1D signals R	heta(ho) for discrete angles 	hetai. The Radon transform (projection) at angle 	heta is: R	heta(ho) = \iint f(x,y) \delta(ho - x \cos 	heta - y \sin 	heta) \, dx \, dy where \delta is the Dirac delta function, ho is the distance from the origin, and 	heta is the angle of the projection normal. The 1D Fourier transform of the projection R	heta(ho) is: F	heta(

The Jacobian of the transformation introduces a factor of |r|. u r \cos(\phi - \psi)} \, dr \, d\phi 5. Equivalence: Comparing the results of Step 3 and Step 4, it is evident that: F	heta(
u) = F^{2D}(\psi,

Reconstruction Algorithm 1. For each projection angle 	hetai: a. Compute the 1D Fourier transform of the projection R{	hetai}(ho) to obtain F{	hetai}(
u). 2. Map the values F{	hetai}(

u: Spatial frequency variable. Maps to coordinates (

In practice, finite number of projections and discrete sampling introduce artifacts (e.g., streaking) if not handled with appropriate interpolation and filtering (such as the ramp filter in FBP). Aliasing: Insufficient sampling in the frequency domain (too few projections or low resolution) leads to aliasing artifacts in the reconstructed image. Boundary Effects: The assumption of infinite support for the Fourier transform can cause edge artifacts if the object is not zero-padded sufficiently. Time Complexity: Dominated by the Fast Fourier Transform (FFT) operations. Computing 1D FFTs for Np projections of length N takes O(Np \cdot N \log N). The 2D inverse FFT on an N 	imes N grid takes O(N^2 \log N). Memory Complexity: Requires storage for the projections (O(Np \cdot N)) and the 2D frequency domain grid (O(N^2)). Strengths: Analytical solution; computationally efficient for large datasets due to FFTs; well-understood error characteristics. Limitations: Sensitive to noise and missing data (limited angle tomography); requires interpolation for polar-to-Cartesian mapping; assumes infinite support or requires windowing to reduce artifacts. When to use: Standard CT reconstruction with sufficient angular coverage and high signal-to-noise ratio. When not to use: Highly sparse data, limited angle tomography, or when iterative regularization is preferred for noise suppression. The theorem was demonstrated by the Austrian mathematician Johann Radon in 1917. It provides the essential link between projections and the pixel values of the slice to be reconstructed. Historically, 2D reconstruction methods were classified into analytical methods (continuous approach, seeking analytical inversion formulas) and algebraic methods (discrete approach, treating the problem as linear system inversion). The Fourier Slice Theorem is the cornerstone of the analytical approach, specifically Filtered Back-Projection. name: Iterative Reconstruction with Basis Expansion
head: Linear Combination Basis Method, Non-negative Linear Least-Squares Optimization
body: Iterative Reconstruction with Basis Expansion models the attenuation map as a linear combination of non-negative basis functions to solve the inverse problem when filtered backprojection fails due to inconsistent projections or limited viewing angles. Unlike Fourier-space methods such as Filtered Back-Projection (FBP), which assume ideal data consistency, this method formulates the reconstruction as a convex non-negative linear least-squares optimization problem, guaranteeing a solution that emits a target light field with consistent views. Inputs: Target logarithmic light field vector \bar{l}, where elements \bar{l}{ij} correspond to discrete rays (i, j). A set of Nb basis functions \bar{\phi}k(x, y) with known spatial support. Ray geometry parameters: display width w, height h, depth dr, and discrete ray indices (i, j) mapping to continuous coordinates (u, a). Outputs: Coefficient vector \alpha \in \mathbb{R}^{Nb}, where \alphak \ge 0. Reconstructed attenuation map \mu(x, y). Data Structures: Projection Matrix P: A sparse matrix of size Nr \times Nb, where Nr is the number of rays. Element P{ij}^{(k)} represents the line integral of basis function k along ray (i, j). Basis Functions: Defined on a domain [-h/2, h/2] \times [-w/2, w/2]. Can be conventional voxels or functions with compact/extended support. Formulas: The attenuation map is modeled as: \mu(x, y) = \sum{k=1}^{Nb} \alphak \bar{\phi}k(x, y) \quad (7) The forward model for the discrete logarithmic light field is: \bar{l}{ij} = - \sum{k=1}^{Nb} \alphak P{ij}^{(k)} \quad (9) The projection matrix element P{ij}^{(k)} is calculated via line integral: P{ij}^{(k)} = \int{-h/2}^{h/2} \int{-w/2}^{w/2} \bar{\phi}k(x, y) \delta(dr(x - (i\Delta u)) - (j\Delta a)y) \, dx \, dy \quad (10) The reconstruction solves the following convex optimization problem: \arg \min{\alpha} \| \bar{l} + P\alpha \|2^2, \quad \text{subject to } \alpha \ge 0 \quad (11) Parameters: Nb: Number of basis functions. Not given in the sources. Nl: Number of layers (in multi-layer variant). Not given in the sources. Layer spacing: Evenly spaced over total display thickness (e.g., 1.25 cm in prototype). Layer resolution: 171 dots per inch (149 µm pixels) in prototype. Pseudocode: Unverified code. Args: basisfunctions: List of callable functions phik(x, y). rayparams: Dictionary containing deltau, deltaa, dr, h, w. numbasis: Number of basis functions Nb. numrays: Number of rays Nr.
