Args: lightfield: Vector lbar of target logarithmic light field values. basisfunctions: List of callable basis functions. rayparams: Geometry parameters. numbasis: Number of basis functions. Returns: alpha: Vector of non-negative coefficients. """ numrays = len(lightfield) # 1. Construct the projection matrix P P = computeprojectionmatrix(basisfunctions, rayparams, numbasis, numrays) # 2. Solve the optimization problem: arg min || lbar + P alpha ||^2 s.t. alpha >= 0 # This is equivalent to: arg min || P alpha - (-lbar) ||^2 # Using scipy's nnls which solves min ||b - Ax||^2 s.t. x >= 0 # Here A = P, b = -lbar b = -lightfield alpha, = nnls(P, b) return alpha def renderlightfield(alpha, basisfunctions, rayparams, numrays): """ Renders the light field from the reconstructed coefficients. Deviations from this linearity may affect perceptual quality. Boundaries: The integration domain is bounded by the display dimensions [-h/2, h/2] \times [-w/2, w/2]. Basis functions extending outside this domain must be handled correctly in the projection matrix calculation. Degenerate Input: If the viewing angles are too limited, the system matrix P may be ill-conditioned, leading to unstable solutions. The non-negativity constraint helps regularize the solution. A tomographic method for reconstructing a volumetric density field from a small number of camera images by modeling the scene as a linear combination of basis functions with local support. It differs from Fourier-space methods like Filtered Back-Projection (FBP) by using basis functions with finite support to create a sparse system matrix, which allows the solution space to be restricted by a visual hull to discard zero-valued variables. A model representing the attenuator as a finite number Nl of discrete attenuation layers (masks) separated by distances dk, where each mask controls spatially-varying transmittance. The forward model for the logarithmic light field is \bar{l}(u, a) = \sum{k=1}^{Nl} \ln tk(u + (dk/dr)a) = - \sum{k=1}^{Nl} ak(u + (dk/dr)a), where ak(\xi) = -\ln tk(\xi) is the absorbance of mask k at position \xi. This leads to a linear system similar to the single-layer case, allowing the use of the same iterative reconstruction algorithm. In the prototype, layers are evenly-spaced over a total display thickness of 1.25 cm, with a resolution of 171 dots per inch (149 µm pixels). Time Complexity: The method requires iterative optimization, which is computationally more complex than direct transform methods like FBP. The complexity depends on the number of basis functions Nb, the number of rays Nr, and the convergence rate of the optimization algorithm. Memory Complexity: Requires storing the projection matrix P, which is Nr \times Nb. If basis functions have local support, P is sparse, reducing memory requirements. Measured Performance: In the prototype, a 5.7 cm × 7.6 cm display with 1.25 cm thickness and 171 dpi resolution was used. The scene was rendered as a light field with 7×7 oblique projections. Strengths: Better accounts for inconsistent projections over limited angles compared to FBP. Guarantees consistent views in the least-squares sense. Limitations: Higher computational complexity than FBP. Requires careful selection of basis functions and optimization parameters. When to use: When projections are inconsistent or viewing angles are limited, making FBP unsuitable. When not to use: When computational resources are limited and projections are consistent. The method was introduced by Wetzstein et al. in 2011 in the paper "Layered 3D: Tomographic Image Synthesis for Attenuation-based Light Field and High Dynamic Range Displays". It builds on the work of Herman [1995] on iterative reconstruction algorithms. The approach is motivated by the need to synthesize attenuation maps for layered 3D displays, where traditional transform methods fail due to the discrete nature of the layers and limited viewing angles. The method leverages the Weber-Fechner law to justify the use of logarithmic light field values in the optimization. name: Iterative Reconstruction with Local Support Basis Functions
head: Algebraic Reconstruction with Visual Hull and Local Basis, Sparse-View Tomographic Reconstruction of Flames
body: A tomographic method for reconstructing a volumetric density field from a small number of camera images by modeling the scene as a linear combination of basis functions with local support. It differs from Fourier-space methods like Filtered Back-Projection (FBP) by using basis functions with finite support to create a sparse system matrix, which allows the solution space to be restricted by a visual hull to discard zero-valued variables. Inputs: A set of N images from different camera viewpoints. Camera calibration data (intrinsics and extrinsics) for each viewpoint. A 3D voxel grid defining the spatial domain. A visual hull mask indicating regions where density is known to be zero. Outputs: A vector of coefficients \mathbf{a} representing the density field. The reconstructed 3D density field \phi. Data Structures: Voxel Grid: A regular 3D grid of resolution Rx \times Ry \times Rz. Basis Functions: Defined on the voxel grid. Two types are described: 1. Box Basis: Defined on a single voxel i. 2. Trilinear Basis: Defined on a 2 \times 2 \times 2 block of voxels, centered at the voxel corner, with one-voxel overlap in every dimension to ensure smooth blending. System Matrix S: A sparse matrix of size N{pixels} \times N{basis}. Rows correspond to pixels, columns to basis functions. Entry s{ni} is the integral of the i-th basis function along the backprojected ray of pixel p. Steps: 1. Define the Image Formation Model: Model the image intensity Ip for pixel p as the line integral of the density field \phi along the backprojected ray c: Ip = \intc \phi \, ds \quad (1) Assumptions: negligible absorption/scattering and proportional self-emission. 2. Basis Expansion: Assume \phi is a linear combination of basis functions \phii with coefficients ai: \phi(\mathbf{x}) = \sumi ai \phii(\mathbf{x}) Substitute into (1) and swap sum and integral: Ip = \sumi ai \left( \intc \phii \, ds \right) \quad (2) This forms the linear system \mathbf{p} = S\mathbf{a}, where \mathbf{p} is the vector of pixel intensities, S{pi} = \intc \phii \, ds, and \mathbf{a} is the vector of coefficients. 3. Construct Matrix S (Sparse Setup): Compute entries s{ni} by intersecting backprojected rays with basis function supports. Use voxel-aligned basis functions to reduce intersection computation from O(n^3) to O(3n) by intersecting 3n planes and performing a lookup. Box Basis: For a box basis function \phii^{Box} defined on voxel i with bounds [x{min}^j, x{max}^j], [y{min}^j, y{max}^j], [z{min}^j, z{max}^j]: \phii^{Box}(x,y,z) = \begin{cases} 1 & \text{if } x{min}^j < x \leq x{max}^j \land y{min}^j < y \leq y{max}^j \land z{min}^j < z \leq z{max}^j \\ 0 & \text{otherwise} \end{cases} \quad (3) Let x1 and x2 be the intersection points of ray cn with voxel i. The entry is the distance between these points: s{ni} = \|x2 - x1\| \quad (4) Trilinear Basis: Arranged on the voxel grid with one-voxel overlap in every dimension. The intersection of the ray with the support is a cubic polynomial. This polynomial is integrated analytically. 4. Restrict Solution Space (Visual Hull): Discard variables (coefficients ai) corresponding to basis functions entirely outside the visual hull (known to be zero). This reduces the size of \mathbf{a} and S. 5. Solve Linear System: Solve for \mathbf{a} using a least-squares approach: \mathbf{a} = (S^T S)^{-1} S^T \mathbf{p} \quad (5) Note: The matrix S is often ill-conditioned with a large condition number (quotient of largest to smallest singular value), making direct inversion difficult. Iterative solvers or regularization may be required in practice, though the source specifies the least-squares formulation. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def reconstructdensity(pixels, cameras, voxelgrid, visualhullmask, basistype='box'): """ Reconstructs density field using iterative reconstruction with local support basis functions. Args: pixels: List of pixel intensities for all cameras. cameras: List of camera objects with projection matrices. voxelgrid: 3D grid defining voxel boundaries. visualhullmask: 3D boolean array, True where density may exist. basistype: 'box' or 'trilinear'. Returns: a: Vector of basis coefficients. """ # 1. Identify active basis functions based on visual hull activebasisindices = [] for i, basis in enumerate(voxelgrid.basisfunctions(basistype)): if basis.intersects(visualhullmask): activebasisindices.append(i) numpixels = len(pixels) numactivebasis = len(activebasisindices) # 2. Construct sparse matrix S # S is numpixels x numactivebasis S = sparsematrix(numpixels, numactivebasis) for pidx, pixel in enumerate(pixels): # Get backprojected ray for this pixel ray = cameras[pixel.cameraid].backprojectray(pixel.u, pixel.v) for basiscol, basisidx in enumerate(activebasisindices): basis = voxelgrid.basisfunctions(basistype)[basisidx] # Compute integral of basis function along ray # For box: distance between intersection points # For trilinear: analytical integral of cubic polynomial if basistype == 'box': x1, x2 = ray.intersectvoxel(basis.voxelbounds) sval = norm(x2 - x1) elif basistype == 'trilinear': # Intersection is cubic polynomial; integrate analytically poly = ray.intersecttrilinearsupport(basis.gridposition) sval = integrateanalytically(poly) else: raise ValueError("Unknown basis type") S[pidx, basiscol] = sval # 3. Solve least squares system: a = (S^T S)^-1 S^T p # Note: S^T S may be ill-conditioned StS = S.transpose() @ S StP = S.transpose() @ pixels # Use a stable solver (e.g., conjugate gradient or SVD) due to ill-conditioning # Direct inversion is discouraged due to large condition number a = solvelinearsystem(StS, StP) return a Time Complexity: Matrix construction is O(3n) per ray/basis pair due to voxel-aligned intersection optimization, where n is the number of planes intersected. Solving the linear system depends on the solver; direct inversion is O(N^3) but unstable due to ill-conditioning. Memory Complexity: The matrix S is sparse, requiring memory proportional to the number of non-zero entries, which is significantly less than the full matrix required by Fourier basis functions. Strengths: Allows high-quality reconstruction from a small number of camera images (sparse-view) by restricting the solution space with a visual hull. Handles perspective projection correctly. Trilinear basis functions allow smooth blending and hardware-accelerated visualization. Limitations: The system matrix S is ill-conditioned, making inversion difficult. Requires a static camera setup for dynamic flames. Assumes negligible absorption/scattering and proportional self-emission. Originated in the paper "Image-based tomographic reconstruction of flames". It was developed to address the difficulty of generating convincing computer-animated fire, which is chaotic and hard to simulate. The method adapts algebraic reconstruction techniques (ART) to tomography, differing from Radon transform methods by using local support basis functions and a visual hull constraint. It is applicable to static camera setups observing dynamic flames, enabling fast processing of multi-video sequences for time-varying models. name: Radon Transform (Direct)
head: Discrete Radon Transform, skradon
body: Computes the Radon transform (sinogram) of a batch of multi-channel images by rotating the image and summing along one axis for each angle. It differs from TorchRadon by providing a specific implementation of the direct projection operator within the torchskradon library, focusing on explicit rotation and summation steps rather than optimized Fourier-space approximations. Inputs: image: A 4-D torch.Tensor of shape (B, C, H, W) representing a batch of multi-channel images. theta: A 1-D torch.Tensor of angles in degrees. If None, defaults to torch.arange(180, dtype=torch.float32). circle: A boolean flag. If True, assumes the image is zero outside the inscribed circle and crops to a square; if False, pads the image to the diagonal size. preserverange: A boolean flag. If True, preserves the original value range by converting to double precision if necessary; if False, scales integer types to [0.0, 1.0] or [-1.0, 1.0]. Outputs: radonimage: A torch.Tensor of shape (B, C, N, M), where B is batch size, C is channels, N is the projection width (padded image size), and M is the number of angles. Data Structures: The implementation uses standard PyTorch tensors. No custom data structures are defined. Steps: 1. Type Conversion: Convert image to float using converttofloat(image, preserverange). If preserverange is true, convert non-float types to double. If false, scale unsigned integers to [0.0, 1.0] and signed integers to [-1.0, 1.0]. 2. Validation: Validate input is 4-D. If theta is None, set theta = torch.arange(180, dtype=torch.float32). Clone theta and move it to the same device as image. 3. Preprocessing (Circle Mode): If circle is True: Calculate shapemin = min(image.size()[2:]) and radius = shapemin // 2. Create a meshgrid x, y for the image coordinates. Calculate distance from center: dist = ((coords - center.view(-1, 1, 1)) 2).sum(0). Identify outsidereconstructioncircle = dist > radius2. Warn if any non-zero values exist outside the circle. Calculate excess = imgshape - shapemin. Create slices to crop the image to a square: paddedimage = image[:,:, slices[0], slices[1]]. 4. Preprocessing (Padding Mode): If circle is False: Calculate diagonal = torch.sqrt(torch.tensor(2)) max(image.size()[2:]). Calculate padding pad = [int(torch.ceil(diagonal - s)) for s in image.size()[2:]]. Calculate new/old centers and pad widths. Apply torch.nn.functional.pad with mode 'constant' and value 0 to get paddedimage. 5. Square Assertion: Assert paddedimage is square. If paddedimage.size()[2] != paddedimage.size()[3], raise ValueError. 6. Center Calculation: If paddedimage.size()[2] is even, center = 0.5; else center = 0.0. 7. Initialization: Initialize radonimage tensor of shape (batch, channels, paddedsize, len(theta)) with zeros. 8. Rotation and Summation: Loop for i, angle in enumerate(torch.deg2rad(theta)): Calculate cosa, sina = torch.cos(angle), torch.sin(angle). Construct 3x3 rotation matrix R: R = \begin{bmatrix} \cosa & \sina & -center \cdot \frac{\cosa + \sina - 1}{padded\size / 2} \\ -\sina & \cosa & -center \cdot \frac{\cosa - \sina - 1}{padded\size / 2} \\ 0 & 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix} Warp image using rotated = warp(paddedimage, R). Sum along axis 2: radonimage[:,:,:, i] = rotated.sum(2). Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import torch import torch.nn.functional as F def radontransform(image, theta=None, circle=True, preserverange=True): # Step 1: Type Conversion if image.dtype == torch.float16: image = image.float() if preserverange: if image.dtype not in [torch.float32, torch.float64]: image = image.double() else: if not image.dtype.isfloatingpoint: if image.dtype == torch.bool: image = image.double() elif image.dtype == torch.uint8: imaxin = torch.iinfo(image.dtype).max image = image / imaxin image = image.double() elif image.dtype in [torch.int8, torch.int16, torch.int32, torch.int64]: # Signed integers -> [-1.0, 1.0] imaxin = torch.iinfo(image.dtype).max image = image / imaxin image = image.double() # Step 2: Validation assert image.dim() == 4, "Input must be 4-D" if theta is None: theta = torch.arange(180, dtype=torch.float32, device=image.device) else: theta = theta.clone().to(image.device) # Step 3 & 4: Preprocessing if circle: shapemin = min(image.size()[2:]) radius = shapemin // 2 # Create meshgrid and calculate distance from center # Note: Exact meshgrid creation depends on image dimensions # Assuming standard coordinate system y, x = torch.meshgrid(torch.arange(image.size(2), device=image.device), torch.arange(image.size(3), device=image.device), indexing='ij') centercoord = shapemin / 2.0 dist = ((x - centercoord) 2 + (y - centercoord) 2) outsidereconstructioncircle = dist > radius 2 if torch.any((image != 0) & outsidereconstructioncircle): import warnings warnings.warn("Non-zero values exist outside the reconstruction circle") excess = [image.size(2) - shapemin, image.size(3) - shapemin] slices = [] for e in excess: if e.item() > 0: slices.append((int(torch.ceil(e / 2).item()), int(torch.ceil(e / 2).item() + shapemin))) else: slices.append(slice(None)) paddedimage = image[:,:, slices[0][0]:slices[0][1], slices[1][0]:slices[1][1]] else: diagonal = torch.sqrt(torch.tensor(2.0, device=image.device)) max(image.size()[2:]) pad = [int(torch.ceil(diagonal - s)) for s in image.size()[2:]] newcenter = [(s + p) // 2 for s, p in zip(image.size()[2:], pad)] oldcenter = [s // 2 for s in image.size()[2:]] padbefore = [nc - oc for oc, nc in zip(oldcenter, newcenter)] padwidth = [(pb, p - pb) for pb, p in zip(padbefore, pad)] # padwidth format for F.pad: (left, right, top, bottom) # padwidth[0] is for dim 2 (height), padwidth[1] is for dim 3 (width) paddedimage = F.pad(image, (padwidth[1][0], padwidth[1][1], padwidth[0][0], padwidth[0][1]), mode="constant", value=0) # Step 5: Square Assertion if paddedimage.size()[2] != paddedimage.size()[3]: raise ValueError("paddedimage must be a square") # Step 6: Center Calculation if paddedimage.size()[2] % 2 == 0: center = 0.5 else: center = 0.0 # Step 7: Initialization radonimage = torch.zeros( (paddedimage.size(0), paddedimage.size(1), paddedimage.size(2), len(theta)), dtype=paddedimage.dtype, device=paddedimage.device,) # Step 8: Rotation and Summation for i, angle in enumerate(torch.deg2rad(theta)): cosa, sina = torch.cos(angle), torch.sin(angle) R = torch.tensor([ [cosa, sina, -center (cosa + sina - 1) / (paddedimage.size(2) / 2)], [-sina, cosa, -center (cosa - sina - 1) / (paddedimage.size(3) / 2)], [0, 0, 1] ], dtype=paddedimage.dtype, device=paddedimage.device) # Warp function is not standard PyTorch, assuming a gridsample based implementation # or a custom warp function. For completeness, we assume a helper warp exists # that applies the affine transform R. rotated = warp(paddedimage, R) radonimage[:,:,:, i] = rotated.sum(2) return radonimage def warp(image, R): # Helper to apply affine transformation R to image # R is 3x3. We extract 2x3 affine matrix. # This is a placeholder for the actual warping logic which typically uses gridsample # with an inverse mapping. # For the purpose of this article, we assume the existence of a valid warp function # as described in the source. pass Parameters: circle: bool, optional. If True, assumes image is zero outside inscribed circle and crops to square. If False, pads to diagonal size. preserverange: bool, optional. Whether to keep original value range or convert via imgasfloat conventions. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: If circle=True and image has non-zero values outside the reconstruction circle, a UserWarning is raised. If circle=False, the padded image must be square. If not, ValueError is raised. Precision issues may arise when converting integer types to float/double, especially with large dynamic ranges. Time and Memory Complexity: Time complexity is O(B \cdot C \cdot N^2 \cdot M), where B is batch size, C is channels, N is image size, and M is number of angles, due to the rotation and summation for each angle. Memory complexity is O(B \cdot C \cdot N \cdot M) for the output sinogram. Measured Performance: Not given in the sources. Scaling: Scales linearly with batch size, channels, and number of angles. Strengths and Limitations: Strengths: Explicit control over rotation and summation; supports multi-channel images. Limitations: Computationally expensive for large images and many angles due to explicit warping; requires square images after preprocessing. When to Use: Use when explicit control over the projection process is needed, or when integrating with other torchskradon operations. When Not to Use: Avoid for large-scale tomographic reconstruction where performance is critical; consider Fourier-space methods instead. The Radon transform is a fundamental tool in tomography, mapping a function to its line integrals. The direct implementation described here is part of the torchskradon library, which provides differentiable Radon transform operations in PyTorch. It is based on the principles outlined in "Principles of Computerized Tomographic Imaging" by Kak and Slaney. tomluetjen/torchskradon, https://github.com/tomluetjen/torchskradon, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial)

name: Gradient w.r.t Source/Detector Geometry
head: Cone Beam Geometry Gradient, Cone Beam Geometry Gradient CUDA Kernel, Gradient of Projection Error w.r.t Source and Detector Positions
body: Computes the gradient of the projection error (or forward projection loss) with respect to the 3D positions of the X-ray source and detector elements in a cone-beam geometry. It differs from standard back-projection by applying the chain rule through the trilinear interpolation derivatives, scattering gradients back to the camera parameters rather than the volume. It is the adjoint operation required for differentiable tomographic reconstruction where geometry is optimized. Inputs: volume: 3D volume data in a bricked layout with a 1-voxel zero border. sources: Array of source positions. detectors: Array of detector element positions. box: 12 floats defining volume centre (3), half-extent (3), inverse voxel spacing (3), and stored centre coordinate (3). grad: Packed gradient tensor for the current group. n: Number of sample points along each ray. Outputs: gradsources: Gradient w.r.t. source positions. graddetectors: Gradient w.r.t. detector positions. Data Structures: ConeRay: Struct containing ray origin (source), direction components (ex, ey, ez), length, entry/exit distances along the ray (entry, exit), entry/exit axes (entryaxis, exitaxis), and sample step parameters in stored coordinates (px, py, pz, sx, sy, sz). Layout: Defines volume dimensions (X, Y, Z) and brick tiling parameters (bricksx, row, plane). Algorithm Steps: 1. Initialization: For each thread handling a ray, initialize F=0 (accumulated value), G[3]={0} (accumulated spatial gradients), M[3]={0} (accumulated weighted spatial gradients), and loaded=0xffffffff (cache invalidation flag). 2. Ray Setup: Construct the ConeRay from source and detector positions. Compute direction vector \vec{e} = \text{detector} - \text{source} and length L = \|\vec{e}\|. If L \le 0, skip. Normalize direction \vec{u} = \vec{e}/L. Clip the ray against the volume box defined by box to find entry, exit, and the axes of intersection (entryaxis, exitaxis). If the ray misses the volume, skip. Compute step size in stored coordinates: weight = (\text{exit} - \text{entry}) / n. Compute starting position in stored coordinates for the first sample midpoint. 3. Sampling Loop: Iterate k from 0 to n-1. Calculate the current sample position in stored coordinates using px, py, pz and steps sx, sy, sz. Determine the 8 neighboring voxel indices (trilinear stencil). If the stencil index has not been loaded (s.index != loaded): fetch the 8 voxel values from the volume for all channels, weight by g[c], store in v[q], and set loaded = s.index. Compute the interpolated value f and its spatial derivatives fx, fy, fz using the precomputed trilinear derivatives. Accumulate: F \leftarrow F + f; G[0] \leftarrow G[0] + fx, G[1] \leftarrow G[1] + fy, G[2] \leftarrow G[2] + fz; M[0] \leftarrow M[0] + w \cdot fx, M[1] \leftarrow M[1] + w \cdot fy, M[2] \leftarrow M[2] + w \cdot fz where w = (k + 0.5) / n. 4. Gradient Accumulation: Let E = [ex, ey, ez] be the ray direction vector. Let \taue = \text{entry} / L and \taux = \text{exit} / L be the normalized entry and exit positions. Let \delta = \taux - \taue be the normalized ray span. Let step = weight. Scale G[a] and M[a] by box[6+a]. Compute GE = \sum{a} G[a] \cdot E[a] and ME = \sum{a} M[a] \cdot E[a]. Compute \text{along} = \delta \cdot F / n and \text{ends} = L \cdot F / n. For each axis a \in \{0, 1, 2\}: H = \taue \cdot G[a] + \delta \cdot M[a]; \text{gd}[a] = \text{along} \cdot E[a] / L + \text{step} \cdot H; \text{gs}[a] = \text{step} \cdot G[a] - \text{gd}[a]. 5. Boundary Corrections: If a == \text{exit\axis}: c = (\text{ends} + \text{step} \cdot ME) / E[a]; \text{gs}[a] \leftarrow \text{gs}[a] - c \cdot (1 - \taux); \text{gd}[a] \leftarrow \text{gd}[a] - c \cdot \taux. If a == \text{entry\axis}: c = (-\text{ends} + \text{step} \cdot (GE - ME)) / E[a]; \text{gs}[a] \leftarrow \text{gs}[a] - c \cdot (1 - \taue); \text{gd}[a] \leftarrow \text{gd}[a] - c \cdot \taue. 6. Writing Results: Write \text{gd}[a] to graddetectors[3r + a] for active rays. Reduce \text{gs}[a] across the warp using warp shuffle instructions. name: Explicit Radon Matrix Construction
head: Explicit Radon Transform Matrix Construction, Forward Projection Matrix, System Matrix
body: Explicit Radon Matrix Construction computes the full forward projection matrix A for a parallel-beam CT geometry, mapping voxel values to sinogram bins. It differs from iterative or approximate methods by materializing the complete linear operator, enabling direct algebraic solutions or explicit adjoint verification. Inputs: Volume dimensions: height v, width h. Projection parameters: number of angles n\angles, maximum angle max\angle, number of detector samples n\samples. SVD mode: boolean sparsesvd (default True). Outputs: Explicit projection matrix A of shape (n\samples \times n\angles, v \times h). Right singular vectors W (if SVD is computed). Data Structures: volgeom: Volume geometry object defining the voxel grid v \times h. projgeom: Projection geometry object defining parallel beam geometry with detector spacing 1.0, n\samples detectors, and n\angles angles. projectorid: Identifier for the 'strip' projector type, linking volgeom and projgeom. Aexp: List of column vectors, each of shape (n\samples \times n\angles, 1). Steps: 1. Define angle vector \thetai = i \cdot \frac{max\angle}{n\angles} for i \in [0, n\angles-1]. 2. Create volume geometry volgeom for dimensions v \times h. 3. Create projection geometry projgeom with type 'parallel', detector spacing 1.0, n\samples samples, and angles \theta. 4. Create projector ID using 'strip' projector type with projgeom and volgeom. 5. Initialize empty list Aexp. 6. For each column col from 0 to v-1: a. For each row row from 0 to h-1: i. Create dummy image dummyimg of shape (v, h) initialized to zeros. ii. Set dummyimg[row][col] = 1.0. iii. Compute sinogram sino by projecting dummyimg.T using projectorid. iv. Reshape sino to shape (-1, 1) using Fortran order. v. Append sino to Aexp. 7. Horizontally stack Aexp into matrix A. 8. If sparsesvd is true, compute right singular vectors W using sparse SVD on A; otherwise, use dense SVD. 9. Return A and W. Pseudocode: Unverified code. name: Dirac Pixel Kernel
head: Dirac interpolator, Noyau de pixel Dirac
body: The Dirac Pixel Kernel is a weighting function used in tomographic back-projection that assigns equal importance to all projection lines traversing a pixel, effectively treating the pixel as a binary switch for ray intersection. It is derived directly from the continuous Radon transform equation but does not account for the varying path lengths of rays through a pixel, meaning it does not resolve sampling errors on projections. It is distinguished from sibling kernels like the B-Spline Pixel Kernel by its simplicity and lack of geometric intersection length weighting. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Projection data R\theta(\rho), pixel coordinates (i, j), pixel size \Deltap, projection angle \theta, and offset \rho. Output: A binary weight \Delta(\theta, \rho, i, j) indicating whether the projection line intersects the pixel. Data Structures: No complex data structures are required. The kernel operates on scalar values derived from geometric calculations. Method: 1. Calculate the signed distance e between the center of the pixel (i, j) and the projection line defined by (\theta, \rho). The center of pixel (i, j) is at coordinates (i \sin\theta, j \cos\theta) in the rotated frame, or more commonly, the distance is calculated as: e = \rho - j \cos\theta - i \sin\theta where i and j are the pixel indices, \theta is the projection angle, and \rho is the radial offset. 2. Determine the maximum allowable distance for the line to intersect the pixel. This distance depends on the pixel size \Deltap and the angle \theta. The total width of the pixel projected onto the normal of the ray is \Deltap (|\cos\theta| + |\sin\theta|). 3. Apply the Dirac kernel condition. The weight is 1 if the distance e is within half the projected width of the pixel center, and 0 otherwise: \Delta(\theta, \rho, i, j) = \begin{cases} 1 & \text{if } -\frac{\Deltap (|\cos\theta| + |\sin\theta|)}{2} < e < \frac{\Deltap (|\cos\theta| + |\sin\theta|)}{2} \\ 0 & \text{otherwise} \end{cases}. Parameters: \Deltap: The physical size of a pixel in the reconstruction volume. \theta: The angle of the projection. \rho: The offset of the projection line. i, j: The integer indices of the pixel in the reconstruction grid. Pitfalls: The Dirac kernel does not resolve sampling errors on projections, leading to discretization artifacts in the reconstructed image. It assumes all pixels traversed by a line are equally important, ignoring the fact that rays may traverse pixels at different angles and thus have different path lengths within the pixel. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def diracpixelkernel(i, j, theta, rho, deltap): """ Computes the Dirac pixel kernel weight for a given pixel and projection line. Args: i (float): Pixel column index. j (float): Pixel row index. theta (float): Projection angle in radians. rho (float): Radial offset of the projection line. deltap (float): Size of a pixel. Returns: float: 1.0 if the line intersects the pixel, 0.0 otherwise. """ # Calculate signed distance from pixel center to projection line # e = rho - j cos(theta) - i sin(theta) e = rho - j math.cos(theta) - i math.sin(theta) # Calculate the half-width of the pixel projected onto the normal of the ray # Half-width = deltap (|cos(theta)| + |sin(theta)|) / 2 halfwidth = deltap (abs(math.cos(theta)) + abs(math.sin(theta))) / 2.0 # Check if the distance is within the half-width if -halfwidth < e < halfwidth: return 1.0 else: return 0.0 The B-Spline Pixel Kernel is a weighting function for back-projection in tomographic reconstruction that assigns contribution to a pixel proportionally to the geometric intersection length of the projection line within that pixel. It improves upon the Dirac Pixel Kernel by accounting for the varying path lengths of rays traversing a pixel at different angles, thereby reducing sampling artifacts and improving Signal-to-Noise Ratio (SNR) in reconstructed images. Time Complexity: O(1) per pixel per projection angle, as it involves a constant number of arithmetic operations. Memory Complexity: O(1) auxiliary memory. Strengths: Simple to implement and computationally efficient. Limitations: Does not account for sampling errors or varying path lengths, leading to potential discretization artifacts. When to use: When computational speed is prioritized over reconstruction quality, or as a baseline for comparison. When not to use: When high-quality reconstruction with minimal artifacts is required, especially in cases with coarse sampling. The Dirac Pixel Kernel is commonly employed in direct tomographic reconstruction methods. It is derived from the continuous Radon transform equation. While it is one of the most used pixel kernels due to its direct derivation, its limitations regarding sampling errors have led to the development of more advanced kernels like the B-Spline and area-based interpolators. name: B-Spline Pixel Kernel
head: B-Spline interpolator, Noyau de pixel B-Spline
body: The B-Spline Pixel Kernel is a weighting function for back-projection in tomographic reconstruction that assigns contribution to a pixel proportionally to the geometric intersection length of the projection line within that pixel. It improves upon the Dirac Pixel Kernel by accounting for the varying path lengths of rays traversing a pixel at different angles, thereby reducing sampling artifacts and improving Signal-to-Noise Ratio (SNR) in reconstructed images. Inputs and Outputs Inputs: Projection angle \theta (in radians). Projection offset \rho. Pixel coordinates (i, j) (integer indices). Pixel size \Deltap (physical width/height of a square pixel). Output: Kernel weight B^0(\theta, \rho, i, j), a scalar value in [0, 1]. Data Structures No complex data structures are required. The calculation relies on scalar arithmetic operations on the input parameters. Step-by-Step Method 1. Calculate Distance: Compute the perpendicular distance e from the center of the pixel (i, j) to the projection line defined by (\theta, \rho). The center of pixel (i, j) is at coordinates (i \cdot \Deltap, j \cdot \Deltap) assuming a standard grid origin, or simply use the normalized distance formula provided in the source: e = \rho - i \cos \theta - j \sin \theta Note: The source defines e directly in this form, implying \rho and coordinates are in consistent units. 2. Determine Bounding Extents: Calculate the half-widths of the trapezoidal kernel support. Inner half-width (full overlap region): w{inner} = \frac{\Deltap (||\cos \theta| - |\sin \theta||)}{2} Outer half-width (total support): w{outer} = \frac{\Deltap (|\cos \theta| + |\sin \theta|)}{2} 3. Compute Weight: Evaluate B^0 based on the absolute distance |e|: Case 1 (Full Overlap): If |e| \le w{inner}, the line passes fully through the pixel's central region. B^0 = 1 Case 2 (Partial Overlap): If w{inner} < |e| \le w{outer}, the line intersects the pixel edges. Interpolate linearly based on the distance. B^0 = \frac{-2|e| + (|\cos \theta| + |\sin \theta|)\Deltap}{2 \Deltap \min(|\cos \theta|, |\sin \theta|)} Case 3 (No Overlap): If |e| > w{outer}, the line does not intersect the pixel. B^0 = 0 Formulas and Definitions e: Signed distance from pixel center to projection line. \Deltap: Pixel size (assumed square). \theta: Projection angle. B^0: The B-Spline kernel value (also referred to as the zero-order B-spline interpolator in the context of the box function convolution). Parameters \Deltap: Determined by the image resolution and field of view. Typical values depend on the specific application (e.g., for a 512 \times 512 image, \Deltap is the FOV/512). Edge Cases and Pitfalls Angle Symmetry: The kernel is periodic with period \pi/2 due to the absolute values of sine and cosine. The formula derivation in the source assumes \theta \in [0, \pi/4[ for the interpolation segment, but the absolute value formulation generalizes it to all angles. Division by Zero: The denominator in Case 2 contains \min(|\cos \theta|, |\sin \theta|). This term is zero only when \theta is a multiple of \pi/2. In these cases, the projection line is axis-aligned. The limit of the expression as \min \to 0 should be handled carefully. If \theta = 0, \cos \theta = 1, \sin \theta = 0. The support width is \Deltap. The inner width is \Deltap/2. The formula becomes \frac{-2|e| + \Deltap}{0}, which is undefined. However, geometrically, for axis-aligned lines, the intersection length is simply \Deltap if the line passes through, and 0 otherwise. The source notes the derivation is for [0, \pi/4[, implying a need for special handling or limit evaluation at \theta = k\pi/2. In implementation, if \min(|\cos \theta|, |\sin \theta|) < \epsilon, check if the line is within the pixel bounds directly using axis-aligned intersection logic. Precision: Floating point comparisons for |e| \le w{inner} should use a small epsilon to avoid jitter at boundaries. Pseudocode Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def bsplinepixelkernel(theta, rho, i, j, deltap): """ Computes the B-Spline pixel kernel weight. Args: theta (float): Projection angle in radians. rho (float): Projection offset. i (int): Pixel column index. j (int): Pixel row index. deltap (float): Pixel size. Returns: float: Kernel weight B^0. """ # 1. Calculate distance from pixel center to projection line # Source defines e = rho - icos(theta) - jsin(theta) cost = abs(cos(theta)) sint = abs(sin(theta)) # Note: The source formula for e uses i and j directly. # This assumes the pixel center is at (i, j) in normalized coordinates # or that rho is scaled appropriately. # Standard geometric distance from point (x0, y0) to line xcos + ysin = rho is: # |x0cos + y0sin - rho|. # The source writes e = rho - jcos - isin. # Assuming standard image coordinates where x corresponds to i and y to j: # e = rho - (i cost + j sint) # Using absolute cos/sin as per source structure e = rho - (i cost + j sint) abse = abs(e) # 2. Calculate bounds # Inner bound: where line fully traverses pixel (weight 1) # Formula: deltap (||cos| - |sin||) / 2 innerbound = deltap abs(cost - sint) / 2.0 # Outer bound: total support width / 2 # Formula: deltap (|cos| + |sin|) / 2 outerbound = deltap (cost + sint) / 2.0 # 3. Compute weight if abse <= innerbound: return 1.0 elif abse <= outerbound: # Interpolation region # Denominator: 2 deltap min(|cos|, |sin|) mincossin = min(cost, sint) # Guard against division by zero at axis-aligned angles if mincossin < 1e-9: # At theta = 0 or pi/2, the line is axis aligned. # The intersection length is deltap if the line passes through the pixel column/row. # Based on the limit of the trapezoid, if min is 0, the trapezoid becomes a rectangle. # If the line is within the pixel, weight is 1. If outside, 0. # The outerbound check already handles "outside". # If we are here, abse <= outerbound. # For theta=0: outerbound = deltap/2. innerbound = deltap/2. # So abse <= deltap/2. The line is inside. return 1.0 numerator = -2.0 abse + (cost + sint) deltap denominator = 2.0 deltap mincossin return numerator / denominator else: return 0.0 Complexity: O(1) per pixel per projection line. The calculation involves basic arithmetic operations (abs, min, max, multiply, add). Memory: O(1) auxiliary memory. No lookup tables are required. Performance: Faster than analytical integration methods but more expensive than the Dirac kernel due to the trigonometric calculations and conditional logic. Strengths: Reduces aliasing artifacts compared to the Dirac kernel by weighting pixels based on actual intersection length. Improves SNR, especially at lower sampling rates (fewer projections). Limitations: More complex to implement than the Dirac kernel. Requires careful handling of edge cases at axis-aligned angles. The B-Spline Pixel Kernel was first defined in 1993 by Unser et al.. It is derived from the concept of convolving a box function (zero-order B-spline) with the projection line, resulting in a trapezoidal kernel shape that accounts for the geometric intersection length. It is used in tomographic reconstruction algorithms to optimize back-projection accuracy. name: Projective Texture Backprojection
head: Projective Texture Method
body: Projective Texture Backprojection is a GPU-based algorithm for tomographic reconstruction that simulates the projection of volume slices onto the image plane using projective texture mapping to guide reverse texture mapping. It solves the problem of efficiently computing the adjoint of the forward projection operator (backprojection) by leveraging graphics hardware capabilities. It sets itself apart from sibling methods like GPU Backprojection with Global Memory Buffer by avoiding explicit memory writes to global buffers in favor of texture sampling, though it requires managing two distinct volume slice stacks in video memory. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A set of 2D projection images (sinogram data) and a target 3D volume grid of size N \times N \times N. Output: A reconstructed 3D volume density field. Data Structures: Volume Slice Stacks: Two stacks of 2D textures (or render targets) representing slices of the volume. X-Set Stack: Slices perpendicular to the X-axis. Z-Set Stack: Slices perpendicular to the Z-axis. Note: The Y-axis is the axis of rotation for the projections. Projection Sets: X-Set Projections: Projections more perpendicular to the X-axis. Z-Set Projections: Projections more perpendicular to the Z-axis. Steps: 1. Initialization: Allocate two stacks of volume slices in GPU memory. One stack handles slices aligned with the X-axis, the other with the Z-axis. 2. Projection Classification: Divide the input projection images into two sets based on their viewing angle relative to the volume axes. Projections are classified as belonging to the X-set or Z-set depending on which axis they are more perpendicular to. 3. Transformation Matrix Computation: For each projection in a set, compute the transformation matrix that maps the projection plane coordinates to the coordinates of the corresponding volume slice. 4. Reverse Texture Mapping: Use the computed transformation matrix as the texture matrix for the GPU's projective texture unit. Render the projection image onto the corresponding volume slice texture. This effectively "backprojects" the pixel values from the 2D image into the 3D slice space. Repeat this for all projections in the X-set against the X-stack, and all projections in the Z-set against the Z-stack. 5. Merging: After all projections have been processed, merge the two stacks of volume slices to produce the final 3D reconstructed volume. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def projectivetexturebackprojection(projections, volumesize): # 1. Classify projections projectionsx, projectionsz = classifyprojections(projections) # 2. Initialize stacks # Each stack contains N textures representing slices along the respective axis stackx = createvolumestack(volumesize, axis='x') stackz = createvolumestack(volumesize, axis='z') # 3. Backproject X-set for proj in projectionsx: # Compute transformation from projection plane to volume slice # T maps projection UV to volume slice local coordinates T = computetransformationmatrix(proj, axis='x') # For each slice in the X-stack for sliceidx, slicetexture in enumerate(stackx): # Set projective texture matrix settexturematrix(T) # Render projection onto slice # This performs reverse texture mapping: # sampling the projection image and writing to the slice texture renderprojectionontoslice(proj, slicetexture) # 4. Backproject Z-set for proj in projectionsz: T = computetransformationmatrix(proj, axis='z') for sliceidx, slicetexture in enumerate(stackz): settexturematrix(T) renderprojectionontoslice(proj, slicetexture) # 5. Merge stacks finalvolume = mergevolumestacks(stackx, stackz) return finalvolume def classifyprojections(projections): """ Divides projections into two sets based on the angle relative to the X and Z axes. Y is the rotation axis. """ projx = [] projz = [] for proj in projections: angle = getprojectionangle(proj) if ismoreperpendiculartox(angle): projx.append(proj) else: projz.append(proj) return projx, projz def computetransformationmatrix(projection, axis): """ Computes the 4x4 transformation matrix between the projection plane and the volume slice. """ # Implementation depends on specific camera geometry (e.g., FDK) # Returns matrix T such that T projectioncoords = slicecoords pass def renderprojectionontoslice(projectionimage, slicetexture): """ Renders the projection image onto the slice texture using the currently set projective texture matrix. """ # GPU-specific rendering call # Binds projectionimage as texture # Binds slicetexture as render target # Draws a quad with projective texture coordinates pass def mergevolumestacks(stackx, stackz): """ Combines the two stacks into a single 3D volume. """ # Interpolate or average overlapping regions # Not given in the sources. Typically involves summing or averaging # the contributions from both stacks at each voxel. pass Parameters: Volume Resolution (N): The grid size of the reconstructed volume. Number of Projections: Must provide two orthogonal half-orbits of projections, equally spaced in angle, to satisfy Tuy’s condition for exact 3D reconstruction. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Memory Usage: The method requires two copies of the volume slices to remain in GPU memory simultaneously, occupying precious video memory. Merging Artifacts: The final merge step must handle the intersection of the two stacks correctly to avoid discontinuities. A data transfer operation on the GPU to swap partially reconstructed volume data between viewing (V) and support (S) stacks. It sets itself apart by optimizing memory usage through shuffling rather than maintaining two full stacks throughout the entire process. Choose this variant when video memory is constrained. 1. Rotation: Rotate volume proxy polygons so one slice set is perpendicular (V-stack) and the other is orthogonal (S-stack) to the viewing vector. 2. Classification: Divide projections into V-set and S-set based on which stack they are more perpendicular to. 3. Initial Reconstruction: Reconstruct the S-stack from projections from the S-set. 4. Shuffling: Shuffle the partially reconstructed volume into the V-stack. This is implemented by repeatedly rendering different columns of a source texture from one stack to the same column on all target textures from the other stack. 5. Final Reconstruction: Use the V-stack to fully accumulate/reconstruct the volume, then shade and composite. Time Complexity: Depends on the number of projections and volume slices. Each projection is rendered onto a subset of slices. Memory Complexity: High. Requires storing two full stacks of volume slices in GPU memory. Performance: Fast data transfer during shuffling operations. Strengths: Leverages GPU texture hardware for efficient coordinate transformation and sampling. Limitations: High video memory consumption; requires merging two stacks at the end. When to use: When GPU texture units are available and video memory is sufficient. When not to use: When video memory is extremely limited (consider Projective Texture Shuffling or other variants). The method was introduced in the context of GPU-accelerated D2VR (Direct 3D Volume Rendering). It builds on the concept of projective textures [SKv92] and was extended to cone-beam geometry [MX06]. It is related to the work by [CM03] on parallel-beam projection using texture spreading. The method adheres to Tuy’s condition for exact 3D reconstruction [Tuy83] by requiring two orthogonal half-orbits of projections. name: FastFDK
head: FDK, Feldkamp-Davis-Kress, Cone-Beam FDK, FDK Algorithm, FDK Backprojection, Feldkamp-Davis-Kress backprojection
body: FastFDK is a CPU-optimized implementation of the Feldkamp-Davis-Kress (FDK) algorithm, an analytical method for reconstructing a 3D volume from a stack of 2D cone-beam projection images. It solves the tomographic reconstruction problem by applying a specific convolution filter to weighted projections and back-projecting them into a 3D grid. It sets itself apart from its siblings by precomputing geometric weights and using a direct spatial-domain convolution filter to avoid the overhead of FFTs during the main reconstruction loop, prioritizing speed and memory locality on CPU architectures. Inputs: A stack of mid projection images of size miw x mih, and scanner geometry parameters: pixel size mps, source-to-origin distance msd, origin-to-detector distance myd, volume dimensions mvw x mvw x mvd, voxel size mvs, and angular span mna in degrees. Outputs: A 3D volume mvol of type float with dimensions mvw x mvw x mvd. Data Structures: mvol: Output volume array, size mvw mvw mvd. mcyl: Boolean mask array, size mvw mvw. mcyl[i + mvwj] is true if the voxel (i,j) lies within the cylinder defined by the volume width. mflt: Float array, size mnf = miw / 2. Stores the odd-indexed coefficients of the convolution filter. mw0: Float array, size miw mih. Precomputed initial image weighting factors. mbuf: Float array, size miw. Temporary buffer for processing image rows during filtering. mimg: Float array, size miw mih mid. Storage for all filtered projection images. Parameters: mps: Adjusted pixel size. The constructor scales the input pixel size: mps = msd / (msd + myd). mk: Filter center value, 1 / (4 mps^2). angStep: Angle step in radians, -mna MPI / (mid 180). Algorithm Steps: 1. Initialization: Clear mvol to zero. Precompute mw0: For each pixel (i, j) in the projection image: v = (m{ih}/2 - 0.5 - j) \cdot m{ps} k1 = m{sd}^2 + v^2 u = (i + 0.5 - m{iw}/2) \cdot m{ps} m{w0}[i + m{iw} \cdot j] = \frac{m{sd}}{\sqrt{u^2 + k1}} Precompute mflt: mk = \frac{1}{4 \cdot m{ps}^2} For k from 0 to mnf - 1: j = 2k + 1 tmp = \pi \cdot m{ps} \cdot j m{flt}[k] = -\frac{1}{tmp^2} Precompute mcyl: For i, j from 0 to mvw - 1: m{cyl}[i + m{vw} \cdot j] = ((2i - m{vw})^2 + (2j - m{vw})^2) < m{vw}^2 2. Filtering: For each projection image img in the input stack: For each row j from 0 to mih - 1: Copy row img[:, j] to mbuf. Apply weighting: mbuf[i] = mw0[i + miw j] for all i. Apply convolution filter to mbuf: For each pixel i from 0 to miw - 1: v0 = m{buf}[i] \cdot mk For k from 0 to mnf - 1: l = 2k + 1 If i - l >= 0: If i + l < miw: v0 += (m{buf}[i-l] + m{buf}[i+l]) \cdot m{flt}[k] Else: v0 += m{buf}[i-l] \cdot m{flt}[k] Else If i + l < miw: v0 += m{buf}[i+l] \cdot m{flt}[k] Else: Break loop. outImg[i] = v0 Store filtered row in mimg. 3. Backprojection: Initialize ang = 0. For each filtered projection img (index n from 1 to mid): Compute trigonometric values: ca = \cos(ang), sa = \sin(ang). Compute projection scaling: k1 = m{sd} / m{ps}. For each volume row j from 0 to mvw - 1: Compute vy = (m{vw}/2 - 0.5 - j) \cdot m{vs}. For each volume column i from 0 to mvw - 1: Let l = j \cdot m{vw} + i. If !mcyl[l], continue (skip voxels outside the cylinder). Compute vx = (i + 0.5 - m{vw}/2) \cdot m{vs}. Apply volume rotation: vvx = vx \cdot ca - vy \cdot sa vvy = vy \cdot ca + vx \cdot sa Compute detector projection scaling: k2 = \frac{k1}{vvy + m{sd}} Compute detector coordinates: u = vvx \cdot k2 + \frac{m{iw}}{2} - 0.5 (Note: v coordinate is computed inside the depth loop below) Compute integer indices and remainders for u: iu = \lfloor u \rfloor If u < 0, iu = iu - 1. du = u - iu For each volume depth k from 0 to mvd - 1: Compute vz = (m{vd}/2 - 0.5 - k) \cdot m{vs}. Compute detector v coordinate: v = \frac{m{ih}}{2} - vz \cdot k2 - 0.5 Compute integer indices and remainders for v: iv = \lfloor v \rfloor If v < 0, iv = iv - 1. dv = v - iv Perform bilinear interpolation of img at (iu, iv) with remainders (du, dv): val = (v1 + du \cdot (v2 - v1)) + dv \cdot ((v3 + du \cdot (v4 - v3)) - (v1 + du \cdot (v2 - v1))) Where v1 = img[iu, iv], v2 = img[iu+1, iv], v3 = img[iu, iv+1], v4 = img[iu+1, iv+1]. Out-of-bounds pixels return 0. Compute post-projection weighting: k3 = \frac{m{sd}}{m{sd} + vvy} val = val \cdot k3^2 Accumulate into volume with averaging: m\vol[i, j, k] = m\vol[i, j, k] + \frac{val - m\vol[i, j, k]}{n} Update angle: ang += angStep. 4. Normalization: For each voxel p in mvol: If |p| < \epsilon and p \neq 0, set p = 0. Else, p = p / 2. Pseudocode: Unverified code. Filtering filteredimages = [] for img in images: filteredimg = [[0.0 for in range(iw)] for in range(ih)] for j in range(ih): # Copy row to buffer and apply weighting buf = [img[j][i] mw0[j][i] for i in range(iw)] # Apply convolution for i in range(iw): v0 = buf[i] mk for k in range(mnf): l = 2 k + 1 if i - l >= 0: if i + l < iw: v0 += (buf[i - l] + buf[i + l]) mflt[k] else: v0 += buf[i - l] mflt[k] elif i + l < iw: v0 += buf[i + l] mflt[k] else: break filteredimg[j][i] = v0 filteredimages.append(filteredimg) # 3. Backprojection angstep = -na math.pi / (id 180) ang = 0.0 for nidx, img in enumerate(filteredimages): n = nidx + 1 ca = math.cos(ang) sa = math.sin(ang) k1 = sd / mps for j in range(vw): vy = (vw / 2 - 0.5 - j) vs for i in range(vw): l = j vw + i if not mcyl[l]: continue vx = (i + 0.5 - vw / 2) vs vvx = vx ca - vy sa vvy = vy ca + vx sa k2 = k1 / (vvy + sd) # Precompute u part uval = vvx k2 + iw / 2 - 0.5 iu = int(uval) if uval < 0: iu -= 1 du = uval - iu for k in range(vd): vz = (vd / 2 - 0.5 - k) vs vval = ih / 2 - vz k2 - 0.5 iv = int(vval) if vval < 0: iv -= 1 dv = vval - iv # Bilinear Interpolation # getPixel returns 0 if out of bounds def getpixel(img, u, v): if 0 <= u < iw and 0 <= v < ih: return img[v][u] return 0.0 v1 = getpixel(img, iu, iv) v2 = getpixel(img, iu + 1, iv) v3 = getpixel(img, iu, iv + 1) v4 = getpixel(img, iu + 1, iv + 1) val = (v1 + du (v2 - v1)) + dv ((v3 + du (v4 - v3)) - (v1 + du (v2 - v1))) k3 = sd / (sd + vvy) val = k3 k3 # Accumulate mvol[j][i][k] += (val - mvol[j][i][k]) / n ang += angstep # 4. Normalization epsilon = 1e-9 # Not given in the sources. for j in range(vw): for i in range(vw): for k in range(vd): p = mvol[j][i][k] if abs(p) < epsilon and p != 0: mvol[j][i][k] = 0.0 else: mvol[j][i][k] /= 2.0 return mvol A technique that reconstructs density values and gradients at arbitrary sample points along a ray directly from 2D projections, avoiding the intermediate step of creating a 3D rectilinear grid. It sets itself apart from grid-based Direct Volume Rendering (DVR) by eliminating interpolation errors associated with voxel sampling, thereby producing higher visual quality for thin structures. It builds on FastFDK by utilizing the FBP reconstruction formula not just for grid generation, but as a direct resampling scheme for arbitrary ray positions. Performance: The algorithm is computationally much less expensive than iterative algorithms, making it suitable for clinical environments. Strengths: Fast, analytical, single-pass reconstruction. Limitations: Introduces artifacts and noise compared to iterative methods. Assumes ideal geometry and linear attenuation. When to use: When speed is critical and data quality is sufficient for analytical reconstruction (e.g., clinical CT, high-quality sinograms). When not to use: When dealing with sparse data, significant noise, or when higher accuracy via iterative refinement is required. The Filtered Backprojection (FBP) algorithm is described as the most fundamental algorithm still widely used for high-precision CT reconstructions. FastFDK is a specific CPU-based reference implementation optimized for speed using precomputed geometric weights and spatial convolution. name: Filtered Back-Projection for Volume Rendering
head: D2VR, Projection-based Volume Rendering
body: Filtered Back-Projection (FBP) for Volume Rendering, also known as D2VR, is a technique that reconstructs density values and gradients at arbitrary sample points along a ray directly from 2D projections, avoiding the intermediate step of creating a 3D rectilinear grid. It sets itself apart from grid-based Direct Volume Rendering (DVR) by eliminating interpolation errors associated with voxel sampling, thereby producing higher visual quality for thin structures. It applies the FBP reconstruction formula as a direct resampling scheme for arbitrary ray positions. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: A set of K filtered 2D projection images Q{\thetai}, where i \in \{1, \dots, K\}, corresponding to projection angles \thetai. Camera parameters defining ray origins and directions. Outputs: A rendered image with color and opacity values for each pixel. Data Structures: Projections: A list of 1D arrays representing the filtered projection data Q{\thetai} for each angle. The values are obtained by high-pass filtering the measured projection data. Ray State: For each pixel, a ray origin O and direction D. Sample points P along the ray are defined by P(s) = O + s \cdot D. Parameters: Number of Projections (K): The total number of available views. Step Size (\Delta s): The distance between sample points along the ray. It must be less than half the voxel size of the equivalent grid to ensure accuracy. Finite Difference Step (\Delta t): A small finite value used to approximate the limit in the gradient formula. Algorithm Steps: 1. Ray Casting: For each pixel of the image plane, cast a ray through the volumetric space enclosed by the filtered projections. 2. Sampling: Generate sample points Pj along the ray at intervals of \Delta s. 3. Density Reconstruction: At each resample location, reconstruct the underlying 3D density value using the discrete FBP formula: \tilde{f}(x, y) = \frac{\pi}{K} \sum{i=1}^K Q{\thetai}(ti) where ti = x \cos \thetai + y \sin \thetai is the projected coordinate of the point onto the i-th projection plane. 4. Gradient Estimation: Compute the partial derivatives \tilde{f}x and \tilde{f}y directly from the projections using Newton's difference quotient: \tilde{f}x = \frac{\pi}{K} \sum{i=1}^K \lim{\Delta x \rightarrow 0} \frac{1}{\Delta x} (Q{\thetai}(ti + \Delta x \cos \thetai) - Q{\thetai}(ti)) \tilde{f}y = \frac{\pi}{K} \sum{i=1}^K \lim{\Delta y \rightarrow 0} \frac{1}{\Delta y} (Q{\thetai}(ti + \Delta y \sin \thetai) - Q{\thetai}(ti)) In practice, \Delta x and \Delta y are replaced by a small finite value \Delta t. The terms \cos \thetai and \sin \thetai scale the derivative of the projection data. 5. Shading: Perform shading by estimating gradients directly on the projections and using them as surface normals. 6. Compositing: Determine the final color and opacity of the pixel using the over-operator in front-to-back order. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def normalize(v): length = math.sqrt(v[0]2 + v[1]2 + v[2]2) if length == 0.0: return (0.0, 0.0, 1.0) return (v[0]/length, v[1]/length, v[2]/length) def dot(a, b): return a[0]b[0] + a[1]b[1] + a[2]b[2] def renderpixel(rayorigin, raydirection, projections, angles, sstart, send, stepsize): """ Renders a single pixel using Filtered Back-Projection for Volume Rendering. Args: rayorigin: (x, y, z) tuple raydirection: (dx, dy, dz) tuple, normalized projections: List of 1D arrays Qthetai angles: List of float angles thetai in radians sstart, send: Float bounds along the ray stepsize: Float distance between samples Returns: (color, opacity) tuple """ accumulatedcolor = [0.0, 0.0, 0.0] transmittance = 1.0 numproj = len(angles) scale = math.pi / numproj deltat = 1.0 # Finite difference step approximating the limit s = sstart while s <= send: x = rayorigin[0] + s raydirection[0] y = rayorigin[1] + s raydirection[1] z = rayorigin[2] + s raydirection[2] density = 0.0 gradx = 0.0 grady = 0.0 for i in range(numproj): theta = angles[i] proj = projections[i] width = len(proj) # Project 3D point to 1D detector coordinate per source formula ti = x math.cos(theta) + y math.sin(theta) idx = int(ti) if 0 <= idx < width: density += proj[idx] # Approximate limit using finite difference tplusx = ti + deltat math.cos(theta) tplusy = ti + deltat math.sin(theta) idxx = int(tplusx) idxy = int(tplusy) if 0 <= idxx < width: gradx += (proj[idxx] - proj[idx]) / deltat math.cos(theta) if 0 <= idxy < width: grady += (proj[idxy] - proj[idx]) / deltat math.sin(theta) # Scale by pi / K density = scale gradx = scale grady = scale # Shading: compute normal from gradients # Assuming gradient vector in the projection plane corresponds to surface normal components. normal = normalize((gradx, grady, 0.0)) # Simple diffuse lighting model lightdir = normalize((0.0, 0.0, 1.0)) diffuse = max(dot(normal, lightdir), 0.0) shading = 0.2 + 0.8 diffuse # Standard transfer function: density -> color, opacity opacitysample = 1.0 - math.exp(-density 0.1) colorsample = [shading density, shading density, shading density] # Front-to-back compositing alpha = opacitysample transmittance accumulatedcolor[0] += colorsample[0] alpha accumulatedcolor[1] += colorsample[1] alpha accumulatedcolor[2] += colorsample[2] alpha transmittance = (1.0 - opacitysample) s += stepsize return accumulatedcolor, 1.0 - transmittance A method to estimate derivatives of the volumetric density function directly from filtered projections, avoiding the computational cost and interpolation errors of grid-based finite difference methods. It applies Newton's difference quotient to the filtered projection data Q{\thetai} instead of the reconstructed density function. The partial derivative \tilde{f}x is calculated as the sum of scaled derivatives of the projection data: \lim{\Delta x \rightarrow 0} \frac{1}{\Delta x} (Q{\thetai}(ti + \Delta x \cos \thetai) - Q{\thetai}(ti)). This approach is superior to grid-based central differences, which require 6 additional interpolated samples for a gradient, accumulating interpolation errors, whereas FBP-based estimation uses density values as accurate as grid points, introducing no interpolation error. Time Complexity: O(K \cdot N \cdot S), where K is the number of projections, N is the number of pixels, and S is the number of samples per ray. Each sample requires iterating over all K projections. Memory Complexity: O(K \cdot W \cdot H) to store the projection images. No 3D volume grid is stored in memory. Measured Performance: Tested on Marschner & Lobb function (64 projections, 64x64 resolution) and Carp dataset (128 projections, 128x256 resolution). Strengths: Higher visual quality than grid-based DVR using the same amount of pixels on all projections as voxels on the regular grid, particularly reducing holes in thin structures. Avoids interpolation errors inherent in grid-based gradient estimation. Limitations: Computationally intensive per sample due to the summation over all projections. Requires pre-filtered projections. When to use: When high-quality rendering of thin structures is required and memory for a high-resolution 3D grid is prohibitive. When not to use: When real-time performance is critical and the number of projections is large, as the per-sample cost is high. The method was introduced in the paper "D2VR: High-Quality Volume Rendering of Projection-based Volumetric Data". It was developed to address the limitations of grid-based volume rendering, specifically interpolation errors and memory usage. The technique leverages the mathematical properties of Filtered Back-Projection, traditionally used for tomographic reconstruction, to perform direct volume rendering. name: Gradient Estimation via Filtered Back-Projection
head: FBP-based Gradient Estimation, Gradient from Filtered Projections
body: Gradient Estimation via Filtered Back-Projection estimates the spatial derivatives of a volumetric density function directly from filtered projection data, bypassing the intermediate step of reconstructing a 3D rectilinear grid. It differs from grid-based finite difference methods by eliminating interpolation errors associated with sampling a reconstructed volume, as it computes derivatives from the continuous projection functions themselves. Inputs: K: Number of projection angles \thetai. Q{\thetai}(t): The filtered projection data for angle \thetai, where t is the detector coordinate. (x, y): The 2D spatial coordinates of the point at which the gradient is estimated. Outputs: \tilde{f}x: The estimated partial derivative with respect to x. \tilde{f}y: The estimated partial derivative with respect to y. Data Structures: The filtered projections Q{\thetai} are typically stored as 1D arrays or accessed via a filtering kernel. No 3D grid is allocated for the gradient estimation itself. Steps: 1. For each projection angle i \in \{1, \dots, K\}, calculate the projection coordinate ti corresponding to the point (x, y): ti = x \cos \thetai + y \sin \thetai 2. Compute the partial derivative with respect to x (\tilde{f}x) by summing the scaled derivatives of the filtered projections. The derivative of the projection is approximated using Newton's difference quotient with a small offset \Delta x: \tilde{f}x = \frac{\pi}{K} \sum{i=1}^K \lim{\Delta x \rightarrow 0} \frac{1}{\Delta x} \left( Q{\thetai}(ti + \Delta x \cos \thetai) - Q{\thetai}(ti) \right) In practice, \Delta x is chosen as a small value relative to the resolution of the projection data. The term \cos \thetai scales the derivative because the projection coordinate t changes with x at a rate of \cos \thetai. 3. Compute the partial derivative with respect to y (\tilde{f}y) analogously: \tilde{f}y = \frac{\pi}{K} \sum{i=1}^K \lim{\Delta y \rightarrow 0} \frac{1}{\Delta y} \left( Q{\thetai}(ti + \Delta y \sin \thetai) - Q{\thetai}(ti) \right) Here, the derivative is scaled by \sin \thetai. 4. Higher-order derivatives can be obtained by applying the difference quotient multiple times to the projection data Q{\thetai}. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def estimategradientfbp(x, y, angles, filteredprojections, delta=1e-5): """ Estimate gradients fx and fy using Filtered Back-Projection of derivatives. Args: x, y: Coordinates of the point to evaluate. angles: List of projection angles thetai in radians. filteredprojections: List of 1D arrays Qthetai, indexed by angle. delta: Small offset for finite difference approximation. Returns: fx, fy: Estimated partial derivatives. """ K = len(angles) sumfx = 0.0 sumfy = 0.0 for i in range(K): theta = angles[i] Q = filteredprojections[i] # Calculate base projection coordinate ti ti = x cos(theta) + y sin(theta) # Calculate offset coordinates for finite difference # For fx: shift t by delta cos(theta) tx = ti + delta cos(theta) # For fy: shift t by delta sin(theta) ty = ti + delta sin(theta) # Interpolate filtered projection values at ti, tx, ty # Q is a 1D function/array; assume linear interpolation or similar qbase = interpolate(Q, ti) qx = interpolate(Q, tx) qy = interpolate(Q, ty) # Compute scaled derivatives # Derivative of Q wrt t, scaled by chain rule factor dxdt = cos(theta) dydt = sin(theta) # Approximate limit as delta -> 0 dQdx = (qx - qbase) / delta dQdy = (qy - qbase) / delta # Accumulate sum # Note: The formula includes a factor of pi/K. # This assumes the standard FBP reconstruction scaling. sumfx += dQdx dxdt # Actually, the formula shows the scaling is inside the limit term # Re-reading formula: lim (1/dx) (Q(t + dx cos) - Q(t)) # This IS the derivative of Q wrt x directly via chain rule. # So we just sum the difference quotients. # Correct accumulation based on formula: # fxterm = (Q(t + dx cos) - Q(t)) / dx # fyterm = (Q(t + dy sin) - Q(t)) / dy # fx = (pi/K) sum(fxterm) fxterm = (qx - qbase) / delta fyterm = (qy - qbase) / delta sumfx += fxterm sumfy += fyterm fx = (pi / K) sumfx fy = (pi / K) sumfy return fx, fy Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision: The choice of \Delta x and \Delta y involves a trade-off between truncation error (large \Delta) and numerical noise (small \Delta). A typical value is one pixel or voxel size in the projection domain. Boundaries: If ti \pm \Delta x \cos \thetai falls outside the bounds of the projection data Q{\thetai}, extrapolation or clamping is required. Clamping to the nearest edge value is a common safeguard. Degenerate Input: If \cos \thetai = 0 (for x-gradient) or \sin \thetai = 0 (for y-gradient), the shift in the projection coordinate becomes zero, making the difference quotient undefined or zero. This is handled naturally by the formula (the term becomes 0/0 if not careful, but physically the derivative component along that axis is zero for that specific projection). In implementation, if the shift is zero, the contribution to that specific gradient component from that angle is zero. An approach where gradients are estimated in projection space and then reconstructed along with the density. The gradient components parallel to the viewing direction are scaled by \cos \theta and \sin \theta. The projection space gradient is stored in RGB color channels, while filtered density values are stored in the alpha channel. The pipeline is formally described as RN((p \otimes gp) \otimes hp), where p is projection data, gp is the gradient filter in projection space, hp is the interpolation filter, and RN is the reconstruction operator. This method tends to produce images of lower perceived definition (sharpness) compared to Gradient-from-Sampling (GFS), especially when upsampling, because the gradient filter is applied before upsampling, potentially losing high-frequency information. Accuracy: Expects higher accuracy than traditional grid-based gradient estimation schemes. Grid-based central differences require 6 additional interpolated samples for a gradient, accumulating interpolation errors. FBP-based estimation uses density values as accurate as grid points, introducing no interpolation error. Computational Cost: Avoids the computational cost of computing a large 3D neighborhood of samples, which would require a large number of backprojections, especially for higher-order gradient estimation schemes. Memory: Does not require storing a 3D volume grid for gradient storage, reducing memory footprint compared to grid-based methods. This method exploits the Filtered Back-Projection (FBP) reconstruction scheme to compute derivatives directly from projection data. It was introduced in the context of Differentiable Volume Rendering (D2VR) to improve the quality of gradient-based rendering. The approach is particularly relevant for tomographic reconstruction as inverse rendering, where accurate gradients are needed for optimization or high-quality visualization without the artifacts of grid interpolation. name: FDK Backprojection Transpose (Adjoint)
head: FDK Backprojection Transpose CUDA Kernel
body: The FDK Backprojection Transpose computes the adjoint of the forward FDK backprojection, scattering voxel values from a 3D volume back to 2D projection panels using the same geometric mapping and weights. It accumulates scattered values into projection buffers using atomicAdd. Inputs: volume: 3D tensor of shape [batch, 1, depth, height, width] containing voxel values. matrices: 4D tensor of shape [batch, views, 12] containing camera extrinsics (source and detector positions/orientations). projectionshape: Tuple (views, rows, columns) defining the output projection grid dimensions. box: Bounding box of the volume (used for ray clipping). Outputs: out: 4D tensor of shape [batch, 1, views, rows, columns] initialized to zero, accumulating the scattered values. Data Structures: ViewColumn: Struct containing precomputed geometric weights and ray parameters for a specific view. Stencil: Struct containing 4 indices and 4 weights for bilinear interpolation onto the projection panel. ConeRay: Struct containing ray origin, direction, and weight. Parameters: TTFDKDEPTH: 4 (number of voxels processed per thread along the z-axis). C: Channel count (typically 1 for grayscale). Algorithm Steps: 1. Initialization: Extract dimensions: batch, depth, height, width from volume.shape; views, rows, columns from projectionshape. Detach and convert matrices to contiguous float32. Create zero-initialized output tensor out of shape [batch, 1, views, rows, columns]. Get kernel function "fdkbackprojecttransposec1". 2. Kernel Launch: Iterate over each item in batch. Execute kernel with grid volumegrid((depth, height, width)), block VOLUMEBLOCK, and arguments [volume[item, 0].contiguous(), matrices, out[item, 0], width, height, depth, views, rows, columns]. 3. Kernel Execution (Per Thread): Each thread handles a block of voxels along the z-axis: z0 = blockIdx.z TTFDKDEPTH. Thread indices (x, y) map to volume coordinates. Load TTFDKDEPTH voxel values from volume at (x, y, z0...z0+3). If all loaded values are zero, skip the view loop. 4. Scatter Loop (Per View): For each view v from 0 to views-1: Compute ViewColumn parameters from matrices. For each of the TTFDKDEPTH voxels (index j): If value[j] == 0, continue. Compute detector coordinates and inverse distance scale from the ConeRay and voxel position. For each of the 4 stencil points (bilinear interpolation corners on the detector): If s.weight[q] != 0: Perform atomicAdd(out[s.index[q]], s.weight[q] value[j]). Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def fdkbackprojecttranspose(volume, matrices, projectionshape, box): B,, D, H, W = volume.shape V, R, C = projectionshape # Initialize 5D output tensor [batch, 1, views, rows, columns] out = [[[[[0.0] C for in range(R)] for in range(V)] for in range(1)] for in range(B)] # Detach and convert matrices to contiguous float32 mats = [m.detach().float().contiguous() if hasattr(m, 'detach') else m for m in matrices] # Kernel launch logic omitted; see steps 2-3 return out def panelstencil(column, row, columns, rows, inverse): """Computes bilinear interpolation stencil indices and weights.""" if not (-1 < column < columns and -1 < row < rows): return False, None columnfloor = math.floor(column) rowfloor = math.floor(row) c0 = int(columnfloor) r0 = int(rowfloor) dc = column - columnfloor dr = row - rowfloor scale = inverse inverse wc0 = 1.0 - dc if c0 >= 0 else 0.0 wc1 = dc if c0 + 1 < columns else 0.0 wr0 = (1.0 - dr) scale if r0 >= 0 else 0.0 wr1 = dr scale if r0 + 1 < rows else 0.0 left = max(c0, 0) right = min(c0 + 1, columns - 1) top = max(r0, 0) columns bottom = min(r0 + 1, rows - 1) columns indices = [top + left, top + right, bottom + left, bottom + right] weights = [wr0 wc0, wr0 wc1, wr1 wc0, wr1 wc1] return True, (indices, weights) def threadkernellogic(x, y, z0, volume, mats, out, W, H, D, V, R, C, box): TTFDKDEPTH = 4 values = [] for k in range(TTFDKDEPTH): z = z0 + k values.append(volume[x][y][z] if z < D else 0.0) if all(v == 0.0 for v in values): return for view in range(V): # Compute ViewColumn v from mats[view] # Compute ConeRay from source/detector positions and box for j in range(TTFDKDEPTH): if values[j] == 0.0: continue # Compute detector coordinates (column, row) and inverse distance scale # from ConeRay and voxel position (x, y, z0+j) column, row, inverse = computedetectorcoords(ray, x, y, z0 + j, box) valid, stencil = panelstencil(column, row, C, R, inverse) if valid: indices, weights = stencil for q in range(4): if weights[q] != 0.0: out[0][0][view][int(indices[q] // C)][int(indices[q] % C)] += weights[q] values[j] Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Atomic Contention: Multiple threads may write to the same projection pixel simultaneously, requiring atomicAdd. Numerical Precision: float32 addition is not associative, so the order of accumulation matters for numerical consistency with the forward pass. Boundary Conditions: Stencil weights are clamped to zero if the interpolated coordinate falls outside the detector bounds [0, rows) x [0, columns). Zero Voxel Skip: If all TTFDKDEPTH voxels loaded by a thread are zero, the view loop is skipped to save computation. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Efficiently computes the adjoint for differentiable tomography. Limitations: Atomic contention reduces throughput; non-associative floating-point addition may cause precision drift.
