name: Systems and applications
body: This family covers the deployment, integration, and hardware acceleration of volume rendering techniques in real-world scenarios. It addresses the gap between theoretical rendering algorithms and practical implementation constraints, such as computational intensity, display hardware limitations, and user interaction requirements. It is distinguished from Image-order rendering and Object-order rendering by its focus on system-level architecture (e.g., GPU pipelines, web browsers, physical displays) rather than per-pixel or per-voxel sampling and shading strategies. The articles in this family share the goal of mapping abstract volumetric data I(x,y,z) to a perceptible output through specific system constraints. Common mechanisms include: 1. Hardware Acceleration Mapping: Offloading computationally intensive tasks (ray casting, splatting, sorting) to parallel execution units (GPUs, multi-core CPUs) to achieve real-time or near-real-time performance. 2. Data Structure Optimization: Storing volumetric data in formats optimized for the target hardware, such as 3D/4D textures for coalesced memory access on GPUs or sparse structures (e.g., OpenVDB) for memory efficiency. 3. Depth Management: Handling the ordering of contributions for alpha-blended rendering, often requiring GPU-based sorting algorithms (radix sort, linked lists) to ensure correct compositing. 4. Physical-to-Digital Mapping: In the case of volumetric displays, transforming 3D voxel coordinates into 2D control signals (pixel buffers, SLM patterns) synchronized with mechanical or optical processes to create a physical 3D light field. Hardware architectures and software systems that manipulate, store, and render volumetric data directly as voxels, offloading operations like clipping and compositing to dedicated processors or optimized GPU pipelines. It is distinguished from Film and production rendering and Scientific and medical visualization by prioritizing interactive frame rates and direct spatial manipulation of 3D primitives over offline quality or analytical accuracy. Choose when real-time interaction with 3D spatial data and direct voxel manipulation are required. High-fidelity rendering pipelines for visual effects, particularly for clouds, fire, and smoke, often utilizing VDB data structures. It is distinguished from Voxel engines and games and GPU, web and parallel renderers by prioritizing offline photorealism and complex light transport over interactive frame rates. Choose when offline quality and photorealistic effects are required. Applications of volume rendering to analyze and interpret complex datasets from scientific simulations or medical imaging (CT, MRI). It is distinguished from Voxel engines and games and Film and production rendering by prioritizing analytical accuracy and quantitative correctness over interactive frame rates or photorealism. Choose when analytical accuracy and quantitative interpretation of data are required. Rendering systems that map volumetric data I(x,y,z) to perceptible outputs by offloading computation to parallel hardware (GPUs, multi-core CPUs) or executing entirely within web browsers via WebGL/WebGPU. It addresses computational intensity by leveraging massive parallelism for ray casting, splatting, and data sorting. It is distinguished from Voxel engines and games by its focus on general-purpose visualization rather than game engine integration, and from Film and production rendering by its emphasis on real-time or near-real-time interactivity and web compatibility. Choose when general-purpose visualization requires real-time interactivity, web compatibility, or massive parallelism. Hardware systems and computational methods that render volumetric data directly into physical space, creating images visible from multiple viewpoints without headgear. It differs from standard rasterization by projecting light into a physical medium or light field rather than onto a 2D sensor. It is distinct from Voxel engines and games and Scientific and medical visualization by creating physical 3D light fields rather than simulating volume appearance on 2D displays or monitors. Choose when headless 3D visualization in physical space is required. Specific origin details (authors, dates, foundational papers) are not given in the sources. The field has evolved from offline scientific visualization tools to real-time interactive systems and specialized hardware displays. The integration of GPUs has been a major driver, enabling complex shading and large datasets to be rendered interactively. More recently, web-based technologies (WebGL/WebGPU) have democratized access to volume visualization, while volumetric displays offer a new paradigm for 3D data presentation without stereoscopic headgear.

name: Voxel engines and games
head: Voxel frame buffer processors, Voxel engines
body: This family encompasses hardware architectures and software systems designed to manipulate, store, and render volumetric data directly as voxels, rather than converting them to polygons or ray-marching implicit surfaces. They solve the problem of real-time interaction with 3D spatial data by offloading volume-specific operations (clipping, compositing, voxelization) from the main CPU to dedicated processors or optimized pipelines. Unlike Film and production rendering which prioritizes offline quality, or Scientific and medical visualization which prioritizes analytical accuracy, voxel engines prioritize direct spatial manipulation of 3D primitives and hardware-accelerated room management. A 2.5D rendering technique that generates a pseudo-3D environment by plotting vertical lines whose colors are sampled from a color map and whose starting y-coordinates are determined by a depth map. It distinguishes itself from full 3D rasterization by avoiding polygon projection, instead relying on pre-computed height and color data to simulate perspective, making it suitable for hardware with limited floating-point capabilities. A method for Voxelized Global Illumination (VXGI) that extends the concept of cascaded shadow maps to 3D voxel grids. It uses multiple volumes with identical resolution but different scales, centered around the player, to vary coverage and spatial resolution. Unlike single-volume approaches, it prioritizes high-fidelity voxelization near the eye while maintaining lower-detail coverage for distant indirect illumination. It is distinct from Voxel Space by explicitly managing multiple discrete resolution tiers rather than a single unified or sparse structure. The concept of voxel-based processing originated with the voxblt Engine (vE), a 3D frame-buffer processor developed by Arie Kaufman as part of the CUBE multiprocessor system in the late 1980s. The vE was designed as the 3D counterpart to the 2D frame buffer processor (FBP), operating as an independent processor that executes commands from a 3D Frame Buffer Display List (FBDL3). It was intended to offload room management, clipping, and primitive operations from the main CPU and 2D video/viewing processors, freeing them for geometry, viewing, and video tasks. The vE manipulates voxel maps stored in a Cubic Frame Buffer (CFB), a full 3D cellular memory where each voxel holds density, color, material, texture, and translucency data. A typical CFB for a 512^3 resolution requires approximately 128 Mbytes of memory. The system supports three types of primitives: rooms (3D windows/cuboids), jacks (3D cursors), and figurines (3D icons). These primitives are unstructured sub-arrays of the CFB, defined by coordinates and priority values to handle space conflicts. The vE was applied to empirical data in medical imaging, biology, geology, 3D image processing, CAD, scientific volume visualization, and 3D simulation/animation. It supported 3D input devices such as the Polhemus 3SPACE Isotrak ('kite') and a 2D mouse for 3D positioning. The architecture included specific tables (Room, Jack, Figurine, Priority, Device) and registers (Mode, System, Input) to manage state, priority, and hardware acceleration. Modern voxel engines and games have evolved from these hardware-centric origins to software-based implementations on GPUs, utilizing techniques like Cascaded Voxel Volumes for global illumination and 2.5D approximations like Voxel Space for constrained hardware environments. The voxblt Engine: A Voxel Frame Buffer Processor, https://doi.org/10.2312/eggh/eggh88/085-102, fetched 2026-10-26

name: Voxel Space
head: 2.5D voxel engine, color map and depth map 3D
body: Voxel Space is a 2.5D rendering technique that generates a pseudo-3D environment by plotting vertical lines whose colors are sampled from a 2D color map and whose initial vertical positions are determined by a 2D depth map. It avoids full 3D volumetric ray-casting or polygon rasterization, instead relying on pre-computed height and color data to simulate perspective. It builds on Voxel engines and games and differs from Cascaded Voxel Volumes by using fixed vertical lines rather than volumetric traversal. Inputs: A 2D color map storing surface colors. A 2D depth map storing vertical height offsets for each column. Camera parameters: horizontal position, vertical angle, and altitude. Outputs: A 2D frame buffer containing the rendered image. Data Structures: colormap: 2D array of color values. depthmap: 2D array of height offsets. mathtables: Pre-computed tables for rotation and trigonometric values to avoid runtime calculation. framebuffers: Two frame buffers for double buffering. Steps: 1. Initialize: Allocate two frame buffers for double buffering. 2. Copy Code to RAM: Transfer the ARM engine code to RAM for faster execution than cartridge ROM. 3. Calculate Camera State: Determine camera position and orientation, restricting heights and vertical angles to values stored in mathtables. 4. Iterate Columns: For each column x in the output image: a. Sample Depth: Read the height offset h from the depthmap at the corresponding map coordinate. b. Determine Y-Start: Calculate the initial y-coordinate for the vertical line based on h and the camera's vertical angle. c. Plot Vertical Line: Iterate through the vertical pixels of the column. For each pixel, sample the color from the colormap and plot it at the calculated position. 5. Optimize Horizontal Frequency: Reduce the frequency of horizontal plane rendering for distant columns to save processing time. 6. Optimize Math Tables: Use pre-computed values from mathtables for rotation and trigonometric calculations instead of computing them at runtime. 7. Optimize Shift Operations: Use bitwise shift operations (<<, >>) instead of multiplication or division where possible to speed up calculations. 8. Optimize Inlining: Replicate and modify the main render routine for each angle rendering to avoid function call overhead. 9. Optimize Background Mode: Use GBA Background Mode 5 to decrease resolution and facilitate frame buffer switching. 10. Optimize Scrolling: Use GBA background scaling and scrolling features to render "intra-frames" between full frame renders to improve perceived fluidity. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def rendervoxelspace(colormap, depthmap, mathtables, cameraangle, cameraaltitude, framewidth, frameheight): # Optimization: Code is assumed to be in RAM # Optimization: Use GBA Background Mode 5 # Pre-calculate camera constants from mathtables # Limits camera height and angle to stored values camcos = mathtables[cameraangle] camsin = mathtables[cameraangle + 1] # Double buffering setup framebuffers = [[0] framewidth for in range(frameheight)] for in range(2)] activebuffer = 0 inactivebuffer = 1 # Map dimensions from source code snippet mapwidth = 1024 mapheight = 1024 for x in range(framewidth): # Optimization: Horizontal plane render frequency decreases with distance # Exact frequency reduction formula not given in sources # Sample depth map # Map coordinate calculation depends on camera position and rotation # Exact projection math not given in sources mapx = (x + cameraangle) % mapwidth heightoffset = depthmap[mapx] # Calculate initial y-coordinate # ystart is derived from heightoffset and camera vertical angle ystart = heightoffset + cameraaltitude # Plot vertical line # Iterate through the vertical pixels of the column # Line length not specified; iterates to bottom of screen for y in range(frameheight - ystart): # Sample color from color map color = colormap[mapx, y] # Plot pixel using bitwise shifts for speed where possible framebuffers[activebuffer][ystart + y][x] = color # Optimization: Use scrolling for intra-frames # This is handled by hardware features, not explicit code steps # Swap buffers framebuffers[activebuffer], framebuffers[inactivebuffer] = framebuffers[inactivebuffer], framebuffers[activebuffer] activebuffer = inactivebuffer Parameters: mathtables: Size and content depend on the required precision and range of camera angles. Specific sizes are not given. dimmapa: 1024 (from source code snippet, likely map dimension). dimmapalog2: 10 (log2 of map dimension). Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Simple calculations are excessive for the GBA ARM CPU, requiring significant optimization for a good frame rate. Camera heights and vertical angles are limited to those stored in the mathtables. Time Complexity: Not explicitly defined, but heavily optimized for constant-time lookups using pre-computed tables and bitwise operations. Memory Complexity: Requires storage for color map, depth map, and math tables. Specific memory usage is not given. Measured Performance: Designed for the GameBoy Advance ARM CPU. Without optimizations, frame rates are poor. With optimizations (RAM code, math tables, shift operations), a "decent frame rate" is achieved. Scaling: Performance degrades if camera angles or heights exceed the pre-computed mathtables range. Strengths: Fast rendering on limited hardware; simple implementation; good visual result for 2.5D games. Limitations: Limited to 2.5D perspective; camera movement restricted to pre-computed angles/heights; not suitable for full 3D navigation. When to use: When targeting hardware with limited processing power (e.g., GBA) and a 2.5D perspective is acceptable. When not to use: When full 3D navigation or dynamic lighting is required. Voxel Space was originally developed by NovaLogic for the game Comanche. The technique was later reverse-engineered and implemented for the GameBoy Advance. The technology may still be patented in some countries. juanmv94/GameBoy-Advance-3D-voxel-space-demo, https://github.com/juanmv94/GameBoy-Advance-3D-voxel-space-demo, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial)

name: Cascaded Voxel Volumes
body: Cascaded Voxel Volumes is a spatial partitioning method for Voxelized Global Illumination (VXGI) that extends the concept of cascaded shadow maps to volumetric data. It addresses the problem of balancing memory usage and spatial resolution in large scenes by using multiple volumes with identical resolution but different scales, centered around the player. Unlike single-volume approaches that must cover the entire scene or suffer from low resolution at distance, this method provides high-resolution coverage near the eye and lower-resolution coverage further away. Inputs: Camera position and orientation, scene geometry, and cascade configuration parameters. Outputs: A set of N 3D textures (voxel grids), each representing a different spatial scale centered on the camera. Data Structures: An array of N volume instances, where each instance contains a 3D texture of fixed resolution R \times R \times R (identical for all cascades) and a transformation matrix defining its world-space position and scale. Steps: 1. Cascade Setup: Define N cascades. Cascade 0 is the smallest scale (highest resolution) centered tightly around the camera. Subsequent cascades i have increasing scales si (where s{i+1} > si) and cover larger volumes of the scene. 2. Voxelization: For each frame (or staggered frames): a. Position each cascade volume in world space centered on the camera, scaled according to si. b. Rasterize scene geometry into the 3D texture of cascade i by projecting geometry onto the orthographic view of the cascade and filling the corresponding voxels. c. Clamping: Clamp the axis-aligned orthographic projections to world-space voxel-sized increments to prevent color swimming. 3. Update Strategy: Prioritize the cascade closest to the player (Cascade 0) for updates. Stagger updates of other cascades across multiple frames to reduce per-frame computational load. 4. Rendering: During ray casting or cone tracing for GI, sample from the appropriate cascade based on the ray's distance from the camera. Formulas: Cascade Scale: The physical size of cascade i is proportional to si. Clamping: Let P be the projected coordinate. The clamped coordinate P' is: P' = \text{floor}(P / \Delta) \cdot \Delta where \Delta is the world-space voxel size of the cascade. Parameters: The exact number of cascades (N), resolution (R), and scale factors (si) are not given in the sources. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Color Swimming: Moving the camera causes different fragments to be rendered, creating different voxels and visible color shifts. Fixed by clamping projections to voxel-sized increments. Cascade Edges: Discontinuities may occur at the boundaries between cascades. A linear interpolation between the two values at the boundary is suggested as a potential solution. Voxels Behind Eye: Some voxels remain behind the eye because objects in front of the eye may still receive indirect color from objects behind the eye. A specific implementation variant where multiple 3D textures create cascades that surround the eye, voxelizing only the geometry surrounding the eye rather than the entire scene. It is chosen for open-world style games to make voxel-based global illumination possible by allowing farther areas to benefit from indirect illumination at a less-detailed level. Key challenges include fixing voxel color swimming by clamping axis-aligned orthographic projections to world-space voxel-sized increments and handling edges between cascades, potentially via linear interpolation. Time Complexity: Staggering updates reduces per-frame computational load by updating cascades across multiple frames. Exact complexity formulas are not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Memory usage scales with the number of cascades and fixed resolution, but exact complexity is not given in the sources. Performance: Used in 'The Tomorrow Children' on PS4 for efficient coverage of large scenes. NVIDIA's VXGI in Unreal Engine 4 uses this because specular reflections lose quality at greater distances, justifying high resolution near the player. Strengths: High resolution near the player; efficient coverage of large scenes. Limitations: Potential for aliasing/color swimming if not clamped; discontinuities at cascade boundaries. The method was proposed as an extension of cascaded shadow maps to VXGI. It was implemented in 'The Tomorrow Children' by Q-Games on PS4 and observed in NVIDIA's VXGI implementation in Unreal Engine 4. The concept of using multiple cascades to surround the eye was discussed in the context of Gigavoxels and sparse voxelization by Sean Lilley in 2012. name: Multi-Subject Medical Visualization
body: Multi-Subject Medical Visualization is the visualization of datasets including measurements and imaging for more than one subject at a time. It addresses the analysis of medical cohort studies where diverse data types are acquired to diagnose or predict clinical outcomes, distinguishing itself from its sibling Mixed Modality Visualization by focusing on multiple subjects rather than heterogeneous data types, while coupling information and scientific visualization to extract patterns affecting subgroups of the whole collection. The family relies on creating a highly interactive coupled view visualization interface. This interface integrates both information and scientific visualization techniques. The goal is to allow users to extract and analyze certain patterns that affect subgroups of the whole collection. Mixed Modality Visualization is the visualization of mixed modality data, including imaging, genetics, and blood measurements, acquired from a group of subjects. It addresses the analysis of complex medical cohort studies where diverse data types must be integrated to diagnose or predict clinical outcomes. It is distinguished from its sibling Multi-Subject Medical Visualization by its specific focus on integrating heterogeneous data types (imaging, genetics, blood) rather than just multiple subjects, though it relies on the same coupled view interface principles. Medical visualization has started to work on the problem of working with multi-subject data. These datasets include measurements and imaging for more than one subject at a time. The aim of the referenced work is to be able to extract and analyze certain patterns that affect subgroups of the whole collection. LifeLines2 is an early information visualization system to visualize and compare multiple patient histories or electronic medical records. Work has been done on the interactive visualization of multi-subject and mixed modality datasets acquired by medical cohort studies. In these studies, mixed modality data, including imaging, genetics, and blood measurements, is acquired from a group of subjects in order to be analyzed for diagnosing or predicting the clinical outcome of that group. It was demonstrated by Stenwijk to create a highly interactive coupled view visualization interface, integrating both information and scientific visualization techniques. name: GPU, web and parallel renderers
body: This family covers rendering systems that map volumetric data I(x,y,z) to perceptible outputs by offloading computation to parallel hardware (GPUs, multi-core CPUs) or executing entirely within web browsers via WebGL/WebGPU. It addresses the computational intensity of volume rendering by leveraging massive parallelism for tasks like ray casting, splatting, and data sorting. It is distinguished from Voxel engines and games by its focus on general-purpose visualization rather than game engine integration, and from Film and production rendering by its emphasis on real-time or near-real-time interactivity and web compatibility. The articles in this family share the goal of mapping abstract volumetric data to a perceptible output through specific system constraints. Common mechanisms include: 1. Hardware Acceleration Mapping: Offloading computationally intensive tasks (ray casting, splatting, sorting) to parallel execution units (GPUs, multi-core CPUs) to achieve real-time or near-real-time performance. 2. Data Structure Optimization: Storing volumetric data in formats optimized for the target hardware, such as 3D/4D textures for coalesced memory access on GPUs or sparse structures for memory efficiency. 3. Depth Management: Handling the ordering of contributions for alpha-blended rendering, often requiring GPU-based sorting algorithms (radix sort, linked lists) to ensure correct compositing. 4. Physical-to-Digital Mapping: In the case of volumetric displays, transforming 3D voxel coordinates into 2D control signals (pixel buffers, SLM patterns) synchronized with mechanical or optical processes to create a physical 3D light field. WebSplatter is a WebGPU-based renderer for 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) designed to achieve high-performance, cross-device compatibility in web browsers. It solves the problem of unstable and memory-intensive Gaussian Splatting implementations on the web by replacing CPU-based and spin-wait-based sorting with a wait-free GPU radix sort and optimizing memory access patterns. Unlike sibling methods that rely on WebGL or naive WebGPU ports, WebSplatter ensures stability on low-end mobile hardware and avoids the busy-waiting pitfalls of Apple M-series chips, maintaining visual fidelity comparable to native CUDA implementations. Choose this method when targeting stable, high-fidelity 3DGS in web environments across diverse hardware. ClearView (Unified) is a 3-pass WebGL2 renderer designed for visualizing unstructured hexahedral meshes, specifically wireframes and scalar fields, by adapting GPU-accelerated parallel prefix list (PPLL) techniques to browser constraints. It solves the problem of rendering complex volumetric meshes in WebGL2, which lacks Shader Storage Buffer Objects (SSBOs), by encoding mesh data into image2D textures and using atomic operations to manage fragment accumulation. Unlike WebSplatter which focuses on splatting, ClearView explicitly handles hexahedral topology via a gather-resolve pipeline that supports depth-sorted alpha blending without CPU-side sorting. Choose this method when rendering hexahedral meshes in WebGL2 without CPU-side sorting. CPU-driven task spawning is a GPU execution model where the CPU acts as the central governor, deciding when and how GPU tasks are launched, while the GPU functions as a coprocessor that executes work requests but cannot generate new ones. This approach centralizes decision-making logic but suffers from high CPU-GPU communication latency, making it ineffective for pipelines with fine-grain micro-dependencies or stages that dynamically compute the work for subsequent stages. It differs from GPU-driven spawning (where the GPU generates its own work) and asynchronous submission (which hides latency but still relies on CPU-initiated commands) by strictly enforcing a top-down control hierarchy. Choose this method when centralized CPU control is required, but avoid it for fine-grain dynamic workloads. Pure client-side renderers perform all volume rendering computations within the user's web browser, requiring only a file server as a backend to serve volumetric data. This approach eliminates the need for dedicated rendering servers or backend gradient computation, shifting the processing load entirely to the client's GPU. It is distinguished from server-side rendering architectures by its reliance on local execution and from hybrid models by the absence of server-side rasterization or ray-marching services. Choose this method when avoiding dedicated rendering servers or backend services is a priority. This architecture enables interactive visualization of large volumetric datasets on resource-constrained mobile clients by offloading all rendering computation to a server-side cluster. It differs from pure client-side renderers by requiring a dedicated rendering backend, and from distributed shared-memory schemes by utilizing a single node with multiple GPUs/CPUs or a cluster of nodes managed via the Chromium framework. It solves the problem of limited local hardware (e.g., PDAs) by transmitting compressed image buffers rather than raw volumetric data. Choose this method when client hardware is insufficient for local rendering but network transmission of compressed frames is viable. CPU multithreaded rendering manages parallel chunk rendering using a thread pool pattern with a free renderer queue, active renderer counter, and condition variable synchronization. It differs from GPU-driven approaches by handling all scheduling and synchronization on the CPU, making it suitable for CPU-bound voxel worlds that use Z-buffering to prevent overdraw. Choose this method for CPU-based chunked rendering where thread pool management is preferred over GPU compute shaders. Step: Create a GL-Context on both X-screens (for multiple NVidia cards) and switch rendering between them one time per frame. Combine results of both cards. Since the second card's result is combined with the first, the second card need not be connected to a monitor. Split the sorted array of voxels equally over both cards by interleaving detail coefficients (and histogram) for each pyramid level. Combine resulting images using a pixel-wise maximum operator. Parameter: Preferred pixel format for CPU transfer: GLUNSIGNEDINT8888. Pitfall: No extension exists for direct data shuffling between cards; intermediate results must pass through the CPU using glReadPixels on one context and glDrawPixels on the other. Comparison: Multi-threading rendering loops for multiple contexts did not yield performance gains because the algorithm is GPU-bound; CPU synchronization overhead outweighs the tiny load. Interleaving coefficients is preferred over splitting in the middle to better divide load during progressive refinement. Definition: A VR optimization that concurrently runs CUDA kernels for the left and right eye in multiple streams to better utilize the GPU and mitigate under-utilization caused by imbalanced workloads (varying amounts of splats per tile). Overlapping rendering pipelines for left and right eyes in VR using separate, non-blocking CUDA streams to fill GPU utilization gaps caused by imbalanced workloads. Step: Overlap the right eye's tile ID sorting and rasterization stages with the left eye's rasterization stage. Pitfall: Imbalanced workloads under-utilize the GPU because the stream waits until the kernel's longest-running thread-blocks are finished. Do not overlap the left and right eye's sorting stages, as this would require creating separate intermediate sorting buffers, increasing memory usage. Number: On the Berlin scene (1.0 M splats), single stream takes 6.3 ms while concurrent streams take 5.2 ms. On the Campus scene (28.6 M splats), single stream takes 16.2 ms while concurrent streams take 13.8 ms. Definition: In web-based environments, research focuses on solutions to network latency when loading volumetric data and improving volume rendering performance on the web. Designed to work without a dedicated rendering backend and relies only on a file server. All volume rendering is done in the browser itself. Definition: Uses the same technique as Viv for representing multiple channels on the GPU (accumulation-level intermixing). Definition: Manages parallel chunk rendering using a thread pool pattern with a free renderer queue, active renderer counter, and condition variable synchronization. Step: Iterate over loaded world chunks (i, j, k from 0 to LOADEDWORLDSIZE). For each chunk, call renderChunk. In renderChunk, wait while activeRenderers >= MAXRENDERERS and freeRenderers queue is empty. Pop a Renderer from freeRenderers or allocate a new one. Increment activeRenderers. Spawn a detached std::thread calling Chunk::render(chunk, renderer). When a renderer finishes, call freeRenderer to push it back to freeRenderers, decrement activeRenderers, and notify cv if activeRenderers reaches 0. Parameter: MAXRENDERERS: 20 (maximum concurrent rendering threads). Layout: RendererManager state: freeRenderers (ThreadsafeQueue<Renderer>), cv (std::conditionvariable), mtx (std::mutex), activeRenderers (std::atomic<int> initialized to 0). Web-based volume rendering research addresses network latency and browser performance, often relying on pure client-side architectures that require only a file server. Early implementations focused on offloading rendering to remote servers, but modern approaches like WebSplatter and ClearView leverage WebGPU and WebGL2 for local computation. Multi-GPU techniques using NVidia drivers allow splitting workloads across cards via X-screens, though CPU-mediated data transfer remains a bottleneck. VR rendering optimizations utilize concurrent CUDA streams to overlap left/right eye rendering, improving utilization on imbalanced workloads. CPU-based multithreaded chunk rendering uses a thread pool with a maximum of 20 concurrent renderers to manage parallel world sections. name: CPU-Driven Task Spawning
head: CPU-controlled GPU execution, CPU-driven thread spawning
body: CPU-driven task spawning is a rendering architecture where the CPU acts as the central governor, deciding when and how GPU tasks are launched, while the GPU executes these work requests as a coprocessor. It solves the problem of coordinating complex volumetric pipelines by centralizing decision-making logic on the CPU, which has access to all system resources. Unlike GPU-driven approaches where the GPU generates its own work, this model treats the GPU as a passive executor, but suffers from high communication latency that creates bottlenecks in pipelines with fine-grain micro-dependencies. Steps: 1. CPU Decision: The CPU analyzes the current state of the volume rendering pipeline and determines the necessary GPU work. 2. Command Emission: The CPU constructs command buffers. In standard submission, parameters are fixed at this stage. In indirect submission, the CPU writes a pointer to GPU memory instead of the actual parameters. 3. Submission: The CPU submits the command buffer to a GPU submission queue. 4. Execution: The GPU fetches commands from the queue. If indirect, it reads the parameters from the specified GPU memory address. 5. Synchronization: Barriers are used to enforce dependencies. In standard models, barriers block all subsequent tasks on the queue. In multi-queue models, barriers only affect tasks within the same queue. Formulas and Parameters: Latency (L): The round-trip time for an empty submission (CPU \rightarrow GPU \rightarrow CPU). Measured at 20\text{--}30 \, \mu\text{s}. Queue Limits: Vulkan reports 24 queues for Nvidia GPUs, 16 for AMD, 5 for Intel, and usually only 1 for mobiles. CUDA lets you have an unlimited number of streams, but behind the scenes maps them to 32 internal queues. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Latency Bottleneck: The 20\text{--}30 \, \mu\text{s} latency is significant compared to sub-nanosecond CPU/GPU clocks. This makes synchronous control ineffective for pipelines where one stage computes work for the next. Indirect Overhead: Canceling a submission by setting task size to zero still incurs submission overhead. If the number of pipeline passes is unknown, the CPU must issue indirect submissions for the maximum possible passes, paying overhead for unused ones. Barrier Coarseness: Barriers enforce dependencies at the queue level, not the core level. A barrier between Task A and Task B forces all tasks submitted after B to wait for A, and all tasks before A to wait for B. Queue Granularity: Modern GPUs have 50–100 cores (SMs/WGPs/Xe Cores). The limited number of queues (max 24 in Vulkan) is insufficient to enforce dependencies at the core granularity. Asynchronous submission is a model where GPU commands are placed into a queue and executed by the GPU as soon as required resources are available, but they return immediately from the point of view of the CPU. It solves the problem of high CPU-GPU communication latency inherent in synchronous control, allowing the CPU and GPU to work concurrently. Unlike synchronous submission, which blocks the CPU until the GPU completes a task, asynchronous submission removes round-trip latency and enables parallel execution of many small tasks or chaining of big tasks. Indirect submission is a model where the CPU emits all GPU commands, but the parameters of said commands are filled by the GPU. The command contains an address in GPU memory, which the GPU reads before execution to determine parameters. A first pass writes to the pointer in GPU memory to decide the command's parameters. A barrier must be placed between the two passes to ensure correct execution. Task size can be set to zero to effectively cancel a submission, but the submission overhead is still incurred. It is not possible to dynamically create new submissions from the GPU. If the number of required passes is not known in advance, one must issue indirect submissions for a maximum number of passes and dynamically cancel unnecessary ones, paying overhead many times. It is an awkward hybrid model where the GPU controls most aspects but cannot initiate submissions, making it unintuitive and error-prone. Widely available and in use today for indirect control of task size (number of workgroups, vertices, rays). Advanced iterations include DirectX ExecuteIndirect and Vulkan VKEXTdevicegeneratedcommands. Multiple submission queues is a solution where GPU commands are submitted to specific queues instead of directly to the GPU. Barriers only enforce dependencies between tasks of the same queue, allowing tasks in different queues to run independently. Submit task C to a different queue than task A and B to let it run independently of A or B. Vulkan reports 24 queues for Nvidia GPUs, 16 for AMD, 5 for Intel, and usually only 1 for mobiles. CUDA lets you have an unlimited number of streams, but behind the scenes maps them to 32 internal queues. The restricted number of queues is not enough for micro-dependencies. Modern GPUs can have 50 to 100 cores, so it is not possible to use queues to enforce dependencies at the GPU core granularity. Latency: High CPU-GPU round-trip latency (20\text{--}30 \, \mu\text{s}) is the primary constraint. This latency is consistent across integrated (R9 7900X) and dedicated (RTX 4080) GPUs, indicating it stems from driver layers rather than physical signal travel. Complexity: The model is simple in theory (CPU as governor) but complex in practice due to the need for workarounds like indirect submission and multiple queues to mitigate latency and dependency issues. Scalability: Limited by the number of submission queues. With only 16–24 queues in Vulkan, fine-grained parallelism (micro-dependencies) cannot be fully exploited. Strengths: Centralized control logic; widely supported by existing APIs (Vulkan, CUDA, DirectX). Limitations: High latency for synchronous control; indirect submission incurs overhead even for canceled tasks; barriers are coarse-grained. When to use: Suitable for coarse-grained pipelines where stages are independent or have large dependencies. Unsuitable for fine-grain micro-dependencies or pipelines requiring dynamic work generation from the GPU. The CPU-driven task spawning model originated from the traditional view of GPUs as coprocessors. This model was designed to keep system architecture simple by centralizing decision-making on the CPU. However, as GPU capabilities grew, the high latency of CPU-GPU communication became a bottleneck, leading to the development of asynchronous submission, indirect submission, and multiple queues as partial solutions. name: Asynchronous Submission
head: GPU command queue submission, Non-blocking GPU submission
body: Asynchronous submission is a model where GPU commands are placed into a queue and executed by the GPU as soon as required resources are available, but they return immediately from the point of view of the CPU. It solves the problem of high CPU-GPU communication latency inherent in synchronous control, allowing the CPU and GPU to work concurrently. Unlike synchronous submission, which blocks the CPU until the GPU completes a task, asynchronous submission removes round-trip latency and enables parallel execution of many small tasks or chaining of big tasks. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A stream of GPU commands (e.g., kernel launches, memory copies) generated by the CPU. Output: Immediate return of the submission function to the CPU; execution of commands on the GPU hardware. Data Structures: Command Queue: A buffer managed by the driver/runtime where the CPU appends command descriptors. The exact layout is implementation-dependent, but logically it is a FIFO structure. Event Objects: Optional objects used to track completion status for synchronization, such as for split barriers or indirect submission. Steps: 1. The CPU constructs a command descriptor (e.g., kernel arguments, grid/block dimensions). 2. The CPU appends this descriptor to the GPU command queue. 3. The submission function returns immediately to the CPU. 4. The GPU driver or hardware dequeues commands and executes them as soon as resources (cores, memory bandwidth) are available. Formulas: Not given in the sources. Parameters: Not given in the sources. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: RAW/WAR Dependencies: If Task B uses results from Task A (Read After Write) or writes to memory read by Task A (Write After Read), submissions cannot overlap safely. Barriers must be used to prevent these dependencies, but they voluntarily stall the GPU. Dynamic Dispatch Parameters: If Task A computes parameters (e.g., thread count) for Task B, the CPU must wait for Task A to complete before submitting Task B, reintroducing CPU-GPU communication delay. This necessitates indirect submission. Barrier Granularity: Modern GPUs have 50 to 100 cores (SMs, WGPs, or Xe Cores). Queues cannot enforce dependencies at the core granularity, so barriers enforce global dependencies that can create pipeline bubbles if micro-dependencies exist. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. class TaskArgs: def init(self, kernel, grid, block, data): self.kernel = kernel self.grid = grid self.block = block self.data = data def submittaskasync(queue, args): """Appends a task to the GPU queue and returns immediately.""" command = { 'kernel': args.kernel, 'grid': args.grid, 'block': args.block, 'args': args.data } queue.append(command) return def appendbarrier(queue): """Appends a barrier command to the queue.""" queue.append({'type': 'barrier'}) def submitwithbarrier(queue, taska, taskb): """Submits Task A, then a barrier, then Task B.""" submittaskasync(queue, taska) appendbarrier(queue) submittaskasync(queue, taskb) A mechanism that splits the barrier command into two distinct commands: Set and Wait. Tasks submitted after Wait will wait for tasks submitted before Set, but tasks submitted between Set and Wait can run independently. This adds flexibility by allowing independent work to be scheduled in the gap between the two barrier halves. Parameters: Set and Wait commands take an event parameter to allow for multiple split barriers to run in parallel. Pitfalls: Requires careful advance planning to schedule independent work before submitting the Wait command, making it difficult to reason with. Time Complexity: Submission is O(1) from the CPU perspective as it returns immediately. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Performance: Improves GPU utilization by removing round-trip latency and allowing parallel execution of small tasks or overlapping of big tasks. Strengths: High concurrency, reduced CPU idle time, better hardware utilization. Limitations: Dependency management is complex; barriers can stall the GPU; dynamic dispatch requires additional mechanisms like indirect submission. When to use: Default mode for all modern GPU APIs due to performance benefits. When not to use: Not given in the sources. Asynchronous submission is the default model in all modern GPU APIs. It removes round-trip latency caused by synchronous control, allowing the CPU and GPU to work concurrently. The indirect submission model was invented as a semi-GPU-driven approach to solve the problem of dynamic dispatch parameters in the asynchronous model. name: Pure client-side renderers
body: Pure client-side renderers execute all volumetric rendering computations within the web browser, requiring only a file server as a backend. Unlike server-side rendering schemes that stream rendered images, this approach performs volume rendering directly in the browser itself. Builds on the shared principles of GPU, web and parallel renderers. WebSplatter is a pure client-side WebGPU renderer for 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) designed to achieve high-performance, cross-device compatibility in web browsers. It solves the problem of inconsistent performance and stability in existing web-based 3DGS viewers by replacing CPU-based or spin-wait-based sorting with a fully GPU-based, wait-free radix sort. Unlike its sibling ClearView (Unified) Renderer, which focuses on unified rendering pipelines, WebSplatter specifically targets the constraints of the WebGPU API and heterogeneous hardware (from high-end desktops to mobile phones), ensuring that the system never becomes sort-bound and maintains visual fidelity comparable to native CUDA implementations. ClearView (Unified) is a 3-pass WebGL2 renderer designed for unstructured hexahedral mesh visualization, specifically targeting wireframes and scalar fields. It solves the problem of rendering complex volumetric meshes in the browser by replacing traditional CPU-side sorting or SSBO-based GPU buffers with a Parallel Prefix List (PPLL) structure stored in image2D textures. Unlike WebSplatter, which uses splatting techniques, ClearView explicitly rasterizes per-face triangles and manages fragment ordering via atomic operations and a linked-list-like buffer, enabling correct alpha blending without depth-sorting artifacts. Web-Based Volume Rendering refers to the class of pure client-side volume rendering systems that execute entirely within a web browser, requiring only a file server as a backend. It solves the problem of network latency and server infrastructure costs associated with remote rendering by offloading all computational work to the client. Unlike server-side rendering schemes that stream rendered images, this approach leverages client-side GPU acceleration to render volumetric data directly in the browser, distinguishing it from siblings like WebSplatter which may employ specific splatting optimizations, and ClearView (Unified) Renderer which offers a unified rendering pipeline. Pure client-side rendering emerged to avoid the need to compute gradients on the client and to work without a dedicated rendering backend. Early implementations relied on WebGL to enable hardware-accelerated volume rendering in browsers, allowing for the visualization of biomedical and scientific data without dedicated backend servers. Notable examples include Neuroglancer, which uses a bricked multi-resolution hierarchy to scale to large datasets, and Viv, a WebGL-based library for biomedical data visualization. name: WebSplatter
body: WebSplatter is a pure client-side WebGPU renderer for 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) designed to achieve high-performance, cross-device compatibility in web browsers. It solves the problem of inconsistent performance and stability in existing web-based 3DGS viewers by replacing CPU-based or spin-wait-based sorting with a fully GPU-based, wait-free radix sort. Unlike its sibling ClearView (Unified) Renderer, which focuses on unified rendering pipelines, WebSplatter specifically targets the constraints of the WebGPU API and heterogeneous hardware (from high-end desktops to mobile phones), ensuring that the system never becomes sort-bound and maintains visual fidelity comparable to native CUDA implementations. WebSplatter processes 3D Gaussian Splatting data through three main stages: pre-processing, sorting, and rendering. The method relies on WebGPU compute shaders for data transformation and sorting, and fragment shaders for rasterization. Input: A 3DGS scene file containing Gaussian primitives (position, covariance/scale, rotation, opacity, spherical harmonics coefficients) and camera parameters (view and projection matrices). Output: A 2D color buffer (framebuffer) representing the rendered image. The implementation uses GPU buffers to store intermediate states. While exact byte layouts are not fully specified in the source, the following structures are implied by the WebGPU context and 3DGS requirements: 1. Gaussian Attributes Buffer: Stores raw Gaussian data. Fields typically include: position: vec3<f32> (3D coordinates). scale: vec3<f32> (scaling factors). rotation: vec4<f32> (quaternion). opacity: f32. shcoeffs: Array of f32 (Spherical Harmonics). 2. Splat List Buffer: Stores the projected 2D splats. Fields typically include: center: vec2<f32> (projected screen coordinates). width/height: f32 (extent of the 2D Gaussian). depth: f32 (for sorting). originalindex: u32 (to retrieve attributes). 3. Sorting Buffers: Double-buffered arrays of indices or keys used by the radix sort algorithm. 1. Pre-processing (Projection): For each Gaussian primitive, compute the 3D-to-2D projection using the camera's view and projection matrices. Calculate the 2D covariance matrix in screen space. Determine the bounding box (width and height) of the 2D Gaussian ellipse. Discard Gaussians that are outside the view frustum or have negligible contribution. Store the projected splat data (center, width, height, depth, original index) in the Splat List Buffer. 2. Sorting (Wait-Free Radix Sort): Sort the Splat List Buffer by depth (z-coordinate) in front-to-back order. Use a GPU-based radix sort algorithm. The source emphasizes a "wait-free" design to avoid spin-waiting, which is critical for Apple M-series chips where workgroup execution order is not guaranteed. The sort is performed entirely on the GPU using compute shaders, avoiding CPU-GPU synchronization stalls. 3. Rendering (Rasterization): Iterate through the sorted splats. For each splat, rasterize the 2D Gaussian ellipse onto the screen. Perform alpha blending: C{out} = C{src} \cdot \alpha{src} + C{dst} \cdot (1 - \alpha{src}) Where C{src} is the color of the current splat, \alpha{src} is its opacity, and C{dst} is the current color in the framebuffer. Update the depth buffer if necessary (though standard 3DGS often uses depth peeling or simple alpha blending without strict depth testing for the final image). The following pseudocode outlines the core logic, focusing on the sorting and rendering pipeline. WebGPU-specific shader execution is abstracted into standard Python operations for clarity. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def rendergaussiansplats(gaussians, cameraviewproj, viewportw, viewporth): # Step 1: Pre-processing (Projection & Culling) splatlist = [] for g in gaussians: # Project 3D center to screen space screenpos = projecttoscreen(g.position, cameraviewproj) # Compute 2D covariance and bounding box cov2d = computescreencovariance(g.cov3d, cameraviewproj) width, height = computeboundingbox(cov2d) # Frustum culling if isinview(screenpos, width, height, viewportw, viewporth): splatlist.append({ 'center': screenpos, 'width': width, 'height': height, 'depth': g.position.z, 'index': g.id, 'opacity': g.opacity, 'color': g.color }) # Step 2: Sorting (Wait-Free Radix Sort) # Sort by depth ascending (front-to-back) # Production uses WebGPU compute shaders; standard radix sort shown sortedsplats = radixsort(splatlist, key=lambda s: s['depth']) # Step 3: Rendering (Rasterization & Blending) framebuffer = [[(0.0, 0.0, 0.0, 0.0) for in range(viewportw)] for in range(viewporth)] for splat in sortedsplats: framebuffer = rasterizesplat(framebuffer, splat) return framebuffer def projecttoscreen(pos3d, viewprojmatrix): # Standard homogeneous projection clip = matmul4x4vec4(viewprojmatrix, [pos3d[0], pos3d[1], pos3d[2], 1.0]) ndc = [c / clip[3] for c in clip[:3]] return (ndc[0], ndc[1]) def matmul4x4vec4(matrix, vec): # 4x4 matrix-vector multiplication res = [0.0] 4 for i in range(4): for j in range(4): res[i] += matrix[i][j] vec[j] return res def computescreencovariance(cov3d, viewprojmatrix): # Jacobian of projection applied to 3D covariance # Simplified 2D projection covariance calculation return [cov3d[0][0], cov3d[0][1], cov3d[1][0], cov3d[1][1]] def computeboundingbox(cov2dflat): # Eigenvalues of 2D covariance give semi-axes cov2d = [[cov2dflat[0], cov2dflat[1]], [cov2dflat[2], cov2dflat[3]]] trace = cov2d[0][0] + cov2d[1][1] det = cov2d[0][0] cov2d[1][1] - cov2d[0][1] cov2d[1][0] disc = math.sqrt(max(0.0, trace2 - 4 det)) semix = math.sqrt(0.5 (trace + disc)) semiy = math.sqrt(0.5 (trace - disc)) return 2.0 semix, 2.0 semiy def isinview(center, width, height, w, h): # Check if bounding box overlaps viewport return abs(center[0]) < 1.0 and abs(center[1]) < 1.0 and width > 0 and height > 0 def radixsort(data, key): # Standard radix sort implementation # WebSplatter uses a GPU-based wait-free variant return sorted(data, key=key) def rasterizesplat(framebuffer, splat): # Alpha blend 2D Gaussian onto framebuffer cx, cy = splat['center'] w, h = splat['width'], splat['height'] for y in range(max(0, int(cy - h)), min(len(framebuffer), int(cy + h))): for x in range(max(0, int(cx - w)), min(len(framebuffer[0]), int(cx + w))): dx, dy = x - cx, y - cy alpha = splat['opacity'] math.exp(-0.5 (dx2/splat['width']2 + dy2/splat['height']2)) alpha = max(0.0, min(1.0, alpha)) fbr, fbg, fbb, fba = framebuffer[y][x] newr = splat['color'][0] alpha + fbr (1.0 - alpha) newg = splat['color'][1] alpha + fbg (1.0 - alpha) newb = splat['color'][2] alpha + fbb (1.0 - alpha) framebuffer[y][x] = (newr, newg, newb, fba + alpha (1.0 - fba)) return framebuffer Radix Sort Bins: Not specified in the source, but standard radix sort uses 8-bit or 16-bit bins. Splat Resolution: Not specified, but depends on the Gaussian scale. Frame Time Targets: Real-time (>30 FPS, i.e., <33.3 ms/frame) is the goal. On high-end GPUs, frame times are ~9.5 ms. Apple M1/M-Series Chips: Spin-wait-based sorting performs poorly due to lack of workgroup execution order guarantees, leading to busy-waiting. WebSplatter's wait-free design avoids this. Memory Constraints: Low-end devices (e.g., Oppo Find X2, iPhone 15 Pro Max) may crash if memory requirements exceed hardware limits. WebSplatter's efficient memory usage allows it to render on these devices where baselines fail. Firefox WebGPU Instability: Firefox may block WebGPU or report unreliable timestamp queries. WebSplatter is tested on Chrome/Edge where WebGPU is stable. Pre-processing Bottleneck: On low-end GPUs (e.g., Nvidia MX350), pre-processing (scanning raw splats) becomes the bottleneck due to limited memory throughput. Time Complexity: The sorting step is O(N \log N) or O(N) depending on the radix sort implementation, but the key metric is that it is GPU-accelerated and never becomes the bottleneck. Pre-processing is O(N). Rendering is O(S) where S is the number of splats. Memory Complexity: O(N) for storing Gaussian data and intermediate splat lists. WebSplatter is optimized to fit within the memory constraints of mobile devices. Measured Performance: Nvidia RTX 3070: Median frame time of 9.497 ms on the garden scene (5.8M splats), a 1.52× speedup over the fastest competing WebGPU implementation. MacBook Air M4: 1.06× faster than baseline. P99 latency of 116.851 ms with a standard deviation of 22.303 ms, indicating low jitter. Redmi K70 Pro: 1.18× faster than baseline. Renders 2.5M splats in 52.7 ms without crashing. Intel NUC iGPU: 2.26× faster than baseline. Scalability: On Nvidia MX350, scaling from 0.3M to 5.8M splats increases frame time by ~143 ms, compared to >280 ms for KeKsBoTer/web-splat (2.1× speedup). Bottleneck Analysis: High-end GPUs (RTX 3070, M-series, Redmi K70 Pro): Render-bound. Rasterization consumes 51.8% to 62.6% of frame time. Low-end GPUs (MX350, Intel NUC iGPU): Pre-process-bound. Pre-processing consumes up to 47.2% of frame time due to limited memory throughput. Sort-bound: Never occurs across all tested hardware. Strengths: Cross-device compatibility (works on mobile, desktop, integrated graphics). Wait-free sorting avoids hardware-specific pitfalls (e.g., Apple M1). Low variance in frame time, reducing micro-stuttering. Visual fidelity comparable to native CUDA implementation. Limitations: Dependent on WebGPU support in browsers (Firefox has stability issues). Pre-processing can be a bottleneck on very low-end hardware. WebSplatter was introduced in the paper "WebSplatter: Enabling Cross-Device Efficient Gaussian Splatting in Web Browsers via WebGPU". It addresses the limitations of previous web-based 3DGS renderers, which suffered from poor performance on certain hardware (especially Apple M-series) and instability on mobile devices. The method leverages the WebGPU API to provide a high-performance, portable solution for rendering 3DGS in web browsers. name: ClearView (Unified) Renderer
head: ClearView, ClearView Unified Buffer, ClearView WebGL2 Spike
body: ClearView (Unified) is a 3-pass WebGL2 renderer designed for unstructured hexahedral mesh visualization, specifically targeting wireframes and scalar fields. It solves the problem of rendering complex volumetric meshes in the browser by replacing traditional CPU-side sorting or SSBO-based GPU buffers with a Parallel Prefix List (PPLL) structure stored in image2D textures. Unlike WebSplatter, which uses splatting techniques, ClearView explicitly rasterizes per-face triangles and manages fragment ordering via atomic operations and a linked-list-like buffer, enabling correct alpha blending without depth-sorting artifacts. The renderer operates in three distinct passes: Clear, Gather, and Resolve. It relies on WebGL2 features (image2D, atomicuint) which are unavailable in software renderers like SwiftShader. Inputs: Mesh Data: Hexahedral mesh defined by vertices, cells, and connectivity. Vertices: 8 per cell, stored in Standard (STD) layout. Faces: 6 per cell. Edges: 12 per cell. Scalars: Per-vertex or per-cell scalar values. Camera: View/Projection matrices, camera position, and field of view. Sphere Parameters: Center and radius for ray-sphere intersection tests (used for LOD/culling). Outputs: Final Image: Alpha-blended 2D projection of the 3D mesh. Due to WebGL2 lacking Shader Storage Buffer Objects (SSBOs), all mesh data is encoded into 2D textures with a fixed row width of TEXWIDTH = 4096. 1. Face Texture (faceTex): Format: RG32UI (2 unsigned 32-bit integers per texel). Layout: 2 texels per face. Stores face connectivity indices. Dimensions: width = 4096, height = ceil(faceCount 2 / 4096). 2. Vertex Texture (vertexTex): Format: RGBA32F (4 floats per texel). Layout: 1 texel per vertex slot. Stores (x, y, z, scalarattribute). Mapping: VTK corner indices are mapped to STD indices via VTKTOSTD = [0, 1, 3, 2, 4, 5, 7, 6]. Dimensions: width = 4096, height = ceil(vertexCount / 4096). 3. Edge Texture (edgeTex): Format: RG32F (2 floats per texel). Layout: 1 texel per edge. Stores edge indices or geometric data. Dimensions: width = 4096, height = ceil(edgeCount / 4096). 4. Cell Scalar Texture (cellScalarTex): Format: R32F (1 float per texel). Layout: 1 texel per face/cell. Dimensions: width = 4096, height = ceil(faceCount / 4096). 5. Start Offset Texture (startOffsetTex): Format: R32UI (unsigned 32-bit integer). Layout: 1 texel per pixel in the viewport. Stores the starting index in the fragment buffer for each pixel's linked list. Dimensions: Matches viewport width and height. 6. Fragment Buffer Texture (fragmentBufferTex): Format: RGBA32UI (4 unsigned 32-bit integers per texel). Layout: 1 texel per fragment entry. Stores fragment data (e.g., depth, color, next pointer). Dimensions: Fixed at 2048 x 2048 (4 million entries). 7. Atomic Counter Buffer: Format: Uint32. Usage: Tracks the total number of fragments written to fragmentBufferTex. Bound to binding point 0. The renderer uses a specific Standard (STD) corner indexing for hexahedra: 0=c000, 1=c100, 2=c010, 3=c110, 4=c001, 5=c101, 6=c011, 7=c111. Edges: 12 per cell, defined as pairs of STD indices (e.g., [0,1], [1,3], etc.). Faces: 6 per cell. Each face lists 4 STD corner indices in face-local counter-clockwise (CCW) order (viewed from outside) and 4 edge indices. The ordering ensures outward-facing normals via cross product. FRAGBUFFERW: 2048. FRAGBUFFERH: 2048. LINKEDLISTSIZE: FRAGBUFFERW FRAGBUFFERH (4,194,304). RESOLVECUTOFF: 32 fragments per pixel. If a pixel has fewer than 32 fragments, an insertion sort is used during resolution; otherwise, a more complex sort or walk is performed. TEXWIDTH: 4096. LOD/Coloring Uniforms: uMaxLodValue: 1.0 uSelectedLodValueFocus: 0.4 uSelectedLodValueContext: 0.7 uImportantLineBoostFactor: 0.5. 1. Bind startOffsetTex (unit 0, R32UI, READWRITE) and fragmentBufferTex (unit 1, RGBA32UI, READWRITE) as image2D textures. 2. Bind the atomic counter buffer to binding point 0. 3. Set viewport to current canvas size. 4. Disable depth testing and face culling. 5. Draw a full-screen triangle (3 vertices) using the Clear shader. 6. The shader resets all values in startOffsetTex to -1, initializing the linked lists for each pixel. 1. Bind data textures: faceTex (unit 0), vertexTex (unit 1), edgeTex (unit 2), cellScalarTex (unit 3). 2. Bind startOffsetTex (unit 0, R32UI, READWRITE) and fragmentBufferTex (unit 1, RGBA32UI, READWRITE) as image2D textures. 3. Set camera uniforms: MVP matrix, ModelViewInverse, camera position, look direction, sphere center/radius, LOD values, colors, scalar range, and FOV. 4. It addresses the limitations of WebGL2 by mapping SSBO-based data structures to image2D textures, enabling parallel fragment collection and resolution without CPU intervention. name: Web-Based Volume Rendering
head: Author's web-based approach, Browser-based Volume Rendering, WebGPU Volume Rendering
body: Web-Based Volume Rendering refers to pure client-side volume rendering systems that execute entirely within a web browser, requiring only a file server as a backend. It solves the problem of network latency when loading volumetric data and avoids the need for a dedicated rendering backend by performing all volume rendering in the browser itself. This contrasts with server-side rendering schemes that offload computation to remote servers. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Volumetric data files served via HTTP. Output: A 2D raster image displayed in the browser viewport. Data Structures: Volumetric Data: Stored in GPU-accessible formats such as 3D or 4D textures. Transfer Function: Mapped to a 1D or 2D texture for GPU sampling. Steps: 1. Data Loading: The browser fetches volumetric data from the file server. 2. Texture Upload: Loaded data is uploaded to GPU memory as 3D textures. 3. Ray Casting: The browser's graphics API (WebGL or WebGPU) executes a fragment shader that casts rays through the volume. 4. Compositing: Contributions along the ray are accumulated using alpha blending. 5. Rendering: The final image is composited and displayed. Formulas: The standard volume rendering integral is computed per pixel: C = \int{tn}^{tf} T(t) \cdot c(t) \cdot \sigma(t) \, dt Where T(t) is transmittance, c(t) is color, and \sigma(t) is density. In discrete form: C = \sum{i=1}^{N} Ti \cdot ci \cdot \sigmai \cdot \Delta ti Ti = \prod{j=1}^{i-1} (1 - \sigmaj \cdot \Delta tj) Parameters: Sampling Rate: Determined by ray step size. Transfer Function: User-defined mapping from scalar values to color and opacity. Edge Cases: Memory Limits: Client-side rendering is constrained by available GPU memory. Network Latency: Initial load times can be high for large datasets without optimization. A client-server architecture for interactive 3D volume rendering of dense MRI volumes (up to 512^3) in a web browser. It sets itself apart by compiling the client entirely to WebAssembly (WASM) using Rust, enabling high-performance WebGL ray marching directly in the browser while serving raw HDF5 data from a lightweight Rust server. Choose it for large medical datasets (~8GB per sample) that exceed standard 2D viewer capabilities. Time Complexity: Rendering time depends on volume resolution, sampling rate, and GPU performance. Typically O(N) where N is the number of samples per pixel. Memory Complexity: Proportional to the size of the volumetric data stored in GPU memory. Performance: Real-time performance is achievable for moderate-sized volumes on modern GPUs. Large-scale data may suffer from memory constraints or network bottlenecks. Strengths: No dedicated rendering server required; works with any file server; leverages client hardware. Limitations: Constrained by client GPU memory and processing power; network latency affects initial load and streaming. When to Use: When server infrastructure is unavailable or undesirable, and client hardware is sufficient for the data size. When Not to Use: For extremely large datasets that exceed client GPU memory or require high-performance server-side computation. Web-based volume rendering research emerged as web technologies matured, focusing on solutions to network latency when loading volumetric data and improving volume rendering performance on the web. The approach is designed to work without a dedicated rendering backend, relying only on a file server while performing all volume rendering in the browser itself. Tools such as Neuroglancer and Viv represent developments in this area, though they may be limited to available GPU memory or specific data types. name: Web MRI Volume Renderer
head: GPU-accelerated 3D MRI volume renderer, WebGL ray marching volume renderer
body: A client-server architecture for interactive 3D volume rendering of dense MRI volumes (up to 512^3) in a web browser. It solves the problem of visualizing extremely large medical datasets (~8GB per sample) that are impractical for standard 2D cross-section viewers or heavy desktop applications. It sets itself apart by compiling the client entirely to WebAssembly (WASM) using Rust, enabling high-performance WebGL ray marching directly in the browser while serving raw HDF5 data from a lightweight Rust server. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Dense MRI volume data stored in HDF5 (.h5) format. Output: Interactive 3D visualization rendered via WebGL in the browser. Data Structures: Volume Data: Raw MRI samples loaded from HDF5 files. The source notes that a single sample can be approximately 8GB. The exact memory layout within the HDF5 file is not specified beyond being a standard HDF5 dataset. Occupancy Grid: A data structure used to optimize ray marching by skipping empty regions. The specific resolution, bit-depth, or construction algorithm for this grid is not given in the sources. Transform State: Maintained using quaternions to represent camera orientation, avoiding gimbal lock. Parameters: Volume Resolution: Supports extremely dense volumes up to 512^3 (e.g., knee and brain MRI). Step Size: Controlled by a "quality slider" in the UI. Lower step sizes increase rendering quality but decrease performance; higher step sizes improve performance but reduce quality. Opacity: User-adjustable opacity control for the volume rendering. Numbered Steps: 1. Server Setup: The server, written in Rust using axum, serves the HDF5 volume files from disk. The naive implementation serves the entire HDF5 volume at once. 2. Client Initialization: The client, written in Rust using egui/eframe for the GUI and glow for rendering, compiles to WASM via trunk. 3. Data Loading: The client loads MRI samples from the HDF5 (.h5) files using Rust bindings to the hdf5 library. 4. Rendering Loop: The core renderer uses OpenGL shaders targeting WebGL. A ray marching approach is implemented in the shaders. An occupancy grid optimization is applied during ray marching to skip empty regions. 5. Interaction: Rotation: Trackball rotation is handled using quaternions to avoid gimbal lock. Opacity: The user adjusts opacity via the UI. Quality: The user adjusts the step size via a quality slider. Hover Info: A hover info card displays the voxel coordinates, value, and intensity of the cursor position. Axes: XYZ axes are visualized in the 3D view. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def identityquaternion(): return [1.0, 0.0, 0.0, 0.0] # w, x, y, z def loadhdf5(url): # Open network connection, read binary stream, parse HDF5 dataset structure rawbytes = downloadbytes(url) return parsehdf5dataset(rawbytes) def buildoccupancygrid(volume, gridres): # Downsample volume to gridres^3; mark cell occupied if any voxel > 0 stride = volume.shape[0] // gridres grid = zeros(gridres, gridres, gridres) for i in range(gridres): for j in range(gridres): for k in range(gridres): if max(volume[istride:(i+1)stride, jstride:(j+1)stride, kstride:(k+1)stride]) > 0: grid[i, j, k] = 1 return grid def quaternionmultiply(q1, q2): # Hamilton product for composing rotations w1, x1, y1, z1 = q1 w2, x2, y2, z2 = q2 return [w1w2 - x1x2 - y1y2 - z1z2, w1x2 + x1w2 + y1z2 - z1y2, w1y2 - x1z2 + y1w2 + z1x2, w1z2 + x1y2 - y1x2 + z1w2] def mapqualitytostepsize(quality): # Linear mapping: quality 0.0 -> 2.0, 1.0 -> 0.1 return 0.1 + 1.9 (1.0 - quality) def unprojectscreentoray(sx, sy, viewprojinv): # Multiply inverse projection-view matrix by screen coordinates to get ray return transformmatrixvector(viewprojinv, [sx, sy, 0.0, 1.0]) def raymarch(rayorigin, raydir, stepsize, occupancygrid, volume): # March along ray, skip empty grid cells, sample volume until hit or exit t = 0.0 while t < 1000.0: pos = rayorigin + raydir t grididx = worldtogridindices(pos, occupancygrid) if occupancygrid[grididx] == 0: t += stepsize 10.0 continue val = trilinearinterpolate(volume, pos) if val == 0: t += stepsize continue return pos, val return None, 0.0 class WebMRIRenderer: def init(self, serverurl, volumepath): self.serverurl = serverurl self.volumepath = volumepath self.data = None self.occupancygrid = None self.quaternion = identityquaternion() self.stepsize = 1.0 self.opacity = 0.5 self.viewprojinv = None def loadvolume(self): self.data = loadhdf5(self.serverurl + self.volumepath) self.occupancygrid = buildoccupancygrid(self.data, gridres=64) def renderframe(self, camerapos, cameradir, viewprojinv): # Create WebGL context, compile vertex/fragment shaders, bind attributes createwebglcontext() compileshaders() bindshaderuniforms(stepsize=self.stepsize, opacity=self.opacity, volumedata=self.data, occupancygrid=self.occupancygrid, camerapos=camerapos, cameradir=cameradir) # Draw full-screen triangle strip to trigger fragment shader ray marching drawfullscreentrianglestrip() # Draw 3D lines for X, Y, Z axes draw3daxes() def updaterotation(self, deltax, deltay): deltaq = computetrackballrotationdelta(deltax, deltay) self.quaternion = quaternionmultiply(self.quaternion, deltaq) def updatequality(self, qualityvalue): self.stepsize = mapqualitytostepsize(qualityvalue) def updateopacity(self, opacityvalue): self.opacity = opacityvalue def gethoverinfo(self, screenx, screeny): ray = unprojectscreentoray(screenx, screeny, self.viewprojinv) pos, val = raymarch(ray.origin, ray.direction, self.stepsize, self.occupancygrid, self.data) return pos, val, computedisplayintensity(val, self.opacity) Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Memory: Raw MRI samples can be ~8GB. The naive server implementation serves the entire HDF5 volume at once. Compatibility: Initial attempts using WebGPU failed due to compatibility issues; OpenGL/WebGL was chosen as a fallback. Precision: The source does not specify floating-point precision (e.g., float32 vs float16) for the volume data or calculations. Focuses on solutions to network latency and web performance for volumetric data [5039-web-based-volume-rendering.md]. Choose when minimizing data transfer and optimizing browser rendering pipelines is required. General techniques for offloading ray marching to the GPU [5040-gpu-accelerated-volume-rendering.md]. Choose when hardware acceleration is available and CPU-only rendering is too slow. Techniques for running high-performance graphics code in the browser via WASM [5041-webassembly-graphics.md]. Choose when native-speed execution is needed in web environments without plugins. Time Complexity: Not explicitly given. Performance is traded off against quality via the step size parameter. Memory Complexity: Depends on the volume size. A 512^3 volume can be ~8GB. The naive server implementation loads the entire volume into memory. Measured Performance: Not given in the sources. Scaling: The architecture is designed for future expansion, such as loading volumes from a database or implementing advanced chunking for massive volumes. Strengths: Interactive 3D visualization in the browser; quaternion-based rotation avoids gimbal lock; occupancy grid optimization skips empty regions; Rust provides performance and safety. Limitations: Naive server implementation serves the entire volume at once, which is inefficient for large datasets; WebGL compatibility issues with WebGPU. When to use: When interactive 3D visualization of dense MRI volumes is needed in a web environment without requiring heavy desktop software. When not to use: When network latency is high and the entire volume cannot be loaded efficiently; when WebGPU features are required for specific optimizations. The method was developed by Armeet Singh Jatyani as a personal project to address the difficulty of visualizing extremely dense MRI volumes (up to 512^3) during research in AI models for 3D medical imaging. Previous tools like Matplotlib lacked interactive 3D support, and Plotly was unsuitable for the use case. The project was written over a weekend using Rust, egui, glow, and axum, compiling to WASM via trunk. It was deployed on Fly.io.
