name: CPU Multithreaded Rendering
head: Multi-core Volume Rendering, Parallel CPU Rendering
body: CPU Multithreaded Rendering maps volumetric data to a 2D output by distributing the computational load of ray casting or projection across multiple CPU cores. It solves the performance bottleneck of single-threaded software rendering by splitting the rendering domain into parallel sections. Unlike GPU, web and parallel renderers, which rely on hardware shaders and coalesced memory access, this method leverages general-purpose CPU instruction sets and explicit thread management, often requiring careful handling of OpenGL context binding if integrated with immediate-mode graphics APIs. Inputs: Volumetric dataset (e.g., 256^3 medical data), rendering parameters (transfer functions, clipping), and scene configuration. Outputs: Rendered image frames (e.g., stereo pairs) or memory buffers. The sources do not specify a universal data structure layout for the volume data itself, noting that performance depends on the "size and structure of the visualized features" rather than the monolithic volume size. For scene management, the VRE engine uses a structure where each scene is associated with two persistent threads. 1. Domain Decomposition: The CPU software version splits the world (or image plane) into sections for parallel rendering. 2. Thread Assignment: For general volume rendering, threads are spawned or managed to process these sections. For scene management with OpenGL, each scene is assigned two persistent threads to handle asynchronous operations. 3. Execution: Synchronous: Execution occurs on the calling thread. Asynchronous: Execution occurs on a separate persistent thread. The thread falls asleep until the next operation request arrives, preserving the OpenGL context binding. 4. Context Handling: One thread operates on a user-provided OpenGL context (e.g., a user-created window). A second thread operates on an internal invisible OpenGL context, used when no context is provided (e.g., command-line applications). 5. Rendering: Standard volume raycasting or projection is performed on the assigned sections. In voxel-set rendering, only voxels representing structures of interest are processed, allowing for object-aware rendering modes (direct volume rendering, MIP, surface rendering) combined via compositing. Stereo pairs can be rendered in parallel using multi-threading. Core Count: Performance scales with the number of cores. Tested on systems ranging from 1 core to 32 cores (Opteron). Data Size: Typical visualizations use 256^3 data sets. The following pseudocode illustrates the persistent thread model for asynchronous OpenGL rendering described in. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import threading import time class SceneRenderer: def init(self, usercontext=None): self.internalcontext = self.createopenglcontext() if usercontext is None else None self.usercontext = usercontext self.requestevent = threading.Event() self.pendingrender = False self.renderdata = None self.lock = threading.Lock() self.threaduser = threading.Thread(target=self.renderloop, args=(self.usercontext,)) self.threadinternal = threading.Thread(target=self.renderloop, args=(self.internalcontext,)) self.threaduser.start() self.threadinternal.start() def createopenglcontext(self): # Sources do not specify OpenGL context creation; standard hidden context initialization would go here. return "OpenGLContextInstance" def renderloop(self, context): data = None while True: self.requestevent.wait() self.requestevent.clear() with self.lock: if self.pendingrender: data = self.renderdata self.pendingrender = False self.renderdata = None if data is not None: # Sources do not specify OpenGL context binding; standard context activation would go here. self.executerender(data) # Sources do not specify OpenGL context unbinding; standard context deactivation would go here. data = None def renderasync(self, data): with self.lock: self.renderdata = data self.pendingrender = True self.requestevent.set() return def executerender(self, data): # Sources do not specify the actual volume rendering logic; standard raycasting/compositing would go here. pass OpenGL Context Binding: Creating a new thread for each asynchronous operation causes costly OpenGL context binding operations. This is mitigated by using persistent threads that fall asleep between requests. Context Availability: If a user does not provide an OpenGL context (e.g., in command-line applications), an internal invisible context must be used. A software-based volume rendering approach that achieves high performance by working with sets of voxels representing structures of interest, rather than rendering the entire monolithic volume. It allows for object-aware rendering modes (direct volume rendering, compositing, MIP, surface rendering, NPR) combined via compositing. It supports multi-threading for stereo pairs. Performance metric: Up to 35 frames per second on a single CPU for typical visualizations of 256^3 data sets from medicine. Choose this when visualization features are sparse or structured, and performance depends on feature size rather than volume size. A threading strategy for managing multiple scenes and asynchronous rendering operations that minimizes the cost of OpenGL context binding by using persistent threads per scene. Each scene uses two persistent threads (one for user context, one for internal context) that fall asleep between requests. Choose this when integrating CPU rendering with OpenGL-based UI frameworks where asynchronous rendering is required without blocking the main thread. Time Complexity: Performance increases with the number of cores. Tested on 1 to 32 cores (Opteron). Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Measured Performance: Up to 35 frames per second on a single CPU for 256^3 medical data sets using voxel-set rendering. Strengths: High flexibility with visualization parameters (e.g., two-level volume rendering). Supports stereo pairs rendered in parallel. Limitations: Performance depends on the structure of visualized features. OpenGL context binding is costly if not managed with persistent threads. When to Use: When hardware acceleration is unavailable or when specific software-based features (like object-aware rendering) are required. When Not to Use: When real-time performance on large monolithic volumes is required without feature sparsity. The concept of CPU multithreaded volume rendering has been implemented in various software frameworks. The Voxel Game Engine describes a CPU software version that splits the world for parallel rendering, tested on Opteron processors. The Real Time Volume Rendering Library (RTVR) introduced voxel-set rendering for interactive volume rendering, achieving high performance by focusing on structures of interest. The VRE volume rendering engine implemented a scene management system with persistent OpenGL contexts to handle asynchronous rendering efficiently. name: Shared-Memory Parallel Raycasting (CPU)
head: Multi-Core CPU Implementation, POSIX Threads Raycasting
body: Shared-memory parallel raycasting on CPUs is a volume rendering technique that distributes the computational load of ray casting and integration across multiple threads within a single process using a shared-memory programming model. It solves the performance bottleneck of sequential raycasting by decomposing the output image into spatially disjoint work blocks, allowing multiple cores to render pixels concurrently. It is distinguished from GPU-based parallel raycasting by its use of explicit thread management (e.g., POSIX threads) and dynamic work queues to handle load imbalance, rather than relying on hardware-level SIMT execution. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A 3D scalar/vector volume dataset, camera parameters (view matrix, projection matrix), and a user-specified number of rendering threads. Output: A 2D final image buffer containing the composited color and opacity for each pixel. Data Structures: 1. Shared-Memory Data Structure: A global memory region visible to all threads. It stores precomputed values common to all rendering tasks, such as the inverse of the model-view matrix. 2. Work Queue: A thread-safe queue containing work assignments (blocks of pixels) to be processed by slave threads. 3. Final Image Buffer: A shared memory buffer where threads write the final pixel color and opacity. Numbered Steps: 1. Initialization: The application launches a user-specified number of rendering threads. Each thread acts as a "slave" and enters an event loop. 2. Precomputation: The master thread computes values common to all slaves (e.g., inverse model-view matrix) and stores them in the shared-memory data structure. 3. Work Assignment Generation: The master thread computes a list of work assignments. Each assignment is a spatially disjoint region of the final image (a work block). 4. Synchronization: A pair of shared-memory barriers synchronizes communication between the master and slave threads in the event loop. 5. Execution Loop (Slave Threads): a. The master thread signals slave threads to begin rendering. b. Each slave thread requests a work block from the work queue. c. The thread performs raycasting over all pixels in the assigned block, performing color and opacity integration along each ray. d. The thread writes the results to the final image buffer. e. The thread returns to step (b) to request the next work block until the queue is empty. 6. Completion: The master thread waits for all slave threads to finish their current blocks (potentially using a barrier if "block synchronization" is enabled) and then proceeds to the next frame or task. Formulas: Ray Casting: For each pixel (u, v) in a work block, a ray is generated. The volume is sampled along the ray. The color C and opacity \alpha are integrated using standard volume rendering integration (Levoy’s formulation): C = \sum{i=0}^{n-1} ci \alphai \prod{j=0}^{i-1} (1 - \alphaj) Where ci and \alphai are the color and opacity at sample i, and n is the number of samples along the ray. Parameters: Work Block Tessellation: The user specifies the size of the work blocks. Examples include 4 \times 4, 8 \times 8, 512 \times 1, or 1 \times 512 pixels. Thread Count: User-specified number of rendering threads, typically matching the number of available CPU cores. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Load Imbalance: Static work assignment (round-robin) can suffer from load imbalance if the volume data or camera view causes some rays to require significantly more computation (e.g., due to empty space skipping or complex transfer functions) than others. Memory Contention: If not managed carefully, concurrent writes to the final image buffer or shared data structures can cause cache thrashing or race conditions. Precision: Standard floating-point precision is used for ray marching and integration. Pseudocode: Unverified code. alpha) t += stepsize return color, alpha def slavethreadeventloop(threadid): """Slave thread event loop.""" while not stopevent.isset(): try: # Request work block from queue block = workqueue.get(timeout=1.0) except queue.Empty: continue xmin, ymin, xmax, ymax = block # Process all pixels in the block for y in range(ymin, ymax): for x in range(xmin, xmax): color, alpha = raycastpixel(x, y, shareddata['invmvmatrix'], volumedata) finalimagebuffer[y][x] = (color, alpha) # Optional: Block synchronization barrier # barrier.wait() workqueue.taskdone() def masterthreadrender(imagewidth, imageheight, numthreads, blocksize): """Master thread manages rendering.""" global finalimagebuffer finalimagebuffer = [[None for in range(imagewidth)] for in range(imageheight)] # 1. Precompute shared data computeshareddata() # 2. Generate work blocks blocks = generateworkblocks(imagewidth, imageheight, blocksize) # 3. Populate work queue for block in blocks: workqueue.put(block) # 4. Launch slave threads threads = [] for i in range(numthreads): t = threading.Thread(target=slavethreadeventloop, args=(i,)) t.start() threads.append(t) # 5. Wait for completion workqueue.join() stopevent.set() for t in threads: t.join() A hybrid parallelism approach that combines image-tile decomposition with domain decomposition to distribute the data volume across groups of threads, allowing testing at varying concurrency levels while maintaining image and data volume size. It uses multiple groups of threads at a given concurrency level, with each group allocating its own memory buffer disjoint from other groups. Thread affinity is enforced using the -Mconcur=numa flag in the PGI compiler to prevent threads from migrating across cores. Data decomposition configurations vary by platform: Intel/Nehalem: 1 thread per buffer, 8 disjoint buffers, buffer size 256 \times 256 \times 256. AMD/MagnyCours: 2 threads per buffer, 4 disjoint buffers, buffer size 256 \times 256 \times 512. Intel/Nehalem (4 threads/buffer): 2 buffers, size 256 \times 512 \times 512. Intel/Nehalem (8 threads/buffer): 1 buffer, size 512 \times 512 \times 512. AMD/MagnyCours (6 threads/buffer): 4 buffers, size 256 \times 256 \times 512. AMD/MagnyCours (24 threads/buffer): 1 buffer, size 512 \times 512 \times 512. Time Complexity: O(N \cdot M \cdot L), where N is the number of pixels, M is the number of rays per pixel (if multi-sampling), and L is the number of samples per ray. Parallelization reduces wall-clock time by a factor approaching the number of threads, subject to overhead and load imbalance. Memory Complexity: O(V + I), where V is the size of the volume data and I is the size of the image buffer. In hybrid parallelism, memory usage scales with the number of disjoint buffers. Measured Performance: Dynamic work assignment performs better than static assignment due to reduced load imbalance. Performance scales with the number of cores but is limited by memory bandwidth and cache contention. Strengths: Flexible work distribution, good load balancing with dynamic queues, easy to implement on standard multi-core CPUs. Limitations: Overhead of thread management and synchronization; static assignment suffers from load imbalance. When to Use: When rendering on multi-core CPUs where load balance is unpredictable or when GPU resources are unavailable. When Not to Use: When extreme scalability on many-core architectures is required (use GPU raycasting) or when memory bandwidth is the primary bottleneck and static assignment with block synchronization might offer better cache locality. The method is based on Levoy’s formulation of volume rendering. It was implemented using POSIX threads as the shared-memory programming model. The approach was explored in the context of multi-core and many-core shared-memory parallel raycasting volume rendering optimization and tuning. The hybrid parallelism approach for concurrency testing was adapted from distributed-memory parallel implementations. name: Threaded Chunk Rendering
head: RendererManager
body: Threaded Chunk Rendering is a CPU-side parallelization strategy that distributes volumetric rendering tasks across a fixed-size thread pool to maximize multi-core utilization while managing synchronization overhead. It differs from CPU Multithreaded Rendering by explicitly decoupling task generation from execution via a queue-based manager, and from Multi-GPU and Cluster Rendering by remaining strictly within a single process and CPU core set. The method solves the problem of dynamic load balancing in chunk-based voxel worlds by reusing renderer instances rather than spawning threads per frame. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A grid of loaded world chunks (dimensions 0 \le i, j, k < \text{LOADED\WORLD\SIZE}) and a pool of pre-allocated or lazily-created Renderer objects. Output: Rendered frames for each chunk, composited into the final image (typically using Z-buffering to handle overdraw). Data Structures: The RendererManager maintains the following state: freeRenderers: A thread-safe queue (ThreadsafeQueue<Renderer>) holding available renderer instances. activeRenderers: An atomic integer (std::atomic<int>) initialized to 0, tracking currently executing render tasks. cv: A condition variable (std::conditionvariable) used to block the main loop or manage synchronization when the pool is idle. mtx: A mutex (std::mutex) protecting the condition variable and queue state. MAXRENDERERS: A constant defining the maximum concurrent threads (typically 20). Algorithm Steps: 1. Initialization: Create MAXRENDERERS Renderer instances and push them all into freeRenderers. Initialize activeRenderers to 0. 2. Task Distribution: Iterate over all loaded chunks (i, j, k). For each chunk, invoke renderChunk(chunk). 3. Renderer Acquisition: Inside renderChunk: Lock mtx and wait on cv while activeRenderers >= MAXRENDERERS AND freeRenderers is empty. This prevents thread explosion and ensures pool reuse. Pop a Renderer from freeRenderers. Increment activeRenderers. Unlock mtx. 4. Execution: Spawn a detached std::thread that executes Chunk::render(chunk, renderer). Inside Chunk::render: Call renderer->renderChunk(this). Upon completion, call rendererManager.freeRenderer(renderer). 5. Renderer Release: Inside freeRenderer(renderer): Lock mtx. Push renderer back into freeRenderers. Decrement activeRenderers. If activeRenderers reaches 0, notify cv (useful for frame synchronization). Unlock mtx. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. class RendererManager: def init(self, maxrenderers=20): self.freerenderers = ThreadsafeQueue() self.activerenderers = AtomicInt(0) self.cv = ConditionVariable() self.mtx = Mutex() self.maxrenderers = maxrenderers # Initialize pool for in range(maxrenderers): self.freerenderers.push(Renderer()) def renderchunk(self, chunk): # Acquire a renderer with self.mtx: while self.activerenderers.get() >= self.maxrenderers and self.freerenderers.isempty(): self.cv.wait(self.mtx) renderer = self.freerenderers.pop() self.activerenderers.increment() # Spawn thread thread = Thread(target=self.executerender, args=(chunk, renderer)) thread.daemon = True thread.start() def executerender(self, chunk, renderer): try: renderer.renderchunk(chunk) finally: self.freerenderer(renderer) def freerenderer(self, renderer): with self.mtx: self.freerenderers.push(renderer) self.activerenderers.decrement() if self.activerenderers.get() == 0: self.cv.notifyall() class Chunk: def render(self, renderer): if renderer is None: raise ValueError("Renderer is null") renderer.renderchunk(self) # Note: In the source, freeRenderer is called here, # but logically it should be called after the thread finishes. # The source code shows: rendererManager.freeRenderer(renderer) inside Chunk::render. # However, Chunk::render is called BY the thread. # To be safe and correct, we assume the thread wrapper handles the free call # or the source implies the renderer is returned immediately after renderChunk returns. # Based on, the thread calls Chunk::render, which calls renderer->renderChunk, # then calls freeRenderer. renderermanager.freerenderer(renderer) The source code snippet shows rendererManager.freeRenderer(renderer) inside Chunk::render, which is executed by the spawned thread. This implies the renderer is returned to the pool immediately after the chunk rendering function returns, not after the thread object is joined. This is safe for detached threads as long as Renderer state is not accessed after return. Parameters: MAXRENDERERS: 20. CHUNKSIZE: 8x8x8 blocks. LOADEDWORLDSIZE: Determined by world segmentation logic. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Deadlock: If activeRenderers is not decremented correctly, the queue will empty and no new threads will spawn. Null Renderer: The source includes a check for renderer == nullptr. Z-Buffering: The method relies on Z-buffering to prevent overdraw artifacts when multiple threads render overlapping chunks or when chunks are rendered out of order. Implements a reader-writer lock using two pthread mutexes (mutexread, mutexwrite) and a readers counter to allow concurrent reads but exclusive writes for chunk data. Acquire Read Lock (chunkopenro): Lock mutexread, increment readers. If readers becomes 1, lock mutexwrite. Unlock mutexread. Release Read Lock (chunkclosero): Lock mutexread, decrement readers. If readers becomes 0, unlock mutexwrite. Unlock mutexread. Acquire Write Lock (chunkopenrw): Directly lock mutexwrite. Release Write Lock (chunkcloserw): Directly unlock mutexwrite. Parameter: c->readers (Integer counter, initialized to 0). Time Complexity: O(N) where N is the number of chunks, with a constant factor reduced by parallelism. Thread creation overhead is amortized by reusing renderers. Memory Complexity: O(M) where M is MAXRENDERERS (20). Performance: Z-buffering provided a 1.33x speedup over the Painters Algorithm in early tests (0.027s vs 0.036s per frame). Strengths: Efficient CPU utilization; avoids thread creation overhead per frame; simple synchronization. Limitations: Fixed thread pool size may not scale to very large worlds without tuning; CPU-bound. When to Use: Single-machine, multi-core CPU rendering of voxel worlds. When Not to Use: When GPU acceleration is available (use GPU, web and parallel renderers variants) or when cluster scaling is required. Originated in the VidFurlan/Voxel1993 project as a "First Major Performance Improvement" over the Painters Algorithm, switching to Z-buffering and multi-threaded chunk management. The approach was part of a broader effort to optimize voxel world rendering by combining chunking, Z-buffering, and multi-threading, with future plans to integrate Voxel Octrees. The mutex-based variant appears in the kosshi-net/voxplat project for managing concurrent access to chunk data. name: Multi-GPU and Cluster Rendering
body: Multi-GPU and Cluster Rendering distributes volumetric rendering workloads across multiple graphics processing units or networked nodes to visualize datasets that exceed the memory or computational capacity of a single machine. It differs from single-node parallel renderers by explicitly managing data partitioning, inter-node communication, and result compositing across distinct hardware contexts, often requiring CPU-mediated data transfer or specialized frameworks like Chromium or Equalizer to synchronize execution. Distributes volumetric rendering workloads across multiple GPUs on a single node to handle datasets exceeding single-card memory or computational capacity. It differs from single-node architectures by explicitly managing data partitioning and result compositing across distinct hardware contexts, often requiring CPU-mediated data transfer due to the lack of direct peer-to-peer GPU communication extensions. Unlike web-based or pure client-side renderers, this method relies on low-level OpenGL context management and specific pixel format optimizations for inter-GPU data exchange. Enables interactive visualization of large volumetric datasets on resource-constrained mobile clients by offloading all storage and computation to a server system. It distinguishes itself from distributed cluster approaches by utilizing a single server node equipped with multiple GPUs and CPUs, managed via the Chromium framework to virtualize OpenGL execution across local hardware. Unlike pure client-side renderers that require significant local GPU power, this method transmits compressed image data to lightweight clients. An OpenGL-based API framework for developing scalable graphics applications for distributed visualization clusters, taking care of distributed execution, synchronization, and final image compositing for both sort-last and sort-first based applications. It is a flexible and transparent OpenGL-based graphics framework for distributed, high-performance visualization systems that allows OpenGL-based applications to display on multi-tile environments by providing a unified OpenGL rendering context. It intercepts and manipulates certain OpenGL directives to provide a unified OpenGL rendering context. It manages the visualization grid without additional implementation requirements to the user. Effectively using these features requires in-depth knowledge of the framework, significant code changes, and application-specific adaptations. Unlike SAGE, CGLX does not impose the pixel read back operation on the system, which can be prohibitively expensive at higher resolutions. A mechanism to synchronize rendering nodes using a barrier before buffer swap to ensure synchronous switching between wavelet levels and reduce artifacts. The system must wait for the slowest node in the cluster, which can be a bottleneck. A cloud rendering system consisting of a Master Node for task scheduling and Sub-nodes (RenderFarm) for high-performance computing, allowing NeRF rendering on user devices without high-end GPUs. Sub-nodes provide color and depth information for each individual NeRF subject. Rendering results from all sub-nodes are synchronized to the Master Node. The Master Node performs fusion/composition between scenes based on the received depth information. The system streams the final composited rendering results to the user’s multi-display terminal. Synchronizes multiple volumetric boards (driving different colored lasers) across single or multiple computers using a master/slave clock architecture. One board (e.g., GREEN) is designated as Master, and its 20-MHz crystal oscillator provides the system clock. Slave boards (RED, BLUE, etc.) receive the master's 20-MHz clock via external cables instead of using their own oscillators. For multi-computer setups, slave computers receive a SYSRESET signal, which clears counter “C” and resets all internal clocks on slave volumetric cards to match the master clock. Synchronization accuracy is within the master board's clock period of 50 nanoseconds (1/20 MHz), assuming short external cables. The J8 Master to Slave cable uses a 1:1 layout: Pin 1=SYS20MHZ, Pin 2=DGND, Pin 3=N/C, Pin 4=SYSRESET, Pin 5=SYS0INDEX, Pin 6=SYS180INDEX. Custom solutions for distributed rendering provide greater support and scalability at the price of inherent inflexibility, as they are specifically built for each application based on parallel rendering algorithms. Frameworks like Chromium were introduced to virtualize OpenGL execution, allowing applications to run on distributed hardware by intercepting command streams. Subsequent frameworks such as Equalizer, SAGE, and CGLX provided more specialized abstractions for distributed execution, synchronization, and compositing, addressing the limitations of earlier generic interceptors. Equalizer handles distributed execution and final image compositing for both sort-last and sort-first based applications. CGLX provides a unified OpenGL rendering context by intercepting directives without imposing expensive pixel read-back operations. body: This method distributes a single volumetric dataset across multiple NVIDIA graphics cards on a single node by interleaving data partitions and switching OpenGL contexts per frame. It enables rendering of large volumes that exceed single-card memory by processing disjoint subsets of the volume data sequentially across the GPUs. It differs from general multi-GPU setups by enforcing a strict sequential context-switching model combined with pixel-wise result combination via CPU-mediated transfers, rather than independent frame rendering or direct inter-GPU communication. Inputs and Outputs Input: A large volumetric dataset represented as a multi-resolution pyramid (e.g., wavelet coefficients). Input: Two or more NVIDIA graphics cards connected to a single X-server. Output: A single composite image combining the results from all GPUs. Data Structures The volume data is organized as a sorted array of voxels with associated detail coefficients for each pyramid level. Voxel Data: Each voxel entry includes position and intensity attributes. For Streaming MIP variants, an extra attribute for the originating pyramid level is required, stored in two bits of the position attribute (4 bytes total for position) plus a short for intensity (2 bytes), totaling 6 bytes per voxel. Partitioning: The sorted array of voxels is split equally among the GPUs. The split is performed by interleaving the detail coefficients (and the histogram) for each pyramid level across the GPUs, rather than splitting the array in the middle. Steps 1. Context Creation: Create a separate OpenGL context for each GPU, targeting distinct X-screens supported by the NVIDIA driver. 2. Data Distribution: Distribute the interleaved voxel data and histogram to the respective GPU memory. 3. Rendering Loop (Per Frame): a. Activate the first GPU's context. b. Render the volume subset assigned to the first GPU. c. Read the resulting image back to system memory using glReadPixels. The preferred pixel format for this transfer is GLUNSIGNEDINT8888. d. Activate the second GPU's context. e. Write the intermediate result from the first GPU into the second GPU's framebuffer using glDrawPixels. f. Render the volume subset assigned to the second GPU, which now composites over the first GPU's result. g. Repeat for additional GPUs if applicable, chaining the read/write operations. 4. Result Combination: The final image is obtained from the last GPU in the chain. The combination is achieved via a pixel-wise maximum operator (Maximum Intensity Projection). Pseudocode Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def rendermultigpu(voxeldata, gpucount): # 1. Partition data by interleaving coefficients and histogram for each pyramid level partitions = [voxeldata[i::gpucount] for i in range(gpucount)] # 2. Initialize contexts and framebuffers contexts = [f"context{i}" for i in range(gpucount)] framebuffers = [f"fb{i}" for i in range(gpucount)] # 3. Render first partition loaddata(contexts[0], partitions[0]) bindframebuffer(contexts[0], framebuffers[0]) executerender(contexts[0]) # 4. Chain subsequent GPUs: read back, switch context, draw pixels, render next partition for i in range(1, gpucount): previmage = readpixelsbacktocpu(framebuffers[i-1], format="GLUNSIGNEDINT8888") switchactivecontext(contexts[i]) bindframebuffer(contexts[i], framebuffers[i]) drawpixelstogpu(previmage) # Composites over previous result via pixel-wise maximum loaddata(contexts[i], partitions[i]) executerender(contexts[i]) # 5. Final readout finalimage = readpixelsbacktocpu(framebuffers[gpucount-1], format="GLUNSIGNEDINT8888") return finalimage def createglcontext(screenid): return f"Context{screenid}" def createframebuffer(): return {"pixels": None} def loaddata(context, data): pass # Upload data to GPU memory def bindframebuffer(context, fb): pass # Set active render target def executerender(context): pass # Dispatch rendering commands def readpixelsbacktocpu(fb, format): return fb["pixels"] # glReadPixels equivalent def switchactivecontext(context): pass # Switch active GL context def drawpixelstogpu(image): pass # glDrawPixels equivalent Parameters Pixel Format: GLUNSIGNEDINT8888 is the preferred format for CPU transfers (glReadPixels/glDrawPixels). Split Strategy: Interleaving coefficients is preferred over contiguous splitting to better divide the load during progressive refinement. Edge Cases and Pitfalls No Direct Inter-GPU Transfer: There is no extension for direct data shuffling between cards. Intermediate results must pass through the CPU using glReadPixels on one context and glDrawPixels on the other. Multi-threading Inefficiency: Attempting to run rendering loops for multiple contexts in separate threads yields no performance gain. The algorithm is GPU-bound, and the CPU synchronization overhead outweighs the minimal CPU load of queuing commands. Monitor Connection: The second (and subsequent) cards do not need to be connected to a monitor, as their output is combined internally via the CPU-mediated transfer. Time Complexity: The rendering time is dominated by GPU computation, which is roughly halved per additional GPU, yielding an almost optimal speedup for large volumes. CPU-mediated data transfers add a constant overhead per frame per GPU pair. Memory Complexity: Memory usage is distributed. Each GPU holds only a fraction (1/N) of the voxel data and histogram, allowing rendering of volumes larger than a single GPU's VRAM. Strengths: Simple implementation using standard OpenGL extensions; supports volumes exceeding single-GPU memory; effective for MIP rendering. Limitations: High CPU bandwidth usage due to intermediate result transfers; sequential chaining in the final composition step; limited to NVIDIA hardware with multi-screen X-server support. When to use: When rendering very large volumes on a single node with multiple NVIDIA GPUs and when the bottleneck is VRAM or single-GPU throughput. When not to use: Not given in the sources. This method originates from research on multiresolution MIP rendering of large volumetric data accelerated on graphics hardware. It was developed to support datasets that exceed the memory capacity of a single graphics card. The approach leverages the NVIDIA driver's support for multiple screens within a single X-server to manage multiple OpenGL contexts. head: Heavy/Light Farm Assignment, Load-balancing Schedule Policy
body: This method is a scheduling policy for distributing rendering jobs for a single user viewing multiple objects in a large scene. It solves the problem of unbalanced GPU workload and I/O bandwidth bottlenecks by separating objects into "Heavy" (larger-sized) and "Light" (smaller-sized) tasks. It distinguishes itself from uniform resource assignment by dynamically allocating dedicated GPUs to heavy tasks and shared GPUs to light tasks, thereby reducing long tail latency for large objects and preventing I/O saturation. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A set of NGP-NOLF objects O to be rendered for a single user view. Output: Assignment of each object i \in O to either HeavyFarm or LightFarm. Data Structures: nhit: Number of rays hit by each object (estimated). npixel: Estimated pixel quantity on the final screen. avgdepth: Average depth of the hit rays. thpixrate: Threshold for pixels per frame. thdepth: Threshold for average depth. frame: Normalization constant or target frame rate used in the pixel rate calculation. Steps: 1. Generate a rough prior scene offscreen using EGL to act as an nhit estimator. 2. Use a preconceived mesh to estimate the pixel quantity and depth on the final rendered screen to predict the number of hit rays (nhit). 3. Calculate npixel and avgdepth from nhit using estimators. 4. Evaluate the condition: if \frac{n\pixel}{frame} > th\pix\rate OR avg\depth < th\depth, assign the object to HeavyFarm (one object per GPU). 5. Assign remaining objects to LightFarm with shared GPU resources. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def scheduleobjects(objects, thpixrate, thdepth, frame): """ Assigns objects to HeavyFarm or LightFarm based on estimated workload. Args: objects: List of object instances. thpixrate: Threshold for pixels per frame. thdepth: Threshold for average depth. frame: Normalization constant for pixel rate calculation. Returns: heavyfarm: List of objects assigned to HeavyFarm. lightfarm: List of objects assigned to LightFarm. """ heavyfarm = [] lightfarm = [] for obj in objects: # Step 1: Generate rough prior scene offscreen using EGL priorscene = renderpriorsceneegl(obj) # Step 2: Use preconceived mesh to predict nhit nhit = counthitraysfrommesh(priorscene, obj) # Step 3: Calculate npixel and avgdepth from nhit npixel = estimatenpixel(nhit) avgdepth = estimateavgdepth(nhit) # Step 4 & 5: Decision logic if (npixel / frame > thpixrate) or (avgdepth < thdepth): heavyfarm.append(obj) else: lightfarm.append(obj) return heavyfarm, lightfarm def renderpriorsceneegl(obj): # Renders a rough prior scene offscreen using EGL return scenedata def counthitraysfrommesh(scene, obj): # Predicts hit rays using a preconceived mesh return nhit def estimatenpixel(nhit): # Maps hit rays to pixel quantity return nhit def estimateavgdepth(nhit): # Maps hit rays to average depth return nhit Parameters: thpixrate: Threshold for pixels per frame. Value not given in the sources. thdepth: Threshold for average depth. Value not given in the sources. nhit: Number of rays hit by each NGP-NOLF object. frame: Denominator for the pixel rate calculation. Value not given in the sources. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: I/O Bandwidth Limits: Simultaneous image transferring for all objects can exceed the Master Node's I/O bandwidth, leading to unacceptable response times. Unbalanced Workload: Uniform resource assignment causes waste for small images and long tail latency for large ones. Extends the scheduling concept to multiple users viewing the same object from adjacent angles by sharing rendered rays. It categorizes tasks into "Heavy" (shareable) and "Light" (necessary) to amortize geometry costs. Time and Memory Complexity: The total time spent on rendering a frame with multiple objects T{frame} is expressed as: T{frame} = \max{i \subset O} (Ti) + \sum{i \subset O} \frac{Di}{BW} + C Where Ti is the rendering time, Di is the result data size of object i, BW is the bandwidth limit of the Master Node, C is the consolidation time, and O is the collection of rendered entities. The scheduler aims to minimize T{frame} by reducing the number of instances in O and choosing a proper subset in the Render Farm. Measured Performance: Not given in the sources. Scaling: Uses Infiniband and CUDA-aware MPI for cross-node communication. Exploits GPU Direct RDMA optimization on Nvidia Advanced GPUs to expedite readout of rendering results, lowering cross-node overhead. Strengths and Limitations: Strengths: Reduces long tail latency for large objects by dedicating GPUs; prevents I/O saturation by separating heavy/light tasks; negligible overhead from the estimation phase. Limitations: Relies on accurate estimation of nhit, npixel, and avgdepth; I/O bandwidth remains a bottleneck if the separation logic fails to sufficiently reduce simultaneous transfers. When to Use: Use when a single user views multiple objects in a large scene with varying sizes and depths. Use when uniform GPU resources are assigned to objects of varying sizes, to prevent waste and long tail latency. When Not to Use: Not suitable for multi-user scenarios without ray sharing, as it does not address repetitive rendering labor for adjacent angles. Origin: Introduced in "NEPHELE: A Neural Platform for Highly Realistic Cloud Radiance Rendering". History and Development: The method addresses obstacles in previous solutions where a Master Node gathers and composites frames from individual renderers, which fails due to I/O bandwidth limits and unbalanced GPU workloads. Where it is used: Cloud radiance rendering platforms using Neural Graphics Primitives (NGP) and Neural Octree Fields (NOLF). name: Multi-User Scheduling with Ray Sharing
head: Multi-user Scheduling Scheme, TaskAssigner Policy
body: A scheduling scheme for cloud-based neural volume rendering that improves efficiency for multiple users viewing the same object from adjacent angles by sharing rendered rays and preventing starvation. It distinguishes itself from single-user scheduling by explicitly categorizing rendering tasks into "Heavy" (shareable) and "Light" (necessary) types, allowing parallel execution of unique view requirements while amortizing the cost of common geometry across users. Inputs: A set of n users requesting views of the same 3D object (e.g., NeRF or i-NOLF model), where each user i specifies a target frame rate FPSi. Outputs: Rendered frames for each user, scheduled to minimize total response time T while maintaining fairness and preventing starvation. 1. Task Classification: Shareable Rays (S): Rays common to adjacent angles or global views. Necessary Rays (i): Rays specific to a user's unique viewing angle. 2. Farms: HeavyFarm: Queue for Heavy Tasks (shareable rays). LightFarm: Pool of available GPUs for Light Tasks (necessary rays). 3. Historical Table: Caches reusable tasks (previously rendered shareable rays) to guide offline rendering. 4. User State: loadedtasks: Number of tasks currently loaded for user u. targettime: Calculated deadline for the next frame, T{\text{last frame}} + wi. starved: Boolean flag indicating if the user is in a starvation state. Layout/Size: Exact memory layouts, sizes, and bit-packing schemes are Not given in the sources. 1. Identify Tasks: For each user, classify rays into Shareable (S) and Necessary (i). 2. Assign to Farms: Place all Shareable Rays (Heavy Tasks) into HeavyFarm. Send Necessary Rays (Light Tasks) to available GPUs in LightFarm for parallel rendering. 3. Cache Management: Maintain a historical table of rendered shareable rays to guide RenderFarm to render shareable rays offline in advance. 4. Calculate Wait Time: For each user i, compute wi using their target FPSi and moving average completion time ti. 5. Check Starvation: If a task has not started within wi after the last frame, mark the user as starved. 6. Resolve Starvation: If any starved tasks exist, enter a starvation state, deny new client requests, render all pending tasks for starved users on RenderFarm until resolved, then allow new requests. 7. Schedule Rendering: Execute the scheduling loop (see Pseudocode). The total response time T is optimized in three stages: 1. Baseline (No Sharing): T = k T{MS} + T{NS} \times n + \sum{i=0}^{n} (k T{Mi} + T{Ni}) Where T{MS} and T{NS} are mesh and neural times for the shared base, and T{Mi}, T{Ni} are per-user specific times. 2. With Ray Sharing (Parallel Light Tasks): Shareable rays are rendered once (Heavy), and necessary rays are rendered in parallel (Light). The total time is dominated by the slowest user's specific task: T = k T{MS} + T{NS} + \max{i=0}^{n} (k T{Mi} + T{Ni}) 3. With Offline Caching: Shareable rays are pre-rendered and cached. The response time depends only on the specific necessary rays for each user: T = \max{i \subset n} (k T{Mi} + T{Ni}) 4. Starvation Wait Time: wi = \frac{1}{FPSi} - ti n: Number of users. k: Constant coefficient for mesh rendering time. TM: Time for mesh rendering. TN: Time for i-NOLF rendering. FPSi: Target frames per second for user i. ti: Moving average of job completion time in seconds for user i. wi: Calculated wait time for user i. Typical Values: Not given in the sources. Precision in Wait Time: If ti approaches or exceeds 1/FPSi, wi becomes zero or negative, immediately triggering starvation. Ray Accounting: The scheduler must track remaining farm capacity accurately to avoid over-subscription when breaking from the user loop. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def nepheleschedulingpolicy(users, renderfarm, currenttime, systemstate): """ Implements the NEPHELE scheduling policy for multi-user ray sharing. users: list of User objects with attributes: loadedtasks, targettime, sharedtasks, dedicatedtasks, Tlastframe, wi, sharingusers renderfarm: object with maxcapacityrays, isavailable(), execute(task) currenttime: float, current simulation time systemstate: dict with 'allownewrequests' boolean """ while renderfarm.isavailable(): # 1. Update user states for user in users: user.loadedtasks = len(user.pendingtasks) user.targettime = user.Tlastframe + user.wi # 2. Sort users by load and urgency users.sort(key=lambda u: (u.loadedtasks, u.targettime)) # 3. Resolve starvation first starvedusers = [u for u in users if u.targettime <= currenttime] while starvedusers: systemstate['allownewrequests'] = False for user in starvedusers: for task in user.alltasks: renderfarm.execute(task) user.updaterendertime() systemstate['allownewrequests'] = True # Re-evaluate starvation condition starvedusers = [u for u in users if u.targettime <= currenttime] # 4. Render until RenderFarm is full remainingrays = renderfarm.maxcapacityrays for user in users: raysneeded = sum(task.raycount for task in user.sharedtasks + user.dedicatedtasks) if remainingrays < raysneeded: break for task in user.sharedtasks: renderfarm.execute(task) for u in task.sharingusers: u.updaterendertime() remainingrays -= task.raycount for task in user.dedicatedtasks: renderfarm.execute(task) user.updaterendertime() remainingrays -= task.raycount Time Complexity: The scheduling loop runs per frame. Sorting users is O(n \log n). Rendering is bounded by the RenderFarm capacity. The theoretical speedup comes from reducing the serial sum \sum (k T{Mi} + T{Ni}) to a parallel max \max (k T{Mi} + T{Ni}). Memory Complexity: Requires storage for the Historical Table (cache of shareable rays) and per-user state. Performance: Improves rendering efficiency E (inverse of T) by maximizing shareable rays. Allows multiple necessary rays for different angles to render in parallel. Strengths: Prevents starvation for users with high latency or slow GPUs; leverages redundancy in adjacent views; supports high FPS targets for VR/AR. Limitations: Requires users to view the same object from adjacent angles to benefit from sharing; overhead of managing Heavy/Light farms and starvation states. When to Use: Multi-user cloud rendering scenarios (e.g., VR/AR, shared NeRF assets) where users view similar content. The method was introduced in the NEPHELE system, a neural platform for cloud radiance rendering, by Luo et al. in 2023. It addresses the limitations of round-robin fairness policies in meeting FPS requirements for multiple users viewing the same 3D asset. The system demonstrates applications in cloud VR/AR and sharing NeRF assets on mobile devices. name: Single Node Multi-GPU/Server Architecture
head: Chromium Framework Cluster Rendering, Cluster rendering with OpenGL Stream Processing Units, Remote visualization via Chromium, Sarton et al. approach, Single node server with multiple GPUs/CPUs (Sarton et al.)
body: This architecture enables interactive visualization of large volumetric datasets on resource-constrained clients by offloading storage and computation to a server system. It utilizes the Chromium framework to unify the rendering power of a graphics accelerator cluster (or a single node with multiple GPUs/CPUs) through a virtualized OpenGL interface. Unlike pure client-side rendering, it relies on server-side compositing and image compression to minimize network bandwidth, distinguishing it from distributed shared-memory schemes that may require more complex synchronization. The method operates in a client-server model where the server handles rendering and the client handles display and interaction. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Large volumetric dataset stored on the server, and user interaction parameters (viewpoint, transfer function) sent from the client. Output: Compressed image stream sent to the client, which decompresses and displays the raw image. Data Structures: OpenGL Stream: A packed representation of OpenGL commands generated by the client or server, transmitted over TCP. Image Buffer: The rendered framebuffer content from each cluster node, read back for compositing. Compression State: Managed by ZLIB (lossless) and JPEG (lossy) encoders/decoders integrated into the client application. Steps: 1. Cluster Setup: Arrange graphics accelerators in a cluster (or configure a single node with multiple GPUs/CPUs). Provide a virtualized interface to the hardware through the OpenGL API. 2. Stream Generation: Client nodes generate OpenGL streams representing the desired scene state and user interactions. 3. Stream Management: Server nodes manage multiple incoming network connections, parsing them as packed representations of OpenGL streams. 4. SPU Execution: Perform stream transformations using OpenGL Stream Processing Units (SPU). SPUs are implemented as dynamically loadable libraries providing the OpenGL interface. Each cluster node renders its portion of the scene directly on its local hardware. 5. Compositing: Read back image buffers from all cluster nodes and transmit them to a final compositing server to combine into a final image. 6. Compression: Compress the resulting composite image using ZLIB and/or JPEG. 7. Transmission: Send the compressed image data stream to the client over a TCP channel established on a wireless link. 8. Client Decompression and Display: The client-side image data decoder receives the encoded information, decompresses it, and renders the raw image to the display. 9. Client Interaction: The visualization interface supervises the render area for framebuffer content received from the remote server. User interactions generate mapping and rendering parameters, which are exchanged over separate TCP socket connections. Parameters: Client RAM: 32 MB of RAM is sufficient for the client application. Compression Algorithms: ZLIB and JPEG are used for sending images to the client. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Hardware Requirements: While the client requires only 32 MB RAM, the server requires significant computational resources. The source explicitly contradicts itself regarding mobile devices, stating the client is not a mobile device and requires a graphics card with at least 128 MB RAM, which conflicts with the 32 MB client claim and the PDA premise. Network Latency: The reliance on TCP for streaming compressed images can introduce latency, affecting interactivity. SAGE (Scalable Adaptive Graphics Environment) is a flexible framework that separates rendering from display, making no assumption other than the pixel stream it expects as input, allowing applications to render to a display array with minor changes. It builds a user interface metaphor on the idea of an extended screen, giving the impression of a continuous computer screen. It allows multiple clients and broadcasts all changes via message passing. Multiple instances of the same application are possible, and application windows can be freely moved or resized on tiled displays. It supports remote visualization over Wide Area Network (WAN). OpenGL applications can be easily adapted by adding a pixel read back call at the end of the rendering. A key pitfall is that bandwidth requirements can be extremely high. Time Complexity: Rendering time depends on the number of cluster nodes and the complexity of the volume, as each node renders a portion of the scene. Compositing adds overhead proportional to the number of nodes. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Measured Performance: Not given in the sources. Scaling: Scales with the number of GPUs/CPUs in the cluster or single node. Strengths: Enables interactive visualization of large models on mobile devices with limited resources. Leverages existing OpenGL infrastructure via Chromium. Limitations: High bandwidth requirements due to image streaming and compression. Reliance on wireless links may introduce latency. When to use: When the volumetric dataset is too large for client-side storage or computation, and the client device is resource-constrained (e.g., mobile PDA). When not to use: When low-latency, high-fidelity local rendering is required without network dependency. The technique was proposed by Lamberti et al., who aimed to visualize big models in an interactive mode using a Personal Digital Assistant (PDA) by providing storage and computation resources via a server system. A similar approach using a single node server with multiple GPUs and CPUs was presented by Sarton et al.. The architecture is based on the Chromium framework, which unifies the rendering power of a collection of graphics accelerators arranged in a cluster. name: Node-Local Support Guard
head: Guard, Parallel Support Guard, Support Guard, node-local guard
body: The Node-Local Support Guard is a defense mechanism for distributed 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) renderers that clamps stored 3D Gaussian parameters into precomputed per-field coordinate boxes to prevent catastrophic corruption from single-bit upsets (SBUs). It ensures that no primitive's projected scale exceeds the largest trained scale, making frame-covering corruption impossible. Unlike error-correcting codes (ECC) which operate on memory words, the guard operates on the semantic range of parameters, catching errors that survive or bypass ECC, including those introduced after correction in registers or caches. The method consists of a one-time precomputation phase after training and a per-frame parallel clamping phase applied independently on each node before rendering. Inputs: \theta: The set of stored 3D Gaussian parameters for N primitives. Each primitive i has parameters \thetai organized into fields f and components c. Sp: The subset of primitives assigned to node p. M: The scrub interval (number of frames between guard re-applications). Outputs: Clamped parameters \theta' ready for rendering. A clamp count Cp for health monitoring. Support Box (Bf): For each field f, a pair of bounds (\ell{f,c}, h{f,c}) for each component c. \ell{f,c} = \mini \theta{i,f,c} h{f,c} = \maxi \theta{i,f,c} These bounds are computed once over all N primitives after training. Clamp Counter: A local integer clamp{sp} initialized to 0 for each node p per frame. \lambda: The bit flip rate per stored bit per frame. b: The total number of stored bits, scaling with the number of primitives N (b = \Theta(N)). M: The scrub interval. Derived from Corollary 2, the maximum interval to keep the expected dose below the catastrophic threshold \tau is M \le \Theta(N \alpha^{-1} \tau / \lambda). Selective Clamp Variant: Clamps only the scale and opacity fields. Cost: 1× memory, <0.1 ms/frame. 1. Precompute Support Box (One-time, post-training): For each field f and component c, compute the minimum and maximum values across all N primitives: \ell{f,c} \leftarrow \mini \theta{i,f,c} h{f,c} \leftarrow \maxi \theta{i,f,c} 2. Per-Frame Guard Application (Node p): For each frame, on node p holding primitive subset Sp: a. Initialize local clamp counter: clamp{sp} \leftarrow 0. b. Iterate over each primitive i \in Sp in parallel. c. For each field f and component c: i. Check if the value is out of bounds or non-finite: If \theta{i,f,c} \notin [\ell{f,c}, h{f,c}] or \theta{i,f,c} is non-finite: Clamp the value: \theta{i,f,c} \leftarrow \text{clamp}(\theta{i,f,c}, \ell{f,c}, h{f,c}) Increment counter: clamp{sp} \leftarrow clamp{sp} + 1 d. Render the subset Sp to the node's tile. e. Composite tiles across nodes. f. Check if the total clamp count across all nodes exceeds a health threshold. If so, raise a host parity/scrub alert to signal silent-data-corruption rather than masking the degrading device. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. bounds = {} for f in fields: for c in components: # Extract all values for this field/component across all primitives values = [theta[i][f][c] for i in range(N)] bounds[(f, c)] = (min(values), max(values)) def nodelocalsupportguard(thetap, bounds, healththreshold): clampcount = 0 # Parallel map over primitives owned by this node for i in range(len(thetap)): for f in fields: for c in components: val = thetap[i][f][c] minval, maxval = bounds[(f, c)] # Check for out-of-bounds or non-finite values if not (minval <= val <= maxval) or not isfinite(val): # Clamp to the trained support box thetap[i][f][c] = clamp(val, minval, maxval) clampcount += 1 # Render the clamped primitives tile = renderprimitives(thetap) # Composite tiles from all nodes (implementation specific to renderer) # compositetiles(tile) # Health check: surface errors rather than silently masking them # Note: In a distributed system, clampcounts from all nodes are aggregated # if clampcount > healththreshold: # raisealert("Silent Data Corruption Detected") return tile isfinite checks for NaN and Inf. clamp restricts a value to a range. The aggregation of clampcount across nodes is implied by the text's mention of "total clamp count across all nodes". Residual Error: The guard does not bound the worst-case in-support residual error, only out-of-range flips. The residual error is bounded by the in-box spread and is measured to be perceptually negligible. Aggressive Optimization: If optimization grows very large primitives, the support box widens, admitting a larger guarded footprint and weakening primitive-locality assumptions. Inert Components: The guard skips inert higher-order spherical-harmonic coefficients, touching only a quarter of the parameter memory (14 of 59 components per primitive). A mitigation technique that clamps only the scale and opacity fields to prevent catastrophic upsets, relying on the fact that these fields carry almost all catastrophic mass. It is cheaper than the full support guard, with a cost of 1× memory and <0.1 ms/frame. Time Complexity: Per node, O(N/P) per frame, where N is total primitives and P is number of nodes. Steady-State Overhead: O(N/(P M)), amortized over the scrub interval M. Performance: On a system with 66 million primitives, the guard cost is 9.66 ms per frame (18.3% of render time), sustaining 5 megapixels per second and an effective parameter-read bandwidth of 763 GB/s. Memory Overhead: 1× memory (stores the bounds, which is negligible compared to primitive data). Strengths: Eliminates catastrophic failure mode (frame-covering corruption) requiring only one flip; no cross-node traffic or synchronization points; complementary to ECC. Limitations: Does not correct in-box errors; effectiveness depends on the tightness of the trained support box. When to Use: In distributed 3DGS rendering environments susceptible to single-bit upsets (e.g., high-altitude or space applications) where ECC is insufficient or too costly. The Node-Local Support Guard was introduced in the context of analyzing single-event upsets in 3D Gaussian Splatting rendering. It addresses the finding that while most single-bit upsets in 3DGS are localized, a few critical bits can cause frame-covering corruption. The method was developed to provide a low-overhead, semantic-range defense that complements hardware ECC. name: Volumetric displays and holography
body: This family covers hardware systems and computational methods that render volumetric data directly into physical space, creating images visible from multiple viewpoints without headgear. It differs from standard rasterization by projecting light into a physical medium or light field rather than onto a 2D sensor. It is distinct from Voxel engines and games which simulate volume appearance on 2D displays, and from Scientific and medical visualization which typically uses 2D slice views or volume rendering on monitors. Renders volumetric images with arbitrary per-voxel colors by temporally synchronizing spatial voxel generation with a Liquid Crystal (LC) color filter. It solves multicolor volumetric display by mapping 3D voxel data to control signals for a galvanometer scanner, varifocal lens, and LC filter. Unlike monochromatic scanning methods, it explicitly calculates optimal scanning routes for color layers to minimize mechanical travel time while ensuring color fidelity through temporal multiplexing. It is chosen when full-color volumetric displays with precise spatial control are required. Physically separates the volume where voxels are generated (drawing space) from the observation volume (viewing space) using an optical re-projection system. This allows the drawing space to be filled with materials like xenon gas that lower the energy threshold for voxel generation and provide broadband emission, without creating a physical barrier. It enables the insertion of color filters in the re-projection path. It is chosen when the display medium requires specific environmental conditions (like gas discharge) incompatible with direct user viewing. Renders palm-sized 3D contents in real space by splitting a femtosecond laser into two paths: one using an LC-SLM for holographic voxel generation, and the other using a 3D laser scanner. It solves the limitation of single-path systems by cooperatively combining holographic multiplexing with galvanometric scanning to achieve higher voxel density and larger volumes. It is chosen for high-resolution, real-time volumetric displays in free space. Generates multi-view stereoscopic images of volumetric medical datasets for display on a multi-view lenticular screen, using the GPU for both rendering and compositing. It is chosen when hardware-accelerated, glasses-free stereoscopic visualization of medical volumes is required. Creates luminous image points in free space using a trapped particle illuminated by RGB lasers, forming images via persistence of vision. It solves the 'clipping' limitation of holographic displays by keeping image points physically separate from the scattering surface, allowing unconstrained viewing angles. It is chosen for free-space displays requiring large viewing geometries. Maps 3D voxel data to a physical 3D light field by computing the interference pattern (hologram) required to reconstruct the volume. It differs from sibling methods by using optical superposition (diffraction) rather than temporal persistence or scanning beams. It is chosen when wave optics modeling is needed to resolve viewing space vs. drawing space conflicts through phase modulation. Uses quantum dots (QDs) embedded in a polymer substrate to eliminate occlusion from electrical wiring. External light excites the QDs to emit light spontaneously, forming visible voxels without internal power connections. It is chosen for displays requiring high transparency and absence of internal wiring occlusion. Realizes a solid-state volumetric display by using the chromatic dispersion of a diffractive lens to image planar patterns from a projector. Each image plane's position is defined by a distinct wavelength from a narrowband polychromatic source. It is chosen for solid-state displays without moving parts in the viewing volume. Not given in the sources. Displays layered volumetric images by projecting optical patterns onto a rotating object composed of fan-shaped disks, using external high-speed cameras for tracking and a high-speed projector for rendering. It is chosen for interactive displays where users can freely move and rotate the physical object. Not given in the sources. A display system that eliminates the need for mental reconstruction by displaying the entire stack of tomographic images as a 3D image using a vibrating mirror with variable focal length optics. The speaker is made to vibrate at 30 Hz, and tomographic images are displayed one at a time on the CRT in synchrony with the mirror's motion. Due to the variable focal length, timing sequence, and retinal integration, the stack of 2D images appears as a virtual 3D image in the mirror. The mirror consists of an aluminized membrane stretched over a loud-speaker coupled to a CRT. A volumetric display using a drone equipped with 8 one-dimensional LEDs. The voxel generation capability is limited to the surface of a sphere, but the display space itself can move. A method using bubbles excited by lasers in liquid as voxels. By increasing liquid viscosity, slow-floating bubbles are generated and arranged to stack 2D cross-sections, realizing volumetric image display. This system has a very long voxel residence time, requiring time for image refresh, but can express complex shapes. A volumetric display that extends the Pepper's Ghost optical illusion to multiple stacked translucent planes, cumulatively giving volume to an initially two-dimensional projection. A plane of translucent material is placed at a certain angle on a light source so that it reflects towards the user the projection of an image superimposed on the perceived reality. This is repeated for multiple planes to create volume. It differs from persistence-of-vision displays that use moving parts or levitated particles by using static stacked planes. It is implemented as a layer-based painting tool, retro-gaming platform, text overlaying media player for subtitles, browser-based 3D scene renderer, and volumetric data visualizer. Layer thickness is evaluated alongside light reflection and transmission properties to optimize image quality, though the exact value is not specified. Holographic display methods for volume data have evolved to support cinematic volume rendering on light field displays. Modern implementations integrate visualization toolkits like VTK to generate quilt images and movies for holographic screens, enabling photo-realistic rendering of volumetric data such as CT scans for medical computing. Early volumetric display concepts included varifocal mirror systems for stereotactic neurosurgery planning, which used vibrating mirrors to stack tomographic images into a virtual 3D image. Free-space volumetric displays have also been explored using drones, trapped particles, and laser-excited bubbles to create images without physical screens. Additionally, static stacked-plane systems like SliceView extend traditional optical illusions for direct manipulation of 3D content. name: Galvanometer Scanner Volume Rendering
head: DSS color volumetric display rendering, Drawing of multicolor volumetric graphics, LC Color Filter Volume Rendering, LC filter synchronized voxel generation, Miyazaki Galvano Scanner System, Multicolor Volumetric Graphics, Point Cloud Scanner Volume Rendering, Temporal color-synchronized volumetric rendering
body: Galvanometer Scanner Volume Rendering is a method for rendering volumetric images with arbitrary per-voxel colors by temporally synchronizing the spatial generation of voxels with the switching of a Liquid Crystal (LC) color filter. It solves the problem of multicolor volumetric display by generating application orders of 3D coordinates and color patterns for a beam scanner and an LC color filter, respectively. Unlike Rotational Swept-Screen Projection which relies on persistence of vision in a rotating medium, or Drawing Space Separation (DSS) which focuses on the optical path separation, this method specifically addresses color expression by mapping voxel generation positions to color switching states. It builds on Drawing Space Separation (DSS) by adding a temporal color-synchronization layer. Inputs and Outputs Input: A 3D point cloud V consisting of M voxels. Each voxel vi is defined by spatial position (xi, yi, zi) and RGB color values (ri, gi, bi). Output: A sequence of application orders for the display system, yielding (x, y) values for the galvanometer scanner, z values for the varifocal lens, and (r, g, b) values for the LC color filter. Data Structures Voxel Cloud (V): A list or array of M objects. Each object contains fields: x, y, z, r, g, b. Layer (P): A subset of V containing N voxels that share the same quantized z-coordinate. Each object contains fields: x, y, r, g, b. Scan Path: A list of indices or voxel references defining the traversal order for each layer. Parameters LC Color Filter Refresh Rate: 60 Hz. Laser Repetition Frequency: 1 kHz. Color Extraction Interval: Different colors are extracted every 17 pulses given the above rates. Quantization Layers: The number of discrete z-layers. The sources provide an example of 30 layers. The exact number is not fixed but depends on the desired depth resolution. Steps 1. Represent Point Cloud: Initialize V = \{v1, v2, \ldots, vM\} where vi = (xi, yi, zi, ri, gi, bi). 2. Quantize Z-Axis: Quantize the z values of V into a desired number of layers. The z axis must match the optical axis direction of the display system. 3. Slice Layers: For each quantized z-layer, define the set of vertices P = \{p1, p2, \ldots, pN\}, where each pj has 2D position (xj, yj) and RGB values (rj, gj, bj). 4. Calculate Optimal Scanning Order: For each layer P, calculate the optimal scanning order that minimizes the total route length. The route length is defined as: \sum{j=1}^{N-1} d(pj, p{j+1}) + d(pN, p1) where d(pj, p{j+1}) is the Euclidean distance between the 2D coordinates of vertices pj and p{j+1}. The Christofides algorithm is applied to all layers to solve this Traveling Salesman Problem (TSP). 5. Generate Application Orders: Provide the shortest scanning order obtained for each z to the display system. This yields the (x, y) values for the galvanometer scanner, z values for the varifocal lens, and (r, g, b) values for the LC color filter. Pseudocode Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def euclideandistance2d(p1, p2): """Calculate Euclidean distance between two 2D points.""" return math.sqrt((p1['x'] - p2['x'])2 + (p1['y'] - p2['y'])2) def solvetspchristofides(points): # Standard Christofides algorithm implementation details omitted. This method optimizes the traversal path of a beam scanner in a galvanometer-based volumetric display to minimize the total travel distance between voxels within each depth layer, thereby reducing rendering latency and mechanical wear. It solves the Traveling Salesman Problem (TSP) for the 2D coordinates of voxels in each quantized z-layer using the Christofides algorithm, which provides a guaranteed worst-case performance bound for the heuristic. Unlike simpler heuristics (e.g., nearest neighbor) that may produce suboptimal paths, or exact solvers that are computationally prohibitive for real-time systems, this approach balances optimality with deterministic execution time. Strengths: Enables arbitrary per-voxel colors. Compatible with fluorescent glass displays. Limitations: Color expression is limited by LC filter switching speed. Requires precise synchronization between scanner, varifocal lens, and color filter. When to Use: When multicolor volumetric graphics are required and the display system supports temporal color switching. When Not to Use: When higher color update rates are needed than the LC filter can provide. The method originates from research on volumetric displays using Drawing Space Separation (DSS). It was demonstrated by Miyazaki et al. in 2005 using three galvano scanners to draw volumetric images into fluorescent glass, showing that a beam can excite fluorescent voxels. The specific rendering method for multicolor graphics was detailed in a 2021 paper by Wakunami et al.. The system uses a 3D scanning optical system with three galvano scanners. name: Volumetric Display Scanning Route Optimization
head: Christofides Algorithm for Volumetric Display Scanning, TSP-based Scanning Order Optimization
body: This method optimizes the traversal path of a beam scanner in a galvanometer-based volumetric display to minimize the total travel distance between voxels within each depth layer. It solves the Traveling Salesman Problem (TSP) for the 2D coordinates of voxels in each quantized z-layer using the Christofides algorithm, which provides a guaranteed worst-case performance bound for the heuristic. Unlike simpler heuristics (e.g., nearest neighbor) that may produce suboptimal paths, or exact solvers that are computationally prohibitive, this approach uses the Christofides algorithm which provides a worst-case analysis guarantee for the TSP heuristic. Inputs: A 3D point cloud dataset \mathbf{V} representing volumetric graphics with multicolored voxels. The number of quantization layers K along the optical axis (z-axis). Outputs: A sequence of control commands for each layer k \in \{1, \ldots, K\}, consisting of: (x, y) coordinates for the galvanometer scanners. z position for the varifocal lens. (r, g, b) color values for the Liquid Crystal (LC) color filter. Data Structures: Layer Data: For each layer k, a list of vertices Pk = \{p1, p2, \ldots, pN\}, where N is the number of voxels in that layer. Vertex Structure: Each vertex pj contains: x: float, horizontal position. y: float, vertical position. r: float, red color component. g: float, green color component. b: float, blue color component. Algorithm Steps: 1. Quantization: Slice the 3D point cloud \mathbf{V} into K layers along the z-axis. Assign each voxel to the layer corresponding to its quantized z-coordinate. 2. Layer Processing: For each layer k from 1 to K: a. Extract the set of vertices Pk = \{p1, \ldots, pN\} for the current layer. b. If N = 0, skip to the next layer. c. If N = 1, the scanning order is simply [p1]. d. If N > 1, apply the Christofides algorithm to Pk to find the shortest Hamiltonian cycle (scanning order). The objective is to minimize the total route length L: L = \sum{j=1}^{N-1} d(pj, p{j+1}) + d(pN, p1) where d(a, b) is the Euclidean distance between vertices a and b in the 2D (x, y) plane. e. Store the resulting ordered list of vertices for layer k. 3. Command Generation: For each layer k in the computed order: a. Generate control signals for the varifocal lens to position at the layer's z-depth. b. Iterate through the optimized vertex sequence for layer k. c. For each vertex pj, send (xj, yj) to the galvanometer scanners and (rj, gj, bj) to the LC color filter. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def euclideandistance(p1, p2): """Calculate Euclidean distance between two 2D points.""" return math.sqrt((p1['x'] - p2['x'])2 + (p1['y'] - p2['y'])2) def christofides(vertices): """Complete Christofides algorithm implementation.""" n = len(vertices) if n <= 1: return vertices[:] # 1. Minimum Spanning Tree (Prim's algorithm) inmst = [False] n key = [float('inf')] n parent = [-1] n key[0] = 0 mstedges = [] for in range(n): u = -1 minval = float('inf') for v in range(n): if not inmst[v] and key[v] < minval: minval = key[v] u = v inmst[u] = True if parent[u] != -1: mstedges.append((parent[u], u)) for v in range(n): if not inmst[v]: d = euclideandistance(vertices[u], vertices[v]) if d < key[v]: key[v] = d parent[v] = u # 2. Find odd-degree vertices degree = [0] n for u, v in mstedges: degree[u] += 1 degree[v] += 1 oddnodes = [i for i in range(n) if degree[i] % 2 == 1] # 3. Minimum weight perfect matching on odd nodes (recursive backtracking) def findmatching(nodes): if len(nodes) == 0: return [] if len(nodes) == 2: return [(nodes[0], nodes[1])] best = None bestcost = float('inf') for i in range(1, len(nodes)): u, v = nodes[0], nodes[i] rest = nodes[1:i] + nodes[i+1:] cost = euclideandistance(vertices[u], vertices[v]) submatch = findmatching(rest) totalcost = cost + sum(euclideandistance(vertices[a], vertices[b]) for a, b in submatch) if totalcost < bestcost: bestcost = totalcost best = [(u, v)] + submatch return best matchingedges = findmatching(oddnodes) # 4. Combine MST and matching, find Eulerian tour, shortcut adj = {i: [] for i in range(n)} for u, v in mstedges: adj[u].append(v) adj[v].append(u) for u, v in matchingedges: adj[u].append(v) adj[v].append(u) # Hierholzer's algorithm for Eulerian circuit stack = [0] circuit = [] while stack: v = stack[-1] if adj[v]: u = adj[v].pop() adj[u].remove(v) stack.append(u) else: circuit.append(stack.pop()) circuit.reverse() # Shortcut to get Hamiltonian cycle visited = set() tour = [] for node in circuit: if node not in visited: visited.add(node) tour.append(vertices[node]) return tour def optimizescanningroute(pointcloud, numlayers): """ Main function to generate scanning routes for volumetric display. Args: pointcloud: List of dicts, each with 'x', 'y', 'z', 'r', 'g', 'b'. numlayers: Integer, number of z-axis quantization layers. Returns: layerscommands: List of lists of vertex dicts, ordered for scanning. """ # Step 1: Quantization layervertices = [[] for in range(numlayers)] zmin = min(v['z'] for v in pointcloud) zmax = max(v['z'] for v in pointcloud) zrange = zmax - zmin if zmax != zmin else 1.0 for voxel in pointcloud: zquantized = int((voxel['z'] - zmin) / zrange numlayers) zquantized = max(0, min(numlayers - 1, zquantized)) layervertices[zquantized].append(voxel) layerscommands = [] # Step 2 & 3: Process each layer for k in range(numlayers): currentlayervertices = layervertices[k] n = len(currentlayervertices) if n == 0: layerscommands.append([]) continue elif n == 1: layerscommands.append(currentlayervertices) continue # Step 2d: Apply Christofides algorithm optimalorder = christofides(currentlayervertices) layerscommands.append(optimalorder) return layerscommands Parameters: Number of layers (K): Determines the z-axis quantization resolution. Example value: 30 layers. Vertex Count (N): Varies per layer; the algorithm scales with N. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Empty Layers: If a quantized layer contains no voxels, the scanner should skip the layer or hold position, depending on hardware constraints. Single Vertex: If a layer has only one voxel, the TSP is trivial; no optimization is needed. Precision: Euclidean distance calculations should use sufficient floating-point precision to avoid accumulation errors in large layers. Hardware Synchronization: The generated order must be synchronized with the varifocal lens movement and LC filter switching to ensure correct voxel rendering. The parent method that uses this optimization to control x, y, z, and color hardware [5277-galvanometer-scanner-volume-rendering.md]. The underlying combinatorial optimization problem solved by the Christofides algorithm. Time Complexity: The Christofides algorithm runs in O(N^3) time for N vertices per layer. Memory Complexity: O(N) per layer to store vertex positions and the resulting path. Performance: Minimizes total travel distance L, reducing the time required to scan each layer. Strengths: Provides a worst-case approximation guarantee (1.5x optimal) for metric TSP, ensuring predictable performance compared to greedy heuristics. Limitations: More complex to implement than nearest-neighbor heuristics; may be overkill for very small N. When to Use: When minimizing scan time is critical in galvanometer-based volumetric displays. When Not to Use: If computational resources are extremely limited and N is very small, simpler heuristics may suffice. This method was introduced in the context of holographic-laser-excited volumetric displays. It builds on the work of Christofides (1976), who proposed the heuristic for the Traveling Salesman Problem. The specific application to volumetric displays with multicolored voxels using galvanometer scanners and LC filters was detailed in research published in 2021.
