name: Drawing Space Separation (DSS)
head: Drawing Space Separation (DSS) Volumetric Display, Holographic-laser-excited graphics
body: Drawing Space Separation (DSS) is a volumetric display technique that physically separates the region where voxels are generated (the drawing space) from the region where the user views the image (the viewing space) using an optical re-projection system. This architecture allows the drawing space to be filled with a material, such as xenon gas, that significantly lowers the energy threshold for voxel generation and provides broadband emission, without creating a physical barrier between the user and the graphics. Unlike sibling methods that rely on capturing scattering particles or direct projection, DSS generates robust, non-contact aerial voxels that can be colored arbitrarily by synchronizing temporal color filtering with spatial beam scanning. Inputs: 3D point cloud data representing the volumetric graphic, defined by vertex coordinates (xi, yi, zi) and target color values (ri, gi, bi) for each voxel i. A femtosecond laser source with center wavelength \lambda = 800 nm, pulse duration \tau = 34 fs, repetition frequency f{rep} = 1 kHz, and average power P{avg} = 7 W. A Liquid Crystal on Silicon Spatial Light Modulator (LCOS-SLM) with resolution 1272 \times 1024 pixels, pixel pitch p = 12.5 \mum, 8-bit depth, and refresh rate \approx 10 Hz. A 3D beam scanning system comprising a galvanometer scanner (deflection angle 40^\circ) and a varifocal lens (aperture 16 mm, variable focal length range -500 to +333 mm). An initial emission lens with focal length f{lens} = 50 mm. An LC color filter capable of switching transmission wavelengths. Outputs: A real, aerial volumetric image in the viewing space, visible from a 360^\circ horizontal angle, composed of voxels with arbitrary colors. The system processes 3D point cloud data. Each voxel i is defined by: Position: \mathbf{p}i = (xi, yi, zi) in the drawing space coordinate system. Color: \mathbf{c}i = (ri, gi, bi), where r, g, b correspond to the transmission states of the LC color filter. The LCOS-SLM stores a Computer-Generated Hologram (CGH) phase pattern \Phi(x, y) calculated to diffract the laser beam into the required focal points. The re-projection system consists of two parabolic mirrors with their concave sides facing each other: 1. Bottom Mirror: Contains a central aperture where the drawing space is located. 2. Top Mirror: Contains a central aperture through which the user views the re-projected image. 3. Alignment: The vertices of the two mirrors are separated by a distance equal to the focal length f{mirror} of the mirrors. 1. Laser Preparation: The femtosecond laser beam passes through a half-wave plate and polarization beamsplitter to control pulse energy, then through the LCOS-SLM. 2. Phase Modulation (Parallel Generation): The LCOS-SLM displays a CGH phase pattern \Phi(x, y) that modulates the phase of the laser pulses, enabling the parallel generation of multiple focal points. 3. 3D Beam Scanning: The modulated beam enters the 3D beam scanning system. The galvanometer scanner adjusts the deflection angle to control the horizontal position of the focal point, while the varifocal lens adjusts the focal length to control the axial position. 4. Voxel Generation in Drawing Space: The focused laser irradiates the Xenon gas in the aperture of the bottom mirror. The incident fluence must exceed the emission threshold. In Xenon, the threshold is 19 mJ/cm^2, which is 34\% lower than in air, and the resulting emission is \approx 200 times brighter than air luminescence at this intensity. The laser pulse energy for rendering typically ranges from 117 \muJ to 271 \muJ depending on the scene. 5. Re-projection: The light emitted from the voxel in the bottom mirror's aperture travels to the top mirror. Due to the parabolic geometry and vertex separation equal to the focal length, the emission is re-projected as a real image through the aperture of the top mirror into the viewing space. 6. Color Extraction: As the light passes through the aperture of the top mirror, it traverses the LC color filter. The filter selectively extracts specific wavelengths from the broad-spectrum emission of the femtosecond-laser-excited Xenon. 7. Temporal Synchronization: The system synchronizes the spatial position of the voxel generation (controlled by the scanner) with the color state of the LC filter. By switching the filter color in time with the arrival of the laser pulse at a specific voxel location, arbitrary colors (ri, gi, bi) are assigned to each voxel. 8. Persistence of Vision: The scanning speed is high enough that the human eye perceives the sequence of emitted voxels as a continuous volumetric image. Unverified code. This implements the CGH beam design technique. """ # Sort points into layers for efficient scanning layers = slicepointcloudintolayers(pointcloud) for layer in layers: # Calculate shortest path between vertices in the layer (TSP-like heuristic) scanpath = calculateshortestscanpath(layer.vertices) for voxel in scanpath: # 1. """ pass Laser: 800 nm center wavelength, 34 fs pulse duration, 1 kHz repetition, 7 W average power. Drawing Space: Cylindrical glass cell, 30 mm diameter, 30 mm height, filled with Xenon (Xe) gas. Threshold: Xe emission threshold is 19 mJ/cm^2; Air emission threshold is higher (Xe reduces threshold by up to 34%). Brightness: Xe emission is \approx 200 times brighter than air at 19 mJ/cm^2. Mirrors: Two parabolic mirrors, vertices separated by focal length. Apertures are central. LCOS-SLM: 1272 \times 1024 resolution, 12.5 \mum pitch, 8-bit, ~10 Hz refresh. Scanner: Galvanometer 40^\circ deflection; Varifocal lens 16 mm aperture, -500 to +333 mm focal range. Rendering Energies: 271 \muJ (Fig 5a), 203 \muJ (Fig 5c, 5f), 219 \muJ (Fig 5e), 117 \muJ (Fig 5g). Physical Barrier: Previous systems filling the space with gas to lower energy thresholds created a physical wall (glass cell) between the user and the image, reducing realism. DSS solves this by re-projecting the image out of the cell, leaving the viewing space as open air. Energy Density vs. Size: In air, high pulse energy is required to form high-energy density, necessitating short focal length lenses, which restricts graphics size to several millimeters. DSS allows the use of lower energy densities in Xe, enabling larger graphics (centimeter-order). Monochromatic Emission: Femtosecond-laser-excited voxels in gas emit bluish-white broadband light. Color is not intrinsic to the voxel but is extracted optically. Synchronization errors between scanner position and filter state will result in incorrect colors or ghosting. Ambient Light: While Xe is 200x brighter than air, the system is demonstrated under ambient room lighting. High ambient light may reduce contrast. Time Complexity: The rendering time is dominated by the scanning speed of the galvanometer and varifocal lens, and the refresh rate of the LCOS-SLM and LC filter. The laser repetition rate (1 kHz) sets an upper bound on voxel emission frequency. The source notes real-time AR demonstration (3D saber) at 20 fps. Memory Complexity: Depends on the size of the point cloud and the CGH pattern stored on the SLM (1272 \times 1024 pixels). Resolution: Demonstrated with up to 5734 voxels (Armadillo model). Size: Centimeter-order images (e.g., 30 mm drawing space). Color: Arbitrary colors achieved via LC filter switching (Cyan, Magenta, Yellow, RGB). Brightness: Visible under ambient room lighting due to Xe enhancement. Strengths: No physical barrier between user and image (open viewing space). Robust graphics that do not disappear upon contact with users or objects (unlike particle traps). Full-color capability from a monochromatic laser source via spectral filtering. Lower energy threshold for voxel generation compared to air. Limitations: Requires complex optical alignment (two parabolic mirrors). Limited by the scanning speed and SLM refresh rate for dynamic content. Drawing space is confined to the 30 mm glass cell aperture at the bottom mirror, not the entire re-projection volume. Use: When robust, interactive, full-color volumetric graphics are needed in open space without physical screens or particle traps. Suitable for AR demonstrations and detailed static/dynamic models. Not Use: When extremely high voxel counts or large-scale graphics (meter-scale) are required, as the scanning mechanism and re-projection optics limit the size and density. Not suitable for applications requiring intrinsic color emission without filtering. Drawing Space Separation (DSS) was introduced in a 2021 paper by researchers publishing in Scientific Reports (Nature Portfolio). The work builds upon previous systems that used femtosecond lasers to create aerial voxels in air, which were limited to monochromatic bluish-white light and small sizes due to high energy requirements. The aerial re-projection method using two parabolic mirrors was reported in a US patent 50 years prior to the DSS paper. The development addressed two main limitations of prior femtosecond-laser volumetric displays: 1. Color: Previous systems emitted monochromatic light. DSS introduced an LC color filter in the re-projection path to extract arbitrary colors. 2. Energy/Size: Previous systems required high energy in air, limiting size. DSS introduced a material-assisted drawing space (Xe gas) separated from the viewing space, lowering the threshold and allowing larger, brighter images. The system has been demonstrated for: Centimeter-order static images (Armadillo, Stanford Bunny). Real-time Augmented Reality (3D light saber). Point cloud visualization with per-voxel coloring. Interaction with physical objects (graphics touching a 3D-printed bunny). name: Dual-Path Holographic Laser Rendering
head: Volumetric display system with LC-SLM and 3D laser scanner
body: Dual-Path Holographic Laser Rendering is a volumetric display method that generates palm-sized 3D contents in real space by splitting a femtosecond laser into two distinct optical paths. One path utilizes a liquid-crystal spatial light modulator (LC-SLM) to generate holographic voxel patterns, while the other employs a 3D laser scanner for positional control. This cooperative dual-path approach solves the limitation of single-path systems by combining the high voxel density of holographic excitation with the flexible spatial scanning of galvanometers, enabling well-filled volumetric graphics and animations within a centimeter-sized volume. It differs from pure holographic methods by integrating mechanical scanning for axial positioning and from pure scanning methods by using CGH for lateral voxel distribution per slice. Inputs and Outputs Input: 3D point cloud data representing the target volumetric content. Output: Visible volumetric graphics formed by multiphoton excitation in a gas-filled rendering space. Data Structures The system processes 3D point cloud data by dividing it into two volumes along the z-direction (the optical axis). Volume Division: The point cloud is split into two subsets, one for each optical path. Slicing: Each subset is sliced in the z-direction to create 2D layers. Sorting: Slices are sorted to minimize the total scanning path length between consecutive slices. Optical Layout and Parameters The system uses a Yb:KGW femtosecond laser (Pharos series PH1SP-10-1M, Light Conversion) with a center wavelength of 1030 nm, a repetition frequency of 10 kHz, and a pulse duration of < 155 fs. The laser beam is split into two optical paths using a half-wave plate and a polarizing beam splitter, delivering 480 µJ of pulse energy to each path. Path 1 (Holographic): The laser passes through an LC-SLM (IL-WU070, JVCKENWOOD) with a pixel pitch of 8 µm and a display area of 1920 × 1200 pixels. The SLM displays Computer-Generated Holograms (CGHs) to modulate the laser phase, controlling the number and position of focal points within the slice. Path 2 (Scanning): The laser passes through a two-axis galvanometer scanner (GVS312, Thorlabs) and a varifocal lens (TL-16-40-TC, Optotune). Common Optics: Both paths use an F-theta lens with a focal length of 100 mm to focus the laser onto the rendering space. A concave lens with a focal length of -568 mm is placed immediately after the varifocal lens to protect optical elements from reflected light from the glass cell surface. Rendering Space: A 100 × 100 × 100 mm³ glass cell filled with Xenon gas at 750 Torr. The gas reduces the threshold energy for excitation and increases brightness intensity. Rendering Area Path 1: Horizontal range of 50 × 50 mm² at an axial position of 88.4 mm from the lens. Path 2: Horizontal range of 60 × 60 mm² at an axial position of 114.4 mm from the lens. Combined Axial Range: 60 mm. Numbered Steps 1. Obtain 3D point cloud data for the target content. 2. Divide the target 3D point cloud data into two volumes along the z-direction (aligned with the optical axes of both paths). 3. Slice the divided point data in the z-direction to create 2D layers for each path. 4. Sort the slices such that the scanning path between consecutive slices is minimized. 5. Form the graphics by stacking these 2D slices in the z-direction. 6. Convert the 3D scanning data (positions for the galvanometer and varifocal lens) into voltage signals via a D/A converter. 7. Apply the voltage signals to the galvanometer scanner and the varifocal lens to position the emission points. 8. Display the corresponding CGH on the LC-SLM for each slice to define the lateral voxel pattern. Formulas The horizontal position (x, y) of an emission point is determined by: (x, y) = (f \thetax, f \thetay) Where: f is the composite focal length of the F-theta lens, concave lens, and varifocal lens. (\thetax, \thetay) is the deflection angle of the galvanometer scanner. This position varies depending on the axial position at which the graphics is rendered. Pseudocode Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def renderdualpath(pointcloud, path1zrange, path2zrange): """ Renders volumetric content using dual-path holographic laser rendering. Args: pointcloud: List of 3D points (x, y, z). path1zrange: Tuple (zmin, zmax) for Path 1. path2zrange: Tuple (zmin, zmax) for Path 2. Accurate calibration of f as a function of z is required. Gas Pressure: The rendering space requires Xenon gas at 750 Torr to reduce excitation threshold and increase brightness. Deviations may affect voxel formation. Liquid-Crystal and Related SLMs are electro-optic or micromechanical devices used to modulate light with computed holographic fringes for volumetric display and holography. They solve the challenge of generating high-resolution fringe patterns by leveraging parallel spatial modulation rather than time-multiplexed scanning. Unlike scanned-AOM systems which require high-speed analog conversion and complex scanning mirrors, LCDs and DMDs are more readily interfaced to digital electronics, requiring only demagnification and optical concatenation. Performance: The system demonstrated animation at 20 fps and static images with an exposure time of 67 ms. Voxel Density: Using CGH to form three voxels achieves higher voxel density compared to graphics rendered by a single voxel. Rendering Volume: The combined axial rendering area is 60 mm, with horizontal ranges of 50 × 50 mm² (Path 1) and 60 × 60 mm² (Path 2). Strengths: Enables palm-sized volumetric contents with well-filled voxels and higher voxel density through holographic excitation. Limitations: Limited to centimeter-sized volumes; requires complex optical alignment and gas-filled chamber. Hardware Specifics: Uses a Yb:KGW femtosecond laser (1030 nm, 10 kHz, <155 fs) and specific commercial components (JVCKENWOOD SLM, Thorlabs scanners, Optotune lens). The method was developed by Kota Kumagai, Hisashi Oka, Kazuki Horikiri, Tetsuji Suzuki, and Yoshio Hayasaki from the Center for Optical Research and Education, Utsunomiya University, Japan. It was presented at SIGGRAPH Emerging Technologies in 2024. The work aims to achieve real-space rendering of palm-sized volumetric contents by optimizing the optical system and scanning path for cooperative dual-path laser rendering. name: Liquid-Crystal and Related SLMs
head: LC-SLM, LCD Holographic Modulation, LCD SLM, Magneto-optic SLM
body: Liquid-Crystal and Related SLMs are electro-optic or micromechanical devices used to modulate light with computed holographic fringes for volumetric display and holography. They solve the challenge of generating high-resolution fringe patterns by leveraging parallel spatial modulation rather than time-multiplexed scanning. Unlike scanned-AOM systems which require high-speed analog conversion and complex scanning mirrors, LCDs and DMDs are more readily interfaced to digital electronics, requiring only demagnification and optical concatenation. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Digitally computed holographic fringe data (amplitude and/or phase values). Output: Modulated light field forming a holographic image (planar or volumetric). Data Structures: LCD SLM: Typically contains approximately one million picture elements ("pixels"). Elements are typically 50 microns wide. Magneto-optic SLM: Contains less than one million elements. DMD: Micromechanical array of tiny mirror elements on a semiconductor chip. Method Steps: 1. Modulation Type Selection: Determine if amplitude or phase modulation is required. LCDs are primarily phase modulators when used without polarizing optics. Phase modulation is optically efficient and most often used. Grayscale modulation (many levels) is desirable for complex images. 2. Demagnification: Apply optical demagnification to reduce the effective sample size of the SLM elements to match the fringe sampling pitch. The fringe sampling pitch is approximately 0.5 micron. The SLM element size is typically 50 microns. This process proportionally reduces the lateral dimensions of the resulting image. 3. Tiling (if necessary): If the required image size exceeds the lateral dimensions reduced by demagnification, tile several modulators together to overcome low pixel count. 4. Digital Interface: Interface the computed fringe data directly to the SLM. LCDs can plug directly into a digital computer or be built on an integrated circuit chip. Parameters: LCD Grayscale Levels: Common LCDs have nominally 9–56 grayscale levels. DMD Latency: Approximately 20 ms. DMD Capacity: Approximately 100 Mb. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def configurelcdslm(fringedata, slmelementsize=50e-6, fringepitch=0.5e-6): """ Configure an LCD SLM for holographic rendering. Args: fringedata: Array of computed fringe values (phase/amplitude). slmelementsize: Physical width of one LCD pixel (meters). fringepitch: Required sampling pitch for the holographic fringe (meters). Returns: config: Dictionary containing optical and digital configuration. """ # Calculate required demagnification factor # The effective sample size must match the fringe pitch demagfactor = slmelementsize / fringepitch # Note: Demagnification proportionally reduces the lateral dimensions of the image # Check if tiling is required based on desired image width vs single SLM width # This is a design decision based on application requirements # Interface setup: Direct digital connection # LCDs are readily interfaced to digital electronics return { "demagnificationfactor": demagfactor, "modulationtype": "phase", # LCDs are basically phase modulators without polarizing optics "grayscalelevels": "9-56", # Typical nominal range "interface": "digital" } def configuredmdslm(fringedata): """ Configure a DMD for holographic rendering. Args: fringedata: Array of computed fringe values. Returns: config: Dictionary containing DMD configuration. """ # DMDs are micromechanical SLMs # Determine modulation mode # Phase-modulating DMDs create small flat holographic images # Binary amplitude-modulating DMDs create small interactive 3D holographic images return { "latencyms": 20, "capacitymb": 100, "costpermbusd": 30, "modulationmodes": ["phase", "binaryamplitude"] } DMDs are micromechanical spatial light modulators fabricated on a semiconductor chip as an electronically addressed array of tiny mirror elements. They modulate the phase or amplitude of reflected light by electrostatically depressing or tilting each element. A phase-modulating DMD was used to create a small flat holographic image, and a binary amplitude-modulating DMD was used to create a small interactive 3D holographic image. DMDs deliver approximately 100 Mb in 20 ms latency time, for a cost of about 3,000 (30 per Mb). Time and Memory Complexity: LCD: Limited by the pixel count (typically ~1 million samples). DMD: Delivers approximately 100 Mb in 20 ms latency. Magneto-optic SLM: Contains less than one million elements. Measured Performance: LCD: Produces small planar images due to low pixel count and demagnification constraints. DMD: Produces small flat or interactive 3D holographic images. Scanned-AOM (for comparison): Produces the largest holovideo images but requires high-speed analog conversion and complex scanning mirrors. Scaling: LCD pixel count can be increased by tiling several modulators together. Future mass production could reduce DMD costs further. Holographic bandwidth compression can increase fringe computation speed by 3000 times for the same hardware implementation. Strengths and Limitations: Strengths: Readily interfaced to digital electronics; avoids high-speed analog conversion; avoids complex scanning mirrors; phase modulation is optically efficient. Limitations: Low pixel count (typically ~1 million); demagnification reduces lateral image dimensions; magneto-optic SLMs have even fewer elements. When to Use: Use LCDs when digital interfacing is preferred and small-to-medium planar or volumetric images are sufficient. Use DMDs when higher capacity (100 Mb) is needed compared to standard LCDs, or for binary amplitude modulation applications. Avoid scanned-AOM if high-speed analog conversion and complex scanning mirrors are undesirable. Early researchers using LCD SLMs or magneto-optic SLMs created small planar images. The challenge in holographic displays arises from the many millions of samples in a fringe, which successful approaches address by exploiting parallelism and/or the time-response of the human visual system (typically 20 ms). Reflective LCDs created directly on semiconductor chips using VLSI technology have also been explored. name: Scanned AOM Holographic Display
head: MIT holovideo display, Scanned Acousto-Optic Modulator (AOM) Holographic Display, Scanned-AOM, Synthetic aperture holography
body: The Scanned AOM Holographic Display is a time-multiplexed volumetric display technique that generates large apparent holographic fringes by rapidly scanning a phase-modulated light beam across the viewer's eye. It solves the hardware limitation of Acousto-Optic Modulators (AOMs), which can only phase-modulate a small number of samples (approximately 1000) at any single instant due to the finite bandwidth and aperture of the acoustic wave. Unlike static SLM-based methods, this approach synthesizes a large hologram by exploiting the human visual system's integration time (typically 20 ms) to merge the scanned, time-multiplexed samples into a coherent 3D image. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A set of computed holographic fringes (complex amplitude data) representing the scene. Output: A real-time 3D holographic image visible to the observer. Data Structures: Fringe Data: Digital representation of the holographic phase/amplitude. The source notes that early systems used 2 MB of fringe data for a 50 ml volume. RF Signal: High-frequency analog signal derived from the fringe data, driving the AOM. Method Steps: 1. Fringe Computation: Compute the holographic fringes for the desired 3D scene. This involves calculating the complex wavefield contributions from scene elements, typically requiring phase-only or phase-amplitude modulation data. 2. Digital-to-Analog Conversion: Convert the digitally computed fringes into high-frequency analog electrical signals. This requires a specialized synchronized high-speed framebuffer system to handle the data rate and synchronization. 3. Acoustic Wave Generation: The analog RF signal is applied to the transducer of an AOM crystal. This generates an acoustic wave that propagates through the crystal, creating a periodic refractive index variation (a phase grating). 4. Phase Modulation: A beam of laser light passes through the AOM. The acoustic wave phase-modulates the light beam. At any instant, the AOM modulates only a small segment of the total holographic fringe (approx. 1000 samples). 5. Optical Processing: Lenses image and demagnify the phase-modulated light beam to a plane in front of the viewer. 6. Horizontal Scanning: A rapidly moving mirror (scanning system) angularly multiplexes the image of the modulated light. This scans the small modulated segment across the horizontal extent of the desired holographic fringe. 7. Vertical Scanning: A vertical scanning system (implied by the need for 2D fringes) addresses the vertical dimension, completing the 2D fringe synthesis. 8. Visual Integration: The human eye, with a latency of typically 20 ms, time-integrates the rapidly scanned light. The brain perceives the superposition of all scanned segments as a single, large, continuous holographic fringe. Parameters: AOM Instantaneous Capacity: ~1000 samples modulated at any one instant. Human Visual Latency: Typically 20 ms. Volume Scaling: Early systems produced 50 ml volumes from 2 MB fringes. Scaled systems with 18 parallel channels produced >1 liter volumes from 36 MB fringes. Pitfalls and Edge Cases: Signal Conversion: Converting digital fringes to high-frequency analog signals is a major practical obstacle, requiring specialized hardware not common in standard digital interfaces. Synchronization: State-of-the-art scanning mirrors must be precisely synchronized with the fringe data stream. Misalignment results in distorted or unviewable images. Complexity: The need for optical processing (mirrors, lenses) and high-speed analog electronics makes the system significantly more complex than LCD-based displays. Acousto-Optic Random Access Scanning with Parallel Channels is a volumetric display technique that uses multiple acousto-optic (AO) deflectors operating in parallel to address voxels in a display volume, thereby increasing the total voxel count and maintaining image intensity. It solves the bottleneck of finite acoustic wave travel time ("access time") in single-channel scanners, which limits the number of addressable voxels per frame at a fixed refresh rate. Unlike single-channel scanners, which suffer from intensity drop-off as voxel density increases due to reduced on-time, this method couples several scanners to distribute the workload. It differs from Four-Channel Scanner Convergence Correction by defining the parallel architecture itself, whereas the sibling method addresses the geometric alignment errors inherent in that architecture. An AOM device variant using multiple ultrasonic transducers (electrodes) fed a complex pattern to launch surface acoustic waves (SAWs) across the device aperture, diffracting light to form a holographic image without time multiplexing. 1. Feed a complex pattern to multiple electrodes on the AOM device. 2. Launch surface acoustic waves (SAWs) across the device aperture. 3. Diffracted light forms a holographic image directly, eliminating the need for time multiplexing and scanning mirrors. Large number of electrodes may be prohibitively expensive. Requires an additional numerical inversion transformation for the array of SAW electrodes, making rapid computation difficult. Time Complexity: The computational complexity is dominated by the fringe generation (CGH calculation) and the high-speed digital-to-analog conversion. The scanning process is hardware-accelerated by the optical system and human integration. Memory Complexity: Early systems required 2 MB of fringe data for a 50 ml volume. Scaled systems used 36 MB for >1 liter volumes. Performance: Produced the world's first real-time 3D holographic display in 1989. Capable of producing the largest holovideo images among contemporary techniques. Strengths: Can be scaled to produce large image volumes (e.g., >1 liter). Provides realistic 3D imagery with full parallax. Limitations: Requires specialized high-speed analog electronics and synchronization with scanning mirrors, making it expensive and complex compared to LCD/DMD-based displays. The need for high-frequency analog signal conversion is a significant barrier. When to Use: When large volume holographic imagery is required and hardware complexity/cost is not a primary constraint. When Not to Use: When low-cost, easily interfaced digital displays (LCD/DMD) are sufficient, or when real-time computation of large fringes is not feasible. The Scanned AOM Holographic Display was invented and exploited by researchers at the MIT Media Laboratory to produce the world's first real-time 3D holographic display in 1989. It was developed to overcome the limitations of static holographic SLMs, which had limited aperture and resolution. The technique leveraged the time-multiplexing capability of AOMs and the temporal integration of the human visual system to synthesize large holographic fringes. Early implementations produced 50 ml volumes, and later scaled versions with 18 parallel channels achieved volumes greater than one liter. name: Acousto-Optic Random Access Scanning with Parallel Channels
head: AO Laser Scanner, Four-Channel Parallel Processing Scanner
body: Acousto-Optic Random Access Scanning with Parallel Channels is a volumetric display technique that uses multiple acousto-optic (AO) deflectors operating in parallel to address voxels in a display volume, thereby increasing the total voxel count and maintaining image intensity. It solves the bottleneck of finite acoustic wave travel time ("access time") in single-channel scanners, which limits the number of addressable voxels per frame at a fixed refresh rate. Unlike single-channel scanners, which suffer from intensity drop-off as voxel density increases due to reduced on-time, this method couples several scanners to distribute the workload. It differs from Four-Channel Scanner Convergence Correction by defining the parallel architecture itself, whereas the sibling method addresses the geometric alignment errors inherent in that architecture. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A single-mode laser beam (e.g., 1.6 mm diameter) and high-speed position/intensity data from a custom computer interface card. Output: A scanned light beam projecting voxels onto a helical display surface. Data Structures: Control Data: High-speed data packets sent to the scanner electronics independent of the host computer speed. Frequency Sets: Each AO deflector is loaded with specific acoustic frequencies corresponding to desired beam deflection angles. Optical Layout and Components: 1. Light Source: An argon ion gas laser (up to 1 W) provides the initial beam. 2. Beam Splitting: The single input beam is split into four paths (Channels A, B, C, D) using beam splitters. 3. Modulation: Each beam is focused into a 440 MHz Tellurium Dioxide (TeO2) Acousto-Optic Modulator (AOM). 4. Collimation: Beams are recollimated to a diameter of 3 mm. 5. Deflection: Beams are sent to x and y TeO2 AO deflectors (50 MHz bandwidth). 6. Combining: Outputs from Channels A and B are combined using a half-wave plate and a polarizing beam splitter. Channels C and D are combined identically. 7. Projection: The two combined outputs are projected downward onto the helix using a final lens pair, which increases angular magnification by ~2.5x. Numbered Steps: 1. Polarization Maintenance: Maintain vertical polarization at the input beam to align parallel to the acoustic wave direction in the deflectors, avoiding corrective wave plates. 2. Beam Reduction: Reduce the optical beam diameter in the AO deflectors from 6 mm to 3 mm. 3. Frequency Loading: Load the x and y deflectors with desired frequencies. The deflectors are swept from 75 to 125 MHz. 4. Blanking: During the "access time" (fill time), blank the laser beam with a modulator to prevent image smearing caused by multiple frequencies being present in the beam deflection path. 5. On-Time Activation: Turn on the modulator for the specified "on-time" after the acoustic wave has traveled across the laser beam to achieve 100% deflection. 6. Channel Combination: Combine A/B and C/D outputs via half-wave plates and polarizing beam splitters to ensure all four channels can overlap anywhere in the helix volume. 7. Projection: Project the combined beams onto the helix using the final lens pair. Formulas and Parameters: Time-Bandwidth Product (TB): TB = \Delta f \times \Delta t Where \Delta f is the deflector sweep range (125 MHz - 75 MHz = 50 MHz) and \Delta t is the sweep time (5 \musec). TB = 50 \times 10^6 \text{ Hz} \times 5 \times 10^{-6} \text{ s} = 250. Access Time Reduction: Reducing beam diameter from 6 mm to 3 mm lowers access time from 10 \musec to 5 \musec. Voxel Capacity: Per Channel: Up to 10,000 voxels/frame. Total System: 4 channels \times 10,000 voxels = 40,000 voxels per color. Refresh Rate: 20 Hz. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. laserpowerwatts = 1.0 inputbeamdiametermm = 1.6 targetbeamdiametermm = 3.0 deflectorfstartmhz = 75.0 deflectorfendmhz = 125.0 sweeptimeus = 5.0 refreshratehz = 20.0 numchannels = 4 voxelsperchannel = 10000 accesstimeus = 5.0 # Reduced from 10 us by halving beam diameter channels = [{"diametermm": inputbeamdiametermm, "polarization": "vertical"} for in range(numchannels)] for i in range(numchannels): channels[i]["modulatorfreqmhz"] = 440.0 for i in range(numchannels): channels[i]["diametermm"] = targetbeamdiametermm for i in range(numchannels): channels[i]["deflectorbwmhz"] = 50.0 combinedab = {"channels": [channels[0], channels[1]], "method": "halfwaveplatepbs"} combinedcd = {"channels": [channels[2], channels[3]], "method": "halfwaveplatepbs"} projectionmagnification = 2.5 for frame in range(refreshratehz): # 1. Blank laser beam during access time modulatorstate = "off" # 2. Load deflectors with frequencies for current voxel positions # Deflectors sweep from 75 to 125 MHz in 5 microseconds currentfreqmhz = deflectorfstartmhz sweepdurationus = sweeptimeus # 3. Wait for acoustic wave to travel across beam (fill time) # Wait for acoustic wave to travel across beam (fill time) # 4. Turn on modulator for on-time modulatorstate = "on" # 5. Display voxels # Display voxels: Not given in the sources. # 6. Turn off modulator modulatorstate = "off" Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Access Time/Smearing: Finite acoustic wave travel time causes an "access time" or "fill time". If the beam is not blanked during this period, image smearing occurs due to multiple frequencies in the beam path. Polarization Mismatch: Misalignment of polarization degrades deflection efficiency. The system solves this by maintaining vertical polarization at the input beam. Intensity Drop-off: In single-channel systems, increasing voxels decreases on-time and overall light level. Parallel coupling prevents this. Four-Channel Scanner Convergence Correction is a geometric alignment method for four-channel acousto-optic (AO) holographic displays, ensuring that four scanned laser beams (organized as two pyramidal sources) intersect uniformly throughout the volumetric display space. It solves the problem of beam separation caused by the physical offset of output lenses, which would otherwise cause the beams to intersect at only a single point rather than throughout the entire volume. Unlike its sibling Acousto-Optic Random Access Scanning with Parallel Channels, which defines the parallel channel architecture, this method specifically addresses the spatial registration errors inherent in that architecture. It differs from Acousto-Optic Modulator R-Factor Analysis by focusing on macroscopic geometric alignment rather than device physics limits. This method evaluates the performance of an Acousto-Optic Modulator (AOM) by calculating the R-factor, defined as the ratio of the acoustical beam spread to the optical beam spread. It determines the output beam eccentricity (ellipticity) to ensure optimal diffraction efficiency and beam quality in scanned volumetric displays. It is distinguished from sibling methods like Four-Channel Scanner Convergence Correction by focusing on the intrinsic beam shaping at the modulator stage rather than the geometric alignment of multiple scanner channels. The Four-Quadrant Helix Optical Layout is an optical system design that distributes four scanner channels across four quadrants of the helix volume, enabling up to 10,000 green and 10,000 red voxels per quadrant, plus 10,000 blue voxels in one quadrant. It differs from the single-quadrant design by making full use of the entire helix volume and improving viewability. Steps: Combine red, green, and blue channels using standard dichroic mirrors before projection. Parameters: Green lasers are diode-pumped Nd:YAG (532 nm), 100 mW each (one pair for channels A/B, another for C/D). Red lasers are helium-neon (20 mW each), one per channel. Blue laser is argon ion (water-cooled). Layout: Projection optics consist of three lenses in series: Lens 1 (300 mm focal length) and Lens 3 (120 mm) provide rough expansion and focusing; Lens 2 (200 mm) acts as an intermediate relay/focusing element. Time Complexity: The system operates at a fixed refresh rate of 20 Hz. The access time per deflection is 5 \musec, allowing for a time-bandwidth product of 250. Memory/Storage: Not given in the sources. Measured Performance: The system supports 40,000 voxels per color at 20 Hz refresh rate. Scaling: Scaling is achieved by coupling multiple scanners in parallel. A four-channel system was built, doubling the voxel count compared to a 2k single-channel system by reducing beam diameter. Strengths: Increases total voxel count without intensity drop-off. Reduces throw distance via angular magnification. Uses efficient laser sources in later variants. Limitations: Requires complex optical alignment. Limited by acoustic wave travel time (access time). Requires beam blanking. When to use: When high voxel count and uniform intensity are required in a volumetric display. When not to use: When simplicity of optical alignment is prioritized over voxel count. The method originated with NEOS Technologies, Inc., of Melbourne, Florida, which built a four-channel 4k voxel system. It was developed as a "Second Generation" improvement to address the bottleneck of finite acoustic wave travel time in random-access scanning. The design was further improved in 1997 to distribute channels across four quadrants of the helix volume, replacing argon ion lasers with diode-pumped Nd:YAG and helium-neon lasers for green and red channels, respectively. name: Four-Channel Scanner Convergence Correction
head: Acousto-Optic Scanner Convergence Correction
body: Four-Channel Scanner Convergence Correction is a geometric alignment method for four-channel acousto-optic holographic displays, ensuring that four scanned laser beams (organized as two pyramidal sources) intersect uniformly throughout the volumetric display space. It solves the problem of beam separation caused by the physical offset of output lenses, which would otherwise cause the beams to intersect at only a single point rather than throughout the entire volume. The method applies linear spatial offsets to the scan coordinates of channels A, B, C, and D to force uniform overlap. Inputs and Outputs Inputs: Scan coordinates for four channels (A, B, C, D) and helix volume geometry. Outputs: Corrected scan deflection angles or pixel addresses for each channel to ensure uniform beam overlap. Data Structures The method operates on normalized scan position variables. Let x be the horizontal scan coordinate (0 to 1, normalized from scan start to end) and y be the vertical helix axis coordinate (0 to 1, normalized from bottom to top). Channels are grouped as {A, B} and {C, D}. Steps 1. X-Axis Correction (Primary): Apply a linear correction across the scan direction to counteract the ~10 mm separation of the pyramidal sources at the helix base. For channels C and D, the correction offset \Delta x is 0 mm at the scan start (x=0) and increases linearly to 10 mm at the scan end (x=1). For channels A and B, the correction offset \Delta x is 10 mm at the scan start (x=0) and decreases linearly to 0 mm at the scan end (x=1). 2. Y-Axis Correction (Secondary): Apply a linear correction along the helix axis (y) to match the intersection point of the pyramidal sources. The correction varies linearly from the bottom (y=0) to the top (y=1). 3. Vertical Line Constraint: If perfectly vertical display lines are required, a slight non-zero correction must be applied even at the beginning of each scan, and both A/B and C/D channels must be corrected in the y-direction. Formulas Formula for C/D: \Delta x{C/D}(x) = 10 \cdot x mm Formula for A/B: \Delta x{A/B}(x) = 10 \cdot (1 - x) mm Formula for Y-axis: \Delta y(y) = k \cdot y mm, where k scales the linear variation from bottom to top. Pseudocode Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def computeconvergenceoffsets(scanx, scany, channelgroup, intersectiontarget='top'): # scanx: float in [0, 1], normalized from scan start to end # scany: float in [0, 1], normalized from bottom to top # channelgroup: 'AB' or 'CD' # intersectiontarget: 'top' or 'bottom' # X-axis correction: linear across scan direction if channelgroup == 'CD': dx = 10.0 scanx # 0 mm at start, 10 mm at end else: # AB dx = 10.0 (1.0 - scanx) # 10 mm at start, 0 mm at end # Y-axis correction: linear along helix axis to match intersection point # Scale factor k not given in sources; apply linear interpolation dy = 10.0 scany # Reverse correction direction if pyramids intersect at bottom if intersectiontarget == 'bottom': dx = -dx dy = -dy return dx, dy Parameters Beam Separation: ~10 mm at the bottom of the helix. Helix Height: 36 inches (3600 mm). Correction Range: 0 to 10 mm for X-axis. Edge Cases and Pitfalls Y-Axis Ignorance: The Y-axis convergence error is barely detectable and can be ignored for general use, simplifying implementation to X-axis correction only. Vertical Lines: If vertical lines are mandatory, ignoring Y-axis correction results in slanted lines. Intersection Point: The correction profile reverses direction if the pyramids are designed to intersect at the bottom of the helix instead of the top. Optical and software correction technique to align red, green, and blue scan beams that diverge due to wavelength-dependent acousto-optic deflection. AO deflection is proportional to wavelength, causing the red scanner to have a wider scan angle than green, which is wider than blue. To correct this, telephoto projection lenses are used to continuously adjust angular magnification, achieving rough alignment of the red, green, and blue scan angles. Software-based minor corrections are then applied to fine-tune color registration. A key pitfall is relying solely on software correction, which causes the red channel to have lower resolution than the blue channel due to the wider red scan angle mapping to the same pixel grid. Complexity: Low, because the correction relies on linear interpolation across scan coordinates. Performance: Effectively corrects the primary geometric distortion (X-axis) while Y-axis errors remain negligible for general viewing. Limitations: Does not address chromatic aberration without additional optical hardware like telephoto lenses. When to use: When operating a four-channel AO holographic display in a helical volume configuration. When not to use: When single-channel or two-channel operation is used, or when color registration is the primary concern without optical correction hardware. This method originates from the development of the Second-Generation 3-D Volumetric Display System, specifically the "big helix" optical system implemented around 1997. The system distributes four channels (two red, two green) into the four quadrants of the helix volume to increase voxel count, providing up to 10,000 green and 10,000 red voxels per quadrant. The convergence problem was identified as one of the most challenging aspects of the immediate future for this design due to the physical separation of output lenses creating non-intersecting pyramidal sources. name: Acousto-Optic Modulator R-Factor Analysis
head: AOM Eccentricity Calculation, Beam Spread Ratio Analysis
body: This method evaluates the performance of an Acousto-Optic Modulator (AOM) by calculating the R-factor, defined as the ratio of the acoustical beam spread to the optical beam spread. It determines the output beam eccentricity (ellipticity) to ensure optimal diffraction efficiency and beam quality in scanned volumetric displays. It focuses on intrinsic beam shaping at the modulator stage rather than geometric alignment of multiple scanner channels. Inputs and Outputs Inputs: Optical beam radius (\omega0), acoustic center frequency (fa), acoustic velocity (V), refractive index (n), and acoustic wavelength (\lambdaa). Outputs: R-factor (R), beam eccentricity (e), and beam diameter ratio (dx/dy). Data Structures No persistent data structures are required. The method is a direct calculation based on physical constants and input beam parameters. Parameters and Constants Typical values for TeO2 modulators used in NEOS scanners: Refractive index (n): 2.26. Acoustic velocity (V): 4.2 mm/\mus. Transducer width (L): 0.67 mm. Acoustic center frequencies (fa): 440 MHz or 260 MHz. Acoustic wavelengths (\lambdaa): 442 nm, 514 nm, or 647 nm. Formulas The R-factor is calculated as: R = \frac{\lambdaa fa}{n V \omega0} Where: \lambdaa is the acoustic wavelength. fa is the acoustic center frequency. n is the refractive index. V is the acoustic velocity. \omega0 is the optical beam radius (waist). For the specific case of a 440-MHz modulator with 514-nm light, this simplifies to: R = 0.0983 \omega0 Note: In this simplified equation, \omega0 must be in microns to yield a dimensionless R-factor. Eccentricity Relationship The eccentricity e is a function of R. Optimal R-factor range: 1.5 to 2.0. Corresponding optimal eccentricity: 0.90 to 0.95. An eccentricity of 1.0 (perfect circle) implies R \approx 6.0, which is impractical as it requires decreasing fa or increasing \omega0 by 3-4x, causing bandwidth loss. Pseudocode Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def calculateaomrfactor(omega0microns, famhz, lambdaanm, n=2.26, Vmmus=4.2): """Calculate the R-factor from physical parameters.""" # Convert to SI units for consistency omega0m = omega0microns 1e-6 fahz = famhz 1e6 lambdaam = lambdaanm 1e-9 Vms = Vmmus 1e3 # R = (lambdaa fa) / (n V omega0) return (lambdaam fahz) / (n Vms omega0m) def analyzebeamquality(omega0microns, famhz, lambdaanm): R = calculateaomrfactor(omega0microns, famhz, lambdaanm) # Eccentricity is obtained from empirical graphs (Figure 1-21 in) # The sources do not provide a closed-form formula for eccentricity. # eccentricity = lookupeccentricity(R) return {"Rfactor": R} Edge Cases and Pitfalls 1. Beam Overfilling: If the input beam diameter exceeds 80 microns for 440-MHz AOMs, it overfills the acoustic beam, causing a vertical aperturing effect and elliptical output. 2. Low R-Factor: A very low R-factor (e.g., R=0.5) results in high eccentricity (e.g., 0.5), meaning a highly elliptical beam. 3. High R-Factor: An eccentricity of 1.0 implies R \approx 6.0. Achieving this requires either decreasing the center frequency or increasing the spot size by 3-4x, which is impractical due to bandwidth loss. 4. Divergence Mismatch: Ideal spot sizes for red scanners (e.g., 45 microns for 440-MHz) do not diverge rapidly enough to reach the required 3.2 mm beam diameter at the X-Y deflectors. This necessitates longer focal length lenses and a 5-10 inch longer scanner body. Corrects geometric alignment errors between multiple scanner channels. Choose this when beam shape is correct but spatial registration is off. Link: Four-Channel Scanner Convergence Correction. Time Complexity: O(1) for calculation. Memory Complexity: O(1). Performance: The method relies on empirical graphs for eccentricity, so precision depends on the resolution of the source figures. Strengths: Provides a direct metric (R-factor) to optimize beam quality and bandwidth. Limitations: Does not account for lens aberrations or mechanical misalignments. Requires precise knowledge of the beam waist at the modulator. When to use: During the design phase of the AOM selection and laser coupling optics. When not to use: When diagnosing spatial artifacts in the final displayed volume (use convergence correction instead). This analysis originates from the design of the NEOS Second-Generation 3-D Volumetric Display System. It is based on the paper "Design Procedure for Wide Bandwidth Acousto-Optic Modulator". The method was developed to optimize the trade-off between beam eccentricity and bandwidth for argon-ion and diode-pumped lasers in holographic displays. name: Holographic Computer-Generated Holography (CGH) Calculation
body: Holographic Computer-Generated Holography (CGH) Calculation is the computational process of synthesizing a hologram fringe pattern (complex amplitude or phase distribution) from 3D scene data, such as voxels, point clouds, or meshes, for display on a Spatial Light Modulator (SLM) or holographic screen. It solves the problem of generating the precise optical wavefront required to reconstruct a 3D image in free space or on a display plane, overcoming the limitations of traditional intensity-based volume rendering which lacks depth cues and parallax. The core mechanism of CGH calculation is the superposition of wavefields originating from scene elements (voxels, points, or primitives) onto a hologram plane. The general mathematical model involves calculating the complex amplitude Uh(x,y) at each pixel (x,y) of the hologram plane by summing the contributions of all M scene elements i: Uh(x,y) = \sum{i=1}^{M} Ai \exp\left(i \phii(x,y)\right) where Ai is the amplitude and \phii(x,y) is the phase of the wavefront from element i arriving at the hologram pixel. The phase typically depends on the distance ri from the element to the hologram pixel: \phii(x,y) = k ri + \phi{0,i} where k = 2\pi/\lambda is the wavenumber and \phi{0,i} is the initial phase of the source element. The final output is often quantized to phase values 0 to 2\pi for phase-only SLMs. Key shared constraints include: 1. Wavelength Dependence: Calculations must account for the specific wavelength \lambda of the reconstruction light source, affecting the wavenumber k and diffraction angles. 2. Computational Complexity: The naive calculation scales with the number of scene elements and hologram pixels, making it extremely expensive for high-resolution holograms and large scenes. Generates CGHs for 3D volume data by treating voxels as transparent objects with diffuse reflection properties. Unlike Maximum Intensity Projection (MIP) methods, it simulates light propagation, attenuation, and diffuse reflection to generate clear holograms for transparent and multi-layer objects. It serves as an alternative to polygon-based methods, offering superior detail for volumetric data at the cost of significantly higher computational complexity. Calculates CGHs by avoiding direct optical interference simulation. It treats the holographic fringe as a signal subsampled spatially into "hogels" and spectrally into "hogel vectors". By leveraging standard 3D computer graphics rendering techniques (orthographic projections), it increases computation speed and achieves bandwidth compression compared to conventional interference-based methods. It is distinguished by its explicit decomposition of the wavefield into hogel vectors and reliance on texture-mapping hardware for decoding. Composed of a series of discrete 2D perspective views of an object scene. It produces a view-dependent image presenting the corresponding perspective view in each horizontally displaced direction, functioning similarly to lenticular or parallax barrier displays. Unlike full-parallax holograms, it restricts vertical parallax, significantly reducing computational complexity compared to direct wavefront simulation. A volumetric display system that generates a 360° horizontal field of view with multiple distinct viewpoints by synchronizing a high-speed projector with a rotating holographic defuser. It solves the occlusion limitation of simple diffusing displays by restricting the reflection angle of the defuser, allowing viewers at different horizontal positions to see different images. Unlike sibling methods that rely on mechanical scanning screens or static parallax barriers, this method uses the angular selectivity of a holographic element to spatially multiplex viewpoints in free space. Generates CGHs by iteratively optimizing the phase profile of a spatial light modulator (SLM) to produce a desired intensity distribution in the reconstruction plane, typically a uniform array of focal spots for volumetric display. It solves the problem of driving phase-only hardware with complex-valued light fields derived from volumetric rendering by discarding amplitude information and encoding required phase variations through iterative optimization. Unlike direct diffraction calculations, this method uses an optimization loop to converge the reconstructed intensity to a target intensity, allowing for precise control over lateral and axial focusing positions. Designs holographic structures that convert N mutually incoherent transverse input modes into N target modes with a one-to-one mapping. It solves the problem of optimizing the refractive index distribution within a 3D volume to achieve specific mode conversion efficiencies. Unlike direct forward calculation methods, this algorithm uses an iterative approach to select voxel distributions that maximize the overlap between propagated fields and target modes. It is distinguished by its reliance on a split-step Fourier Beam Propagation Method (BPM) and a local multi-objective criterion to select from a discrete set of pre-defined transverse voxel profiles. Generates CGHs for point clouds by distributing the calculation across multiple parallel wavefront recording planes (WRPs) to handle occlusion and reduce computational load, specifically adapted for Horizontal Parallax Only (HPO) displays. It differs from full-parallax WRP methods by computing point contributions to 1D hololines rather than the full 2D plane, and from naive point-source summation by using pre-computed look-up tables (LUTs) and band-limited angular spectrum propagation to manage the high spatial bandwidth product required for wide viewing angles. Calculates CGHs by decomposing a 3D scene into discrete parallel depth layers and computing the hologram plane wavefield as the superposition of contributions from each layer. It differs from point-based methods by processing spatially coherent planar slices rather than individual voxels, and from full volume rendering approaches by restricting propagation to a fixed set of discrete depths. This method is particularly suited for real-time embedded systems and AR applications with isolated models, though it introduces visible separation artifacts in scenes with continuous depth ranges. Computes the complex wavefield at a specific depth plane from a recorded hologram matrix, effectively "refocusing" the light to visualize the 3D scene. It distinguishes itself from sibling methods by operating in the frequency domain (ASM) or using quadratic phase approximations (Fresnel) to propagate the field, rather than summing individual voxel contributions. Generates holograms by discretizing a 3D scene into a set of points, treating each as a light-emitting primitive, and summing their individual wavefield contributions onto the hologram plane. It is distinguished by its direct geometric summation of point sources, offering simplicity and the ability to process real-world scanned data, but suffers from high computational costs for large scenes compared to convolution-based or layer-based approaches. Definition: Calculates computer-generated holograms by simulating ray paths to remove hidden surfaces and render realistic material properties. Steps: Cast rays from every elementary hologram into virtual objects. Determine the traveling paths of the rays. Consider intersection with objects, absorption, reflection, and refraction during path calculation. Express multiple reflections and refractions by casting additional rays into the reflection and transmission directions. Calculate the length of the light path for each ray. Apply the Phong reflection model and Cook–Torrance reflection model to express material quality. Pitfall: Hidden surfaces must be explicitly removed to avoid incorrect holographic fringe generation. Definition: Reduces reconstruction error and blur in holographic stereograms by assigning reference planes to different depth segments of a 3D scene. Steps: Divide the 3D scene into several parts along its depth direction. Set a reference plane for each of the object parts. Resynthesize all effectively synthetic perspective images referred to their own reference planes of the object parts. Generate the finally effectively synthetic perspective image exposed to one holographic elemental by only once exposure. Pitfall: Traditional EPISM causes distortion and blur for object points located far away from the reference plane. Definition: Production of full-color holographic images by computing three separate fringes for additive primary colors (red, green, blue) accounting for different wavelengths, and modulating three separate laser beams. Steps: 1. Compute three separate fringes, one for each additive primary color (red, green, blue), considering their specific wavelengths. 2. Use each fringe to modulate a separate beam of light corresponding to that primary color. Definition: A technique to measure the complex light field (amplitude and phase) at the output facet of a CGVH by interfering the signal with a tilted reference wave, allowing characterization of mode sorting quality. Steps: Tilt the reference wave such that interference fringes have a period of about 3 pixels. Capture the intensity image (interferogram). Compute the Fast Fourier Transform (FFT) of the intensity image. Crop a 60x60 pixel region around one sideband in the frequency domain. Compute the inverse FFT of the cropped sideband to obtain the complex field. Apply corrections using a Nelder-Mead optimizer to maximize the overlap integral between the measured field (at 0° AOI) and the target mode (e.g., HG1,1). The seven optimized parameters are then used to correct all experimentally recorded fields. Pitfall: The retrieved field may show poor overlap with target modes due to: 1) imperfect centering on the pixel grid, 2) small geometric rotation in experimental images, 3) global phase tilt and defocus, and 4) slight differences in mode waist compared to simulation. Steps: The apodized aperture is zero-padded to the size of the full hologram to represent the hologram from that specific viewing position. It is then back-propagated using BL-ASM to reconstruct the hologram for the corresponding view. To visualize the reconstructed object, the magnitude (square root of the intensity) of the complex wavefield computed by the back propagation is extracted. This magnitude matches the gamma curves for displays and is stored as a 2D image. Definition: A method to construct a target wave field for multiple viewpoints by coherently superposing wave fields of all viewpoints, where each viewpoint's wave field is encoded with a blazed grating corresponding to its viewing angle. Steps: Encode the propagation characteristics of the target wave field into the phase via blazed gratings for each viewpoint's viewing angles. Apply a filtering mechanism (iris) at the Fourier plane to the target spectrum, which acts as a mask allowing only waves corresponding to specific angles to traverse, enabling recording of the wavefront from a particular viewpoint. Formula: u{\text{target}}(x, y) = \sum{i=1}^{n} ui(x, y) u{\thetai, \etai}(x, y), where u{\thetai, \etai}(x, y) represents the blazed grating for view angles of \thetai, \etai, and ui(x, y) is the wave field for the ith viewpoint. Definition: A method to encode a phase pattern (hologram) as a binary amplitude hologram, allowing the use of a Digital Micromirror Device (DMD) as a fast phase modulator. Steps: Encode the phase pattern of the tiled hologram into a binary amplitude pattern suitable for the DMD. Definition: A method exploiting an intermediate light-ray sampling (RS) plane between the scene and hologram plane. The light field is sampled in the RS plane, Fourier-transformed, and the resulting wavefront is propagated to the hologram plane to simulate the object wave. Steps: 1. Sample the light field in the RS plane (often as images from different perspectives). 2. Fourier-transform these images. 3. Propagate the wavefront to the hologram plane. 4. Interfere the object wave with a reference wave. 5. Record the interference in the hologram plane. Pitfall: Computational cost can be high for high-resolution holograms. Speed-up solutions include using multiple GPUs or tile segmentation of the hologram. Comparison: Can be applied to both synthetic and real scenes (via camera arrays). Reflections and occlusion effects are easily taken into account. Definition: A method where the scene is composed of 2D surfaces, each considered a light-emitter whose contribution is propagated to the hologram plane; the final hologram is the sum of all surface contributions. Pitfall: When scene complexity is high, a large number of polygons are present, requiring advanced techniques to speed up calculations. Additionally, hidden-surface removal can be very computationally intensive. Comparison: Typically less computationally expensive than point-cloud synthesis because the number of polygons needed to approximate a scene is lower than the number of points in a point-cloud representation. The concept of Computer-Generated Holography (CGH) originated from the work of Emmett N. Leith and Juris Upatnieks in 1962, who described the process of constructing holograms from a communication-theory viewpoint, involving modulation and diffraction operations. Early CGH methods focused on point-source models and interference-based calculations. Over time, the field has expanded to include various computational strategies to handle the immense computational load of full-parallax holography. Recent developments include the use of ray-tracing for realistic material rendering, hogel-vector approaches for compression, and iterative optimization algorithms like ORA for phase-only SLMs. The integration of CGH with volumetric displays has led to techniques like scanned AOM displays for large-scale holographic fringes and voxel-based inverse design for mode conversion in glass. name: Volume Rendering based CGH Calculation
head: Direct volume rendering method for holograms, Approximate Volume Rendering Based CGH Calculation, Approximate Volume Rendering Based CGH Calculation with Elemental Holograms, Approximate volume rendering based CGH calculation method with elemental holograms
body: Volume Rendering based CGH Calculation generates Computer-Generated Holograms (CGH) for 3D volume data by treating voxels as transparent objects with diffuse reflection properties. Unlike Maximum Intensity Projection (MIP) methods which only display objects with maximum voxel values, this approach simulates light propagation from a source to the voxel, diffuse reflection at the voxel, and propagation from the voxel to the viewpoint, allowing for the generation of clear holograms for transparent and multi-layer objects. It serves as an alternative to polygon-based methods, offering superior detail for volumetric data at the cost of significantly higher computational complexity. The method calculates the complex amplitude at the hologram plane by summing contributions from all voxels, modeled as point light sources after rendering. The process involves initializing voxel properties, simulating light transport with attenuation and diffuse reflection, and finally computing the holographic interference pattern. Inputs: Volume data grid of size M \times M \times M (or general dimensions), where each voxel i has a scalar value Ii. Color map and Alpha (\alpha) map definitions. Light source position and intensity I{d0}. Viewpoint position (for the standard method) or Elemental Hologram grid parameters (for the approximate method). Wavelength \lambda and wavenumber k = 2\pi/\lambda. Outputs: Complex amplitude distribution \mu(\xi, \eta) for each pixel (\xi, \eta) on the hologram plane. Voxel Array: Stores R, G, B, \alpha for each voxel. Hologram Plane: 2D grid of complex numbers. Elemental Holograms (Approximate Method): A subset of the hologram plane, where each elemental hologram is represented by its center pixel for propagation calculations. 1. Initialize Color and Opacity: For each voxel x with value Ix, calculate its color components Cx (where C \in \{R, G, B, \alpha\}) using linear interpolation on the provided maps: Cx = C3 - (C3 - C2) \frac{I3 - Ix}{I3 - I2} where C2, C3 are known parameters of the color/alpha map at endpoints with voxel values I2, I3. 2. Light Propagation to Voxel (Attenuation): For a voxel eli, calculate the incident light intensity I{di} from the light source. Light attenuates as it passes through preceding voxels j along the path: I{di} = I{d0} \prod{j=0} (1 - \alphaj) where I{d0} is the source intensity and \alphaj is the opacity of voxel j. 3. Diffuse Reflection Calculation: Calculate the reflected light intensity I{ri} using the Lambertian reflection model: I{ri} = k{di} I{di} \max(0, \mathbf{L} \cdot \mathbf{N}) where: k{di} is the ratio of Lambert light. \mathbf{L} is the unit vector pointing from the voxel to the light source. \mathbf{N} is the normal unit vector, derived from the gradient of the \alpha map in x, y, z directions. 4. Light Propagation to Viewpoint (Attenuation): Calculate the final reflected light intensity I{rLi} reaching the viewpoint from voxel eli. Light attenuates through subsequent voxels j between the voxel and the viewpoint: I{rLi} = I{ri} \prod{j=i+1} (1 - \alphaj) Note: I{di} and I{ri} are independent of the viewpoint direction, but I{rLi} must be recalculated for each viewpoint. 5. CGH Calculation (Point Light Source Method): Treat each voxel as a point light source. The complex amplitude \mui(\xi, \eta) contributed by voxel i at hologram pixel (\xi, \eta) is: \mui(\xi, \eta) = \frac{\sqrt{I{rLi}}}{ri} \exp\left(-j(k ri + \phii)\right) where ri is the distance from voxel i to the hologram pixel, and \phii is the initial phase. The total complex amplitude Uh(\xi, \eta) is the superposition of all voxels: Uh(\xi, \eta) = \sum{i=1}^{M} \mui(\xi, \eta) 6. Approximate Calculation with Elemental Holograms (Optional Optimization): To reduce computation, divide the hologram plane into Ne elemental holograms. For each elemental hologram k, use only the center pixel to represent the entire elemental hologram for the final light propagation calculation. The amplitude for elemental hologram k is I{ek{rLi}}. The complexity is reduced from O(M^2 N) to O(M^2 Ne) for the propagation step. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math import cmath def volumerenderingcgh(volumedata, colormap, alphamap, lightsourcepos, viewpointpos, wavelength, hologramplane): """ Calculate CGH using Volume Rendering based method. Args: volumedata: 3D array of voxel values I. colormap: function(I) -> (R, G, B) alphamap: function(I) -> alpha lightsourcepos: 3D vector (Lx, Ly, Lz) viewpointpos: 3D vector (Vx, Vy, Vz) wavelength: float, lambda hologramplane: 2D array of complex numbers, shape (H, W) Returns: hologramplane: Complex amplitude distribution. """ k = 2.0 math.pi / wavelength Mx, My, Mz = volumedata.shape voxellist = [] # Pre-calculate voxel properties and positions for iz in range(Mz): for iy in range(My): for ix in range(Mx): val = volumedata[iz, iy, ix] R, G, B = colormap(val) alpha = alphamap(val) pos = (ix, iy, iz) voxellist.append({'pos': pos, 'R': R, 'G': G, 'B': B, 'alpha': alpha, 'val': val}) # Step 2-4: Light Transport for each voxel voxelcontributions = [] for v in voxellist: pos = v['pos'] alpha = v['alpha'] # Step 2: Light Propagation to Voxel (Attenuation) Idi = raymarchattenuation(lightsourcepos, pos, volumedata, alphamap) Idi = 1.0 # Scaled by Id0 (assumed normalized to 1.0 in this implementation) # Step 3: Diffuse Reflection N = computealphagradient(pos, volumedata, alphamap) L = normalize(subtract(lightsourcepos, pos)) kdi = 1.0 dotval = max(0.0, dot(L, N)) Iri = kdi Idi dotval # Step 4: Light Propagation to Viewpoint (Attenuation) IrLi = Iri raymarchattenuation(pos, viewpointpos, volumedata, alphamap) voxelcontributions.append({'pos': pos, 'intensity': IrLi}) # Step 5: CGH Calculation H, W = hologramplane.shape for y in range(H): for x in range(W): pixelpos = (x, y, 0.0) totalamplitude = complex(0.0, 0.0) for vc in voxelcontributions: vpos = vc['pos'] IrLi = vc['intensity'] ri = distance(vpos, pixelpos) phii = 0.0 phase = k ri + phii amplitude = math.sqrt(IrLi) / ri complexcontrib = amplitude cmath.exp(-1j phase) totalamplitude += complexcontrib hologramplane[y, x] = totalamplitude return hologramplane def subtract(a, b): return (a[0]-b[0], a[1]-b[1], a[2]-b[2]) def add(a, b): return (a[0]+b[0], a[1]+b[1], a[2]+b[2]) def dot(a, b): return a[0]b[0] + a[1]b[1] + a[2]b[2] def normalize(v): mag = math.sqrt(dot(v, v)) return (v[0]/mag, v[1]/mag, v[2]/mag) if mag > 0 else (0.0, 0.0, 0.0) def distance(a, b): return math.sqrt(dot(subtract(a, b), subtract(a, b))) def scale(v, s): return (v[0]s, v[1]s, v[2]s) def computealphagradient(pos, volumedata, alphamap): ix, iy, iz = pos Mx, My, Mz = volumedata.shape dx = alphamap(volumedata[min(ix+1, Mx-1), iy, iz]) - alphamap(volumedata[max(ix-1, 0), iy, iz]) dy = alphamap(volumedata[ix, min(iy+1, My-1), iz]) - alphamap(volumedata[ix, max(iy-1, 0), iz]) dz = alphamap(volumedata[ix, iy, min(iz+1, Mz-1)]) - alphamap(volumedata[ix, iy, max(iz-1, 0)]) return normalize((dx, dy, dz)) def raymarchattenuation(start, end, volumedata, alphamap): steps = max(abs(end[i]-start[i]) for i in range(3)) 10 if steps == 0: return 1.0 attenuation = 1.0 for t in range(steps + 1): frac = t / steps curr = add(start, scale(subtract(end, start), frac)) ix, iy, iz = int(curr[0]), int(curr[1]), int(curr[2]) if 0 <= ix < volumedata.shape[0] and 0 <= iy < volumedata.shape[1] and 0 <= iz < volumedata.shape[2]: alpha = alphamap(volumedata[ix, iy, iz]) attenuation = (1.0 - alpha) return attenuation Wavelength (\lambda): Determines the wavenumber k. Color/Alpha Maps: Define the mapping from voxel intensity to RGB and opacity. Number of Viewpoints (n): The method calculates intensity for each voxel and each viewpoint. Number of Elemental Holograms (Ne): Used in the approximate method. If Ne is small relative to N, calculation time is greatly shortened. Computational Complexity: The calculation amount is very large, making the method computationally expensive compared to polygon-based or MIP-based methods. Precision: Attenuation products \prod (1-\alphaj) can underflow if many semi-transparent voxels are traversed. Boundary Conditions: Ray marching must handle voxels outside the volume grid gracefully. A layered rendering method for generating computer-generated holograms (CGH) of 3D objects that uses view volume transformation to avoid shape distortion and size deviation in the reconstructed image, preserving the real size of the original model. Unlike conventional layer-based methods where sampling pitch in Fresnel diffraction is proportional to reconstruction distance (causing inconsistent sizes), this method preserves the real size of the original model. A calculating method that generates a 3D hologram by encoding 2D projection images of an object captured from multiple angles. Method 1 adds inclination factors to each 2D projection image, conducts an integral calculation, uses the integrals as pixel values for corresponding points in the projection image, and combines pixel values to form the hologram. Method 2 transforms 2D projection images into 2D spectral matrices via Fourier transform, combines all 2D matrices into a 3D matrix, extracts a 2D matrix indicating 3D characteristics by analyzing the functional expression of the optical field distribution, and encodes the 2D matrix to obtain the hologram. Time Complexity: Incident light calculation: O(M^2). Reflected light calculation: O(M). Final light propagation: O(M^2 \cdot Ne) for the approximate method with elemental holograms, or O(M^2 \cdot N) for the standard method. Total CGH calculation complexity: O(M^2 \cdot N). Memory Complexity: Proportional to the number of voxels M and hologram pixels N. Measured Performance: In experiments, the proposed method took 24.3 hours for rendering and 3.8 minutes for CGH calculation, compared to 1.5 hours/0.3 seconds for polygon-based and 0.2 hours/0.6 seconds for MIP-based methods. The approximate method with elemental holograms reduced rendering time to 3.6 hours and CGH calculation to 3.7 minutes. Strengths: Generates clear holograms for transparent and multi-layer objects; better detail than polygon-based methods. Limitations: Extremely high computational cost; requires special lighting conditions for reconstruction (point monochrome light source at a specific angle). Holography is a form of lensless photography based on the recording of amplitude and phase of light illuminating an object. Computed holograms are created by calculating the interference pattern and recording it on film. However, output devices often cannot transfer the pattern to film at the required resolution, and fully computed holograms are difficult and expensive to record. This method was proposed to address the limitations of MIP-based methods, which only show objects with maximum voxel values, by applying direct volume rendering with transparency and diffuse reflection.
