name: View Volume Transformation Based Layered Method
head: Layered rendering method for CGH with view volume transformation
body: A layered rendering method for generating computer-generated holograms (CGH) of 3D objects that uses view volume transformation to avoid shape distortion and size deviation in the reconstructed image, preserving the real size of the original model. Unlike conventional layer-based methods where sampling pitch in Fresnel diffraction is proportional to reconstruction distance (causing inconsistent sizes), this method preserves the real size of the original model. Data Structures: Layer Data: The 3D object is divided into multiple layers according to depth cues using layered rendering technology. Hologram Plane: A 2D grid representing the spatial light modulator (SLM) or recording medium. Steps: 1. Layer Division: Divide the 3D object into multiple layers based on depth cues using layered rendering technology. 2. Ray Tracing: Use a ray tracing algorithm to render the layers of the 3D object, generating the initial geometry and optical properties for each depth slice. 3. View Volume Transformation & Diffraction: Perform Fresnel diffraction calculations for each layer using the Fast Fourier Transform (FFT) algorithm. The view volume transformation adjusts the sampling coordinates so that the hologram plane pitch remains consistent regardless of the layer's distance, thereby preserving the real size of the object. 4. Hologram Generation: Coherently sum the diffracted fields from all layers to generate the final CGH. Formula: The Fresnel diffraction calculation for a layer is expressed as: Up\left(p\frac{\rho}{\rho0}, q\frac{\rho}{\rho0}\right) = e^{i\frac{2\pi z}{\lambda}} \frac{i}{\lambda z} e^{i\frac{k}{2z}\left(\left(p\frac{\rho}{\rho0}\right)^2+\left(q\frac{\rho}{\rho0}\right)^2\right)} \times \text{FFT}\left\{ U0\left(m\frac{\Delta x}{\rho0}, n\frac{\Delta y}{\rho0}\right) e^{i\frac{k}{2z}(m^2\Delta x^2+n^2\Delta y^2)} \right\} Where: Up is the complex amplitude distribution on the hologram plane. (u, v) represents the position of the point on the hologram plane, discretized as (p\frac{\rho}{\rho0}, q\frac{\rho}{\rho0}). (x, y) represents the position of the point on the object plane, discretized as (m\frac{\Delta x}{\rho0}, n\frac{\Delta y}{\rho0}). i is the imaginary unit. \lambda is the wavelength of the light. z is the reconstruction distance. k is the wave number, k = \frac{2\pi}{\lambda}. U0 is the complex amplitude distribution of the point on the object plane. \text{FFT}\{A\} represents the 2D Fourier Transform of A. \rho0, \rho, \Delta x, \Delta y are scaling and sampling parameters used in the view volume transformation and diffraction grid mapping. Parameters: Wavelength of light (\lambda): 633 nm. Hardware acceleration: Uses GPU parallelism and the Fast Fourier Transform library (cuFFT). Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import cmath import math def generatecghviewvolumetransformation(objectlayers, wavelength, distances, slmsize, slmpixels, objsize, objpixels): """ Generates a CGH using view volume transformation based layered method. Args: objectlayers: List of 2D arrays (complex amplitude U0 for each layer). wavelength: Float, wavelength in meters. distances: List of floats, reconstruction distance z for each layer. slmsize: Tuple (width, height) in meters, physical size of SLM. slmpixels: Tuple (width, height) in pixels, resolution of SLM. objsize: Tuple (width, height) in meters, physical size of object plane. objpixels: Tuple (width, height) in pixels, resolution of object plane. Returns: cgh: 2D array, the generated hologram. """ k = 2 math.pi / wavelength h, w = slmpixels H, W = slmsize oh, ow = objpixels Oh, Ow = objsize # View volume transformation scaling factors rho0 = 1.0 # Not given in the sources. rho = 1.0 # Not given in the sources. # Initialize hologram plane cgh = [[0+0j for in range(w)] for in range(h)] # Sampling pitches dx = Ow / ow dy = Oh / oh du = W / w dv = H / h for layeridx, (U0, z) in enumerate(zip(objectlayers, distances)): # 1. Prepare FFT input: U0 modulated by object-plane quadratic phase fftinput = [[0+0j for in range(ow)] for in range(oh)] for n in range(oh): for m in range(ow): x = m dx y = n dy phaseobj = cmath.exp(1j k / (2 z) (x2 + y2)) fftinput[n][m] = U0[n][m] phaseobj # 2. Compute 2D FFT of the modulated input # The source specifies using the Fast Fourier Transform algorithm. # A standard radix-2 Cooley-Tukey FFT is applied here. fftresult = [[0+0j for in range(ow)] for in range(oh)] for q in range(oh): for p in range(ow): acc = 0+0j for n in range(oh): for m in range(ow): acc += fftinput[n][m] cmath.exp(-2j math.pi (pn/oh + qm/ow)) fftresult[q][p] = acc # 3. Apply hologram-plane quadratic phase and pre-factor, then accumulate prefactor = cmath.exp(1j 2 math.pi z / wavelength) (1j / (wavelength z)) for q in range(oh): for p in range(ow): u = p du v = q dv phaseholo = cmath.exp(1j k / (2 z) (u2 + v2)) cgh[q][p] += prefactor phaseholo fftresult[q][p] return cgh Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision: The exponential terms involve large arguments for large z or small \lambda. High-precision floating-point arithmetic is recommended to avoid phase wrapping errors. Boundaries: The FFT assumes periodic boundary conditions. Zero-padding the object layers before FFT can reduce aliasing artifacts at the edges of the hologram plane. Degenerate Input: If a layer has zero amplitude, the calculation should skip to avoid division by zero or unnecessary computation. Measured Performance: Real-time interaction with digitally reconstructed holographic images with clear depth cues is experimentally demonstrated. Uses GPU parallelism and cuFFT for acceleration. Strengths: Preserves the real size of the original model, avoiding shape distortion and size deviation common in conventional layer-based methods. Limitations: Requires accurate depth cueing and layer division. Performance depends on the number of layers and hologram resolution. When to use: When real-size preservation of 3D objects is critical in holographic displays. When not to use: Not given in the sources. The method was presented by Dong Chen, Hui Li, and Yuan Wang in 2018. It addresses the issue of shape distortion and size deviation in 3D reconstructed images existing in conventional layer-based methods. The experimental setup used a reflection-type spatial light modulator (SLM) and a laser with a wavelength of 633 nm. Three letters (A, B, C) with height and width of 6 mm, positioned at near, middle, and far distances, were reconstructed to verify real-size preservation. name: Diffraction-Specific Approach
head: Hogel Vector Approach, Hogel-based CGH, Interference-Based Approach
body: The Diffraction-Specific Approach is a method for calculating Computer-Generated Holograms (CGH) that avoids the direct simulation of optical interference between object and reference waves. Instead, it treats the holographic fringe as a signal that can be subsampled spatially into functional elements called "hogels" and spectrally into an array of "hogel vectors". By working backwards from the 3D image and leveraging standard 3D computer graphics rendering techniques (orthographic projections), this approach significantly increases computation speed and achieves bandwidth compression compared to conventional interference-based methods. It is distinguished from its sibling Volume Rendering based CGH Calculation by its explicit decomposition of the wavefield into hogel vectors and its reliance on texture-mapping hardware for decoding. The method consists of two main stages: encoding (generation of the hogel-vector array) and decoding (reconstruction of the fringe). Inputs: A 3D scene defined by primitives (points, polygons) with attributes including color, lighting, shading, and occlusion information. Outputs: A holographic fringe pattern (complex amplitude or phase-only data) suitable for display on a Spatial Light Modulator (SLM). 1. Hogel: A spatially subsampled functional holographic element that partitions the hologram plane. 2. Hogel Vector: A spectral subsampling of the wavefront information associated with a single hogel, storing values for each projection direction. 3. Basis Fringes: A precomputed set of reference fringe patterns corresponding to the spectral samples, used during the decoding step. Compression Ratio (CR): The ratio between the size of the fringe and the hogel-vector array. Typical values are 8:1, 16:1, and 32:1. Spatial Subsampling: Determines the hogel grid resolution. Spectral Subsampling: Determines the number of components in each hogel vector. 1. 3D Scene Preparation: Perform a 3D filling operation to generate a list of 3D points or primitives, including color, lighting, shading, and occlusion data. 2. Orthographic Projections: Render a series of orthographic projections of the 3D scene. Each projection corresponds to a specific spectral sample (direction) of the hogels, providing a discrete sampling of space (pixels) and spectrum (projection direction). 3. Vector Conversion: Convert the rendered orthographic projections into a hogel-vector array by mapping the pixel values from the projections to the components of the hogel vectors. 1. Basis Fringe Retrieval: Retrieve the precomputed basis fringes corresponding to the spectral samples used during encoding. 2. Inner Product Calculation: Compute the inner product between the array of hogel vectors and the basis fringes to reconstruct the interference fringe. Implementation Note: This is accelerated using graphics hardware. The texture mapping function multiplies a component from each hogel vector by a replicated array of a single basis fringe. This operation is repeated for each hogel-vector component, and the results are accumulated in an accumulation buffer. 3. Output Generation: The accumulated result forms the final holographic fringe. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def diffractionspecificcgh(scene, hogelgrid, spectraldirections, basisfringes): """ Generates a holographic fringe using the Diffraction-Specific Approach. Args: scene: List of 3D primitives with color/lighting data. hogelgrid: Grid definition for spatial subsampling (hogels). spectraldirections: List of viewing directions for spectral subsampling. basisfringes: Precomputed array of basis fringe patterns. Returns: fringe: The reconstructed holographic fringe. """ # Step 1: Encoding - Generate Hogel-Vector Array # Render orthographic projections for each spectral direction projections = [] for direction in spectraldirections: # Standard 3D rendering of scene along direction proj = renderorthographic(scene, direction) projections.append(proj) # Convert projections into hogel-vector array # Each hogel in the grid stores a vector of values, one per spectral direction hogelvectors = createemptyhogelarray(hogelgrid, len(spectraldirections)) for idx, proj in enumerate(projections): # Map projection pixels to hogel grid cells for cell in hogelgrid.cells(): # Aggregate projection data for this cell into the vector component hogelvectors[cell][idx] = aggregateprojectiondata(proj, cell) # Step 2: Decoding - Recover Fringe # Initialize output fringe buffer fringe = createzeroslike(basisfringes[0]) # Compute inner product between hogel vectors and basis fringes # Exploits texture mapping: multiply each vector component by its basis fringe for cell in hogelgrid.cells(): hv = hogelvectors[cell] for compidx in range(len(hv)): # Multiply hogel vector component by corresponding basis fringe contribution = hv[compidx] basisfringes[compidx] # Accumulate result in buffer fringe += contribution return fringe def renderorthographic(scene, direction): # Standard computer graphics rendering of scene using orthographic projection return render(scene, projectiontype="orthographic", viewdirection=direction) def createemptyhogelarray(grid, numcomponents): # Initialize array where each grid cell holds a list of numcomponents values return {cell: [0.0] numcomponents for cell in grid.cells()} def aggregateprojectiondata(projection, cell): # Sample or average pixel values from the projection corresponding to the cell return mean(projection[cell.region]) def createzeroslike(array): # Create a new array of the same shape filled with zeros return [[0.0] len(row) for row in array] Image Sharpness vs. Compression: Higher compression ratios (e.g., 32:1) result in acceptable but degraded image quality due to added blur. For CR \le 8:1, the blur is invisible to the Human Visual System (HVS). Hardware Dependency: The decoding step relies heavily on multiplication-accumulation (MAC) operations, making performance significantly tied to the availability of hardware acceleration (e.g., texture mapping and accumulation buffers). Basis Fringe Precomputation: The method requires precomputed basis fringes, and reconstruction accuracy depends on their fidelity. Techniques to increase fringe computation speed and reduce data volume, including spatial subsampling, nonuniform sampling, and standard video compression algorithms. Nonuniformly sampled fringes provide lossless bandwidth compression, whereas standard MPEG algorithms can be used for encoding/decoding computed fringes. This approach increases fringe computation speed by 3000 times for the same hardware implementation. A technique within the diffraction-specific approach where the fringe is subsampled spatially into hogels and spectrally into hogel vectors. It uses standard 3D computer graphics rendering (orthographic projections) to generate the data. The inner product between hogel vectors and precomputed basis fringes is performed rapidly by exploiting texture mapping and accumulation buffers. This achieved a computation time of 0.9 seconds for fringes of 6-MB with CR=32:1 using Silicon Graphics RealityEngine2 (RE2). A variant that further subsamples the hogel in the spatial domain. Each hogel is encoded as a spatially smaller "fringelet". Using a simple sample-replication decoding scheme, fringelets provide the fastest method of fringe computation. Complex images have been generated in under one second for 6 MB fringes. Additionally, a "fringelet display" can optically decode fringelets to produce a CR-times greater image volume without increased electronic bandwidth. Computational Complexity: The encoding stage involves standard 3D rendering, which is efficient. The decoding stage involves many multiplication-accumulation (MAC) calculations, which can be slow on general-purpose CPUs but are accelerated by specialized hardware (DSP cards, graphics subsystems). Performance: For a 6-MB fringe with CR=32:1, computation time was 0.9 seconds on Silicon Graphics RealityEngine2 (RE2). With specialized DSP hardware, computation times of about one second were achieved for similar fringe sizes. Bandwidth Compression: Achieves significant bandwidth reduction. Compression ratios of 8:1, 16:1, and 32:1 are typical. Image Quality: Accompanied by a loss in image sharpness (added blur). For CR \le 8:1, blur is invisible to the HVS. For CR 16:1 or 32:1, good images are achieved with acceptable degradation. Strengths: Fast computation for interactive displays, bandwidth compression, leverages existing 3D graphics hardware. Limitations: Loss of image sharpness at high compression ratios, reliance on precomputed basis fringes, decoding complexity without hardware acceleration. The Diffraction-Specific Approach was introduced as an alternative to the conventional Interference-Based Approach for computing holographic fringes. It was developed to address the high computational cost of simulating optical interference, which requires billions of complex arithmetic operations (trigonometric functions and square roots) for small simple holographic images. The approach was pioneered by researchers who recognized that the fringe could be treated as a subsampled signal (hogels and hogel vectors) and reconstructed using standard 3D graphics techniques. It was presented in the context of interactive three-dimensional holographic displays, aiming to achieve computation speeds sufficient for real-time or near-real-time holographic video. name: Holographic Stereogram
head: HPO Stereogram, Horizontal-Parallax-Only Stereogram, Stereogram
body: A Holographic Stereogram is a type of computer-generated hologram composed of a series of discrete 2D perspective views of an object scene. It produces a view-dependent image that presents the corresponding perspective view in each horizontally displaced direction, functioning similarly to lenticular or parallax barrier displays. It restricts vertical parallax to achieve this horizontal-only view dependency. Inputs: A 3D scene model or point cloud; camera parameters (field of view, resolution). Outputs: A 2D fringe pattern (hologram) suitable for display on an SLM or printed medium. Data Structures: Not given in the sources. Steps: 1. View Generation: Generate a sequence of perspective views by moving a virtual camera laterally in discrete steps across the scene. 2. Fringe Combination: Combine the generated views to generate the holographic fringe for display. This involves mapping each view to a specific horizontal segment or column of the hologram plane. 3. Display: Output the resulting fringe pattern to a spatial light modulator (SLM) or print medium. Formulas: Not given in the sources. Parameters: Number of Views (N): Must be large enough to create a high-quality image free from sampling artifacts. The exact number N depends on the target horizontal field of view (FOV), with larger FOVs requiring more views and increasing computational complexity. Camera Step Size: Determines the angular separation between views. Smaller steps improve smoothness but increase computation. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Sampling Artifacts: A small number of perspective views leads to visible artifacts and poor image quality. Computational Load: The need for a large number of views limits computation speed, although specialized hardware can achieve nearly interactive rates. A technique used to acquire sub-holograms that simulate a pinhole camera view. A window with the resolution of the vertical axis of the hologram moves along the horizontal axis to extract different views. The apertures can be chosen densely enough to overlap, as increasing the number of views improves final rendering quality. However, larger targeted FOVs require more views and increased computational complexity. Complexity: Computationally expensive due to the need for a large number of perspective views. Complexity scales with the number of views required for the target FOV. Performance: Allows computation at nearly interactive rates when implemented on specialized hardware. Strengths: Suitable for horizontal parallax applications. Limitations: Limited to horizontal parallax; requires many views for high quality, impacting speed. The holographic stereogram approach was introduced as a method to produce 3D images with resolution finer than can be utilized by the human visual system, avoiding the need for supercomputers in some implementations. It is based on the principle of combining discrete 2D perspective views to form a holographic fringe. name: Computational Phase Modulation (CGH Generation)
head: Fresnel Holography, Lens Phase Function Method, ORA method, Optimization with Random Phase Algorithm
body:
Computational Phase Modulation generates Computer-Generated Holograms (CGH) by calculating the complex wavefield contributions of scene elements (points or voxels) to a hologram plane, typically displayed on a Spatial Light Modulator (SLM). It solves the problem of reconstructing 3D light fields from digital scene data by explicitly modeling the diffraction of light from source elements to the modulator plane. It is distinguished from Point-Cloud Based CGH Calculation by its specific reliance on the "lens phase function" abstraction for sub-holograms and the "point-wise integration" summation model, and from Layer-Based Holographic Algorithm by its direct point-to-plane propagation model rather than layer-by-layer accumulation. Inputs: Scene definition: A set of M object points \vec{o}j = (xj, yj, zj) with desired intensities aj. Hologram plane parameters: Resolution (W, H), pixel pitch p, wavelength \lambda. SLM constraints: Maximum supported spatial frequency, which determines the maximum radius of a sub-hologram. Outputs: A complex-valued hologram pattern H(\vec{p}) or phase-only pattern \phih(x,y) ready for SLM display. Data Structures: Hologram Plane: A 2D grid of complex values H(x,y) or phase values \phih(x,y), size W 	imes H. Sub-hologram Map: A mapping from hologram pixel coordinates \vec{p} to the set of object points 	ext{sp}(\vec{p}) whose sub-holograms cover \vec{p}. Method: The method computes the hologram by summing the contributions of all object points. Each object point j contributes a "lens phase function" fj(\vec{p}) to every hologram pixel \vec{p} that falls within its designated sub-hologram region. 1. Initialize the hologram plane H(\vec{p}) = 0 for all \vec{p}. 2. For each object point j in the scene: a. Determine Sub-hologram Region: Calculate the bounding box on the hologram plane that contains the spatial frequencies supported by the SLM for the distance zj and wavelength \lambda. Let this region be Rj. b. For each pixel \vec{p} in Rj: i. Calculate the distance r{j,\vec{p}} = \|\vec{p} - \vec{o}j\|. ii. Calculate the lens phase function contribution: fj(\vec{p}) = \exp\left(i \left(\phi{0,j} +  rac{2\pi}{\lambda} r{j,\vec{p}}ight)ight) where \phi{0,j} is an initial phase offset (often 0). iii. Add the weighted contribution to the hologram plane: H(\vec{p}) \leftarrow H(\vec{p}) + aj fj(\vec{p}) 3. Post-processing (Optional): If the SLM is phase-only, convert the complex H(\vec{p}) to a phase-only pattern \phih(x,y) using an approximation method (e.g., Amplitude Discard or Iterative Fourier Transform). Note: The source describes an iterative optimization (ORA) to refine phase \phih for uniform intensity spot arrays, which is a specific variant of this post-processing step. Formulas: Lens Phase Function: fo(\vec{p}) = e^{i(\phio +  rac{2\pi}{\lambda} \|\vec{p}-\vec{o}\|)} where \vec{o} is the object point, \vec{p} is the hologram pixel, \lambda is wavelength, and \phio is phase offset. Hologram Summation: H(\vec{p}) = \sum{j \in 	ext{sp}(\vec{p})} aj fj(\vec{p}) where 	ext{sp}(\vec{p}) is the set of object points whose sub-holograms include \vec{p}, and aj is the intensity weight. Reconstruction (Verification): Ur(
ux, 
uy) = \iint Uh(x, y) e^{-i 2\pi (x
ux + y
uy)} dx dy where Uh is the hologram pattern and Ur is the reconstructed complex amplitude. Parameters: \lambda: Wavelength of reconstruction light. aj: Desired intensity of object point j. \phio: Phase offset, typically 0. Sub-hologram size: Determined by SLM spatial frequency limits. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Sub-hologram Overlap: Sub-holograms for different object points may overlap on the hologram plane. The method handles this by simple complex summation of their contributions. Spatial Frequency Limits: If a sub-hologram is too large, the phase gradient exceeds the SLM's Nyquist limit. The sub-hologram must be confined to a size supported by the SLM. Amplitude Loss: If using phase-only SLMs without iterative optimization, significant energy is lost in diffraction orders or zero-order. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def computecghphasemodulation(objectpoints, hologramwidth, hologramheight, pixelpitch, wavelength): """ Computes the complex hologram H(p) using the lens phase function method. Args: objectpoints: List of tuples (x, y, z, intensity) for each point in the scene. hologramwidth: Width of the hologram plane in pixels. hologramheight: Height of the hologram plane in pixels. pixelpitch: Physical size of one pixel (e.g., in meters). wavelength: Wavelength of the reconstruction laser (e.g., in meters). Returns: H: 2D numpy array of complex values representing the hologram plane. """ import numpy as np # Initialize hologram plane with zeros H = np.zeros((hologramheight, hologramwidth), dtype=np.complex128) # Create coordinate grids for the hologram plane # Center the coordinates at (0,0) for easier distance calculation xcoords = np.arange(hologramwidth) pixelpitch - (hologramwidth pixelpitch) / 2 ycoords = np.arange(hologramheight) pixelpitch - (hologramheight pixelpitch) / 2 X, Y = np.meshgrid(xcoords, ycoords) k = 2 np.pi / wavelength for point in objectpoints: ox, oy, oz, intensity = point # Calculate distance from object point to each hologram pixel # r = sqrt((x - ox)^2 + (y - oy)^2 + (z - oz)^2) # Note: ox, oy are typically 0 if object is on axis, or relative to center dx = X - ox dy = Y - oy dz = -oz # Assuming hologram is at z=0 and object is at z=oz R = np.sqrt(dx2 + dy2 + dz2) # Calculate lens phase function # fo(p) = exp(i (phi0 + k R)) # phi0 is set to 0 for simplicity as per source phase = k R fo = np.exp(1j phase) # Add weighted contribution to hologram H += intensity fo return H def applyphaseonlyconstraint(H): """ Converts complex hologram to phase-only using Amplitude Discard method. This is a simple approximation; iterative methods like ORA are more complex. """ # Extract phase phase = np.angle(H) # Return phase-only pattern (amplitude set to 1) return np.exp(1j phase) Uses phase-only CGHs on an LCOS-SLM to split a laser beam into multiple focal spots simultaneously, increasing voxel generation density for volumetric displays. It differs from single-point rendering by enabling parallel voxel generation, though it requires optimization of scanning trajectories and hardware constraints. Methods for encoding complex-valued object waves into phase-only holograms for LCSLMs without iterative optimization. Includes Amplitude Discard (simplest), Double Phase (encodes amplitude and phase into two adjacent values), and Binary Phase (quantizes to two levels). Trades image quality and energy efficiency for computational simplicity. Mitigates depth replicas in simultaneous color holography by exploiting the wavelength-dependent phase response of LCoS SLMs. Uses SLMs with phase ranges > 2\pi to break wavelength-depth ambiguity, differing from Computational Phase Modulation by addressing multi-wavelength crosstalk via physical device dispersion rather than algorithmic approximation. A model for the phase delay \phi\lambda imparted by an LCoS SLM, accounting for wavelength dispersion. The phase delay is \phi\lambda =  rac{2\pi d}{\lambda} n(s, \lambda), where d is the LC layer thickness, n(s, \lambda) is the refractive index controlled by digital input s and dependent on \lambda. Quantization errors increase with larger phase ranges, requiring at least 6 bits of granularity per 2\pi range to maintain PSNR/SSIM. Complexity: The naive point-wise integration scales with O(M \cdot N), where M is the number of object points and N is the number of hologram pixels. This is extremely expensive for high-resolution holograms and large scenes. Memory: Requires storing the complex hologram plane H(\vec{p}), size W 	imes H complex values. Strengths: Physically accurate modeling of diffraction from point sources; supports arbitrary 3D point distributions. Limitations: Computationally intensive; sub-hologram overlap can cause interference artifacts if not managed; phase-only conversion leads to energy loss. When to use: When high-fidelity point-source reconstruction is required and computational resources allow for direct summation. When not to use: For real-time applications with very large scenes or high-resolution SLMs without acceleration techniques (e.g., GPU parallelization, FFT-based approximations). Originating from the principles of Fresnel holography, this method was formalized in the context of holographic near-eye displays and volumetric graphics. The "lens phase function" and "point-wise integration" terminology was popularized by Maimone et al. for holographic projectors. The ORA (Optimization with Random Phase Algorithm) variant was developed by Hayasaki et al. for femtosecond laser processing and volumetric graphics. The extended phase range approach was introduced to address color crosstalk in simultaneous color holography. name: CGH-based parallel focal point generation
head: CGH-Based Multi-Voxel Generation, Computer Generated Hologram parallel voxel generation, Computer Generated Holography multi-point rendering
body: This method uses phase-only Computer-Generated Holograms (CGH) displayed on a Liquid Crystal on Silicon Spatial Light Modulator (LCOS-SLM) to split a single laser beam into multiple focal spots simultaneously. It solves the bottleneck of low voxel generation density in holographic volumetric displays by increasing the number of voxels generated per frame. Unlike single-point rendering, it allows for parallel voxel generation, though it introduces trade-offs in scanning trajectory optimization and hardware constraints. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Target voxel distribution (number of focal points P), laser parameters (repetition frequency, pulse energy), LCOS-SLM specifications (maximum spatial frequency, grayscale range). Output: A phase-only CGH pattern displayed on the SLM, resulting in P simultaneous focal points in the drawing space. Data Structures: CGH Pattern: A 2D array of phase values. Layout: Grayscale values 0 to 255 (8-bit). Mapping: Grayscale value g \in [0, 255] maps linearly to phase modulation \phi \in [0, 2\pi]. Spatial Frequency Constraint: The encoded focal points must be arranged within a spatial frequency range up to 1/8 of the LCOS-SLM's maximum spatial frequency. Algorithm Steps: 1. CGH Generation: Generate a phase-only hologram to create P focal points. Use the Gerchberg–Saxton algorithm with 50 Fourier iterative calculations to optimize the phase distribution. Ensure the spatial frequency of the generated pattern does not exceed 1/8 of the SLM's maximum spatial frequency. 2. SLM Display: Load the calculated CGH onto the LCOS-SLM. The SLM modulates the phase of the incident laser beam according to the grayscale values. 3. Optical Focusing: Pass the modulated beam through a lens (focal length f{lens}) and a varifocal lens. The lens focuses the light into separated focal points in the drawing space at an effective infinite distance. 4. Scanning: Apply the scanning trajectory to the beam. Note: If using a trajectory optimized for single-point rendering, blur may occur when rendering multiple spatially separated focal points. Optimizing the scanning trajectory for multi-point rendering is required to resolve this. Formulas: The estimated number of voxels generated per frame N is calculated as: N = \frac{P \cdot n}{fr} Where: P: Number of focal points (voxels) generated in parallel per pulse. n: Number of voxels generated in 1 second, dependent on the laser repetition frequency. fr: Refresh rate of the display system. Estimated Parallel Voxels (P): 708 (theoretical estimate based on D=50\% and E{th}). Actual Achieved Parallel Voxels (P): 4 (due to hardware constraints). Refresh Rate (fr): 20 Hz. Solution for Damage: Use a varifocal lens with higher light resistance or combine with dynamic optimization for CGH diffraction efficiency to improve P. name: Phase-Only Hologram Approximations
head: Amplitude Discard Method, Binary Phase Method, DPE, Direct Amplitude Encoding, Double Phase Encoding, Double Phase Method, Double-phase holograms
body: Phase-only hologram approximations are methods for generating holograms compatible with Liquid Crystal Spatial Light Modulators (LCSLMs) that can only modulate the phase of light, not its amplitude. They solve the problem of encoding a complex-valued object wave O(x,y;c) into a phase-only hologram H without using computationally expensive iterative optimization. The Amplitude Discard Method is the simplest approach, retaining only the phase of the object wave, while the Double Phase Method explicitly encodes both amplitude and phase into two adjacent phase values. The Binary Phase Method quantizes the phase to two levels. These methods trade off image quality and energy efficiency for computational simplicity and real-time capability. Input: Complex-valued object wave O(x, y; c), where x, y are spatial coordinates and c is the color channel index. The wave is defined as O(x, y; c) = A(x, y; c) e^{j \phi(x, y; c)}, where A is amplitude and \phi is phase. Output: Phase-only hologram H(x, y), representing the phase values to be displayed on the SLM. Object Wave: A 2D array of complex numbers, one per pixel per color channel. Hologram: A 2D array of phase values. For Amplitude Discard and Binary Phase: One phase value per pixel. For Double Phase: Two phase values per logical pixel, typically arranged in a checkerboard pattern or sub-hologram block. This method discards the amplitude of the object wave and quantizes the phase. H(x, y; c) = Q \left( \frac{L}{2\pi} \arg \{ O(x, y; c) \} \right) \arg \{ O \}: The phase angle of the complex object wave. L: Number of discrete quantization levels (typically L=256). Q: A uniform mid-rise quantizer mapping the scaled phase to integer levels. Parameters: L=256. Characteristics: Does not produce unwanted diffraction order artifacts, so no spatial filter is required in the optical system. This method discards the amplitude and quantizes the phase to two levels. Formula: The phase is quantized to two levels (e.g., 0 and \pi, or mapped to two discrete SLM levels). Parameters: 2 quantization levels. Characteristics: Requires temporal averaging and a single-sideband filter. This method encodes the complex value O into the sum of two complex numbers with constant amplitude and variable phase. O(x, y; c) = 0.5 e^{j \theta1(x, y; c)} + 0.5 e^{j \theta2(x, y; c)} \theta1, \theta2: The two phase values to be encoded. Derivation: Let O = a e^{j p}, where a = |O| is the amplitude and p = \arg \{ O \} is the phase. The two phase values are calculated as: Pa(r) = p - \arccos(a) Pb(r) = p + \arccos(a) where a \in [0, 1]. Parameters: Quantization levels L=256. Characteristics: Requires spatial filtering by a pupil aperture to remove unwanted diffraction orders. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import numpy as np def amplitudediscardhologram(objectwave, L=256): """ Generates a phase-only hologram using the Amplitude Discard Method. Args: objectwave: 2D numpy array of complex numbers representing O(x,y;c). L: Number of quantization levels (default 256). Returns: hologram: 2D numpy array of phase values in [0, 2pi). """ # Extract phase angle from complex object wave phase = np.angle(objectwave) # Scale phase to [0, L) and quantize # Q is a uniform mid-rise quantizer scaledphase = (L / (2 np.pi)) phase # Quantize to integer levels quantized = np.round(scaledphase) # Map back to phase range [0, 2pi) # Note: np.angle returns in [-pi, pi], so we adjust for mid-rise quantization # Typically, we just take the phase directly if continuous, # but for discrete levels: hologram = (quantized / L) 2 np.pi # Ensure phase is in [0, 2pi) hologram = hologram % (2 np.pi) return hologram def binaryphasehologram(objectwave, numlevels=2): """ Generates a phase-only hologram using the Binary Phase Method. Args: objectwave: 2D numpy array of complex numbers. numlevels: Number of phase levels (default 2). Returns: hologram: 2D numpy array of phase values. """ phase = np.angle(objectwave) # Quantize phase to numlevels # Map phase from [-pi, pi] to [0, numlevels) # Shift phase to [0, 2pi] phaseshifted = phase % (2 np.pi) # Scale to [0, numlevels) scaled = (numlevels / (2 np.pi)) phaseshifted # Quantize quantized = np.round(scaled) % numlevels # Map back to phase range hologram = (quantized / numlevels) 2 np.pi return hologram def doublephasehologram(objectwave, L=256): """ Generates a double phase hologram using Direct Amplitude Encoding. Args: objectwave: 2D numpy array of complex numbers. L: Number of quantization levels (default 256). Returns: holograma: 2D numpy array of phase values Pa. hologramb: 2D numpy array of phase values Pb. """ # Extract amplitude and phase amplitude = np.abs(objectwave) phase = np.angle(objectwave) # Calculate Pa and Pb # Pa = p - arccos(a) # Pb = p + arccos(a) # Note: arccos is defined for a in [0, 1] acosa = np.arccos(amplitude) Pa = phase - acosa Pb = phase + acosa # Quantize to L levels # Scale to 0, L) Pascaled = (L / (2 np.pi)) Pa Pbscaled = (L / (2 np.pi)) Pb # Quantize Paquant = np.round(Pascaled) % L Pbquant = np.round(Pbscaled) % L # Map back to phase range holograma = (Paquant / L) 2 np.pi hologramb = (Pbquant / L) 2 np.pi return holograma, hologramb Amplitude > 1: The Double Phase Method requires |O| \le 1 for \arccos(|O|) to be real. If the object wave amplitude exceeds 1, normalization or [clamping is required. Resolution Loss: The Double Phase Method requires two phase values for each complex value, leading to a corresponding loss in resolution. Ringing Artifacts: The Double Phase Method may produce subtle ringing artifacts. Simple Text Only: The Amplitude Discard Method may produce acceptable results only for simple text and symbology consisting of thin lines, as phase encodes high frequencies like object edges; it is not a practical general solution. Phase Wrapping: Real-world SLMs may have imperfections in phase wrapping from 2\pi back to 0. Centering the distribution of phase values to fill the full phase range (> 2\pi) and scaling to taper off to zero near max/min rotation can improve contrast. One Step Phase Retrieval (OSPR) is a technique for generating phase-only holograms by replacing iterative phase optimization with random phase assignment, relying on temporal averaging to recover the target image intensity. It differs from standard amplitude discard methods by explicitly managing the resulting high-frequency noise through the rapid playback of multiple randomized sub-frames, rather than attempting to minimize noise within a single static hologram. Amplitude Discard: O(N) time and memory, where N is the number of pixels. Trivial computation. Binary Phase: O(N) time and memory. Trivial computation. Double Phase: O(N) time and memory. Trivial computation after complex hologram is obtained. Iterative Methods: Not considered in these approximations due to high computational burden. PSNR (dB): Binary Phase: 25.2 dB. Double Phase: 27.6 dB, 30.57 dB (red), 30.05 dB (green), 27.26 dB (blue) in simulation. Amplitude Discard: 27.7 dB. Amplitude Holograms (for comparison): 40.2 dB at \Delta=0.5. SSIM: Binary Phase: 0.30. Double Phase: 0.40. Amplitude Discard: 0.62. Amplitude Holograms (for comparison): 0.97 at \Delta=0.5. Energy Efficiency: Amplitude Discard: 100%. Binary Phase: 50%. Double Phase: 21.6%. Amplitude Holograms: 1.4% at \Delta=0.5. Amplitude Discard: Strengths: Highest energy efficiency (100%), no spatial filter needed, simple computation. Limitations: Lower SSIM than binary phase, not practical for general images due to high-frequency noise. Binary Phase: Strengths: Superior SSIM compared to other phase methods due to temporal averaging reducing speckle noise. Limitations: Lower PSNR, requires temporal averaging and single-sideband filter, significant per-pixel error. Double Phase: Strengths: Higher contrast and less high-frequency noise than iterative methods, smooth phase profile. Limitations: Lowest energy efficiency (21.6%), requires spatial filtering, resolution loss, ringing artifacts. Use Amplitude Discard for simple text/symbology or when energy efficiency is critical and no spatial filter is available. Use Binary Phase when structural preservation (SSIM) is more important than PSNR and temporal averaging is feasible. Use Double Phase when high contrast and smooth phase are required, and spatial filtering is available. The Amplitude Discard Method is described as the most trivial way of computing a phase-only hologram. The Double Phase Method was described by Hsueh and Sawchuk in 1978. These methods are used in holographic near-eye displays for virtual and augmented reality, where real-time embedded rendering is required. name: One Step Phase Retrieval (OSPR)
head: Temporal averaging
body: One Step Phase Retrieval (OSPR), also known as temporal averaging, generates phase-only holograms by playing back multiple sub-frames with randomized object phases to approximate a target complex wavefield. Unlike iterative methods that optimize phase to match a target amplitude, OSPR discards amplitude entirely and relies on the temporal averaging of uncorrelated pseudo-random noise patterns to reveal the target image. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Target complex object wavefield O(x,y) = A(x,y)e^{i\phio(x,y)}, where A is amplitude and \phio is phase. Output: A sequence of binary or multi-level phase-only hologram sub-frames Hk(x,y) displayed in rapid succession. Data Structures: Each hologram sub-frame is a 2D grid of phase values, typically quantized to binary levels (0, \pi) or a small discrete set, suitable for high-speed binary SLMs. Steps: 1. Randomize Object Phase: Instead of optimizing the object phase \phio to match the target amplitude, assign \phio(x,y) random values uniformly distributed over [0, 2\pi) for each sub-frame generation. 2. Generate Hologram Sub-frames: Compute the hologram Hk using the randomized phase \phio^{(k)}. The required amplitude on the hologram plane becomes a pseudo-random uniform noise pattern because the object phase is random. 3. Discard Amplitude: On playback, the amplitude information is discarded, leaving only the phase component of Hk to be displayed by the SLM. 4. Temporal Playback: Display the sequence of hologram sub-frames H1, H2, \dots, HN in random succession on a high-speed display. 5. Noise Averaging: The human eye or a low-pass optical system averages the intensity of these rapidly changing sub-frames. Since the noise patterns are uncorrelated across sub-frames, they average out, revealing the target image. Parameters: Number of sub-frames N: Several sub-frames must be calculated for each image frame. Display Switching Speed: Must be high enough to meet bandwidth requirements and prevent flicker. Pitfalls: Low contrast of noisy hologram sub-frames cannot be recovered by temporal averaging. Requires high bandwidth and switching speed from the display (SLM). Iteratively optimized holograms tend to include undesirable high frequency noise or speckle, which OSPR aims to mitigate through averaging. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math import random def generateosprsubframes(targetamplitude, targetphase, numsubframes): """Generates phase-only hologram sub-frames using OSPR.""" rows = len(targetamplitude) cols = len(targetamplitude[0]) subframes = [] for in range(numsubframes): # Step 1: Randomize object phase uniformly over [0, 2pi) randomphase = [[random.uniform(0, 2 math.pi) for in range(cols)] for in range(rows)] # Step 2: Generate hologram sub-frame using randomized phase # The source indicates the hologram is computed from the randomized phase, # making the required amplitude a pseudo-random uniform noise pattern. # The exact hologram computation formula is not given in the sources. hologramphase = [[random.uniform(0, 2 math.pi) for in range(cols)] for in range(rows)] # Step 3: Discard amplitude; output is phase-only subframes.append(hologramphase) return subframes def displayosprsequence(subframes, refreshratehz): """Plays back sub-frames in random succession on a high-speed SLM.""" frameduration = 1.0 / refreshratehz for frame in subframes: # Step 4: Display holograms in random succession # Step 5: Human eye or low-pass optical system averages intensity # Hardware-specific display call is omitted as it is implementation-specific pass This method models and mitigates phase noise inherent to liquid crystal amplitude-only Spatial Light Modulators (SLMs) by analyzing the coupling between amplitude modulation and unwanted phase modulation. It establishes a mathematical framework using Jacobi-Anger expansions to separate signal terms from noise terms in the Fourier domain, allowing for the design of grating frequencies that prevent noise overlap with the reconstructed signal. It sets it apart from sibling methods by providing a rigorous analytical derivation of noise spectra based on the specific physical properties of the liquid crystal, rather than relying solely on empirical averaging or iterative phase retrieval. Time Complexity: Requires calculating multiple hologram sub-frames for each image frame, increasing computational load compared to single-frame methods. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Performance: The primary downside is that the low contrast of the noisy hologram sub-frames cannot be recovered by temporal averaging. Hardware Requirements: Requires high bandwidth and switching speed from the display (SLM). Binary phase holograms may be produced for playback on a high-speed binary SLM to facilitate these requirements. Strengths: Mitigates undesirable high-frequency noise or speckle associated with iteratively optimized holograms. Limitations: Cannot recover low contrast from noisy sub-frames; requires multiple sub-frames per image frame; dependent on high-speed display hardware. One Step Phase Retrieval (OSPR), also known as temporal averaging, was introduced by Cable et al. in 2004. It is used in holographic near-eye displays for virtual and augmented reality to generate phase-only holograms that approximate complex wavefields by averaging out noise over time. name: Phase Noise Handling in Amplitude-Only SLMs
head: Phase Noise Mitigation in Amplitude-Only SLMs
body: This method models and mitigates phase noise inherent to liquid crystal amplitude-only Spatial Light Modulators (SLMs) by analyzing the coupling between amplitude modulation and unwanted phase modulation. It establishes a mathematical framework using Jacobi-Anger expansions to separate signal terms from noise terms in the Fourier domain, allowing for the design of grating frequencies that prevent noise overlap with the reconstructed signal. It sets it apart from sibling methods by providing a rigorous analytical derivation of noise spectra based on the specific physical properties of the liquid crystal, rather than relying solely on empirical averaging or iterative phase retrieval. Inputs and Outputs Input: The amplitude modulation function f(x) applied to the SLM pixels. Output: A derived expression for the wave field at the SLM plane, identifying signal and noise components, and a constraint on the grating phase frequency to avoid aliasing. Data Structures Amplitude Function: Represented as a Fourier series f(x) = \sumk Fk \cos(kx + \phik), where Fk are amplitude coefficients and \phik are phase coefficients for spatial frequency k. Phase Noise Model: Unwanted phase modulation is modeled as a second-order polynomial of the amplitude: \exp(i p1 f(x) + i p2 f(x)^2), where p1 and p2 are coefficients characterizing the liquid crystal's phase-amplitude coupling. Steps 1. Model the Wave Field: Define the complex wave field U(x) at the SLM plane as the product of the amplitude modulation and the unwanted phase modulation: U(x) = f(x) e^{i p1 f(x) + i p2 f(x)^2} 2. Expand Phase Terms: Apply the Jacobi-Anger expansion, e^{iz \cos \theta} = \sum{n=-\infty}^{\infty} i^n Jn(z) e^{in\theta}, to the exponential terms. Here, Jn(z) is the n-th Bessel function of the first kind. 3. Substitute Fourier Series: Substitute the Fourier series expansion of f(x) into the phase terms. The term f(x) becomes \sumk Fk \cos(kx + \phik). This transforms the wave field into a product of sums involving Bessel functions and complex exponentials. 4. Derive Expanded Expression: The full expanded wave field is given by: U(x) = f(x) \prodk \sumn i^n Jn(p1 Fk) e^{in(kx + \phik)} \prod{k,l} \sumn i^n Jn\left(\frac{p2 Fk Fl}{2}\right) e^{in((k+l)x + \phik + \phil)} \prod{k,l} \sumn i^n Jn\left(\frac{p2 Fk Fl}{2}\right) e^{in((k-l)x + \phik - \phil)} 5. Approximate for Small Parameters: In typical experimental conditions, p1, p2, Fk < 1 and |n| \ll 1. Under these conditions, higher-order Bessel functions Jn(z) for |n| \gg 1 are negligible. The expression approximates to: U(x) \approx f(x) \prodk J0(p1 Fk) \prod{k,l} J0\left(\frac{p2 Fk Fl}{2}\right) \left[ \summ J1(p1 Fm) e^{i(mx + \phim)} J1(pm Fm) + \sum{m,n} 2i J1\left(\frac{p1 F1 F2}{2}\right) e^{i((m+n)x + \phim + \phin)} J0\left(\frac{p0 F0 F2}{2}\right) + O(p1 Fk^2) + O(p2 Fk^2) \right] Note: The source text contains specific indices in the approximation (Eq. 6) which appear to contain typos (e.g., J(p1 Fk) instead of J1, mixed indices F1, F2, F0). The implementer should use the general structure derived in Step 4 and truncate based on the magnitude of p1 Fk and p2 Fk Fl. 6. Identify Noise Terms: Analyze the frequency components of the expanded expression. The signal term is typically the first-order diffraction e^{ik{prism}x}. Noise terms arise from higher-order interactions, such as e^{ik{pitch}x - 2ik{prism}x}, where k{pitch} is the wavenumber of the SLM pixel pitch and k{prism} is the grating frequency. 7. Set Grating Frequency Constraint: To ensure noise terms do not overlap with the signal term in the Fourier domain, set the grating phase frequency k{prism} to one-quarter or less of the spatial frequency of the pixel pitch k{pitch}: k{prism} \le \frac{1}{4} k{pitch} Parameters p1, p2: Phase noise coefficients. Values are typically < 1 in experimental setups. Fk: Fourier coefficients of the amplitude pattern. Values are typically < 1. Grating Frequency: Must be \le 1/4 of the pixel pitch spatial frequency. Edge Cases and Pitfalls Noise Overlap: If the grating phase frequency is set to one-third of the spatial frequency of the pixel pitch, the signal term e^{ik{prism}x} overlaps with the noise term e^{ik{pitch}x - 2ik{prism}x}. This makes the noise unfilterable. High-Order Terms: If p1 Fk or p2 Fk Fl are not small, the approximation in Step 5 fails, and higher-order Bessel terms must be retained, increasing computational complexity. Pseudocode Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import numpy as np from scipy.special import jv def calculatewavefieldspectrum(fouriercoeffs, p1, p2, kmax): """ Calculate the spectral components of the wave field at an amplitude-only SLM with phase noise, using the Jacobi-Anger expansion. Parameters: fouriercoeffs: dict mapping spatial frequency k to (amplitude Fk, phase phik) p1: Phase noise linear coefficient p2: Phase noise quadratic coefficient kmax: Maximum spatial frequency to consider for truncation Returns: spectrum: dict mapping spatial frequency k to complex amplitude """ spectrum = {} # Iterate through all combinations of k and l within kmax ks = list(fouriercoeffs.keys()) for k in ks: if abs(k) > kmax: continue Fk, phik = fouriercoeffs[k] # Term 1: Linear phase noise contribution (from p1) # Sum over n, but truncate for small p1Fk # Dominant term is n=1 for first-order diffraction if abs(p1 Fk) < 1.0: # Small argument approximation # J1(p1Fk) is the dominant non-zero term for n=1 coeff = jv(1, p1 Fk) freq = k phase = phik spectrum[freq] = spectrum.get(freq, 0) + coeff np.exp(1j phase) # Term 2: Quadratic phase noise contribution (from p2) # Involves products of Fk and Fl for l in ks: if abs(l) > kmax: continue Fl, phil = fouriercoeffs[l] # Sum over n for (k+l) and (k-l) terms # Dominant term is n=1 arg = p2 Fk Fl / 2 if abs(arg) < 1.0: coeff = jv(1, arg) # Frequency component for (k+l) freqsum = k + l phasesum = phik + phil spectrum[freqsum] = spectrum.get(freqsum, 0) + 2j coeff np.exp(1j phasesum) # Frequency component for (k-l) freqdiff = k - l phasediff = phik - phil spectrum[freqdiff] = spectrum.get(freqdiff, 0) + 2j coeff np.exp(1j phasediff) return spectrum def checkgratingconstraint(kprism, kpitch): """ Check if the grating frequency avoids noise overlap. Parameters: kprism: Grating phase frequency kpitch: Spatial frequency of the pixel pitch Returns: bool: True if constraint is satisfied """ return kprism <= 0.25 kpitch A method to obtain amplitude in a phase-only device by playing back several holograms with randomized object phases in random succession, allowing noise to average out. Link A broader approach that uses the physical properties of the SLM and optical system to engineer the diffraction pattern, often incorporating phase noise models. Link Time Complexity: The analytical derivation is O(1), but the numerical evaluation of the spectrum depends on the number of Fourier components N. The pseudocode is O(N^2) due to the double loop over k and l. Memory Complexity: O(N) to store the Fourier coefficients and the resulting spectrum. Measured Performance: In experiments using an IRIS-U62 LCoS SLM (3840 × 2160 resolution, 3.6 μm pixel pitch, binned to 7.2 μm effective pitch), the method successfully mitigated phase noise by setting the grating frequency to \le 1/4 of the pixel pitch spatial frequency. Strengths: Provides a rigorous physical model for phase noise; allows for precise design of grating frequencies to avoid aliasing; analytical solution avoids iterative computation. Limitations: Relies on the assumption that p1, p2, Fk < 1; higher-order terms may become significant for large amplitude modulations or strong phase coupling; requires accurate characterization of p1 and p2 for the specific SLM. When to Use: When using amplitude-only SLMs for holography and phase noise is a significant artifact; when analytical design of the grating frequency is preferred over empirical tuning. When Not to Use: When the SLM has negligible phase noise; when the amplitude modulation is large enough to violate the small argument approximation for Bessel functions. This method originates from research into diffraction-engineered holography, specifically addressing the limitations of amplitude-only SLMs in volumetric displays and holographic computer-generated holography. The work was published in Nature Communications in 2022 by researchers investigating the depth representation limit of holographic displays. name: Extended Phase Range SLM Modulation
head: Depth Replica Removal via Extended Phase Range, Extended Phase Range, Extended Phase Range SLM for Depth Replica Reduction, Replica reduction, Wavelength-Dependent Phase SLM
body: Extended Phase Range SLM Modulation is a technique used in simultaneous color holography to mitigate depth replicas (ghost images) by exploiting the wavelength-dependent phase response of Liquid Crystal Spatial Light Modulators (SLSMs). Unlike standard 0-2\pi SLMs which produce perfect intensity copies of the target image at specific replica planes, this method uses SLMs with extended phase ranges (greater than 2\pi) that vary significantly across RGB wavelengths to break the wavelength-depth ambiguity. This approach sets it apart from Computational Phase Modulation (CGH Generation) by specifically addressing the multi-wavelength crosstalk inherent in single-SLM color holography, and differs from Phase-Only Hologram Approximations by relying on physical device dispersion rather than algorithmic approximation to suppress artifacts. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Target RGB image data; SLM physical parameters (thickness d, refractive index range n{max}, n{min}, dispersion -dn/d\lambda). Output: Phase-only hologram pattern \phi(x,y) optimized for the specific SLM's wavelength-dependent phase response. Data Structures: SLM Model: A mapping function R(\lambda) returning the maximum phase shift \phi{max}(\lambda) for a given wavelength \lambda. Fields: wavelength (float, nm), phaserange (float, multiples of \pi). Typical values for Holoeye Pluto-2.1-Vis-016: Red (\lambda \approx 630 nm): 2.4\pi Green (\lambda \approx 532 nm): 5.9\pi Blue (\lambda \approx 450 nm): 7.4\pi Method Steps: 1. Characterize SLM Dispersion: Determine the phase response \phi\lambda for each primary color channel. The phase shift introduced by the LC layer is defined as: \phi\lambda = \frac{2\pi d \Delta n(\lambda)}{\lambda} where d is the LC layer thickness and \Delta n(\lambda) = n(\lambda) - n{min} is the change in refractive index relative to the minimum state. Note that n depends on \lambda due to material dispersion. 2. Analyze Wavelength Dependence: Calculate the derivative of phase with respect to wavelength to quantify replica suppression potential: \frac{d\phi}{d\lambda} A larger magnitude of this derivative indicates stronger wavelength dependence, which diminishes the coherence of replica planes across different colors. This derivative increases with larger \Delta n = n{max} - n{min} and higher dispersion -dn/d\lambda. 3. Generate Hologram: Compute the phase pattern \phi(x,y) using a standard CGH algorithm (e.g., Gerchberg-Saxton or direct calculation) but constrain the phase values to the specific extended range [0, \phi{max}(\lambda)] for each channel during the optimization or quantization step. Unlike standard methods that wrap phase to 2\pi, this method allows the phase to exceed 2\pi according to the device's physical limits. 4. Quantization: Map the continuous phase values to the SLM's bit depth. Simulation indicates that PSNR and SSIM remain stable for 6 bits and above, but lower bit depths exacerbate quantization errors as the phase range increases. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def calculateextendedphasehologram(targetrgb, slmparams, wavelength): """ Generates a hologram pattern accounting for extended phase range. Args: targetrgb: 3D array (H, W, 3) representing the target image intensity for R, G, B. slmparams: Object containing 'd' (thickness), 'nmin', 'nmaxlambda' (dict mapping lambda to nmax). wavelength: Array of wavelengths [lambdar, lambdag, lambdab] in nm. Returns: phasepattern: 2D array (H, W) of phase values in radians. """ # 1. Calculate max phase shift for each channel based on SLM physics # phimax = 2 pi d (nmax(lambda) - nmin) / lambda phaseranges = [] for lam in wavelength: nmax = slmparams.nmaxlambda[lam] deltan = nmax - slmparams.nmin phimax = (2 math.pi slmparams.d deltan) / lam phaseranges.append(phimax) # 2. Initialize phase pattern (e.g., using Gerchberg-Saxton or direct calculation) # This step depends on the parent method [Computational Phase Modulation] # We assume a standard iterative Fourier transform algorithm is used here. phasepattern = initializephasepattern(targetrgb) # 3. Apply extended phase constraints during iteration # In standard 2pi SLMs, phase is wrapped: phase = phase % (2pi) # Here, we do not wrap to 2pi, but allow it to scale with the channel's specific range. # However, since a single SLM pattern is displayed for all colors simultaneously, # the physical phase shift is determined by the LC orientation 's'. # The effective phase for color c is phic = phipattern (phimaxc / 2pi) # The optimization must ensure the resulting intensities match targetrgb. for iteration in range(maxiterations): # Forward propagation to sensor plane for each color for c, lam in enumerate(wavelength): # Propagate phasepattern modulated by the specific wavelength's efficiency # The physical phase shift is phiphys = phasepattern (phaseranges[c] / (2pi)) # Note: phasepattern is normalized to [0, 2pi] for the SLM input, # but the optical effect scales by phaseranges[c]. fieldc = propagate(phasepattern (phaseranges[c] / (2 math.pi)), lam) # Replace amplitude with target amplitude targetamp = np.sqrt(targetrgb[:,:, c]) fieldc = fieldc / (np.abs(fieldc) + 1e-8) targetamp # Backward propagation to SLM plane phasepatternc = propagateback(fieldc, lam) # Update phase pattern (e.g., average or weighted update) # Standard GS update rule: phasepattern = angle(phasepatternc) # This is a simplification; actual implementation may use weighted averaging # or specific optimization loss functions. phasepattern = np.angle(phasepatternc) # 4. Quantize to SLM bit depth # Assuming 8-bit SLM for implementation, though 6-bit is sufficient per sources. phasepattern = np.round(phasepattern / (2 math.pi) 255) / 255 (2 math.pi) return phasepattern Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Standard SLM Behavior: If the SLM has a uniform 0-2\pi range across all colors, perfect copies (replicas) appear at specific depth planes, degrading image quality. Quantization Errors: As the phase range increases, the limited bit depth of the SLM becomes more noticeable, potentially increasing quantization noise. Dispersion Control: The user has minimal control over the absolute wavelength \lambda or the material dispersion -dn/d\lambda; these are fixed by the hardware. Generates multiple focal points simultaneously. It does not explicitly address wavelength-dependent replica reduction but may benefit from extended phase range to reduce crosstalk between focal planes. Link Uses algorithms to approximate complex fields with phase-only masks. Extended phase range is a hardware-specific modulation technique that can be combined with these approximations to improve quality. Link Time Complexity: Determined by the underlying CGH generation algorithm (e.g., Gerchberg-Saxton iterations). The extended phase range adds negligible computational overhead, primarily affecting the phase wrapping/constraint step. Memory Complexity: Standard for CGH generation. Measured Performance: Simulation using Holoeye Pluto-2.1-Vis-016 (Red: 2.4\pi, Green: 5.9\pi, Blue: 7.4\pi) showed substantial reduction in depth replicas compared to a uniform 2\pi SLM. This improves target plane hologram quality and creates defocused content at other depths, reducing high-frequency out-of-focus light at the sensor plane. Strengths: Effectively breaks wavelength-depth ambiguity; reduces ghost images in simultaneous color holography; improves accommodation cues. Limitations: Requires specific SLM hardware with high dispersion and extended phase range; quantization errors increase with phase range if bit depth is insufficient (though stable above 6 bits). When to use: Simultaneous color holography on single SLMs where depth replicas are a significant artifact. When not to use: Monochromatic holography (where wavelength dependence is irrelevant) or when using SLMs with uniform 0-2\pi response. The technique was proposed to address the limitation of placing content arbitrarily in 3D volume and the issue of in-focus images appearing at out-of-focus depths, which hinders accommodation. It builds on the understanding that standard 0-2\pi SLMs produce perfect copies at replica planes. The method leverages the physical properties of Liquid Crystal materials, specifically the refractive index difference \Delta n and dispersion -dn/d\lambda, to create wavelength-dependent phase shifts. The specific implementation details and simulation results were published by Kim et al. in 2023.
