name: Inverse Design Algorithm for Voxel-based CGVHs
head: Iterative Propagation Algorithm (IPA) for mode conversion
body: The Inverse Design Algorithm for Voxel-based Computer-Generated Volume Holograms (CGVHs) is a method for designing holographic structures that convert N mutually incoherent transverse input modes \{un\} into N target modes \{vn\} with a one-to-one mapping. It optimizes the refractive index distribution within a 3D volume to achieve specific mode conversion efficiencies. Unlike direct forward calculation methods, this algorithm uses an iterative approach to select voxel distributions that maximize the overlap between propagated fields and target modes. It is distinguished from sibling methods by its reliance on a split-step Fourier Beam Propagation Method (BPM) and a local multi-objective criterion to select from a discrete set of pre-defined transverse voxel profiles. Inputs: N: Number of input/target mode pairs. \{un\}{n=1}^N: Input mode field distributions defined at plane z{in} = z1. \{vn\}{n=1}^N: Target mode field distributions defined at plane z{out} = z{K+1}. \lambdan: Wavelength associated with mode pair n. nn: Bulk refractive index of the sample at wavelength \lambdan. D: Number of available transverse voxel distributions \{\Delta RId\}{d=0}^D. \Delta RI0 is the null modification. I, J, K: Grid dimensions of the sample volume. Dx, Dy, Dz: Spatial extensions of sub-volumes v{ijk}. dx, dy, dz: Simulation spatial resolutions. Outputs: Selected voxel distribution index d^{ijk} for each sub-volume v{ijk} (1 \le i \le I, 1 \le j \le J, 1 \le k \le K). The sample volume is virtually split into sub-volumes v{ijk} acting as placeholders for elementary voxel distributions. Grid: 3D array of indices (i, j, k). Sub-volume v{ijk}: Defined by spatial extent Dx \times Dy \times Dz. Voxel Distributions: A discrete set of D+1 transverse refractive index change profiles \Delta RId(x,y). These are relative to the bulk index nn. Field Storage: Complex 2D arrays storing transverse field distributions u{ijk}^n and v{ijk}^n at each plane zk. Elementary Length: Dz = 10 \mu m (typical). Simulation Resolution: dx = dy = 0.25 \mu m, dz = 0.5 \mu m (typical). Coordinate System: Rectangular (O, x, y, z), with z as the propagation direction. Phase multiplication model: Crossing a layer of thickness dz through a homogeneous medium nn, followed by a local phase \phi{ijk}, is modeled as: \phi{ijk}(\lambdan) = \exp\left(i \frac{2\pi}{\lambdan} \Delta RI{ijk}^d(\lambdan) dz\right), \quad 0 \le d \le D. Maximization criterion: The squared l2 distance minimization O{min} = \min \sum{n=1}^N \|un - vn\|2^2 is transformed into a maximization problem for lossless designs (where \|un\|^2 and \|vn\|^2 are conserved): O{max} = \max{\Delta RI{ijk}^d} \sum{n=1}^N \int{z{out}} \Re(vn^ un). Local selection criterion: The optimal distribution for sub-volume v{ijk} maximizes: O{ijk}^{max} = \maxd \sum{n=1}^N \int{z{k+1}} \Re\left((v{ijk+1}^n)^ u{ijk+1}^n(d)\right) where u{ijk+1}^n(d) is the input mode propagated from zk to z{k+1} through \Delta RI{ijk}^d. 1. Initialization: Set all sub-volumes v{ijk} to the null distribution \Delta RI0. 2. Forward Propagation: Propagate input modes \{un\} from z1 to z{K+1} using split-step Fourier BPM with resolutions dx, dy, dz. Cross sub-volumes v{ijk} layer by layer for k from 1 to K. During propagation, save the transverse distributions \{un\} before crossing each v{ijk}, noting them \{u{ijk}^n\} for reference. Note \{zk\} as the common transverse planes where distributions are saved. 3. Convergence Check: Compute the final overlap criterion O{max} to monitor convergence. If satisfactory or stagnant, exit and consider the current selection optimal. 4. Backward Propagation and Voxel Selection: Iteratively backpropagate target modes \{vn\} from z{out}=z{K+1} to z{in}=z1. For a given k, select the distribution d that maximizes the local multi-objective criterion O{ijk}^{max}. To find d, try all distributions \{\Delta RI{ijk}^d\} for each sub-volume v{ijk} (k fixed). After selecting \{\Delta RI{ijk}^d\} for a given k, backpropagate target modes \{v{ijk+1}^n\} to plane zk, and repeat iteratively until k=1. 5. Iteration: Repeat steps 2-4. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import numpy as np def splitstepbpm(fieldin, dz, nbulk, wavelength): """Standard split-step Fourier BPM propagation through homogeneous medium.""" k0 = 2 np.pi / wavelength # Propagation phase in frequency domain kx = np.fft.fftfreq(fieldin.shape[1], d=0.25e-6) 2 np.pi ky = np.fft.fftfreq(fieldin.shape[0], d=0.25e-6) 2 np.pi KX, KY = np.meshgrid(kx, ky) kz = np.sqrt((nbulk k0)2 - KX2 - KY2) phase = np.exp(1j kz dz) fieldfft = np.fft.fft2(fieldin) fieldfft = phase return np.fft.ifft2(fieldfft) def backpropagatelayer(fieldin, dz, deltari, wavelength, nb): """Reverse phase multiplication and reverse homogeneous propagation.""" phase = np.exp(-1j 2 np.pi / wavelength deltari dz) fieldprop = fieldin phase return splitstepbpm(fieldprop, -dz, nb, wavelength) def inversedesignCGVH(N, modesu, modesv, wavelengths, nbulk, voxeldistributions, I, J, K, Dz, dx, dy, dz): """ Inverse design algorithm for voxel-based CGVHs. """ H, W = modesu[0].shape selectedvoxels = np.zeros((I, J, K), dtype=int) # ufields[k][n] stores field at plane zk for mode n ufields = [np.zeros((I, J, N, H, W), dtype=complex) for in range(K + 1)] # vfields[k][n] stores field at plane zk for mode n vfields = [np.zeros((I, J, N, H, W), dtype=complex) for in range(K + 1)] prevoverlap = 0.0 maxiterations = 100 for iteration in range(maxiterations): # Step 1: Forward Propagation for n in range(N): ufields[0][:,:, n,:,:] = modesu[n] for k in range(K): for i in range(I): for j in range(J): d = selectedvoxels[i, j, k] deltari = voxeldistributions[d] for n in range(N): # Propagate from zk to z{k+1} ufields[k+1][i, j, n,:,:] = splitstepbpm( ufields[k][i, j, n,:,:], dz, nbulk, wavelengths[n]) # Local phase multiplication phase = np.exp(1j 2 np.pi / wavelengths[n] deltari dz) ufields[k+1][i, j, n,:,:] = phase # Step 2: Convergence Check totaloverlap = 0.0 for n in range(N): overlap = np.sum(np.conj(modesv[n]) ufields[K][:,:, n,:,:]) totaloverlap += np.real(overlap) if iteration > 0 and abs(totaloverlap - prevoverlap) < 1e-6: break prevoverlap = totaloverlap # Step 3: Backward Propagation and Voxel Selection for n in range(N): vfields[K][:,:, n,:,:] = modesv[n] for k in range(K - 1, -1, -1): for i in range(I): for j in range(J): bestd = 0 bestcriterion = -np.inf uin = ufields[k][i, j,:,:,:] vtarget = vfields[k+1][i, j,:,:,:] for d in range(len(voxeldistributions)): deltari = voxeldistributions[d] localcriterion = 0.0 for n in range(N): unext = splitstepbpm(uin[n,:,:], dz, nbulk, wavelengths[n]) phase = np.exp(1j 2 np.pi / wavelengths[n] deltari dz) unext = phase overlap = np.real(np.sum(np.conj(vtarget[n,:,:]) unext)) localcriterion += overlap if localcriterion > bestcriterion: bestcriterion = localcriterion bestd = d selectedvoxels[i, j, k] = bestd deltaribest = voxeldistributions[bestd] for n in range(N): vfields[k][i, j, n,:,:] = backpropagatelayer( vtarget[n,:,:], dz, deltaribest, wavelengths[n], nbulk) return selectedvoxels Precision: The simulation resolution dx, dy, dz must be much smaller than the feature size to ensure numerical accuracy. Typical values are dx=dy=0.25 \mu m and dz=0.5 \mu m. Wavelength Dependence: The voxel distributions \Delta RId may be wavelength-dependent, requiring the algorithm to use the correct \Delta RId(\lambdan) for each mode n. Convergence Monitoring: The algorithm monitors stagnation of the overlap metric to determine termination. Complexity: Each iteration involves K forward propagation steps and K backward propagation steps. In each step, for each sub-volume, all D voxel distributions are tested. The complexity per iteration is O(K \cdot I \cdot J \cdot D \cdot N \cdot \text{BPM\cost}). Memory: Requires storing fields at all K+1 planes for all N modes, plus the voxel distributions. Memory complexity is O(K \cdot I \cdot J \cdot N \cdot H \cdot W). Strengths: Allows for the design of complex 3D structures for multi-mode conversion using a discrete set of transverse voxel profiles. Limitations: The solution depends on the initial guess (all null) and the set of available voxel distributions. The maximization criterion is derived specifically for lossless designs where \|un\|^2 and \|vn\|^2 are conserved. The algorithm was proposed in the context of designing computer-generated volume holograms (CGVHs) in glass for mode conversion. It is based on the Iterative Propagation Algorithm (IPA) [50], which maximizes the overlap integral between propagated fields and target fields. Design and manufacturing of efficient computer-generated volume holograms in glass, https://www.researchgate.net/publication/363920430Designandmanufacturingofefficientcomputer-generatedvolumehologramsinglass, fetched 2026-11-03 (unofficial)

name: Multiple Wavefront Recording Planes (WRP) with Horizontal Parallax Only (HPO)
head: Fast CGH method for point clouds, HPO WRP method
body: This method generates computer-generated holograms (CGH) for point clouds by distributing the calculation across multiple parallel wavefront recording planes (WRPs) to handle occlusion and reduce computational load, specifically adapted for Horizontal Parallax Only (HPO) displays. It differs from full-parallax WRP methods by computing point contributions to 1D hololines rather than the full 2D plane, and from naive point-source summation by using pre-computed look-up tables (LUTs) and band-limited angular spectrum propagation to manage the high spatial bandwidth product (SBP) required for wide viewing angles. Inputs: Point cloud data: Set of M points, each with 3D coordinates (xi, yi, zi) and RGB color values. Display parameters: Pixel pitch px, py, resolution Nx, Ny, wavelength \lambda, and number of WRPs. Hologram geometry: HPO configuration where diffraction is computed only along horizontal lines (hololines). Outputs: Complex-valued hologram data for the HPO display. Data Structures: Point Cloud: Array of structures containing position (x, y, z) and color (R, G, B). Look-Up Table (LUT): Pre-computed complex propagation kernels for a specific distance z. The LUT stores the complex amplitude H(u, v; z) in the frequency domain, modified by a random phase mask for diffuse reflection modeling. Wavefront Recording Planes (WRPs): A set of parallel planes positioned between the object (point cloud) and the hologram plane. Each WRP holds a complex field representing the wavefront at that depth. Hololines: 1D arrays representing the hologram data for a single vertical row of the display. Parameters: \lambda: Wavelength of reconstruction light (e.g., 640 nm). px, py: Horizontal and vertical pixel pitches (e.g., 0.55 µm, 23.4 µm). Nx, Ny: Resolution of the hologram plane (e.g., 32,768 × 768). z{min}: Minimum object-to-hologram distance to satisfy Shannon criterion, calculated as z{min} = \frac{N p^2}{\lambda}. \theta: Maximum diffraction angle, determined by \sin \theta = \frac{\lambda}{2p}. Steps: 1. Point Volume Attribution: Assign a Gaussian distribution profile to each point in the point cloud to model a continuous volume rather than a singular point. This generates smoother, continuous surface reconstructions. The amplitude Ai of point i at a distance r from its center is modeled as: Ai(r) = A{0,i} \exp\left(-\frac{r^2}{2\sigma^2}\right) where \sigma controls the spread [G: \sigma is typically chosen based on the desired surface smoothness and pixel pitch; not explicitly defined in sources, but implied by "Gaussian distribution profile"]. 2. LUT Generation (Source Plane to First WRP): Pre-compute the propagation kernel from the point source plane to the first WRP distance z{LUT}. Calculate the angular spectrum transfer function H(u, v; z{LUT}) using the Band-Limited Angular Spectrum Method (BL-ASM). Apply a random phase mask to the LUT content to account for diffuse reflections, scattering light over a wide angular range. Store the complex kernel H{LUT}(u, v) in the LUT. 3. Inter-WRP Propagation: Propagate the wavefield from one WRP to the next parallel WRP using BL-ASM. For each WRP pair separated by distance \Delta z, compute the transfer function H(u, v; \Delta z). Apply BL-ASM constraints: double the calculation window area in the source plane by padding with zeros, perform FFT, multiply by the transfer function, and IFFT, then crop the output to the original window size to avoid edge errors from circular convolution. 4. HPO Hololine Computation: Adapt the standard WRP method for HPO by computing contributions only to 1D hololines. For each point i, determine its contribution to the hololines on the hologram plane. Instead of propagating to the full 2D hologram plane, propagate the wavefield from the last WRP to the hologram plane along the horizontal direction only. Use inverted Gaussian filters during propagation to model occlusions, locally blocking light from points behind others. 5. Superposition: Sum the complex contributions from all points i onto the respective hololines of the hologram plane [G: Standard superposition principle for CGH]. 6. Color Channel Handling: For colour holograms, compute the hologram for a single reference wavelength (e.g., red, 640 nm) but assign RGB intensity values to the points. The final hologram consists of three channels computed with the same wavelength but different intensities per point to maintain colour information and wide viewing angle. 7. Quantization (Optional): If using a phase-only SLM, quantize the complex field Uh(x, y) to phase values 0 to 2\pi [G: Standard phase-only encoding techniques such as detour phase or error diffusion may be applied, but specific algorithm details are not provided in the source]. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import numpy as np def computetransferfunction(distance, wavelength, px, Ny, Nx): """Compute the band-limited angular spectrum transfer function H(u,v;z).""" u = np.fft.fftfreq(Nx, d=px) v = np.fft.fftfreq(Ny, d=px) U, V = np.meshgrid(u, v) # w calculation: w = (lambda^-2 - u^2 - v^2)^0.5 wsq = (1.0 / wavelength2) - U2 - V2 w = np.zeroslike(wsq) w[wsq >= 0] = np.sqrt(wsq[wsq >= 0]) H = np.exp(1j 2 np.pi w distance) # Band-limiting: H'(u,v;z) = H(u,v;z) rect(u/2ulimit) rect(v/2vlimit) ulimit = 1.0 / (2 px) vlimit = 1.0 / (2 px) rectu = np.abs(U) <= ulimit rectv = np.abs(V) <= vlimit H = H rectu rectv return H def propagateblasm2d(field, transferfunc, wavelength, px, Ny, Nx): """Band-Limited Angular Spectrum propagation with zero-padding and cropping.""" # Double the calculation window area by padding with zeros Nypad, Nxpad = 2 Ny, 2 Nx fieldpadded = np.zeros((Nypad, Nxpad), dtype=complex) fieldpadded[:Ny,:Nx] = field # Resize transfer function to match padded grid spacing upad = np.fft.fftfreq(Nxpad, d=px / 2) vpad = np.fft.fftfreq(Nypad, d=px / 2) Upad, Vpad = np.meshgrid(upad, vpad) wsqpad = (1.0 / wavelength2) - Upad2 - Vpad2 wpad = np.zeroslike(wsqpad) wpad[wsqpad >= 0] = np.sqrt(wsqpad[wsqpad >= 0]) Hpad = np.exp(1j 2 np.pi wpad transferfunc.shape[0] / Ny) # Scale distance proportionally ulimit = 1.0 / (2 (px / 2)) vlimit = 1.0 / (2 (px / 2)) Hpad = Hpad (np.abs(Upad) <= ulimit) (np.abs(Vpad) <= vlimit) # FFT, multiply, IFFT F = np.fft.fft2(fieldpadded) G = F Hpad fieldoutpadded = np.fft.ifft2(G) # Crop to original window size return fieldoutpadded[:Ny,:Nx] def propagateblasm1d(fieldrow, distance, wavelength, px, Nx): """1D BL-ASM propagation for HPO hololines.""" u = np.fft.fftfreq(Nx, d=px) U = u.reshape(1, -1) wsq = (1.0 / wavelength2) - U2 w = np.zeroslike(wsq) w[wsq >= 0] = np.sqrt(wsq[wsq >= 0]) H = np.exp(1j 2 np.pi w distance) # Band-limiting ulimit = 1.0 / (2 px) H = H (np.abs(U) <= ulimit) F = np.fft.fft(fieldrow) G = F H return np.fft.ifft(G) def applyinvertedgaussianocclusion(field, centerx, centery, sigma): """Locally block light using an inverted Gaussian filter to model occlusions.""" Ny, Nx = field.shape y, x = np.mgrid[0:Ny, 0:Nx] distsq = (x - centerx)2 + (y - centery)2 occlusion = 1.0 - np.exp(-distsq / (2 sigma2)) return field occlusion def generatehpowrpcgh(points, displayparams, wrpdistances, lutdistance): """ Generate HPO CGH using Multiple WRP method. Args: points: List of dicts with keys 'x', 'y', 'z', 'r', 'g', 'b'. displayparams: Dict with 'lambda', 'px', 'py', 'Nx', 'Ny'. wrpdistances: List of z-distances for each WRP plane. lutdistance: Distance for LUT generation. Returns: hologram: 2D array (Ny, Nx) of complex values. """ wavelength = displayparams['lambda'] px = displayparams['px'] Nx = displayparams['Nx'] Ny = displayparams['Ny'] # Initialize hologram plane hologram = np.zeros((Ny, Nx), dtype=complex) # Step 1 & 2: LUT Generation lut = computetransferfunction(lutdistance, wavelength, px, Ny, Nx) randomphase = np.exp(1j 2 np.pi np.random.rand(Ny, Nx)) lut = randomphase # Initialize WRPs wrpfields = [np.zeros((Ny, Nx), dtype=complex) for in range(len(wrpdistances))] # Step 1: Project points to first WRP for point in points: dz = wrpdistances[0] - point['z'] if dz <= 0: continue # Map point to grid indices ix = int(point['x'] / px) iy = int(point['y'] / px) sigma = px # [G: Typical spread relative to pixel pitch] # Create sparse source field with Gaussian attribution sourcefield = np.zeros((Ny, Nx), dtype=complex) y, x = np.mgrid[0:Ny, 0:Nx] distsq = (x - ix)2 + (y - iy)2 amp = point['r'] np.exp(-distsq px2 / (2 sigma2)) sourcefield = amp # Propagate to first WRP using LUT (BL-ASM) wrpfields[0] += propagateblasm2d(sourcefield, lut, wavelength, px, Ny, Nx) # Step 3: Inter-WRP Propagation for i in range(len(wrpdistances) - 1): dz = wrpdistances[i+1] - wrpdistances[i] h = computetransferfunction(dz, wavelength, px, Ny, Nx) wrpfields[i+1] = propagateblasm2d(wrpfields[i], h, wavelength, px, Ny, Nx) # Step 4: HPO Hololine Computation & Step 5: Superposition dzfinal = displayparams['zhologram'] - wrpdistances[-1] for y in range(Ny): fieldrow = wrpfields[-1][y,:] # 1D BL-ASM propagation to hologram plane hologramrow = propagateblasm1d(fieldrow, dzfinal, wavelength, px, Nx) # Apply inverted Gaussian occlusion filter if needed # [G: Occlusion centers would be derived from point cloud depth ordering] hologramrow = applyinvertedgaussianocclusion(hologramrow, Nx//2, 0, px) hologram[y,:] += hologramrow return hologram POS-WRP is a rendering pipeline that encodes mesh-based 3D scenes into complex-valued wave fields with fine-grained textures, photo-realistic shadings, and perspective depth cues. It solves the problem of maintaining continuous depth cues and realistic illumination when projecting from perspective scene space to the orthogonal space of a Spatial Light Modulator (SLM). Unlike standard wave propagation which assumes paraxial orthogonal propagation, POS-WRP explicitly transforms mesh coordinates and textures to correct for projection discrepancies, delivering high-fidelity data with reduced speckle artifacts. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Requires storage for the point cloud, K WRP fields, and the LUT. Each WRP field is O(N) complex numbers. The LUT is O(N). Total memory is O(K \cdot N + N). For high-resolution holograms (e.g., 32,768 × 768), this can be significant. Measured Performance: Demonstrated on a Holografika HoloVizio 722RC light field display with 32,768 × 768 pixel resolution, 0.55 µm horizontal pitch, and 640 nm wavelength. The method supports a viewing angle of 70°. Strengths: Handles occlusion naturally through the WRP structure and inverted Gaussian filters. High-quality reconstructions with smooth surfaces due to Gaussian volume attribution. Wide field of view achieved through diffuse reflection modeling (random phase LUTs). Efficient for HPO by reducing 2D propagation to 1D hololines. Limitations: HPO results in constrained viewing zones and astigmatic output due to diminished vertical resolution. Small pixel pitch leads to strong light field diffusion beyond computation window borders, requiring BL-ASM and zero-padding, which increases computational overhead. Aperiodic functions cause edge errors in FFT, mitigated by BL-ASM but not eliminated. Limited to point clouds; mesh-based scenes require different handling (see POS-WRP). When to Use: Use for point cloud data on HPO displays requiring wide viewing angles and high resolution. When Not to Use: Avoid for full-parallax holography, mesh-based scenes with complex textures (use POS-WRP), or when computational resources are too limited for BL-ASM overhead. The Multiple WRP method was originally proposed for fast computation of holograms supporting full parallax. It was adapted for HPO displays to leverage the specific constraints of light field displays, such as the Holografika HoloVizio 722RC. The method builds on the Angular Spectrum method for wave propagation and incorporates Band-Limited Angular Spectrum (BL-ASM) to handle the high spatial bandwidth product of modern holographic displays. name: Phase-Only Wave Field Reconstruction/Propagation (POS-WRP)
head: POS-WRP, Perspective-to-Orthogonal Smooth Wave field Rendering Pipeline (POS-WRP)
body: POS-WRP is a rendering pipeline that encodes mesh-based 3D scenes into complex-valued wave fields with fine-grained textures, photo-realistic shadings, and perspective depth cues. It solves the problem of maintaining continuous depth cues and realistic illumination when projecting from perspective scene space to the orthogonal space of a Spatial Light Modulator (SLM). Unlike standard wave propagation which assumes paraxial orthogonal propagation, POS-WRP explicitly transforms mesh coordinates and textures to correct for projection discrepancies, delivering high-fidelity data with reduced speckle artifacts. Inputs: 3D scene data: Mesh geometry (vertices, faces) and lighting data captured through a perspective camera. Pre-defined output texture dimensions. Outputs: Complex-valued wave field representation of the scene at the hologram plane. Specifically, the amplitude is derived from baked textures, and the phase is processed for SLM compatibility. Data Structures: Mesh: Standard polygonal mesh representation. Texture: 2D array storing physical illumination values (amplitude). Wave Field: Complex-valued array U(x,y) representing the field at the SLM plane. Parameters: Processing time for POS-WRP component: 24.96 seconds per hologram. Spatial sampling rate: Assumed sufficient such that visual loss from ignoring diffraction at occlusion edges is negligible. Steps: 1. Input Acquisition: Load the 3D scene comprising meshes and lighting data from a perspective camera view. 2. Texture Baking (Amplitude Generation): Employ a Physically Based Rendering (PBR) pipeline to bake rendering outcomes onto a pre-defined output texture. The texture stores physical illumination, which serves as the amplitude A(x,y) of the wave field across mesh facets. Occlusion Handling: During baking, obstructed portions of a facet are rendered black (zero amplitude). This adheres to geometric optics principles. Diffraction at occlusion edges is not explicitly accounted for, relying on facet size and sampling rate to render visual loss negligible. 3. Coordinate Transformation: Transform mesh coordinates and textures from perspective scene space to orthogonal SLM space to maintain consistency with the orthogonal projection required for wave field propagation from the SLM. 4. Tilted Plane Propagation & Phase Smoothing: Process the transformed meshes and textures through tilted plane propagation. Incorporate an additional phase smoothing step to generate a relatively smooth target phase. This mitigates artifacts caused by SLM crosstalk. 5. Wave Field Propagation: Use spectral resampling and the Angular Spectrum Method (ASM) to propagate each tilted facet of the mesh scene to the hologram plane. This creates the final complex-valued wave field representation of the entire scene. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def poswrppipeline(meshscene, lightingdata, cameraparams, textureresolution): """ Implements the Phase-Only Wave Field Reconstruction/Propagation (POS-WRP) pipeline. Args: meshscene: List of mesh objects with geometry and material properties. lightingdata: Light sources and environment map. cameraparams: Perspective camera intrinsics and extrinsics. textureresolution: (width, height) of the output texture. Returns: complexwavefield: Complex-valued array representing the wave field at the hologram plane. """ # Step 1: Input 3D scene comprises meshes and lighting data captured through a perspective camera. # (Data is already in input variables) # Step 2: Texture Baking # Employ physically based rendering (PBR) pipelines to bake rendering outcomes onto a pre-defined output texture. # The texture contains physical illumination serving as the amplitude. amplitudetexture = bakepbrtexture( meshes=meshscene, lights=lightingdata, camera=cameraparams, resolution=textureresolution) # Occlusion handling is naturally integrated during baking. # Obstructed portions are rendered black (zero amplitude). # Note: Diffraction at occlusion edges is not explicitly accounted for. # Step 3: Coordinate Transformation # Transform mesh coordinates and textures from perspective scene space to orthogonal SLM space. # This ensures consistency with the orthogonal projection during wave field propagation. transformedmeshes = transformtoorthogonalspace( meshes=meshscene, cameraparams=cameraparams) transformedtexture = transformtexturecoordinates( texture=amplitudetexture, cameraparams=cameraparams) # Step 4: Tilted Plane Propagation and Phase Smoothing # Process transformed meshes and textures through tilted plane propagation. # Incorporate phase smoothing to mitigate SLM crosstalk artifacts. # This step generates a relatively smooth target phase. # Implementation detail: The specific smoothing algorithm is not detailed in the source, # but it is applied to the phase component derived from the tilted propagation. smoothedphase = applyphasesmoothing( meshes=transformedmeshes, texture=transformedtexture) # Step 5: Wave Field Propagation using ASM # Use spectral resampling and Angular Spectrum Method (ASM) to propagate each tilted facet # to the hologram plane. complexwavefield = propagatewithasm( meshes=transformedmeshes, amplitude=transformedtexture, phase=smoothedphase, method="spectralresamplingasm") return complexwavefield def bakepbrtexture(meshes, lights, camera, resolution): """ Simulates PBR baking. Returns a 2D array of amplitude values. Obstructed areas are 0.0. """ # Standard rasterization and shading calculation. # For each pixel in the output texture: # 1. Ray trace from camera through pixel into scene. # 2. If intersection with mesh: # a. Calculate shading using PBR model (lights, material). # b. Store result as amplitude. # 3. Else (occluded or no intersection): # a. Store 0.0 (black). return np.zeros(resolution) # Placeholder for actual PBR engine call def transformtoorthogonalspace(meshes, cameraparams): """ Transforms mesh vertices from perspective projection to orthogonal space compatible with SLM. """ # Apply inverse perspective projection and re-project to orthogonal coordinates. # The exact mathematical transformation depends on the specific camera-to-SLM mapping. # The source states this is done to maintain consistency with orthogonal propagation. return meshes # Placeholder for actual transformation logic def applyphasesmoothing(meshes, texture): """ Applies phase smoothing to mitigate SLM crosstalk. """ # The source mentions an "additional phase smoothing step" but does not provide the algorithm. # This would typically involve low-pass filtering the phase map or optimizing phase continuity. # Since the specific method is not given, we assume a generic smoothing operation. return np.zeroslike(texture) # Placeholder def propagatewithasm(meshes, amplitude, phase, method): """ Propagates the wave field from the mesh plane to the hologram plane using ASM. """ # Angular Spectrum Method implementation. # 1. Initialize complex field U = amplitude exp(i phase). # 2. Compute FFT of U. # 3. Multiply by transfer function H(fx, fy) = exp(i kz z). # 4. Compute IFFT to get propagated field. # The source specifies "spectral resampling" is used, implying interpolation in frequency domain. return np.zeroslike(amplitude) # Placeholder Time Complexity: The POS-WRP component takes 24.96 seconds per hologram. The total time for generating one phase-only hologram (including the subsequent PAGD optimization) is 54.96 seconds. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Delivers high-fidelity wave field data with continuous depth cues. Reduces speckle artifacts. Maintains perspective depth cues and realistic shadings which are typically lost in orthogonal propagation. Computationally efficient occlusion handling by using geometric optics (PBR) rather than wave-based masking. Limitations: Does not explicitly account for diffraction at occlusion edges, assuming visual loss is negligible due to sampling rate. Real-time hologram generation remains a goal for future exploration; current performance is not real-time. When to use: When high-fidelity, photo-realistic holographic reconstruction from mesh data is required, and continuous depth cues are critical. When not to use: When real-time performance is strictly required, or when diffraction effects at occlusion edges are visually significant for the specific resolution and scene scale. Origin: The method was introduced in the paper "Mesh-represented and learning-empowered hologram synthesis for full 3D holographic displays". Context: It is part of a framework that also includes the Phase-Aware Gradient Descent (PAGD) algorithm for encoding the complex wave field into phase-only holograms. Development: The method addresses challenges in end-to-end holographic display frameworks where tightly coupled approaches may lack robustness. It aims to bridge the disparity in wavefront propagation between simulation and physical display systems. name: Layer-Based Holographic Algorithm
head: Layer-Based Hologram Calculation, Layer-based CGH Calculation
body: The Layer-Based Holographic Algorithm calculates Computer-Generated Holograms (CGHs) by slicing a 3D scene into discrete parallel depth layers and numerically propagating their wavefields to the hologram plane. It distinguishes itself from point-cloud or volume-rendering methods by leveraging 2D Fourier transforms to efficiently compute the superposition of these layers, enabling real-time binocular color holography. Unlike continuous depth methods, it introduces visible separation artifacts at layer boundaries when applied to scenes with continuous depth ranges. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A 3D model represented as an 8-bit Computer Generated Depth Map (CGDM), where depth values range from 0 to 255. The model is sliced into L=256 parallel layers. Output: A complex amplitude distribution E{com}(x,y) on the holographic plane, which is subsequently quantized to a phase-only distribution Ep(x,y) for display on a Spatial Light Modulator (SLM). Data Structures: Layer Amplitude Map Ul(x,y): A 2D array representing the amplitude of the l-th depth layer. Random Phase Map r(x,y): A 2D array of random phase values superposed on each layer to simulate the diffusive effect of the object surface. Layer Distance zl: The scalar distance between the l-th layer and the holographic plane. Parameters: L = 256: Number of layers, derived from the 8-bit CGDM. \lambda: Wavelength of the reconstruction light. u, v: Spatial frequencies defined as u = \frac{\cos \alpha}{\lambda} and v = \frac{\cos \beta}{\lambda}, where \alpha and \beta are the angles between the incident wave and the x- and y-directions, respectively. FT: Fourier Transform operator. FT^{-1}: Inverse Fourier Transform operator. Algorithm Steps: 1. Slicing: Divide the 3D model into 256 parallel layers based on the 8-bit CGDM. 2. Phase Superposition: For each layer l, superpose a random phase r(x,y) onto the layer's amplitude Ul(x,y) to simulate surface diffusion. 3. Propagation Calculation: Compute the complex amplitude distribution E{com}(x,y) on the holographic plane by summing the contributions of all layers. The contribution of each layer is calculated by transforming the modulated layer amplitude to the frequency domain, applying a phase shift term representing propagation, and transforming back: E{com}(x,y) = \sum{l=0}^{255} FT^{-1} \left\{ FT \left\{ Ul(x,y) \exp[i r(x,y)] \right\} \exp \left[ i \frac{2\pi}{zl} \left( 1 - \lambda u - \frac{\lambda v}{\lambda} \right) \right] \right\} Note: The source formula contains the term \frac{\lambda v}{\lambda} which simplifies to v. The term \left( 1 - \lambda u - \frac{\lambda v}{\lambda} \right) appears in the source. 4. Phase Extraction: Extract the phase-only distribution Ep(x,y) from the complex amplitude E{com}(x,y) for use with a phase-only SLM. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def layerbasedhologram(layers, zl, lambdawavelength, alpha, beta): """ Calculate hologram using layer-based algorithm. Args: layers: List of 2D arrays Ul(x,y) for l in 0..255. zl: List of distances zl for each layer. lambdawavelength: Scalar wavelength lambda. alpha: Angle between incident wave and x-direction. beta: Angle between incident wave and y-direction. Returns: Ep: Phase-only hologram distribution. """ # Constants L = 256 u = cos(alpha) / lambdawavelength v = cos(beta) / lambdawavelength # Initialize complex amplitude sum Ecom = zeroslike(layers[0], dtype=complex) for l in range(L): Ul = layers[l] z = zl[l] # Generate random phase map r(x,y) for this layer # In practice, r(x,y) is typically generated per layer or globally. # The source implies superposition on each layer. r = randomphasemap(shape=Ul.shape) # Modulate amplitude with random phase modulatedlayer = Ul exp(1j r) # Forward Fourier Transform freqdomain = FT(modulatedlayer) # Propagation phase shift # Source formula: exp[i (2pi/zl) (1 - lambdau - lambdav/lambda)] # Note: lambdav/lambda simplifies to v. phaseshift = exp(1j (2 pi / z) (1 - lambdawavelength u - v)) # Apply phase shift propagatedfreq = freqdomain phaseshift # Inverse Fourier Transform propagatedspace = FTinverse(propagatedfreq) # Sum contributions Ecom += propagatedspace # Extract phase-only distribution Ep = angle(Ecom) return Ep Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Continuous Depth Artifacts: When applied to VR scenes with continuous depth ranges, the discrete layering creates visible separation artifacts at layer boundaries. This makes the method suitable for AR content with isolated 3D models but not ideal for continuous VR scenes. Optical Misalignment: Experimental prototypes may suffer from reduced imaging quality due to optical component misalignment, geometric aberrations, and chromatic aberrations. Computes left and right holograms by propagating light waves from compensated depth layers to the hologram plane using 2D IFFTs. Distinguished by its specific reliance on 2D IFFTs for high-resolution binocular color holography on hardware accelerators. Performance: Capable of computing binocular color holograms at over 35 frames per second on an NVIDIA Jetson AGX Orin embedded platform for a resolution of 2048 \times 1024. Strengths: Enables real-time, standalone holographic near-eye displays with full-color reconstruction and accurate focus cues. Reduces speckle noise when combined with SLED illumination. Limitations: Not suitable for scenes with continuous depth extents due to layer boundary artifacts. Limited field-of-view remains a challenge for holographic near-eye displays. Imaging quality may be lower than consumer stereoscopic displays due to optical imperfections. The method is described as a real-time hologram calculation technique for binocular color holograms. It employs an 8-bit CGDM to slice 3D models into 256 parallel layers. The approach is utilized in holographic near-eye displays and 3D display systems using depth maps generated by 2D-to-3D rendering. name: Layer-based diffraction
head: FFT-based holographic computation, Layer-based CGH Calculation, Layer-based hologram generation, Layer-based holographic rendering method, Layer-based method
body: Layer-based diffraction computes left and right holograms by numerically propagating light waves from compensated depth layers towards the hologram plane and summing them. It generates high-quality holographic patterns for a Spatial Light Modulator (SLM) from RGB-D 3D scene data by computing optical field distributions on the eye lens plane using 2D Inverse Fast Fourier Transforms (IFFTs). It is distinguished from sibling methods by its specific reliance on 2D IFFTs for both the optical field distribution and hologram pattern computations, enabling high-resolution binocular color holography on hardware accelerators. Inputs and Outputs Input: RGB-D 3D image data representing the 3D image projected onto the viewer's retina plane. The data format consists of Red, Green, Blue, and Depth channels. Output: A single combined hologram pattern for the SLM, derived from simultaneously processed left and right eye images. Data Structures Complex Numbers: Stored in memory using exactly 32 bits. Number Representation: Fixed-point number representation is used for all data processing and IFFT multiplications. Hologram Levels: The amplitude-only hologram is quantized onto L=256 discrete levels. Steps 1. Receive Input: Obtain the RGB-D 3D image data from rendering software or a 3D camera. 2. Compute Optical Field: Compute the optical field distribution on the eye lens plane from the retina plane image. 3. Compute Hologram Patterns: Compute the holographic patterns to be applied to the SLM from the eye lens plane distributions. 4. Execute 2D IFFTs: Perform 2D IFFT computations for the field distribution and pattern computations. The 2D IFFTs are computed using the row-column method, where 1-D IFFTs are performed on rows and then columns. 5. Process Binocular Images: Process right and left eye images simultaneously. 6. Combine: Combine the two eye images into a single hologram. 7. Quantize: Obtain the amplitude-only hologram H by shifting, scaling, and quantizing the real part of the complex-valued object wave O onto L=256 discrete levels. Formulas The complex-valued object wave O(x, y; c) is the sum of propagated waves from Nz compensated depth layers: O(x, y; c) = \sum{i=0}^{Nz-1} P{\hat{z}i} \{ Ui \} (x, y; c) where c is the color channel. The propagation of a layer Ui from depth \hat{z}i is given by the Fourier transform: P{\hat{z}i} \{ Ui \} = \frac{\exp(j \lambdac \hat{z}i)}{j \lambdac \hat{z}i} \mathcal{F} \left\{ Ui(\xi, \eta; c) \exp\left( \frac{j \pi (\xi^2 + \eta^2)}{\lambdac \hat{z}i} \right) \exp\left( -\frac{j \pi (x^2 + y^2)}{\lambdac \hat{z}i} \right) \right\} where: \lambdac is the wavelength of color channel c. \mathcal{F} is the forward Fourier transform. \hat{z}i is the intermediate compensated layer depth. Ui(\xi, \eta; c) is the field at the layer. The final amplitude-only hologram H is: H(x, y; c) = Q(\Re \{ O(x, y; c) \}, L, \Delta) where \Re \{ O \} is the real part of the object wave, L=256 is the number of discrete levels, and Q represents the quantization operation. Parameters Output Resolution: 3840 × 2160 pixels. Refresh Rate: 30 frames per second (fps). Quantization Levels: L = 256. Pitfalls Hardware Complexity: FFT-based layer methods are traditionally unsuitable for CGH hardware accelerators because large-scale FFT processors are difficult to build. This implementation overcomes that using a highly parallel architecture and hardware-reducing techniques. Precision: Fixed-point arithmetic is used to minimize bit depth, requiring careful management of precision to avoid artifacts in the IFFT multiplications. Pseudocode Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def layerbaseddiffraction(rgbddata, retinaplaneimage, eyelensparams, slmparams): """ Computes hologram from RGB-D data using layer-based diffraction. """ # Step 1: Receive Input (RGB-D format) # Step 2 & 3: Compute optical field on eye lens plane and SLM patterns # Step 5: Process right and left eyes simultaneously rightfield = computeeyelensfield(retinaplaneimage, eyelensparams, eye='right') rightpattern = computeslmpattern(rightfield, slmparams) leftfield = computeeyelensfield(retinaplaneimage, eyelensparams, eye='left') leftpattern = computeslmpattern(leftfield, slmparams) # Step 6: Combine into single hologram combinedhologram = combineholograms(rightpattern, leftpattern) # Step 7: Quantize to L=256 levels finalhologram = quantizehologram(combinedhologram, levels=256) return finalhologram def computeeyelensfield(retinaimage, params, eye): # Initialize complex field sum fieldsum = 0.0 + 0.0j Nz = params.numlayers for i in range(Nz): # Extract layer data Ui(xi, eta) for depth zhati Ui = getlayerdata(retinaimage, params.zhat[i]) # Propagate layer using diffraction formula propagated = propagatelayer(Ui, params.lambdac, params.zhat[i]) fieldsum += propagated return fieldsum def propagatelayer(Ui, lambdac, zhati): # Pre-computation phase factor phasefactor = math.exp(1j lambdac zhati) / (1j lambdac zhati) # Apply quadratic phase modulation to source coordinates (xi, eta) # The evidence formula includes a term with (x^2+y^2) inside the transform argument modulated = Ui math.exp(1j math.pi (Ui.coordsx2 + Ui.coordsy2) / (lambdac zhati)) modulated = math.exp(-1j math.pi (Ui.coordsx2 + Ui.coordsy2) / (lambdac zhati)) # Execute 2D IFFT/FFT as per row-column method fftresult = forwardfouriertransform(modulated) return phasefactor fftresult def forwardfouriertransform(data): # Standard 2D Discrete Fourier Transform (row-column method) rowtransformed = [fft1d(row) for row in data] coltransformed = [fft1d(col) for col in zip(rowtransformed)] return coltransformed def fft1d(signal): N = len(signal) result = [0.0 + 0.0j] N for k in range(N): for n in range(N): result[k] += signal[n] math.exp(-2j math.pi k n / N) return result def getlayerdata(retinaimage, depth): # Extract pixels matching the compensated layer depth zhati return retinaimage.filterbydepth(depth) def computeslmpattern(lensfield, slmparams): # FSU performs filtering, scaling, and pixel encoding # Pixel encoding converts complex number to integer using fixed-point representation encoded = pixelencodefixedpoint(lensfield) return encoded def pixelencodefixedpoint(complexval): # Fixed-point representation uses 32 bits for complex numbers # Convert real and imaginary parts to fixed-point integers realfixed = int(complexval.real (215)) & 0xFFFF imagfixed = int(complexval.imag (215)) & 0xFFFF return (realfixed << 16) | imagfixed def combineholograms(rightpattern, leftpattern): # Combine right and left eye images into a single hologram return rightpattern + leftpattern def quantizehologram(hologram, levels=256): # Shift, scale, and quantize the real part of O onto L discrete levels realpart = [[row.real for row in col] for col in hologram] minval = min(min(row) for row in realpart) maxval = max(max(row) for row in realpart) scale = (levels - 1) / (maxval - minval) if maxval != minval else 1.0 quantized = [[int((val - minval) scale) for val in row] for row in realpart] return quantized CGH algorithms that process the light field using Fresnel or other wavefront propagation methods. Unlike holographic stereograms, these can be applied globally or within hogels. Requires different propagation kernels for different depths, resulting in a different calculation per pixel, which may make parallelization more difficult. True depth-varying Fresnel method takes roughly O(m^4) operations. A single-plane approximation takes only O(m^2 \log m) operations. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Complex numbers are stored using exactly 32 bits. Fixed-point representation is used to minimize bit depth. Measured Performance: A single-chip FPGA implementation generates binocular holographic colour images with 3840 × 2160 pixels at 30 fps. Scenes with 8 million voxels are rendered at 30 fps. Scaling: The method is implemented on a single-chip FPGA, suggesting scalability through parallel architecture. Strengths: Generates high-quality holograms for real scenes. Enables real-time embedded rendering. Limitations: Historically, FFT-based layer methods were considered unsuitable for CGH hardware accelerators due to the difficulty of building large-scale FFT processors. When to use: When high-quality binocular color holography is required for real scenes, and hardware acceleration via FPGA is available. When not: When computational resources are limited to CPUs without specialized FFT hardware, as large-scale FFT processors are difficult to build. Origin: The method is used in holographic near-eye displays and slim-panel holographic video displays. History: Layer-based methods using FFTs were traditionally considered unsuitable for CGH hardware accelerators because FFT processors were difficult to build in large scale. Recent implementations have overcome this using highly parallel architectures. Usage: Implemented in a single-chip FPGA holographic video processor. Used to calculate CGH from Unity-rendered 3D scenes. name: Digital Hologram Numerical Reconstruction
head: ASM, Angular Spectrum Method, Fresnel Method
body: Digital Hologram Numerical Reconstruction computes the complex wavefield at a target plane from a recorded or computed hologram matrix, solving the inverse problem of optical propagation. It differs from sibling methods by focusing on the mathematical inversion of the diffraction integral (via Angular Spectrum or Fresnel approximations) rather than the physical setup [13993-holographic-reconstruction-system-setup.md] or the generation of the hologram itself Parent. The core mechanism propagates a complex field Uh(x,y) defined on the hologram plane to a reconstruction plane at distance z. The propagation is modeled in the spatial frequency domain. Let Uh(u,v) be the 2D Fourier Transform of the hologram field, where u,v are spatial frequencies. The transfer function H(u,v,z) depends on the chosen approximation: 1. Angular Spectrum Method (ASM): Exact for scalar diffraction, valid for near-field. H{ASM}(u,v,z) = \exp\left(i 2\pi z \sqrt{\frac{1}{\lambda^2} - u^2 - v^2}\right) Valid when \frac{1}{\lambda^2} - u^2 - v^2 \ge 0. Otherwise, the term is evanescent and decays. 2. Fresnel Method: Approximation for far-field or paraxial regimes. H{Fresnel}(u,v,z) = \exp\left(i \frac{2\pi z}{\lambda}\right) \exp\left(-i \pi \lambda z (u^2 + v^2)\right) The reconstructed field Uz(x,y) is obtained by: Uz(x,y) = \mathcal{F}^{-1} \left\{ \mathcal{F}\{Uh(x,y)\} \cdot H(u,v,z) \right\} Key shared constraints include: 1. Sampling Requirements: The pixel pitch \Delta x and wavelength \lambda must satisfy the Nyquist criterion for the highest spatial frequency in the transfer function to avoid aliasing. 2. Complexity: The FFT-based approach scales as O(N^2 \log N) for an N \times N hologram, significantly faster than direct summation. Describes the physical apparatus (SLM, lenses, cameras) required to convert the numerically reconstructed complex wavefield into a visible optical image [13993-holographic-reconstruction-system-setup.md]. It addresses hardware-specific constraints like phase-only encoding, pixel crosstalk, and diffraction order filtering, which are absent in pure numerical methods. A post-processing step applied after the absolute value extraction of the reconstructed wavefield. It involves clipping extreme intensity values at a user-defined percentile threshold and applying linear histogram stretching to enhance contrast before final image generation. The method is implemented in tools that allow users to configure wavelength, pixel pitch, and reconstruction method (ASM or Fresnel) via external configuration files to avoid re-declaration. It is used to reconstruct datasets such as "Dices 8K" (using ASM at z=0.004 m) and "Skull" (using Fresnel at z=0.169 m). The output is typically saved as a standard PNG image. Recent Advances in the Processing and Rendering Algorithms for Computer-Generated Holography, https://doi.org/10.3390/electronics8050556, fetched 2026-10-26

name: Holographic Reconstruction System Setup
head: Experimental setup for holographic reconstruction, Optical setup for holographic reconstruction, Phase-Only Holographic Display
body: This article describes the physical optical apparatus required to reconstruct a complex wavefield computed numerically (see Digital Hologram Numerical Reconstruction) into a visible image. It solves the problem of converting digital hologram matrices into optical fields using spatial light modulators (SLMs), handling the constraints of phase-only or amplitude-only modulation, and filtering out diffraction artifacts. It differs from pure numerical reconstruction by introducing physical components (lasers, lenses, SLMs, cameras) and their calibration. The system converts a digital hologram into a physical wavefront using coherent illumination, spatial light modulation, and optical filtering. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Digital hologram matrix (complex or real-valued), system parameters (wavelength, pixel pitch, distance). Output: Reconstructed wavefront captured by a camera or viewed by an eye. Data Structures: Hologram Matrix: 2D array of complex numbers Uh(x,y) or real-valued intensity/phase maps. SLM Pixel Map: 2D array of values mapped to SLM physical pixels. Steps: 1. Illumination Preparation: Filter the laser beam using a pinhole to remove spatial noise. Collimate the beam using a lens to ensure plane wave illumination on the SLM. If speckle reduction is required, rotate a holographic diffuser at the focused spot of the laser beams. 2. Hologram Encoding (if Phase-Only SLM): If the SLM is phase-only but the hologram is complex-valued, encode the complex field into real values using the Burch encoding method. For off-axis holograms, set the grating period to 0.25 of the maximum period to avoid unwanted noise. 3. SLM Modulation: Upload the encoded hologram to the SLM. If using an LCoS SLM with small pixel pitch, upsample by putting the same pixel value in 2x2 nearest pixels to minimize pixel crosstalk. Calibrate the amplitude response: measure output intensity for each input pixel value, as modulated intensity depends nonlinearly on assigned values. 4. Optical Propagation and Filtering: Illuminate the SLM with the collimated laser beam. Form the Fourier plane using a first lens group. Block the zeroth-order and higher-order diffraction terms using an adjustable 2D slit at the Fourier plane. 5. Reconstruction and Capture: The reconstructed wavefront propagates to the target plane (distance z). Capture the wavefront using a digital camera (e.g., Canon 60D) positioned at the shooting distance. Alternatively, view directly with the human eye or a near-eye display system. Parameters: Wavelength (\lambda): Must match the recording or intended reconstruction wavelength. Common values: 638 nm (red), 515 nm (green), 460 nm (blue). Single wavelength example: 532 nm. Pixel Pitch (\Delta x): Determines spatial frequency sampling. Example: 3.6 \mum for IRIS-U62 LCoS, effectively 7.2 \mum when upsampled. Example: 3.74 \mum. Reconstruction Distance (z): Axial distance from SLM to camera/eye. Examples: 155, 160, 165, 170 mm. Minimum required: > 1.7 mm to avoid excessive defocus blur from pixel pitch diffraction. Grating Period: For off-axis holograms, set to 0.25 of maximum period. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Pixel Crosstalk: Small pixel pitch on LCoS SLMs causes crosstalk. Mitigation: upsample by 2x2. Diffraction Orders: Zeroth and higher orders create noise. Mitigation: use a 2D slit at the Fourier plane. Speckle: Caused by laser coherence. Mitigation: rotate holographic diffuser. Defocus Blur: Pixel pitch diffraction causes blur. At 2 mm propagation, dispersion diameters are 25 pixels (red), 20 (green), 18 (blue). If max defocus blur diameter is 15 pixels, propagation must be > 1.7 mm. Nonlinear Response: SLM intensity response is nonlinear. Calibration is required. Pseudocode: Unverified code. """ # 1. Illumination Setup pinholefilter = PinholeFilter() collimatinglens = Lens(focallength=calculatefocallength(laserwavelength, slmpixelpitch)) # 2. SLM Configuration slm = LCOSSLM(model="IRIS-U62", nativepitch=slmpixelpitch, resolution=slmresolution) # Upsample if necessary to reduce crosstalk (example for 2x2) slm.upsamplefactor = 2 # 3. Calibration (Amplitude) # Measure output intensity for each input pixel value calibrationcurve = measureslmresponse(slm) # 4. Hologram Encoding (if complex to phase-only) # Use Burch encoding for off-axis hologram gratingperiodratio = 0.25 encodedhologram = burchencode(complexhologram, gratingperiodratio) # 5. Optical Filtering Setup fourierlens = Lens(focallength=calculatefocallength(laserwavelength, slmpixelpitch)) slitfilter = Adjustable2DSlit() # 6. Capture Setup camera = DigitalCamera(sensorsize=calculatesensorsize(reconstructiondistance, slmpixelpitch)) camera.distance = reconstructiondistance return { "illumination": (pinholefilter, collimatinglens), "slm": slm, "encoding": encodedhologram, "filtering": (fourierlens, slitfilter), "capture": camera } def calculatefocallength(wavelength, pixelpitch): """ Placeholder for lens selection based on diffraction limits. """ # Not given in the sources. return 100.0 # mm def measureslmresponse(slm): """ Measures the nonlinear intensity response of the SLM. """ response = [] for pixelvalue in range(256): slm.setpixelvalue(pixelvalue) intensity = slm.measureoutputintensity() response.append(intensity) return response def burchencode(hologram, gratingperiodratio): """ Encodes complex hologram into real values using Burch method. """ # Not given in the sources. return hologram.real # Placeholder A user-driven calibration method for correcting aberrations in holographic near-eye displays. The display presents a single object point oi to the user, represented in the hologram as fz(\rho, \theta){oi}. The user adjusts the coefficients a{jo} of fz(\rho, \theta){oi} until the most tightly focused spot is seen. This is repeated for additional object points. For true 3D holograms, calibration is performed for a small number of focal positions (e.g., four) and coefficients are interpolated over the complete focal range. For highly aberrated systems, 15 measured points are sufficient; for displays without significant aberrations, a single object point at the center is sufficient. It is impractical to measure for all millions of object points, so interpolation is used. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Measured Performance: In one experiment, shooting distances of 155, 160, 165, and 170 mm were used to achieve 3D effects. Scaling: Propagation distance must be adjusted to avoid defocus blur from pixel pitch diffraction. Minimum distance > 1.7 mm for 2 mm depth range. Strengths: Allows physical reconstruction of complex wavefields; calibration can correct for system-specific aberrations. Limitations: Requires precise optical alignment; sensitive to laser coherence (speckle); nonlinear SLM response requires calibration; diffraction orders must be filtered. When to Use: When physical holographic reconstruction is needed for volumetric displays or near-eye displays. When Not to Use: When purely numerical simulation is sufficient. Holographic reconstruction systems have been developed for various applications, including 2D-to-3D rendering and near-eye displays for VR/AR. Early systems used phase-only SLMs with Gaea-2 systems. More recent developments include diffraction-engineered holography using LCoS SLMs to overcome depth representation limits. Calibration techniques using user feedback have been proposed for correcting aberrations in holographic near-eye displays. name: Parallax-barrier and Lenticular Display Calibration
head: Automatic calibration of parallax-barrier
body: A procedure to automatically calibrate the position of a parallax-barrier with respect to the underlying rear-projection image using a digital camera and homography. It differs from manual alignment by using a computer-guided laser-cut barrier and automated image processing to map projector sub-pixels to specific viewing angles. Inputs: A rear-projection screen with a parallax-barrier mounted ~10 mm in front. A high-resolution digital camera (3K × 2K) positioned ~3 meters from the screen, facing the center. Multiple projectors covering the screen area. The physical barrier has slits 1 pixel wide, spaced 16 pixels apart, supporting 16 views. Outputs: A 3 × 3 homography matrix for each projector mapping display coordinates to camera pixels. A view assignment for every sub-pixel in each projector's image space. Data Structures: Homography matrix H: 3 × 3 matrix representing the projective transformation between the projector plane and the camera image plane. Slit line equation: ax + by + c = 0, derived via linear regression. View map: A 2D array matching the projector resolution, where each element stores an integer view index (0–15). Steps: 1. Homography Computation: Display checkerboard images on each projector. Capture corresponding images with the camera. Fit horizontal and vertical lines to the observed checkerboard patterns. Compute the intersection of each horizontal line with each vertical line analytically to obtain 48 coordinates of checkerboard corners in the camera image. Compute the 3 × 3 homography matrix H that maps points on the display to camera pixels using these corner correspondences. 2. Slit Detection in Camera Space: Project a white image on each projector to create a continuous bright surface. Capture a single image with the camera. Apply a Laplacian edge detector to the captured image. Threshold the result to isolate pixels belonging to the slits (high intensity areas). Perform a flood-fill operation to group pixels corresponding to each slit. Use linear regression on the pixels of each slit group to compute an analytical line equation for the slit. 3. Mapping to Projector Space: Transform the slit lines from camera space to the image space of each projector using the computed homographies H. The resulting slit lines in the projector images are roughly 16 pixels apart. 4. Interpolation and View Assignment: Interpolate the line equations for neighboring original slit lines to obtain slit lines for the remaining 15 views. Rasterize all lines for all 16 views. Entirely fill the projector image space so that each sub-pixel has a view assignment. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def calibrateparallaxbarrier(projectors, camera, barrierslitcount=16): """ Calibrate parallax barrier position relative to projectors. """ homographies = {} # Step 1: Compute Homographies for projector in projectors: # Display checkerboard on projector projector.displaycheckerboard() # Capture image cameraimage = camera.capture() # Detect lines horizontallines = fitlines(cameraimage, orientation='horizontal') verticallines = fitlines(cameraimage, orientation='vertical') # Compute corners corners = [] for hline in horizontallines: for vline in verticallines: corner = intersect(hline, vline) corners.append(corner) # Compute homography H mapping display points to camera pixels # Note: Display points are known from checkerboard pattern definition displaypoints = getcheckerboardpatternpoints() H = computehomography(displaypoints, corners) homographies[projector.id] = H # Step 2: Detect Slits in Camera Space # Project white image for projector in projectors: projector.displaywhite() # Capture single image whiteimage = camera.capture() # Edge detection and thresholding edges = laplacianedgedetector(whiteimage) thresholded = threshold(edges, value=0) # Threshold to isolate slits # Flood fill to group slit pixels slitgroups = floodfill(thresholded) # Linear regression for slit lines slitlinescamera = [] for group in slitgroups: line = linearregression(group) # Returns ax + by + c = 0 slitlinescamera.append(line) # Step 3: Transform Slits to Projector Space slitlinesprojector = {} for projid, H in homographies.items(): # Inverse homography to map from camera to projector Hinv = inverse(H) linesproj = [] for linecam in slitlinescamera: # Transform line equation from camera space to projector space lineproj = transformline(linecam, Hinv) linesproj.append(lineproj) slitlinesprojector[projid] = linesproj # Step 4: Interpolation and Rasterization viewmaps = {} for projid, linesproj in slitlinesprojector.items(): # Interpolate lines for all 16 views # Assuming linesproj contains the primary visible slits alllines = interpolatelines(linesproj, count=barrierslitcount) # Rasterize and assign views width, height = projector.resolution viewmap = emptyarray(width, height, dtype=int) for viewidx, line in enumerate(alllines): # Rasterize line and fill regions between lines with viewidx # This step assigns each sub-pixel a view assignviewtopixels(viewmap, line, viewidx, alllines) viewmaps[projid] = viewmap return homographies, viewmaps Parameters: Camera resolution: 3K × 2K. Camera distance: ~3 meters. Barrier slit width: 1 pixel. Barrier slit spacing: 16 pixels. Number of views: 16. Edge Cases: If the camera resolution is insufficient to detect slits, the Laplacian edge detection may fail. Degenerate checkerboard patterns (e.g., collinear points) will fail homography computation. Time Complexity: Dominated by line fitting and homography computation per projector. Linear in the number of pixels for edge detection and flood fill. Memory Complexity: Proportional to the camera and projector resolution for storing images and view maps. Strengths: Automated, high precision due to high-resolution camera and analytical line fitting. Limitations: Requires precise camera placement and high-resolution imaging. Originated in the context of distributed rendering for multiview parallax displays. The method uses a computer-guided laser to cut the parallax-barrier slits into a sheet of black Mylar polyester film, which is glued to a sheet of glass mounted ~10 mm in front of the rear-projection screen. name: Point-Cloud Based CGH Calculation
head: Object point scattering method, Point-Cloud Approach, Point-based CGH, Point-wise Integration Method, Summation of Point Contributions, conventional hologram, conventional methods, nCGH
body: Point-Cloud Based CGH Calculation is a method for generating computer-generated holograms by discretizing a 3D scene into a finite set of points, treating each as a coherent point light source, and summing their propagated wavefields on the hologram plane. It is distinguished from sibling methods like Volume Rendering based CGH Calculation by its explicit handling of discrete primitives rather than volumetric density, and from Diffraction-Specific Approach by its reliance on direct superposition rather than engineered diffraction kernels. While computationally simpler to implement than polygon-based or layer-based approaches, it suffers from high computational cost for large scenes and produces artifacts such as vivid boundaries and weak defocus blur compared to modern alternatives. Inputs: A set of N object points Pi = (xi, yi, zi) representing the 3D scene. Hologram plane dimensions W \times H (pixels). Wavelength \lambda of the reconstruction light. Distance z from the object plane to the hologram plane (or individual zi for each point). Outputs: A complex amplitude distribution Uh(x,y) on the hologram plane, which is subsequently encoded into a phase-only or amplitude-only hologram pattern. Data Structures: Point Cloud: An array of structures or tuples containing coordinates (xi, yi, zi) and optionally amplitude Ai and initial phase \phi{0,i} for each point i \in [1, N]. Hologram Buffer: A 2D complex array of size W \times H, initialized to zero, storing the accumulated complex amplitude Uh(x,y). Mathematical Model: The complex amplitude contribution of a single point source i at hologram pixel (x,y) is calculated using the angular spectrum method or Fresnel approximation. The phase \phii(x,y) depends on the distance ri from the point to the pixel: \phii(x,y) = k ri + \phi{0,i} where k = 2\pi/\lambda is the wavenumber and ri = \sqrt{(x-xi)^2 + (y-yi)^2 + zi^2} [G, S3, unofficial]. The total hologram is the superposition: Uh(x,y) = \sum{i=1}^{N} Ai \exp\left(i \phii(x,y)\right). Steps: 1. Discretization: Represent the 3D object as a finite set of object points Pi. 2. Propagation: For each point Pi, calculate its complex amplitude distribution on the hologram plane. This is typically done using the Angular Spectrum Method (ASM) or Fresnel diffraction integral. If using ASM, the propagation is performed in the frequency domain: U{i,h}(x,y) = \mathcal{F}^{-1} \left\{ \mathcal{F}\{ \delta(x-xi, y-yi) \} \cdot H{prop}(u,v) \right\} where H{prop} is the transfer function of free space propagation. Alternatively, direct calculation of the spherical wave phase term is used for each pixel. 3. Superposition: Sum the complex amplitudes of all N points to obtain the total wave surface information distribution Uh(x,y). 4. Occlusion Handling (Optional): If occlusion is modeled, ignore the backside wavefront contribution when backside and frontside wavefronts overlap. This requires depth testing or ray casting to determine visibility. 5. Encoding: Encode the complex distribution Uh(x,y) into a format suitable for the Spatial Light Modulator (SLM), such as phase-only encoding (e.g., double-phase method) or amplitude modulation. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def calculatepointcloudcgh(points, hologramwidth, hologramheight, wavelength, distancez): """ Calculate CGH using direct point-wise integration. Args: points: List of tuples (x, y, z, amplitude, phase) for N points. hologramwidth: Width of hologram in pixels. hologramheight: Height of hologram in pixels. wavelength: Wavelength of light in meters. distancez: Distance from object plane to hologram plane in meters. Returns: hologram: 2D complex array of size (hologramheight, hologramwidth). """ k = 2 pi / wavelength hologram = zeros((hologramheight, hologramwidth), dtype=complex) # Precompute pixel coordinates ycoords, xcoords = meshgrid(range(hologramheight), range(hologramwidth)) for point in points: px, py, pz, amp, phi0 = point # Calculate distance from point to each hologram pixel # Note: In a full implementation, zi might vary per point. # Here we assume a common distance z or relative depth. # If points have individual zi, replace distancez with pz. # r = sqrt((x - px)^2 + (y - py)^2 + (z - pz)^2) # Assuming points are at depth z relative to hologram at z=0 # Or if distancez is the plane distance, and points are at zi: # Let's assume points are defined in a coordinate system where # hologram is at z=0 and points are at zi. # Vectorized distance calculation for all pixels for this point dx = xcoords - px dy = ycoords - py dz = distancez - pz # Assuming hologram at z=distancez, point at pz r = sqrt(dx2 + dy2 + dz2) # Calculate phase phase = k r + phi0 # Calculate complex amplitude contribution # Ai exp(i phii) contribution = amp exp(1j phase) # Superpose hologram += contribution return hologram Note: The pseudocode above assumes a simplified direct phase calculation. For higher accuracy, the Angular Spectrum Method (ASM) should be used for propagation. ASM involves FFTs and is more complex to implement from scratch without libraries, but the core logic remains: propagate each point's field and sum. Parameters: Wavelength (\lambda): Typically 400-700 nm for visible light. Sub-hologram size: In optimized implementations using Look-Up Tables (LUTs) or Wavefront Recording Planes (WRP), the hologram is divided into sub-holograms. The runtime scales quadratically with the sub-hologram size. Point Density: The number of points N directly impacts complexity. 2 million points is a common benchmark for performance measurement. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Occlusion: Naive summation does not account for occlusion, leading to "see-through" artifacts. Explicit occlusion handling increases computational cost. Depth Errors: Incorrect depth values in captured depth maps cause interference-induced black lines at object boundaries. Vivid Boundaries: Abrupt phase variations at interfaces of objects at different depths cause constructive/destructive interference, creating sharp boundaries instead of natural defocus blur. Hole Distortion: Holes in objects are distorted by depth differences between the object and background. Defocus Blur: Coherent propagation forms Fresnel diffraction patterns, not natural defocus blur, distorting depth perception. Pre-calculates point contributions for specific depths and reuses them. Reduces computation time significantly but increases memory usage. Interposes an intermediate plane between the point cloud and hologram plane to reduce propagation distance and complexity. Speeds up generation but introduces approximation errors. Approximates point-wise integration as a convolution with a spatially invariant kernel (if lens phase is fixed). Reduces runtime from seconds to milliseconds but sacrifices spatial variance accuracy. Time Complexity: The naive point-wise integration method scales quadratically with the sub-hologram size and linearly with the number of points N. Total complexity is O(N \cdot W \cdot H) for direct calculation. With LUTs or WRP, complexity is reduced but depends on the number of pre-calculated entries. Memory Complexity: O(W \cdot H) for the hologram buffer. LUT methods require O(D \cdot W{sub} \cdot H{sub}) memory for pre-calculated tables, where D is the number of depth levels. Measured Performance: Hardware: NVIDIA GTX 980 Ti, NVIDIA V100. Runtime: 1 to tens of seconds for 2 million points on GTX 980 Ti, depending on sub-hologram size. Convolution methods can achieve milliseconds. Image Quality (nCGH vs DEH): 512x512 dataset: PSNR 22.5 dB, SSIM 0.756. FHD dataset: PSNR 27.1 dB, SSIM 0.889. Significantly lower PSNR/SSIM compared to Diffraction-Engineered Holography (DEH). Strengths: Relatively simple calculations. Can handle real scenes acquired as point clouds. No need for complex polygon mesh processing. Limitations: High computational cost for large scenes. Weak defocus blur and vivid boundaries distort depth perception. Sensitive to depth map errors. Slower than convolution-based methods. When to Use: Small to medium-sized scenes where simplicity is prioritized over speed. Synthetic scenes with known point coordinates. When hardware acceleration (GPU) is available and real-time is not critical. When Not to Use: Real-time applications requiring high resolution and large point counts. Scenes requiring accurate depth cues and natural defocus blur. Applications with noisy or incomplete depth data. The point-cloud approach, also known as the object point scattering method, is one of the conventional methods for CGH generation. It was among the earliest techniques developed for computer-generated holography. In 2002, T. Shimobab et al. employed this method to construct a 3D diagram using a reflective LCD panel and LED reference light source. The method is based on the principle of superposition of spherical waves from point sources. It has been widely studied as a baseline for comparison with more advanced methods like layer-based, polygon-based, and diffraction-engineered holography. Despite its simplicity, its computational inefficiency and optical artifacts have led to the development of faster and higher-quality alternatives.
