name: HORN-8 Point-Cloud Hologram Generation
head: HORN-8 algorithm, HORN-8 pipeline
body: HORN-8 is a hardware-accelerated method for generating computer-generated holograms (CGH) from point-cloud data using a dedicated FPGA pipeline. It solves the computational bottleneck of point-cloud CGH by employing a normalized Fresnel approximation that enables integer arithmetic and incremental phase calculation, thereby eliminating the need for memory-intensive look-up tables for trigonometric operations. Unlike the layer method, which relies on FFTs and is unsuitable for hardware implementation, HORN-8 is optimized for localized models and achieves high parallelization through a memoryless pipeline architecture. Inputs and Outputs Input: A set of N{obj} object points, where each point j has a depth Zj. The hologram plane has dimensions N{hol} pixels. The system supports a maximum of 65,536 object points per calculation block. Output: A hologram intensity map I(X\alpha, Y\alpha) for all pixels \alpha on the acquisition plane. Data Structures The system is implemented on an FPGA with a specific pipeline structure: FPGA Board: Contains 7 parallel pipelines. Pipeline: Consists of 1 Basic Processing Unit (BPU) and 639 Additional Processing Units (APU). Total Cores: Each board has 640 \times 7 = 4,480 parallel calculation circuits (cores). Memory: The design is memoryless for the calculation pipeline itself, using Block RAM only for input/output data buffering. Formulas The core calculation uses the normalized Fresnel approximation. The intensity I(X\alpha, Y\alpha) at pixel (X\alpha, Y\alpha) is the sum of contributions from all object points: I ( X\alpha, Y\alpha) = \sum{j=1}^{N{obj}} \cos \left[ 2\pi \left( \frac{p}{2\lambda Zj} (X\alpha^2 + Y\alpha^2) \right) \right] = \sum{j=1}^{N{obj}} \cos (2\pi \theta{\alpha j}) Where: p is the hologram pixel pitch. \lambda is the wavelength of the reference light. Zj is the depth of object point j. X\alpha, Y\alpha are the pixel coordinates normalized by the pixel pitch p (i.e., integer indices). Aj (intensity of point j) is set to 1 and excluded from the equation. \theta{\alpha j} is the normalized phase term for point j at pixel \alpha: \theta{\alpha j} = \frac{p}{2\lambda Zj} (X\alpha^2 + Y\alpha^2). Parameters Operating Frequency (f): 0.25 GHz. Parallel Circuits (C): 4,480 per board. Max Points per Block: 65,536 (2^{16}). Algorithm Steps The calculation proceeds pixel by pixel across the hologram plane. For each pixel, the contributions of all active object points are summed. 1. Initialization (BPU): For the first pixel (X1, Y1), the Basic Processing Unit (BPU) calculates the initial phase \theta{1j} and the corresponding cosine value for each object point j. 2. Increment Calculation: Compute the phase difference increment \Deltaj for each object point j. This value is constant for a given object point and depth: \Deltaj = \frac{p}{2\lambda Zj} 3. Phase Update (APU): For subsequent pixels, the Additional Processing Units (APU) update the phase incrementally. The difference \Gamma between adjacent pixels is summed to create the next phase value. The text defines this difference logic as \Gamma = 2\Delta X\alpha (referring to the change in the squared coordinate term or specific hardware increment logic). The APU sums this difference to update the phase for the next pixel. 4. Cosine Approximation: Calculate the cosine of the updated phase using a novel approximate algorithm implemented with two adder-subtractor gates. This avoids memory look-up tables, allowing the pipeline to be memoryless. 5. Summation: Sum the cosine contributions from all object points to determine the hologram pixel intensity. 6. Iteration: Repeat steps 3-5 for all pixels in the hologram plane. 7. Block Processing: If the number of object points exceeds 65,536, divide the object into blocks of up to 65,536 points each and process them sequentially or in parallel across multiple boards. Pseudocode The following pseudocode represents the logic of a single pipeline core (BPU or APU) processing one object point's contribution to the hologram plane. Note that in the actual hardware, these operations are parallelized across 4,480 cores per board. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def horn8pipeline(objectpoints, hologramwidth, hologramheight, p, lambdawavelength, f, C): """ Simulates the HORN-8 pipeline logic for a single object point contribution. In hardware, this is parallelized across many cores. """ # Constants # p: pixel pitch # lambdawavelength: wavelength # objectpoints: list of depths Zj # Pre-calculate constant increment for this object point # Deltaj = p / (2 lambda Zj) # Note: In hardware, this is fixed per point hologram = [[0.0 for in range(hologramheight)] for in range(hologramwidth)] for x in range(hologramwidth): for y in range(hologramheight): # Normalized coordinates (integers) X = x Y = y # Calculate phase theta for this pixel and object point # theta = (p / (2 lambda Z)) (X^2 + Y^2) # This is done incrementally in hardware, but here we compute directly for clarity # However, the hardware uses: # 1. BPU for first pixel # 2. APU for subsequent pixels using difference Gamma # For implementation completeness, we use the direct formula # as the incremental logic is hardware-specific (add/sub gates) intensitysum = 0.0 for point in objectpoints: Z = point['z'] if Z == 0: continue # Avoid division by zero # Normalized phase term theta = (p / (2 lambdawavelength Z)) (X2 + Y2) # Cosine approximation using adder-subtractors (hardware specific) # Here we use standard math for the 'output' of the approximation cosval = math.cos(2 math.pi theta) intensitysum += cosval hologram[x][y] = intensitysum return hologram def theoreticaltime(Nobj, Nhol, f, C): """ Calculates the theoretical time for HORN-8 generation. """ return (Nobj Nhol) / (f C) Edge Cases and Pitfalls Memory Bottleneck: Previous systems used look-up tables for cosine operations, which consumed significant Block RAM (up to 94% usage) and limited parallelism. HORN-8 avoids this by using an approximate algorithm with adder-subtractors, keeping slice usage at 98% and Block RAM at 94% but freeing up memory for I/O. Object Size Limit: The maximum number of object points per calculation block is 65,536. Larger objects must be divided into blocks. Precision: The use of integer arithmetic and approximate cosine algorithms may introduce quantization errors, but the design prioritizes speed and hardware efficiency. Time and Memory Complexity Time Complexity: The theoretical calculation time for one board is T{horn} = \frac{N{obj} \times N{hol}}{f \times C}. Memory Complexity: The pipeline is memoryless for calculation, using Block RAM only for input/output data buffering. Measured Performance Single Board: Generating a 1,920x1,080 hologram (2 million pixels) from 10,000 points took 0.019 seconds (155 fps). This is 160x faster than a CPU (Core i7-6700K, 2.951 seconds) and 6x faster than a GPU (GTX TITAN X, 0.106 seconds). Cluster Performance: An 8-board cluster generated a 100-million-pixel hologram from 10,000 points in 100 ms (10 fps). Large-Scale Generation: Generating a 100-million-pixel hologram from 10-million points took 125 seconds on an 8-board cluster, with the object divided into 160 blocks of ~65,000 points each. Scaling Performance scales linearly with the number of parallel circuits (cores) and boards. The system is designed to output hologram data in parallel with calculation, concealing transfer time T{out}. Strengths and Limitations Strengths: High speed, suitable for hardware implementation, memoryless pipeline, effective for localized models (simulations, medical data). Limitations: Requires division of large objects into blocks, approximate cosine algorithm may have precision trade-offs, not suitable for complete spaces (real scenes) which are better handled by the layer method. HORN-8 was developed as a next-generation holographic imaging system to demonstrate real-time generation of large-scale holograms. It builds on the point-cloud based CGH calculation method, which is effective for localized models and suitable for hardware implementation due to its independence from FFTs. The system was designed to overcome the memory and speed limitations of previous HORN computers by implementing a memoryless pipeline with a novel cosine approximation algorithm. name: True 3D Hologram Calculation
head: Fresnel holography with phase correction
body: True 3D Hologram Calculation generates a hologram where scene elements are positioned at their actual 3D coordinates, providing accurate depth cues and parallax for all viewing angles. It differs from planar hologram methods by explicitly correcting the object phase to maintain consistency across the hologram plane, preventing the noise and artifacts that arise when using a constant object phase for objects at varying depths. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: A point cloud of object points \mathbf{o} derived from color and depth buffers, with occluded points culled from the viewer's eye position. The wavelength \lambda of the reconstruction light. The position of the hologram plane. Outputs: A complex amplitude distribution or phase-only hologram pattern ready for upload to a Spatial Light Modulator (SLM). Data Structures: Point Cloud: A list of 3D coordinates \mathbf{o} = (xo, yo, zo) and associated color/intensity values. Hologram Plane: A 2D grid of pixels (x, y) at a specific depth zh. Method Steps: 1. Point Cloud Generation: Form a point cloud from the viewer's eye position using standard rendering pipeline color and depth buffers. Cull occluded points to ensure only visible surfaces contribute to the hologram. 2. Phase Correction Calculation: For each object point \mathbf{o}, calculate the corrected object phase \phio. This correction ensures that the phase contribution is consistent across the sub-hologram associated with that point, mitigating the wide variation in phase that occurs with true 3D depth. 3. Hologram Synthesis: Calculate the total complex amplitude at each hologram pixel by summing the contributions of all object points, using the corrected phase \phio and the actual 3D position of each point in the wave propagation model. Formulas: The corrected object phase \phio is calculated as: \phio = -\frac{2\pi}{\lambda} \left( k|\mathbf{p}c^o - \mathbf{o}| - k|\mathbf{p}c^o - \mathbf{k}| \right) Where: \lambda is the wavelength of the reconstruction light. k is the wavenumber (2\pi/\lambda). \mathbf{o} is the 3D position of the object point. \mathbf{p}c^o is the center point of the sub-hologram corresponding to object point \mathbf{o}. \mathbf{k} is a reference vector or position used to define the phase reference (often related to the optical axis or a reference beam origin, though the source text implies a geometric correction term involving the distance from the sub-hologram center to the object and a reference point). Note: The source text presents the formula as \phio = -\frac{2\pi}{\lambda} (k|\mathbf{p}c^o - \mathbf{o}| - k|\mathbf{p}c^o - \mathbf{k}|). The term |\mathbf{p}c^o - \mathbf{k}| appears to be a constant reference distance for the sub-hologram, ensuring phase continuity. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def calculatetrue3dhologram(pointcloud, wavelength, hologramplane, subhologramcenters): """ Calculate a true 3D hologram with phase correction. Args: pointcloud: List of object points o with 3D coordinates. wavelength: Float, lambda of reconstruction light. hologramplane: Grid of pixels (x, y) at depth zh. subhologramcenters: Dictionary mapping object point index to center point pc^o. Returns: hologram: Complex amplitude array for the hologram plane. """ k = 2 pi / wavelength hologram = zeroslike(hologramplane, dtype=complex) for o in pointcloud: # Get the center of the sub-hologram for this object point pco = subhologramcenters[o.index] # Calculate corrected object phase phio # Distance from sub-hologram center to object point distobj = norm(pco - o) # Reference distance term (constant for the sub-hologram) # Assuming k in the formula refers to a reference point or axis origin # The source formula is: phio = - (2pi/lambda) (k |pco - o| - k |pco - k|) # Note: The variable 'k' in the source formula inside the parenthesis # likely represents a reference point vector, distinct from wavenumber k. # Let's denote reference point as refk. distref = norm(pco - refk) phio = - (2 pi / wavelength) (k distobj - k distref) # Calculate contribution to hologram plane for pixel in hologramplane: # Distance from object point to hologram pixel dist = norm(pixel - o) # Phase at pixel due to propagation from object phiprop = k dist # Total phase at pixel totalphase = phio + phiprop # Amplitude Ao (from point cloud data, e.g., intensity) Ao = o.intensity # Add contribution hologram[pixel] += Ao exp(1j totalphase) return hologram Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Constant Phase Error: Using a constant object phase \phio for true 3D holograms results in widely varying object phase at the hologram plane, producing poor quality results with high noise. Intra-pupil Effects: The method assumes view-dependent effects are handled by head-tracked rendering. It does not account for intra-pupil view-dependent effects (e.g., differences in occlusion between the left and right edges of the eye pupil). Holographic Defocus Blur Matching calculates the maximum propagation distance \Delta z and the diameter of the blur circle of a human eye CoC{eye} in display pixels. It ensures that the holographic defocus blur matches the optical defocus blur of the human eye. It sets itself apart by linking SLM and lens array optical constraints to the physiological limits of the human pupil, allowing for the determination of rendering camera aperture sizes that produce perceptually correct depth cues. A processing method that captures 2D elemental images via a micro lens array, calculates holograms using a corrected Iterative Fourier Transform Algorithm (IFTA), uploads them to an SLM, and reconstructs a 3D image using output-side micro lens array imaging. Implemented by Choi et al. (2005) to construct a full-parallax wide-viewing-angle 3D holographic display system. Steps: 1. Capture 2D elemental images of a 3D object using a CCD and input micro lens array. 2. Calculate the hologram of the elemental images using a corrected IFTA. 3. Upload the calculated hologram to an SLM. 4. Reconstruct the 3D image using image formation from the output micro lens array. Complexity: The calculation scales with the number of object points and hologram pixels. For true 3D, every point contributes to every pixel, leading to O(N \cdot M) complexity where N is points and M is hologram pixels. Performance: Achieving good results with phase-only modulation is difficult without phase correction. The phase correction method allows for high-quality holograms with widely varying depth, but requires careful computation of the reference distances. Strengths: Provides accurate 3D depth cues and parallax. Corrects for phase inconsistencies inherent in naive true 3D Fresnel holography. Limitations: Computationally expensive. Does not account for intra-pupil view-dependent effects. The method is described in the context of holographic near-eye displays for virtual and augmented reality. It addresses the challenge of generating high-quality true 3D holograms using phase-only modulation, where naive approaches fail due to phase variation across the hologram plane. The phase correction formula was introduced to improve consistency on the hologram plane. name: Holographic Defocus Blur Matching
head: Blur Circle Diameter Calculation, CoC Eye Matching, Determining the diameter of the blur circle
body: Holographic Defocus Blur Matching is a method for calculating the maximum propagation distance of a hologram (\Delta z) and the diameter of the blur circle of a human eye (CoC{eye}) in display pixels, ensuring that the holographic defocus blur matches the optical defocus blur of the human eye. It sets apart from sibling methods by explicitly linking the physical constraints of the spatial light modulator (SLM) and lens array optics to the physiological limits of the human pupil, allowing for the determination of rendering camera aperture sizes that produce perceptually correct depth cues. Inputs and Outputs Inputs: Pixel pitch of the SLM (\Delta x), display resolution (res), system field of view (FoV), virtual image distance of the floating object (d), and human pupil diameter (A). Outputs: Maximum hologram propagation distance (\Delta z) and the eye's blur circle diameter in pixels (CoC{eye}). Data Structures No complex data structures are required; the method relies on scalar geometric and optical parameters. Steps and Formulas 1. Calculate Maximum Propagation Distance (\Delta z): The maximum distance the hologram can propagate while still reconstructing a virtual image from distance d to infinity is determined by approximating the lens array as a thin lens. The formula is: \Delta z \approx \frac{1}{\Delta x^2 res^2} \frac{d}{4 \tan^2(FoV/2)} Where: \Delta x: Pixel pitch of the SLM. res: Resolution of the display. FoV: Field of view of the system. d: Virtual image distance of the floating object synthesized by the hologram. The virtual image distance of the display is assumed to be infinity. 2. Calculate Eye Blur Circle Diameter (CoC{eye}): Calculate the diameter of the blur circle of a human eye when focused at infinity, while the holographic object is at distance d, expressed in units of display pixels: CoC{eye} = \frac{A \cdot res}{2d \cdot \tan(FoV/2)} Where: A: Pupil diameter. 3. Determine Rendering Aperture: Set the aperture size of the rendering camera to satisfy the calculated CoC{eye} diameter to ensure the rendered images match the human eye's defocus blur. Parameters and Typical Values Pupil Diameter (A): Set to 1.5 mm. This value is chosen to avoid image degradation originating from a partially blocked wave field, as the pupil diameter is larger than 1.5 mm in the majority of cases. Typical Scenario: For a 55° FoV, 4K resolution, \Delta x = 7.2 \, \mu\text{m}, and d = 0.35 \, \text{m}: \Delta z = 2 \, \text{mm}. CoC{eye} = 15 \, \text{pixels}. Pitfalls and Edge Cases FoV Dependency: Achieving a blur circle equivalent to that of a human eye is only possible under a small FoV (~10°). Propagation Distance Trade-off: Increasing the propagation distance to enlarge the defocus blur diameter causes the virtual image distance (d) to come closer, which also increases CoC{eye}. Consequently, an increase in the diameter of the defocus blur under a fixed propagation distance is required to attain a human eye-equivalent defocus blur with a holographic display. Wave Field Blocking: If the wave field of the hologram is partially blocked by the iris, image quality degrades due to noise from the blocked wave field. Complexity: The method involves constant-time arithmetic operations and trigonometric functions. Strengths: Provides a direct mapping between hardware parameters (SLM, lens array) and perceptual parameters (pupil size, defocus), enabling physically accurate depth cue synthesis in volumetric displays. Limitations: The method's ability to match human eye defocus is constrained by the system's Field of View; it is difficult to match under small FoV conditions when adjusting propagation distance. Use Cases: Holographic optical tweezers, one-step volumetric printings, and volumetric displays requiring accurate depth perception. The method originates from research into diffraction-engineered holography, specifically addressing the depth representation limits of holographic displays. It was developed to support time applications such as holographic optical tweezers, one-step volumetric printings, and volumetric displays by ensuring that the synthesized holographic defocus matches the optical defocus of the human eye. The work was published in Nature Communications in 2022. name: Diffraction-Engineered Holography (DEH)
head: optimized DEH
body: Diffraction-Engineered Holography (DEH) is a hologram synthesis method that optimizes a single complex wave field to reconstruct sharply focused images at object-existing planes and blurred images at other focal planes, thereby providing real-world-like defocus blur and photorealistic reconstruction. It sets itself apart from conventional methods by explicitly optimizing diffracted patterns at out-of-focus planes to enhance defocus blur while maintaining high image quality at in-focus planes, unlike siblings such as nCGH which exhibit weak defocus blur. Inputs: N target varifocal images I{dn}, where n=1 \dots N, rendered for specific propagation distances dn using a physically-based renderer to ensure occluded surfaces are correctly handled. An all-in-focus image I{AIF} of the scene. A depth map D of the scene. A depth attention factor \eta. Initial complex wave field at the hologram plane (z=0): U0(x,y) = A(x,y)e^{i\phi(x,y)}, typically initialized with constant amplitude and random phase. Outputs: Optimized complex wave field U{DEH}(x,y) = A(x,y)e^{i\phi{opt}(x,y)} at the hologram plane. Data Structures: Wave Field: Complex array of size H \times W (hologram resolution), stored as two real arrays: Amplitude A and Phase \phi. Varifocal Images: Array of N intensity images of size H{img} \times W{img} corresponding to depths dn. Depth Map: Array of size H{img} \times W{img} containing depth values D(x,y). Parameters: N: Number of varifocal planes. The benchmark dataset uses 21 planes. \eta: Depth attention factor. Value not explicitly given in sources. Iterations: Optimization steps. Typical value: 500. Wavelength \lambda: Required for wavenumber k = 2\pi/\lambda. Steps: 1. Render Varifocal Images: Generate target intensity images I{dn} for each propagation distance dn using a physically-based renderer. The camera focal distance is changed to match dn to capture accurate blur circles and occlusions. 2. Initialize Wave Field: Initialize the complex wave field U0(x,y) at z=0. 3. Optimization Loop: Repeat for iter = 1 to MaxIter: a. Propagation: For each target plane n=1 \dots N: i. Calculate the propagated wave field Prop{dn} at distance dn using the Angular Spectrum Method (ASM): Prop{dn}(U0) = \mathcal{F}^{-1} \left[ \mathcal{F}[U0(x,y)] \cdot e^{i kz dn} \right] where \mathcal{F} and \mathcal{F}^{-1} are the Fourier and inverse Fourier transform operators, k = 2\pi/\lambda, and kz = \sqrt{k^2 - kx^2 - ky^2} is the axial wavenumber, with kx, ky being the angular wavenumbers in the lateral directions. ii. Calculate the propagated intensity: I{prop,n} = |Prop{dn}(U0)|^2. b. Loss Calculation: Compute the total loss L: L = \sum{n=1}^{N} \text{MSE}(I{prop,n}, I{dn}) + \lambda{AIF} \cdot \text{MSE}(I{prop,closest}, I{AIF\weighted}) The first term is the MSE between propagated intensity and varifocal images. The second term is the MSE between propagated intensity and a depth-weighted all-in-focus image, weighted by \eta and D. I{AIF\weighted}(x,y) = I{AIF}(x,y) \cdot w(D(x,y)) where w is a depth-dependent weight function emphasizing planes close to object depths. The index closest refers to the plane dn closest to the object depth for each pixel. c. Gradient Descent: Update the phase \phi(x,y) of the wave field using gradient descent to minimize L. \phi{new}(x,y) = \phi{old}(x,y) - \alpha \frac{\partial L}{\partial \phi(x,y)} where \alpha is the learning rate. d. Convergence Check: If the change in the wave field (e.g., phase difference) is negligible, stop. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import numpy as np from scipy.fft import fft2, ifft2 def angularspectrumpropagation(U0, dz, wavelength, pixelsize): """ Propagates a complex wave field U0 by distance dz using Angular Spectrum Method. """ k = 2 np.pi / wavelength H, W = U0.shape fx = np.fft.fftfreq(W, d=pixelsize) fy = np.fft.fftfreq(H, d=pixelsize) Fx, Fy = np.meshgrid(fx, fy) kx = 2 np.pi Fx ky = 2 np.pi Fy kx2plusky2 = kx2 + ky2 # Handle evanescent waves by setting imaginary kz for exponential decay kz = np.where(kx2plusky2 <= k2, np.sqrt(k2 - kx2plusky2), 1j np.sqrt(kx2plusky2 - k2)) kernel = np.exp(1j kz dz) Ufreq = fft2(U0) Upropfreq = Ufreq kernel return ifft2(Upropfreq) def computemse(img1, img2): return np.mean((img1 - img2)2) def dehoptimization(varifocalimages, depths, aifimage, depthmap, eta, wavelength, pixelsize, numiterations=500, learningrate=0.1): """ Optimizes a hologram wave field using Diffraction-Engineered Holography. """ H, W = varifocalimages[0].shape A = np.ones((H, W)) phi = np.random.uniform(0, 2 np.pi, (H, W)) U = A np.exp(1j phi) for i in range(numiterations): totalloss = 0.0 # Term 1: MSE against varifocal images for n in range(len(varifocalimages)): dn = depths[n] Itarget = varifocalimages[n] Uprop = angularspectrumpropagation(U, dn, wavelength, pixelsize) Iprop = np.abs(Uprop)2 totalloss += computemse(Iprop, Itarget) # Term 2: MSE against depth-weighted all-in-focus image # Source does not specify exact weighting function w(D) or closest-plane selection # Assuming a simplified global comparison to a reference depth dref dref = np.median(depths) Upropaif = angularspectrumpropagation(U, dref, wavelength, pixelsize) Ipropaif = np.abs(Upropaif)2 Iaifweighted = aifimage (1.0 - depthmap / np.max(depthmap)) eta totalloss += computemse(Ipropaif, Iaifweighted) # Gradient descent update # The exact gradient dL/dphi requires backpropagation through the ASM operators # Sources do not provide the explicit analytical derivative gradL = np.zeroslike(phi) # Placeholder for backprop result phi = phi - learningrate gradL if i % 100 == 0: print(f"Iteration {i}, Loss: {totalloss}") return A np.exp(1j phi) DEHNet is a convolutional neural network designed to synthesize Diffraction-Engineered Hologram (DEH) wave fields directly from an all-in-focus color image and an all-in-focus depth map. It solves the computational bottleneck of traditional DEH generation, which requires multiple varifocal images and iterative optimization, by replacing the optimization procedure with a direct inference step. Unlike its sibling method nCGH, which also uses RGB-D inputs but lacks depth-aware defocus control, DEHNet produces wave fields that correctly reconstruct defocus blur and sharp focus while suppressing interference artifacts at object boundaries. Time Complexity: The optimization-based DEH is computationally expensive. It requires synthesizing multiple varifocal images and performing iterative optimization (e.g., 500 iterations). Synthesis takes more than 1 minute for a single hologram on an NVIDIA V100 GPU. DEHNet achieves 62 Hz inference on FHD resolution images. Memory Complexity: Requires storing the complex wave field, varifocal images, and depth maps. The optimization process requires memory for gradients and intermediate propagated fields. Performance: General dataset: PSNR 26.1 dB, SSIM 0.88. 512x512 dataset: PSNR 29.0 dB, SSIM 0.909. FHD dataset: PSNR 33.4 dB, SSIM 0.955. Strengths: Provides clear defocus blur even if the blur circle diameter is slightly smaller than the rendered image, enhancing depth perception. Maintains high image quality at in-focus planes. Limitations: High computational load for the optimization-based method makes it impractical for real-time applications without neural network acceleration. When to use: When photorealistic depth expression with accurate defocus blur is required and computational resources allow for offline synthesis or neural network inference. When not to use: For real-time applications requiring rapid hologram generation without pre-trained models, or when hardware constraints prevent the use of large neural networks. Diffraction-Engineered Holography (DEH) was introduced to address the limitations of conventional CGH algorithms that only optimize intensity at object-existing planes, failing to provide realistic defocus blur at other planes. It leverages the fact that phase variation steers light propagation without affecting the image seen by the eyes, allowing adaptive phase changes to enhance defocus blur. The method was demonstrated in a 2022 paper published in Nature Communications. name: DEHNet
head: Neural Diffraction-Engineered Holography Network
body: DEHNet is a convolutional neural network designed to synthesize Diffraction-Engineered Hologram (DEH) wave fields directly from an all-in-focus color image and an all-in-focus depth map. It solves the computational bottleneck of traditional DEH generation, which requires multiple varifocal images and iterative optimization, by replacing the optimization procedure with a direct inference step. Unlike its sibling method nCGH, which also uses RGB-D inputs but lacks depth-aware defocus control, DEHNet produces wave fields that correctly reconstruct defocus blur and sharp focus while suppressing interference artifacts at object boundaries. Inputs and Outputs Input: An all-in-focus color image (I{color}) and an all-in-focus depth map (D). Output: A DEH wave field (complex amplitude). Data Structures The network consists of 34 convolutional layers. Hidden Layers: Layers 1 through 33 are standard convolutional layers. Each layer has 12 channels. Output Layer: Layer 34 is the final layer. It includes a concatenated shortcut (skip connection) from earlier in the network. It outputs the DEH wave field. Channels: The number of channels is set to 12. This value is selected as small as possible to maximize the number of convolutions and activations under restricted computational resources, prioritizing non-linearity and wide receptive field over hidden feature capacity. Parameters Quantization: After training, weights are quantized to 8-bit integers to reduce computational load during inference. Training Data: The dataset consists of 3000 different scenes. Each scene contains: 21 varifocal images 1 all-in-focus color image 21 varifocal depth maps 1 all-in-focus depth map Algorithm Steps 1. Preprocessing: Obtain an all-in-focus color image and an all-in-focus depth map for the target scene. 2. Inference: Pass the color image and depth map into the quantized DEHNet. 3. Synthesis: The network computes the optimal wave field directly. 4. Encoding: Encode the resulting amplitude-only hologram for display. Pseudocode Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def dehnetinference(colorimage, depthmap, quantizedweights): """ Synthesizes a DEH wave field using the quantized DEHNet. Args: colorimage (Tensor): All-in-focus color image. depthmap (Tensor): All-in-focus depth map. quantizedweights (List[Tensor]): Quantized 8-bit integer weights for 34 layers. Returns: Tensor: The synthesized DEH wave field. """ # Input concatenation or processing is implied by the architecture # The network takes RGB-D as input x = concatenate(colorimage, depthmap) # Layers 1 to 33: Convolutional layers with 12 channels for i in range(33): # Conv2d, 3x3 kernel, 12 channels x = conv2d(x, quantizedweights[i], kernelsize=3, channels=12) # PReLU activation is used in the residual blocks described in Fig 2 x = prelu(x) # Layer 34: Output layer with concatenated shortcut # The last layer includes a concatenated shortcut (skip connection) # Assuming the shortcut connects to an earlier feature map, # typically the input or a specific intermediate layer. # Based on "concatenated shortcut", we concatenate the input or a previous feature map. # Note: The exact skip connection source (e.g., input vs layer 1) is not explicitly # detailed in the text beyond "includes a concatenated shortcut". # Standard residual/skip logic implies concatenating with a previous representation. # For implementation, we assume a standard skip from input or early layer. # Given the text "last layer which includes a concatenated shortcut", # we concatenate the input feature map to the current feature map before the final conv. xshortcut = concatenate(colorimage, depthmap) # Placeholder for specific skip source x = concatenate(x, xshortcut) # Final convolution to output DEH wave field # Output channels correspond to the complex wave field components dehwavefield = conv2d(x, quantizedweights[33], kernelsize=3) return dehwavefield Edge Cases and Pitfalls Depth Map Errors: Real-world captured depth maps often contain incorrect values or depth holes. These errors induce severe noise and distort objects in the reconstructed hologram due to interference-induced black lines at boundaries. DEHNet is designed to suppress this noise at boundaries, unlike nCGH which produces visible black lines at noisy depth interfaces. Occlusion: The method must handle occluded surfaces correctly to provide appropriate blur and sharp focus. Time and Memory Complexity Inference Time: DEHNet (quantized, qNET) achieves a frame rate of 62 Hz. Total Frame Rate: Including the encoding of amplitude-only holograms (0.89 ms), the total frame rate is 57 Hz. Comparison to Optimization: DEHNet is 8600 times faster than the optimization-based DEH method (OPT), which requires more than 1 minute per hologram. Comparison to nCGH: DEHNet is 70 times faster than nCGH. Measured Performance 512x512 Dataset: DEHNet (qNET): PSNR 28.5 dB, SSIM 0.894. nCGH: PSNR 22.5 dB, SSIM 0.756. DEHNet provides a 6.5 dB enhancement in PSNR and 0.15 enhancement in SSIM compared to nCGH. FHD Dataset: DEHNet (qNET): PSNR 32.7 dB, SSIM 0.939. nCGH: PSNR 27.1 dB, SSIM 0.889. DEHNet provides a 6.3 dB enhancement in PSNR and 0.07 enhancement in SSIM compared to nCGH. Comparison to OPT: DEHNet (qNET) has a PSNR of 28.5 dB, compared to OPT's 29.0 dB, representing a loss of only ~0.5 dB. Strengths and Limitations Strengths: Real-time performance (62 Hz); superior image quality compared to nCGH; robustness to noisy depth maps from real-world sensors; correct depth perception and defocus blur. Limitations: Requires training data (3000 scenes); performance depends on the quality of the input depth map, though it is more robust than nCGH. DEHNet was introduced to address the impracticality of optimization-based DEH generation for real-time applications, which requires numerous varifocal images and extensive computation. It builds on the Diffraction-Engineered Holography (DEH) method, which synthesizes optimal wave fields for clear defocus blur and correct depth perception. The method was developed by the authors of the source paper, published in Nature Communications in 2022. name: Holographic 3D display system based on SLM
head: Holographic 3D display system based on liquid crystal spatial light modulator or digital micromirror device, LC/DMD Holographic Display, SLM-based Holographic Display
body: This method describes a hardware architecture for reconstructing computer-generated holograms using a Spatial Light Modulator (SLM) and a coherent or semi-coherent light source. It solves the problem of converting calculated holographic data into a visible 3D optical field by modulating incident light via electro-optic effects (LC) or mechanical reflection (DMD). It differs from pure calculation methods (like Volume Rendering based CGH Calculation) by focusing on the physical reconstruction pipeline, specifically addressing the trade-offs between modulator type and light source coherence. Inputs: 1. Hologram Data: A 2D complex amplitude or phase map generated by a CGH algorithm (e.g., object point scattering method). 2. Light Source: A reference light source, typically an LED or laser. 3. Modulator: A reflective Liquid Crystal Display (LCD) panel or a Digital Micromirror Device (DMD). Outputs: A reconstructed 3D optical wavefield visible to an observer or camera. Data Structures: Hologram Plane: A 2D array of pixels corresponding to the active area of the SLM. Each pixel stores a value representing the modulation state (phase shift for LC, tilt angle/state for DMD). SLM Panel: The physical device. For reflective LCDs, the data is uploaded as an image intensity or phase pattern. For DMDs, the data is uploaded as a binary bitmap controlling mirror states. Steps: 1. Hologram Generation: The system computer generates a 3D diagram of the target object. This is typically done using the object point scattering method, where the hologram is calculated by summing the wave contributions from discrete points representing the object. 2. Data Upload: The calculated hologram data is uploaded to the reflective LCD panel (acting as the light modulator). The panel maps the calculated phase/amplitude values to its physical modulation capabilities. 3. Illumination: An LED is used as the reference light source to illuminate the SLM. The light reflects off the modulated surface. 4. Reconstruction: The modulated light diffracts, reconstructing the 3D diagram of the object in space. Pitfalls: Computational Load: The object point scattering method involves calculating the interference of every object point with every hologram pixel. This results in a high calculation amount, which hinders the generation of high-resolution holograms in real-time. Coherence Length: The use of LEDs as reference sources introduces a shorter coherence length compared to lasers. This degrades the reconstruction quality, particularly for deep 3D scenes or high-contrast interference patterns. A variant that replaces standard SLM pixelation with a pseudorandom mask of pinholes to overcome narrow diffraction angle limits. Complexity: The calculation complexity is dominated by the object point scattering method, scaling poorly with resolution and object point count. This makes high-resolution reconstruction difficult without optimization. Hardware Constraints: LC-SLMs: Rely on the electro-optic effect. They can modulate phase and amplitude but are limited by pixel pitch and fill factor. DMDs: Rely on mechanical mirror tilting. They are binary modulators (on/off), requiring specific encoding schemes (e.g., pulse-width modulation or spatial dithering) to achieve grayscale or phase control, which is not detailed in the primary source but implied by the "on/off state" description. Image Quality: Reconstruction quality is significantly affected by the coherence length of the light source. LEDs provide better eye safety and lower cost than lasers but suffer from speckle reduction at the cost of contrast and depth fidelity. The specific system configuration described was employed by T. Shimobaba et al. from Japan in 2002. It represents an early practical implementation of computer-generated holography using readily available components (LCDs and LEDs) rather than specialized laser interferometry setups. The method is cited in the context of advances in digital holography and 3D display technologies. Principle and Outlook of Holography, https://doi.org/10.2991/icmmita-16.2016.54, fetched 2026-10-26

name: Non-periodic Photon Sieve Holographic Display
head: Deterministic pseudorandom mask holography, Photon sieve display
body: The Non-periodic Photon Sieve Holographic Display is a flat-panel wavefront modulation technique that combines a transmissive liquid crystal display (LCD) with a deterministically generated pseudorandom mask of pinholes to generate large dynamic holographic images with a wide viewing angle. It solves the fundamental limitation of standard Spatial Light Modulators (SLMs), which are restricted to narrow diffraction angles and small space-bandwidth products due to pixel pitch constraints. By diffracting light at wide angles through the pinholes, the method expands the optical mode space significantly, enabling large-area projection and multi-color holography without the bulky complexity of SLM multiplexing or time-consuming calibration processes. Inputs: Collimated laser beams at specific wavelengths (Red: 639 nm, Green: 532 nm, Blue: 473 nm). Target 3D scene defined by desired focal positions (xf, yf, zf). LCD panel parameters: Resolution N \times M (e.g., 1024 \times 768), pixel pitch p. Photon sieve parameters: Pinhole size d, pinhole positions \mathbf{r}k, and LCD pixel positions \mathbf{p}k. Outputs: Phase modulation pattern displayed on the LCD panel. Reconstructed 3D holographic image in the volume between the observer and the screen. 1. LCD Panel: A 2D array of pixels with resolution W \times H. Each pixel k has a center position \mathbf{p}k = (xk, yk) in the x-y plane. 2. Photon Sieve Mask: A binary transmission mask defined by a set of pinholes. Layout: One-to-one correspondence with LCD pixels. There is exactly one pinhole per LCD pixel. Pinhole Position: The lateral displacement of the k-th pinhole from the center of the k-th LCD pixel follows a continuous uniform distribution. Pinhole Size: Diameter d (e.g., 2.2 μm). Orientation: Pseudo-randomly oriented to suppress spatial aliasing. 3. Optical Path Data: For each pinhole k and target focus j, the optical path length L{k,j} from the pinhole position to the focal point. 1. System Setup: Place the non-periodic photon sieve close to the transmissive LCD panel to maintain a small form factor. Illuminate the LCD panel with collimated laser beams. 2. Pattern Generation (for each target focus j): Calculate the required phase shift for each LCD pixel k to direct light from the pinhole k to the target focal position \mathbf{f}j = (xj, yj, zj). The phase value \phik is determined by the optical path length from the pinhole to the focus: \phik = \frac{2\pi}{\lambda} L{k,j} where \lambda is the wavelength of the light. The optical path length L{k,j} is the Euclidean distance between the pinhole position and the focal point. 3. LCD Modulation: Convert the calculated phase values \phik into bias values suitable for the LCD panel. Display the bias values on the LCD panel. The LCD acts as a wavefront modulator; its non-ideal amplitude/phase response is scrambled by the photon sieve's randomness, allowing efficient modulation upon precise calibration. 4. Diffraction: Light passes through the LCD and the photon sieve pinholes. The pinholes act as a spectrally uncorrelated optical transformation, diffracting light at wide angles. 5. Projection: Project the holographic images onto a large volume. The images are formed in the space between the observer's eyes and the scattering surface (photon sieve) because the light is emitted from the screen. Unverified code. Args: lcdwidth (int): Number of pixels in x-direction. lcdheight (int): Number of pixels in y-direction. pinholepositions (list of tuples): List of (x, y) coordinates for each pinhole. Length must equal lcdwidth lcdheight. Positions are pseudo-randomly displaced from pixel centers. pinholesizes (float): Diameter of each pinhole in meters. targetfoci (list of tuples): List of (x, y, z) coordinates for desired focal points. wavelengths (list of float): List of wavelengths (e.g., [639e-9, 532e-9, 473e-9]) for RGB. Returns: dict: A dictionary mapping each wavelength to a 2D numpy array of phase values (radians). """ # Initialize phase patterns for each wavelength phasepatterns = {w: np.zeros((lcdheight, lcdwidth)) for w in wavelengths} # Map linear index to 2D coordinates numpixels = lcdwidth lcdheight for w in wavelengths: phasepattern = phasepatterns[w] for idx in range(numpixels): # Get pinhole position for this pixel px, py = pinholepositions[idx] # Calculate phase contribution for each target focus # Note: In a multi-focus scenario, phases are typically summed or optimized. # The source describes generating foci at "different spatial positions" by displaying # "optimal patterns". For a single focus j: for focus in targetfoci: fx, fy, fz = focus # Calculate optical path length from pinhole to focus # L = sqrt((fx - px)^2 + (fy - py)^2 + fz^2) dx = fx - px dy = fy - py dz = fz opticalpathlength = np.sqrt(dx2 + dy2 + dz2) # Calculate phase shift required # phi = 2 pi L / lambda phaseshift = (2 np.pi opticalpathlength) / w # Accumulate phase (simplified superposition) # In practice, LCDs are phase-only or amplitude-only; # here we assume phase modulation is the primary mechanism described. phasepattern[idx // lcdwidth, idx % lcdwidth] += phaseshift # Normalize or wrap phase if necessary for LCD driver phasepatterns[w] = phasepattern % (2 np.pi) return phasepatterns def displayandproject(phasepatterns, lcdpanel, photonsieve, lasers): """ Displays the patterns and projects the hologram. """ for w, pattern in phasepatterns.items(): # Find corresponding laser laser = lasers[w] # Illuminate LCD with laser lcdpanel.illuminate(laser) # Display phase pattern on LCD lcdpanel.display(pattern) # Light passes through LCD and Photon Sieve # The sieve diffracts light at wide angles lightfield = photonsieve.transmit(lcdpanel.getoutput()) # Project to volume # The actual projection geometry depends on the optical setup. # The source states images lie between observer and screen. projecttovolume(lightfield) Pinhole Size (d): 2.2 μm (standard demonstration); variable sizes tested include 2 μm, 3 μm, and 5 μm. LCD Resolution: XGA (1024 \times 768 pixels), providing \sim 10^6 controlled optical modes. Wavelengths: Red (\lambda = 639 nm), Green (\lambda = 532 nm), Blue (\lambda = 473 nm). Numerical Aperture (NA): 0.75 (used in measurement system). Low Light Efficiency: The active area of the LCD pixel is confined by the pinhole size, resulting in low transmittance (e.g., 0.16% for 2.2 μm pinholes). Viewing Angle Reduction with Distance: When the distance between the screen and focus increases beyond a certain distance (Z{1,2}), the effective viewing angle decreases inversely proportional to the distance due to the limited supported spatial frequency range. Contrast Degradation with Multiple Foci: When a large number of optical modes are addressed simultaneously, the signal level decreases proportionally to the number of optical modes while background noise remains constant. Spatial Aliasing: If pinholes are periodically aligned, reconstructed holograms carry optical information only within the Nyquist frequency defined by pixel pitches, causing unwanted multiple cloned images. This is avoided by using pseudo-randomly oriented pinholes. Background Noise: Pseudo-random pinhole orientation suppresses image duplication but introduces background noise. Time Complexity: The calculation of the optimal pattern requires O(\sim 10^6) computations, equal to the number of LCD pixels, rather than O(>10^9) for the large optical mode space. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Performance: Viewing Angle: Approximately 30^\circ achieved with a single flat-panel wavefront modulator. Contrast Factor: Approximately 2.0 \times 10^5 achieved using all pixels in XGA resolution. Transmittance: 0.16% measured for a photon sieve with 2.2 μm sized pinholes. Enhancement: The product of screen size and diffraction angle was enhanced by a factor of \sim 1200 compared to using only a wavefront modulator with XGA resolution. Scaling: Larger pinhole sizes or a larger number of pinholes per LCD pixel can increase transmittance, but this compromises viewing angles and increases calculation burden linearly. A demonstration with 7.8 million pinholes successfully generated a holographic tetrahedron with 60 foci. Strengths: Wide viewing angle, large screen size, multi-color projection, small form factor, no time-consuming calibration. Limitations: Low light efficiency, contrast degradation with many foci, viewing angle reduction at large distances, background noise. When to Use: When a wide viewing angle and large holographic image area are required from a compact, flat-panel device without complex SLM multiplexing. When Not to Use: When high light efficiency is critical, or when complex holographic images requiring many simultaneous foci are needed without sacrificing contrast. Origin: Published in Nature Communications, 2019, Volume 10, Article 1304. History: The method addresses the limitations of standard SLMs, which have limited diffraction angles (\theta = 2\sin^{-1}(\lambda/2p)) and small space-bandwidth products. Unlike wavefront shaping through disordered systems, which requires time-consuming calibration, this method uses a deterministically generated pseudorandom mask. It overcomes the challenges of transmissive SLMs (narrow pixel pitch difficulties due to embedded electrodes) by using an off-the-shelf LCD combined with a photon sieve. name: Simultaneous Color Holography via End-to-End Optimization
head: Simultaneous RGB Holography, Single SLM Pattern RGB Holography
body: This method generates a full RGB hologram using a single Spatial Light Modulator (SLM) pattern illuminated simultaneously by red, green, and blue light sources, eliminating the need for field sequential color or multiple SLMs. It sets itself apart from Depth Division Multiplexing by directly optimizing the output hologram end-to-end rather than assigning colors to different depths, and from Bit Division Multiplexing by using a flexible framework with a perceptual loss function for direct optimization rather than a two-step lookup table process. The method formulates hologram generation as an end-to-end differentiable optimization problem. It maps target RGB intensities to SLM voltage values by minimizing a perceptual loss function through gradient descent. Inputs and Outputs Input: Target RGB intensity image I{target}(x,y); SLM physical parameters (wavelengths \lambdaR, \lambdaG, \lambdaB; phase range). Output: SLM voltage matrix V(x,y); Reconstructed RGB complex wavefield at the sensor plane. Data Structures SLM Voltage Matrix: 2D array of floating-point values representing digital input levels to the SLM. Complex Wavefield: 2D array of complex numbers representing amplitude and phase at the sensor plane for each color channel. Perceptual Loss Weights: Scalars or matrices weighting luminance and chrominance channels based on human visual acuity. Steps 1. SLM Modeling: Map the current SLM voltage values V to a complex field U{SLM} at the SLM plane. This model accounts for the SLM's wavelength-dependent response and cross-talk. It uses a learned cross-talk kernel and a linear lookup table to map voltage to complex amplitude. U{SLM} = \text{SLMModel}(V, \lambda) 2. Propagation: Propagate the complex wavefield from the SLM plane to the sensor plane. This uses a modified propagation model [Gopakumar et al. 2021] that separates the zeroth and first diffraction orders and combines them through a U-Net architecture to simulate the optical system's point spread function. U{sensor} = \text{PropagationModel}(U{SLM}, \lambda) 3. Loss Calculation: Compute the color-specific perceptual loss between the reconstructed intensity I{recon} and the target intensity I{target}. The loss function incorporates human color perception, specifically the difference in visual acuity between chrominance and luminance channels. L = \text{PerceptualLoss}(I{recon}, I{target}) 4. Gradient Update: Calculate gradients of the loss with respect to the SLM voltages using automatic differentiation (e.g., PyTorch’s autograd). \frac{\partial L}{\partial V} = \text{Autograd}(L, V) 5. Optimization: Update the SLM voltages V using a gradient-based optimizer (e.g., Adam or SGD) to minimize the loss. V{new} = V{old} - \eta \frac{\partial L}{\partial V} Repeat steps 1-5 until convergence or a maximum number of iterations is reached. Parameters SLM Phase Range: The method leverages the extended phase range of Liquid Crystal on Silicon (LCoS) SLMs, up to 10\pi, to create diversity in phase triplets for RGB. Perceptual Loss Weights: Weights for luminance and chrominance channels based on human visual acuity. Learning Rate (\eta): Step size for gradient descent. Optimization Iterations: Number of optimization steps. Pitfalls Depth Replicas: Simultaneous color holography suffers from "depth replicas" artifacts due to the ambiguity between color and propagation distance. This is mitigated by using the extended phase range of the SLM. Wavelength Dependence: The SLM response varies with wavelength, requiring accurate modeling in the SLM model step. Pseudocode Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def optimizehologram(targetrgb, slmparams, wavelengths, numiterations): """ End-to-end optimization for simultaneous color holography. Args: targetrgb: Target RGB intensity image (H, W, 3) slmparams: Dictionary containing SLM physical parameters wavelengths: Tuple of wavelengths (lambdaR, lambdaG, lambdaB) numiterations: Number of optimization steps Returns: optimizedvoltages: Optimized SLM voltage matrix (H, W) """ # Initialize SLM voltages randomly or with a baseline pattern voltages = torch.randn(H, W, requiresgrad=True) for i in range(numiterations): voltages.retaingrad() # Step 1: SLM Model # Maps voltage to complex field using learned cross-talk kernel and LUT # Assumes slmmodel is a differentiable module defined elsewhere complexfieldslm = slmmodel(voltages, wavelengths) # Step 2: Propagation Model # Propagates wavefield to sensor plane using modified Gopakumar et al. model # Assumes propagationmodel is a differentiable module defined elsewhere complexfieldsensor = propagationmodel(complexfieldslm, wavelengths) # Compute reconstructed intensity from complex field reconstructedrgb = torch.abs(complexfieldsensor) 2 # Step 3: Perceptual Loss # Loss function based on human color perception (luminance/chrominance acuity) # Assumes perceptualloss is a differentiable function defined elsewhere loss = perceptualloss(reconstructedrgb, targetrgb) # Step 4: Gradient Calculation loss.backward() # Step 5: Update Voltages # Using a simple gradient descent step; in practice, use Adam/SGD with torch.nograd(): voltages -= learningrate voltages.grad # Clear gradients for next iteration voltages.grad.zero() return voltages.detach() Time Complexity: The optimization process is iterative and computationally expensive, scaling with the number of optimization iterations and the complexity of the U-Net propagation model. Memory Complexity: Requires storing the SLM voltage matrix, complex wavefields at each step, and gradients for backpropagation. Strengths: Eliminates the need for field sequential color or multiple SLMs; allows for extended phase range utilization; improves color fidelity via perceptual loss. Limitations: Computationally intensive optimization; sensitive to accurate SLM and propagation models; potential for depth replica artifacts if phase range is not sufficiently extended. When to use: When a single SLM pattern is required for simultaneous RGB illumination, and computational resources for optimization are available. When not to use: When real-time hologram generation is required without pre-computation; when SLM phase range is limited to 2\pi. This method was introduced by researchers at Reality Labs Research, Meta, USA. It addresses the limitations of traditional color holography methods such as field sequential color, depth division multiplexing, and bit division multiplexing. The work builds on prior research in differentiable holography and perceptual loss functions for image optimization. It was validated experimentally on 2D and 3D content using a custom camera-calibrated model. name: Simultaneous Color Focal Stack Optimization
head: Learned Wave Propagation SLM Optimization, Multi-plane Focal Stack Optimization
body: Simultaneous Color Focal Stack Optimization is a method for generating computer-generated holograms (CGH) that reconstruct a full-color image across multiple depth planes using a single spatial light modulator (SLM) pattern illuminated by simultaneous red, green, and blue light sources. It solves the problem of creating volumetric color displays without the complexity of field-sequential color or multiple SLMs. Unlike methods that optimize for a single focal plane, this approach uses a learned wave propagation model and gradient descent to jointly optimize the SLM pattern for a stack of target intensities at different depths. It builds on Simultaneous Color Holography via End-to-End Optimization by extending the optimization target from a single plane to a multi-plane focal stack. Inputs: Learned wave propagation model Holo(\cdot) for the unfiltered holography system. Initial SLM pattern P{SLM}. Target intensity images I{target}[d] for each depth plane d in the focal stack. Outputs: Optimized SLM pattern P{SLM}. Captured simultaneous color focal stack FocalStack. Data Structures: P{SLM}: The complex or phase-only pattern on the SLM. The specific bit depth and phase range constraints are discussed in SLM Bit Depth Analysis. I{target}[d]: A 2D image array representing the desired intensity at depth d. FocalStack: A list or array of captured images, one for each depth plane. Algorithm: 1. Initialization: Load the learned wave propagation model. Initialize P{SLM} and define I{target} for each depth plane in the focal stack. 2. Optimization Loop: Iterate while P{SLM} has not converged. 3. Plane-wise Optimization: For each depth plane d in the focal stack hologram: 4. Gradient Clearing: Clear previous gradients with respect to P{SLM}. 5. Forward Propagation: Generate the optical field from the current P{SLM} and propagate it to depth plane d using the learned model: Field{out} = Holo(P{SLM}, \text{depth}=d) 6. Loss Computation: Compute the loss using a custom perceptual loss function: Loss = LossFunc(Field{out}, I{target}[d]) 7. Backpropagation: Backpropagate the gradient of Loss with respect to P{SLM}. 8. Update: Update P{SLM} using the calculated gradients (e.g., via gradient descent). 9. Capture: Experimentally capture the simultaneous color focal stack. 10. For each depth plane d in the focal stack hologram: 11. Move the camera to depth plane d. 12. Capture the hologram image: Hologram = CaptureImage(camera) 13. Add the captured hologram to the focal stack: FocalStack.append(Hologram) 14. Output: Return the optimized P{SLM} and the captured FocalStack. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def SimultaneousColorFocalStackOptimization(learnedmodel, initialpslm, targetintensities): """ Optimizes an SLM pattern for a multi-plane focal stack using a learned wave propagation model. Args: learnedmodel: A callable Holo(PSLM, depth) that propagates the field to a specific depth. initialpslm: The initial SLM pattern (tensor/array). targetintensities: A list or dictionary of target intensity images Itarget[d] for each depth plane d. Returns: optimizedpslm: The optimized SLM pattern. focalstack: A list of captured images for each depth plane. """ # 1. Initialize pslm = initialpslm focalstack = [] # 2. Optimize while not converged(pslm): for d in targetintensities.keys(): # 3. Clear gradients cleargradients(pslm) # 4. Forward propagation # Fieldout is the complex field at depth d fieldout = learnedmodel(pslm, depth=d) # 5. Compute loss # LossFunc is the custom perceptual loss function defined in [Perceptual Loss Function for Color Holography] loss = LossFunc(fieldout, targetintensities[d]) # 6. Backpropagation loss.backward() # 7. Update SLM pattern # Update rule depends on the optimizer (e.g., SGD, Adam) updateparameters(pslm, learningrate=0.01) # Typical learning rate placeholder; specific optimizer not given in sources. # 8. Capture (Experimental Step) # Note: This step requires physical hardware interaction. # In a pure simulation context, this would be replaced by evaluating the field at each depth. for d in targetintensities.keys(): # Move camera to depth plane d movecameratodepth(d) # Capture hologram hologram = captureimage() # Add to focal stack focalstack.append(hologram) return pslm, focalstack def converged(pslm): """ Check for convergence. Not explicitly defined in sources. Typically checks for change in loss or pattern magnitude below a threshold. """ # Placeholder for convergence check logic return False Parameters: Convergence Criteria: Not given in the sources. Learning Rate: Not given in the sources. Optimizer: Not given in the sources. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Convergence Failure: If the optimization fails to converge, or if the product of initial source power and weighting function exceeds 100% (in the context of Source Power Optimization), the exposure time should be increased and the source power optimization restarted. Bit Depth Quantization: Significant drop-off in image quality (PSNR and SSIM) occurs between 5 and 6 bits. An effective bit depth of at least 6 bits is required for adequate image quality. An active camera-in-the-loop iterative process to optimize the power of each color channel of the SLED source for color fidelity. It is chosen when precise color balance is required and the source power cannot be perfectly calibrated beforehand. It sets the source power to an arbitrary value (<100%), captures a baseline reference image, debayers it, and maps it to SLM space. Three learnable weighting parameters (one per color channel) are initialized to unity and applied to the reference image as a proxy for source power. The process iteratively captures an image, calculates loss against the target, and backpropagates through the weighting parameters to update the initial source power. It repeats until the color weighting parameters converge (typically 15-30 iterations). If convergence fails or the product of initial source power and weighting function exceeds 100%, the exposure time is increased and the optimization restarted. An analysis defining the effective bit depth as the number of bits contained in a 2\pi interval of the extended phase range. It determines the minimum quantization level required for adequate image quality. It simulates holograms by optimizing with gradient descent and then quantizing to the target bit depth. Significant drop-off in PSNR and SSIM is observed between 5 and 6 bits. The minimum effective bit depth required is 6 bits. For 6-bit SLM simulation, PSNR is 31.00 and SSIM is 0.856; for 8-bit, PSNR is 34.98 and SSIM is 0.943. No image quality improvement is achieved for simultaneous color holograms once each color channel has a bit depth of at least 6 bits across a 2\pi phase range. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Measured Performance: For 6-bit SLM simulation, PSNR is 31.00 and SSIM is 0.856. For 8-bit SLM simulation, PSNR is 34.98 and SSIM is 0.943. Scaling: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Allows for the creation of volumetric color displays using a single SLM and simultaneous RGB illumination, eliminating the need for field-sequential color or multiple SLMs. Uses a learned model which may be faster or more accurate than analytical propagation for unfiltered systems. Limitations: Requires a learned wave propagation model which must be trained for the specific unfiltered holography system. Requires experimental capture for validation, which involves moving the camera. Sensitive to source power calibration, requiring active optimization. When to use: When creating volumetric color holograms with a single SLM and simultaneous RGB illumination is desired, and a learned propagation model is available. When not to use: When high bit-depth SLMs are not available (minimum 6 bits effective required). When real-time performance is critical and the optimization time is prohibitive (not given). The method was introduced by Markley et al. in "Simultaneous Color Computer Generated Holography". It addresses the challenges of near-eye holographic displays and volumetric imaging by enabling simultaneous color reconstruction across multiple depth planes. The approach relies on a learned wave propagation model for the unfiltered holography system, which accounts for system-specific aberrations and filtering effects. The research highlights the importance of source power optimization and SLM bit depth analysis for achieving high-fidelity color holograms. name: Physics-Informed Deep Learning Framework for Multi-Plane CGH
head: Multi-Plane Neural CGH with Physics-Informed Self-Supervision, Neural Multi-Plane CGH, Physics-Informed Neural Holography
body: This method generates phase-only computer-generated holograms (CGH) for multi-plane 3D targets by mapping spatial intensity distributions to depth-dependent reconstructions using a trainable Fourier transform layer. It explicitly addresses axial crosstalk (unwanted intensity diffraction from adjacent planes) by combining a physics-informed training strategy with a specialized network architecture that expands the receptive field. Unlike traditional iterative optimization methods, it achieves significant speedups while maintaining structural fidelity in sparse 3D volumes. Input: A discretized 3D target volume I{tar} with dimensions m \times m \times p, where m is the lateral resolution (matching the SLM pixel grid) and p is the number of axial depth planes. The input is a binary or sparse intensity stack representing the desired focal spots at each depth Zk. Output: A phase-only hologram \phi{SLM}(x, y) defined on the SLM plane, where x, y are lateral coordinates. The network processes the input as a tensor of shape (p, m, m) or (m, m, p) depending on channel ordering, but logically represents p channels of m \times m intensity values. The internal feature maps utilize space-to-depth (interleave) operations to reshape spatial regions into channel groups, effectively increasing the channel dimension while reducing spatial resolution to expand the receptive field. The model is a U-Net-style encoder-decoder architecture: 1. Encoder: Consists of six convolutional blocks. Instead of standard max-pooling, it uses space-to-depth (interleave) operations to preserve high-frequency fringe details and expand the receptive field for global diffraction modeling. 2. Bottleneck: A central structure that reduces feature map channels to enhance computational efficiency. 3. Decoder: Uses two up-sampling stages and depth-to-space (deinterleave) operations to restore spatial resolution. 4. Output Layer: Produces the complex optical field at the focal plane Z=0, denoted as U(X, Y; 0). The framework integrates a differentiable physics model within the training loop to constrain solutions to wave optics. 1. SLM Field: The complex field immediately after the SLM is defined as: U{SLM}(x, y) = \exp[i \phi{SLM}(x, y)] where the input beam has unit amplitude. 2. Propagation: The field at image space depth Z is calculated. In the far-field regime (valid when Z \ge f, where f is the focal length of the focusing lens), the field is expressed using the 2D Fourier transform \mathcal{F}: U(X, Y; Z) = A0 \times \mathcal{F}\{U{SLM}\} where the amplitude factor is: A0 = \frac{\exp(ikZ)\exp\left(\frac{ik(X^2+Y^2)}{2Z}\right)}{i\lambda Z} Here, k = 2\pi/\lambda is the wavenumber and \lambda is the wavelength. 3. Intensity: The reconstructed intensity at each depth plane is: I(X, Y; Z) = |U(X, Y; Z)|^2. The training involves a two-phase strategy to balance initialization and physical consistency: 1. Phase 1 (Supervised): Reference holograms are computed using an angular spectrum-based CGH algorithm for the target volumes. These serve as supervisory targets for the network output during initial epochs. 2. Phase 2 (Self-Supervised): The reference targets are gradually phased out. The loss is evaluated directly on the reconstructed intensity volumes I{recon} generated by the physics model. The primary loss is the cosine similarity loss, which is scale-invariant and emphasizes structural similarity over absolute intensity: L = 1 - \frac{\langle I{tar}, I{recon} \rangle}{|I{tar}| |I{recon}|} where \langle \cdot \rangle is the inner product and |\cdot| is the modulus, computed across all pixels and all p depth planes. Regularization: A regularization term is applied to the reconstructed background lying outside a narrow mask defined around the target points to suppress background noise. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import torch import torch.nn as nn import torch.nn.functional as F class SpaceToDepth(nn.Module): """Reshuffles local spatial regions into separate channel groups.""" def init(self, blocksize=2): super().init() self.blocksize = blocksize def forward(self, x): # x shape: (B, C, H, W) b, c, h, w = x.size() bs = self.blocksize # Reshape to (B, C, H//bs, bs, W//bs, bs) x = x.view(b, c, h // bs, bs, w // bs, bs) # Permute to (B, C, H//bs, W//bs, bs, bs) x = x.permute(0, 1, 3, 5, 2, 4).contiguous() # View to (B, C bs^2, H//bs, W//bs) x = x.view(b, c bs bs, h // bs, w // bs) return x class DepthToSpace(nn.Module): """Inverse of SpaceToDepth.""" def init(self, blocksize=2): super().init() self.blocksize = blocksize def forward(self, x): # x shape: (B, C, H, W) b, c, h, w = x.size() bs = self.blocksize # Reshape to (B, C, H, W) -> (B, C, H, W) # We need to reverse the view logic # From (B, Cout, H, W) where Cout = Cin bs^2 # View to (B, Cin, bs, bs, H, W) cin = c // (bs bs) x = x.view(b, cin, bs, bs, h, w) # Permute to (B, Cin, H, bs, W, bs) x = x.permute(0, 1, 4, 2, 5, 3).contiguous() # View to (B, Cin, Hbs, Wbs) x = x.view(b, cin, h bs, w bs) return x class PhysicsInformedMultiPlaneCGH(nn.Module): def init(self, m, p, kernelsize=3): """ Args: m: Lateral dimension of the SLM/target (m x m). p: Number of depth planes. """ super().init() self.m = m self.p = p # Encoder self.enc1 = nn.Conv2d(p, 64, kernelsize, padding=1) self.sto1 = SpaceToDepth() self.enc2 = nn.Conv2d(64 4, 128, kernelsize, padding=1) # 4x channels due to ST # Bottleneck self.bottleneck = nn.Conv2d(128 4, 256, kernelsize, padding=1) # Decoder self.d2 = nn.Conv2d(256, 128, kernelsize, padding=1) self.dto2 = DepthToSpace() self.d1 = nn.Conv2d(128, 64, kernelsize, padding=1) self.dto1 = DepthToSpace() # Output layer: predicts complex field at Z=0 # Output is complex, so 2 channels (real, imag) self.outconv = nn.Conv2d(64, 2, kernelsize, padding=1) # Initialize weights using He initialization self.initweights() def initweights(self): for m in self.modules(): if isinstance(m, nn.Conv2d): nn.init.kaimingnormal(m.weight, mode='fanout', nonlinearity='relu') def forward(self, targetvolume): """ Args: targetvolume: Tensor of shape (B, p, m, m) representing Itar Returns: phislm: Tensor of shape (B, m, m) representing phase hologram """ # Encoder x = self.enc1(targetvolume) x = F.relu(x) x = self.sto1(x) x = self.enc2(x) x = F.relu(x) # Bottleneck x = self.bottleneck(x) x = F.relu(x) # Decoder x = self.d2(x) x = F.relu(x) x = self.dto2(x) x = self.d1(x) x = F.relu(x) x = self.dto1(x) # Output complex field at focal plane Z=0 complexfieldz0 = self.outconv(x) # Shape (B, 2, m, m) # The network outputs the estimated complex field U(X,Y;0) # We need to back-propagate to SLM plane via Inverse Fourier Transform # Note: In a fully differentiable PyTorch implementation, # we would compute the loss in the physical domain. # However, the network directly outputs the hologram in some variants, # but the source states: "Once trained, the network establishes an end-to-end mapping... # to a physically realizable approximation of the complex optical field at the focal plane... # This estimated field is subsequently back-propagated to the SLM plane via an inverse 2D Fourier transform" # Therefore, the network output is Uz0. We must compute phislm here # if this is the inference step, or keep Uz0 for loss calculation during training. # For the final output of the method (the hologram): # 1. Get Uz0 from network # 2. Compute Uslm = Finv(Uz0 / A0) # 3. Extract phase # Since A0 depends on Z, and here Z=0, A0 is singular in the formula provided # for Z>0. However, the source says "at the focal plane... name: Phase Range Optimization for Simultaneous Color
head: Differentiated Phase Range RGB Holography, RGB Phase Range Optimization, SLM Phase Range Optimization
body: This method determines the optimal phase modulation range for each color channel (Red, Green, Blue) in a Simultaneous Color Holography system to overcome depth-wavelength ambiguity inherent in the Angular Spectrum Method (ASM) kernel. It ensures that the holographic patterns for each wavelength are sufficiently distinct to reconstruct unique color channels, while minimizing the phase range to preserve effective bit depth and refresh rate. It sets apart from sibling methods by focusing specifically on the magnitude of the phase excursion per channel rather than the loss function or focal stack geometry. Inputs: Target RGB image I{target}. Wavelengths for Red (\lambdaR), Green (\lambdaG), and Blue (\lambdaB). Propagation distance z. SLM pixel pitch p. SLM resolution N \times N. Outputs: Optimal phase range values \PhiR, \PhiG, \PhiB for each channel. The optimized SLM phase pattern \Phi{SLM}(x,y) (composite of all channels). Data Structures: Phase range vector \mathbf{\Phi} = [\PhiR, \PhiG, \PhiB]. SLM phase map \Phi{SLM} of size N \times N, values in [0, \Phi{max}] or normalized [0, 1]. Parameters: Red channel phase range \PhiR: Fixed at 2\pi. Blue channel phase range \PhiB: Variable, searched in range [2\pi, 8\pi]. Green channel phase range \PhiG: Set as the arithmetic mean of \PhiR and \PhiB. Loss function: L2 norm between target and simulated hologram. Algorithm: The method uses an experimental search procedure via gradient descent to find the minimal \PhiB that yields acceptable image quality. 1. Initialize: Set \PhiR = 2\pi. Set initial \PhiB = 2\pi. 2. Calculate Green: Compute \PhiG = (\PhiR + \PhiB) / 2. 3. Forward Model: For the current \mathbf{\Phi}, simulate the hologram reconstruction for each channel using the Angular Spectrum Method (ASM). Compute the complex field UR for Red using phase modulation limited to \PhiR. Compute the complex field UG for Green using phase modulation limited to \PhiG. Compute the complex field UB for Blue using phase modulation limited to \PhiB. Combine fields to form the total intensity I{sim} at the target plane. 4. Compute Loss: Calculate the L2 norm loss L = || I{target} - I{sim} ||2^2. 5. Optimize: Use gradient descent to adjust the SLM phase pattern \Phi{SLM} to minimize L, keeping \mathbf{\Phi} fixed for this inner loop. 6. Evaluate Quality: If the loss L is below a predefined threshold (indicating sufficient quality), record the current \PhiB as a candidate. 7. Increment: Increase \PhiB by a small step (e.g., 0.1\pi). 8. Loop: Repeat steps 2-7 until \PhiB reaches 8\pi or a maximum iteration count. 9. Select Optimal: Choose the smallest \PhiB that achieved the target quality threshold. For unnatural images (high color contrast/unique channels), the minimum sufficient \PhiB is typically 5\pi. For natural images (similar color channels), a phase difference of 4\pi (i.e., \PhiB = 6\pi if \PhiR=2\pi) is adequate. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def optimizephaserange(targetimage, wavelengths, distance, slmpitch, slmres): """ Determines optimal phase ranges for R, G, B channels. Returns (PhiR, PhiG, PhiB) and the optimized SLM pattern. """ PhiR = 2 math.pi PhiBmin = 2 math.pi PhiBmax = 8 math.pi step = 0.1 math.pi # Thresholds derived from experimental findings # These represent the minimum quality required to stop searching # In practice, this is determined by the L2 loss value corresponding # to "adequate quality" in the reference study. thresholdunnatural = 0.05 # Placeholder for specific L2 value from S1 Fig S9 thresholdnatural = 0.05 # Placeholder for specific L2 value from S1 Fig S9 bestphib = PhiBmax bestslmpattern = None isunnatural = detectimagetype(targetimage) # Helper to classify image type for PhiB in range(PhiBmin, PhiBmax + step, step): PhiG = (PhiR + PhiB) / 2 # Inner optimization: Find SLM pattern for these fixed phase ranges slmpattern = optimizeslmpattern(targetimage, wavelengths, distance, slmpitch, slmres, PhiR, PhiG, PhiB) # Simulate reconstruction to get loss simulatedimage = simulatereconstruction(slmpattern, wavelengths, distance, slmpitch, slmres, PhiR, PhiG, PhiB) loss = l2norm(targetimage, simulatedimage) # Check if quality is sufficient # Note: The source states "minimum phase range... is sufficient", implying we want the smallest PhiB # that meets the quality criteria. if loss < thresholdunnatural if isunnatural else thresholdnatural: bestphib = PhiB bestslmpattern = slmpattern break # Found the minimal sufficient range PhiGfinal = (PhiR + bestphib) / 2 return PhiR, PhiGfinal, bestphib, bestslmpattern def optimizeslmpattern(target, wavelengths, z, pitch, res, PhiR, PhiG, PhiB): """ Gradient descent to find SLM phase map minimizing L2 loss. """ # Initialize SLM phase map randomly or with zero phase slmphase = np.zeros((res, res)) learningrate = 0.01 epochs = 1000 # Typical value for such optimization for epoch in range(epochs): # Forward pass: Simulate ASM for each channel with constrained phase # Channel R: Phase modulated in [0, PhiR] # Channel G: Phase modulated in [0, PhiG] # Channel B: Phase modulated in [0, PhiB] # Compute complex fields UR, UG, UB using ASM propagation UR = angularspectrumpropagation(slmphase, wavelengths[0], z, pitch) maskphase(slmphase, PhiR) UG = angularspectrumpropagation(slmphase, wavelengths[1], z, pitch) maskphase(slmphase, PhiG) UB = angularspectrumpropagation(slmphase, wavelengths[2], z, pitch) maskphase(slmphase, PhiB) # Combine intensities (incoherent sum for color) Isim = np.abs(UR)2 + np.abs(UG)2 + np.abs(UB)2 # Loss loss = np.sum((target - Isim)2) # Backpropagation to update slmphase # Standard gradient descent step on the phase variable grad = computegradient(loss, slmphase, target, wavelengths, z, pitch, PhiR, PhiG, PhiB) slmphase -= learningrate grad return slmphase def maskphase(phasemap, maxphase): """ Constrains phase values to the specified range. """ return np.clip(phasemap, 0, maxphase) Time Complexity: The optimization is iterative (gradient descent). The search over \PhiB adds a linear factor relative to the number of steps in the range [2\pi, 8\pi]. Each step requires a full hologram optimization. Memory Complexity: Requires storing the SLM phase map and intermediate complex fields for three wavelengths. Complexity is O(N^2) where N is the SLM resolution. Performance: Larger phase ranges degrade image quality by reducing effective bit depth and tend to have slower refresh rates on physical SLMs. Strengths: Overcomes depth-wavelength ambiguity; provides a systematic way to select SLMs or configure phase ranges for simultaneous color. Limitations: Requires empirical tuning or simulation to determine the "minimal" range; unnatural images require significantly larger phase ranges (5\pi) than natural images (4\pi difference). When to use: When using an SLM with extended phase range capability for simultaneous RGB holography, or when selecting an SLM for such a system. This method originates from research into Simultaneous Color Computer Generated Holography (CGH). It addresses the specific challenge that the Angular Spectrum Method (ASM) kernel introduces depth-wavelength ambiguity, meaning different wavelengths can produce similar diffraction patterns for different depths. By ensuring the phase ranges are sufficiently different, unique holograms are produced for each color channel. The experimental procedure was detailed in studies involving Holoeye Pluto SLMs and standard simulated SLMs, comparing performance against depth division and bit division methods.
