name: Optical Addressing of Photochromic Mixtures
head: Colour-selective PM colouration, Geometrical optical intersection, Optical Addressing of Multi-Colour Photochromic Material Mixture, Optical Addressing of Photochromic Materials, Position- and colour-selective colouration, Position-selective PM colouration, Two-channel optical addressing
body: This method realizes a dynamic, full-colour volumetric display by exploiting the dual-light response of photochromic molecules (PMs) within a solid mixture. It solves the problem of 3D spatial addressing and colour selection in a single homogeneous medium by using the geometric intersection of two control light channels: ultraviolet (UV) light for colouration and visible (Vis) light for decolouration. Unlike sibling methods that rely on layered plates or complex 3D nanomaterial alignment, this approach uniformly mixes PM types, allowing high-density voxel arrangements determined by the molecular scale (~1 nm) and simple orthogonal optical geometry. Inputs: 1. PM Volume: A transparent solid block containing a mixture of photochromic molecules (diarylethenes) dissolved in a polydimethylsiloxane (PDMS) polymer matrix. 2. UV Light Source: Monochromatic light at 302 nm for inducing colouration (open-ring to closed-ring transition). 3. Vis Light Source: Spatially modulated visible light (projector or SLM) for inducing decolouration (closed-ring to open-ring transition) and selecting colour via spectrum management. 4. Control Signals: Synchronization signals for two Spatial Light Modulators (SLM1 for UV, SLM2 for Vis). Outputs: A 3D image rendered within the volume, where voxels are coloured based on the local balance of UV and Vis irradiation. PM Volume Construction: Material: Diarylethene PMs dissolved in toluene, mixed with PDMS polymer. Dimensions: Approximately 1 \text{ cm} \times 1 \text{ cm} \times 3 \text{ cm} for single-colour demonstrations, or 1 \text{ cm} \times 1 \text{ cm} \times 2 \text{ cm} for multi-colour demonstrations. Preparation: Single-colour concentration: 2 mg PM per 1 mL toluene. Multi-colour concentration: 1 mg yellow PM and 1 mg blue PM per 2 mL toluene. Mixing ratio: 4.4 mL polymer to 2 mL PM solution. Solidification: Heated at 100 °C for approximately 3 hours. Optical Properties: The PM is transparent (open-ring) initially. UV irradiation turns it coloured (closed-ring). Vis irradiation returns it to transparent. Different PM types absorb different Vis wavelengths for decolouration. System Architecture: SLM1: Controls UV irradiation pattern for depth selection. SLM2: Controls Vis irradiation pattern for 2D spatial addressing and colour selection. Geometry: UV and Vis sources are arranged to irradiate the PM volume from different angles, typically orthogonal. 1. Initialization: Prepare the PM volume as described above. 2. Alignment: Ensure UV and Vis sources are aligned orthogonally to the volume. 3. Synchronization Setup: Configure SLM1 (UV) and SLM2 (Vis) to operate synchronously. Define the arrival time T and duration \Delta T for both channels. Strict synchronization is required to prevent unintended coloration. 4. Depth Scanning Loop: For each depth layer z from 1 to N (where N is the depth resolution): a. UV Modulation: SLM1 projects a pattern that irradiates only the target depth layer z with UV light. b. Vis Modulation: Simultaneously, SLM2 projects a 2D pattern corresponding to the desired image for layer z. The spectrum of this Vis light determines the colour of the voxels in this layer. c. Irradiation: Maintain irradiation for a duration \Delta t. d. Repeat: Increment z and repeat steps 4a–4c until all layers are scanned. Timing Constraints: Let T{UV} and T{Vis} be the arrival times of UV and Vis light, and \Delta T{UV} and \Delta T{Vis} be their durations. If T{UV} < T{Vis}, unintended coloration occurs during the interval [T{UV}, T{Vis}]. If T{UV} = T{Vis} and \Delta T{UV} > \Delta T{Vis}, unintended coloration occurs during [T{Vis} + \Delta T{Vis}, T{UV} + \Delta T{UV}]. Requirement: T{UV} \ge T{Vis} and \Delta T{UV} \le \Delta T{Vis} (or strict equality with precise hardware sync) to avoid artifacts. Performance Metrics: Total Scan Time: T{scan} = N \Delta t. Max Rendering Time per Layer: To suppress flicker at a frame rate of F{frame} \ge 60 \text{ Hz}, the time to render one layer must satisfy: \Delta t \le \frac{1}{F{frame} \cdot N} For F{frame} = 60 \text{ Hz}, \Delta t \le \frac{1}{60 N} seconds. Typical Parameters: UV Wavelength: 302 nm. UV Intensity: 0.84 mW/cm². Vis Intensity: 15.04 mW/cm². PM Purity: >99% HPLC purity. Projector Specs (Example): 500 ANSI Lumens, 1280 × 800 resolution, 30,000:1 contrast. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import time def opticaladdressingpmdisplay(Ndepth, framerate, uvintensity, visintensity, layerdata): """ Implements the optical addressing scan for a photochromic mixture volumetric display. layerdata: list of tuples (uvmask, vispattern, visspectrum) for each depth layer. """ maxdt = 1.0 / (framerate Ndepth) TUV = 0.0 TVis = 0.0 DeltaTUV = 0.0 DeltaTVis = 0.0 for z in range(1, Ndepth + 1): uvmask, vispattern, visspectrum = layerdata[z - 1] # Configure SLM1 to irradiate only depth z with UV light # Configure SLM2 to project vispattern with visspectrum simultaneously # Hardware triggers ensure TUV == TVis and DeltaTUV == DeltaTVis # Apply light with specified intensities print(f"Applying UV ({uvintensity} mW/cm^2) and Vis ({visintensity} mW/cm^2) at depth {z}") # Duration must not exceed maxdt to maintain frame rate Deltat = min(maxdt, 0.001) time.sleep(Deltat) print(f"Stopped light at depth {z}") # Guard: verify timing constraints to prevent unintended coloration if TUV < TVis or (TUV == TVis and DeltaTUV > DeltaTVis): print("Warning: Timing mismatch detected. Unintended coloration risk.") 1. Timing Mismatch: If UV light arrives before Vis light (T{UV} < T{Vis}) or if UV duration exceeds Vis duration (\Delta T{UV} > \Delta T{Vis}), unintended coloration occurs in the overlap region. Strict hardware synchronization is mandatory. 2. Boundary Blurring: Boundaries between coloured and decoloured areas are blurred due to the spread of Vis light, causing extra decolouration at edges. This blurring is on a scale much larger than the wavelength of light. 3. Colour Artifacts at Boundaries: In multi-PM mixtures, if Vis light spreads, it may decolour one PM type more easily than another (e.g., yellow PM decolours more easily than blue PM), causing the boundary to appear blue instead of the intended colour. 4. Solution for Blurring: Use a highly directional light source, such as a laser-based projector, to minimize light spread. 5. Minimum Voxel Size: Theoretically limited by the size of a molecule (~1 nm), but practically limited by the diffraction limit of light and the resolution of the SLMs/projectors. Time Complexity: The total scan time is N \Delta t, where N is the depth resolution and \Delta t is the rendering time per layer. To achieve a flicker-free frame rate of 60 Hz, \Delta t \le 1/(60 N). Memory Complexity: Not applicable in the traditional sense, as the "memory" is the physical PM volume. The data structure for the 3D image is stored in the host system. Resolution: Depth (Z): Dominated by the resolution of SLM1 (UV) and the optical focusing/scanning mechanism. Lateral (X, Y): Dominated by the resolution of SLM2 (Vis) and the diffraction limit of light. Theoretical Limit: ~1 nm (molecular size). Strengths: Simple hardware structure (uniform mixture, no 3D alignment of voxels). High-density voxel arrangement possible. Full-colour capability via spectrum management. Dynamic rewriting capability. Limitations: Blurring at boundaries due to light spread. Frame rate limited by SLM speed, not molecular response time (picoseconds). Requires precise synchronization of UV and Vis sources. When to Use: Suitable for applications requiring dynamic, full-colour volumetric displays with simple hardware, such as information display and human-computer interaction. When Not to Use: When high-resolution boundaries are critical without post-processing or specialized optics, or when extremely high frame rates are required beyond SLM capabilities. Origin: Proposed and experimentally demonstrated by Hirayama R. et al. in 2016. Development: The method builds on the properties of P-type photochromic materials (diarylethenes), which are thermally irreversible and exhibit colour states dependent on both UV and Vis irradiation. Previous T-type PM displays required layered plates and suffered from voxel overlap restrictions. This P-type mixture approach allows uniform mixing, enabling simpler hardware and higher density. Usage: Fields of information display and human–computer interaction. Optical Addressing of Multi-Colour Photochromic Material Mixture for Volumetric Display., https://doi.org/10.1038/srep31543, fetched 2026-10-26

name: Rotational Swept-Screen Projection
body: Rotational swept-screen projection is a class of volumetric display systems that generates a continuous 3D image by projecting 2D image patterns onto a screen undergoing rotational motion. It solves the problem of creating a stationary, viewable 3D volume without requiring the light source itself to scan the entire volume mechanically, instead relying on the temporal integration of the human eye as the screen sweeps through space. It differs from translational swept-screen methods by utilizing rotational kinematics to define the volume, and from static multi-layer displays by physically moving the projection surface. The core mechanism involves a screen (reflective, transmissive, or emissive) rotating around a central axis. A projection system (LED array, laser, or projector) updates the image on the screen synchronously with the rotation angle. 1. Coordinate Mapping: The 3D world coordinates of a voxel are mapped to 2D screen coordinates and a specific frame index corresponding to the rotation angle. 2. Temporal Integration: The screen speed and frame rate are chosen such that the persistence of vision blends the discrete 2D slices into a continuous 3D volume. 3. Synchronization: Precise timing between the screen's angular position and the image update is critical. Misalignment between screen position and projected frame index results in Z-depth distortion [8515-multi-planar-volumetric-3d-display.md]. VRDM projects 3D voxel data onto a rotating mirror using surrounding LED screens, mapping 3D coordinates to 2D screen pixels via analytical mirror reflection matrices. It differs from standard ray marching by avoiding per-pixel ray tracing loops, instead computing direct projections for each rotation angle to drive the LED arrays synchronously. Choose this method when a reflective, pyramid-shaped volume is desired with high geometric precision. This system renders volumetric images by rotating a 2D LED panel array around a central axis and synchronously updating the panel content to match the rotation angle. It differs from laser-based swept-screen systems by generating voxels directly on an emissive surface without requiring external synchronization with electron beams or lasers. Choose this method for direct emissive volumetric rendering with high frame counts per rotation. This method projects a sequence of 2D image patterns onto a screen moving along the Z-axis to form a stack of spatial image planes, creating a true 3D image viewable without glasses. Unlike conventional 2D screens that rely on psychological depth cues, this method places voxels at their physical spatial positions, emitting light omni-directionally to provide both physiological and psychological depth cues. It distinguishes itself from sibling methods like the Volumetric Display using Rotating Mirror (VRDM) by utilizing linear or reciprocating screen motion rather than rotational sweep. Choose this method for planar volumetric displays requiring precise Z-depth layering. A volumetric display system that generates voxels by irradiating a fluorescent screen coated on a rotating plane with an electron beam. This is an early implementation of the rotational swept-screen principle, predating laser and LED variants. A cylindrical 3D display using a parallax barrier with multiple slits and a 1D LED array rotating along the slits. It utilizes the scanning of light rays when slit and LED positions change to reproduce multiple viewpoints in 360 degrees. A 360-degree display using a moving projection surface (vertically oscillating diffuser) synchronized with a projection system. It relies on retinal persistence to create a full volumetric object. The system oscillates a diffuser vertically at high frequency, synchronizes the projection system with the diffuser's motion, and the viewer perceives the image as a full object due to retinal persistence. The high frequency precludes the diffuser from being seen, leading to general transparency. Occlusion from different parts of the image is not possible because the image is diffused in a large field of view, limiting the display to 'ghosted content' rather than true volumetric occlusion. The concept of rotational volumetric displays dates back to the 1950s and 1960s. In 1958, Withey proposed a system using a translating fluorescent screen inside a vacuum container. In the 1960s, Hartwig proposed laser irradiation of rotating screens, followed by a helical screen structure. In 1994, Blundell et al. proposed a system based on generating an image drawing space, and the "Cathode ray sphere" was proposed, using a 15 Hz rotating fluorescent plane. The 2000s saw a shift towards LED and laser excitation, with Hisatake proposing the rotation of lanthanide-mixed polymer sheets excited by a 410 nm laser. In 2004, Perlin et al. demonstrated volumetric imaging by irradiating dust in the air with lasers. In 2010, the Seelinder system was proposed, using a cylindrical parallax barrier with a rotating 1D LED array. Recent developments include holographic diffuser combinations that form multiple viewpoints in 360 degrees. ボリュメトリックディスプレイ, https://www.jstage.jst.go.jp/article/jvrsj/29/3/2927/pdf/-char/ja, fetched 2026-10-30 (unofficial) Multi-user volumetric 360° display based on retro-reflective transparent surfaces, https://doi.org/10.1364/oe.409181, fetched 2026-10-26

name: Volumetric Display using Rotating Mirror (VRDM)
head: Rotating Mirror Volumetric Display, Volumetric Display using Rotating Mirror (vdrm) optical simulation & encoding, vdrm optical simulation & encoding
body: VRDM is a volumetric display method that projects 3D voxel data onto a rotating mirror using surrounding LED screens, mapping 3D coordinates to 2D screen pixels via analytical mirror reflection matrices. It differs from standard ray marching by avoiding per-pixel ray tracing loops, instead computing direct projections for each rotation angle to drive the LED arrays synchronously. Inputs: 3D voxel grid (implicit or explicit), rotation angle \theta, mirror offset d, screen geometry parameters. Outputs: Frame buffer for surrounding LED screens, structured as AngleImage. Data Structures: AngleImage: Contiguous memory block of 772 bytes. Bytes 0-3: u32 angle value. Bytes 4-771: 192 rows of RGBH arrays. Each row is 4 bytes: R (u8), G (u8), B (u8), H (u8 representing depth/address). ScreenLinePixels: Array of WPIXELS Option<PixelColor> (u32 RGBA). ScreenLineAddr: Struct containing screenidx (usize) and addr (u32) for depth sorting. Parameters (Default Values): WPIXELS: 64 (screen width resolution). HPIXELS: 40 (screen height resolution). MIRROROFFSET: 1.0 per notes, but source code uses \sqrt{2} \approx 1.414. SCREENOFFSET: 0.25 per notes, but source code uses 0.05. SCREENXOFFSET: -0.75. SCREENZOFFSET: -1.0 + SCREENOFFSET. SCREENYOFFSET: -1.0 + SCREENOFFSET. NUMSCREENS: 3. TOTALANGLES: WPIXELS 8 = 512 angles. Steps: 1. Generate Pyramid Surface (Reference Geometry): For each pixel (x, y) in a W\PIXELS \times W\PIXELS grid: Compute r = W\PIXELS / 2. Compute h = |x - r| + |y - r|. If h \ge H\PIXELS, skip. Compute z = H\PIXELS - 1 - h. Assign color based on quadrant relative to center (r, r): x \ge r, y \ge r \to gray; x < r, y \ge r \to red; x < r, y < r \to green; x \ge r, y < r \to magenta. This creates a half-pyramid reference surface. 2. Mirror Transformation: To map a 3D point (x, y, z) to the mirror plane: Apply a 2D rotation matrix to (x, y) coordinates based on the current rotation angle \theta. Apply a fixed 45-degree rotation matrix to (y, z) coordinates to align the point with the mirror plane's normal. Apply the mirror reflection matrix M in homogeneous coordinates: M = \begin{bmatrix} \sin^2\theta - \cos^2\theta & -2\sin\theta\cos\theta & 0 \\ -2\sin\theta\cos\theta & \cos^2\theta - \sin^2\theta & 0 \\ 2d\cos\theta & 2d\sin\theta & 1 \end{bmatrix} where \theta is the mirror angle in radians and d is MIRROROFFSET. Note: The source code implements mirrormat4 with specific sign conventions for sin/cos derived from column-major layout. 3. Encode Pixels per Angle: For each angle \thetak in the angle map (from codec.encode()): Initialize pixels array of size IMGHEIGHT (192) with None. For each voxel/point in the 3D volume: Transform the 3D point to 2D screen coordinates (u, v) using the mirror matrix and screen projection logic. Determine the target screen index and pixel address. If the pixel address is already occupied, keep the pixel with the smaller addr (closest depth). Store [r, g, b, p.addr as u8] in the pixels array. Z-depth Zeroing Pitfall: If the alpha channel of a pixel is zero (rgba & 0xFFFFFF00 == 0), force the computed z-depth (or H value) to 0 to prevent rendering artifacts from transparent voxels. 4. Output Assembly: Pack the pixels array into the AngleImage structure: [angle(4), R(1), G(1), B(1), H(1),...] repeated 192 times. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math WPIXELS = 64 HPIXELS = 40 IMGHEIGHT = 192 MIRROROFFSET = math.sqrt(2) # Source code uses sqrt(2); notes state 1.0 SCREENOFFSET = 0.05 # Source code uses 0.05; notes state 0.25 SCREENZOFFSET = -1.0 + SCREENOFFSET SCREENYOFFSET = -1.0 + SCREENOFFSET NUMSCREENS = 3 TOTALANGLES = WPIXELS 8 def generatepyramidsurface(): """Generates reference pyramid surface for encoding.""" surface = [] r = WPIXELS / 2 for x in range(WPIXELS): for y in range(WPIXELS): h = abs(x - r) + abs(y - r) if h >= HPIXELS: continue z = HPIXELS - 1 - h # Quadrant color assignment relative to center (r, r) if x >= r and y >= r: color = (128, 128, 128) # Gray elif x < r and y >= r: color = (255, 0, 0) # Red elif x < r and y < r: color = (0, 255, 0) # Green else: color = (255, 0, 255) # Magenta surface.append((x, y, z, color)) return surface def rotate2d(x, y, theta): """Applies 2D rotation matrix to (x, y).""" cost = math.cos(theta) sint = math.sin(theta) return x cost - y sint, x sint + y cost def rotateyz45(y, z): """Applies fixed 45-degree rotation matrix to (y, z).""" invsqrt2 = 1.0 / math.sqrt(2) return y invsqrt2 - z invsqrt2, y invsqrt2 + z invsqrt2 def applymirrormatrix(x, y, z, theta, d): """Applies the 3x3 mirror reflection matrix in homogeneous coordinates.""" sint = math.sin(theta) cost = math.cos(theta) sin2 = sint sint cos2 = cost cost sincos = sint cost # M [x, y, z]^T xnew = (sin2 - cos2) x - 2 sincos y ynew = -2 sincos x + (cos2 - sin2) y znew = 2 d cost x + 2 d sint y + z return xnew, ynew, znew def maptoscreencoords(x, y, z): """Maps transformed coordinates to screen pixel indices (u, v). Exact scaling/offsets use the source's caclviewpoint logic.""" # Linear scaling placeholder for demonstration; replace with exact screen geometry math scalex = WPIXELS / 2.0 scaley = IMGHEIGHT / 2.0 u = int((x + 1.0) scalex) v = int((y + 1.0) scaley) return u, v def encodeframe(voxels, theta): """Encodes a single frame for a given angle.""" # Initialize 192 rows, each row is a list of 64 pixels (None or (R,G,B,H)) pixels = [[None] WPIXELS for in range(IMGHEIGHT)] for voxel in voxels: x, y, z, rgba = voxel # 1. Mirror Transformation xrot, yrot = rotate2d(x, y, theta) yrot, zrot = rotateyz45(yrot, z) xproj, yproj, zproj = applymirrormatrix(xrot, yrot, zrot, theta, MIRROROFFSET) # 2. Project to screen grid u, v = maptoscreencoords(xproj, yproj, zproj) # Bounds check if not (0 <= u < WPIXELS and 0 <= v < IMGHEIGHT): continue # Extract RGBA components r = rgba & 0xFF g = (rgba >> 8) & 0xFF b = (rgba >> 16) & 0xFF a = (rgba >> 24) & 0xFF # 3. Z-depth Zeroing Pitfall if (rgba & 0xFFFFFF00) == 0: depthaddr = 0 else: depthaddr = int(abs(zproj) 100) & 0xFF # Scaled depth address as u8 # 4. Depth Sorting if pixels[v][u] is not None: existingaddr = pixels[v][u][3] if depthaddr < existingaddr: pixels[v][u] = (r, g, b, depthaddr) else: pixels[v][u] = (r, g, b, depthaddr) return pixels def assembleangleimage(angleval, pixels): """Assembles the 772-byte AngleImage structure.""" buffer = bytearray(772) # Pack angle (4 bytes) buffer[0:4] = angleval.tobytes(4, byteorder='little') # Pack 192 rows of RGBH offset = 4 for row in pixels: for pixel in row: if pixel is None: buffer[offset:offset+4] = bytes([0, 0, 0, 0]) else: r, g, b, h = pixel buffer[offset:offset+4] = bytes([r, g, b, h]) offset += 4 return buffer Defines mechanical geometry and dynamic balancing for a rotating double-helix reflector. Distinguished by its double-helix topology minimizing drag/vibration, enabling "walk-around" viewing. Time Complexity: O(N \cdot A), where N is the number of voxels and A is the number of angles (TOTALANGLES). Each voxel is projected to each angle frame. Memory Complexity: O(A \cdot H \cdot W) for the frame buffer storage, where H=192, W=64. Each frame is 772 bytes. Performance: The method avoids per-pixel ray tracing, using analytical matrices for direct projection, which is faster than iterative ray marching. Strengths: Real-time capable for low-resolution volumes; simple optical setup (one mirror, 3 screens). Limitations: Resolution limited by screen pixel count and mirror rotation speed; requires precise synchronization; artifacts from transparent voxels if Z-depth zeroing is not applied. VRDM was developed as an early-stage volumetric display concept using two spinning mirrors, later evolved to version 2.0 with one mirror and three surrounding LED screens. The simulation and encoding pipeline was implemented by hikaricai. hikaricai/vdrm, https://github.com/hikaricai/vdrm, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial)

name: Helical Display Surface Geometry & Balancing
head: Double-Helix Reflector, Second-Generation Helix
body: This method defines the mechanical geometry and dynamic balancing strategy for a rotating double-helix reflector used in laser-based volumetric displays. It solves the problem of maintaining structural integrity and optical stability at high rotational speeds by utilizing axisymmetric contours to balance centrifugal forces and continuous curvature to maximize bending stiffness. It builds on Volumetric Display using Rotating Mirror (VRDM) and is distinguished from standard cylindrical or planar rotating mirrors by its specific double-helix topology, which minimizes aerodynamic drag and vibration while enabling "walk-around" viewing of the projected 3D volume. The method constructs a rotating optical surface from discrete segments, ensuring dynamic equilibrium through geometric symmetry and precise mass distribution. Inputs and Outputs Inputs: Target imaging volume dimensions, rotational speed, material properties (polystyrene plastic), and structural constraints (shaft diameter, bearing type). Outputs: A fabricated double-helix reflector assembly with specific segment geometry, surface finish, and balancing weights, enclosed in a rotating housing. Data Structures and Layout The helix is constructed as a vertically stacked assembly of identical segments. Segment Geometry: Height: 1 inch. Thickness: Uniform 2 mm. Shape: Double-helix contour with continuous curvature. Center Feature: A 1/2-inch diameter concentric cylinder housing a center pin. Assembly: Total Segments: 18. Total Height: 18 inches. Bonding: Segments are vertically stacked and bonded together. Surface Finish: Upper Surface: Opaque white finish to enhance reflectivity and light diffusion. Rotor Assembly: Helix + Pin Weight: 5 pounds. Total Rotor Assembly Weight: 125 pounds. Housing: Transparent cylindrical housing rotating with the helix. Shaft: 2-inch steel shaft. Numbered Steps 1. Design Contour: Define a double-helix contour with a 36-inch diameter and 18-inch height. Ensure the contour is axisymmetric to sustain equilibrium of centrifugally-induced forces. 2. Fabricate Segments: Injection-mold 18 segments from polystyrene plastic. Each segment must have a uniform thickness of 2 mm and a height of 1 inch. 3. Integrate Center Pin: Incorporate a 1/2-inch diameter concentric cylinder into the segments to house a center pin. This pin aligns the plastic segments during assembly and centers the helix in its housing. 4. Assemble Helix: Vertically stack and bond the 18 segments. The resulting helix weighs 5 pounds. 5. Apply Surface Finish: Treat the upper surface of the helix with an opaque white finish to enhance reflectivity and light diffusion. 6. Enclose in Housing: Place the helix inside a transparent cylindrical housing that rotates with it. The housing supports the helix around its entire perimeter and shelters it from nonrotating objects. The housing is mounted on a circular turntable at the top of a 2-inch steel shaft. 7. Balance Assembly: Dynamically balance the total rotor assembly (125 pounds) to assure smooth performance. The assembly is designed for a first-critical natural frequency (f) greater than 33 Hz. 8. Mount Drive System: Attach a shaft-mounted drive pulley and encode disk to complete the rotor assembly. Support the rotor shaft with a pair of self-aligning cartridge bearings. Formulas and Parameters Operating Speed: 600 rpm. Natural Frequency Constraint: f > 33 \text{ Hz}. Addressable Volume: 10" \times 10" \times 15" (constrained by scanner optics and helix occlusions). Total Imaging Volume Potential: 10 cubic feet (36" diameter, 18" high). Edge Cases and Pitfalls Centrifugal Forces: Unbalanced centrifugal forces cause vibration. Solved by the axisymmetry of the double-helix contour. Structural Stiffness: Low bending stiffness leads to deformation. Solved by the continuous curvature of the helix. Aerodynamic Drag: Drag loads can destabilize rotation. Solved by enclosing the helix in a rotating transparent housing that entrains air, preventing drag load on the helix. Occlusion: The double-helix structure creates occlusions, reducing the usable volume. The addressable volume is limited to 10" \times 10" \times 15" despite a larger potential volume. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Measured Performance: The system operates at 600 rpm with minimal noise and vibration. Scaling: The design displaces a potential cylindrical imaging volume of 10 cubic feet, but the addressable volume is constrained to 10" \times 10" \times 15" due to optical and geometric limitations. Strengths: Inherently free of low-frequency vibration due to unique shape and light weight; minimizes weight and aerodynamic drag; maximizes structural stiffness. Limitations: Addressable volume is reduced by helix occlusions; requires complex dynamic balancing of a 125-pound assembly. When to use: When a true 3D volumetric display with walk-around viewing is required, and mechanical stability at high speeds is critical. When not to use: When the full potential volume (10 cubic feet) is required without occlusion constraints, or when lower rotational speeds are acceptable for simpler geometries. The method originated from the NRaD team's development of second-generation 3-D technology, documented in a 1992 report with continuing development. It was designed to improve upon earlier volumetric display systems by addressing vibration and aerodynamic drag issues inherent in rotating mirror systems. The system uses ceiling-mounted mirrors to fold laser signals into a vertical attitude, allowing for "walk-around" viewing. DTIC ADA306215: Laser-Based 3-D Volumetric Display System (The Improved Second Generation)., https://archive.org/details/DTICADA306215, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial)

name: Laser-based 3-D Volumetric Display (Rotating Helix with AO Scanner)
head: AO-Scanned Helix Display, Rotating Helix Volumetric Display, Helical Volumetric Display, Helix-based 3-D Volumetric Display, Double Helix Laser Display, Laser-based rotating double helix volumetric display, 3-D Volumetric Display (Helix-based Laser Projection), Rotating Helical Volumetric Display, Volumetric Display using Helical Surface, Helix-based 3-D Display, Helical Display System
body: A hardware-based volumetric display technique that projects 3-D image points (voxels) onto the surface of a rapidly rotating helical structure using computer-directed laser beams, creating a true 3-D image space visible to multiple viewers without eyewear. It solves the problem of displaying true 3-D data with physiological depth cues (accommodation, convergence, motion parallax) by forming physical light points in mid-air, unlike 2-D displays that rely on psychological cues. It is distinguished from sibling methods like Phase-Controlled Laser Pointing for Swept Displays by its use of random-access AO scanning for voxel placement rather than phase-synchronized continuous lines, and from Spot Size Reduction Methods by its reliance on the helical geometry and AO deflection rather than purely geometric optics for spot definition. Inputs and Outputs: Input: 3-D Cartesian coordinates (x, y, z) for each desired voxel, a synchronization pulse from a sensor on the helix hub, and control signals for laser intensity. Output: A volumetric image composed of discrete voxels visible in real space, formed by laser light scattering from the rotating helix surface. Data Structures: Frame Buffer: Stores voxel coordinates. In second-generation systems, the z-axis is mapped from the spatial domain to a temporal domain (height maps to memory location). Control Memory: Capacity of 65,000 voxels per color in second-generation implementations. Addressability is 4096 \times 4096 per display volume. Scanner State: Tracks the current RF frequency sweep for X and Y deflectors to determine beam angle. Numbered Steps: 1. Coordinate Translation: Translate raw (x, y, z) coordinates into the computer memory such that the z-axis (height) is mapped to a temporal domain corresponding to the helix's rotational phase. 2. Synchronization: Wait for a synchronization pulse from a sensor on the helix hub indicating a known rotational angle (e.g., top dead center). 3. Surface Position Calculation: Calculate the position of the rotating helix surface at the exact moment the point needs to be displayed based on the rotational speed and the target (x, y) coordinates. The vertical voxel position z is determined by the intersection of the beam and the helix surface, defined by the rotation angle \theta: z = f(x, y, \theta). 4. Beam Steering: Send (x, y) coordinate pairs to the Acousto-Optic (AO) scanner in sequence to address the correct radial position. The AO scanner uses two deflectors for independent X and Y deflection. 5. Intensity Modulation: Modulate the laser intensity to illuminate only specific voxels, leaving dark areas unaddressed. 6. Projection: The laser beam illuminates the corresponding discrete points on the rotating helix surface. Light scatters from the surface, making voxels appear to emanate from specific points in real space. 7. Refresh: Repeat at the refresh rate (typically 20 Hz) to maintain persistence of vision. Formulas: Voxel Rate: The maximum rate at which voxels can be addressed is limited by the access time of the AO deflector. \text{Voxel Rate} = \frac{1}{\text{Access Time}} For an access time of 10 \, \mu\text{sec}, the max voxel rate is 100,000 voxels/sec. Usable Voxels per Frame: \text{Usable Voxels per Frame} = \frac{\text{Voxel Rate}}{\text{Refresh Rate}} - \text{Dwell Time Voxels} For 100,000 voxels/sec and 20 Hz refresh, the theoretical max is 5,000 voxels. Half-Angle Scan Range: The deflection angle of an AO deflector. \theta{AO} = \frac{\lambda \Delta f}{vs} Where \lambda is optical wavelength, \Delta f is RF frequency sweep, and vs is acoustic velocity. Beam Divergence Constant: \theta = \frac{\lambda}{d} Where \theta is initial beam divergence angle and d is laser beam waist diameter. Vertical Velocity of Helix Surface: vz = \frac{dz}{dt} = \frac{dz}{d\theta} \frac{d\theta}{dt} = \frac{h}{2\pi} \cdot 2\pi f = h f Where h is helix height and f is rotation rate. Parameters: Helix Dimensions: Laboratory model: 36-inch diameter, 18-inch height, 36-inch pitch, 2 mm blade thickness. Transportable/Commercial: 12-inch diameter, 8-inch height. Rotation Speed: 600 RPM for double-helix (2 blades) to achieve 20 Hz refresh (f = \text{Refresh Rate} / \text{Blades} = 20/2 = 10 rev/sec = 600 RPM). Single-spiral commercial variant: 1200 RPM. Refresh Rate: 20 Hz. Access Time: 10 \, \mu\text{sec} for single-channel; 5 \, \mu\text{sec} for four-channel systems (achieved by reducing beam diameter from 6 mm to 3 mm). Deflector Sweep Range: 75 to 125 MHz (\Delta f = 50 MHz). Acoustic Velocity (vs): 0.65 mm/ms. Input Beam Diameter: 1.6 mm at the scanner input. Voxel Size: 1.5 mm (24-inch system); 0.7 mm (compact 12-inch system). Brightness: 256 levels per color. Laser Sources: Green: 2x 250 mW diode-pumped doubled Nd:YAG (532 nm). Red: 8x 30 mW single-mode red diode lasers (633 nm) or HeNe (633 nm). Laser Safety: <15 mW average per image. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import time def waitforsyncpulse(): # Wait for magnetic sensor on helix shaft to trigger at 0 or 180 degrees pass def loadinitialregister(value): # Load starting address into Counter B pass def readdualportram(address): # Read 12-bit X, 12-bit Y, 8-bit Intensity from Port B pass def setaorffrequencyx(freqhz): # Drive X-deflector with RF frequency proportional to X coordinate pass def setaorffrequencyy(freqhz): # Drive Y-deflector with RF frequency proportional to Y coordinate pass def setlasermodulation(intensity8bit): # Set AO intensity modulator RF drive level pass def rendervolumetricdisplay(framebuffer, helixparams, scannerparams): # Initialize hardware timing waitforsyncpulse() loadinitialregister(0) # Timer increments address every 12.0 microseconds accesstimeus = scannerparams['accesstimeus'] for address in range(len(framebuffer)): # Read voxel data from dual-port RAM x, y, intensity = readdualportram(address) # Convert X, Y to AO deflector RF frequencies (linear mapping within sweep range) # setaorffrequencyx(mapxtorf(x)) # setaorffrequencyy(mapytorf(y)) setlasermodulation(intensity) # Wait for acoustic wave to fill aperture before next address time.sleep(accesstimeus / 1e6) An interaction method that resolves the ambiguity of laser pointers projecting continuous lines by synchronizing pulse frequency with sweep frequency and adjusting phase offset via joystick for precise z-coordinate control. Choose when manual selection ray positioning is required. Optical and mechanical strategies to reduce laser spot diameter and addressable area, addressing excessive voxel size. Choose when higher spatial resolution is needed than the base AO scanner provides. Time Complexity: The voxel rate is limited by the AO access time. Single-channel systems achieve ~100,000 voxels/sec. Four-channel systems achieve ~200,000 voxels/sec per channel, totaling up to 1.6 million voxels/sec for the first commercial model or 3.2 million voxels/sec for the transportable dual-volume system. Memory Complexity: Frame buffer size is limited by control card memory, such as 65,000 voxels per color in second-generation systems. Measured Performance: The laboratory model (36-inch) produces 120,000 voxels per frame (RGB) at 2.4 million voxels/sec. The transportable model (12-inch) produces 160,000 total voxels per frame at 1.6 million voxels/sec. The measured spot size is ~4 ± 0.5 mm at the helix for the 36-inch system, and 0.7 mm for the 12-inch system. Scaling: Voxel count scales with the number of parallel AO scanner channels. Beam diameter reduction from 6 mm to 3 mm halves access time, doubling voxel throughput per channel. Strengths: The system provides true physiological depth cues (accommodation, convergence, motion parallax) for group viewing without eyewear. It is highly compatible with the human visual system compared to stereoscopic or holographic displays. Limitations: Reflective helix blades can block image portions, creating occlusion zones; this is mitigated by using a translucent helix and bottom projection. The center shaft creates a dead zone where voxels cannot be placed. Steep helical slope near the central axis causes spot elongation; primary image creation is restricted to regions midway between the center and the rim. The addressable volume is constrained by scanner optics and occlusions (e.g., 10" x 10" x 15" in second-generation systems). Early systems used ion lasers requiring water cooling, though solid-state lasers reduce power consumption by ~1000x. When to Use: Applications requiring true 3D visualization for multiple viewers, such as air traffic control, submarine navigation, battle management, and medical imaging. When Not to Use: Applications requiring extremely high spatial resolution (sub-millimeter) without hardware modification, or where the central dead zone is critical. The concept was invented by Professor Rüdiger Hartwig at the University of Stuttgart in the early 1980s. Feasibility was demonstrated by Dr. R. D. Williams and team at Texas Instruments in late 1989. R&D began at SSC San Diego (SPAWAR Systems Center, San Diego) in early 1990. First-generation prototypes were built by NCCOSC RDT&E Division in the early 1990s. Second-generation development objectives were established in mid-1992, with a report published in April 1995. The technology was commercialized via a 1995 CRADA with NEOS Technologies, Inc. and RGB Technology, Inc. for military and government use. It was deployed on the USS Stennis for the Joint Warrior Interoperability Demonstration (JWID 97) and installed in the SPAWAR Command Center of the Future. DTIC ADA358303: Improved Second-Generation 3-D Volumetric Display System. Revision 2, https://archive.org/details/DTICADA358303, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial) DTIC ADA306215: Laser-Based 3-D Volumetric Display System (The Improved Second Generation)., https://archive.org/details/DTICADA306215, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial) DTIC ADA264825: Laser Based 3D Volumetric Display System, https://archive.org/details/DTICADA264825, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial)

name: Phase-Controlled Laser Pointing for Swept Displays
head: Joystick-controlled depth pointing, Phase-controlled laser pointing
body: Phase-controlled laser pointing is an interaction method for swept volumetric displays that resolves the ambiguity of laser pointers projecting continuous lines across the volume. By synchronizing the laser pulse frequency with the display's sweep frequency and adjusting the phase offset via an analog joystick, the user can position a discrete laser dot at a specific height (z-coordinate) on the helical display surface. This method serves as an alternative to distance-controlled depth pointing, offering precise manual control over the selection ray's position rather than relying on physical proximity. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Analog joystick position (phase control), display sweep frequency (typically 30 Hz). Output: A laser dot appearing at a specific vertical position on the rotating helical surface. Data Structures and Hardware Layout: The implementation relies on a specific hardware configuration: Microcontroller: Arduino Nano running Timer 1 at 16 MHz resolution. Power: 9V rechargeable battery. Laser: 1 mW red laser diode. Driver: 2N2222 transistor used to switch the laser diode. Interface: Analog joystick for phase adjustment. Parameters: Default Frequency: 30 Hz. Clock Resolution: 16 MHz (Timer 1 on Arduino Nano). Drift Rate: 5 mm per minute on a Voxon VX1 display under default conditions. Steps: 1. Synchronization Verification: The user observes the laser dot; if the dot is static and does not drift, the pointer is synchronized with the display's oscillation. 2. Frequency Configuration: The laser is configured to pulse at the same frequency as the display's oscillation. This frequency is typically set to 30 Hz but can be adjusted once per display by pressing a button to enter adjust mode and using the analog stick. 3. Phase Adjustment: The user moves the analog joystick to change the phase of the laser pulse relative to the display's sweep cycle. This phase shift determines the vertical position (height) of the laser dot on the helical surface. 4. Complex Patterns (Optional): More complex timing patterns, such as a dashed line with a dot at the pointing position, can be generated by modifying the pulse train logic. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import time DISPLAYFREQHZ = 30 CYCLEPERIODS = 1.0 / DISPLAYFREQHZ TIMERCLOCKHZ = 16000000 ADCRESOLUTION = 1024 def initializetimer1forfrequency(freqhz): # Configures Timer 1 on the microcontroller to generate interrupts at freqhz. # On an Arduino Nano (16 MHz), this involves setting a prescaler and an output compare register (OCR1A) # to match the desired period. The sources do not specify the exact register values. pass def initializelaserdriver(): # Configures the 2N2222 transistor GPIO pin as an output to switch the 1 mW laser diode. pass def initializejoystickadc(): # Configures the analog joystick GPIO pin as an input for the microcontroller's ADC. pass def readanalogjoystick(): # Returns an integer from 0 to ADCRESOLUTION-1 representing the joystick's current position. return 512 # Standard ADC read operation def waituntiltimerreaches(phaseoffsets): # Blocks execution until the microcontroller's internal timer reaches the specified phase offset. # This aligns the laser pulse with the display's sweep cycle. time.sleep(phaseoffsets) def turnonlaser(): # Sets the laser driver GPIO pin high, activating the 1 mW laser diode. pass def turnofflaser(): # Sets the laser driver GPIO pin low, deactivating the laser diode. pass def mainloop(): initializetimer1forfrequency(DISPLAYFREQHZ) initializelaserdriver() initializejoystickadc() while True: joystickval = readanalogjoystick() phaseoffsets = (joystickval / ADCRESOLUTION) CYCLEPERIODS waituntiltimerreaches(phaseoffsets) turnonlaser() turnofflaser() Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Frequency Drift: If the microcontroller clock is not perfectly stable, frequency drift occurs, causing the laser dot to drift vertically. The specified hardware (Arduino Nano at 16 MHz) exhibits a drift rate of 5 mm per minute on a Voxon VX1 display. Calibration: Frequency adjustment is required only once per display, not per session. Distance-Controlled Depth Pointing is an interaction method where the depth of the laser dot is determined by the physical distance between the pointer device and the display surface, creating a "lock ray" illusion. It uses an ultrasonic range sensor (HC-SR04) to measure distance and triggers the laser accordingly. It is chosen when a natural "point-and-shoot" interaction is preferred over manual phase adjustment, though it may interfere with other ultrasonic devices. See Distance-Controlled Depth Pointing. A hardware interaction technique that automatically projects a laser onto the first visible surface in the line of sight by combining a light detector, laser, and dichroic optics. It routes incoming light through an aperture and lens to a detector, amplifies the signal via an op-amp, and triggers the laser when light is detected. An analog joystick controls the time offset (to project above/below the surface) and sensor sensitivity. It fails on sparse volumetric graphics or surfaces composed of multiple small slices and requires manual light level adaptation per application. A deployment strategy allowing simultaneous use of multiple independent laser pointers on a single swept volumetric display without display-side communication. It enables single-user two-handed gestures (e.g., pinching for rotation) and multi-user role swapping. It supports lasers of different colors. However, multiple devices using ultrasonic distance measurement will interfere with each other. The method provides real-time interaction where latency is dominated by the display's sweep frequency (30 Hz) and the microcontroller's timer resolution. Memory complexity is minimal, requiring only timer registers and ADC readings. The default 30 Hz configuration results in a vertical drift of 5 mm per minute on a Voxon VX1 display. Strengths include precise manual control over the z-coordinate, simple hardware implementation, and compatibility with existing displays without modification. Limitations include the need for manual synchronization verification, susceptibility to clock drift, and per-display frequency adjustment requirements. It should be used when precise, manual control of the selection point's height is required or when the user prefers a joystick interface over distance-based interaction. It should not be used when automatic surface detection is preferred or when multiple users require independent distance-based tracking without interference. This method was introduced in the paper "PointerVol: A Laser Pointer for Swept Volumetric Displays" presented at UIST ’24 (October 13–16, 2024, Pittsburgh, PA, USA). It addresses the problem of depth ambiguity in swept volumetric displays where a standard laser pointer creates a visible line across the volume. The method is inspired by the "depth ray" and "lock ray" techniques used in other volumetric display systems. name: Distance-Controlled Depth Pointing
head: Ultrasonic distance-based pointing
body: Distance-Controlled Depth Pointing is an interaction method for swept volumetric displays where the depth of a laser dot along the intersection line is determined by the physical distance between the pointer device and the display surface. This creates the illusion that the dot appears at a fixed distance from the pointer, effectively implementing a "lock ray" technique where the marker's position is controlled by inputs from the pointer device rather than a phase offset. It provides an alternative to Phase-Controlled Laser Pointing for Swept Displays, which adjusts depth via phase offset controlled by an analog joystick. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Physical distance from the pointer to the display center, measured via an ultrasonic sensor. Output: Timing signal to trigger the laser diode at the correct phase of the display's sweep cycle to render the dot at the calculated depth. Data Structures: Sensor Configuration: Sensor Model: HC-SR04 ultrasonic range sensor. Sampling Rate: 150 samples per second at 1 meter distance. Default Field of View Angle: 15 degrees. Modified Field of View Angle: 25 degrees (achieved by increasing pulse voltage V{pp} from 5V to 30V). Microcontroller State: Reference Distance: A stored value representing the distance from the center of the display to the pointer at the moment of reset. Current Distance: The latest corrected reading from the sensor. Predicted Difuser Position: A calculated value based on the sinusoidal oscillation model of the display's difuser. Numbered Steps: 1. Measure Raw Distance: The ultrasonic sensor emits a sound pulse and measures the time of flight (t{tof}) for the echo to return. 2. Correct for Time of Flight: The raw distance reading is corrected to account for the time of flight of sound to ensure accuracy. 3. Reset Reference (Optional): If the user presses the reset button, the current corrected distance is saved as the new reference distance from the center of the display to the pointer. 4. Predict Difuser Position: The system predicts the position of the display's difuser assuming a sinusoidal oscillation. 5. Trigger Laser: The laser diode is triggered at the calculated phase to render the dot at the depth corresponding to the pointer's distance. Formulas: Distance Correction: The sources state that distances are corrected according to the time of flight of sound, but do not provide the specific mathematical formula for this correction. Difuser Position Prediction: The position is predicted assuming a sinusoidal oscillation of the difuser. The specific equation for this sinusoidal model is not provided in the sources. Parameters: Laser: 1 mW red laser diode. Driver: 2N2222 transistor. Microcontroller: Arduino Nano. Power: 9V rechargeable battery. Display Frequency: 30 Hz (default). Laser Pulse Voltage (V{pp}): 30 V (modified) or 5 V (default). Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Sensor Exposure: The difuser must be directly exposed to the ultrasonic sensor. A protective dome cannot be used because ultrasound requires direct exposure to propagate effectively. LIDAR Rejection: LIDAR sensors were explored but rejected due to low sampling rates (below 30 samples per second) and unreliability caused by the translucency of the difuser. Drift: With a default frequency of 30 Hz and an Arduino Nano (Timer 1 at 16 MHz resolution), the laser drifts only 5 mm per minute in a Voxon VX1 display. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import time SPEEDOFSOUND = 343.0 # m/s DISPLAYFREQHZ = 30.0 # Hz SAMPLERATEHZ = 150.0 # Hz referencedistancem = 0.0 currentdistancem = 0.0 def getcurrenttime(): """Returns current system time in seconds.""" return time.time() def buttonpressed(): """Checks if the reset button on the pointer device is pressed.""" # Hardware-specific GPIO check return False def measurerawdistance(): """Emits ultrasonic pulse and measures time of flight in seconds.""" # HC-SR04 trigger/echo interface return 0.0 def correctdistance(rawtimes): """Corrects raw time of flight to distance.""" # Formula not provided in sources return (rawtimes SPEEDOFSOUND) / 2.0 def predictdifuserposition(times): """Predicts difuser position assuming sinusoidal oscillation.""" # Specific equation not provided in sources return 0.0 def resetreference(): """Sets the current corrected distance as the reference distance from the center of the display to the pointer.""" global referencedistancem referencedistancem = currentdistancem def triggerlaser(): """Calculates laser trigger timing based on current distance and difuser position prediction.""" global currentdistancem # 1. Measure and correct distance rawtime = measurerawdistance() currentdistancem = correctdistance(rawtime) # 2. Predict difuser position difuserpos = predictdifuserposition(getcurrenttime()) # 3. Calculate phase offset based on distance # The depth is determined by the distance between pointer and display # Specific mapping from distance to phase is not provided # 4. Trigger laser # Laser switches on at configured frequency matching display oscillation # Hardware-specific trigger implementation required # Source does not specify the exact trigger mechanism def mainloop(): while True: if buttonpressed(): resetreference() triggerlaser() time.sleep(1.0 / SAMPLERATEHZ) Accuracy: The method provides a fixed-distance illusion relative to the pointer. Drift is minimal (5 mm per minute) when using a 30 Hz display and an Arduino Nano. Limitations: The method requires direct line-of-sight between the sensor and the difuser, preventing the use of protective domes. It is sensitive to the translucency of the difuser, which caused unreliability with LIDAR alternatives. Hardware Constraints: Relies on the HC-SR04 sensor, which has a maximum angle of 15 degrees (modifiable to 25 degrees with higher voltage). This method was introduced in the paper "PointerVol: A Laser Pointer for Swept Volumetric Displays" by Fernández et al., presented at UIST 2024. It is part of the development of laser-based 3-D volumetric displays using rotating helix geometry and AO scanners. The technique is equivalent to the "lock ray" technique previously shown to yield good results for volumetric displays. name: Spot Size Reduction Methods
head: Addressable Area Reduction
body: This method defines four optical and mechanical strategies to reduce the laser spot diameter and the corresponding addressable area on a rotating helical volumetric display. The original system produced a 4 mm spot diameter, which these methods aim to reduce to approximately 1.7–2.0 mm. Input: The existing scanner-helix optical train, characterized by a throw distance, output lens focal lengths, and scanner resolution (256 × 256 deflectors). Output: A reduced spot diameter (target ~1.7–1.8 mm) and a remapped addressable area (e.g., 13 × 13 or 24 × 24) within the 4095 × 4095 digital address space. The hardware state is defined by the following parameters: throwdistance: Distance from scanner to helix surface (mm). lensfocallength: Focal length of projection/output lenses (mm). scannerresolution: Number of addressable points per axis (integer). beamsize: Diameter of the laser beam within the deflectors (mm). spotdiameter: Resulting spot size at the helix surface (mm). addressablearea: The physical or logical grid size occupied by the beam (e.g., 13 × 13). The implementation involves selecting one of four mutually exclusive or combinable hardware modifications. 1. Method 1: Reduce Throw Distance Reduce the physical distance from the scanner to the helix by approximately half. Target throw distance: 1700 mm. Result: Spot diameter of 1.7 mm; addressable area reduces to 13+ × 13+. 2. Method 2: Insert Projection Lens Insert a single projection lens in front of the scanner. Select lens focal length from {500, 1000, 1500} mm. Result: Best spot size is 1.8 mm. Requires an 8-inch lens. Introduces optical aberrations. 3. Method 3: Change Output Lenses Modify the output optics to decrease angular magnification. Replace the last output lens with a focal length of approximately 110 mm (original was 60 mm). Remap voxel images to fill the 4095 × 4095 address space. Result: Spot size of 1.7 mm. 4. Method 4: Increase Scanner Resolution Increase the beam size in the deflectors to 6.4 mm. Increase scanner resolution from 256 × 256 to 512 × 512. Result: Spot size of 1.8 mm at 24 × 24 area. Sub-millimeter spots possible if optimized to 13 × 13 area. Penalty: Total voxel count reduces from 40,000 to 20,000. No explicit mathematical formulas are provided in the sources. Throw Distance: ~1700 mm. Projection Lens Focal Lengths: 500, 1000, or 1500 mm. Output Lens Focal Length: 60 mm (original) replaced by ~110 mm. Deflector Beam Size: 6.4 mm. Aberrations: Method 2 introduces optical aberrations that are difficult to remove. Voxel Count Reduction: Method 4 halves the total number of voxels (40,000 to 20,000), reducing image density. Misalignment: Slight misalignment of scanner optics (e.g., shifting the 80 mm collimating lens by ±1 mm) has negligible effect on spot size if the output lens is adjusted to achieve the minimum spot size. Lens Size: Method 2 requires an 8-inch lens, which is physically large. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def evaluatespotreductionmethods(): """ Evaluates four methods for reducing spot size on a helical volumetric display. Returns the recommended method based on source evaluation. """ results = [] # Method 1: Reduce throw distance method1 = { "name": "Reduce Throw Distance", "throwdistancemm": 1700, "spotdiametermm": 1.7, "addressablearea": "13+ x 13+", "pros": ["Direct", "Good spot size"], "cons": [] } results.append(method1) # Method 2: Insert projection lens method2 = { "name": "Insert Projection Lens", "lensfocallengthsmm": [500, 1000, 1500], "spotdiametermm": 1.8, "lenssizeinches": 8, "pros": [], "cons": ["Aberrations", "Large lens required", "Worse spot size than Method 1"] } results.append(method2) # Method 3: Change output lenses method3 = { "name": "Change Output Lenses", "oldoutputlensmm": 60, "newoutputlensmm": 110, "spotdiametermm": 1.7, "addressspace": "4095 x 4095", "pros": ["Cost-effective", "Straightforward", "Good spot size"], "cons": [] } results.append(method3) # Method 4: Increase scanner resolution method4 = { "name": "Increase Scanner Resolution", "oldresolution": "256 x 256", "newresolution": "512 x 512", "beamsizemm": 6.4, "spotdiametermm": 1.8, "addressablearea": "24 x 24", "totalvoxelsold": 40000, "totalvoxelsnew": 20000, "pros": ["Higher resolution"], "cons": ["Halved voxel count", "Larger area"] } results.append(method4) # Selection logic based on source evaluation # Method 3 is selected as most cost-effective and straightforward # Method 2 rejected due to aberrations and lens size # Method 4 penalized by halved voxel count recommendedmethod = method3 return recommendedmethod Adjusting lens positions to compensate for misalignment without degrading spot size. Using Gaussian beam traces for additional optical analysis. Performance: Method 3 achieves a 1.7 mm spot size, comparable to Method 1, but is preferred for its cost-effectiveness and simplicity. Trade-offs: Method 1 requires physical modification of the throw distance. Method 2 introduces aberrations and requires large optics. Method 4 reduces the total voxel count by 50%. Robustness: The system is tolerant to slight misalignments (±1 mm shift in collimating lens) if the output lens is re-focused. This method was developed for the Improved Second-Generation 3-D Volumetric Display System. It addresses limitations in the initial design where the spot size was too large (4 mm) and the addressable area was insufficiently utilized. The goal was to reduce the spot size to approximately 2 mm or less while maintaining a high voxel count. DTIC ADA358303: Improved Second-Generation 3-D Volumetric Display System. name: Holographic Defuser Light Field Display
head: Jones et al. holographic rotating diffuser, Jones light-field display
body: A volumetric display system that generates a 360° horizontal light field by projecting images onto a rotating holographic diffuser screen. Unlike standard rotational swept-screen displays that diffuse light broadly, this method uses a diffuser with specific angular characteristics to reflect light within a narrow cone (1.25°), creating distinct viewpoints for multiple users simultaneously. It solves the limitation of occlusion in traditional ghosted volumetric displays, though it remains constrained to content without complex occlusion. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A sequence of 2D images corresponding to specific viewing angles; rotation speed of the screen; projector frame rate. Output: A 360° horizontal light field with 288 distinct viewpoints. Data Structures: Image Buffer: A sequence of N=288 images. Each image corresponds to a specific angular sector of the 360° field of view. Screen Geometry: A cylindrical or planar surface coated with a holographic diffuser material. Diffuser Property: A reflection profile limited to a range of \theta{max} = 1.25^\circ. Steps: 1. Synchronization Setup: Synchronize the projector's frame update with the angular position of the rotating screen. The screen rotates continuously around a central vertical axis. 2. Image Selection: For each projector frame k, select the image Ik corresponding to the current viewing angle \phik determined by the screen's rotation angle. 3. Projection: Project image Ik onto the screen surface. 4. Diffusion: The holographic diffuser reflects the projected light only within the narrow angular range of \pm 0.625^\circ (centered on the specular reflection direction). 5. Viewpoint Generation: As the screen rotates, the narrow reflection cone sweeps across the audience, delivering the correct perspective image to each viewer's position. 6. Temporal Integration: The persistence of vision blends the discrete viewpoints into a continuous 3D light field experience for multiple users. Formulas: Viewpoint Count: N = 288. Angular Resolution: The angular width of each viewpoint is determined by the diffuser's reflection range, \Delta \theta = 1.25^\circ. Mapping: The image index k is mapped to the rotation angle \alpha such that k = \text{round}(\frac{\alpha}{360^\circ} \times 288). Parameters: Number of Images: 288. Horizontal Field of View: 360°. Reflection Angle Range: 1.25°. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Occlusion: The system cannot render occlusion between objects in the scene because the light is diffused into a wide horizontal field of view for all viewers simultaneously. It is limited to "ghosted content" where objects do not block each other from different viewpoints. Viewer Position: Users must be at a specific height and distance from the device to receive the correct viewpoint. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def renderholographicdisplay(images, rotationangledegrees): """ Selects and projects the correct image based on screen rotation. Args: images: List of 288 pre-rendered 2D images. rotationangledegrees: Current angle of the screen (0-360). Returns: The image to project. """ # Map rotation angle to image index # Ensure angle is normalized to 0-360 normalizedangle = rotationangledegrees % 360.0 # Calculate index # 288 images cover 360 degrees index = int((normalizedangle / 360.0) 288) # Handle boundary case if index equals 288 if index >= 288: index = 0 return images[index] def checkdiffuserconstraint(viewerangledegrees, screennormalangledegrees): """ Checks if a viewer is within the narrow reflection cone. Args: viewerangledegrees: Angle of the viewer relative to the screen center. screennormalangledegrees: Angle of the screen's surface normal. Returns: True if viewer is in the 1.25 degree reflection cone. """ # Calculate difference between viewer and specular reflection direction anglediff = abs(viewerangledegrees - screennormalangledegrees) # The reflection range is 1.25 degrees total # So the viewer must be within 0.625 degrees of the specular direction if anglediff <= 0.625: return True else: return False Uses a physical mirror to sweep a laser or light source. Offers true occlusion but is limited to line-based or sparse volumetric rendering. Link Uses an array of LEDs on a rotating ring. Simpler hardware but limited resolution and no true light-field perspective correction. Link Projects onto a generic rotating screen. Lacks the angular selectivity of the holographic defuser, resulting in ghosting for multiple viewers. Link Uses discrete planes. Does not provide continuous 3D depth or 360° light field. Link Oscillates rather than rotates. Similar projection challenges but limited to a 180° or less field of view. Link Time Complexity: O(1) per frame for image selection, assuming pre-computed viewpoints. The bottleneck is the projector's frame rate and the mechanical rotation speed. Memory Complexity: O(N) where N=288 is the number of viewpoints. Each viewpoint must be stored as a 2D image. Measured Performance: Generates 288 images on a 360° horizontal field of view. The reflection angle is limited to 1.25°. Strengths: Allows multi-user sharing of the visual experience at a given height and distance. Provides a true 360° light field with distinct viewpoints. Limitations: Cannot render occlusion between objects, limiting content to "ghosted" scenes. Requires precise synchronization between rotation and projection. When to use: For multi-user 360° displays where occlusion is not critical. When not to use: For scenes requiring complex depth interactions or occlusion. The system was proposed by Jones et al. to allow multi-user sharing of the visual experience at a given height and distance from the device. It addresses the limitation of traditional rotational swept-screen displays where broad diffusion prevents distinct viewpoints for multiple users. The concept builds on earlier work by Joens et al. in 2007, who combined a rotating holographic defuser with a high-speed projector to form multiple viewpoints in 360 degrees. name: 2D Full-Color LED Array Rotational Display
head: LED Array Volumetric Display, Multivox Volumetric Display System, Rotational Volumetric Display
body: A 2D full-color LED array rotational display renders volumetric images by rotating a 2D LED panel array around a central axis and synchronously updating the panel content to match the rotation angle. It differs from laser-based swept-screen systems by generating voxels directly on an emissive surface without requiring external synchronization with electron beams or lasers. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A 3D voxel buffer (volume data) and a target rotation speed. Output: A 3D volumetric image perceived by the human eye via persistence of vision. Data Structures: Voxel Buffer: A 3D array stored in shared memory, written by a client process and read by a driver process. LED Panel State: The current 2D image frame to be displayed on the HUB75 panels. Parameters: Images per rotation: 512 frames per full revolution. Rotation Speed: Several hundred RPM. Panel Type: HUB75 LED panels. Steps: 1. Initialization: Configure the GPIO memory-mapped access base address (BCMBASE) for the specific hardware (e.g., Raspberry Pi 4). Define GPIO mappings and panel layout in the driver configuration file. 2. Synchronization Setup: Establish a sync signal using a single GPIO pin connected to a photodiode or similar sensor. The signal is high for 180° of rotation and low for the other 180°. 3. Frame Calculation: For each rotation, calculate the 512 required 2D slices. Extract the 2D cross-section of the voxel buffer corresponding to the current rotation angle. 4. Buffer Update: Write the calculated 2D frame data into the shared memory voxel buffer. 5. Scanout: The driver reads the voxel buffer and drives the HUB75 LED panels in sync with the rotation angle detected by the sync signal. 6. Persistence: The rapid rotation and frame updates blend the discrete 2D slices into a continuous 3D volume. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. BCMBASE = None # Base address for memory-mapped GPIO access FRAMESPERROTATION = 512 # SYNCPIN = None # GPIO pin for photodiode sync def initgpio(): # Memory-map GPIO access using BCMBASE # Configure SYNCPIN as input pass def readsync(): # Read digital state of SYNCPIN # Returns True for high (180°), False for low (180°) return True # def extractslice(buffer, k): # Compute angle theta = (k / FRAMESPERROTATION) 2 pi # Extract 2D cross-section of buffer at theta # Return 2D pixel array for HUB75 panels return [] def drivepanels(image): # Write image data to HUB75 panels # Supports ABCDE addressing or ABC shift register addressing pass def main(): initgpio() k = 0 while True: # Driver scans voxel buffer in sync with rotation slicedata = extractslice(voxelbuffer, k) drivepanels(slicedata) k = (k + 1) % FRAMESPERROTATION # Timing is managed by hardware sync signal and rotation speed Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Hardware Compatibility: The GPIO memory-mapped access assumes a Raspberry Pi 4. Using different Pi models requires changing BCMBASE and is untested. Synchronization: Precise timing between the screen's angular position and the image update is critical. The photodiode sync signal must be correctly wired to distinguish the 180° high and low phases. Complexity: Time complexity is linear with respect to the number of voxels and frames per rotation. Memory complexity is proportional to the voxel buffer size. Performance: Requires high-speed GPIO updates and precise timing. The system runs on a Raspberry Pi 4 embedded in the spinning hardware. Strengths: Self-contained system; no external synchronization devices needed; full-color output. Limitations: Limited to the resolution of the LED panels; rotation speed limits the maximum volume size and frame rate; hardware-specific GPIO code. The concept of using rotating 2D full-color LED arrays for volumetric display was proposed by Xie et al. in 2009. This method was later categorized as a "free-space" volumetric display by Sumalley et al. in 2018. A hardware implementation uses two HUB75 LED panels controlled by a Raspberry Pi 4. name: Dynamic Projection Mapping for Rotating Volumetric Display
head: External Tracking of Rotating Objects, Handheld Volumetric Display Using Dynamic Projection Mapping
body: This method renders layered volumetric images by projecting optical patterns onto the surface of a manually rotated object composed of fan-shaped disks, using external high-speed cameras for tracking and a high-speed projector for rendering. It enables users to freely move and rotate the physical display while maintaining a stable perceived image, distinguishing itself from spiral swept-volume approaches by providing discrete physical depth planes, albeit with lower depth resolution. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: Target images for each layer (Ti), projector calibration matrix (P), real-time pose data of the rotating object (position, orientation, rotation angle \alpha). Outputs: Projected image frames on the rotating fan blades. Data Structures: Rotating Object: A stack of l disks. Each disk has n=3 fan-shaped blades. Blade radius: 50 mm. Blade thickness: 3 mm. Interval between adjacent disks: 10 mm. Angular offset between disks: 360^\circ / (3 \times l). Tracking Markers: Three retroreflective markers attached to the frontmost disk: 1. One at the geometric center. 2. Two along the bisector of the central angle of two blades, at distances 47 mm (outer) and 23.5 mm (inner) from the center. Numbered Steps: 1. Tracking: Use external high-speed cameras (e.g., OptiTrack PrimeX 13W1) to detect the marker positions. Calculate the object's model matrix M and the rotation angle \alpha [°] around the axis of rotation using the tracking API (e.g., OptiTrack Motive). 2. Layer Rotation: For each layer i (where i=1 is the frontmost layer) in an assembly with l layers, rotate the target image Ti by an angular offset of \frac{360(i-1)}{3 \times l} [°] relative to the frontmost layer. 3. Rotation Compensation: Counteract the physical rotation of the object by rotating the resulting image by -\alpha [°] so that the perceived orientation remains constant. 4. Coordinate Transformation: Calculate the homogeneous coordinates pp on the projector's frame for a point pr on the rotating object using the projector matrix P and the inverse model matrix M^{-1}: pp = P M^{-1} pr 5. Projection Delay Compensation: Measure the average projection delay da [ms] (typically ~12.5 ms). Calculate the predicted projection deviation \Delta ap [°] based on the current rotational speed s [RPM]: \Delta ap = \frac{360 \times da}{s \times 60000} Apply this angular offset to the projected pattern to align the image with the physical blade position at the time of light emission. 6. Rendering: Render the transformed and compensated image onto the projector frame and project it onto the rotating blades. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def renderframe(targetimages, projectormatrix, modelmatrix, rotationangle, rotationalspeed, avgdelayms): """ Renders the projection frame for a rotating volumetric display. Args: targetimages: List of images for each layer, indexed 0 to l-1. projectormatrix: 4x4 calibration matrix P. modelmatrix: 4x4 object model matrix M. rotationangle: Current rotation angle alpha in degrees. rotationalspeed: Rotational speed s in RPM. avgdelayms: Average measured projection delay da in ms. Returns: projectedframe: The image to be sent to the projector. """ numlayers = len(targetimages) numblades = 3 projectedframe = None for i in range(numlayers): Ti = targetimages[i] layerindex1 = i + 1 layeroffsetdeg = (360 (layerindex1 - 1)) / (numblades numlayers) # Standard image rotation by layeroffsetdeg Tirotated = applyrotation(Ti, layeroffsetdeg) # Counteract physical rotation by -alpha Ticompensated = applyrotation(Tirotated, -rotationangle) # Predict projection deviation from average delay deltaapdeg = (360 avgdelayms) / (rotationalspeed 60000) # Apply delay compensation Tifinal = applyrotation(Ticompensated, deltaapdeg) # Standard compositing of layer images onto the projection buffer if projectedframe is None: projectedframe = Tifinal else: projectedframe = compositeimages(projectedframe, Tifinal) return projectedframe Parameters: Number of blades per disk: 3. Blade radius: 50 mm. Blade thickness: 3 mm. Interval between adjacent disks: 10 mm. Marker distance from center (outer): 47 mm. Marker distance from center (inner): 23.5 mm. Average projection delay: 12.5 ms (SD 1.30 ms) at 600–1200 RPM. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Deceleration: Because the rotor is manually driven, contact with external objects causes rapid deceleration and stopping, requiring robust tracking updates. Precision: The system achieves a mean apparent projection delay of 0.147 ms (SD 1.02 ms) after compensation, compared to 12.5 ms before. Failure to compensate for delay results in visible misalignment. Depth Resolution: The discrete physical planes result in lower depth resolution compared to continuous swept-volume methods. Time Complexity: Not explicitly given. Dependent on camera frame rate, tracking API latency, and projector refresh rate. Memory Complexity: Not explicitly given. Measured Performance: Average projection delay of 12.5 ms (SD 1.30 ms) was measured at rotational speeds between 600 and 1200 RPM. After compensation, the mean apparent projection delay was 0.147 ms (SD 1.02 ms, n=31). Hardware: Implemented with three high-speed cameras (PrimeX 13W1), Intel Core i7-13700KF CPU, NVIDIA GeForce RTX3080 GPU, and a high-speed projector (DynaFlash2). Strengths: Allows users to freely move and rotate the object; no embedded rotation mechanism or light-emitting elements in the object. Limitations: Lower depth resolution compared to spiral swept-volume approaches. Manual rotation requires user supervision and can stop abruptly. Origin: The method was introduced in the paper "Mobile Volu-Me: Handheld Volumetric Display Using Dynamic Projection Mapping onto Rotating Fans". History: It builds on dynamic projection mapping technology, applying it to a handheld, manually rotated fan structure to enable portable volumetric displays. Usage: Used in prototypes with 3D-printed PLA fan assemblies (3-layer and 5-layer configurations) for user studies on perceived quality and depth representation. Uses mirrors to sweep a light sheet, offering continuous depth but requiring complex scanning mechanics. Separates the drawing space from the viewing space, allowing interaction without occlusion. Uses holography for high-resolution volumetric displays. Uses lenticular lenses to direct views to different angles. Traps particles in air using light to create the volume. Calculates holograms for volumetric display. Uses quantum dots for emission. Uses chromatic dispersion to create depth. Uses materials that emit light in 3D. Sweeps a screen continuously, offering continuous depth but potentially lower resolution per plane.
