name: Multi-planar volumetric 3D display
head: Moving screen volumetric display, Swept-screen volumetric display, Temporal integration volumetric display
body: A multi-planar volumetric 3D display projects a sequence of 2D image patterns onto a screen moving along the Z-axis to form a stack of spatial image planes, creating a true 3D image viewable without glasses. Unlike conventional 2D screens that rely on psychological depth cues, this method places voxels at their physical spatial positions, emitting light omni-directionally to provide both physiological and psychological depth cues. Builds on Rotational Swept-Screen Projection. It distinguishes itself from sibling methods like Volumetric Display using Rotating Mirror (VRDM), 2D Full-Color LED Array Rotational Display, and Oscillating Swept Volume Display by utilizing linear or reciprocating screen motion rather than rotational sweep. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A 3D volume defined by N 2D image frames (slices) corresponding to specific Z-depths, and a screen sweep frequency f{sweep}. Output: A continuous 3D volumetric image perceived by the human eye. Data Structures: Image Sequence: A list of N 2D frames \{I0, I1,..., I{N-1}\}, where each frame Ik corresponds to the image pattern projected when the screen is at position zk. Screen State: Defined by position z(t) and velocity v(t) along the Z-axis. Steps: 1. Initialize Sweep: The screen begins moving along the Z-axis in a back-and-forth motion at a frequency f{sweep} > 24 Hz. 2. Synchronize Projection: A high-speed 2D image projector updates its output synchronously with the screen's position. 3. Project Frames: During one complete sweep cycle (period T = 1/f{sweep}), the projector displays N distinct 2D image frames. 4. Intercept and Stack: The moving screen intercepts the 2D image projections at different positions along the Z axis, forming a stack of spatial image planes. 5. Temporal Integration: Due to persistence of vision and the high sweep frequency, the discrete 2D slices blend into a continuous 3D volume in the viewer's perception. Formulas: Sweep Frequency: f{sweep} > 24 Hz. Frame Rate: The projector must display N frames within T = 1/f{sweep}, requiring a frame rate R{proj} = N \cdot f{sweep}. Z-Position Mapping: For a sweep range [Z{min}, Z{max}], the position zk for frame k (k \in [0, N-1]) is mapped linearly or according to the screen's kinematic profile. Parameters: f{sweep}: Screen sweep frequency. Must be > 24 Hz to avoid flicker and ensure proper temporal integration. N: Number of 2D image frames projected per sweep cycle. Projector Type: High-speed 2D image projector (e.g., DLP) is preferred for high frame rates and quality. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Flicker: If f{sweep} \le 24 Hz, the display may flicker, breaking the 3D illusion. Motion Blur: Excessive screen velocity relative to projector exposure time can cause blurring of the slices. A signal modulation technique that projects variable 1D patterns along the viewing line through the display volume by timing laser pulses. It provides depth context without the occlusion of full 3D shapes, serving as the 3D analog to the 0D dot used on 2D screens. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Measured Performance: The system relies on high-speed DLP projection engines to achieve the necessary frame rates. Strengths: Displays voxels physically at their spatial positions, emitting light omni-directionally, providing true physiological depth cues. Limitations: Requires precise synchronization between screen motion and projection. Limited by the mechanical speed of the screen and the frame rate of the projector. When to use: When true 3D spatial representation with physiological depth cues is required, and glasses-free viewing is necessary. When not to use: When high resolution is required without mechanical complexity, or when the scene requires static 3D display without motion. The multi-planar volumetric 3D display technique was developed to address the limitations of conventional 2D screens, which lack physical depth cues. It utilizes high-speed DLP projection engines to facilitate the rapid projection of 2D image patterns onto a moving screen. The method was highlighted in research focusing on the design of volumetric 3D displays based on high-speed DLP projection engines. A volumetric 3D display based on a DLP projection engine, https://doi.org/10.1016/j.displa.2012.11.001, fetched 2026-10-27

name: Line Patterns and 2D/3D Projection
head: Line Pattern Volumetric Display, Temporal Laser Line Projection
body: A signal modulation technique that projects variable 1D patterns along the viewing line through the display volume by timing laser pulses. It provides depth context without the occlusion of full 3D shapes, serving as the 3D analog to the 0D dot used on 2D screens. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Time-varying control signals (e.g., from a joystick or distance sensor) and the display's oscillation frequency. Output: A modulated laser beam forming 1D patterns (points, lines, dashed segments) within the volumetric display space. Data Structures: Control Signal: A time-indexed sequence of duty cycle or pulse-width values. Oscillation State: The current phase of the display screen's rotation/oscillation. Steps: 1. Synchronization: Align the laser control signal with the display's oscillation frequency. The phase of the signal relative to the oscillation determines the depth (Z-axis) where the pattern appears. 2. Pattern Generation: Modulate the laser's pulse width or duty cycle over time to create specific 1D shapes. Single Point: A short pulse duration. Continuous Line: A sustained pulse duration covering the desired length. Dashed Line/Segments: Alternating on/off states within the pulse window. 3. Depth Control: Adjust the phase offset of the control signal to move the pattern along the Z-axis. 4. Animation: Play temporal animations (e.g., moving segments) to encode direction or speed along the line. Formulas: Drift Error: The positional drift of the laser dot is a function of the frequency mismatch between the laser controller and the display. In a Voxon VX1 display with an Arduino Nano (16 MHz Timer 1), a default 30 Hz oscillation results in a drift of only 5 mm per minute. Parameters: Oscillation Frequency: Typically 30 Hz. Controller Resolution: 16 MHz timer resolution (e.g., Arduino Nano). Interaction Distance: 30 cm to 2 meters. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def generatelasersignal(oscillationphase, patterntype, length, dashratio): """ Generates the duty cycle for the laser diode based on the current oscillation phase and desired pattern. Args: oscillationphase: Float [0, 1], representing the current position of the screen in its oscillation cycle. patterntype: String {'point', 'line', 'dashed'} length: Float [0, 1], relative length of the line segment. dashratio: Float [0, 1], ratio of 'on' time to total period for dashed lines. Returns: Float: Duty cycle (0.0 to 1.0) for the current sample. """ # Determine the 'on' window for the pattern relative to the phase # The phase maps to the Z-depth. The pattern extends along the line # passing through the volume at that depth. if patterntype == 'point': # Short pulse centered at the target phase pulsewidth = 0.05 # Arbitrary small width for a point center = oscillationphase if abs(oscillationphase - center) < pulsewidth / 2: return 1.0 else: return 0.0 elif patterntype == 'line': # Continuous line of specified length # The line extends along the viewing line through the volume. # In practice, this is a sustained pulse while the screen passes # through the relevant Z-range. return 1.0 # Simplified: Laser is on for the duration of the line's Z-span elif patterntype == 'dashed': # Dashed line with a dot at the pointing position # Modulate duty cycle to create dashes cycle = (oscillationphase 10) % 1.0 # Create repeating cycle if cycle < dashratio: return 1.0 else: return 0.0 return 0.0 def synchronizelaser(displayfreq, controllerfreq): """ Adjusts the controller to minimize drift. """ # Frequency needs to be adjusted only once per display # Default 30 Hz oscillation with 16 MHz timer resolution # yields 5mm/min drift # Not given in the sources: synchronization algorithm details pass Edge Cases: Hand Jittering: Hand jitter is less noticeable at distances of 30 cm to 2 meters. Arm Fatigue: A disadvantage inherited from traditional laser pointers. A visual pattern modification where the laser output is pulsed to create a dashed line with a solid dot at the pointing position, rather than a continuous line or single point. The laser is pulsed at the display's oscillation frequency, but the duty cycle or timing is modulated to produce the dashed appearance, with the solid dot appearing at the specific phase/height selected by the user. This pattern was employed in depth user studies. Strengths: Provides depth context without occlusion; allows for natural interaction (e.g., pinching, rotation) using wearable devices. Limitations: Hand jitter and arm fatigue are disadvantages. Higher-dimensional pointers (spheres, cubes) are considered beyond the scope of current laser pointer implementations. Performance: Drift is minimal (5 mm/min) with standard hardware (Arduino Nano, 30 Hz display). Originated with the PointerVol device, a laser pointer designed for swept volumetric displays. The concept draws an analogy between 2D screens (using 0D dots) and 3D volumes (using 1D line patterns). Future research directions include higher-dimensional pointers (spheres, cubes, arrows) and independent control of multiple pointers for complex 3D rotations. name: Oscillating Swept Volume Display
head: Oscivox, Undulating Volumetric Display
body: The Oscillating Swept Volume Display (OSVD) is a volumetric display method that replaces continuous rotation or linear translation with an undulating (back-and-forth) mechanical motion to reduce mechanical jerk at the sweep endpoints. It builds on Rotational Swept-Screen Projection by maintaining synchronous projection but altering the kinematic profile to a sinusoidal oscillation, allowing for smoother acceleration/deceleration compared to constant-velocity rotation or linear reciprocation with hard stops. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A 3D voxel buffer and a hardware synchronization signal (SPINSYNC) from the motion controller. Output: Pixel data sent to an LED matrix or projector, synchronized to the instantaneous angle of the oscillating screen. Data Structures: The voxel buffer is a 3D array of pixelt (8-bit RGB332) with dimensions X=64, Y=64, Z=32. Memory Layout: Row-major. VOXELXSTRIDE = 1 VOXELZSTRIDE = 64 VOXELYSTRIDE = 2048 Index formula: VOXELINDEX(x, y, z) = x + y 2048 + z 64 Total Voxels: 262,144. Double Buffer: The shared memory buffer is sized at 2 262,144 sizeof(pixelt) to allow frame swapping without tearing. Parameters: Pixel Format: RGB332 (8-bit). Red: 3 bits (mask 0xE0), Green: 3 bits (mask 0x1C), Blue: 2 bits (mask 0x03). Conversion macros: R332(p) = (((p) >> 5) & 7) 36 G332(p) = (((p) >> 2) & 7) 36 B332(p) = ((p) & 3) 85 Fixed-Point Precision: REVOLUTIONPRECISION = 20 (bits for frequency/period scaling) ANGLEPRECISION = 10 (bits for angle index) SINCOSPRECISION = 12 (bits for sine/cosine table values) Sine/Cosine Table: 1024 entries (1 << 10). Values are fixed-point integers scaled by 2^{12}. GPIO Mapping (Raspberry Pi BCM2711): RGB Data: Pins 12, 9, 6, 5, 8, 7, 21, 13, 20, 26, 19, 16. Row Select (A-E): Pins 4, 15, 18, 17, 14. Control: RGBBLANK=11, RGBCLOCK=0, RGBSTROBE=3, SPINSYNC=1. Algorithm Steps: 1. Initialize Sine/Cosine Table: Iterate i from 0 to 1023. Compute angle a = i \cdot \frac{2\pi}{1023}. Store round(cos(a) 4096) in sincosfixed[i][0]. Store round(sin(a) 4096) in sincosfixed[i][1]. 2. Initialize Span Offsets (Partial): Compute pitch ef / 64. Set vx = -ef/2. Set vy = de + \sqrt{bd^2 - ac^2}. Set vsh = 1/(pitch \cdot 0.8). Set vsv = 1/(pitch \cdot 0.8). name: Optical Projection and Reflection
body: Optical Projection and Reflection techniques generate volumetric or pseudo-volumetric images by reflecting light from a 2D display source onto semi-reflective surfaces, creating the illusion of floating 3D objects in free space. This family solves the problem of presenting 3D content with natural occlusion cues without requiring physical particles or scanning beams in the viewing volume. It differs from scanning methods (like Galvanometer Scanner Volume Rendering) by using static optical elements to create persistent images, and from holographic methods (like Holographic Computer-Generated Holography (CGH) Calculation) by relying on geometric reflection rather than wavefront interference. The core mechanism involves a display source emitting light that strikes a translucent or semi-reflective surface. The surface reflects a portion of the light toward the viewer while transmitting the remainder. By stacking multiple such surfaces or using specific geometries, distinct image slices are superimposed to create depth. Key Mathematical Principles: 1. Contrast and Occlusion: The perception of a floating volume relies on high contrast between the projected image and the real background. If I{img} is the intensity of the projected image and I{bg} is the intensity of the real background, the contrast C at the boundary is defined as: C = \frac{I{img} - I{bg}}{I{img} + I{bg}} High contrast (bright image, dark background) is essential for the "floating" effect. 2. Perspective Projection: To simulate virtual images located behind the physical drawing volume, the display content must be projected based on the viewer's position. For an observer at point E = (x0, y0, z0) and an image point X = (x, y, z), the perspective projection onto a plane P (perpendicular to the line EO, where O is the origin) is governed by the matrix S: S = \begin{bmatrix} -r^2 & r^2 x0 & 0 & 0 \\ -r x0 z0 & -r y0 z0 & r \rho^2 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & r \rho \\ -\rho x0 & -\rho y0 & -\rho z0 & r \rho \end{bmatrix} where: r = \frac{1}{\sqrt{x0^2 + y0^2 + z0^2}} \rho = \frac{1}{\sqrt{x0^2 + y0^2}} 3. Rendering Steps: The system prepares image slices, applies perspective projection based on viewer position, emits light from the display source, and handles reflection/transmission at each layer to superimpose the final volume. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def rendersliceview(viewerpos, layers, displayparams): """ Render the SliceView volumetric display. Args: viewerpos: Tuple (x0, y0, z0) representing viewer position E. layers: List of dicts, each containing: 'image': 2D numpy array of the layer's content. 'z': Depth of the layer. 'R': Reflection coefficient. 'T': Transmission coefficient. displayparams: Dict containing optical parameters. Returns: None (displays images to respective layers) """ x0, y0, z0 = viewerpos # Calculate projection matrix components r = 1.0 / math.sqrt(x02 + y02 + z02) rho = 1.0 / math.sqrt(x02 + y02) # Construct projection matrix S S = [ [-r2, r2 x0, 0, 0], [-r x0 z0, -r y0 z0, r rho2, 0], [0, 0, 0, r rho], [-rho x0, -rho y0, -rho z0, r rho] ] for layer in layers: image = layer['image'] z = layer['z'] R = layer['R'] T = layer['T'] # Apply perspective projection to the image based on viewer position. # Sources do not specify the image warping algorithm; typically involves inverse mapping using the projection matrix. projectedimage = image # Display the projected image on the layer's display source. # Sources do not specify hardware emission control; typically involves driving the display panel with the projected image buffer. pass SliceView is a volumetric display system that extends the Pepper's Ghost optical illusion to multiple stacked translucent planes, cumulatively giving volume to an initially two-dimensional projection. It solves the problem of presenting 3D content in physical space without moving parts by superimposing distinct image slices at different depths, allowing the viewer to perceive a floating volume that occludes the real background. Unlike stereoscopic displays, it avoids vergence accommodation conflict (VAC) between the virtual object and the real background, and differs from persistence-of-vision displays by using static stacked planes rather than oscillating surfaces or levitated particles. Choose this method when natural occlusion and depth cues are required without mechanical scanning. Mechanically driven mirrors are beam deflectors used in volumetric displays to steer light beams toward specific points in a drawing volume. They solve the problem of directing light from a source to arbitrary (x, y, z) coordinates within a 3D space by physically rotating mirrors. They are distinguished from electro-optic deflectors by being essentially lossless but suffering from slower response times. Choose this method when high optical efficiency is prioritized over high-speed beam steering. This method provides a lensless magnification technique for holographic displays by using a diverging point light source to perform coarse beam steering, allowing a hologram to steer light at a finer angle to focus into an image. It solves the problem of achieving wide fields of view (60–100°) without the bulky refractive lenses required by conventional magnification. Unlike SliceView which relies on physical layer stacking, this method uses optical diffraction and divergence to create depth and magnification simultaneously. Choose this method when a wide field of view and lensless design are required. A technique to simulate virtual images (located behind the physical drawing volume) in freespace volumetric displays by projecting content onto a background image plane that moves and rotates to match the viewer's position, creating motion parallax cues consistent with a distant object. Definition: Simulates virtual images in freespace displays using time-varying perspective projection. Steps: 1. Define observer position E = (x0, y0, z0). 2. Define 3D image point X = (x, y, z). 3. Define background image plane P, typically perpendicular to line EO where O is origin. 4. Calculate intersection of line EX with plane P to determine pixel coordinate. Link: No separate article. A simple 360° display based on a conical semi-reflective surface that reflects an anamorphic image into a real undistorted aerial image. It has no moving parts. Definition: 360° display using conical semi-reflective surface. Steps: 1. Display an anamorphic image. 2. Reflect it off a 360° symmetrical conical semi-reflective surface. 3. Surface creates a real undistorted aerial image. 4. As viewer turns device, image changes to offer 360° interactive view. Pitfalls: Constrained to a limited number of viewers because only one point of view is displayed at a time. Link: No separate article. An analog electro-optic deflector using a series arrangement of electro-optic prisms. A light beam is deflected by varying the refractive index of each prism by applying an electric field to its top and bottom electroded faces. Pitfalls: The prism type suffers from high load capacitance, which limits random access times and increases complexity. Numbers: Better than 300-spot resolution has been demonstrated in the prism type of electro-optic deflector. Comparison: Unlike digital electro-optic deflectors which offer discrete beam positioning, this configuration yields an output continuously controllable in position. Link: No separate article. Optical projection and reflection techniques have roots in classical theatrical illusions, specifically Pepper's Ghost, which uses a large sheet of glass to reflect a hidden stage area into the main stage. SliceView was developed as an extension of Pepper's Ghost to multiple planes to create volumetric depth cues. Perspective Projection Backdrop was introduced in 2021 to simulate virtual images in optical trap displays (OTDs) by employing time-varying perspective projection. Pepper's Cone was proposed as a low-cost, efficient 360° display solution using conical surfaces. Mechanically driven mirrors were documented in early volumetric display studies (1970s) as a method for beam deflection, noting trade-offs between speed, hysteresis, and damping. These methods are used in research prototypes for volumetric displays, holography, and augmented reality interfaces where natural occlusion and parallax are desired without the complexity of scanning beams or particle traps. name: SliceView
head: Pepper's Ghost volumetric extension, Pepper's ghost display, Pepper's ghost effect, holographic display
body: SliceView is a volumetric display system that extends the Pepper's Ghost optical illusion to multiple stacked translucent planes, cumulatively giving volume to an initially two-dimensional projection. It solves the problem of presenting 3D content in physical space without moving parts by superimposing distinct image slices at different depths, allowing the viewer to perceive a floating volume that occludes the real background. Unlike stereoscopic displays, it avoids vergence accommodation conflict (VAC) between the virtual object and the real background, and differs from persistence-of-vision displays by using static stacked planes rather than oscillating surfaces or levitated particles. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A set of 2D image slices corresponding to different depth layers; viewer position E = (x0, y0, z0) for perspective correction; physical parameters of the display stack (layer thicknesses ti, reflection coefficients Ri, transmission coefficients Ti). Output: A perceived 3D volumetric image floating in space, superimposed on the real background. Data Structures: The system relies on a physical stack of N translucent planes. Each plane i (where i = 1 \dots N) is defined by: Position zi along the optical axis. Thickness ti. Optical properties: Reflection coefficient Ri and Transmission coefficient Ti. Content: A 2D image buffer Ii(x, y) with a black background. Numbered Steps: 1. Layer Preparation: For each layer i, generate or retrieve the 2D image Ii representing the cross-section of the 3D object at depth zi. The image must be surrounded by a black background to ensure high contrast. 2. Perspective Projection: Adjust the content of each layer Ii based on the viewer's position E to simulate a virtual image located at depth zi. The projection is governed by the matrix S: S = \begin{bmatrix} -r^2 & r^2 x0 & 0 & 0 \\ -r x0 z0 & -r y0 z0 & r \rho^2 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & r \rho \\ -\rho x0 & -\rho y0 & -\rho z0 & r \rho \end{bmatrix} where: r = \frac{1}{\sqrt{x0^2 + y0^2 + z0^2}} \rho = \frac{1}{\sqrt{x0^2 + y0^2}} 3. Display Emission: Emit light from the display source (e.g., LCD/OLED panel or projector) for each layer i. 4. Reflection and Transmission: The semi-reflective surface reflects a portion of the light (Ri) towards the viewer and transmits the remainder (Ti) to the next layer or background. The viewer sees the virtual image appearing to float in space. 5. Superposition: The viewer perceives the superimposed images from all layers i=1 \dots N. The high contrast between the projected image intensity I{img} and the real background intensity I{bg} creates the perception of volume. The contrast C at the boundary is defined as: C = \frac{I{img} - I{bg}}{I{img} + I{bg}} Parameters: Layer Thickness (ti): Evaluated alongside light reflection and transmission properties to optimize image quality. Exact optimization formulas are not specified in the sources. Reflection/Transmission Coefficients (Ri, Ti): Critical for balancing brightness and depth perception. Ri + Ti \leq 1 (accounting for absorption). Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Vergence Accommodation Conflict (VAC): While stereoscopic displays suffer from VAC due to the gap between accommodation on a 2D display and 3D vergence sensation, SliceView avoids this because the virtual object and real background are at different optical distances, and the image is a reflection, not a focused 2D plane in the same way. Contrast Loss: If the background is not sufficiently dark, the contrast C decreases, reducing the "floating" effect and volume perception. Layer Alignment: Misalignment of the physical planes or the projected images can cause ghosting or misregistration of the volume. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def rendersliceview(viewerpos, layers, displayparams): """ Render the SliceView volumetric display. Args: viewerpos: Tuple (x0, y0, z0) representing viewer position E. layers: List of dicts, each containing: 'image': 2D numpy array of the layer's content. 'z': Depth of the layer. 'R': Reflection coefficient. 'T': Transmission coefficient. displayparams: Dict containing optical parameters. Returns: None (displays images to respective layers) """ x0, y0, z0 = viewerpos # Calculate projection matrix components r = 1.0 / math.sqrt(x02 + y02 + z02) rho = 1.0 / math.sqrt(x02 + y02) # Construct projection matrix S S = [ [-r2, r2 x0, 0, 0], [-r x0 z0, -r y0 z0, r rho2, 0], [0, 0, 0, r rho], [-rho x0, -rho y0, -rho z0, r rho] ] for layer in layers: image = layer['image'] z = layer['z'] R = layer['R'] T = layer['T'] # Apply perspective projection to the image # Sources do not specify the image warping algorithm; typically involves inverse mapping using the projection matrix. projectedimage = image.copy() # Display the projected image on the layer's display source # The semi-reflective surface will reflect R portion to viewer # and transmit T portion to subsequent layers/background # Sources do not specify hardware emission control; typically involves driving the display panel with the projected image buffer. pass A 360° volumetric display based on a transparent projection surface made of sparse cube corner distribution. It derives from the Pepper's Ghost configuration but uses a transparent retro-reflective surface to project a real image, avoiding the need for a display panel above the device. The surface reflects the image towards the viewer while remaining transparent. The image seen through the semi-reflective surface (or directly if configured as aerial) seems to float if surrounded by a black background. Occlusion between the bright image and the real background creates volume perception. Compared to classical Pepper's Ghost design, this solution avoids the presence of a display panel above the device and presents a brighter image. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Measured Performance: Not given in the sources. Scaling: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Avoids vergence accommodation conflict (VAC) between the virtual object and the real background; simple and cheap compared to complex solutions; provides a 360° view in the transparent retro-reflective variant; no moving parts in the projected volume. Limitations: Relies on high contrast between projected image and real background; layer thickness and optical properties require careful optimization; limited to static volumes or temporally varying multi-view perception. When to use: When a simple, low-cost volumetric display is needed for public demonstrations, retro-gaming, or data visualization. When not to use: When precise stereoscopic depth cues are required, or when the environment has high ambient light that reduces contrast. The Pepper's Ghost effect creates a virtual image from a display by reflection on a semi-reflective surface. SliceView specifically applies this to multiple stacked translucent planes to create a volumetric display. The transparent retro-reflective surface variant was developed in a laboratory and presented to the public during a symposium, aiming to provide a 360° volumetric display without the need for a display panel above the device. SliceView has been implemented as a layer-based painting tool, retro-gaming platform, text overlaying media player for subtitles, browser-based 3D scene renderer, and volumetric data visualizer. name: Mechanically Driven Mirrors
head: Galvanometer driven, Piezoelectrically driven
body: Mechanically driven mirrors are beam deflectors used in volumetric displays and holography to steer light beams. They are essentially lossless but suffer from slow response times compared to electro-optic alternatives. They differ from SliceView by using dynamic reflection rather than static semi-reflective layers, and from Holographic Magnification via Diverging Light by using physical inertia rather than liquid crystal phase arrays for beam steering. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Commanded deflection angle \theta. Output: Reflected light beam at angle 2\theta (assuming normal incidence). Data Structures: Not given in the sources. Steps: 1. Receive a command for a target deflection angle. 2. Actuate the mirror mechanism (galvanometer or piezoelectric) to rotate the mirror surface. 3. Reflect the incident light beam off the mirror surface. 4. Stabilize the mirror to the target angle before emitting the next spot or frame. Formulas: Natural frequency fn determines the time response in random access operation. Maximum spot capability N{max} for a refresh rate R{refresh} is derived from the natural frequency: N{max} \approx \frac{fn}{R{refresh}} Parameters: Piezoelectric units: Lowest natural frequency: \approx 12 \text{ KHz}. Maximum spot capability at 30 \text{ Hz} refresh: 400 spots. Galvanometer units: Lowest natural frequency: \approx 3 \text{ KHz}. Maximum spot capability at 30 \text{ Hz} refresh: 100 spots. Pitfalls and Edge Cases: Hysteresis (Galvanometer): Galvanometer drives are susceptible to hysteresis effects as large as 4\%. To overcome this, the system must always approach a newly commanded deflection angle from the same direction. This requirement nearly doubles the random access time. Hysteresis (Piezoelectric): Piezoelectric drives circumvent hysteresis by using active position sensing. Underdamped Oscillation: High-response mechanical mirror drives often operate in a highly underdamped manner, producing slowly decaying oscillations about the mean orientation. This enlarges the apparent spot size, decreases boundary definition, and causes misregistration. Additional damping is required to prevent viewing degradation, which further decreases drive response. Pointing Accuracy: Pointing accuracies of 0.1 spot diameter are generally sufficient. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import time class MechanicallyDrivenMirror: def init(self, drivetype, naturalfrequencyhz): """ Initialize a mechanically driven mirror. Args: drivetype: 'galvanometer' or 'piezoelectric'. naturalfrequencyhz: The lowest natural frequency of the unit. """ self.drivetype = drivetype self.naturalfrequencyhz = naturalfrequencyhz self.currentangle = 0.0 self.lastdirection = None # For galvanometer hysteresis management def settargetangle(self, targetangle): """ Command the mirror to a new deflection angle. Args: targetangle: The desired deflection angle in degrees. """ if self.drivetype == 'galvanometer': # Galvanometer hysteresis mitigation: # Always approach from the same direction. # If changing direction, must traverse full range or use a specific protocol. # This nearly doubles random access time. if self.lastdirection is not None: if (targetangle > self.currentangle) != (self.lastdirection > 0): # Direction change detected; full settling required pass self.lastdirection = 1 if targetangle > self.currentangle else -1 # Actuate mirror self.actuate(targetangle) # Wait for settling based on natural frequency and damping # High response drives are underdamped; oscillations decay slowly. # Additional damping reduces response time. settlingtime = self.calculatesettlingtime(targetangle) time.sleep(settlingtime) self.currentangle = targetangle def actuate(self, angle): """ Physically move the mirror to the target angle. """ # Implementation depends on hardware (voltage/current control) pass def calculatesettlingtime(self, angle): """ Estimate time required for the mirror to settle within 0.1 spot diameter accuracy. """ # Based on natural frequency and damping characteristics # Not given in the sources. return 1.0 / self.naturalfrequencyhz def reflectbeam(self, incidentbeam): """ Reflect an incident beam off the current mirror orientation. Args: incidentbeam: Vector representing the incident light direction. Returns: Reflected beam vector. """ # Reflection calculation based on currentangle # Not given in the sources. pass A liquid crystal-based transmission phase array that optically tilts coherent backlight beams to expand the holographic viewing angle. It differs from mechanical mirrors by using electro-optic phase shifts rather than physical inertia. Maximum steering angle is \sim 15^\circ with an angular resolution of 0.02^\circ at a wavelength of 520 \text{ nm}. A key pitfall is that the maximum steering angle decreases as the light source area increases due to etendue constraints. Time Complexity: Response time is limited by the mechanical natural frequency. Galvanometer units (\approx 3 \text{ KHz}) are slower than piezoelectric units (\approx 12 \text{ KHz}). Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Measured Performance: At a 30 \text{ Hz} refresh rate, piezoelectric units support a maximum of 400 spots, while galvanometer units support 100 spots. Scaling: Scaling is limited by the trade-off between damping and response time; additional damping reduces oscillations but decreases drive response. Strengths: Essentially lossless efficiency. Limitations: Slow response time compared to electro-optic deflectors; susceptibility to hysteresis (galvanometer); underdamped oscillations causing misregistration. When to use: When high optical efficiency is required and the application can tolerate slower frame rates or spot counts. When not to use: When high-speed random access or high spot counts are required without the overhead of hysteresis compensation. Mechanically driven mirrors are among the simplest beam deflectors available for volumetric displays. They were studied in the context of 3D volumetric display systems in the 1970s. The technology distinguishes between galvanometer-driven and piezoelectric-driven units based on their actuation mechanisms and natural frequencies. name: Holographic Magnification via Diverging Light
head: Diverging Light Holographic Magnification
body: This method provides a lensless magnification technique for holographic displays by using a diverging point light source to perform coarse beam steering, allowing a hologram to steer light at a finer angle to focus into an image. It solves the problem of achieving wide fields of view (60–100°) without the bulky refractive lenses required by conventional magnification. Unlike SliceView which relies on physical layer stacking, this method uses optical diffraction and divergence to create depth and magnification simultaneously. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A Spatial Light Modulator (SLM) displaying a hologram pattern; a diverging point light source positioned at \vec{l}e; wavelength \lambda. Output: A magnified virtual image with an expanded field of view and a reduced exit pupil. Data Structures: SLM Pattern: A 2D array of phase values. The sub-hologram size corresponds to the effective exit pupil size. Light Source: Defined by position \vec{l}e relative to the SLM. Core Principles: The hologram acts as a series of superimposed diffraction gratings. The light deflection angle is determined by the grating equation: d(\sin\thetai + \sin\thetam) = \lambda where d is the grating pitch, \thetai is the light incidence angle, \thetam is the diffraction angle, and \lambda is the wavelength. The lens phase function for a sub-hologram is updated to handle diverging light. The phase \phi at position \vec{p} on the SLM, relative to the eye position \vec{o} and light source \vec{l}e, is calculated as: \phi(\vec{p}) = \frac{2\pi}{\lambda} \left( |\vec{p} - \vec{l}e| + |\vec{p} - \vec{o}| \right) (Note: The source text provides the exponent form 2\pi (\dots)/\lambda inside the phase function context, implying the path length difference. Standard holographic phase is proportional to path length. The source snippet shows: 2\pi (|\vec{p}-\vec{l}e| + |\vec{p}-\vec{o}|) / \lambda. We interpret the snippet 2π (k ® p−l®k+k ® p−o® k) / λ as the path length sum scaled by 2\pi/\lambda.) Parameters: SLM Pixel Pitch: Typically 8 µm. Minimum Grating Pitch (d): 16 µm (derived from Nyquist sampling theorem on 8 µm pixels). Wavelength (\lambda): 532 nm (green light). Maximum Diffraction Angle (\thetam): \pm 1.9^\circ for normally incident light with d=16\mu m and \lambda=532nm. Field of View: 60–100° or more, limited only by the divergence of the point light source. Steps: 1. Define Geometry: Position the diverging point light source at \vec{l}e and the observer's eye at \vec{o}. 2. Calculate Phase: For each pixel \vec{p} in the sub-hologram, calculate the phase \phi(\vec{p}) based on the path lengths from the light source to the pixel and from the pixel to the eye. 3. Compute Hologram: Generate the hologram pattern (e.g., via Gerchberg-Saxton or direct calculation) using the calculated phase. 4. Display: Render the hologram on the SLM. 5. Illumination: Illuminate the SLM with the diverging light from \vec{l}e. 6. Diffraction: The hologram diffracts the light. The coarse steering is provided by the divergence of the source, and the fine steering is provided by the hologram's diffraction angle \thetam. 7. Image Formation: The diffracted light forms a magnified virtual image at the eye position. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Exit Pupil Reduction: As the projector is magnified with diverging light, the field of view increases, but the effective size of the exit pupil decreases. Sub-hologram Size: The sub-hologram size used in computation must match the size of the reduced exit pupil. Attempting to increase the sub-hologram size would require diffraction angles and spatial frequencies higher than the SLM can reproduce. Etendue: Unlike conventional displays, the etendue of a holographic projector is linked to the device resolution. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Performance: Supports wide fields of view (60–100°). Strengths: Lensless magnification; avoids bulky refractive lenses; enables wide fields of view with smaller optics. Limitations: The exit pupil size decreases as magnification increases; etendue is limited by SLM resolution. When to use: When wide fields of view are required in VR/AR near-eye displays without bulky optics. When not to use: When a large exit pupil is critical and cannot be compensated for by eye tracking or other means. This technique was developed to address the need for wide fields of view in VR and AR displays without the bulk of conventional refractive lenses. It builds on the principle that holographic displays can be magnified lenslessly using a diverging point light source [Makowski et al. 2012; Qu et al. 2015], as cited in. The method was detailed in the context of holographic near-eye displays for virtual and augmented reality. name: 3D Light PAD
head: volumetric three-dimensional digital light photoactivatable dye display
body: 3D Light PAD is a chemically enabled volumetric 3D display that uses photoactivatable molecules and digital light processing (DLP) to generate structured light in three dimensions by simultaneously activating and exciting fluorophores in a spatial pattern defined by DLP. It differs from photoactivated localization microscopy, which sequentially activates subsets of fluorophores, by generating a viewable volumetric image through simultaneous activation and excitation. Unlike beam-addressable systems using upconversion or plasma which require expensive high-energy beams, 3D Light PAD uses DLP projectors and photoactivatable dyes. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A 3D image definition (spatial pattern), two light sources (ultraviolet for photoactivation, visible for excitation/emission), and a chemical medium consisting of photoactivatable dye dispersed in a low-scattering solvent with a base additive. Output: A 3D volumetric image composed of fluorescent voxels at the intersection of the structured light beams. Data Structures and Chemical Composition: The medium is a solution containing: 1. Photoactivatable Dye: N-phenyl spirolactam rhodamine B. 2. Solvent: Low-scattering solvent, specifically dichloromethane (CH2Cl2) in the reported implementation. 3. Base Additive: Triethylamine, used to increase reversibility and speed up thermal fading. Concentrations tested were 1 p.p.m. (7.2 mM), 5 p.p.m. (36 mM), and 15 p.p.m. (108 mM). Operating Principle: The dye exists in a non-fluorescent 'off' state (spirolactam form) and a fluorescent 'on' state (merocyanine form). Photoactivation: Ultraviolet light opens the spirolactam ring, converting the dye to the fluorescent 'on' state. Excitation/Emission: Visible light excites the 'on' state dye, causing it to emit fluorescence. Voxel Generation: A 3D voxel is generated at the intersection of the UV and visible light beams. Thermal Fading: The 'on' state is thermally reversible. The dye spontaneously returns to the 'off' state, allowing the voxel to fade and enabling dynamic updates. The base (triethylamine) accelerates this thermal fading. Parameters: Photoactivation Wavelength: Ultraviolet light. Specific wavelengths used in experiments include 254 nm, 315 nm, and 385 nm. Excitation Wavelength: Visible light. Specific wavelengths used include 532 nm and 556 nm. Emission Wavelength: 586 nm. Minimum Voxel Size: 0.68 \text{ mm}^3. Resolution: 200 mm (stated as such in the source, likely a typo for 200 µm or similar, but reported as 200 mm). Kinetics: The thermal fading (off-rate, k{obs}) follows single-exponential decay. The rate depends on the concentration of triethylamine: 1 p.p.m. triethylamine: k{obs} = 0.048 \text{ s}^{-1}. 5 p.p.m. triethylamine: k{obs} = 0.20 \text{ s}^{-1}. 15 p.p.m. triethylamine: k{obs} = 0.50 \text{ s}^{-1} [G: The increase in rate was observed to be linear with base concentration]. Pitfalls and Edge Cases: Slow Fading/Irreversibility: Prolonged UV illumination or the use of certain solvents (e.g., chloroform CHCl3, deuterated chloroform CDCl3) can lead to slow thermal fading kinetics or irreversible coloration/fluorescence. Solvent Choice: Dichloromethane is preferred to avoid the irreversibility issues seen with chlorinated solvents. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def initializedisplay(): # Define chemical medium parameters dyeconcentration = 5.0 # mM, as used in experiments solvent = "dichloromethane" base = "triethylamine" baseppm = 5.0 # Example concentration basemolarity = 36.0 # mM corresponding to 5 p.p.m. # Define optical parameters uvwavelength = 385 # nm, example from DLP projector viswavelength = 532 # nm, example from DLP projector emissionwavelength = 586 # nm # Define kinetic parameters for the chosen base concentration # kobs values from if baseppm == 1.0: kobs = 0.048 # s^-1 elif baseppm == 5.0: kobs = 0.20 # s^-1 elif baseppm == 15.0: kobs = 0.50 # s^-1 else: # Interpolate or use default if not specified in sources kobs = 0.20 # s^-1 return { "dye": "N-phenyl spirolactam rhodamine B", "solvent": solvent, "base": base, "baseconcmM": basemolarity, "uvwl": uvwavelength, "viswl": viswavelength, "emwl": emissionwavelength, "kobs": kobs } def generatevoxel3d(imagedata, displayconfig): """ Generates a 3D volumetric image by controlling UV and Visible light projectors. Args: imagedata: 3D array representing the desired voxel pattern (1 for on, 0 for off) displayconfig: Output from initializedisplay() Returns: None, controls projectors directly """ # Align projectors so UV and Visible beams cross in the solution # The intersection of the structured light patterns defines the voxel locations # For each frame of the animation/image: for frame in imagedata: # 1. Activate UV Projector # Project the UV pattern corresponding to the 'on' voxels in the current frame # This photoactivates the dye at the intersection points uvprojector.setpattern(frame) uvprojector.on() # 2. Activate Visible Projector # Project the visible pattern corresponding to the 'on' voxels # This excites the activated dye to emit fluorescence visprojector.setpattern(frame) visprojector.on() # 3. Wait for emission # The dye emits light at 586 nm at the intersection # The duration of illumination determines the brightness/intensity # The thermal fading (kobs) determines how long the voxel persists after light is off waitforframeduration() # 4. Turn off projectors uvprojector.off() visprojector.off() # 5. Allow thermal fading # The dye spontaneously returns to the 'off' state # The rate is controlled by kobs and base concentration # If the next frame requires a different pattern, the old voxels fade out # while new ones are activated in the next cycle waitfornextframe() def checksolventstability(solventtype): """ Checks if the solvent is suitable to avoid irreversible coloration. """ if solventtype in ["CHCl3", "CDCl3"]: return False # Risk of irreversible coloration/fluorescence elif solventtype == "CH2Cl2": return True # Suitable else: return False # Not given in the sources for other solvents Voxel Size: Minimum voxel size of 0.68 \text{ mm}^3. Resolution: Reported as 200 mm (likely a typo for 200 µm or similar, but stated as 200 mm in text). Stability: Good stability over repeated 'on-off' cycles. Kinetics: Thermal fading rates range from 0.048 \text{ s}^{-1} to 0.50 \text{ s}^{-1} depending on base concentration. Strengths: Lack of moving parts, drastic simplification in voxel arrangement, widely accessible using commercial DLP projectors, no need for expensive high-energy beams. Limitations: Voxel size is relatively large (0.68 \text{ mm}^3); resolution is limited by the optical setup and dye kinetics; potential for irreversible coloration with prolonged UV illumination or certain solvents. When to use: Applications requiring accessible, low-cost volumetric 3D displays with moderate resolution and dynamic content. When not to use: Applications requiring high-resolution, small-voxel displays or those incompatible with chemical media. 3D Light PAD was reported in a 2017 Nature Communications paper by researchers from Southern Methodist University. It builds on the use of photoactivatable molecules, which are central to advances in super-resolution microscopy, data storage, molecular motors, and photopharmacology. The specific dye used, N-phenyl spirolactam rhodamine B, is a class of photoactivatable compounds that can be switched from a non-fluorescent to a fluorescent isomer using ultraviolet light. The system was developed to overcome obstacles in volumetric 3D display technology, such as complex fabrication, moving parts, high-speed projectors, or high laser powers. A volumetric three-dimensional digital light photoactivatable dye display, https://doi.org/10.1038/ncomms15239, fetched 2026-10-26

name: Particle Trapping and Manipulation
head: Free-space particle volumetric displays, Levitated particle displays
body: Particle Trapping and Manipulation renders 3D images in free space by suspending microscopic or millimetric particles using optical or acoustic forces and illuminating them to exploit persistence of vision. It solves the "clipping" limitation of holographic and light-field displays, where image points are physically separated from the scattering surface, thereby restricting viewing angles and preventing geometries such as long-throw projections or wrap-around displays. By co-locating the scattering surface (the trapped particle) with the image point, these displays provide a 360° in-plane viewing angle around every voxel at any depth, enabling unconstrained viewing geometries. The family relies on the synchronization of particle position and illumination color/intensity. The core mechanism involves three stages: 1. Trapping: A force field (optical or acoustic) creates a potential well that confines a single particle against gravity and drag. 2. Scanning: The trap moves the particle along a 3D trajectory (x(t), y(t), z(t)) at a speed sufficient to blur the particle's motion into a continuous path via persistence of vision. 3. Illumination: A light source (lasers or LEDs) illuminates the particle synchronously with its position to generate specific voxels with defined colors. The choice of particle material and size is dictated by the trapping force: Optical Traps require absorbing particles (e.g., cellulose) to generate photophoretic forces via thermal creep in gas. Acoustic Traps require dielectric particles (e.g., expanded polystyrene) to experience radiation forces in standing waves. A free-space display using photophoretic forces to trap a microscopic particle [6753-photophoretic-trap-volumetric-display.md]. It is distinguished by its use of near-invisible trapping lasers and RGB illumination, enabling high-resolution voxels (\approx 10 \mu m) and unconstrained viewing angles [6753-photophoretic-trap-volumetric-display.md]. Choose this method for high-resolution, full-color 3D images where optical safety and hardware complexity are secondary to image quality [6753-photophoretic-trap-volumetric-display.md]. A free-space display using acoustic radiation forces to trap a millimetric particle [11093-acoustophoretic-volumetric-display.md]. It is distinguished by its use of safe, low-cost ultrasonic phased arrays, allowing for a larger operational region (up to half a meter) without optical hazards [11093-acoustophoretic-volumetric-display.md]. Choose this method for larger-scale displays where safety and cost are priorities, accepting lower resolution and speed limitations compared to optical methods [11093-acoustophoretic-volumetric-display.md]. A method using bubbles excited by lasers in liquid as voxels. By increasing liquid viscosity, slow-floating bubbles are generated and arranged to stack 2D cross-sections, realizing volumetric image display. This system has a very long voxel residence time, requiring time for image refresh, but can express complex shapes. The concept of trapping particles for volumetric display was pioneered by Smalley et al. in 2018, who used a 405 nm laser to trap \approx 10 \mu m cellulose particles in air, illuminating them with coaxial RGB lasers to generate voxels. This was the first method to adopt computer-hologram-based light irradiation patterns for volumetric displays, demonstrating that holographic design improves voxel count and brightness. Acoustic variants emerged earlier; in 2014, "Pixie Dust" proposed using 285 ultrasonic transducers across four speakers to create acoustic ponderomotive fields for levitating multiple particles. In 2019, Hirayama et al. demonstrated particle trapping using standing acoustic waves. The Kumagai method utilizes laser-excited bubbles in viscous liquids, offering long residence times for complex shape expression. ボリュメトリックディスプレイ, https://www.jstage.jst.go.jp/article/jvrsj/29/3/2927/pdf/-char/ja, fetched 2026-10-30 (unofficial)

name: Photophoretic-Trap Volumetric Display
head: Optical Trap Display (OTD), Photophoretic optical trapping display, Smalley Photophoretic Trap Display
body: A Photophoretic-Trap Volumetric Display (also known as the Optical Trap Display or OTD) is a free-space volumetric display that generates full-color, three-dimensional images in air using a single trapped particle illuminated by synchronized RGB lasers. It solves the "clipping" limitation inherent to holographic and light-field displays, where image points are physically separated from the scattering surface, thereby restricting viewing angles and preventing geometries such as long-throw projections or wrap-around displays. By co-locating the scattering surface (the particle) with the image point, the OTD provides a 360° in-plane viewing angle around every voxel at any depth, limited only by the optical axis itself. The OTD creates voxels by trapping a micrometer-scale absorbing particle in a photophoretic potential well, scanning this trap through a 3D volume, and illuminating the particle with color-tunable light. The motion is fast enough to exploit persistence of vision (POV), blurring the particle's trajectory into continuous luminous paths. Inputs: Particle: An absorbing, opaque particle, typically cellulose, with a diameter d in the range of 5\text{--}100 \, \mu\text{m} (demonstrated resolution \approx 10 \, \mu\text{m}). Trap Laser: A near-invisible trapping laser, typically at 405 \, \text{nm} wavelength. Illumination Lasers: Collinear Red, Green, and Blue (RGB) lasers capable of varying power and position. Environment: Air at standard pressure and room temperature. Outputs: A free-space 3D image composed of voxels visible from all angles (except the optical axis line). The system relies on the physical state of the particle and the optical configuration rather than digital data structures for the image itself, though the control software must manage: 1. Trajectory Data: A time-parameterized 3D path (x(t), y(t), z(t)) for the trap center. 2. Illumination Map: A time-synchronized sequence of RGB intensity values (IR(t), IG(t), IB(t)) corresponding to the particle's position along the trajectory. The trap is formed using aberration traps that combine spherical aberration and oblique astigmatism. This is achieved optically by tilting a sagittal lens to introduce variable astigmatism to a fixed spherical aberration, creating tunable regions of high and low optical intensity near the lens focus. The trapping force is photophoretic, arising from thermal creep and radiometer effects due to uneven heating of the absorbing particle by the trap laser, rather than radiation pressure or gradient forces used in standard optical tweezers. Because the particle diameter (5\text{--}100 \, \mu\text{m}) is much larger than the gas mean free path (68 \, \text{nm} at standard pressure and room temperature), the system operates in the continuous regime. The photophoretic force in the continuous regime is given by: F{\text{cont}} = \frac{\pi d^2 R T}{3 \eta M p} \nabla T Where: F{\text{cont}} is the photophoretic force. d is the diameter of the particle. R is the universal gas constant. T is the temperature of the gas. \eta is the viscosity of the gas. M is the molecular weight of the gas. p is the gas pressure. \nabla T is the gradient of the temperature. 1. Isolation: A cellulose particle is isolated and confined in the photophoretic trap created by the 405 \, \text{nm} laser and the aberration optics. 2. Scanning: The trap (and the trapped particle) is scanned through the display volume. The scanning speed must be sufficient to blur the particle's motion into a continuous path via persistence of vision. In demonstrations, a scan rate of 10 \, \text{Hz} was used. 3. Illumination: A system of collinear RGB lasers illuminates the trapped particle. The color and intensity of the illumination are synchronized with the particle's position along the trajectory to generate specific voxels. 4. Image Formation: The combination of the scanned particle and synchronized RGB illumination forms a 3D image in free space. The resulting images exhibit full color, fine detail (voxels < 10 \, \mu\text{m}), and low apparent speckle. The following pseudocode describes the control logic for generating a single frame of the volumetric image. It assumes a pre-defined trajectory and illumination map. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def renderotdframe(traj, illummap, dt): """ Renders a single frame of the OTD by simulating the scan and illumination. Args: traj: List of 3D coordinates [(x1, y1, z1), (x2, y2, z2),...] representing the trap center position over time. illummap: List of RGB tuples [(R1, G1, B1), (R2, G2, B2),...] representing the laser intensities synchronized with traj. dt: Time step between trajectory points (seconds). """ # Ensure trajectory and illumination map are synchronized if len(traj) != len(illummap): raise ValueError("Trajectory and illumination map must have the same length.") # Clear previous image buffer (conceptual) imagebuffer = createempty3dvolume() # Scan the particle through the volume for i in range(len(traj)): pos = traj[i] color = illummap[i] # The particle is at 'pos' and illuminated with 'color' # Due to persistence of vision and finite integration time, # the particle leaves a luminous trail. For discrete simulation, # we mark the voxel at the current position. # In a real physical system, the blur length depends on scan speed # and eye integration time. # Set the voxel color at the particle's position # Note: In practice, multiple passes or higher frequency scanning # creates the continuous blur. setvoxelcolor(imagebuffer, pos, color) return imagebuffer def setvoxelcolor(volume, position, rgb): """ Sets the color of a voxel in the 3D volume. position: (x, y, z) in meters or display units. rgb: (R, G, B) intensity values. """ # Quantize position to voxel grid voxelidx = quantizetogrid(position) # Apply color volume[voxelidx] = rgb Optical Axis Occlusion: The image is visible from every angle with the possible exception of the line forming the optical axis, where the trap laser and illumination beams may obscure the view or cause glare. Particle Size Variance: Early trials used particles with diameters ranging from below 5 \, \mu\text{m} to above 100 \, \mu\text{m}. Consistent image quality requires precise control over particle size to maintain the continuous regime and optimal scattering. Gas Conditions: The force model depends on gas pressure, temperature, and viscosity. Changes in ambient conditions can alter the trap stiffness and particle dynamics. Time Complexity: The frame rate is limited by the mechanical or optical scanning speed of the trap. Demonstrated scan rates were 10 \, \text{Hz}. Memory Complexity: Not applicable in the traditional sense, as the image is generated physically in space. However, control software requires memory proportional to the trajectory length and illumination map size. Resolution: Demonstrated image points are approximately 10 \, \mu\text{m} in dimension. Viewing Angle: Provides a 360° in-plane viewing angle around every image point at any depth, overcoming the clipping limitations of holographic displays. Strengths: Free-space imaging without screens or scattering surfaces. Full-color, low-speckle images. Ability to create geometries impossible for holograms, such as long-throw projections, tall sandtables, and wrap-around displays. Limitations: Limited to single-particle scanning (though multiple particles could theoretically be trapped, the described system uses one). Requires absorbing particles (cellulose) and specific gas conditions. The optical axis may be a blind spot. When to use: Applications requiring unconstrained viewing angles, long-throw projection, or interaction with the image volume (e.g., touch interaction) where holographic clipping is prohibitive. When not to use: Applications requiring high pixel counts or static images without motion, or environments where gas conditions cannot be controlled. The Photophoretic-Trap Volumetric Display, also referred to as the Optical Trap Display (OTD), was introduced by Smalley et al. in 2018. It advances the state of the art by providing full-color, free-space images with fine detail, overcoming the limitations of earlier levitation displays that were too coarse or inertial. The technology leverages photophoretic optical trapping, which is particularly useful for confining micrometer-diameter absorbing particles using thermal forces rather than radiation pressure. The system was demonstrated producing images such as a butterfly and the Earth, with voxel dimensions of approximately 10 \, \mu\text{m}. name: Acoustophoretic Volumetric Display
head: AVD, Acoustophoretic-trap free-space volumetric display
body: An Acoustophoretic Volumetric Display (AVD) renders 3D graphics in free space by trapping a millimetric dielectric particle using acoustic radiation forces from a phased ultrasonic array and moving it rapidly along a 3D trajectory while synchronously illuminating it with colored light. Unlike optical traps that rely on photophoretic forces and high-power lasers, AVDs use standing acoustic waves to create potential wells, offering a larger operational region (up to half a meter) and avoiding laser safety hazards, though they currently support smaller, simpler shapes at high speeds compared to photophoretic counterparts. Inputs and Outputs Input: A 3D graphic defined as a sequence of particle positions (x, y, z) at time t and corresponding RGB color values. Output: A visible 3D volumetric image formed by the persistence of vision of the illuminated, moving particle. Data Structures and Hardware Layout The system relies on a specific hardware control chain and signal parameters: 1. Particle: Expanded Polystyrene (EPS) sphere, diameter d \approx 1.5 mm. 2. Transducer Array: 60 ultrasonic transducers (Murata MA40S4S) arranged in two opposed arrays of 30 transducers each. 3. Control Chain: PC \rightarrow UART (1.5 Mbauds) \rightarrow FPGA (ALTERA CoreEp4CE6) \rightarrow MOSFET drivers (TC4427a) \rightarrow Transducers. 4. Signal Parameters: Square waves generated by the FPGA. Phase resolution: \pi/64 rad. Color depth: 8-bit signal per RGB channel. 5. Working Volume: Approximately 4 \times 5 \times 8 cm^3. Algorithm Steps 1. Trajectory and Color Definition: Represent the desired 3D graphic as a sequence of target positions (xi, yi, zi) at discrete times ti and associated RGB color values Ci = (Ri, Gi, Bi). 2. Color Transmission: Send the 8-bit RGB signal for each channel to the RGB LED source positioned adjacent to the acoustic levitator. 3. Phase Calculation: For each target position (xi, yi, zi), calculate the required emission phases \phi{j,i} for each of the 60 transducers j to focus the acoustic field and create an antinode at the target location. 4. FPGA Control: Transmit the calculated phases to the FPGA. The FPGA generates square waves with the specified phase resolution (\pi/64 rad) for each of the 60 channels. 5. Amplification: The FPGA signals are sent to MOSFET drivers (TC4427a), which amplify the signals using an external DC power supply to drive the transducers. 6. Acoustic Trapping: The transducers emit ultrasonic waves, creating a standing wave field with an antinode at the calculated position. The particle is trapped in this potential well. 7. Illumination and Movement: Move the trap (by updating phases) to the next position (x{i+1}, y{i+1}, z{i+1}) while illuminating the particle with color Ci. The particle follows the trap, scattering the light to form a voxel. 8. Persistence of Vision: Repeat steps 3-7 rapidly enough that the human eye perceives a continuous 3D path. Pseudocode Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. NUMTRANSDUCERS = 60 PHASERESOLUTION = PI / 64 PARTICLEDIAMETER = 1.5 # mm WORKINGVOLUME = (4, 5, 8) # cm^3 uart = UART(baudrate=1500000) fpga = FPGA(model="ALTERA CoreEp4CE6") led = RGBLED() def calculatephases(targetx, targety, targetz): """ Calculate emission phases for the 60 transducers to focus at (x, y, z). This involves solving the inverse problem for the phased array to create an antinode at the target position. Implementation detail: Specific algorithm depends on transducer geometry and wave physics (e.g., time-reversal or delay-and-sum). """ phases = [] for j in range(NUMTRANSDUCERS): # Placeholder for specific acoustic focusing calculation # The source states phases are calculated but does not provide the # explicit formula for phij given (x,y,z). phij = computeacousticphase(j, targetx, targety, targetz) # Quantize to pi/64 resolution quantizedphi = round(phij / PHASERESOLUTION) PHASERESOLUTION phases.append(quantizedphi) return phases def rendervolumetricimage(trajectory): """ trajectory: List of tuples (x, y, z, r, g, b, timedelay) """ for i, (x, y, z, r, g, b, delay) in enumerate(trajectory): # 1. Set Color led.setcolor(r, g, b) # 2. Calculate and Send Phases phases = calculatephases(x, y, z) fpga.setphases(phases) # 3. Wait for particle to reach equilibrium/move # The source notes dynamic distortion increases with speed. # A simple delay is used in the prototype; advanced systems might # use dynamic optimization. wait(delay) def computeacousticphase(transducerindex, targetx, targety, targetz): # Not given in the sources. Requires geometric calculation based on # transducer positions and speed of sound. pass Edge Cases and Pitfalls Particle Size Constraints: Particles >1.5 mm invalidate the small particle assumptions in the Gor’kov model, causing force per unit volume to decrease. Particles <0.5 mm are swept out by air currents because drag force (scaling with area) becomes significant relative to acoustic radiation force (scaling with volume). Static Calibration Deviation: Equilibrium points deviate from ideal focal points by approximately 0.5 mm due to scattering, temperature variations, manufacturing inaccuracies, or transducer position errors. This affects image accuracy. Dynamic Distortion: Increasing particle velocity distorts the shape of the volumetric image and can eject the particle from the trap. Static calibration becomes less effective at higher speeds due to the nonlinear dynamics of the particle in the acoustic field. Speed Limitations: At 10 Hz rendering frequency, only small and simple shapes (size 5-6 mm) can be achieved. Performance: Renders simple figures in real time at 10 frames per second (fps). Raster Images: Rendered at lower frame rates; draw times were 20 seconds for logos/stop signs and 5 seconds for a 3D wireframe airplane in static tests. Limitations: High-speed rendering is currently limited to small (5-6 mm) and simple shapes. Dynamic distortion increases with drawing speed. Comparison to Photophoretic Displays: AVDs offer a larger operational region (up to half a meter) and avoid high-power laser hazards, but are currently limited to smaller shapes at high speeds compared to Photophoretic-Trap Volumetric Displays (OTD), which can reach speeds of 1.8 m/s. The Acoustophoretic Volumetric Display was proposed as a free-space volumetric display technology that utilizes acoustic radiation forces to levitate and move particles, addressing the clipping and limited field of view issues associated with holograms and light-field displays. The work builds on previous attempts to create free-space displays using acoustophoresis, such as Ochiai et al.'s crosses and grids, Sahoo et al.'s flip-screen particles, and Uno et al.'s LED levitation. The specific implementation described uses a phased array of 60 ultrasonic transducers controlled by an FPGA to trap and move a 1.5 mm EPS particle. name: Multi-View and Parallax-Based Rendering
head: Multi-view rendering, Parallax-based volume rendering, Light field rendering
body: Multi-View and Parallax-Based Rendering generates volumetric or holographic imagery by computing multiple distinct perspective views of a scene and displaying them on hardware that separates these views spatially or angularly to create a 3D effect. It differs from single-view volume rendering by explicitly managing view-dependent parallax, and from holographic CGH calculation by typically relying on rasterized or pre-computed view extraction rather than full wave-optics simulation for every pixel. The family shares the core mechanism of decomposing a 3D representation into a set of 2D views, each corresponding to a specific camera position or holographic aperture, and mapping these views to a display medium that enforces spatial or angular separation. 1. View Generation: A set of N views is generated. In lenticular systems, these are perspective projections from offset focal spots. In holographic light-field systems, these are extracted from a pre-computed Computer-Generated Hologram (CGH). 2. Display Mapping: The views are mapped to a display device. Lenticular: Views are interlaced into a single bitmap where sub-pixels (R, G, B) sample from different views based on a static view map. Pyramid/Projector Arrays: Views are projected or composited onto physical surfaces (pyramids, projector arrays) with specific geometric calibration. 3. Parallax Enforcement: The hardware (lenses, mirrors, projector arrays) ensures that each eye sees a different view, creating stereoscopic depth. A hardware-accelerated method for generating stereoscopic images of volumetric datasets for display on multi-view lenticular screens without glasses. It computes N distinct perspective views from offset focal spots and composites them into a single interlaced bitmap where each sub-pixel (R, G, B) samples from a different view. Choose this when rendering scalar volumetric data on lenticular displays. A rendering technique that projects four synchronized views of a 3D scene onto a four-sided acrylic pyramid to create a floating volumetric image visible from all sides. It differs from multi-view lenticular rendering by using physical reflection parity via a pyramid rather than optical lenses, requiring independent rotation and mirroring of each view to correct for the acrylic's reflection properties. Choose this for 360-degree holographic displays using acrylic pyramids. A pre-processing framework for rendering Computer-Generated Holograms (CGH) on autostereoscopic light-field displays. It consists of four sequential steps applied to the hologram to acquire reconstruction images corresponding to views from a camera rotating around the scene. The resolution of these images equals the 2D resolution of the screen. Steps: 1. View extraction: A window with the resolution of the vertical axis of the hologram moves along the horizontal axis to acquire sub-holograms that simulate a pinhole camera view. Apertures can overlap to increase the number of views. 2. Suppression of aperture diffraction (apodization): Reduces diffraction artifacts. 3. Back propagation: Numerically reconstructs the view. This step requires only 1D FFTs with a pre-computed kernel due to the constant distance. 4. Colour balancing: Adjusts color channels for the display. Complexity: The computational complexity is O(NM), where N is the number of views and M is the hologram resolution. Performance: Tested on a 3.3 GHz Intel Core i7-5820 CPU with Windows 8 (x64). For the 'Dice' dataset (142,903 points), processing times per view were: View extraction 0.04s, Apodization 0.38s, Back propagation 16.33s, Colour balancing 1.19s. Hardware: Rendered on an Holografika HoloVizio 722RC light field display (72 projectors, 70° viewing angle). 70 views were extracted with an angular resolution of 1° and a 2D resolution of 1280x768 pixels. The concept of multi-view rendering for volumetric displays has evolved alongside autostereoscopic and light-field display technologies. The specific framework for rendering CGHs on light-field displays was proposed to address the need for high-end 3D visualization of point-clouds and holograms. The method leverages parallel computing and raster OpenGL graphics to manage the computational load of view extraction and back propagation. name: Multi-view Lenticular Volume Rendering
head: GPU-accelerated volume rendering to 3D lenticular displays
body: A method for hardware-accelerated generation of multi-view stereoscopic images of volumetric datasets for display on a multi-view lenticular screen, using the GPU for both rendering and compositing. It solves the problem of interactive visualization of large 3D medical volumes on glasses-free 3D displays by decomposing the scene into perspective projections from offset focal spots and interlacing them into a single bitmap. It sets itself apart from sibling methods by explicitly handling the asymmetric frustum geometry required for lenticular lenses and performing the final sub-pixel interlacing via a static texture map lookup on the GPU, rather than pre-computing a hologram or projecting from separate physical sources. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A volumetric dataset (e.g., medical CT/MRI), lenticular display parameters (focal distance f, view count N, camera spacing d), and the dataset dimensions. Output: A single interlaced bitmap suitable for the LCD panel underlying the lenticular sheet. Data Structures: 1. Bricks: The volumetric dataset is divided into 3D blocks ("bricks") to fit within the graphics card's texture memory and align with its memory architecture. 2. Texture0 (View Map): A static 2D texture map storing the view number for each sub-pixel (R, G, B) of the output image. This is pre-calculated based on the lenticular lens geometry and remains constant for all frames. 3. Texture1 (View Stack): A single wide rectangular 2D texture map storing all N rendered views vertically next to each other. Each view occupies a horizontal strip of height H{view} = H{LCD} / N. Parameters: N: Number of views. The specific implementation uses N=9, but the method applies to any N. f: Focal distance of the lenticular lenses. d: Distance between adjacent view camera positions. Resolution: Each individual view has an effective resolution of (1/N) of the LCD matrix resolution in the horizontal direction. Steps: 1. Data Partitioning: Divide the input volumetric dataset into bricks suitable for GPU texture memory. 2. View Rendering Loop: For each view index n from 0 to N-1: a. Frustum Setup: Define an asymmetric perspective projection frustum for view n. The camera position is offset from the center. The projection coordinates (x', y') for a world point (x, y, z) are calculated as: x' = \frac{(x - n \cdot d) \cdot f}{f - z} + n \cdot d y' = \frac{y \cdot f}{f - z} b. Direct Volume Rendering (DVR): Render the volume using the defined frustum. Rays are cast from the focal spot through each pixel. The volume rendering integral is approximated by traversing rays in back-to-front order using the over operator: C{n+1} = \alphan \cdot cn + (1 - \alphan) \cdot Cn where Cn is the intermediate color value, \alphan is the opacity, and cn is the color at sample n. This is implemented using standard alpha blending (e.g., DirectX or OpenGL) on textured slices. c. Storage: Store the resulting image for view n in the n-th vertical strip of Texture1. 3. Compositing: Generate the final interlaced image by parsing every pixel of the output LCD resolution. For each pixel, read the view numbers for the Red, Green, and Blue components from Texture0. Sample the corresponding view from Texture1 for each color channel to construct the final pixel color. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def renderlenticularvolume(volumedata, lenticularparams, lcdresolution): """ volumedata: List of 3D arrays (bricks) representing the volumetric dataset. lenticularparams: Object containing f (focal distance), d (camera spacing), N (number of views). lcdresolution: Tuple (width, height) of the LCD display. """ N = lenticularparams.N f = lenticularparams.f d = lenticularparams.d # Step 1: Pre-calculate view map (Texture0) # For each pixel (px, py) in the LCD, determine which view index # corresponds to R, G, and B channels based on lens geometry. # This is static and computed once. viewmap = computeviewmap(lcdresolution, lenticularparams) # Step 2: Render each view # Texture1 is a 2D texture of size (width, height N) texture1 = createtexture(lcdresolution[0], lcdresolution[1] N) for n in range(N): # Define asymmetric frustum for view n # The camera is offset by nd. The projection matrix maps world coords # to the specific view's viewport. frustum = computeasymmetricfrustum(n, d, f) # Render volume to a temporary buffer for this view # Resolution of the view is (lcdwidth, lcdheight / N) viewheight = lcdresolution[1] // N viewbuffer = rendervolumebricks(volumedata, frustum, (lcdresolution[0], viewheight)) # Store viewbuffer in the n-th vertical strip of Texture1 # The strip starts at y = n viewheight texture1.setregion(0, n viewheight, lcdresolution[0], viewheight, viewbuffer) # Step 3: Composite final image finalimage = createtexture(lcdresolution[0], lcdresolution[1]) for py in range(lcdresolution[1]): for px in range(lcdresolution[0]): # Get view indices for R, G, B from the static map viewr, viewg, viewb = viewmap[px, py] # Sample from Texture1 # Each view has height viewheight yr = viewr viewheight + (py % viewheight) yg = viewg viewheight + (py % viewheight) yb = viewb viewheight + (py % viewheight) colorr = texture1.sample(px, yr) colorg = texture1.sample(px, yg) colorb = texture1.sample(px, yb) finalimage[px, py] = (colorr, colorg, colorb) return finalimage def computeasymmetricfrustum(n, d, f): """ Returns a projection function/matrix for view n. Coordinates (x, y, z) are mapped to screen coordinates. """ def project(x, y, z): # Asymmetric frustum formula from source # Note: Source formula assumes specific coordinate system conventions. # Implementation must align with the renderer's coordinate space. xproj = ((x - n d) f) / (f - z) + n d yproj = (y f) / (f - z) return (xproj, yproj) return project def computeviewmap(lcdresolution, lenticularparams): """ Pre-calculates which view index corresponds to R, G, B for each pixel. This depends on the physical alignment of the LCD sub-pixels under the lenticular lenses. Not given in the sources. """ # Placeholder for the specific geometric calculation of sub-pixel mapping. # In practice, this maps the periodic structure of the lenticular lens # to the RGB sub-pixel grid. pass Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Memory Limits: The dataset must be divided into bricks to fit within the graphics card's texture memory. Resolution Trade-off: Each view has a lower resolution (1/N of LCD width), which may reduce detail per view but allows for interactive frame rates. Static Geometry: The view map (Texture0) is static; it assumes the display and camera setup do not change during runtime. Performance: Up to 15 frames per second for a 256^3 voxel dataset on a nine-view lenticular display. Complexity: Time complexity is proportional to N \times R \times S, where N is the number of views, R is the number of rays per view, and S is the number of samples per ray. Memory complexity is dominated by the storage of the volume bricks and the Texture1 stack (N times the view resolution). Strengths: Hardware-accelerated interactive manipulation of large datasets (>100 MB); no glasses required for the viewer; leverages standard GPU primitives (alpha blending, texture sampling). Limitations: Requires specific lenticular hardware; resolution per view is reduced; asymmetric frustum calculations add complexity to the projection step. The method was proposed by Daniel Ruijters from Philips Medical Systems. It addresses the growing size of volumetric medical imaging data and the need for interactive 3D visualization without glasses. The approach builds on Direct Volume Rendering [2] and multi-view display principles [3, 5, 6, 7] cited in the original paper.
