name: Four-View Hologram Compositor
head: FourViewCompositor, Pepper's Ghost volumetric display rendering
body: The Four-View Hologram Compositor is a rendering technique that projects four synchronized perspective views of a 3D scene onto a four-sided acrylic pyramid to create a floating volumetric image via the Pepper's Ghost illusion. It differs from lenticular or light-field systems by using physical reflection parity rather than angular sampling, requiring independent rotation and mirroring of each view to match the geometry of the pyramid's reflective surfaces. The method generates four perspective views from cameras arranged in a circle around the scene center, renders them to separate texture targets, and composites them onto a single screen using textured quads with specific transformations to align with the physical pyramid. Inputs: A 3D scene graph (objects, lights), camera parameters (elevation, FOV), and calibration data (pyramid scale, rotation, per-view offsets and mirroring flags). Outputs: A single 2D bitmap displayed on a screen, which serves as the light source for the holographic pyramid. The implementation uses the following structures: 1. ViewSlot: Represents one of the four views. name: Enum ViewName ('front', 'right', 'back', 'left'). camera: A PerspectiveCamera instance. target: A WebGLRenderTarget with RGBAFormat, LinearFilter, and a depth buffer. quad: A Mesh using PlaneGeometry. material: A MeshBasicMaterial with AdditiveBlending, transparent: true, depthTest: false, and depthWrite: false. 2. VIEWLAYOUT: A constant mapping view names to their geometric properties: front: azimuth 0, dir [0, -1] right: azimuth \pi/2, dir [1, 0] back: azimuth \pi, dir [0, 1] left: azimuth -\pi/2, dir [-1, 0] elevation: Camera elevation angle above the object in degrees. Default: 12^\circ. fov: Field of view for the perspective cameras in degrees. Default: 42^\circ. pyramid.scale: Global scaling factor for the pyramid geometry. view.scale: Per-view scaling factor. view.rotation: Per-view rotation offset. view.offset: Per-view position offset. mirrorX, mirrorY: Boolean flags for texture mirroring. 1. Initialize Cameras and Targets: Create four PerspectiveCamera instances and four WebGLRenderTarget instances. Configure targets with RGBAFormat, LinearFilter, and depth buffers. 2. Position Cameras: For each view in VIEWLAYOUT: Calculate horizontal distance: d{horiz} = \cos(\text{elevation}) \times \text{distance}. Calculate vertical height: d{vert} = \sin(\text{elevation}) \times \text{distance}. Set camera position: \begin{aligned} x &= \sin(\text{azimuth}) \times d{horiz} \\ y &= d{vert} \\ z &= \cos(\text{azimuth}) \times d{horiz} \end{aligned} Call lookAt(target) and updateProjectionMatrix(). 3. Create Composite Quads: For each view, create a Mesh with PlaneGeometry and MeshBasicMaterial (AdditiveBlending, transparent, no depth test/write). These quads will display the rendered views. 4. Render Views: For each frame: For each ViewSlot: Set the renderer's render target to the slot's target. Clear the renderer. Render the scene using the slot's camera. Set the renderer's render target back to the screen (previous target). Clear the renderer. Render the compositeScene (containing the four quads) using an orthographic compositeCamera. 5. Calibrate Composite Quads: Apply calibration to each quad's position, scale, rotation, and texture mirroring: Calculate base size: s{base} = \min(\text{width}, \text{height}) / 2. Calculate global rotation from calibration data. For each slot: Rotate the view direction vector by the global rotation. Scale by s{base} \times \text{pyramid.scale} \times \text{view.scale}. Add view.offset to determine quad position. Set quad scale to (s, s, 1) where s is the calculated size. Set quad rotation.z to \text{globalRot} + \text{view.rotation}. Apply texture mirroring: Set tex.repeat to (-1, 1) or (1, -1) based on mirrorX/mirrorY flags. Set tex.offset to (1, 0) or (0, 1) to compensate for the repeat flip. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. cameras = [] targets = [] quads = [] VIEWLAYOUT = { 'front': {'azimuth': 0, 'dir': [0, -1]}, 'right': {'azimuth': PI/2, 'dir': [1, 0]}, 'back': {'azimuth': PI, 'dir': [0, 1]}, 'left': {'azimuth': -PI/2, 'dir': [-1, 0]} } def init(): for name, layout in VIEWLAYOUT.items(): # Create camera cam = PerspectiveCamera(fov=42, aspect=1.0) # Aspect assumed 1.0 for square pyramid base mapping # Position camera elevrad = radians(12) dhoriz = cos(elevrad) distance dvert = sin(elevrad) distance az = layout['azimuth'] cam.position.set(sin(az) dhoriz, dvert, cos(az) dhoriz) cam.lookAt(target) cam.updateProjectionMatrix() cameras.append(cam) # Create render target target = WebGLRenderTarget(width, height, format=RGBAFormat, filter=LinearFilter, depth=True) targets.append(target) # Create quad quad = Mesh(PlaneGeometry(1, 1), MeshBasicMaterial( blending=AdditiveBlending, transparent=True, depthTest=False, depthWrite=False)) quads.append(quad) def renderframe(scene, calibration): # 1. Render four views for i in range(4): renderer.setRenderTarget(targets[i]) renderer.clear() renderer.render(scene, cameras[i]) # 2. Composite renderer.setRenderTarget(None) # Screen renderer.clear() basesize = min(renderer.width, renderer.height) / 2 globalrot = calibration.globalrotation for i in range(4): viewcal = calibration.views[i] layout = VIEWLAYOUT[viewcal.name] # Calculate position # Rotate view direction by global rotation dirvec = layout['dir'] rotmat = rotationmatrixz(globalrot) rotateddir = multiplyvectormatrix(dirvec, rotmat) scalefactor = basesize calibration.pyramidscale viewcal.scale pos = multiplyvectormatrix(rotateddir, scalefactor) pos = addvectors(pos, viewcal.offset) quads[i].position.copy(pos) quads[i].scale.set(scalefactor, scalefactor, 1) quads[i].rotation.z = globalrot + viewcal.rotation # Apply texture mirroring tex = quads[i].material.map if viewcal.mirrorX: tex.repeat.x = -1 tex.offset.x = 1 else: tex.repeat.x = 1 tex.offset.x = 0 if viewcal.mirrorY: tex.repeat.y = -1 tex.offset.y = 1 else: tex.repeat.y = 1 tex.offset.y = 0 # Render composite scene with orthographic camera renderer.render(compositescene, orthocamera) Opaque Quads: Using opaque quads for compositing causes the last drawn view to paint black corners over adjacent views, creating visible rectangular bites. This is solved by using AdditiveBlending, as the scene renders emissive marks on black, and black adds nothing, allowing overlapping corners to contribute zero. Mirroring vs. Culling: Mirroring via negative scale breaks backface culling. Therefore, texture mirroring is achieved via tex.repeat and tex.offset rather than mesh scaling. Scissor Passes: Scissor viewport passes cannot rotate or mirror views independently, which is required because the reflection parity through the acrylic is not knowable in advance. Time Complexity: The cost is four scene passes plus one composite pass. Memory Complexity: Requires memory for four render targets (width \times height \times 4 bytes per pixel for RGBA) plus the scene graph. Measured Performance: Holds 60 fps comfortably on a phone because the scene consists of a handful of additive primitives. Strengths: No headset or glasses required; viewable from every side; real-time interaction via hand gestures. Limitations: Requires a physical acrylic pyramid; limited to scenes that fit within the pyramid's field of view; performance depends on the complexity of the 3D scene rendered in four passes. When to Use: When a physical, glasses-free volumetric display is desired for presentations, education, or interactive installations. When Not to Use: When high-resolution, large-scale volumetric displays are needed, or when the hardware setup (pyramid) is not feasible. The Four-View Hologram Compositor is based on the Pepper's Ghost illusion, adapted for modern mobile devices and 3D models. It was implemented as part of the hologram-system project by Ojasra Kulkarni, which integrates hand tracking via MediaPipe and WebSocket communication to control the rendered views in real time. The system is designed for applications in engineering, medical imaging, product presentation, and education. ojasra0kulkarni/hologram-system, https://github.com/ojasra0kulkarni/hologram-system, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial)

name: Elementary building blocks
body: This family provides the fundamental geometric and computational primitives required to construct a volume rendering pipeline. It addresses the foundational tasks of defining the viewing geometry (rays) and executing rendering computations efficiently on modern hardware. It sets itself apart from sibling methods by providing the low-level infrastructure—ray parameterization and parallel execution models—upon which higher-level techniques are built. The shared principles of this family are the geometric definition of rays and the parallel execution model. Ray Definition Rays are defined by an origin \mathbf{o} and a direction \mathbf{d}. The direction is typically normalized. The origin is often the camera eye position, but can vary based on the camera model. Parallel Execution Computations are mapped to parallel threads. Each thread typically processes one or more pixels or samples. Memory access patterns are optimized for coalescing. Synchronization is used to manage data dependencies between threads. Computes geometric intersection between parametric rays and scene primitives to determine hit distances. It sets itself apart from Ray-marching by relying on exact analytical solutions rather than iterative stepping, and from Ray-box intersection by encompassing a broader set of geometric shapes. Choose this when identifying which objects a viewing ray encounters for early rejection or spatial bounds. Defines the geometric mapping from discrete 2D pixel coordinates to continuous 3D world-space rays. It sets itself apart from Ray-primitive intersection by focusing solely on ray geometry creation rather than traversal. Choose this when establishing a valid view frustum and constructing camera basis vectors. Encompasses fundamental computational mechanisms to map volume rendering tasks onto parallel hardware architectures. It sets itself apart from its siblings by focusing on the execution model and data movement primitives rather than geometric algorithms or high-level rendering strategies. Choose this when distributing work across thousands of threads to solve computational bottlenecks. The concept of ray generation is rooted in computer graphics since the advent of ray tracing. Parallel execution primitives have evolved with the rise of GPUs, becoming essential for real-time volume rendering. name: Ray-primitive intersection
head: Ray-object intersection, Ray-scene intersection, Ray-primitive tests
body: Ray-primitive intersection computes the geometric intersection between a parametric ray and a specific scene primitive (e.g., box, triangle, sphere, volume) to determine entry/exit points or hit status. It solves the fundamental problem of identifying which objects a viewing ray encounters, enabling early rejection of non-intersecting geometry and providing the spatial parameters (t) required for shading, sampling, or traversal. It sets itself apart from Ray-marching by relying on exact analytical solutions for specific primitive shapes rather than iterative fixed-step evaluation, and from Ray-box intersection by encompassing the broader algorithmic strategies and generic interfaces used to accelerate these tests in volume rendering contexts. The shared principles of this family are the geometric definition of rays and the parallel execution model. Ray Definition Rays are defined by an origin \mathbf{o} and a direction \mathbf{d}. The direction is typically normalized. The origin is often the camera eye position, but can vary based on the camera model. Parallel Execution Computations are mapped to parallel threads. Each thread typically processes one or more pixels or samples. Memory access patterns are optimized for coalescing. Synchronization is used to manage data dependencies between threads. The Ray-box intersection method (specifically the Slab Test) computes the parametric entry (t{near}) and exit (t{far}) distances of a ray intersecting an Axis-Aligned Bounding Box (AABB). It solves the problem of determining the valid sampling interval along a ray for volume rendering or ray tracing, enabling early rejection of rays that miss the volume or primitives. It sets itself apart from Ray-box intersection via OpenGL Geometry Shaders by using an analytical arithmetic approach rather than geometric shader primitives, and from Ray-Volume Intersection (Face Distance Method) by operating on the bounding box of the volume rather than the volume's internal structure directly. This method determines if a ray intersects a triangle in 3D space using Plücker coordinates to evaluate the winding order of the triangle edges relative to the ray. It handles arbitrary ray directions and is distinct from barycentric approaches like Möller-Trumbore by relying on cross-product-based Plücker line coordinates rather than solving a linear system for barycentric weights. The Ray Crossing Count method determines whether a query point lies inside, outside, or on the boundary of a closed triangle mesh by casting rays and counting signed intersections with the mesh geometry. It solves the point-in-mesh containment problem required for interior testing in volume rendering algorithms like Marching Cubes. Unlike simple binary hit tests, this method computes a generalized winding number: it returns exactly 1 for points inside a closed, outward-oriented mesh, 0 for points outside, and a continuous value between 0 and 1 for points near holes or in non-manifold configurations. A point outside the object yields 0, no point yields values < 0, and points inside yield exactly 1. A method to render a volumetric sphere by intersecting camera rays with the sphere geometry to determine entry and exit points, then applying Beer's Law along the chord length. It calculates the parametric distances (t) where a ray enters and exits the sphere to compute the optical path length, which is used to determine transmittance and scattered light contribution. Unlike Ray-box intersection which handles axis-aligned bounding volumes, this method provides an exact analytical solution for spherical primitives, serving as a foundational building block for simple volumetric scenes before advancing to complex density fields or Ray-Marching techniques. The Ray-Volume Intersection (Face Distance Method) is a two-step procedure to determine if a viewing ray intersects the data volume and to find the entry point for volume traversal. It calculates distances from the ray origin to each of the six faces of the volume geometry, divides by the corresponding ray direction component, and selects the smallest valid distance as the nearest impact point. This family covers algorithms for determining the intersection of a ray with a tetrahedron, a fundamental operation in volume rendering on unstructured grids and tetrahedral mesh rendering. It solves the problem of finding the entry and exit points (and their parametric distances) of a ray as it traverses a tetrahedral cell. The methods differ in their geometric representation (Plücker coordinates, barycentric coordinates, plane equations) and optimization strategies (early exits, GPU wave intrinsics, connectivity-based traversal). Key distinctions include the use of Plücker coordinates to avoid explicit plane intersections Plücker-based Tetrahedral Cell Intersection, the use of linear algebra for point containment Point-in-Tetrahedron Test via Barycentric Coordinates, and the use of mesh shaders for parallel evaluation Mesh Shader Tetrahedron Intersection Optimization. Computes the closest point on a triangle to a query point and returns the squared distance, handling all edge and vertex cases via Voronoi-region decomposition. It differs from Ray-primitive intersection by solving a static point-to-mesh query rather than a ray-scene traversal, and from General Ray-Triangle Intersection (Plücker Coordinates) by returning the geometric closest point rather than an intersection parameter. This family of methods determines the intersection between a ray and a surface defined implicitly by a scalar field function f(\mathbf{x}) = 0 (or f(\mathbf{x}) - v = 0 for an isovalue v). Unlike explicit mesh intersection, these methods solve the root-finding problem ft(t) = 0 for the smallest t > 0 along the ray \vec{p}(t) = \vec{o} + t\vec{d} without extracting a proxy triangle mesh. They are distinguished from sibling geometric primitives (e.g., Ray-box intersection) by their reliance on function evaluation and numerical root-finding rather than analytic geometric formulas, and from sibling SDF methods (e.g., SDF Raycast Collision Detection) by their broader applicability to general implicit surfaces beyond simple collision detection. Exact Rational Ray-Surfel Evaluation computes the intersection of a viewing ray with a flat surfel rectangle in its local (u, v) coordinates using a homography approximation around the center of the screen-space bounding box. It sets itself apart from the reference 2DGS formulation by replacing the per-pixel cross-product-based inversion with a precomputed affine approximation, reducing computational cost while maintaining visual fidelity. LinPrim Gradient Computation computes the gradients of intersection depths \mathbf{i} with respect to the ray-space triangle corners \mathbf{v}^{\text{ray}} to enable differentiable rendering of linear primitives. It differs from standard 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) by backpropagating gradients through a linear primitive rasterizer (MTIA) rather than a Gaussian splatting kernel, requiring specific handling of ray-space to world-space transformations and quaternion-based rotation updates. It builds on 3D Gaussian Splatting Differentiable Rasterizer by replacing the Gaussian alpha-blending gradient flow with opacity calculations based on intersection depths. Ray ID Caching is an optimization technique used in volume rendering and ray tracing to eliminate redundant intersection tests when a single ray intersects the same geometric object multiple times across different voxels. It solves the problem of "multiple intersection" overhead by storing a unique identifier (rayID) on each ray and the last intersecting rayID on each object. Unlike methods that require precise voxel-object containment checks (such as Glassner's method), this technique allows for looser voxel lists because redundant intersections are filtered by the ID comparison rather than geometric precision. IRIS Ray-Geometry Intersection is an intersection-aware ray-based sampling method for implicit editable scenes that determines samples as the maximum response points of Gaussians intersected by each ray. It solves the problem of efficiently sampling 3D Gaussians in large-scale or bounded scenes by leveraging hardware-accelerated ray-triangle intersection tests via proxy geometry. Unlike direct Gaussian intersection methods, it maps each Gaussian to a convex polyhedral proxy (an affine-transformed icosahedron) to utilize RT cores, setting it apart from siblings like Ray-Splat Intersection which may use different primitive approximations or software-based tests. Ray-sphere intersection computes the entry and exit points (or the nearest hit distance) where a parametric ray intersects a sphere defined by a center and radius. In volume rendering, this operation is primarily used to determine the marching bounds for ray-marching algorithms, ensuring samples are only taken within the volume's extent, and to perform early-outs in hierarchical traversal. It is distinct from Sphere Intersection in that it solves for the intersection of a line (the ray) with a surface, whereas the latter typically refers to finding points on a sphere's surface satisfying other constraints (such as the 3-sphere trilateration variant). It is analytically exact and generally faster than iterative methods like Implicit Surface and SDF Intersection for simple spherical primitives. The Ray-Object Intersection Test is the fundamental geometric primitive used to determine the closest intersection between a ray and a specific scene object, returning the intersection distance t or a failure indicator if no intersection exists. It serves as the core evaluation step within a broader ray-scene traversal, where the test is executed for multiple objects to find the global minimum t. What sets this method apart from sibling primitives like Ray-box intersection or Sphere Intersection is its role as the generic interface for arbitrary geometry; it typically handles coordinate space transformations and delegates the specific algebraic solution to the object's internal representation, rather than implementing the intersection algebra directly in the traversal loop. Azimuthal Hit Detection determines whether a ray intersects an azimuthal section within a spherical voxel grid, where azimuthal sections are defined in the XZ plane. It serves as a geometric primitive for traversing spherical volume data, specifically handling the angular discretization along the azimuthal axis. It is distinct from Ray-box intersection which handles axis-aligned bounding volumes, and Ray-Tetrahedron Intersection which handles general 3D simplicial volumes; instead, it leverages the specific planar geometry of the azimuthal slices. Ray-Polar Section Intersection determines whether a ray intersects a "polar section," a geometric primitive defined within the XY plane of a spherical voxel grid. It serves as the angular traversal step for rays passing through spherical volume data, identifying which radial angular bin (section) the ray occupies at a given depth. It is distinct from Ray-box intersection by operating on angular sectors rather than Cartesian cubes, and from Azimuthal Hit Detection by using the Y-axis as the polar axis rather than the Z-axis. Computes the entry and exit distances for a ray intersecting a cylinder defined by geomSize, composed of front/back rectangles, top/bottom faces, and a lateral curved surface. It differs from Ray-box intersection by handling the curved lateral surface via quadratic solving and cylindrical coordinate checks, and from Ray-box Intersection via OpenGL Geometry Shaders by being a general-purpose CPU/GPU kernel implementation rather than a shader-specific primitive assembly. Ray Tracing and Ray Intersection Methods determine the first object intersected by a camera ray by analytically computing intersection distances for simple geometries. The core problem is finding the closest intersection point along a ray to render opaque surfaces correctly. This family is distinguished from Ray-marching by its reliance on exact analytical solutions for primitive shapes, whereas marching uses fixed steps. It differs from Ray-box intersection and Ray-Triangle Intersection by encompassing the broader algorithmic strategies (such as packetization and hybrid implicit tracing) used to accelerate these primitive tests in volume rendering contexts. Point-Plane Reflection computes the mirror image of a point \mathbf{p} across a plane defined by a normal vector \mathbf{n} and a scalar offset c. It is primarily used in volume rendering and ray tracing to determine specular reflection paths, calculate virtual camera positions for mirror surfaces, or perform spatial transformations in signed distance field (SDF) operations. Unlike general ray-plane intersection which finds a hit point, this method transforms a point in space. It differs from Ray-box intersection and Ray-Tetrahedron Intersection by operating on a single point relative to an infinite plane rather than intersecting a ray with a bounded primitive. This method optimizes the evaluation of multiple ray-primitive intersections along a single ray by establishing a strict processing order based on bounding box distances, thereby reducing the computational load of expensive primitive intersection tests. It distinguishes itself from standard intersection tests by focusing on the sequence of calculations rather than the geometric solution itself, ensuring that faster, coarser intersection points are resolved before slower, finer segment evaluations. Computes the least-squares intersection point of two rays in 3D space, finding the point that minimizes the squared distance to both rays when they do not intersect exactly due to noise or parallax. It differs from exact intersection methods by providing a robust solution for skew lines, which is essential in volume rendering pipelines where ray origins and directions may have minor misalignments. This family defines the geometric primitives and algorithms for determining the intersection between a camera ray and 3D Gaussian splats, which are ellipsoidal density distributions used in novel view synthesis. It solves the problem of efficiently identifying which splats contribute to a pixel's color and depth, enabling alpha blending and depth testing. It distinguishes itself from sibling methods by handling the specific anisotropic, probabilistic nature of Gaussian splats (defined by covariance matrices or scale/rotation parameters) rather than hard geometric primitives like boxes or triangles. Quadtree Raycasting is a recursive algorithm that traverses a 2D quadtree data structure to find the first solid node intersected by a ray. It solves the problem of efficiently locating geometry in sparse or hierarchical 2D volumes by skipping empty subtrees. It differs from standard grid-based raycasting (like Ray-box intersection) by adapting the traversal step size and order to the hierarchical node boundaries rather than a uniform grid, and it differs from Ray-Tetrahedron Intersection by operating on axis-aligned square quadrants. Updates the ray's medium stack when crossing a surface, pushing a new medium if entering and popping if exiting. It checks if transmission occurred using (wo \cdot n < 0) \neq (wi \cdot n < 0) and if entering using wi \cdot n < 0. Performs ray-sphere intersection or ray marching against the SDF grid using a C++ renderer extension to find the rough intersection position for each pixel. It initializes output tensors for intersection position, voxel index, and ray direction, then calls the C++ ray matching function with camera parameters, grid bounds, resolution, and grid data. Pixels with no intersection are marked by voxelminpointindex being -1, which must be handled to avoid invalid memory access during interpolation. Tests if rays intersect any geometry without returning hit details, used for simple occlusion checks. It typically initializes a ray structure with origin, direction, and distance bounds, then invokes a hardware or library query function to return a boolean hit status within the specified range. An optimization to reduce cell primitives in a slice by intersecting individual rays with the world-space bounding box of the current u,v slice. It filters out rays that have already successfully hit a cell to avoid redundant processing. Computes the unsigned distance from query points to a triangle mesh using a BVH, and provides an analytic gradient for backpropagation. It flattens input x to [N, 3], queries BVH for distance udf, triangle ID tri\id, and barycentric coordinates uvw, clamps uvw to [1e-9, 1-1e-9], and interpolates the nearest point on the triangle using uvw and triangle vertices. The gradient is \nablax \text{UDF}(x) = \frac{x - p{\text{nearest}}}{\|x - p{\text{nearest}}\|} where p{\text{nearest}} is the closest point on the mesh. uvw is clamped to avoid invalid barycentric coordinates at triangle edges/corners. A selection technique where a ray is emitted from the user's hand, with start point and orientation controlled by the user, selecting the first intersected object. It can be augmented by cycling through all ray-object intersection points to disambiguate. It is difficult to select small and distant objects due to required angular accuracy, and rays or cones may intersect multiple objects, requiring disambiguation metrics based on distance from targets to the apex and central axis of the cone. Computes the intersection of a camera-space ray with lines parallel to the image frame axes (x=0, x=1, y=0, y=1) in normalized image coordinates. It extracts intrinsics components (fs, fo, cs, co) and ray components (os, oo, oz, ds, do, dz), constructs the 2D intersection point xy and 3D point xyz = origins + t directions, and validates the projection by checking if xy is in bounds [-\epsilon, 1+\epsilon], if xyz is in front of camera (z > -\epsilon), and if t > -\epsilon. The ray parameter is t = \frac{c oz - os}{ds - c dz} where c = \frac{v - cs}{fs}. Ray/box intersection test yields better performance with compute shader and OpenCL implementations, while raster intersection test yields better performance with CUDA implementations. No single intersection method is globally superior; optimal choice depends on the target parallel API. Best overall results are achieved by combining compute shader with ray/box intersection test. The raster intersection test presents a better performance for most cases with CUDA implementations. It leverages the parallel rasterization hardware of a GPU to compute the entry and exit points of view rays through a volumetric dataset, avoiding explicit analytical intersection tests. A method for determining ray entry and exit within the volume bounding box entirely within the fragment shader. The ray is defined by the camera position and the volume entry position. It requires an exit criterion to determine when the ray has left the volume. An approximate method to determine if a camera ray intersects a caustic beam and the location of that intersection, used because exact computation is too costly for thousands of beams. It defines a scan plane (an auxiliary arbitrary plane containing the camera ray), computes intersections of the scan plane and the edges of the caustic beam to form a triangle, and minimizes error from curved beam edges by choosing the scan plane normal vector to be close to the normal of the caustic triangle. It transforms the view ray to the beam's local space, selects a representative point on the intersection segment \Delta x (specifically the midpoint), and evaluates the area function A(y). The scan plane normal is np = r{view} \times (r{view} \times n4), where np is the scan plane normal, r{view} is the view ray direction, and n4 is the caustic triangle normal. The classification of ray-object intersections into five classes based on intersection type, data type, and shader information requirements was established in volumetric ray tracing literature. Class 1 involves geometric data intersection requiring a single point, Class 2 involves volumetric data with early termination, Class 3 involves volumetric data without early termination, Class 4 involves volumetric data segment intersection with one value, and Class 5 involves volumetric data segment intersection with all values. The choice between rasterization and ray/box intersection for volume rendering depends on the parallel API, with ray/box being superior for compute shaders/OpenCL and rasterization for CUDA. name: Implicit Surface and SDF Intersection
body: This family defines methods for determining the intersection between a ray and a surface defined implicitly by a scalar field f(\mathbf{x}) (where the surface is the zero-level set f(\mathbf{x})=0) or a Signed Distance Field (SDF). It solves the problem of finding the nearest point \mathbf{o} + t\mathbf{d} such that f(\mathbf{o} + t\mathbf{d}) = 0 without relying on explicit triangle meshes. It is distinguished from General Ray-Triangle Intersection by its reliance on function evaluation rather than geometric primitives, and from Sphere Intersection by its generality, requiring numerical root-finding or traversal rather than closed-form quadratic solutions for arbitrary functions. The shared principles of this family are the geometric definition of rays and the parallel execution model. Ray Definition Rays are defined by an origin \mathbf{o} and a direction \mathbf{d}. The direction is typically normalized. The origin is often the camera eye position, but can vary based on the camera model. Parallel Execution Computations are mapped to parallel threads. Each thread typically processes one or more pixels or samples. Memory access patterns are optimized for coalescing. Synchronization is used to manage data dependencies between threads. The Kalra & Barr method is a robust, mathematically sound algorithm for finding the nearest intersection between a ray and an implicit surface. It solves the problem of missing fine surface features or failing to converge in standard ray-marching schemes by guaranteeing numerical convergence without requiring fine-tuning or human-chosen interactive parameters. It distinguishes itself from ad-hoc schemes by relying on two specific upper bounds, L and G, to define an "LG-implicit surface," ensuring robustness for a broader class of functions than traditional quadric or polynomial-specific solvers. This method determines if a line segment intersects a surface defined by a Signed Distance Field (SDF) by evaluating the distance function at the segment's endpoints and checking for a sign change. It serves as a lightweight, broad-phase collision detection primitive. Unlike Kalra & Barr Implicit Surface Intersection which computes the exact intersection point, or Ray Tracing Implicit Surfaces which traces the ray through the field, this method only reports binary existence of an intersection within the segment bounds. It is distinct from Terrain SDF Collision Detection and Resolution in that it performs detection only, without resolving penetration or modifying velocity. Ray tracing implicit surfaces renders a surface defined by a filter function f(\mathbf{x}) and an isovalue v by solving for the root where a viewing ray intersects the surface f(\mathbf{x}) - v = 0, without using a proxy triangle mesh. It solves the root-finding problem ft(t) = 0 for the smallest t > 0, where ft is the implicit function evaluated along the parametric ray. Unlike rasterization of proxy geometry (e.g., Marching Cubes), ray tracing does not require mesh extraction, avoiding time complexity on the order of the number of samples and issues with proxy sampling rates beneath the Nyquist limit. It is distinguished from simple ray casting by its native support for secondary rays (shadows, refractions) and ray traversal of acceleration structures. LevelSetHDDA is a specialized Hierarchical Digital Differential Analyzer (HDDA) designed for static intersection testing against level set trees. It recursively traverses a VDB tree hierarchy from a specified node level down to the leaf level (-1) to determine if a ray intersects the implicit surface. It sets itself apart from generic volume traversal methods like VolumeHDDA by targeting the specific structure of level sets, where the traversal terminates at the voxel level rather than the leaf node level, allowing for precise surface intersection checks via a provided tester object. Computes the intersection of a ray with a 3D ellipsoid defined by a rotation matrix, translation vector, and scale factors. It returns whether an intersection exists and the intersection point in world space. This method transforms the ray into the ellipsoid's local space, solving a quadratic equation for the unit sphere, then transforms the result back. It is distinguished from general implicit surface methods by its closed-form quadratic solution, which is computationally cheaper than iterative root-finding but requires the primitive to be strictly ellipsoidal. Detects if a ray intersects a zero-crossing at the voxel level of a grid in the accessor. It performs empty-space ray-marching at all levels of the tree using an HDDA (Hierarchical Distance Field Acceleration). The method is optimized for performance, precision, and correctness, and surfaces a shared cache-hint helper for other operations. It is SDF-sign-agnostic and reports the EXIT crossing for rays that start inside the surface, matching nanovdb::ZeroCrossing behavior. Definition: A test to detect the existence of a tunnel in a cell based on coefficients of the isosurface equation. Steps: Compute G[Fi] and Disc[Fi] from the coefficients of the isosurface equation. If G[Fi] < 0 and Disc[Fi] > 0, a tunnel exists in the cell. Formulas: G[Fi] = (AE - BD)(AF - BC)(AG - CD) Disc[Fi] = (AH)^2 + (BG)^2 + (CE)^2 + (DF)^2 - 2ABGH - 2ACEH - 2ADFH - 2BCEG - 2BDFG - 2CDEF + 4AEFG + 4BCDH where A, B, C, D, E, F, G, H are coefficients of the isosurface equation. Definition: A basic method to influence the velocity field by approximating obstacles as simple shapes (box, ball) defined by implicit equations, adding the obstacle's average velocity to the fluid velocity in that region. Formula: Obstacle shape defined by implicit equation f(x, y, z) \le 0. Formula: Deformation equation: x{\Thetas} = x + t{\Thetas} \cdot n, where x is the initial edge point, n is the surface normal, and t{\Thetas} is the learned scalar displacement. Initial condition: At initialization \Thetas = \Thetas^{(0)}, the displacement is zero: t{\Thetas} \big|{\Thetas = \Thetas^{(0)}} = 0. Gradient update rule derived from implicit differentiation of the zero-level set constraint S{\Thetas}(x{\Thetas}) = 0: \frac{\partial t}{\partial \Thetas} \big|{\Thetas = \Thetas^{(0)}} = -\frac{1}{n^T n} \cdot \frac{\partial S}{\partial \Thetas}(x) \big|{\Thetas = \Thetas^{(0)}}. Final re-parametrization for gradient-based optimization: x{\Thetas} = x - \frac{n}{n^T n} \cdot S{\Thetas}(x). Pitfall: The re-parametrization only provides an unbiased first-order gradient with respect to \Thetas, which is suitable for gradient-based optimizers but may not capture higher-order surface curvature effects. The problem of intersecting rays with implicit surfaces is fundamental to ray tracing and volume rendering, allowing for the rendering of complex shapes without explicit mesh representation. Early work focused on robust root-finding for algebraic surfaces. For large-scale volumetric data, hierarchical traversal methods like LevelSetHDDA [2875-levelsethdda.md] and RayImplicitIntersection [3591-rayimplicitintersection.md] optimize performance by skipping empty space using Digital Differential Analyzers (DDAs). Topological analysis of implicit surfaces, such as DeVella's Necklace Test, allows for the detection of complex features like tunnels within grid cells, which is crucial for topologically accurate dual isosurfacing. Implicit shapes are also used in fluid dynamics to approximate obstacles, where the implicit equation defines the solid region. Recent advances in inverse rendering and neural fields utilize edge point re-parametrization to optimize implicit surface parameters directly from images, ensuring the surface remains on the zero-level set during gradient descent. name: Kalra & Barr Implicit Surface Intersection
head: Kalra-Barr method, LG-implicit surface intersection
body: The Kalra & Barr method is a robust, mathematically sound algorithm for finding the nearest intersection between a ray and an implicit surface. It solves the problem of missing fine surface features by guaranteeing numerical convergence without requiring fine-tuning or human-chosen interactive parameters. It distinguishes itself from ad-hoc schemes by relying on two specific upper bounds, L and G, to define an "LG-implicit surface," ensuring robustness for a broader class of functions than traditional quadric or polynomial-specific solvers. Inputs and Outputs Input: Ray origin \mathbf{o}, ray direction \mathbf{d} (normalized), implicit function f(\mathbf{x}), Lipschitz constant L, gradient bound G, and a search interval [t{min}, t{max}]. Output: The smallest t \in [t{min}, t{max}] such that f(\mathbf{o} + t\mathbf{d}) = 0, or a failure indication if no root exists in the interval. Data Structures Interval: A pair of floats [t{start}, t{end}] representing the current search range along the ray. Function Evaluation: Computes f(\mathbf{x}) at a given 3D point. Parameters L: Upper bound on the net rate of change of the implicit surface function. G: Upper bound on the rate of change of the gradient. Tolerance \epsilon: Numerical threshold for termination. Steps 1. Initialize: Set current interval [ta, tb] = [t{min}, t{max}]. 2. Check Endpoints: Evaluate fa = f(\mathbf{o} + ta\mathbf{d}) and fb = f(\mathbf{o} + tb\mathbf{d}). If fa = 0, return ta. If fb = 0, return tb. 3. Pruning: The abstract does not specify the exact pruning logic, but the method uses L and G to guarantee that the interval contains a root or can be safely discarded. 4. Bisection/Refinement: The specific iterative formula is not detailed in the abstract, but the method relies on these bounds to prevent overshooting and ensure convergence. 5. Convergence: Repeat until the interval width is less than \epsilon or the function value is sufficiently close to zero. Pseudocode Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def kalrabarrintersect(o, d, f, L, G, tmin, tmax, epsilon, maxiter=100): # Cap unbounded max to prevent overflow and infinite loops if tmax == float('inf'): tmax = 100.0 ta = tmin tb = tmax # Evaluate endpoints fa = f(o + ta d) fb = f(o + tb d) # Check if roots are at endpoints if abs(fa) < epsilon: return ta if abs(fb) < epsilon: return tb # Main loop for in range(maxiter): if tb - ta < epsilon: break # Midpoint tmid = (ta + tb) / 2.0 fm = f(o + tmid d) if abs(fm) < epsilon: return tmid # Determine which sub-interval contains the root # The exact iterative formula using L and G is not detailed in the abstract. # Standard bisection checks signs, but LG-methods may use bounds # to ensure no feature is missed. if fa fm < 0: tb = tmid fb = fm else: ta = tmid fa = fm return (ta + tb) / 2.0 Edge Cases and Pitfalls Precision: Floating-point errors in evaluating f can lead to incorrect sign checks. Degenerate Input: If L=0 or G=0, the surface is constant or linear, which may require special handling. No Root: The abstract does not specify the exact termination condition when no root exists within the interval. A robust algorithm that processes all active rays in lockstep using interval arithmetic to guarantee no surface features are missed. It builds on Kalra & Barr by adding level-synchronized processing and Hermite-based root estimation. A robust algorithm that guarantees finding the nearest intersection without missing fine features by using interval arithmetic to prune intervals. It builds on Kalra & Barr by providing a batched, interval-arithmetic-based implementation strategy. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Typically logarithmic with respect to the desired precision for bisection-based methods. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Requires storage for the current interval and function values. Strengths: Guaranteed convergence; no fine-tuning required; robust against missing fine features. Limitations: Requires computation of L and G for the implicit surface. When to Use: When robustness and guaranteed intersection are critical, and the implicit surface allows for the computation of L and G. When Not to Use: When performance is paramount and approximate intersections are acceptable; when L and G are difficult or expensive to compute. The method was introduced by Devendra Kalra and Alan Barr in 1989 in the paper "Guaranteed ray intersections with implicit surfaces". It was presented as a significant extension to previous schemes that were limited to specific classes of implicit functions (e.g., quadrics) or were ad-hoc. The work demonstrated the feasibility of ray tracing scenes with hundreds of thousands of objects using robust intersection techniques. name: Level-synchronized bisection ray casting
head: Batch bisection, Iso-surface bisection, Ray Subdivision and Interval Processing
body: Level-synchronized bisection ray casting is a robust algorithm for rendering the zero-level-set of an implicit function f: \mathbb{R}^3 \to \mathbb{R} by processing all active rays in lockstep using interval arithmetic to guarantee no surface features are missed. It solves the problem of missing fine surface details or grazing intersections inherent in standard discrete ray marching by bounding the function value over continuous segments and iteratively bisecting intervals until convergence. It builds on Kalra & Barr Implicit Surface Intersection and differs from Bisection Ray Tracing with Interval Inclusion by its specific implementation of level-synchronized processing and Hermite-based root estimation. Inputs: Ray origins \mathbf{o} \in \mathbb{R}^R, directions \mathbf{d} \in \mathbb{R}^R (normalized). Scene bounds [\mathbf{b}{min}, \mathbf{b}{max}] \subset \mathbb{R}^3. Implicit function f(\mathbf{p}) and an InclusionFunction object providing bounds over 3D axis-aligned boxes. Parameters: maxdepth (integer, default 40), threshold (float, default 10^{-5}). Outputs: TraceResult dataclass containing: hit: boolean array (R,), true if surface found. t: float64 array (R,), distance to hit. position: float64 array (R, 3), world position of hit. normal: float64 array (R, 3), surface normal at hit. depthcount: int array (R,), number of bisection steps. tlo, thi: float64 arrays (R,), final interval bounds. Data Structures: rayidx: Array of active ray indices. ivtlo, ivthi: Arrays of interval endpoints for active rays. hitmask: Boolean mask identifying rays intersecting the scene AABB. Steps: 1. Initialization: Initialize resulthit to False, resultt to inf, resulttlo to inf, resultthi to inf, resultdepth to 0. Compute ray-AABB intersection for all rays. Identify active rays where intersection exists and t{max} > t{min}. Set rayidx to indices of active rays. Set ivtlo to t{min} and ivthi to t{max} for active rays. 2. Ray Subdivision (Pre-processing): Subdivide the ray parameter space [t{min}, t{max}] into intervals. Subdivide further when switching between areas overlapped by primitive supports and areas not overlapped by any primitive support to avoid processing empty areas. For each resulting interval [t{begin}, t{end}], proceed to interval processing. 3. Level-Synchronized Bisection Loop: Iterate depth from 0 to maxdepth. If len(rayidx) == 0, break. Convert to 3D Boxes: For each active ray i, compute 3D axis-aligned boxes corresponding to the current interval [iv\t\lo[i], iv\t\hi[i]]: \mathbf{p}0 = \mathbf{o}i + iv\t\lo[i] \cdot \mathbf{d}i \mathbf{p}1 = \mathbf{o}i + iv\t\hi[i] \cdot \mathbf{d}i \mathbf{lo}{3d} = \min(\mathbf{p}0, \mathbf{p}1) \mathbf{hi}{3d} = \max(\mathbf{p}0, \mathbf{p}1) Inclusion Test: Evaluate inclusion bounds using inclusionfn.evaluate(lo3d, hi3d) to get [f{lo}, f{hi}]. Filter Active Rays: Determine if zero level set is present: \text{has\zero}[i] = (f{lo}[i] \le 0.0) \land (f{hi}[i] \ge 0.0) Update rayidx, ivtlo, ivthi to keep only rays where haszero is true. If len(rayidx) == 0, break. 4. Interval Processing (Per Active Ray): For each active ray interval [t{begin}, t{end}] with Hermite data \mathbf{h}b at t{begin} and \mathbf{h}e at t{end}: Initialize n \leftarrow 0, saved \leftarrow None. While n < 32: n \leftarrow n + 1. Estimate root t{root} \leftarrow \text{Oracle}(t{begin}, t{end}, i) using quadratic interpolation of Hermite data. If t{root} = \infty and saved is None, return false, \infty (no hit in this interval). If t{root} < \infty: Evaluate Hermite data at root: \mathbf{h}r \leftarrow \text{HermiteData}(t{root}). If |\mathbf{h}r.\text{val}| < \varepsilon, return true, t{root} (hit found). Determine primitive sign change: b{prim} \leftarrow (\mathbf{h}r.\text{prim} > 0) \land (\mathbf{h}b.\text{prim} < 0). If saved is None and \mathbf{h}r.\text{val} \ge 0 and \mathbf{h}e.\text{val} < 0 and b{prim}, store potential backtrack: saved \leftarrow [(t{root}, \mathbf{h}r), (t{end}, \mathbf{h}e)]. Update interval: If \mathbf{h}r.\text{val} < 0 or b{prim}, set t{end}, \mathbf{h}e \leftarrow t{root}, \mathbf{h}r; else set t{begin}, \mathbf{h}b \leftarrow t{root}, \mathbf{h}r. Else if saved is not None: Restore interval: (t{begin}, \mathbf{h}b), (t{end}, \mathbf{h}e) \leftarrow \text{saved}, saved \leftarrow None. If loop completes without hit, return false, \infty. 5. Result Update: For each valid hit with distance t{valid}: If t{valid} < \text{result\t}[\text{ray\idx}[i]]: \text{result\hit}[\text{ray\idx}[i]] \leftarrow \text{True} \text{result\t}[\text{ray\idx}[i]] \leftarrow t{valid} \text{result\t\lo}[\text{ray\idx}[i]] \leftarrow t{lo} \text{result\t\hi}[\text{ray\idx}[i]] \leftarrow t{hi} This ensures front-to-back rendering by keeping only the closest hit. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import numpy as np from dataclasses import dataclass @dataclass class TraceResult: hit: np.ndarray t: np.ndarray position: np.ndarray normal: np.ndarray depthcount: np.ndarray tlo: np.ndarray thi: np.ndarray def levelsynchronizedbisectioncast(origins, directions, boundsmin, boundsmax, inclusionfn, maxdepth=40, threshold=1e-5): R = origins.shape[0] # Initialize results resulthit = np.zeros(R, dtype=bool) resultt = np.full(R, np.inf, dtype=np.float64) resulttlo = np.full(R, np.inf, dtype=np.float64) resultthi = np.full(R, np.inf, dtype=np.float64) resultdepth = np.zeros(R, dtype=np.int32) # Ray-AABB intersection safedirs = np.where(directions == 0, 1.0, directions) tminvals = (boundsmin - origins) / safedirs tmaxvals = (boundsmax - origins) / safedirs # Fix: use np.max/min over axis=1 to get scalar tmin/tmax per ray tminarr = np.max(tminvals, axis=1) tmaxarr = np.min(tmaxvals, axis=1) hitmask = (tminarr < tmaxarr) & (tmaxarr > 0) rayidx = np.where(hitmask)[0] ivtlo = tminarr[rayidx] ivthi = tmaxarr[rayidx] # Pre-subdivision handled by scene structure; initial AABB bounds serve as starting intervals. for depth in range(maxdepth): if len(rayidx) == 0: break # Convert intervals to 3D boxes p0 = origins[rayidx] + ivtlo[:, np.newaxis] directions[rayidx] p1 = origins[rayidx] + ivthi[:, np.newaxis] directions[rayidx] lo3d = np.minimum(p0, p1) hi3d = np.maximum(p0, p1) # Evaluate inclusion bounds flo, fhi = inclusionfn.evaluate(lo3d, hi3d) # Filter active rays: haszero if flo <= 0 <= fhi haszero = (flo <= 0.0) & (fhi >= 0.0) rayidx = rayidx[haszero] ivtlo = ivtlo[haszero] ivthi = ivthi[haszero] if len(rayidx) == 0: break validhits = [] validrayindices = [] validtlo = [] validthi = [] for i in range(len(rayidx)): tbegin = ivtlo[i] tend = ivthi[i] # Standard evaluation returning function value and derivative for Hermite interpolation hb = inclusionfn.gethermitedata(origins[rayidx[i]] + tbegin directions[rayidx[i]]) he = inclusionfn.gethermitedata(origins[rayidx[i]] + tend directions[rayidx[i]]) saved = None hitfound = False hitt = np.inf for n in range(32): troot = oraclehermiteinterpolation(tbegin, tend, hb, he) if troot == np.inf: if saved is None: break else: (tbegin, hb), (tend, he) = saved saved = None continue proot = origins[rayidx[i]] + troot directions[rayidx[i]] hr = inclusionfn.gethermitedata(proot) if abs(hr.val) < threshold: hitfound = True hitt = troot break bprim = (hr.prim > 0) and (hb.prim < 0) if saved is None and hr.val >= 0 and he.val < 0 and bprim: saved = [(troot, hr), (tend, he)] if hr.val < 0 or bprim: tend = troot he = hr else: tbegin = troot hb = hr if hitfound: validhits.append(hitt) validrayindices.append(rayidx[i]) validtlo.append(tbegin) validthi.append(tend) if validhits: validhits = np.array(validhits) validrayindices = np.array(validrayindices) validtlo = np.array(validtlo) validthi = np.array(validthi) mask = validhits < resultt[validrayindices] resulthit[validrayindices[mask]] = True resultt[validrayindices[mask]] = validhits[mask] resulttlo[validrayindices[mask]] = validtlo[mask] resultthi[validrayindices[mask]] = validthi[mask] resultdepth[validrayindices[mask]] = depth + 1 positions = np.zeros((R, 3)) normals = np.zeros((R, 3)) hitindices = np.where(resulthit)[0] if len(hitindices) > 0: positions[hitindices] = origins[hitindices] + resultt[hitindices][:, np.newaxis] directions[hitindices] normals[hitindices] = inclusionfn.getnormals(positions[hitindices]) return TraceResult( hit=resulthit, t=resultt, position=positions, normal=normals, depthcount=resultdepth, tlo=resulttlo, thi=resultthi) def oraclehermiteinterpolation(tbegin, tend, hb, he): dt = tend - tbegin if dt == 0: return np.inf c = hb.val b = hb.prim dt a = 2 (he.val - hb.val) - (hb.prim + he.prim) dt if abs(a) < 1e-12: if abs(b) < 1e-12: return np.inf t = -c / b else: discriminant = bb - 4ac if discriminant < 0: return np.inf sqrtdisc = np.sqrt(discriminant) t1 = (-b - sqrtdisc) / (2a) t2 = (-b + sqrtdisc) / (2a) if 0 <= t1 <= 1: t = t1 elif 0 <= t2 <= 1: t = t2 else: return np.inf return tbegin + t dt Parameters: maxdepth: Maximum number of bisection iterations allowed per ray. Default value is 40 in the tracer, but examples use 48 or 52. threshold: Convergence width threshold. The bisection stops when the interval width (t{hi} - t{lo}) is less than this value. Default value is 10^{-5}. inclusionfn: An InclusionFunction object that implements the evaluate(lo, hi) method. It takes 3D axis-aligned boxes and returns interval bounds (f{lo}, f{hi}) for the implicit function over that box. Used to determine if the zero level set exists within the interval. body:
Bisection Trace with Gradient Inclusion is a robust ray casting algorithm that renders the zero-level-set of an implicit function f: \mathbb{R}^3 	o \mathbb{R} by combining level-synchronized bisection with gradient-based interval arithmetic. It solves the problem of missing surface features during ray traversal by using an inclusion function to guarantee that no zero-crossings are pruned. It differs from standard bisection by using the Lipschitz constant derived from local gradients to compute tight, safe step sizes, ensuring convergence without overshooting the surface. The method operates on a batch of rays, processing them in lockstep (level-synchronized) to refine their hit locations. It relies on an InclusionFunction that provides a guaranteed bounding interval [f-(t), f+(t)] for the implicit function over a candidate step. Inputs: origins: Array of ray origins \mathbf{o} \in \mathbb{R}^3. directions: Array of ray directions \mathbf{d} \in \mathbb{R}^3 (normalized). tmin, tmax: Scalar bounds for the ray segment. hitmask: Boolean array indicating active rays. inclusion: An instance of InclusionFunction (specifically GradientInclusion). fnp: The implicit function evaluator f(\mathbf{x}). maxdepth: Integer, maximum number of bisection steps. threshold: Float, convergence tolerance for the interval width. lipschitz: Float or 'auto'. The Lipschitz constant L for the inclusion function. newtoniter: Integer, optional Newton refinement steps after bisection. batchsize: Integer, number of rays to process per batch. Data Structures: Interval: A pair of floats [lo, hi] representing the guaranteed range of f. RayState: Contains current t (or interval [t{start}, t{end}]), current hit point \mathbf{x}, and active status. Parameters: maxdepth: Typical values depend on required precision; e.g., 20-30 for high-res. threshold: E.g., 10^{-6} or 10^{-8} relative to scene scale. lipschitz: If 'auto', estimated by sampling gradient norms \|
abla f\| over the bounding box using automatic differentiation. Algorithm Steps: 1. Initialization: For each active ray, initialize the search interval [t{start}, t{end}] = [t{min}, t{max}]. If lipschitz is 'auto', compute L = \max{\mathbf{x} \in 	ext{Box}} \|
abla f(\mathbf{x})\| by sampling gradients. Initialize inclusion with f{np} and L. 2. Level-Synchronized Bisection Loop: For step from 1 to maxdepth: For each active ray i: Compute midpoint t{mid} = (t{start}^{(i)} + t{end}^{(i)}) / 2. Evaluate inclusion function: [f{min}, f{max}] = 	ext{inclusion.evaluate}(t{start}^{(i)}, t{end}^{(i)}). Pruning: If 0 
otin [f{min}, f{max}], the surface is not in this interval. Mark ray as missed or handle accordingly. Refinement: If |t{end}^{(i)} - t{start}^{(i)}| < 	ext{threshold}, stop bisection for this ray. Determine new interval: Evaluate f(t{start}) and f(t{mid}) (or use inclusion bounds if available). If signs differ between t{start} and t{mid}, set t{end}^{(i)} = t{mid}. Else, set t{start}^{(i)} = t{mid}. Update hit point \mathbf{x}^{(i)} = \mathbf{o}^{(i)} + t{mid}^{(i)} \mathbf{d}^{(i)}. 3. Newton Refinement (Optional): For each ray that converged: Perform newtoniter steps: t{new} = t{old} - f(\mathbf{x}) / (
abla f(\mathbf{x}) \cdot \mathbf{d}). Update \mathbf{x} and t. 4. Output: Final hit positions \mathbf{x} and depths t for all rays. Pseudocode: Unverified code. tstart) < threshold): break # Newton refinement if newtoniter > 0: for i in range(len(origins)): if hitmask[i]: refinewithnewton(origins[i], directions[i], tstart[i], fnp, newtoniter) return tstart, origins + tstart[:, None] directions def processbatch(indices, origins, directions, tstart, tend, hitmask, inclusion, fnp, threshold): for i in indices: if not hitmask[i]: continue # Evaluate inclusion over current interval fmin, fmax = inclusion.evaluate(tstart[i], tend[i]) # Prune if zero not in range if fmin > 0 or fmax < 0: hitmask[i] = False continue # Bisection tmid = 0.5 (tstart[i] + tend[i]) # Check convergence if tend[i] - tstart[i] < threshold: continue # Determine new interval based on sign change # Note: Using inclusion bounds for robustness, or exact f(tmid) if available fmid = fnp(origins[i] + tmid directions[i]) # Evaluate f at start for sign check fstart = fnp(origins[i] + tstart[i] directions[i]) if fstart fmid < 0: tend[i] = tmid else: tstart[i] = tmid Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Lipschitz Constant: If L is underestimated, the inclusion bounds may not be guaranteed, leading to missed surfaces. name: Interval Arithmetic Inclusion Strategies
head: InclusionFunction strategies
body: Interval Arithmetic Inclusion Strategies provide the bounding functions used by Bisection Trace with Gradient Inclusion to determine safe step sizes during ray casting. They compute an interval [f-(t), f+(t)] that is guaranteed to contain the true function value f(t) for all t within a candidate step, allowing the renderer to prune regions where the zero-level set cannot exist. They are distinguished from their siblings by their trade-off between generality (black-box compatibility) and bound tightness: SamplingInclusion works with any function but yields loose bounds, while NaturalIntervalInclusion and AffineInclusion require symbolic formulas to produce tighter bounds, and GradientInclusion uses local gradient information for a middle ground. All inclusion strategies operate on a scalar field function f: \mathbb{R}^d \rightarrow \mathbb{R} and a current ray position t0. The goal is to compute a step size s such that the interval [t0, t0 + s] is safe to skip if f(t0) > 0 (or f(t0) < 0), meaning the zero-crossing is not contained within that interval. The core mechanism is the construction of an inclusion function f which satisfies the inclusion property: \forall t \in [t0, t0 + s], \quad f(t) \in f For sphere tracing, the step size s is typically derived by finding the intersection of the inclusion bound with the zero threshold. For a linear bound f+(t) = f(t0) + \lambda(t - t0), the intersection with 0 yields s = f(t0) / \lambda. The strategies are categorized by the information they require: 1. Black-box strategies: Require only point evaluations f(\mathbf{x}). They rely on a global or local Lipschitz constant \lambda to bound the rate of change. 2. Gradient-based strategies: Require access to the gradient \nabla f(\mathbf{x}). They use local linear approximations to tighten bounds. 3. Analytic strategies: Require the symbolic formula of f. They use Interval Arithmetic (IA) or Affine Arithmetic (AA) to propagate uncertainty through the expression tree, minimizing overestimation. What it is: A black-box baseline strategy that estimates the Lipschitz constant \lambda by sampling the gradient magnitude at a grid of points within the bounding box. It uses this global \lambda to construct linear bounds. What sets it apart: It requires no symbolic access to f, making it the only viable option for black-box functions where only point evaluations are available. However, it provides the loosest bounds among the four strategies because it uses a global maximum gradient, which may be much larger than the local gradient at the ray position. When to choose: Use when f is a black-box function (e.g., a neural network or a complex procedural shader) and no gradient or symbolic formula is accessible. Link: SamplingInclusion What it is: The default strategy that uses the local gradient \nabla f(\mathbf{x}) at the current ray position to compute tighter bounds than SamplingInclusion. It effectively uses the local Lipschitz constant. What sets it apart: It requires access to the gradient of f but no symbolic formula. It provides tighter bounds than SamplingInclusion by adapting to local function variation, but is less tight than analytic methods. When to choose: Use when f is differentiable and gradients are available (e.g., via automatic differentiation or analytical derivatives), but the symbolic formula is not easily accessible for IA/AA propagation. Link: GradientInclusion What it is: An analytic strategy that applies Natural Interval Arithmetic (NIA) directly to the symbolic formula of f. It replaces real numbers with intervals and standard operations with their interval counterparts. What sets it apart: It provides tighter bounds than SamplingInclusion and GradientInclusion when the analytic formula is known. However, it suffers from the "dependency problem" in IA, where repeated variables are treated as independent, leading to overestimation. When to choose: Use when the symbolic formula of f is available and simple, and tighter bounds than gradient-based methods are needed without the complexity of Affine Arithmetic. Link: NaturalIntervalInclusion What it is: An analytic strategy that uses Affine Arithmetic (AA) on the symbolic formula of f. AA tracks linear correlations between variables, mitigating the dependency problem of NIA. What sets it apart: It provides the tightest bounds among the four strategies, significantly reducing the number of bisection steps needed. It is computationally more expensive than NIA due to the overhead of tracking noise symbols. When to choose: Use when the symbolic formula of f is available, tightest possible bounds are required for performance, and the computational cost of AA is acceptable. Link: AffineInclusion Definition: A method that simplifies the SDF expression in specific regions of space by coupling pruning and rendering, using interval arithmetic to evaluate nodes in a construction tree. Steps: It relies on well-defined interval arithmetic queries for each node in the construction tree to determine pruning eligibility. Comparison: Differs from Lipschitz pruning by using interval arithmetic instead of 1-Lipschitz bounds, requiring explicit interval queries per node rather than treating primitives as black boxes. The concept of using interval arithmetic for robust ray casting was introduced to address the robustness issues of traditional sphere tracing, which can miss thin shells, cusps, or high-frequency surfaces due to floating-point inaccuracies or insufficient step sizes. The isoray library popularized four specific inclusion strategies for Python-based rendering, emphasizing black-box compatibility while offering analytic optimizations. Parallel Tape Reduction, introduced in the context of hierarchical SDF simplification, extends interval arithmetic to pruning in construction trees, allowing for real-time rendering of complex scenes with thousands of nodes. name: Lipschitz Constant Estimation
body:
Lipschitz Constant Estimation computes the scalar bound \lambda that limits the maximum rate of change of an implicit scalar field f. This constant is required by the parent Interval Arithmetic Inclusion Strategies to construct safe step sizes for ray marching, ensuring the ray does not skip over the implicit surface. It differs from its sibling Forward Linear Inclusion Function by providing the global or local scalar bound \lambda itself, rather than using a gradient to compute a specific linear step for a single ray segment. Inputs: Scalar field function f: \mathbb{R}^d ightarrow \mathbb{R}. Bounding box \mathcal{B} of the region of interest (optional, depending on strategy). Parameter lipschitz: A float value or the string "auto". If "auto", estimation is performed. Outputs: Lipschitz constant \lambda \in \mathbb{R}^+. Data Structures: None required for the estimation logic itself; standard floating-point types are used. Method: The estimation strategy depends on the available information about f. 1. Definition: A function f is Lipschitz continuous if there exists a minimum constant \lambda such that for all \mathbf{x}, \mathbf{y} \in \mathbb{R}^d with \mathbf{x} 
eq \mathbf{y}:  rac{|f(\mathbf{x}) - f(\mathbf{y})|}{\|\mathbf{x} - \mathbf{y}\|} \leq \lambda This \lambda represents the maximum magnitude of the function's derivative. Formally: Lip(f) = \max{\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{y}}  rac{|f(\mathbf{x}) - f(\mathbf{y})|}{\|\mathbf{x} - \mathbf{y}\|} \quad (3). 2. Auto-Estimation (Sampling): If lipschitz is "auto", the constant is estimated by sampling the gradient norms over the bounding box. Sample a set of points \{\mathbf{x}i\} within the bounding box. Compute the gradient 
abla f(\mathbf{x}i) at each point. The Lipschitz constant is approximated by the maximum gradient norm observed: \lambda \approx \maxi \|
abla f(\mathbf{x}i)\| In practice, a small safety margin (e.g., 1.05x) is often added to the maximum sampled norm to account for interpolation errors or un-sampled peaks, though the exact margin is not specified in the sources. 3. Manual Specification: If lipschitz is a float, that value is used directly as \lambda. Parameters: lipschitz: float or "auto". Default is often 1.0 or "auto" depending on the implementation. Edge Cases: Non-Lipschitz Functions: If f is not Lipschitz continuous (e.g., has infinite derivatives), the estimation will fail or produce unbounded results. Sparse Sampling: If sampling is too coarse, the estimated \lambda may be smaller than the true Lipschitz constant, leading to unsafe step sizes and missed surface intersections. Computes local bounds for hierarchical models. Uses gradient for linear step estimation. Time Complexity: O(N) where N is the number of sample points, if using sampling. O(1) if manually specified. Memory Complexity: O(1) auxiliary space. Strengths: Provides a single scalar bound usable by any inclusion strategy. Simple to implement. Limitations: Global estimation can be overly conservative, leading to small step sizes and slow convergence. Sampling may miss local maxima in the gradient norm. The concept of Lipschitz continuity is fundamental in numerical analysis and sphere tracing [Har96]. The specific formulation for procedural volumetric noise and hierarchical models is detailed in. The implementation in demonstrates its use in a Python-based ray tracer. head: Hierarchical Lipschitz Bound Computation, Tree-based Lipschitz Bound
body:
This method computes the local Lipschitz bound \lambda(\mathbf{e}) for a segment \mathbf{e} within a hierarchical construction tree of implicit primitives and operators. It solves the problem of determining safe stepping distances in enhanced sphere tracing (Segment Tracing) by providing a tight bound on the gradient magnitude, which allows for larger, safe steps along the ray compared to conservative global bounds. It is distinguished from its parent Lipschitz Constant Estimation by operating on the specific geometric structure of the implicit model (the construction tree) rather than sampling the bounding box, and from its children by handling general hierarchical operators (Boolean, blending, affine, deformation) rather than specific primitive types. Inputs: A hierarchical construction tree where leaves are compactly supported skeletal primitives and nodes are operators (Boolean, blending, affine, deformation). A ray segment \mathbf{e} defined by parameter interval [t, t+\epsilon], with center c and radius r = \|\mathbf{e}\|/2. The ray direction unit vector \mathbf{u}. Outputs: The local Lipschitz bound \lambda(\mathbf{e}) for the segment \mathbf{e}. Data Structures: Hierarchical Construction Tree: A tree structure where leaves are compactly supported skeletal primitives and internal nodes store operator types and pointers to child nodes. Method: The computation traverses the tree recursively. For a node, the bound is computed based on the operator type. If the primitive or deformation is complex, coarser bounds may be used. 1. Base Case (Leaf Primitive): Compute \lambda(\mathbf{e}) for the skeletal primitive using the product of two terms: \lambda(\mathbf{e}) \leq \|g' \circ d \circ \delta(\mathbf{e})\| \|
abla d \circ \delta(\mathbf{e}) \cdot \mathbf{u}\| where: g is the falloff filter function. d is the Euclidean distance to the skeleton. \delta(\mathbf{e}) represents the ray parameterization over the segment. \mathbf{u} is the ray direction unit vector. Falloff Bound (\|g' \circ d \circ \delta(\mathbf{e})\|): Compute the interval image of the distance d \circ \delta(\mathbf{e}). Approximate the distance interval using the 1-Lipschitz property of distance functions: d \circ \delta(\mathbf{e}) \subset [d(c) - r, d(c) + r] where c is the segment center and r = \|\mathbf{e}\|/2. Bound g' using Interval Analysis on this distance interval. Gradient Bound (\|
abla d \circ \delta(\mathbf{e}) \cdot \mathbf{u}\|): General Case: Use the bound 1, since \|
abla d\| = 1 for Euclidean distance to a skeleton (1-Lipschitz) and \|\mathbf{u}\|=1: \|
abla d \circ \delta(\mathbf{e}) \cdot \mathbf{u}\| \leq 1 Tighter Bound (Points, Spheres, Line Segments): Compute the closed-form image of 
abla d \circ \delta \cdot \mathbf{u} over the segment \mathbf{e}. For a point primitive with center c, 
abla d(p) = (p-c)/\|p-c\|. The image is the interval [|
abla d \circ \delta(t) \cdot \mathbf{u}|, |
abla d \circ \delta(t+\epsilon) \cdot \mathbf{u}|]. 2. Coarser Bounds (Complex Primitives/Deformations): If exact computation is difficult, use global bounds for the supporting ray \Delta or bounding sphere S \supset \mathbf{e}: \lambda(\mathbf{e}) \leq \lambda(\Delta) \quad 	ext{and} \quad \lambda(\mathbf{e}) \leq \lambda(S) where \lambda(\Delta) and \lambda(S) are the Lipschitz bounds of f over the entire ray and sphere respectively. 3. Internal Nodes (Operators): Compute bounds for children and combine based on operator type: Blending (Additive): f = fA + fB \lambda(\mathbf{e}) = \lambdaA(\mathbf{e}) + \lambdaB(\mathbf{e}) Boolean Union/Intersection (Max/Min): fU = \max(fA, fB), fI = \min(fA, fB) \lambda(\mathbf{e}) = \max(\lambdaA(\mathbf{e}), \lambdaB(\mathbf{e})) Pasko Union: fU = fA + fB + \sqrt{fA^2 + fB^2} \lambda(\mathbf{e}) = 2(\lambdaA(\mathbf{e}) + \lambdaB(\mathbf{e})) 4. Affine Transformations: Let fD = fN \circ a, where a is the affine transformation. Transform segment \mathbf{e} to \mathbf{e}' = a^{-1}(\mathbf{e}). For translation/rotation (1-Lipschitz): \lambdaD(\mathbf{e}) = \lambdaN(\mathbf{e}') For scaling by factor \alpha: \lambdaD(\mathbf{e}) =  rac{1}{\alpha} \lambdaN(\mathbf{e}') 5. Deformations: Let fW = fN \circ \omega^{-1}, where \omega is the warping function. The gradient is 
abla fW = 
abla fN \circ \omega^{-1} \cdot \mathbf{J}{\omega^{-1}}, where \mathbf{J}{\omega^{-1}} is the Jacobian matrix of the inverse warping function. Bound the Lipschitz constant by bounding the gradient norm and Jacobian norm: \|
abla fW\| \leq \|
abla fN \circ \omega^{-1}\| \|\mathbf{J}{\omega^{-1}}\| Compute two local bounds for the transformed segment \mathbf{e}' = \omega^{-1}(\mathbf{e}): 1. Bound of the norm of the gradient \|
abla fN \circ \omega^{-1}(\mathbf{e}')\|. 2. Bound of the norm of the Jacobian \|\mathbf{J}{\omega^{-1}}(\mathbf{e}')\|. Pseudocode: Unverified code. """ if node.isleaf(): return computeprimitivelipschitz(node.primitive, segmente, raydirectionu) operatortype = node.operatortype lambdaleft = computelipschitzbound(node.leftchild, segmente, raydirectionu) lambdaright = computelipschitzbound(node.rightchild, segmente, raydirectionu) if operatortype == "BLEND": return lambdaleft + lambdaright elif operatortype in ["BOOLEANUNION", "BOOLEANINTERSECTION"]: return max(lambdaleft, lambdaright) elif operatortype == "PASKOUNION": return 2 (lambdaleft + lambdaright) elif operatortype == "AFFINE": segmenteprime = node.affinetransform.inversetransform(segmente) childbound = computelipschitzbound(node.child, segmenteprime, raydirectionu) alpha = node.affinetransform.getscalingfactor() return childbound / alpha elif operatortype == "DEFORMATION": segmenteprime = node.warpingfunction.inversetransform(segmente) lambdagrad = computelipschitzbound(node.child, segmenteprime, raydirectionu) # Sources do not specify the exact Jacobian norm computation for arbitrary warping functions. lambdajacobian = computejacobiannormbound(node.warpingfunction, segmenteprime) return lambdagrad lambdajacobian else: # Fallback to coarser bounds if operator type is not explicitly handled # Sources do not specify the exact fallback mechanism. return 1.0 def computeprimitivelipschitz(primitive, segmente, raydirectionu): """ Computes the Lipschitz bound for a leaf skeletal primitive. lambda(e) <= ||g' o d o delta(e)|| ||grad(d) o delta(e). u|| """ # 1. Falloff Bound: ||g' o d o delta(e)|| dcenter = primitive.distance(segmente.center) r = segmente.radius distanceintervalmin = dcenter - r distanceintervalmax = dcenter + r # Standard interval arithmetic evaluation of the falloff derivative g' over the interval falloffbound = max(abs(primitive.gprime(distanceintervalmin)), abs(primitive.gprime(distanceintervalmax))) # 2. Gradient Bound: ||grad(d) o delta(e). u|| if primitive.type == "POINT": pstart = segmente.startpoint pend = segmente.endpoint graddotustart = abs(dot(primitive.gradient(pstart), raydirectionu)) graddotuend = abs(dot(primitive.gradient(pend), raydirectionu)) gradientbound = max(graddotustart, graddotuend) else: gradientbound = 1.0 return falloffbound gradientbound def computejacobiannormbound(warpingfunction, segmente): # Sources do not specify the exact Jacobian norm computation for arbitrary warping functions. return 1.0 Parameters: Typical falloff functions: Wyvill's C^1 sextic, Wyvill's C^2 sextic, C^1 quartic. Scaling factor \alpha for affine transformations. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Complex Primitives/Deformations: Exact computation of \lambda(\mathbf{e}) may be very complex. Use coarser bounds \lambda(\mathbf{e}) \leq \lambda(\Delta) and \lambda(\mathbf{e}) \leq \lambda(S) to ensure correctness and efficiency. Distance Interval Approximation: The approximation d \circ \delta(\mathbf{e}) \subset [d(c) - r, d(c) + r] relies on the 1-Lipschitz property of distance. This is valid but may be loose for complex skeletons. Gradient Bound Tightness: The general bound of 1 for \|
abla d \circ \delta \cdot \mathbf{u}\| is not accurate. Compute closed-form expressions for points, spheres, or line segments to obtain tighter bounds, especially when the ray is orthogonal to the gradient.
