name: Screen-Space Ray Tracing with Depth Buffer
head: SSRT, Single depth-buffer tracing
body: Screen-Space Ray Tracing with Depth Buffer (SSRT) traces rays in screen space against a depth buffer to find surface intersections, supporting up to four depth layers per pixel. It solves the problem of efficiently determining ray-surface intersections for effects like reflections, refractions, and ambient occlusion without traversing complex scene graphs or voxel structures. What sets it apart from Binary Search IsoSurface Extraction and Trilinear Isosurface Intersection is that it operates directly on the rendered depth buffer rather than a volumetric or implicit representation, allowing it to capture any geometry already present in the frame buffer. Unlike Ray Tracing which traverses acceleration structures, SSRT traverses the 2D screen grid, making it highly parallelizable on GPUs but limited to visible surfaces. Inputs and Outputs Inputs: csOrig: Camera-space ray origin (vec3). csDir: Camera-space ray direction (vec3). proj: Matrix projecting from camera-space position to pixel screen position (mat4x4). nearPlaneZ: Explicit negative near plane Z value (float). csZBuffer: The depth buffer (sampler2D). csZBufferSize: Dimensions of the depth buffer (vec2). csZBufferIsHyperbolic: Boolean flag indicating if the depth buffer uses hyperbolic encoding (bool). zThickness: Camera-space Z thickness ascribed to each point in the depth buffer (float). maxDistance: Maximum trace distance in camera-space (float). maxSteps: Maximum number of steps to trace (float/int). stride: Step size multiplier in screen space (float). jitter: Random value in [0,1] used to conceal banding (float). clipInfo: Information used for reconstructing camera-space Z from hyperbolic depth values (vec3). Outputs: hitPixel: Screen-space coordinates of the hit (out point2). hitLayer: Index of the hit layer in the depth buffer (out int). csHitPoint: Camera-space hit point (out point3). Return value: Boolean indicating if the hit pixel is within buffer bounds. Data Structures The method tracks up to four depth-buffer layers in sceneZMax at each pixel. If csZBufferIsHyperbolic is true, the buffer contains hyperbolically encoded depth values; otherwise, it is assumed to contain precomputed negative camera-space Z values for performance. Algorithm Steps 1. Clip to Near Plane: Calculate the ray length within the valid range. If the ray endpoint exceeds the near plane, clip it. \text{rayLength} = \begin{cases} \frac{\text{nearPlaneZ} - \text{csOrig}.z}{\text{csDir}.z} & \text{if } (\text{csOrig}.z + \text{csDir}.z \times \text{maxDistance}) > \text{nearPlaneZ} \\ \text{maxDistance} & \text{otherwise} \end{cases} Compute the clipped endpoint: \text{csEndPoint} = \text{csOrig} + \text{csDir} \times \text{rayLength}. 2. Project to Screen Space: Convert endpoints to homogeneous coordinates and then to screen space. H0 = \text{proj} \times \text{vec4}(\text{csOrig}, 1.0), \quad H1 = \text{proj} \times \text{vec4}(\text{csEndPoint}, 1.0) k0 = \frac{1.0}{H0.w}, \quad k1 = \frac{1.0}{H1.w} P0 = H0.xy \times k0, \quad P1 = H1.xy \times k1 Q0 = \text{csOrig} \times k0, \quad Q1 = \text{csEndPoint} \times k1 Here, P represents screen-space coordinates and Q represents camera-space coordinates scaled by 1/w. 3. Handle Single-Pixel Lines: Ensure the ray has a non-zero delta to avoid division by zero. P1 += \text{vec2}((\text{distanceSquared}(P0, P1) < 0.0001) ? 0.01: 0.0). 4. Determine Traversal Direction and Derivatives: Compute delta: \Delta = P1 - P0. If |\Delta.x| < |\Delta.y|, permute coordinates (swap x/y for P0, P1, \Delta) and set permute = true. Compute step direction and inverse delta x: \text{stepDir} = \text{sign}(\Delta.x), \quad \text{invdx} = \frac{\text{stepDir}}{\Delta.x} Compute derivatives per unit step in the dominant axis: dP = \text{vec2}(\text{stepDir}, \Delta.y \times \text{invdx}) \times \text{stride} dQ = (Q1 - Q0) \times \text{invdx} \times \text{stride} dk = (k1 - k0) \times \text{invdx} \times \text{stride}. 5. Apply Jitter: Bump the starting position to conceal banding artifacts caused by stride > 1. P0 += dP \times \text{jitter}, \quad Q0 += dQ \times \text{jitter}, \quad k0 += dk \times \text{jitter}. 6. Initialize Loop Variables: \text{prevZMaxEstimate} = \text{csOrig}.z Q = Q0, \quad k = k0, \quad \text{stepCount} = 0.0 \text{end} = P1.x \times \text{stepDir}. 7. Loop Over Pixels: Iterate while the ray is within bounds and steps remain. Condition: (P.x \times \text{stepDir}) \le \text{end} \land \text{stepCount} < \text{maxSteps} Update: P += dP, \quad Q.z += dQ.z, \quad k += dk, \quad \text{stepCount} += 1.0. 8. Inside Loop - Compute Ray Z Bounds: Compute ray Z bounds for the current step. The ray covers the interval [\text{rayZMin}, \text{rayZMax}]. \text{rayZMin} = \text{prevZMaxEstimate} \text{rayZMax} = \frac{dQ.z \times 0.5 + Q.z}{dk \times 0.5 + k} \text{prevZMaxEstimate} = \text{rayZMax} If \text{rayZMin} > \text{rayZMax}, swap them. 9. Inside Loop - Fetch Depth & Check Intersection: Determine hit pixel coordinates: \text{hitPixel} = \text{permute} ? P.yx: P. Fetch depth values: \text{sceneZMax} = \text{texelFetch}(\text{csZBuffer}, \text{int2}(\text{hitPixel}), 0). If csZBufferIsHyperbolic is true, reconstruct camera-space Z for each layer: \text{sceneZMax}[L] = \text{reconstructCSZ}(\text{sceneZMax}[L], \text{clipInfo}) \quad \text{for } L \in [0, 3]. Compute scene Z bounds: \text{sceneZMin} = \text{sceneZMax} - \text{zThickness}. Check for overlap with any layer L: If (\text{rayZMax} \ge \text{sceneZMin}[L] \land \text{rayZMin} \le \text{sceneZMax}[L]) \lor (\text{sceneZMax}[L] == 0), then a hit is found. Set hitLayer = L and break out of both loops. 10. Post-Loop - Compute Hit Point: Advance Q.xy based on steps taken: Q.xy += dQ.xy \times \text{stepCount} Compute final hit point: \text{hitPoint} = Q \times \frac{1.0}{k}. 11. Return Result: Check if hitPixel is within buffer bounds: \text{return all}(\text{lessThanEqual}(|\text{hitPixel} - (\text{csZBufferSize} \times 0.5)|, \text{csZBufferSize} \times 0.5)). Pseudocode Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. class Vec2: def init(self, x, y): self.x, self.y = x, y def add(self, o): return Vec2(self.x + o.x, self.y + o.y) def sub(self, o): return Vec2(self.x - o.x, self.y - o.y) def mul(self, s): return Vec2(self.x s, self.y s) def truediv(self, s): return Vec2(self.x / s, self.y / s) def abs(self): return Vec2(abs(self.x), abs(self.y)) @property def yx(self): return Vec2(self.y, self.x) @property def xy(self): return Vec2(self.x, self.y) class Vec3: def init(self, x, y, z): self.x, self.y, self.z = x, y, z def add(self, o): return Vec3(self.x + o.x, self.y + o.y, self.z + o.z) def sub(self, o): return Vec3(self.x - o.x, self.y - o.y, self.z - o.z) def mul(self, s): return Vec3(self.x s, self.y s, self.z s) def truediv(self, s): return Vec3(self.x / s, self.y / s, self.z / s) @property def xy(self): return Vec2(self.x, self.y) @xy.setter def xy(self, v): self.x, self.y = v.x, v.y class Vec4: def init(self, x, y, z, w): self.x, self.y, self.z, self.w = x, y, z, w def add(self, o): return Vec4(self.x + o.x, self.y + o.y, self.z + o.z, self.w + o.w) def sub(self, o): return Vec4(self.x - o.x, self.y - o.y, self.z - o.z, self.w - o.w) def mul(self, s): return Vec4(self.x s, self.y s, self.z s, self.w s) def tracescreenspaceray(csOrig, csDir, proj, csZBuffer, csZBufferSize, zThickness, csZBufferIsHyperbolic, clipInfo, nearPlaneZ, stride, jitter, maxSteps, maxDistance): def distancesquared(a, b): return (a.x - b.x)2 + (a.y - b.y)2 def int2(v): return (int(v.x), int(v.y)) def swap(a, b): return b, a def texelfetch(tex, coord, level): return [0.0, 0.0, 0.0, 0.0] # Placeholder for texture fetch def reconstructcsz(depth, clipInfo): # Formula for reconstructing camera-space Z from hyperbolic depth not provided in sources return depth # 1. Clip to near plane if (csOrig.z + csDir.z maxDistance) > nearPlaneZ: rayLength = (nearPlaneZ - csOrig.z) / csDir.z else: rayLength = maxDistance csEndPoint = csOrig + csDir rayLength # 2. Project to screen space H0 = proj Vec4(csOrig.x, csOrig.y, csOrig.z, 1.0) H1 = proj Vec4(csEndPoint.x, csEndPoint.y, csEndPoint.z, 1.0) k0 = 1.0 / H0.w k1 = 1.0 / H1.w Q0 = Vec3(csOrig.x k0, csOrig.y k0, csOrig.z k0) Q1 = Vec3(csEndPoint.x k1, csEndPoint.y k1, csEndPoint.z k1) P0 = Vec2(H0.x k0, H0.y k0) P1 = Vec2(H1.x k1, H1.y k1) # 3. Handle single-pixel lines if distancesquared(P0, P1) < 0.0001: P1 = P1 + Vec2(0.01) delta = P1 - P0 permute = False if abs(delta.x) < abs(delta.y): permute = True delta = delta.yx P0 = P0.yx P1 = P1.yx stepDir = 1.0 if delta.x > 0 else (-1.0 if delta.x < 0 else 0.0) invdx = stepDir / delta.x dP = Vec2(stepDir, delta.y invdx) stride dQ = (Q1 - Q0) invdx stride dk = (k1 - k0) invdx stride # 4. Apply jitter P0 = P0 + dP jitter Q0 = Q0 + dQ jitter k0 = k0 + dk jitter # 5. Initialize loop variables prevZMaxEstimate = csOrig.z Q = Q0 k = k0 stepCount = 0.0 end = P1.x stepDir hitPixel = Vec2(-1, -1) hitLayer = -1 csHitPoint = Vec3(0, 0, 0) # 6. Loop over pixels P = P0 while (P.x stepDir) <= end and stepCount < maxSteps: # Compute ray Z bounds rayZMin = prevZMaxEstimate rayZMax = (dQ.z 0.5 + Q.z) / (dk 0.5 + k) prevZMaxEstimate = rayZMax if rayZMin > rayZMax: rayZMin, rayZMax = swap(rayZMin, rayZMax) # Determine hit pixel hitPixel = P.yx if permute else P # Fetch depth buffer sceneZMax = texelfetch(csZBuffer, int2(hitPixel), 0) if csZBufferIsHyperbolic: for layer in range(4): sceneZMax[layer] = reconstructcsz(sceneZMax[layer], clipInfo) # Check intersection sceneZMin = [sceneZMax[i] - zThickness for i in range(4)] hitfound = False for L in range(4): if (rayZMax >= sceneZMin[L] and rayZMin <= sceneZMax[L]) or (sceneZMax[L] == 0): hitLayer = L hitfound = True break if hitfound: break # Update loop variables P = P + dP Q.z = Q.z + dQ.z k = k + dk stepCount = stepCount + 1.0 # 7. Post-Loop - Compute Hit Point Q.xy = Q.xy + dQ.xy stepCount csHitPoint = Vec3(Q.x (1.0 / k), Q.y (1.0 / k), Q.z (1.0 / k)) # 8. Return Result boundscheck = all(abs(hitPixel.x - (csZBufferSize.x 0.5)) <= (csZBufferSize.x 0.5)) and all(abs(hitPixel.y - (csZBufferSize.y 0.5)) <= (csZBufferSize.y 0.5)) return boundscheck, hitPixel, hitLayer, csHitPoint Edge Cases and Pitfalls Division by Zero: Avoided because the ray is clipped to the near plane (no w=0 singularity) and delta.x is guaranteed non-zero for single-pixel lines. Coordinate System: The method assumes pixel (0,0) is the upper-left corner. To switch to lower-left, modify the final hit point by hitPoint.y = csZBufferSize.y - hitPoint.y. Performance: Converting hyperbolic depth values per iteration is expensive. It is preferred to use a floating-point buffer of precomputed negative camera-space values. Miss Handling: Rays that miss the depth buffer (travel farther than maxDistance or towards the camera) require a fallback strategy, such as sparse voxels or environment cube maps. Time and Memory Complexity The time complexity is linear with respect to the number of iterations before a hit is encountered or the maxDistance is reached. The method tracks up to four depth-buffer layers in sceneZMax at each pixel. Measured Performance At 1920x1080 resolution, casting a diagonal ray for 25 iterations per pixel costs 1.2 ms on an NVIDIA GeForce Titan and 6.4 ms on a MacBook NVIDIA GeForce 650M. Ambient occlusion and radiosity examples, which cast 25 rays per pixel, spend about 30 ms on ray casts, making them not viable for real-time pipelines with other tasks. Scaling Performance scales linearly with resolution and the number of rays per pixel. Using stride > 1 reduces the number of samples, improving performance at the cost of quality. Strengths and Limitations Strengths: Efficient for single-ray-per-pixel effects like reflections and refractions. Captures any geometry present in the depth buffer without additional scene traversal. Limitations: Limited to visible surfaces. High ray counts (e.g., for global illumination) are too slow for real-time. Stride > 1 introduces banding artifacts. When to Use Use for reflection and refraction (one ray cast per pixel) where real-time performance is critical. Not recommended for ambient occlusion or radiosity if other graphics tasks are present. Origin The method was introduced in the paper "Efficient GPU screen-space ray tracing". It is a feature of the G3D Innovation Engine. History and Development The technique has been used in commercial games such as Killzone: Shadow Fall for reflections and volumetrics. It was presented at SIGGRAPH Advances in Real-Time Rendering in Games course. Usage It is used for reflection and refraction (one ray cast per pixel) and ambient occlusion/radiosity (25 rays per pixel). Efficient GPU screen-space ray tracing, https://jcgt.org/published/0003/04/04/paper.pdf, fetched 2026-10-25 (unofficial)

name: Parabolic Ray Tracing in Heterogeneous Media
head: Non-linear ray tracing, Piecewise polynomial ray tracing
body: Parabolic Ray Tracing is a method for computing light ray trajectories in media with spatially varying Refractive Index Fields (RIF) by approximating the RIF such that ray paths are second-order polynomials within tetrahedral cells. It solves the problem of exact intersection computation with cell boundaries, which is difficult when ray trajectories involve transcendental functions, by reducing the intersection problem to solving quadratic equations. It differs from linear ray tracing methods by accounting for continuous curvature within cells, and from general non-linear solvers by providing closed-form analytical solutions for the trajectory. Inputs: A tetrahedral mesh defining the spatial domain. A Refractive Index Field (RIF) \eta(\mathbf{x}) defined per cell. A ray origin \mathbf{x}0 and initial direction \mathbf{p}0 satisfying the Eikonal equation. Outputs: The trajectory of the ray as it traverses the medium. Intersection points with cell boundaries. Data Structures: Cell Coefficients: For each tetrahedral cell, the squared RIF is defined as a linear function: \eta^2(\mathbf{x}) = A0 + A1 \mathbf{x}x + A2 \mathbf{x}y + A3 \mathbf{x}z = A0 + \boldsymbol{\gamma} \cdot \mathbf{x} where \boldsymbol{\gamma} = [A1, A2, A3]^T is the constant gradient of the squared RIF, and A0 is a scalar offset. Ray State: Position \mathbf{x}(\tau) and direction \mathbf{p}(\tau) at parameter \tau. Algorithm Steps: 1. Initialize Ray State: Set initial position \mathbf{x}0 and initial direction \mathbf{p}0. Ensure \|\mathbf{p}0\| = \eta(\mathbf{x}0). 2. Determine Current Cell: Identify the tetrahedral cell containing the current ray position \mathbf{x}(\tau). 3. Compute Cell Coefficients: Calculate \boldsymbol{\gamma} and A0 for the current cell based on the RIF definition. 4. Compute Ray Trajectory within Cell: The ray trajectory \mathbf{x}(\tau) and direction \mathbf{p}(\tau) are second-order polynomials in the parameter \tau: \mathbf{x}(\tau) = \frac{1}{4}\boldsymbol{\gamma} \tau^2 + \mathbf{p}0\tau + \mathbf{x}0 \mathbf{p}(\tau) = \frac{1}{2}\boldsymbol{\gamma} \tau + \mathbf{p}0 where \tau is a parameter related to arc length s by ds = \eta d\tau. 5. Intersect with Cell Boundary: Solve for the intersection of the parabolic ray subsection with the cell boundary. This is done by solving a quadratic equation exactly. Let the cell boundary be defined by a plane equation \mathbf{n} \cdot \mathbf{x} + d = 0. Substitute \mathbf{x}(\tau) into the plane equation: \mathbf{n} \cdot \left( \frac{1}{4}\boldsymbol{\gamma} \tau^2 + \mathbf{p}0\tau + \mathbf{x}0 \right) + d = 0 Rearrange into standard quadratic form a\tau^2 + b\tau + c = 0: a = \frac{1}{4} (\mathbf{n} \cdot \boldsymbol{\gamma}) b = \mathbf{n} \cdot \mathbf{p}0 c = \mathbf{n} \cdot \mathbf{x}0 + d Solve for \tau using the quadratic formula. Select the smallest positive \tau that corresponds to the exit point from the current cell. 6. Update Ray State: Update position: \mathbf{x}{new} = \mathbf{x}(\tau{exit}). Update direction: \mathbf{p}{new} = \mathbf{p}(\tau{exit}). Reset \tau to 0 for the next cell, adjusting \mathbf{x}0 and \mathbf{p}0 accordingly. 7. Repeat: Repeat steps 2-6 until the ray exits the medium or reaches a termination condition. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def solvequadratic(a, b, c): """Solve ax^2 + bx + c = 0. Returns smallest positive root or None.""" if a == 0: if b == 0: return None root = -c / b return root if root > 0 else None discriminant = b b - 4 a c if discriminant < 0: return None sqrtdisc = math.sqrt(discriminant) root1 = (-b - sqrtdisc) / (2 a) root2 = (-b + sqrtdisc) / (2 a) roots = [r for r in [root1, root2] if r > 0] return min(roots) if roots else None def parabolicraytrace(rayorigin, raydirection, tetmesh, riffunction): """ Trace a ray through a tetrahedral mesh with a piecewise linear squared RIF. Args: rayorigin: Initial position x0. raydirection: Initial direction p0. tetmesh: List of tetrahedra, each with vertices and plane equations for faces. riffunction: Function returning (gamma, A0) for a given position. Returns: List of intersection points. """ x = rayorigin p = raydirection intersections = [] # Ensure initial direction satisfies Eikonal equation # pnorm = norm(p) # etax0 = riffunction(x)[1] # A0 is not eta, need to compute eta from A0 + gamma.x # etax0 = math.sqrt(A0 + dot(gamma, x)) # p = p (etax0 / pnorm) # Normalize to match eta currenttet = findtetrahedroncontainingpoint(tetmesh, x) while currenttet is not None: gamma, A0 = riffunction(x) # Get coefficients for current cell # Find exit point from current tetrahedron mintau = float('inf') exitface = None for face in currenttet.faces: # Plane equation: n. x + d = 0 n = face.normal d = -dot(n, face.vertices[0]) # Coefficients for quadratic equation a = 0.25 dot(n, gamma) b = dot(n, p) c = dot(n, x) + d tau = solvequadratic(a, b, c) if tau is not None and tau < mintau: mintau = tau exitface = face if mintau == float('inf'): # Ray stays within tetrahedron (should not happen in convex mesh) break # Compute exit position and direction exitx = 0.25 gamma (mintau 2) + p mintau + x exitp = 0.5 gamma mintau + p intersections.append(exitx) # Update state for next cell x = exitx p = exitp # Find next tetrahedron currenttet = findadjacenttetrahedron(tetmesh, currenttet, exitface) return intersections Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision: Solving the quadratic equation exactly is crucial for boundary intersection accuracy. Eikonal Equation: The initial direction must satisfy \|\mathbf{p}0\| = \eta(\mathbf{x}0) to ensure physical correctness. Degenerate Input: If the ray is tangent to a cell boundary, the quadratic equation may have a double root or no positive root, requiring careful handling. Time Complexity: Linear in the number of cells traversed, with constant time per cell for intersection computation (solving a quadratic equation). Memory Complexity: Linear in the size of the tetrahedral mesh and RIF data. Strengths: Exact intersection computation with cell boundaries; analytical solutions for ray trajectories within cells. Limitations: Limited to media where the squared RIF can be approximated as a linear function within tetrahedral cells; may require fine mesh resolution for accurate RIF representation. When to Use: When accurate ray tracing in heterogeneous media with smooth refractive index variations is required, and the medium can be discretized into tetrahedral cells with linear squared RIF profiles. When Not to Use: When the RIF varies rapidly or non-linearly within cells, or when the medium is not naturally represented as a tetrahedral mesh. Parabolic Ray Tracing was introduced in the context of seismic wave propagation, where Virieux and Farra demonstrated that a well-chosen expression for the slowness profile within tetrahedral cells yields simple second-order polynomial solutions for ray trajectories. This approach was later adapted for computer graphics to model light propagation in heterogeneous media, such as old glass, by assembling multiple tetrahedral cells and tracing piecewise polynomial rays. It generalizes the concept of ray differentials used in computer graphics for building two-point tracing methods. Parabolic Sphere Tracing of Signed Distance Fields for Old Glass Modelling and Rendering, https://doi.org/10.1109/tvcg.2025.3613853, fetched 2026-11-05

name: Surface Area Heuristic (SAH)
head: Crofton’s Theorem based cost model, Surface Area Heuristic (SAH) / Crofton’s Theorem
body: The Surface Area Heuristic (SAH) is a cost model used to determine the optimal partitioning of primitives in Bounding Volume Hierarchy (BVH) construction, both for top-down recursive splitting and iterative insertion. It minimizes the estimated ray tracing cost by leveraging the probability that a ray intersects a bounding volume, which is proportional to its surface area. It sets itself apart from sibling methods like Binary Search IsoSurface Extraction or Trilinear Isosurface Intersection by operating on the acceleration structure's topology rather than the geometric intersection logic itself, providing a general framework for spatial partitioning efficiency. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A set of primitives P (e.g., triangles) enclosed in a parent Bounding Volume B with surface area Area(B). Output: A partition of P into subsets B1 and B2 (and potentially more) that minimizes the SAH cost function, or the decision to attach a primitive directly to the current node in iterative insertion. Data Structures: Bounding Volume (BV): Typically an Axis-Aligned Bounding Box (AABB) or Oriented Bounding Box (OBB). The layout includes minimum and maximum coordinates defining the volume. The surface area is calculated from these extents. Primitive Set: A list of primitives associated with each node. Core Formula: The cost C(B) of a node containing a set of polygons B is estimated by the weighted sum of the surface areas of its children multiplied by the number of primitives they contain: C(B) = \min{B1 \subseteq P(B)} \left[ Area(B1) \cdot N(B1) + Area(B2) \cdot N(B2) \right] Where: B is the set of polygons in the parent BV. B1 and B2 are the subsets of primitives assigned to the left and right children, respectively. Area(Bi) is the surface area of the bounding volume enclosing subset Bi. N(Bi) is the number of primitives in subset Bi. Theoretical Basis: The heuristic relies on Crofton’s Theorem, which states that for a convex body, the total number of rays hitting an object is proportional to its surface area. Consequently, the probability of a ray hitting an object completely inside a cell is proportional to the object's surface area relative to the cell's properties. The cost model assumes that the traversal cost is proportional to the surface area of the bounding volumes tested. Algorithm Steps: 1. Bounding Volume Calculation: Calculate the bounding volume for the given set of objects. 2. Partitioning (Top-Down): Partition the set of objects into two (or more) subsets. Calculate the bounding volumes for each subset. Compute the cost C(B) for the partition using the formula above. Seek the optimal split that minimizes this cost. Note: Exhaustively searching all possible partitions is not practical. Heuristic approaches, such as representing objects by their centroids, determining the axis of largest extent, sorting points along this axis, and using a plane-sweep to find the minimum cost split, are typically employed. 3. Recursive Construction: Recursively construct BVHs for each subset. 4. Iterative Insertion (Goldsmith/Salmon): For each new object, propagate it into the subtree that causes the smallest cost increase for ray tracing. Tie-Breaking: If both subtrees cause equal costs (e.g., 0), use a secondary heuristic, such as the number of triangles in the subtree. Non-Binary Fallback: If all subtrees cause too high costs (e.g., area increase reaches 90% of the parent's area), attach the object as a direct child of the current node, allowing for non-binary BVHs. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def calculatesahcost(subsetprimitives, boundingvolume): """ Calculates the SAH cost for a node. Note: The formula in defines the cost of the split (children). Here we assume the cost contribution of a node is proportional to Area(BV) NumPrimitives, which is minimized by the split choice. """ area = boundingvolume.surfacearea() numprims = len(subsetprimitives) return area numprims def findoptimalsplittopdown(primitives, parentbv): """ Finds the split that minimizes SAH cost for top-down construction. Uses a heuristic plane-sweep approach as exhaustive search is impractical. """ # 1. Represent objects by centroids centroids = [p.centroid() for p in primitives] # 2. Determine axis of largest extent extent = parentbv.extent() axis = argmax(extent) # 3. Sort points along this axis sortedindices = sortindicesbyaxis(centroids, axis) # 4. Plane-sweep to find minimum cost mincost = infinity bestsplitindex = -1 # Initialize left and right subsets leftprims = [] rightprims = primitives # Initially all in right # Calculate initial right BV and cost rightbv = computeboundingvolume(rightprims) currentrightcost = calculatesahcost(rightprims, rightbv) for i in range(len(primitives) - 1): # Split between i and i+1 # Move primitive i from right to left prim = primitives[sortedindices[i]] leftprims.append(prim) rightprims.remove(prim) # Update bounding volumes leftbv = computeboundingvolume(leftprims) rightbv = computeboundingvolume(rightprims) # Calculate split cost cost = calculatesahcost(leftprims, leftbv) + calculatesahcost(rightprims, rightbv) if cost < mincost: mincost = cost bestsplitindex = i return bestsplitindex, leftprims, rightprims def insertiterative(node, primitive): """ Inserts a primitive into an existing BVH using SAH for iterative insertion. """ # Calculate cost increase for inserting into each child costincreases = [] for child in node.children: # Estimate new BV if primitive is added newbv = computeboundingvolume(child.primitives + [primitive]) oldcost = calculatesahcost(child.primitives, child.bv) newcost = calculatesahcost(child.primitives + [primitive], newbv) costincrease = newcost - oldcost costincreases.append((child, costincrease)) # Find child with smallest cost increase bestchild, minincrease = min(costincreases, key=lambda x: x[1]) # Check for high cost increase (fallback to non-binary) # Threshold: area increase to 90% of parent's area parentarea = node.bv.surfacearea() newbvarea = computeboundingvolume(bestchild.primitives + [primitive]).surfacearea() if newbvarea > 0.9 parentarea: # Attach as direct child of current node node.children.append(Node([primitive])) return # Recursively insert into best child insertiterative(bestchild, primitive) Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Exhaustive Search: Finding the true global minimum split is computationally expensive and not practical. Heuristics like plane-sweep on sorted centroids are necessary. Non-Binary Trees: The heuristic allows for non-binary BVHs if the cost of splitting is too high (e.g., >90% area increase). Tie-Breaking: Equal costs require a secondary heuristic, such as primitive count. A cost model for ray intersection with a subset of the scene enclosed in a Bounding Volume (BV), used to evaluate the trade-off between BV simplicity and compactness. The total cost T is defined as T = n \cdot B + m \cdot I, where n is the number of rays tested against the BV, B is the cost for one ray-BV intersection test, m is the number of rays that actually intersect the BV, and I is the cost for testing the objects in the BV. The goal is to minimize T. Simple BVs (e.g., sphere or box) have small intersection costs B but usually result in a large number of ray hits m, while compact BVs (e.g., exact convex hull) have small m but high intersection costs B. Time Complexity: The cost calculation for a single split is O(N) where N is the number of primitives, assuming bounding volume updates are efficient. Finding the optimal split via plane-sweep is O(N \log N) due to sorting. Memory Complexity: Depends on the BVH structure; typically O(N) for N primitives. Strengths: Provides a robust, geometry-independent metric for balancing the BVH tree, leading to efficient ray traversal. It effectively balances the number of nodes visited against the cost of intersection tests. Limitations: The heuristic assumes uniform ray distribution and may not be optimal for all scene types or ray distributions. Exhaustive optimization is impractical. When to use: Standard choice for BVH construction in ray tracers. When not to use: When scene-specific heuristics (e.g., density-based) are known to be more accurate, or when build time is extremely constrained and simpler splits are acceptable. The Surface Area Heuristic is based on Crofton’s Theorem, which relates the number of rays hitting an object to its surface area. It was popularized in the context of BVH construction by Goldsmith and Salmon for iterative insertion and is widely used in top-down construction methods. It addresses the problem of efficiently organizing primitives for ray tracing by minimizing the expected number of intersection tests. name: Ray Occlusion Test
head: hitSomething, hitSomething8, rtcOccluded1, rtcOccluded8
body: The Ray Occlusion Test determines whether a ray intersects any geometry within a specified distance range, returning only a binary result rather than detailed intersection data. Inputs and Outputs Input: Ray origin \mathbf{o}, ray direction \mathbf{d}, minimum distance t{near}, maximum distance t{far} (typically infinity), and an acceleration structure context. Output: Boolean indicating if any geometry was intersected within [t{near}, t{far}]. Data Structures The method uses a ray structure (e.g., RTCRay or RTCRay8) containing: origin: 3D vector (x, y, z) direction: 3D vector (x, y, z), typically normalized. tnear: float, minimum intersection distance. tfar: float, maximum intersection distance; modified by the kernel to a negative value on hit. Steps 1. Initialize the ray structure with origin \mathbf{o} and direction \mathbf{d}. 2. Set t{near} to the specified minimum distance. 3. Set t{far} to the maximum valid distance (typically infinity). 4. Initialize the acceleration structure context if not already done. 5. Invoke the occlusion query function (rtcOccluded1 for single rays or rtcOccluded8 for batched rays). 6. Return true if an intersection occurred within the range, false otherwise. Pseudocode Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def rayocclusiontest(origin, direction, mindist, maxdist, context): # Initialize ray structure ray = {'origin': origin, 'direction': direction, 'tnear': mindist, 'tfar': maxdist} # Initialize context if not already done if context is None: context = {} # # Call rtcOccluded1 or rtcOccluded8 # Standard ray tracing kernel call to update ray state # ray.tfar is set to a negative value if an intersection occurs # Acceleration structure traversal logic is not provided in the sources ray['tfar'] = queryaccelerationstructure(ray, context) # Return result based on intersection status return ray['tfar'] < 0.0 Parameters mindist: Minimum ray distance for intersection. Edge Cases If t{near} > t{far}, the test should return false immediately. Degenerate rays (zero-length direction) should be handled or rejected. An optimized variant using pre-generated sampling masks to efficiently update occlusion values along a ray direction, designed to accelerate local density averages in 3D volumes. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Not given in the sources. Limitations: Not given in the sources. When to use: Not given in the sources. When not to use: Not given in the sources. The method is commonly associated with the Embree ray tracing kernel, which provides rtcOccluded1 and rtcOccluded8 functions for efficient occlusion queries. whu-lyh/flod, https://github.com/whu-lyh/flod, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial)

name: Ray-cast Occlusion with Sampling Masks
head: Slab-based Occlusion Accumulation, VolumeManager::calcOcclusion, VolumeManager::initSlice, calcOcclusion, initSlice
body: Ray-cast Occlusion with Sampling Masks is an optimized method for calculating volume occlusion values by using pre-generated sampling masks to efficiently update occlusion values along a ray direction, rather than re-sampling the entire sphere for each voxel. It builds on Ray Occlusion Test by providing the actual occlusion intensity values required for ray casting, specifically designed to accelerate the computation of local density averages in 3D volumes. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A 3D volume data structure (mvolume), a sampling radius (rad or radius), pre-computed sampling masks (idxadd and idxremove), and a direction vector (dir) with step increment (stepInc). Output: An occlusion value for each voxel, stored in mocclusion. Data Structures: mvolume: The 3D volume grid, accessed via getVoxel(mvolume, pos). idxadd and idxremove: osg::Vec3Array objects containing offset vectors for voxels entering and leaving the sampling sphere as the ray progresses. occprev: An array storing the occlusion value for the previous slice along the primary accumulation axis (e.g., y-slice or x-slice). addprev, subtprev: Accumulators for the net voxel intensity entering and leaving the sampling window along the secondary axes. msphereSamples: The count of voxels actually inside the sampling sphere. Formulas: Total voxels in cubic bounding box: w = (2 \cdot rad + 1)^3. Net difference in intensity: diff = \frac{add - rem}{m\sphereSamples}. The source specifies dividing by w in intermediate slab-based updates, but the final formula section specifies dividing by m\sphereSamples (the actual voxel count inside the sphere). Parameters: rad: The radius of the spherical sampling kernel, determining the window size for occlusion calculation. radius: The radius of the sampling sphere. dir: The direction vector of the ray along which occlusion is accumulated. stepInc: The starting coordinate offset for the ray. Steps: The method typically involves initialization and incremental updates using masks. The implementation iterates through volume dimensions z from 0 to mvolume->r(), x from 0 to mvolume->s(), and y from 0 to mvolume->t(). 1. Initialization: Initialize occprev[y] to store occlusion for the previous y-slice. Initialize addprev and subtprev to 0. For the base case (x=0, y=0), compute the full occlusion for the first voxel by summing all voxels in the sphere centered at pos. Store this in occprev[0] and set mocclusion for that voxel. This step also sets msphereSamples. 2. First Column Update (x=0, y>0): Calculate the difference between voxels entering the sphere at the top (y+rad) and leaving at the bottom (y-rad) along the y-axis. Sum these into temporary accumulators add and subt. Compute diff = \frac{add - subt}{w}. Update occlusion: occ = diff + occprev[y-1]. Store result in occprev[y] and set mocclusion voxel. 3. First Row Reset (y=0, x>0): Reset addprev and subtprev to 0. Calculate the difference between voxels entering at the right (x+rad) and leaving at the left (x-rad) along the x-axis for the current z-slice. This prepares the accumulators for the main loop. 4. Main Loop Update (x>0, y>0): Update addprev by adding voxels entering at x+rad and subtracting voxels leaving at x-rad for each z in [-rad, rad]. Update subtprev similarly. This effectively slides the sampling window along the x-axis. Compute final occlusion for current voxel: diff = \frac{addprev - subtprev}{w}. occ = occprev[y] + diff. Set mocclusion voxel and update occprev[y] for the next y iteration. 5. Alternative Mask-Based Update: For each voxel at pos (iterating y from 0 to t(), x from 0 to s()): Base case (x=0): Compute initial occlusion using getOcclusion(pos, radius). Set mocclusion and store in occold. Update case (x>0): Define prev position as (x-1, y, stepInc). Initialize add=0, rem=0. Subtract old voxels: Iterate through remmask (equivalent to idxremove). For each offset, calculate tmp = prev + offset. Add getVoxel(mvolume, tmp) to rem. Add new voxels: Iterate through addmask (equivalent to idxadd). For each offset, calculate tmp = pos + offset. Add getVoxel(mvolume, tmp) to add. Compute diff = \frac{add - rem}{m\sphereSamples}. Update occlusion based on previous value. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def computeocclusionmasks(volume, radius, idxadd, idxremove, stepinc): occprev = [0.0] volume.t() addprev = 0.0 subtprev = 0.0 mspheresamples = 0 occold = 0.0 for z in range(volume.r()): for x in range(volume.s()): for y in range(volume.t()): pos = (x, y, z) # Base case: first voxel if x == 0 and y == 0: occold = getocclusion(pos, radius, volume) occprev[0] = occold volume.setocclusion(pos, occold) continue # Alternative mask-based update (simplified view from source) if x == 0: occold = getocclusion(pos, radius, volume) volume.setocclusion(pos, occold) continue # Update case (x > 0) prevpos = (x - 1, y, stepinc) addval = 0.0 remval = 0.0 # Subtract old voxels for offset in idxremove: tmp = (prevpos[0] + offset.x, prevpos[1] + offset.y, prevpos[2] + offset.z) remval += volume.getvoxel(tmp) # Add new voxels for offset in idxadd: tmp = (pos[0] + offset.x, pos[1] + offset.y, pos[2] + offset.z) addval += volume.getvoxel(tmp) # Compute difference and update occlusion diff = (addval - remval) / mspheresamples occ = occold + diff volume.setocclusion(pos, occ) occold = occ Pitfalls: Boundary Conditions: Specific if/else branches are required for x=0 and y=0 to handle the initialization of the sliding window accumulators correctly, preventing out-of-bounds access or incorrect accumulation logic. Normalization: msphereSamples is set by getOcclusion and represents the number of voxels in the sampling sphere, used as the divisor for the difference calculation. A method to calculate occlusion values for a volume, serving as the base case for the incremental mask-based method. It computes the average intensity of all voxels within a sphere of radius rad centered at pos. Definition: Computes res by iterating through a cube bounding the sphere (x, y, z from -rad to rad), incrementing msphereSamples for each valid voxel inside the sphere, and summing their values. Returns res / msphereSamples. Parameters: radius (sphere radius), dir (direction vector for sampling in calcOcclusion), stepInc (step increment, default 1). Usage: Implemented in VolumeManager.cpp, used by the VolumeManager singleton to provide occlusion data for the ray casting renderer and to initialize values for the faster mask-based method. Not given in the sources. The method originates from the volume-occlusion-editor project by MPanknin. It is designed to support ray casting renderers by providing efficient local density estimates. MPanknin/volume-occlusion-editor, https://github.com/MPanknin/volume-occlusion-editor, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial)

name: Point-Plane Reflection
head: Reflect Point Across Plane, Space Reflection
body: Point-Plane Reflection computes the mirror image of a point \mathbf{p} across a plane defined by a normal vector \mathbf{n} and a scalar offset c. It serves as a fundamental geometric primitive for ray-primitive intersection, specifically for determining specular reflection directions or mirroring geometry in volumetric and differentiable rendering contexts. It is distinct from Mirror, which applies this reflection operation to entire volumetric datasets for symmetry filling, whereas Point-Plane Reflection operates on individual geometric entities. Inputs and Outputs Input: Point \mathbf{p} \in \mathbb{R}^3, plane normal \mathbf{n} \in \mathbb{R}^3, plane offset c \in \mathbb{R}. Output: Modified point \mathbf{p}' (the reflected point) and a signed distance indicator s = \text{sign}(t). Data Structures \mathbf{p}: 3-component floating-point vector. \mathbf{n}: 3-component floating-point vector. c: Single floating-point scalar. t: Single floating-point scalar representing the signed distance. Steps 1. Compute the signed distance t from the point to the plane using the dot product and offset: t = \mathbf{p} \cdot \mathbf{n} + c 2. Check if the point lies on the negative side of the plane relative to the normal. If t < 0: Reflect the point across the plane by subtracting twice the signed distance along the normal: \mathbf{p} \leftarrow \mathbf{p} - 2t\mathbf{n} 3. Return the sign of t: s = \text{sign}(t) where \text{sign}(t) is -1 if t < 0, 0 if t = 0, and 1 if t > 0. Pseudocode Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def pointplanereflection(p, n, c): # Step 1: Compute signed distance t t = p[0]n[0] + p[1]n[1] + p[2]n[2] + c # Step 2: Reflect if t < 0 if t < 0: p[0] = p[0] - 2.0 t n[0] p[1] = p[1] - 2.0 t n[1] p[2] = p[2] - 2.0 t n[2] # Step 3: Return sign of t signt = -1 if t < 0 else (1 if t > 0 else 0) return p, signt Parameters Normalization of \mathbf{n}: The formula assumes \mathbf{n} is a unit vector. If \mathbf{n} is not normalized, the offset c and the distance t are scaled by \|\mathbf{n}\|, and the reflection vector 2t\mathbf{n} becomes geometrically incorrect unless \mathbf{n} is normalized first. Edge Cases and Pitfalls Non-normalized Normal: If \mathbf{n} is not normalized, the reflection is geometrically incorrect. Precision: For points very close to the plane (t \approx 0), floating-point errors may cause oscillation if this operation is repeated iteratively. Degenerate Input: If \mathbf{n} is the zero vector, the plane is undefined. The Mirror method is a volumetric filling tool that copies content from a source region to a target region across a user-defined reflection plane. It is designed to exploit symmetry in structures, such as the human body or head, by allowing users to interactively define a plane that divides the volume into two parts. Unlike the parent Point-Plane Reflection which reflects a single point, Mirror operates on volumetric data, copying material values from one side of the plane to the other. The Image Method for Specular Reflection is a geometric technique to determine the specular hit point and path length by mirroring the receiver (or source) across the reflecting surface, converting the broken path into a straight line. It provides a deterministic, closed-form solution for the hit point and angles without iterative optimization, unlike angle search methods. Formula The path length \ell(h) is given by: \ell(h) = \sqrt{\Delta x^2 + (2h - yS - yR)^2} where h is the wall height, yS and yR are source and receiver y-coordinates, and \Delta x is the horizontal distance. The hit point xB is: xB = xS + \frac{(h - yS)(xR - xS)}{2h - yS - yR} The reflection angle \thetai = \thetar is: \thetai = \thetar = \arctan\left[ \frac{|xR - xS|}{|2h - yS - yR|} \right] Pitfall The derivative \frac{\partial \ell}{\partial h} = \frac{2(2h - yS - yR)}{\ell(h)} applies only to a nonzero-length path while the same valid reflection branch is retained. If the path topology changes (e.g., hit point moves off the surface), the derivative is invalid. Time and Memory Complexity Time: O(1) per point reflection. The operation involves a dot product, a few multiplications, and a conditional update. Memory: O(1) auxiliary space. Measured Performance Not given in the sources. Scaling The method scales linearly with the number of points to be reflected. It is highly suitable for parallel execution on GPUs, as each point reflection is independent. Strengths and Limitations Strengths: Exact, closed-form solution; computationally inexpensive; easy to implement. Limitations: Only applicable to planar surfaces; requires normalized normal vector; does not handle curved or complex geometries directly. When to Use Use when reflecting points across flat planes, such as in specular reflection calculations, symmetry operations, or simple geometric transformations. When Not to Use Do not use for curved surfaces, non-planar boundaries, or when the normal vector is not available or not normalized. The Point-Plane Reflection method is a standard geometric transformation used in computer graphics, particularly in ray tracing and volume rendering for specular reflections and symmetry operations. It is derived from basic linear algebra and vector geometry. The Image Method variant is used in differentiable ray tracing to compute specular paths deterministically. tdhooper/glsl-marching-cubes, https://github.com/tdhooper/glsl-marching-cubes, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial) Differentiable ray tracing — from paths to gradients | Bai Liping, https://bailiping.com/differentiable-ray-tracing/, fetched 2026-10-28 (unofficial)

name: Mirror
head: Mirror Tool, Mirroring tool
body: The Mirror method is a volumetric filling tool that copies content from a source region to a target region across a user-defined reflection plane. It is designed to exploit symmetry in structures, such as the human body or head, by allowing users to interactively define a plane that divides the volume into two parts. Unlike the parent Point-Plane Reflection which reflects a single point, Mirror operates on volumetric data, copying material values from one side of the plane to the other. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A 3D volume dataset, a user-defined reflection plane (position and orientation), and a mirroring direction. Output: A modified volume where the target region contains copied material from the source region. Data Structures: The implementation uses a texture-based system. The volume data is stored in VolumeTex (3D texture). A SculptMap (3D texture) acts as a mask representing visibility and inserted material, using the alpha channel (Col.a) for visibility and the blue channel (Col.b) for inserted material. A PolygonCoord (2D texture) provides texture coordinates for sampling the volume data. Steps: 1. The user interactively selects the position and orientation of the reflection plane. 2. The direction of mirroring, represented by an arrow on the plane, defines the target area for copying. The opposite direction defines the source region. 3. For each voxel V in the selected part of the volume, calculate the coordinates of its reflected voxel V'. Let P be the orthogonal projection of V onto the reflection plane. Let d be the distance between voxel V and its orthogonal projection P. The mirrored voxel V' is located at an absolute distance |d| from P, in the same direction as the vector \vec{v}(V-p). 4. Access the voxel at V' in the source region. 5. If visible material exists at V', copy its content to V. Formula: Let d be the distance between voxel V and its orthogonal projection P on the reflection plane. The mirrored voxel V' is located at absolute distance |d| from P, in the same direction as the vector \vec{v}(V-p). Pseudocode: The source provides a fragment shader implementation (FSMirror) applied to proxy geometry fragments, noting it considers a plane moving along the X axis. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def FSMirror(v2fTexCoord, P, SculptMap, PolygonCoord, VolumeTex): # Map fragment to volume coordinates via 2D texture sampling texCoord = PolygonCoord.sample(v2fTexCoord) # Get current volume voxel value via 3D texture sampling volumevoxel = VolumeTex.sample(texCoord.xyz) # Get current mask state (visibility in alpha, insertion in blue) Col = SculptMap.sample(texCoord.xyz) # Calculate 3D Euclidean distance from the plane point P to the current voxel # P.a is used as a divisor for normalization or scaling D = ((P.x - texCoord.x)2 + (P.y - texCoord.y)2 + (P.z - texCoord.z)2)0.5 / P.a # Check if the voxel is within the influence of the mirror tool if D < Col.a: # Do not overwrite existing material if it is not background # Col.a == 0.0 implies no visibility/mask active # volumevoxel.r == 0.0 implies background/no material if volumevoxel.r == 0.0 or Col.a == 0.0: # Mark this voxel as having inserted material (using blue channel) Col.b = 1.0 return Col Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Overwriting: The tool does not overwrite existing material. It checks the current value of voxels; they are filled only if they have background values (e.g., volumevoxel.r == 0.0). Visibility: The tool relies on a visibility mask (Col.a) to determine which voxels are affected. Time and Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Measured Performance: Not given in the sources. Strengths and Limitations: Strengths: Exploits symmetry in structures like the human body, reducing manual effort for symmetric modeling. Integrated into a texture-based volume rendering system, allowing users to manipulate only a 3D mask before concluding the sculpting process. Limitations: Limited to structures with symmetry. Does not overwrite existing material, which may require pre-cleaning of the target region. When to Use: Use when working with symmetric anatomical structures (e.g., human head) and when the target region is empty or contains background values. The Mirror tool was developed as part of a volume sculpting system based on geometric tools, specifically integrated with 3D Clipper and Digger tools. It was designed to provide direct insertion of material in voxels by exploiting the existing symmetry of many structures of the human body. The implementation uses specific shaders (FSMirror) applied to fragments of proxy geometry within a texture-based volume rendering pipeline. The tool was assessed in a practical application reported in Section 7 of the source paper. Volume sculpting based on geometric tools, https://doi.org/10.1007/bf03194498, fetched 2026-10-26

name: Ray-Image Frame Intersection
head: Ray-Box Edge Intersection, Ray-Frame Intersection
body: Ray-Image Frame Intersection computes the intersection of a camera-space ray with the four lines parallel to the image frame axes (the boundaries x=0, x=1, y=0, y=1) in normalized image coordinates. It serves as a geometric primitive to determine where a ray exits or enters the image plane boundaries, which is essential for culling rays that miss the image or for mapping ray parameters to image-space coordinates. It differs from Ray-Volume and Bounding Box Intersection by operating specifically on the normalized image frame boundaries rather than a 3D volumetric bounding box, and from Implicit Surface and SDF Intersection by using analytic linear solutions rather than iterative root finding. Inputs and Outputs Inputs: Ray origin \mathbf{o} = (os, oo, oz), ray direction \mathbf{d} = (ds, do, dz), and camera intrinsics consisting of focal lengths fs, fo and principal points cs, co. The dimension to intersect is specified (e.g., horizontal or vertical). A target coordinate value v (typically 0.0 or 1.0) is provided for the boundary line. Outputs: The ray parameter t, the 2D image coordinate of the intersection point (x, y), and the 3D world coordinate \mathbf{xyz}. A validity flag indicating if the intersection is within bounds and in front of the camera. Data Structures The method operates on scalar components extracted from tensors representing ray origins, directions, and intrinsics. No complex data structures are required; computations are element-wise. Steps 1. Extract Intrinsics and Ray Components: Retrieve focal lengths fs, fo, principal points cs, co, ray origin components os, oo, oz, and ray direction components ds, do, dz. 2. Compute Normalized Coordinate c: Calculate the normalized coordinate c corresponding to the target boundary value v (e.g., 0.0 or 1.0) along the intersected dimension: c = \frac{v - cs}{fs} 3. Compute Ray Parameter t: Solve for the ray parameter t where the ray intersects the plane defined by the normalized coordinate c. The formula is: t = \frac{c oz - os}{ds - c dz} 4. Compute Other Coordinate: Calculate the coordinate value for the orthogonal dimension at the intersection point. Let oo and do be the origin and direction components for the other dimension, and co be its principal point: \text{coordinate\other} = co + \frac{fo (oo (c dz - ds) + do (os - c oz))}{dz os - ds oz} 5. Construct Intersection Points: 2D Image Point: Construct the 2D point \mathbf{xy} by placing the computed coordinateother in the orthogonal dimension and the target value v in the intersected dimension. 3D World Point: Compute the 3D point \mathbf{xyz} using the ray equation: \mathbf{xyz} = \mathbf{o} + t \mathbf{d} 6. Validate Intersection: The intersection is valid if: The 2D point \mathbf{xy} is within bounds [-\epsilon, 1+\epsilon] for both dimensions. The 3D point \mathbf{xyz} is in front of the camera (z > -\epsilon). The ray parameter t > -\epsilon. Pseudocode Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def rayimageframeintersection(os, oo, oz, ds, do, dz, fs, fo, cs, co, v, dim): """ Computes intersection of a ray with an image frame boundary. Args: os, oo, oz: Ray origin components. ds, do, dz: Ray direction components. fs, fo: Focal lengths. cs, co: Principal points. v: Target coordinate value (0.0 or 1.0). dim: 's' for horizontal (x), 'o' for vertical (y). Returns: t: Ray parameter. xy: 2D image coordinates. xyz: 3D world coordinates. valid: Boolean validity flag. """ epsilon = 1e-6 # Step 1 & 2: Compute normalized coordinate c c = (v - cs) / fs # Step 3: Compute ray parameter t # Note: Division by zero if ds - c dz is zero, handled by validity check denominatort = ds - c dz if abs(denominatort) < epsilon: return None, None, None, False t = (c oz - os) / denominatort # Step 4: Compute other coordinate # The formula uses specific variable names from sources: # coordinateother = co + (fo (oo (c dz - ds) + do (os - c oz))) / (dz os - ds oz) numeratorother = fo (oo (c dz - ds) + do (os - c oz)) denominatorother = dz os - ds oz if abs(denominatorother) < epsilon: return None, None, None, False coordinateother = co + numeratorother / denominatorother # Step 5: Construct points if dim == 's': # Intersecting horizontal boundary (x = v) x = v y = coordinateother else: # Intersecting vertical boundary (y = v) x = coordinateother y = v xy = (x, y) xyz = (os + t ds, oo + t do, oz + t dz) # Step 6: Validate # Check bounds [-epsilon, 1+epsilon] inbounds = (-epsilon <= x <= 1 + epsilon) and (-epsilon <= y <= 1 + epsilon) # Check in front of camera infront = xyz[2] > -epsilon # Check t is positive (or near zero) tvalid = t > -epsilon valid = inbounds and infront and tvalid return t, xy, xyz, valid Parameters \epsilon: Epsilon for floating-point comparisons. Typical value: 10^{-6}. v: Target coordinate. Values are typically 0.0 or 1.0. Edge Cases and Pitfalls Division by Zero: If ds - c dz = 0 or dz os - ds oz = 0, the ray is parallel to the intersection plane or the geometry is degenerate. The method should return invalid. Precision: Floating-point errors may cause points slightly outside [0, 1] to be considered valid if \epsilon is not used. Conversely, strict bounds may reject valid intersections due to precision loss. Degenerate Input: If the ray origin is on the image plane or the direction is zero, the intersection is undefined. Time Complexity: O(1) per ray per boundary. The computation involves a fixed number of arithmetic operations. Memory Complexity: O(1) auxiliary space. Performance: Highly efficient for parallel execution on GPUs due to lack of branching and simple arithmetic. Strengths: Exact analytic solution; no iteration required; suitable for culling and boundary checks. Limitations: Only computes intersections with the image frame boundaries, not with arbitrary geometry. Requires valid camera intrinsics. The method is used in sparse voxel and volume rendering pipelines, particularly in implementations like VolSplat and VoLoDSplat, for efficient ray-culling and coordinate mapping. It is a fundamental building block in ray-primitive intersection families for image-space based rendering. ziplab/VolSplat, https://github.com/ziplab/VolSplat, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial) pulangk97/VoLoDSplat, https://github.com/pulangk97/VoLoDSplat, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial)

name: Image Bounds Check
body: Image Bounds Check verifies whether 2D coordinates lie within the normalized image plane boundaries (0 to 1). It serves as a guard clause in ray-image frame intersection logic to prevent out-of-bounds memory access or invalid sampling when projecting rays onto the image plane. Unlike sibling methods that compute intersection points, this method performs a simple validity test with epsilon tolerance to handle floating-point precision errors near the edges. Inputs and Outputs: Input: xy, a tensor or array of 2D coordinates with shape (N, 2) or (2,), representing normalized image coordinates (u, v). Input: epsilon, a float tolerance value. Output: A boolean value or boolean tensor indicating whether all coordinates are within the valid range. Data Structures: xy: Floating-point array/tensor. No specific bit-packing is required beyond standard float representation. Steps: 1. Define the tolerance epsilon. The typical value is 10^{-6}. 2. Check if all coordinates in xy are greater than or equal to -\epsilon. 3. Check if all coordinates in xy are less than or equal to 1 + \epsilon. 4. Return the logical AND of the two conditions. Formula: \text{valid} = \left( \min(xy) \ge -\epsilon \right) \land \left( \max(xy) \le 1 + \epsilon \right) Where xy represents the coordinate vector(s). Parameters: epsilon: Float. Default value 10^{-6}. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Coordinates exactly at 0 or 1 are considered valid due to the epsilon tolerance. Negative coordinates slightly below 0 (within epsilon) are treated as valid. Coordinates slightly above 1 (within epsilon) are treated as valid. If xy is empty, the result depends on the implementation of.all(), but typically returns True for an empty set in many tensor libraries. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def imageboundscheck(xy, epsilon=1e-6): """ Check if 2D coordinates are within the normalized image plane [0, 1] with epsilon tolerance. Args: xy: Array-like of shape (..., 2) or (2,) containing u, v coordinates. epsilon: Float tolerance for boundary checks. Returns: Boolean: True if all coordinates are within [-epsilon, 1+epsilon]. """ # Check if all coordinates are >= -epsilon lowerboundcheck = (xy >= -epsilon) # Check if all coordinates are <= 1 + epsilon upperboundcheck = (xy <= 1 + epsilon) # Combine checks: all elements must satisfy both conditions #.all(dim=-1) ensures the check applies to the last dimension (coordinates) # and returns a boolean for each sample if xy is batched return (lowerboundcheck.all(dim=-1) & upperboundcheck.all(dim=-1)) Resolves the color of a sampled point by sampling an image texture at given UV coordinates if a material image index is provided, otherwise returning the base color. It handles boundary clamping and coordinate wrapping for flat image arrays. Choose this when you need to map 3D points to 2D image colors using UV coordinates. Link: Image Sampling (hypothetical link). Definition: Samples a single pixel color from a flat image array given UV coordinates, handling boundary clamping and coordinate wrapping. If material.imageindex is None or uv is None, returns material.basecolor. Steps: 1. If material.imageindex is None or uv is None, return material.basecolor. 2. Get image width and height from the image data associated with material.imageindex. 3. If width or height is less than or equal to 0, return None. 4. Wrap UV coordinates to the [0, 1) range using modulo: u = uv[0] \% 1.0, v = uv[1] \% 1.0. 5. Compute pixel coordinates x and y by multiplying u and v by width and height respectively, casting to integer, and clamping to [0, \text{width}-1] and [0, \text{height}-1]. 6. Calculate the linear index in the pixel array assuming RGBA layout (4 bytes per pixel): \text{index} = (y \times \text{width} + x) \times 4. 7. Retrieve the pixel data at index and return the first three channels (RGB) converted to a byte tuple. Pitfalls: If width or height is \le 0, the function returns None. Coordinate wrapping uses modulo, which can cause discontinuities at image boundaries if not handled carefully. Time and Memory Complexity: Time: O(1) for a single point check, O(N) for N points, where N is the number of coordinates. Memory: O(1) auxiliary space. Measured Performance: Not given in the sources. Scaling: Scales linearly with the number of points checked. Strengths and Limitations: Strengths: Simple, fast, and robust against floating-point errors near boundaries. Limitations: Only checks bounds; does not perform interpolation or sampling. When to Use: Use when validating UV coordinates before texture sampling or when ensuring ray intersections stay within the image plane. When Not to Use: Do not use if you need to clamp coordinates or perform texture sampling; use Image Sampling instead. Origin: The method is implemented in the NoPoSplat project. It is used in volume rendering and neural rendering pipelines to ensure that projected points remain within the valid image domain. cvg/NoPoSplat, https://github.com/cvg/NoPoSplat, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial) yumehiko/3dgs-dataset-builder, https://github.com/yumehiko/3dgs-dataset-builder, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial)

name: Ray-Splat/Gaussian Intersection
body: This family defines the geometric intersection between a camera ray and 3D Gaussian splats, which are ellipsoidal primitives used in novel view synthesis. It solves the problem of accurately determining which splats contribute to a pixel and at what depth, enabling alpha blending and depth-based operations. It distinguishes itself from sibling methods by handling the specific quadratic nature of Gaussian density fields, supporting both exact ellipsoid intersection and numerical stabilization for degenerate cases, unlike Sphere Intersection which assumes constant radius or Ray-Triangle Intersection which handles planar surfaces. The shared principles are inherited from Ray-primitive intersection. Exact Rational Ray-Surfel Evaluation computes the precise intersection point of a viewing ray with a flat surfel rectangle in the surfel's local (u, v) coordinates. It solves the problem of determining where a pixel's ray hits the surfel plane to evaluate the 2D Gaussian opacity, avoiding the per-pixel cross products and divisions required by the original 2DGS formulation. It sets itself apart from Ray-Splat/Gaussian Intersection by using a homography approximation around the screen-space bounding box center to replace the exact ray-plane intersection with a rational function, significantly reducing computational cost while maintaining visual fidelity. SPaGS is a real-time rendering method for 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) that supports arbitrary spherical camera models, specifically equirectangular panoramas, by replacing the standard local affine approximation with a numerically stable ray-splat intersection approach. It solves the problem of rendering artifacts and numerical instability inherent in standard 3DGS when applied to wide-field-of-view or distorted panoramic views, where first-order affine projections fail to accurately represent the Gaussian distribution. Unlike ODGS, which uses suboptimal tangent plane approximations, or 3DGUT, which relies on the Unscented Transform, SPaGS achieves higher quality and speed by representing each viewing ray as the intersection of two perpendicular planes in camera space, thereby avoiding matrix inversion of the covariance. Ray-Splat Intersection determines which 3D Gaussian splats in a scene are intersected by a camera ray, returning the closest hit for depth testing, picking, or alpha blending. It distinguishes itself from sibling methods by supporting both approximate spherical intersection (for performance) and true ellipsoid intersection (for geometric accuracy) within a hierarchical Bounding Volume Hierarchy (BVH) structure. Unlike Splat Raycasting Dispatch, which focuses on the parallel dispatch mechanism, this method defines the geometric traversal and intersection logic itself. Splat Raycasting Dispatch manages the buffer preparation and dispatch call for ray-splat intersection tests, returning hit distances and splat indices. It operates on pre-transformed, packed buffer structures optimized for batched processing, distinguishing it from Ray-Splat Intersection, and targets standard Euclidean camera models rather than spherical panoramas like Spherical Panoramic Gaussian Splatting (SPaGS). This method computes the intersection depths between camera rays and quadric splats, providing a numerically stable solution when the quadratic coefficient is near zero. It differs from standard quadratic solvers by detecting degenerate cases where the quadric surface is nearly flat or the ray is nearly perpendicular to the principal axes, switching to a linear approximation to prevent floating-point overflow. It builds on Ray-Splat/gaussian Intersection by handling the specific numerical instability inherent in second-order primitives. Quadratic Gaussian Splatting (QGS) is a surface reconstruction method that replaces static Gaussian primitives with deformable quadric surfaces (specifically paraboloids) to capture intricate geometry. Unlike standard Gaussian Splatting which uses Euclidean distance for density modeling, QGS employs geodesic distance-based density distributions to maintain spatial coherence during deformation. It sets itself apart from its siblings by generalizing 3D Gaussian primitives to higher-order surfaces, allowing adaptive curvature modeling while retaining the efficiency of ray-splat intersection. The Ray-Point Distance Test is a fragment shader technique that tests whether a viewing ray passes within a specified radius of up to 10 pre-selected 3D points, outputting a binary highlight color to indicate selection proximity. It differs from general ray-primitive intersection methods by operating on a discrete, small constant number of points rather than continuous geometric primitives, and by explicitly using the ray segment endpoints to compute perpendicular distance. Intersect the RBFs of the density representation with slices of thickness \Delta x that are perpendicular to the view direction. Render the slices from far to near using alpha blending with GLONE and GLSRCALPHA. Render the bounding quad of all intersections with the RBFs in each slice. For each pixel, retrieve D(x) and Lx from 3D textures. Set the RGB channels of the output to D(x)Lx. Set the alpha channel to the differential transmittance of the slice, computed as \exp(-\frac{\tau}{t} D(x) \Delta x). A technique to discard Gaussians that do not directly intersect with the ray, based on the intersection points identified during depth reinitialization. Identify \mathcal{I}{max}, the collection of all indexes i{max}(x) for all pixels x. Retain only Gaussians whose index i is in \mathcal{I}{max}. \mathcal{G}^{int} = \{\mathcal{G}i | i \in \mathcal{I}{max} \wedge i \in [1, N]\}, where \mathcal{G}^{int} is the set of intersected Gaussians and \mathcal{I}{max} is the collection of all indexes i{max}(x) in the rendered indexes. The concept of ray-splat intersection evolved from the need to render 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) efficiently in real-time. Standard 3DGS uses a rasterization-based approach that approximates the projection of Gaussians onto the image plane. For wide-field-of-view cameras or spherical panoramas, this first-order affine approximation introduces significant artifacts, leading to Spherical Panoramic Gaussian Splatting (SPaGS) which uses exact ray-splat intersection with perpendicular planes to avoid covariance matrix inversion. Concurrently, Ray-Splat Intersection introduced BVH-based traversal for more complex scenes, supporting both spherical approximations and true ellipsoid intersections. Numerical stability issues in quadratic solvers for quadric splats led to Ray-splat Intersection with Numerical Stabilization, which switches to linear approximations when the quadratic coefficient is negligible. Quadratic Gaussian Splatting further generalized this by using paraboloids and geodesic distances for surface reconstruction. Additionally, Intersection Preserving discards Gaussians that do not directly intersect with the ray based on depth reinitialization, while Ray Marching with RBF Intersection intersects RBFs with slices perpendicular to the view direction for volume rendering. name: Exact Rational Ray-Surfel Evaluation
head: 2DGS Ray-Surfel Intersection, Homography-based Ray-Surfel Intersection, Screen-space Homography Surfel Intersection
body: Exact Rational Ray-Surfel Evaluation computes the precise intersection point of a viewing ray with a flat surfel rectangle in the surfel's local (u, v) coordinates. It solves the problem of determining where a pixel's ray hits the surfel plane to evaluate the 2D Gaussian opacity, avoiding the per-pixel cross products and divisions required by the original 2DGS formulation. It sets itself apart from Ray-Splat/Gaussian Intersection by using a homography approximation around the screen-space bounding box center to replace the exact ray-plane intersection with a rational function, significantly reducing computational cost while maintaining visual fidelity. Inputs and Outputs Inputs: Ray origin \mathbf{o} and direction \mathbf{d} (normalized). Surfel-to-world homogeneous transformation matrix H \in \mathbb{R}^{4\times4}. World-to-screen homogeneous transformation matrix W \in \mathbb{R}^{4\times4}. Pixel coordinates (xp, yp) in screen space. Surfel center (u0, v0) in local coordinates. Jacobian matrix \mathbf{J} of the homography approximation. Offset vector \Delta from the bounding box center to the pixel. Ray direction vector d (used in the denominator term). Base opacity oi. Outputs: Local intersection coordinates (uj, vj). Per-pixel opacity \alphai. Data Structures Matrices: H and W are 4\times4 homogeneous transformation matrices. H maps local surfel coordinates (u, v, 1, 1)^\top to world space. W maps world space to screen space. Vectors: \mathbf{h}x, \mathbf{h}y, \mathbf{h}u, \mathbf{h}v are 4D homogeneous plane vectors. \mathbf{J} is a 2\times2 Jacobian matrix. \Delta is a 2D offset vector. Steps 1. Define Screen-Space Planes: Construct two plane vectors representing the pixel boundaries in screen space: \mathbf{h}x = (-1, 0, 0, xp)^\top \mathbf{h}y = (0, -1, 0, yp)^\top 2. Transform to Surfel-Local Frame: Transform these planes into the surfel's local coordinate system using the combined transformation WH. Note that the transformation is applied via the transpose of the inverse (or adjoint) of the matrix product, effectively transforming planes: \mathbf{h}u = (WH)^\top \mathbf{h}x \mathbf{h}v = (WH)^\top \mathbf{h}y 3. Compute Intersection Coordinates: Solve the 2\times2 linear system derived from the intersection of the ray with the surfel plane defined by \mathbf{h}u and \mathbf{h}v. Let hu^i and hv^i denote the i-th component of vectors \mathbf{h}u and \mathbf{h}v respectively (1-indexed): uj = \frac{hu^2 hv^4 - hu^4 hv^2}{hu^1 hv^2 - hu^2 hv^1} vj = \frac{hu^4 hv^1 - hu^1 hv^4}{hu^1 hv^2 - hu^2 hv^1} Alternative Approximation (Homography): For hardware rasterization or performance optimization, the intersection can be approximated using a homography expansion around the center of the screen-space bounding box (u0, v0): u = u0 + \frac{(\mathbf{J}\Delta)u}{1 + d^\top\Delta} v = v0 + \frac{(\mathbf{J}\Delta)v}{1 + d^\top\Delta} Here, \Delta is the offset from the bounding box center, \mathbf{J} is the precomputed Jacobian, and d is the ray direction. This avoids per-pixel cross products and divisions. 4. Evaluate Opacity: Compute the per-pixel opacity using the 2D Gaussian falloff in the local frame: \alphai = oi \exp\left(-\frac{uj^2 + vj^2}{2}\right) Parameters Gaussian Variance: The exponent uses a variance of 1 (implicit in the formula -(u^2+v^2)/2). Base Opacity oi: A scalar parameter per surfel. Edge Cases and Pitfalls Division by Zero: In the exact formulation, the denominator hu^1 hv^2 - hu^2 hv^1 represents the determinant of the system. If this is zero, the ray is parallel to the surfel plane or the planes are degenerate. Precision: The homography approximation is valid near the center of the bounding box. Far from the center, the rational function may deviate from the exact intersection. Hardware Rasterization: When using the homography approximation with hardware rasterization, the comparison with 2DGS was timed only on the CUDA renderer because the hardware rasterizer does not have a native ray-surfel variant. Pseudocode Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def exactraysurfelintersection(rayorigin, raydirection, H, W, xp, yp, oi): """ Computes exact ray-surfel intersection using plane transformation. Args: rayorigin: (3,) list, ray origin. raydirection: (3,) list, normalized ray direction. H: (4, 4) list of lists, surfel-to-world homogeneous matrix. W: (4, 4) list of lists, world-to-screen homogeneous matrix. xp: float, pixel x coordinate. yp: float, pixel y coordinate. oi: float, base opacity. Returns: alpha: float, per-pixel opacity. """ # Step 1: Define screen-space planes hx = [-1.0, 0.0, 0.0, xp] hy = [0.0, -1.0, 0.0, yp] # Step 2: Transform to surfel-local frame # Note: (WH)^T transforms planes from screen to local WH = [[sum(W[i][k] H[k][j] for k in range(4)) for j in range(4)] for i in range(4)] WHT = [[WH[j][i] for j in range(4)] for i in range(4)] def matvecmul(M, v): return [sum(M[i][j] v[j] for j in range(4)) for i in range(4)] hu = matvecmul(WHT, hx) hv = matvecmul(WHT, hy) # Step 3: Solve 2x2 system for uj, vj # Denominator: hu^1 hv^2 - hu^2 hv^1 (1-indexed) # In 0-indexed Python: hu[0] hv[1] - hu[1] hv[0] denom = hu[0] hv[1] - hu[1] hv[0] if abs(denom) < 1e-9: # Degenerate case: ray parallel to surfel or invalid geometry return 0.0 # Formula indices 1,2,4 -> Python indices 0,1,3 uj = (hu[1] hv[3] - hu[3] hv[1]) / denom vj = (hu[3] hv[0] - hu[0] hv[3]) / denom # Step 4: Evaluate opacity import math alpha = oi math.exp(-(uj2 + vj2) / 2.0) return alpha def homographyraysurfelintersection(u0, v0, J, delta, d, oi): """ Computes approximate ray-surfel intersection using homography. Args: u0: float, center u coordinate of bounding box. v0: float, center v coordinate of bounding box. J: (2, 2) list of lists, Jacobian matrix. delta: (2,) list, offset from center. d: (3,) list, ray direction (used in denominator term). oi: float, base opacity. Returns: alpha: float, per-pixel opacity. """ import math # Compute denominator term: 1 + d^T delta # delta is 2D, d is 3D. We pad delta with 0 for the dot product. delta3d = delta + [0.0] dotproduct = sum(d[i] delta3d[i] for i in range(3)) denomterm = 1.0 + dotproduct if abs(denomterm) < 1e-9: return 0.0 # Compute J delta Jdelta = [sum(J[i][j] delta[j] for j in range(2)) for i in range(2)] u = u0 + Jdelta[0] / denomterm v = v0 + Jdelta[1] / denomterm alpha = oi math.exp(-(u2 + v2) / 2.0) return alpha A rasterization technique for planar surfels that computes screen-space texture coordinates (u, v) using an algebraically exact rational function of pixel position, avoiding per-pixel cross products and vector constructions. It sets itself apart from the reference 2DGS formulation by replacing the per-pixel cross-product-based inversion with a precomputed affine approximation, reducing computational cost while maintaining visual fidelity. It is chosen for fragment-bound scenes where the saving per fragment yields significant performance gains (+47% on stump and flowers scenes) compared to scenes bound by sorting and binning (+20% on train scene). The hardware rasterizer has no ray–surfel variant, so performance comparisons were made on the CUDA renderer. Time Complexity: The exact method involves matrix-vector multiplications and a 2\times2 solve, which is constant time O(1) per pixel per surfel. The homography approximation reduces this to a few multiplications and additions, also O(1) but with a smaller constant factor. Memory Complexity: Requires storing the 4\times4 matrices H and W per surfel or globally, and per-pixel temporary vectors. Memory usage is low and constant per surfel. Measured Performance: On Mip-NeRF 360, Tanks & Temples, and Deep Blending datasets, the hardware rasterizer implementation achieved 2698, 3016, and 4413 FPS respectively, which is 1.8× faster than the CUDA software rasterizer implementation. The method remains 1.1–1.5× faster than Speedy-Splat at lower LPIPS on matched hardware rasterizers. Strengths: Avoids expensive per-pixel cross products and divisions of the original 2DGS method. Compatible with hardware rasterization for significant speedups. Limitations: The homography approximation is local to the bounding box center; accuracy may degrade far from the center. The exact method still requires more computation than simple splatting if not optimized. When to Use: Use when high-quality surfel rendering is required and performance is critical, especially on hardware rasterizers. Use the exact method when precision is paramount and the homography approximation is insufficient. The method originates from 2DGS (2D Gaussian Splatting), which introduced the surfel parameterization and ray-plane intersection for evaluating Gaussian opacity. Fourier Splatting inherits this ray-surfel intersection method but replaces the fixed Gaussian falloff with Fourier encoded boundaries. The homography-based approximation was introduced in "Bake It Till You Make It: Ultrafast Spatial Texture-Atlas Splatting" to enable hardware rasterization of surfels by leveraging perspective-correct texturing principles.
