name: Fragment Shader Volume Ray Casting
head: Direct Ray Casting (Volume with Light), GLSL Ray Casting, GPU Ray Casting via Rasterization, OpenGL Fragment Shader Volume Rendering, Shader Type 2: RAY CASTING Method
body: Fragment Shader Volume Ray Casting is a volume rendering technique implemented via a fragment shader that samples a 3D texture along rays cast from the camera through a unit cube geometry to produce a final color. It solves the problem of mapping screen-space fragments to 3D ray parameters and evaluating the volume rendering equation efficiently on the GPU by leveraging OpenGL rasterization. It builds on Intersection using Rasterization by using two rendering passes to decouple the calculation of ray entry/exit points from the volumetric integration. The method requires two rendering passes. The first pass calculates the exit point of the ray. The second pass calculates the entry point, ray direction, and numerically evaluates the volume rendering equation. Inputs: Volume Data: A 3D texture (volume) containing the scalar field, formatted as unsigned byte (GLubyte) with no header. Transfer Function: A 1D texture (transferFunction) mapping scalar values to color and opacity. Exit Point Texture: A 2D texture (lastHit) storing the exit point of the ray for each pixel, generated in the first pass. Camera Position: A vec3 uniform (ucameraPosition) representing the camera position in world space. Model-View-Projection Matrix: A mat4 uniform (uMVPMatrix) combining perspective and model-view transformations. Step Size: A scalar float h representing the step size for ray traversal. A related vec3 uniform ustepSize may also be passed, calculated as (1.0/XDIM, 1.0/YDIM, 1.0/ZDIM) where XDIM, YDIM, ZDIM are the volume dataset dimensions. Outputs: Final Color: A vec4 output (vFragColor) containing the accumulated color and opacity. Geometry: A unit cube defined by 8 vertices at coordinates (\pm 0.5, \pm 0.5, \pm 0.5) and 36 indices forming 12 triangles (GLTRIANGLES). The cube is stored in a Vertex Array Object (VAO) with two Vertex Buffer Objects (VBOs): one for vertex positions (GLARRAYBUFFER) and one for indices (GLELEMENTARRAYBUFFER). Textures: volume: uniform sampler3D at binding 3. transferFunction: uniform sampler1D at binding 2. lastHit: uniform sampler2D at binding 1. 1. Initialization: Create and compile vertex and fragment shaders from the source files. Link them into a shader program. Bind attribute aPosition to location ATTRIBUTEPOSITION. Retrieve uniform locations for uMVPMatrix, uVolume3DSampler, ucameraPosition, and ustepSize. 2. First Pass (Exit Point): Render the volume bounding box geometry to calculate and store the ray exit points in the lastHit texture. 3. Second Pass Setup: Enable blending. Set the shader program. Pass the Model-View-Projection matrix, camera position, and step size. Bind the 3D volume texture to unit 0, the exit point texture to binding 1, and the transfer function to binding 2. 4. Second Pass Rendering: Draw the unit cube using the 36 indices. For each fragment: a. Fetch Exit Point: Retrieve the exit point from the lastHit texture using texelFetch based on the fragment coordinates. b. Calculate Ray Parameters: Let first be the entry point (interpolated from the front face rendering). Calculate direction: \vec{d} = \text{last}.xyz - \text{first}.xyz. Calculate length: D = \|\vec{d}\|. Normalize direction: \vec{d} = \frac{\vec{d}}{\|\vec{d}\|}. c. Initialize Accumulators: \text{color} = (0.0, 0.0, 0.0, 1.0). \vec{tr} = \text{first}. \vec{rayStep} = \vec{d} \times h. d. Ray Marching Loop: Iterate for t from 0 to D with step h: i. Sample Volume: Sample the scalar field from the volume texture at \vec{tr}: v = \text{texture}(\text{volume}, \vec{tr}). ii. Sample Transfer Function: Map the scalar value to color and opacity: \text{samp} = \text{texture}(\text{transferFunction}, v.x).rgba. iii. Calculate Alpha: Apply the opacity model: \text{samp}.a = 1.0 - \exp(-0.5 \times \text{samp}.a). iv. Pre-multiply Color: \text{samp}.rgb = \text{samp}.rgb \times \text{samp}.a. v. Accumulate Color (Under Operator): \text{color}.rgb += \text{samp}.rgb \times \text{color}.a. \text{color}.a = 1.0 - \text{samp}.a. vi. Early Ray Termination: If 1.0 - \text{color}.a > \text{opacityThreshold} (where \text{opacityThreshold} = 0.99), break the loop. vii. Advance Ray: \vec{tr} += \vec{rayStep}. e. Finalize: \text{color}.a = 1.0 - \text{color}.a. Store \text{color} in vFragColor. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def main(): # 1. Fetch exit point from the texture generated in the first pass tcoord = ivec2(glFragCoord.xy) last = texelFetch(lastHit, tcoord, 0).xyz # 2. Calculate ray direction and length direction = last - first D = length(direction) direction = normalize(direction) # 3. Initialize accumulators color = vec4(0.0, 0.0, 0.0, 1.0) tr = first rayStep = direction h # 4. Ray marching loop t = 0.0 while t <= D: # Sample scalar field samp = texture(volume, tr) # Map scalar to color and alpha via transfer function samp = texture(transferFunction, samp.x) # Calculate alpha using the exponential model samp.a = 1.0 - exp(-0.5 samp.a) # Pre-multiply color by alpha samp.rgb = samp.rgb samp.a # Accumulate using the under operator color.rgb += samp.rgb color.a color.a = 1.0 - samp.a # Early ray termination if 1.0 - color.a > opacityThreshold: break # Advance ray position tr += rayStep t += h # 5. Finalize opacity color.a = 1.0 - color.a # 6. Output final color vFragColor = color Step Size (h): Determines the resolution of the ray march. A smaller h increases accuracy but reduces performance. It can be derived from the volume dimensions as (1/XDIM, 1/YDIM, 1/ZDIM). Opacity Threshold: Set to 0.99 for early ray termination. Precision: The use of texelFetch for lastHit ensures exact sampling of the exit point texture, avoiding interpolation artifacts that might occur with texture(). Boundaries: The method assumes the ray intersects the unit cube. The entry point first must be correctly interpolated from the front face rasterization in the second pass. A volume rendering technique implemented on consumer graphics boards using fragment programs to simulate ray tracing per pixel, approximating the volume rendering integral via discrete sampling. It differs from modern GLSL implementations by being constrained by older fragment program limitations, specifically a maximum loop count of 256 iterations. This restriction requires volume traversal to be implemented using nested loops. Unlike software ray tracing, it lacks recursion and flexible loop structures, making secondary rays for advanced shading (e.g., reflections) difficult or impossible to implement. However, it fully exploits the built-in parallelism of modern graphics boards. First presented by Stegmaier et al. in 2005. Time Complexity: Linear with respect to the number of samples per ray (N) and the number of pixels (P). O(P \times N). Memory Complexity: O(V) for the volume texture, O(T) for the transfer function, and O(P) for the intermediate lastHit texture. Performance: Highly parallel on the GPU due to fragment shader execution. Strengths: Simple implementation using standard OpenGL rasterization. Early ray termination can significantly reduce computation for opaque regions. Limitations: Requires two rendering passes. Limited by the maximum loop count in older fragment program architectures (256 iterations). No support for recursion, limiting advanced shading effects. When to Use: Real-time volume rendering on GPUs where hardware ray tracing is not available or when a simple, rasterization-based approach is preferred. When Not to Use: When advanced shading effects requiring recursion (e.g., reflections, refractions) are needed. The method originated from the need to perform volume rendering on programmable graphics hardware. Early implementations used fragment programs to simulate ray tracing on consumer graphics boards, as presented by Stegmaier et al. in 2005. This approach exploited the parallelism of GPUs to approximate the volume rendering integral. Later implementations, such as those described in 2017, refined the technique using two-pass rasterization to decouple ray intersection calculation from volumetric integration, allowing for efficient use of OpenGL fragment shaders. name: Rasterization-based Ray Setup
head: Raycast Shader Setup, RenderVolume, bounding box rasterization
body: Rasterization-based ray setup generates ray origins and directions for volume ray casting by rasterizing the volume's bounding box. It maps screen-space fragments to 3D ray parameters efficiently on the GPU. Unlike procedural intersection methods, this approach uses identical ray setup logic for both orthogonal and perspective projections. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Volume 3D texture, transfer function texture, camera position (camerapos), inverted model matrix (invertedmodel), and a quad vertex buffer. Output: Ray start position and direction vector (or start/exit positions) for subsequent ray marching. Data Structures: Vertex Buffer: Quad with two attributes per vertex: position (2 floats at offset 0 bytes) and UV coordinates (2 floats at offset 8 bytes). Textures: Unit 0 holds the volume 3D texture, unit 1 holds the front face depth texture, unit 2 holds the back face depth texture, and unit 3 holds the transfer function texture. Parameters: camerapos: World space camera position. invertedmodel: Inverted model matrix for transforming camera space to world space. transferindex: Uniform index for transfer function lookup. Steps: 1. Bind the raycast program. 2. Bind the volume 3D texture to texture unit 0. 3. Bind the front face depth texture to texture unit 1. 4. Bind the back face depth texture to texture unit 2. 5. Bind the transfer function texture to texture unit 3. 6. Set the uniform transferindex. 7. Set the uniform camerapos (world space). 8. Set the uniform invertedmodel. 9. Bind the quad vertex buffer with vertex attribute at offset 0 (2 floats) and UV attribute at offset 8 bytes (2 floats). 10. Draw GLTRIANGLESTRIP with 4 vertices. Formulas: The ray start position is computed by reconstructing the world-space intersection of the view ray with the front face of the bounding box. The ray direction is computed from the camera position to the fragment's world position. The exact reconstruction depends on the projection matrix used during depth texture generation. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def matvecmul(M, v): return [sum(M[i][j] v[j] for j in range(4)) for i in range(4)] def normalize(v, origin): diff = [v[i] - origin[i] for i in range(3)] length = sum(d2 for d in diff)0.5 return [d / length for d in diff] def rasterizationraysetup(uv, frontdepth, camerapos, invertedmodel, invprojmatrix): clipx = uv[0] 2.0 - 1.0 clipy = uv[1] 2.0 - 1.0 clipz = frontdepth clipw = 1.0 viewpos = matvecmul(invprojmatrix, [clipx, clipy, clipz, clipw]) viewpos = [v / viewpos[3] for v in viewpos] worldpos = matvecmul(invertedmodel, viewpos)[:3] raystart = worldpos raydirection = normalize(worldpos, camerapos) return raystart, raydirection Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Not given in the sources. Computes ray-box intersection analytically in the shader. It is chosen when avoiding the extra render pass for depth textures is preferred, but requires different logic for orthogonal versus perspective projections. Procedural Ray/Box Intersection Stops ray casting when a surface is hit or opacity threshold is reached. It is chosen when computational savings from early exit outweigh the overhead of per-sample checks. Early Ray Termination Skips transparent regions to reduce sample count. It is chosen when the volume contains large transparent areas and hierarchical structures or tighter bounding geometry are available. Empty Space Skipping Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Requires storage for front and back face depth textures plus the volume texture. Strengths: Identical logic for orthogonal and perspective projections. Limitations: Requires an additional render pass to generate depth textures. When to Use: Suitable for real-time volume rendering where simplicity and compatibility with standard rasterization pipelines are prioritized. When Not to Use: Not given in the sources. The rasterization-based ray setup approach was introduced by Krüger and Westermann in 2003. It emerged as an alternative to procedural ray/box intersection methods proposed by Röttger et al. (2003) and Green (2004). This method leverages the GPU's rasterization capabilities to generate ray parameters, simplifying the shader logic and ensuring consistency across different projection types. mversiotech/volume-rendering-demo, https://github.com/mversiotech/volume-rendering-demo, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial) PDF Volume Rendering - Isenberg, https://tobias.isenberg.cc/graphics/uploads/Class/07-volume-rendering.pdf, fetched 2026-10-28 (unofficial)

name: View-Ray Intersection via Hardware Tessellation
body: This method computes the intersection points between view-rays and the boundary surfaces of volume blocks by reformulating the zero-finding problem as a surface approximation problem, utilizing GPU hardware tessellation for parallel efficiency. It differs from Fragment Shader Volume Ray Casting by deferring the ray-marching computation to a later stage; instead, it focuses on generating precise entry and exit points for the volume blocks using rasterization primitives. Inputs: Volume blocks G\alpha, each defined by spline surfaces. Camera parameters defining the view-rays. Outputs: A texture buffer containing an unordered list of intersections per pixel, structured for subsequent depth-sorting. Data Structures: Intersection List Entry: A linked list node stored in a texture buffer (populated via atomic operations). Each entry contains: Parameter value (position in the parameter domain). Depth value (distance to the screen). Block number (\alpha). Orientation flag (front-facing or back-facing). Steps: 1. Render Boundary Surfaces: Render all boundary surfaces of all volume blocks G\alpha (6 surfaces per block) using a single-pass algorithm based on Hjelmervik. The algorithm uses hardware tessellation to create a view-dependent triangulation of the spline surfaces, guaranteeing water-tightness and satisfying the approximation error requirements for pixel-accurate rendering. 2. Store Intersections: Store the resulting intersection data into a texture buffer. The rasterization process effectively finds all ray-surface intersections of the triangulation in parallel. 3. Populate Linked Lists: For each pixel, populate a linked list of intersections using atomic operations in a single pass, adapted from order-independent transparency techniques. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. class IntersectionEntry: def init(self, paramvalue, depth, blocknumber, isfrontfacing): self.paramvalue = paramvalue self.depth = depth self.blocknumber = blocknumber self.isfrontfacing = isfrontfacing self.used = False def blockwisedepthsort(intersectionlists): """ Processes the unordered list of intersections per pixel according to Algorithm 2. intersectionlists: dict mapping pixel coordinates to a list of IntersectionEntry. """ for pixel, entries in intersectionlists.items(): # Continue until no unused entries remain while any(not e.used for e in entries): # 1) Find pOut: closest to screen (min depth), not used, not front facing pOut = None mindepth = float('inf') for entry in entries: if not entry.used and not entry.isfrontfacing: if entry.depth < mindepth: mindepth = entry.depth pOut = entry # 2) Exit if list is effectively empty (no valid pOut found) if pOut is None: break # 3) Find pIn: closest to screen, not used, front facing, matches block number of pOut pIn = None mindepth = float('inf') for entry in entries: if not entry.used and entry.isfrontfacing and entry.blocknumber == pOut.blocknumber: if entry.depth < mindepth: mindepth = entry.depth pIn = entry # 4) Render volume between pIn and pOut if pIn is not None: rendervolumesegment(pIn, pOut) # 5) Mark pOut and pIn as used pOut.used = True if pIn is not None: pIn.used = True def rendervolumesegment(pIn, pOut): """Conceptual step: composites the volume between the entry and exit points.""" pass Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Neighboring Blocks: In Isogeometric Analysis (IGA), surfaces of neighboring blocks match exactly, producing entries in the intersection list with approximately the same depth value. The depth-sorting algorithm ensures that paired entry and exit points correspond to the same block number to avoid incorrect pairing. Non-Convex Objects: View-rays may intersect the geometry multiple times per block, leading to multiple entry and exit points. The linked list approach handles this by iterating through all entries. Multi-Block Objects: Each volume block adds further intersections, requiring the block number check in the pairing logic. A method to pair entry and exit points from an unordered list of intersections per view-ray, handling non-convex objects and multi-block structures using atomic operations for linked lists. It differs from simple depth-sorting by explicitly checking block numbers to ensure pairs correspond to the same volume block, which is critical when neighboring blocks produce nearly identical depth values. Choose this method when dealing with multi-block volumes or non-convex geometries where simple front-to-back sorting is insufficient. Time Complexity: The intersection finding is performed in a single rasterization pass, leveraging parallel GPU hardware tessellation. The depth-sorting step requires iterating through the intersection list per pixel, which depends on the number of intersections determined by the view-angle, non-convexity, and multi-block structures. Memory Complexity: Requires a texture buffer to store the intersection lists. Strengths: Highly parallel and efficient due to hardware tessellation. Guarantees water-tightness and pixel-accurate approximation error. Single-pass intersection finding. Limitations: Requires post-processing to sort and pair intersections. Precision issues may arise with neighboring blocks having identical surfaces, requiring careful block-number matching. When to use: When pixel-accurate geometry is required for volume rendering, especially with spline-based volumes (IGA). When not to use: Not given in the sources. The method originates from Interactive Isogeometric Volume Visualization with Pixel-Accurate Geometry. It builds on the work of Hjelmervik [11] for single-pass hardware tessellation and Yeo et al. [26] for view-dependent triangulation. The linked list approach for handling multiple intersections is adapted from order-independent transparency techniques by Yang et al. [25], Everitt [10], Carpenter and Ii [1], and Myers and Bavoil [20]. name: Ray-Volume and Bounding Box Intersection
body: This family provides geometric methods to determine if a viewing ray intersects a volume's bounding region and to calculate the entry/exit intervals for subsequent sampling. It solves the problem of early rejection, ensuring that rays missing the data volume are discarded before expensive traversal occurs. The shared principles of this family are the geometric definition of rays and the parallel execution model. Ray Definition Rays are defined by an origin \mathbf{o} and a direction \mathbf{d}. The direction is typically normalized. The origin is often the camera eye position, but can vary based on the camera model. Parallel Execution Computations are mapped to parallel threads. Each thread typically processes one or more pixels or samples. Memory access patterns are optimized for coalescing. Synchronization is used to manage data dependencies between threads. The Ray-box intersection method computes the parametric entry (t{near}) and exit (t{far}) distances where a ray intersects an Axis-Aligned Bounding Box (AABB). It solves the problem of determining the valid sampling interval along a ray for volume rendering, enabling early rejection of rays that miss the volume entirely. It sets itself apart by exploiting axis-alignment to perform the test analytically with minimal arithmetic operations. Choose it when rendering axis-aligned volumes for maximum performance. This method determines if a viewing ray intersects the bounding volume of a dataset and calculates the entry point for subsequent volume traversal. It serves as the initial geometric culling step in ray casting, ensuring that rays missing the data volume are discarded before expensive sampling occurs. It sets itself apart by explicitly computing distances to the six faces of the data volume to determine a planar impact coordinate rather than using slab intervals. Choose it when volume boundaries are defined by explicit planar faces. Ray filtering reduces computational load by discarding rays that do not intersect with the scene's geometry or alpha mask before expensive volume rendering steps. It distinguishes itself from sibling methods by operating as a pre-processing culling stage on a batch of rays, often integrating alpha-mask density checks alongside axis-aligned bounding box (AABB) intersection tests. Choose it when optimizing batch ray processing pipelines. Procedural Ray/Box Intersection determines ray entry and exit within a volume's bounding box entirely within the fragment shader, without pre-rendering geometry. It computes the ray's intersection parameters directly in the shader, allowing the volume to be rendered without rasterized bounding box primitives. It sets itself apart by being self-contained in the shader, placing the full computational load of intersection and marching there instead of using rasterization setup. Choose it when avoiding explicit geometry buffers is required. An optimization to reduce cell primitives in a slice by intersecting individual rays with the world-space bounding box of the current u,v slice. It sets itself apart by ignoring rays that have already successfully hit a cell (inactive rays), even if they intersect the slice bounding box. Choose it when optimizing octree-based slice rendering. Originated in interactive volume rendering research, specifically within octree-based ray tracing pipelines for implicit surfaces. Used to optimize slice rendering by culling empty macrocells and filtering rays against bounding volumes. name: Ray-Volume Intersection (Face Distance Method)
head: Six-face intersection check, Volume::intersect
body: This method determines if a viewing ray intersects the bounding volume of a dataset and calculates the entry point for subsequent volume traversal. It serves as the initial geometric culling step in ray casting, ensuring that rays missing the data volume are discarded before expensive sampling occurs. Unlike Ray-box intersection, which typically uses slab-based interval intersection for axis-aligned bounding boxes, this method explicitly computes distances to the six faces of the data volume to determine a planar impact coordinate. It is distinct from Homogeneous Volume Intersection by not assuming uniform density for analytical free-path calculation, and from Near/Far Distance Precomputation Pass by using analytical geometry rather than rasterization to find bounds. Inputs and Outputs Input: Ray origin \mathbf{o}, ray direction \mathbf{d} (normalized to unit length). The volume is represented by its geometric boundaries, specifically six faces defining a rectangular prism. Output: Boolean indicating intersection; if intersecting, the entry point (impact point) on the volume surface. Data Structures The volume is defined by its six faces. The ray is defined by origin \mathbf{o} and direction \mathbf{d}. Steps 1. Check Origin Inside: Test if the ray origin \mathbf{o} lies within the data volume. If yes, the impact point is set to \mathbf{o}. If no, proceed to step 2. 2. Calculate Face Distances: For each of the six faces of the data volume, calculate the distance from the ray origin to the face. Let di be the distance from \mathbf{o} to face i. Let ci be the corresponding component of the ray direction vector \mathbf{d} associated with that face's normal or axis. Compute the parameter ti = di / ci. 3. Compute Planar Impact Coordinates: Multiply each calculated distance parameter ti by the corresponding eye positional ordinate (coordinate component) to create a planar impact coordinate. Impact point candidate \mathbf{p}i = \mathbf{o} + ti \mathbf{d}. 4. Select Nearest Intersection: Filter valid intersections (where ti > 0 and the point lies on the face segment). Select the smallest valid ti (or corresponding impact point) as the nearest ray-volume impact point. 5. Miss Handling: If no intersection points are found, the ray misses the volume entirely, and processing proceeds to the next pixel. Pseudocode Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def rayvolumeintersectfacedistance(rayorigin, raydirection, bounds): """ rayorigin: tuple (ox, oy, oz) raydirection: tuple (dx, dy, dz) bounds: tuple ((xmin, xmax), (ymin, ymax), (zmin, zmax)) Returns: (hit: bool, tmin: float, impactpoint: tuple) """ ox, oy, oz = rayorigin dx, dy, dz = raydirection xmin, xmax = bounds[0] ymin, ymax = bounds[1] zmin, zmax = bounds[2] # Step 1: Check if origin is inside volume if xmin <= ox <= xmax and ymin <= oy <= ymax and zmin <= oz <= zmax: return True, 0.0, rayorigin tmin = float('inf') hit = False bestpoint = None # Step 2 & 3: Calculate distances to each of the six faces # Each entry: (axisindex, facelimit, directioncomponent, origincomponent, rangestocheck) faces = [ (0, xmin, dx, ox, [(ymin, ymax), (zmin, zmax)]), (0, xmax, dx, ox, [(ymin, ymax), (zmin, zmax)]), (1, ymin, dy, oy, [(xmin, xmax), (zmin, zmax)]), (1, ymax, dy, oy, [(xmin, xmax), (zmin, zmax)]), (2, zmin, dz, oz, [(xmin, xmax), (ymin, ymax)]), (2, zmax, dz, oz, [(xmin, xmax), (ymin, ymax)]), ] for axis, limit, dircomp, origincomp, checkranges in faces: # Handle division by zero for rays parallel to face if dircomp == 0.0: continue # Distance from origin to face divided by corresponding ray component t = (limit - origincomp) / dircomp # Filter valid intersections (must be in front of ray) if t <= 0.0: continue # Compute planar impact coordinate px, py, pz = ox + t dx, oy + t dy, oz + t dz # Validate if point lies on the face segment valid = True if axis == 0: if not (ymin <= py <= ymax and zmin <= pz <= zmax): valid = False elif axis == 1: if not (xmin <= px <= xmax and zmin <= pz <= zmax): valid = False else: if not (xmin <= px <= xmax and ymin <= py <= ymax): valid = False # Select nearest intersection if valid and t < tmin: tmin = t hit = True bestpoint = (px, py, pz) # Step 5: Miss handling if not hit: return False, float('inf'), None return True, tmin, bestpoint Parameters Ray direction normalization: Unit length. Volume definition: Six faces. Edge Cases and Pitfalls Ray Parallel to Face: If the ray direction component corresponding to a face normal is zero, division by zero occurs. Such rays do not intersect that specific infinite plane unless contained within it, which is handled by the origin-inside check. Miss Handling: If no valid ti is found, the ray misses the volume entirely. The algorithm must return a miss status to avoid invalid traversal. Precision: Floating-point precision issues may cause rays to miss thin volumes or intersect incorrectly near boundaries. Assumes uniform density, allowing direct analytical sampling without majorant-based rejection sampling. Uses rasterization to compute entry/exit depths, differing from this analytical face-distance approach. Time Complexity: O(1) per ray, as it involves a fixed number of face checks (6 for a hexahedron). Memory Complexity: O(1) auxiliary memory for storing face parameters. Strengths: Simple, fast culling for rectangular volumes; avoids rasterization overhead. Limitations: Requires explicit face definitions; less efficient for complex non-convex geometries compared to hierarchical methods. When to Use: Initial culling for axis-aligned or simple convex volumes in ray casting. This method originates from early volumetric rendering techniques for displaying 3D aerodynamic flow field data. It implements a two-step process to determine ray-volume intersection before incremental ray extension through the data. Early versions of VRVE (Volumetric Rendering of Volume Elements) used similar approaches, though they faced aliasing issues with uniform resampling. The method is also referenced in CUDA-based volume rendering implementations. name: Homogeneous Volume Intersection
head: Constant-density volume intersection, Ray-Volume Intersection, Volume Intersection, Volume::intersect
body: Homogeneous Volume Intersection computes the first interaction point of a ray within a constant-density volume, or determines if the ray exits the medium without interacting. It differs from Heterogeneous Volume Intersection by assuming a uniform density field, which allows direct analytical sampling of the free path length without majorant-based rejection sampling. Inputs: World-space ray with origin \mathbf{o}, direction \mathbf{d}, and valid interval [t{\min}, t{\max}]. Volume boundary entry t{\text{in}} and exit t{\text{out}} relative to the world ray. Constant density \sigmat. Random number generator for sampling free path length. Outputs: A hit structure containing t (distance along the world ray), T (transmittance), and istransmission (boolean). Or std::nullopt if the ray does not intersect the volume or the index-space bounding box. Data Structures: Ray defined by origin \mathbf{o} and direction \mathbf{d}. Hit structure containing t, T, and istransmission. Index ray with parameters transformed into the voxel grid's index space. Steps: 1. Boundary Intersection: Intersect ray with volume boundary to obtain entry (t{\text{in}}) and exit (t{\text{out}}) hits. 2. Clamping: Clamp t{\text{in}} to t{\min} and t{\text{out}} to t{\max}. If t{\text{in}} < 0, set t{\text{in}} = 0. 3. Coordinate Conversion: Convert world ray origin and direction to index space using the grid's transform. 4. Index Space Clipping: Clip the index ray against the density grid's index bounding box; if it fails, return std::nullopt. 5. Distance Calculation: Compute ray length \|\mathbf{d}\| and distance inside boundary L{\text{inside}} = (t{\text{out}} - t{\text{in}}) \cdot \|\mathbf{d}\|. 6. Free Path Sampling: Sample interaction distance d{\text{hit}} = -\frac{1}{\sigmat} \ln(r) where r is a random value. 7. Interaction Decision: If d{\text{hit}} > L{\text{inside}}, compute T = \exp(-\sigmat \cdot L{\text{inside}}), return exit hit at t{\text{out}} with istransmission = true. Otherwise, compute t{\text{hit}} = t{\text{in}} + \frac{d{\text{hit}}}{\|\mathbf{d}\|}, T = \exp(-\sigmat \cdot d{\text{hit}}), return hit at t{\text{hit}} with istransmission = false. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math class Hit: def init(self, t, transmittance, istransmission): self.t = t self.transmittance = transmittance self.istransmission = istransmission def vectornorm(v): return math.sqrt(v[0]2 + v[1]2 + v[2]2) def homogeneousvolumeintersect(rayorigin, raydirection, tmin, tmax, tin, tout, sigmat, randomgenerator): # Step 1 & 2: Clamping tinclamped = max(tmin, tin) if tinclamped < 0: tinclamped = 0 toutclamped = min(tmax, tout) if tinclamped >= toutclamped: return None # Step 3: Coordinate Conversion (Index Space) # Apply grid's world-to-index affine transform # indexrayorigin = (rayorigin - gridorigin) / gridspacing # indexraydirection = raydirection / gridspacing # indexray = Ray(indexrayorigin, indexraydirection) # Step 4: Index Space Clipping # if not indexray.clipagainstindexboundingbox(): # return None # Step 5: Distance Calculation dirnorm = vectornorm(raydirection) distanceinsideboundary = (toutclamped - tinclamped) dirnorm # Step 6: Free Path Sampling r = randomgenerator() hitdistance = -1.0 / sigmat math.log(r) # Step 7: Interaction Decision if hitdistance > distanceinsideboundary: transmittance = math.exp(-sigmat distanceinsideboundary) return Hit(t=toutclamped, transmittance=transmittance, istransmission=True) else: thit = tinclamped + hitdistance / dirnorm transmittance = math.exp(-sigmat hitdistance) return Hit(t=thit, transmittance=transmittance, istransmission=False) Parameters: \sigmat: Extinction coefficient. Must be > 0. r: Random number. Standard inverse transform sampling requires r \in (0, 1]. Edge Cases: Zero Density: If \sigmat = 0, the formula for d{\text{hit}} divides by zero. Ray Origin Inside: If the ray origin is inside the volume, t{\text{in}} may be negative or zero. The clamping logic handles this by ensuring t{\text{in}} \ge 0 relative to the ray's valid range. Degenerate Ray: If \|\mathbf{d}\| = 0, the ray has no direction. Division by zero occurs in t{\text{hit}} calculation. Time Complexity: O(1) for the intersection calculation itself, assuming constant-time random number generation and bounding box checks. Memory Complexity: O(1) auxiliary space. Performance: Significantly faster than heterogeneous intersection because it avoids the overhead of querying a density field and performing rejection sampling with a majorant. Strengths: Simple implementation, low computational cost, exact sampling for uniform media. Limitations: Cannot model spatially varying density. When to use: When simulating uniform fog, smoke, or participating media where density is constant. When not to use: For clouds, smoke with varying density, or complex atmospheric effects requiring spatial variation. Homogeneous volume intersection is a fundamental technique in volumetric path tracing. It relies on the analytical solution to the radiative transfer equation for constant coefficients. The method of sampling the free path length using the inverse transform sampling of the exponential distribution is standard in Monte Carlo rendering. The integration of index-space clipping ensures robustness against grid boundaries. name: Heterogeneous Volume Intersection
head: Majorant-based Ray Marching
body: Heterogeneous Volume Intersection computes the first interaction point of a ray within a participating medium with spatially varying density, or determines if the ray exits the medium without interacting. It differs from Homogeneous Volume Intersection by handling non-constant density fields using a constant majorant density for rejection sampling. Inputs: Ray r(t) = o + t \cdot d, where o is the origin, d is the direction, and t \ge 0. A heterogeneous volume object containing: A boundary geometry defining the spatial extent of the medium. A density texture function returning the local density at a point. A majorant density, a constant value such that the local density is bounded by it. A material for scattering properties. Outputs: A hit record indicating the first interaction point and the distance along the ray, if an interaction occurs. A flag indicating whether the ray exited the volume without interaction. The transmittance from the entry point to the interaction point (or exit point), set to 1.0 in the reference implementation. Data Structures: The volume is represented by a class HeterogeneousVolume inheriting from Object. Fields: Object boundary (enclosing geometry), double densitymajorant (constant upper bound on density), Texture densitytexture (spatial density function). Constructor: HeterogeneousVolume(Object boundary, double densitymajorant, Texture densitytexture, Material material). Steps: 1. Ray-Volume Boundary Intersection: Intersect the ray with the boundary geometry (boundary) to obtain entry and exit distances, t{in} and t{out}. Clamp t values to the ray interval, and handle cases where t{in} < 0 (ray starts inside). If the ray misses or t{in} \ge t{out}, return no hit. 2. Initialization: Set the current distance along the ray, t{current} = t{in}. 3. Ray Marching Loop: Loop indefinitely: a. Sample Step Size: Generate a uniform random number u \in (0, 1) and calculate the step size \Delta t = -\ln(u) / \rho{max}. b. Advance Ray: Update the current distance: t{current} \leftarrow t{current} + \Delta t / \|d\|. c. Check Exit: If t{current} \ge t{out}, the ray has exited the volume without an interaction. Return an exit hit with transmittance = 1.0 and istransmission = true. d. Evaluate Local Density: Compute the point p = r(t{current}) and evaluate the density texture at p. Calculate the local density as \rho{local} = \rho{max} \cdot (tex\val.r + tex\val.g + tex\val.b) / 3.0. e. Rejection Sampling: Generate a new uniform random number v \in (0, 1). If v < \rho{local} / \rho{max}, accept as an interaction. Return a hit at p with transmittance = 1.0 and istransmission = false. f. Otherwise: If the rejection test fails, continue the loop from step 3a. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math import random class HitRecord: def init(self, point, t, transmittance, istransmission): self.point = point self.t = t self.transmittance = transmittance self.istransmission = istransmission def randomdouble(): return random.random() def rayat(rayorigin, raydirection, t): raylength = math.sqrt(raydirection.x2 + raydirection.y2 + raydirection.z2) return rayorigin + raydirection (t / raylength) def heterogeneousvolumeintersection(rayorigin, raydirection, volume): # Intersect ray with boundary to get hitin and hitout hitint, hitoutt = volume.boundary.intersect(rayorigin, raydirection) if hitint is None or hitoutt is None: return None # No intersection with volume tin = hitint tout = hitoutt # Handle ray starting inside the volume if tin < 0: tin = 0 if tin >= tout: return None # Tangent or miss tcurrent = tin rhomax = volume.densitymajorant raylength = math.sqrt(raydirection.x2 + raydirection.y2 + raydirection.z2) # Step 3: Ray Marching Loop while True: # Step 3a: Sample step size u = randomdouble() dt = -math.log(u) / rhomax # Step 3b: Advance ray tcurrent += dt / raylength # Step 3c: Check exit if tcurrent >= tout: return HitRecord(rayat(rayorigin, raydirection, tout), tout, 1.0, True) # Step 3d: Evaluate local density p = rayat(rayorigin, raydirection, tcurrent) texval = volume.densitytexture.value(p) rholocal = rhomax (texval.r + texval.g + texval.b) / 3.0 # Step 3e: Rejection sampling v = randomdouble() if v < rholocal / rhomax: return HitRecord(p, tcurrent, 1.0, False) Parameters: densitymajorant: Must be \ge \max(\rho(p)) for all p in the volume. densitytexture: A texture object implementing a value(Point3) method that returns the density at a point. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision: If \rho{local} is very close to \rho{max}, floating-point errors may affect the rejection test. Boundary Intersection: The boundary intersection must be robust. If the ray originates exactly on the boundary, t{in} should be handled carefully to avoid infinite loops or missed interactions. Majorant Selection: If \rho{max} is too large, the acceptance rate \rho{local} / \rho{max} becomes low, leading to many rejected steps. Represents a participating medium with spatially varying density using a texture, bounded by geometry, and using a majorant density for null rejection. It inherits from Object and includes fields for the boundary, majorant density, density texture, and material. The constructor takes these four parameters. This representation is essential for the intersection method to function, as it provides the necessary data for density evaluation and boundary intersection. Time Complexity: The expected number of steps depends on the ratio of local density to the majorant density. Memory Complexity: O(1) additional memory beyond the storage for the density texture and boundary geometry. Strengths: Handles arbitrary density distributions without requiring a uniform grid. Simple to implement. Exact sampling (no discretization error in the density field). Limitations: Requires a robust boundary intersection routine. When to Use: When the density field is complex and cannot be easily approximated by a uniform grid. When Not to Use: When the density field is uniform (use Homogeneous Volume Intersection). The method implements null rejection sampling for spatially varying density volumes. It is used in volumetric path tracing for rendering participating media. The implementation follows the logic from the provided source code. TakTikFR/Volumetric-Path-Tracing, https://github.com/TakTikFR/Volumetric-Path-Tracing, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial)

name: Near/Far Distance Precomputation Pass
head: Voxel Brick Distance Pass, tNear-tFar Rendering
body: The Near/Far Distance Precomputation Pass renders voxel bricks to a render target to compute the entry (t{Near}) and exit (t{Far}) distances of viewing rays intersecting the volume for each pixel. This prepares the bounds for the subsequent raymarching pass, allowing the main rendering pass to skip empty space and focus computation only on occupied regions. It differs from Homogeneous Volume Intersection by explicitly rasterizing the volume geometry to derive depth bounds rather than analytically solving for intersections with a homogeneous bounding box. Inputs: A flag volume texture (mpFlagVolumeSRV) indicating which bricks are active. Camera matrices (cbmView, cbmViewProj) and view position (cbf4ViewPos). Volume parameters: VOXELNUMX/Y/Z, VOXELBRICKRATIO, VOXELSIZE, gcf3VoxelReso, gcf3HalfBrickSize. A render target view (mpFarNearRTV) for output. Outputs: A render target where each pixel stores t{Near} in the RGB channels and t{Far} in the Alpha channel. Data Structures: Render Target (mpFarNearRTV): Format not given in the sources. Vertex Buffer (mpPassVB): Contains point primitives with stride sizeof(short). The content acts as a dummy list of primitive indices, as the actual geometry is generated in the Geometry Shader. Flag Volume (texFlagVolume): A 3D texture where active bricks are marked with 1 and inactive with 0. Numbered Steps: 1. Clear Render Target: Clear mpFarNearRTV with {50.0f, 50.0f, 50.0f, -10.0f}. This sets an initial background value where RGB=50 and Alpha=-10. 2. Set Topology: Set primitive topology to D3D11PRIMITIVETOPOLOGYPOINTLIST. 3. Bind Resources: Bind input layout mpOutVL, vertex buffer mpPassVB (stride sizeof(short)), vertex shader mpPassVS, geometry shader mpActiveCellAndSOGS, and pixel shader mpFarNearPS. 4. Bind Shaders: Bind GS constant buffer mpCBperFrame and GS shader resource mpFlagVolumeSRV. 5. Set States: Set rasterizer state mpBackFaceRS and blend state mpBlendState. 6. Draw: Issue a draw call for VOXELNUMX VOXELNUMY VOXELZ / VOXELBRICKRATIO^3 primitives. 7. Restore: Restore previous blend state. Blend State Configuration (mpBlendState): BlendEnable = true RGB Channels (t{Near}): SrcBlend=D3D11BLENDONE, DestBlend=D3D11BLENDONE, BlendOp=D3D11BLENDOPMIN. Result: t{Near} = \min(t{Near}, \text{new\value}). Alpha Channel (t{Far}): SrcBlendAlpha=D3D11BLENDONE, DestBlendAlpha=D3D11BLENDONE, BlendOpAlpha=D3D11BLENDOPMAX. Result: t{Far} = \max(t{Far}, \text{new\value}). RenderTargetWriteMask=D3D11COLORWRITEENABLEALL. Pseudocode (Geometry Shader Logic): The Geometry Shader iterates over active bricks, generates a cube for each, transforms it to clip space, and outputs it. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def geometryshader(primID, flagvolume, VOXELNUMY, VOXELBRICKRATIO, gcf3VoxelReso, VOXELSIZE, gcf3HalfBrickSize, cbmViewProj): # Decode brick coordinates from primitive ID u3Idxz = primID // (gcuFlagVolSliceStep gcuFlagVolStripStep) u3Idxy = (primID % gcuFlagVolSliceStep) // gcuFlagVolStripStep u3Idxx = primID % gcuFlagVolStripStep # Check if the current cell is active, discard if inactive if flagvolume[u3Idxz, u3Idxy, u3Idxx] != 1: return # Adjust Y coordinate (source flips Y) u3Idxy = (VOXELNUMY // VOXELBRICKRATIO) - 1 - u3Idxy # Calculate the offset vector to move (0,0,0,1) to current cell center centeroffset = (float3(u3Idxx, u3Idxy, u3Idxz) - float3(gcf3VoxelReso.x, gcf3VoxelReso.y, gcf3VoxelReso.z) 0.5 / VOXELBRICKRATIO + 0.5) VOXELSIZE VOXELBRICKRATIO # Get half cell size to expand the cell center point to full cell cube geometry halfcellsize = float3(gcf3HalfBrickSize.x, gcf3HalfBrickSize.y, gcf3HalfBrickSize.z) # Define cube vertices in local space (-1 to 1) verts = [ float3(-1, -1, -1), float3(-1, 1, -1), float3(1, 1, -1), float3(1, -1, -1), float3(-1, -1, 1), float3(-1, 1, 1), float3(1, 1, 1), float3(1, -1, 1) ] # Output front face vertices as a line strip for i in range(4): output = PSINPUT() v = verts[i] halfcellsize + centeroffset output.Pos = float4(v.x, v.y, v.z, 1.0) output.projPos = mul(output.Pos, cbmViewProj) lineStream.Append(output) lineStream.RestartStrip() # Output back face vertices as a line strip for i in range(4, 8): output = PSINPUT() v = verts[i] halfcellsize + centeroffset output.Pos = float4(v.x, v.y, v.z, 1.0) output.projPos = mul(output.Pos, cbmViewProj) lineStream.Append(output) lineStream.RestartStrip() def pixelshader(input): # Convert clip space position to view space depth zclip = input.projPos.z / input.projPos.w # Convert to linear view space depth (standard D3D11 mapping) lineardepth = -(zclip 2.0 - 1.0) return float4(lineardepth, lineardepth, lineardepth, lineardepth) Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Back-Face Culling: The use of mpBackFaceRS means only front-facing triangles are rendered. The sources enable back-face culling but do not explain how t{Far} is correctly accumulated when back faces are discarded, given the Alpha channel uses a MAX blend operation. Precision: Using float for depth calculations may introduce precision errors for large scenes. The clear value of {50.0f, 50.0f, 50.0f, -10.0f} must lie outside the expected range of valid depths to ensure correct min/max accumulation. Empty Bricks: Inactive bricks (flag != 1) are discarded early in the GS, preventing unnecessary rendering and blending operations. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Performance: Depends on the number of active bricks and the resolution of the render target. Rasterizing wireframes can be expensive if the number of active bricks is high. Strengths: Efficiently culls empty space using standard rasterization hardware. Limitations: Requires a second raymarching pass; accuracy depends on the rasterization of the cube geometry; back-face culling complicates t{Far} derivation. Origin: Part of the Dynamic Volume Raycasting implementation. History: The technique leverages the GPU's rasterization pipeline to compute depth bounds, avoiding the need for complex CPU-side bounding volume hierarchy traversal or analytical intersection tests for every ray. Usage: It is used in real-time volume rendering applications where efficient culling of empty space is critical for performance. pengliu916/DynamicVolumeRayCasting, https://github.com/pengliu916/DynamicVolumeRayCasting, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial)

name: Ray Filtering
head: Filtering Rays, Ray Culling, Ray Filtering Outside Bounding Box, Ray Filtering using Alpha Mask, TensorBase Ray Filtering
body: Ray filtering reduces computational load by discarding rays that do not intersect with the scene's geometry or alpha mask before expensive volume rendering steps. It distinguishes itself from sibling methods by operating as a pre-processing culling stage on a batch of rays, often integrating alpha-mask density checks alongside axis-aligned bounding box (AABB) intersection tests. Inputs and Outputs Inputs: A batch of rays defined by origins \mathbf{o} \in \mathbb{R}^{N \times 3} and directions \mathbf{d} \in \mathbb{R}^{N \times 3}; an AABB defined by minimum corner \mathbf{min} \in \mathbb{R}^3 and maximum corner \mathbf{max} \in \mathbb{R}^3; an optional alpha mask volume for density-based culling; a boolean flag bboxonly. Outputs: A boolean mask validmask of size N indicating which rays intersect the scene; optionally, filtered ray origins and directions. Data Structures AABB: Two 3D vectors, aabb[0] (min) and aabb[1] (max). Alpha Mask: A 3D tensor sampled at query points, returning scalar alpha values. Steps 1. Split the total number of rays N into chunks of size chunk for batched processing. 2. For each chunk, extract ray origins and directions. 3. Compute the intersection parameter range [t{min}, t{max}] with the AABB using the slab method: \text{rate}a = \frac{\mathbf{aabb}[1] - \mathbf{o}}{\mathbf{d}} \text{rate}b = \frac{\mathbf{aabb}[0] - \mathbf{o}}{\mathbf{d}} t{min} = \max(\min(\text{rate}a), \min(\text{rate}b)) t{max} = \min(\max(\text{rate}a), \max(\text{rate}b)) A ray intersects the box if t{max} > t{min}. 4. Determine the initial mask: maskinbbox = (tmax > tmin). 5. If bboxonly is False, sample points along the rays within the bounding box interval and check if any sample has an alpha value > 0 in the alpha mask. Update maskinbbox to true only if the ray intersects the box AND passes through a non-zero alpha region. 6. If bboxonly is True, maskinbbox remains based solely on AABB intersection. 7. Reinitialize the ray sampler with the filtered ray count to ensure subsequent rendering steps only process valid rays. Pseudocode Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def filterrays(rayso, raysd, aabbmin, aabbmax, alphamask=None, bboxonly=False, Nsamples=64): """ Filter rays based on AABB intersection and optionally alpha mask density. Args: rayso: (N, 3) ray origins raysd: (N, 3) ray directions aabbmin: (3,) minimum corner of AABB aabbmax: (3,) maximum corner of AABB alphamask: Object with method samplexyz(xyz) returning alpha values bboxonly: Boolean, if True skip alpha mask check Nsamples: Number of points sampled along each ray Returns: validmask: (N,) boolean mask of valid rays """ N = len(rayso) validmask = [False] N for i in range(N): o = rayso[i] d = raysd[i] # Avoid division by zero for degenerate rays dsafe = [1e-10 if abs(dx) < 1e-10 else dx for dx in d] # Compute rate arrays ratea = [(aabbmax[j] - o[j]) / dsafe[j] for j in range(3)] rateb = [(aabbmin[j] - o[j]) / dsafe[j] for j in range(3)] # Compute tmin and tmax tmin = max(min(ratea), min(rateb)) tmax = min(max(ratea), max(rateb)) # Initial bbox mask if tmax > tmin: if bboxonly: validmask[i] = True else: # Clamp startt to 0 if origin is inside the box startt = max(tmin, 0.0) endt = tmax if endt > startt: # Sample points along the ray tvals = [startt + k (endt - startt) / (Nsamples - 1) for k in range(Nsamples)] xyzsampled = [[o[j] + d[j] t for j in range(3)] for t in tvals] # Check alpha mask alphavalues = [alphamask.samplexyz(pt) for pt in xyzsampled] if any(a > 0 for a in alphavalues): validmask[i] = True else: validmask[i] = False else: validmask[i] = False else: validmask[i] = False return validmask Parameters bboxonly: Boolean. If True, only AABB intersection is checked. If False, alpha mask density is also checked. Nsamples: Number of points sampled along each ray for alpha mask checking. Not given in the sources. Edge Cases and Pitfalls Degenerate Rays: Rays with zero direction components cause division by zero in ratea and rateb. Handle by clamping zero direction components to a small epsilon before division. Origin Inside Box: If the ray origin is inside the AABB, t{min} may be negative. Ensure sampling starts at \max(0, t{min}) to avoid sampling behind the camera. Precision: Floating-point errors in t{max} > t{min} comparisons can lead to incorrect culling. Use a small epsilon if necessary. Standard AABB intersection test. Used as the primary culling step. Ray-box intersection Alternative to AABB for non-box volumes. Not used in this method. Ray-Volume Intersection (Face Distance Method) Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Performance: Reduces computation for rays that do not pass through the scene. Strengths: Not given in the sources. Limitations: Not given in the sources. Ray filtering is used in TensorBase and Collaborative NeRF to cull rays outside the bounding box or alpha mask. The method is typically applied during training iterations when the alpha mask is updated. name: Procedural Ray/Box Intersection
body: Procedural Ray/Box Intersection determines ray entry and exit within a volume's bounding box entirely within the fragment shader, without pre-rendering geometry. Unlike rasterization-based setup methods like Ray-box intersection or Ray-Volume Intersection (Face Distance Method), it computes intersection parameters directly in the shader, making it self-contained but placing the full computational load on the fragment shader. Inputs and Outputs Input: Camera position \mathbf{o}{cam}, volume entry position \mathbf{p}{entry}, and bounding box corners \mathbf{b}{min} and \mathbf{b}{max}. Output: Ray origin \mathbf{o}, ray direction \mathbf{d}, and exit parameter t{exit} for the marching loop. Data Structures Ray: Defined by origin \mathbf{o} and direction \mathbf{d}. Bounding Box: Axis-aligned box defined by \mathbf{b}{min} and \mathbf{b}{max}. Steps 1. Define the Ray: Set \mathbf{o} = \mathbf{o}{cam}. Compute \mathbf{d} = \mathbf{p}{entry} - \mathbf{o}{cam}. 2. Compute Exit Criterion: Calculate t{exit} to determine when the ray leaves the bounding box. 3. Marching Loop: Use \mathbf{o}, \mathbf{d}, and t{exit} to march through volume data, terminating when the exit criterion is met. Formulas \mathbf{d} = \mathbf{p}{entry} - \mathbf{o}{cam} where \mathbf{o}{cam} is the camera position and \mathbf{p}{entry} is the volume entry position. Pseudocode def proceduralrayboxintersection(camerapos, volumeentrypos, boxmin, boxmax): """ Computes ray parameters for volume marching within a bounding box. """ rayorigin = camerapos raydirection = volumeentrypos - camerapos # Compute t values for intersection with all 6 planes (slab method) t1 = (boxmin - rayorigin) / raydirection t2 = (boxmax - rayorigin) / raydirection tmin = min(t1, t2) tmax = max(t1, t2) tenter = max(tmin.x, tmin.y, tmin.z) texit = min(tmax.x, tmax.y, tmax.z) if tenter > texit: return None, None, -1.0 return rayorigin, raydirection, texit Parameters Exit Criterion: Required to determine when the ray has left the volume. Edge Cases and Pitfalls Precision: Division by zero in direction components is handled by floating-point infinity and min/max operations. Boundaries: The method assumes the volume entry position lies on the near face of the bounding box. Performance: The entire computational load for intersection and marching is placed on the fragment shader, which is a disadvantage compared to rasterization-based setup. Strengths: Simple and self-contained implementation. Limitations: Full computational load on the fragment shader. The method was introduced by Röttger et al. in 2003 and Green in 2004. GPU-Based Volume Ray-Casting with Advanced Illumination, https://doi.org/10.2312/egt.20091069, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial) GPU-Based Volume Ray-Casting with Advanced Illumination, https://www.uni-ulm.de/fileadmin/websiteuniulm/iui.inst.100/institut/Papers/viscom/2008/advancedillumination.pdf, fetched 2026-10-29 (unofficial)

name: Ray-Box Intersection via OpenGL Geometry Shaders
head: CubeIntersection, Front/Back Hit Textures
body: This method computes the 3D entry and exit points of view rays intersecting a volume's bounding box by rasterizing the box geometry to textures, thereby avoiding procedural intersection calculations in the fragment shader. It leverages the GPU's parallel rasterization pipeline to generate ray setup data as a byproduct of rendering a simple color cube. Unlike analytical ray-box intersection tests, it relies on face culling and depth testing to separate front and back intersections across two rendering passes. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A camera projection matrix (Model-View-Projection, MVP), a boolean flag mbFront indicating whether to compute the front (entry) or back (exit) intersection, and the geometry of a unit cube centered at the origin. Output: Two 2D textures (TEXTUREFRONTHIT and TEXTUREBACKHIT) storing the 3D world-space intersection coordinates for each pixel. Data Structures: Hit Textures: Two 2D textures of size W \times H (matching the viewport resolution). Format: GLRGBA16F Internal Format: GLRGBA16F Type: GLFLOAT Layout: Each texel stores a 4-component vector (x, y, z, w). The x, y, z components store the world-space intersection point. The w component is typically unused or set to 1.0. Framebuffer Object (FBO): Contains the color attachment (the hit texture) and a depth renderbuffer. Depth Buffer: Format GLDEPTHCOMPONENT16. Numbered Steps: 1. Initialize FBO: Create a Framebuffer Object (FBO). Attach a GLRGBA16F texture as the color attachment (either TEXTUREFRONTHIT or TEXTUREBACKHIT). Attach a GLDEPTHCOMPONENT16 renderbuffer as the depth attachment. Clear both the color buffer and the depth buffer. 2. Configure Rasterization State: Enable GLCULLFACE and GLDEPTHTEST. Set the culling mode based on the mbFront flag: if mbFront is true, cull GLBACK faces to capture only the front-facing intersections (entry points); if mbFront is false, cull GLFRONT faces to capture only the back-facing intersections (exit points). 3. Render Geometry: Bind the hit shader program. Pass the MVP matrix as a uniform variable to the shader program. Draw the cube geometry using the hit shader program. 4. Shader Execution: The shader consists of a Vertex Shader, a Geometry Shader, and a Fragment Shader. The Vertex Shader passes vertex positions to the geometry shader. The Geometry Shader receives the triangle vertices, computes the intersection of the view ray with the triangle plane, and outputs the intersection point as a single point primitive. The position is transformed into clip space and written to glPosition to ensure correct depth testing. The world-space intersection coordinates are passed to the fragment shader as varying/interpolated values. The Fragment Shader receives the interpolated world-space intersection coordinates and writes them to the output color buffer (the hit texture). Since the depth test is enabled and the geometry shader outputs points at the correct depth, only the closest intersection (front or back) is written per pixel. 5. Repeat: Repeat steps 1-4 for the back hit texture by toggling the mbFront flag to false. Formulas: Ray Definition: For a pixel at screen coordinates (u, v), the view ray origin \mathbf{o} and direction \mathbf{d} in world space are derived from the inverse projection and view matrices. The geometry shader typically computes the intersection of this ray with the triangle plane defined by vertices \mathbf{v}0, \mathbf{v}1, \mathbf{v}2. Plane Intersection: Given a triangle plane with normal \mathbf{n} and a point \mathbf{p}0 on the plane, the intersection distance t along the ray \mathbf{o} + t\mathbf{d} is: t = \frac{(\mathbf{p}0 - \mathbf{o}) \cdot \mathbf{n}}{\mathbf{d} \cdot \mathbf{n}} The intersection point is \mathbf{p}{hit} = \mathbf{o} + t\mathbf{d}. Depth Writing: The geometry shader must transform \mathbf{p}{hit} into clip space to set glPosition, ensuring the depth buffer correctly resolves occlusions between front and back faces if they were rendered simultaneously (though they are rendered separately here) or between multiple triangles. Parameters: mbFront: Boolean flag. true for entry points, false for exit points. MVP: Model-View-Projection matrix uniform. Width, Height: Resolution of the hit textures. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Depth Buffer Precision: The depth buffer is cleared along with the color buffer, but the depth test is enabled, requiring correct depth writing from the geometry shader. Using GLDEPTHCOMPONENT16 may lead to precision issues for large bounding boxes or small depth differences. Degenerate Triangles: Ensure the cube geometry does not produce degenerate triangles that could cause undefined behavior in the geometry shader. Ray-Box Tangency: Rays that are tangent to the box edges or corners may produce unstable intersection results. The rasterization approach handles this via depth testing, but precision limits may cause flickering or missed hits. Face Culling: Incorrect culling configuration (e.g., culling both front and back) will result in empty hit textures. The culling mode must be explicitly set based on the desired hit type. Shader Compilation: Ensure the hit shader program is correctly compiled and linked. Shader compilation errors should be checked and reported. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def renderhittextures(cubevertices, cubeindices, mvpmatrix, width, height, frontflag): """ Renders the front or back hit textures for ray-box intersection. Args: cubevertices: Array of vertex positions for a unit cube. cubeindices: Array of triangle indices. mvpmatrix: 4x4 Model-View-Projection matrix. width: Width of the output texture. height: Height of the output texture. frontflag: Boolean, True for front (entry) hits, False for back (exit) hits. Returns: hittexture: 2D texture containing the intersection points. """ # 1. Create and configure FBO fbo = createframebuffer() hittexture = create2dtexture(width, height, format="GLRGBA16F") depthbuffer = createrenderbuffer(width, height, format="GLDEPTHCOMPONENT16") bindframebuffer(fbo) attachtexturetoattachment(fbo, "GLCOLORATTACHMENT0", hittexture) attachrenderbuffertoattachment(fbo, "GLDEPTHATTACHMENT", depthbuffer) clearbuffers("GLCOLORBUFFERBIT | GLDEPTHBUFFERBIT") # 2. Configure rasterization state enable("GLCULLFACE") enable("GLDEPTHTEST") if frontflag: setcullface("GLBACK") else: setcullface("GLFRONT") setdepthfunc("GLLEQUAL") # 3. Bind and use hit shader program shader = loadshaderprogram(vertexshadercode, geometryshadercode, fragmentshadercode) useshader(shader) setuniformmatrix4(shader, "mvpmatrix", mvpmatrix) # 4. Draw cube geometry drawelements("GLTRIANGLES", cubeindices) # 5. Unbind FBO bindframebuffer(0) return hittexture This method determines the 3D entry and exit points of view rays intersecting a volume’s bounding box by rasterizing the box geometry to textures, thereby avoiding procedural intersection calculations in the fragment shader. It sets apart from analytical ray-box intersection tests by leveraging the GPU's parallel rasterization pipeline to generate ray setup data as a byproduct of rendering a simple color cube. Unlike the parent method which uses geometry shaders to output hit positions, this approach relies on standard vertex/fragment pipelines with face culling to separate front and back intersections. Time Complexity: O(N) where N is the number of pixels in the viewport. The cost is dominated by the rasterization of the cube geometry, which is constant per frame regardless of scene complexity. Memory Complexity: O(W \times H) for the hit textures and depth buffer, where W and H are the viewport dimensions. Measured Performance: Performance depends on the GPU's rasterization speed and the resolution of the hit textures. For high-resolution viewports, the cost can be significant. However, it is generally faster than per-ray analytical intersection tests for large numbers of rays. Scaling: Scales linearly with viewport resolution. Does not scale with scene complexity (number of volumes) as it only renders the bounding box. Strengths: Avoids complex ray-box intersection math in shaders. Leverages GPU parallelism for ray setup. Simple to implement using standard OpenGL features. Limitations: Requires two passes (front and back) or a more complex single-pass approach. Precision issues with depth buffer can affect accuracy. Only works for axis-aligned boxes (or requires transformation to align with axes). Dependent on OpenGL geometry shaders, which may not be available or performant on all hardware (e.g., mobile GPUs). When to Use: Suitable for volume rendering applications where ray-box intersection is a bottleneck and the bounding boxes are axis-aligned. Best for desktop GPUs with robust geometry shader support. When Not to Use: Not suitable for mobile GPUs without geometry shader support. Not ideal for non-axis-aligned boxes without additional transformation overhead. This method is implemented in the VRCUDA project, an unofficial implementation of volume rendering using CUDA and OpenGL interoperability. It was developed to optimize the ray-box intersection step in volume rendering pipelines by offloading the computation to the GPU's rasterization hardware. The technique is particularly useful in real-time volume rendering applications where performance is critical. franjaviersans/VRCUDA, https://github.com/franjaviersans/VRCUDA, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial)

name: Two-Pass Ray Entry/Exit Determination
head: Krüger and Westermann approach, Object-order ray setup, Rasterize bounding box, Rasterized Bounding Box Ray Setup, Ray Setup Pass, Ray casting setup rendering, Two-Pass Rasterization Intersection, Two-Pass Raycasting with Back-Face Depth Buffering
body: This method determines the 3D entry and exit points of view rays intersecting a volume’s bounding box by rasterizing the box geometry to textures, thereby avoiding procedural intersection calculations in the fragment shader. It sets apart from analytical ray-box intersection tests by leveraging the GPU's parallel rasterization pipeline to generate ray setup data (origins and directions) as a byproduct of rendering a simple color cube. Unlike the parent method which uses geometry shaders to output hit positions, this approach relies on standard vertex/fragment pipelines with face culling to separate front and back intersections. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: A unit cube (or scaled bounding box) representing the volume boundaries; the concatenated World-View-Projection matrix (M{WVP}); the camera position in world space (P{cam}); and the volume texture dimensions. Outputs: Two textures storing the 3D texture coordinates of the ray entry point and the ray exit point for every pixel. From these, the ray direction is derived. Data Structures: 1. Bounding Box Geometry: A cube with 8 vertices. In model space, vertices are typically in the range [-0.5, 0.5]^3 or [0, 1]^3. Each vertex is assigned a color equal to its 3D texture coordinate (e.g., vertex at (0,0,0) has color (0,0,0), vertex at (1,1,1) has color (1,1,1)). 2. Ray Setup Textures: Two 2D textures (Resolution: W \times H, matching the screen) to store the 3D coordinates. 3. Constant Buffer: Contains the M{WVP} matrix. Numbered Steps: 1. Prepare Geometry: Create a cube mesh. Assign vertex colors corresponding to the volume's texture coordinate space. If the volume texture coordinates are [0,1]^3, map the cube's corners accordingly: (0,0,0) is black, (1,0,0) is red, (0,1,0) is green, (0,0,1) is blue, etc.. 2. Pass 1: Determine Exit Point (Back Faces): Enable face culling to cull front faces (GLFRONT or equivalent). Render the cube to the "Exit Point" texture. The fragment shader outputs the interpolated vertex color (which represents the 3D texture coordinate of the intersection) as RGB, with alpha set to 1.0. Because front faces are culled, the depth buffer retains the farthest intersection (the exit point) for each ray. 3. Pass 2: Determine Entry Point (Front Faces) and Compute Direction: Disable face culling or enable culling to cull back faces (GLBACK). Render the cube to the "Entry Point" texture. The fragment shader outputs the interpolated vertex color (entry point texture coordinate) as RGB. In some implementations, Pass 2 reads the Exit Point texture from Pass 1. The fragment shader computes the direction vector D = P{exit} - P{entry} and stores the direction in a separate texture or computes it on-the-fly during the main raycasting pass. 4. Compute Ray Direction: For each pixel, retrieve the entry point texture coordinate T{entry} and exit point texture coordinate T{exit} from the setup textures. The ray direction in texture space is D{tex} = T{exit} - T{entry}. Note that T{entry} and T{exit} are in normalized texture coordinates [0,1]^3. 5. Main Raycasting Pass: Use the entry point and direction to traverse the volume. Accumulate color and opacity along the ray using the volume rendering equation. Formulas: Vertex Shader Transformation: Pos{clip} = M{WVP} \times Pos{model} Where Pos{model} is the vertex position in model space. Texture Coordinate Mapping (if model space is [-0.5, 0.5]): T{xyz} = Pos{model}.xyz + (0.5, 0.5, 0.5) This shifts coordinates to [0.0, 1.0]. Ray Direction: D = P{exit} - P{entry} Where P{exit} and P{entry} are the 3D texture coordinates retrieved from the setup textures. Volume Rendering Equation (Discrete): C \approx \sum{i=0}^{n-1} \left( (1 - \alphai) \sum{j=0}^{i-1} (1 - \alphaj) \alphai ci \right) Where \alphai is opacity, ci is color, and n is the number of samples. Parameters: Matrix M{WVP}: Concatenated World-View-Projection matrix. Must be updated every frame to reflect camera movement. Culling Mode: GLFRONT for exit point pass, GLBACK or none for entry point pass. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Depth Buffer: The method relies on the depth buffer to resolve front/back intersections. Ensure the depth buffer is cleared and enabled correctly between passes. Orthographic vs. Perspective: The two-pass method works for both. In orthographic projection, the entry and exit points are simply the front and back faces of the box along the view direction. In perspective, they are the intersections with the near and far clipping planes of the box. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def setuprayentryexit(screenwidth, screenheight, volumebbox, mwvp): # Pass 1: Render back faces to get exit point texture coordinates exittexture = createtexture(screenwidth, screenheight, format=RGB32F) bindfbo(exittexture) cleardepthbuffer() enableculling() setcullface(FRONT) # Cull front faces, render back faces rendercube(mwvp) # Vertices colored by texture coordinates in [0,1]^3 exittex = readfbo() # Pass 2: Render front faces to get entry point texture coordinates entrytexture = createtexture(screenwidth, screenheight, format=RGB32F) bindfbo(entrytexture) cleardepthbuffer() enableculling() setcullface(BACK) # Cull back faces, render front faces rendercube(mwvp) entrytex = readfbo() return entrytex, exittex def computeraydirection(entrytex, exittex, x, y): tentry = sampletexture(entrytex, x, y) # RGB vector in [0,1]^3 texit = sampletexture(exittex, x, y) # RGB vector in [0,1]^3 return texit - tentry Computes intersections analytically in the fragment shader. Simpler to implement but more computationally expensive per pixel. Choose when memory bandwidth for setup textures is a bottleneck or when the volume shape is not a simple box. Uses geometry shaders to output ray data directly from primitive assembly. Avoids the need for two rasterization passes but requires hardware support for geometry shaders and may have higher overhead for simple boxes. Choose when using modern OpenGL/DirectX and avoiding FBO binds is desired [Parent]. Time Complexity: O(W \times H) for the setup passes (rasterizing a constant-size cube) plus O(W \times H \times N) for the main raycasting pass, where N is the number of samples per ray. The setup cost is negligible compared to the traversal. Measured Performance: The rasterization setup is extremely fast, leveraging the GPU's fixed-function rasterizer. It avoids the overhead of branch-heavy procedural intersection tests in the fragment shader. Strengths: Simple to implement on older GPUs that lack advanced shader features. Efficient use of parallel rasterization hardware. Independent of projection type (orthographic or perspective). Limitations: Requires two additional render passes and FBO binds. Only works for convex, box-like volumes. When to use: When the volume is axis-aligned or can be tightly bounded by a box, and when procedural intersection is too slow or complex. Ideal for real-time raycasting on GPUs with limited shader complexity. When not to use: For non-convex volumes, or when memory bandwidth is extremely constrained and FBO binds are costly. Also less suitable if the volume is not box-shaped. The method was introduced by Krüger and Westermann in 2003 as an efficient way to perform volume raycasting on GPUs by leveraging rasterization. It was developed as an alternative to procedural ray-box intersection, which placed a heavy load on fragment shaders. The technique has been widely adopted in GPU-based volume rendering pipelines, particularly in early implementations of real-time raycasting.
