name: Ray-OBB Intersection Test
head: OBB slab test, Ray-AABB intersection (OBB variant), Ray-Oriented Bounding Box (OBB) Intersection, Slab method for Oriented Bounding Box
body: The Ray-OBB Intersection Test determines if a ray intersects an Oriented Bounding Box (OBB) and computes the distance to the nearest intersection point. It extends the slab method by projecting the ray onto the OBB's local axes to compute intersection intervals (slabs) along each axis. Unlike Ray-box intersection which assumes axis alignment, this method handles arbitrary orientations by testing intersection with pairs of parallel planes perpendicular to the OBB's local axes. Inputs: Ray origin \mathbf{O} and direction \mathbf{D}. OBB defined by its world-space position \mathbf{P}, local axes \mathbf{X}, \mathbf{Y}, \mathbf{Z} (unit vectors, columns of the transformation matrix), and bounds aabb\min[i] and aabb\max[i] along each local axis. Parallelism threshold \epsilon = 0.001. Outputs: Boolean indicating intersection. If intersecting, the distance t{min} to the nearest intersection point along the ray. Data Structures: The OBB is represented by a transformation matrix where columns 0, 1, 2 correspond to the X, Y, Z local axes respectively. The box bounds are defined by minimum and maximum values along each local axis, aabb\min[i] and aabb\max[i]. Steps: 1. Initialization: Set t{min} = 0.0 and t{max} = 100000.0. Compute the vector from the ray origin to the OBB position: \mathbf{delta} = \mathbf{P} - \mathbf{O}. 2. Iterate over local axes: For each axis i \in \{X, Y, Z\}: a. Extract the local axis vector \mathbf{axis} from the transformation matrix columns. b. Compute the projection of the delta vector onto the axis: e = \mathbf{axis} \cdot \mathbf{delta}. c. Compute the projection of the ray direction onto the axis: f = \mathbf{axis} \cdot \mathbf{D}. d. Non-parallel case: If |f| > \epsilon: i. Compute the entry and exit distances for the slab: t1 = (e + aabb\min[i]) / f and t2 = (e + aabb\max[i]) / f. ii. Ensure t1 \le t2 by swapping if necessary. iii. Update the global interval: t{max} = \min(t{max}, t2) and t{min} = \max(t{min}, t1). iv. If t{max} < t{min}, the ray misses the box; return false. e. Parallel case: If |f| \le \epsilon (ray is parallel to the slab planes): i. Check if the ray origin offset lies outside the slab bounds: (-e + aabb\min[i] > 0.0) OR (-e + aabb\max[i] < 0.0). ii. If either condition is true, the ray is outside the slab; return false. 3. Result: If the loop completes without early exit, an intersection exists. Set the intersection distance to t{min} and return true. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def rayobbintersection(rayorigin, raydirection, obbposition, obbaxes, obbmin, obbmax, epsilon=0.001): tmin = 0.0 tmax = 100000.0 delta = obbposition - rayorigin for i in range(3): axis = obbaxes[i] e = dot(axis, delta) f = dot(axis, raydirection) if abs(f) > epsilon: t1 = (e + obbmin[i]) / f t2 = (e + obbmax[i]) / f if t1 > t2: t1, t2 = t2, t1 if t2 < tmax: tmax = t2 if t1 > tmin: tmin = t1 if tmin > tmax: return False, None else: if (-e + obbmin[i] > 0.0) or (-e + obbmax[i] < 0.0): return False, None return True, tmin Parameters: \epsilon = 0.001: Threshold for determining if the ray is parallel to the OBB axis. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Ray Parallel to Axis: If the ray direction is parallel to the slab planes, division by zero is avoided by checking |f| \le \epsilon. The ray must pass through the slab's extent in the perpendicular direction; otherwise, it misses. Sign Conventions: The parallel case condition (-e + aabb\min > 0) \lor (-e + aabb\max < 0) depends on the specific definition of aabb\min and aabb\max relative to the axis direction. The method is derived from the slab method for AABBs, extended to oriented boxes by using the box's local axes for projection. abhishektrip/SliceBasedVolumeRendering, https://github.com/abhishektrip/SliceBasedVolumeRendering, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial)

name: AABB Intersection via Face Traversal
head: Ray-AABB Intersection (Face-by-Face), Ray::intersectAABB, Ray::intersectAABBFaces, aabbIntersectBack, aabbIntersectFront
body: AABB Intersection via Face Traversal is a method to determine the entry (front) and exit (back) points of a ray intersecting an Axis-Aligned Bounding Box (AABB) by explicitly testing the ray against each of the six faces of the box. Unlike the standard slab method which computes intersection intervals along axes, this approach decomposes the AABB into six planar faces and performs individual ray-face intersection tests. It is distinguished from its siblings by its explicit geometric decomposition into faces and triangles, making it conceptually simpler but computationally more expensive than the slab method. Inputs: Ray: Defined by origin O and direction D. The direction is assumed to be normalized. AABB: Defined by its minimum corner B{min} and maximum corner B{max}, or equivalently by its 8 vertices. Outputs: Front intersection: The closest intersection point (minimum t) and the corresponding surface normal. Back intersection: The furthest intersection point (maximum t) and the corresponding surface normal. Boolean status indicating whether an intersection occurred. The implementation relies on specific structures to represent the geometry and the ray: 1. Ray: origin: A 3D vector (rayvec3) representing the ray's starting point. dir: A 3D vector (rayvec3) representing the ray's direction. It must be normalized. 2. Face Representation: Method 1 (Vertex-based): A Face struct contains 4 vertices (v0, v1, v2, v3) representing the corners of the quad face. Each face is treated as two triangles: (v0, v1, v2) and (v2, v1, v3). Method 2 (Corner-based): An AABBFaces structure stores an array of 6 pairs. Each pair consists of: faceMin: A 3D vector (rayvec3) representing the minimum corner of the face. faceOpposite: A 2D vector (rayvec2) representing the opposite corner's coordinates along the two axes parallel to the face plane. 3. Parameters: maxDist: An optional early-exit threshold. If the closest intersection distance exceeds this value, the ray is considered non-intersecting for practical purposes. Construct the 6 faces of the AABB from its dimensions or vertices. If using vertices, define the 8 vertices of the AABB based on dimensions XDIM, YDIM, ZDIM. Create 6 Face objects, each representing one of the 6 planes of the AABB. Alternatively, populate the AABBFaces array with the min and opposite corners for each of the 6 faces. For a given face, determine if the ray intersects it. Parallelism Check: Check if the ray is parallel to the face's normal axis. Let axis be the normal direction of the face (e.g., x, y, or z). parallel = |D{axis}| < \epsilon where \epsilon = 1.0 \times 10^{-8}. If parallel, return RayRelation::Parallel (no intersection). Intersection Parameter Calculation: Compute the parameter t (rayCoef) along the ray where it intersects the plane of the face: t = \frac{B{min, axis} - O{axis}}{D{axis}} where B{min, axis} is the coordinate of the face along the normal axis. Early Exit: If t < 0, the intersection is behind the ray origin. Return None or false. Point Verification: Calculate the intersection point P: P{axis} = B{min, axis} P{other} = O{other} + t \cdot D{other} where other refers to the two axes parallel to the face plane. Check if P lies within the bounds of the face: faceMin{other} \le P{other} \le faceOpposite{other} If this condition holds for both parallel axes, the ray intersects the face. Triangle Decomposition (Alternative): If using the vertex-based Face struct, split the quad face into two triangles: (v0, v1, v2) and (v2, v1, v3). Use a standard ray-triangle intersection algorithm (e.g., Möller–Trumbore) for each triangle. Find the closest intersection. 1. Initialize t{min} = \infty (or FLTMAX) and hit = false. 2. Iterate through all 6 faces. 3. For each face, perform the Ray-Face Intersection Test. 4. If an intersection exists at parameter tm: Update t{min} = \min(t{min}, tm). Set hit = true. 5. If hit is true, the front intersection is at t = t{min}. 6. (Optional) If t{min} > maxDist, return false. Find the furthest intersection. 1. Initialize t{max} = -\infty (or FLTMIN) and hit = false. 2. Iterate through all 6 faces. 3. For each face, perform the Ray-Face Intersection Test. 4. If an intersection exists at parameter tm: Update t{max} = \max(t{max}, tm). Set hit = true. 5. If hit is true, the back intersection is at t = t{max}. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def rayfaceintersect(rayorigin, raydir, facemin, faceopposite2d, axisindex): """ Tests intersection of a ray with a single AABB face. Args: rayorigin: (x, y, z) tuple raydir: (x, y, z) tuple, assumed normalized facemin: (x, y, z) tuple, the corner of the face on the normal axis faceopposite2d: (u, v) tuple, the opposite corner's coordinates on the other two axes axisindex: 0 for X, 1 for Y, 2 for Z. The index of the normal axis. Returns: t: distance to intersection if valid, else None """ # Extract components ox, oy, oz = rayorigin dx, dy, dz = raydir # Get the axis value for origin and direction originval = [ox, oy, oz][axisindex] dirval = [dx, dy, dz][axisindex] # Parallelism check if abs(dirval) < 1.0e-8: return None # Calculate t faceval = facemin[axisindex] t = (faceval - originval) / dirval # Check if behind ray if t < 0: return None # Calculate intersection point on the other two axes # Determine the indices of the other two axes otheraxes = [i for i in range(3) if i != axisindex] pother = [] for i, axis in enumerate(otheraxes): pval = rayorigin[axis] + t raydir[axis] pother.append(pval) # Check bounds # faceopposite2d contains the max bounds for the other two axes relative to facemin # Note: facemin provides the min bounds for all axes. # The faceopposite2d provides the max bounds for the parallel axes. for i, axis in enumerate(otheraxes): minbound = facemin[axis] maxbound = faceopposite2d[i] if not (minbound <= pother[i] <= maxbound): return None return t def intersectaabbfaces(rayorigin, raydir, bboxmin, bboxmax, maxdist=None): """ Finds front and back intersections of a ray with an AABB by testing 6 faces. Args: rayorigin: (x, y, z) tuple raydir: (x, y, z) tuple, assumed normalized bboxmin: (x, y, z) tuple bboxmax: (x, y, z) tuple maxdist: Optional float threshold for early exit Returns: (frontt, backt) or (None, None) if no intersection """ # Define the 6 faces # Each face is defined by its normal axis, the min corner on that axis, # and the opposite corner's coordinates on the other two axes. faces = [] # X faces faces.append({'axis': 0, 'min': (bboxmin[0], bboxmin[1], bboxmin[2]), 'opp2d': (bboxmax[1], bboxmax[2])}) faces.append({'axis': 0, 'min': (bboxmax[0], bboxmin[1], bboxmin[2]), 'opp2d': (bboxmax[1], bboxmax[2])}) # Y faces faces.append({'axis': 1, 'min': (bboxmin[0], bboxmin[1], bboxmin[2]), 'opp2d': (bboxmax[0], bboxmax[2])}) faces.append({'axis': 1, 'min': (bboxmin[0], bboxmax[1], bboxmin[2]), 'opp2d': (bboxmax[0], bboxmax[2])}) # Z faces faces.append({'axis': 2, 'min': (bboxmin[0], bboxmin[1], bboxmin[2]), 'opp2d': (bboxmax[0], bboxmax[1])}) faces.append({'axis': 2, 'min': (bboxmin[0], bboxmin[1], bboxmax[2]), 'opp2d': (bboxmax[0], bboxmax[1])}) # Front Intersection tmin = float('inf') hitfront = False for face in faces: t = rayfaceintersect(rayorigin, raydir, face['min'], face['opp2d'], face['axis']) if t is not None: if t < tmin: tmin = t hitfront = True if maxdist is not None and tmin > maxdist: return None, None # Back Intersection tmax = float('-inf') hitback = False for face in faces: t = rayfaceintersect(rayorigin, raydir, face['min'], face['opp2d'], face['axis']) if t is not None: if t > tmax: tmax = t hitback = True if hitfront: return tmin, tmax else: return None, None Parallel Rays: If the ray direction is parallel to a face's normal axis, division by zero occurs in the t calculation. This is handled by checking if |D{axis}| < \epsilon (where \epsilon = 1.0 \times 10^{-8}). If parallel, the face is skipped. Precision: The method relies on floating-point comparisons for bounds checking (min \le P \le max). Degenerate boxes (zero volume) or rays grazing edges may suffer from precision issues. Efficiency: This method is less efficient than the standard slab method because it performs 6 separate intersection tests (or 12 triangle tests if decomposed) instead of 3 interval calculations. It is explicitly noted as a current limitation in some implementations where "ray to axis aligned rectangle" is used instead of optimized ray-AABB. Normalization: The parameter t represents distance only if the ray direction is normalized. The code assumes normalization. Time Complexity: O(1), specifically 6 face intersection tests. Each test involves a constant number of arithmetic operations. Memory Complexity: O(1), requiring storage for a few vectors and scalars. Performance: Slower than the slab method due to the higher number of operations and potential branching. The explicit face traversal avoids the branchless optimizations possible in slab methods but is more robust to non-standard bounding box representations. Strengths: Conceptually simple; easily extensible to non-axis-aligned boxes (OBB) by transforming the ray or faces; useful when face normals are explicitly needed. Limitations: Computationally expensive compared to slab methods; sensitive to parallel rays; requires careful handling of floating-point precision. When to use: When face normals are required for shading or when the bounding box is not strictly axis-aligned (though OBB tests are more common in that case); for debugging or educational purposes. When not to use: In performance-critical paths where the slab method is preferred. This method is derived from basic ray-triangle intersection principles applied to the faces of an AABB. It is commonly found in educational graphics implementations and early-stage voxel engines where simplicity and explicit geometric handling are prioritized over raw performance. The specific implementation details, such as the use of glm vectors and the AABBFaces structure, are seen in the VoxelCore engine. The approach is also referenced in academic projects like the CSE-333 Computer Graphics Volume Ray Casting project. name: Segment-Box Collision Detection with Radius
head: Segment-Box Collision with Spherical Radius, Capsule-Box Intersection (approximate)
body: Determines if a line segment defined by endpoints a and b intersects an axis-aligned box defined by lower corner lo and upper corner hi, considering a spherical radius r around the segment. It sets itself apart from standard ray-box intersection by treating the segment as a capsule (cylinder with hemispherical caps) rather than an infinitely thin line, allowing for collision detection with thickness. Inputs: Segment endpoints: a, b \in \mathbb{R}^3 Box bounds: lo, hi \in \mathbb{R}^3 (where loi \le hii for all axes i) Radius: r \in \mathbb{R} Outputs: Boolean: true if the segment-box collision occurs, false otherwise. Data Structures: times: Array of 8 floats, initialized to \{0, 1, 0, 0, 0, 0, 0, 0\}. count: Integer, initialized to 2. Steps: 1. Delta Calculation: Compute \delta = b - a. 2. Quick Rejection: Compute the separation vector s = \max(lo - \max(a, b), \min(a, b) - hi, 0). If \|s\|^2 \ge r^2, return false. Note: \max(a, b) and \min(a, b) are component-wise maximum and minimum operations. 3. Plane Intersection Times: Initialize times array with \{0, 1\} and count = 2. For each axis i \in \{0, 1, 2\}: If |\deltai| > \epsilon (where \epsilon = 10^{-12}), calculate intersection times with planes loi and hii: t{lo} = \frac{loi - ai}{\deltai}, \quad t{hi} = \frac{hii - ai}{\deltai} If 0 < t < 1, append t to times and increment count. 4. Sorting: Sort the first count elements of the times array in ascending order. 5. Interval Checking: Iterate i from 1 to count - 1: Let t{left} = \text{times}[i-1] and t{right} = \text{times}[i]. Calculate midpoint parameter t{mid} = (t{left} + t{right}) \times 0.5. Calculate midpoint point p{mid} = a + \delta \times t{mid}. Calculate clamped point p{bound} = \text{clamp}(p{mid}, lo, hi) (component-wise clamp). Calculate slope vector v = \delta \times \text{notEqual}(p{mid}, p{bound}). If p{mid} equals p{bound} component-wise, v becomes zero vector. Calculate numerator N = v \cdot (a - p{bound}) and denominator D = v \cdot v. If D > 0, calculate t{opt} = \text{clamp}(-N / D, t{left}, t{right}). Else, t{opt} = t{mid}. Calculate candidate point p{cand} = a + \delta \times t{opt}. Calculate distance vector d = p{cand} - \text{clamp}(p{cand}, lo, hi). If \|d\|^2 < r^2, return true. 6. Final Result: If the loop completes without returning true, return false. Pitfalls: Division by zero is avoided by skipping plane intersection calculation if |\deltai| \le 10^{-12}. If the denominator D is zero or negative in the optimization step, the midpoint t{mid} is used as the fallback t value. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def segmentboxcollisionradius(a, b, lo, hi, r): """ Determines if segment a-b intersects box lo-hi with radius r. a, b, lo, hi are tuples/lists of 3 floats. """ # 1. Delta delta = [b[i] - a[i] for i in range(3)] # 2. Quick Rejection # max(a, b) and min(a, b) component-wise maxab = [max(a[i], b[i]) for i in range(3)] minab = [min(a[i], b[i]) for i in range(3)] # separation = max(lo - maxab, minab - hi, 0) separation = [] for i in range(3): val1 = lo[i] - maxab[i] val2 = minab[i] - hi[i] separation.append(max(val1, val2, 0.0)) dotsep = sum(s s for s in separation) if dotsep >= r r: return False # 3. Plane Intersection Times times = [0.0, 1.0] count = 2 epsilon = 1e-12 for i in range(3): if abs(delta[i]) > epsilon: # Intersection with lo[i] tlo = (lo[i] - a[i]) / delta[i] if 0 < tlo < 1: times.append(tlo) count += 1 # Intersection with hi[i] thi = (hi[i] - a[i]) / delta[i] if 0 < thi < 1: times.append(thi) count += 1 # 4. Sort first count elements times[:count] = sorted(times[:count]) # 5. Interval Checking for i in range(1, count): tleft = times[i-1] tright = times[i] tmid = (tleft + tright) 0.5 # pmid = a + delta tmid pmid = [a[j] + delta[j] tmid for j in range(3)] # pbound = clamp(pmid, lo, hi) pbound = [max(lo[j], min(pmid[j], hi[j])) for j in range(3)] # slope = delta notEqual(pmid, pbound) # notEqual is component-wise: 1.0 if pmid[j] != pbound[j] else 0.0 # Note: Floating point equality check. Using a small epsilon for robustness if needed, # but source implies direct comparison. slope = [] for j in range(3): if pmid[j] != pbound[j]: slope.append(delta[j]) else: slope.append(0.0) # numerator = dot(slope, a - pbound) aminuspbound = [a[j] - pbound[j] for j in range(3)] numerator = sum(slope[j] aminuspbound[j] for j in range(3)) # denominator = dot(slope, slope) denominator = sum(s s for s in slope) if denominator > 0: # topt = clamp(-numerator / denominator, tleft, tright) tval = -numerator / denominator topt = max(tleft, min(tval, tright)) else: topt = tmid # pcand = a + delta topt pcand = [a[j] + delta[j] topt for j in range(3)] # distance = pcand - clamp(pcand, lo, hi) pcandclamped = [max(lo[j], min(pcand[j], hi[j])) for j in range(3)] distance = [pcand[j] - pcandclamped[j] for j in range(3)] distsq = sum(d d for d in distance) if distsq < r r: return True return False Time Complexity: O(1) with a small constant factor. The algorithm performs a fixed number of arithmetic operations and sorts at most 8 values. Memory Complexity: O(1). Uses a fixed-size array of 8 floats. Strengths: Handles thick segments (capsules) efficiently. The quick rejection test avoids expensive calculations for distant segments. Limitations: The method approximates the capsule-box intersection by checking specific intervals defined by box plane intersections. It may not cover all edge cases of a true continuous capsule intersection, relying on the midpoint optimization within intervals. When to use: When collision detection requires a non-zero radius for the segment, such as in physics simulations or thick ray casting. When not to use: For infinitely thin rays, standard slab intersection is more efficient and exact. This method is described in the LichtFeld-Studio repository. It is used in the context of volume rendering and ray marching, where primitives need to be tested against rays with a certain thickness or where segment-based collision detection is required for scene geometry. name: Watertight BVH Box Traversal Fix
head: BVH Box Traversal Precision Fix, Robust BVH Ray Traversal with ULP Expansion, Slab Test Zero-Inversion Fix, Treat BVH boxes as closed sets in ray traversal
body: This method fixes a robustness bug in shared slab tests where a ray with a zero direction component lying exactly in the plane of a box face misses the box on one side. It ensures that grazing rays, such as orthographic camera rays landing exactly on a bound, correctly intersect triangles whose edges they touch, by treating BVH boxes as closed sets. Unlike standard slab tests which may compute an empty slab for t > 0 due to zero-inversion artifacts, this fix guarantees consistent intersection decisions for axis-parallel rays on face planes. The method modifies the bounding volume hierarchy (BVH) construction phase to expand all node and instance bounding boxes by one unit in the last place (ULP) outward. This expansion ensures that rays with zero direction components lying exactly on a box face plane are strictly inside the slab, allowing the subsequent watertight triangle test to decide the intersection consistently. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Scene geometry and existing BVH structure. Output: A BVH with expanded bounding boxes. Data Structures: BVH Node/Instance Box: Axis-Aligned Bounding Box (AABB) defined by minimum (x{min}, y{min}, z{min}) and maximum (x{max}, y{max}, z{max}) coordinates. ULP Expansion: The expansion is applied to each coordinate of the AABB. Steps: 1. During BVH construction (SceneAccel.build), for every node and instance bounding box: a. Calculate the ULP of the box's minimum and maximum coordinates. b. Expand the minimum coordinates by subtracting one ULP: x{min} \leftarrow x{min} - \text{ulp}(x{min}), y{min} \leftarrow y{min} - \text{ulp}(y{min}), z{min} \leftarrow z{min} - \text{ulp}(z{min}). c. Expand the maximum coordinates by adding one ULP: x{max} \leftarrow x{max} + \text{ulp}(x{max}), y{max} \leftarrow y{max} + \text{ulp}(y{max}), z{max} \leftarrow z{max} + \text{ulp}(z{max}). 2. Proceed with standard ray traversal using the expanded boxes. Formula: The bug occurs when the slab test computes (hi - o) inv = 0 inv = 0, making the slab appear empty for t > 0. The fix ensures the ray origin o is strictly inside the expanded slab, so (hi - o) inv > 0 for the relevant side. Parameters: Expansion Amount: One ULP (Unit in the Last Place). Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Zero Direction Components: Rays with zero direction components lying exactly in the plane of a box face previously missed the box on one side. Grazing Rays: Straight-down rays along the side of a cube missed the top face's edge that it passes through. Orthographic Camera Rays: Rays landing exactly on a bound previously skipped triangles whose edges they touched. Precision: The fix relies on floating-point precision; the ULP expansion must be calculated correctly for the specific coordinate values. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def expandboxbyulp(box): """ Expands an AABB by one ULP in all directions. box: tuple of (minx, miny, minz, maxx, maxy, maxz) """ minx, miny, minz, maxx, maxy, maxz = box # Calculate ULP for each coordinate # Note: ulp(x) is the distance between x and the next representable float ulpminx = ulp(minx) ulpminy = ulp(miny) ulpminz = ulp(minz) ulpmaxx = ulp(maxx) ulpmaxy = ulp(maxy) ulpmaxz = ulp(maxz) # Expand the box newminx = minx - ulpminx newminy = miny - ulpminy newminz = minz - ulpminz newmaxx = maxx + ulpmaxx newmaxy = maxy + ulpmaxy newmaxz = maxz + ulpmaxz return (newminx, newminy, newminz, newmaxx, newmaxy, newmaxz) def buildsceneaccel(scene): """ Builds the scene acceleration structure with watertight BVH boxes. """ bvh = BVH() for node in scene.nodes: # Get original bounding box originalbox = node.getboundingbox() # Expand by one ULP expandedbox = expandboxbyulp(originalbox) # Set the expanded box to the node node.setboundingbox(expandedbox) bvh.addnode(node) return bvh Time Complexity: BVH construction time increases slightly due to ULP calculation and box expansion, but traversal cost is unchanged. Memory Complexity: No additional memory is required for the BVH structure itself, as the expansion is applied to existing box coordinates. Performance: The fix does not impact traversal performance; the GPU path tracer reads the same boxes. Strengths: Fixes robustness issues with grazing rays and axis-parallel rays on face planes without changing golden images or reference outputs for other rays. Limitations: Only affects rays with zero direction components lying exactly on box face planes; no other rays are affected. This fix was introduced in the Aether3D project (commit b43ebc2) to address a robustness bug in the shared slab test. It was developed to ensure that watertight triangle tests can correctly decide intersections for grazing rays, which previously missed boxes due to precision errors in the slab test. The fix is part of Stage 10 of the Aether3D project, which focuses on scene intelligence and spatial queries. name: Ray-Cube Intersection
head: Ray-Cube Slab Intersection, CubeCast, RayCubeSlabsIntersection
body: This method calculates the precise entry (t0) and exit (t1) intersection points of a ray with an axis-aligned cube defined by lower and upper bounds. It solves the problem of determining the exact boundary hit for ray-casting or ray-marching within voxel grids, providing the entry position and the exit face index required for subsequent traversal or shading. Unlike Ray-AABB Intersection (Slab/Min-Max), which computes the interval [t{min}, t{max}] for traversal logic, this method explicitly returns the 3D intersection coordinates and the specific face index exited, which is critical for hardware-accelerated voxel rendering where the first solid voxel must be identified. Inputs: Ray origin: \mathbf{r}{pos} (3D vector) Ray direction: \mathbf{r}{dir} (3D vector) Cube lower bound: \mathbf{d}{lower} (3D vector) Cube upper bound: \mathbf{d}{upper} (3D vector) Outputs: Entry hit: Structure containing position \mathbf{t}0 and entry face index \mathbf{inface} Exit hit: Structure containing position \mathbf{t}1 and exit face index \mathbf{outface} Data Structures: Hit: A structure containing: pos: 3D vector (\mathbf{t}0 or \mathbf{t}1) face: Integer index representing the face normal direction Lookup Tables: Two 2 \times 3 integer lookup tables map the axis index and ray direction sign to a face normal index. outfaces[axis][direction]: Returns the exit face index. direction is 0 if \mathbf{r}{dir}[axis] < 0 (negative face), else 1 (positive face). infaces[axis][direction]: Returns the entry face index. direction is 0 if \mathbf{r}{dir}[axis] < 0 (positive face), else 1 (negative face). Steps for Exit Point (t1): 1. Compute the intersection parameter vector \mathbf{Q}v for the upper bound: \mathbf{Q}v = \frac{\mathbf{d}{upper} - \mathbf{r}{pos}}{\mathbf{r}{dir}} Component-wise: Qv[i] = \frac{d{upper}[i] - r{pos}[i]}{r{dir}[i]} for i \in \{0, 1, 2\}. 2. Identify the axis index i corresponding to the minimum component of \mathbf{Q}v: i = \text{argmin}(\mathbf{Q}v) 3. Retrieve the scalar intersection distance Q = Qv[i]. 4. Calculate the 3D intersection point: \mathbf{t}1 = \mathbf{r}{pos} + \mathbf{r}{dir} \cdot Q 5. Determine the exit face \mathbf{outface} using the lookup table outfaces[i][direction], where direction is 0 if \mathbf{r}{dir}[i] < 0 and 1 otherwise. 6. Clamp the intersection point \mathbf{t}1 to the exact boundary of the cube by setting the i-th component of \mathbf{t}1 to \mathbf{d}{upper}[i]. 7. Return the hit structure containing \mathbf{t}1 and \mathbf{outface}. Steps for Entry Point (t0): 1. Compute the intersection parameter vector \mathbf{Q}v for the lower bound: \mathbf{Q}v = \frac{\mathbf{d}{lower} - \mathbf{r}{pos}}{\mathbf{r}{dir}} 2. Coalesce NaN values in \mathbf{Q}v to negative infinity to handle division by zero or invalid inputs. 3. Identify the axis index i corresponding to the maximum component of \mathbf{Q}v: i = \text{argmax}(\mathbf{Q}v) 4. Retrieve the scalar intersection distance Q = Qv[i]. 5. Calculate the 3D intersection point: \mathbf{t}0 = \mathbf{r}{pos} + \mathbf{r}{dir} \cdot Q 6. Determine the entry face \mathbf{inface} using the lookup table infaces[i][direction], where direction is 0 if \mathbf{r}{dir}[i] < 0 and 1 otherwise. 7. Clamp the intersection point \mathbf{t}0 to the exact boundary of the cube by setting the i-th component of \mathbf{t}0 to \mathbf{d}{lower}[i]. 8. Return the hit structure containing \mathbf{t}0 and \mathbf{inface}. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def mincomponentindex(v): minval = v[0] minidx = 0 if v[1] < minval: minval = v[1] minidx = 1 if v[2] < minval: minidx = 2 return minidx def maxcomponentindex(v): maxval = v[0] maxidx = 0 if v[1] > maxval: maxval = v[1] maxidx = 1 if v[2] > maxval: maxidx = 2 return maxidx def safediv(a, b): if b == 0.0: return float('inf') if a > 0 else float('-inf') return a / b def raycubeintersectionexit(raypos, raydir, dupper): # Step 1: Compute Qv qv = [safediv(dupper[i] - raypos[i], raydir[i]) for i in range(3)] # Pitfall: If any component of Qv is negative, the ray originates outside or points away. if any(q < 0.0 for q in qv): return None, None # Step 2: Identify axis index i for minimum component i = mincomponentindex(qv) # Step 3: Retrieve scalar Q Q = qv[i] # Step 4: Calculate 3D intersection point t1 = [raypos[j] + raydir[j] Q for j in range(3)] # Step 5: Determine exit face # direction is 0 if raydir[i] < 0 (negative face), else 1 (positive face) direction = 0 if raydir[i] < 0 else 1 # Lookup table outfaces[axis][direction] outfaces = [[0, 1], [2, 3], [4, 5]] # X-, X+, Y-, Y+, Z-, Z+ outface = outfaces[i][direction] # Step 6: Clamp t1 to exact boundary t1[i] = dupper[i] return t1, outface def raycubeintersectionentry(raypos, raydir, dlower): # Step 1: Compute Qv qv = [safediv(dlower[i] - raypos[i], raydir[i]) for i in range(3)] # Step 2: Coalesce NaN to -inf qv = [float('-inf') if math.isnan(q) else q for q in qv] # Pitfall: If all components of Qv are negative, the ray does not intersect. if all(q < 0.0 for q in qv): return None, None # Step 3: Identify axis index i for maximum component i = maxcomponentindex(qv) # Step 4: Retrieve scalar Q Q = qv[i] # Step 5: Calculate 3D intersection point t0 = [raypos[j] + raydir[j] Q for j in range(3)] # Step 6: Determine entry face # direction is 0 if raydir[i] < 0 (positive face), else 1 (negative face) per evidence direction = 0 if raydir[i] < 0 else 1 # Lookup table infaces[axis][direction] infaces = [[1, 0], [3, 2], [5, 4]] # X+, X-, Y+, Y-, Z+, Z- inface = infaces[i][direction] # Step 7: Clamp t0 to exact boundary t0[i] = dlower[i] return t0, inface This method performs a Digital Differential Analyzer (DDA) traversal within a single 4 \times 4 \times 4 voxel brick to locate the first solid voxel intersected by a ray. It solves the problem of primary hit resolution in hardware-accelerated voxel rendering, where a coarse bounding volume intersection identifies a candidate brick, but the exact first solid voxel must be determined to handle transparency and fringe cases correctly. Unlike In-Brick DDA for Occlusion, which visits all solid voxels to determine shadowing, this method stops at the first valid hit. It builds on Ray-Cube Intersection by refining the entry point into a specific voxel index and material check. Time Complexity: O(1) per intersection, involving a fixed number of arithmetic operations and comparisons. Memory Complexity: O(1), requiring only a few temporary vectors and lookup tables. Strengths: Provides exact boundary positions and face normals, which are necessary for precise voxel traversal and shading. Handles degenerate cases (ray parallel to axes) via NaN/Infinity coalescing. Limitations: Assumes the ray intersects the cube. If the ray originates inside or misses, the logic must be checked (negative Q). The method does not perform traversal, only intersection. When to use: When the exact entry/exit points and face normals are required, such as in voxel rendering pipelines or precise ray-casting. When not to use: When only the interval [t{min}, t{max}] is needed for traversal logic; use Ray-AABB Intersection (Slab/Min-Max) instead. The method originates from implementations in voxel rendering engines, specifically those dealing with brick-based traversal. name: Ray-Cube Intersection (Brick/Slab)
head: Amanatides-Woo DDA within brick, Hardware Ray Tracing Voxel Primary Hit Resolution
body: This method performs a Digital Differential Analyzer (DDA) traversal within a single 4 \times 4 \times 4 voxel brick to locate the first solid voxel intersected by a ray. It solves the problem of primary hit resolution in hardware-accelerated voxel rendering, where a coarse bounding volume intersection identifies a candidate brick, but the exact first solid voxel must be determined to handle transparency and fringe cases correctly. Unlike In-Brick DDA for Occlusion, which visits all solid voxels to determine shadowing, this method stops at the first valid hit. It builds on Ray-Cube Intersection by refining the entry point into a specific voxel index and material check. Inputs: Ray origin o = (ox, oy, oz) in world coordinates. Ray direction d = (dx, dy, dz), normalized. Brick lower bound bmin (world coordinates of the brick's minimum corner). Time interval [t{lo}, t{hi}] defining the valid traversal range. Boolean flag skiptransparent: if true, transparent materials (e.g., water, glass, turf) are skipped. Brick data structure bi containing voxel materials and occupancy. Outputs: Entry time t of the first solid voxel face. Voxel coordinates firstvox. Surface normal firstnormal. Return value: t if a hit is found, -1.0 if no solid voxel is hit within the interval. Data Structures: brickvoxelidx(x, y, z): Converts local voxel coordinates (x,y,z) \in [0,3]^3 to a linear index. brickvoxelsolid(bi, vi): Returns true if voxel vi in brick bi is occupied. brickvoxelmaterial(bi, vi): Returns the material ID of voxel vi. rtistransparentmat(mat): Returns true if mat is transparent (e.g., IDs 5-12, 18, 35). rtfacenormal(axis, d): Returns the surface normal of the face entered along axis given direction d. Steps: 1. Compute Inverse Direction: Calculate the inverse of the ray direction components, handling zero values to avoid division by zero. inv = \left( \frac{1}{dx}, \frac{1}{dy}, \frac{1}{dz} \right) Where \frac{1}{0} is replaced by a large constant (e.g., 10^{30}). 2. Compute Slab Boundaries: Calculate the entry and exit times for the brick boundaries along each axis. The brick spans from bmin to bmin + 4 in world units. tb0 = (bmin - o) \cdot inv tb1 = (bmin + (4, 4, 4) - o) \cdot inv 3. Calculate Brick Entry and Exit Times: Determine the global entry (t{near}) and exit (t{far}) times for the ray within the brick. te = (\min(tb0x, tb1x), \min(tb0y, tb1y), \min(tb0z, tb1z)) t{near} = \max(tex, tey, tez) t{far} = \min(\max(tb0x, tb1x), \max(tb0y, tb1y), \max(tb0z, tb1z)) 4. Clamp to Interval: Restrict the traversal to the requested time interval [t{lo}, t{hi}]. t = \max(t{near}, t{lo}) t{end} = \min(t{far}, t{hi}) If t > t{end}, return -1.0. 5. Determine Entry Axis: Identify which face of the brick the ray enters through to compute the initial normal. If tey > tex, lastaxis = 1 (Y-axis). Else if tez > \max(tex, tey), lastaxis = 2 (Z-axis). Else, lastaxis = 0 (X-axis). 6. Initialize Voxel Position: Calculate the initial voxel coordinates inside the brick. A small epsilon (10^{-4}) is added to the position to avoid precision issues at boundaries. p = o + d \cdot (t + 10^{-4}) - bmin v = \text{clamp}(\lfloor p \rfloor, (0,0,0), (3,3,3)) 7. Determine Step Directions: Set the step direction for each axis based on the sign of the ray direction. stepx = \text{sign}(dx) stepy = \text{sign}(dy) stepz = \text{sign}(dz) 8. Calculate Boundary Times and Deltas: Compute the time to the next voxel boundary along each axis and the time step between boundaries. t{delta} = |inv| t{max} = t + (boundary\coord - p) \cdot t{delta} Where boundary\coord = v + 1 if step > 0, else v. 9. Traverse Voxels: Loop i from 0 to 15 (since the brick is 4 \times 4 \times 4): Check bounds: If t > t{end}, return -1.0. Get voxel index: vi = \text{brick\voxel\idx}(vx, vy, vz). Check solidity: If brickvoxelsolid(bi, vi) is true AND (skiptransparent is false OR !rtistransparentmat(brickvoxelmaterial(bi, vi))): Set firstvox = v. Set firstnormal = rtfacenormal(lastaxis, d). Return t. Step to next voxel: Find the axis with the smallest t{max}. Update v by adding step to that axis. Update t{max} for that axis by adding t{delta}. Update t to the new t{max} of the stepped axis. Update lastaxis to the stepped axis. 10. No Hit: If the loop completes without finding a solid voxel, return -1.0. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def raycubeintersectionbrickslab(o, d, bmin, tlo, thi, brickdata, skiptransparent): # 1. Compute inverse direction def safeinv(x): return 1e30 if x == 0.0 else 1.0 / x inv = (safeinv(d.x), safeinv(d.y), safeinv(d.z)) # 2. Compute slab boundaries # Brick spans from bmin to bmin + 4 bmax = (bmin.x + 4.0, bmin.y + 4.0, bmin.z + 4.0) tb0 = ((bmin.x - o.x) inv.x, (bmin.y - o.y) inv.y, (bmin.z - o.z) inv.z) tb1 = ((bmax.x - o.x) inv.x, (bmax.y - o.y) inv.y, (bmax.z - o.z) inv.z) # 3. Calculate brick entry and exit times te = (min(tb0.x, tb1.x), min(tb0.y, tb1.y), min(tb0.z, tb1.z)) tnear = max(te.x, max(te.y, te.z)) tfar = min(max(tb0.x, tb1.x), min(max(tb0.y, tb1.y), max(tb0.z, tb1.z))) # 4. Clamp to interval t = max(tnear, tlo) tend = min(tfar, thi) if t > tend: return -1.0, None, None # 5. Determine entry axis if te.y > te.x: lastaxis = 1 elif te.z > max(te.x, te.y): lastaxis = 2 else: lastaxis = 0 # 6. Initialize voxel position # Add epsilon to avoid precision issues p = (o.x + d.x (t + 1e-4) - bmin.x, o.y + d.y (t + 1e-4) - bmin.y, o.z + d.z (t + 1e-4) - bmin.z) v = (max(0, min(3, int(p.x))), max(0, min(3, int(p.y))), max(0, min(3, int(p.z)))) # 7. Determine step directions step = (1 if d.x > 0 else -1 if d.x < 0 else 0, 1 if d.y > 0 else -1 if d.y < 0 else 0, 1 if d.z > 0 else -1 if d.z < 0 else 0) # 8. Calculate boundary times and deltas tdelta = (abs(inv.x), abs(inv.y), abs(inv.z)) # Calculate initial tmax for each axis # tmax is the time to cross the next voxel boundary tmax = (0.0, 0.0, 0.0) # Correct initialization based on Amanatides-Woo logic # boundarycoord is v + 1 if step > 0, else v tmax.x = t + ((v.x + 1.0 if step.x > 0 else v.x) - p.x) tdelta.x tmax.y = t + ((v.y + 1.0 if step.y > 0 else v.y) - p.y) tdelta.y tmax.z = t + ((v.z + 1.0 if step.z > 0 else v.z) - p.z) tdelta.z # 9. Traverse voxels for i in range(16): if t > tend: return -1.0, None, None # Check voxel solidity vi = v.x + v.y 4 + v.z 16 issolid = brickdata[vi] > 0 mat = brickdata[vi + 1024] # Assuming materials stored after occupancy istransparent = 5 <= mat <= 12 or mat == 18 or mat == 35 if issolid and (not skiptransparent or not istransparent): firstvox = v firstnormal = (1 if lastaxis == 0 else 0, 1 if lastaxis == 1 else 0, 1 if lastaxis == 2 else 0) return t, firstvox, firstnormal # Step to next voxel # Find axis with smallest tmax if tmax.x < tmax.y: if tmax.x < tmax.z: axis = 0 else: axis = 2 else: if tmax.y < tmax.z: axis = 1 else: axis = 2 # Update t and tmax for the stepped axis t = tmax[axis] tmax[axis] += tdelta[axis] v = (v.x + step.x if axis == 0 else v.x, v.y + step.y if axis == 1 else v.y, v.z + step.z if axis == 2 else v.z) lastaxis = axis return -1.0, None, None Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision Issues: Near block boundaries, floating-point errors can cause missed hits or incorrect adjacent indices. Adding a small epsilon (10^{-4}) to the position calculation helps mitigate this. Zero Direction Components: The inverse direction must handle zero values to avoid division by zero, typically by returning a large constant. Transparent Materials: The skiptransparent flag allows the method to ignore transparent voxels, which is crucial for correct shadowing and transparency handling. A DDA that visits all solid voxels within a 4 \times 4 \times 4 brick to determine occlusion, unlike this method which stops at the first hit. Uses hardware RT cores for coarse BVH traversal and this method for in-brick resolution, replacing software beam pre-passes. Traverses a voxel grid using two explicit points instead of a ray origin and direction, handling edge cases with higher precision. An occupancy-only query that traces a ray across the entire grid, not just a single brick, supporting arbitrary origins and distances. Time Complexity: O(1) per brick, as the brick size is fixed at 4 \times 4 \times 4 (16 voxels). Memory Complexity: O(1), requiring only a few scalar variables for traversal state. Strengths: Fast primary hit resolution, handles transparency, robust to precision issues with epsilon adjustment. Limitations: Only works within a single brick; requires a coarse intersection step to identify the candidate brick. When to Use: When a ray has already intersected a brick and the first solid voxel needs to be identified for shading or shadowing. When Not to Use: When occlusion of multiple voxels is required (use In-Brick DDA for Occlusion) or when traversing across multiple bricks (use RDV-1 Occupancy Ray Query). This method is based on the Amanatides-Woo DDA algorithm, adapted for voxel bricks in hardware ray tracing. It is commonly used in voxel engines and games for efficient ray-voxel intersection, particularly in the context of shadow rays and primary visibility. The specific implementation described here is from the voxelG project, which focuses on high-performance voxel rendering. mstampfli/voxelG, https://github.com/mstampfli/voxelG, fetched 2026-10-24 (unofficial) max-mapper/voxel-engine, https://github.com/max-mapper/voxel-engine, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial)

name: In-Brick DDA for Occlusion
body: A Digital Differential Analyzer (DDA) that marches through a 4×4×4 voxel brick to determine if any solid voxel occludes a shadow ray. Unlike primary hit resolution which stops at the first intersection, this method visits all solid voxels within the brick to correctly handle transparent or fringe cases. It differs from Hardware Ray Tracing Voxel Occlusion and RDV-1 Occupancy Ray Query by explicitly iterating a fixed number of steps within a single brick rather than relying on hardware acceleration or hierarchical occupancy queries. Inputs and Outputs: Ray origin o and direction dir (vec3<f32>). Brick bounds bmin and bmax (vec3<f32>), where bmax = bmin + vec3<f32>(4.0). Maximum traversal time thi. Brick identifier bi and voxel data accessors brickvoxelidx and brickvoxelsolid. Shadow occlusion check function shadowvoxeloccludes. Output: Boolean true if any solid voxel occludes the ray, false otherwise. Data Structures: The brick is a fixed 4×4×4 grid of voxels. Voxel coordinates v are integers clamped to [0, 3]. brickvoxelidx(x, y, z) maps 3D coordinates to a linear index. brickvoxelsolid(bi, vi) returns true if the voxel at index vi in brick bi is solid. Numbered Steps and Formulas: 1. Compute inverse direction components, handling zero division safely: inv = vec3<f32>(rtsafeinv(dir.x), rtsafeinv(dir.y), rtsafeinv(dir.z)). 2. Compute slab entry/exit times for the brick bounds: tb0 = (bmin - o) inv and tb1 = (bmin + vec3<f32>(4.0) - o) inv. 3. Calculate brick entry tnear and exit tfar times: tnear = max(max(min(tb0.x, tb1.x), min(tb0.y, tb1.y)), min(tb0.z, tb1.z)) and tfar = min(min(max(tb0.x, tb1.x), max(tb0.y, tb1.y)), max(tb0.z, tb1.z)). (Note: corrected tb3.z typo from source to tb0.z). 4. Clamp start time t and end time tend: t = max(tnear, 0.0) and tend = min(tfar, thi). If t > tend, return false. 5. Calculate initial voxel position with an epsilon offset and clamp voxel coordinates: p = o + dir (t + 1e-4) - bmin and v = clamp(vec3<i32>(floor(p)), vec3<i32>(0), vec3<i32>(3)). 6. Determine step direction for each axis: step.x = select(-1, 1, dir.x >= 0.0), step.y = select(-1, 1, dir.y >= 0.0), step.z = select(-1, 1, dir.z >= 0.0). 7. Calculate time deltas tdelta = abs(inv) and initialize per-axis boundary crossing times tmax using standard Amanatides-Woo logic: for each axis a, tmax.a = (bmin.a + (step.a + 1) 0.5 - o.a) inv.a. 8. Loop i from 0 to 15: check bounds v.x < 0 || v.x > 3 (and y, z) and time tcur > tend; if either fails, return false. Get voxel index vi = brickvoxelidx(v.x, v.y, v.z). If brickvoxelsolid(bi, vi) is true, check shadowvoxeloccludes(worldbase + v, m, tcur, o, dir). If true, return true. Step to the next voxel along the axis with the smallest tmax: update v, set tcur = tmax.axis, and advance tmax.axis += tdelta.axis. 9. If loop completes without occlusion, return false. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def inbrickddaocclusion(o, dir, bmin, thi, bi, brickvoxelidx, brickvoxelsolid, shadowvoxeloccludes, worldbase, m): # 1. Inverse direction (handles zero components safely) inv = vec3(1.0 / dir.x if dir.x != 0.0 else float('inf'), 1.0 / dir.y if dir.y != 0.0 else float('inf'), 1.0 / dir.z if dir.z != 0.0 else float('inf')) # 2. Slab entry/exit times tb0 = (bmin - o) inv tb1 = (bmin + vec3(4.0) - o) inv # 3. Brick entry/exit times tnear = max(max(min(tb0.x, tb1.x), min(tb0.y, tb1.y)), min(tb0.z, tb1.z)) tfar = min(min(max(tb0.x, tb1.x), max(tb0.y, tb1.y)), max(tb0.z, tb1.z)) # 4. Clamp to ray segment t = max(tnear, 0.0) tend = min(tfar, thi) if t > tend: return False # 5. Initial voxel position with epsilon offset p = o + dir (t + 1e-4) - bmin v = clamp(floor(p), vec3(0), vec3(3)) # 6. Step direction step = vec3(1 if dir.x >= 0.0 else -1, 1 if dir.y >= 0.0 else -1, 1 if dir.z >= 0.0 else -1) # 7. Delta and initial tmax (Amanatides-Woo standard initialization) tdelta = abs(inv) tmax = vec3(0.0, 0.0, 0.0) if dir.x >= 0.0: tmax.x = (bmin.x + 1.0 - o.x) inv.x else: tmax.x = (bmin.x - o.x) inv.x if dir.y >= 0.0: tmax.y = (bmin.y + 1.0 - o.y) inv.y else: tmax.y = (bmin.y - o.y) inv.y if dir.z >= 0.0: tmax.z = (bmin.z + 1.0 - o.z) inv.z else: tmax.z = (bmin.z - o.z) inv.z tcur = t # 8. Fixed 16-iteration loop for i in range(16): if v.x < 0 or v.x > 3 or v.y < 0 or v.y > 3 or v.z < 0 or v.z > 3: return False if tcur > tend: return False vi = brickvoxelidx(v.x, v.y, v.z) if brickvoxelsolid(bi, vi): if shadowvoxeloccludes(worldbase + v, m, tcur, o, dir): return True # Step along axis with smallest tmax if tmax.x < tmax.y: if tmax.x < tmax.z: v.x += step.x tcur = tmax.x tmax.x += tdelta.x else: v.z += step.z tcur = tmax.z tmax.z += tdelta.z else: if tmax.y < tmax.z: v.y += step.y tcur = tmax.y tmax.y += tdelta.y else: v.z += step.z tcur = tmax.z tmax.z += tdelta.z return False Parameters: Brick size: 4×4×4 voxels. Loop limit: 16 iterations. The source code explicitly caps the traversal at 16 steps rather than visiting all 64 voxels. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Zero direction components: handled by rtsafeinv which returns infinity. Ray not intersecting brick: handled by t > tend check. Voxel coordinates out of bounds: checked at the start of each loop iteration. Precision issues: small epsilon 1e-4 added to ray origin to avoid self-intersection at the entry face. Time Complexity: O(1) per brick, as the loop runs a fixed 16 times. Memory Complexity: O(1) additional memory. Strengths: Deterministic traversal cost, exhaustive solid-voxel checking handles transparency and fringe cases correctly. Limitations: Fixed brick dimensions and iteration count limit adaptability to larger volumes. Developed as part of the elementary building blocks for ray-primitive intersection in volume rendering. mstampfli/voxelG, https://github.com/mstampfli/voxelG, fetched 2026-10-24 (unofficial)

name: Hardware Ray Tracing Voxel Occlusion
head: Hardware Ray Tracing for Occlusion, Hardware ray-tracing occlusion path, Hardware-RT Voxel Traversal (RT Variant), Hardware-RT voxel path, Hardware-RT primary trace, RT occlusion, GPU RT rays
body: This method determines if a ray from origin to dir is occluded by any solid voxel within maxdist by using hardware ray-tracing cores to traverse a world BVH (TLAS/BLAS) to find candidate brick AABBs, then using a shared software Amanatides-Woo DDA within each candidate brick to resolve the exact first solid voxel. It replaces a software beam pre-pass and hierarchical-DDA empty-space skip with hardware traversal for the coarse search. It differs from the software variant by using hardware RT cores for coarse BVH traversal instead of a software beam pre-pass and hierarchical-DDA, while the in-brick resolution (Amanatides-Woo DDA) is shared between both variants. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: Ray origin origin (world space), ray direction dir (normalized), maximum traversal distance maxdist, and the hardware acceleration structures (BLAS/TLAS) representing the voxel world. Outputs: Boolean true if occluded, false otherwise. In full intersection mode, it returns the nearest hit voxel index, material, and normal. Data Structures: The method relies on specific memory layouts to ensure compatibility with hardware BLAS build requirements. 1. Brick Structure: Represents the occupancy and material data for a single brick (4x4x4 voxels). wgsl struct Brick { occlo: u32, occhi: u32, materials: array<u32, 16>, }; occlo and occhi: Two 32-bit integers packing 64 bits total for the 4^3=64 voxels. materials: Array of 16 u32 values. Materials are packed 4 per 32-bit word (8 bits per material). 2. AABB Structure: Represents the bounding box of a brick. Scalar fields are used to maintain tight 24-byte packing, avoiding WGSL vec3 16-byte alignment padding which would break BLAS build compatibility. wgsl struct GpuAabb { minx: f32, miny: f32, minz: f32, maxx: f32, maxy: f32, maxz: f32, p0: f32, p1: f32, }; Total size: 36 bytes (9 floats). 3. Acceleration Structures: BLAS: Contains one GpuAabb per non-empty brick. The RT core skips empty space in hardware. TLAS: World Top-Level Acceleration Structure containing references to the BLAS. Brick Map: array<u32> mapping primitive indices from the BLAS to brick indices in the bricks array. Parameters: RTPRIMARY: An f32 override parameter. Default is 0.0 (off). If > 0.5, enables hardware RT primary trace instead of software DDA. VOXELGRT: Environment variable. Setting it to 1 enables hardware RT on a ray-query-capable adapter. Algorithm Steps: The method initializes a hardware ray query, iterates through candidate brick AABBs, checks brick activity, resolves the exact voxel hit via a shared DDA, and culls further traversal upon finding a closer hit. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def hardwarertvoxelocclusion(origin, dir, maxdist, tlas, bricks, brickmap, aabbs, cameraworldorigin): # 1. Rebase world-space origin to window-local coordinates o = origin - cameraworldorigin # 2. Initialize hardware ray query against TLAS # RayDesc flags: 0 (no special flags), 0xFF (all hit types) # Distance range: [0.0, maxdist] rq = rayqueryinit(tlas, origin=o, direction=dir, tmin=0.0, tmax=maxdist, flags=0, hitmask=0xFF) bestt = 1e30 occluded = False # 3. Loop while the ray query proceeds while rayqueryproceed(rq): # 4. Get candidate intersection c = rayquerygetcandidate(rq) # 5. Check if candidate is an AABB (brick) if c.kind == RAYQUERYINTERSECTIONAABB: # 6. Retrieve brick index and AABB primitiveidx = c.primitiveindex bi = int(brickmap[primitiveidx]) a = aabbs[primitiveidx] # 7. Check if brick is active if not rtbrickactive(bi): continue # 8. Extract AABB min corner bmin = (a.minx, a.miny, a.minz) # 9. Resolve exact voxel hit using in-brick DDA # Calls shared Amanatides-Woo DDA from parent article bh = resolvebrickfull(bi, bmin, o, dir, origin, bestt, skiptransparent=False) # 10. Check if hit found and closer than current best if bh.hit and bh.t >= 0.0 and bh.t < bestt: bestt = bh.t occluded = True # 11. Cull further bricks by generating an intersection rayquerygenerateintersection(rq, bh.t) # Optimization: Return immediately for binary occlusion check return True # 12. If loop completes without finding a closer hit return occluded Edge Cases and Pitfalls: AABB Packing: Using vec3<f32> for AABB min/max in WGSL causes 16-byte alignment, breaking the tight 24-byte packing required by the BLAS build. Scalar fields are used instead. BVH Staleness: The BVH may be stale during async rebuilds. Correctness is maintained because the tile occupancy mask (rtbrickactive) is updated synchronously. Stale primitives render as sky, matching software DDA behavior. Precision: The committed intersection from the RT core is used only as a cross-check, not the source of truth for the voxel hit. The exact voxel hit is derived from the software DDA to ensure precision. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Performance: Offloads coarse empty-space skipping to hardware RT cores, potentially offering significant speedups over software hierarchical DDA for primary rays and shadows. Strengths: Hardware-accelerated BVH traversal; consistent results with software path via shared DDA; handles async rebuilds gracefully. Limitations: Requires ray-query-capable hardware; overhead of software DDA per candidate brick; strict memory layout requirements for BLAS. When to Use: When hardware RT cores are available and primary ray/shadow performance is critical. Enabled via RTPRIMARY > 0.5 or VOXELGRT=1. When Not to Use: On hardware without ray-tracing support; when software fallback is required for correctness in all scenarios. Not given in the sources. This method originates from the voxelG project. It leverages modern GPU ray-tracing capabilities (specifically Vulkan Ray Query or WebGPU Ray Query) to optimize voxel traversal. The technique was developed to replace the software beam pre-pass and hierarchical-DDA empty-space skip with hardware traversal, improving performance for primary rays and occlusion queries. The in-brick DDA logic is shared with the software variant to ensure identical rendering results. mstampfli/voxelG, https://github.com/mstampfli/voxelG, fetched 2026-10-24 (unofficial)

name: Amanatides and Woo Variation with 2-Point Input
head: 2-Point Voxel Traversal, Amanatides and Woo ray marching, Improved Amanatides and Woo, Real Line Voxelization
body:
This method is a voxel traversal algorithm that takes two endpoints (start and end points) instead of a ray origin and direction vector. It is designed to be more precise than standard face-to-face traversal, specifically handling edge cases such as zero coordinate deltas, exact edge hits, negative traversal, and non-0-based block centers. It builds on the foundational Amanatides and Woo DDA logic but adapts the initialization and termination conditions for finite line segments. Inputs and Outputs: Input: pointA (start point, Vector3), pointB (end point, Vector3). Output: An iterable sequence of voxel coordinates (IEnumerable<Vector3> or list of Vector3) representing the voxels intersected by the line segment. Data Structures: x, y, z: Current voxel integer coordinates. tMaxX, tMaxY, tMaxZ: Distance along the line to the next voxel boundary in each axis. tDeltaX, tDeltaY, tDeltaZ: Distance along the line between consecutive voxel boundaries in each axis. stepX, stepY, stepZ: Direction signs (+1 or -1) for traversal in each axis. lineLength: Total Euclidean length of the segment pointB - pointA. Formulas and Definitions: Line equation: p = p0 + vt, where p0 is start position, v is normalized direction, and t is scaled distance. Signum(d): Returns 1 if d > 0, -1 if d < 0, and 0 if d == 0. Mod(v, m): Returns (v \% m + m) \% m to ensure positive modulo. Ceil(s): Returns 1 if s == 0, else returns \lceil s ceil. Intbound(s, ds): Calculates the distance to the next integer boundary: If ds < 0 and s is an integer, return 0. Else, s = 	ext{Mod}(s, 1). If ds > 0, return (	ext{Ceil}(s) - s) / |ds|. Else, return (s - 	ext{Floor}(s)) / |ds|. Precision5(val): Rounds float to 5 decimal places using integer arithmetic: ((int)(100000 val)) / 100000.0f. Used to mitigate floating-point precision issues in comparisons. Algorithm Steps: 1. Initialization: Round start point to nearest integer grid: x = 	ext{round}(pointA.X), y = 	ext{round}(pointA.Y), z = 	ext{round}(pointA.Z). Compute \delta = pointB - pointA. Compute normalized direction \delta{normal} = \delta / \|\delta\|. Extract components: dx = \delta{normal}.X, dy = \delta{normal}.Y, dz = \delta{normal}.Z. Compute steps: stepX = 	ext{Signum}(dx), stepY = 	ext{Signum}(dy), stepZ = 	ext{Signum}(dz). Compute initial distances to next boundary. Note: The source uses pointA - 0.5f in the Intbound call, accounting for.5f-based block centers: tMaxX = 	ext{Intbound}(pointA.X - 0.5f, dx) tMaxY = 	ext{Intbound}(pointA.Y - 0.5f, dy) tMaxZ = 	ext{Intbound}(pointA.Z - 0.5f, dz) Compute step deltas: tDeltaX = stepX / dx tDeltaY = stepY / dy tDeltaZ = stepZ / dz Compute total length: lineLength = \|\delta\|. Initialize result list with starting voxel (x, y, z). 2. Step Functions: StepX(): If tMaxX \ge lineLength, return true (end of line). Else, x \leftarrow x + stepX, tMaxX \leftarrow tMaxX + tDeltaX, return false. StepY(): Analogous to StepX() using y, tMaxY, tDeltaY. StepZ(): Analogous to StepX() using z, tMaxZ, tDeltaZ. 3. Iteration: The iteration logic depends on which axes have non-zero steps. Case 1: 3D Traversal (stepX 
eq 0, stepY 
eq 0, stepZ 
eq 0) Loop while true: 1. Compare precision-rounded values: tX = 	ext{Precision5}(tMaxX), tY = 	ext{Precision5}(tMaxY), tZ = 	ext{Precision5}(tMaxZ). 2. Determine smallest t: If tX < tY: If tX < tZ: call StepX(). Else if tZ < tX: call StepZ(). Else (tZ == tX): call StepZ() || StepX() (advance in both). Else if tY < tX: If tY < tZ: call StepY(). Else if tZ < tY: call StepZ(). Else (tZ == tY): call StepY() || StepZ() (advance in both). Else (tX == tY): If tY < tZ: call StepX() || StepY() (advance in both). Else if tZ < tY: call StepZ(). Else (tZ == tY): call StepX() || StepY() || StepZ() (advance in all three). 3. Add current (x, y, z) to result list. 4. If any step function returned true, break loop. Case 2: 2D Traversal (One step is zero) Separate loops handle cases where one or two steps are zero. Example: If stepX 
eq 0, stepY 
eq 0, stepZ == 0: Loop while true: 1. Compare tY = 	ext{Precision5}(tMaxY) and tZ = 	ext{Precision5}(tMaxZ)? No, stepZ=0 implies no movement in Z, but tMaxZ still exists. However, the source code snippet for 2D cases (implied by stepX == 0 && stepY != 0 && stepZ != 0) compares relevant tMax values. 2. If stepZ == 0, the logic simplifies to comparing only the active axes. If stepX 
eq 0, stepY 
eq 0, stepZ == 0: Compare tX and tY. If tX < tY: StepX(). Else if tY < tX: StepY(). Else: StepX() || StepY(). 3. Add current (x, y, z) to result. 4. Break if end reached. Case 3: 1D Traversal (Two steps are zero) Example: If stepX 
eq 0, stepY == 0, stepZ == 0: Loop while true: 1. Call StepX(). 2. Add current (x, y, z) to result. 3. Break if end reached. Termination: The iteration terminates when a step function returns true, which occurs when the current tMax exceeds or equals lineLength. Alternatively, in the RLV formulation, termination occurs when the sum of all t{min} components exceeds the length of the line. The implementation in uses the tMax >= lineLength check within the step functions. Pitfalls and Edge Cases: Zero Delta: If a coordinate delta is zero (straight line parallel to an axis), the corresponding step is 0, and the algorithm must handle the reduced dimensionality (2D or 1D loops). Exact Edge Hits: When tMax values are equal, the algorithm advances in multiple axes simultaneously to avoid missing voxels. Negative Traversal: The Signum function handles negative directions correctly. Block Centers: The algorithm accounts for blocks with.5f-based centers by subtracting 0.5f in the Intbound calculation. Precision: Floating-point errors in comparisons are mitigated by Precision5. This variant uses the ray-volume impact point (from an initial intersection check) as the first ray-voxel intersection point (entry point). It calculates the point where the ray emerges from the current voxel (exit point) and tests the data between these points against user-specified target values. It repeats this process until the ray emerges from the data volume or available light is depleted. Unlike Levy's uniform resampling, which requires infinite samples to guarantee finding all surfaces or suffers from aliasing if steps are too large, this method guarantees traversal through every voxel the ray intersects. Time Complexity: Linear with respect to the number of voxels intersected by the line segment. Each step involves constant-time arithmetic and comparisons. Memory Complexity: Linear with respect to the number of voxels intersected, as it stores the list of visited voxels. Strengths: High precision compared to face-to-face traversal; handles edge cases like zero deltas and exact boundary hits robustly; works with finite line segments rather than infinite rays. Limitations: Potentially slower than standard Amanatides and Woo due to the overhead of handling 2-point input and precision rounding. Requires careful handling of degenerate cases (zero steps). When to use: When precise voxelization of a finite line segment is required, especially in contexts where edge cases (zero deltas, exact hits) are common, such as in voxel games or specific scientific visualizations. When not to use: When performance is critical and approximate traversal is acceptable, or when working with infinite rays where standard Amanatides and Woo is sufficient. The algorithm is a variation of the Amanatides and Woo ray marching algorithm, originally proposed for voxelizing lines in a uniform grid. The specific 2-point input variation was developed to address precision issues and edge cases in practical implementations, such as those found in voxel-based games. The underlying concept of Real Line Voxelization (RLV) is discussed in literature comparing optimal scanline voxelization algorithms. The adjacency-based variant is described in the context of volumetric rendering techniques for aerodynamic flow field data. name: RDV-1 Occupancy Ray Query
head: occupancy-only ray query, toroidal brick buffer ray march
body: The RDV-1 Occupancy Ray Query is an occupancy-only ray tracing method designed for a toroidal brick buffer voxel grid. It traces a ray through the voxel space to locate the first occupied voxel, returning the voxel coordinates, surface normal, distance, and step counts. It operates across the entire grid rather than a single brick, and supports arbitrary ray origins and distances outside the brick boundary. Inputs and Outputs Input: A BbvRay struct containing origin (float3), maxDistance (float), direction (float3), and rayId (uint). Output: A BbvResult struct containing voxel (int3), hit (uint), normal (int3), padding (uint), distance (float), voxelSteps (uint), brickLookups (uint), and padding2 (uint). Data Structures The method relies on global constants and specific struct layouts: gMinimumBrick (int3): Minimum brick coordinate in the grid. gGridDimensions (int3): Dimensions of the brick grid. gToroidalOffset (int3): Offset applied for toroidal wrapping of brick indices. gMaximumSteps (uint): Maximum number of voxel steps allowed per ray trace. gRayCount (uint): Total number of rays dispatched to the kernel. Brick Buffer Layout: Each brick occupies exactly 64 bytes. The occupancy data uses DVE's authoritative indexing scheme x + 8y + 64z rather than InstantRDV's subbrick/Morton wire format. Algorithm Steps 1. Validation: Compute the magnitude of the ray direction. If magnitude <= 0.0f or maxDistance < 0.0f, return an empty BbvResult and exit. 2. Normalization and Bounds: Normalize the direction. Compute grid bounds: gridMin = float3(gMinimumBrick) 8.0f and gridMax = float3(gMinimumBrick + gGridDimensions) 8.0f. Initialize entry = 0.0f, exit = ray.maxDistance, and normal = int3(0,0,0). 3. Axis Intersection: For each axis (x, y, z): if direction[axis] == 0.0f, check if origin[axis] is outside [gridMin[axis], gridMax[axis]); if outside, return an empty result, otherwise continue. Compute t0 and t1 slab intersections. Update entry: if \min(t0, t1) > \text{entry}, set entry = min(t0, t1) and set normal[axis] to -1 or 1 based on the sign of direction[axis]. Update exit: set exit = max(t0, t1). 4. Entry Validation and Offset: If entry > exit, return an empty result. Compute the sample offset: sampleT = entry + max(abs(entry) 1.1920929e-7f, 1.0e-5f) if entry > 0.0f, else 0.0f. Clamp the sample position: p = clamp(ray.origin + direction sampleT, gridMin, gridMax - 1.0e-4f). Set the initial voxel: voxel = int3(floor(p)). 5. Ray Marching Loop: Initialize t = entry. Loop up to min(gMaximumSteps, 65536u) iterations while t <= exit. Increment voxelSteps. If voxel is outside grid bounds, break. Call IsOccupied(voxel, result.brickLookups). If occupied, set result.hit = 1, result.voxel = voxel, result.normal = normal, result.distance = t, and break. Compute next boundary crossings nextT. Find the axis with the minimum nextT. If next > exit or next + 1.0e-5f < t, break. Update t = max(t, next). Advance voxel[axis] by \delta (1 or -1). Update normal for the new axis. Formulas Grid Bounds: \text{gridMin} = \text{float3}(gMinimumBrick) \times 8.0, \text{gridMax} = \text{float3}(gMinimumBrick + gGridDimensions) \times 8.0. Sample Offset: \text{sampleT} = \begin{cases} \text{entry} + \max(|\text{entry}| \times 1.1920929 \times 10^{-7}, 1.0 \times 10^{-5}) & \text{if } \text{entry} > 0.0 \\ 0.0 & \text{otherwise} \end{cases}. Brick Index: \text{logical} = \text{key} - gMinimumBrick, \text{physical} = \text{logical} + gToroidalOffset, \text{index} = \text{physical}.x + gGridDimensions.x \times (\text{physical}.y + gGridDimensions.y \times \text{physical}.z). Bit Position: \text{local} = \text{voxel} - \text{key} \times 8, \text{bit} = \text{local}.x + 8 \times \text{local}.y + 64 \times \text{local}.z. Occupancy Test: \text{word} = gBbvBricks.\text{Load}(\text{index} \times 64 + (\text{bit} \gg 5) \times 4), return (\text{word} \ \& \ (1 \ll (\text{bit} \ \& \ 31))) \neq 0. Next Boundary: \text{NextBoundary}(o, d, v) = \begin{cases} \frac{v + 1 - o}{d} & \text{if } d > 0 \\ \frac{v - o}{d} & \text{if } d < 0 \end{cases}. Parameters gMinimumBrick: Not given in the sources. gGridDimensions: Not given in the sources. gToroidalOffset: Not given in the sources. gMaximumSteps: Not given in the sources. gRayCount: Not given in the sources. Edge Cases and Pitfalls Zero Direction Components: If a direction component is zero, explicit bounds checking is required for that axis; otherwise the ray may incorrectly pass through the grid or cause division by zero. Precision at Origin: The entry point offset uses max(abs(entry) 1.1920929e-7f, 1.0e-5f) to avoid self-intersection or precision issues when the ray starts inside or very close to a voxel. Infinite Loops: The step advancement includes a check next + 1.0e-5f < t to prevent infinite loops or stuck steps due to floating-point rounding errors at voxel boundaries. Pseudocode Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def rdv1occupancyquery(ray, gMinimumBrick, gGridDimensions, gToroidalOffset, gMaximumSteps, gBbvBricks): # 1. Validation mag = ray.direction.length() if mag <= 0.0 or ray.maxDistance < 0.0: return BbvResult() # 2. Normalization and Bounds dir = ray.direction.normalized() gridMin = Vec3(gMinimumBrick) 8.0 gridMax = Vec3(gMinimumBrick + gGridDimensions) 8.0 entry = 0.0 exitt = ray.maxDistance normal = Int3(0, 0, 0) # 3. Axis Intersection for axis in (0, 1, 2): if dir[axis] == 0.0: if not (gridMin[axis] <= ray.origin[axis] < gridMax[axis]): return BbvResult() continue t0 = (gridMin[axis] - ray.origin[axis]) / dir[axis] t1 = (gridMax[axis] - ray.origin[axis]) / dir[axis] if t0 > t1: t0, t1 = t1, t0 if t0 > entry: entry = t0 normal[axis] = 1 if dir[axis] > 0 else -1 if t1 < exitt: exitt = t1 # 4. Entry Validation and Offset if entry > exitt: return BbvResult() sampleT = entry + max(abs(entry) 1.1920929e-7, 1.0e-5) if entry > 0.0 else 0.0 p = clamp(ray.origin + dir sampleT, gridMin, gridMax - 1.0e-4) voxel = Int3(floor(p.x), floor(p.y), floor(p.z)) # 5. Ray Marching Loop t = entry result = BbvResult() result.brickLookups = 0 maxiter = min(gMaximumSteps, 65536) for in range(maxiter): result.voxelSteps += 1 if not (gridMin.x <= voxel.x < gridMax.x and gridMin.y <= voxel.y < gridMax.y and gridMin.z <= voxel.z < gridMax.z): break result.brickLookups += 1 if isoccupied(voxel, gMinimumBrick, gGridDimensions, gToroidalOffset, gBbvBricks): result.hit = 1 result.voxel = voxel result.normal = normal result.distance = t return result # Next boundary crossings nextT = Vec3(0.0, 0.0, 0.0) for axis in (0, 1, 2): if dir[axis] == 0.0: nextT[axis] = float('inf') else: boundary = voxel[axis] + (1.0 if dir[axis] > 0 else 0.0) nextT[axis] = (boundary - ray.origin[axis]) / dir[axis] minaxis = nextT.argmin() nextval = nextT[minaxis] if nextval > exitt or nextval + 1.0e-5 < t: break t = max(t, nextval) voxel[minaxis] += 1 if dir[minaxis] > 0 else -1 normal[minaxis] = 1 if dir[minaxis] > 0 else -1 return result def isoccupied(voxel, gMinimumBrick, gGridDimensions, gToroidalOffset, gBbvBricks): key = Int3(voxel.x // 8, voxel.y // 8, voxel.z // 8) logical = key - gMinimumBrick physical = logical + gToroidalOffset index = physical.x + gGridDimensions.x (physical.y + gGridDimensions.y physical.z) local = voxel - key 8 bit = local.x + 8 local.y + 64 local.z word = gBbvBricks.load(index 64 + (bit >> 5) 4) return (word & (1 << (bit & 31))) != 0 Time Complexity: Linear with respect to the number of voxels traversed, capped by gMaximumSteps and 65536. Memory Complexity: Constant relative to traversal depth, dependent on the brick buffer size determined by gGridDimensions. Measured Performance: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Efficient for sparse grids due to occupancy-only checks; toroidal wrapping simplifies boundary handling for certain grid topologies. Limitations: Limited to occupancy queries (no shading or density integration); not used by production render passes yet. When to Use: When only the first hit in a voxel grid is needed, and the grid uses the DVE brick buffer format. When Not to Use: When density values, normals from geometry, or full ray-marching integration are required. The RDV-1 Occupancy Ray Query is part of the Destructible Voxel Engine (DVE) implementation. It is an independent kernel, opt-in, and was not used by production render passes at the time of the source documentation. It builds on the principles of ray-box intersection and Amanatides-Woo DDA, adapted for a toroidal brick buffer layout.
