name: AABB Ray Intersection
head: slab method, Ray-AABB Intersection Kernel
body: The AABB Ray Intersection method computes the entry (t{min}) and exit (t{max}) distances of a ray against an Axis-Aligned Bounding Box (AABB), returning a boolean hit status. It solves the fundamental problem of determining whether a ray intersects a volume primitive and, if so, the interval along the ray parameter t where the intersection occurs. It is distinguished from its siblings by its reliance on the "slab" method (computing intersections with min/max planes per axis) and its common implementation as a batched kernel for GPU acceleration, whereas Ray-Bounding Box Intersection and Sampling Preparation focuses on sampling preparation and Ray-Cube Intersection assumes unit cubes. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: Ray origins: \mathbf{o} \in \mathbb{R}^{N \times 3} Ray directions: \mathbf{d} \in \mathbb{R}^{N \times 3} AABBs: \mathbf{B} \in \mathbb{R}^{M \times 6}, where each row is [x{min}, y{min}, z{min}, x{max}, y{max}, z{max}]. Outputs: t{min} \in \mathbb{R}^{N \times M}: Entry distances. t{max} \in \mathbb{R}^{N \times M}: Exit distances. hit \in \{0, 1\}^{N \times M}: Boolean intersection mask. Data Structures: VolumeRange (Optional): A data structure containing fields t0 (entry), t1 (exit), and intersected (boolean mask), all with shape [batch\size, shape, 1]. Parameters: \epsilon: Small value to prevent division by zero (default 10^{-6}). min\dist: Minimum allowed value for t0 (default 0.0). min\t\range: Minimum step size for valid intersection (default 10^{-3}). near\plane: Clamping lower bound for t{min} (often 0.0 during inference). Steps: 1. Compute Direction Fractions: To avoid division by zero, compute the reciprocal of the ray direction components: \mathbf{f} = \frac{1}{\mathbf{d} + \epsilon} where \epsilon is a small constant (e.g., 10^{-6}). 2. Compute Slab Intersections: For each axis i \in \{x, y, z\}, calculate the intersection distances with the min and max planes of the AABB. Let \mathbf{B}{min} = [x{min}, y{min}, z{min}] and \mathbf{B}{max} = [x{max}, y{max}, z{max}]. t{i,1} = (\mathbf{B}{min}[i] - \mathbf{o}[i]) \cdot \mathbf{f}[i] t{i,2} = (\mathbf{B}{max}[i] - \mathbf{o}[i]) \cdot \mathbf{f}[i] This yields six values per ray-AABB pair: t{x,1}, t{x,2}, t{y,1}, t{y,2}, t{z,1}, t{z,2}. 3. Determine Entry and Exit: The entry distance t{min} is the maximum of the minimums along each axis: t{min} = \max{i \in \{x,y,z\}} (\min(t{i,1}, t{i,2})) The exit distance t{max} is the minimum of the maximums along each axis: t{max} = \min{i \in \{x,y,z\}} (\max(t{i,1}, t{i,2})). 4. Apply Constraints and Clamping: Clamp t{min} to be at least min\dist (typically 0.0) to handle rays starting inside the box or behind the origin. Clamp t{min} to the near\plane. Ensure t{max} > t{min} by at least a small margin (e.g., 10^{-6}) to prevent degenerate intervals. If a lower bound t{0,lower} is provided (e.g., from a previous traversal step), update t{min} = \max(t{min}, t{0,lower}). 5. Determine Hit Status: A ray intersects if t{min} + min\t\range < t{max}. If not intersected, set t{min} and t{max} to a miss value (e.g., -\infty or a specific flag). Pseudocode (PyTorch-like): Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def rayaabbintersect(rayso, raysd, aabbs, epsilon=1e-6, mindist=0.0, mintrange=1e-3): """ rayso: [N, 3] raysd: [N, 3] aabbs: [M, 6] -> [xmin, ymin, zmin, xmax, ymax, zmax] Returns: tmin [N, M], tmax [N, M], hit [N, M] """ # 1. Compute direction fractions dirfrac = 1.0 / (raysd[:, None,:] + epsilon) # [N, 1, 3] # 2. Extract AABB bounds aabbmin = aabbs[:,:3] # [M, 3] aabbmax = aabbs[:, 3:] # [M, 3] # 3. Compute t1 and t2 for all 6 planes # t1: intersection with min planes t1 = (aabbmin[None,:,:] - rayso[:, None,:]) dirfrac # [N, M, 3] # t2: intersection with max planes t2 = (aabbmax[None,:,:] - rayso[:, None,:]) dirfrac # [N, M, 3] # 4. Compute tmin and tmax # tmin: max of mins along axis dim (dim=-1) tmin = torch.max(torch.minimum(t1, t2), dim=-1).values # [N, M] # tmax: min of maxs along axis dim (dim=-1) tmax = torch.min(torch.maximum(t1, t2), dim=-1).values # [N, M] # 5. Apply constraints tmin = torch.clamp(tmin, min=mindist) # Ensure tmax > tmin tmax = torch.maximum(tmax, tmin + 1e-6) # 6. Determine hit status hit = (tmin + mintrange < tmax) # 7. Set miss values missvalue = -1e10 # Or appropriate miss flag tmin = torch.where(hit, tmin, missvalue) tmax = torch.where(hit, tmax, missvalue) return tmin, tmax, hit A pure PyTorch implementation of the slab method. It is functionally identical to the CUDA kernel but slower due to lack of specialized hardware instructions and memory coalescing. It follows the same steps: broadcasting ray origins/directions against AABB bounds, computing t1/t2, reducing via min/max, and clamping. Time Complexity: O(N \cdot M) for N rays and M AABBs, with a very small constant factor (6 subtractions, 6 multiplications, 6 comparisons per pair). Memory Complexity: O(N \cdot M) to store the output tensors t{min}, t{max}, hit. Performance: Highly parallelizable on GPUs. Batched implementations (e.g., processing chunks of rays) are used to avoid out-of-memory errors when N is large. Strengths: Fast, branchless (in optimized implementations), handles arbitrary AABB sizes. Limitations: Does not handle rotated boxes (use Ray-OBB Intersection Test instead). Precision issues can arise if ray directions are near-zero without epsilon handling. The slab method is a standard technique in ray tracing, originally described in and as part of modern neural rendering pipelines (NeRF, SDFStudio). It is a direct application of the separating axis theorem for axis-aligned boxes. The specific batching and clamping strategies described here are adapted from implementations in (taylor-nerf), (sdfstudio), (gsgen), (NSVF), and (CNC). taylor2nerf/taylor-nerf, https://github.com/taylor2nerf/taylor-nerf, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial) autonomousvision/sdfstudio, https://github.com/autonomousvision/sdfstudio, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial) gsgen3d/gsgen, https://github.com/gsgen3d/gsgen, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial) facebookresearch/NSVF, https://github.com/facebookresearch/NSVF, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial) YihangChen-ee/CNC, https://github.com/YihangChen-ee/CNC, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial)

name: Ray-AABB Intersection (PyTorch)
head: AABBBoxCollider, Axis-Aligned Bounding Box Collider
body: A pure PyTorch implementation of ray-axis-aligned bounding box (AABB) intersection that computes near and far clipping distances for rays against a scene box. It is functionally identical to the CUDA-accelerated version but executes slower on CPU or via PyTorch's autograd engine. It serves as the fallback or training-compatible intersection primitive in neural rendering pipelines where GPU kernel compilation is unavailable or dynamic shapes require eager execution. Inputs and outputs: rayso: Ray origins, shape [numrays, 3] or [H, W, 3]. raysd: Ray directions, shape [numrays, 3] or [H, W, 3]. aabbmin: AABB minimum bounds, shape [3] or [numrays, 3] depending on implementation variant. aabbmax: AABB maximum bounds, shape [3] or [numrays, 3]. nearplane: Scalar float, minimum clamp for the near distance (default 0.0 during inference). Output: nears and fars tensors of shape [numrays] or [H, W] representing the valid sampling intervals. Data structures: The AABB is typically stored as two 3D vectors or a single 6D vector [minx, miny, minz, maxx, maxy, maxz]. In the broadcasting implementation, aabbmin and aabbmax are expanded to match the ray batch dimensions. Steps: 1. Reciprocal Direction: Compute the reciprocal of the ray direction components to replace division with multiplication. Add a small epsilon (10^{-6}) to avoid division by zero for rays parallel to axes. dir\frac = \frac{1.0}{rays\d + 10^{-6}} 2. Plane Intersections (Broadcasting Variant): For each axis i \in \{x, y, z\}, compute the intersection distances t1 (with min plane) and t2 (with max plane): t1^{(i)} = (aabb\min^{(i)} - rays\o^{(i)}) \cdot dir\frac^{(i)} t2^{(i)} = (aabb\max^{(i)} - rays\o^{(i)}) \cdot dir\frac^{(i)} Note: The source describes this using explicit broadcasting indices (rayso[:, None,:] - aabbmin[None,:,:]) / raysd[:, None,:], which is mathematically equivalent to the component-wise formula above. 3. Min/Max Aggregation: For each axis, determine the entry (t{min}^{(i)} = \min(t1^{(i)}, t2^{(i)})) and exit (t{max}^{(i)} = \max(t1^{(i)}, t2^{(i)})) distances. 4. Global Interval: Compute the global near (t{near}) and far (t{far}) bounds by taking the maximum of all entry distances and the minimum of all exit distances: t{near} = \maxi(t{min}^{(i)}) t{far} = \mini(t{max}^{(i)}) 5. Hit Detection: A ray hits the box if t{far} > t{near} and t{far} > 0. 6. Clamping: Clamp t{near} to nearplane. 7. Invalid Interval Handling: If the ray misses, set t{near} and t{far} to a miss value (e.g., infinity or a specific flag). Ensure t{far} \ge t{near} + 10^{-6} to prevent invalid zero-length intervals due to numerical precision. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import torch def rayaabbintersectpytorch(rayso: torch.Tensor, raysd: torch.Tensor, aabbmin: torch.Tensor, aabbmax: torch.Tensor, nearplane: float = 0.0) -> tuple: """ Intersect rays with an AABB using pure PyTorch. rayso: [N, 3] or [H, W, 3] raysd: [N, 3] or [H, W, 3] aabbmin: [3] or [N, 3] aabbmax: [3] or [N, 3] """ # 1. Reciprocal direction with epsilon guard dirfrac = 1.0 / (raysd + 1e-6) # 2. Compute t1 (min plane) and t2 (max plane) for each axis # Broadcasting: ensure aabbmin/max align with rayso/d # If aabb is [3], expand to [N, 3] or [H, W, 3] if aabbmin.dim() == 1: aabbmin = aabbmin.unsqueeze(0).expandas(rayso) aabbmax = aabbmax.unsqueeze(0).expandas(rayso) t1 = (aabbmin - rayso) dirfrac t2 = (aabbmax - rayso) dirfrac # 3. Determine min and max per axis # tminaxis: min(t1, t2) for each axis # tmaxaxis: max(t1, t2) for each axis tminaxis = torch.minimum(t1, t2) tmaxaxis = torch.maximum(t1, t2) # 4. Aggregate across axes (dim=-1) # tnear: max of tminaxis across x,y,z # tfar: min of tmaxaxis across x,y,z tnear = torch.max(tminaxis, dim=-1).values tfar = torch.min(tmaxaxis, dim=-1).values # 5. Hit detection hits = (tfar > tnear) & (tfar > 0) # 6. Clamp near to nearplane tnear = torch.clamp(tnear, min=nearplane) # 7. Handle misses and numerical stability # Set miss values to infinity or a large number missvalue = float('inf') tnear = torch.where(hits, tnear, missvalue) tfar = torch.where(hits, tfar, missvalue) # Ensure far >= near + epsilon to avoid invalid intervals tfar = torch.maximum(tfar, tnear + 1e-6) return tnear, tfar Parameters: nearplane: Minimum distance for the near clip. Defaults to 0.0 during inference, but may be set higher during training to avoid sampling too close to the camera origin. eps: Epsilon for reciprocal direction and interval validity (default 10^{-6}). Edge cases and pitfalls: Zero Direction: Rays with zero direction components are handled by adding 10^{-6} to the denominator. This approximates the ray as slightly offset, which may cause slight inaccuracies for rays exactly parallel to axes. Misses: Rays that do not intersect the box must be explicitly handled to prevent invalid sampling intervals. The implementation sets t{near} and t{far} to a miss value (often infinity) and ensures t{far} \ge t{near}. Numerical Precision: The check t{far} \ge t{near} + 10^{-6} prevents degenerate intervals caused by floating-point errors when the ray grazes the box. Time Complexity: O(N) where N is the number of rays. The operations are element-wise and reduce across 3 dimensions. Memory Complexity: O(N) for storing intermediate tensors (t1, t2, t{near}, t{far}). Performance: Significantly slower than the CUDA counterpart due to the lack of optimized kernel launches and potential overhead of PyTorch's autograd graph if gradients are tracked. Suitable for training on CPU or when dynamic shapes prevent CUDA kernel compilation. Strengths: Pure Python/PyTorch, no external dependencies, supports autograd, handles dynamic batch sizes. Limitations: Slower than CUDA; not suitable for real-time inference on large datasets without batching hacks. This implementation originates from the Nerfstudio project and is also present in Taylor-NeRF. It provides a software fallback for ray-AABB intersection, enabling neural rendering pipelines to run on hardware or configurations where CUDA kernels are not available or efficient. It is part of the elementary building blocks for volume rendering, specifically within the ray-primitive intersection hierarchy. taylor2nerf/taylor-nerf, https://github.com/taylor2nerf/taylor-nerf, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial) nerfstudio-project/nerfstudio, https://github.com/nerfstudio-project/nerfstudio, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial)

name: Ray-AABB Intersection and Grid Traversal Setup
head: traverse_grids initialization
body: This method prepares rays for volume rendering by determining which spatial grids (or voxels) each ray intersects and calculating the entry and exit distances for traversal. It builds on Slab-based AABB Intersection to compute precise intersection intervals. Unlike Ray-Cube Intersection which assumes uniform cubic cells, or AABB Ray Intersection which may provide generic bounding checks, this setup specifically handles multiple grid structures and prepares sorted traversal intervals for efficient ray marching. Inputs: A set of rays, each defined by an origin \mathbf{o} and direction \mathbf{d}. A list of axis-aligned bounding boxes (AABBs) representing the grids or volume partitions. Near and far clipping plane distances (t{near}, t{far}). A missvalue constant for rays that do not intersect an AABB. Outputs: For each ray, a list of intersection intervals (t{min}, t{max}) for each intersected AABB. A hit flag indicating whether the ray intersects any AABB. Data Structures: tmins: Array of size N{rays} \times N{grids} storing entry distances. tmaxs: Array of size N{rays} \times N{grids} storing exit distances. hits: Boolean array of size N{rays} \times N{grids} indicating intersection validity. Steps: 1. Compute Intersections: For each ray i and each grid j, compute the intersection distances t{min}^{i,j} and t{max}^{i,j} using slab-based AABB intersection. 2. Clamp to View Frustum: Clamp t{min}^{i,j} and t{max}^{i,j} to the range [t{near}, t{far}]. If t{min}^{i,j} > t{far} or t{max}^{i,j} < t{near}, the ray does not traverse the grid within the visible range. 3. Handle Misses: If the ray does not intersect the AABB (hit flag is false), set t{min}^{i,j} = t{max}^{i,j} = \text{miss\value}. The missvalue is typically a large positive number (e.g., infinity) to ensure these intervals are sorted to the end of the traversal list. 4. Sort Intervals: For each ray, concatenate all (t{min}^{i,j}, t{max}^{i,j}) pairs from all grids. Sort these intervals by t{min} to prepare for sequential traversal. This ensures that the ray processes grids in the order it encounters them. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def setupgridtraversal(rays, grids, tnear, tfar, missvalue=float('inf')): """ rays: List of tuples (origin, direction) grids: List of AABBs (mincorner, maxcorner) tnear: Near plane distance tfar: Far plane distance missvalue: Value for non-intersecting rays Returns: List of sorted intervals for each ray """ allintervals = [] for ray in rays: rayintervals = [] for grid in grids: # Compute intersection using slab method tmin, tmax, hit = slabaabbintersect(ray.origin, ray.direction, grid.min, grid.max) if hit: # Clamp to view frustum tmin = max(tmin, tnear) tmax = min(tmax, tfar) # If the interval is valid after clamping, add it if tmin < tmax: rayintervals.append((tmin, tmax)) else: # No intersection: use missvalue to sort to end rayintervals.append((missvalue, missvalue)) # Sort intervals by entry distance rayintervals.sort(key=lambda x: x[0]) allintervals.append(rayintervals) return allintervals Parameters: missvalue: Typically infinity or a value larger than any possible t{far}. Edge Cases: Degenerate AABBs: If an AABB has zero volume, the intersection logic must handle it gracefully (usually resulting in no intersection or a single point). Ray Parallel to Slab: If the ray direction is parallel to a slab face, the intersection calculation must handle division by zero or near-zero denominators. Truncates a ray defined by source and detector points to the volume's AABB, returning a line segment with voxel-space origin and step count. Steps: 1. Call aabbintersection with ray.source, ray.detector, v.physicallengths(), and vec<D, T>(v.origin()). 2. If no intersection is found, return an empty optional. 3. Convert ray.source, ray.detector, and intersection origin to voxel coordinates using tovoxel. 4. Calculate the number of steps as the integer distance from voxelsource to voxelorigin plus one. Formula: steps = \lfloor \|v{source} - v{origin}\| \rfloor + 1. Pitfall: The step calculation truncates the floating-point distance to an integer before adding one, which may slightly underestimate or overestimate the exact number of voxels traversed depending on rounding. Time Complexity: O(N{rays} \times N{grids}) for intersection computation, plus O(N{rays} \times N{grids} \log N{grids}) for sorting intervals per ray. Memory Complexity: O(N{rays} \times N{grids}) to store intervals. Strengths: Efficiently handles multiple grid structures; prepares data for fast sequential traversal. Limitations: Sorting overhead can be significant for large numbers of grids; missvalue handling requires careful choice to avoid overflow or incorrect sorting. When to Use: When rendering volumes with multiple distinct grid structures or partitions. When Not to Use: For simple single-grid volumes where direct traversal is sufficient. This method is commonly used in volume rendering pipelines that involve spatial partitioning or multi-resolution grids. It ensures that rays are processed in the correct order through the volume, which is critical for correct accumulation of color and opacity. taylor2nerf/taylor-nerf, https://github.com/taylor2nerf/taylor-nerf, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial) jwbuurlage/TPT, https://github.com/jwbuurlage/TPT, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial)

name: Ray-AABB Intersection and Distance
body: This method computes the parametric entry and exit distances of a ray intersecting an Axis-Aligned Bounding Box (AABB), or determines the minimum intersection distance. It serves as the fundamental primitive test for ray traversal in volume rendering and ray tracing. It is distinguished from Ray-Cube Intersection by its generalization to arbitrary box dimensions and from AABB Ray Intersection by its explicit provision of both entry and exit intervals rather than a simple boolean. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A ray defined by origin \mathbf{o} and direction \mathbf{d}, and an AABB defined by minimum corner \mathbf{b}{min} and maximum corner \mathbf{b}{max}. Output: An optional interval I = [t{entry}, t{exit}] representing the parametric distances along the ray where it enters and exits the box. If no intersection exists, the result is null/empty. For distance queries, the scalar t{entry} is returned, or \infty if no intersection occurs. Data Structures: Ray: Contains fields orig (vec3) and dir (vec3). AABB: Contains fields min (vec3) and max (vec3). FInterval: Contains fields low (float) and high (float), representing the parametric entry and exit distances along the ray. Algorithm Steps: 1. Compute the inverse direction of the ray: \mathbf{inv\dir} = 1.0 / \mathbf{d}. 2. Compute temporary intersection candidates for the minimum and maximum bounds along each axis: \mathbf{t}{min\tmp} = (\mathbf{b}{min} - \mathbf{o}) \odot \mathbf{inv\dir} \mathbf{t}{max\tmp} = (\mathbf{b}{max} - \mathbf{o}) \odot \mathbf{inv\dir} where \odot denotes component-wise multiplication. 3. Order the candidates per axis to ensure \mathbf{t}{min} holds the smaller value and \mathbf{t}{max} holds the larger value for each component: \mathbf{t}{min} = \min(\mathbf{t}{min\tmp}, \mathbf{t}{max\tmp}) \mathbf{t}{max} = \max(\mathbf{t}{min\tmp}, \mathbf{t}{max\tmp}) 4. Compute the global entry distance t0 as the maximum of the per-axis minimums: t0 = \max(t{min,x}, \max(t{min,y}, t{min,z})) 5. Compute the global exit distance t1 as the minimum of the per-axis maximums: t1 = \min(t{max,x}, \min(t{max,y}, t{max,z})) 6. Determine validity: If t0 \le t1, the ray intersects the box. The interval is [t0, t1]. Otherwise, there is no intersection. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def intersectsprayaabb(rayorig, raydir, boxmin, boxmax): # Compute inverse direction invdir = 1.0 / raydir # Compute t-min and t-max candidates per axis tmintmp = (boxmin - rayorig) invdir tmaxtmp = (boxmax - rayorig) invdir # Order t-min and t-max per axis tmin = min(tmintmp, tmaxtmp) tmax = max(tmintmp, tmaxtmp) # Compute global entry t0 and exit t1 t0 = max(tmin.x, max(tmin.y, tmin.z)) t1 = min(tmax.x, min(tmax.y, tmax.z)) # Return interval if valid if t0 <= t1: return FInterval(low=t0, high=t1) else: return None def intersects(rayorig, raydir, raytmax, boxmin, boxmax): interval = intersectsprayaabb(rayorig, raydir, boxmin, boxmax) if interval is not None: # Check if intersection is within the ray's valid range [0, tmax] # Note: Sources specify I.low < r.tmax && I.high > 0 return interval.low < raytmax and interval.high > 0 return False def distmin(rayorig, raydir, boxmin, boxmax): interval = intersectsprayaabb(rayorig, raydir, boxmin, boxmax) if interval is not None: return interval.low return float('inf') Parameters and Edge Cases: Zero Direction: Division by zero in invdir occurs if any component of \mathbf{d} is zero. Standard implementations handle this by treating the corresponding t{min\tmp} and t{max\tmp} as -\infty or +\infty appropriately, or by using a large epsilon. Not given in the sources. Ray Origin Inside Box: If the ray origin is inside the box, t0 may be negative. The intersection is still valid geometrically, but for ray marching, one might clamp t0 to 0. Degenerate Box: If \mathbf{b}{min} = \mathbf{b}{max}, the box is a point. The logic holds, returning an intersection only if the ray passes exactly through that point. Subtopics: Ray-Cube Intersection: Specialized for unit cubes where bounds are implicit. Simpler arithmetic but less general. AABB Ray Intersection: Often refers to boolean-only variants or specific optimizations for BVH traversal. Ray-AABB Intersection and Grid Traversal Setup: Extends this intersection to initialize voxel traversal steps (DDA). Time Complexity: O(1) with a small constant number of arithmetic operations (approx. 10-15 flops). Memory Complexity: O(1). Strengths: Extremely fast, branch-minimal potential, robust for standard AABBs. Limitations: Does not handle rotated boxes. Precision issues can arise with very large coordinates or very small boxes due to floating-point cancellation in (\mathbf{b} - \mathbf{o}). When to use: As the primary primitive test in ray tracers, BVH traversal, and volume rendering ray marching. The slab method for AABB intersection is a classic technique in computer graphics. It is widely used in ray tracing kernels and volume rendering engines. The specific implementation details provided here are drawn from modern implementations in graphics libraries and research codebases. rordenlab/MRIcroWeb, https://github.com/rordenlab/MRIcroWeb, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial) Decoupling Data Layouts from Bounding Volume Hierarchies, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2511.15028, fetched 2026-10-29

name: Multi-Hit BVH Traversal
head: Multi-Hit BVH Traversal for Volume Clipping, Multi-hit intersection, Multi-hit query, Ray Traced Volume Clipping Using Multi-Hit BVH Traversal
body: Multi-Hit BVH Traversal is a technique to determine the N closest intersections of a viewing ray with compound clip objects (geometric primitives organized in a Bounding Volume Hierarchy) to construct clip intervals for volume rendering. It sets itself apart from all-hit queries by using a preallocated static array to avoid costly dynamic memory reallocation, which is essential for real-time implementation. Unlike texture-based approaches that require multiple rendering passes or depth peeling, this method calculates intervals directly in on-chip GPU memory. Inputs and Outputs Input: A ray defined by origin \mathbf{o} and direction \mathbf{d}; a set of clip primitives (planes, spheres, triangle meshes) organized in a BVH; an integer N representing the maximum number of intersections to retrieve. Output: An array of N intersection distances (or hit records) sorted by proximity to the ray origin, used to construct clip intervals. Data Structures Clip Primitives: Stored as Plain Old Data (POD) objects in a C array to avoid virtual inheritance and vtable lookups, reducing indirection overhead. BVH: Manages triangle meshes. The BVH is rebuilt completely if the triangle mesh changes, as dynamic updates are not supported in this implementation. Result Array: A static memory array of size N. The size N must be decided a priori. Parameters N: The maximum number of intersections to retrieve. This value determines the size of the static result array. Algorithm Steps 1. Preallocation: Allocate a static array of size N to store the intersection results. This avoids dynamic memory allocation during the traversal loop. 2. Traversal: Execute the multi-hit query on the BVH. The traversal visits nodes and primitives, collecting hit distances. 3. Sorting/Selection: The implementation ensures the N closest hits are returned. 4. Interval Construction: Use the resulting hit distances to define clip intervals (e.g., [t1, t2], [t3, t4]) for the volume rendering pass. Pseudocode The following pseudocode illustrates the usage pattern, assuming a generic ray-tracing library interface that supports multi-hit queries with a fixed-size buffer. Vector operations are standard. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def multihitbvhtraversal(rayorigin, raydirection, bvhroot, maxhits): # Preallocate a static array for the results hits = [None] maxhits hitcount = 0 maxhitt = float('inf') # Standard BVH traversal stack stack = [bvhroot] while stack: node = stack.pop() # Check bounding box intersection using slab method tmin = (node.bbox.min - rayorigin) / raydirection tmax = (node.bbox.max - rayorigin) / raydirection tenter = max(min(tmin), min(tmax)) texit = min(max(tmin), max(tmax)) if tenter > texit or texit < 0: continue if tenter >= maxhitt: continue if node.isleaf(): # Intersect primitives in leaf for primitive in node.primitives: t = intersectprimitive(primitive, rayorigin, raydirection) if t is not None and t < maxhitt: # Insert into sorted static buffer if hitcount < maxhits: hits[hitcount] = t # Bubble sort insertion i = hitcount while i > 0 and hits[i] < hits[i-1]: hits[i], hits[i-1] = hits[i-1], hits[i] i -= 1 hitcount += 1 else: if t < hits[maxhits - 1]: hits[maxhits - 1] = t i = maxhits - 1 while i > 0 and hits[i] < hits[i-1]: hits[i], hits[i-1] = hits[i-1], hits[i] i -= 1 maxhitt = hits[maxhits - 1] else: # Push children to stack stack.append(node.left) stack.append(node.right) return hits[:hitcount] def intersectprimitive(primitive, origin, direction): # Generic dispatch to specific intersect() functions for POD objects # Avoids dynamic branching in the innermost traversal loop if primitive.type == 0: # PLANE return intersectplane(primitive, origin, direction) elif primitive.type == 1: # SPHERE return intersectsphere(primitive, origin, direction) elif primitive.type == 2: # TRIANGLE return intersecttriangle(primitive, origin, direction) return None def intersectplane(plane, origin, direction): denom = plane.normal.dot(direction) if abs(denom) < 1e-8: return None t = (plane.d - origin.dot(plane.normal)) / denom return t if t > 0 else None def intersectsphere(sphere, origin, direction): oc = origin - sphere.center b = oc.dot(direction) c = oc.dot(oc) - sphere.radius sphere.radius disc = b b - c if disc < 0: return None sq = disc 0.5 t = -b - sq return t if t > 0 else (-b + sq if -b + sq > 0 else None) def intersecttriangle(tri, origin, direction): # Möller–Trumbore algorithm e1 = tri.v1 - tri.v0 e2 = tri.v2 - tri.v0 h = direction.cross(e2) a = e1.dot(h) if a < 1e-8 and a > -1e-8: return None f = 1.0 / a s = origin - tri.v0 u = f s.dot(h) if u < 0.0 or u > 1.0: return None q = s.cross(e1) v = f direction.dot(q) if v < 0.0 or u + v > 1.0: return None t = f e2.dot(q) return t if t > 0 else None Edge Cases and Pitfalls Dynamic Branching: Switching over primitive types in the innermost traversal loop causes performance degradation. The implementation avoids this by using generic routines that call specific intersect() functions for POD objects. Register Pressure: Storing clip intervals in on-chip GPU memory increases register demand per thread on the shading multi-processor (SM), which may impact kernel performance. Static Geometry: Triangle meshes must be static. Changing them requires a complete BVH rebuild. Precision: The method avoids the need for a tiny epsilon \Delta that varies per query, which can cause artifacts and unnecessary BVH traversals in other methods. Time Complexity: Depends on the BVH traversal depth and the number of primitives. The multi-hit query is generally more efficient than an all-hit query for large scenes because it stops after finding N hits. The asymptotic behavior is reduced to average logarithmic in the number of geometric primitives due to the BVH. Memory Complexity: O(N) for the result array, where N is the maximum number of hits. The BVH structure itself is O(P) where P is the number of primitives. Performance: Evaluated on a 1024x1024 resolution MRI dataset (MNI152, 0.5mm³ voxel size, 364x436x364 voxels) clipped with Utah teapot models. Level 1: 2,464 triangles, 1,559 BVH nodes. Level 2: 14,784 triangles, 9,771 BVH nodes. Level 3: 59,136 triangles, 39,063 BVH nodes. Level 4: 236,544 triangles, 151,637 BVH nodes. Strengths: Real-time capable; avoids dynamic memory allocation; no multiple rendering passes or depth peeling required; on-chip memory access is faster than DDR3. Limitations: Requires a priori knowledge of the maximum number of intersections N; increased register pressure on GPU; triangle meshes must be static (BVH rebuild required on change). The method was proposed in the context of real-time volume rendering for neurosurgical applications. It builds on the Visionaray ray tracing template library and the BVH construction scheme from [31] (cited in S1). It is conceptually aligned with the approach by Weiskopf et al. [34] (cited in S1), but differs by using a multi-hit query instead of hardware depth buffers and multiple render passes. name: Ray-Primitive Intersection (Analytic/Geometric)
body: This family computes exact intersection parameters between camera rays and standard geometric primitives by solving their implicit or parametric equations. It sets itself apart from iterative approaches like Ray-Marching by avoiding root-finding loops, and from bounding volume methods like Ray-Volume and Bounding Box Intersection by operating directly on specific primitive shapes. The shared principles of this family are the geometric definition of rays and the parallel execution model. Ray Definition Rays are defined by an origin \mathbf{o} and a direction \mathbf{d}. The direction is typically normalized. The origin is often the camera eye position, but can vary based on the camera model. Parallel Execution Computations are mapped to parallel threads. Each thread typically processes one or more pixels or samples. Memory access patterns are optimized for coalescing. Synchronization is used to manage data dependencies between threads. Intersects camera rays with spherical geometry to determine entry and exit points, then applies Beer's Law along the chord length for volumetric rendering. Determines entry and exit points for rays traversing tetrahedral cells, exploiting the primitive's topology for early termination and shared edge computations in unstructured grids. Returns the closest valid intersection distance or a failure indicator, serving as the core decision unit that filters non-intersections and self-intersections via epsilon thresholds. Optimizes multiple ray-primitive evaluations along a single ray by establishing a strict processing order based on bounding box distances to reduce computational load. Computes intersections with planar primitives using linear algebra and plane equations, distinguishing itself from curved primitives by avoiding quadratic surface definitions. Computes intersections with triangular meshes using barycentric coordinate validation, explicitly testing against finite arbitrary surfaces rather than infinite planes. Provides geometric primitives for structured voxel grids and approximate intersections with complex volumetric structures, relying on angular decomposition and scan-plane approximations. Not given in the sources.

name: Sphere Intersection
head: Ray-Marching: Sphere Intersection and Path Calculation, Ray-Sphere Intersection for Volume Rendering, Volumetric Sphere Rendering
body: Sphere Intersection is a method to render a volumetric sphere by intersecting camera rays with the sphere geometry to determine entry and exit points, then applying Beer's Law along the chord length. It calculates the entry and exit t-values for a ray intersecting a sphere, returning sentinel values if no intersection occurs. Unlike Ray-Triangle Intersection which handles discrete surfaces, this method computes the path length through a participating medium to determine transmittance and scattered light contribution. Inputs and Outputs Input: Ray origin \mathbf{o}, ray direction \mathbf{d} (typically normalized), sphere center \mathbf{c}, sphere radius r. Output: Entry and exit t-values (t{min}, t{max}) for chord calculation, or the smallest positive t for the closest hit. If no intersection occurs, returns a sentinel value indicating failure. Data Structures Ray: Struct containing origin (vec3) and direction (vec3). Sphere: Struct containing center (vec3) and radius (float). Steps 1. Vector Calculation: Compute the vector from the sphere center to the ray origin: \mathbf{l} = \mathbf{o} - \mathbf{c}. 2. Quadratic Coefficients: Solve the quadratic equation derived from the sphere implicit function \|\mathbf{o} + t\mathbf{d} - \mathbf{c}\|^2 = r^2. A = \mathbf{d} \cdot \mathbf{d} B = 2.0 \cdot (\mathbf{l} \cdot \mathbf{d}) C = (\mathbf{l} \cdot \mathbf{l}) - r^2 3. Discriminant Check: Compute d = B^2 - 4AC. If d < 0, there is no intersection. Return a sentinel value (e.g., None, nullopt, or large floats). 4. Root Calculation: Compute \sqrt{d}. Calculate t1 = \frac{-B - \sqrt{d}}{2A} and t2 = \frac{-B + \sqrt{d}}{2A}. 5. Validity Check: If both t1 and t2 are negative, the sphere is behind the ray origin. Return no intersection. For volume rendering, t{min} = \min(t1, t2) is the entry point and t{max} = \max(t1, t2) is the exit point. 6. Chord Length: Compute the distance the ray travels through the sphere: L = t{max} - t{min}. If t{min} < 0 < t{max}, the ray starts inside the sphere, and the chord length is t{max}. 7. Beer's Law: Apply Beer's Law using the chord length L and uniform density \rho to determine transmittance T = e^{-\rho L}. 8. Scattering: Assume uniform scattered light from the sphere and blend with the transmitted background. Pseudocode Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def raysphereintersection(rayorigin, raydirection, spherecenter, sphereradius): # Vector from sphere center to ray origin lx = rayorigin.x - spherecenter.x ly = rayorigin.y - spherecenter.y lz = rayorigin.z - spherecenter.z # Quadratic coefficients: At^2 + Bt + C = 0 A = (raydirection.x raydirection.x + raydirection.y raydirection.y + raydirection.z raydirection.z) B = 2.0 ((lx raydirection.x) + (ly raydirection.y) + (lz raydirection.z)) C = (lx lx + ly ly + lz lz) - (sphereradius sphereradius) # Discriminant discriminant = (B B) - (4.0 A C) if discriminant < 0.0: return None sqrtdisc = math.sqrt(discriminant) # Calculate t values t1 = (-B - sqrtdisc) / (2.0 A) t2 = (-B + sqrtdisc) / (2.0 A) # Ensure tmin is the smaller value if t1 > t2: tmin = t2 tmax = t1 else: tmin = t1 tmax = t2 # If both t are negative, the sphere is behind the ray if tmax < 0.0: return None return (tmin, tmax) def computetransmittance(tmin, tmax, density): if tmin is None: return 1.0 # Chord length calculation if tmin < 0.0: chordlength = tmax else: chordlength = tmax - tmin # Beer's Law transmittance = math.exp(-density chordlength) return transmittance Parameters EPS: Epsilon value used for normal calculation and offsetting, typically 0.0001. Density: Uniform particle density assumed for the sphere. Edge Cases and Pitfalls No Intersection: If discriminant < 0, return sentinel values (e.g., 1e2, -1e5). Ray Behind Sphere: If both t values are negative, the sphere is behind the ray origin. Return false/no intersection. Ray Origin Inside: If t{min} < 0 < t{max}, the ray originates inside the sphere. The chord length is t{max} (distance to exit). Tangential Intersection: If discriminant = 0, the ray is tangent to the sphere. t{min} = t{max}. Chord length is 0. Shadow Ignorance: This specific implementation ignores shadows cast by objects outside or inside the volume. Varying Densities: This specific implementation assumes uniform density and does not handle varying densities. A technique to render a 3D sphere as a 2D billboard by calculating a spherical contribution factor based on the fragment's distance from the center. It calculates sphereContrib = distance(center, fragPos)/radius, then sphereContrib = sqrt(max(0, 1 - sphereContrib sphereContrib)). If showQuad is true, it sets color to vec4(sphereContrib) and discards fragments near edges (< 0.01 or > 0.99). Time Complexity: O(1) per ray, as it involves a fixed number of arithmetic operations (dot products, square root). Memory Complexity: O(1), requiring only local variables for ray and sphere parameters. Performance: Extremely fast due to the simplicity of the quadratic formula, making it suitable for real-time rendering and GPU parallel execution. Strengths: Analytical solution, no iteration required, and robust for simple volumetric spheres. Limitations: Only applies to spheres, does not handle complex geometries or varying densities without extension, and ignores shadows and inter-volume scattering. Originating from basic ray tracing techniques, sphere intersection is a fundamental building block for volume rendering. It is widely used in introductory volume rendering tutorials to demonstrate the application of Beer's Law. The algorithm appears in educational tutorials, Shadertoy examples, Rust-based raytracers, and WebGL implementations. The billboard variant is used in cloud rendering for efficient sprite-based volume approximation. name: Ray-Tetrahedron Intersection
body: Ray-tetrahedron intersection determines the entry and exit points of a ray as it traverses a tetrahedral cell, which is the fundamental geometric primitive for rendering unstructured volumetric data. It solves the problem of efficiently computing the intersection segment [t{enter}, t{exit}] required for volume integration, distinguishing itself from sibling methods by handling the specific topology of four triangular faces and the potential for non-convex or deformed geometries. The shared principles of this family are the geometric definition of rays and the parallel execution model. Ray Definition Rays are defined by an origin \mathbf{o} and a direction \mathbf{d}. The direction is typically normalized. The origin is often the camera eye position, but can vary based on the camera model. Parallel Execution Computations are mapped to parallel threads. Each thread typically processes one or more pixels or samples. Memory access patterns are optimized for coalescing. Synchronization is used to manage data dependencies between threads. The Fast Convex Polygon Wrapper (FCPW) Accelerator is a geometric query structure designed to efficiently compute ray-tetrahedron edge intersections and closest-point projections on polygonal meshes. It solves the problem of robustly determining intersection parameters and surface normals for tetrahedral cells defined by polygonal boundaries, serving as the core geometric engine for the MeshQueryHandler. It sets itself apart from sibling methods by wrapping convex polygonal geometry into an accelerated structure that supports both single-edge intersection finding and closest-point queries, enabling efficient rasterization of ambient occlusion volumes via the Convex Polygon Falloff Function. This method determines the entry and exit points of a ray intersecting a tetrahedron by representing the ray and tetrahedron edges as Plücker coordinates, computing permuted inner products to classify faces, and deriving scaled barycentric coordinates directly from these products. It sets itself apart from plane-intersection approaches by avoiding explicit plane calculations and divisions until the final normalization step, and from ray-triangle decomposition methods (like Moller-Trumbore) by leveraging shared edge computations and early termination logic specific to the tetrahedron's topology. This method determines whether a set of query points lies inside a set of tetrahedra by solving for barycentric coordinates. It serves as the core geometric primitive for Ray-Tetrahedron Intersection, allowing volume rendering engines to identify which cells contain sample points for density accumulation. Unlike Plücker-based Tetrahedral Cell Intersection which operates on ray primitives, this method operates on explicit point positions, making it suitable for post-intersection validation or direct point-in-volume queries. Computes the four planar faces (unit normals and distances to the origin) from a four-vertex description of a tetrahedron. It serves as the geometric preprocessing step for Ray-Tetrahedron Intersection, converting vertex-based topology into plane-based primitives suitable for analytic ray intersection tests. Unlike sibling methods that optimize traversal or use Plücker coordinates, this method focuses strictly on the algebraic derivation of face planes from vertex coordinates. This method computes the intersection of a ray with a Scale-Invariant Integral Surface (SCALIS) primitive by minimizing the squared distance from the ray to the skeleton curve, normalized by the local radius, rather than solving the implicit surface equation directly. It sets itself apart from direct sphere-cone intersection approaches by reducing the problem to finding the root of a linear equation, offering superior numerical stability and lower computational cost. This method determines the ray segments that intersect deformed finite elements, addressing the problem where the mapping from a standard element shape (e.g., a regular tetrahedron) to physical simulation space is non-linear. It is distinct from linear tetrahedron intersection methods because it handles higher-order polynomial mappings, requiring the calculation of multiple intersection segments and an approximate inverse mapping to evaluate scalar functions. This method optimizes the ray-tetrahedron intersection test by leveraging mesh shader wave intrinsics to share geometric data among the four vertices of a single tetrahedron. It reduces redundant memory loads by a factor of four and lowers the computational cost of the intersection routine to approximately 12 floating-point operations (FLOPs). Unlike naive implementations that load tetrahedron data independently for each vertex, this approach precomputes plane parameters in the mesh shader and interpolates them in the fragment shader, building on the standard Cyrus-Beck algorithm. This method renders volumetric data defined by unstructured or irregular cell grids (such as tetrahedra or hexahedra) by traversing the cell structure along a ray. It solves the problem of efficiently visiting cells intersected by a ray in non-uniform geometries where regular grid acceleration structures (like uniform grids or octrees) are not applicable or efficient. It differs from sibling methods by explicitly handling the topological connectivity of irregular cells and managing concave dataset boundaries, which can cause rays to exit and re-enter the volume multiple times. Definition: An interface method that computes edge intersection t-values and normals for a tetrahedron in a subgrid context. Parameters: useRobust (bool, default false) enables robust intersection computation; recordNormals (bool, default true) skips normal calculation when false to save computation. Layout: Input is std::array<Vector3,4> tetpositions (or tetindices + positions). Output is std::array<std::vector<double>,6> edgeisectts and std::array<std::vector<Vector3>,6> edgeisectnormals, where each array has size 6 corresponding to the tetrahedron edges. Code: virtual void queryintersections(const std::array<Vector3,4>& tetpositions, std::array<std::vector<double>,6>& edgeisectts, std::array<std::vector<Vector3>,6>& edgeisectnormals, bool useRobust = false, bool recordNormals = true) = 0;. Definition: A method that uses the geometric property that if a ray misses the first face (F3), it intersects the supporting plane in one of six regions defined by edge lines, determining potential entry/exit faces based on barycentric coordinates. Steps: If the ray does not intersect F3 (V0V1V2), determine which of the six regions (A–F) on the supporting plane the intersection point lies in, based on barycentric coordinates. Determine if the ray 'enters' the plane using the test: \sum{j=0}^{2} (\boldsymbol{\pi}r \odot \boldsymbol{\pi}{3j}) > 0, which is equivalent to \mathbf{L} \cdot \mathbf{N} < 0 where \mathbf{N} is the face normal. Based on the region and ray direction, restrict potential entry/exit faces; e.g., entering in region (E) allows entry only through F1 (V2V3V0), entering in region (A) allows exit only through F0 (V3V2V1). Performance: The modifications have a negative impact on performance compared to the optimized Plücker-based algorithm because it requires computing all three products \boldsymbol{\pi}r \odot \boldsymbol{\pi}{3j} and involves an involved examination of barycentric coordinates. Definition: Clips a polyhedron against four clip planes, effectively finding its intersection with a tetrahedron defined by those planes. Parameters: poly is the polyhedron to be clipped, where distances to the clip plane and bit flags in poly.verts[...].orient must be set prior to calling. andcmp is a set of bit flags; face f will be skipped if andcmp & (1 << f) evaluates to true. Definition: A geometric test to determine if a point P lies in the interior of a tetrahedron ABCD by evaluating the signs of determinants of sub-vectors formed by the tetrahedron's vertices and P. Steps: Calculate the signed volume of the tetrahedron using one sixth of the determinant of the three vectors spanning it. Compute Da, Db, Dc, and Dd as determinants of matrices formed by the other three vertices for each respective vertex (e.g., Da uses b, c, d). Formula: Da = \det(Va) where Va = \{b, c, d\}; Db = \det(Vb) where Vb = \{a, c, d\}; Dc = \det(Vc) where Vc = \{a, b, d\}; Dd = \det(Vd) where Vd = \{a, b, c\}. Definition: A method to classify tetrahedra in a volume mesh as interior or exterior to a closed surface by casting a ray from each tetrahedron's centroid and counting intersections with the surface mesh. Steps: For each tetrahedron in the mesh, compute its centroid. Cast a ray from the centroid in the specified direction against all triangles of the closed surface mesh. Count only forward intersections where the intersection parameter t > 0. Apply the parity test: if the total intersection count is odd, the tetrahedron is interior; if even, it is exterior. Remove all tetrahedra classified as exterior (even hit count) from the mesh. Rebuild adjacency structures for the remaining tetrahedra to maintain mesh consistency. Parameters: Ray direction is a fixed vector [1.0, 10^{-4}, 10^{-8}] used for all rays to minimize edge/vertex grazing ambiguities. Intersection tolerance (\epsilon) is 10^{-12}, used for numerical stability in the Möller–Trumbore algorithm. Accuracy: The computed volume of the interior mesh matches analytical values within 5% for a unit box and a unit sphere. The problem of ray-tetrahedron intersection is central to the visualization of unstructured grid data, such as that produced by finite element analysis (FEA) or computational fluid dynamics (CFD). Early methods relied on decomposing the tetrahedron into four triangles and applying ray-triangle intersection tests, such as the Möller–Trumbore algorithm, which is computationally redundant due to shared edges. The use of Plücker coordinates was introduced to optimize this process by representing lines in 6D space, allowing for the computation of face orientations and intersection parameters without explicit plane equations or divisions until the final step. This approach leverages the topological connectivity of the tetrahedron to enable early termination and shared edge computations. In the context of GPU rendering, mesh shaders have been utilized to optimize the intersection test by sharing geometric data among the four vertices of a single tetrahedron within a wave group, significantly reducing memory bandwidth requirements. For deformed elements, where the mapping from a reference element to physical space is non-linear, the intersection problem becomes more complex, requiring the solution of polynomial equations and the use of approximate inverse mappings to evaluate scalar fields. Additionally, ray-tetrahedron intersection is used in mesh processing tasks, such as classifying tetrahedra as interior or exterior to a surface by ray-casting from centroids, which is a critical step in generating valid volumetric meshes for simulation. hbaktash/subgrid-marching, https://github.com/hbaktash/subgrid-marching, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial) Fast Ray–Tetrahedron Intersection using Plücker..., https://users.uop.gr/~nplatis%20/files/PlatisTheoharisRayTetra.pdf, fetched 2026-10-29 (unofficial) devonmpowell/r3d, https://github.com/devonmpowell/r3d, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial) Robust Voxelization and Visualization by Improved Tetrahedral Mesh Generation, https://doi.org/10.48550/arxiv.2106.01326, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial) Implement interior/exterior classification for tetrahedral meshes, https://github.com/mkofler96/KoFEM/pull/51, fetched 2026-10-29 (unofficial)

name: Fast Convex Polygon Wrapper (FCPW) Accelerator
head: Mesh Handler Implementation, MeshQueryHandler
body: The Fast Convex Polygon Wrapper (FCPW) Accelerator is a geometric query structure used within the MeshQueryHandler to process polygonal meshes. It provides accelerated queries for finding ray-tetrahedron edge intersections and computing closest-point projections on mesh surfaces. It sets itself apart from sibling methods by wrapping convex polygonal geometry into a single structure that supports both intersection finding and closest-point queries, which is utilized by the Convex Polygon Falloff Function. The FCPW accelerator is constructed from a set of polygons and their vertex positions. It provides two primary query operations: finding the single intersection of a ray with tetrahedron edges, and finding the closest point on the mesh surface to a query point. name: Convex Polygon Falloff Function
head: Convex Polygon Distance Falloff, Falloff Function g
body: The Convex Polygon Falloff Function computes a scalar occlusion weight for a point in space based on its distance from a convex polygon P. It solves the problem of defining a smooth, monotonic falloff from a surface (mapping distance 0 to weight 1, and distance \delta to weight 0) for arbitrary convex polygons, not just triangles. It sets itself apart from sibling methods by using a product of linear clamped terms defined by edge and face normals, enabling efficient rasterization of the ambient occlusion volume (AOV) via the Fast Convex Polygon Wrapper (FCPW) Accelerator. Inputs: Polygon vertices \{\vec{p}0, \dots, \vec{p}{k-1}\}, where no three vertices are collinear. Falloff distance parameter \delta > 0. Surface type flag \bar{\alpha} (1 for solid surfaces). Outputs: Scalar falloff value g(\vec{x}) \in [0, 1] for a query point \vec{x}. Data Structures: Edge normals \hat{m}i for i \in \{0, \dots, k-1\}. Face normal \hat{m}k. These are precomputed vectors stored in memory. Steps: 1. Compute the negative face normal \hat{m}k using the first three vertices \vec{p}0, \vec{p}1, \vec{p}2: \hat{m}k = S((\vec{p}2 - \vec{p}0) \times (\vec{p}1 - \vec{p}0)) where S(\vec{v}) = \vec{v} / \|\vec{v}\| is the normalization function. 2. Compute the inward-facing edge normals \hat{m}i for each edge i \in \{0, \dots, k-1\}: \hat{m}i = S\left((\vec{p}{(i+1) \bmod k} - \vec{p}i) \times \hat{m}k\right) 3. Evaluate the falloff function g(\vec{x}) for a point \vec{x}: g(\vec{x}) = \bar{\alpha} \prod{i=0}^k \max(0, \min(1, (\vec{x} - \vec{p}{i \bmod k}) \cdot \hat{m}i / \delta + 1)) The product index i runs from 0 to k. The term for i=k uses \hat{m}k and vertex \vec{p}{k \bmod k} = \vec{p}0. Parameters: \delta: The distance at which the falloff reaches 0. Not given in the sources. \bar{\alpha}: Set to 1 for solid surfaces. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Collinear Vertices: The method assumes no three vertices are collinear. Degenerate polygons may produce zero-length normals, causing division by zero during normalization. Implementers should check for zero-length cross products and handle degenerate edges. Precision: The clamping \max(0, \min(1, \dots)) ensures numerical stability but may introduce artifacts if \delta is very small relative to vertex precision. Vertex Indexing: The formula uses i \bmod k for vertex indexing in the product. For i=k, this refers to \vec{p}0. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def computefalloff(pvertices, delta, x, alpha=1.0): """ Compute convex polygon falloff for point x. pvertices: list of k 3D vectors (p0,..., p{k-1}) delta: falloff distance parameter x: query 3D vector alpha: surface alpha (1.0 for solid) """ k = len(pvertices) # Step 1: Compute negative face normal mk v0 = pvertices[0] v1 = pvertices[1] v2 = pvertices[2] edge1 = v1 - v0 edge2 = v2 - v0 crossface = cross(edge2, edge1) # (p2 - p0) x (p1 - p0) normface = length(crossface) if normface < 1e-10: return 0.0 # Degenerate polygon mk = crossface / normface # Step 2: Compute edge normals mi for i in 0..k-1 medge = [] for i in range(k): pi = pvertices[i] pnext = pvertices[(i + 1) % k] edgevec = pnext - pi crossedge = cross(edgevec, mk) normedge = length(crossedge) if normedge < 1e-10: return 0.0 # Degenerate edge mi = crossedge / normedge medge.append(mi) # Step 3: Evaluate falloff function result = alpha for i in range(k + 1): pidx = pvertices[i % k] if i < k: mi = medge[i] else: mi = mk diff = x - pidx dotval = dot(diff, mi) / delta + 1.0 clamped = max(0.0, min(1.0, dotval)) result = clamped return result The Bounding Volume {B} defines the spatial extent of the ambient occlusion volume (AOV) generated by a convex polygon P using the Convex Polygon Falloff Function. It solves the problem of efficiently rasterizing the region where occlusion is non-zero by constructing a closed polyhedron V bounded by k+2 planes. It sets itself apart from sibling methods by explicitly computing the displacement vectors required to extrude the polygon's vertices into a 3D volume suitable for depth-buffer-based occlusion queries. Time Complexity: O(k) per query point, where k is the number of vertices. Memory Complexity: O(k) to store precomputed normals. Strengths: Efficient evaluation; works for any convex polygon, not just triangles; monotonic falloff. Limitations: Requires precomputation of normals; degenerate polygons cause issues. When to use: When generating ambient occlusion volumes for convex polygonal occluders in real-time rendering. When not to use: For non-convex polygons or when higher-order falloff functions are required. The Convex Polygon Falloff Function was introduced by Matt McGuire in the paper "Ambient Occlusion Volumes". It is part of the AOV framework for real-time ambient occlusion, allowing static and dynamic geometry to correctly occlude each other. The method is designed for efficiency on GPUs, leveraging the fact that the falloff function can be rasterized as a volume. name: Bounding Volume {B}
head: AO Bounding Polyhedron, Polyhedral Bounding Volume for AO [S1, unofficial]
body: The Bounding Volume {B} method defines the spatial extent of the ambient occlusion volume (AOV) for a convex polygon P by constructing a closed polyhedron V bounded by k+2 planes. It enables efficient rasterization-based occlusion queries by explicitly computing vertex displacement vectors to extrude the polygon into a 3D volume. Inputs: Convex polygon P with k vertices \{\vec{p}0, \dots, \vec{p}{k-1}\}, no three collinear. Maximum occlusion distance \delta. Edge normals \hat{m}i for i \in [0, k-1], pointing inward relative to the polygon projection. Face normal \hat{m}k (normal to the plane containing P). Outputs: A polyhedron V defined by 2k vertices \{\vec{v}0, \dots, \vec{v}{2k-1}\}. The bounding planes \{B0, \dots, B{k+1}\}. Data Structures: Vertices: Array of 2k 3D vectors. Indices 0 to k-1 lie in the plane of P. Indices k to 2k-1 are displaced along \hat{m}k. Normals: Array of k+2 3D unit vectors. \hat{m}0 \dots \hat{m}{k-1} are edge normals; \hat{m}k is the face normal; \hat{m}{k+1} is the normal for the "above" plane. Steps: 1. Define Plane Normals and Reference Points: Set \hat{m}0, \dots, \hat{m}{k-1} as the inward-facing normals of the polygon edges. Set \hat{m}k as the unit normal to the plane containing P. Define \vec{p}k = \vec{p}0 and \vec{p}{k+1} = \vec{p}0 + \delta \hat{m}{k+1}, where \hat{m}{k+1} is the normal of the plane B{k+1} containing P. 2. Compute Extension Vectors \vec{e}i for Base Vertices (0 \le i < k): The extension vector \vec{e}i displaces polygon vertex \vec{p}i to volume vertex \vec{v}i. It is constrained by the geometry of the bounding planes: \vec{e}i \cdot -\hat{m}i = \delta \quad (9) \vec{e}i \cdot -\hat{m}{(i-1+k) \bmod k} = \delta \quad (10) \vec{e}i \cdot \hat{m}k = 0 \quad (11) Solve for \vec{e}i using the linear system: \vec{e}i = \begin{bmatrix} \hat{m}i \\ \hat{m}{(i-1+k) \bmod k} \\ \hat{m}k \end{bmatrix}^{-1} \begin{bmatrix} -\delta \\ -\delta \\ 0 \end{bmatrix} \quad (12). 3. Clamp Extension Vectors: To prevent sliver polygons from creating excessively long volumes with negligible occlusion, clamp the magnitude of each extension vector: \|\vec{e}i\| \le 2\delta for all i < k. 4. Compute Top Extension Vectors (k \le i < 2k): The vertices in the "top" plane are displaced from the base vertices along the face normal: \vec{e}i = \vec{e}{i-k} - \delta \hat{m}k \quad (13). 5. Construct Volume Vertices: For 0 \le i < k: \vec{v}i = \vec{p}i + \vec{e}i. For k \le i < 2k: \vec{v}i = \vec{p}{i-k} + \vec{e}i. 6. Define Bounding Planes: Planes B0, \dots, B{k-1} correspond to polygon edges with normal \hat{m}i. Plane Bk is above P. Plane B{k+1} contains P. The plane equation is given by (\vec{x} - \vec{p}i) \cdot \hat{m}i = \delta. Simplified Falloff Evaluation: When evaluating the falloff function g for a point at the origin, the formula simplifies to: g(\vec{0}) = \bar{\alpha} \prod{i=0}^k \max(0, \min(1, 1 - \vec{p}{i \bmod k} \cdot \hat{m}i / \delta)) \quad (8) Here, \bar{\alpha} is the average alpha of the polygon. Pitfalls: Sliver polygons produce long, thin volumes that are computationally expensive to rasterize but contribute little occlusion; the clamp \|\vec{e}i\| \le 2\delta is critical. Incorrect normals invert the volume or create empty intersections. Solving the 3 \times 3 linear system may suffer from numerical instability if the polygon is nearly degenerate. Not given in the sources. The Bounding Volume {B} method was introduced in the paper "Ambient Occlusion Volumes". It was developed to enable efficient rasterization-based ambient occlusion for complex geometry, particularly foliage and fences, by converting polygonal occluders into volumetric primitives that can be processed by standard graphics pipelines. The method relies on the Convex Polygon Falloff Function to define the occlusion intensity within the volume. name: Hexahedral Mesh Traversal (Plücker Space)
head: Hex-P, Hexahedral Plücker traversal
body: A traversal method for hexahedral meshes that uses Plücker coordinates to determine the exit face of a ray intersecting a hexahedral cell, requiring face decomposition into triangles for interpolation. It sets itself apart from its sibling Hexahedral Mesh Traversal (Bilinear Patch-Extension) by relying on triangular decomposition for interpolation, which introduces parametric discontinuities along the diagonal but allows unambiguous face determination. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A ray defined by origin \mathbf{o} and direction \mathbf{d}; a hexahedral mesh where each cell has 8 vertices v0, \dots, v7. The entry face is defined by vertices v0, v1, v2, v3 and the opposite face by v4, v5, v6, v7. Output: The index of the next hexahedron in the traversal path and the barycentric coordinates on the exit face for interpolation. Data Structures: The mesh topology is implicit in the grid structure; no extra connectivity memory is required. Boundary faces are preprocessed and decomposed into two triangles each for efficient kd-tree initialization. Steps: 1. Initialization: Find the initial hexahedron along the ray using a kd-tree built from the decomposed boundary faces. 2. First Plücker Test: Perform a Plücker test using edges v4 \to v5 and v6 \to v7. This test partitions the possible exit faces into three areas A0, A1, A2, each containing exactly three faces of the hexahedron. 3. Second Plücker Test (Conditional): If the first test does not uniquely identify the exit face, perform a second Plücker test based on the determined area: For area A0: test edges v2 \to v6 and v3 \to v7. For area A1: test edges v4 \to v6 and v5 \to v7. For area A2: test edges v0 \to v4 and v1 \to v5. 4. Face Determination: Determine the correct exit face using simple sign comparisons from the second test. 5. Traversal Step: Modify the index pointer by incrementing or decrementing with respect to the dimension corresponding to the exit face to fetch the next cell. Stop if the pointer exits volume bounds. 6. Interpolation: Decompose the intersected exit face into two triangles. Compute barycentric coordinates for the intersection point on the selected triangle. Note that Plücker values cannot be directly scaled to receive parametric coordinates for quadrilaterals, necessitating this decomposition. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def cross(a, b): return (a[1]b[2] - a[2]b[1], a[2]b[0] - a[0]b[2], a[0]b[1] - a[1]b[0]) def dot(a, b): return a[0]b[0] + a[1]b[1] + a[2]b[2] def sub(a, b): return (a[0]-b[0], a[1]-b[1], a[2]-b[2]) def pluckersign(o, d, p1, p2): # Standard Plücker sign test: sign(dot(d x (p1-o), p2-p1)) vectop1 = sub(p1, o) vecedge = sub(p2, p1) crossprod = cross(d, vectop1) val = dot(crossprod, vecedge) return 1 if val > 0 else (-1 if val < 0 else 0) def barycentriccoords(p, a, b, c): # Standard 2D barycentric computation for triangle abc v0 = sub(c, a) v1 = sub(b, a) v2 = sub(p, a) d00 = dot(v0, v0) d01 = dot(v0, v1) d11 = dot(v1, v1) d20 = dot(v2, v0) d21 = dot(v2, v1) denom = d00 d11 - d01 d01 v = (d11 d20 - d01 d21) / denom w = (d00 d21 - d01 d20) / denom u = 1.0 - v - w return (u, v, w) def traversehexahedron(rayo, rayd, mesh, currentidx, bounds, dimoffsets): # 1. Fetch vertices for current cell v = mesh.vertices[currentidx] v0, v1, v2, v3 = v[0], v[1], v[2], v[3] v4, v5, v6, v7 = v[4], v[5], v[6], v[7] # 2. First Plücker test: edges v4->v5 and v6->v7 # Sum of Plücker signs determines the area region areaval = pluckersign(rayo, rayd, v4, v5) + pluckersign(rayo, rayd, v6, v7) if areaval > 0: area = 0 # A0 elif areaval < 0: area = 2 # A2 else: area = 1 # A1 exitface = None # 3. Second Plücker test if area is ambiguous if area == 0: s1 = pluckersign(rayo, rayd, v2, v6) s2 = pluckersign(rayo, rayd, v3, v7) exitface = 0 if (s1 > 0 and s2 > 0) else (1 if s1 > 0 else 2) elif area == 1: s1 = pluckersign(rayo, rayd, v4, v6) s2 = pluckersign(rayo, rayd, v5, v7) exitface = 0 if (s1 > 0 and s2 > 0) else (1 if s1 > 0 else 2) elif area == 2: s1 = pluckersign(rayo, rayd, v0, v4) s2 = pluckersign(rayo, rayd, v1, v5) exitface = 0 if (s1 > 0 and s2 > 0) else (1 if s1 > 0 else 2) # 4. Traversal Step: Modify index pointer # Grid index update based on exit face dimension nextidx = currentidx + dimoffsets[exitface] if nextidx < bounds.min or nextidx >= bounds.max: return None, None # 5. Interpolation: Decompose exit face into two triangles # Select triangle based on exitface index and compute barycentrics tria, trib, tric = getexitfacevertices(exitface, v) barycentric = barycentriccoords(rayo + rayd intersectiont, tria, trib, tric) return nextidx, barycentric Parameters: Typical performance: 3.2 million hexahedra per second on a Dual-core Opteron 2 GHz. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Decomposing a face into two triangles leads to parametric discontinuities along the diagonal. Unwanted artifacts may appear if hexahedra values are badly distributed. Plücker values are only suitable for triangles; they cannot be directly scaled to receive parametric coordinates for quadrilaterals. A hybrid traversal algorithm that combines Plücker-based face selection with bilinear patch intersection tests. It avoids the geometric singularities and discontinuities of pure Plücker traversal by using parametric coordinates (u, v) from bilinear patches for interpolation. Choose this when smooth interpolation across face boundaries is critical and performance overhead of bilinear tests is acceptable. Time Complexity: The method requires at most four Plücker tests to decide the exit face. However, the need to decompose faces and compute barycentric coordinates reduces performance significantly compared to tetrahedral traversal. Memory Complexity: No extra memory for connectivity is required as topology is implicit. Measured Performance: 3.2 million hexahedra per second on a Dual-core Opteron 2 GHz. Scaling: Data fetching costs are 7 times higher than tetrahedral traversal because more than one vertex and scalar value must be fetched per step. Strengths: Unambiguous determination of intersected faces; optimized for convex hexahedral faces; easily extendable to concave faces. Limitations: Parametric discontinuities along the diagonal of decomposed faces; artifacts with badly distributed values; higher data fetching costs. When to use: When unambiguous face determination is prioritized over interpolation smoothness and performance overhead is acceptable. When not to use: When smooth interpolation across face boundaries is required or when performance is critical and tetrahedral meshes are an option. Originated in the paper "Fast Ray Traversal of Tetrahedral and Hexahedral Meshes for Direct Volume Rendering" (2006). The method extends the Plücker test introduced for tetrahedral traversal to hexahedral grids. It is used in direct volume rendering for hexahedral meshes. name: Hexahedral Mesh Traversal (Bilinear Patch-Extension)
head: Bilinear Patch Traversal, Hex-H, Hybrid Hexahedral Traversal
body: This method is a hybrid traversal algorithm for hexahedral meshes that combines Plücker-based face selection with bilinear patch intersection tests. It solves the problem of geometric singularities and interpolation discontinuities inherent in pure Plücker traversal by utilizing the parametric coordinates (u, v) derived directly from bilinear patch intersections to compute interpolated scalar values. It sets itself apart from the parent Hexahedral Mesh Traversal (Plücker Space) by avoiding triangle decomposition for interpolation and instead using the known parametric coordinates to compute values continuously across hexahedral faces. Inputs: Ray origin \mathbf{o}, ray direction \mathbf{d}, hexahedron vertices \mathbf{v}0 \dots \mathbf{v}7. Outputs: Exit face index, parametric coordinates (u, v) on the exit face, and interpolated scalar values at entry and exit points. Data Structures: Vertices: Array of 8 3D vectors representing the hexahedron corners. Plücker Values: Three scalar areas A0, A1, A2 derived from cross products of edge vectors and the ray direction. Bilinear Patch Parameters: u, v \in \mathbb{R} representing the parametric hit location on the face. Steps: 1. Plücker Face Selection: Compute the Plücker values for the lines \mathbf{v}4 \to \mathbf{v}5, \mathbf{v}6 \to \mathbf{v}7, and the ray direction to determine the three areas A0, A1, A2. This identifies the three candidate exit faces. 2. Bilinear Patch Intersection: For each of the three candidate exit faces, perform a bilinear patch intersection test. An edge of the bilinear patch depends on all four face vertices. 3. Exit Determination: Stop as soon as a patch is hit, i.e., when parametric coordinates (u, v) \in [0, 1]^2. This provides the exit face and the parametric coordinates (u, v) for the exit point. 4. Numerical Consistency Check: If numerical inconsistencies occur due to insufficient floating-point accuracy, perform two additional Plücker tests equivalent to the second step of the pure Plücker method to resolve the correct exit face. 5. Interpolation: Use the known parametric coordinates (u, v) from the bilinear patch test to compute interpolated scalar values on the entry and exit faces. This completely avoids discontinuities in the interpolated field. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def cross(a, b): return [a[1]b[2] - a[2]b[1], a[2]b[0] - a[0]b[2], a[0]b[1] - a[1]b[0]] def dot(a, b): return a[0]b[0] + a[1]b[1] + a[2]b[2] def sub(a, b): return [a[0]-b[0], a[1]-b[1], a[2]-b[2]] def traversehexahedron(rayorigin, raydirection, hexvertices): # Step 1: Compute Plücker areas for candidate faces edge1 = sub(hexvertices[5], hexvertices[4]) edge2 = sub(hexvertices[7], hexvertices[6]) # Standard Plücker coordinate computation for ray-cell face intersection A0 = dot(cross(edge1, raydirection), cross(edge1, raydirection)) A1 = dot(cross(edge2, raydirection), cross(edge2, raydirection)) A2 = dot(cross(edge1, edge2), cross(edge1, edge2)) # Identify candidate faces based on signs of A0, A1, A2 candidatefaces = [0, 1, 2] # Indices of the three candidate exit faces exitface = None u, v = 0.0, 0.0 # Step 2 & 3: Check bilinear patch intersection for each candidate for faceidx in candidatefaces: # Standard algebraic solution for ray-bilinear patch intersection # Solves P(u,v) = rayorigin + traydirection for the bilinear face hit, u, v = solvebilinearpatchintersection(rayorigin, raydirection, hexvertices, faceidx) if hit and 0.0 <= u <= 1.0 and 0.0 <= v <= 1.0: exitface = faceidx break # Step 4: Handle numerical inconsistencies if exitface is None: # Perform two additional Plücker tests (pure Plücker fallback) # Equivalent to the second step of the pure Plücker method exitface = resolvepluckerfallback(rayorigin, raydirection, hexvertices) # Recompute (u, v) by projecting the exit point onto the exit face plane exitpoint = add(rayorigin, scale(raydirection, computetexit(rayorigin, raydirection, hexvertices, exitface))) u, v = projecttofaceuv(exitpoint, hexvertices, exitface) # Step 5: Interpolation # Compute scalar at entry point (previous cell exit or ray origin) # Compute scalar at exit point using u, v on exitface scalarexit = interpolatescalarbilinear(hexvertices, exitface, u, v) return exitface, u, v, scalarexit def solvebilinearpatchintersection(rayorigin, raydirection, hexvertices, faceidx): # Standard bilinear patch intersection: constructs the 4-vertex bilinear surface, # forms a quadratic equation in t and u/v, solves for valid intersections. return False, 0.0, 0.0 def resolvepluckerfallback(rayorigin, raydirection, hexvertices): # Two additional Plücker tests equivalent to pure Plücker method return 0 def computetexit(rayorigin, raydirection, hexvertices, faceidx): # Standard ray-plane intersection return 1.0 def projecttofaceuv(point, hexvertices, faceidx): # Standard projection onto bilinear patch parameter space return 0.0, 0.0 def interpolatescalarbilinear(hexvertices, faceidx, u, v): # Standard bilinear interpolation return 0.0 def add(a, b): return [a[0]+b[0], a[1]+b[1], a[2]+b[2]] def scale(v, s): return [v[0]s, v[1]s, v[2]s] Parameters: Floating-point precision: Standard double precision is recommended to minimize numerical inconsistencies. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Holes in Hexahedron: Bilinear patches are generally not flat, introducing holes in the hexahedron because the implicit edge representation depends on all four face vertices, unlike Plücker coordinates which depend solely on two edge points. This can cause rays to miss the exit face or produce invalid (u, v) coordinates. Numerical Inconsistencies: Insufficient floating-point accuracy can lead to incorrect face selection. The method requires a fallback to Plücker tests in these cases. Discontinuities: Using bilinear patches with known parametric coordinates completely avoids discontinuities in the interpolated field. A method to calculate normals for hexahedral meshes using trilinear interpolation of vertex normals, converted from computational space to physical space via the Jacobian matrix. It is chosen when accurate shading is required for curvilinear hexahedral meshes. It operates on vector fields and requires Jacobian transformation for correct physical-space orientation. Steps: 1. Interpolate a vector at the entry and exit faces using the same parametric coordinates (u, v) used for scalar interpolation. 2. Perform a linear interpolation between the two interpolated vectors based on their distance to the isosurface to yield the final normal. 3. Calculate three vectors in physical space corresponding to the normal in computational space Nc and convert them to physical space Np using the Jacobian matrix. Formulas: Convert physical coordinates xi to computational coordinates \tilde{\rho}j using the Jacobian matrix J{ij}: xi = J{ij} \tilde{\rho}j J{ij} = \frac{\partial xi}{\partial \tilde{\rho}j} Approximate the Jacobian matrix J{ij} for a grid node n using central differences: J{ij} = \frac{1}{2} \left( \frac{xi(n) - xi(n-1)}{\tilde{\rho}j(n) - \tilde{\rho}j(n+1)} + \frac{xi(n+1) - xi(n)}{\tilde{\rho}j(n+1) - \tilde{\rho}j(n)} \right) A linear combination of the three vectors with the normal in computational space Nc results in the converted normal Np. Time Complexity: Raw traversal performance is 15% lower compared to the pure Plücker traverser due to the cost of bilinear patch intersection tests. However, overall performance gains 25% on average because time is saved in interpolation (no triangle decomposition needed). Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Measured Performance: The hybrid algorithm processes up to 4.5 million hexahedra per second on a Dual-core Opteron 2 GHz. Strengths: Better quality and significantly faster overall performance than the pure Plücker approach for hexahedral meshes due to avoided discontinuities and efficient interpolation. Limitations: Raw traversal is slower; numerical inconsistencies may require fallback tests, though this is rare. When to Use: Recommended for traversing curvilinear grids on a ray tracing basis, especially when high-quality rendering and continuous interpolation are prioritized over raw traversal speed. Originated in the paper "Fast Ray Traversal of Tetrahedral and Hexahedral Meshes for Direct Volume Rendering" (2006) by Ramsey et al.. The method was developed to address singularities and discontinuities in hexahedral mesh traversal for direct volume rendering. It builds on the Plücker-based traversal method but integrates bilinear patch tests to improve interpolation quality.
