name: Point-in-Tetrahedron Test via Barycentric Coordinates
head: Barycentric Point-in-Tetrahedron Test
body: This method determines whether a set of query points lies inside a set of tetrahedra by solving for barycentric coordinates. It serves as the core geometric primitive for Ray-Tetrahedron Intersection, allowing volume rendering engines to identify which cells contain sample points for density accumulation. Unlike Plücker-based Tetrahedral Cell Intersection which operates on ray primitives, this method operates on explicit point positions, making it suitable for post-intersection validation or direct point-in-volume queries. Inputs: points: Tensor of shape (P, 3) containing P query points in 3D space. vertices: Tensor of shape (V, 3) containing the vertices of the tetrahedral mesh. tetrahedra: Tensor of shape (T, 4) containing indices into vertices defining T tetrahedra. Outputs: insidetet: Tensor of shape (P,) storing the index of the first tetrahedron containing each point, or -1 if no containing tetrahedron exists. barycentriccoords: Tensor of shape (P, 4) storing the barycentric weights (\lambda0, \lambda1, \lambda2, \lambda3) for each point within its containing tetrahedron, or zeros if outside. The implementation relies on dense tensor layouts optimized for batched linear algebra operations. mat: A (T, 3, 3) tensor representing the system of linear equations for a chunk of points, where columns are the edge vectors. d: A (K, T, 3) tensor representing the vector from the reference vertex to the query points in the current chunk. 1. Initialization: Initialize insidetet with -1 and barycentriccoords with 0. 2. Chunking: To manage memory efficiency, process points in chunks of size chunksize. Iterate start from 0 to P with step chunksize. Let end = min(start + chunksize, P). 3. Vertex Extraction: For the current chunk, extract the vertices of all tetrahedra. Let v0, v1, v2, v3 be the vertices of a specific tetrahedron t. 4. Edge Vector Computation: Compute edge vectors relative to vertex v3 (the reference vertex): \mathbf{a} = \mathbf{v}0 - \mathbf{v}3 \mathbf{b} = \mathbf{v}1 - \mathbf{v}3 \mathbf{c} = \mathbf{v}2 - \mathbf{v}3 5. Point Vector Computation: Compute the vector from v3 to the query point \mathbf{p}: \mathbf{d} = \mathbf{p} - \mathbf{v}3 6. Barycentric Solving: Solve the linear system \mathbf{M} \boldsymbol{\lambda}{0:2} = \mathbf{d} for the first three barycentric coordinates, where \mathbf{M} = [\mathbf{a}, \mathbf{b}, \mathbf{c}]. \begin{bmatrix} \lambda0 \\ \lambda1 \\ \lambda2 \end{bmatrix} = \mathbf{M}^{-1} \mathbf{d} The fourth coordinate is derived by the constraint \sum \lambdai = 1: \lambda3 = 1 - \lambda0 - \lambda1 - \lambda2 7. Inside Test: A point is inside the tetrahedron if all barycentric coordinates are non-negative: \text{inside} = (\lambda0 \ge 0) \land (\lambda1 \ge 0) \land (\lambda2 \ge 0) \land (\lambda3 \ge 0) 8. Selection: For each point, identify the first tetrahedron satisfying the inside condition. If no tetrahedron contains the point, the result is -1. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def pointintetrahedron(points, vertices, tetrahedra, chunksize): """ Determines if points lie inside tetrahedra using barycentric coordinates. Args: points: Array (P, 3) vertices: Array (V, 3) tetrahedra: Array (T, 4) chunksize: Integer, number of points to process per batch Returns: insidetet: Array (P,) index of containing tetrahedron or -1 barycentriccoords: Array (P, 4) barycentric weights """ P = len(points) insidetet = [-1] P barycentriccoords = [[0.0, 0.0, 0.0, 0.0] for in range(P)] # Pre-fetch tetrahedron vertices: shape (T, 4, 3) tetvertices = [[vertices[tetrahedra[t][v]] for v in range(4)] for t in range(len(tetrahedra))] for start in range(0, P, chunksize): end = min(start + chunksize, P) chunkpoints = points[start:end] K = len(chunkpoints) # Extract vertices v0..v3 for all T: shape (T, 3) v0 = [row[0] for row in tetvertices] v1 = [row[1] for row in tetvertices] v2 = [row[2] for row in tetvertices] v3 = [row[3] for row in tetvertices] # Edge vectors: shape (T, 3) a = [[v0[t][i] - v3[t][i] for i in range(3)] for t in range(len(tetvertices))] b = [[v1[t][i] - v3[t][i] for i in range(3)] for t in range(len(tetvertices))] c = [[v2[t][i] - v3[t][i] for i in range(3)] for t in range(len(tetvertices))] # Matrix M: shape (T, 3, 3) where columns are a, b, c M = [[[a[t][i][j] for i in range(3)] for j in range(3)] for t in range(len(tetvertices))] # Point vectors relative to v3: shape (K, T, 3) d = [[[chunkpoints[k][i] - v3[t][i] for i in range(3)] for t in range(len(tetvertices))] for k in range(K)] # Transpose d to (T, 3, K) to match solve signature dT = [[[d[k][t][i] for k in range(K)] for i in range(3)] for t in range(len(tetvertices))] # Solve M @ lambda = dT for each T using standard linear algebra routine # sol shape: (T, 3, K) sol = solvelinearsystem(M, dT) # Transpose sol to (K, T, 3) chunkbary = [[[sol[t][i][k] for i in range(3)] for t in range(len(tetvertices))] for k in range(K)] # Extract lambdas l0 = [[chunkbary[k][t][0] for t in range(len(tetvertices))] for k in range(K)] l1 = [[chunkbary[k][t][1] for t in range(len(tetvertices))] for k in range(K)] l2 = [[chunkbary[k][t][2] for t in range(len(tetvertices))] for k in range(K)] l3 = [[1.0 - l0[k][t] - l1[k][t] - l2[k][t] for t in range(len(tetvertices))] for k in range(K)] # Inside condition: shape (K, T) inside = [[(l0[k][t] >= 0) and (l1[k][t] >= 0) and (l2[k][t] >= 0) and (l3[k][t] >= 0) for t in range(len(tetvertices))] for k in range(K)] # Find first containing tetrahedron for each point validexists = [any(inside[k]) for k in range(K)] tetidx = [] for k in range(K): if validexists[k]: # argmax on float representation of boolean array scores = [1.0 if inside[k][t] else 0.0 for t in range(len(tetvertices))] tetidx.append(scores.index(max(scores))) else: tetidx.append(-1) # Update outputs for valid points validmask = [k for k in range(K) if validexists[k]] for k in validmask: globalidx = start + k t = tetidx[k] insidetet[globalidx] = t barycentriccoords[globalidx][0:3] = [l0[k][t], l1[k][t], l2[k][t]] return insidetet, barycentriccoords chunksize: Controls memory usage during the batched solve. Not given in the sources. Degenerate Tetrahedra: If the volume of the tetrahedron is zero (coplanar vertices), the matrix \mathbf{M} is singular and the solve will fail or produce NaNs. Implementers should check for zero volume or use a pseudo-inverse with a tolerance threshold. Precision: Barycentric coordinates sum to 1. Floating-point errors may cause \sum \lambdai \ne 1 exactly. It is recommended to renormalize \lambda3 = 1 - \lambda0 - \lambda1 - \lambda2 after solving for the first three, as done in the algorithm, to ensure the constraint is satisfied. Boundary Conditions: Points exactly on the face or edge have \lambdai = 0. The condition \lambdai \ge 0 includes boundaries. Time Complexity: O(P \cdot T) for a naive implementation checking all tetrahedra, where P is the number of points and T is the number of tetrahedra. With spatial acceleration (e.g., BVH), this reduces to O(P \log T) or better. The linear algebra solve is O(T \cdot K) per chunk for K points. Memory Complexity: O(T \cdot K) for the intermediate matrices in the chunked solve. Strengths: Simple to implement, numerically stable for non-degenerate tetrahedra, easily vectorizable. Limitations: Naive search is slow for large T. Requires a spatial accelerator for performance in dense volumes. This method is a standard geometric technique used in computer graphics and scientific visualization. It is employed in TetWeave for resampling and interpolation in 3D reconstruction pipelines. name: Tetrahedron Face Extraction
body: Computes the four planar faces (unit normals and distances to the origin) from a four-vertex description of a tetrahedron. It provides the exact plane representation required for analytic ray-tetrahedron intersection tests. Inputs and Outputs Input: verts, an array of four r3drvec3 vectors representing the tetrahedron vertices V0, V1, V2, V3. Output: faces, an array of four r3dplane structures. Data Structures The internal layout of r3drvec3 and r3dplane is not given in the sources. The implementation uses standard 3D vector and plane representations. Algorithm For each face i (where i \in \{0, 1, 2, 3\}), the face is defined by the three vertices excluding Vi. Let the vertices of face i be A, B, C. 1. Compute Edge Vectors: Calculate two edge vectors from the face vertices: \mathbf{e}1 = B - A \mathbf{e}2 = C - A 2. Compute Normal: Calculate the unnormalized normal vector using the cross product: \mathbf{n}{raw} = \mathbf{e}1 \times \mathbf{e}2 3. Normalize: Compute the magnitude |\mathbf{n}{raw}| and normalize: \mathbf{n} = \frac{\mathbf{n}{raw}}{|\mathbf{n}{raw}|} 4. Compute Distance: The distance d to the origin is derived from the plane equation \mathbf{n} \cdot \mathbf{x} + d = 0. Using any vertex A on the plane: d = -(\mathbf{n} \cdot A) 5. Store: Assign \mathbf{n} and d to faces[i]. Pseudocode Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def tetrahedronfaceextraction(verts): """ verts: list of 4 Vec3 objects (V0, V1, V2, V3) returns: list of 4 Plane objects """ faces = [] # Face indices: each face excludes one vertex faceindices = [[1, 2, 3], [0, 2, 3], [0, 1, 3], [0, 1, 2]] for idx in faceindices: A = verts[idx[0]] B = verts[idx[1]] C = verts[idx[2]] # 1. Edge vectors e1 = Vec3sub(B, A) e2 = Vec3sub(C, A) # 2. Raw normal (cross product) nraw = Vec3cross(e1, e2) # 3. Normalize mag = Vec3length(nraw) if mag == 0.0: # Degenerate face: return zero vector to avoid division by zero n = Vec3(0.0, 0.0, 0.0) else: n = Vec3scale(nraw, 1.0 / mag) # 4. Distance to origin # Plane equation: n. x + d = 0 => d = -(n. A) dotproduct = Vec3dot(n, A) d = -dotproduct # 5. Store faces.append(Plane(n, d)) return faces def Vec3sub(a, b): return Vec3(a.x - b.x, a.y - b.y, a.z - b.z) def Vec3cross(a, b): return Vec3( a.y b.z - a.z b.y, a.z b.x - a.x b.z, a.x b.y - a.y b.x) def Vec3length(v): return (v.x2 + v.y2 + v.z2) 0.5 def Vec3scale(v, s): return Vec3(v.x s, v.y s, v.z s) def Vec3dot(a, b): return a.x b.x + a.y b.y + a.z b.z class Vec3: def init(self, x, y, z): self.x, self.y, self.z = x, y, z class Plane: def init(self, normal, distance): self.normal = normal self.distance = distance Parameters and Edge Cases Degenerate Input: If the four vertices are coplanar, the volume is zero, and at least one face will have a zero-length normal vector. The pseudocode guards against division by zero during normalization. Winding Order: The direction of the normal depends on the winding order of the vertices A, B, C. Consistent winding is required for correct inside/outside tests in subsequent intersection steps. Calculates the signed volume of a tetrahedron defined by four input vertices Pa, Pb, Pc, Pd. The return value is the signed volume; a positive value indicates a specific winding order, while a negative value indicates the opposite. This is often used to verify vertex ordering or to correct winding by swapping vertices if the volume is negative. The volume is computed as \frac{1}{6} |(\mathbf{b}-\mathbf{a}) \cdot ((\mathbf{c}-\mathbf{a}) \times (\mathbf{d}-\mathbf{a}))|. Time and Memory Complexity Time: O(1) per tetrahedron. It involves a constant number of vector operations (3 subtractions, 2 cross products, 1 dot product, 1 normalization). Memory: O(1) auxiliary space. The output size is fixed at 4 planes. Measured Performance and Scaling Not given in the sources. Strengths and Limitations Strengths: Simple, deterministic, and numerically stable for non-degenerate tetrahedra. It provides the exact plane representation needed for analytic ray intersection. Limitations: Does not handle degenerate tetrahedra (zero volume) gracefully without explicit checks. The normal direction depends on vertex winding, which must be consistent across the mesh. When to Use Not given in the sources. Originates from the r3d library ecosystem. It is used for tetrahedral mesh preprocessing in ray tracing pipelines. Specific historical development details and authorship are not given in the sources. devonmpowell/r3d, https://github.com/devonmpowell/r3d, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial)

name: Skeleton Parameter Minimization for Ray Intersection
head: Inverted Minima Computation, Rational Function Root Finding for SCALIS
body: This method computes the intersection of a ray with a Scale-Invariant Integral Surface (SCALIS) primitive by minimizing the squared distance from the ray to the skeleton curve, normalized by the local radius, rather than solving the implicit surface equation directly. It sets itself apart from direct sphere-cone intersection approaches by reducing the problem to finding the root of a linear equation, offering superior numerical stability and lower computational cost. Inputs and Outputs Input: Ray origin \mathbf{o}, ray direction \mathbf{d} (normalized), skeleton segment endpoints \mathbf{p}0, \mathbf{p}1, skeleton segment radius at start \tau0, and radius change \Delta \tau over the segment length L = \|\mathbf{p}1 - \mathbf{p}0\|. Output: The ray parameter t{min} corresponding to the closest intersection point on the SCALIS surface. Data Structures No complex data structures are required. The method operates on scalar values and 3D vectors. Steps 1. Define Geometry: Let \mathbf{u} = \mathbf{p}1 - \mathbf{p}0 be the skeleton direction vector. Let \mathbf{m} = \mathbf{p}0 - \mathbf{o} be the vector from the ray origin to the skeleton start point. The skeleton point at parameter s \in [0, L] is \mathbf{p}(s) = \mathbf{p}0 + s \frac{\mathbf{u}}{L}. The radius at parameter s is \tau(s) = \tau0 + s \frac{\Delta \tau}{L}. 2. Define Objective Function: Minimize the rational function f(s) representing the squared distance from the ray to the skeleton point, normalized by the squared radius: f(s) = \frac{d{\mathbf{r}}^2(\mathbf{p}(s))}{\tau(s)^2} where d{\mathbf{r}}(\mathbf{p}) is the perpendicular distance from point \mathbf{p} to the ray. The squared distance is given by: d{\mathbf{r}}^2(\mathbf{p}(s)) = \| (\mathbf{m} + s \frac{\mathbf{u}}{L}) - ((\mathbf{m} + s \frac{\mathbf{u}}{L})^T \mathbf{d}) \mathbf{d} \|^2 3. Compute Derivative Coefficients: Find the critical points by setting the derivative f'(s) = 0. This results in a linear equation b s + c = 0. The coefficients b and c are calculated as follows: b = \tau0 L^2 (1 - (\mathbf{u}^T \mathbf{d})^2) - \Delta \tau L \mathbf{u}^T (\mathbf{m} - (\mathbf{m}^T \mathbf{d}) \mathbf{d}) c = \Delta \tau \|\mathbf{m} - (\mathbf{m}^T \mathbf{d}) \mathbf{d}\|^2 + \tau0 L \mathbf{u}^T (\mathbf{m} - (\mathbf{m}^T \mathbf{d}) \mathbf{d}) Note: The term \mathbf{m} - (\mathbf{m}^T \mathbf{d}) \mathbf{d} represents the projection of \mathbf{m} onto the plane perpendicular to \mathbf{d}. 4. Solve for Candidate Minimum: If b \neq 0, compute the candidate parameter: s{cand} = -\frac{c}{b} If b = 0, there is no internal critical point (the function is monotonic or constant), so s{cand} is undefined. 5. Determine Global Minimum: Evaluate f(s) at the boundaries s=0 and s=L. If s{cand} exists and 0 < s{cand} < L, evaluate f(s{cand}). Select the s{min} that yields the smallest value of f(s) among the valid candidates (boundaries and internal critical point). 6. Compute Ray Parameter: Calculate the skeleton point \mathbf{p}(s{min}). Project \mathbf{p}(s{min}) orthogonally onto the ray to find t{min}: t{min} = (\mathbf{p}(s{min}) - \mathbf{o})^T \mathbf{d} Ensure t{min} is non-negative if the ray is treated as a half-ray; otherwise, clamp or reject based on application requirements. Pseudocode Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def skeletonparamminimization(rayo, rayd, p0, p1, tau0, deltatau): """ rayo: 3D vector, ray origin rayd: 3D vector, normalized ray direction p0: 3D vector, skeleton start point p1: 3D vector, skeleton end point tau0: float, radius at p0 deltatau: float, change in radius from p0 to p1 """ L = dot(p1 - p0, p1 - p0) 0.5 if L == 0: return None # Degenerate segment u = (p1 - p0) / L # Unit skeleton direction m = p0 - rayo # Vector from ray origin to skeleton start # Precompute projection of m onto plane perpendicular to rayd mdotd = dot(m, rayd) mperp = m - rayd mdotd # Precompute projection of u onto plane perpendicular to rayd udotd = dot(u, rayd) uperp = u - rayd udotd # Coefficient b # b = tau0 L^2 (1 - (u. d)^2) - deltatau L (u. mperp) term1 = tau0 (L 2) (1 - (udotd 2)) term2 = deltatau L dot(u, mperp) b = term1 - term2 # Coefficient c # c = deltatau ||mperp||^2 + tau0 L (u. mperp) normmperpsq = dot(mperp, mperp) term3 = deltatau normmperpsq term4 = tau0 L dot(u, mperp) c = term3 + term4 # Evaluate f(s) helper # f(s) = ||mperp + s uperp||^2 / (tau0 + s deltatau/L)^2 def f(s): radius = tau0 + s (deltatau / L) if radius == 0: return float('inf') distsq = dot(mperp + uperp s, mperp + uperp s) return distsq / (radius 2) # Find smin scandidates = [0.0, L] if abs(b) > 1e-9: # Numerical guard for b=0 scand = -c / b if 0 < scand < L: scandidates.append(scand) # Evaluate and pick minimum bests = scandidates[0] minval = f(bests) for s in scandidates[1:]: val = f(s) if val < minval: minval = val bests = s # Compute intersection point on skeleton pmin = p0 + u bests # Project pmin onto ray to get tmin tmin = dot(pmin - rayo, rayd) return tmin Parameters L: Length of the skeleton segment. \tau0: Radius at the start of the segment. \Delta \tau: Total radius change over the segment. Edge Cases and Pitfalls Degenerate Segment: If L=0, the method is undefined. Return early or handle as a sphere intersection. Zero Radius: If \tau(s) = 0 within [0, L], the function f(s) has a pole. The sources state poles are not in the range of interest for valid SCALIS primitives, but numerically, if \tau(s) approaches zero, precision issues may arise. Check for near-zero radii and handle appropriately (e.g., clamp or reject). Numerical Stability: The linear equation approach is preferred over solving the implicit surface equation (Equation 16 in) because the latter involves finding scaling factors for sphere-cone intersections, which is computationally heavier and less numerically stable. Time Complexity: O(1) per primitive. The method involves a constant number of vector operations and a single linear solve. Memory Complexity: O(1) auxiliary memory. Strengths: Numerically stable, computationally efficient, avoids complex geometric logic for sphere-cone intersections. Limitations: Specific to SCALIS primitives defined by linear skeleton segments with linearly varying radii. Not directly applicable to general implicit surfaces without adaptation. When to use: When rendering SCALIS volumes where performance and stability are critical. When not to use: For primitives that do not fit the SCALIS model or when higher-order skeleton curves are used. This method originates from the work on Fast Ray Tracing of Scale-Invariant Integral Surfaces (SCALIS). It was developed to address the computational cost and numerical instability associated with direct intersection methods for SCALIS primitives, which involve sphere-cone intersections. The approach inverts the minimization order, focusing on the skeleton parameter first. Fast Ray Tracing of Scale‐Invariant Integral Surfaces, https://doi.org/10.1111/cgf.14208, fetched 2026-10-26

name: Deformed element ray intersection
head: Wiley et al. method for deformed quadratic tetrahedra
body: This method determines the ray segments that intersect deformed finite elements, addressing the problem where the mapping from a standard element shape (e.g., a regular tetrahedron) to physical simulation space is non-linear. It is distinct from linear tetrahedron intersection methods because it handles higher-order polynomial mappings, requiring the calculation of multiple intersection segments and an approximate inverse mapping to evaluate scalar functions. Inputs and Outputs Input: A ray defined by origin \mathbf{o} and direction \mathbf{d}; a deformed finite element (specifically a quadratic tetrahedron) defined by its control points/vertices in physical space and their corresponding coordinates in the standard reference element. Output: A set of ray parameter intervals [t{start}, t{end}] representing the segments of the ray that lie within the deformed element. Data Structures The deformed element is represented by its vertices. For a quadratic tetrahedron, this includes the 4 corner vertices and 6 mid-edge vertices, defining the non-linear mapping. The mapping function \mathbf{x}(\mathbf{u}) maps a point \mathbf{u} in the standard reference tetrahedron to physical space \mathbf{x}. Steps 1. Formulate the Intersection Equation: The intersection of the ray \mathbf{r}(t) = \mathbf{o} + t\mathbf{d} with the deformed element boundary is found by solving for t such that \mathbf{r}(t) lies on the boundary of the element. Since the element is defined by a non-linear mapping, this involves solving a polynomial equation derived from the element's geometry. 2. Solve for Intersection Parameters: For deformed quadratic tetrahedra, the boundary conditions lead to polynomial equations in t. Wiley et al. [57] provide the method to determine these segments. This typically involves finding the roots of the polynomial that define the entry and exit points of the ray into the deformed volume. 3. Identify Valid Segments: Collect all real, positive roots t. Sort them. The intervals between consecutive roots (or from the first root to infinity, bounded by the element's extent) represent the segments where the ray intersects the deformed element. Note that a ray can intersect a deformed element in more than one segment due to the non-linear deformation. 4. Approximate Inverse Mapping: For any point \mathbf{x} on a valid ray segment within the element, the scalar function (e.g., density) is evaluated in the standard reference space. This requires the inverse map \mathbf{u} = \mathbf{x}^{-1}(\mathbf{x}). Since an analytical inverse may not exist or be complex, it is approximated using polynomial splines along the ray segments. 5. Evaluate Scalar Function: Use the approximated inverse map to find the coordinates \mathbf{u} in the standard element. Evaluate the scalar function defined on the standard element at \mathbf{u}. Formulas Ray: \mathbf{r}(t) = \mathbf{o} + t\mathbf{d} Deformed Element Mapping: \mathbf{x}(\mathbf{u}), where \mathbf{u} are barycentric coordinates in the reference tetrahedron. Inverse Mapping Approximation: \mathbf{u} \approx S(\mathbf{x}), where S is a polynomial spline approximation. Scalar Evaluation: f(\mathbf{x}) = f{ref}(S(\mathbf{x})), where f{ref} is the function defined on the reference element. Parameters Polynomial degree: Determined by the finite element order (e.g., quadratic for quadratic tetrahedra). Integration method: After segments are found, integration can use equally spaced sampling or Gaussian integration for smoother transfer functions. Edge Cases and Pitfalls Multiple Segments: A ray may intersect a deformed element in multiple disjoint segments. The method must correctly identify all such segments. Inverse Mapping: An inverse map is strictly required to evaluate the scalar function at a point on the ray, as the function is typically defined on the standard element. Precision: Solving high-order polynomials for intersection can be numerically sensitive. Pseudocode Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def deformedelementrayintersection(rayorigin, raydirection, element): """ Determines ray segments intersecting a deformed quadratic tetrahedron. Args: rayorigin: 3D vector, origin of the ray. raydirection: 3D vector, direction of the ray. element: Object containing the deformed quadratic tetrahedron data, including vertex positions in physical space and reference space mapping coefficients. Returns: List of tuples (tstart, tend) representing valid ray segments. """ # Step 1: Formulate the polynomial equation for intersection # The boundary of the deformed element is defined by the mapping. # For a quadratic tetrahedron, this results in a polynomial in t. # The exact coefficients depend on the specific deformation and element geometry. # This step involves deriving the polynomial P(t) = 0 where P represents # the condition that the ray point lies on the element boundary. # In practice, this requires solving the intersection of the ray with # the curved faces of the deformed element. polynomialcoeffs = computeintersectionpolynomial(rayorigin, raydirection, element) # Step 2: Solve for roots # Find all real, positive roots of the polynomial. roots = solvepolynomialroots(polynomialcoeffs) validroots = [t for t in roots if t > 0] validroots.sort() # Step 3: Identify segments # Intervals between consecutive roots are potential segments. segments = [] if not validroots: return segments # The first root is an entry point. The next is an exit, etc. # We assume the ray starts outside the element. for i in range(0, len(validroots) - 1, 2): tstart = validroots[i] tend = validroots[i+1] segments.append((tstart, tend)) # Note: If the ray starts inside, the first segment might start at t=0. # This requires a point-in-element test for the ray origin. # A point-in-deformed-element test is needed to handle this case. return segments def evaluatescalaratraypoint(rayorigin, raydirection, t, element): """ Evaluates the scalar function at a point on the ray within a deformed element. Args: rayorigin: 3D vector. raydirection: 3D vector. t: Parameter along the ray. element: Deformed element data. Returns: Scalar value at the point. """ # Point in physical space pointphysical = rayorigin + t raydirection # Approximate inverse mapping to reference space # Using polynomial splines as per Wiley et al. pointreference = approximateinversemap(pointphysical, element) # Evaluate scalar function in reference space scalarvalue = evaluatescalarinreferencespace(pointreference, element) return scalarvalue This variant is used in NeRF editing contexts where a deformed tetrahedral mesh T' corresponds to an original mesh T. It bends casting rays by calculating the displacement of sampled points via barycentric interpolation. Rays are cast to the space containing the deformed mesh T'. For each sampled point, the tetrahedron in T' containing it is identified. Using the correspondence between T and T', the displacement \Delta p from the deformed vertices to the original vertices is obtained via barycentric interpolation of the four vertices of the containing tetrahedron. The displacement \Delta p is added to the sampled point's coordinate p to predict density and RGB values using a network \zeta: (\zeta(p + \Delta p), \zeta(d)) \rightarrow (\sigma, c). A pitfall is that sampled points outside the tetrahedral mesh T' are not moved, meaning parts of the ray outside the mesh are not bent. Complexity: The complexity is dominated by solving high-order polynomial equations for intersection, which is more expensive than linear intersection. The number of segments can be greater than one, increasing the number of evaluations. Performance: Accuracy is higher for smoothly varying transfer functions when combined with Gaussian integration. Strengths: Handles non-linear deformations accurately, essential for finite element visualization. Limitations: Requires complex inverse mapping approximations; multiple intersection segments increase computational cost. When to use: When visualizing data on deformed finite element meshes where linear approximations are insufficient. The method was introduced by Wiley et al. [57] for determining ray segments intersecting deformed quadratic tetrahedra. It addresses the challenges of volume rendering with finite elements where the mapping to physical space is non-linear. Local and Global Illumination in the Volume Rendering Integral, https://avishek.net/assets/papers/nerfs/local-and-global-illumination-rendering-integral.pdf, fetched 2026-10-27 (book) NeRF-Editing: Geometry Editing of Neural Radiance Fields, https://doi.org/10.1109/cvpr52688.2022.01781, fetched 2026-10-26

name: Mesh Shader Tetrahedron Intersection Optimization
head: Accelerated intersections using wave intrinsics within a mesh shader, Optimized Cyrus-Beck for tetrahedra
body: This method optimizes the ray-tetrahedron intersection test by leveraging mesh shader wave intrinsics to share geometric data among the four vertices of a single tetrahedron. It reduces redundant memory loads by a factor of four and lowers the computational cost of the intersection routine to approximately 12 floating-point operations (FLOPs). Unlike naive implementations that load tetrahedron data independently for each vertex, this approach precomputes plane parameters in the mesh shader and computes final distances in the fragment shader, building on the standard Cyrus-Beck algorithm. The method splits the intersection calculation between a mesh shader (for precomputation) and a fragment shader (for final distance calculation). It assumes a tetrahedron is defined by four vertices and four outward-facing triangular faces. Inputs: Ray origin \mathbf{o} and direction \mathbf{d}, passed as uniform or per-ray data. Vertex positions of the tetrahedron, accessible via wave intrinsics. tetVertexId: An identifier for the current vertex within the tetrahedron (0–3). Outputs: planeN: A vector of four numerators for the plane equations, one per face. planeD: A vector of four denominators for the plane equations, one per face. Static Lookup Table (kTetTriangles) A constant array of 4 uint4 vectors defining the vertex indices for the 4 faces of a tetrahedron. The indices are ordered to ensure outward-facing normals. \text{kTetTriangles} = \begin{bmatrix} 0, 2, 1, 3 \\ 1, 2, 3, 0 \\ 0, 3, 2, 1 \\ 3, 0, 1, 2 \end{bmatrix} Each row i corresponds to the face opposite vertex i. The three indices define the triangle vertices. 1. Face Index Retrieval: For the current vertex tetVertexId, retrieve the face index tri from kTetTriangles[tetVertexId]. 2. Normal Computation: Compute the outward-facing normal \mathbf{n} for the triangle defined by tri. The vertices of the triangle are accessed using wave intrinsics to read the positions of the other lanes in the wave group. \mathbf{n} = (\mathbf{v}{\text{tri}[2]} - \mathbf{v}{\text{tri}[0]}) \times (\mathbf{v}{\text{tri}[1]} - \mathbf{v}{\text{tri}[0]}) Where \mathbf{v}{\text{idx}} is the position of the vertex with index idx, retrieved via WaveReadLaneAt. 3. Plane Numerator: Compute the numerator for the plane equation. Let \mathbf{v}0 be the position of the first vertex of the triangle (tri[0]). \text{num} = \mathbf{n} \cdot (\mathbf{v}0 - \mathbf{o}) Broadcast this scalar num to all lanes in the wave group to populate the planeN vector. 4. Plane Denominator: Compute the denominator for each lane. The normal \mathbf{n} is broadcasted to the specific lane. \text{planeD}{\text{lane}} = \mathbf{n}{\text{lane}} \cdot \mathbf{d} 5. Normalization: In the fragment shader, normalize the denominator by the length of the ray direction \mathbf{d}. \text{planeD}' = \frac{\text{planeD}}{\|\mathbf{d}\|} 6. Intersection Parameters: Compute the intersection parameter t for each plane. ti = \frac{\text{planeN}i}{\text{planeD}'i} 7. Entry and Exit Distances: t{\text{enter}} = \max \{ ti \mid \text{planeD}'i > 0 \}. If no such i exists, t{\text{enter}} = -\infty. t{\text{exit}} = \min \{ ti \mid \text{planeD}'i < 0 \}. If no such i exists, t{\text{exit}} = +\infty. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def meshshaderintersect(rayorigin, raydir, tetvertexid, vertexpositions): # Static lookup table for outward-facing faces kTetTriangles = [ (0, 2, 1, 3), (1, 2, 3, 0), (0, 3, 2, 1), (3, 0, 1, 2) ] # Base lane index for this tetrahedron baselane = (wavegetlaneindex() // 4) 4 # Helper to read vertex position from another lane def getvertex(idx): return wavereadlaneat(vertexpositions, baselane + idx) # Get face indices for the current vertex tri = kTetTriangles[tetvertexid] # Compute outward facing normal n v0 = getvertex(tri[0]) v1 = getvertex(tri[1]) v2 = getvertex(tri[2]) edge1 = v2 - v0 edge2 = v1 - v0 n = cross(edge1, edge2) # Compute numerator num = dot(n, v0 - rayorigin) num = dot(n, v0 - rayorigin) # Each lane constructs a vector of 4 numerators by reading num from all 4 lanes planeN = [wavereadlaneat(num, baselane + i) for i in range(4)] # Each lane constructs a vector of 4 denominators by reading n from all 4 lanes and dotting with raydir planeD = [dot(wavereadlaneat(n, baselane + i), raydir) for i in range(4)] return planeN, planeD def fragmentshaderintersect(planeN, planeD, raydir): # Normalize denominator by ray direction length dlen = length(raydir) planeDnorm = [d / dlen for d in planeD] # Compute t for each plane allt = [n / d for n, d in zip(planeN, planeDnorm)] # Compute tenter: max t where planeD > 0 tenter = float('-inf') for i in range(4): if planeDnorm[i] > 0.0: if allt[i] > tenter: tenter = allt[i] # Compute texit: min t where planeD < 0 texit = float('inf') for i in range(4): if planeDnorm[i] < 0.0: if allt[i] < texit: texit = allt[i] return tenter, texit kTetTriangles: Static constant array. Values are fixed as shown in the Data Structures section. Redundant Loads: The naive version loads tetrahedron information for each of the 4 vertices separately, leading to redundant memory loads. This method avoids this by sharing information between vertices in the mesh shader. Wave Size: The method assumes a wave size of at least 4 to accommodate the 4 vertices of a tetrahedron. Parallel Gather Semantics: The pseudocode uses list comprehensions for clarity, but in hardware these operations execute in parallel across the wave lanes to gather num and n values. Time Complexity: The optimized implementation reduces the runtime cost to only 12 FLOPs for the intersection calculation. Memory Access: Reduces memory loads by a factor of four compared to the naive version by leveraging wave intrinsics to share data among vertices. Strengths: Significant reduction in computational cost and memory bandwidth usage for tetrahedral mesh rendering. Limitations: Requires hardware support for mesh shaders and wave intrinsics. The method is specific to tetrahedral primitives. This method addresses the inefficiency of naive ray-tetrahedron intersection tests in volumetric rendering by exploiting the parallel execution model of mesh shaders. It is a specialized application of the Cyrus-Beck algorithm. Radiance Meshes for Volumetric Reconstruction, https://arxiv.org/abs/2512.04076v1, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial)

name: Raytracing Cell-Organized Irregular Volumes
head: Cell-based volume raytracing, Raytracing irregular volume data
body: This method renders volumetric data defined by unstructured or irregular cell grids (such as tetrahedra or hexahedra) by traversing the cell structure along a ray. It solves the problem of efficiently visiting cells intersected by a ray in non-uniform geometries where regular grid acceleration structures are not applicable. It differs from sibling methods by explicitly handling the topological connectivity of irregular cells and managing concave dataset boundaries, which can cause rays to exit and re-enter the volume multiple times. The method traverses a cell-organized irregular volume by stepping from cell to cell along a ray. It relies on the geometric intersection of the ray with the faces of the cells to determine entry and exit points. Input: Ray defined by origin \mathbf{d} and direction \mathbf{c}; irregular volume dataset composed of cells (e.g., tetrahedra, hexahedra) with associated vertex positions and face connectivity; scalar or vector field values at vertices. Output: Integrated optical properties (color, opacity) along the ray path within the volume. Cell: Contains a list of vertices and a list of faces. Face: Defined by three vertices for tetrahedra or four for hexahedra; for tetrahedra, a face is a triangle. The face stores the precomputed cross product of its edge vectors to accelerate intersection tests. Exposed Faces: The set of faces on the boundary of the dataset that are not shared with another cell. These define the entry and exit points for the ray when it leaves the volume. 1. Initial Intersection: Intersect the ray against all exposed faces of the dataset to find the first entry point. 2. Cell Traversal: Identify the cell adjacent to the current face. Intersect the ray with all faces of the current cell to find the exit face. Use the barycentric coordinate test to verify if the intersection point lies within the triangular face. If the intersection point is inside the face, the ray passes through to the adjacent cell. If the face is not shared by another cell, the ray has exited the dataset. 3. Re-entry Handling: If the ray exits the dataset, intersect the ray against all remaining exposed faces to find a new entry point. This is necessary because irregular volumes can be concave, allowing the ray to intersect the surface in multiple locations. 4. Integration: For each cell traversed, integrate the volume properties along the segment inside the cell. 5. Termination: Stop when the ray has exited the dataset and no further re-entries are found, or when the ray direction parameter exceeds a maximum distance. Plane Intersection: The intersection parameter t for a ray defined by point \mathbf{d} and vector \mathbf{c} with a plane defined by points \mathbf{a}, \mathbf{b}, \mathbf{c} is given by: t = \frac{(\mathbf{Ab} \times \mathbf{Ac}) \cdot \mathbf{a} - (\mathbf{Ab} \times \mathbf{Ac}) \cdot \mathbf{d}}{(\mathbf{Ab} \times \mathbf{Ac}) \cdot \mathbf{c}} where \mathbf{Ab} = \mathbf{b} - \mathbf{a} and \mathbf{Ac} = \mathbf{c} - \mathbf{a}. The cross product \mathbf{Ab} \times \mathbf{Ac} is the plane normal and can be precomputed and stored with the face. (Note: The source uses \mathbf{c} for both the ray direction vector and a plane vertex; implementations must distinguish them, e.g., ray direction \mathbf{r} and plane vertex \mathbf{p}3.) Barycentric Coordinate Test: To verify if an intersection point lies inside a triangular face defined by \mathbf{a}, \mathbf{b}, \mathbf{c} and ray direction \mathbf{e}, calculate: u = \frac{(\mathbf{Ac} \times \mathbf{e}) \cdot \mathbf{d} - (\mathbf{Ac} \times \mathbf{e}) \cdot \mathbf{a}}{(\mathbf{Ac} \times \mathbf{e}) \cdot \mathbf{b}} v = \frac{(\mathbf{Ab} \times \mathbf{e}) \cdot \mathbf{d} - (\mathbf{Ab} \times \mathbf{e}) \cdot \mathbf{a}}{(\mathbf{Ab} \times \mathbf{e}) \cdot \mathbf{c}} where \mathbf{d} denotes the intersection point in this context. If u > 0, v > 0, and u + v < 1, the point is inside the face. Tessellation: For hexahedral cells, if symmetric tessellation is not possible, add a new vertex at the center of each face and subdivide into twenty-four tetrahedra. Concave Volumes: Rays may exit and re-enter the dataset. After exiting, re-intersect with all exposed faces to find new entry points. Degenerate Tetrahedra (Coincident Vertices): Two zero-area triangles and two non-degenerate triangles. Ignore zero-area triangles. If the ray enters through a non-degenerate face, it exits through the other. The distance difference dt=0, so no integration is required. Degenerate Tetrahedra (Planar): All face intersection distances are the same. Determine which two triangular faces the ray passes through the interior of (entry and exit). dt=0, so no integration is required. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def raytraceirregularvolume(rayorigin, raydirection, volume): INF = float('inf') EPS = 1e-9 # Adjacency: face -> list of adjacent cells facetocells = {} for cell in volume.cells: for face in cell.faces: facetocells.setdefault(face, []).append(cell) # 1. Initial Intersection: Find first entry point among exposed faces mint = INF entryface = None for face in volume.exposedfaces: t = intersectrayplane(rayorigin, raydirection, face) if t > EPS and t < mint: mint = t entryface = face if entryface is None: return None currentt = mint currentface = entryface accumulatedcolor = (0.0, 0.0, 0.0) accumulatedopacity = 0.0 while True: # 2. Identify current cell adjacent to the entry face currentcell = facetocells[currentface][0] # 3. Find exit face among cell faces exitface = None exitt = INF for face in currentcell.faces: if face is currentface: continue t = intersectrayplane(rayorigin, raydirection, face) if t > currentt + EPS: intersectionpoint = rayorigin + t raydirection if ispointintriangle(intersectionpoint, face.vertices, raydirection): if t < exitt: exitt = t exitface = face # 4. Handle exit from volume if exitface is None: # Ray exited the dataset; re-intersect with all exposed faces reentryt = INF reentryface = None for face in volume.exposedfaces: t = intersectrayplane(rayorigin, raydirection, face) if t > currentt + EPS and t < reentryt: reentryt = t reentryface = face if reentryface is not None: currentt = reentryt currentface = reentryface continue else: break # 5. Integrate through the cell dt = exitt - currentt if dt > EPS: color, opacity = integratecellproperties(currentcell, rayorigin, raydirection, currentt, exitt) accumulatedcolor = accumulatedcolor + color (1.0 - accumulatedopacity) accumulatedopacity = accumulatedopacity + opacity (1.0 - accumulatedopacity) # 6. Move to next cell currentt = exitt currentface = exitface return accumulatedcolor, accumulatedopacity def intersectrayplane(rayorigin, raydirection, face): # Source formula: t = ((Ab x Ac). a - (Ab x Ac). d) / ((Ab x Ac). c) # Note: Source uses d for ray origin and c for ray direction (and plane point) a, b, c = face.vertices Ab = b - a Ac = c - a N = cross(Ab, Ac) # Denominator uses raydirection (source calls it c) denom = dot(N, raydirection) if abs(denom) < EPS: return INF # Numerator: N. a - N. rayorigin num = dot(N, a) - dot(N, rayorigin) return num / denom def ispointintriangle(point, vertices, raydirection): a, b, c = vertices Ab = b - a Ac = c - a e = raydirection d = point # Intersection point term1 = cross(Ac, e) unum = dot(term1, d) - dot(term1, a) uden = dot(term1, b) term2 = cross(Ab, e) vnum = dot(term2, d) - dot(term2, a) vden = dot(term2, c) if abs(uden) < EPS or abs(vden) < EPS: return False u = unum / uden v = vnum / vden return u > 0 and v > 0 and (u + v) < 1 def integratecellproperties(cell, rayorigin, raydirection, tstart, tend): # Integration logic depends on the specific scalar/vector field representation return (0.0, 0.0, 0.0), 0.0 Time Complexity: Depends on the number of cells intersected by the ray. Memory Complexity: Proportional to the number of cells and faces in the volume. Strengths: Handles irregular and unstructured grids efficiently. Can handle concave volumes correctly by re-entering the dataset. Limitations: Requires explicit connectivity information. Degenerate cells must be handled explicitly. Performance may degrade for highly complex or concave geometries due to multiple re-entries. This method was introduced in the paper "Raytracing irregular volume data". It addresses the need for rendering techniques that can handle non-uniform volumetric data, such as those arising from finite element analysis or geological modeling, where regular grid structures are not suitable. name: Ray-Object Intersection Test
head: Child Ray Intersection with Transformation, Ray Intersection Update, Ray-Object Intersection, raytrace
body: The Ray-Object Intersection Test determines if and where a ray intersects a specific scene object, returning the closest valid intersection distance or a failure indicator. It serves as the core decision unit in ray tracing and volume rendering pipelines, filtering out non-intersections and self-intersections via epsilon thresholds to ensure robustness. Unlike sibling primitives that solve for specific analytic shapes (e.g., Sphere Intersection), this test is a generic interface that may involve coordinate space transformations to handle arbitrary object orientations and positions. Inputs and Outputs Input: A ray defined by origin \mathbf{o} and direction \mathbf{d}, and an object (geometry definition, optional transformation matrix \mathbf{M}). Output: Distance t to the closest intersection point, hit status, object index, and surface normal. Data Structures The ray state is maintained in a structure containing: origin: Vector3D (x, y, z) direction: Vector3D (x, y, z), typically normalized. normal: Vector3D, the surface normal at the hit point. t: Float, the current closest hit distance. hit: Boolean, indicating if a valid hit has been recorded. Steps 1. Transformation (Optional): If the object has a transformation matrix \mathbf{M}, transform the ray into the object's local coordinate space. New origin: \mathbf{o}' = \mathbf{M} \cdot [\mathbf{o}, 1]^T New direction: \mathbf{d}' = \mathbf{M} \cdot [\mathbf{d}, 0]^T 2. Intersection Solve: Solve the system of equations representing the ray and the object's surface geometry to find potential intersection parameters t{obj}. 3. Filtering: Check if the computed t{obj} is valid: t{obj} > \epsilon (where \epsilon is 1.0 \times 10^{-5} or 0.001) to prevent self-intersection or near-origin artifacts. t{obj} < t{current} (if tracking the closest hit among multiple objects). 4. Update: If valid, update the ray's hit state: Set hit = true. Set t = t{obj}. Store the object index. Transform the normal back to world space using the matrix transpose: \mathbf{n}{world} = \text{normalize}(\mathbf{M}^\top \cdot [\mathbf{n}{local}, 1]^T). 5. Return: Return the boolean hit status and the distance t. Formulas Ray Equation: \mathbf{p}(t) = \mathbf{o} + t\mathbf{d}, \quad t \in \mathbb{R}^+. Unit Sphere Surface: \{(x, y, z) \mid x^2 + y^2 + z^2 = 1\}. Optimization Criterion: Find object o that minimizes t such that t = \text{intersection test}(\mathbf{r}, o) and t > 0. Parameters \epsilon (SMALLESTDIST): Minimum distance threshold to accept a hit. Typical values are 1.0 \times 10^{-5} or 0.001. Edge Cases and Pitfalls Self-Intersection: Intersections very close to the ray origin or previous hit point (t \le \epsilon) must be discarded to avoid artifacts. Degenerate Rays: If \mathbf{d} is not normalized, t does not represent Euclidean distance. Transformation Precision: Normal transformation uses the matrix transpose, not the inverse-transpose, to map local normals to world space per the provided implementation. Pseudocode Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def rayobjectintersection(ray, objects, epsilon=1e-5): """ Finds the closest intersection between a ray and a list of objects. """ closestt = float('inf') hitindex = -1 for index, obj in enumerate(objects): # 1. Transform ray to object's local space if matrix M exists if hasattr(obj, 'transform'): M = obj.transform localo = M.transformpoint(ray.origin) locald = M.transformvector(ray.direction) else: localo = ray.origin locald = ray.direction # 2. Solve system of equations between the ray and the object geometry # Returns distance tobj or None if no intersection tobj = solveintersection(localo, locald, obj.geometry) # 3. Filter: must be in front of ray origin and closer than current best if tobj is not None and tobj > epsilon and tobj < closestt: closestt = tobj hitindex = index # 4. Update ray state if a valid hit was found if hitindex != -1: ray.t = closestt ray.hit = True ray.objindex = hitindex # Transform normal back to world space using matrix transpose if hasattr(objects[hitindex], 'transform'): M = objects[hitindex].transform localn = computenormal(objects[hitindex].geometry, closestt) worldn = M.transpose().transformvector(localn) ray.normal = normalize(worldn) else: localn = computenormal(objects[hitindex].geometry, closestt) ray.normal = normalize(localn) return ray.hit, ray.t def solveintersection(o, d, geometry): # Solves the parametric ray equation p(t) = o + td against the object's implicit/surface equation. # The sources do not give the specific solver implementation for arbitrary geometry. return None def computenormal(geometry, t): # Computes the surface normal at the intersection point. # The sources do not give the specific normal computation implementation. return Vector3(0, 0, 1) A recursive ray traversal algorithm for a binary bounding box tree (BBNode) that determines the closest surface intersection by testing the node's bounding box, then recursing into left and right children, and finally comparing hit distances. It solves the problem of efficiently finding the nearest primitive in a hierarchical scene structure by pruning branches whose bounding volumes do not intersect the ray. Unlike Ray-Object Intersection Test which tests a single object, this method navigates a tree structure to find the global minimum intersection distance among all contained primitives. Time Complexity: O(1) per object for analytic primitives (spheres, planes, triangles). O(N) for a naive test against N objects. Memory Complexity: O(1) auxiliary space per test. Strengths: Core decision unit for ray tracing and volume rendering; handles coordinate transformations; robust with epsilon filtering. Limitations: Linear scan does not scale to large scenes. When to use: For small scenes, debugging, or as the leaf node test in acceleration structures. When not to use: For large-scale rendering without acceleration; for complex CSG operations without decomposition. The concept originates from early ray tracing algorithms, where the intersection of a ray with primitive shapes (spheres, planes) was solved analytically. The term "raytrace" in this context refers to the iterative process of casting rays and updating intersection states. The use of epsilon thresholds to prevent self-intersection is a standard practice in computer graphics to handle floating-point precision errors. name: Bounding Box Node Intersection
head: BBNode::intersect
body: Bounding Box Node Intersection is a recursive ray traversal algorithm for a binary bounding box tree (BBNode) that determines the closest surface intersection by testing the node's bounding box, then recursing into left and right children, and finally comparing hit distances. It solves the problem of efficiently finding the nearest primitive in a hierarchical scene structure by pruning branches whose bounding volumes do not intersect the ray. Unlike Ray-Object Intersection Test which tests a single object, this method navigates a tree structure to find the global minimum intersection distance among all contained primitives. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A ray R (origin O, direction D), a pointer to the current BBNode root, and a small epsilon constant \epsilon = 0.001f. Output: The closest intersection distance t along the ray, or a sentinel value (e.g., -\infty or infinity) if no intersection is found within the subtree. Data Structures: The BBNode structure contains the following fields: min: A Vec3 representing the minimum corner of the axis-aligned bounding box (AABB). max: A Vec3 representing the maximum corner of the AABB. childl: A pointer to SceneObject (left child). childr: A pointer to SceneObject (right child). getType(): A method returning an enum indicating if the node is a NODE (internal) or a leaf type. Algorithm Steps: 1. Bounding Box Test: Test if the ray intersects the current node's AABB defined by min and max. If no intersection occurs, return the "no hit" value. 2. Left Child Recursion: If the left child (childl) exists, determine its type. If childl is a NODE (castable to BBNode), recursively call intersect on it. Otherwise, call the primitive intersection function childintersect on the leaf object. Store the resulting distance as t{left}. 3. Right Child Recursion: If the right child (childr) exists, perform the same type check and recursion/intersection logic as step 2. Store the resulting distance as t{right}. 4. Distance Comparison: Compare t{left} and t{right} to find the closest intersection. To handle floating-point precision issues, add \epsilon to t{left} before comparing. If t{left} + \epsilon < t{right}, return t{left}. Otherwise, return t{right}. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def bbnodeintersect(ray, node, epsilon=0.001): # 1. Bounding Box Test # Assuming rayaabbintersect returns tmin, tmax or None hit = rayaabbintersect(ray, node.min, node.max) if hit is None: return INFINITY tleft = INFINITY tright = INFINITY # 2. Left Child Recursion if node.childl is not None: if node.childl.getType() == NODE: tleft = bbnodeintersect(ray, node.childl, epsilon) else: tleft = childintersect(ray, node.childl) # 3. Right Child Recursion if node.childr is not None: if node.childr.getType() == NODE: tright = bbnodeintersect(ray, node.childr, epsilon) else: tright = childintersect(ray, node.childr) # 4. Distance Comparison with Epsilon # Handle floating-point precision issues if tleft + epsilon < tright: return tleft else: return tright Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Floating-Point Precision: Direct comparison of hit distances can lead to incorrect pruning due to precision errors. The algorithm explicitly adds \epsilon to the left hit distance before comparison to mitigate this. Empty Children: The algorithm checks for the existence of childl and childr before recursion, handling leaf nodes or incomplete trees gracefully. No Intersection: If neither child intersects, the function must correctly propagate the "no hit" value up the recursion stack. Generalizes this node intersection test to arbitrary bounding volumes and hierarchical traversal, adapting to spatial distribution rather than uniform grids. Time Complexity: O(\log N) on average for balanced trees, where N is the number of primitives, but degrades to O(N) in worst-case scenarios (e.g., highly unbalanced trees or rays intersecting many nodes). Memory Complexity: O(N) to store the tree structure and bounding boxes. Strengths: Significantly reduces the number of primitive intersection tests compared to brute-force linear search. Limitations: Performance depends heavily on the quality of the bounding volume hierarchy construction. When to use: Ideal for scenes with many static primitives where acceleration structures can be precomputed. Originating from implementations such as cgibson/Mr-Voxel, this method is a fundamental component of ray tracing acceleration structures. It builds on the concept of Ray-Object Intersection Test by applying it recursively within a tree hierarchy. cgibson/Mr-Voxel, https://github.com/cgibson/Mr-Voxel, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial)

name: Hierarchical Bounding Volumes (HBV)
head: Bounding Volume Hierarchy
body: Hierarchical Bounding Volumes (HBV) is an acceleration structure for ray-primitive intersection that organizes scene primitives into a tree of nested bounding volumes to reduce the number of expensive primitive intersection tests. It solves the problem of linear search complexity in brute-force ray tracing by allowing rays to quickly discard large portions of the scene that do not intersect the current bounding volume. Unlike regular 3D grids which partition space uniformly and may suffer from high memory overhead or empty cells, HBV adapts its structure to the spatial distribution of primitives, typically storing primitives only at leaf nodes and partitioning the primitive set at internal nodes. It builds on Bounding Box Node Intersection by generalizing the node intersection test to arbitrary bounding volumes and hierarchical traversal. Inputs: A set of primitives P (e.g., triangles, spheres); a ray r = (o, d) where o is the origin and d is the direction. Outputs: A list of intersection hits, sorted by distance from o. Data Structures: The HBV is a tree where each node N contains: 1. Bounding Volume (BV): A geometric enclosure B that contains all primitives in the subtree rooted at N. Common types include Axis-Aligned Bounding Boxes (AABB), Oriented Bounding Boxes (OBB), or spheres. 2. Primitives: A list of primitives PN associated with the node. In standard implementations, internal nodes do not store primitives; primitives are stored only at leaf nodes. 3. Children: Pointers to left and right child nodes (for binary trees) or an array of children (for higher arity). Parameters: BV Type: The shape of the bounding volume (e.g., AABB, Sphere, OBB). Arity: The number of children per internal node (typically 2 for binary trees). Stopping Criterion: The maximum number of primitives allowed in a leaf node (e.g., 1–10 triangles). Partitioning Criterion: The heuristic used to split primitives during construction (e.g., Median Cut, Surface Area Heuristic). Algorithm Steps: 1. Construction (Preprocessing): If a model hierarchy exists, derive the tree from it. Otherwise, use automatic clustering. A common heuristic is Median Cut: 1. Construct a BV around all primitives in the current set. 2. Sort primitives by the center coordinate along a chosen axis (e.g., x-axis). 3. Partition the set into two subsets at the median. 4. Recursively repeat for each subset. 5. Terminate when a node contains fewer than n primitives (the stopping criterion). Variant: Cyclically choose the axis (x, y, z) at each level. Variant: Choose the axis with the longest extent of the current BV. Other methods include bottom-up clustering or iterative insertion. 2. Traversal (Intersection Test): The traversal determines which primitives intersect the ray r. The standard recursive depth-first approach is defined as follows: python def intersect(node, ray, hits): # Test if the ray intersects the node's bounding volume if intersectp(node.bound, ray): if isleaf(node): # Test all primitives in the leaf node intersectprimitives(node.prims, ray, hits) else: # Recurse into children for child in node.children: intersect(child, ray, hits) Priority Queue Traversal (Optimization): Pure depth-first search (DFS) order depends only on tree topology, not spatial layout. To improve efficiency, a priority queue (heap) can be used to visit nodes in order of their distance to the ray origin. 1. Initialize a min-heap with the root node. 2. While the heap is not empty: a. Extract the node N with the smallest distance t{BV} from the ray origin to its BV intersection. b. If t{BV} is greater than the distance t{hit} of the closest primitive intersection found so far, discard N and its subtree (pruning). c. Otherwise, if N is a leaf, test its primitives and update t{hit} if a closer intersection is found. d. If N is internal, calculate the intersection distance for each child, and insert valid children into the heap. e. Note: A complete ordering among all BVs is not required; only the ability to extract the minimum element is needed, which a heap provides in O(\log n) time. Formulas: Ray-BV Intersection: For an AABB defined by [minx, maxx] \times [miny, maxy] \times [minz, maxz], the ray o + t \cdot d intersects if: t{min} = \max \left( \frac{minx - ox}{dx}, \frac{miny - oy}{dy}, \frac{minz - oz}{dz} \right) t{max} = \min \left( \frac{maxx - ox}{dx}, \frac{maxy - oy}{dy}, \frac{maxz - oz}{dz} \right) Intersection exists if t{min} \le t{max} and t{max} \ge 0. Heap Complexity: Insertion and extraction of the minimal element cost O(\log n). Edge Cases and Pitfalls: False Positives: A "false positive" occurs when the BV is hit but the object inside is not. This requires further testing of the primitives within the node. Ordering Ambiguity: The closest ray-BV intersection and the closest ray-primitive intersection can happen in different BVs. The priority queue must handle this correctly by not assuming that the closest BV contains the closest primitive. Precision: Numerical stability in ray-BV intersection tests can affect pruning efficiency. This method accelerates the computation of physically-based indirect illumination for Gaussian splatting representations by treating Gaussians as ellipsoidal surfels and organizing them into a BVH. It solves the problem of unnatural indirect lighting in unconstrained spherical harmonic (SH) methods by enforcing physical constraints via ray tracing. Unlike standard Gaussian splatting which uses screen-space rasterization, this approach explicitly traces rays through the 3D Gaussian field to calculate visibility and accumulated radiance, enabling true inverse rendering and relighting. This method constructs a BVH using a recursive top-down approach that optimizes a cost function based on surface area and object count, rather than seeking the mathematically optimal partition which is computationally infeasible. It distinguishes itself from iterative bottom-up methods by generally yielding better BVH quality, and from exact optimal partitioning by using a heuristic plane-sweep strategy to find a near-optimal split. It builds on Hierarchical Bounding Volumes (HBV). The choice of bounding volume affects the trade-off between construction time, traversal speed, and tightness of fit. Common types include AABBs (fast intersection, slow construction), Spheres (very fast intersection, loose fit), OBBs (tighter fit, slower intersection), and convex hulls (tightest, slowest). A traversal algorithm that uses a priority queue (heap) to visit BV nodes in order of their distance to the ray origin, improving upon pure depth-first search. It calculates the distance between the ray origin and the intersection point of the ray with the currently visited BV. If this distance is greater than the distance to an already found intersection with an object, the BV and its subtree are ignored. Otherwise, it recurses into the children. All remaining BVs are sorted by their distance to the ray origin in a heap, and the closest BV is always selected as the next candidate. The pitfall is that the closest ray-BV intersection and the closest ray-primitive intersection can happen in different BVs, so a complete ordering among BVs is not needed, only the ability to extract the closest one. A simple heuristic for top-down construction. It constructs a BV around all objects in the current set, sorts all objects according to their center along a chosen axis (e.g., x-axis), and partitions the scene along the median on that axis, assigning half of the objects to the left and right subtrees. This is repeated recursively until a node contains less than n objects. Variants include cyclically choosing a different axis on each level or choosing the axis with the longest extent. Time Complexity: Construction: Depends on the heuristic. Median Cut is O(n \log n) due to sorting at each level. Bottom-up or iterative insertion can vary. Traversal: Worst-case O(n) if the tree is unbalanced or the ray passes through all nodes. Average case is significantly better, often O(\log n) for well-balanced trees. Priority queue traversal adds O(\log k) overhead per node visit, where k is the number of nodes in the queue. Memory Complexity: O(n) for storing the tree nodes and primitives, where n is the number of primitives. Measured Performance: For a scene with 66,430 spheres, brute-force rendering took 24,891.0 seconds, while a Goldsmith/Salmon BVH took 7.4 seconds on an Athlon XP 1900+. This demonstrates a significant speedup for large scenes. Strengths and Limitations: Strengths: Adapts to scene density; reduces intersection tests significantly for sparse scenes; flexible BV types. Limitations: Construction can be expensive; dynamic scenes require frequent updates or rebuilding; false positives still require primitive tests. When to Use: Use for static scenes with many primitives where acceleration is critical. Use when primitives are clustered, allowing tight bounding volumes. When Not to Use: Use for highly dynamic scenes where rebuilding the tree is too costly. Use for very simple scenes where the overhead of traversal outweighs the benefit. The Bounding Volume Hierarchy was introduced as an acceleration data structure for ray tracing to save costs by precomputations on the scene and filtering of rays during run-time. The concept of using bounding volumes to filter rays dates back to early ray tracing research. The specific term "Bounding Volume Hierarchy" and its application to hierarchical scene graphs became prominent in the 1980s and 1990s. Goldsmith and Salmon (1987) proposed an iterative insertion method for BVHs. The structure is widely used in modern ray tracers and global illumination engines. name: BVH for Gaussian Surfels
head: BVH over ellipses representing Gaussians, Gaussian Surfels BVH, Indirect illumination via BVH ray tracing, Physically-based Illumination with Raytracing
body: This method accelerates the computation of physically-based indirect illumination for Gaussian splatting representations by treating Gaussians as ellipsoidal surfels and organizing them into a Bounding Volume Hierarchy (BVH). It solves the problem of unnatural indirect lighting in unconstrained spherical harmonic (SH) methods by enforcing physical constraints via ray tracing. Unlike standard Gaussian splatting which uses screen-space rasterization, this approach explicitly traces rays through the 3D Gaussian field to calculate visibility and accumulated radiance, enabling true inverse rendering and relighting. Inputs: A set of N Gaussians, each defined by center \mathbf{x}, covariance matrix (defining the ellipse shape/orientation), color c, and transparency \alpha. A visibility threshold \epsilon = 0.8. A sampling count K for directions. Outputs: For each Gaussian vertex, the outgoing radiance Lo(\mathbf{x}, \omegao) computed via the rendering equation. Data Structures: BVH: A hierarchical tree where each node contains an axis-aligned bounding box (AABB) enclosing its children. The leaf nodes represent the Gaussians. Gaussian Representation: Each Gaussian is treated as an ellipse (2D projection of a 3D ellipsoid) for intersection purposes. The axis lengths of these ellipses are scaled by a factor of three to ensure robust intersection testing. Steps: 1. BVH Construction: Construct a BVH over the set of Gaussians. To do this, represent each Gaussian as an ellipse. Scale the axis lengths of each Gaussian's ellipse by a factor of three. Insert these scaled ellipses into the BVH structure. 2. Ray Emission: For each Gaussian vertex \mathbf{x} with geometry normal \mathbf{n}: Define the upper hemisphere \Omega relative to \mathbf{n}. Uniformly sample K directions \{\omega{ik}\}{k=1}^K within \Omega. 3. Ray Tracing and Accumulation: For each sampled direction \omega{ik}: Emit a ray R(t) = \mathbf{x} + t\omega{ik} starting from the Gaussian center \mathbf{x}. Query the BVH to find intersecting Gaussians along the ray. Accumulate transmittance T and indirect radiance Li^{ind} as the ray traverses the scene. The transmittance T is calculated based on the opacity of the intersected Gaussians (referenced as Eqn. 3 in the source, typically T = \prod (1 - \alphal)). Compute visibility V(\mathbf{x}, \omegai): V(\mathbf{x}, \omegai) = \begin{cases} 0 & \text{if } T \le \epsilon \\ 1 & \text{if } T > \epsilon \end{cases} where \epsilon = 0.8. Compute indirect incoming radiance Li^{ind}(\mathbf{x}, \omegai) by summing the contributions of the intersected Gaussians: Li^{ind}(\mathbf{x}, \omegai) = \sum{l=0}^{n} cl \alphal Tl where cl is the color, \alphal is the transparency, and Tl is the transmittance up to Gaussian l. 4. Final Radiance Computation: Compute the total incoming radiance Li(\mathbf{x}, \omegai): Li(\mathbf{x}, \omegai) = Li^{dir}(\mathbf{x}, \omegai)V(\mathbf{x}, \omegai) + Li^{ind}(\mathbf{x}, \omegai) where Li^{dir} is direct illumination from an environment map. Finally, compute the outgoing radiance Lo(\mathbf{x}, \omegao) using the rendering equation: Lo(\mathbf{x}, \omegao) = \int{\Omega} f(\mathbf{x}, a, r, \omegai, \omegao) Li(\mathbf{x}, \omegai) (\omegai \cdot \mathbf{n}) d\omegai where f is the Disney Principled BRDF, a is albedo, r is roughness, and \omegao is the view direction. This integral is approximated by the sum over the K sampled directions. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math import numpy as np def scalegaussianaxes(gaussian, scalefactor=3.0): """ Returns an ellipse representation with axis lengths scaled by scalefactor. Gaussian is assumed to have a covariance matrix or axis lengths/orientation. """ # Extract axis lengths from Gaussian covariance # Eigen decomposition of covariance matrix Sigma gives axes and orientations eigenvalues, eigenvectors = np.linalg.eigh(gaussian.covariance) axislengths = 2.0 np.sqrt(eigenvalues) # Standard convention for 2-sigma or similar scaledaxislengths = axislengths scalefactor return Ellipse(axislengths=scaledaxislengths, orientation=eigenvectors, center=gaussian.center) def buildbvh(gaussians): """ Constructs a BVH from a list of Gaussians. Each Gaussian is converted to a scaled ellipse. """ ellipses = [scalegaussianaxes(g) for g in gaussians] # Standard BVH construction algorithm (e.g., SAH or simple split) # Returns root node of BVH return BVHConstructor(ellipses) def rayellipseintersection(rayorigin, raydir, ellipse): """ Computes intersection of a ray with an ellipse. Returns distance t if intersected, else None. """ # Analytic intersection of ray and ellipse # Ellipse equation: (x-c)^T S (x-c) = 1 where S is shape matrix # Ray: x = o + td # Solve quadratic for t c = ellipse.center d = raydir o = rayorigin # Shape matrix S from ellipse axes and orientation S = ellipse.shapematrix # Quadratic coefficients for (o + td - c)^T S (o + td - c) = 1 # t^2 (d^T S d) + 2t (d^T S (o-c)) + ((o-c)^T S (o-c) - 1) = 0 A = np.dot(d, np.dot(S, d)) B = 2.0 np.dot(d, np.dot(S, o - c)) C = np.dot(o - c, np.dot(S, o - c)) - 1.0 discriminant = BB - 4AC if discriminant < 0: return None sqrtd = math.sqrt(discriminant) t1 = (-B - sqrtd) / (2A) t2 = (-B + sqrtd) / (2A) # Return smallest positive t if t1 > 0: return t1 elif t2 > 0: return t2 else: return None def traceray(rayorigin, raydir, bvhroot, epsilon=0.8): """ Traces a ray through the BVH. Returns visibility V and indirect radiance Lind. """ t = 0.0 transmittance = 1.0 Lind = 0.0 # Query BVH for intersections intersections = bvhroot.query(rayorigin, raydir) # Sort intersections by distance intersections.sort(key=lambda x: x.t) for hit in intersections: gaussian = hit.gaussian # Update transmittance # Tl is transmittance up to this Gaussian # Contribution is cl alphal Tl Lind += gaussian.color gaussian.alpha transmittance # Update transmittance for next Gaussian transmittance = (1.0 - gaussian.alpha) # Early exit if transmittance is too low? # The source defines V based on final T, so we continue or break if T is negligible if transmittance < 1e-6: break # Visibility if transmittance <= epsilon: V = 0.0 else: V = 1.0 return V, Lind, transmittance def computeglobalillumination(gaussians, bvhroot, K=16, epsilon=0.8): """ Computes global illumination for all Gaussian vertices. """ results = [] for gaussian in gaussians: center = gaussian.center normal = gaussian.normal # Geometry normal Nig # Sample K directions on upper hemisphere directions = samplehemisphere(normal, K) Losum = 0.0 for omegai in directions: # Ray from Gaussian center rayorigin = center raydir = omegai V, Lind, T = traceray(rayorigin, raydir, bvhroot, epsilon) # Direct illumination (from environment map) Ldir = getenvironmentradiance(raydir) # Total incoming radiance Li = Ldir V + Lind # BRDF evaluation # f is Disney Principled BRDF # omegao is view direction (assumed known or averaged) # For simplicity, assuming we compute for a specific view direction or average # The integral is approximated by sum/K f = evaluatedisneybrdf(gaussian.albedo, gaussian.roughness, omegai, omegao, normal) # Rendering equation term: f Li (omegai. n) dotproduct = max(0.0, np.dot(omegai, normal)) Losum += f Li dotproduct Lo = Losum / K results.append(Lo) return results Time Complexity: BVH construction is typically O(N \log N) or O(N \log^2 N) depending on the build algorithm. Ray tracing is O(N) in the worst case but typically O(\log N) per ray for sparse scenes. The total cost is O(N \cdot K \cdot \log N) for N Gaussians and K samples per Gaussian. Memory Complexity: O(N) to store the Gaussians and the BVH structure. Strengths: Enables physically-based indirect illumination and relighting, which is not possible with standard SH-based Gaussian splatting. The BVH acceleration makes ray tracing through the Gaussian field feasible. Limitations: Computationally expensive due to ray tracing and sampling. The approximation of Gaussians as scaled ellipses may introduce intersection errors. The visibility threshold \epsilon=0.8 is a heuristic that may cause artifacts in transparent regions. When to use: When physically-based inverse rendering and relighting are required for Gaussian splatting scenes. When not to use: For real-time rendering where performance is critical, or when indirect lighting is not needed. The method was introduced in "SVG-IR: Spatially-Varying Gaussian Splatting for Inverse Rendering". It addresses the limitation of previous unconstrained SH-based methods which produce unnatural indirect lighting. By introducing physically-based illumination via ray tracing through a learned radiance field represented by Gaussians, it enforces physical constraints. The use of BVH over ellipses is a specific optimization for this ray tracing task.
