name: Heuristic BVH Construction (Top-Down with Plane-Sweep)
head: Heuristic Aufbau einer BVH, Top-down BVH construction
body: This method constructs a Bounding Volume Hierarchy (BVH) using a recursive top-down approach that optimizes a cost function based on surface area and object count, rather than seeking the mathematically optimal partition which is computationally infeasible. It distinguishes itself from iterative bottom-up methods by generally yielding better BVH quality, and from exact optimal partitioning by using a heuristic plane-sweep strategy to find a near-optimal split. It builds on Hierarchical Bounding Volumes (HBV). Inputs: A set of n geometric primitives (e.g., triangles) B. Outputs: A root node of a BVH tree representing the bounding volume of B. Data Structures: Primitive Representation: Each primitive is represented by its centroid (center point) ci. Bounding Volume (BV): An axis-aligned bounding box (AABB) enclosing a set of primitives. For a single primitive bj, the elementary BV is the bounding box of that primitive. For a set, it is the union of its children's BVs. Cost Function: A scalar value estimating the rendering cost (e.g., ray intersection probability). Algorithm Steps: 1. Calculate Parent BV: Compute the bounding volume B for the current set of objects. 2. Base Case / Leaf Check: If the set contains a single primitive, create a leaf node containing that primitive and return. 3. Select Split Axis: Determine the axis (x, y, or z) with the greatest extent (largest dimension) of the current bounding volume B. 4. Sort Primitives: Sort the primitives in the current set based on the centroid coordinates along the selected axis. Let the sorted list be p1, p2, \dots, pn. 5. Plane-Sweep for Optimal Split: Initialize the left set L = \emptyset and right set R = \{p1, \dots, pn\}. Initialize the bounding box of the left set BL to empty (or the first primitive's BV). Iterate through split index j from 1 to n-1: Move primitive pj from R to L. Update BL to include pj. Calculate the cost for the split at j: Cost(j) = \frac{\text{Area}(BL)}{\text{Area}(B)} \cdot j + \frac{\text{Area}(BR)}{\text{Area}(B)} \cdot (n-j) where BR is the bounding box of the remaining primitives in R, \text{Area}(\cdot) is the surface area of the bounding box, and j and n-j are the number of objects in the left and right child sets, respectively. Track the minimum cost and the corresponding split index k. Note: The formula provided in the source uses j and n-j as weights. This implies a cost model where the probability of a ray hitting a child is proportional to its surface area relative to the parent, and the cost of traversing that child is proportional to the number of primitives it contains. 6. Partition: Split the primitives into two subsets B1 = \{p1, \dots, pk\} and B2 = \{p{k+1}, \dots, pn\} based on the optimal split index k. 7. Recursive Construction: Recursively construct the BVH for B1 to get left child node N1. Recursively construct the BVH for B2 to get right child node N2. 8. Non-Binary Fallback (Heuristic Check): If the resulting children nodes result in prohibitively high costs (e.g., the area increase is approximately 90% of the parent's area, or the cost function indicates poor separation), attach the primitives directly as children of the current node instead of creating binary children. This allows the BVH to be non-binary. Alternatively, if both potential splits yield equal costs (e.g., 0), use an alternative heuristic such as the number of triangles in the subtree to select the split. 9. Return Node: Create a node with the bounding volume B and children N1, N2 (or the direct primitives if the fallback was triggered). Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def buildbvhtopdownprimitives(primitives): """ Recursively builds a BVH using top-down plane-sweep heuristic. primitives: list of primitive objects, each having a centroid (x,y,z) and a method to get its elementary bounding box. """ if not primitives: return None # Step 1: Calculate Parent BV parentbv = computeboundingvolume(primitives) # Base Case: Single primitive if len(primitives) == 1: return Node(bv=parentbv, children=[primitives[0]]) # Step 3: Select Split Axis extent = parentbv.max - parentbv.min axis = argmax(extent) # Returns 0, 1, or 2 for x, y, z # Step 4: Sort Primitives # Sort based on centroid coordinate along the selected axis sortedprimitives = sorted(primitives, key=lambda p: p.centroid[axis]) # Step 5: Plane-Sweep n = len(sortedprimitives) mincost = infinity bestsplitindex = -1 # Initialize left set bounding box with the first primitive leftbv = sortedprimitives[0].elementarybv() # Right set initially contains all primitives, but we will subtract from it # To efficiently compute rightbv, we can precompute total BV or update dynamically. # Since we need Area(BR), and BR is the BV of primitives[j+1...n], # we can maintain a running right BV or compute it. # For simplicity in this pseudocode, we assume a function to compute BV of a list. # Optimization: Precompute suffix BVs or use a segment tree, but O(N) sweep is standard for this heuristic description. # To match the formula exactly, we need Area(BL) and Area(BR) at each step j. # BL is BV of primitives[0...j] # BR is BV of primitives[j+1...n-1] # Precompute total BV for the whole set to help? No, BR changes. # Efficient approach: # 1. Compute BV for all primitives. # 2. Iterate j from 0 to n-2. # Update leftbv by adding primitives[j]. # Compute rightbv from primitives[j+1:]. # Note: Computing rightbv from scratch is O(N) per step, leading to O(N^2). # The source cites O(N log N) for the sweep, implying an efficient implementation # (e.g., maintaining counts and bounds, or precomputed suffixes). # We will write the logical step. for j in range(n - 1): # Add primitive j to left set leftbv = union(leftbv, sortedprimitives[j].elementarybv()) # Compute right set BV (primitives j+1 to end) # In a real implementation, this would be optimized. rightbv = computeboundingvolume(sortedprimitives[j+1:]) arealeft = surfacearea(leftbv) arearight = surfacearea(rightbv) areaparent = surfacearea(parentbv) # Cost function from source # k = arg minj ( Area(b1...bj)/Area(B) j + Area(bj+1...bn)/Area(B) (n-j)) # Note: The source formula indices are 1-based. Here j is 0-based index of the last element in left set. # Number of elements in left set = j + 1 # Number of elements in right set = n - (j + 1) countleft = j + 1 countright = n - countleft cost = (arealeft / areaparent) countleft + (arearight / areaparent) countright if cost < mincost: mincost = cost bestsplitindex = j # Step 6: Partition leftprimitives = sortedprimitives[:bestsplitindex + 1] rightprimitives = sortedprimitives[bestsplitindex + 1:] # Step 8: Non-Binary Fallback Check # Check if the split is "bad" based on area increase or cost. # Source: "Falls alle Unterbäume zu hohe Kosten verursachen (z.B. Flächenzunahme auf 90% der Fläche von Vater)" # This implies checking if the children's BVs are too large relative to parent. # If the split results in poor separation, we might attach directly. # However, the standard top-down split is performed first. The fallback is usually # checked if the recursive calls return high cost or if the split itself is degenerate. # We will assume the split is performed, and the recursion handles leaf creation. # The "90% area" rule is likely a pruning criterion for the recursion or a check # before splitting. If the potential children BVs are > 90% of parent area, # it might be better to not split. # Let's implement the check: if the sum of children areas is not significantly smaller # or if the cost is too high, treat as leaf. # A common interpretation: if the split does not reduce the bounding volume significantly, # or if the cost is above a threshold. # For this implementation, we proceed with the split. The "90%" rule is a heuristic # for when to stop splitting or when to attach directly if the split is bad. # We will add a check: if the best cost is very high (e.g., close to n, meaning no separation), # we might attach directly. But the source says "attach object as direct child". # This suggests a non-binary node. # Let's stick to the binary split as the primary method, with the fallback # being a check on the result of the split or a pre-check. # Given the ambiguity, we perform the split. The recursive calls will handle # the base cases. The "90%" rule is likely a specific optimization for # "if the split doesn't help, don't split". # Re-reading source: "Falls alle Unterbäume zu hohe Kosten verursachen... hänge Objekt als direktes Kind an" # This implies: If the calculated cost for the best split is too high (indicating # the children are almost as big as the parent), then don't split, just attach primitives. # Threshold: If mincost > threshold? The source says "Flächenzunahme auf 90%". # This likely refers to the ratio of child BV area to parent BV area. # If Area(BL)/Area(B) + Area(BR)/Area(B) is close to 1 (or specific ratio), # it means no reduction. # Let's define a threshold for the cost. If mincost is high, we treat as leaf. # A simple heuristic: if the best split cost is greater than a certain value, # or if the area reduction is minimal. # We will implement a check: if the best split does not reduce the bounding volume # significantly (e.g., children BVs are > 90% of parent area combined? No, they are subsets). # Actually, if the split is bad, the children BVs might still be large. # Let's assume the standard split is done. The "90%" rule is a specific condition # for creating a non-binary leaf. # Check: If the cost is too high, attach directly. # What is the threshold? Not given explicitly as a number, but "90% of parent area". # This likely means: if Area(BL) > 0.9 Area(B) OR Area(BR) > 0.9 Area(B)? # Or if the sum of areas is close to parent? # We will implement a generic check: if mincost > somethreshold, treat as leaf. # Since no threshold is given, we will skip the explicit check in the code # and rely on the recursive base case (single primitive) and the general heuristic. # The source mentions this as a fallback for "prohibitively high costs". # Step 7: Recursive Construction leftchild = buildbvhtopdownprimitives(leftprimitives) rightchild = buildbvhtopdownprimitives(rightprimitives) # Step 9: Return Node return Node(bv=parentbv, children=[leftchild, rightchild]) def computeboundingvolume(primitives): """Computes the AABB for a list of primitives.""" if not primitives: return BoundingVolume() minx = min(p.centroid.x for p in primitives) miny = min(p.centroid.y for p in primitives) minz = min(p.centroid.z for p in primitives) maxx = max(p.centroid.x for p in primitives) maxy = max(p.centroid.y for p in primitives) maxz = max(p.centroid.z for p in primitives) # Include primitive extents? The source says "elementary BVs". # Usually, the BV of a set is the union of the BVs of its elements. # For simplicity, we use centroids. For accuracy, we should use the full primitive bounds. # Let's assume primitives have a method to get their full AABB. fullminx = min(p.fullbv().min.x for p in primitives) fullminy = min(p.fullbv().min.y for p in primitives) fullminz = min(p.fullbv().min.z for p in primitives) fullmaxx = max(p.fullbv().max.x for p in primitives) fullmaxy = max(p.fullbv().max.y for p in primitives) fullmaxz = max(p.fullbv().max.z for p in primitives) return BoundingVolume(min=(fullminx, fullminy, fullminz), max=(fullmaxx, fullmaxy, fullmaxz)) def surfacearea(bv): """Calculates the surface area of an AABB.""" dx = bv.max.x - bv.min.x dy = bv.max.y - bv.min.y dz = bv.max.z - bv.min.z return 2 (dx dy + dy dz + dz dx) def union(bv1, bv2): """Returns the union of two AABBs.""" minx = min(bv1.min.x, bv2.min.x) miny = min(bv1.min.y, bv2.min.y) minz = min(bv1.min.z, bv2.min.z) maxx = max(bv1.max.x, bv2.max.x) maxy = max(bv1.max.y, bv2.max.y) maxz = max(bv1.max.z, bv2.max.z) return BoundingVolume(min=(minx, miny, minz), max=(maxx, maxy, maxz)) Time Complexity: O(n \log^2 n), derived from the recurrence T(n) = T(\alpha n) + T((1-\alpha)n) + O(n \log n). The O(n \log n) term comes from sorting the primitives at each node. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Performance: Top-down methods generally yield better BVHs than iterative methods. Strengths: Heuristic approach is computationally feasible compared to exact optimal partitioning. Limitations: The mathematically optimal partition is not practical, so this method is a heuristic approximation. When to use: When a good quality BVH is needed and O(n \log^2 n) is acceptable. When not to use: When exact optimal partitioning is required (infeasible) or when O(n \log n) is strictly required (consider SAH or other methods). This method is described in the context of "Advanced Computer Graphics" lectures by G. Zachmann. It is based on the work of Salmon and Goldsmith, as referenced in the source. The source also references a comparison of data structures by Havran. name: Volume BVH
head: Volume Bounding Volume Hierarchy, Scene-level Volume BVH
body: Volume BVH is a hierarchical acceleration structure for volume rendering that handles multiple objects, instances, and transformations by using bounding boxes to quickly identify which volume instances overlap a given ray segment. It solves the problem of efficiently determining which potentially transformed or instanced volume sources contribute to a specific ray, serving as a coarse-level filter before detailed voxel traversal. It sets itself apart from sibling methods by focusing on the scene-level management of multiple distinct volume objects and instances, rather than optimizing the construction of a single object's hierarchy or handling specific primitive types like Gaussian surfels. The family relies on a tree of axis-aligned bounding boxes (AABBs) where each node contains a bounding volume enclosing its children. The core mechanism involves traversing this tree to find all leaf nodes (representing volume instances or objects) that intersect a ray segment defined by points A and B. Key shared properties: 1. Bounding Volumes: Nodes store AABBs. These can represent full object bounds or finer inner/leaf node bounds to reduce false positives. 2. Instance Handling: The structure must robustly detect overlap for objects that are rotated, scaled, or instanced multiple times. 3. Gathering: The traversal result is a list of overlapping object instances, which is gathered into an array in the kernel before volume shading begins. 4. Orthogonality: The BVH operates at a level orthogonal to the internal voxel traversal (e.g., HDDA), which may be used subsequently for fine-grained stepping. Optimizes BVH construction and traversal specifically for Gaussian surfel primitives, differing from the general object-instance focus of the main Volume BVH. Provides a specific algorithm for building the BVH tree using plane-sweep heuristics, which can be applied to Volume BVH construction but is not unique to it. The concept was proposed for Blender's Cycles renderer to optimize

name: Bit-stealing for Strand-Based Geometry
head: Mixed Bounding Volume Strategy, Woop et al. mixed BVH
body: Bit-stealing for strand-based geometry is a heterogeneous Bounding Volume Hierarchy (BVH) representation designed for hair and fur, which combines Axis-Aligned Bounding Boxes (AABBs) near the root for fast traversal with Oriented Bounding Boxes (OBBs) at deeper levels for tighter volume fits. It distinguishes itself from standard BVHs by using bit-field exploitation to encode node type, primitive counts, and offsets within a single 64-bit index, while leveraging a merged-parent quantization frame for OBB children to reduce memory footprint. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A set of Bezier segments representing hair/fur strands. Output: A BVH tree stored in a compact, bit-packed layout using indirect addressing. Data Structures: The BVH is defined by the type BVHm, which supports three node variants: AABBNode, OBBNode, and Leaf. 1. Index Layout (I): A 64-bit unsigned integer (u64) serves as the node identifier. The bits are partitioned as follows: Bits 0–1: Node type discriminator. Bits 1–4: Primitive count (nprims) for Leaf nodes; unused for interior nodes. Bits 5–63: Offset. For Leaf nodes, this is the primitive offset into the primitive buffer. For interior nodes, this is the offset into the respective interior node buffer (AABBs or OBBs). 2. Node Variants: AABBNode: Stores uncompressed 32-bit floating-point bounds (low: f32x3x4, high: f32x3x4) and four child pointers (C: u64x4). OBBNode: Stores a merged-parent bounding volume (mlo: f323, mex: f323), per-child quantized offsets (qlo: u8x3x4, qhi: u8x3x4), a shared quantized orientation matrix (qo: i8x4x3), and four child pointers (C: u64x4). Leaf: Stores a primitive count (nprims: u4) and an array of BezierSegment data. Algorithm Steps: 1. Construct Tree: Build a BVH where the top levels use AABBs and deeper levels transition to OBBs. 2. Encode Index: For each node, compute the 64-bit index I by setting bits 0–1 to the node type code, bits 1–4 to the primitive count (if leaf), and bits 5–63 to the memory offset. 3. Store Interior Nodes: If AABBNode, store low, high, and C in the AABB indirect group. If OBBNode, store mlo, mex, qlo, qhi, qo, and C in the OBB indirect group. 4. Store Primitives: Store BezierSegment data in the primitive buffer, indexed by the leaf offset. 5. Traverse: Decode I to determine node type and offset. If Leaf, access primitives using the offset. If AABBNode, access bounds and children from the AABB buffer. If OBBNode, access merged bounds and quantized data from the OBB buffer. Dequantize child bounds using mlo, mex, qlo, qhi, and qo to perform intersection tests. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. AABBTYPE = 0 OBBTYPE = 1 LEAFTYPE = 2 def decodeindex(I: u64) -> dict: nodetype = I & 0x3 nprims = (I >> 1) & 0xF offset = I >> 5 return {'type': nodetype, 'nprims': nprims, 'offset': offset} def traverse(nodeindex: u64, ray: Ray) -> bool: info = decodeindex(nodeindex) if info['type'] == LEAFTYPE: # Access BezierSegments from primitive buffer primitives = getprimitives(info['offset'], info['nprims']) for prim in primitives: if intersect(prim, ray): return True return False elif info['type'] == AABBTYPE: # Access AABB data from AABB buffer aabbdata = getaabbdata(info['offset']) # Check intersection with AABB bounds if not intersectsaabb(aabbdata.low, aabbdata.high, ray): return False # Recurse children for childidx in aabbdata.C: if traverse(childidx, ray): return True return False elif info['type'] == OBBTYPE: # Access OBB data from OBB buffer obbdata = getobbdata(info['offset']) # Dequantize child bounds using merged parent frame # Note: Exact dequantization formulas are not provided in sources for i in range(4): childlow = dequantize(obbdata.mlo, obbdata.mex, obbdata.qlo[i], obbdata.qo) childhigh = dequantize(obbdata.mlo, obbdata.mex, obbdata.qhi[i], obbdata.qo) if intersectsobb(childlow, childhigh, obbdata.qo, ray): if traverse(obbdata.C[i], ray): return True return False return False Parameters and Edge Cases: Quantization: OBB bounds are quantized to 8-bit integers (u8) relative to a merged parent frame. Orientation: The orientation matrix qo is quantized to 8-bit signed integers (i8) and shared among all four children of an OBB node. Pitfall: The specific dequantization functions for OBB bounds and orientation are not defined in the source specification. Implementers must derive these from Woop et al. [105, Sec 3.5]. Memory: Reduces memory footprint by using quantized 8-bit offsets and shared orientation matrices for OBBs, compared to storing full 32-bit floats for every child bound. Performance: AABBs at the root provide fast, simple traversal, while OBBs at deeper levels offer tighter bounds for complex strand geometry, improving culling efficiency. Complexity: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Compact representation for high-primitive-count hair/fur; flexible layout decoupling. Limitations: Requires complex dequantization logic for OBBs; bit-stealing requires careful index management. The method is based on the mixed bounding volume strategy from Woop et al. [105], which addresses the challenges of ray tracing hair and fur, such as high primitive counts and poor spatial coherence. It is implemented in the Scion language to demonstrate decoupling data layouts from BVH structures. Decoupling Data Layouts from Bounding Volume Hierarchies, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2511.15028, fetched 2026-10-29

name: BVH with 8-bit Quantized Bounds and Indirect Interior Storage
head: bvh8-q8-ci, bvh8i, qbvh8i
body: This method defines an 8-ary Bounding Volume Hierarchy (BVH) layout optimized for memory efficiency and traversal speed by storing interior node bounds in a separate indirect array and quantizing child bounding boxes to 8-bit integers. It solves the problem of high memory bandwidth consumption and cache pressure during ray traversal by reducing the footprint of interior nodes and leveraging SIMD-friendly integer arithmetic for intersection tests. It differs from its sibling BVH for Gaussian Surfels by targeting triangle primitives with a specific 8-ary topology, and from Heuristic BVH Construction (Top-Down with Plane-Sweep) by defining the storage layout and quantization scheme rather than the construction heuristic. It extends Hierarchical Bounding Volumes (HBV) by introducing indirect interior storage and 8-bit quantization. Inputs: A set of geometric primitives (specifically triangles) and a target BVH topology (8-ary). Outputs: A serialized BVH structure containing a primitive array and an indirect interior array, along with a root index. The layout is defined by two main groups: Interiors and the main indexed group. 1. Global Header: primitivecount: u32 primitives: Array of Triangle of size primitivecount. interiorcount: u32 2. Indirect Interior Group (Interiors): Size: interiorcount Fields per node: mlo: f32x3 (Merged Low bounds of children) mex: f32x3 (Merged Extent of children, mhi - mlo) childbounds: qbox3x8 (Quantized bounds for 8 children) children: u32x8 (Pointers/indices to children) Derived fields (for traversal logic): lo = \text{dequantize\bounds\lo}(mlo, mex, child\bounds) hi = \text{dequantize\bounds\hi}(mlo, mex, child\bounds) 3. Main Indexed Group (indexed by I): Default root index I is 1. The index I is a 32-bit integer split as follows: Bit 0: Tag bit. 1 indicates an Interior node; 0 indicates a Leaf node. Bits 1-31: Payload. If Tag is 1 (Interior): Bits 2-31 store the index into the Interiors array. Bit 1 is unused/reserved. If Tag is 0 (Leaf): Bits 7-31 store the primitive offset O. Bits 2-6 store nprims - 1. 4. Quantized Box (qbox3): Represents a 3D bounding box quantized to 8 bits per axis. Fields: lo: u8x3, hi: u8x3. Values are clamped to [0, 255]. 5. Quantized Box Array (qbox3x8): Array of 8 qbox3 structures, one for each child of an interior node. 1. Quantization of Child Bounds For each interior node with 8 children, the bounds are quantized relative to the merged bounds of all children. Merged Bounds: mlo = \mini(lowi) mhi = \maxi(highi) mex = mhi - mlo Where i \in [0, 7] indexes the children. Reciprocal: rcp = \frac{255.0}{mex} Quantization Function: For each child i and axis d \in \{x, y, z\}: q{lo}^{(i,d)} = \text{tfloor}((lowi^{(d)} - mlo^{(d)}) \times rcp^{(d)}) q{hi}^{(i,d)} = \text{tceil}((highi^{(d)} - mlo^{(d)}) \times rcp^{(d)}) Where \text{tfloor}(v) and \text{tceil}(v) clamp the result to [0, 255]: \text{tfloor}(v) = \text{clamp}(\lfloor v \rfloor, 0, 255) \text{tceil}(v) = \text{clamp}(\lceil v \rceil, 0, 255) Dequantization (for intersection tests): lo^{(i,d)} = mlo^{(d)} + (q{lo}^{(i,d)} \times rcp^{(d)}) \times mex^{(d)} hi^{(i,d)} = mlo^{(d)} + (q{hi}^{(i,d)} \times rcp^{(d)}) \times mex^{(d)} Note: The source specifies dequantization uses the stored mlo, mex, and quantized bounds. The formula in the notes is \text{lo} = \text{mlo} + (\text{bound.lo} \times \text{rcp}) \times \text{mex}. This implies the stored bound.lo is the integer index, and it is scaled back to float space. 2. Index Packing Interior Node Index: I = (\text{interior\array\index} \ll 2) \mid 1 Leaf Node Index: I = (\text{primitive\offset} \ll 7) \mid ((\text{nprims} - 1) \ll 2) \mid 0 3. Build Procedure The build process constructs the tree bottom-up or via a specified topology, generating the packed indices. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def tfloor(f: f32x3) -> u8x3: """Floor and clamp to [0, 255]""" f1 = floor(f) f2 = max(0.0, min(f1, 255.0)) return f2 as u8x3 def tceil(f: f32x3) -> u8x3: """Ceil and clamp to [0, 255]""" f1 = ceil(f) f2 = max(0.0, min(f1, 255.0)) return f2 as u8x3 def computemergedlow(low: f32x3x8) -> f32x3: """Compute element-wise minimum across 8 children's low bounds.""" mlo = low[0] for i in range(1, 8): mlo = min(mlo, low[i]) return mlo def computemergedextent(low: f32x3x8, high: f32x3x8) -> f32x3: """Compute max(high) - min(low) across 8 children.""" mlo = computemergedlow(low) mhi = high[0] for i in range(1, 8): mhi = max(mhi, high[i]) return mhi - mlo def quantizebounds(low: f32x3x8, high: f32x3x8) -> qbox3x8: """Quantize 8 children's bounds to 8-bit integers.""" mlo = computemergedlow(low) mex = computemergedextent(low, high) rcp = (1.0 / mex) 255.0 childbounds = qbox3x8() for i in range(8): # Quantize each axis for child i qlo = tfloor((low[i] - mlo) rcp) qhi = tceil((high[i] - mlo) rcp) childbounds[i] = qbox3(lo=qlo, hi=qhi) return childbounds def buildinteriornode(children: BVH[8], lo: f32x3x8, hi: f32x3x8) -> u32: """ Build an interior node. Returns the packed index for this node. """ # 1. Compute merged bounds mlo = computemergedlow(lo) mex = computemergedextent(lo, hi) # 2. Quantize child bounds childbounds = quantizebounds(lo, hi) # 3. Store in Interiors array # The index in the Interiors array is determined by the build order/allocator. # Let's assume 'interiorindex' is the next available slot in Interiors. interiorindex = allocateinteriorslot() Interiors[interiorindex].mlo = mlo Interiors[interiorindex].mex = mex Interiors[interiorindex].childbounds = childbounds Interiors[interiorindex].children = [child.index for child in children] # 4. Return packed index: shift by 2, set bit 0 to 1 return (interiorindex << 2) | 1 def buildleafnode(nprims: u8, data: Triangle[nprims]) -> u32: """ Build a leaf node. Returns the packed index for this node. """ # 1. Append primitives to global array primitiveoffset = appendprimitives(data, nprims) # 2. Return packed index: # Bits 7-31: primitiveoffset # Bits 2-6: nprims - 1 # Bit 0: 0 (Leaf tag) # Bit 1: 0 (reserved) return (primitiveoffset << 7) | ((nprims - 1) << 2) | 0 4. Intersection Method For the quantized layout, the Möller-Trumbore algorithm is used for ray-triangle intersection. The dequantized bounds are used for the BVH traversal step (AABB intersection), and the quantized bounds may be used for early rejection or SIMD optimization if the hardware supports integer AABB tests. Zero Extent: If mex is zero (degenerate bounding box), division by zero occurs in rcp. The implementation must handle this, likely by treating the extent as a small epsilon or skipping quantization. Not given in the sources. Quantization Error: Quantization to 8 bits introduces error. The dequantized bounds are an approximation. This may lead to false negatives in intersection tests if the approximation is too coarse, though the source notes that Möller-Trumbore is used for the final primitive test, mitigating this risk for correctness. Index Overflow: The leaf index packs nprims - 1 into 5 bits (bits 2-6). This limits nprims to 2^5 = 32 primitives per leaf. If a leaf has more than 32 primitives, the layout cannot represent it directly. Not given in the sources if this is a hard limit or if larger leaves are split. Interior Index Overflow: The interior index is stored in 30 bits (bits 2-31), allowing for 2^{30} interior nodes. Memory Footprint: Significantly reduced compared to unquantized layouts (e.g., bvh8i) because child bounds are stored as 8-bit integers instead of 32-bit floats, and interior nodes are stored in a separate compact array. The source notes that qbvh8i uses less memory than bvh8i. Traversal Speed: The use of 8-bit quantization and integer arithmetic can improve SIMD performance. name: Ray-Primitive and Segment Intersection
head: Intersection Ordering Optimization, Ray-Primitive and Segment Intersection Ordering
body: This method optimizes the evaluation of volumetric ray primitives by determining the correct processing order of intersection points and segments along a ray, and provides the geometric primitives for intersecting rays with line segments. It solves the problem of redundant or incorrect shading calculations when multiple objects or data structures intersect a single ray. It sets itself apart from sibling methods like Sphere Intersection and Ray-Triangle Intersection by focusing on the ordering and culling of intersection results rather than the analytic solution of a single primitive, and from Voxel selection via pick ray intersection by handling general bounding box hierarchies rather than specific voxel grid traversal. The method consists of two distinct components: an optimization strategy for ordering intersection evaluations based on bounding boxes, and the geometric algorithm for intersecting a ray with a line segment. Inputs: Ray defined by origin \mathbf{o} = (ox, oy) and direction \mathbf{d} = (dx, dy). List of objects, each with an axis-aligned bounding box (AABB). For segment intersection: Segment endpoints \mathbf{A} = (ax, ay) and \mathbf{B} = (bx, by). Outputs: Sorted list of intersection points and segments to be processed by the shader. For segment intersection: Intersection parameter t, segment parameter s, and validity flag. 1. Intersection Point List (P): Contains objects classified as Class 1 (surface intersections). Each entry stores the object ID and the distance to the entry point of its bounding box. 2. Intersection Segment List (S): Contains objects classified as Class 2 or 3 (volumetric/average/max-value projections). Each entry stores the object ID and the distance to the exit point of its bounding box. 3. Bounding Box: Defined by minimum and maximum coordinates. Used to compute entry and exit distances for the ray. 1. Bounding Box Intersection: For each object, compute the entry and exit points of the ray with its bounding box. Determine if the ray intersects the box. 2. Classification: Class 1: Surface intersection objects. Distance metric is the entry point of the bounding box. Class 2: Average-value projection objects. Distance metric is the exit point of the bounding box. Class 3: Max-value projection objects. Distance metric is the exit point of the bounding box. 3. Sorting: Sort the lists P and S by distance. P is sorted by entry distance. S is sorted by exit distance. Note: The sources imply a unified processing order where Class 1 points are processed before Class 2/3 segments that might contain them, or segments that are occluded by closer Class 1 points. 4. Initialize Tracker: Set D{min} = \infty. This variable tracks the closest intersection point found so far. 5. Process Intersection Points (Class 1): Iterate through the sorted list P. For each point, if its distance is less than D{min}, update D{min} to this distance. This establishes the closest surface intersection Pt. 6. Process Intersection Segments (Class 2/3): Iterate through the sorted list S. Use D{min} to cull or terminate calculations: If a Class 1 intersection occurs within a Class 4 (or general) segment, compute the average value only for the sub-segment outside the Class 1 intersection, not the entire segment. If a Class 1 intersection occurs after a Class 2 or 3 intersection start, perform the Class 1 calculation first. This reduces the segment length for the Class 2/3 calculation or allows early termination of Class 3. Class 3 Early Termination: For max-value projection, if the maximum value encountered along the ray up to point Pt is vt, the Class 3 calculation can terminate as soon as a value v2 is encountered such that v2 > vt. This requires the Class 1 calculation to be performed first to establish Pt. 1. Compute Segment Vector: \mathbf{s} = \mathbf{B} - \mathbf{A} = (sx, sy) = (bx - ax, by - ay). 2. Compute Denominator: denom = dx sy - dy sx. 3. Check Parallelism: If |denom| < \epsilon (e.g., 10^{-9}), the ray and segment are parallel. Return invalid/null. 4. Compute Parameters: t = \frac{(ax - ox) sy - (ay - oy) sx}{denom} s = \frac{(ax - ox) dy - (ay - oy) dx}{denom} 5. Validate: The intersection is valid if t \ge 0 (ray direction) AND 0 \le s \le 1 (segment bounds). 6. Compute Intersection Point: \mathbf{hit} = \mathbf{o} + t \mathbf{d} = (ox + dx t, oy + dy t). Ray-Segment Intersection Parameters: sx = bx - ax sy = by - ay denom = dx sy - dy sx t = \frac{(ax - ox) sy - (ay - oy) sx}{denom} s = \frac{(ax - ox) dy - (ay - oy) dx}{denom} valid = (t \ge 0) \land (0 \le s \le 1) hitx = ox + dx t hity = oy + dy t Bounding Box Distance (Implicit): The distance to entry/exit is derived from standard ray-AABB intersection, where t{min} and t{max} are computed for each axis and combined. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def raysegmentintersect2d(ox, oy, dx, dy, ax, ay, bx, by): """ Computes intersection between ray (O, D) and segment (A, B) in 2D. Returns dict with t, s, x, y, valid or None if parallel. """ sx = bx - ax sy = by - ay denom = dx sy - dy sx # Check for parallelism if math.abs(denom) < 1e-9: return None t = ((ax - ox) sy - (ay - oy) sx) / denom s = ((ax - ox) dy - (ay - oy) dx) / denom valid = (t >= 0) and (s >= 0) and (s <= 1) hitx = ox + dx t hity = oy + dy t return { "t": t, "s": s, "x": hitx, "y": hity, "valid": valid } def processintersectionordering(rayorigin, raydir, objects): """ Optimizes processing order of intersection points and segments. objects: list of dicts with 'bbox' (min, max), 'class' (1, 2, 3), 'id'. Returns sorted lists of points and segments to process. """ points = [] # Class 1 segments = [] # Class 2, 3 for obj in objects: # Compute ray-AABB intersection # tmin, tmax are entry and exit distances tmin, tmax = computerayaabbintersection(rayorigin, raydir, obj['bbox']) if tmax < 0: continue # Behind ray if tmin < 0: tmin = 0 # Ray starts inside if obj['class'] == 1: # Class 1: Surface. Distance is entry point. points.append({ 'id': obj['id'], 'distance': tmin, 'tmin': tmin, 'tmax': tmax }) else: # Class 2/3: Volumetric. Distance is exit point. segments.append({ 'id': obj['id'], 'class': obj['class'], 'distance': tmax, 'tmin': tmin, 'tmax': tmax }) # Sort points by entry distance points.sort(key=lambda p: p['distance']) # Sort segments by exit distance segments.sort(key=lambda s: s['distance']) # Process Points to find closest intersection dmin = float('inf') closestpoint = None for p in points: if p['distance'] < dmin: dmin = p['distance'] closestpoint = p # Process Segments with culling processedsegments = [] for seg in segments: # Check if segment is completely behind the closest point if seg['tmax'] < dmin: continue # Cull # Check if segment contains the closest point if seg['tmin'] <= dmin <= seg['tmax']: # The closest point is inside this segment. # If Class 1, it overrides the segment value at that point. # For Class 2 (Average), compute average for sub-segments outside the point. # For Class 3 (Max), check early termination logic. # Simplified logic: Split segment or mark for partial evaluation # Note: Exact sub-segment calculation depends on specific shader requirements processedsegments.append({ 'id': seg['id'], 'type': 'partial', 'tstart': seg['tmin'], 'tend': dmin, 'tstart2': dmin, 'tend2': seg['tmax'] }) else: # Segment is entirely before or after the closest point processedsegments.append({ 'id': seg['id'], 'type': 'full', 'tmin': seg['tmin'], 'tmax': seg['tmax'] }) return points, processedsegments def computerayaabbintersection(origin, direction, bbox): """ Computes tmin and tmax for ray-AABB intersection. bbox: {'min': (x,y,z), 'max': (x,y,z)} Returns (tmin, tmax). """ # Implementation of standard slab method # Not given in sources, standard graphics algorithm tmin = -float('inf') tmax = float('inf') for i in range(3): if direction[i] == 0: if origin[i] < bbox['min'][i] or origin[i] > bbox['max'][i]: return (float('inf'), -float('inf')) # No intersection else: t1 = (bbox['min'][i] - origin[i]) / direction[i] t2 = (bbox['max'][i] - origin[i]) / direction[i] tenter = min(t1, t2) texit = max(t1, t2) tmin = max(tmin, tenter) tmax = min(tmax, texit) return (tmin, tmax) Epsilon: A threshold of 10^{-9} is used to detect parallel rays and segments. Inside Ray: If a ray starts inside a solid, it must report the exit point to prevent holes or inside-out meshes from passing as outside intersections. Class 1 vs Class 2/3: Class 1 calculations are generally faster and should be performed first to reduce segment lengths or enable early termination for Class 3. Linear Edge Intersection determines the precise position where an isosurface intersects a grid edge by linearly interpolating between the scalar field values at the two vertices defining that edge. It solves the problem of locating surface geometry within a discrete voxel grid, serving as the fundamental geometric primitive for contouring algorithms like Marching Cubes and ray-marching isosurface extraction. It sets itself apart from its siblings by assuming a strictly linear variation of the scalar field along the edge, providing an exact algebraic solution for the intersection point under that assumption, whereas Iterative Bisection Intersection Refinement uses numerical approximation and Hermite Interpolation for Isosurface Extraction uses gradient data for higher-order accuracy. This method extracts spatial information from a simulation by mapping 2D screen coordinates to 3D voxel indices, serving as a direct manipulation interface for tasks such as segmentation seed selection. It differs from Reverse Index Map for Voxel Location by computing the intersection dynamically rather than relying on a pre-computed index texture, and from Ray-Box Intersection for Interaction by focusing on identifying the specific seed voxel for segmentation rather than just the entry point for fluid injection. Boundary Segment Validity Conditions define the geometric and topological constraints required for a line segment connecting two points on a polygonal mesh to be classified as a valid spatial boundary segment. These conditions ensure that the segment represents a true visibility boundary (e.g., a silhouette or occlusion edge) rather than a segment penetrating the geometry. This method is distinct from sibling methods like Linear Edge Intersection and Voxel selection via pick ray intersection by explicitly validating the segment against the mesh normals and intersection geometry to prevent self-intersection or penetration artifacts in volume rendering integrals. Ordering Optimization: Sorting the intersection lists takes O(N \log N) where N is the number of objects intersected by the ray. The processing step is O(N). Ray-Segment Intersection: O(1) per segment. Specific performance metrics are not given in the sources. However, the method is designed to reduce total computation by avoiding unnecessary segment evaluations. The method scales with the number of objects intersected by the ray. Efficient bounding box hierarchies (BVH) are implied to reduce the number of bounding box tests. Strengths: Reduces redundant shading calculations; enables early termination for max-value projections; handles complex ordering of surface and volumetric intersections. Limitations: Requires classification of objects into classes; relies on accurate bounding box intersection; does not solve the analytic intersection itself but orders the results. Use when rendering scenes with multiple overlapping volumetric objects or mixed surface/volume data where shading costs are high and early termination is possible. Use when ray-segment intersection is required for 2D grid traversal or wall detection. Use when only a single primitive intersection is needed (use sibling methods). Use when the scene is static and pre-computed index maps are more efficient for interaction. The intersection ordering optimization was introduced by Sobierajski et al. in "Volumetric Ray Tracing". The ray-segment intersection formula is a standard 2D geometric primitive often implemented in raycasting tutorials. The ray query interface for general shapes was developed as part of the EBGeometry project. The method evolved from the need to optimize volumetric ray tracing, where shading calculations are expensive. By ordering intersections and culling segments, significant performance gains are achieved. The ray-segment intersection is a foundational component in 2D raycasting engines. The EBGeometry project extended ray queries to support various shape types with device-callable interfaces. Volumetric ray tracers. 2D raycasting engines and maze renderers. name: Linear Edge Intersection
head: Linear Edge Interpolation, Linear Interpolation, Midpoint Intersection (variant), Inverse Linear Interpolation (algebraic form)
body: Linear Edge Intersection determines the precise position where an isosurface intersects a grid edge by linearly interpolating between the scalar field values at the two vertices defining that edge. It solves the problem of locating surface geometry within a discrete voxel grid, serving as the fundamental geometric primitive for contouring algorithms like Marching Cubes and ray-marching isosurface extraction. It sets itself apart from its siblings by assuming a strictly linear variation of the scalar field along the edge, providing an exact algebraic solution for the intersection point under that assumption, whereas Iterative Bisection Intersection Refinement uses numerical approximation and Hermite Interpolation for Isosurface Extraction uses gradient data for higher-order accuracy. Inputs: Two edge endpoints: \mathbf{p}1 and \mathbf{p}2 (3D coordinates). Scalar field values at endpoints: v1 = f(\mathbf{p}1) and v2 = f(\mathbf{p}2). Target isovalue (threshold): iso (or k, T, Y). Outputs: Intersection point \mathbf{p} on the edge segment [\mathbf{p}1, \mathbf{p}2]. Data Structures: Points are represented as 3D vectors (x, y, z). Scalar values are floating-point numbers. Steps: 1. Identify Intersection: Check if the edge crosses the isosurface. This occurs if (v1 - iso) and (v2 - iso) have opposite signs, or equivalently, if (v1 - iso)(v2 - iso) < 0. If both values are on the same side of the isovalue, there is no intersection on this edge segment. 2. Handle Degeneracy: If the scalar values are nearly identical (|v1 - v2| < \epsilon), the denominator in the interpolation formula approaches zero. In this case, return \mathbf{p}1 (or \mathbf{p}2, as they are effectively the same point relative to the surface) to avoid division by zero. Typical \epsilon values are 10^{-7} or 10^{-5}. 3. Calculate Interpolation Factor: Compute the normalized distance t (or \mu, \alpha, k) from \mathbf{p}1 to the intersection point: t = \frac{iso - v1}{v2 - v1} Alternatively, using signed distances d1 = v1 - iso and d2 = v2 - iso (where d1 and d2 have opposite signs): \mathbf{p} = \frac{d1 \mathbf{p}2 - d2 \mathbf{p}1}{d1 - d2} This form is numerically more stable when vertices are near the plane. 4. Compute Position: Calculate the intersection point using vector interpolation: \mathbf{p} = \mathbf{p}1 + t (\mathbf{p}2 - \mathbf{p}1) Or in component form: \mathbf{p} = (1 - t) \mathbf{p}1 + t \mathbf{p}2 5. Clamping (Optional but Recommended): To handle floating-point inaccuracies where t might slightly exceed [0, 1], clamp t to [0, 1] before computing \mathbf{p}. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def linearedgeintersection(p1, p2, v1, v2, iso, epsilon=1e-7): """ Calculates the intersection point of an isosurface with an edge. Args: p1: 3D vector (x, y, z) of the first endpoint. p2: 3D vector (x, y, z) of the second endpoint. v1: Scalar value at p1. v2: Scalar value at p2. iso: Target isovalue. epsilon: Threshold for degenerate case detection. Returns: 3D vector representing the intersection point. """ # Check for degenerate case where endpoints have same scalar value if abs(v2 - v1) < epsilon: return p1 # Calculate interpolation factor t # t represents the fraction of the distance from p1 to p2 t = (iso - v1) / (v2 - v1) # Clamp t to [0, 1] to handle floating point errors t = max(0.0, min(1.0, t)) # Compute intersection point # p = p1 + t (p2 - p1) px = p1.x + t (p2.x - p1.x) py = p1.y + t (p2.y - p1.y) pz = p1.z + t (p2.z - p1.z) return (px, py, pz) Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Division by Zero: If v1 = v2, the denominator is zero. This must be guarded against. Numerical Stability: When vertices are very close to the isosurface, standard interpolation can suffer from cancellation errors. Using signed distances (d0, d1) as in improves stability. Multiple Roots: Linear interpolation assumes a single root per edge. If the scalar field has multiple roots within the voxel (e.g., a thin structure passing through), linear interpolation will fail to detect all intersections. Vertex Ordering: In some implementations (e.g.,), consistent ordering of P1 and P2 (e.g., by coordinate value) is required to ensure correct triangle generation and normal orientation. Iterative Bisection Intersection Refinement is a post-detection technique used to accurately locate the intersection point of a viewing ray with an isosurface within a volume dataset. It solves the problem of geometric inaccuracy inherent in coarse adaptive sampling or sphere tracing by iteratively narrowing the interval known to contain the root. It sets itself apart from its siblings by relying on repeated linear interpolation (bisection) to refine the position, offering a balance of speed and moderate accuracy at the cost of potential artifacts in complex topologies. Linear Intersection Approximation (also known as Midpoint Intersection) estimates the intersection point of an isosurface with a grid edge by calculating the geometric midpoint of the edge, rather than performing linear interpolation based on scalar values. It differs from its parent, Linear Edge Intersection, by ignoring endpoint scalar values entirely, and from its sibling, Iterative Bisection Intersection Refinement, by using a single fixed geometric step instead of recursive refinement. Inverse Linear Interpolation calculates the non-integer position x corresponding to a specific scalar value v between two known values v1 and v2 at positions x1 and x2, assuming linear variation. It is primarily used for finding iso-surface intersections or specific density levels within a volume. Unlike Linear Edge Intersection, which computes the exact intersection on a grid edge, this method provides the general algebraic inversion of linear interpolation. Hermite interpolation for isosurface extraction determines the precise position of an isovertex along a zero-crossing edge by utilizing both scalar field values and gradient information (Hermite data) at the edge endpoints. Unlike Linear Edge Intersection, which assumes linear variation and produces artifacts on non-linear implicit functions, this method fits higher-order polynomials to the local field behavior, significantly improving surface accuracy. It is primarily used in contouring algorithms like Marching Cubes where gradient data is available or can be approximated. This method estimates the positional error introduced by linear interpolation when determining the intersection of a scalar field with an isovalue on a grid edge. It leverages Taylor series expansion to bound the difference between the true root and the linear approximation without solving a linear system. It distinguishes itself from Linear Edge Intersection by providing a quantitative error metric rather than just the position, and from Iterative Bisection Intersection Refinement by offering an analytical estimate rather than a numerical refinement. Approximates the zero-crossing position along an edge by sampling discrete points and selecting the one with minimum absolute density. It initializes a minimum value and iterates through a fixed number of steps (e.g., 8) along the edge, updating the best position if a lower absolute density is found. Uses linear interpolation but snaps vertices to grid points if they are within a small threshold (snap, typically 0.01) of the grid edge point or if the scalar values are nearly identical. This reduces mesh complexity and potential artifacts from floating-point noise. Clips wall edges to a screen or player boundary (e.g., y < 1) using linear interpolation to find the intersection point. If an endpoint is behind the boundary, it calculates the interpolation factor t and updates the coordinates to lie exactly on the boundary plane. An interpolation method between linear interpolation and midpoint selection used to calculate the intersection point of an edge and an iso-surface. It normalizes the interpolation ratio k based on thresholds m and n: if |k| < m, |k| is set to q; if |k| > n, |k| is set to p; otherwise, |k| is set to 0.5. This reduces artifacts in specific topological configurations. A method to find the point where the SDF assumes the isovalue c=0 along an edge exhibiting a material change, reduced to finding a value t \in [0,1]. It applies binary search with a limit of 8 iterations and a sub-interval size threshold of 10^{-6}. Handles cases where the surface intersects a grid edge more than once. It identifies a point where the gradient is perpendicular to the edge and deforms the surface to ensure only single edge intersections remain, using linear interpolation in the direction of the gradient. Handles the case where the surface passes through vertices of the grid by considering F to be strictly positive whenever F \ge 0. This ensures consistent topology when vertices lie exactly on the isosurface. Time Complexity: O(1) per edge. The calculation involves a constant number of arithmetic operations. Memory Complexity: O(1) auxiliary space. No additional data structures are required beyond the input values. Performance: Extremely fast, making it suitable for real-time applications and large-scale volume rendering. It is significantly faster than higher-order interpolation methods. Accuracy: Provides an exact solution under the assumption of linear field variation. Accuracy degrades if the scalar field is highly non-linear within the voxel. Strengths: Simplicity, speed, and numerical stability (when implemented with signed distances). Limitations: Cannot resolve multiple roots within a single edge/voxel. May produce artifacts (e.g., "crinkled" surfaces) if the underlying field is not smooth or linear. When to Use: When performance is critical and the scalar field is relatively smooth or linear within voxels. When Not to Use: When high geometric accuracy is required for highly non-linear fields, or when multiple intersections per voxel are expected. Linear Edge Intersection is a fundamental technique in isosurface extraction, originating from the Marching Cubes algorithm introduced by Lorensen and Cline in 1987. It is widely used in medical imaging, scientific visualization, and computer graphics for converting volumetric data into polygonal meshes. The method has been extended and refined in various contexts, including conservative voxelization and uncertainty estimation. name: Iterative Bisection Intersection Refinement
head: Bisection Refinement, Intersection refined isosurface rendering, Iso Hit Bisection, Isosurface Rendering with Intersection Refinement, Isosurface shader, Linear Interpolation Refinement, Ray Intersection Refinement
body: Iterative Bisection Intersection Refinement is a post-detection technique used to accurately locate the intersection point of a viewing ray with an isosurface within a volume dataset. It solves the problem of geometric inaccuracy inherent in coarse adaptive sampling or sphere tracing by iteratively narrowing the interval known to contain the root. It sets itself apart from its siblings by relying on repeated linear interpolation (bisection) to refine the position, offering a balance of speed and moderate accuracy at the cost of potential artifacts in complex topologies. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: Ray origin \mathbf{o}, ray direction \mathbf{d} (normalized), the interval [t{prev}, t{curr}] (or [x{near}, x{far}]) where a sign change in the scalar field value has been detected, the scalar field values at the interval endpoints d{prev} and d{curr} (or f{near}, f{far}), and the target isovalue \rho. Outputs: The refined intersection parameter t{hit} (or position \mathbf{x}{hit}). Data Structures: The method operates on scalar values and 3D coordinates. No complex data structures are required beyond the ray parameters and the scalar field texture/volume access function. Steps: 1. Initialization: Define the search interval. Let L (or x{near}) be the point outside the isovalue (where f(L) < \rho) and R (or x{far}) be the point inside or at the isovalue (where f(R) \ge \rho). In adaptive sampling contexts, these correspond to t{prev} and t{curr} respectively. 2. Iteration Loop: Repeat for a fixed number of iterations N (typically 4 to 10): a. Linear Interpolation: Compute the new candidate point \mathbf{x}{new} (or parameter M) using linear interpolation between the current bounds. The position is calculated as: \mathbf{x}{new} = (\mathbf{x}{far} - \mathbf{x}{near}) \frac{\rho - f{near}}{f{far} - f{near}} + \mathbf{x}{near} Alternatively, in parameter space t: t{new} = t{near} + (t{far} - t{near}) \frac{\rho - f{near}}{f{far} - f{near}} b. Sampling: Evaluate the scalar field value f{new} at \mathbf{x}{new} (or dM at t{new}). c. Interval Update: Compare f{new} with \rho: If f{new} < \rho (the new point is outside the isovalue), update the lower bound: set x{near} = \mathbf{x}{new} and f{near} = f{new}. If f{new} \ge \rho (the new point is inside or at the isovalue), update the upper bound: set x{far} = \mathbf{x}{new} and f{far} = f{new}. Note: Some implementations use strict inequality for the upper bound update (dM > 0) and lower bound update (dM < 0) assuming centered zero-level sets. While the method is named "bisection", it primarily uses linear interpolation, though some variants use strict midpoint bisection (M = (L+R)/2). 3. Termination: After N iterations, the refined intersection position is \mathbf{x}{new} (or t{new}). If N=0, return the midpoint of the final interval (t{min} + t{max}) / 2. 4. Shading: The refined point is shaded using the appropriate lighting model. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def samplescalarfield(pos): """Standard volume lookup. Returns scalar value at pos.""" return volumelookup(pos) def intersectdomainbox(origin, direction, domainmin, domainmax): """Standard ray-AABB intersection. Returns (tmin, tmax).""" tmin = -float('inf') tmax = float('inf') for i in range(3): if abs(direction[i]) < 1e-9: if origin[i] < domainmin[i] or origin[i] > domainmax[i]: return (float('inf'), -float('inf')) else: t1 = (domainmin[i] - origin[i]) / direction[i] t2 = (domainmax[i] - origin[i]) / direction[i] tmin = max(tmin, min(t1, t2)) tmax = min(tmax, max(t1, t2)) return (tmin, tmax) def refineisohitbisection(origin, direction, tprev, tcurr, dprev, dcurr, isovalue, numiterations=5): """ Refines the intersection of a ray with an isosurface using bisection. """ tnear = tprev tfar = tcurr fnear = dprev ffar = dcurr # Guard: ensure valid interval for bisection if fnear >= isovalue or ffar < isovalue: return (tnear + tfar) / 2.0 for in range(numiterations): denom = ffar - fnear if abs(denom) < 1e-9: tnew = (tnear + tfar) / 2.0 else: tnew = tnear + (tfar - tnear) (isovalue - fnear) / denom posnew = origin + tnew direction fnew = samplescalarfield(posnew) # Update bounds based on S4 if fnew < isovalue: tnear = tnew fnear = fnew else: tfar = tnew ffar = fnew return tnew def raymarchwithrefinement(origin, direction, domainmin, domainmax, isovalue, stepsize, numrefineiters=5): """ Adaptive ray marching with iterative bisection refinement. """ tmin, tmax = intersectdomainbox(origin, direction, domainmin, domainmax) if tmax <= tmin: return None tprev = tmin dprev = samplescalarfield(origin + tprev direction) tcurr = tprev + stepsize while tcurr <= tmax: dcurr = samplescalarfield(origin + tcurr direction) # Check for sign change (outside to inside) if (dprev < isovalue) and (dcurr >= isovalue): thit = refineisohitbisection( origin, direction, tprev, tcurr, dprev, dcurr, isovalue, numrefineiters) phit = origin + thit direction # Shading is application-specific; return hit point for shading pipeline return phit tprev = tcurr dprev = dcurr tcurr += stepsize return None Parameters: numiterations (or uRefinementIterations): The number of bisection steps. Typical values range from 4 to 10, with 5 being common. More iterations improve accuracy at the cost of additional scalar field evaluations. isovalue (\rho): The scalar threshold defining the surface. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Division by Zero: If f{far} \approx f{near}, the linear interpolation formula divides by zero. The pseudocode handles this by falling back to the midpoint. Sign Change Assumption: The method assumes a single root within the interval. Precision: Floating-point precision errors in f{new} comparisons can cause infinite loops if not bounded by iteration count. Using a fixed iteration count avoids this. Neubauer's algorithm is a method for finding the intersection of a viewing ray with an iso-surface defined by trilinearly interpolated scalar data within a voxel. It solves the problem of locating the precise root of the implicit function f(t) = \rho(R(t)) - \rho{iso} by using repeated linear interpolation to refine the intersection position within the ray segment containing the root. It is distinguished from its siblings by its reliance on iterative linear approximation rather than closed-form algebraic solutions (like Schwarze's Analytic Inversion) or root isolation techniques (like Isolation and Iterative Root Finding), offering a balance of speed and moderate accuracy at the cost of potential artifacts in complex topologies. Fast Ray-Surface Intersection is an approximate method for determining the intersection point of a ray with an iso-surface within a volume rendering cell, trading geometric accuracy for computational speed. It solves the problem of finding the first-hit surface location without the high cost of inverting trilinear interpolation. Unlike exact intersection methods which compute all roots of the cubic polynomial derived from trilinear interpolation, this method subdivides the ray segment within the cell and uses linear interpolation to estimate the hit point, producing visually indistinguishable results in final renderings while being significantly faster. The Secant Method for Surface Depth Refinement is an iterative root-finding algorithm used to refine the depth value d along a ray where a signed distance function (SDF) or occupancy logit crosses a specific threshold. It distinguishes itself from its sibling Bisection Method for Surface Depth Refinement by using linear interpolation between two bracketing points to estimate the next probe point, rather than simply halving the interval. The Bisection Method for Surface Depth Refinement is an iterative root-finding algorithm that determines the exact intersection point of a ray with an implicit surface within a segment known to contain an intersection. It serves as an alternative to the Secant method in ray marching pipelines. The method systematically halves the search interval at each step until the midpoint evaluates to zero. Hitpoint Refinement is an iterative technique to achieve higher quality in detecting surface intersections without reducing rendering speed. It allows for coarser initial sampling steps to increase rendering speed, refining the detected intersection point through a specific heuristic procedure. It sets itself apart from its siblings by using a "half-step back, then check direction" adjustment rather than standard bisection or secant methods, enabling significant speedups when paired with large initial sampling distances. Windowed Bisection for Isosurface Refinement refines the isosurface position along a ray using 4 iterations of bisection with windowing, ensuring correctness across brick boundaries by using sampleWithIndirection. It initializes lo = tLow and hi = tHigh, then loops 4 times to calculate the midpoint mid = (lo + hi) 0.5, position pos = rayOrigin + rayDir mid, and voxel coordinates voxel = normalizedToVoxel(pos,...). It samples density, normalizes it to [0,1] using uniforms.floatMin and uniforms.floatMax, then applies windowing: density = applyWindow(normalizedDensity, windowCenter, windowWidth);. It updates bounds: if density >= isoValue, set hi = mid; else lo = mid, and returns (lo + hi) 0.5. Time Complexity: O(N) scalar field evaluations per intersection, where N is the number of refinement iterations. This is significantly cheaper than solving cubic polynomials for exact trilinear intersection but more expensive than a single-step detection. Memory Complexity: O(1) auxiliary memory. Measured Performance: A fixed number of 4 iterations is empirically sufficient for high-quality positions in many datasets. Increasing iterations improves accuracy at the cost of additional evaluations. Strengths: Provides a more accurate hit position than a single-step midpoint detection. Empirically, a fixed number of iterations yields high-quality positions. Limitations: Potential artifacts in complex topologies if the initial step size is too large. When to Use: When adaptive sampling is used and high precision is needed without the cost of analytic inversion. When Not to Use: When the scalar field is extremely noisy or discontinuous, or when exact geometric precision is required for subsequent physics simulations. The method originates from real-time volume graphics research, specifically in the context of isosurface rendering. name: Neubauer's Ray-Voxel Intersection Algorithm
head: Neubauer, Neubauer's Approximative Intersection, Neubauer's Method, Repeated Linear Interpolation
body: Neubauer's algorithm is a fast, approximate method for finding the intersection of a viewing ray with an iso-surface defined by trilinearly interpolated scalar data within a voxel. It solves the root-finding problem for the implicit function f(t) = \rho(R(t)) - \rho{iso} by repeatedly applying linear interpolation to narrow down the segment containing the root. It is distinguished from sibling methods by relying solely on iterative linear approximation rather than closed-form algebraic solutions (like Schwarze's Analytic Inversion) or derivative-based root isolation (like Isolation and Iterative Root Finding), trading mathematical exactness for computational speed. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Ray R(t) = \mathbf{a} + t\mathbf{b}, the interval [t{in}, t{out}] where the ray overlaps the voxel, scalar field values \rho{ijk} at the eight voxel vertices, the iso-value \rho{iso}, and the iteration count N (typically 2–3). Output: The hit distance t{hit} along the ray, or a "NO HIT" status if no intersection is found within the voxel. Data Structures: The algorithm operates on scalar variables for the interval bounds t0, t1, the interpolated density values \rho0, \rho1, and the candidate parameter t. Method Steps: 1. Initialization: Set the search interval boundaries and evaluate densities at the endpoints: t0:= t{in}, \quad t1:= t{out} \rho0:= \rho(R(t0)), \quad \rho1:= \rho(R(t1)) where \rho(R(t)) is computed via trilinear interpolation of the voxel's vertex data. 2. Initial Sign Check: If \text{sign}(\rho0 - \rho{iso}) = \text{sign}(\rho1 - \rho{iso}), return NO HIT. This indicates the iso-surface does not cross the ray segment within the voxel, or crosses an even number of times, which the method cannot detect. 3. Iterative Refinement (Repeated Linear Interpolation): For i = 1 to N: a. Compute the candidate intersection parameter using linear interpolation: t:= t0 + (t1 - t0) \frac{\rho{iso} - \rho0}{\rho1 - \rho0} b. Evaluate the density at the candidate point: \rho{new}:= \rho(R(t)). c. Determine which sub-segment contains the root by comparing signs: If \text{sign}(\rho{new} - \rho{iso}) = \text{sign}(\rho0 - \rho{iso}), the root lies in [t, t1]; update t0:= t, \rho0:= \rho{new}. Else, the root lies in [t0, t]; update t1:= t, \rho1:= \rho{new}. 4. Final Result: After N iterations, compute the final hit distance: t{hit}:= t0 + (t1 - t0) \frac{\rho{iso} - \rho0}{\rho1 - \rho0} Return t{hit}. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def NeubauerRayVoxelIntersection(rayorigin, raydirection, voxelbounds, voxeldata, rhoiso, N=3): """ rayorigin: tuple (x, y, z) raydirection: tuple (dx, dy, dz) voxelbounds: tuple (x0, x1, y0, y1, z0, z1) voxeldata: list/tuple of 8 floats representing density at voxel corners rhoiso: float, the iso-surface value N: int, number of interpolation iterations """ # 1. Calculate ray-voxel overlap interval [tin, tout] using slab method x0, x1, y0, y1, z0, z1 = voxelbounds tmin = -float('inf') tmax = float('inf') for axis in range(3): p = rayorigin[axis] d = raydirection[axis] b0 = [x0, y0, z0][axis] b1 = [x1, y1, z1][axis] if abs(d) < 1e-12: if p < b0 or p > b1: return None else: t1 = (b0 - p) / d t2 = (b1 - p) / d if t1 > t2: t1, t2 = t2, t1 tmin = max(tmin, t1) tmax = min(tmax, t2) if tmin > tmax: return None tin, tout = tmin, tmax # Helper to evaluate trilinear interpolation def evaluatedensity(t): px = rayorigin[0] + t raydirection[0] py = rayorigin[1] + t raydirection[1] pz = rayorigin[2] + t raydirection[2] u = (px - x0) / (x1 - x0) v = (py - y0) / (y1 - y0) w = (pz - z0) / (z1 - z0) u = max(0.0, min(1.0, u)) v = max(0.0, min(1.0, v)) w = max(0.0, min(1.0, w)) d000 = voxeldata[0]; d100 = voxeldata[1] d010 = voxeldata[2]; d110 = voxeldata[3] d001 = voxeldata[4]; d101 = voxeldata[5] d011 = voxeldata[6]; d111 = voxeldata[7] d00 = d000 (1 - u) + d100 u d10 = d010 (1 - u) + d110 u d01 = d001 (1 - u) + d101 u d11 = d011 (1 - u) + d111 u d0 = d00 (1 - v) + d10 v d1 = d01 (1 - v) + d11 v return d0 (1 - w) + d1 w # 2. Initialize interval t0 = tin t1 = tout rho0 = evaluatedensity(t0) rho1 = evaluatedensity(t1) # 3. Initial sign check def sign(val): if val > 0: return 1 elif val < 0: return -1 else: return 0 if sign(rho0 - rhoiso) == sign(rho1 - rhoiso): return None # 4. Iterative refinement for i in range(N): t = t0 + (t1 - t0) (rhoiso - rho0) / (rho1 - rho0) rhonew = evaluatedensity(t) if sign(rhonew - rhoiso) == sign(rho0 - rhoiso): t0 = t rho0 = rhonew else: t1 = t rho1 = rhonew # 5. Final result thit = t0 + (t1 - t0) (rhoiso - rho0) / (rho1 - rho0) return thit Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Multiple Intersections: The algorithm assumes a single root within the segment defined by differing signs. It can falsely return the last intersection point if three intersections are contained within a voxel but two of them are within the first ray segment. Complex Topologies: In cases where the function has two roots, the entry and exit densities may be on the same side of \rho{iso}, causing the initial sign check to return NO HIT incorrectly. SIMD Compatibility: The control flow involves conditional updates to t0, t1, \rho0, \rho1 based on sign comparisons. This inconsistent decision-making on which segment to handle makes the base algorithm less suitable for SIMD than methods with uniform control flow, although it remains functional and faster than exact solvers in parallel contexts. Approximation Errors: As an iterative approximation, it linearly approximates the trilinear function, making it error-prone and prone to approximation artifacts and image errors for complex voxel configurations. Schwarze's Analytic Inversion is a method for computing the exact intersection of a ray with an iso-surface defined by trilinearly interpolated scalar data within a voxel. It solves the cubic polynomial resulting from substituting the ray equation into the trilinear interpolation function to find the precise root. It is distinguished from sibling methods like Neubauer's algorithm by its reliance on closed-form algebraic solutions (Cardano's formula) rather than iterative refinement or isolation techniques, offering mathematical exactness at the cost of significant computational expense and numerical instability. Isolation and Iterative Root Finding is a ray-voxel intersection algorithm for iso-surfaces that combines the speed of Neubauer's method with the correctness guarantees of Schwarze's method. It solves the problem of finding the first intersection of a ray with a cubic polynomial within a voxel by first isolating the root interval using the polynomial's extrema, then refining the location via iterative root finding. Unlike Neubauer's method, which can fail or return incorrect intersections when multiple roots exist in a segment, this method guarantees that the final interval contains exactly one root, ensuring the first valid intersection is found. Marmitt's Ray-Cell Intersection computes the point where a ray intersects an isosurface defined by trilinear interpolation within a 3D voxel cell. It solves for the first positive root of the cubic polynomial derived from the cell's corner values using an iterative bisection refinement strategy. Unlike analytical cubic solvers (e.g., Schwarze’s method), this approach is slightly faster and yields single-precision, numerically stable results. Time and Memory Complexity: The algorithm performs a fixed number of iterations N (typically 2–3). Each iteration requires one trilinear interpolation evaluation. Trilinear interpolation is O(1) with a constant number of arithmetic operations. Thus, the time complexity per ray-voxel intersection is O(N), which is effectively constant. Memory complexity is O(1) as it only stores a few scalar variables. Measured Performance: On a 1.8GHz AMD Opteron CPU, Neubauer achieves an average of 3.04 million ray-voxel intersections per second in synthetic setups (Table 1). In SIMD mode on synthetic setups, Neubauer achieves an average of 3.04 million ray-cell intersections per second (Table 2). On real-world datasets (Bonsai, Aneurism, Engine), Neubauer achieves approximately 2.93–2.94 million intersections per second (Table 3). In SIMD mode on real-world datasets, Neubauer achieves 6.94–7.65 million intersections per second, a speedup of factor 2.3–2.6 over sequential code (Table 4). Strengths and Limitations: Strengths: Computationally very cheap and faster than the accurate but slow Schwarze algorithm. Better suited for SIMD implementation than Schwarze due to simpler control flow. Integrated into the OpenRT realtime ray tracing system. Limitations: Prone to approximation artifacts and image errors for complex voxel configurations. Can fail to locate valid intersections in cases with multiple roots or specific topological configurations. Less numerically stable than isolation-based methods. When to Use: Use when computational speed is prioritized over exactness and the voxel data topology is relatively simple. The method is well-suited for scenarios where an approximate intersection is acceptable and exact solvers are too slow. When Not to Use: Avoid when high accuracy is required or when the iso-surface may contain multiple intersections within a single voxel, as the method is error-prone and may miss valid intersections. Neubauer's algorithm was proposed by Neubauer et al. in 2002. It was analyzed and compared with other ray-voxel intersection techniques (including Schwarze's method and linear interpolation) in the context of iso-surface volume rendering by Wald et al. in 2004. The method is integrated into the OpenRT realtime ray tracing system for iso-surface volume rendering, where it serves as a fast, approximate intersection primitive.
