name: Schwarze's Analytic Inversion
head: Accurate Ray-Isosurface Intersection via Cubic Polynomial, Cardano's formula method, Cubic Intersection Search, Exact Projection, Exact Ray-Surface Intersection, Schwarze approach
body: Schwarze's Analytic Inversion is a method for computing the exact intersection of a viewing ray with an isosurface defined by trilinear interpolation within a voxel. It solves the cubic polynomial representing the scalar value along the ray using Cardano's formula. It is distinguished from its siblings by its reliance on closed-form algebraic solutions for cubic roots, whereas Isolation and Iterative Root Finding uses root isolation and bisection, and Marmitt's Ray-Cell Intersection uses extrema-based splitting. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A ray defined by an origin point p\lambda and a direction vector \tilde{d}, and a voxel containing the ray segment. The scalar field values at the voxel corners are assumed to be available for trilinear interpolation. Output: The ray parameter t corresponding to the first intersection with the isosurface within the voxel, and the intersection point p'\lambda = p\lambda + t\tilde{d}. Data Structures: The method operates on the coefficients of a cubic polynomial At^3 + Bt^2 + Ct + D = 0. These coefficients are derived from the eight trilinear interpolation coefficients \rho{ijk} (where i,j,k \in \{0,1\}) and the ray direction components dx, dy, dz. The exact mapping from \rho{ijk} to A,B,C,D is not explicitly detailed in the provided notes, but the polynomial form is standard for trilinear interpolation along a line. Steps: 1. Ray Definition: Define the ray \tilde{r}(t) = p\lambda + t\tilde{d}. The direction \tilde{d} can be determined by shooting from the sample point p\lambda to a subset of the eight cell corners (determined by the Marching Cubes case table) or by using the gradient at p\lambda. Note: Using the gradient may result in a ray that does not intersect the isosurface inside the cell. 2. Voxel Traversal: Use voxel-based ray traversal (e.g., 3DDDA) to identify the voxel containing the intersection. 3. Segment Definition: Within the identified voxel, define the ray segment entering at p0 and exiting at p3. 4. Coefficient Estimation (Alternative Approach): Some implementations estimate the cubic polynomial coefficients by fetching scalar values at four points along the ray: the entry point p0, the exit point p3, and two trisection points p1 and p2. The coefficients are then estimated from these four values. 5. Special Case Check: Check if coefficients A and/or B are small, indicating the polynomial does not have full degree (e.g., quadratic or linear). Solve these cases directly. 6. Cardano's Solution: For a full cubic polynomial, solve for the roots using Cardano's formula. This involves computing cosines and inverse cosines. 7. Root Selection: Compute all roots of the polynomial. Identify the first root along the ray (smallest positive t) that lies within the current voxel segment [t{in}, t{out}]. 8. Intersection Point: Calculate the intersection point p'\lambda = p\lambda + t\tilde{d}. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def schwarzeanalyticinversion(rayorigin, raydirection, voxelbounds, scalarfield): """ Computes the exact ray-isosurface intersection using Schwarze's method. """ # 1. Define ray segment within voxel tmin, tmax = computerayvoxelintersection(rayorigin, raydirection, voxelbounds) if tmin > tmax: return None # No intersection with voxel # 2. Get trilinear coefficients or sample points # Note: Exact derivation of A, B, C, D from rhoijk is not provided in sources. # Alternative: Sample 4 points to estimate coefficients p0 = rayorigin + tmin raydirection p3 = rayorigin + tmax raydirection p1 = rayorigin + (tmin + tmax) / 3 raydirection p2 = rayorigin + (tmin + 2 tmax) / 3 raydirection # Fetch scalar values at these points val0 = scalarfield.evaluate(p0) val1 = scalarfield.evaluate(p1) val2 = scalarfield.evaluate(p2) val3 = scalarfield.evaluate(p3) # Estimate cubic coefficients A, B, C, D from values # This step requires solving a linear system or using Lagrange interpolation # to find the polynomial P(t) = At^3 + Bt^2 + Ct + D such that # P(0) = val0, P(1/3) = val1, P(2/3) = val2, P(1) = val3 # Then adjust for isovalue. # Since exact formula is not in sources, we assume a function exists: A, B, C, D = estimatecubiccoefficients(val0, val1, val2, val3) # 3. Check for special cases (low degree) if issmall(A) and issmall(B): # Linear case: Ct + D = 0 if issmall(C): return None # No unique solution or constant t = -D / C elif issmall(A): # Quadratic case: Bt^2 + Ct + D = 0 t = solvequadratic(B, C, D, tmin, tmax) else: # Full cubic case: Cardano's formula roots = solvecubiccardano(A, B, C, D) t = findfirstvalidroot(roots, tmin, tmax) if t is None: return None return rayorigin + t raydirection def solvecubiccardano(A, B, C, D): """ Solves At^3 + Bt^2 + Ct + D = 0 using Cardano's formula. Involves cosines and inverse cosines. """ # Normalize to monic polynomial t^3 + a2t^2 + a1t + a0 = 0 a2 = B / A a1 = C / A a0 = D / A # Depressed cubic substitution t = x - a2/3 p = a1 - a22 / 3 q = 2 a23 / 27 - a1 a2 / 3 + a0 # Discriminant delta = (q/2)2 + (p/3)3 roots = [] if delta > 0: # One real root u = cbrt(-q/2 + sqrt(delta)) v = cbrt(-q/2 - sqrt(delta)) x = u + v t = x - a2 / 3 roots.append(t) elif delta == 0: # Multiple real roots if q == 0: t = -a2 / 3 roots.append(t) else: u = cbrt(-q/2) t1 = 2 u - a2 / 3 t2 = -u - a2 / 3 roots.append(t1) roots.append(t2) else: # Three real roots (Casus irreducibilis) - requires trigonometric solution r = sqrt(-(p/3)3) theta = acos(-q / (2 r)) # Note: Sources mention cosines and inverse cosines m = 2 cbrt(r) t1 = m cos(theta / 3) - a2 / 3 t2 = m cos((theta + 2 pi) / 3) - a2 / 3 t3 = m cos((theta + 4 pi) / 3) - a2 / 3 roots.append(t1) roots.append(t2) roots.append(t3) return roots def findfirstvalidroot(roots, tmin, tmax): """ Returns the smallest root t such that tmin <= t <= tmax. """ validroots = [t for t in roots if tmin <= t <= tmax] if not validroots: return None return min(validroots) Parameters: Floating Point Precision: Single precision is often targeted for interactive rendering, but this exacerbates numerical stability issues. Epsilon: Not explicitly defined for Schwarze's method in the sources, but related iterative methods use \epsilon = 4.0 \cdot 10^{-3}. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Numerical Stability: The algebraic solution is prone to numerical problems, especially in single precision floating point. It is difficult to tune to avoid incorrectly computed intersections. Ray Direction: Using the gradient as the ray direction may result in a ray that does not intersect the isosurface inside the cell. Special Cases: Coefficients A and/or B may be small, requiring direct solution of lower-degree polynomials. A voxel intersection method that solves the cubic polynomial for ray-SDF intersection by first splitting the polynomial using the method proposed by Marmitt et al. [2004] and then using repeated linear interpolation for iteration. It uses a maximum of 50 iterations and an epsilon threshold of \epsilon = 4.0 \cdot 10^{-3}. It is often faster than Newton-Raphson because Newton-Raphson can take longer to converge in harder cases where the derivative is small. A method to find the intersection of a ray with an iso-surface defined by trilinear interpolation within a cell. It solves the resulting cubic polynomial by isolating roots via extrema, avoiding the numerical instability and cost of Cardano's formula. It splits the ray segment into at most three parts using extrema, steps through them to find the interval containing zero, and uses recursive bisection (3-4 steps) to find the root. It is approximately three times faster than Schwarze's algorithm and more numerically stable in single precision. Time Complexity: High computational cost due to the determination of roots of a cubic polynomial. Cardano's formula involves several cosines and inverse cosine operations, which are costly. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Measured Performance: It is mathematically the most accurate solution but has too many drawbacks for interactive volume rendering due to speed and numerical stability issues compared to the isolation method. Marmitt's method is approximately three times faster than Schwarze's. Strengths: Mathematically exact intersection. Limitations: Computationally very expensive. Prone to numerical problems, especially in single precision. Difficult to tune to avoid incorrect intersections. When to use: When exact intersection is required and performance is not a primary constraint, or in double precision environments where stability is less of an issue. When not to use: For interactive volume rendering where speed and single-precision stability are critical. Schwarze's Analytic Inversion was introduced by Schwarze [Sch90] and further discussed by Parker et al. [PSL+98]. It is a technique for inverting trilinear interpolation to find the precise intersection point of a ray with an isosurface. It is commonly applied in volume ray tracing. name: Isolation and Iterative Root Finding
head: Isolation method, New intersection algorithm
body: Isolation and Iterative Root Finding is a ray-voxel intersection algorithm that finds the first intersection of a viewing ray with an implicit surface within a voxel cell. It balances the correctness of analytical solvers with the speed of iterative refinement by isolating the root interval via polynomial extrema before applying iterative refinement, guaranteeing exactly one root in the final interval. This approach is roughly three times faster than Schwarze's method while maintaining correctness and improving numerical stability. The method operates on a ray segment [t{in}, t{out}] parameterized by t, where the implicit function is f(t). The algorithm proceeds in two phases: root isolation via extrema analysis, followed by iterative root refinement. Inputs: Ray segment endpoints t{in}, t{out}; polynomial coefficients A, B, C, D for f(t) = At^3 + Bt^2 + Ct + D; isovalue \rho{iso}. Outputs: Intersection parameter t{hit} or a no-hit indicator. The algorithm uses scalar variables for parameters and coefficients. 1. Initialization: Set t0 = t{in}, t1 = t{out}. Compute f0 = f(t0) and f1 = f(t1). 2. Extrema Isolation: Compute the derivative f'(t) = 3At^2 + 2Bt + C. Solve the quadratic equation f'(t) = 0 for real roots. Let the roots be e0 (smaller) and e1 (larger). If no real roots exist, skip to Step 4. 3. Segment Advancement: Iterate through the extrema to isolate the interval containing the first root. First Extremum (e0): If e0 \in [t0, t1]: Compute f(e0). If \text{sign}(f(e0)) == \text{sign}(f0): The root is in the segment after e0. Advance: t0:= e0 f0:= f(e0) Else: The root is in the segment before e0. Constrain: t1:= e0 f1:= f(e0) Second Extremum (e1): If e1 \in [t0, t1]: Compute f(e1). If \text{sign}(f(e1)) == \text{sign}(f0): The root is in the segment after e1. Advance: t0:= e1 f0:= f(e1) Else: The root is in the segment before e1. Constrain: t1:= e1 f1:= f(e1) 4. Hit Test: If \text{sign}(f0) == \text{sign}(f1), return NO HIT. Otherwise, the interval [t0, t1] contains exactly one root. 5. Iterative Refinement: Apply repeated linear interpolation (regula falsi) for a fixed number of iterations N (typically 2–3). For i = 1 to N: Compute candidate t: t = t0 + (t1 - t0) \frac{-f0}{f1 - f0} Compute f(t). If \text{sign}(f(t)) == \text{sign}(f0): t0:= t f0:= f(t) Else: t1:= t f1:= f(t) 6. Return Result: t{hit} = t0 + (t1 - t0) \frac{-f0}{f1 - f0} Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def isolationanditerativerootfinding(tin, tout, A, B, C, D, rhoiso): # f(t) = At^3 + Bt^2 + Ct + D - rhoiso # f'(t) = 3At^2 + 2Bt + C t0 = tin t1 = tout f0 = At03 + Bt02 + Ct0 + D - rhoiso f1 = At13 + Bt12 + Ct1 + D - rhoiso # Solve 3At^2 + 2Bt + C = 0 aquad = 3 A bquad = 2 B cquad = C discriminant = bquad2 - 4 aquad cquad if discriminant >= 0: sqrtdisc = discriminant 0.5 e0 = (-bquad - sqrtdisc) / (2 aquad) e1 = (-bquad + sqrtdisc) / (2 aquad) # Process first extremum e0 if t0 <= e0 <= t1: fe0 = Ae03 + Be02 + Ce0 + D - rhoiso if sign(fe0) == sign(f0): t0 = e0 f0 = fe0 else: t1 = e0 f1 = fe0 # Process second extremum e1 if t0 <= e1 <= t1: fe1 = Ae13 + Be12 + Ce1 + D - rhoiso if sign(fe1) == sign(f0): t0 = e1 f0 = fe1 else: t1 = e1 f1 = fe1 if sign(f0) == sign(f1): return None # NOHIT # Iterative refinement (Regula Falsi) N = 3 # Typical value for i in range(1, N + 1): # Guard against division by zero if f1 == f0 if f1 == f0: t = (t0 + t1) / 2.0 else: t = t0 + (t1 - t0) (-f0) / (f1 - f0) ft = At3 + Bt2 + Ct + D - rhoiso if sign(ft) == sign(f0): t0 = t f0 = ft else: t1 = t f1 = ft # Final estimate if f1 == f0: thit = (t0 + t1) / 2.0 else: thit = t0 + (t1 - t0) (-f0) / (f1 - f0) return thit def sign(x): if x > 0: return 1 elif x < 0: return -1 else: return 0 N (Iterations): Typically 2–3. A fixed number is faster than an adaptive termination criterion. No Real Extrema: If the discriminant of the derivative is negative, the function is monotonic. Extrema Outside Interval: Extrema outside [t0, t1] are ignored. Sign Equality: If f0 and f1 have the same sign after isolation, no root exists in the segment. Division by Zero: If f1 \approx f0 during refinement, the denominator becomes small. Multiple Roots: The method isolates the first root. This method finds the intersection of a viewing ray with an isosurface defined by a trivariate polynomial in Bernstein form by iteratively subdividing the control polygon using the de Casteljau algorithm at the intersection with the zero axis. It distinguishes itself from sibling methods like Neubauer Iterative Root Finder and Knot insertion root finding by offering quadratic convergence speed and constant memory usage without index operations, making it significantly faster and more suitable for GPU architectures than linear-convergence knot insertion approaches. The Neubauer Iterative Root Finder is a numerical method for finding the intersection of a ray with an implicit surface (typically defined by a trivariate polynomial or spline) within a voxel cell. It solves the problem of determining the parameter t along the ray where the implicit function f(t) equals zero. It sets itself apart from analytical solvers like Schwarze’s cubic solver by using iterative bisection/refinement, which yields single-precision, numerically stable results and is slightly faster in practice. It builds on Isolation and Iterative Root Finding by using root isolation via sign changes within sub-intervals. A root finding approach based on Sturm Series working in power form. It uses the Sturm Series to count multiplicities of roots in a given interval and employs binary subdivision of the search interval. The algorithm computes the Sturm Series at the beginning, evaluates it once per iteration, and subdivides the interval. It offers exponential convergence with constant memory consumption during iteration, but high overall memory consumption as the whole Sturm Series must be kept in memory. Numerical problems inherent to power form implementations become more severe with more iterations. For degree 9 (tri-cubic), it has a relative execution time of 0.077, MSE of 0.003, and max error of 1.0. Time Complexity: Roughly a factor of three faster than Schwarze's analytical method. The cost is dominated by solving the quadratic derivative and evaluating the cubic polynomial. Memory Complexity: Constant memory usage, requiring only scalar storage for coefficients and parameters. Strengths: Guarantees correctness (one root in the final interval), better numerical stability than Neubauer's method, and is well suited for data parallel SIMD implementations due to simple branching and lack of complex control flow. Limitations: Requires computing polynomial coefficients and extrema upfront. Not suitable if the polynomial form is not available or if the cost of coefficient computation outweighs the intersection benefit. When to Use: When high performance and correctness are both required, especially in SIMD/GPU environments. When Not to Use: When the polynomial coefficients are not pre-computed or when the overhead of computing them is prohibitive. The method was introduced as a new intersection algorithm to address the trade-off between speed and correctness in ray-voxel intersection for isosurface rendering. It builds on the observation that repeated linear interpolation is reliable if the starting interval contains exactly one root. By isolating roots via extrema, it guarantees this condition. The method is well-suited for data parallel SIMD implementations, as it avoids the complex control flow of analytical solvers like Schwarze's. name: de Casteljau-based root finding
head: Root Finding: de Casteljau Subdivision (LR81), de Casteljau Subdivision
body: This method finds the intersection of a viewing ray with an isosurface defined by a trivariate polynomial in Bernstein form by iteratively subdividing the control polygon using the de Casteljau algorithm at the intersection with the zero axis. It distinguishes itself from sibling methods like Neubauer Iterative Root Finder and Knot insertion root finding by offering quadratic convergence speed and constant memory usage without index operations, making it significantly faster and more suitable for GPU architectures than linear-convergence knot insertion approaches. Inputs: Polynomial coefficients in Bernstein basis defining the distance field or implicit function f(t) along the ray parameter t \in [0, 1]. Isosurface value c (typically 0 for normalized distance fields). Maximum number of iterations N{iter} (typically 3 to 7). Outputs: The smallest root t^ \in [0, 1] such that f(t^) - c = 0. Data Structures: The algorithm operates on the control polygon of the Bernstein polynomial. For a polynomial of degree d, the control polygon consists of d+1 control points Pi. In the context of volume rendering, the polynomial is often univariate along the ray, derived from the trivariate field. The values are represented as scalars bi corresponding to the Bernstein coefficients. Steps: 1. Initialization: Let the current control points be Pi^{(0)} = bi for i = 0, \dots, d. Let the current parameter interval be [t{min}, t{max}] = [0, 1]. 2. Iteration Loop: Repeat for k = 1 to N{iter}. a. Find Intersection: Identify the index j where the control polygon crosses the zero axis (or the value c). Specifically, find j such that Pj^{(k-1)} - c and P{j+1}^{(k-1)} - c have opposite signs or one is zero. b. Compute Subdivision Parameter: Calculate t{sub} = \frac{Pj^{(k-1)} - c}{Pj^{(k-1)} - P{j+1}^{(k-1)}} using linear interpolation at the crossing segment. c. De Casteljau Subdivision: Perform the de Casteljau algorithm to split the control polygon at t{sub}. This generates two new sets of control points: left polygon P^{(L)} and right polygon P^{(R)}. d. Selection: Select the sub-polygon (P^{(L)} or P^{(R)}) that contains the root by checking the signs of the control points relative to c. e. Update: Set the current control points to the selected sub-polygon and update [t{min}, t{max}] to the corresponding sub-interval. 3. Result: The root is approximated by the midpoint of the final interval [t{min}, t{max}]. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def decasteljaurootfinding(bernsteincoeffs, targetvalue, maxiterations): """ Finds the root of a polynomial in Bernstein form using de Casteljau subdivision. Args: bernsteincoeffs: List of float coefficients b0,..., bd. targetvalue: The isosurface value c (e.g., 0). maxiterations: Integer, typically 3-7. Returns: float: Approximate root t in [0, 1]. """ # Current control points (constant memory for fixed degree d) p = list(bernsteincoeffs) degree = len(p) - 1 # Interval bounds tmin = 0.0 tmax = 1.0 # Pre-allocate buffers to satisfy constant memory claim left = [0.0] (degree + 1) right = [0.0] (degree + 1) for in range(maxiterations): # 1. Find the segment crossing the target value crossingindex = -1 for i in range(degree): vali = p[i] - targetvalue valnext = p[i+1] - targetvalue if vali valnext <= 0: crossingindex = i break # Fallback if no crossing found (root at boundary or degenerate) if crossingindex == -1: return (tmin + tmax) / 2.0 # 2. Calculate subdivision parameter tsub at the intersection v1 = p[crossingindex] - targetvalue v2 = p[crossingindex+1] - targetvalue denom = v1 - v2 tsub = v1 / denom if abs(denom) > 1e-12 else 0.5 # 3. Perform de Casteljau subdivision at tsub # Compute Left Polygon PL (for interval [0, tsub]) left[0] = p[0] for j in range(1, degree + 1): left[j] = left[j-1] (1.0 - tsub) + p[j] tsub # Compute Right Polygon PR (for interval [tsub, 1]) right[degree] = p[degree] for j in range(degree - 1, -1, -1): right[j] = right[j+1] tsub + p[j] (1.0 - tsub) # 4. Determine which side contains the root # Check sign change in the left polygon relative to target valleftstart = left[0] - targetvalue valleftend = left[degree] - targetvalue # Value at tsub if valleftstart valleftend <= 0: # Root is in the left polygon for j in range(degree + 1): p[j] = left[j] tmax = tsub else: # Root is in the right polygon for j in range(degree + 1): p[j] = right[j] tmin = tsub # Return the midpoint of the final interval return (tmin + tmax) / 2.0 Parameters: maxiterations: 3 to 7, depending on the interpolation type. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: CUDA Divergence: Combined isolation methods using Regula Falsi suffer from diverging branches on CUDA architectures, whereas LR81 itself remains well-suited for GPU execution. Precision: Not given in the sources. Boundaries: Not given in the sources. Multiple Roots: Not given in the sources. A root finding algorithm based on knot insertion. It has linear convergence speed and linear complexity per step. It requires index operations and memory usage grows with every iteration step, limiting the maximum number of iterations. For degree 9 (tri-cubic), it has an execution time of 1.0 (relative), MSE 0.034, and max error 0.85. The MR07 knot insertion variant is more than 10 times slower than LR81. A root finding method using Regula Falsi combined with De Casteljau subdivision for root isolation. Although the second phase (Regula Falsi) outperforms LR81 when a root is isolated, the isolation step is not well suited for CUDA due to diverging branches. Time Complexity: Quadratic complexity per step due to the de Casteljau algorithm. Convergence: Quadratic convergence speed. Memory Complexity: Constant memory usage. It can be implemented without index operations. Performance: For degree 9 (tri-cubic), execution time is 0.076 (relative to worst result 1.0), MSE 0.003, max error 0.66. It is more than 10 times faster than the MR07 (knot insertion) algorithm. Strengths: Fast, constant memory, no index operations, suitable for GPU (CUDA). Limitations: Requires a fixed number of iterations (3-7) chosen based on interpolation type; combined isolation methods suffer from CUDA branch divergence. The method is based on the idea of subdividing the control polygon using the de Casteljau algorithm at the intersection of the control polygon with the zero axis. It is referenced as [LR81] in the literature. It is used in volume rendering for finding the first intersection of a viewing ray with an isosurface defined by trivariate polynomials in Bernstein form. name: Recursive Short-Stack Bézier Clipping
head: Modified Bézier Clipping, Optimized Bézier Clipping
body: Recursive Short-Stack Bézier Clipping is a GPU-optimized algorithm for finding the intersection of a ray with a Bézier curve or surface parameterized as a curve in the clipping dimension. It solves the problem of efficiently locating roots of a polynomial function defined by Bézier control points while minimizing register usage and avoiding expensive convex hull intersection tests. It distinguishes itself from standard iterative Bézier Clipping by using a fixed-size stack to limit recursion depth and by aggressively splitting the control polygon when sign changes exceed two, thereby reducing the number of expensive geometric tests required. Inputs: A set of Bézier control points P0, P1, \dots, Pn defining the curve segment. A convergence threshold \epsilon (typically 10^{-4}). A maximum stack size S{\text{max}} (typically 3). Outputs: The parameter t \in [0, 1] where the curve intersects the axis (zero-crossing), or an indication that no intersection exists within the segment. Data Structures: Stack: A fixed-size array of control point sets with capacity S{\text{max}}. The stack stores sub-segments of the control polygon that require further processing. Control Points: Represented as scalar values along the axis of interest (e.g., signed distance from the ray to the surface, or polynomial value). Algorithm Steps: 1. Count the number of sign changes k in the sequence of control point values along the axis. 2. If k = 0, the convex hull does not intersect the axis; discard the segment and do not solve. 3. If k > 2, split the control polygon into two halves beforehand; push both resulting sub-segments onto the stack. 4. If k = 1, perform the relatively expensive intersection test between the convex hull and the axis to find the root. 5. Push control points onto the stack only after ensuring their convex hull intersects the axis. 6. Repeat until the stack is empty or a root is found within \epsilon. Formulas: Sign Change Count: For a sequence v0, v1, \dots, vn, the number of sign changes is the count of indices i such that vi \cdot v{i+1} < 0. Subdivision (de Casteljau): To split a Bézier curve at parameter t, the new control points Qi are computed recursively: Qi^{(0)} = Pi, \quad Qi^{(r)} = (1-t)Qi^{(r-1)} + tQ{i+1}^{(r-1)} The left sub-curve control points are the first elements of each iteration level, and the right sub-curve control points are the last elements of each iteration level. Convergence: The segment width is measured as \max(P) - \min(P). Iteration stops when width \le \epsilon. Parameters: Convergence threshold: 10^{-4}. Stack size: 3. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision: Floating-point precision errors may cause sign changes to be detected incorrectly near zero. Robust handling of zero values (e.g., treating them as positive or skipping) is required. Degenerate Input: If all control points are zero, the curve lies on the axis. The algorithm should handle this by returning the midpoint or a valid range. Stack Overflow: The fixed stack size limits recursion depth. The method assumes a stack size of 3 is sufficient for typical cases. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def recursiveshortstackbezierclipping(controlpoints, epsilon=1e-4, stacksize=3): """ Finds the root of a Bézier curve defined by controlpoints. controlpoints: list of scalar values representing control points along the axis. epsilon: convergence threshold. stacksize: maximum size of the stack. Returns: t (float) or None if no intersection found. """ stack = [controlpoints] while stack: currentpoints = stack.pop() n = len(currentpoints) - 1 # Count sign changes signchanges = 0 for i in range(n): if currentpoints[i] currentpoints[i+1] < 0: signchanges += 1 if signchanges == 0: # No intersection continue elif signchanges > 2: # Split the polygon into two halves beforehand leftpoints, rightpoints = decasteljausubdivide(currentpoints, 0.5) if len(stack) < stacksize: stack.append(leftpoints) stack.append(rightpoints) elif signchanges == 1: # Perform expensive intersection test between convex hull and axis t = convexhullaxisintersection(currentpoints) if t is not None: # Check convergence width = max(currentpoints) - min(currentpoints) if width <= epsilon: return t else: # Split at t and push sub-segments leftpoints, rightpoints = decasteljausubdivide(currentpoints, t) if len(stack) < stacksize: stack.append(leftpoints) stack.append(rightpoints) else: # Fallback for signchanges == 2: split to refine leftpoints, rightpoints = decasteljausubdivide(currentpoints, 0.5) if len(stack) < stacksize: stack.append(leftpoints) stack.append(rightpoints) return None def decasteljausubdivide(points, t): """ Subdivides a Bézier curve at parameter t using de Casteljau's algorithm. Returns (leftcontrolpoints, rightcontrolpoints). """ n = len(points) - 1 left = [] right = [] currentlevel = points[:] for in range(n + 1): left.append(currentlevel[0]) right.append(currentlevel[-1]) nextlevel = [] for j in range(len(currentlevel) - 1): nextlevel.append((1 - t) currentlevel[j] + t currentlevel[j + 1]) currentlevel = nextlevel return left, right def convexhullaxisintersection(points): """ Finds the intersection of the convex hull of the control points with the axis. Since signchanges == 1, exactly one pair of adjacent points straddles zero. Returns t in [0, 1] or None. """ for i in range(len(points) - 1): if points[i] points[i+1] < 0: # Linear interpolation between the straddling control points t = points[i] / (points[i] - points[i+1]) return t return None Time Complexity: The algorithm reduces the number of iterations significantly compared to standard Bézier Clipping. Pabst et al.'s method used 16.4 iterations on average (max 29), while this method uses 2.3 iterations on average (max 8). Memory Complexity: Uses a fixed-size stack of size 3, minimizing register usage on the GPU. Performance: Achieves approximately double the overall speedup of standard Bézier Clipping. Strengths: Efficient on GPU due to fixed stack size and reduced intersection tests. Robust against degenerate cases where the convex hull barely intersects the axis. Limitations: The fixed stack size may require careful handling if the recursion depth exceeds the limit, though the source claims a size of 3 is sufficient. The method is presented in. It builds on the iterative Bézier Clipping method by Pabst et al. [PSS∗06] and the recursive algorithm by Nishita et al. [NSK90]. The key innovation is the modification of the splitting strategy to occur early when sign changes exceed two, addressing a flaw pointed out by Campagna et al. [CSS97] where the convex hull barely intersects the axis. The method was tested on an NVIDIA GeForce 8800 Ultra graphics card using Wyvill et al.'s degree-six polynomial for metaballs [WMW86]. name: Neubauer Iterative Root Finder
head: Neubauer's method
body: The Neubauer Iterative Root Finder is a numerical method for finding the intersection of a ray with an implicit surface within a voxel cell. It determines the parameter t along the ray where the implicit function f(t) equals zero. It sets itself apart from analytical solvers like Schwarze’s cubic solver by using iterative re-parameterization into sub-intervals, which yields single-precision, numerically stable results and is slightly faster in practice. It builds on Isolation and Iterative Root Finding by isolating roots via sign changes within sub-intervals. Inputs: Ray origin \mathbf{o} and direction \mathbf{d}. Implicit surface function f(t), where t is the ray parameter. Initial search interval [t{min}, t{max}] (typically the entry and exit parameters of the current voxel/cell). Convergence tolerance \epsilon and maximum number of iterations N{max}. Outputs: The smallest positive root t^ \in [t{min}, t{max}] such that f(t^) \approx 0. Data Structures: Standard floating-point variables for interval bounds and function evaluations. Steps: 1. Evaluate Endpoints: Compute f{min} = f(t{min}) and f{max} = f(t{max}). 2. Check for Sign Change: If f{min} and f{max} have the same sign, no root is guaranteed in this interval. 3. Iterative Refinement: Initialize t{left} = t{min}, t{right} = t{max}, f{left} = f{min}, f{right} = f{max}. Loop until convergence or N{max}: calculate midpoint t{mid} = \frac{t{left} + t{right}}{2}, evaluate f{mid} = f(t{mid}). If |t{right} - t{left}| < \epsilon or |f{mid}| < \epsilon, return t{mid}. If f{left} \cdot f{mid} < 0, set t{right} = t{mid}, f{right} = f{mid}; else set t{left} = t{mid}, f{left} = f{mid}. 4. Return Result: Return t{mid} or the final interval midpoint. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def neubauerrootfinder(f, tmin, tmax, epsilon=4.0e-3, maxiter=50): """ Finds the root of f(t) in [tmin, tmax] using iterative bisection. f: callable, returns scalar value for parameter t. """ fleft = f(tmin) fright = f(tmax) # Check if a root exists in the interval if fleft fright > 0: return None # No sign change, root not guaranteed # Handle exact zero at boundaries if abs(fleft) < epsilon: return tmin if abs(fright) < epsilon: return tmax tleft = tmin tright = tmax for in range(maxiter): tmid = (tleft + tright) / 2.0 fmid = f(tmid) # Check convergence based on interval width or function value if abs(tright - tleft) < epsilon or abs(fmid) < epsilon: return tmid # Bisection step if fleft fmid < 0: tright = tmid fright = fmid else: tleft = tmid fleft = fmid return (tleft + tright) / 2.0 # Return best estimate if max iter reached Parameters: \epsilon: Convergence threshold. Typical value: 4.0 \cdot 10^{-3}. N{max}: Maximum iterations. Typical value: 50. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: No Sign Change: If the ray grazes the surface or misses it, f(t{min}) and f(t{max}) may have the same sign. Multiple Roots: The basic bisection finds one root; handling multiple intersections requires additional logic not covered by the core method. Precision: Single-precision arithmetic is numerically stable, unlike some analytical cubic solvers which may suffer from catastrophic cancellation. A voxel intersection method using the Newton–Raphson iterative solver. It uses the polynomial split from Marmitt et al. [2004] but replaces repeated linear interpolation with Newton–Raphson iteration. Maximum number of iterations: 50. Epsilon threshold for convergence: \epsilon = 4.0 \cdot 10^{-3}; iteration stops if the difference between two subsequent t-values is less than this value. Handling the case where the line between entry point g{In} and exit point g{Out} intersects the boundary of the volume block, which can cause surface approximation to miss intersections in tessellation. Handling spline degeneracies where the Jacobian J\phi is singular at the entry point g{In}, causing linear systems in root finding and ODE methods to have singular matrices. For Explicit Runge-Kutta methods, clamp the approximated solution values to remain in parameter domain P. Find the new entry point \tilde{p}{In} in parameter domain P using the root finding method with a different starting point for Newton-Raphson iterations: x0 = p{In} + \epsilon \frac{p{Out} - p{In}}{\|p{Out} - p{In}\|{L2}}, with an appropriately chosen \epsilon. For Implicit Euler and Root Finding methods, the Newton-Raphson method fails to converge and repeatedly tries to exit the parameter domain P; detect this behavior and step along the boundary of the parameter domain until the view-ray is within the domain again. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: O(1), requiring only a few scalar variables. Performance: Slightly faster than the analytical Schwarze cubic solver. Strengths: Numerically stable in single-precision arithmetic. Limitations: Not given in the sources. When to Use: Not given in the sources. When Not to Use: Not given in the sources. Proposed by Marmitt et al. [13] (also cited as [75] in), based on the Neubauer iterative root finder. It was used in the context of interactive isosurface ray tracing of large octree volumes. The method was compared against analytical solvers like Schwarze's cubic solver. name: Marmitt's Ray-Cell Intersection
head: Marmitt et al. 03 method, Marmitt et al. root finder, Marmitt Iso-Surface Ray Tracing
body: Marmitt's Ray-Cell Intersection is a method for computing the intersection of a ray with an isosurface defined by trilinear interpolation within a 3D voxel cell. It solves for the first positive root of the cubic polynomial derived from the cell's corner values, using an iterative bisection refinement strategy. It is distinguished from analytical cubic solvers (e.g., Schwarze’s method) by being slightly faster and yielding single-precision, numerically stable results. Inputs: Ray origin \mathbf{o} and direction \mathbf{d} (normalized). Cell corner scalar values v{ijk} for i,j,k \in \{0,1\}. Isosurface threshold T. Ray parameter interval [t{in}, t{out}] representing the ray's overlap with the cell. Outputs: Boolean indicating intersection. If true, the hit parameter t{hit} along the original ray. Data Structures: The scalar field is sampled at the 8 corners of the cell. The implementation in uses the ordering [v{000}, v{100}, v{010}, v{110}, v{001}, v{101}, v{011}, v{111}]. Algorithm Steps: 1. Preconditioning: If t{out} \le t{in}, return false. To avoid numerical precision issues when the ray origin is near a cell boundary, re-center the local coordinate system. Let \mathbf{p}{cell} be the midpoint of the ray's overlap with the cell: \mathbf{p}{cell} = \mathbf{o} + \mathbf{d} \cdot \frac{t{in} + t{out}}{2} Define the local ray direction \mathbf{d}{local} = \mathbf{d} (normalized). Calculate the local parameter bounds relative to \mathbf{p}{cell}: t'{in} = -\frac{t{out} - t{in}}{2} \|\mathbf{d}\| t'{out} = \frac{t{out} - t{in}}{2} \|\mathbf{d}\| Note: Since \mathbf{d} is normalized, \|\mathbf{d}\|=1, simplifying the bounds to \pm \frac{t{out} - t{in}}{2}. 2. Polynomial Construction: Construct the cubic polynomial P(t) such that P(t) = 0 corresponds to the isosurface. The polynomial coefficients are derived from the trilinear interpolation of the corner values along the ray. Let the ray in local cell coordinates be \mathbf{r}(t) = \mathbf{p}{cell} + t \cdot \mathbf{d}{local}. The trilinear interpolation of the scalar field S(\mathbf{r}) can be expressed as a cubic polynomial in t: P(t) = A t^3 + B t^2 + C t + D The coefficients A, B, C, D are computed from the 8 corner values v{ijk} and the geometry of the cell relative to \mathbf{p}{cell}. Specifically, the implementation in computes these via a helper function computepolynomial which maps the cell geometry and values to the cubic coefficients. The constant term is adjusted for the isovalue: D' = D - T So, P(t) = A t^3 + B t^2 + C t + D'. 3. Critical Point Analysis: Evaluate P(t) at the boundaries: f{in} = P(t'{in}) and f{out} = P(t'{out}). Solve for the critical points (roots of the derivative P'(t) = 3At^2 + 2Bt + C = 0). Use the quadratic formula to find roots t{c1}, t{c2}: t{c} = \frac{-2B \pm \sqrt{4B^2 - 12AC}}{6A} Filter roots that lie within [t'{in}, t'{out}]. If a root exists within the interval, evaluate P(t) at that root. If the sign of P(t{root}) differs from the sign of the adjacent boundary (f{in} or f{out}), update the search interval [t'{in}, t'{out}] to exclude the region where the sign does not change, effectively isolating the root. 4. Iterative Bisection Refinement: If sign(f{in}) \neq sign(f{out}), a root exists in [t'{in}, t'{out}]. Perform iterative bisection (linear interpolation refinement) to find the root. While the interval width is above a tolerance or for a fixed number of iterations (e.g., 3 iterations as noted in): t{mid} = \frac{t'{in} + t'{out}}{2} f{mid} = P(t{mid}) If sign(f{mid}) == sign(f{in}), set t'{in} = t{mid}. Else, set t'{out} = t{mid}. Standard bisection logic applies. The source mentions "3 iterations of linear interpolation (bisection)", implying a fixed-depth refinement for performance. 5. Result Mapping: The refined local parameter is t'{hit} = \frac{t'{in} + t'{out}}{2}. The hit position in world space is: \mathbf{p}{hit} = \mathbf{p}{cell} + t'{hit} \cdot \mathbf{d}{local} The final ray parameter t{hit} is: t{hit} = \|\mathbf{p}{hit} - \mathbf{o}\| Since \mathbf{d} is normalized and points in the direction of the ray, and t'{hit} is relative to the midpoint, the distance calculation holds. More precisely, t{hit} = \frac{t{in} + t{out}}{2} + t'{hit} if \mathbf{d} is normalized. The source uses length(hitp - rayorg) / length(raydir). Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def marmittraycellintersection(rayorg, raydir, cellcorners, isovalue, tin, tout): """ rayorg: float3, ray origin raydir: float3, ray direction (assumed normalized) cellcorners: array<f32, 8>, corner values in order [v000, v100, v010, v110, v001, v101, v011, v111] isovalue: f32 tin: f32, entry parameter tout: f32, exit parameter Returns: (hit: bool, thit: f32) """ if tout <= tin: return (False, 0.0) # 1. Preconditioning: Center at midpoint tmid = (tin + tout) / 2.0 cellp = rayorg + raydir tmid dlocal = raydir # Already normalized # Local bounds relative to midpoint tprimein = -(tout - tin) / 2.0 tprimeout = (tout - tin) / 2.0 # 2. Polynomial Construction # Compute coefficients A, B, C, D for P(t) = At^3 + Bt^2 + Ct + D # where P(t) represents the scalar field value along the ray relative to cellp poly = computetrilinearpolynomial(cellp, dlocal, cellcorners) # Adjust constant term for isovalue poly.D -= isovalue # Helper to evaluate polynomial def evalpoly(t): return poly.A t3 + poly.B t2 + poly.C t + poly.D fin = evalpoly(tprimein) fout = evalpoly(tprimeout) # 3. Critical Point Analysis # Solve derivative 3At^2 + 2Bt + C = 0 roots = solvequadratic(3.0 poly.A, 2.0 poly.B, poly.C) # Filter roots within [tprimein, tprimeout] validroots = [r for r in roots if tprimein <= r <= tprimeout] # Update bounds if critical points indicate sign changes for r in validroots: fr = evalpoly(r) if sign(fr) == sign(fin): tprimein = r fin = fr else: tprimeout = r fout = fr # 4. Iterative Bisection Refinement # Check if a root exists if sign(fin) != sign(fout): # Perform fixed iterations of bisection for in range(3): tmidprime = (tprimein + tprimeout) / 2.0 fmid = evalpoly(tmidprime) if sign(fmid) == sign(fin): tprimein = tmidprime fin = fmid else: tprimeout = tmidprime fout = fmid tprimehit = (tprimein + tprimeout) / 2.0 hitp = cellp + dlocal tprimehit thit = length(hitp - rayorg) # Assuming raydir is normalized return (True, thit) return (False, 0.0) def computetrilinearpolynomial(cellp, d, corners): """ Computes the cubic polynomial coefficients for the trilinear field along the ray passing through cellp with direction d. Assumes a unit cell aligned with axes, with corner v000 at cellp - 0.5dcell? Note: The exact mapping of cellp to the trilinear basis depends on the coordinate system. In, cellp is the midpoint of the ray overlap, and the polynomial is computed relative to the cell geometry. """ # This is a placeholder for the specific coefficient calculation. # The source uses a function computepolynomial # which takes cellp, cellraydir, v000, and values. # It maps the cell corners to the polynomial basis. # For implementation, one must map the 8 corners to the trilinear basis # functions evaluated along the ray. pass def solvequadratic(a, b, c): """Solves ax^2 + bx + c = 0. Returns array of roots.""" if a == 0: if b == 0: return [] return [-c / b] disc = b2 - 4ac if disc < 0: return [] sqrtdisc = sqrt(disc) r1 = (-b + sqrtdisc) / (2a) r2 = (-b - sqrtdisc) / (2a) return [r1, r2] Parameters: isovalue: The scalar threshold for the isosurface. deltastep: Step size for numerical gradient computation, typically 0.005. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Cell Boundaries: Numerical issues arise when the ray origin is near the edge of a cell. The method mitigates this by setting the local cell position to the midpoint of the ray's overlap with the cell. Gradient Artifacts: When computing normals, clamping in the gradient computation can produce artifacts at cell boundaries. Reducing deltastep reduces these artifacts but may make the surface appear bumpier due to less smooth normals. Sign Changes: The algorithm relies on detecting sign changes. If the isovalue is exactly equal to a corner value or a critical point, special handling (e.g., epsilon comparison) is required. Time Complexity: The polynomial evaluation and bisection are constant time per cell, O(1). The bisection is fixed to a small number of iterations (e.g., 3). Memory Complexity: O(1) auxiliary memory per ray-cell intersection. Performance: It is slightly faster than analytical cubic solvers like Schwarze’s method. Precision: Yields single-precision, numerically stable results. Strengths: Suitable for real-time rendering (e.g., WebGPU). Limitations: Approximate due to fixed bisection iterations; may miss roots if the function is highly oscillatory within the cell (though trilinear interpolation is generally well-behaved). Origin: Proposed by Marmitt et al. in 2003/2004. The method is described in "Fast and Accurate Ray-Voxel Intersection Techniques for Iso-Surface Ray Tracing". History: It is often compared to Parker et al.'s use of Schwarze’s cubic solver. Usage: Used in WebGPU implicit isosurface raycasters. name: Fast Ray-Surface Intersection
head: Fast Intersection, Linear Interpolation Approximation for Ray-Surface Intersection
body: Fast Ray-Surface Intersection is an approximate method for determining the intersection point of a ray with an iso-surface within a volume rendering cell, trading geometric accuracy for computational speed. It solves the problem of finding the first-hit surface location without the high cost of inverting trilinear interpolation. Unlike exact intersection methods which compute all roots of the cubic polynomial derived from trilinear interpolation, this method subdivides the ray segment within the cell and uses linear interpolation to estimate the hit point, producing visually indistinguishable results in final renderings while being significantly faster. Inputs: Ray segment parameters: entry point R(t{in}) and exit point R(t{out}) of the ray within the current voxel/cell. Iso-value threshold \rho{iso}. Density field \rho(x,y,z), accessible via trilinear interpolation at arbitrary points. Outputs: Approximate intersection parameter t{hit} along the ray. Boolean flag indicating whether an intersection was found. Data Structures: Fields, sizes, and bit packing: Not given in the sources. The method operates on the scalar density values sampled at specific points along the ray. No complex data structures are required beyond the volume grid and the ray parameters. Steps: 1. Subdivision: Divide the complete path of the ray through the surface cell into two parts of equal length. Let the midpoint parameter be t{mid} = \frac{t{in} + t{out}}{2}. The two sub-segments are [t{in}, t{mid}] and [t{mid}, t{out}]. 2. Sampling: Calculate the density values at the end points of each part of the path. Specifically, evaluate \rho(t{in}), \rho(t{mid}), and \rho(t{out}). 3. Intersection Check: Determine if any iso-surface is intersected by the corresponding part of the ray based on the density values. An intersection exists in a segment [ta, tb] if the iso-value \rho{iso} lies between the density values at the endpoints. Mathematically, for a segment with endpoints ta and tb, an intersection is indicated if: (\rho(ta) - \rho{iso}) \cdot (\rho(tb) - \rho{iso}) \le 0. 4. Refinement: If an intersection exists, find an approximation of the intersection point by linear interpolation. If the intersection is in [t{in}, t{mid}], compute t{hit} based on \rho(t{in}) and \rho(t{mid}). If it is in [t{mid}, t{out}], compute t{hit} based on \rho(t{mid}) and \rho(t{out}). The linear interpolation formula is: t{hit} = ta + (\rho{iso} - \rho(ta)) \frac{tb - ta}{\rho(tb) - \rho(ta)} 5. Termination: Compute the color value and assign it to the pixel. If no intersection exists for a part, continue voxel traversal. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def fastraysurfaceintersection(tin, tout, rhoiso, sampledensity): """ Approximates ray-surface intersection by subdividing the ray segment and using linear interpolation. Args: tin (float): t parameter at ray entry into the cell. tout (float): t parameter at ray exit from the cell. rhoiso (float): The density threshold for the iso-surface. sampledensity (callable): Function that returns density at a given t along the ray, i.e., sampledensity(t). Returns: float or None: The approximate t value of the intersection, or None if not found. """ # Step 1: Divide the path into two equal parts tmid = (tin + tout) / 2.0 # Step 2: Calculate density values at endpoints rhoin = sampledensity(tin) rhomid = sampledensity(tmid) rhoout = sampledensity(tout) # Helper for linear interpolation of t given two densities and their t values def linearinterpolate(t1, rho1, t2, rho2, targetrho): # Avoid division by zero if abs(rho1 - rho2) < 1e-9: return (t1 + t2) / 2.0 # Linear interpolation formula: t = t1 + (target - rho1) (t2 - t1) / (rho2 - rho1) return t1 + (targetrho - rho1) (t2 - t1) / (rho2 - rho1) # Step 3 & 4: Check first half [tin, tmid] if (rhoin - rhoiso) (rhomid - rhoiso) <= 0: thit = linearinterpolate(tin, rhoin, tmid, rhomid, rhoiso) return thit # Check second half [tmid, tout] if (rhomid - rhoiso) (rhoout - rhoiso) <= 0: thit = linearinterpolate(tmid, rhomid, tout, rhoout, rhoiso) return thit # Step 5: No intersection found in either part return None Parameters: Subdivision count: Fixed at 2 (one midpoint). Interpolation method: Linear. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision: Linear interpolation assumes the density function is linear within the sub-segment. The method produces visible differences in some pixels compared to exact intersection, but these are not visible in the final visualization results. Boundaries: If the ray grazes the iso-surface exactly at a sample point, the product term becomes zero, correctly identifying an intersection. Degenerate Input: If the density values at the endpoints are identical and equal to the iso-value, the interpolation denominator is zero. A simplistic approximate intersection method that assumes an intersection for every voxel where the iso-value is within the range of data values at the vertices. The intersection point is set to the midpoint between the ray's entry point (t{in}) and exit point (t{out}). This method is fast but leads to blocky artifacts of the size of voxels, so it is typically used only as a reference for performance comparisons rather than in production. Time and Memory Complexity: Time complexity is O(1) per cell, requiring only 3 density samples and basic arithmetic operations. Memory complexity is O(1), requiring no additional storage beyond local variables. Measured Performance: The method is significantly faster than exact intersection methods which invert trilinear interpolation. Visual comparison shows that while there are pixel-level differences between fast and exact intersection, these differences are not visible in the final visualization results. Strengths and Limitations: Strengths: High speed, low computational overhead, visually acceptable results for many applications. Limitations: Lower geometric accuracy compared to exact methods; potential for small artifacts in high-frequency density regions. When to Use: Use when rendering speed is critical and the visual difference between exact and approximate intersection is imperceptible in the final image. Avoid when precise geometric accuracy is required, such as in scientific visualization where exact surface location is critical for measurement. The Fast Ray-Surface Intersection method was introduced as a faster alternative to exact ray-surface intersection techniques in the context of cell-based first-hit ray casting. Exact methods, such as those by Lin et al. and Parker et al., invert trilinear interpolation to find all points assigned a specific density value, which is computationally expensive. The fast intersection method trades this accuracy for speed by using linear interpolation on subdivided paths. It is part of the broader family of approximate ray-surface intersection techniques used in volume rendering to optimize performance. (PDF) Cell-Based First-Hit Ray Casting - ResearchGate, https://www.researchgate.net/publication/2521319Cell-BasedFirst-HitRayCasting, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial) PDF Fast and Accurate Ray-Voxel Intersection Techniques for Iso-Surface Ray..., https://www.sci.utah.edu/~wald/Publications/2004/iso/IsoIsecVMV2004.pdf, fetched 2026-10-29 (unofficial)

name: Secant Method for Surface Depth Refinement
head: Linear Interpolation Root Finding for SDF, Secant Refinement
body: The Secant Method for Surface Depth Refinement is an iterative root-finding algorithm used to refine the depth value d along a ray where a signed distance function or occupancy logit crosses a specific threshold. It solves the problem of locating the precise zero-crossing of a scalar field by using linear interpolation between two bracketing points to estimate the next candidate point. Inputs: Ray origin ray0 (3D vector). Ray direction ray\direction (normalized 3D vector). Initial bracketing depths d{low} and d{high} (scalars or vectors) such that the function values f{low} and f{high} have opposite signs. A scalar field evaluation function decoder(p, c, only\occupancy=True) that returns occupancy logits or SDF values at point p given camera parameters c. A threshold logit\tau (scalar). Number of refinement iterations n{secant\steps} (integer). Outputs: Refined depth d{pred} (scalar or vector) representing the estimated intersection point. Data Structures: Vectors d{low}, d{high}, f{low}, f{high}, d{pred} of size N (where N is the number of rays processed in parallel). Boolean mask ind{low} of size N identifying rays where the current prediction fell below the threshold. Steps: 1. Initialization: Compute the initial prediction d{pred} using linear interpolation between the initial bracketing points: d{pred} = - f{low} \cdot \frac{d{high} - d{low}}{f{high} - f{low}} + d{low} 2. Iteration Loop: For i from 0 to n{secant\steps} - 1: a. Sample Point: Compute the 3D position p{mid} for each ray: p{mid} = ray0 + d{pred} \cdot ray\direction b. Evaluate Field: Evaluate the scalar field at p{mid} without tracking gradients: f{mid} = decoder(p{mid}, c, only\occupancy=True) - logit\tau c. Identify Bracketing Side: Determine indices where the function value is negative: ind{low} = (f{mid} < 0) d. Update Lower Bracket: For all indices in ind{low}, update the lower bound: d{low}[ind{low}] = d{pred}[ind{low}] f{low}[ind{low}] = f{mid}[ind{low}] e. Update Upper Bracket: For all indices where f{mid} \ge 0 (i.e., ind{low} is false): d{high}[ind{low} == 0] = d{pred}[ind{low} == 0] f{high}[ind{low} == 0] = f{mid}[ind{low} == 0] f. Recalculate Prediction: Update d{pred} using the new bracketing values: d{pred} = - f{low} \cdot \frac{d{high} - d{low}}{f{high} - f{low}} + d{low} 3. Return: The final d{pred} is the refined depth. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def secantrefine(ray0, raydirection, dlow, dhigh, flow, fhigh, decoder, c, logittau, nsecantsteps): """ Refine surface depth using the Secant Method. Args: ray0: Array of shape (N, 3), ray origins. raydirection: Array of shape (N, 3), normalized ray directions. dlow: Array of shape (N,), initial lower depth bounds. dhigh: Array of shape (N,), initial upper depth bounds. flow: Array of shape (N,), function values at dlow. fhigh: Array of shape (N,), function values at dhigh. decoder: Function that takes (point, cameraparams, onlyoccupancy) and returns logits. c: Camera parameters. logittau: Threshold for zero-crossing. nsecantsteps: Number of iterations. Returns: dpred: Array of shape (N,), refined depths. """ # Step 1: Initialize prediction denom = fhigh - flow # Guard against division by zero: if denominator is near zero, fallback to midpoint safedenom = where(abs(denom) > 1e-8, denom, oneslike(denom)) dpred = - flow ((dhigh - dlow) / safedenom) + dlow for in range(nsecantsteps): # Step 2a: Compute 3D point pmid = ray0 + dpred[:, None] raydirection # Step 2b: Evaluate function without gradient tracking fmid = decoder(pmid, c, onlyoccupancy=True) - logittau # Step 2c: Identify indices where fmid < 0 indlow = fmid < 0 # Step 2d: Update lower bracket dlow[indlow] = dpred[indlow] flow[indlow] = fmid[indlow] # Step 2e: Update upper bracket (where fmid >= 0) maskhigh = ~indlow dhigh[maskhigh] = dpred[maskhigh] fhigh[maskhigh] = fmid[maskhigh] # Step 2f: Recalculate prediction denom = fhigh - flow safedenom = where(abs(denom) > 1e-8, denom, oneslike(denom)) dpred = - flow ((dhigh - dlow) / safedenom) + dlow return dpred Parameters: n{secant\steps}: Integer specifying the number of refinement iterations. Typical value: 8. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Division by Zero: If f{high} == f{low}, the denominator in the secant formula becomes zero. The implementation must handle this, typically by falling back to the midpoint or clamping the denominator. Non-Bracketing Inputs: The method assumes f{low} and f{high} have opposite signs. If the initial guess does not bracket the root, the method may diverge or converge to an incorrect root. A procedure to detect surface points along rays by evaluating a neural decoder at proposal points, identifying sign changes in occupancy logits, and refining the depth using a root-finding method. It distinguishes itself from its siblings by combining coarse uniform sampling with a specific sign-change detection logic to locate the first entry into the volume, followed by secant refinement. It builds on Secant Method for Surface Depth Refinement. Parabolic root-finding with gradients is an iterative refinement technique that estimates the zero-crossing of a scalar field F(x) along a line segment by fitting a parabola to the function values and directional derivatives (gradients) at the endpoints. It solves for the root of this parabola to determine the intersection depth. It sets itself apart from its sibling, the Secant Method for Surface Depth Refinement, by utilizing gradient information to model curvature, thereby avoiding the need for an additional function evaluation to estimate the second derivative, while offering higher accuracy for non-linear fields. A root-finding algorithm combining linear interpolation and the midpoint algorithm. It finds the exact intersection point even if the field function is not continuous. Implementation is in IsoMesher::intersectxaxis(), IsoMesher::intersectyaxis(), and IsoMesher::intersectzaxis(). The algorithm used is determined by the preprocessor symbol FALSEPOSITION. It is no worse than the midpoint algorithm in terms of iterations and usually better, making it the preferred choice for finding exact intersection points. Methods to find the grazing point (where the ray is tangent to the SDF surface) along a ray segment [tmin, tmax] using secant or bisection iteration on the directional derivative. Secant Method: Initialize L = ray(tmin), R = ray(tmax). Loop up to utils.NUMGRZ iterations: compute directional derivatives dL = dirderiv(L, d), dR = dirderiv(R, d). Compute midpoint M = R - dR (R - L) / (dR - dL). Compute dM = dirderiv(M, d). Update L[dM < 0] = M, R[dM > 0] = M. Return dr.detach(L). Bisection Method: Initialize L = ray(tmin), R = ray(tmax). Loop up to utils.NUMGRZ iterations: compute M = (L + R) / 2. Compute dM = dirderiv(M, d). Update L[dM < 0] = M[dM < 0], R[dM > 0] = M[dM > 0]. Return dr.detach(L). Selection: Method is selected based on utils.GRZMODE: 'secant' or 'bisection'. Parameter: utils.GRZMODE: String specifying grazing point method, 'secant' or 'bisection'. Pitfall: Gradient computation is suspended during grazing point search using dr.suspendgrad() to prevent differentiability issues in the iterative root-finding process. Refines the rough intersection position obtained from ray marching by stepping along the ray direction by the SDF value at the current position, effectively performing one Newton-Raphson step or gradient descent step for surface finding. Step 1: Compute the SDF value at the rough intersection position using trilinear interpolation. Step 2: Update the intersection position: P{new} = P{rough} + d \cdot SDF(P{rough}), where d is the ray direction. Step 3: For pixels with no intersection (mask=0), preserve the original rough position or handle appropriately. The code adds (1-mask) which implies adding 1 if no intersection, but this seems like a placeholder or specific handling for non-intersecting rays. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Performance: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Not given in the sources. Limitations: Not given in the sources. When to Use: Not given in the sources. When Not to Use: Not given in the sources. The Secant Method is a classic root-finding algorithm that approximates the derivative using finite differences. In the context of volume rendering and neural implicit surfaces, it is used to refine the depth of surface intersections detected by coarse sampling. The specific implementation described here is found in the autonomousvision/differentiablevolumetricrendering repository. The False Position variant is discussed in the context of isosurface extraction in IsoMesher. The grazing point refinement using secant methods is detailed in zichenwang01/relaxed-boundary. The Newton-Raphson approach for SDF refinement is presented in YueJiang-nj/CVPR2020-SDFDiff. autonomousvision/differentiablevolumetricrendering, https://github.com/autonomousvision/differentiablevolumetricrendering, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial) http://www.oocities.org/tzukkers/isosurf/isosurfaces.html, http://www.oocities.org/tzukkers/isosurf/isosurfaces.html, fetched 2026-10-30 (unofficial) zichenwang01/relaxed-boundary, https://github.com/zichenwang01/relaxed-boundary, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial) YueJiang-nj/CVPR2020-SDFDiff, https://github.com/YueJiang-nj/CVPR2020-SDFDiff, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial)

name: Ray Marching with Secant Refinement
body:
A procedure to detect surface points along rays by evaluating a neural decoder at proposal points, identifying sign changes in occupancy logits, and refining the depth using a root-finding method. It distinguishes itself from its siblings by combining coarse uniform sampling with a specific sign-change detection logic to locate the first entry into the volume, followed by secant refinement. It builds on Secant Method for Surface Depth Refinement. Inputs: ray0: Origin of rays, shape (B, N, 1, 3). raydirection: Direction of rays, shape (B, N, 1, 3). depthrange: Tuple (d{min}, d{max}) defining the sampling interval. nsteps: Tuple (n{min}, n{max}) defining the range for sampling the number of steps. maxpoints: Integer, maximum number of points loaded to GPU memory per batch to prevent OOM. checkcubeintersection: Boolean, whether to intersect with a unit cube. decoder: Neural network function decoder(p, c) returning occupancy logits. c: Latent codes or context, shape (B, N, 1, C). tau: Probability threshold for occupancy. Outputs: dpred: Refined depth values, shape (B, N, 1, 1). ptpred: 3D points on the surface, shape (B, N, 1, 3). Data Structures: dproposal: Linearly spaced depth proposals, shape (B, N, n{steps}, 1). val: Occupancy logits minus logit threshold, shape (B, N, n{steps}, 1). signmatrix: Matrix indicating sign changes, shape (B, N, n{steps}). costmatrix: Matrix for finding the first sign change, shape (B, N, n{steps}). Steps: 1. Threshold Conversion: Convert probability threshold 	au to logit threshold: logit	au = 	ext{get\logits rom\prob}(	au). getlogitsfromprob is the inverse sigmoid function: \log( rac{	au}{1-	au}). 2. Step Sampling: Sample number of steps n{steps} uniformly from integer range [n{steps}[0], n{steps}[1]]. 3. Proposal Generation: Create linearly spaced depth proposals d{proposal} from depthange[0] to depthange[1] with n{steps} points, shaped (B, N, n{steps}, 1). 4. Cube Intersection (Optional): If checkcubeintersection is true, compute intersection with unit cube and replace d{proposal} values inside the cube with cube-intersection depths. Exact intersection logic depends on the renderer's bounding volume implementation. 5. Point Evaluation: Compute 3D proposal points: p{proposal} = ray0 + ray\direction \cdot d{proposal}. Evaluate decoder at all proposal points in parallel, splitting into chunks of size max\points / batch\size to manage GPU memory. Compute: val = decoder(p, c, only\occupancy=True) - logit	au. Shape of val is (B, N, n{steps}, 1). 6. Initial Occupancy Mask: Create mask for rays where the first point is not occupied: mask\0
ot\occupied = val[:,:, 0] < 0. 7. Sign Change Detection: Compute sign change matrix: sign\matrix = [	ext{sign}(val[:,:,:-1] \cdot val[:,:, 1:]), 1]. The last element is padded with 1 to maintain shape. Compute cost matrix: cost\matrix = sign\matrix \cdot [n{steps}, n{steps}-1,..., 1]. This weights earlier indices higher to find the first sign change. 8. Index Identification: Find the first sign change index: (values, indices) = 	ext{argmin}(cost\matrix). Identify valid sign changes: mask\sign\change = values < 0. 9. Transition Verification: Identify negative-to-positive transitions: mask
eg	o\pos = val[batch\indices, point\indices, indices] < 0. batchindices and pointindices are the batch and point indices corresponding to the argmin result. 10. Final Mask: Combine masks for valid depth detection: mask = mask\sign\change \land mask
eg	o\pos \land mask\0
ot\occupied. 11. Bracket Extraction: Extract bracketing depths and function values for valid rays: d{low}, f{low} at indices d{high}, f{high} at indices + 1 (clamped to n{steps}-1). 12. Refinement: Apply refinement method (Secant or Bisection) on the masked rays to get d{pred}. See Secant Method for Surface Depth Refinement. 13. Point Reconstruction: Compute final 3D points: pt{pred}[mask] = ray0{masked} + d{pred} \cdot ray\direction{masked}. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import torch def performraymarching(ray0, raydirection, depthrange, nstepsrange, maxpoints, checkcubeintersection, decoder, c, tau): """ ray0: (B, N, 1, 3) or list raydirection: (B, N, 1, 3) or list depthrange: (dmin, dmax) nstepsrange: (nmin, nmax) maxpoints: int decoder: callable c: (B, N, 1, C) or list tau: float """ device = ray0.device if hasattr(ray0, 'device') else torch.device('cpu') ray0 = torch.astensor(ray0, device=device) raydirection = torch.astensor(raydirection, device=device) c = torch.astensor(c, device=device) B, N,, = ray0.shape # 1. Threshold Conversion logittau = torch.log(torch.tensor(tau, device=device) / (1 - tau)) # 2. Step Sampling nsteps = torch.randint(nstepsrange[0], nstepsrange[1] + 1, (1,), device=device).item() # 3. Proposal Generation dproposal = torch.linspace(depthrange[0], depthrange[1], nsteps, device=device) dproposal = dproposal.view(1, 1, nsteps, 1).expand(B, N, nsteps, 1) # 4. Cube Intersection if checkcubeintersection: # Compute intersection with unit cube and replace dproposal values inside the cube. # Implementation depends on specific bounding volume logic. pass # 5. Point Evaluation pproposal = ray0 + raydirection dproposal val = evaluatedecoderchunks(pproposal, c, decoder, maxpoints, logittau) # 6. Initial Occupancy Mask mask0notoccupied = val[:,:, 0, 0] < 0 # 7. Sign Change Detection valprev = val[:,:,:-1, 0] valcurr = val[:,:, 1:, 0] signchanges = torch.sign(valprev valcurr) signmatrix = torch.cat([signchanges, torch.ones(B, N, 1, device=device)], dim=2) weights = torch.arange(nsteps, 0, -1, device=device).float().view(1, 1, nsteps) costmatrix = signmatrix weights # 8. Index Identification values, indices = torch.min(costmatrix, dim=2) masksignchange = values < 0 # 9. Transition Verification batchindices = torch.arange(B, device=device).view(B, 1, 1).expand(B, N, 1) pointindices = torch.arange(N, device=device).view(1, N, 1).expand(B, N, 1) valatindices = val[batchindices, pointindices, indices, 0] masknegtopos = valatindices < 0 # 10. Final Mask mask = masksignchange & masknegtopos & mask0notoccupied # 11. Bracket Extraction dlow = dproposal[batchindices, pointindices, indices, 0] flow = val[batchindices, pointindices, indices, 0] idxhigh = torch.clamp(indices + 1, max=nsteps - 1) dhigh = dproposal[batchindices, pointindices, idxhigh, 0] fhigh = val[batchindices, pointindices, idxhigh, 0] # 12. Refinement dpred = secantrefine(dlow, flow, dhigh, fhigh, mask) # 13. Point Reconstruction ptpred = torch.zeroslike(ray0) ptpred[mask] = ray0[mask] + dpred[mask] raydirection[mask] return dpred, ptpred def evaluatedecoderchunks(pproposal, c, decoder, maxpoints, logittau): B, N, nsteps, = pproposal.shape totalpoints = B N nsteps if totalpoints <= maxpoints: val = decoder(pproposal, c, onlyoccupancy=True) return val - logittau else: numchunks = (totalpoints + maxpoints - 1) // maxpoints chunksize = totalpoints // numchunks valchunks = [] # Tile c along nsteps dimension to match pproposal shape ctiled = c.repeat(1, 1, nsteps, 1) for i in range(numchunks): start = i chunksize end = min((i + 1) chunksize, totalpoints) pchunk = pproposal.view(-1, 3)[start:end] cchunk = ctiled.view(-1, ctiled.shape[-1])[start:end] valchunk = decoder(pchunk, cchunk, onlyoccupancy=True) valchunks.append(valchunk - logittau) val = torch.cat(valchunks, dim=0) return val.view(B, N, nsteps, 1) def secantrefine(dlow, flow, dhigh, fhigh, mask): # Standard secant step denom = fhigh - flow denom = torch.where(denom == 0, torch.oneslike(denom), denom) dnew = dhigh - fhigh (dhigh - dlow) / denom return dnew Parameters: maxpoints: Integer, maximum number of points loaded to GPU memory per batch to prevent OOM. Typical value: 3,500,000. nsteps: Tuple of integers defining the range for sampling the number of evaluation steps. Typical value: [128, 129]. depthrange: Tuple of floats defining the range of possible depth values. Typical value: [0.0, 2.4]. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: No Sign Change: If no sign change is detected, the ray does not intersect the surface within the sampled range. The mask will be false, and no depth is predicted. Occupied Start: If the first point is occupied (val[:,:, 0] \ge 0), the ray is ignored. This assumes the ray starts outside the volume. Division by Zero: In secant refinement, if f{high} \approx f{low}, division by zero can occur. Guard against this by clamping the denominator or falling back to bisection. GPU Memory: Large batches or high n{steps} can exceed GPU memory. Chunking is necessary.
