name: Differentiable Depth Function Forward/Backward Pass
head: DepthFunction.backward, DepthFunction.forward
body: This method implements the forward and backward passes for a differentiable depth prediction module in neural volume rendering. It wraps the ray marching process (specifically Ray Marching with Secant Refinement) within a PyTorch autograd.Function to enable gradient flow from the rendered depth output back to the neural decoder parameters and latent codes. It distinguishes itself by explicitly reconstructing the occupancy gradient along the ray direction to compute the depth sensitivity, allowing end-to-end training of implicit surface representations. Inputs: ray0: Origin of rays, shape (N, 3). raydirection: Unit direction vectors of rays, shape (N, 3). decoder: Neural network module (implicit decoder) taking position and latent code. c: Latent codes for each ray, shape (N, Dc). nsteps: Number of coarse sampling steps. nsecantsteps: Number of secant refinement steps. tau: Temperature parameter for soft thresholding. depthrange: Tuple (d{min}, d{max}) defining the sampling interval. method: String specifying the marching algorithm. checkcubeintersection: Boolean flag for bounding box checks. maxpoints: Maximum number of points to store. gradoutput: Gradient tensor from the loss function w.r.t the forward output, shape (N). Outputs: dpred: Predicted depth values, shape (N). ppred: Predicted 3D positions corresponding to dpred, shape (N, 3). mask: Boolean mask indicating valid depth predictions, shape (N). Data Structures: dpred: Float tensor. Invalid depths are set to \infty or 0 based on specific masks. ppred: Float tensor. Saved for backward pass. mask: Boolean tensor. Tracks validity. Steps: 1. Forward Pass: 1. Call performraymarching(ray0, raydirection, decoder, c, nsteps, nsecantsteps, tau, depthrange, method, checkcubeintersection, maxpoints) to obtain raw depth predictions draw, positions praw, and validity masks. 2. Apply invalid depth handling: If a ray fails to intersect or is invalid (mask == 0), set d{pred}[mask==0] = \infty. If a ray is valid but the surface is not occupied (mask0notoccupied == 0), set d{pred}[mask\0\not\occupied==0] = 0. 3. Save ray0, raydirection, dpred, ppred, and c for the backward pass. 4. Return dpred. 2. Backward Pass: 1. Retrieve saved tensors: ray0, raydirection, dpred, ppred, c. 2. Enable gradient computation for ppred: ppred.requiresgrad(True). 3. Evaluate the decoder's occupancy logit at the predicted positions: fp = \text{decoder}(p{pred}, c, \text{only\occupancy}=\text{True}) Here, fp is the scalar occupancy value (logit) for each point. 4. Compute the gradient of the occupancy w.r.t. the positions: \text{grad\p} = \frac{\partial fp}{\partial p{pred}} Shape: (N, 3). 5. Compute the directional derivative along the ray direction (dot product): \text{grad\p\dot\v} = \sum{dim=1}^{3} (\text{grad\p}{:, dim} \cdot \text{ray\direction}{:, dim}) Shape: (N). This represents the rate of change of occupancy along the ray. 6. Clamp small gradients to avoid division by zero: \text{grad\p\dot\v}[|\text{grad\p\dot\v}| < \epsilon] = \epsilon where \epsilon = 10^{-3}. 7. Set gradients for invalid masks to 1 to prevent gradient flow into invalid regions: \text{grad\p\dot\v}[mask==0] = 1. 8. Compute the gradient w.r.t the depth output: \text{grad\outputs} = - \frac{\text{grad\output}}{\text{grad\p\dot\v}} \cdot mask Shape: (N). The negative sign arises from the chain rule through the depth-position mapping. 9. Compute gradient w.r.t. latent code c: \text{grad\c} = \frac{\partial fp}{\partial c} Specifically, compute the gradient of fp w.r.t c using gradoutputs as the upstream gradient. 10. Compute gradient w.r.t. decoder parameters \phi: \text{grad\\phi} = \frac{\partial fp}{\partial \phi} Specifically, compute the gradient of fp w.r.t \phi using gradoutputs as the upstream gradient. 11. Return None for ray0, raydirection, decoder, nsteps, etc., and gradc, grad\\phi for the latent code and decoder parameters respectively. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import torch import torch.nn as nn class DepthFunction(torch.autograd.Function): @staticmethod def forward(ctx, ray0, raydirection, decoder, c, nsteps, nsecantsteps, tau, depthrange, method, checkcubeintersection, maxpoints, gradoutput): # 1. Perform Ray Marching (defined in Ray Marching with Secant Refinement) dpred, ppred, mask, mask0notoccupied = performraymarching( ray0, raydirection, decoder, c, nsteps, nsecantsteps, tau, depthrange, method, checkcubeintersection, maxpoints) # 2. Handle Invalid Depths dpred[mask == 0] = float('inf') dpred[mask0notoccupied == 0] = 0.0 # 3. Save for Backward ctx.saveforbackward(ray0, raydirection, dpred, ppred, c) ctx.gradoutput = gradoutput ctx.mask = mask ctx.decoder = decoder return dpred @staticmethod def backward(ctx, gradoutput): ray0, raydirection, dpred, ppred, c = ctx.savedtensors mask = ctx.mask decoder = ctx.decoder # 1. Enable gradients for ppred ppred.requiresgrad(True) # 2. Evaluate Occupancy fp = decoder(ppred, c, onlyoccupancy=True) # 3. Gradient of fp w.r.t ppred gradp = torch.autograd.grad( fp, ppred, gradoutputs=torch.oneslike(fp), creategraph=True, retaingraph=True)[0] # 4. Dot product with ray direction gradpdotv = torch.sum(gradp raydirection, dim=1) # 5. Clamp small gradients epsilon = 1e-3 gradpdotv = torch.where( torch.abs(gradpdotv) < epsilon, torch.fulllike(gradpdotv, epsilon), gradpdotv) # 6. Set invalid mask gradients to 1 gradpdotv[mask == 0] = 1.0 # 7. Compute output gradients (depth gradient) gradfpupstream = - (gradoutput / gradpdotv) mask.float() # 8. Compute gradient w.r.t latent code c gradc = torch.autograd.grad( fp, c, gradoutputs=gradfpupstream, retaingraph=True)[0] # 9. Compute gradient w.r.t decoder parameters phi gradphi = torch.autograd.grad( fp, decoder.parameters(), gradoutputs=gradfpupstream, retaingraph=True) # 10. Return gradients return ( None, None, None, gradc, None, None, None, None, None, None, None, None) Parameters: \epsilon = 10^{-3}: Clamping threshold for gradient stability. Edge Cases: Invalid Rays: Rays that do not intersect the volume or fail to find a surface are masked out. Their depth is set to \infty or 0, and their gradient contribution is nullified or clamped to prevent instability. Zero Gradient: If the occupancy gradient along the ray is near zero (e.g., inside a uniform volume or far from surface), clamping prevents division by zero. A neural network module that predicts a depth distribution for each ray from image features, sampling discrete depth values and probability density function (PDF) values to represent surface geometry. It differs from the standard DepthPredictor by explicitly modeling multiple surfaces and using a distribution sampler to handle the stochastic nature of depth estimation, building on the differentiable forward/backward pass of Differentiable Depth Function Forward/Backward Pass. The DepthPredictor is a PyTorch nn.Module that implements the depth prediction pipeline for differentiable volume rendering. It integrates a distribution sampler with conversion functions to transform raw feature tensors into probabilistic depth estimates and associated opacities. It differs from sibling methods like Monocular Depth Predictor with Distribution Sampling by explicitly handling the unbinding of PDF and offset channels, sampling from the resulting discrete distribution, and computing opacity via a cumulative transmittance formulation. Time Complexity: Dominated by the forward ray marching step, which involves N \times (n{steps} + n{secant\steps}) decoder evaluations. The backward pass requires an additional N decoder evaluations to compute the occupancy gradient and potentially more for the latent code/decoder gradients depending on implementation. Memory Complexity: Stores intermediate positions and gradients for all sampled points. The backward pass requires storing the graph for the decoder evaluation at p{pred}. Strengths: Enables end-to-end training of implicit surfaces by providing gradients through the depth prediction. Handles invalid rays gracefully. Limitations: Sensitive to the clamping parameter \epsilon. Requires the decoder to be differentiable. Performance depends on the efficiency of the underlying ray marching implementation. When to Use: When training neural radiance fields or implicit surface representations where depth supervision is available or desired. When Not to Use: If non-differentiable rendering is sufficient, or if the decoder is not differentiable. This method is part of the differentiable volumetric rendering framework, specifically designed to integrate depth prediction into the training loop. It builds upon the Ray Marching with Secant Refinement method to provide a differentiable interface for depth estimation. The approach allows gradients to flow from the depth loss to the neural decoder, enabling the optimization of implicit surface representations. autonomousvision/differentiablevolumetricrendering, https://github.com/autonomousvision/differentiablevolumetricrendering, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial)

name: Monocular Depth Predictor with Distribution Sampling
head: Depth Prediction via Discrete Distribution Sampling, DepthPredictorMonocular
body: A neural network module that predicts a depth distribution for each ray from image features by discretizing the depth range into buckets, predicting a probability density function (PDF) and intra-bucket offsets, and sampling from this distribution to determine depth values. It differs from the sibling DepthPredictor by explicitly modeling depth uncertainty via a discrete probability distribution over sampled buckets rather than predicting a single deterministic depth value. It is wrapped in a PyTorch Autograd Function to enable gradient flow, building on Differentiable Depth Function Forward/Backward Pass. Inputs: features: Tensor of shape (batch, view, ray, surface, depth, 2) containing projected features, where the last dimension holds raw PDF logits and raw offset logits. near: Tensor of shape (batch, view) specifying the near plane distance. far: Tensor of shape (batch, view) specifying the far plane distance. deterministic: Boolean flag controlling whether sampling is deterministic (argmax) or stochastic. gaussiansperpixel: Integer specifying the number of samples (buckets) to draw from the depth distribution. usetransmittance: Boolean flag determining whether opacity is computed via the transmittance formula or taken directly from the PDF density. Outputs: depth: Tensor of shape (batch, view, ray, surface, sample) containing the predicted absolute depth values. opacity: Tensor of shape (batch, view, ray, surface, sample) containing the predicted opacity values. pdf: Tensor of shape (batch, view, ray, surface, sample) containing the sampled PDF values. Data Structures: The module DepthPredictorMonocular contains: projection: An nn.Sequential module consisting of nn.ReLU() followed by nn.Linear(din, 2 numsamples numsurfaces). topdf: nn.Softmax(dim=-1) hook to normalize raw logits into a valid PDF. tooffset: nn.Sigmoid() hook to normalize raw logits into the range [0, 1]. numsamples: Integer, the number of depth samples (buckets) per surface. numsurfaces: Integer, the number of distinct surfaces to model. Parameters: numsamples: Number of depth samples per surface. Not given in the sources. numsurfaces: Number of distinct surfaces to model. Not given in the sources. gaussiansperpixel: Number of samples to draw. Not given in the sources. Steps: 1. Project input features through self.projection to obtain raw logits of shape (batch, view, ray, surface, depth, 2) where the last dimension corresponds to pdfraw and offsetraw. 2. Rearrange the projected features from shape... (dpt srf c) to c... srf dpt where c=2, separating pdfraw and offsetraw tensors. 3. Apply self.topdf (Softmax) to pdfraw along the last dimension (depth dimension) to obtain normalized PDF values pdf. 4. Apply self.tooffset (Sigmoid) to offsetraw to obtain intra-bucket offsets offset in the range [0, 1]. 5. Sample depth indices and corresponding PDF densities from the distribution using self.sampler.sample(pdf, deterministic, gaussiansperpixel). This returns index (sampled bucket indices) and pdfi (PDF values at sampled indices). 6. Gather the intra-bucket offsets corresponding to the sampled indices: offset = self.sampler.gather(index, offset). 7. Calculate the relative disparity for each sample: relative\disparity = \frac{index + offset}{s} where s is numsamples (the number of buckets). 8. Convert relative disparity to absolute depth using the near and far plane values: depth = relativedisparitytodepth(relativedisparity, near, far). 9. Compute opacity based on the usetransmittance flag: If usetransmittance is true: a. Calculate the cumulative sum of the PDF along the depth dimension: partial = pdf.cumsum(dim=-1). b. Shift the cumulative sum to align with the previous bucket's transmittance: partial = torch.cat((torch.zeroslike(partial[...,:1]), partial[...,:-1]), dim=-1). c. Compute opacity using the PDF and the shifted cumulative sum (approximating transmittance): opacity = \frac{pdf}{1 - partial + 10^{-10}} The epsilon 10^{-10} is added for numerical stability in the denominator. d. Gather the computed opacity values for the sampled indices: opacity = self.sampler.gather(index, opacity). If usetransmittance is false: a. Set opacity directly to the sampled PDF density: opacity = pdfi. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import torch import torch.nn as nn from typing import Tuple class DepthPredictorMonocular(nn.Module): def init(self, din: int, numsamples: int, numsurfaces: int, usetransmittance: bool = True): super().init() self.numsamples = numsamples self.numsurfaces = numsurfaces self.usetransmittance = usetransmittance self.projection = nn.Sequential( nn.ReLU(), nn.Linear(din, 2 numsamples numsurfaces)) self.topdf = nn.Softmax(dim=-1) self.tooffset = nn.Sigmoid() def forward( self, features: torch.Tensor, near: torch.Tensor, far: torch.Tensor, deterministic: bool = False, gaussiansperpixel: int = 1) -> Tuple[torch.Tensor, torch.Tensor, torch.Tensor]: # features: (batch, view, ray, surface, depth, 2) projected = self.projection(features) # projected: (batch, view, ray, surface, depth, 2 numsamples numsurfaces) # Rearrange to (2, batch, view, ray, numsurfaces, depth) B, V, R, S, D, C = projected.shape projected = projected.view(B, V, R, S, D, self.numsurfaces, 2) projected = projected.permute(6, 0, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5) pdfraw = projected[0] offsetraw = projected[1] pdf = self.topdf(pdfraw) offset = self.tooffset(offsetraw) index, pdfi = self.sample(pdf, deterministic, gaussiansperpixel) offset = self.gather(index, offset) relativedisparity = (index + offset) / self.numsamples depth = self.relativedisparitytodepth(relativedisparity, near, far) if self.usetransmittance: partial = pdf.cumsum(dim=-1) partial = torch.cat((torch.zeroslike(partial[...,:1]), partial[...,:-1]), dim=-1) opacityfull = pdf / (1 - partial + 1e-10) opacity = self.gather(index, opacityfull) else: opacity = pdfi return depth, opacity, pdfi def sample(self, pdf: torch.Tensor, deterministic: bool, gaussiansperpixel: int) -> Tuple[torch.Tensor, torch.Tensor]: # pdf shape: (2, batch, view, ray, numsurfaces, numsamples) # Sample over the last dimension if deterministic: index = torch.argmax(pdf, dim=-1) else: index = torch.multinomial(pdf, numsamples=gaussiansperpixel, replacement=True) # Gather PDF values at sampled indices indexexpanded = index.unsqueeze(0).expand(2, index.shape) pdfi = torch.gather(pdf, dim=-1, index=indexexpanded).squeeze(0) return index, pdfi def gather(self, index: torch.Tensor, tensor: torch.Tensor) -> torch.Tensor: # tensor shape: (2, batch, view, ray, numsurfaces, numsamples) # index shape: (batch, view, ray, numsurfaces, gaussiansperpixel) indexexpanded = index.unsqueeze(0).expand(2, index.shape) return torch.gather(tensor, dim=-1, index=indexexpanded).squeeze(0) def relativedisparitytodepth(self, relativedisparity: torch.Tensor, near: torch.Tensor, far: torch.Tensor) -> torch.Tensor: # Standard inverse depth interpolation invnear = 1.0 / near invfar = 1.0 / far invdepth = (1 - relativedisparity) invnear + relativedisparity invfar return 1.0 / invdepth A 3D CNN converts the cost volume Vc into a depth probability volume Vp and a 3D feature volume F{cv}. Vp is used to calculate estimated depth D and confidence interval S. The number of layers L in the depth probability volume typically equals 16. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Provides a probabilistic estimate of depth, allowing for uncertainty quantification and multi-modal surface prediction via numsurfaces. Limitations: Numerical stability must be handled in opacity calculation. When to use: Not given in the sources. When not to use: Not given in the sources. The method originates from the PixelSplat project, which uses monocular depth prediction for novel view synthesis. It was developed to handle the ambiguity in monocular depth estimation by modeling depth as a distribution rather than a point estimate. dcharatan/pixelsplat, https://github.com/dcharatan/pixelsplat, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial) NeRF-SDP: Efficient Generalizable Neural Radiance Field with Scene Depth Perception, https://doi.org/10.1145/3595916.3626380, fetched 2026-10-30

name: Depth Probability Volume Estimation
head: Depth Probability Volume, Vp Estimation, Disparity Probability Volume (DPV) Estimation
body: Depth Probability Volume (DPV) Estimation constructs a 3D representation where each voxel encodes the probability density of surface depth along a ray, derived from multi-view feature consistency. It solves the problem of robust depth estimation in multi-view stereo and novel view synthesis by converting a cost volume into a probabilistic distribution, enabling the calculation of expected depth and confidence intervals. It differs from standard cost volume aggregation by explicitly modeling the uncertainty of depth hypotheses via a 3D CNN, allowing for differentiable depth extraction. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A set of N feature volumes \{Vi^f\} extracted from N source views, and camera parameters (intrinsics, extrinsics). Output: A Depth Probability Volume Vp of dimensions H \times W \times L, where H, W are spatial dimensions and L is the number of depth layers. Optionally, an initial disparity map D{init}. Data Structures: Cost Volume (Vc): A 3D tensor where each element represents the aggregated feature distance at a specific spatial location and depth hypothesis. Depth Probability Volume (Vp): A 3D tensor Vp(x, y, j) where j \in \{1, \dots, L\} indexes the depth layer. The values represent probabilities pj. Depth Layers: L discrete depth planes (or disparity planes) spanning the scene's depth range [t{near}, t{far}]. Parameters: L: Number of depth layers. Typical value: 16. N: Number of source views. t{near}, t{far}: Near and far clipping planes defining the depth range. Steps: 1. Feature Extraction: Extract 2D feature volumes Vi^f for each source view i \in \{1, \dots, N\}. 2. Cost Volume Construction: Compute the cost volume Vc by aggregating feature distances across views. For each spatial location (x,y) and depth hypothesis, calculate the squared element-wise difference between the reference view feature and the mean of other views' features: Vc = \sum{i=1}^{N} (Vi^f - \bar{V}^f)^2 where \bar{V}^f is the mean feature volume of N views. 3. 3D CNN Processing: Pass Vc through a 3D Convolutional Neural Network (3D CNN) to produce the Depth Probability Volume Vp and a 3D feature volume F{cv}. The 3D CNN learns to map cost values to probability distributions. 4. Depth and Confidence Calculation: Compute the expected depth d and confidence interval (standard deviation) s for each pixel by taking the expectation and variance over the probability distribution Vp: d = \sum{j=1}^{L} pj dj s = \sqrt{\sum{j=1}^{L} pj (dj - d)^2} where pj is the probability at layer j in Vp, and dj is the depth value at layer j. 5. Initial Disparity Map (Optional): Calculate an initial disparity map D{init} from the DPV Vt (or Vp) using standard peak-picking or integration methods. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Scale Consistency: DPVs from different captures have varying disparity intervals due to different focal lengths and baselines. A Scale-Consistent Volume Rescaling (SCVR) algorithm is required to realign DPVs using reliable 3D anchors (e.g., from COLMAP) before fusion. Precision: Sub-pixel level parallax estimation requires efficient algorithms to handle high-precision disparity values. Depth Range: The depth range [t{near}, t{far}] must be carefully set; incorrect bounds lead to truncated depth distributions. Time Complexity: Dominated by the 3D CNN inference on the cost volume. The cost volume construction is O(N \cdot H \cdot W \cdot L). The 3D CNN complexity depends on its architecture but is generally O(H \cdot W \cdot L \cdot C^2) where C is the feature dimension. Memory Complexity: Requires storing the cost volume Vc and the DPV Vp. Memory usage is O(H \cdot W \cdot L \cdot C), where C is the feature channel size. Performance: On LLFF datasets, methods using DPV (e.g., NeRF-SDP) achieve competitive PSNR (22.99 for 64 points) and SSIM (0.745) with significantly lower rendering times (5.38s) compared to some baselines. Strengths: Provides explicit depth uncertainty estimates (s); differentiable; efficient generalizable neural rendering. Limitations: Requires multi-view inputs; sensitive to camera pose accuracy; requires scale-consistent fusion for heterogeneous captures. DPV estimation originated in the context of multi-view stereo and light field processing. Early work used the slope of Epipolar Plane Image (EPI) lines to estimate disparity, where the confidence of the slope estimation represented the probability of the corresponding disparity value. Modern implementations integrate this probabilistic representation into neural rendering pipelines like NeRF-SDP to enable efficient generalizable novel view synthesis with depth perception. The method is used in immersive rendering and 3D reconstruction from heterogeneous light field captures. name: DepthPredictor
body: The DepthPredictor is a PyTorch nn.Module that implements a depth prediction pipeline by integrating a distribution sampler with conversion functions. It transforms raw feature tensors containing probability density function (PDF) and offset channels into probabilistic depth estimates and associated opacities, differing from sibling methods by explicitly handling discrete distribution sampling and transmittance-based opacity computation. Inputs and Outputs: Input: features tensor of shape Float[Tensor, "batch view ray surface depth 2"]. The last dimension contains two channels: raw PDF values and raw offset values. Outputs: depth: Float[Tensor, "batch view ray surface sample"]. opacity: Float[Tensor, "batch view ray surface sample"]. index: Int64[Tensor, "batch view ray surface sample"]. Data Structures: The method uses a sampler object that provides sample and gather methods to handle discrete sampling from the PDF and retrieval of corresponding offset values. Parameters: numdepths: Integer specifying the number of discrete depth buckets (size of the depth dimension in input). near: Near plane distance for depth conversion. far: Far plane distance for depth conversion. deterministic: Boolean flag controlling sampling mode. gaussiansperpixel: Integer specifying the number of samples to draw per pixel/ray. usetransmittance: Boolean flag controlling the opacity calculation method. Steps: 1. Unbind Features: Separate the last dimension of features into pdfraw and offsetraw tensors. 2. Normalize PDF: Apply a Softmax function to pdfraw to obtain the probability density function pdf. 3. Normalize Offsets: Apply a Sigmoid function to offsetraw to obtain bounded offsets offset. 4. Sample: Draw index and corresponding PDF densities pdfi from pdf using the sampler, with the sample count determined by gaussiansperpixel. 5. Gather Offsets: Retrieve the offsets corresponding to the sampled indices: offset = sampler.gather(index, offset). 6. Calculate Relative Disparity: Compute relative disparity using the sampled indices and offsets: \text{relative\disparity} = \frac{\text{index} + \text{offset}}{\text{num\depths}} 7. Convert to Depth: Map relative disparity to absolute depth using the near and far planes: \text{depth} = \text{relative\disparity\to\depth}(\text{relative\disparity}, \text{near}, \text{far}) 8. Compute Opacity: If usetransmittance is true: a. Compute cumulative sum of PDF: partial = pdf.cumsum(dim=-1). b. Shift cumulative sum to align with transmittance: partial = torch.cat((torch.zeroslike(partial[...,:1]), partial[...,:-1]), dim=-1). c. Compute opacity per bucket: opacityraw = pdf / (1 - partial + 1e-10). d. Gather opacity values: opacity = sampler.gather(index, opacityraw). If usetransmittance is false: a. Set opacity directly to the sampled PDF density: opacity = pdfi. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import torch import torch.nn as nn class DepthPredictor(nn.Module): def init(self, sampler, numdepths, near, far, usetransmittance=True): super().init() self.sampler = sampler self.numdepths = numdepths self.near = near self.far = far self.usetransmittance = usetransmittance def forward(self, features, deterministic=False, gaussiansperpixel=1): pdfraw, offsetraw = features.unbind(dim=-1) pdf = torch.softmax(pdfraw, dim=-1) offset = torch.sigmoid(offsetraw) index, pdfi = self.sampler.sample(pdf, deterministic, gaussiansperpixel) offset = self.sampler.gather(index, offset) relativedisparity = (index + offset) / self.numdepths depth = relativedisparitytodepth(relativedisparity, self.near, self.far) if self.usetransmittance: partial = pdf.cumsum(dim=-1) partial = torch.cat((torch.zeroslike(partial[...,:1]), partial[...,:-1]), dim=-1) opacity = pdf / (1 - partial + 1e-10) opacity = self.sampler.gather(index, opacity) else: opacity = pdfi return depth, opacity, index def relativedisparitytodepth(relativedisparity, near, far): # Standard linear mapping from normalized disparity to depth return near + relativedisparity (far - near) Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Division by Zero: The opacity calculation includes a small epsilon (1e-10) to prevent division by zero when 1 - partial approaches zero. Near/Far Plane Boundaries: The near and far parameters define the valid depth range; values outside this range produce invalid depth estimates. A sibling method that also uses distribution sampling but may differ in the specific architecture of the predictor or the sampling strategy. Choose this when a monocular prior is integrated directly into the sampling process Link. Not given in the sources. name: Parabolic Root-Finding with Gradients
head: Gradient-based parabola interpolation, Least-squares parabolic root finding
body:
Parabolic root-finding with gradients is an iterative refinement technique that estimates the zero-crossing of a scalar field F(x) along a line segment by fitting a parabola to the function values and directional derivatives (gradients) at the endpoints. It solves for the root of this parabola to determine the intersection depth. It sets itself apart from its sibling, the Secant Method for Surface Depth Refinement, by utilizing gradient information to model curvature, thereby avoiding the need for an additional function evaluation to estimate the second derivative, while offering higher accuracy for non-linear fields. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: Two endpoints x1 and x2 on the ray, the scalar field values F(x1) and F(x2), and the gradients 
abla F(x1) and 
abla F(x2) at these points. Output: The parameter t \in [0, 1] representing the position of the root along the segment x(t) = x1 + t(x2 - x1). Data Structures: Not given in the sources. Steps: 1. Define the Line Segment: Parameterize the segment between x1 and x2 as v(t) = x1 + t(x2 - x1) for t \in [0, 1]. 2. Compute Directional Derivatives: Calculate the directional derivative of F along the vector (x2 - x1) at both endpoints. The directional derivative is defined as D{x2-x1} F(x) = 
abla F(x) \cdot (x2 - x1). Let d1 = D{x2-x1} F(x1) and d2 = D{x2-x1} F(x2). 3. Fit Parabola Coefficients: Define the parabola F(t) interpolating the endpoints: F(t) = F(x1) + (F(x2) - F(x1) - b)t + bt^2. The derivative of this parabola is F'(t) = F(x2) - F(x1) - b + 2bt. Determine the coefficient b by minimizing the least-squares error between the parabola's derivatives and the actual directional derivatives. The system of equations for the derivatives is d1 \approx F(x2) - F(x1) - b and d2 \approx F(x2) - F(x1) + b. Solving for b by averaging the two estimates yields b =  rac{d1 - d2}{2}. 4. Solve for Root: Solve F(t) = 0 using the quadratic formula. The equation is bt^2 + (F(x2) - F(x1) - b)t + F(x1) = 0. t =  rac{-(F(x2) - F(x1) - b) \pm \sqrt{(F(x2) - F(x1) - b)^2 - 4bF(x1)}}{2b} Select the root t that lies within the interval [0, 1]. The source guarantees exactly one root in this interval for valid zero-crossings. 5. Handle Degeneracy: If d1 = d2, then b=0. The method degenerates to the linear secant method. In this case, use linear interpolation: t =  rac{-F(x1)}{F(x2) - F(x1)} Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def parabolicrootfindingwithgradients(x1, x2, f1, f2, grad1, grad2): """ Finds the root t in [0, 1] along the segment x1->x2. x1, x2: 3D vectors (endpoints) f1, f2: scalar field values at x1, x2 grad1, grad2: gradient vectors at x1, x2 """ # 1. Direction vector dirvec = [x2[i] - x1[i] for i in range(len(x1))] # 2. Directional derivatives: D = grad. dirvec d1 = sum(g d for g, d in zip(grad1, dirvec)) d2 = sum(g d for g, d in zip(grad2, dirvec)) # 3. Compute parabola coefficient b: b = (d1 - d2) / 2 b = (d1 - d2) / 2.0 # 4. Solve quadratic equation: bt^2 + (f2 - f1 - b)t + f1 = 0 acoeff = b bcoeff = f2 - f1 - b ccoeff = f1 # Handle linear case (degeneracy) when b is effectively zero if abs(acoeff) < 1e-9: # Linear interpolation (Secant method) if abs(bcoeff) < 1e-9: return 0.5 # Fallback if both f1 and f2 are effectively equal and flat t = -ccoeff / bcoeff # Clamp to [0, 1] to handle numerical noise return max(0.0, min(1.0, t)) # Quadratic formula discriminant = bcoeff2 - 4 acoeff ccoeff # Clamp negative discriminant due to floating-point precision if discriminant < 0: discriminant = 0.0 sqrtdisc = math.sqrt(discriminant) # Two possible roots t1 = (-bcoeff + sqrtdisc) / (2 acoeff) t2 = (-bcoeff - sqrtdisc) / (2 acoeff) # Select the root in [0, 1] if 0.0 <= t1 <= 1.0: return t1 elif 0.0 <= t2 <= 1.0: return t2 else: # Not given in the sources: fallback behavior when no root is in [0, 1] return 0.5 Parameters: Not given in the sources. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Equal Gradients: If d1 = d2, b=0, and the quadratic formula fails. The method must fall back to linear interpolation. Precision: If the discriminant is slightly negative due to floating-point errors, it should be clamped to zero. No Root in Interval: If neither root lies in [0, 1], the segment does not contain a zero-crossing (or the field is not monotonic/convex in a way that guarantees one). A quadratic interpolation method that guarantees a root along an edge if the implicit function has a root, by interpolating function values and least-squares fitting derivatives. It enforces value constraints a0 = v0 and a0 + a1 + a2 = v1, and minimizes (a1 - d0)^2 + (a1 + 2a2 - d1)^2. The resulting coefficients are a1 =  rac{d0 - d1}{2} + v1 - v0 and a2 =  rac{d1 - d0}{2}. The second order term a2 vanishes if the implicit function is locally linear (d0 = d1). This solution is equivalent to the Third Order Elimination with additive offset. Time Complexity: O(1) per segment, involving a few arithmetic operations and a square root. Memory Complexity: O(1), requiring storage for the two endpoints, function values, and gradients. Strengths: Higher accuracy than linear interpolation for curved surfaces; avoids the cost of an additional function evaluation compared to 3-point parabolic fitting. Limitations: Requires gradient information, which may not always be available or cheap to compute. Degenerates to linear interpolation if gradients are equal. When to use: When gradients are available (e.g., from pre-computed textures or analytic implicit functions) and high accuracy is needed with minimal extra function evaluations. When not to use: When gradients are unavailable and computing them is expensive, or when the field is known to be linear. The method was introduced in "Real-Time Isosurface Extraction Using the GPU Programmable Geometry Pipeline". It leverages the fact that gradients are often already computed for shading or are easily available in static volume textures. It is used in real-time isosurface extraction to refine intersection points on GPU pipelines. Real-Time Isosurface Extraction Using the GPU Programmable Geometry Pipeline, https://doi.org/10.1145/1281500.1361219, fetched 2026-11-03 Accurate Isosurface Interpolation with Hermite Data, https://ieeexplore.ieee.org/document/7335492/, fetched 2026-11-05

name: Joint Root-Finding
head: Joint Root-Finding for Ray-Surface Intersection, Simultaneous Ray-Surface and Correspondence Search
body: Joint Root-Finding is a hybrid algorithm for simultaneous ray-surface intersection search and canonical correspondence search in articulated implicit surface representations. It solves for the precise intersection point \hat{\mathbf{x}} and depth d in a single Newton iteration, avoiding the high memory and runtime costs of alternating sphere tracing and root finding. Unlike Secant Method for Surface Depth Refinement which refines depth for a known surface, or Parabolic Root-Finding with Gradients which uses gradient information for faster convergence, this method couples the surface constraint with the geometric correspondence constraint (forward skinning) to handle articulated deformations. Inputs: Camera ray defined by center \mathbf{c} and unit direction vector \mathbf{v}. Canonical Signed Distance Function (SDF) network \sigmaf evaluating f{\sigmaf}(\hat{\mathbf{x}}). Forward Linear Blend Skinning (LBS) network \sigma\omega evaluating LBS{\sigma\omega}(\hat{\mathbf{x}}). Initial rough estimation of canonical point \hat{\mathbf{x}}0 and depth d0. Outputs: Converged canonical point \hat{\mathbf{x}}^ and depth d^. Data Structures: State vector \mathbf{u}k = [\hat{\mathbf{x}}k, dk]^T \in \mathbb{R}^4 (assuming 3D space). Residual vector \mathbf{g}(\mathbf{u}k) \in \mathbb{R}^4. Jacobian matrix \mathbf{J}k \in \mathbb{R}^{4 \times 4}. Formulas: The system to solve is defined as: g{\sigmaf, \sigma\omega}(\hat{\mathbf{x}}, d) = \begin{bmatrix} f{\sigmaf}(\hat{\mathbf{x}}) \\ LBS{\sigma\omega}(\hat{\mathbf{x}}) - (\mathbf{c} + \mathbf{v} \cdot d) \end{bmatrix} = \mathbf{0} where: f{\sigmaf}(\hat{\mathbf{x}}) is the scalar SDF value at canonical point \hat{\mathbf{x}}. LBS{\sigma\omega}(\hat{\mathbf{x}}) is the 3D position in observation space predicted by forward skinning from canonical point \hat{\mathbf{x}}. \mathbf{c} + \mathbf{v} \cdot d is the 3D position on the camera ray at depth d. The Jacobian matrix \mathbf{J}k at iteration k is: \mathbf{J}k = \begin{bmatrix} \frac{\partial f{\sigmaf}}{\partial \hat{\mathbf{x}}}(\hat{\mathbf{x}}k) & 0 \\ \frac{\partial LBS{\sigma\omega}}{\partial \hat{\mathbf{x}}}(\hat{\mathbf{x}}k) & -\mathbf{v} \end{bmatrix} where \frac{\partial f{\sigmaf}}{\partial \hat{\mathbf{x}}} is the gradient of the SDF (scalar), \frac{\partial LBS{\sigma\omega}}{\partial \hat{\mathbf{x}}} is the Jacobian of the skinning function (3x3 matrix), and -\mathbf{v} is the negative ray direction vector (3x1 column). Pseudocode: The implementation uses Broyden’s method to approximate the Jacobian inverse, avoiding explicit computation of \mathbf{J}k at each iteration. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def jointrootfinding(c, v, sigmaf, sigmaw, xinit, dinit, maxiter=10): """ Solves for canonical point xhat and depth d simultaneously. Args: c: Camera center (3,) v: Ray direction unit vector (3,) sigmaf: SDF network function f(xhat) -> scalar sigmaw: LBS network function LBS(xhat) -> 3D point xinit: Initial canonical point estimate (3,) dinit: Initial depth estimate (scalar) maxiter: Maximum number of Newton/Broyden steps Returns: xhat: Converged canonical point (3,) d: Converged depth (scalar) """ # Initialize state xhat = xinit.copy() d = dinit # Initialize Jacobian approximation Jinv # J = [ gradf 0 ] # [ gradLBS -v ] # We need Jinv. A simple initialization is the inverse of the diagonal # or identity scaled, but Broyden updates it. # For the first step, we compute the exact Jacobian inverse or use a # pseudo-inverse if singular. Using identity as initial guess for # Broyden's rank-1 update is standard, but computing the first exact # inverse is safer for convergence. # Compute initial residual fval = sigmaf(xhat) lbsval = sigmaw(xhat) raypos = c + v d residual = np.array([fval, lbsval[0] - raypos[0], lbsval[1] - raypos[1], lbsval[2] - raypos[2]]) # Compute initial Jacobian J # gradf is scalar, treated as 1x3 row vector gradf = computegradientsigmaf(xhat) # gradLBS is 3x3 matrix gradLBS = computejacobiansigmaw(xhat) # Construct J # J shape: 4x4 # Row 0: [gradf, 0, 0, 0] # Rows 1-3: [gradLBS, -v] J = np.zeros((4, 4)) J[0,:3] = gradf J[0, 3] = 0 J[1:4,:3] = gradLBS J[1:4, 3] = -v # Invert J for the first step Jinv = np.linalg.inv(J) for k in range(maxiter): # Newton/Broyden update: u{k+1} = uk - Jinv g(uk) # u = [xhat; d] update = Jinv @ residual xhatnew = xhat - update[:3] dnew = d - update[3] # Check convergence if np.linalg.norm(update) < 1e-6: return xhatnew, dnew # Update state xhat = xhatnew d = dnew # Compute new residual fval = sigmaf(xhat) lbsval = sigmaw(xhat) raypos = c + v d residual = np.array([fval, lbsval[0] - raypos[0], lbsval[1] - raypos[1], lbsval[2] - raypos[2]]) # Broyden's Rank-1 Update for Jinv # y = g(u{k+1}) - g(uk) # s = u{k+1} - uk = -update # Jinv{k+1} = Jinvk + (s - Jinvk @ y) @ s^T / (s^T @ s) # Note: Standard Broyden updates J, not Jinv. # The "Good" Broyden method updates Jinv directly: # Jinv{k+1} = Jinvk + (s - Jinvk @ y) @ s^T / (s^T @ s) s = -update # u{k+1} - uk # We need y = g(u{k+1}) - g(uk). We have residual for uk. # We need to compute residual for u{k+1} (which is now xhat, d) # But we already computed residual for the NEW xhat, d above? # No, the residual variable holds g(uk) from the start of the loop. # Let's re-evaluate residual for the NEW point to get y. fvalnew = sigmaf(xhat) lbsvalnew = sigmaw(xhat) rayposnew = c + v d residualnew = np.array([fvalnew, lbsvalnew[0] - rayposnew[0], lbsvalnew[1] - rayposnew[1], lbsvalnew[2] - rayposnew[2]]) y = residualnew - residual # Broyden update for Jinv # Jinv = Jinv + (s - Jinv @ y) @ s.T / (s.T @ s) term1 = s - Jinv @ y denom = np.dot(s, s) if abs(denom) < 1e-12: break # Singular update Jinv = Jinv + np.outer(term1, s) / denom residual = residualnew return xhat, d def computegradientsigmaf(x): # Standard automatic differentiation or finite difference for scalar field pass def computejacobiansigmaw(x): # Standard automatic differentiation for vector field pass Parameters: maxiter: Typically small, as the method converges quadratically. Initialization: A single initialization is sufficient; multiple initializations incur drastic overhead without noticeable improvement. The rough estimation is obtained by combining approximate backward mapping (inverse of linearly combined forward bone transforms) with sphere tracing. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Initialization Quality: The method relies on a rough estimation from inverse transformations using SMPL skinning weights rather than rigid bone transformations. Poor initialization may lead to convergence failure. Singular Jacobian: If the Jacobian is singular, Broyden's update may fail. Guard against division by zero in the denominator s^T @ s. Multiple Initializations: Adding more initializations incurs drastic memory and runtime overhead without noticeable improvements. Uses secant method for depth refinement after ray marching. Simpler but slower convergence than joint root-finding. Link Uses second-order (parabolic) approximation for faster convergence. Requires gradient computation. Link Time Complexity: Amortized complexity is O(M) where M is the number of root-finding steps. Naive alternation between sphere-tracing and root-finding is O(MN) where N is sphere-tracing steps. Measured Performance: Results in approximately 5x speedup compared to naive alternation between sphere-tracing and root-finding. Convergence: Quadratic convergence theoretically, compared to superlinear convergence for secant-method-based root-finding. Strengths: Efficient simultaneous search for intersection and correspondence; generalizes well to unseen poses; avoids high memory/runtime cost of alternating methods. Limitations: Requires differentiable SDF and LBS networks; relies on good initialization from inverse transformations. When to Use: When rendering articulated human avatars with detailed geometry and pose-dependent appearance from sparse multi-view RGB videos. When Not to Use: When rigid geometry is assumed (simpler methods suffice); when computational resources are extremely limited and initialization quality is poor. Originated in the paper "ARAH: Animatable Volume Rendering of Articulated Human SDFs". The method addresses the challenge of rendering clothed human avatars with detailed geometry that generalizes well to out-of-distribution poses. It combines articulated implicit surface representation with volume rendering. The joint root-finding algorithm enables efficient point sampling and accurate point canonicalization. It is used in the context of 3D Computer Vision, Clothed Human Modeling, and Cloth Motion Capture. ARAH: Animatable Volume Rendering of Articulated Human SDFs, https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-031-19824-31, fetched 2026-10-26

name: Bisection Method for Surface Depth Refinement
head: Bisection Method, Iterative Bisection, Midpoint (Bisection) Algorithm
body: The Bisection Method for Surface Depth Refinement is an iterative root-finding algorithm that determines the exact intersection point of a ray with an implicit surface within a segment known to contain an intersection. It serves as an alternative to the Secant method in ray marching pipelines. The method systematically halves the search interval at each step until the midpoint evaluates to zero. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Two endpoints of a line segment, P{low} and P{high}, bracketing the intersection. Output: A point P{hit} on the segment where the field function evaluates to zero. Data Structures: Endpoints: 3D vectors or 1D coordinates along an axis-aligned edge. Field Values: Scalars f(P{low}) and f(P{high}) indicating signed distance or occupancy relative to the isosurface threshold. Algorithm Steps: 1. Initialization: Set P{low} and P{high} to the segment endpoints and evaluate f{low} = f(P{low}) and f{high} = f(P{high}). 2. Midpoint Calculation: Compute P{mid} = (P{low} + P{high}) / 2. 3. Evaluation: Evaluate the field function at the midpoint: f{mid} = f(P{mid}). 4. Convergence Check: If f{mid} = 0, the exact intersection point is found. 5. Interval Update: Replace the endpoint whose field value has the same sign as f{mid} with the midpoint. 6. Iteration: Repeat from Step 2 until convergence. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def bisectionintersection(Plow, Phigh, fieldfunction): """Refines the intersection point on a segment using the bisection method.""" flow = fieldfunction(Plow) fhigh = fieldfunction(Phigh) while True: Pmid = (Plow + Phigh) / 2.0 fmid = fieldfunction(Pmid) if fmid == 0: return Pmid if fmid flow > 0: Plow = Pmid flow = fmid else: Phigh = Pmid fhigh = fmid # Convergence check (tolerance/maxiter) not specified in sources Parameters: Tolerance: Not given in the sources. Max Iterations: Not given in the sources. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Non-Bracketing Segments: The method requires the initial segment to bracket a root. Discontinuous Functions: The method requires continuity. Multiple Roots: Not given in the sources. Combines bisection with Newton’s method for high-degree polynomials, ensuring all real roots are found by isolating them in monotonic intervals. Choose when dealing with complex implicit surfaces defined by high-degree polynomials where simple bisection might miss roots or converge slowly. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Performance: The false position algorithm is "no worse than the midpoint algorithm, and usually better" in terms of iteration count. Strengths: Guaranteed convergence for continuous functions by systematically halving the search interval. Limitations: Requires the field function to be continuous and the initial segment to bracket a root. When to Use: Not given in the sources. When Not to Use: Not given in the sources. The bisection method is a classic root-finding algorithm. In isosurface extraction, it is cited as a "far better choice" than simple linear interpolation for finding exact intersection points on edges. It is implemented in the IsoMesher class methods intersectxaxis(), intersectyaxis(), and intersectzaxis(), controlled by the preprocessor symbol BISECTION. It is also used in differentiable volumetric rendering pipelines as an alternative to the Secant method. autonomousvision/differentiablevolumetricrendering, https://github.com/autonomousvision/differentiablevolumetricrendering, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial) http://www.oocities.org/tzukkers/isosurf/isosurfaces.html, http://www.oocities.org/tzukkers/isosurf/isosurfaces.html, fetched 2026-10-30 (unofficial)

name: Bracketed Newton Bisection
head: BNB
body: Bracketed Newton Bisection is a root-finding algorithm that combines bisection and Newton’s methods with a preliminary step that splits the polynomial into monotonic pieces. It finds all possible real roots of high-degree polynomials, ensuring no solutions are missed by guaranteeing at most one root per interval. Unlike simple numerical solvers that may converge to a single root or fail on high-degree cases, this method systematically partitions the domain using derivative roots to isolate and solve each root independently. Inputs: A polynomial P(x) of degree n, its first derivative P'(x), a list of higher-order derivative functions P^{(k)}(x) for k=2 \dots n-2, and a search domain [x{min}, x{max}]. Outputs: A list of all real roots of P(x) within the domain. Data Structures: A list of interval boundaries (initially [x{min}, x{max}]) and a list to accumulate found roots. Steps: 1. Base Interval Resolution: Start with the (n-2)-th derivative P^{(n-2)}, which is a quadratic polynomial (degree 2). Solve P^{(n-2)}(x) = 0 algebraically to find its real roots within the domain. These roots become the initial interval boundaries for the next level. If P^{(n-2)} has no real roots, the domain remains a single interval [x{min}, x{max}]. 2. Bottom-Up Interval Refinement: Iterate k from n-3 down to 1. For each derivative P^{(k)}, evaluate it at the current interval boundaries. If P^{(k)} changes sign between two adjacent boundaries, a root of P^{(k)} exists in that sub-interval. Find this root using the Bracketed Newton Bisection method. This root becomes a new boundary for the next derivative P^{(k-1)}. If P^{(k)} does not change sign, the existing boundaries are retained. 3. Final Root Finding: After reaching k=0, the boundaries define monotonic segments of P(x). For each segment [a, b] where P(a) \cdot P(b) < 0, apply the Bracketed Newton Bisection method to find the single root of P(x). Root Finding Formula (Mixture of Bisection and Newton): For a monotonic interval [x{min}, x{max}] with P(x{min}) \cdot P(x{max}) < 0: 1. Initialize x = (x{min} + x{max}) / 2. 2. Iterate until convergence: Compute f = P(x) and f' = P'(x). Compute Newton step: x{new} = x - f / f'. Bracketing Guard: If x{new} \notin [x{min}, x{max}] or the Newton step does not reduce |f| sufficiently, fall back to bisection: x{new} = (x{min} + x{max}) / 2. Update interval: If P(x{new}) \cdot P(x{min}) < 0, set x{max} = x{new}; else set x{min} = x{new}. Set x = x{new}. Parameters: Convergence tolerance and maximum iterations are not given in the sources. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: The method can find at most 9 monotonic intervals for a degree-9 polynomial (e.g., tricubic SDFs). BNB does not offer an early skip strategy, unlike Affine Arithmetic tests. High-degree polynomials require evaluating multiple derivative chains, increasing computational cost. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def bracketednewtonbisection(P, Pprime, derivs, domain, degree): """ Finds all real roots of polynomial P in the given domain. P: callable for P(x) Pprime: callable for P'(x) derivs: list of callables [P, P', P'',..., P^(n-2)] domain: tuple (xmin, xmax) degree: integer n """ xmin, xmax = domain # Step 1: Base case - solve quadratic P^(n-2) = 0 algebraically # Extract coefficients a, b, c for f(x) = ax^2 + bx + c from derivs[degree-2] c = derivsdegree - 2 b = (derivsdegree - 2 - derivsdegree - 2) / 2.0 a = (derivsdegree - 2 + derivsdegree - 2) / 2.0 - c quadroots = [] if abs(a) < 1e-12: if abs(b) > 1e-12: root = -c / b if xmin <= root <= xmax: quadroots.append(root) else: disc = b b - 4 a c if disc >= 0: sqrtd = disc 0.5 r1 = (-b + sqrtd) / (2 a) r2 = (-b - sqrtd) / (2 a) if xmin <= r1 <= xmax: quadroots.append(r1) if xmin <= r2 <= xmax: quadroots.append(r2) boundaries = sorted(list(set([xmin, xmax] + quadroots))) # Step 2: Bottom-up refinement from k = n-3 down to 1 for k in range(degree - 3, 0, -1): newboundaries = [] fk = derivs[k] fkplus1 = derivs[k + 1] for i in range(len(boundaries) - 1): aint, bint = boundaries[i], boundaries[i + 1] fa, fb = fk(aint), fk(bint) if fa fb < 0: root = findrootbnb(fk, fkplus1, aint, bint) newboundaries.append(root) else: newboundaries.append(aint) newboundaries.append(bint) boundaries = sorted(list(set(newboundaries))) # Step 3: Final root finding for P^(0) = P roots = [] for i in range(len(boundaries) - 1): aint, bint = boundaries[i], boundaries[i + 1] if P(aint) P(bint) < 0: root = findrootbnb(P, Pprime, aint, bint) roots.append(root) return roots def findrootbnb(f, fprime, xmin, xmax, tol=1e-7, maxiter=100): """Mixture of Bisection and Newton's method for a monotonic interval.""" x = (xmin + xmax) / 2.0 for in range(maxiter): fx = f(x) if abs(fx) < tol: return x fpx = fprime(x) if abs(fpx) < 1e-12: x = (xmin + xmax) / 2.0 continue xnew = x - fx / fpx # Bracketing Guard if xnew < xmin or xnew > xmax: xnew = (xmin + xmax) / 2.0 fxnew = f(xnew) if fxnew f(xmin) < 0: xmax = xnew else: xmin = xnew x = xnew return x The Analytic Ray-Intersection Polynomial Solver finds the intersection parameter t where a ray intersects the polynomial approximation of a Signed Distance Function (SDF) leaf node. It solves the problem of slow convergence in sphere marching when rays pass near parallel surfaces or graze the isosurface. Unlike sphere marching, which evaluates the SDF iteratively, this method computes a single polynomial in t per node and solves for its roots, offering a significant performance improvement near the surface at the cost of higher initial coefficient computation. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Measured Performance: BNB provides an average 12% speedup over basic Sphere Marching in the narrow band for trilinear interpolation, primarily by skipping nodes early on silhouettes where Sphere Marching converges slowly. However, it is the slowest method for tricubic interpolation because it must search monotonic intervals of seven previous derivatives. Strengths: Guarantees finding all real roots of high-degree polynomials by splitting into monotonic intervals. Limitations: Requires computing and solving lower-degree derivative polynomials iteratively; lacks an early skip strategy. When to use: When high-degree polynomial approximations of SDFs are used and all real roots must be found. When not to use: When lower-degree polynomials are sufficient, analytical solutions are available, or an early skip strategy is required. Bracketed Newton Bisection is a root-finding algorithm named by Peters et al. and first proposed by Yuksel. Rendering piecewise approximations of SDFs through analytic intersections, https://doi.org/10.1016/j.cag.2024.103981, fetched 2026-10-27

name: Analytic Ray-Intersection Polynomial Solver
head: Polynomial SDF Intersection Solver
body: The Analytic Ray-Intersection Polynomial Solver finds the intersection parameter t where a ray intersects the polynomial approximation of a Signed Distance Function (SDF) leaf node. It solves the problem of slow convergence in sphere marching when rays pass near parallel surfaces or graze the isosurface. Unlike sphere marching, which evaluates the SDF iteratively, this method computes a single polynomial in t per node and solves for its roots, offering a significant performance improvement near the surface at the cost of higher initial coefficient computation. Inputs: Ray origin \mathbf{p} and direction \mathbf{v}. SDF leaf node coefficients defining the polynomial PN: \mathbb{R}^3 \to \mathbb{R}. Node type: Trilinear (8 coefficients) or Tricubic (64 coefficients). Outputs: The smallest positive real root t of the intersection polynomial, representing the first intersection point. A boolean indicating if an intersection exists within the node. Data Structures: Trilinear Node: Array of 8 scalar coefficients c{ijk} for i,j,k \in \{0,1\}. Tricubic Node: Array of 64 scalar coefficients c{ijkl} for i,j,k,l \in \{0,1,2,3\}. Intersection Polynomial Coefficients: Array of size 4 for trilinear (c{l3} \dots c{l0}) or size 10 for tricubic (c{c9} \dots c{c0}). Steps: 1. Compute Intersection Polynomial Coefficients: Substitute the ray equation \mathbf{x}(t) = \mathbf{p} + \mathbf{v}t into the node's polynomial PN(\mathbf{x}) and expand by powers of t. For Trilinear interpolation, the result is a cubic polynomial: c{l3}t^3 + c{l2}t^2 + c{l1}t + c{l0} = 0 Computing these 4 coefficients requires 26 multiplications. For Tricubic interpolation, the result is a degree 9 polynomial: c{c9}t^9 + c{c8}t^8 + \dots + c{c1}t + c{c0} = 0 Computing these 10 coefficients requires 492 multiplications. 2. Early Skip Test (Tricubic Only): For tricubic nodes, apply an Affine Arithmetic-based early skip test to detect non-collisions in constant time or provide a better starting point. Factorize the function as a degree 2 polynomial: PN(\mathbf{p}+\mathbf{v}t) \approx at^2 + bt + c = 0 where: a = c{c9}t^7 + c{c8}t^6 + \dots + c{c3}t + c{c2} b = c{c1} c = c{c0} Since a depends on t, approximate it with a fixed bound to form a real quadratic equation. If starting outside the object, check if the quadratic evaluates to negative values for t \ge 0; if it does not, return "No Intersection". 3. Identify Monotonic Intervals: Use the Bracketed Newton Bisection method to find all real roots of the derivative polynomials, which define the boundaries of monotonic intervals for the original polynomial. Start from the (n-2)-th derivative (degree 2), find its roots algebraically, and iteratively use them to bound the roots of the (n-3)-th derivative up to the original polynomial. Trilinear: The derivative is quadratic (degree 2) with at most 2 roots, creating at most 3 monotonic intervals for the cubic polynomial. Tricubic: The solver searches monotonic intervals of the seven previous derivatives, identifying up to 9 monotonic intervals for the degree 9 polynomial. 4. Root Finding: For each monotonic interval [t{min}, t{max}]: Check for a sign change between the polynomial values at the interval bounds. If signs differ, a root exists in this interval. Apply Bracketed Newton Bisection to find the root within this interval. Discard analytical formulas like Cardano's method due to instability in certain situations. 5. Select Intersection: Return the smallest positive t found among all intervals. If no sign changes are detected in any monotonic interval, the node does not intersect the surface. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def solveanalyticintersection(p, v, nodecoeffs, nodetype): """ p: list[float, float, float], ray origin v: list[float, float, float], ray direction (normalized) nodecoeffs: list[float], SDF node coefficients nodetype: 'trilinear' or 'tricubic' Returns: (t, hit) where t is the intersection distance and hit is a boolean """ # Step 1: Compute intersection polynomial coefficients if nodetype == 'trilinear': poly = expandtrilinear(p, v, nodecoeffs) degree = 3 elif nodetype == 'tricubic': poly = expandtricubic(p, v, nodecoeffs) degree = 9 else: raise ValueError("Unsupported node type") # Step 2: Early Skip Test (Tricubic only) if nodetype == 'tricubic': c9, c8, c7, c6, c5, c4, c3, c2, c1, c0 = poly # Approximate 'a' with a fixed bound for t >= 0 aapprox = sum(abs(c) for c in poly[:8]) b, c = c1, c0 # If quadratic at^2+bt+c has no real roots or stays positive for t>=0, skip if aapprox > 0 and c >= 0 and -b / (2 aapprox) < 0: return (float('inf'), False) disc = b b - 4 aapprox c if disc < 0: return (float('inf'), False) # Step 3: Identify Monotonic Intervals intervals = findmonotonicintervals(poly, degree) # Step 4 & 5: Root Finding & Selection mint = float('inf') hit = False for tmin, tmax in intervals: if tmax <= 0: continue valmin = evaluatepoly(poly, tmin) valmax = evaluatepoly(poly, tmax) if valmin valmax < 0: troot = bracketednewtonbisection(poly, max(0.0, tmin), tmax) if troot < mint: mint = troot hit = True return (mint, hit) def expandtrilinear(p, v, c): # Expands trilinear basis with ray x(t)=p+vt. Requires 26 multiplications. # Standard polynomial composition of basis functions px, py, pz = p vx, vy, vz = v # Basis polynomials for each axis: (1-p-vt) and (p+vt) def basis(pval, vval): return [[1.0 - pval, -vval], [pval, vval]] ax = [basis(px, vx), basis(py, vy), basis(pz, vz)] # Combine with node coefficients using polynomial convolution poly = [0.0] 4 for i in range(2): for j in range(2): for k in range(2): coeff = c[i 4 + j 2 + k] # Multiply three linear polynomials and add to result for d1, a1 in enumerate(ax[i]): for d2, a2 in enumerate(ax[j]): for d3, a3 in enumerate(ax[k]): deg = d1 + d2 + d3 poly[deg] += coeff a1 a2 a3 return poly def expandtricubic(p, v, c): # Expands tricubic basis with ray x(t)=p+vt. Requires 492 multiplications. # Standard polynomial composition of basis functions px, py, pz = p vx, vy, vz = v def basis(pval, vval): # Returns coefficients for (1-p-vt)^3 and (p+vt)^3 etc. # Direct expansion of cubic basis return [ [1.0 - pval, -vval], [3.0 (1.0 - pval)2, -6.0 (1.0 - pval) vval], [3.0 (1.0 - pval), 3.0 vval2], [1.0, -vval] ] # Simplified to direct expansion for completeness # Full expansion requires convolving 1D bases across 3 dimensions # Returns array of 10 coefficients [cc9,..., cc0] # Implementation follows the same basis expansion pattern as trilinear but for degree 9 # Sources do not provide exact coefficient formulas # Placeholder for full basis expansion return [0.0]10 # Sources do not provide exact coefficient formulas def findmonotonicintervals(poly, degree): # Iteratively finds derivative roots to bound monotonic intervals # Start with the full polynomial and compute derivatives up to degree 2 derivs = [poly] current = poly while len(current) > 3: current = getderivativecoeffs(current) derivs.append(current) # Start from degree 2 derivative (index len(derivs)-3) up to original intervals = [[0.0, float('inf')]] for d in range(len(derivs) - 3, -1, -1): roots = solvequadraticroots(derivs[d]) if len(derivs[d]) == 3 else solvehigherderivativeroots(derivs[d]) newintervals = [] for tmin, tmax in intervals: splitpoints = sorted([tmin] + [r for r in roots if tmin < r < tmax] + [tmax]) for i in range(len(splitpoints) - 1): newintervals.append([splitpoints[i], splitpoints[i+1]]) intervals = newintervals return intervals def solvequadraticroots(deriv): # Returns real roots of quadratic derivative a, b, c = deriv[0], deriv[1], deriv[2] if a == 0: return [-c/b] if b != 0 else [] disc = bb - 4ac if disc < 0: return [] r1 = (-b + disc0.5) / (2a) r2 = (-b - disc0.5) / (2a) return [r1, r2] def solvehigherderivativeroots(deriv): # Recursively finds roots of higher derivatives if len(deriv) == 3: return solvequadraticroots(deriv) return solvehigherderivativeroots(getderivativecoeffs(deriv)) def getderivativecoeffs(poly): # Returns coefficients of derivative polynomial return [poly[i] (len(poly) - 1 - i) for i in range(len(poly) - 1)] def bracketednewtonbisection(poly, tmin, tmax): # Standard Bracketed Newton Bisection algorithm for in range(100): if abs(tmax - tmin) < 1e-7: break tmid = (tmin + tmax) / 2.0 fmid = evaluatepoly(poly, tmid) fmin = evaluatepoly(poly, tmin) if fmin fmid < 0: tmax = tmid else: tmin = tmid return (tmin + tmax) / 2.0 def evaluatepoly(coeffs, t): # Horner's method result = 0.0 for c in reversed(coeffs): result = result t + c return result Parameters: Trilinear Node: 8 coefficients. Evaluating the polynomial requires 7 multiplications. Computing intersection coefficients requires 26 multiplications. Tricubic Node: 64 coefficients. Evaluating the polynomial requires 84 multiplications. Computing intersection coefficients requires 492 multiplications. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Instability of Analytical Solvers: Analytical formulas like Cardano's method for cubic roots are found to be unstable in some situations; therefore, numerical methods (Bracketed Newton Bisection) are preferred. Parallel Surfaces: Sphere marching fails when rays pass close to parallel surfaces without colliding. This method handles such cases by solving the polynomial directly, avoiding the slow convergence of iterative distance estimation. Coefficient Computation Cost: Computing the intersection coefficients is significantly more expensive than evaluating the SDF directly (e.g., 492 vs 84 multiplications for tricubic). However, this cost is amortized if the polynomial is evaluated multiple times before exiting the node. Time Complexity: The initial coefficient computation is O(1) but with a high constant factor (26 or 492 multiplications). Root finding is O(1) due to the fixed number of monotonic intervals (at most 3 for trilinear, 9 for tricubic). Memory Complexity: O(1), storing only the polynomial coefficients and derivative roots. Measured Performance: Improves performance when sphere marching requires many iterations (near surface or grazing rays) because the intersection polynomial is computed only once per ray and node, then evaluated multiple times. Strengths: Robust near the surface; avoids slow convergence of sphere marching; constant-time early skip for tricubic nodes. Limitations: High initial computational cost for coefficient generation; analytical cubic solvers are unstable. When to Use: When rays are likely to intersect or graze the isosurface within a leaf node, particularly in high-resolution SDF representations (tricubic). When Not to Use: When the ray is far from the surface and sphere marching converges quickly, as the overhead of polynomial computation is not justified. The method was introduced in the paper "Rendering piecewise approximations of SDFs through analytic intersections". It addresses the limitations of sphere marching, which can be slow when rays pass near parallel surfaces or graze the isosurface. The approach leverages the known polynomial representation of the SDF within leaf nodes to replace iterative distance estimation with direct root finding. Rendering piecewise approximations of SDFs through analytic intersections, https://doi.org/10.1016/j.cag.2024.103981, fetched 2026-10-27
