name: Hitpoint Refinement
body: Hitpoint Refinement is an iterative technique to achieve higher quality in detecting surface intersections without reducing rendering speed. It allows for coarser initial sampling steps to increase rendering speed, refining the detected intersection point through a specific heuristic procedure. It sets itself apart from its siblings by using a "half-step back, then check direction" adjustment rather than standard bisection or secant methods, enabling significant speedups when paired with large initial sampling distances. Inputs and outputs: Input: A ray, a surface function evaluating to a scalar (e.g., distance to surface or threshold crossing indicator), and an initial coarse intersection estimate found via sparse sampling. Output: A refined intersection parameter. Data structures: Not given in the sources. Numbered steps: 1. Sample along the ray with a relatively small sampling rate (large steps between sampling points) to detect a rough intersection. 2. Upon detecting an intersection, step back by half a step. 3. Check if moving closer to the target value or further away. 4. If closer, move back another half-step (quarter step total). If further, move forward one such step. 5. Repeat steps 3–4 five to six times. Formulas: Let t be the ray parameter and \Delta t be the current step size. Initial coarse hit: t0, coarse step: \Delta t0. Backstep: t1 = t0 - \frac{\Delta t0}{2}, \Delta t1 = \frac{\Delta t0}{2}. Iteration i = 1 to k (where k \in \{5, 6\}): Evaluate surface at ti. Compare absolute error to target. If closer: t{i+1} = ti - \frac{\Delta ti}{2}, \Delta t{i+1} = \frac{\Delta ti}{2}. If further: t{i+1} = ti + \Delta ti, \Delta t{i+1} = \frac{\Delta ti}{2}. Final refined parameter: t{k+1}. Parameters: Initial sampling distance: Can be increased to 400% or 500% of the original fine sampling distance when Hitpoint Refinement is used. Iteration count: 5 to 6 times. Edge cases and pitfalls: Not given in the sources. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def hitpointrefinement(tinit, dtcoarse, surfacefunc, target=0.0, iterations=6): """ Refines a coarse intersection point tinit found with step size dtcoarse. Args: tinit: Initial coarse intersection estimate. dtcoarse: Step size used during initial coarse sampling. surfacefunc: Function f(t) returning scalar value (e.g., distance to surface). target: Target scalar value for intersection (e.g., 0.0 for zero-crossing). iterations: Number of refinement steps (typically 5-6). Returns: Refined intersection parameter t. """ # Step 2: Step back by half a step tcurr = tinit - dtcoarse / 2.0 dtcurr = dtcoarse / 2.0 # Evaluate current position valcurr = surfacefunc(tcurr) errcurr = abs(valcurr - target) # Steps 3-4: Refinement loop for in range(iterations): # Tentative backstep tnext = tcurr - dtcurr / 2.0 valnext = surfacefunc(tnext) errnext = abs(valnext - target) if errnext < errcurr: # Closer to target: move back, halve step size tcurr = tnext valcurr = valnext errcurr = errnext dtcurr /= 2.0 else: # Further away: move forward by one current step size, halve step size tcurr = tcurr + dtcurr valcurr = surfacefunc(tcurr) errcurr = abs(valcurr - target) dtcurr /= 2.0 return tcurr Time complexity: O(k) where k is the number of iterations (typically 5–6). Memory complexity: Not given in the sources. Measured performance: Using Hitpoint Refinement allows the initial sampling distance to be increased to 400% or 500% of the original, significantly increasing rendering speed. The refinement yields a 64-fold better intersection accuracy compared to the initially chosen point. Strengths: High accuracy with minimal additional cost; allows for coarser initial sampling. Limitations: Not given in the sources. Hitpoint Refinement was introduced as an optimization technique for raycasters to improve intersection detection quality without sacrificing rendering speed. It is described in the context of volume raycasting optimization. Volume Raycasting mit OpenCL, https://arxiv.org/abs/1609.01317v1, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial)

name: Linear Intersection Approximation
head: Midpoint Intersection [S1, unofficial]
body: Linear Intersection Approximation (also known as Midpoint Intersection) estimates the intersection point of an isosurface with a grid edge by calculating the geometric midpoint of the edge, rather than performing linear interpolation based on scalar values. It differs from its parent, Linear Edge Intersection, by ignoring endpoint scalar values entirely, and from its sibling, Iterative Bisection Intersection Refinement, by using a single fixed geometric step instead of recursive refinement. Inputs: Voxel corner coordinates (x, y, z) and an integer edge index identifying the specific edge of the unit cube. Outputs: Intersection point P{mid} = (x{mid}, y{mid}, z{mid}). Data Structures: Coordinates are stored as floating-point values. Edge indices are integers mapping to cube edges. Steps: 1. Initialize edge endpoints (x1, y1, z1) and (x2, y2, z2) to the voxel corner (x, y, z). 2. Adjust endpoints based on the edge number to define the specific edge of the unit cube. For example, Edge 0 goes from (x, y, z) to (x, y+1, z), so y2 \leftarrow y2 + 1. Edge 1 goes from (x, y+1, z) to (x+1, y+1, z), so y1 \leftarrow y1 + 1, x2 \leftarrow x2 + 1, y2 \leftarrow y2 + 1. 3. Return the midpoint of the edge as the intersection point. Formulas: x{mid} = \frac{x1 + x2}{2}, \quad y{mid} = \frac{y1 + y2}{2}, \quad z{mid} = \frac{z1 + z2}{2} Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def linearintersectionapproximation(voxelorigin, edgeindex): x, y, z = voxelorigin x1, y1, z1 = float(x), float(y), float(z) x2, y2, z2 = float(x), float(y), float(z) # Adjust endpoints based on edge number (standard Marching Cubes edge enumeration) if edgeindex == 0: y2 += 1.0 elif edgeindex == 1: y1 += 1.0; x2 += 1.0; y2 += 1.0 elif edgeindex == 2: x1 += 1.0; x2 += 1.0 elif edgeindex == 3: x1 += 1.0 elif edgeindex == 4: y2 += 1.0; z2 += 1.0 elif edgeindex == 5: y1 += 1.0; x2 += 1.0; y2 += 1.0; z2 += 1.0 elif edgeindex == 6: x1 += 1.0; x2 += 1.0; z2 += 1.0 elif edgeindex == 7: x1 += 1.0; z2 += 1.0 elif edgeindex == 8: z2 += 1.0 elif edgeindex == 9: x1 += 1.0; x2 += 1.0; z2 += 1.0 elif edgeindex == 10: x1 += 1.0; x2 += 1.0; y1 += 1.0; y2 += 1.0; z2 += 1.0 elif edgeindex == 11: y1 += 1.0; y2 += 1.0; z2 += 1.0 # Calculate midpoint xmid = (x1 + x2) / 2.0 ymid = (y1 + y2) / 2.0 zmid = (z1 + z2) / 2.0 return (xmid, ymid, zmid) Parameters: None. The method is deterministic and requires no tuning parameters. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: The method assumes the edge is a straight line segment. No special handling is needed for degenerate edges (zero-length) as the midpoint will simply be the endpoint. It does not account for curved edges or non-linear scalar fields. Recursive Bisection Interpolation refines edge intersection points by recursively bisecting the edge until the midpoint crosses the isovalue, reducing geometric holes between different Level of Detail (LOD) representations. It differs from its parent Linear Intersection Approximation by using a binary search on the scalar field values to locate the intersection, rather than assuming a linear gradient across the edge. Time Complexity: O(1) per edge, involving only basic arithmetic operations. Memory Complexity: O(1), requiring no additional data structures. Measured Performance: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Simplicity and speed. Limitations: Low accuracy compared to linear interpolation, as it ignores scalar field values. When to use: When performance is critical and accuracy is secondary, or when scalar field data is unavailable. When not to use: When high-fidelity isosurfaces are required. The method is described in the context of marching cubes implementations, specifically in the ilastik/marchingcubes repository. It is presented as a simple alternative to linear interpolation for edge intersections. The term "Midpoint Intersection" is used interchangeably. The method is part of a broader set of techniques for isosurface extraction, where accurate edge intersection is crucial for generating correct triangle meshes. ilastik/marchingcubes, https://github.com/ilastik/marchingcubes, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial)

name: Recursive Bisection Interpolation
head: Midpoint Refinement, Surface Shifting
body: Recursive Bisection Interpolation refines edge intersection points by recursively bisecting the edge until the midpoint crosses the isovalue, reducing geometric holes between different Levels of Detail (LODs). It sets itself apart from its parent Linear Intersection Approximation by using a binary search on the scalar field values rather than a single linear interpolation step, ensuring the intersection point lies within a sub-segment that contains the zero-crossing. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Edge endpoints a and b, their scalar field values valuea and valueb, and the target isovalue iso. Output: Intersection point p on the edge. Data Structures: Not given in the sources. Parameters: surfaceshift (int): Boolean flag (0 or 1) to enable recursive bisection interpolation instead of standard linear interpolation. Steps: 1. Compute the midpoint c = \frac{a + b}{2} and its scalar value valuec. 2. Check if (valuea - iso)(valuec - iso) < 0; if true, recurse on half [a, c]. 3. Else check if (valueb - iso)(valuec - iso) < 0; if true, recurse on half [b, c]. 4. Otherwise, return linear interpolation on [a, b]. Formula: Linear interpolation fallback: p = a + \frac{iso - valuea}{valueb - valuea}(b - a) Midpoint crossing check: (valuea - iso)(valuec - iso) < 0 Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def recursivebisectioninterpolation(a, b, valuea, valueb, iso): # Compute midpoint c = (a + b) / 2.0 # Scalar field evaluation at c is not specified in the sources. valuec = 0.0 # Placeholder for field value # Check first half [a, c] if (valuea - iso) (valuec - iso) < 0: return recursivebisectioninterpolation(a, c, valuea, valuec, iso) # Check second half [b, c] if (valueb - iso) (valuec - iso) < 0: return recursivebisectioninterpolation(b, c, valueb, valuec, iso) # Fallback to linear interpolation if valueb == valuea: return a # Guard for degenerate case where values are identical t = (iso - valuea) / (valueb - valuea) return a + t (b - a) Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Not given in the sources. A geometric constraint technique used during hierarchical isosurface extraction to prevent refinement dependencies and topological artifacts at the interfaces of adjacent sub-blocks. It extends the standard time lag method by enforcing a local inclusion check against block boundaries, ensuring that edge contractions do not create geometric inconsistencies between neighbors. Unlike the original time lag which applies globally, this extension specifically targets the borders of current sub-blocks to maintain consistency in parallel or partitioned rendering environments. Strengths: Reduces geometric holes between different LODs by ensuring intersection points are more accurately located within the scalar field's zero-crossing. Recursive Bisection Interpolation, also known as Surface Shifting, is implemented in the OpenGL Marching Cubes/Tetrahedra Geometry Shader framework by AnBenLa. It is used in conjunction with Simple LOD and Transvoxel algorithm implementations to improve mesh quality. The method was described in the context of a GitHub repository for real-time volume visualization. AnBenLa/OpenGL-MarchingCubes-MarchingTetrahedra-GeometryShader, https://github.com/AnBenLa/OpenGL-MarchingCubes-MarchingTetrahedra-GeometryShader, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial)

name: Extended Time Lag for Parallel Boundaries
head: Border time lag, Prevention sphere, Time Lag Extension for Block Borders
body: Extended Time Lag for Parallel Boundaries is a geometric constraint technique used during hierarchical isosurface extraction to prevent refinement dependencies and topological artifacts at the interfaces of adjacent sub-blocks. It extends the standard time lag method by enforcing a local inclusion check against block boundaries, ensuring that edge contractions do not create geometric inconsistencies between neighbors. Unlike the original time lag which applies globally, this extension specifically targets the borders of current sub-blocks to maintain consistency in parallel or partitioned rendering environments. The method operates during the edge collapse phase of simplification algorithms within a hierarchical block structure. It prevents the contraction of an edge if the resulting geometric influence sphere would extend outside the current block's boundaries. Inputs and Outputs: Input: An edge ab to be considered for collapse, the current block boundary definition, and the radii of the edge endpoints rad(a) and rad(b). Output: A boolean decision indicating whether the edge contraction is permitted or prevented. Data Structures: Edge: Defined by endpoints a and b. Block: Defined by its spatial boundaries, typically represented as an axis-aligned bounding box with minimum and maximum extents. Radius Field: Each vertex x stores a scalar value rad(x). Formulas: The radius of a point c, which is the result of collapsing edge ab into a single vertex, is calculated as: rad(c) = \frac{\|a - b\| + rad(a) + rad(b)}{2} Where: \|a - b\| is the Euclidean distance between vertices a and b. rad(a) and rad(b) are the radii associated with vertices a and b. For original vertices of the isosurface, the radius is defined as: rad(x) = 1 Algorithm Steps: 1. Identify the edge ab to be collapsed. 2. Calculate the midpoint m of the edge: m = \frac{a + b}{2}. 3. Calculate the radius rad(c) of the potential new vertex c using the formula above. 4. Define a sphere S centered at m with radius rad(c). 5. Check if sphere S is totally included within the current block's boundaries. If S is not totally included (i.e., it intersects or crosses the block boundary), prevent the contraction of edge ab. If S is totally included, allow the contraction. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def norm(v): return math.sqrt(v[0]2 + v[1]2 + v[2]2) def lerp(a, b, t): return (a[0] + t (b[0] - a[0]), a[1] + t (b[1] - a[1]), a[2] + t (b[2] - a[2])) def issphereinsideaabb(center, radius, minpt, maxpt): if center[0] - radius < minpt[0] or center[0] + radius > maxpt[0]: return False if center[1] - radius < minpt[1] or center[1] + radius > maxpt[1]: return False if center[2] - radius < minpt[2] or center[2] + radius > maxpt[2]: return False return True def isedgecontractionallowed(apos, bpos, rada, radb, minpt, maxpt): """ Determines if edge ab can be collapsed based on Extended Time Lag constraints. Args: apos: Tuple (x, y, z) of vertex a position. bpos: Tuple (x, y, z) of vertex b position. rada: Radius of vertex a. radb: Radius of vertex b. minpt: Tuple (x, y, z) of block minimum extent. maxpt: Tuple (x, y, z) of block maximum extent. Returns: bool: True if contraction is allowed, False if prevented. """ distab = norm([bpos[0] - apos[0], bpos[1] - apos[1], bpos[2] - apos[2]]) radc = (distab + rada + radb) / 2.0 center = lerp(apos, bpos, 0.5) return issphereinsideaabb(center, radc, minpt, maxpt) Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision: Floating-point errors in distance calculations may cause a sphere that is mathematically inside to be flagged as outside, or vice versa. A small epsilon tolerance may be required in the inclusion check. Original Vertices: The radius definition rad(x)=1 applies strictly to original vertices. If intermediate vertices are created, their radii must be propagated correctly using the formula to maintain the prevention sphere logic. name: Triangle Point Generation (Linear Interpolation with Snap)
head: Linear Interpolation with Snap, Snap Interpolation
body: This method computes the precise intersection point on a triangle edge where a scalar field equals a threshold, using linear interpolation between two grid vertices. It distinguishes itself from siblings like Iterative Bisection Intersection Refinement by avoiding iterative convergence, instead applying a deterministic "snap" heuristic to vertices near the threshold to stabilize the interpolation result. It serves as the geometric foundation for Triangle Point Sampling, which requires robust point generation to ensure uniform spatial distribution. Inputs: p1, p2: 3D coordinates of the two vertices defining the edge. v1, v2: Scalar field values at p1 and p2 respectively. snap: Threshold parameter for snapping. Default: 0.01. Outputs: point: The 3D coordinate of the intersection point on the edge. Data Structures: No complex structures required; operates on scalar values and 3D vectors. Steps: 1. Check if |v1| < snap. If true, return p1. 2. Check if |v2| < snap. If true, return p2. 3. Check if |v2 - v1| < snap. If true, return p1. 4. Calculate the interpolation factor \mu: \mu = \frac{v2}{v2 - v1} 5. Calculate the intersection point: point = \mu \cdot p1 + (1 - \mu) \cdot p2 Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def trianglepointgeneration(p1, v1, p2, v2, snap=0.01): # Step 1: Check if v1 is close to zero if abs(v1) < snap: return p1 # Step 2: Check if v2 is close to zero if abs(v2) < snap: return p2 # Step 3: Check if the difference between v1 and v2 is small if abs(v2 - v1) < snap: return p1 # Step 4: Calculate mu mu = v2 / (v2 - v1) # Step 5: Calculate point point = mu p1 + (1 - mu) p2 return point Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Division by Zero: The formula for \mu divides by v2 - v1. The check |v2 - v1| < snap prevents this when the denominator is near zero. Precision: The snap threshold handles numerical instability when values are very close to the threshold or to each other. Provides probabilistic selection and coordinate transformation for uniform mesh sampling, building on this method's point generation. Time Complexity: O(1) constant time. Memory Complexity: O(1) constant space. Strengths: Simple, fast, and stable for edges near the threshold due to snapping. Limitations: The snapping behavior may introduce small geometric inaccuracies compared to pure linear interpolation when high precision is required away from the threshold. When to use: When robustness near the threshold is more critical than perfect geometric accuracy, or when performance is paramount. When not to use: When exact linear interpolation is required without heuristic snapping. Originated in the context of marching tets reconstruction algorithms, specifically within the marchingtets-reconstruction project. It is used in surface reconstruction pipelines where stable edge intersection points are needed for generating triangle meshes from scalar fields. mwrazam/marchingtets-reconstruction, https://github.com/mwrazam/marchingtets-reconstruction, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial)

name: Triangle Point Sampling
head: Barycentric Coordinate Sampling, Barycentric Triangle Sampling, Triangle Sampling, Uniform Triangle Sampling
body: Triangle Point Sampling is a method to uniformly sample points over a mesh surface by selecting triangles proportional to their area and then sampling a point uniformly within the selected triangle using barycentric coordinates. It builds on Triangle Point Generation (Linear Interpolation with Snap) by providing the probabilistic selection and coordinate transformation logic required to ensure uniform spatial distribution across the entire mesh surface, correcting for the non-linear area distortion inherent in simple linear interpolation of random variables. The method consists of two phases: triangle selection based on cumulative area, and point generation within the selected triangle using square-root-transformed barycentric coordinates. Inputs: vertices: A list of N triangles, where each triangle is defined by 3 vertices. Each vertex is a 3D vector (Vx, Vy, Vz). areas: A list of N floats, where areas[i] is the area of triangle i. cumulativeareas: A list of N floats, where cumulativeareas[i] is the sum of areas of triangles 0 through i. totalarea is cumulativeareas[-1]. rng: A seeded random number generator capable of producing uniform random numbers in [0, 1). uvs (optional): A list of N triangles, where each triangle has 3 UV coordinates corresponding to the vertices. Outputs: point: A 3D vector (Px, Py, Pz) representing the sampled point on the mesh surface. uv (optional): A 2D vector (U, V) representing the interpolated UV coordinate at the sampled point. cumulativeareas: An array of floats. cumulativeareas[i] = \sum{k=0}^{i} areas[k]. The last element is totalarea. vertices: A list of lists or arrays. vertices[i] contains 3 vertices. vertices[i][j] is the j-th vertex of the i-th triangle. Each vertex is a tuple or array of 3 floats (x, y, z). uvs: Optional. Same structure as vertices, but each vertex is a tuple or array of 2 floats (u, v). 1. Triangle Selection: 1. Generate a random number pick in the range [0, \text{total\area}) using rng. 2. Find the index of the triangle containing pick using binary search on cumulativeareas. Specifically, find the first index triangleindex such that cumulativeareas[triangleindex] > pick. 3. Handle the boundary case: if triangleindex equals the number of triangles (which can happen if pick is very close to totalarea due to floating-point precision), clamp it to the last valid index (len(vertices) - 1). 2. Point Generation: 1. Generate two independent uniform random numbers r1 and r2 in [0, 1) using rng. 2. Compute sqrtr1 as the square root of r1. 3. Calculate barycentric weights: wA = 1 - \sqrt{r1} wB = \sqrt{r1}(1 - r2) wC = \sqrt{r1}r2 4. Retrieve the vertices of the selected triangle: VA = \text{vertices}[\text{triangle\index}][0], VB = \text{vertices}[\text{triangle\index}][1], VC = \text{vertices}[\text{triangle\index}][2]. 5. Compute the 3D point coordinates by linear combination: Px = wA V{A,x} + wB V{B,x} + wC V{C,x} Py = wA V{A,y} + wB V{B,y} + wC V{C,y} Pz = wA V{A,z} + wB V{B,z} + wC V{C,z} 6. If uvs is available, interpolate UV coordinates using the same weights: U = wA UV{A,u} + wB UV{B,u} + wC UV{C,u} V = wA UV{A,v} + wB UV{B,v} + wC UV{C,v} 7. Return point and uv (or None if uvs is not provided). Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math import random def trianglepointsampling(vertices, cumulativeareas, totalarea, rng, uvs=None): """ Samples a point uniformly on the mesh surface defined by vertices. Args: vertices: List of triangles, each triangle is a list of 3 vertices. Each vertex is a tuple/list of 3 floats (x, y, z). cumulativeareas: List of floats, cumulativeareas[i] is sum of areas[0..i]. totalarea: Float, total area of all triangles. rng: Random number generator with method 'random()' returning float in [0, 1). uvs: Optional list of triangles, each triangle is a list of 3 UVs. Each UV is a tuple/list of 2 floats (u, v). Returns: point: Tuple of 3 floats (x, y, z). uv: Tuple of 2 floats (u, v) or None. """ # Step 1: Triangle Selection pick = rng.random() totalarea # Binary search for the first index where cumulativeareas[i] > pick triangleindex = 0 left, right = 0, len(cumulativeareas) - 1 while left <= right: mid = (left + right) // 2 if cumulativeareas[mid] > pick: triangleindex = mid right = mid - 1 else: left = mid + 1 # Handle boundary case: if pick >= totalarea, clamp to last triangle if triangleindex >= len(vertices): triangleindex = len(vertices) - 1 # Step 2: Point Generation r1 = rng.random() r2 = rng.random() sqrtr1 = math.sqrt(r1) # Barycentric weights wA = 1.0 - sqrtr1 wB = sqrtr1 (1.0 - r2) wC = sqrtr1 r2 # Get vertices of the selected triangle triverts = vertices[triangleindex] VA = triverts[0] VB = triverts[1] VC = triverts[2] # Compute 3D point Px = wA VA[0] + wB VB[0] + wC VC[0] Py = wA VA[1] + wB VB[1] + wC VC[1] Pz = wA VA[2] + wB VB[2] + wC VC[2] point = (Px, Py, Pz) # Interpolate UVs if available uv = None if uvs is not None: triuvs = uvs[triangleindex] UVA = triuvs[0] UVB = triuvs[1] UVC = triuvs[2] U = wA UVA[0] + wB UVB[0] + wC UVC[0] V = wA UVA[1] + wB UVB[1] + wC UVC[1] uv = (U, V) return point, uv Random Number Generator: Must produce uniform random numbers in 0, 1). The seed should be set appropriately for reproducibility. Boundary Case: If pick is exactly totalarea (or very close due to floating-point error), triangleindex might exceed the array bounds. [Clamping to the last index is required. Degenerate Triangles: Triangles with zero area (collinear vertices) will have zero probability of being selected if areas are computed correctly. However, if areas are not precomputed or are incorrect, degenerate triangles may cause issues. The method assumes valid, non-degenerate triangles with positive area. Precision: Floating-point precision in cumulativeareas can affect triangle selection probability for very large meshes. Using double precision is recommended for cumulativeareas and pick. A technique to select a triangle with probability proportional to its area by using a precomputed array of cumulative triangle areas and binary search. It uses binary search (bisectleft or equivalent) on the cumulativeareas array to find the first index where the cumulative area exceeds the random pick value. The data structure cumulativeareas is a sequence of floats where cumulativeareas[i] is the sum of areas of triangles 0 through i, and totalarea is the last element. This method ensures that triangles with larger areas have a higher probability of being selected, which is necessary for uniform sampling over the mesh surface. Time Complexity: Triangle selection is O(\log N) due to binary search, where N is the number of triangles. Point generation is O(1). Total time per sample is O(\log N). Memory Complexity: O(N) to store cumulativeareas and vertices. If uvs are stored, an additional O(N) memory is required. Measured Performance: Performance depends on the efficiency of the random number generator and the binary search implementation. For large meshes, the O(\log N) selection cost is negligible compared to the cost of ray tracing or shading. Strengths: Guarantees uniform sampling over the mesh surface. Simple to implement. Efficient for static meshes. Limitations: Requires precomputation of triangle areas and cumulative areas. Binary search adds a small overhead. Not suitable for dynamic meshes where topology changes frequently. When to Use: When uniform sampling over a mesh surface is required, such as in Monte Carlo integration for rendering, physics simulations, or texture mapping. When Not to Use: When the mesh is dynamic and triangles are frequently added/removed. When non-uniform sampling is desired (e.g., sampling based on material properties). Triangle Point Sampling is a fundamental technique in computer graphics for generating uniformly distributed points on mesh surfaces. It is widely used in rendering algorithms, particularly in path tracing and Monte Carlo integration, where uniform sampling is required to reduce variance. The method relies on the mathematical property that barycentric coordinates with square-root-transformed random variables yield a uniform distribution within a triangle. The technique is commonly implemented in 3D asset processing tools and dataset builders for neural rendering methods like 3D Gaussian Splatting. yumehiko/3dgs-dataset-builder, https://github.com/yumehiko/3dgs-dataset-builder, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial)

name: Inverse Linear Interpolation
head: Inverse Linear Interpolation for Isosurface Location, Inverse interpolation problem, Isosurface location calculation, Linear Interpolation Position
body:
Inverse Linear Interpolation calculates the non-integer position x corresponding to a specific scalar value v between two known values v1 and v2 at positions x1 and x2. It solves the inverse interpolation problem for isosurface extraction by determining the exact location along a grid line segment where an interpolated scalar field takes on a specific isosurface value Tm. Unlike forward linear interpolation which estimates a value at a known position, this method inverts the relationship to find the exact position for a known value, which is necessary for precise isosurface mesh generation. It builds on Linear Edge Intersection by providing the specific arithmetic to resolve the intersection point analytically. Inputs: x1, x2: The coordinates of the two endpoints of the grid line segment (typically integers or grid-aligned floats). T1, T2: The scalar data values at x1 and x2 respectively. Tm: The target isosurface level value. Outputs: xm: The interpolated coordinate along the segment where the scalar value equals Tm. Data Structures: No complex data structures are required. The method operates on scalar values and coordinates. If implemented within a grid context, x1 and x2 are often derived from grid indices i, j, k and cell dimensions. Steps: 1. Validate Monotonicity: Check if Tm lies between T1 and T2. Specifically, verify that (Tm - T1)(Tm - T2) \le 0. If not, the isosurface does not cross this segment (or the segment is degenerate/flat). 2. Check for Degeneracy: Check if T1 = T2. If true, the denominator in the interpolation parameter calculation is zero. This case represents zero data variation across the segment. The method is undefined here; typically, the segment is skipped or handled as a special case (e.g., no intersection or midpoint assignment depending on application logic). 3. Compute Interpolation Parameter \alpha: Calculate the normalized distance parameter \alpha using the formula: \alpha =  rac{Tm - T1}{T2 - T1} This parameter represents the fractional distance from x1 to x2. 4. Compute Intersection Position xm: Calculate the final position using the weighted average of the endpoints: xm = (1 - \alpha)x1 + \alpha x2 Alternatively, this can be computed directly as: xm = x1 + (x2 - x1) 	imes  rac{Tm - T1}{T2 - T1} Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def inverselinearinterpolation(x1: float, x2: float, t1: float, t2: float, tm: float) -> float: """ Calculates the position xm along the segment [x1, x2] where the scalar value equals tm. Args: x1: Start coordinate of the segment. x2: End coordinate of the segment. t1: Scalar value at x1. t2: Scalar value at x2. tm: Target isosurface value. Returns: The coordinate xm where the interpolated value is tm. Raises: ValueError: If t1 equals t2 (division by zero) or if tm is not between t1 and t2. """ # Step 1: Check for degeneracy (zero gradient) if t1 == t2: # The segment has constant value. If tm equals t1, the whole segment is on the isosurface. # If tm != t1, there is no intersection. # For standard marching cubes/edges logic, we usually return None or handle outside. # Here we raise to indicate undefined behavior for a single point intersection. raise ValueError("Division by zero: t1 equals t2. No unique intersection point.") # Step 2: Check if the isosurface crosses the segment # The value tm must be between t1 and t2 (inclusive) if not ((t1 <= tm <= t2) or (t2 <= tm <= t1)): # No intersection along this edge for this isovalue return None # Step 3: Calculate the interpolation parameter alpha # alpha is the fraction of the distance from x1 to x2 alpha = (tm - t1) / (t2 - t1) # Step 4: Calculate the intersection position xm # Using the weighted average form: xm = (1 - alpha)x1 + alphax2 # Or the direct form: xm = x1 + alpha (x2 - x1) xm = x1 + alpha (x2 - x1) return xm Sensitivity and Error Analysis: The position xm is sensitive to uncertainties \Delta T1 and \Delta T2 in the data values. The error \Delta xm is given by: \Delta xm =  rac{\partial xm}{\partial T1} \Delta T1 +  rac{\partial xm}{\partial T2} \Delta T2 The partial derivatives are:  rac{\partial xm}{\partial T1} =  rac{Tm - T2}{(T2 - T1)^2}(x2 - x1)  rac{\partial xm}{\partial T2} =  rac{T1 - Tm}{(T2 - T1)^2}(x2 - x1) The relative error can be expressed as:  rac{\Delta xm}{x2 - x1} = -\left(1 - \alphaight) rac{\Delta T1}{T2 - T1} + \alpha  rac{\Delta T2}{T2 - T1} The error bound is: |\Delta xm| \le |x2 - x1|  rac{\max(|\Delta T1|, |\Delta T2|)}{|T2 - T1|} Uncertainty in isosurface location is proportional to the magnitude of data uncertainty and inversely proportional to the data variation |T2 - T1|. A variant that uses Newton-Raphson iteration to refine the intersection point by projecting a sample point onto the isosurface using the gradient. It calculates a displacement parameter t =  rac{fI - f(x0)}{
abla f(x0) \cdot 
abla f(x0)} and updates the point p'\lambda = x0 + t 
abla f(x0). It applies a displacement criterion \Delta d (based on cell dimensions) to discard points projected too far, avoiding convergence to distant roots near local extrema. Time Complexity: O(1). The method involves a constant number of arithmetic operations (subtraction, division, multiplication, addition). Memory Complexity: O(1). No additional memory is required beyond the input variables. Strengths: Exact analytical solution for linear interpolation. Extremely fast computation, suitable for real-time rendering or large-scale mesh generation. Simple to implement. Limitations: Assumes linear variation between grid points. Accuracy degrades if the scalar field varies non-linearly within the cell. Numerical instability or division by zero when T1 = T2 (zero gradient). Sensitivity to data noise increases as |T2 - T1| approaches zero. When to use: Standard isosurface extraction (e.g., Marching Cubes) where linear interpolation is the standard assumption. Real-time volume rendering requiring precise ray-primitive intersection. When not to use: When high-order continuity or non-linear field behavior is critical and higher-order interpolation (e.g., Hermite) is available Siblings: [Hermite Interpolation for Isosurface Extraction]. When the gradient is known to be zero or near-zero, requiring fallback logic. Inverse Linear Interpolation is a fundamental technique in scientific visualization and computer graphics, particularly in isosurface extraction algorithms like Marching Cubes. The method is formally described in the verification guide for Smokeview (Version 6), a tool for visualizing Fire Dynamics Simulation data, where it is referred to as the "inverse interpolation problem". The sensitivity analysis provided in highlights the importance of understanding error propagation in isosurface location due to data uncertainty. The basic implementation is also found in open-source volume rendering projects. The concept is distinct from iterative refinement methods like Approximate Projection or bisection Siblings: [Iterative Bisection Intersection Refinement]. joshcodd/volume-rendering, https://github.com/joshcodd/volume-rendering, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial) Smokeview (Version 6) A Tool for Visualizing Fire Dynamics Simulation Data Volume III: Verification Guide, https://doi.org/10.6028/nist.sp.1017-3, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial) Iso-splatting: a point-based alternative to isosurface visualization, https://doi.org/10.1109/pccga.2003.1238274, fetched 2026-10-26

name: Hermite Interpolation for Isosurface Extraction
head: Hermite contouring, Hermite interpolation
body:
Hermite interpolation for isosurface extraction determines the precise position of an isovertex along a zero-crossing edge by utilizing both scalar field values and gradient information (Hermite data) at the edge endpoints. Unlike Linear Edge Intersection, which assumes linear variation and produces artifacts on non-linear implicit functions, this method fits higher-order polynomials to the local field behavior, significantly improving surface accuracy. It is primarily used in contouring algorithms like Marching Cubes where gradient data is available or can be approximated. Inputs: Edge endpoints: \mathbf{x}0, \mathbf{x}1 \in \mathbb{R}^3. Scalar field values at endpoints: v0 = F(\mathbf{x}0), v1 = F(\mathbf{x}1). Gradient vectors at endpoints: 
abla F0 = 
abla F(\mathbf{x}0), 
abla F1 = 
abla F(\mathbf{x}1). Target isovalue: T (typically 0 for zero-level sets). Outputs: Isovertex position \mathbf{x}{iso} along the edge such that F(\mathbf{x}{iso}) \approx T. No complex data structures are required beyond standard vector and scalar types. The method operates on a per-edge basis. 1. Normalize the Edge Interval: Map the physical edge segment [\mathbf{x}0, \mathbf{x}1] to the parametric interval [0, 1]. Let e = \mathbf{x}1 - \mathbf{x}0. The length is L = \|e\|. If L \approx 0, the edge is degenerate; return \mathbf{x}0 or handle as an error. 2. Compute Directional Derivatives: Calculate the derivative of the scalar field along the direction of the edge at each endpoint. The directional derivative f' is the projection of the gradient onto the edge direction, normalized by the squared length of the edge to account for the parametric scaling. f'0 =  rac{
abla F0 \cdot e}{\|e\|^2} f'1 =  rac{
abla F1 \cdot e}{\|e\|^2} If the edge is axis-aligned, f' is simply the corresponding component of 
abla F. 3. Scale Derivatives for Unit Interval: To fit a polynomial p(t) where t \in [0, 1], the derivatives must be scaled by the edge length L because p'(t) =  rac{dF}{dt} =  rac{dF}{ds}  rac{ds}{dt} = f' \cdot L. d0 = f'0 \cdot L = 
abla F0 \cdot  rac{e}{\|e\|} d1 = f'1 \cdot L = 
abla F1 \cdot  rac{e}{\|e\|} Note: d0 and d1 represent the rate of change with respect to the parametric coordinate t. 4. Adjust Values for Target Isovalue: The interpolation targets the zero-crossing of the shifted function. Define the target values v0, v1 relative to the isovalue T. v0 \leftarrow v0 - T v1 \leftarrow v1 - T 5. Select Interpolation Order and Solve: Choose between Cubic or Quadratic Hermite interpolation based on the nature of the implicit function. Option A: Cubic Hermite Interpolation (General Case) Fit a cubic polynomial p(t) = a0 + a1 t + a2 t^2 + a3 t^3 satisfying: p(0) = v0, \quad p'(0) = d0, \quad p(1) = v1, \quad p'(1) = d1 The coefficients are uniquely determined: a0 = v0 a1 = d0 a2 = 3v1 - 3v0 - 2d0 - d1 a3 = 2v0 - 2v1 + d0 + d1 Solve p(t) = 0 for t \in [0, 1]. Since p(t) is cubic, it may have up to three real roots. Select the root that lies within [0, 1]. If multiple roots exist, select the one closest to the midpoint or consistent with the sign change. Option B: Quadratic Hermite Interpolation (Least-Squares Derivatives) Use this if the implicit function is known to be quadratic (e.g., PSR with B-splines). Fit p(t) = a0 + a1 t + a2 t^2. Interpolate values exactly: a0 = v0 a0 + a1 + a2 = v1 \implies a2 = v1 - v0 - a1 Fit derivatives in a least-squares sense to minimize (a1 - d0)^2 + (a1 + 2a2 - d1)^2. Substituting a2: a1 =  rac{d0 - d1}{2} + v1 - v0 a2 =  rac{d1 - d0}{2} Solve the quadratic equation a2 t^2 + a1 t + a0 = 0 for t \in [0, 1]. 6. Compute Isovertex Position: \mathbf{x}{iso} = \mathbf{x}0 + t \cdot e Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def hermiteisovertex(x0, x1, v0, v1, grad0, grad1, T=0.0): """ Calculate isovertex position using Hermite interpolation. Args: x0, x1: Endpoints of the edge (vectors). v0, v1: Scalar field values at endpoints. grad0, grad1: Gradient vectors at endpoints. T: Target isovalue. Returns: xiso: Position of the isovertex. """ # 1. Edge vector and length e = x1 - x0 Lsq = dot(e, e) # Handle degenerate edge if Lsq < 1e-12: return x0 L = math.sqrt(Lsq) # 2. Directional derivatives (projected onto edge direction) # f' = (grad. e) / ||e||^2 df0 = dot(grad0, e) / Lsq df1 = dot(grad1, e) / Lsq # 3. Scale derivatives for unit interval [0, 1] # d = df L d0 = df0 L d1 = df1 L # 4. Adjust values for target isovalue v0adj = v0 - T v1adj = v1 - T # 5. Solve for t # Using Cubic Hermite as the general robust method a0 = v0adj a1 = d0 a2 = 3 v1adj - 3 v0adj - 2 d0 - d1 a3 = 2 v0adj - 2 v1adj + d0 + d1 # Solve cubic a3t^3 + a2t^2 + a1t + a0 = 0 t = solvecubicrootinrange(a3, a2, a1, a0, 0.0, 1.0) if t is None: # Fallback to linear if cubic fails to find root in range # Linear interpolation: t = -v0 / (v1 - v0) denom = v1adj - v0adj if abs(denom) < 1e-12: return x0 t = -v0adj / denom t = max(0.0, min(1.0, t)) # 6. Compute position xiso = x0 + t e return xiso def solvecubicrootinrange(a3, a2, a1, a0, low, high): """ Finds a real root of a3t^3 + a2t^2 + a1t + a0 = 0 within [low, high]. Returns the root or None if no root exists in range. """ # Use standard cubic formula or numerical solver # For implementation simplicity, we assume a robust cubic solver exists # or implement Cardano's method. Here we outline the logic. roots = [] # Normalize if a3 is 0 (quadratic) if abs(a3) < 1e-12: if abs(a2) < 1e-12: # Linear: a1t + a0 = 0 if abs(a1) > 1e-12: t = -a0 / a1 if low <= t <= high: return t return None else: # Quadratic: a2t^2 + a1t + a0 = 0 disc = a1a1 - 4a2a0 if disc < 0: return None sqrtdisc = math.sqrt(disc) t1 = (-a1 + sqrtdisc) / (2 a2) t2 = (-a1 - sqrtdisc) / (2 a2) if low <= t1 <= high: return t1 if low <= t2 <= high: return t2 return None # Cubic case # Convert to depressed cubic u^3 + pu + q = 0 # t = u - a2/(3a3) p = (3a3a1 - a2a2) / (3a3a3) q = (2a2a2a2 - 9a3a2a1 + 27a3a3a0) / (27a3a3a3) # Discriminant delta = (qq/4 + ppp/27) if delta > 0: # One real root sqrtdelta = math.sqrt(delta) u = cbrt(-q/2 + sqrtdelta) + cbrt(-q/2 - sqrtdelta) t = u - a2 / (3 a3) if low <= t <= high: return t elif delta == 0: # Multiple roots if p == 0 and q == 0: t = -a2 / (3 a3) # Triple root if low <= t <= high: return t else: u = cbrt(-q/2) t1 = 2u - a2/(3a3) t2 = -u - a2/(3a3) if low <= t1 <= high: return t1 if low <= t2 <= high: return t2 else: # Three real roots (casus irreducibilis) r = math.sqrt(-ppp/27) theta = math.acos(-q / (2 r)) m = 2 math.cbrt(r) t1 = m math.cos(theta/3) - a2/(3a3) t2 = m math.cos((theta + 2math.pi)/3) - a2/(3a3) t3 = m math.cos((theta + 4math.pi)/3) - a2/(3a3) candidates = [t1, t2, t3] for t in candidates: if low <= t <= high: return t return None def cbrt(x): if x >= 0: return x (1/3) else: return -((-x) (1/3)) Target Isovalue (T): Typically 0. Interpolation Order: Cubic is the default for general implicit functions; Quadratic is used for known quadratic fields (e.g., B-splines). Degenerate Edges: If \|\mathbf{x}0 - \mathbf{x}1\| \approx 0, the derivative calculation involves division by zero. Guard against this by returning one of the endpoints. Multiple Roots: A cubic polynomial can have up to three real roots. The method must select the root corresponding to the actual zero-crossing of the implicit function. In a zero-crossing edge, there is an odd number of roots. If multiple roots fall in [0, 1], additional context or higher-order analysis may be needed, but typically the root closest to the linear estimate or the one consistent with the sign change is chosen. Least-Squares Pitfall: Do not use the standard least-squares solution for all four constraints (values and derivatives) in the quadratic case. This solution does not guarantee that the polynomial p(t) has a root along the edge even if F(t) does. The value-interpolating, derivative-least-squares approach described above is preferred. Gradient Availability: Hermite data (gradients) may not be available in all datasets. In such cases, gradients can be approximated using finite differences, though accuracy may decrease. Cubic Hermite Interpolation fits a cubic polynomial to the four Hermite constraints (two values, two derivatives). It is the general-purpose method for non-linear implicit functions, offering higher accuracy than linear interpolation by reducing artifacts. It requires solving a cubic equation, which may yield up to three roots, necessitating a strategy to select the correct isovertex. Choose this when the implicit function is not known to be quadratic and high accuracy is required. See Cubic Hermite Interpolation. This variant fits a quadratic polynomial that interpolates the endpoint values exactly and fits the endpoint derivatives in a least-squares sense. It is specifically designed for implicit functions known to be quadratic, such as those represented by linear combinations of second-order B-splines (e.g., PSR). It is computationally cheaper than cubic interpolation (solving a quadratic vs. cubic equation) and avoids the multiple-root ambiguity of cubics. Choose this when the underlying field is known to be quadratic. Time Complexity: O(1) per edge. Cubic interpolation involves solving a cubic equation (constant number of operations). Quadratic interpolation involves solving a quadratic equation (constant number of operations). Memory Complexity: O(1) per edge. No additional storage is required beyond the input values and gradients. Measured Performance: Not given in the sources. Scaling: Scales linearly with the number of edges in the mesh. Strengths: Significantly reduces reconstruction artifacts compared to linear interpolation for non-linear implicit functions. Provides mathematically precise isovertex positions given gradient data. Limitations: Requires gradient data (Hermite data), which may need to be computed via finite differences if not available, adding overhead and potential noise. Cubic interpolation can have multiple roots, requiring careful selection logic. When to Use: When high-quality isosurfaces are required for non-linear implicit functions and gradient information is available or can be efficiently approximated. When Not to Use: When gradient data is unavailable and finite difference approximation is too expensive or noisy, or when the implicit function is strictly linear (linear interpolation is sufficient and faster). Hermite interpolation for isosurface extraction was proposed to address the inaccuracies of linear interpolation in contouring algorithms like Marching Cubes when applied to non-linear implicit functions. The method utilizes the gradient of the implicit function to generate more accurate isosurfaces by means of higher-order interpolation techniques. The approach was demonstrated to provide clear quality improvements, even when Hermite data is not directly available and gradients are approximated using finite differences. name: Cubic Hermite Interpolation
head: Third Order Polynomial, Cubic polynomial interpolation
body: Cubic Hermite Interpolation is a method for determining precise isovertex positions along zero-crossing edges in contouring algorithms by fitting a cubic polynomial to both function values and gradients (Hermite data) at the edge endpoints. It improves upon linear interpolation by reducing artifacts caused by the non-linear nature of implicit functions, offering higher accuracy at the cost of solving for polynomial coefficients and finding cubic roots. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: Two scalar field values v0 = f(x0) and v1 = f(x1) at edge endpoints x0 and x1; two derivative estimates d0 = f'(x0) and d1 = f'(x1); and the target isovalue k. Outputs: The position x^ along the edge where the interpolated function equals k. Data Structures: The method operates on scalar values and a single cubic polynomial defined by four coefficients. Steps: 1. Compute Coefficients: Determine the coefficients a0, a1, a2, a3 of the cubic polynomial p(x) = a0 + a1 x + a2 x^2 + a3 x^3 such that it satisfies the Hermite constraints: \begin{aligned} p(x0) &= v0 \\ p(x1) &= v1 \\ p'(x0) &= d0 \\ p'(x1) &= d1 \end{aligned} The closed-form solution for these coefficients is: \begin{aligned} a0 &= v0 \\ a1 &= d0 \\ a2 &= 3v1 - 3v0 - 2d0 - d1 \\ a3 &= 2v0 - 2v1 + d0 + d1 \end{aligned} These formulas assume the edge is parameterized such that x0=0 and x1=1. 2. Solve for Roots: Find all real roots of the equation p(x) = k, which is equivalent to finding roots of q(x) = a0 + a1 x + a2 x^2 + a3 x^3 - k = 0. 3. Select Isovertex: If multiple real roots exist within the edge interval, select the "middle" root to uniquely define the isovertex position. This choice is based on the observation that a zero-crossing edge must contain an odd number of roots, and the middle root best represents the primary crossing. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def cubichermiteinterpolation(v0, v1, d0, d1, k): """ Computes the isovertex position along an edge [0, 1] using cubic Hermite interpolation. Args: v0: Function value at x=0 v1: Function value at x=1 d0: Derivative estimate at x=0 d1: Derivative estimate at x=1 k: Target isovalue Returns: xstar: The position of the isovertex along the edge [0, 1] """ # Step 1: Compute cubic coefficients # p(x) = a0 + a1x + a2x^2 + a3x^3 a0 = v0 a1 = d0 a2 = 3 v1 - 3 v0 - 2 d0 - d1 a3 = 2 v0 - 2 v1 + d0 + d1 # Adjust for isovalue k: solve a0 + a1x + a2x^2 + a3x^3 = k # Equivalent to: a3x^3 + a2x^2 + a1x + (a0 - k) = 0 c3 = a3 c2 = a2 c1 = a1 c0 = a0 - k # Step 2: Find real roots of the cubic equation roots = solvecubicreal(c0, c1, c2, c3) # Step 3: Filter roots within the edge interval [0, 1] validroots = [r for r in roots if 0.0 <= r <= 1.0] if not validroots: # Fallback: If no roots found, return midpoint or handle error # This can happen if the cubic approximation fails to capture the crossing return 0.5 if len(validroots) == 1: return validroots[0] # Select the middle root if multiple roots exist validroots.sort() return validroots[len(validroots) // 2] def solvecubicreal(c0, c1, c2, c3): """ Solves c3x^3 + c2x^2 + c1x + c0 = 0 for real roots. Uses Cardano's method with robust sign handling for cube roots. """ if c3 == 0: if c2 == 0: if c1 == 0: return [] return [-c0 / c1] disc = c12 - 4 c2 c0 if disc < 0: return [] sqrtdisc = math.sqrt(disc) return [(-c1 - sqrtdisc) / (2 c2), (-c1 + sqrtdisc) / (2 c2)] a = c2 / c3 b = c1 / c3 c = c0 / c3 p = b - a2 / 3 q = 2 a3 / 27 - a b / 3 + c disc = q2 / 4 + p3 / 27 roots = [] if disc > 0: # One real root uval = -q / 2 + math.sqrt(disc) vval = -q / 2 - math.sqrt(disc) u = math.copysign(abs(uval)(1/3), uval) v = math.copysign(abs(vval)(1/3), vval) roots.append(u + v - a / 3) elif disc == 0: # Multiple real roots if q == 0: roots.append(-a / 3) else: uval = -q / 2 u = math.copysign(abs(uval)(1/3), uval) roots.append(2 u - a / 3) roots.append(-u - a / 3) else: # Three distinct real roots r = math.sqrt(-p3 / 27) theta = math.acos(-q / (2 r)) m = 2 r(1/3) roots.append(m math.cos(theta / 3) - a / 3) roots.append(m math.cos((theta + 2 math.pi) / 3) - a / 3) roots.append(m math.cos((theta + 4 math.pi) / 3) - a / 3) return roots Parameters: Derivative Estimation: Derivatives f'(x0) and f'(x1) are often not directly available and must be approximated using finite difference methods. The quality of these estimates significantly impacts accuracy. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Multiple Roots: A cubic polynomial can have up to three real roots. The location and count of these roots may be sensitive to small perturbations in function coefficients. Root Selection: If multiple roots exist, the "middle" root is selected to ensure a unique isovertex position. Missing Roots: If the cubic polynomial p(x) does not have a root along the edge despite f(x) having a zero-crossing, the interpolation fails to capture the crossing. This can occur if the derivative estimates are poor or the function is highly non-linear. Kochanek-Bartels spline interpolation is an interpolation method used to generate smooth tour paths through a series of keyframes in Smokeview. Each interval is uniquely specified using a function value and a derivative at both endpoints, requiring four data values. Derivatives at endpoints are computed in terms of three parameters: bias, continuity, and tension. Each parameter ranges from -1 to 1 with a default value of 0, though bias and continuity are set to zero internally by Smokeview. A tension value of 1 results in a linear spline, removing smoothness. Unlike standard cubic splines, Kochanek-Bartels allows local control via bias, continuity, and tension parameters to adjust path smoothness or create abrupt changes. Solving the 4x4 system is constant time O(1) per edge due to the closed-form solution. Finding cubic roots is also O(1) but involves more arithmetic operations than linear interpolation. Memory complexity is O(1) additional memory per edge. The method provides higher accuracy than linear interpolation, especially for non-linear implicit functions. It is sensitive to derivative estimation errors. It may fail to find a root if the cubic approximation is poor. It should be used when high accuracy is required and derivative information (or good estimates) is available. Cubic Hermite Interpolation was proposed as a higher-order interpolation method to improve the accuracy of level crossing detection in isosurface extraction algorithms like Marching Cubes. It builds on the concept of Hermite interpolation, which uses both function values and derivatives to construct a polynomial. The specific closed-form coefficients for the edge case are detailed in, while the broader context of high-order interpolation methods is discussed in. name: Edge-Crossing Error Approximation
head: Linear interpolation error estimation, Taylor series error approximation
body: This method estimates the positional error introduced by linear interpolation when determining the intersection of a scalar field with an isovalue on a grid edge. It leverages Taylor series expansion to bound the difference between the true root and the linear approximation without solving a linear system. It distinguishes itself from Linear Edge Intersection by providing a quantitative error metric rather than just the position, and from Iterative Bisection Intersection Refinement by offering an analytical estimate rather than a numerical refinement. Inputs: Scalar field values at grid vertices xi, x{i+1}, the isovalue k, and the linear crossing position \bar{x}^ computed via Linear Edge Intersection. Outputs: The estimated edge-crossing error e (or bound eb). Data Structures: The method requires the first-order divided differences U[i, i+1] and second-order divided differences U[i-1, i+1] and U[i, i+2]. U[i] = f(xi) U[i, i+1] = \frac{U[i+1] - U[i]}{x{i+1} - xi} U[i-1, i+1] = \frac{U[i, i+1] - U[i-1, i]}{x{i+1} - x{i-1}} U[i, i+2] = \frac{U[i+1, i+2] - U[i, i+1]}{x{i+2} - xi} Steps: 1. Compute the divided differences U[i, i+1], U[i-1, i+1], and U[i, i+2] using the scalar values at vertices x{i-1}, xi, x{i+1}, x{i+2}. 2. Calculate the maximum second-order divided difference magnitude: M = \max(|U[i-1, i+1]|, |U[i, i+2]|). 3. Compute the tighter vertex approximation error estimate e using the linear crossing position \bar{x}^: e = \frac{M}{U[i, i+1]} (\bar{x}^ - xi)(\bar{x}^ - x{i+1}) 4. (Optional) Compute the standard bound approximation eb for a conservative upper bound: eb = \frac{M}{U[i, i+1]} (xi - x{i+1})^2 Formulas: The theoretical error bound is derived from the Taylor series remainder: |x^ - \bar{x}^| \le \frac{\max{\xi \in [xi, x{i+1}]} |f''(\xi)|}{2 U[i, i+1]} (x^ - xi)(x^ - x{i+1}) where x^ is the true root and \xi is an unknown point in the interval. Since f''(\xi) and x^ are unknown, they are approximated as described in Steps 2-3. Parameters: Grid spacing: Implicit in xi coordinates. Typical performance: Error computation takes <1ms for the Tangle dataset, compared to seconds for isosurface comparison methods. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Division by Zero: If U[i, i+1] \approx 0, the denominator becomes small, leading to large error estimates or numerical instability. This occurs when the scalar values at the edge endpoints are equal. Overestimation: The standard bound eb tends to significantly overestimate the error compared to the measured error. The vertex approximation e is much tighter. Hidden Features: Linear interpolation may miss isosurface patches (hidden features) entirely. This method estimates error on existing crossings but does not detect missing features; see Hidden Features Detection and Reconstruction for that capability. This variant detects and reconstructs isosurface patches (hidden features) not captured by standard linear interpolation by analyzing slopes on cell edges. Definition: Identifies cells where linear interpolation fails to capture topology changes due to opposite slopes surrounding a feature. Detection Condition: A hidden feature is detected in a cell if for any of its edges, two of the three slopes (divided differences) of neighboring edges have opposite signs. In 1D, this is indicated by U[i-1, i+1] \cdot U[i+1, i+2] < 0. Reconstruction: The detected cell is subdivided into smaller subcells using tri-cubic Lagrange polynomial interpolation. Linear interpolation for refinement does not recover these features. The Marching Cubes (or Squares) algorithm is then applied to each subcell. Pitfalls: Cell refinements lead to cracks in the reconstructed isosurface where refined cells meet unrefined neighbors. Crack-free techniques from adaptive mesh refinement are required to resolve these mismatches. Time Complexity: O(1) per edge, as it involves a constant number of arithmetic operations and divided difference calculations. Memory Complexity: O(1) auxiliary memory per edge, requiring storage of local scalar values and divided differences. Performance: The approximated error computation is computationally efficient, taking less than 1ms for the Tangle example, whereas measuring error via isosurface comparison takes a few seconds. This efficiency scales well with grid resolution, unlike comparison-based methods. Strengths: Provides quick insight into isosurface quality without additional sampling or solving linear systems. The vertex approximation e is significantly closer to the measured error than the standard bound eb. Limitations: It only estimates error for existing crossings; it does not detect missing features (hidden features) on its own. The standard bound eb is a loose overestimate. The method originates from the analysis of interpolation errors in volume rendering and isosurface extraction. It builds on the observation that Taylor series expansion can estimate local function error. Previous work by Moller et al. used Taylor series for smooth filters and error estimation in volume data approximation. This specific application to edge-crossing error in Marching Cubes algorithms was proposed to visualize isosurface discrepancies and guide decisions on using higher-order interpolation or higher-resolution data. Estimation and Visualization of Isosurface Uncertainty from Linear and High-Order Interpolation Methods, https://arxiv.org/abs/2409.00043v1, fetched 2026-10-26

name: Voxel selection via pick ray intersection
head: Basic picker, Pick ray intersection for voxel selection, Voxel Picking with Bresenham's Algorithm, Voxel Selecting
body: This method extracts spatial information from a simulation by mapping 2D screen coordinates to 3D voxel indices, serving as a direct manipulation interface for tasks such as segmentation seed selection. It differs from Reverse Index Map for Voxel Location by computing the intersection dynamically rather than relying on a pre-computed index texture, and from Ray-Box Intersection for Interaction by focusing on identifying the specific seed voxel for segmentation rather than just the entry point for fluid injection. Inputs: Screen coordinates (x{screen}, y{screen}) from user input (mouse click/drag). Camera projection parameters (orthographic view matrix and viewport dimensions). Volume bounding box definition (min/max extents in world space). Voxel grid resolution (dimensions Nx, Ny, Nz). Outputs: 3D voxel index (i, j, k) corresponding to the intersected voxel. Data Structures: Pick Ray: Defined by origin \mathbf{o} and direction \mathbf{d}. In orthographic projection, \mathbf{o} is derived from the screen position mapped to the near plane, and \mathbf{d} is constant (view direction). Volume Bounding Box: Axis-aligned box defined by \mathbf{B}{min} and \mathbf{B}{max}. Steps: 1. Ray Generation: Construct the pick ray from screen coordinates. For orthographic projection, map (x{screen}, y{screen}) to world space coordinates on the camera's near plane to determine ray origin \mathbf{o}. The ray direction \mathbf{d} is the negative view vector (or forward vector depending on coordinate system). 2. Bounding Box Intersection: Perform ray-box intersection tests to find the closest point of intersection between the pick ray and the volume's rectangular solid. This uses standard ray-tracing techniques. 3. Voxel Selection: If an intersection exists, determine the voxel index (i, j, k) at the intersection point. The sources indicate this can be implemented using a modified Bresenham's Algorithm to traverse the voxel grid from the entry point. Alternatively, direct coordinate conversion from the intersection point to voxel indices is used. 4. Return Index: Output the integer voxel coordinates (i, j, k). Formulas: Ray Origin (Orthographic): \mathbf{o} = \mathbf{C} + x{world} \mathbf{R} + y{world} \mathbf{U} + z{near} \mathbf{D}, where \mathbf{C} is camera center, \mathbf{R}, \mathbf{U} are right/up vectors, and z{near} is the near plane distance. Ray-Box Intersection: Standard slab method or parametric intersection to find t{min} and t{max}. Voxel Index: i = \lfloor \frac{x{intersect} - B{min,x}}{Vx} \rfloor, j = \lfloor \frac{y{intersect} - B{min,y}}{Vy} \rfloor, k = \lfloor \frac{z{intersect} - B{min,z}}{Vz} \rfloor, where Vx, Vy, Vz are voxel dimensions. Parameters: Projection Type: Orthographic only. Grid Resolution: Depends on simulation volume. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Perspective Projection: The described implementation does not support perspective projections; it is limited to orthographic views. Out-of-Bounds: If the screen coordinate does not intersect the volume bounding box, no voxel is selected. Precision: Integer voxel indices must be clamped to valid grid ranges [0, Nx-1], [0, Ny-1], [0, Nz-1]. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def selectvoxel(screenx, screeny, camera, volumebounds, voxelsize): # Step 1: Generate pick ray (Orthographic only) # Map screen coordinates to world space on near plane # Assuming camera has right (R), up (U), forward (F) vectors and position (C) # and viewport width/height are known aspect = camera.viewportwidth / camera.viewportheight # Normalize screen coords to [-1, 1] range (adjust based on actual API) nx = (2.0 screenx / camera.viewportwidth) - 1.0 ny = (2.0 screeny / camera.viewportheight) - 1.0 # Scale by view frustum dimensions at near plane # For orthographic, this is often fixed or based on ortho width/height viewwidth = camera.orthowidth viewheight = viewwidth / aspect rayorigin = camera.position + \ (nx viewwidth 0.5) camera.right + \ (ny viewheight 0.5) camera.up raydirection = -camera.forward # Orthographic ray direction is constant # Step 2: Ray-Box Intersection # Standard slab method tmin = -float('inf') tmax = float('inf') for axis in range(3): if abs(raydirection[axis]) < 1e-8: # Ray is parallel to slab if rayorigin[axis] < volumebounds.min[axis] or rayorigin[axis] > volumebounds.max[axis]: return None # No intersection else: invd = 1.0 / raydirection[axis] t1 = (volumebounds.min[axis] - rayorigin[axis]) invd t2 = (volumebounds.max[axis] - rayorigin[axis]) invd tmin = max(tmin, min(t1, t2)) tmax = min(tmax, max(t1, t2)) if tmin > tmax: return None # No intersection if tmax < 0: return None # Box is behind ray # Use closest intersection point t = tmin if tmin > 0 else tmax # Prefer positive t intersectionpoint = rayorigin + t raydirection # Step 3: Convert intersection point to voxel index # Assuming volume bounds align with voxel grid start voxelx = int((intersectionpoint.x - volumebounds.min.x) / voxelsize.x) voxely = int((intersectionpoint.y - volumebounds.min.y) / voxelsize.y) voxelz = int((intersectionpoint.z - volumebounds.min.z) / voxelsize.z) # Clamp to valid range voxelx = max(0, min(voxelx, volumebounds.resolution.x - 1)) voxely = max(0, min(voxely, volumebounds.resolution.y - 1)) voxelz = max(0, min(voxelz, volumebounds.resolution.z - 1)) return (voxelx, voxely, voxelz) Uses a pre-computed index texture for direct lookup from screen to voxel, avoiding runtime ray casting. Choose when performance is critical and memory allows for the index map. Uses DDA raycasting for dynamic voxel painting/erasing with brush volumes. Choose when editing voxel data directly is required. Focuses on geometric intersection for fluid injection or placement. Choose when the specific voxel index is less important than the world position for simulation effects. Uses face normals from mesh geometry to determine voxel indices. Choose when working with voxelized meshes rather than regular grids. Time Complexity: O(1) for ray-box intersection and coordinate conversion. Bresenham's traversal is O(N) where N is the number of voxels traversed, but typically only the entry voxel is needed for seed selection. Memory Complexity: O(1) auxiliary memory. Performance: Quick and reliable for orthographic views. Strengths: Intuitive user interface for segmentation; simple implementation for orthographic projections. Limitations: Does not support perspective projections. Accuracy depends on voxel grid alignment. The method originated in the context of volume visualization and segmentation applications, specifically the SIV (Segmentation of Isosurfaces in Volumes) system. It was also independently implemented in homebrew voxel engines for real-time simulation interaction. The technique leverages the regular structure of voxel grids to simplify ray-primitive intersection, often employing Bresenham's algorithm for grid traversal. It is used in medical imaging and scientific visualization for seed point selection during isosurface segmentation. name: Reverse Index Map for Voxel Location
head: P->V Mapping
body: The Reverse Index Map (P->V) is a technique used to determine the 3D voxel location in volume coordinates from a 2D fragment location in the framebuffer and a current slice z-offset. It serves as the inverse of the forward mapping used during texture sampling, enabling direct manipulation and segmentation by linking screen pixels to volumetric data. Inputs: 1. Fragment location in the framebuffer (x{fb}, y{fb}). 2. Current slice z-offset (z{slice}). Outputs: 1. Voxel location in volume coordinates (V = (xv, yv, zv)). Data Structures: Reverse Index Texture: A 2D texture mapping packed coordinates (P) to volume coordinates (V). The texture stores the 3D voxel coordinates corresponding to each 2D screen position. The layout typically stores xv, yv, zv as components (e.g., RGBA or RGB with one component unused or packed) in the texture units. Steps: 1. Retrieve the fragment's 2D coordinates (x{fb}, y{fb}) from the framebuffer. 2. Combine these coordinates with the current slice z-offset to form the packed coordinate P. In the context of slice-based rendering, P typically represents the 2D screen position (x{fb}, y{fb}) which indexes into the Reverse Index Texture. 3. Sample the Reverse Index Texture at P to retrieve the volume coordinates V. V = \text{TextureLookup}(\text{ReverseIndexTexture}, P) 4. Use V as the seed voxel for subsequent ray integration or segmentation operations. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def getvoxellocation(fragmentx, fragmenty, slicezoffset, reverseindextexture): """ Determines the 3D voxel location from 2D framebuffer coordinates. Args: fragmentx (int): X coordinate in the framebuffer. fragmenty (int): Y coordinate in the framebuffer. slicezoffset (float): The current z-offset for the slice being rendered. reverseindextexture (Texture): A 2D texture mapping 2D screen coords to 3D volume coords. Returns: tuple: (xv, yv, zv) volume coordinates. """ # Packed coordinates P are derived from the fragment location. # In slice-based rendering, P typically corresponds to (fragmentx, fragmenty). p = (fragmentx, fragmenty) # Sample the reverse index texture to get volume coordinates V. # The texture stores (xv, yv, zv) for each 2D position. v = reverseindextexture[p] # v is expected to be a vector (xv, yv, zv). return v Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision: The accuracy of the voxel location depends on the resolution of the Reverse Index Texture. Boundaries: Fragments outside the volume bounds will return invalid or undefined coordinates. Slice Offset: The slice z-offset must be consistent with the data used to generate the Reverse Index Texture. A technique used during ray integration to map volume coordinates to packed texture coordinates via a forward mapping index texture (V \to P). It is the inverse of the Reverse Index Map. While the Reverse Index Map is used for interaction (screen to volume), the Forward Index Map is used for sampling (volume to texture). The layout is a texture mapping volume coordinates (V) to packed texture coordinates (P). A method to map 2D mouse clicks on a Maximum Intensity Projection (MIP) image to 3D voxel coordinates by maintaining a depth buffer of the current projection. Unlike the Reverse Index Map which uses a pre-computed texture, this method maintains a 2D buffer Z(i, j) = (x, y, z) that records the voxel position for each projected MIP value or surface color. When a user selects a point [i, j] in the MIP, the appropriate voxel address (x, y, z) is looked up from the buffer. This is used to redefine slice positions in orthogonal viewers or provide initial points for analysis.
