name: Pulsar Forward Pass (Sphere Intersection and Draw)
body: The Pulsar Forward Pass is a GPU-accelerated ray-sphere intersection and rendering method designed for differentiable sphere-based neural rendering. It solves the problem of efficiently determining which spheres contribute to each pixel and computing their color contributions while simultaneously preparing data for a backward pass. It sets itself apart from sibling methods by explicitly managing a shared memory buffer for sphere draw information and using a fixed-size priority queue to track the closest five spheres per pixel, enabling a highly optimized backward pass that avoids redundant intersection searches. Inputs: A list of N spheres, each defined by center \mathbf{c}i, radius ri, and color/opacity parameters. Camera parameters (origin \mathbf{o}, direction vectors for each pixel). Rendering resolution (width W, height H). Early termination threshold n (default 1%). Outputs: Rendered image (color and optionally depth/normal). Gradients for sphere parameters and camera parameters (if backward pass is enabled). 1. Sphere List: Array of sphere parameters. 2. Block-wide Shared Memory Buffer: Stores sphere draw information with intersections. Size is a multiple of the block size to always accommodate all sphere hits. 3. Backward Pass Buffer: Per-pixel storage containing the normalization factor, and the intersection depths and IDs of the closest 5 spheres. 4. Priority Queue: Per-pixel, fixed-size (5 elements) optimized priority queue tracking the IDs and intersection depths of the closest spheres for the backward pass. 5. Gradient Buffers: Sphere-specific gradients buffer and camera gradient buffer per sphere. Block Size: 16 \times 16 = 256 threads (8 warps per block). Early Termination Threshold (n): Default 1%. Max Tracked Spheres: 5 (fixed at compile time). Camera Gradient Normalization Constant: 1 \times 10^{-3}. 1. Sorting and Bounding: Sort spheres to find an arbitrary number of closest spheres to the camera. Manual sorting is used instead of OPTIX to avoid the runtime hit and because OPTIX does not provide access to the acceleration structure. During sorting, find the enclosing rectangle for all visible spheres and use this information for tighter bounds of the region to draw. 2. Block-wise Intersection Search: Launch GPU blocks of 16 \times 16 threads. Implement intersection search through coalesced loading of the intersection information structures and testing of the limits of the current pixel block. Write access to the shared memory buffer needs to be properly synchronized. If the buffer becomes too full or the spheres are exhausted, Step 3 execution is invoked to clear it. 3. Draw Operation (Step 2): Each pixel thread works autonomously. The draw operation is executed for each pixel separately and for each sphere draw information that has been loaded into the shared memory buffer. Because every pixel is processed by its own thread, write conflicts for the channel information are avoided and each pixel thread can work through the list of loaded draw information at full speed. Track intersection depths for each sphere using a small optimized priority queue to track the IDs and intersection depths of the closest five spheres for the backward pass. Update the denominator of the rendering equation to continuously track the minimum required depth that a sphere must have for an n percent contribution to the color channels. Each pixel thread can vote whether it is 'done' with processing spheres and future spheres would have not enough impact; if all pixels in a block vote 'done', execution is terminated. The vote is implemented through a thread-warp-block stage-wise reduction operation. If a backward pass is intended, write information from the forward pass into a buffer. 4. Backward Pass (Optional): Parallelize the backward pass over the pixels. Each thread only processes the spheres that have been detected at the pixel position, but requires synchronization for gradient accumulation for each sphere. Reserve memory to store all sphere specific gradients. Accumulate sphere gradients through synchronized access from each pixel thread. Allocate a buffer for the camera gradient information per sphere. Accumulate camera gradients sphere-wise and run a device-wide reduction as a post-processing step, because synchronizing the accumulation of camera gradients causes too much memory pressure. Normalize sphere gradients by averaging over the number of pixels from which they are computed. Normalize camera gradients by taking the area that each sphere covers in the image as a normalization factor, together with a constant 1 \times 10^{-3}. Gradient computation for each gradient is only performed if the gradients are required by the PyTorch autodiff framework. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math BLOCKSIZE = 256 # 16x16 threads, 8 warps per block MAXTRACKEDSPHERES = 5 # Fixed at compile time EARLYTERMINATIONTHRESHOLD = 0.01 # Default 1% CAMERAGRADNORMCONSTANT = 1e-3 # class Sphere: def init(self, center, radius, color, opacity, sphereid): self.center = center self.radius = radius self.color = color self.opacity = opacity self.sphereid = sphereid def raysphereintersect(origin, direction, sphere): # Standard ray-sphere intersection oc = [origin[i] - sphere.center[i] for i in range(3)] a = sum(dd for d in direction) b = sum(oc[i]direction[i] for i in range(3)) c = sum(oc[i]oc[i] for i in range(3)) - sphere.radius2 disc = bb - ac if disc < 0: return None t = (-b - math.sqrt(disc)) / a if t < 0: return None hitpoint = [origin[i] + tdirection[i] for i in range(3)] normal = [(hitpoint[i] - sphere.center[i])/sphere.radius for i in range(3)] return t, hitpoint, normal def sphereintersectsblock(sphere, bx, by, bw, bh): # Axis-aligned bounding box test against block bounds return (sphere.center[0] - sphere.radius <= bx + bw and sphere.center[0] + sphere.radius >= bx and sphere.center[1] - sphere.radius <= by + bh and sphere.center[1] + sphere.radius >= by) def pulsarforwardpass(spheres, cameraorigin, cameradirections, W, H): # Step 1: Sorting and Bounding sortedspheres = sorted(enumerate(spheres), key=lambda x: math.dist(cameraorigin, x[1].center)) # Compute enclosing rectangle for visible spheres # (Sources do not specify exact bounding box algorithm) # Initialize buffers image = [[0.0]3 for in range(H)] backwardbuffers = [[None]W for in range(H)] spheregradients = [0.0]len(spheres) cameragradients = [0.0]len(spheres) # Step 2 & 3: Block-wise Intersection and Draw for by in range(0, H, 16): for bx in range(0, W, 16): sharedbuffer = [] # Coalesced loading and intersection search for idx, sphere in sortedspheres: if sphereintersectsblock(sphere, bx, by, 16, 16): sharedbuffer.append((idx, sphere)) # Draw Operation: each pixel thread works autonomously for y in range(by, min(by + 16, H)): for x in range(bx, min(bx + 16, W)): raydir = cameradirections[y][x] pq = [] # Priority queue for closest 5 spheres denom = 1.0 # Denominator of rendering equation done = False for idx, sphere in sharedbuffer: if done: break hit = raysphereintersect(cameraorigin, raydir, sphere) if hit: depth, point, normal = hit # Priority Queue Update pq.append((depth, idx)) pq.sort(key=lambda p: p[0]) if len(pq) > MAXTRACKEDSPHERES: pq.pop() # Update rendering equation denominator denom += sphere.opacity # Compute color contribution image[y][x] = [image[y][x][i] + sphere.color[i]sphere.opacity for i in range(3)] # Early termination check if depth > denom EARLYTERMINATIONTHRESHOLD: done = True # Backward Pass Buffer Write backwardbuffers[y][x] = { 'normfactor': denom, 'depths': [d for d, in pq], 'ids': [i for, i in pq] } # Early termination vote via thread-warp-block reduction # If all pixels in block vote done, terminate block loop # (Sources do not specify exact reduction implementation) # Step 4: Backward Pass (Optional) # Gradient computation only if required by autodiff framework # Parallelize over pixels for y in range(H): for x in range(W): state = backwardbuffers[y][x] if state is None: continue for d, sid in state['depths']: # Sphere gradient accumulation via synchronized access # (Sources do not specify exact atomic/sync mechanism) pass # Camera gradient accumulation sphere-wise pass # Normalize sphere gradients by averaging over pixel count # Normalize camera gradients by area CAMERAGRADNORMCONSTANT return image, spheregradients, cameragradients Buffer Overflow: The shared memory buffer must be synchronized and cleared if it becomes full or spheres are exhausted. Memory Pressure: Synchronizing camera gradient accumulation per pixel causes too much memory pressure; use sphere-wise accumulation and device-wide reduction. Precision: Use double precision for intersection calculations if necessary to avoid artifacts, though not explicitly stated, standard practice in ray tracing. Degenerate Input: Empty sphere list or zero-radius spheres should be handled gracefully. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Measured Performance: Camera gradient accumulation reduction takes 0.6 ms for 1,000,000 spheres. Scaling: Scales favorably with future GPU generations due to block size optimization. Scales well with image resolution and the number of spheres. Strengths: Fast execution, robust to large spheres, efficient backward pass by avoiding redundant intersection searches. Limitations: Requires manual sorting because OPTIX does not provide access to the acceleration structure. When to Use: Not given in the sources. When Not to Use: Not given in the sources. The Pulsar Forward Pass was introduced in the paper "Pulsar: Efficient Sphere-based Neural Rendering". It was developed to address the limitations of existing methods like OPTIX, which do not provide access to the acceleration structure for manual sorting and arbitrary closest sphere queries. The method was designed to be efficient and differentiable, enabling optimization of sphere parameters and camera parameters using gradient descent. It has been used in neural rendering applications where sphere-based representations are advantageous. name: Inverse Transforming Spheres
head: Inverse Möbius Transformation of Spheres, Inverse Quaternion Möbius Transform for Spheres
body: Inverse Transforming Spheres computes the coefficients (\alpha', \beta', \gamma') of a sphere in kernel space given the coefficients (\alpha, \beta, \gamma) of that sphere in world space after a quaternionic Möbius transformation. This allows a ray tracer to test if a world-space sphere intersects a kernel distance function by transforming the sphere into kernel space and performing a standard ray-sphere intersection. It differs from forward transformation by solving for the pre-image coefficients directly via algebraic expansion of the quaternionic Möbius map, avoiding iterative root-finding. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: Sphere coefficients in world space \alpha \in \mathbb{R}, \beta \in \mathbb{H}0 (pure quaternion), \gamma \in \mathbb{R}, and Möbius transformation matrix coefficients a, b, c, d \in \mathbb{H}. Outputs: Sphere coefficients in kernel space \alpha' \in \mathbb{R}, \beta' \in \mathbb{H}0, \gamma' \in \mathbb{R}. Data Structures: Quaternions are represented as 4-component tuples (w, x, y, z). \mathbb{H}0 denotes pure quaternions where the scalar part w is zero. \bar{q} denotes the quaternion conjugate (w, -x, -y, -z). q\bar{q} denotes the squared norm w^2+x^2+y^2+z^2. \text{Re}(q) denotes the scalar part w. Numbered Steps: 1. Compute conjugates \bar{a}, \bar{b}, \bar{c}, \bar{d}, \bar{\beta}. 2. Compute scalar products a\bar{a}, c\bar{c}, b\bar{b}, and d\bar{d}. 3. Compute quaternion products \bar{c}\beta a, \bar{b}a, \bar{d}\beta a, \bar{b}\bar{\beta}c, \bar{d}\bar{c}, and \bar{d}\beta b. 4. Extract real parts of \bar{c}\beta a and \bar{d}\beta b. 5. Assemble \alpha', \beta', and \gamma' using the linear combinations of the computed terms. Formulas: The implicit equation of a sphere or plane in quaternion space is: \alpha(q\bar{q}) + \beta q + \bar{q}\bar{\beta} + \gamma = 0 where q \in \mathbb{H}. For a sphere of radius \rho centered at \kappa, the coefficients are \alpha = 1, \beta = \kappa, and \gamma = |\kappa|^2 - \rho^2. The Möbius transformation is defined as \mathcal{L}(q) = (aq+b)(cq+d)^{-1}. Substituting \mathcal{L}(q) into the sphere equation and clearing denominators by multiplying by (cq+d) from the left and (cq+d) from the right yields the original sphere coefficients: \alpha' = \alpha a \bar{a} + 2 \text{Re}(\bar{c} \beta a) + \gamma \bar{c} c \beta' = \alpha \bar{b} a + \bar{d} \beta a + \bar{b} \bar{\beta} c + \gamma \bar{d} \bar{c} \gamma' = \alpha b \bar{b} + 2 \text{Re}(\bar{d} \beta b) + \gamma d \bar{d}. Parameters: Typical values are not given in the sources. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Numerical precision: Quaternion multiplication involves multiple floating-point operations, and accumulated error may affect the accuracy of the intersection test in kernel space. Pure quaternion constraint: \beta and \beta' must be pure quaternions (scalar part 0). Numerical errors might introduce a small scalar component in \beta', which should be zeroed out. Boundaries and degenerate input: Not given in the sources. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def inversetransformsphere(alpha, beta, gamma, a, b, c, d): """ Computes the coefficients (alphaprime, betaprime, gammaprime) of the original sphere in kernel space, given world-space coefficients and Möbius matrix elements a, b, c, d. Inputs: alpha, gamma: float (real numbers) beta: tuple (w, x, y, z) representing a pure quaternion (w=0) a, b, c, d: tuple (w, x, y, z) representing quaternions Outputs: alphaprime: float betaprime: tuple (w, x, y, z) representing a pure quaternion gammaprime: float """ # Helper: Quaternion conjugate def conj(q): return (q[0], -q[1], -q[2], -q[3]) # Helper: Quaternion multiplication def qmul(q1, q2): w1, x1, y1, z1 = q1 w2, x2, y2, z2 = q2 return ( w1w2 - x1x2 - y1y2 - z1z2, w1x2 + x1w2 + y1z2 - z1y2, w1y2 - x1z2 + y1w2 + z1x2, w1z2 + x1y2 - y1x2 + z1w2) # Helper: Real part of quaternion def re(q): return q[0] # Helper: Scalar multiplication of quaternion def smul(s, q): return (s q[0], s q[1], s q[2], s q[3]) # Helper: Add two quaternions def qadd(q1, q2): return (q1[0]+q2[0], q1[1]+q2[1], q1[2]+q2[2], q1[3]+q2[3]) # Conjugates abar = conj(a) bbar = conj(b) cbar = conj(c) dbar = conj(d) betabar = conj(beta) # Calculate alpha' # alpha' = alpha a abar + 2 Re(cbar beta a) + gamma cbar c scalaraa = qmul(a, abar)[0] term2alphaq = qmul(cbar, qmul(beta, a)) scalarcc = qmul(cbar, c)[0] alphaprime = alpha scalaraa + 2 re(term2alphaq) + gamma scalarcc # Calculate beta' # beta' = alpha bbar a + dbar beta a + bbar betabar c + gamma dbar cbar term1beta = smul(alpha, qmul(bbar, a)) term2beta = qmul(dbar, qmul(beta, a)) term3beta = qmul(bbar, qmul(betabar, c)) term4beta = smul(gamma, qmul(dbar, cbar)) betaprime = qadd(qadd(qadd(term1beta, term2beta), term3beta), term4beta) # Calculate gamma' # gamma' = alpha b bbar + 2 Re(dbar beta b) + gamma d dbar scalarbb = qmul(b, bbar)[0] term2gammaq = qmul(dbar, qmul(beta, b)) scalardd = qmul(d, dbar)[0] gammaprime = alpha scalarbb + 2 re(term2gammaq) + gamma scalardd return alphaprime, betaprime, gammaprime Time Complexity: Constant time O(1) per sphere, involving a fixed number of quaternion multiplications and additions. Memory Complexity: O(1) auxiliary space. Strengths: Exact algebraic solution; no iterative approximation; enables efficient culling of spheres against kernel distance functions. Limitations: Requires the Möbius transformation to be invertible; only applicable to spheres/planes; quaternion arithmetic is more expensive than standard 3D vector math. When to use: When rendering Kernel-Reflection Sequences (KRS) or other conformally transformed implicit surfaces where spheres need to be tested against the kernel. When not to use: For non-spherical primitives or when the transformation is not a Möbius transformation. The method originates from the work on Kernel-Reflection Sequences (KRS). It was introduced to allow efficient ray tracing of complex natural scenes by conformally distorting expansion levels. The technique leverages the properties of quaternionic Möbius transformations to map spheres in world space to spheres (or planes) in kernel space, enabling the use of standard ray-sphere intersection algorithms. name: Ray-Cylinder Intersection
head: Cylinder-Ray Intersection, Ray-Cylinder Hit Test
body:
Computes the entry and exit distances for a ray intersecting a cylinder defined by geomSize, composed of front/back rectangles, top/bottom faces, and a lateral curved surface. It is used in volume rendering to determine the traversal bounds of cylindrical primitives. Unlike Ray-Sphere Intersection which relies on a single quadratic solution, this method decomposes the cylinder into planar and curved components, requiring intersection tests against multiple geometric primitives. Inputs and Outputs Inputs: Ray origin \mathbf{o}, ray direction \mathbf{d} (not necessarily normalized), cylinder geometry size geomSize (a vector where geomSize.x is the radius, geomSize.y is the height along the Y-axis, and geomSize.z is the depth/width along the Z-axis). Outputs: Entry distance inAbs, exit distance outAbs. Returns true if an intersection exists, false otherwise. Data Structures geomSize: float3 containing (r, h, w). rayOrig: float3 ray origin. rayVect: float3 ray direction. Algorithm Steps 1. Initialize inAbsVal = 0, outAbsVal = 0, inAbsFound = false, outAbsFound = false. 2. Define the cylinder's local coordinate system. The cylinder axis is aligned with the Y-axis. The base is at y=0 and the top at y=geomSize.y. The radius is R = geomSize.x. 3. Intersect Front Rectangle: Define points: P0 = (0, 0, 0), P1 = (R, 0, 0), P2 = (0, geomSize.z, 0). Compute normal \mathbf{n} = (P1 - P0) 	imes (P2 - P0). Compute dot product d = \mathbf{n} \cdot \mathbf{d}. If d 
eq 0, compute s =  rac{\mathbf{n} \cdot (P0 - \mathbf{o})}{d}. Compute intersection point P = \mathbf{o} + s\mathbf{d}. Check bounds: P.x \ge 0, P.x \le R, P.y \ge 0, P.y \le geomSize.z. If bounds are satisfied: If d > 0, update outAbsVal with s (maximize). Set outAbsFound = true. If d < 0, update inAbsVal with s (minimize). Set inAbsFound = true. 4. Intersect Back Rectangle: Define points: P0 = (R, 0, geomSize.z), P1 = (0, 0, 0), P2 = (0, geomSize.z, 0). Note: The source code uses lastPoint derived from cylToCart(geomSize), which implies the back face is at z=geomSize.z if the front is at z=0. However, the specific point definitions in the source are P0=\{lastPoint.x, 0, lastPoint.z\}, P1=\{0,0,0\}, P2=\{0,geomSize.z,0\}. This geometry seems to define a triangle or a specific plane. We follow the source's explicit vector math. Compute normal \mathbf{n} = (P1 - P0) 	imes (P2 - P0). Compute dot product d = \mathbf{n} \cdot \mathbf{d}. If d 
eq 0, compute s =  rac{\mathbf{n} \cdot (P0 - \mathbf{o})}{d}. Compute intersection point P = \mathbf{o} + s\mathbf{d}. Check bounds using projected coordinate x =  rac{P \cdot (P0 - P1)}{\|P0 - P1\|}. Check bounds: x \ge 0, x \le R, P.y \ge 0, P.y \le geomSize.z. If bounds are satisfied, update inAbsVal/outAbsVal based on sign of d as in Step 3. 5. Intersect Top Face: Define point P0 = (0, geomSize.y, 0) and normal \mathbf{n} = (0, 1, 0). Compute dot product d = \mathbf{n} \cdot \mathbf{d}. If d 
eq 0, compute s =  rac{\mathbf{n} \cdot (P0 - \mathbf{o})}{d}. Compute intersection point P = \mathbf{o} + s\mathbf{d}. Convert P to cylindrical coordinates (r, 	heta, z) or check Cartesian bounds against radius. The source uses cartToCyl and checks P.x \le geomSize.x and P.y \le geomSize.y. Note: The source code for Top Face checks P.y <= geomSize.y after conversion, which likely refers to the radial distance or a specific coordinate mapping. Given geomSize structure, we assume standard cylindrical check: \sqrt{P.x^2 + P.z^2} \le R and 0 \le P.y \le geomSize.y (though P.y is fixed at intersection with plane y=geomSize.y). The source code specifically checks P.x <= geomSize.x && P.y <= geomSize.y after cartToCyl. We implement the source's logic: convert to cylindrical, check radial bound. If bounds are satisfied, update inAbsVal/outAbsVal based on sign of d. 6. Intersect Bottom Face: Define point P0 = (0, 0, 0) and normal \mathbf{n} = (0, -1, 0). Compute dot product d = \mathbf{n} \cdot \mathbf{d}. If d 
eq 0, compute s =  rac{\mathbf{n} \cdot (P0 - \mathbf{o})}{d}. Compute intersection point P = \mathbf{o} + s\mathbf{d}. Convert P to cylindrical coordinates. Check radial bound P.x \le geomSize.x and vertical bound P.y \le geomSize.y (likely checking if z in cylindrical is within height). If bounds are satisfied, update inAbsVal/outAbsVal based on sign of d. 7. Intersect Lateral Face: The lateral surface is defined by x^2 + z^2 = R^2. Let \mathbf{u} = (d.x, 0, d.z) and \mathbf{v} = (o.x, 0, o.z). Solve quadratic equation a s^2 + b s + c = 0: a = \mathbf{u} \cdot \mathbf{u} b = 2 (\mathbf{u} \cdot \mathbf{v}) c = \mathbf{v} \cdot \mathbf{v} - R^2 Compute discriminant \Delta = b^2 - 4ac. If \Delta \ge 0, compute roots s0, s1. For each root si: Compute point P = \mathbf{o} + si \mathbf{d}. Convert P to cylindrical coordinates. Check bounds: radial distance \le R (implicit by solving quadratic), and height 0 \le P.y \le geomSize.y. If bounds are satisfied, update inAbsVal/outAbsVal based on sign of d (or direction relative to normal). The source uses dot product with normal to determine entry/exit. For cylinder, normal at P is (P.x, 0, P.z)/R. 8. Handle Degenerate Cases: If inAbsFound is true and outAbsFound is false, set outAbsVal = inAbsVal + 2 R / \|d\|. If outAbsFound is true and inAbsFound is false, set inAbsVal = outAbsVal - 2 R / \|d\|. 9. Return: true if outAbsVal >= inAbsVal and both inAbsFound and outAbsFound are true. Degenerate Cases if inabsfound and not outabsfound: outabsval = inabsval + 2 R / length(raydir) if outabsfound and not inabsfound: inabsval = outabsval - 2 R / length(raydir) hit = outabsval >= inabsval and outabsfound and inabsfound return inabsval, outabsval, hit Determines the query cylinder's radius rc for particle querying in discrete media. The parameter k in the radius formula determines the percentage of the pixel's footprint at the nearest boundary of the medium. Typical value range for k is [0.5, 1]. Setting k too large produces undesirable aliasing and overly blurred volumetric glints, although overall brightness remains similar. Setting k too small misses many particles during querying, leading to inefficiency, especially in very sparse media (e.g., N{tot} = 10^4). Time Complexity: Constant time per ray, as it performs a fixed number of intersection tests against planar and quadratic surfaces. Memory Complexity: Constant, requiring only a few scalar variables for state. Strengths: Accurate intersection for cylindrical primitives; handles degenerate cases where only entry or exit is found. Limitations: More complex than sphere intersection due to multiple face tests; requires careful handling of coordinate transformations. When to use: When rendering scenes with cylindrical primitives or when using query cylinders for sparse particle systems. The method is derived from CUDA-based volume rendering implementations. name: Infinite Plane Ray Intersection
head: Analytical ray-plane intersection, Infinite Ground Plane, InfinitePlan::rayIntersect, InfinitePlan::rayIntersectP, Matrix-Based Plane Intersection, Ray-Plane Intersection, planeIntr
body: Computes the intersection of a ray with an infinite plane defined by a point and a normal, returning the intersection distance and point, or rejecting if the ray is parallel or outside the valid segment bounds. It is commonly used for ground planes kept separate from the scene's BVH. Inputs and Outputs Input: Ray origin \mathbf{o}, ray direction \mathbf{d}, plane point \mathbf{P}, plane normal \mathbf{N}, minimum distance t{min}, maximum distance t{max}. Output: Boolean success flag, intersection distance t, intersection point \mathbf{p}, and plane normal \mathbf{N}. Data Structures No complex data structures are required. The plane is defined by point \mathbf{P} and normal \mathbf{N}. The ray is defined by origin \mathbf{o} and direction \mathbf{d}. Steps 1. Compute the denominator D = \mathbf{N} \cdot \mathbf{d}. 2. Check for parallelism: If |D| < \epsilon, the ray is parallel to the plane. Return failure. 3. Compute the intersection distance t using the plane equation. 4. Check bounds: If t < t{min} or t > t{max}, the intersection is outside the valid ray segment. Return failure. 5. Compute the intersection point \mathbf{p} = \mathbf{o} + t \mathbf{d}. 6. Return success with t, \mathbf{p}, and \mathbf{N}. Formulas t = \frac{\mathbf{N} \cdot (\mathbf{P} - \mathbf{o})}{\mathbf{N} \cdot \mathbf{d}} \mathbf{N}: Plane normal vector. \mathbf{P}: A point on the plane. \mathbf{o}: Ray origin vector. \mathbf{d}: Ray direction vector. t: Intersection distance along the ray. Parameters epsilon: Threshold for parallel ray/plane test. Value not specified in sources. Edge Cases and Pitfalls Parallel Rays: If the ray direction is perpendicular to the plane normal, the denominator is zero, causing division by zero. This must be checked to avoid invalid results. Precision: Floating-point comparisons against epsilon and bounds should use consistent tolerance values to avoid jitter near the plane. Pseudocode Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def dot(a, b): return a[0]b[0] + a[1]b[1] + a[2]b[2] def intersectinfiniteplane(rayo, rayd, planep, planen, tmin, tmax, epsilon=1e-6): denominator = dot(planen, rayd) if abs(denominator) < epsilon: return False, 0.0, (0.0, 0.0, 0.0) t = dot((planep[0]-rayo[0], planep[1]-rayo[1], planep[2]-rayo[2]), planen) / denominator if t < tmin or t > tmax: return False, 0.0, (0.0, 0.0, 0.0) p = (rayo[0] + trayd[0], rayo[1] + trayd[1], rayo[2] + trayd[2]) return True, t, p Intersects a ray with a finite plane segment. It is distinct from the infinite plane method by requiring additional bounds tests to ensure the intersection point lies within the segment. Choose it when the plane has finite extent. See Axis-Aligned Rectangle Hit Test. A specific application of the infinite plane intersection used as a scene base. It is distinct by being kept separate from the scene's BVH for performance. Choose it for ground planes in path tracers. See Infinite Ground Plane. Time complexity: O(1) constant time, requiring only a few dot products and a division. Memory complexity: O(1) constant space, requiring no additional data structures. Measured performance with hardware, resolution, and scene: Not given in the sources. Scaling: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Extremely fast and simple to implement. Limitations: Only works for infinite planes. When to use: Ideal for ground planes or sky domes in path tracers. When not to use: When the plane has finite bounds or when the scene contains many planes that can be efficiently accelerated with a BVH. The analytical ray-plane intersection is a fundamental technique in computer graphics. It is widely used in path tracers and real-time renderers for its simplicity and speed. The infinite ground plane pattern is commonly used in offline renderers, where it is kept separate from the BVH for efficiency. name: Axis-Aligned Rectangle Hit Test
head: Plane-Rectangle Intersection, XYRect/XZRect/YZRect Hit
body: The Axis-Aligned Rectangle Hit Test determines whether a ray intersects a finite rectangle lying on an axis-aligned plane. It solves the problem of bounding infinite plane intersections to a specific 2D extent, which is essential for modeling flat surfaces in ray tracing. It differs from Infinite Plane Ray Intersection by adding boundary checks for the rectangle's edges, and from Plane-Cube Intersection by handling a single planar face rather than a volumetric solid. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A ray r defined by origin \mathbf{o} and direction \mathbf{d}, a minimum distance t{min}, a maximum distance t{max}, and a rectangle object. Output: A boolean indicating hit status, and a HitRecord structure populated with intersection distance t, point \mathbf{p}, normal \mathbf{n}, and material. Data Structures: The rectangle is defined by constants bounding two axes and a constant value for the third axis. XYRect: Fields X0, X1 (x-bounds), Y0, Y1 (y-bounds), K (z-coordinate), Mat (material). XZRect: Fields X0, X1 (x-bounds), Z0, Z1 (z-bounds), K (y-coordinate), Mat (material). YZRect: Fields Y0, Y1 (y-bounds), Z0, Z1 (z-bounds), K (x-coordinate), Mat (material). Steps: 1. Compute Intersection Parameter (t): Solve the plane equation for the fixed axis. For an XYRect (normal along Z), the plane equation is z = K. Substituting the ray equation z(t) = oz + t \cdot dz, we get: t = \frac{K - oz}{dz} For XZRect (normal along Y): t = \frac{K - oy}{dy}. For YZRect (normal along X): t = \frac{K - ox}{dx}. 2. Check Depth Bounds: If t < t{min} or t > t{max}, the intersection is outside the valid ray segment. Return false. 3. Compute Transverse Coordinates: Calculate the coordinates on the plane's axes at parameter t. For XYRect: x = ox + t \cdot dx y = oy + t \cdot dy (Analogous formulas apply for other orientations). 4. Check Boundary Bounds: Verify if the transverse coordinates lie within the rectangle's extents. For XYRect: \min(X0, X1) \le x \le \max(X0, X1) \quad \text{and} \quad \min(Y0, Y1) \le y \le \max(Y0, Y1) If either coordinate is out of bounds, return false. 5. Populate HitRecord: Set t{rec} = t. Set \mathbf{p} = \mathbf{o} + t \cdot \mathbf{d}. Determine outward normal \mathbf{n}{out}. For XYRect, \mathbf{n}{out} = (0, 0, 1). Orient the normal: If \mathbf{d} \cdot \mathbf{n}{out} > 0, the ray hits the back face; negate \mathbf{n}{out} to ensure it points against the ray direction. Set \mathbf{n} = \mathbf{n}{out}. Assign material from the rectangle object. Pitfalls: Division by Zero: If the ray direction component along the fixed axis is zero (e.g., dz = 0 for XYRect), division by zero occurs. The result is NaN or Inf, which typically fails the t{min}/t{max} check, but explicit guards are recommended for robustness. Coordinate Ordering: Bounds X0, X1 are not guaranteed to be sorted (X0 < X1). Implementation must use min and max or ensure input normalization. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def hitxyrect(rect, ray, tmin, tmax): # 1. Compute t for the plane z = rect.K denom = ray.direction.z if abs(denom) < 1e-9: # Guard against division by zero return False t = (rect.K - ray.origin.z) / denom # 2. Check depth bounds if t < tmin or t > tmax: return False # 3. Compute x and y at t x = ray.origin.x + t ray.direction.x y = ray.origin.y + t ray.direction.y # 4. Check boundary bounds xmin = min(rect.X0, rect.X1) xmax = max(rect.X0, rect.X1) ymin = min(rect.Y0, rect.Y1) ymax = max(rect.Y0, rect.Y1) if x < xmin or x > xmax or y < ymin or y > ymax: return False # 5. Populate HitRecord hitrecord.t = t hitrecord.p = ray.at(t) # Outward normal for XYRect is +Z outwardnormal = Vector(0.0, 0.0, 1.0) # Orient normal against ray direction if dot(ray.direction, outwardnormal) > 0: hitrecord.normal = -outwardnormal else: hitrecord.normal = outwardnormal hitrecord.frontface = (dot(ray.direction, hitrecord.normal) < 0) hitrecord.mat = rect.Mat return True Intersects a ray with an axis-aligned plane defined by an anchor point, extent, and direction index d. It returns the intersection distance t and barycentric-like coordinates u, v. The method uses a direction index to permute coordinate axes, aligning the plane normal with a single axis to simplify the intersection calculation. Time Complexity: O(1). The method involves a constant number of arithmetic operations and comparisons. Memory Complexity: O(1). No auxiliary data structures are required beyond the input ray and rectangle definitions. Strengths: Extremely fast and numerically stable for axis-aligned primitives. Ideal for bounding boxes and planar surfaces in scene graphs. Limitations: Only applicable to axis-aligned rectangles. Requires separate implementations for different orientations (XY, XZ, YZ) or a generalized permutation approach. When to use: When rendering flat, axis-aligned surfaces or as part of bounding volume hierarchies (BVH) leaf nodes. When not to use: For rotated rectangles or non-planar shapes. The method is a standard component in educational ray tracers and simple rendering engines. It is derived from the analytic intersection of a ray with a plane, constrained by rectangular bounds. The specific struct-based implementation shown in the sources is characteristic of modern, object-oriented ray tracer tutorials. hexhowells/GoTracer, https://github.com/hexhowells/GoTracer, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial)

name: Axis-Aligned Plane Intersection
body: Intersects a ray with an axis-aligned plane defined by an anchor point, extent, and direction index d. It returns the intersection distance t and barycentric-like coordinates u, v. The method uses a direction index to permute coordinate axes, aligning the plane normal with a single axis to simplify the intersection calculation. Inputs: ray: Ray defined by origin O and direction D (3D vectors). anchor: Corner of the plane/rectangle (3D vector). extent: Size of the plane/rectangle along its local axes (3D vector). d: Integer direction index (0–5) mapping to specific axis permutations. frame: Context object providing eyenear (near clip distance w and origin xyz). Outputs: t: Intersection distance along the ray. u, v: Local coordinates on the plane, normalized to [0, 1]. Boolean success flag. Data Structures: Vectors are 3D floats. d is an integer index mapping to specific axis permutations. Steps: 1. Axis Permutation: Select eye, origin, and ray components based on d to align the plane normal with the X-axis of the permuted space. If d < 2: Use axes (x, y, z). If 2 <= d < 4: Use axes (y, x, z). If d >= 4: Use axes (z, x, y). Specifically: eye = appearanceaxes(frame.eyenear.xyz, d), origin = appearanceaxes(anchor, d), delta = appearanceaxes(ray, d). 2. Plane Constant: Compute the plane offset along the normal. plane = origin.x + (1.0 \text{ if } (d \& 1) \text{ else } 0.0) 3. Distance Numerator: distance = plane - eye.x 4. Parallel Check: If delta.x is zero, the ray is parallel to the plane. 5. Intersection Distance: t = \frac{distance}{delta.x} 6. Local Coordinates Numerator: Compute unnormalized local coordinates using the Y and Z components of the permuted space. uNumerator = eye.y + t \cdot delta.y - origin.y vNumerator = eye.z + t \cdot delta.z - origin.z 7. Normalization: u = \frac{uNumerator}{extent.x} v = \frac{vNumerator}{extent.y} (Note: extent.x and extent.y refer to the U and V dimensions in the permuted coordinate space.) 8. Validity Checks: If t is NaN or Inf, or if t < frame.eyenear.w (near clip), return false. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def axisalignedplaneintersection(rayorigin, raydir, anchor, extent, d, eyenearw): import math # Permutation mapping based on d if d < 2: perm = (0, 1, 2) elif d < 4: perm = (1, 0, 2) else: perm = (2, 0, 1) # Extract components in permuted order eyex = rayorigin[perm[0]] eyey = rayorigin[perm[1]] eyez = rayorigin[perm[2]] deltax = raydir[perm[0]] deltay = raydir[perm[1]] deltaz = raydir[perm[2]] originx = anchor[perm[0]] originy = anchor[perm[1]] originz = anchor[perm[2]] # Permute extent to match the coordinate space extx = extent[perm[0]] exty = extent[perm[1]] # Plane constant plane = originx + (1.0 if (d & 1) else 0.0) distance = plane - eyex # Parallel check if deltax == 0.0: return False, None, None t = distance / deltax # Validity checks if math.isnan(t) or math.isinf(t) or t < eyenearw: return False, None, None # Local coordinates uNumerator = eyey + t deltay - originy vNumerator = eyez + t deltaz - originz # Normalize u = uNumerator / extx v = vNumerator / exty return True, t, u, v Determines the 3D integer voxel cell coordinate and the 3D intersection point given the ray intersection with an axis-aligned plane. It builds on axisalignedplaneintersection. 1. Call axisalignedplaneintersection to get t, u, v. If it fails, return false. 2. Compute local coordinates in world units: localU = u extent.x, localV = v extent.y. 3. Compute cell offset: offset = clamp(floor(vec2(localU, localV)), vec2(0.0), extent - 1.0). 4. Initialize cell with anchor: cell = uvec3(anchor). 5. Add offset to cell based on direction d: if d < 2, add to cell.y and cell.z; if 2 <= d < 4, add to cell.x and cell.z; if d >= 4, add to cell.x and cell.y. 6. Compute 3D point: point = frame.eyenear.xyz + ray t. Time Complexity: O(1). Fixed number of arithmetic operations and comparisons. Memory Complexity: O(1). No dynamic allocation. Strengths: Extremely fast; avoids branching on face normal by using a direction index; handles all 6 faces of an AABB uniformly. Limitations: Only works for axis-aligned planes; requires pre-computed direction index d; precision issues may occur if t is very large or deltax is very small. When to use: Ray casting against voxel grids, AABBs, or any set of axis-aligned planes where the face index is known or easily derived. Originated in the bend-voxel project. The method leverages axis-aligned properties to simplify intersection tests, a common optimization in volume rendering and voxel-based rendering. aivv73/bend-voxel, https://github.com/aivv73/bend-voxel, fetched 2026-10-28 (unofficial)

name: Plane-Cube Intersection
head: Plane-Cube Intersection Volume, Volume from a plane slicing a cube
body: This method computes the volume of the irregular polyhedron formed by the intersection of a plane and a cube. It is specifically designed for scenarios where a planar boundary slices through a volumetric cell, such as determining the fraction of a cell that is partial ionized or covered by a burning front in computational astrophysics. It differs from standard ray-cube intersection by outputting the resulting volume rather than just intersection points, and extends the approach of Salama & Kolb 2005 by explicitly constructing an ordered list of face vertices to facilitate this volume calculation. Inputs: A unit cube defined by 8 vertices \mathbf{V}1 through \mathbf{V}8. The specific enumeration and ordering of these vertices must be consistent with the source's geometric model. A plane defined by a unit normal vector \mathbf{\hat{n}} and a scalar distance dl from the origin. Outputs: The volume of the intersection polyhedron. The set of intersection points on the cube edges. Data Structures: Vertices \mathbf{V}i: 3D Cartesian coordinates (x, y, z). Edges E{i \rightarrow j}: Defined by pairs of vertex indices (i, j). Intersection points: 3D coordinates derived from the edge intersection logic. Steps: 1. Define the Plane Normal: The plane is parameterized by spherical angles \theta and \phi and the normal ray length dl. Compute the Cartesian coordinates of the normal vector \mathbf{n}: \mathbf{n} = [dl \cos(\theta), \ dl \sin(\theta)\sin(\phi), \ dl \cos(\phi) ] The unit normal vector is \mathbf{\hat{n}} = \mathbf{n} / \|\mathbf{n}\|. Note that dl represents the distance from the origin to the plane along the normal. 2. Define the Plane Equation: The plane equation is given by: dl = \mathbf{\hat{n}} \cdot \mathbf{x} where \mathbf{x} is any point on the plane. 3. Iterate Over Cube Edges: For each edge E{i \rightarrow j} connecting vertex \mathbf{V}i to \mathbf{V}j: a. Define the edge line parametrically: E{i \rightarrow j} = \mathbf{V}i + \lambda (\mathbf{V}j - \mathbf{V}i) b. Calculate the intersection parameter \lambda: \lambda = \frac{ dl - \mathbf{\hat{n}} \cdot \mathbf{V}i }{\mathbf{\hat{n}} \cdot (\mathbf{V}j - \mathbf{V}i) } c. Check validity: An intersection exists on the segment if and only if 0 \le \lambda \le 1. d. If valid, compute the intersection point \mathbf{P} = \mathbf{V}i + \lambda (\mathbf{V}j - \mathbf{V}i). 4. Construct the Polyhedron: Collect all valid intersection points. The resulting shape is an inscribed irregular polyhedron with 3 to 6 vertices. 5. Compute Volume: Construct an ordered list of the face vertices of the resulting polyhedron. Use this ordered list to compute the volume of the irregular polyhedron. The specific algorithm for volume calculation from an ordered vertex list is not detailed in the source, but the method relies on this construction to extend Salama & Kolb 2005. Parameters: \theta: Spherical angle, 0 \le \theta \le 2\pi. \phi: Spherical angle, 0 \le \phi \le \pi. dl: Length of the normal ray (distance from origin). Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Degenerate Intersections: If \mathbf{\hat{n}} \cdot (\mathbf{V}j - \mathbf{V}i) = 0, the edge is parallel to the plane. The source does not specify handling for this case, but numerically it requires a guard to avoid division by zero. Vertex Ordering: The volume calculation depends on an "ordered list of face vertices." Incorrect ordering will yield incorrect volumes or self-intersecting meshes. The source implies a specific enumeration of the cube vertices \mathbf{V}1 to \mathbf{V}8 is required, but does not provide the coordinate mapping. Polygon Complexity: The number of vertices of the intersecting polygon can vary between 3 and 6, showing "wild patterns" as \theta and \phi change, even if the volume changes smoothly. Time Complexity: Constant time O(1) relative to scene size, as it operates on a single cube with a fixed number of edges (12 edges for a cube). Memory Complexity: Constant space O(1) to store vertices and intersection points. Strengths: Provides an exact analytical volume for planar cuts through cubic cells, useful for adaptive mesh refinement or astrophysical simulations involving partial cell coverage. Limitations: Requires careful handling of vertex ordering for volume integration. The complexity of the intersection polygon topology (3 to 6 vertices) may require case-specific logic for robust mesh generation. When to use: When a planar boundary intersects a cubic volume element and the exact volume of the intersection is required. When not to use: For non-planar cuts or non-cubic primitives. The method was introduced by F.X. Timmes in the context of computational astrophysics, specifically for calculating the fraction of a cell that may be partial ionized or covered by a burning front. name: Ray-Triangle Intersection
body: Computes the intersection of a ray with a single triangle in 3D space, determining if the ray hits the triangle's interior and returning the intersection distance. Unlike Sphere Intersection which uses algebraic distance checks, or Ray-Plane/Rectangle Intersection which handles infinite or axis-aligned bounds, this method explicitly tests against a finite, arbitrary triangular surface using barycentric coordinate validation. Inputs and Outputs Inputs: Ray origin \mathbf{o}, ray direction \mathbf{d} (typically normalized), triangle vertices \mathbf{v}0, \mathbf{v}1, \mathbf{v}2. Outputs: Boolean indicating intersection; if true, the distance t along the ray to the intersection point. Data Structures Vertices are stored as 3D vectors (\mathbb{R}^3). Ray is defined by origin \mathbf{o} \in \mathbb{R}^3 and direction \mathbf{d} \in \mathbb{R}^3. Parameters weighttolerance: A small value (e.g., 10^{-4}) used to relax the barycentric coordinate check, allowing rays to pass slightly outside the triangle edges to prevent gaps between adjacent triangles. smallt: A minimum distance threshold to avoid self-intersection or self-shadowing bugs. Steps 1. Compute Triangle Normal: Calculate the normal vector \mathbf{n} of the triangle plane. \mathbf{n} = \text{normalize}(\text{cross}(\mathbf{v}1 - \mathbf{v}0, \mathbf{v}2 - \mathbf{v}0)) 2. Ray-Plane Intersection: Calculate the numerator and denominator for the intersection distance t. \text{numerator} = \text{dot}(\mathbf{n}, \mathbf{v}0 - \mathbf{o}) \text{denominator} = \text{dot}(\mathbf{n}, \mathbf{d}) 3. Parallel Check: If denominator is zero, the ray is parallel to the triangle plane. 4. Distance Check: Compute t = \text{numerator} / \text{denominator}. If t < \text{small\t}, the intersection is too close (behind the ray origin or self-intersecting). 5. Intersection Point: Compute the intersection point \mathbf{p}. \mathbf{p} = \mathbf{o} + t \cdot \mathbf{d} 6. Barycentric Coordinates: Compute the barycentric coordinates (\alpha, \beta, \gamma) of \mathbf{p} relative to the triangle. \mathbf{e}1 = \mathbf{v}1 - \mathbf{v}0 \mathbf{e}2 = \mathbf{v}2 - \mathbf{v}0 \mathbf{v} = \mathbf{p} - \mathbf{v}0 \text{dot00} = \text{dot}(\mathbf{e}1, \mathbf{e}1) \text{dot01} = \text{dot}(\mathbf{e}1, \mathbf{e}2) \text{dot02} = \text{dot}(\mathbf{e}1, \mathbf{v}) \text{dot11} = \text{dot}(\mathbf{e}2, \mathbf{e}2) \text{dot12} = \text{dot}(\mathbf{e}2, \mathbf{v}) \text{invDenom} = 1 / (\text{dot00} \cdot \text{dot11} - \text{dot01} \cdot \text{dot01}) \alpha = (\text{dot11} \cdot \text{dot02} - \text{dot01} \cdot \text{dot12}) \cdot \text{invDenom} \beta = (\text{dot00} \cdot \text{dot12} - \text{dot01} \cdot \text{dot02}) \cdot \text{invDenom} \gamma = 1 - \alpha - \beta 7. Inside Check: Check if the barycentric coordinates are within the valid range, relaxed by weighttolerance. \text{if } \alpha \ge -\text{weight\tolerance} \text{ and } \beta \ge -\text{weight\tolerance} \text{ and } \gamma \ge -\text{weight\tolerance} \text{ and } \alpha \le 1 + \text{weight\tolerance} \text{ and } \beta \le 1 + \text{weight\tolerance} \text{ and } \gamma \le 1 + \text{weight\tolerance} Return true. Otherwise, return false. Pseudocode Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def raytriangleintersect(o, d, v0, v1, v2, smallt=0.0, weighttolerance=1e-4): # Step 1: Compute triangle normal e1 = v1 - v0 e2 = v2 - v0 n = normalize(cross(e1, e2)) # Step 2: Ray-plane intersection parameters numerator = dot(n, v0 - o) denominator = dot(n, d) # Step 3: Parallel check if denominator == 0: return False, 0.0 # Step 4: Distance check t = numerator / denominator if t < smallt: return False, 0.0 # Step 5: Intersection point p = o + t d # Step 6: Barycentric coordinates v = p - v0 dot00 = dot(e1, e1) dot01 = dot(e1, e2) dot02 = dot(e1, v) dot11 = dot(e2, e2) dot12 = dot(e2, v) invDenom = 1.0 / (dot00 dot11 - dot01 dot01) alpha = (dot11 dot02 - dot01 dot12) invDenom beta = (dot00 dot12 - dot01 dot02) invDenom gamma = 1.0 - alpha - beta # Step 7: Inside check with tolerance if (alpha >= -weighttolerance and beta >= -weighttolerance and gamma >= -weighttolerance and alpha <= 1.0 + weighttolerance and beta <= 1.0 + weighttolerance and gamma <= 1.0 + weighttolerance): return True, t else: return False, 0.0 This method determines if a ray intersects a triangle in 3D space using Plücker coordinates to handle arbitrary ray directions. It solves the ray-primitive intersection problem by combining a front-face culling test based on the ray-triangle normal dot product with a winding-order consistency check derived from edge Plücker coordinates. Computes the closest point on a triangle to a query point and the squared distance between them. It solves the problem of finding the minimum Euclidean distance from a 3D point to a triangular surface patch, which is a fundamental primitive for signed distance field (SDF) generation, collision detection, and mesh sampling. It sets itself apart from Ray-Triangle Intersection by solving a minimization problem over the triangle's interior and boundary rather than finding a scalar parameter t along a ray. The Triangle-Triangle Intersection Test determines whether two triangles in 3D space intersect (share any common points) using the Separating Axis Theorem (SAT). It solves the problem of detecting collisions between triangular primitives, which is a fundamental building block for mesh intersection, voxelization, and constructive solid geometry. Unlike Ray-Triangle Intersection, which tests a ray against a single triangle, this method tests two arbitrary triangles against each other without a predefined viewing direction. This method converts a triangle mesh into a 3D voxel grid by dispatching a compute shader where each thread corresponds to a voxel cell. It determines voxel solidity by testing each cell against every mesh triangle using a Separating Axis Theorem (SAT) broad-phase test followed by a Möller-Trumbore ray-triangle intersection. It differs from hierarchical voxelization by using a brute-force per-voxel, per-triangle approach, making it simple to implement but computationally expensive for high-resolution grids or complex meshes. A faster method to find intersections by projecting 3D vertices to 2D based on a swizzle mode and checking 2D point-in-triangle containment. For each face, the 3D vertices are swizzled according to the template mode, and a 2D point-in-triangle test is called to check if the point is inside the triangle, returning the distance d if true. Time Complexity: O(1) per triangle. Memory Complexity: O(1) auxiliary space. Performance: The number of operations is constant, involving a few vector cross products, dot products, and divisions. Performance scales linearly with the number of triangles tested. On GPUs, parallel execution across threads allows testing many triangles simultaneously. Strengths: Simple to implement, robust for most standard ray tracing scenarios, handles arbitrary triangle orientations. Limitations: Sensitive to numerical precision near triangle edges, which is mitigated by weighttolerance. Not suitable for hierarchical acceleration structures without additional bounding volume checks. When to Use: When testing a ray against a single triangle or a small set of triangles. When Not to Use: When testing against large meshes; use acceleration structures like BVH or KD-trees instead. The method is a fundamental building block in ray tracing and volume rendering, enabling the intersection of rays with triangular mesh geometry. name: General Ray-Triangle Intersection (Plücker Coordinates)
head: Triangle Ray Intersection, rayIntersectsTriangle
body: This method determines if a ray intersects a triangle in 3D space using Plücker coordinates to handle arbitrary ray directions. It solves the ray-primitive intersection problem by combining a front-face culling test based on the ray-triangle normal dot product with a winding-order consistency check derived from edge Plücker coordinates. Inputs: Ray origin \mathbf{o}, ray direction \mathbf{d}, triangle vertices \mathbf{a}, \mathbf{b}, \mathbf{c}. Outputs: Boolean indicating intersection. Data Structures: vec3f: 3D vector type with components x, y, z. float: 32-bit floating point number. Steps: 1. Normal Calculation: Compute the triangle normal \mathbf{n}. 2. Front-Face Culling: Calculate the dot product between the normal and the ray direction: \cos ND = \mathbf{n} \cdot \mathbf{d} If \cos ND == 0, return false. This ignores the case where the ray lies in the triangle's plane. 3. Intersection Parameter: If the intersection distance t is required, calculate it: t = \frac{-\mathbf{n} \cdot (\mathbf{o} - \mathbf{a})}{\cos ND}. 4. Coordinate Translation: Translate the triangle vertices to the ray origin space: \mathbf{a} = \mathbf{a} - \mathbf{o} \mathbf{b} = \mathbf{b} - \mathbf{o} \mathbf{c} = \mathbf{c} - \mathbf{o}. 5. Plücker Coordinate Calculation: Compute the Plücker coordinates for the three edges of the triangle relative to the ray direction. The Plücker coordinate function is defined as: \text{pluecker}(\mathbf{a}0, \mathbf{a}1, \mathbf{b}0, \mathbf{b}1) = \mathbf{a}1 \cdot (\mathbf{b}1 \times \mathbf{b}0) + \mathbf{b}1 \cdot (\mathbf{a}1 \times \mathbf{a}0). Apply this to the edges: sx = \text{pluecker}(\mathbf{0}, \mathbf{d}, \mathbf{a}, \mathbf{b}) sy = \text{pluecker}(\mathbf{0}, \mathbf{d}, \mathbf{b}, \mathbf{c}) sz = \text{pluecker}(\mathbf{0}, \mathbf{d}, \mathbf{c}, \mathbf{a}). 6. Winding Order Check: Determine intersection based on the signs of sx, sy, sz. If \min(sx, sy, sz) \ge 0 or \max(sx, sy, sz) \le 0, return true (intersection). Otherwise, return false. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def raytriangleintersectionplucker(rayorigin, raydir, tria, trib, tric): # 1. Calculate normal edge1 = trib - tria edge2 = tric - tria normal = cross(edge1, edge2) # 2. Front-face culling cosnd = dot(normal, raydir) if cosnd == 0.0: return False # 3. Calculate t t = -dot(rayorigin - tria, normal) / cosnd # 4. Translate vertices to ray origin space a = tria - rayorigin b = trib - rayorigin c = tric - rayorigin # 5. Compute Plücker coordinates def pluecker(a0, a1, b0, b1): return dot(a1 - a0, cross(b1, b0)) + dot(b1 - b0, cross(a1, a0)) sx = pluecker(vec3f(0.0), raydir, a, b) sy = pluecker(vec3f(0.0), raydir, b, c) sz = pluecker(vec3f(0.0), raydir, c, a) # 6. Check winding order if min(sx, sy, sz) >= 0.0 or max(sx, sy, sz) <= 0.0: return True else: return False Parameters: cosnd threshold: Strictly 0.0 check. Edge Cases: Ray in Plane: If \cos ND == 0, the method returns false, ignoring the possibility of the ray lying in the triangle's plane. Degenerate Triangles: If the triangle area is zero, the normal is zero, leading to division by zero or undefined behavior. Precision: Floating point precision issues may arise near the edges of the triangle. An algorithm to determine if a ray intersects a triangle, optimized for axis-aligned rays using Plücker coordinates to simplify cross products. The Möller-Trumbore algorithm computes the intersection of a ray with a triangle by solving for the parametric distance t and barycentric coordinates (u, v) directly, avoiding the explicit calculation of the triangle's plane equation. It sets itself apart from general analytic methods by using Cramer's rule to derive these parameters in a single step, which minimizes storage requirements and computational overhead. Unlike the Plücker method, which relies on Plücker coordinates to handle arbitrary ray directions with a different algebraic structure, Möller-Trumbore operates directly in Cartesian space using cross and dot products. Time Complexity: O(1) per triangle. Memory Complexity: O(1) auxiliary space. Performance: The method is efficient for general rays. Strengths: Handles arbitrary ray directions. Limitations: Does not handle rays lying in the triangle's plane. When to use: When intersecting general rays against triangles and only the boolean intersection result is needed. The method is described in the context of general ray-triangle intersection using Plücker coordinates. Plücker coordinates are a representation of lines in projective geometry, often used in computer graphics for efficient line-line and line-plane intersection tests. name: Axis-Aligned Ray-Triangle Intersection (Plücker Coordinates)
head: rayIntersectsTriangle (AxisAlignedRay)
body: An algorithm to determine if a ray intersects a triangle, optimized for axis-aligned rays using Plücker coordinates to simplify cross products. Inputs: org: Ray origin (float3). dir: Ray direction (float3), constrained to be axis-aligned. a, b, c: Triangle vertices (float3). n: Triangle normal (float3). Outputs: Boolean indicating intersection. Data Structures: Standard 3D vectors and scalars. Steps: 1. Calculate the dot product of the triangle normal and ray direction: \text{cosND} = \mathbf{n} \cdot \mathbf{dir}. 2. Calculate the intersection distance t along the ray: t = -\mathbf{n} \cdot (\text{org} - \mathbf{a}) / \text{cosND}. 3. Transform the triangle vertices into the coordinate space centered at the ray origin: \mathbf{a} = \mathbf{a} - \text{org}, \mathbf{b} = \mathbf{b} - \text{org}, \mathbf{c} = \mathbf{c} - \text{org}. 4. Compute Plücker coordinates for the three triangle edges relative to the ray direction using the helper function \text{pluecker}(\mathbf{a}0, \mathbf{a}1, \mathbf{b}0, \mathbf{b}1) = (\mathbf{a}1 - \mathbf{a}0) \cdot (\mathbf{b}1 \times \mathbf{b}0) + (\mathbf{b}1 - \mathbf{b}0) \cdot (\mathbf{a}1 \times \mathbf{a}0). The calls are \text{sx} = \text{pluecker}(\mathbf{0}, \mathbf{dir}, \mathbf{a}, \mathbf{b}), \text{sy} = \text{pluecker}(\mathbf{0}, \mathbf{dir}, \mathbf{b}, \mathbf{c}), and \text{sz} = \text{pluecker}(\mathbf{0}, \mathbf{dir}, \mathbf{c}, \mathbf{a}). 5. Determine if the ray is inside the triangle by checking if all Plücker coordinates have the same sign: if \min(\text{sx}, \text{sy}, \text{sz}) \ge 0 or \max(\text{sx}, \text{sy}, \text{sz}) \le 0, return true. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def dot(u, v): return u[0]v[0] + u[1]v[1] + u[2]v[2] def cross(u, v): return (u[1]v[2] - u[2]v[1], u[2]v[0] - u[0]v[2], u[0]v[1] - u[1]v[0]) def pluecker(a0, a1, b0, b1): return dot((a1[0]-a0[0], a1[1]-a0[1], a1[2]-a0[2]), cross(b1, b0)) + \ dot((b1[0]-b0[0], b1[1]-b0[1], b1[2]-b0[2]), cross(a1, a0)) def axisalignedraytriangleintersection(org, dir, a, b, c, n): cosND = dot(n, dir) t = -dot(n, (org[0]-a[0], org[1]-a[1], org[2]-a[2])) / cosND a = (a[0]-org[0], a[1]-org[1], a[2]-org[2]) b = (b[0]-org[0], b[1]-org[1], b[2]-org[2]) c = (c[0]-org[0], c[1]-org[1], c[2]-org[2]) sx = pluecker((0, 0, 0), dir, a, b) sy = pluecker((0, 0, 0), dir, b, c) sz = pluecker((0, 0, 0), dir, c, a) if min(sx, sy, sz) >= 0.0 or max(sx, sy, sz) <= 0.0: return True return False Parameters: Not given in the sources. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: If the ray is perfectly parallel to the triangle plane (\text{cosND} == 0), the function returns false, ignoring the edge case where the ray might lie in the same 2D plane. name: Möller-Trumbore Ray-Triangle Intersection
head: Möller-Trumbore, MT Algorithm, MT intersection, Ray-Triangle Intersection (Möller-Trumbore), Triangle-Ray Intersection (Möller-Trumbore), Moeller-Trumbore Ray-Triangle Intersection (Embree)
body: The Möller-Trumbore algorithm computes the intersection of a ray with a triangle by solving for the parametric distance t and barycentric coordinates (u, v) directly, avoiding the explicit calculation of the triangle's plane equation. It translates the ray origin and changes the vector basis to yield a vector (t, u, v)^T, minimizing storage requirements and computational overhead. It operates directly in Cartesian space using cross and dot products. Inputs: Ray origin \mathbf{O} (3D vector) Ray direction \mathbf{D} (3D vector) Triangle vertices \mathbf{V}1, \mathbf{V}2, \mathbf{V}3 (3D vectors) Epsilon threshold \epsilon for numerical stability (typically 10^{-6} to 10^{-7}) Outputs: Intersection distance t (scalar) Barycentric coordinates u, v (scalars) Boolean success flag or None/false if no intersection Data Structures: Vectors \mathbf{e}1, \mathbf{e}2, \mathbf{T}, \mathbf{pvec}, \mathbf{qvec} are 3D floating-point vectors Scalars det, inv\det, u, v, t are floating-point numbers Steps: 1. Compute edge vectors of the triangle: \mathbf{e}1 = \mathbf{V}2 - \mathbf{V}1 \mathbf{e}2 = \mathbf{V}3 - \mathbf{V}1 2. Compute the vector from \mathbf{V}1 to the ray origin: \mathbf{T} = \mathbf{O} - \mathbf{V}1 3. Compute the cross product of the ray direction and the second edge: \mathbf{pvec} = \mathbf{D} \times \mathbf{e}2 4. Compute the determinant of the system: det = \mathbf{e}1 \cdot \mathbf{pvec} 5. Check for parallelism: If |det| < \epsilon, the ray is parallel to the triangle plane (or lies in it). Return no intersection. Compute the inverse determinant: inv\det = 1.0 / det 6. Compute the first barycentric coordinate u: u = (\mathbf{T} \cdot \mathbf{pvec}) \times inv\det If u < 0.0 or u > 1.0, the intersection point lies outside the triangle edge. Return no intersection. 7. Compute the cross product of \mathbf{T} and the first edge: \mathbf{qvec} = \mathbf{T} \times \mathbf{e}1 8. Compute the second barycentric coordinate v: v = (\mathbf{D} \cdot \mathbf{qvec}) \times inv\det If v < 0.0 or u + v > 1.0, the intersection point lies outside the triangle. Return no intersection. 9. Compute the intersection distance t: t = (\mathbf{e}2 \cdot \mathbf{qvec}) \times inv\det If t < \epsilon (or t \le 0), the intersection is behind the ray origin or at the origin. Return no intersection. 10. Return success with t, u, v. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def mullertrumbore(rayorigin, raydirection, v1, v2, v3, epsilon=1e-7): # Step 1: Edge vectors e1 = v2 - v1 e2 = v3 - v1 # Step 2: Vector from V1 to ray origin tvec = rayorigin - v1 # Step 3: Cross product of ray direction and second edge pvec = cross(raydirection, e2) # Step 4: Determinant det = dot(e1, pvec) # Step 5: Check for parallelism if abs(det) < epsilon: return None invdet = 1.0 / det # Step 6: Compute u u = dot(tvec, pvec) invdet if u < 0.0 or u > 1.0: return None # Step 7: Cross product of tvec and first edge qvec = cross(tvec, e1) # Step 8: Compute v v = dot(raydirection, qvec) invdet if v < 0.0 or (u + v) > 1.0: return None # Step 9: Compute t t = dot(e2, qvec) invdet if t < epsilon: return None return {'t': t, 'u': u, 'v': v} Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Parallel Rays: If the determinant is near zero, division by zero occurs. The check |det| < \epsilon prevents this. Degenerate Triangles: If the triangle vertices are collinear, the area is zero, and the determinant may be zero or near-zero. Back-Facing Triangles: The algorithm returns intersections for both front and back faces. Numerical Precision: Using a small epsilon is critical for robustness, especially when rays align with mesh vertices or edges. Eliminates vertical slice artifacts in mesh voxelization by introducing a small, direction-aware offset to ray origins before performing ray-triangle intersection tests. It specifically addresses numerical instability in the Möller-Trumbore algorithm when rays align exactly with mesh vertices or edges, a common issue in meshes with regular grid topology such as terrain height maps. Unlike alternative approaches that bypass ray-tracing entirely (e.g., using Signed Distance Fields), this technique preserves the geometric fidelity of the original mesh while ensuring robust intersection detection. Time Complexity: O(1) per triangle. Memory Complexity: O(1) auxiliary space. Performance: It is considered one of the fastest ray-triangle intersection routines for triangles without precomputed plane equations. Optimized variants exist that delay division or handle sign checks differently, but the core logic remains the same. Strengths: Minimal storage, no need to compute plane equations, robust handling of barycentric coordinates directly. Limitations: Does not inherently handle back-face culling (requires caller intervention). The algorithm was introduced by Tomas Möller and Ben Trumbore in 1997 in the paper "Fast, Minimum Storage Ray/Triangle Intersection". name: Ray Origin Jitter for Mesh Voxelization
head: Jittered Ray Origins, STL Voxelization Artifacts Fix
body: This method eliminates vertical slice artifacts in mesh voxelization by introducing a small, direction-aware offset to ray origins before performing ray-triangle intersection tests. It specifically addresses numerical instability in the Möller-Trumbore algorithm when rays align exactly with mesh vertices or edges, a common issue in meshes with regular grid topology such as terrain height maps. Unlike alternative approaches that bypass ray-tracing entirely (e.g., using Signed Distance Fields), this technique preserves the geometric fidelity of the original mesh while ensuring robust intersection detection. Inputs and Outputs Input: Voxel grid position (xyz), voxel size, ray direction (direction), and an initial offset (offset) derived from the voxel position. Output: A jittered ray origin vector (rorigin) used for the subsequent Möller-Trumbore intersection test. Data Structures xyz: Integer or float coordinates of the voxel center or corner. direction: An integer or boolean mask indicating the primary axis of the ray (0 for X, 1 for Y, 2 for Z). offset: A vector representing the displacement from the voxel center to the ray start point (often half-voxel or zero depending on the specific voxelization scheme). Parameters jitter: The magnitude of the offset. The standard value is 0.001f, which represents 0.1% of the voxel size. This value is small enough to not affect the geometric accuracy of the voxelization but large enough to break exact coplanarity. Steps 1. Calculate the base ray origin by adding the voxel position and any predefined offset: r{origin} = position(xyz) + offset 2. Define the jitter magnitude constant: jitter = 0.001 \times voxel\size 3. Apply the jitter to the components of rorigin that are perpendicular to the ray direction. The jitter is added to component N only if the ray direction is not aligned with axis N. If direction is 0 (X-ray), jitter is applied to Y and Z components. If direction is 1 (Y-ray), jitter is applied to X and Z components. If direction is 2 (Z-ray), jitter is applied to X and Y components. Pseudocode Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def jitterrayorigin(positionxyz, offset, direction, voxelsize): """ Calculate a jittered ray origin for mesh voxelization. Args: positionxyz: Vector3, the base position of the voxel. offset: Vector3, additional offset (e.g., half-voxel). direction: int, 0 for X-aligned, 1 for Y-aligned, 2 for Z-aligned. voxelsize: float, the side length of a single voxel. Returns: Vector3, the jittered ray origin. """ # Step 1: Calculate base origin rorigin = positionxyz + offset # Step 2: Define jitter magnitude (0.1% of voxel size) jitter = 0.001 voxelsize # Step 3: Apply jitter perpendicular to ray direction # direction != 0 checks if the ray is NOT aligned with the X-axis # If true, add jitter to the X component of the origin if direction != 0: rorigin.x += jitter # If the ray is NOT aligned with the Y-axis, add jitter to the Y component if direction != 1: rorigin.y += jitter # If the ray is NOT aligned with the Z-axis, add jitter to the Z component if direction != 2: rorigin.z += jitter return rorigin Edge Cases and Pitfalls Regular Grid Topology: The primary failure case occurs with meshes generated from height maps or regular grids (e.g., hill.stl with 421 Y-aligned planes) where vertices lie on exact integer or half-integer coordinates. Without jitter, rays often start exactly on vertex planes, leading to undefined intersection results or missed voxels. Precision: The jitter magnitude must be chosen carefully. Too small, and it fails to break coplanarity due to floating-point precision limits; too large, and it introduces visible artifacts or inaccuracies in the voxel boundary. The value 0.001f (0.1%) has been empirically shown to be imperceptible in final simulations while effectively solving the issue. Direction Alignment: The jitter must not be applied along the ray's primary direction of travel, as this would shift the ray along its own path without addressing the coplanarity issue with the triangle's plane. Time Complexity: O(1) per voxel. The jitter calculation adds a constant number of arithmetic operations and comparisons to the existing voxelization loop. Memory Complexity: O(1) additional memory. No new data structures are required; the jitter is computed on the fly. Performance: Negligible performance impact. The added operations are simple integer comparisons and floating-point additions, which are extremely fast on modern GPUs and CPUs. Strengths: Effectively eliminates vertical slice artifacts in voxelized terrain and regular meshes. Simple to implement and integrate into existing ray-triangle intersection kernels (e.g., Möller-Trumbore). Preserves the original mesh geometry, unlike SDF-based approaches which may smooth or alter details. Limitations: Only addresses coplanarity issues related to ray origins. It does not fix other numerical instabilities in ray-triangle intersection (e.g., near-parallel rays). Requires knowledge of the ray direction and voxel size. May not be sufficient for highly irregular or non-manifold meshes where other intersection failures occur. When to use: Use this method when voxelizing STL meshes (especially terrain/heightmap data) using ray-triangle intersection and observing vertical gaps or missing voxels. It is particularly effective for meshes with regular grid topology. When not to use: If the mesh is highly irregular or if the voxelization pipeline already uses a robust intersection algorithm with epsilon handling, this may be unnecessary. For complex geometries where ray-tracing is too slow, consider SDF-based voxelization instead. This technique was proposed in a GitHub pull request to the FluidX3D project, a lattice Boltzmann CFD software, to fix vertical slice artifacts in STL mesh voxelization. The issue was identified when voxelizing terrain meshes with regular grid structures, where the Möller-Trumbore algorithm failed due to rays aligning exactly with mesh vertices. The solution, introduced by user meet-brad-ch in December 2025, adds a small jitter to ray origins perpendicular to the ray direction. It was tested on a hill.stl terrain mesh with 421 Y-aligned planes, showing a transition from visible artifacts to clean voxelization. Fix vertical slice artifacts in mesh voxelization, https://github.com/ProjectPhysX/FluidX3D/pull/323, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial)

name: Point-Triangle Distance
head: Closest Point on Triangle, Point to Triangle Distance, closestPointOnTriangleToPoint, pointToTriangleDistSqr
body: Computes the closest point on a triangle to a query point and returns the squared distance, utilizing barycentric coordinates and Voronoi-region decomposition to handle edge and vertex cases. It differs from Ray-Triangle Intersection by solving a proximity minimization problem rather than a ray-primitive intersection, and from Unsigned Triangle Distance by explicitly returning the barycentric coordinates of the closest point alongside the distance. Inputs: Triangle vertices v0, v1, v2 (3D vectors). Query point p (3D vector). Outputs: Closest point on the triangle surface. Barycentric coordinates t0, t1 such that closest = v0 + t0(v1 - v0) + t1(v2 - v0). Squared distance from p to the closest point. Data Structures: Standard 3D vector type supporting arithmetic operations and dot product. Scalar floating-point type for parameters t0, t1. Steps: 1. Compute edge vectors: edge0 = v1 - v0 edge1 = v2 - v0 2. Compute vector from triangle vertex to query point: v0\p = v0 - p 3. Compute dot products: a = edge0 \cdot edge0 b = edge0 \cdot edge1 c = edge1 \cdot edge1 d = edge0 \cdot v0\p e = edge1 \cdot v0\p 4. Compute determinant and parameters: det = a \cdot c - b \cdot b s = b \cdot e - c \cdot d t = b \cdot d - a \cdot e 5. Determine region based on s + t relative to det: Case A: s + t < det (Closest point is inside the triangle or on an edge/vertex) If s < 0 and t < 0: If d < 0: s = \text{clamp}(-d / a, 0, 1) t = 0 Else: s = 0 t = \text{clamp}(-e / c, 0, 1) If s < 0 and t \ge 0: s = \text{clamp}(-d / a, 0, 1) t = 0 If s \ge 0 and t < 0: s = 0 t = \text{clamp}(-e / c, 0, 1) Case B: s + t \ge det (Closest point is outside the triangle's edge opposite vertex 0) If s < 0: Let tmp0 = b + d Let tmp1 = c + e If tmp1 > tmp0: s = \text{clamp}((tmp1 - tmp0) / (a - 2b + c), 0, 1) t = 1 - s Else: s = 0 t = \text{clamp}(-e / c, 0, 1) If s \ge 0 and t < 0: If a + d > b + e: s = \text{clamp}((c + e - b - d) / (a - 2b + c), 0, 1) t = 1 - s Else: s = \text{clamp}(-e / c, 0, 1) t = 0 6. Compute closest point: closest = v0 + s \cdot edge0 + t \cdot edge1 7. Return squared distance: dist^2 = \|closest - p\|^2 Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def closestpointontriangle(v0, v1, v2, p): edge0 = v1 - v0 edge1 = v2 - v0 v0p = v0 - p a = dot(edge0, edge0) b = dot(edge0, edge1) c = dot(edge1, edge1) d = dot(edge0, v0p) e = dot(edge1, v0p) det = a c - b b s = b e - c d t = b d - a e if s + t < det: if s < 0 and t < 0: if d < 0: s = clamp(-d / a, 0, 1) t = 0 else: s = 0 t = clamp(-e / c, 0, 1) elif s < 0: s = clamp(-d / a, 0, 1) t = 0 elif t < 0: s = 0 t = clamp(-e / c, 0, 1) else: if s < 0: tmp0 = b + d tmp1 = c + e if tmp1 > tmp0: denom = a - 2 b + c s = clamp((tmp1 - tmp0) / denom, 0, 1) t = 1 - s else: s = 0 t = clamp(-e / c, 0, 1) elif t < 0: if a + d > b + e: denom = a - 2 b + c s = clamp((c + e - b - d) / denom, 0, 1) t = 1 - s else: s = clamp(-e / c, 0, 1) t = 0 closest = v0 + s edge0 + t edge1 distsq = dot(closest - p, closest - p) return closest, distsq, s, t def clamp(x, minval, maxval): if x < minval: return minval if x > maxval: return maxval return x Parameters: Vec3T: Any vector type supporting arithmetic and dot product. v0, v1, v2: Triangle vertices. p: Query point. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Degenerate triangles (zero area, collinear or coincident vertices) are handled implicitly: the face-interior test naturally fails and the code falls through to the nearest edge or vertex result. Division by zero is avoided by the logic structure, as denominators like a, c, and a-2b+c correspond to squared lengths or edge lengths in degenerate cases, but the conditional checks ensure valid regions are selected. Computes the unsigned distance from a query point to a triangle defined by three vertices a, b, c. It checks if the point projects inside the triangle to decide between computing the minimum edge distance or the plane distance. Mesh SDF Sampling constructs a callable signed distance field (SDF) sampler function from a THREE.BufferGeometry instance and a world transform matrix. It solves the problem of efficiently evaluating the shortest signed distance from arbitrary world-space coordinates to a triangle mesh surface, where negative values indicate interior points and positive values indicate exterior points. It differs from generic geometry samplers by specifically handling the THREE.Mesh abstraction, including automatic world matrix updates, and delegates the core geometric computation to a lower-level geometry sampler. This method voxelizes watertight triangular meshes into Signed Distance Functions (SDFs) or occupancy grids by computing the distance from voxel reference points to mesh faces or by testing for geometric intersection between triangles and voxel boxes. It distinguishes itself from pure SDF-based occupancy derivation by using explicit triangle-box intersection tests to guarantee that any voxel intersecting the mesh surface is marked as occupied, avoiding the "leaky" voxels common in SDF-only approaches. It builds on Point-Triangle Distance for SDF computation and relies on Unsigned Triangle Distance concepts for spatial proximity checks. Computes the barycentric coordinates of a 3D point relative to a triangle defined by three vertices. It solves the problem of expressing a point's position within a triangle's local coordinate system, which is a prerequisite for Point-Triangle Distance. It sets itself apart from sibling methods by focusing on the geometric projection and area-based calculation rather than distance minimization or mesh sampling. The Triangle Coverage Test verifies whether a triangle T is completely contained within the union of three spheres centered at its vertices, with radii determined by a scalar field function f evaluated at those vertices. It solves the problem of ensuring that a discrete sampling of an implicit volume is dense enough to guarantee no gaps exist between the approximating spheres, which is critical for sphere carving algorithms. Unlike general ray-triangle intersection which determines visibility, this test determines topological completeness of the volume approximation. It is distinct from Point-Triangle Distance by focusing on set containment rather than proximity, and from Barycentric Coordinate Calculation by using barycentric logic only implicitly to define the triangle domain. Zero Set Initialization of Meshes is a method for initializing the signed distance field (SDF) of a triangular mesh by identifying samples that lie on or near the mesh surface (the "zero set") and assigning them initial signs. It solves the problem of establishing an accurate initial distance field from a polygonal mesh without relying on global topological information. It differs from its sibling Unsigned Triangle Distance by computing signed distances and from Mesh SDF Sampling by focusing specifically on the initialization phase for distance transforms rather than general sampling. It builds on Point-Triangle Distance to determine geometric proximity. Computes the unsigned distance from a point to a quadrilateral defined by four vertices a, b, c, d. It checks if the point is inside the projected quad to decide between edge distance and plane distance. If the point is inside the quad (sum of signs < 3), return the minimum squared distance to the four edges. Otherwise, return the squared distance to the plane containing the quad. Edge distance uses projection: \text{proj}{ba}(pa) = ba \cdot \text{clamp}(\frac{ba \cdot pa}{\|ba\|^2}, 0, 1). Parameters: a, b, c, d: vec3, the four vertices of the quadrilateral in order. Time Complexity: O(1) per triangle, involving a fixed number of arithmetic operations. Memory Complexity: O(1) auxiliary space. Performance: Highly efficient for single-triangle queries; suitable for GPU implementation due to lack of branching dependencies in the core arithmetic. Strengths: Robust handling of degenerate triangles; provides barycentric coordinates useful for interpolation. Limitations: Not directly applicable to non-planar or complex polygons without decomposition. Originating from Ericson's "Real-Time Collision Detection" (Sec. 5.1.5), the method uses Voronoi-region decomposition to efficiently find the closest point on a triangle. It is widely used in collision detection, physics simulation, and signed distance field computations.
