name: Unsigned Triangle Distance
head: Unsigned Triangle, udTriangle
body: Computes the unsigned distance from a query point to a triangle defined by three vertices a, b, c. It checks if the point projects inside the triangle to decide between computing the minimum edge distance or the plane distance. Inputs: p: Query point (vec3). a, b, c: Triangle vertices (vec3). Outputs: d: Unsigned distance (float). Data Structures: Intermediate vectors ba, pa, cb, pb, ac, pc, nor (all vec3). Steps: 1. Compute edge vectors and point-to-vertex vectors: ba = b - a, \quad pa = p - a cb = c - b, \quad pb = p - b ac = a - c, \quad pc = p - c. 2. Compute the triangle normal: nor = ba \times ac. 3. Determine if the point projects inside the triangle by summing the signs of the cross products of each edge with the normal against the corresponding point vector: inside = (\text{sign}(\text{dot}(\text{cross}(ba, nor), pa)) + \text{sign}(\text{dot}(\text{cross}(cb, nor), pb)) + \text{sign}(\text{dot}(\text{cross}(ac, nor), pc))) < 2.0. 4. If inside, compute the minimum squared distance to the three edges. For each edge (e.g., ba), project pa onto ba clamped to [0, 1]: proj = ba \cdot \text{clamp}\left(\frac{ba \cdot pa}{\|ba\|^2}, 0.0, 1.0\right) dist^2 = \|proj - pa\|^2. 5. If not inside, compute the squared distance to the plane containing the triangle: dist^2 = \frac{(nor \cdot pa)^2}{\|nor\|^2}. 6. Return \sqrt{dist^2}. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def dot(v1, v2): return v1[0]v2[0] + v1[1]v2[1] + v1[2]v2[2] def cross(v1, v2): return (v1[1]v2[2] - v1[2]v2[1], v1[2]v2[0] - v1[0]v2[2], v1[0]v2[1] - v1[1]v2[0]) def clamp(x, lo, hi): return max(lo, min(hi, x)) def sign(x): return 1 if x > 0 else (-1 if x < 0 else 0) def dot2(v): return dot(v, v) def udTriangle(p, a, b, c): ba = (b[0]-a[0], b[1]-a[1], b[2]-a[2]) pa = (p[0]-a[0], p[1]-a[1], p[2]-a[2]) cb = (c[0]-b[0], c[1]-b[1], c[2]-b[2]) pb = (p[0]-b[0], p[1]-b[1], p[2]-b[2]) ac = (a[0]-c[0], a[1]-c[1], a[2]-c[2]) pc = (p[0]-c[0], p[1]-c[1], p[2]-c[2]) nor = cross(ba, ac) s1 = sign(dot(cross(ba, nor), pa)) s2 = sign(dot(cross(cb, nor), pb)) s3 = sign(dot(cross(ac, nor), pc)) inside = (s1 + s2 + s3) < 2.0 if inside: projba = (ba[0]clamp(dot(ba, pa)/dot2(ba), 0.0, 1.0), ba[1]clamp(dot(ba, pa)/dot2(ba), 0.0, 1.0), ba[2]clamp(dot(ba, pa)/dot2(ba), 0.0, 1.0)) distba = dot2((projba[0]-pa[0], projba[1]-pa[1], projba[2]-pa[2])) projcb = (cb[0]clamp(dot(cb, pb)/dot2(cb), 0.0, 1.0), cb[1]clamp(dot(cb, pb)/dot2(cb), 0.0, 1.0), cb[2]clamp(dot(cb, pb)/dot2(cb), 0.0, 1.0)) distcb = dot2((projcb[0]-pb[0], projcb[1]-pb[1], projcb[2]-pb[2])) projac = (ac[0]clamp(dot(ac, pc)/dot2(ac), 0.0, 1.0), ac[1]clamp(dot(ac, pc)/dot2(ac), 0.0, 1.0), ac[2]clamp(dot(ac, pc)/dot2(ac), 0.0, 1.0)) distac = dot2((projac[0]-pc[0], projac[1]-pc[1], projac[2]-pc[2])) return math.sqrt(min(distba, min(distcb, distac))) else: return math.sqrt(dot(nor, pa)dot(nor, pa) / dot2(nor)) Parameters: a, b, c: vec3. Vertices of the triangle. Order does not affect unsigned distance magnitude, but affects normal direction (used only for the inside check logic which is robust to winding). Edge Cases: Degenerate Triangle: If a, b, c are collinear, nor is zero. The plane distance formula divides by \|nor\|^2, causing division by zero. A guard should check dot2(nor) < epsilon and fallback to point-to-segment distance on the longest edge. Point on Plane: If the point lies on the plane but outside the triangle, the plane distance formula yields 0 because nor \cdot pa = 0. This correctly represents the distance to the infinite plane, though the point is outside the triangle boundary. Precision: Clamping prevents extrapolation errors on edges. Computes the center and radius of the unique circle passing through three non-collinear vertices a, b, c of a triangle. This method is primarily used in volume rendering to define the bounding sphere (splat) for triangle-based leaf nodes, as described in Unsigned Triangle Distance. It is distinguished by its formulation using vector cross products and coordinate differences, which minimizes numerical error for vertices far from the origin, and by a specific fallback strategy for obtuse triangles. Time Complexity: O(1). Fixed number of vector operations. Memory Complexity: O(1). No dynamic allocation. Strengths: Robust handling of edge/vertex proximity without explicit case branching for barycentric coordinates. Fast execution suitable for ray marching. Limitations: Does not provide signed distance (orientation). Degenerate triangles cause division by zero. When to use: When only magnitude of distance is needed, e.g., for blending or collision response. When not to use: When surface normal orientation is required (use Signed Triangle Distance). Originated in the GLSL SDF primitives library by Marklundin. It is a standard primitive in ray marching and distance field rendering. marklundin/glsl-sdf-primitives, https://github.com/marklundin/glsl-sdf-primitives, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial)

name: Triangle Circum-Center Calculation
head: Circum-center, Circumcircle Center
body: Computes the circum-center and circum-radius of a triangle defined by three vertices a, b, c. It is used to derive bounding spheres for triangle-based leaf nodes in volume rendering. Inputs: Three vertices a, b, c \in \mathbb{R}^3. Outputs: Absolute circum-center C and circum-radius R. Data Structures: No persistent data structures are required. Parameters: Not given in the sources. Steps: 1. Compute edge vectors relative to a: ab = b - a, ac = c - a. 2. Compute A(b, c) = ab \times ac. Evaluate the denominator 2|A(b, c)|^2. If near zero, the vertices are co-linear (degenerate). 3. For non-degenerate triangles, determine if the triangle is obtuse. If obtuse, approximate the circum-center as the midpoint of the longest edge and the circum-radius as half the length of that edge. 4. For non-obtuse triangles, compute the relative circum-center m{tri} using the analytic formula. 5. Compute the absolute center C = a + m{tri} and the radius R = |m{tri}|. Formula: Let A(u, v) = (u - a) \times (v - a). The relative circum-center m{tri} is: m{tri} = \frac{|c - a|^2 A(b, c) \times (b - a) + |b - a|^2 (c - a) \times A(b, c)}{2 |A(b, c)|^2} Where: | \cdot | denotes the Euclidean norm. \times denotes the cross product. The denominator is 2 |A(b, c)|^2. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Degeneracy: The denominator vanishes when vertices are co-linear. Numerical Stability: The formula uses differences of coordinates rather than absolute values, which reduces relative error since vertices are typically closer to each other than to the origin. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math from typing import Tuple, List def crossproduct(u: List[float], v: List[float]) -> List[float]: return [ u[1]v[2] - u[2]v[1], u[2]v[0] - u[0]v[2], u[0]v[1] - u[1]v[0] ] def dotproduct(u: List[float], v: List[float]) -> float: return u[0]v[0] + u[1]v[1] + u[2]v[2] def vectorsub(u: List[float], v: List[float]) -> List[float]: return [u[0]-v[0], u[1]-v[1], u[2]-v[2]] def vectornormsq(u: List[float]) -> float: return dotproduct(u, u) def trianglecircumcenter(a: List[float], b: List[float], c: List[float]) -> Tuple[List[float], float]: ab = vectorsub(b, a) ac = vectorsub(c, a) Abc = crossproduct(ab, ac) denomsq = 2.0 vectornormsq(Abc) # Fallback for degenerate (co-linear) vertices if denomsq < 1e-12: lenab = math.sqrt(vectornormsq(ab)) lenac = math.sqrt(vectornormsq(ac)) lenbc = math.sqrt(vectornormsq(vectorsub(c, b))) maxlen = max(lenab, lenac, lenbc) if maxlen == lenab: return [(a[0]+b[0])/2, (a[1]+b[1])/2, (a[2]+b[2])/2], lenab / 2.0 elif maxlen == lenac: return [(a[0]+c[0])/2, (a[1]+c[1])/2, (a[2]+c[2])/2], lenac / 2.0 else: return [(b[0]+c[0])/2, (b[1]+c[1])/2, (b[2]+c[2])/2], lenbc / 2.0 # Check for obtuse triangle ba = vectorsub(a, b) bc = vectorsub(c, b) ca = vectorsub(a, c) cb = vectorsub(b, c) dota = dotproduct(ab, ac) dotb = dotproduct(ba, bc) dotc = dotproduct(ca, cb) if dota < 0 or dotb < 0 or dotc < 0: lenab = math.sqrt(vectornormsq(ab)) lenac = math.sqrt(vectornormsq(ac)) lenbc = math.sqrt(vectornormsq(bc)) maxlen = max(lenab, lenac, lenbc) if maxlen == lenab: return [(a[0]+b[0])/2, (a[1]+b[1])/2, (a[2]+b[2])/2], lenab / 2.0 elif maxlen == lenac: return [(a[0]+c[0])/2, (a[1]+c[1])/2, (a[2]+c[2])/2], lenac / 2.0 else: return [(b[0]+c[0])/2, (b[1]+c[1])/2, (b[2]+c[2])/2], lenbc / 2.0 term1vec = crossproduct(Abc, ab) term2vec = crossproduct(ac, Abc) term1 = vectornormsq(ac) term1vec term2 = vectornormsq(ab) term2vec numerator = [term1[0] + term2[0], term1[1] + term2[1], term1[2] + term2[2]] mtri = [numerator[0] / denomsq, numerator[1] / denomsq, numerator[2] / denomsq] center = [a[0] + mtri[0], a[1] + mtri[1], a[2] + mtri[2]] radius = math.sqrt(vectornormsq(mtri)) return center, radius Computes the center and radius of the sphere passing through four vertices a, b, c, d. It is chosen when tetrahedral primitives are used instead of triangles. The relative circum-center m{tet} is: m{tet} = \frac{|d - a|^2 A(b, c) + |c - a|^2 A(d, b) + |b - a|^2 A(c, d)}{2 \det\begin{pmatrix} [b-a]x & [b-a]y & [b-a]z \\ [c-a]x & [c-a]y & [c-a]z \\ [d-a]x & [d-a]y & [d-a]z \end{pmatrix}} Where A(u, v) = (u - a) \times (v - a) and [u]k is the k-th component. The absolute center is a + m{tet} and radius is |m{tet}|. Using differences of coordinates rather than absolute values reduces relative error, as vertices are usually nearer to each other than to the origin. The formula becomes unstable if the denominator vanishes, which occurs when the tetrahedron is nearly degenerate (flat or needle-shaped). Constant-time evaluation per primitive. Numerically stable for non-degenerate triangles when using coordinate differences. Unstable for degenerate inputs. Not given in the sources for measured performance or scaling behavior. Originated in the TetSplat paper by Museth and Lombeyda (2004) for real-time rendering and volume clipping of large meshes. The method is adapted from reference [19] in the original paper. It is used to derive leaf nodes for hierarchical volume representations from triangle meshes. TetSplat: Real-time Rendering and Volume Clipping of Large... - Museth, https://ken.museth.org/Publicationsfiles/Museth-LombeydaVIS04.pdf, fetched 2026-10-28 (unofficial)

name: Mesh SDF Sampling
head: Signed Distance Field Sampler from Geometry, createGeometrySdfSampler
body: Mesh SDF Sampling constructs a callable signed distance field (SDF) sampler function from a THREE.BufferGeometry instance and a world transform matrix. It solves the problem of evaluating the shortest signed distance from arbitrary world-space coordinates to a triangle mesh surface, where negative values indicate interior points and positive values indicate exterior points. It differs from raw mesh intersection tests by providing continuous distance gradients essential for smooth shading and anti-aliasing. Inputs: geometry: A THREE.BufferGeometry instance. Must be indexed. matrix: A THREE.Matrix4 representing the world transform of the mesh. Outputs: A function sampler(x, y, z) returning a number (the signed distance). Data Structures: worldPositions: An array of vertices transformed into world space. Size equals geometry.attributes.position.count. index: An integer array from geometry.index.array. position: The THREE.BufferAttribute from geometry.attributes.position. Temporary Vectors (allocated once, reused): va, vb, vc: Vertices of the current triangle. ab, ac, bc: Edge vectors. ap, bp, cp: Vectors from vertices to point p. n: Normal vector. p, q: Point p (query), q (closest point on triangle). bestPoint: The closest point found so far. bestNormal: The normal at bestPoint. toPoint: Vector from bestPoint to p. Steps: 1. Validation: Check if geometry.index exists. If not, throw an error "Geometry must be indexed". 2. Precomputation: Extract position and index arrays. Initialize worldPositions array. Iterate i from 0 to position.count - 1: create a vector from position at index i, apply matrix to transform it to world space, and store in worldPositions[i]. 3. Sampler Function Definition: Return a function sampler(x, y, z). 4. Query Execution: Inside the function, set p to (x, y, z) and initialize closestDistance2 to Infinity. 5. Triangle Iteration: Iterate i from 0 to index.length - 1 with step 3: get indices ia = index[i], ib = index[i+1], ic = index[i+2]. Retrieve va = worldPositions[ia], vb = worldPositions[ib], vc = worldPositions[ic]. 6. Closest Point & Distance: Compute q as the closest point on triangle va, vb, vc to p. Compute distance2 = p.distanceToSquared(q). 7. Update Best: If distance2 < closestDistance2: update closestDistance2 = distance2. Copy q to bestPoint. Compute edge vectors ab = vb - va, ac = vc - va. Compute bestNormal = ab.cross(ac).normalize(). 8. Sign Calculation: After the loop, compute toPoint = p - bestPoint. Compute dot = toPoint.dot(bestNormal). Set sign = 1 if dot >= 0, else sign = -1. 9. Return: Return Math.sqrt(closestDistance2) sign. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math class Vec3: def init(self, x=0.0, y=0.0, z=0.0): self.x, self.y, self.z = x, y, z def set(self, x, y, z): self.x, self.y, self.z = x, y, z def copy(self, other): self.x, self.y, self.z = other.x, other.y, other.z def sub(self, other): return Vec3(self.x - other.x, self.y - other.y, self.z - other.z) def add(self, other): return Vec3(self.x + other.x, self.y + other.y, self.z + other.z) def scale(self, s): return Vec3(self.x s, self.y s, self.z s) def dot(self, other): return self.x other.x + self.y other.y + self.z other.z def cross(self, other): return Vec3(self.y other.z - self.z other.y, self.z other.x - self.x other.z, self.x other.y - self.y other.x) def lengthsq(self): return self.dot(self) def length(self): return math.sqrt(self.lengthsq()) def normalize(self): l = self.length() return self.scale(1.0 / l) if l > 1e-12 else Vec3() def lerp(self, other, t): return self.add(other.sub(self).scale(t)) def closestpointontriangle(p, a, b, c): # Standard algorithm based on Christer Ericson's Real-Time Collision Detection ab = b.sub(a) ac = c.sub(a) ap = p.sub(a) d1 = ab.dot(ap) d2 = ac.dot(ap) if d1 <= 0.0 and d2 <= 0.0: return a.copy() bp = p.sub(b) d3 = ab.dot(bp) d4 = ab.dot(ab) if d3 >= 0.0 and d1 <= d3: t = d1 / d4 return a.lerp(b, t) vc = ap.sub(ab.scale(d1 / d4)) if vc.dot(vc) <= 0.0: t = d1 / d4 return a.lerp(b, t) cp = p.sub(c) d5 = ac.dot(cp) d6 = ac.dot(ac) if d5 <= 0.0 and d2 <= d5: t = d2 / d6 return a.lerp(c, t) vb = ap.sub(ac.scale(d2 / d6)) if vb.dot(vb) <= 0.0: t = d2 / d6 return a.lerp(c, t) # name: Signed Distance Field Sampler from Mesh
head: createMeshInstanceSdfSampler
body: This method constructs a signed distance field (SDF) sampler function from a THREE.Mesh instance, enabling efficient ray-marching or point-query operations against complex geometry in volume rendering pipelines. It solves the problem of converting explicit triangle meshes into implicit distance functions, where negative values indicate interior points and positive values indicate exterior points. Unlike raw mesh intersection tests which return binary hit/miss results, this method provides continuous distance gradients essential for smooth shading and anti-aliasing. It acts as a thin abstraction layer over the underlying geometry sampler, delegating the core distance computation to Mesh SDF Sampling while handling mesh-specific state management like world matrix updates. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A THREE.Mesh instance containing a THREE.BufferGeometry and a transformation matrix. Output: A JavaScript function (x, y, z) => number that returns the signed distance in world space. Data Structures: The method relies on the internal structure of THREE.Mesh and THREE.BufferGeometry. No new data structures are created by this specific wrapper; it references the geometry's index and attribute arrays directly via the delegated sampler. Steps: 1. Validation: Check if the input object is an instance of THREE.Mesh. If not, throw an error with the message 'Expected a THREE.Mesh instance'. 2. Matrix Update: Call instance.updateMatrixWorld(true) to ensure the mesh's world transformation matrix is up-to-date, including any parent hierarchy transformations. 3. Delegation: Invoke the helper function createGeometrySdfSampler passing instance.geometry and instance.matrixWorld as arguments. The result of this call is the returned sampler function. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def createmeshinstancesdfsampler(mesh): # Step 1: Validation if not isinstance(mesh, THREE.Mesh): raise ValueError("Expected a THREE.Mesh instance") # Step 2: Update World Matrix # The boolean argument ensures parent matrices are also updated if necessary mesh.updatematrixworld(true) # Step 3: Delegate to Geometry Sampler # This returns a function (x, y, z) -> distance sampler = creategeometrysdfsampler(mesh.geometry, mesh.matrixworld) return sampler Parameters: None explicitly defined in the wrapper logic; parameters are inherited from the underlying geometry sampler. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Non-Mesh Input: Passing a THREE.Object3D or other non-mesh object will cause an immediate runtime error. Stale Transforms: If updateMatrixWorld is not called, the sampler will use outdated world coordinates, leading to incorrect distance calculations for animated or parented meshes. Empty Geometry: If the mesh has no vertices or indices, the delegated sampler may return undefined behavior or constant values depending on the implementation of createGeometrySdfSampler. Time Complexity: The wrapper itself is O(1), dominated by the matrix update and function call overhead. The actual distance computation complexity depends on the underlying Mesh SDF Sampling implementation, which typically scales with the number of triangles or the efficiency of the spatial acceleration structure (e.g., BVH) used within the geometry sampler. Memory Complexity: O(1) additional memory for the wrapper function. The geometry data is already resident in memory. Strengths: Simple API; handles world-space transformation automatically; integrates seamlessly with Three.js ecosystem. Limitations: Relies on the performance of the underlying geometry sampler; requires explicit matrix updates for dynamic scenes. This method is part of the three.js-volume-renderer project, an unofficial implementation of volume rendering techniques using Three.js. It was developed to provide a convenient way to sample signed distances from mesh-based objects for use in ray-marched volume rendering scenes. name: Surface Distance Query
head: Minimum Surface Distance Query, Closest Surface Search
body: Surface Distance Query is a method for determining the minimum Euclidean distance from a query point to a collection of geometric surfaces, while optionally identifying the specific surface responsible for that minimum distance. It solves the problem of proximity detection in scenes containing multiple distinct objects or mesh parts, serving as the foundational lookup mechanism for Signed Distance Field (SDF) Samplers built from meshes [Parent]. Unlike single-mesh distance queries, this method aggregates results across a list of surfaces, enabling complex scene representations where the global distance is the minimum of local surface distances. Inputs: point: A 3D coordinate (x, y, z) in world space. surfaces: A list or array of surface objects. Each surface object must implement a method distance(p) that returns the signed or unsigned distance from point p to that specific surface. Outputs: mindist: The scalar minimum distance found. closestsurface: The reference to the surface object that yielded mindist. Data Structures: surfaces: An iterable collection of surface handles. mindist: Initialized to a large constant representing "infinity" or the maximum search radius. closestsurface: Initialized to null or None. Algorithm Steps: 1. Initialize mindist to MAXDISTANCE (a value larger than any expected scene dimension, e.g., 2000.0f). 2. Initialize closestsurface to null. 3. Iterate through each surface in the surfaces list: a. Compute d = surface.distance(point). b. If d < mindist: i. Set mindist = d. ii. Set closestsurface = surface. 4. Return mindist and closestsurface. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def surfacedistancequery(point, surfaces, maxdistance=2000.0): """ Finds the minimum distance from point to any surface in the list. Args: point: Tuple or array of (x, y, z). surfaces: List of objects with a.distance(p) method. maxdistance: Upper bound for initialization. Returns: mindist: Float, the minimum distance. closestsurface: Object, the surface yielding the minimum distance. """ mindist = maxdistance closestsurface = None for surface in surfaces: # Call the surface-specific distance function d = surface.distance(point) if d < mindist: mindist = d closestsurface = surface return mindist, closestsurface Parameters: maxdistance: Typical value depends on scene scale. In the reference implementation, MAXDISTANCE is set to 2000f. MINDISTANCE: A lower bound threshold used in ray marching contexts to terminate early if the distance is sufficiently small (e.g., 0.2f). Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Empty List: If surfaces is empty, the function returns maxdistance and null. The caller must handle this case to avoid dereferencing a null surface. Precision: Floating-point comparison d < mindist is standard. For signed distances, negative values (inside geometry) will correctly update the minimum if they are smaller than the current positive minimum. Performance: This is a linear scan O(N) where N is the number of surfaces. For large N, spatial partitioning (BVH, Grid) is required before querying individual surfaces, but the query logic itself remains a reduction. Definition: A variant configuration for high-density meshes (e.g., vegetation with masked materials like leaves/branches) where surfaces contain many holes and cannot be treated as solid opaque boundaries. It generates distance fields for both sides of the geometry. When to choose: Use for semi-transparent or highly perforated geometry like trees and grass where standard one-sided distance fields fail to capture the interior/exterior relationship correctly. Pitfall: Enabling this increases ray marching cost because the surface becomes semi-transparent in the distance field representation, requiring more steps to find the mesh intersection compared to opaque surfaces. Definition: A rendering technique that colors a surface based on the geodesic (mesh-path) distance from a query point, computed via Dijkstra's algorithm on the surface mesh connectivity. Steps: 1. Find the closest mesh vertex to the query point using a spatial locator. 2. Run Dijkstra's algorithm on the surface mesh from the closest vertex to a dummy end vertex (0) to compute cumulative edge weights. 3. Extract cumulative weights as a numpy array and replace uncomputed/infinite distances with -1.0. 4. Normalize distances based on climmax (default 'ptile95'): supports 'max', 'mean', 'median', 'ptileN' (percentile), or a float. Divide by climmax, scale to 0-255, clip, and mark negatives as -1. 5. Construct a 257-entry LUT: index 0 is white with specified alpha; indices 1-256 map to the colormap. 6. Create a polydata mapper, set input, override scalar range to (-1.0, maxdatarange), and bind the LUT. Parameters: climmax: Normalization target, default 'ptile95'. Layout: vtk.vtkLookupTable: 257 entries. Index 0 stores white (1.0, 1.0, 1.0, alpha). Indices 1-256 store colormap colors. Pitfall: Unreachable mesh regions or uncomputed Dijkstra weights exceed VTKDOUBLEMAX/10.0 and must be explicitly replaced with -1.0 to avoid rendering artifacts. Time Complexity: O(N) per query, where N is the number of surfaces in the list. Each surface distance calculation is O(1) for analytic primitives or O(M) for mesh queries depending on the surface implementation. Memory Complexity: O(N) to store the list of surface references. No additional temporary memory is required beyond scalar variables. Strengths: Simple to implement; agnostic to the underlying surface representation (triangle, sphere, plane) as long as a distance() method exists. Limitations: Linear scan does not scale to scenes with thousands of surfaces without spatial acceleration structures. Does not handle self-occlusion or visibility; it returns the geometric minimum, not the visible minimum. When to use: Small to medium-sized scenes, or as a backend for SDF samplers where the number of constituent meshes is manageable [Parent, S1]. When not to use: Large-scale open worlds with millions of objects; use spatial hashing or BVH-based distance queries instead. The method originates from basic ray-marching shader implementations where multiple surface types (planes, spheres, meshes) are queried per pixel to determine the closest hit. It is a core component of the "Signed Distance Field Sampler from Mesh" pipeline, allowing a single sampler function to abstract over a THREE.Mesh instance composed of multiple geometries [Parent]. The specific implementation details (MAXDISTANCE=2000f, MINDISTANCE=0.2f) come from a Java-based ray marching engine. The variant "Geodesic Distance Rendering" utilizes VTK's Dijkstra implementation for path-based distance visualization. conradplake/ray-marching-shader, https://github.com/conradplake/ray-marching-shader, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial) 虚幻引擎网格体距离场, https://dev.epicgames.com/documentation/unreal-engine/mesh-distance-fields-in-unreal-engine?lang=zh-CN, fetched 2026-10-30 Volume Renderer with VTK - yuta-hi, https://github.com/yuta-hi/volume-renderer, fetched 2026-10-29 (unofficial)

name: 3D Empty Space Supervision
head: 3D emptiness supervision, object field emptiness loss
body: 3D Empty Space Supervision is a method for regularizing the non-occupied regions of a learned radiance field by supervising the "object code" using estimated surface distances. It solves the problem of ambiguous empty space in neural rendering, where the model may incorrectly assign object semantics to background voxels. It sets itself apart from standard volume rendering losses by explicitly computing a "surfaceness" and "emptiness" score for every sample point along a ray, allowing for targeted supervision of the object field's background channel. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: A set of K 3D sample points \{pk\}{k=1}^K along a query ray; the learned density \sigmak and distance intervals \deltak for each sample; the camera-to-sample distance dk; the hyperparameter \Delta d; the object code vector ok \in \mathbb{R}^{H+1} for each sample point. Outputs: The 3D empty space loss \ell{3d\empty} and the 3D object field loss \ell{3d\obj}, which are combined with 2D losses to optimize the object field MLP. Data Structures: Object Code (ok): A one-hot vector of dimension H+1. The first H dimensions represent specific object classes, and the (H+1)-th dimension represents the "empty" or "background" class. Sample Point Data: For each k \in \{1, \dots, K\}: dk: Distance from camera center to sample point k. \sigmak: Learned density at sample point k. \deltak: Distance between sample point k and k+1 (or to the ray end). Step-by-Step Method: 1. Compute Transmittance and Alpha: For each sample point k, compute the transmittance Tk and alpha \alphak using the standard volume rendering equations: Tk = \exp\left(-\sum{i=1}^{k-1} \sigmai \deltai\right) \alphak = 1 - \exp(-\sigmak \deltak) Note: T1 = 1. 2. Estimate Surface Distance (d): Calculate the approximate distance from the camera center to the surface hit point along the ray: d = \sum{k=1}^K Tk \alphak \deltak 3. Compute Surfaceness Score (sk): For each sample point k, compute the surfaceness score, which measures how close the sample is to the estimated surface distance d: sk = \exp\left(-(dk - d)^2\right) 4. Compute Emptiness Score (ek): For each sample point k, compute the emptiness score. This score is high for points in front of the surface (empty space) and zero for points behind the surface: ek = (1 - sk) \cdot \mathbbm{1}(d - \Delta d - dk > 0) Where \mathbbm{1}(\cdot) is the indicator function: 1 if the condition is true, 0 otherwise. \Delta d is a hyperparameter compensating for distance estimation inaccuracy. 5. Compute 3D Empty Loss (\ell{3d\empty}): Supervise the last dimension of the object code (o^{H+1}k), which corresponds to the empty class: \ell{3d\empty} = -\frac{1}{K} \sum{k=1}^K \Big ( ek \log(o^{H+1}k) + sk \log(1 - o^{H+1}k) \Big) Note: The term sk \log(1 - o^{H+1}k) encourages the empty class probability to be low at the surface. 6. Compute 3D Object Field Loss (\ell{3d\obj}): Push the first H dimensions of the object code (o^hk for h=1 \dots H) to zero in empty space: \ell{3d\obj} = - \frac{1}{K} \sum{k=1}^K \Big ( ek \sum{h=1}^H \log(1 - o^hk) \Big) 7. Total Loss: The total object field loss is the sum of the 2D object loss (\ell{2d\obj}), the 3D empty loss, and the 3D object field loss: \ell = \ell{2d\obj} + \ell{3d\empty} + \ell{3d\obj} Parameters: \Delta d: Hyperparameter to compensate for inaccuracy in the estimated surface distance d. Typical value: 0.05 meters. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def compute3demptysupervision(dk, sigma, delta, objectcode, deltad=0.05): """ Computes 3D empty space supervision losses for a single ray. Args: dk: Array of shape (K,), distance from camera to each sample point. sigma: Array of shape (K,), learned density at each sample point. delta: Array of shape (K,), distance between consecutive sample points. objectcode: Array of shape (K, H+1), object code for each sample point. Last dimension (H+1) is the empty/background class. deltad: Float, hyperparameter for distance inaccuracy compensation. Returns: loss3dempty: Float, emptiness supervision loss. loss3dobj: Float, object field suppression loss in empty space. """ K = len(sigma) # Step 1: Compute Transmittance Tk # Tk = exp(-sum{i=1}^{k-1} sigmai deltai) # We compute cumulative sum of sigma delta sigmadelta = sigma delta cumsum = np.cumsum(sigmadelta) # Tk corresponds to exp(-cumsum[k-1]) for k > 0, T0 = 1 # To align with formula Tk for sample k, we need sum of previous intervals # Let's define T array where T[k] is transmittance arriving at sample k T = np.exp(np.concatenate(([0.0], cumsum[:-1]))) # T[0] = exp(0) = 1 # Step 2: Compute Alpha alphak alpha = 1.0 - np.exp(-sigma delta) # Step 3: Estimate Surface Distance d # d = sum{k=1}^K Tk alphak deltak # Note: The formula uses Tk and alphak for the k-th sample. # In standard volume rendering, contribution of sample k is Tk alphak deltak? # Actually, standard color is sum Tk alphak colork. # Here d is weighted average of distances. # The formula says d = sum Tk alphak deltak. # Wait, deltak is the interval length. The distance contribution is usually Tk alphak dk? # Let's re-read: "d = sum{k=1}^K Tk alphak deltak". # This seems to be an approximation of the mean depth. # Usually mean depth is sum Tk alphak dk. # However, the source explicitly writes deltak. # Let's stick strictly to the source formula provided in. d = np.sum(T alpha delta) # Step 4: Compute Surfaceness Score sk # sk = exp(-(dk - d)^2) s = np.exp(-(dk - d)2) # Step 5: Compute Emptiness Score ek # ek = (1 - sk) 1(d - deltad - dk > 0) indicator = (d - deltad - dk > 0).astype(float) e = (1.0 - s) indicator # Step 6: Compute Losses # Object code shape: (K, H+1) # ok^{H+1} is the last column oempty = objectcode[:, -1] oobjects = objectcode[:,:-1] # First H dimensions # l3dempty = -1/K sum( ek log(ok^{H+1}) + sk log(1 - ok^{H+1})) # Add epsilon to log to avoid NaN eps = 1e-7 term1 = e np.log(oempty + eps) term2 = s np.log(1.0 - oempty + eps) loss3dempty = -np.mean(term1 + term2) # l3dobj = -1/K sum( ek sum{h=1}^H log(1 - ok^h)) # sum over H dimensions for each k log1minusoobjects = np.log(1.0 - oobjects + eps) sumh = np.sum(log1minusoobjects, axis=1) # Shape (K,) loss3dobj = -np.mean(e sumh) return loss3dempty, loss3dobj Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision: The indicator function \mathbbm{1}(d - \Delta d - dk > 0) creates a hard boundary. Small errors in d can cause discontinuous changes in loss gradients. The hyperparameter \Delta d smooths this by creating a buffer zone. Degenerate Input: If \sigmak = 0 for all k, then Tk=1, \alphak=0, d=0. The surfaceness scores will be based on distance from camera. This is valid but may not provide useful surface supervision if no geometry is present. Boundary Conditions: The formula assumes K samples are sufficient to capture the surface. If the surface is between samples, d is an approximation. A supervision signal using HD map ground height fields to guide density field reconstruction, partitioning ray termination into uncertain, ground, and certain regions to avoid applying supervision where map data is unreliable. It differs from 3D Empty Space Supervision by using external map data (height fields) rather than estimated surface distances from the radiance field itself. It is chosen when high-definition maps are available for driving scenes. The method partitions the ray termination distribution into: 1) Uncertain region (obstacles not in map), 2) Ground region (surface within error tolerance \epsilon \approx 30cm), 3) Certain region (beneath ground). It generates a dense triangle mesh Mc from the ground height map M using Delaunay triangulation and renders it to get pseudo ground truth depth D{pgt}. The loss is: L{gd} = \mathbb{E}{r \in Ii} \left[ \int{D{pgt} - \epsilon}^{D{pgt} + \epsilon} h(t) \frac{(t - D{pgt})^2}{2\epsilon^2} \exp\left(-\frac{(t - D{pgt})^2}{2\epsilon^2}\right) dt + \int{D{pgt} + \epsilon}^{\infty} h(t)^2 dt \right] where h(t) is the ray termination distribution, and \epsilon is the uncertainty parameter (typical average error ~30cm). It also improves smoothness by sampling 2x2 patches for depth gradient computation. Time Complexity: Linear in the number of samples K per ray. The computation of d, sk, and ek involves simple arithmetic operations and exponentials. Memory Complexity: Requires storing K samples of density, distance, and object codes. No additional large data structures are needed beyond the object field MLP. Strengths: Explicitly handles empty space, preventing the model from assigning object semantics to background. Complements 2D supervision by providing 3D geometric constraints. Limitations: Relies on the accuracy of the estimated surface distance d. If the density field is poor, d is inaccurate, leading to incorrect emptiness scores. The hard indicator function can cause gradient instability without \Delta d. When to use: When learning object fields in scenes with significant empty space and 2D object masks are available. Particularly useful for geometry manipulation tasks. When not to use: When no object field representation is used, or when high-quality 3D ground truth geometry is available (in which case direct geometric losses might be preferred). 3D Empty Space Supervision was introduced in DM-NeRF (Deep Model-based Neural Radiance Fields) by Liu et al., published at ICLR 2023. The method addresses the limitation of standard NeRF which only optimizes for photometric consistency, often resulting in ambiguous geometry in empty regions. By introducing an object field and supervising it with 3D emptiness scores derived from estimated surface distances, DM-NeRF enables 3D scene geometry decomposition and manipulation from 2D images. DM-NeRF: 3D Scene Geometry Decomposition and Manipulation from 2D Images, https://arxiv.org/abs/2208.07227v2, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial) MapNeRF: Incorporating Map Priors into Neural Radiance Fields for Driving View Simulation, https://doi.org/10.1109/iros55552.2023.10341681, fetched 2026-10-26

name: Triangle-Box Intersection Voxelization
head: Mesh Voxelization via SDF and Occupancy, Triangle-Point Distance Voxelization, Watertight Mesh Voxelization
body: This method voxelizes watertight triangular meshes into Signed Distance Functions (SDFs) or occupancy grids by computing distances from voxel reference points to mesh faces or by testing for geometric intersection between triangles and voxel boxes. It distinguishes itself from pure SDF-based occupancy derivation by using explicit triangle-box intersection tests to guarantee that any voxel intersecting the mesh surface is marked as occupied, avoiding voxels that might be missed by SDF-only approaches. It builds on Point-Triangle Distance for SDF computation. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A watertight triangular mesh in OFF format (or a directory of such files). Output: An HDF5 tensor of shape N \times C \times H \times W \times D (or C \times H \times W \times D for a single file), where N is the number of input meshes, C=2 is the number of channels, H is height (y-axis), W is width (x-axis), and D is depth (z-axis). Optional Output: If the --color flag is set, an additional [int]color.h5 file stores original face colors, indexed by face IDs stored in the occupancy grid. Data Structures: Voxel Grid: A 3D array indexed by (h, w, d) corresponding to spatial coordinates. Mesh Representation: A list of triangles, each defined by 3 vertices (x, y, z). HDF5 Tensor: Dimensions [N, C, H, W, D]. C=2 holds SDF sign/distance or occupancy/color data. Values are signed distances in SDF mode, or 0/face IDs in occupancy mode. Formulas: Voxel size: \Delta x = \frac{1}{W}, \Delta y = \frac{1}{H}, \Delta z = \frac{1}{D}. Voxel bounds for index (h, w, d): x \in [w\Delta x, (w+1)\Delta x], y \in [h\Delta y, (h+1)\Delta y], z \in [d\Delta z, (d+1)\Delta z]. Voxel center: cx = (w+0.5)\Delta x, cy = (h+0.5)\Delta y, cz = (d+0.5)\Delta z. SDF sign: d{signed} = -d{min} if point is interior, d{signed} = d{min} if exterior. Parameters: --mode: 'occ' (default) or 'sdf'. --height, --width, --depth: Resolution H, W, D. Default 32 \times 32 \times 32. --center: Boolean. If set, use voxel centers for SDF computation; otherwise, use voxel corners (default). --color: Boolean. If set, store face IDs in occupancy grid and save colors to a separate file. Numbered Steps: 1. Preprocessing and Scaling: Load the input mesh. Normalize the mesh to [-0.5, 0.5]^3. Scale and translate the mesh to fit the volume bounds [0, H] \times [0, W] \times [0, D]. The coordinate system assumes x= right, y= up, z= forward. The output volume maps H \to y, W \to x, D \to z. 2. Voxelization Loop: Iterate over each voxel (h, w, d) in the grid. Determine the reference point P: if --center is false, P is the voxel corner (e.g., top-left-front); if true, P is the voxel center. If --mode is 'sdf': Compute the distance from P to the nearest triangle face using the triangle-point distance algorithm. Determine the sign: negative if P is inside the mesh, positive if outside. Store the signed distance in the output tensor. If --mode is 'occ': Perform a triangle-box intersection test between the voxel box (defined by center and half-size) and all mesh triangles. If any intersection is detected, mark the voxel as occupied. If --color is set, store the ID of the intersecting face instead of a simple binary 1. 3. Output Generation: Save the resulting tensor to an HDF5 file. If --color is set, save the face colors to [int]color.h5. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def voxelizemesh(meshtriangles, height, width, depth, mode='occ', usecenter=False, color=False): # Initialize output tensor: N=1, C=2, H, W, D outputtensor = [[[[[0.0 for in range(depth)] for in range(width)] for in range(height)] for in range(2)] for in range(1)] colordata = {} dx, dy, dz = 1.0 / width, 1.0 / height, 1.0 / depth for h in range(height): for w in range(width): for d in range(depth): # Voxel bounds in world space [0, H]x[0, W]x[0, D] # y maps to h, x maps to w, z maps to d miny, maxy = h dy, (h + 1) dy minx, maxx = w dx, (w + 1) dx minz, maxz = d dz, (d + 1) dz centery = (miny + maxy) / 2.0 centerx = (minx + maxx) / 2.0 centerz = (minz + maxz) / 2.0 halfy, halfx, halfz = dy / 2.0, dx / 2.0, dz / 2.0 if usecenter: refpoint = (centerx, centery, centerz) voxelcenter = (centerx, centery, centerz) voxelhalf = (halfx, halfy, halfz) else: refpoint = (minx, miny, minz) voxelcenter = (centerx, centery, centerz) voxelhalf = (halfx, halfy, halfz) if mode == 'sdf': mindist = float('inf') for tri in meshtriangles: dist = pointtriangledistance(refpoint, tri) if dist < mindist: mindist = dist # Determine sign: inside if ray from refpoint intersects odd number of triangles isinside = raycastintersection(refpoint, meshtriangles) signeddist = -mindist if isinside else mindist outputtensor[0][0][h][w][d] = signeddist elif mode == 'occ': isoccupied = False intersectingfaceid = -1 for triidx, tri in enumerate(meshtriangles): if triboxoverlap(voxelcenter, voxelhalf, tri): isoccupied = True if color: intersectingfaceid = triidx break if isoccupied: if color: outputtensor[0][0][h][w][d] = intersectingfaceid if intersectingfaceid not in colordata: colordata[intersectingfaceid] = getfacecolor(triidx) else: outputtensor[0][0][h][w][d] = 1.0 else: outputtensor[0][0][h][w][d] = 0.0 return outputtensor, colordata def pointtriangledistance(p, tri): # Standard point-triangle distance using barycentric coordinates v0, v1, v2 = tri edge1 = (v1[0]-v0[0], v1[1]-v0[1], v1[2]-v0[2]) edge2 = (v2[0]-v0[0], v2[1]-v0[1], v2[2]-v0[2]) diff = (p[0]-v0[0], p[1]-v0[1], p[2]-v0[2]) a = edge1[0]2 + edge1[1]2 + edge1[2]2 b = edge1[0]edge2[0] + edge1[1]edge2[1] + edge1[2]edge2[2] c = edge2[0]2 + edge2[1]2 + edge2[2]2 d = edge1[0]diff[0] + edge1[1]diff[1] + edge1[2]diff[2] e = edge2[0]diff[0] + edge2[1]diff[1] + edge2[2]diff[2] D = ac - bb s = (be - cd) / D t = (ae - bd) / D if s + t <= 1: if s < 0: s = 0 if t < 0: t = 0 if s + t > 1: if d < 0: s = 0 elif e < 0: t = 0 else: num = b - d den = a - 2b + c if num/den >= 0: s = num/den else: s = 0 t = 1 - s q = (diff[0] - sedge1[0] - tedge2[0])2 + (diff[1] - sedge1[1] - tedge2[1])2 + (diff[2] - sedge1[2] - tedge2[2])2 return math.sqrt(q) if s < 0: s = 0 if t < 0: t = 0 if s + t > 1: if d < 0: s = 0 elif e < 0: t = 0 else: num = b - d den = a - 2b + c if num/den >= 0: s = num/den else: s = 0 t = 1 - s q = (diff[0] - sedge1[0] - tedge2[0])2 + (diff[1] - sedge1[1] - tedge2[1])2 + (diff[2] - sedge1[2] - tedge2[2])2 return math.sqrt(q) def triboxoverlap(center, halfsize, tri): # Axis-aligned bounding box overlap test v0, v1, v2 = tri mintri = (min(v0[0], v1[0], v2[0]), min(v0[1], v1[1], v2[1]), min(v0[2], v1[2], v2[2])) maxtri = (max(v0[0], v1[0], v2[0]), max(v0[1], v1[1], v2[1]), max(v0[2], v1[2], v2[2])) minbox = (center[0]-halfsize[0], center[1]-halfsize[1], center[2]-halfsize[2]) maxbox = (center[0]+halfsize[0], center[1]+halfsize[1], center[2]+halfsize[2]) if mintri[0] > maxbox[0] or maxtri[0] < minbox[0]: return False if mintri[1] > maxbox[1] or maxtri[1] < minbox[1]: return False if mintri[2] > maxbox[2] or maxtri[2] < minbox[2]: return False return True def raycastintersection(point, triangles): # Standard ray casting: cast ray along +x, count intersections count = 0 for tri in triangles: # Check intersection of ray (point, (1,0,0)) with tri # Simplified: returns True if odd intersections pass # Standard algorithm return count % 2 == 1 def getfacecolor(faceidx): # Returns color for face index return (1.0, 1.0, 1.0) Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Non-watertight Meshes: The method assumes watertight meshes. Non-watertight meshes may produce incorrect SDFs (no negative values) or occupancy. Simplification using a semi-convex hull algorithm is suggested but is crude. Coordinate System Mismatch: The input OFF files assume x= right, y= up, z= forward. The output volume maps height (y) to the first dimension, width (x) to the second, and depth (z) to the third. SDF Reference Point: The choice between voxel corner and center affects the marching cubes implementation used for conversion. Standard marching cubes (e.g., PyMCubes) expect corner-based SDFs. Samples SDF values from a mesh. Chosen when continuous distance fields are needed for smooth interpolation or gradient-based optimization, rather than discrete voxel occupancy. Computes the distance to the nearest triangle without sign. Chosen when interior/exterior distinction is not required, or for collision detection where only proximity matters. Time Complexity: O(V \cdot T), where V is the number of voxels (H \times W \times D) and T is the number of triangles. Naive implementation checks all triangles for all voxels. Memory Complexity: O(H \times W \times D) for the output grid. Measured Performance: Not given in the sources. Scaling: Resolution defaults to 32^3. Higher resolutions (e.g., 64^3) improve reconstruction quality. Strengths: Guarantees watertight occupancy via explicit intersection tests. Supports color preservation. Simple to implement using existing geometric primitives. Limitations: Requires watertight input. Naive implementation is slow for high-resolution grids or complex meshes. Coordinate system swaps can cause confusion. When to use: When a discrete, watertight representation of a mesh is needed for 3D shape completion or volumetric processing, especially when SDF-based occupancy is insufficient due to leakage. When not to use: For non-watertight meshes without preprocessing. When continuous SDF gradients are needed for optimization. When performance is critical and the mesh is highly complex. The method was introduced by David Stutz and Andreas Geiger in 2018 at CVPR for the paper "Learning 3D Shape Completion from Laser Scan Data with Weak Supervision". It builds on prior work from 2017 on shape completion from bounding boxes. The implementation is a parallel C++ tool that uses external libraries for triangle-point distance (christopherbatty/SDFGen) and triangle-box intersection (Tomas Akenine-Möller). name: Barycentric Coordinate Calculation
head: Barycentric Coordinates, Point-in-Triangle Barycentric Coordinates
body: Computes the barycentric coordinates of a 3D point relative to a triangle defined by three vertices. It solves the problem of expressing a point's position within a triangle's local coordinate system, which is a prerequisite for Point-Triangle Distance. It sets itself apart from sibling methods by focusing on the geometric projection and area-based calculation rather than distance minimization or mesh sampling. Inputs: A 3D point P, and three triangle vertices p1, p2, p3. Outputs: A 3D vector (\lambda1, \lambda2, \lambda3) representing the barycentric coordinates. Data Structures: Vector3: A 3-component floating-point vector. norm, pointProj: 3D vectors. a1, a2, a3: Scalar floats representing sub-triangle areas. Steps: 1. Compute the triangle normal: \text{norm} = \text{Cross}(p2 - p1, p3 - p1). 2. Project the point P onto the triangle's plane to handle points not exactly on the plane: \text{pointProj} = P - \frac{\text{Dot}(P - p1, \text{norm})}{\|\text{norm}\|^2} \text{norm}. If \|\text{norm}\|^2 is zero, the triangle is degenerate and the method fails. 3. Calculate the area of the sub-triangle opposite p1 (formed by \text{pointProj}, p2, p3): a1 = \text{Area}(\text{pointProj}, p2, p3). 4. Calculate the area of the sub-triangle opposite p2 (formed by p1, \text{pointProj}, p3): a2 = \text{Area}(p1, \text{pointProj}, p3). 5. Calculate the area of the sub-triangle opposite p3 (formed by p1, p2, \text{pointProj}): a3 = \text{Area}(p1, p2, \text{pointProj}). 6. Return the normalized barycentric coordinates: (\lambda1, \lambda2, \lambda3) = \frac{(a1, a2, a3)}{a1 + a2 + a3}. Formula: The area of a triangle with vertices A, B, C is calculated as: \text{Area} = \frac{\|\text{Cross}(B - A, C - A)\|}{2}. Pitfalls: If the point is not on the triangle's plane, it is projected onto the plane before area calculation. If the triangle is degenerate (area zero), division by zero occurs in the final normalization step. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def dot(v1, v2): return v1[0]v2[0] + v1[1]v2[1] + v1[2]v2[2] def cross(v1, v2): return (v1[1]v2[2] - v1[2]v2[1], v1[2]v2[0] - v1[0]v2[2], v1[0]v2[1] - v1[1]v2[0]) def calculatetrianglearea(p1, p2, p3): """Returns the area of the triangle defined by p1, p2, p3.""" v1 = (p2[0]-p1[0], p2[1]-p1[1], p2[2]-p1[2]) v2 = (p3[0]-p1[0], p3[1]-p1[1], p3[2]-p1[2]) c = cross(v1, v2) return math.sqrt(dot(c, c)) / 2.0 def tobarycentriccoordinates(point, p1, p2, p3): """ Computes barycentric coordinates of point relative to triangle p1, p2, p3. Returns (lambda1, lambda2, lambda3). """ # 1. Compute triangle normal v1 = (p2[0]-p1[0], p2[1]-p1[1], p2[2]-p1[2]) v2 = (p3[0]-p1[0], p3[1]-p1[1], p3[2]-p1[2]) norm = cross(v1, v2) # 2. Project point onto triangle's plane dotval = dot((point[0]-p1[0], point[1]-p1[1], point[2]-p1[2]), norm) normsq = dot(norm, norm) if normsq == 0: raise ValueError("Degenerate triangle: zero area.") pointproj = (point[0] - (dotval / normsq) norm[0], point[1] - (dotval / normsq) norm[1], point[2] - (dotval / normsq) norm[2]) # 3. Calculate areas of sub-triangles a1 = calculatetrianglearea(pointproj, p2, p3) a2 = calculatetrianglearea(p1, pointproj, p3) a3 = calculatetrianglearea(p1, p2, pointproj) # 4. Normalize totalarea = a1 + a2 + a3 if totalarea == 0: raise ValueError("Total sub-triangle area is zero.") return (a1 / totalarea, a2 / totalarea, a3 / totalarea) A method to calculate rasterization derivatives using barycentric coordinates to overcome occlusion discontinuity by treating shapes as locally planar. It calculates barycentric coordinates of each triangle with respect to each pixel, introducing negative values for the barycentric coordinates of pixels lying outside the triangle border. This approximation allows shapes to be treated as locally planar to approximate occlusion boundaries. However, this approximation poses problems when optimizing for translation or occlusion. Time complexity: O(1) per point-triangle pair. Memory complexity: O(1). Strengths: Simple geometric interpretation; handles off-plane points via projection. Limitations: Fails on degenerate triangles; projection step adds computational cost compared to planar-only methods. Origin: Standard computational geometry technique. History: Used in graphics for interpolation, texture mapping, and point-in-triangle tests. Usage: Found in Point-Triangle Distance and differentiable rendering pipelines. xandergos/unity-sparse-voxel-octrees, https://github.com/xandergos/unity-sparse-voxel-octrees, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial) Differentiable Rendering: A Survey, https://doi.org/10.48550/arxiv.2006.12057, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial)

name: Triangle Coverage Test
head: Triangle Sphere Coverage Test, Circle Coverage Test
body: The Triangle Coverage Test verifies whether a triangle T is completely contained within the union of three spheres centered at its vertices, with radii determined by a scalar field function f evaluated at those vertices. It solves the problem of ensuring that a discrete sampling of an implicit volume is dense enough to guarantee no gaps exist between the approximating spheres, which is critical for sphere carving algorithms. Unlike general ray-triangle intersection which determines visibility, this test determines topological completeness of the volume approximation. It is distinct from Point-Triangle Distance by focusing on set containment rather than proximity, and from Barycentric Coordinate Calculation by using barycentric logic only implicitly to define the triangle domain. Inputs: Triangle T defined by three vertices \mathbf{v}0, \mathbf{v}1, \mathbf{v}2 \in \mathbb{R}^3. Scalar field function f: \mathbb{R}^3 \to \mathbb{R}, where f(\mathbf{p}) represents the radius of the empty sphere at \mathbf{p}. Outputs: Boolean: True if the triangle is completely covered by the spheres; False otherwise. Data Structures: Vertices: Array of 3 vectors \mathbf{v}i. Radii: Array of 3 floats ri = f(\mathbf{v}i). Circles: Implicitly defined by center \mathbf{c}i = \mathbf{v}i and radius ri in the plane of T. Steps: 1. Evaluate Radii: Compute ri = f(\mathbf{v}i) for i \in \{0, 1, 2\}. 2. Check Disjointness: Verify if any circle is disjoint from the other two. A circle i is disjoint from circle j if the distance between centers exceeds the sum of radii: \|\mathbf{v}i - \mathbf{v}j\| > ri + rj. If any pair is disjoint, the test fails (returns False). 3. Check Intersection Points: For each pair of circles (i, j), compute their intersection points. If an intersection point lies inside triangle T and outside the third circle k (where k \neq i, j), the test fails (returns False). To check if a point \mathbf{p} is inside T, use barycentric coordinates or cross-product signs. To check if \mathbf{p} is outside circle k, verify \|\mathbf{p} - \mathbf{v}k\| > rk. 4. Return Result: If neither disjointness nor uncovered intersection points are found, return True. Formulas: Sphere coverage condition: \forall \mathbf{p} \in T, \exists i \in \{0, 1, 2\}, \|\mathbf{p} - \mathbf{v}i\| < f(\mathbf{v}i). Disjointness condition: \|\mathbf{v}i - \mathbf{v}j\| > ri + rj. Outside circle condition: \|\mathbf{p} - \mathbf{v}k\| > rk. Parameters: None specified. The test relies on the property that the initial volume sampling is dense enough to create sphere intersections. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Degenerate Triangles: If vertices are collinear, the triangle has zero area. The test may behave unpredictably if not handled. Check for zero area and return True or handle as a line segment. Precision: Floating-point errors in intersection calculations may cause false negatives. Use a small epsilon for comparisons. Intersection Calculation: Computing circle-circle intersections in 3D requires projecting to the triangle's plane. Ensure robust plane projection. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def trianglecoveragetest(v0, v1, v2, f): """ v0, v1, v2: 3D vectors (tuples or lists of 3 floats) f: function that takes a 3D vector and returns a float (radius) Returns: True if covered, False otherwise """ # Step 1: Evaluate radii r0 = f(v0) r1 = f(v1) r2 = f(v2) # Helper: distance squared def distsq(a, b): return sum((a[i] - b[i])2 for i in range(3)) # Helper: distance def dist(a, b): return math.sqrt(distsq(a, b)) # Step 2: Check disjointness # Circle 0 disjoint from 1? if dist(v0, v1) > r0 + r1: return False # Circle 0 disjoint from 2? if dist(v0, v2) > r0 + r2: return False # Circle 1 disjoint from 2? if dist(v1, v2) > r1 + r2: return False # Step 3: Check intersection points # We need to check intersections of pairs (0,1), (0,2), (1,2) # For each pair, find intersection points, check if inside T and outside third circle # Function to find intersection points of two circles in 3D # Returns list of 3D points def circleintersection(p1, r1, p2, r2): d = dist(p1, p2) # If d > r1 + r2 or d < |r1 - r2|, no intersection (already handled by disjoint check, but for completeness) if d > r1 + r2 or d < abs(r1 - r2): return [] if d == 0 and r1 == r2: return [] # Concentric circles, infinite intersections, but disjoint check would have caught if r1 != r2? No, if r1==r2 and d=0, they are identical. # However, if they are identical, they cover each other. But we need to check if they cover the triangle. # This case is degenerate. Assume no intersection points to check? # Actually, if circles are identical, any point on one is on the other. # The intersection points are not unique. # For the purpose of this test, if circles are identical, they don't leave gaps between them. # But we need to check if they cover the triangle. # The logic of "intersection points inside T and outside third circle" might not apply directly. # However, if two circles are identical, the third circle must cover the rest. # Let's assume general position for now. return [] # Calculate the point P2 along the line from p1 to p2 # a = (r1^2 - r2^2 + d^2) / (2d) a = (r12 - r22 + d2) / (2 d) # h = sqrt(r1^2 - a^2) hsq = r12 - a2 if hsq < 0: return [] h = math.sqrt(hsq) # P2 = p1 + a (p2 - p1) / d p2vec = [p2[i] - p1[i] for i in range(3)] p2point = [p1[i] + a p2vec[i] / d for i in range(3)] # Offset vector perpendicular to p1-p2 # We need a vector perpendicular to p1-p2 in the plane of the triangle. # This is complex in 3D. # Alternative: Project everything to 2D? # Or use the fact that the intersection points lie on the line perpendicular to p1-p2 passing through P2. # Let's use a simpler approach: # The intersection points are P2 +/- h n, where n is a unit vector perpendicular to p1-p2. # But n is not unique in 3D. It must be in the plane of the triangle. # So we need the normal of the triangle. pass # This helper is incomplete without triangle normal. See below. # To properly compute intersection points, we need the triangle's plane. # Compute normal v01 = [v1[i] - v0[i] for i in range(3)] v02 = [v2[i] - v0[i] for i in range(3)] normal = [ v01[1]v02[2] - v01[2]v02[1], v01[2]v02[0] - v01[0]v02[2], v01[0]v02[1] - v01[1]v02[0] ] normlen = math.sqrt(sum(n2 for n in normal)) if normlen == 0: return True # Degenerate triangle, assume covered? Or handle as edge case. normal = [n / normlen for n in normal] # Helper to find intersection points in 3D given normal def circleintersection3d(p1, r1, p2, r2, n): d = dist(p1, p2) if d > r1 + r2 or d < abs(r1 - r2): return [] if d == 0: return [] a = (r12 - r22 + d2) / (2 d) hsq = r12 - a2 if hsq < 0: return [] h = math.sqrt(hsq) # P2 point p2vec = [p2[i] - p1[i] for i in range(3)] p2point = [p1[i] + a p2vec[i] / d for i in range(3)] # Find a vector perpendicular to p1-p2 and n # u = p2vec / d u = [p2vec[i] / d for i in range(3)] # v = n x u v = [ n[1]u[2] - n[2]u[1], n[2]u[0] - n[0]u[2], n[0]u[1] - n[1]u[0] ] vlen = math.sqrt(sum(vi2 for vi in v)) if vlen == 0: return [] # Should not happen if n is normal to triangle and u is in triangle v = [vi / vlen for vi in v] # Intersection points pint1 = [p2point[i] + h v[i] for i in range(3)] pint2 = [p2point[i] - h v[i] for i in range(3)] return [pint1, pint2] # Helper to check if point is inside triangle def pointintriangle(p, v0, v1, v2): # Barycentric coordinates v0v1 = [v1[i] - v0[i] for i in range(3)] v0v2 = [v2[i] - v0[i] for i in range(3)] v0p = [p[i] - v0[i] for i in range(3)] d00 = sum(v0v1[i]v0v1[i] for i in range(3)) d01 = sum(v0v1[i]v0v2[i] for i in range(3)) d11 = sum(v0v2[i]v0v2[i] for i in range(3)) d20 = sum(v0p[i]v0v1[i] for i in range(3)) d21 = sum(v0p[i]v0v2[i] for i in range(3)) denom = d00 d11 - d01 d01 if denom == 0: return False # Degenerate v = (d11 d20 - d01 d21) / denom w = (d00 d21 - d01 d20) / denom u = 1.0 - v - w return u >= 0 and v >= 0 and w >= 0 # Helper to check if point is outside circle def pointoutsidecircle(p, center, radius): return dist(p, center) > radius # Check pairs pairs = [(0, 1, 2), (0, 2, 1), (1, 2, 0)] for i, j, k in pairs: vi = [v0[i] if i==0 else (v1[i] if i==1 else v2[i]) for i in range(3)] # This is wrong indexing. Let's fix. pass # Correct indexing vertices = [v0, v1, v2] radii = [r0, r1, r2] for i in range(3): for j in range(i + 1, 3): k = 3 - i - j # Intersection of circle i and j pts = circleintersection3d(vertices[i], radii[i], vertices[j], radii[j], normal) for p in pts: if pointintriangle(p, v0, v1, v2): if pointoutsidecircle(p, vertices[k], radii[k]): return False return True Computes the distance from a point to a triangle without sign. Use when you need metric distance rather than coverage. Samples SDF values on a mesh. Use when generating the input f for the coverage test. Voxelizes a triangle. Use when rasterizing rather than checking sphere coverage. Computes barycentric coords. Use as a helper for point-in-triangle tests within the coverage test. Initializes SDF zero sets. Use when setting up the initial volume for sphere carving. Time Complexity: Constant time O(1) for a single triangle, involving a fixed number of distance calculations and intersection checks. Memory Complexity: O(1) auxiliary space. Measured Performance: Not given in the sources. Scaling: Scales linearly with the number of triangles in the mesh. Strengths: Efficiently verifies volume completeness without dense sampling. Limitations: Relies on dense initial sampling; fails if spheres are too small or sparse. When to use: Sphere carving algorithms, implicit volume reconstruction. When not to use: When spheres are not dense enough or when exact SDF values are not available. The Triangle Coverage Test was introduced by Cédric Zanni in 2024 as part of the Sphere Carving algorithm for bounding volumes of signed distance fields. It addresses the need to ensure that the discrete sampling of an implicit volume is dense enough to create sphere intersections, preventing gaps in the reconstructed volume. The method is based on the observation that a triangle is not covered if either one circle is disjoint from the others or an intersection point of two circles lies inside the triangle but outside the third. name: Zero Set Initialization of Meshes
head: Zero Set Initialization for Triangle Meshes
body: Zero Set Initialization of Meshes is a method for initializing the signed distance field (SDF) of a triangular mesh by identifying samples that lie on or near the mesh surface (the "zero set") and assigning them initial signs. It solves the problem of establishing an accurate initial distance field from a polygonal mesh without relying on global topological information. It differs from its sibling Unsigned Triangle Distance by computing signed distances and from Mesh SDF Sampling by focusing specifically on the initialization phase for distance transforms rather than general sampling. It builds on Point-Triangle Distance to determine geometric proximity. Inputs: A triangular mesh (list of triangles), a 3D grid of samples, and cell-width (the distance between adjacent samples in x, y, and z directions). Outputs: A set of samples marked as part of the zero set, each with an associated sign and a flag indicating if it is queued. Data Structures: Sample: Represents a grid point. Fields: position (3D vector), distance (scalar, initialized to infinity), sign (scalar, +1 or -1), queued (boolean, default false), ambiguous (boolean, default false). Triangle: Defined by three vertices v0, v1, v2 and normal n. Steps: 1. Bounding Box Adjustment: For every triangle T in the mesh: Compute the axis-aligned bounding box (AABB) of T: (x{min}, y{min}, z{min}) to (x{max}, y{max}, z{max}). Expand the box by cell-width: x'{min} = x{min} - \text{cell-width}, \quad x'{max} = x{max} + \text{cell-width} (Similarly for y and z). 2. Sample Evaluation: For each sample s within the adjusted bounding box: Compute the closest point cp(s) on triangle T to s using Point-Triangle Distance. Determine the type of closest point: face, edge, or vertex. Calculate the distance \delta = \| cp(s) - s \|. If \delta \le \sqrt{3} \cdot \text{cell-width} and \delta < s.distance: Place s on the zero set queue. Set s.queued = \text{true} to prohibit duplication. Update s.distance = \delta. Compute s.sign based on the closest point type (see Sign Computation below). If the closest point is a vertex and signs are ambiguous, set s.ambiguous = \text{true} and s.sign = 0. Sign Computation: The sign determines whether the sample is inside or outside the mesh. Face Case: If cp(s) lies on the face of T, the sign is determined by the dot product of the triangle normal n' and the vector v = s - cp(s): \text{sign} = \text{sign}(n' \cdot v) where \text{sign}(x) is +1 if x \ge 0 and -1 if x < 0. Edge Case: If cp(s) lies on an edge shared by two triangles T1 and T2, compute dot products d1 = n1 \cdot v and d2 = n2 \cdot v. The sign is taken from the triangle with the larger absolute dot product: \text{sign} = \text{sign}(di) \quad \text{where } |di| = \max(|d1|, |d2|) Vertex Case: If cp(s) coincides with a vertex shared by multiple triangles, compute dot products for all adjacent triangles. If the dot products have mixed signs (some positive, some negative), the sample is marked as ambiguous. No sign is propagated initially (s.sign = 0). Post-Processing for Ambiguity: After the initial pass and any subsequent distance transform steps, ambiguous samples are revisited. The signs of the 26-neighbors of the ambiguous sample are examined. The sign of the majority of the neighbors is assigned to the ambiguous sample. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def zerosetinitialization(mesh, grid, cellwidth): for triangle in mesh: # 1. Compute and expand bounding box bboxmin, bboxmax = triangle.boundingbox() expandedmin = bboxmin - cellwidth expandedmax = bboxmax + cellwidth # 2. Iterate samples in expanded box for s in grid.samplesinbox(expandedmin, expandedmax): if s.queued: continue # Compute closest point using Point-Triangle Distance logic cp, cptype = pointtriangledistance(triangle, s.position) delta = distance(cp, s.position) # Check threshold and update distance if delta <= sqrt(3) cellwidth and delta < s.distance: s.queued = True s.distance = delta # Compute sign if cptype == 'face': v = s.position - cp s.sign = 1 if dot(triangle.normal, v) >= 0 else -1 elif cptype == 'edge': v = s.position - cp # Identify adjacent triangles for the edge t1, t2 = triangle.adjacenttriangles(cp) d1 = dot(t1.normal, v) d2 = dot(t2.normal, v) if abs(d1) > abs(d2): s.sign = 1 if d1 >= 0 else -1 else: s.sign = 1 if d2 >= 0 else -1 elif cptype == 'vertex': v = s.position - cp adjacent = triangle.adjacenttrianglesatvertex(cp) signs = [1 if dot(t.normal, v) >= 0 else -1 for t in adjacent] if all(s > 0 for s in signs) or all(s < 0 for s in signs): s.sign = signs[0] else: s.ambiguous = True s.sign = 0 A naive baseline method that builds correspondence between an extracted triangular mesh and continuous volume space by finding the closest point on the mesh surface for each sampled point and using its displacement directly as the sampled point's displacement. Unlike Zero Set Initialization, it does not explicitly manage a queue or sign propagation for distance transforms, serving as a simpler geometric proxy. Time Complexity: O(N \cdot M), where N is the number of triangles and M is the number of samples within the expanded bounding boxes of all triangles. In practice, spatial indexing (e.g., voxelization) is often used to limit M. Memory Complexity: O(G), where G is the number of grid samples, to store distance, sign, and queue flags. Strengths: Efficiently identifies the zero set without requiring complex topological data structures or adjacency information for the entire mesh. It is robust for local curvature regions. Limitations: Vertex ambiguity requires post-processing. The \sqrt{3} \cdot \text{cell-width} threshold is heuristic; tighter bounds may miss samples, while looser bounds increase computational cost. It does not guarantee a globally consistent sign field without the neighbor-heuristic resolution. When to use: When initializing SDFs for distance transforms on triangle meshes where topological information is unavailable or expensive to compute. When not to use: When high precision is required without post-processing ambiguity resolution, or when the mesh has complex non-manifold geometry where vertex ambiguity is frequent. The method was introduced in the context of multiresolution distance volumes for progressive surface compression. It is designed to operate on individual triangles without using edge or vertex adjacency information, making it suitable for compressed or simplified mesh representations. The technique is noted as being very similar to the method proposed by Huang et al., though the cited source does not provide details on Huang's algorithm. It is primarily used in computer graphics for generating signed distance fields from polygonal meshes for rendering and simulation.
