name: Triangle-Triangle Intersection Test
head: SAT Triangle Intersection, Separating Axis Theorem (SAT) for triangles, testIntersection
body: The Triangle-Triangle Intersection Test determines whether two triangles in 3D space intersect using the Separating Axis Theorem (SAT). It solves the problem of detecting collisions between triangular primitives by projecting them onto potential separating axes and checking for interval overlap. Unlike Ray-Triangle Intersection, which tests a ray against a single triangle, this method tests two arbitrary triangles against each other without a predefined viewing direction. It is distinct from General Ray-Triangle Intersection (Plücker Coordinates) in that it relies on interval projection rather than line-plane duality, and from Point-Triangle Distance as it returns a boolean intersection status rather than a distance metric. Input: Two triangles, T1 and T2. Output: A boolean value: true (or 1) if the triangles intersect, false (or 0) if they do not. Each triangle is defined by three vertices in 3D space, stored in a vt[3][3] array where each row is a 3D float vector. Vertices are indexed 0, 1, 2. The test projects both triangles onto a set of potential separating axes. If the projections (intervals) on any axis are disjoint, the triangles do not intersect. If all tested axes show overlap, the triangles intersect. 1. Compute Edge Vectors: For each triangle Ti (i \in \{1, 2\}), compute the three edge vectors: e{i,0} = Ti.vt[1] - Ti.vt[0], e{i,1} = Ti.vt[2] - Ti.vt[1], e{i,2} = Ti.vt[0] - Ti.vt[2]. 2. Compute Face Normals: Compute the unnormalized face normals: n1 = e{1,0} \times e{1,1} and n2 = e{2,0} \times e{2,1}. 3. Check for Co-planarity: Compute n = n1 \times n2. If n is the zero vector, the triangles are co-planar. Co-planar Case: Check if the triangles lie in the same plane by comparing n1 \cdot T1.vt[0] and n1 \cdot T2.vt[0]. If n1 \cdot T1.vt[0] \neq n1 \cdot T2.vt[0], the planes are distinct and the triangles do not intersect; return false. If they are in the same plane, test separation along the 6 edge normals: n1 \times e{1,i} and n2 \times e{2,i} for i \in \{0, 1, 2\}. If any axis separates the triangles, return false; otherwise return true. Non-Co-planar Case: Test separation along the face normals n1 and n2. If either separates them, return false. Test separation along the 9 cross products of every edge of T1 with every edge of T2: axis{i,j} = e{1,i} \times e{2,j} for i,j \in \{0, 1, 2\}. If any separates them, return false. If no axis separates the triangles, return true. 4. Projection and Separation Check: For each candidate axis A, project both triangles to min/max intervals: min1 = A \cdot T1.vt[0], max1 = min1; loop k \in \{1, 2\}: temp = A \cdot T1.vt[k]; update min1 = \min(min1, temp), max1 = \max(max1, temp); repeat for T2. If any axis shows disjoint intervals (min1 \ge max2 or min2 \ge max1), return false; else return true. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def triangletriangleintersect(t1, t2, epsilon=1e-5): # 1. Compute edge vectors e1 = [t1.vt[1] - t1.vt[0], t1.vt[2] - t1.vt[1], t1.vt[0] - t1.vt[2]] e2 = [t2.vt[1] - t2.vt[0], t2.vt[2] - t2.vt[1], t2.vt[0] - t2.vt[2]] # 2. Compute face normals n1 = cross(e1[0], e1[1]) n2 = cross(e2[0], e2[1]) # 3. Check co-planarity n = cross(n1, n2) if iszerovector(n, epsilon): # Co-planar case if dot(n1, t1.vt[0]) != dot(n1, t2.vt[0]): return False axes = [] for i in range(3): axes.append(cross(n1, e1[i])) axes.append(cross(n2, e2[i])) for axis in axes: if testseparation(axis, t1, t2, epsilon): return False return True else: # Non-co-planar case if testseparation(n1, t1, t2, epsilon): return False if testseparation(n2, t1, t2, epsilon): return False for i in range(3): for j in range(3): axis = cross(e1[i], e2[j]) if testseparation(axis, t1, t2, epsilon): return False return True def testseparation(axis, t1, t2, epsilon): min1 = dot(axis, t1.vt[0]) max1 = min1 for k in range(1, 3): proj = dot(axis, t1.vt[k]) if proj < min1: min1 = proj if proj > max1: max1 = proj min2 = dot(axis, t2.vt[0]) max2 = min2 for k in range(1, 3): proj = dot(axis, t2.vt[k]) if proj < min2: min2 = proj if proj > max2: max2 = proj if min1 > max2 + epsilon or min2 > max1 + epsilon: return True return False def iszerovector(v, epsilon): return abs(v.x) < epsilon and abs(v.y) < epsilon and abs(v.z) < epsilon Note: dot and cross are standard vector operations. Epsilon: A small floating-point tolerance (e.g., 0.00001f) used to handle numerical instability in separation checks and zero-vector detection. Co-planar Triangles: Handling co-planar triangles correctly is critical. Some implementations use a hack where co-planar triangles are explicitly regarded as not intersecting to avoid degenerate cases. The full SAT test requires testing the 6 edge normals in the co-planar case. Numerical Precision: Floating-point errors can cause false negatives or positives. Using an epsilon in the separation check (min1 > max2 + \epsilon) helps mitigate this. Degenerate Triangles: If a triangle has zero area (collinear vertices), its normal is zero. The algorithm assumes non-degenerate triangles; degenerate inputs may require pre-validation. An early-out optimization where the axis-aligned bounding boxes (AABBs) of the two triangles are tested for intersection. If the AABBs do not intersect, the triangles do not intersect. This is an O(1) check that can save the more expensive SAT test. An extension of the intersection test that computes the area of intersection between two triangles, useful for rendering and physics. Time Complexity: O(1) per pair of triangles. The algorithm tests at most 11 axes (2 face normals + 9 edge-edge cross products) for non-co-planar triangles, and up to 6 axes for co-planar triangles. Memory Complexity: O(1). Only a few temporary vectors and scalars are required. Measured Performance: The SAT method is generally fast and robust for single pair tests. Strengths: No division by zero issues; handles all relative orientations; robust with epsilon tuning. Limitations: Does not provide the intersection curve or area; co-planar cases require special handling; less efficient than bounding volume hierarchies for large scenes. When to Use: When testing a small number of triangle pairs, or as a leaf-node test in a spatial partitioning structure. When Not to Use: For large-scale scene intersection, use a BVH or grid-based approach. For ray-triangle intersection, use Ray-Triangle Intersection. The Triangle-Triangle Intersection Test using SAT is a standard technique in computational geometry and computer graphics. It is implemented in various open-source dual contouring and mesh processing libraries, including work by Tao Ju. The method relies on the Separating Axis Theorem, which states that two convex objects are disjoint if and only if there exists a plane (axis) onto which their projections do not overlap. For triangles, the potential separating axes are the face normals and the cross products of their edges. aewallin/dualcontouring, https://github.com/aewallin/dualcontouring, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial) jbayardo/tao-ju-dual-contouring, https://github.com/jbayardo/tao-ju-dual-contouring, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial) ChessQian/DualContouring, https://github.com/ChessQian/DualContouring, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial)

name: GPU Mesh Voxelization via SAT Ray Casting
head: Ray-Triangle Intersection for Voxelization, UnityGPUMeshVoxelizer, VoxelizeMesh
body: This method converts a triangle mesh into a 3D voxel grid by dispatching a compute shader where each thread corresponds to a voxel cell. It determines voxel solidity by testing each cell against every mesh triangle using a Separating Axis Theorem (SAT) broad-phase test followed by a Möller-Trumbore ray-triangle intersection. It differs from hierarchical voxelization by using a brute-force per-voxel, per-triangle approach, making it simple to implement but computationally expensive for high-resolution grids or complex meshes. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A triangle mesh defined by vertex positions and triangle indices. Input: Voxel grid dimensions (W, H, D) and cell size (s). Input: World-space bounds of the voxelization volume. Output: A structured buffer of voxels, each containing a position and a boolean isSolid flag. Data Structures: The implementation uses the following structures in HLSL/C#: 1. Voxel: hlsl struct Voxel { Vector3 position; float isSolid; }; Stored in a RWStructuredBuffer<Voxel>. 2. Triangle: hlsl struct Triangle { float3 a, b, c; }; Triangles are not stored as a single struct buffer but are fetched from vertex and index buffers. 3. Mesh Buffers: MeshVertices: StructuredBuffer<float3>, size Nv (number of vertices). MeshTriangleIndices: StructuredBuffer<int>, size Nt \times 3 (number of triangles \times 3). 4. Grid Parameters: GridWidth, GridHeight, GridDepth: Integers defining the voxel count per axis. CellHalfSize: Float, half the side length of a voxel (default 0.05f). BoundsMin: Float3, minimum corner of the voxel grid in world space. WorldToLocalMatrix: Matrix, transforms world coordinates to local mesh coordinates. TriangleCount: Integer, total number of triangles. Algorithm Steps: 1. Grid Initialization: Calculate grid dimensions from the mesh collider bounds and CellHalfSize. W = \lceil \text{bounds.extents.x} / \text{CellHalfSize} \rceil H = \lceil \text{bounds.extents.y} / \text{CellHalfSize} \rceil D = \lceil \text{bounds.extents.z} / \text{CellHalfSize} \rceil Allocate voxelsBuffer of size W \times H \times D. 2. Buffer Upload: Upload mesh vertices to MeshVertices and indices to MeshTriangleIndices. 3. Compute Dispatch: Dispatch the VoxelizeMesh kernel with thread groups: \text{Groups}x = \lceil W / \text{GroupSize} \rceil, \quad \text{Groups}y = \lceil H / \text{GroupSize} \rceil, \quad \text{Groups}z = \lceil D / \text{GroupSize} \rceil. 4. Voxelization Kernel (VoxelizeMesh): For each thread with global ID (id.x, id.y, id.z): a. Bounds Check: If id.x \ge W or id.y \ge H or id.z \ge D, return. b. Compute Cell Center: \text{cellSize} = \text{CellHalfSize} \times 2.0 \text{centerPos} = (id.x \times \text{cellSize} + \text{CellHalfSize} + \text{BoundsMin}.x, \dots) (Repeat for y and z components). c. Initialize Solidity: Set isSolid = 0. d. Triangle Iteration: Iterate through all triangles i from 0 to TriangleCount - 1. i. Fetch vertices A, B, C from MeshVertices using indices from MeshTriangleIndices. ii. SAT Broad-Phase: Test if the voxel AABB (centered at centerPos, extents CellHalfSize) intersects the triangle's AABB. iii. Ray-Triangle Intersection: If SAT passes, cast a ray from centerPos towards the triangle centroid. If a hit is found, set isSolid = 1 and break. e. Write Output: Write the voxel to voxelsBuffer[id.z W H + id.y W + id.x]. 5. Fill Volume (Optional): Dispatch a subsequent kernel to propagate solidity to neighboring empty voxels if a "filled" volume is required rather than a surface shell. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. EPSILON = 0.0000001 def dot(a, b): return a[0]b[0] + a[1]b[1] + a[2]b[2] def cross(a, b): return (a[1]b[2] - a[2]b[1], a[2]b[0] - a[0]b[2], a[0]b[1] - a[1]b[0]) def raytriangleintersect(rayorigin, raydirection, tria, trib, tric): ab = (trib[0]-tria[0], trib[1]-tria[1], trib[2]-tria[2]) ac = (tric[0]-tria[0], tric[1]-tria[1], tric[2]-tria[2]) h = cross(raydirection, ac) a = dot(ab, h) if a > -EPSILON and a < EPSILON: return False f = 1.0 / a s = (rayorigin[0]-tria[0], rayorigin[1]-tria[1], rayorigin[2]-tria[2]) u = f dot(s, h) if u < 0.0 or u > 1.0: return False q = cross(s, ab) v = f dot(raydirection, q) if v < 0.0 or u + v > 1.0: return False t = f dot(ac, q) if t <= EPSILON: return False return True def sattest(voxelcenter, voxelextents, tria, trib, tric): axes = [ (1, 0, 0), (0, 1, 0), (0, 0, 1), cross((trib[0]-tria[0], trib[1]-tria[1], trib[2]-tria[2]), (tric[0]-tria[0], tric[1]-tria[1], tric[2]-tria[2])) ] for axis in axes: p0 = dot(tria, axis) p1 = dot(trib, axis) p2 = dot(tric, axis) maxP = max(p0, max(p1, p2)) minP = min(p0, min(p1, p2)) r = voxelextents[0]abs(axis[0]) + voxelextents[1]abs(axis[1]) + voxelextents[2]abs(axis[2]) if max(-maxP, minP) > r: return False return True def voxelizemeshkernel(idx, idy, idz, gridw, gridh, gridd, cellhalfsize, boundsmin, meshvertices, meshindices, trianglecount, voxelsbuffer): if idx >= gridw or idy >= gridh or idz >= gridd: return cellsize = cellhalfsize 2.0 centerpos = ( idx cellsize + cellhalfsize + boundsmin[0], idy cellsize + cellhalfsize + boundsmin[1], idz cellsize + cellhalfsize + boundsmin[2]) issolid = 0.0 voxelextents = (cellhalfsize, cellhalfsize, cellhalfsize) for i in range(trianglecount): idx0 = meshindices[i 3] idx1 = meshindices[i 3 + 1] idx2 = meshindices[i 3 + 2] tria = meshvertices[idx0] trib = meshvertices[idx1] tric = meshvertices[idx2] if not sattest(centerpos, voxelextents, tria, trib, tric): continue centroid = ((tria[0]+trib[0]+tric[0])/3.0, (tria[1]+trib[1]+tric[1])/3.0, (tria[2]+trib[2]+tric[2])/3.0) direction = (centroid[0]-centerpos[0], centroid[1]-centerpos[1], centroid[2]-centerpos[2]) lensq = direction[0]2 + direction[1]2 + direction[2]2 if lensq > 0.0: lensqinv = 1.0 / (lensq 0.5) direction = (direction[0]lensqinv, direction[1]lensqinv, direction[2]lensqinv) else: direction = (0.0, 0.0, 1.0) if raytriangleintersect(centerpos, direction, tria, trib, tric): issolid = 1.0 break voxelsbuffer[idz gridw gridh + idy gridw + idx] = (centerpos, issolid) Parameters: CellHalfSize: Default 0.05f. Determines voxel resolution. GridWidth, GridHeight, GridDepth: Derived from mesh bounds and CellHalfSize. BoundsMin: World-space minimum corner of the voxelization volume. WorldToLocalMatrix: Used if mesh vertices are in local space and need transformation to world space for intersection tests. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Ray Parallel to Triangle: If the ray direction is parallel to the triangle plane, the denominator a in Möller-Trumbore becomes zero. Handled by checking if (a > -epsilon && a < epsilon) return false;. Barycentric Coordinates: If u or v are outside [0, 1] or u+v > 1, the ray misses the triangle. Handled by explicit bounds checks. Back-facing/Degenerate Hits: Hits with t \le \epsilon are rejected to avoid self-intersection or degenerate cases. Handled by return t > epsilon;. Time Complexity: O(V \times T), where V is the total number of voxels (W \times H \times D) and T is the number of triangles. Each voxel thread iterates over all triangles. Memory Complexity: O(V + V{mesh} + T{mesh}), where V is the voxel buffer size, V{mesh} is the vertex buffer size, and T{mesh} is the index buffer size. Performance: Performance degrades linearly with grid resolution and triangle count. Suitable for real-time visualization of moderate-resolution grids on modern GPUs. Strengths: Simple implementation, no complex data structures required, fully parallelizable. Limitations: No spatial acceleration, leading to poor performance on dense meshes or high-resolution grids. This method is implemented in the Unity engine using ComputeShaders and Graphics.DrawProceduralIndirect / Graphics.DrawMeshInstancedIndirect for visualization. It is part of the "UnityGPUMeshVoxelizer" project series. bzgeb/UnityGPUMeshVoxelizerPart5, https://github.com/bzgeb/UnityGPUMeshVoxelizerPart5, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial) 3DStuff/voxelizer, https://github.com/3DStuff/voxelizer, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial)

name: Coordinate System and Parametric Intersection
body: Coordinate System and Parametric Intersection provides geometric primitives for determining ray intersections within structured voxel grids and for computing approximate intersections with complex volumetric structures. It is distinguished from sibling methods like Ray-Tetrahedron Intersection by its specific handling of spherical grid topology and from Exact Rational Ray-Surfel Evaluation by its reliance on angular decomposition and scan-plane approximations. Determines whether a ray intersects an azimuthal section within a spherical voxel grid. An azimuthal section is defined as a surface segment living in the XZ plane, bounded by radial and polar extents. This method serves as the core primitive intersection test for the azimuthal dimension, complementing radial and polar hit detection. It is distinguished from Ray-Polar Section Intersection by operating on the XZ plane geometry rather than the XY plane, and from Ray-Ray Intersection by specifically handling the curved, sector-based boundaries of spherical coordinates rather than straight line segments. Choose it when traversing spherical voxel grids requiring azimuthal boundary checks. See Azimuthal Hit Detection. Determines whether a ray intersects a polar section, which is a volumetric primitive defined within the XY plane of a spherical voxel grid. It serves as the specific implementation for polar coordinates within the broader Ray-Primitive Intersection framework. It distinguishes itself from Azimuthal Hit Detection by operating on the Y-axis plane rather than the Z-axis, and from Ray-Ray Intersection by handling planar sector boundaries rather than linear line segments. Choose it when traversing spherical voxel grids requiring polar boundary checks. See Ray-Polar Section Intersection. Computes the least-squares intersection point of two rays in 3D space. Used when rays do not intersect exactly due to noise or parallax, finding the point that minimizes the squared distance to both rays. It differs from exact intersection methods by providing a robust estimate for skew lines, which is essential in volumetric reconstruction where ray origins and directions are derived from noisy camera poses. Choose it when resolving non-intersecting lines in 3D space. See Ray-Ray Intersection. An approximate method to determine if a camera ray intersects a caustic beam and the location of that intersection, used because exact computation is too costly for thousands of beams. Definition: An approximate method to determine if a camera ray intersects a caustic beam and the location of that intersection, used because exact computation is too costly for thousands of beams. Steps: 1. Define a scan plane, which is an auxiliary arbitrary plane containing the camera ray. 2. Compute the intersections of the scan plane and the edges of the caustic beam to form a triangle. 3. Minimize error from curved beam edges by choosing the scan plane normal vector to be close to the normal of the caustic triangle. 4. Transform the view ray to the beam's local space. 5. Select a representative point on the intersection segment \Delta x (specifically the midpoint) and evaluate the area function A(y). 6. Compute the fraction of light scattered towards the viewer based on the cross-section area (determining radiance scaling) and scattering in the participating medium. Formula: The scan plane normal \mathbf{n}p is computed as \mathbf{n}p = \mathbf{r}{view} \times (\mathbf{r}{view} \times \mathbf{n}4), where \mathbf{r}{view} is the view ray direction and \mathbf{n}4 is the caustic triangle normal. Choose it when rendering real-time volume caustics where exact ray-bilinear patch intersection is too expensive. The spherical coordinate intersection methods are part of the infrastructure for spherical voxel grid traversal, often used in global illumination and caustic rendering where spherical symmetry or specific grid structures are advantageous. The Ray-Ray intersection method is a standard technique in computer graphics for finding the closest approach between skew lines, frequently used in ray tracing acceleration structures and multi-view geometry. The Scan Plane Beam Intersection method originates from real-time volume caustics rendering, where exact ray-bilinear patch intersection is too expensive for the large number of caustic beams present in typical scenes. name: Azimuthal Hit Detection
head: azimuthalHit
body: Azimuthal Hit Detection determines whether an azimuthal hit occurs for a given ray. An azimuthal hit is an intersection between the ray and an azimuthal section, where azimuthal sections live in the XZ plane. This method projects the 3D ray and voxel boundaries onto the XZ plane to perform 2D intersection tests, serving as one of the two angular components required to traverse a spherical volume. It differs from Ray-Polar Section Intersection by operating on the XZ plane rather than the XY plane, and from Ray-Ray Intersection by handling curved grid boundaries via planar projection. Inputs: grid: The spherical voxel grid object containing bounds, center, and angular resolution. ray: The ray being tested, containing origin, direction, and segment endpoints. currentazimuthalvoxel: The integer index of the current azimuthal voxel being traversed. collineartimes: Output container for collinear intersection times. t: Output parameter for the intersection distance. maxt: Maximum valid intersection distance. raysegment: Ray segment object with.P1() (start point) and.vector() (direction vector) methods. Outputs: Boolean indicating if an azimuthal hit occurred. Updated t and collineartimes if a hit is found. Data Structures: BoundVec3: A 3D vector structure where the Y-component is explicitly set to 0.0 for azimuthal calculations. grid.centerToAzimuthalBound(v): Returns a BoundVec3 representing the boundary vector for voxel v. grid.pMaxAzimuthal(v): Returns a structure with fields P1 and P2 representing the azimuthal bounds for voxel v. Steps: 1. Calculate pone: BoundVec3 with x = grid.pMaxAzimuthal(currentazimuthalvoxel).P1, y = 0.0, z = grid.pMaxAzimuthal(currentazimuthalvoxel).P2. 2. Calculate ptwo: BoundVec3 with x = grid.pMaxAzimuthal(currentazimuthalvoxel + 1).P1, y = 0.0, z = grid.pMaxAzimuthal(currentazimuthalvoxel + 1).P2. 3. Set umin pointer to &grid.centerToAzimuthalBound(currentazimuthalvoxel). 4. Set umax pointer to &grid.centerToAzimuthalBound(currentazimuthalvoxel + 1). 5. Calculate wmin = pone - raysegment.P1(). 6. Calculate wmax = ptwo - raysegment.P1(). 7. Calculate perpuvmin = umin->x() raysegment.vector().z() - umin->z() raysegment.vector().x(). 8. Calculate perpuvmax = umax->x() raysegment.vector().z() - umax->z() raysegment.vector().x(). 9. Calculate perpuwmin = umin->x() wmin.z() - umin->z() wmin.x(). 10. Calculate perpuwmax = umax->x() wmax.z() - umax->z() wmax.x(). 11. Calculate perpvwmin = raysegment.vector().x() wmin.z() - raysegment.vector().z() wmin.x(). 12. Calculate perpvwmax = raysegment.vector().x() wmax.z() - raysegment.vector().z() wmax.x(). 13. Return angularHit(grid, ray, perpuvmin, perpuvmax, perpuwmin, perpuwmax, perpvwmin, perpvwmax, raysegment, collineartimes, t, maxt, ray.direction().z(), grid.sphereCenter().z(), grid.pMaxAzimuthal(), currentazimuthalvoxel). Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. class Vec3: def init(self, x, y, z): self.x = x self.y = y self.z = z class RaySegment: def init(self, start, direction): self.start = start self.dir = direction def P1(self): return self.start def vector(self): return self.dir def azimuthalHit(grid, ray, currentazimuthalvoxel, collineartimes, t, maxt, raysegment): # 1. Define boundary points in XZ plane (y=0) pone = Vec3(grid.pMaxAzimuthal(currentazimuthalvoxel).P1, 0.0, grid.pMaxAzimuthal(currentazimuthalvoxel).P2) ptwo = Vec3(grid.pMaxAzimuthal(currentazimuthalvoxel + 1).P1, 0.0, grid.pMaxAzimuthal(currentazimuthalvoxel + 1).P2) # 2. Get boundary vectors umin = grid.centerToAzimuthalBound(currentazimuthalvoxel) umax = grid.centerToAzimuthalBound(currentazimuthalvoxel + 1) # 3. name: Ray-Polar Section Intersection
head: Polar Hit Detection, polarHit
body: Determines whether a ray intersects a polar section of a spherical voxel grid, where polar sections are defined within the XY plane. It differs from Azimuthal Hit Detection by operating on the polar coordinate boundaries (Y-axis projection) rather than azimuthal ones (Z-axis projection), and from Ray-Ray Intersection by utilizing precomputed grid boundary vectors rather than solving for arbitrary line-line crossings. Inputs: A ray segment (defined by origin P1 and direction vector \vec{v}), the current polar voxel index i, the spherical voxel grid data (including pMaxPolar boundary definitions and centerToPolarBound mappings), and traversal parameters (t, max\t, collinear times). Outputs: Boolean or status indicating a polar hit, with updated intersection parameters. Data Structures: BoundVec3: A 3D vector structure where the Z component is explicitly set to 0.0 for polar calculations. LineSegment: Defined by points P1 and P2. raysegment: Contains P1 (origin) and \vec{v} (direction vector). Steps: 1. Retrieve Boundary Points: Let P{1, i} be grid.pMaxPolar(i).P1 and P{2, i} be grid.pMaxPolar(i).P2. Let P{1, i+1} be grid.pMaxPolar(i+1).P1 and P{2, i+1} be grid.pMaxPolar(i+1).P2. Construct 2D vectors in the XY plane (Z=0): \vec{p}{one} = (P{1, i}, P{2, i}, 0.0) \vec{p}{two} = (P{1, i+1}, P{2, i+1}, 0.0) 2. Retrieve Center-to-Bound Vectors: Let \vec{u}{min} be the vector pointed to by grid.centerToPolarBound(i). Let \vec{u}{max} be the vector pointed to by grid.centerToPolarBound(i+1). 3. Calculate Displacement Vectors: Let \vec{w}{min} = \vec{p}{one} - ray\segment.P1. Let \vec{w}{max} = \vec{p}{two} - ray\segment.P1. 4. Calculate Perpendicular Components (2D Cross Products): These values represent the signed area of parallelograms formed by the vectors in the XY plane. perp\uv\min = u{min}.x \cdot v.y - u{min}.y \cdot v.x perp\uv\max = u{max}.x \cdot v.y - u{max}.y \cdot v.x perp\uw\min = u{min}.x \cdot w{min}.y - u{min}.y \cdot w{min}.x perp\uw\max = u{max}.x \cdot w{max}.y - u{max}.y \cdot w{max}.x perp\vw\min = v.x \cdot w{min}.y - v.y \cdot w{min}.x perp\vw\max = v.x \cdot w{max}.y - v.y \cdot w{max}.x 5. Invoke Generalized Angular Hit Logic: Pass the calculated perpendicular components to angularHit along with grid context, ray data, and traversal state. Pseudocode: Unverified code. Retrieve boundary points for current and next polar voxel p1curr = grid.pMaxPolar(currentpolarvoxel).P1 p2curr = grid.pMaxPolar(currentpolarvoxel).P2 p1next = grid.pMaxPolar(currentpolarvoxel + 1).P1 p2next = grid.pMaxPolar(currentpolarvoxel + 1).P2 # 2. Construct pone and ptwo vectors (Z=0) pone = BoundVec3(x=p1curr, y=p2curr, z=0.0) ptwo = BoundVec3(x=p1next, y=p2next, z=0.0) # 3. Retrieve umin and umax pointers umin = grid.centerToPolarBound(currentpolarvoxel) umax = grid.centerToPolarBound(currentpolarvoxel + 1) # 4. Calculate w vectors wmin = pone - raysegment.P1() wmax = ptwo - raysegment.P1() # 5. Calculate perpendicular components (2D cross products in XY plane) v = raysegment.vector() perpuvmin = umin.x v.y - umin.y v.x perpuvmax = umax.x v.y - umax.y v.x perpuwmin = umin.x wmin.y - umin.y wmin.x perpuwmax = umax.x wmax.y - umax.y wmax.x perpvwmin = v.x wmin.y - v.y wmin.x perpvwmax = v.x wmax.y - v.y wmax.x # 6. Call generalized angular hit function # The angularHit helper is not detailed in the sources. # It processes the perpendicular components to determine the hit. # return angularHit(grid, ray, perpuvmin, perpuvmax, perpuwmin, perpuwmax, # perpvwmin, perpvwmax, raysegment, collineartimes, t, maxt, # ray.direction().y(), grid.sphereCenter().y(), grid.pMaxPolar(), currentpolarvoxel) Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Not given in the sources. name: Ray-Ray Intersection
head: Least-squares ray intersection, Ray vs. Ray Intersection
body: Computes the least-squares intersection point of two rays in 3D space. It is used when rays do not intersect exactly (e.g., due to noise or parallax), finding the point that minimizes the squared distance to both rays. It sets itself apart from standard ray-casting which assumes exact intersection by minimizing the squared distance to both rays, making it robust to noise or parallax errors. Inputs: origins: Tensor of shape (2, shape, 3) containing the origins of the two rays. directions: Tensor of shape (2, shape, 3) containing the direction vectors of the two rays. eps: Float threshold for detecting parallel rays (default 1e-5). infval: Float value returned for parallel ray intersections (default 1e10). Outputs: result: Tensor of shape (shape, 3) containing the least-squares intersection points; parallel ray pairs are assigned infval. Data Structures: The algorithm operates on batched tensors where shape represents the batch dimensions (e.g., number of ray pairs). Intermediate tensor n has shape (2, shape, 3, 3) representing the matrix n{r,b,i,j}. Intermediate tensor lhs has shape (shape, 3, 3). Intermediate tensor rhs has shape (shape, 3). Steps: 1. Broadcast origins and directions to a common shape. 2. Stack origins and directions into tensors of shape (2, shape, 3). 3. Detect parallel rays by computing the dot product of the direction vectors for each ray pair; a pair is considered parallel if the dot product exceeds 1 - \text{eps}. 4. Filter out parallel rays from the origins and directions tensors. 5. Compute the outer product matrix n{r,b,i,j} = d{r,b,i} d{r,b,j} - \delta{i,j} for each ray, where d is the direction vector and \delta is the Kronecker delta (identity matrix). 6. Compute the left-hand side L{b,i,j} = \sum{r=0}^{1} n{r,b,i,j} by summing n over the ray dimension. 7. Compute the right-hand side R{b,i} = \sum{r=0}^{1} \sum{j=0}^{2} n{r,b,i,j} o{r,b,j} by multiplying n with the origins o and summing over the ray and inner indices. 8. Solve the linear system L p = R for p using least squares. 9. Initialize the output tensor with infval. 10. Assign the computed solution p to the non-parallel indices. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import torch def intersectrays(origins, directions, eps=1e-5, infval=1e10): """ Computes the least-squares intersection point of two rays in 3D space. Args: origins: Tensor of shape (2, shape, 3) directions: Tensor of shape (2, shape, 3) eps: Threshold for parallel ray detection infval: Value for parallel ray results Returns: result: Tensor of shape (shape, 3) """ origins = torch.astensor(origins, dtype=torch.float32) directions = torch.astensor(directions, dtype=torch.float32) shape = origins.shape[1:-1] # Step 3: Detect parallel rays dotproduct = torch.sum(directions[0] directions[1], dim=-1) parallel = dotproduct > (1.0 - eps) # Step 4: Filter parallel rays nonparallelmask = ~parallel if not torch.any(nonparallelmask): return torch.full((shape, 3), infval, dtype=origins.dtype, device=origins.device) # Flatten batch dimensions for indexing (not in sources) originsflat = origins.reshape(2, -1, 3) directionsflat = directions.reshape(2, -1, 3) parallelflat = parallel.reshape(-1) nonparallelflat = ~parallelflat originsfiltered = originsflat[:, nonparallelflat,:] directionsfiltered = directionsflat[:, nonparallelflat,:] # Step 5: Compute n n = torch.einsum("r b i, r b j -> r b i j", directionsfiltered, directionsfiltered) eye3 = torch.eye(3, dtype=n.dtype, device=n.device) n = n - eye3.unsqueeze(0).unsqueeze(0) # Step 6: Compute LHS lhs = torch.sum(n, dim=0) # Step 7: Compute RHS rhstemp = torch.einsum("r b i j, r b j -> r b i", n, originsfiltered) rhs = torch.sum(rhstemp, dim=0) # Step 8: Solve linear system solution = torch.linalg.lstsq(lhs, rhs).solution # Step 9 & 10: Initialize and assign results result = torch.full((shape, 3), infval, dtype=origins.dtype, device=origins.device) resultflat = result.reshape(-1, 3) resultflat[nonparallelflat,:] = solution result = resultflat.reshape(shape, 3) return result Parameters: eps: Float, default 1e-5. Threshold for detecting parallel rays based on dot product proximity to 1. infval: Float, default 1e10. Value returned for parallel ray intersections. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Parallel Rays: If rays are parallel, the dot product threshold detects them and the algorithm returns infval. Degenerate Input: If origins or directions contain NaN or Inf, standard floating-point propagation rules apply. Computes 3D ray origins and directions from 2D pixel coordinates and camera parameters, and finds the least-squares intersection point of two rays in 3D space. It extends Ray-Ray Intersection by batching the computation over multiple pixel locations and handling the transformation from camera to world space. It is distinct from standard ray-casting which assumes exact intersection; this method minimizes the squared distance to both rays, making it robust to noise or parallax errors. A filter to eliminate inaccurate correspondences by computing the minimal distance between two rays; true correspondences should converge at a single point (distance ~ 0). It discards paired rays where d{ray} > \tau{ray}. The distance d{ray} is computed as \|o1 - o2 + m d1 - n d2\|2, where o1, o2 are origins, d1, d2 are directions, and m, n are distances from origins to the closest points on the respective rays. The values m and n are solved from the system: \begin{cases} m(d1 \cdot d2) - n(d1 \cdot d2) = d1 \cdot o2 - d1 \cdot o1 \\ m(d1 \cdot d2) - n(d2 \cdot d2) = d2 \cdot o2 - d2 \cdot o1 \end{cases} The solution is: m = \frac{be + cf - cg - bd}{ab - c^2}, \quad n = \frac{ce + af - cd - ag}{ab - c^2} where a = d1 \cdot d1, b = d2 \cdot d2, c = d1 \cdot d2, d = d1 \cdot o1, e = d1 \cdot o2, f = d2 \cdot o1, g = d2 \cdot o2. It is used to establish robust correspondences between rays from different views, which is crucial for geometry regularization in neural radiance fields (NeRF). cvg/NoPoSplat, https://github.com/cvg/NoPoSplat, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial) ziplab/VolSplat, https://github.com/ziplab/VolSplat, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial) SGCNeRF: Few-Shot Neural Rendering via Sparse Geometric Consistency Guidance, https://doi.org/10.1109/tcsvt.2025.3610950, fetched 2026-10-30

name: Ray Casting and Intersection
head: Least-squares ray intersection, Ray Intersection, Ray intersection via least squares, Ray-Ray Intersection
body: Computes 3D ray origins and directions from 2D pixel coordinates and camera parameters, and finds the least-squares intersection point of two rays in 3D space. It extends Ray-Ray Intersection by batching the computation over multiple pixel locations and handling the transformation from camera to world space. It is distinct from standard ray-casting which assumes exact intersection; this method minimizes the squared distance to both rays, making it robust to noise or parallax errors. Inputs: intrinsics: Camera intrinsic matrix K (typically 3 \times 3). extrinsics: Camera extrinsic matrix T (typically 4 \times 4), containing rotation R and translation t. pixelcoords: 2D pixel coordinates (u, v) for the rays to be cast. paralleleps: Epsilon threshold for detecting parallel rays (default 10^{-5}). infval: Value used to represent infinity for parallel ray intersections (default 10^{10}). Outputs: intersectionpoints: 3D coordinates (x, y, z) of the least-squares intersection points for each pixel/ray pair. Data Structures: Ray directions are stored as unit vectors in world space. Ray origins are stored as 3D points (camera centers). Matrices N are 3 \times 3 matrices derived from ray directions. Steps: 1. Unproject to Camera Space: Convert 2D pixel coordinates (u, v) to homogeneous coordinates \mathbf{p}{cam} = [u, v, 1]^T. Multiply by the inverse intrinsic matrix K^{-1} to get unprojected direction vectors in camera space: \mathbf{d}{cam} = K^{-1} \mathbf{p}{cam} Normalize these vectors by dividing by their z-component (depth) to ensure they point forward in the camera frustum: \mathbf{d}{cam} = \frac{\mathbf{d}{cam}}{\mathbf{d}{cam}[2]} 2. Transform to World Space: Transform the ray directions from camera space to world space using the rotation component R of the extrinsic matrix: \mathbf{d}{world} = R \mathbf{d}{cam} Normalize \mathbf{d}{world} to obtain unit direction vectors \mathbf{u}: \mathbf{u} = \frac{\mathbf{d}{world}}{\|\mathbf{d}{world}\|} 3. Compute Ray Origins: The origin of each ray is the camera center. Extract the translation vector t from the extrinsic matrix T. Tile this origin to match the batch shape of the rays. 4. Detect Parallel Rays: For a pair of rays with directions \mathbf{u}1 and \mathbf{u}2, compute the dot product. If the dot product is greater than 1 - \text{parallel\eps}, the rays are considered parallel. \text{parallel} = \mathbf{u}1 \cdot \mathbf{u}2 > 1 - \text{parallel\eps} 5. Construct Least-Squares System: For each ray i with direction \mathbf{u}i, compute the matrix Ni: Ni = \mathbf{u}i \mathbf{u}i^T - I where I is the 3 \times 3 identity matrix. Compute the Left-Hand Side (LHS) of the linear system A \mathbf{x} = \mathbf{b} by summing Ni over all rays involved in the intersection (typically two rays per pixel): A = \sumi Ni Compute the Right-Hand Side (RHS) by summing Ni \mathbf{o}i over all rays, where \mathbf{o}i is the origin of ray i: \mathbf{b} = \sumi Ni \mathbf{o}i 6. Solve for Intersection: Solve the linear system A \mathbf{x} = \mathbf{b} for \mathbf{x} using least squares: \mathbf{x} = \text{argmin}{\mathbf{x}} \| A \mathbf{x} - \mathbf{b} \|^2 7. Handle Parallel Rays: If rays are parallel (detected in Step 4), the system is singular. Set the intersection point for these rays to \text{inf\val} (default 10^{10}) to indicate no valid intersection. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import torch import torch.linalg def raycastingandintersection( intrinsics: torch.Tensor, extrinsics: torch.Tensor, pixelcoords: torch.Tensor, paralleleps: float = 1e-5, infval: float = 1e10) -> torch.Tensor: """ Computes the least-squares intersection of rays cast from pixel coordinates. Args: intrinsics: (B, 3, 3) Camera intrinsic matrices. extrinsics: (B, 4, 4) Camera extrinsic matrices. pixelcoords: (B, 2) Pixel coordinates (u, v). paralleleps: Epsilon for parallel ray detection. infval: Value for parallel ray results. Returns: intersectionpoints: (B, 3) 3D intersection points. """ B = pixelcoords.shape[0] # Step 1: Unproject to camera space # Convert pixel coords to homogeneous [u, v, 1] ones = torch.ones(B, 1, device=pixelcoords.device) pcam = torch.cat([pixelcoords, ones], dim=1) # (B, 3) # Multiply by inverse intrinsics Kinv = torch.inverse(intrinsics) # (B, 3, 3) dcam = torch.bmm(Kinv, pcam.unsqueeze(2)).squeeze(2) # (B, 3) # Normalize by z-component dcamz = dcam[:, 2:3] # (B, 1) dcam = dcam / dcamz # (B, 3) # Step 2: Transform to world space R = extrinsics[:,:3,:3] # (B, 3, 3) dworld = torch.bmm(R, dcam.unsqueeze(2)).squeeze(2) # (B, 3) # Normalize to unit vectors norms = torch.norm(dworld, dim=1, keepdim=True) # (B, 1) u = dworld / norms # (B, 3) # Step 3: Compute origins (camera centers) t = extrinsics[:,:3, 3] # (B, 3) origins = t # (B, 3) # Step 4: Detect parallel rays # Assuming we are intersecting ray i with ray j. # In a typical batched setup for stereo/NeRF, we might have two rays per pixel. # However, the source notes imply a general "two rays" context for the least squares. # If the input is a single ray per pixel, this function likely expects pairs or # is used in a context where rays are paired. # Based on S1/S2, it seems to handle a batch of ray pairs or a single ray # intersecting with itself (which is degenerate). # Let's assume the input pixelcoords defines two rays per batch item # or the function is called for pairs. # The notes describe directionsx and directionsy, implying two sets of rays. # Re-reading S1/S2: "Computes 3D ray origins and directions... and finds the least-squares intersection point of two rays" # This implies the function takes two rays as input. # Let's adjust inputs to accept two rays per batch item. # If the function signature is fixed to single rays, it might be part of a larger loop. # But the notes say "intersectrays" and "getworldrays". # Let's assume the standard case: two rays are provided. # If the input is just one ray per pixel, we cannot compute intersection. # The source S1 mentions "viewsampler.sample" which returns context and target views. # This function likely computes intersection between a context ray and a target ray. # Let's assume inputs are: # directions1: (B, 3) # origins1: (B, 3) # directions2: (B, 3) # origins2: (B, 3) # Since the prompt asks for "Ray Casting and Intersection" based on S1/S2, # and S1 mentions "intersectrays", I will write the function to take two rays. # However, the "Inputs" section in the prompt's structure asks for "pixel coordinates". # This suggests the function generates rays from pixels. # If it intersects two rays, it likely needs two sets of pixels or cameras. # Let's stick to the most general interpretation from S1/S2: # It computes intersection for a batch of ray pairs. # The "pixelcoords" might be for one ray, and another set is implied or passed separately. # Given the ambiguity, I will write the core least-squares solver for two rays, # assuming they are passed as directions and origins. # If the function must take pixel coords, it likely takes two sets. # Let's assume pixelcoords is for ray 1, and we need ray 2. # This is complex. Let's look at S2: intersectrays takes directionsx, directionsy. # I will write the function to take two rays (directions and origins) directly, # as the "casting" part is just coordinate transformation. # Let's redefine inputs for the pseudocode to match the "How it works" steps precisely. # Inputs: directions1, origins1, directions2, origins2 # But the prompt says "Inputs:... pixelcoords". # I will assume the function takes two sets of pixel coordinates and two sets of cameras. # To keep it simple and aligned with S1/S2's intersectrays: # I will write a helper that takes two rays. pass def intersectrays( directions1: torch.Tensor, origins1: torch.Tensor, directions2: torch.Tensor, origins2: torch.Tensor, paralleleps: float = 1e-5, infval: float = 1e10) -> torch.Tensor: """ Computes the least-squares intersection of two rays. Args: directions1: (B, 3) Unit direction vectors of ray 1. origins1: (B, 3) Origins of ray 1. directions2: (B, 3) Unit direction vectors of ray 2. origins2: (B, 3) Origins of ray 2. paralleleps: Epsilon for parallel ray detection. infval: Value for parallel ray results. Returns: intersectionpoints: (B, 3) 3D intersection points. """ B = directions1.shape[0] # Step 4: Detect parallel rays dotproducts = torch.sum(directions1 directions2, dim=1) # (B,) isparallel = dotproducts > (1.0 - paralleleps) # (B,) # Step 5: Construct Least-Squares System # Ni = ui ui^T - I # For ray 1 u1 = directions1.unsqueeze(2) # (B, 3, 1) u1T = directions1.unsqueeze(1) # (B, 1, 3) N1 = torch.bmm(u1, u1T) - torch.eye(3, device=directions1.device).unsqueeze(0) # (B, 3, 3) # For ray 2 u2 = directions2.unsqueeze(2) # (B, 3, 1) u2T = directions2.unsqueeze(1) # (B, 1, 3) N2 = torch.bmm(u2, u2T) - torch.eye(3, device=directions2.device).unsqueeze(0) # (B, 3, 3) # LHS: A = N1 + N2 A = N1 + N2 # (B, 3, 3) # RHS: b = N1 o1 + N2 o2 b1 = torch.bmm(N1, origins1.unsqueeze(2)).squeeze(2) # (B, 3) b2 = torch.bmm(N2, origins2.unsqueeze(2)).squeeze(2) # (B, 3) b = b1 + b2 # (B, 3) # Step 6: Solve for intersection # Use lstsq # result = torch.linalg.lstsq(A, b).solution # Note: lstsq might fail for singular matrices. We handle parallel rays separately. # Filter out parallel rays for solving nonparallelmask = ~isparallel # (B,) # Initialize result with infval result = torch.full((B, 3), infval, device=directions1.device) # Solve for non-parallel rays if nonparallelmask.any(): Anp = A[nonparallelmask] # (K, 3, 3) bnp = b[nonparallelmask] # (K, 3) # Solve least squares # torch.linalg.lstsq returns a solution, residuals, rank, singular values # We only need the solution try: sol = torch.linalg.lstsq(Anp, bnp).solution # (K, 3) result[nonparallelmask] = sol except RuntimeError: # If lstsq fails (e.g., due to numerical issues), keep infval pass return result def raycastingandintersection( intrinsics1: torch.Tensor, extrinsics1: torch.Tensor, intrinsics2: torch.Tensor, extrinsics2: torch.Tensor, pixelcoords1: torch.Tensor, pixelcoords2: torch.Tensor, paralleleps: float = 1e-5, infval: float = 1e10) -> torch.Tensor: """ Main function: Casts rays from pixels and computes their intersection. Args: intrinsics1: (B, 3, 3) extrinsics1: (B, 4, 4) intrinsics2: (B, 3, 3) extrinsics2: (B, 4, 4) pixelcoords1: (B, 2) pixelcoords2: (B, 2) paralleleps: Epsilon for parallel ray detection. infval: Value for parallel ray results. Returns: intersectionpoints: (B, 3) """ # Cast rays for camera 1 rays1 = castrays(intrinsics1, extrinsics1, pixelcoords1) # Cast rays for camera 2 rays2 = castrays(intrinsics2, extrinsics2, pixelcoords2) # Intersect return intersectrays( rays1['directions'], rays1['origins'], rays2['directions'], rays2['origins'], paralleleps, infval) def castrays(intrinsics: torch.Tensor, extrinsics: torch.Tensor, pixelcoords: torch.Tensor) -> dict: B = pixelcoords.shape[0] # Step 1: Unproject to camera space ones = torch.ones(B, 1, device=pixelcoords.device) pcam = torch.cat([pixelcoords, ones], dim=1) # (B, 3) Kinv = torch.inverse(intrinsics) # (B, 3, 3) dcam = torch.bmm(Kinv, pcam.unsqueeze(2)).squeeze(2) # (B, 3) # Normalize by z-component dcamz = dcam[:, 2:3] # (B, 1) dcam = dcam / dcamz # (B, 3) # Step 2: Transform to world space R = extrinsics[:,:3,:3] # (B, 3, 3) dworld = torch.bmm(R, dcam.unsqueeze(2)).squeeze(2) # (B, 3) # Normalize to unit vectors norms = torch.norm(dworld, dim=1, keepdim=True) # (B, 1) u = dworld / norms # (B, 3) # Step 3: Compute origins t = extrinsics[:,:3, 3] # (B, 3) origins = t # (B, 3) return {'directions': u, 'origins': origins} Time Complexity: O(B) where B is the batch size, dominated by matrix multiplications and the least-squares solve. The solve is O(1) per batch item since the system is 3 \times 3. Memory Complexity: O(B) for storing directions, origins, and intermediate matrices. Performance: Efficient on GPU due to batched operations. The use of torch.linalg.lstsq is optimized for CUDA. Strengths: Robust to noise and parallax errors. Handles non-intersecting rays gracefully. Limitations: Fails for parallel rays (returns infinity). Numerical stability depends on the condition number of the matrix A. When to use: Stereo matching, multi-view geometry, NeRF training where rays from different views need to intersect. When not to use: When exact intersection is guaranteed and performance is critical (simple geometric intersection is faster). Originated in the context of multi-view stereo and neural radiance fields (NeRF) to handle the discrepancy between rays from different cameras that do not intersect exactly due to calibration errors or scene depth variations. The method is commonly used in libraries like depthsplat and VoLoDSplat for efficient ray intersection computation. cvg/depthsplat, https://github.com/cvg/depthsplat, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial) pulangk97/VoLoDSplat, https://github.com/pulangk97/VoLoDSplat, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial)

name: Topological/Inside Tests
head: Inside/Outside Tests, Point-in-Mesh Tests, Winding Number Tests
body: Topological/Inside Tests determine whether a query point lies inside or outside a closed volume or triangle mesh, resolving the ambiguity of depth-based occlusion tests which fail on self-intersecting or complex geometries. Unlike Ray-primitive intersection, which computes geometric hit points, these tests evaluate the topological relationship between a point and a boundary, often serving as a preprocessing step for sculpting or boolean operations. They differ from Ray Occlusion Test by returning a boolean state for a static point rather than a binary hit/miss for a ray segment, and from Implicit Surface and SDF Intersection by relying on explicit mesh topology rather than scalar field gradients. The family shares the geometric definition of rays and the parallel execution model. Ray Definition Rays are defined by an origin \mathbf{o} and a direction \mathbf{d}. The direction is typically normalized. The origin is often the camera eye position, but can vary based on the camera model. Parallel Execution Computations are mapped to parallel threads. Each thread typically processes one or more pixels or samples. Memory access patterns are optimized for coalescing. Synchronization is used to manage data dependencies between threads. Determines if a point is inside a closed triangle mesh by counting ray-surface intersections. It solves the topological "inside/outside" ambiguity that plagues simpler depth-based tests. Unlike Region Nesting Merge, which relies on hierarchical containment logic, this method uses a direct parity or signed accumulation of ray-triangle hits. Choose this for general point-in-mesh queries on closed meshes. A post-processing step that removes nested inner regions from a sorted list of ray samples. It solves the problem of redundant geometry resulting from boolean unions or subtractions where one volume is entirely contained within another. It differs from Ray Crossing Count (Winding Number) by using a simple nesting depth counter based on normal direction rather than a cumulative winding number, making it suitable for specific sculpting and boolean contexts where only the outermost boundary of nested structures is required. Choose this when processing pre-computed ray samples for sculpting or boolean operations. A procedure that checks if a vertex is inside or outside the volume by finding the closest sample along the ray and checking its normal direction. Step 1. Calculate the signed distance between the vertex v and the ray origin. 2. Find the sample s in R.list where the distance from s.position to R.origin is less than or equal to the vertex distance and is the maximum such distance. 3. If the dot product of s.normal and R.direction is less than 0, return False (outside). Code Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def IsInside(Ray R, Vertex v): dist = Dist(v, R.origin) # signed dist. between 2 points # find sample s in R.list where Dist(s.position, R.origin) <= dist # and Dist(s.position, R.origin) is maximum s = None maxdist = -infinity for sample in R.list: d = Dist(sample.position, R.origin) if d <= dist and d > maxdist: maxdist = d s = sample if s is None: return False # No sample found within distance if Dot(s.normal, R.direction) < 0: return False else: return True Originating from sculpting applications requiring precise topological queries, this family was detailed in "Detail sculpting using cubical marching squares". The methods allow for efficient visual quality improvements in sculpting by providing robust inside/outside tests for vertices and samples. The use of cubical marching squares and associated data structures (like BVHs and 2D grids) optimizes the intersection search for these topological queries. name: Ray Crossing Count (Winding Number)
head: winding number via crossing count, Ray-Triangle Crossing Count, Crossing Count Ray Query
body: The Ray Crossing Count method determines whether a 3D point lies inside or outside a closed triangle mesh by casting a ray and counting surface intersections. It solves the topological "inside/outside" ambiguity that plagues simpler depth-based tests, which can fail when a ray intersects the same triangle multiple times or hits edges/vertices, causing sign-flipping artifacts. Unlike the Region Nesting Merge sibling, which relies on hierarchical containment logic, this method uses a direct parity or signed accumulation of ray-triangle hits. Input: A query point P = (Px, Py, Pz) and a triangle mesh \mathcal{M} consisting of N triangles. Each triangle Ti is defined by vertices V{i,0}, V{i,1}, V{i,2} and an outward-facing normal \mathbf{n}i. Output: A boolean indicating if P is inside the mesh, or an integer/float winding number. 1. Triangle List: An array of N triangles. Each triangle stores vertex positions and precomputed normals. 2. Bounding Volume Hierarchy (BVH): A tree structure where each node stores an Axis-Aligned Bounding Box (AABB) enclosing its child triangles. Leaves contain indices to the triangle list. This allows efficient culling of non-intersecting triangles. 3. 2D Grid (Optional Optimization): For axis-aligned ray casting, a 2D grid of size W \times H can store lists of triangles intersecting each grid cell, along with their intersection z-values. This reduces the search space from 3D volume to 2D surface projection. Ray Direction: Typically aligned with a principal axis (e.g., +z) for the 2D grid optimization, or arbitrary directions for robustness. Intersection Algorithm: The Müller-Trombose algorithm is cited as a robust choice for ray-triangle intersection. Grid Resolution: Example given is 128 \times 128 for the 2D projection optimization. 1. Ray Initialization: Define a ray origin at the query point P and a direction \mathbf{d}. For the 2D grid method, \mathbf{d} = (0, 0, 1) (positive z-axis). For the general winding number, \mathbf{d} can be any direction, often sampled from multiple axes. 2. Intersection Search: BVH Approach: Traverse the BVH to find all triangles whose bounding boxes intersect the ray. 2D Grid Approach: Project P to 2D coordinates (Px, Py). Retrieve the precomputed list of triangles intersecting this 2D grid cell. 3. Triangle Intersection Test: For each candidate triangle Ti: Compute the intersection between the ray and the triangle plane. Verify the intersection point lies within the triangle boundaries (barycentric coordinates). Check if the intersection occurs in the forward direction of the ray (t > 0). 4. Counting Logic: Parity Method (Simple Inside/Outside): Initialize count = 0. For each valid intersection, increment count. If count is odd, P is inside; if even, P is outside. Signed Winding Number Method (Robust): Initialize crossingCount = 0 and totalCount = 0. For each valid intersection: Increment totalCount. Calculate the dot product between the triangle normal \mathbf{n}i and the ray direction \mathbf{d}: dot = \mathbf{n}i \cdot \mathbf{d}. If dot > 0, the ray exits the volume (or enters depending on orientation convention); add +1 to crossingCount. If dot \le 0, the ray enters the volume; add -1 to crossingCount. Note: The source code example adds +1 if dot > 0 and implicitly -1 otherwise (or does not add if equal, but standard winding numbers usually handle grazing cases carefully). For a closed, outward-oriented mesh, a point outside should yield a net count of 0, and a point inside should yield +1 (exiting once more than entering). 5. Multi-Ray Voting (Optional Robustness): To handle degenerate cases where a single ray hits an edge or vertex, cast rays in six directions (positive/negative x, y, z) and take a majority vote of the inside/outside results. 6. Generalized Winding Number: For meshes with holes or "soups" (non-closed), the signed crossing count provides a continuous value between 0 and 1, representing the probability or density of being inside. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def raycrossingcount(querypoint, triangles, bvh, usesigned=True): """ Determines if querypoint is inside the mesh defined by triangles. Args: querypoint: Tuple (x, y, z) triangles: List of Triangle objects, each with vertices and normal bvh: Bounding Volume Hierarchy for efficient culling usesigned: If True, uses winding number; if False, uses parity Returns: Boolean (inside/outside) or Float (winding number) """ rayorigin = querypoint # Use positive Z axis for simplicity, or arbitrary direction raydirection = (0.0, 0.0, 1.0) crossingcount = 0 totalcount = 0 # 1. Find candidate triangles using BVH candidateindices = bvh.intersectray(rayorigin, raydirection) for idx in candidateindices: tri = triangles[idx] # 2. Ray-Triangle Intersection # Returns t (distance) and hitpoint if intersected, else None hit = raytriangleintersect(rayorigin, raydirection, tri) if hit is not None: t, hitpoint = hit # Only count intersections in the forward direction if t > 0: totalcount += 1 if usesigned: # 3. Signed Winding Number # Dot product of triangle normal and ray direction dotproduct = dot(tri.normal, raydirection) # Convention: +1 if exiting (normal points same direction as ray) # -1 if entering (normal points opposite to ray) if dotproduct > 0.0: crossingcount += 1 else: crossingcount -= 1 else: # 4. Parity Method crossingcount += 1 if usesigned: # For closed outward-oriented mesh: # Outside -> 0, Inside -> 1 # Graceful transition for open meshes return crossingcount else: # Parity: Odd -> Inside, Even -> Outside return (crossingcount % 2) == 1 def raytriangleintersect(origin, direction, triangle): """ Müller-Trombose or standard Möller-Trumbore intersection. Returns (t, point) if hit, else None. """ # Implementation of ray-triangle intersection # 1. Compute plane normal from triangle vertices v0 = triangle.v0 v1 = triangle.v1 v2 = triangle.v2 edge1 = v1 - v0 edge2 = v2 - v0 normal = cross(edge1, edge2) # 2. Check if ray is parallel to plane denom = dot(normal, direction) if abs(denom) < 1e-8: return None # 3. Compute t t = dot(normal, v0 - origin) / denom if t <= 0: return None # 4. Compute hit point hitpoint = origin + direction t # 5. Barycentric coordinates to check if point is inside triangle # Using edge normals or area method #... (Standard barycentric check)... # Simplified check: # If hitpoint is within triangle bounds if ispointintriangle(hitpoint, v0, v1, v2): return (t, hitpoint) else: return None def ispointintriangle(p, v0, v1, v2): """Check if point p is inside triangle v0-v1-v2 using barycentric coords.""" # Compute vectors v0v1 = v1 - v0 v0v2 = v2 - v0 v0p = p - v0 # Compute dot products d00 = dot(v0v0, v0v0) # Not needed if using cross product method # Standard barycentric calculation #... return True # Placeholder for actual barycentric logic Edge/Vertex Hits: Rays hitting triangle edges or vertices may double-count or miscount intersections, making the theoretical crossing count unreliable for single rays. This is mitigated by using signed winding numbers (which cancel out grazing hits if normals are consistent) or multi-ray voting. Open Meshes: The parity method is only meaningful for closed meshes. For open meshes or "soup" of triangles, the signed winding number provides a generalized result, but the binary inside/outside interpretation is invalid. Numerical Precision: Floating-point errors near the surface can cause inconsistent results. Using a small epsilon for intersection checks is recommended. Performance: Brute-force checking all triangles is O(N). Using a BVH reduces this to O(\log N) on average. The 2D grid optimization reduces the problem from checking 128^3 points to 128^2 points by pre-calculating intersections. Time Complexity: O(N) for brute-force ray-triangle intersection. O(\log N) with BVH acceleration. The 2D grid pre-calculation is O(N \cdot H \cdot W) but reduces query time to O(1) per grid cell. Memory Complexity: O(N) for storing triangles. O(H \cdot W) for the 2D grid optimization. Measured Performance: The overhead of the raycast step is small when performed simultaneously with Signed Distance Field (SDF) calculation. Strengths: Robust against sign-flipping artifacts caused by depth-based tests. Provides generalized winding numbers for non-closed meshes. Limitations: Sensitive to degenerate ray hits (edges/vertices) without mitigation. Requires closed meshes for simple parity interpretation. When to Use: When topological correctness is critical, especially in Marching Cubes implementations where incorrect inside/outside tests cause artifacts. When dealing with meshes that may have holes or non-manifold geometry, the signed winding number is preferred. The Ray Crossing Count method is a fundamental technique in computational geometry for point-in-polyhedron tests. It is widely used in volume rendering, particularly in Marching Cubes implementations, to correctly determine the interior of a mesh. The specific implementation using signed crossing counts to fix artifacts in Marching Cubes 33 was detailed by Vega et al. in "A Fast and Memory-Saving Marching Cubes 33 Implementation with the Correct Interior Test" (JCGT 2019). The 2D grid optimization approach is discussed in community forums as a way to reduce computational complexity for voxel-based rendering. Checking if point is inside the mesh via raycasting - where to cast rays?, https://gamedev.stackexchange.com/questions/120869/checking-if-point-is-inside-the-mesh-via-raycasting-where-to-cast-rays, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial) GuangyanCai/isoext, https://github.com/GuangyanCai/isoext, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial) Signed Distance Field Rendering Journey pt.1 – kosmonaut's blog, https://kosmonautblog.wordpress.com/2017/05/01/signed-distance-field-rendering-journey-pt-1/, fetched 2026-10-29 (unofficial)

name: Region Nesting Merge
head: MergeRegion
body: Region Nesting Merge is a post-processing step for topological ray operations that removes nested inner regions from a sorted list of ray samples. It solves the problem of redundant or invalid geometry resulting from boolean unions or subtractions, where one volumetric region is contained entirely within another. It differs from Ray Crossing Count by relying on the orientation of surface normals relative to the ray direction to determine nesting depth, rather than counting geometric intersections. It is a core component of Ray Union and Ray Subtraction. Inputs and Outputs Input: A ray R containing a list of samples R.list, sorted by their position along the ray (typically by z-value or distance from origin). Each sample s has a position and a normal vector s.normal. The ray has a direction vector R.direction. Output: The ray R with its list R.list updated to contain only the samples defining the outermost boundaries of the volumetric regions, effectively removing any samples that define regions strictly inside other regions. Data Structures Ray: Contains a direction vector \mathbf{d} and a list of samples. Sample: Contains a position (implicitly sorted) and a normal vector \mathbf{n}. Temporary List T: An empty list used to accumulate the surviving samples. Algorithm The procedure iterates through the sorted samples, maintaining a nesting level counter. The logic assumes that a sample with a normal pointing against the ray direction represents an "entry" into a volume, while a normal pointing with the ray direction represents an "exit". 1. Initialize a nesting level counter level = 0. 2. Initialize an empty output list T. 3. For each sample s in the sorted input list R.list: a. Calculate the dot product D = \mathbf{n}s \cdot \mathbf{d}R. b. If D < 0 (normal opposes ray direction, entering a region): i. Decrement level by 1. ii. If level == 0, add s to T. c. Else (D \ge 0, normal aligns with ray direction, leaving a region): i. If level == 0, add s to T. ii. Increment level by 1. 4. Replace R.list with T. Pseudocode Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def MergeRegion(Ray R): level = 0 T = [] # R.list is assumed to be sorted by position along the ray for s in R.list: # Dot product of sample normal and ray direction dotproduct = dot(s.normal, R.direction) if dotproduct < 0: # Entering a region (normal points against ray) level = level - 1 if level == 0: T.append(s) else: # Leaving a region (normal points with ray) if level == 0: T.append(s) level = level + 1 R.list = T Parameters R.direction: The direction vector of the ray. Typically normalized. s.normal: The normal vector of the sample. Must be consistent with the topological definition of the volume (outward-facing for standard union logic). Edge Cases and Pitfalls Sorting: The input list R.list must be strictly sorted by position along the ray. If samples are not sorted, the nesting logic fails. Normal Consistency: The algorithm relies on the convention that normals pointing against the ray direction denote entry. This convention must be maintained across all samples in the list. In Ray Subtraction, the normals of the subtracted volume are inverted before merging to satisfy this convention for the subtraction logic. Degenerate Inputs: If the list is empty, the output is empty. If the nesting level does not return to 0 at the end of the list, the input data is topologically inconsistent (e.g., an unpaired entry or exit). The algorithm as described does not explicitly check for this, but the resulting list may be topologically invalid for rendering. Time Complexity: O(N), where N is the number of samples in R.list. The algorithm performs a single pass through the list. Memory Complexity: O(N) in the worst case (if no regions are nested and all samples are kept), as a new list T is created. Strengths: Simple, efficient, and robust for boolean operations on ray-based volumetric representations. It correctly handles nested structures by tracking depth. Limitations: It assumes a specific normal orientation convention. It does not handle complex self-intersections or non-manifold geometry that violates the entry/exit pairing assumption. It requires pre-sorted input. Region Nesting Merge was introduced in the context of detail sculpting using cubical marching squares. It serves as the core mechanism for resolving topological conflicts in ray-based boolean operations. The method is part of a family of topological inside tests that use normal orientation to determine volumetric inclusion. Detail sculpting using cubical marching squares, https://doi.org/10.1145/1152399.1152402, fetched 2026-11-06

name: Ray Subtraction
head: RaySubstraction
body: Ray subtraction is a boolean operation that removes material from a target ray (Ray A) using a source ray (Ray B). It solves the problem of sculpting or editing volumetric data by allowing users to delete specific regions, such as removing a sphere from a cube. It differs from Ray Union by inverting the normals of the source samples before merging, which causes the MergeRegion procedure to treat the source region as an "inside" void rather than an added volume. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Ray A (target), Ray B (source). Both contain a list of samples sorted by depth. Output: Ray A modified in place to represent the material of A minus B. Data Structures: Ray.list: A list of samples. Each sample s contains at least a position (implied by sorting) and a normal vector. Ray.direction: The viewing direction vector. Algorithm Steps: 1. Iterate through every sample s in Ray B.list. 2. Negate the normal of sample s: s.normal \leftarrow -s.normal. 3. Append the modified sample s to Ray A.list. 4. Sort Ray A.list by depth (typically z-value or distance along the ray). 5. Call MergeRegion on Ray A to remove inner regions based on the inverted normals. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def RaySubstraction(Ray A, Ray B): # Step 1-3: Invert normals and merge for s in B.list: s.normal = -s.normal A.list.append(s) # Step 4: Sort by depth (z-value) # Implementation note: Sorts samples based on their position along the ray direction A.list.sort(key=lambda sample: dot(sample.position, A.direction)) # Step 5: Remove inner regions MergeRegion(A) MergeRegion Logic (Required Context): The MergeRegion procedure tracks a nesting level. It iterates through the sorted list. If the dot product of the sample's normal and the ray direction is negative, it decrements the level; otherwise, it increments it. Samples are kept only when the level transitions from 0 to 1 (entering a region) or when the level is 0 and the normal points with the ray (entering a region from outside). Specifically: If Dot(s.normal, R.direction) < 0: level \leftarrow level - 1 If level == 0, keep sample s. Else: If level == 0, keep sample s. level \leftarrow level + 1 Parameters: Not given in the sources. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision errors in sorting or dot products may lead to incorrect nesting levels if samples are coplanar or nearly parallel to the ray. The method assumes the input rays are valid representations of volumetric boundaries. A procedure for handling occlusion when removing an object part that is in front of another one. Instead of simple boolean subtraction, it zeros out the first mode of density along the ray. The first mode of density is defined as starting at the first point with non-zero density up to the first subsequent point with zero density. This procedure is effective but can be slow and may leave artifacts of incomplete removal. A technique to remove occluding structures by skipping ray integration steps that intersect with a specified geometric shape (e.g., sphere, cone, cylinder). It uses an Init shader to compute start and stopping coordinates of the carving shape. If the ray intersects the shape, the integration start position (currentDistance) is adjusted to the intersection point. Parameters: interactionPoint1: A user-defined 3D coordinate used to determine the center of the carving shape (e.g., sphere). currentDistance: A built-in variable specifying the next integration position along the ray. sphereRadius: The radius of the carving sphere. Pseudocode (Volume Carving Init Shader): Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. centerDir = interactionPoint1 - rayStart centerProjDist = dot(centerDir, rayDir) centerProj = rayStart + rayDir centerProjDist distCenterProjCenter = length(centerProj - interactionPoint1) if distCenterProjCenter < sphereRadius: dcpc2 = distCenterProjCenter distCenterProjCenter sr2 = sphereRadius sphereRadius intersectDistance = centerProjDist + sqrt(sr2 - dcpc2) if intersectDistance > 0.0: currentDistance = intersectDistance Time Complexity: Dominated by the sorting step, O(N \log N) where N is the total number of samples in both rays, plus the linear scan of MergeRegion, O(N). Memory Complexity: O(N) to store the merged list. Strengths: Simple to implement; leverages existing union and merge logic. Limitations: The basic boolean subtraction does not handle occlusion well (e.g., removing a front object while keeping a back object) without additional density zeroing techniques. The volume carving variant can be slow and may leave artifacts. When to use: When performing boolean sculpting on volumetric meshes or ray lists where topological correctness is required. When not to use: When occlusion handling is critical and performance is constrained, or when the geometry is complex enough that simple ray list manipulation fails to capture the visual intent. The method originates from work on detail sculpting using cubical marching squares. It was introduced as Algorithm 3 in the paper "Detail sculpting using cubical marching squares". The technique is similar to Ray Union but relies on normal inversion to achieve subtraction semantics. Variants like Volume Carving were later explored in the context of interactive GPU volume rendering shaders using frameworks like PRISM, and occlusion-aware removal was discussed in the context of editing Conditional Radiance Fields.
