name: Ray generation and camera models
body: Ray generation and camera models define the geometric mapping from discrete 2D pixel coordinates to continuous 3D world-space rays, serving as the foundational input for volume rendering, ray marching, and ray tracing pipelines. This family solves the problem of establishing a valid view frustum by constructing camera basis vectors and projecting pixel locations onto a virtual image plane. It differs from sibling methods like Ray-primitive intersection by focusing solely on the creation of the ray geometry rather than its traversal, and from Parallel and GPU primitives by defining the logical data flow rather than the hardware execution model. The shared principles of this family are the geometric definition of rays and the parallel execution model. Ray Definition Rays are defined by an origin \mathbf{o} and a direction \mathbf{d}. The direction is typically normalized. The origin is often the camera eye position, but can vary based on the camera model. Parallel Execution Computations are mapped to parallel threads. Each thread typically processes one or more pixels or samples. Memory access patterns are optimized for coalescing. Synchronization is used to manage data dependencies between threads. Sky Gradient generates a background color for rays that miss the primary volume or reach infinite distance by interpolating between a horizon color and a zenith color based on the ray's vertical direction component. It is a lightweight, non-geometry effect often implemented as a handful of sine waves or simple color blending in a sky shader. The Arcball Camera is an interactive camera control technique that maps 2D screen coordinates to a 3D virtual sphere to compute rotation quaternions for smooth orbiting around a center point. It decouples 2D input from 3D orientation, allowing intuitive rotation without gimbal lock. It differs from First-Person Camera Control by orbiting a fixed center rather than moving the eye position directly. Uniform Sphere Sampling generates a random direction vector uniformly distributed over the surface of a unit sphere. It solves the problem of creating isotropic ray directions for global illumination, sky sampling, or volume scattering where no preferred direction exists. It sets itself apart from Random Hemisphere Sampling by covering the full 4\pi steradians rather than restricting samples to a half-sphere, and from Rejection Sampling for Uniform Sphere Sampling by using a direct transformation method that avoids discarding samples. First-Person Camera Control manages camera position, orientation (yaw and pitch), and projection parameters, translating discrete user input (mouse movement, keyboard presses) into continuous 3D transformations. It packs these state variables into a GPU-friendly structure to minimize bandwidth overhead during rendering passes. The Arbitrary Source-Detector Geometry Projector is a CT geometry type that allows the user to define the 3D location and orientation of every individual source-detector pair, overriding standard geometric assumptions. It supports flexible specification including arbitrary 3D detector shifts and non-equispaced projection angles, covering planar or curved detectors (axial) and arbitrary source/detector placement (flexible). It differs from fixed-camera models by explicitly defining every source-detector pair, supporting complex trajectories and parameterized detector surfaces while maintaining exact cell-constant integration. The Camera Class Structure defines the geometric state and rendering parameters required to generate rays for volume rendering. It serves as the primary interface between the application's scene graph and the ray generation kernel, encapsulating position, orientation, field of view, and clipping boundaries. Unlike sibling methods that focus on specific sampling strategies or traversal setups, this structure provides the foundational data layout necessary to compute ray origins and directions for any camera model. Ray Angle Computation calculates the geometric angular relationship between a query ray and reference rays intersecting the same 3D point. It is primarily used in multi-view stereo and NeRF-based methods to generate features that encode viewing geometry. Unlike methods that rely solely on coordinate transformations, this approach explicitly computes the dot product and difference vectors between ray directions to capture angular similarity. The Sky Radiance Model generates background illumination for ray-traced scenes by sampling a precomputed equirectangular sky texture and adding a direct sun disk contribution based on ray direction relative to the sun direction. It solves the problem of providing sky lighting without performing real-time atmospheric integration per ray. It differs from the Sky Gradient by using a high-resolution precomputed texture for complex atmospheric effects rather than a simple analytic gradient, and from the Uniform Sphere Sampling by including directional sun intensity and atmospheric attenuation. This method initializes the compute shader pipeline for volumetric ray marching, specifically handling camera ray reconstruction and dispatch parameters for a voxel-based smoke renderer. It differs from general ray generation by explicitly detailing the reconstruction of world-space rays from screen coordinates via inverse projection matrices and the two-stage marching logic (empty-space skipping vs. density accumulation). It serves as the computational core that bridges the camera model and the voxel data structures. The Grid Ray Sampler generates camera rays by mapping pixel coordinates from an image grid to 3D space, producing either a uniform set of rays covering the entire resolution or a random subset of rays for sparse sampling. It differs from its siblings by providing the foundational geometric mapping from 2D pixel indices to 3D ray origins and directions, whereas methods like Sky Gradient or Arcball Camera focus on specific camera models or environmental lighting, and Refined Ray Generation via PDF Sampling builds upon this uniform base by re-weighting samples based on opacity. Fisheye Distortion Correction eliminates the visual bowing of flat surfaces in ray-cast scenes caused by using raw Euclidean ray lengths for perspective projection. It replaces the naive distance with the perpendicular distance to the projection plane, ensuring that a flat wall renders as a straight line across the entire field of view. Unlike Sky Gradient or Arcball Camera which define viewing geometry, this method specifically corrects the depth value used for screen-space projection in planar scenes. Ray casting is the fundamental image synthesis technique that generates primary rays through image pixels to determine visible geometry and accumulate light contributions, serving as the base layer for more complex ray tracing algorithms. It is distinguished from full ray tracing by its exclusive use of primary (viewing) rays, omitting secondary rays for shadows, reflections, or refractions. This family defines the geometric mapping from discrete pixel coordinates to continuous 3D rays, establishing the camera's extrinsic parameters and projection model. It solves the problem of generating valid ray origins and directions for volume rendering by constructing an orthonormal basis from eye/target/up vectors and applying the appropriate projection, differing from sibling methods by focusing on fundamental algebraic construction rather than traversal optimizations or control interfaces. This family implements optical effects that deviate from the ideal pinhole camera model, primarily depth of field (blur based on focal distance) and geometric lens distortions. It sets itself apart from sibling ray generation methods by introducing a finite aperture for ray origins, requiring sampling over a 2D area rather than a single point, and by modifying ray directions to simulate optical phenomena like magnification or shift. Camera Trajectory and Path Generation defines the sequence of camera poses (positions and orientations) used to sample rays for volume rendering or novel view synthesis. It solves the problem of determining where to place virtual cameras to capture a scene from desired viewpoints, ranging from static orbits to complex helical fly-throughs. It differs from Ray generation and camera models by focusing on the temporal/spatial sequence of poses rather than the instantaneous ray construction, and from Novel View Synthesis Rendering by excluding the actual rendering and encoding steps, providing only the geometric path. Camera Ray Generation computes the 3D origin \mathbf{o} and direction \mathbf{d} for primary rays corresponding to each pixel (or sample) in an image, mapping 2D raster coordinates to 3D world-space rays for volume rendering or ray tracing. It differs from Orthographic (Parallel) Camera Ray Generation by supporting perspective projection (converging rays) and from Pinhole Camera Ray Generation by explicitly constructing and utilizing camera parameters (intrinsic/extrinsic or basis vectors) rather than assuming a canonical pinhole model. It serves as the foundational step for Ray Casting and Ray Marching. Definition: Minimizes aliasing caused by ray divergence by adjusting the distance between the viewer's eye and the viewing plane, reducing the angle between neighboring rays. Steps: Increase the distance between the viewer's eye and the viewing plane. As distance increases, the angle of divergence between rays decreases. As distance approaches infinity, ray divergence approaches zero. Steps: Initialize bounds with scene.sceneBounds. Iterate over scene.splatSets, merging each set's bounds into bounds using MergeBounds. If bounds is invalid, return default view with center {0, 0, 2.5} and radius 1.0. Otherwise, return view with center = ComputeAabbCenter(bounds) and radius = max(ComputeAabbRadius(bounds), 0.5f). Call EstimateSceneView(scene) to get view. Calculate aspect = width / height. Calculate distance = max(view.radius 2.5f, 1.5f). Set eye = {view.center.x, view.center.y, view.center.z - distance}. Set input.view = LookAt(eye, view.center, {0.0f, 1.0f, 0.0f}). Set input.proj = Perspective(1.0f, aspect, 0.01f, max(100.0f, distance + view.radius 4.0f)). Set input.cameraPosition = eye. Set input.viewportWidth = width, input.viewportHeight = height. Set input.nearPlane = 0.01f. Set input.farPlane = max(100.0f, distance + view.radius 4.0f). Set input.frameIndex = frameIndex. Set input.settings.antialiasing = true, input.settings.fastCulling = true. The pinhole camera model, which simulates depth by positioning the eye behind the image plane at a distance f (focal length), is the standard geometric foundation for ray generation in computer graphics. Early implementations in ray marching focused on simple perspective projection to create depth illusions, moving beyond orthographic parallel casting. The field has expanded to include arbitrary source-detector geometries for medical imaging (CT). name: Sky Gradient
head: Aurora Rendering, Aurora curtains, Horizon-Zenith Gradient, Neon Sky, Sky gradient texture, Synthwave Sky Gradient, getSky
body: Sky Gradient generates a background color for rays that do not intersect the primary volume, interpolating between a horizon color and a zenith color based on the ray's vertical direction component. It differs from SkyboxRendering by lacking time-dependent sun/moon arcs or procedural starfields in its core definition. Inputs and Outputs Input: Ray direction vector \mathbf{d} (typically normalized). Input: Horizon color \mathbf{C}{horizon} (RGB). Input: Zenith color \mathbf{C}{zenith} (RGB). Input: Optional transition parameters (bounds, power, glow intensity). Output: Background color \mathbf{C}{sky} (RGB). Data Structures No persistent data structures are required. The method is a pure function of the ray direction and uniform color parameters. Steps 1. Normalize Direction: Ensure the ray direction \mathbf{d} is normalized. If the input is a point \mathbf{p} relative to the camera, compute \mathbf{d} = \text{normalize}(\mathbf{p}). 2. Compute Vertical Component: Extract the vertical component y = \mathbf{d}y (the y-component of the normalized direction vector). 3. Compute Interpolation Factor: Calculate a factor t that maps the vertical range to [0, 1]. Two common variations exist: Linear Mapping: t = 0.5 \times (y + 1.0). This maps y=-1 (nadir) to t=0 and y=1 (zenith) to t=1. Smoothstep Mapping: t = \text{smoothstep}(0.0, 0.7, y). This creates a smooth transition starting at y=0 and completing at y=0.7. Clamped Linear: h = \text{clamp}(0.5 \times y + 0.5, 0.0, 1.0). 4. Apply Power (Optional): Some implementations apply a power function to the factor to adjust the gradient curve. For example, use h^{0.55} instead of h. 5. Interpolate Colors: Compute the base sky color using linear interpolation (mix): \mathbf{C}{base} = (1 - t) \mathbf{C}{horizon} + t \mathbf{C}{zenith} Or using the power-adjusted factor h: \mathbf{C}{base} = (1 - h^p) \mathbf{C}{horizon} + h^p \mathbf{C}{zenith} where p is the mix power (e.g., 0.55). 6. Add Ground Glow (Optional): Enhance the horizon with a glow effect. Compute the glow intensity based on the distance from the horizon: \mathbf{C}{glow} = \mathbf{C}{horizon} \times I \times (1.0 - |y|)^g where I is intensity (e.g., 0.4) and g is the glow power (e.g., 6.0). 7. Combine: Add the glow to the base color: \mathbf{C}{sky} = \mathbf{C}{base} + \mathbf{C}{glow}. Pseudocode Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def normalize(v): length = math.sqrt(v[0]2 + v[1]2 + v[2]2) if length == 0.0: return (0.0, 0.0, 0.0) return (v[0]/length, v[1]/length, v[2]/length) def smoothstep(edge0, edge1, x): t = max(0.0, min(1.0, (x - edge0) / (edge1 - edge0))) return t t (3.0 - 2.0 t) def mix(a, b, t): return (a[0](1.0-t) + b[0]t, a[1](1.0-t) + b[1]t, a[2](1.0-t) + b[2]t) def clamp(x, minval, maxval): return max(minval, min(maxval, x)) def skygradient(direction, horizon, zenith, usesmoothstep=False, smoothstepmax=0.7, mixpower=1.0, glowintensity=0.0, glowpower=6.0): d = normalize(direction) y = d[1] if usesmoothstep: t = smoothstep(0.0, smoothstepmax, y) else: t = 0.5 (y + 1.0) t = clamp(t, 0.0, 1.0) tpow = t mixpower basecolor = mix(horizon, zenith, tpow) if glowintensity > 0.0: glowfactor = (1.0 - abs(y)) glowpower glowcolor = (horizon[0]glowintensityglowfactor, horizon[1]glowintensityglowfactor, horizon[2]glowintensityglowfactor) basecolor = (basecolor[0]+glowcolor[0], basecolor[1]+glowcolor[1], basecolor[2]+glowcolor[2]) return basecolor Parameters Horizon Color: RGB vector. Example: (0.80, 0.90, 1.0), (0.55, 0.06, 0.32), (255, 100, 80). Zenith Color: RGB vector. Example: (0.35, 0.60, 0.95), (0.02, 0.01, 0.05), (10, 20, 60). Smoothstep Bounds: Transition range for d.y. Example: (0.0, 0.7). Mix Power: Exponent for interpolation factor. Example: 0.55. Default: 1.0. Glow Intensity: Multiplier for ground glow. Example: 0.4. Default: 0.0. Glow Power: Exponent for glow falloff. Example: 6.0. Default: 1.0. Edge Cases and Pitfalls Non-normalized Input: If the direction vector is not normalized, the y-component will not accurately represent the vertical angle, leading to incorrect gradient placement. Always normalize. Precision: When y is close to 0 or 1, floating-point precision errors might cause slight color shifts. Clamping t to [0, 1] mitigates this. Degenerate Input: If horizon and zenith colors are identical, the result is constant regardless of direction. Generates a dynamic sky color with time-dependent sun/moon arcs, day/night palettes, and a hashed starfield. Choose when you need a realistic day/night cycle or starfield. Uses a learnable/procedural 3D grid sampled on spherical shells with volumetric attenuation. Choose when you need density-based background sampling or volumetric fog effects in the background. Time Complexity: O(1) per ray. The computation involves a few arithmetic operations and trigonometric functions (if normalization is required). Memory Complexity: O(1). No additional memory is required beyond the input parameters. Performance: Extremely fast. Suitable for real-time rendering on any hardware. Strengths: Simple to implement, computationally inexpensive, easy to tune visually. Limitations: Lacks physical accuracy (no scattering, no sun position), no temporal variation (static unless manually animated), no starfields or complex atmospheric effects. When to Use: Simple backgrounds, stylized rendering, performance-critical applications, or as a base for more complex sky models. When Not to Use: When physical accuracy is required, when dynamic sun/moon positions are needed, or when volumetric background effects are desired. Variations include "Aurora Rendering" which adds sine-wave based aurora effects, and implementations featuring ground glow and specific color palettes. name: SkyboxRendering
head: NoisyStarField, Procedural sky, SampleStars, Sky Gradient with Day/Night Cycle, Sky Shader, Skybox, Skybox Rendering with Day/Night Cycle, StableStarField
body: SkyboxRendering generates a dynamic sky color for a ray or fragment based on the viewing direction, simulating a day/night cycle with sun position, atmospheric blending, and a procedural starfield. It differs from the parent Sky Gradient by introducing time-dependent sun/moon arcs, distinct day/night color palettes blended via light direction, and a hashed starfield component. Inputs: raydir: Normalized ray direction in world space (\mathbf{r}). sundir: Normalized direction to the sun (\mathbf{s}). time: Current simulation time (for star twinkle). Outputs: skycolor: Final RGB color of the sky. Data Structures: Not given in the sources. Parameters: SunSize: Exponent for sun disk falloff. Default: 10.0. StarThreshold: Hash threshold for star presence. Default: 0.99514. StarGridScale: Scaling factor for star coordinate mapping. Default: 4096.0. Day/Night Colors: Pre-defined RGB vectors for zenith and horizon for both cycles. Blend Bounds: Smoothstep boundaries for vertical blending. Default: -0.5 to 1.5. Steps: 1. Calculate Day/Night Blend Factor: Determine the intensity of daylight based on the sun's vertical position or dot product with the world up vector (\mathbf{y} = (0,1,0)): Using sun direction Y component: \text{mixFactor} = 1.0 - (1.0 - \mathbf{s}y)^4 Or using light dot normalization: \text{lightDot} = \text{dot}(\mathbf{s}, \mathbf{y}) \text{lightDotNormalized} = \frac{\text{lightDot} + 1.0}{2.0} \text{cycleBlendValue} = 1.0 - \text{lightDotNormalized} 2. Compute Day Sky Gradient: Interpolate between day bottom and top colors based on ray vertical component \mathbf{r}y: \text{day} = \text{mix}(\text{DayBottomColor}, \text{DayTopColor}, \text{smoothstep}(D{start}, D{end}, \mathbf{r}y + 0.5)) Where D{start} = -0.5, D{end} = 1.5. 3. Compute Night Sky Gradient: Interpolate between night bottom and top colors: \text{night} = \text{mix}(\text{NightBottomColor}, \text{NightTopColor}, \text{smoothstep}(N{start}, N{end}, \mathbf{r}y + 0.5)) Where N{start} = -0.5, N{end} = 1.5. 4. Compute Sun Contribution: Calculate the dot product between the ray and sun direction: \text{sundot} = \text{clamp}(\text{dot}(\mathbf{r}, \mathbf{s}), 0.0, 1.0) \text{sun} = \text{SunColor} \times \text{pow}(\text{sundot}, \text{SunSize}) \text{SunColor} may vary based on time of day (e.g., mix between down/up sun colors). 5. Blend Day and Night: Combine the day and night gradients using the cycle blend value: \text{cycleColor} = \text{mix}(\text{day}, \text{night}, \text{cycleBlendValue}) 6. Add Sun to Cycle Color: Blend the sun contribution into the cycle color: \text{cycleColor} = \text{mix}(\text{cycleColor} + \text{sun}, \text{sun}, \text{clamp}(\text{pow}(\text{sundot}, \text{SunSize}), 0, 1)) 7. Generate Starfield: Coordinate Mapping: Convert ray direction to 2D UV for hashing: u = \text{fract}\left(0.5 + \frac{\text{atan2}(\mathbf{r}z, \mathbf{r}x)}{2\pi}\right) v = (\mathbf{r}y \times 0.5) + 0.5 \text{sample\pos} = (u \times 4096.0, v \times 4096.0) Stable Sampling: Use bilinear interpolation of a noisy hash field to prevent star flickering. 1. Calculate integer base coordinates: \text{base} = \text{floor}(\text{sample\pos}). 2. Calculate fractional parts: \text{fract\x} = \text{fract}(\text{sample\pos}x), \text{fract\y} = \text{fract}(\text{sample\pos}y). 3. Sample NoisyStarField at four corners: (0,0), (0,1), (1,0), (1,1) relative to base. 4. Bilinearly interpolate the results using \text{fract\x} and \text{fract\y}. NoisyStarField Logic: 1. Hash the integer position to get a value h \in 0, 1). 2. If h \ge \text{threshold} (0.99514), return \text{pow}\left(\frac{h - \text{threshold}}{1.0 - \text{threshold}}, 6.0\right), else return 0.0. Fade Stars: Apply horizon fade and night fade: \text{horizonFade} = \text{smoothstep}(0.0, 0.2, \mathbf{r}y) \text{nightFade} = \text{smoothstep}(1.0, 0.0, \text{mixFactor}) \text{starValue} = \text{StableStarField}(\text{sample\pos}) \times \text{horizonFade} \times \text{nightFade} 8. Final [Color Composition: Mix ground and sky colors if ground is visible (ray \mathbf{r}y is low): \text{groundColor} = \text{mix}(\text{NIGHT\GROUND\COLOR}, \text{DAY\GROUND\COLOR}, \text{mixFactor}) \text{skyColor} = \text{mix}(\text{NIGHT\SKY\COLOR}, \text{DAY\SKY\COLOR}, \text{mixFactor}) \text{baseColor} = \text{mix}(\text{groundColor}, \text{skyColor}, \mathbf{r}y) \text{finalColor} = \text{baseColor} + \text{starValue} 9. Post-Processing (Optional): Apply contrast and saturation adjustments: \text{contrast} = \text{rgb} \times \text{rgb} \times (3.0 - 2.0 \times \text{rgb}) \text{saturation} = \text{rgb} \times (1.0 + \text{sat}) - \text{sat} \times \text{dot}(\text{rgb}, (0.33, 0.33, 0.33)) Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def mix(a, b, t): return a + t (b - a) def smoothstep(edge0, edge1, x): t = max(0.0, min(1.0, (x - edge0) / (edge1 - edge0))) return t t (3.0 - 2.0 t) def fract(x): return x - math.floor(x) def dot(v1, v2): return v1[0]v2[0] + v1[1]v2[1] + v1[2]v2[2] def clamp(x, mn, mx): return max(mn, min(mx, x)) def vec3(x, y, z): return (x, y, z) def vec2(x, y): return (x, y) def Hash2D(pos): # Standard hash implementation p = vec2(dot(pos, vec2(127.1, 311.7)), dot(pos, vec2(269.5, 183.3))) return fract(math.sin(p[0]) 43758.5453123) def NoisyStarField(pos, threshold): val = Hash2D(pos) if val >= threshold: return pow((val - threshold) / (1.0 - threshold), 6.0) return 0.0 def StableStarField(samplepos, threshold): basex = math.floor(samplepos[0]) basey = math.floor(samplepos[1]) fx = fract(samplepos[0]) fy = fract(samplepos[1]) h00 = NoisyStarField(vec2(basex, basey), threshold) h10 = NoisyStarField(vec2(basex + 1, basey), threshold) h01 = NoisyStarField(vec2(basex, basey + 1), threshold) h11 = NoisyStarField(vec2(basex + 1, basey + 1), threshold) return mix(mix(h00, h10, fx), mix(h01, h11, fx), fy) def SkyboxRendering(raydir, sundir, time): # 1. Day/Night Blend Factor mixfactor = 1.0 - pow(1.0 - sundir[1], 4.0) lightdot = dot(sundir, vec3(0.0, 1.0, 0.0)) lightdotnormalized = (lightdot + 1.0) / 2.0 cycleblendvalue = 1.0 - lightdotnormalized # 2. Day Sky Gradient daybottom = vec3(205.0, 200.0, 252.0) / 255.0 1.3 daytop = vec3(85.0, 105.0, 170.0) / 255.0 day = mix(daybottom, daytop, smoothstep(-0.5, 1.5, raydir[1] + 0.5)) # 3. Night Sky Gradient nightbottom = vec3(205.0, 220.0, 255.0) / 255.0 0.5 nighttop = vec3(0.0, 10.0, 51.0) / 255.0 0.7 night = mix(nightbottom, nighttop, smoothstep(-0.5, 1.5, raydir[1] + 0.5)) # 4. Sun Contribution sundot = clamp(dot(raydir, sundir), 0.0, 1.0) suncolordown = vec3(1.0, 1.0, 1.0) 0.7 suncolorup = vec3(1.0, 1.0, 1.0) 0.8 suncolor = mix(suncolordown, suncolorup, 1.0 - smoothstep(1.0, 0.5, lightdotnormalized)) sunsize = 10.0 sun = suncolor pow(sundot, sunsize) # 5. Blend Day and Night cyclecolor = mix(day, night, cycleblendvalue) # 6. Add Sun cyclecolor = mix(cyclecolor + sun, sun, clamp(pow(sundot, sunsize), 0.0, 1.0)) # 7. Starfield u = fract(0.5 + math.atan2(raydir[2], raydir[0]) / (2.0 3.14159265)) v = (raydir[1] 0.5) + 0.5 samplepos = vec2(u 4096.0, v 4096.0) threshold = 0.99514 starval = StableStarField(samplepos, threshold) # Fade Stars horizonfade = smoothstep(0.0, 0.2, raydir[1]) nightfade = smoothstep(1.0, 0.0, mixfactor) starval = horizonfade nightfade # 8. Final Color nightground = vec3(0.1, 0.1, 0.2) dayground = vec3(0.5, 0.4, 0.3) groundcolor = mix(nightground, dayground, mixfactor) skycolor = mix(nightground, dayground, mixfactor) basecolor = mix(groundcolor, skycolor, raydir[1]) finalcolor = basecolor + starval return finalcolor A procedural star field generated by hashing sky directions into cells, with a sparse probability of holding a star, jittered position within the cell, and twinkle animation. It differs from the StableStarField by using a single hash lookup per cell rather than bilinear interpolation, resulting in sharper but potentially flickering stars if not animated. Choose this when visual sharpness is prioritized over temporal stability, or when twinkle effects are desired. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Performance: Not given in the sources. Strengths: No texture memory usage, fully procedural, supports dynamic day/night cycles. Limitations: Not given in the sources. SkyboxRendering is a common technique in real-time graphics, particularly in voxel engines and raymarched scenes, to provide a dynamic background without loading large skybox textures. The specific implementation details provided here are derived from various open-source voxel raymarching projects and voxel engines. jamestkiernan/webgpu-voxel-raymarching, https://github.com/jamestkiernan/webgpu-voxel-raymarching, fetched 2026-10-24 (unofficial) SamCZ/RayTracer, https://github.com/SamCZ/RayTracer, fetched 2026-10-24 (unofficial) DanielWLiu07/voxel-engine, https://github.com/DanielWLiu07/voxel-engine, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial) PIGJET/neon-raymarcher, https://github.com/PIGJET/neon-raymarcher, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial)

name: Background Rendering
body:
Background Rendering renders the environment behind a volume by sampling a 3D grid representing the background field along concentric spheres. It handles infinite distance or skybox-like backgrounds by mapping spherical coordinates to a 2D equirectangular texture. Unlike standard equirectangular sampling which may alias distant features, this method uses a structured traversal of background layers to mitigate aliasing. It serves as the final compositing stage, accumulating color from background layers and adding a constant ambient term based on remaining transmission. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: Ray origin ray.origin, ray direction ray.dir, background grid resolution grid.backgroundreso, number of background layers grid.backgroundnlayers, background data grid grid.backgrounddata (density and color), log-transmittance logtransmit from the volume pass, optimization options opt (including stepsize, stopthresh, backgroundbrightness), and ray world step size ray.worldstep. Outputs: Background color out (RGB) and updated log-transmittance. Data Structures: grid.backgrounddata: A 3D grid of size backgroundreso x backgroundreso x backgroundnlayers. Each voxel stores 4 channels: 3 for color (RGB) and 1 for density (\sigma). ray.l: Integer lattice indices for trilinear interpolation. ray.pos: Fractional offsets for trilinear interpolation. Parameters: innerradius: Minimum sampling radius, calculated as \max(	ext{dist}(	ext{ray.origin}, 	ext{ray.dir}) + 10^{-3}, 1.0). nsteps: Number of sampling steps, calculated as \lfloor 	ext{grid.background
layers} / 	ext{opt.step\size} floor + 2. C0: Spherical Harmonic DC factor, typically  rac{1}{\sqrt{4\pi}}. Steps: 1. Early Termination Check: If logtransmit < -25.0, return early to avoid numerical instability for fully opaque rays. 2. Initialization: Compute innerradius and nsteps. Initialize output color outv[3] to zeros. Set invrlast and invrmid to track inverse radii across steps. 3. Sampling Loop: Iterate i from 0 to nsteps - 1: a. Radius Calculation: Compute sampling radius r =  rac{n\steps}{n\steps - i - 0.5}. This creates non-linear spacing, denser near the origin and sparser at infinity. b. Intersection: Intersect the ray with a sphere of radius r centered at the origin. If intersection fails or r < 	ext{inneradius}, skip to next step. c. Position Calculation: Calculate ray position ray.pos at intersection t: ray.pos[j] = ray.origin[j] + t ray.dir[j]. d. Normalization: Normalize ray.pos and compute invrmid = 1.0 / \|ray.pos\|. e. Depth Coordinate: Set the z-coordinate (layer index) based on inverse radius: ray.pos[2] = 	ext{clamp}((1.0 - 	ext{invr\mid}) 	imes 	ext{grid.background
layers} - 0.5, 0.0, 	ext{grid.background
layers} - 1). f. Grid Indices: Compute integer grid indices ray.l from ray.pos and clamp them to valid bounds: ray.l[0] to 2 	imes 	ext{backgroundeso} - 1, ray.l[1] to backgroundeso - 1, ray.l[2] to background
layers - 2. g. Fractional Offsets: Compute fractional offsets ray.pos by subtracting integer indices: ray.pos[j] -= ray.l[j]. h. Trilinear Interpolation: Sample density \sigma and color from grid.backgrounddata using trilinear interpolation with ray.l and ray.pos. i. Optical Depth: If \sigma > 0, calculate optical depth pcnt = (	ext{invr\last} - 	ext{invr\mid}) 	imes 	ext{ray.world\step} 	imes \sigma. j. Weight Calculation: Calculate weight weight = e^{	ext{log	ransmit}} 	imes (1 - e^{-pcnt}). Update logtransmit -= pcnt. k. Color Accumulation: For each color channel i (0-2), interpolate color, scale by C0, add 0.5, clamp to [0, \infty), and accumulate: outv[i] += weight 	imes \max(	ext{color} 	imes C0 + 0.5, 0.0). l. Update Inverse Radius: Set invrlast = invrmid. m. Termination Check: If e^{	ext{log	ransmit}} < 	ext{opt.stop	hresh}, break loop. 4. Final Output: For each channel i, add ambient term: out[i] = outv[i] + e^{	ext{log	ransmit}} 	imes 	ext{opt.background rightness}. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def renderbackgroundforward(grid, rayspec, opt, logtransmit, out): """ Renders the background color for a single ray using concentric sphere sampling. Args: grid: Background grid data structure containing backgroundreso, backgroundnlayers, backgrounddata. rayspec: Ray specification containing origin, dir, worldstep. opt: Optimization options containing stepsize, stopthresh, backgroundbrightness. logtransmit: Current log-transmittance of the ray. out: Output array for background color (size 3). Returns: Updated logtransmit. """ # Early termination for fully opaque rays if logtransmit < -25.0: return logtransmit outv = [0.0, 0.0, 0.0] disttoorigin = math.sqrt(sum(rayspec.origin[j]2 for j in range(3))) innerradius = max(disttoorigin + 1e-3, 1.0) nsteps = int(grid.backgroundnlayers / opt.stepsize) + 2 C0 = 1.0 / math.sqrt(4.0 math.pi) invrlast = 0.0 invrmid = 0.0 for i in range(nsteps): # Calculate sampling radius r = nsteps / (nsteps - i - 0.5) # Check if radius is valid if r < innerradius: continue # Ray-sphere intersection for sphere centered at origin with radius r ox, oy, oz = rayspec.origin dx, dy, dz = rayspec.dir a = dxdx + dydy + dzdz b = 2.0 (oxdx + oydy + ozdz) c = oxox + oyoy + ozoz - rr disc = bb - 4.0ac if disc < 0.0: continue sqrtdisc = math.sqrt(disc) t = (-b - sqrtdisc) / (2.0 a) if t < 0.0: t = (-b + sqrtdisc) / (2.0 a) if t < 0.0: continue # Calculate ray position at intersection raypos = [ox + tdx, oy + tdy, oz + tdz] # Normalize position and compute inverse radius norm = math.sqrt(sum(v2 for v in raypos)) invrmid = 1.0 / norm raypos = [v invrmid for v in raypos] # Calculate depth coordinate (layer index) depthcoord = (1.0 - invrmid) grid.backgroundnlayers - 0.5 raypos[2] = max(min(depthcoord, grid.backgroundnlayers - 1), 0.0) # Compute integer grid indices rayl = [int(raypos[j]) for j in range(3)] # Clamp indices to valid bounds rayl[0] = max(min(rayl[0], 2 grid.backgroundreso - 1), 0) rayl[1] = max(min(rayl[1], grid.backgroundreso - 1), 0) rayl[2] = max(min(rayl[2], grid.backgroundnlayers - 2), 0) # Compute fractional offsets rayfrac = [raypos[j] - rayl[j] for j in range(3)] # Sample density sigma = trilinearinterpolate(grid.backgrounddata, rayl, rayfrac, channel=3) if sigma > 0.0: # Calculate optical depth pcnt = (invrlast - invrmid) rayspec.worldstep sigma # Calculate weight weight = math.exp(logtransmit) (1.0 - math.exp(-pcnt)) # Update log-transmittance logtransmit -= pcnt # Accumulate color for ich in range(3): color = trilinearinterpolate(grid.backgrounddata, rayl, rayfrac, channel=ich) # Scale by SH DC factor and add bias colorval = color C0 + 0.5 # Clamp and accumulate outv[ich] += weight max(colorval, 0.0) # Update inverse radius for next step invrlast = invrmid # Termination check if math.exp(logtransmit) < opt.stopthresh: break # Final output with ambient term for ich in range(3): out[ich] = outv[ich] + math.exp(logtransmit) opt.backgroundbrightness return logtransmit def trilinearinterpolate(grid, l, frac, channel): """Standard 3D trilinear interpolation over a 4D grid (depth, height, width, channels).""" x0, y0, z0 = l x1, y1, z1 = x0 + 1, y0 + 1, z0 + 1 fx, fy, fz = frac def fetch(x, y, z): x = max(0, min(x, grid.width - name: Background Rendering Kernel (Forward)
body: A CUDA kernel that renders the background color for rays that have transmitted through the volume. It serves as the final compositing stage in the background rendering kernel, accumulating color from the background layers and adding a constant ambient term based on remaining transmission. It differs from standard equirectangular sampling by using concentric spheres to distribute samples, which helps mitigate aliasing and provides a structured traversal of the background layers. Inputs and Outputs: grid: Background environment data structure (e.g., layered spherical map). rayspec: Ray origins and directions. options: Rendering configuration parameters. logtransmit: Per-ray logarithmic transmission values. output: Buffer for the resulting background color. Data Structures: logtransmit: Array of floats, indexed by rayid. Stores the natural logarithm of the accumulated transmission along the ray through the volume. Steps: 1. Initialize Ray Specification: Extract ray origins and directions from the input buffers for the current thread's rayid. 2. Find Background Bounds: Call rayfindboundsbg to determine the intersection interval of the ray with the background environment bounds. 3. Check Occlusion: If logtransmit[rayid] < -25.0f, the ray is considered highly occluded. The kernel returns early, skipping background rendering for this ray. 4. Render Background Forward: Call renderbackgroundforward with the grid, rayspec, options, logtransmit, and output buffers. This function samples the background using concentric spheres and composites the result with the transmission. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. @cuda.kernel def renderbackgroundkernelforward(grid, rayorigins, raydirections, options, logtransmit, output): rayid = cuda.grid(1) if rayid >= numrays: return # Step 1: Initialize ray specification origin = rayorigins[rayid] direction = raydirections[rayid] rayspec = Ray(origin, direction) # Step 2: Find background bounds tmin, tmax = rayfindboundsbg(rayspec, grid) # Step 3: Check occlusion if logtransmit[rayid] < -25.0f: return # Step 4: Render background forward renderbackgroundforward(grid, rayspec, options, logtransmit, output, rayid) Parameters: logtransmit threshold: -25.0f. Rays with transmission less than e^{-25} are skipped. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: High Occlusion: Rays with very low transmission (log value < -25) are skipped to save computation. This assumes that the background contribution is negligible for such rays. Precision: The use of logarithmic transmission requires careful handling of underflow. The threshold of -25 is chosen to balance precision and performance. This method renders the background environment for rays that have transmitted through the volume by sampling a layered spherical map. It differs from standard equirectangular sampling by using concentric spheres to distribute samples, which helps mitigate aliasing and provides a structured traversal of the background layers. It serves as the final compositing stage in the background rendering kernel, accumulating color from the background layers and adding a constant ambient term based on remaining transmission. Time Complexity: Linear with respect to the number of rays, O(N), where N is the number of pixels/rays. The cost per ray depends on the number of samples taken in the background rendering step. Memory Complexity: O(N) for storing logtransmit and output buffers. Performance: The early exit for highly occluded rays can significantly reduce computation time in scenes with dense volumes. Strengths: Efficient handling of occluded rays; structured sampling reduces aliasing. Limitations: Dependent on the efficiency of rayfindboundsbg and renderbackgroundforward. When to Use: Suitable for real-time or near-real-time volume rendering where background quality is important but computational resources are limited. When Not to Use: Not suitable for offline rendering where maximum quality is required without performance constraints. The Background Rendering Kernel (Forward) is part of the nerf-factory project by Kakao Brain. It is designed to integrate background rendering into the volume rendering pipeline, specifically for rays that have passed through the volume. body: This method renders the background environment for rays that have transmitted through the volume by sampling a layered spherical map. It differs from standard equirectangular sampling by using concentric spheres to distribute samples, which helps mitigate aliasing and provides a structured traversal of the background layers. It serves as the final compositing stage in the background rendering kernel, accumulating color from the background layers and adding a constant ambient term based on remaining transmission. Inputs: ray.origin: 3D vector, ray origin. ray.dir: 3D vector, ray direction. grid.backgroundlinks: Array of integers defining the connectivity or structure of the background data layers. grid.backgrounddata: Array of floats containing the background density (\sigma) and color values. grid.backgroundreso: Integer, resolution of the background spherical map (W \times H). grid.backgroundnlayers: Integer, number of layers in the background representation. opt.stepsize: Float, control parameter for step count calculation. opt.stopthresh: Float, termination threshold for transmission. opt.backgroundbrightness: Float, constant color added at the end. Outputs: outv[3]: Accumulated background color (RGB). logtransmit: Logarithmic transmission factor (updated during loop). out[3]: Final output color (updated after loop). The background data is stored in a 3D lattice structure implied by grid.backgrounddata. The interpolation function trilerpbgone assumes a layout where the first two dimensions correspond to the equirectangular map (W \times H) and the third dimension corresponds to the layers (N{layers}). The exact memory layout (e.g., row-major vs column-major) is not specified in the sources, but the indices ray.l[0], ray.l[1], and ray.l[2] map to these dimensions respectively. grid.backgroundreso: Typical values depend on the scene, e.g., 512 or 1024. grid.backgroundnlayers: Number of layers, e.g., 10-100. opt.stepsize: Control parameter, value not explicitly given but used in calculation. opt.stopthresh: Termination threshold, value not explicitly given. opt.backgroundbrightness: Constant color, value not explicitly given. 1. Initialization: Create ConcentricSpheresIntersector csi with ray.origin and ray.dir. Calculate innerradius = max(distance(ray.origin, ray.dir) + 1e-3, 1.0). Note: distance(ray.origin, ray.dir) likely refers to the distance from the ray origin to the nearest intersection with the inner sphere of the concentric structure, or a fixed offset. Given the context of "Concentric Spheres", this likely defines the inner boundary of the background volume. However, the code snippet fmaxf(distraytoorigin(ray.origin, ray.dir) + 1e-3f, 1.f) suggests distraytoorigin is a helper function. Without its definition, we assume it returns the distance from the ray origin to the center of the concentric spheres. If the ray origin is the camera, this might be 0, making innerradius 1.0. Calculate nsteps = int(grid.backgroundnlayers / opt.stepsize) + 2. Initialize outv[3] = {0, 0, 0}. Initialize logtransmit = 0.0 (implied, as it is used in exp(logtransmit)). Standard initialization for log transmission is 0 (transmission = 1). 2. Loop: For i from 0 to nsteps - 1: Calculate radius r = nsteps / (nsteps - i - 0.5). If r < innerradius or !csi.intersect(r, &t), continue to next iteration. Calculate position ray.pos = ray.origin + t ray.dir. Calculate invrmid = 1.0 / length(ray.pos). Normalize position: ray.pos = ray.pos invrmid. Convert to equirectangular coordinates: ray.pos = unitvec2equirect(ray.pos, grid.backgroundreso). This maps the normalized 3D vector to 2D coordinates (u, v) in the range [0, W-1] \times [0, H-1]. Convert to integer lattice: ray.l[j] = floor(ray.pos[j]) for j \in \{0, 1, 2\}. Clamp indices: ray.l[0] = clamp(ray.l[0], 0, grid.backgroundreso 2 - 1). Calculate fractional part: ray.pos[j] -= ray.l[j] for j \in \{0, 1, 2\}. However, the snippet updates invrlast = invrmid at the end of the loop. We assume invrlast is initialized to invrmid of the first valid sample or a default value. Let's assume invrlast is initialized to 1.0 / innerradius or invrmid of the first step. Actually, looking at the formula pcnt = (invrlast - invrmid)..., if invrlast is not set, this is undefined. Initialize invrlast = 1.0 / innerradius before the loop. Calculate weight = exp(logtransmit) (1.0 - exp(-pcnt)). Update logtransmit -= pcnt. For each color channel i (0 to 2): Interpolate color: color = trilerpbgone(...) C0. The C0 is not defined. Assume C0 is a scaling factor, possibly 1.0 or a specific constant. The source does not specify. We will assume C0 = 1.0 for now, or that the color is stored directly. Accumulate: outv[i] += weight max(color + 0.5, 0.0). The + 0.5 and max(..., 0.0) suggest a specific color space or bias. Check termination: if (exp(logtransmit) < opt.stopthresh) break;. Update invrlast = invrmid. 3. name: Skybox Rendering with Procedural Shading
head: Procedural Sky, Shader-based Sky
body: A procedural sky rendered on a back-face culled sphere using a custom shader material, combining horizon/zenith gradients, ground reflection, tiling noise clouds, and a sun disk with glow. It differs from kernel-based forward rendering by computing the background color per-fragment via analytical functions and noise sampling rather than precomputing or accumulating contributions in a separate pass. Inputs and outputs: Input: Camera view direction vector \mathbf{dir} (normalized). Input: Sun direction vector \mathbf{sunDir} (normalized). Input: Cloud texture (2D noise map). Input: Color constants for horizon, zenith, ground, and sun. Output: Final background color \mathbf{col}. Data structures: Sphere geometry: Radius R = 440 units. Resolution: 32x16 segments. Cloud texture: 2D noise texture, sampled via bilinear interpolation. Parameters: Horizon blend exponent: 0.55 Ground blend threshold: 0.25 (smoothstep range start) Cloud UV scale: 0.22 Cloud UV offset: (0.31, 0.17) Cloud noise threshold: 0.5 to 0.78 Cloud vertical fade: 0.02 to 0.22 Cloud opacity multiplier: 0.85 Cloud color mix threshold: 0.55 to 0.9 Sun glow exponents: 12 (weight 0.25), 220 (weight 0.6) Sun disk smoothstep: 0.99935 to 0.9997 Sun disk intensity multiplier: 18 Cloud masking factor for sun: 0.8 Steps: 1. Calculate normalized camera direction \mathbf{dir}. 2. Compute vertical component y = \mathbf{dir}.y. 3. Determine sun direction \mathbf{sunDir}. 4. Calculate horizon blend factor up = \max(y, 0). 5. Mix horizon and zenith colors: \mathbf{col} = \text{mix}(\text{color}(\text{HORIZON}), \text{color}(\text{ZENITH}), \text{pow}(up, 0.55)). 6. Blend with ground color based on negative y: \mathbf{col} = \text{mix}(\mathbf{col}, \text{color}(\text{GROUND}), \text{smoothstep}(0, 0.25, -y)). 7. Generate cloud layer by projecting direction onto a high plane. Calculate UVs: \mathbf{cuv} = (\mathbf{dir}.xz / (y + 0.12)) \times 0.22 + (0.31, 0.17). 8. Sample tiling noise texture n = \text{texture}(\text{cloudTexture}, \mathbf{cuv}).r. 9. Compute cloud opacity: \mathbf{cloud} = \text{smoothstep}(0.5, 0.78, n) \times \text{smoothstep}(0.02, 0.22, y) \times 0.85. 10. Compute cloud color based on noise: \mathbf{cloudCol} = \text{mix}((0.82, 0.86, 0.93), (1.15, 1.15, 1.15), \text{smoothstep}(0.55, 0.9, n)). 11. Blend cloud into sky: \mathbf{col} = \text{mix}(\mathbf{col}, \mathbf{cloudCol}, \mathbf{cloud}). 12. Render sun disk and glow. Calculate dot product s = \max(\mathbf{dir} \cdot \mathbf{sunDir}, 0). 13. Compute glow using power functions: \mathbf{glow} = \text{pow}(s, 12) \times 0.25 + \text{pow}(s, 220) \times 0.6. 14. Compute disk using smoothstep threshold: \mathbf{disk} = \text{smoothstep}(0.99935, 0.9997, s) \times (1 - \mathbf{cloud} \times 0.8) \times 18. 15. Add sun color to sky: \mathbf{col} = \mathbf{col} + \text{color}(\text{SUN\COLOR}) \times (\mathbf{glow} + \mathbf{disk}). Pitfalls: Sun disk must be masked by clouds to avoid rendering through them. Implemented by multiplying disk intensity by 1 - \mathbf{cloud} \times 0.8. Precision issues may arise near the horizon due to the y+0.12 term in cloud UV calculation; ensure y does not cause division by zero or extreme UV stretching. The sphere must be rendered with depth write disabled and behind all other geometry (render order -1000) to avoid z-fighting with foreground objects. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def renderskybox(dir: Vec3, sunDir: Vec3, cloudTexture: Texture2D) -> Vec3: # Constants HORIZONCOLOR = Vec3(0.5, 0.7, 0.9) ZENITHCOLOR = Vec3(0.1, 0.3, 0.6) GROUNDCOLOR = Vec3(0.4, 0.3, 0.2) SUNCOLOR = Vec3(1.0, 0.9, 0.7) # Step 1-3: Basic setup y = dir.y up = max(y, 0.0) # Step 4-5: Sky gradient col = mix(HORIZONCOLOR, ZENITHCOLOR, pow(up, 0.55)) # Step 6: Ground blend groundblend = smoothstep(0.0, 0.25, -y) col = mix(col, GROUNDCOLOR, groundblend) # Step 7-8: Cloud UVs and sampling # Avoid division by zero by adding small epsilon uvx = dir.x / (y + 0.12) 0.22 + 0.31 uvy = dir.z / (y + 0.12) 0.22 + 0.17 cuv = Vec2(uvx, uvy) # Sample noise texture (assuming normalized coordinates) n = cloudTexture.sample(cuv).r # Step 9: Cloud opacity cloudalpha = smoothstep(0.5, 0.78, n) smoothstep(0.02, 0.22, y) 0.85 # Step 10: Cloud color cloudcol = mix(Vec3(0.82, 0.86, 0.93), Vec3(1.15, 1.15, 1.15), smoothstep(0.55, 0.9, n)) # Step 11: Blend clouds col = mix(col, cloudcol, cloudalpha) # Step 12-15: Sun disk and glow s = max(dot(dir, sunDir), 0.0) # Glow glow = pow(s, 12.0) 0.25 + pow(s, 220.0) 0.6 # Disk with cloud masking disk = smoothstep(0.99935, 0.9997, s) (1.0 - cloudalpha 0.8) 18.0 # Add sun col = col + SUNCOLOR (glow + disk) return col Procedural background with sky gradient, sun glow, volumetric light shafts, and vignette. Kernel-based forward rendering approach. Time complexity: O(1) per fragment, independent of scene complexity. Memory complexity: O(1) for sphere geometry, plus texture memory for cloud noise. Performance: Fast, as it avoids complex ray marching or volumetric integration. Strengths: Simple to implement, visually appealing for stylized or low-poly scenes, no need for complex lighting calculations. Limitations: Lacks physical accuracy, no atmospheric scattering, limited detail compared to volumetric methods. When to use: Stylized games, low-end hardware, simple scenes. When not to use: Realistic simulations, complex atmospheric effects. Originated in early 3D graphics for efficient sky rendering. Popularized by voxel-based games and indie titles for its simplicity and visual appeal. Used in games like Voxel Wars for its lightweight nature and customizable appearance. sh1ftmaker/voxel-wars, https://github.com/sh1ftmaker/voxel-wars, fetched 2026-10-28 (unofficial)

name: Environment Rendering Setup
head: Daytime Lighting System, Sky and Fog Configuration
body: Configures the global lighting, atmospheric fog, and shadow parameters for a bright, saturated daytime look, typically targeting mobile-specific quality adjustments. It sets up the sky dome, directional sun, hemisphere light, and fog density, distinct from sibling methods like SkyboxRendering which use pre-rendered cubemaps, or Background Rendering which handles static backdrops without volumetric interaction. Inputs: Scene object, camera object, platform type (mobile/desktop), and optional anisotropy parameters for fog. Outputs: Configured scene with sky dome, lights, fog, and shadow settings. Data Structures: Color: 24-bit integer (0xRRGGBB) or RGB tuple. Vector3: Normalized direction vector (x, y, z). ShadowCamera: Defines frustum bounds [-H, H] for left/right/top/bottom, near plane n=1, far plane f=260. Fog: Linear or exponential height fog with near distance d{near} and far distance d{far}. Parameters: Zenith Color: 0x2a78e0. Horizon Color: 0xb6daf5. Ground Color: 0xb9cfdc. Sun Color: 0xfff2dc. Sun Direction: (0.36, 0.7, 0.6) normalized. Hemisphere Sky Color: 0xcfe4ff. Hemisphere Ground Color: 0x8d7a5c. Hemisphere Intensity: 1.35. Sun Intensity: 3.2. Shadow Map Size: 2048 \times 2048 (mobile), 4096 \times 4096 (desktop). Shadow Camera Half-Size H: 32 (mobile), 48 (desktop). Shadow Bias: -0.0004. Shadow Normal Bias: 0.04. Shadow Radius (Softness): 2. Tone Mapping: ACES Filmic. Exposure: 1.1. Pixel Ratio Cap: 1.25 (mobile), 1.5 (desktop). Steps: 1. Background: Set the scene background color to the Horizon Color (0xb6daf5). 2. Fog: Configure scene fog using the Horizon Color. Set near distance d{near} = 70 and far distance d{far} = 330. 3. Hemisphere Light: Create a hemisphere light with sky color 0xcfe4ff, ground color 0x8d7a5c, and intensity 1.35. Add to scene. 4. Sun Light: a. Create a directional light with color 0xfff2dc and intensity 3.2. b. Enable shadows. c. Set shadow map size based on platform: 2048^2 for mobile, 4096^2 for desktop. d. Configure shadow camera frustum: bounds [-H, H] for left/right/top/bottom, near 1, far 260, where H is 32 (mobile) or 48 (desktop). e. Set shadow bias parameters: bias -0.0004, normal bias 0.04, radius 2. f. Add sun light and its target to the scene. 5. Sky Dome: Create the sky dome using the sky() method (which interpolates between Zenith and Horizon colors based on ray vertical component, building on Sky Gradient). Add to scene. 6. Post-Processing: Apply ACES Filmic tone mapping with exposure 1.1. 7. Pixel Ratio: Cap pixel ratio to 1.25 (mobile) or 1.5 (desktop). Pitfalls: Shadow Camera Snapping: The shadow camera position must be snapped to whole shadow texels to prevent shadow edges from "crawling" or jittering as the camera moves. This is achieved by aligning the camera bounds to the shadow map grid. A configuration for controlling global fog density and color via Anisotropy and Radial blend parameters in the Environment Editor. It distinguishes between atmospheric fog (isotropic, low anisotropy) and sun radial scattering (anisotropic, high anisotropy). The Radial blend factor (range 0–1) blends these components: 0.0 shows atmosphere only, 1.0 shows radial only. Anisotropy controls the directionality of light scattering. Performance: Mobile targets 2048^2 shadow maps and lower pixel ratios (1.25) for real-time performance on constrained hardware. Desktop targets 4096^2 maps and higher ratios (1.5) for quality. Memory: Shadow map memory scales with resolution (2048^2 vs 4096^2). Strengths: Provides a consistent, bright daytime look with integrated volumetric fog and shadowing. Limitations: Specific to mobile/desktop presets; not a general-purpose lighting solver. Originated in the Voxel Wars project, an unofficial voxel-based game engine, providing a standardized daytime lighting setup. name: Arcball Camera

body: The Arcball Camera is a camera control technique that maps 2D screen coordinates to a 3D virtual sphere to compute rotation quaternions for smooth orbiting around a center point. It differs from First-Person Camera Control by decoupling rotation from the camera's local forward vector, instead rotating the view around a fixed center. It builds on Camera Matrix and Coordinate Transformation to apply the resulting rotation to the view matrix. Inputs: Mouse position (x, y) in screen/pixel coordinates. Viewport dimensions: width W, height H. Previous mouse position (x{prev}, y{prev}) and previous arcball state (rotation quaternion q{old}). Camera configuration: eye position \mathbf{e}, center point \mathbf{c}, up vector \mathbf{u}, zoom speed k{zoom}, minimum/maximum camera distance d{min}, d{max}. Outputs: Updated camera view matrix M{cam}. Updated rotation quaternion q{new}. Updated translation vector for zoom/pan. ArcballState rotation: Quaternion q (w, x, y, z), normalized. translation: 4x4 matrix T or vector \mathbf{t}, representing zoom/pan offset. centerTranslation: 4x4 matrix Tc, representing the translation to the orbit center. invCamera: 4x4 matrix, inverse of the current camera matrix. invScreen: Array [1/W, 1/H] used to normalize pixel coordinates. lastPosition: 2D vector (x{prev}, y{prev}). isRotating: Boolean flag. CameraConfig eye: 3D vector \mathbf{e}. center: 3D vector \mathbf{c}. up: 3D vector \mathbf{u} (typically [0, 1, 0]). zoomSpeed: Scalar k{zoom} (e.g., 0.1). minDist: Float d{min} (e.g., 1.25). maxDist: Float d{max} (e.g., 8.0). 1. Initialize Camera Basis: Compute the camera's local coordinate system. \mathbf{z}{axis} = \text{normalize}(\mathbf{c} - \mathbf{e}) \mathbf{x}{axis} = \text{normalize}(\text{cross}(\mathbf{z}{axis}, \mathbf{u})) \mathbf{y}{axis} = \text{normalize}(\text{cross}(\mathbf{x}{axis}, \mathbf{z}{axis})) Construct the rotation matrix R from these axes and convert to initial quaternion q. Store translation \mathbf{t} = \mathbf{e} - \mathbf{c}. 2. Normalize Mouse Coordinates: Convert screen pixel coordinates to normalized device coordinates in the range [-1, 1]. u = \text{clamp}\left( \frac{2x}{W} - 1, -1, 1 \right) v = \text{clamp}\left( 1 - \frac{2y}{H}, -1, 1 \right) The y-axis inversion accounts for top-left origin screen coordinates. 3. Project to Arcball Surface (Screen-to-Arcball): Map the 2D point (u, v) to a 3D point \mathbf{p} on the virtual trackball. Calculate squared distance from center: d^2 = u^2 + v^2. If d^2 \le 1.0: The point is inside the unit circle. Project onto the upper hemisphere of the sphere: pz = \sqrt{1.0 - d^2} \mathbf{p} = (u, v, pz) If d^2 > 1.0: The point is outside the unit circle. Normalize the XY components and set z = 0. \mathbf{p}{xy} = \text{normalize}((u, v)) pz = 0 \mathbf{p} = \mathbf{p}{xy} Some implementations use a spherical cap projection where z = \cos(\frac{\pi}{2} \min(d, 1)), or a hyperboloid fallback z = 1/\sqrt{u^2+v^2} for constant angular velocity. 4. Compute Rotation Delta: Let \mathbf{p}{prev} be the arcball point from the previous frame and \mathbf{p}{curr} be the current point. Compute the rotation axis \mathbf{a} and angle \theta between these two vectors. \mathbf{a} = \text{cross}(\mathbf{p}{prev}, \mathbf{p}{curr}) d = \text{dot}(\mathbf{p}{prev}, \mathbf{p}{curr}) Edge Case Handling: If d > 1 - \epsilon: Vectors are parallel. Return identity quaternion. If d < -1 + \epsilon: Vectors are anti-parallel. Find an orthogonal axis to \mathbf{p}{prev} by crossing with [1,0,0] or [0,1,0], normalize, and create a 180-degree quaternion. Else: Normalize \mathbf{a} and construct delta quaternion q{\Delta} = [1+d, \mathbf{a}], then normalize q{\Delta}. 5. Update Rotation Quaternion: q{new} = q{\Delta} \times q{old} Normalize q{new}. 6. Update Camera Matrix: Convert q{new} to rotation matrix R{quat}. The camera matrix M{cam} is constructed as: M{cam} = T{trans} \cdot R{quat} \cdot T{center}^{-1} Where T{center} translates the center \mathbf{c} to the origin, R{quat} applies the rotation, and T{trans} translates the eye back to its position relative to the center. 7. Handle Zoom and Pan: Zoom: Compute translation vector \mathbf{v}{zoom} = [0, 0, \text{amount} \cdot k{zoom}]. Update T{trans} and clamp the distance component to [d{min}, d{max}] to prevent passing through the center. Pan: Compute delta in screen space, transform to world space using M{cam}^{-1}, and update T{center} or the eye position relative to the center. Unverified code. return [0.0, 0.0, 0.0] return [v[0]/l, v[1]/l, v[2]/l] def dot(v1, v2): return v1[0]v2[0] + v1[1]v2[1] + v1[2]v2[2] def cross(v1, v2): return [ v1[1]v2[2] - v1[2]v2[1], v1[2]v2[0] - v1[0]v2[2], v1[0]v2[1] - v1[1]v2[0] ] def quatmul(q1, q2): w1, x1, y1, z1 = q1 w2, x2, y2, z2 = q2 return [ w1w2 - x1x2 - y1y2 - z1z2, w1x2 + x1w2 + y1z2 - z1y2, w1y2 - x1z2 + y1w2 + z1x2, w1z2 + x1y2 - y1x2 + z1w2 ] def quattomat4(q): w, x, y, z = q xx, yy, zz = xx, yy, zz xy, xz, yz = xy, xz, yz wx, wy, wz = wx, wy, wz return [ [1 - 2(yy + zz), 2(xy - wz), 2(xz + wy), 0], [2(xy + wz), 1 - 2(xx + zz), 2(yz height)) distsq = uu + vv if distsq <= 1.0: z = math.sqrt(1.0 - distsq) else: length = math.sqrt(distsq) u /= length v /= length z = 0.0 return [u, v, z] def rotationbetweenvectors(v1, v2): v1 = normalize(v1) v2 = normalize(v2) d = dot(v1, v2) if d > 1.0 - 1e-6: return [1.0, 0.0, 0.0, 0.0] if d < -1.0 + 1e-6: axis = cross(v1, [1.0, 0.0, 0.0]) if math.sqrt(axis[0]2 + axis[1]2 + axis[2]2) < 1e-6: axis = cross(v1, [0.0, 1.0, 0.0]) axis = normalize(axis) return [0.0, axis[0], axis[1], axis[2]] axis = cross(v1, v2) quat = [1.0 + d, axis[0], axis[1], axis[2]] l = math.sqrt(quat[0]2 + quat[1]2 + quat[2]2 + quat[3]2) return [quat[0]/l, quat[1]/l, quat[2]/l, quat[3]/l] def mat4mul(A, B): C = [[0.0]4 for in range(4)] for i in range(4): for j in range(4): for k in range(4): C[i][j] += A[i][k] B[k][j] return C class ArcballCamera: def init(self, eye, center, up, width, height): self.eye = eye self.center = center self.up = up self.width = width self.height = height zaxis = normalize([center[0]-eye[0], center[1]-eye[1], center[2]-eye[2]]) xaxis = normalize(cross(zaxis, up)) yaxis = normalize(cross(xaxis, zaxis)) self.rotation = [1.0, 0.0, 0.0, 0.0] self.translation = [eye[0]-center[0], eye[1]-center[1], eye[2]-center[2]] self.lastmouse = [0, 0] self.lastarcball = screentoarcball(0, 0, width, height) def updaterotation(self, x, y): currarcball = screentoarcball(x, y, self.width, self.height) deltaquat = rotationbetweenvectors(self.lastarcball, currarcball) self.rotation = quatmul(deltaquat, self.rotation) self.lastmouse = [x, y] self.lastarcball = currarcball def updatezoom(self, amount, zoomspeed, mindist, maxdist): zoomfactor = amount zoomspeed viewdir = normalize([self.center[0]-self.eye[0], self.center[1]-self.eye[1], self.center[2]-self.eye[2]]) neweye = [ self.eye[0] + viewdir[0] zoomfactor, self.eye[1] + viewdir[1] zoomfactor, self.eye[2] + viewdir[2] zoomfactor ] dist = math.sqrt((neweye[0]-self.center[0])2 + (neweye[1]-self.center[1])2 + (neweye[2]-self.center[2])2) if dist < mindist: scale = mindist / dist neweye = [self.center[0] + (neweye[0]-self.center[0])scale, self.center[1] + (neweye[1]-self.center[1])scale, self.center[2] + (neweye[2]-self.center[2])scale] elif dist > maxdist: scale = maxdist / dist neweye = [self.center[0] + (neweye[0]-self.center[0])scale, self.center[1] + (neweye[1]-self.center[1])scale, self.center[2] + (neweye[2]-self.center[2])scale] self.eye = neweye self.translation = [neweye[0]-self.center[0], neweye[1]-self.center[1], neweye[2]-self.center[2]] def getcameramatrix(self): R = quattomat4(self.rotation) T = [ [1, 0, 0, self.translation[0]], [0, 1, 0, self.translation[1]], [0, 0, 1, self.translation[2]], [0, 0, 0, 1] ] Tcinv = [ [1, 0, 0, -self.center[0]], [0, 1, 0, -self.center[1]], [0, 0, 1, -self.center[2]], [0, 0, 0, 1] ] return mat4mul(T, mat4mul(R, Tcinv)) width, height: Viewport dimensions in pixels. zoomSpeed: Scalar multiplier for zoom magnitude (e.g., 0.1). minDist, maxDist: Minimum and maximum camera distance from center (e.g., 1.25, 8.0). eye, center, up: Initial camera position, target, and up vector. Gimbal Lock: Avoided by using quaternions instead of Euler angles. Parallel/Anti-parallel Vectors: When the mouse moves such that the arcball vectors are parallel or anti-parallel, the cross product is zero. Handle by checking the dot product against thresholds (1-\epsilon, -1+\epsilon) and using a fallback orthogonal axis for 180-degree rotations. Boundary Clamping: Mouse coordinates must be clamped to [-1, 1] before projection to prevent artifacts at screen edges. Zoom Clamping: The camera distance must be clamped to prevent the eye from passing through the center point. Projection Boundary: For points outside the unit circle, the provided sources normalize the XY components and set z=0 in their code. Alternative projections use a spherical cap z = \cos(\frac{\pi}{2} \min(d, 1)) or a hyperboloid z = 1/\sqrt{u^2+v^2}. Time Complexity: O(1) per frame for rotation update. Memory Complexity: O(1) for state storage (quaternion, translation, matrices). Performance: Very fast, suitable for real-time interaction. Strengths: Intuitive control, no gimbal lock, smooth rotation. Limitations: Can be disorienting if the center point is not visible or if the rotation axis is not aligned with user expectations. When to use: Interactive volume exploration and medical imaging viewers. When not to use: When precise, axis-aligned rotation is required, or when the camera needs to follow a specific path. The Arcball Camera is implemented in various volume rendering and 3D visualization applications. It maps 2D mouse movements to a 3D sphere, allowing users to rotate the view as if interacting with a physical trackball. The method is used in web-based marching cubes renderers, Qt-based medical volume viewers, and WebGL raycasting implementations. name: First-Person Camera Control
head: Camera Control, Camera Controller, Camera State & GPU Data Packing, Input Handler, Mouse and Keyboard Input Controller
body: First-Person Camera Control manages the position, orientation (yaw/pitch), and projection parameters of a virtual camera, mapping user input (mouse/keyboard) to transformations for 3D rendering. It differs from spherical or arcball models by maintaining a fixed "up" vector and allowing free translation along the camera's local axes, which is essential for immersive exploration or precise volumetric inspection. It builds on Ray generation and camera models by providing the specific \mathbf{o} and \mathbf{d} generation logic for a perspective view. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: Mouse movement deltas (\Delta x, \Delta y), keyboard state (active keys), time delta (\Delta t), and initial camera state (position, yaw, pitch). Outputs: Updated camera position, orientation vectors (front, right, up), and a packed GPU buffer containing these parameters for ray generation shaders. Data Structures: The camera state is typically maintained in CPU memory for logic and packed into a GPU-friendly struct for rendering passes. CPU State (S3, unofficial): position: vec3 (x, y, z) front: vec3 (normalized direction vector) right: vec3 (normalized right vector) up: vec3 (normalized up vector) yaw: float (horizontal rotation, default \pi/2) pitch: float (vertical rotation, default 0.0) speed: float (movement speed) sensitivity: float (mouse sensitivity) zoom: float (field of view factor) aspectRatio: float nearPlane: float farPlane: float worldUp: vec3 (default (0, 1, 0)) GPU Struct (S1, unofficial): position: array<f32, 4> (xyz position, w unused or padding) rot: array<array<f32, 4>, 3> (3 rows of 4 floats, representing the rotation matrix columns or basis vectors) sinhalfvfov: f32 framecount: u32 width: f32 height: f32 prevposition: array<f32, 4> Parameters (Typical Values): Vertical Field of View (vfov): \pi/2 radians (90^\circ). Movement Speed: 1.0 units/sec. Mouse Sensitivity/Rotation Factor: 0.01 or 0.0025. Pan Factor: 1.0. Zoom Factor: 0.0025. Algorithm Steps: 1. Process Input: Read mouse deltas (\Delta x, \Delta y) and active keyboard keys. If mouse button is left and Control key is held, update lighting parameters (if applicable). If mouse button is left and Control is not held, update rotation: \Delta \text{yaw} = \Delta x \times \text{ROTATION\FACTOR} \Delta \text{pitch} = \Delta y \times \text{ROTATION\FACTOR} If mouse button is right, update pan (position offset): \Delta \text{pan}x = \Delta x \times \text{PAN\FACTOR} \Delta \text{pan}y = \Delta y \times \text{PAN\FACTOR} Store active keys on key-down; clear on key-up. 2. Update Orientation (Yaw/Pitch): Apply rotation deltas to yaw and pitch. Clamp pitch to [-\pi/2 + \epsilon, \pi/2 - \epsilon] to prevent gimbal lock or flipping. Recalculate basis vectors using the new angles: \text{front}x = \cos(\text{pitch}) \sin(\text{yaw}) \text{front}y = -\sin(\text{pitch}) \text{front}z = \cos(\text{pitch}) \cos(\text{yaw}) \text{front} = \text{normalize}(\text{front}) \text{right} = \text{normalize}(\text{cross}(\text{front}, \text{worldUp})) \text{up} = \text{cross}(\text{right}, \text{front}) Note: Some implementations compute vecx and vecy from vecz (front) using cross products with a fixed up vector. 3. Update Position: Determine movement direction based on active keys (WASD/Arrows). Calculate displacement vector \mathbf{v}: \mathbf{v} = (\text{forward} \times \text{front} + \text{right} \times \text{right} + \text{up} \times \text{up}) \times \text{speed} \times \Delta t Update position: \text{position} = \text{position} + \mathbf{v} Note: If pan mode is active (right mouse), apply \Delta \text{pan} to position directly or relative to view plane. 4. Pack GPU Data: Compute sinhalfvfov = sin(0.5 vfov). Construct the rotation matrix rows/columns from front, right, up. Fill CameraGpuData struct with position, rot, sinhalfvfov, framecount, width, height, and prevposition. Upload to GPU buffer (e.g., Uniform Buffer Object or Storage Buffer). Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math class FirstPersonCamera: def init(self, position=[0.0, 0.0, 0.0], yaw=math.pi / 2, pitch=0.0): self.position = list(position) self.yaw = yaw self.pitch = pitch self.worldup = [0.0, 1.0, 0.0] self.front = [0.0, 0.0, 0.0] self.right = [0.0, 0.0, 0.0] self.up = [0.0, 0.0, 0.0] self.speed = 1.0 self.sensitivity = 0.01 self.vfov = math.pi / 2 self.updatevectors() def updatevectors(self): # Calculate front vector x = math.cos(self.pitch) math.sin(self.yaw) y = -math.sin(self.pitch) z = math.cos(self.pitch) math.cos(self.yaw) self.front = self.normalize([x, y, z]) # Calculate right and up vectors self.right = self.normalize(self.cross(self.front, self.worldup)) self.up = self.normalize(self.cross(self.right, self.front)) def normalize(self, v): length = math.sqrt(v[0]2 + v[1]2 + v[2]2) if length == 0: return [0, 0, 0] return [v[0]/length, v[1]/length, v[2]/length] def cross(self, a, b): return [ a[1]b[2] - a[2]b[1], a[2]b[0] - a[0]b[2], a[0]b[1] - a[1]b[0] ] def processmouse(self, dx, dy): self.yaw += dx self.sensitivity self.pitch += dy self.sensitivity # Clamp pitch to avoid flipping if self.pitch > 89.0 math.pi / 180.0: self.pitch = 89.0 math.pi / 180.0 if self.pitch < -89.0 math.pi / 180.0: self.pitch = -89.0 math.pi / 180.0 self.updatevectors() def processkeyboard(self, direction, deltatime): velocity = self.speed deltatime if direction == 'FORWARD': self.position[0] += self.front[0] velocity self.position[1] += self.front[1] velocity self.position[2] += self.front[2] velocity elif direction == 'BACKWARD': self.position[0] -= self.front[0] velocity self.position[1] -= self.front[1] velocity self.position[2] -= self.front[2] velocity elif direction == 'RIGHT': self.position[0] += self.right[0] velocity self.position[1] += self.right[1] velocity self.position[2] += self.right[2] velocity elif direction == 'LEFT': self.position[0] -= self.right[0] velocity self.position[1] -= self.right[1] velocity self.position[2] -= self.right[2] velocity def getgpudata(self, width, height, framecount): sinhalfvfov = math.sin(self.vfov / 2.0) # Rotation matrix rows (or columns depending on shader expectation) # Here we pack basis vectors as rows for simplicity rot = [ self.front, # Row 0 self.right, # Row 1 self.up # Row 2 ] # Pad to 4 floats per row if required by struct rotpacked = [ self.front + [0.0], self.right + [0.0], self.up + [0.0] ] return { "position": self.position + [0.0], "rot": rotpacked, "sinhalfvfov": sinhalfvfov, "framecount": framecount, "width": float(width), "height": float(height), "prevposition": self.position + [0.0] # Update prev in actual loop } The Cinematic Camera Metaphor is a navigation technique for non-immersive 3D environments where user input manipulates the position and orientation of a virtual camera to control the viewpoint. It enables users to "tumble, track, and dolly" the view, allowing for precise framing of the scene. It is distinguished from direct manipulation metaphors (like Scene-in-Hand) by treating the camera as an independent entity controlled via standard input devices, often requiring modifier keys or specific gestures to invoke different camera motions. A programmatic interface for setting camera state, often used in scientific visualization toolkits (e.g., VTK.js). It handles synchronization between requested state and applied state, ensuring that changes are only applied if they differ from the last request. It supports setting position, focal point, view up, and zoom (parallel scale). A key pitfall is handling XR mode, where headset pose should override programmatic control, and ensuring that unchanged camera steps do not reset the view unexpectedly. Time Complexity: O(1) per frame for input processing and matrix updates. Memory Complexity: O(1) for camera state storage. Performance: Highly efficient; the primary cost is the CPU-to-GPU upload of the camera uniform buffer, which can be batched or updated only when state changes. Strengths: Intuitive for exploration; supports free movement and rotation; standard in FPS games and medical imaging viewers. Limitations: Prone to gimbal lock if not implemented with quaternions or careful clamping (though yaw/pitch avoids singularity at poles, it restricts full spherical rotation). Not suitable for orbiting around a specific point without additional logic (pan/trackball hybrid). When to use: Immersive navigation, medical volume inspection, FPS-style viewers. When not to use: When a fixed orbit around a center point is required (use Arcball) or when spherical sampling is needed (use Uniform Sphere Sampling). First-person camera control is a standard technique in computer graphics, originating from first-person shooter games and virtual reality applications. In the context of volume rendering, it allows users to navigate through volumetric datasets (e.g., medical CT/MRI scans) with intuitive controls. The specific implementation details (yaw/pitch decomposition, GPU struct packing) are common in modern WebGL and WebGPU-based volume renderers. newDINO/voxelraydemo, https://github.com/newDINO/voxelraydemo, fetched 2026-10-24 (unofficial) fraserlove/ossium, https://github.com/fraserlove/ossium, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial) Justinj68/OM3DPROJECT, https://github.com/Justinj68/OM3DPROJECT, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial) kevinkunkel98/reinforcement-learning-volume-rendering-transfer-function, https://github.com/kevinkunkel98/reinforcement-learning-volume-rendering-transfer-function, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial)

name: Cinematic Camera Metaphor
head: Eyeball-in-Hand Metaphor, Flying Vehicle Metaphor, StyleCam, Unicam, cinematic camera
body: The Cinematic Camera Metaphor is a navigation technique for non-immersive 3D environments where user input manipulates the position and orientation of a virtual camera to control the user's viewpoint. It enables users to tumble, track, and dolly the view for precise scene framing. It is distinguished from direct manipulation metaphors by treating the camera as an independent entity controlled via standard input devices, often requiring modifier keys or specific gestures to invoke different camera motions. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Mouse movements with modifier keys, or 6DoF input device position/orientation. Output: Updated virtual camera position and orientation applied to the rendering pipeline. Data Structures: CameraState: Holds position (vec3), orientation (quat or euler angles), and projectionparams (fov, aspect ratio). InputEvent: Holds deltaposition (vec2/vec3), buttonstate (bool), modifierkeys (bitmask), and device pose data. Steps: 1. Initialize: Set CameraState to an initial view. 2. Read Input: Capture InputEvent from mouse or 6DoF device. 3. Map Input to Motion: If using mouse + keys: Map specific key combinations to tumble (rotation), track (pan), or dolly (zoom) operations. If using 6DoF device: Map device position directly to camera position for Eyeball-in-Hand, or map input to spatial/angular velocity for Flying Vehicle. 4. Update Camera: Apply the calculated transformation to CameraState. 5. Render: Use updated CameraState to generate the view matrix for ray generation. Parameters: Mapping Mode: Absolute or Relative. Relative mapping requires a button press to activate movement. Gestures: Specific mouse movements or button sequences can invoke predefined camera paths or positions (e.g., StyleCam). Pitfalls: Relative Mapping Confusion: Using relative mapping for eyeball-in-hand navigation can destroy the user's mental model of a fixed, invisible scene, leading to confusion. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. KEYTUMBLE = 0x01 KEYTRACK = 0x02 KEYDOLLY = 0x04 def updatecinematiccamera(camera: dict, inputevent: dict) -> dict: """ Updates the camera state based on input using the Cinematic Camera Metaphor. camera: dict with 'position' (list[float]), 'orientation' (list[float]), 'projectionparams' (dict) inputevent: dict with 'devicetype' (str), 'deltaposition' (list[float]), 'buttonpressed' (bool), 'modifierkeys' (int), 'deviceposition' (list[float]), 'deviceorientation' (list[float]) """ if inputevent["devicetype"] == "MOUSE": if inputevent["modifierkeys"] & KEYTUMBLE: camera["orientation"][0] += inputevent["deltaposition"][0] camera["orientation"][1] += inputevent["deltaposition"][1] elif inputevent["modifierkeys"] & KEYTRACK: camera["position"][0] += inputevent["deltaposition"][0] camera["position"][1] += inputevent["deltaposition"][1] elif inputevent["modifierkeys"] & KEYDOLLY: camera["position"][2] += inputevent["deltaposition"][1] elif inputevent["devicetype"] == "6DOF": if inputevent.get("relativemode", False): if inputevent["buttonpressed"]: camera["position"] = [camera["position"][i] + inputevent["deltaposition"][i] for i in range(3)] camera["orientation"] = [camera["orientation"][i] + inputevent.get("deltaorientation", [0,0,0])[i] for i in range(3)] else: camera["position"] = inputevent["deviceposition"] camera["orientation"] = inputevent["deviceorientation"] return camera A variant where the input device's position is directly mapped to the virtual camera's position. It supports absolute mapping (continuous control) or relative mapping (movement only when a button is depressed). Absolute mapping is preferred to maintain the user's mental model of a fixed scene; relative mapping can cause confusion. Example: Chameleon display device. The scene is perceived from the position and orientation of a virtual vehicle. The input device controls the spatial and angular velocity of this vehicle, allowing it to move through the scene. Commonly used in 3D games where the "player position" is the vehicle. Enhancements include rapid and controlled movement techniques. The 3D world moves in correspondence with the 6DoF input device. Rotating the device clockwise rotates the scene clockwise. Large movements can be achieved by ratcheting using a button as a clutch. Useful for hierarchical scenes. An extension, "World-in-Miniature," involves manipulating a hand-held miniature copy of the virtual environment. Strengths: Intuitive for users familiar with standard 2D mouse interactions; allows for precise control over framing and composition (tumble, track, dolly). Limitations: Can be less applicable for immersive 3D environments compared to other navigation tasks; relative mapping can break spatial awareness. Usage: Implemented in Unicam (mouse + single button + gestures) and StyleCam (tailored camera positions/paths). The Cinematic Camera Metaphor was introduced in the context of non-immersive 3D environments, such as 3D graphics and animation programs. It is based on the concept of tumbling, tracking, and dollying a viewpoint, as described by Burtnyk et al.. Variations using 6DoF input devices were explored by Ware and Osborne. Specific implementations include Unicam by Zeleznik and Forsberg and StyleCam by Burtnyk et al.. The Eyeball-in-Hand and Scene-in-Hand metaphors were also discussed by Ware and Osborne, with the Chameleon device by Fitzmaurice and World-in-Miniature by Stoakley et al. serving as examples.
