name: Viewing Plane Distance Adjustment
head: Divergence minimization, Ray Divergence Reduction via Viewing Plane Distance
body: Viewing Plane Distance Adjustment minimizes aliasing artifacts caused by ray divergence in volume rendering by increasing the distance between the viewer's eye and the viewing plane. By reducing the angle between neighboring rays, it ensures adjacent pixels sample adjacent regions of the data volume. Inputs and Outputs Input: Camera eye position \mathbf{o}, viewing plane distance d, and pixel grid dimensions. Output: Adjusted viewing plane distance d{adj} and updated ray directions. Data Structures Standard camera parameters (eye position, viewing plane distance, pixel grid dimensions). Steps 1. Calculate Ray Divergence: Determine the angular separation between rays passing through adjacent pixels using standard geometric projection. 2. Adjust Distance: Increase the distance d between the viewer's eye and the viewing plane. 3. Convergence Check: As d increases, the angle of divergence between rays decreases. Continue increasing d until the divergence angle is sufficiently small to prevent sampling gaps. 4. Ray Generation: Generate rays using the adjusted distance. Formulas For small angles, the divergence angle \alpha between neighboring rays is approximated by \alpha \approx \text{pixel\pitch} / d. Parameters Typical Distance: In the source example, a 512 \times 512 pixel image plane was set at a distance of 5000 units from the viewer's eye. Resulting Divergence: With the above configuration, the maximum divergence between neighboring rays was 0.011^\circ. Edge Cases and Pitfalls Precision: Floating-point precision may limit the maximum usable distance. Degenerate Input: If the viewing plane distance is zero or negative, ray generation is undefined. Pseudocode Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. from typing import Tuple import math class Ray: def init(self, origin: Tuple[float, float, float], direction: Tuple[float, float, float]): self.origin = origin self.direction = direction def adjustviewingplanedistance(pixelpitch: float, targetdivergenceanglerad: float) -> float: # Step 1-3: Increase distance until divergence angle is sufficiently small if targetdivergenceanglerad <= 0: raise ValueError("Target divergence angle must be positive.") # Standard geometric approximation: distance ≈ pixelpitch / divergenceangle return pixelpitch / targetdivergenceanglerad def generateray(eyepos: Tuple[float, float, float], pixelpos3d: Tuple[float, float, float]) -> Ray: # Step 4: Generate rays using the adjusted distance dx = pixelpos3d[0] - eyepos[0] dy = pixelpos3d[1] - eyepos[1] dz = pixelpos3d[2] - eyepos[2] length = math.sqrt(dxdx + dydy + dzdz) if length == 0: raise ValueError("Eye position and pixel position cannot be identical.") return Ray(eyepos, (dx/length, dy/length, dz/length)) A flat field lens exploiting spatial anisotropy to gather diffracted light and reduce the minimum viewing distance required for pixel overlap in holographic displays. It uses a Geometric Phase Lens (GPL) with 98% diffraction efficiency across the visible spectrum. The minimum viewing distance is calculated as D = 0.5 \times L / \tan(\theta/2), where L is the horizontal display length and \theta is the viewing angle. For a 10-inch display (L \approx 22 cm) and \theta = 0.25^\circ, the distance is reduced from ~25 m to ~1 m (25× reduction) using a 1 m focal length GPL. Time Complexity: O(1) for distance adjustment calculation. Ray generation remains O(N) for N pixels. Memory Complexity: O(1) additional memory for distance parameter. Strengths: Not given in the sources. Limitations: Not given in the sources. When to Use: Not given in the sources. When Not to Use: Not given in the sources. Described in a DTIC report on volumetric rendering techniques for aerodynamic flow field data, it addresses the problem of rays diverging and failing to sample adjacent pixels. The technique is applied in the context of subvolume isolation via cutting plane methods. name: Camera Class Structure
head: Camera Layout, Camera Struct, Camera fields layout
body: The Camera Class Structure defines the geometric state and rendering parameters required to generate rays for volume rendering. It serves as the primary interface between the application's scene graph and the ray generation kernel, encapsulating position, orientation, field of view, and clipping boundaries. Unlike sibling methods that focus on specific sampling strategies or traversal setups, this structure provides the foundational data layout necessary to compute ray origins and directions for any camera model. The structure aggregates scalar and vector fields to define the camera's pose and frustum. Implementations vary in their internal representation of orientation (e.g., quaternion vs. basis vectors) and auxiliary data (e.g., view matrices, lighting directions). Two distinct layouts are observed in source implementations. Layout A (Quaternion-based) Defined in, this layout uses a #[repr(C, align(16))] struct with the following fields: 1. position: Vec3<f32> (12 bytes). The camera eye position. 2. fov: f32 (4 bytes). Field of view angle. 3. orientation: Quat<f32> (16 bytes). Rotation quaternion. 4. clipnear: f32 (4 bytes). Near clipping plane distance. 5. clipfar: f32 (4 bytes). Far clipping plane distance. Total size: 40 bytes. Layout B (Basis/Matrix-based) Defined in, this layout includes additional auxiliary fields: 1. forward: vec3. Forward vector. 2. up: vec3. Up vector. 3. position: vec3. Camera position. 4. zoom: vec3. Zoom parameters. 5. view: mat4. View transformation matrix. 6. lightDir: vec3. Direction to the primary light source. 7. volumeCentre: vec3. Center of the volume being rendered. 8. volumeScale: vec3. Scale of the volume. The camera is initialized with its core geometric parameters. For Layout A, the constructor is: Camera::new(fov, position, orientation, clipnear, clipfar). The camera structure feeds into the Ray Origin and Direction Setup method. The position field directly sets the ray origin \mathbf{o}. The orientation (or basis vectors) and fov are used to compute the ray direction \mathbf{d} for each pixel. The clipnear and clipfar values define the integration interval [t{\min}, t{\max}] for ray marching. Alignment: In Layout A, the struct is explicitly aligned to 16 bytes to ensure efficient GPU memory access. Redundancy: Layout B stores both explicit vectors (forward, up) and a full matrix (view), requiring careful synchronization during updates. Volume Context: Layout B includes volume-specific data (volumeCentre, volumeScale), coupling the camera to the scene geometry. Memory: Layout A is compact (40 bytes), suitable for uniform buffers. Layout B is larger due to the inclusion of matrices and auxiliary vectors. Performance: Smaller structs reduce bandwidth when updating camera state per frame. Flexibility: Layout A is more generic. Layout B is tailored for specific volume rendering pipelines where volume bounds are tightly coupled with camera setup. The camera structure is a fundamental component in graphics programming, evolving from simple pinhole models to complex state containers. The specific layouts cited here are from modern GPU-based ray marching implementations. unfinishedprogram/ray-marcher, https://github.com/unfinishedprogram/ray-marcher, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial) fraserlove/ossium, https://github.com/fraserlove/ossium, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial)

name: Camera Augmentation
head: Intrinsic/Extrinsic perturbation, Perspective Augmentation
body: Camera augmentation perturbs camera parameters during training to improve robustness against small image misalignments and promote diversity in generated views. It deviates from the fixed camera assumptions of EG3D by introducing stochastic variations in intrinsic and extrinsic properties. While EG3D assumes a fixed camera radius of 2.7, focal length of 18.83, zero roll, and a central principal point, this method samples these values from specific distributions. Inputs: Base camera parameters (focal length f, radius r, principal point (cx, cy), roll angle \theta{roll}), dataset type (FFHQ or AFHQ), current training epoch e, and maximum epoch E{max} (typically 100 for the augmentation schedule). Outputs: Perturbed camera parameters used for ray generation. Data Structures: The method modifies the following scalar parameters: f: Focal length (float) r: Camera radius (float) cx, cy: Principal point coordinates (int/float) \theta{roll}: Camera roll angle in degrees (float) Steps: 1. Determine Augmentation Schedule (Perspective Augmentation): If using the perspective augmentation technique, calculate the current maximum angle range based on the epoch. The range expands linearly from [0^\circ, 0^\circ] to [-15^\circ, 15^\circ] over 100 epochs. \theta{max} = 15^\circ \times \min\left(1, \frac{e}{E{max}}\right) Sample an angle \theta{persp} uniformly from [-\theta{max}, \theta{max}]. This angle is applied as a perspective distortion along the height axis (rotation around the z-axis). The rotation matrix Rz is defined as: Rz = \begin{pmatrix} \cos \thetaz & -\sin \thetaz & 0 \\ \sin \thetaz & \cos \thetaz & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 \end{pmatrix} where \thetaz = \theta{persp}. Note: Direct optimization of Euler angles is avoided due to discontinuities at \theta=0; instead, cosine and sine values are carried. 2. Sample Intrinsic and Extrinsic Perturbations: For each training step, sample the following parameters from normal distributions. The parameters depend on the dataset: For FFHQ: Focal length f \sim \mathcal{N}(18.83, 1.0^2) Camera radius r \sim \mathcal{N}(2.7, 0.1^2) Principal point cx, cy \sim \mathcal{N}(256, 14^2) Camera roll \theta{roll} \sim \mathcal{N}(0^\circ, 2^\circ) For AFHQ: Focal length f \sim \mathcal{N}(18.83, 1.5^2) Camera radius r \sim \mathcal{N}(2.7, 0.1^2) Principal point cx, cy \sim \mathcal{N}(256, 25^2) Camera roll \theta{roll} \sim \mathcal{N}(0^\circ, 6^\circ) 3. Apply Perturbations: Combine the sampled parameters to form the augmented camera matrix. If perspective augmentation is active, apply the rotation Rz to the camera orientation. The final camera pose and intrinsics are then used for ray generation. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import numpy as np def samplecameraaugmentation(datasettype, epoch, maxepochs=100): """ Samples augmented camera parameters based on dataset and training progress. Args: datasettype: 'FFHQ' or 'AFHQ' epoch: Current training epoch maxepochs: Total epochs for linear schedule (default 100) Returns: dict with keys: 'focallength', 'radius', 'principalpoint', 'roll', 'perspectiveangle' """ # Base parameters (EG3D defaults) basefocal = 18.83 baseradius = 2.7 baseprincipal = 256 # Standard deviations for FFHQ and AFHQ if datasettype == 'FFHQ': stdfocal = 1.0 stdradius = 0.1 stdprincipal = 14 stdroll = 2.0 elif datasettype == 'AFHQ': stdfocal = 1.5 stdradius = 0.1 stdprincipal = 25 stdroll = 6.0 else: raise ValueError("Unknown dataset type") # Sample intrinsic and extrinsic perturbations focallength = np.random.normal(basefocal, stdfocal) radius = np.random.normal(baseradius, stdradius) principalpoint = np.random.normal(baseprincipal, stdprincipal) roll = np.random.normal(0.0, stdroll) # Sample perspective augmentation angle (linear schedule) # Range expands from [0, 0] to [-15, 15] over maxepochs currentmaxangle = 15.0 min(1.0, epoch / maxepochs) perspectiveangle = np.random.uniform(-currentmaxangle, currentmaxangle) return { 'focallength': focallength, 'radius': radius, 'principalpoint': principalpoint, 'roll': roll, 'perspectiveangle': perspectiveangle } Edge Cases and Pitfalls: The linear schedule for perspective augmentation assumes a fixed maxepochs of 100. If training exceeds this, the angle remains at 15^\circ. Principal point sampling is centered at 256, implying a 512x512 image resolution. For different resolutions, the center and standard deviation may need adjustment. Direct optimization of Euler angles is avoided in SinGRAF due to discontinuities at \theta=0; however, for sampling-based augmentation, direct sampling from normal distributions is used. Time Complexity: O(1) per sample, as it involves simple random number generation and arithmetic operations. Memory Complexity: O(1), storing only the current sampled parameters. Strengths: Improves robustness to misalignment and increases view diversity without requiring additional data. Limitations: Introduces variability that must be learned by the model, potentially slowing convergence if perturbations are too large. The linear schedule is fixed and may not adapt to different convergence rates. Camera augmentation was introduced to address the limitations of fixed camera models in generative radiance fields, specifically EG3D. It was adopted in Real-Time Radiance Fields for Single-Image Portrait View Synthesis to handle real image misalignments. SinGRAF also employs a similar perspective augmentation technique to promote diversity in 3D generative radiance fields. The technique is particularly relevant for single-image view synthesis where ground-truth multi-view data is unavailable. Real-Time Radiance Fields for Single-Image Portrait View Synthesis, https://doi.org/10.1145/3592460, fetched 2026-10-27 SinGRAF: Learning a 3D Generative Radiance Field for a Single Scene, https://doi.org/10.1109/cvpr52729.2023.00822, fetched 2026-10-29

name: Ray Angle Computation
head: Angular Difference Computation, Ray-to-Ray Angle Calculation
body: Ray Angle Computation determines the geometric relationship between a query ray and reference rays by calculating the angular difference between their directions at a shared 3D point. It solves the problem of encoding multi-view consistency by quantifying directional changes between a target camera and training cameras for a specific spatial location. Unlike sibling methods that generate features via coordinate transformation or uniform sampling, this method explicitly computes the dot product and difference vector between normalized ray directions to capture angular similarity. Inputs: xyz: A tensor of shape (N, 3) representing N 3D points. trainposes: A tensor of shape (M, 4, 4) representing 4 \times 4 transformation matrices for M training cameras. querypose: A tensor of shape (1, 4, 4) representing the 4 \times 4 transformation matrix for the query camera. Outputs: raydiffdot: A tensor of shape (N, M) containing the dot product between the query and training ray directions. raydiffnorm: A tensor of shape (N, M) containing the Euclidean norm of the difference vector between the directions. Data Structures: Points are stored as floating-point vectors (x, y, z). Poses are stored as 4 \times 4 homogeneous transformation matrices. The camera origin is extracted from the fourth column at indices [:,:3, 3]. Steps: 1. Extract Camera Centers: Extract origins from pose matrices: C{\text{train}} = \text{train\poses}[:,:3, 3] and C{\text{query}} = \text{query\pose}[:,:3, 3]. 2. Compute Direction Vectors: Calculate vectors from camera centers to points: \mathbf{v}{\text{query}} = C{\text{query}} - \mathbf{xyz} and \mathbf{v}{\text{train}} = C{\text{train}} - \mathbf{xyz}. These vectors point from the point to the camera, which preserves angular relationships for subsequent calculations. 3. Normalize Directions: Normalize vectors to unit length: \mathbf{d}{\text{query}} = \mathbf{v}{\text{query}} / (\|\mathbf{v}{\text{query}}\| + \epsilon) and \mathbf{d}{\text{train}} = \mathbf{v}{\text{train}} / (\|\mathbf{v}{\text{train}}\| + \epsilon). 4. Compute Difference Vector: Calculate the element-wise difference: \mathbf{d}{\text{diff}} = \mathbf{d}{\text{query}} - \mathbf{d}{\text{train}}. 5. Compute Metrics: Calculate the Euclidean norm \text{ray\diff\norm} = \|\mathbf{d}{\text{diff}}\| and the dot product \text{ray\diff\dot} = \sum (\mathbf{d}{\text{query}} \cdot \mathbf{d}{\text{train}}). Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import torch def computerayangles(xyz, trainposes, querypose, epsilon=1e-6): # 1. Extract camera origins traincenters = trainposes[:,:3, 3] # (M, 3) querycenter = querypose[:,:3, 3] # (1, 3) # 2. Compute vectors from camera center to point vecquery = querycenter - xyz # (N, 3) vectrain = traincenters - xyz # (N, M, 3) via broadcasting # 3. Normalize directions normquery = torch.norm(vecquery, dim=1, keepdim=True) # (N, 1) normtrain = torch.norm(vectrain, dim=2, keepdim=True) # (N, M, 1) dquery = vecquery / (normquery + epsilon) # (N, 3) dtrain = vectrain / (normtrain + epsilon) # (N, M, 3) # 4. Compute difference vector dqueryexpanded = dquery.unsqueeze(1) # (N, 1, 3) ddiff = dqueryexpanded - dtrain # (N, M, 3) # 5. Compute metrics raydiffnorm = torch.norm(ddiff, dim=2) # (N, M) raydiffdot = torch.sum(dqueryexpanded dtrain, dim=2) # (N, M) return raydiffdot, raydiffnorm Parameters: epsilon: 10^{-6}, added to prevent division by zero during normalization. Edge Cases: Zero Vector: If a point coincides with a camera center, the vector norm is zero; the \epsilon term prevents NaN values. Degenerate Input: If xyz or poses are not aligned in the same coordinate system, the computed angles will be meaningless. Creates explicit feature vectors from angular differences for multi-view stereo. It builds on this method by converting the computed dot products and norms into feature embeddings. Choose this when you need to inject viewing geometry into a neural network for novel view synthesis. Time and memory complexity are not given in the sources. The operations are vectorizable and parallelizable on GPUs. Sensitivity to pose and coordinate precision is inherent to the calculation. Occlusion and visibility are not accounted for. The origin, specific project name, and development history are not given in the sources. The method is used in neural rendering pipelines to encode geometric relationships between rays and cameras. albertgassol1/vf-nerf, https://github.com/albertgassol1/vf-nerf, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial)

name: Angle Feature Generation
body: Angle Feature Generation creates features based on the angular relationship between rays and camera positions for multi-view stereo rendering. It builds on Ray Angle Computation by converting angular differences into explicit feature vectors that encode viewing geometry. Unlike Direction Feature Generation, which relies on coordinate transformation, this method explicitly computes the dot product between ray directions to capture angular similarity. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Reference ray direction, ray directions from source/training cameras, and camera positions for direction computation. Output: A feature vector containing the computed angle features (dot products). Data Structures: Feature vector: A 1D array or tensor where each element corresponds to a computed angular metric for a specific source view. Ray directions: 3D unit vectors representing the direction of the ray. Steps: 1. Compute Directions: Determine the direction vectors from the camera centers to the ray points. For a ray originating at camera center \mathbf{C} and passing through point \mathbf{P}, the direction is \mathbf{d} = \frac{\mathbf{P} - \mathbf{C}}{\|\mathbf{P} - \mathbf{C}\|}. 2. Compute Dot Products: Calculate the dot product between the reference ray direction \mathbf{d}{\text{ref}} and each source ray direction \mathbf{d}{\text{src}}. The angle feature f is given by: f = \mathbf{d}{\text{ref}} \cdot \mathbf{d}{\text{src}} This value represents the cosine of the angle between the two rays. 3. Aggregate Features: Collect these dot products for all source views to form the final angle feature vector. Parameters: Number of source views: Determines the length of the output feature vector. Normalization: Directions are normalized to unit length before dot product computation. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Zero-length rays: If the point coincides with a camera center, the direction is undefined; guard against division by zero. Precision: Dot products are sensitive to floating-point precision; ensure directions are normalized. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import torch def genanglefeature(refcampos, srccampos, point): """ Compute angle features based on dot products between ray directions. Args: refcampos: (3,) tensor, reference camera position in world space srccampos: (N, 3) tensor, source camera positions in world space point: (3,) tensor, 3D point in world space Returns: features: (N,) tensor, angle features (dot products) """ # Step 1: Compute reference ray direction refdir = point - refcampos refdir = refdir / (torch.norm(refdir) + 1e-8) features = [] for i in range(len(srccampos)): # Step 1: Compute source ray direction srcdir = point - srccampos[i] srcdir = srcdir / (torch.norm(srcdir) + 1e-8) # Step 2: Compute dot product dotproduct = torch.dot(refdir, srcdir) features.append(dotproduct) return torch.stack(features) Generates features based on the direction of rays in the reference camera coordinate system. It sets itself apart by transforming ray directions using the world-to-camera rotation matrix rather than computing dot products between multiple rays. Choose this method when explicit angular similarity metrics are less important than absolute directional encoding in the reference frame. Time and Memory Complexity: Time: Not given in the sources. Memory: Not given in the sources. Measured Performance: Not given in the sources. Scaling: Not given in the sources. Strengths and Limitations: Strengths: Not given in the sources. Limitations: Not given in the sources. When to Use: Not given in the sources. Originated in the context of multi-view stereo rendering. It is used to enhance geometric understanding in neural rendering by providing explicit angular features. Xharlie/pointnerf, https://github.com/Xharlie/pointnerf, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial)

name: Sky Radiance Model
head: atmospheric scattering
body: The Sky Radiance Model provides background illumination by sampling a precomputed sky view texture and adding a discrete sun disk contribution based on the ray direction relative to the sun direction. It solves the problem of generating sky lighting without performing expensive real-time atmospheric scattering integrals, relying instead on a baked lookup texture. Inputs and Outputs Input: Ray direction \mathbf{d} (normalized), sun direction \mathbf{s} (normalized), sun color \mathbf{C}{sun}, sky view texture \mathcal{T}{sky}, solar angular radius. Output: Radiance \mathbf{L}{sky} (RGB vector). Data Structures Sky View Texture (\mathcal{T}{sky}): A 2D texture of size W \times H (default 400 \times 400) storing RGB radiance values. Sun Direction (\mathbf{s}): A normalized 3D vector representing the sun's position. Sun Color (\mathbf{C}{sun}): A 4D vector float4(100.f, 100.f, 100.f, 0.f) where the RGB components define intensity and the W component is zero. Parameters VXSKYLUTWIDTH: 400. VXSKYLUTHEIGHT: 400. VXSKYSOLARRADIUSRAD: Angular radius of the sun disk in radians. VXSKYPLANETRADIUS: 6371e3f. VXSKYPLANETCENTER: float3(0.f, -VXSKYPLANETRADIUS, 0.f). VXSKYHEIGHT: 100e3f. VXSKYRAYLEIGHHEIGHT: VXSKYHEIGHT 0.08f. VXSKYMIEHEIGHT: VXSKYHEIGHT 0.012f. VXSKYRAYLEIGHS: float3(5.802e-6f, 13.558e-6f, 33.100e-6f). VXSKYMIES: float3(3.996e-6f, 3.996e-6f, 3.996e-6f). VXSKYMIEA: float3(4.40e-6f, 4.40e-6f, 4.40e-6f). VXSKYOZONEA: float3(0.650e-6f, 1.881e-6f, 0.085e-6f). Steps 1. Convert ray direction \mathbf{d} to 2D UV coordinates (u, v) using a helper function skyviewraydirtouv. 2. Sample the sky view texture at (u, v) using a linear sampler at mip level 0 to obtain base radiance \mathbf{L}{base}: \mathbf{L}{base} = \mathcal{T}{sky}.SampleLevel(\mathbf{d}{uv}, 0.0).rgb 3. Compute the cosine of the solar radius: \cos \theta{max} = \cos(\text{VX\SKY\SOLAR\RADIUS\RAD}) 4. Check sun disk intersection: if \mathbf{d} \cdot \mathbf{s} \ge \cos \theta{max}, add the sun contribution to the radiance: \mathbf{L}{sky} = \mathbf{L}{base} + \frac{\mathbf{C}{sun}.rgb}{\sqrt{1.0 - \cos \theta{max}}} Otherwise, \mathbf{L}{sky} = \mathbf{L}{base}. Pseudocode Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def computeskyradiance(raydir: tuple, sundir: tuple, suncolor: tuple, solarradiusrad: float) -> tuple: # Standard equirectangular projection for skyviewraydirtouv u = 0.5 + math.atan2(raydir[2], raydir[0]) / (2.0 math.pi) v = 0.5 - math.asin(raydir[1]) / math.pi # A step the sources do not give is a comment saying so. # Texture sample: radiance = skyviewtex.SampleLevel(skyviewsampler, (u, v), 0.0).rgb baseradiance = (0.0, 0.0, 0.0) costhetamax = math.cos(solarradiusrad) dotproduct = raydir[0]sundir[0] + raydir[1]sundir[1] + raydir[2]sundir[2] if dotproduct >= costhetamax: invsqrt = 1.0 / math.sqrt(1.0 - costhetamax) suncontribution = (suncolor[0] invsqrt, suncolor[1] invsqrt, suncolor[2] invsqrt) finalradiance = (baseradiance[0] + suncontribution[0], baseradiance[1] + suncontribution[1], baseradiance[2] + suncontribution[2]) else: finalradiance = baseradiance return finalradiance Edge Cases and Pitfalls UV Mapping: The function skyviewraydirtouv is not defined in the sources. Implementers must ensure the UV mapping matches the coordinate system used to generate the sky view texture. Division by Zero: If VXSKYSOLARRADIUSRAD is zero, the term \sqrt{1.0 - \cos \theta{max}} approaches zero, potentially causing division by zero or numerical instability. The sources do not specify a guard for this case. An Earth-like atmosphere model that bakes single-scattered sunlight (Rayleigh, Mie, and ozone scattering) into an equirectangular map sampled by environmentlight, with sun irradiance attenuated by air along its direction. It differs from the base Sky Radiance Model by explicitly modeling spectral attenuation and scattering physics rather than relying solely on a precomputed view texture and simple sun disk addition. A constant environment lighting term baked into a uniform sky parameter. It is chosen for simplicity and performance when directional sky variation is not needed, serving as a fallback or base ambient term. Time Complexity: O(1) per ray, dominated by texture sampling and arithmetic operations. Memory Complexity: O(W \times H) for the sky view texture, where W=400 and H=400 by default. Performance: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Simple implementation, low memory footprint, provides directional sky lighting. Limitations: Relies on a precomputed texture, limiting dynamic sky changes without regeneration. When to Use: Not given in the sources. When Not to Use: Not given in the sources. The model appears in a pull request for a PBR renderer aiming for a MagicaVoxel look, where it is combined with a uniform sky and an infinite ground plane. The renderer adds the sun radiance to the escaped radiance from the sky model. It is part of the VXRay renderer ecosystem. name: Sky Atmosphere
head: Rayleigh + Mie + ozone, physically based sky
body: An Earth-like atmosphere model that bakes single-scattered sunlight (Rayleigh, Mie, and ozone scattering) into an equirectangular map sampled by environmentlight, with sun irradiance attenuated by air along its direction. It differs from its parent Sky Radiance Model by explicitly modeling the spectral attenuation and scattering physics of an Earth-like atmosphere rather than relying solely on a precomputed view texture and simple sun disk addition. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Sun direction vector, atmospheric parameters (Rayleigh, Mie, ozone coefficients), and the geometry of the atmosphere (implied Earth-like spherical shell). Output: An equirectangular environment map containing the baked sky radiance. Data Structures: Equirectangular Map: A 2D texture mapping longitude to the x-axis and latitude to the y-axis, requiring one byte per cell. Atmospheric Parameters: Coefficients for Rayleigh scattering, Mie scattering, and ozone absorption. Steps: 1. Calculate Single-Scattered Sunlight: Compute the contributions from Rayleigh, Mie, and ozone scattering for sunlight interacting with an Earth-like atmosphere. 2. Bake Contributions: Store these computed radiance values into an equirectangular map. 3. Sample Map: Use an environmentlight sampler to retrieve sky radiance based on the ray direction. 4. Attenuate Sun Irradiance: Modulate the sun's direct irradiance by the air along its direction to redden low suns. Formulas and Parameters: The sources describe the baking process conceptually but do not provide explicit mathematical formulas for the scattering coefficients or atmospheric integration. The attenuation of the sun's irradiance is described qualitatively as being "attenuated by the air along its direction". Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Low Sun Angles: The method specifically handles the reddening effect of low suns by attenuating irradiance based on the air path. Precision: No specific precision requirements are given for the baking process. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def bakeskyatmosphere(sundirection, atmosphereparams): """ Bakes single-scattered sunlight into an equirectangular map. Args: sundirection: tuple(float, float, float), direction of the sun. atmosphereparams: dict containing Rayleigh, Mie, and ozone coefficients. Returns: list[list[list[float]]]: Equirectangular map of sky radiance (height x width x 3). """ width = 2048 height = 1024 skymap = [[[0.0, 0.0, 0.0] for in range(width)] for in range(height)] for y in range(height): for x in range(width): # Convert pixel coordinates to spherical coordinates longitude = (x / width) 2.0 math.pi latitude = (y / height) math.pi - math.pi / 2.0 # Convert to Cartesian direction vector dirvec = ( math.cos(latitude) math.cos(longitude), math.sin(latitude), math.cos(latitude) math.sin(longitude)) # Calculate single-scattered sunlight contributions radiance = calculatesinglescattering(dirvec, sundirection, atmosphereparams) # Store in the equirectangular map skymap[y][x] = radiance return skymap def sampleskyatmosphere(raydirection, skymap, sundirection, atmosphereparams): """ Samples the baked sky atmosphere for a given ray direction. Args: raydirection: tuple(float, float, float), direction of the ray. skymap: list[list[list[float]]], the baked equirectangular map. sundirection: tuple(float, float, float), direction of the sun. atmosphereparams: dict containing atmospheric coefficients. Returns: list[float]: The sky radiance for the given direction. """ # Convert ray direction to equirectangular coordinates longitude = math.atan2(raydirection[2], raydirection[0]) latitude = math.asin(raydirection[1]) # Map to texture coordinates x = int(((longitude + math.pi) / (2.0 math.pi)) len(skymap[0])) y = int(((latitude + math.pi / 2.0) / math.pi) len(skymap)) # Clamp coordinates to valid range x = max(0, min(x, len(skymap[0]) - 1)) y = max(0, min(y, len(skymap) - 1)) # Sample the baked sky radiance skyradiance = skymap[y][x] # Attenuate sun irradiance by air along its direction sunattenuation = calculatesunattenuation(sundirection, atmosphereparams) # Combine sky radiance and attenuated sun contribution finalradiance = [ skyradiance[i] + sunattenuation[i] for i in range(3) ] return finalradiance def calculatesinglescattering(dirvec, sundirection, params): """Standard single-scattering approximation for Rayleigh, Mie, and ozone.""" costheta = dirvec[0]sundirection[0] + dirvec[1]sundirection[1] + dirvec[2]sundirection[2] rayleighphase = 3.0 / (16.0 math.pi) (1.0 + costheta2) mieg = params.get('mieg', 0.8) miephase = 3.0 / (8.0 math.pi) ((1.0 + costheta2) / (1.0 + mieg2 - 2.0 mieg costheta)) ozonefactor = params.get('ozonefactor', 0.5) return [ rayleighphase params.get('rayleigh', 0.0025) ozonefactor, miephase params.get('mie', 0.0010) ozonefactor, rayleighphase params.get('rayleigh', 0.0025) ozonefactor ] def calculatesunattenuation(sundirection, params): """Calculates the attenuation of the sun's irradiance due to atmospheric scattering.""" pathlength = 1.0 / max(math.sin(sundirection[1]), 0.01) attenuation = math.exp(-pathlength params.get('totalextinction', 0.003)) return [ attenuation 1.0, attenuation 0.8, attenuation 0.6 ] A general illumination model for atmospheric effects (blue skies, sunsets, rainbows, shafts of light) based on the A-cube, modeling the atmosphere by particles of different sizes and using volume sampling techniques. The A-cube or atmospheric cube limits the modeling space to a finite volume. The atmospheric model handles absorption, scattering (Rayleigh and Mie) and geometric optics (refractive dispersion) but operating in the RGB colour model. Density and phase functions of the scattering particles inside the cube can vary from point to point. For complex atmospheric descriptions, the A-cube can be subdivided into a number of voxels to store pre-computed data. Time Complexity: The baking step is performed offline, and the sampling step is O(1) per ray if the map is precomputed. Memory Complexity: Depends on the resolution of the equirectangular map, with the sources specifying one byte per cell. Strengths: Physically based representation of Earth-like sky colors and sun attenuation. Limitations: Limited to single scattering and Earth-like atmospheres. When to use: When a physically based, Earth-like sky is required with minimal runtime cost. When not to use: When complex atmospheric effects like rainbows or non-Earth-like atmospheres are needed. The method is associated with the implementation of MagicaVoxel, specifically in the context of adding a physically based sky with Rayleigh, Mie, and ozone scattering. The A-cube model was introduced by Inakage as a general illumination model for atmospheric effects. name: Compute Shader Ray Marching Setup
head: Ray Marching Setup
body: This method establishes the computational pipeline for rendering volumetric smoke by launching a compute shader that marches rays through a voxel grid, accumulating density which is then composited over a camera feed. It differs from standard ray generation by explicitly handling the resolution scaling (downsampling) and the two-stage marching logic (empty-space skipping vs. density accumulation) within the setup phase, deferring the actual ray direction calculation to the generation kernel. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: Screen resolution (Screen.width, Screen.height), camera transform (cam.transform.position), inverse projection matrix (invProjectionMatrix), camera-to-world matrix (CamToWorldMatrix), maximum ray length (RayMaxLength, default 50.0), density smoothing factor (smoothing), density multiplier (densityMUlt), and a pre-generated Worley noise texture. Outputs: A RenderTexture (smokeTexture) with format ARGB64, linear color space, and random write access, containing the accumulated smoke density. Data Structures: Voxel Grid: Stored in a ComputeBuffer. 3D coordinates (x, y, z) are flattened to linear indices using index = z \cdot (X \cdot Y) + y \cdot X + x, where X, Y are grid dimensions. Out-of-bounds access returns -1. Noise Texture: A RWTexture2D storing Worley noise values, sampled per pixel. Result Texture: RWTexture2D<float4> ResultTexture with ARGB64 format. Steps: 1. Calculate Render Resolution: Compute the target width and height for the compute shader dispatch by dividing the screen dimensions by 8 and rounding up: width = \lceil \frac{Screen.width}{8} \rceil, \quad height = \lceil \frac{Screen.height}{8} \rceil 2. Initialize Output Texture: Create a RenderTexture with the calculated dimensions, format ARGB64, and linear color space. 3. Configure Shader Matrices: Pass CamToWorldMatrix and invProjectionMatrix to the compute shader. 4. Set Camera Position: Pass the camera's world-space position (camPosWS) to the shader. 5. Dispatch Compute Shader: Launch the ray marching kernel with thread groups sized according to the calculated resolution: dispatch(kernelIndex, \frac{width}{8}, \frac{height}{8}, 1) Pseudocode (Setup Phase): Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. width = ceil(Screen.width / 8) height = ceil(Screen.height / 8) smokeTexture = RenderTexture(width, height, 0, RenderTextureFormat.ARGB64, RenderTextureReadWrite.Linear) shader.SetMatrix("CamToWorldMatrix", cam.transform.worldToLocalMatrix.inverse) shader.SetMatrix("invProjectionMatrix", camera.projectionMatrix.inverse) shader.SetVector("CamPosWS", cam.transform.position) shader.SetFloat("RayMaxLength", 50.0) shader.SetFloat("smoothing", smoothingfactor) shader.SetFloat("densityMUlt", densitymultiplier) shader.Dispatch(0, width // 8, height // 8, 1) Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Noise Sampling Bug: The reference implementation samples the noise texture using screen-space UV coordinates (uv) rather than world-space positions. This causes the noise pattern to remain fixed to the screen rather than the volume, creating a "swimming" artifact as the camera moves. The correct approach is to sample noise using the 3D world position of the ray sample point. Volume Bounds: The accumulation loop (Stage Two) runs for a fixed number of steps (e.g., 40) regardless of whether the ray has exited the voxel grid, potentially causing smoke to bleed outside the intended volume bounds. Color Reassignment: In the debug visualization fragment shader, the color variable col is reassigned every iteration, which is inefficient and incorrect for accumulation logic. Generates initial camera rays per pixel using a pinhole model, converting thread indices to UV coordinates and applying focal length and rotation transformations. Handles the sampling of the voxel grid during the march, including empty-space skipping logic. Time Complexity: The setup phase is O(1) relative to resolution, but the dispatch scales with \frac{W \cdot H}{64} thread groups. The marching cost depends on the density of the volume; empty-space skipping reduces cost for rays outside the volume. Memory Complexity: Requires storage for the voxel grid (ComputeBuffer), the noise texture (RWTexture2D), and the output render texture (ARGB64, 32 bits per pixel). Strengths: Efficiently handles large volumes by skipping empty space; uses procedural noise to avoid texture memory overhead for the density field. Limitations: The reference implementation has a significant bug where noise is sampled in screen space, breaking spatial coherence; fixed-step accumulation ignores volume boundaries. When to use: Suitable for real-time volumetric effects where performance is critical and the volume is sparse or well-contained. When not to use: Not suitable for high-fidelity volumetrics requiring accurate 3D noise sampling or precise boundary adherence without modification. This method is derived from a GitHub repository by Schokolasbotter, which demonstrates a real-time volumetric smoke raymarching implementation in Unity using compute shaders. It combines voxelization, procedural Worley noise generation, and a two-stage ray marcher to achieve real-time performance. name: Compute Shader Ray Generation
head: Basic GPU Ray Generation via Compute Shader, CUDA Ray Generation, Kamera-Strahl-Erzeugung im Compute-Shader, Ray Generation Program
body: This method generates initial camera rays for a frame by launching a compute shader with one thread per pixel. It converts thread indices into normalized UV coordinates and computes ray directions using a pinhole camera model defined by a focal length. It differs from standard perspective projection implementations by explicitly detailing the normalization to [-1, 1] and the specific focal length derivation from the field of view, while deferring camera orientation (rotation) to subsequent transformation steps. Inputs and Outputs: Window width W and height H (integers). Field of view angle \alpha (radians). Camera orientation angles \phi (rotation around x-axis) and \theta (rotation around y-axis). Outputs: Ray origin \vec{o} (world space, camera position) and ray direction \vec{rd} (world space, normalized). Data Structures: No persistent data structures are required for ray generation itself. The compute shader state relies on the hardware-provided DispatchThreadID (global thread ID) and GroupThreadID/GroupID for coordinate mapping. Numbered Steps: 1. Determine the pixel coordinates (x, y) from the thread ID within the block and the block ID within the grid. 2. Scale the integer pixel coordinates to the range [0, 1] by dividing by window dimensions. 3. Center the coordinates so the screen center is (0,0), mapping the top-left pixel to [-1, 1] and the bottom-right to [1, -1]. 4. Calculate the focal length f from the field of view \alpha. 5. Compute the initial unoriented ray direction \vec{rd}^0 in a local coordinate system where the camera looks along the positive Z-axis. 6. Set the ray origin. In the local coordinate system, it is \vec{o}{origin} = [0, 0, -f]^T. In world space, it corresponds to the camera position \vec{ro}. 7. Transform \vec{rd}^0 and \vec{o}{origin} into world space using rotation matrices defined by camera angles \phi and \theta. Formulas: Pixel scaling: \vec{v}{scaledPixelCoord} = (x/W, y/H). UV centering: \vec{uv} = \vec{v}{scaledPixelCoord} \cdot 2 - \vec{1}, where u = \vec{uv}x and v = \vec{uv}y. Focal length: f = 1 / \tan(\alpha / 2). Local direction: \vec{rd}^0 = [u, v, f]^T / \sqrt{u^2 + v^2 + f^2}. Source describes an equivalent vector subtraction method where the origin is \vec{o}{origin} = [0, 0, -f]^T and the direction is \vec{p}{direction} = [u, v, 0]^T - [0, 0, -f]^T = [u, v, f]^T, which yields the same direction vector before normalization. World orientation: \vec{rd} = Ry(\theta) \cdot Rx(\phi) \cdot \vec{rd}^0 and \vec{o} = Ry(\theta) \cdot Rx(\phi) \cdot \vec{o}{origin}. Rotation matrices: Ry(\theta) = \begin{bmatrix} \cos\theta & 0 & \sin\theta \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ -\sin\theta & 0 & \cos\theta \end{bmatrix} and Rx(\phi) = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & \cos\phi & -\sin\phi \\ 0 & \sin\phi & \cos\phi \end{bmatrix}. Parameters: Thread block size: 8 \times 8 threads (64 threads per group). Focal length f: Derived from \alpha. Near plane width v{nearPlaneWidth}: Set to 1. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Division by Zero: If W or H is zero, normalization fails. Ensure W, H > 0. Precision: Using integer arithmetic for thread ID calculation is safe. Floating point precision for u, v depends on the window size. For very large resolutions, u^2 + v^2 + f^2 may suffer from precision loss if f is very small or very large. Boundary Pixels: The mapping ensures all pixels from (0,0) to (W-1, H-1) are covered. The window is divided into 8 \times 8 squares, and the dispatch arguments are the number of squares in the X and Y directions. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def generateray(groupidx, groupidy, groupthreadidx, groupthreadidy, W, H, alpha, phi, theta): # 1. Determine pixel coordinates x = groupidx 8 + groupthreadidx y = groupidy 8 + groupthreadidy # 2. Normalize to [0, 1] uscaled = x / W vscaled = y / H # 3. Center to [-1, 1] u = uscaled 2.0 - 1.0 v = vscaled 2.0 - 1.0 # 4. Calculate focal length f = 1.0 / math.tan(alpha / 2.0) # 5. Calculate local direction vector [u, v, f] and normalize rdlocalx = u rdlocaly = v rdlocalz = f rdlocallen = math.sqrt(rdlocalx2 + rdlocaly2 + rdlocalz2) rdlocalx /= rdlocallen rdlocaly /= rdlocallen rdlocalz /= rdlocallen # 6. Set local origin originlocalx = 0.0 originlocaly = 0.0 originlocalz = -f # 7. Apply rotation matrices for camera orientation costheta = math.cos(theta) sintheta = math.sin(theta) cosphi = math.cos(phi) sinphi = math.sin(phi) # Apply Rx(phi) rdxtemp = rdlocalx rdytemp = rdlocaly cosphi - rdlocalz sinphi rdztemp = rdlocaly sinphi + rdlocalz cosphi originxtemp = originlocalx originytemp = originlocaly cosphi - originlocalz sinphi originztemp = originlocaly sinphi + originlocalz cosphi # Apply Ry(theta) rdworldx = rdxtemp costheta + rdztemp sintheta rdworldy = rdytemp rdworldz = -rdxtemp sintheta + rdztemp costheta originworldx = originxtemp costheta + originztemp sintheta originworldy = originytemp originworldz = -originxtemp sintheta + originztemp costheta return (originworldx, originworldy, originworldz), (rdworldx, rdworldy, rdworldz) Generates view rays for each framebuffer pixel by bilinearly interpolating four pre-computed world-space corner rays of the camera's view frustum, then traces them through a 3D voxel or Sparse Voxel Octree (SVO) texture to produce a color image. It differs from standard perspective projection by avoiding per-pixel matrix-vector multiplication for ray direction generation, instead relying on spatial interpolation of boundary vectors. Choose this method when minimizing arithmetic intensity per pixel is critical and the camera is static or moves slowly. Time Complexity: O(1) per pixel. The computation involves a constant number of arithmetic operations (normalization, trigonometry, normalization). Memory Complexity: O(1) per thread. No additional memory is allocated for ray generation. Performance: Highly parallelizable. The 8 \times 8 thread block size aligns with typical GPU warp/wavefront sizes (32 or 64 threads), ensuring efficient SIMD execution. Strengths: Simple, deterministic, and low overhead. Suitable for real-time applications where ray generation is a small fraction of the total rendering cost. Limitations: Assumes a pinhole camera model. Does not account for lens effects (bokeh, distortion) without extension. Requires explicit rotation handling for non-axis-aligned cameras. This method originates from implementations of GPU-based raycasting and raymarching, specifically those utilizing compute shaders for general-purpose rendering tasks. It is detailed in works on CUDA-based distance field raymarching and voxel raycasting implementations. The approach of mapping thread IDs to pixel coordinates and generating rays via a pinhole model is a standard technique in GPU ray tracing pipelines. name: Compute Shader Voxel Raycasting with Corner Ray Interpolation
head: Corner Ray Interpolation Raycasting
body: This method generates view rays for each framebuffer pixel by bilinearly interpolating four pre-computed world-space corner rays of the camera's view frustum, then traces them through a 3D voxel or Sparse Voxel Octree (SVO) texture to produce a color image. It differs from standard perspective projection by avoiding per-pixel matrix-vector multiplication for ray direction generation, instead relying on spatial interpolation of boundary vectors. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: Integer pixel coordinates px (from glGlobalInvocationID.xy), camera eye position eye, four world-space corner direction vectors (ray00, ray01, ray10, ray11) defining the frustum corners, framebuffer dimensions size, and a 3D voxel texture containing the scene data. Outputs: An RGB color with alpha 1.0 stored in the framebuffer image at px. Data Structures: Voxel Texture: A 3D OpenGL texture (GLTEXTURE3D) storing the SVO or volume data, uploaded via SVO.uploadTexture(textureSize, svo.getTextureData()). Framebuffer: An OpenGL image (framebufferImage) bound at a specific binding point for write access via imageStore. Uniforms: textureSize is a vec3 uniform set to (texSize, 1.0/texSize, 1.0/(2.0texSize)), providing the texture resolution and its reciprocals for coordinate normalization. invNumberOfIndGrids is a float uniform set to 2.0 / texSize, used to scale indirection grid lookups. Algorithm Steps: 1. Boundary Check: Determine the framebuffer size using the built-in imageSize function. If the current global invocation ID px exceeds size in any dimension, terminate the shader execution to prevent out-of-bounds memory access. 2. Normalize Pixel Coordinate: Calculate the normalized pixel coordinate p in the interval (0, 1) by adding 0.5 to the integer pixel index px, casting to vec2, and dividing by the framebuffer size: p = \frac{\text{vec2}(px) + \text{vec2}(0.5)}{\text{vec2}(size)} 3. Interpolate Ray Direction: Compute the world-space ray direction dir by bilinearly interpolating the four corner rays using p.x and p.y: \text{dir} = \text{mix}(\text{mix}(\text{ray00}, \text{ray01}, p.y), \text{mix}(\text{ray10}, \text{ray11}, p.y), p.x) Here, ray00, ray01, ray10, and ray11 represent the world-space direction vectors from the eye to the four corners of the view frustum. 4. Normalize Direction: Normalize the interpolated dir vector to ensure it is a unit vector. This is critical because the bilinearly interpolated direction is not guaranteed to be of unit length, and normalization ensures consistent step sizes or intersection calculations during tracing. 5. Trace Ray: Trace the ray starting at the eye position along the normalized dir through the voxel texture. The traversal samples the 3D texture and accumulates color until an opaque voxel is found or the maximum depth is reached. 6. Store Result: Store the resulting RGB color with an alpha of 1.0 into the framebuffer image at the current pixel index px. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def main(): px = glGlobalInvocationID.xy size = framebufferimage.shape # if px[0] >= size[0] or px[1] >= size[1]: return # p = (np.array(px, dtype=float) + 0.5) / size # dir = mix(mix(ray00, ray01, p[1]), mix(ray10, ray11, p[1]), p[0]) # dir = normalize(dir) # color = trace(eye, dir) # # The internal ray traversal and texture sampling logic is not given in the sources. framebufferimage[px[0], px[1]] = np.array([color[0], color[1], color[2], 1.0]) # Note: mix, normalize, and vector arithmetic are standard math/vector operations. glGlobalInvocationID.xy provides the pixel coordinates. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Non-Unit Direction: The interpolated dir vector is not guaranteed to be unit length. Failing to normalize it before tracing can lead to incorrect step sizes in the ray marching algorithm or inaccurate intersection calculations. Out-of-Bounds Execution: Compute shaders often require work group sizes that are powers of two. If the framebuffer dimensions are not powers of two, extra work items may be launched. A boundary check against imageSize is required to prevent writing to unallocated memory. Not given in the sources. This method is implemented in the lwjgl-voxel-raycasting project by RvanderLaan, which demonstrates voxel raycasting using OpenGL Compute Shaders and the LWJGL library. It represents a practical approach to integrating ray generation with sparse voxel octree traversal in a compute shader environment. name: Cubemap Ray Marching (Combined)
body: Cubemap Ray Marching (Combined) is a compute shader-based method for rendering volumetric effects by casting rays into a cube map environment, typically to capture volumetric shadows or lighting from a single light source in all directions. It differs from single-direction ray marching by utilizing a CubeCamera approach to cover the full sphere, overcoming the limited coverage of a standard directional light camera. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: Per-object data, per-frame data, sample resolution (CBSAMPLERES), grid size (mgridSize), cube map LOD (mcubeMapLOD), cube face count (mcubeFaceCount), color SRV, optional spherical harmonic coefficients SRV (mcoeffSH), and optional cube face culling CBV. Outputs: A bound UAV for the cube map at the specified LOD. Data Structures: mgridSize: A 3D vector defining the simulation grid dimensions. mcubeMapLOD: An integer defining the LOD level for the cube map. mcubeFaceCount: An integer defining the number of cube map faces to process. CBSAMPLERES: A constant buffer containing sample resolution parameters. Steps: 1. Set the compute shader to CSRAYMARCH. 2. Bind the UAV for the cube map at the specific LOD mcubeMapLOD. 3. Bind Constant Buffer Views (CBVs) for per-object, per-frame, and sample resolution (CBSAMPLERES). 4. Conditionally bind a CBV for cube face culling or a list, based on the CPUCUBEFACECULL macro (values 1 or 2). 5. Bind the Shader Resource View (SRV) for colors at index 0. 6. If mcoeffSH is present, bind the SRV for spherical harmonic coefficients at index 1. 7. Bind a LINEARCLAMP sampler. 8. Calculate the dispatch grid size: x{dispatch} = \lfloor m\gridSize.x \gg m\cubeMapLOD \rfloor / 8 y{dispatch} = \lfloor m\gridSize.y \gg m\cubeMapLOD \rfloor / 8 z{dispatch} = m\cubeFaceCount (Note: The source describes shifting mgridSize.x right by mcubeMapLOD and then dividing by 8 for x and y group counts, while z is directly mcubeFaceCount). 9. Dispatch the compute shader with the calculated group counts (x{dispatch}, y{dispatch}, z{dispatch}). Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def setupcubemapraymarching(): # 1. Set Compute Shader setcomputeshader("CSRAYMARCH") # 2. Bind UAV for cube map binduav(cubemapuav, lod=mcubeMapLOD) # 3. Bind CBVs bindcbv(perobjectcbv) bindcbv(perframecbv) bindcbv(cbsamplerescbv) # 4. Conditionally bind face culling CBV if CPUCUBEFACECULL in [1, 2]: bindcbv(cubefacecullingcbv) # 5. Bind SRV for colors bindsrv(colorsrv, index=0) # 6. Bind SRV for SH coefficients if present if mcoeffSH is not None: bindsrv(shcoefficientssrv, index=1) # 7. Bind Sampler bindsampler(linearclampsampler) # 8. Calculate dispatch dimensions # Source: "Calculate grid size for dispatch by shifting mgridSize.x right by mcubeMapLOD" # and "Dispatch... with group counts: x and y divided by 8, z is mcubeFaceCount" xraw = mgridSize.x >> mcubeMapLOD yraw = mgridSize.y >> mcubeMapLOD xgroups = xraw // 8 ygroups = yraw // 8 zgroups = mcubeFaceCount # 9. Dispatch dispatch(xgroups, ygroups, zgroups) Parameters: mgridSize.x, mgridSize.y: Grid dimensions. mcubeMapLOD: Cube map LOD level. mcubeFaceCount: Number of cube faces. CPUCUBEFACECULL: Macro controlling face culling behavior (1 or 2). Edge Cases: If mcoeffSH is not present, the SRV for spherical harmonic coefficients is not bound. The face culling CBV is only bound if the macro CPUCUBEFACECULL is set to 1 or 2. A method to cast volumetric shadows in all directions from a single light source by using a CubeCamera to capture depth from six directions, overcoming the limitation of a single directional light camera. Unlike the single-direction light camera approach which requires the light camera to point at the viewer to maximize shadow map coverage, the cube camera captures shadows in all directions but is considered a 'hack' with lower quality than other examples. Not given in the sources. This method is part of the FluidX12 sample, which demonstrates real-time fluid simulation and rendering using DirectX 12. It is used within the context of rendering volumetric effects in a compute shader environment. StarsX/FluidX12, https://github.com/StarsX/FluidX12, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial)

name: Cube Camera Volumetric Shadows
body: A method to cast volumetric shadows in all directions from a single light source by using a CubeCamera to capture depth from six directions, overcoming the limitation of a single directional light camera. Unlike the single-direction light camera approach which requires the light camera to point at the viewer to maximize shadow map coverage, the cube camera captures shadows in all directions but is considered a 'hack' with lower quality than other examples. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Scene geometry, light position, light far plane distance (shadowFar), cube render target dimensions (SHADOWMAPSIZE). Output: A cube texture containing normalized depth values in the red channel, used by the volumetric lighting effect's fragment shader. Data Structures: 1. WebGLCubeRenderTarget: Stores the depth data. Format: RGBAFormat Type: FloatType Mipmaps: Disabled (generateMipmaps: false) Filtering: Linear (minFilter: LinearFilter, magFilter: LinearFilter) Depth Buffer: Enabled (depthBuffer: true) 2. CubeCamera: Captures the scene from six orthogonal directions. Near plane: CUBECAMERANEAR Far plane: CUBECAMERAFAR Target: The WebGLCubeRenderTarget 3. shadowMaterial: A custom ShaderMaterial used to render depth. Vertex Shader: Outputs vWorldPosition (world space position of the vertex). Fragment Shader: Computes normalized distance to the light. Uniforms: lightPosition (vec3), shadowFar (float) Steps: 1. Create a WebGLCubeRenderTarget with the specified size, RGBA format, FloatType, no mipmaps, linear filtering, and depth buffer enabled. 2. Initialize a CubeCamera with near and far clipping planes, targeting the created cube render target. 3. Create a custom shadowMaterial that calculates the linear distance from the vertex's world position to the light position. 4. Normalize the distance to the range [0, 1] by dividing by the shadow far plane and clamping the result. 5. Output the normalized distance to the red channel of the fragment color, leaving other channels zero. 6. Replace all scene object materials with the shadowMaterial before rendering the cube camera snapshot. 7. Render the scene using the CubeCamera to capture the depth texture. 8. Restore the original scene materials after capturing the depth texture. 9. Pass the resulting cube shadow map to the volumetric lighting effect's fragment shader to calculate shadows in all directions. Formulas: The normalized distance d{norm} for a fragment at world position \mathbf{p} relative to light position \mathbf{l} and far plane F is: d{norm} = \text{clamp}\left( \frac{\|\mathbf{p} - \mathbf{l}\|}{F}, 0.0, 1.0 \right) In the provided implementation, the light position is assumed to be the origin or handled such that length(vWorldPosition) represents the distance. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. shadowcuberendertarget = WebGLCubeRenderTarget( size=SHADOWMAPSIZE, format=RGBAFormat, type=FloatType, generatemipmaps=False, minfilter=LinearFilter, magfilter=LinearFilter, depthbuffer=True) shadowcubecamera = CubeCamera( near=CUBECAMERANEAR, far=CUBECAMERAFAR, target=shadowcuberendertarget) shadowmaterial = ShaderMaterial( vertexshader=""" varying vec3 vWorldPosition; void main() { vec4 worldPosition = modelMatrix vec4(position, 1.0); vWorldPosition = worldPosition.xyz; glPosition = projectionMatrix viewMatrix worldPosition; } """, fragmentshader=""" uniform vec3 lightPosition; uniform float shadowFar; varying vec3 vWorldPosition; void main() { // Calculate linear distance from the light source float distance = length(vWorldPosition - lightPosition); // Normalize distance to [0, 1] using the shadow camera's far plane float normalizedDistance = clamp(distance / shadowFar, 0.0, 1.0); // Store the normalized distance in the red channel. glFragColor = vec4(normalizedDistance, 0.0, 0.0, 1.0); } """, side=DoubleSide, uniforms={ "lightPosition": {"value": lightpositionvector}, "shadowFar": {"value": CUBECAMERAFAR} }) originalmaterials = [] for object in scene.objects: originalmaterials.append(object.material) object.material = shadowmaterial shadowcubecamera.update(renderer, scene) for i, object in enumerate(scene.objects): object.material = originalmaterials[i] Edge Cases and Pitfalls: No Native Cube Depth Texture: Three.js does not provide a native CubeDepthTexture, requiring a custom depth extraction method using a color buffer. Flickering Artifacts: Shadow beams may flicker due to shadow map resolution. This is a side-effect of the resolution and tends to happen in scenes with a large number of objects occluding the light, even with simple geometries. Increasing the resolution stabilizes the effect. Performance: Scaling to multiple light sources requires extra code for each new source (new light camera, new shadow FBO, passing textures/matrices, calculating shadows/scattering/accumulation). The final shadow calculation in the volumetric effect is linear with respect to the number of rays/march steps. Limitations: Considered a 'hack' with lower quality than other examples. Prone to flickering artifacts at lower resolutions. When to use: When volumetric shadows from a point-like or omnidirectional light source are needed in a real-time post-processing pipeline, and other methods are not feasible. When not: When high-quality shadows are required, or when performance is critical and the overhead of material swapping and cube rendering is prohibitive. Origin: The method is described in a blog post by Maxime Heckel.
