name: Rigid Parametric Alignment
head: Closed-form Rigid Alignment, Horn's Method, Horn's Method for Trajectory Alignment, Rigid Alignment via SVD
body: Rigid Parametric Alignment computes the optimal 3D rigid transformation T \in SE(3) that aligns a set of model points to a set of data points by minimizing the sum of squared Euclidean distances between corresponding landmarks. It solves the absolute orientation problem in a single closed-form step using Singular Value Decomposition (SVD), distinguishing it from iterative methods like ICP or optimization-based approaches that require gradient descent. Unlike Homography Parametric Alignment, which estimates a 2D projective transformation for planar distortions, this method operates in 3D Euclidean space to preserve metric distances and angles. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Two sets of N corresponding 3D points: model points X = \{x1, \dots, xN\} and data points Y = \{y1, \dots, yN\}. Each set is represented as a 3 \times N matrix where columns are points. Output: A rotation matrix R \in SO(3) and a translation vector t \in \mathbb{R}^3, forming the transformation T = [R|t]. Data Structures: Points are stored as 3D vectors. In implementation, they are often packed into 3 \times N matrices for batched linear algebra operations. Steps: 1. Centroid Calculation: Compute the centroid (mean) of the model points \bar{x} and the data points \bar{y}: \bar{x} = \frac{1}{N} \sum{i=1}^{N} xi, \quad \bar{y} = \frac{1}{N} \sum{i=1}^{N} yi 2. Centering: Subtract the centroids from the respective points to obtain zero-centered coordinates: x'i = xi - \bar{x}, \quad y'i = yi - \bar{y} 3. Covariance Matrix: Compute the 3 \times 3 covariance matrix H (also denoted as W in some implementations) between the centered points: H = \sum{i=1}^{N} x'i (y'i)^T (Note: Source defines H as \sum (xj - \bar{x})(Tj yj - T\bar{x})^T in the context of general registration, but for standard rigid alignment where T is the unknown, the cross-covariance of centered points is the standard derivation. Source computes W as sum of outer products of centered columns.) 4. SVD: Perform Singular Value Decomposition on H: H = U S V^T where U and V are orthogonal matrices and S is a diagonal matrix of singular values. 5. Rotation Correction: Initialize a correction matrix D as the identity matrix I3. To ensure a proper rotation (determinant +1) and avoid reflection: If \det(U V^T) < 0, set the last element of D to -1 (i.e., D = \text{diag}(1, 1, -1)). This handles the case where the SVD yields a reflection. Specifically, if \det(U) \cdot \det(V) < 0, flip the sign of the smallest singular value's corresponding axis in the rotation calculation. 6. Rotation Calculation: Compute the optimal rotation matrix: R = V D U^T (Source states R = V U^T, assuming no reflection or implicit handling. Source explicitly includes the sign flip logic.) 7. Translation Calculation: Compute the optimal translation vector: t = \bar{y} - R \bar{x} 8. Transformation Construction: The final rigid transformation is: T = \begin{bmatrix} R & t \\ 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix} \in SE(3) Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import numpy as np def rigidparametricalignment(modelpoints, datapoints): """ Aligns modelpoints to datapoints using closed-form SVD. Args: modelpoints: np.ndarray of shape (N, 3) datapoints: np.ndarray of shape (N, 3) Returns: R: np.ndarray of shape (3, 3), rotation matrix t: np.ndarray of shape (3,), translation vector """ # 1. Centroids meanmodel = np.mean(modelpoints, axis=0) meandata = np.mean(datapoints, axis=0) # 2. Centering modelcentered = modelpoints - meanmodel datacentered = datapoints - meandata # 3. Covariance Matrix H # H = sum(x'i y'i^T) H = np.dot(modelcentered.T, datacentered) # 4. SVD U, S, Vt = np.linalg.svd(H) # 5. Rotation Correction # Check for reflection detUVt = np.linalg.det(np.dot(U, Vt)) if detUVt < 0: # Flip the sign of the last column of V (or last row of Vt) # Corresponds to flipping the sign of the smallest singular value's axis Vt[-1,:] = -1 # 6. Rotation R = np.dot(Vt.T, U.T) # 7. Translation t = meandata - np.dot(R, meanmodel) return R, t Parameters: Landmark Count: Minimum 4 non-coplanar points are required for a unique solution in 3D. More points improve robustness to noise. Hidden Units (Contextual): In specific neural field implementations (e.g., L2G-NeRF), the rigid alignment is parameterized by a ReLU MLP with six 256-dimensional hidden units. This is a specific architectural choice for differentiable alignment, not a general parameter of the SVD method itself. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Reflection: If the point sets have different handedness, the SVD may yield a rotation with determinant -1. The correction step (flipping the sign of the last singular value's axis) is critical to enforce R \in SO(3). Degenerate Configurations: If all points are collinear or coplanar, the covariance matrix H is rank-deficient, leading to ambiguous rotation solutions. At least 4 non-coplanar points are required. Precision: Floating-point errors in SVD can occasionally result in R not being perfectly orthogonal. Re-orthogonalization (e.g., via SVD of R) may be needed for strict numerical stability. Estimates a 2D projective transformation T \in SL(3) from point correspondences by solving a homogeneous linear least squares problem via SVD. It is employed in camera-in-the-loop optimization to map captured camera coordinates to Spatial Light Modulator (SLM) pattern coordinates, ensuring the captured wavefront and SLM pattern reside in the same coordinate system. Unlike Rigid Parametric Alignment, which estimates a 3D rigid transformation in SE(3), this method operates in 2D homogeneous space to handle planar or perspective distortions between the sensor and the display plane. A registration algorithm used to align two point sets, typically a reconstructed point cloud and a ground truth mesh, by finding an optimal rigid transformation. It builds on Rigid Parametric Alignment by iteratively refining the transformation estimate through correspondence matching, rather than solving for a transformation from pre-established correspondences in a single step. Unlike differentiable renderers which optimize pose via gradient descent on pixel errors, ICP operates directly in geometric space. An incremental registration method that estimates the initial extrinsic parameters (camera pose) for unposed target images relative to a registered reference image using a learned scene regressor. It solves the problem of initializing camera poses in neural radiance field training by converting predicted 3D points into 2D-3D correspondences and solving for the pose via Perspective-n-Point (PnP). It differs from ICP by relying on a neural scene representation to provide dense 3D structure rather than iterative point-to-point alignment, and from Structure-from-Motion (SfM) by operating incrementally on a learned regressor rather than globally on feature matches. An automatic registration tool that aligns source and destination objects by finding a transformation that minimizes the error between corresponding landmarks. It requires identifying at least four corresponding landmarks in both the source and destination objects and computes the transformation using the least-square approximation method based on these landmarks. The more landmarks specified, the better the fit. Time Complexity: O(N) for centroid and covariance calculation, and O(1) for the fixed-size 3 \times 3 SVD. Thus, the overall complexity is linear in the number of points N. Memory Complexity: O(N) to store the point sets and O(1) for the covariance matrix. Performance: Provides an exact closed-form solution, making it extremely fast and deterministic compared to iterative methods like ICP. Strengths: No initialization required; robust to moderate noise; computationally efficient. Limitations: Requires known correspondences between points; sensitive to outliers in the point sets (minimizes squared error, so outliers have large influence); fails if points are degenerate (collinear/coplanar). When to Use: When correspondences are known and the transformation is strictly rigid (no scaling or shear). When Not to Use: When correspondences are unknown (use ICP or feature matching); when the transformation includes scaling (use Sim(3) Alignment); when outliers are prevalent (use RANSAC-based variants). Rigid Parametric Alignment, often referred to as Horn's Method, originates from the work of B. K. P. Horn in 1987, who published a closed-form solution for the absolute orientation problem using quaternions, later shown to be equivalent to the SVD approach. It is a fundamental building block in computer vision and robotics for pose estimation and registration. In the context of neural rendering, it is used in methods like L2G-NeRF to align local neural fields to a global coordinate system, and in SplaTAM for trajectory alignment. spla-tam/SplaTAM, https://github.com/spla-tam/SplaTAM, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial) Local-to-Global Registration for Bundle-Adjusting Neural Radiance Fields, https://doi.org/10.1109/cvpr52729.2023.00799, fetched 2026-10-29 Multimodal volume-based tumor neurosurgery planning in the virtual workbench, https://doi.org/10.1007/bfb0056289, fetched 2026-10-26

name: Homography Parametric Alignment
head: Camera Space to SLM Space Homography, Camera-to-SLM Homography, SLM Camera Homography
body: Homography Parametric Alignment estimates a 2D projective transformation T \in SL(3) from point correspondences by solving a homogeneous linear least squares problem via Singular Value Decomposition (SVD). It is specifically employed in camera-in-the-loop optimization to map captured camera coordinates to Spatial Light Modulator (SLM) pattern coordinates, ensuring the captured wavefront and SLM pattern reside in the same coordinate system. Unlike Rigid Parametric Alignment, which estimates a 3D rigid transformation in SE(3), this method operates in 2D homogeneous space to handle planar or perspective distortions between the sensor and the display plane. Inputs: A set of N point correspondences \{x^j\}{j=1}^N, where each x^j consists of a source point in camera space and a target point in SLM space. The source points x^j are detected centers of dots on the sensor in camera coordinates. The target points are the known centers of the same dots in SLM space, derived from the target image used to generate the dot grid. Outputs: A 3 \times 3 homography matrix T representing the affine/projective transform mapping camera space to SLM space. Data Structures: The homography matrix T is a 3 \times 3 matrix with elements T{ij} for i,j \in \{1,2,3\}. The unknown parameter vector h contains the 9 elements of T stacked into a column vector. Steps: 1. Generate Reference Pattern: Calculate an SLM pattern that produces a grid of dots. 2. Capture and Detect: Capture the wavefront on the sensor. Detect the dots and estimate their centers in camera space coordinates. 3. Define Correspondences: Establish correspondences between the detected camera-space centers and the known SLM-space centers of the dot grid. 4. Construct Linear System: For each correspondence j, construct the constraint equation in homogeneous coordinates. The transformation is defined as: \begin{bmatrix} 0 & x^j1 & x^j2 & 1 \end{bmatrix} = T \begin{bmatrix} x^j1 & x^j2 & 1 \end{bmatrix} Note: The source text presents this constraint in a specific rearranged form leading to Aj h = 0. The standard homography constraint x' \sim T x implies x'1 (T{31} x1 + T{32} x2 + T{33}) = T{11} x1 + T{12} x2 + T{13} and x'2 (T{31} x1 + T{32} x2 + T{33}) = T{21} x1 + T{22} x2 + T{23}. The source explicitly cites Eq. (15) as the basis for Aj h = 0. 5. Aggregate System: Stack the constraints from all N points into a global linear system A h = 0, where A is a 2N \times 9 matrix. 6. Solve via SVD: Perform Singular Value Decomposition on A (or the covariance matrix H = A^T A) to find the null space vector corresponding to the smallest singular value. This vector h forms the optimal transformation matrix T that minimizes the algebraic error. 7. Reshape: Reshape the vector h into the 3 \times 3 matrix T. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import numpy as np def computehomography(camerapoints, slmpoints): """ Computes the 3x3 homography matrix T mapping camerapoints to slmpoints. camerapoints: Nx2 array of (x, y) in camera space. slmpoints: Nx2 array of (x, y) in SLM space. Returns: 3x3 matrix T. """ N = camerapoints.shape[0] A = np.zeros((2 N, 9)) for j in range(N): x, y = camerapoints[j] u, v = slmpoints[j] # Construct rows for the linear system Ah = 0 # Based on the constraint: u = (T11x + T12y + T13) / (T31x + T32y + T33) # and v = (T21x + T22y + T23) / (T31x + T32y + T33) # Rearranged to linear form: # T11x + T12y + T13 - T31xu - T32yu - T33u = 0 # T21x + T22y + T23 - T31xv - T32yv - T33v = 0 # Row 1 (for u) A[2j, 0] = x A[2j, 1] = y A[2j, 2] = 1 A[2j, 3] = 0 A[2j, 4] = 0 A[2j, 5] = 0 A[2j, 6] = -x u A[2j, 7] = -y u A[2j, 8] = -u # Row 2 (for v) A[2j+1, 0] = 0 A[2j+1, 1] = 0 A[2j+1, 2] = 0 A[2j+1, 3] = x A[2j+1, 4] = y A[2j+1, 5] = 1 A[2j+1, 6] = -x v A[2j+1, 7] = -y v A[2j+1, 8] = -v # Solve Ah = 0 using SVD # The solution is the right singular vector corresponding to the smallest singular value U, S, Vt = np.linalg.svd(A) h = Vt[-1,:] # Last row of V^T corresponds to smallest singular value # Reshape into 3x3 matrix T = h.reshape(3, 3) return T Parameters: A unique homography is calculated for each depth location and color channel. Edge Cases: Degenerate configurations (e.g., collinear points) may result in a singular matrix A, making the SVD solution unstable or ambiguous. Precision issues may arise if the coordinates are not normalized before solving the linear system. An iterative algorithm for registering two point clouds by minimizing the distance between corresponding points. It differs from Homography Parametric Alignment by operating in 3D and using iterative optimization rather than a closed-form SVD solution for 2D homographies. Choose ICP for general 3D rigid registration when correspondences are not known a priori. Iterative Closest Point (ICP) Estimates the initial camera pose from image features. It serves as a precursor to fine alignment methods. Choose it when an initial guess is needed before applying parametric alignment. Coarse Camera Pose Estimation Time Complexity: The SVD of a 2N \times 9 matrix is O(N), making it very fast for typical numbers of dots (N). Memory Complexity: O(N) to store the matrix A. Strengths: Closed-form solution ensures deterministic results; differentiable, allowing gradient flow for optimization. Limitations: Only models 2D projective transformations; assumes planar correspondence or negligible depth variation within the field of view. When to use: When mapping between two 2D planes (camera sensor and SLM) with known point correspondences. When not to use: When 3D rigid body motion is the primary concern (use Rigid Parametric Alignment) or when correspondences are unknown and require iterative matching (use Iterative Closest Point (ICP)). The method originates from research on local-to-global registration for Neural Radiance Fields (NeRF) and simultaneous color computer-generated holography. It was introduced to enable camera-in-the-loop optimization by aligning captured wavefronts with SLM patterns. The mathematical foundation relies on solving homogeneous linear systems via SVD, a standard technique in computer vision for homography estimation. name: Iterative Closest Point (ICP)
head: ICP Alignment
body: Iterative Closest Point (ICP) is a registration algorithm used to align two point sets, typically a reconstructed point cloud and a ground truth mesh, by finding an optimal rigid transformation. It builds on Rigid Parametric Alignment by iteratively refining the transformation estimate through correspondence matching, rather than solving for a transformation from pre-established correspondences in a single step. Unlike differentiable renderers which optimize pose via gradient descent on pixel errors, ICP operates directly in geometric space. Inputs: 1. Source point set P = \{pi\}{i=1}^N, where pi \in \mathbb{R}^3. 2. Target point set Q = \{qj\}{j=1}^M, where qj \in \mathbb{R}^3. In mesh evaluation, Q may represent the surface of a reference mesh. 3. Initial transformation estimate T0 \in SE(3) (often the identity matrix). 4. Convergence threshold \epsilon and maximum iterations K. Outputs: 1. Final rigid transformation T^ \in SE(3) that minimizes the distance between corresponding points in P and Q. Data Structures: KD-Tree: A spatial index structure built on Q to enable efficient nearest-neighbor search. Transformation Matrix: A 4 \times 4 homogeneous matrix T = \begin{bmatrix} R & t \\ 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix}, where R \in SO(3) is the rotation matrix and t \in \mathbb{R}^3 is the translation vector. Algorithm Steps: 1. Initialization: Set T = T0. 2. Iteration Loop: For k = 0 to K-1: a. Transformation: Apply current transformation to source points: P' = T P. b. Correspondence: For each point p'i \in P', find the nearest neighbor qi \in Q using the KD-Tree. Let C = \{(p'i, qi)\} be the set of correspondences. c. Error Calculation: Compute the mean squared error: Ek = \frac{1}{N} \sum{i=1}^N \| p'i - qi \|^2. d. Convergence Check: If |E{k-1} - Ek| < \epsilon, terminate and return T. e. Optimization: Solve for the optimal rigid transformation T{new} that minimizes the distance between the matched pairs in P' and Q. This is typically done using Singular Value Decomposition (SVD) as described in Rigid Parametric Alignment. f. Update: Set T = T{new}. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def icp(sourcepoints, targetpoints, initialtransform, maxiter=100, tol=1e-4): # sourcepoints: Nx3 array, targetpoints: Mx3 array, initialtransform: 4x4 matrix T = initialtransform preverror = float('inf') targettree = KDTree(targetpoints) # Standard spatial index for k in range(maxiter): # 1. Transform source points transformedsource = applytransform(sourcepoints, T) # 2. Find correspondences (Nearest Neighbor) distances, indices = targettree.query(transformedsource, k=1) correspondences = targetpoints[indices] # 3. Calculate error (Mean Squared Error) errors = [[transformedsource[i][j] - correspondences[i][j] for j in range(3)] for i in range(len(transformedsource))] currenterror = sum(e[0]2 + e[1]2 + e[2]2 for e in errors) / len(errors) # 4. Check convergence if abs(preverror - currenterror) < tol: break preverror = currenterror # 5. Compute optimal rigid transformation using SVD T = computerigidtransform(transformedsource, correspondences) return T def applytransform(points, T): # Apply 4x4 homogeneous transformation to Nx3 points return [[sum(T[i][j] (points[k][j] if j < 3 else 1.0) for j in range(4)) for i in range(3)] for k in range(len(points))] def computerigidtransform(P, Q): # Standard Procrustes SVD alignment meanp = [sum(P[i][j] for i in range(len(P)))/len(P) for j in range(3)] meanq = [sum(Q[i][j] for i in range(len(Q)))/len(Q) for j in range(3)] Pc = [[P[i][j] - meanp[j] for j in range(3)] for i in range(len(P))] Qc = [[Q[i][j] - meanq[j] for j in range(3)] for i in range(len(Q))] H = [[sum(Pc[i][j] Qc[i][k] for i in range(len(Pc))) for k in range(3)] for j in range(3)] U, S, Vt = svd(H) # Standard linear algebra routine R = transpose(Vt) @ transpose(U) if determinant(R) < 0: # Handle reflection Vt[2] = [-x for x in Vt[2]] R = transpose(Vt) @ transpose(U) t = [meanq[j] - sum(R[j][k] meanp[k] for k in range(3)) for j in range(3)] return [[R[0][0], R[0][1], R[0][2], t[0]], [R[1][0], R[1][1], R[1][2], t[1]], [R[2][0], R[2][1], R[2][2], t[2]], [0, 0, 0, 1]] Parameters: maxiter: Typically 10–100. tol: Typically 10^{-4} to 10^{-6}. initialtransform: Critical for convergence. ICP can find poor local minima on average. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Local Minima: ICP is sensitive to initialization and can converge to suboptimal alignments. Singularities: In noise-free, dense point clouds, ICP can exhibit singularities and establish bad correspondences due to symmetry. Noise Sensitivity: Point-to-Plane ICP degrades significantly under synthetic depth noise, while Point-to-Point ICP suffers from poor local minima on average. Matches each source point to the nearest target point based on Euclidean distance. It is robust in noise-free conditions and outperforms Point-to-Plane ICP and differentiable renderers, achieving errors to fractions of a degree. However, it is prone to poor local minima on average. Matches source points to target points and utilizes the surface normal of the target point to define the error metric (distance to the tangent plane). It performs better than Point-to-Point ICP when synthetic depth noise is present, as it incorporates geometric orientation information. This variant integrates ICP concepts within differentiable rendering pipelines. While ICP methods can achieve order-of-magnitude better precision than differentiable renderers in noise-free cases, differentiable renderers remain robust under noise where ICP degrades. Fuzzy Metaballs, a low-fidelity algebraic surface model, often outperforms both in noisy scenarios, achieving lower mean and percentile errors (typically 2x better than ICP). Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Measured Performance: Noise-Free: Point-to-Point ICP achieves errors to fractions of a degree, outperforming differentiable renderers. Fuzzy Metaballs show higher median and 25th percentile errors but lower 75th percentile errors, indicating higher robustness. Noisy: Under synthetic depth noise, ICP performance degrades significantly. Fuzzy Metaballs and differentiable renderers remain robust, with Fuzzy Metaballs achieving the lowest mean, median, and percentile errors (typically 2x better than ICP). Scaling: Performance is highly dependent on the density of the point clouds. Dense clouds improve ICP accuracy in noise-free settings but increase susceptibility to local minima. Strengths: High precision in noise-free scenarios. Direct geometric optimization without gradient approximation. Limitations: Sensitive to initialization and local minima. ICP degrades significantly under synthetic depth noise, while differentiable renderers remain robust. Can suffer from singularities in symmetric, noise-free dense clouds. ICP was introduced as a standard method for aligning 3D point clouds to ground truth meshes for geometric evaluation. It is widely used in 3D reconstruction pipelines to quantify accuracy (precision) and completeness (recall) by aligning reconstructed data to reference models. The method relies on the iterative minimization of the distance between corresponding points, often solved via SVD for the rigid transformation component. Recent comparisons highlight its limitations in noisy environments compared to differentiable rendering and algebraic surface methods. name: Coarse Camera Pose Estimation
head: Coarse Pose Estimation, Initial Pose Registration
body: Coarse Camera Pose Estimation is an incremental registration method that estimates the initial extrinsic parameters (camera pose) for unposed target images relative to a registered reference image using a learned scene regressor. It solves the problem of initializing camera poses in neural radiance field training by converting predicted 3D points into 2D-3D correspondences and solving for the pose via Perspective-n-Point (PnP). It differs from Iterative Closest Point (ICP) by relying on a neural scene representation to provide dense 3D structure rather than iterative point-to-point alignment, and from Structure-from-Motion (SfM) by operating incrementally on a learned regressor rather than globally on feature matches. Inputs: Registered reference image I{ref} (or Ii). Target image Ik to be registered. Camera intrinsic matrix K. Inlier threshold s{inlier} (typically 5,000). Reprojection error threshold (typically 6 pixels). Outputs: Coarse camera pose T{coarse} for Ik. Inlier count Sk. Data Structures: Scene Regressor f{SCR}: A neural network (e.g., Transformer-based) that takes two images and outputs a set of 3D points \{Xk\} in the global coordinate frame. Pixel Coordinates \{uk\}: 2D coordinates of pixels in Ik. 3D Points \{Xk\}: Predicted 3D coordinates corresponding to \{uk\}. Steps: 1. Scene Regression: Pass I{ref} and Ik to the scene regressor f{SCR} to obtain the set of 3D points \{Xk\} in the global coordinate frame. \{Xk\} = f{SCR}(I{ref}, Ik) 2. Correspondence Generation: Construct 2D-3D correspondences \{(uk, Xk)\} using the pixel coordinates \{uk\} from Ik and the predicted 3D points \{Xk\}. 3. Pose Solving: Solve for the coarse camera pose T{coarse} using a PnP solver with RANSAC (specifically DSAC, modified for non-square focal lengths). T{coarse}, Sk = \text{PnP}(K, \{(uk, Xk)\}) where Sk is the number of inliers. 4. Validation: If Sk > s{inlier}, add Ik to the training buffer and register it. Otherwise, discard the pose. Parameters: s{inlier}: Inlier threshold. Set to 5,000. Reprojection error threshold: Set to 6 pixels. DSAC Modification: Supports different focal lengths for x and y axes. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Gauge Ambiguity: The camera pose of the seed image is fixed during optimization to resolve gauge ambiguity. Scale Ambiguity: The scaling factor between the seed image and its most similar adjacent image is fixed. Pose Accuracy: Coarse poses may be inaccurate if the scene regressor has not seen the target images. A separate MLP pose refiner (as in ACE0) was found ineffective for transformer-based regressors. Initialization: The seed image is selected as the reference image. Subsequent reference images are selected from registered images that connect to the most unregistered images. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def coarsecameraposeestimation(Iref, Ik, K, sinlier=5000, reprojthresh=6.0): # Step 1: Get 3D points from scene regressor # fscr is the learned scene regressor Xk = fscr(Iref, Ik) # Step 2: Get 2D pixel coordinates from Ik # Assuming uk is extracted from image grid or provided uk = getpixelcoordinates(Ik) # Step 3: Form 2D-3D correspondences correspondences = list(zip(uk, Xk)) # Step 4: Solve PnP with RANSAC (DSAC variant) # DSAC is modified to support different fx and fy Tcoarse, Sk = solvepnpransac(K, correspondences, inlierthresh=reprojthresh, supportnonsquarefocal=True) # Step 5: Validate against inlier threshold if Sk > sinlier: return Tcoarse, True else: return None, False SfM recovers poses globally from uncalibrated photos, providing the geometric constraints for radiance fields. It differs from Coarse Camera Pose Estimation by not relying on a sequential learned regressor but on feature matching and triangulation. Time Complexity: Depends on the inference time of the scene regressor f{SCR} and the PnP solver. The regressor is typically a Transformer, which is computationally expensive compared to traditional feature extraction. Memory Complexity: Requires storing the scene regressor parameters and the 3D points \{Xk\} for the current batch. Performance: The method relies on the accuracy of the scene regressor. If the regressor has not seen the images, poses may be inaccurate. Strengths: Enables training from unposed images without traditional SfM pipelines. Incremental registration allows scaling to large datasets. Limitations: Requires a trained scene regressor. Performance degrades if the regressor is not well-trained on the target domain. The fixed threshold of 5,000 inliers may not be optimal for all scenes. When to use: When initializing neural radiance field training from unposed images and a scene regressor is available. When not to use: When high-precision initial poses are required without further refinement, or when computational resources for the regressor are limited. Coarse Camera Pose Estimation is part of the ZeroGS pipeline, which trains 3D Gaussian Splatting from unposed images. It was introduced in the paper "ZeroGS: Training 3D Gaussian Splatting from Unposed Images". The method builds on the idea of using a learned scene regressor to predict 3D structure, which is then used to solve for camera poses via PnP. It addresses the limitation of previous methods that required posed images or relied on less accurate pose refinement techniques. name: Structure-from-Motion (SfM)
body: Structure-from-Motion (SfM) is a sparse reconstruction technique that estimates camera poses (extrinsics), camera calibration (intrinsics), and a sparse 3D point cloud from a set of uncalibrated photographs. It serves as the foundational "load-bearing" preprocessing step for modern implicit and explicit radiance field methods (such as NeRF and Gaussian Splatting), providing the known camera positions required to optimize scene representations against source images. Unlike methods that anchor the coordinate system to semantic features, SfM establishes the global frame through geometric consistency across the scene. The method reconstructs the scene incrementally by recovering the relative and absolute geometry of cameras and 3D points. Input: A set of N images \{I1, \dots, IN\}. Output: Camera poses: A rotation matrix Ri \in SO(3) and translation vector ti \in \mathbb{R}^3 for each image i, forming the projection matrix Pi = K [Ri | ti]. Intrinsics: The camera calibration matrix K (focal lengths fx, fy, principal point cx, cy, and distortion coefficients). Sparse point cloud: A set of 3D points Xj \in \mathbb{R}^3 with associated color/normal data. 1. Keypoints: For each image i, a list of 2D points u{i,k} \in \mathbb{R}^2 and their descriptors d{i,k} \in \mathbb{R}^D (typically D=128 for SIFT). 2. Matches: A list of correspondences (u{i,k}, u{j,l}) between images i and j. 3. Reconstruction: Cameras: Array of (Ri, ti, K). Points: Array of Xj with visibility mask V{j,i} \in \{0, 1\} indicating if point j is visible in image i. 1. Feature Extraction: Detect distinctive keypoints (corners, spots, texture) in each image and compute descriptors robust to rotation, scale, and brightness changes. SIFT is the classic detector; it is monochrome, discarding hue and saturation. Pseudocode: python keypoints = [] descriptors = [] for image in images: # Detect distinctive patches and compute descriptor vectors kp = detectkeypoints(image) desc = computedescriptor(image, kp) keypoints.append(kp) descriptors.append(desc) 2. Pairwise Matching: Compare descriptors between image pairs to find candidate matches. For large N, use a vocabulary tree to avoid O(N^2) comparisons. Pseudocode: python matches = [] for i in range(N): for j in range(i + 1, N): candidates = [] for u, du in zip(keypoints[i], descriptors[i]): bestv, mindist = None, float('inf') for v, dv in zip(keypoints[j], descriptors[j]): dist = sum((a - b) 2 for a, b in zip(du, dv)) if dist < mindist: mindist = dist bestv = v candidates.append((u, bestv)) matches.append((i, j, candidates)) 3. Geometric Verification (RANSAC): Discard incorrect matches using epipolar geometry. True matches must satisfy the constraint that a point in one image lies on a specific line (epipolar line) in the other. Use the Fundamental Matrix F (uncalibrated) or Essential Matrix E (calibrated). RANSAC iteratively guesses a model from a minimal subset, counts inliers (matches satisfying the geometric constraint within a threshold), and selects the model with the most inliers. Pseudocode: python verifiedmatches = [] for (i, j, candidates) in matches: bestmodel = None bestinliers = [] for in range(1000): # Standard iteration count subset = random.sample(candidates, 4) # Minimal sample for F matrix F = estimatefundamentalmatrix(subset) # Standard 8-point algorithm inliers = [] for u, v in candidates: # Epipolar constraint: v^T F u = 0 if abs(v[0] (F[0][0] u[0] + F[0][1] u[1] + F[0][2]) + v[1] (F[1][0] u[0] + F[1][1] u[1] + F[1][2]) + 1 (F[2][0] u[0] + F[2][1] u[1] + F[2][2])) < 1.0: inliers.append((u, v)) if len(inliers) > len(bestinliers): bestinliers = inliers bestmodel = F if len(bestinliers) > 10: # Minimum inlier threshold verifiedmatches.append((i, j, bestmodel, bestinliers)) 4. Incremental Reconstruction: Pick a good starting pair with a wide baseline and many matches. Reconstruct those two cameras and triangulate their shared points. Find another image that sees a bunch of the points you already have. Because you know where those points are in 3D and where they landed in the new image, you can solve for that camera's position using Perspective-n-Point (PnP). Triangulate the new points that camera adds, then repeat. Triangulation finds the closest approach of rays from camera centers through feature locations. Pseudocode: python cameras = [] points3d = [] # Initialize with best pair imga, imgb, Fab, inliersab = verifiedmatches[0] Ra, ta = np.eye(3), np.zeros(3) # First camera at origin Rb, tb = recoverposefromepipolar(Fab, inliersab) # Standard recovery cameras.append((imga, Ra, ta)) cameras.append((imgb, Rb, tb)) points3d = triangulatepoints(keypoints[imga], keypoints[imgb], Ra, ta, Rb, tb) # Linear triangulation registeredimages = {imga, imgb} unregisteredimages = set(range(N)) - registeredimages while unregisteredimages: nextimg = max(unregisteredimages, key=lambda x: countsharedpoints(x, points3d, cameras)) Rnew, tnew = solvepnp(keypoints[nextimg], points3d, cameras) # Standard PnP solver cameras.append((nextimg, Rnew, tnew)) newpoints = triangulatenewpoints(keypoints[nextimg], Rnew, tnew, points3d, cameras) points3d.extend(newpoints) registeredimages.add(nextimg) unregisteredimages.remove(nextimg) 5. Bundle Adjustment (BA): Periodically optimize all camera poses and 3D points simultaneously to minimize the total reprojection error. The error is the pixel distance between the actual 2D projection and the estimated projection of each 3D point. Intrinsics are often treated as unknowns to be recovered via self-calibration within BA, rather than relying solely on EXIF metadata. If photos come from the same physical camera with a fixed lens, intrinsics are shared across the whole set. Pseudocode: python def bundleadjustment(cameras, points3d): # Non-linear least squares optimization (e.g., Levenberg-Marquardt) while not converged: residuals = computereprojectionerrors(cameras, points3d) jacobian = computejacobian(cameras, points3d) update = solvelinearsystem(jacobian, residuals) applyupdate(cameras, points3d, update) return cameras, points3d Feature Detector: SIFT (default in COLMAP) or SuperPoint. Matcher: Brute-force or LightGlue. Baseline: Initial pair selection should maximize baseline to improve triangulation accuracy. Segmentation Interval: In progressive motion sequences, the trajectory may be segmented (e.g., every 5 frames) to introduce a local prior, initializing new poses using the last frame of the previous segment: [R|t]{p+1} \leftarrow [R|t]p. Zooming: If photos are taken with zooming, intrinsics change, violating the shared-intrinsics assumption. Rolling Shutter: Fast motion with rolling-shutter sensors smears geometry, violating the pinhole model assumption. Cropped/Resized Images: Invalidate principal point and focal length relative to the original sensor. Motion Blur: Smears feature points, causing bad matches. Mitigation: detect/drop blurriest frames or shoot at high shutter speeds. Tiny Baselines: Processing too many nearly-identical video frames wastes compute and provides little new triangulation information. This method estimates a canonical coordinate frame for selfie and full-body captures using facial landmarks, enabling the automatic generation of novel view trajectories for NeRF training. It serves as a preprocessing step that aligns all input camera poses to a canonical coordinate system using 3D facial keypoints and similarity transformation. Unlike general Structure-from-Motion (SfM) alignment which relies on scene geometry, this method anchors the coordinate system to specific semantic features of the subject (the face), ensuring consistent orientation regardless of the initial camera pose. This method establishes the geometric foundation for neural volume rendering by estimating camera poses and initializing the spatial data structures (binoctree) from raw input video or images. It solves the problem of aligning unstructured input data into a coherent global coordinate frame and initializing the scene representation with a sparse but accurate 3D point cloud. It differs from sibling methods like Canonical Frame Estimation via Facial Landmarks by relying on general Structure-from-Motion (SfM) pipelines rather than semantic landmarks, making it applicable to general 3D scenes rather than just faces. An initialization pipeline that replaces traditional sparse SfM methods with a deep learning framework to construct a robust initial point cloud. It uses SuperPoint as the feature extractor to detect keypoints and compute descriptors, and LightGlue as the feature matcher to match descriptors between images. This approach replaces SfM/MVS which have limitations in robustness, efficiency, and scalability compared to deep learning methods. A method for online feature matching and pose estimation. It performs Hierarchical Weighted Local Bundle Adjustment (BA) incorporating only neighboring connected and registered images after acquiring a new image, reducing time complexity compared to global BA. It achieves online feature matching via global feature retrieval on HNSW (Hierarchical Navigable Small World) to enable efficient dynamic updates for the matching matrix. Time Complexity: Incremental SfM is generally O(N^2) for matching and O(N \cdot M) for BA, where N is the number of images and M is the number of points. Global SfM (e.g., GLOMAP) can be dramatically quicker on large sets. Measured Performance: On a machine with an RTX A6000 GPU and 128 GB RAM: For 310 frames: COLMAP took 00:08:26, HLOC took 01:08:39, LocalRF took 23:20:52. For 1392 frames: COLMAP took 00:49:29, HLOC took 21:51:34, LocalRF took 75:10:54. For 2784 frames: COLMAP took 04:32:53. Scaling: COLMAP performs well with dense views (2784 frames) but is slower than HLOC on sparse views (310, 1392 frames). HLOC is slower but more effective on sparse views. LocalRF handles long-range trajectories but has extensive running time. Strengths: Robust to viewpoint changes; provides accurate initial poses for downstream optimization. Limitations: Struggles with repetitive textures, low-texture regions, and significant motion blur. Requires sufficient overlap and baseline between images. Structure-from-Motion is a classic computer vision technique that predates Gaussian Splats by decades. It is the same math that builds the sparse point clouds in classic photogrammetry. The de facto standard tool for SfM is COLMAP, an open-source package by Schönberger and Frahm (CVPR 2016). It is used to generate the camera poses and sparse point cloud that serve as the seed for Gaussian Splatting training. name: Canonical Frame Estimation via Facial Landmarks
head: Camera Alignment via Procrustes, Facial Landmark-based Canonical Frame
body: This method estimates a canonical coordinate frame for selfie and full-body captures using facial landmarks, enabling the automatic generation of novel view trajectories for NeRF training. It serves as a preprocessing step that aligns all input camera poses to a canonical coordinate system using 3D facial keypoints and similarity transformation. Unlike general Structure-from-Motion (SfM) alignment which relies on scene geometry, this method anchors the coordinate system to specific semantic features of the subject (the face), ensuring consistent orientation regardless of the initial camera pose. Inputs: 1. A set of N images with associated camera poses Pi \in \mathbb{R}^{4 \times 4} (extrinsics) and intrinsics, obtained from SfM. 2. 2D facial landmark detections for each image. Outputs: 1. A canonical coordinate frame defined by a rotation matrix R{can}, translation vector t{can}, and scale factor s. 2. Transformed camera poses P'i aligned to this canonical frame. Data Structures: 2D Landmarks: For each image i, a set of K 2D points l{i,k} = (u{i,k}, v{i,k}) where k \in \{1, \dots, K\}. MediaPipe’s face mesh is used to extract these. 3D Keypoints: A set of M=5 3D points Xk = (xk, yk, zk) representing the outer eye corners, nose, mouth, and chin. Canonical Keypoints: A fixed set of 5 reference points X^{ref}k computed as the median location of these keypoints across the first 260 subjects in the training set. Steps: 1. 2D Landmark Detection: For each input image i, compute 2D facial landmarks l{i,k} using MediaPipe’s face mesh. 2. 3D Triangulation: Triangulate the 2D landmarks into 3D space using the SfM camera poses Pi and intrinsic parameters. Let the resulting 3D points for image i be \hat{X}{i,k}. Note: This step assumes the subject is static. If the subject moves, the triangulation is technically incorrect but observed to be sufficiently good for defining the frame even with head rotation. 3. Keypoint Selection: From the triangulated points, identify the 5 specific keypoints corresponding to the outer eye corners, nose, mouth, and chin. Let the set of 3D points for image i be Xi = \{\hat{X}{i,1}, \dots, \hat{X}{i,5}\}. 4. Similarity Transform Calculation: Calculate a similarity transform (rotation R, translation t, scale s) that maps the subject's 3D keypoints Xi to the canonical reference keypoints X^{ref} using Procrustes analysis. The canonical frame is centered at the face mesh. The orientation is defined as: +y up, +x right, -z into the face. The scale is set such that the distance between the eyes (interpupillary distance) matches 6 cm. 5. Pose Transformation: Apply the computed similarity transform to all camera poses Pi to obtain the canonical poses P'i. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import numpy as np def estimatecanonicalframe(imageposes, intrinsics, imagepaths): """ Estimates a canonical frame and transforms camera poses. Args: imageposes: List of 4x4 numpy arrays (extrinsics) from SfM. intrinsics: Camera intrinsic matrix K. imagepaths: List of image file paths. Returns: canonicaltransform: 4x4 similarity transform matrix. transformedposes: List of transformed 4x4 pose matrices. """ # Step 1: Detect 2D landmarks and Triangulate to 3D # Note: In practice, this requires a face detection library (e.g., MediaPipe) # and a triangulation function. We assume get2dlandmarks and triangulate3d # are available helpers. all3dlandmarks = [] for i, imgpath in enumerate(imagepaths): # Get 2D landmarks for image i landmarks2d = get2dlandmarks(imgpath) # Returns Nx2 array # Triangulate using the i-th camera pose and intrinsics # This projects 2D points back to 3D rays and intersects them # across multiple views or uses the known pose if multi-view is not # explicitly handled in this simplified loop. # The source implies triangulation using SfM poses. landmarks3d = triangulate3d(landmarks2d, imageposes[i], intrinsics) all3dlandmarks.append(landmarks3d) # Step 2: Select 5 specific keypoints # Indices depend on MediaPipe face mesh ordering. # We assume indices for: left eye outer, right eye outer, nose tip, mouth center, chin. keypointindices = [33, 263, 1, 61, 152] subjectkeypoints = [] for landmarks3d in all3dlandmarks: kp = landmarks3d[keypointindices] subjectkeypoints.append(kp) # Step 3: Define Canonical Reference Keypoints # Computed as median across first 260 subjects # For implementation, these are pre-computed constants. canonicalkeypoints = getcanonicalreferencekeypoints() # Step 4: Calculate Similarity Transform via Procrustes # We align the subject's keypoints to the canonical keypoints. # Since the subject may be in different poses, we align the set of keypoints # from a representative frame (or average if available) to the canonical frame. # The source implies a single transform per subject/session. # Using the first frame's keypoints as the representative subject geometry Xsubject = subjectkeypoints[0] # Procrustes analysis to find R, t, s such that: # s R Xsubject + t = Xcanonical R, t, s = procrustesanalysis(Xsubject, canonicalkeypoints) # Step 5: Enforce Metric Scale (Interpupillary Distance = 6 cm) # The Procrustes solution provides relative scale. We adjust s to match 6cm. currentipd = np.linalg.norm(Xsubject[1] - Xsubject[0]) # Distance between eyes targetipd = 0.06 # 6 cm in meters s = s (targetipd / currentipd) # Construct the 4x4 similarity transform matrix # T = [ sR t ] # [ 0 1 ] canonicaltransform = np.eye(4) canonicaltransform[:3,:3] = s R canonicaltransform[:3, 3] = t # Step 6: Transform all camera poses transformedposes = [] for pose in imageposes: # The camera pose P transforms world to camera. # To align the world (subject) to canonical, we apply the inverse of the # subject-to-canonical transform to the world coordinates. # Alternatively, if P is [Rcam|tcam], the new pose P' is: # P' = Tcanonical P # This assumes P is in the original SfM world frame. newpose = canonicaltransform @ pose transformedposes.append(newpose) return canonicaltransform, transformedposes def procrustesanalysis(X, Y): """ Computes the similarity transform (R, t, s) to map X to Y. X, Y are (M, 3) arrays. """ # Center points Xmean = np.mean(X, axis=0) Ymean = np.mean(Y, axis=0) Xc = X - Xmean Yc = Y - Ymean # Compute scale s = np.sum(Yc2) / np.sum(Xc2) s = np.sqrt(s) # Compute rotation using SVD H = Xc.T @ Yc U, S, Vt = np.linalg.svd(H) R = Vt.T @ U.T # Ensure proper rotation (det(R) = 1) if np.linalg.det(R) < 0: Vt[-1,:] = -1 R = Vt.T @ U.T # Compute translation t = Ymean - s R @ Xmean return R, t, s Parameters: Interpupillary Distance: 6 cm. Canonical Keypoints: Median location of 5 keypoints (outer eye corners, nose, mouth, chin) across the first 260 subjects in the training set. Orientation: +y up, +x right, -z into the face. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Subject Motion: 3D triangulation of facial landmarks is only strictly correct if the subject is static. However, it is observed to be sufficiently good for defining the coordinate frame even when the subject rotates their head side-to-side. Missing Segmentation: This step is skipped for captures where segmentation masks cannot be obtained (e.g., BADMINTON and B ROOM datasets in the original study). Animal Captures: For animal captures, manual virtual camera paths are generated instead of using this automatic method. Time Complexity: Dominated by 2D landmark detection (MediaPipe) and 3D triangulation. Procrustes analysis is negligible (O(M) for M=5 keypoints). Memory Complexity: Low. Requires storing 2D landmarks and 5 3D keypoints per image. Strengths: Provides a consistent, semantically meaningful canonical frame for human subjects, enabling automatic novel view trajectory generation (e.g., figure-eight paths). It is robust to initial camera pose variations. Limitations: Relies on the accuracy of facial landmark detection and SfM poses. Performance degrades if the subject moves significantly during capture, though head rotation is tolerated. Not applicable to non-human subjects without manual intervention. This method was introduced in the context of NeRFies, a framework for reconstructing and animating humans from video. It addresses the challenge of camera registration in the presence of a moving foreground by anchoring the coordinate system to the subject's face rather than the static background. The use of Procrustes analysis for alignment is a standard technique in computer vision for shape matching. The canonical keypoints are derived from a large dataset of 1450 volunteers, with the reference frame computed from the first 260 subjects. name: Preprocessing and Initialization
body: This method establishes the geometric foundation for neural volume rendering by estimating camera poses and initializing the spatial data structures (binoctree) from raw input video or images. It solves the problem of aligning unstructured input data into a coherent global coordinate frame and initializing the scene representation with a sparse but accurate 3D point cloud. It differs from sibling methods like Canonical Frame Estimation via Facial Landmarks by relying on general Structure-from-Motion (SfM) pipelines rather than semantic landmarks, making it applicable to general 3D scenes rather than just faces. Inputs: Raw video frames or image sequence. (Optional) Pre-trained disparity estimation network weights. Outputs: Camera poses (extrinsics) and intrinsics for each frame. A global 3D point cloud in metric units. An initialized spherical binoctree structure. Scaling coefficient for unit sphere normalization. 1. Camera Pose: 4 \times 4 matrix P representing world-to-camera transformation. 2. Intrinsics: 3 \times 3 matrix K containing focal lengths and principal points. 3. Point Cloud: Set of 3D points C = \{ci\} where ci \in \mathbb{R}^3. 4. Binoctree: Hierarchical structure where each node (sphoxel) stores SDF and color information. Initialized via subdivision. 1. Camera Pose Estimation: Use a Structure-from-Motion (SfM) algorithm (e.g., OpenVSLAM or COLMAP) to estimate per-frame camera poses from the input video/images. If using COLMAP, configure a "simple radial" camera model with a single radial distortion coefficient and shared intrinsic parameters across all images. Enable "sift feature guided matching" in the exhaustive matcher step. Refine principal points of the intrinsic parameters during bundle adjustment. 2. Depth and Point Cloud Extraction: For each frame, extract a dense 3D point cloud using spherical rectification and a fine-tuned disparity estimation network. Combine per-frame poses and calibrated depth maps to form a global coordinate frame in metric units. 3. Coordinate Frame Construction: Place the origin at the center of all camera positions. Set the near sphere bound to contain all camera positions. Set the far sphere bound per scene to fit the recovered point cloud inside the sphere. Place a final sphere at the far plane with view-independent color decoded by a background MLP to represent scene elements at infinity (e.g., sky). 4. Normalization: Scale both the binoctree coordinates and the point cloud coordinates into a unit sphere. Store the scaling coefficient for later metric re-scaling during rendering or evaluation. 5. Binoctree Initialization: Use the scaled initial 3D point cloud to subdivide the binoctree to its finest level. Continue subdivision until all sphoxels reach a minimum solid angle \alpha{min}. Derive \alpha{min} per scene from baseline and image sizes, typically setting \alpha{min} between 5 \times 10^{-4} and 1 \times 10^{-3}. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def preprocessandinitialize(videoframes, disparitymodel=None): # Step 1: Estimate Camera Poses # Use OpenVSLAM or COLMAP if useopenvslam: poses = OpenVSLAM.estimateposes(videoframes) elif usecolmap: # Configure COLMAP with simple radial model colmapconfig = { "cameramodel": "simpleradial", "radialdistortioncoeff": 1, "sharedintrinsic": True, "matcher": "siftfeatureguided", "refineprincipalpoints": True } poses, intrinsics = COLMAP.run(videoframes, colmapconfig) # Step 2: Extract Point Cloud pointclouds = [] for frame, pose in zip(videoframes, poses): # Rectify and estimate disparity rectifiedframe = sphericalrectification(frame) if disparitymodel: disparitymap = disparitymodel.predict(rectifiedframe) else: disparitymap = estimatedisparity(rectifiedframe) # Convert to 3D points using pose and intrinsics points = depthto3d(disparitymap, pose, intrinsics) pointclouds.append(points) # Step 3: Form Global Coordinate Frame # Combine all point clouds globalpointcloud = concatenate(pointclouds) # Calculate center of cameras cameracenters = [pose.translation for pose in poses] origin = mean(cameracenters) # Set bounds nearbound = maxdistancefromorigin(cameracenters) farbound = maxdistancefromorigin(globalpointcloud) # Step 4: Normalize to Unit Sphere scalecoefficient = 1.0 / farbound scaledpointcloud = globalpointcloud scalecoefficient scaledbinoctreebounds = [-1, 1] # Unit sphere # Step 5: Initialize Binoctree alphamin = 1e-3 # Typical value from binoctree = Binoctree() binoctree.initializefrompoints(scaledpointcloud, alphamin) return poses, intrinsics, scaledpointcloud, binoctree, scalecoefficient \alpha{min}: Minimum solid angle for sphoxels. Typical range: 5 \times 10^{-4} to 1 \times 10^{-3}. Camera Model: "simpleradial" with 1 distortion coefficient. Inaccurate Poses: Errors in camera poses and intrinsic parameters lead to poor synthesis results. Boundary Conditions: The near sphere must contain all camera positions; the far sphere must contain the point cloud. Infinity Representation: Scene elements at infinity (e.g., sky) require a separate background MLP at the far plane. A specific implementation of the pose estimation step using the COLMAP software package. It differs from other SfM implementations by its specific configuration options for neural rendering pipelines. It is chosen when high-accuracy intrinsic refinement is required. Key steps include using a "simple radial" camera model, "sift feature guided matching," and refining principal points during bundle adjustment. Pitfall: Inaccurate poses/intrinsics lead to poor results. Time Complexity: Dominated by SfM feature matching and depth estimation. COLMAP's exhaustive matching is O(N^2) in worst case but optimized with SIFT. Memory Complexity: Proportional to the number of frames and the density of the point cloud. The binoctree initialization scales with the number of points and the target resolution (\alpha{min}). Strengths: Provides a metric global coordinate frame; handles omnidirectional video; initializes structure accurately from sparse data. Limitations: Requires accurate SfM; fails if feature matching is poor (e.g., textureless regions); depth estimation network may fail on untrained domains. When to Use: When starting from raw video/images and a global metric frame is needed. When Not to Use: When camera poses are already known and accurate, or when semantic landmarks are more appropriate (e.g., faces). Originating from the need to initialize neural radiance fields (NeRF) and related methods from unstructured video, this method combines traditional SfM with modern depth estimation. OpenVSLAM is used for omnidirectional video, while COLMAP is used for standard image sets. The binoctree initialization strategy was introduced to efficiently represent sparse 3D data in a hierarchical structure suitable for neural rendering. name: Pose Registration Metrics
head: Pose Error Metrics, Rotation Error, Translation Error
body: Pose Registration Metrics quantify the alignment accuracy between estimated camera poses and ground-truth poses, serving as the evaluation standard for methods like Sim(3) Alignment via Procrustes Analysis. They solve the problem of measuring how well an estimated trajectory matches reality in terms of both orientation and position. Unlike sibling methods that focus on alignment optimization or parametric fitting, these metrics provide the scalar error values used to judge the success of the alignment. The method computes two primary error components: translation error and rotation error. These are calculated per pose pair or aggregated over a trajectory. Inputs: T{gt}: Ground-truth translation vector (3D position). \hat{T}: Estimated translation vector (3D position). R{gt}: Ground-trotation rotation matrix (3 \times 3). \hat{R}: Estimated rotation matrix (3 \times 3). Outputs: T{err}: Translation error (scalar). R{err}: Rotation error (scalar, in radians). Data Structures: Rotation matrices are stored as 3 \times 3 orthogonal matrices with determinant 1. Translation vectors are stored as 3-element floating-point arrays. Formulas: 1. Translation Error (T{err}): The Euclidean distance between the estimated and ground-truth positions: T{err} = \| \hat{T} - T{gt} \|2 Note: On datasets where positions are not in metric space, this error has no physical units. 2. Rotation Error (R{err}): The geodesic distance on the rotation manifold, representing the angle required to align the estimated rotation with the ground truth: R{err} = \arccos \left( \frac{\text{tr}(R{gt}^\top \hat{R}) - 1}{2} \right) Alternatively expressed using the inverse: R{err} = \arccos \left( \frac{\text{tr}(R{gt}^{-1} \hat{R}) - 1}{2} \right) Where \text{tr}(\cdot) denotes the trace of a matrix. The result is in radians. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math import numpy as np def computetranslationerror(estpos: np.ndarray, gtpos: np.ndarray) -> float: """ Computes Euclidean distance between estimated and ground truth positions. Args: estpos: 3D array, estimated position [x, y, z] gtpos: 3D array, ground truth position [x, y, z] Returns: float: Euclidean distance """ diff = estpos - gtpos return np.linalg.norm(diff) def computerotationerror(estrot: np.ndarray, gtrot: np.ndarray) -> float: """ Computes geodesic rotation error in radians. Args: estrot: 3x3 numpy array, estimated rotation matrix gtrot: 3x3 numpy array, ground truth rotation matrix Returns: float: Rotation error in radians """ # Compute trace of Rgt^T Rest # Note: Rgt^T is equivalent to Rgt^-1 for rotation matrices product = gtrot.T @ estrot traceval = np.trace(product) # Clamp value to [-1, 1] to handle floating point errors in arccos cosangle = (traceval - 1.0) / 2.0 cosangle = np.clip(cosangle, -1.0, 1.0) return math.acos(cosangle) def evaluateposepair(estpose, gtpose): """ Evaluates a single pose pair. Args: estpose: dict or object with 'pos' (3D) and 'rot' (3x3) gtpose: dict or object with 'pos' (3D) and 'rot' (3x3) Returns: tuple: (translationerror, rotationerror) """ terr = computetranslationerror(estpose['pos'], gtpose['pos']) rerr = computerotationerror(estpose['rot'], gtpose['rot']) return terr, rerr Parameters: No specific tuning parameters for the basic error calculation. Aggregation metrics (like RMSE) may require trajectory length N. Edge Cases: Numerical Stability: The argument to \arccos must be clamped to [-1, 1] to prevent NaNs due to floating-point precision errors in matrix multiplication. Non-Metric Space: Translation error units are undefined if the coordinate system is not metric. Computes the Root Mean Square Error (RMSE) of the translation component between a ground truth trajectory and an estimated trajectory after optimal alignment. It quantifies the global scale and drift of an ego-motion estimation system by measuring the integrated distance between pose estimates and ground truth. Unlike relative error metrics, ATE evaluates the absolute consistency of the trajectory in the world frame. Time Complexity: O(N) for N poses, as each pose is processed independently. Memory Complexity: O(1) per pose pair; O(N) if storing all errors for aggregation. Strengths: Simple to implement; provides intuitive geometric interpretation (meters for translation, radians for rotation). Limitations: Translation error lacks physical meaning in non-metric spaces. Does not account for temporal consistency or drift direction. When to use: Standard evaluation for pose estimation accuracy after alignment. When not to use: When relative drift or scale consistency is the primary concern (use Relative Pose Error instead). Originating from the evaluation of visual odometry and SLAM systems, these metrics have become standard in novel view synthesis and 3D reconstruction papers. The specific formulation of rotation error as the geodesic distance on the rotation manifold is widely cited in recent works such as SPARF and VoxelTTO. The translation error is a standard Euclidean norm, though its interpretation varies based on the dataset's coordinate system. name: Absolute Trajectory Error Computation
head: ATE, ATE RMSE Calculation, ATE RMSE Computation, Absolute Trajectory Error Measurement, Absolute Trajectory Error RMSE, Ego-Motion Estimation Evaluation
body: Computes the Root Mean Square Error (RMSE) of the translation component between a ground truth trajectory and an estimated trajectory after optimal alignment. It quantifies the global scale and drift of an ego-motion estimation system by measuring the integrated distance between pose estimates and ground truth. Unlike relative error metrics, ATE evaluates the absolute consistency of the trajectory in the world frame. Inputs: Ground truth trajectory: A sequence of N poses T{gt} = \{P{gt,1}, \dots, P{gt,N}\}, where each P{gt,i} \in SE(3) is a 4 \times 4 transformation matrix (typically world-to-camera or camera-to-world, must be consistent with estimated poses). Estimated trajectory: A sequence of N poses T{est} = \{P{est,1}, \dots, P{est,N}\}, aligned to the same coordinate frame convention. Correspondence: The i-th pose in T{est} corresponds to the i-th pose in T{gt}. Outputs: atermse: The scalar ATE RMSE value in meters (or units of the ground truth scale). transerror: An array of per-frame translation errors. Data Structures: Translation vectors: Extracted from the 4th row, 3rd column (or 3rd row, 4th column depending on convention) of the 4 \times 4 pose matrices. Let t{gt} \in \mathbb{R}^{3 \times N} and t{est} \in \mathbb{R}^{3 \times N} be the stacked translation vectors. Steps: 1. Preprocessing and Alignment: Filter out invalid poses. If a ground truth pose contains NaN values, skip the corresponding frame in the estimated trajectory. Normalize estimated rotation quaternions if the input is provided in quaternion form. Align the estimated trajectory to the ground truth trajectory using a similarity transformation (Sim(3)) or rigid transformation (SE(3)) to minimize the alignment error. The standard approach uses Horn's method for absolute orientation. Let s, R, t be the scale, rotation, and translation parameters of the alignment transform. Compute aligned estimated translations: t{est, aligned} = s \cdot R \cdot t{est} + t. 2. Compute Per-Frame Translation Error: For each frame i, compute the translation error vector: e{trans, i} = t{gt, i} - t{est, aligned, i} Compute the magnitude of the error: e{trans, i} = \| e{trans, i} \|2 = \sqrt{\sum{j=1}^{3} (e{trans, i, j})^2} Store e{trans, i} in an array transerror. 3. Compute ATE RMSE: Calculate the mean of the squared translation errors: \text{MSE} = \frac{1}{N} \sum{i=1}^{N} (e{trans, i})^2 The ATE RMSE is the square root of the MSE: \text{ATE RMSE} = \sqrt{\text{MSE}} Alternatively, some implementations compute the mean of the errors directly (Mean ATE), but RMSE is the standard metric for "Absolute Trajectory Error" in the context of SLAM evaluation. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import numpy as np def computeatermse(gtposes, estposes): """ Compute Absolute Trajectory Error (ATE) RMSE. Args: gtposes: List of N 4x4 numpy arrays (ground truth poses). estposes: List of N 4x4 numpy arrays (estimated poses). Returns: atermse: Float, the ATE RMSE. transerror: Array of N floats, per-frame translation errors. """ N = len(gtposes) if N == 0: return 100.0, np.array([]) # Pitfall: Return default error if evaluation fails # 1. Extract translation vectors # Assuming poses are 4x4 matrices. Translation is typically row 3, cols 0-2 or col 3, rows 0-2. # We assume standard column-major or row-major consistency. # Here we assume translation is in the 4th column (indices [0:3, 3]) for column-major # or 4th row (indices [3, 0:3]) for row-major. # The source mentions "3rd column, 4th row", which implies row 3, cols 0-2 in 0-indexed notation # if the matrix is stored as [row][col]. Let's assume standard numpy array indexing: # t = pose[3, 0:3] for row-major (common in OpenGL/Python) or pose[0:3, 3] for column-major. # We will use pose[3, 0:3] as per common Python/NumPy convention for row-major matrices. gttrans = np.array([pose[3, 0:3] for pose in gtposes]) esttrans = np.array([pose[3, 0:3] for pose in estposes]) # Filter NaNs validmask = ~np.any(np.isnan(gttrans), axis=1) gttrans = gttrans[validmask] esttrans = esttrans[validmask] Nvalid = len(gttrans) if Nvalid == 0: return 100.0, np.array([]) # 2. Align estimated trajectory to ground truth # Using Horn's method for Sim(3) or SE(3). # For ATE, often a similarity transform (scale, rotation, translation) is used to align the trajectories. # This step is critical to remove global scale and drift differences. # We implement a simplified SE(3) alignment (Procrustes) here. # For full Sim(3), scale estimation is added. # Compute centroids mugt = np.mean(gttrans, axis=0) muest = np.mean(esttrans, axis=0) # Center the data gtcentered = gttrans - mugt estcentered = esttrans - muest # Compute covariance matrix H = estcentered.T @ gtcentered # SVD U, S, Vt = np.linalg.svd(H) # Rotation d = np.linalg.det(Vt.T @ U.T) D = np.eye(3) D[2, 2] = d R = Vt.T @ D @ U.T # Translation t = mugt - R @ muest # Scale (Optional for Sim(3), but often ATE is computed after SE(3) alignment in some contexts, # or Sim(3) in others. The source mentions "Align... using Horn's method". # Horn's method can solve for Sim(3). We will assume Sim(3) alignment for robustness. # Scale factor scale = np.sum(np.square(gtcentered)) / np.sum(np.square(estcentered)) scale = np.sqrt(scale) # Apply alignment estaligned = scale (estcentered @ R.T) + mugt # 3. Compute translation errors etransvec = gttrans - estaligned transerror = np.sqrt(np.sum(etransvec2, axis=1)) # 4. Compute RMSE atermse = np.sqrt(np.mean(transerror2)) return atermse, transerror Parameters: baseline: In some evaluations, a baseline map processed with a Gaussian blur kernel (size 9 \times 9 \times 9 voxels, \sigma=4/3) is used to compute ATE. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: If trajectory evaluation fails (e.g., no valid poses), ATE RMSE is set to 100.0. Ensure coordinate frame conventions (world-to-camera vs. camera-to-world) are consistent between GT and estimated poses before alignment. Precision issues may arise if trajectories are very large or very small; normalization during alignment helps. Time Complexity: O(N) for error computation, where N is the number of frames. Alignment is O(N) or O(N \log N) depending on the solver, but typically dominated by the linear scan for error calculation. Memory Complexity: O(N) to store translation vectors and errors. Strengths: Provides a single scalar metric for global trajectory accuracy. Simple to compute and interpret. Limitations: Sensitive to global scale errors if Sim(3) alignment is not used. Does not capture local drift or oscillations as well as relative error metrics. When to use: Evaluating the global consistency of SLAM systems, visual odometry, or pose estimation pipelines. When not to use: When local accuracy or drift over short intervals is more important than global consistency. Origin: The Absolute Trajectory Error (ATE) was introduced as a standard metric for evaluating ego-motion estimation in SLAM and visual odometry. It is widely used in benchmarks such as the TUM RGB-D dataset. Development: Initially proposed to measure the integrated distance between pose estimates and ground truth, it has become a de facto standard in the field. Usage: Commonly used in RGB-D SLAM, Structure from Motion (SfM), and NeRF/Gaussian Splatting pose estimation evaluations.
