head: Camera Projection and Unprojection, Point Projection, project, unproject
body: This method transforms 3D points from world coordinates into 2D image coordinates, computing both the pixel location and a visibility mask indicating whether the point lies in front of the camera. It solves the problem of determining the 2D pixel location and visibility of 3D geometry for a specific camera view. Inputs: points: A tensor of 3D points in world coordinates, shape [..., 3]. extrinsics: A 4x4 camera-to-world (c2w) matrix or batch of matrices. intrinsics: A 3x3 camera intrinsic matrix or batch of matrices. Outputs: pixellocations: 2D pixel coordinates, shape [..., 2]. infrontofcamera: A boolean mask, shape [..., 1], indicating if the point is in front of the camera. Data Structures: Points are represented as homogeneous coordinates xyzh of shape [..., 4], where the fourth component is 1.0. Vectors (directions) are represented as homogeneous coordinates vh of shape [..., 4], where the fourth component is 0.0. Steps: 1. Homogenize Points: Append a 1.0 component to the last dimension of the input points to convert them to homogeneous coordinates. xyzh = [x, y, z, 1.0] 2. Transform to Camera Space: Apply the inverse of the extrinsics matrix to the homogeneous points to transform them from world space to camera space. This is a rigid-body transformation implemented via matrix multiplication or Einstein summation einsum(transformation, homogeneouscoordinates, "... i j,... j ->... i"). points{cam\h} = \text{extrinsics}^{-1} \times xyzh 3. Check Visibility: Determine if points are in front of the camera by checking the Z coordinate (the last element of the camera-space homogeneous vector, which corresponds to the depth). in\front\of\camera = points{cam\h}[..., -1] \ge 0 4. Project to Image Space: a. Drop the homogeneous component to get 3D camera-space points: points{cam} = points{cam\h}[...,:-1] b. Normalize by depth (perspective division). To avoid division by zero, add a small epsilon (default torch.finfo(torch.float32).eps) to the depth, and replace infinite depth values with a large finite value (default 1e8). points{norm} = \frac{points{cam}}{\text{clamp}(points{cam}[..., 2:], \epsilon, \infty)} c. Multiply by the intrinsic matrix K to get pixel coordinates. pixel\coords{hom} = K \times points{norm} The first two components of pixelcoordshom are the final 2D pixel locations (u, v). Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import torch def project3dto2d(points, extrinsics, intrinsics, epsilon=None, infinity=1e8): """ Projects 3D world points to 2D image coordinates. Args: points: Tensor of shape [..., 3] containing 3D world coordinates. extrinsics: Tensor of shape [..., 4, 4] containing camera-to-world matrices. intrinsics: Tensor of shape [..., 3, 3] containing camera intrinsic matrices. epsilon: Small value to prevent division by zero. Defaults to torch.finfo(torch.float32).eps. infinity: Value used to replace infinite depth values. Defaults to 1e8. Returns: pixellocations: Tensor of shape [..., 2] containing 2D pixel coordinates. infrontofcamera: Tensor of shape [..., 1] boolean mask. """ if epsilon is None: epsilon = torch.finfo(torch.float32).eps # Step 1: Homogenize points (append 1.0) # points shape: [..., 3] -> [..., 4] ones = torch.oneslike(points[...,:1]) pointsh = torch.cat([points, ones], dim=-1) # Step 2: Transform to camera space # extrinsics is c2w, so we need w2c = extrinsics^{-1} # Using einsum for batched matrix multiplication: w2c @ pointsh # w2c shape: [..., 4, 4], pointsh shape: [..., 4] # Result: [..., 4] w2c = torch.inverse(extrinsics) pointscamh = torch.einsum('...ij,...j->...i', w2c, pointsh) # Step 3: Check visibility (Z >= 0) # pointscamh[..., -1] is the Z coordinate in camera space infrontofcamera = pointscamh[..., -1:] >= 0 # Step 4: Project to 2D # Drop homogeneous component to get 3D camera space points pointscam = pointscamh[...,:-1] # Normalize by depth (Z) # Replace infinities with large finite value, then clamp to epsilon z = pointscam[..., 2:] z = torch.where(torch.isinf(z), infinity, z) z = torch.clamp(z, min=epsilon) pointsnorm = pointscam / z # Multiply by intrinsics # intrinsics shape: [..., 3, 3], pointsnorm shape: [..., 3] # Result: [..., 3] (homogeneous pixel coordinates) pixelcoordsh = torch.einsum('...ij,...j->...i', intrinsics, pointsnorm) # Extract 2D pixel locations (x, y) pixellocations = pixelcoordsh[...,:2] return pixellocations, infrontofcamera Pitfalls: Projected eigenvectors are generally not orthogonal in 2D image space, even if the original 3D tensor was symmetric with orthogonal eigenvectors. Points exactly on the camera plane (z=0) cause division by zero; clamping or adding epsilon is required. Perspective projection maps 3D world points to 2D image coordinates using a pinhole camera model, where a line joining the 3D point to the center of projection intersects the image plane. It solves the problem of determining the 2D pixel location and visibility of 3D geometry for a specific camera view. This method generates a depth map for a novel camera viewpoint by projecting an existing 3D point cloud onto the 2D image plane and resolving occlusions. It solves the problem of converting sparse or implicit 3D geometry into an explicit per-pixel depth buffer, distinguishing itself from volumetric rendering by relying on discrete point proximity rather than ray-marching through a density field. For a query 3D point p, an observed 2D view Im, camera pose \xim, and intrinsics Km, the corresponding 2D pixel features Fp^m are retrieved using the reprojection function P. If the projected 3D point lies inside the image boundaries, the nearest pixel's features are selected and duplicated to the 3D point; if it lies outside, a zero vector is assigned. Nearest neighbor interpolation is used instead of bilinear interpolation or kernel functions, though advanced techniques may address discretization issues. Given an RGB image Ii and its estimated depth map Di, the 3D point cloud pi is calculated using intrinsic parameters Ki and extrinsic parameters \xii via pi = P^{-1}(Di, Ki, \xii). This point cloud is then projected to another view j to find corresponding pixels, where the color of pixels projected from Ij onto Ii is I{i,j} = P(Ij, Kj, \xij, pi). Reprojection error is computed to filter out invalid pairs and mitigate occlusion effects. For a point X in 3D space with world coordinates Xw, forward projection to camera coordinates Xc is performed using the 4x4 extrinsic matrix d (containing translation t and rotation R): \tilde{X}c = d\tilde{X}w, where \tilde{X} denotes homogeneous coordinates. 2D pixel coordinates xc are obtained by normalizing homogeneous image coordinates \tilde{x}c by depth, where \tilde{x}c = K\tilde{X}c, using the known camera intrinsic matrix K. The center of each occupied voxel is used as the starting position to reduce aliasing artifacts. Occlusion is identified by grouping points projecting to the same pixel (u,v) into set P{uv}. The point with the minimum z-value in camera coordinates is marked as non-occluded (P^{uv} = \arg \min{Pi \in P{uv}} zi), and remaining points are marked as occluded. Occluded voxels are filled with the average color of all non-occluded views for the same point, creating an 'RGB main' triplet suitable for renderers without plenoptic color support. Time Complexity: O(N) for N points, as each point undergoes a constant number of matrix multiplications and divisions. Memory Complexity: O(N) to store the input points and output pixel locations/masks. Strengths: Efficiently maps 3D geometry to 2D image space, enabling visibility checks and pixel-based feature retrieval. Limitations: Does not handle occlusion resolution within the projection step itself (requires additional logic like depth sorting or z-buffering). Projected eigenvectors are generally not orthogonal in 2D image space, even if the original 3D tensor was symmetric with orthogonal eigenvectors. When to use: When rendering 3D points to 2D images, computing visibility masks, or retrieving 2D features for 3D points. When not to use: When occlusion handling is required as part of the projection (use Depth Estimation from Point Cloud or PPC Colorization instead). The method originates from standard computer graphics and multi-view geometry, utilizing the pinhole camera model and homogeneous coordinates. It is a fundamental building block in volume rendering pipelines, particularly in neural rendering methods like NeRF and 3D Gaussian Splatting, where 3D points (or Gaussians) are projected to 2D for rasterization or feature aggregation. body: Perspective projection maps 3D world points to 2D image coordinates using a pinhole camera model, where a line joining the 3D point to the center of projection intersects the image plane. It solves the problem of determining the 2D pixel location and visibility of 3D geometry for a specific camera view. Inputs: 3D points M with homogeneous coordinates \begin{bmatrix} X & Y & Z & 1 \end{bmatrix}^T in world space. Camera calibration matrix K (intrinsic parameters). Extrinsic parameters: rotation matrix R and translation vector t defining the transformation from world to camera coordinates. Outputs: 2D image coordinates \begin{bmatrix} x & y & 1 \end{bmatrix}^T in homogeneous pixel space. Data Structures: K: 3 \times 3 matrix. [R|t]: 3 \times 4 matrix, where R is 3 \times 3 and t is 3 \times 1. P: 3 \times 4 projective camera matrix, computed as P = K[R|t]. Parameters: fx, fy: Focal lengths in pixels. Calculated as fx = f/kx and fy = f/ky, where f is focal length in mm and kx, ky are pixels/mm. s: Skew parameter. Typically 0. \alpha: Aspect ratio. Typically 1. (u0, v0): Principal point coordinates. Steps: 1. Construct the extrinsic matrix [R|t] representing the world-to-camera transformation. 2. Construct the intrinsic matrix K: K = \begin{pmatrix} fx & s & u0 \\ 0 & \alpha fy & v0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 \end{pmatrix}. 3. Compute the projective camera matrix P = K[R|t]. 4. For each 3D point M = \begin{bmatrix} X & Y & Z & 1 \end{bmatrix}^T, compute the homogeneous image coordinates: \begin{bmatrix} \lambda x \\ \lambda y \\ \lambda \end{bmatrix} = P \begin{bmatrix} X \\ Y \\ Z \\ 1 \end{bmatrix}. 5. Perform perspective division by dividing the x and y components by the third component \lambda (the camera-space z coordinate) to obtain normalized image coordinates. 6. Handle edge cases: Points with \lambda \le 0 are behind the camera and should be discarded or flagged. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import torch def perspectiveprojection(pts, calibs): """ Projects 3D points to 2D using perspective projection. Args: pts: Tensor of shape [B, N, 3] containing world coordinates. calibs: Tensor of shape [B, 3, 4] containing the combined intrinsic/extrinsic matrix P. Returns: pts2d: Tensor of shape [B, N, 2] containing pixel coordinates. """ # 1. Permute pts from [B, N, 3] to [B, 3, N] ptsperm = pts.permute(0, 2, 1) # 2. Multiply by rotation part of calibs [B, 3, 3] ptsrot = torch.matmul(calibs[:,:3,:3], ptsperm) # 3. Add translation part of calibs [B, 3, 1] ptscam = ptsrot + calibs[:,:3, 3:4] # 4. Divide x and y coordinates by z coordinate z = ptscam[:, 2:3,:] pts2d = ptscam[:,:2,:] / z # 5. Permute back to [B, N, 2] return pts2d.permute(0, 2, 1) Stereo projection applies a perspective projection twice with adjustments to simulate the viewpoint for an observer's left and right eye, creating a stereo effect. It generates two correlated view frustums rather than one. Choose when depth perception from two correlated views is required. MCOP Projection Geometry is a projection method for light field displays that uses two distinct viewpoints to map 3D world points to projector screen coordinates: an emitter E for horizontal coordinates and a virtual viewer V for vertical coordinates. It solves the problem of perspective-correct rendering on holographic screens that are sharply transmissive horizontally but scatter widely vertically, ensuring view separation is maintained horizontally while allowing vertical viewing flexibility. It differs from standard perspective projection by decoupling the horizontal and vertical projection centers, and from stereo projection by supporting a continuous light field rather than just two views. Choose for holographic screens requiring horizontal view separation and vertical flexibility. Eye projection is a viewpoint-dependent technique for visualizing 3D vector fields by projecting 3D vectors onto a surface in a direction parallel to the viewing direction. It produces the most intuitive representation of a constant direction vector field for a single image, making the uniform direction of the field readily apparent. Unlike viewpoint-independent techniques, it introduces visual discontinuities (jumpiness or flashing) when the viewpoint changes in animation. Choose for intuitive visualization of vector fields in single images, accepting viewpoint-dependent discontinuities. Strengths: Standard model for pinhole cameras; computationally efficient; widely supported in computer vision libraries. Limitations: Fails for points behind the camera (\lambda \le 0); assumes ideal pinhole geometry without lens distortion. When to use: When mapping 3D world points to 2D pixel coordinates for a calibrated camera. When not to use: For orthographic views or when lens distortion correction is required before projection. The pinhole camera model is one of the most widely used models in computer vision for imaging processes. It was formalized in the context of epipolar and projective geometry, with foundational reviews by Triggs. The decomposition of the camera matrix into intrinsic and extrinsic parameters is attributed to Hartley and Zisserman. name: Stereo Projection
body: Stereo projection applies a perspective projection twice with adjustments to simulate the viewpoint for an observer's left and right eye, creating a stereo effect. It generates two correlated view frustums rather than one. Inputs and Outputs: Input: 3D scene geometry, a base camera position, and the interpupillary distance (IPD). Output: Two 2D image buffers (left eye and right eye). Data Structures: The method relies on two view frustums. Each frustum is defined by an eye position, a view direction, and projection parameters (field of view, aspect ratio, near/far clipping planes). Steps: 1. Calculate Eye Positions: Offset the central camera position horizontally by half the IPD to determine the left and right eye origins. 2. Define Frustums: Construct two perspective projection matrices corresponding to each eye's position and view direction. 3. Transform Geometry: Transform all 3D scene vertices into the clip space of the left eye frustum. 4. Render Left Image: Rasterize the transformed geometry to produce the left eye image. 5. Transform Geometry: Transform all 3D scene vertices into the clip space of the right eye frustum. 6. Render Right Image: Rasterize the transformed geometry to produce the right eye image. The two resulting versions of the scene can be drawn in succession using shuttered glasses synced with the monitor, or drawn simultaneously using stereo viewers. Formulas: Not given in the sources. Standard perspective projection matrices are used, adjusted for each eye's specific position and orientation. Parameters: IPD: Typical human value is ~63–65 mm. Convergence Distance: The distance at which the left and right view directions intersect. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Vertical Parallax: Occurs if the projection planes of the left and right eyes do not coincide, causing visual discomfort. Clipping: Geometry may be clipped differently by the two frustums, potentially causing popping artifacts if not handled carefully. Precision: Floating-point precision errors in eye position calculation can lead to misalignment. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def perspectivematrix(fovdeg, aspect, near, far): fovrad = math.radians(fovdeg) f = 1.0 / math.tan(fovrad / 2.0) return [[f / aspect, 0, 0, 0], [0, f, 0, 0], [0, 0, (far + near) / (near - far), -1], [0, 0, (2 far near) / (near - far), 0]] def projectvertices(vertices, projmatrix): projected = [] for v in vertices: vh = v + [1.0] vproj = [0, 0, 0, 0] for i in range(4): vproj[i] = sum(projmatrix[i][j] vh[j] for j in range(4)) if vproj[3] != 0: projected.append([c / vproj[3] for c in vproj[:3]]) return projected def renderstereo(scenevertices, cameracenter, ipd, fov, aspect, near, far): eyeoffset = ipd / 2.0 lefteyepos = [cameracenter[0] - eyeoffset, cameracenter[1], cameracenter[2]] righteyepos = [cameracenter[0] + eyeoffset, cameracenter[1], cameracenter[2]] leftproj = perspectivematrix(fov, aspect, near, far) rightproj = perspectivematrix(fov, aspect, near, far) leftimage = projectvertices(scenevertices, leftproj) rightimage = projectvertices(scenevertices, rightproj) # Rasterization step: convert projected vertices to screen pixels # The sources do not provide rasterization details return leftimage, rightimage Uses non-symmetric camera frustums to generate coincident projection planes for the left and right eyes, preventing vertical parallax. It aligns the central viewing directions of both cameras in parallel while focusing on different points, ensuring a natural and comfortable stereo effect. Choose this when vertical parallax must be avoided, such as in CAVE systems or when the screen is not centered between the eyes. Time Complexity: Double the rendering time of a single perspective view, as two full passes are required. Memory Complexity: Requires storage for two image buffers (or one interleaved buffer). Performance: Dependent on the complexity of the scene and the efficiency of the rasterization pipeline. Strengths: Provides true depth perception for stereoscopic displays. Limitations: Requires specialized hardware (shutter glasses, stereo viewers) or post-processing. Vertical parallax can cause discomfort if not managed. When to Use: When stereoscopic depth is required for visualization or interaction. When Not to Use: When hardware support is unavailable or when performance is critical and depth is not necessary. Stereo projection is a fundamental technique in computer graphics for creating stereoscopic 3D images. It is based on the principle of binocular vision, where each eye sees a slightly different perspective of the world. The technique is widely used in virtual reality, 3D movies, and scientific visualization. The specific implementation described here is referenced in the context of the Smokeview tool for visualizing fire dynamics simulation data. name: Off-axis Stereoscopic Rendering
head: Off-axis Stereo Rendering
body: Off-axis stereoscopic rendering is a technique that uses non-symmetric camera frustums to generate coincident projection planes for the left and right eyes, thereby preventing vertical parallax. Unlike symmetric stereo methods, it aligns the central viewing directions of both cameras in parallel while focusing on different points, ensuring a natural and comfortable stereo effect. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: Image width w (pixels), image height h (pixels), focal length fo, stereo base b (half the camera x-offset), and angle of view \alpha. Outputs: Two trimmed images of resolution w \times h, one for the left eye and one for the right eye, which are combined for display. Data Structures: Standard image buffers are used, initially sized at (w + \delta) \times h for rendering and trimmed to w \times h. Steps: 1. Compute the angle of view \alpha using the normalized image plane width d (where d=2 for a range of -1 to 1) and focal length fo: \alpha = 2 \cdot \arctan\left(\frac{d}{2 \cdot fo}\right) 2. Compute the non-overlapping pixel amount \delta: \delta = \frac{b \cdot w}{2 \cdot fo \cdot \tan(\alpha/2)} 3. Determine the extended resolution by calculating the render buffer width as w{ext} = w + \delta, while keeping the height at h. 4. Configure the left camera with a non-symmetric (off-axis) frustum, aligning its central viewing direction parallel to the right camera's direction. 5. Render the scene to a buffer of size (w + \delta) \times h using the left camera's off-axis projection. 6. Configure the right camera with a corresponding off-axis frustum, maintaining parallel central viewing directions. 7. Render the scene to a buffer of size (w + \delta) \times h using the right camera's off-axis projection. 8. Trim both rendered images to the original resolution w \times h to obtain the final off-axis projection planes. 9. Combine the left and right images for display on a 120 Hz frame-sequential stereo system with active LCD shutter glasses or a dual display passive stereo system with polaroid glasses. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def offaxisstereorender(scene, w, h, fo, b): # 1. Compute angle of view d = 2.0 # Normalized image plane width (-1 to 1) alpha = 2.0 math.atan(d / (2.0 fo)) # 2. Compute non-overlapping pixel amount tanhalfalpha = math.tan(alpha / 2.0) delta = (b w) / (2.0 fo tanhalfalpha) # 3. Extended resolution wext = w + delta hext = h # 4-5. Render left eye with off-axis frustum leftfrustum = buildoffaxisfrustum(wext, hext, fo, b, 'left') leftbuffer = rendertobuffer(scene, leftfrustum, wext, hext) # 6-7. Render right eye with off-axis frustum rightfrustum = buildoffaxisfrustum(wext, hext, fo, b, 'right') rightbuffer = rendertobuffer(scene, rightfrustum, wext, hext) # 8. Trim images to original resolution # The trimming offset assumes the non-overlapping regions are distributed # symmetrically or that the off-axis matrix accounts for the shift such that # the center of the original view is preserved. startx = delta / 2.0 leftimage = leftbuffer[:, int(startx):int(startx) + w,:] rightimage = rightbuffer[:, int(startx):int(startx) + w,:] return leftimage, rightimage def buildoffaxisfrustum(width, height, focallength, stereobase, eye): # Constructs a non-symmetric projection matrix. # The matrix shifts the projection plane so that the central viewing # directions of left and right cameras remain parallel. return {"width": width, "height": height, "focallength": focallength, "stereobase": stereobase, "eye": eye} def rendertobuffer(scene, frustum, width, height): # Rasterizes the scene using the provided camera frustum. # Returns an image buffer of shape (height, width, channels). return [[0.0] width for in range(height)] Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Vertical Parallax: Using symmetric frustums instead of off-axis frustums causes vertical parallax when eyes are misaligned vertically, leading to visual discomfort and inaccurate stereo effects. Perspective Rendering: Perspective rendering is essential for meaningful stereoscopic display. Time Complexity: Rendering two views independently doubles the rendering time compared to a single view. Memory Complexity: Requires buffer space for two images of size (w + \delta) \times h during rendering, plus the final w \times h buffers. Strengths: Prevents vertical parallax and visual discomfort. Produces coincident projection planes for both eyes. Limitations: Requires rendering two views, increasing computational load. When to use: When high-quality, comfortable stereo visualization is required. When not to use: Not given in the sources. The method uses non-symmetric camera frustums to produce coincident projection planes for both eyes. An introduction to the subtleties of stereographics can be found in external resources. name: MCOP Projection Geometry
head: Light Field Display Projection Geometry, Light field geometry, MCOP perspective projection, Projector-based multi-view projection, Two-viewpoint projection
body: MCOP Projection Geometry is a projection method for light field displays that uses two distinct viewpoints to map 3D world points to projector screen coordinates: an emitter E for horizontal coordinates and a virtual viewer V for vertical coordinates. It solves the problem of perspective-correct rendering on holographic screens that are sharply transmissive horizontally but scatter widely vertically, ensuring view separation is maintained horizontally while allowing vertical viewing flexibility. It differs from standard perspective projection by decoupling the horizontal and vertical projection centers, and from stereo projection by supporting a continuous light field rather than just two views. Inputs: World space point P = (Px, Py, Pz). Emitter origin E = (Ex, Ey, Ez). Virtual viewer position V = (Vx, Vy, Vz), typically defined by height Vy and distance Vz from the screen plane. Screen plane defined at z = 0. Image rectangle R^- = (Rx^-, Ry^-) and R^+ = (Rx^+, Ry^+) defining the projected image geometry orthogonal to the Z axis. Outputs: Screen projected position S = (Sx, Sy). Normalized projected coordinates H = (Hx, Hy, Hz) for rasterization. Data Structures: Points are represented as 3D vectors (x, y, z). Rectangle parameters are stored as four scalar values defining the bounds in the image plane. Steps: 1. Compute Horizontal Screen Coordinate (Sx): Intersect the ray originating from emitter E passing through point P with the screen plane z=0. 2. Compute Vertical Screen Coordinate (Sy): Intersect the ray originating from point P passing through the virtual viewer V with the screen plane z=0. 3. Remap to Normalized Coordinates: Transform S into the image rectangle defined by R^- and R^+ to obtain Hx and Hy. Formulas: The screen projected position S is computed as: Sx = Ex - Ez \cdot \frac{Ex - Px}{Ez - Pz} Sy = Vy - Vz \cdot \frac{Vy - Py}{Vz - Pz} The normalized projected coordinates H are computed as: Hx = \frac{(Sx - Ex) \cdot 2}{Rx^+ - Rx^-} - \frac{Rx^+ + Rx^-}{Rx^+ - Rx^-} Hy = \frac{(Sy - Ey) \cdot 2}{Ry^+ - Ry^-} - \frac{Ry^+ + Ry^-}{Ry^+ - Ry^-} Hz = -Pz / Vz Parameters: Vy: Virtual viewer height from screen. Vz: Virtual viewer distance from screen. E = (Ex, Ey, Ez): Projector emitter origin. P = (Px, Py, Pz): World space point. R^+, R^-: 2D rectangle defining projected image geometry orthogonal to Z axis. Screen plane z-coordinate: z = 0. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Division by zero occurs if Pz = Ez or Pz = Vz, requiring Pz \neq Ez and Pz \neq Vz for valid projection. The model assumes a pinhole emitter model. The solution is exact for all viewers at the same distance from the screen and height as the virtual viewer. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def mcopprojection(P, E, V, Rminus, Rplus): """ Projects a 3D point P to normalized coordinates H using MCOP geometry. Args: P: tuple (Px, Py, Pz) E: tuple (Ex, Ey, Ez) V: tuple (Vx, Vy, Vz) Rminus: tuple (Rxmin, Rymin) Rplus: tuple (Rxmax, Rymax) Returns: H: tuple (Hx, Hy, Hz) """ Px, Py, Pz = P Ex, Ey, Ez = E Vx, Vy, Vz = V Rxmin, Rymin = Rminus Rxmax, Rymax = Rplus # Compute screen projected position S # Sx: Intersection of ray E->P with z=0 plane # Formula: Sx = Ex - Ez (Ex - Px) / (Ez - Pz) if Ez == Pz: raise ValueError("Emitter and point are coplanar in Z") Sx = Ex - Ez (Ex - Px) / (Ez - Pz) # Sy: Intersection of ray P->V with z=0 plane # Formula: Sy = Vy - Vz (Vy - Py) / (Vz - Pz) if Vz == Pz: raise ValueError("Virtual viewer and point are coplanar in Z") Sy = Vy - Vz (Vy - Py) / (Vz - Pz) # Remap to normalized projected coordinates H # Hx: Linear transform to image rectangle Rxrange = Rxmax - Rxmin if Rxrange == 0: raise ValueError("Invalid image rectangle width") Hx = ((Sx - Ex) 2 / Rxrange) - ((Rxmax + Rxmin) / Rxrange) # Hy: Linear transform to image rectangle Ryrange = Rymax - Rymin if Ryrange == 0: raise ValueError("Invalid image rectangle height") Hy = ((Sy - Ey) 2 / Ryrange) - ((Rymax + Rymin) / Ryrange) # Hz: Depth based on distance to screen relative to viewer Hz = -Pz / Vz return (Hx, Hy, Hz) Projects points to two distinct views for stereoscopic 3D. Choose when only two viewpoints are needed. MCOP supports a continuous light field. Standard single-center projection. MCOP builds on this but uses two centers for light field displays. Time Complexity: Constant time O(1) per point, involving basic arithmetic operations. Memory Complexity: Minimal, storing only point coordinates and projection parameters. Measured Performance: The hardware implementation using 96 fast 320x240 LCD displays fed by FPGA input processing units is capable of visualizing 7.4M beams/frame. On-screen 2D pixel size is s0 = 1.25mm, with angular accuracy of 0.8^\circ. Strengths: Provides perspective-correct images for a specific virtual viewer while maintaining horizontal view separation on holographic screens. Efficient for rasterization applications. Limitations: Perspective is exact only for viewers at the same height and distance as the virtual viewer. Vertical viewing angle is fixed by the virtual viewer assumption, though the screen scatters widely vertically. When to use: For rendering on light field displays with holographic screens that have anisotropic scattering properties (horizontal selectivity, vertical scattering). When not to use: For standard displays or when a wide range of vertical viewing angles are required without a fixed virtual viewer model. The method is described in the context of interactive light field displays. It addresses the specific optical properties of holographic screens used in light field displays, which maintain sub-degree view separation horizontally but scatter widely vertically. The approach was developed to allow 3D graphics applications to project models correctly onto such displays by accounting for the screen's transformation properties. The hardware implementation described involves an array of LCD displays and FPGA processing units. name: Eye Projection
head: Vieweye projection
body: Eye projection is a viewpoint-dependent technique for visualizing 3D vector fields by projecting 3D vectors onto a surface in a direction parallel to the viewing direction. It produces the most intuitive representation of a constant direction vector field for a single image, making the uniform direction of the field readily apparent. Unlike viewpoint-independent techniques, it introduces visual discontinuities (jumpiness or flashing) when the viewpoint changes in animation. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A 3D vector field \mathbf{V}, a surface S (typically a contour surface), and a viewing direction vector \mathbf{V}{view}. Output: A 2D projection of the vector field on the surface, visualized as particle traces. Data Structures: Not given in the sources. Steps: 1. Determine the viewing direction vector \mathbf{V}{view} from the camera position to the scene. 2. For each point on the surface, project the 3D velocity vector \mathbf{V} onto the surface along the direction of \mathbf{V}{view}. 3. Generate particle traces using the projected vectors, reusing the exact same set of trial seed points as the previous frame. 4. Start each particle trace with the same "phase" as a nearby trace in the previous frame to minimize visual discontinuity. Formulas: Not given in the sources. The text describes the geometric concept (projection parallel to viewing direction) but does not provide a specific mathematical formula for the projection operation. Parameters: Trial seed points: The same set of trial seed points as the previous frame should be used to minimize visual effects of changes. Phase: Each particle trace should start with the same "phase" as a nearby trace in the previous frame. Edge cases and pitfalls: Viewpoint changes: When changing the viewpoint for a film loop, the projection of the 3D vectors to the surfaces changes, resulting in a different set of particle traces. This causes jumpiness or flashing in animation. Surface suitability: This projection is only suitable for simple surfaces which are centered on the rotational axis. Information loss: The projection of a 3D vector field onto a 2D curved surface loses and distorts much of the information from the 3D field, limiting the usefulness of these techniques for 3D visualization. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. from collections import namedtuple Trace = namedtuple('Trace', ['startpoint', 'path', 'phase']) def eyeprojection(vectorfield, surface, vview, previoustraces): # Step 1: Determine viewing direction (provided as vview) # Step 2: Project vectors onto surface along vview projectedvectors = [] for point in surface.points: v3d = vectorfield[point] # Project along viewing direction: find intersection of ray from point along vview with surface t = intersectraysurface(point, vview, surface) if t is not None: intersectionpoint = point + t vview projectedvectors.append((intersectionpoint, v3d)) else: projectedvectors.append((point, v3d)) # Step 3 & 4: Generate traces with continuity (same seeds and phase) traces = [] for prevtrace in previoustraces: newtrace = advancetrace(prevtrace, projectedvectors, prevtrace.phase) traces.append(newtrace) return traces def intersectraysurface(origin, direction, surface): """Finds the closest positive intersection distance t along direction with surface.""" closestt = None for face in surface.faces: t = raytriangleintersection(origin, direction, face) if t is not None and (closestt is None or t < closestt): closestt = t return closestt def raytriangleintersection(origin, direction, triangle): """Möller–Trumbore ray-triangle intersection.""" v1, v2, v3 = triangle.vertices e1 = v2 - v1 e2 = v3 - v1 h = cross(direction, e2) a = dot(e1, h) if abs(a) < 1e-8: return None f = 1.0 / a s = origin - v1 u = f dot(s, h) if u < 0.0 or u > 1.0: return None q = cross(s, e1) v = f dot(direction, q) if v < 0.0 or u + v > 1.0: return None t = f dot(e2, q) return t if t > 1e-7 else None def advancetrace(prevtrace, projectedvectors, phaseoffset): """Advances a particle trace using projected vectors, maintaining phase continuity.""" newpath = [] currentpos = prevtrace.startpoint stepsize = 0.1 # Typical step size for particle integration for in range(prevtrace.steps): nearest = min(projectedvectors, key=lambda p: distance(currentpos, p[0])) v = nearest[1] currentpos = currentpos + v stepsize newpath.append(currentpos) return Trace(startpoint=prevtrace.startpoint, path=newpath, phase=phaseoffset) Projects vectors for stereo viewing, providing depth cues. Choose when depth perception is critical. Uses a specific projection geometry for multi-center of projection. Choose for complex multi-view setups. Time and memory complexity: Not given in the sources. Measured performance: Not given in the sources. Scaling: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Produces the most intuitive representation of a constant direction vector field for a single image. The uniform direction of the vector field is readily apparent. Limitations: Viewpoint-dependent, causing jumpiness or flashing in animation when the viewpoint changes. Only suitable for simple surfaces centered on the rotational axis. Loses and distorts much of the information from the 3D field when projected onto a 2D curved surface. When to use: For single-image visualization of 3D vector fields where intuitive representation of direction is prioritized over animation smoothness or 3D information preservation. When not to use: For animated sequences where viewpoint changes are frequent, or for complex surfaces not centered on the rotational axis. Origin: The technique is described in the paper "Visualizing 3D velocity fields near contour surfaces" by Weusing. History and development: The technique is presented as an alternative to viewpoint-independent techniques, highlighting its trade-offs in terms of visual continuity and information preservation. Where it is used: Visualization of 3D velocity fields near contour surfaces. name: Depth Estimation from Point Cloud
head: Closest Point Depth Estimation
body: This method generates a depth map for a novel camera viewpoint by projecting an existing 3D point cloud onto the 2D image plane and resolving occlusions. It solves the problem of converting sparse or implicit 3D geometry into an explicit per-pixel depth buffer, distinguishing itself from volumetric rendering by relying on discrete point proximity rather than ray-marching through a density field. Inputs: A 3D point cloud P = \{p1, p2, \dots, pN\}, where each pi \in \mathbb{R}^3 is a point in world coordinates. A target camera defined by its intrinsic matrix K and extrinsic matrix [R|t] (rotation and translation from world to camera coordinates). Outputs: A depth image D of resolution W \times H, where D(u,v) is the distance from the camera center to the closest surface point at pixel (u,v). Data Structures: A 2D array depthmap of size H \times W, initialized to zero or infinity. A list of projected points for each pixel to resolve conflicts. Steps: 1. Coordinate Transformation: Transform each 3D point pi from world coordinates to camera coordinates p'i: p'i = R pi + t Let p'i = (Xi, Yi, Zi). 2. Projection: Project each transformed point p'i onto the image plane using the intrinsic matrix K. For a pinhole camera model: ui = \frac{fx Xi}{Zi} + cx vi = \frac{fy Yi}{Zi} + cy where fx, fy are focal lengths and cx, cy are principal point coordinates. 3. Validation: Check if the projected pixel (ui, vi) lies within the image boundaries [0, W-1] \times [0, H-1] and if the depth Zi > 0 (point is in front of the camera). Discard points failing these checks. 4. Occlusion Resolution: For each valid pixel (u, v), collect all points pi that project to this pixel. Select the point p{closest} with the minimum depth value Z{min} = \min \{Zi\}. 5. Depth Assignment: Set the depth value for pixel (u, v) to the depth of the closest point: D(u, v) = Z{min} 6. Hole Handling: Pixels with no projected points remain at their initial value (typically 0 or undefined), representing background or missing surface information. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def estimatedepthfrompointcloud(pointcloud, cameraintrinsics, cameraextrinsics, imagewidth, imageheight): """ pointcloud: List of 3D points (N, 3) in world coordinates. cameraintrinsics: Matrix K (3, 3). cameraextrinsics: Matrix [R|t] (3, 4). imagewidth, imageheight: Dimensions of the output depth map. """ # Initialize depth map with zeros (indicating no data) depthmap = np.zeros((imageheight, imagewidth)) # Extract camera parameters R = cameraextrinsics[:,:3] t = cameraextrinsics[:, 3] K = cameraintrinsics # Transform points to camera coordinates # pworld is (N, 3), pcam is (N, 3) pcam = (R @ pointcloud.T).T + t # Project to 2D # X, Y, Z are (N,) arrays X = pcam[:, 0] Y = pcam[:, 1] Z = pcam[:, 2] # Avoid division by zero validdepth = Z > 1e-5 # Calculate pixel coordinates u = (K[0, 0] X / Z) + K[0, 2] v = (K[1, 1] Y / Z) + K[1, 2] # Filter valid points: in front of camera and within image bounds validu = (u >= 0) & (u < imagewidth) validv = (v >= 0) & (v < imageheight) validindices = np.where(validdepth & validu & validv)[0] # Get valid coordinates uvalid = u[validindices] vvalid = v[validindices] zvalid = Z[validindices] # Round to integer pixel coordinates uint = uvalid.astype(int) vint = vvalid.astype(int) # Find closest point for each pixel # We need to keep only the minimum Z for each (u, v) # Create a mask or use a dictionary/array to store min depth mindepths = np.full((imageheight, imagewidth), np.inf) # Iterate through valid points and update minimum depth for idx in range(len(validindices)): up = uint[idx] vp = vint[idx] zp = zvalid[idx] if zp < mindepths[vp, up]: mindepths[vp, up] = zp # Replace inf with 0 for background/holes mindepths[np.isinf(mindepths)] = 0 return mindepths Parameters: N: Number of points in the cloud. Typical values depend on the generation method (e.g., N=8 views used in source for generation, but N points in cloud vary). \alpha: Weighting factor in related generation steps, not directly used in projection. Edge Cases: Holes: Pixels with no projected points result in zero depth. The source notes that these holes cannot be automatically distinguished from background areas without additional context. Precision: Floating-point errors in projection may cause slight misalignments. Integer rounding of (u,v) is required for array indexing. Computes 3D position by finding the closest intersection to multiple camera rays, using least-squares optimization and visibility masks. Choose when multi-view consistency is required. Reconstructs dense depth by evaluating photo-consistency across depth planes. Choose for textureless regions or when explicit point clouds are unavailable. Time Complexity: O(N) for projection and O(W \cdot H) for depth map initialization and hole filling. The bottleneck is typically the projection of N points. Memory Complexity: O(N) to store the point cloud and O(W \cdot H) for the depth map. Performance: The source reports a PSNR of 31.44 dB on the Pavillon dataset using this method, compared to 30.27 dB for standard MVS. Strengths: Simple, fast, and directly utilizes existing 3D points. Limitations: Produces sparse depth maps with holes if the point cloud is incomplete. Cannot infer depth in regions without 3D points. This method is used in the test stage of neural radiance field improvements that incorporate point cloud generation. It serves as a bridge between implicit/explicit 3D representations and explicit 2D depth buffers for novel view synthesis. Improving Neural Radiance Fields Using Near-Surface Sampling with Point Cloud Generation, https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s11063-024-11654-5, fetched 2026-10-30

name: Triangulation for Closest Point
head: Depth-based visibility verification via triangulation, Least-squares closest point triangulation
body: This method computes the 3D position of a point by finding the closest intersection to a set of N camera rays originating from 2D projections. It formulates the problem as a least-squares optimization, converting it into a linear system solved via a weighted sum of projections. It is distinguished from simple back-projection by incorporating a visibility mask \gammai derived from 2D tracking occlusion checks and depth-based verification against rendered Gaussian splats, ensuring robustness in dynamic scenes. Inputs: A set of N camera rays, where each ray i is defined by an origin \mathbf{o}i \in \mathbb{R}^3 and a direction \mathbf{d}i \in \mathbb{R}^3 (normalized). A visibility mask \gammai \in \{0, 1\} for each ray, indicating if the corresponding 2D point is visible and unoccluded in the i-th view. Outputs: The closest point \mathbf{x}c \in \mathbb{R}^3 to all rays. Depth scalars \lambdai \in \mathbb{R} for each ray, representing the distance along the ray to \mathbf{x}c. Data Structures: Ray origins: Array of vectors \mathbf{o}i. Ray directions: Array of normalized vectors \mathbf{d}i. Visibility mask: Array of integers/booleans \gammai. Accumulators: A 3 \times 3 matrix A and a 3 \times 1 vector b for the linear system. Steps: 1. Initialize Accumulators: Set A = \mathbf{0}{3 \times 3} and b = \mathbf{0}{3 \times 1}. 2. Iterate Rays: For each ray i from 0 to N-1: a. Check visibility: If \gammai = 0, skip this ray. b. Compute the projection matrix term: Pi = I3 - \mathbf{d}i \mathbf{d}i^T, where I3 is the 3 \times 3 identity matrix. c. Update the system matrix: A \leftarrow A + \gammai Pi. d. Update the system vector: b \leftarrow b + \gammai Pi \mathbf{o}i. 3. Solve Linear System: Solve the linear equation A \mathbf{x} = b for \mathbf{x}. The solution \mathbf{x}c is the closest point. 4. Compute Depths: For each ray i, compute \lambdai = (\mathbf{x}c - \mathbf{o}i) \cdot \mathbf{d}i. Formula: The optimization problem is: \mathbf{x}c, \lambdai = \arg \min{\mathbf{x}, \lambdai} \sumi \|(\mathbf{o}i + \lambdai \mathbf{d}i) - \mathbf{x}\|^2 This converts to the linear system: \left( \sumi \gammai (I3 - \mathbf{d}i \mathbf{d}i^T) \right) \mathbf{x} = \sumi \gammai (I3 - \mathbf{d}i \mathbf{d}i^T) \mathbf{o}i Parameters: \gammai: Visibility mask. \gammai=1 if the point is visible, 0 otherwise. Determined by combining 2D tracking occlusion masks and depth-based verification. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Visibility Mask Accuracy: Incorrect \gammai values (false positives) introduce bias. The mask relies on TAPIR for 2D occlusion and alpha-blended depth rendering for depth verification. Depth Verification: Depth-based visibility compares the projected depth of a splat with the rendered depth map. If the projected depth is smaller, the splat is unoccluded. This requires rendering all splats to the view using alpha blending. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import numpy as np def triangulateclosestpoint( origins: np.ndarray, # Shape (N, 3) directions: np.ndarray, # Shape (N, 3), normalized visibilitymask: np.ndarray # Shape (N,), integers 0 or 1) -> tuple[np.ndarray, np.ndarray]: """ Computes the closest point to a set of camera rays using least-squares optimization with visibility masking. Args: origins: Array of ray origins oi. directions: Array of ray directions di. visibilitymask: Array of gammai values. Returns: xc: The 3D closest point. lambdas: Array of depth scalars lambdai. """ N = origins.shape[0] A = np.zeros((3, 3)) b = np.zeros(3) for i in range(N): gamma = visibilitymask[i] if gamma == 0: continue d = directions[i] o = origins[i] # Compute projection matrix: I3 - d d^T outerdd = np.outer(d, d) P = np.eye(3) - outerdd # Update A and b A += gamma P b += gamma (P @ o) # Solve linear system A x = b xc = np.linalg.solve(A, b) # Compute depth scalars lambdai lambdas = np.dot(origins - xc, directions) return xc, lambdas Provides initial 3D points and rays for refinement. Sets apart from multi-view methods by establishing a baseline visibility before consistency is enforced. Choose when initial sparse reconstructions are available. [8043-depth-estimation-from-point-cloud.md] Generates the initial occlusion mask for \gammai by processing query points and video frames. Sets apart from static occlusion methods by handling temporal motion. Choose when dynamic scene tracking is required. Derives rendered depths via alpha blending of splat depths for visibility verification. Sets apart from ray-marching or mesh-based rendering by leveraging implicit Gaussian primitives. Choose when differentiable rasterization of Gaussians is available. Time Complexity: O(N) for the accumulation step, where N is the number of rays. Solving the 3 \times 3 linear system is O(1). Memory Complexity: O(N) to store ray origins, directions, and visibility masks. Strengths: Robust to noise by using least-squares. Incorporates temporal consistency via 2D tracking and depth verification, reducing flickering artifacts in dynamic scenes. Limitations: Relies on accurate visibility masks. If the 2D tracker fails or depth verification is incorrect, the triangulation result will be biased. When to use: When reconstructing dynamic scenes with multiple views where temporal consistency and occlusion handling are critical. Suitable for history-aware streaming reconstruction. When not to use: For static scenes with perfect visibility or when computational resources for depth rendering are unavailable. This method is part of the "History-aware Streaming Reconstruction" pipeline for 3D Gaussian Splatting. It was introduced in. The method addresses flickering artifacts in per-frame reconstruction by merging previous and current frame information, achieving state-of-the-art visual quality and temporal consistency at interactive rates (15 fps with 350ms delay on 320x240 resolution). Learning Efficient Fuse-and-Refine for Feed-Forward 3D Gaussian Splatting, https://arxiv.org/abs/2503.14698v2, fetched 2026-10-27

name: Dense Depth Estimation via Plane Sweep
head: GPU Plane Sweep Depth Estimation, Live Image Capturing and Dense Depth Estimation, WoeKoch04, Woetzel and Koch
body: Dense Depth Estimation via Plane Sweep estimates per-pixel depth by projecting a series of depth planes into multiple camera views and evaluating photometric consistency across views. It solves the problem of recovering dense 3D geometry from multi-view imagery by replacing explicit volumetric storage with a single-pass rendering approach. Unlike Triangulation for Closest Point, which computes depth from point correspondences, this method operates directly on image pixels and is distinct from Binocular Depth Estimation (Stereo Matching) by generalizing the cost-volume concept to arbitrary numbers of views (though practical implementations may limit this) and combining rendering with reconstruction in a single step without producing an explicit intermediate volume. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: A set of N rectified images I1, \dots, IN with known camera projection matrices. Outputs: A dense depth map D for a reference view (typically the first camera). Data Structures: Depth planes: Defined by a minimum depth d{min}, maximum depth d{max}, and step size \Delta d. Cost Volume: Implicitly computed per pixel during the sweep; no explicit 3D texture is stored. Steps: 1. Initialization: For each pixel (u, v) in the reference image, initialize a consistency score C(u, v) = 0. 2. Plane Sweep: Iterate through depth values d from d{min} to d{max} with step \Delta d: a. Construct a depth plane at distance d in the reference camera coordinate system. b. For each other camera k \in \{2, \dots, N\}: i. Project the 3D point corresponding to (u, v, d) from the reference view into camera k's image plane to obtain coordinates (uk, vk). ii. Sample the intensity or color value Ik(uk, vk) from image k. iii. Compare Ik(uk, vk) with the reference pixel value I1(u, v). iv. Accumulate a photometric consistency cost (e.g., sum of absolute differences or gradient correlation) into C(u, v) for this depth hypothesis. 3. Silhouette/Background Test: Optionally, reject depth hypotheses that project outside the image boundaries or fail a background consistency check. Note that in the GPU-accelerated implementation, the photo-consistency check is performed on each fragment regardless of rejection by silhouette tests. 4. Depth Selection: For each pixel (u, v), select the depth d that minimizes the accumulated cost C(u, v). 5. Refinement: Apply local smoothing or winner-takes-all selection to produce the final depth map. Formulas: Projection: \mathbf{x}k = Pk \mathbf{X}1, where \mathbf{X}1 is the 3D point at depth d for pixel (u,v) in camera 1, and Pk is the projection matrix of camera k. Cost: C(u, v) = \sum{d} \sum{k=2}^{N} \text{Cost}(I1(u, v), Ik(uk, vk)). Parameters: d{min}, d{max}: Depth range. \Delta d: Depth resolution. N: Number of views. Edge Cases: Occlusions: Points visible in the reference view may be occluded in other views, leading to inconsistent costs. Textureless Regions: Lack of distinctive features causes ambiguous minima in the cost function. Precision: Floating-point precision in projection calculations can cause sampling errors at large depths. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def planesweepdepthestimation(images, cameras, dmin, dmax, dstep): """ images: list of N images (reference is images[0]) cameras: list of N camera projection matrices dmin, dmax, dstep: depth range parameters """ height, width = images[0].shape[:2] depthmap = np.zeros((height, width)) # Initialize cost volume implicitly # In GPU implementation, this is done in a shader loop for d in np.arange(dmin, dmax, dstep): for y in range(height): for x in range(width): # Get 3D point in reference camera Xref = unproject(x, y, d, cameras[0]) cost = 0 for k in range(1, len(images)): # Project to other camera Xk = cameras[k] @ Xref uk, vk = Xk[0]/Xk[2], Xk[1]/Xk[2] # Check bounds if not (0 <= uk < width and 0 <= vk < height): continue # Sample intensity Iref = images[0][y, x] Ik = images[k][int(vk), int(uk)] # Accumulate cost cost += abs(Iref - Ik) # Store cost for this depth # In practice, keep track of min cost and corresponding depth if d == dmin or cost < mincost[y, x]: mincost[y, x] = cost depthmap[y, x] = d return depthmap Note: The above pseudocode is a simplified CPU version. The GPU implementation processes these steps in parallel shaders. Binocular depth estimation estimates scene depth from a pair of rectified left and right images by computing a disparity map, which is inversely proportional to depth. It solves the problem of recovering 3D structure from 2D imagery using geometric constraints between two viewpoints. Unlike monocular depth estimation, which relies on learned priors from single images, this method leverages explicit pairwise multi-view consistency, making it more effective for scenes with weak texture or repetitive patterns where local photometric costs are ambiguous. It builds on Dense Depth Estimation via Plane Sweep by providing the foundational cost-volume-based approach that plane sweep generalizes to multiple views. Time Complexity: O(H \cdot W \cdot N \cdot D), where H, W are image dimensions, N is number of views, and D is number of depth planes. Memory Complexity: O(H \cdot W) for the cost accumulation per pixel, as no explicit 3D volume is stored. Performance: Dense depth maps can be computed with up to 20 frames per second on GPU hardware. Strengths: High speed due to GPU acceleration; no explicit volume storage reduces memory footprint; works with uncalibrated views if projection matrices are known. Limitations: Limited to only four camera views in the original implementation; sensitive to occlusions and textureless regions; requires rectified images or known camera poses. When to use: Real-time dense reconstruction with limited views and GPU resources. When not to use: Scenes with significant occlusions, very large depth ranges, or when more than four views are available and CPU resources are abundant. Woetzel and Koch proposed a live system for image capturing and dense depth estimation in [WoeKoch04]. Their plane-sweep algorithm runs almost entirely on the GPU, leaving the main CPU free for other tasks such as image capture and higher level recognition. This approach was developed to address the computational bottlenecks of traditional volumetric reconstruction methods. Accelerated volumetric reconstruction from uncalibrated camera views, http://doras.dcu.ie/157/, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial)

name: Binocular Depth Estimation (Stereo Matching)
head: DLNR Stereo Matching, Disparity computation, Stereo Depth Estimation with DLNR, Stereo Matching, Stereo depth
body: Binocular depth estimation estimates scene depth from a pair of left and right images by computing a disparity map. It solves the problem of recovering 3D structure from 2D imagery using geometric constraints between two viewpoints. It builds on Dense Depth Estimation via Plane Sweep by providing the foundational cost-volume-based approach that plane sweep generalizes to multiple views. The method follows a four-stage pipeline: feature extraction, cost volume construction, cost aggregation, and disparity computation. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Left image Il and right image Ir. Output: Disparity map d. Data Structures: Feature maps: Dense tensors output by the feature extraction network f\theta, sharing spatial dimensions with the input images. Cost volume: A tensor constructed by the cost volume construction operator \partial. Steps: 1. Feature Extraction: Encode Il and Ir into feature representations using a shared-weight network f\theta. Fl = f\theta(Il), \quad Fr = f\theta(Ir) 2. Cost Volume Construction: Compute the similarity between features from the left and right views using the operator \partial. C = \partial(Fl, Fr) 3. Cost Aggregation: Smooth the cost volume to resolve ambiguities and enforce consistency using the operator \delta. C{agg} = \delta(C) 4. Disparity Computation: Extract the final disparity map from the aggregated cost volume using the operator \eta. d = \eta(C{agg}) Formula: The entire process is represented as: d = \eta(\delta(\partial(f\theta(Il), f\theta(Ir)))) where: Il, Ir: Input left and right images. f\theta: Feature extraction network. \partial: Cost volume construction operator. \delta: Cost aggregation operator. \eta: Disparity computation operator. Parameters: Depth range: Valid depth is considered in the range 4B \le Z \le 20B to enhance accuracy and reliability. Baseline: A horizontal baseline of 7% of the scene radius yields optimal results. Network architecture: Representative methods include CFNet [47] and PCWNet [48]. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Occlusions: Pixels visible in only one camera create unreliable disparities. An occlusion mask is calculated by applying a threshold on the difference between left-to-right and right-to-left disparities to mask these regions. Depth limits: Objects too close to the camera exceed maximum disparity limits, causing error, while distant objects result in quadratic error. The stereo matching error relationship is \epsilon(Z) \approx \frac{\epsilon(d)^2 fx}{Z^2 B}, where \epsilon(d) is disparity output error, Z is ground-truth depth, fx is horizontal focal length, and B is baseline. Baseline trade-off: A larger baseline allows for a wider “sweet spot” for the stereo model, but 3DGS limits how far the camera can stray from original training images without producing noisy renders. head: MASt3R
body:
MASt3R Feature Integration is a method for enriching stereo matching cost volumes with deep multi-view features to improve depth estimation and subsequent mesh reconstruction accuracy. It addresses the limitation of traditional cost volumes by injecting semantically rich correspondences learned by the MASt3R foundation model, which establishes dense pointmap and stereo feature correspondences between image pairs. Unlike monocular feature integration (e.g., DINOv2), which extracts features from single images, this method leverages pairwise multi-view consistency, making it particularly effective for scenes with weak texture or repetitive patterns where local photometric costs are ambiguous. The method integrates features predicted by the MASt3R model into a downstream reconstruction pipeline (such as a Gaussian Splatting regression network or a cost volume aggregator). Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: A set of N input images \{I1, I2, \dots, IN\} of the same scene. Outputs: Enriched feature representations for each image, typically concatenated with the original image data, ready for injection into a feature pyramid network (FPN) or cost volume construction module. Data Structures: Stereo Feature Map (F): A 4D tensor with layout R^{H 	imes W 	imes 24}. H, W: Height and width of the input images. 24: The dimensionality of the MASt3R feature vector per pixel. Enriched Image Representation: For image Ii, the enriched input is the concatenation of the original image Ii and all its pairwise stereo feature maps with other views Ik (k 
eq i). Numbered Steps: 1. Pairwise Feature Extraction: For every unique pair of input images (Ii, Ij) where i 
eq j, compute the stereo feature maps using the MASt3R model: F{ij}, F{ji} = F{	ext{MASt3R}}(Ii, Ij) where F{ij} \in R^{H 	imes W 	imes 24} contains features for Ii conditioned on Ij, and F{ji} contains features for Ij conditioned on Ii. 2. Feature Aggregation per Image: For each image Ii, concatenate its original image data with the stereo feature maps obtained from all other N-1 views. The resulting feature representation for Ii is: [Ii, F{ik}]{k=1, k 
eq i}^{N} For example, if N=3, the representation for I1 is [I1, F{12}, F{13}]. 3. Injection into Downstream Pipeline: Feed the concatenated enriched representation into the target network. In Gaussian Splatting pipelines, this is typically done by feeding the enriched features as input to a Feature Pyramid Network (FPN) to regress Gaussian attributes (position, scale, rotation, color, opacity). Parameters: Feature Dimension: 24 (fixed for MASt3R). Number of Views (N): Variable, depending on the input set. Typical evaluations use N=3 or more. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Memory Constraints: Computing pairwise features for all N images requires O(N^2) forward passes through MASt3R. For large N, this becomes computationally expensive. Pose Dependency: While MASt3R can estimate poses, the feature integration itself assumes geometric consistency between the paired views. Significant misalignment or large baseline changes may reduce feature correspondence quality. Not Given in the sources: Specific normalization or scaling applied to the 24-dimensional features before concatenation is not specified. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def integratemast3rfeatures(images: List[Image], mast3rmodel: Model) -> List[EnrichedInput]: """ Integrates MASt3R multi-view features into input images for downstream reconstruction. Args: images: List of N input images [I1,..., IN]. mast3rmodel: The pre-trained MASt3R model. Returns: List of enriched inputs for each image, ready for FPN/network injection. """ n = len(images) enrichedinputs = [] # Step 1: Compute pairwise stereo features for all unique pairs # Fij is the feature map for image i given image j pairwisefeatures = {} for i in range(n): for j in range(n): if i != j: # Fij, Fji = FMASt3R(Ii, Ij) # Note: The model returns features for both views in one forward pass fij, fji = mast3rmodel(images[i], images[j]) pairwisefeatures[(i, j)] = fij pairwisefeatures[(j, i)] = fji # Step 2: Aggregate features for each image for i in range(n): # Start with the original image currentfeatures = [images[i]] # Concatenate stereo features from all other views for k in range(n): if k != i: # Get Fik fik = pairwisefeatures[(i, k)] currentfeatures.append(fik) # Concatenate along the channel/dimension axis # Result shape: [H, W, Cimg + (N-1)24] enrichedinput = concatenatealongchannels(currentfeatures) enrichedinputs.append(enrichedinput) return enrichedinputs A baseline evaluation method that directly rasterizes MASt3R's predicted 3D points as a colored point cloud without confidence filtering. It assigns each predicted 3D point the color of its corresponding source pixel from the input images and renders the entire unfiltered point cloud to reconstruct and visualize the full 3D scene. This approach exhibits visible artifacts compared to learned Gaussian representations, such as those produced by Splatt3R, due to the lack of smoothness and density estimation inherent in point-based rendering. Time Complexity: O(N^2) forward passes through the MASt3R model for N images, as pairwise features are computed for all combinations. Memory Complexity: High, due to storing O(N^2) feature maps of size H 	imes W 	imes 24 and the concatenated enriched inputs. Performance: Improves depth estimation accuracy and mesh reconstruction quality compared to methods using only monocular features (like DINOv2) or standard photometric cost volumes. Strengths: Leverages strong semantic correspondences learned from large-scale data, robust to textureless regions. Limitations: Computationally expensive for large numbers of views; requires significant memory for feature storage. When to use: When high-fidelity 3D reconstruction is required from a moderate number of unposed or calibrated images, and computational resources allow for pairwise feature computation. When not to use: When real-time performance is critical or the number of input views is very large, due to the quadratic scaling. MASt3R is a state-of-the-art 3D foundation model trained on a large dataset to establish correspondences in feature space between pairs of images of the same scene. It was introduced as a tool for dense pointmap and stereo feature prediction, enabling downstream tasks like depth estimation and 3D reconstruction. The integration of MASt3R features into cost volumes or Gaussian Splatting pipelines represents a shift towards leveraging pre-trained 3D foundation models for generalizable reconstruction. name: Arbitrary Source-Detector Geometry Projector
head: Arbitrary Source-Detector Geometry, Axial cone-beam, Cone-Beam Geometry Projector, Flexible cone-beam, Parallel Beam Geometry, Parallel-Beam Geometry Projector
body: The Arbitrary Source-Detector Geometry Projector is a flexible CT forward/backward projection model that allows the user to define the 3D location and orientation of every individual source-detector pair, overriding standard geometric assumptions. It supports planar or curved detectors (axial) and arbitrary source/detector placement, enabling complex trajectories and non-equispaced projection angles. Unlike standard Radon models which assume parallel rays, this geometry handles point-source cone-beam and fan-beam configurations where projection lines are non-parallel. It builds on Camera Matrix and Coordinate Transformation by mapping world-space voxel intersections to arbitrary detector coordinates. Inputs: Volume data V (3D array of voxel values, units \text{mm}^{-1}). Geometry specification: Source positions \mathbf{s}i for each projection angle i. Detector plane parameters: center, normal vector, pixel size, resolution. Projection angles \Theta = \{\theta1, \dots, \thetaN\}. Optional: Source-to-Isocenter Distance (DSO), Source-to-Detector Distance (DSD). Outputs: Projection data P (2D array per angle, representing line integrals or attenuated intensity). Data Structures: Detector Grid: A 2D array of pixel centers in world coordinates. Ray Representation: Origin \mathbf{o} = \mathbf{s}i, Direction \mathbf{d} = \text{normalize}(\mathbf{p}{\text{pixel}} - \mathbf{s}i). Steps: 1. Compute Detector Pixel Positions in World Coordinates: a. Calculate y{\text{coords}} and x{\text{coords}} using linear spacing based on detectorsize and pixelsize. b. Create a meshgrid with 'ij' indexing to form 2D coordinate arrays X, Y. c. Set the z coordinate to centeroffsetz (SID). d. Stack into a (H, W, 3) array with order [Z, Y, X]. 2. Compute Ray Directions: For each pixel p at position \mathbf{p}{\text{world}} and source \mathbf{s}: \mathbf{d} = \mathbf{p}{\text{world}} - \mathbf{s} \mathbf{d} = \frac{\mathbf{d}}{\|\mathbf{d}\|} 3. Ray Casting / Integration: Trace rays from \mathbf{s} along \mathbf{d} through the volume V. Use a projector model such as Siddon, Joseph, or Distance Driven (DD). Accumulate the integral of voxel values along the ray segment within the volume bounds. 4. Handle Geometry Variants: Parallel Beam: Rays are parallel; source is at infinity. Cone Beam: Point source, diverging rays. Flexible: Arbitrary source/detector positions. Parameters: DSO (Source-to-Isocenter Distance): Default 500. DSD (Source-to-Detector Distance): Default 800. detpixels: Detector pixel count per side (assumed square). Default 256. pixelsize: Physical size of a detector pixel. Default 1.0. angles: Array of rotation angles from 0 to 2\pi. Default 180 angles. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Non-Parallel Rays: Standard Radon models assume parallel rays. Cone-beam and fan-beam geometries use a point source, making projection lines non-parallel. Precision: Floating-point errors in ray-volume intersection calculations can cause artifacts. Use robust intersection algorithms (e.g., Siddon). Boundary Conditions: Rays may miss the volume entirely. Handle these by setting projection value to 0 or background intensity. Args: volume: 3D list of lists of lists (H, W, D) of voxel values. sources: List of 3D source positions (N, 3). detectorcenters: List of detector center positions (N, 3). detectornormals: List of detector normal vectors (N, 3). pixelsize: Physical size of a detector pixel. detres: Tuple (height, width) of detector resolution. Returns: projections: List of 2D lists (N, H, W). """ projections = [] for i in range(len(sources)): s = sources[i] center = detectorcenters[i] normal = detectornormals[i] # 1. Compute detector pixel positions in world coordinates ycoords = [j pixelsize for j in range(-detres[0]//2, detres[0]//2 + 1)] xcoords = [j pixelsize for j in range(-detres[1]//2, detres[1]//2 + 1)] # Construct basis vectors for the detector plane arbitraryvec = [0, 0, 1] if abs(dot(normal, arbitraryvec)) > 0.9: arbitraryvec = [1, 0, 0] u = normalize(cross(normal, arbitraryvec)) v = cross(u, normal) # 2. Compute ray directions raydirs = [] for yidx, yval in enumerate(ycoords): rowdirs = [] for xidx, xval in enumerate(xcoords): pixelpos = [center[0] + xvalu[0] + yvalv[0], center[1] + xvalu[1] + yvalv[1], center[2] + xvalu[2] + yvalv[2]] raydir = normalize([pixelpos[k] - s[k] for k in range(3)]) rowdirs.append(raydir) raydirs.append(rowdirs) # 3. Project projection = [[0.0 for in range(detres[1])] for in range(detres[0])] for y in range(detres[0]): for x in range(detres[1]): integral = integrateray(volume, s, raydirs[y][x]) projection[y][x] = integral projections.append(projection) return projections def integrateray(volume, origin, direction): # The sources do not specify the exact integration method (Siddon, Joseph, DD). # This placeholder would calculate intersections with voxel boundaries # and sum the weighted path lengths or sample along the ray. return 0.0 t-beam projectors integrate the source-to-pixel segment along a ray for volume rendering or projection in arbitrary source-detector geometries. name: t-beam projectors
head: t-beam
body: t-beam projectors integrate the source-to-pixel segment along a ray for volume rendering or projection in arbitrary source-detector geometries. They differ from standard fixed-camera models by allowing explicit definition of every source-detector pair, supporting complex trajectories (circular, spiral, saddle) and parameterized detector surfaces while maintaining exact cell-constant integration. Inputs: Source positions S, detector centers C, detector axes eu, ev, volume grid x, and optional trajectory parameters \Theta. Outputs: Projection values p (forward) or gradients (backward). Data Structures: Ray: Defined by origin o and direction d. Grid Face Crossings: Ordered list t^0 < \dots < t^M where the ray intersects volume boundaries. Surface Offsets: (au, av, an) mapping pixel indices to world coordinates. Steps: 1. Geometry Setup: Define source S(\beta) and detector frame based on trajectory. For circular cone-beam: S(\beta) = (-\text{sid} \sin \beta, \text{sid} \cos \beta, 0) C(\beta) = ((\text{sdd} - \text{sid}) \sin \beta, -(\text{sdd} - \text{sid}) \cos \beta, 0) eu(\beta) = (\cos \beta, \sin \beta, 0), \quad ev = (0, 0, 1) where \text{sid} is source-to-isocenter distance and \text{sdd} is source-to-detector distance. 2. Detector Point Calculation: For a pixel with offsets (au, av, an), the world point D is: D = C + au eu + av ev + an (eu \times ev) For flat surfaces, (au, av, an) = (u, v, 0). For cylindrical offsets of radius r: (au, av, an) = (r \sin(u/r), v, r[\cos(u/r) - 1]). 3. Ray Definition: The ray direction is \hat{a} = (D - S)/\|D - S\|2. The segment is clipped to the volume box. Rays must not extend through the detector or behind the source. 4. Siddon Integration: Find axis-q grid face crossings at t = (b - oq)/dq. Order crossings t^0 < \dots < t^M. The projection is: (A{\Theta} x)j = \sum{m=0}^{M-1} x{\text{cell}(m)} (t{m+1} - tm) This is exact integration of the cell-constant representation. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def tbeamforward(S, C, eu, ev, au, av, an, volume, gridbounds): # 1. Calculate detector point D normal = cross(eu, ev) D = C + au eu + av ev + an normal # 2. Define ray Dvec = D - S L = sqrt(sum(d2 for d in Dvec)) if L == 0: raise ValueError("Source and detector coincide") dhat = tuple(d / L for d in Dvec) # 3. Clip to volume box tmin, tmax = clipraytobox(S, dhat, gridbounds) if tmin >= tmax: return 0.0 # 4. Siddon Integration projection = 0.0 tcurrent = tmin for cell in traversegrid(S, dhat, gridbounds, tmin, tmax): tnext = nextfacecrossing(S, dhat, cell, tcurrent) chordlength = tnext - tcurrent projection += volume[cell] chordlength tcurrent = tnext return projection def cross(a, b): return (a[1]b[2] - a[2]b[1], a[2]b[0] - a[0]b[2], a[0]b[1] - a[1]b[0]) def clipraytobox(origin, direction, bounds): tmin = -float('inf') tmax = float('inf') for i in range(3): if direction[i] == 0: if origin[i] < bounds[i][0] or origin[i] > bounds[i][1]: return (1.0, 0.0) else: t1 = (bounds[i][0] - origin[i]) / direction[i] t2 = (bounds[i][1] - origin[i]) / direction[i] tmin = max(tmin, min(t1, t2)) tmax = min(tmax, max(t1, t2)) return (tmin, tmax) def traversegrid(origin, direction, bounds, tstart, tend): # Amanatides & Woo 3D grid traversal stepx = 1 if direction[0] > 0 else -1 stepy = 1 if direction[1] > 0 else -1 stepz = 1 if direction[2] > 0 else -1 cellx = int(origin[0]) celly = int(origin[1]) cellz = int(origin[2]) tmaxx = ((cellx + (1 if stepx > 0 else 0)) - origin[0]) / direction[0] if direction[0] != 0 else float('inf') tmaxy = ((celly + (1 if stepy > 0 else 0)) - origin[1]) / direction[1] if direction[1] != 0 else float('inf') tmaxz = ((cellz + (1 if stepz > 0 else 0)) - origin[2]) / direction[2] if direction[2] != 0 else float('inf') dtx = stepx / direction[0] if direction[0] != 0 else float('inf') dty = stepy / direction[1] if direction[1] != 0 else float('inf') dtz = stepz / direction[2] if direction[2] != 0 else float('inf') while tstart < tend: yield (cellx, celly, cellz) if tmaxx < tmaxy: if tmaxx < tmaxz: cellx += stepx tmaxx += dtx else: cellz += stepz tmaxz += dtz else: if tmaxy < tmaxz: celly += stepy tmaxy += dty else: cellz += stepz tmaxz += dtz tstart = max(tmaxx, tmaxy, tmaxz) def nextfacecrossing(origin, direction, cell, tcurrent): minx, maxx = cell[0], cell[0] + 1 miny, maxy = cell[1], cell[1] + 1 minz, maxz = cell[2], cell[2] + 1 texit = float('inf') if direction[0] != 0: texit = min(texit, (maxx if direction[0] > 0 else minx - origin[0]) / direction[0]) if direction[1] != 0: texit = min(texit, (maxy if direction[1] > 0 else miny - origin[1]) / direction[1]) if direction[2] != 0: texit = min(texit, (maxz if direction[2] > 0 else minz - origin[2]) / direction[2]) return max(texit, tcurrent) Parameters: \text{sid}, \text{sdd}: Distances in voxel units. Stability: At least one source or detector-center endpoint must lie within 10^6 voxel lengths of the volume center, and both must lie within 10^{15} for stable float32 setup. Edge Cases: Source/detector coincidences are invalid. Detectors viewed edge-on from the source are rejected in the native flat path. At a ray through a cell edge or corner, crossings coincide and the kernel returns a derivative from one adjacent side. Time Complexity: Linear in the number of ray-cell intersections. Memory: Low; no sparse matrix storage required. Strengths: Exact cell-constant integration; supports arbitrary trajectories and differentiable geometry. Limitations: Does not enforce Tuy–Smith completeness; geometry second derivatives are not defined. Use When: Arbitrary source-detector geometry is required; differentiable projection is needed. Avoid When: Standard parallel/fan-beam assumptions suffice and performance is critical without differentiation. Implemented in differentiable CT operator frameworks to support arbitrary trajectories from circular orbits to complex paths. Developed to enable gradient-based optimization in CT reconstruction with flexible geometry. diffct: Differentiable CT Operators from Circular Orbits to Arbitrary Trajectories, https://doi.org/10.20944/preprints202605.1446.v2, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial)

body: Configures a TIGRE geometry object from a configuration dictionary, setting detector, voxel, and offset parameters for cone or parallel beam modes. Data Structures: The geo object stores scanner parameters: geo.mode: Scanner mode, either "parallel" or "cone". geo.DSD: Source-to-detector distance. geo.DSO: Source-to-origin distance. geo.nDetector: Number of detector elements. geo.sDetector: Size of a single detector element. geo.dDetector: Total detector size. geo.nVoxel: Number of voxels. geo.sVoxel: Size of a single voxel. geo.dVoxel: Total voxel size. geo.offset: Offset for origin and detector. geo.accuracy: Accuracy setting for forward projection. geo.filter: Reconstruction filter type. Steps: 1. Initialize geo based on cfg["mode"] ("parallel" or "cone"). 2. Set geo.nVoxel from cfg. 3. Set geo.DSD and geo.DSO. 4. Set geo.nDetector, geo.sDetector, and geo.dDetector. 5. Set geo.nVoxel, geo.sVoxel, and geo.dVoxel. 6. Set offsets for origin and detector. 7. Store cfg["accuracy"] and cfg["filter"]. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def setuptigregeometry(cfg): geo = {} # 1. Initialize geometry based on mode geo["mode"] = cfg["mode"] # 2. Set nVoxel from config geo["nVoxel"] = cfg["nVoxel"] # 3. Set source-detector and source-origin distances geo["DSD"] = cfg["DSD"] geo["DSO"] = cfg["DSO"] # 4. Set detector parameters geo["nDetector"] = cfg["nDetector"] geo["sDetector"] = cfg["sDetector"] geo["dDetector"] = cfg["dDetector"] # 5. Set image/voxel parameters geo["nVoxel"] = cfg["nVoxel"] geo["sVoxel"] = cfg["sVoxel"] geo["dVoxel"] = cfg["dVoxel"] # 6. Set offsets for origin and detector geo["offset"] = cfg["offset"] # 7. Store additional configuration parameters geo["accuracy"] = cfg["accuracy"] geo["filter"] = cfg["filter"] return geo Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Not given in the sources.
