name: Camera Trajectory and Path Generation
head: Camera Path Generation, Trajectory Sampling, Novel View Trajectory
body: This family defines methods for generating sequences of camera poses (position and orientation) for volume rendering, novel view synthesis, and 3D reconstruction. It solves the problem of determining valid viewing geometries when real-world capture data is unavailable, insufficient, or requires optimization for specific computational constraints. What sets this family apart from sibling methods like Sky Gradient or Arcball Camera is the focus on generating temporal sequences or structured multi-view sets rather than interactive single-view controls or static background models. It differs from Camera Ray Generation by operating at the pose level (defining the camera's world transform) rather than the ray level (defining individual pixel rays), although it feeds directly into ray generation. The shared principles of this family are the geometric definition of rays and the parallel execution model. Ray Definition Rays are defined by an origin \mathbf{o} and a direction \mathbf{d}. The direction is typically normalized. The origin is often the camera eye position, but can vary based on the camera model. Parallel Execution Computations are mapped to parallel threads. Each thread typically processes one or more pixels or samples. Memory access patterns are optimized for coalescing. Synchronization is used to manage data dependencies between threads. Generates multi-view camera poses for large-scale outdoor elongated structures (e.g., ancient city walls) from a 3D point cloud. It fits a principal axis via Principal Component Analysis (PCA) to the point cloud's XY coordinates, samples stations along this axis, and validates positions against a density grid to ensure coverage. It replaces indoor room-centric hardcoded poses with data-driven trajectories aligned to the structure's geometry. It differs from Spiral Camera Path Generation by following a linear principal axis rather than a helical path, and from Orbit Camera Path Generation by maintaining a fixed distance from a linear centerline rather than orbiting a central point. Generates a continuous video of novel views by traversing a predefined camera trajectory (typically a spiral path) and rendering each frame using a trained Neural Radiance Field (NeRF). It differs from static novel view synthesis by outputting a temporal sequence (MP4) rather than a single image, and from diffusion-based methods like iNVS by relying on volumetric ray marching through a learned implicit representation rather than warping and inpainting. Reduces the computational load of trajectory-based rendering methods by selecting a subset of frames from a full trajectory based on a predefined mapping file. It serves as a preprocessing step for algorithms like 2D Gaussian Splatting, allowing for efficient training or rendering on hardware with limited memory or compute resources by skipping redundant or intermediate camera poses. Unlike continuous path generation methods such as Spiral Camera Path Generation or Orbit Camera Path Generation, this method operates on discrete, existing trajectory data, acting as a filter rather than a generator. Creates a sequence of camera poses for volume rendering or novel view synthesis when real-world capture data is unavailable or insufficient. It solves the problem of defining valid viewing geometries by sampling positions and orientations from a structured distribution, typically using low-discrepancy sequences like Sobol samplers to ensure uniform coverage of the scene volume. It differs from spiral or orbit generation by decoupling position and direction sampling to allow arbitrary spherical coverage, and from random pose selection by providing deterministic, space-filling trajectories rather than stochastic samples. Creates training data for volume rendering and 3D reconstruction models by simulating sensor observations in computer-generated environments. It solves the problem of lacking real-world labeled data by providing ground-truth geometry, semantic labels, and controlled noise characteristics. Unlike methods that generate camera trajectories for active planning or reconstruct scenes from sparse inputs, this method focuses on the pipeline of rendering, augmenting, and cleaning synthetic data to match the statistical properties of real sensors. It differs from Elongated Structure Camera Trajectory Generation by prioritizing data quality and label correctness over trajectory coverage, and from Novel View Synthesis Rendering by providing explicit geometric and semantic ground truth rather than just photometric consistency. Constructs camera trajectories by evaluating explicit mathematical functions of a scalar parameter (typically angle or time) to produce a sequence of camera poses. It solves the problem of generating smooth, continuous novel views from a sparse set of training images by defining the geometry of the path analytically rather than interpolating between discrete keyframes. It differs from Sparse Trajectory Generation by relying on closed-form equations for position and orientation, and from Synthetic Camera Trajectory Generation by deriving parameters directly from scene statistics (e.g., camera bounding boxes) rather than arbitrary artistic constraints. An initialization method for the transformation T \in SE(3) between Scene A and Scene B. It generates good camera viewpoints for Scene A using its Viewshed Field (VFA), transforms them by candidate T, and scores them based on their viewshed likelihood in Scene B (VFB). Generate a set of N good camera viewpoints CA for Scene A using VFA. For a candidate transformation T, transform each camera Ci in CA to get T(Ci). Calculate the viewshed score for all oriented points p originating from these transformed cameras in Scene B. Sample multiple random transformations T. Select the T with the highest Score{init} as the initialization. Calculate the initialization score for T as the median over all transformed cameras of the sum of viewshed values in Scene B: Score{init}(CA; T) = Median{CA}(\sum{p \in T(Ci)} VFB(p)). A method proposing multi-timestep sampling for multi-stage scene-level generation. Multi-timestep sampling is used for multi-stage scene-level generation. Surrounding environment, ground, and objects are synthesized. A method to generate two distinct camera paths for stereoscopic visualization by calculating a second eye position based on a separation angle and the primary view vector. Define the primary camera position c, look-at point l, and sky vector s. Calculate the viewing vector v = l - c. Calculate the right direction vector r using the cross product: r = S × v. Calculate the orthogonal component S of the sky vector s using: S = s - \cos(\alpha) v \frac{|s|}{|v|}, where \alpha is the angle between s and v. Calculate \cos(\alpha) using: \cos(\alpha) = \frac{v \cdot s}{|v| |s|}. Calculate the right eye position C using: C = c + \frac{r}{|r|} \frac{\beta 2\pi}{360} |v|, where \beta is the separation angle. The sky vector s does not need to be orthogonal to the view vector v for Splotch, but orthogonalization is performed for the stereo calculation. Creates a smooth spline path between input keyframe camera poses using multidimensional B-spline interpolation. Convert poses to (position, lookat, up) format using posestopoints(poses, dist=rotweight). Run multidimensional B-spline interpolation via scipy.interpolate.splprep on reshaped points with degree k and smoothness s. Evaluate spline at ninterp(points.shape[0]-1) points using splev. Reshape back to (n, 3, 3) format. Convert back to pose matrices using pointstoposes(newpoints). Parameters: ninterp (interpolation factor per segment), splinedegree (polynomial degree, default 5), smoothness (smoothing factor, default 0.03), rotweight (relative weighting of rotation/translation, default 0.1). Initialize camera selection scores: selected cameras get s=1.0, others get s=0.0. Apply temporal filtering to scores si^t to get weights wi^t using the exponential moving average formula with \lambda=0.05. Select the N views with the highest updated weights wi^t for rendering. Refine weights across all views using element-wise subtraction of the minimum weight, followed by normalization, to ensure zero weight for views entering/leaving the set and move C0 discontinuity to C1. Formula: wi^t = \lambda si^t + (1.0 - \lambda) wi^{t-1}. Formula: w^{CS} = \frac{w - \mini wi}{\sum (w - \mini wi)}. Parameters: \lambda (temporal filtering adaptation speed, typical 0.05), N (number of highest weighted views, typical 9). Pitfall: Temporal instability when cameras appear/disappear. Handled by smooth fading and weight refinement to ensure gradients of weights become discontinuous instead of actual values. Camera trajectory generation is fundamental to novel view synthesis (NVS) and 3D reconstruction, where the goal is to render views from angles not captured during data acquisition. Early methods relied on manual keyframe definition or simple geometric paths (spirals, orbits). With the advent of Neural Radiance Fields (NeRF) and 3D Gaussian Splatting, the demand for high-quality, dense, and uniformly distributed camera poses increased to ensure robust training and rendering. For specific applications like stereoscopic visualization, specialized paths are required to maintain correct interocular geometry. In large-scale outdoor scenarios, data-driven approaches using PCA on point clouds have been developed to align trajectories with elongated structures. Furthermore, computational efficiency has led to sparse trajectory selection methods to reduce training time for large datasets. name: Novel View Synthesis Rendering
head: Video Rendering Pipeline
body: This method generates a continuous video of novel views by traversing a predefined camera trajectory (typically a spiral path) and rendering each frame using a trained Neural Radiance Field (NeRF). It differs from static novel view synthesis by outputting a temporal sequence (MP4) rather than a single image, and from diffusion-based methods like iNVS by relying on volumetric ray marching through a learned implicit representation rather than warping and inpainting. Inputs: A trained NeRF model (MLP mapping (\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{d}) \to (\sigma, \mathbf{c})). Camera metadata: focal length, image dimensions, near/far clipping planes, and initial pose. A camera trajectory definition (e.g., spiral parameters). Outputs: A sequence of RGB frames concatenated into an MP4 video file. Data Structures: allrays: A 2D array of shape (N{total}, 6), where each row is [\mathbf{o}x, \mathbf{o}y, \mathbf{o}z, \mathbf{d}x, \mathbf{d}y, \mathbf{d}z]. allrgb: Ground truth RGB values for training validation, shape (N{total}, 3). frames: List of rendered image arrays. Steps: 1. Initialization: Load the trained NeRF checkpoint and set the model to evaluation mode (eval()). 2. Metadata Loading: Load camera intrinsics (focal length) and extrinsics (poses, near, far) from a JSON configuration file specific to the dataset (e.g., Blender). 3. Trajectory Generation: Generate a sequence of camera poses along a spiral path using generatespiralpath. 4. Ray Generation: For each camera pose in the trajectory, compute the origin \mathbf{o} and direction \mathbf{d} for every pixel in the image plane using getrays. 5. Rendering Loop: Iterate through the generated poses. For each pose, invoke renderrays with the corresponding rays. Inside renderrays: Sample Nc points along each ray for coarse density estimation. Sample Nf points for fine color and density estimation. Compute volume rendering integral and composite color. Render rays in chunks to manage memory. 6. Post-processing: Concatenate RGB chunks. Clamp values to [0, 1]. Convert to uint8. Append to the frames list. 7. Video Export: Write the frames list to an MP4 file using imageio.mimwrite. Parameters: Nc: Number of coarse samples per ray. Default: 64. Nf: Number of fine samples per ray. Default: 128. whitebg: Boolean flag for background color. Default: True (white) for Blender dataset. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision: Floating-point accumulation during transmittance calculation can cause artifacts; standard implementations use cumulative products with careful dtype handling. Boundaries: Rays near the near/far clipping planes require explicit delta padding to avoid zero-length intervals. Degenerate input: Invalid poses or missing metadata will cause ray generation to fail; robust implementations validate JSON keys before execution. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import torch import numpy as np import imageio def rendernovelviewvideo(model, metadata, trajectoryparams): """ Renders a novel view synthesis video from a trained NeRF. """ model.eval() focal = metadata['focal'] near = metadata['near'] far = metadata['far'] height = metadata['height'] width = metadata['width'] poses = generatespiralpath(trajectoryparams, numframes=100) frames = [] for pose in poses: rays = getrays(pose, height, width, focal) chunksize = 1000 rgbchunks = [] for i in range(0, rays.shape[0], chunksize): chunkrays = rays[i:i+chunksize] chunkrgb = renderrays( model=model, rays=chunkrays, Nc=64, Nf=128, whitebg=True, near=near, far=far) rgbchunks.append(chunkrgb) rgb = torch.cat(rgbchunks, dim=0).reshape(height, width, 3) rgb = torch.clamp(rgb, 0.0, 1.0) frame = (rgb.cpu().numpy() 255).astype(np.uint8) frames.append(frame) imageio.mimwrite('output.mp4', frames, fps=30) def getrays(pose, height, width, focal): """ Generates camera rays from a 4x4 pose matrix. Returns rays of shape (height, width, 6). """ i, j = torch.meshgrid(torch.arange(width), torch.arange(height), indexing='xy') dirs = torch.stack([(i - width / 2) / focal, -(j - height / 2) / focal, -torch.oneslike(i)], dim=-1) dirs = dirs / torch.norm(dirs, dim=-1, keepdim=True) raysd = (dirs @ pose[:3,:3].T).reshape(height, width, 3) rayso = pose[:3, 3].reshape(1, 1, 3).expand(height, width, 3) return torch.cat([rayso, raysd], dim=-1) def generatespiralpath(params, numframes): """ Generates a standard spiral camera trajectory for Blender dataset evaluation. Returns a list of 4x4 pose matrices. """ poses = [] for i in range(numframes): t = i / numframes angle = 2 np.pi t radius = params.get('radius', 1.0) heightoffset = params.get('height', 0.0) rot = torch.tensor([ [np.cos(angle), 0, np.sin(angle), 0], [0, 1, 0, heightoffset], [-np.sin(angle), 0, np.cos(angle), 0], [0, 0, 0, 1] ]) poses.append(rot) return poses def renderrays(model, rays, Nc, Nf, whitebg, near, far): """ Renders a batch of rays using coarse and fine sampling. rays: (N, 6) """ N = rays.shape[0] rayso = rays[:,:3] raysd = rays[:, 3:] # Sample coarse points tvalscoarse = torch.linspace(0., 1., Nc, device=rayso.device) zvalscoarse = near (1. - tvalscoarse) + far tvalscoarse ptscoarse = rayso.unsqueeze(1) + raysd.unsqueeze(1) zvalscoarse.unsqueeze(2) sigmacoarse, rgbcoarse = model(ptscoarse, raysd) # Sample fine points tvalsfine = torch.linspace(0., 1., Nf, device=rayso.device) zvalsfine = near (1. - tvalsfine) + far tvalsfine ptsfine = rayso.unsqueeze(1) + raysd.unsqueeze(1) zvalsfine.unsqueeze(2) sigmafine, rgbfine = model(ptsfine, raysd) # Volume rendering deltas = zvalsfine[:, 1:] - zvalsfine[:,:-1] deltainf = torch.tensor(1e10, device=rayso.device) deltas = torch.cat([deltas, deltainf.unsqueeze(0)], dim=1) alpha = 1.0 - torch.exp(-sigmafine[:,:-1] deltas) T = torch.cumprod(torch.exp(-sigmafine[:,:-1] deltas), dim=1) T = torch.cat([torch.oneslike(T[:,:1]), T], dim=1) weights = alpha T rgbfinal = torch.sum(weights.unsqueeze(-1) rgbfine[:,:-1], dim=1) if whitebg: bgcolor = torch.tensor([1.0, 1.0, 1.0], device=rayso.device) rgbfinal = rgbfinal + bgcolor (1.0 - torch.sum(weights, dim=1, keepdim=True)) return rgbfinal.reshape(-1, 3) A variant that does not use volumetric rendering. Instead, it warps a source view to the novel view and uses a Diffusion model to complete/inpaint the novel view image. This approach is noted as being more robust to lighting inconsistencies and sparse input views compared to standard NeRF. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Performance: Rendering speed is limited by the MLP inference time. On modern GPUs, this can be slow for high-resolution videos without acceleration structures (like hash grids or octrees). Strengths: Produces high-quality, continuous novel views; leverages the robustness of trained NeRFs for geometry and appearance. Limitations: Computationally expensive for real-time video generation; requires a pre-trained NeRF model; sensitive to input data quality (e.g., lighting consistency) unless augmented (e.g., NeRF-W). The method originates from the implementation of Neural Radiance Fields (NeRF) by Mildenhall et al. (ECCV 2020). The specific "Video Rendering Pipeline" or rendervideo script is a common utility in open-source NeRF implementations (e.g., nerf-from-scratch) to visualize the learned scene by traversing a spiral camera path. The spiral path is a standard trajectory for evaluating novel view synthesis on synthetic datasets like Blender. emmanueladutwum123/nerf-from-scratch, https://github.com/emmanueladutwum123/nerf-from-scratch, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial) NeRF的基础及后续扩展, https://pengsida.net/files/NeRFTutorial.pdf, fetched 2026-10-30 (unofficial)

name: Sparse Trajectory Generation
head: Mapping-based Trajectory Selection
body: Sparse Trajectory Generation reduces a dense camera path to a subset of frames by filtering based on a predefined mapping file. It differs from Parametric Path Generation by relying on discrete frame indices rather than continuous mathematical functions. It differs from Synthetic Camera Trajectory Generation by acting as a post-processing filter rather than a generative model. Inputs and Outputs Input: ftrajectory, a list of camera frames; mapping, a list of entries where each entry contains a frame index. Output: sparsetraj, a list of camera frames corresponding to the selected indices. Data Structures ftrajectory: A sequence of frame objects. mapping: A sequence of entries. Each entry m is structured such that m[1] holds the 1-based frame index. sparsetraj: A dynamic list of frame objects. Steps 1. Initialize an empty list sparsetraj. 2. Iterate through each entry m in mapping. 3. Convert m[1] to an integer, then subtract 1 to adjust for 0-based indexing. 4. Append ftrajectory[index] to sparsetraj. 5. Return sparsetraj. Pseudocode Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def generatesparsetrajectory(ftrajectory, mapping): sparsetraj = [] for m in mapping: frameindex1based = int(m[1]) index = frameindex1based - 1 sparsetraj.append(ftrajectory[index]) return sparsetraj Parameters and Edge Cases If mapping is empty, the result is an empty list. If index is out of bounds for ftrajectory, a robust implementation should check bounds before access. The 1600-frame threshold for optional sparsification applies only to the alignment variant, not the general generation method. Aligns a sparse camera trajectory to a ground truth trajectory using RANSAC-based point cloud registration. It differs from standard global alignment by handling sparse, potentially noisy inputs through iterative sampling, and optionally sparsifies the input trajectory if a mapping file is provided and the trajectory length exceeds 1600 frames. For the Waymo dataset, generates testing views by translating the camera by 2 to 3 meters or rotating it by 10 to 15 degrees horizontally. For LLFF and Mip-NeRF 360, partitions the full trajectory into training and testing sets to ensure ground truth images exist for extrapolated views. For scenes lacking obvious extrapolated trajectories, sparsifies the training views to create relative extrapolated trajectories. Time Complexity: Linear with respect to the size of the mapping list, O(N), where N is the number of entries. Memory Complexity: Linear with respect to the number of selected frames, O(K), where K is the length of sparsetraj. Strengths: Simple to implement; computationally inexpensive; deterministic based on the mapping file. Limitations: Does not optimize for view coverage or redundancy; relies entirely on the quality of the provided mapping file. When to use: When a specific subset of frames is known a priori to be sufficient or required. name: Trajectory Alignment (RANSAC)
head: RANSAC Trajectory Alignment, Trajectory Alignment via RANSAC
body: Aligns a sparse camera trajectory to a ground truth trajectory using RANSAC-based point cloud registration. It differs from standard global alignment by handling sparse, potentially noisy inputs through iterative sampling, and optionally sparsifies the input trajectory if a mapping file is provided and the trajectory length exceeds 1600 frames. Inputs: gttrajcol: Ground truth trajectory (column-major format). mapfile: Optional mapping file containing nsampledframes, ntotalframes, and a mapping array where each row is [frameindex, totalframeindex]. gttrans: Optional transformation matrix to apply to the ground truth point cloud. randomvar: Noise magnitude multiplier. Default: 0.0. If < 1e-5, no noise is added. Outputs: Aligned trajectory poses. Data Structures: Point Cloud: A set of 3D points derived from trajectory camera positions. Correspondence Vector: A list of index pairs [i, i] indicating self-correspondence between the source and target point clouds. Steps: 1. Parse Mapping: If mapfile exists, parse nsampledframes, ntotalframes, and the mapping array. 2. Sparsify (Conditional): If mapfile is provided AND the trajectory length > 1600, use the mapping to select specific frames. If trajectory length <= 1600 or no mapfile is present, use the full trajectory. 3. Convert to Point Cloud: Convert the selected ground truth trajectory gttrajcol into a point cloud trajpcdcol. 4. Transform Ground Truth: If gttrans is provided, apply it to trajpcdcol. 5. Create Correspondences: Generate a correspondence vector corres where each point in the source trajectory corresponds to itself in the target trajectory: corres = [[0,0], [1,1],..., [N-1, N-1]]. 6. RANSAC Alignment: Perform RANSAC registration using trajpcdcol and the source trajectory point cloud with the following parameters: maxiteration: 100,000. maxvalidation: 100,000. Add noise to the source points scaled by randomvar if randomvar >= 1e-5. 7. Apply Transformation: Apply the best-fit transformation found by RANSAC to the source trajectory. Returns: Aligned trajectory. Typical for point-to-point. # checks=100000, # criteria=o3d.pipelines.registration.RANSACConvergenceCriteria(100000, 100000) #) # Apply result transformation to source trajectory # alignedtraj = applytransformation(sourcetrajectory, result.transformation) return selectedtraj # Placeholder return def converttrajectorytopointcloud(traj): """ Converts a trajectory to a point cloud. Implementation detail not provided in source. Assumes extraction of 3D positions. """ pcd = o3d.geometry.PointCloud() # Extract positions from traj # pcd.points = o3d.utility.Vector3dVector(trajpositions) return pcd For fewer than 9 input views, performs alignment by sampling every possible pair of cameras in one set, computing the Sim(3) transformation relating it to the same camera pair in the other trajectory. The global Sim(3) transformation leading to the lowest average camera alignment error is kept. For 9 or more views, it uses the standard Umeyama algorithm. Time Complexity: High for the RANSAC variant due to 100,000 iterations and validation steps. The RANSAC-inspired variant for <9 views involves checking all camera pairs, which is O(N^2) for N views. Memory Complexity: Linear with respect to the number of trajectory points for point cloud storage. Strengths: Robust to noise and outliers in sparse trajectories. Handles very few views (<9) where standard algorithms fail. Limitations: Unstable for very few views if not using the RANSAC-inspired approach. Sparsification is only applied if trajectory length > 1600. When to use: When aligning sparse, noisy trajectories where standard global alignment (e.g., Umeyama) is unstable due to insufficient views. Originated in the context of 2D Gaussian Splatting and sparse pose alignment for NeRF reconstruction. The RANSAC-based approach was adopted to handle the instability of standard alignment methods (like Umeyama) when dealing with very few input views (<9). name: Synthetic Camera Trajectory Generation
head: Colmap Dataset Generation, Sobol Camera Sampling
body: Synthetic Camera Trajectory Generation creates a structured set of camera poses for volume rendering or 3D reconstruction by sampling positions on a sphere surrounding the scene center. It differs from Sparse Trajectory Generation by using quasi-random Sobol sequences to ensure uniform coverage of the viewing sphere, and from B-Spline Camera Path Interpolation by generating discrete, independent poses rather than a continuous smooth path. Inputs: Volume bounding box (AABB) defined by minimum and maximum coordinates. Renderer resolution (width W, height H). Number of views N{VIEWS}. Focal length calculation function (e.g., based on sensor size or field of view). Outputs: A list of camera poses, each containing a position \mathbf{p}, orientation (quaternion \mathbf{q}), and translation vector \mathbf{t}. Metadata compatible with COLMAP format (camera model, intrinsic parameters). Data Structures: 1. Volume AABB: Stored as a single point or structure with position and RGB values representing bounds. 2. Camera Record: id: Integer identifier. model: String, e.g., "SIMPLEPINHOLE". width, height: Integer resolution. focallength: Float. qvec: Quaternion components [w, x, y, z]. tvec: Translation vector [x, y, z]. Steps: 1. Initialize Volume Metadata: Write the world-space AABB of the volume as a single entry (id=0) with position and RGB values derived from the AABB bounds. 2. Initialize Camera Intrinsics: Write a single camera definition (id=0) with model SIMPLEPINHOLE. Set resolution to the renderer's output dimensions. Calculate the focal length f using the renderer's focal length function, typically based on the sensor width and field of view. 3. Sample Camera Positions (Sphere Sampling): For each view index i from 0 to N{VIEWS}-1: a. Use a Sobol sequence sampler (samplerOut) to generate a 3D point on the unit sphere. b. Scale this point by the desired radius R (distance from volume center) to get the camera position \mathbf{p}i. c. The volume center \mathbf{c} is the origin of this coordinate system. 4. Sample Camera Orientation: a. Define the target direction \mathbf{d}{target} = \mathbf{c} - \mathbf{p}i. b. Use a Sobol sequence sampler (samplerIn) to generate a small random offset vector \mathbf{o}i in the tangent plane or as a spherical perturbation. c. Compute the final viewing direction \mathbf{d}i = \text{normalize}(\mathbf{d}{target} + \mathbf{o}i). d. Construct a rotation matrix or quaternion \mathbf{q}i that aligns the camera's local Z-axis with \mathbf{d}i. 5. Store Pose Metadata: a. Compute the translation vector \mathbf{t}i = -\mathbf{R}i \mathbf{p}i, where \mathbf{R}i is the rotation matrix derived from \mathbf{q}i. b. Store the quaternion. Note that COLMAP expects quaternions in the order [w, x, y, z], but some internal representations may use [x, y, z, w] or other permutations. The source specifies reordering from [3, 0, 1, 2] which likely maps from a specific internal layout to COLMAP's [w, x, y, z] or vice versa. Specifically, if the internal format is [x, y, z, w], reordering indices [3, 0, 1, 2] yields [w, x, y, z]. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import numpy as np def generatesobolcameratrajectory(nviews, volumecenter, radius, resolution, focallengthfunc): """ Generates camera poses using Sobol sequence sampling on a sphere. Args: nviews: Number of camera views to generate. volumecenter: 3D vector (x, y, z) of the volume center. radius: Distance from center to camera positions. resolution: Tuple (width, height). focallengthfunc: Function returning focal length based on resolution. Returns: List of dictionaries containing 'position', 'quaternion', 'translation', 'cameraid'. """ poses = [] # Initialize Sobol sampler for 3D points # Note: In a real implementation, use a library like scipy.stats.qmc.Sobol # or a custom low-discrepancy sequence generator. sobolsampler = SobolSequence(dim=3) # Camera intrinsic setup (simplified) camid = 0 width, height = resolution focallength = focallengthfunc(width, height) for i in range(nviews): # Step 3: Sample position on sphere # Sobol sequence returns values in [0, 1), map to sphere surface # Using inverse transform sampling or rejection sampling for uniform sphere distribution # is complex with Sobol; typically, Sobol points are mapped to sphere via # specific transformations or used as indices for pre-computed sphere distributions. # Here we assume a helper samplespherepoint that uses Sobol indices. # Generate uniform point on unit sphere using Sobol sequence # A common method is to use Sobol for angles or use a specific sphere Sobol sequence. # For simplicity, we assume a function that maps Sobol sequence to sphere. u = sobolsampler.next() # Returns 3D vector in [0,1)^3 # Map to sphere (example: using spherical coordinates or rejection) # This is a placeholder for the specific Sobol-to-sphere mapping logic. # A robust implementation would use a low-discrepancy sequence specifically for the sphere. theta = 2 np.pi u[0] phi = np.arccos(2 u[1] - 1) x = np.sin(phi) np.cos(theta) y = np.sin(phi) np.sin(theta) z = np.cos(phi) position = volumecenter + radius np.array([x, y, z]) # Step 4: Sample orientation # Direction towards center directiontocenter = volumecenter - position directiontocenter = directiontocenter / np.linalg.norm(directiontocenter) # Small random offset using Sobol offsetu = sobolsampler.next() # Create a small perturbation vector orthogonal to directiontocenter # This is a simplified approximation of the "small random offset" # In practice, one might generate a random vector and project it. randomvec = np.array([offsetu[0] - 0.5, offsetu[1] - 0.5, offsetu[2] - 0.5]) # Project randomvec to be orthogonal to directiontocenter proj = randomvec - np.dot(randomvec, directiontocenter) directiontocenter proj = proj / np.linalg.norm(proj) if np.linalg.norm(proj) > 1e-6 else np.array([1, 0, 0]) # Scale offset by a small factor (e.g., 0.1 radians) offsetangle = 0.1 offsetvec = offsetangle proj finaldirection = directiontocenter + offsetvec finaldirection = finaldirection / np.linalg.norm(finaldirection) # Construct rotation matrix/quaternion # Assume camera looks down -Z axis in local space # We need a rotation matrix R such that R [0, 0, -1]^T = finaldirection # And R aligns the local X and Y axes appropriately. # Using scipy.spatial.transform.Rotation for robustness from scipy.spatial.transform import Rotation as R # Define a reference up vector, e.g., [0, 1, 0] # If finaldirection is parallel to up, choose a different up vector. up = np.array([0, 1, 0]) if np.abs(np.dot(finaldirection, up)) > 0.99: up = np.array([1, 0, 0]) # Create rotation that aligns local Z with finaldirection # Note: OpenGL/Colmap often use -Z as forward. rot = R.frommatrix(buildrotationmatrix(finaldirection, up)) # Quaternion in [w, x, y, z] format q = rot.asquat() # Returns [x, y, z, w] qcolmap = np.array([q[3], q[0], q[1], q[2]]) # Reorder to [w, x, y, z] # Step 5: Store metadata # Translation vector t = -R p t = -rot.asmatrix() @ position poses.append({ 'id': camid, 'position': position, 'quaternion': qcolmap, 'translation': t, 'cameramodel': 'SIMPLEPINHOLE', 'width': width, 'height': height, 'focallength': focallength }) return poses def buildrotationmatrix(forward, up): """ Constructs a rotation matrix given a forward vector and an up vector. """ z = forward / np.linalg.norm(forward) x = np.cross(up, z) x = x / np.linalg.norm(x) y = np.cross(z, x) return np.columnstack((x, y, z)) Parameters: N{VIEWS}: Number of views. Typical values depend on scene complexity, e.g., 100-1000. Radius: Distance from center. Must be large enough to encompass the volume but small enough to maintain resolution. Offset Scale: Magnitude of the random orientation offset. Small values (e.g., 0.1 radians) prevent gimbal lock and ensure stable viewing. Edge Cases: Degenerate Up Vector: If the viewing direction is parallel to the up vector, the cross product for the X-axis becomes zero. A fallback up vector must be selected. Sobol Sequence Dimension: Sobol sequences are sensitive to dimension. Ensure the sampler is initialized with the correct dimension (3 for position, 3 for offset). Quaternion Ordering: COLMAP uses [w, x, y, z]. Many libraries return [x, y, z, w]. Incorrect ordering leads to rotated views. Inpainting Trajectory Sampling generates camera poses for RGBD inpainting by defining a closed curve on the horizontal plane based on depth values at zero elevation angle from a single panoramic depth map. It differs from standard spherical sampling by constraining the camera to a 2D curve that adapts to the scene's geometry, ensuring the camera stays within observable regions. Definition: Samples camera positions on shrunk curves derived from a smoothed depth-based curve. Steps: 1. Extract distance values of all pixels at zero elevation angle from the panoramic depth map. 2. Apply 1D Gaussian filtering to these distances to obtain a smoothed closed curve C. 3. Define shrunk curves \{Ci\} scaled by factors \{si\} relative to C. 4. Uniformly sample 8 camera positions on each shrunk curve. Parameters: Number of shrunk curves: 4. Scale factors \{si\}: 0.15, 0.3, 0.45, 0.6. Positions per curve: 8. Total positions: 32. Time Complexity: O(N{VIEWS}) for generating poses, assuming constant-time Sobol sequence generation. Memory Complexity: O(N{VIEWS}) to store the pose list. Performance: Sobol sequences provide better coverage than random sampling with fewer samples, reducing the number of views needed for high-quality reconstruction. Strengths: Uniform coverage of the viewing sphere; deterministic and reproducible; simple to implement. Limitations: Assumes a central volume; not suitable for scenes with significant depth variation where a fixed radius is inappropriate; does not account for occlusions or visibility constraints. When to Use: When a uniform set of views around a central object is required for volume rendering or NeRF training. When Not to Use: For scenes with large depth variations, indoor environments with complex geometry, or when specific viewpoints are required. Synthetic Camera Trajectory Generation using Sobol sequences for volume rendering was described in the context of the volren project. The method leverages low-discrepancy sequences to ensure efficient sampling of the camera sphere. The COLMAP format for storing poses is widely used in 3D reconstruction pipelines. nihofm/volren: Simple OpenGL-based renderer for..., https://github.com/nihofm/volren, fetched 2026-10-29 (unofficial) PERF: Panoramic Neural Radiance Field From a Single Panorama, https://doi.org/10.1109/tpami.2024.3387307, fetched 2026-10-26

name: Random Pose Selection
head: Random Pose Generation
body: Random Pose Selection generates intermediate camera poses by interpolating between two randomly chosen training poses to ensure rendering occurs within observed regions, avoiding failures on unobserved parts of the scene. It differs from Nearest Camera Pose Selection, which explicitly ranks existing training data by geometric proximity to a query pose, by instead synthesizing new poses that lie between existing training views to guarantee visibility. Inputs: P = \{ \{Ri, ti\} \}{i=1}^{N}: The set of N training poses, where Ri \in \mathbb{R}^{3 \times 3} is the rotation matrix and ti \in \mathbb{R}^3 is the translation vector. \theta: Rotation distance threshold. d: Translation distance threshold. Outputs: p{out} \in \mathbb{R}^{4 \times 4}: The output homogeneous transformation matrix. Intrinsic matrix and image shape: Randomly selected from the training set corresponding to the selected poses. Data Structures: Pose pi: Represented as a pair (Ri, ti). Distance functions DR and Dt compute the separation between two poses. Parameters: \theta = \pi/24: Rotation threshold. d = 0.5: Translation threshold. s \sim U[0, 1]: Interpolation factor, uniformly sampled. Formulas: 1. Rotation Distance: DR(R1, R2) = \arccos\left(\frac{\text{Tr}(R2^{-1} R1)}{2} - 1\right) where \text{Tr}(\cdot) is the trace of the matrix. 2. Translation Distance: Dt(t1, t2) = \|t2 - t1\|2^2 where \|\cdot\|2 is the Euclidean norm. 3. Axis-Angle Conversion: \text{AA2R}(v, \theta): Converts axis v and angle \theta to a rotation matrix. \text{R2AA}(R): Converts rotation matrix R to axis v and angle \theta. 4. Reduced Angle Rotation: \text{ReduceAngle}(R, s) = \text{AA2R}\left(\text{R2AA}(R)v, s \cdot \text{R2AA}(R)\theta\right) This scales the rotation angle of R by factor s while keeping the axis constant. 5. Intermediate Rotation: \text{IntermediateRot}(R1, R2, s) = \text{ReduceAngle}(R2 R1^{-1}, s) R1 This computes the relative rotation from R1 to R2, scales it by s, and applies it to R1. Algorithm Steps: 1. Initialize output pose p{out} as a 4 \times 4 matrix. 2. Randomly select two indices j and k from the range [1, N]. 3. While DR(Rj, Rk) \ge \theta AND Dt(tj, tk) \ge d: Re-randomly select j and k from [1, N]. 4. Compute the intermediate rotation R{jk} = \text{IntermediateRot}(Rj, Rk, s). 5. Set the upper-left 3 \times 3 block of p{out} to R{jk}. 6. Set the translation column of p{out} to s tk + (1 - s) tj. 7. Set the bottom-right element p{out}[3, 3] to 1. 8. Randomly select an intrinsic matrix and image shape from the training set for the output pose. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import numpy as np def randomposeselection(P, theta, d): """ Generate a random intermediate pose from a set of training poses. Args: P: List of tuples (R, t), where R is 3x3 rotation matrix, t is 3x1 translation vector. theta: Rotation distance threshold (default pi/24). d: Translation distance threshold (default 0.5). Returns: pout: 4x4 homogeneous transformation matrix. """ N = len(P) def rotationdist(R1, R2): val = np.trace(R2.T @ R1) / 2.0 - 1.0 val = np.clip(val, -1.0, 1.0) return np.arccos(val) def translationdist(t1, t2): return np.linalg.norm(t2 - t1)2 def aa2r(v, angle): vx, vy, vz = v c = np.cos(angle) s = np.sin(angle) C = 1 - c return np.array([ [c + vxvxC, vxvyC - vzs, vxvzC + vys], [vyvxC + vzs, c + vyvyC, vyvzC - vxs], [vzvxC - vys, vzvyC + vxs, c + vzvzC] ]) def r2aa(R): angle = np.arccos((np.trace(R) - 1) / 2.0) angle = np.clip(angle, 0, np.pi) if angle < 1e-6: return np.array([1.0, 0.0, 0.0]), 0.0 axis = np.array([ R[2, 1] - R[1, 2], R[0, 2] - R[2, 0], R[1, 0] - R[0, 1] ]) axis = axis / (2 np.sin(angle)) return axis, angle def reduceangle(R, s): v, theta = r2aa(R) return aa2r(v, s theta) def intermediaterot(R1, R2, s): Rrel = R2 @ R1.T Rred = reduceangle(Rrel, s) return Rred @ R1 j = np.random.randint(0, N) k = np.random.randint(0, N) # Loop condition matches source exactly: continues only if BOTH distances exceed thresholds while rotationdist(P[j][0], P[k][0]) >= theta and translationdist(P[j][1], P[k][1]) >= d: j = np.random.randint(0, N) k = np.random.randint(0, N) s = np.random.uniform(0, 1) Rjk = intermediaterot(P[j][0], P[k][0], s) pout = np.eye(4) pout[:3,:3] = Rjk pout[:3, 3] = s P[k][1] + (1 - s) P[j][1] pout[3, 3] = 1.0 return pout Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Unobserved Regions: If the selected poses are too far apart, the interpolated pose may lie in an unobserved region, causing rendering failures. The distance thresholds mitigate this. Intrinsic Parameters: The method requires randomly selecting intrinsic matrices and image shapes from the training set to accompany the generated pose. Nearest Camera Pose Selection identifies the most relevant training images for a novel view by finding camera poses with minimal positional and angular distance. It selects a subset of training poses that maximizes image content overlap with the novel view, serving as a prerequisite for feature reprojection in enhancement pipelines. Unlike Random Pose Selection, which interpolates between random poses to ensure visibility, this method explicitly ranks existing training data by geometric proximity to the query pose. Random Pose Perturbation generates random pose perturbations from the SE(3) group biased around a reference pose to ensure feature visibility and uniform coverage of the local pose space. It samples rotation axes uniformly on a unit-2 sphere in the neighborhood of a reference axis \tilde{e} as \tilde{e} + \Delta \tilde{e}. It samples rotation angles from a non-uniform distribution in [0, \theta] for small \theta to yield uniform random rotation matrices. These rotation matrices are converted to Gibbs vectors (q) for orientation representation. Translation components are sampled from a bounded uniform random distribution along each axis, covering transverse and forward motions. If tracking of at least four features is unsuccessful, the method re-initializes with conservative pose samples. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Not given in the sources. Limitations: Not given in the sources. When to Use: When generating novel views for training or rendering where visibility is guaranteed by interpolation between known views. When Not to Use: When precise alignment with specific training views is required (use Nearest Camera Pose Selection instead). When local Jacobian approximation around a specific reference pose is needed (use Random Pose Perturbation instead). Random Pose Selection was proposed in the context of PeRFception, a method for perception using radiance fields. It addresses the issue of rendering failures when attempting to render extremely unobserved parts of a scene that are significantly out of train-view coverage. The method is used within the PeRFception pipeline to generate training views for 3D ResUNets implemented with sparse convolutional layers on the PeRFception-ScanNet dataset. PeRFception: Perception using Radiance Fields, https://doi.org/10.48550/arxiv.2208.11537, fetched 2026-10-26 Differentiable Rendering for Pose Estimation in Proximity Operations, https://core.ac.uk/download/552738213.pdf, fetched 2026-10-30

name: Nearest Camera Pose Selection
head: Nearest Neighbor Pose Selection, Pose Selection by Distance
body: Nearest Camera Pose Selection identifies the most relevant training images for a novel view by finding camera poses with minimal positional and angular distance. It addresses the problem of selecting appropriate context for feature reprojection or rendering enhancement by ensuring the selected neighbors share significant image content overlap with the target view. Unlike its parent Random Pose Selection, which interpolates between random poses to stay within observed regions, this method explicitly selects discrete existing training frames based on geometric proximity. It differs from Pose Grouping and Representative View Selection by selecting the single most relevant subset based on minimal distance rather than partitioning the dataset into clusters to ensure geometric coverage. Inputs: A novel camera pose Ck, defined by a rotation matrix Rk and a translation vector \bm{t}k. A set of M training camera poses \{Cj\}{j=1}^M, where each Cj consists of rotation matrix Rj and translation vector \bm{t}j. Outputs: A subset of n training poses \{Ci\}{i=1}^n considered the closest neighbors to Ck. Data Structures: Camera Pose: A tuple or object containing R \in \mathbb{R}^{3 \times 3} and \bm{t} \in \mathbb{R}^3. Distance Metrics: Scalar values computed per training pose. Formulas: 1. Angular Distance: dist^{i}{ang}(R{k}, R{i}) = \frac {1}{3} \lvert \pi (R{k}) - \pi (R{i}) \rvert {1} where \pi(Ri) returns the three Euler angles of the rotation matrix Ri, and \lvert \cdot \rvert1 is the L1 norm (sum of absolute differences). 2. Positional Distance: dist^{i}{pos}(\bm {t}{k}, \bm {t}{i}) = \frac {1}{3} \lvert \bm {t}{k} - \bm {t}{i} \rvert {1} where \bm{t}k and \bm{t}i are the translation vectors of the novel and training cameras, respectively. 3. Selection Logic: Empirically, positional distance is the strongest indicator for image content overlap, followed by angular distance. First, select the 5 poses \{Cp\}{p=1}^5 with the smallest positional distances: \{C{p}\}{p=1}^{5} = \{C{j}\} \mid \ j \in \text{min}{5}\{dist^{j}{pos}(\bm {t}{k}, \{\bm {t}j\}{j=1}^M)\} Second, from these 5 candidates, select the n poses \{Ci\}{i=1}^n with the smallest angular distances: \{C{i}\}{i=1}^{n} = \{C{p}\} \mid \ p \in \text{min}{n}\{dist^{p}{ang}(R{k},\{Rp\}{p=1}^5)\} Parameters: Number of initial positional candidates: 5. This value is used for LLFF and 360v2 datasets. Number of final angular neighbors n: 2. This value is used for the DTU dataset. Leniency threshold: 0.25 is used for visibility testing in conjunction with this selection. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import numpy as np def euleranglesfromrotationmatrix(R): """ Extracts Euler angles (roll, pitch, yaw) from a 3x3 rotation matrix. Assumes a specific convention (e.g., ZYX or similar) consistent with the source. Note: The source uses pi(R) to denote Euler angles. Implementation detail: Standard decomposition is required. """ # Placeholder for specific Euler angle extraction logic. # The source defines distang using the L1 norm of the difference of these angles. # Common convention for NeRF literature often assumes specific axis order. # For implementation, ensure consistency with how R was generated. sy = np.sqrt(R[0,0]2 + R[1,0]2) singular = sy < 1e-6 if not singular: x = np.arctan2(R[2,1], R[2,2]) y = np.arctan2(-R[2,0], sy) z = np.arctan2(R[1,0], R[0,0]) else: x = np.arctan2(-R[1,2], R[1,1]) y = np.arctan2(-R[2,0], sy) z = 0 return np.array([x, y, z]) def nearestcameraposeselection(novelpose, trainingposes, kpos=5, nang=2): """ Selects the nearest training camera poses to a novel view. Args: novelpose: Tuple (Rk, tk) trainingposes: List of tuples [(R1, t1),..., (RM, tM)] kpos: Number of initial candidates based on position (default 5) nang: Number of final neighbors based on angle (default 2) Returns: List of nang training poses closest to novelpose. """ Rk, tk = novelpose piRk = euleranglesfromrotationmatrix(Rk) # Step 1: Compute positional distances posdistances = [] for i, (Rj, tj) in enumerate(trainingposes): # dist^ipos = (1/3) L1norm(tk - ti) diff = np.abs(tk - tj) distpos = np.sum(diff) / 3.0 posdistances.append((distpos, i)) # Sort by positional distance and pick top kpos posdistances.sort(key=lambda x: x[0]) topkindices = [idx for, idx in posdistances[:kpos]] # Step 2: Compute angular distances for the top kpos candidates angdistances = [] for idx in topkindices: Rj, tj = trainingposes[idx] piRj = euleranglesfromrotationmatrix(Rj) # dist^iang = (1/3) L1norm(pi(Rk) - pi(Ri)) diff = np.abs(piRk - piRj) distang = np.sum(diff) / 3.0 angdistances.append((distang, idx)) # Sort by angular distance and pick top nang angdistances.sort(key=lambda x: x[0]) finalindices = [idx for, idx in angdistances[:nang]] # Return the selected training poses return [trainingposes[idx] for idx in finalindices] Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Euler Angle Ambiguity: The formula relies on \pi(Ri), the Euler angles of the rotation matrix. Different Euler angle conventions (ZYX, XYZ, etc.) yield different values. The implementation must use the same convention as the source data generation. Gimbal Lock: If the rotation matrices approach singularities, Euler angle extraction may become unstable. However, for typical camera trajectories in NeRF datasets, this is less common than in robotic kinematics. Scale Sensitivity: Positional distance is linear. If the scene scale varies significantly between datasets, the relative weight of position vs. angle may need adjustment, though the source fixes the selection counts (5 and 2) empirically. Selects a subset of representative training viewpoints by clustering camera poses and filtering for image quality. It partitions the dataset to ensure geometric coverage, whereas Nearest Camera Pose Selection selects the single most relevant image based on minimal distance. Complexity: The method requires computing distances for all M training poses. Positional distance computation is O(M). Angular distance computation is limited to the top k candidates (k=5), so it is O(k). Total time complexity is O(M). Memory complexity is O(M) to store distances or O(k) if streaming. Performance: The method is computationally lightweight compared to feature-matching or SfM-based splitting methods. It relies on known camera pose priors, avoiding failures in texture-less regions where feature matching might fail. Strengths: Empirically, positional distance is the strongest indicator for image content overlap. It is simple to implement and does not require additional feature extraction or matching pipelines. Limitations: It assumes accurate camera poses are available. It does not account for occlusion or scene content directly, only geometric proximity. The fixed parameters (5 and 2) are dataset-specific and may not generalize without tuning. The method was introduced in the context of RoGUENeRF, a robust geometry-consistent universal enhancer for NeRF. It was developed to leverage relevant information from neighboring training images for feature reprojection and enhancement, allowing the enhancer to handle novel views effectively. The approach was evaluated on LLFF, 360v2, and DTU datasets. RoGUENeRF: A Robust Geometry-Consistent Universal Enhancer for NeRF, https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-031-73254-64, fetched 2026-10-29

name: Pose Grouping and Representative View Selection
head: AABB Expansion, Block Splitting, Clustering-based View Selection, KMeans Block Splitting, Representative View Selection
body: This method selects a subset of representative training viewpoints from a large set of rendered images by clustering camera poses and filtering for image quality. It addresses the problem of visual inconsistencies, amplified exposure differences, and noise propagation that arise when using all available frames for subsequent training rounds. Unlike its parent Nearest Camera Pose Selection, which selects the single most relevant image based on minimal distance, this method partitions the entire dataset into groups to ensure geometric coverage and selects the sharpest image from each group. It differs from SfM-based splitting methods (e.g., Mega-NeRF) by leveraging known camera pose priors and KMeans clustering on centers rather than feature-metric correspondences, avoiding failures in texture-less regions. Inputs: Set of N camera poses P = \{P1, \dots, PN\}, where each Pi consists of rotation matrix Ri and translation vector ti. Set of rendered images I = \{I1, \dots, IN\} corresponding to the poses. Number of clusters K (typically 12). Bounding box scale factor vector s{AABB} = [sx, sy, sz]^T (default sx=sy=sz=1.0). Outputs: A set of K representative images, one from each cluster/block. Data Structures: Camera Center: cn = -Rn^T tn. Forward Direction: zn = Rn^T [0,0,1]^T. Feature Vector: vn = [cn, zn] \in \mathbb{R}^6. Axis-Aligned Bounding Box (AABB): Defined by minimum corner A and maximum corner B. Steps: 1. Extract Geometric Features: For each image i, compute the camera center ci and forward direction zi from the extrinsic parameters Ri, ti. Construct the 6D feature vector vi = [ci, zi]. 2. Initial Clustering: Perform KMeans clustering on the set of feature vectors \{vi\} with K clusters. Assign each image i to an initial block Bk based on its cluster ID. LIi = \text{KMeans}(vi, K) where LIi is the block ID of image i. 3. Compute Bounding Boxes: For each cluster k, determine the spatial extent of the camera centers Pk = \{Pi \mid LIi = k\}. Compute the initial AABB bounds Ak and Bk: Ak = \min(Pk), \quad Bk = \max(Pk) where min/max are taken component-wise over the 3D coordinates of the camera centers in the cluster. 4. Expand Bounding Boxes (AABB Expansion): To introduce overlap between blocks, expand the AABBs using the scale factor s{AABB}. Compute the diagonal midpoint Ck: Ck = \frac{Ak + Bk}{2} Compute the diagonal direction rk and half-length lenk: rk = \frac{Bk - Ak}{\|Bk - Ak\|}, \quad lenk = \frac{\|Bk - Ak\|}{2} Recompute the expanded bounds A'k and B'k: A'k = Ck + s{AABB} \cdot rk \cdot lenk B'k = Ck - s{AABB} \cdot rk \cdot lenk Note: The source notation uses A and B for the final bounds after expansion. 5. Regroup Images: Reassign images to blocks based on the expanded bounds. If the camera pose Pi of image i lies within the expanded bounds [A'k, B'k] (component-wise), add image i to block Bk. This allows images to belong to multiple overlapping blocks. \text{If } A'k \le Pi \le B'k, \text{ then } Bk \leftarrow Bk \cup \{Ii\} 6. Select Representative Views: For each block Bk, calculate the Laplacian variance for every image Ii \in Bk. Select the image with the highest variance as the representative view for that block. \text{Representative}k = \arg \max{Ii \in Bk} \text{Var}{Lap}(Ii) Formula: The sharpness metric is the variance of the Laplacian gradient: \text{Var}{Lap}(I) = \text{Var}(\nabla^2 I) where \nabla^2 I is the Laplacian gradient of image I. Higher values indicate richer high-frequency details (texture/edges). Parameters: K: Number of clusters/blocks. Default 12. s{AABB}: Scale factor vector. Default [1, 1, 1]^T (no overlap). \gamma: Hyperparameter for Inverse Distance Weighting (used in blending, not selection). Default 1. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Texture-less Regions: SfM-based splitting fails here; this method uses pose priors, making it robust. Overlap Ratio: If s{AABB} \to \infty, blocks encompass all training images. If s{AABB} = 1.0, there is no overlap. Blurring: If blocks are too close, blending methods like Inverse Distance Weighting (IDW) can produce blurry images due to similar weights for outliers. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import numpy as np from sklearn.cluster import KMeans def posegroupingandrepresentativeviewselection(poses, images, K=12, sAABB=np.array([1.0, 1.0, 1.0])): """ Selects representative views by clustering camera poses and expanding bounding boxes. Args: poses: List of tuples (R, t) for N images. R is 3x3 rotation, t is 3x1 translation. images: List of image arrays (for Laplacian calculation). K: Number of clusters. sAABB: Scale factor vector for AABB expansion. Returns: List of K representative images. """ N = len(poses) # Step 1: Extract geometric features # cn = -Rn^T tn # zn = Rn^T [0, 0, 1]^T featurevectors = [] for R, t in poses: RT = R.T c = -RT @ t z = RT @ np.array([0, 0, 1]) # Concatenate to form 6D vector v = np.concatenate([c, z]) featurevectors.append(v) featurematrix = np.array(featurevectors) # Shape (N, 6) # Step 2: Initial Clustering kmeans = KMeans(nclusters=K, randomstate=42) clusterlabels = kmeans.fitpredict(featurematrix) # Step 3 & 4: Compute and Expand Bounding Boxes # We need to track which images fall into which expanded AABBs # Initialize block membership as empty sets blockimages = [set() for in range(K)] for k in range(K): # Get indices of images in cluster k clusterindices = np.where(clusterlabels == k)[0] if len(clusterindices) == 0: continue # Get camera centers for this cluster # Camera center is the first 3 components of the feature vector clustercenters = featurematrix[clusterindices,:3] # Compute initial AABB bounds (min and max of centers) A = np.min(clustercenters, axis=0) B = np.max(clustercenters, axis=0) # Compute diagonal properties midpoint = (A + B) / 2.0 diagonalvec = B - A diagonallen = np.linalg.norm(diagonalvec) if diagonallen == 0: # Degenerate case: all centers are identical # Use a small epsilon or just the point itself Aexpanded = A - sAABB 0.001 Bexpanded = B + sAABB 0.001 else: direction = diagonalvec / diagonallen halflen = diagonallen / 2.0 # Expand bounds # A' = C + s r len # B' = C - s r len # Note: Source says A = C + s r len and B = C - s r len # But typically A is min and B is max. # If s > 1, the expansion might flip min/max depending on direction. # We compute the new bounds and then take min/max to ensure A <= B component-wise # for the containment check. # Actually, the source defines A and B as the corners. # Let's compute the two corners explicitly. corner1 = midpoint + sAABB direction halflen corner2 = midpoint - sAABB direction halflen Aexpanded = np.minimum(corner1, corner2) Bexpanded = np.maximum(corner1, corner2) # Step 5: Regroup images based on expanded AABB for i in range(N): # Check if camera center of image i is within [Aexpanded, Bexpanded] centeri = featurematrix[i,:3] if np.all(centeri >= Aexpanded) and np.all(centeri <= Bexpanded): blockimages[k].add(i) # Step 6: Select representative views representatives = [] for k in range(K): if not blockimages[k]: # Fallback: if a block is empty, pick a random image or the cluster centroid's image # This is a gap not explicitly covered, so we pick the first image of the original cluster originalclusterindices = np.where(clusterlabels == k)[0] if len(originalclusterindices) > 0: idx = originalclusterindices[0] else: idx = 0 # Fallback else: # Calculate Laplacian variance for each image in the block bestidx = None maxvar = -1 for i in blockimages[k]: # Compute Laplacian variance # Laplacian gradient is approximated by standard kernel # Var(Laplacian(I)) laplacianimg = computelaplacian(images[i]) var = np.var(laplacianimg) if var > maxvar: maxvar = var bestidx = i representatives.append(images[bestidx]) return representatives def computelaplacian(image): """ Computes the Laplacian gradient of an image. Uses a standard 3x3 Laplacian kernel. """ # Convert to grayscale if necessary if len(image.shape) == 3: gray = np.mean(image, axis=2) else: gray = image # Normalize to 0-1 gray = gray.astype(np.float64) if gray.max() > 1.0: gray = gray / 255.0 # Apply Laplacian kernel kernel = np.array([[0, 1, 0], [1, -4, 1], [0, 1, 0]]) # Convolve from scipy.signal import convolve2d laplacian = convolve2d(gray, kernel, mode='same', boundary='symm') return laplacian A data-driven spatial decomposition strategy that uses K-Means clustering on 3D camera center positions to partition large-scale scenes into sub-scenes for parallel training. It adapts to the actual distribution of viewpoints rather than using heuristic grids, providing a principled solution for decomposing large-scale scenes in 3D reconstruction tasks. Unlike Sub-scene Extension, which augments cluster radii to ensure overlap, this method performs only static spatial partitioning based on camera center positions. Time Complexity: Dominated by KMeans clustering, which is O(N \cdot K \cdot D \cdot I) where N is number of images, K is clusters, D is dimension (6), and I is iterations. Regrouping is O(N \cdot K) for checking bounds. Laplacian calculation is O(N \cdot H \cdot W) per image. Memory Complexity: O(N \cdot D) for feature vectors. O(N) for block assignments. Strengths: Robust in texture-less regions compared to SfM-based splitting. Ensures geometric coverage by clustering positions and directions. Computationally efficient. Limitations: Requires known camera poses (not suitable for pre-SfM stages). Blurring can occur if blocks are too close and blending is used. When to use: When training a second round of reconstruction/denoising with a fixed number of input views (e.g., 12) and needing to ensure diversity and sharpness. When not to use: When camera poses are unknown or unreliable. Originating from methods for large-scale NeRF reconstruction and sparse-view Gaussian Splatting, this technique addresses the scalability and stability issues of training on all available views. introduces it for "Denoise-GS" to select representative viewpoints for fine-grained denoising. introduces "Block Splitting" for "SCALAR-NeRF" to enable distributed training of local NeRF models. It differs from Mega-NeRF by using pose priors instead of feature-metric correspondences. name: K-Means Spatial Partitioning for Camera Clustering
head: Camera Center Clustering, Initial spatial partitioning
body: A data-driven spatial decomposition strategy that uses K-Means clustering on 3D camera center positions to partition large-scale scenes into sub-scenes for parallel training. It adapts to the actual distribution of viewpoints rather than using heuristic grids, providing a principled solution for decomposing large-scale scenes in 3D reconstruction tasks. Unlike Sub-scene Extension, which augments cluster radii to ensure overlap, this method performs only static spatial partitioning based on camera center positions. Inputs: Intrinsic and extrinsic camera parameters, and a sparse point cloud. Outputs: A set of camera clusters C1, \dots, CK, where each cluster corresponds to a sub-scene for separate training. Data Structures: Camera Positions: A list or array of 3D coordinates X \in \mathbb{R}^3 derived from the extrinsic parameters of all input cameras. Centroids: A list of K 3D coordinates Oi \in \mathbb{R}^3, representing the center of each cluster. Clusters: A mapping or list of sets Ci, where each Ci contains the indices or objects of cameras assigned to cluster i. Parameters: K (Number of clusters): Determined by the available GPU memory during training. Maximum Iterations: A preset limit for the K-Means loop. Threshold: A preset value for the change in error E to determine convergence. Steps: 1. Initialization: Choose K camera positions from the input set as the initial centroids (\mathbf{O1}, \mathbf{O2}, \dots, \mathbf{OK}). 2. Assignment: For each camera position X, assign it to the cluster Cj whose centroid Oj is closest to X. 3. Update: Recalculate the centroid for each cluster j as the mean of all camera positions X currently in that cluster: Oj = \frac{1}{|Cj|} \sum{X \in Cj} X 4. Convergence Check: Calculate the total within-cluster squared error E: E = \sum{i=1}^{K} \sum{X \in Ci} ||X - Oi||^22 where E is the total error, K is the number of clusters, Ci is the set of cameras in cluster i, X is a camera position, and Oi is the centroid of cluster i. Repeat steps 2–4 until the change in error E falls below the preset threshold or the maximum number of iterations is reached. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def kmeansspatialpartitioning(camerapositions, k, maxiterations, threshold): """ Partitions camera positions into K clusters using K-Means. Args: camerapositions: List of 3D vectors (numpy arrays or lists) representing camera centers. k: Integer, number of clusters (determined by GPU memory). maxiterations: Integer, maximum number of K-Means iterations. threshold: Float, minimum change in error to continue. Returns: clusters: List of lists, where clusters[i] contains indices of cameras in cluster i. centroids: List of 3D vectors, the final centroids of each cluster. """ n = len(camerapositions) # Step 1: Initialize centroids by choosing K camera positions # Using a simple deterministic selection for reproducibility if random seed not specified # In practice, random selection or K-Means++ is common, but source specifies "choosing K camera positions" indices = list(range(n)) # Simple selection: pick every n/K-th element or first K if n < K # To be robust, we select K distinct indices. # Note: Source does not specify the exact selection heuristic (e.g., random, first K). # We assume a standard random selection for initialization. import random initialindices = random.sample(indices, k) centroids = [camerapositions[i] for i in initialindices] clusters = [[] for in range(k)] for iteration in range(maxiterations): # Step 2: Assignment # Clear previous assignments for i in range(k): clusters[i] = [] for idx, pos in enumerate(camerapositions): # Find closest centroid mindist = float('inf') closestcluster = -1 for cidx, centroid in enumerate(centroids): # Euclidean distance squared dist = sum((p - c)2 for p, c in zip(pos, centroid)) if dist < mindist: mindist = dist closestcluster = cidx clusters[closestcluster].append(idx) # Step 3: Update newcentroids = [] for cidx in range(k): clusterpoints = [camerapositions[idx] for idx in clusters[cidx]] if not clusterpoints: # If a cluster is empty, keep the old centroid or reinitialize newcentroids.append(centroids[cidx]) else: # Calculate mean meanpos = [0.0, 0.0, 0.0] for p in clusterpoints: for d in range(3): meanpos[d] += p[d] for d in range(3): meanpos[d] /= len(clusterpoints) newcentroids.append(meanpos) # Step 4: Convergence Check # Calculate change in error or change in centroids # Source specifies "change in error E" # E = sum{i=1}^{K} sum{X in Ci} ||X - Oi||^22 currenterror = 0.0 for cidx, centroid in enumerate(newcentroids): for idx in clusters[cidx]: pos = camerapositions[idx] distsq = sum((p - c)2 for p, c in zip(pos, centroid)) currenterror += distsq # Calculate change in error from previous iteration if iteration == 0: preverror = currenterror else: errorchange = abs(currenterror - preverror) if errorchange < threshold: break preverror = currenterror centroids = newcentroids return clusters, centroids A post-processing step applied to initial K-Means clusters to ensure sufficient overlap between neighboring sub-scenes for robust image registration and multi-block rendering. It sets itself apart from its sibling, K-Means Spatial Partitioning for Camera Clustering, by actively augmenting cluster radii and adding nearby cameras to prevent registration failures, whereas the parent method only performs static spatial partitioning based on camera center positions. Time Complexity: Standard K-Means complexity O(I \cdot N \cdot K \cdot D), where I is iterations, N is number of cameras, K is clusters, D=3 is dimensionality. Memory Complexity: O(N + K \cdot D) to store positions and centroids. Strengths: Adapts to the actual spatial distribution of camera viewpoints, providing a principled and efficient solution for decomposing large-scale scenes. Limitations: The initial clustering does not guarantee sufficient camera overlap between clusters, meaning overlap between sub-scenes cannot be ensured, which can negatively impact the quality of the final rendered results if not handled by subsequent steps like Sub-scene Extension. When to use: When decomposing large-scale scenes for parallel training where GPU memory limits the size of each sub-scene. When not to use: When uniform grid-based partitioning is sufficient or when overlap is critical and not handled by post-processing. Originated in the context of BirdNeRF, a method for fast neural reconstruction of large-scale scenes from aerial imagery. It was introduced to address the limitations of traditional heuristic or grid-based spatial decomposition methods by leveraging K-Means clustering on camera center positions. name: Sub-scene Extension
head: Camera division, Cluster expansion, Spatial Decomposition with Conservative Expansion, Spatial partitioning extension
body: Sub-scene extension is a post-processing step applied to initial K-Means clusters to ensure sufficient overlap between neighboring sub-scenes for robust image registration and multi-block rendering. It sets itself apart from its sibling, K-Means Spatial Partitioning for Camera Clustering, by actively augmenting cluster radii and adding nearby cameras to prevent registration failures, whereas the parent method only performs static spatial partitioning based on camera center positions. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A set of initial clusters C1, \dots, CK produced by K-Means, where each cluster contains a set of cameras with 3D positions and parameters. Parameters: \sigma = 1.1: The expansion threshold (10% expansion). \text{MaxNum}: The maximum number of cameras the hardware can handle per cluster. \text{TopNum}: The hard upper bound on cameras per cluster after expansion, typically set to \text{MaxNum} or slightly below to ensure safety. Output: Expanded clusters C'1, \dots, C'K containing augmented camera sets. Data Structures: Each cluster Ck is a list of camera objects. Each camera object contains: position: 3D vector (x, y, z) representing the camera center. parameters: Additional camera intrinsics/extrinsics required for rendering. Steps: 1. Initialize Initial Size: Set the target size for initial K-Means clustering to 80\% of \text{MaxNum}. This reserves headroom for the expansion phase. 2. Calculate Intra-Cluster Radius: For each initial cluster Ck, calculate the maximum distance from the cluster centroid (or center of mass) to any camera position within the cluster. Let this be Rk. Formula: Rk = \max{c \in Ck} \| \text{position}(c) - \text{centroid}(Ck) \| 3. Expand Radius: Multiply the radius by the expansion threshold \sigma to get the new radius R'k. Formula: R'k = Rk \times \sigma 4. Add Neighboring Cameras: Identify all cameras not currently in Ck that fall within the new radius R'k from the cluster centroid. Add these cameras to Ck. 5. Enforce Hard Cap: If the number of cameras in the expanded cluster |C'k| exceeds \text{TopNum}, remove cameras from the cluster until |C'k| = \text{TopNum}. The specific selection criteria for removal (e.g., furthest from centroid) are not specified in the sources. 6. Repeat: Apply steps 2–5 for all initial clusters K. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def subsceneextension(clusters, maxnum, topnum, sigma=1.1): """ clusters: List of lists, where clusters[k] is a list of camera dicts. Each camera dict has 'position' (list of 3 floats). maxnum: int, hardware limit for initial clustering size. topnum: int, hard cap after expansion. sigma: float, expansion factor (default 1.1). Returns: List of expanded clusters. """ expandedclusters = [] for k in range(len(clusters)): currentcameras = clusters[k] if not currentcameras: expandedclusters.append([]) continue # Step 2: Calculate centroid n = len(currentcameras) centroid = [0.0, 0.0, 0.0] for cam in currentcameras: pos = cam['position'] centroid[0] += pos[0] centroid[1] += pos[1] centroid[2] += pos[2] centroid[0] /= n centroid[1] /= n centroid[2] /= n # Step 2: Calculate max intra-cluster radius Rk maxdistsq = 0.0 for cam in currentcameras: pos = cam['position'] dx = pos[0] - centroid[0] dy = pos[1] - centroid[1] dz = pos[2] - centroid[2] distsq = dxdx + dydy + dzdz if distsq > maxdistsq: maxdistsq = distsq Rk = maxdistsq 0.5 # Step 3: Expand radius Rprime = Rk sigma # Step 4: Add neighboring cameras # Identify all cameras in the entire scene not already in currentcameras # Note: In practice, 'allcameras' would be a global list passed in or indexed. # Here we assume a global list 'allscenecameras' is available. newcameras = [] for cam in allscenecameras: if cam in currentcameras: continue pos = cam['position'] dx = pos[0] - centroid[0] dy = pos[1] - centroid[1] dz = pos[2] - centroid[2] distsq = dxdx + dydy + dzdz if distsq <= Rprime Rprime: newcameras.append(cam) # Combine existing and new cameras expandedcluster = currentcameras + newcameras # Step 5: Enforce hard cap TopNum if len(expandedcluster) > topnum: # Removal strategy not specified in source. # Common practice is to remove cameras furthest from centroid. # Sorting by distance descending and keeping topnum. expandedcluster.sort(key=lambda c: (c['position'][0]-centroid[0])2 + (c['position'][1]-centroid[1])2 + (c['position'][2]-centroid[2])2, reverse=True) expandedcluster = expandedcluster[:topnum] expandedclusters.append(expandedcluster) return expandedclusters Edge Cases and Pitfalls: GPU Memory Overflow: Expansion may cause the number of cameras to exceed the initial \text{MaxNum} limit. This is handled by enforcing the hard upper bound \text{TopNum}. Degenerate Input: If a cluster has only one camera, the radius is 0. Expansion will still create a non-zero radius based on \sigma, potentially adding neighbors. Time Complexity: O(K \cdot N), where K is the number of clusters and N is the total number of cameras in the scene, as each cluster expansion requires checking distances to all other cameras. Memory Complexity: Increases memory usage per cluster due to added overlapping cameras, but bounded by \text{TopNum}. Strengths: Enhances the success rate of image registration and multi-block rendering by ensuring spatial overlap. Balances memory utilization and hardware reliability. Limitations: Requires careful tuning of \text{TopNum} to avoid memory overflow. The specific algorithm for removing cameras when capping is not defined. When to use: When using K-Means for large-scale scene partitioning and subsequent image registration is required. When not to use: If GPU memory is extremely constrained and overlap is not critical for the downstream task. Origin: Introduced in BirdNeRF for fast neural reconstruction of large-scale scenes from aerial imagery. History: Developed to address failures in image registration caused by insufficient overlap between spatially partitioned sub-scenes. Usage: Used in aerial imagery reconstruction pipelines where multiple blocks are rendered and aligned.
