name: Random Camera Sampling
head: Camera Sampling
body: Random Camera Sampling selects a fixed number of cameras from a predefined viewpoint stack by uniformly sampling indices without replacement. It solves the problem of generating a diverse set of training views for 3D reconstruction or novel view synthesis when a limited pool of existing captures is available. It differs from its sibling Random Pose Selection by drawing exclusively from a discrete, existing list of poses rather than generating continuous pose parameters from a distribution. Inputs: myviewpointstack: A list of camera objects or pose data structures representing available viewpoints. numcams: An integer specifying the number of cameras to sample. Outputs: camlist: A list of numcams camera objects, shuffled relative to their original order in the stack. Data Structures: myviewpointstack: A dynamic array (list) of camera poses. camlist: A dynamic array (list) of selected camera poses. Parameters: numcams: The count of cameras to extract. The source implementation fixes this value at 10. Steps: 1. Initialize an empty list camlist. 2. Set numcams to 10. 3. Loop numcams times: a. Generate a random integer loc uniformly distributed in the range [0, \text{len}(my\viewpoint\stack) - 1]. b. Remove the camera at index loc from myviewpointstack using a pop operation. c. Append the removed camera to camlist. 4. Return camlist. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def randomcamerasampling(myviewpointstack, numcams=10): """ Samples numcams cameras from myviewpointstack without replacement. Args: myviewpointstack: List of camera pose objects. numcams: Number of cameras to sample (default 10). Returns: List of sampled camera pose objects. """ camlist = [] # Note: The source implementation hardcodes numcams = 10 # but the function signature accepts it for flexibility. for in range(numcams): if len(myviewpointstack) == 0: raise ValueError("Not enough viewpoints in stack to sample requested number.") # Generate random index in [0, len(stack) - 1] loc = random.randint(0, len(myviewpointstack) - 1) # Pop camera at loc and append to result list camera = myviewpointstack.pop(loc) camlist.append(camera) return camlist Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Stack Exhaustion: If numcams exceeds the length of myviewpointstack, the algorithm will fail or return fewer cameras than requested. The implementation must guard against this. Replacement: The use of pop ensures sampling without replacement, preventing duplicate cameras in the output list. Structured Camera Batch Generation creates a list of camera samples for a 3D dataset by distributing them between close-up and general views based on a configurable ratio, sampling directions uniformly or within a hemisphere. It differs from basic Random Camera Sampling by introducing a structured bias towards specific viewing distances (close-up vs. general) and shuffling the final list to randomize order. It is chosen when the application requires a balanced mix of detailed and contextual views. Definition: Generates camera samples with a mix of close-up and general views. Steps: 1. Initialize a random number generator rng if not provided. 2. Calculate closeupcount as int(round(totalframes closeupratio)). 3. Loop index from 0 to totalframes - 1: a. Determine iscloseup as index < closeupcount. b. Sample radius using sampleradius with minradius, maxradius, iscloseup, and rng. c. Sample direction using sampledirection with radius, viewdistribution, and rng. d. Create a CameraSample with the computed position and iscloseup flag. e. Append the sample to the samples list. 4. Shuffle the samples list. 5. Return the shuffled samples. Parameters: CLOSEUPBANDFRACTION: A constant fraction of the radius span used for the close-up maximum radius, defaulting to 0.15. Time Complexity: O(N) where N is the number of cameras sampled, as each sample involves a constant-time random index generation and a list pop operation. Memory Complexity: O(N) to store the output list of sampled cameras. Strengths: Simple to implement; guarantees no duplicate views; efficient for small to medium-sized viewpoint stacks. Limitations: Does not guarantee spatial coverage of the scene; performance depends entirely on the diversity of the input myviewpointstack. When to use: When a fixed, small set of diverse training views is needed from a pre-existing capture set, such as in FastGS training. When not to use: When continuous pose generation is required or when the input stack is too small to provide adequate coverage. Random Camera Sampling is a technique used in Gaussian Splatting and 3D reconstruction pipelines to select training viewpoints. It is implemented in the FastGS repository, which provides optimized tools for training 3D Gaussian Splatting models. The method is often used in conjunction with other sampling strategies like Structured Camera Batch Generation to ensure balanced dataset creation. fastgs/FastGS, https://github.com/fastgs/FastGS, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial) yumehiko/3dgs-dataset-builder, https://github.com/yumehiko/3dgs-dataset-builder, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial)

name: Active Learning Scene Sampling
head: Bayesian Optimization Scene Sampler
body: Active Learning Scene Sampling finds optimal camera poses (position and rotation) that minimize the deviation of median render time from a target time budget using Bayesian optimization. It differs from its parent, Random Camera Sampling, by intelligently selecting viewpoints based on performance feedback rather than uniform random selection. Inputs: timebudget (float): Target render time in seconds or milliseconds. numsamples (int): Number of initialization and iteration points for the Bayesian optimizer. defaultlodparams (List[float]): Default Level-of-Detail parameters, typically [1.0, 1.0, 1.0, 1.0]. samplerparams: Object containing minpoint and maxpoint defining the spatial bounds for camera positions. Outputs: Best position and rotation keys starting with p and r extracted from the optimizer's maximum result. Data Structures: Search bounds pbounds: Dictionary mapping parameter names to (min, max) tuples for position (x, y, z) and rotation (rx, ry, rz). State object: Contains pos (position vector) and quaternion representation of rotation. Steps: 1. Define search bounds pbounds for position coordinates (x, y, z) and rotation Euler angles (rx, ry, rz) using samplerparams.minpoint and samplerparams.maxpoint. 2. Initialize a BayesianOptimization instance with a loss function. 3. The loss function computes the absolute difference between the measured render time and the timebudget: \text{loss} = | \text{render\time} - \text{time\budget} | 4. Inside the loss function, for each set of optimizer kwargs: a. Set samplestate.pos from the optimizer's position kwargs. b. Convert Euler angles to a quaternion using the standard library: \text{quat}{xyzw} = \text{Rotation.from\euler}("XYZ", [rx, ry, rz]).\text{as\quat}() c. Reorder quaternion components from [x, y, z, w] to [w, x, y, z] to match the engine's expected format: \text{quat}{engine} = \text{vkgs\py.quat}(w, x, y, z) d. Pass the state to the model to predict LOD parameters using defaultlodparams if not specified. e. Call engine.sample() to perform the rendering and measure the actual render time. 5. Run the optimization loop with initpoints=numsamples and niter=numsamples. 6. Extract the best position and rotation from optimizer.max["params"], filtering keys starting with p and r. Pitfalls: Quaternion component ordering varies between libraries. The implementation explicitly reorders [x, y, z, w] to [w, x, y, z] before passing to the engine. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. from scipy.spatial.transform import Rotation from bayesopt import BayesianOptimization def activelearningscenesampling(timebudget, numsamples, defaultlodparams, samplerparams): """ Finds optimal camera poses minimizing deviation from target render time. """ # Define search bounds # Note: Exact bounds logic depends on samplerparams structure pbounds = { 'px': (samplerparams.minpoint[0], samplerparams.maxpoint[0]), 'py': (samplerparams.minpoint[1], samplerparams.maxpoint[1]), 'pz': (samplerparams.minpoint[2], samplerparams.maxpoint[2]), 'rx': (-180, 180), # Typical Euler range, adjust if specified 'ry': (-180, 180), 'rz': (-180, 180) } def lossfunction(px, py, pz, rx, ry, rz): # 1. Set position pos = [px, py, pz] # 2. Convert Euler to Quaternion [x, y, z, w] rot = Rotation.fromeuler("XYZ", [rx, ry, rz]) quatxyzw = rot.asquat() # 3. Reorder to [w, x, y, z] for engine w, x, y, z = quatxyzw[3], quatxyzw[0], quatxyzw[1], quatxyzw[2] quatengine = (w, x, y, z) # 4. Predict LOD params (placeholder for model logic) lodparams = defaultlodparams # 5. Measure render time # engine.sample() is assumed to be available in context rendertime = engine.sample(pos, quatengine, lodparams) # 6. Return negative loss (BayesianOptimization maximizes) return -abs(rendertime - timebudget) optimizer = BayesianOptimization( f=lossfunction, pbounds=pbounds, randomstate=1) # Run optimization optimizer.maximize( initpoints=numsamples, niter=numsamples,) # Extract best params bestparams = optimizer.max['params'] bestpos = [bestparams['px'], bestparams['py'], bestparams['pz']] bestrot = [bestparams['rx'], bestparams['ry'], bestparams['rz']] return bestpos, bestrot Time Complexity: Depends on the number of iterations (numsamples) and the cost of each render evaluation. Bayesian optimization typically requires fewer evaluations than grid search but each evaluation is expensive (full render). Memory Complexity: Low, storing only the optimizer state and current sample parameters. Strengths: Automatically tunes camera poses to meet specific performance budgets (e.g., frame rate targets). Limitations: Requires a differentiable or measurable render time metric; sensitive to the choice of numsamples and search bounds. When to use: When rendering performance is critical and camera viewpoints need to be optimized for a specific time budget. When not to use: When uniform coverage is required regardless of performance, or when render time is not a reliable metric for scene complexity. This method originates from the CLOD-3DGS project by Facebook Research, which uses Bayesian optimization to manage Level-of-Detail (LOD) parameters and camera sampling for 3D Gaussian Splatting. It addresses the need for efficient rendering of large-scale 3D scenes by adapting camera poses to maintain target frame rates. facebookresearch/CLOD-3DGS, https://github.com/facebookresearch/CLOD-3DGS, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial)

name: Elliptic Cylinder Sampled Views
head: Elliptic Cylinder View Sampling
body: Elliptic Cylinder Sampled Views is a camera trajectory generation method that creates random viewpoints directed at a scene center for computing SDS (Score Distillation Sampling) loss, using an elliptical cylinder that fits the training view positions. It differs from its sibling Active Learning Scene Sampling by relying on a geometric fit of existing views rather than an active learning loop, and from Warped Views by generating novel, uncorrelated positions rather than rotating existing ones. Inputs: A set of N training camera poses \{Pi\}{i=1}^N, where each pose Pi consists of a translation vector ti and a rotation matrix Ri. Outputs: A single new camera pose P{new} = (t{new}, R{new}). Data Structures: Camera Pose: Struct containing translation (vec3) and rotation (3x3 matrix). Scene Center: vec3, typically the mean of all training camera positions. Steps: 1. Coordinate Alignment: Transform all training camera positions to align with a world coordinate system where the positive Z-axis is perpendicular to the ground. This is achieved using Principal Component Analysis (PCA) on the training camera positions. Let the transformed positions be t'i. 2. Ellipse Fitting: Determine the scaling factors for the elliptical axes in the X-Y plane. Calculate the absolute displacements of each transformed position from the scene center: di = \sqrt{(x'i)^2 + (y'i)^2}. The scaling factors are the 90th percentile of these displacements. Let these factors be a (semi-major axis) and b (semi-minor axis). 3. Vertical Bounds: Set the vertical bounds for the Z-coordinate. The lower bound z{min} and upper bound z{max} are the 10th and 90th percentiles of the Z-coordinates of the transformed training views, respectively. 4. Random Translation Sampling: Uniformly randomly select a camera translation vector t{new}. Select an angle \phi \in [0, 2\pi). Set x{new} = a \cos \phi and y{new} = b \sin \phi. Set z{new} uniformly at random within [z{min}, z{max}]. t{new} = [x{new}, y{new}, z{new}]^T in the aligned coordinate system. 5. Rotation Computation: Compute the camera’s rotation matrix R{new}. Look-at Vector: Direct the look-at vector towards the scene center. In the aligned system, if the scene center is at the origin (or known offset), the direction is -\text{normalize}(t{new} - \text{center}). Up Vector: Align the up vector with the average up vector of the input views. Compute the average up vector \bar{u} from the training cameras' rotation matrices and normalize it. Construct R{new} such that its columns correspond to the right, up, and forward vectors derived from the look-at and up vectors. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import numpy as np def generateellipticcylinderview(trainingposes, scenecenter): """ Generate a single random camera view using the Elliptic Cylinder method. Args: trainingposes: List of dicts with 'translation' (vec3) and 'rotation' (3x3). scenecenter: vec3 representing the center of the scene. Returns: dict with 'translation' (vec3) and 'rotation' (3x3). """ # Step 1: Coordinate Alignment via PCA positions = np.array([p['translation'] for p in trainingposes]) # Center positions for PCA meanpos = np.mean(positions, axis=0) centeredpos = positions - meanpos # Compute covariance matrix and eigenvectors cov = np.cov(centeredpos.T) eigenvalues, eigenvectors = np.linalg.eigh(cov) # Sort eigenvectors by eigenvalue (descending) to align Z with ground normal # Assuming the smallest eigenvalue corresponds to the ground normal direction (Z) # Reorder: Z axis is the eigenvector with the smallest eigenvalue idx = np.argsort(eigenvalues) zaxis = eigenvectors[:, idx[0]] # Construct rotation matrix to align world Z with zaxis # We need a rotation matrix Ralign such that Ralign @ [0,0,1] = zaxis # This is complex; simpler approach: rotate points so zaxis becomes [0,0,1] # Let's define the alignment transform as rotating the space so zaxis aligns with world Z # For simplicity in implementation, we assume we can compute a rotation matrix Ralign # that maps the principal component basis to the world basis. # Here we assume zaxis is the normal to the ground. # Create a basis where the third column is zaxis # We need two other orthogonal vectors. # Let's pick an arbitrary vector not parallel to zaxis arbitrary = np.array([0, 0, 1]) if abs(zaxis[2]) < 0.9 else np.array([1, 0, 0]) xaxis = np.cross(zaxis, arbitrary) xaxis = xaxis / np.linalg.norm(xaxis) yaxis = np.cross(xaxis, zaxis) Ralign = np.columnstack((xaxis, yaxis, zaxis)) # Transform positions to aligned system alignedpositions = (Ralign.T @ (positions - meanpos).T).T # Step 2: Determine scaling factors (90th percentile of absolute displacements in XY) xydisplacements = np.sqrt(alignedpositions[:, 0]2 + alignedpositions[:, 1]2) scalex = np.percentile(xydisplacements, 90) scaley = np.percentile(xydisplacements, 90) # Step 3: Set vertical bounds (10th and 90th percentiles of Z) zcoords = alignedpositions[:, 2] zmin = np.percentile(zcoords, 10) zmax = np.percentile(zcoords, 90) # Step 4: Uniformly randomly select a camera translation vector phi = np.random.uniform(0, 2 np.pi) xnew = scalex np.cos(phi) ynew = scaley np.sin(phi) znew = np.random.uniform(zmin, zmax) taligned = np.array([xnew, ynew, znew]) # Step 5: Compute rotation matrix # Look-at vector: towards scene center. # In aligned system, scene center is effectively at origin relative to the fit? # The notes say "directing its look-at vector towards the scene center". # Assuming scenecenter is in original coordinates, we must transform it or assume it's the origin of the fit. # Let's assume the scene center is the mean of the training positions, which is now at origin in aligned space? # Actually, meanpos was subtracted. So the center of the distribution is origin. lookatdir = -taligned # Looking back towards origin/center lookatdir = lookatdir / np.linalg.norm(lookatdir) # Average up vector of input views upvectors = np.array([p['rotation'][:, 1] for p in trainingposes]) avgup = np.mean(upvectors, axis=0) avgup = avgup / np.linalg.norm(avgup) # Compute right vector right = np.cross(avgup, lookatdir) right = right / np.linalg.norm(right) # Recompute up to ensure orthogonality up = np.cross(lookatdir, right) Raligned = np.columnstack((right, up, lookatdir)) # Transform back to original coordinate system tnew = (Ralign @ taligned) + meanpos Rnew = (Ralign @ Raligned).T # Rotation matrices are orthogonal, inverse is transpose return {'translation': tnew, 'rotation': Rnew} Parameters: Percentile for ellipse scaling: 90th. Percentile for vertical bounds: 10th and 90th. Number of sampled views: Fixed number, as per Random Camera Sampling. Edge Cases: Degenerate Input: If all training views are collinear or coplanar, PCA may fail to produce a stable ground normal. Add a check for singular covariance matrix and fallback to a default up vector (e.g., [0,1,0]). Precision: Ensure numerical stability when computing cross products for near-parallel vectors. A view sampling strategy creating novel viewpoints by rotating training cameras around an estimated center axis to provide large view overlapping, unlike SDS sampled views. It extracts the up-vector of each camera as Y = [R{11}, R{21}, R{31}]^T where R is the rotation matrix. It computes the normalized average up-vector across all cameras to serve as an estimate of the scene center and orientation: \bar{Y} = \frac{1}{N} \sum Yi, normalized to \frac{\bar{Y}}{||\bar{Y}||}. Novel viewpoints are created by rotating the training cameras around this estimated center axis by various angles using the Rodrigues’ rotation formula: P' = P \cos \theta + (P \times \bar{Y}) \sin \theta + \bar{Y} (\bar{Y} \cdot P) (1 - \cos \theta), where P represents the original camera pose. Angles \theta selected are -3°, -1.5°, 1.5°, and 3°, resulting in four warped viewpoints for each training camera. Time Complexity: O(N) for PCA and percentile calculations, where N is the number of training views. Sampling a single view is O(1). Memory Complexity: O(N) to store training poses and intermediate statistics. Strengths: Ensures sampled views are geometrically consistent with the input data distribution, providing good coverage for SDS loss. Limitations: Does not provide the large view overlapping required for depth warping losses, which is why Warped Views are used for those. When to use: When computing SDS loss for 3D Gaussian Splatting from sparse input views. When not to use: When large view overlapping is required for depth consistency losses. Originating from the SparseGS paper, this method is part of the UVR (Unsupervised View Regularization) framework designed to regularize 3DGS training from sampled views. It is specifically applied to compute the SDS loss, complementing other components like Pearson Depth Loss and Depth Warping Loss which use different sampling strategies. name: Structured Camera Batch Generation
head: Camera Sample Generation
body: Generates a deterministic list of camera samples (positions) for a 3D dataset, distributing them between close-up views and general views based on a specified ratio, and sampling directions uniformly or within a hemisphere. It differs from its parent Random Camera Sampling by enforcing a structured ratio of close-up to general views rather than purely random selection, and from siblings like Elliptic Cylinder Sampled Views by using spherical radius constraints rather than elliptic cylinder geometry. Inputs: totalframes: Integer, total number of camera samples to generate. closeupratio: Float, fraction of totalframes designated as close-up views. minradius: Float, minimum distance from the center for any camera. maxradius: Float, maximum distance from the center for general views. viewdistribution: String or enum, specifying "uniform" (full sphere) or "hemisphere" (upper/lower half). rng: Random number generator instance. If None, a new default RNG is initialized. Outputs: A list of CameraSample objects, each containing: position: 3D vector (x, y, z) representing the camera location. iscloseup: Boolean flag indicating if the sample is a close-up view. Data Structures: CameraSample: A simple struct or class with fields position (vec3) and iscloseup (bool). samples: A list of CameraSample objects. Parameters: CLOSEUPBANDFRACTION: Constant fraction of the radius span used to determine the maximum radius for close-up views. Default value is 0.15. Steps: 1. Initialize rng if it is None. 2. Calculate closeupcount as int(round(totalframes closeupratio)). 3. Calculate closeupmaxradius as minradius + (maxradius - minradius) CLOSEUPBANDFRACTION. 4. Initialize an empty list samples. 5. Loop index from 0 to totalframes - 1: a. Determine if the current frame is a close-up view: iscloseup = (index < closeupcount). b. Determine the radius bounds: If iscloseup is true, set radiusmin = minradius and radiusmax = closeupmaxradius. If iscloseup is false, set radiusmin = closeupmaxradius and radiusmax = maxradius. (Note: The source implies a split in the radius span based on the band fraction, though exact boundary handling at closeupmaxradius is implementation-dependent.) c. Sample radius using sampleradius(radiusmin, radiusmax, rng). d. Sample direction using sampledirection(radius, viewdistribution, rng). e. Compute position as direction radius (assuming origin at 0,0,0). f. Create a CameraSample with position and iscloseup. g. Append the sample to samples. 6. Shuffle the samples list in place using rng. 7. Return samples. Helper Functions: sampleradius(minr, maxr, rng): Samples a scalar radius uniformly between minr and maxr. sampledirection(radius, distribution, rng): If distribution is "uniform": Samples a point uniformly on the surface of a sphere of radius. If distribution is "hemisphere": Samples a point uniformly on the surface of a hemisphere of radius. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: If totalframes is 0, return an empty list. If closeupratio is 0, closeupcount is 0, and all samples are general views. If closeupratio is 1, closeupcount equals totalframes, and all samples are close-up views. Precision issues may arise if minradius equals maxradius; in this case, the radius is constant. The shuffle step ensures that the structured ratio is not preserved in the output order, which is critical for training stability in stochastic optimization. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import random import math def structuredcamerabatchgeneration( totalframes: int, closeupratio: float, minradius: float, maxradius: float, viewdistribution: str, rng: random.Random = None) -> list: """ Generates a batch of structured camera samples. Args: totalframes: Total number of samples. closeupratio: Fraction of samples that are close-up. minradius: Minimum camera distance from center. maxradius: Maximum camera distance from center. viewdistribution: 'uniform' or 'hemisphere'. rng: Random number generator. If None, uses global random. Returns: List of dicts with 'position' (vec3) and 'iscloseup' (bool). """ if rng is None: rng = random.Random() closeupcount = int(round(totalframes closeupratio)) closeupbandfraction = 0.15 # Default constant radiusspan = maxradius - minradius closeupmaxradius = minradius + radiusspan closeupbandfraction samples = [] for index in range(totalframes): iscloseup = index < closeupcount if iscloseup: rmin = minradius rmax = closeupmaxradius else: rmin = closeupmaxradius rmax = maxradius # Sample radius uniformly radius = rng.uniform(rmin, rmax) # Sample direction if viewdistribution == "uniform": direction = samplespheredirection(rng) elif viewdistribution == "hemisphere": direction = samplehemispheredirection(rng) else: raise ValueError(f"Unknown viewdistribution: {viewdistribution}") position = [direction[i] radius for i in range(3)] samples.append({"position": position, "iscloseup": iscloseup}) rng.shuffle(samples) return samples def samplespheredirection(rng: random.Random) -> list: """Sample a point uniformly on the unit sphere.""" # Using normal distribution method for uniform sphere sampling x = rng.gauss(0, 1) y = rng.gauss(0, 1) z = rng.gauss(0, 1) norm = math.sqrt(xx + yy + zz) return [x/norm, y/norm, z/norm] def samplehemispheredirection(rng: random.Random) -> list: """Sample a point uniformly on the upper hemisphere (z > 0).""" while True: x = rng.uniform(-1, 1) y = rng.uniform(-1, 1) z = rng.uniform(0, 1) norm = math.sqrt(xx + yy + zz) if norm > 0: return [x/norm, y/norm, z/norm] A variant that refines camera positions based on rendering error. Initial sampling uses farthest point sampling on a hulling sphere with random perturbations, looking at the object center. Refinement involves downsampling reference and rendered images, finding the pixel with the largest error, identifying K points projecting closest to this pixel, and setting the new focal center to the mean 3D position of these points. New cameras are sampled on a small sphere around this focal point. This is chosen for complex topologies where uniform sampling fails to converge quickly. Time Complexity: O(N) where N is totalframes, for generation and shuffling. Memory Complexity: O(N) to store the list of samples. Strengths: Ensures balanced coverage of close-up and general views, which is critical for high-fidelity reconstruction. The shuffle prevents order bias. Limitations: Does not adapt to scene content during generation (unlike Error-aware View Sampling). The fixed ratio may not suit all scenes. When to use: When a balanced dataset of close-up and general views is required for training or evaluation. When not to use: When the scene has complex topology requiring adaptive refinement. Originated in the context of 3D Gaussian Splatting dataset generation, specifically in the 3dgs-dataset-builder tool. It addresses the need for structured camera trajectories that provide both detailed close-ups and broader context views. The method is distinct from error-aware approaches proposed in differentiable surface splatting literature, which focus on iterative refinement based on image loss. yumehiko/3dgs-dataset-builder, https://github.com/yumehiko/3dgs-dataset-builder, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial) Differentiable surface splatting for point-based geometry processing, https://doi.org/10.1145/3355089.3356513, fetched 2026-10-26

name: Error-aware View Sampling
head: error-guided camera refinement
body: Error-aware view sampling is a dynamic camera trajectory generation method that refines camera positions based on the current rendering error, ensuring focused coverage of complex or poorly reconstructed regions. Unlike static structured batches, it adapts to the optimization state by targeting areas of high discrepancy between rendered and reference images. The method operates in two phases: initial global coverage and iterative local refinement. Inputs: Reference images (ground truth). Current rendered images. A set of 3D points (e.g., from a point cloud or mesh). Hyperparameters: K (number of points to consider for focal center), V (number of views per step, if applicable), sampling radius for refinement. Outputs: A new set of camera poses (position and orientation). Data Structures: Reference Image: 2D array of pixel values. Rendered Image: 2D array of pixel values. 3D Points: List of (x, y, z) coordinates. Camera Pose: Position \mathbf{c} and look-at target \mathbf{t}. Steps: 1. Initial Sampling (Global Coverage): Sample camera positions on a hulling sphere surrounding the object using Farthest Point Sampling (FPS) to ensure uniform initial distribution. Randomly perturb these sampled positions to break symmetry. Set the camera look-at target to the center of the object (centroid of the 3D points). Repeat this process periodically during optimization to maintain global coverage. 2. Error-Aware Refinement (Local Focus): Compute Error: Downsample the reference image and the current rendered image to a manageable resolution. Compute the pixel-wise error (e.g., L2 norm or L1 norm) between the downsampled reference and rendered images. Identify Max Error: Find the pixel coordinates (u{max}, v{max}) with the largest error value. Back-Project to 3D: Identify K 3D points whose projection onto the image plane is closest to (u{max}, v{max}). This requires knowing the current camera projection matrix or ray directions. Determine Focal Center: Calculate the mean 3D position \mathbf{c}{focus} of these K points: \mathbf{c}{focus} = \frac{1}{K} \sum{i=1}^{K} \mathbf{p}i where \mathbf{p}i are the selected 3D points. Sample New Poses: Sample new camera positions on a sphere centered at \mathbf{c}{focus} with a relatively small radius (distance). Set Orientation: Set the new camera look-at target to \mathbf{c}{focus}. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def errorawareviewsampling(points, refimg, renderimg, K, radius, fpscount): # Phase 1: Initial Global Sampling (performed periodically) # 1. Sample fpscount positions on a hulling sphere using Farthest Point Sampling globalpositions = farthestpointsamplingonsphere(fpscount) # 2. Randomly perturb positions globalpositions += randomperturbation(globalpositions) # 3. Set look-at to object center objectcenter = mean(points) globalcameras = [Camera(pos, objectcenter) for pos in globalpositions] # Phase 2: Error-Aware Refinement (performed every step or frequently) # 1. Downsample images refdown = downsample(refimg, factor=4) renderdown = downsample(renderimg, factor=4) # 2. Compute pixel-wise error errormap = abs(refdown - renderdown) # 3. Find pixel with largest error maxerrorpixel = argmax(errormap) # 4. Find K points closest to this pixel's projection # Assuming we have a function to project 3D points to 2D for the current camera projectedpoints = projectpointstoimage(points, currentcamera) distances = computedistancetopixel(projectedpoints, maxerrorpixel) kindices = argsort(distances)[:K] kpoints = [points[i] for i in kindices] # 5. Compute focal center focalcenter = mean(kpoints) # 6. Sample new camera positions on a sphere around focal center localpositions = sampleonsphere(focalcenter, radius, count=V) # 7. Set look-at to focal center localcameras = [Camera(pos, focalcenter) for pos in localpositions] return globalcameras, localcameras Parameters: K: Number of points to average for the focal center. Not given in the sources. Radius: Distance from the focal center for sampling new cameras. Described as "relatively small". FPS Count: Number of initial global samples. Not given in the sources. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision: Downsampling images may smooth out high-frequency errors, leading to suboptimal focal points. The sources do not specify the downsampling factor. Boundaries: If the object has complex topology, the initial uniform sampling may be insufficient, necessitating the error-aware step. Degenerate Input: If K points are not available (e.g., too few points), the method fails. Not given in the sources. This variant uses a target mesh and camera poses to sample views. At each training step, V camera views are sampled. All rays hitting the mesh across these views are identified. A random subset of these rays is selected to provide uniform coverage around the object. The rendering error against ground-truth pixels at the ray intersections is minimized to drive optimization (e.g., HKTex optimization). This approach is suitable when a mesh is available and the goal is to optimize texture or material properties rather than geometry from scratch. Time Complexity: The initial FPS sampling is O(N \log N) or O(N^2) depending on implementation, where N is the number of points. The error-aware step involves image downsampling (O(W \times H)), error computation (O(W \times H)), and finding K closest points (O(M) where M is the number of points). Overall, it is efficient per step but requires rendering at each step to compute error. Memory Complexity: Requires storing reference and rendered images, and the 3D points. Not given in the sources. Strengths: Quickly converges on complex shapes by focusing on high-error regions. Improves point positions in small holes during large shape deformation. Limitations: Requires rendering at each step to compute error, which can be computationally expensive. Performance depends on the quality of the initial sampling. When to use: When optimizing geometry or texture for complex shapes where uniform sampling is insufficient. When not to use: When computational resources are limited and rendering is too slow. The method was introduced in "Differentiable surface splatting for point-based geometry processing" by. It addresses the challenge of quick convergence in differentiable rendering for point-based geometry editing. The authors found that simple uniform sampling on a hulling sphere was insufficient for shapes with complex topology, leading to the development of the error-aware refinement strategy. name: Multi-timestep Sampling for Scene Generation
head: DreamScene
body: Multi-timestep sampling is a method for multi-stage scene-level generation that synthesizes a surrounding environment, ground, and objects simultaneously. It is distinguished from sibling methods like GALA3D, which generates objects separately and composes them, by avoiding complicated object composition through joint synthesis. Inputs and Outputs Input: A text prompt or image condition defining the desired scene. Output: A 3D scene representation comprising the surrounding environment, ground plane, and constituent objects. Data Structures Not given in the sources. Steps 1. Initialize the scene generation process using a diffusion model. 2. Apply multi-timestep sampling to guide the generation process across multiple stages. 3. Synthesize the surrounding environment, ground, and objects concurrently within the multi-stage framework. 4. Refine the generated scene components to ensure consistency. Formulas Not given in the sources. Parameters Not given in the sources. Edge Cases and Pitfalls Not given in the sources. Uses object-level text-to-3D models to generate objects and a scene-level diffusion model to compose them. Choose when modular object generation is preferred. Utilizes diffusion priors from inpainting and depth estimation to generate different viewpoints iteratively. Choose when iterative viewpoint refinement is needed. Generates a 360-degree panoramic image and converts it into a 3D scene with depth estimation. Choose when panoramic consistency is required. Not given in the sources. The method was proposed in the paper "DreamScene". It is used in the context of 3D scene generation, specifically to address the complexity of composing separate objects into a coherent scene. name: Synthetic Dataset Generation
head: RealEstate10K stratification, Stratified Scene Dataset Generation, Synthetic stratified dataset creation, Training Data Generation, Training dataset generation for DEH
body: Synthetic dataset generation is the procedure of creating labeled training images by rendering 3D scenes with controlled variations in lighting, camera poses, and material properties. It solves the problem of insufficient or biased real-world data for training neural rendering and computer vision models by providing ground-truth annotations (depth, normals, segmentation) and diverse appearance variations. It differs from sibling methods like Synthetic Camera Trajectory Generation by focusing on the full pipeline of scene composition, texture/lighting randomization, and dataset balancing, rather than just the geometric path of the camera. The method varies significantly by application domain (volume visualization, holography, SLAM, NeRF). The following steps cover the common patterns found in the sources. Inputs: 3D scene geometry (meshes/volumes), texture libraries, camera parameters (FOV, resolution), lighting models, and scene layout constraints. Outputs: A dataset D consisting of tuples (I, A, P), where I is the rendered image (RGB/Depth), A are annotations (depth, normals, instance masks), and P are camera poses. Scene Graph: Nested structure levels (e.g., exterior, interior, object). Dataset Sample: For SDDF models, a sample is defined as sj = (pj, vj, f^j, i^j, s^j), where pj is ray origin, vj is direction, f^j is signed distance, i^j is intersection indicator, and s^j is sign indicator. View Space: Defined as a hemisphere (radius 4) for Synthetic-NeRF or a 3D bounding box for Tanks & Temple. 1. Scene Composition: For stratified scenes, define nested levels (Level 0: exterior, Level 1: interior, Level 2: object). For indoor scenes, compose rooms using object meshes (e.g., from free3d.com) with scale/pose transformations. For holography, ensure distances between camera and objects are significantly longer than distances between different objects to symmetrically blur either side of the focal plane. 2. Texture and Lighting Randomization: Sample textures from CC0 libraries for training and benchmark datasets for evaluation. Randomly sample light source colors, orientations, and intensities. Restrict maximum intensity (e.g., <1000W or specific bounds) to prevent overexposure. For volume visualization, uniformly sample Phong reflection coefficients: Ambient=1, Diffuse \in [0.25, 0.75], Specular \in [0.5, 1], Shininess \in [20, 100]. 3. Camera Trajectory and Pose Sampling: Define trajectories using Catmull-Rom splines on control points or Bézier curves. Sample poses from curved hemispheres centered on focal objects. For active mapping, sample waypoints uniformly from the trajectory (e.g., 100 waypoints) and select a subset (e.g., 10) for information gain calculation. 4. Rendering: Render color and depth images using a renderer (e.g., Blender, BlenderProc). Apply noise to depth maps to simulate real sensor noise. For holography, render varifocal images with symmetric blur consistent with eye optics. 5. Dataset Augmentation (SDDF Specific): Convert sensor poses and range measurements into dataset samples. Generate negative samples to balance sign indicators: for each sample (pj, vj, f^j, i^j, s^j), generate (p', vj, -\epsilon, 1, -1) where p' = pj + (f^j + \epsilon)vj and \epsilon > 0. Ray Generation (SDDF): pj = pt, vj = Rt vi, f^j = r{t,i}, i^j = 1, s^j = 1. Negative Sample Origin: p' = pj + (f^j + \epsilon)vj. Holographic Blur Condition: Distance(Camera, Object) \gg Distance(Object 1, Object 2). Resolution: 256x256, 400x400. FOV: 50 degrees. Viewpoints: N=2,352 for volume categories; 100 waypoints for NeRF. Split: Typically 30/15/15 or 30/10/10 images per level. Overexposure: If light intensity is too high, intensity sums vary across varifocal images, violating energy conservation and preventing single wave field construction. Depth Overfitting: Pixel-wise depth distribution must be almost uniform (except background) to prevent overfitting to specific depths. Sign Imbalance: Raw SDDF data has all s^j=1 and f^j \ge 0. Negative samples are required for training stability. Dynamic Motion: Real scenes must filter out clips with dynamic motion to ensure static scene assumption. A procedure to convert sensor poses and range measurements into a dataset D suitable for training the SDDF model, including augmentation for sign balance. It is distinct by its focus on balancing signed distance function signs through negative sample generation. Choose this when training signed distance field networks that require balanced positive/negative samples. Defines the camera view space (hemisphere or bounding box) and sampling strategy for active viewpoint generation and information gain calculation. It is distinct by its use of spherical coordinates constrained to point at the object center and sparse 3D point sampling for efficiency. Choose this for active NeRF mapping where viewpoint selection is critical. Synthetic dataset creation for evaluating geometry manipulation, using 8 types of complex indoor rooms. It is distinct by its focus on instance-level rendering and object manipulation within composed indoor scenes. Choose this for tasks requiring instance segmentation and geometry decomposition. Time Complexity: Training time scales with dataset size and scene complexity. For example, Strata-NeRF takes 6h 20m for 150k iterations on an RTX 3090 for a specific scene, compared to 5h 30m for mipNeRF-360. Memory Complexity: Depends on the number of rendered images and annotations. Volume categories can generate up to 6.0 \times 10^5 images. Strengths: Provides perfect ground truth; allows controlled variation of lighting and camera poses; avoids real-world sensor noise and occlusion ambiguities. Limitations: Domain gap between synthetic and real data; computationally expensive to render large datasets; requires careful randomization to avoid overfitting to synthetic artifacts. When to Use: When real data is scarce, expensive to collect, or lacks precise annotations. When Not to Use: When the target application is highly sensitive to real-world sensor noise or complex lighting interactions not captured by the synthetic renderer. Synthetic dataset generation originated from the need for labeled data in computer vision and volume visualization. Early work focused on volume rendering for medical imaging, using opacity and color transfer functions to generate training data for viewpoint estimation. Later, it expanded to neural rendering (NeRF) and SLAM, where synthetic scenes are used to train and evaluate reconstruction algorithms. Recent developments include stratified scene generation for hierarchical modeling and holographic display training data with specific optical constraints. name: Replica Dataset Preparation
head: Replica Data Processing
body: Replica Dataset Preparation filters and corrects the synthetic Replica indoor scan dataset for neural rendering training and evaluation. It addresses unrealistic camera poses (e.g., inside furniture), label ambiguity, and coordinate system misalignment by filtering invalid renders, normalizing poses to the origin, and semi-automatically correcting semantic labels. Inputs: RGB images, camera poses, semantic labels, and point clouds from the Replica dataset. Outputs: Filtered image sets, corrected semantic labels, normalized camera poses, and near/far clipping parameters. The input data consists of: Images: RGB arrays of resolution 340 \times 600. Poses: Camera poses for the rendered images. Labels: Semantic segmentation maps aligned with images. Point Clouds: 3D coordinates associated with the scene. 1. Scene Selection: Select specific scenes from the Replica dataset. Standard preparation uses room0, room1, office3, and office4. For sparse-view variants, use room0, room1, room2, office0, office1, office2, and office3. 2. Geometric Filtering: Render images from the provided camera poses. Filter out any images where the camera position is inside furniture or other geometry, as these are unrealistically rendered. 3. Coordinate Normalization: Adjust the camera poses so that the 3D points visible in the selected training images are centered around the world origin (0,0,0). This is critical for pose refinement stability. 4. Clipping Plane Setup: Set NeRF near/far clipping planes. Default is (0.1, 10.0). For office3, use (0.1, 15.0). 5. Semantic Label Correction (Semi-Automatic): Apply LSeg to predict semantic label maps for each RGB image. Evaluate the accuracy of LSeg predictions against the original Replica label map. Ignore points with labels having accuracy almost or exactly zero from evaluation/training. Manually fix label ambiguities by ignoring specific labels or merging them (e.g., merge 'rug' and 'floor'). 6. Sparse-View Sub-sampling (Variant): Sub-sample every k-th frame from the video sequence. Adapt k per scene to ensure a minimum of 20% covisible regions between any selected view and its neighbors. Randomly select a triplet of consecutive training images from the sub-sampled set. Image Resolution: 340 \times 600 pixels. Near/Far Clipping: (0.1, 10.0) generally; (0.1, 15.0) for office3. Covisibility Threshold: Minimum 20% overlap between selected views. Collapsed Geometry: Replica data suffers from collapsed geometry and less photo-realistic appearances compared to real scans. Label Ambiguity: Objects may have bad appearance or intrinsic indistinguishability (e.g., rug vs. floor). Unobserved Regions: Training images may not cover all scene regions; evaluation must account for generalization to unobserved areas via propagation. A variant designed for sparse-view reconstruction tasks. It uses 7 scenes (room0, room1, room2, office0, office1, office2, office3). It sub-samples every k-th frame from the original video (1500–3000 frames per scene) to create wide-baseline scenarios. The sampling rate k is adapted per scene to ensure at least 20% covisible regions between selected views. It randomly selects a triplet of consecutive training images from these sub-sampled frames. Poses are adjusted to center the scene around the origin to benefit pose refinement. Data Quality: The source dataset is moderate-quality, suffering from collapsed geometry, less photo-realistic appearances, and defective annotations. Pose Refinement: Centering the scene around the origin significantly benefits pose refinement stability. Evaluation Scope: Training images may not cover all regions; evaluation measures generalization to unobserved regions via propagation. Limitations: Label quality requires manual intervention to resolve ambiguities like 'rug' vs 'floor'. The Replica dataset is a moderate-quality indoor reconstruction dataset with semantic segmentation labels, originally created for proof-of-concept work in neural rendering. It is based on synthetic scans with randomly generated pose trajectories. The preparation method was introduced to address issues like camera-in-geometry poses and label inaccuracies. The sparse-view variant was developed to evaluate methods under realistic sparse-input conditions. name: Light Cone Construction
head: Light cone projection, Light rays
body: Light Cone Construction is a method for generating synthetic astronomical observations (imaging or spectroscopy) from cosmological simulation data by stacking discrete redshift slices into a continuous line-of-sight volume. It solves the problem of creating realistic light cones from periodic simulation boxes that do not natively span the required redshift range, while minimizing redundant sampling of the same physical structures. It is distinguished from standard volume rendering by its specific handling of cosmological distance metrics, periodic domain wrapping, and the statistical generation of unique, non-overlapping sightlines. Inputs: Observer redshift (z{obs}). Redshift interval [z{min}, z{max}]. Simulation dataset stack (periodic boxes at various redshifts). Cosmological parameters: \OmegaM (matter density), \Omegak (curvature density), \Omega\Lambda (cosmological constant density). For Light Cone Projections: Angular field of view (\theta), image resolution, and maximum allowed common volume between projections. For Light Rays: Number of sightlines and maximum allowed common volume. Outputs: A stack of datasets ordered by redshift. For Projections: A 2D image or data cube representing the integrated signal along the line of sight. For Rays: A list of ray segments, each containing intersected pixels, path lengths (dl), and assigned redshifts. Dataset Stack: A list of simulation data objects, ordered from highest redshift (z{max}) to lowest (z{min}). Each object represents a simulation box at a specific redshift. Ray Segment (for Light Rays): An array containing: Indices of all pixels intersected by the ray within the dataset. The path length dl through each intersected pixel. Projection Object (for Light Cone Projections): A pre-computed projection of the entire lateral domain of a dataset. This allows multiple light cone projections to sample different regions of the same box without re-projecting the full volume. Expansion Factor E(z): E(z) \equiv \sqrt{\OmegaM (1 + z)^3 + \Omegak (1 + z)^2 + \Omega\Lambda} where \OmegaM, \Omegak, \Omega\Lambda are the energy density contributions of matter, curvature, and the cosmological constant, respectively. Angular Size Distance DA: The width of the sampled region in the image plane for a field of view \theta is (1+z) DA \theta. DA is defined as: DA = \begin{cases} \frac{DH}{\sqrt{|\Omegak|}} \frac{\sinh(\sqrt{|\Omegak|} DC)}{(1+z)} & \text{for } \Omegak > 0 \\ \frac{DC}{1+z} & \text{for } \Omegak = 0 \\ \frac{DH}{\sqrt{|\Omegak|}} \frac{\sin(\sqrt{|\Omegak|} DC)}{(1+z)} & \text{for } \Omegak < 0 \end{cases} where DC is the comoving distance and DH is the Hubble distance. Column Density: For a ray segment, the column density N contributed by a physical density \rho over a path length element dl is: N = \rho \times dl. Fraction of Box Length: The user may specify a fraction of the total simulation box length to calculate the maximum allowable redshift step \delta z between datasets, rather than using the full box length. Maximum Common Volume: A user-specified limit on the volume overlap between different light cone projections or rays to ensure statistical independence. 1. Select Datasets: Use time series machinery to select simulation datasets appropriate for the requested redshift interval [z{min}, z{max}]. 2. Build Stack: Initialize an empty stack. Add the dataset with the redshift closest to z{max} as the first element. 3. Iterate Downward: a. Calculate \delta z, the redshift interval corresponding to the length of the simulation box. Note that \delta z varies with redshift. b. Determine the target redshift for the next dataset: z{target} = z{current} - \delta z. c. Select the dataset whose redshift is closest to, but no less than, z{target}. d. Add this dataset to the stack. e. Repeat until the lower limit z{min} is reached. Note: The user may constrain the maximum \delta z to be a fraction of the full box length to ensure smoother transitions. 4. Generate Sightlines (Randomization): a. For each dataset in the stack, choose a random projection axis and center for the projected region. This exploits the periodicity of the computational domain to minimize sampling the same structures multiple times. b. For Light Rays, assign a random orientation to each ray segment. 5. Compute Projections/Rays: a. For Projections: Project the full lateral domain of each dataset. The comoving radial distance determines the fraction of the box used in the line of sight. The image width is determined by (1+z) DA \theta. b. For Rays: For each ray segment, identify all intersected pixels and calculate the path length dl through each. 6. Assign Redshifts: For each length element in a ray, assign a unique redshift based on the dataset's redshift and the point's position along the ray, assuming a smooth Hubble flow. 7. Ensure Uniqueness (Optional): If generating multiple projections/rays, use a unique solution generator to find realizations with a user-specified maximum common volume. This generator first attempts to vary only the lateral randomization (reusing projection objects) before attempting fully unique randomization. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def constructlightcone(observerredshift, zmin, zmax, datasets, cosmology): """ Constructs a stack of datasets for light cone observation. Args: observerredshift: Redshift of the observer (typically 0). zmin: Lower bound of redshift interval. zmax: Upper bound of redshift interval. datasets: List of available simulation datasets, each with a 'redshift' attribute. cosmology: Object containing OmegaM, Omegak, OmegaLambda, H0. Returns: stack: List of datasets ordered from zmax to zmin. """ # Step 1: Preliminary selection of datasets # Filter datasets that fall within or near the requested interval relevantdatasets = [d for d in datasets if d.redshift >= zmin and d.redshift <= zmax] # Sort by redshift descending relevantdatasets.sort(key=lambda d: d.redshift, reverse=True) stack = [] currentz = zmax # Step 2: Add first dataset # Find dataset closest to zmax firstdataset = min(relevantdatasets, key=lambda d: abs(d.redshift - zmax)) stack.append(firstdataset) currentz = firstdataset.redshift # Step 3: Iterate down to zmin while currentz > zmin: # Calculate deltaz for the current redshift # deltaz corresponds to the length of the simulation box # Note: deltaz is not constant with redshift deltaz = calculatedeltaz(currentz, cosmology, boxlength) # Determine target redshift targetz = currentz - deltaz # Select next dataset: closest to, but no less than, targetz # Filter candidates that are >= targetz candidates = [d for d in relevantdatasets if d.redshift >= targetz] if not candidates: break # Should not happen if datasets are dense enough # Choose the one closest to targetz nextdataset = min(candidates, key=lambda d: abs(d.redshift - targetz)) # Avoid duplicates if the same dataset is selected multiple times if nextdataset not in stack: stack.append(nextdataset) currentz = nextdataset.redshift else: # If the closest valid dataset is already in the stack, # we might need to pick the next closest or handle overlap. # The source implies a strict selection process. # For implementation robustness, we pick the next closest unique one. remainingcandidates = [d for d in candidates if d not in stack] if remainingcandidates: nextdataset = min(remainingcandidates, key=lambda d: abs(d.redshift - targetz)) stack.append(nextdataset) currentz = nextdataset.redshift else: break return stack def calculatedeltaz(z, cosmology, boxlength): """ Calculates the redshift interval corresponding to the comoving distance of the simulation box length. """ # Comoving distance calculation depends on cosmology # This is a placeholder for the specific integral of 1/E(z) # DC = integral from 0 to z of c/H(z) dz # deltaz is derived from the box length in comoving coordinates # The source notes that deltaz is not constant with redshift. # Implementation detail: Calculate comoving distance for boxlength at z. # Then find dz such that DC(z+dz) - DC(z) = boxlengthcomoving # For simplicity in this pseudocode, we assume a helper exists. return computeredshiftstepfromcomovingdistance(boxlength, z, cosmology) def generatelightray(dataset, numrays, maxcommonvolume): """ Generates light rays for a single dataset in the stack. """ rays = [] for in range(numrays): # Random orientation for the ray segment direction = randomunitvector() origin = randompointinbox() # Intersect ray with the dataset's grid # Returns array of intersected pixels and path lengths dl intersections = intersectraywithgrid(origin, direction, dataset.grid) raysegment = { 'intersections': intersections, # Array of (pixelindex, dl) 'direction': direction, 'origin': origin, 'redshift': dataset.redshift # Base redshift for this segment } rays.append(raysegment) return rays def assignredshifts(raysegment, datasetredshift, positionalongray): """ Assigns unique redshift to each length element assuming smooth Hubble flow. """ # For each intersection in raysegment['intersections']: # Calculate physical distance from observer # Map distance to redshift using cosmological model # This allows creation of synthetic spectra with properly redshifted lines pass Non-constant \delta z: The redshift interval corresponding to the simulation box length changes with redshift. Failing to recalculate \delta z at each step will lead to incorrect stacking. Periodicity: The method relies on the periodicity of the computational domain. If the simulation is not periodic, the randomization of projection axes and centers may result in discontinuities or artifacts at the boundaries of the stacked boxes. Sampling Redundancy: Without randomizing the projection axis and center for each dataset, the same large-scale structures may be sampled multiple times, biasing statistical analyses. Common Volume: If the maximum common volume is not specified or set too high, multiple light cone projections may sample the same volume, violating the assumption of independent realizations. Time Complexity: The initial dataset stacking is linear with respect to the number of datasets in the stack. Projection of the full lateral domain is performed once per dataset, making subsequent light cone projections computationally cheap (only sampling different regions). Ray intersection calculations are proportional to the number of rays and the complexity of the grid. Memory Complexity: Requires storing the full lateral projection for each dataset in the stack if multiple light cone projections are to be generated efficiently. This can be memory-intensive for large boxes. Strengths: Efficiently generates multiple independent sightlines from a limited set of simulation boxes. The pre-computation of full lateral projections allows for rapid generation of statistical samples. Limitations: Relies on the assumption of a smooth Hubble flow for redshift assignment along rays, which may not capture local velocity distortions (redshift-space distortions) unless explicitly modeled. The quality depends on the density of available simulation datasets at different redshifts. When to Use: When generating synthetic observations (imaging or spectroscopy) from cosmological simulations that do not span the full redshift range of interest, or when statistical independence of multiple sightlines is required. When Not to Use: When high-fidelity modeling of local velocity fields or non-periodic boundary conditions is critical, or when computational resources are insufficient to store full lateral projections for all datasets. Light Cone Construction was implemented in the yt analysis toolkit, building on earlier work by Hallman et al. (2007, 2009). The method leverages yt's projection machinery to handle the complexities of projecting data from periodic simulation boxes onto a light cone. It is primarily used in astrophysics for creating synthetic surveys of the universe, such as quasar absorption line studies or galaxy distribution maps, allowing researchers to compare simulation predictions directly with observational data. name: B-Spline Camera Path Interpolation
head: B-Spline Camera Path, Multidimensional B-Spline Interpolation for Camera Poses, Spline Interpolated Camera Path
body: B-Spline Camera Path Interpolation generates a smooth, continuous camera trajectory between discrete input keyframe poses using multidimensional B-spline interpolation. It solves the problem of jittery or discontinuous motion in volume rendering and novel view synthesis by ensuring positional and rotational continuity across the entire path. It differs from linear interpolation by providing C^2 continuity (smooth acceleration) and from least-squares approximation by allowing exact interpolation of keyframes when the smoothing factor is zero, avoiding the introduction of artifacts not present in the source data. Inputs: poses: Array of shape (N, 3, 4) representing N input camera poses in world-to-camera or camera-to-world format (typically extrinsic matrix columns 0-2 and translation vector column 3). ninterp: Integer, number of interpolated poses to generate between each pair of consecutive keyframes. splinedegree: Integer, polynomial degree of the B-spline. Default 5. smoothness: Float, smoothing factor for the spline fit. 0 forces exact interpolation through all points. Default 0.03. rotweight: Float, relative weighting of rotation vs. translation in the pose decomposition. Default 0.1. Outputs: newposes: Array of shape (M, 3, 4), where M = n\interp \times (N - 1), containing the interpolated camera poses. Data Structures: The method internally converts 3 \times 4 pose matrices into a structured point representation (P, L, U) where P is position, L is look-at, and U is up vector. These are treated as a single multidimensional array of shape (N, 9) for interpolation. Steps: 1. Pose Decomposition: Convert each input pose matrix W \in \mathbb{R}^{3 \times 4} into three 3D vectors: Position (pos), Look-at (lookat), and Up (up). pos = W[:, 0:3, 3] lookat = W[:, 0:3, 3] - rot\weight \times W[:, 0:3, 2] up = W[:, 0:3, 3] + rot\weight \times W[:, 0:3, 1] Here, W[:, 0:3, 2] is the z-axis (forward/look direction) and W[:, 0:3, 1] is the y-axis (up direction) of the camera basis. 2. Spline Fitting: Construct a multidimensional B-spline curve S(u) that fits the sequence of points (posi, lookati, upi) for i=0 \dots N-1. Input to spline fitter: Transposed array of shape (9, N) containing all position, look-at, and up coordinates. Degree k = \min(spline\degree, N - 1). Smoothness parameter s = smoothness. The fitter returns a tuple (tck, u), where tck contains the knots, coefficients, and degree, and u are the parameter values (typically uniform or chord-length). 3. Evaluation: Sample the spline curve at M = n\interp \times (N - 1) points. Parameter vector u{eval} = \text{linspace}(0, 1, M, \text{endpoint=False}). Evaluate S(u{eval}) to get interpolated points of shape (M, 9). 4. Pose Reconstruction: Convert the interpolated (pos, lookat, up) vectors back into 3 \times 4 pose matrices. Extract pos, lookat, up from the interpolated points. Reconstruct the camera basis vectors: z{axis} = -(lookat - pos) / \|lookat - pos\| (normalized forward vector). x{axis} = z{axis} \times up / \|z{axis} \times up\| (normalized right vector). y{axis} = x{axis} \times z{axis} (normalized up vector). Construct the pose matrix W{new} with columns [x{axis}, y{axis}, z{axis}, pos]. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import numpy as np from scipy.interpolate import splprep, splev def posestopoints(poses, rotweight=0.1): """ Convert N poses of shape (N, 3, 4) to (N, 9) array of (pos, lookat, up). """ pos = poses[:,:3, 3] lookat = pos - rotweight poses[:,:3, 2] up = pos + rotweight poses[:,:3, 1] return np.concatenate([pos, lookat, up], axis=-1) def pointstoposes(points): """ Convert (N, 9) array of (pos, lookat, up) back to (N, 3, 4) poses. """ pos = points[:,:3] lookat = points[:, 3:6] up = points[:, 6:9] # Reconstruct basis vectors # Forward vector (negative z-axis in standard OpenGL/Camera coords) forward = lookat - pos zaxis = -forward / np.linalg.norm(forward, axis=1, keepdims=True) # Right vector (x-axis) right = np.cross(zaxis, up) xaxis = right / np.linalg.norm(right, axis=1, keepdims=True) # Up vector (y-axis) yaxis = np.cross(xaxis, zaxis) # Construct pose matrix [x, y, z, pos] poses = np.zeros((points.shape[0], 3, 4)) poses[:,:3, 0] = xaxis poses[:,:3, 1] = yaxis poses[:,:3, 2] = zaxis poses[:,:3, 3] = pos return poses def generateinterpolatedpath(poses, ninterp=10, splinedegree=5, smoothness=0.03, rotweight=0.1): """ Generate smooth camera path using B-spline interpolation. Args: poses: (N, 3, 4) array of input poses. ninterp: Number of interpolated poses between keyframes. splinedegree: Degree of B-spline. smoothness: Smoothing factor (0 for exact interpolation). rotweight: Weight for rotation vs translation in decomposition. Returns: newposes: (M, 3, 4) array of interpolated poses, M = ninterp (N-1). """ N = poses.shape[0] # Step 1: Decompose poses points = posestopoints(poses, rotweight=rotweight) # Step 2: Fit B-spline # splprep expects points in shape (ndim, N), so we transpose tck, u = splprep(points.T, k=min(splinedegree, N - 1), s=smoothness) # Step 3: Evaluate spline M = ninterp (N - 1) ueval = np.linspace(0, 1, M, endpoint=False) newpoints = splev(ueval, tck) # splev returns list of arrays, one for each dimension. Stack them. newpoints = np.array(newpoints).T # Step 4: Reconstruct poses newposes = pointstoposes(newpoints) return newposes This variant extends the base B-spline interpolation to simultaneously interpolate per-frame exposure values, preventing flickering in rendered sequences. It identifies keyframe indices from a configuration file or directory listing, generates the camera path using the standard B-spline method, and then applies a separate 1D B-spline interpolation to the logarithm of exposure values. If exposure interpolation is enabled but exposure data is missing, it raises an error. A higher smoothness value (e.g., 20) is typically used for exposure interpolation to ensure stability. Time Complexity: O(N \cdot M), where N is the number of keyframes and M is the number of output poses. The spline fitting is O(N) and evaluation is O(M). Memory Complexity: O(N) for storing the spline coefficients and O(M) for the output poses. Strengths: Produces visually smooth camera motion with continuous derivatives; handles both position and orientation in a unified framework; configurable smoothness allows trade-off between fidelity to keyframes and path smoothness. Limitations: Requires at least k+1 keyframes for a spline of degree k; exact interpolation (s=0) may lead to oscillations if keyframes are noisy or poorly distributed; the linear approximation of rotation via look-at/up vectors does not guarantee unit quaternion interpolation, potentially introducing slight scaling artifacts in the basis vectors. When to use: When generating smooth fly-throughs or orbit paths from sparse keyframes in volume rendering or NeRF training. When not to use: When exact physical camera constraints (e.g., fixed focal length, specific lens distortion) must be preserved without post-processing, or when the input poses are highly erratic and require robust fitting rather than interpolation. The method originates from the need to generate smooth camera trajectories for novel view synthesis and volume rendering, particularly in the context of NeRF (Neural Radiance Fields) and Gaussian Splatting pipelines. It was popularized by implementations in Google's MultiNeRF repository and adapted in various open-source Gaussian Splatting frameworks like mrGSplat. The approach leverages the mathematical properties of B-splines, specifically their local control and smoothness, to interpolate multidimensional data (position and orientation) simultaneously. google-research/multinerf, https://github.com/google-research/multinerf, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial) meshroomHub/mrGSplat, https://github.com/meshroomHub/mrGSplat, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial)

name: Streamline Approximation via Iterative B-spline Fitting
head: Data reduction scheme for B-splines, Iterative curve fitting
body: This method computes a B-spline curve \gamma(u) that approximates a set of input samples X, specifically designed to avoid the oscillations ("wriggles") introduced by standard interpolation or least-squares approximation. These artifacts are problematic for generating tubular geometry and ambient occlusion in volume rendering. It sets itself apart from Least-squares approximation by leveraging Schönberg’s approximation properties to prevent new perturbations, and from Interpolation by strictly avoiding the introduction of features not present in the original data. Inputs: X = \{x1, \dots, xn\}: A set of n 3D points representing a sampled streamline or path. \epsilon: User-specified accuracy threshold for termination. Outputs: \gamma(u): A cubic (C^2 continuous) B-spline curve approximating X. k: The number of iterations performed in the data reduction scheme. Data Structures: B-spline Curve \gammai(u): Defined by a set of control points (coefficients). For a cubic B-spline, the curve is a linear combination of basis functions weighted by these coefficients. Sample Set Xi: A list of points generated by evaluating the previous curve \gamma{i-1}(u). Parameters: \epsilon: Termination threshold. Typical value: 10^{-4}. n: Initial number of samples in X. Algorithm Steps: 1. Initialization (Schönberg’s Approximation): Construct an initial cubic B-spline curve \gamma1(u) using the input samples X directly as its control point coefficients. This step relies on the variation diminishing property of B-splines to approximate X without introducing new perturbations. 2. Iterative Data Reduction: Repeat the following steps for i = 2, 3, \dots until termination: a. Calculate Sample Count: Compute the number of samples mi for the current iteration: mi = \left\lfloor \frac{n}{2^{i-1}} \right\rfloor At each step, the number of samples is halved. b. Construct New Sample Set Xi: Generate Xi by regularly sampling the parameter space of the previous curve \gamma{i-1}(u). The j-th sample in Xi is obtained by evaluating \gamma{i-1} at parameter value uj = \frac{j-1}{mi-1}: x'j = \gamma{i-1}\left( \frac{j-1}{mi-1} \right), \quad j = 1, \dots, mi This process samples a C^2 curve, smoothing out high-frequency features. c. Iterative Curve Fitting: Compute the new curve \gammai(u) by applying an iterative curve fitting algorithm to the sample set Xi. The coefficients of \gammai(u) are updated so that the curve moves closer to the samples in Xi until a user-specified accuracy is achieved. The specific details of this iterative update and its convergence properties are defined in [14] (see Sources). d. Error Check: Calculate the maximum error \epsilon{\max} between the original samples X and the current curve \gammai(u). The error is defined as: \epsilon{\max}:= \max{1 \le j \le n} \| x'j - xj \|2 where xj \in X and x'j is the projection of xj onto the current curve \gammai(u). e. Termination: If \epsilon{\max} \le \epsilon, terminate. The final curve is \gamma(u):= \gammai(u) and k = i. Otherwise, increment i and repeat. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def streamlineapproximation(X, epsilon): """ Approximates a set of points X using iterative B-spline fitting. Args: X: List of n 3D points (samples). epsilon: Termination threshold (e.g., 1e-4). Returns: gamma: Final B-spline curve object. k: Number of iterations. """ n = len(X) # Step 1: Initialize with Schönberg's approximation # Construct cubic B-spline gamma1 using X as control points gammaprev = createcubicbspline(controlpoints=X) i = 1 while True: i += 1 # Step 2a: Calculate number of samples mi = floor(n / (2 (i - 1))) # Step 2b: Construct new sample set Xi by sampling gammaprev Xi = [] for j in range(1, mi + 1): u = (j - 1) / (mi - 1) point = evaluatebspline(gammaprev, u) Xi.append(point) # Step 2c: Iterative curve fitting to get gammai # Note: The specific iterative update algorithm is detailed in [14]. # This function updates coefficients of gammaprev to fit Xi. gammacurr = iterativefitbspline(Xi, gammaprev) # Step 2d: Calculate max error against original samples X # x'j is the projection of xj onto gammacurr maxerror = 0.0 for xj in X: # Projection of a point onto a B-spline curve # This typically involves finding the parameter u that minimizes distance # or using the closest point on the curve. xprimej = projectpointontocurve(xj, gammacurr) dist = l2norm(xprimej - xj) if dist > maxerror: maxerror = dist # Step 2e: Termination check if maxerror <= epsilon: return gammacurr, i # Prepare for next iteration gammaprev = gammacurr Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Division by Zero: If mi = 1, the parameter calculation \frac{j-1}{mi-1} involves division by zero. This occurs if n < 2^{i-1}. The algorithm assumes n is sufficiently large such that mi \ge 2 for all relevant iterations. If mi < 2, the sampling step is undefined. Projection Cost: Calculating the projection x'j of each original sample onto the curve can be computationally expensive if not optimized. Convergence: The iterative fitting step (Step 2c) relies on the algorithm from [14]. If this sub-algorithm fails to converge or oscillates, the overall method may not terminate or may produce unstable curves. Time Complexity: The method involves k iterations. In each iteration, the number of samples is halved. The iterative fitting step (Step 2c) is non-trivial and depends on the specific algorithm from [14]. The error calculation requires projecting n points onto the curve. Memory Complexity: Requires storing the control points for the current and previous curves, and the sample sets Xi. Performance: For the data sets shown in the source, k < 4 with \epsilon = 10^{-4}. Strengths: Effectively reduces wriggles and oscillations compared to least-squares approximation, leading to cleaner tubular geometry and ambient occlusion. Limitations: Requires the iterative fitting algorithm from [14] to be implemented correctly. The projection step can be costly. This method was proposed in the context of visualizing streamlines and generating stream tubes for volume rendering, where visual artifacts from curve approximation can significantly impact the quality of ambient occlusion. It builds on Schönberg’s approximation properties and the iterative curve fitting algorithm described in [14].
