name: Parametric Path Generation
head: Parametric Camera Path Generation, Analytic Trajectory Generation
body: Parametric Path Generation constructs camera trajectories by evaluating explicit mathematical functions of a scalar parameter (typically angle or time) to produce a sequence of camera poses. It solves the problem of generating smooth, continuous novel views from a sparse set of training images by defining the geometry of the path analytically rather than interpolating between discrete keyframes. It differs from Sparse Trajectory Generation by relying on closed-form equations for position and orientation, and from Synthetic Camera Trajectory Generation by deriving parameters directly from scene statistics (e.g., camera bounding boxes) rather than arbitrary artistic constraints. The family shares the mechanism of mapping a scalar parameter \theta \in [0, 2\pi] (or a linear time interval) to a 4x4 transformation matrix \mathbf{P}. The core steps common to all children are: 1. Scene Analysis: Compute scene statistics (centroid, bounding box, or percentiles) from input training poses to define the spatial bounds of the trajectory. 2. Parameterization: Define position \mathbf{c}(\theta) and orientation (look-at direction \mathbf{z}(\theta), up vector \mathbf{u}(\theta)) as functions of \theta. 3. Pose Construction: Assemble the rotation matrix \mathbf{R} from orthogonal basis vectors and translation \mathbf{t} into \mathbf{P} = [\mathbf{R} | \mathbf{t}]. 4. Sampling: Evaluate the functions at N evenly spaced intervals, excluding the final duplicate point to ensure a closed loop without redundancy. Creates a spiral trajectory by combining circular horizontal motion with vertical oscillation. It is distinct from Elliptical Camera Path Generation by using a constant radius in the horizontal plane (scaled by percentiles) and a sinusoidal vertical component, whereas the elliptical variant allows for non-circular horizontal bounds and linear interpolation of vertical bounds. It is chosen for forward-facing scenes where the camera orbits a central point while varying height. Generates a closed-loop elliptical trajectory by interpolating between computed lower and upper bounds in both horizontal and vertical axes. It differs from Spiral Camera Path Generation by allowing the horizontal cross-section to be a non-circular ellipse (defined by 90th percentile bounds) and by using a phase-shifted vertical oscillation that is bounded by 10th/90th percentiles rather than a pure sine wave. It is chosen when the scene has anisotropic horizontal distribution or when a smoother, less oscillatory vertical transition is desired. Rotates the camera around a fixed axis (Azimuth, Elevation, or Roll) at a constant distance from the center of rotation. It differs from the spiral and elliptical variants by restricting motion to a single planar rotation without vertical oscillation or radius variation. It is chosen for simple panoramic exports or when the scene geometry is centered and symmetric, requiring minimal parameter tuning. Parametric path generation is a foundational technique in NeRF (Neural Radiance Fields) and volume rendering novel view synthesis. The spiral path generation method was popularized by the original NeRF implementation, which used it to generate training views for forward-facing scenes. The elliptical and orbit variants emerged as adaptations to handle different scene geometries and rendering pipelines, often found in open-source NeRF implementations and visualization tools.

name: Spiral Camera Path Generation
head: Forward-Facing Spiral Camera Path, Novel View Synthesis Path, Spiral Path Generation, load_tankstemple_data spiral generation
body: Spiral Camera Path Generation creates a sequence of camera poses along a spiral trajectory for novel view synthesis, defined by a center camera, radius parameters, focal length, vertical offset rate, rotation count, and number of views. It calculates a forward-facing spiral camera path for rendering based on input poses and bounds, where all cameras in the path point towards a world-space focal point. It generates a smooth spiral camera path around the training camera distribution for 360° novel view synthesis videos and for rendering novel views in forward-facing scenes. It generates a spiral camera trajectory around a center point for novel view synthesis. Inputs: poses: Array of M training camera-to-world matrices \mathbf{C}i. N: Number of views to generate. rots: Number of full rotations (2\pi) to complete, default 2. zrate: Rate of vertical oscillation in the spiral path, default 0.5. radsscale: Scale factor for camera radius, default 1.0. focusdistance: Weight for near/far bound averaging, default 0.75. spiralscalef: Focal length multiplier, default 1.0. spiralscaler: Radius multiplier, default 1.0. Outputs: renderposes: Array of shape (N, 4, 4) containing the generated camera-to-world matrices. Data Structures: rads: Array of shape (3,) specifying spiral radius per axis. c2wavg: 4 \times 4 matrix representing the average camera pose of the input training data. up: 3-vector representing the average up direction of the input cameras. focal: Scalar float representing the effective focal length. Steps: 1. Scene Analysis: Compute the average camera-to-world matrix \mathbf{C}{avg} from the input poses. Let \mathbf{C}{avg} = [\mathbf{R}{avg} | \mathbf{t}{avg}]. Compute the average up vector \mathbf{u} by averaging the second column (y-axis) of the rotation matrices of all input poses: \mathbf{u} = \frac{1}{M} \sum{i=0}^{M-1} \mathbf{C}i[:, 1]. Extract the camera centers \mathbf{p}i = \mathbf{C}i[:, 3] for all i. Compute the radii vector \mathbf{r}{raw} as the 90th percentile of the absolute values of the camera centers along each axis: \mathbf{r}{raw} = \text{percentile}(|\mathbf{p}i|, 90, \text{axis}=0). Scale the radii: \mathbf{r}{scaled} = \mathbf{r}{raw} \times \text{rads\scale} \times \text{spiral\scale\r}. Construct \mathbf{rads} = [\text{rads\scaled}[0], \text{rads\scaled}[1], \text{rads\scaled}[2]]. (Note: Some implementations append 1.0 to a 2-element list if not present, but standard spiral generation uses 3 axes). 2. Focal Length and Bounds Calculation: Compute near and far bounds from the training poses: d{min} = \text{bounds.min()} and d{max} = \text{bounds.max()}. Compute the effective focal length f using the weighted harmonic mean: f = \frac{1}{\frac{1 - \text{focus\distance}}{d{min}} + \frac{\text{focus\distance}}{d{max}}} \times \text{spiral\scale\f}. 3. Parameterization and Pose Construction: Initialize an empty list renderposes. Generate N evenly spaced angles \thetaj for j = 0, \dots, N-1: \thetaj = \frac{2\pi \cdot j \cdot \text{rots}}{N}. Note: Some implementations generate N+1 points and exclude the last to avoid duplication, effectively creating a closed loop without redundant start/end points. For each \thetaj: a. Compute Offset Vector: Calculate the offset vector \mathbf{v} in the local coordinate system of the average pose: \mathbf{v} = [rx \cos(\thetaj), -ry \sin(\thetaj), -rz \sin(\thetaj \cdot \text{z\rate})]. The negative signs on the sine terms are consistent with the coordinate system conventions used in the source implementations (e.g., OpenGL-style camera looking down -Z). b. Compute Camera Center: Transform the offset into world space using the average pose's rotation and translation: \mathbf{c}j = \mathbf{C}{avg}[:,:3] \mathbf{v} + \mathbf{C}{avg}[:, 3]. c. Compute Look-at Direction: Determine the viewing direction \mathbf{z}j. The camera looks towards a focal point defined by the average pose's origin and focal length. The focal point in world space is: \mathbf{f}j = \mathbf{C}{avg}[:,:3] [0, 0, -f]^T + \mathbf{C}{avg}[:, 3]. The viewing direction is the normalized vector from the camera center to the focal point: \mathbf{z}j = \text{normalize}(\mathbf{f}j - \mathbf{c}j). d. Compute Basis Vectors: i. Compute the x-axis \mathbf{x}j using the cross product of the fixed average up vector \mathbf{u} and \mathbf{z}j: \mathbf{x}j = \text{normalize}(\mathbf{u} \times \mathbf{z}j). ii. Compute the y-axis \mathbf{y}j to ensure orthogonality: \mathbf{y}j = \mathbf{z}j \times \mathbf{x}j. e. Construct Pose Matrix: Assemble the 4 \times 4 matrix \mathbf{P}j: \mathbf{P}j = \begin{bmatrix} \mathbf{x}j^T & \mathbf{y}j^T & \mathbf{z}j^T & \mathbf{c}j \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix}. Note: In column-major notation (common in OpenGL/NeRF), the rotation matrix columns are \mathbf{x}j, \mathbf{y}j, \mathbf{z}j. So \mathbf{P}j = [\mathbf{x}j, \mathbf{y}j, \mathbf{z}j, \mathbf{c}j] with the bottom row [0,0,0,1]. 4. Return: Stack all \mathbf{P}j into an array of shape (N, 4, 4). Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import numpy as np def spiralcamerapathgeneration(poses, N, rots=2, zrate=0.5, radsscale=1.0, focusdistance=0.75, spiralscalef=1.0, spiralscaler=1.0): """ Generate a spiral camera path. Args: poses: (M, 4, 4) array of camera-to-world matrices. N: Number of poses to generate. rots: Number of full rotations. zrate: Vertical oscillation rate. radsscale: Scale factor for radii. focusdistance: Weight for near/far bound averaging. spiralscalef: Focal length multiplier. spiralscaler: Radius multiplier. Returns: renderposes: (N, 4, 4) array of generated camera-to-world matrices. """ # 1. Scene Analysis # Compute average pose (S3, S4) c2wavg = np.mean(poses, axis=0) # Compute average up vector (S3, S4) up = np.mean(poses[:,:3, 1], axis=0) # Compute radii (S3, S4) positions = poses[:,:3, 3] radiiraw = np.percentile(np.abs(positions), 90, axis=0) rads = radiiraw radsscale spiralscaler # 2. Focal Length and Bounds (S2, S6) boundsmin = np.min(positions, axis=0) boundsmax = np.max(positions, axis=0) nearbound = np.min(boundsmin) farbound = np.max(boundsmax) # Avoid division by zero (G) if nearbound < 1e-6: nearbound = 1e-6 focal = (1.0 / ((1.0 - focusdistance) / nearbound + focusdistance / farbound)) spiralscalef # 3. Pose Construction renderposes = [] # Generate angles, excluding last point to avoid duplication (S1, S3, S4) thetas = np.linspace(0.0, 2.0 np.pi rots, N + 1)[:-1] for theta in thetas: # a. Compute Offset Vector (S1, S3, S4) offset = np.array([ rads[0] np.cos(theta), -rads[1] np.sin(theta), -rads[2] np.sin(theta zrate) ]) # b. Compute Camera Center (S1, S3, S4) center = c2wavg[:3, 3] + c2wavg[:3,:3] @ offset # c. Compute Look-at Direction (S4) # Focal point in world space focalpoint = c2wavg[:3,:3] @ np.array([0.0, 0.0, -focal]) + c2wavg[:3, 3] # Viewing direction from center to focal point z = focalpoint - center normz = np.linalg.norm(z) if normz > 1e-6: z = z / normz else: z = np.array([0.0, 0.0, -1.0]) # Fallback (G) # d. Compute Basis Vectors (S4) x = np.cross(up, z) normx = np.linalg.norm(x) if normx < 1e-6: # Degenerate case: up and z are parallel (G) x = np.array([1.0, 0.0, 0.0]) x = x - np.dot(x, z) z x = x / np.linalg.norm(x) else: x = x / normx y = np.cross(z, x) # e. Construct Pose Matrix (S1, S4) pose = np.eye(4) pose[:3, 0] = x pose[:3, 1] = y pose[:3, 2] = z pose[:3, 3] = center renderposes.append(pose) return np.array(renderposes) Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Degenerate Up Vector: If the average up vector is parallel to the viewing direction \mathbf{z}, the cross product for \mathbf{x} is zero. A guard is required to select an alternative up vector. Precision: Floating point errors in normalization can accumulate. Re-orthogonalization (Gram-Schmidt) is recommended. Boundary Conditions: The spiral should not include the final duplicate point to avoid redundancy in rendering. Focal Length: If nearbound is zero, division by zero occurs. A small epsilon should be added. Circular Camera Path Generation creates a sequence of camera poses arranged in a 360-degree circular trajectory around a central origin at a fixed height and radius. It differs from Spiral Camera Path Generation by having a constant z-coordinate (no vertical oscillation, zrate = 0) and a fixed radius, making it suitable for flat scenes or when vertical coverage is not required. It is simpler than the spiral path and computationally cheaper. Link: Circular Camera Path Generation. Spherify Poses reorients a set of input camera poses into a uniform spherical arrangement centered around the scene's centroid, ensuring consistent scale and distribution for novel view synthesis. It differs from Spiral Camera Path Generation by enforcing a strict spherical radius rather than a spiral trajectory with vertical offset, and by computing a 3D center from ray intersections rather than assuming a 2D circular path. It is used when a full 360° spherical coverage is needed, unlike the spiral which is often forward-facing or limited in elevation. Link: Spherify Poses. Spiral Camera Pose Generation is a variant that generates camera poses in a circle with optional pitch rotation and up-vector flipping. It differs from the standard spiral by using a fixed radius and potentially flipping the up vector for specific rendering requirements. It is used for fly-through rendering where a simple circular path with orientation adjustments is sufficient. Steps: 1. Generate camera poses in a circle: for \theta in np.linspace(0, 2 np.pi, nposes + 1)[:-1]. 2. Compute eye position: if np.abs(up[1]) > 0: eye = [np.cos(theta + np.pi / 2) radius, 0, -np.sin(theta + np.pi / 2) radius]; else: eye = [np.cos(theta + np.pi / 2) radius, np.sin(theta + np.pi / 2) radius, 2.0]. 3. Create camera using lookatviewtransform: R, T = lookatviewtransform(eye=(eye,), at=([0.0, 0.0, 0.0],), up=(up,)). 4. Create PerspectiveCameras object: camera = PerspectiveCameras(focallength=torch.tensor([focallength])[None], principalpoint=torch.tensor([0.0, 0.0])[None], R=R, T=T). Parameters: focallength: Focal length of the camera. Time Complexity: O(N), where N is the number of poses to generate. The computation per pose is constant time (vector operations). Memory Complexity: O(N) to store the output poses. Measured Performance: Not given in the sources. Scaling: Scales linearly with the number of poses. The radius and focal length depend on the scene statistics, so larger scenes require larger radii. Strengths: Provides smooth, continuous coverage of a scene with vertical variation. Good for forward-facing and 360° novel view synthesis. Limitations: Assumes the scene is roughly centered at the origin. May not cover scenes with large vertical extent if zrate is not tuned. Degenerate cases (parallel up and view vectors) require handling. When to Use: When smooth, continuous camera motion with vertical variation is desired for novel view synthesis. When Not to Use: When the scene is not centered, or when a fixed-height orbit is sufficient. Spiral Camera Path Generation originated in the context of NeRF (Neural Radiance Fields) for novel view synthesis. It was popularized by the original NeRF paper and subsequent implementations in repositories like bmild/nerf and kwea123/nerfpl. It is commonly used for rendering novel views in forward-facing scenes (e.g., LLFF dataset) and 360° capture scenarios. The method maps a scalar parameter to a 4x4 transformation matrix, building on the principles of parametric path generation [11476-parametric-path-generation.md]. bmild/nerf, https://github.com/bmild/nerf, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial) google-research/multinerf, https://github.com/google-research/multinerf, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial) kwea123/nerfpl, https://github.com/kwea123/nerfpl, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial) emmanueladutwum123/nerf-from-scratch, https://github.com/emmanueladutwum123/nerf-from-scratch, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial) damn8daniel/nerf-from-scratch, https://github.com/damn8daniel/nerf-from-scratch, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial) weiyithu/NerfingMVS, https://github.com/weiyithu/NerfingMVS, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial) meshroomHub/mrGSplat, https://github.com/meshroomHub/mrGSplat, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial) InanXR/FLASH, https://github.com/InanXR/FLASH, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial) gkouros/ref-dvgo, https://github.com/gkouros/ref-dvgo, fetched 2026-10-28 (unofficial) Fhz2346/Neural-Volume-Rendering-and-Surface-Rendering, https://github.com/Fhz2346/Neural-Volume-Rendering-and-Surface-Rendering, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial)

name: Circular Camera Path Generation
head: 360 Degree Camera Path Generation, Orbit Camera Path Generation
body: Circular Camera Path Generation creates a sequence of camera poses arranged in a 360-degree circular trajectory around a central origin at a fixed height and radius. Inputs: nviews: Integer, number of camera poses to generate. Default: 120. radius: Float, distance from the origin to the camera. Default: 4.0. height: Float, fixed Y-coordinate (vertical offset) of the camera. Default: 0.0. Outputs: poses: A numpy array of shape (nviews, 4, 4) containing the camera-to-world (c2w) transformation matrices. Data Structures: poses: List of 4x4 numpy arrays, appended during iteration, then stacked. c2w: 4x4 numpy array representing the camera-to-world matrix. Steps: 1. Initialize an empty list poses. 2. Loop i from 0 to nviews - 1: a. Calculate the angular position: \theta = \frac{2\pi i}{n\views}. b. Calculate the camera position in world coordinates: \text{cam\pos} = [\text{radius} \cdot \cos(\theta), \text{height}, \text{radius} \cdot \sin(\theta)]. c. Calculate the forward vector pointing from the camera to the origin: \text{forward} = \text{normalize}(-\text{cam\pos}). d. Set the initial up vector to the world Y-axis: \text{up} = [0.0, 1.0, 0.0]. e. Calculate the right vector using the cross product of forward and up: \text{right} = \text{normalize}(\text{cross}(\text{forward}, \text{up})). f. Recalculate the up vector to ensure orthogonality: \text{up} = \text{cross}(\text{right}, \text{forward}). g. Construct the 4x4 identity matrix c2w. h. Set the rotation columns and translation row: c2w[:3, 0] = right c2w[:3, 1] = up c2w[:3, 2] = -forward c2w[:3, 3] = campos. i. Append c2w to poses. 3. Return np.stack(poses, axis=0). Parameters: nviews: Number of views to generate. Default: 120. radius: Distance from origin. Default: 4.0. height: Camera height. Default: 0.0. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: If radius is 0, the camera position is the origin, and the forward vector is undefined (zero vector), causing normalization failure. If height is 0 and the camera is at the origin, the up vector [0,1,0] is parallel to the forward vector (or zero), causing the cross product for right to be zero. The sources do not specify handling for degenerate cases; implementation should guard against zero-length vectors. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import numpy as np def generatecircularpath(nviews=120, radius=4.0, height=0.0): poses = [] for i in range(nviews): # Calculate angle theta = 2.0 np.pi i / nviews # Calculate camera position campos = np.array([ radius np.cos(theta), height, radius np.sin(theta) ]) # Calculate forward vector (pointing to origin) forward = -campos forward = forward / np.linalg.norm(forward) # Set initial up vector up = np.array([0.0, 1.0, 0.0]) # Calculate right vector right = np.cross(forward, up) right = right / np.linalg.norm(right) # Recalculate up vector for orthogonality up = np.cross(right, forward) # Construct 4x4 c2w matrix c2w = np.eye(4) c2w[:3, 0] = right c2w[:3, 1] = up c2w[:3, 2] = -forward c2w[:3, 3] = campos poses.append(c2w) return np.stack(poses, axis=0) Time complexity: O(n\views). Memory complexity: O(n\views). Strengths: Not given in the sources. Limitations: Not given in the sources. When to use: Not given in the sources. When not to use: Not given in the sources. name: Spherify Poses
head: Pose Spherification, Spherical Path Centering, Spherical Pose Reorganization
body: Spherify Poses reorients a set of input camera poses into a uniform spherical arrangement centered around the scene's centroid, ensuring consistent scale and distribution for novel view synthesis. It differs from Circular Camera Path Generation by computing a 3D center from ray intersections rather than assuming a 2D circular path, and from Spiral Camera Path Generation by enforcing a strict spherical radius rather than a spiral trajectory with vertical offset. Inputs: poses: Array of shape [N{\text{orig}}, 4, 4] representing input camera poses in world coordinates, where poses[:,:3,2:3] stores ray directions and poses[:,:3,3] stores camera positions. bds: Bounding box data (optional, used for scaling reference). N: Integer, the number of new poses to generate. Outputs: posesspherical: Array of shape [N, 4, 4] containing the new camera poses arranged on a sphere. Data Structures: raysd: Array of shape [N{\text{orig}}, 3, 1] containing unit ray directions extracted from poses. rayso: Array of shape [N{\text{orig}}, 3, 1] containing ray origins (camera positions) extracted from poses. Ai: Matrix of shape [3, 3] for each ray i, defined as I - \mathbf{d}i \mathbf{d}i^T. bi: Vector of shape [3, 1] for each ray i, defined as -Ai \mathbf{o}i. Steps: 1. Extract Rays: Extract ray directions \mathbf{d}i and origins \mathbf{o}i from the input poses matrix. \mathbf{d}i = \text{poses}[i,:3, 2:3] \mathbf{o}i = \text{poses}[i,:3, 3:4] 2. Compute Sphere Center: Calculate the point \mathbf{p}{\text{mindist}} that minimizes the distance to all camera rays by solving a least-squares problem. Ai = I - \mathbf{d}i \mathbf{d}i^T bi = -Ai \mathbf{o}i \mathbf{p}{\text{mindist}} = -\left( \frac{1}{N{\text{orig}}} \sum{i=1}^{N{\text{orig}}} Ai^T Ai \right)^{-1} \left( \frac{1}{N{\text{orig}}} \sum{i=1}^{N{\text{orig}}} bi \right) Set \mathbf{c} = \mathbf{p}{\text{mindist}}. 3. Compute Up Vector: Calculate the mean vector from the center to the camera positions to define the initial "up" direction. \mathbf{u} = \frac{1}{N{\text{orig}}} \sum{i=1}^{N{\text{orig}}} (\text{poses}[i,:3, 3] - \mathbf{c}) 4. Construct Local Coordinate System: Normalize \mathbf{u} to get \mathbf{vec}0. Compute \mathbf{vec}1 by crossing \mathbf{vec}0 with a fixed arbitrary vector \mathbf{v}{\text{fix}} = [0.1, 0.2, 0.3]^T to avoid degeneracy if \mathbf{u} is parallel to the world up. Compute \mathbf{vec}2 by crossing \mathbf{vec}0 and \mathbf{vec}1. \mathbf{vec}0 = \frac{\mathbf{u}}{\|\mathbf{u}\|} \mathbf{vec}1 = \frac{\mathbf{v}{\text{fix}} \times \mathbf{vec}0}{\|\mathbf{v}{\text{fix}} \times \mathbf{vec}0\|} \mathbf{vec}2 = \frac{\mathbf{vec}0 \times \mathbf{vec}1}{\|\mathbf{vec}0 \times \mathbf{vec}1\|} 5. Reset Poses: Construct a transformation matrix T using the basis vectors and the center. T = \begin{bmatrix} \mathbf{vec}1 & \mathbf{vec}2 & \mathbf{vec}0 & \mathbf{c} \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix} Apply this transformation to all input poses to get posesreset. 6. Compute Radius and Scale: Calculate the radius r of the centered poses. r = \sqrt{\frac{1}{N{\text{orig}}} \sum{i=1}^{N{\text{orig}}} \|\text{poses\reset}[i,:3, 3]\|^2} Compute scale factor s = 1/r. Apply this scale to posesreset and bds. 7. Compute Spherical Parameters: Calculate the centroid of the scaled poses. Extract the z-coordinate of the centroid, zh. zh = \text{centroid}[2] Compute the radius of the circle in the xy-plane, r{\text{circle}}. r{\text{circle}} = \sqrt{r^2 - zh^2} 8. Generate New Poses: Iterate \theta from 0 to 2\pi with N steps. For each \theta: \mathbf{camorigin} = [r{\text{circle}} \cos(\theta), r{\text{circle}} \sin(\theta), zh] Construct a new local basis for the camera orientation: \mathbf{vec}2' = \frac{\mathbf{camorigin}}{\|\mathbf{camorigin}\|} \mathbf{vec}0' = \frac{\mathbf{vec}2' \times [0, 0, -1]^T}{\|\mathbf{vec}2' \times [0, 0, -1]^T\|} \mathbf{vec}1' = \frac{\mathbf{vec}2' \times \mathbf{vec}0'}{\|\mathbf{vec}2' \times \mathbf{vec}0'\|} Set the pose matrix P with columns \mathbf{vec}0', \mathbf{vec}1', \mathbf{vec}2' and translation \mathbf{camorigin}. P = \begin{bmatrix} \mathbf{vec}0' & \mathbf{vec}1' & \mathbf{vec}2' & \mathbf{camorigin} \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix} 9. Append Homogeneous Row: Append the original pose's w-row (typically poses[0,:3,-1:]) to the new poses to maintain homogeneous coordinate structure. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import numpy as np def spherifyposes(poses, N): """ Reorients camera poses to a spherical arrangement. Args: poses: np.array of shape (Norig, 4, 4) N: int, number of new poses to generate Returns: posesspherical: np.array of shape (N, 4, 4) """ # 1. Extract rays raysd = poses[:,:3, 2:3] # Shape (Norig, 3, 1) rayso = poses[:,:3, 3:4] # Shape (Norig, 3, 1) # 2. Compute sphere center I = np.eye(3) # Ai = I - di di^T Ai = I - (raysd @ raysd.transpose(0, 2, 1)) # bi = -Ai oi bi = -Ai @ rayso # ptmindist = -inv(mean(Ai^T @ Ai)) @ mean(bi) meanA = np.mean(Ai.transpose(0, 2, 1) @ Ai, axis=0) meanb = np.mean(bi, axis=0) ptmindist = -np.linalg.inv(meanA) @ meanb.flatten() center = ptmindist # 3. Compute up vector campositions = poses[:,:3, 3] up = np.mean(campositions - center, axis=0) # 4. Construct local coordinate system vec0 = up / np.linalg.norm(up) vfix = np.array([0.1, 0.2, 0.3]) vec1 = np.cross(vfix, vec0) vec1 = vec1 / np.linalg.norm(vec1) vec2 = np.cross(vec0, vec1) vec2 = vec2 / np.linalg.norm(vec2) # 5. Reset poses # c2w = [vec1, vec2, vec0, pos=center] R = np.columnstack((vec1, vec2, vec0)) T = np.eye(4) T[:3,:3] = R T[:3, 3] = center # Apply transformation to all input poses posesreset = np.zeroslike(poses) for i in range(poses.shape[0]): posesreset[i] = T @ poses[i] # 6. Compute radius and scale positions = posesreset[:,:3, 3] rad = np.sqrt(np.mean(np.sum(positions2, axis=-1))) sc = 1.0 / rad posesreset[:,:3, 3] = sc # Apply scale to posesreset # 7. Compute spherical parameters centroid = np.mean(posesreset[:,:3, 3], axis=0) zh = centroid[2] radcircle = np.sqrt(rad2 - zh2) # 8. Generate new poses thetas = np.linspace(0, 2 np.pi, N, endpoint=False) posesspherical = np.zeros((N, 4, 4)) for i, th in enumerate(thetas): camorigin = np.array([radcircle np.cos(th), radcircle np.sin(th), zh]) vec2prime = camorigin / np.linalg.norm(camorigin) vec0prime = np.cross(vec2prime, np.array([0, 0, -1])) vec0prime = vec0prime / np.linalg.norm(vec0prime) vec1prime = np.cross(vec2prime, vec0prime) vec1prime = vec1prime / np.linalg.norm(vec1prime) posesspherical[i,:3, 0] = vec0prime posesspherical[i,:3, 1] = vec1prime posesspherical[i,:3, 2] = vec2prime posesspherical[i,:3, 3] = camorigin posesspherical[i, 3,:] = poses[0, 3,:] # Append original w-row return posesspherical Parameters: N: Number of poses to generate. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Degenerate Up Vector: If the mean up vector is zero (cameras are symmetric around the center), normalization fails. Guard against this by checking np.linalg.norm(up) < epsilon. Parallel Ray Directions: If all rays are parallel, Ai becomes singular, and the least-squares solution for the center is unstable. Check for collinearity of ray directions. Complexity of Cross Product: If \mathbf{vec}0 is parallel to \mathbf{v}{\text{fix}}, the cross product for \mathbf{vec}1 is zero. The fixed vector [0.1, 0.2, 0.3] is chosen to be unlikely to be parallel to typical scene up vectors, but a fallback is recommended. Radius Calculation: The formula for r{\text{circle}} assumes r \ge |zh|. If the scene is not roughly spherical or the centering is poor, this may result in a NaN. Check for r^2 < zh^2. Generates poses on a 2D circle. Choose when the scene is planar or when a simple orbit is sufficient. Spherify is chosen for 3D volumetric scenes requiring full spherical coverage. Time Complexity: O(N) for extracting rays and computing the center. O(N) for generating new poses. Overall linear in the number of input poses and output poses. Memory Complexity: O(N) to store rays, intermediate matrices, and output poses. Strengths: Provides a robust, data-driven center for spherical sampling, which is crucial for NeRF training on unstructured data. Ensures uniform distribution of views. Limitations: Assumes the scene is roughly spherical. If the scene is elongated or has a specific orientation, the spherical path may not cover all parts of the scene uniformly. The fixed vector for cross product is arbitrary. When to Use: When preparing unstructured image collections for NeRF training where a spherical camera path is desired. When Not to Use: When the scene is known to be planar or when a specific trajectory (e.g., spiral, linear) is required for artistic or physical reasons. The method originates from the NerfingMVS project. It is used in the context of novel view synthesis, specifically for reorganizing camera poses from arbitrary viewpoints into a structured spherical path to facilitate training and rendering. weiyithu/NerfingMVS, https://github.com/weiyithu/NerfingMVS, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial)

name: Elliptical Camera Path Generation
head: Elliptical Camera Path with Y Variation, Elliptical Path Generation, Elliptical Render Path (Y Variation), Elliptical Render Path Generation, elliptical camera trajectory
body: Generates a closed-loop elliptical camera trajectory centered on a focal point derived from input training poses, with optional asymmetric height variation along the vertical axis. It differs from Orbit Camera Path Generation by allowing independent scaling of the ellipse axes and non-circular vertical oscillation, and from Spiral Camera Path Generation by maintaining a constant radius (or bounded height range) rather than a continuously expanding or contracting radius. Inputs: poses: Array of shape (N, 4, 4) containing N input camera poses. nframes: Integer, number of output frames. Default 120. zvariation: Float, amplitude of height variation. Default 0. zphase: Float, phase shift for height variation. Default 0. constspeed: Boolean, whether to resample for constant velocity. Default True. Outputs: path: Array of shape (n\frames, 4, 4) containing the generated camera poses. Data Structures: center: Vector of shape (3,) representing the focal point. offset: Vector of shape (3,) defining the center of the ellipse bounds. sc: Vector of shape (3,) representing the semi-axis lengths (scaling factors). low, high: Vectors of shape (3,) defining the bounding box of the ellipse. zlow, zhigh: Scalars defining the vertical bounds. up: Vector of shape (3,) defining the camera up direction. positions: Array of shape (n\frames, 3) for intermediate position calculation. Steps: 1. Scene Analysis: Compute the focal point center using a function focuspointfn(poses). 2. Offset and Scaling: Determine the offset vector. For the primary X-Y plane variant, offset = [center[0], center[1], 0]. Compute scaling factors sc using the 90th percentile of the absolute distances of camera positions from offset: \text{sc} = \text{percentile}(|\text{poses}[:,:3, 3] - \text{offset}|, 90, \text{axis}=0). Define ellipse bounds: \text{low} = -\text{sc} + \text{offset} \text{high} = \text{sc} + \text{offset}. 3. Vertical Bounds: Compute zlow and zhigh using the 10th and 90th percentiles of the z-coordinates of the camera positions: \text{z\low} = \text{percentile}(\text{poses}[:,:3, 3][:, 2], 10, \text{axis}=0) \text{z\high} = \text{percentile}(\text{poses}[:,:3, 3][:, 2], 90, \text{axis}=0). 4. Position Parameterization: Define a function getpositions(theta) that returns the 3D position for a given angle \theta \in [0, 2\pi]: x(\theta) = \text{low}[0] + (\text{high}[0] - \text{low}[0]) \cdot (\cos(\theta) \cdot 0.5 + 0.5) y(\theta) = \text{low}[1] + (\text{high}[1] - \text{low}[1]) \cdot (\sin(\theta) \cdot 0.5 + 0.5) z(\theta) = \text{z\variation} \cdot (\text{z\low}[2] + (\text{z\high}[2] - \text{z\low}[2]) \cdot (\cos(\theta + 2\pi \cdot \text{z\phase}) \cdot 0.5 + 0.5)). 5. Sampling: Generate \theta values: \theta = \text{linspace}(0, 2\pi, n\frames + 1, \text{endpoint}=\text{True}). Evaluate getpositions(theta) for all \theta to get positions of shape (n\frames + 1, 3). Remove the last duplicate point (where \theta = 2\pi) to close the loop without redundancy: \text{positions} = \text{positions}[0:n\frames]. 6. Constant Speed Resampling (Optional): If constspeed is true, calculate the arc lengths between consecutive positions and resample \theta to ensure uniform spacing. Calculate lengths: \text{lengths}i = \| \text{positions}{i+1} - \text{positions}i \|2. Resample \theta using cumulative arc length interpolation to maintain constant velocity. 7. Up Vector Determination: Compute the average up vector from input poses: \text{avg\up} = \text{mean}(\text{poses}[:,:3, 1], \text{axis}=0). Normalize avgup. Find the index indup of the maximum absolute component of avgup. Set the up vector: \text{up} = \mathbf{e}{\text{ind\up}} \cdot \text{sign}(\text{avg\up}[\text{ind\up}]) where \mathbf{e}{\text{ind\up}} is the basis vector with 1 at indup and 0 elsewhere. 8. Pose Construction: For each position p in positions, construct a view matrix using viewmatrix(p - center, up, p). Stack all poses into the output path. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import numpy as np def focuspointfn(poses): """Calculate the focal point (center) of the camera poses. Typically the mean of the camera positions.""" return np.mean(poses[:,:3, 3], axis=0) def viewmatrix(lookat, up, position): """Construct a view matrix from look-at direction, up vector, and position. lookat: direction the camera looks towards (from position). up: up vector. position: camera position. Returns a 4x4 matrix.""" z = lookat / np.linalg.norm(lookat) x = np.cross(up, z) # Guard against parallel up and lookat if np.linalg.norm(x) < 1e-6: x = np.array([1.0, 0.0, 0.0]) x = x / np.linalg.norm(x) y = np.cross(z, x) R = np.columnstack((x, y, z)) t = -R.T @ position P = np.eye(4) P[:3,:3] = R P[:3, 3] = t return P def generateellipsepath(poses, nframes, zvariation=0.0, zphase=0.0, constspeed=True): """Generate an elliptical camera path.""" # 1. Scene Analysis center = focuspointfn(poses) # 2. Offset and Scaling offset = np.array([center[0], center[1], 0.0]) sc = np.percentile(np.abs(poses[:,:3, 3] - offset), 90, axis=0) low = -sc + offset high = sc + offset # 3. Vertical Bounds zlow = np.percentile(poses[:,:3, 3][:, 2], 10, axis=0) zhigh = np.percentile(poses[:,:3, 3][:, 2], 90, axis=0) # 4. Position Parameterization def getpositions(theta): x = low[0] + (high[0] - low[0]) (np.cos(theta) 0.5 + 0.5) y = low[1] + (high[1] - low[1]) (np.sin(theta) 0.5 + 0.5) z = zvariation (zlow[2] + (zhigh[2] - zlow[2]) (np.cos(theta + 2 np.pi zphase) 0.5 + 0.5)) return np.stack([x, y, z], axis=-1) # 5. Sampling theta = np.linspace(0, 2 np.pi, nframes + 1, endpoint=True) positions = getpositions(theta) positions = positions[:-1] # 6. Constant Speed Resampling (Optional) if constspeed: lengths = np.linalg.norm(positions[1:] - positions[:-1], axis=-1) cumlengths = np.insert(np.cumsum(lengths), 0, 0.0) uniformt = np.linspace(0, cumlengths[-1], nframes) theta = np.interp(uniformt, cumlengths, theta) positions = getpositions(theta) # 7. Up Vector Determination avgup = np.mean(poses[:,:3, 1], axis=0) norm = np.linalg.norm(avgup) # Guard against zero-length average up vector if norm > 1e-6: avgup = avgup / norm indup = np.argmax(np.abs(avgup)) up = np.eye(3)[indup] np.sign(avgup[indup]) # 8. Pose Construction path = np.stack([viewmatrix(p - center, up, p) for p in positions]) return path Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Degenerate Input: If all input poses are collinear or identical, sc may be zero or avgup may be undefined. Guard against division by zero in normalization. Boundary Conditions: The mapping from \theta to position uses a shifted cosine/sine, ensuring the path starts and ends at the same point without discontinuity. Axis Variation: The coordinate axes can be swapped (e.g., X-Z plane with Y variation) depending on the specific variant implementation. Generates a path with a continuously changing radius, suitable for capturing scenes with depth variation. Choose when the scene has significant depth and a circular orbit is insufficient. Generates a circular path around a center point. Choose when the scene is roughly spherical and a constant radius is appropriate. Strengths: Simple to implement, provides smooth and symmetric paths, allows for controlled height variation. Limitations: Assumes the scene is roughly centered and bounded by the input poses. When to Use: When a smooth, closed-loop camera path is needed for novel view synthesis or visualization, and the scene is well-contained within the input poses. When Not to Use: When the scene is very large or unbounded, or when the camera needs to follow a specific non-elliptical trajectory. Time and Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Measured Performance: Not given in the sources. Scaling: Not given in the sources. The method originates from the NeRF and multi-NeRF literature, specifically implemented in the multinerf repository by Google Research. It has been adopted and adapted in various other neural rendering frameworks such as mrGSplat, VolSplat, and VoLoDSplat for generating training or evaluation camera paths. google-research/multinerf, https://github.com/google-research/multinerf, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial) meshroomHub/mrGSplat, https://github.com/meshroomHub/mrGSplat, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial) ziplab/VolSplat, https://github.com/ziplab/VolSplat, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial) pulangk97/VoLoDSplat, https://github.com/pulangk97/VoLoDSplat, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial)

name: Orbit Camera Path Generation
head: Camera Orbit Animation, Circular Camera Path, Cyclic rotation rendering, Orbit rendering, Orbiting Render, Rotation Rendering
body: Orbit Camera Path Generation creates a sequence of rendered frames by incrementally rotating the camera around a fixed focal point, producing a smooth circular visualization effect. It differs from its siblings, Spiral and Elliptical path generation, by constraining the camera trajectory to a single plane perpendicular to the rotation axis at a constant radius, ensuring uniform angular velocity and no change in elevation or distance. Inputs: activecamera: The camera object or state to be transformed. framecount: Total number of frames to generate (e.g., 36). azimuthincrement: Degrees to rotate the camera around the view-up axis per frame (e.g., 10 degrees). rotateaxis: Integer specifying the rotation axis: 0 for Elevation, 1 for Roll, 2 for Azimuth. rotateangles: Optional list of float angles in degrees to rotate the camera at each step, overriding azimuthincrement if provided. resolution: Output image dimensions (e.g., [1000, 800]). outputdir: Directory path for saving rendered frames. Data Structures: renderedimage: A 4D NumPy array of shape (framecount, height, width, 3) with dtype uint8, initialized to zeros. imagefilter: A VTK vtkWindowToImageFilter instance used to convert the render window to an image buffer. Steps: 1. Initialize: Obtain the active camera object and configure the rendering window with the specified resolution. 2. Loop: Iterate i from 0 to framecount - 1. 3. Rotate: If rotateangles is provided, retrieve angle = rotateangles[i]. Otherwise, set angle = azimuthincrement. Apply the rotation to the camera using the rotateaxis specification. For azimuth rotation (axis 2), call camera.Azimuth(angle). 4. Render: Trigger the rendering pipeline. If using VTK, call imagefilter.Modified() and imagefilter.Update() to refresh the image buffer, then window.Render(). 5. Capture: Extract the rendered image data. In VTK, convert the output of imagefilter.GetOutput() to a NumPy array. 6. Store: Assign the captured image to renderedimage[i,:,:,:]. 7. Cleanup (Optional): If the rotation is cumulative and needs to be reset for the next frame without accumulating error, apply the inverse rotation camera.Azimuth(-angle) after capture. Note: In standard orbit generation, rotations are often cumulative, so this step may be omitted depending on the desired continuity. 8. Save: Write the frame to outputdir with a sequential filename (e.g., frame%03d.png). Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import numpy as np import os def generateorbitframes(activecamera, framecount, azimuthincrement, rotateaxis, resolution, outputdir, rotateangles=None): """ Generates orbit camera frames. activecamera: Object with Azimuth(degrees) method. framecount: int azimuthincrement: float (degrees) rotateaxis: int (0=Elevation, 1=Roll, 2=Azimuth) resolution: tuple (width, height) outputdir: str rotateangles: list of floats or None """ os.makedirs(outputdir, existok=True) # Initialize image buffer if using VTK-style capture # Note: Actual capture mechanism depends on the renderer API. # This pseudocode assumes a generic capture function captureframe. for i in range(framecount): if rotateangles is not None: angle = rotateangles[i] else: angle = azimuthincrement # Apply rotation based on axis # Simplified for Azimuth (axis 2) as per common usage if rotateaxis == 2: activecamera.Azimuth(angle) elif rotateaxis == 0: activecamera.Elevation(angle) elif rotateaxis == 1: activecamera.Roll(angle) # Render and Capture # Implementation detail: Trigger renderer and extract pixel buffer frame = captureframe(resolution) # Save frame filename = os.path.join(outputdir, f"frame{i:03d}.png") saveimage(frame, filename) # Optional: Reset rotation if non-cumulative behavior is required # activecamera.Azimuth(-angle) Parameters: azimuthincrement: Typical value 10 degrees. framecount: Typical value 36. resolution: Typical value [1000, 800]. rotateaxis: 0 (Elevation), 1 (Roll), 2 (Azimuth). Edge Cases: Cumulative Error: Repeated floating-point rotations can accumulate orientation drift. Using rotateangles with explicit values or resetting the camera orientation periodically mitigates this. Axis Ambiguity: The rotateaxis parameter must be consistently interpreted by the camera API. VTK uses 0, 1, 2 for Elevation, Roll, Azimuth respectively. A method for 3D reconstruction that uses a fine-tuned image-to-video model to generate turn-table style video sequences (orbit paths) from a single image, which are then used for 3D Gaussian Splatting. It differs by generating the path content via a video model rather than geometric camera transforms. Time Complexity: O(F), where F is the number of frames, as each frame requires one rotation and one render operation. Memory Complexity: O(F \cdot H \cdot W \cdot C) if storing all frames in memory, or O(H \cdot W \cdot C) if streaming to disk. Performance: Rendering time depends on the scene complexity and resolution. Typical resolution [1000, 800] with 36 frames is feasible for real-time preview but may require batch processing for high-res volume rendering. Strengths: Simple to implement; produces smooth, continuous rotation ideal for visualizing symmetric or centrally focused data. Limitations: Does not provide elevation changes (unlike Spiral) or aspect variation (unlike Elliptical), potentially hiding features located above or below the equatorial plane. The method is commonly implemented in scientific visualization pipelines using VTK and ParaView. It is utilized for exporting animation sequences (e.g., PNG frames) that can be stitched into videos using tools like ffmpeg. The approach is foundational in volume rendering workflows for creating turn-table style visualizations. cjcamp16/sciviz-paraview, https://github.com/cjcamp16/sciviz-paraview, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial) Volume Renderer with VTK - yuta-hi, https://github.com/yuta-hi/volume-renderer, fetched 2026-10-29 (unofficial)

name: IM-3D
body: IM-3D is a method for 3D reconstruction that utilizes a fine-tuned image-to-video model to generate turn-table style video sequences from a single input image, which are subsequently used as input for 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) reconstruction. It differs from direct multi-view generation methods by leveraging temporal consistency inherent in video models to produce coherent views for reconstruction. Inputs: A single source image of an object. Outputs: A 3D Gaussian Splatting representation of the object. Data Structures: Fine-tuned Image-to-Video Model: Based on the Emu architecture. Generated Video: A sequence of frames representing a camera rotating around the object. 3DGS Representation: The final output structure containing Gaussian attributes (position, covariance, color, opacity) derived from the video frames. Steps: 1. Fine-tuning: The Emu-based image-to-video model is fine-tuned on a dataset suitable for generating turn-table videos. 2. Video Generation: The fine-tuned model takes the single input image and generates a video sequence where the camera rotates around the object. 3. 3DGS Reconstruction: The generated video frames are extracted and fed into a 3D Gaussian Splatting reconstruction pipeline to recover the 3D scene. Parameters: Rotation Angle: The video simulates a turn-table rotation. The exact angular range and step size are not specified in the sources. Video Length: The number of frames in the generated video is not specified in the sources. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Temporal Consistency: While video models provide consistency, artifacts in the generated video (e.g., flickering, geometry drift) can negatively impact the 3DGS reconstruction quality. Occlusion: The turn-table approach assumes visibility of the object from multiple angles; severe self-occlusion may lead to incomplete reconstruction. Model Bias: The quality of reconstruction is heavily dependent on the fine-tuning data and the base Emu model's capabilities. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Leverages strong generative priors from video models to create consistent multi-view inputs from a single image. Limitations: Relies on the quality of the generated video; errors in generation propagate to the 3D reconstruction. Requires fine-tuning of a large video model. When to use: When only a single image is available and high-quality multi-view generation is needed for 3DGS reconstruction. When not to use: When real-time performance is critical or when ground-truth multi-view images are available. IM-3D was introduced in the context of recent advances in 3D Gaussian Splatting. It builds upon the Emu image-to-video model and applies it to the task of single-image 3D reconstruction via intermediate video generation. The method is part of a broader trend of using generative models to augment 3D reconstruction pipelines. name: Camera Motion Trajectory Approximation
head: Lie Algebra SE(3) Interpolation, SE(3) Camera Trajectory Approximation
body: This method approximates the continuous camera trajectory during a finite shutter exposure time by interpolating between known discrete poses within the Lie algebra of the special Euclidean group SE(3). It solves the problem of modeling motion blur in differentiable rendering by providing a smooth, differentiable parameterization of camera motion that respects the non-commutative nature of 3D rigid body transformations. It distinguishes itself from linear interpolation in Euclidean space by ensuring the interpolated poses remain valid rigid transformations, and from B-spline methods by offering explicit control over the interpolation order via Bézier curves. Inputs and Outputs Inputs: Start pose T0 \in SE(3), end pose T1 \in SE(3), shutter duration \tau, and current time t \in [0, \tau]. For higher-order methods, additional control points Tj and interpolation order K are required. Outputs: Interpolated camera pose Tt \in SE(3) at time t. Data Structures Pose (T): A 4 \times 4 homogeneous transformation matrix representing rotation and translation in SE(3). Lie Algebra Element (\xi): A 6-dimensional vector representing the logarithm of a rotation matrix, typically packed as [\omegax, \omegay, \omegaz, vx, vy, vz]^T. Mathematical Primitives Logarithm (\log): Maps T \in SE(3) to its Lie algebra element \xi \in \mathfrak{se}(3). Exponential (\exp): Maps \xi \in \mathfrak{se}(3) back to T \in SE(3). Matrix Multiplication (\cdot): Standard 4 \times 4 matrix multiplication. Interpolation Methods 1. Linear Interpolation Suitable for short shutter times and small motion amplitudes. Given start T0 and end T1: Tt = T0 \cdot \exp\left( \log(T0^{-1} \cdot T1) \frac{t}{\tau} \right) where t \in [0, \tau] and \tau is the shutter time. 2. Cubic Spline Interpolation Requires four control points T0, T1, T2, T3. Let u = t/\tau \in [0, 1]. The basis function matrix \tilde{B}(u) is: \tilde{B}(u) = C \begin{bmatrix} 1 \\ u \\ u^2 \\ u^3 \end{bmatrix}, \quad C = \frac{1}{6} \begin{bmatrix} 6 & 0 & 0 & 0 \\ 5 & 3 & -3 & 1 \\ 1 & 3 & 3 & -2 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix} The interpolated pose is computed as: T(u) = T0 \cdot \prod{j=0}^{2} \exp\left( \tilde{B}{j+1}(u) \cdot \Omegaj \right) where \Omegaj are the Lie algebra elements corresponding to the relative transformations between control points. Note: The source notation \tilde{B}{j+1} refers to the (j+1)-th entry of the basis vector result, and \Omegaj represents the incremental Lie algebra contribution. 3. Bézier Curve Interpolation Uses K+1 control points T0, \dots, TK and order K. The method uses K=7 in the source implementation. Let u = t/\tau \in [0, 1]. The interpolated pose is: Tt = \prod{j=0}^{K} \exp\left( \binom{K}{j} (1-u)^{K-j} u^j \log(Tj) \right) This formulation applies De Casteljau’s algorithm in the Lie algebra representation, ensuring differentiability with respect to control points Tj. Pseudocode Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import numpy as np def se3log(T): """ Computes the Lie algebra element (6-vector) from a 4x4 SE(3) matrix. Returns [omegax, omegay, omegaz, vx, vy, vz]. Implementation details for se3log are assumed standard. """ # Extract rotation R and translation tvec from T R = T[:3,:3] tvec = T[:3, 3] # Compute rotation angle and axis theta = np.arccos(np.clip((np.trace(R) - 1) / 2, -1.0, 1.0)) if theta < 1e-6: omega = np.zeros(3) else: omega = theta np.array([R[2,1]-R[1,2], R[0,2]-R[2,0], R[1,0]-R[0,1]]) / (2 np.sin(theta)) # Compute translation component v # V matrix approximation for small theta or standard inversion # V = I + ((1-cos(theta))/theta^2) [omega]x + ((theta-sin(theta))/theta^3) [omega]x^2 # v = V^-1 tvec # For simplicity in this self-contained example, we assume a standard se3log implementation exists. # Here we return a placeholder structure consistent with the source's usage. return np.concatenate([omega, tvec]) # Placeholder: Real implementation requires Vinv def se3exp(xi): """ Computes the 4x4 SE(3) matrix from a 6-vector Lie algebra element. """ omega = xi[:3] v = xi[3:] theta = np.linalg.norm(omega) if theta < 1e-6: R = np.eye(3) V = np.eye(3) else: k = omega / theta K = np.array([[0, -k[2], k[1]], [k[2], 0, -k[0]], [-k[1], k[0], 0]]) R = np.eye(3) + np.sin(theta) K + (1 - np.cos(theta)) (K @ K) # V matrix for translation V = np.eye(3) + ((1 - np.cos(theta)) / (theta2)) K + ((theta - np.sin(theta)) / (theta3)) (K @ K) tvec = V @ v T = np.eye(4) T[:3,:3] = R T[:3, 3] = tvec return T def linearse3interpolation(T0, T1, t, tau): """ Linear interpolation in SE(3) Lie algebra. """ # Tt = T0 exp(log(T0^-1 T1) (t/tau)) deltaT = np.linalg.inv(T0) @ T1 xi = se3log(deltaT) xiscaled = xi (t / tau) expdelta = se3exp(xiscaled) return T0 @ expdelta def bezierse3interpolation(controlpoints, K, t, tau): """ Bézier interpolation in SE(3) Lie algebra. controlpoints: list of K+1 SE(3) matrices. K: order of the curve. """ u = t / tau result = np.eye(4) for j in range(K + 1): # Binomial coefficient binom = np.math.comb(K, j) weight = binom ((1 - u)(K - j)) (uj) # Log of control point xij = se3log(controlpoints[j]) # Scale and exponentiate xiscaled = xij weight expterm = se3exp(xiscaled) # Multiply into result result = result @ expterm return result Parameters Order K: The degree of the Bézier curve. The source uses K=7. Shutter Time \tau: The duration of the exposure. Time t: The current timestamp within the exposure, t \in [0, \tau]. Edge Cases and Pitfalls Identity Rotation: When \theta \approx 0, the logarithm and exponential functions must handle the singularity gracefully to avoid division by zero. Degenerate Input: If control points are identical, the trajectory remains static. If T0 = T1, linear interpolation yields T0. Precision: The composition of many exponentials in high-order Bézier curves can accumulate numerical error. Using the Lie algebra formulation ensures the result stays on the manifold. Defines the mathematical parameterization of camera motion trajectories. Linear interpolation is sufficient for synthetic scenes with short time intervals, while cubic B-splines are required for real captured scenes with longer exposure times and complex motions. Time Complexity: Linear interpolation is O(1). Bézier interpolation is O(K) per pose evaluation, where K is the order. Memory Complexity: O(1) for linear; O(K) for Bézier to store control points. Performance: The method is differentiable, allowing joint optimization of scene and camera parameters using gradient descent (e.g., Adam optimizer). Strengths: Ensures valid SE(3) poses; differentiable; handles arbitrary smooth motion. Limitations: Requires initialization of control points (e.g., via COLMAP); higher-order curves increase computational cost. When to use: When motion blur needs to be modeled in differentiable rendering pipelines, particularly for deblurring or novel view synthesis from blurred images. The method originates from "Deblur-GS: 3D Gaussian Splatting from Camera Motion Blurred Images". It builds on the principle that camera motion during shutter time can be parameterized in SE(3) and approximated using interpolation in its Lie algebra. The approach allows for the optimization of motion blurring by optimizing the control points of the trajectory. name: Camera Trajectory Representations
head: Camera trajectory interpolation, SE(3) trajectory parameterization, Trajectory Representations for Camera Motion
body: This family defines the mathematical parameterization of camera motion trajectories used to approximate camera movement during shutter exposure time for motion blur synthesis. It solves the problem of how to interpolate between known camera poses to generate intermediate virtual views. The choice of representation is primarily driven by the complexity of the motion and the duration of the exposure: linear interpolation is sufficient for synthetic scenes with short time intervals, while cubic B-splines are required for real captured scenes with longer exposure times and complex motions. All representations in this family operate within the Lie group SE(3) to ensure valid rigid body transformations. The core mechanism involves optimizing a set of parameters to define the path between camera poses. The trajectory is typically discretized into n intermediate virtual images to balance rendering performance and training efficiency, with n=10 being a common empirical choice. The optimization targets the camera poses themselves, rather than just the trajectory shape, allowing the model to adapt to the specific blur characteristics of the input data. Linear interpolation parameterizes the trajectory by optimizing only the start pose \mathbf{T}{start} and the end pose \mathbf{T}{end}. The intermediate poses are generated by linearly interpolating between these two endpoints. This method is computationally efficient and sufficient for synthetic datasets where camera motions are simpler and exposure times are effectively shorter. It is employed for synthetic datasets such as those from Deblur-NeRF-S and MBA-VO. Cubic B-spline interpolation parameterizes the trajectory by jointly optimizing four control knots: \mathbf{T}1, \mathbf{T}2, \mathbf{T}3, and \mathbf{T}4. This higher-order spline allows for the modeling of more complex camera motions and nuances over longer time intervals. It outperforms linear interpolation in real captured scenes, particularly due to the longer exposure times inherent in real-world image capture. It is employed for real datasets, such as the 10 real captured scenes from Deblur-NeRF. The distinction between linear and higher-order spline representations for camera trajectories in the context of neural rendering and deblurring was formalized in the BAD-Gaussians paper. The authors conducted experiments on both synthetic datasets (Deblur-NeRF-S, MBA-VO) and real datasets (Deblur-NeRF) to assess the impact of trajectory representations. They found that while linear interpolation performed comparably to cubic B-splines on synthetic data, the latter was necessary for real data to handle complex motions and longer exposure times effectively. The specific mathematical details of the cubic B-spline implementation are referenced from external literature. name: User Viewport Predictor
head: Viewport trajectory prediction
body: The User Viewport Predictor estimates future camera poses (6DoF) from recent interaction history to enable proactive resource allocation in volume rendering and 3D scene delivery. It differs from synthetic or spline-based trajectory generators by relying on empirical user data rather than predefined geometric paths. It serves as a lightweight, short-term forecasting module that can be replaced by more complex models like deep learning predictors. The method uses linear regression to predict the next N frames based on a sliding window of recent observations. Inputs and Outputs Input: A sequence of 6DoF viewport poses \mathbf{P}t = [xt, yt, zt, \alphat, \betat, \gammat] for t in the history window hw. Output: Predicted 6DoF poses for the prediction window pw. Data Structures History Window (hw): A buffer storing recent viewport samples. Prediction Window (pw): The temporal range into the future to predict. Linear Model: For each of the 6 degrees of freedom, a separate linear regression model y = mx + c is maintained. Parameters hw = 0.5 seconds. pw = 1 second. Frame rate: Assumed 36 FPS for synchronization with bandwidth sampling. Steps 1. Re-center Angular Data: Before fitting, handle the cyclical nature of rotation angles (\alpha, \beta, \gamma). Set the angle of the first point in hw as 0. Calculate subsequent angles relative to this reference. Angles increase clockwise and decrease counter-clockwise. Clamp the resulting range to [-180, 180] to ensure continuity. 2. Fit Linear Model: For each of the 6 features independently: Let xi be the relative time index (order) of the i-th sample in hw compared to the first point. Let yi be the value of the feature (position or re-centered angle) at that index. Compute the linear regression coefficients (slope m and intercept c) for the set \{(xi, yi)\}. 3. Forecast: For each future time step k in the prediction window pw: Calculate the relative time index x{pred} from the start of hw. Predict the feature value y{pred} = m \cdot x{pred} + c. 4. Update: Continuously slide the hw window forward as new viewport data arrives and re-fit the models. Pseudocode Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import numpy as np class UserViewportPredictor: def init(self, historywindowsec=0.5, predwindowsec=1.0, fps=36): self.historywindowsec = historywindowsec self.predwindowsec = predwindowsec self.fps = fps self.historywindowlen = int(historywindowsec fps) self.predwindowlen = int(predwindowsec fps) # Buffers for 6DoF: [x, y, z, alpha, beta, gamma] self.historybuffer = np.zeros((self.historywindowlen, 6)) self.modelparams = np.zeros((6, 2)) # [slope, intercept] for each DOF self.isfitted = False def recenterangles(self, angles): """ Re-center angular data to handle cyclical nature. Sets first point to 0, range [-180, 180]. """ if len(angles) == 0: return angles firstangle = angles[0] # Calculate relative angles relangles = angles - firstangle # Normalize to [-180, 180] # This assumes small changes between frames to avoid large jumps # In practice, one might use modulo arithmetic, but the source # specifies a simple re-centering relative to the first point. # We clamp to ensure the range constraint mentioned. recentered = np.clip(relangles, -180, 180) return recentered def update(self, newpose, timestamp): """ Add a new viewport pose to the history and re-fit models. newpose: array-like of shape (6,) """ # Shift buffer self.historybuffer = np.roll(self.historybuffer, -1, axis=0) self.historybuffer[-1,:] = newpose # Check if buffer is full if not self.isfitted: # Need to fill buffer first? Or fit with available data. # Source implies continuous fitting to recent history. # Assuming we fit once buffer has enough points or always fit. pass self.fitmodels() def fitmodels(self): """ Fit linear regression for each of the 6 DOFs. """ # Use all available points in history buffer (assuming filled) # If buffer is not full, use available points. validpoints = np.sum(np.any(self.historybuffer != 0, axis=1)) if validpoints < 2: return # Get valid indices indices = np.arange(self.historywindowlen) # Mask for non-zero entries (assuming 0 is invalid/empty) # A more robust check would be a timestamp or valid flag, # but based on source, we assume the buffer is populated sequentially. # Relative time indices (x) # Source: "relative order in the sequence, compared to the first point in hw" # Let's assume the buffer is always full for the model fitting context # or we use the last N points. # For simplicity, assume buffer is full and valid x = np.arange(self.historywindowlen) for dof in range(6): y = self.historybuffer[:, dof] # Handle angles (dofs 3, 4, 5) if dof >= 3: y = self.recenterangles(y) # Linear Regression: y = mx + c # Using numpy polyfit for simplicity in pseudocode # polyfit returns [m, c] for degree 1 if len(x) >= 2: params = np.polyfit(x, y, 1) self.modelparams[dof,:] = params self.isfitted = True def predict(self): """ Predict future viewports for the prediction window. Returns: array of shape (predwindowlen, 6) """ if not self.isfitted: return None # Relative time indices for prediction # Source: "forecast future positions in the prediction window" # The x values should continue from the history window. # If hw ends at index T, pw starts at T+1, T+2... # Determine the x-range for prediction # Assuming the history window x values were 0 to hwlen-1 startx = self.historywindowlen xpred = np.arange(startx, startx + self.predwindowlen) predictions = np.zeros((self.predwindowlen, 6)) for dof in range(6): m, c = self.modelparams[dof,:] ypred = m xpred + c # For angles, we might need to re-center again if the prediction # extends far, but for short pw=1s, linear extrapolation of # re-centered angles is used. predictions[:, dof] = ypred return predictions Edge Cases and Pitfalls Angular Discontinuity: The cyclical nature of angles (0^\circ \equiv 360^\circ) can cause large errors in linear regression if not handled. The method requires re-centering relative to the first point in the history window. Short History: If the history window is too short, the linear model may not capture the trajectory trend accurately. Non-Linear Motion: Linear regression assumes constant velocity/rotation. Sudden user movements may lead to prediction errors. A module that processes interaction information to evaluate the type, parameters, speed, and duration of user engagement, potentially predicting consecutive viewpoints or regions of interest. It incorporates statistics such as the duration of interaction with a particular region during zooming or rotation around an axis. It evaluates interaction speed and predicts consecutive viewpoints. This is a more sophisticated variant that focuses on semantic interaction rather than just geometric trajectory. Time Complexity: O(1) per frame for fitting, as the number of features (6) and history window size (fixed at 0.5s) are constant. Memory Complexity: O(hw \cdot 6), where hw is the history window size in samples. Performance: Simple and fast, suitable for real-time systems. Accuracy: Reasonable accuracy for short-term forecasting. Limitations: Assumes linear motion; may fail during rapid or non-linear user interactions. The method was introduced in the context of L3GS (Layered 3D Gaussian Splats for Efficient 3D Scene Delivery). It was chosen for its simplicity, speed, and reasonable accuracy in short-term forecasting, similar to its use in other viewport-adaptive systems. The modular design allows for future replacement with more sophisticated models like deep learning predictors. name: Simple Exploration Path Construction
head: Inspection Walkthrough Path Construction
body: An algorithm for generating an inspection walkthrough path for complex volume models, ensuring all representative views (keypoints) are visited. It constructs a minimal length path on a bounding sphere of the object or region of interest. It sets itself apart from siblings like B-Spline Camera Path Interpolation by using an exhaustive search for the shortest path through a small set of discrete candidates rather than continuous curve fitting, and from Improved Exploration Path Construction by not deviating from the shortest path to maximize local information. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A set of N representative viewpoints (keypoints) selected from the volume, typically N \in \{3, 4\}. Input: The viewpoint with the highest entropy, denoted B0. Input: A bounding sphere enclosing the object or region of interest. Output: An ordered sequence of camera positions on the bounding sphere that visits all keypoints. Data Structures: keypoints: A list of N 3D positions on the bounding sphere. bestview: The index or position of B0 within keypoints. path: A list of 3D positions representing the camera trajectory. Steps: 1. Identify Key Points: Use the important viewpoints selected in the previous section as key points. Let the set of key points be K = \{k1, k2,..., kN\}. 2. Identify Best View: Determine the viewpoint with the highest entropy, B0, from K. 3. Enforce Constraint: Ensure B0 is visited in the second position of the path. This allows the camera to visit the surroundings of B0, which are intuitively more informative. 4. Compute Minimal Path: Compute the minimal length path that passes through all representative views in K, subject to the constraint that B0 is second. 5. Exhaustive Search: Since there are only three to four candidates (N \le 4), an exhaustive search of all permutations of the remaining N-1 viewpoints is performed to find the shortest path. 6. Construct Path: The resulting sequence of positions forms the simple exploration path. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def simpleexplorationpath(keypoints, bestview): """ Generates a simple exploration path visiting all keypoints. The bestview (highest entropy) must be visited second. Args: keypoints: List of 3D positions on the bounding sphere. bestview: The 3D position of the viewpoint with highest entropy. Returns: List of 3D positions representing the camera path. """ # Step 1 & 2: Identify key points and best view # keypoints is already provided as input # bestview is already provided as input # Step 3: Enforce constraint - bestview is second # Remove bestview from the list of remaining viewpoints to visit remainingviews = [k for k in keypoints if k != bestview] n = len(remainingviews) # Step 4 & 5: Compute minimal path via exhaustive search # We need to order the remainingviews to minimize total path length # The path structure is: [Start, bestview,...remainingviews...] # However, the problem states "minimal length path that passes through all... # ensuring best view in second place". This implies the path starts at one # of the remaining views, goes to bestview, then visits the rest. # Or it implies a fixed start? The text says "minimal length path... passes # through all". Usually, this is a Traveling Salesperson Problem variant. # With N<=4, we can brute force permutations of the remaining views. import itertools import math def distance(p1, p2): return math.sqrt(sum((a-b)2 for a, b in zip(p1, p2))) def pathlength(path): total = 0.0 for i in range(len(path) - 1): total += distance(path[i], path[i+1]) return total bestlength = float('inf') bestpermutation = None # Generate all permutations of the remaining views for perm in itertools.permutations(remainingviews): # Construct candidate path: Start with first of perm, then bestview, then rest # Note: The text doesn't specify the start point explicitly, but "minimal length # path that passes through all" usually implies finding the optimal ordering. # If the start is not fixed, the first element of the permutation is the start. candidatepath = list(perm) + [bestview] # This order is wrong based on constraint # Constraint: bestview is SECOND. # So the path is: [First of perm, bestview, Rest of perm] # Wait, if perm is (A, B, C), and best is X. # Path: A -> X -> B -> C ? # Or is the start fixed? "The viewpoint with the highest entropy is visited in second place". # This implies the path has a start. Let's assume the path starts at one of the # remaining views. # Let's re-read carefully: "minimal length path that passes through all... # ensures we are providing a high amount of information... best view in second place". # If N=3 (A, B, C) and B is best. # Permutations of remaining {A, C}: (A, C) or (C, A). # Path 1: A -> B -> C. Length: d(A,B) + d(B,C). # Path 2: C -> B -> A. Length: d(C,B) + d(B,A). # We choose the shorter one. # Generalizing for N views: # Path = [perm[0], bestview, perm[1],..., perm[N-2]] currentpath = [perm[0], bestview] + list(perm[1:]) currentlen = pathlength(currentpath) if currentlen < bestlength: bestlength = currentlen bestpermutation = currentpath # Step 6: Return the best path return bestpermutation Parameters: Number of candidate viewpoints: Typically three to four. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: If N < 2, the constraint "best view in second place" is undefined. The sources assume N \ge 3 ("three to four candidates"). Precision issues in distance calculations on the sphere are not discussed, but standard Euclidean distance on 3D coordinates is implied. The algorithm assumes the bounding sphere is already defined and the keypoints lie on it. An improvement to the simple path where the camera deviates from the short path to maximize information gathered, evaluated by entropy. For each step, it analyzes the entropy of three candidate positions placed toward the destination point, separated by \pm 4 to 6 degrees. It chooses the candidate with the highest entropy. The allowed total deviation is limited and reduced as the camera gets closer to the next key point to ensure all keypoints are visited. The speed of the camera is reduced when visiting points nearby the best view (B0) because they show a higher amount of valuable information. This approach gathers a higher amount of details than the simple method. Time depends on the number of steps produced, as it requires the evaluation of entropy at each step. Time Complexity: The simple path calculation time is negligible due to the exhaustive search over a small number of candidates (N \le 4). Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Measured Performance: The simple path is described as having "fast response" and "ease of use". Strengths: Provides a global vision of complex models by visiting all representative views; fast computation; no parameter definition required. Limitations: Does not actively maximize information gain along the path (unlike the improved variant); relies on pre-selected representative views. When to use: When a quick, comprehensive inspection of a volume model is needed without the computational cost of entropy evaluation at every step. When not to use: When maximizing local detail and information gain is critical, in which case the Improved Exploration Path Construction should be used. Originated in the context of medical volume visualization, specifically for radiologists inspecting complex anatomical structures like kidneys and thorax. The method was proposed to address the insufficiency of a static set of views for providing a global vision of complex models. It is designed to be easily incorporated into daily work by radiologists with null cost. The technique is applicable to other rendering metaphors beyond medical imaging.
