name: Scene View Estimation
head: Estimate Scene View, Make Render Input
body: Scene View Estimation computes the camera position, orientation, and projection parameters required to render a 3D scene into a target viewport. It solves the problem of automatically framing the scene content within the camera's view frustum by analyzing the spatial extent of the scene data. It differs from sibling methods like Arcball Camera or First-Person Camera Control by being fully automatic and data-driven, rather than user-controlled or trajectory-based. It builds on Camera Matrix and Coordinate Transformation for the final matrix assembly. Inputs: scene: A scene object containing sceneBounds (global bounds) and splatSets (a list of splat sets, each with its own bounds). width, height: Target viewport dimensions in pixels. frameIndex: Current frame identifier. Outputs: input: A render input structure containing: view: View matrix (look-at). proj: Projection matrix (perspective). cameraPosition: Eye position vector. viewportWidth, viewportHeight: Viewport dimensions. nearPlane, farPlane: Clipping plane distances. frameIndex: Frame ID. settings: Configuration flags (antialiasing, fastCulling). Data Structures: bounds: Axis-Aligned Bounding Box (AABB) defined by minimum and maximum 3D vectors. view: A struct containing center (3D vector) and radius (float). Steps: 1. Initialize bounds with scene.sceneBounds. 2. Iterate over each set in scene.splatSets, merging each set's bounds into bounds using MergeBounds. 3. If bounds is invalid, return a default view with center = {0, 0, 2.5} and radius = 1.0. 4. Otherwise, compute center = ComputeAabbCenter(bounds) and radius = max(ComputeAabbRadius(bounds), 0.5). 5. Calculate aspect = width / height. 6. Calculate distance = max(view.radius 2.5, 1.5). 7. Set eye = {view.center.x, view.center.y, view.center.z - distance}. 8. Set input.view = LookAt(eye, view.center, {0.0, 1.0, 0.0}). 9. Set input.proj = Perspective(1.0, aspect, 0.01, max(100.0, distance + view.radius 4.0)). 10. Set input.cameraPosition = eye, input.viewportWidth = width, input.viewportHeight = height, input.nearPlane = 0.01, input.farPlane = max(100.0, distance + view.radius 4.0), input.frameIndex = frameIndex. 11. Set input.settings.antialiasing = True, input.settings.fastCulling = True. Formulas: aspect = \frac{width}{height} distance = \max(view.radius \times 2.5, 1.5) eye = (view.center.x, view.center.y, view.center.z - distance) farPlane = \max(100.0, distance + view.radius \times 4.0) Parameters and Typical Values: aspect: Derived from viewport dimensions. distance: Scaled by view.radius 2.5, minimum 1.5. nearPlane: Fixed at 0.01. farPlane: Scaled by distance + view.radius 4.0, minimum 100.0. FOV: Fixed at 1.0 radian. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Invalid Bounds: If the scene has no splats or invalid bounds, a default view is returned to prevent crashes. Small Scenes: The max(..., 0.5) and max(..., 1.5) guards prevent the camera from getting too close to small or zero-sized scenes, which could cause numerical instability or clipping issues. Large Scenes: The max(..., 100.0) guard for the far plane ensures that very large scenes do not result in excessively large far planes that could reduce depth buffer precision. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def EstimateSceneView(scene, width, height, frameIndex): # Step 1: Compute Scene Bounds bounds = scene.sceneBounds for splatset in scene.splatSets: bounds = MergeBounds(bounds, splatset.bounds) # Step 2: Validate Bounds and Compute View Parameters if bounds is invalid: # Check if bounds is invalid (e.g., empty or uninitialized) viewcenter = Vector3(0, 0, 2.5) viewradius = 1.0 else: viewcenter = ComputeAabbCenter(bounds) viewradius = max(ComputeAabbRadius(bounds), 0.5) # Step 3: Calculate Camera Distance aspect = width / height distance = max(viewradius 2.5, 1.5) # Step 4: Set Eye Position eye = Vector3(viewcenter.x, viewcenter.y, viewcenter.z - distance) # Step 5: Construct View Matrix upvector = Vector3(0.0, 1.0, 0.0) viewmatrix = LookAt(eye, viewcenter, upvector) # Step 6: Construct Projection Matrix farplane = max(100.0, distance + viewradius 4.0) projmatrix = Perspective(1.0, aspect, 0.01, farplane) # Step 7: Populate Render Input input = RenderInput() input.view = viewmatrix input.proj = projmatrix input.cameraPosition = eye input.viewportWidth = width input.viewportHeight = height input.nearPlane = 0.01 input.farPlane = farplane input.frameIndex = frameIndex input.settings.antialiasing = True input.settings.fastCulling = True return input Hybrid module for estimating and refining per-pixel depth maps from image inputs, resolving scaling/shifting ambiguities and mitigating MVS inaccuracies on sparse views. Combines initial MVS estimation with U-Net refinement using multi-view stereo cues and image features for consistent depth maps. Estimates camera viewpoint (azimuth and elevation) by classifying rendered volume images into discrete regions on a viewing sphere using HEALPix division, evaluating loss via geodesic distance. Provides probabilities for each interval to capture viewpoint ambiguity, unlike regression methods. Predicts viewpoint label via classification, estimates viewpoint residual via regression, and combines them for the final viewpoint. Uses a K-means dictionary size K=24 and geodesic distance importance \alpha=10 for best performance. Modified to be category-specific rather than category-independent. Viewpoint estimation method based on AlexNet that ignores the camera-lit angle and focuses only on azimuth and elevation. Achieves lower classification accuracy than VGGNet (UD+GS) across all tested categories and angle tolerances (2° to 15°). Selects a batch of B views to capture new images, avoiding similar views via a greedy optimization algorithm that is 1/e-approximate in Fisher Information. Initializes selected set S0 = \emptyset and Fisher Information matrix H0 = H[w^|D{train}]. Iteratively selects view i maximizing \text{tr}(H''[y{i,acq}|x{acqi}, w^] H{b-1}^{-1}), adds it to Sb, and updates Hb = H{b-1} + H''[y{i,acq}|x{acqi}, w^]. Time Complexity: Linear with respect to the number of splat sets, O(N), where N is the number of sets in scene.splatSets. The bounding box merge and center/radius computations are constant time per set. Memory Complexity: Constant, O(1), as it only stores temporary bounds and view parameters. Strengths: Simple, fast, and automatic. Ensures the entire scene is visible within the frustum. Limitations: Does not account for camera orientation preferences (always looks from -Z). May not frame aesthetically pleasing views for complex scenes with sparse distributions. When to Use: When an automatic, data-driven camera setup is required for rendering 3D Gaussian Splatting scenes. When Not to Use: When user-controlled camera movement or specific artistic framing is required. This method is implemented in the DirectXSplat project, a DirectX 12 implementation of 3D Gaussian Splatting. It provides a standardized way to initialize the camera for rendering splat sets. pbkx/DirectXSplat, https://github.com/pbkx/DirectXSplat, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial) CNNs Based Viewpoint Estimation for Volume Visualization, https://doi.org/10.1145/3309993, fetched 2026-10-29 FisherRF: Active View Selection and Mapping with Radiance Fields Using Fisher Information, https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-031-72624-824, fetched 2026-10-31

name: Depth Network
head: Depth Network d
body: The Depth Network is a component in sparse-view novel view synthesis systems that refines initial depth estimates to construct accurate 3D point clouds for rendering. It solves the problem of inaccurate depth estimation in sparse input scenarios, where traditional Multi-View Stereo (MVS) fails due to limited overlap and large baselines, and single-image estimation suffers from scaling/shifting ambiguity. It distinguishes itself from sibling methods like Viewpoint Estimation via Sphere Classification and Batch Active View Selection by explicitly regressing geometric depth maps from image features rather than estimating camera poses or selecting views. The Depth Network takes an input image and an initial depth map (derived from MVS or sensor data) and outputs a refined depth map. It employs a hybrid design that cascades a lightweight MVS module with a U-Net refinement network. Inputs and Outputs: Input Image (Ii): The i-th input view. Initial Depth (D{init}): Either MVS-estimated depths or sensor depths (D^{sen}). Output (Di): Refined depth map for building the point cloud. Data Structures: Binary Mask (Mi): A mask indicating valid sensor depth pixels. If sensor depth is not used, this is not applicable. U-Net: The core refinement architecture. It takes the image Ii and initial depth as inputs. Steps: 1. Initial Estimation: Use PatchmatchNet [77] to generate initial depth estimations from the sparse input views. If sensor depth D^{sen} is available, it is used directly as the initial input instead of MVS output. 2. Feature Encoding: The image Ii is processed by a spatial feature encoder (built on BigGAN architecture [3]) to generate per-pixel feature vectors Fi. Each vector is 61-dimensional and concatenated with RGB channels, resulting in 64 dimensions total. 3. Refinement: The U-Net takes the image Ii and the initial depth map (D{init}) as inputs. It refines the depth using multi-view stereo cues and image cues. 4. Output: The U-Net outputs the refined depth Di, which is used to build the point cloud. Formulas: During training, if sensor depth is available, a loss function Ls is used to encourage the U-Net output to match the sensor depth: Ls = \| Mi Di - Mi D^{sen} \| where Mi is the binary mask of valid sensor depths, Di is the network output, and D^{sen} is the sensor depth. Parameters: MVS Module: PatchmatchNet [77] is used for its speed and lightweight nature. Feature Encoder: Based on BigGAN [3], producing 64-dimensional features per pixel. Loss Weight: Not given in the sources. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Sparse Inputs: Applying MVS solely on sparse inputs is challenging due to limited overlap and huge baselines, leading to inaccurate and low-confidence estimations. Ambiguity: Single-image depth estimation suffers from scaling/shifting ambiguity, losing valuable multi-view cues and causing inconsistent estimations across views. Sensor Noise: Sensor depths are often noisy and incomplete; the U-Net acts as a completion and refinement module in this setting. A multi-branch ResNet backbone that predicts intrinsic properties (albedo, normals, depth) and a global lighting feature from a single input image. It distinguishes itself by predicting a global lighting feature vector alongside geometric properties, enabling downstream volumetric lighting prediction. Choose this when inverse rendering of indoor scenes with spatially-varying lighting is required. Definition: Predicts albedo \tilde{A}, surface normals \tilde{N}, depth \tilde{D}, and a global lighting feature \tilde{f}L from a single linearized RGB image I. Formula: \tilde{A}, \tilde{N}, \tilde{D}, \tilde{f}L = h{DP} (I; \Theta{DP}) where h{DP} is the ResNet backbone and \Theta{DP} are the network parameters. Parameters: Input: Single linearized RGB image I \in \mathbb{R}^{3 \times H \times W}. Output: Albedo \tilde{A} \in \mathbb{R}^{3 \times H \times W}, Normals \tilde{N} \in \mathbb{R}^{3 \times H \times W}, Depth \tilde{D} \in \mathbb{R}^{H \times W}, Global Feature \tilde{f}L \in \mathbb{R}^C. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Measured Performance: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Handles sparse input views where traditional MVS fails; refines noisy sensor data; integrates multi-view cues with single-image appearance cues. Limitations: Relies on the quality of the initial MVS estimate or sensor data; single-image estimation alone is ambiguous. When to use: When synthesizing novel views from a sparse set of images and accurate geometry is required for point cloud construction. When not to use: When dense input views are available and standard MVS is sufficient, or when camera pose estimation is the primary goal rather than depth refinement. The Depth Network was introduced in the context of Forward Warping and Depth (FWD) for real-time novel view synthesis. It addresses the limitations of learning 3D geometry end-to-end by relying on rendering and refinement. The method uses PatchmatchNet for initial MVS and a U-Net for refinement, leveraging the BigGAN architecture for feature extraction. The Direct Prediction Module variant was introduced in the context of learning indoor inverse rendering with 3D spatially-varying lighting. name: GPS-Gaussian Network Architecture
head: GPS-Gaussian, Generalizable Pixel-Wise 3D Gaussian Splatting
body: The GPS-Gaussian Network Architecture is a single-image regression method that predicts pixel-wise 3D Gaussian parameter maps (position, rotation, scaling, opacity, and color) to enable real-time novel view synthesis. It distinguishes itself from classic binocular stereo methods by making the image encoder independent from the depth estimator and re-indexing the correlation volume for both lookup procedures, achieving a compact parallelized implementation with over 30% efficiency gain. Inputs and Outputs Input: A single source image I of resolution 1024 \times 1024. Output: Five pixel-wise maps: Position map Mp (3 channels) Rotation map Mr (4 channels, quaternion) Scaling map Ms (3 channels) Opacity map M\alpha (1 channel) Color map Mc (3 channels) Data Structures Correlation Volume C: A 3D tensor used for depth estimation. It is re-indexed to support both reference and target view lookups in a single parallelized pass. Feature Maps: Intermediate representations fS (source image features) and f'S (features from other views, if applicable, though the primary architecture described is single-image generalizable). Gaussian Feature \Gamma: The decoded pixel-wise feature vector before final parameter prediction. Algorithm Steps 1. Image Encoding: The input image I is processed by an image encoder to produce image features fS. This encoder is designed to be independent from the depth estimator. 2. Depth Estimation: A depth estimator processes the features to predict a coarse depth map. The correlation volume C is re-indexed to allow efficient lookup for both reference and target view operations. A refinement module iteratively refines the depth map. This module runs for T = 3 iterations, chosen as a trade-off between performance and computational cost. The output is a predicted depth map D. Note that depth prediction operates on a lower resolution and is upsampled to the full image resolution (1024 \times 1024). 3. Depth Encoding: The predicted depth map D is passed through a depth encoder E{depth}. This encoder has an identical architecture to the image encoder. 4. Feature Aggregation: Image features (from Step 1) and depth features (from Step 3) are aggregated into a U-Net-like Gaussian parameter decoder D{parm} via skip connections. 5. Parameter Prediction: The decoder outputs a pixel-wise Gaussian feature \Gamma. Three specific prediction heads process \Gamma to produce: Rotation map Mr Scaling map Ms Opacity map M\alpha The position map Mp is computed directly from the predicted depth map D and the camera intrinsics (implied by the projection of depth to 3D position). The color map Mc is directly borrowed from the RGB values of the input image I. Pseudocode Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def gpsgaussiannetwork(sourceimage: Tensor) -> Dict[str, Tensor]: """ Predicts 3D Gaussian parameters from a single source image. Args: sourceimage: RGB image tensor of shape (3, 1024, 1024). Returns: Dictionary containing maps Mp, Mr, Ms, Malpha, Mc. """ # 1. Image Encoding # Encoder is independent from depth estimator imagefeatures = imageencoder(sourceimage) # 2. Depth Estimation # Re-index correlation volume C for parallelized lookup # Refinement runs for T=3 iterations depthmap = depthestimator(imagefeatures, T=3) # 3. Depth Encoding # Edepth has identical architecture to imageencoder depthfeatures = depthencoder(depthmap) # 4. Feature Aggregation # Concatenate image and depth features, pass through U-Net decoder gaussianfeature = gaussianparameterdecoder(imagefeatures, depthfeatures) # 5. Parameter Prediction # Predict rotation, scaling, and opacity from Gaussian feature rotationmap = rotationhead(gaussianfeature) scalingmap = scalinghead(gaussianfeature) opacitymap = opacityhead(gaussianfeature) # Position is derived directly from depth # Assumes camera intrinsics K are available or fixed for the generalizable model positionmap = depthtoposition(depthmap) # Color is borrowed directly from input colormap = sourceimage return { "Mp": positionmap, "Mr": rotationmap, "Ms": scalingmap, "Malpha": opacitymap, "Mc": colormap } Parameters T = 3: Number of refinement iterations in the depth estimator. Input Resolution: 1024 \times 1024 pixels. Edge Cases and Pitfalls Upsampling Artifacts: Depth prediction operates on low resolution and is upsampled to full resolution. This causes drastically changed depth in margin areas (e.g., crossed limbs, legs), leading to ambiguous predictions and rendering noise. Ambiguous Depth Handling: The network handles ambiguous depth predictions at margins by jointly regressing extremely low opacity values for outlier Gaussian points. This makes the outliers invisible in novel view rendering. Generalization: The model is trained on uniformly placed 8-camera setups but generalizes to random camera setups with pitch in [-20^\circ, +20^\circ] and yaw in [-25^\circ, +25^\circ]. Performance may degrade outside these ranges or with significantly different camera distributions, requiring re-training with synthetic data covering those setups. Time Complexity: The method is designed for real-time performance. The source view processing takes 14 ms, and each novel view takes 5 ms on an RTX 3090 GPU. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Performance: On an RTX 3090 GPU, the total run-time for source view processing and one novel view is 27 ms. The re-indexing of the correlation volume and independent encoder design provide an efficiency increase exceeding 30% compared to classic binocular stereo methods that do not share these optimizations. Strengths: Real-time novel view synthesis from a single image; robust handling of ambiguous depth via learned opacity; efficient parallelized implementation. Limitations: Depth upsampling artifacts in complex geometries (margins); generalization limited to specific camera angle ranges unless re-trained; relies on accurate single-image depth estimation. When to use: Real-time novel view synthesis for human subjects or dynamic scenes where multiple views are not available or latency is critical. When not to use: When high-precision geometry is required in complex margin areas without opacity masking; when camera poses are outside the trained distribution [-20^\circ, +20^\circ] pitch and [-25^\circ, +25^\circ] yaw without re-training. The GPS-Gaussian architecture was introduced in the paper "GPS-Gaussian: Generalizable Pixel-Wise 3D Gaussian Splatting for Real-Time Human Novel View Synthesis". It builds upon the Depth Network module, which estimates depth from a single image using a hybrid design to resolve scaling/shifting ambiguity and inconsistent estimations across views [Parent]. The method was tested with randomly placed camera setups to demonstrate generalization capabilities. name: Viewpoint Estimation via Sphere Classification
head: Geodesic loss viewpoint estimation, HEALPix-based viewpoint classification
body: This method estimates the camera viewpoint (azimuth and elevation) of a rendered volume image by classifying the image into discrete regions on a viewing sphere, rather than regressing continuous angles. It differs from previous classification methods that divide azimuth and elevation domains independently by dividing the sphere uniformly using HEALPix, allowing loss evaluation via geodesic distance. It differs from regression methods, which fail to capture viewpoint ambiguity (e.g., similar rendered images for nearby viewpoints), by providing probabilities for each interval. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A rendered volume image. Output: A predicted viewpoint label corresponding to one of N discrete regions on the viewing sphere, or a probability distribution over these regions. Data Structures: Viewpoint Label: An integer index k \in \{0, \dots, N-1\} corresponding to a specific HEALPix region. HEALPix Regions: The viewing sphere is discretized into N uniform regions using Hierarchical Equal Area isoLatitude Pixelization (HEALPix). Each region serves as a class label. Viewpoint Parameterization: A viewpoint is parameterized as a tuple (\theta, \phi), where \theta is the azimuth (longitude) angle and \phi is the elevation (latitude) angle. The viewing sphere is centered at the volume center. Algorithm Steps: 1. Dataset Generation (Training Phase): Select a category of volumes (e.g., head, engine). For each volume in the category, generate a large number of rendered images with viewpoint annotations. Viewpoint Sampling: Sample viewpoints uniformly on the viewing sphere using HEALPix. These sampled viewpoints serve as the ground-truth labels for the generated images. Rendering Parameter Variation: For each viewpoint label, render images with varying parameters to ensure robustness: Camera-Tilt: Randomly rotate the camera-tilt angle for each image to handle CNN's lack of rotation invariance. Projection Type: Randomly select between parallel and perspective projection for each image. Background Color: Randomly choose black or white for each image to account for alpha blending effects. Scale: Uniformly sample scale from 1 to 1.8 for rendering volumes to reduce scale influence. Lighting Mode: Mode 1: Environment light only. Mode 2: Environment light + one headlight at camera position; headlight intensity sampled uniformly from 0.7 to 1. Mode 3: Environment light + headlight + scene light; scene light position sampled on a sphere with radius 3-5x the viewing sphere radius; headlight and scene light intensities sampled uniformly from 0.35 to 0.5. Phong Coefficients: Ambient reflection fixed at 1; Diffuse sampled uniformly from 0.25 to 0.75; Specular sampled uniformly from 0.5 to 1; Shininess sampled uniformly from 20 to 100. Transfer Functions: Opacity: Manually designed to highlight specific features (e.g., skin, skull, tooth) rather than randomly generated, to avoid missing important features. Add a small random disturbance: for each feature, move the keypoint of the 1D transfer function left or right by distance d \sim N(0, 1). Color: Randomly sample color for each feature for each image, biased towards high contrast with the background. Train a category-specific CNN on this dataset. 2. Inference (Testing Phase): Input a new rendered volume image into the trained CNN. The CNN outputs a classification result, identifying the HEALPix region (viewpoint label) most likely to have generated the image. The predicted viewpoint is the center (or representative point) of the predicted HEALPix region. Loss Function: The loss is computed using the geodesic distance between the predicted viewpoint label and the ground-truth viewpoint label. Let y be the ground-truth label and \hat{y} be the predicted label (or probability distribution). The loss L is based on the geodesic distance dG(y, \hat{y}) on the sphere. Note: A variant, the Geometric Structure-Aware Loss Function, modifies the Softmax loss by incorporating geometric constraints between neighbor viewpoints to exploit continuity on the viewing sphere [Child: Geometric Structure-Aware Loss Function]. Pitfalls and Edge Cases: Keypoint-based methods are unsuitable: They require known camera intrinsic parameters to solve perspective-n-point, whereas this method estimates viewpoints with unknown/different intrinsic parameters (parallel vs perspective). Random Opacity Transfer Functions: Randomly generated opacity functions may miss important features completely, reducing performance. Therefore, opacity functions are manually designed with slight random disturbances. Azimuth/Elevation Non-Uniformity: Previous methods dividing azimuth and elevation independently fail because these are not uniform units of measure and cannot directly evaluate distance. HEALPix solves this by providing uniform regions. A loss function for viewpoint estimation that modifies the Softmax loss by incorporating geometric constraints between neighbor viewpoints to exploit continuity on the viewing sphere. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Measured Performance: Experiments show that classification performance is better than regression performance for viewpoint estimation. Strengths: Captures viewpoint ambiguity by providing probabilities for each interval, unlike regression which returns only predicted parameters. Handles different intrinsic parameters (parallel vs perspective projection). Uses geodesic distance for loss, which correctly evaluates distance on the sphere, unlike independent azimuth/elevation classification. Limitations: Requires a large number of viewpoint-annotated images to avoid overfitting deep CNNs. Requires generating a training dataset via "Render for CNN" approach since no public training dataset exists for this specific problem. Performance may depend on the specific category of volumes (e.g., head vs engine). When to use: When estimating viewpoint for volume visualization where camera intrinsics are unknown or variable, and when capturing viewpoint ambiguity is important. When not to use: When keypoints are available and camera intrinsics are known (keypoint-based methods may be more suitable). Origin: The method was introduced in "CNNs Based Viewpoint Estimation for Volume Visualization". History: It uses HEALPix [7] for sphere pixelization and references the 'Render for CNN' [35] approach for dataset generation. It addresses limitations of previous classification methods that divided azimuth and elevation independently and regression methods that failed to capture ambiguity. Usage: Used for viewpoint estimation of rendered volume images in volume visualization contexts. CNNs Based Viewpoint Estimation for Volume Visualization, https://doi.org/10.1145/3309993, fetched 2026-10-29

name: Geometric Structure-Aware Loss Function
head: GS Loss
body: The Geometric Structure-Aware Loss Function (GS Loss) is a classification loss designed for viewpoint estimation in volume rendering that modifies the standard Softmax loss by incorporating geometric constraints between neighboring viewpoints on the viewing sphere. Unlike standard Softmax, which treats all incorrect classes as equally wrong, GS Loss assigns non-zero weights to neighbor viewpoints based on their geodesic distance from the ground truth, explicitly exploiting the continuity and correlation inherent in spherical camera parameterizations. Inputs and Outputs Input: A rendered volume image s and its ground-truth viewpoint label vs from a discrete set of viewpoints V (typically arranged via HEALPix). Output: A scalar loss value L{vp}(\{s\}) used to update the neural network weights. Data Structures Viewpoint Set (V): A discrete set of viewpoints covering the viewing sphere. The specific topology depends on the discretization method (e.g., HEALPix), which defines neighbor relationships. Neighbor Viewpoint Set (V(vs, n)): A subset of V containing viewpoints within a relative distance bandwidth n of the ground-truth viewpoint vs. For n=1, this includes vs and its first-order neighbors. Ground-Truth Distribution (q): A vector of weights over the viewpoint set V, where q(v) is the target probability weight for viewpoint v. Parameters Bandwidth Parameter (n): Determines the size of the neighbor set V(vs, n). Typical Value: n=1. Effect: Includes the ground-truth viewpoint and its first-order neighbors. n=0 includes only the ground truth. Geodesic Distance (d): The distance metric between two viewpoints on the sphere, d: V \times V \to \mathbb{R}. Algorithm The loss is computed in three steps: 1. Determine Neighbor Set: Identify the set of viewpoints V(vs, n) surrounding the ground-truth viewpoint vs based on the bandwidth parameter n. 2. Compute Ground-Truth Distribution Weights: Calculate the weight q(v) for each viewpoint v \in V(vs, n) using the exponential decay of the geodesic distance: q(v) = e^{-d(v, vs)} For viewpoints outside the neighbor set, q(v) = 0. 3. Compute Loss: Calculate the weighted cross-entropy loss using the predicted probabilities Pv(s) and the weights q(v): L{vp}(\{s\}) = - \sum{v \in V(vs, n)} \sum{\{s\}} q(v) \log Pv(s) Where Pv(s) is the probability that image s is classified as viewpoint v. Pseudocode Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def geometricstructureawareloss(predictedprobabilities, groundtruthviewpoint, neighborviewpoints, bandwidthn): """ Computes the Geometric Structure-Aware Loss. Args: predictedprobabilities: dict or array mapping viewpoint labels to probabilities Pv(s). groundtruthviewpoint: The label of the ground-truth viewpoint vs. neighborviewpoints: A list/set of viewpoint labels in V(vs, n). bandwidthn: The relative distance bandwidth parameter (e.g., 1). Returns: loss: Scalar loss value. """ loss = 0.0 # Step 1 & 2: Iterate over the neighbor set and compute weights for v in neighborviewpoints: # Calculate geodesic distance d(v, vs) # Note: The exact implementation of geodesic distance depends on the # spherical coordinate system or HEALPix indexing used. distance = computegeodesicdistance(v, groundtruthviewpoint) # Calculate weight q(v) = exp(-d) weight = math.exp(-distance) # Get predicted probability Pv(s) prob = predictedprobabilities[v] # Add to loss: -q(v) log(Pv(s)) # Guard against log(0) if prob > 0: loss -= weight math.log(prob) else: # Handle numerical stability: if prob is 0, loss is infinite. # In practice, a small epsilon is added to probabilities during training. loss -= weight math.log(epsilon) return loss def computegeodesicdistance(viewpointa, viewpointb): """ Computes the geodesic distance between two viewpoints. Implementation depends on the specific sphere discretization (e.g., HEALPix). For HEALPix, this may involve converting pixel indices to 3D vectors and computing the angle, or using precomputed neighbor distance tables. """ # Placeholder for specific distance metric implementation. # The source states d is geodesic distance but does not provide # the closed-form formula for the specific HEALPix resolution used. pass Edge Cases and Pitfalls Zero Probability: If Pv(s) = 0 for any v with q(v) > 0, the log term becomes undefined. Standard practice is to add a small epsilon to probabilities or clamp log inputs. Neighbor Definition: The definition of "neighbor" is strictly tied to the sphere discretization (HEALPix). Incorrect neighbor identification breaks the geometric constraint. Bandwidth Selection: The choice of n affects the smoothness of the loss landscape. n=1 is used in experiments to balance local continuity with computational cost. Complexity: The complexity is proportional to the size of the neighbor set |V(vs, n)|. For n=1, this is a small constant (e.g., 7 nodes for HEALPix level 1, though exact count depends on resolution), making it O(1) relative to the total number of viewpoints |V|. Performance: In experiments on volume visualization datasets (engine, fish, head, tooth, tree, vessel), GS Loss with n=1 improved prediction accuracy compared to standard Softmax loss. Strengths: Explicitly models the continuity of the viewing sphere, preventing the model from treating distant viewpoints as equally "wrong" as immediate neighbors. Limitations: Requires a discretization scheme that provides neighbor relationships (e.g., HEALPix). Not directly applicable to continuous regression without discretization. The Geometric Structure-Aware Loss Function was introduced in the context of CNN-based viewpoint estimation for volume visualization. It addresses the limitation of standard classification losses that ignore the geometric structure of the viewing sphere. The method leverages the fact that neighboring viewpoints share significant geometric information, which is particularly important for volume rendering where small viewpoint changes can result in similar visual features. The approach was evaluated on six volume categories extracted from public databases (VolVis, The Volume Library). name: Batch Active View Selection
head: Greedy Batch Selection
body: Batch Active View Selection selects a batch of B camera views to capture new images for volume reconstruction, specifically avoiding the selection of highly similar views by using a greedy optimization algorithm based on Fisher Information. It differs from single-view selection methods by planning a trajectory for an agent to acquire multiple training views simultaneously, addressing the combinatorial explosion of directly maximizing expected information gain across a batch. Unlike sibling methods like Depth Network or Viewpoint Estimation via Sphere Classification which may rely on learned heuristics or geometric classification, this method relies on the statistical properties of the current model's uncertainty. The method uses a greedy approximation to maximize the trace of the product of the new view's Hessian and the inverse of the accumulated Fisher Information matrix, providing a 1/e-approximation of the optimal solution. Inputs: D{pool}: The pool of candidate acquisition views. H''[w^ | D{train}]: The Fisher Information matrix (Hessian) computed from the initial training dataset D{train} at the current optimal weights w^. B: The number of views to select in the batch. Outputs: SB: The set of B selected views. Data Structures: Sb: A set containing the indices of views selected in steps 0 to b. Hb: The accumulated Fisher Information matrix after step b. Algorithm Steps: 1. Initialize the selected set S0 to the empty set \emptyset. 2. Initialize the accumulated Fisher Information matrix H0 to the Hessian of the training data: H0 \leftarrow H''[w^ | D{train}]. 3. For each batch step b from 1 to B: a. Identify the candidate view i from the remaining pool D{pool} \setminus S{b-1} that maximizes the trace of the product of its Hessian and the inverse of the current accumulated matrix: i \leftarrow \arg \max{x{acq} \in D{pool} \setminus S{b-1}} \text{tr} \left( H''[y{i{acq}} | x{acqi}, w^] H{b-1}^{-1} \right) where H''[y{i{acq}} | x{acqi}, w^] is the Hessian (Fisher Information contribution) of the candidate view i. b. Add the selected view i to the set: Sb \leftarrow S{b-1} \cup \{i\}. c. Update the accumulated Fisher Information matrix by adding the selected view's Hessian: Hb \leftarrow H{b-1} + H''[y{i{acq}} | x{acqi}, w^]. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def batchactiveviewselection(Dpool, Htrain, B): """ Selects B views from Dpool using greedy Fisher Information maximization. Args: Dpool: List of candidate view indices. Htrain: Initial Fisher Information matrix (Hessian) from training data. B: Number of views to select. Returns: SB: List of selected view indices. """ S = [] # Selected views H = Htrain.copy() # Accumulated Fisher Information matrix for b in range(1, B + 1): bestview = None maxtrace = -float('inf') # Iterate over remaining candidates for viewidx in Dpool: if viewidx in S: continue # Compute Hessian for this candidate view at current weights w # Note: w is assumed to be fixed or updated externally; # here we assume H'' is pre-computed or accessible via viewidx. Hview = gethessianforview(viewidx) # Compute trace(Hview H^{-1}) # Inverse of H must be computed. For efficiency, # one might maintain H^{-1} directly, but the formula uses H^{-1}. Hinv = inverse(H) traceval = trace(matrixmultiply(Hview, Hinv)) if traceval > maxtrace: maxtrace = traceval bestview = viewidx # Add best view to selection S.append(bestview) # Update accumulated Fisher Information Hviewbest = gethessianforview(bestview) H = matrixadd(H, Hviewbest) return S Parameters: B: Batch size. When B=1, the algorithm is equivalent to single-view active selection. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Matrix Inversion: Computing H{b-1}^{-1} at every step can be computationally expensive. In practice, maintaining the inverse explicitly or using Cholesky decomposition updates is recommended for stability and speed. Degenerate Input: If the pool D{pool} becomes empty before B views are selected, the algorithm terminates early. Precision: The trace operation sums eigenvalues; numerical instability may occur if H{b-1} is ill-conditioned. A greedy scheme to select a set of views that show information not captured in the best view, avoiding similar information under different directions. It selects the best view B0 first, then measures distances from B0 to remaining views, selecting B1 as the one at the highest distance. For subsequent views, it computes distances from remaining views against all previously selected views and chooses the view X that maximizes the geometric average of the distances to the selected views. This approach is preferred over global maximization because global maximization has a quadratic cost in the number of views, while this approach yields similar results with lower cost. Usually, three or four representative views are enough for most models. Time Complexity: The greedy selection requires B iterations. In each iteration, it evaluates all remaining candidates. If N is the number of candidates, the complexity is roughly O(B \cdot N \cdot C), where C is the cost of computing the trace and matrix inverse. The matrix inverse is O(M^3) where M is the dimension of the parameter space. Memory Complexity: Requires storing the Fisher Information matrix H (O(M^2)) and the pool of candidates. Strengths: Provides a 1/e-approximation guarantee for the Fisher Information objective. It is more related to real-world scenarios where an agent plans a trajectory to acquire more training views. Limitations: Greedy optimization may get stuck in local optima compared to global search, though the approximation bound mitigates this. The cost of matrix operations can be high for large parameter spaces. When to use: When batch acquisition is required and the computational cost of global optimization is prohibitive. When not to use: When single-view selection is sufficient (B=1) or when the parameter space is too large for efficient matrix inversion. The method was introduced in the context of active mapping with 3D Gaussian Splatting and Radiance Fields, specifically in the paper "FisherRF: Active View Selection and Mapping with Radiance Fields Using Fisher Information". It addresses the problem of selecting informative views for reconstruction by leveraging Fisher Information to quantify the information gain of potential new views. The approach is designed to avoid the combinatorial explosion of directly maximizing expected information gain between training and acquisition samples. name: Greedy Representative View Selection
head: Greedy view selection, Representative view selection
body: Greedy Representative View Selection is a method for selecting a small, diverse subset of camera views to represent a 3D scene, ensuring that selected views capture information not present in previously chosen ones. It solves the problem of redundant view selection by maximizing geometric diversity among a candidate set. It differs from global maximization approaches by offering a linear-time approximation that yields similar results with significantly lower computational cost. The method selects a set of M representative views from a candidate pool using a greedy strategy based on view similarity distances. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A set of candidate views V{cand}, a similarity metric d(X, Y) between two views, and the desired number of representative views M. Output: A subset R = \{B0, B1, \dots, B{M-1}\} \subset V{cand}. Data Structures: V{cand}: List of candidate view indices or identifiers. R: List of selected view indices. D{rem}: List of remaining candidate views not yet selected. Similarity Metric: The distance d(X, Y) between two views X and Y is typically computed using the Normalized Compression Distance (NCD). NCD is chosen because it is robust to image transformations such as rotation and translation, which simple metrics like Mean Squared Error (MSE) are sensitive to. Algorithm Steps: 1. Initialization: Select the first representative view B0 using an adaptive algorithm or by choosing the view with the highest information content from V{cand}. 2. First Selection: Compute the distance d(B0, v) for all v \in V{cand} \setminus \{B0\}. Select B1 as the view with the maximum distance from B0. 3. Iterative Selection: For k = 2 to M-1: a. For each remaining candidate view v \in V{cand} \setminus R, compute the geometric average of its distances to all currently selected views B0, \dots, B{k-1}: G(v) = \left( \prod{j=0}^{k-1} d(v, Bj) \right)^{\frac{1}{k}} b. Select Bk as the view v that maximizes G(v). c. Add Bk to R. Parameters: M: Number of representative views. Typically, 3 or 4 views are sufficient for most models. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def greedyrepresentativeviews(candidates, similarityfunc, m): """ Select m representative views from candidates using greedy geometric average distance. Args: candidates: List of view identifiers. similarityfunc: Function d(X, Y) returning distance between two views. m: Number of representative views to select. Returns: List of selected view identifiers. """ if not candidates: return [] # Step 1: Select B0 using an adaptive algorithm or heuristic. # Note: The specific adaptive algorithm for B0 is not detailed in the source. # Assuming B0 is selected as the first candidate or via a separate metric. # Here we assume a placeholder selection for B0. In practice, this might be # the view with highest entropy or a predefined "best" view. b0 = candidates[0] # Placeholder for adaptive selection logic selected = [b0] remaining = [v for v in candidates if v != b0] if m == 1: return selected # Step 2: Select B1 as the view furthest from B0 maxdist = -1 b1 = None for v in remaining: dist = similarityfunc(b0, v) if dist > maxdist: maxdist = dist b1 = v selected.append(b1) remaining = [v for v in remaining if v != b1] if m == 2: return selected # Step 3: Iteratively select remaining views for k in range(2, m): bestview = None maxgeoavg = -1 for v in remaining: # Compute geometric average of distances to all selected views product = 1.0 for b in selected: product = similarityfunc(v, b) # Geometric average geoavg = product (1.0 / len(selected)) if geoavg > maxgeoavg: maxgeoavg = geoavg bestview = v selected.append(bestview) remaining = [v for v in remaining if v != bestview] return selected Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision: The geometric average can suffer from underflow if distances are small. Log-space computation (\frac{1}{k} \sum \log d(v, Bj)) is recommended for numerical stability. Boundary: If M > |V{cand}|, the algorithm cannot proceed. The sources do not specify handling for this case. Degenerate Input: If multiple views have identical distances to selected views, the selection is arbitrary. The sources do not specify a tie-breaking rule. A supervision strategy for 3D Gaussian Splatting that favors target cameras with optical axes significantly different from input cameras to constrain Gaussian scales and orientations. It prunes Gaussians with opacity below \tau\alpha from the voxel-based scene G{vox} to yield G^0. Candidate target views v are scored by their angular separation from the nearest input direction i \in C: a(v, C) = \min{i \in C} \arccos(fv^\top fi), where fv = Rv^\star (0, 0, 1)^\top is the unit optical axis in the common reference frame. The target set T is sampled with a bias toward larger scores a(v, C). Supervision is applied to renderings from input views and T, using GT-depth warp masks to restrict loss to valid regions. Opacity pruning threshold \tau\alpha values tested include 0.01, 0.02, and 0.05. Time Complexity: Linear with respect to the number of views, as the comparison process is the most costly part, but each step only compares remaining views against the fixed set of selected views. Global maximization has a quadratic cost in the number of views. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Avoids redundant information capture; computationally efficient compared to global optimization; robust to image transformations via NCD. Limitations: Greedy approach may not find the globally optimal set of views; relies on the quality of the similarity metric. When to use: When a small, diverse set of views is needed for volume model representation or initialization, and computational resources are limited. When not to use: When the globally optimal view set is required and computational cost is not a constraint. The method was proposed in the context of generating representative views and paths for volume models, aiming to avoid preprocessing steps like segmentation. It was developed to address the limitations of simple image metrics (like MSE) which are sensitive to rotations and translations, and to improve upon methods like those by Bordoloi and Shen which use Jensen-Shannon divergence but do not exploit dataset symmetry. name: Stereo Rendering
head: Anaglyph Stereo, Red-Blue (Anaglyph) Stereo, Red-cyan stereo, Red-green stereo
body: Stereo rendering generates a pair of images to simulate binocular parallax, where each eye sees a slightly different picture to determine depth. It differs from standard rendering by requiring two distinct camera viewpoints separated by an inter-ocular distance. Unlike Depth of Field and Lens Effects which simulates focus, stereo rendering simulates disparity. The presentation method determines how these images are combined and viewed. Inputs: Scene geometry, camera parameters (position, orientation, frustum), eye separation distance, and display type (single vs. dual). Outputs: A stereo image pair (either separate buffers, a combined anaglyph, or interlaced frames). The implementation relies on standard camera frustum data structures extended with stereo parameters. Camera Frustum: Defined by origin \mathbf{o}, direction \mathbf{d}, and projection matrix. For single-display systems, the frustum must be sheared to account for the non-perpendicular view plane relative to the combined image. Image Buffers: Standard RGB uses 24 bits per pixel (8 bits per channel). Stereo double buffering requires quad buffering (Left Front, Left Back, Right Front, Right Back). Memory for a 1Kx1K display with 24-bit RGB, 24-bit back buffer color, and 24-bit z-buffer per view is 144 bits per pixel or 18 MB total. 1. Calculate Eye Positions: Determine left and right eye origins based on the center eye position and eye separation distance. 2. Set Camera Configuration: For two-display systems, perform camera azimuths to reach the left and right eye positions. For single-display systems, translate and shear the camera's viewing frustum to handle the non-perpendicular view plane. 3. Generate Images: Render the scene from both eye positions to generate the left and right eye images. 4. Convert to Intensity: Convert the RGB values of both views into grayscale intensities. 5. Combine Channels (Anaglyph): Create the resulting image where red values are taken from left eye image intensities and blue values (mixture of blue and green) are taken from right eye image intensities. 6. Display: Invoke stereo rendering mode on the render window. The anaglyph channel mapping converts intensities IL (left) and IR (right) into output channels: R{out} = IL B{out} = IR G{out} = IR \quad \text{(Red-green variant utilizes eye sensitivity to green)} This discards original hue and saturation. Eye Separation Distance: The distance between the left and right eye positions. Controlling this amount directly controls the generated parallax. Typical values approximate human inter-ocular distance (~6.5 cm) but are often adjusted for virtual scale. Precision: High bits-per-pixel requirements for double-buffered stereo can exhaust video memory (e.g., 144 bits/pixel for 1Kx1K). Screen Coverage: Time-multiplexed techniques require the application to take up the entire screen while rendering. Color Loss: Anaglyph methods discard original hue and saturation. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def setupstereorendering(renderwindow, stereotype="RedBlue"): renderwindow.StereoRenderOn() if stereotype == "RedBlue": renderwindow.SetStereoTypeToRedBlue() # Further rendering will be done in stereo Generates a stereo pair from a pre-existing 2D image stack to simulate binocular parallax and volumetric depth perception using standard web technologies. It is distinguished from full ray-casting volume rendering by relying on image overlay and CSS positioning rather than per-pixel shading, and from single-slice viewers by allowing simultaneous visibility of multiple depth layers. Choose when visualizing scientific volumetric data in a browser without specialized hardware. Stereo Pseudo 3D Rendering via Image Stacks Each eye is updated at the original refresh rate (e.g., 60Hz) with full horizontal resolution but half vertical resolution. Renders the left eye image to the top half of the screen and the right eye image to the bottom half, then enters a special stereo mode on the graphics card to double the monitor's refresh rate (e.g., from 60Hz to 120Hz). Choose when full horizontal resolution is prioritized over vertical resolution and screen takeover is acceptable. Uses TV standards (NTSC/PAL) interlacing, rendering left eye to even lines and right eye to odd lines. Viewed with liquid crystal shutter glasses synchronized to the interlacing rate. Choose for television display compatibility, though it suffers from low resolution and flicker because each eye is updated at half the refresh rate. Displays both left and right images simultaneously on two separate screens (one per eye). Requires two graphics cards or one card with two outputs. Choose when simultaneous full-resolution views are required and hardware cost is not a constraint. Preserves all color information by separating views using polarized light: one eye's image projected through a vertical filter, the other through a horizontal filter. User wears glasses with a vertical filter over one eye and a horizontal filter over the other. Choose when color fidelity is critical and polarized projection hardware is available. Uses separate left and right image buffers, allowing stereo rendering without taking over the entire screen. Requires more memory or lower resolution (e.g., 144 bits per pixel for 1Kx1K with quad buffering). Choose for high-quality interactive applications on supported hardware without full-screen takeover. Displays both views in a single image using repeating dot patterns, where depth is incorporated by changing the interval between patterns. Viewed by focusing in front of or behind the image until two triangular cutouts in the top appear as one. Choose for static, depth-only images requiring no special hardware. Time Complexity: Linear with respect to pixels and scene complexity, multiplied by the number of eyes (typically 2). Memory Complexity: Increases significantly for double-buffered stereo; quad buffering can require up to 144 bits per pixel. Performance: Time multiplexed methods halve vertical resolution per eye. Interlaced methods halve vertical resolution and suffer from flicker. Anaglyph methods have minimal performance overhead but poor color fidelity. Scaling: Resolution scales with display hardware; interlaced and split-screen methods halve vertical resolution per eye, while dual buffer maintains full resolution at the cost of memory. Strengths: Anaglyph is low-cost and works on any display (monitor, paper, or film) with inexpensive glasses. Dual buffer preserves full resolution and color but requires hardware support. Limitations: Anaglyph loses color. Interlaced has low resolution and flicker. Time parallel requires expensive hardware. SIRDS requires user effort to focus and loses texture/color. When to use: Use Anaglyph for low-cost distribution. Use Dual Buffer for high-quality interactive applications with supported hardware. Use SIRDS for static depth-only images. Stereo rendering originated from the need to simulate binocular vision in computer graphics. Foundational concepts of camera azimuths for two-display systems and frustum shearing for single-display systems were detailed in early computer graphics literature, specifically in the context of the Visualization Toolkit (VTK) and general advanced computer graphics textbooks. The term encompasses various methods including anaglyph, interlaced, and polarized techniques, adapted from television and display technologies. Chapter 7 - Advanced Computer Graphics - VTK, https://examples.vtk.org/site/VTKBook/07Chapter7/, fetched 2026-10-29 (book)

name: Stereo Pseudo 3D Rendering via Image Stacks
head: Pseudo Stereo Pair Generation, Web-based Stereo Pseudo 3D
body:
This method generates a stereo pair of images from a pre-existing 2D image stack to simulate binocular parallax and volumetric depth perception using standard web technologies. It solves the problem of visualizing scientific volumetric data (e.g., medical scans) in a browser without specialized hardware or client-side rendering engines. It is distinguished from full ray-casting volume rendering by relying on image overlay and CSS positioning rather than per-pixel shading, and from single-slice viewers like BrainMaps.org by allowing simultaneous visibility of multiple depth layers. Inputs and Outputs Input: A stack of N 2D images (e.g., PNG slices) representing cross-sections of a volume. Output: Two HTML DOM trees (stacks) containing positioned elements that, when viewed with stereo merging techniques (e.g., cross-viewing), produce a 3D effect. Data Structures The implementation relies on the HTML Document Object Model (DOM). Containers: Two
elements with position: absolute CSS styling. One serves as the base stack (imgstacks), the other as the offset stack (imgoffsets). Image Elements: nodes created dynamically. Each has position: absolute, and explicit top, left, width, and height style properties. Preprocessing: Input images must have alpha channels added, with background pixels set to transparent to allow proper overlay blending. Parameters Opacity of interleaving layer (\alpha): Typically 10% (0.1) for the semi-opaque white image. Horizontal offset per slice (\Delta x): Typically 1 pixel relative to the previous slice's position. Image Resolution: Example usage subsampled to 180x180 pixels from 512x512 source. Steps 1. Preprocess Images: Convert input slices to PNG format with transparent backgrounds. Generate a single semi-opaque white image (e.g., 180x180 pixels, 10% opacity) to be reused for distance attenuation. 2. Initialize DOM: Create two absolute-positioned
containers in the HTML structure: one for the base stack and one for the offset stack. 3. Generate Base Stack: Iterate through the image stack from i = 0 to N-1. For each data slice i: Create an element. Set src to the data slice. Set position to absolute. Set top and left to the base coordinates (e.g., 0,0 relative to container). Append to the base stack container. Insert the semi-opaque white image between every pair of data slices to simulate distance attenuation (aerial perspective). 4. Generate Offset Stack: Iterate through the image stack from i = 0 to N-1. For each data slice i: Create an element. Set src to the data slice. Set position to absolute. Calculate horizontal position: xi = x{i-1} + \Delta x. For the first slice, x0 is the base left position. Set left to xi. Keep top identical to the base stack. Append to the offset stack container. Insert the semi-opaque white image between every pair of data slices in the offset stack as well. 5. Display: Load both stacks into the browser. The user views the combined result using stereo merging (e.g., crossing eyes for parallel view or diverging for crossed view). Pseudocode Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def generatestereopseudo3d(imagestack, numslices, offsetperslice=1, opacity=0.1): """ Generates DOM structures for stereo pseudo 3D rendering. imagestack: List of image data/paths. numslices: Number of data slices N. offsetperslice: Horizontal pixel shift per slice depth. opacity: Opacity of the interleaving attenuation layer. """ # 1. Preprocessing assumed done: images are transparent PNGs. # Generate a single semi-opaque white image for attenuation. # In a real implementation, this is a static asset downloaded once. attenuationimage = createsemiopaquewhiteimage(opacity) # 2. Initialize DOM containers basecontainer = createdomelement("div", id="imgstacks", position="absolute") offsetcontainer = createdomelement("div", id="imgoffsets", position="absolute") contentcontainer = createdomelement("div", id="imgcontent", position="absolute") contentcontainer.append(basecontainer) contentcontainer.append(offsetcontainer) # 3. Build Base Stack currenttop = 0 currentleft = 0 for i in range(numslices): # Add data slice imgelem = createdomelement("img") imgelem.src = imagestack[i] imgelem.style.position = "absolute" imgelem.style.top = str(currenttop) + "px" imgelem.style.left = str(currentleft) + "px" basecontainer.append(imgelem) # Add attenuation layer between slices (except after the last one) if i < numslices - 1: attimg = createdomelement("img") attimg.src = attenuationimage.src attimg.style.position = "absolute" attimg.style.top = str(currenttop) + "px" attimg.style.left = str(currentleft) + "px" basecontainer.append(attimg) # 4. Build Offset Stack # The offset stack mirrors the base stack but with horizontal shifts # The shift accumulates or is relative to the previous slice. # Note: The source implies offsetting relative to the previous location. # We need to track the position for the offset stack independently offsettop = 0 offsetleft = 0 for i in range(numslices): # Add data slice with offset imgelem = createdomelement("img") imgelem.src = imagestack[i] imgelem.style.position = "absolute" imgelem.style.top = str(offsettop) + "px" # Apply horizontal offset. # Source says "offsetted by 1 pixel from the previous location". # This implies a cumulative shift or a shear. # If it's a shear, the shift depends on depth (i). # Source: "images on the top of the stack will be shifted the most" # This implies cumulative offset: offset = i offsetperslice currentoffsetx = i offsetperslice imgelem.style.left = str(currentoffsetx) + "px" offsetcontainer.append(imgelem) # Add attenuation layer if i < numslices - 1: attimg = createdomelement("img") attimg.src = attenuationimage.src attimg.style.position = "absolute" attimg.style.top = str(offsettop) + "px" attimg.style.left = str(currentoffsetx) + "px" offsetcontainer.append(attimg) return contentcontainer Edge Cases and Pitfalls Pseudo-Accuracy: Fixed linear offsetting produces "pseudo" accurate stereo pairs, not fully accurate geometric projections. Nonlinear offsetting based on a depth function can improve accuracy but is not implemented in the basic method. Viewpoint Rigidity: The viewpoint is predetermined by the image stack organization. Interactive viewpoint changes (rotation, zoom) are not supported on the fly. Viewer Strain: Stereo merging requires the user to perform cross-viewing or parallel viewing, which can cause eye strain. Optical aids (mirrors/prisms) may be required. Performance Scaling: Memory and load time scale linearly with the number of images. Large stacks (e.g., 500+ images) may require significant bandwidth and memory. Time Complexity: Linear O(N) with respect to the number of images N for loading and DOM construction. Memory Complexity: Linear O(N), as each image is stored in the browser cache and DOM. Measured Performance: On a 1.7 GHz PC with 1GB RAM, displaying 50 overlayed images took approximately 3 seconds after download. Load time and memory usage scaled linearly for 15, 30, and 50 images (95kB–126kB each) on Firefox 2.0 and IE 7.0. Strengths: Requires no specialized software, hardware, or client-side computation; works in standard web browsers with CSS/JS support. Allows viewing multiple stacked images simultaneously to perceive volumetric structures. Limitations: No interactive viewpoint changes; stereo accuracy is approximate; requires user ability to merge stereo images; potential eye strain. When to Use: Web-based display of static scientific volumetric data where interactive 3D rendering is not feasible or necessary. When Not to Use: When interactive viewpoint rotation, high-precision geometric stereo, or real-time animation is required. The method was developed by D. C.-Y. Eng and Y. Choe and presented at the Pacific Graphics 2008 conference. It was applied to visualize 50 slices of mouse spinal cord scans from the KESM (Kavli Institute for the Exploration of the Spinal Cord) dataset, where blood vessels were stained with India ink. The approach contrasts with BrainMaps.org, which displays one slide at a time, and other web-based 3D approaches that require specialized software or hardware. Stereo Pseudo 3D Rendering for Web-based Display of Scientific Volumetric Data, https://doi.org/10.2312/vg/vg-pbg08/073-080, fetched 2026-10-26

name: Camera Model with Radial/Tangential Distortion
head: nerfies Camera
body: This camera model defines the geometric relationship between 2D pixel coordinates and 3D world rays, incorporating standard pinhole camera intrinsics (focal length, principal point, skew, aspect ratio) and lens distortion (radial and tangential). It is used to convert between pixel coordinates and 3D world rays or points. It distinguishes itself from simple pinhole models by including an iterative undistortion step to recover ideal normalized coordinates from distorted pixel measurements. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: Pixel coordinates with shape [..., 2] and camera parameters (intrinsics and extrinsics). Outputs: Normalized ray directions in world coordinates with shape [..., 3]. Data Structures: The Camera object stores the following fields: orientation: 3 \times 3 matrix (world-to-camera rotation). position: 3-vector (camera center in world coordinates). focallength: float. principalpoint: 2-vector [u0, v0]. skew: float. pixelaspectratio: float. radialdistortion: 3-vector [k1, k2, k3]. tangentialdistortion: 2-vector [p1, p2]. imagesize: 2-vector [width, height] (uint32). dtype: data type (e.g., float32). Formulas: 1. Pixel to Local Undistorted Coordinates: The mapping from ideal normalized coordinates (x, y) to distorted pixel coordinates (u, v) is: u = f \cdot x + s \cdot y + u0 v = f \cdot \text{aspect} \cdot y + v0 Where f is focal length, s is skew, and \text{aspect} is pixel aspect ratio. 2. Radial Distortion Factor: r^2 = x^2 + y^2 d(r) = 1 + r^2 (k1 + r^2 (k2 + k3 r^2)) 3. Tangential and Radial Distortion Application: The distorted coordinates (xd, yd) are related to ideal coordinates (x, y) by: xd = x \cdot d(r) + 2 p1 x y + p2 (r^2 + 2 x^2) yd = y \cdot d(r) + 2 p2 x y + p1 (r^2 + 2 y^2) 4. World Ray Direction: \mathbf{d}{\text{world}} = \text{Orientation}^\top \mathbf{d}{\text{local}} Algorithm Steps: 1. Validation: Ensure pixel coordinates have a last dimension of 2 and match the camera's dtype. 2. Reshape: Flatten pixel coordinates to (-1, 2) for batch processing. 3. Normalize to Principal Point: Calculate intermediate y and x values: y = \frac{v - v0}{f \cdot \text{aspect}} x = \frac{u - u0 - s \cdot y}{f} 4. Undistortion: If radial or tangential distortion parameters are non-zero, apply radialandtangentialundistort to (x, y) using Newton's method to solve for ideal (x, y) given distorted (xd, yd). 5. Local Ray Direction: Stack [x, y, 1] and normalize by L2 norm. 6. World Transformation: Multiply local directions by the transpose of the orientation matrix. 7. Final Normalization: Normalize the resulting world directions by L2 norm. 8. Reshape: Restore the original batch shape plus (3,). Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import numpy as np def computeresidualandjacobian(x, y, xd, yd, k1, k2, k3, p1, p2): """Computes residuals and Jacobian for undistortion.""" r = x x + y y d = 1.0 + r (k1 + r (k2 + k3 r)) # Distorted projection equations fx = d x + 2 p1 x y + p2 (r + 2 x x) - xd fy = d y + 2 p2 x y + p1 (r + 2 y y) - yd # Derivatives of d dr = k1 + r (2.0 k2 + 3.0 k3 r) dx = 2.0 x dr dy = 2.0 y dr # Jacobian entries fxx = d + dx x + 2 p1 y + 6 p2 x fxy = dx y + 2 p1 x + 2 p2 y fyx = dx y + 2 p2 y + 2 p1 x fyy = d + dy y + 2 p2 x + 6 p1 y return fx, fy, fxx, fxy, fyx, fyy def radialandtangentialundistort(xd, yd, k1=0.0, k2=0.0, k3=0.0, p1=0.0, p2=0.0, eps=1e-9, maxiterations=10): """Undistorts pixel coordinates using Newton's method.""" x = xd.copy() y = yd.copy() for in range(maxiterations): fx, fy, fxx, fxy, fyx, fyy = computeresidualandjacobian( x, y, xd, yd, k1, k2, k3, p1, p2) denominator = fyx fxy - fxx fyy xnumerator = fx fyy - fy fxy ynumerator = fy fxx - fx fyx # Avoid division by zero stepx = np.where(np.abs(denominator) > eps, xnumerator / denominator, 0.0) stepy = np.where(np.abs(denominator) > eps, ynumerator / denominator, 0.0) x = x + stepx y = y + stepy return x, y def pixelstorays(pixels, camera): """ Convert pixel coordinates to world-space ray directions. Args: pixels: np.ndarray of shape (..., 2) camera: Camera object with attributes orientation, position, focallength, principalpoint, skew, pixelaspectratio, radialdistortion, tangentialdistortion. Returns: np.ndarray of shape (..., 3) containing normalized ray directions. """ # 1. Validation if pixels.shape[-1] != 2: raise ValueError("Pixels must have shape (..., 2)") pixels = pixels.astype(camera.dtype) # 2. Reshape originalshape = pixels.shape pixelsflat = pixels.reshape(-1, 2) # 3. Normalize to principal point u = pixelsflat[:, 0] v = pixelsflat[:, 1] scalefactorx = camera.focallength scalefactory = camera.focallength camera.pixelaspectratio u0, v0 = camera.principalpoint s = camera.skew y = (v - v0) / scalefactory x = (u - u0 - s y) / scalefactorx # 4. Undistortion if np.any(camera.radialdistortion) or np.any(camera.tangentialdistortion): k1, k2, k3 = camera.radialdistortion p1, p2 = camera.tangentialdistortion x, y = radialandtangentialundistort(x, y, k1, k2, k3, p1, p2) # 5. Local Ray Direction dirs = np.stack([x, y, np.oneslike(x)], axis=-1) dirs = dirs / np.linalg.norm(dirs, axis=-1, keepdims=True) # 6. World Transformation raysdir = np.matmul(camera.orientation.T, dirs[..., np.newaxis]).squeeze(-1) # 7. Final Normalization raysdir = raysdir / np.linalg.norm(raysdir, axis=-1, keepdims=True) # 8. Reshape return raysdir.reshape(originalshape[:-1] + (3,)) Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Zero Denominator: In undistortion, if the Jacobian determinant is near zero, the step is clamped to zero to prevent NaNs. Degenerate Look-At: If the look-at vector and up vector are parallel, the right vector calculation fails (norm < eps). Cropping: If cropping the camera domain results in non-positive resolution, an error is raised. A parameterization variant where pixel-valued parameters (focal length, principal point) are scaled by the initial camera focal length f. This encodes camera residual parameters as world coordinates, making additive biases invariant to the absolute scale of the scene. For example, a residual \Delta u0 is applied as u0' = u0 + f \Delta u0. Not given in the sources. The camera model is implemented in the Nerfies library by Google. It is based on standard computer vision camera models with radial and tangential distortion. The Pixel Scale variant is described in the CamP paper for camera preconditioning in neural radiance fields. google/nerfies, https://github.com/google/nerfies, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial) CamP: Camera Preconditioning for Neural Radiance Fields, https://doi.org/10.1145/3618321, fetched 2026-10-30

name: Camera Ray Projection
head: Inverse Projection with Distortion, Pixel to Ray Conversion with Distortion
body: Camera Ray Projection converts 2D pixel coordinates into 3D world-space rays by applying inverse intrinsic mapping, radial/tangential distortion correction, and extrinsic transformation. It solves the inverse camera distortion equations to map distorted normalized coordinates to undistorted ones using Newton-Raphson iteration, then constructs normalized ray directions. It differs from its sibling Camera Model with Radial/Tangential Distortion by explicitly handling the iterative inversion of the distortion model and providing the final world-space ray geometry (origins, directions, and optional radii) required for volume rendering sampling. Inputs: Pixel coordinates: P = (u, v), shape (H, W) or batched. Intrinsics: Focal length fx, fy, principal point (cx, cy), skew s, pixel aspect ratio r. Distortion parameters: Radial k1, k2, k3 (and optionally k4), Tangential p1, p2. Extrinsics: Camera orientation matrix R \in \mathbb{R}^{3 \times 3} and position T \in \mathbb{R}^3 (or camera-to-world matrix C2W). Optional: Camera type (Perspective/Fisheye), NDC inverse intrinsic matrix. Outputs: Rays dataclass containing: origins: Camera positions in world space, shape (..., 3). directions: Unnormalized ray directions in world space, shape (..., 3). viewdirs: Normalized ray directions, shape (..., 3). radii: Optional cone radii for mip-NeRF, shape (..., 1). imageplane: Original pixel coordinates, shape (..., 2). Data Structures: Distortion coefficients are stored as floats. Default values are 0.0 for all ki, pi. Camera orientation is a 3 \times 3 orthonormal matrix. Pixel coordinates are typically integer indices; half-pixel offset is applied to target pixel centers. Steps: 1. Pixel to Normalized Coordinates: Compute pixel centers by adding 0.5 to integer indices. Convert to normalized image plane coordinates (x{raw}, y{raw}) using intrinsics: x{raw} = \frac{u - cx - s \cdot y{raw}}{fx} \quad \text{(Note: } y{raw} \text{ is computed first)} y{raw} = \frac{v - cy}{fy \cdot r} 2. Inverse Distortion (Undistortion): Solve for undistorted normalized coordinates (x, y) from distorted (xd, yd) = (x{raw}, y{raw}) using Newton-Raphson. Distortion Model: The forward distortion maps undistorted (x, y) to distorted (xd, yd): r^2 = x^2 + y^2 d(x, y) = 1 + k1 r^2 + k2 r^4 + k3 r^6 \quad (\text{or } 1 + k4 r^8 \text{ if } k4 \text{ is present}) xd = x \cdot d(x, y) + 2 p1 x y + p2 (r^2 + 2 x^2) yd = y \cdot d(x, y) + 2 p2 x y + p1 (r^2 + 2 y^2) Newton-Raphson Iteration: Initialize x = xd, y = yd. Iterate up to maxiterations (default 10 or 100): a. Compute residuals fx, fy: fx = x \cdot d(x, y) + 2 p1 x y + p2 (r^2 + 2 x^2) - xd fy = y \cdot d(x, y) + 2 p2 x y + p1 (r^2 + 2 y^2) - yd b. Compute Jacobian elements J{xx}, J{xy}, J{yx}, J{yy}: Let d' = \frac{d(r^2)}{d(r^2)} = k1 + 2 k2 r^2 + 3 k3 r^4. J{xx} = d + 2 x^2 d' + 2 p1 y + 6 p2 x J{xy} = 2 x y d' + 2 p1 x + 2 p2 y J{yx} = J{xy} J{yy} = d + 2 y^2 d' + 6 p1 y + 2 p2 x Note: Some implementations approximate or simplify the Jacobian. uses a simplified Jacobian calculation in code comments but the logic follows the derivative of the distortion function. c. Compute Newton step using Cramer's rule: \text{det} = J{xx} J{yy} - J{xy} J{yx} \Delta x = \frac{fx J{yy} - fy J{xy}}{\text{det}} \Delta y = \frac{fy J{xx} - fx J{yx}}{\text{det}} d. Handle singular Jacobian: If |\text{det}| < \epsilon (default 10^{-9}), set \Delta x = 0, \Delta y = 0. e. Trust Region (Optional): Compute step norm squared S = \Delta x^2 + \Delta y^2. If S > \max(r^2 \cdot k{RelStepRadius}^2, k{StepRadius}^2) (defaults 0.1), scale step: \text{scale} = \sqrt{\frac{\text{radiusSqr}}{S}} \Delta x \leftarrow \Delta x \cdot \text{scale}, \quad \Delta y \leftarrow \Delta y \cdot \text{scale} f. Update: x \leftarrow x + \Delta x y \leftarrow y + \Delta y g. Convergence: If step norm squared < 10^{-10} or max iterations reached, break. 3. Local Ray Direction Construction: Stack undistorted coordinates with z=1: \mathbf{v}{local} = [x, y, 1]^T Normalize: \mathbf{v}{local} \leftarrow \frac{\mathbf{v}{local}}{\|\mathbf{v}{local}\|} 4. Fisheye Correction (Optional): If camera type is FISHEYE: \theta = \sqrt{x^2 + y^2} Clamp \theta to \pi. \text{scale} = \frac{\sin(\theta)}{\theta} x \leftarrow x \cdot \text{scale}, \quad y \leftarrow y \cdot \text{scale} z = \cos(\theta) Reconstruct and normalize \mathbf{v}{local} = [x, y, z]^T. 5. Coordinate System Flip: Flip from OpenCV to OpenGL convention if necessary: \mathbf{v}{local} \leftarrow \text{diag}(1, -1, -1) \cdot \mathbf{v}{local} 6. World Space Transformation: Apply camera rotation R (orientation matrix): \mathbf{v}{world} = R \cdot \mathbf{v}{local} Normalize: \mathbf{v}{world} \leftarrow \frac{\mathbf{v}{world}}{\|\mathbf{v}{world}\|} 7. Ray Origins: Set origins to camera position T (from extrinsics). 8. Ray Radii (Optional): For mip-NeRF, compute radii using neighbor rays. Compute directions for right neighbor (u+1, v) and bottom neighbor (u, v+1). dx{norm} = \|\mathbf{v}{right} - \mathbf{v}{current}\| dy{norm} = \|\mathbf{v}{bottom} - \mathbf{v}{current}\| \text{radii} = 0.5 \cdot (dx{norm} + dy{norm}) \cdot \frac{2}{\sqrt{12}} If NDC space is used, compute radii from NDC origin differences. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import numpy as np def camerarayprojection( pixels: np.ndarray, # Shape (H, W, 2) or (N, 2), integer pixel coords fx: float, # Focal length x fy: float, # Focal length y cx: float, # Principal point x cy: float, # Principal point y skew: float = 0.0, # Skew aspectratio: float = 1.0,# Pixel aspect ratio k1: float = 0.0, # Radial distortion k1 k2: float = 0.0, # Radial distortion k2 k3: float = 0.0, # Radial distortion k3 p1: float = 0.0, # Tangential distortion p1 p2: float = 0.0, # Tangential distortion p2 R: np.ndarray = None, # 3x3 Rotation matrix (world from camera) T: np.ndarray = None, # 3x1 Translation vector (camera position in world) maxiterations: int = 10, # Max Newton iterations eps: float = 1e-9 # Epsilon for Jacobian check): """ Projects pixel coordinates to world-space rays with distortion correction. Returns origins, directions, viewdirs. """ # 1. Pixel to Normalized Coordinates # Add half-pixel offset u = pixels[..., 0] + 0.5 v = pixels[..., 1] + 0.5 # Compute y first to handle skew yraw = (v - cy) / (fy aspectratio) xraw = (u - cx - skew yraw) / fx # 2. Inverse Distortion x = xraw.copy() y = yraw.copy() for in range(maxiterations): r2 = xx + yy # Distortion factor d d = 1.0 + r2 (k1 + r2 (k2 + r2 k3)) # Residuals fx = x d + 2.0 p1 x y + p2 (r2 + 2.0 xx) - xraw fy = y d + 2.0 p2 x y + p1 (r2 + 2.0 yy) - yraw # Jacobian derivative of d w.r.t r2 dddr2 = k1 + r2 (2.0 k2 + 3.0 r2 k3) # Jacobian elements jxx = d + 2.0 xx dddr2 + 2.0 p1 y + 6.0 p2 x jxy = 2.0 x y dddr2 + 2.0 p1 x + 2.0 p2 y jyx = jxy jyy = d + 2.0 yy dddr2 + 6.0 p1 y + 2.0 p2 x # Determinant det = jxx jyy - jxy jyx # Newton Step if np.abs(det) > eps: dx = (fx jyy - fy jxy) / det dy = (fy jxx - fx jyx) / det else: dx = 0.0 dy = 0.0 x = x + dx y = y + dy # Convergence check (optional, based on step size) if dxdx + dydy < 1e-10: break # 3. Local Ray Direction # Stack with z=1 dirslocal = np.stack([x, y, np.oneslike(x)], axis=-1) # Normalize norms = np.linalg.norm(dirslocal, axis=-1, keepdims=True) dirslocal = dirslocal / norms # 4. World Space Transformation if R is not None: # Rotate: R is 3x3, dirslocal is (..., 3) # matmul: (..., 3) @ (3, 3).T or np.dot # Standard: vworld = R @ vlocal # If R is stored as rows, vworld = vlocal @ R.T dirsworld = np.matmul(dirslocal, R.T) else: dirsworld = dirslocal # Normalize again (numerical stability) normsworld = np.linalg.norm(dirsworld, axis=-1, keepdims=True) viewdirs = dirsworld / normsworld # 5. Origins if T is not None: origins = np.broadcastto(T, (dirsworld.shape[:-1], 3)) else: origins = np.zeroslike(dirsworld) return origins, dirsworld, viewdirs The core iterative solver. Use when lens distortion parameters are non-zero. Sets it apart by solving the non-linear inverse problem rather than applying forward distortion. Variant for fisheye cameras. Use when camtype is FISHEYE. Applies \theta-based scaling instead of polynomial radial distortion. Variant for Normalized Device Coordinates. Use when rendering to NDC space (e.g., for neural radiance fields in NDC). Maps origins to NDC space for radius calculation. Time Complexity: O(N \cdot I) where N is number of pixels and I is number of Newton iterations (typically 10-100). The Jacobian computation is constant time per iteration. Memory Complexity: O(N) for storing ray origins, directions, and residuals. Performance: Newton-Raphson converges quadratically near the solution. For small distortions, 5-10 iterations are sufficient. For large distortions (e.g., wide-angle lenses), up to 100 iterations may be needed. Strengths: Handles arbitrary radial/tangential distortion models. Provides accurate ray directions for volume rendering. Limitations: Iterative solver can be slow on CPU. Singular Jacobians (rare, near optical center with high distortion) require fallback. When to use: When camera calibration includes non-zero distortion coefficients. When not to use: For pinhole cameras with negligible distortion, skip undistortion for performance. Originating from computer vision camera calibration models (Brown), the inverse distortion method is widely used in photogrammetry and SLAM. In volume rendering, it was popularized by NeRF and its variants (NeRF-W, Mip-NeRF) to handle real-world camera distortions. The Newton-Raphson approach is standard for inverting the polynomial distortion model.
