name: Near-Far Linear Ray Generation
head: NeRF Near-Far Linear Ray Generation, Near-Far Disparity Linear Ray Generation
body: Near-Far Linear Ray Generation generates a list of 3D sampling points along a camera ray segment defined by near (t{min}) and far (t{max}) distances for a specified number of samples. It solves the problem of discretizing the continuous ray domain into a finite set of query points for volume rendering or neural radiance field evaluation. It sets itself apart from its siblings by providing the foundational uniform or disparity-based spacing logic upon which stratified, probabilistic, or depth-guided variants build. Unlike Inverse CDF Ray Sampling which adapts density to learned probabilities, or Depth-Guided Supersampling which uses external depth priors, this method relies on fixed geometric intervals. Inputs: rayso: Ray origins, shape (N{rays}, 3). raysd: Ray directions, shape (N{rays}, 3). near: Near plane distances, shape (N{rays}, 1). far: Far plane distances, shape (N{rays}, 1). Nsamples: Integer, number of depth samples per ray. lindisp: Boolean. If True, samples in disparity space (1/z); if False, samples in linear depth space. perturb: Float. Amount of random jitter to add to samples (0.0 for no jitter). bbox3D: Optional 3D Axis-Aligned Bounding Box (AABB) for clipping. Outputs: xyzcoarsesampled: 3D coordinates of sampled points, shape (N{rays}, N{samples}, 3). Data Structures: Tensors for ray parameters and sampled depths. No specific bit-packing is mandated; standard floating-point tensors are used. Steps: 1. Decompose Ray Parameters: Extract origins, directions, near, and far values from the input tensor. \text{rays}o, \text{rays}d = \text{rays}[:, 0:3], \text{rays}[:, 3:6] \text{near}, \text{far} = \text{rays}[:, 6:7], \text{rays}[:, 7:8] 2. Generate Normalized Depth Steps: Create a linearly spaced vector from 0 to 1 with N{samples} steps. z{steps} = \text{linspace}(0, 1, N{samples}) 3. Compute Depth Values (z{vals}): If lindisp is False (linear depth): z{vals} = \text{near} \cdot (1 - z{steps}) + \text{far} \cdot z{steps} If lindisp is True (linear disparity): z{vals} = \frac{1}{\frac{1}{\text{near}} \cdot (1 - z{steps}) + \frac{1}{\text{far}} \cdot z{steps}} 4. Expand Dimensions: Expand z{vals} to match the batch dimension of rays. z{vals} = \text{expand}(z{vals}, (N{rays}, N{samples})) 5. Apply Bounding Box Clipping (Optional): If bbox3D is provided, compute intersection intervals using the slab method (DDA) and clamp z{vals} to valid ranges. Compute inverse direction: \text{inv\rays\d} = 1.0 / (\text{rays}d + \epsilon). Calculate t{min}, t{max} for the AABB and clamp to [\text{near}, \text{far}]. Note: If clipping alters the valid range, z{vals} must be re-sampled or interpolated within the new bounds. The sources describe clipping as a constraint step but do not provide the explicit re-sampling formula for clipped rays in the main linear generation block. 6. Perturb Samples (Optional): If perturb > 0, add uniform random noise to break sampling symmetry. Compute interval midpoints: z{vals\mid} = 0.5 \cdot (z{vals}[:,:-1] + z{vals}[:, 1:]) Define interval bounds: \text{upper} = \text{concat}([z{vals\mid}, z{vals}[:, -1:]], \text{dim}=-1) \text{lower} = \text{concat}([z{vals}[:,:1], z{vals\mid}], \text{dim}=-1) Generate random noise: \text{perturb\rand} = \text{perturb} \cdot \text{rand}(z{vals}.shape) Apply jitter: z{vals} = \text{lower} + (\text{upper} - \text{lower}) \cdot \text{perturb\rand} 7. Compute 3D Coordinates: Combine ray origin, direction, and sampled depths. \text{xyz\coarse\sampled} = \text{rays}o.\text{unsqueeze}(1) + \text{rays}d.\text{unsqueeze}(1) \cdot z{vals}.\text{unsqueeze}(2) Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import torch def nearfarlinearraygeneration(rays, Nsamples, lindisp=False, perturb=1.0, bbox3d=None): """ Generate 3D sampling points along camera rays. Args: rays: Tensor of shape (Nrays, 8). Columns 0-2: origin (x,y,z), Columns 3-5: direction (x,y,z), Column 6: near distance, Column 7: far distance. Nsamples: int, number of samples per ray. lindisp: bool, if True sample in disparity space. perturb: float, amount of jitter (0.0 to disable). bbox3d: tuple (minxyz, maxxyz) or None. Returns: xyzcoarsesampled: Tensor of shape (Nrays, Nsamples, 3). """ # 1. Decompose ray parameters rayso = rays[:, 0:3] # (Nrays, 3) raysd = rays[:, 3:6] # (Nrays, 3) near = rays[:, 6:7] # (Nrays, 1) far = rays[:, 7:8] # (Nrays, 1) # 2. Generate normalized depth steps zsteps = torch.linspace(0, 1, Nsamples, device=rays.device) # (Nsamples,) # 3. Compute depth values if not lindisp: # Linear depth zvals = near (1 - zsteps) + far zsteps else: # Linear disparity zvals = 1.0 / (1.0 / near (1 - zsteps) + 1.0 / far zsteps) # 3b. Expand dimensions to match batch # zvals is currently (Nrays, Nsamples) if near/far were broadcast, # but near/far are (Nrays, 1) and zsteps is (Nsamples,). # In PyTorch broadcasting, (Nrays, 1) (1, Nsamples) -> (Nrays, Nsamples) # However, explicit expand is safer if dimensions don't align perfectly in all frameworks. # Assuming standard broadcasting works: # zvals shape is (Nrays, Nsamples) # 4. Apply Bounding Box Clipping (Optional) if bbox3d is not None: # Note: The sources mention AABB clipping via DDA but do not provide # the full re-sampling logic for clipped rays in this specific function. # This step is marked as a placeholder for implementation details found in. # Typically, one would compute tmin/tmax for the AABB intersection # and clamp zvals to the valid range [tmin, tmax]. pass # 5. Perturb samples if perturb > 0: # Compute midpoints zvalsmid = 0.5 (zvals[:,:-1] + zvals[:, 1:]) # (Nrays, Nsamples - 1) # Compute upper and lower bounds # upper: last column is the last zval, others are midpoints upper = torch.cat([zvalsmid, zvals[:, -1:]], dim=-1) # (Nrays, Nsamples) # lower: first column is the first zval, others are midpoints lower = torch.cat([zvals[:,:1], zvalsmid], dim=-1) # (Nrays, Nsamples) # Generate random noise perturbrand = perturb torch.rand(zvals.shape, device=rays.device) # Apply jitter zvals = lower + (upper - lower) perturbrand # 6. Compute 3D coordinates # rayso: (Nrays, 3), raysd: (Nrays, 3), zvals: (Nrays, Nsamples) # Unsqueeze to broadcast: (Nrays, 1, 3) and (Nrays, 1, 3) and (Nrays, Nsamples, 1) xyzcoarsesampled = rayso.unsqueeze(1) + raysd.unsqueeze(1) zvals.unsqueeze(2) return xyzcoarsesampled Parameters: Nsamples: Default 64. lindisp: Default False (linear depth). perturb: Default 1.0 (full jitter). Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Division by Zero: When computing disparity (1/z), if near is 0, division by zero occurs. Add a small epsilon (\epsilon) to denominators. Precision: Floating-point precision issues may arise when near and far differ significantly in magnitude, especially in disparity space. Boundary Conditions: If bbox3D is used, rays that do not intersect the box must be handled (e.g., by discarding or clamping to the box boundaries). Constrains ray sampling intervals to a specified viewing volume defined by fixed global near and far distances. Ensures samples are only generated within valid bounds, preventing rays from sampling empty space beyond the far plane or artifacts near the camera origin. Applies rigid, uniform bounds to all rays. Samples points along rays using inverse CDF sampling based on probability distributions associated with depth intervals. Maps uniform random noise to depth intervals using the cumulative distribution function derived from per-hit probabilities. Replaces uniform spacing with probability-weighted stratification. Generates sample points along camera rays by sampling z-values (depths) either linearly or in disparity space, with optional stratification to reduce variance. Extends the base method by supporting disparity-based spacing and depth-guided supersampling. Generates sample positions along a ray by perturbing a depth estimate with Gaussian noise, encouraging the renderer to sample around the estimated surface location. Relies on an external depth prior rather than a learned density distribution. Computes the near and far clipping planes for ray sampling based on the dataset type and Normalized Device Coordinates (NDC) configuration. Ensures that the ray sampler operates within a geometrically valid range appropriate for the scene's scale and projection model. Samples a fixed number of points along each ray globally, then filters out samples that fall outside of occupied Sparse Point Cloud (SPC) cells. Prioritizes a uniform global sampling density, using the SPC structure solely as a validity mask. Generates ray samples along a near-far segment by dividing the depth range into equal intervals and drawing one uniform random sample from each interval, ensuring low-discrepancy coverage. Guarantees that every sub-interval contributes exactly one sample, reducing variance. Generates ray samples using disparity spacing with random jitter within segments, similar to NeRF's sampling but with explicit segment length calculation. It creates linear t{vals} from 0 to 1 with pointcount steps, converts them to disparity space using t{vals} = 1. / (1. / \text{near} \cdot (1 - t{vals}) + 1. / \text{far} \cdot t{vals}), and applies jitter if jitter > 0 by computing midpoints, upper/lower bounds, and random t{rand} to jitter t{vals}. Segment lengths are computed by differencing t{vals}, appending a large value (1e10), and multiplying by ray direction norm. Ray positions are computed directly from t{vals} as \text{raypos} = \text{campos} + \text{raydir} \cdot t{vals}. A method to generate seed points along a line segment between mstartPt and mendPt. It calculates delta as (\text{m\endPt} - \text{m\startPt}) / \text{count} and loops i from 0 to count - 1, setting \text{m\h\seeds}[i] = \text{m\startPt} + i \cdot \text{delta}. The parameter count specifies the number of seed points to generate. Generates samples in NDC space by initializing sample count N{samples}, retrieving near/far clipping planes, and generating linearly spaced depth values interpx between near and far. If training, uniform random noise is added to interpx scaled by step size (\text{far}-\text{near})/N{samples}. Linear depth is converted to NDC depth using \text{ndc\depth} = 2 \cdot \text{ndc\near\plane} / (1 - \text{ndc\near\plane} - \text{interpx}). The depth is then rescaled to simulated Euclidean depth using util.gradrescale(interpx, ndcdepth). Ray points are computed using either simulated or linear depth, and a mask is generated to check if points are outside the AABB defined by self.aabb[0] and self.aabb[1]. The parameter ndcnearplane is typically 1.0. Time Complexity: O(N{rays} \cdot N{samples}) for generating depth values and 3D coordinates. Memory Complexity: O(N{rays} \cdot N{samples}) to store the sampled points. Measured Performance: Not given in the sources. Scaling: Scales linearly with the number of rays and samples. Strengths: Simple to implement; provides uniform coverage of the ray segment; disparity sampling is beneficial for scenes with large depth variations. Limitations: Uniform sampling may waste samples in empty space; disparity sampling can introduce precision issues near the camera. When to use: When a simple, uniform sampling strategy is sufficient; when disparity sampling is needed for deep scenes. When not to use: When the scene has complex geometry requiring adaptive sampling; when computational resources are limited and stratified or importance sampling is preferred. Near-Far Linear Ray Generation is a fundamental technique in volume rendering and neural radiance fields (NeRF) for discretizing camera rays into sample points. It was popularized by the NeRF paper and is widely used in various implementations such as TensoRF and PointNeRF. The method allows for efficient evaluation of neural networks along rays to render images or extract 3D structures. name: Near-Far Clipping
head: Fixed Near/Far Plane Collider, NearFar Collider
body: Near-Far Clipping is a post-processing step in ray generation that constrains ray sampling intervals to a specified viewing volume defined by fixed global near and far distances. It ensures that samples are only generated within valid bounds, preventing rays from sampling empty space beyond the far plane or artifacts near the camera origin. Unlike Inverse CDF Ray Sampling which adapts sampling density to scene content, or Near-Far Linear/Disparity Ray Generation with Stratification which handles stratified intervals, this method applies rigid, uniform bounds to all rays. Inputs: raybundle: A data structure containing ray origins, directions, and currently assigned near/far distances. self.nearplane: The minimum distance from the camera origin for valid samples. self.farplane: The maximum distance from the camera origin for valid samples. self.resetnearplane: A boolean flag (default True). Outputs: Updated raybundle with nears and fars tensors overwritten. Data Structures: raybundle.nears: Tensor of shape (batchsize, 1) or matching raybundle.origins[..., 0:1], storing the start distance of each ray. raybundle.fars: Tensor of shape (batchsize, 1) or matching raybundle.origins[..., 0:1], storing the end distance of each ray. Steps: 1. Create a tensor ones of ones with shape matching raybundle.origins[..., 0:1]. 2. Determine the effective nearplane value: if self.training is True OR self.resetnearplane is False, use self.nearplane; otherwise use 0.0. 3. Set raybundle.nears to ones nearplane. 4. Set raybundle.fars to ones self.farplane. 5. Return the updated raybundle. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def applynearfarclipping(raybundle, nearplane, farplane, resetnearplane, training): """ Clips ray samples to specified near and far planes. Args: raybundle: Object containing ray origins and near/far tensors. nearplane: Float, the configured near distance. farplane: Float, the configured far distance. resetnearplane: Bool, whether to reset near to 0 during inference. training: Bool, whether currently in training mode. Returns: Updated raybundle. """ # 1. Create ones array matching the shape of ray origins' first dimension # raybundle.origins is assumed to be a list/array of shape (N, 3) numrays = len(raybundle.origins) ones = [1.0] numrays # 2. Determine effective near plane if training or not resetnearplane: effectivenear = nearplane else: effectivenear = 0.0 # 3. Set near distances raybundle.nears = [o effectivenear for o in ones] # 4. Set far distances raybundle.fars = [o farplane for o in ones] # 5. Return updated bundle return raybundle Parameters: nearplane: Minimum distance from camera origin. Typical values vary by scene; e.g., 2.00 for kitchen, 5.00 for playroom. farplane: Maximum distance from camera origin. Not given in the sources. resetnearplane: Boolean flag (default True). Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Clipping Artifacts: Using a non-zero nearplane during inference can cause clipping artifacts if the evaluation or viewer camera moves closer to the object than the nearplane distance. This is mitigated by resetnearplane=True. Precision: Not given in the sources. Boundaries: Not given in the sources. A technique to reduce the visual impact of floaters (noisy Gaussians near the camera) by using near clipping planes. For ray tracers, tracing starts further along the initial ray; for splatting, Gaussians with centroids closer than d{\text{near}} are culled. Choose this when dense initialization produces visible floaters near the camera. It is a variant of near clipping focused on artifact suppression rather than volume definition. Time and Memory Complexity: Time: O(N) where N is the number of rays, due to tensor operations. Memory: O(N) to store the updated near/far tensors. Measured Performance: Metrics (PSNR, SSIM, LPIPS) are measured without clipping planes to ensure fair comparison, as clipping planes offer negligible improvements to quality metrics. PSNR improvement for TreeHill at d{\text{near}}=1.0 is negligible (26.91 → 26.93). PSNR improvement for Garden at d{\text{near}}=2.0 is negligible (21.89 → 21.94). Strengths and Limitations: Strengths: Simple to implement; effectively culls irrelevant geometry near the camera. Limitations: Does not improve standard quality metrics; requires careful tuning of d{\text{near}} per scene. When to Use: Use during inference or rendering to hide floaters in dense Gaussian splatting or ray tracing. Do not use for metric evaluation to maintain fairness. Originating from techniques to handle floaters in 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS), near clipping planes were adopted to mitigate visual artifacts caused by dense initialization. The method is implemented in toolkits like Gaussian-Splatting-Toolkit and referenced in ray tracing optimizations like GRay. barbararoessle/ganerf, https://github.com/barbararoessle/ganerf, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial) Gaussian-Splatting-Toolkit/Gaussian-Splatting-Toolkit, https://github.com/Gaussian-Splatting-Toolkit/Gaussian-Splatting-Toolkit, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial) GRay: Ray Tracing 3D Gaussians Near the Speed of Splats, https://doi.org/10.1145/3804496, fetched 2026-10-29

name: Inverse CDF Ray Sampling
body: Inverse CDF Ray Sampling is a CUDA kernel that samples points along rays using inverse CDF sampling based on probability distributions (probs) associated with depth intervals (hits), supporting optional fixed step size. It maps uniform random noise to depth intervals using the cumulative distribution function derived from per-hit probabilities. It builds on Near-Far Linear Ray Generation by replacing uniform spacing with probability-weighted stratification. Inputs: probs: Probability distribution for each hit along the ray. Shape: [batchsize, numrays, maxhits]. steps: Target number of samples per ray. Shape: [batchsize, numrays]. mindepth: Minimum depth of the current hit interval. Shape: [batchsize, numrays, maxhits]. maxdepth: Maximum depth of the current hit interval. Shape: [batchsize, numrays, maxhits]. ptsidx: Index of the primitive/vertex associated with each hit. Shape: [batchsize, numrays, maxhits]. fixedstepsize: Optional scalar. If > 0, overrides dynamic step calculation for uniform spacing within bins. If -1, uses dynamic calculation. Outputs: sampledidx: Primitive indices for each sample. Shape: [batchsize, numrays, maxsamplesperray]. sampleddists: Distance from the start of the current bin to the sample. Shape: [batchsize, numrays, maxsamplesperray]. sampleddepth: Absolute depth of the sample. Shape: [batchsize, numrays, maxsamplesperray]. The method processes data in chunks to manage memory. Chunk Size (G): 200. Batch Chunk Size: 4 \times G = 800 rays processed per CUDA kernel launch to avoid Out-Of-Memory (OOM) errors. Padding: Inputs are padded to multiples of G. Let H be the padded ray count. Reshaping: Data is viewed as (G, -1, P) for 3D tensors and (G, -1) for 2D tensors, where P is the point dimension (e.g., 3 for depth/idx). 1. Set batch chunk size G = 200. 2. Determine ray count N and point dimension P. 3. Pad inputs to size H (multiple of G). 4. Reshape inputs to (G, -1, P) for data and (G, -1) for steps. 5. Calculate maxsteps = steps.ceil().long().max() + P. 6. Generate noise tensor of shape [H, maxsteps]. 7. If deterministic, set noise to 0.5; else, sample uniform u \in [0, 1) and clamp to [0.001, 0.999]. 8. Process in chunks of 4 \times G to avoid OOM. 9. Call CUDA extension ext.inversecdfsampling with ptsidx, mindepth, maxdepth, noise, probs, steps, and fixedstepsize. 10. Concatenate results from chunks. 11. Reshape outputs to (H, -1). 12. Truncate to N rays if padded. 13. Trim outputs to maxlen (max valid samples per ray). 14. Mark outputs as non-differentiable. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math import random def inversecdfsampling(probs, steps, mindepth, maxdepth, ptsidx, fixedstepsize=-1, deterministic=False): batchsize, numrays, maxhits = len(probs), len(probs[0]), len(probs[0][0]) G = 200 H = ((numrays + G - 1) // G) G P = 3 # Pad inputs to multiple of G probspad = [row + [0.0] (H - numrays) for row in probs] stepspad = steps + [0] (H - numrays) mindepthpad = [row + [0.0] (H - numrays) for row in mindepth] maxdepthpad = [row + [0.0] (H - numrays) for row in maxdepth] ptsidxpad = [row + [-1] (H - numrays) for row in ptsidx] maxstepsval = math.ceil(max(stepspad)) + P noise = [] for in range(H): row = [] for in range(maxstepsval): u = 0.5 if deterministic else random.random() row.append(max(0.001, min(0.999, u))) noise.append(row) results = [] chunksize = 4 G for start in range(0, H, chunksize): end = min(start + chunksize, H) chunklen = end - start # The actual implementation calls a CUDA extension ext.inversecdfsampling # Below is the Python-equivalent logic for the kernel: chunksamples = [] for k in range(start, end): raysamples = [] s = 0 zlow = mindepthpad[k][0] currbin = 0 currmincdf = 0.0 currmaxcdf = probspad[k][0] currmindepth = mindepthpad[k][0] currmaxdepth = maxdepthpad[k][0] done = False stepsize = fixedstepsize if fixedstepsize > 0 else 1.0 / stepspad[k] for currstep in range(int(stepspad[k])): if done: break currcdf = (float(currstep) + noise[k][currstep]) stepsize while currcdf > currmaxcdf: raysamples.append((ptsidxpad[k][currbin], currmaxdepth - zlow, (currmaxdepth + zlow) 0.5)) currbin += 1 s += 1 if currbin >= maxhits or ptsidxpad[k][currbin] == -1: done = True break currmindepth = mindepthpad[k][currbin] currmaxdepth = maxdepthpad[k][currbin] currmincdf = currmaxcdf currmaxcdf += probspad[k][currbin] zlow = currmindepth if done: break u = (currcdf - currmincdf) / (currmaxcdf - currmincdf) z = currmindepth + u (currmaxdepth - currmindepth) raysamples.append((ptsidxpad[k][currbin], z - zlow, (z + zlow) 0.5)) zlow = z s += 1 while zlow < currmaxdepth and not done: raysamples.append((ptsidxpad[k][currbin], currmaxdepth - zlow, (currmaxdepth + zlow) 0.5)) currbin += 1 s += 1 if currbin >= maxhits or ptsidxpad[k][currbin] == -1: break currmindepth = mindepthpad[k][currbin] currmaxdepth = maxdepthpad[k][currbin] zlow = currmindepth chunksamples.append(raysamples) results.extend(chunksamples) allsamples = results[:numrays] finalsamples = [ray[:max(steps[i])] for i, ray in enumerate(allsamples)] return finalsamples fixedstepsize: If > 0, overrides dynamic step calculation. If -1, uses dynamic calculation. probs: Shape [b, numrays, maxhits]. steps: Shape [b, numrays]. Noise Clamping: Noise must be clamped to [0.001, 0.999] to prevent division by zero or invalid CDF lookups at the exact boundaries. Padding: Inputs must be padded to multiples of G=200 to align with the kernel's block structure. Invalid Hits: Check for ptsidx == -1 to handle rays with fewer hits than maxhits. Time Complexity: O(N \cdot S), where N is the number of rays and S is the number of samples per ray. The bin-skipping loop adds overhead proportional to the number of hits, but typically S \ll \text{max\hits}. Memory Complexity: O(N \cdot S) for outputs. Intermediate padding adds O(G \cdot S) overhead. Performance: Chunking by 4 \times G (800 rays) balances GPU occupancy and memory usage. The method is efficient on CUDA hardware due to parallel ray processing. Strengths: Provides stratified sampling with arbitrary probability distributions, reducing variance compared to uniform sampling. Limitations: Requires pre-computed probabilities and hit intervals. Less flexible than pure random sampling for highly dynamic scenes where probabilities change rapidly. Inverse CDF sampling is a standard technique in Monte Carlo integration, applied to volume rendering to sample along rays according to the estimated density or opacity distribution. In the context of Neural Volume Rendering (NSVF), it is used to efficiently sample points within the reconstructed volume based on the learned probability distribution of surface intersections. facebookresearch/NSVF, https://github.com/facebookresearch/NSVF, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial) YihangChen-ee/CNC, https://github.com/YihangChen-ee/CNC, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial)

name: Near-Far Linear/Disparity Ray Generation with Stratification
head: Coarse Stratified Sampling, Near-Far Linear Ray Generation with Stratification, Stratified Sampling Along Rays, linear/disparity sampling
body: Generates sample points along camera rays for volume rendering by sampling z-values (depths) either linearly or in disparity space, with optional stratification to reduce variance. It extends Near-Far Linear Ray Generation by supporting disparity-based spacing and depth-guided supersampling, distinguishing it from Inverse CDF Ray Sampling which uses probabilistic distributions rather than fixed geometric spacing. Inputs: origins: Ray origins, shape [batchsize, 3]. directions: Ray directions, shape [batchsize, 3]. near: Float, near clip plane distance. far: Float, far clip plane distance. numcoarsesamples: Integer, number of base samples to generate along each ray. uselineardisparity: Boolean, if True, samples linearly in disparity (1/z) rather than depth (z). usestratifiedsampling: Boolean, if True, adds uniform random noise to sample positions within intervals to reduce variance. randomized: Boolean flag to use randomized stratified sampling. sigmadepth: Optional float, if not None, triggers depth-guided supersampling. rays: Object containing origins, directions, radii, and rayshape for supersampling context. Outputs: tsamples: Sorted sample positions along the ray parameter t \in [0, 1], shape [batchsize, numtsamples]. means, covs: Radiance and covariance outputs from ray casting. Data Structures: tvals: 1D tensor of base sample positions in [0, 1]. zvals: 1D tensor of depth values corresponding to tvals. sstsamples: Tensor of additional samples from depth-guided supersampling. Steps: 1. Compute Base Linear Samples: Generate numcoarsesamples + 1 evenly spaced values in [0, 1]: t{base} = \text{linspace}(0.0, 1.0, \text{num\coarse\samples} + 1). 2. Convert to Depth (z{val}): For each t \in t{base}, compute depth using linear or disparity spacing: If uselineardisparity is False: z{val} = near \cdot (1 - t) + far \cdot t. If uselineardisparity is True: z{val} = \frac{1}{\frac{1}{near}(1 - t) + \frac{1}{far}t}. 3. Apply Stratification (if usestratifiedsampling is True): Compute midpoints mids = 0.5 \cdot (z{vals}[1:] + z{vals}[:-1]), upper bounds upper = [mids, z{vals}[-1]], and lower bounds lower = [z{vals}[0], mids]. Generate random uniform noise t{rand} \sim U[0, 1] with shape matching zvals, then update z{vals} = lower + (upper - lower) \cdot t{rand}. 4. Compute 3D Points: Calculate points using the stratified depth values: points = origins + z{vals} \cdot directions. 5. Determine Sample Counts: If sigmadepth is not None, set numtsamples = numcoarsesamples // 4 3 + 1 and numsssamples = numcoarsesamples // 4; otherwise set numtsamples = numcoarsesamples + 1 and numsssamples = 0. 6. Generate Base t Samples: Create t{samples} = \text{linspace}(0., 1., \text{num\t\samples}) on the same device as origins. 7. Convert t Samples to Depth: If uselineardisparity is True, transform to disparity: t{samples} = \frac{1}{\frac{1}{near}(1 - t{samples}) + \frac{1}{far}t{samples}}; otherwise transform to depth: t{samples} = near + (far - near) \cdot t{samples}. 8. Apply Randomized Stratification (if randomized is True): Compute midpoints mids = 0.5 \cdot (t{samples}[:, 1:] + t{samples}[:,:-1]), upper bounds upper = \text{concat}([mids, t{samples}[:, -1:]]), and lower bounds lower = \text{concat}([t{samples}[:,:1], mids]). Generate random uniform noise t{rand} \sim U[0, 1] with shape matching tsamples, then update t{samples} = lower + (upper - lower) \cdot t{rand}. 9. Depth-Guided Supersampling (if sigmadepth is not None): Call depthguidedsupersampling(rays=rays, nsamples=numsssamples, startsigma=sigmadepth) to get sstsamples, then concatenate and sort: t{samples} = \text{sort}(\text{concat}([t{samples}, ss{tsamples}]), \text{axis}=-1). 10. Cast Rays: Call castrays(tsamples, origins, directions, radii, rayshape, a, f, l) to get means and covariances. 11. Return Results: Output tsamples, (means, covs). Pseudocode: Unverified code. Args: origins: Tensor [B, 3] directions: Tensor [B, 3] near: float far: float numcoarsesamples: int uselineardisparity: bool usestratifiedsampling: bool randomized: bool sigmadepth: float or None rays: Object with origins, directions, radii, rayshape Returns: tsamples: Tensor [B, N] means: Tensor from castrays covs: Tensor from castrays """ device = origins.device # Step 1: Base linear samples in t-space [0, 1] tbase = torch.linspace(0.0, 1.0, numcoarsesamples + 1, device=device) # Step 2: Convert to depth zvals if uselineardisparity: invnear = 1.0 / near invfar = 1.0 / far denom = invnear (1.0 - tbase) + invfar tbase zvals = 1.0 / denom else: zvals = near (1.0 - tbase) + far tbase # Step 3: Stratification on zvals if usestratifiedsampling: mids = 0.5 (zvals[1:] + zvals[:-1]) upper = torch.cat([mids, zvals[-1:]], dim=0) lower = torch.cat([zvals[:1], mids], dim=0) trand = torch.randlike(zvals) zvals = lower + (upper - lower) trand # Step 4: Compute 3D points # zvals shape [N], origins [B, 3], directions [B, 3] # Broadcasting yields [B, N, 3] points = origins[:, None,:] + zvals[None,:, None] directions[:, None,:] # Step 5: Determine sample counts if sigmadepth is not None: numtsamples = numcoarsesamples // 4 3 + 1 numsssamples = numcoarsesamples // 4 else: numtsamples = numcoarsesamples + 1 numsssamples = 0 # Step 6: Generate base tsamples tsamples = torch.linspace(0., 1., numtsamples, device=device) # Step 7: Convert tsamples to depth/disparity if uselineardisparity: invnear = 1.0 / near invfar = 1.0 / far denom = invnear (1.0 - tsamples) + invfar tsamples tsamples = 1.0 / denom else: tsamples = near + (far - near) tsamples # Step 8: Randomized stratification on tsamples if randomized: mids = 0.5 (tsamples[..., 1:] + tsamples[...,:-1]) upper = torch.cat([mids, tsamples[..., -1:]], dim=-1) lower = torch.cat([tsamples[...,:1], mids], dim=-1) trand = torch.randlike(tsamples) tsamples = lower + (upper - lower) trand # Step 9: Depth-guided supersampling if sigmadepth is not None and rays is not None: # Sources do not provide implementation for depthguidedsupersampling. # Standard implementation uses sigma field to allocate additional samples. sstsamples = depthguidedsupersampling(rays, numsssamples, sigmadepth) tsamples = torch.sort(torch.cat([tsamples, sstsamples], dim=-1), dim=-1).values # Step 10: Cast rays # Sources do not provide implementation for castrays. # Standard implementation evaluates volume rendering integral at sample positions. means, covs = castrays(tsamples, origins, directions, rays.radii, rays.rayshape, 0.02, 0.1, 0.6) # Step 11: Return results return tsamples, means, covs Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Division by Zero: If near or far is 0, disparity calculation (1/z) will fail. Ensure near > 0. Precision: Floating-point precision issues may arise when near and far differ significantly, especially in disparity space. Use double precision if necessary. Degenerate Input: If numcoarsesamples is 0, no samples are generated. Handle this case explicitly. Time Complexity: O(N) where N is the number of samples per ray. Supersampling adds O(N{ss}) where N{ss} is the number of additional samples. Memory Complexity: O(N) for storing sample positions and points. Performance: Stratification reduces variance compared to uniform sampling, potentially requiring fewer samples for similar quality. Strengths: Simple to implement, supports both depth and disparity sampling, reduces variance with stratification. Limitations: Requires external implementations for depthguidedsupersampling and castrays to complete the pipeline. Disparity sampling may be less intuitive for scenes with large depth ranges. name: Depth-Guided Supersampling
body: Depth-Guided Supersampling generates sample positions along a ray by perturbing a depth estimate with Gaussian noise. Inputs: rays: Tensor containing ray origins, directions, and near/far bounds. depth: Tensor of estimated depth values for each ray, shape [batchsize] or [batchsize, 1]. nsamples: Integer, number of samples per ray. startsigma: Float, initial standard deviation for noise (default 0.1). Outputs: zvals: Tensor of sample depths along the ray, shape [batchsize, nsamples]. Data Structures: zvals: Float tensor. mean: Tensor of shape [batchsize, nsamples], initialized with the depth estimate. sigma: Tensor of shape [1, nsamples], initialized to startsigma. noise: Tensor of shape [batchsize, nsamples], drawn from \mathcal{N}(0, 1). Steps: 1. Extract near, far, and depth from the ray data. 2. Set mean to depth (cloned and detached). 3. Set sigma to a tensor of ones multiplied by startsigma, shape [1, nsamples]. 4. Generate noise from \mathcal{N}(0, 1) with shape [batchsize, nsamples]. 5. Compute zvals0level as noise sigma + mean. 6. For rays with depth == 0, replace zvals0level with random points uniformly distributed between near and far. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import torch def depthguidedsupersampling(rays, depth, nsamples, startsigma=0.1): """ Generate sample positions along a ray guided by a depth estimate. Args: rays: Tensor or object containing.near and.far attributes of shape [B]. depth: Tensor of shape [B] or [B, 1] with depth estimates. nsamples: int, number of samples per ray. startsigma: float, standard deviation of noise. Returns: zvals: Tensor of shape [B, nsamples] with sample depths. """ near = rays.near far = rays.far if depth.dim() == 2: depth = depth.squeeze(1) mean = depth.clone().detach().unsqueeze(1) sigma = torch.ones(1, nsamples, device=depth.device) startsigma noise = torch.randn(mean.shape[0], nsamples, device=depth.device) zvals = noise sigma + mean zerodepthmask = (depth == 0) if zerodepthmask.any(): uniformnoise = torch.rand(mean.shape[0], nsamples, device=depth.device) nearexpanded = near.unsqueeze(1).expand(-1, nsamples) farexpanded = far.unsqueeze(1).expand(-1, nsamples) uniformzvals = nearexpanded + uniformnoise (farexpanded - nearexpanded) zvals[zerodepthmask] = uniformzvals[zerodepthmask] return zvals Parameters: startsigma: Float, default 0.1. Controls the spread of noise around the depth estimate. Edge Cases: If depth == 0, the method falls back to uniform sampling between near and far. Samples K{fd} positions around a specified depth value with Gaussian noise, clamped to ray bounds. It repeats the input depth tensor of shape (B,) along dimension 1 to shape (B, K{fd}), adds Gaussian noise with standard deviation depthstd, and clamps the resulting values between near and far bounds from the rays. name: Dataset-Specific Near/Far Bound Calculation
head: Dataset-dependent Near/Far Clipping, Near/Far Bound Calculation per Dataset, Scene Normalization, Scene contraction strategy
body: Computes the near and far clipping planes for ray sampling based on the dataset type and Normalized Device Coordinates (NDC) configuration. It ensures that the ray sampler operates within a geometrically valid range appropriate for the scene's scale and projection model, serving as the parameterization layer for Near-Far Linear Ray Generation. Inputs: datasettype: String identifier for the dataset ('llff', 'blender', 'deepvoxels'). nondc: Boolean flag. If True, disables NDC projection for non-forward-facing scenes. bds: Array of bounding box min/max values derived from camera poses. poses: Array of camera transformation matrices. Outputs: near: Float, the near clipping plane distance. far: Float, the far clipping plane distance. Data Structures: bds: Shape [3] or [numcameras, 3] containing min/max extents. In LLFF loading, bds is rescaled by bdfactor (default 0.75) if provided. poses: Shape [numcameras, 4, 4] or [numcameras, 3, 4] representing camera extrinsics. Steps: 1. LLFF Dataset (datasettype == 'llff'): If nondc is True: Calculate near = min(bds) 0.9 and far = max(bds) 1.0. If nondc is False: Set near = 0.0 and far = 1.0. 2. Blender Dataset (datasettype == 'blender'): Set near = 2.0 and far = 6.0. 3. DeepVoxels Dataset (datasettype == 'deepvoxels'): Compute hemiR = mean(norm(poses[:,:3, -1])). Calculate near = hemiR - 1.0 and far = hemiR + 1.0. 4. Scene Normalization (Unbounded Scenes): Calculate the maximum distance D{max} between any two camera positions in the training log. Determine sphere diameter D{sphere} = D{max} + 50 meters. Model the scene of interest with a sphere of this diameter for scene contraction. Pitfalls: LLFF NDC vs. Non-NDC: Using fixed [0, 1] bounds for LLFF when nondc=True causes incorrect sampling ranges because the physical scale is not normalized. Conversely, using physical bounds with nondc=False breaks the NDC assumption. Pose Extraction: Ensure poses[:,:3, -1] correctly extracts the translation component from the transformation matrix. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def computenearfar(datasettype, nondc, bds, poses): """ Compute near and far clipping planes based on dataset type. Args: datasettype (str): 'llff', 'blender', or 'deepvoxels'. nondc (bool): If True, disable NDC projection. bds (list or array): Bounding box min/max values. poses (list or array): Camera poses. Returns: float: near float: far """ if datasettype == 'llff': if nondc: near = min(bds) 0.9 far = max(bds) 1.0 else: near = 0.0 far = 1.0 elif datasettype == 'blender': near = 2.0 far = 6.0 elif datasettype == 'deepvoxels': translations = [pose[:3, -1] for pose in poses] norms = [sum(t2 for t in trans)0.5 for trans in translations] hemiR = sum(norms) / len(norms) near = hemiR - 1.0 far = hemiR + 1.0 else: raise ValueError(f"Unsupported datasettype: {datasettype}") return near, far Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Not given in the sources. Limitations: Hardcoded for specific dataset types. Does not generalize to arbitrary unstructured point clouds without scene normalization (contraction). This method originates from the implementation details of early NeRF variants and their derivatives. The LLFF and Blender bounds are standard conventions established in the original NeRF paper and subsequent repositories. The DeepVoxels approach adapts to spherical camera trajectories. The scene normalization strategy (sphere diameter + 50m) is introduced in LidaRF to handle unbounded street scenes using scene contraction. name: Uniform Ray Marching with Occupancy Filtering
head: SPC Ray Raymarching
body: Uniform Ray Marching with Occupancy Filtering is a raymarching strategy that samples a fixed number of points along each ray globally, then filters out samples that fall outside of occupied Sparse Point Cloud (SPC) cells. It builds on Near-Far Linear Ray Generation by applying a global uniform grid and discarding empty-space samples via occupancy queries. Inputs: origins: Tensor of ray origins, shape (N, 3). directions: Tensor of normalized ray directions, shape (N, 3). distmin: Scalar or tensor of near-plane distances for each ray. distmax: Scalar or tensor of far-plane distances for each ray. numsamples: Integer, the number of base samples to generate per ray. spc: The Sparse Point Cloud acceleration structure supporting point index queries. Outputs: samples: Filtered 3D coordinates, shape (M, 3), where M \le N \times \text{num\samples}. depths: Filtered depths along rays, shape (M,). deltas: Filtered step sizes between consecutive samples, shape (M,). rayindices: Indices mapping each sample back to its originating ray, shape (M,). packboundaries: Boolean mask marking the start of each ray's sample pack in the flattened output. Data Structures: The SPC structure maps 3D coordinates to integer point indices (pidx). mask: Boolean tensor of length N \times \text{num\samples}, true where pidx > -1. Steps: 1. Generate Base Depths: Create linearly spaced depths in [0, 1] and add jitter. d{\text{base}} = \text{linspace}(0, 1.0, \text{num\samples}) d{\text{jitter}} = \text{rand}(0, 1, \text{num\samples}) / \text{num\samples} d{\text{norm}} = d{\text{base}} + d{\text{jitter}} The jitter ensures stratification within each uniform interval. 2. Normalize to Ray Range: Map normalized depths to the ray's [dist\min, dist\max] range. d{\text{final}} = d{\text{norm}} \times (dist\max - dist\min) + dist\min Shape: (N, \text{num\samples}). 3. Compute Sample Coordinates: Calculate 3D positions using origins, directions, and depths. \text{samples} = \text{origins} + d{\text{final}} \times \text{directions} Shape: (N, \text{num\samples}, 3). 4. Query Occupancy: Query the SPC structure for all sample coordinates to get point indices. \text{pidx} = \text{SPC.query}(\text{samples}) Shape: (N, \text{num\samples}). 5. Create Occupancy Mask: Identify samples inside occupied cells. \text{mask} = (\text{pidx} > -1) Shape: (N, \text{num\samples}). 6. Compute Depth Deltas: Calculate distances between consecutive samples and prepend the near plane. \Delta d = \text{diff}(d{\text{final}}, \text{axis}=1) \Delta d{\text{full}} = [dist\min, \Delta d{0}, \Delta d{1}, \dots] Shape: (N, \text{num\samples}). 7. Filter Samples: Flatten tensors and filter using the mask. \text{flat\samples} = \text{flatten}(\text{samples}) \text{flat\depths} = \text{flatten}(d{\text{final}}) \text{flat\deltas} = \text{flatten}(\Delta d{\text{full}}) \text{flat\ray\idx} = \text{repeat}(0..N-1, \text{num\samples}) \text{flat\mask} = \text{flatten}(\text{mask}) Apply fastfiltermethod to keep only elements where flatmask is true. \text{out\samples} = \text{flat\samples}[\text{flat\mask}] \text{out\depths} = \text{flat\depths}[\text{flat\mask}] \text{out\deltas} = \text{flat\deltas}[\text{flat\mask}] \text{out\ray\idx} = \text{flat\ray\idx}[\text{flat\mask}] 8. Mark Pack Boundaries: Identify the start of each ray's samples in the filtered output. Boundaries are marked where the ray index changes or at the first element. Parameters: numsamples: Number of samples generated per ray. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Empty Occupancy: If NUMHITSAMPLES (the count of true values in mask) is 0, the output tensors will be empty. Precision: Jitter addition must be performed carefully to avoid precision loss when distmax - distmin is very large or very small. Boundary Conditions: The first delta is explicitly set to distmin. Ensure distmin is correctly passed for rays that may have varying near planes. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import torch def uniformraymarchingwithoccupancyfilter( origins: torch.Tensor, directions: torch.Tensor, distmin: torch.Tensor, distmax: torch.Tensor, numsamples: int, spcqueryfunc) -> dict: """ Performs uniform ray marching with occupancy filtering. Args: origins: (N, 3) Ray origins. directions: (N, 3) Normalized ray directions. distmin: (N,) or scalar Near plane distance. distmax: (N,) or scalar Far plane distance. numsamples: int Number of samples per ray. spcqueryfunc: Callable that takes (N numsamples, 3) coordinates and returns (N numsamples,) pidx. Returns: Dictionary containing filtered samples, depths, deltas, rayindices, and packboundaries. """ N = origins.shape[0] # 1. Generate base depths with jitter basedepths = torch.linspace(0.0, 1.0, numsamples, device=origins.device) jitter = torch.rand(numsamples, device=origins.device) / numsamples normdepths = basedepths + jitter # (numsamples,) # 2. Normalize to ray range normdepths = normdepths.unsqueeze(0) # (1, numsamples) distminexp = distmin.unsqueeze(1) if distmin.dim() == 1 else distmin distmaxexp = distmax.unsqueeze(1) if distmax.dim() == 1 else distmax depths = normdepths (distmaxexp - distminexp) + distminexp # (N, numsamples) # 3. Compute sample coordinates depths3d = depths.unsqueeze(2) # (N, numsamples, 1) samples = origins.unsqueeze(1) + depths3d directions.unsqueeze(1) # (N, numsamples, 3) # 4. Query SPC flatsamples = samples.reshape(-1, 3) # (N numsamples, 3) pidx = spcqueryfunc(flatsamples) # (N numsamples,) # 5. Create mask mask = pidx > -1 # (N numsamples,) # 6. Compute deltas deltasdiff = torch.diff(depths, dim=1) # (N, numsamples - 1) deltas = torch.cat([distminexp, deltasdiff], dim=1) # (N, numsamples) # 7. Filter flatdepths = depths.reshape(-1) flatdeltas = deltas.reshape(-1) flatrayindices = torch.arange(N, device=origins.device).repeatinterleave(numsamples) validsamples = flatsamples[mask] validdepths = flatdepths[mask] validdeltas = flatdeltas[mask] validrayindices = flatrayindices[mask] # 8. Mark pack boundaries shiftedrayindices = torch.roll(validrayindices, 1) shiftedrayindices[0] = -1 packboundaries = validrayindices != shiftedrayindices return { "samples": validsamples, "depths": validdepths, "deltas": validdeltas, "rayindices": validrayindices, "packboundaries": packboundaries } A raymarching strategy that intersects rays with SPC cells and samples points at uniform distances determined by the cell geometry. It calls raytrace(rays, level, withexit=True) to get intersection depths. It calculates stepsize as 2\sqrt{3} / \text{num\samples}, scales it to an integer scale, and normalizes stepsize to 1.0/\text{scale}. It calculates interval counts for each intersection by scaling depth intervals and taking the ceiling difference. It filters out intersections with zero interval counts. It computes an inclusive sum of interval counts for indexing. It calls uniformsamplecuda kernel with scale, filtered indices, depths, and inclusive sum. It computes deltas as constant stepsize for all samples. It computes sample coordinates using ray origins, directions, and depth samples. Parameter: numsamples determines the uniform step distance, calculated as 2\sqrt{3}/\text{num\samples} initially. Pitfall: NUMINTERSECTIONS can be 0. A raymarching strategy that first intersects rays with Sparse Point Cloud (SPC) cells, then samples a fixed number of points within each intersected cell. It calls raytrace(rays, level, withexit=True) to get ray indices (ridx), point indices (pidx), and depth intervals (depth) for each intersection. It generates depth samples within each interval by calling samplefromdepthintervals(depth, numsamples) and appending a dimension. It computes depth deltas by taking the difference of depthsamples along the last dimension, prepending the start depth of the interval. It computes sample coordinates by adding the product of ray origins/directions and depth samples using torch.addcmul. It creates a boundary mask marking the start of each sample pack by expanding the first-hit mask of each intersection. It flattens ridx, samples, and depthsamples to a single list of size numintersections numsamples. Parameter: numsamples is the number of samples generated per voxel intersection. Pitfall: NUMINTERSECTIONS can be 0, meaning no cells were hit by any ray. Time Complexity: O(N \cdot S) for generating samples and querying the SPC, where N is the number of rays and S is numsamples. Filtering is O(N \cdot S). The SPC query cost depends on the structure. Memory Complexity: O(N \cdot S) for storing intermediate tensors before filtering. The output size is variable but bounded by N \cdot S. Performance: Efficient for scenes with high occupancy where most samples are valid. In sparse scenes, the filtering step discards many samples, but the initial generation cost remains. Strengths: Simple to implement; provides uniform sampling density in space; jitter reduces banding. Limitations: Wastes computation on empty space if the scene is sparse; numsamples must be chosen to balance coverage and performance; potential for NUMHITSAMPLES = 0 in empty scenes. When to use: When a uniform sampling distribution is desired and the scene has significant occupied volume. When not to use: In very sparse scenes where most rays hit empty space, as the filtering overhead may not justify the uniform sampling benefit; consider SPC Voxel Raymarching instead. This method is part of the NVIDIA Kaolin-Wisp framework, specifically within the wisp.tracers module, designed for efficient neural radiance field rendering. It builds on the concept of uniform ray sampling but integrates occupancy filtering via Sparse Point Cloud (SPC) structures to optimize computation in sparse environments. name: Near-Far Linear Ray Generation with Stratified Sampling
head: Stratified Ray Sampling
body: This method generates ray samples along a near-far segment by dividing the depth range into equal intervals and drawing one uniform random sample from each interval, ensuring low-discrepancy coverage. It differs from uniform jittered sampling by guaranteeing that every sub-interval contributes exactly one sample, reducing variance in scenes with high-frequency detail. It builds on Near-Far Linear Ray Generation by adding stratification logic to the base linear spacing. Inputs: tmin: Near plane distance (scalar or tensor). tmax: Far plane distance (scalar or tensor). numsamples: Integer count of samples per ray. depthmode: String specifying interpolation space: 'linear', 'geometric', or 'harmonic'. epsilon: Small constant to prevent division by zero or log(0) in non-linear modes. Default: 10^{-3}. Outputs: samples: Tensor of shape [..., numsamples, 1] containing the final 3D positions along the ray. Data Structures: ts: Intermediate tensor of shape [..., numsamples] storing interpolated depth values. trand: Tensor of shape [..., numsamples] storing uniform random noise in [0, 1]. Steps: 1. Base Timestamps: Generate base timestamps ts{base} using linear spacing from 0 to 1. ts{base} = \text{linspace}(0, 1, \text{num\samples}) Reshape to [..., numsamples]. 2. Interpolation: Compute interpolated timestamps ts based on depthmode: Linear: ts = t{min} (1 - ts{base}) + t{max} ts{base}. Geometric: Interpolate in log-space. Clamp t{min}, t{max} by \epsilon first. ts = \exp\left( \log(\max(t{min}, \epsilon)) (1 - ts{base}) + \log(\max(t{max}, \epsilon)) ts{base} \right) This samples closer points more densely. Harmonic: Interpolate in inverse-space. Clamp t{min}, t{max} by \epsilon first. ts = \frac{1}{\frac{1}{\max(t{min}, \epsilon)} (1 - ts{base}) + \frac{1}{\max(t{max}, \epsilon)} ts{base}} Recommended for spherical scenes. 3. Interval Bounds: Define the boundaries of each stratified interval. Compute midpoints: mids = 0.5 (ts{1:} + ts{:-1}). Lower bounds: lower = [t{min}, mids]. Upper bounds: upper = [mids, t{max}]. Note: If depthmode is 'linear', ts represents the sorted sample positions. The intervals are defined by these sorted positions. For 'geometric' and 'harmonic', ts are the sorted positions in their respective metric spaces, but the physical interval bounds for stratification are derived from the sorted ts values. 4. Stratified Sampling: Draw uniform random noise t{rand} \sim U[0, 1] with shape [..., numsamples]. Compute final depth values: t{final} = lower + (upper - lower) \cdot t{rand} This ensures one sample per interval. 5. Position Calculation: Compute step size for verification or alternative implementation: dt = (t{max} - t{min}) / \text{num\samples}. Compute sample position: p = \text{ray\origin} + \text{ray\direction} \cdot t{final} Note: The sources describe two slightly different approaches. computes positions from the stratified t{final} derived from sorted ts. describes a loop-based approach: t = t{min} + dt \cdot (i + \text{random}()). The vectorized approach is preferred for implementation as it avoids loops and handles arbitrary depthmode interpolation consistently. 6. Output: Return positions unsqueezed at the last dimension: samples = tfinal.unsqueeze(-1). Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import torch import math def stratifiedsampleray(tmin, tmax, numsamples, depthmode='linear', epsilon=1e-3): """ Generate stratified samples along a ray segment. Args: tmin: Tensor of near distances. tmax: Tensor of far distances. numsamples: int, number of samples per ray. depthmode: str, 'linear', 'geometric', or 'harmonic'. epsilon: float, small value for clamping. Returns: samples: Tensor of shape [..., numsamples, 1] with 3D positions relative to origin (depth values). """ # 1. Generate base timestamps # linspace(0, 1, numsamples) creates [0, 1/(N-1),..., 1] tsbase = torch.linspace(0, 1, numsamples, device=tmin.device) # Reshape to broadcast correctly if tmin/tmax are batched # Assuming tmin/tmax shape [...], tsbase shape [numsamples] # We need tsbase to broadcast: [..., numsamples] tsbase = tsbase.view([1] tmin.dim() + [numsamples]) # 2. Interpolate based on depthmode if depthmode == 'linear': ts = tmin (1.0 - tsbase) + tmax tsbase elif depthmode == 'geometric': # Clamp to epsilon to avoid log(0) tminc = torch.clamp(tmin, min=epsilon) tmaxc = torch.clamp(tmax, min=epsilon) logtmin = torch.log(tminc) logtmax = torch.log(tmaxc) ts = torch.exp(logtmin (1.0 - tsbase) + logtmax tsbase) elif depthmode == 'harmonic': # Clamp to epsilon to avoid division by zero tminc = torch.clamp(tmin, min=epsilon) tmaxc = torch.clamp(tmax, min=epsilon) invtmin = 1.0 / tminc invtmax = 1.0 / tmaxc ts = 1.0 / (invtmin (1.0 - tsbase) + invtmax tsbase) else: raise ValueError(f"Unknown depthmode: {depthmode}") # 3. Compute interval bounds from sorted ts # ts is already sorted because tsbase is sorted and interpolation is monotonic # Midpoints between adjacent samples # ts shape: [..., numsamples] # mids shape: [..., numsamples - 1] mids = 0.5 (ts[..., 1:] + ts[...,:-1]) # Lower bounds: [tmin, mids0, mids1,...] # Upper bounds: [mids0, mids1,..., tmax] # We need to stack these to get [..., numsamples] # Construct lower bounds # lower[0] = tmin, lower[1:] = mids lower = torch.cat([tmin.unsqueeze(-1), mids], dim=-1) # Construct upper bounds # upper[0:-1] = mids, upper[-1] = tmax upper = torch.cat([mids, tmax.unsqueeze(-1)], dim=-1) # 4. Draw uniform random noise trand = torch.randlike(ts) # 5. Sample final positions tsfinal = lower + (upper - lower) trand # 6. Return unsqueezed return tsfinal.unsqueeze(-1) Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Harmonic Interpolation: Edge cases occur when the observer crosses from the inner to outer volume, potentially causing discontinuities or invalid depths if t{min} or t{max} are negative or zero. Clamping with \epsilon mitigates this. Zero Distance: If t{min} = 0, geometric and harmonic modes require clamping to \epsilon to avoid \log(0) or 1/0. Ordering: The method assumes t{min} < t{max}. If not, results are undefined. Filters samples outside the viewing frustum. Use when rays must be discarded before marching. Samples based on a learned or analytical distribution. Use when importance sampling is required. Extends stratification to disparity space. Use for stereo or multi-view consistency. Adaptive sampling based on depth variance. Use for high-detail regions. Computes t{min}, t{max} from scene data. Use when bounds are not known a priori. Skips empty space. Use with stratified sampling to improve efficiency in sparse volumes. Time Complexity: O(N) per ray, where N is numsamples. The vectorized implementation avoids loops, making it efficient on GPUs. Memory Complexity: O(N) per ray for storing ts, lower, upper, and trand. Performance: Typical numsamples is 384. Performance scales linearly with resolution and sample count. Strengths: Low variance compared to pure random sampling; simple to implement; supports multiple interpolation modes. Limitations: Does not adapt to scene content; harmonic mode can be unstable near zero. When to Use: General-purpose volume rendering where uniform coverage is desired; spherical scenes (use harmonic mode). When Not to Use: Scenes with highly non-uniform density where importance sampling is needed; use Inverse CDF Ray Sampling instead. Originating from computer graphics literature on stratified sampling, this method is implemented in modern neural rendering frameworks. (gsgen3d/gsgen) uses it for 3D generation, supporting linear, geometric, and harmonic modes. (OctaNeRF) uses a loop-based variant for distillation. The method is widely used in NeRF and Gaussian Splatting pipelines for ray sampling. gsgen3d/gsgen, https://github.com/gsgen3d/gsgen, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial) mdmubarak/OctaNeRF, https://github.com/mdmubarak/OctaNeRF, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial)

name: SpacedSampler
head: Spaced Ray Sampler
body: The SpacedSampler is a base class for sampling points along a ray according to a user-defined spacing function and its inverse. It generalizes linear, disparity, and logarithmic sampling by mapping Euclidean distances to a "spacing space," performing uniform stratified sampling in that space, and mapping the results back to Euclidean space. It builds on Near-Far Linear Ray Generation by allowing arbitrary non-linear spacing functions rather than just linear interpolation. Inputs: near: Tensor of shape (numrays,) containing near-plane distances. far: Tensor of shape (numrays,) containing far-plane distances. numsamples: Integer, number of samples per ray. spacingfn: Callable mapping Euclidean distance d to spacing coordinate s. spacingfninv: Callable mapping spacing coordinate s back to Euclidean distance d. trainstratified: Boolean, default True. singlejitter: Boolean, default False. Outputs: RaySamples object containing: starts: Tensor of shape (numrays, numsamples) with Euclidean start positions. ends: Tensor of shape (numrays, numsamples) with Euclidean end positions. spacingstarts: Tensor of shape (numrays, numsamples) with spacing-space start positions. spacingends: Tensor of shape (numrays, numsamples) with spacing-space end positions. spacingtoeuclideanfn: Helper function for interpolation. Data Structures: bins: Tensor of shape (numrays, numsamples + 1) in spacing space. bincenters: Tensor of shape (numrays, numsamples) in spacing space. binlower, binupper: Tensors of shape (numrays, numsamples) in spacing space. trand: Random jitter tensor. Steps: 1. Compute uniform bins in spacing space: \text{bins} = \text{linspace}(0.0, 1.0, \text{num\samples} + 1) Shape: (numrays, numsamples + 1). 2. Generate stratified jitter if training and stratified sampling is enabled: If singlejitter is True: trand has shape (numrays, 1). Otherwise: trand has shape (numrays, numsamples + 1). Values are drawn from a uniform distribution U(0, 1). 3. Calculate bin centers in spacing space: \text{bin\centers} = \frac{\text{bins}[:, 1:] + \text{bins}[:,:-1]}{2.0} Shape: (numrays, numsamples). 4. Construct bin lower and upper bounds in spacing space: \text{bin\lower} = \text{concat}([\text{bins}[:,:1], \text{bin\centers}], \text{axis}=-1) \text{bin\upper} = \text{concat}([\text{bin\centers}, \text{bins}[:, -1:]], \text{axis}=-1) Shapes: (numrays, numsamples). 5. Apply stratified jitter to bins: \text{bins} = \text{bin\lower} + (\text{bin\upper} - \text{bin\lower}) \times \text{t\rand} Shape: (numrays, numsamples). 6. Transform ray near and far distances into spacing space: s{\text{near}} = \text{spacing\fn}(\text{near}) s{\text{far}} = \text{spacing\fn}(\text{far}) Shapes: (numrays,). 7. Define helper function for mapping spacing-space interpolation to Euclidean space: \text{spacing\to\euclidean\fn}(x) = \text{spacing\fn\inv}(x \cdot s{\text{far}} + (1 - x) \cdot s{\text{near}}) This function interpolates linearly in spacing space between s{\text{near}} and s{\text{far}}, then maps the result back to Euclidean distance. 8. Map the spacing-space bins to Euclidean space: \text{euclidean\bins} = \text{spacing\to\euclidean\fn}(\text{bins}) Shape: (numrays, numsamples). 9. Create RaySamples using: starts: euclideanbins ends: euclideanbins shifted by one index (or computed similarly for bin ends) spacingstarts: bins spacingends: bins shifted by one index spacingtoeuclideanfn: The helper function defined in step 7. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import torch def spacedsampler(near, far, numsamples, spacingfn, spacingfninv, trainstratified=True, singlejitter=False): """ Samples points along a ray using a user-defined spacing function. Args: near: Tensor of shape (numrays,) with near-plane distances. far: Tensor of shape (numrays,) with far-plane distances. numsamples: Integer, number of samples per ray. spacingfn: Callable mapping Euclidean distance to spacing coordinate. spacingfninv: Callable mapping spacing coordinate to Euclidean distance. trainstratified: Boolean, default True. singlejitter: Boolean, default False. Returns: RaySamples object with starts, ends, spacingstarts, spacingends, and spacingtoeuclideanfn. """ numrays = near.shape[0] # Step 1: Compute uniform bins in spacing space # bins shape: (numrays, numsamples + 1) bins = torch.linspace(0.0, 1.0, numsamples + 1, device=near.device).unsqueeze(0).expand(numrays, -1) # Step 2: Generate stratified jitter if trainstratified: if singlejitter: trand = torch.rand(numrays, 1, device=near.device) else: trand = torch.rand(numrays, numsamples + 1, device=near.device) else: trand = torch.zeroslike(bins) # Step 3: Calculate bin centers # bincenters shape: (numrays, numsamples) bincenters = (bins[:, 1:] + bins[:,:-1]) / 2.0 # Step 4: Construct bin lower and upper bounds # binlower, binupper shape: (numrays, numsamples) binlower = torch.cat([bins[:,:1], bincenters], dim=-1) binupper = torch.cat([bincenters, bins[:, -1:]], dim=-1) # Step 5: Apply stratified jitter to bins # bins shape: (numrays, numsamples) bins = binlower + (binupper - binlower) trand # Step 6: Transform ray near and far distances into spacing space # snear, sfar shape: (numrays,) snear = spacingfn(near) sfar = spacingfn(far) # Step 7: Define helper function def spacingtoeuclideanfn(x): # x shape: (numrays, numsamples) # Interpolate in spacing space and map back to Euclidean # snear, sfar need to be broadcasted to (numrays, numsamples) snearexpanded = snear.unsqueeze(-1) sfarexpanded = sfar.unsqueeze(-1) sinterp = x sfarexpanded + (1 - x) snearexpanded return spacingfninv(sinterp) # Step 8: Map the spacing-space bins to Euclidean space # euclideanbins shape: (numrays, numsamples) euclideanbins = spacingtoeuclideanfn(bins) # Step 9: Create RaySamples # Note: The source describes creating RaySamples with starts, ends, spacingstarts, spacingends. # For simplicity, we assume starts/ends are the bin centers or bin edges. # The source says "Create RaySamples using the Euclidean bin starts and ends". # We will use bincenters as the sample points, and binlower/binupper as the intervals. # However, RaySamples typically expects start and end of each interval. # Let's assume the samples are the intervals defined by binlower and binupper in spacing space, # mapped to Euclidean space. # Euclidean starts and ends for each sample interval euclideanstarts = spacingtoeuclideanfn(binlower) euclideanends = spacingtoeuclideanfn(binupper) # Spacing starts and ends spacingstarts = binlower spacingends = binupper return { 'starts': euclideanstarts, 'ends': euclideanends, 'spacingstarts': spacingstarts, 'spacingends': spacingends, 'spacingtoeuclideanfn': spacingtoeuclideanfn } Parameters: spacingfn: A callable that maps Euclidean distance to spacing coordinate. spacingfninv: A callable that maps spacing coordinate back to Euclidean distance. trainstratified: Boolean flag, default True, to use stratified sampling during training. singlejitter: Boolean flag, default False, to use a single random jitter value for all samples along a ray instead of one per sample. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision: When spacingfn or spacingfninv involve logarithms or square roots, ensure inputs are positive to avoid NaNs or complex numbers. Boundaries: Ensure near and far are positive and near < far. Degenerate Input: If numsamples is 0, the method should return empty tensors. A piecewise sampler that allocates the first half of samples uniformly and the second half using linearly in disparity spacing. It uses the spacing function s(x) = x/2 if x < 1 else 1 - 1/(2x) and its inverse s^{-1}(s) = 2s if s < 0.5 else 1/(2 - 2s). Parameters: numsamples, trainstratified (default True), singlejitter (default False). Samples points uniformly along a ray in Euclidean space. It initializes SpacedSampler with spacingfn = lambda x: x and spacingfninv = lambda x: x. Samples points linearly in disparity (inverse depth) along a ray. It initializes SpacedSampler with spacingfn = lambda x: 1/x and spacingfninv = lambda x: 1/x. Samples points using a square root spacing function along a ray. It initializes SpacedSampler with spacingfn = torch.sqrt and spacingfninv = lambda x: x2. Samples points using a logarithmic spacing function along a ray. It initializes SpacedSampler with spacingfn = torch.log and spacingfninv = torch.exp. Not given in the sources. The SpacedSampler is part of the nerfstudio project, a collaboration-friendly studio for NeRFs. It was introduced as part of the nerfstudio codebase to provide a flexible way to sample points along rays for volume rendering. nerfstudio-project/nerfstudio, https://github.com/nerfstudio-project/nerfstudio, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial)

name: Batch Stratified Pixel Sampling
head: Pixel Sampling and Ground Truth Retrieval
body: Batch Stratified Pixel Sampling is a method used in neural reconstruction pipelines to select a subset of pixels for optimization at each training iteration. Inputs: Target image (texture) containing ground-truth color values. Batch size Nb. Image dimensions W \times H. Outputs: A set of Nb pixel coordinates (u, v) and their corresponding ground-truth color values. Data Structures: Pixel coordinates: Floating-point pairs (u, v) representing sub-pixel locations. Ground-truth values: Floating-point vectors (e.g., RGB) retrieved via interpolation. Steps: 1. Stratified Sampling: Divide the image grid into a grid of strata and sample pixel coordinates within each stratum. 2. Ground-Truth Retrieval: Obtain ground-truth values at the sampled coordinates via bilinear interpolation on the target image. 3. Efficient Lookup: Implement the bilinear interpolation as a CUDA texture lookup for hardware-accelerated efficiency. Parameters: Batch size Nb: Number of pixels to sample. Strata count: Not specified in sources. Edge Cases: Boundary conditions and precision behavior: Not given in the sources. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import random def batchstratifiedpixelsampling(targetimage, batchsize, width, height): """ Samples a batch of pixels using stratified sampling and retrieves ground truth. Args: targetimage: 2D array of pixel values. batchsize: Number of pixels to sample. width: Image width in pixels. height: Image height in pixels. Returns: pixels: List of (u, v) coordinates. gtvalues: List of interpolated color values. """ pixels = [] gtvalues = [] # Standard stratified sampling: divide image into strata grid strataside = int(round(batchsize 0.5)) if strataside strataside < batchsize: strataside += 1 strataw = width / strataside stratah = height / strataside for i in range(strataside): for j in range(strataside): if len(pixels) >= batchsize: break # Sample uniform sub-pixel coordinate within stratum u = (i + random.uniform(0, 1)) strataw v = (j + random.uniform(0, 1)) stratah # Clip to image bounds u = max(0.0, min(u, float(width - 1))) v = max(0.0, min(v, float(height - 1))) pixels.append((u, v)) # Bilinear interpolation via CUDA texture lookup gtvalues.append(bilinearinterpolate(targetimage, u, v, width, height)) if len(pixels) >= batchsize: break return pixels, gtvalues def bilinearinterpolate(image, x, y, width, height): x0, y0 = int(x), int(y) x1, y1 = min(x0 + 1, width - 1), min(y0 + 1, height - 1) dx, dy = x - x0, y - y0 c00 = image[y0][x0] c01 = image[y0][x1] c10 = image[y1][x0] c11 = image[y1][x1] return (1 - dx) (1 - dy) c00 + dx (1 - dy) c01 + (1 - dx) dy c10 + dx dy c11 A variant used in interaction-aware pruning of 3D Gaussian Splatting. It selects view-pixel pairs by sampling around projected Gaussian centers and their neighbors to evaluate opacity responses, rather than using uniform stratified sampling. Definition: Selects a set of view-pixel pairs Pb for a block Cb by sampling around projected Gaussian centers and their neighbors. Steps: 1. Initialize Pb \leftarrow \emptyset and D \leftarrow \{(0, 0), (\pm0.5, 0), (0, \pm0.5), (\pm0.35, \pm0.35)\}. 2. For each selected view v: a. Obtain projected centers u{vi} and screen radii h{vi} for i \in Cb. b. Generate pixel locations p = \text{round}(u{vi} + \max(h{vi}, 1)\delta) for h{vi} > 0 and \delta \in D. c. Remove duplicate pixels and discard those outside the image boundaries. d. Add remaining view-pixel pairs (v, p) to Pb. 3. Return Pb. Formula: Candidate locations: u{vi} + \max(h{vi}, 1)\delta, where \delta \in D = \{(0, 0), (\pm0.5, 0), (0, \pm0.5), (\pm0.35, \pm0.35)\}. Parameters: D: Set of 9 offset vectors (center + 8 neighbors) used for pixel sampling. Not given in the sources. Not given in the sources.
