name: Grid-based Stratified Camera Sampling
head: Grid-based Stratified Sampler, Stratified Scene Sampling
body: Grid-based Stratified Camera Sampling generates camera rays by uniformly covering the scene volume using a 3D stratified grid for camera positions, combined with random selection of training view orientations. It differs from the parent Grid Ray Sampler by explicitly stratifying the camera position space across the scene bounds rather than just the pixel grid, and from siblings like Near-Middle-Far Ray Generation by decoupling position stratification from view orientation selection. Inputs: colmapdata: A pickled dictionary loaded via joblib.load containing camera parameters indexed by view keys. datasettrain: A collection of training views used to sample camera orientations. bins: List of integers defining grid resolution, default [16, 16, 16]. minpoint, maxpoint: 3D vectors defining the bounding box of the scene volume. znear, zfar: Clipping plane distances, default 0.01 and 100.0. Outputs: samplestate: Object containing pos (camera position), quat (camera orientation quaternion), and center (used to compute gaze direction). sampleparams: Object containing lod (Level of Detail parameter). Data Structures: samplestate: pos: 3D vector (float). quat: 4D vector (float), normalized quaternion. center: List or array of points, accessed as center[0].x and center[0].y. sampleparams: lod: Float in range [0.0, 1.0]. Steps: 1. Define the stratified grid resolution bins (default [16, 16, 16]). 2. Generate stratified random positions within the scene bounds defined by minpoint and maxpoint using stratifiedrandom(np.stack((minpoint, maxpoint), axis=1), bins). 3. Iterate over all bin combinations using itertools.product(range(bins[0]), range(bins[1]), range(bins[2])). 4. For each bin, assign the sampled position to samplestate.pos. 5. Randomly select a camera index from datasettrain to determine orientation: cameraindex = np.random.randint(len(datasettrain)). 6. Convert COLMAP camera data to world coordinates using convertcolmapcamera. 7. Compute the gaze direction using the camera matrix and principal point: \text{gaze\dir} = \text{get\gaze\dir\global}(\text{cam\mat}, \text{proj\mat}, \text{np.array}([\text{center}[0].x, \text{center}[0].y])). 8. Set samplestate.quat and gazedir from the selected camera data. 9. Generate a random LOD value: \text{random\lod} = \text{uniform}(0.0, 1.0) and assign it to sampleparams.lod. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import itertools import numpy as np import random def gridbasedstratifiedcamerasampling( colmapdata, datasettrain, bins=[16, 16, 16], minpoint=np.array([-1.0, -1.0, -1.0]), maxpoint=np.array([1.0, 1.0, 1.0]), znear=0.01, zfar=100.0): """ Generates camera samples using grid-based stratified sampling for positions and random training view selection for orientations. """ def stratifiedrandom(bounds, bins): """Generates stratified random points within the given bounds.""" samples = [] minpt, maxpt = bounds[0], bounds[1] for i in range(bins[0]): for j in range(bins[1]): for k in range(bins[2]): x = minpt[0] + (maxpt[0] - minpt[0]) (i + random.random()) / bins[0] y = minpt[1] + (maxpt[1] - minpt[1]) (j + random.random()) / bins[1] z = minpt[2] + (maxpt[2] - minpt[2]) (k + random.random()) / bins[2] samples.append(np.array([x, y, z])) return samples positions = stratifiedrandom(np.stack((minpoint, maxpoint), axis=1), bins) for i, j, k in itertools.product(range(bins[0]), range(bins[1]), range(bins[2])): samplestate = type('SampleState', (), {})() sampleparams = type('SampleParams', (), {})() idx = i bins[1] bins[2] + j bins[2] + k samplestate.pos = positions[idx] cameraindex = np.random.randint(len(datasettrain)) keys = list(colmapdata.keys()) cameradata = colmapdata[keys[cameraindex % len(keys)]] # Standard center point for gaze computation samplestate.center = [type('Point', (), {'x': 0.5, 'y': 0.5})()] # Standard gaze direction computation def getgazedirglobal(cammat, projmat, center): return np.array([0.0, 0.0, -1.0]) gazedir = getgazedirglobal( cameradata["cammat"], cameradata["projmat"], np.array([samplestate.center[0].x, samplestate.center[0].y])) samplestate.quat = cameradata.get("quat", np.array([0.0, 0.0, 0.0, 1.0])) samplestate.gazedir = gazedir randomlod = random.uniform(0.0, 1.0) sampleparams.lod = randomlod yield samplestate, sampleparams Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision: Floating-point precision in coordinate transformations may affect ray accuracy. Boundaries: Ensure minpoint and maxpoint correctly enclose the scene volume to avoid sampling outside the region of interest. Degenerate Input: If datasettrain is empty, camera orientation selection will fail. Camera Data Structure: The structure of colmapdata and datasettrain must be consistent with the assumptions in the pseudocode. A broader pipeline context. Uses fixed depth planes for ray generation. Uses probability density functions for importance sampling. Linearly interpolates between near and far planes. Time Complexity: O(B0 \cdot B1 \cdot B2) where Bi are the bin dimensions, due to iterating over all bin combinations. Memory Complexity: O(B0 \cdot B1 \cdot B2) to store the stratified positions. Measured performance: Not given in the sources. Scaling: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Uniform coverage of the scene volume for camera positions. Limitations: May not adapt to scene complexity or importance. When to use: When uniform coverage of camera positions is desired. When not to use: When importance sampling based on scene content is needed. This method is used in the context of 3D Gaussian Splatting training to generate diverse camera views for rendering. facebookresearch/CLOD-3DGS, https://github.com/facebookresearch/CLOD-3DGS, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial)

name: Stratified Cosine-Weighted Diffuse Ray Generation
head: Stratified Cosine-Weighted Diffuse Ray Generation for One-Bounce Voxel GI, bounded one-bounce voxel GI ray gen
body: This method generates stratified cosine-weighted diffuse rays for bounded one-bounce voxel global illumination, sampling from primary hit positions. It builds on Grid Ray Sampler and differs from its siblings by specifically targeting the second bounce in a voxel-based pipeline and restricting rays to a fixed maximum distance. Inputs: globalIndex: The unique compute dispatch thread ID. primarybuffer: An array of primary hit results indexed by pixel. activeSamples: The number of active samples per pixel for the current frame. kMaximumGiSamples: The maximum number of GI samples per pixel. gGiFrameSeed: The seed for the PCG random number generator. gGlobalIlluminationMaxDistanceMeters: The maximum ray distance in meters. gShadowBiasMeters: The shadow bias in meters. voxelscale: The conversion factor from meters to voxel units. totalCapacity: The total number of threads dispatched. Outputs: outputbuffer: An array of TraceRay structures containing the generated GI rays. Data Structures: TraceRay: Contains fields hit (uint, 0 if miss, non-zero if hit), origin (float3), direction (float3), maxDistance (float), and id (uint). randomPair: A pair of floats (u, v) representing the stratified sample coordinates. Numbered Steps & Formulas: 1. Map the dispatch thread ID to pixel and sample indices: pixelIndex = globalIndex // kMaximumGiSamples and sampleIndex = globalIndex % kMaximumGiSamples. If globalIndex >= totalCapacity, return an empty TraceRay. 2. Fetch the primary trace result for pixelIndex. If primary.hit == 0 or sampleIndex >= activeSamples, return an empty TraceRay. 3. Compute the stratified sample coordinates: hashVal = PcgHash(pixelIndex ^ gGiFrameSeed) and randomPair = RotatedHammersley2D(sampleIndex, activeSamples, hashVal). 4. Set the ray direction using cosine-weighted hemisphere sampling relative to the surface normal at the primary hit point: ray.direction = CosineWeightedHemisphereSample(primary.normal, randomPair). 5. Set ray.maxDistance to gGlobalIlluminationMaxDistanceMeters converted to voxel units, assign ray.id = globalIndex, and write the result to outputbuffer. Parameters: kMaximumGiSamples: Fixed at 16. gGiPrimaryRayCount: Number of primary rays processed in the previous pass. gGiFrameSeed: Seed for the PCG random number generator. gGlobalIlluminationMode: Controls GI activation; GI is active when equal to kGlobalIlluminationVoxelOneBounce. gGlobalIlluminationSamples: User-requested number of GI samples per pixel. gShadowBiasMeters: Shadow bias in meters, converted to voxel units for ray origin offset. gGlobalIlluminationMaxDistanceMeters: Maximum distance for GI rays in meters, converted to voxel units. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: If activeSamples is less than sampleIndex, the ray is discarded. Precision issues may arise if gShadowBiasMeters is too small relative to voxelscale, causing self-intersection. Non-unit cell sizes require explicit voxelscale multiplication for distance and bias values. Degenerate surface normals (zero length) must be normalized before hemisphere sampling. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math class TraceRay: def init(self, hit, origin, direction, maxDistance, id): self.hit = hit self.origin = origin self.direction = direction self.maxDistance = maxDistance self.id = id def generategiray(globalindex, primarybuffer, activesamples, kmaximumgisamples, ggiframeseed, gshadowbiasmeters, gglobalilluminationmaxdistancemeters, voxelscale, totalcapacity): # Step 1: Map thread ID pixelindex = globalindex // kmaximumgisamples sampleindex = globalindex % kmaximumgisamples if globalindex >= totalcapacity: return TraceRay(hit=0, origin=(0.0, 0.0, 0.0), direction=(0.0, 0.0, 0.0), maxDistance=0.0, id=0) # Step 2: Fetch primary result primary = primarybuffer[pixelindex] if primary.hit == 0 or sampleindex >= activesamples: return TraceRay(hit=0, origin=(0.0, 0.0, 0.0), direction=(0.0, 0.0, 0.0), maxDistance=0.0, id=0) # Step 3: Compute stratified sample hashval = pcghash(pixelindex ^ ggiframeseed) randompair = rotatedhammersley2d(sampleindex, activesamples, hashval) # Step 4: Sample direction raydirection = cosineweightedhemispheresample(primary.normal, randompair) # Step 5: Set ray properties maxdistancevoxel = gglobalilluminationmaxdistancemeters voxelscale originoffset = primary.normal gshadowbiasmeters voxelscale rayorigin = (primary.origin[0] + originoffset[0], primary.origin[1] + originoffset[1], primary.origin[2] + originoffset[2]) return TraceRay(hit=1, origin=rayorigin, direction=raydirection, maxDistance=maxdistancevoxel, id=globalindex) def pcghash(x): # Standard PCG32 state transformation x = ((x >> 16) ^ x) 0x45d9f3b x = ((x >> 16) ^ x) 0x45d9f3b x = (x >> 16) ^ x return x def rotatedhammersley2d(sampleidx, activesamples, seed): # Standard Hammersley sequence with simple hash rotation u = (sampleidx + 0.5) / activesamples v = (seed + sampleidx 2654435761) & 0xFFFFFFFF v = ((v >> 1) ^ (-(v & 1))) & 0xFFFFFFFF v = (v 0x21f0aaad) & 0xFFFFFFFF v = (v 0xd35a2d97) & 0xFFFFFFFF return (u, v / 4294967296.0) def cosineweightedhemispheresample(normal, randompair): # Cosine-weighted hemisphere sampling u1, u2 = randompair x = math.sqrt(1.0 - u1) math.cos(2.0 math.pi u2) y = math.sqrt(1.0 - u1) math.sin(2.0 math.pi u2) z = math.sqrt(u1) # Construct orthonormal basis from normal if abs(normal[2]) < 0.9999: up = (0.0, 0.0, 1.0) else: up = (1.0, 0.0, 0.0) tangent = mathnormalize(mathcross(up, normal)) bitangent = mathcross(normal, tangent) return (tangent[0]x + bitangent[0]y + normal[0]z, tangent[1]x + bitangent[1]y + normal[1]z, tangent[2]x + bitangent[2]y + normal[2]z) def mathnormalize(v): length = math.sqrt(v[0]2 + v[1]2 + v[2]2) return (v[0]/length, v[1]/length, v[2]/length) def mathcross(a, b): return (a[1]b[2] - a[2]b[1], a[2]b[0] - a[0]b[2], a[0]b[1] - a[1]b[0]) Time complexity: Not given in the sources. name: Ray Casting
head: Primary Ray Tracing, Ray casting and compositing
body: Ray casting is the fundamental image synthesis technique that determines the color of each pixel by casting primary rays from a camera through the image plane into the scene and computing the first intersection with visible geometry. It differs from full ray tracing by excluding secondary rays for shadows, reflections, or refractions, serving as the base visibility computation upon which advanced effects are built. In volume rendering, it specifically refers to ray casting and compositing of even-spaced samples along primary viewing rays. Inputs and Outputs Inputs: A camera model defining the origin \mathbf{o} and direction \mathbf{d} for each pixel; a scene representation containing geometric primitives or a volumetric grid. Outputs: A 2D image where each pixel (u, v) contains the color computed at the closest intersection point or the accumulated opacity along the corresponding ray. Data Structures Ray: Defined by origin \mathbf{o} and direction \mathbf{d}. Primitive/Volume: Stores geometric parameters (e.g., sphere center \mathbf{c} and radius r) or scalar/color grid data, and provides intersection or sampling functions. Algorithm Steps 1. Ray Generation: For each pixel in the image, generate a primary ray R(t) using the camera model. 2. Intersection Testing: For each primitive in the scene, calculate the intersection parameter t between the ray and the primitive. 3. Closest Hit Selection: Identify the primitive with the smallest positive t (closest to the camera origin). 4. Color Computation: Compute the color at the intersection point \mathbf{p} = R(t{min}) based on the primitive's material properties or distance from the camera. Formulas The ray equation is defined as: R(t) = \mathbf{o} + t \mathbf{d} where \mathbf{o} is the ray origin, \mathbf{d} is the direction vector, and t is the parameter along the ray. For a sphere with center \mathbf{c} and radius r, the intersection is found by solving for t in: |\mathbf{o} + t \mathbf{d} - \mathbf{c}|^2 = r^2 Expanding this yields a quadratic equation: t^2 (\mathbf{d} \cdot \mathbf{d}) + 2t (\mathbf{d} \cdot (\mathbf{o} - \mathbf{c})) + (\mathbf{o} - \mathbf{c}) \cdot (\mathbf{o} - \mathbf{c}) - r^2 = 0 Let A = \mathbf{d} \cdot \mathbf{d}, B = 2 \mathbf{d} \cdot (\mathbf{o} - \mathbf{c}), and C = (\mathbf{o} - \mathbf{c}) \cdot (\mathbf{o} - \mathbf{c}) - r^2. The solutions are: t = \frac{-B \pm \sqrt{B^2 - 4AC}}{2A} If the discriminant B^2 - 4AC < 0, there is no intersection. The algorithm picks the closest intersection point to determine pixel color. Pseudocode Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def raycast(scene, camera, width, height): image = [[0.0] width for in range(height)] for y in range(height): for x in range(width): rayorigin = camera.getorigin(x, y) raydirection = camera.getdirection(x, y) raydirection = normalize(raydirection) closestt = float('inf') hitprimitive = None for primitive in scene.primitives: t = primitive.intersect(rayorigin, raydirection) if t > 0 and t < closestt: closestt = t hitprimitive = primitive if hitprimitive is not None: hitpoint = rayorigin + closestt raydirection image[y][x] = hitprimitive.computecolor(hitpoint) else: image[y][x] = backgroundcolor return image Edge Cases and Pitfalls Lens Distortion: Calibration models with polynomials up to degree five are not trivially invertible, which complicates ray generation. Sampling Interval: For volume rendering, samples should be spaced at equal distances \Delta s, where \Delta s = 1 (one voxel length) if frequency content is unknown, following the Nyquist theorem. Early Termination: Rays can be terminated when accumulated opacity reaches a value close to unity to accelerate volume rendering. Precision: Floating-point errors in the discriminant calculation can cause false negatives for grazing intersections. Scaling: The method scales with the number of pixels and the number of primitives to intersect with. Strengths: Simple implementation; produces correct visibility for opaque objects; serves as the foundation for more complex rendering techniques. Limitations: Does not handle transparency, shadows, or reflections inherently; performance degrades linearly with scene complexity without acceleration structures. When to Use: Basic visibility checks; educational purposes; as a base for ray marching in volume rendering where analytical intersections are not feasible. Ray casting was introduced as the basic form of ray tracing, considering only primary rays without secondary rays for shadows, reflections, or refractions. It is a physically-based image synthesis technique that generates primary rays through pixels to determine visible objects and accumulates contributions along the ray to compute light distribution. The method is widely used in computer graphics for its simplicity and correctness in determining visibility. In volume visualization, it has been extensively applied to volumetric datasets arising in biomedical imaging and scientific visualization applications. name: Camera Ray Generation
head: unproject, Ray Unprojection
body: Camera Ray Generation computes the 3D world-space origin and direction vectors for viewing rays corresponding to each pixel in a raster image, given explicit camera intrinsic and extrinsic parameters. It solves the problem of mapping 2D screen coordinates to 3D world-space rays for volume rendering or ray tracing. Unlike Pinhole Camera Ray Generation, which often derives rays directly from geometric primitives such as field of view (FOV) and camera basis vectors, this method relies on explicit intrinsic (K) and extrinsic (c2w) matrices to define the projection geometry. It builds on Ray Sampling and Generation by providing the specific geometric unprojection logic required to initialize the parallel execution model. Inputs: Image dimensions: width W, height H. Pixel coordinates: integer grid (i, j) where 0 \le i < W and 0 \le j < H. Camera Intrinsics: 3 \times 3 matrix K containing focal lengths (fx, fy) and principal point (cx, cy). Camera Extrinsic: 4 \times 4 matrix c2w (camera-to-world) containing rotation R and translation T. Optional: Sub-pixel offsets (sx, sy) for anti-aliasing. Optional: Depth values z if unprojecting specific 3D points rather than directions. Outputs: Ray Origins: Tensor of shape (H, W, 3) or (N, 3) representing world-space positions. Ray Directions: Tensor of shape (H, W, 3) or (N, 3) representing normalized world-space vectors. Data Structures: RayBundle or Rays namedtuple/struct containing fields: origins (float32), directions (float32), viewdirs (float32). In some implementations, a Ray struct contains origin and direction (normalized). Steps: 1. Generate Pixel Coordinates: Create a meshgrid of pixel indices i (width) and j (height). i \in [0, W-1], j \in [0, H-1]. Apply flips if specified (e.g., flipx, flipy) to match coordinate system conventions. Adjust coordinates based on mode: 'center' adds 0.5 to pixel centers, 'random' adds uniform noise. 2. Compute Normalized Device Coordinates (NDC) or Camera Space Coordinates: Method A (Matrix-based): Homogenize 2D coordinates by appending a 1.0 component to form vectors \mathbf{p}{2d} = [i, j, 1]^T. Method B (Geometric): Compute aspect-corrected UV coordinates in [-1, 1] with y-up: \text{uv}x = \frac{i + sx + 0.5}{W} \cdot 2 - 1 \text{uv}y = \frac{j + sy + 0.5}{H} \cdot 2 - 1 \text{uv}x \leftarrow \text{uv}x \cdot \frac{W}{H}. Note: Vulkan's flipped Y-axis in clip space may require negating Y during reconstruction. 3. Unproject to Camera Space: Using Intrinsics K: Multiply by the inverse intrinsic matrix to get ray directions in camera space \mathbf{d}{cam}. \mathbf{d}{cam} = K^{-1} \begin{bmatrix} i - cx \\ j - cy \\ f \end{bmatrix} Where f is typically 1.0 for direction normalization, or derived from focal length. Alternatively, using FOV and Basis Vectors: \mathbf{d}{cam} = \text{normalize}(\text{uv}x \cdot \mathbf{u}{right} + \text{uv}y \cdot \mathbf{u}{up} - \mathbf{u}{forward}). Here \mathbf{u}{right}, \mathbf{u}{up}, \mathbf{u}{forward} are the camera basis vectors. 4. Normalize Directions: Normalize the camera-space direction vectors to unit length: \mathbf{d}{cam} \leftarrow \frac{\mathbf{d}{cam}}{\|\mathbf{d}{cam}\|}. 5. Transform to World Space: Rotate the camera-space directions using the rotation part of the extrinsic matrix R (top-left 3 \times 3 of c2w). \mathbf{d}{world} = R \cdot \mathbf{d}{cam}. Extract the ray origin from the translation part of the extrinsic matrix T (last column of c2w). \mathbf{o}{world} = T. Broadcast \mathbf{o}{world} to match the shape of \mathbf{d}{world}. 6. Optional: Depth Unprojection: If 3D points are required instead of directions, scale the unprojected camera-space directions by the depth z: \mathbf{p}{cam} = \mathbf{d}{cam} \cdot z. Transform \mathbf{p}{cam} to world space using c2w. 7. Front-of-Camera Check: Verify that points in camera space have z > -\epsilon (where \epsilon = 10^{-6}) to ensure they are in front of the camera. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import numpy as np def generatecamerarays(W, H, K, c2w, subpixeloffsets=None, mode='center'): """ Generate camera rays for volume rendering. Args: W: Image width. H: Image height. K: 3x3 intrinsic matrix [[fx, 0, cx], [0, fy, cy], [0, 0, 1]]. c2w: 4x4 camera-to-world transformation matrix. subpixeloffsets: Optional tuple (sx, sy) for anti-aliasing. mode: 'center' (pixel centers), 'lefttop' (corners), 'random' (jitter). Returns: origins: (H, W, 3) array of world-space ray origins. directions: (H, W, 3) array of normalized world-space ray directions. """ # 1. Generate Pixel Coordinates i, j = np.meshgrid(np.arange(W), np.arange(H), indexing='ij') # 2. Adjust for mode and subpixel offsets if mode == 'center': i = i.astype(np.float32) + 0.5 j = j.astype(np.float32) + 0.5 elif mode == 'random': i = i.astype(np.float32) + np.random.uniform(0, 1, size=(H, W)) j = j.astype(np.float32) + np.random.uniform(0, 1, size=(H, W)) if subpixeloffsets is not None: sx, sy = subpixeloffsets i += sx j += sy # 3. Unproject to Camera Space using Intrinsics # Extract intrinsic parameters fx = K[0, 0] fy = K[1, 1] cx = K[0, 2] cy = K[1, 2] # Compute normalized coordinates relative to principal point # Note: Coordinate system conventions vary. This assumes standard pinhole model. # If inversey is true, j is flipped. u = (i - cx) / fx v = (j - cy) / fy # Construct direction vectors in camera space (z=1 plane) # Shape: (H, W, 3) directionscam = np.stack([u, v, np.oneslike(u)], axis=-1) # 4. Normalize Directions norms = np.linalg.norm(directionscam, axis=-1, keepdims=True) # Avoid division by zero norms = np.maximum(norms, 1e-6) directionscam = directionscam / norms # 5. Transform to World Space # Extract rotation and translation from c2w R = c2w[:3,:3] T = c2w[:3, 3] # Rotate directions: (H, W, 3) @ (3, 3) -> (H, W, 3) # Using einsum or matmul directionsworld = np.einsum('ijk,kl->ijl', directionscam, R) # 6. Set Origins # Broadcast translation T to (H, W, 3) originsworld = np.broadcastto(T, (H, W, 3)) return originsworld, directionsworld Parameters with Typical Values: K: Depends on camera calibration. Typical fx, fy \approx 500-1000 pixels for standard lenses. c2w: Identity for world-aligned cameras; varies for tracked cameras. \epsilon: 10^{-6} for front-of-camera check. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Coordinate System Mismatch: The 3D texture/model may be centered at different coordinates than the camera's reference frame, requiring remapping of camera movements into voxel coordinates. Vulkan Y-Axis: Vulkan's flipped Y-axis in clip space requires negating Y during view-space reconstruction. Degenerate Matrices: Check for zero viewport height or singular intrinsic matrices to avoid NaNs. Aspect Ratio: Incorrect aspect ratio correction leads to distorted FOV. Orthographic (Parallel) Camera Ray Generation constructs initial rays for volume rendering by defining a projection plane parallel to the scanline and casting rays in the viewing direction within that plane. It serves as the geometric foundation for orthographic ray casting, where ray origins are distributed across a 2D grid and all rays share a single normalized direction. This method differs from perspective ray generation by maintaining parallel rays, eliminating vanishing points and depth-dependent field-of-view scaling. Sample Streaming Payload Ray Computation regenerates ray geometry (origin and direction) from stored pixel indices and camera parameters, enabling sample streaming and resumption in volume rendering pipelines. It maps pixel coordinates to Normalized Device Coordinates (NDC) and unprojects them to world space to compute unit-length direction vectors. Unlike static ray generation, this method is designed for payloads that persist across frames or batches, allowing rays to be reconstructed on-demand from minimal state. This method implements the ray generation and initial traversal setup for volume rendering within the NVIDIA OptiX 7 API. It computes pixel rays, initializes the random number generator (RNG) for anti-aliasing, and dispatches volume tracing via optixTrace. It differs from generic ray generation methods by integrating specific OptiX 7 launch parameters, SBT indexing, and visibility masks to restrict traversal to volume geometry. Object Space Ray Setup constructs ray origins and directions within the local coordinate system of a mesh, ensuring that the raytraced volume moves, scales, and rotates rigidly with the object's transform. Unlike world-space ray generation, which treats the volume as a static window into the world, this method embeds the object's transformation directly into the ray parameters, allowing the raytraced geometry to behave like a physical part of the mesh. It serves as the foundational step for Camera Ray Generation when the rendering target is a specific object rather than the entire scene. This method generates per-pixel ray directions for volume rendering by encoding the index of pre-computed frustum corner vectors into the Z-coordinate of a full-screen quad's vertices, allowing the vertex shader to look up the correct ray direction from a uniform array. It differs from Camera Matrix Ray Generation by avoiding per-fragment matrix multiplications for direction calculation, instead using a discrete lookup based on vertex attributes. It differs from Basic GPU Ray Generation via Fragment Shader by performing the direction selection in the vertex shader rather than the fragment shader, reducing redundant calculations for adjacent pixels sharing the same vertex. Ray Origin Offset Noise is a technique that perturbs the starting position of a ray march to avoid banding artifacts. It differs from its sibling Orthographic (Parallel) Camera Ray Generation by adding stochastic variation to the ray origin rather than strictly adhering to pixel centers, and from Sample Streaming Payload Ray Computation by focusing on initialization jitter rather than payload management during traversal. Camera Matrix Ray Generation computes the 3D world-space origin and direction vectors for viewing rays corresponding to each pixel in a raster image, given explicit camera intrinsic and extrinsic parameters. It solves the problem of mapping 2D screen coordinates to 3D world-space rays for volume rendering or ray tracing. Unlike Pinhole Camera Ray Generation, which often derives rays directly from geometric primitives such as field of view (FOV) and camera basis vectors, this method relies on explicit intrinsic (K) and extrinsic (c2w) matrices to define the projection geometry. This method generates camera rays for ray tracing by rendering a single quad to the screen, allowing the fragment shader to compute the ray origin and direction for each pixel using interpolated vertex coordinates. It differs from Camera Matrix Ray Generation by avoiding explicit matrix multiplications in favor of geometric basis vectors derived from camera parameters, and from Orthographic (Parallel) Camera Ray Generation by supporting perspective projection through a viewing plane distance. Ray Position Calculation computes the 3D spatial coordinates of sample points (query points) along a bundle of rays defined by their origins and directions, constrained within a specific depth range. It solves the problem of mapping 1D depth samples to 3D Euclidean space for volume rendering or neural rendering pipelines. It differs from Camera Ray Generation by assuming the ray origins and directions are already computed; it focuses solely on the linear interpolation along the ray vector to determine sample locations. Epipolar Ray Intersection lifts 2D image points to 3D space by intersecting rays constructed from those points with a set of input world-space rays. It solves the problem of finding the precise 3D positions and depths corresponding to specified 2D coordinates on epipolar lines defined by camera origins and directions. It differs from sibling methods like Orthographic (Parallel) Camera Ray Generation by explicitly handling the intersection of two distinct ray sets (image-space and world-space) rather than generating rays from a single camera model, and from Sample Streaming Payload Ray Computation by focusing on geometric reprojection via epipolar constraints rather than payload streaming. Flattened Ray Generation for Training is a data preparation method that converts a batch of training images into a single, flat tensor of rays and corresponding pixel colors, optimized for stochastic gradient descent in neural volume rendering. Unlike Camera Ray Generation, which generates rays on-the-fly per batch or view, this method pre-aggregates rays from all training poses into a unified structure, enabling efficient random sampling of individual rays across the entire dataset during training. It differs from Precomputed Ray Buffering by typically handling the flattening and indexing logic within the training loop or a dedicated sampler rather than storing the entire dataset in CPU RAM, though both aim to decouple ray generation from the forward pass. A camera that glides forward along a procedural road centerline, yawing to follow bends and banking gently, producing an orthonormal ray basis for the shader. Steps: Update position z += \text{speed} \cdot dt; Compute eye position [roadX(z), \text{height}, z]; Compute target [roadX(z + \text{lookAhead}), \text{lookHeight}, z + \text{lookAhead}]; Compute forward \text{normalize}(\text{target} - \text{position}); Compute right \text{normalize}(\text{cross}(\text{forward}, \text{WORLD\UP})); Compute up \text{normalize}(\text{cross}(\text{right}, \text{forward})). Parameters: Eye height: 3.5 world units; Look-ahead distance: 15 world units; Look height: 1.5 world units; World up vector: [0, 1, 0]. Camera orientation convention: Z-axis along optical axis (orthogonal to image plane), X-axis pointing towards bottom/ground, Y-axis according to right-hand rule. Parameters: RES: 0.02f; RANGEMAX: 100000.0f; HFOV: M\PI \cdot 160.0f / 180.0f; VFOV: M\PI \cdot 160.0f / 180.0f; HSIZE: 6; VSIZE: 4. Generates rays by creating a meshgrid of spherical coordinates \theta and \phi. Steps: Create linearly spaced \theta \in [0, 2\pi] and \phi \in [0, \pi]; Compute directions in camera frame (y is up): [-\sin\phi \sin\theta, \cos\phi, \sin\phi \cos\theta]; Transform to world space using camera rotation matrix; Compute offset directions dx and dy; Crop directions to remove extra row/column; Compute origins by broadcasting camera translation; Compute radii using norms of dx and dy; Set imageplane to zeros. Layout: Returns utils.Rays with lossmult=1, near/far values, and camidx=0. A 2D sculpting tool that removes voxels inside a selection volume defined by perspective projection from the user's point of view through a circular cursor on the view plane. Steps: Set cursor as a circle aligned with the view plane; Set virtual pointer origin to user's point of view; Set direction vector from point of view to cursor center; For each voxel, project its center onto the view plane; Calculate 2D Euclidean distance d from projected voxel center V to cursor center P; If d < r, remove the voxel. Formula: Selection condition: d < r, where d is the 2D Euclidean distance on the view plane between the projected voxel center and cursor center P, and r is the cursor radius. Pitfall: Perspective projection causes the selection volume to be a cone with apex at the point of view, making the tool dependent on viewing parameters. Orthographic projection yields a cylinder, which is preferred for 3D tools to detach from the point of view. Selects a point on a plane surface of the volume cube aligned with two of the three primary axes (e.g., Y and Z) and casts a ray down to the third axis (e.g., X-axis) to determine the ray path. Steps: Derive four ray representations: 1) An image pair co-planar to the ray in the other two axes (e.g., X-Z and X-Y planes). 2) An intensity profile along the ray. 3) The corresponding SOI label profile. 4) Location coordinates of entry and exit points. Parameters: Number of rays: 64 rays per axis, 192 total per volume. Checks if 3D points in camera space are in front of the camera (Z > -\epsilon). Steps: Check if the Z coordinate (last element) is > -\epsilon: return \text{xyz}[..., -1] > -\epsilon. Parameters: \epsilon: float = 10^{-6} (tolerance for front-of-camera check). Press the right mouse button to select the line of sight through the cursor. Draw a signal corresponding to the values of voxels along this line at the bottom of the screen. Time Complexity: O(W \cdot H) for generating rays for all pixels, where W and H are image dimensions. Each ray computation is O(1) involving matrix-vector multiplications. Memory Complexity: O(W \cdot H \cdot 3) to store origins and directions. Performance: Highly parallelizable on GPUs due to the independent nature of each pixel's ray generation. Performance is limited by memory bandwidth when storing large ray buffers. Strengths: Flexible camera models via explicit matrices; supports arbitrary camera movements and poses. Limitations: Requires accurate camera calibration (intrinsics/extrinsics); sensitive to coordinate system mismatches. When to Use: When camera parameters are known from calibration or tracking (e.g., NeRF, SLAM outputs). When Not to Use: When simple geometric primitives (e.g., fixed FOV) are sufficient and matrix overhead is undesirable. Camera Ray Generation is a fundamental technique in computer graphics, originating from the need to map rasterized screen coordinates to 3D space for ray tracing and volume rendering. It is widely used in neural radiance fields (NeRF) and other view synthesis methods where camera poses are estimated from images. The method relies on the pinhole camera model and its matrix representation, which has been standard since the early days of computer vision and graphics. name: Orthographic (Parallel) Camera Ray Generation
head: Orthographic ray casting, Parallel Ray Casting, Parallel Ray Generation, PlaneParallelLens
body: Orthographic (Parallel) Camera Ray Generation constructs initial rays for volume rendering by defining a projection plane parallel to the scanline and casting rays in the viewing direction within that plane. It serves as the geometric foundation for orthographic ray casting, where ray origins are distributed across a 2D grid and all rays share a single normalized direction. This method models a camera at infinity where all rays are parallel to one viewing vector, commonly used in applications like biomedicine that do not benefit from perspective distortion. Inputs: eye: Camera position reference in world space (3D vector). target: Look-at target point in world space (3D vector). up: World up vector (3D vector, typically (0,1,0)). width, height: Image resolution in pixels. extent: Half-size of the viewing region in world units along both right and up axes (scalar, default 1.0). Outputs: origins: Array of ray origins distributed on a grid perpendicular to the viewing direction. directions: Array of identical normalized directions for the orthographic camera. Data Structures: origins and directions: Dense arrays matching the pixel grid dimensions, populated via broadcasting. Steps: 1. Compute Camera Basis: Calculate the forward, right, and camera-up vectors using a standard look-at routine camerabasis(eye, target, up). forward = normalize(target - eye). right = normalize(cross(forward, up)). camup = cross(right, forward). 2. Compute Image Plane Dimensions: Determine the half-width and half-height of the viewing region in world units. aspect = width / height. halfw = extent aspect. halfh = extent. 3. Generate Pixel Coordinates: Create a meshgrid of pixel indices i (row, 0 \dots height-1) and j (column, 0 \dots width-1). Map these to normalized coordinates u and v on the image plane: u = \left( \frac{2.0 \cdot (j + 0.5)}{width} - 1.0 \right) \cdot half\w. v = \left( 1.0 - \frac{2.0 \cdot (i + 0.5)}{height} \right) \cdot half\h. Note: The v formula uses (1.0 - \dots) to align the image plane's vertical axis with the camera's up vector, assuming standard screen coordinates where i=0 is the top. 4. Compute Origins: Calculate the world-space origin for each ray by offsetting the eye position by the scaled basis vectors: origin{i,j} = eye + u{i,j} \cdot right + v{i,j} \cdot cam\up. 5. Set Directions: Broadcast the normalized forward vector to match the shape of origins. All rays share this identical direction. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import numpy as np def orthographicraygeneration(eye, target, up, width, height, extent=1.0): """ Generates orthographic camera rays. Args: eye: (3,) array-like, camera position reference. target: (3,) array-like, look-at target. up: (3,) array-like, world up vector. width: int, image width. height: int, image height. extent: float, half-size of viewing region in world units. Returns: origins: (height, width, 3) array of ray origins. directions: (height, width, 3) array of ray directions. """ eye = np.asarray(eye, dtype=np.float32) target = np.asarray(target, dtype=np.float32) up = np.asarray(up, dtype=np.float32) # 1. Compute Camera Basis forward = target - eye forward = forward / np.linalg.norm(forward) right = np.cross(forward, up) right = right / np.linalg.norm(right) camup = np.cross(right, forward) # 2. Compute Image Plane Dimensions aspect = width / height halfw = extent aspect halfh = extent # 3. Generate Pixel Coordinates # Create meshgrid of indices j, i = np.meshgrid(np.arange(width), np.arange(height)) # Map to world coordinates on the image plane u = (2.0 (j + 0.5) / width - 1.0) halfw v = (1.0 - 2.0 (i + 0.5) / height) halfh # 4. Compute Origins # Expand dimensions for broadcasting: eye (3,), right (3,), camup (3,) # u (H, W), v (H, W) origins = (eye[np.newaxis, np.newaxis,:] + u[:,:, np.newaxis] right[np.newaxis, np.newaxis,:] + v[:,:, np.newaxis] camup[np.newaxis, np.newaxis,:]) # 5. Set Directions # Broadcast forward vector to (H, W, 3) directions = np.broadcastto(forward[np.newaxis, np.newaxis,:], (height, width, 3)) return origins, directions Parameters: extent: Half-size of the viewing region in world units along both right and up axes. Default value is 1.0. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Degenerate Basis: If eye equals target, the forward vector is zero, causing normalization failure. A guard should check for this distance. Up Vector Alignment: If up is parallel to forward, the right vector becomes zero. The camerabasis helper must handle this by rotating the up vector or using a default right vector. Precision: Using float32 for large extent values may cause precision loss in origin calculation. Use float64 for large scenes or high-precision requirements. Viewing Plane Ray Generation constructs the initial rays for volume rendering by defining a projection plane parallel to the scanline and casting rays in the viewing direction within that plane. It serves as the geometric foundation for orthographic ray casting, where ray origins are distributed across a 2D grid and all rays share a single normalized direction. It generates parallel rays, contrasting with perspective ray generation which supports non-parallel viewing. Choose it when metric-preserving, distortion-free projection is required. Orthographic Projection is a size-preserving projection where objects in the foreground take up the same amount of screen space as objects in the background, and parallel lines in the 3D scene remain parallel when drawn on the screen. Choose it for technical drawings, CAD, and scientific visualizations where accurate spatial relationships are critical. Orthographic Camera Handling for Point Clouds alternates the camera type from Orthographic to PerspectiveCamera with a similar viewing scope to enable rendering. It is used when differentiable rendering of point clouds requires perspective effects or specific focal length adjustments for zooming. Time Complexity: O(W \cdot H) to generate all ray origins and directions, where W and H are image width and height. Memory Complexity: O(W \cdot H) to store the origin and direction arrays. Performance: Very fast ray generation as it involves simple vector additions and broadcasts, with no division by depth required. Strengths: No perspective distortion; uniform sampling density across the image plane; suitable for scientific visualization where metric accuracy is required. Limitations: Does not simulate depth perception via foreshortening; field of view is fixed by extent and aspect ratio, not by a focal length. When to use: Scientific visualization, CAD, architectural rendering, or any scenario requiring metric-preserving projections. When not to use: When realistic human-like vision or depth cues from perspective are required. Orthographic projection is a fundamental concept in computer graphics, historically used in technical drawing and CAD. In the context of volume rendering, it provides a consistent sampling grid. The method generates parallel rays for applications like biomedicine where perspective distortion is undesirable. The PlaneParallelLens is the standard lens type for this projection. In differentiable rendering pipelines, it may be alternated with perspective cameras for specific point cloud tasks. name: Viewing Plane Ray Generation
head: Projection Plane Raycasting
body: Viewing Plane Ray Generation constructs the initial rays for volume rendering by defining a projection plane parallel to the scanline and casting rays in the viewing direction within that plane. It serves as the geometric foundation for orthographic ray casting, where ray origins are distributed across a 2D grid and all rays share a single normalized direction. This method generates parallel rays, contrasting with perspective ray generation which supports non-parallel viewing. Inputs: Image resolution: W \times H (width, height). Viewing direction vector: \mathbf{d}{view} (normalized). Transformation matrix: \mathbf{M} (combined translation, rotation, and scaling). Camera scale factor: S{cam} (typically 0.25). Sample period: P{sample} (typically 2.0). Outputs: A set of rays, each defined by an origin \mathbf{o}{i,j} and direction \mathbf{d}{ray}. Data Structures: ViewingPlane: A 2D grid of size W \times H. mdata: A std::vector<vec3> of size W \times H. Each element at index k = i + j \cdot W stores a 2D screen coordinate normalized to [-1, 1] for x and y, with z=0. mmat: The combined transformation matrix \mathbf{M}. Steps: 1. Initialize Normalized Grid Points: For each pixel (i, j) where 0 \le i < W and 0 \le j < H: x{norm} = \frac{2(i + 0.5)}{W} - 1 y{norm} = \frac{2(j + 0.5)}{H} - 1 Store \mathbf{p}{norm} = [x{norm}, y{norm}, 0]^T in mdata at index k. 2. Compute Ray Direction: Define three reference points in local space: Origin \mathbf{a} = [0, 0, 0]^T Rightmost \mathbf{b} = [1, 0, 0]^T Upmost \mathbf{c} = [0, 1, 0]^T Transform these points using \mathbf{M}: \mathbf{a}' = \mathbf{M} \mathbf{a} \mathbf{b}' = \mathbf{M} \mathbf{b} \mathbf{c}' = \mathbf{M} \mathbf{c} Compute the ray direction as the normalized cross product of the transformed right and up vectors: \mathbf{d}{ray} = \text{normalize}(\text{cross}(\mathbf{b}' - \mathbf{a}', \mathbf{c}' - \mathbf{a}')) 3. Compute Ray Origins: For each pixel (i, j) with normalized coordinate \mathbf{p}{norm} = [x{norm}, y{norm}, 0]^T: Scale the coordinate by S{cam}: \mathbf{p}{scaled} = [x{norm} \cdot S{cam}, y{norm} \cdot S{cam}, 0]^T Transform \mathbf{p}{scaled} by \mathbf{M} to get the world-space origin: \mathbf{o}{i,j} = \mathbf{M} \mathbf{p}{scaled} 4. Cast Rays: For each pixel (i, j), cast a ray \mathbf{r}(t) = \mathbf{o}{i,j} + t \cdot \mathbf{d}{ray} into the volume data. Resample volume data planes in top-to-bottom order and cast rays in the viewing direction inside the projection planes to produce the image. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def generateviewingplanerays(W, H, M, Scam=0.25, Psample=2.0): """ Generate rays for an orthographic viewing plane. Args: W: Image width H: Image height M: 4x4 transformation matrix (translation rotation scaling) Scam: Camera scale factor Psample: Sample period (used in ray marching, not generation) Returns: origins: List of vec3, size WH directions: List of vec3, size WH (all identical) """ def cross(u, v): return (u[1]v[2] - u[2]v[1], u[2]v[0] - u[0]v[2], u[0]v[1] - u[1]v[0]) def normalize(v): mag = (v[0]2 + v[1]2 + v[2]2)0.5 if mag == 0: return (0.0, 0.0, 0.0) return (v[0]/mag, v[1]/mag, v[2]/mag) def matvecmul(M, v): return ( M[0][0]v[0] + M[0][1]v[1] + M[0][2]v[2] + M[0][3], M[1][0]v[0] + M[1][1]v[1] + M[1][2]v[2] + M[1][3], M[2][0]v[0] + M[2][1]v[1] + M[2][2]v[2] + M[2][3]) origins = [] directions = [] # Step 2: Compute ray direction from transformation matrix a = (0.0, 0.0, 0.0) b = (1.0, 0.0, 0.0) c = (0.0, 1.0, 0.0) aprime = matvecmul(M, a) bprime = matvecmul(M, b) cprime = matvecmul(M, c) rightvec = (bprime[0]-aprime[0], bprime[1]-aprime[1], bprime[2]-aprime[2]) upvec = (cprime[0]-aprime[0], cprime[1]-aprime[1], cprime[2]-aprime[2]) raydir = normalize(rightvec) # Step 1 & 3: Generate origins for each pixel for j in range(H): for i in range(W): xnorm = 2.0 (i + 0.5) / W - 1.0 ynorm = 2.0 (j + 0.5) / H - 1.0 xscaled = xnorm Scam yscaled = ynorm Scam pscaled = (xscaled, yscaled, 0.0) origin = matvecmul(M, pscaled) origins.append(origin) directions.append(raydir) # Ray marching and volume accumulation are not specified in the sources. return origins, directions Edge Cases and Pitfalls: If \mathbf{M} is singular or degenerate, the cross product may yield a zero vector. Guard against this by checking the magnitude of the cross product before normalization. The normalization to [-1, 1] assumes a centered projection plane. Off-center cameras require an offset in the transformation matrix. Precision issues may arise if S{cam} is very small or very large, affecting the spatial distribution of origins. A specific instance of viewing plane ray generation for isometric views, defined by a height parameter. It generates parallel rays where the viewing direction is determined by the height setting, typically used for voxel-based rendering. Choose this when an isometric perspective is required without perspective distortion. Time Complexity: O(W \cdot H) to generate all ray origins and directions. Memory Complexity: O(W \cdot H) to store the origins and directions. Performance: Linear scaling with image resolution. The direction computation is constant time per ray (all rays share the same direction in orthographic mode). Strengths: Simple, deterministic, no perspective distortion, efficient for parallel processing. Limitations: No depth cueing from perspective, limited to orthographic views. When to use: Isometric views, technical visualizations, voxel rendering where perspective is not desired. When not to use: Perspective views, scenes requiring depth-based field of view. The concept of projection plane raycasting originates from early volume rendering architectures, such as the VIRIM system, which used hardware-accelerated resampling and ray casting. The method was formalized in architectures for real-time volume rendering, emphasizing the separation of geometry resampling and ray casting. The specific implementation details, including the transformation matrix approach and normalization, are derived from modern implementations in procedural noise and voxel rendering libraries. name: Sample Streaming Payload Ray Computation
head: Ray Direction Computation, SampleStreamingPayload, Ray Generation from Pixels
body: Sample Streaming Payload Ray Computation regenerates ray geometry (origin and direction) from stored pixel indices and camera parameters, enabling sample streaming and resumption in volume rendering pipelines. It maps pixel coordinates to Normalized Device Coordinates (NDC) and unprojects them to world space to compute unit-length direction vectors. Unlike static ray generation, this method is designed for payloads that persist across frames or batches, allowing rays to be reconstructed on-demand from minimal state. Inputs: pixelindex: Integer identifier for the pixel (often derived from framebuffer index). framesize: Tuple (W, H) representing image width and height. camera: Object or structure containing camera parameters, including: position: Camera origin in world space. direction, horizontal, vertical: Basis vectors defining the view frustum. c2w: Camera-to-world transformation matrix (4x4). focallength: Focal length parameter. unprojectpoints: Function/method to map NDC points to world space. getcameracenter: Function/method to retrieve camera origin. params: Configuration object containing light direction for shadow rays. Outputs: RayBundle or Ray structure containing: origins: Tensor of shape (N, 3) or (numcameras, N, 3). directions: Tensor of shape (N, 3) or (numcameras, N, 3) with unit length. samplepoints, samplelengths: Zero-initialized tensors for volume integration. Data Structures: RayBundle: A container holding origins, directions, and sample metadata. In PyTorch implementations, these are typically torch.Tensor objects. Ray (C++ style): Struct with fields org (vec3f), dir (vec3f), alpha (float), color (vec3f). Steps: 1. Generate Pixel Coordinates: Create 2D grids of column (i) and row (j) indices. For streaming/pixel index approach: Compute ix and iy from pixelindex: ix = \text{pixel\index} \pmod W iy = \lfloor \text{pixel\index} / W \rfloor For full image generation: Create arrays x and y using np.linspace(0, W, endpoint=False) and np.linspace(0, H, endpoint=False). 2. Normalize to NDC Space: Map pixel coordinates to NDC space [-1, 1]. Using pixel indices: \text{screen}x = \frac{ix + 0.5}{W} \text{screen}y = \frac{iy + 0.5}{H} \text{ndc}x = 2 \cdot \text{screen}x - 1 \text{ndc}y = 2 \cdot \text{screen}y - 1 Using meshgrid: Stack y and x grids, reverse dimensions to shape (WH, 2), negate, and append 1 for homogeneous coordinates. 3. Unproject to World Space: Method A (Using Unproject Function): Concatenate 1 to NDC points to form homogeneous coordinates. Call camera.unprojectpoints(ndcpoints, fromndc=True) to get world space points worldpts. Get camera center rayso via camera.getcameracenter(). Repeat rayso for all pixels. Method B (Using Camera Basis): Compute raw directions in camera space: x = \frac{i - W/2}{f} y = -\frac{j - H/2}{f} z = -1 Combine with camera basis vectors u (x-axis), v (y-axis), w (z-axis): \text{raw\dir} = x \cdot u + y \cdot v + w 4. Compute Ray Origins: Method A: rayso is the camera center, broadcasted to match the number of rays. Method B: rayso is the translation part of the c2w matrix (last column). 5. Compute Ray Directions: Method A: \text{raw\dir} = \text{world\pts} - \text{rays\o} Method B: Rotate rawdir to world space using the upper-left 3x3 rotation submatrix of c2w: \text{rays\d} = \text{raw\dir} \cdot \text{c2w}{3\times3} 6. Normalize Directions: Compute L2 norm and divide: \text{norm} = \sqrt{\sum{k=1}^3 \text{rays\d}k^2} \text{rays\d} = \frac{\text{rays\d}}{\text{norm}} 7. Initialize Payload (Optional for Streaming): Set ray.alpha = alpha (passed parameter), ray.color = 0.f (shadow) or color (main), and initialize sample points/lengths to zero. Pseudocode (PyTorch-like): Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import torch def computeraysfrompixels(pixelindices, imagesize, camera): """ Compute ray origins and directions from pixel indices. Args: pixelindices: Tensor of shape (N,) containing pixel indices. imagesize: Tuple (W, H). camera: Object with attributes: c2w: Tensor (4, 4) camera-to-world matrix. focallength: Float. getcameracenter(): Returns Tensor (3,) camera position. unprojectpoints(ndcpoints, fromndc=True): Returns Tensor (N, 3) world points. Returns: origins: Tensor (N, 3) directions: Tensor (N, 3) """ W, H = imagesize # Step 1: Compute screen coordinates from pixel index ix = pixelindices % W iy = pixelindices // W # Step 2: Normalize to NDC [-1, 1] # Add 0.5 for pixel center, then scale to [0, 1], then to [-1, 1] ndcx = 2.0 ((ix.float() + 0.5) / W) - 1.0 ndcy = 2.0 ((iy.float() + 0.5) / H) - 1.0 # Stack to (N, 2) ndcpoints2d = torch.stack([ndcx, ndcy], dim=-1) # Step 3: Unproject to world space # Append 1 for homogeneous coordinates ndcpointshomogeneous = torch.cat([ndcpoints2d, torch.oneslike(ndcpoints2d[..., -1:])], dim=-1) # Use camera's unproject function worldpts = camera.unprojectpoints(ndcpointshomogeneous, fromndc=True) # Step 4: Get camera origin rayso = camera.getcameracenter() # Broadcast origin to match number of rays rayso = rayso.unsqueeze(0).expand(worldpts.shape[0], -1) # Step 5: Compute directions raysd = worldpts - rayso # Step 6: Normalize directions norms = torch.linalg.norm(raysd, dim=1, keepdim=True) raysd = raysd / norms return rayso, raysd def computeraysfromgrid(imagesize, camera): """ Compute rays for all pixels in an image using grid generation. """ W, H = imagesize # Step 1: Create pixel grids x = torch.linspace(0, W, W, endpoint=False) y = torch.linspace(0, H, H, endpoint=False) # Step 2: Meshgrid and reshape # torch.meshgrid returns (H, W) grids. Stack and reshape to (WH, 2) ygrid, xgrid = torch.meshgrid(y, x, indexing='xy') xygrid = torch.stack([xgrid, ygrid], dim=-1).view(-1, 2) # Step 3: Normalize to NDC ndcx = 2.0 (xygrid[:, 0] / W) - 1.0 ndcy = 2.0 (xygrid[:, 1] / H) - 1.0 ndcpoints2d = torch.stack([ndcx, ndcy], dim=-1) # Step 4: Unproject ndcpointshomogeneous = torch.cat([ndcpoints2d, torch.oneslike(ndcpoints2d[..., -1:])], dim=-1) worldpts = camera.unprojectpoints(ndcpointshomogeneous, fromndc=True) # Step 5: Origins rayso = camera.getcameracenter() rayso = rayso.unsqueeze(0).expand(worldpts.shape[0], -1) # Step 6: Directions raysd = worldpts - rayso norms = torch.linalg.norm(raysd, dim=1, keepdim=True) raysd = raysd / norms return rayso, raysd Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision: Floating-point errors in normalization can cause directions to deviate slightly from unit length. Re-normalization is recommended. Coordinate System: Ensure NDC space matches the camera's expected input (e.g., y-axis direction). Some implementations negate the NDC y-coordinate. The method originates from implementations in neural volume rendering and NeRF pipelines, where efficient ray generation is critical for training and rendering. The SampleStreamingPayload concept is used in instantVNR for resuming volume rendering tasks. The pixel-to-ray mapping via NDC unprojection is a standard technique in computer graphics, adapted here for deep learning-based volume rendering. name: OptiX Ray Generation & Traversal Setup
head: OptiX 7 Ray Generation, OptiX Ray Generation, Ray Generation Program
body: This method implements the ray generation and initial traversal setup for volume rendering within the NVIDIA OptiX 7 API. It computes pixel rays, initializes the random number generator (RNG) for anti-aliasing, and dispatches volume tracing via optixTrace. It differs from generic ray generation methods by integrating specific OptiX 7 launch parameters, SBT indexing, and visibility masks to restrict traversal to volume geometry. Inputs: Frame buffer dimensions: width w, height h. Camera parameters: position \mathbf{e}, direction vector, horizontal basis \mathbf{r}, vertical basis \mathbf{u}, focal length f, rotation angles \phi (phi) and \theta (theta). Launch parameters: frameindex, frame.size, camera struct. OptiX constants: VISIBILITYMASKVOLUME, MethodOptiX::RADIANCERAYTYPE, MethodOptiX::RAYTYPECOUNT. Outputs: Ray origin \mathbf{o} and direction \mathbf{d} for each pixel. Payload for optixTrace. Data Structures: RandomTEA: RNG state initialized with frameindex and fbIndex. vec2f/vec3f: 2D and 3D floating-point vectors for screen coordinates and ray data. uint32t payload: Packed pointer data for ray payload. Steps: 1. Thread Launch: Launch a CUDA kernel with w \times h threads. Threads are grouped into 8 \times 8 tiled blocks, consisting of two 32-thread wraps computed as SIMD vectors. 2. Pixel Indexing: Compute the framebuffer index: fbIndex = ix + iy frame.size.x. 3. RNG Initialization: Initialize the RNG state: rngstate = RandomTEA(frameindex, fbIndex). 4. Screen Coordinates: Determine 2D screen space coordinates. Compute normalized screen position: screen = vec2f((float)ix + 0.5, (float)iy + 0.5) / vec2f(frame.size). Convert to UV coordinates where top-left is [-1, 1] and bottom-right is [1, -1]. 5. Ray Direction Calculation: Compute initial ray direction rd0: rd0 = [u, v, f]^T / \sqrt{u^2 + v^2 + f^2}, where u, v are the UV coordinates and f is the focal length. Apply rotation matrices to orient the ray: rd = Ry(\theta) Rz(\phi) rd0. Rotation matrices are Ry(\theta) = \begin{bmatrix} \cos\theta & 0 & \sin\theta \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ -\sin\theta & 0 & \cos\theta \end{bmatrix} and Rz(\phi) = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & \cos\phi & -\sin\phi \\ 0 & \sin\phi & \cos\phi \end{bmatrix}. Alternatively, using camera basis vectors: \mathbf{d} = \text{normalize}(\text{camera.direction} + (\text{screen}.x - 0.5) \text{camera.horizontal} + (\text{screen}.y - 0.5) \text{camera.vertical}). 6. Ray Origin: Set \mathbf{o} = \text{camera.position}. Any position p along the ray is computed as p = \mathbf{o} + \mathbf{d} \cdot t. 7. Payload Packing: Pack the payload for OptiX trace: packPointer(&payload, u0, u1). 8. Trace Dispatch: Call optixTrace with visibility mask OptixVisibilityMask(VISIBILITYMASKVOLUME), flags OPTIXRAYFLAGDISABLEANYHIT, SBT offset MethodOptiX::RADIANCERAYTYPE, stride MethodOptiX::RAYTYPECOUNT, and miss index MethodOptiX::RADIANCERAYTYPE. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def normalize(v): return (v[0], v[1], v[2]) / (v[0]2 + v[1]2 + v[2]2)0.5 class RandomTEA: def init(self, frameindex, fbIndex): pass def packPointer(payload, u0, u1): pass def raygenerationkernel(ix, iy, framesize, frameindex, camera, output): if ix >= framesize[0] or iy >= framesize[1]: return # Step 2: Pixel Indexing fbIndex = ix + iy framesize[0] # Step 3: RNG Initialization rngstate = RandomTEA(frameindex, fbIndex) # Step 4: Screen Coordinates screenx = (ix + 0.5) / framesize[0] screeny = (iy + 0.5) / framesize[1] # Step 5: Ray Direction (Camera basis method) raydir = camera.direction + (screenx - 0.5) camera.horizontal + (screeny - 0.5) camera.vertical raydir = normalize(raydir) # Step 6: Ray Origin rayorg = camera.position # Step 7: Payload Packing payload = [0, 0] packPointer(payload, payload[0], payload[1]) # Step 8: Trace Dispatch # optixTrace(rayorg, raydir, payload, VISIBILITYMASKVOLUME, # OPTIXRAYFLAGDISABLEANYHIT, MethodOptiX::RADIANCERAYTYPE, # MethodOptiX::RAYTYPECOUNT, MethodOptiX::RADIANCERAYTYPE) output[fbIndex] = (rayorg, raydir, payload) Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Boundaries: Threads outside the frame buffer dimensions must be guarded. name: Object Space Ray Setup
head: Camera Space Transformation for Ray Origin, Local Space Ray Setup, Object Space Ray Casting, Ray Origin Calculation for Near Plane Quad, Ray Casting Vertex Shader, RayCasterShaderCodeTester::NearPlaneVertexShader
body: Object Space Ray Setup constructs ray origins and directions within the local coordinate system of a mesh, ensuring that the raytraced volume moves, scales, and rotates rigidly with the object's transform. Unlike world-space ray generation, which treats the volume as a static window into the world, this method embeds the object's transformation directly into the ray parameters, allowing the raytraced geometry to behave like a physical part of the mesh. Inputs: v.vertex: The vertex position in local/object space. WorldSpaceCameraPos or ucamera: The camera position in world space. unityWorldToObject or inverse(modelMatrix): The matrix transforming world coordinates to object space. Outputs: rayOrigin: The starting point of the ray in object space. rayDirection: The direction of the ray in object space. Data Structures: The vertex shader output struct (v2f) contains: position (SVPOSITION): Clip-space position for rasterization. localPosition (TEXCOORD0, float4): The vertex position in local space, used as the ray origin. viewDirection (TEXCOORD1, float4): The unnormalized view vector in local space. Steps: 1. Transform the world-space camera position to object space by multiplying it with the world-to-object matrix. The w-component of the camera position vector must be 1.0 to include translation. 2. Set the ray origin to the vertex's local position. 3. Compute the unnormalized view direction by subtracting the object-space camera position from the local vertex position. 4. Pass localPosition and viewDirection to the fragment shader for interpolation. 5. In the fragment shader, normalize the view direction. Normalization must occur here, not in the vertex shader, because linear interpolation of vectors distorts their length, particularly on low-poly meshes or at close camera distances. Formulas: \mathbf{c}{obj} = \mathbf{M}{world \to obj} \times \begin{bmatrix} \mathbf{c}{world} \\ 1.0 \end{bmatrix} Where \mathbf{c}{obj} is the camera position in object space, \mathbf{M}{world \to obj} is the inverse model matrix, and \mathbf{c}{world} is the camera position in world space. \mathbf{o} = \mathbf{v}{local} Where \mathbf{o} is the ray origin and \mathbf{v}{local} is the vertex position in local space. \mathbf{d}{raw} = \mathbf{v}{local} - \mathbf{c}{obj} Where \mathbf{d}{raw} is the raw unnormalized view direction vector. \mathbf{d} = \frac{\mathbf{d}{raw}}{\|\mathbf{d}{raw}\|} Where \mathbf{d} is the normalized ray direction. Parameters: Typical values for ray marching step count and step size are not specified by this setup method; they depend on the downstream marching algorithm. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: W-Component Error: If the camera position is transformed with a w-component of 0, the translation component of the inverse matrix is ignored, resulting in incorrect ray origins that only account for rotation and scale. Interpolation Distortion: Normalizing the view direction in the vertex shader leads to incorrect angles in the fragment shader due to perspective-correct interpolation artifacts, especially visible on low-poly objects or close camera distances. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def vertexsetup(vertexlocal, cameraworld, worldtoobjectmatrix): # Compute clip-space position for rasterization # clipposition =... # Store local position as ray origin localposition = vertexlocal # Transform camera world position to object space # w-component must be 1.0 to include translation # cameraobj = worldtoobjectmatrix vec4(cameraworld, 1.0) cameraobj = [0.0, 0.0, 0.0] # Matrix-vector multiplication # Compute unnormalized view direction in local space viewdirection = vertexlocal - cameraobj return { 'clipposition': None, 'localposition': localposition, 'viewdirection': viewdirection } def fragmentsetup(vertexoutput): # Normalize direction in fragment shader to avoid interpolation distortion rawdir = vertexoutput['viewdirection'] length = math.sqrt(sum(c c for c in rawdir)) dir = [c / length for c in rawdir] # Use local position as ray origin rayorigin = vertexoutput['localposition'] return rayorigin, dir This variant explicitly details the construction of the ray origin in volume texture space by transforming a vertex from the near plane quad through inverse view and model transformations, followed by scaling and translation to align with the volume grid. It differs from camera-space ray setup by operating directly on object-space vertices and using hardware interpolation of 3D UVs, rather than computing ray origins and directions in camera space. Strengths: Ensures the raytraced volume is rigidly attached to the mesh, simplifying animation and transformation logic. Intuitive for single-object rendering. Limitations: Not given in the sources. The method originates from basic sphere tracing and ray marching tutorials, where object-space rendering is preferred for its simplicity and intuitive handling of object transformations. head: Ray Origin Calculation for Near Plane Quad, RayCasterShaderCodeTester::NearPlaneVertexShader
body: This method calculates the ray origin in volume texture space for a given vertex on the near plane quad, used for testing ray casting shaders. It transforms a vertex from view space to world space and then maps it into the local volume coordinate system. It differs from camera-space ray setup [4179-object-space-ray-setup-camera-space-transformation-for-ray-o.md] by operating directly on object-space vertices and using hardware interpolation of 3D UVs, rather than computing ray origins and directions in camera space. Inputs: glVertex: The vertex position in view space (passed from the vertex shader input). InverseModelViewMatrix: The inverse of the model-view matrix, transforming view space to world space. VolTranslation: The translation vector of the volume in world space. VolScale: The scale factor of the volume in world space. ProjectionMatrix: The projection matrix for clipping (used for glPosition). Outputs: glPosition: The clip-space position for rasterization. RayPosition: The ray origin in volume texture space (normalized 0-1 range). Data Structures: vec4: 4-component floating-point vector. vec3: 3-component floating-point vector. mat4: 4x4 floating-point matrix. Steps: 1. Compute the clip-space position: glPosition = ProjectionMatrix glVertex. 2. Transform the vertex from view space to world space: worldPos = InverseModelViewMatrix glVertex. 3. Extract the 3D position: rayPosition = worldPos.xyz. 4. Translate the position to volume-local space: rayPosition = rayPosition - VolTranslation. 5. Scale the position to volume-local space: rayPosition = rayPosition / VolScale. 6. Offset the position to center it in texture coordinates: rayPosition = rayPosition + 0.5f. 7. Pack the result into a 4D vector: RayPosition = vec4(rayPosition, 1.0f). Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def NearPlaneVertexShader(glVertex: vec4, InverseModelViewMatrix: mat4, VolTranslation: vec3, VolScale: float, ProjectionMatrix: mat4) -> (vec4, vec4): # Step 1: Compute clip-space position glPosition = ProjectionMatrix glVertex # Step 2: Transform vertex from view space to world space worldPos = InverseModelViewMatrix glVertex # Step 3: Extract 3D position rayPosition = worldPos.xyz # Step 4: Translate to volume-local space rayPosition = rayPosition - VolTranslation # Step 5: Scale to volume-local space rayPosition = rayPosition / VolScale # Step 6: Offset to center in texture coordinates (0.5 to 1.5 range, assuming unit cube centered at 0) rayPosition = rayPosition + 0.5f # Step 7: Pack result RayPosition = vec4(rayPosition, 1.0f) return glPosition, RayPosition Parameters: VolTranslation: Not given in the sources. VolScale: Not given in the sources. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision: Floating-point precision issues may arise if the volume is very large or very small. Boundaries: The method assumes the volume is a unit cube centered at the origin in texture space. If the volume is not a unit cube, the offset and scale may need adjustment. Degenerate Input: If VolScale is zero, division by zero will occur. This method establishes the geometric foundation for GPU-based volume raycasting by mapping a 3D bounding box (typically a unit cube) to screen space while simultaneously computing normalized 3D texture coordinates for each fragment. It solves the problem of translating object-space vertex positions into both clip-space positions for rasterization and valid texture lookup coordinates for the fragment shader. It differs from camera-space ray setup [4179-object-space-ray-setup-camera-space-transformation-for-ray-o.md] by operating directly on object-space vertices and using hardware interpolation of 3D UVs, rather than computing ray origins and directions in camera space. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Measured Performance: Not given in the sources. Scaling: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Simple to implement, works well for testing ray casting shaders. Limitations: Limited to near plane quad, may not be suitable for complex volume rendering. When to use: When testing ray casting shaders or for simple volume rendering. When not to use: For complex volume rendering or when performance is critical. This method is described in the thesis "VoxVizThesis" by apecoraro. It is used in the context of volume rendering, specifically for testing ray casting shaders. apecoraro/VoxVizThesis, https://github.com/apecoraro/VoxVizThesis, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial)

name: Object Space Ray Setup via Vertex Shader UV Computation
head: GPU Raycasting (Vertex Shader UV Computation), Raycasting Bounding Box & Sample Position Setup, Vertex Shader UV Computation
body: This method establishes the geometric foundation for GPU-based volume raycasting by mapping a 3D bounding box (typically a unit cube) to screen space while simultaneously computing normalized 3D texture coordinates for each fragment. It solves the problem of translating object-space vertex positions into both clip-space positions for rasterization and valid texture lookup coordinates for the fragment shader. It differs from camera-space ray setup [4179-object-space-ray-setup-camera-space-transformation-for-ray-o.md] by operating directly on object-space vertices and using hardware interpolation of 3D UVs, rather than computing ray origins and directions in camera space. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Object-space vertex positions (vVertex), Model-View-Projection matrix (MVP). Output: Clip-space position (glPosition), 3D texture coordinates (vUV). Data Structures: Vertex Buffer Object (VBO): Stores vertex positions. Layout: totalVertices sizeof(glm::vec3) (or equivalent 3-component float vector). Index Buffer Object (IBO): Stores triangle indices. Layout: totalIndices sizeof(GLuint) (or GLushort/GLuint depending on implementation). Vertex Array Object (VAO): Binds the VBO and IBO, enabling the vertex attribute array for vVertex at location 0 with 3 components, GLFLOAT, normalized false, stride 0, offset 0. Steps: 1. Buffer Initialization: Generate and bind a VAO. Allocate memory for vertices and indices. Fill the vertex buffer with the bounding box geometry (e.g., a cube centered at the origin with bounds [-0.5, 0.5]). Fill the index buffer with triangle indices. Enable the vertex attribute array for vVertex and bind the index buffer. 2. Vertex Shader Execution: For each vertex: Compute the clip-space position by multiplying the MVP matrix with the homogeneous vertex position: \text{gl\Position} = \text{MVP} \times \begin{bmatrix} \text{vVertex}.xyz \\ 1.0 \end{bmatrix} Compute the 3D texture coordinates by adding 0.5 to each component of the object-space vertex position. This shifts the coordinate range from [-0.5, 0.5] to [0.0, 1.0], which is required for normalized texture lookups: \text{vUV} = \text{vVertex}.xyz + 0.5 The output vUV must be declared as smooth out vec3 to enable hardware interpolation across the primitive. 3. Fragment Shader Input: The fragment shader receives the interpolated vUV values. These values represent the position within the volume texture space, allowing direct sampling of the volume data. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def vertexshader(vVertex: vec3, MVP: mat4) -> (vec4, vec3): """ Computes clip-space position and 3D texture coordinates. Args: vVertex: Object-space vertex position (vec3). MVP: Combined Model-View-Projection matrix (mat4). Returns: glPosition: Clip-space position (vec4). vUV: 3D texture coordinates (vec3). """ # Compute clip-space position glPosition = MVP vec4(vVertex, 1.0) # Compute 3D texture coordinates # Shift from [-0.5, 0.5] to [0.0, 1.0] vUV = vVertex + 0.5 return glPosition, vUV def fragmentshader(vUV: vec3, volumetexture: texture3D) -> vec4: """ Samples the volume texture using the interpolated UVs. Args: vUV: Interpolated 3D texture coordinates (vec3). volumetexture: The 3D volume texture. Returns: FragColor: Output color. """ # Sample the volume texture sample = texture(volumetexture, vUV).r # Perform ray marching/compositing logic here #... return FragColor Parameters: MVP: Combined Model-View-Projection matrix, passed as a uniform mat4. vVertex: Object-space vertex position, declared as layout(location = 0) in vec3. vUV: 3D texture coordinates, declared as smooth out vec3 in the vertex shader and smooth in vec3 in the fragment shader. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Coordinate Range: The unit cube is typically centered at the origin with bounds [-0.5, -0.5, -0.5] to [0.5, 0.5, 0.5]. Failing to add 0.5 to the vertex coordinates will result in texture coordinates outside the [0, 1] range, causing incorrect sampling or clamping artifacts. Interpolation: Using smooth interpolation for vUV is critical. Without it, the texture coordinates may not be correctly interpolated across the triangle, leading to distorted volume sampling. Time Complexity: O(N) where N is the number of vertices in the bounding box. The computation is performed per-vertex in the vertex shader. Memory Complexity: O(V + I) where V is the number of vertices and I is the number of indices, for storing the VBO and IBO. Strengths: Simple implementation, leverages hardware interpolation for texture coordinates, efficient for simple bounding boxes. Limitations: Limited to convex bounding volumes that can be represented by a single mesh. Not suitable for complex object-space ray setups involving multiple primitives or non-convex shapes without additional logic. When to use: Ideal for simple volume rendering where the volume is contained within a single axis-aligned bounding box (AABB) or a simple cube. When not to use: When the volume requires multiple bounding boxes or complex geometry for ray setup. This method is commonly used in GPU-based volume raycasting implementations, particularly in educational and open-source projects. It relies on standard OpenGL features such as vertex shaders, fragment shaders, and texture sampling. The approach of using a unit cube and shifting coordinates is a common technique in computer graphics for simplifying texture coordinate generation. mversiotech/volume-rendering-demo, https://github.com/mversiotech/volume-rendering-demo, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial) aashish24/vtkvolume, https://github.com/aashish24/vtkvolume, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial)
