name: Camera Intrinsics Simplification
head: FOV from Intrinsics, Field of View Calculation, Simplified Camera Intrinsics, Square Pixel Camera Model
body: This method computes the horizontal and vertical field of view (FOV) angles, focal lengths, and principal point offsets from a camera's intrinsic calibration matrix and sensor parameters. It solves the problem of deriving geometric camera parameters required for ray generation when only the intrinsic matrix K and physical sensor/lens specifications are available, bypassing the need for explicit FOV inputs. It differs from Pinhole Camera Ray Generation by explicitly handling sensor fit modes and pixel aspect ratios to resolve ambiguities in focal length scaling, and from Camera Matrix Ray Generation by deriving the intrinsic parameters from raw sensor data rather than assuming a pre-computed matrix. Inputs: Intrinsic matrix K (typically 3 \times 3). Image width W and height H in pixels. Camera lens focal length f{lens} (in mm). Sensor width Sw and sensor height Sh (in mm). Pixel aspect ratio p{aspect} = px / py. Sensor fit mode: "AUTO", "HORIZONTAL", or "VERTICAL". Principal point shifts cx^{shift}, cy^{shift} (normalized coordinates, typically -1 to 1 or 0 to 1 depending on convention; here assumed normalized relative to image dimensions). Outputs: Dictionary containing: cameraanglex: Horizontal FOV in radians. cameraangley: Vertical FOV in radians. flx: Focal length in pixels (X). fly: Focal length in pixels (Y). cx: Principal point X coordinate in pixels. cy: Principal point Y coordinate in pixels. w: Effective image width. h: Effective image height. Data Structures: K: 3 \times 3 matrix. Standard layout: K = \begin{bmatrix} fx & s & cx \\ 0 & fy & cy \\ 0 & 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix} where fx, fy are focal lengths in pixels, s is skew (usually 0), and cx, cy are principal points. intrinsicsinv: 3 \times 3 matrix, inverse of K. Steps: 1. Compute Effective Resolution: Calculate the effective width w and height h based on the scene resolution and percentage scaling: w = \left\lfloor \text{scene.render.resolution\x} \times \frac{\text{scene.render.resolution\percentage}}{100} \right\rfloor h = \left\lfloor \text{scene.render.resolution\y} \times \frac{\text{scene.render.resolution\percentage}}{100} \right\rfloor 2. Determine Sensor Fit Mode: If sensorfit is "AUTO", determine the fit direction based on the aspect ratio: If w \times p{aspect} \ge h, set sensorfit = "HORIZONTAL". Else, set sensorfit = "VERTICAL". 3. Compute Focal Lengths in Pixels: Calculate the focal length in pixels (f{px}) based on the lens focal length f{lens}, sensor dimensions, and fit mode: If sensorfit == "HORIZONTAL": flx = \frac{f{lens}}{Sh} \times h \times p{aspect} fly = \frac{f{lens}}{Sh} \times h If sensorfit == "VERTICAL": flx = \frac{f{lens}}{Sw} \times w fly = \frac{f{lens}}{Sw} \times \frac{w}{p{aspect}} Note: Some implementations derive flx, fly directly from the inverse intrinsic matrix corner vectors (see Pseudocode). 4. Compute Principal Point: Calculate the principal point coordinates in pixels: cx = \frac{w}{2.0} - (cx^{shift} \times w) cy = \frac{h}{2.0} + (cy^{shift} \times h) 5. Compute Field of View (FOV): Two methods are cited. Method A uses the derived focal lengths. Method B uses the inverse intrinsic matrix and corner vectors. Method A (Direct): \text{camera\angle\x} = 2.0 \times \arctan\left(\frac{w}{2.0 \times flx}\right) \text{camera\angle\y} = 2.0 \times \arctan\left(\frac{h}{2.0 \times fly}\right) Method B (Vector-based): Define corner vectors in homogeneous coordinates: v{left} = [0, 0.5, 1]^T v{right} = [1, 0.5, 1]^T v{top} = [0.5, 0, 1]^T v{bottom} = [0.5, 1, 1]^T Compute the inverse intrinsic matrix K^{-1}. Transform and normalize the vectors to camera space: \hat{v} = \text{normalize}(K^{-1} v) Compute FOV as the angle between the transformed left/right and top/bottom vectors: \text{fov\x} = \arccos(\hat{v}{left} \cdot \hat{v}{right}) \text{fov\y} = \arccos(\hat{v}{top} \cdot \hat{v}{bottom}) Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math import numpy as np def computecameraintrinsicssimplification( K: np.ndarray, resolutionx: float, resolutiony: float, resolutionpercentage: float, lensfocallengthmm: float, sensorwidthmm: float, sensorheightmm: float, pixelaspectx: float, pixelaspecty: float, sensorfit: str, shiftx: float, shifty: float, cameratype: str) -> dict: """ Computes camera intrinsics (FOV, focal lengths, principal point) from intrinsic matrix and sensor data. Args: K: 3x3 intrinsic matrix. resolutionx, resolutiony: Base resolution. resolutionpercentage: Scaling factor (0-100). lensfocallengthmm: Lens focal length in mm. sensorwidthmm, sensorheightmm: Sensor physical dimensions. pixelaspectx, pixelaspecty: Pixel aspect ratio components. sensorfit: "AUTO", "HORIZONTAL", or "VERTICAL". shiftx, shifty: Normalized principal point shifts. cameratype: "PERSP" or other. Returns: Dictionary with cameraanglex, cameraangley, flx, fly, cx, cy, w, h. """ # Pitfall: Check camera type if cameratype != "PERSP": raise ValueError("3DGS export requires a perspective camera.") # Step 1: Effective Resolution w = int(resolutionx resolutionpercentage / 100) h = int(resolutiony resolutionpercentage / 100) # Step 2: Pixel Aspect Ratio pixelaspect = pixelaspectx / pixelaspecty # Step 3: Sensor Fit Mode if sensorfit == "AUTO": if w pixelaspect >= h: sensorfit = "HORIZONTAL" else: sensorfit = "VERTICAL" # Step 4: Focal Lengths in Pixels (Method A from) if sensorfit == "HORIZONTAL": flx = (lensfocallengthmm / sensorheightmm) h pixelaspect fly = (lensfocallengthmm / sensorheightmm) h else: # VERTICAL flx = (lensfocallengthmm / sensorwidthmm) w fly = (lensfocallengthmm / sensorwidthmm) (w / pixelaspect) # Step 5: Principal Point cx = w / 2.0 - (shiftx w) cy = h / 2.0 + (shifty h) # Step 6: FOV (Method A from) cameraanglex = 2.0 math.atan(w / (2.0 flx)) cameraangley = 2.0 math.atan(h / (2.0 fly)) return { "cameraanglex": cameraanglex, "cameraangley": cameraangley, "flx": flx, "fly": fly, "cx": cx, "cy": cy, "w": w, "h": h } def computefovfromintrinsicmatrix(K: np.ndarray) -> tuple: """ Alternative method using inverse intrinsic matrix and corner vectors. Returns (fovx, fovy) in radians. """ # Inverse intrinsic matrix Kinv = np.linalg.inv(K) # Corner vectors in homogeneous coordinates left = np.array([0, 0.5, 1]) right = np.array([1, 0.5, 1]) top = np.array([0.5, 0, 1]) bottom = np.array([0.5, 1, 1]) def processvector(v): # Transform to camera space and normalize vec = Kinv @ v return vec / np.linalg.norm(vec) leftcam = processvector(left) rightcam = processvector(right) topcam = processvector(top) bottomcam = processvector(bottom) # Compute angles using dot product fovx = math.acos(np.dot(leftcam, rightcam)) fovy = math.acos(np.dot(topcam, bottomcam)) return fovx, fovy Parameters: sensorfit: Determines which sensor dimension scales the lens focal length. Values: "AUTO", "HORIZONTAL", "VERTICAL". lensfocallengthmm: Physical focal length of the lens. sensorwidthmm, sensorheightmm: Physical dimensions of the camera sensor. pixelaspectx, pixelaspecty: Pixel aspect ratio components. shiftx, shifty: Normalized principal point offsets. degree: Degree of spherical harmonics for intrinsic embedding (variant). downsample: Factor to downsample image grid dimensions (variant). mergehw: If True, merge height and width dimensions into a single sequence dimension (variant). Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Non-perspective cameras: If camera.type != "PERSP", the method raises an error and aborts. Precision: The acos function in the vector-based FOV calculation is sensitive to normalization errors; ensure vectors are strictly normalized. Sensor Fit Ambiguity: In "AUTO" mode, the decision boundary is w \times p{aspect} == h. This method transforms 3D world-space vertices of geometric primitives (specifically cube faces) into 2D screen-space coordinates using a simplified perspective projection model [15857-optimized-3d-to-2d-projection.md]. It solves the problem of determining which faces are visible on the screen by combining coordinate transformation, perspective division, and visibility culling (backface, near-plane, and screen-boundary checks) [15857-optimized-3d-to-2d-projection.md]. It differs from general-purpose graphics pipelines by operating on raw vertex arrays with explicit yaw/pitch rotations and a custom visibility mask calculation, rather than relying on a full view-projection matrix multiplication [15857-optimized-3d-to-2d-projection.md]. This variant generates an embedding of camera intrinsic parameters by converting ray directions to spherical harmonics coefficients. It extracts batch, views, and image dimensions, calculates target dimensions after downsampling, and samples image grid coordinates. It converts local ray directions to spherical harmonics coefficients based on a specified degree (0, 2, 4, or 8). The output shape depends on the mergehw parameter: if True, shape is [b, v, (h w), d]; otherwise [b, v, d, h, w]. Time Complexity: O(1) for the direct calculation of FOV from focal lengths. O(1) for the vector-based calculation, involving a fixed number of matrix-vector multiplications and normalizations. Memory Complexity: O(1), requiring only temporary storage for a few vectors and the inverse intrinsic matrix. Performance: Extremely fast, suitable for per-pixel or per-camera initialization in real-time applications. Strengths: Handles sensor fit modes and pixel aspect ratios explicitly, providing robust focal length calculation from physical sensor data. The vector-based method is robust to skew and non-square pixels if the intrinsic matrix is accurate. Limitations: Requires accurate knowledge of sensor dimensions and lens focal length for the physical method. The vector method assumes the intrinsic matrix correctly models the camera. When to use: When initializing a camera model from physical sensor specifications or when deriving FOV from a known calibration matrix. When not to use: When the camera is not perspective. The method originates from implementations in 3D Gaussian Splatting dataset builders and novel view synthesis frameworks. The physical sensor-based calculation is detailed in the 3dgs-dataset-builder repository. The vector-based FOV calculation from intrinsic matrices is used in depth estimation and splatting frameworks like depthsplat and NoPoSplat. The spherical harmonics embedding variant is used in NoPoSplat for intrinsic parameter representation. cvg/depthsplat, https://github.com/cvg/depthsplat, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial) cvg/NoPoSplat, https://github.com/cvg/NoPoSplat, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial) yumehiko/3dgs-dataset-builder, https://github.com/yumehiko/3dgs-dataset-builder, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial) NeRF: A Volume Rendering Perspective | Yue Yu - GitHub Pages, https://yconquesty.github.io/blog/ml/nerf/nerfrendering.html, fetched 2026-10-29 (unofficial)

name: Optimized 3D to 2D Projection
head: 3D to 2D Projection, Screen Space Transform
body: This method transforms 3D world-space vertices of geometric primitives (specifically cube faces) into 2D screen-space coordinates using a simplified perspective projection model. It solves the problem of determining which faces are visible on the screen by combining coordinate transformation, perspective division, and visibility culling (backface, near-plane, and screen-boundary checks). It differs from general-purpose graphics pipelines by operating on raw vertex arrays with explicit yaw/pitch rotations and a custom visibility mask calculation, rather than relying on a full view-projection matrix multiplication. Inputs: verts: Array of shape (numfaces, 4, 3) containing 3D world coordinates for the 4 vertices of each face. origin: 3D vector representing the camera position in world space. yaw: Float, rotation angle around the Y-axis (radians). pitch: Float, rotation angle around the Z-axis (radians). settings: Object containing NEARPLANE (float), FOV (float), WIDTH (int), HEIGHT (int). constants: Object containing HALFWIDTH, HALFHEIGHT. Outputs: projpoints: Array of shape (numfaces, 4, 2) containing integer screen coordinates (x, y). depthperface: Array of shape (numfaces,) containing the average depth of each face. visibilitymask: Boolean array of shape (numfaces,) indicating visible faces. Data Structures: Vertices are stored as contiguous float32 arrays. Screen coordinates are packed as int32. Depth is stored as float32. Parameters: NEAR: settings.NEARPLANE. FOVVAL: settings.FOV. AREAEPSILON: 1e-6. Steps: 1. Translation: Translate vertices relative to the camera origin. v{local} = verts - origin Reshape verts to (numfaces 4, 3) for vectorized subtraction. 2. Yaw Rotation (XY Plane): Rotate the local X and Y components around the Y-axis. rxy = vx \cos(yaw) - vy \sin(yaw) ry{temp} = vx \sin(yaw) + vy \cos(yaw) Where vx, vy are the X and Y components of v{local}. 3. Pitch Rotation (YZ Plane): Rotate the temporary Y and Z components around the Z-axis. ryp = vz \sin(pitch) + ry{temp} \cos(pitch) rzp = vz \cos(pitch) - ry{temp} \sin(pitch) Where vz is the Z component of v{local}. Resulting coordinates are (rxy, ryp, rzp). 4. Perspective Projection: Clamp depth to prevent division by zero or negative depth artifacts: depth{safe} = \max(ryp, NEAR) Calculate screen coordinates: screenx = \left( \frac{HALF\WIDTH + rxy \cdot \frac{FOV\VAL}{depth{safe}}}{1} \right){int32} screeny = \left( \frac{HALF\HEIGHT - rzp \cdot \frac{FOV\VAL}{depth{safe}}}{1} \right){int32} Note: The source implementation uses np.maximum for clamping and explicit casting to np.int32. 5. Pack Projections: Reshape screenx and screeny back to (numfaces, 4, 2). Calculate average depth per face: depth{per\face} = \text{mean}(ryp, \text{axis}=1) 6. Visibility Mask Calculation: Compute a boolean mask for each face based on four criteria: Behind Near Plane: Face is behind the camera if all vertices have depth < NEAR. is\behind = \text{all}(depths < NEAR, \text{axis}=1) Off Screen X: Face is off-screen if all vertices are outside horizontal bounds. is\off\x = \text{all}(screenx < 0) \lor \text{all}(screenx > WIDTH) Off Screen Y: Face is off-screen if all vertices are outside vertical bounds. is\off\y = \text{all}(screeny < 0) \lor \text{all}(screeny > HEIGHT) Backface Culling: Use the Shoelace formula on screen-space vertices to determine orientation. dx1 = sx1 - sx0, \quad dy1 = sy1 - sy0 dx2 = sx2 - sx0, \quad dy2 = sy2 - sy0 area = (dx1 \cdot dy2) - (dy1 \cdot dx2) is\backface = area > -\AREA\EPSILON A face is considered a backface if the signed area is non-negative (or close to zero). Final mask: visibility\mask = \neg (is\behind \lor is\off\x \lor is\off\y \lor is\backface) Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import numpy as np def optimized3dto2dprojection( verts: np.ndarray, # Shape: (numfaces, 4, 3) origin: np.ndarray, # Shape: (3,) yaw: float, pitch: float, settings: dict, constants: dict) -> tuple: """ Transforms 3D face vertices to 2D screen space and calculates visibility. """ numfaces = verts.shape[0] if numfaces == 0: return ( np.empty((0, 4, 2), dtype=np.int32), np.empty((0,), dtype=np.float32), np.empty((0,), dtype=np.bool)) NEAR = settings['NEARPLANE'] FOVVAL = settings['FOV'] WIDTH = settings['WIDTH'] HEIGHT = settings['HEIGHT'] HALFWIDTH = constants['HALFWIDTH'] HALFHEIGHT = constants['HALFHEIGHT'] AREAEPSILON = 1e-6 # 1. Translation # Reshape to (numfaces 4, 3) for broadcasting vertsflat = verts.reshape(-1, 3) vlocal = vertsflat - origin # Extract components vx = vlocal[:, 0] vy = vlocal[:, 1] vz = vlocal[:, 2] # 2. Yaw Rotation (XY Plane) cosy = np.cos(yaw) siny = np.sin(yaw) rxy = (vx cosy) - (vy siny) rytemp = (vx siny) + (vy cosy) # 3. Pitch Rotation (YZ Plane) cosp = np.cos(pitch) sinp = np.sin(pitch) ryp = (vz sinp) + (rytemp cosp) rzp = (vz cosp) - (rytemp sinp) # 4. Perspective Projection depthsafe = np.maximum(ryp, NEAR) # Calculate screen coordinates # Note: Source uses integer casting directly screenx = (HALFWIDTH + (rxy FOVVAL / depthsafe)).astype(np.int32) screeny = (HALFHEIGHT - (rzp FOVVAL / depthsafe)).astype(np.int32) # 5. Pack Projections # Reshape back to (numfaces, 4, 2) projpoints = np.stack([screenx, screeny], axis=1).reshape(numfaces, 4, 2) # Calculate depth per face (mean of ryp for the 4 vertices) depthperface = ryp.reshape(numfaces, 4).mean(axis=1) # 6. Visibility Mask # Reshape for per-face checks sxf = screenx.reshape(numfaces, 4) syf = screeny.reshape(numfaces, 4) depths = ryp.reshape(numfaces, 4) # Behind near plane: all vertices behind near plane isbehind = np.all(depths < NEAR, axis=1) # Off screen X: all vertices outside [0, WIDTH] isoffx = np.all(sxf < 0, axis=1) | np.all(sxf > WIDTH, axis=1) # Off screen Y: all vertices outside [0, HEIGHT] isoffy = np.all(syf < 0, axis=1) | np.all(syf > HEIGHT, axis=1) # Backface culling using Shoelace formula # Vertices are assumed to be ordered 0, 1, 2, 3 # Use vertices 0, 1, 2 for triangle area calculation sx0 = sxf[:, 0] sx1 = sxf[:, 1] sx2 = sxf[:, 2] sy0 = syf[:, 0] sy1 = syf[:, 1] sy2 = syf[:, 2] dx1 = sx1 - sx0 dy1 = sy1 - sy0 dx2 = sx2 - sx0 dy2 = sy2 - sy0 area = (dx1 dy2) - (dy1 dx2) isbackface = area > -AREAEPSILON visibilitymask = ~(isbehind | isoffx | isoffy | isbackface) return projpoints, depthperface, visibilitymask Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Zero Faces: If numfaces is 0, the function returns empty arrays immediately. Depth Clamping: Using np.maximum with NEAR prevents division by zero and negative depth issues, but may cause z-fighting if NEAR is too large. Backface Orientation: The Shoelace formula assumes a specific vertex winding order (counter-clockwise or clockwise). The source defines backfaces as those with area > -1e-6, implying a specific winding convention. Integer Overflow: Screen coordinates are cast to int32. If FOV or world coordinates are extremely large, overflow may occur. Time Complexity: O(N) where N is the number of faces. All operations are vectorized numpy operations. Memory Complexity: O(N) for storing intermediate arrays and outputs. Performance: Highly optimized for bulk processing of voxel faces. The use of vectorized numpy operations avoids Python loops. Strengths: Simple, fast, and explicit. No matrix library dependencies. Limitations: Limited to perspective projection with fixed FOV. Not suitable for complex camera models (e.g., fisheye, orthographic). Backface culling is approximate due to epsilon. This method is derived from the pyvorengi-sdk-demo project, an unofficial SDK for a voxel-based game engine. It implements a simplified screen-space transform for rendering voxel chunks. The approach is tailored for real-time voxel rendering where performance is critical and complex camera models are unnecessary. herbal1st/pyvorengi-sdk-demo, https://github.com/herbal1st/pyvorengi-sdk-demo, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial)

name: Camera Intrinsic Matrix Construction
head: Camera Intrinsic Extraction for Open3D, Intrinsic Matrix Construction, K matrix construction, camera intrinsic matrix
body: Builds a 3x3 camera intrinsic matrix K from focal length and image dimensions. Inputs: focal: Focal length in pixels. H: Image height. W: Image width. Outputs: K: A 3x3 matrix of dtype float32 representing the intrinsic matrix. Data Structures: K: 3x3 matrix. K{0,0}: fx (focal length in x) K{1,1}: fy (focal length in y) K{0,2}: cx (principal point x) K{1,2}: cy (principal point y) K{2,2}: 1.0 All other entries: 0.0 Steps: 1. Initialize a 3x3 matrix K with zeros. 2. Set K{0,0} = \text{focal}. 3. Set K{1,1} = \text{focal}. 4. Set K{0,2} = 0.5 \times W. 5. Set K{1,2} = 0.5 \times H. 6. Set K{2,2} = 1.0. 7. Return K. Alternative Derivation (from NDC): Construct the NDC-to-pixel transformation matrix T{\text{ndc2pix}} using image width W and height H: T{\text{ndc2pix}} = \begin{bmatrix} W/2 & 0 & 0 & (W-1)/2 \\ 0 & H/2 & 0 & (H-1)/2 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix} If a projection matrix P is available, compute K as the top-left 3x3 submatrix of P \times T{\text{ndc2pix}}, transposed: K = (P \times T{\text{ndc2pix}})[0:3, 0:3]^T where P is a 4x4 projection matrix. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import numpy as np def constructintrinsicmatrix(focal: float, H: int, W: int) -> np.ndarray: """ Construct the 3x3 camera intrinsic matrix K. Args: focal: Focal length in pixels. H: Image height. W: Image width. Returns: K: 3x3 numpy array, dtype float32. """ K = np.zeros((3, 3), dtype=np.float32) K[0, 0] = focal K[1, 1] = focal K[0, 2] = 0.5 W K[1, 2] = 0.5 H K[2, 2] = 1.0 return K Parameters: focal: Focal length in pixels. H: Image height. W: Image width. Edge Cases: Not given in the sources. Not given in the sources. Not given in the sources. damn8daniel/nerf-from-scratch, https://github.com/damn8daniel/nerf-from-scratch, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial) hbb1/2d-gaussian-splatting, https://github.com/hbb1/2d-gaussian-splatting, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial)

name: Pinhole Camera Ray Generation
head: Pinhole Camera, Pinhole Ray Casting
body: The Pinhole Camera Ray Generation method computes the origin and direction vectors for viewing rays corresponding to each pixel in a raster image, assuming an ideal pinhole camera model where all rays pass through a single center point. It solves the problem of mapping 2D screen coordinates to 3D world-space rays for volume rendering or ray tracing. Unlike Camera Matrix Ray Generation, which relies on explicit intrinsic and extrinsic matrices, this method often derives rays directly from geometric primitives such as field of view (FOV), aspect ratio, and camera basis vectors, or uses a simplified look-at formulation. It provides no depth of field, ensuring all objects are in focus. Inputs: Image dimensions: width W, height H. Camera position (origin): \mathbf{p}. Camera orientation: defined by a forward vector \mathbf{f} (look-at direction), a world up vector \mathbf{u}{world}, and optionally a rotation matrix \mathbf{R}. Field of View: Vertical FOV \theta{v} (in radians or degrees) or Horizontal FOV \theta{h}. Focal length f or focal distance (distance from pinhole to image plane). Outputs: For each pixel (i, j) where i \in [0, W-1] and j \in [0, H-1]: Ray origin \mathbf{o}{i,j} = \mathbf{p}. Ray direction \mathbf{d}{i,j} (normalized). Data Structures: Ray arrays: Two contiguous arrays of size W \times H \times 3 storing origins and directions as floating-point vectors. Camera Basis: Three orthonormal vectors \mathbf{w} (backward/forward), \mathbf{u} (right), \mathbf{v} (up) forming the local camera coordinate system. Steps: 1. Compute Camera Basis Vectors: Define the camera's local coordinate system. The camera looks along the negative Z-axis in its local space, which maps to the forward vector in world space. \mathbf{w} = \text{normalize}(\mathbf{p} - \mathbf{target}) \quad \text{or} \quad \mathbf{w} = -\text{normalize}(\mathbf{target} - \mathbf{p}) \mathbf{u} = \text{normalize}(\text{cross}(\mathbf{u}{world}, \mathbf{w})) \mathbf{v} = \text{cross}(\mathbf{w}, \mathbf{u}) Here, \mathbf{w} points from the target to the eye (or negative forward), \mathbf{u} is the right vector, and \mathbf{v} is the up vector. 2. Determine View Plane Dimensions: Calculate the physical extent of the image plane at a unit focal distance or based on the specified FOV. If using FOV directly: \text{viewport\height} = 2 \cdot \tan\left(\frac{\thetav}{2}\right) \text{viewport\width} = \text{viewport\height} \cdot \frac{W}{H} Alternatively, if using focal length f: \text{viewport\height} = \frac{H}{2f} \quad \text{(scaled appropriately)} defines the viewport at unit focal distance. derives focal distance from FOV: f{dist} = \frac{1.0}{2 \tan(\thetav \pi / 360)}. 3. Compute Pixel Offsets: Map pixel indices to coordinates on the view plane. Two common conventions exist: Convention A (Centered, Normalized): Map pixel (i, j) to Normalized Device Coordinates (NDC) or a centered offset. x{ndc} = \frac{2(i + 0.5)}{W} - 1 y{ndc} = 1 - \frac{2(j + 0.5)}{H} (Note: y is often inverted depending on whether image coordinates increase downwards or upwards). Convention B (Tangent Division): Sample the FOV by dividing the tangent of the half-FOV by the resolution. \Delta x = \frac{\tan(\thetah / 2)}{W} \Delta y = \frac{\tan(\thetav / 2)}{H} x{local} = (i - \frac{W}{2}) \cdot \Delta x y{local} = (\frac{H}{2} - j) \cdot \Delta y 4. Construct Local Ray Direction: Combine the offsets with the camera basis. Using Convention A and Viewport dimensions: \mathbf{d}{local} = \mathbf{w} + x{ndc} \cdot \frac{\text{viewport\width}}{2} \cdot \mathbf{u} + y{ndc} \cdot \frac{\text{viewport\height}}{2} \cdot \mathbf{v} Using Convention B (Tangent): \mathbf{d}{local} = \Delta y \cdot \mathbf{v} + \Delta x \cdot \mathbf{u} + \mathbf{w} constructs rayd << dv v, dh h, 1.0 where h, v are loop indices centered at 0. 5. Normalize and Transform: Normalize the direction vector to ensure unit length. If the basis vectors are already orthonormal and the forward vector is \mathbf{w}, the resulting vector from the linear combination in step 4 is generally not unit length before normalization if offsets are large, or is unit length if constructed via rotation matrix. \mathbf{d}{world} = \text{normalize}(\mathbf{d}{local}) If a rotation matrix \mathbf{R} is provided instead of explicit basis vectors: \mathbf{d}{world} = \mathbf{R} \cdot \mathbf{d}{local} applies rayd = rot rayd. 6. Handle Anti-Aliasing (Optional): To reduce aliasing, jitter the pixel coordinates by adding a random value \epsilon \in [0, 1) to i and j before computing offsets. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math import numpy as np def generatepinholerays(width, height, position, target, worldup, fovdegrees): """ Generates ray origins and directions for a pinhole camera. Args: width (int): Image width in pixels. height (int): Image height in pixels. position (np.array): Camera origin (3,). target (np.array): Look-at point (3,). worldup (np.array): World up vector (3,). fovdegrees (float): Vertical field of view in degrees. Returns: origins (np.array): Shape (H, W, 3). directions (np.array): Shape (H, W, 3). """ # 1. Compute Camera Basis # Forward vector points from camera to target forward = target - position forward = forward / np.linalg.norm(forward) # Right vector is perpendicular to forward and worldup right = np.cross(forward, worldup) right = right / np.linalg.norm(right) # Up vector is perpendicular to forward and right up = np.cross(right, forward) # 2. Compute Viewport Dimensions at unit focal distance # Using vertical FOV fovrad = math.radians(fovdegrees) viewportheight = 2.0 math.tan(fovrad / 2.0) aspectratio = width / height viewportwidth = viewportheight aspectratio # 3. Create Pixel Grid # Create meshgrid for x and y coordinates # x corresponds to columns (0 to W-1), y to rows (0 to H-1) # Using half-pixel offset for centering xcoords = np.arange(width) + 0.5 ycoords = np.arange(height) + 0.5 X, Y = np.meshgrid(xcoords, ycoords, indexing='xy') # 4. Map to NDC [-1, 1] # X: -1 to 1, Y: 1 to -1 (assuming image y goes down, but NDC y goes up) # Or simply map to viewport coordinates directly # Let's map to viewport coordinates relative to center # Center is at (W/2, H/2) # Offset from center in pixel units dx = (X - width / 2.0) / (width / 2.0) # Range approx -1 to 1 dy = (height / 2.0 - Y) / (height / 2.0) # Range approx -1 to 1 (inverted Y) # Scale by viewport dimensions # The factor 0.5 is included in viewportwidth/height definition? # viewportheight = 2 tan(fov/2). So tan(fov/2) is half-height. # dx (viewportwidth / 2) gives the offset in world units at focal distance 1? # Let's use the explicit formula from: # raydir = normalize(forward + ndc.x (viewportwidth / 2.0) right + ndc.y (viewportheight / 2.0) up) ndcx = (2.0 X / width) - 1.0 ndcy = 1.0 - (2.0 Y / height) # 5. Compute Directions # Vector addition in world space # Note: forward is the Z-axis of the camera (looking down -Z in local, but here forward is the direction vector) # In the basis {right, up, forward}, the ray direction is: # d = forward + ndcx (vw/2) right + ndcy (vh/2) up dirx = ndcx (viewportwidth / 2.0) right diry = ndcy (viewportheight / 2.0) up dirz = forward directions = dirx + diry + dirz directions = directions / np.linalg.norm(directions, axis=-1, keepdims=True) # 6. Origins # All rays originate from the camera position origins = np.broadcastto(position, (height, width, 3)) return origins, directions Parameters with Typical Values: fovdegrees: 60° (telephoto/normal), 90° (wide), 120° (very wide). near, far: Depth bounds for ray marching, typically near=2.0, far=6.0 for synthetic datasets. worldup: Usually (0, 1, 0). Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Degenerate Up Vector: If worldup is parallel to forward, the cross product for right becomes zero. Guard against this by checking the dot product or using a default up vector if alignment is detected. Precision: On some mobile Intel Graphics 6xx chipsets, compute shaders generating these rays may fail silently or throw AccessViolationException, resulting in a purple screen. FOV Definition: Sources disagree on whether FOV is horizontal or vertical. Most modern engines (e.g., Godot,) use Vertical FOV. Ensure consistency with the rendering API. Also known as Thin Lens Camera. This variant introduces a finite aperture to simulate realistic lens behavior, creating a focal plane where objects are sharp and others are blurred (bokeh). What it is: Extends the pinhole model by sampling ray origins from a disk (the lens) rather than a single point. What sets it apart: It requires additional parameters: aperture (lens diameter) and focusdistance. The ray origin is offset by a random vector on the lens disk, and the direction is calculated towards a focus point on the focal plane. When to choose it: When realistic blur effects are required for depth perception or artistic style. Link: Pinhole Camera with Depth of Field (Hypothetical link as no article exists, but described here). Time Complexity: O(W \cdot H) to generate rays for all pixels. The computation per pixel is constant time (vector operations). Memory Complexity: O(W \cdot H) to store the ray origins and directions arrays. Measured Performance: Generating rays is generally fast and CPU/GPU parallelizable. However, implementation errors (e.g., incorrect basis vectors) lead to completely incorrect rendering. The method is efficient compared to matrix inversion methods if the basis is precomputed. Strengths: Simple to implement; intuitive geometric interpretation; no need for explicit intrinsic matrix inversion if FOV is known. Limitations: Does not account for lens distortion, chromatic aberration, or depth of field (unless extended). When to use: Standard volume rendering, ray marching, and simple ray tracing where ideal perspective projection is sufficient. When not: When using calibrated real-world camera data with known intrinsics/extrinsics (use Camera Matrix Ray Generation) or when depth of field is required. The pinhole camera model is the simplest mathematical model of image formation, dating back to the camera obscura. In computer graphics, it is the standard assumption for perspective projection. The specific implementation of generating rays by sampling the tangent of the FOV equally is a common technique in ray tracers to ensure uniform angular sampling. The relationship between focal length and FOV, fov = 2 \cdot \arctan(\frac{sensor\height}{2 \cdot focal\length}), is derived from basic trigonometry. A 50mm lens on a 35mm sensor yields approximately 39.6° FOV, considered a "normal" lens. name: Basic GPU Ray Generation via Fragment Shader
head: Fragment shader ray tracing, Fragment Shader Ray Generation, Ray Tracing Fragment Shader
body: This method generates camera rays for ray tracing by rendering a single quad to the screen, allowing the fragment shader to compute the ray origin and direction for each pixel using interpolated vertex coordinates. It differs from Camera Matrix Ray Generation by avoiding explicit matrix multiplications in favor of geometric basis vectors derived from camera parameters, and from Orthographic (Parallel) Camera Ray Generation by supporting perspective projection through a viewing plane distance. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: Window resolution (iResolution), camera position (iRayOrigin), camera facing direction (iRayDir), camera up direction (iRayUp), distance to viewing plane (iPlaneDist), and interpolated texture coordinates (texCoord) ranging from (0,0) to (1,1) across the quad. Outputs: A ray (origin and direction) for each pixel, which is then used for intersection testing and shading. Data Structures: Uniforms: iResolution (vec2), iRayOrigin (vec3), iRayDir (vec3), iRayUp (vec3), iPlaneDist (float). Varying/Input: texCoord (vec2) interpolated from vertex attributes (0,0) to (1,1). Steps: 1. Setup Geometry: Render a single quad (two triangles covering the screen) using a minimal vertex shader that performs no transformations. 2. Compute Normalized Coordinates: In the fragment shader, convert the interpolated texCoord (range [0,1]) to a normalized device coordinate p (range [-1,1]): p = 2.0 \cdot \text{texCoord} - 1.0 3. Apply Aspect Ratio: Scale the x-component of p by the aspect ratio to prevent distortion: p.x = p.x \cdot \frac{\text{iResolution}.x}{\text{iResolution}.y} 4. Compute Camera Basis Vectors: Calculate the camera's right vector (camSide) using the cross product of the forward (iRayDir) and up (iRayUp) vectors: \text{camSide} = \text{normalize}(\text{cross}(\text{iRayDir}, \text{iRayUp})) 5. Calculate Ray Direction: Compute the ray direction by combining the basis vectors scaled by p and the viewing plane distance: \text{raydir} = \text{normalize}(p.x \cdot \text{camSide} + p.y \cdot \text{iRayUp} + \text{iPlaneDist} \cdot \text{iRayDir}) 6. Set Ray Origin: The ray origin is the camera position: \text{rayorig} = \text{iRayOrigin} 7. Trace and Shade: Use the generated ray to perform intersection tests (e.g., sphere tracing) and compute the final color. Apply Lambertian shading with albedo 0.8, light intensity 8.0, light direction vec3(-0.2, 1.0, -0.3), and shadow bias 0.0001. Formulas: Normalized coordinates: p = 2.0 \cdot \text{texCoord} - 1.0. Aspect-scaled coordinates: p.x = p.x \cdot \frac{\text{iResolution}.x}{\text{iResolution}.y}. Ray direction: \text{raydir} = \text{normalize}(p.x \cdot \text{camSide} + p.y \cdot \text{iRayUp} + \text{iPlaneDist} \cdot \text{iRayDir}). Sphere intersection parameter: t = \begin{cases} t1 & \text{if } t1 < t2 \land t1 \ge 0 \\ t2 & \text{otherwise} \end{cases}, where t1 = -OdotD + \sqrt{\text{base}}, t2 = -OdotD - \sqrt{\text{base}}, \text{base} = OdotD^2 - OdotO + \text{radius}^2, OdotD = \text{dot}(\text{rayorig} - \text{pos}, \text{raydir}), and OdotO = \text{dot}(\text{rayorig} - \text{pos}, \text{rayorig} - \text{pos}). Lambertian diffuse shading: L = \frac{\text{albedo}}{\pi} \max(0, \mathbf{n} \cdot -\mathbf{l}) I{\text{light}}. Parameters: iPlaneDist: Controls the field of view. A smaller value results in a wider FOV. iResolution: Window dimensions in pixels. albedo: 0.8. lightintensity: 8.0. lightdirection: vec3(-0.2, 1.0, -0.3). shadowbias: 0.0001. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Aspect Ratio Distortion: Failing to scale the x-coordinate by the aspect ratio (width/height) will distort the field of view, making circles appear as ellipses. Camera Basis Orthogonality: The camSide vector is computed via cross(iRayDir, iRayUp). If iRayUp is not orthogonal to iRayDir, the resulting basis is not orthonormal, leading to skewed rays. Winding Order: The quad's vertex winding order determines the interpolation direction of texCoord. Ensure the quad covers the screen correctly (e.g., vertices at (0,0), (1,0), (1,1), (0,1)) and that the interpolation maps to screen space correctly (bottom-left to top-right). Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def computeraydirection(texcoord, resolution, raydir, rayup, planedist): p = [2.0 texcoord[0] - 1.0, 2.0 texcoord[1] - 1.0] p[0] = resolution[0] / resolution[1] camside = normalize(cross(raydir, rayup)) raydir = normalize([p[0] camside[0] + p[1] rayup[0] + planedist raydir[0], p[0] camside[1] + p[1] rayup[1] + planedist raydir[1], p[0] camside[2] + p[1] rayup[2] + planedist raydir[2]]) return raydir def tracesphere(rayorig, raydir, pos, radius): OdotD = dot(rayorig, raydir) - dot(pos, raydir) OdotO = dot(rayorig, rayorig) - 2.0 dot(rayorig, pos) + dot(pos, pos) base = OdotD OdotD - OdotO + radius radius if base >= 0: root = math.sqrt(base) t1 = -OdotD + root t2 = -OdotD - root if t1 >= 0 or t2 >= 0: t = t1 if (t1 < t2 and t1 >= 0) else t2 pt = [rayorig[i] + raydir[i] t for i in range(3)] normal = normalize([pt[i] - pos[i] for i in range(3)]) return {"point": pt, "normal": normal, "t": t, "hit": True} return {"point": [0.0, 0.0, 0.0], "normal": [0.0, 0.0, 0.0], "t": -1.0, "hit": False} def shadelambertian(hitpoint, normal, lightdir, albedo, lightintensity, shadowbias): lightdirnorm = normalize(lightdir) diff = max(0.0, dot(normal, [-lightdirnorm[i] for i in range(3)])) return (albedo / math.pi) diff lightintensity def main(): rayorig = iRayOrigin raydir = computeraydirection(texCoord, iResolution, iRayDir, iRayUp, iPlaneDist) hit = tracesphere(rayorig, raydir, spherepos, sphereradius) if hit["hit"]: lightdir = [-0.2, 1.0, -0.3] color = shadelambertian(hit["point"], hit["normal"], lightdir, 0.8, 8.0, 0.0001) else: color = [0.0, 0.0, 0.0] fragColor = [color[0], color[1], color[2], 1.0] Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Performance: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Simple to implement, leverages GPU interpolation, minimal geometry overhead. Limitations: Not given in the sources. When to Use: Not given in the sources. When Not to Use: Not given in the sources. It allows developers to implement ray tracing in the fragment shader without complex vertex transformations, making it accessible for learning and simple applications. gabrielmuller/zazen, https://github.com/gabrielmuller/zazen, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial) mxbrt/svo, https://github.com/mxbrt/svo, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial) unfinishedprogram/ray-marcher, https://github.com/unfinishedprogram/ray-marcher, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial) PDF Further Graphics - University of Cambridge, https://www.cl.cam.ac.uk/teaching/1819/FGraphics/1.%20Ray%20Marching%20and%20Signed%20Distance%20Fields.pdf, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial) Ray Marching with Signed Distance Fields - Scribd, https://www.scribd.com/document/831412915/1-Ray-Marching-and-Signed-Distance-Fields, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial)

name: Ray Position Calculation
head: Query Point Sampling
body: Ray Position Calculation computes the 3D spatial coordinates of sampling points (query points) along camera rays within specified near and far depth bounds. It solves the problem of discretizing a continuous ray into a finite set of 3D locations for volume rendering or neural radiance field (NeRF) evaluation. It differs from its siblings, such as Camera Matrix Ray Generation which produces the ray vectors themselves, by taking those rays and sampling specific positions along them. It differs from World Space Position Reconstruction by generating positions along a parametric ray direction rather than reconstructing a single point from depth buffers. Inputs: rayorigins: Tensor of shape (W, H, 3), where W is width and H is height. Contains the 3D origin for each pixel's ray. raydirections: Tensor of shape (W, H, 3). Contains the normalized direction vector for each pixel's ray. nearthresh: Float. The minimum distance along the ray to sample. farthresh: Float. The maximum distance along the ray to sample. numsamples: Integer. The number of discrete points to generate along each ray. randomize: Boolean. If true, adds uniform noise to the depth values to reduce aliasing (jittering). Default is True. Outputs: querypoints: Tensor of shape (W, H, num\samples, 3). The 3D coordinates of the sampling points. Data Structures: depthvalues: A 1D tensor of shape (num\samples) containing the sampled distances along the ray. Steps: 1. Generate a linearly spaced array of distances between nearthresh and farthresh with numsamples elements. Let this be d. di = \text{linspace}(near\thresh, far\thresh, num\samples)i 2. If randomize is true, add uniform noise \epsilon \sim U(0, \frac{far\thresh - near\thresh}{num\samples}) to each di to jitter the samples. 3. Compute the query points using the ray equation: Q{w,h,s} = O{w,h} + ds \cdot D{w,h} Where: Q{w,h,s} is the query point at pixel (w,h) and sample index s. O{w,h} is the ray origin at pixel (w,h). D{w,h} is the ray direction at pixel (w,h). ds is the distance value for sample s. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import torch import numpy as np def raypositioncalculation(rayorigins, raydirections, nearthresh, farthresh, numsamples, randomize=True): """ Computes 3D query points along rays. Args: rayorigins: torch.Tensor, shape (width, height, 3) raydirections: torch.Tensor, shape (width, height, 3) nearthresh: float, nearest depth coordinate farthresh: float, farthest depth coordinate numsamples: int, number of samples per ray randomize: bool, whether to add jitter noise Returns: querypoints: torch.Tensor, shape (width, height, numsamples, 3) """ # Step 1: Create linearly spaced depth values # torch.linspace(start, end, steps) depthvalues = torch.linspace(nearthresh, farthresh, numsamples, device=rayorigins.device) # Step 2: Optional jittering if randomize: # Add uniform noise in range 0, stepsize) stepsize = (farthresh - nearthresh) / numsamples noise = torch.randlike(depthvalues) stepsize depthvalues = depthvalues + noise # Step 3: Expand dimensions for broadcasting # rayorigins: (W, H, 1, 3) # raydirections: (W, H, 1, 3) # depthvalues: (1, 1, numsamples, 1) rayoriginsexp = rayorigins.unsqueeze(2) raydirectionsexp = raydirections.unsqueeze(2) depthvaluesexp = depthvalues.unsqueeze(0).unsqueeze(0).unsqueeze(3) # Step 4: Compute query points # Q = O + d D querypoints = rayoriginsexp + raydirectionsexp depthvaluesexp return querypoints Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision: When numsamples is very large, depthvalues may suffer from floating-point precision issues if nearthresh and farthresh are large. Ensure nearthresh and farthresh are consistent with the coordinate system scale. Zero Direction: If raydirections contains zero vectors, the result will be invalid. Ray directions should be normalized before this step. Near/Far Order: If nearthresh > farthresh, torch.linspace will produce decreasing values, which is mathematically valid but semantically incorrect for [ray marching. Validate nearthresh < farthresh. Reconstructs 3D world-space positions from 2D screen-space UV coordinates and depth values. Choose this when working with post-processing raymarching or deferred rendering pipelines where depth buffers are available, rather than parametric camera rays. Time Complexity: O(W \cdot H \cdot N), where W is width, H is height, and N is numsamples. The operation is highly parallelizable on GPUs. Memory Complexity: O(W \cdot H \cdot N \cdot 3) for the output querypoints tensor. Intermediate tensors are minimal. Performance: On modern GPUs, this is a memory-bound operation dominated by tensor allocation and broadcasting. It is extremely fast compared to the subsequent volume rendering steps (e.g., density/color evaluation). Strengths: Simple, differentiable, and easily vectorized. Supports jittering for anti-aliasing. Limitations: Does not handle ray-object intersections or adaptive sampling. It assumes a uniform or linear spacing along the ray unless modified. When to use: Standard volume rendering, NeRF training, and any method requiring fixed-step ray marching. When not to use: When adaptive sampling based on scene complexity is required, or when ray-object intersection is needed before sampling. This method is a fundamental building block in neural radiance fields (NeRF) and volume rendering. It was popularized by the original NeRF paper [Mildenhall et al., 2020] and is implemented in many open-source NeRF repositories. The specific implementation details, including the use of torch.linspace and jittering, are commonly found in PyTorch-based NeRF implementations. The concept of sampling along rays is central to classical volume rendering [Levoy, 1988], but the explicit tensor-based calculation for differentiable rendering is a hallmark of modern neural rendering pipelines. rigved-sanku/NeRF-Implementation-for-Efficient-3D-Scene-Reconstruction, https://github.com/rigved-sanku/NeRF-Implementation-for-Efficient-3D-Scene-Reconstruction, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial) hopexn/VolumeRenderingParallel, https://github.com/hopexn/VolumeRenderingParallel, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial) bennyguo/instant-nsr-pl, https://github.com/bennyguo/instant-nsr-pl, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial)

name: World Space Position Reconstruction
head: Coordinate system transformations, Screen-to-World Ray Reconstruction, World position reconstruction
body: World Space Position Reconstruction is a method to reconstruct 3D world-space positions from 2D screen-space UV coordinates and depth values, enabling raymarching in post-processing by converting screen space to world space. It differs from direct ray generation by first establishing the precise 3D location of the current fragment in the world, which serves as the origin for subsequent raymarching steps. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: uv: UV coordinate of the current fragment in the post-processing pass. depth: Depth value of the underlying scene sampled at uv. projectionMatrixInverse: Inverse of the camera projection matrix. viewMatrixInverse: Inverse of the view matrix (equivalent to camera.matrixWorld). CameraPosition: The 3D position of the camera. ViewDir: The view direction vector for the current pixel. Outputs: worldSpace: The reconstructed 3D position in world coordinates. Data Structures: Clip Space Vector: A 4D vector {xNDC, yNDC, zNDC, 1.0}. View Space Vector: A 4D vector resulting from matrix multiplication. World Space Vector: A 4D vector resulting from matrix multiplication, requiring perspective division. Depth Texture Index: An integer 3-vector (int3) constructed from the pixel's screen-space x and y coordinates and a z of 0, used for direct texture loading. Steps: 1. Convert UV to NDC: Calculate Normalized Device Coordinates (NDC) for x and y. x{NDC} = uv.x \times 2.0 - 1.0 y{NDC} = uv.y \times 2.0 - 1.0 2. Convert Depth to NDC Z: Transform the linear or depth-buffer value to NDC Z. z{NDC} = depth \times 2.0 - 1.0 3. Construct Clip Space Vector: Assemble the 4D clip-space vector. clipSpace = \{x{NDC}, y{NDC}, z{NDC}, 1.0\} 4. Transform to View Space: Multiply the clip-space vector by the inverse projection matrix. view = projectionMatrixInverse \times clipSpace 5. Transform to World Space: Multiply the view-space vector by the inverse view matrix. world = viewMatrixInverse \times view 6. Perspective Divide: Divide the x, y, and z components by the w component to obtain the final world position. worldSpace = \frac{world.xyz}{world.w} Alternative Linear Depth Method: If linear depth is available, the position can be calculated directly without matrix inversion for the Z component, using the view direction and camera position: Position{WS} = Depth{linear} \times ViewDir + CameraPosition Parameters: cameraFar: The depth limit beyond which nothing is visible. lightDirection: A normalized vector representing the direction the light points toward. lightPosition: A vector representing the position of the light. coneAngle: Represents the width of the spotlight aperture. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Texture Filtering: Hardware texture filtering must not be used for depth sampling in this context because it interpolates across edges of different blocks, leading to incorrect depth values. Point filtering (e.g., Texture.Load) must be used instead. Precision: Standard floating-point precision is assumed for matrix operations. Degenerate inputs (e.g., world.w being zero) should be handled, though not explicitly detailed in sources. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def getworldposition(uv: vec2, depth: float, projectionmatrixinverse: mat4, viewmatrixinverse: mat4) -> vec3: # Step 1 & 2: Convert to NDC clipz = depth 2.0 - 1.0 ndc = uv 2.0 - 1.0 # Step 3: Construct clip space vector clip = vec4(ndc.x, ndc.y, clipz, 1.0) # Step 4: Transform to view space view = projectionmatrixinverse clip # Step 5: Transform to world space world = viewmatrixinverse view # Step 6: Perspective divide return world.xyz / world.w Time Complexity: O(1) per pixel, involving a fixed number of arithmetic operations and two matrix-vector multiplications. Memory Complexity: O(1) auxiliary memory per pixel, requiring storage for intermediate vectors. Strengths: Enables post-processing volumetric effects by accurately placing ray origins in world space without requiring geometry traversal. Limitations: Requires access to the inverse projection and view matrices, as well as a valid depth buffer. Accuracy is limited by the precision of the depth buffer and the inverse matrix calculations. When to use: When implementing post-processing volumetric lighting or raymarching effects that need to interact with scene geometry depth. When not to use: When forward rendering geometry directly or when depth information is unavailable. This method is fundamental to real-time volumetric lighting techniques that rely on post-processing. It allows the conversion of screen-space coordinates into world-space coordinates, facilitating the calculation of light rays originating from the camera or light sources. The technique is commonly used in shaders for volumetric fog, god rays, and other atmospheric effects. name: Epipolar Ray Intersection
head: Epipolar 3D Lifting and Depth Computation, Get Depth, Lift 2D Points to 3D via Epipolar Lines, Lift to 3D, depth from 2D points, lift_to_3d / get_depth
body: Epipolar Ray Intersection lifts 2D image points to 3D space by intersecting rays constructed from those points with a set of input world-space rays. It solves the problem of finding the precise 3D positions and depths corresponding to specified 2D coordinates on epipolar lines defined by camera origins and directions. It differs from sibling methods like Orthographic (Parallel) Camera Ray Generation by explicitly handling the intersection of two distinct ray sets (image-space and world-space) rather than generating rays from a single camera model, and from Sample Streaming Payload Ray Computation by focusing on geometric reprojection via epipolar constraints rather than payload streaming. Inputs and Outputs: origins: Float tensor of shape (#batch, 3) representing ray origins in world space. directions: Float tensor of shape (#batch, 3) representing ray directions in world space. xy: Float tensor of shape (#batch, 2) representing 2D image coordinates. extrinsics: Float tensor of shape (#batch, 4, 4) representing camera extrinsic matrices. intrinsics: Float tensor of shape (#batch, 3, 3) representing camera intrinsic matrices. Output xyz: Float tensor of shape (#batch, 3) representing the lifted 3D points. Output depth: Float tensor of shape (#batch) representing the distance from the camera origin to the 3D point. Data Structures: The method relies on standard 3D vector and matrix operations. The getworldrays helper constructs ray origins and directions from 2D points using camera parameters. The intersectrays helper computes the intersection between two rays. Steps: 1. Construct World Rays from 2D Points: Convert the 2D image coordinates xy and camera parameters (extrinsics, intrinsics) into world-space ray origins (xyorigins) and directions (xydirections) using the getworldrays function. 2. Intersect Rays: Intersect the input world-space rays (origins, directions) with the newly constructed world rays (xyorigins, xydirections) using the intersectrays function to find the 3D point xyz. 3. Compute Depth: Calculate the depth as the L2 norm (Euclidean distance) between the lifted 3D point xyz and the input ray origins. Formulas: The depth is computed as: \text{depth} = \| \text{xyz} - \text{origins} \|2 where \| \cdot \|2 denotes the L2 norm. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import torch from typing import Tuple def getworldrays( xy: torch.Tensor, extrinsics: torch.Tensor, intrinsics: torch.Tensor) -> Tuple[torch.Tensor, torch.Tensor]: """ Converts 2D image coordinates to world-space ray origins and directions. Args: xy: Float tensor of shape (batch, 2), 2D image coordinates. extrinsics: Float tensor of shape (batch, 4, 4), camera extrinsics. intrinsics: Float tensor of shape (batch, 3, 3), camera intrinsics. Returns: xyorigins: Float tensor of shape (batch, 3), ray origins in world space. xydirections: Float tensor of shape (batch, 3), ray directions in world space. """ # Expand dimensions for broadcasting if necessary # Assuming xy is (batch, 2), extrinsics is (batch, 4, 4), intrinsics is (batch, 3, 3) # Homogeneous coordinates for xy (add 1s) xyhom = torch.cat([xy, torch.oneslike(xy[...,:1])], dim=-1) # (batch, 3) # Invert intrinsics to go from pixel to camera coordinates # Note: Standard pinhole model: xcam = K^-1 xpixel Kinv = torch.inverse(intrinsics) # (batch, 3, 3) # Camera space directions (assuming origin at camera center) directionscam = torch.bmm(Kinv, xyhom.unsqueeze(-1)).squeeze(-1) # (batch, 3) # Normalize directions directionscam = directionscam / torch.norm(directionscam, dim=-1, keepdim=True) # Transform directions to world space using rotation part of extrinsics # Extrinsics: [R | t; 0 0 0 1] R = extrinsics[...,:3,:3] # (batch, 3, 3) t = extrinsics[...,:3, 3] # (batch, 3) directionsworld = torch.bmm(R, directionscam.unsqueeze(-1)).squeeze(-1) # (batch, 3) # Origins are the camera centers in world space originsworld = t # (batch, 3) return originsworld, directionsworld def intersectrays( origins1: torch.Tensor, directions1: torch.Tensor, origins2: torch.Tensor, directions2: torch.Tensor) -> torch.Tensor: """ Computes the intersection point of two rays in 3D space. Finds the point that minimizes the distance between the two rays. Args: origins1: Float tensor of shape (batch, 3), first ray origins. directions1: Float tensor of shape (batch, 3), first ray directions. origins2: Float tensor of shape (batch, 3), second ray origins. directions2: Float tensor of shape (batch, 3), second ray directions. Returns: intersection: Float tensor of shape (batch, 3), the 3D intersection point. """ # Vector between origins d1 = directions1 / torch.norm(directions1, dim=-1, keepdim=True) d2 = directions2 / torch.norm(directions2, dim=-1, keepdim=True) # Normalize directions d1 = directions1 d2 = directions2 # Cross product of directions n = torch.cross(d1, d2, dim=-1) # (batch, 3) nnormsq = torch.sum(n n, dim=-1, keepdim=True) # (batch, 1) # Avoid division by zero for parallel rays nnormsq = torch.clamp(nnormsq, min=1e-8) # Vector between origins v = origins2 - origins1 # (batch, 3) # Project v onto the normal vector n c1 = torch.sum(v n, dim=-1, keepdim=True) / nnormsq # (batch, 1) # Intersection point on ray 1 intersection = origins1 + d1 c1 # (batch, 3) return intersection.squeeze(-1) def liftto3d( origins: torch.Tensor, directions: torch.Tensor, xy: torch.Tensor, extrinsics: torch.Tensor, intrinsics: torch.Tensor) -> torch.Tensor: """ Lifts 2D points to 3D space via epipolar ray intersection. Args: origins: Float tensor of shape (batch, 3), input ray origins. directions: Float tensor of shape (batch, 3), input ray directions. xy: Float tensor of shape (batch, 2), 2D image coordinates. extrinsics: Float tensor of shape (batch, 4, 4), camera extrinsics. intrinsics: Float tensor of shape (batch, 3, 3), camera intrinsics. Returns: xyz: Float tensor of shape (batch, 3), lifted 3D points. """ # Step 1: Get world rays from 2D points xyorigins, xydirections = getworldrays(xy, extrinsics, intrinsics) # Step 2: Intersect input rays with world rays xyz = intersectrays(origins, directions, xyorigins, xydirections) return xyz def getdepth( xyz: torch.Tensor, origins: torch.Tensor) -> torch.Tensor: """ Computes depth as the L2 norm of the difference between the 3D point and the ray origin. Args: xyz: Float tensor of shape (batch, 3), 3D points. origins: Float tensor of shape (batch, 3), ray origins. Returns: depth: Float tensor of shape (batch), depth values. """ diff = xyz - origins depth = torch.norm(diff, dim=-1) return depth Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Parallel Rays: If the input ray and the constructed world ray are parallel, the cross product in intersectrays will be zero, leading to division by zero. The pseudocode handles this by clamping the denominator to a small epsilon. Out-of-Bounds Coordinates: The 2D coordinates xy should be within the valid image bounds. Some implementations check if xy is within [-epsilon, 1+epsilon] for normalized coordinates. Points Behind Camera: The Z coordinate of the lifted point in the camera frame should be positive (in front of the camera). Checks like Z > -epsilon can be used to validate this. Negative Ray Parameter: The intersection parameter t should be positive, indicating the intersection is in the direction of the ray. This variant involves rendering depth labels along the epipolar line. It interpolates epipolar line endpoints in pixel space using pt = projection["xymin"] t + (1 - t) projection["xymax"] for t in [0, 1]. The depth is computed as the Euclidean distance from the camera center to the 3D point: depth = (xyz - extrinsics[0,:3, 3]).norm(dim=-1). Finally, it renders depth labels along the epipolar line with white backer rectangles and rotated text. This variant focuses on validating the projection of points onto epipolar lines. It checks if XY coordinates are in bounds (normalized 0 to 1) by verifying xy >= -epsilon and xy <= 1 + epsilon for all dimensions. It also checks if points are in front of the camera by verifying the Z coordinate is greater than -epsilon. Additionally, it verifies if the ray parameter t is positive by checking t > -epsilon. Time Complexity: The complexity is dominated by the matrix inversions and multiplications in getworldrays and the cross product and division in intersectrays. For N points, it is O(N) assuming fixed-size matrix operations. Memory Complexity: O(N) for storing the input and output tensors. Strengths: Provides a geometrically precise method for lifting 2D points to 3D using epipolar constraints, which is robust for multi-view stereo and novel view synthesis tasks. Limitations: Requires accurate camera intrinsics and extrinsics. Performance may degrade if rays are nearly parallel or if the intersection is numerically unstable. When to Use: Use when you need to lift 2D points to 3D space using epipolar geometry, particularly in multi-view settings. When Not to Use: Avoid if camera parameters are inaccurate or if the rays are likely to be parallel. Epipolar Ray Intersection is a fundamental technique in computer vision and graphics, particularly in multi-view stereo and structure from motion. It leverages the epipolar constraint to find corresponding points in different views. name: Depth to 3D Points Conversion
head: 3D Point Cloud Generation from Depth
body: This method converts a 2D depth map and associated pseudo-focal lengths into a 3D point cloud in absolute coordinates. It solves the problem of mapping per-pixel depth values from a 2D image plane into 3D space, enabling the construction of geometric scene representations from RGB-D data. Unlike sibling methods that may rely on explicit mesh extraction or virtual laser scans, this approach directly unprojects per-pixel depth values into 3D space, preserving high-dimensional semantic information alongside geometry. It builds on Epipolar Ray Intersection by providing the specific reprojection logic required to convert rendered buffers into 3D points. Inputs: depth: Depth map of shape (B, H, W) or (B, H, W, n). pseudofocal: Pseudo focal lengths of shape [B, H, W], [B, 2, H, W], or [B, 1, H, W]. pp (optional): Principal point coordinates. If None, defaults are used. Outputs: A 3D point cloud represented as coordinates (x, y, z) for each pixel in the depth map. Data Structures: Grid coordinates gridx, gridy: 2D arrays of shape (H, W) representing the pixel indices. pseudofocalx, pseudofocaly: Extracted focal length components from pseudofocal. Steps: 1. Generate grid coordinates gridx and gridy using an xygrid function, which creates coordinate matrices for the image dimensions H \times W. 2. Adjust grid coordinates by subtracting the principal point. If pp is provided, subtract pp; otherwise, subtract (W-1)/2 for x and (H-1)/2 for y. 3. Extract pseudofocalx and pseudofocaly from pseudofocal based on its shape. 4. Compute the x coordinate: x = \text{depth} \times \text{grid\x} / \text{pseudo\focalx}. 5. Compute the y coordinate: y = \text{depth} \times \text{grid\y} / \text{pseudo\focaly}. 6. Compute the z coordinate: z = \text{depth}. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import numpy as np def depthto3dpoints(depth, pseudofocal, pp=None): """ Converts a depth map and pseudo-focal lengths to a 3D point cloud. Args: depth: np.ndarray of shape (B, H, W) or (B, H, W, n) pseudofocal: np.ndarray of shape [B, H, W], [B, 2, H, W], or [B, 1, H, W] pp: tuple (px, py) for principal point. If None, uses image center. Returns: points: np.ndarray of shape (B, H, W, 3) containing x, y, z coordinates """ # Get dimensions B, H, W = depth.shape[:3] # Generate grid coordinates # Create meshgrid for x and y indices yindices, xindices = np.meshgrid(np.arange(H), np.arange(W), indexing='ij') # Adjust grid coordinates by subtracting principal point if pp is None: px = (W - 1) / 2.0 py = (H - 1) / 2.0 else: px, py = pp gridx = xindices - px gridy = yindices - py # Extract pseudo focal lengths # Handle different shapes of pseudofocal if pseudofocal.ndim == 4: if pseudofocal.shape[1] == 2: pseudofocalx = pseudofocal[:, 0,:,:] pseudofocaly = pseudofocal[:, 1,:,:] else: # Assume single channel or broadcastable pseudofocalx = pseudofocal[:, 0,:,:] pseudofocaly = pseudofocal[:, 0,:,:] else: # Shape [B, H, W] pseudofocalx = pseudofocal pseudofocaly = pseudofocal # Compute coordinates # x = depth gridx / pseudofocalx # y = depth gridy / pseudofocaly # z = depth # Ensure broadcasting works correctly # depth shape: (B, H, W) # gridx, gridy shape: (H, W) -> broadcast to (B, H, W) # pseudofocalx, pseudofocaly shape: (B, H, W) x = depth gridx / pseudofocalx y = depth gridy / pseudofocaly z = depth # Stack into (B, H, W, 3) points = np.stack([x, y, z], axis=-1) return points Parameters: depth: Depth map of shape (B, H, W) or (B, H, W, n). pseudofocal: Pseudo focal lengths of shape [B, H, W], [B, 2, H, W], or [B, 1, H, W]. pp: Principal point. If None, defaults to image center (W-1)/2, (H-1)/2. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Division by zero if pseudofocalx or pseudofocaly is zero. Guard against zero focal lengths. Shape mismatches between depth and pseudofocal. Ensure broadcasting compatibility. Principal point offset if not centered. Use provided pp or default to center. This method converts 2D rasterized depth and color images into a 3D point cloud using camera intrinsics and extrinsics. It solves the problem of mapping per-pixel depth values from a 2D image plane into 3D world coordinates, enabling the construction of geometric scene representations from multi-view RGB-D data. Unlike sibling methods that may rely on explicit mesh extraction or virtual laser scans, this approach directly unprojects per-pixel depth and learned feature vectors into 3D space, preserving high-dimensional semantic information alongside geometry. It builds on Depth to 3D Points Conversion by providing the specific reprojection logic required to convert rendered buffers into 3D points. An offline process that generates and refines a 3D point cloud from a subset of training images to improve depth estimation accuracy for novel views in neural rendering. It differs from standard Multi-View Stereo (MVS) by iteratively validating points against ground-truth depth from adjacent views, allowing it to generate a denser, more accurate point cloud for similar computational time, which leads to higher rendering quality (PSNR). Global Scene Point Cloud Construction aggregates depth maps from multiple calibrated views into a single, unified 3D point cloud in world coordinates. It solves the problem of redundant and inconsistent primitives that arise when unprojecting overlapping depth maps independently. It differs from Depth to 3D Points Conversion by handling the accumulation and cleaning of multiple views rather than processing a single depth map, and from Point Cloud Generation and Refinement by focusing specifically on the initial global assembly and noise removal steps. This method generates a fixed-size, colored 3D point cloud initialization for volume rendering primitives by backprojecting RGB-D data. It differs from its parent Depth to 3D Points Conversion by applying explicit downsampling factors and stride ratios to control point density, and from its sibling Point Cloud Generation and Refinement by relying on direct geometric backprojection rather than implicit field refinement. Time complexity: O(B \cdot H \cdot W) for processing all pixels in the batch. Memory complexity: O(B \cdot H \cdot W) to store the output point cloud. Measured performance: Not given in the sources. Scaling: Linear with respect to image resolution and batch size. Strengths: Simple, direct conversion from 2D depth to 3D points. Limitations: Relies on accurate depth maps and pseudo-focal lengths. When to use: When converting single-view depth maps to 3D points. When not: When multi-view consistency or refinement is required. The method originates from the InstantSplat project, which uses depth maps and pseudo-focal lengths to generate 3D point clouds for neural rendering. It is also referenced in the context of surface-based sampling for improving NeRF models, where depth images from the training set are used to generate point clouds for inference.
