name: Depth Map to Absolute Camera Coordinates
head: Depth Map Unprojection, RGBD to Point Cloud Back-Projection, camera back-projection, depth-to-3D conversion, depth2pc
body: This method converts 2D rasterized depth and color images into a 3D point cloud using camera intrinsics and extrinsics. It solves the problem of mapping per-pixel depth values from a 2D image plane into 3D world coordinates, enabling the construction of geometric scene representations from multi-view RGB-D data. Unlike sibling methods that may rely on explicit mesh extraction or virtual laser scans, this approach directly unprojects per-pixel depth and learned feature vectors into 3D space, preserving high-dimensional semantic information alongside geometry. It builds on Depth to 3D Points Conversion by providing the specific reprojection logic required to convert rendered buffers into 3D points. Inputs: depth: A tensor of shape (B, H, W) or (H, W) containing depth values z (distance from camera center). intrinsics: A 3x3 camera intrinsic matrix K. K{0,0} = fx (focal length in x) K{1,1} = fy (focal length in y) K{0,2} = cx (principal point x) K{1,2} = cy (principal point y) K{2,2} = 1 extrinsic (optional): A 4x4 world-to-camera transformation matrix W2C or its inverse C2W. If not provided, points remain in camera space. Outputs: points: A tensor of shape (B, H \times W, 3) or (H \times W, 3) containing 3D coordinates in world space (or camera space if extrinsics are omitted). Data Structures: Pixel grid indices xx, yy: 1D tensors of shape (H \times W) representing column and row indices. Homogeneous coordinate vector pixones: 1D tensor of shape (H \times W, 1) filled with ones. Steps: 1. Generate Pixel Grid: Create 2D meshgrid indices for all pixels. For a depth map of size H \times W, generate coordinates u \in [0, W-1] and v \in [0, H-1]. Flatten these into 1D arrays xx and yy of length H \times W. Note: Some implementations normalize these to [-1, 1] range first, while others keep integer indices. The standard pinhole model uses integer indices or normalized device coordinates depending on the intrinsic definition. We follow the standard pinhole projection formula. 2. Compute Camera Space Coordinates: For each pixel (u, v) with depth z: xc = (u - cx) \frac{z}{fx} yc = (v - cy) \frac{z}{fy} zc = z Stack these into a tensor ptscam of shape (H \times W, 3). 3. Handle Depth Scaling (Variant): Some pipelines (e.g., AtomGS) apply a depth scaling factor using elements f1, f2 from the projection matrix to adjust for specific rendering artifacts or inverse depth representations. If applicable: s{d{i,j}} = \frac{f1 d{i,j} + f2}{d{i,j}} Replace zc with s{d{i,j}} in ptscam. 4. Transform to World Space (Optional): If extrinsic is provided: Construct homogeneous coordinates pts4 by appending a column of ones to ptscam: pts4 = [xc, yc, zc, 1]. Compute the camera-to-world matrix C2W = (W2C)^{-1}. Transform points: P{world} = C2W \times pts4^T. Extract the first three rows to get Cartesian world coordinates. Reshape to (B, H \times W, 3). Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import torch def depthmaptoabsolutecameracoordinates(depth, intrinsics, extrinsic=None): """ Converts a depth map to 3D world coordinates. Args: depth: Tensor of shape (B, H, W) or (H, W). Depth values in meters. intrinsics: Tensor of shape (B, 3, 3) or (3, 3). Camera intrinsic matrix K. extrinsic: Tensor of shape (B, 4, 4) or (4, 4). World-to-Camera matrix W2C. Optional. Returns: points: Tensor of shape (B, HW, 3). 3D points in world space. """ # Handle batch dimension if depth.dim() == 2: depth = depth.unsqueeze(0) intrinsics = intrinsics.unsqueeze(0) if extrinsic is not None: extrinsic = extrinsic.unsqueeze(0) B, H, W = depth.shape # 1. Generate pixel grid indices # Create meshgrid: u in [0, W-1], v in [0, H-1] # Note: Using torch.arange and meshgrid u = torch.arange(0, W, device=depth.device).float() v = torch.arange(0, H, device=depth.device).float() uu, vv = torch.meshgrid(u, v, indexing='xy') # Flatten to 1D xx = uu.reshape(-1) # Column indices (u) yy = vv.reshape(-1) # Row indices (v) # Repeat for batch dimension if needed, or broadcast # Assuming intrinsics are per-batch xx = xx.unsqueeze(0).expand(B, -1) yy = yy.unsqueeze(0).expand(B, -1) zdepth = depth.reshape(B, -1) # 2. Extract intrinsics fx = intrinsics[:, 0, 0] fy = intrinsics[:, 1, 1] cx = intrinsics[:, 0, 2] cy = intrinsics[:, 1, 2] # 3. Compute camera space coordinates # xc = (u - cx) z / fx # yc = (v - cy) z / fy # zc = z # Broadcasting: xx, yy, zdepth are (B, HW) # fx, fy, cx, cy are (B,) xcam = (xx - cx.unsqueeze(1)) zdepth / fx.unsqueeze(1) ycam = (yy - cy.unsqueeze(1)) zdepth / fy.unsqueeze(1) zcam = zdepth # Stack into (B, HW, 3) ptscam = torch.stack([xcam, ycam, zcam], dim=-1) # 4. Transform to world space if extrinsic is provided if extrinsic is not None: # Compute C2W = inv(W2C) # Note: Inverse of 4x4 matrix c2w = torch.inverse(extrinsic) # Append homogeneous coordinate 1 ones = torch.ones(B, ptscam.shape[1], 1, device=ptscam.device) pts4 = torch.cat([ptscam, ones], dim=-1) # (B, HW, 4) # Transform: Pworld = C2W @ Pcamhom # pts4 is (B, N, 4). We need to multiply C2W (B, 4, 4) by pts4^T (B, 4, N) # Result is (B, 4, N). Then transpose to (B, N, 4) ptsworldhom = torch.bmm(c2w, pts4.transpose(1, 2)) # (B, 4, HW) ptsworldhom = ptsworldhom.transpose(1, 2) # (B, HW, 4) # Discard homogeneous coordinate pts = ptsworldhom[:,:,:3] else: pts = ptscam return pts Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Zero Depth: Pixels with z=0 result in undefined coordinates. Mask these out or set to NaN. Invalid Intrinsics: Ensure fx, fy \neq 0. Coordinate System: Verify if the depth map represents distance along the optical axis or Euclidean distance from the camera center. Standard pinhole assumes optical axis distance. Precision: Use float32 or float64 for coordinate calculations to avoid precision loss in large scenes. Point Cloud Construction converts 2D input views into 3D point clouds containing both geometric positions and view-dependent semantic features. It solves the problem of representing complex scenes in a format that is memory-efficient and scalable, serving as the foundational representation for subsequent differentiable rendering and multi-view fusion. Unlike sibling methods that may rely on explicit mesh extraction or virtual laser scans, this approach directly unprojects per-pixel depth and learned feature vectors into 3D space, preserving high-dimensional semantic information alongside geometry. A method to generate a point cloud with normals from a mesh by rendering normal and depth buffers from a specific camera viewpoint and reprojecting the buffer data into world space. It differs from direct mesh sampling by relying on rasterization to handle visibility and occlusion, effectively acting as a "virtual laser scan" from a single viewpoint. It builds on Depth Map to Absolute Camera Coordinates by providing the specific reprojection logic required to convert rendered buffers into 3D points. In scenarios where LiDAR data is available, depth maps can be generated by projecting LiDAR points onto the image plane. For a given image frame, LiDAR points from the ten closest LiDAR frames are selected and transformed into world coordinates. These points are then projected onto the image coordinates. The depth value for each pixel is derived from the distance along the ray from the camera center to the nearest LiDAR point. If multiple LiDAR points project to the same pixel, the depth value is taken from the closest point. Time Complexity: O(H \times W) per image, as each pixel is processed independently. Memory Complexity: O(H \times W) to store the resulting point cloud. Performance: Highly parallelizable on GPU. Typical performance depends on resolution; for 1080p images, processing is nearly instantaneous on modern GPUs. Strengths: Simple, differentiable (if depth is learned), and preserves per-pixel correspondence. Limitations: Sensitive to depth errors; noisy depth maps result in noisy point clouds. Does not handle occlusions or missing depth data automatically (requires masking). The method originates from standard computer vision techniques for back-projecting depth maps to 3D space using pinhole camera models. It is widely used in RGB-D reconstruction, SLAM, and NeRF/Gaussian Splatting pipelines to initialize point clouds or supervise depth predictions. Key implementations include SplaTAM, InstantSplat, and GPS+. The specific depth scaling variant is described in AtomGS. spla-tam/SplaTAM, https://github.com/spla-tam/SplaTAM, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial) NVlabs/InstantSplat, https://github.com/NVlabs/InstantSplat, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial) YaourtB/GPSplus, https://github.com/YaourtB/GPSplus, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial) AtomGS: Atomizing Gaussian Splatting for High-Fidelity Radiance Field, https://core.ac.uk/works/391753628, fetched 2026-10-30 (unofficial) LidaRF: Delving into Lidar for Neural Radiance Field on Street Scenes, https://doi.org/10.1109/cvpr52733.2024.01850, fetched 2026-10-26

name: Point Cloud Construction
head: Depth and Feature Unprojection, Multi-view Point Cloud Generation
body: Point Cloud Construction converts 2D input views into 3D point clouds containing both geometric positions and view-dependent semantic features. It solves the problem of representing complex scenes in a format that is memory-efficient and scalable, serving as the foundational representation for subsequent differentiable rendering and multi-view fusion. Unlike sibling methods that may rely on explicit mesh extraction or virtual laser scans, this approach directly unprojects per-pixel depth and learned feature vectors into 3D space, preserving high-dimensional semantic information alongside geometry [S1, 16278-virtual-laser-scan-for-point-cloud-generation.md]. Inputs: Input image view Ii. Camera intrinsics matrix K. Camera pose (extrinsics) T{world \to camera} or T{camera \to world} (implied by "Absolute Camera Coordinates" parent context, but specifically "known camera intrinsics" are cited for projection). Estimated depth map Di (output of depth network d). Spatial feature vectors Fi^{raw} (output of spatial feature encoder f). Outputs: Point cloud Pi, a set of points where each point contains 3D coordinates and a 64-dimensional feature vector. Data Structures: Point Cloud Pi: A list or array of points. Each point stores: 3D coordinates (X, Y, Z) in world or camera space (consistent with the parent method's output coordinate system). Feature vector F \in \mathbb{R}^{64}. Feature Vector Layout: Dimensions 0-60 (61 dims): Semantic features from encoder f. Dimensions 61-63 (3 dims): RGB color channels from input image Ii. Steps: 1. Depth Estimation: For each input view Ii, estimate the per-pixel depth map Di using a depth network d. This network may combine multi-view stereo cues with a U-Net refinement to resolve scaling ambiguities. 2. Feature Encoding: Compute per-pixel spatial feature vectors Fi^{raw} using a spatial feature encoder f (e.g., BigGAN-based). 3. Feature Concatenation: For each pixel, concatenate the 61-dimensional feature vector Fi^{raw} with the 3 RGB channels of the input image Ii to form the final 64-dimensional feature vector Fi. Fi = \text{Concat}(Fi^{raw}, \text{RGB}(Ii)) 4. 3D Unprojection: For each pixel (u, v) with depth d{uv} and feature F{uv}: a. Convert pixel coordinates to normalized camera coordinates using intrinsics K. b. Scale by depth d{uv} to get camera-space coordinates. c. Transform to world coordinates using the camera pose (as per parent method [7984-depth-map-to-absolute-camera-coordinates.md]). d. Create a point p = (X, Y, Z, F{uv}) and add to Pi. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def constructpointcloud(Ii, K, Tworldtocamera, Di, Firaw): """ Constructs a 3D point cloud from a single view. Args: Ii: Input image (H, W, 3) with RGB values in [0, 1] or [0, 255]. K: Camera intrinsic matrix (3, 3). Tworldtocamera: 4x4 transformation matrix from world to camera coordinates. Di: Estimated depth map (H, W). Firaw: Spatial feature vectors (H, W, 61). Returns: Pi: List of points, each being a tuple (X, Y, Z, F64). """ H, W = Di.shape Pi = [] # Precompute inverse intrinsics for unprojection Kinv = np.linalg.inv(K) for y in range(H): for x in range(W): # 1. Get depth and raw features depth = Di[y, x] featraw = Firaw[y, x] # Shape: (61,) rgb = Ii[y, x] # Shape: (3,) # 2. Concatenate features: 61-dim + 3 RGB = 64-dim featfull = np.concatenate([featraw, rgb]) # 3. Unproject pixel to 3D # Convert pixel (x, y) to homogeneous normalized coordinates # Assuming standard pinhole model: x = (u - cx) / fx, y = (v - cy) / fy # Or using Kinv: [xnorm, ynorm, 1.0] = Kinv @ [u, v, 1] pixelhom = np.array([x, y, 1.0]) camcoordshom = Kinv @ pixelhom # Scale by depth to get camera-space coordinates # Note: Depth Di is assumed to be in the same scale as the Z-axis in camera space camcoords = camcoordshom depth # Transform to world coordinates # camcoords is (3,), need to make it (4,1) for matrix mult camcoordshom = np.append(camcoords, 1.0) worldcoordshom = np.linalg.inv(Tworldtocamera) @ camcoordshom X, Y, Z = worldcoordshom[:3] # 4. Add point to cloud Pi.append((X, Y, Z, featfull)) return Pi Parameters: Feature vector base dimension: 61. Total feature dimension per point: 64 (61 + 3 RGB). Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Depth Ambiguity: Single-image depth estimation suffers from scaling/shifting ambiguity, which can lead to inconsistent 3D points across views. The method relies on the depth network d to mitigate this, often using multi-view stereo cues. Missing Depth: Pixels with invalid or missing depth values should be excluded from the point cloud to avoid artifacts. Coordinate System Consistency: The depth values must be consistent with the camera coordinate system defined by K and the transformation T [S1, 7984-depth-map-to-absolute-camera-coordinates.md]. Projects 2D features from a source view to a target view using estimated depth and camera poses. It differs by handling depth uncertainty through a depth volume and aggregating features across multiple depth hypotheses, rather than a single plane. Choose when multi-view consistency checks or feature aggregation for depth estimation are required. Time Complexity: Linear with respect to the number of pixels in the input image O(H \times W) per view, as each pixel is processed independently during unprojection. Memory Complexity: Proportional to the number of pixels times the feature dimension size. For an image of size H \times W, memory is O(H \times W \times 64) for the point cloud data. Strengths: Efficient, compact memory usage, and scalable to complex scenes compared to dense voxel grids. Preserves view-dependent semantics. Limitations: Relies heavily on the accuracy of the estimated depth Di and feature encoder f. Inaccurate depth leads to geometric errors in the point cloud. Sparse inputs with large baselines can lead to inaccurate depth estimations if not properly refined. When to Use: When a compact, semantically rich 3D representation is needed for differentiable rendering or novel view synthesis. When Not to Use: When high-precision geometric reconstruction is required without semantic features, or when depth estimation is unreliable. The method originates from the FWD (Forward Warping and Depth) model for real-time novel view synthesis. It was introduced to leverage the efficiency and scalability of point clouds for representing scenes with complex geometry and view-dependent appearance. The approach integrates a differentiable neural point cloud renderer, allowing end-to-end training with photometric and perceptual losses. FWD: Real-time Novel View Synthesis with Forward Warping and Depth, https://doi.org/10.1109/cvpr52688.2022.01526, fetched 2026-10-29

name: Depth-aware Feature Warping
body: Depth-aware Feature Warping projects 2D features from a source view to a target view using estimated depth and camera poses, enabling multi-view consistency checks or feature aggregation for depth estimation. It differs from standard geometric warping by explicitly handling depth uncertainty through a depth volume, allowing the method to aggregate features across multiple depth hypotheses rather than a single depth plane. Inputs: Source feature map Fs \in \mathbb{R}^{B \times C \times H \times W}, where B is batch size, C is channels, H is height, W is width. Source camera intrinsics K \in \mathbb{R}^{B \times 3 \times 3}. Relative pose from source to target view P \in \mathbb{R}^{B \times 4 \times 4}, composed of rotation R \in \mathbb{R}^{B \times 3 \times 3} and translation t \in \mathbb{R}^{B \times 3 \times 1}. Depth volume D \in \mathbb{R}^{B \times D \times H \times W}, where D is the number of depth candidates. Outputs: Warped feature map Fw \in \mathbb{R}^{B \times C \times D \times H \times W} (or flattened spatial dimensions depending on implementation). Data Structures: Homogeneous pixel coordinate grid: Shape [B, 3, H, W]. The first two channels are normalized coordinates (x, y), and the third channel is all ones. 3D points in camera space: Shape [B, 3, H \times W]. Transformed 3D points: Shape [B, 3, D, H \times W]. Sampling grid: Shape [B, D \times H, W, 2] or [B, D, H, W, 2] depending on gridsample requirements. Parameters: clampmindepth: Minimum depth value for clamping z during reprojection to prevent division by zero. Default is 10^{-3}. Steps: 1. Generate Pixel Grid: Create a homogeneous grid of pixel coordinates. For each pixel (u, v) in the source image, construct a vector [u, v, 1]^T. This results in a tensor of shape [B, 3, H, W]. 2. Back-project to 3D Camera Space: Flatten the spatial dimensions of the grid to [B, 3, H \times W]. Multiply by the inverse of the source camera intrinsics K^{-1} to obtain 3D points in the source camera coordinate system (normalized by depth, effectively rays): P{cam} = K^{-1} \cdot G{flat} Resulting shape: [B, 3, H \times W]. 3. Transform to Target Coordinate System: a. Apply the rotation R from the relative pose P: P{rot} = R \cdot P{cam} b. Repeat the rotated points along the depth dimension to match the depth volume shape [B, 3, D, H \times W]. c. Scale by the depth values di from the depth volume D: P{scaled} = P{rot} \cdot D{reshaped} where D{reshaped} has shape [B, 1, D, H \times W]. 4. Translate by Pose Translation: Add the translation vector t from the relative pose to the scaled points: P{target} = P{scaled} + t Resulting shape: [B, 3, D, H \times W]. 5. Reproject to Target Image Plane: Multiply the 3D points in the target coordinate system by the target camera intrinsics K{target} (often assumed same as source or provided separately). Reshape points to [B, 3, D \times H \times W] before multiplication: P{proj} = K{target} \cdot P{target, flat} Reshape back to [B, 3, D, H \times W]. 6. Compute Normalized Pixel Coordinates: Divide the x and y coordinates by the z coordinate (depth in target view). Clamp z to clampmindepth to avoid division by zero: u{norm} = \frac{P{proj, x}}{\max(P{proj, z}, \text{clamp\min\depth})} v{norm} = \frac{P{proj, y}}{\max(P{proj, z}, \text{clamp\min\depth})} Resulting shape for u{norm}, v{norm}: [B, D, H \times W]. 7. Normalize to [-1, 1] Range: Convert normalized pixel coordinates to the range [-1, 1] required by bilinear sampling functions: x{grid} = \frac{2 u{norm}}{W - 1} - 1 y{grid} = \frac{2 v{norm}}{H - 1} - 1 Resulting shape: [B, D, H \times W]. 8. Construct Sampling Grid: Stack x{grid} and y{grid} to form a sampling grid. The grid must be shaped appropriately for the interpolation function, typically [B, D \times H, W, 2] or [B, D, H, W, 2] with channels last. 9. Sample Features: Use bilinear interpolation (gridsample) to sample features from the source feature map Fs using the computed grid. Use zero padding for out-of-bounds pixels: Fw = \text{grid\sample}(Fs, \text{Grid}, \text{mode}=\text{"bilinear"}, \text{padding\mode}=\text{"zeros"}, \text{align\corners}=\text{True}) Resulting shape: [B, C, D, H, W]. Pitfalls: Large feature maps (e.g., >1,000,000 elements) can cause CUDNN errors in gridsample. In such cases, disable CUDNN for the sampling operation. Division by zero must be handled via clamping z. Coordinate system conventions (e.g., origin at center vs. corner, axis directions) must be consistent between back-projection and reprojection. Time Complexity: O(B \cdot D \cdot H \cdot W), dominated by the 3D point transformation and bilinear sampling. Memory Complexity: O(B \cdot D \cdot H \cdot W) for storing the transformed 3D points and sampling grids. Strengths: Enables robust feature aggregation across views by accounting for depth uncertainty. Allows for multi-view consistency checks by warping features from multiple source views to a target view. Limitations: Computationally expensive for high-resolution images and large depth volumes. Sensitive to errors in depth estimation and camera pose accuracy. When to use: Multi-view stereo depth estimation, novel view synthesis, and 3D reconstruction tasks requiring feature alignment across views. When not to use: Real-time applications with strict latency constraints and limited depth uncertainty. Depth-aware Feature Warping is a fundamental technique in multi-view geometry and computer vision, particularly in deep learning-based multi-view stereo (MVS) and novel view synthesis. It allows neural networks to leverage information from multiple viewpoints by aligning features in a common coordinate system. The method is widely used in frameworks like DepthSplat for efficient depth estimation and feature aggregation. cvg/depthsplat, https://github.com/cvg/depthsplat, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial)

name: Virtual Laser Scan for Point Cloud Generation
head: Scan class, get_surface_point_cloud via scan
body: A method to generate a point cloud with normals from a mesh by rendering normal and depth buffers from a specific camera viewpoint and reprojecting the buffer data into world space. It differs from direct mesh sampling by relying on rasterization to handle visibility and occlusion, effectively acting as a "virtual laser scan" from a single viewpoint. It builds on Depth Map to Absolute Camera Coordinates by providing the specific reprojection logic required to convert rendered buffers into 3D points. Inputs: mesh: The input 3D mesh object. cameratransform: A 4 \times 4 transformation matrix representing the camera's pose in world space. resolution: Integer, width and height of the rendered buffers (default 400). calculatenormals: Boolean, whether to compute and store normals (default True). fov: Field of view in radians (default 1). znear: Near plane distance (default 0.1). zfar: Far plane distance (default 10). Outputs: self.points: Array of shape (N, 3) containing 3D coordinates in world space. self.normals: Array of shape (N, 3) containing unit normals in world space (if calculatenormals is True). Data Structures: depthbuffer: Rendered depth values from the graphics API. colorbuffer: Rendered normal buffer (RGB8 format) if calculatenormals is True. projectionmatrix: 4 \times 4 matrix derived from camera intrinsics. cameraposition: 3 \times 1 vector derived from cameratransform. Steps: 1. Initialize Camera: Compute cameraposition from cameratransform: \text{camera\position} = (\text{camera\transform} \times [0, 0, 0, 1]^T)[:3] Create a perspective camera with yfov=fov, aspectRatio=1.0, znear=znear, zfar=zfar. Extract the projectionmatrix. 2. Render Buffers: Render the mesh using the camera. Obtain depthbuffer and colorbuffer (if calculatenormals is True) at the specified resolution. 3. Filter Valid Pixels: Find indices where depth is non-zero: \text{indices} = \text{argwhere}(\text{depth\buffer} \neq 0) Set depth values equal to 0 to infinity to exclude them from further processing: \text{depth\buffer}[\text{depth\buffer} == 0] = \infty 4. Revert Depth Processing: The rendered depth is typically non-linear. Revert to linear clip-space depth z{clip} using: z{clip} = \frac{z{far} + z{near} - \frac{2 z{near} z{far}}{depth{buffer}}}{z{far} - z{near}} Store this as self.depth. 5. Map to Clip Space: Create a points array of shape (N, 4) initialized with ones in the w-component. Map pixel indices to normalized device coordinates (NDC) clip space: \text{points}[:, [1, 0]] = \frac{\text{indices}}{\text{resolution} - 1} \times 2 - 1 Negate the y-component to account for coordinate system differences (e.g., screen vs. clip space): \text{points}[:, 1] = -1 Set the z-component to the calculated clip-space depth: \text{points}[:, 2] = \text{self.depth}[\text{indices}[:, 0], \text{indices}[:, 1]] 6. Transform to World Space: Compute the clipping-to-world matrix: \text{clipping\to\world} = \text{camera\transform} \times \text{inv}(\text{projection\matrix}) Transform points: \text{points} = \text{points} \times \text{clipping\to\world}^T Perform perspective divide: \text{points} = \text{points} / \text{points}[:, 3][:, \text{newaxis}] Store the final 3D points: \text{self.points} = \text{points}[:,:3] 7. Compute Normals (Optional): If calculatenormals is True: Decode normals from the color buffer (assuming RGB8 encoding where [0, 255] maps to [-1, 1]): \text{normals} = \frac{\text{color\buffer}[\text{indices}[:, 0], \text{indices}[:, 1]]}{255} \times 2 - 1 Compute vector from camera to points: \text{camera\to\points} = \text{camera\position} - \text{self.points} Determine orientation via dot product: \text{normal\orientation} = \text{einsum}('ij,ij->i', \text{camera\to\points}, \text{normals}) Flip normals pointing away from the camera: \text{normals}[\text{normal\orientation} < 0] = -1 Store normals: \text{self.normals} = \text{normals} Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import numpy as np import pyrender import trimesh class Scan: def init(self, mesh, cameratransform, resolution=400, calculatenormals=True, fov=1.0, znear=0.1, zfar=10.0): self.mesh = mesh self.cameratransform = cameratransform self.resolution = resolution self.calculatenormals = calculatenormals self.znear = znear self.zfar = zfar # Compute camera position self.cameraposition = np.matmul(self.cameratransform, np.array([0, 0, 0, 1]))[:3] # Create camera and get projection matrix # Note: pyrender PerspectiveCamera expects yfov, aspectRatio, znear, zfar self.camera = pyrender.PerspectiveCamera( yfov=fov, aspectRatio=1.0, znear=znear, zfar=zfar) self.projectionmatrix = self.camera.getprojectionmatrix() # Render buffers # rendernormalanddepthbuffers is a helper that returns depth and color buffers depthbuffer, colorbuffer = self.renderbuffers() # Filter valid pixels indices = np.argwhere(depthbuffer != 0) depthbuffer[depthbuffer == 0] = float('inf') if indices.size == 0: self.points = np.empty((0, 3)) self.normals = None return # Revert depth processing to get clip-space depth # Formula: zclip = (zfar + znear - (2 znear zfar) / depth) / (zfar - znear) self.depth = (zfar + znear - (2.0 znear zfar) / depthbuffer) / (zfar - znear) # Map pixel indices to clip space coordinates points = np.ones((indices.shape[0], 4)) points[:, [1, 0]] = indices.astype(float) / (resolution - 1) 2 - 1 points[:, 1] = -1 # Negate y points[:, 2] = self.depth[indices[:, 0], indices[:, 1]] # Transform to world space clippingtoworld = np.matmul(self.cameratransform, np.linalg.inv(self.projectionmatrix)) points = np.matmul(points, clippingtoworld.transpose()) # Perspective divide points /= points[:, 3][:, np.newaxis] self.points = points[:,:3] if calculatenormals: # Decode normals from color buffer normals = colorbuffer[indices[:, 0], indices[:, 1]] / 255.0 2.0 - 1.0 # Compute vector from camera to points cameratopoints = self.cameraposition - self.points # Determine normal orientation normalorientation = np.einsum('ij,ij->i', cameratopoints, normals) # Flip normals pointing away from camera normals[normalorientation < 0] = -1 self.normals = normals else: self.normals = None def renderbuffers(self): """Helper to render depth and normal buffers using pyrender.""" scene = pyrender.Scene() scene.add(pyrender.Mesh.fromtrimesh(self.mesh)) scene.add(self.camera) # Render depth r = pyrender.OffscreenRenderer(self.resolution, self.resolution) color, depth = r.render(scene, flags=pyrender.constants.RenderFlags.RGBA | pyrender.constants.RenderFlags.DEPTHONLY) # Extract normal buffer if needed (pyrender doesn't natively support normal buffer rendering # in standard OffscreenRenderer without custom shaders or extensions. # Assuming a helper exists that renders normals to color buffer if calculatenormals is True) if self.calculatenormals: # Placeholder for actual normal buffer rendering logic which might require # a custom shader or library extension not detailed in standard pyrender API. # In the source context, this is handled by rendernormalanddepthbuffers. # We assume 'color' here represents the normal buffer if calculated, # but standard pyrender returns RGBA color. # For implementation fidelity based on, we assume a specific rendering path # that outputs normals to the color buffer. pass return depth, color def isvisible(self, points): """Check if points are visible from this scan's perspective.""" # Visibility check logic: transform points to clip space, check depth buffer # This requires projecting points and comparing against self.depth # Implementation details omitted as per source brevity, but involves: # 1. Transform points to camera space # 2. Project to clip space # 3. Check if projected depth is less than stored depth buffer value at that pixel # pass A variant that generates a complete surface point cloud by aggregating scans from multiple viewpoints. It uses a Fibonacci sphere distribution to generate camera angles, ensuring uniform coverage. For each angle, a Scan object is created with specific parameters: fov=1.0472, znear=boundingradius, zfar=3boundingradius, and resolution=400. The points and normals from all scans are concatenated to form the final SurfacePointCloud. Time Complexity: Linear with respect to the number of pixels in the resolution (O(R^2)) for rendering and reprojection. Aggregating multiple scans scales linearly with the number of scans. Memory Complexity: Linear with respect to the number of visible pixels. The depth and color buffers require O(R^2) memory. Performance: Depends heavily on the rendering engine's speed. Pyrender is relatively slow for high-resolution scans compared to GPU-based rasterization libraries. Strengths: Handles occlusion naturally via the depth buffer. Provides normals aligned with the view direction (corrected to face outward). Simple to implement using standard graphics libraries. Limitations: Resolution-dependent; high resolution is needed for smooth surfaces. Single-scan scans suffer from occlusion and back-face visibility issues. Requires the camera to be outside the mesh for accurate visibility checks. When to use: When a view-dependent point cloud is sufficient, or when generating a multi-view point cloud for SDF reconstruction. When not to use: When a complete, watertight, and resolution-independent surface representation is required (use mesh sampling or SDF instead). Originated in the meshtosdf library by marian42, which uses virtual laser scans to generate point clouds for Signed Distance Field (SDF) reconstruction. The method leverages standard graphics pipeline operations (projection, rasterization, depth testing) to sample the mesh surface. meshtosdf, https://github.com/marian42/meshtosdf, fetched 2026-10-28 (unofficial)

name: Lidar Depth Generation
head: LiDAR Depth Map Generation, LiDAR-to-Image Depth Projection
body: Lidar Depth Generation converts sparse, unstructured 3D LiDAR point clouds into dense, pixel-aligned depth maps for synchronized RGB images. It solves the problem of generating high-quality depth supervision for neural rendering or vision tasks by leveraging the geometric accuracy of LiDAR sensors. Unlike direct depth sensing, this method projects accumulated LiDAR points from multiple time steps onto the 2D image plane, resolving occlusions and sparsity by selecting the nearest point per pixel. It builds on Depth Map to Absolute Camera Coordinates by providing the raw depth values and projection logic required to establish the camera-space depth map. Inputs: A target RGB image frame I with known camera intrinsics K and extrinsics T{cam}^{world} (pose). A set of N LiDAR frames \{L1, L2,..., LN\}, where each frame Li contains a set of 3D points Pi = \{(x, y, z)\} in the LiDAR sensor coordinate system. A synchronization window parameter W (number of closest LiDAR frames to consider). Outputs: A depth map D of size H \times W, where D{u,v} is the depth value for pixel (u, v). A validity mask M indicating which pixels have valid depth. Data Structures: Depth Map: A 2D array of floats, initialized to infinity or a sentinel value (e.g., -1) to indicate no depth. Point Cloud: A list of 3D vectors. Steps: 1. Selection: Identify the W LiDAR frames closest in time to the target image frame. Let this subset be L{selected}. 2. Transformation: For each LiDAR frame Li \in L{selected}, transform its points from the LiDAR sensor frame to the world coordinate frame using the sensor-to-world transformation matrix T{lidar}^{world}. Let the transformed points be Pi^{world}. 3. Projection: For each point p \in Pi^{world}, project it onto the image plane using the camera intrinsics K and the camera-to-world pose T{cam}^{world}. Compute the camera-relative point: p{cam} = T{cam}^{world^{-1}} \cdot p. Project to normalized device coordinates: p{ndc} = K \cdot p{cam}. Convert to pixel coordinates (u, v): u = \frac{p{ndc,x}}{p{ndc,z}} v = \frac{p{ndc,y}}{p{ndc,z}} Check if (u, v) lies within the image bounds [0, W{img}) \times [0, H{img}) and if p{ndc,z} > 0 (point is in front of the camera). 4. Depth Calculation: For valid projections, compute the depth value d as the Euclidean distance from the camera center to the point: d = \| p{cam} \|2 = \sqrt{p{cam,x}^2 + p{cam,y}^2 + p{cam,z}^2} 5. Aggregation: For each pixel (u, v), if multiple points project to it, select the point with the smallest depth value d. Update the depth map: D{u,v} = \min(D{u,v}, d) Mark M{u,v} = 1 if D{u,v} was updated. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def generatelidardepth(imageintrinsics, camerapose, lidarframes, numframes=10): """ imageintrinsics: 3x3 matrix K camerapose: 4x4 matrix Tcamworld lidarframes: list of (timestamp, points3d, lidarpose) numframes: number of closest lidar frames to use """ # 1. Select closest frames targettimestamp = getimagetimestamp() sortedlidar = sortbytimediff(lidarframes, targettimestamp) selectedlidar = sortedlidar[:numframes] # Initialize depth map with infinity height, width = getimageshape() depthmap = np.full((height, width), np.inf) validmask = np.zeros((height, width), dtype=bool) # Inverse camera pose for world-to-camera transformation caminv = np.linalg.inv(camerapose) for frame in selectedlidar: lidarpoints = frame.points lidarpose = frame.pose # 2. Transform to world coordinates # lidarpoints are Nx3, lidarpose is 4x4 # Homogeneous coordinates for batch transformation ones = np.ones((lidarpoints.shape[0], 1)) lidarpointshomo = np.hstack([lidarpoints, ones]) worldpointshomo = (lidarpose @ lidarpointshomo.T).T worldpoints = worldpointshomo[:,:3] # 3. Project to image coordinates # Transform world points to camera coordinates campointshomo = (caminv @ worldpointshomo.T).T campoints = campointshomo[:,:3] # Check if points are in front of camera validz = campoints[:, 2] > 0 # Project using intrinsics # u = fx x/z + cx, v = fy y/z + cy x, y, z = campoints[validz].T u = (imageintrinsics[0, 0] x / z) + imageintrinsics[0, 2] v = (imageintrinsics[1, 1] y / z) + imageintrinsics[1, 2] # Check image bounds validu = (u >= 0) & (u < width) validv = (v >= 0) & (v < height) validindices = np.where(validz & validu & validv)[0] if len(validindices) == 0: continue uvalid = u[validindices].astype(int) vvalid = v[validindices].astype(int) zvalid = z[validindices] # 4. Compute depth (distance from camera center) # Depth is Euclidean distance in camera coordinates depths = np.sqrt(x[validindices]2 + y[validindices]2 + zvalid2) # 5. Update depth map with minimum depth for idx in range(len(validindices)): ui, vi = uvalid[idx], vvalid[idx] d = depths[idx] if d < depthmap[vi, ui]: depthmap[vi, ui] = d validmask[vi, ui] = True return depthmap, validmask Parameters: numframes: Typically 10, as used in PandaSet. lidarpose: Must be synchronized and calibrated relative to the camera. Edge Cases: No LiDAR points: If no points project to a pixel, the depth remains infinity/invalid. Multiple points: The nearest point (smallest depth) is chosen, handling occlusions. Precision: Floating-point precision in depth calculation should be sufficient to distinguish close points. Simulates real LiDAR sensor rays by defining ray origin and direction based on sensor parameters and ego-vehicle motion to generate 3D points. Time Complexity: O(N \cdot W), where N is the number of LiDAR points in the selected frames and W is the number of frames. Projection and aggregation are linear in the number of points. Memory Complexity: O(H \cdot W) for the depth map, plus storage for the selected LiDAR points. Strengths: Provides accurate depth supervision by leveraging LiDAR's direct range measurement. Handles sparse LiDAR data by accumulating points over time. Limitations: Requires synchronized LiDAR and camera data. Performance depends on the density of LiDAR points and the number of frames used. Occlusions may still result in missing depth if the nearest point is not captured. When to use: When generating depth maps for neural rendering or vision tasks where LiDAR data is available but sparse. When not to use: When real-time performance is critical and LiDAR data is not available or too sparse. Lidar Depth Generation is a technique used in datasets like PandaSet to provide depth supervision for neural radiance fields (NeRF) and other vision tasks. It was introduced in the LidaRF paper, which delves into the use of LiDAR for neural radiance fields on street scenes. The method addresses the challenge of unbounded scenes by normalizing the scene based on the camera trajectory radius. LidaRF: Delving into Lidar for Neural Radiance Field on Street Scenes, https://doi.org/10.1109/cvpr52733.2024.01850, fetched 2026-10-26

name: LiDAR Ray Simulation
head: NeRF-LiDAR Ray Simulation
body: Simulates real LiDAR sensor rays by defining ray origin and direction based on sensor parameters and ego-vehicle motion to generate 3D points. It differs from standard ray casting by explicitly modeling the temporal evolution of the sensor origin due to vehicle velocity and incorporating a learned "raydrop" probability to mimic real-world signal loss, rather than assuming perfect reflection. Inputs and Outputs Inputs: NeRF implicit representation (for depth/distance \hat{D}), LiDAR sensor parameters (channels, FOV, spin rate), ego-vehicle velocity v, and time interval \Delta t. Outputs: A set of 3D points p and their associated semantic/depth labels, forming a simulated LiDAR frame \hat{P}. Data Structures Ray Parameters: Defined by azimuth \theta and vertical angle \phi. Equirectangular Grid: A 2D image grid of resolution H \times W used for point-wise alignment. For a 32-channel LiDAR (e.g., nuScenes), this is 32 \times 1024. Numbered Steps 1. Determine Ray Direction: For each laser channel, calculate the azimuth \theta and vertical angle \phi based on the LiDAR's mechanical settings and the time interval \Delta t within the scan cycle. Compute the direction vector d using: d = (\cos \theta \cos \phi, \sin \theta \sin \phi, \cos \phi)^T 2. Update Ray Origin: Calculate the current sensor origin o by updating the previous origin o0 with the ego-vehicle's velocity v over the time interval \Delta t: o = o0 + \Delta t \cdot v 3. Query NeRF for Distance: Cast the ray defined by o and d into the NeRF. Sample along the ray to find the distance \hat{D} from the sensor to the nearest surface (or integrate density to find the expected depth). 4. Compute 3D Point: Calculate the simulated point p in 3D space: p = o + \hat{D}d 5. Apply Raydrop (Optional/Learned): To match real-world sensor behavior where points are dropped due to low reflectance or incidence angle, apply a learned probability mask. This is often done by projecting both real point cloud P and simulated point

name: Distance-from-Center (DFC) Map Generation
head: DFC maps
body: Distance-from-Center (DFC) map generation converts per-view depth maps into a global radial distance representation relative to a scene center. It solves the problem of separating foreground and background elements in outdoor scenes by providing a unified metric that is invariant to camera position. Unlike sibling methods that operate in local camera coordinates or raw point clouds, DFC maps express depth in a common global reference frame, enabling a single distance threshold to segment foreground and background regions across all views. Inputs: A set of camera poses (extrinsics) and intrinsic parameters for N views. A depth map Dv for each view v, where Dv(u, v) is the depth value at pixel coordinates (u, v). A defined scene center O (typically the origin of the world coordinate system or the centroid of the sparse point cloud). Outputs: A set of DFC maps, one per view, where each pixel stores the Euclidean distance from the unprojected 3D point to O. Data Structures: Scene Center O: A 3D vector (Ox, Oy, Oz). DFC Map Mv: A 2D array of floats, same dimensions as Dv. Mv(u, v) stores the distance. Steps: 1. Unprojection: For each view v and each pixel (u, v) in the depth map Dv: Retrieve the depth value d = Dv(u, v). If d is invalid (e.g., zero or infinity), set Mv(u, v) to invalid and continue. Convert pixel coordinates (u, v) to normalized device coordinates (xn, yn) using intrinsics. Construct the ray direction \mathbf{r} in camera coordinates. Transform \mathbf{r} and the camera origin Cv to world coordinates using the camera pose. Compute the 3D point P in world coordinates: P = Cv + d \cdot \mathbf{r}. 2. Distance Calculation: Compute the Euclidean distance from P to the scene center O: \text{dist} = \| P - O \|2 = \sqrt{(Px - Ox)^2 + (Py - Oy)^2 + (Pz - Oz)^2} Store \text{dist} in Mv(u, v). Parameters: Scene Center O: Not given in the sources. Typically derived from the centroid of the initial COLMAP sparse point cloud or set to (0,0,0) if the scene is centered. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Invalid Depth: Pixels with missing depth must be handled to avoid NaNs in the DFC map. Precision: Floating-point precision in distance calculation should be sufficient to distinguish foreground/background boundaries. Degenerate Input: If the scene center O is poorly chosen (e.g., far from the scene), the DFC values may not effectively separate foreground/background. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import numpy as np def generatedfcmaps(depthmaps, poses, intrinsics, scenecenter): """ depthmaps: list of 2D numpy arrays, shape (H, W), values in meters. poses: list of 4x4 numpy arrays, world-to-camera or camera-to-world? Assuming poses are camera-to-world matrices Tcam2world. intrinsics: 3x3 numpy array, camera intrinsic matrix K. scenecenter: 3D numpy array, shape (3,), coordinates of O. Returns: dfcmaps: list of 2D numpy arrays, same shape as depthmaps. """ dfcmaps = [] # Precompute inverse intrinsics for unprojection Kinv = np.linalg.inv(intrinsics) for depthmap, Tcam2world in zip(depthmaps, poses): H, W = depthmap.shape dfcmap = np.zeros((H, W)) # Create meshgrid for pixel coordinates u, v = np.meshgrid(np.arange(W), np.arange(H)) # Normalize pixel coordinates to camera space # x = (u - cx) / fx, y = (v - cy) / fy, z = 1 fx, fy = intrinsics[0, 0], intrinsics[1, 1] cx, cy = intrinsics[0, 2], intrinsics[1, 2] xcam = (u - cx) / fx ycam = (v - cy) / fy zcam = np.oneslike(u) # Stack to form ray directions in camera coordinates rayscam = np.stack([xcam, ycam, zcam], axis=-1) # Shape (H, W, 3) # Transform rays to world coordinates # Rcam2world is the upper-left 3x3 of Tcam2world Rcam2world = Tcam2world[:3,:3] raysworld = np.einsum('ijk,ljk->ijl', rayscam, Rcam2world) # Shape (H, W, 3) # Camera origin in world coordinates Cworld = Tcam2world[:3, 3] # Shape (3,) # Unproject: P = C + d r # depthmap is (H, W), raysworld is (H, W, 3) # Pworld = Cworld + depthmap[..., None] raysworld Pworld = Cworld + depthmap[:,:, np.newaxis] raysworld # Shape (H, W, 3) # Compute distance to scene center # diff = Pworld - scenecenter diff = Pworld - scenecenter[np.newaxis, np.newaxis,:] distances = np.sqrt(np.sum(diff2, axis=-1)) # Shape (H, W) dfcmap = distances dfcmaps.append(dfcmap) return dfcmaps This variant uses the DFC maps to automatically determine a threshold for separating foreground and background. It estimates the histogram of DFC values from the original point cloud with a binning interval of 10 meters. The threshold Ri is set at the first bin interval where the point count is less than 2.5% of the total reconstructed points. This threshold is then used to generate masked background images (removing foreground pixels) and filtered foreground points (keeping points within distance Ri from the center). The parameter Ri is scene-dependent but the heuristic is robust; manual override is possible. Changing Ri within reasonable ranges has minimal impact on novel view synthesis metrics but may affect reconstruction detail in moved regions. Time Complexity: O(N \cdot H \cdot W), where N is the number of views, and H, W are image dimensions. Each pixel is processed once for unprojection and distance calculation. Memory Complexity: O(N \cdot H \cdot W) to store the DFC maps. Strengths: Provides a global, view-invariant metric for depth, simplifying foreground/background segmentation in outdoor scenes. Limitations: Relies on accurate depth maps and camera poses. The heuristic for Ri may fail in scenes with unusual depth distributions. When to use: Outdoor scene reconstruction where background separation is critical, such as in Gaussian Splatting with environment map baking. When not to use: Indoor scenes with complex lighting or where global center is ambiguous. The DFC map generation method was introduced in the context of EnvMap-GS, a two-stage outdoor Gaussian reconstruction method that bakes background into an environment map. It was proposed by D. Pintani et al. to address the challenge of separating foreground and background in outdoor scenes for 3D Gaussian Splatting. EnvMap-GS: two-stage outdoor Gaussian reconstruction with background-to-environment map baking, https://doi.org/10.1007/s00371-026-04593-w, fetched 2026-10-29

name: Point Cloud Generation and Refinement
head: Depth-guided Point Cloud Refinement
body: An offline process that generates and refines a 3D point cloud from a subset of training images to improve depth estimation accuracy for novel views in neural rendering. It differs from standard Multi-View Stereo (MVS) by iteratively validating points against ground-truth depth from adjacent views, allowing it to generate a denser, more accurate point cloud for similar computational time, which leads to higher rendering quality (PSNR). Inputs: A subset of training images with known camera poses and ground-truth depth maps. A threshold parameter \tau controlling the tolerance for depth consistency. Outputs: A refined 3D point cloud used for surface-based sampling during novel view synthesis. Data Structures: Point Cloud: A list of 3D points P = \{p1, p2, \dots, pN\} in absolute coordinates. Depth Map: A 2D array of ground-truth depth values d{GT} for each pixel in the training views. Steps: 1. Initialization: Select a subset of training views with sufficient and uniform distance between adjacent viewpoints to ensure efficiency. 2. Iterative Generation: For each viewpoint Vi in the subset, sequentially follow the trajectory: a. Generate: Create an initial point cloud using the depth image from viewpoint Vi. b. Project: Project the 3D points of the generated point cloud onto the image plane of the next viewpoint V{i+1}. c. Calculate Distance: For each projected point, calculate the distance \tilde{d} between the 3D point and the camera location of V{i+1} using multiple view geometry. d. Validate: Compare \tilde{d} with the ground-truth depth value d{GT} of the corresponding pixel in V{i+1}'s depth map. Check if the condition is satisfied: |\tilde{d} - d{GT}| \le \tau where \tilde{d} is the calculated distance, d{GT} is the ground-truth depth, and \tau is the specified threshold. e. Refine: If the condition is not satisfied, discard the current point and generate a new 3D point by back-projecting the pixel with value d{GT} from V{i+1}. 3. Finalization: Repeat the iteration for all viewpoints in the subset to produce the final refined point cloud. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def generateandrefinepointcloud(trainingviews, tau): """ Generate and refine a 3D point cloud from a subset of training views. Args: trainingviews: List of view objects containing camera pose, depthmap (2D array), and image dimensions. tau: Threshold for depth consistency check. Returns: pointcloud: List of 3D points. """ pointcloud = [] # Iterate through the subset of training views sequentially for i in range(len(trainingviews) - 1): currentview = trainingviews[i] nextview = trainingviews[i + 1] # Step 1: Generate initial point cloud from current view's depth # Back-project pixels using currentview's camera intrinsics/extrinsics currentpoints = backprojectdepth(currentview.depthmap, currentview.camera) # Step 2: Project these points to the next view's image plane # and calculate distances to the next camera center for point in currentpoints: # Project 3D point to 2D pixel coordinates in nextview pixeluv = projecttoimage(point, nextview.camera) # Check if pixel is within image bounds if not isvalidpixel(pixeluv, nextview.width, nextview.height): continue # Get ground truth depth at projected pixel dgt = nextview.depthmap[pixeluv.y][pixeluv.x] # Calculate distance from 3D point to next camera location # dtilde is the Euclidean distance between point and nextview.camera.position dtilde = calculatedistance(point, nextview.camera.position) # Step 3: Validate against threshold if abs(dtilde - dgt) <= tau: # Condition satisfied: keep the point pointcloud.append(point) else: # Condition not satisfied: generate new point from ground truth # Back-project the ground truth depth from nextview newpoint = backprojectpixelwithdepth( pixeluv, dgt, nextview.camera) pointcloud.append(newpoint) return pointcloud Parameters: \tau: Threshold for comparing calculated distance and ground-truth depth. Controls point cloud density and hole filling. Too large: fewer points, faster rendering, more holes. Too small: overlapping points, slower rendering, fewer holes. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Threshold Selection: An inappropriate \tau leads to either excessive holes (if too large) or overlapping points causing slow rendering (if too small). Background Filling: If the hole-filling kernel size \kappa (used in subsequent refinement) is too small, holes in background areas may be filled, blurring the depth image. Subset Selection: Using the entire training view set is less efficient; a subset with uniform spacing is recommended. A strategy that uses sparse Structure-from-Motion (SfM) and dense PatchMatch Stereo point clouds to guide depth prediction in few-shot novel view synthesis, preventing overfitting to training views. It differs from standard depth-supervised methods by computing adaptive weights based on multiview color consistency to mitigate inaccuracies in estimated 3D points, and by restricting its application to early training stages. A method to obtain accurate depth images for novel views by refining a rough depth image projected from a 3D point cloud, specifically by removing unnecessary points and filling holes. Steps: 1. Project the saved 3D point cloud onto a novel view to generate a rough depth image. 2. Remove unnecessary 3D points from the point cloud to refine the depth estimation. 3. Fill the holes in the projected depth image. 4. Use the refined depth image for surface-based sampling during novel view rendering. Time Complexity: Similar to standard MVS. On a GPU with 20 views, processing time is approximately 87.12 s, compared to 86.78 s for standard MVS. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Performance: Generates more points than standard MVS for similar computational time, leading to higher PSNR (31.44 dB vs 30.27 dB on the Pavillon dataset). Strengths: Improves rendering quality by providing a denser, more accurate point cloud for surface-based sampling. Limitations: Requires ground-truth depth maps for training views; performance is sensitive to the threshold \tau. When to use: When high-quality novel view synthesis is required and ground-truth depth data is available for training views. When not to use: When computational resources are extremely limited and slight quality degradation is acceptable, or when ground-truth depth is unavailable. Originated in the work by H. B. Yoo et al., titled "Improving Neural Radiance Fields Using Near-Surface Sampling with Point Cloud Generation". The method was developed to address the limitations of original NeRF's wide-range sampling by introducing surface-based sampling guided by a refined point cloud. It leverages multiple view geometry to iteratively correct point positions based on depth consistency across training views. name: Projected Depth Refining
head: Diffusion-based iterative depth refinement, Generative Depth Refinement Module, Scale-consistent depth integration
body: Projected Depth Refining is a post-processing technique that enhances the geometric fidelity of depth maps projected from a 3D point cloud, addressing the loss of fine details and scale ambiguity inherent in initial projections. It sets itself apart from sibling methods like Depth-Guided Optimization by explicitly integrating high-resolution RGB priors via diffusion models to recover high-frequency geometric details, rather than relying solely on geometric consistency or optimization constraints. The method operates in two primary contexts: a generative refinement for high-fidelity reconstruction and a computational refinement for efficient surface sampling. The core algorithm described in follows these steps: 1. Initial Projection: The dense 3D point cloud (obtained from a prior step such as Neural Bundle Adjustment) is projected into a 2D depth map D0 for a target view. This initial map is limited by the resolution of the source geometry estimator (e.g., DUSt3R) and lacks fine details. 2. Latent Encoding: The initial depth map D0 and the corresponding RGB image I are encoded into latent representations z^{(D)} and z^{(I)} using separate latent encoders. 3. Diffusion-Based Refinement: The latent depth representation z^{(D)} is refined iteratively in the latent code space using a diffusion model. Forward Process: Gaussian noise is added to the initial latent z0^{(D)} over T steps. At step t, the noisy latent zt^{(D)} is computed as: zt^{(D)} = \sqrt{\bar{\alpha}t} z0^{(D)} + \sqrt{1 - \bar{\alpha}t} \epsilon where \epsilon \sim \mathcal{N}(0, I), and \bar{\alpha}t = \prod{s=1}^{t} (1 - \betas), with \{\beta1, \dots, \betaT\} being the noise variance schedule. Reverse Process: The noise is progressively removed to recover the refined latent representation. This process is guided by the RGB latent z^{(I)} to ensure texture-consistent geometric details. 4. Scale-Consistent Integration: To prevent scale drift during diffusion, a scale-consistent integration path constrains the depth scale at each iteration. 5. Output: The result is a scale-consistent, detail-rich depth map (and optionally normal maps). In the context of, the refinement focuses on computational efficiency for NeRF sampling: 1. Projection: Project the saved 3D point cloud onto a novel view to generate a rough depth image. 2. Point Removal: Remove unnecessary 3D points from the point cloud to reduce noise and ambiguity in the depth estimation. 3. Hole Filling: Fill holes in the projected depth image using computationally efficient methods. 4. Usage: The refined depth image is used for surface-based sampling during novel view rendering, restricting 3D sampling to the vicinity of the estimated surface. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def projecteddepthrefining(pointcloud, rgbimage, cameraparams, diffusionmodel, latentencoderdepth, latentencoderrgb, noiseschedule): """ Refines a projected depth map using diffusion-based iterative refinement. Args: pointcloud: 3D point cloud (N, 3) rgbimage: Input RGB image (H, W, 3) cameraparams: Camera intrinsic and extrinsic parameters diffusionmodel: Pre-trained diffusion model for depth refinement latentencoderdepth: Encoder for depth maps latentencoderrgb: Encoder for RGB images noiseschedule: List of beta values {beta1,..., betaT} Returns: refineddepthmap: Refined depth map (H, W) """ # Step 1: Initial Projection # Project point cloud to 2D depth map D0 # Handle occlusions by keeping the closest point per pixel D0 = projectpointcloudtodepth(pointcloud, cameraparams) # Step 2: Latent Encoding # Encode depth and RGB into latent space zD = latentencoderdepth(D0) zI = latentencoderrgb(rgbimage) # Step 3: Diffusion-Based Refinement T = len(noiseschedule) zcurrent = zD # Forward process: Add noise # Note: In implementation, this is often done by sampling noise at step T # and then reversing. Here we simulate the iterative reverse process # guided by the RGB prior. # Initialize with noisy latent at step T epsilon = randomgaussiannoiselike(zD) alphabarT = product(1 - beta for beta in noiseschedule) zT = sqrt(alphabarT) zD + sqrt(1 - alphabarT) epsilon # Reverse process: Denoise for t in reversed(range(1, T + 1)): betat = noiseschedule[t-1] alphat = 1 - betat alphabart = product(1 - beta for beta in noiseschedule[:t]) alphabarprev = product(1 - beta for beta in noiseschedule[:t-1]) if t > 1 else 1 # Predict noise or mean from diffusion model # The model takes noisy latent zt, step t, and condition zI predictednoise = diffusionmodel.predictnoise(zcurrent, t, zI) # Compute mean for reverse step # Standard DDIM or DDPM reverse step formula # zprev = 1/sqrt(alphat) (zt - (1-alphat)/sqrt(1-alphabart) predictednoise) # + sigmat epsilonpred # For simplicity, using a standard reverse update: coeff1 = sqrt(alphabarprev) (1 - alphat) / (1 - alphabart) coeff2 = sqrt(alphat) (1 - alphabarprev) / (1 - alphabart) zprev = coeff1 zcurrent + coeff2 predictednoise # Add noise if t > 1, else deterministic if t > 1: sigmat = sqrt((1 - alphabarprev) / (1 - alphabart) (1 - alphat)) epsilont = randomgaussiannoiselike(zcurrent) zprev = zprev + sigmat epsilont zcurrent = zprev # Step 4: Scale-Consistent Integration # Apply scale constraints during the process or post-process # This ensures the global scale matches the point cloud zrefined = applyscaleconsistency(zcurrent, D0) # Decode back to depth map refineddepthmap = latentencoderdepth.decode(zrefined) return refineddepthmap def projectpointcloudtodepth(pointcloud, cameraparams): """ Projects 3D points to 2D depth map. Returns depth map with infinity for empty pixels. """ H, W = cameraparams.imagesize depthmap = np.full((H, W), np.inf) # Project each point for point in pointcloud: # Transform point to camera coordinates pointcam = transformtocamera(point, cameraparams.extrinsics) # Project to 2D u, v = project3dto2d(pointcam, cameraparams.intrinsics) # Check bounds if 0 <= u < W and 0 <= v < H: depth = pointcam.z if depth < depthmap[v, u]: depthmap[v, u] = depth return depthmap A module that employs a diffusion model to integrate high-resolution RGB information into the point cloud, enhancing geometric details and smoothness. It is chosen when high-fidelity mesh reconstruction is required. It differs from standard hole-filling by using generative priors to hallucinate plausible geometric details consistent with the RGB texture. It includes a diffusion model for iterative refinement and a scale-consistent integration path to constrain the depth scale for each iteration. A method focused on efficiency for NeRF-based rendering. It involves removing unnecessary 3D points and filling holes in the projected depth image. It is chosen when the goal is to enable surface-based sampling for novel view synthesis rather than explicit mesh generation. It sets itself apart by prioritizing computational speed and robustness for sampling over high-frequency detail recovery. Time Complexity: The generative variant is computationally expensive due to the iterative diffusion process (T steps) and latent encoding/decoding. The computational variant is efficient, relying on simple projection and hole-filling. Memory Complexity: Requires storing the 3D point cloud, RGB images, and latent representations. The diffusion model adds significant memory overhead during inference. Strengths: The generative variant produces scale-consistent, detail-rich depth and normal maps, overcoming the resolution limits of initial geometry estimators like DUSt3R. The computational variant enables efficient surface-based sampling, improving NeRF rendering quality with minimal overhead. Limitations: The generative variant depends on the quality of the RGB prior and the diffusion model's training data. It may hallucinate details not present in the scene. The computational variant may leave artifacts if the point cloud is sparse or noisy. When to use: Use the generative variant for high-fidelity 3D reconstruction and mesh extraction. Use the computational variant for efficient novel view synthesis with NeRF. The concept of refining projected depth maps originated from the need to improve NeRF rendering by restricting sampling to the object surface. The generative approach was introduced in GBR (Generative Bundle Refinement) to address geometry accuracy challenges in Gaussian Splatting by integrating diffusion models with neural bundle adjustment. name: Depth-Guided Optimization
head: Depth-Guided Optimization with 3D Point Clouds
body: Depth-Guided Optimization is a strategy that uses sparse Structure-from-Motion (SfM) and dense PatchMatch Stereo point clouds to guide depth prediction in few-shot novel view synthesis, preventing overfitting to training views. It differs from standard depth-supervised methods by computing adaptive weights based on multiview color consistency to mitigate inaccuracies in estimated 3D points, and by restricting its application to early training stages. Inputs: Reference images Ik (k=1 \dots M). Camera intrinsics Kk and extrinsics Ek (world-to-camera) for each reference view. A hybrid representation model (e.g., TriDF) parameterized by density fields \sigma and features fm. A set of 3D points P = \{pi\} derived from SfM and PatchMatch Stereo. Combine or select points for optimization. For each point pi, compute its average color ci across all M views where it is visible. Outputs: Depth loss term L{depth} used in the total optimization objective. Data Structures: 3D Point Cloud: A list of 3D coordinates pi = [Xw, Yw, Zw, 1]^T in world space. Sparse SfM cloud: \approx 10^2 points. Dense Stereo cloud: \approx 10^3 points. Keypoint Data: For each 3D point pi and view k, store projected pixel coordinates (u, v) and the rendered depth \hat{d}i. Parameters: Ns: Number of key points sampled per iteration (64). \lambda1: Depth loss weight. Initial: 0.001; Later: 0. \lambda2: Smoothness loss weight. Initial: 0; Later: 1.0. Training Schedule: Depth guidance active for the first 10,000 iterations of a 30,000-iteration process. Steps: 1. Point Cloud Generation: Estimate sparse 3D points using SfM (e.g., via COLMAP). Generate dense 3D points using PatchMatch Stereo and COLMAP fusion. Combine or select points for optimization. The method uses approximately 10^3 dense points for guidance. 2. Projection and Rendering: For each 3D point pi in the cloud: Transform to camera coordinates for view k: \begin{bmatrix} Xc \\ Yc \\ Zc \\ 1 \end{bmatrix} = Ek pi = \begin{bmatrix} R & T \\ 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} Xw \\ Yw \\ Zw \\ 1 \end{bmatrix} where R \in \mathbb{R}^{3 \times 3} and T \in \mathbb{R}^{3 \times 1}. Project to image plane to get pixel coordinates (u, v): \begin{bmatrix} u \\ v \\ 1 \end{bmatrix} \propto Kk \begin{bmatrix} Xc \\ Yc \\ Zc \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} fx & 0 & cx \\ 0 & fy & cy \\ 0 & 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} Xc \\ Yc \\ Zc \end{bmatrix} where Zc is the depth value. Render predicted depth \hat{d}i at this location using volume rendering: \hat{d}i = \sum{j=1}^{N} Tj (1 - \exp(-\sigmaj \deltaj)) tj where tj is the position of the j-th sample, \sigmaj is density, \deltaj is distance, and Tj is transmittance. 3. Error and Weight Calculation: For each point pi, compute its average color ci across all M views where it is visible. Let c{ij} be the color of point i projected on view j, and pi be the color of the point cloud itself. Compute the color difference metric S(ca, cb): S(ca, cb) = \frac{1}{3} \| ca - cb \|1 Calculate the error e{ik} for point i on view k: e{ik} = \left( \frac{1}{M-1} \sum{j=1}^{M} S(c{ij}, ci) + S(c{ik}, pi) \right)^{1/2} This quantifies multiview inconsistency and edge sensitivity. Compute adaptive weight \alpha{ki}: \alpha{ki} = 1 - e{ik} Clamp the weight: w{ki} = \text{clamp}(\alpha{ki}, 0, 1) 4. Loss Computation: Compute the weighted depth loss L{depth}: L{depth} = \sqrt{ \frac{1}{Ns} \sum{i=1}^{Ns} wi (\hat{d}i - di)^2 } where di is the depth of the 3D point cloud (from stereo/SfM) and wi is the computed weight. 5. Integration into Training: The total loss is: L{total} = L{color} + \lambda1 L{depth} + \lambda2 L{smooth} During the first 10,000 iterations, set \lambda1 = 0.001 and \lambda2 = 0. After 10,000 iterations, set \lambda1 = 0 and \lambda2 = 1.0 to switch to edge-aware smoothness regularization. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def l1norm(a, b): return sum(abs(x - y) for x, y in zip(a, b)) def colordist(c1, c2): return (1.0 / 3.0) l1norm(c1, c2) def samplecolor(image, u, v): h, w, = image.shape uint = max(0, min(w - 1, int(round(u)))) vint = max(0, min(h - 1, int(round(v)))) return image[vint, uint] def computedepthguidedloss(model, points3d, cameraparams, referenceimages, iteration): """ Computes the depth-guided loss for early training stages. model: Neural network providing renderdepth(u, v). points3d: List of 3D points [X, Y, Z, 1] in world coordinates. cameraparams: List of dicts with 'K' (3x3) and 'E' (4x4) for each view. referenceimages: List of HxWx3 RGB arrays. iteration: Current training iteration number. Returns: Scalar depth loss Ldepth. """ if iteration >= 10000: return 0.0 M = len(referenceimages) Ns = 64 totalweightederror = 0.0 count = 0 for pi in points3d[:Ns]: visiblecolors = [] Zc = 0.0 for k in range(M): K = cameraparams[k]['K'] E = cameraparams[k]['E'] # Transform to camera coordinates pcam = [sum(E[r][c] pi[c] for c in range(4)) for r in range(4)] Xc, Yc, Zc = pcam[0], pcam[1], pcam[2] # Project to image plane uvhom = [sum(K[r][c] (Xc if c < 3 else 1) for c in range(3)) for r in range(3)] u = uvhom[0] / uvhom[2] v = uvhom[1] / uvhom[2] if 0 <= u < referenceimages[k].shape[1] and 0 <= v < referenceimages[k].shape[0]: visiblecolors.append(samplecolor(referenceimages[k], u, v)) if len(visiblecolors) < 2: continue # Average color across visible views ci = [sum(c[j] for c in visiblecolors) / len(visiblecolors) for j in range(3)] # Color of the point cloud itself picolor = visiblecolors[0] # Compute error ei (averaged over visible views to match loss formula) sumS = sum(colordist(cvis, ci) for cvis in visiblecolors) term1 = sumS / (len(visiblecolors) - 1) term2 = colordist(visiblecolors[0], picolor) ei = math.sqrt(term1 + term2) # Weight alphai = 1.0 - ei wi = max(0.0, min(1.0, alphai)) # Render predicted depth at this location dhat = model.renderdepth(u, v) # Depth loss contribution di = Zc totalweightederror += wi (dhat - di) 2 count += 1 if count == 0: return 0.0 return math.sqrt(totalweightederror / count) Time Complexity: Adds overhead per iteration for projecting points, rendering depth at specific locations, and computing multiview color consistency. The projection and rendering are done for Ns points (64) per iteration. Memory Complexity: Requires storing the 3D point cloud (\approx 10^3 points) and reference image features. Performance: Improves geometric accuracy in few-shot settings by preventing overfitting to training views, which manifests as excessive density near the ray origin. Limitations: Relies on the accuracy of SfM and PatchMatch Stereo. Inaccuracies in point clouds (spatial position errors, edge ambiguities) can compromise geometry if not weighted correctly. When to use: Early training stages (first 10k iterations) of few-shot novel view synthesis where depth guidance is needed to anchor geometry. When not to use: Later training stages, where it is replaced by edge-aware smoothness regularization to refine geometry without the noise of potentially inaccurate point clouds. Depth-Guided Optimization was introduced in the context of TriDF (Triplane-Accelerated Density Fields) for few-shot remote sensing novel view synthesis. It addresses the issue of overfitting in hybrid representations (combining implicit density fields with explicit features) when training data is limited. The method leverages the fact that SfM is often already performed for camera pose estimation, adding minimal computational overhead. It was developed to handle the sparse nature of SfM points by augmenting them with dense PatchMatch Stereo points generated via COLMAP. name: Global Scene Point Cloud Construction
head: Global Point Cloud Construction, Multi-view Point Cloud Generation
body: Global Scene Point Cloud Construction aggregates depth maps from multiple calibrated views into a single, unified 3D point cloud in world coordinates. It solves the problem of redundant and inconsistent primitives that arise when unprojecting overlapping depth maps independently. It differs from Depth to 3D Points Conversion by handling the accumulation and cleaning of multiple views rather than processing a single depth map, and from Point Cloud Generation and Refinement by focusing specifically on the initial global assembly and noise removal steps. Inputs: N RGB images \{In\}{n=1}^N. N corresponding metric depth maps \{Dn\}{n=1}^N. Intrinsic matrices \{Kn\}{n=1}^N. Extrinsics matrices \{Tn = [Rn | tn]\}{n=1}^N, where Rn is rotation and tn is translation. Ego-vehicle poses for registration (if LiDAR is used for bounds, see). Outputs: A global scene point cloud \mathcal{P} \in \mathbb{R}^{Np \times 3} in world coordinates. Data Structures: Raw point cloud P{raw}: List or array of 3D points. Filtered point cloud P{final}: List or array of 3D points. Steps: 1. Unprojection: For each view n \in \{1, \dots, N\}, unproject the depth map Dn using In, Dn, Tn, Kn to obtain local 3D points. Pn = \pi^{-1}(In, Dn, Tn, Kn) Where \pi^{-1} denotes the pixel unprojection operation, mapping each pixel (u, v) with depth d to world coordinates via Kn^{-1} and Tn^{-1}. 2. Accumulation: Union all local point clouds: P{raw} = \bigcup{n=1}^N Pn 3. Uniform Filtering: Apply a uniform filter in 3D space to P{raw} to delete duplicate primitives while keeping the scene structure. This addresses redundancy in overlapping regions. 4. Statistical Filtering: Apply a statistical filter to P{final} (output of step 3) to remove floaters (noise). 5. LiDAR Integration (Optional/Contextual): If using LiDAR for scene bounds: Filter LiDAR points to keep only those within 80 meters from the ego-vehicle. Register filtered LiDAR points in the global world frame using ego-vehicle poses. Compute scene bounds from the resulting global point cloud. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def globalpointcloudconstruction(images, depths, intrinsics, extrinsics): """ images: List of N RGB images depths: List of N depth maps intrinsics: List of N intrinsic matrices Kn extrinsics: List of N extrinsic matrices Tn = [Rn | tn] """ rawpoints = [] # Step 1 & 2: Unproject and Accumulate for n in range(len(images)): # Unproject depth map to 3D points in world coordinates # piinv handles: pixel -> normalized camera coords -> world coords localpoints = unprojectdepthmap(images[n], depths[n], intrinsics[n], extrinsics[n]) rawpoints.extend(localpoints) # Step 3: Uniform Filter # Removes duplicates in overlapping regions filteredpoints = uniformfilter3d(rawpoints) # Step 4: Statistical Filter # Removes noise/floaters finalcloud = statisticalfilter3d(filteredpoints) return finalcloud def unprojectdepthmap(image, depthmap, K, T): """ Unprojects a depth map to 3D points in world coordinates. K: 3x3 intrinsic matrix T: 4x4 extrinsic matrix [R|t] """ h, w = depthmap.shape points = [] # Precompute inverse intrinsic Kinv = np.linalg.inv(K) # Precompute inverse extrinsic (world to camera) # T maps world to camera: Pcam = T Pworld # So Pworld = Tinv Pcam Tinv = np.linalg.inv(T) for y in range(h): for x in range(w): d = depthmap[y, x] if d <= 0: # Skip invalid depth continue # Pixel to normalized camera coordinates # Assuming pixel center at (x+0.5, y+0.5) u, v = x + 0.5, y + 0.5 # Back-project to camera frame # [u, v, 1] are homogeneous coordinates in image plane camcoords = Kinv @ np.array([u, v, 1]) # Scale by depth camcoords = camcoords d # Transform to world coordinates # camcoords is 3D, so we use homogeneous 4D for Tinv worldcoords = Tinv @ np.append(camcoords, 1) # Extract 3D point point = worldcoords[:3] points.append(point) return points def uniformfilter3d(points, radius=0.01): """ Removes duplicate points within a radius. """ # Implementation depends on spatial data structure (e.g., KDTree) # For each point, if there is another point within radius, remove one # This is a simplified description; actual implementation uses efficient spatial hashing or grid pass def statisticalfilter3d(points, k=50, stdratio=2.0): """ Removes outliers based on distance to k-nearest neighbors. """ # For each point, compute mean distance to k nearest neighbors # If mean distance > stdratio globalmeandistance, remove point pass Parameters: Maximum distance for LiDAR filtering: 80 meters. Uniform filter radius: Not given in the sources. Statistical filter k and standard deviation ratio: Not given in the sources. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Overlapping regions generate redundant primitives; uniform filtering is required. Noise/floaters remain after uniform filtering; statistical filtering is required. Dynamic objects may receive invalid depth supervision if not handled; LiDAR measurements are used as ground truth only at the time of camera sensor recording. Converts a single depth map to 3D points. Use this as the base unprojection step for each view. Refines the locations of primitives after global construction. Use this after statistical filtering. Alternative initialization method. Use this if fixed-size grids are preferred over sparse point clouds. Time Complexity: O(N \cdot H \cdot W) for unprojection, where N is number of views, H, W are image dimensions. Filtering complexity depends on implementation (e.g., O(Np \log Np) for KDTree-based filtering). Memory Complexity: O(N \cdot H \cdot W) for raw points, reduced after filtering. Strengths: Handles overlapping views efficiently; removes redundancy and noise. Limitations: Requires accurate calibration; sensitive to depth errors. When to use: When constructing a global scene representation from multiple calibrated views. When not to use: When real-time single-view reconstruction is required. Originated in works on urban environment modeling, such as and. uses LiDAR for scene bounds and ego-vehicle poses for registration. focuses on accumulating predicted metric depth maps into a global point cloud for Gaussian Splatting.
