name: Fixed-size initialization from RGB-D backprojection
head: Explicit Geometry Recovery, RGB-D backprojection initialization, RGBD Backprojection
body: This method generates a fixed-size, colored 3D point cloud initialization for volume rendering primitives by backprojecting RGB-D data. It differs from its parent Depth to 3D Points Conversion by applying explicit downsampling factors and stride ratios to control point density, and from its sibling Point Cloud Generation and Refinement by relying on direct geometric backprojection rather than implicit field refinement. Inputs: Training RGB-D images, camera intrinsics (focal lengths, principal point), camera extrinsics (rotation, translation), downsampling factor ds, and stride ratio. Outputs: A colored point cloud with a fixed number of primitives (e.g., \sim 1.1 billion, \sim 102 million, or \sim 25 million). Data Structures: A point cloud storing 3D coordinates and RGB colors per primitive, and 2D depth maps aligned with input images. Steps: 1. Downsample input RGB-D images by factor ds to reduce point density. 2. Backproject valid depth points into 3D space using camera intrinsics and extrinsics to form a colored point cloud. 3. Uniformly subsample the valid backprojected points using the stride ratio to regulate point count. 4. Derive smaller initializations (e.g., 102M or 25M points) by uniformly downsampling the largest generated cloud (e.g., 1.1B points), ensuring all scales share the same underlying geometry distribution. Parameters: ds: Image downsampling factor applied during projection to reduce point density. Typical value: Not given in the sources. Stride ratio: Uniform subsampling stride applied to valid depth points to regulate point count. Typical value: Not given in the sources. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def downsampleimage(image, factor): return image[::factor,::factor] def fixedsizeinitialization(rgbdimages, intrinsics, extrinsics, ds, strideratio): allpoints = [] allcolors = [] fx = intrinsics[0][0] fy = intrinsics[1][1] cx = intrinsics[0][2] cy = intrinsics[1][2] for rgbimg, depthimg, pose in rgbdimages: rgbdown = downsampleimage(rgbimg, ds) depthdown = downsampleimage(depthimg, ds) h, w = len(rgbdown), len(rgbdown[0]) for y in range(h): for x in range(w): z = depthdown[y][x] if z > 0: px = (x - cx) z / fx py = (y - cy) z / fy pz = z R = [row[:3] for row in pose[:3]] t = [row[3] for row in pose[:3]] wx = R[0][0]px + R[0][1]py + R[0][2]pz + t[0] wy = R[1][0]px + R[1][1]py + R[1][2]pz + t[1] wz = R[2][0]px + R[2][1]py + R[2][2]pz + t[2] allpoints.append((wx, wy, wz)) allcolors.append(rgbdown[y][x]) points = allpoints[::strideratio] colors = allcolors[::strideratio] return points, colors def derivesmallerscale(points, colors, targetcount): step = len(points) // targetcount return points[::step][:targetcount], colors[::step][:targetcount] Time and memory complexity: Not given in the sources. Measured performance: The method generates initializations at three scales: Standard (\sim 25M), Large (\sim 102M), and Billion (\sim 1.1B). Strengths: Deriving smaller initializations from a larger one ensures all scales share the same underlying geometry distribution. Limitations: Not given in the sources. When to use: When explicit geometric initialization is required for large-scale volumetric representations. When not to use: Not given in the sources. This method originates from the TideGS paper, which trains over one billion 3D Gaussian Splatting primitives using out-of-core optimization on the MatrixCity BigCity/Aerial training split (51,623 images). It is also applied in neural rendering for stereo 3D reconstruction of deformable tissues in robotic surgery, where optimized radiance fields are rendered to RGB-D maps, smoothed via bilateral filtering, and backprojected into point clouds based on calibrated endoscope intrinsics. name: Voxel Initialization via PI3
head: PI3-based Voxel Initialization
body: Voxel Initialization via PI3 is a method for establishing a geometrically accurate Signed Distance Field (SDF) prior for volume rendering or reconstruction tasks using unposed images. It solves the problem of initializing sparse voxel grids from depth maps by leveraging a visual geometry model (PI3) to estimate 3D points in world coordinates, transforming them to ground truth poses, and allocating voxels with SDF values derived from minimum distances to these points. It differs from sibling methods like Depth Map to Absolute Camera Coordinates by explicitly handling camera pose misalignment via Umeyama’s method and using PI3’s world-coordinate estimates rather than direct backprojection from known poses. Inputs: Unposed images (or depth maps derived from them). PI3 model outputs: Point maps in world coordinates (P{world}). Ground truth camera poses (or estimated poses to align with). Voxel grid parameters: Corner position v{min}, side length vl. Outputs: Initialized sparse voxel grid with SDF values. Data Structures: Voxel: Parameterized by corner SDF values. A voxel v is defined by its corner closest to the world origin v{min} and side length vl. Point Map: Set of 3D points p in world coordinates. Steps: 1. Estimate World Points: Use the PI3 model to estimate 3D points in world coordinates from the unposed images. Let this set be P{world}. 2. Transform to Ground Truth Poses: Transform the points P{world} into the coordinate system of the ground truth camera poses using Umeyama’s method. Let the transformed points be P{transformed}. 3. Allocate Voxels: Allocate voxels in the sparse grid at the locations of P{transformed}. 4. Compute SDF: For each allocated voxel, compute the SDF value by calculating the minimum Euclidean distance from the voxel to the points in P{transformed}. Formulas: The SDF for a voxel is based on the minimum distance to the transformed points. The local coordinate q of a point p within a voxel v is defined as: q = \frac{p - v{min}}{vl} where v{min} is the voxel corner closest to the world origin and vl is the voxel side length. The SDF value is derived from the minimum distance from the transformed points to the voxel geometry. Parameters: v{min}: Voxel corner position. vl: Voxel side length. PI3 Model: Visual geometry model for 3D point estimation. Umeyama’s Method: Rigid body transformation estimation. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision: The accuracy of the initialization depends heavily on the PI3 model's ability to estimate correct world coordinates and the precision of Umeyama’s transformation. Boundaries: Voxels are only allocated at transformed points; empty space is not explicitly initialized via free-space carving in this specific PI3-based step, relying on the SDF formulation for convergence. Degenerate Input: If PI3 fails to estimate points or Umeyama’s method encounters degenerate configurations, the initialization will be incomplete or incorrect. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def initializevoxelsviapi3(unposedimages, groundtruthposes, pi3model, umeyamatransform, voxelconfig): """ Initialize voxels using PI3 and Umeyama's method. Args: unposedimages: List of unposed images or depth maps. groundtruthposes: Ground truth camera poses. pi3model: PI3 visual geometry model. umeyamatransform: Function to apply Umeyama's method. voxelconfig: Configuration for voxel grid (vmin, vl). Returns: voxelgrid: Initialized sparse voxel grid with SDF values. """ # Step 1: Estimate 3D points in world coordinates using PI3 # PI3 outputs point maps in world coordinates pointsworld = pi3model.estimate3dpoints(unposedimages) # Step 2: Transform points to ground truth camera poses using Umeyama's method # Umeyama's method computes the rigid transformation between two point sets # Here, we assume we are aligning PI3's world points to the ground truth coordinate system # If groundtruthposes are in a different frame, we compute the transformation # Note: The exact implementation of Umeyama's method involves finding rotation R and translation t # that minimize the error between two point sets. transformedpoints = umeyamatransform(pointsworld, groundtruthposes) # Step 3: Allocate voxels at the transformed points voxelgrid = SparseVoxelGrid(voxelconfig) for point in transformedpoints: voxelgrid.allocatevoxelat(point) # Step 4: Compute SDF for each allocated voxel # SDF is the minimum distance from the voxel to the transformed points for voxel in voxelgrid: mindist = infinity for point in transformedpoints: dist = euclideandistance(voxel.center, point) if dist < mindist: mindist = dist voxel.sdf = mindist return voxelgrid A method to generate testing points P{t\{i\}} from P{v\{i\}} and sensor origin to update distance information for voxels within the current sensor field of view, improving efficiency over conventional free-space carving. It ray-casts from the sensor origin to each voxel in P{v\{i\}}, queries only voxels with previous surface measurements, generates voxels along surface normals up to a certain distance, and uses L-GPDF to infer distance, surface properties, and variances. Time Complexity: Depends on the PI3 model inference time and the number of points. Umeyama’s method is O(N) for N points. SDF computation is O(N \cdot M) where N is points and M is voxels, but optimized by allocating only at points. Memory Complexity: Proportional to the number of allocated voxels and points. Strengths: Provides a stable and physically meaningful initialization, enabling faster convergence for SDF-based learning. Handles unposed images effectively. Limitations: Relies on the accuracy of PI3 and Umeyama’s method. Does not explicitly handle free-space carving in the initialization step. When to Use: When initializing SDF-based reconstruction from unposed images is required, and a geometric prior is beneficial for convergence. When Not to Use: When ground truth poses are not available for Umeyama’s alignment, or when PI3 is not suitable for the scene. Originated in SVRecon, which uses PI3, a visual geometry model, to estimate 3D points in world coordinates from unposed images, transforming them via Umeyama’s method to initialize SDF-based voxel grids. It is used in sparse voxel rasterization for surface reconstruction. SVRecon: Sparse Voxel Rasterization for Surface Reconstruction, https://doi.org/10.48550/arxiv.2511.17364, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial) VDB-GPDF: Online Gaussian Process Distance Field With VDB Structure, https://doi.org/10.1109/lra.2024.3505814, fetched 2026-10-26

name: Flattened Ray Generation for Training
head: Ray Generation for Training Views, Training Ray Sampling
body: Flattened Ray Generation for Training is a data preparation method that converts a batch of training images into a single, flat tensor of rays and corresponding pixel colors, optimized for stochastic gradient descent in neural volume rendering. Unlike Camera Ray Generation, which generates rays on-the-fly per batch or view, this method pre-aggregates rays from all training poses into a unified structure, enabling efficient random sampling of individual rays across the entire dataset during training. It differs from Precomputed Ray Buffering by typically handling the flattening and indexing logic within the training loop or a dedicated sampler rather than storing the entire dataset in CPU RAM, though both aim to decouple ray generation from the forward pass. The method processes a set of training images and camera poses to produce flattened tensors of ray origins, directions, view directions, and target RGB values. It supports both regular grid-based scenes and irregular shapes, and can downsample rays to reduce memory usage. Inputs: rgbtr: Tensor of training images, shape [B, V, H, W, 3] or list of images, where B is batch size, V is views per batch, H is height, W is width. trainposes: List or tensor of camera-to-world transformation matrices (c2w), shape [BV, 4, 4]. K: Intrinsic camera matrix, shape [3, 3]. worldsize: Size of the voxel grid, used for sampling step calculation. xyzmin, xyzmax: Bounding box of the scene. near, far: Near and far plane distances for ray clipping. stepsize: Base step size for ray sampling. downrate: Downsampling factor for rays (optional). irregularshape: Boolean flag indicating if images have varying dimensions. DEVICE: Target device (e.g., cuda). Outputs: raysotr: Flattened ray origins, shape [N, 3]. raysdtr: Flattened ray directions, shape [N, 3]. viewdirstr: Flattened view directions, shape [N, 3]. rgbtr: Flattened target RGB colors, shape [N, 3]. imsz: List of image sizes (number of pixels per image). raysotr, raysdtr, viewdirstr, rgbtr: PyTorch tensors on the target device. imsz: List of integers, storing HW for each image in the training set. top: Integer, current offset in the flattened tensors. 1. Initialize Output Tensors: Calculate total number of pixels N across all training images. Initialize raysotr, raysdtr, viewdirstr, and rgbtr as zero tensors of shape [N, 3] on the target device. 2. Iterate Over Training Poses: For each training pose index i (from 0 to BV - 1): a. Extract Pose and Image: Get c2w from trainposes[i] and corresponding image img from rgbtr. b. Generate Rays: Call getraysofaview(H, W, K, c2w, ndc=False, inversey=False, flipx=False, flipy=False) to obtain rayso, raysd, and viewdirs for this view. These are tensors of shape [H, W, 3]. c. Flatten and Copy: Flatten rayso, raysd, viewdirs, and img from [H, W, 3] to [HW, 3]. Copy them into the global output tensors starting at index top: python n = H W rgbtr[top:top+n].copy(img.flatten(0,1)) raysotr[top:top+n].copy(rayso.flatten(0,1).to(DEVICE)) raysdtr[top:top+n].copy(raysd.flatten(0,1).to(DEVICE)) viewdirstr[top:top+n].copy(viewdirs.flatten(0,1).to(DEVICE)) d. Update Indices: Append n to imsz and update top += n. 3. Handle Irregular Shapes or Downsampling (Optional): If irregularshape is True, split the rays by image size. If downrate is specified, downsample the rays by selecting every downrate-th pixel, then flatten and split by 10000 for batch processing. 4. Ray Sampling for Training (Runtime): During training, sample random ray indices from the flattened tensors: a. Calculate numpossiblerays = sum(imsz). b. Generate numrays random indices: rayindices = torch.randint(numpossiblerays, (batchsize, numrays), device=device). c. Retrieve the corresponding rays and colors using these indices. Ray Generation (via getraysofaview): For a pixel at (u, v), the ray origin o and direction d are computed from the camera matrix K and pose c2w. \begin{aligned} \text{pixel\center} &= (u + 0.5, v + 0.5) \\ \text{cam\coord} &= K^{-1} \cdot \text{pixel\center} \\ o &= c2w{0:3, 3} \\ d &= c2w{0:3, 0:3} \cdot \text{cam\coord} \\ d &= \frac{d}{\|d\|} \end{aligned} Ray Sampling Step (for volume rendering): \begin{aligned} N{\text{samples}} &= \lfloor \| \text{world\size} + 1 \| / \text{stepsize} \rfloor + 1 \\ \text{vec} &= \text{where}(rays\d == 0, 1e-6, rays\d) \\ \text{rate\a} &= (\text{xyz\max} - rays\o) / \text{vec} \\ \text{rate\b} &= (\text{xyz\min} - rays\o) / \text{vec} \\ t{\text{min}} &= \text{clamp}(\min(\text{rate\a}, \text{rate\b}), \text{min}=near, \text{max}=far) \\ t{\text{max}} &= \text{clamp}(\max(\text{rate\a}, \text{rate\b}), \text{min}=near, \text{max}=far) \\ \text{step} &= \text{stepsize} \cdot \text{voxel\size} \cdot \text{rng} \\ \text{interpx} &= t{\text{min}} + \text{step} / \|rays\d\| \\ \text{rays\pts} &= rays\o + rays\d \cdot \text{interpx} \end{aligned} near: Near plane distance. Default overwritten to 1e9 in some implementations for unbounded scenes. far: Far plane distance. stepsize: Step size for sampling. downrate: Downsampling rate for rays. irregularshape: Boolean flag for irregular ray shapes. Precision: When raysd is zero, a small epsilon (1e-6) is used to avoid division by zero in step calculation. Boundaries: Ray clipping to near and far planes is essential to prevent sampling outside the scene bounds. Memory: Flattening all rays into a single tensor can consume significant GPU memory for high-resolution datasets. Irregular Shapes: If images have different sizes, imsz must be tracked to correctly index into the flattened tensors. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import torch import torch.nn.functional as F def gettrainingraysflatten(rgbtr, trainposes, K, worldsize, xyzmin, xyzmax, near, far, stepsize, downrate=1, irregularshape=False, DEVICE='cuda'): """ Generate flattened ray tensors for training. Args: rgbtr: Tensor of shape [B, V, H, W, 3] or list of images. trainposes: Tensor of shape [BV, 4, 4] or list of c2w matrices. K: Intrinsic matrix [3, 3]. worldsize: Size of the voxel grid. xyzmin, xyzmax: Scene bounding box. near, far: Near and far plane distances. stepsize: Base step size. downrate: Downsampling factor. irregularshape: Flag for irregular image sizes. DEVICE: Target device. Returns: raysotr, raysdtr, viewdirstr, rgbtrflat, imsz """ # Calculate total number of pixels if isinstance(rgbtr, list): imsz = [im.shape[0] im.shape[1] for im in rgbtr] N = sum(imsz) else: B, V, H, W, = rgbtr.shape imsz = [H W] (B V) N = B V H W # Initialize output tensors raysotr = torch.zeros(N, 3, device=DEVICE) raysdtr = torch.zeros(N, 3, device=DEVICE) viewdirstr = torch.zeros(N, 3, device=DEVICE) rgbtrflat = torch.zeros(N, 3, device=DEVICE) top = 0 for i, (c2w, img) in enumerate(zip(trainposes, rgbtr.flatten(0,1))): # Assuming img is already flattened to [HW, 3] if irregular, else reshape if irregularshape: H, W = int(img.shape[0]0.5), int(img.shape[1]0.5) # Approximate, better to store H,W # In practice, H and W should be known or stored else: H, W = img.shape[0], img.shape[1] # Generate rays for this view # getraysofaview is a helper that computes rayso, raysd, viewdirs rayso, raysd, viewdirs = getraysofaview(H, W, K, c2w, ndc=False, inversey=False, flipx=False, flipy=False) # Flatten and copy n = H W rgbtrflat[top:top+n].copy(img.flatten(0,1)) raysotr[top:top+n].copy(rayso.flatten(0,1).to(DEVICE)) raysdtr[top:top+n].copy(raysd.flatten(0,1).to(DEVICE)) viewdirstr[top:top+n].copy(viewdirs.flatten(0,1).to(DEVICE)) top += n return raysotr, raysdtr, viewdirstr, rgbtrflat, imsz def getraysofaview(H, W, K, c2w, ndc=False, inversey=False, flipx=False, flipy=False): """ Helper function to generate rays for a single view. """ # Create pixel coordinates i, j = torch.meshgrid(torch.arange(W, device=c2w.device), torch.arange(H, device=c2w.device), indexing='ij') dirs = torch.stack([(i - K[0,2])/K[0,0], (j - K[1,2])/K[1,1], torch.oneslike(i)], dim=-1) # Transform to world space raysd = (dirs @ c2w[:3,:3].T).to(c2w.device) rayso = c2w[:3,3].expandas(raysd).to(c2w.device) # Normalize directions raysd = F.normalize(raysd, dim=-1) # View directions (same as raysd for perspective) viewdirs = raysd return rayso, raysd, viewdirs Precomputed Ray Buffering stores all rays and RGB values in CPU RAM before training. It iterates over training images, computes rays for each, and concatenates them into large tensors (self.allrays of shape (B, 8) and self.allrgbs of shape (B, 3)). This approach simplifies the training loop by providing pre-computed data but can exhaust CPU RAM for high-resolution datasets (e.g., 800x800). Validation and test splits often bypass this buffer to save memory. Time Complexity: O(N) for initial ray generation, where N is the total number of pixels. Sampling is O(1) per ray. Memory Complexity: O(N) for storing flattened rays and colors. This can be significant for large datasets. Performance: Efficient for training as it avoids per-batch ray generation overhead. However, memory usage can be a bottleneck. Strengths: Simplifies data loading, enables random ray sampling across the entire dataset. Limitations: High memory consumption, especially for high-resolution images. Not suitable for very large datasets without downsampling or chunking. When to Use: When training on a fixed dataset with manageable memory requirements. When Not to Use: When memory is constrained or when dealing with extremely high-resolution images. Flattened Ray Generation for Training is a common technique in neural radiance fields (NeRF) and related volume rendering methods. It was popularized by early NeRF implementations and is widely used in frameworks like kwea123/nerfpl and Jumpat/SegmentAnythingin3D. The method addresses the need for efficient data access during stochastic gradient descent, where random ray sampling is crucial for learning. sjtuytc/UnboundedNeRFPytorch, https://github.com/sjtuytc/UnboundedNeRFPytorch, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial) Jumpat/SegmentAnythingin3D, https://github.com/Jumpat/SegmentAnythingin3D, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial) cvg/NoPoSplat, https://github.com/cvg/NoPoSplat, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial) kwea123/nerfpl, https://github.com/kwea123/nerfpl, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial)

name: Spherical Ray Casting
body: Spherical Ray Casting generates camera rays by mapping a 2D grid of pixel coordinates to spherical angles (\theta, \phi), creating a cylindrical-spherical projection suitable for 360-degree video and dome-based presentations. It differs from standard pinhole models by using angular spacing rather than linear perspective projection, and from orthographic models by maintaining a central viewpoint with varying ray density. Inputs: width, height: Integer resolution of the output image. camtoworld: 4 \times 4 extrinsic camera pose matrix (rotation and translation). xnp: Numerical array library (e.g., NumPy). Outputs: utils.Rays object containing: origins: Array of shape (H, W, 3), camera positions. directions: Array of shape (H, W, 3), normalized ray directions in world space. lossmult: Scalar 1. near, far: Not given in the sources. camidx: Scalar 0. Data Structures: theta, phi: 2D arrays of shape (H+1, W+1) representing angular coordinates. directions: 3D array of shape (H+1, W+1, 3) representing untransformed directions in the camera frame. dx, dy: 2D arrays of shape (H, W+1, 3) and (H+1, W, 3) representing finite differences. radii: 2D array of shape (H, W, 1) representing pixel radii for sampling. Steps: 1. Generate Angular Grids: Create linearly spaced values for azimuth \theta and elevation \phi: \theta{\text{vals}} = \text{linspace}(0, 2\pi, W + 1) \phi{\text{vals}} = \text{linspace}(0, \pi, H + 1) Create a meshgrid using 'xy' indexing: \theta, \phi = \text{meshgrid}(\theta{\text{vals}}, \phi{\text{vals}}, \text{indexing}='xy') 2. Compute Camera-Frame Directions: Calculate unit vectors in the camera reference frame where y is up: dx = -\sin(\phi) \sin(\theta) dy = \cos(\phi) dz = \sin(\phi) \cos(\theta) Stack into directions array: \mathbf{D}{\text{cam}} = [\dots, dx, dy, dz] Shape: (H+1, W+1, 3). 3. Transform to World Space: Apply the camera rotation matrix R{\text{cam}} (top-left 3 \times 3 of camtoworld) to each direction vector: \mathbf{D}{\text{world}} = R{\text{cam}} \cdot \mathbf{D}{\text{cam}}^T Reshape to (H+1, W+1, 3). 4. Compute Finite Differences: Calculate differences along axes to estimate pixel extent: \Deltay = \text{diff}(\mathbf{D}{\text{world}}[:,:-1], \text{axis}=0) \Deltax = \text{diff}(\mathbf{D}{\text{world}}[:-1,:], \text{axis}=1) Shapes: \Deltay is (H, W+1, 3), \Deltax is (H+1, W, 3). 5. Crop Directions: Remove the extra row and column introduced by the meshgrid and diff operations to align with pixel centers: \mathbf{D}{\text{final}} = \mathbf{D}{\text{world}}[:-1,:-1] Shape: (H, W, 3). 6. Compute Origins: Broadcast the camera translation vector \mathbf{t} (last column of camtoworld) to match the shape of \mathbf{D}{\text{final}}: \mathbf{O} = \text{broadcast\to}(\mathbf{t}, (H, W, 3)) 7. Compute Radii: Calculate norms of difference vectors: \|\Deltay\| = \text{norm}(\Deltay, \text{axis}=-1) \|\Deltax\| = \text{norm}(\Deltax, \text{axis}=-1) Compute average radius scaled by geometric factor: r = 0.5 \cdot (\|\Deltay\| + \|\Deltax\|) \cdot \frac{2}{\sqrt{12}} Reshape to (H, W, 1). 8. Initialize Image Plane: Set placeholder image plane coordinates to zeros: \text{imageplane} = \text{zeros}(\text{shape}(\mathbf{D}{\text{final}}[...,:2])) Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def sphericalraycasting(width, height, camtoworld, xnp): # 1. Generate Angular Grids thetavals = xnp.linspace(0, 2 xnp.pi, width + 1) phivals = xnp.linspace(0, xnp.pi, height + 1) theta, phi = xnp.meshgrid(thetavals, phivals, indexing='xy') # 2. Compute Camera-Frame Directions (y is up) sinphi = xnp.sin(phi) cosphi = xnp.cos(phi) sintheta = xnp.sin(theta) costheta = xnp.cos(theta) dxcam = -sinphi sintheta dycam = cosphi dzcam = sinphi costheta directionscam = xnp.stack([dxcam, dycam, dzcam], axis=-1) # 3. Transform to World Space Rcam = camtoworld[:3,:3] # Matmul expects last dim to be vector; Rcam is (3,3), directionscam is (H+1, W+1, 3) directionsworld = xnp.matmul(Rcam, directionscam[..., None])[..., 0] # 4. Compute Finite Differences # diff along axis 0 (rows) for dy, axis 1 (cols) for dx dydiff = xnp.diff(directionsworld[:,:-1], axis=0) dxdiff = xnp.diff(directionsworld[:-1,:], axis=1) # 5. Crop Directions directions = directionsworld[:-1,:-1] # 6. Compute Origins camtranslation = camtoworld[:3, -1] origins = xnp.broadcastto(camtranslation, directions.shape) # 7. Compute Radii dynorm = xnp.linalg.norm(dydiff, axis=-1) dxnorm = xnp.linalg.norm(dxdiff, axis=-1) radii = (0.5 (dynorm + dxnorm))[..., None] 2 / xnp.sqrt(12) # 8. Image Plane Placeholder imageplane = xnp.zeroslike(directions[...,:2]) # Return Rays object structure return utils.Rays( origins=origins, directions=directions, radii=radii, imageplane=imageplane, lossmult=1, near=None, far=None, camidx=0) Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Boundary Precision: The meshgrid includes boundaries 0 and 2\pi for \theta and 0 and \pi for \phi. The cropping step [:-1,:-1] is critical to align rays with pixel centers; failing to crop results in shape mismatch with the image buffer. Singularity at Poles: At \phi=0 and \phi=\pi, the \theta variation collapses to a point. The finite difference method naturally handles this by reducing the effective pixel width, but numerical stability should be monitored. Coordinate System: The method assumes a camera frame where y is up. If the downstream renderer expects z-forward or y-down, the direction computation must be adjusted. Produces a cylindrical-spherical projection specifically designed for 360-degree video content. Unlike the basic spherical ray casting which maps pixels to angles linearly, this variant is optimized for playback on platforms like YouTube 360. It supports stereo rendering via StereoSphericalLens, which generates two images from nearby camera positions for VR headsets (e.g., Oculus Rift, Google Cardboard). Time Complexity: O(H \cdot W) for grid generation and vector transformations. Memory Complexity: O(H \cdot W) for storing origins, directions, and auxiliary difference arrays. Performance: Efficient on GPU due to vectorized operations (meshgrid, matmul, diff). No iterative ray marching is performed here; this is purely ray generation. Strengths: Naturally handles full 360-degree fields of view; uniform angular sampling simplifies spherical harmonics integration if used later. Limitations: Pixel density is not uniform in world space (higher density near poles if \phi is linear, though the diff-based radius calculation attempts to account for this); not suitable for perspective-correct rendering of flat scenes without distortion correction. When to use: 360-degree video rendering, planetarium dome presentations, spherical environment mapping. When not to use: Standard perspective camera rendering, orthographic projections, or when linear pixel spacing is required. Originated in the context of spherical video rendering and 360-degree media pipelines. The specific implementation details (angular grid generation, finite difference radius calculation) are documented in the multinerf repository by Google Research, which adapts spherical sampling for neural radiance field rendering. The concept of spherical lenses for dome-based presentations (e.g., Hayden Planetarium) dates back to early virtual reality and planetarium software. google-research/multinerf, https://github.com/google-research/multinerf, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial) https://yt-project.org/docs/dev/visualizing/volumerendering.html#volume-rendering-components, https://yt-project.org/docs/dev/visualizing/volumerendering.html, fetched 2026-10-29

name: Voxel Picking
head: BrainGazer picking, Bruckner et al. method, Contribution-Based Picking, voglPick
body: Voxel Picking is a volume rendering interaction technique that selects a specific position along a camera ray based on the sample that contributes most significantly to the final pixel color. Unlike methods that select the maximum data value or opacity threshold, this approach targets the sample with the highest accumulated contribution to the rendered image. It is distinct from Camera Ray Generation by adding a selection criterion to the generated ray, and differs from Orthographic (Parallel) Camera Ray Generation by focusing on contribution-based selection rather than geometric projection alone. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A 2D screen coordinate (cursor position) and the current volume rendering state (ray, transfer function, accumulation buffer). Output: A 3D voxel position along the ray that maximizes the contribution to the pixel color. Data Structures: Not given in the sources. Steps: 1. Ray Generation: Generate a 3D ray originating from the camera eye position and passing through the 2D cursor coordinates on the screen. This builds on Camera Ray Generation. 2. Sampling: Traverse the volume along the generated ray, sampling voxel values at regular intervals. 3. Contribution Calculation: For each sample i along the ray, calculate its contribution Ci to the final pixel color. The contribution is typically defined by the product of the sample's opacity \alphai and the accumulated transmittance Ti from the eye to that sample: Ci = \alphai \cdot Ti where Ti = \prod{j=0}^{i-1} (1 - \alphaj). 4. Selection: Identify the sample index k that maximizes the contribution: k = \arg \maxi (Ci) 5. Output: Return the 3D position of the voxel at index k. Parameters: Ray step size: Not given in the sources. Transfer function: Depends on the specific rendering technique (e.g., BrainGazer system). Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Visibility vs. Contribution: The sample contributing most to the final pixel does not necessarily belong to the most visible object (the group of samples contributing most to the final pixel). Arbitrary Positioning: Because the method considers only one sample, the resulting position may lie at an arbitrary location within a perceivable structure rather than at the front or center of the perceived structure. Interaction: In the voglPick implementation, the user selects the line of sight by pressing the right mouse button. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def voxelpick(cursorx, cursory, volume, transferfunction): # 1. Generate ray from camera through cursor # Assumes camera ray generation is handled by parent module rayorigin, raydirection = generatecameraray(cursorx, cursory) maxcontribution = -1.0 bestposition = None accumulatedtransmittance = 1.0 # 2. Traverse volume along ray # Step size and bounds depend on volume implementation stepsize = 0.1 for t in range(0, volume.maxdistance, stepsize): position = rayorigin + raydirection t # Check if position is within volume bounds if not volume.contains(position): break # 3. Sample voxel value voxelvalue = volume.sample(position) # 4. Calculate opacity and contribution # Transfer function maps value to color and opacity color, opacity = transferfunction(voxelvalue) contribution = opacity accumulatedtransmittance # 5. Track maximum contribution if contribution > maxcontribution: maxcontribution = contribution bestposition = position # Update transmittance for next sample accumulatedtransmittance = (1.0 - opacity) return bestposition The specific implementation used in the BrainGazer system, noted for working well with the special volume rendering technique employed there. An example implementation in the SGI Volumizer suite that illustrates picking individual voxels by drawing a signal of voxel values along the selected line of sight at the bottom of the screen. Time Complexity: Linear with respect to the number of samples along the ray, O(N), where N is the number of steps taken during traversal. Memory Complexity: O(1) auxiliary memory, as only the current contribution and best position need to be tracked. Strengths: Directly targets the most visually significant part of the ray in terms of color contribution. Limitations: May select positions that are not at the front or center of a structure, leading to potentially unintuitive user feedback. It is sensitive to the transfer function and may not correspond to the "most visible" object if that object has low opacity but high color intensity. When to use: When the goal is to identify the voxel that most strongly influences the pixel's color in the final image. When not to use: When precise localization to the surface or center of a structure is required, or when the most visible object has low opacity. Voxel Picking was introduced by Bruckner et al. in the context of the BrainGazer system. The technique was designed to work with the specific volume rendering method used in that system. It is also referenced in the WYSIWYP (What You See Is What You Pick) paper, which critiques the method for its potential to select arbitrary positions within structures rather than intuitive ones like the front or center. An early example of similar functionality is found in the SGI Volumizer's voglPick utility, which allows users to select a line of sight and view a signal of voxel values along that line. name: Ray Sample Generation
head: Frustum Generation
body: Ray Sample Generation constructs RaySamples from a RayBundle and bin boundaries, projecting points along ray directions to create frustums for volume rendering. It serves as the bridge between camera geometry and volumetric integration, defining the spatial extent and sampling intervals for each ray. Unlike sibling methods that define ray origins or directions (e.g., Camera Ray Generation), this method focuses on the discretization of the ray path into manageable segments (frustums) with associated geometric properties. Inputs and Outputs Input: A RayBundle containing ray origins, directions, and camera parameters (e.g., focal length, image dimensions); bin boundaries defining the sampling intervals along the ray. Output: A RaySamples object containing the geometric representation of the sampled frustums. Data Structures The RaySamples structure contains the following fields: frustums: The geometric representation of the frustums (e.g., Frustums object). cameraindices: Integer tensor of shape (bs, 1) indicating the camera index for each sample. deltas: Float tensor of shape (bs, 1) representing the distance between consecutive sample points. spacingstarts: Float tensor of shape (bs, numsamples, 1) indicating the start distance of each interval. spacingends: Float tensor of shape (bs, numsamples, 1) indicating the end distance of each interval. spacingtoeuclideanfn: A callable function to convert spacing to Euclidean distance. metadata: A dictionary for additional context. times: Float tensor of shape (batch, 1) for temporal information. Steps 1. Extract Ray Parameters: Retrieve ray origins \mathbf{o} and directions \mathbf{d} from the RayBundle. Determine the number of samples N and the bin boundaries t0, t1, \dots, tN along the ray. 2. Compute Interval Boundaries: For each sample i \in [0, N-1], define the start t{start}^{(i)} and end t{end}^{(i)} of the interval using the bin boundaries. 3. Calculate Deltas: Compute the delta \Delta^{(i)} = t{end}^{(i)} - t{start}^{(i)} for each interval. 4. Generate Frustums: Construct the frustum geometry for each interval. This involves projecting the interval boundaries onto the image plane to determine the frustum's base and top areas, using the camera's intrinsic parameters (focal length, aspect ratio). 5. Assemble RaySamples: Populate the RaySamples object with the computed frustums, deltas, spacing starts/ends, and metadata. Formulas Interval Delta: \Delta^{(i)} = t{end}^{(i)} - t{start}^{(i)}. Frustum Geometry: The frustum is defined by the ray direction \mathbf{d}, origin \mathbf{o}, and the projected radii at t{start}^{(i)} and t{end}^{(i)}. The radius r at distance t is proportional to t \cdot \frac{\text{pixel\size}}{\text{focal\length}}. Parameters numsamples: The number of intervals per ray. Typical values range from 128 to 1024 depending on desired accuracy and performance. binboundaries: The specific distances along the ray where samples are taken. Can be uniform or non-uniform (e.g., linear spacing, depth-based). Edge Cases and Pitfalls Precision: Floating-point precision errors can accumulate when computing large distances or small deltas. Use double precision for intermediate calculations if necessary. Boundaries: Ensure that bin boundaries are strictly increasing and within the valid viewing range (near and far planes). Degenerate Input: Handle cases where ray directions are zero or origins are undefined. Pseudocode Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def generateraysamples(raybundle, binboundaries): """ Generates RaySamples from a RayBundle and bin boundaries. Args: raybundle: Object containing ray origins (o) and directions (d). binboundaries: Array of shape (numsamples + 1,) containing t0, t1,..., tN. Returns: RaySamples object. """ o = raybundle.origins # Shape: (batchsize, 3) d = raybundle.directions # Shape: (batchsize, 3) numsamples = len(binboundaries) - 1 # Initialize tensors spacingstarts = binboundaries[:-1] # Shape: (numsamples,) spacingends = binboundaries[1:] # Shape: (numsamples,) deltas = spacingends - spacingstarts # Shape: (numsamples,) # Compute frustum geometry # This step involves projecting the interval boundaries to image plane # to determine the frustum's base and top radii. # The exact implementation depends on the camera model (e.g., pinhole). # For a pinhole camera, radius r at distance t is: # r = t (pixelwidth / focallength) # Frustums are constructed from these radii and the ray direction. frustums = computefrustums(o, d, spacingstarts, spacingends, raybundle.cameraparams) # Assemble RaySamples raysamples = RaySamples( frustums=frustums, cameraindices=raybundle.cameraindices, deltas=deltas, spacingstarts=spacingstarts, spacingends=spacingends, spacingtoeuclideanfn=raybundle.spacingtoeuclideanfn, metadata=raybundle.metadata, times=raybundle.times) return raysamples Approximates a frustum as a Gaussian distribution (mean + covariance) to enable efficient featurization of ray sections. It assumes the ray originates from the origin and casts cone- or cylinder-shaped rays. Choose this variant when using Gaussian-based rendering or when smooth, differentiable approximations of ray segments are required. It sets itself apart by converting distance intervals into Gaussian parameters rather than keeping them as geometric frustums. Steps: 1. Extract interval boundaries t0 and t1 from the ray samples. 2. Compute the mean distance t{\text{mean}} = (t0 + t1) / 2. 3. Compute the variance of the distance t{\text{var}} = (t1 - t0)^2 / 12. 4. Compute the radius variance r{\text{var}} = \text{radius}^2 / 4. 5. Select the Gaussian conversion function based on rayshape: 'cone' uses conicalfrustumtogaussian, 'cylinder' uses cylindertogaussian. 6. Call the selected function with directions, t0, t1, radii, and variances to get means and covariances. 7. Add the ray origins to the means: \text{means} = \text{means} + \text{origins}[\dots, \text{None},:]. 8. Return the means and covariances. Formulas: t{\text{mean}} = \frac{t0 + t1}{2}. t{\text{var}} = \frac{(t1 - t0)^2}{12}. r{\text{var}} = \frac{\text{radius}^2}{4}. Time Complexity: Linear in the number of samples N and batch size B, i.e., O(B \cdot N). Memory Complexity: Linear in B \cdot N for storing frustum parameters and deltas. Performance: Performance depends on the efficiency of the frustum construction and the underlying tensor operations. GPU acceleration is typically used for parallel generation. Strengths: Provides a structured representation of ray segments suitable for volume rendering and integration. Limitations: Memory usage can be high for large numbers of samples. Precision issues may arise with very small or large distances. When to Use: When volume rendering requires explicit discretization of rays into segments. When Not to Use: When continuous ray integration is preferred or when memory is constrained. Ray Sample Generation is a fundamental component in modern volume rendering and neural radiance fields (NeRF) pipelines. It was popularized by frameworks like Gaussian-Splatting-Toolkit and CaSE-NeRF, which require explicit ray segment definitions for efficient rendering and optimization. The method builds on the principles of ray generation and camera models. name: Parallel and GPU primitives
head: GPU acceleration primitives, parallel rendering primitives
body: This family encompasses the low-level algorithms and hardware mechanisms used to execute volume rendering computations on parallel architectures, primarily GPUs and multi-core CPUs. It solves the performance bottleneck of sequential ray casting and compositing by distributing work across thousands of threads. What sets this family apart from sibling methods like Ray-primitive intersection and Ray generation and camera models is its focus on the execution model, memory synchronization, and data parallelism infrastructure rather than the geometric or optical mathematics of the ray itself. The core mechanism of this family is the mapping of computational tasks (pixels, rays, or data elements) to parallel execution units (threads, warps, or cores). Common principles include: 1. Thread Mapping: Assigning one or more threads to process specific data elements (e.g., one thread per pixel or one thread per voxel sample). 2. Memory Hierarchy Utilization: Leveraging global memory for large datasets, shared/local memory for intermediate results (reductions), and registers for per-thread state. 3. Synchronization: Managing concurrency conflicts using atomic operations, barriers, or spatial partitioning (tiles) to ensure data consistency without excessive serialization. 4. Data Parallelism: Performing identical operations on different data elements simultaneously, often requiring coalesced memory access patterns to maximize bandwidth. A rendering strategy that divides the framebuffer into disjoint spatial tiles to enable lock-free, zero-synchronization parallel processing of semi-transparent primitives. It solves the concurrency conflict inherent in alpha compositing by ensuring that each tile is written to by only one thread, eliminating the need for atomics or locks. This approach is distinct from Parallel Direct Compositing which may use global atomic counters, and from Y-Bucket Parallelization which groups pixels by depth rather than spatial locality. A GPU compute shader kernel is a program executed on the GPU that processes data in parallel using thread IDs to map work items to data elements. It serves as a fundamental primitive for general-purpose GPU (GPGPU) computing, such as generating gradient textures or performing initial volume data preprocessing. It differs from higher-level volume rendering techniques by operating at the raw hardware execution level, requiring manual management of thread indexing and memory access patterns. CUDA-OpenGL Interoperability is a mechanism that allows CUDA kernels to read from and write to OpenGL resources (textures, buffers) directly in GPU memory, eliminating the need for CPU-mediated data transfers. It solves the bottleneck of copying rendered volume data or simulation results from CUDA device memory back to system memory for display. It sets itself apart from standard interop methods by supporting both read-only access (via mapped arrays/texture objects) and write access (via surface objects or direct buffer pointers), enabling zero-copy rendering pipelines. Y-Bucket Parallelization is a two-pass parallel algorithm for direct volume rendering that processes polygonal representations of isosurfaces or volume slices by grouping them into scanline-based "y-buckets". It solves the problem of efficiently rendering irregular and multiple grids in software by maximizing spatial coherence and avoiding the computational difficulties associated with ray-casting intersecting cells. Unlike tile-based parallelization methods that break scanlines and lose coherence, this method parallelizes on a scanline basis to limit duplication. Atomic Fragment List Insertion is a GPU-side algorithm for building a per-pixel linked list of fragments using atomic operations to handle concurrent writes from multiple fragments without locks. It solves the problem of accumulating geometry fragments into a dynamic acceleration structure (A-buffer) for subsequent compositing or ray processing. It differs from brute-force ray marching by avoiding empty space evaluation and from Tiled Parallel Compositing by using a global atomic counter for list construction rather than tiled accumulation buffers. Hardware and Platform Specific methods execute volume rendering algorithms directly on the GPU using shader languages (GLSL/HLSL) or compute models (CUDA/OpenCL), bypassing the CPU for the heavy lifting of ray marching and compositing. This approach solves the performance bottleneck of CPU-based ray casting by leveraging massive parallelism. It is distinguished from sibling methods like Tiled Parallel Compositing and Compute Shader Kernel by its specific reliance on the graphics pipeline's fragment/vertex shaders or specific vendor APIs (CUDA) rather than generic compute abstractions or tile-based memory optimizations. Parallel Prefix Sum (Scan) Orchestration is a GPU-based method for computing prefix sums (scans) of an input array using a multi-timestep iterative reduction strategy with ping-pong buffers. It solves the problem of efficiently aggregating data across parallel threads without race conditions, serving as a foundational primitive for operations like voxel compaction and vertex indexing in volume rendering pipelines. It sets itself apart from sibling methods like Tiled Parallel Compositing by focusing on the low-level data movement and synchronization required for global aggregation, rather than high-level compositing logic. A multi-core parallel rendering method that divides screen space into contiguous regions for Phase I (BONO tree traversal to build block lists) and partitions ray casting tasks into Z-ordered tiles grouped by weight for Phase II (dynamic load-balanced ray casting). It sets itself apart from static tile allocation methods by using dynamic, weight-based grouping of Z-ordered tiles to achieve better load balancing and cache performance while minimizing synchronization overhead. Parallel Vector Multiplication is a fundamental GPU primitive where each thread independently multiplies corresponding elements from two input arrays to produce an output array. It solves the problem of element-wise vector scaling or Hadamard product computation at massive scale by mapping one thread per data element. It is distinct from sibling primitives like Parallel Prefix Sum (which requires inter-thread dependency) or Atomic Fragment List Insertion (which requires synchronization), as it involves no communication between threads. A parallel volume rendering technique where image compositing is performed directly across processors in a distributed memory environment, specifically analyzed for block data subdivision on a bidirectional torus topology. A lifecycle management technique for Buffer Objects (BOs) shared between OpenGL and CUDA. After allocation in OpenGL, the buffer is registered with CUDA. It alternates accessibility for integration (CUDA) or rendering (OpenGL). Operations performed across a subgroup (NVIDIA warp, AMD wave), which are hardware-synchronized groups of threads. Unlike atomics, they do not involve global memory synchronization and are faster. A technique to safely write to global memory from multiple GPU threads simultaneously by avoiding race conditions (collisions) using atomic operations. A warp-level reduction technique using warp shuffling operations (Kepler+) to communicate register values, allocating a single float4 buffer from the register space of each thread. step: Bind renderPipeline with descriptor set indices {0, currentImageIndex}. Push width and height as uint32t[2] constants. Transition swapchain image layout from eUndefined to eGeneral. Dispatch compute shader: (width + 15) / 16 by (height + 15) / 16 workgroups. Transition image layout to eColorAttachmentOptimal if GUI is enabled, else ePresentSrcKHR. If GUI enabled, draw ImGui, then transition from eColorAttachmentOptimal back to ePresentSrcKHR. code: Render pass dispatch and layout transitions. definition: Calculation of vector dot products using NVIDIA's CUDA CUBLAS library. A method to calculate vector dot products using point-wise multiplication followed by a parallel reduction operation within each thread block. step: Create a dot product handler. Calculate the dot product of arbitrary sized vectors using the cublasSDot function with necessary parameters. Write the result into device memory. Point-wise multiplication is performed in the kernel, storing results in shared memory sized to the number of threads in the block. Parallel reduction is performed using a tree-based approach within each thread block to sum the multiplied values. layout: Shared memory is used to store intermediate results for each variable, with each block maintaining its own copy. complexity: Complexity of parallel reduction is O(log n), compared to O(n) for traditional summation. definition: A parallel scheme exploiting parallelism in object space by dividing the volume into p subvolumes assigned to processors. step: Divide the volume into p subvolumes. Assign tasks associated with each subvolume to processors. Parallel render each subvolume to generate p distributed subimages. Merge subimages into the final image via image compositing. Parallel and GPU primitives have evolved alongside the development of General-Purpose computing on Graphics Processing Units (GPGPU). Early volume rendering relied on CPU-based ray casting, which was computationally prohibitive for high-resolution volumes. The introduction of programmable shaders (GLSL/HLSL) and compute APIs (CUDA, OpenCL) allowed for massive parallelization of the ray marching and compositing steps. Techniques like tiled compositing and atomic fragment lists emerged to solve specific concurrency issues in alpha blending and fragment accumulation. Object parallel rendering was developed to handle large-scale datasets by distributing volume data across processors, contrasting with screen-space parallelism. Modern implementations leverage hardware-specific features like warp shuffling and subgroup operations for efficient intra-thread-block communication. name: Tiled Parallel Compositing
body: Tiled parallel compositing partitions the output framebuffer into disjoint spatial tiles, enabling independent, parallel processing of each tile with zero synchronization, no atomics, and no locks. It solves concurrency conflicts in parallel volume rendering or splatting by ensuring each thread writes exclusively to its assigned pixel region. It sets itself apart from Atomic Fragment List Insertion by avoiding atomic contention, and from Parallel Direct Compositing by relying on spatial partitioning rather than data partitioning for parallelism. Inputs: wi, hi: Framebuffer width and height in pixels. TILEW, TILEH: Tile dimensions in pixels. bins.offsets: An array of size numtiles + 1 defining the start and end indices of splats assigned to each tile. projected: An array of projected splat data (position, covariance, color) indexed by splat ID. fb: A framebuffer buffer storing color and alpha values (e.g., Vec3 color and f32 alpha). Data Structures: ScratchBuffers: Reusable memory for intermediate calculations. sortaux: Vec<Projected>: Auxiliary storage for sorting or temporary projection data. tiles: TileBins: Structure containing the offsets array mapping tiles to splat ranges. FbPtr: A Send + Sync wrapper around mut (Vec3, f32) that enables safe concurrent mutable access to the framebuffer across threads, relying on the geometric guarantee that tile (tx, ty) only writes to pixels [tx \cdot TILE\W.. (tx+1) \cdot TILE\W, ty \cdot TILE\H.. (ty+1) \cdot TILE\H]. Parameters: TILEW, TILEH: Tile grid dimensions in pixels. AlphaThreshold: Minimum alpha value required to contribute to the framebuffer, used to skip transparent pixels during compositing. Steps: 1. Parallel Iteration: Iterate over all tile indices t in parallel using a thread pool or parallel iterator. 2. Tile Bounds Calculation: For each tile index t, determine grid coordinates (tx, ty) and pixel bounds: \begin{aligned} px0 &= tx \cdot TILE\W \\ py0 &= ty \cdot TILE\H \\ px1 &= \min(px0 + TILE\W - 1, wi - 1) \\ py1 &= \min(py0 + TILE\H - 1, hi - 1) \end{aligned}. 3. Validity Check: If px0 > px1 or py0 > py1, the tile is invalid or outside bounds; return immediately. 4. Splat Range Retrieval: Retrieve the splat index range for this tile: \begin{aligned} start &= bins.offsets[t] \\ end &= bins.offsets[t + 1] \end{aligned}. 5. Empty Check: If start == end, the tile has no splats; return immediately. 6. Splat Processing: For each splat ID sid in the range [start, end): a. Retrieve the projected splat p using projected.getunchecked(sid). b. Calculate the intersection of the splat's bounding box [bx0, by0, bx1, by1] with the tile's pixel bounds [px0, py0, px1, py1]: \begin{aligned} ix0 &= \max(bx0, px0) \\ iy0 &= \max(by0, py0) \\ ix1 &= \min(bx1, px1) \\ iy1 &= \min(by1, py1) \end{aligned}. c. If ix0 > ix1 or iy0 > iy1, the splat does not intersect the tile; continue to the next splat. d. Call compositesplatregion(p, fb, wi, ix0, iy0, ix1, iy1) to render the splat into the intersecting pixels. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def tiledparallelcompositing(wi, hi, TILEW, TILEH, bins, projected, fb): numtilesx = (wi + TILEW - 1) // TILEW numtilesy = (hi + TILEH - 1) // TILEH numtiles = numtilesx numtilesy # Parallel loop over tile indices for t in range(numtiles): # 1. Calculate tile coordinates and pixel bounds tx = t % numtilesx ty = t // numtilesx px0 = tx TILEW py0 = ty TILEH px1 = min(px0 + TILEW - 1, wi - 1) py1 = min(py0 + TILEH - 1, hi - 1) # 2. Check validity if px0 > px1 or py0 > py1: continue # 3. Get splat range start = bins.offsets[t] end = bins.offsets[t + 1] # 4. Check if empty if start == end: continue # 5. Process splats in this tile for sid in range(start, end): # Get projected splat data p = projected[sid] # Calculate intersection with tile bounds ix0 = max(p.bx0, px0) iy0 = max(p.by0, py0) ix1 = min(p.bx1, px1) iy1 = min(p.by1, py1) # Check intersection validity if ix0 > ix1 or iy0 > iy1: continue # Composite splat into framebuffer compositesplatregion(p, fb, wi, ix0, iy0, ix1, iy1) def compositesplatregion(p, fb, width, ix0, iy0, ix1, iy1): # Standard front-to-back alpha compositing for the intersecting region for y in range(iy0, iy1 + 1): for x in range(ix0, ix1 + 1): idx = y width + x # Blend splat color/alpha into framebuffer at (x, y) fb[idx].color = p.color p.alpha + fb[idx].color (1.0 - p.alpha) fb[idx].alpha = p.alpha + fb[idx].alpha (1.0 - p.alpha) Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Borrow Checker/Concurrency: In languages like Rust, multiple threads cannot hold &mut references to the same buffer. This is handled by wrapping the raw framebuffer pointer in a Send + Sync newtype (FbPtr) and using unsafe blocks, relying on the disjoint tile geometry to guarantee no data races. Tile Bounds: Tiles at the image boundary must clamp pixel bounds to prevent out-of-bounds memory access. Empty Tiles: Tiles with no overlapping geometry must be skipped early to avoid unnecessary overhead. Tile-Based Alpha Compositing blends multiple semi-transparent primitives into a final image by processing them in depth order from nearest to farthest within disjoint tiles. It is distinguished from back-to-front compositing by its tile-based parallelization, which allows independent processing of each tile without synchronization. Choose this when rendering overlapping splats or Gaussians that require strict depth ordering per tile. Dynamic Load Balancing via Tile Queue splits screen space into tiles and assigns them to processors via a shared queue to ensure high processor utilization over a wide range of views. It addresses the unpredictability of isosurface extraction complexity per pixel, which static partitioning cannot handle efficiently. It sets itself apart from static partitioning by dynamically adjusting task granularity to balance load and reduce contention. Choose this when rendering scenes with highly variable geometric density. A strategy to select between two tile dimensions (16x16 and 16x32) based on the number of pixels to render to optimize performance. It sets itself apart from fixed-size tiling by adapting to resolution, reducing duplicated Gaussians at high resolutions while avoiding excessive sequential load per tile at low resolutions. Choose this when rendering at variable resolutions. This method initializes the data structures required for tiled parallel compositing by computing the spatial extent (boundaries) of each tile within the framebuffer. It solves the problem of determining which input primitives or data elements contribute to which output tiles, enabling subsequent parallel processing stages to operate on disjoint subsets of the image without synchronization. It differs from sibling methods like Coarse Raster by focusing on the setup of the boundary metadata itself rather than the rasterization of geometry, and from Dynamic Load Balancing via Tile Queue by being a static setup phase rather than a runtime scheduling mechanism. Choose this during the initialization phase before parallel execution begins. Parallel Image Assembly is the final step in spatial decomposition volume rendering where sub-images rendered by independent threads or processes are combined into a single final image. It solves the problem of merging disjoint spatial data portions into a coherent visual output by placing sub-images at their correct spatial coordinates and blending them along the z-axis using front-to-back alpha compositing. Unlike temporal sequencing, which has minimal overhead, spatial compositing incurs significant overhead due to the data collection and blending requirements. Choose this when combining results from spatially partitioned rendering passes. Multi-Threaded Tile-Based Rendering is a parallelization strategy that divides the screen height into tiles and processes each tile in a separate thread to parallelize the rasterization workload. It differs from Tile-Based Alpha Compositing by focusing on the rasterization phase itself rather than just compositing pre-rasterized fragments, and from Screen Parallel Rendering by dividing the screen into tiles processed by threads on a single machine rather than subscreens distributed across multiple processors. Choose this when offloading rasterization to CPU threads. Manages tile assignment and synchronization across worker threads using wave indices and tokens. It sets itself apart from lock-free tiling by providing explicit synchronization points for tasks requiring global consistency or progress tracking. Choose this when implementing a path tracer or ray caster that requires wave-based synchronization. Parallel Binary-Swap Compositing is a method for combining independently rendered image tiles from multiple processors in a massively parallel environment. It solves the synchronization and communication bottlenecks of naive parallel compositing by reducing the data volume at each step, ensuring all processors remain busy with useful work. Unlike approaches where communication dominates or processors idle, this method maintains full processor utilization by pairing processors in a binary-swap fashion. Choose this in distributed or multi-GPU environments where inter-processor communication is a bottleneck. A tile-grouping architecture that merges adjacent tiles into larger work units, reducing redundant sorting and improving data reuse within GPU streaming multiprocessors. It sets itself apart from single-tile processing by increasing the working set size per multiprocessor to hide memory latency and improve cache hit rates. Choose this when targeting modern GPU architectures with large shared memory and high memory bandwidth. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Measured Performance: Not given in the sources. Scaling: Scales with the number of tiles and available threads, provided the workload is balanced. Strengths: Zero synchronization overhead, no atomics, no locks, effective on CPU. Simple to implement with standard parallel loops. Limitations: Load imbalance occurs if geometry clusters in specific tiles. When to use: When rendering large numbers of independent primitives (e.g., Gaussians, splats) with minimal inter-tile dependencies. When not to use: When global synchronization is required between tiles. Tiled parallel compositing is a standard spatial decomposition technique for parallel rendering. It leverages spatial decomposition to enable lock-free parallelism. The approach has been adapted for various hardware architectures, including CPU multi-threading (e.g., using rayon in Rust) and GPU compute shaders. name: Tile-Based Alpha Compositing
head: Tsplat compositing
body: Tile-Based Alpha Compositing is a rendering technique that blends multiple semi-transparent primitives (such as 2D Gaussians or splats) into a final image by processing them in depth order from nearest to farthest within disjoint tiles. It is distinguished from back-to-front compositing by its tile-based parallelization, which allows independent processing of each tile without synchronization. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A list of splats, each defined by a 2D center (sx, sy), an inverse 2D covariance matrix cov2d\inv, an opacity \alpha{splat}, and a color C{splat}. Output: A framebuffer containing accumulated color C{accum} and accumulated opacity \alpha{accum} for each pixel. Data Structures: Framebuffer: Parallel arrays or a 2D array of structs for C{accum} (RGB floats) and \alpha{accum} (float). Initialized to (0, 0, 0) and 0 respectively. Splat: Struct containing: sx, sy: Float center coordinates in pixel space. cov2d\inv: 2x2 inverse covariance matrix represented by elements a, b, d where cov2d\inv = \begin{bmatrix} a & b \\ b & d \end{bmatrix}. \alpha{splat}: Float opacity. C{splat}: RGB color vector. Steps: 1. Initialization: Initialize the framebuffer's C{accum} to (0, 0, 0) and \alpha{accum} to 0 for all pixels. 2. Sorting: Sort all splats by depth (distance from camera) in descending order (front-to-back). 3. Tile Processing: Divide the image into disjoint tiles. For each tile: 4. Splat Rasterization: For each splat overlapping the tile: 5. Bounding Box: Compute the axis-aligned bounding box (AABB) of the splat's 2D Gaussian projection within the tile. 6. Pixel Loop: Iterate over each pixel (px, py) within the AABB: 7. Displacement: Calculate dx = px - sx and dy = py - sy. 8. Optimization: For a fixed row py, dy is constant. Precompute coefficients for the quadratic form in dx to optimize the inner loop. 9. Gaussian Evaluation: Compute the power term: power = -\frac{1}{2} (a \cdot dx^2 + 2b \cdot dx \cdot dy + d \cdot dy^2) where a = cov2d\inv.x\axis.x, b = cov2d\inv.x\axis.y, d = cov2d\inv.y\axis.y. 10. Alpha Calculation: Compute the splat's alpha at this pixel: \alpha = \alpha{splat} \cdot \exp(power). 11. Clamping: Clamp \alpha to [0, 1]. 12. Compositing: Update the framebuffer using front-to-back alpha blending: T = 1 - \alpha{accum} contrib = T \cdot \alpha C{accum} += contrib \cdot C{splat} \alpha{accum} += contrib. radius), int(splat.sx + radius) ymin, ymax = int(splat.sy - radius), int(splat.sy + radius) # Clip to tile bounds clipxmin = max(tx, xmin) clipxmax = min(tileendx, xmax) clipymin = max(ty, ymin) clipymax = min(tileendy, ymax) if clipxmin >= clipxmax or clipymin >= clipymax: continue a = splat.cov2dinv[0][0] b = splat.cov2dinv[0][1] d = splat.cov2dinv[1][1] for py in range(clipymin, clipymax): dy = py - splat.sy term1 = d dy dy term2 = 2.0 b dy for px in range(clipxmin, clipxmax): # Skip if pixel is already fully opaque if accumalpha[py][px] >= 1.0: continue dx = px - splat.sx power = -0.5 (a dx dx + term2 dx + term1) alpha = splat.opacity math.exp(power) alpha = max(0.0, min(1.0, alpha)) if alpha < 1e-6: continue T = 1.0 - accumalpha[py][px] contrib = T alpha r, g, bval = accumcolor[py][px] cr, cg, cb = splat.color accumcolor[py][px] = (r + contrib cr, g + contrib cg, bval + contrib cb) accumalpha[py][px] += contrib Front-to-Back Alpha Compositing is a rendering technique that blends multiple semi-transparent primitives (such as 2D Gaussians or splats) into a final image by processing them in depth order from nearest to farthest, ensuring correct occlusion where near primitives paint over far ones. It is distinguished from back-to-front compositing by its ability to use early termination: once the accumulated transmittance drops below a threshold, the pixel is considered fully opaque and remaining splats are skipped, providing a significant computational speedup. Time Complexity: O(N \cdot K) where N is the number of splats and K is the average number of pixels per splat's bounding box. Memory Complexity: O(W \cdot H) for the framebuffer, where W, H are image dimensions. Strengths: Parallelizable across tiles; no synchronization needed between tiles; effective on CPU architectures. Limitations: Requires sorting splats by depth; performance depends on splat density and overlap. When to use: Real-time rendering of large numbers of semi-transparent primitives, especially on CPU or GPU where tile-based parallelism is beneficial. When not to use: Scenes with very low opacity where early termination is ineffective; when strict back-to-front order is required for specific artistic effects. Tile-Based Alpha Compositing is implemented in the Tsplat renderer. The method leverages the spatial coherence of splats and the efficiency of tile-based processing to minimize overhead and maximize throughput.
