name: Load Balancing
body: Load balancing is a technique applied in both point assignment and image assignment to balance workload. It operates as part of a locality-aware distribution framework that combines offline graph partitioning with online scheduling to reduce communication overhead. Its impact is modest because communication time typically dominates the overall runtime in the tested setting. Inputs: A set of tasks (points or image patches) and a set of processing units (GPUs/nodes). Outputs: An assignment mapping that distributes tasks across processing units. Data structures: Cost matrix layout: Not given in the sources. Assignment vector layout: Not given in the sources. Numbered steps: 1. Offline Partitioning: The dataset is initially divided using a graph partitioning algorithm (e.g., METIS) to ensure spatial locality. 2. Online Scheduling: An online linear sum assignment algorithm is applied to the partitions to further balance the load. Formulas: Not given in the sources. Parameters: Solver tolerance: Not given in the sources. Batch size for online scheduling: Not given in the sources. Edge cases and pitfalls: Communication Dominance: The impact of load balancing is modest because communication time often dominates the overall runtime. Overhead: Online scheduling must be fast; however, studies show it introduces no significant overhead. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def solveloadbalancing(costmatrix): # Solve linear sum assignment to minimize total cost # rowindices, colindices = standardlinearsumassignmentsolver(costmatrix) assignment = [-1] len(costmatrix) # The sources do not specify the exact solver implementation return assignment An online scheduling technique paired with offline METIS partitioning to assign points or images, reducing communication overhead. End-to-end speedups across scenes indicate that this online scheduling introduces no significant overhead. Time and Memory Complexity: The exact complexity depends on the solver used for the linear sum assignment and is not given in the sources. METIS partitioning time varies by scene complexity, ranging from 1.9s to 31.0s for large scenes. Measured Performance: Removing load balancing causes performance reductions ranging from 1% to 14%. In contrast, removing hierarchical assignment ("w/o Hier.") results in 16% to 35% slower performance, and removing patching ("w/o Patch") results in 10% to 52% slower performance. The modest effect of load balancing stems from the fact that communication time dominates the overall runtime in the tested setting. Strengths and Limitations: Strengths: Reduces communication overhead; complements hierarchical assignment; no significant scheduling overhead. Limitations: Modest impact compared to hierarchical partitioning and patching; less effective when communication is not the bottleneck. The technique is implemented within a locality-aware distribution framework for large-scale point-based rendering. The framework combines offline METIS bipartite graph partitioning with online linear sum assignment to significantly reduce communication overhead compared to random distribution strategies. Prior work in point cloud partitioning includes manual heuristics, graphics data structures like KD-Trees, and clustering techniques like k-means. name: Adaptive Tile Sizing
head: Dynamic Tile Sizing
body: Adaptive Tile Sizing is a strategy for selecting tile dimensions in tiled parallel compositing based on the total number of pixels to render, aiming to optimize performance by balancing memory access patterns and computational load. It differs from sibling methods like Tile-Based Alpha Compositing by treating tile dimensions as tunable parameters subject to empirical thresholds rather than fixed constants, addressing the trade-off where larger tiles reduce duplicated primitive processing but increase sequential load per tile. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Total number of pixels to render (N{pix}). Input: Memory indexing scheme (column-major or row-major). Output: Selected tile dimensions (W \times H). Data Structures: Tile dimensions are represented as a pair of integers (W, H). The method evaluates two candidate configurations: Small tile: 16 \times 16 pixels. Large tile: 16 \times 32 pixels. Parameters: Threshold (T): 1,500,000 pixels. This value is determined experimentally. Steps: 1. Calculate the total number of pixels N{pix} to be rendered in the current frame or batch. 2. Compare N{pix} against the threshold T. 3. If N{pix} < T, select the 16 \times 32 tile configuration. 4. If N{pix} \ge T, select the 16 \times 16 tile configuration. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def selecttiledimensions(numpixels: int, indexing: str) -> tuple[int, int]: """ Selects tile dimensions based on pixel count and memory indexing. Args: numpixels: Total number of pixels to render. indexing: Memory indexing scheme, either 'column-major' or 'row-major'. Returns: A tuple (width, height) representing the selected tile dimensions. """ threshold = 1500000 # Base selection based on pixel count threshold if numpixels < threshold: width, height = 16, 32 else: width, height = 16, 16 # Adjust orientation based on memory indexing # Column-major: 16x32 is efficient (contiguous memory access along height) # Row-major: 32x16 is efficient (contiguous memory access along width) if indexing == 'row-major': # Swap dimensions to align the larger dimension with the row stride width, height = height, width return width, height Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Memory Indexing Dependency: The performance advantage of 16 \times 32 over 32 \times 16 (or vice versa) is strictly dependent on memory indexing. In column-major indexing, 16 \times 32 outperforms 32 \times 16 because the larger dimension (32) aligns with the contiguous memory stride. In row-major indexing, this relationship is reversed. Implementers must swap dimensions if the rendering backend uses row-major storage. Resolution Sensitivity: The threshold of 1.5 million pixels is specific to the hardware and implementation context described in the source. Blindly using 16 \times 16 tiles for all resolutions can lead to suboptimal performance, as larger tiles are not always faster. Performance Degradation: Using larger tiles (e.g., 16 \times 32) on low-resolution scenes can increase render time. For example, on the Bicycle scene at low resolution, using 16 \times 32 tiles increased average render time to 9.77 ms, demonstrating that larger tiles are not universally superior. Image-Space Partitioning divides the output image into rectangular tiles to distribute ray-casting work among parallel threads, balancing the trade-off between mutex contention (small tiles) and load imbalance (large tiles). It differs from sibling methods by explicitly treating tile dimensions as tunable parameters subject to empirical sweep, rather than fixed constants, to identify performance "sweet spots" on specific hardware. An adaptive tiling method based on hybrid saliency detection that divides each Group of Frames (GoF) into fine-grained uniform tiles, extracts static and dynamic saliency metrics, fuses them into a distribution map, and clusters tiles to group salient regions into larger tiles for higher quality representation. It divides each GoF into fine-grained uniform tiles. It extracts static saliency consisting of: 1) Intra-tile dispersion (SI) capturing geometric features within tiles. 2) Inter-tile variability (SE) capturing geometric features between tiles. It extracts dynamic saliency (SD) by comparing matching tiles between the first and last frames to represent motion changes. It computes a weighted fusion of SI, SE, and SD to yield a comprehensive saliency distribution map for all tiles within a single GoF. It employs a clustering algorithm to group tiles with similar saliency values. Tiles with high saliency and proximal distances are prioritized and merged into larger tiles representing regions of greater user interest. Time Complexity: The selection logic is O(1), involving a single comparison and potential dimension swap. The impact on overall render time depends on the chosen tile size's efficiency in reducing duplicated Gaussian processing versus increasing sequential load per tile. Memory Complexity: O(1) for the selection logic. The tile size choice affects the granularity of shared memory usage and cache efficiency, but no additional data structures are required for the selection itself. Measured Performance: On the Bicycle scene, using 16 \times 32 tiles at low resolution resulted in an average render time of 9.77 ms, which was slower than the alternative, indicating that larger tiles are not always faster. The threshold of 1.5 million pixels was determined experimentally to optimize performance across varying resolutions. Strengths: Adapts to resolution changes without manual tuning; accounts for memory indexing architecture; reduces duplicated Gaussian processing at higher resolutions. Limitations: The threshold is hardware-specific and may not generalize across all architectures; requires knowledge of memory indexing scheme; may not account for scene complexity or content distribution. When to use: When rendering 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) or similar tile-based compositing workloads where resolution varies significantly and memory access patterns are critical. When not to use: When scene complexity or content distribution (e.g., saliency) is the primary bottleneck, in which case saliency-based methods may be more appropriate. Adaptive Tile Sizing was introduced in the context of optimizing 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) rendering performance. The method addresses the inefficiency of fixed tile sizes by empirically determining a pixel-count threshold that balances the benefits of larger tiles (reduced duplicate processing) against their costs (increased sequential load). The specific threshold of 1.5 million pixels and the 16 \times 16 vs. 16 \times 32 configurations were derived from experiments on the Bicycle scene using a Julia-based implementation. The importance of memory indexing (column-major vs. row-major) was also highlighted as a critical factor in tile orientation performance. name: Image-Space Partitioning (Tile Size Optimization)
head: Image Tile Sizing and Work Assignment Strategy, Image Tile Tuning, Work Block Sizing
body: Image-Space Partitioning divides the output image into rectangular tiles to distribute ray-casting work among parallel threads, balancing the trade-off between mutex contention (small tiles) and load imbalance (large tiles). It differs from sibling methods by explicitly treating tile dimensions as tunable parameters subject to empirical sweep, rather than fixed constants, to identify performance "sweet spots" on specific hardware. Inputs: Image dimensions (W \times H). Hardware constraints (e.g., max threads per block, register limits). Memory layout (e.g., row-major). Outputs: Optimal tile width (Tw) and height (Th). Work assignment strategy (static or dynamic). Data Structures: Work List: A queue of tiles to be processed. For dynamic assignment, this requires synchronization primitives (e.g., mutex). Tile Grid: The image is decomposed into a grid of tiles. If W is not divisible by Tw or H by Th, boundary tiles are handled by clamping coordinates or processing partial tiles. Steps: 1. Define Search Space: Select ranges for tile width and height. Typical sweeps use powers of two: \{1, 2, 4, \dots, 256, 512\}. 2. Filter Invalid Configurations: Exclude combinations that result in fewer than 2 total work blocks. For a 512 \times 512 image, configurations like 256 \times 512, 512 \times 512, and 512 \times 256 are invalid as they produce only 1 or 2 blocks, preventing effective parallelization. 3. Benchmark: For each valid (Tw, Th) pair: a. Render multiple views (e.g., 30 views) using the chosen work assignment strategy. b. Measure Frame Rendering Time (FRT). 4. Normalize Performance: Calculate normalized FRT for each configuration: \text{Normalized FRT} = \frac{\text{FRT}{config}}{\min(\text{FRT}{all})} Values range from 1.0 (optimal) to \infty. 5. Identify Sweet Spot: Select the configuration with the lowest normalized FRT. In the reference study, 32 \times 32 was optimal for CPU pthreads, and 4 \times 2 (thread block dimensions) was optimal for CUDA FX5800. 6. Select Work Assignment: For small block sizes, static assignment may be slightly faster. For medium and large block sizes (e.g., 32 \times 32), dynamic assignment is preferred due to better load balance. Parameters: Optimal Tile Size (CPU): 32 \times 32 pixels. Optimal Thread Block Size (GPU, FX5800): 4 \times 2 threads. GPU Constraints: Max 512 threads/block, 16KB register memory per block. Pitfalls: Small Tiles: Cause serialized access to the work list via mutex, degrading performance. Large Tiles: Result in insufficient tiles for good load balance. Cache Misses: Block widths of 1, 2, and 4 exhibit poor performance due to high L1, L2, and TLB cache miss rates caused by degraded spatial/temporal locality in row-major memory layouts. Invalid Decompositions: Configurations yielding 1 or 2 total blocks are invalid for parallelization. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def findoptimaltilesize(imagewidth, imageheight, hardwareconstraints): """ Finds optimal tile dimensions by sweeping a parameter space. Returns (optimalw, optimalh, strategy). """ # Define search space: powers of 2 up to image dimensions widths = [1, 2, 4, 8, 16, 32, 64, 128, 256, 512] heights = [1, 2, 4, 8, 16, 32, 64, 128, 256, 512] # Filter widths/heights to not exceed image dimensions widths = [w for w in widths if w <= imagewidth] heights = [h for h in heights if h <= imageheight] minfrt = float('inf') bestconfig = None for w in widths: for h in heights: # Calculate total number of tiles numtilesw = (imagewidth + w - 1) // w numtilesh = (imageheight + h - 1) // h totaltiles = numtilesw numtilesh # Pitfall: Invalid block sizes (1 or 2 total blocks) if totaltiles < 2: continue # Pitfall: GPU hardware constraints (example for FX5800) # If using CUDA, ensure thread block size fits register/memory limits # e.g., max 512 threads, 16KB registers if isgpuhardware(hardwareconstraints): if w h > 512: # Max threads per block continue # Additional register/memory checks would go here # Benchmark this configuration frt = measureframerenderingtime(w, h, imagewidth, imageheight) if frt < minfrt: minfrt = frt bestconfig = (w, h) # Determine work assignment strategy # Dynamic is preferred for medium/large tiles for better load balance strategy = "dynamic" if bestconfig[0] bestconfig[1] >= 3232 else "static" return bestconfig, strategy def measureframerenderingtime(tilew, tileh, imgw, imgh): """ Renders multiple views and returns the minimum Frame Rendering Time (FRT). """ frts = [] for view in range(30): # Sweep over 30 views # Initialize work list with tiles worklist = createtilegrid(imgw, imgh, tilew, tileh) # Render using parallel threads # If dynamic: threads pop from worklist (mutex protected) # If static: threads are assigned fixed ranges of worklist rendertime = parallelraycast(worklist) frts.append(rendertime) return min(frts) # Minimum times represent optimal, contention-free conditions Performance Variation: The worst-performing tile size can be up to 3.0 times slower than the best configuration (normalized FRT max ~3.0). Complexity: The optimization phase is O(N \cdot V \cdot T), where N is the number of tile configurations, V is the number of views, and T is the render time per view. This is a one-time or infrequent cost. Strengths: Identifies hardware-specific optimal parameters; dynamic assignment handles load imbalance well for medium/large tiles. Limitations: Requires empirical tuning; small tiles suffer from mutex overhead; large tiles suffer from load imbalance; row-major memory layout exacerbates cache misses for certain tile shapes (e.g., width 1, 2, 4). When to Use: When deploying to specific hardware architectures where tile size significantly impacts cache behavior and synchronization overhead. The method originates from studies on hybrid parallelism for volume rendering on multi-core systems, specifically analyzing shared-memory raycasting on AMD Opteron CPUs and CUDA GPUs (FX5800). It addresses the need to balance parallel efficiency with memory access patterns in image-space partitioning. name: Tile Boundary Computation Setup
head: Tile Boundary Buffer Setup, Tile Boundary Generation
body: This method initializes the data structures required for tiled parallel compositing by computing the spatial extent (boundaries) of each tile within the framebuffer. It solves the problem of determining which input primitives or data elements contribute to which output tiles, enabling subsequent parallel processing stages to operate on disjoint subsets of the image without synchronization. It differs from sibling methods like Coarse Raster by focusing on the setup of the boundary metadata itself rather than the rasterization of geometry, and from Dynamic Load Balancing via Tile Queue by being a static setup phase rather than a runtime scheduling mechanism. Inputs: Swapchain extent (width W, height H) in pixels. Tile dimensions Tx = 16, Ty = 16 (fixed in source). Sorted key buffer (sortKBufferEven) containing pre-sorted data indices. Outputs: tileBoundaryBuffer: A storage buffer containing boundary indices for each tile. Data Structures: tileBoundaryBuffer: A storage buffer of size N{tiles} \times 2 \times \text{sizeof(uint32t)}. Layout: For each tile (i, j), the buffer stores two uint32t values. The stride is 2 uint32s per tile. The exact semantic meaning of the two values (e.g., start/end indices) is implied by the name "boundary" but not explicitly defined in the source beyond the storage size. Total size: T{tilesX} \times T{tilesY} \times 8 bytes. Steps: 1. Calculate Tile Grid Dimensions: Compute the number of tiles in the X and Y directions using ceiling division: T{tilesX} = \left\lceil \frac{W}{16} \right\rceil = \frac{W + 15}{16} T{tilesY} = \left\lceil \frac{H}{16} \right\rceil = \frac{H + 15}{16} 2. Allocate Buffer: Allocate tileBoundaryBuffer with size T{tilesX} \times T{tilesY} \times 2 \times \text{sizeof(uint32t)}. 3. Initialize Buffer: Zero out tileBoundaryBuffer using a fill operation. 4. Synchronization: Apply a pipeline barrier transitioning tileBoundaryBuffer from eTransfer to eComputeShader access. 5. Bind Resources: Bind sortKBufferEven (sorted key buffer) and tileBoundaryBuffer to the compute pipeline descriptor set. 6. Dispatch Compute Shader: Bind tileBoundaryPipeline and dispatch workgroups. Push constant: numInstances (likely related to the number of data elements or tiles, source does not specify exact derivation). Workgroup size: 256 threads. Number of workgroups: N{workgroups} = \left\lceil \frac{N{instances}}{256} \right\rceil = \frac{N{instances} + 255}{256} 7. name: Coarse Raster
head: Coarse Rasterizer
body: The Coarse Rasterizer performs triangle setup and emits a conservative list of all triangles touching each tile in a tiled volume rendering pipeline. It differs from typical chunkers by avoiding per-tile queues and expensive tile coverage tests during the setup phase, instead relying on a global radix-sort to organize triangle-tile relationships. This approach minimizes inter-thread communication and leverages the high compute-to-bandwidth ratio of modern GPUs by recomputing setup data per tile rather than caching it. The method consists of three main phases: Triangle Setup, Tile Sorting, and Tile Splitting. Input: A list of triangles defined in world or voxel space. Output: A set of virtual tiles, each containing a bounded number of triangles, ready for the Fine Raster stage. 1. Triangle Descriptor: A word-sized integer used for sorting. Bits [0:1]: Dominant axis of the triangle (2 bits). Bits [2:31]: Tile ID (remaining bits). 2. Unsorted List: An array of pairs (triangleindex, descriptor). 3. Per-Tile Ranges: After sorting, a compact list of (begin, end) indices into the sorted list for each physical tile. 4. Virtual Tile Arena: Memory allocated per virtual tile during the fine raster stage. M{tile}: The maximum number of triangles allowed in a virtual tile. 1. Triangle Setup and Emission For each triangle, a single CUDA thread processes the triangle. a. Compute the integer bounding box of the triangle. b. Determine the dominant axis of the triangle. c. Identify all physical tiles whose voxel grid intersects the triangle's integer bounding box. This is a conservative estimate; expensive precise coverage tests are skipped. d. For each touched tile, compute the 12 floats required for the cheapest 6-separating triangle-voxel coverage test. These floats are recomputed for each tile rather than computed once and reused, optimizing for GPU compute-to-bandwidth ratios. e. Construct the descriptor: combine the dominant axis (2 bits) and the tile ID. f. Emit a pair (triangleindex, descriptor) to a global unsorted list. 2. Tile Sorting a. Perform a global radix sort on the unsorted list of (triangleindex, descriptor) pairs based on the descriptor. b. The sorting groups triangles by tile ID, and within each tile, by dominant axis. This grouping increases SIMD efficiency in the subsequent fine raster stage. c. Generate a compact list of per-tile (begin, end) ranges that point to the start and end indices of each tile's triangles in the sorted array. 3. Tile Splitting a. Iterate through the physical tiles. b. If a physical tile contains more than M{tile} triangles, split it into multiple virtual tiles. c. Each virtual tile contains at most M{tile} triangles. d. Virtual tiles may overlap on the voxel grid. During the fine raster stage, a separate memory arena is created for each virtual tile. A final merging pass blends the results of all virtual tiles mapping to the same physical framebuffer entry. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def coarseraster(triangles, Mtile): # Phase 1: Triangle Setup and Emission outputlist = [] for tri in triangles: # 1. Compute integer bounding box bboxmin = [int(tri.min[i]) for i in range(3)] bboxmax = [int(tri.max[i]) for i in range(3)] # 2. Determine dominant axis (0=x, 1=y, 2=z) extents = [bboxmax[i] - bboxmin[i] for i in range(3)] dominantaxis = max(range(3), key=lambda i: extents[i]) # 3. Find all tiles intersecting the bounding box touchedtiles = [] for x in range(bboxmin[0], bboxmax[0] + 1): for y in range(bboxmin[1], bboxmax[1] + 1): for z in range(bboxmin[2], bboxmax[2] + 1): touchedtiles.append((x, y, z)) # 4. Emit for each touched tile for tileid in touchedtiles: # Recompute 12 floats for this specific tile setupdata = computesetupfloats(tri, tileid) # Construct descriptor: 2 bits for axis, rest for tile ID descriptor = (tileid << 2) | dominantaxis outputlist.append((tri.id, descriptor)) # Phase 2: Tile Sorting # Represents the global radix sort counting and scattering phase sortedlist = sorted(outputlist, key=lambda x: x[1]) tileranges = {} currenttile = -1 startidx = 0 for i, (triidx, descriptor) in enumerate(sortedlist): tileid = descriptor >> 2 if tileid != currenttile: if currenttile != -1: tileranges[currenttile] = (startidx, i) currenttile = tileid startidx = i if currenttile != -1: tileranges[currenttile] = (startidx, len(sortedlist)) # Phase 3: Tile Splitting virtualtiles = [] for tileid, (start, end) in tileranges.items(): numtriangles = end - start if numtriangles <= Mtile: virtualtiles.append({ 'physicaltileid': tileid, 'triangles': sortedlist[start:end], 'isvirtual': False }) else: numsplits = (numtriangles + Mtile - 1) // Mtile for i in range(numsplits): chunkstart = start + i Mtile chunkend = min(start + (i + 1) Mtile, end) virtualtiles.append({ 'physicaltileid': tileid, 'triangles': sortedlist[chunkstart:chunkend], 'isvirtual': True, 'virtualindex': i }) return virtualtiles, tileranges def computesetupfloats(triangle, tileid): # Recompute the 12 floats required for the cheapest 6-separating triangle-voxel coverage test # for the specific tile. Implementation uses standard geometric calculations. return [0.0] 12 Low-resolution voxelizations: May have too few occupied tiles to fill the GPU machine, or skewed triangle distributions. Tile splitting addresses this by creating more virtual tiles to improve load balancing. Degenerate ranges: If a scanline range is degenerate, it does not intersect the triangle. The coarse rasterizer avoids this by using conservative bounding box tests, potentially emitting triangles to tiles they do not strictly intersect, which is handled by the fine rasterizer's precise tests. Time Complexity: Efficient due to low data amplification; triangles often touch one or a few tiles only. The sorting phase dominates complexity, typically O(N \log N) or O(N) with radix sort, where N is the number of triangle-tile pairs. Memory Complexity: Requires storage for the unsorted list, sorted list, and per-tile ranges. Virtual tile arenas are allocated during fine raster. Strengths: Avoids inter-thread communication primitives like per-tile queues by using global radix-sort counting and scattering. The recomputation of setup data exploits high compute-to-bandwidth ratios. Sorting by dominant axis improves SIMD efficiency in the fine raster stage. Limitations: Conservative bounding box tests may emit more triangles than necessary, increasing the workload for the fine rasterizer. The need for a global sort adds latency compared to queue-based approaches if the number of triangle-tile pairs is small. When to use: When running on GPUs with high compute-to-bandwidth ratios and when tile sizes are large enough that triangles touch few tiles. Especially useful for low-resolution voxelizations where load balancing is critical. The Coarse Rasterizer is part of the VoxelPipe pipeline. It was designed to address the inefficiencies of previous tiled volume rendering approaches that relied on per-tile queues and inter-thread communication. The method leverages the parallel sorting capabilities of GPUs to efficiently organize triangle data for subsequent rasterization stages. name: Tile-Based Neural Material Classification and Sorting
head: ClassificationA, ClassificationB, Mixed Tile Repacking, Tile-based classification
body: This method is a two-pass compute shader pipeline that classifies 8x4 pixel tiles based on the neural material (MLP) index used by their pixels, separating them into uniform tiles (single MLP) and mixed tiles (multiple MLPs), then sorts mixed tiles to ensure uniform MLP usage per tile for efficient hardware matrix multiplication. It solves the problem of thread divergence in cooperative vector matrix multiplication by ensuring all pixels in a same workgroup use the same base matrix. Unlike Coarse Raster, which focuses on early visibility culling, this method operates on the output of the Visibility pass to reorganize pixel data for the Lighting pass. The method consists of two compute shader passes: ClassificationA and ClassificationB. Inputs: Visibility buffer containing material IDs for each pixel. Screen resolution (ScreenSize). Tile dimensions (TileSize), fixed at 8x4 pixels. Outputs: UniformTileAppendBuffer: Append buffer for uniform tiles. ComplexTileAppendBuffer: Append buffer for mixed tiles. ActiveTileAppendBuffer: Append buffer for all active tiles. IndexedTilesBufferRW: Read-write buffer storing sorted pixel coordinates. MLPUsageBufferRW: Read-write buffer tracking MLP usage counts and offsets. 1. UniformTileAppendBuffer: Append buffer storing workgroup IDs of tiles where all valid pixels share the same MLP index. 2. ComplexTileAppendBuffer: Append buffer storing workgroup IDs of tiles containing pixels with multiple different MLP indices. 3. ActiveTileAppendBuffer: Append buffer storing workgroup IDs of all tiles with at least one valid pixel. 4. ComplexTileConsumeBuffer: Consume buffer derived from ComplexTileAppendBuffer, used by Pass 2 to process mixed tiles. 5. MLPUsageBufferRW: A read-write buffer indexed by material ID (matID). Index matID: Stores the atomic usage count (number of pixels assigned to this MLP in the current batch). Index UNIQUEMLPCOUNT + matID: Stores the group offset for the specific material ID. 6. IndexedTilesBufferRW: A read-write buffer storing linearized pixel coordinates. Index: tileGroupOffset WORKGROUPSIZE + targetSlot. Value: Linearized screen coordinate x + y ScreenSize.x. Tile Size: 8x4 pixels, matching the workgroup size [numthreads(8, 4, 1)]. Valid Pixel Threshold: A tile is considered uniform only if it has more than 16 valid pixels (validPixelsCount > 16). WORKGROUPSIZE: The size of a work group (32 threads), used as a multiplier for the tile group offset in the indexed tiles buffer. UNIQUEMLPCOUNT: An offset index into MLPUsageBufferRW used to retrieve the group offset for a specific material ID. This pass classifies each 8x4 tile (workgroup) based on the material IDs of its valid pixels. 1. For each thread in the workgroup, retrieve the material ID for the current pixel using visibilitybuffermatid(pixelCoords). 2. Check if the material ID is valid. 3. If valid, use wave-level intrinsics to find the minimum and maximum material IDs within the workgroup: maxID = WaveActiveMax(matID) minID = WaveActiveMin(matID) 4. Count the number of valid pixels in the workgroup: validPixelsCount = WaveActiveSum(1) 5. If the thread is the first lane in the wave (WaveIsFirstLane()): Calculate the flattened workgroup ID: wgID = groupID.x + groupID.y TileSize.x. If maxID == minID and validPixelsCount > 16, append wgID to UniformTileAppendBuffer. Otherwise, append wgID to ComplexTileAppendBuffer. Always append wgID to ActiveTileAppendBuffer. This pass processes only the mixed tiles identified in Pass 1, sorting their pixels into uniform groups based on MLP index. 1. Consume a workgroup ID from ComplexTileConsumeBuffer. 2. Convert the workgroup ID to coordinates: wgX = workGroupID % TileSize.x wgY = workGroupID / TileSize.x 3. Compute pixel coordinates for each thread in the 8x4 workgroup: pixelCoords = uint2(wgX 8 + groupThreadID.x, wgY 4 + groupThreadID.y) 4. For each thread, retrieve the material ID: matID = visibilitybuffermatid(pixelCoords). 5. If the material ID is valid: Atomically increment the usage count for that material ID in MLPUsageBufferRW and book a slot: InterlockedAdd(MLPUsageBufferRW[matID], 1, targetSlot) Retrieve the offset for the current MLP group from MLPUsageBufferRW: mlpGroupOffset = MLPUsageBufferRW[UNIQUEMLPCOUNT + matID] Store the pixel's linearized coordinate into IndexedTilesBufferRW at the calculated offset: IndexedTilesBufferRW[mlpGroupOffset WORKGROUPSIZE + targetSlot] = pixelCoords.x + pixelCoords.y ScreenSize.x Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. [numthreads(8, 4, 1)] def ClassificationA(groupID: uint2, pixelCoords: uint2): # Get the material ID of the pixel matID = visibilitybuffermatid(pixelCoords) if validmatid(matID): # Find min and max material IDs within the workgroup maxID = WaveActiveMax(matID) minID = WaveActiveMin(matID) # Count valid pixels in the workgroup validPixelsCount = WaveActiveSum(1) # Flatten the work group ID wgID = groupID.x + groupID.y TileSize.x # Only the first lane classifies the tile if WaveIsFirstLane(): # Append to active tiles list always ActiveTileAppendBuffer.Append(wgID) # Classify as uniform or complex if maxID == minID and validPixelsCount > 16: UniformTileAppendBuffer.Append(wgID) else: ComplexTileAppendBuffer.Append(wgID) [numthreads(8, 4, 1)] def ClassificationB(groupThreadID: uint2): # Consume a workgroup ID from the complex tile buffer workGroupID = ComplexTileConsumeBuffer.Consume() # Convert workgroup ID to coordinates wgX = workGroupID % TileSize.x wgY = workGroupID / TileSize.x # Compute pixel coordinates for this thread pixelCoords = uint2(wgX 8 + groupThreadID.x, wgY 4 + groupThreadID.y) # Get material ID matID = visibilitybuffermatid(pixelCoords) if validmatid(matID): # Book a slot for this pixel in the right tile group using atomic add targetSlot = InterlockedAdd(MLPUsageBufferRW[matID], 1) # Get the group offset for this material ID mlpGroupOffset = MLPUsageBufferRW[UNIQUEMLPCOUNT + matID] # Store the linearized pixel coordinate IndexedTilesBufferRW[mlpGroupOffset WORKGROUPSIZE + targetSlot] = \ pixelCoords.x + pixelCoords.y ScreenSize.x Global Atomics: The method uses global atomics for sorting mixed tiles. This is inefficient if the screen is filled with mixed tiles; shared memory atomics would be more suitable in that case. Uniform Tile Threshold: A tile is only classified as uniform if it has more than 16 valid pixels. Tiles with fewer valid pixels, even if they share a single MLP, are treated as complex tiles. MLP Sharing: The current implementation does not share unique MLPs for different materials. Sharing MLPs could reduce the number of mixed tiles and improve performance at the expense of quality. Time Complexity: The method requires two passes over the tiles. Pass 1 is O(N) where N is the number of tiles. Pass 2 is O(M) where M is the number of mixed tiles. Memory Complexity: Requires additional buffers for classification (UniformTileAppendBuffer, ComplexTileAppendBuffer, ActiveTileAppendBuffer) and sorting (MLPUsageBufferRW, IndexedTilesBufferRW). Performance: When using wider MLPs (D >= 32), using cooperative vectors permits up to a ×40 speedup compared to software FMA. The classification itself takes approximately 0.035 ms for L=1 layer and D=16, scaling with MLP dimensions. Strengths: Avoids divergence in the Lighting pass by ensuring all pixels in a workgroup use the same MLP, which is required for efficient cooperative vector matrix multiplication. Limitations: Scaling issue: The classification is not optimal for screens filled with mixed tiles due to global atomics. This method was introduced by L. Belcour & A. Benyoub in the paper "Hardware Accelerated Neural Block Texture Compression with Cooperative Vectors" (Eurographics 2025). It is part of the HW NBTC pipeline, designed to handle neural material compression and rendering efficiently on hardware supporting cooperative vectors. name: Parallel Image Assembly
head: Final Image Assembly & Alpha Blending, Image Stitching, Spatial Compositing, Z-Order Compositing
body: Parallel Image Assembly is the final step in spatial decomposition volume rendering where sub-images rendered by independent threads or processes are combined into a single final image. It solves the problem of merging disjoint spatial data portions into a coherent visual output by placing sub-images at their correct spatial coordinates and blending them along the z-axis using front-to-back alpha compositing. Unlike temporal sequencing, which has minimal overhead, spatial compositing incurs significant overhead due to the data collection and blending requirements. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A set of composited sub-images (RGBA) and their corresponding opacities from all participating ranks/threads. Each sub-image corresponds to a specific spatial tile (px, py) and potentially a depth slice pz. Output: A single final image array of shape (X, Y, 4) with dtype float32, representing the fully composited volume, often saved as uint8 PNG. Data Structures: finalimage: A numpy array of shape (x\dim, y\dim, 4) storing the accumulated color and opacity. zsplitimages: A collection of sub-images arranged by their spatial coordinates. totalopacity: An array tracking the accumulated opacity for each pixel location. Parameters: LOCATIONOFZ: A sorted list of unique z-start coordinates for each process chunk, used to determine depth ordering. PZ: Total number of depth slices. Steps: 1. Gather Sub-images: Collect the composited subdomain images and opacities from all ranks to a root rank (typically Rank 0). 2. Initialize Final Image: On the root rank, initialize finalimage with zeros and shape (PX \times sub\height, PY \times sub\width, 3) for color, and a corresponding opacity array. 3. Place Sub-images: Iterate through all gathered ranks. 4. Depth Handling: For each rank, determine its spatial coordinates (px, py, pz). If the rank corresponds to the middle depth slice (pz == PZ // 2), place its composited color image into the finalimage grid at the appropriate (px, py) location. Add the opacity from this slice to the totalopacity map for the corresponding (px, py) location. 5. Compositing: For each z-slice (or depth layer), blend the sub-image into the finalimage using front-to-back alpha compositing. The blending follows the standard volume rendering equation: C{final} = C{prev} + C{z} \cdot (1 - \alpha{prev}) \alpha{final} = \alpha{prev} + \alpha{z} \cdot (1 - \alpha{prev}) Where C is color (RGB) and \alpha is opacity. 6. Finalization: Convert the finalimage from float32 to uint8 RGBA and save as a PNG file. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def parallelimageassembly(gatheredsubimages, gatheredopacities, px, py, pz, subwidth, subheight, xdim, ydim, PZ): """ Assembles sub-images into a final image using spatial compositing. Args: gatheredsubimages: List of arrays from all ranks, each of shape (subwidth, subheight, 4) gatheredopacities: List of arrays from all ranks, each of shape (subwidth, subheight, 1) px, py, pz: Spatial coordinates of the current rank's sub-image subwidth, subheight: Dimensions of each sub-image xdim, ydim: Total dimensions of the final image PZ: Total number of depth slices Returns: finalrgba: List of lists of lists representing uint8 RGBA image of shape (xdim, ydim, 4) """ # Initialize final image arrays with zeros def createzeros(shape): return [[[0.0 for in range(shape[2])] for in range(shape[1])] for in range(shape[0])] finalcolor = createzeros((xdim, ydim, 3)) finalopacity = createzeros((xdim, ydim, 1)) # Place sub-images into the final image grid at spatial coordinates startx = px subwidth starty = py subheight for dy in range(subheight): for dx in range(subwidth): finalcolor[startx + dx][starty + dy] = gatheredsubimages[dy][dx][:3] finalopacity[startx + dx][starty + dy] = [gatheredopacities[dy][dx][0]] # Depth handling: if middle slice, accumulate opacity to totalopacity map if pz == PZ // 2: for dy in range(subheight): for dx in range(subwidth): finalopacity[startx + dx][starty + dy][0] += gatheredopacities[dy][dx][0] # Front-to-back alpha compositing across z-slices # Sources do not specify the exact iteration order for multiple slices beyond front-to-back for zidx in range(len(gatheredsubimages)): zimg = gatheredsubimages[zidx] zop = gatheredopacities[zidx] for dy in range(ydim): for dx in range(xdim): cprev = finalcolor[dx][dy] aprev = finalopacity[dx][dy][0] cz = zimg[dy][dx][:3] az = zop[dy][dx][0] # Apply compositing formulas finalcolor[dx][dy] = [cprev[j] + cz[j] (1.0 - aprev) for j in range(3)] finalopacity[dx][dy][0] = aprev + az (1.0 - aprev) # Convert to uint8 RGBA with clipping to avoid overflow finalrgba = createzeros((xdim, ydim, 4)) for dy in range(ydim): for dx in range(xdim): for j in range(3): val = finalcolor[dx][dy][j] 255.0 finalrgba[dx][dy][j] = max(0, min(255, int(val))) val = finalopacity[dx][dy][0] 255.0 finalrgba[dx][dy][3] = max(0, min(255, int(val))) return finalrgba Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Overhead: Spatial compositing has huge overhead compared to temporal sequencing. Precision: Using float32 for intermediate calculations is standard, but conversion to uint8 must be clipped to avoid overflow. Boundary Conditions: Ensure sub-images are placed at correct (px, py) coordinates to avoid gaps or overlaps. A technique for rendering high-resolution viewports that intersect multiple display tiles (projectors) by tiling the image and reassembling it, requiring dynamic progress properties for frame reassembly. It renders a single image stream (e.g., 1600x1200 RGBA) at the target resolution and distributes the image tiles to the appropriate projectors based on viewport intersection. If the viewport intersects multiple logical pipelines, a new routability proof is required to account for image sources contributing to more than one pipeline, and a dynamic progress property must be implemented for frame reassembly. Time Complexity: Dominated by the communication cost of gathering sub-images to the root rank and the compositing step, which is O(X \cdot Y) per depth slice. Memory Complexity: Requires storing the full final image (X \cdot Y \cdot 4) and all sub-images during the gather phase. Strengths: Produces a single, coherent final image suitable for display or storage. Limitations: High overhead due to data collection and potential bottleneck at the root rank. Not suitable for real-time animation without optimization. Parallel Image Assembly, also known as spatial compositing, is a technique used in parallel volume rendering to combine results from spatially decomposed data. It involves collecting sub-images from different threads and compositing them in a front-to-back order. The method is applied when each thread has completely processed its own data portion and the main thread must merge the separate ray segments into one final image. name: Multi-Threaded Tile-Based Rendering
head: threaded rasterization
body: Multi-Threaded Tile-Based Rendering is a parallelization strategy that divides the screen height into tiles and processes each tile in a separate thread to parallelize the rasterization workload. It differs from Tile-Based Alpha Compositing by focusing on the rasterization phase itself rather than just compositing pre-rasterized fragments, and from Screen Parallel Rendering by dividing the screen into tiles processed by threads on a single machine rather than subscreens distributed across multiple processors. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Screen height (H), screen width (W), and the number of available hardware threads. Output: A fully rasterized framebuffer. Data Structures: Tile Struct: Contains four integer fields defining the rectangular region of the screen to render: xmin, xmax, ymin, and ymax. Algorithm Steps: 1. Determine Thread Count: Calculate the number of threads (T) as the maximum of 1 and the system's reported hardware concurrency. If std::thread::hardwareconcurrency() returns 0, T is set to 1 to prevent division by zero or empty thread vectors. 2. Calculate Tile Height: Compute the height of each tile (h{tile}) as H / T. 3. Initialize Threads: For each thread index i from 0 to T-1: Calculate the vertical range for the tile. Set ymin = i \times h{tile}. Set ymax = (i == T-1) ? H-1: (i+1) \times h{tile} - 1. Set xmin = 0 and xmax = W-1 (assuming full width per tile). Launch a worker thread executing the renderTile function with this tile's coordinates. 4. Join Threads: Wait for all worker threads to complete. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import threading def hardwareconcurrency(): """Returns the number of logical processors available.""" import os return os.cpucount() or 1 def rendertile(tile): """Renders the specific tile region. Actual rasterization logic is not provided in the sources.""" # Process pixels within tile.xmin, tile.xmax, tile.ymin, tile.ymax pass def multithreadedtilerendering(screenheight, screenwidth): # Step 1: Determine number of threads threadscount = max(1, hardwareconcurrency()) # Step 2: Calculate tile height tileheight = screenheight // threadscount threads = [] # Step 3: Create and launch threads for i in range(threadscount): ymin = i tileheight # Last tile extends to the end of the screen to handle non-divisible heights if i == threadscount - 1: ymax = screenheight - 1 else: ymax = (i + 1) tileheight - 1 tile = { 'xmin': 0, 'xmax': screenwidth - 1, 'ymin': ymin, 'ymax': ymax } thread = threading.Thread(target=rendertile, args=(tile,)) threads.append(thread) thread.start() # Step 4: Join all worker threads for thread in threads: thread.join() Parameters: threadscount: Typically equal to std::thread::hardwareconcurrency(). Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Zero Hardware Concurrency: If the system reports 0 cores, the algorithm defaults to 1 thread to avoid runtime errors. Non-Divisible Heights: The last tile must explicitly extend to screenheight - 1 to ensure all pixels are covered when H is not evenly divisible by T. Screen Parallel Rendering is a parallelization technique that exploits parallelism in screen space by dividing the screen into regions and assigning each region to a processor. It solves the problem of rendering large scenes by distributing the workload of ray traversal across multiple processors, where each processor is responsible for the entire ray for its assigned subscreen. Unlike object-parallel methods that partition the volume data, this approach partitions the image space, allowing each processor to access the full dataset. It is a form of sort-first parallel rendering, where primitives are distributed based on their projected screen location. Tile-Based Rasterization is a GPU-accelerated rendering primitive that divides the image plane into fixed-size tiles, assigning one CUDA thread block to each tile to process all fragments within that region. It solves the parallelization bottleneck of global rasterization by localizing the workload, allowing threads within a block to share splat data in fast shared memory and blend them in front-to-back order. Unlike Screen Parallel Rendering, which assigns individual threads to pixels without explicit tile-level coordination, this method leverages the spatial coherence of tiles to optimize memory access patterns for splat blending. Not given in the sources. This method is described in the context of CPU rasterizers, specifically referenced in the whudsontosh/CPU-Rasterizer repository. name: Screen Parallel Rendering
head: Demand-Driven Ray-Parallel Rendering, Demand-driven, Sort-First Parallel Rendering, Image Space Partitioning, Parallel Row Rendering
body: Screen Parallel Rendering is a parallelization technique that exploits parallelism in screen space by dividing the screen into regions (tasks) and assigning each region to a processor. It solves the problem of rendering large scenes by distributing the workload of ray traversal across multiple processors, where each processor is responsible for the entire ray for its assigned subscreen. Unlike object-parallel methods that partition the volume data, this approach partitions the image space, allowing each processor to access the full dataset. It is a form of sort-first parallel rendering, where primitives are distributed based on their projected screen location. Inputs: A volume dataset (or scene primitives). A camera view (viewpoint and projection). A set of p processors. Outputs: A final composite image. Data Structures: Screen Partitioning: The screen is divided into p disjoint subscreens or tiles. Task Queue: A master node maintains a queue of tasks (subscreen regions). Volume Data: The entire volume dataset must be accessible to every processor. Steps: 1. Partitioning: Divide the screen into p subscreens, where p is the number of available processors. 2. Assignment: Assign tasks associated with each subscreen to processors. Tasks are assigned in a cyclic manner to statically balance processing workloads. 3. Execution: Each processor takes responsibility for the entire ray for its subscreen. All voxels along a ray are processed simultaneously by the respective processor. 4. Demand-Driven Scheduling: Processors execute tasks and request new ones from a master node upon completion of the current task. This is referred to as the "demand-driven" approach. 5. Compositing: Rendered portions are assembled or pasted together to form the final image. Formulas: Ray direction computation per pixel (x, y): rx = (x - \text{res}[0]/2) \cdot fx ry = (y - \text{res}[1]/2) \cdot fy rz = 1.0 fx = \frac{\tan(\text{fov})}{\text{res}[0]/2} fy = \frac{\tan(\text{fov})}{\text{res}[1]/2} \cdot \frac{\text{res}[1]}{\text{res}[0]} The ray direction is then rotated using Rodrigues' rotation formula around the camera rotation vector. Parameters: p: Number of processors. Must match the number of subscreens. RENDERINGTHREADS: Number of threads, typically set to 8. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Memory Requirements: Every processor needs to load the entire volume into memory, requiring large main memory. This makes the approach infeasible for massive datasets where data cannot be replicated. Load Balancing: Primitives may cluster into specific regions, causing load balancing problems between renderers. Boundary Processing: Primitives overlapping screen region boundaries may be processed by more than one renderer, leading to redundant computation. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def screenparallelrendering(volume, camera, numprocessors): # Step 1: Partition screen into p subscreens resolution = camera.resolution subscreens = [] for i in range(numprocessors): ystart = (i resolution[1]) // numprocessors yend = ((i + 1) resolution[1]) // numprocessors if i < numprocessors - 1 else resolution[1] subscreens.append({'id': i, 'xstart': 0, 'xend': resolution[0], 'ystart': ystart, 'yend': yend}) # Step 2 & 4: Demand-driven task queue taskqueue = list(subscreens) renderedportions = [None] numprocessors while taskqueue: subscreen = taskqueue.pop(0) procid = subscreen['id'] portion = rendersubscreen(subscreen, camera, volume) renderedportions[procid] = portion # Step 5: Compositing finalimage = compositeportions(renderedportions, resolution) return finalimage def rendersubscreen(subscreen, camera, volume): resolution = camera.resolution fov = camera.fov resx, resy = resolution[0], resolution[1] xfactor = math.tan(fov) / (resx / 2) yfactor = (math.tan(fov) / (resy / 2)) (resy / resx) image = [[0.0] 3 for in range(subscreen['yend'] - subscreen['ystart'])] for y in range(subscreen['ystart'], subscreen['yend']): for x in range(subscreen['xstart'], subscreen['xend']): # Compute ray direction rx = (x - resx / 2) xfactor ry = (y - resy / 2) yfactor rz = 1.0 raydir = normalize([rx, ry, rz]) rayorigin = camera.origin # Cast ray through volume color = raycastvolume(rayorigin, raydir, volume) image[y - subscreen['ystart']][x] = color return image def raycastvolume(rayorigin, raydirection, volume): # Standard ray-marching for volume rendering color = [0.0, 0.0, 0.0] alpha = 0.0 t = 0.0 stepsize = 0.1 while t < 10.0 and alpha < 1.0: point = [rayorigin[i] + raydirection[i] t for i in range(3)] density = samplevolume(point, volume) if density > 0: transmittance = math.exp(-density stepsize) color = [color[i] + (1.0 - alpha) density stepsize colormap(density)[i] for i in range(3)] alpha = 1.0 - (1.0 - alpha) transmittance t += stepsize return color def compositeportions(portions, resolution): final = [[0.0] 3 for in range(resolution[1])] for portion in portions: if portion is None: continue for y in range(len(portion)): for x in range(len(portion[0])): final[y][x] = portion[y][x] return final def normalize(v): mag = math.sqrt(sum(cc for c in v)) return [c/mag for c in v] def samplevolume(point, volume): # Placeholder for volume trilinear interpolation return 0.0 def colormap(density): # Placeholder for transfer function return [density, density, density] Time Complexity: Linear with respect to the number of pixels in the subscreen and the number of voxels along the ray for each processor. The total time is dominated by the slowest processor if load balancing is poor. Memory Complexity: O(N) per processor, where N is the size of the entire volume dataset. This is a significant limitation as memory usage scales with the dataset size, not the subscreen size. Measured Performance: Effective for small datasets that require no data decomposition. Performance degrades for large-scale datasets due to memory constraints. Strengths: Exploits parallelism in screen space. Each processor has all information needed for complete rendering, allowing use of any rendering algorithm. Takes advantage of frame-to-frame coherence, as few primitives move between tiles from one frame to the next. Limitations: Requires large main memory because every processor needs to load the entire volume. Infeasible for massive volumes where data cannot be replicated. Load balancing issues due to primitive clustering. Redundant processing of primitives at region boundaries. When to Use: Small datasets where memory is not a constraint and frame-to-frame coherence is high. When Not to Use: Large-scale datasets requiring out-of-core processing or distributed memory management. Screen Parallel Rendering is one of the earliest parallel schemes for volume rendering, classified under screen parallel rendering as opposed to object parallel rendering. It is a form of sort-first parallel rendering, a concept identified by Molnar et al.. The Chromium System uses the sort-first approach to distribute rendering work to cluster nodes before the transformation and lighting stages. The technique is also known as demand-driven ray-parallel rendering, where processors request new tasks from a master upon completion. A broader category that includes Screen Parallel Rendering. It distributes raw primitives during geometry preprocessing by dividing the 2D screen into disjoint regions. It takes advantage of frame-to-frame coherence well. Sort-First Parallel Rendering Contrasts with screen parallel rendering by dividing the volume into subvolumes. It requires image compositing to merge subimages. name: Tile-Based Rasterization
head: CUDA tile rasterization
body: Tile-Based Rasterization is a GPU rendering primitive that assigns one CUDA thread block per image tile to process fragments locally. It parallelizes the rasterization workload by having threads within a block share splat data in fast shared memory and blend them in front-to-back order. Unlike Screen Parallel Rendering, which assigns threads directly to pixels without tile-level coordination, this method groups pixels into fixed-size tiles to optimize shared memory reuse. Inputs: A list of splats (e.g., 3D Gaussians) projected to screen space. A tile grid covering the resolution (16×16 pixels). For each tile, a sorted list of splat indices assigned to that tile. Outputs: Final color and opacity values for each pixel in the tile. Data Structures: Shared Memory Buffer: A 1D array storing up to 128 splats per iteration. Thread Block: A CUDA thread block of 256 threads, mapped one-to-one to the 16×16 pixel tile. Parameters: Tile size: 16×16 pixels. Threads per block: 256. Load batch size: 128 splats. Steps: 1. Assign one CUDA thread block per tile, with 256 threads mapping to the 16×16 pixel grid. 2. Initialize pixel buffers for color and accumulated opacity. 3. Ping-pong blending loop: Phase 1 uses 128 threads to load the next batch of up to 128 splats from global memory into shared memory. Phase 2 uses all 256 threads to iterate through the loaded splats and blend them in front-to-back order. Repeat until all assigned splats are processed. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def tilerasterize(tilesplats, threadid, numpixels=256, loadbatch=128): # Map thread index to pixel coordinates in the 16x16 tile pixelcoords = (threadid % 16, threadid // 16) pixelcolor = [0.0, 0.0, 0.0] pixelalpha = 0.0 splatidx = 0 numsplats = len(tilesplats) sharedsplats = [None] loadbatch while splatidx < numsplats: # Phase 1: Load loadcount = 0 if threadid < loadbatch: endload = min(splatidx + loadbatch, numsplats) for i in range(splatidx, endload): sharedsplats[loadcount] = tilesplats[i] loadcount += 1 splatidx = endload # Synchronize all 256 threads syncthreads() # Determine how many splats were actually loaded numloaded = loadcount if threadid < loadbatch else 0 # Broadcast numloaded from thread 0 to all threads if threadid == 0: broadcastnumloaded = numloaded syncthreads() numloaded = broadcastnumloaded # Phase 2: Blend for s in range(numloaded): splat = sharedsplats[s] if pixelinsplatfootprint(splat, pixelcoords): contribution = computesplatcontribution(splat, pixelcoords) pixelcolor, pixelalpha = fronttobackblend( pixelcolor, pixelalpha, contribution['color'], contribution['alpha']) syncthreads() def syncthreads(): # Simulates CUDA syncthreads() barrier pass def pixelinsplatfootprint(splat, coords): # Checks if coords are within the splat's 2D bounding box return True def computesplatcontribution(splat, coords): # Computes color and alpha at coords return {'color': [0.0, 0.0, 0.0], 'alpha': 0.0} def fronttobackblend(c1, a1, c2, a2): # Standard alpha compositing outa = a1 + a2 (1.0 - a1) outc = [c1[i] + c2[i] a2 (1.0 - a1) for i in range(3)] return outc, outa Edge Cases: Fewer than 128 splats: The load phase handles partial batches. The blend phase must correctly determine the number of valid splats in shared memory to avoid reading garbage data. Empty Tile: If no splats are assigned to a tile, the loop does not execute, and the pixel retains its background value. Binned Raster Traversal is a GPU-accelerated rasterization method for Gaussian Splatting that replaces the baseline's single globally depth-sorted scan with a linear scan over a concatenation of K coarse, tile-local depth bins. It solves the performance bottleneck of global sorting by deferring depth ordering to a tile-local binning phase, allowing the rasterizer to process a contiguous memory interval without per-bin branching or complex control flow. Unlike the baseline traversal, which requires a single sorted range, this method scans the concatenated bins in front-to-back order, relying on pre-computed offsets to define the scan interval. Time Complexity: Linear with respect to the number of splats assigned to the tile and the number of pixels in the tile. Memory Complexity: O(N{splat\per\tile}) for shared memory, where N{splat\per\tile} is capped at 128. Strengths: Reduces global memory bandwidth pressure by reusing splat data in shared memory. Scales well with tile size and splat density. Limitations: Requires efficient binning of splats to tiles beforehand. Performance may degrade if splat distribution is highly uneven across tiles. Tile-Based Rasterization for Gaussian Splatting adapts the standard 3DGS rasterization approach to a tile-based parallel model on CUDA, leveraging the hardware's thread block architecture to optimize the blending process. name: Binned Raster Traversal
head: Binned CUDA Rasterization
body: Binned Raster Traversal is a GPU-accelerated rasterization method for Gaussian splatting that replaces the global depth-sorted scan of the baseline with a tile-local, bin-based linear scan. It solves the performance bottleneck of global sorting by partitioning the pair stream into coarse bins per tile, allowing each CUDA thread block to process a contiguous interval of pre-ordered data without per-bin branching. Unlike the baseline which scans a single globally depth-sorted range, this method scans the concatenation of K coarse bins laid out back to back in front-to-back bin order. Inputs: Repaired pair stream P (containing Gaussian IDs and sidecar data). Bin offsets array binOffsets[t, k] for each tile t and bin index k \in [0, K]. Optional flat-ID sidecar. Gaussian attributes (position, covariance, color, opacity). Image and tile dimensions. Outputs: Rendered colors, alphas, and last contributing IDs for each pixel. Data Structures: binOffsets: A 2D array of size T \times (K+1), where T is the number of tiles and K is the number of coarse bins per tile. binOffsets[t, k] stores the start index in the pair stream for the k-th bin of tile t. The interval for tile t is [binOffsets[t, 0], binOffsets[t, K]). Shared memory: Used for candidate Gaussian IDs and optionally for staging candidate colors. Parameters: K: Number of coarse bins per tile. Default: 64. Early-termination threshold: Transmittance Tp below which a pixel is marked inactive. Tile-alpha culling threshold: Minimum contribution threshold for tile-level culling. Configuration flags: colorstaging (enabled by default), tilealphaculling (enabled by default), traversalprofiling (disabled by default). Steps: 1. Launch one CUDA block per tile in parallel. 2. Determine tile pixel coordinates and skip masked tiles. 3. For all pixels p in tile t: Initialize color accumulator Cp \leftarrow 0 and transmittance accumulator Tp \leftarrow 1. 4. Set scan interval [a, b) \leftarrow [binOffsets[t, 0], binOffsets[t, K]). 5. Iterate through batches within the interval a, b): If all pixels in the tile have terminated, break the loop. 6. Load candidate Gaussian IDs into shared memory. 7. If tile-alpha culling is enabled, remove candidates below the tile-level contribution threshold. 8. If color staging is enabled, stage candidate colors cooperatively in shared memory. 9. For all Gaussians g in the surviving batch order, iterate over all active pixels p in the tile. 10. If traversal profiling is enabled, count candidate visits. 11. Evaluate the same opacity/conic test as the baseline. 12. Update Cp and Tp using baseline alpha [compositing. 13. If Tp reaches the early-termination threshold, mark pixel p as inactive. 14. Write final color, alpha, and last contributing ID for each pixel. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def binnedrastertraversal(repairedpairstream, binoffsets, gaussianattrs, tiledims, K=64, batchsize=256, earlyterminationthreshold=1e-4, tilealphacullingenabled=True, tilealphathreshold=0.01, colorstagingenabled=True, traversalprofilingenabled=False): # Constants EARLYTERMINATIONTHRESHOLD = earlyterminationthreshold TILEALPHATHRESHOLD = tilealphathreshold candidatevisits = 0 # 1. Launch one CUDA block per tile in parallel for tilet in range(numtiles): # 2. Determine tile pixel coordinates; skip masked tiles if tilet.ismasked: continue tilepixels = tilet.getpixelcoordinates() # 3. Initialize accumulators for all pixels in the tile for p in tilepixels: p.Cp = 0.0 p.Tp = 1.0 p.isactive = True # 4. Set scan interval a = binoffsets[tilet.id, 0] b = binoffsets[tilet.id, K] # 5. Iterate through batches within the interval [a, b) batchstart = a while batchstart < b: # Check if all pixels terminated if not any(p.isactive for p in tilepixels): break # Determine batch end batchend = min(batchstart + batchsize, b) # 6. Load candidate Gaussian IDs into shared memory candidateids = [] for idx in range(batchstart, batchend): candidateids.append(repairedpairstream[idx].gaussianid) # 7. Tile-alpha culling if tilealphacullingenabled: survivingids = [] for gid in candidateids: g = gaussianattrs[gid] # Estimate tile-level contribution contribution = g.opacity g.scalefactor if contribution >= TILEALPHATHRESHOLD: survivingids.append(gid) candidateids = survivingids # 8. Color staging if colorstagingenabled: stagedcolors = [gaussianattrs[gid].color for gid in candidateids] # 9. For all Gaussians g in surviving batch order, iterate over all active pixels p for gid in candidateids: g = gaussianattrs[gid] for p in tilepixels: if not p.isactive: continue # 10. Traversal profiling if traversalprofilingenabled: candidatevisits += 1 # 11. Evaluate opacity/conic test alpha = computealpha(p, g) if alpha < 1e-6: continue # 12. Update Cp and Tp using baseline alpha compositing color = computecolor(p, g) p.Cp += color alpha p.Tp p.Tp = (1.0 - alpha) # 13. Early termination if p.Tp < EARLYTERMINATIONTHRESHOLD: p.isactive = False batchstart = batchend # 14. Write final results for p in tilepixels: p.finalcolor = p.Cp p.finalalpha = 1.0 - p.Tp p.lastcontributingid = candidateids[-1] if candidateids else -1 def computealpha(pixel, gaussian): # Evaluates opacity/conic test as in baseline rasterization return gaussian.opacity gaussian.scalefactor def computecolor(pixel, gaussian): # Computes projected color contribution as in baseline rasterization return gaussian.color Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Bin Order: Entries within a bin are not depth-sorted unless selective exact repair has restored the order. The method relies on the concatenation of bins being in front-to-back bin order, not necessarily within each bin. Precision: Standard floating-point precision is used for accumulators. Early termination thresholds must be chosen carefully to avoid visual artifacts from premature culling. Boundaries: The scan interval a, b) is exclusive of b. Ensure binOffsets array is sized correctly to avoid out-of-bounds access. The [CUDA Tile-and-Bin Implementation is a parallelization strategy for computing the forward and backward passes of 2D bitmap primitive rendering on a GPU. It partitions the image plane into tiles and assigns primitives to the tiles they overlap, using one CUDA thread block per tile to achieve complete pixel-level parallelism. It sets itself apart from parent Binned Raster Traversal by explicitly managing the tile-to-primitive assignment on the CPU and staging primitive parameters in shared memory for cooperative compositing within the block, rather than relying on a linear scan of a pre-binned pair stream. Time Complexity: Linear with respect to the number of candidates in the tile's concatenated bins. Memory Complexity: Requires storage for the pair stream, bin offsets, and Gaussian attributes, plus shared memory for candidate IDs and optionally colors. Measured Performance: Evaluated on an RTX 4090 with a synthetic scale-up diagnostic from 5M to 30M Gaussians. Not given in the sources. Strengths: Eliminates global sorting overhead; enables efficient tile-local processing; supports early termination. Limitations: Performance depends on the quality of binning; poor binning can lead to unbalanced workloads. When to Use: Suitable for high-resolution rendering with large numbers of Gaussians where global sorting is a bottleneck. When Not to Use: For small scenes or low Gaussian counts where global sorting overhead is negligible. head: Tile-and-Bin CUDA Pipeline, Tile-and-Bin CUDA Pipeline for 2D Bitmaps, tile-based differentiable splatting for 2D bitmaps
body:
The CUDA Tile-and-Bin Implementation is a parallelization strategy for computing the forward and backward passes of 2D bitmap primitive rendering on a GPU. It partitions the image plane into tiles and assigns primitives to the tiles they overlap, using one CUDA thread block per tile to achieve complete pixel-level parallelism. It sets itself apart from parent Binned Raster Traversal by explicitly managing the tile-to-primitive assignment on the CPU and staging primitive parameters in shared memory for cooperative compositing within the block, rather than relying on a linear scan of a pre-binned pair stream. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A set of N primitives, each defined by parameters \{(xi, yi, si, 	hetai, 
ui, ci)\}{i=1}^N, where (xi, yi) is position, si is scale, 	hetai is rotation, 
ui is opacity logit, and ci is color logits. A tile-primitive mapping generated on the CPU. Output: Rendered image I \in [0,1]^3 and alpha channel I\alpha. Data Structures: Tile-Primitive Mapping: A list associating each tile with the indices of primitives whose bounding boxes overlap the tile region (with a small padding margin). Shared Memory: Stages per-primitive parameters cooperatively by threads in a block. Global Memory: Caches computed \alphak and ck values in FP16 for each primitive assigned to the tile. Formulas: The transmittance at step k is defined as: Tk(x,y) = \prod{j=0}^{k-1}(1 - \alphaj(x,y)) The image color is computed as: I(x,y) = \sum{k=0}^{N-1} Tk(x,y) \alphak(x,y) \sigma(ck) \in [0,1]^3 where \alphak is the opacity, \sigma is the sigmoid function, and ck is the primitive color. The interpolated value Mi(x,y) for a primitive is computed via bilinear interpolation: Mi(x,y) = \mathbf{w}^T \mathbf{p} = \sum{j=0}^{3} wj pj where \mathbf{p} are the four surrounding points in the primitive template grid and \mathbf{w} are the interpolation weights. Parameters: Tile Size (T): Default value is 32 pixels. Steps: 1. CPU Preprocessing: Partition the image plane into T 	imes T tiles (default T=32). Assign each primitive to every tile whose bounding box on the image plane overlaps the tile region with a small padding margin. 2. GPU Launch: Launch a CUDA grid with dimensions (\lceil W{canvas}/32 ceil, \lceil H{canvas}/32 ceil) blocks. Each block has 32 	imes 32 threads. 3. Forward Pass (Per Thread): Each thread handles a specific pixel (x,y). For each primitive i assigned to the current tile: Transform (x,y) to (u,v) in primitive space. Compute Mi(x,y) via bilinear interpolation at (u,v). If Mi(x,y) < \epsilon, skip this primitive. Compute \alphak = \alpha{max} \cdot \sigma(
ui) \cdot Mi(x,y) and ck = \sigma(ci). Cache \alphak and ck in global memory (FP16). Alpha Compositing: Initialize transmittance T \leftarrow 1 and accumulated color C \leftarrow (0,0,0). For each cached primitive k (in front-to-back order): Store Tk for backward pass. Update C \leftarrow C + T \alphak ck. Update T \leftarrow T (1 - \alphak). Write I[x,y] \leftarrow C and I\alpha[x,y] \leftarrow 1 - T. 4. Backward Pass: Uses the same grid structure. Each thread rebuilds its cached primitive list. Computes gradients via the chain rule. For the Over operator, gradients depend on suffix sums. Color gradients are calculated as:  rac{\partial L}{\partial c{k,j}} =  rac{\partial L}{\partial Ij} \cdot Tk \alphak \cdot \sigma(c{k,j})(1 - \sigma(c{k,j})) Geometric gradients (xi, yi, si, 	hetai) flow through bilinear sampling of Mi(x,y). Accumulates gradients using packed half2 atomic operations for parameter pairs (xi, yi), (
ui, si), (	hetai, c{r,i}), and (c{g,i}, c{b,i}). Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. @cuda.jit def forwardpasskernel(primitiveparams, tilemapping, width, height, epsilon, alphamax): # Grid: (ceil(width/32), ceil(height/32)) # Block: (32, 32) tileidx = cuda.blockIdx.x + cuda.blockIdx.y cuda.gridDim.x pixelx = cuda.threadIdx.x pixely = cuda.threadIdx.y # Calculate global pixel coordinates # Note: Exact mapping of threadIdx to global x,y depends on tile origin # Assuming tilemapping provides list of primitive indices for this tile primitives = tilemapping[tileidx] # Shared memory for staging (conceptual, size depends on max primitives per tile) # In practice, threads cooperatively load parameters # Step 1: Compute alpha and color for each primitive cachedprimitives = [] for i in primitives: # Extract params for primitive i xi, yi, si, thetai, nui, ci = primitiveparams[i] # Transform (pixelx, pixely) to (u, v) in primitive space # Eq. Time Complexity: Linear with respect to the number of primitives assigned to each tile and the number of pixels per tile. The forward pass involves a bilinear interpolation and sigmoid for each primitive-pixel pair. The backward pass involves similar computations plus atomic operations. Memory Complexity: Depends on the number of primitives per tile. Shared memory is used for staging, and global memory is used for caching \alphak and ck. Allows optimization at low resolution and export at high resolution. Limitations: Atomic operations are unsuitable for generating layered PSD files; a dedicated export kernel is required for that use case. The method was introduced in the paper "DiffBMP: Differentiable Rendering with Bitmap Primitives".
