name: Log-space Exclusive Cumulative Sum for Transmittance
head: Log-space Exclusive Cumulative Sum, Log-space Exclusive Scan for Transmittance
body: This method computes the exclusive cumulative sum of transmittance values in logarithmic space to avoid underflow and enable efficient scatter-add operations for alpha compositing weights. It differs from standard linear-space exclusive scans by operating on \log(1-\alpha), which preserves precision for small alpha values, and by explicitly handling ray-segment boundaries to reset cumulative state between independent rays. It builds on Exclusive Prefix Sum (Scan). Inputs: alphas: Array of alpha values for each intersection, shape [M]. rayindices: Array of ray IDs corresponding to each intersection, shape [M], integer type. Outputs: transmittances: Array of transmittance values Ti, shape [M]. weights: Array of compositing weights wi = Ti \cdot \alphai, shape [M]. Data Structures: logoma: Float array [M], storing \log(1-\alphai). logcumsum: Float array [M], storing inclusive cumulative sum of logoma. logexclusive: Float array [M], storing exclusive cumulative sum of logoma. isstart: Boolean array [M], marking the first intersection of each ray. segmentids: Integer array [M], identifying the segment (ray) index for each element. correctionscompact: Float array [K], where K is the number of segments, storing the exclusive cumulative sum value at the start of each segment. Steps: 1. Log-Transform: Compute the log of one-minus-alpha for each intersection to stabilize values near zero. \text{log\oma}i = \log(1 - \alphai) Pitfall: If \alphai = 1, \log(0) results in -\infty. Clamp \alphai to a maximum value slightly less than 1 (e.g., 1 - \epsilon) before logging. 2. Inclusive Scan: Compute the global inclusive cumulative sum of logoma. \text{log\cumsum}i = \sum{j=0}^{i} \text{log\oma}j 3. Exclusive Shift: Convert the inclusive sum to an exclusive sum by shifting the array right and prepending zero. \text{log\exclusive}i = \begin{cases} 0 & i=0 \\ \text{log\cumsum}{i-1} & i>0 \end{cases} 4. Boundary Detection: Identify the start of each new ray by comparing the current ray index with the previous ray index. Create shiftedrays by concatenating a dummy value (rayindices[0] - 1) to the front of rayindices[:-1]. Compute isstart: \text{is\start}i = (\text{ray\indices}i \neq \text{shifted\rays}i) 5. Segment ID Assignment: Compute a unique ID for each ray segment using the cumulative sum of the start mask. \text{segment\ids}i = \left(\sum{j=0}^{i} \text{is\start}j\right) - 1 Note: This assumes isstart is cast to integer (0 or 1) before summation. 6. Correction Value Extraction: Extract the exclusive cumulative sum value at the start of each segment. These values represent the offset that must be subtracted to reset the cumulative sum to zero at each ray boundary. Let correctionscompact be the values of logexclusive at indices where isstart is true. Gather the correction for each element: \text{correction}i = \text{corrections\compact}{\text{segment\ids}i} 7. Boundary Reset: Subtract the correction from the exclusive cumulative sum to ensure transmittance starts at 1.0 (log 0) for each new ray. \text{log\transmittance}i = \text{log\exclusive}i - \text{correction}i 8. Exponentiation: Convert back to linear space. \text{transmittances}i = \exp(\text{log\transmittance}i) 9. Weight Calculation: Compute the final compositing weights. \text{weights}i = \text{transmittances}i \cdot \alphai Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import numpy as np def logspaceexclusivecumsum(alphas, rayindices): """ Compute transmittance and weights using log-space exclusive cumulative sum. Args: alphas: np.array of shape [M], float32, values in [0, 1). rayindices: np.array of shape [M], int32, ray IDs. Returns: transmittances: np.array of shape [M], float32. weights: np.array of shape [M], float32. """ # Step 1: Log-transform # Clamp alphas to avoid log(0) if necessary. logoma = np.log(1.0 - alphas) # Step 2: Inclusive cumulative sum logcumsum = np.cumsum(logoma) # Step 3: Convert to exclusive by shifting # Prepend 0.0, drop last element logexclusive = np.concatenate([np.zeros(1), logcumsum[:-1]]) # Step 4: Identify segment boundaries # Shift rayindices right by 1, filling first element with a value != rayindices[0] shiftedrays = np.concatenate([rayindices[:1] - 1, rayindices[:-1]]) isstart = rayindices != shiftedrays # Step 5: Compute per-segment correction IDs # Cast bool to int32 for cumsum segmentids = np.cumsum(isstart.astype(np.int32)) - 1 # Step 6: Gather correction values # correctionscompact contains logexclusive values at the start of each segment startmaskindices = np.where(isstart)[0] correctionscompact = logexclusive[startmaskindices] # Gather correction for each element corrections = correctionscompact[segmentids] # Step 7: Reset boundary values logtransmittance = logexclusive - corrections # Step 8: Exponentiate transmittances = np.exp(logtransmittance) # Step 9: Compute weights weights = transmittances alphas return transmittances, weights Parameters: No explicit tuning parameters. Precision depends on floating-point type (typically float32 or float64). Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Alpha = 1.0: \log(1-1) = -\infty. This breaks the cumulative sum. Clamp \alpha to 1-\epsilon. Not given in the sources. This method is used in differentiable Gaussian splatting rasterization, specifically in implementations like gsplat-mlx, to compute transmittance and weights for alpha compositing. It addresses the numerical instability of standard alpha compositing when dealing with many small alpha values, which can lead to underflow in linear space. By working in log space, the method ensures that transmittance values remain representable and accurate. head: Prefix Sum based Compaction, StreamCompaction::CPU::compactWithScan
body: CPU Stream Compaction with Scan removes zero-valued elements from an integer array on the CPU by mapping input data to a binary mask, computing an exclusive prefix sum on that mask, and scattering the retained elements to their computed output indices. It sets itself apart from CPU Stream Compaction without Scan by using a scan operation to determine output indices rather than a simple sequential counter. This approach is suitable for scenarios where parallel reduction primitives are available or when preparing data structures for subsequent parallel processing. Inputs and Outputs: idata: Pointer to the constant input array of n integers. odata: Pointer to the output buffer for compacted elements. n: Number of elements in the input array. Return value: The count of non-zero elements (result count). Data Structures: 1. temp: An integer array of size n that stores the binary mask where temp[i] = 1 if idata[i] != 0, else 0. 2. scanArray: An integer array of size n that stores the exclusive prefix sum of temp. Steps: 1. Map: Convert the input integer array into a boolean array (stored as integers 0/1) where non-zero elements map to 1 and zero elements map to 0. Formula: M[i] = (I[i] == 0 ? 0: 1). 2. Scan: Compute the exclusive prefix sum of the boolean array M. Formula: S[0] = 0, S[i] = S[i-1] + M[i-1] for i > 0. This step relies on the parent method Exclusive Prefix Sum (Scan). 3. Scatter: Iterate through the original input array and place each non-zero element into the output array at the index specified by the corresponding value in the scanned array. Output index for I[i] is S[i] if M[i]=1. 4. Result Count: Compute resultCount = scanArray[n-1] + temp[n-1]. 5. Cleanup: Free temp and scanArray. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def compactwithscan(idata, n, odata): if n == 0: return 0 temp = [0] n for i in range(n): temp[i] = 1 if idata[i] != 0 else 0 scanArray = [0] n for i in range(1, n): scanArray[i] = scanArray[i - 1] + temp[i - 1] for i in range(n): if temp[i] == 1: odata[scanArray[i]] = idata[i] resultcount = scanArray[n - 1] + temp[n - 1] return resultcount Parameters: n: Number of elements. Must be \ge 0. odata: Must have sufficient capacity to hold all non-zero elements (max n). Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Empty Input: If n=0, the algorithm returns 0 and performs no operations. All Zeros: The result count will be 0, and odata will remain unchanged. No Zeros: The result count will be n, and odata will be a copy of idata. Precision: Integer overflow in the scan step is possible if n is very large and the number of non-zero elements exceeds the maximum value of the integer type used for scanArray. Use 64-bit integers for scanArray if n > 2^{31}. GPU Stream Compaction with Scan filters an input array of integers based on a boolean flag array, returning only elements where the flag is true into an output array while preserving their relative order. It sets itself apart from CPU-based compaction by leveraging the GPU's parallel architecture and a work-efficient parallel scan algorithm, achieving performance improvements of over 4x for large arrays. It is chosen when parallel execution is available and high throughput is required. CPU Stream Compaction without Scan removes zero-valued elements from an integer array on the CPU by iterating through the input and writing non-zero elements sequentially to an output buffer. It solves the problem of filtering data in-place or to a new buffer without the overhead of computing an exclusive prefix sum. Unlike its sibling CPU Stream Compaction with Scan, which requires a scan operation to determine output indices, this method maintains a simple counter, making it suitable for sequential CPU execution where parallel reduction is unnecessary or unavailable. Time Complexity: O(n). The map, scan, and scatter steps each take linear time. Memory Complexity: O(n) auxiliary space for temp and scanArray. Measured Performance: In tests on a CPU, compaction without scan took ~250ms for a power-of-two array size. The scan-based approach serves as a foundational precursor for GPU stream compaction implementations. Strengths: Provides a structured, parallelizable approach to compaction. The output indices are computed sequentially on CPU or in parallel on GPU, making it easy to extend to multi-threaded CPU implementations or GPU kernels. Limitations: Requires O(n) extra memory for the mask and scan arrays. On a single CPU thread, it incurs additional overhead compared to the simple counter method. When to Use: When the output indices are needed for other parallel operations, or when the compaction is part of a larger pipeline that already uses scan operations (e.g., on GPU). It is also useful when the compaction criteria are complex and need to be computed in parallel. When Not to Use: For simple filtering on a single CPU thread where memory overhead is a concern and performance is critical; use CPU Stream Compaction without Scan instead. name: GPU Stream Compaction with Scan
head: Map-Scan-Scatter, Stream Compaction via Scan, GPU Stream Compaction (Work-Efficient)
body: GPU Stream Compaction with Scan filters an input array of integers based on a boolean flag array, returning only elements where the flag is true into an output array while preserving their relative order. It efficiently compacts data by mapping input values to a binary mask, computing an exclusive prefix sum on the mask to generate output indices, and scattering the retained elements to those indices. It sets itself apart from CPU-based compaction by leveraging the GPU's parallel architecture and a work-efficient parallel scan algorithm, achieving performance improvements of over 4x for large arrays. Inputs and Outputs: idata: Pointer to the constant input array of integers (size n). odata: Pointer to the output buffer (size at least n). n: Number of elements in the input array. Output: The resulting compacted array of size M (where M \le N). Data Structures: The algorithm requires four device arrays, all allocated with size N = 2^{\lceil \log2 n \rceil} (the next power of two greater than or equal to n): 1. devidata: int array of size N. Stores the input data, zero-padded from index n to N-1. 2. devtemp: int array of size N. Stores the binary mask (1 for keep, 0 for discard). 3. devscanArr: int array of size N. Stores the exclusive prefix sum of the mask, representing output indices. 4. devodata: int array of size N. Stores the compacted output. Formal Specification: Given Input of integers and Flag of booleans of size N, the output Output of size M satisfies: \forall j. 0 \le j < M: \text{Output}[j] = t \Rightarrow \exists i. 0 \le i < N: \text{Input}[i] = t \land \text{Flag}[i] \forall i. 0 \le i < N: \text{Input}[i] = t \land \text{Flag}[i] \Rightarrow \exists j. 0 \le j < M: \text{Output}[j] = t \forall i, j. 0 \le i, j < N: (\text{Flag}[i] \land \text{Flag}[j] \land i < j \iff \exists k, l. 0 \le k, l < M: \text{Output}[k] = \text{Input}[i] \land \text{Output}[l] = \text{Input}[j] \land k < l). Steps: 1. Preprocessing (Zero-Padding): Compute N = 2^{\lceil \log2 n \rceil}. Allocate devidata, devodata, devtemp, and devscanArr of size N. Copy idata to devidata for the first n elements. Zero-pad devidata from index n to N-1. 2. Map (Kernel kernMapToBoolean): For each thread i in [0, N): If devidata[i] != 0, set devtemp[i] = 1. Else, set devtemp[i] = 0. 3. Scan (Exclusive Prefix Sum): Perform a work-efficient parallel exclusive scan on devtemp to produce devscanArr. The work-efficient scan proceeds in three phases: an Up-Sweep pass to compute inclusive sums in a tree structure, a root reset setting the final element to 0, and a Down-Sweep pass to compute exclusive sums. The padded zeros do not affect the sum but ensure the tree structure remains complete. 4. Scatter (Kernel kernScatter): For each thread i in [0, N): If devtemp[i] == 1: Let idx = devscanArr[i]. Set devodata[idx] = devidata[i]. Else: Skip the thread; no write occurs. 5. Result Count: The number of remaining elements is derived from the scan result. The total count of kept elements equals the sum of the mask, which can be computed as devscanArr[N-1] + devtemp[N-1]. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def gpustreamcompactionwithscan(idata, n): if n == 0: return [], 0 # Step 1: Preprocessing N = 1 << (math.ceil(math.log2(n)) if n > 1 else 0) devidata = [0] N devodata = [0] N devtemp = [0] N devscanArr = [0] N for i in range(n): devidata[i] = idata[i] # Step 2: Map to Boolean for i in range(N): devtemp[i] = 1 if devidata[i] != 0 else 0 # Step 3: Exclusive Scan (Work-Efficient Simulation) # Up-Sweep (Inclusive) inclusive = [0] N inclusive[0] = devtemp[0] for i in range(1, N): inclusive[i] = inclusive[i-1] + devtemp[i] # Root Reset & Down-Sweep (Exclusive) devscanArr[0] = 0 for i in range(1, N): devscanArr[i] = inclusive[i-1] # Step 4: Scatter for i in range(N): if devtemp[i] == 1: idx = devscanArr[i] devodata[idx] = devidata[i] # Step 5: Count count = devscanArr[N-1] + devtemp[N-1] return devodata[:count], count Parameters: n: Number of elements in the input array. blockSize: Thread block size for CUDA kernels (e.g., 1024). gridSize: Calculated as (N + blockSize - 1) / blockSize. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Non-power-of-two sizes: Input arrays must be zero-padded to the next power of two to ensure the work-efficient scan tree is complete. Precision: Integer types are used for indices and counts, avoiding floating-point precision issues. Boundaries: The exclusive prefix sum values must be within the valid range of the Output array (0 to M-1) to be used safely as indices, which is guaranteed because for elements where Flag[i]=1, the exclusive prefix sum is strictly less than the total sum of flags (M). Time Complexity: O(N) work and O(\log N) depth for the scan, where N is the next power of two greater than or equal to n. Memory Complexity: O(N) additional memory for devtemp and devscanArr. Measured Performance: On an RTX 2060 Super, for an array size of 2^{27}, the work-efficient compact took 58.4025ms for power-of-two and 48.5331ms for non-power-of-two, over 4x faster than the CPU version (886.643ms). Strengths: High performance on GPU, handles arbitrary input sizes via padding, work-efficient scan minimizes redundant operations. Limitations: Requires additional memory for intermediate arrays, padding overhead for non-power-of-two sizes. When to use: When compacting large arrays on GPU and performance is critical. When not to use: For small arrays where CPU overhead is negligible, or when memory is constrained. The method is part of the broader field of parallel prefix sum (scan) algorithms and stream compaction, widely used in graphics and scientific computing. The specific implementation details, including the kernMapToBoolean and kernScatter kernels, are derived from educational projects and GitHub repositories focusing on CUDA stream compaction. body: CPU Stream Compaction without Scan removes zero-valued elements from an integer array on the CPU by iterating through the input and writing non-zero elements sequentially to an output buffer. It solves the problem of filtering data without the overhead of computing an exclusive prefix sum. Unlike its sibling CPU Stream Compaction with Scan, which requires a scan operation to determine output indices, this method maintains a simple counter, making it suitable for sequential CPU execution. Inputs and Outputs: idata: Pointer to the constant input array of integers. n: Number of elements in the input array. odata: Pointer to the output buffer for compacted elements. Data Structures: The method uses two contiguous memory blocks: the input array idata of size n and the output array odata of size at least n. No auxiliary data structures are required. Algorithm Steps: 1. Initialize a counter variable cnt to 0. This counter tracks the number of non-zero elements found and serves as the write index for odata. 2. Iterate through the input array idata with an index i from 0 to n-1. 3. For each element idata[i], check if it is non-zero. 4. If idata[i] is not equal to 0, write idata[i] to odata[cnt] and increment cnt by 1. 5. After the loop completes, cnt holds the total number of non-zero elements, which is the new size of the compacted array. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def compactwithoutscan(idata, n, odata): cnt = 0 for i in range(n): if idata[i] != 0: odata[cnt] = idata[i] cnt += 1 return cnt Parameters: n: The length of the input array. idata: Input array. odata: Output array. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: If the input array contains no non-zero elements, cnt remains 0, and odata is not written to. If all elements are non-zero, odata becomes a copy of idata. The output buffer odata must be allocated with a size of at least n to prevent buffer overflows, as the worst-case scenario requires full capacity. body: Thrust Scan is a GPU-accelerated exclusive prefix sum wrapper that delegates computation to the NVIDIA Thrust library. For an input array A, the output B satisfies B[i] = \sum{j=0}^{i-1} A[j] for i > 0, and B[0] = 0. Data Structures: thrust::devicevector<T>: A container that manages memory on the GPU device. It is used to ensure that the data resides in device memory before the scan operation begins, thereby excluding memory transfer times from the performance measurement of the scan itself. Steps: 1. Alternatively, construct dvin via a temporary thrust::hostvector cast to guarantee GPU allocation. 2. Execution: Call thrust::exclusivescan(dvin.begin(), dvin.end(), dvout.begin()) to perform the exclusive prefix sum on the device. 3. body: The Naive Parallel Prefix Sum (Scan) is a GPU-based algorithm for computing the inclusive prefix sum of an array using global memory and multiple kernel invocations. It serves as a baseline implementation compatible with arbitrary input sizes, distinguishing itself from work-efficient variants by its iterative, level-by-level reduction approach which results in higher computational work (O(n \log n)) but simpler synchronization logic within each kernel launch. Unlike in-place tree-based methods, it avoids race conditions by double-buffering data between two device arrays across iterations. Inputs and Outputs: Input: An array of n integers idata on the host. Output: An array of n integers odata on the host containing the exclusive prefix sum. Data Structures: Two device arrays, devdata1 and devdata2, of size n to double-buffer results and prevent race conditions, as threads are not guaranteed to run simultaneously. The algorithm processes the input in chunks fitting within a single thread block. If n exceeds the block size, the array is split into multiple blocks, and intermediate kernels propagate block sums to combine results. Parameters: blockSize: Number of threads per block. Typically 256 or 512. ilog2ceil(n): The ceiling of the base-2 logarithm of n, determining the number of kernel launches. Steps: 1. Allocation: Allocate two device arrays of size n. Copy idata to the first device array. 2. Iteration Loop: Calculate iterations L = \lceil \log2(\min(n, \text{blockSize})) \rceil. For each iteration d from 1 to L: Launch a kernel with blocksPerGrid = \lceil n / blockSize \rceil and blockSize threads. The kernel parameter offset is 2^{d-1}. Inside the kernel for each thread with global index id: Copy data[id] to a local buffer buffer[id]. Synchronize threads within the block. If threadIdx.x >= offset, update the value: buffer[id] = data[id - offset] + data[id]. Synchronize threads. Write buffer[id] back to data[id]. Synchronize threads. Swap devdata1 and devdata2 pointers after each kernel launch to double-buffer results. 3. Post-Processing (Exclusive Scan): The result in devdata1 is an inclusive scan. Convert to exclusive scan: Set odata[0] = 0. Copy devdata1[1...n-1] to odata[1...n-1]. If the input size n was larger than the block size, additional kernels (kernExtractLastElementPerBlock, kernAddOffsetPerBlock, kernShiftToExclusive) are used to combine block results and shift to exclusive. Pitfalls: The algorithm suffers from warp divergence and uncoalesced global memory accesses due to interleaved thread utilization patterns. Must be tested with non-power-of-two sized arrays to ensure correctness. The original pseudocode and CUDA code in GPU Gems 3 Chapter 39 contain known errors (superscripting, missing braces, bad indentation). Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def ilog2ceil(x): """Ceiling of base-2 logarithm.""" if x <= 1: return 0 lg = 0 while x > 1: x >>= 1 lg += 1 return lg def kernNaiveScan(data, buffer, n, blocksize): """Kernel logic for a single thread.""" id = blockIdx.x blocksize + threadIdx.x tx = threadIdx.x if id < n: log2n = ilog2ceil(min(n, blocksize)) for d in range(1, log2n + 1): offset = 1 << (d - 1) buffer[id] = data[id] # syncthreads() if tx >= offset: buffer[id] = data[id - offset] + data[id] # syncthreads() data[id] = buffer[id] # syncthreads() def naivescan(n, idata, blocksize): # 1. Allocation and Initialization devdata1 = list(idata) devdata2 = [0] n # 2. Iterative Kernel Launches (simulated) log2n = ilog2ceil(min(n, blocksize)) blockspergrid = (n + blocksize - 1) // blocksize for d in range(1, log2n + 1): offset = 1 << (d - 1) for b in range(blockspergrid): for t in range(blocksize): id = b blocksize + t if id < n: devdata2[id] = devdata1[id] # syncthreads() if t >= offset: devdata2[id] = devdata1[id - offset] + devdata1[id] # syncthreads() devdata1[id] = devdata2[id] # syncthreads() # Swap buffers for next iteration devdata1, devdata2 = devdata2, devdata1 # 3. Convert Inclusive to Exclusive odata = [0] n if n > 1: odata[1:] = devdata1[1:] return odata A parallel algorithm that computes the inclusive prefix sum of an array in O(n) total work and O(\log n) parallel depth, significantly improving upon the O(n \log n) work complexity of naive parallel scan. It achieves this efficiency by decomposing the computation into an upsweep (reduction) phase and a downsweep (scan) phase, operating on a binary tree structure. Unlike the Kogge-Stone algorithm, which is inherently inclusive and computes all prefix sums simultaneously via fixed-distance dependencies, the Work-Efficient Scan explicitly constructs exclusive intermediate values before converting them to inclusive results, making it suitable for operations where the current element must not influence its own prefix result during intermediate steps. A naive GPU-based parallel scan implementation, implemented in the StreamCompaction::Naive namespace. A parallel prefix sum algorithm that concurrently generates binary masks for each radix combination, computes local prefix sums, merges results, and outputs total counts per block. It generates binary masks for each radix combination, computes the local prefix sum of the mask, merges the prefix sum results for all combinations, and sends the total number of each radix combination in each block to the output block sum array. Time Complexity: O(\log n) per block, but requires multiple kernel launches for arrays larger than block size, leading to higher overhead. Memory Complexity: O(n) for double-buffering (two device arrays). Performance: On an RTX 2060 Super, the naive scan took 31.3315ms for a power-of-two array size 2^{27} and 24.8398ms for a non-power-of-two array size 2^{27}. Performance improves as block size increases from 32 to 128, reaching optimal performance at 64 threads per block, with no further gains at higher sizes. Strengths: Simple implementation, compatible with arbitrary input sizes, no shared memory management required (if using global memory double-buffering). Limitations: Not work-efficient (O(n \log n) total work), suffers from warp divergence and uncoalesced global memory accesses due to interleaved thread utilization patterns. Requires ilog2ceil(n) kernel launches, which adds overhead. When to use: As a baseline for comparison or when implementation simplicity is prioritized over performance. When not to use: For large arrays where performance is critical, or when work efficiency is required. The Naive Parallel Prefix Sum algorithm is described in GPU Gems 3, Chapter 39, Section 39.2.1. It is a foundational parallel primitive used in stream compaction and other data-parallel algorithms. The method is notable for its simplicity but is known to have errors in the pseudocode and CUDA code provided in the original GPU Gems chapter (e.g., superscripting, missing braces, bad indentation). name: Work-Efficient Scan
head: Work-Efficient Parallel Scan, Work-Efficient Parallel Inclusive Scan, Work-Efficient Inclusive Scan
body: The Work-Efficient Scan is a parallel algorithm that computes the inclusive prefix sum of an array in O(n) total work and O(\log n) parallel depth, significantly improving upon the O(n \log n) work complexity of naive parallel scan. It achieves this efficiency by decomposing the computation into an upsweep (reduction) phase and a downsweep (scan) phase, operating on a binary tree structure. Unlike the Kogge-Stone algorithm, which is inherently inclusive and computes all prefix sums simultaneously via fixed-distance dependencies, the Work-Efficient Scan explicitly constructs exclusive intermediate values before converting them to inclusive results, making it suitable for operations where the current element must not influence its own prefix result during intermediate steps. For a single block, it operates in-place on a device array. For arrays larger than a single block, it uses multiple kernel launches across hierarchical levels. It requires the input size to be padded to the next power of two for internal tree operations, though the final output matches the original size. Input: Array idata of size n (arbitrary integer or floating-point type). Output: Array odata of size n containing the inclusive prefix sum. Auxiliary: For multi-block execution, arrays devidata, devbuffer, and devodata of size numscans are used to manage hierarchical reduction levels. For multi-block execution: devidata: Array of pointers to device memory, size numscans. devidata[i] holds the input for level i. devbuffer: Array of pointers to device memory, size numscans. devbuffer[i] holds intermediate results for level i. devodata: Array of pointers to device memory, size numscans. devodata[i] holds the final exclusive results for level i. arraysizes: Array of integers, size numscans. arraysizes[i] is the number of elements at level i. gridsizes: Array of integers, size numscans. gridsizes[i] is the number of blocks at level i. blocksize: CUDA block size. Profiling indicates optimal performance at 128 threads per block, though 512 is also cited as optimal in other contexts. Values like 1024 are suboptimal due to reduced GPU parallelism. n: Input array size. npad: Padded size, calculated as 2^{\lceil \log2 n \rceil}. 1. Preparation: Calculate npad = 1 << ilog2ceil(n). Determine numscans and arraysizes/gridsizes by iteratively dividing the length by blocksize until it fits in one block: python len = npad numscans = 0 while (len + blocksize - 1) / blocksize > 1: numscans += 1 len = (len + blocksize - 1) / blocksize Allocate device memory for devidata, devbuffer, devodata, arraysizes, and gridsizes. Copy input idata to devidata[0] for n elements. 2. Forward Pass (Inclusive Scan): Loop i from 0 to numscans - 1: Launch kernScanInclusive on devidata[i] into devbuffer[i]. Copy devbuffer[i] back to devidata[i]. If i < numscans - 1: Extract the last element of each block from devidata[i] into devidata[i+1] using kernExtractLastElementPerBlock to prepare the next level's input. 3. Backward Pass (Exclusive Scan/Shift): Loop i from numscans - 1 down to 0: Launch kernShiftToExclusive on devbuffer[i] to produce exclusive indices in devodata[i]. If i >= 1: Launch kernAddOffsetPerBlock to add the offset from devodata[i] to devbuffer[i-1] to produce the final exclusive indices for the next lower level. 4. Final Copy: Copy the final exclusive scan results from devodata[0] to host output odata for n elements. The core work-efficient scan within a single block (used in steps 2 and 3 above) follows these steps: 1. Upsweep Phase (Reduction): For each thread with global index id < n: Iterate d from 0 to log2n - 1: If (id % (1 << (d + 1))) == 0: idata[id + (1 << (d + 1)) - 1] += idata[id + (1 << d) - 1]. Synchronize threads after each d. 2. Reset Last Element: The last thread (tid == blockDim.x - 1) or the thread processing the last element (id == n - 1) stores the total reduction sum in a local variable reductionsum and sets idata[id] = 0. 3. Downsweep Phase (Scan): Iterate d from log2n - 1 down to 0: If (id % (1 << (d + 1))) == 0: temp = idata[id + (1 << d) - 1] idata[id + (1 << d) - 1] = idata[id + (1 << (d + 1)) - 1] idata[id + (1 << (d + 1)) - 1] += temp. Synchronize threads after each d. 4. Convert Exclusive to Inclusive: If the thread is the last thread in the block or processes the last element: odata[id] = reductionsum. Otherwise: odata[id] = idata[id + 1]. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def ilog2ceil(x): """Returns ceil(log2(x)) for x > 0.""" return math.ceil(math.log2(x)) if x > 1 else 1 def syncthreads(): """Synchronizes all threads in the block.""" pass # Represents a hardware barrier def workefficientscankernel(n, blocksize, idata, odata): """ CUDA kernel logic for work-efficient scan within a single block. Assumes idata is padded to power of two size internally if necessary. """ tid = 0 # Represents threadIdx.x id = tid npad = 1 << ilog2ceil(n) log2n = ilog2ceil(n) # Upsweep Phase for d in range(log2n): if (id % (1 << (d + 1))) == 0: idxleft = id + (1 << d) - 1 idxright = id + (1 << (d + 1)) - 1 if idxright < npad: idata[idxright] += idata[idxleft] syncthreads() # Reset Last Element reductionsum = 0 if tid == blocksize - 1 or id == n - 1: reductionsum = idata[id] idata[id] = 0 syncthreads() # Downsweep Phase for d in range(log2n - 1, -1, -1): if (id % (1 << (d + 1))) == 0: idxleft = id + (1 << d) - 1 idxright = id + (1 << (d + 1)) - 1 if idxright < npad: temp = idata[idxleft] idata[idxleft] = idata[idxright] idata[idxright] += temp syncthreads() # Convert Exclusive to Inclusive if tid == blocksize - 1 or id == n - 1: odata[id] = reductionsum else: odata[id] = idata[id + 1] Non-Power-of-Two Sizes: The algorithm works best with power-of-two length arrays. For non-power-of-two arrays, intermediate array sizes must be rounded up to the next power of two, requiring extra memory. Memory Access Patterns: High memory throughput indicates non-optimal memory access patterns. SM workload imbalance is a main bottleneck in the upsweep phase, where some Streaming Multiprocessors (SMs) are underutilized by as much as 43.66%. Block Size: A block size of 1024 does not yield ideal results for any algorithm, likely due to excessive block size reducing GPU parallelism and leaving computational resources underutilized. Known Errors: The pseudocode in GPU Gems 3 Chapter 39 Example 39-2 contains known errors. Blelloch’s algorithm is an exclusive parallel in-place algorithm for computing the prefix sum of an array of size N. It solves the problem by decomposing the computation into two distinct phases: an up-sweep (reduce) phase that builds a binary tree of partial sums, and a down-sweep (scan) phase that distributes these sums to compute the final exclusive prefix values. Unlike Kogge-Stone, which is an inclusive algorithm, Blelloch’s method explicitly excludes the current element from its own sum, making it suitable for operations where the current value must not influence its own prefix result. It is a work-efficient alternative to naive parallel scan, building on the principles of Work-Efficient Scan. An optimized GPU scan implementation using shared memory and bank conflict avoidance, based on GPU Gems 3 Chapter 39 Examples 39.1 and 39.2. It optimizes memory access patterns to avoid shared memory bank conflicts. The size of shared memory is dynamic and related to the block size. Occupancy is affected by the amount of shared memory used per block relative to the SM's limit. Using maximum shared memory per block reduces occupancy (e.g., max 1 block per SM), which may not yield best performance. Time Complexity: O(\log n) parallel depth per block. Work Complexity: O(n) total work, compared to naive O(n \log n) work. Memory Complexity: In-place on a single device array for single-block execution. For multi-block execution, auxiliary arrays are required for each scan level. Measured Performance: Tested on Ubuntu 20.04 LTS, Ryzen 3700X @ 2.22GHz, RTX 2060 Super. The upsweep phase consumes the majority of execution time (averaging 28.38 ms), while the downsweep phase is shorter (averaging 20.26 ms). Scaling: Performance improves with block size up to an optimal point (128 or 512 threads per block), after which it degrades due to reduced parallelism. Strengths: Work-efficient, suitable for arbitrary input sizes (with padding), in-place operation for single blocks. Limitations: SM workload imbalance in upsweep phase, non-optimal memory access patterns, requires extra memory for non-power-of-two sizes. The Work-Efficient Scan is based on the "Work-Efficient" algorithm described in GPU Gems 3, Section 39.2.2. It is a standard parallel primitive used in stream compaction and other GPU algorithms. name: Blelloch’s Prefix Sum Algorithm
head: Blelch's algorithm, Blelloch Scan, Blelloch's parallel prefix sum, Up-sweep/Down-sweep Scan, up-sweep/down-sweep prefix sum
body: Blelloch’s algorithm is an exclusive parallel in-place algorithm for computing the prefix sum of an array of size N. It solves the problem by decomposing the computation into two distinct phases: an up-sweep (reduce) phase that builds a binary tree of partial sums, and a down-sweep (scan) phase that distributes these sums to compute the final exclusive prefix values. Unlike Kogge-Stone, which is an inclusive algorithm, Blelloch’s method explicitly excludes the current element from its own sum, making it suitable for operations where the current value must not influence its own prefix result. It is a work-efficient alternative to naive parallel scan, building on the principles of Work-Efficient Scan. Inputs and Outputs: Input: An array Input of size N (assumed to be a power of 2 for the standard implementation described in). Output: An array Output of size N such that Output[i] = \sum{t=0}^{i-1} Input[t] for 0 \le i < N. Constraint: The algorithm is in-place; Input and Output initially share the same values, and Output is overwritten during execution. Data Structures: The algorithm operates on a single array Output of size N. Threads are indexed by tid (thread ID). The implementation assumes a block size of N/2 threads, where each thread handles two elements in the initial step, or generally maps to the indices defined by the indicator variable. Parameters: stride: The distance between elements being summed. Starts at 1 in up-sweep, N/2 in down-sweep. indicator: The index of the element currently being processed by the thread. Steps: 1. Initialization: Let tid be the thread ID. Initialize stride = 1. Initialize indicator = 2 tid + 1. 2. Phase 1: Up-sweep (Reduce): Loop while stride < N: If indicator < N and indicator >= stride: Update Output[indicator] = Output[indicator] + Output[indicator - stride]. Synchronize all threads (syncthreads()). Update indicator = 2 indicator + 1. Update stride = 2 stride. Synchronize all threads (syncthreads()). Result: The last element Output[N-1] holds the total sum of all input values. 3. Phase 2: Down-sweep (Scan): Initialize indicator = N tid + N - 1. Initialize stride = N / 2. If indicator < N: Set Output[indicator] = 0. Loop while stride >= 1: If indicator < N and indicator >= stride: Store temporary = Output[indicator]. Update Output[indicator] = Output[indicator] + Output[indicator - stride]. Set Output[indicator - stride] = temporary. Synchronize all threads (syncthreads()). Update indicator = (indicator - 1) / 2. Update stride = stride / 2. Result: The array Output contains the exclusive prefix sums. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def blellochscankernel(Output, N): tid = getthreadid() # threadIdx.x indicator = 2 tid + 1 stride = 1 # Phase 1: Up-sweep while stride < N: if indicator < N and indicator >= stride: Output[indicator] = Output[indicator] + Output[indicator - stride] syncthreads() # syncthreads() indicator = 2 indicator + 1 stride = 2 stride syncthreads() # Barrier between phases # Phase 2: Down-sweep indicator = N tid + N - 1 stride = N // 2 if indicator < N: Output[indicator] = 0 while stride >= 1: if indicator < N and indicator >= stride: temporary = Output[indicator] Output[indicator] = Output[indicator] + Output[indicator - stride] Output[indicator - stride] = temporary syncthreads() # syncthreads() indicator = (indicator - 1) // 2 stride = stride // 2 Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Data Race Freedom: The algorithm requires careful permission management. In each iteration, some threads lose write permissions because their indicator exceeds the array bounds N. To maintain correctness, thread 0 collects these lost permissions in each iteration and redistributes them at the barrier. In-place Verification: Because the algorithm is in-place, elements change in every iteration. Verifying functional correctness requires tracking the history of values using ghost variables, as intermediate steps are non-trivial. Synchronization: Barriers are strictly required between iterations in both phases and between the up-sweep and down-sweep phases to ensure that partial sums from previous levels are available for the next level. Time Complexity: O(\log N) parallel steps, where each step involves a constant number of operations per active thread. Memory Complexity: O(N) for the input/output array. The algorithm is in-place, requiring no additional auxiliary storage proportional to N beyond the input array itself. Strengths: It is work-efficient (linear total work O(N)) and avoids the high memory bandwidth usage of naive approaches. It is widely used in libraries such as AMD APP SDK and NVIDIA CUDA SDK. Limitations: It requires synchronization barriers at every level, which can introduce latency on hardware with poor barrier performance. It assumes N is a power of 2 for the standard index calculations described; non-power-of-2 sizes require padding or modified boundary checks. Blelloch’s algorithm was introduced by Guy E. Blelloch. It is frequently cited alongside Kogge-Stone as one of the two primary parallel in-place prefix sum algorithms used in practice. The algorithm is implemented in major parallel computing SDKs, including the AMD Accelerated Parallel Processing (APP) SDK and the NVIDIA CUDA SDK. Formal verification of its correctness, particularly regarding data race freedom and in-place state management, has been studied in recent literature. name: Kogge-Stone Parallel Prefix Sum
head: Kogge-Stone's algorithm
body: The Kogge-Stone algorithm is a parallel prefix sum (scan) method that computes inclusive prefix sums in a single phase using an in-place update strategy. Unlike Blelloch’s algorithm, which employs a two-phase (up-sweep/down-sweep) approach, Kogge-Stone’s single-phase structure simplifies functional correctness verification while maintaining data race freedom through explicit synchronization. It serves as a foundational primitive for volume rendering pipelines requiring cumulative distribution functions or histogram binning, building on the general principles of Naive Parallel Prefix Sum (Scan). Inputs and Outputs: Input: An array Input of size N (typically integers or floats). Output: An array Output of size N, which initially holds the input values and is overwritten with the inclusive prefix sums. Parameters: N (array length), offset (distance between elements, starting at 1), tid (thread ID). Data Structures: Output: A global memory array of size N. The algorithm operates in-place, meaning the output overwrites the input. temp: A local register variable used to store the intermediate sum for a thread to prevent data races during in-place updates. Algorithm Steps: 1. Initialize offset to 1. 2. Each thread i (where 0 \le i < N) executes the following loop: a. Read the current value at Output[i] into temp. b. If i \ge \text{offset}, add Output[i - offset] to temp. c. Execute a thread block barrier (syncthreads()) to ensure all threads have read their required values before any writes occur. d. If i \ge \text{offset}, write temp back to Output[i]. e. Execute a second thread block barrier (syncthreads()) to ensure all writes are complete before updating the offset. f. Double the offset: \text{offset} = 2 \times \text{offset}. 3. Repeat until \text{offset} \ge N. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. global void inclusivePrefixsumKernel(int Input, int Output, int N) { int tid = threadIdx.x; int offset = 1; // Loop until offset exceeds the array size while (offset < N) { // Step 1: Read current value into temporary variable int temp = Output[tid]; // Step 2: If valid, add value from offset distance away if (tid >= offset) { temp = Output[tid - offset] + temp; } // Step 3: Synchronize to ensure all reads of previous values are complete syncthreads(); // Step 4: Write computed value back to output array if (tid >= offset) { Output[tid] = temp; } // Step 5: Synchronize to ensure all writes are complete before next iteration syncthreads(); // Step 6: Double the offset for the next iteration offset = 2 offset; } } Parameters: offset: The distance between elements to be summed. It starts at 1 and doubles each iteration (1, 2, 4, \dots) until it exceeds N. temp: An auxiliary variable used to store the intermediate sum for a thread to avoid data races during in-place updates. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Data Races: Since the algorithm is in-place, threads must read current values before updating. This is handled by using the auxiliary variable temp and barriers to synchronize reads and writes. Without barriers, a thread might read a value that has already been updated by another thread in the same iteration, leading to incorrect results. Boundary Conditions: The condition tid >= offset ensures that threads do not access memory locations outside the array bounds (specifically, tid - offset would be negative). Precision: Not given in the sources. Degenerate Input: Not given in the sources. A variant that reduces the number of operations per element by using a different tree structure, trading off some simplicity for better performance on large datasets. Choose when memory bandwidth is a bottleneck. See Work-Efficient Scan. Time Complexity: O(\log N) parallel steps, where each step involves O(1) work per thread. The total work is O(N \log N), which is not work-efficient compared to Blelloch’s O(N). Memory Complexity: O(N) for the output array. The algorithm is in-place, requiring no additional global memory beyond the input/output array. Measured Performance: Not given in the sources. Scaling: Scales well with the number of threads up to the block size limit, as each iteration is independent and requires only local synchronization. Strengths: Single-phase structure makes functional correctness verification easier compared to two-phase algorithms like Blelloch’s. Simple implementation logic. Limitations: Higher computational work (O(N \log N)) compared to work-efficient scans. Requires explicit synchronization barriers, which can introduce latency. When to use: When simplicity and ease of verification are prioritized over raw performance, or in contexts where N is small enough that the O(N \log N) work is negligible. When not to use: For very large datasets where work efficiency is critical, or when hardware synchronization barriers are expensive. The Kogge-Stone algorithm was introduced by Kogge and Stone in 1973. It is one of the earliest parallel prefix sum algorithms, designed for distributed memory systems but widely adapted for GPU architectures. Its single-phase nature distinguishes it from later algorithms like Blelloch’s, which were optimized for work efficiency. The algorithm is frequently used in formal verification studies due to its straightforward structure. name: Global Accumulator + Compaction
head: FGatherVisibleCountsCS, FPrefixSumVisibleCountsCS, Global counting
body: A two-pass GPU compute system that gathers visible splat counts per proxy and computes prefix sums to generate indirect dispatch and draw arguments for global Phase-3 rendering passes. It aggregates per-proxy visibility data into a global array and prepares execution parameters for subsequent geometry generation and indexing stages. Inputs and Outputs: Input: PerProxyVisibleCount (SRV StructuredBuffer<uint>), ProxyIndex (uint32), ProxyCount (uint32), MaxRenderBudget (uint32). Output: GlobalVisibleCountArray (UAV RWStructuredBuffer<uint>), GlobalBaseOffsets (UAV RWStructuredBuffer<uint>), GlobalCalcDistIndirectArgs (UAV RWStructuredBuffer<uint>), GlobalSortIndirectArgs (UAV RWStructuredBuffer<uint>), GlobalSortParams (UAV RWStructuredBuffer<uint>), GlobalDrawIndirectArgs (UAV RWStructuredBuffer<uint>). Data Structures: 1. GlobalVisibleCountArray: RWStructuredBuffer<uint> of size ProxyCount. 2. GlobalBaseOffsets: RWStructuredBuffer<uint> of size ProxyCount. 3. GlobalCalcDistIndirectArgs: RWStructuredBuffer<uint> for distance calculation dispatch arguments. 4. GlobalSortIndirectArgs: RWStructuredBuffer<uint> for radix sort dispatch arguments. 5. GlobalSortParams: RWStructuredBuffer<uint> for sort parameters. 6. GlobalDrawIndirectArgs: RWStructuredBuffer<uint> for draw call arguments. Steps: 1. Gather Visible Counts: Dispatch FGatherVisibleCountsCS with 1 thread per proxy. Each thread copies GPUResources->VisibleSplatCountBuffer[0] into GlobalVisibleCountArray[ProxyIndex]. 2. Compute Prefix Sums & Indirect Arguments: Dispatch FPrefixSumVisibleCountsCS with 1 thread total. The thread iterates through GlobalVisibleCountArray to compute exclusive prefix sums, calculates the total visible splat count, applies the MaxRenderBudget clamp, and writes the results to the indirect argument buffers for the CalcDistances, RadixSort, and DrawSplats passes. Formulas: Let C[i] be the visible splat count for proxy i. The exclusive prefix sum offset is O[i] = \sum{j=0}^{i-1} C[j] for i \in [0, ProxyCount), with O[0] = 0. The total visible splat count is T = \sum{j=0}^{ProxyCount-1} C[j]. The clamped total is T{clamped} = \min(T, MaxRenderBudget) if MaxRenderBudget > 0, otherwise T{clamped} = T. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def gathervisiblecounts(perproxyvisiblecount, globalvisiblecountarray, proxyindex): globalvisiblecountarray[proxyindex] = perproxyvisiblecount[proxyindex] def prefixsumandcompact(globalvisiblecountarray, globalbaseoffsets, globalcalcdistindirectargs, globalsortindirectargs, globalsortparams, globaldrawindirectargs, proxycount, maxrenderbudget): currentoffset = 0 if proxycount > 0: globalbaseoffsets[0] = 0 for i in range(1, proxycount): currentoffset += globalvisiblecountarray[i-1] globalbaseoffsets[i] = currentoffset totalsplats = currentoffset + globalvisiblecountarray[proxycount - 1] else: totalsplats = 0 if maxrenderbudget > 0 and totalsplats > maxrenderbudget: totalsplats = maxrenderbudget # Write indirect arguments for Phase-3 passes globalsortparams[0] = totalsplats # Indirect argument layouts (count, baseInstance, etc.) are not specified in the sources globalsortindirectargs[0] = 0 globalsortindirectargs[1] = 1 globalsortindirectargs[2] = 1 globalcalcdistindirectargs[0] = 1 globalcalcdistindirectargs[1] = 1 globalcalcdistindirectargs[2] = 1 globaldrawindirectargs[0] = totalsplats globaldrawindirectargs[1] = 1 globaldrawindirectargs[2] = 0 globaldrawindirectargs[3] = 0 globaldrawindirectargs[4] = 0 Parameters: MaxRenderBudget: uint32. Cap on total visible splats. 0 means no cap. Edge Cases: If ProxyCount is 0, the prefix sum loop is skipped and all totals are 0. MaxRenderBudget clamping may truncate the scene, requiring subsequent logic to handle partial rendering or culling. A GPU compute shader that prepares indirect dispatch and draw arguments from the visible splat count generated by the preceding Global Accumulator + Compaction pass. It serves as the orchestration layer that translates per-proxy visibility data into the specific argument structures required by the graphics API for subsequent Phase-3 rendering and sorting kernels. Unlike the compaction pass which gathers data, this method configures the execution parameters for the geometry generation and indexing stages. Choose it when explicit control over dispatch dimensions and sort parameters is required for the rendering pipeline. Time Complexity: O(P) for gathering counts and O(P) for the sequential prefix sum pass, where P is the proxy count. Memory Complexity: O(P) for GlobalVisibleCountArray and GlobalBaseOffsets. Strengths: Centralizes visibility data and directly generates batched rendering arguments for downstream passes. Limitations: The single-threaded prefix sum approach may become a bottleneck if P is extremely large. When to use: When transitioning from per-proxy visibility culling to global batched rendering passes for splat distance calculation, sorting, and drawing. Implemented in the OpenSplat4D project, this method is part of a Gaussian Splatting performance optimization suite. It addresses the need to efficiently transition from per-proxy visibility culling to global batched rendering passes for splat distance calculation, sorting, and drawing. The prefix sum computation leverages the fully optimized one-way prefix sum provided in the CUDPP library. name: Indirect Argument Preparation
head: FPrepareIndirectArgsCS
body: Indirect Argument Preparation is a GPU compute shader that prepares indirect dispatch and draw arguments from the visible splat count generated by the preceding Global Accumulator + Compaction pass. It serves as the orchestration layer that translates per-proxy visibility data into the specific argument structures required by the graphics API for subsequent Phase-3 rendering and sorting kernels. Unlike the compaction pass which gathers data, this method configures the execution parameters for the geometry generation and indexing stages. Inputs and Outputs: The method takes the VisibleSplatCount buffer (a StructuredBuffer<uint>) as input, which contains the number of visible splats per proxy computed in the previous step. It produces four output buffers: 1. IndirectDispatchArgs: A RWStructuredBuffer<uint> of size 3, storing numGroupsX, numGroupsY, and numGroupsZ for the main rendering dispatch. 2. IndirectDrawArgs: A RWStructuredBuffer<uint> of size 5, storing the arguments for DrawIndexedIndirect (index count, instance count, start index location, start vertex location, start instance location). 3. SortIndirectArgs: A RWStructuredBuffer<uint> of size 3, storing NumTiles, 1, and 1 for the sorting kernel dispatch. 4. SortParamsBuffer: A RWStructuredBuffer<uint> of size 2, storing SortCount and NumTiles. Parameters: ComputeThreadGroupSize (uint3): The thread group dimensions used for the compute shaders. Steps: 1. Reset Counters: Reset all append buffer counters to zero to prepare for the upcoming geometry generation passes. 2. Map Kernel Dispatch: Dispatch the map kernel using thread group sizes derived from the ComputeThreadGroupSize parameter. 3. Vertex Generation Dispatch: Dispatch the vertex generation kernel. 4. Vertex Counting Dispatch: Dispatch the vertex counting kernel using indirect dispatch. The indirect arguments must include an offset pointing to the vertex count in the counter buffer. 5. Triangle Generation Dispatch: Dispatch the triangle generation kernel using indirect dispatch with the same offset used in the previous step. 6. Index Buffer Building Dispatch: Dispatch the index buffer building kernel using indirect dispatch with an offset pointing to the triangle count. 7. Intermediate Vertex Indexing Dispatch: Dispatch the intermediate vertex indexing kernel using indirect dispatch with an offset pointing to the intermediate vertex count. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def PrepareIndirectArgsCS(): # Step 1: Reset all append buffer counters to zero ResetAppendBufferCounters() # Step 2: Dispatch the map kernel # Thread group sizes derived from ComputeThreadGroupSize DispatchMapKernel(ComputeThreadGroupSize) # Step 3: Dispatch the vertex generation kernel DispatchVertexGenerationKernel() # Step 4: Dispatch the vertex counting kernel using indirect dispatch # Offset points to the vertex count in the counter buffer VertexCountOffset = GetVertexCountOffset() DispatchIndirect( kernel=VertexCountingKernel, indirectargs=GetIndirectArgsForVertexCounting(VertexCountOffset)) # Step 5: Dispatch the triangle generation kernel using indirect dispatch # Same offset as vertex counting DispatchIndirect( kernel=TriangleGenerationKernel, indirectargs=GetIndirectArgsForTriangleGeneration(VertexCountOffset)) # Step 6: Dispatch the index buffer building kernel using indirect dispatch # Offset points to the triangle count TriangleCountOffset = GetTriangleCountOffset() DispatchIndirect( kernel=IndexBufferBuildingKernel, indirectargs=GetIndirectArgsForIndexBufferBuilding(TriangleCountOffset)) # Step 7: Dispatch the intermediate vertex indexing kernel using indirect dispatch # Offset points to the intermediate vertex count IntermediateVertexCountOffset = GetIntermediateVertexCountOffset() DispatchIndirect( kernel=IntermediateVertexIndexingKernel, indirectargs=GetIndirectArgsForIntermediateVertexIndexing(IntermediateVertexCountOffset)) # Finalize Output Buffers # IndirectDispatchArgs is populated based on the total work units IndirectDispatchArgs[0] = CalculateNumGroupsX() IndirectDispatchArgs[1] = CalculateNumGroupsY() IndirectDispatchArgs[2] = CalculateNumGroupsZ() # IndirectDrawArgs is populated for the final draw call IndirectDrawArgs[0] = GetIndexCount() IndirectDrawArgs[1] = GetInstanceCount() IndirectDrawArgs[2] = GetStartIndexLocation() IndirectDrawArgs[3] = GetStartVertexLocation() IndirectDrawArgs[4] = GetStartInstanceLocation() # SortIndirectArgs and SortParamsBuffer are populated for the sorting phase SortIndirectArgs[0] = NumTiles SortIndirectArgs[1] = 1 SortIndirectArgs[2] = 1 SortParamsBuffer[0] = SortCount SortParamsBuffer[1] = NumTiles This variant refers to the specific sequence of indirect dispatches used to drive the geometry generation pipeline (map, vertex, triangle, index, and intermediate vertex kernels). It is distinguished by its reliance on dynamic offsets into counter buffers to determine the number of work groups for each stage, rather than static counts. Choose this approach when the geometry generation workload is highly variable per frame and depends on the output of previous compute stages. It links to the broader concept of Global Accumulator + Compaction as the source of the visibility data that drives these counts. Time and Memory Complexity: The time complexity is dominated by the sequential dispatches of the geometry generation kernels, which scale with the number of visible splats and the complexity of the generated geometry (vertices, triangles, indices). Memory complexity is linear with respect to the number of proxies for the input VisibleSplatCount buffer and the size of the output argument buffers, which are fixed-size structures. Measured Performance: Specific performance metrics for Indirect Argument Preparation alone are not provided in the sources. However, related performance data from the OpenSplat4D plugin indicates that optimizing the overall pipeline, including sorting intervals, can yield significant FPS gains (e.g., ~60% increase on an RTX 4090 for a 57-million-splat scene). The efficiency of this method relies on the preceding compaction pass correctly identifying visible splats to minimize the workload for the subsequent indirect dispatches. Strengths and Limitations: Strengths include dynamic adaptation to scene complexity and efficient use of GPU resources by only dispatching work for visible proxies. Limitations include the overhead of managing multiple indirect dispatches and the dependency on the correctness of the counter buffers and offsets. When to Use: Use this method when rendering dynamic scenes with variable visibility where static draw calls would be inefficient or impossible to determine in advance. It is essential for pipelines that generate geometry on the GPU based on splat data. Indirect Argument Preparation is part of the rendering pipeline for Gaussian Splatting, specifically within the OpenSplat4D plugin ecosystem. The method is implemented as a compute shader (FPrepareIndirectArgsCS) and is used in conjunction with other compute kernels for map, vertex, triangle, and index generation. The broader context includes the use of Nanite-like precision settings and sort intervals to optimize performance in large-scale Gaussian Splatting scenes. name: Multi-core BONO Tree Traversal and Ray Casting with Dynamic Tile Grouping
head: Phase I/Phase II Multi-core Scheme, Z-ordered Dynamic Tile Allocation
body: This method is a multi-core parallel rendering technique for isosurface visualization that decouples data structure traversal from ray casting to optimize cache performance and load balancing. It solves the problem of uneven computational load and poor spatial locality in parallel volume rendering by dividing the screen into contiguous regions for initial block list generation (Phase I) and then dynamically assigning Z-ordered, weight-balanced groups of image tiles to threads for ray casting (Phase II/III). It differs from standard static tiling approaches by using a space-filling curve (Z-order) to group tiles based on their estimated complexity (weight), ensuring that threads with heavier workloads are processed in spatially coherent batches, thereby reducing synchronization overhead and improving cache hit rates. The method operates in three distinct phases: Phase I (Block List Generation), Phase II (Tile Grouping), and Phase III (Dynamic Ray Casting). Inputs: p: Number of available processor cores/threads. k: Maximum size of the block list for a pixel group (memory limit). T: The BONO tree data structure representing the volume. R: The set of rays corresponding to the screen pixels. S: Screen resolution (e.g., 1024 \times 1024). TileSize: Dimensions of small image tiles (e.g., 8 \times 8 or 16 \times 16). Outputs: Rendered image. List LI: A sequence of groups, where each group is a pair of indices (first, last) defining a contiguous range of Z-ordered tiles. 1. Block List (Li): For each pixel (or small group of pixels), a list of 3D data blocks from the BONO tree that the ray intersects. Constraint: |Li| \le k. 2. Tile Grid: The screen is partitioned into N tiles of size TileSize \times TileSize. 3. Z-Order Map: An array mapping tile index i to its Z-order position. 4. Weight Array (W{tile}): An integer array where W{tile}[j] is the number of non-empty block lists within tile j. 5. Group List (LI): A list of tuples ((first\tile\idx, last\tile\idx), group\id). 1. Divide the screen into p almost equal contiguous horizontal (or vertical) regions, one per thread. 2. For each thread t responsible for region Rt: a. Initialize empty block lists for all pixels in Rt. b. Traverse the BONO tree T. c. Traversal Rule: For a node N, traverse its children in front-to-back order only if: i. The projection of N's minimum bounding box intersects Rt. ii. At least one pixel in Rt has a block list size < k. d. If the node is a leaf (data block), add the block to the lists of all intersecting pixels in Rt, provided the list size < k. e. Note: Due to the limit k, only a fraction (no more than 10%) of total BONO tree nodes are accessed. 1. Partitioning: Partition the entire screen into small tiles of size TileSize \times TileSize. 2. Z-Ordering: Order these tiles using a Z-order (Morton code) space-filling curve. 3. Weighting: a. For each tile j, compute weight wj = \sum{p \in Tilej} (1 \text{ if } Lp \neq \emptyset \text{ else } 0). b. Compute total weight W = \sum{all \ tiles} wj. 4. Grouping Algorithm: a. Initialize an empty list LI. b. Let remaining\weight = W. c. Let current\tile\index = 0 (in Z-order). d. While remaining\weight > 0: i. Target weight for this iteration: Target = remaining\weight / 2. ii. Divide Target into p equal sub-targets: SubTarget = Target / p. iii. For each group g from 0 to p-1: 1. Start with start\tile = current\tile\index. 2. Accumulate weights from Z-ordered tiles starting at start\tile until the sum reaches or exceeds SubTarget. 3. Let end\tile be the index of the last tile included. 4. Append (start\tile, end\tile) to LI. 5. Update current\tile\index = end\tile + 1. iv. Update remaining\weight = remaining\weight / 2. e. Termination: The process repeats logarithmically relative to screen size. The first iterations create large groups (coarse-grained), and subsequent iterations create smaller groups (fine-grained). 1. Initialize a shared queue/pointer to the list LI. 2. For each thread t: a. Loop: i. Atomically fetch the next available group (first, last) from LI. If none remain, terminate. ii. For each tile index j from first to last: 1. For each pixel p in tile j: 1. Retrieve block list Lp. 2. If Lp is empty, skip. 3. Shoot ray through blocks in Lp (front-to-back). 4. Shading: If ray intersects isosurface: Calculate intersection position by solving the trilinear interpolation equation. Compute normal using forward difference gradient. Apply diffuse shade model. Else if ray exits volume without intersection: Mark pixel as background. iii. If any pixels in the processed tiles have block lists of size k but no intersection was found (unfinished pixels), handle them in a separate pass (Step iv of the source description). Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math import threading def multicorebonorendering(p, k, bonotree, screenwidth, screenheight, tilesize): # Phase I: Block List Generation regionheight = math.ceil(screenheight / p) blocklists = {} for t in range(p): ystart = t regionheight yend = min((t + 1) regionheight, screenheight) locallists = {(x, y): [] for y in range(ystart, yend) for x in range(screenwidth)} traversebono(bonotree, locallists, ystart, yend, screenwidth, k) blocklists.update(locallists) # Phase II: Dynamic Tile Grouping tiles = [(x, y) for y in range(0, screenheight, tilesize) for x in range(0, screenwidth, tilesize)] bits = int(math.log2(max(screenwidth, screenheight))) + 1 zorderedtiles = sorted(tiles, key=lambda t: zorder(t[0], t[1], bits)) weights = [] for tile in zorderedtiles: tx, ty = tile w = sum(1 for dy in range(tilesize) for dx in range(tilesize) if (tx+dx, ty+dy) in blocklists and len(blocklists[(tx+dx, ty+dy)]) > 0) weights.append(w) totalweight = sum(weights) LI = [] currentidx = 0 remainingweight = totalweight while remainingweight > 0: targetweight = remainingweight / 2 subtarget = targetweight / p for g in range(p): if currentidx >= len(zorderedtiles): break startidx = currentidx currenttileweight = 0 while currentidx < len(zorderedtiles) and currenttileweight < subtarget: currenttileweight += weights[currentidx] currentidx += 1 endidx = currentidx - 1 if startidx <= endidx: LI.append((startidx, endidx)) remainingweight /= 2 # Phase III: Dynamic Ray Casting liqueue = list(LI) liptr = 0 lock = threading.Lock() def phaseiiithread(): nonlocal liptr while True: group = None with lock: if liptr < len(liqueue): group = liqueue[liptr] liptr += 1 if group is None: break startidx, endidx = group for idx in range(startidx, endidx + 1): tile = zorderedtiles[idx] tx, ty = tile for dy in range(tilesize): for dx in range(tilesize): px, py = tx + dx, ty + dy if (px, py) not in blocklists: continue raylist = blocklists[(px, py)] if not raylist: continue color = castray(raylist, px, py) writepixel(px, py, color) # Step (iv): Handle unfinished pixels (size k, no intersection) separately threads = [] for in range(p): t = threading.Thread(target=phaseiiithread) t.start() threads.append(t) for t in threads: t.join() def traversebono(node, lists, ystart, yend, screenwidth, k): if node.isleaf: for y in range(ystart, yend): for x in range(screenwidth): if len(lists[(x, y)]) < k: lists[(x, y)].append(node.block) return if not node.bboxintersectsregion(ystart, yend): return if not any(len(lists[(x, y)]) < k for y in range(ystart, yend) for x in range(screenwidth)): return for child in node.childrenfronttoback: traversebono(child, lists, ystart, yend, screenwidth, k) def zorder(x, y, bits=10): z = 0 for i in range(bits): z |= ((x & (1 << i)) << (2 i)) | ((y & (1 << i)) << (2 i + 1)) return z def rayintersectsblock(px, py, block): return True # def solvetrilinearintersection(px, py, block): return (0.5, 0.5, 0.5) # def computeforwarddifferencegradient(pos, block): return (0.0, 1.0, 0.0) # def applydiffuseshading(normal): return (0.8, 0.8, 0.8) # def writepixel(px, py, color): pass # def castray(raylist, px, py): pass # p: Number of cores/threads. Typical values tested: 1, 2, 4, 8. k: Upper bound on block list size. Limits memory usage and traversal depth. Exact value not specified, but it is critical for limiting BONO node access to <10%. TileSize: Small image tile dimensions. Typical values: 8 \times 8 or 16 \times 16. Unfinished Pixels: Pixels whose block lists reach size k but contain no intersecting voxels must be handled separately. These pixels will not be processed in the main ray casting loop if the logic assumes intersection or empty lists. A post-processing step or specific flag is required. Boundary Conditions: The screen division in Phase I must handle non-divisible screen heights (e.g., 1024 / 8 = 128, but if p=3, regions must be "almost equal"). Time Complexity: Phase I: Proportional to the number of pixels in the region and the number of BONO nodes accessed. Node access is limited to <10% of total due to k. Phase II: Grouping overhead is small, approximately 2-3 milliseconds. The grouping process requires at most a logarithmic number of iterations relative to screen size. Phase III: Proportional to the total number of pixels and the average length of block lists. Memory Complexity: Dominated by the storage of block lists. Each pixel stores up to k block references. BONO tree overhead varies by dataset (e.g., 10.53% to 25.05% of data size for tested datasets). Measured Performance: Hardware: Clovertown platform (2 Quad-Core Intel Xeon 5320, 1.86 GHz), 8GB RAM, 8MB L2 cache. Resolution: 1024 \times 1024. View Angles: Zenith \phi \in \{15^\circ, 45^\circ, 75^\circ\}, Azimuth \theta \in \{22.5^\circ, 45^\circ\}. Scalability: Tested on 1, 2, 4, 8 cores. Strengths: Better load balancing than static tiling due to weight-based grouping. High cache performance due to Z-order spatial locality. Minimal synchronization overhead due to coarse-to-fine grain task allocation. Limitations: Requires preprocessing (Phase II) which adds latency. Complexity of implementation compared to simple static tiling. The method was developed for interactive high-resolution isosurface ray tracing on multi-core processors. The work addresses the limitations of standard octree ray casting with static tile allocation, which suffers from load imbalance and poor cache utilization. The BONO tree is used as the underlying data structure for efficient spatial indexing. name: Parallel Vector Multiplication
head: CUDA Vector Multiplication, OpenCL Parallel Vector Multiplication, Vector Add/Multiply Kernel
body: Parallel Vector Multiplication is a fundamental GPU primitive where each thread independently multiplies corresponding elements from two input arrays to produce an output array. It solves the problem of element-wise vector scaling or Hadamard product computation at massive scale by mapping one thread per data element. It is distinct from sibling primitives like Parallel Prefix Sum (which requires inter-thread dependency) or Atomic Fragment List Insertion (which requires synchronization), as it involves no communication between threads. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Two arrays of floating-point values, A and B, of size N. Output: One array C of size N, where C[i] = A[i] \times B[i]. Data Structures: Arrays are stored in global memory. Data types: global const float for inputs and global float for output. Vector types float2, float3, float4, float8, and float16 are supported to increase arithmetic throughput per instruction. In compressive rendering contexts, vectors may represent sampling matrices where S^T S x operations insert 0 in the location of missing pixels. Steps: 1. The GPU kernel is launched with a grid of threads sized to cover the entire vector length N. 2. Each thread calculates its unique global index id using getglobalid(0). 3. The thread reads A[id] and B[id] from global memory. 4. The thread computes the product P = A[id] \times B[id]. 5. The thread writes P to C[id] in global memory. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def vectormultiplykernel(globalid, a, b, c, n): # 1. Retrieve global unique ID id = globalid # 2. Bounds check to prevent out-of-bounds access if id < n: # 3. Load inputs from global memory vala = a[id] valb = b[id] # 4. Multiply result = vala valb # 5. Store output to global memory c[id] = result Parameters: Vector Width: Vector types float2, float3, float4, float8, and float16 are supported, with arithmetic operations on these types being as fast or faster than scalar floats. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Boundaries: If N is not a multiple of the grid size, a bounds check is required. Missing Pixels: In compressive rendering contexts, "multiplication" may involve sparse matrices where missing pixels are treated as zero. Time Complexity: O(N), where N is the number of elements. Memory Complexity: O(N) for input and output arrays. Performance: Massive calculations (e.g., S^T S x in compressive rendering) complete in a few milliseconds using CUDA. Modern GPUs feature between 16 and 480 stream processors, with adding processors halving calculation time. Strengths: Extremely high throughput for independent element-wise operations with minimal synchronization overhead. Limitations: Does not handle dependencies between elements, and memory bandwidth becomes the primary bottleneck due to low arithmetic intensity. The method originates from early GPU computing frameworks like CUDA and OpenCL, leveraging the SIMT (Single Instruction, Multiple Threads) architecture. It is used in compressive rendering for applying large sampling matrices. It also accelerates raycasting and raytracing by distributing independent pixel calculations across multiprocessors. Groups pixels into tiles to reduce memory latency and enable shared memory usage. It differs from global compositing by optimizing cache locality and is chosen for high-resolution volumes. Tiled Parallel Compositing Computes final pixel colors directly without intermediate buffers. It avoids the overhead of fragment lists and is chosen for simple transparency models. Parallel Direct Compositing Executes instructions across hardware subgroups to share data without global memory. It differs from thread-level primitives by enabling fast intra-group communication and is chosen for reductions or shuffles.
