name: Data Distribution via k-d Trees and Multicast
head: Top-down data distribution layout, k-d Tree Based Data Distribution
body: This method is a data distribution strategy for sort-last parallel volume rendering that minimizes network redundancy by assigning volume data based on k-d tree leaf nodes, ensuring each worker node is responsible for exactly one leaf. It differs from its siblings by using a top-down distribution from a master node that holds comprehensive knowledge of the dataset's distribution, rather than relying on static block-splitting or distributed pipeline stages. Unlike Block-Splitting (BS) method which may imply static spatial partitioning without visibility sorting, this approach integrates k-d trees as a visibility sorting structure to guide data assignment. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: A volume dataset, a set of worker nodes, a master node, and optionally a parallel file system. Outputs: Distributed volume data on worker nodes, ready for local rendering and subsequent compositing. Data Structures: k-d Tree: A binary tree structure used for visibility sorting, where each worker node is responsible for exactly one leaf node. Axis-Aligned Bounding Box (AABB): Associated with each k-d tree leaf node, defining the spatial extent of the data assigned to a worker. Multicast Group: A network group identifier used for UDP-based data transmission. Steps: 1. Tree Construction and Assignment: A k-d tree is constructed for the volume dataset. Each worker node is assigned responsibility for exactly one leaf node of this tree. 2. AABB Distribution: The master node distributes the axis-aligned bounding box (AABB) of each leaf node to the corresponding worker node. 3. Dataset Location Communication: The master node communicates the location of the volume dataset on the parallel file system to the worker nodes. 4. Data Loading (Option A - Parallel File System): Worker nodes load their own copy of the volume dataset directly from the parallel file system. This imposes network load on the connection between worker nodes and the file server, but allows the master node to be used solely for alpha compositing without storing the dataset permanently. 5. Data Loading (Option B - Multicast): The master node sends the whole dataset using IP Multicast. Worker nodes register to the same Multicast group. Each worker node retrieves UDP packages from the Multicast stream. A worker node stores a package permanently only if the data contained in the package is within the AABB of its assigned leaf node. Each worker node allocates enough main memory to accommodate its share of the volume dataset. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def masterdistribute(dataset, workernodes, kdtree): # Each worker node is responsible for exactly one leaf node assert len(kdtree.leaves) == len(workernodes) for i, leaf in enumerate(kdtree.leaves): worker = workernodes[i] # Distribute AABB of the leaf to the responsible worker sendmessage(worker, "AABB", leaf.aabb) # Communicate dataset location on parallel file system sendmessage(worker, "FSPATH", dataset.path) # Option B: Multicast distribution # Multicast group address and port are not given in the sources multicastgroup = "239.1.1.1" multicastport = 5000 joinmulticastgroup(multicastgroup, multicastport) for chunk in dataset.getchunks(): sendmulticastpacket(multicastgroup, multicastport, chunk) # Fallback to TCP per worker if Multicast fails def workerreceive(workerid, assignedleaf, datasetpath): aabb = assignedleaf.aabb # Allocate enough main memory to accommodate its share of the volume dataset memorybuffer = allocatememory(aabb.volume) # Option A: Load from parallel file system loaddatafromfilesystem(datasetpath, aabb, memorybuffer) # Option B: Receive via Multicast multicastgroup = "239.1.1.1" multicastport = 5000 joinmulticastgroup(multicastgroup, multicastport) while True: packet = receivemulticastpacket(multicastgroup, multicastport) # Store permanently only if contained in the AABB of its leaf node if iswithinaabb(packet.data, aabb): storepermanently(packet.data, memorybuffer) else: discard(packet.data) # Ensure datagram delivery via additional meta information if checkmissingdata(): requestdataviatcp(workerid, assignedleaf) def sendmessage(target, msgtype, data): pass def joinmulticastgroup(group, port): pass def sendmulticastpacket(group, port, chunk): pass def allocatememory(size): return bytearray(size) def loaddatafromfilesystem(path, aabb, buffer): pass def receivemulticastpacket(group, port): return {"data": b""} def iswithinaabb(data, aabb): return True def storepermanently(data, buffer): buffer.extend(data) def discard(data): del data def checkmissingdata(): return False def requestdataviatcp(workerid, leaf): pass Parameters: Multicast Group Address: Not given in the sources. Multicast Port: Not given in the sources. k-d Tree Splitting Criteria: Not given in the sources. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Unreliability of UDP: IP Multicast uses UDP, which is unreliable. The system ensures datagram delivery by communicating additional meta information. If Multicast fails, the system falls back to sending the dataset to individual worker nodes using TCP. However, because worker nodes are usually in the same local network as the master node, this fallback happens infrequently. Master Node Knowledge: The master node must maintain comprehensive knowledge of how the dataset is distributed among worker nodes. Memory Allocation: Worker nodes must allocate enough main memory to accommodate their share of the volume dataset. A data partitioning strategy for distributed memory parallel rendering that ensures proper view ordering for all processes by creating a KD-tree and clipping straddling cells to partition boundaries. Unlike regular grids where KD-tree planes do not intersect cells, unstructured grids require cells to be copied and clipped because KD-tree planes inevitably intersect general unstructured cells. The process involves creating a KD-tree that partitions cells evenly, identifying cells that straddle multiple KD-tree regions, copying straddling cells to all regions they intersect, and clipping the copied cells by the bounds of each region to ensure every region completely contains all cells within it. Hardware clipping planes are avoided because they do not support algorithms like projected tetrahedra well, causing artifacts along cutting planes in transparent regions. This method ensures load balancing as data is split evenly amongst processes cell-wise. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Worker nodes must allocate enough main memory to accommodate their share of the volume dataset. Measured Performance: Not given in the sources. Scaling: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Reduces network redundancy by assigning volume data based on k-d tree leaf nodes. Allows the master node to be used for alpha compositing only if workers load from a parallel file system. Ensures reasonable load balancing in the KD-tree clipping variant. Limitations: Requires the master node to maintain comprehensive knowledge of the dataset distribution. IP Multicast is unreliable, requiring fallback mechanisms. When to Use: Distributed volume rendering on HPC clusters where reducing network redundancy is critical. When Not to Use: When the master node cannot maintain comprehensive knowledge of the distribution. This method was implemented in a described distributed volume rendering architecture to manage large datasets across HPC clusters. It is part of a software architecture that supports various usage scenarios, ranging from remote data exploration using thin clients to virtual reality applications. The k-d tree based partitioning with clipping variant was developed for parallel unstructured volume rendering in ParaView. name: Distributed Volume Rendering Pipeline
head: Virvo system, Virvo Architecture
body: The Distributed Volume Rendering Pipeline is a parallel software architecture that structures distributed direct volume rendering as a loosely coupled pipeline of sequential and parallel stages to hide I/O costs and achieve interactive framerates on heterogeneous High-Performance Computing (HPC) systems. It solves the problem of limited local hardware performance and data locality by decoupling elementary renderers from parallelism and resource management, allowing the system to scale across distributed memory clusters and Multi-GPU nodes. Unlike sibling methods that focus primarily on data distribution algorithms or compositing optimizations, this architecture emphasizes a modular pipeline design with a dedicated display phase and Zero Configuration Networking (ZCN) for dynamic resource allocation, enabling seamless integration of new resources without system restarts. The pipeline consists of four distinct stages: data distribution, rendering, compositing, and display. Data distribution and display are sequential tasks assigned to a single processor (or host), while rendering and compositing are performed by multiple processors in parallel. The architecture supports two primary operational modes: single-resource mode (where compositing is omitted) and multi-resource mode (sort-last parallel rendering). Inputs: Raw volume data stored on a parallel file system, transfer functions, and viewing transformation matrices. Outputs: A final composited image displayed on a client device or stored to disk. Spatial Encoding: For time-varying data with static mesh structures, a one-time preprocessing step generates a spatial octree encoding of the raw data. Each block of elements is associated with a subtree of the global octree. Resource List: A dynamic list of available computing resources managed via ZCN, tracking hardware metrics such as available/used video memory and CUDA compute capability. Image Portions: Partially composited images held by each node after the compositing phase, which are sent back to the host for final assembly. Partition Sizes: Tested on CM-5 with 32, 64, 128, 256, and 512 nodes. Data Sets: 256³ voxel vorticity data, 128³ voxel head data, and 256×256×128 voxel vessel data. 1. Initialization and Resource Discovery: The resource manager monitors socket connections and uses Zero Configuration Networking (ZCN) to dynamically discover and add idle resources to the active resource list. If a connection breaks, the client is notified, and the resource is removed from the list without affecting the management subsystem. 2. Data Distribution (Sequential): Input processors read data files from the parallel file system storage device. Input processors prepare raw data for rendering calculations, such as quantization from 32-bit to smaller types. Using the precomputed octree and workload estimation, input processors partition the data and distribute data blocks to rendering processors using non-blocking send and receive operations. In the host-node model, the host broadcasts data-space partitioning information and the portion of data to each node. The host also broadcasts transfer functions and transform matrices to all nodes. 3. Rendering (Parallel): Rendering processors (or nodes) receive their local data blocks. Nodes update their local transfer functions and transform matrices. Each node executes its own copy of the renderer. If a single resource is assigned, an elementary renderer is used. If multiple resources are assigned, a parallel brick renderer is instantiated, configured for sort-last parallel Multi-GPU or distributed memory rendering. The renderer superimposes a k-d tree search structure and threading logic on top of elementary renderers to handle parallelism. 4. Compositing (Parallel): Nodes synchronize after rendering and before entering the compositing phase. Rendering processors deliver their rendered images to output processors or other nodes. A parallel compositing method, specifically a binary-swap algorithm, combines the independently rendered results. If only one resource is assigned, this stage is omitted, and execution proceeds directly to display. 5. Display (Sequential): Output processors send the final images to a display or storage device. In the host-node model, once compositing is finished, each node holds a portion of the image and sends it back to the host for display. The host performs an I/O servicing loop to receive these portions. The display phase determines how the image is presented, accommodating varying requirements such as high-frame-rate VR head tracking or low-frame-rate HPC monitoring. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def runpipeline(resources, datapath, transferfunction, transformmatrix): # 1. Resource Discovery via ZCN activeresources = discoverresourcesviazcn() if not activeresources: return None # 2. Data Distribution (Sequential) # Check for static mesh to apply one-time octree preprocessing if isstaticmesh(datapath): octree = precomputeoctree(datapath) else: octree = None # Partition data using octree subtrees and workload estimation partitions = partitiondata(datapath, octree, activeresources) # Broadcast control parameters to all nodes broadcastparams(activeresources, transferfunction, transformmatrix) # 3. Rendering (Parallel) renderfutures = [] for node in activeresources: # Send data partition and control parameters sendpartition(node, partitions[node]) # Execute renderer on node future = node.executerenderer() renderfutures.append(future) # Synchronize after rendering synchronize(renderfutures) # 4. Compositing (Parallel or Omitted) if len(activeresources) > 1: # Collect rendered images and perform binary-swap compositing renderedimages = [f.result() for f in renderfutures] imageportions = binaryswapcomposite(renderedimages) # Send portions back to host for node, portion in zip(activeresources, imageportions): sendimagetohost(node, portion) else: # Single resource: skip compositing, proceed to display finalimage = renderfutures[0].result() displayimage(finalimage) return # 5. Display (Sequential) # Host performs I/O servicing loop to receive portions finalimage = hostassembleimages(activeresources) displayimage(finalimage) def discoverresourcesviazcn(): # Uses Zero Configuration Networking to dynamically add idle resources # and removes unavailable ones on socket break return [] def isstaticmesh(datapath): # Returns True if mesh structure does not change across time steps return True def precomputeoctree(datapath): # Generates spatial octree encoding for static mesh data return None def partitiondata(datapath, octree, resources): # Distributes data blocks using octree subtrees and workload estimation return {r: None for r in resources} def broadcastparams(resources, tf, tm): # Host broadcasts transfer function and transform matrices to nodes pass def sendpartition(node, data): # Sends data-space partitioning information and data portion to node pass def synchronize(futures): # Waits for all rendering tasks to complete before compositing for f in futures: f.result() def binaryswapcomposite(images): # Parallel binary-swap compositing that keeps processors busy return [None] len(images) def sendimagetohost(node, image): # Sends composited image portion back to host for display pass def hostassembleimages(resources): # Host I/O loop receives and assembles image portions return None def displayimage(image): # Displays final image or handles VR/monitoring requirements pass Pipeline Fill Time: The pipeline is not efficient until all stages are filled; performance improves significantly once the pipeline is full. Load Balancing: Datasets with many empty voxels (e.g., head, vessel) cause load imbalance and non-linear speedup, whereas dense datasets (e.g., vorticity) exhibit nearly linear speedup. Communication Costs: On heterogeneous shared workstations, communication costs are highly variable due to Ethernet sharing, which can degrade performance. Communication dominates compositing costs on workstations (~97% of compositing time). Small Image Overhead: Rendering small images (e.g., 64×64) exhibits less speedup due to overhead costs associated with rendering and compositing steps. Resource Unavailability: The system is tolerant to resource failure; if a socket connection breaks, the client is notified, and the resource is removed from the list without affecting the management subsystem. Separates the rendering engine into a computation server and an interaction client, serving as the foundational communication layer for this pipeline. Time Complexity: Rendering time dominates the overall process. Communication costs dominate compositing costs on workstations (~97% of compositing time). Memory Complexity: Nodes must store their portion of the data in local memory. The architecture allows nodes to store the whole dataset in main memory if data parallelism is abandoned, though the default is data parallelism. Performance: On CM-5, nearly linear speedup was achieved for dense datasets (vorticity) across various image sizes, except for small images (64×64) where overhead reduced speedup. Speedup for compositing was lower (1.46 from 32 to 512 nodes) due to communication overhead. Strengths: Hides I/O costs, supports interactive framerates, scales to heterogeneous hardware (from workstations to Multi-GPU clusters), and allows dynamic resource addition via ZCN. Limitations: Not efficient until pipeline is full; sensitive to load imbalance from sparse data; communication costs can be high on shared networks; resource management is handcrafted and lacks generality for non-direct volume rendering methods. When to Use: Interactive visualization of large, time-varying volume data on distributed HPC systems or clusters with heterogeneous hardware. When Not to Use: Not suitable when the storage infrastructure lacks a parallel file system, as input processors require it for efficient data retrieval. Performance degrades on datasets with many empty voxels due to load imbalance. The Distributed Volume Rendering Pipeline was introduced as a parallel pipeline architecture for visualizing time-varying volume data, aiming to hide I/O costs and achieve interactive framerates. It was implemented on the CM-5 and a network of scientific workstations using PVM. A later software architecture extension emphasized loose coupling, ZCN for dynamic node allocation, and a dedicated display phase to support diverse scenarios from VR to HPC monitoring. The architecture is also known as the Virvo system or Virvo Architecture. name: Remote Rendering Client/Server Architecture
head: Client/Server Volume Rendering, I/O subsystem, Network Rendering, Remote Rendering, Remote client, Remote server, Thin Client Remote Rendering
body: Remote Rendering Client/Server Architecture separates the volume rendering engine into a server and a client connected via a network, allowing rendering computation to be performed on a remote machine while the user interacts locally. It solves the problem of limited local hardware performance or data accessibility by centralizing data storage and rendering power on a server, while the client handles user interface and display. It distinguishes itself from client-side compositing approaches (like Visapult) by performing all rendering and compositing remotely, resulting in a "thin client" that only receives final composited RGB images. The architecture relies on a transparent API where the client exposes the same interface as a local renderer, encoding function calls into network messages and deserializing results as if they were computed locally. Inputs and Outputs: Input: User interaction events (viewpoint changes, parameter adjustments) from the client; volume data and scene definition stored on the server. Output: Final composited RGB images (optionally compressed) sent from server to client for display. Data Structures: Command Stream: A sequence of serialized function calls (e.g., setViewpoint, setTransferFunction, render) sent from client to server. Result Buffer: Binary image data (RGB pixels) generated by the server's renderer, serialized and transmitted back to the client. Communication Protocol: Configurable to support TCP/IP, InfiniBand, or shared memory (if client and server are on the same physical machine). Steps: 1. Client Initialization: The client establishes a network connection to the remote server. 2. Command Encoding: The client encodes user commands (scene modifications or rendering requests) into a binary format. 3. Transmission: The client sends the serialized commands over the network to the server. 4. Server Interpretation: The server receives the commands, interprets them, and executes corresponding local calls (e.g., modifying scene elements, assigning data files, or triggering the renderer). 5. Rendering: The server executes the volume rendering algorithm (e.g., ray casting, 3D texture mapping) using the local data and scene parameters. 6. Result Serialization: The server serializes the resulting image buffer (binary pixel data). 7. Result Transmission: The server sends the serialized image data back to the client. 8. Client Display: The client deserializes the image data and renders it to an OpenGL context or provides it directly to the user interface. Parameters: Network Bandwidth: The architecture assumes network overhead is acceptable for use cases involving low-performance workstations or very large data volumes. Compression: On-the-fly JPEG compression can be applied to transient images to mitigate bandwidth constraints. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Latency: The thin client approach requires a full round-trip for each update during interactive rendering, which can introduce latency if the network is slow. Synchronization: In standard implementations, the client waits for the result of each command before sending the next, unlike asynchronous variants that ignore intermediate updates. Data Locality: Data is stored centrally on the server; clients do not hold copies of the volume data, ensuring consistency but requiring sufficient server storage and I/O bandwidth. This variant decouples user navigation from rendering by using UDP/IP to transfer rendered images. It solves interaction latency by ignoring intermediate update requests during active rendering, processing only the youngest message upon completion, which yields lower latency than synchronous TCP cycles. In this variant, a thin client communicates via TCP/IP as an image viewer, while server nodes synchronize using MPI. Partial images are sent to the client either gathered and composited or directly without compositing, with optional compression of the final image. Time Complexity: Rendering time depends on the server's hardware and the volume size. For a 128x256x256 volume rendered to a 512x512 image using a 3D texture GPU renderer, the remote configuration over a 100Mbit/s network took 557.12 ms. Memory Complexity: The server must hold the entire volume dataset in memory or accessible storage; clients hold only the UI state and the current frame buffer. Performance: Interactive visualization of large AMR data sets has been achieved at several frames per second under the latency and bandwidth constraints of a consumer-level DSL Internet connection, leveraging on-the-fly JPEG compression. Strengths: Platform-independent clients (e.g., Java applets); centralized data management; ability to use high-end server hardware for rendering. Limitations: Requires a full round-trip for each update in synchronous modes, potentially limiting interactivity on high-latency networks; dependent on network stability. When to use: When local hardware is insufficient for the data size or rendering complexity, or when data is too large to distribute to multiple clients. When not to use: When ultra-low latency is critical and network conditions are poor, or when client-side compositing is required to guarantee limited interactivity during network disruptions. The architecture originated from the need to support remote visualization on HPC systems and heterogeneous clusters. It was formalized in the VRE volume rendering engine, which separated user interaction, scene management, and rendering into distinct components to facilitate remote extension. It has been used in systems like Visapult (as a contrast point) and various AMR rendering frameworks to enable sort-last parallel rendering on distributed memory systems. name: Asynchronous UDP Client-Server Volume Rendering
body: This method is a distributed rendering architecture where volume rendering computation is offloaded to a separate server PC, with rendered images transferred to a client via UDP/IP. It solves the problem of interaction latency in virtual environments by decoupling user navigation from rendering, allowing the client to handle input smoothly while the server updates the view asynchronously. It distinguishes itself from synchronous request/acknowledge cycles by ignoring intermediate update requests during active rendering, processing only the youngest message upon completion, which yields lower latency. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Visualization parameters (viewpoint, transparency) from the client; volume data on the server. Output: Rendered image pairs (stereo) sent to the client. Data Structures: Message: Contains visualization parameters. Format is not specified in the sources. Image: Rendered image pair. Format is not specified in the sources. Steps: 1. The client detects a change in visualization parameters (e.g., viewpoint or transparency). 2. The client sends an update-request message to the server via UDP/IP. 3. The server receives the message and stores it as the latest parameter set. 4. If the server is currently rendering, it ignores the incoming packet. 5. Only when an image pair is completed, the server processes the youngest received message and starts a new rendering. 6. The server renders the image pair using the latest parameters. 7. The server sends the completed image pair to the client via UDP/IP. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def sendudp(data, targetaddress, targetport): """Standard UDP datagram transmission.""" # Implementation sends data as an unbuffered, message-oriented packet pass def rendervolume(params): """Standard volume rendering step using viewpoint and transparency.""" # Implementation computes the stereo image pair from params return b"imagepairdata" class Server: def init(self, clientaddress, clientport): self.clientaddress = clientaddress self.clientport = clientport self.latestparams = None self.isrendering = False def receivemessage(self, message): # Store the youngest message; ignore if currently rendering if not self.isrendering: self.latestparams = message # If rendering, the message is effectively ignored per spec def renderloop(self): while True: if self.latestparams is not None: self.isrendering = True imagepair = rendervolume(self.latestparams) self.latestparams = None self.isrendering = False sendudp(imagepair, self.clientaddress, self.clientport) else: # Wait for next message pass class Client: def onparameterchange(self, params, serveraddress, serverport): sendudp(params, serveraddress, serverport) Parameters: Protocol: UDP/IP. Reliability: Unreliable (packets may be lost), but continuous transmission guarantees idempotent updates. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Packet Loss: Since UDP is unreliable, lost packets result in stale views, but continuous transmission ensures idempotent updates rather than eventual consistency. Network Congestion: High throughput is required; UDP minimizes protocol overhead but does not handle congestion control. Multi-frame rate volume rendering is an asynchronous parallel rendering technique that distributes workload across multiple GPUs to balance high frame rates with high visual quality. A fast display GPU handles user input and low-latency feedback, while one or more backend GPUs asynchronously compute high-quality views. It distinguishes itself from earlier multi-frame rate systems by using layered image warping to preserve motion parallax and enable view-dependent lighting for transparent volumetric structures, rather than reconstructing the scene as a single surface. Latency: Lower than complete request/acknowledge cycles because the server does not wait for acknowledgments and processes only the youngest message. Throughput: High, due to UDP's unbuffered, message-oriented communication minimizing protocol overhead. Scalability: Supports multi-user environments by distributing client and server processes on different machines without performance reduction. Reliability: Lower than TCP; suitable for LANs where packet loss is rare. Originated in the context of distributed software-based volume visualization in virtual environments, specifically within the "Studierstube" and "RTVR" systems. It was developed to provide flexible coupling between Java and C++ components and to ensure that rendering delays do not impair VR interaction. The approach builds on previous experience in distributed visualization [FLS97] but distinguishes itself by using a dedicated server for volume rendering. name: Multi-Frame Rate Volume Rendering
head: Asynchronous Multi-GPU Volume Rendering, Fast/Slow GPU Volume Rendering
body: Multi-frame rate volume rendering is an asynchronous parallel rendering technique that distributes workload across multiple GPUs to balance high frame rates with high visual quality. A fast display GPU handles user input and low-latency feedback, while one or more backend GPUs asynchronously compute high-quality views. It distinguishes itself from earlier multi-frame rate systems by using layered image warping to preserve motion parallax and enable view-dependent lighting for transparent volumetric structures, rather than reconstructing the scene as a single surface. The method operates on a client-server architecture where the "fast node" (client) manages display and interaction, and the "slow node" (server) performs heavy raycasting. Inputs and Outputs Input: Volumetric dataset, camera parameters, and user input (mouse/keyboard). Output: Final composited image displayed on the fast node's monitor. Data Structures Ring Buffer: Process-local heap memory on the host, used as an intermediate storage for images transferred from the slow node to the fast node. G-Buffers: Stored on the fast node GPU. Each G-Buffer stores three channels: Color, Normal, and Depth. Multiple G-Buffers may exist to hold reference frames or intermediate warping results. Pipeline Steps The rendering pipeline executes five main steps in order: 1. Raycasting (Slow Node): The slow node GPU performs volume raycasting. It produces three buffers: Color, Depth, and Normal. The raycaster supports complex translucent objects and CSG intersections. 2. Transfer: The image buffers are downloaded from the slow node's GPU memory to the host memory (ring buffer) and then uploaded to the fast node's GPU memory. 3. Latency Compensation (Warping): The fast node warps the reference frames (stored in G-Buffers) to compensate for camera movement since the last raycast. This involves projecting the depth and normal information to estimate new pixel positions and colors. 4. Shading: View-dependent lighting is computed on the warped data. This step is critical for transparent objects to correctly light inner structures revealed by motion parallax. 5. Compositing: Fragments are sorted per pixel, blended front-to-back, and written to the frame buffer. Pseudocode The following pseudocode outlines the asynchronous loop on the fast node and the raycasting loop on the slow node. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. class GBuffer: def init(self, color, normal, depth): self.color = color self.normal = normal self.depth = depth class Camera: def init(self, viewmatrix, projmatrix): self.viewmatrix = viewmatrix self.projmatrix = projmatrix def projectpoint(point3d, camera): """Projects a 3D world point to normalized device coordinates [-1, 1]""" # Standard matrix multiplication: clip = proj view point return applymatrices(point3d, camera.projmatrix, camera.viewmatrix) def unprojectpixel(u, v, depth, camera): """Reconstructs a 3D world point from screen coordinates and depth""" # Standard inverse projection using camera matrices return inverseprojection(u, v, depth, camera.projmatrix, camera.viewmatrix) def isinviewport(x, y, width, height): return 0 <= x < width and 0 <= y < height def fastnodeloop(gbuffers, ringbuffer, camera, screenwidth, screenheight): while True: # Step 1: Process user input (camera updated externally) # Step 2: Check for new frames from slow node if ringbuffer.hasnewframe(): newcolor, newdepth, newnormal = ringbuffer.read() refgbuffer = GBuffer(newcolor, newdepth, newnormal) gbuffers.append(refgbuffer) if len(gbuffers) > 2: gbuffers.pop(0) # Step 3: Latency Compensation (Warping) if gbuffers: ref = gbuffers[-1] warpedcolor = [[0.0] screenwidth for in range(screenheight)] warpednormal = [[(0.0, 0.0, 0.0)] screenwidth for in range(screenheight)] warpeddepth = [[float('inf')] screenwidth for in range(screenheight)] srch, srcw = len(ref.depth), len(ref.depth[0]) for ysrc in range(srch): for xsrc in range(srcw): depthval = ref.depth[ysrc][xsrc] if depthval == float('inf'): continue # Unproject reference pixel to 3D world space pworld = unprojectpixel(xsrc, ysrc, depthval, ref.camera) # Project to current camera view pclip = projectpoint(pworld, camera) xdst = int(pclip.x screenwidth / 2.0 + screenwidth / 2.0) ydst = int(pclip.y screenheight / 2.0 + screenheight / 2.0) if isinviewport(xdst, ydst, screenwidth, screenheight): # Depth test handles occlusion for layered warping if pclip.z < warpeddepth[ydst][xdst]: warpeddepth[ydst][xdst] = pclip.z warpedcolor[ydst][xdst] = ref.color[ysrc][xsrc] warpednormal[ydst][xdst] = ref.normal[ysrc][xsrc] warpedgbuffer = GBuffer(warpedcolor, warpednormal, warpeddepth) # Step 4: Shading shadedcolor = [[0.0] screenwidth for in range(screenheight)] for y in range(screenheight): for x in range(screenwidth): if warpeddepth[y][x] == float('inf'): continue normal = warpednormal[y][x] viewdir = normalize(camera.viewmatrix[2][:3]) lightintensity = max(0.0, dot(normal, viewdir)) shadedcolor[y][x] = [c lightintensity for c in warpedcolor[y][x]] shadedgbuffer = GBuffer(shadedcolor, warpednormal, warpeddepth) # Step 5: Compositing # Front-to-back blending for multiple layers finalimage = [[0.0] screenwidth for in range(screenheight)] alphaaccum = 0.0 for gbuf in gbuffers: for y in range(screenheight): for x in range(screenwidth): if gbuf.depth[y][x] == float('inf'): continue color = gbuf.color[y][x] alpha = 1.0 - alphaaccum finalimage[y][x] = [c alpha for c in color] alphaaccum += alpha if alphaaccum >= 1.0: break # Display displayimage(finalimage) else: displayimage(previousframe) def slownodeloop(volumedata, ringbuffer, camera): while True: # Step 1: Raycasting color, depth, normal = raycastvolume(volumedata, camera) # Step 2: Transfer to Host Memory (Ring Buffer) ringbuffer.write(color, depth, normal) Parameters Ring Buffer Size: Not given in the sources. Must be large enough to hold at least one full frame of color, depth, and normal data. Layer Separation: The system uses feature peeling to separate layers for transparent objects, adapting to dataset features rather than using regular intervals. Edge Cases and Pitfalls Data Transfer Bottleneck: Transfer through host memory is a major performance limitation, especially when the slow node's frame rate approaches the fast node's frame rate. Economic Viability: Due to transfer costs, the system is only economic for large rendering problems until fast inter-GPU links are available. Transparent Objects: Previous systems failed to preserve motion parallax for transparent objects by using a single surface representation. This method avoids that by warping layered G-Buffers. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Measured Performance: Not given in the sources. Scaling: Scales by adding backend GPUs for higher quality or resolution, while the fast node maintains display latency. Strengths: High frame rates and low latency for user input; preserves motion parallax and view-dependent lighting for transparent volumes. Limitations: Performance limited by host memory bandwidth for inter-GPU transfer; requires large rendering problems to be economic. When to use: Medical visualization or scientific visualization of transparent volumetric data where user interaction latency is critical but high-quality rendering is also required. When not to use: Small datasets where single-GPU rendering is sufficient, or when fast inter-GPU links are not available and transfer overhead dominates. Multi-frame rate volume rendering was introduced by Stefan Hauswiesner, Denis Kalkofen, and Dieter Schmalstieg from Graz University of Technology. It was presented in the context of the Eurographics Symposium on Parallel Graphics and Visualization (EGPGV) in 2010. The work addresses limitations in previous multi-frame rate systems that used single-surface reconstruction, which destroyed motion parallax for transparent objects. name: Parallel Brick Renderer
head: Sort-last parallel brick renderer
body: The Parallel Brick Renderer is a sort-last parallel volume rendering method that subdivides a large dataset into convex objects (bricks) small enough to fit into GPU video memory, renders these bricks concurrently using multiple threads, and composites the results via sort-last alpha blending. It differs from the serial brick renderer by using multiple threads to render bricks concurrently instead of processing leaf nodes sequentially. Inputs: A volume dataset, the number of available rendering threads, and the GPU video memory limit. Outputs: A final composited 2D image. Data Structures: Brick: A convex subset of the volume data that fits entirely within GPU video memory. k-d Tree: Organizes the bricks to facilitate the traversal required for the compositing visitor. Steps: 1. Subdivision: Subdivide the volume dataset into convex bricks that fit into GPU video memory. 2. Assignment: Assign the generated bricks to rendering threads. 3. Parallel Rendering: Each assigned thread renders its brick using an elementary renderer. 4. Compositing: Once all threads have finished rendering, the main thread performs sort-last alpha compositing using a visitor invoked during k-d tree traversal. Parameters: Brick Size: Determined by available GPU video memory; must be small enough to fit entirely in VRAM. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Memory Overflow: If a brick exceeds available VRAM, it cannot be rendered by the GPU. Thread Synchronization: The main thread must wait for all worker threads to complete before initiating compositing. A parallel volume rendering strategy for AMR meshes where MultiFABs are processed independently by a GPU renderer and results are combined via MPI reduction. It differs from standard brick renderers by explicitly handling the topological dependencies and non-convexities inherent in AMR grids through a "convexification" preprocessing step, ensuring correct alpha blending for color and emissivity cases. Choose this variant when rendering Adaptive Mesh Refinement datasets that require explicit handling of non-convex grid topologies. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Measured Performance: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Enables parallel thread execution for brick rendering instead of sequential leaf node processing. Limitations: Requires subdivision into convex bricks; compositing relies on a k-d tree traversal visitor. When to use: When parallel thread execution is desired for brick rendering. When not to use: Not given in the sources. The Parallel Brick Renderer was introduced as part of a software architecture for distributed volume rendering. It builds on the concept of brick renderers, which handle large datasets by subdivision and can connect to remote servers running arbitrary renderers. The method was developed to address the sequential processing limitation of the serial brick renderer. name: MultiFAB Convexification and Parallel Volume Rendering
body: A parallel volume rendering strategy for Adaptive Mesh Refinement (AMR) meshes where MultiFABs are processed independently by a GPU renderer (Viskores) and results are combined via MPI reduction. It differs from standard brick renderers by explicitly handling topological dependencies and non-convexities inherent in AMR grids through a convexification preprocessing step, ensuring correct alpha blending for color and emissivity cases. Inputs: A MultiFAB dataset representing an AMR mesh, consisting of a hierarchy of boxes (grids) at various refinement levels. Optical properties: absorption coefficient, emission coefficient, and/or color/opacity data associated with the cells. Camera parameters: viewing direction and projection type (assumed orthogonal for tie-breaking logic). Outputs: A final composite image (e.g., PNG) representing the volume rendering. Data Structures: MultiFAB: A collection of Box objects. Each Box defines a contiguous chunk of 3D grid data. Image Buffer: A 2D array of pixels, typically RGBA, initialized to zero (or background color) for accumulation. Algorithm Steps: 1. Convexify the MultiFABs: The raw AMR boxes may overlap or be non-convex due to the hierarchy. To enable independent processing and correct merging: Remove Covered Parts: For any box, identify regions covered by coarser parent cells. These regions are excluded from the current box's data to prevent double-counting. Split Disconnected Pieces: If removing covered parts leaves a box topologically disconnected, split it into multiple separate boxes. Break Dependency Loops: In 3D AMR meshes, dependency loops can form where grid A depends on B, B on C, and C on A. Break these loops by splitting grids using cutting planes perpendicular to the z-axis. This reduces the layout to 2D layers where no loops are possible. Split Size-Mismatched Boxes: If boxes of different sizes prevent a valid topological ordering, split the problematic boxes along a Cartesian axis. The preferred axis is the one most nearly orthogonal to the viewing plane. For BoxLib grids, the z-axis is preferred because it leaves two contiguous chunks of data, which is more efficient for underlying numerical routines. 2. Render Each FAB Independently: Call the GPU volume renderer (e.g., Viskores) separately for each resulting FAB (Family of Arrays). Each renderer produces a partial image containing the accumulated color and opacity for the rays passing through that FAB's boxes. 3. Merge Partial Images (Local): Attenuation Only: If the volume only has absorption (no color/emissivity), simply add the images from all local FABs together. Color/Emissivity: If color or emissivity is present, simple addition is insufficient. The boxes must be topologically sorted and merged in back-to-front order using alpha blending. Use a binary tree merge structure since the merge operator is associative. Topological Sort: Sort boxes based on their depth relative to the viewer. Tie-Breaking: For geometrically degenerate cases where boxes are at the same depth, sort by maximum distance from the viewer (assuming orthogonal projection). Boxes with the same maximum distance are tied; one is picked arbitrarily to go first. For tied boxes A and C, the order can be either (A \text{ merge } C) \text{ merge } B or (C \text{ merge } A) \text{ merge } B. 4. MPI Reduction: Perform an MPI reduction operation to sum all images from all MPI ranks. This combines the contributions from different nodes in the distributed system. 5. Output: Write the final composite image (e.g., PNG file) from rank 0. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def multifabconvexifyrender(multifab, camera, renderer, mpicomm, rank, hascolororemissivity): # Step 1: Convexify MultiFABs # Remove covered parts, split disconnected pieces, break dependency loops (z-axis), # split size-mismatched boxes (axis most orthogonal to view). convexifiedfabs = [] # Standard AMR box decomposition not detailed in sources # Step 2: Render each FAB independently localimages = [] for fab in convexifiedfabs: img = renderer.render(fab, camera) # GPU volume rendering call localimages.append((fab, img)) # Step 3: Merge partial images locally if hascolororemissivity: # Topological sort with tie-breaking # Sort by maximum distance from viewer (orthogonal projection) sortedfabs = sorted(localimages, key=lambda x: -x[0].maxdistancefrom(camera)) # Merge in back-to-front order using a binary tree mergedimage = mergebinarytree(sortedfabs) else: # Attenuation only: simple addition mergedimage = sumimages([img for, img in localimages]) # Step 4: MPI reduction globalimage = mpicomm.allreduce(mergedimage, op=mpicomm.SUM) # Standard MPI reduction # Step 5: Output if rank == 0: writepng(globalimage, "output.png") # Standard image encoding return globalimage def mergebinarytree(sortedfabs): if len(sortedfabs) == 1: return sortedfabs[0].image mid = len(sortedfabs) // 2 left = mergebinarytree(sortedfabs[:mid]) right = mergebinarytree(sortedfabs[mid:]) return alphablend(left, right) # Standard back-to-front alpha blending def sumimages(images): result = zeroimage() for img in images: result += img return result def zeroimage(): return [[0.0, 0.0, 0.0, 0.0] for in range(width height)] # Standard initialization Time and Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Measured Performance: Not given in the sources. Scaling: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Handles complex AMR topologies correctly, including dependency loops and non-convex shapes. Efficient for large-scale parallel rendering using MPI and GPUs. Limitations: The convexification step adds CPU overhead. Splitting boxes may increase the number of boxes. Dependency loop breaking requires cutting planes. When to Use: Suitable for AMR meshes where topological correctness is crucial, especially for color and emissivity rendering. When Not to Use: For octree meshes, which do not have the dependency loop problem. If a physically-accurate solution is not required, alternative tie-breaking or pixel-independent merging might be considered, though this increases MPI communication. This method was proposed in the context of the Quokka astro codebase for outputting volume renderings of AMR data. It builds on the Parallel Brick Renderer concept but adapts it for the specific challenges of AMR grids, such as dependency loops and non-convexity. The approach leverages the Viskores GPU renderer and MPI for parallelism. The idea of breaking dependency loops by cutting along the z-axis to reduce to 2D layers is a key insight for handling 3D AMR meshes. output volume renderings, https://github.com/quokka-astro/quokka/issues/1078, fetched 2026-10-28 (unofficial)

name: Parallel Sort-Last Image Compositing for Volumes
head: Sort-last Volume Rendering with Associative Compositing, Sort-last volume rendering on PC clusters
body: This method extends sort-last image compositing, traditionally used for opaque surfaces via libraries like IceT, to translucent volumes by leveraging the associativity of the Porter-Duff 'over' operator. Inputs: A distributed dataset partitioned into blocks, each accessible to a single process; a viewing ray \vec{v}; and a serial volume rendering algorithm capable of computing the color contribution of a cell. Outputs: A final composited image where each pixel represents the accumulated color along the viewing ray. Data Structures: Data Partition: Each process holds a contiguous set of intersected cells for any viewing ray. The partitioning must ensure a consistent view ordering of processes for all viewing rays to simplify composition. Communication Schedule: A map of overlapping pixels between processes, computed to manage data transfer during compositing. Steps: 1. Data Distribution: Distribute equal blocks of data among rendering nodes to ensure an initial even distribution of work. 2. Local Rendering: Each process locally combines colors from its assigned cells using a serial volume rendering algorithm. 3. Late Visibility Test: Nodes that render data but do not contribute to the final image are identified and discarded. 4. Communication Schedule Computation: Compute a schedule of overlapping pixels to perform compositing. The traversal is done in scanline order to provide better load balancing. 5. Associative Compositing: Composite the results from individual processes using a sort-last image compositing algorithm. Formula: The composite color for a viewing ray \vec{v} intersecting cells C1, \dots, Cn is: \text{color}(C1, \vec{v}) \text{ over } \text{color}(C2, \vec{v}) \text{ over } \dots \text{ over } \text{color}(Cn, \vec{v}) The 'over' operator is associative: a \text{ over } (b \text{ over } c) = (a \text{ over } b) \text{ over } c This allows grouping cells into blocks C1 \dots Ca, C{a+1} \dots Cz, etc., such that: (\text{color}(C1, \vec{v}) \text{ over } \dots \text{ over } \text{color}(Ca, \vec{v})) \text{ over } (\text{color}(C{a+1}, \vec{v}) \text{ over } \dots \text{ over } \text{color}(Cn, \vec{v})) The order of operations is important (non-commutative), but the grouping is flexible. Parameters: Block Size: Arbitrarily sized blocks of cells. Traversal Order: Scanline order is used for the communication schedule to improve load balancing. Pitfalls: OpenGL Blending: The OpenGL over operator blending function must be explicitly set to (GL ONE, GL ONE MINUS SRCALPHA) because it is not the default. View Ordering: On distributed memory machines, it is best to have the same view ordering of processes for all viewing rays to avoid complicating the image composition. Load Imbalance: While sort-last systems are generally less prone to load imbalance than sort-first, late visibility tests can cause some nodes to render without contributing to the final image. A method for blending snapshots of sub-volumes rendered independently by distributed nodes, allowing any geometrically coherent group of sub-volumes to be blended together while respecting distance/priority order. It sets itself apart from sibling methods like SH-RS-CO-RD by treating the compositing step as a direct blend of rendered snapshots rather than separating shading/resampling from global blending, effectively extending classic ray casting to distributed environments by replacing geometric surfaces with images. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Leverages existing sort-last infrastructure (like IceT) for volumes; associative property allows flexible grouping of cells; generally less prone to load imbalance than sort-first methods. Limitations: Requires careful partitioning to ensure contiguous intersected cells and consistent view ordering; late visibility tests can lead to wasted computation on some nodes. When to use: Large-scale distributed rendering of translucent volumes where existing sort-last infrastructure is available or when flexible cell grouping is beneficial. When not to use: When strict front-to-back or back-to-front ordering is required and associativity cannot be exploited (though the 'over' operator is associative, commutativity is not, so order within a block matters). The method builds on the observation that the Porter-Duff 'over' operator is associative, allowing image compositing to be applied to rendered volumes similarly to opaque surfaces. It extends earlier work on sort-last rendering for surfaces (e.g., IceT) and systems like those by Stompel et al. on PC clusters, which used communication schedules of overlapping pixels traversed in scanline order. It is used in systems like ParaView for parallel unstructured volume rendering. name: Associative Image Compositing
head: Concurrent Composition Operator F, Parallel Image Compositing with Associative Operator
body: Associative Image Compositing is a method for blending snapshots of sub-volumes rendered independently by distributed nodes, allowing any geometrically coherent group of sub-volumes to be blended together while respecting distance/priority order. It sets itself apart from sibling methods like SH-RS-CO-RD by treating the compositing step as a direct blend of rendered snapshots rather than separating shading/resampling from global blending, effectively extending classic ray casting to distributed environments by replacing geometric surfaces with images. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A set of sub-images i1, i2, \dots, in, where each sub-image ik contains an accumulated color C{ik} and accumulated opacity \alpha{ik} for every pixel. The sub-images must be geometrically coherent and ordered by their distance to the viewpoint (priority order). Output: A single composite image with accumulated color C{total} and accumulated opacity \alpha{total}. Data Structures: Each sub-image i is represented as a pair (Ci, \alphai), where: Ci: A vector representing the accumulated color (typically RGB). \alphai: A scalar value in the range [0, 1] representing the accumulated opacity. The Concurrent Composition Operator F: The core of the method is the operator F, which combines two sub-images i1 and i2. The operator is defined as: F(i1, i2) = (C{i1} + (1 - \alpha{i1})C{i2}, \alpha{i1} + (1 - \alpha{i1})\alpha{i2}) Where: i1 is the sub-image closer to the viewpoint (higher priority). i2 is the sub-image further from the viewpoint (lower priority). C{i1}, \alpha{i1} are the color and opacity of i1. C{i2}, \alpha{i2} are the color and opacity of i2. Numbered Steps: 1. Render Sub-volumes: Each distributed node renders its assigned sub-volume independently, producing a snapshot (sub-image) for each pixel. This snapshot consists of the accumulated color C and accumulated opacity \alpha along the ray segment within that sub-volume. 2. Order Sub-images: For each pixel, identify the set of sub-images covering that pixel. Sort these sub-images based on their distance to the viewpoint (priority order). Let the sorted sequence be i1, i2, \dots, ik, where i1 is closest and ik is furthest. 3. Apply Associative Composition: Combine the sorted sub-images using the operator F. Due to the associativity of F, the order of application does not affect the final result, enabling parallel reduction. The composite result for a pixel is: Result = F(\dots F(F(i1, i2), i3) \dots, ik) Alternatively, using the associative property, any grouping can be used: Result = F(i1, F(i2, F(i3, \dots, ik)\dots)) 4. Output Composite Image: The resulting (C{total}, \alpha{total}) for each pixel forms the final composite image. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def composesubimages(subimages): """ Compose a list of subimages using the associative operator F. subimages: list of tuples (C, alpha), ordered by distance to viewpoint (closest first). C is a vector/list of color components. alpha is a scalar. Returns: (Ctotal, alphatotal) """ if not subimages: return ([0.0, 0.0, 0.0], 0.0) currentC, currentalpha = subimages[0] for i in range(1, len(subimages)): nextC, nextalpha = subimages[i] # Apply operator F: F(i1, i2) where i1 is current (closer), i2 is next (further) # Cnew = Ccurrent + (1 - alphacurrent) Cnext # alphanew = alphacurrent + (1 - alphacurrent) alphanext newalpha = currentalpha + (1.0 - currentalpha) nextalpha newC = [c1 + (1.0 - currentalpha) c2 for c1, c2 in zip(currentC, nextC)] currentC = newC currentalpha = newalpha return (currentC, currentalpha) def parallelcomposite(allsubimagesperpixel): """ For each pixel, compose its subimages. allsubimagesperpixel: dict mapping pixelid to list of (C, alpha) tuples, sorted by distance. Returns: dict mapping pixelid to (Ctotal, alphatotal) """ compositeimage = {} for pixelid, subimages in allsubimagesperpixel.items(): compositeimage[pixelid] = composesubimages(subimages) return compositeimage Parameters: Distance Order: Critical. The operator is not commutative; F(i1, i2) \neq F(i2, i1) if i1 and i2 are at different depths. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Non-commutativity: Applying F in the wrong order (e.g., furthest first) yields an incorrect result. Precision: Accumulated opacity \alpha should be clamped to [0, 1] to avoid numerical issues. Moves 2D image data during redistribution, reducing transfer volume compared to 3D data movement. Unlike Associative Image Compositing, it explicitly separates shading/resampling from global blending, allowing for distributed or centralized global compositing strategies. Choose this variant when minimizing network bandwidth for large volume datasets is a higher priority than maximizing compositing parallelism, as it decouples the shading phase from the final blend. Time Complexity: The compositing step for each pixel is linear in the number of sub-images covering that pixel, O(k), where k is the number of sub-images. Due to associativity, this can be parallelized using a tree reduction, reducing the critical path to O(\log k). Measured Performance: Rendering time for a given image size is roughly proportionate to the size of the volume rendered. Strengths: Allows independent rendering of sub-volumes, enabling efficient parallelization. The associativity of F ensures arithmetic equivalence to serial composition, simplifying parallel implementation. Limitations: Requires careful handling of depth ordering. Not commutative, so order matters. When to Use: When rendering large volumes distributed across multiple nodes where independent rendering of sub-volumes is beneficial, and geometric coherence allows for clear depth ordering. The method was proposed by Lombeyda et al. [71] (cited in), who demonstrated the arithmetic equivalence of a single ray casting composite computation and the combined result of a set of smaller composite computations. The concept extends classic ray casting to distributed environments by treating distributed ray casting as an extension of classic ray casting, where geometric surfaces are replaced with images from sub-volumes. name: SHade -> ReSample -> Composite -> ReDistribute
head: RD-RS-SH-CO, RD-SH-RS-CO, RS-SH-CO-RD, SH-RS-CO-RD, SH-RS-RD-CO
body: SHade -> ReSample -> Composite -> ReDistribute (SH-RS-CO-RD) is a parallel volume rendering algorithm where each node independently shades its local 3D data, resamples it into 2D projections, performs local compositing, and redistributes the resulting 2D image sub-images for global compositing. It differs from its siblings by moving 2D image data rather than 3D volume data during the redistribution phase, which reduces the volume of data transferred. Unlike Associative Image Compositing, which blends snapshots of sub-volumes, this method explicitly separates shading and resampling from the final global blend, supporting both distributed and centralized global compositing strategies. Inputs and Outputs: Input: 3D volume data statically distributed evenly among N nodes, and view parameters. Output: A single composited 2D image on the screen. Data Structures: Local Volume Data: 3D array of voxels, distributed evenly among nodes. Shaded Data: 4-tuples (R, G, B, \alpha) for each voxel or sample point. Sub-images: 2D arrays of pixels (or regions thereof) generated by local compositing. Global Image: The final composited frame buffer. Steps: 1. Shade: Each node shades its local 3D data samples to compute R, G, B, \alpha four-tuples. 2. Resample: Each node resamples the shaded data to compute its projection onto the view plane. This can be done via ray-casting or splatting. Ray-casting requires a reconstruction filter kernel with a maximum size such that eight nearest neighbors are sufficient. Splatting projects volume elements onto the image plane. 3. Composite (Local): Each node performs local compositing of its projected points to generate one or more sub-images. The order is typically front-to-back or back-to-front. 4. Redistribute: The sub-images from all nodes are globally collected. 5. Composite (Global): The collected sub-images are composited in front-to-back or back-to-front order to produce the final image. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def nodetask(localvoxels, viewparams): # Step 1: Shade shadedvoxels = [] for voxel in localvoxels: rgba = computeshading(voxel, viewparams) shadedvoxels.append((voxel.position, rgba)) # Step 2: Resample projectedpoints = [] if viewparams.method == "raycasting": for ray in viewparams.rays: for step in ray.steps: if not step.shaded: shadestepneighbors(step, shadedvoxels) sample = resamplestep(step, shadedvoxels) projectedpoints.append(sample) else: # splatting for voxel in shadedvoxels: splat = splatvoxel(voxel, viewparams) projectedpoints.append(splat) # Step 3: Local Composite subimage = localcomposite(projectedpoints, viewparams.tile) # Step 4: Redistribute return subimage def computeshading(voxel, viewparams): # Standard volume shading: compute RGBA from voxel properties and view parameters return (voxel.color, voxel.alpha) def shadestepneighbors(step, shadedvoxels): # Shade voxels adjacent to the current ray step pass def resamplestep(step, shadedvoxels): # Apply reconstruction filter kernel to eight nearest neighbors return interpolateandfilter(step, shadedvoxels) def splatvoxel(voxel, viewparams): # Project voxel onto image plane using splat kernel return projectsplat(voxel, viewparams) def localcomposite(points, tile): # Sort points by depth, blend into tile buffer using front-to-back or back-to-front order sortedpoints = sortbydepth(points) buffer = inittilebuffer(tile) for p in sortedpoints: blendpixel(buffer, p) return buffer Parameters: Macro Size: In the Goldwasser et al. implementation, the macro size was 64^3. Resampling Method: Ray-casting with interpolation or splatting. Compositing Order: Front-to-back or back-to-front. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Load Balance: Load balance is statically set by the data distribution since no 3D data samples move. It depends on the relative effects of the efficiency techniques at each node, and the view dependent compositing sequence. Medium granularity random or interleaved macro grouping improves load balance due to spatial coherence of interesting voxels, but increases memory requirement and redistribution cost. Centralized vs. Distributed Compositing: Centralized compositing is a serial operation and may be a poor match for machines with many nodes. Distributed compositing allows parallel processing of sub-regions but requires complex coordination. Alpha Cutoff: Alpha cutoff efficiencies can be realized in distributed compositing if sub-region propagation prioritizes ray scheduling. A variant where shading is performed locally, then data is redistributed, followed by resampling and global compositing. Unlike SH-RS-CO-RD, this moves 3D volume data (macros) rather than 2D image data, which increases the volume of data transferred. It allows perspective projections and arbitrary resampling points because resampling is done after redistribution. Implemented by Westover (1989) and Levoy (1989) on Pixel-Planes 5. Time and Memory Complexity: Memory: Includes average number of data samples at each node, shaded and resampled points (same count as samples), screen region memory, and memory for incoming regions in distributed compositing (at least size of own region). Communication: Each node may produce a full screen array of pixels as its sub-image if slab-shaped macros are used, requiring each node to send and receive an entire screen array. More cubic macro aspect ratios produce smaller sub-images and lower bandwidth requirements. Measured Performance: Not explicitly given for SH-RS-CO-RD in the sources, but related variants achieved 1.4 frames per second for 128^3 data sets on Pixel-Planes 5. Strengths and Limitations: Strengths: Reduces data transfer volume by moving 2D image data instead of 3D volume data. Supports alpha cutoff, adaptive refinement, and octtrees within a node's local data. Limitations: Centralized compositing is a serial bottleneck. Load balance is statically set by the data distribution since no 3D data samples move. It depends on the relative effects of the efficiency techniques at each node, and the view dependent compositing sequence. Origin: Implemented by Goldwasser et al. in 1985 in custom hardware with a macro size of 64^3. Used by Yazdy et al. in 1990 on an array of transputers. Described as a general approach in the taxonomy of volume rendering algorithms on multicomputers. History and Development: Part of a taxonomy of 8 possible orderings of Shade, Resample, Composite, and Redistribute tasks. The method is one of the four primary approaches analyzed in the taxonomy, distinguished by moving 2D image data during redistribution. DTIC ADA236632: Taxonomy and Algorithms for Volume Rendering on Multicomputers, https://archive.org/details/DTICADA236632, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial)

name: Block-Splitting (BS) method
head: BS method, Binary Splitting (BS) Method
body: The Block-Spliting (BS) method is a parallel compositing technique for sort-last parallel volume rendering that reduces the number of communication steps to \log2 P by doubling the block size at each stage. It serves as a baseline for comparison against hierarchical variants like the DSH method. Unlike the Parallel Pipeline (PP) method, BS is optimal when the processor count P is a power of two, offering fewer communication steps for square processor grids. Inputs and Outputs: Input: P processors, each holding a partial image of size A/P pixels. The total image size is A. Output: One complete composite image held by a designated root processor (or distributed, though the time formula assumes a single final merge point or equivalent load). Data Structures: Partial Image: A 2D array of pixels. Block: A rectangular sub-region of the partial image. Initially, each processor holds one block of size A/P. Steps: 1. Initialization: Each processor Pi (0 \le i < P) holds a partial image block Bi of size A/P. 2. Communication Loop: Perform k = 1 to \log2 P steps: a. Pairing: In step k, processors are paired based on their indices. Specifically, processor i communicates with processor i \oplus 2^{k-1} (where \oplus is bitwise XOR). Only one processor in each pair sends, and the other receives. Typically, the processor with the higher index sends to the lower index, or vice versa, following a butterfly topology. b. Block Size: In step k, the block size being transmitted is Ak = A / 2^k. c. Transmission: The sending processor transmits its current block to the receiving processor. d. Compositing: The receiving processor composites the received block with its own local block using the "over" operator. The result replaces the local block. 3. Termination: After \log2 P steps, the root processor (or the designated final accumulator) holds the fully composite image. Formulas: Block Size at Step k: Ak = \frac{A}{2^k}. Communication Time per Step: Ts (latency) + Ak \times Tp (pixel transfer time). Compositing Time per Step: Ak \times To (pixel operation time). Total Time: T{total}(BS) = \sum{k=1}^{\log P} \left( Ts + \frac{A}{2^k} Tp \right) + \sum{k=1}^{\log P} \frac{A}{2^k} To Simplifying the geometric series \sum{k=1}^{\log P} \frac{1}{2^k} = 1 - \frac{1}{2^{\log P}} = 1 - \frac{1}{P}: T{total}(BS) = (\log P) Ts + \left(1 - \frac{1}{P}\right) (Tp + To) A Parameters: P: Number of processors. Must be a power of two for the standard binary splitting topology. A: Total number of pixels in the final image. Ts: Communication latency per message. Tp: Pixel transfer time per unit area. To: Compositing operation time per unit area. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Non-Power-of-Two Processors: The standard BS method assumes P is a power of two. If P is not a power of two, the topology must be adapted (e.g., using the Rotate-Tiling method which generalizes BS). Load Imbalance: If the "over" operation is not uniform (e.g., sparse data), the actual computation time may vary, but the BS model assumes uniform To. Precision: Standard floating-point compositing is assumed. No specific precision handling is detailed in the source. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def blocksplittingcomposite(partialimage, processorid, totalprocessors, A, Ts, Tp, To): """ Performs Block-Splitting compositing. partialimage: The initial partial image block held by this processor. processorid: Unique ID of this processor (0 to P-1). totalprocessors: P, must be a power of 2. A: Total pixels in the final image. Ts, Tp, To: Timing parameters. Returns: The final composite image. """ import math import socket # Assuming a generic send/recv interface for illustration currentblock = partialimage currentblocksize = A / totalprocessors # Number of steps is log2(P) numsteps = int(math.log2(totalprocessors)) for k in range(1, numsteps + 1): # Determine partner in the butterfly network # In step k, we XOR with 2^(k-1) partnerid = processorid ^ (1 << (k - 1)) # Determine if we send or receive # Convention: Higher ID sends to Lower ID, or vice versa. # Let's assume even IDs send to odd IDs in step 1, etc. # Actually, standard butterfly: if (processorid & mask) == 0, send; else receive. mask = 1 << (k - 1) if (processorid & mask) == 0: # Sender # Send currentblock to partnerid senddata(currentblock, partnerid) # Wait for acknowledgment or just proceed if synchronous # Note: The receiver will composite. The sender's block is no longer needed for this step's result # but the sender does not composite in this step. else: # Receiver # Receive block from partnerid receivedblock = receivedata(partnerid) # Composite receivedblock with currentblock # "Over" operator: result = received + current (1 - receivedalpha) currentblock = compositeover(receivedblock, currentblock) # Update block size for next step (conceptually, though not used in code logic directly) currentblocksize /= 2 return currentblock def compositeover(blocka, blockb): """ Standard alpha compositing: A over B. """ # Implementation depends on pixel format. Assuming RGBA. # This is a placeholder for the actual pixel-wise operation. # Standard Porter-Duff 'over' operator. pass def senddata(data, destid): # Placeholder for network send. pass def receivedata(srcid): # Placeholder for network receive. pass Eliminates redundant communication by dividing the screen into non-overlapping tiles and dynamically assigning processors. Choose when P is large and data coverage is sparse to avoid transmitting blank regions. Generalizes BS to arbitrary P and N (number of blocks) using ring rotations. Choose when P is not a power of two or when performance tuning via N is required. Time and Memory Complexity: Communication Steps: \log2 P. Total Time: T{total}(BS) = (\log P) Ts + (1 - 1/P) (Tp + To) A. Memory: Each processor holds one block of size A/P at any time. No significant additional memory for buffering is required beyond the block being transmitted. Measured Performance: BS is faster than the Parallel Pipeline (PP) method when P is a power of two, because T{total}(BS) \le T{total}(PP) in this case. BS transmits more pixels than the DSH method as the number of regions n increases, because DSH avoids transmitting redundant blank regions. Strengths and Limitations: Strengths: Simple topology (butterfly), minimal communication steps (\log P), optimal for power-of-two processor counts. Limitations: Inefficient for non-power-of-two processor counts without modification. Transmits all data regardless of sparsity (unlike DSH), leading to higher bandwidth usage on sparse volumes. When to Use: Use when P is a power of two and the dataset is dense enough that the simplicity of the butterfly network outweighs the benefit of hierarchical tiling. Use as a baseline for comparison. When Not to Use: Use when P is not a power of two (use RT instead). Use when the volume is sparse and significant bandwidth can be saved by avoiding transmission of blank regions (use DSH instead). The Block-Splitting method is a foundational sort-last parallel compositing algorithm. It is cited in the context of comparing various parallel volume rendering compositing strategies, specifically against the Parallel Pipeline (PP) and Rotate-Tiling (RT) methods. It is also used as a baseline for the Divided-Screenwise Hierarchical (DSH) method. The specific origin paper is not explicitly named in the provided notes, but the analysis is attributed to and.
