name: DSH (Divided-Screenwise Hierarchical) method
head: Divided-Screenwise Hierarchical (DSH) Compositing
body: The DSH method is a sort-last parallel volume rendering compositing technique designed for high performance on distributed memory multiprocessors with a large number of processors. It solves the problem of redundant communication and inefficient load balancing in hierarchical compositing by dividing the screen into non-overlapping tile-shaped regions, dynamically assigning processors to these regions based on their data coverage, and compositing each region concurrently in a hierarchical order. Unlike the Block-Splitting (BS) method, DSH eliminates redundant communication between processors that lack common non-blank regions and allows up to D processors to merge the final image simultaneously, avoiding the bottleneck where only one processor merges the final image as in the BT method. The DSH method operates in three phases: preprocessing, dynamic assignment, and concurrent hierarchical compositing. Inputs: n: Number of processors (nodes). D: Number of screen divisions (regions). B = \{\tilde{B}^dq \mid 1 \le q \le n, 1 \le d \le D\}: Set of bounding rectangles of divided-subimages \tilde{I}^dq. Z = \{\tilde{B}q \mid 1 \le q \le n\}: Set of bounding rectangles of projected subvolumes \tilde{V}q. \tilde{I}q: The rendered subimage for processor q. Outputs: O = \{Od \mid 1 \le d \le D\}: Set of compositing order lists for each region. The final composited image. Bounding Rectangle (\tilde{B}): Defined by coordinates (x{min}, y{min}, x{max}, y{max}) and area A(\tilde{B}) = (x{max}-x{min})(y{max}-y{min}). Processor Set (Wd): A set of processor indices q that have non-blank pixels within region d. Compositing Order (Od): A list of stages, where each stage contains pairs (qs, ql) representing sender-receiver relationships for region d. 1. Screen Division: For each processor q (1 \le q \le n), divide the subimage \tilde{I}q into D non-overlapping tile-shaped regions to obtain divided-subimages \tilde{I}^1q, \tilde{I}^2q, \dots, \tilde{I}^Dq. 2. Preprocessing (Broadcast): Broadcast the coordinates of all bounding rectangles \tilde{B}q and \tilde{B}^dq from all processors to all other processors at the beginning of the compositing phase. This allows every processor to determine the processor sets Wd. 3. Determine Processor Sets and Compositing Order: For each region d (1 \le d \le D): a. Initialize Wd = \emptyset and Od = \emptyset. b. Identify processors with non-blank pixels in region d. A processor q is included in Wd if the bounding rectangle \tilde{B}^dq is within region d. The search space is reduced by referring to the coordinates of \tilde{B}q. c. While Wd is not empty, determine the compositing stage for region d: i. Let W{d,stg} = Wd. ii. Select the processor ql \in W{d,stg} with the largest bounding rectangle area A(\tilde{B}^d{ql}) as the receiver. iii. Select the processor qs \in W{d,stg} \setminus \{ql\} with the smallest bounding rectangle area A(\tilde{B}^d{qs}) as the sender. iv. Pair (qs, ql) and add to Od. v. Remove qs and ql from W{d,stg}. If |W{d,stg}| is odd, one processor remains unpaired (isolated) and stays in Wd for the next stage. vi. Update Wd = W{d,stg} for the next stage. Note: In the worst case, isolated processors exist between every pair, reducing |Wd| by a factor of 2/3 per stage. 4. Concurrent Hierarchical Compositing: For each region d (1 \le d \le D), execute the compositing stages defined in Od concurrently across all regions. a. For each stage k in Od: i. For each pair (qs, ql) in stage k: Processor qs transmits its non-blank pixels within \tilde{B}^d{qs} to ql. Processor ql composites the received pixels with its current buffer for region d. b. Use the Receiver First (RF) scheme: The receiver ql is selected first based on having the largest bounding rectangle, and the sender qs is selected from the remaining processors based on having the smallest bounding rectangle. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def area(rect): return (rect.xmax - rect.xmin) (rect.ymax - rect.ymin) def isempty(rect): return area(rect) == 0 def cropimage(img, rect): return img[rect.ymin:rect.ymax, rect.xmin:rect.xmax] def fronttobackcomposite(dst, src): return src + dst (1 - src.alpha) def determinecompositingorder(n, D, Bdivided, Bsubvolume): O = {} W = {} for d in range(1, D + 1): W[d] = set() for q in range(1, n + 1): Bdq = Bdivided[(q, d)] if Bdq is not None and not isempty(Bdq): W[d].add(q) for d in range(1, D + 1): Od = [] Wd = set(W[d]) while len(Wd) > 0: Wdstg = set(Wd) stagepairs = [] if len(Wdstg) == 0: break ql = max(Wdstg, key=lambda q: area(Bdivided[(q, d)])) remaining = Wdstg - {ql} if len(remaining) == 0: Wd = set() break qs = min(remaining, key=lambda q: area(Bdivided[(q, d)])) stagepairs.append((qs, ql)) Wdstg.remove(qs) Wdstg.remove(ql) Od.append(stagepairs) Wd = Wdstg O[d] = Od return O def compositeregiondsh(regiond, Wd, Od, Bdivided, images): localbuffers = {} for q in Wd: Bdq = Bdivided[(q, regiond)] localbuffers[q] = cropimage(images[q], Bdq) for stage in Od[regiond]: for qs, ql in stage: Bqs = Bdivided[(qs, regiond)] pixelstosend = cropimage(localbuffers[qs], Bqs) localbuffers[ql] = fronttobackcomposite(localbuffers[ql], pixelstosend) return localbuffers D: Number of screen divisions. Optimal Dm is determined by increasing D from n until T{DSH} starts to increase; Dm is the value giving the last decrease. Constraint D \ge n^{2/3}. c: Proportionality constant for the number of non-blank pixels transmitted by a processor at a stage. e: Proportionality constant for the number of processors engaged in a region. p: Number of pixels in the final image (context implies p n^{-2/3} is non-blank pixels per processor). g: Network latency or per-pixel transmission time constant. tc: Compositing time per pixel. o: Overhead per compositing stage. Bounding Rectangle Growth: If D is too small, bounding rectangles can grow to the size of the entire region, causing repeated transmission of large areas. Increasing D mitigates this. Excessive Division: If D is extremely large relative to n, the number of compositing stages increases rapidly, decreasing performance. Isolated Processors: In the worst case, isolated processors exist between every pair, reducing the effective processor set size by a factor of 2/3 per stage. A compositing pairing scheme used within DSH where the receiver ql is selected first (based on having the largest bounding rectangle) and the sender qs is selected from the remaining processors (based on having the smallest bounding rectangle). This scheme transmits 4% fewer pixels on average than the Sender First (SF) scheme because it allows fewer bounding rectangles to grow during compositing. A compositing pairing scheme compared against RF in DSH where the sender is selected first. It transmits slightly more pixels on average than RF and is not used in the optimal DSH implementation. Time Complexity (Stages): The number of compositing stages s{DSH} is bounded by s{DSH} \le D n^{-2/3} \lceil \log{3/2}(c n^{1/3}) \rceil. If concurrent compositing is performed in serial, s{DSH} = D n^{-2/3} \log{3/2}|Wd|. If performed fully independently, s{DSH} = \max(D n^{-2/3}, \log{3/2}|Wd|). Communication Complexity (Pixels): The number of transmitted pixels per processor c{DSH} is c{DSH} = s{DSH} \cdot (e p n^{-2/3} / D). Total Time: t{DSH} \le p (g + tc) \cdot \{ e n^{-4/3} \lceil \log{3/2}(c n^{1/3}) \rceil \} + o \cdot \{ D n^{-2/3} \lceil \log{3/2}(c n^{1/3}) \rceil \}. Performance: On a 64-node PC cluster, DSH renders a 512x512x224 voxel volume at approximately 8 fps. The maximum speedup of DSH over BS ranges from 1.4 to 2.2 when n=64 and D=64. The ratio of transmitted pixels C{DSH}/C{BS} decreases from 0.87 at n=2 to 0.22 at n=64. The compositing time ratio r{DSH} reaches a maximum of 22.2% of total rendering time as n increases. Strengths: Eliminates redundant communication; simplifies communication patterns via tile-shaped regions; allows parallel final merge; scales well with increasing n. Limitations: Requires preprocessing broadcast of bounding rectangles; performance depends on the efficiency of concurrent compositing; requires careful tuning of D. The DSH method was developed by Ino et al. and presented in 2003. It was designed for sort-last parallel volume rendering on distributed memory multiprocessors to address the limitations of existing methods like BS and BT, specifically focusing on maintaining high performance as the number of processors n increases. It builds on the DS method's screen division and the BT method's hierarchical compositing, but introduces dynamic assignment and tile-shaped regions to optimize communication. name: Rotate-Tiling (RT) Method
head: RT method
body: The Rotate-Tiling (RT) method is a sort-last parallel volume rendering compositing algorithm that allows the number of processors (P) and the number of initial image blocks (N) to be arbitrary positive integers. It solves the performance optimization problem of image compositing by deriving send/receive equations based on the indexing operations of the Block-Splitting (BS) method and the ring rotation topology of the Parallel Pipeline (PP) method. Unlike the BS method, which fixes N=2 and requires P to be a power of two, the RT method allows N to vary, enabling performance tuning for any P. Inputs and Outputs Inputs: P: Number of processors (P > 0). A: Final image size in pixels (assumed square or uniform distribution). N: Number of initial blocks per partial image (N > 0). Ts: Startup time of a communication channel. Tp: Data transmission time per byte. To: Computation time of the “over” operation per pixel. Outputs: A composite final image distributed across P processors. Data Structures Partial Image: Each processor Pr (rank r, 0 \le r \le P-1) holds a partial image A. Blocks: The partial image is divided into N equal blocks. Notation: Ar^k(b) represents the block of processor Pr with block number b in the k-th communication step. 0 \le b \le N-1 (initially), expanding as compositing proceeds. 0 \le r \le P-1. 1 \le k \le \lceil \log2 P \rceil. Algorithm Steps 1. Initialization: Each processor Pr partitions its partial image A into N equal blocks, numbered Ar^1(0) to Ar^1(N-1). 2. Communication Loop: For each communication step k from 1 to \lceil \log2 P \rceil: a. Determine Partners: Each processor Pr calculates the rank of the processor to send to (Pi) and the rank of the processor to receive from (Pj), along with the block indices m (send) and n (receive), using the equations below. b. Send/Receive: Pr sends block Ar^k(m) to Pi and receives block Aj^k(n) from Pj. c. Composite: Pr composites the received block Aj^k(n) with its local block Ar^k(n) using the standard volume rendering "over" operation. d. Tiling (Partition): For each block Ar^k(b) held by Pr, divide it into two equal sub-blocks: Ar^{k+1}(2b) and Ar^{k+1}(2b+1). This prepares the data for the next step where blocks are effectively merged and redistributed. Formulas The send and receive indices are calculated as follows, where l = 0 \dots k-1, w = 0 \dots P/N - 1, and v = 0 \dots P/2: Send Equation: m = ((r - 2 + 2l) \bmod 2^k) \times 2^{k-1} + v \times 2^{k-1} + l + P \times w i = (r - 2 + l) \bmod P Processor Pr sends block Ar^k(m) to processor Pi. Receive Equation: n = ((r + l) \bmod 2^k) \times 2^{k-1} + v \times 2^{k-1} + l + P \times w j = (r + 2 - l) \bmod P Processor Pr receives block Aj^k(n) from processor Pj. Block Size Evolution: Let Bk be the number of blocks associated with the tiling hierarchy at step k. B1 = N For k > 1: Bk = B{k-1} - \lfloor B{k-1} / P \rfloor. The size of the block sent/received in step k is proportional to A \cdot Bk / 2^{k-1}. Total Time Complexity: The total compositing time T{total}(RT) is given by: T{total}(RT) = \left( \left\lceil \frac{N}{P} \right\rceil + \left\lceil \frac{2N}{P} \right\rceil \right) Ts + \sum{k=1}^{\lceil \log2 P \rceil} \left[ \left\lceil \frac{2 Bk}{P} \right\rceil \frac{A}{2^{k-1}} (Tp + To) \right] Note: The source provides a more detailed expansion involving ceiling functions for communication steps and computation steps. The simplified form above captures the dominant terms derived from the cost model where communication and computation are summed. A more precise formulation from the source for T{RT}(N) is: T{RT}(N) = \left( \sum{k=1}^{\lceil \log2 P \rceil} \left\lceil \frac{2 Bk}{P} \right\rceil + \left\lceil \frac{A}{P} \right\rceil - \left\lceil \frac{N}{P} \right\rceil \right) Ts + N \left( \sum{k=1}^{\lceil \log2 P \rceil} \left\lceil \frac{2 Bk}{P} \right\rceil \frac{1}{2^{k-1}} + \left\lceil \frac{2N}{P} \right\rceil - \left\lceil \frac{N}{P} \right\rceil \right) (Tp + To) where Bk depends on N. Optimization of N: To find the optimal N, calculate the difference \Delta T = T{RT}(N+1) - T{RT}(N). Set \Delta T = 0 to solve for the theoretical best N. The equation is: \left( \sum{k'=1}^{\lceil \log2 P \rceil} \left\lceil \frac{2 B{k'}}{P} \right\rceil + \left\lceil \frac{A}{P} \right\rceil - \left\lceil \frac{N+1}{P} \right\rceil \right) - \left( \sum{k=1}^{\lceil \log2 P \rceil} \left\lceil \frac{2 Bk}{P} \right\rceil + \left\lceil \frac{A}{P} \right\rceil - \left\lceil \frac{N}{P} \right\rceil \right) + (N+1)\left(\sum{k'=1}^{\lceil \log2 P \rceil} \left\lceil \frac{2 B{k'}}{P} \right\rceil \frac{1}{2^{k'-1}} + \left\lceil \frac{2N+2}{P} \right\rceil - \left\lceil \frac{N+1}{P} \right\rceil \right) - N\left(\sum{k=1}^{\lceil \log2 P \rceil} \left\lceil \frac{2 Bk}{P} \right\rceil \frac{1}{2^{k-1}} + \left\lceil \frac{2N}{P} \right\rceil - \left\lceil \frac{N}{P} \right\rceil \right) = \frac{Tp + To}{Ts} A Solving this yields the theoretical best N. name: Direct Send Compositing
head: Direct Send
body: Direct Send Compositing is the simplest parallel image compositing technique for sort-last volume rendering, where each processor sends its partial image pixel data directly to the specific processor responsible for compositing that image partition. It solves the problem of global image assembly in a distributed memory system by avoiding the exchange of full-size images, instead exchanging only the specific tiles assigned to each processor. Unlike Binary Swap, which uses a hierarchical tree structure to reduce network congestion, Direct Send performs a single stage of all-to-all communication, making it easier to implement but potentially prone to link contention. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Partial image tiles rendered by N processors. Each processor p holds a full-size image of resolution S \times S, but is responsible for compositing only a specific tile (partition) of the final image. Output: The final composited image, assembled from the tiles processed by each processor. Data Structures: Image Tile: A 2D array of pixel values (e.g., RGBA). The size of the tile depends on the number of processors N and the total image resolution. If the image is divided into N equal tiles, the tile dimensions are S \times (S/N) (assuming horizontal striping) or similar partitioning. Message Buffer: A contiguous block of memory containing the pixel data for the tile that processor p needs to send to processor q. Steps: 1. Tile Assignment: The final image is divided into N screen-space tiles. Each processor p is assigned one unique tile Tp to composite. 2. Data Exchange (All-to-All): Each processor p sends its rendered partial image data for every tile Tq (where q \neq p) to the processor q responsible for compositing Tq. Simultaneously, each processor p receives the partial image data for its assigned tile Tp from all other N-1 processors. This constitutes a single stage of all-to-all communication. 3. Local Compositing: Once all required tiles have arrived, each processor p composites its assigned tile Tp independently. Compositing involves sorting the volume samples (ray-casting fragments) by depth and blending them according to the volume rendering integral equation (e.g., standard front-to-back alpha blending). 4. Final Gathering: Each processor sends its fully composited tile Tp to a designated master process (or all processors, depending on the implementation) for final assembly into the complete image. Formulas: Let N be the number of processors. Let P be the total number of pixels in the final image. Let P{sendrecv} be the number of pixels a processor sends and receives. Let N{sendrecv} be the number of messages a processor sends and receives. Number of messages per processor: N{sendrecv} = N - 1 Number of pixels sent/received per processor: P{sendrecv} = P \times \left(1 - \frac{1}{N}\right) Total compositing time for a processor (T{comp}): T{comp} = T{exchange} + T{blend} Where T{exchange} is the time for sending and receiving, and T{blend} is the time for blending. Assuming full-duplex communication and equal latency/bandwidth for send/receive: T{exchange} = \max(L{send} + T{send}, L{recv} + T{recv}) With: L{send} = N{sendrecv} \times l{sendrecv} T{send} = \frac{P{sendrecv}}{B{sendrecv}} And blending time: T{blend} = \frac{P{blend}}{B{blend}} Where: l{sendrecv}: Latency per message. B{sendrecv}: Network bandwidth for sending/receiving. B{blend}: Blending speed (pixels per second). P{blend}: Number of pixels to blend (typically P/N). Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def directsendcompositing(rank, numprocs, imageresolution, renderfunction, compositefunction): """ rank: Current processor ID (0 to numprocs - 1) numprocs: Total number of processors N imageresolution: Tuple (width, height) of the final image renderfunction: Function that renders the volume and returns partial image tiles compositefunction: Function that composites a tile from received partial images """ # 1. Render the volume # Each processor renders the entire volume but only stores/keeps the fragments # relevant to its assigned tile. However, for Direct Send, it must send # all its rendered fragments to all other processors. # In practice, this means rendering the full image but partitioning the output. mypartialimage = renderfunction(rank, numprocs) # Determine tile assignment # Assuming horizontal striping for simplicity tileheight = imageresolution[1] // numprocs mytileid = rank mytileystart = mytileid tileheight mytileyend = mytileystart + tileheight # 2. All-to-All Communication # Each processor sends its partial image to all other processors # and receives partial images from all other processors. # In MPI, this is MPIAlltoall. # Prepare send buffer: list of partial images to send to each rank # Each processor sends its entire rendered partial image to everyone. sendbuffers = [mypartialimage] numprocs # Prepare receive buffer: list to store received partial images recvbuffers = [None] numprocs # Perform all-to-all exchange # Note: In a real implementation, this would be an MPI call. # Here we simulate the data flow. for targetrank in range(numprocs): if targetrank != rank: # Send mypartialimage to targetrank # Receive partial image from targetrank into recvbuffers[targetrank] pass # MPIAlltoall(sendbuffers, recvbuffers) # 3. Local Compositing # Each processor composites its assigned tile using the received partial images # from all other processors. # Collect all partial images relevant to mytileid # Since every processor sent its full partial image, we need to extract # the fragments that fall within mytileystart to mytileyend. # However, the standard Direct Send model assumes each processor sends # the specific tile data it rendered. If the render function returns # the full image, we must slice it. receivedfragments = [] for sourcerank in range(numprocs): # Extract the portion of the received image that corresponds to my tile # This assumes the received image is the full resolution or properly partitioned fragment = extracttile(recvbuffers[sourcerank], mytileystart, mytileyend) receivedfragments.append(fragment) # Composite the tile compositedtile = compositefunction(receivedfragments, mytileystart, mytileyend) # 4. Final Gathering # Send the composited tile to the master process if rank == 0: mastertile = compositedtile # Receive tiles from all other ranks for r in range(1, numprocs): othertile = receivetilefrom(r) # Assemble the final image pass else: sendtileto(0, compositedtile) return compositedtile if rank == 0 else None Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Link Contention: Because all processors send to all other processors simultaneously, link contention is likely to occur, especially on networks with limited bandwidth or non-full-duplex capabilities. Message Size Limits: On some systems (e.g., Cray XT4 with MPICH), large data sizes and all-to-all communication can exceed MPI capabilities, causing failures beyond a certain number of processors (e.g., 1021 processors for 4096^2 images). Protocol Switching: Timing drops can occur when the message size exceeds the MPICHMAXSHORTMSGSIZE (default 128000 bytes), switching from short (eager) to long message protocols, which increases latency. Power of Two: Unlike Binary Swap, Direct Send does not require the number of processors to be a power of two. Tiling Compositing is a parallel compositing strategy for distributed volume rendering where processing elements (PEs) hold tiles of the final image and pass partial results to adjacent PEs in a staggered, linear fashion to merge them into the final image. It solves the problem of global image assembly in a distributed memory system by avoiding the exchange of full-size images, instead exchanging only the specific tile assigned to each PE. Unlike the inverted binary tree method, which leaves a majority of PEs idle during latter cycles, tiling keeps all PEs working on the problem until the final image is completed. Parallel Compositing is a distributed rendering technique that partitions the final image into spatial tiles, assigning each tile to a specific compositing task. It solves the bottleneck of global image assembly by exchanging only the ray-casting fragments relevant to each tile, performing local compositing, and gathering the result. It differs from Direct Send Compositing by using a collective MPIAlltoallv communication pattern rather than explicit point-to-point sends, and from Tiling Compositing by its specific reliance on the Alltoallv primitive for fragment exchange. SLIC Parallel Image Compositing is an optimized parallel image compositing algorithm for sort-last rendering that minimizes the number of messages exchanged among processors using a view-dependent precomputed compositing schedule. It solves the bottleneck of Direct Send by reducing the total amount of data sent over the network. The algorithm involves a preprocessing step (overhead < 10ms) to compute a compositing schedule for each new view, which is then used to minimize data transmission. SLIC outperforms previous algorithms, especially for high-resolution images (1024x1024 pixels or larger). On low-bandwidth networks, care must be taken to avoid many-to-one or many-to-many communication patterns inherent in direct send. Time and Memory Complexity: Communication Steps: Direct Send requires only one stage of all-to-all communication. Messages: In the worst case, N \times (N - 1) messages are exchanged among N compositing processors. Data Volume: Each processor sends and receives P \times (1 - 1/N) pixels, where P is the total number of pixels in the image. Memory: Each processor must store the full partial image it rendered and the partial images received from all other processors before compositing. Measured Performance: On the Cray XT4 machine, Direct Send failed beyond 1021 processors for 4096^2 images due to MPI limitations with large data sizes. Performance drops significantly when message sizes exceed the short message protocol threshold (e.g., 128000 bytes in MPICH). Direct Send scales poorly compared to Binary Swap or 2-3 Swap as the number of processors increases, due to the O(N^2) message complexity and network congestion. Strengths and Limitations: Strengths: Simplest implementation; requires only one communication stage; does not require the number of processors to be a power of two; works well for small numbers of processors or high-bandwidth networks. Limitations: Prone to link contention; poor scalability for large N; high communication overhead; sensitive to network topology and MPI implementation limits. When to Use: Use Direct Send when the number of processors is small, the network bandwidth is high, and implementation simplicity is prioritized over scalability. Avoid Direct Send when the number of processors is large, the network is congested, or the image resolution is very high, leading to large message sizes. Direct Send Compositing was introduced as the simplest image compositing technique for sort-last parallel rendering. It has been used often in prior work. The method is based on the idea that each processor sends its pixel data directly to the processor responsible for the corresponding image partition in a single stage of communication. It is often compared with Binary Swap, which was proposed to reduce network congestion by using a hierarchical communication scheme. name: Tiling Compositing
head: Linear Tiling, Staggered Tiling
body: Tiling Compositing is a parallel compositing strategy for distributed volume rendering where processing elements (PEs) hold tiles of the final image and pass partial results to adjacent PEs in a staggered, linear fashion to merge them into the final image. Unlike the inverted binary tree method, which leaves a majority of PEs idle during latter cycles, tiling keeps all PEs working on the problem until the final image is completed. Inputs and Outputs: Input: n processing elements (PEs), indexed 0 to n-1. Each PE i initially holds a local tile Ti of the final image. Output: A fully composited final image distributed across the PEs. Data Structures: Tile (Ti): A 2D array of pixels representing a portion of the screen. For typical views, a tile might be 100 pixels wide with 4 floating-point values per pixel, totaling ~150 KB. Parameters: n: The number of processing elements in the system. Cycle count: n-1 cycles are required to complete the compositing. Steps: 1. Initialization: Each PE i holds its local tile Ti. 2. Loop over Cycles: Repeat for c = 0 to n-2: a. Communication: Each PE sends its current tile to its right neighbor and receives a tile from its left neighbor. In each of the n-1 cycles, n messages are sent across the network (each PE must receive one message). b. Compositing: The PE composites the received tile with its local tile. The standard volume rendering compositing operation (e.g., front-to-back alpha compositing) is applied. 3. Termination: After n-1 cycles, all tiles have been propagated and composited across the network. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def tilingcompositing(n, myid, mytile): currenttile = mytile # The algorithm requires n-1 cycles for cycle in range(n - 1): # Linear staggered shift: PE i sends to i+1, receives from i-1 neighborsend = myid + 1 neighborrecv = myid - 1 # Send current tile to right neighbor if neighborsend < n: # Standard point-to-point message send operation pass # Receive tile from left neighbor if neighborrecv >= 0: # Standard point-to-point message receive operation receivedtile = None # Placeholder for receive # Apply standard front-to-back compositing currenttile = composite(currenttile, receivedtile) return currenttile def composite(tilea, tileb): # Standard volume rendering compositing operator (e.g., front-to-back alpha blending) return tilea # Stub Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Network Contention: Network contention becomes a severe concern due to the high volume of traffic: n messages are sent across the network in every cycle. Memory Contention: Memory contention is eliminated by the staggered nature of the tiling approach. Small n: For 8 or fewer PEs, there is no discernible difference in compositing times compared to the inverted binary tree method. A technique that generalizes screen tiles to be composites of multiple stacked tiles, adding an additional composite phase at the end of rendering algorithms to allow machines with many nodes to maintain larger tiles and minimize volume data replication during redistribution. This technique allows machines with large numbers of nodes to maintain larger tiles, thereby minimizing the replication of volume data during redistribution compared to using smaller tiles. A method to perform the global gather operation with minimal communication by keeping volume blocks stationary (except for load balancing) and transferring the 2D tiles generated by projection, rather than transferring 3D volume blocks. Step 1 (Projection): Each node generates projected two-dimensional tiles from the blocks it holds. Step 2 (Composition): Overlapping sets of tiles are collected at some location to be composited together. An image partition is used to assign single large regions of the screen to processors for the composition step; each processor receives a copy of all tiles that overlap its region of the screen. This method transfers tiles rather than blocks because typical blocks (2-4 MB) are larger than typical tiles (150 KB). It differs from the alternative image partition method where volume blocks are sent to nodes, which may require the entire dataset to move for each frame. Time Complexity: The algorithm requires n-1 communication cycles, where n is the number of PEs. Memory Contention: Memory contention is eliminated by the staggered nature of the tiling approach. Network Traffic: n messages are sent across the network in every cycle, leading to high network occupancy. Performance: For 8 or fewer PEs, there is no discernible difference in compositing times compared to the inverted binary tree method. As the number of PEs increases, the tiling approach is superior because it keeps all PEs working, whereas the inverted binary tree leaves a majority of PEs idle during latter cycles. Strengths: Eliminates memory contention; maintains high PE utilization for large n. Limitations: Severe network contention due to high message volume. When to use: Suitable for large-scale systems with many PEs where PE utilization is critical and network bandwidth is sufficient to handle the linear traffic pattern. When not to use: Unsuitable for small numbers of PEs (≤8) where the overhead is not justified, or in systems with severe network contention issues. Tiling Compositing was examined in the context of high-resolution interactive volume rendering on the Cray T3D. It was compared against an inverted binary tree method for compositing partially completed raster images in a distributed memory environment. The approach is intuitively appropriate for distributed systems as it keeps all processing elements working on the problem until the final image is completed. name: Parallel Compositing
head: Fragment Compositing, MPI Alltoallv Compositing
body: Parallel Compositing is a distributed rendering technique that partitions the final image into spatial tiles, assigning each tile to a specific compositing task. It solves the bottleneck of global image assembly by exchanging only the ray-casting fragments relevant to each tile, performing local compositing, and gathering the result. It differs from Direct Send Compositing by using a collective MPIAlltoallv communication pattern rather than explicit point-to-point sends, and from Tiling Compositing by its specific reliance on the Alltoallv primitive for fragment exchange. Inputs: A set of N tasks. Ray-casting fragments generated by each task, where each fragment contains color, opacity, and depth information for a ray segment. The final image resolution and the partitioning scheme. Outputs: The final composited image, gathered on the root task. Data Structures: Fragment Buffer: A contiguous memory block holding all fragments generated by a task. The layout is not explicitly defined in the sources, but fragments are packed into a single buffer per socket in hybrid implementations. Image Partition: The image is divided into K tiles. Each task owns one or more tiles. Parameters: Compositing Tasks Ratio: The ratio of total tasks to active compositing tasks. Typical values are 4 or 5, depending on memory constraints. Max Receiving Tasks: To mitigate scaling issues, the number of tasks receiving fragments is limited. Emulated values cap this at 2,000, though higher values were experimented with. Steps: 1. Partition: Divide the pixels of the final image across the available tasks. Each task is assigned a specific region (tile) of the image. 2. Exchange: Perform an MPIAlltoallv call to exchange fragments. Each task sends its generated fragments to the tasks that own the image regions where those fragments lie. In hybrid-memory implementations, only one thread per socket participates in compositing. This thread gathers fragments from all other threads in the same socket, packs them into a single buffer, and transmits it. 3. Composite: For each pixel in its assigned region, perform the final compositing using the 'over' operator (C{out} = C{in} + C{frag}(1 - \alpha{in})). 4. Gather: Collect the final composited image tiles from all tasks onto the root task. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def parallelcompositing(taskid, numtasks, fragments, imagewidth, imageheight, compositingratio): # 1. Partition # Determine which image tiles this task owns based on taskid and compositingratio. # The sources do not specify the exact partitioning algorithm (e.g., block, cyclic). # Assume a simple block distribution for illustration. tilespertask = numtasks // compositingratio mytilestart = (taskid % compositingratio) tilespertask mytileend = mytilestart + tilespertask # 2. Exchange (MPIAlltoallv) # In hybrid mode, gather fragments from local threads first. # Assuming 'gatherlocalfragments' is a local operation. localbuffer = gatherlocalfragments(fragments) # MPIAlltoallv sends localbuffer to all compositing tasks. # The sendcounts and recvcounts depend on the number of fragments # destined for each task. # The exact send/recv counts are not provided in sources. receivedfragments = mpialltoallv(localbuffer, sendcounts, recvcounts) # 3. Composite # For each pixel in my tiles, composite the received fragments. # The 'over' operator is standard: Cout = Cin + Cfrag (1 - alphain) for tile in range(mytilestart, mytileend): for pixel in getpixelsintile(tile, imagewidth, imageheight): pixelcolor = compositeover(receivedfragments, pixel) # 4. Gather # Gather the final image tiles to the root task. # Assuming a standard MPIGather or MPIGatherv. finalimage = mpigather(mytileresults, root=0) return finalimage Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Scaling Limits: Using more than 8,000 tasks causes scaling difficulties due to communication overhead. This is mitigated by limiting the number of tasks receiving fragments to ~2,000. Message Size: The total message size in MPIAlltoallv is greater than in binary swap algorithms because intermediate compositing is not performed during exchange. Time Complexity: Dominated by the MPIAlltoallv communication step. The number of messages is similar to sophisticated algorithms like binary swap, but the total data volume is higher. Memory Complexity: Depends on the fragment buffer size. Hybrid implementations reduce memory pressure by aggregating fragments per socket. Performance: On small scales, this method performs well. However, optimized binary swap or Radix-K implementations can outperform this approach by up to 40%. Strengths: Simpler implementation than binary swap; leverages MPI optimizations for collective operations; effective in hybrid-memory environments by reducing message count. Limitations: Higher total message size than binary swap; scaling issues beyond 8,000 tasks without fragment receiver limiting. Parallel Compositing was analyzed in the context of hybrid parallelism for volume rendering on large multi- and many-core systems. The approach emulates techniques from Peterka et al.. The study compared this method against binary swap and direct send strategies, highlighting the trade-offs between communication volume and algorithmic complexity. name: Sort-middle Parallel Rendering
body: Sort-middle parallel rendering is a distributed rendering strategy that partitions the workload between the geometry processing (transformation and lighting) stage and the rasterization stage. Unlike sort-first methods, which distribute primitives before transformation, sort-middle allows geometry processors to handle arbitrary subsets of primitives and then routes the transformed primitives to specific rasterizers based on screen-space coverage. This approach is chosen when high-bandwidth interconnects are available to handle the transfer of transformed primitives, offering a frame-rate advantage over sort-first by avoiding network delays associated with pre-transformation distribution. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A set of 3D primitives (e.g., triangles, voxels) and a set of geometry processors (G1 \dots Gm) and rasterizers (R1 \dots Rn). Output: A composite image. Data Structures: Primitive List: Unsorted collection of primitives. Transformed Primitive Buffer: Stores primitives after transformation and lighting. Screen Partition Map: Defines which rasterizer is responsible for which region of the screen. Steps: 1. Assignment: Distribute the input primitives arbitrarily among the available geometry processors. 2. Geometry Processing: Each geometry processor Gi performs transformation and lighting on its assigned primitives. 3. Routing: Determine the screen-space bounding box or coverage of each transformed primitive. Send each transformed primitive to the rasterizer(s) responsible for the screen regions it overlaps. 4. Rasterization: Each rasterizer Rj rasterizes the subset of primitives routed to it. 5. Compositing: Combine the results from all rasterizers to form the final image. If rasterizers write to separate framebuffers, a final compositing step merges them. Pitfalls: Load Imbalance: Primitives may cluster in specific screen regions, causing uneven workloads among rasterizers. Bandwidth: High bandwidth is required for transferring transformed primitives from geometry processors to rasterizers. Combines shared-memory and distributed-memory parallelism to balance scalability and communication overhead. Performance: Achieves approximately twice the frame-rate of sort-first approaches by reducing network delays associated with sending primitives before transformation. Scalability: Scales well with the number of geometry processors, but is limited by the bandwidth of the interconnect between geometry and rasterization stages. Limitations: Suffers from load imbalance if primitives are unevenly distributed over the screen. Requires high-bandwidth networks for data transfer between stages. The sort-middle approach was developed to address the inefficiencies of sort-first rendering in distributed systems, such as the Chromium system, where network delays for pre-transformation primitive distribution were significant. Williams and Hiromoto modified Chromium to implement sort-middle, allowing it to achieve higher frame-rates. The approach became popular due to the availability of high-end graphics machines capable of handling the required data transfer rates. name: Parallel Rendering (Hybrid Systems)
head: Hybrid Parallel Rendering, Shared-Distributed Memory Hybrid Rendering
body: Parallel Rendering (Hybrid Systems) is a sort-middle parallel rendering approach that combines shared-memory and distributed-memory parallelism to render volume data on clusters of multicore processors or heterogeneous systems. It solves the scalability and communication overhead limitations of pure distributed-memory systems by reducing the number of distributed compositing nodes while leveraging high-concurrency shared-memory threads. Unlike pure shared-memory systems, which are limited by single-node memory capacity, or pure distributed-memory systems, which suffer from high communication traffic, hybrid systems balance these by partitioning both data and image space to maintain work coherence. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Volume dataset, camera parameters, rendering resolution. Output: Composite image. Data Structures: The system partitions the image space (pixels) and potentially the data space (voxels) across nodes. Each node manages a local shared-memory pool (e.g., GPU memory or CPU cache) and communicates with other nodes via distributed memory interfaces (e.g., MPI). Steps: 1. Partitioning: Distribute the image space across the available nodes using an image-space partitioning scheme. Optionally, partition the data space as well to keep the distribution of work coherent. 2. Raycasting (Shared Memory): Within each node, perform raycasting using dynamically-scheduled, image-based decomposition. This phase utilizes shared-memory parallelism (e.g., CUDA threads, pthreads, or OpenMP) to scale to high concurrencies per node (thousands of threads). 3. Compositing (Distributed Memory): Composite the partial results from the raycasting phase. The number of compositing tasks (nodes) is kept relatively low compared to the total number of rendering threads to reduce communication overhead. 4. Cache Coherence: Maintain cache coherence throughout execution to prevent performance deterioration. Parameters and Optimization: Concurrency: The number of compositing tasks (nodes) should be optimized. Peterka et al. observed that 1,000 to 2,000 compositors were optimal for up to 32,768 total tasks in strong scaling studies. Weak Scaling: In weak scaling scenarios, using a larger subset of compositing tasks (2,000 to 30,000) is optimal, as smaller subsets lead to overallocation of temporary data structures and MPI buffers. Hardware: The method benefits from high core-to-node ratios, such as multi-core CPUs or many-core GPUs. Pitfalls: Failing to maintain cache coherence throughout execution progressively deteriorates overall system performance. Setting the number of compositing tasks too small in weak scaling studies leads to overallocation from temporary data structures and MPI buffers, as additional data is concentrated in fewer compositors. A parallelism strategy combining distributed memory (MPI) and shared memory (pthreads/OpenMP/CUDA) to enable performance gains and reduced resource usage compared to distributed-memory-only implementations on large supercomputers. Advantages include reduced memory footprint, reduced MPI overhead, and reduced communication traffic. It uses dynamically-scheduled, image-based decomposition in the raycasting phase to scale well to high concurrencies per node (thousands of threads in CUDA). Peterka et al. first observed that the reduced number of compositors at higher concurrencies increased overall performance, concluding 1,000 to 2,000 compositors were optimal for up to 32,768 total tasks. Time Complexity: The raycasting phase scales well with the number of shared-memory threads per node. The compositing phase performance is influenced by the number of nodes; decreasing the absolute number of nodes improves communication performance during compositing. Memory Complexity: Reduced memory footprint compared to pure distributed-memory implementations. Performance: Hybrid parallelism enables performance gains and uses less resources than distributed-memory implementations on large supercomputers. For example, hybrid/CUDA runs showed compositing times half that of hybrid-memory runs at high concurrency. Strengths: Reduced MPI overhead, reduced communication traffic, and ability to leverage high-concurrency shared-memory resources. Limitations: Scalability is limited by the need to maintain cache coherence. Pure shared-memory systems are prohibitively expensive to build with large amounts of memory and cannot easily be extended. Hybrid systems were developed to address the limitations of pure shared-memory and pure distributed-memory rendering systems. Shared-memory systems offer faster communication but are limited by scalability and memory capacity. Distributed-memory systems scale better but suffer from high communication overhead. Hybrid approaches mix features of both, using clusters of multicore processors. Peterka et al. [4] were among the first to observe the performance benefits of reducing the number of compositors at higher concurrencies. The approach is particularly relevant for multi-core CPU systems with increasing core counts and heterogeneous systems with many-core GPUs. name: Temporal Division of Uniform Resolution Data
head: Data streaming, Frame multiplexing, Temporal Decomposition, Time-step Parallelism
body: Temporal division of uniform resolution data is a parallelism strategy for time-varying volume rendering where computational tasks are distributed across processors based on time steps rather than spatial regions. It solves the problem of rendering large, multi-frame datasets by assigning unique groups of time steps to each processor, ensuring all processors remain busy and the frame generation rate matches the display rate. Unlike spatial decomposition methods such as Parallel Image Compositing with Overlapping, temporal division does not require breaking up a single data file between processors, which reduces preprocessing overhead and allows different time steps to reside on different processors. The approach encompasses two variants: frame multiplexing, where each processor is assigned a unique group of time steps, and data streaming, where all processors work jointly on each time step. Inputs: A sequence of N time steps of volume data, each of uniform resolution. A set of P processors. Outputs: A sequence of rendered frames displayed in temporal order (1, 2, \dots, N). Frame Pool: A buffer that stores completed frames from processors, indexed by their time step ID. Assignment Map: A mapping of processor IDs to their assigned time step indices. For uniform interleaving, Processor p (where 1 \le p \le P) is assigned time steps t such that p = ((t - 1) \pmod P) + 1. 1. Assignment: Assign time steps to processors in a round-robin or interleaved fashion. For example, with 3 processors and 9 time steps: Processor 1 gets steps 1, 4, 7; Processor 2 gets steps 2, 5, 8; Processor 3 gets steps 3, 6, 9. 2. Rendering: Each processor renders its assigned time steps sequentially. Upon completion, it adds the resulting image to the Frame Pool. 3. Sequencing: A display system or sequencer picks frames from the pool in increasing time order. It displays frame t, then increments the target time to t+1 and waits for that frame if it is not yet available. 4. Loop: Processors continue rendering their next assigned time step immediately after finishing the previous one. The pipeline aims to ensure a frame is ready before it is needed, eliminating lag after an initial startup delay. Interleaving Assignment: For Processor p (1-indexed) and Time Step t (1-indexed): p = ((t - 1) \pmod P) + 1 Pipeline Timing: Ideally, the system ensures a frame is ready before it is needed, eliminating lag after an initial startup delay. P (Number of Processors): Determines the stride of the interleaving. N (Total Time Steps): The total number of frames in the sequence. Late Frames: If a processor slows down, its assigned frame may arrive late. This causes the sequencer to wait, resulting in fluctuating frame rates or animation pauses. Initial Lag: There is an initial startup delay while the first set of frames is generated. Variable Rendering Time: If time steps have varying computational costs (e.g., due to adaptive resolution), simple interleaving leads to load imbalance. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. P = 3 # Number of processors N = 9 # Total time steps framepool = {} # Dictionary mapping timestepid -> imagedata def renderloop(processorid): """Each processor runs this loop. processorid is 1-indexed (1 to P).""" for t in range(processorid, N + 1, P): # Load volume data for time step t (standard I/O) # Render volume step (standard ray-casting/compositing) image = rendervolumestep(t) framepool[t] = image # Loop continues to next assigned step immediately def displayloop(): """The sequencer runs this loop.""" currentdisplaytime = 1 while currentdisplaytime <= N: # Wait for the frame to be available while currentdisplaytime not in framepool: pass # Synchronization wait # Display frame from pool displayimage(framepool[currentdisplaytime]) currentdisplaytime += 1 1D Input Processors (1DIP) is a parallel I/O strategy that uses multiple input processors to fetch and preprocess a single complete time step of volume data, maximizing parallel file system bandwidth. It differs from its sibling 2D Input Processors (2DIP) by focusing on parallelizing the read of one time step rather than concurrently reading multiple time steps, making it suitable when sending time per time step is the bottleneck. 2D Input Processors (2DIP) is a parallel I/O strategy for rendering large time-varying volume data that addresses the bottleneck where the data sending time (Ts) exceeds the rendering time (Tr). Unlike 1D Input Processors (1DIP), which distributes a single time step across multiple input processors to reduce send time, 2DIP concurrently reads and distributes multiple time steps using a two-dimensional configuration of input processors. This ensures that rendering processors remain busy by overlapping I/O and preprocessing of future time steps with the rendering of the current one. A technique to hide latency by decoupling the display phase from the rendering and I/O phases, showing only approximate images while no reliable image information is available. The system displays and warps approximate images based on 2.5D data while no newly rendered image data is available from the remote servers. This approach achieves interactive frame rates of approximately 30 Hz, necessary for virtual reality applications. A load-balancing strategy for temporal division where time steps are assigned to processors based on their resolution (computational cost) rather than simple interleaving. The system calculates the relative cost/resolution of each time step and assigns fewer high-resolution time steps to processors and more low-resolution time steps to balance the total workload. In a specific example, Processor 1 was assigned 3 high-resolution frames and Processor 2 was assigned 6 low-resolution frames to achieve equal work distribution. A post-processing step for temporal division where completed frames from a pool are displayed in increasing time order. The sequencer maintains a pool of frames; when a processor finishes a time step, it adds the image to the pool. The sequencer picks the frame for the current time step from the pool and displays it, then increments the time and repeats. To mitigate late frames, a time lag can be introduced at the start to ensure enough frames are in the pool, or a fixed display time for each frame can be set equal to the max rendering time of any resolution. A pitfall is that if a processor slows down, frames arrive late, causing the animation to wait and resulting in fluctuating frame rates. Time Complexity: Each processor renders its assigned time steps sequentially, dividing the workload equally among processors. Memory Complexity: Each processor stores only the time steps assigned to it, allowing very large datasets that do not fit in one processor's memory to be rendered by placing only a few time steps on each computer. Performance: STARVolume uses this method to render huge datasets at high speeds, allowing equal workload division among processors. Strengths: Reduces preprocessing work by avoiding file splitting; allows large datasets that do not fit in one processor's memory to be rendered by distributing time steps across nodes. Limitations: Requires synchronization for display sequencing; susceptible to frame rate fluctuations if rendering times vary significantly between time steps. Temporal division techniques were described by Bhaniramka et al.. Two primary techniques were identified: frame multiplexing (where each processor is assigned a group of unique time steps) and data streaming (where all processors work jointly on each time step). STARVolume uses the frame multiplexing approach for temporal parallel rendering. This method is distinct from spatial decomposition approaches like sort-last rendering, which require complex compositing algorithms. name: 1D Input Processors (1DIP)
head: 1D Input Processing, 1DIP, 1DIP strategy
body: 1D Input Processors (1DIP) is a parallel I/O strategy that uses multiple input processors to fetch and preprocess a single complete time step of volume data, maximizing parallel file system bandwidth. It differs from its sibling 2D Input Processors (2DIP) by focusing on parallelizing the read of one time step rather than concurrently reading multiple time steps, making it suitable when sending time per time step is the bottleneck. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Raw volume data for a single time step stored on a parallel file system. Output: Preprocessed data blocks sent to rendering processors. Data Structures: Rendering processors maintain local buffers to merge incoming data into complete octree blocks. Steps: 1. Fetch: m input processors concurrently read the complete single time step from the parallel file system. 2. Preprocess: Each input processor preprocesses its fetched data, which may include load balancing calculations and data quantization. 3. Send: Input processors send the preprocessed data to rendering processors. 4. Merge: Each rendering processor merges incoming data from the input processors to form complete local octree blocks without inter-processor communication. Formula: The optimal number of input processors m is calculated to hide I/O and preprocessing costs behind rendering time: m = \frac{Tf + Tp}{Ts} + 1 Where: Tf: Time to fetch the data from the file system. Tp: Preprocessing time (including load balancing and quantization). Ts: Time to send the data to a rendering processor. If the sending time Ts is smaller than the rendering time Tr, the formula can be adjusted to use fewer input processors while keeping rendering processors busy: m = \frac{Tf + Tp}{Tr} + 1 Parameters: Tf, Tp, Ts, Tr: Measured in seconds. On LeMieux with 64 rendering processors and 512×512 image resolution, Tr \approx 2\text{s}, Tf \approx 12.32\text{s}, and Tp \approx 9.06\text{s} for complex quantization. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: If Ts becomes larger than Tr, 1DIP becomes less scalable compared to 2DIP. Preprocessing cost can vary significantly; using simpler quantization methods can reduce Tp substantially. The strategy assumes that the overhead of collective I/O is too high, making independent reads preferable. Time Complexity: The total time per time step is dominated by the rendering time when m is optimal, effectively hiding I/O and preprocessing costs. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Measured Performance: On LeMieux (HP/Compaq AlphaServer, 3,000 processors) with 64 rendering processors and 512×512 image resolution: 1 input processor: I/O+preprocessing \approx 22\text{s}, rendering \approx 2\text{s}. 12 input processors: I/O+preprocessing \approx 2\text{s}, matching rendering time. At 1024×1024 resolution, rendering time increases to 3.63s, requiring only 7 input processors to match total time. Scaling: 1DIP is less scalable than 2DIP at high processor counts. With 256 rendering processors, 2DIP can hide I/O with m=14, but 1DIP cannot. Strengths: Maximizes file system bandwidth for single time steps; effective when sending time is significant. Limitations: Less scalable than 2DIP at high processor counts; requires careful tuning of m. When to use: When rendering time is significant and sending time per time step is a bottleneck, and when collective I/O overhead is high. When not to use: When rendering processor counts are high enough that 2DIP can hide I/O/preprocessing costs while 1DIP cannot. 1DIP was introduced by Hongfeng Yu, Kwan-Liu Ma, and Joel Welling in their 2004 paper "I/O Strategies for Parallel Rendering of Large Time-Varying Volume Data". It was tested on the LeMieux system at the Pittsburgh Supercomputing Center. The strategy addresses the I/O problem in massively parallel rendering by employing multiple data servers to fetch a single time step. name: 2D Input Processors (2DIP)
head: 2D Input Processing, 2DIP strategy
body: 2D Input Processors (2DIP) is a parallel I/O strategy for rendering large time-varying volume data that addresses the bottleneck where the data sending time (Ts) exceeds the rendering time (Tr). Unlike 1D Input Processors (1DIP), which distributes a single time step across multiple input processors to reduce send time, 2DIP concurrently reads and distributes multiple time steps using a two-dimensional configuration of input processors. This ensures that rendering processors remain busy by overlapping I/O and preprocessing of future time steps with the rendering of the current one. Inputs: Large time-varying volume dataset; number of rendering processors (Pr); estimated rendering time per frame (Tr); estimated total sending time for one time step (Ts); estimated total preprocessing time for one time step (Tp); estimated frame fetch time (T{f0}). Outputs: A configuration of input processors organized into groups, and a stream of time steps delivered to rendering processors such that T{s0} < Tr. The input processors are organized into a two-dimensional logical structure: Groups: n groups of input processors. Processors per Group: m input processors per group. Total Input Processors: n \times m. Each group is responsible for reading, preprocessing, and distributing one complete time step of the data to all rendering processors. 1. Estimate Costs: Determine Ts (sending time for one time step), Tp (preprocessing time for one time step), and Tr (rendering time per frame). 2. Calculate m: Determine the number of input processors per group (m) to ensure the send time per group (T{s0}) is less than the rendering time (Tr). m \ge \frac{Ts}{Tr} 3. Calculate n: Determine the number of groups (n) required to keep the rendering processors busy. This is derived from the condition that the time to fetch and preprocess n-1 time steps equals the time to render n frames (assuming T{s0} = Tr for the boundary case): n = \frac{T{f0} + T{p0}}{Tr} + 1 where T{p0} = Tp / m and T{f0} is the frame fetch time. Assuming ideal load balancing where each input processor handles 1/m of the data, T{f0} = Ts / m and T{p0} = Tp / m. 4. Configure Input Processors: Organize the available input processors into n groups of m processors. 5. Concurrent Execution: Each group i (where 0 \le i < n) reads, preprocesses, and distributes time step i to all rendering processors. With m input processors working on one time step, the send time per group is: T{s0} = \frac{Ts}{m} The preprocessing cost per group is spread across m processors: T{p0} = \frac{Tp}{m} The rendering processors render time step i while input processors for group i+1 (if available) prepare time step i+1. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def calculate2dipparameters(Ts, Tp, Tr, Tf0): """ Calculates the required number of input processors per group (m) and the number of groups (n) to hide I/O and preprocessing latency. """ # m ensures send time per group Ts0 = Ts / m is less than rendering time Tr m = math.ceil(Ts / Tr) # Per-group times are divided by m Ts0 = Ts / m Tp0 = Tp / m # n ensures the pipeline stays full: (Tf0 + Tp0) (n - 1) = Tr n (approx) # Simplified from source: n = (Tf0 + Tp0) / Tr + 1 n = math.ceil((Tf0 + Tp0) / Tr) + 1 return m, n def execute2dippipeline(m, n, timesteps): """ Executes the 2DIP strategy. timesteps: list of time step data to render. """ # Input processors are organized into n groups of m processors. # Each group i reads, preprocesses, and distributes time step i. for i in range(n): # 1. Read data for time step i # Independent Contiguous Read is used for superior performance rawdata = timesteps[i] # 2. Preprocess data (spread across m processors, cost Tp0 = Tp / m) processeddata = preprocess(rawdata, m) # 3. Distribute to all rendering processors (cost Ts0 = Ts / m) distribute(processeddata, m) # 4. Rendering processors render the current time step # While rendering, the next group prepares the next time step render(processeddata) def preprocess(data, m): # Spreads preprocessing cost Tp0 = Tp / m across m processors return data def distribute(data, m): # Spreads sending cost Ts0 = Ts / m across m processors pass def render(data): # Performs volume rendering on the distributed data pass m: Must be at least \lceil Ts / Tr \rceil. In tests with 256 rendering processors, m=14 was sufficient to completely hide I/O and preprocessing. n: Depends on T{f0}, Tp, and Tr. Typically n > 1 to allow pipelining. Hardware: Tested with up to 256 rendering processors and 8+ input processors. Ts \le Tr: If sending time is less than rendering time, 1DIP is sufficient and more efficient. 2DIP is only needed when Ts > Tr. Insufficient Input Processors: If the total number of available input processors is less than n \times m, the pipeline stalls. The send time per group is strictly determined by m (T{s0} = Ts / m), so T{s0} cannot be reduced by changing n. To reduce T{s0}, m must be increased, which may require adjusting n to maintain pipeline occupancy. Read Strategy: Using Collective Noncontiguous Read is inferior to Independent Contiguous Read for 2DIP, resulting in higher sending and total times. Time Complexity: The send time per group is reduced to T{s0} = Ts / m. The total time for rendering N frames is dominated by the rendering time Tr once the pipeline is full, as I/O and preprocessing are hidden. Memory Complexity: Requires storing n time steps in the input processor groups' memory buffers simultaneously. Measured Performance: With 8 or more input processors, total time drops below 10 seconds, and sending time drops below 1 second, enabling multiple frames per second. At 256 rendering processors, 2DIP with m=14 completely hides I/O and preprocessing cost, whereas 1DIP does not scale as well. Strengths: Effectively hides I/O and preprocessing latency when Ts > Tr; enables interactive frame rates for large time-varying datasets. Limitations: Requires a significant number of input processors (n \times m); less scalable than 1DIP if Ts is not significantly larger than Tr. When to Use: Use when Ts > Tr or when 1DIP limits the reduction of Ts. When Not to Use: Use 1DIP when Tr > Ts. 2D Input Processors were introduced by Hongfeng Yu, Kwan-Liu Ma, and Joel Welling in their 2004 paper "I/O Strategies for Parallel Rendering of Large Time-Varying Volume Data". The work was presented at the Eurographics Symposium on Parallel Graphics and Visualization (EGPGV). The strategy was developed to address the I/O bottleneck in massively parallel rendering of large time-varying volume data, where the time to send data to rendering processors exceeded the time to render the image. It builds on the 1DIP strategy by adding a second dimension of parallelism (multiple time steps) to overcome the limitations of 1DIP when send times are high. name: Breakable Integrals
head: Distributable Integral Functions
body: Breakable integrals are a family of integral functions defined over a domain [t1, t{N+1}] that can be decomposed into a sum of products of integrals over individual segments [tk, t{k+1}]. This decomposition enables the parallel or distributed computation of the total integral by allowing partial results from independent segments to be combined. Unlike standard parallel primitives that distribute data elements, this family distributes the mathematical structure of the integral itself, making it suitable for multi-GPU implementations where segments are processed independently and aggregated. The core mechanism of this family is the mapping of computational tasks (pixels, rays, or data elements) to parallel execution units (threads, warps, or cores). Common principles include: 1. Thread Mapping: Assigning one or more threads to process specific data elements (e.g., one thread per pixel or one thread per voxel sample). 2. Memory Hierarchy Utilization: Leveraging global memory for large datasets, shared/local memory for intermediate results (reductions), and registers for per-thread state. 3. Synchronization: Managing concurrency conflicts using atomic operations, barriers, or spatial partitioning (tiles) to ensure data consistency without excessive serialization. 4. Data Parallelism: Performing identical operations on different data elements simultaneously, often requiring coalesced memory access patterns to maximize bandwidth. The transmittance function T(t1 \rightarrow t{N+1}) = \exp \left( - \int{t1}^{t{N+1}} \sigma(t) dt \right) is a breakable integral because the exponential of an integral over a union of segments equals the product of the exponentials (transmittances) over each segment. Specifically, T(t1 \rightarrow t{N+1}) = \prod{i=1}^N T(ti \rightarrow t{i+1}). This property allows transmittance to be computed segment-wise and multiplied across GPUs. The volume rendering equation C(t1 \rightarrow t{N+1}) = \int{t1}^{t{N+1}} T(t1 \rightarrow t) \sigma(t) c(t) dt is a breakable integral because it is an integral of the product of transmittance T(t1 \rightarrow t) (which is breakable) and the source term \sigma(t)c(t). It fits the general form of the family by leveraging the breakability of transmittance. The distortion loss \mathcal{L}{dist}(t1 \rightarrow t{N+1}) = 2 \int{t1}^{t{N+1}} T(t1 \rightarrow u) \sigma(u) S(t1 \rightarrow u) du is a breakable integral. The inner component S(t1 \rightarrow u) = \int{t1}^u T(t1 \rightarrow v) \sigma(v) (u - v) dv is breakable. The product T(t1 \rightarrow u)S(t1 \rightarrow u) is breakable due to the closure properties of the family, and the outer integral preserves this property. The concept of breakable integrals was introduced in the context of scaling Neural Radiance Fields (NeRFs) across multiple GPUs. The primary motivation was to enable efficient distributed training and inference by partitioning the ray integration domain. The family is characterized by its ability to decompose complex integrals into segment-wise operations that can be aggregated, facilitating parallel processing in distributed systems.
