name: Tiled Matrix Multiplication with Shared Memory
body: A GPU kernel that optimizes matrix multiplication C = A \times B by tiling data into block-private shared memory to reduce global memory bandwidth pressure. It differs from the naive kernel by loading each tile once into shared memory and reusing it for TILE\WIDTH multiplications, whereas the naive kernel accesses global memory for every element in the inner loop. Inputs and Outputs: Matrix A of size M \times N in global memory. Matrix B of size N \times P in global memory. Matrix C of size M \times P in global memory (output). TILEWIDTH: The dimension of the square tile loaded into shared memory. Default value is 32. Data Structures: shared float As[TILEWIDTH][TILEWIDTH]: Block-private array storing a tile of matrix A. shared float Bs[TILEWIDTH][TILEWIDTH]: Block-private array storing a tile of matrix B. Algorithm: 1. Calculate global row and column indices for the output matrix C using block and thread indices: row = blockIdx.y \times TILE\WIDTH + ty col = blockIdx.x \times TILE\WIDTH + tx where tx = threadIdx.x and ty = threadIdx.y. 2. Initialize accumulator: accumulate = 0.0f. 3. Calculate total number of tiles along the reduction dimension N: total\tiles = \lceil N / TILE\WIDTH \rceil = (N + TILE\WIDTH - 1) / TILE\WIDTH using integer division rounding up. 4. Loop over tiles: for \ (int \ tile\idx = 0; \ tile\idx < total\tiles; \ tile\idx++). 5. Load tile of A into shared memory: Each thread (tx, ty) loads one element from global memory A into shared memory As. The global index for A is (row, tile\idx \times TILE\WIDTH + tx). If row < M and tile\idx \times TILE\WIDTH + tx < N, load A[row][tile\idx \times TILE\WIDTH + tx] into As[ty][tx]. Otherwise, write 0.0f to As[ty][tx] to prevent garbage values from corrupting the dot product accumulation. 6. Load tile of B into shared memory: Each thread (tx, ty) loads one element from global memory B into shared memory Bs. The global index for B is (tile\idx \times TILE\WIDTH + ty, col). If tile\idx \times TILE\WIDTH + ty < N and col < P, load B[tile\idx \times TILE\WIDTH + ty][col] into Bs[ty][tx]. Otherwise, write 0.0f to Bs[ty][tx]. 7. Synchronize threads within the block to ensure all shared memory loads are complete: \\syncthreads(). 8. Compute partial dot product for the current tile: Loop k from 0 to TILE\WIDTH - 1: accumulate += As[ty][k] \times Bs[k][tx]. 9. Synchronize threads again before loading the next tile: \\syncthreads(). 10. Write final result to global memory: If row < M and col < P, write accumulate to d\c[row \times P + col]. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. shared float As[TILEWIDTH][TILEWIDTH] shared float Bs[TILEWIDTH][TILEWIDTH] tx = threadIdx.x ty = threadIdx.y bx = blockIdx.x by = blockIdx.y row = by TILEWIDTH + ty col = bx TILEWIDTH + tx accumulate = 0.0f totaltiles = (N + TILEWIDTH - 1) // TILEWIDTH for tileidx in range(totaltiles): # Load tile of A acol = tileidx TILEWIDTH + tx if row < M and acol < N: As[ty][tx] = dA[row N + acol] else: As[ty][tx] = 0.0f # Load tile of B brow = tileidx TILEWIDTH + ty if brow < N and col < P: Bs[ty][tx] = dB[brow P + col] else: Bs[ty][tx] = 0.0f # Synchronize to ensure all threads have loaded their data syncthreads() # Compute partial dot product for the current tile for k in range(TILEWIDTH): accumulate += As[ty][k] Bs[k][tx] # Synchronize before loading the next tile syncthreads() if row < M and col < P: dC[row P + col] = accumulate Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Boundary Conditions: If matrix dimensions M, N, or P are not multiples of TILEWIDTH, threads accessing out-of-bounds global memory indices must write 0.0f to shared memory to prevent garbage values from corrupting the dot product accumulation. Precision: The use of float (single precision) is standard, but accumulation order can affect precision in large tiles. Not given in the sources. Synchronization: Failure to call syncthreads() after loading shared memory and before computing the dot product, or after computing and before loading the next tile, will result in race conditions and incorrect results. Time Complexity: O(M \times P \times N), same as naive matrix multiplication, but with reduced memory access overhead. Memory Complexity: O(TILE\WIDTH^2) per block for shared memory, plus O(M \times N + N \times P + M \times P) for global memory. Measured Performance: Not given in the sources. Scaling: Performance scales with the number of blocks and threads, limited by shared memory capacity and occupancy. Larger TILEWIDTH reduces global memory accesses but increases shared memory usage and may reduce occupancy. Strengths: Significantly reduces global memory bandwidth pressure by reusing data in shared memory. Limitations: Requires shared memory, which is limited on GPUs. Not suitable for very large tiles or matrices that exceed shared memory capacity. Boundary handling adds conditional logic. When to Use: When matrix dimensions are large enough to benefit from shared memory reuse and fit within the tile size. When global memory bandwidth is a bottleneck. When Not to Use: When matrices are small, or when shared memory is constrained. When dimensions are not multiples of TILEWIDTH and boundary handling overhead is significant. Origin: The tiled matrix multiplication with shared memory is a standard optimization technique in GPU programming, often attributed to early CUDA programming guides and textbooks. The specific implementation details and code structure are found in. History: Developed as part of the broader effort to optimize GPU performance by leveraging the memory hierarchy. Usage: Widely used in scientific computing, machine learning, and graphics applications where matrix multiplication is a core operation. wyh1309/hpcfoundationaldemos, https://github.com/wyh1309/hpcfoundationaldemos, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial)

name: Batched Fault Injection Engine
head: throughput-bound parallel workload
body: The Batched Fault Injection Engine is a parallel workload that batches multiple corrupted variants of a scene into a single rasterizer call to saturate device throughput, removing latency bounds associated with host control between renders. It differs from standard fault injection by treating the injection campaign itself as a data-parallel rendering task rather than a sequence of latency-bound host-driven calls, allowing it to sustain near-maximum hardware utilization. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A scene representation (e.g., 3D Gaussian Splatting primitives) and a set of bit-flip patterns. Output: A batch of rendered images, each corresponding to a specific corrupted variant of the scene. Data Structures: Batched Scene Data: The scene primitives are duplicated K times (where K is the batch size) to hold independent corruption states. Bit-Flip Patterns: A vectorized structure defining which bits to flip in each variant. Steps: 1. Prepare Batch: Duplicate the scene data K times to create K independent variants. 2. Apply Corruption: Apply bit flips to the batch using a vectorized scatter operation. This operation targets specific memory locations corresponding to the primitive attributes for each variant in the batch. 3. Rasterize: Issue a single rasterizer call processing all K variants simultaneously. 4. Collect Results: Read back the rendered outputs for each variant. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def batchedfaultinjection(sceneprimitives, bitflippatterns, batchsize): # Duplicate scene primitives for each variant in the batch batchedprimitives = repeat(sceneprimitives, batchsize) # Apply bit flips to the batch using a vectorized scatter operation # bitflippatterns is a structured array defining flips for each variant corruptedprimitives = vectorizedscatter(batchedprimitives, bitflippatterns) # Render all variants in a single call # The rasterizer processes the batched primitives in parallel renderedimages = rasterizercall(corruptedprimitives) return renderedimages Parameters: Batch Size (K): The number of corrupted variants processed per call. Typical values saturate the device (e.g., 32 variants per launch). Bit-Flip Patterns: Defined by the fault injection campaign (e.g., single-bit upsets). Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Throughput Saturation: The method is designed to saturate device throughput; if the batch size is too small, the device remains underutilized due to host control latency. Memory Bandwidth: High memory bandwidth is required to handle the duplicated scene data and bit-flip operations efficiently. Hardware Specificity: Throughput varies by hardware (e.g., Blackwell vs. L40S), but bit-level criticality remains consistent across architectures with identical floating-point layouts. Simulates transient bit flips in GPU memory to measure rendering corruption in 3D Gaussian Splatting. It differs from neural network weight perturbation because 3DGS primitives are spatially localized and redundant, whereas network weights are shared globally; this method quantifies whether such redundancy provides robustness or concentrates risk into rare catastrophic failures. Time Complexity: The method is throughput-bound, not latency-bound. It processes K variants in a single call, reducing overhead per variant to near zero. Memory Complexity: Requires K times the memory for scene primitives, where K is the batch size. Performance: Sustains 2,515 single-bit injections per second on Blackwell hardware. Processes 4.3 million primitive instances per launch. Reaches 6,081 single-bit injections per second on 4 L40S accelerators (4.00x speedup) with 100% parallel efficiency. Saturates device at 99% utilization and 386 W. Strengths: Eliminates host control latency between renders. Embarrassingly parallel across devices (no communication needed). Achieves near-maximum hardware utilization. Limitations: Requires significant memory for batched scene data. Throughput is hardware-dependent (e.g., 1,522 injections/sec on L40S vs. 2,515 on Blackwell). When to Use: When the goal is to measure bit-level criticality or fault tolerance at scale, and hardware throughput is the bottleneck rather than host control latency. When Not to Use: When the number of variants is small, or when host control latency is negligible compared to rendering time. The Batched Fault Injection Engine was introduced in the context of analyzing Single-Event Upsets (SEUs) in 3D Gaussian Splatting rendering. It was developed to address the latency-bound nature of traditional fault injection campaigns, where each corrupted render is small relative to the host control between renders. The method was validated on Blackwell and Ada-generation (L40S) hardware, demonstrating that bit-level criticality is a property of the representation and floating-point layout rather than specific architecture. name: Single-Event Upset (SEU) Fault Injection in 3DGS
head: Bit-flip injection, Single-bit upset injection
body: Single-Event Upset (SEU) fault injection in 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) simulates transient bit flips in GPU memory to measure the rendering corruption caused by hardware errors. It differs from neural network weight perturbation because 3DGS primitives are spatially localized and redundant, whereas network weights are shared globally; this method quantifies whether such redundancy provides robustness or concentrates risk into rare catastrophic failures. Inputs and Outputs Input: A trained 3DGS model with N primitives stored in GPU memory, a set of K held-out camera views, and a fault site tuple (field, primitive, component, bit). Output: Corruption metrics (peak pixel error, LPIPS, SSIM, PSNR, non-finite flag, corruption footprint) for the rendered views. Data Structures A trained 3DGS model consists of N primitives. Primitive i stores six fields in memory: 1. Mean \mui \in \mathbb{R}^3 2. Logarithmic scale si \in \mathbb{R}^3 (renderer applies \exp) 3. Quaternion qi \in \mathbb{R}^4 (normalized at render time) 4. Opacity logit oi \in \mathbb{R} (renderer applies logistic \sigma) 5. DC color term c{0i} \in \mathbb{R}^3 6. Higher-order spherical harmonic coefficients c{Ni} \in \mathbb{R}^{((\ell+1)^2-1) \times 3} IEEE-754 Bit Layouts The bit positions determine the impact of a flip: fp32: Sign is bit 31, exponent is bits 23–30, mantissa is bits 0–22. fp16: 5-bit exponent, 10-bit mantissa. bf16: 8-bit exponent (from fp32), 7-bit mantissa. Algorithm Steps 1. Reinterpret: Cast the stored floating-point value at the fault site to an unsigned integer of the matching width. 2. Flip: XOR the integer with a mask having a single bit set at the target position. 3. Restore: Reinterpret the modified integer back to the original floating-point format. 4. Render: Render the K held-out views using the corrupted parameter. 5. Measure: Compute metrics on the GPU. 6. Cleanup: Restore the original value to the working copy. Pseudocode Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import numpy as np import struct def flipbitfp32(value: float, bitindex: int) -> float: """Flip a single bit in an fp32 value. Args: value: The original floating-point value. bitindex: The bit position to flip (0-31). Returns: The value with the specified bit flipped. """ # Reinterpret float as unsigned 32-bit integer # struct.unpack returns a tuple, so we take the first element bits = struct.unpack('I', struct.pack('f', value))[0] # Flip the bit using XOR bits ^= (1 << bitindex) # Reinterpret back to float return struct.unpack('f', struct.pack('I', bits))[0] def injectseuandrender(model, faultsite, cameras, renderer): """Inject a single-bit upset and render metrics. Args: model: Object containing primitive parameters in GPU memory. faultsite: Tuple (fieldname, primitiveindex, componentindex, bitindex). cameras: List of K camera poses. renderer: Function that renders primitives to images given cameras. Returns: Dictionary of metrics. """ fieldname, primidx, compidx, bitidx = faultsite # 1. Get clean value from model # Assuming model.params[fieldname][primidx][compidx] accesses the value cleanvalue = model.params[fieldname][primidx][compidx] # 2. Inject fault corruptedvalue = flipbitfp32(cleanvalue, bitidx) # 3. Write to working copy model.params[fieldname][primidx][compidx] = corruptedvalue # 4. Render K views # Assuming renderer returns a list of images or a batched tensor corruptedimages = renderer(model.params, cameras) # 5. Render clean views (or use cached clean render) # Assuming cleanimages are pre-computed or re-rendered cleanimages = renderer(model.params, cameras) # Note: In practice, cleanimages should be from the uncorrupted model state. # The pseudocode above re-reads from model.params which is now corrupted. # Correct approach: Store cleanvalue, render clean once, then swap. # 6. Compute metrics metrics = computemetrics(corruptedimages, cleanimages) # 7. Restore value model.params[fieldname][primidx][compidx] = cleanvalue return metrics def computemetrics(corruptedimgs, cleanimgs): """Compute corruption metrics.""" # Standard image processing functions assumed available peakerror = np.max(np.abs(corruptedimgs - cleanimgs)) psnr = 10 np.log10(1.0 / np.mean((corruptedimgs - cleanimgs)2)) # Corruption footprint: fraction of pixels changing > 1/255 diff = np.abs(corruptedimgs - cleanimgs) footprint = np.mean(diff > (1.0/255.0)) # Non-finite check isnonfinite = np.any(np.isnan(corruptedimgs)) or np.any(np.isinf(corruptedimgs)) return { 'peakerror': peakerror, 'psnr': psnr, 'footprint': footprint, 'nonfinite': isnonfinite } Parameters and Typical Values Precision: fp32 is the baseline; fp16 and bf16 are tested by casting clean parameters to the target format before injection. Views (K): Multiple held-out views are averaged to compute the corruption footprint. Catastrophic Threshold: An upset is catastrophic if the corruption footprint exceeds 1% of the frame or produces non-finite values. Edge Cases and Pitfalls Exponent Overflow: Flipping high exponent bits in fp32 can cause overflow to non-finite values. Scale Sign Flip: For the scale field, the activation is \phi = \exp. A sign flip on a typical log scale \theta \approx -3 changes it to +3, multiplying the primitive size by e^6 \approx 4 \times 10^2. Global Metrics: Full-frame PSNR is a poor discriminator for single upsets in large scenes because a single corrupted primitive among hundreds of thousands barely moves the global average. Analyzes the mathematical impact of bit flips on specific fields. For the scale field, the relative change is |\Delta s|/s = |\Delta \theta|, meaning a mantissa flip changes scale by a fixed relative amount 2^{b-p} independent of the exponent e. For a normal fp32 value \theta = (-1)^\epsilon 2^e (1+m), flipping mantissa bit b changes the value by |\Delta \theta| = 2^{e+b-p}. Flipping the sign bit gives \Delta \theta = -2\theta, and flipping exponent bit j multiplies magnitude by 2^{\pm 2^j}. Time and Memory Complexity Time: The parallel injection engine keeps the GPU busy with a stream of independent corrupted renders, saturating device throughput. Memory: Clean parameters remain resident on the GPU; only one working copy is modified at a time. Measured Performance Redundancy Scaling: For a converged model of N primitives, the typical (median) image error of one uniform-random single-bit upset scales as \sigma^2(N) = \Theta(N^{-\alpha}) for a scene-dependent exponent \alpha > 0. Dose Budget: Under k independent uniform single-bit upsets, the expected squared image error is E\|\Delta I\|^2 = k \sigma^2(N). The dose k\tau at which error exceeds threshold \tau scales as k\tau = \Theta(N^\alpha \tau). Strengths and Limitations Strengths: Directly measures hardware vulnerability; identifies critical bit positions (e.g., scale sign bit). Limitations: Full-frame PSNR is insensitive to local corruption; catastrophic upsets are rare but dominant in mean error. When to Use Use for evaluating robustness of 3DGS deployments against hardware errors. Do not use for optimizing model accuracy; use for safety-critical validation. Originated from the paper "Single-Event Upsets in 3D Gaussian Splatting Rendering: Bit-Level Criticality, Spatial Extent, and a Parallel Support Guard". It addresses the gap in understanding whether the redundancy of 3DGS primitives provides robustness against transient faults, contrasting with extensive prior work on neural network weight perturbation.
